title: Microstructural development of human newborn cerebral white matter assessed in vivo by diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging.
text:
Changes in the structure of the white matter in the developing human brain can impact the development of the cortex and lead to functional disabilities. We used a specialized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique called line scan diffusion-weighted MRI with diffusion tensor analysis to measure the apparent diffusion coefficient, calculate relative anisotropy, and map the three-dimensional fiber architecture in the white matter of preterm (n = 17) and full-term infants (n = 7). To understand the effects of prematurity on white matter development, we studied early gestation preterm infants (n = 10) a second time when they reached full term. 

We found that the mean apparent diffusion coefficient in the central white matter was high at 28 weeks gestation (1.8 microm2/ms) and decreased towards full term (1.2 microm2/ms). In the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the mean apparent diffusion coefficients were similar at both time points (1.2 versus 1.1 microm2/ms). Relative anisotropy, which indicates the directionality of water diffusion, was higher the closer the infants were to full term, with greater values in the internal capsule compared to the central white matter. 

At full term, preterm infants had higher mean diffusion coefficients in the central white matter (1.4 +/- 0.24 versus 1.15 +/- 0.09 microm2/ms, p = 0.016) and lower relative anisotropy in both areas compared to full-term infants (white matter, 10.9 +/- 0.6 versus 22.9 +/- 3.0%, p = 0.001; internal capsule, 24.0 +/- 4.44 versus 33.1 +/- 0.6% p = 0.006). We were able to visualize nonmyelinated fibers in the corpus callosum as early as 28 weeks gestation using diffusion tensor MRI, and there were significant differences in white matter fiber organization between full-term and preterm infants at term. 

These findings demonstrate that quantitative assessment of water diffusion using diffusion tensor MRI can provide valuable information about the microstructural development of the white matter in living infants.

title: Induction of myelodysplasia by myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text: We have discovered that myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), which are stem cell malignancies that occur with age, exhibit characteristics of an activated adaptive immune response and ineffective hematopoiesis. In our study, we observed a significant increase in myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) in the bone marrow of MDS patients. MDSC are typically associated with immunosuppression, inflammation, and cancer, but in this case, they played a role in the development of ineffective hematopoiesis. These MDSC produce excessive amounts of cytokines that suppress hematopoiesis and have the ability to induce apoptosis in hematopoietic progenitor cells. Through our experiments with transfected cell models, we discovered that the expansion of MDSC is driven by the interaction between the proinflammatory molecule S100A9 and CD33. These two proteins form a functional ligand/receptor pair that activates CD33's immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM), leading to the secretion of suppressive cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β by immature myeloid cells. We also observed that mice with S100A9 overexpression developed an accumulation of MDSC in the bone marrow, along with progressive multilineage cytopenias and cytological dysplasia. Importantly, we found that early maturation of MDSC through treatment with all-trans-retinoic acid or interruption of CD33 signaling using an adapter protein (DAP12) that bears an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) rescued the hematologic abnormalities. These findings suggest that the expansion of MDSC in the bone marrow, driven by the S100A9/CD33 pathway, disrupts hematopoiesis and contributes to the development of MDS.

title: BC1 RNA, the transcript from a master gene for ID element amplification, is able to prime its own reverse transcription.
text: ID elements are a type of short interspersed elements (SINEs) that are present in high numbers in the genomes of many rodents. BC1 RNA, which is a transcript related to ID elements, is produced from a single copy gene called BC1 RNA gene. The BC1 RNA gene has been identified as a key gene responsible for the amplification of ID elements in rodent genomes. The dispersal of ID elements occurs through a process known as retroposition, which involves several regulatory steps. These steps may include transcription in specific tissues, stability of the transcript, preparation of the RNA transcript for reverse transcription, and integration. This research specifically focuses on the preparation of the RNA transcript for reverse transcription. It has been demonstrated that BC1 RNA gene transcripts have the ability to efficiently prime their own reverse transcription in a specific manner within the same molecule. This self-priming capability is a result of the unique structure of the 3'-end region. The fact that a gene that has been actively amplified throughout rodent evolution produces an RNA molecule capable of efficient self-primed reverse transcription strongly suggests that self-priming is one of the characteristics that establish the BC1 RNA gene as a master gene for the amplification of ID elements.

title: The DNA Methylome of Human Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
text:
DNA methylation plays a crucial role in various biological processes related to human health and disease. Thanks to recent technological advancements, it is now possible to conduct unbiased analysis of the entire DNA methylation pattern (known as the methylome) in human cells. In this study, we utilized whole-genome bisulfite sequencing to analyze the methylome of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from an Asian individual whose genome was previously decoded in the YH project. PBMCs are widely used in clinical blood tests.

Our analysis revealed that 68.4% of CpG sites and less than 0.2% of non-CpG sites were methylated in human PBMCs, indicating that non-CpG cytosine methylation is not significant in these cells. We also identified 20 distinct genomic features, including regulatory regions, protein-coding genes, non-coding genes, RNA-coding genes, and repetitive sequences, within the PBMC methylome. By integrating our methylome data with the YH genome sequence, we were able to assess allele-specific methylation (ASM) between the two haploid methylomes of the individual. This analysis led to the identification of 599 haploid differentially methylated regions (hDMRs) covering 287 genes. Among these genes, 76 had hDMRs located within 2 kb of their transcriptional start sites, and more than 80% of them exhibited allele-specific expression (ASE).

Our findings demonstrate that ASM is a recurring phenomenon and is strongly associated with ASE in human PBMCs. Alongside similar studies, our research provides a valuable resource for future epigenomic investigations and confirms the efficacy of new sequencing technologies for large-scale epigenomics studies.

title: The human myelin basic protein gene is included within a 179-kilobase transcription unit: expression in the immune and central nervous systems.
text: Two cDNAs of human Golli-MBP (myelin basic protein) genes, expressed in the oligodendrocyte lineage, have been discovered in a human oligodendroglioma cell line. Through analysis of these cDNAs, the complete structure of the human Golli-MBP gene has been determined. The Golli-MBP gene, which includes the MBP transcription unit, spans approximately 179 kb and consists of 10 exons, with seven of them being part of the MBP gene. The human Golli-MBP gene contains two transcription start sites, each giving rise to a set of alternatively spliced transcripts. The first transcription start site produces at least two Golli-MBP transcripts, containing the initial three exons of the gene and one or more MBP exons. The second set of transcripts solely consists of MBP exons and generates the well-known MBPs. In humans, RNA blot analysis has shown that Golli-MBP transcripts are expressed in the fetal thymus, spleen, human B-cell and macrophage cell lines, as well as the fetal spinal cord. These findings establish a clear connection between the expression of exons encoding the autoimmunogen/encephalitogen MBP in the central nervous system and cells and tissues of the immune system through the normal expression of the Golli-MBP gene. Furthermore, they confirm that this genetic locus, which includes the MBP gene, is conserved across species, providing additional evidence that the MBP transcription unit is an essential component of the Golli transcription unit. This structural arrangement is likely crucial for the genetic function and/or regulation of these genes.

title: Targeting A20 Decreases Glioma Stem Cell Survival and Tumor Growth
text: Glioblastomas are highly lethal cancers that have a functional cellular hierarchy maintained by self-renewing glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs). These GSCs are regulated by distinct molecular pathways from the rest of the tumor, which could potentially be targeted for therapy. Our research revealed that A20 (TNFAIP3), a regulator of cell survival and the NF-kappaB pathway, is overexpressed in GSCs compared to non-stem glioblastoma cells at both the mRNA and protein levels. To understand the importance of A20 in GSCs, we used lentiviral-mediated delivery of short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to target A20 expression. Inhibiting A20 expression resulted in decreased growth and survival of GSCs, primarily due to reduced cell-cycle progression and phosphorylation of p65/RelA. The elevated levels of A20 in GSCs contributed to their resistance to apoptosis, as they were less susceptible to TNFalpha-induced cell death compared to non-stem glioma cells. However, knocking down A20 sensitized GSCs to TNFalpha-mediated apoptosis. The decreased survival of GSCs upon A20 knockdown also led to a reduced ability of these cells to self-renew in primary and secondary neurosphere formation assays. Targeting A20 in GSCs decreased their tumorigenic potential, resulting in improved survival of mice with human glioma xenografts. Analysis of a glioma patient genomic database showed an inverse correlation between A20 overexpression/amplification and survival. These findings suggest that A20 plays a role in maintaining glioma through its effects on the GSC subpopulation. While A20 has been identified as a tumor suppressor in lymphoma, we did not find similar mutations in glioma genomic sequencing. In fact, our data suggests that A20 may enhance tumor growth in glioma by promoting GSC survival. Therefore, caution should be exercised when considering A20 as a therapeutic target for glioma, as its effects may vary depending on the tumor type.

title: Efficient targeting of expressed and silent genes in human ESCs and iPSCs using zinc-finger nucleases
text: Efficient methods for genetic modification are essential to fully harness the potential of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs). However, current techniques for generating cell type-specific lineage reporters and tools for disrupting, repairing, or overexpressing genes through gene targeting are largely inefficient and not commonly used. In this study, we present a highly efficient approach to target three genes in human pluripotent cells using zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN)-mediated genome editing. Firstly, we utilized ZFNs specific to the OCT4 (POU5F1) locus to create OCT4-eGFP reporter cells, enabling us to monitor the pluripotent state of hESCs. Secondly, we successfully inserted a transgene into the AAVS1 locus, resulting in a robust drug-inducible overexpression system in hESCs. Lastly, we targeted the PITX3 gene, demonstrating the ability of ZFNs to generate reporter cells by targeting non-expressed genes in both hESCs and hiPSCs.

title: Empirical Bayesian models for analysing molecular serotyping microarrays
text:
In this study, we utilized microarrays as a potential platform for molecular diagnostics in infectious diseases. Specifically, we used a microarray designed for molecular serotyping of Streptococcus pneumoniae to identify the presence of 91 known pneumococcal serotypes from DNA extracts. The microarray contained oligonucleotide probes for all known capsular polysaccharide synthesis genes and required a statistical analysis of the microarray intensity data to determine the serotype(s) present in a sample based on the detected genes.

To calculate the probabilities of serotype combinations from the microarray data, we propose an empirical Bayesian model. This model takes into account the dependencies between serotypes, which are induced by shared genes and homologous genes with similar sequences. In cases where serotypes have very similar capsular gene compositions, we included extra probes on the microarray to provide additional information for the Bayesian model. For serotype combinations with high probabilities, we applied a Bayesian random effects model to determine the relative abundance of each serotype.

To evaluate the accuracy of our analysis, we applied our methods to experimental data from samples containing individual serotypes and samples containing combinations of serotypes with known abundance levels. The Bayesian model successfully determined all but two of the known serotypes of S. pneumoniae tested as individual samples. Additionally, the model enabled the identification of serotype combinations within samples. Even serotypes with very low abundance within a combination (down to 2% in this study) could be detected. Furthermore, the model provided an approximate measure of the percentage abundance of each serotype within the combination.

title: Bayesian measures of model complexity and fit
text:
In this summary, we address the issue of comparing complex hierarchical models that do not have a clearly defined number of parameters. We propose a measure called pD, which represents the effective number of parameters in a model. This measure is derived using an information theoretic argument and is calculated as the difference between the posterior mean of the deviance and the deviance at the posterior means of the parameters of interest. In most cases, pD can be approximated by the trace of the product of Fisher's information and the posterior covariance. In normal models, this corresponds to the trace of the 'hat' matrix that projects observations onto fitted values. We explore the properties of pD in exponential families. 

We suggest using the posterior mean deviance as a Bayesian measure of fit or adequacy. By examining the contributions of individual observations to the fit and complexity, we can create a diagnostic plot of deviance residuals against leverages. To compare models, we propose adding pD to the posterior mean deviance, resulting in a deviance information criterion. This criterion is related to other information criteria and has an approximate decision theoretic justification. 

We provide examples to illustrate the procedure and compare it with alternative Bayesian and classical proposals. Throughout, we emphasize that the required quantities can be easily computed in a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis.

title: Simplifying likelihood ratios
text: The use of likelihood ratios is considered one of the most effective ways to assess diagnostic accuracy. However, they are not commonly utilized due to the complexity of interpreting them, which involves converting between the "probability" and "odds" of disease using a calculator. This article presents a simpler approach to interpreting likelihood ratios that eliminates the need for calculators, nomograms, and conversions to disease odds. Through various examples, it demonstrates how clinicians can employ this method to enhance diagnostic decision-making directly at the patient's bedside.

title: induction of early IFN-inducible genes in the absence of type
text: TLR7 recognition of the influenza virus (Flu) leads to significant production of type I IFN by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs). Synthetic TLR7 ligands can induce pDC maturation, as shown by the expression of costimulatory molecules and proinflammatory cytokine production. However, these ligands only result in low-level production of IFN-alpha. To understand the TLR7 signaling in pDCs and how it induces different profiles, we investigated the effects of two TLR7 ligands (Flu and CL097) on blood-isolated pDCs and the human GEN2.2 pDC cell line. The production of type I IFN by pDCs is associated with the differential translocation of interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7) into the nucleus, which is induced by the two TLR7 ligands. Surprisingly, both activators rapidly induced the expression of IFN-inducible genes mxa, cxcl10, and trail within four hours of stimulation. This expression, regulated by STAT1 phosphorylation, occurred independently of type I IFN. We discovered that STAT1 activation relies on the PI3K-p38MAPK pathway, revealing a novel signaling pathway that leads to the rapid expression of IFN-inducible genes after TLR7 activation. Therefore, pDCs possess the ability to promptly respond to viral infection during the early stages of the innate immune response through this unique TLR7 signaling mechanism.

title: Arteriolar function in visceral adipose tissue is impaired in human obesity.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between the characteristics of adipose tissue and the function of microvessels in different fat compartments. In a group of 30 obese individuals undergoing bariatric surgery, we collected samples of visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue and analyzed their specific characteristics. We used videomicroscopy to assess the vasomotor function of small arterioles isolated from these fat compartments. We found that endothelium-dependent vasodilation was significantly impaired in visceral arterioles compared to subcutaneous ones. However, nonendothelium dependent responses were similar. Inhibition of endothelial nitric oxide synthase had no effect on the impaired vasodilation in visceral arterioles. Visceral fat also exhibited higher expression of proinflammatory, oxidative stress-related, hypoxia-induced, and proangiogenic genes, as well as increased populations of activated macrophages and a greater capacity for cytokine production. These findings suggest that the microenvironment of visceral fat may be toxic to arterial health, potentially contributing to the development of atherosclerotic vascular disease. Furthermore, our results support the idea that both the quality and quantity of adipose tissue play important roles in shaping cardiovascular phenotypes in obesity.

title: Common Carotid Intima Media Thickness and Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index Correlate with Local but Not Global Atheroma Burden: A Cross Sectional Study Using Whole Body Magnetic Resonance Angiography
text:
BACKGROUND
Carotid intima media thickness (CIMT) and ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) are commonly used as surrogate markers of atherosclerosis. They have been found to be associated with arterial stiffness, but their correlation with overall atherosclerotic burden has not been previously examined. In this study, we compared CIMT and ABPI with atheroma burden as measured by whole body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA).

METHODS
We recruited 50 patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease. CIMT was measured using ultrasound, while rest and exercise ABPI were performed. WB-MRA was conducted using a 1.5T MRI scanner and intravenous gadolinium gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem, Guerbet, FR). The WB-MRA data was divided into 31 arterial segments, and each segment was scored based on the degree of luminal narrowing: 0 = normal, 1 = <50%, 2 = 50-70%, 3 = 70-99%, 4 = vessel occlusion. The segment scores were summed to calculate a standardized atheroma score.

RESULTS
The atherosclerotic burden was found to be high, with a standardized atheroma score of 39.5±11. Common CIMT showed a positive correlation with the overall atheroma score (β 0.32, p = 0.045), but this was primarily driven by its strong correlation with the neck and thoracic segments (β 0.42 p = 0.01), with no correlation observed with the rest of the body. ABPI correlated with the overall atheroma score (β -0.39, p = 0.012), mainly due to a strong correlation with the ilio-femoral vessels, but no correlation was found with the thoracic or neck vessels. Multiple linear regression analysis revealed no correlation between CIMT and global atheroma burden (β 0.13 p = 0.45), while the correlation between ABPI and atheroma burden remained significant (β -0.45 p = 0.005).

CONCLUSION
In a population with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease, ABPI but not CIMT was found to correlate with global atheroma burden as measured by whole body contrast enhanced magnetic resonance angiography. However, this correlation was primarily driven by the strong association between ABPI and ilio-femoral atheroma burden.

title: Loss of immune escape mutations during persistent HCV infection in pregnancy enhances replication of vertically transmitted viruses
text: Globally, approximately 1% of pregnant women are chronically infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV). The transmission of HCV from mother to child occurs in 3-5% of pregnancies and is responsible for the majority of new childhood infections. CD8(+) cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) that specifically target HCV play a crucial role in eliminating acute HCV infections. However, in the 60-80% of cases where the infection persists, these CTLs become exhausted or the virus mutates to evade recognition by the immune system. The replication of HCV is known to increase during pregnancy, suggesting that the immune tolerance mechanisms between mother and fetus may further hinder the function of HCV-specific CTLs, reducing their ability to exert selective pressure on persistent viruses. To investigate this possibility, we studied the genetic diversity of circulating HCV strains during and after consecutive pregnancies in two women. Our analysis revealed a decrease in the presence of certain genetic mutations that allow the virus to evade CTL recognition during pregnancy, which coincided with the emergence of more robust viral strains. However, after childbirth, the selective pressure from CTLs was reinstated, leading to a sharp decline in viral load and a resurgence of escape mutations in these genetic regions. Importantly, the viruses transmitted from mother to child during childbirth were those with enhanced fitness due to the reversal of escape mutations. These findings suggest that the immune changes that occur during pregnancy reduce the selective pressure exerted by CTLs on specific regions of the HCV genome, thereby facilitating the vertical transmission of viruses that are optimized for replication.

title: The journey of developing hematopoietic stem cells.
text: The development of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) is a complex process that occurs during embryogenesis and involves multiple anatomical sites. After HSC precursors are determined from mesoderm, they must mature into functional HSCs and undergo divisions that allow them to renew themselves and create a pool of HSCs. Throughout this process, developing HSCs move through different areas in the embryo that provide signals for their establishment and the preservation of their ability to renew themselves. To generate HSCs from embryonic stem cells, these processes need to be replicated. Understanding the interactions between developing HSCs and their environments will aid in the production and expansion of HSCs in a laboratory setting, allowing for the exploration of their clinical potential.

title: The sacroiliac joint in the spondyloarthropathies.
text: Spondyloarthropathy (SpA) is a term used to describe a group of inflammatory joint diseases that have similar clinical features and are uniquely associated with the major histocompatibility complex class I molecule HLA-B27. There are five subgroups within SpA: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and undifferentiated SpA. The sacroiliac joints are primarily affected in SpA, particularly in ankylosing spondylitis where early onset is common. To aid in the diagnosis of early sacroiliitis, dynamic magnetic resonance imaging has been used to visualize both acute and chronic changes in the sacroiliac joints. Recent examination of inflammation in the sacroiliac joints of SpA patients has revealed the presence of T cells, macrophages, and various cytokines through immunohistology and in situ hybridization. Biopsy specimens obtained under guided computed tomography have also shown successful intra-articular corticosteroid treatment. Further investigation of these biopsy specimens has shown the absence of DNA from bacteria associated with reactive arthritis. The exact cause of SpA and its specific affinity for the sacroiliac joints is still unknown. The relationship between the genetic background of SpA and initial bacterial infections that trigger the disease has yet to be established. In chronic cases, autoimmune mechanisms may play a more significant role.

title: A rapid method for extraction of cotton (Gossypium spp.) genomic DNA suitable for RFLP or PCR analysis
text: Obtaining high-quality genomic DNA from Gossypium (cotton) species poses challenges due to the presence of polysaccharides, oxidizable quinones, and other substances that interfere with the extraction process. However, we have developed a reliable method that consistently allows for the isolation of cotton genomic DNA with satisfactory size and quality. This DNA can be used for RFLP and PCR analysis, as well as for various routine cloning applications. To achieve this, we employ a series of antioxidants, phenol-binding reagents, and phenol oxidase inhibitors throughout the procedure. Additionally, we eliminate most polysaccharides early on by isolating the nuclei.

title: Cross sectional stature and weight reference curves for the UK, 1990.
text: The stature and weight reference curves for the UK, which have been in use since 1966, are being questioned for their accuracy in describing the growth of present-day British children. To address this concern, new reference curves have been developed using data from seven sources, covering the period from birth to 20 years for children born in 1990. The majority of the data used is nationally representative. The analysis employed Cole's LMS method, resulting in efficient estimates of the conventional centiles and a good fit to the data. Notably, these new curves differ from the currently used curves at important ages for both stature and weight. Given the concerns raised about the current curves and the disparities between them and the new curves, it is recommended that the curves presented here be adopted as the new reference curves for the UK.

title: The suture provides a niche for mesenchymal stem cells of craniofacial bones
text: Stem cells play a crucial role in the constant turnover of bone tissue. Recent research has revealed that perivascular mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are involved in the renewal of long bones. However, the specific identity and regulating environment for MSCs in craniofacial bones, which are flat bones originating from a different embryonic source than long bones, remain unknown. In this study, we have identified Gli1+ cells within the suture mesenchyme as the primary MSC population responsible for craniofacial bones. These cells are not associated with blood vessels, but they give rise to all craniofacial bones in adult individuals and are activated during the healing process of injuries. In vitro experiments have confirmed that Gli1+ cells exhibit typical MSC characteristics. When Gli1+ cells are eliminated, craniosynostosis occurs, leading to a halt in skull growth. This demonstrates that these cells are an essential population of stem cells. Additionally, Twist1(+/-) mice with craniosynostosis exhibit a reduction in Gli1+ MSCs in sutures, suggesting that diminished suture stem cells may contribute to the development of craniosynostosis. Our findings highlight the unique role of craniofacial sutures as a niche for MSCs involved in the maintenance and repair of craniofacial bones.

title: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to the dormant multipotent stem cell in the mammalian heart
text:
A population of cells derived from the heart, known as Arodent cardiac side population cells, were able to form clonal spheroids in a medium without serum. These cells expressed certain genes, such as nestin, Musashi-1, and multi-drug resistance transporter gene 1, which are markers of undifferentiated neural precursor cells. However, these markers were no longer present once the cells underwent differentiation. Instead, the cells started expressing proteins specific to neurons, glial cells, smooth muscle cells, or cardiomyocytes.

When these cells were transplanted into chick embryos, they migrated to specific areas of the heart, such as the truncus arteriosus and cardiac outflow tract. Additionally, they also contributed to the development of dorsal root ganglia, spinal nerves, and aortic smooth muscle cells. Further studies using double transgenic mice revealed the presence of both undifferentiated and differentiated neural crest-derived cells in the fetal myocardium. The undifferentiated cells expressed GATA-binding protein 4 and nestin, but not actinin, while the differentiated cells were identified as cardiomyocytes.

These findings suggest that cells derived from the cardiac neural crest have the ability to migrate into the heart and remain there as dormant multipotent stem cells. Under certain conditions, these cells can differentiate into cardiomyocytes and other types of neural crest-derived cells, including neurons, glia, and smooth muscle cells.

title: The mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway mediates epileptogenesis in a model of temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: Developing more effective therapies for epilepsy requires a deep understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved in epileptogenesis. Our recent research has revealed the involvement of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway in epileptogenesis. In a mouse model of tuberous sclerosis complex, we found that mTOR inhibitors can prevent epilepsy. Building on this, we conducted a study using a rat model of temporal lobe epilepsy induced by status epilepticus to investigate the potential role of mTOR. We observed a biphasic activation of the mTOR pathway following acute kainate-induced seizures, as indicated by an increase in phospho-S6 (P-S6) expression. The initial rise in P-S6 expression occurred around 1 hour after seizure onset, reached its peak at 3-6 hours, and returned to baseline within 24 hours in both the hippocampus and neocortex. This suggests a widespread stimulation of mTOR signaling during acute seizure activity. After the resolution of status epilepticus, we observed a second increase in P-S6 expression specifically in the hippocampus. This increase began at 3 days, peaked at 5-10 days, and persisted for several weeks after kainate injection. This correlated with the development of chronic epileptogenesis within the hippocampus. By administering the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin before kainate, we were able to block both the acute and chronic phases of seizure-induced mTOR activation. Additionally, rapamycin reduced kainate-induced neuronal cell death, neurogenesis, mossy fiber sprouting, and the development of spontaneous epilepsy. When rapamycin was administered after the termination of status epilepticus, it only blocked the chronic phase of mTOR activation and reduced mossy fiber sprouting and epilepsy, but not neurogenesis or neuronal death. These findings demonstrate that mTOR signaling plays a crucial role in the mechanisms of epileptogenesis in the kainate rat model, and that mTOR inhibitors have potential antiepileptogenic effects in this model.

title: Acute administration of recombinant Angiopoietin-1 ameliorates multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome and improves survival in murine sepsis.
text:
INTRODUCTION
The breakdown of the vascular barrier due to endothelial activation is a crucial factor in the development of multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in sepsis. Recent evidence suggests that Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), a vessel-protective factor that binds to the endothelial-specific Tie2 receptor, is inhibited by its antagonist Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2) during sepsis. To investigate whether intravenous injection of recombinant human (rh) Ang-1 can reverse the effects of sepsis-induced suppression of Ang-1 and elevation of Ang-2, we aimed to study its protective effects against MODS in a murine sepsis model.

METHODS
We induced polymicrobiological abdominal sepsis using cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) in mice. The mice were then treated with either 1 μg of intravenous rhAng-1 or a control buffer immediately after CLP induction and every 8 hours thereafter. Sham-operated animals were used as time-matched controls.

RESULTS
Compared to the control group treated with the buffer, septic mice treated with rhAng-1 showed significant improvements in various hematologic and biochemical indicators of MODS. Additionally, rhAng-1 treatment stabilized endothelial barrier function, as demonstrated by the inhibition of protein leakage from lung capillaries into the alveolar compartment. Histological analysis revealed that rhAng-1 treatment reduced leukocyte infiltration in the lungs and kidneys of septic mice, likely due to decreased expression of endothelial adhesion molecules. Furthermore, rhAng-1 treatment improved survival time in a lethal CLP model.

CONCLUSIONS
In a clinically relevant murine sepsis model, intravenous rhAng-1 treatment alone was found to significantly improve various sepsis-associated organ dysfunctions and survival time, most likely by preserving endothelial barrier function. Further research is needed to facilitate the clinical application of this therapeutic approach.

title: Mechanisms linking obesity to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
text: Obesity is linked to a higher likelihood of developing insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. In individuals who are obese, the adipose tissue releases larger quantities of non-esterified fatty acids, glycerol, hormones, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and other substances that contribute to the development of insulin resistance. When insulin resistance occurs alongside dysfunction of pancreatic islet β-cells, which are responsible for releasing insulin, it becomes difficult to regulate blood glucose levels. Consequently, the malfunctioning of β-cell function plays a crucial role in determining the risk and progression of type 2 diabetes. This understanding has prompted further investigation into the molecular and genetic factors underlying the disease, as well as the development of novel approaches for its treatment and prevention.

title: Tracking the fate of glomerular epithelial cells in vivo using serial multiphoton imaging in novel mouse models with fluorescent lineage tags
text: The maintenance of a healthy glomerular filter relies heavily on podocytes, but studying them in the intact kidney has been challenging due to technical limitations. However, we have made a breakthrough by developing a method called serial multiphoton microscopy (MPM) that allows us to observe the movement of podocytes and parietal epithelial cells (PECs) in real-time. Using podocin-GFP mice, we observed that podocytes formed sporadic clusters and migrated into the parietal Bowman's capsule after unilateral ureteral ligation. By tracking individual cells in podocin-confetti mice, which express different fluorescent proteins, we discovered that multiple podocytes migrate simultaneously. Additionally, in phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK)-GFP mice, we observed PEC-to-podocyte migration and nanotubule connections using serial MPM. These findings suggest that the glomerular environment and cellular composition are highly dynamic rather than static. This new approach has the potential to greatly enhance our understanding of glomerular injury and regeneration mechanisms in the future.

title: CTCF binding at the H19 imprinting control region mediates maternally inherited higher-order chromatin conformation to restrict enhancer access to Igf2.
text: The H19 imprinting control region (ICR) is believed to be responsible for silencing the maternally inherited Igf2 allele through a chromatin insulator that depends on CTCF. The ICR has been observed to physically interact with a silencer region called differentially methylated region (DMR)1 in Igf2, but the exact role of CTCF in this chromatin loop and whether it restricts the access of distal enhancers to Igf2 is still unknown. To investigate this, we conducted comprehensive chromosome conformation capture analyses in the Igf2/H19 region spanning over 160 kb. Through this analysis, we identified specific sequences that physically interact with the distal enhancers and the ICR. Our findings indicate that on the paternal chromosome, enhancers interact with the Igf2 promoters, but on the maternal allele, this interaction is prevented by CTCF binding within the H19 ICR. CTCF binding in the maternal ICR controls its interaction with matrix attachment region (MAR)3 and DMR1 at Igf2, creating a tight loop around the maternal Igf2 locus, which likely contributes to its silencing. Furthermore, when the CTCF binding sites in the H19 ICR are mutated, CTCF binding is lost, and de novo methylation occurs at a CTCF target site within Igf2 DMR1. This demonstrates that CTCF can coordinate regional epigenetic marks. Overall, our systematic chromosome conformation capture analysis of an imprinting cluster highlights the critical role of CTCF in the epigenetic regulation of higher-order chromatin structure and gene silencing across significant distances in the genome.

title: De novo assembly of a PML nuclear subcompartment occurs through multiple pathways and induces telomere elongation.
text: Tumor cells that lack telomerase use an alternative pathway called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) to maintain their ability to divide. This pathway involves DNA recombination and repair, and a key feature of this process is the accumulation of a protein called promyelocytic leukemia (PML) at the ends of telomeric DNA, forming structures known as ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs). In this study, we investigated the formation of a telomeric PML subcompartment by recruiting proteins involved in APB formation. We found that specific proteins were able to initiate the formation of APBs efficiently and in a self-organizing and self-propagating manner. These proteins included PML, Sp100, telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2 (TRF1 and TRF2), the DNA repair protein NBS1, and the SUMO E3 ligase MMS21, as well as the isolated SUMO1 domain through interaction with another protein factor. On the other hand, other repair factors such as Rad9, Rad17, and Rad51 were less effective in initiating APB formation but were recruited to preassembled APBs. The artificially created APBs induced telomeric extension through a DNA repair mechanism, as evidenced by their colocalization with sites of non-replicative DNA synthesis and histone H2A.X phosphorylation, and an increase in telomere length. These activities were not observed when the APB factors were recruited to a different location in the cell, indicating that APBs are functional intermediates of the ALT pathway.

title: Effects of an opal termination codon preceding the nsP4 gene sequence in the O'Nyong-Nyong virus genome on Anopheles gambiae infectivity.
text: The genomic RNA of an alphavirus encodes four nonstructural proteins: nsP1, nsP2, nsP3, and nsP4. When translation stops at an opal termination codon between nsP3 and nsP4, the polyprotein P123 is produced. If translational readthrough occurs or if the opal termination codon is replaced by a sense codon in the alphavirus genome, the polyprotein P1234 is produced. The O'nyong-nyong virus (ONNV) genome contains both a stop codon (opal) and an open reading frame (arginine), indicating that both are necessary. The predominance of a particular codon at this locus in the viral quasispecies may be determined by the alternate replication of ONNVs in vertebrate and invertebrate hosts. However, this hypothesis has not been systematically tested in whole animals before. In this study, we investigated the functional significance of the opal stop codon in an alphavirus genome using a natural mosquito host. We created mutants of ONNV by replacing the arginine between nsP3 and nsP4 with an opal, ochre, or amber stop codon using a full-length cDNA clone of ONNV. The presence of an opal stop codon upstream of nsP4 increased the infectivity of ONNV by almost double (75.5%) compared to the virus with a codon for arginine at the same position (39.8%). Although the opal virus did not significantly differ from the arginine virus in terms of dissemination from the mosquito midgut on days 8 and 10, dissemination started earlier in mosquitoes infected with the opal virus. The presence of an opal codon between nsP3 and nsP4 provided a clear fitness advantage to ONNV in Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes. However, sequence analysis of ONNV RNA extracted from mosquito bodies and heads showed that codon usage at this position corresponded to the virus administered in the blood meal. These results suggest that while ONNV variants are being selected, spontaneous mutation at the position between nsP3 and nsP4 does not readily occur in mosquitoes. Overall, the primary fitness advantage provided by the opal codon between nsP3 and nsP4 in ONNV is related to mosquito infectivity.

title: Down-regulation of a host microRNA by a Herpesvirus saimiri noncoding RNA.
text: T cells infected with Herpesvirus saimiri produce seven viral U-rich noncoding RNAs called HSURs, but their function is still unknown. We discovered that HSURs 1 and 2 contain conserved sequences that could potentially bind to three microRNAs (miRNAs) from the host cell. Through coimmunoprecipitation experiments, we confirmed that HSURs 1 and 2 indeed interact with these predicted miRNAs in the infected T cells. Interestingly, the abundance of one of these miRNAs, miR-27, is significantly reduced in the infected cells, leading to changes in the expression of genes targeted by miR-27. By temporarily reducing or artificially increasing the levels of HSUR 1, we demonstrated that it specifically degrades mature miR-27 in a sequence-specific and binding-dependent manner. This viral strategy highlights the use of a noncoding RNA to manipulate gene expression in the host cell through the miRNA pathway.

title: HTRF: A Technology Tailored for Drug Discovery –A Review of Theoretical Aspects and Recent Applications
text: HTRF, or Homogeneous Time Resolved Fluorescence, is a commonly used assay technology for measuring analytes in a homogenous format. It is particularly useful for drug target studies in high-throughput screening (HTS). This technology combines fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) with time-resolved measurement (TR). In TR-FRET assays, a signal is generated when a donor and an acceptor molecule are in close proximity, resulting in fluorescent resonance energy transfer. Dual-wavelength detection reduces interference from buffer and media, and the final signal is proportional to the amount of product formed. The HTRF assay is highly sensitive and robust, and can be miniaturized into 384 and 1536-well plate formats. It has been applied to various antibody-based assays, including GPCR signaling, kinases, cytokines, biomarkers, bioprocesses, and protein interactions. Since its introduction over ten years ago, HTRF has been used to expedite the study of GPCRs, kinases, biomarkers, protein interactions, and other targets of interest. It has also been used as an alternative method for bioprocess monitoring. The first-generation HTRF technology used Europium cryptate as a fluorescence donor, but in 2008, a second-generation donor, Terbium cryptate (Tb), was introduced to enhance screening performance. Terbium cryptate has different photophysical properties compared to Europium, including increased quantum yield and a higher molar extinction coefficient. It can also serve as a donor fluorophore to green-emitting fluors because it has multiple emission peaks. Additionally, Terbium HTRF assays can be read on the same instruments as Europium HTRF assays. Overall, HTRF is a highly sensitive and robust technology for detecting molecular interactions in vitro, and it is widely used in the primary and secondary screening phases of drug development. This review discusses the general principles of HTRF and its current applications in drug discovery.

title: Chk1 inhibits replication factory activation but allows dormant origin firing in existing factories
text: Loading MCM2-7 hexamers onto replication origins is necessary before entering S phase. However, only about 10% of these licensed origins are typically utilized during S phase, while the rest remain inactive. When the progression of replication forks is hindered, dormant origins nearby are triggered to ensure complete replication of all DNA. Interestingly, replicative stress activates the ATR and Chk1 checkpoint kinases, which inhibit the firing of replication origins. In this study, we demonstrate that under mild replication stress, ATR/Chk1 primarily suppresses the initiation of origins by preventing the activation of new replication factories, thereby reducing the number of active factories. Simultaneously, inhibition of replication fork progression allows dormant origins to initiate within existing replication factories. Consequently, ATR/Chk1's inhibition of new factory activation redirects replication towards active factories where fork progression is hindered, while avoiding regions that have not yet started replication. This strategy minimizes the harmful effects of fork stalling and prevents similar issues from occurring in unreplicated regions of the genome.

title: Fra-1 protooncogene regulates IL-6 expression in macrophages and promotes the generation of M2d macrophages
text: The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a significant role in the growth of tumor cells. M2d macrophages, as the main inflammatory component of the TME, are influenced by the TME to adopt an immunosuppressive role that supports tumor metastasis and progression. Fra-1, in partnership with Jun, forms activator protein-1 heterodimers and regulates gene transcription. Fra-1 is believed to strongly contribute to tumorigenesis and progression. However, the specific role of Fra-1 in the development of M2d macrophages remains poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that when co-cultured with RAW264.7 macrophage cells, 4T1 mammary carcinoma cells alter the differentiation of RAW264.7 macrophages, leading to the formation of M2d macrophages. The 4T1 cells induce the overexpression of Fra-1 in RAW264.7 cells, which then binds to the interleukin 6 (IL-6) promoter, resulting in increased production of the cytokine IL-6 in RAW264.7 cells. IL-6 acts in an autocrine manner to skew the differentiation of RAW264.7 macrophages towards M2d macrophages. These findings provide new insights into reversing M2d macrophage-induced immune tolerance to enhance the effectiveness of immunotherapeutic approaches.

title: Analysis of SiO2 nanoparticles binding proteins in rat blood and brain homogenate
text: Numerous nanoparticles, including titanium oxide (TiO2), zinc oxide, aluminum oxide, gold oxide, silver oxide, iron oxide, and silica oxide, are present in various chemical, cosmetic, pharmaceutical, and electronic products. Recently, it has been determined that SiO2 nanoparticles have a non-toxic profile and do not cause irreversible toxicological changes in animal models. As a result, exposure to SiO2 nanoparticles is increasing. These nanoparticles are commonly used in a wide range of materials, such as strengthening fillers for concrete and other construction composites, as well as non-toxic platforms for biomedical applications like drug delivery and theragnostics. However, recent in vitro experiments have shown that SiO2 nanoparticles can be cytotoxic. Therefore, we conducted a study to identify potentially toxic pathways by analyzing the protein corona that forms on the surface of SiO2 nanoparticles in the blood and brain of rats. We selected four types of SiO2 nanoparticles for investigation and used liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry technology to analyze the protein corona of each type. In total, we identified 115 plasma proteins bound to negatively charged 20 nm SiO2 nanoparticles and 48 plasma proteins bound to negatively charged 100 nm SiO2 nanoparticles. Additionally, we found 50 proteins bound to 20 nm arginine-coated SiO2 nanoparticles and 36 proteins bound to 100 nm arginine-coated SiO2 nanoparticles. Interestingly, a higher number of proteins were adsorbed onto the 20 nm SiO2 nanoparticles compared to the 100 nm nanoparticles, regardless of charge. Furthermore, when comparing the two charges, we observed a higher number of proteins bound to the positively charged arginine-coated SiO2 nanoparticles compared to the negatively charged nanoparticles. We further analyzed the proteins identified in the corona using ClueGO, a Cytoscape plugin that helps identify biological interaction pathways and protein ontology. The proteins bound to the surface of nanoparticles can potentially impact functional and conformational properties, as well as distributions, in complex biological processes.

title: Inferring nucleosome positions with their histone mark annotation from ChIP data
text:
MOTIVATION: The nucleosome, consisting of core histones and DNA, is the fundamental unit of chromatin. Histone proteins undergo various post-translational modifications, such as methylation or acetylation. Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) is a technique that provides genome-wide data on these modified histones, requiring computational methods. 

RESULTS: We introduce NucHunter, an algorithm that utilizes ChIP-seq data from multiple histone modification experiments to determine the positioning of nucleosomes. NucHunter assigns intensity values of histone modifications to each nucleosome, allowing for the inference of distinct nucleosomal states correlated with genomic features and chromatin-related processes, including transcriptional start sites, enhancers, RNA polymerase II elongation, and chromatin-mediated repression. NucHunter is a versatile tool for predicting nucleosome positions and identifying specific histone modification patterns associated with different chromatin states. 

AVAILABILITY: The software can be accessed at http://epigen.molgen.mpg.de/nuchunter/.

title: Generation of large numbers of dendritic cells from mouse bone marrow cultures supplemented with granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor
text: Dendritic cells, which are rich in major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II antigens, are known to originate from the bone marrow. However, mature dendritic cells are not found in the marrow, and there is still a need to identify a significant number of proliferating less-mature cells. Recently, a method for inducing dendritic cell growth in mouse blood has been adapted to MHC class II-negative precursors in the marrow. A crucial step in this process is to remove most of the nonadherent granulocytes that are newly formed through gentle washes during the first 2-4 days of culture. This leaves behind clusters of proliferating cells that are loosely attached to a more firmly adherent "stroma." By days 4-6, these clusters can be dislodged, isolated through sedimentation, and when recultured, a large number of dendritic cells are released. These dendritic cells can be easily identified by their unique cell shape, ultrastructure, and repertoire of antigens using a panel of monoclonal antibodies. The dendritic cells express high levels of MHC class II products and serve as potent accessory cells for initiating the mixed leukocyte reaction. However, if macrophage colony-stimulating factor is used instead of granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), neither the clusters nor mature dendritic cells are generated. Therefore, GM-CSF is responsible for generating all three lineages of myeloid cells (granulocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells). It is worth noting that more than 5 x 10(6) dendritic cells can develop within one week from precursors in the large hind limb bones of a single animal, indicating that marrow progenitors can serve as a significant source of dendritic cells. This characteristic will be valuable for future molecular and clinical studies involving this relatively rare cell type.

title: Insulin action and resistance in obesity and type 2 diabetes
text: Excessive nutrition plays a significant role in the development of type 2 diabetes. It increases the production of insulin, but weakens its effectiveness in the liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. However, there is conflicting evidence regarding the timing of these events during the progression of obesity and diabetes, highlighting a crucial gap in our understanding of metabolic disease. This Perspective examines different perspectives and recent findings on the timing and mechanisms linking hyperinsulinemia, obesity, and insulin resistance. While much attention has been focused on early stages of insulin signaling, insulin resistance in obesity appears to primarily occur downstream of these stages. Recent discoveries also reveal a strong connection between insulin resistance and extensive metabolic communication among the liver, adipose tissue, pancreas, and skeletal muscle. These advancements, along with others made in the last 5 years, present both exciting opportunities and daunting challenges in the development of new therapeutic approaches for treating type 2 diabetes.

title: Effect of lowering blood pressure on cardiovascular events and mortality in patients on dialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
Patients undergoing dialysis are at a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity. While there have been trials demonstrating the cardiovascular benefits of lowering blood pressure in the general population, it remains uncertain whether this approach is effective and well-tolerated in dialysis patients. To address this, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the impact of blood pressure reduction in dialysis patients.

We conducted a comprehensive search of Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library database for trials published between 1950 and November 2008, without any language restrictions. We extracted data from randomized controlled trials that focused on blood pressure lowering in dialysis patients and reported cardiovascular outcomes. Meta-analysis was performed using a random effects model.

We identified eight relevant trials, which included a total of 1679 patients and 495 cardiovascular events. The actively treated patients had a mean systolic blood pressure that was 4.5 mm Hg lower and a mean diastolic blood pressure that was 2.3 mm Hg lower compared to the control group. Blood pressure lowering treatment was associated with a reduced risk of cardiovascular events (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92; p=0.009), all-cause mortality (RR 0.80, 0.66-0.96; p=0.014), and cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.71, 0.50-0.99; p=0.044) compared to control regimens. These effects were consistent across various patient groups included in the studies.

In conclusion, the routine consideration of blood pressure-lowering agents for dialysis patients is recommended to mitigate the significantly elevated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality rates observed in this population.

title: Interaction of an adenovirus E3 14.7-kilodalton protein with a novel tumor necrosis factor alpha-inducible cellular protein containing leucine zipper domains.
text: The E3 region 3 (E3) of group C human adenoviruses (Ad) contains genes that produce inhibitors of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) cytolysis. These inhibitors include a 14.7-kDa protein called E3-14.7K and a heterodimer made up of two polypeptides weighing 10.4 and 14.5 kDa. To understand how these viral proteins block TNF-alpha functions, researchers used the E3-14.7K protein to screen a HeLa cell cDNA library in the yeast two-hybrid system. They discovered a new protein, named FIP-2 (short for 14.7K-interacting protein), which contains multiple leucine zipper domains and does not resemble any known protein. FIP-2 was found to interact with E3-14.7K both in vitro and in vivo. It was observed that FIP-2 and Ad E3-14.7K colocalized in the cytoplasm, particularly near the nuclear membrane, and caused a redistribution of the viral protein. FIP-2 alone did not induce cell death, but it could reverse the protective effect of E3-14.7K on cell killing caused by overexpression of the intracellular domain of the 55-kDa TNF receptor or by RIP, a death protein involved in the TNF-alpha and Fas apoptosis pathways. Further analysis revealed that the reversal effect of FIP-2 depended on its interaction with E3-14.7K. Three major forms of FIP-2 mRNA were detected in various human tissues, and the expression of these transcripts was induced by TNF-alpha treatment in a time-dependent manner in two different cell lines. FIP-2 also contains consensus sequences for potential posttranslational modifications. These findings suggest that FIP-2 is a target of Ad E3-14.7K and that its mechanism of action in cell death involves the TNF receptor, RIP, or a downstream molecule influenced by either of these two molecules.

title: PML induces compaction, TRF2 depletion and DNA damage signaling at telomeres and promotes their alternative lengthening.
text: The mechanism known as alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) enables cancer cells to evade senescence and apoptosis even without active telomerase. A key aspect of this process is the formation of ALT-associated promyelocytic leukemia (PML) nuclear bodies (APBs) at telomeres. In this study, we investigated the role of APBs in a human ALT cell line using an automated 3D fluorescence microscopy platform and advanced 3D image analysis through an RNA interference screen. Our analysis revealed 29 proteins that influenced APB formation, including proteins involved in telomere and chromatin organization, protein sumoylation, and DNA repair. Building upon these findings, we discovered that APB formation led to the clustering of telomere repeats, compaction of telomeres, and a decrease in the shelterin protein TRF2 (also known as TERF2). These changes induced by APBs were accompanied by a DNA damage response at telomeres, as evidenced by a significant increase in the phosphorylated form of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase. Consequently, we propose that APBs facilitate telomere maintenance in ALT-positive tumor cells by triggering a DNA damage response through alterations in the telomeric chromatin state, ultimately leading to ATM phosphorylation.

title: Gr-1+CD11b+ myeloid cells tip the balance of immune protection to tumor promotion in the premetastatic lung.
text: The exact ways in which a primary tumor affects a distant organ before the arrival of tumor cells are still unknown. However, this study demonstrates that Gr-1+CD11b+ cells are significantly increased in the lungs of mice with mammary adenocarcinomas before the tumor cells arrive. These immature myeloid cells in the premetastatic lungs decrease the production of IFN-gamma and increase the levels of proinflammatory cytokines. Additionally, they produce large amounts of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and contribute to vascular remodeling. By deleting MMP9, the abnormal vasculature in the premetastatic lung is normalized and lung metastasis is reduced. The production and activity of MMP9 are specifically limited to the lungs and organs with a high number of Gr-1+CD11b+ cells. This research uncovers a new mechanism by which Gr-1+CD11b+ cells promote tumor growth, creating an inflammatory and proliferative environment in the premetastatic lung, weakening immune protection, and facilitating metastasis through the formation of abnormal blood vessels. Therefore, inhibiting Gr-1+CD11b+ cells could restore the normal environment of the premetastatic lung, enhance immune surveillance, and hinder tumor metastasis.

title: Activin/Nodal signalling in stem cells.
text: The Activin/Nodal growth factors have a significant impact on various biological processes, such as early cell fate determination, organ development, and maintaining the balance of adult tissues. In this article, we aim to provide an overview of how the Activin/Nodal signaling pathway regulates the function of stem cells during different stages of growth. We will also explore recent discoveries linking Activin/Nodal signaling to disease conditions, particularly its involvement in the formation of cancer stem cells and its potential as a target for therapeutic interventions. Additionally, we will address the unanswered questions and future research directions regarding the role of Activin/Nodal signaling in the self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation of stem cells.

title: Distinct RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are required for RNAi triggered by double-stranded RNA versus truncated transgenes in Paramecium tetraurelia
text: RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs) are important players in the RNAi pathway in many eukaryotes. They are involved in recognizing and processing abnormal transcripts, initiating the silencing process, and amplifying the silencing response. We conducted experiments to investigate the roles of RdRP genes from the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia in both experimentally induced and naturally occurring gene silencing mechanisms. In Paramecium, RNAi can be triggered by high-copy, truncated transgenes or by directly feeding cells with double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Surprisingly, we found that dsRNA-induced silencing relies on the functional RDR1 and RDR2 genes, which are necessary for the accumulation of primary siRNAs and a distinct class of small RNAs that may be secondary siRNAs. On the other hand, a third gene, RDR3, with a significantly different catalytic domain, is required for siRNA accumulation when RNAi is triggered by truncated transgenes. Our findings also suggest that RDR3 is involved in the accumulation of previously identified endogenous siRNAs and in regulating the surface antigen gene family. While only one of these genes is typically expressed in each clonal cell line, reducing the expression of RDR3 leads to the simultaneous expression of multiple antigens. These results provide evidence for the specialized functions of Paramecium RdRP genes in distinct RNAi pathways that operate during vegetative growth.

title: Mechanisms of Renal Cell Apoptosis Induced by Cyclosporine A: A Systematic Review of in vitro Studies
text:
Background: Chronic nephrotoxicity caused by cyclosporine A (CsA) is a significant contributor to chronic renal dysfunction, and effective clinical interventions for this condition are currently lacking. 

Objective: Our objective was to investigate the mechanisms of renal cell apoptosis in chronic CsA nephrotoxicity by analyzing relevant in vitro studies. 

Methods: We conducted a comprehensive search of Medline (1966 to July 2010), Embase (1980 to July 2010), and ISI (1986 to July 2010) to identify all in vitro studies on the mechanisms of renal cell apoptosis induced by CsA. We assessed the quality of these studies according to in vitro standards, extracted data following the PICOS principles, and synthesized the findings. 

Results: Our analysis revealed several key findings. Firstly, CsA was found to increase the expression of Fas and Fas-L, as well as apoptosis enzymes (caspase-2, -3, -4, -7, -8, -9, and -10), while downregulating Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL. Secondly, CsA induced oxidative stress and impaired the antioxidant defense system. Thirdly, CsA increased the expression of HERP, GRP78, and CHOP. Lastly, CsA induced renal cell apoptosis and upregulated iNOS and p53 expression in cultured cells. 

Conclusions: Our findings suggest that CsA-induced renal cell apoptosis involves at least four distinct pathways in different cell species. Caspases may serve as the final common pathway in vitro. These findings provide potential targets for interventions, although further confirmation in vivo is necessary.

title: Blood stem cells emerge from aortic endothelium by a novel type of cell transition
text: The debate surrounding the development of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) during embryonic growth, particularly their potential connection to vascular endothelial cells, remains ongoing. The aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM), specifically the area near the dorsal aortic floor, is the first known location where cells with long-term HSC potential have been discovered. While some researchers argue that HSCs originate directly from the aortic floor and enter the dorsal aortic lumen, others propose that HSCs first appear within the underlying mesenchyme. Through non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of live zebrafish embryos, we demonstrate that HSCs emerge directly from the aortic floor. This process involves a consistent sequence of events, including the bending and exit of individual endothelial cells from the aortic ventral wall into the sub-aortic space, where they transform into haematopoietic cells. The process is not only polarized in the dorso-ventral direction but also in the rostro-caudal versus medio-lateral direction. Furthermore, this process relies on the expression of Runx1. In embryos lacking Runx1, the exit events are initially similar but much less frequent, often resulting in the death of the exiting cell. These findings provide evidence that the aortic floor possesses haemogenic properties and that HSCs emerge from it into the sub-aortic space. This occurs not through asymmetric cell division but through a novel type of cell behavior, which we refer to as an endothelial haematopoietic transition.

title: Probable person to person transmission of novel avian influenza A (H7N9) virus in Eastern China, 2013: epidemiological investigation
text:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the potential transmission of the avian influenza H7N9 virus from person to person and assess its efficiency.

DESIGN: Epidemiological investigations were conducted following a family cluster of two patients with avian H7N9 in March 2013.

SETTING: The study took place in Wuxi, Eastern China.

PARTICIPANTS: The study included two patients, their close contacts, and relevant environments. Samples from the patients and environments were collected and tested using real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR), viral culture, and haemagglutination inhibition assay. Contacts who became ill were tested for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. Paired serum samples were obtained from contacts for serological testing using haemagglutination inhibition assays.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The study assessed clinical data, history of exposure before illness onset, laboratory testing results of pathogens, and further analysis of sequences and phylogenetic tree to isolated strains.

RESULTS: The index patient became ill five to six days after his last exposure to poultry. The second patient, his 32-year-old daughter who provided unprotected bedside care in the hospital, had no known exposure to poultry. She developed symptoms six days after her last contact with her father. Two strains were successfully isolated from the two patients. Genome sequence and phylogenetic tree analysis showed that both viruses were almost genetically identical. Forty-three close contacts of both patients were identified. One contact had mild illness but tested negative for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. All 43 close contacts tested negative for haemagglutination inhibition antibodies specific for avian H7N9.

CONCLUSIONS: The daughter's infection likely resulted from contact with her father (the index patient) during unprotected exposure, indicating person-to-person transmission in this cluster. However, the transmissibility was limited and non-sustainable.

title: Genetic Variation in the Interleukin-28B Gene Is Associated with Spontaneous Clearance and Progression of Hepatitis C Virus in Moroccan Patients
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of genetic variations in the IL28B gene on the progression and outcome of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in a population from Morocco. A total of 438 individuals were included in the analysis, including 232 patients with persistent HCV infection (115 with mild chronic hepatitis and 117 with advanced liver disease), 68 individuals who had naturally cleared HCV, and 138 healthy subjects. The IL28B SNPs rs12979860 and rs8099917 were genotyped using a TaqMan 5' allelic discrimination assay. 

The results showed that the protective rs12979860-C and rs8099917-T alleles were more common in individuals who had spontaneously cleared HCV infection compared to those with persistent infection (77.9% vs 55.2% and 95.6% vs 83.2%, respectively). Individuals with clearance were significantly more likely to have the C/C genotype for the rs12979860 polymorphism (4.69 times more likely) and the T/T genotype for rs8099917 (3.55 times more likely). Patients with advanced liver disease were more likely to carry the rs12979860-T/T genotype compared to those with mild chronic hepatitis C, and this risk was even higher when compared to healthy controls. The rs8099917-G allele was also associated with advanced liver disease. 

In conclusion, in the Moroccan population, genetic variations near the IL28B gene are involved in both the spontaneous clearance and progression of HCV infection.

title: CD127 expression inversely correlates with FoxP3 and suppressive function of human CD4+ T reg cells
text: Regulatory T (T reg) cells play a crucial role in maintaining immune tolerance. Traditionally, T reg cells have been identified based on the expression of CD4, CD25, and the transcription factor, FoxP3. However, these markers have posed challenges in accurately defining this specialized T cell subset in humans. Our research has revealed that a subset of CD4+ T cells in peripheral blood exhibit down-regulation of the IL-7 receptor (CD127). Importantly, we have demonstrated that the majority of these cells are FoxP3+, even those with low levels or no CD25 expression. By combining CD4, CD25, and CD127 markers, we have successfully isolated a highly purified population of T reg cells, which significantly surpasses the number of cells previously identified using other cell surface markers. These cells have shown strong suppressive activity in functional suppressor assays. Interestingly, T cells separated solely based on CD4 and CD127 expression were found to be anergic. Despite representing at least three times the number of cells compared to the "classic" CD4+CD25hi T reg cell subset (including both CD25+CD4+ and CD25−CD4+ T cell subsets), they exhibited similar suppressive capabilities. Lastly, we have demonstrated that CD127 can be utilized as a biomarker to quantify T reg cell subsets in individuals with type 1 diabetes, further supporting its potential as a valuable tool for studying human T reg cells.

title: Environmental factors that influence the cutaneous production of vitamin D
text: Most vertebrates, including humans, primarily obtain their daily vitamin D requirement from casual exposure to sunlight. When exposed to sunlight, ultraviolet B photons from the sun penetrate the skin and cause the breakdown of 7-dehydrocholesterol into precholecalciferol. This precholecalciferol then undergoes a rearrangement of its double bonds to form cholecalciferol. However, factors such as skin pigmentation, aging, and the use of sunscreen can reduce the production of cholecalciferol in the skin. Additionally, the amount of solar ultraviolet B photons that reach the earth's surface is influenced by latitude, season, time of day, and ozone pollution, all of which can affect the production of cholecalciferol. In places like Boston, exposure to sunlight between November and February does not result in significant production of cholecalciferol in the skin. Sunlight that passes through glass windows is also unable to produce cholecalciferol due to the absorption of ultraviolet B radiation by windowpane glass. It is now known that vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency are common in elderly individuals, particularly those who are immobile, lack sunlight exposure, or live in regions with limited sunlight during the winter months. Insufficient or deficient levels of vitamin D can worsen osteoporosis, cause osteomalacia, and increase the risk of bone fractures. To prevent vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency, it is recommended to encourage responsible sunlight exposure or consume a multivitamin tablet containing 10 micrograms (400 IU) of vitamin D.

title: Genomic imprinting in development, growth, behavior and stem cells.
text: Imprinted genes in mammals are genes that are selectively expressed from only one parental allele. This selective expression plays a vital role in normal development, as these genes directly control the growth of the fetus. Moreover, recent research has uncovered the intricate involvement of imprinted genes in brain function, impacting behavior and neuronal activity. Additionally, recent studies have emphasized the significance of correct expression of specific imprinted genes in induced pluripotent stem cells and adult stem cells. In summary, these discoveries underscore the intricate nature and developmental significance of imprinted genes.

title: Quantitative Detection of Hepatitis C Virus RNA by Light Cycler PCR and Comparison with Two Different PCR Assays
text: We utilized the innovative Light Cycler technology to detect hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA in clinical samples. A total of 81 patient sera were examined using Light Cycler PCR, AMPLICOR HCV Monitor assay, and in-house PCR. Our findings unequivocally establish that Light Cycler is a rapid and dependable approach for the precise detection and quantification of HCV RNA.

title: Targeting arginine metabolism pathway to treat arginine-dependent cancers.
text: The significant differences in metabolism between tumor cells and normal cells have sparked the development of anti-tumor treatments based on metabolism. Arginine, an amino acid, is considered semi-essential because normal cells can produce it on their own and also absorb it from outside sources. However, certain types of tumors have abnormalities in their arginine metabolism enzymes and rely solely on external sources of arginine for their biological processes. This reliance on arginine is known as arginine auxotrophy. Researchers have explored the use of arginine deprivation, achieved through the use of arginine deiminase (ADI) and arginase I, as a novel approach to cancer therapy, taking advantage of the characteristic arginine auxotrophy in tumors. Arginine deprivation has shown promising effectiveness against arginine-auxotrophic tumors. This article provides a comprehensive review of arginine deprivation as a potential anticancer therapy, incorporating insights from both clinical oncologists and laboratory scientists.

title: Rank Signaling Links the Development of Invariant γδ T Cell Progenitors and Aire+ Medullary Epithelium
text: During the embryonic-neonatal period, the thymic medulla plays a crucial role in the negative selection of T cells. This process relies on the presence of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) that express autoimmune regulator (Aire). Our study reveals that the establishment of long-lasting tolerance is dependent on the emergence of the first cohorts of Aire(+) mTECs during this developmental stage, before the selection of αβ T cell repertoire. This emergence is jointly directed by Rankl(+) lymphoid tissue inducer cells and invariant Vγ5(+) dendritic epidermal T cell (DETC) progenitors, which are the first thymocytes to express the products of gene rearrangement. Subsequently, the generation of Aire(+) mTECs promotes the maturation of DETC progenitors in a Skint-1-dependent manner, independent of Aire, leading to the emergence of an invariant DETC repertoire. Our findings highlight the functional importance of the temporal development of Vγ5(+) γδ T cells during thymus medulla formation in inducing αβ T cell tolerance. Additionally, we demonstrate a reciprocal link between DETC and Aire(+) mTEC maturation mediated by Rank.

title: Long-term immune deficiency after allogeneic stem cell transplantation: B-cell deficiency is associated with late infections.
text: We analyzed immune reconstitution in a group of 140 patients who had undergone myeloablative allogeneic transplantation and were disease-free for two years. We observed a defect in both CD4 and CD8 cells, affecting naive, terminally differentiated, memory, and competent cells, as well as elevated levels of activated subsets. Natural killer cells returned to normal levels after six months, while CD19(+)/CD5(+) B cells showed expansion after three months and a persistent defect in memory B cells. The presence of chronic graft-versus-host disease did not significantly impact CD8 subsets, but had a strong effect on naive and competent CD4 subsets. However, the most significant impact of chronic graft-versus-host disease was on B-cell subsets, particularly memory B cells. The incidence of severe infections occurring later on was relatively low (14% at four years). Cox's models revealed that low B-cell counts at 12 (P=0.02) and 24 (P=0.001) months were associated with a higher risk of developing late infections, especially in patients without chronic graft-versus-host disease.

title: The stimulatory potency of T cell antigens is influenced by the formation of the immunological synapse.
text: The activation of T cells relies on the interaction between the T cell receptor and peptide-major histocompatibility (pMHC) ligands. However, the factors that determine how potent a pMHC molecule is in stimulating T cells are still not fully understood. In our study, we present findings that demonstrate how a peptide with characteristics of a weak agonist can actually stimulate T cell proliferation more effectively than the wild-type agonist ligand. Through an in silico approach, we discovered that the lack of formation of the central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC) may be responsible for this increased proliferation. This conclusion was further supported by experiments that showed enhancing cSMAC formation reduced the stimulatory capacity of the weak peptide. Our research emphasizes the intricate interplay of various factors in determining the quality of a T cell antigen.

title: Control of glutamate clearance and synaptic efficacy by glial coverage of neurons.
text: The examination of excitatory synaptic transmission in the rat hypothalamic supraoptic nucleus demonstrated that the removal of glutamate, along with its concentration and spread in the space outside the cells, is linked to the extent of astrocytic protection around the neurons.
