In this study, we focus on ANKTM1, a channel that is activated by cold and has a lower activation temperature compared to TRPM8, the receptor for cold and menthol. ANKTM1 belongs to a different family of TRP channels and has very little similarity in amino acid composition to TRPM8. It is found in a specific group of sensory neurons that detect pain and is coexpressed with TRPV1/VR1, the receptor for capsaicin and heat, but not with TRPM8. Our findings suggest that there are sensory neurons that are sensitive to both noxious cold and capsaicin, but not to menthol.

title: Plasma vitamin D metabolites and risk of colorectal cancer in women.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the potential role of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and its precursor, 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], in preventing colorectal cancer. We conducted a nested case-control study among women in the Nurses' Health Study, identifying 193 cases of colorectal cancer in women aged 46 to 78 years, diagnosed within 11 years after blood collection. Two controls were matched to each case based on year of birth and month of blood draw. We used conditional logistic regression to calculate odds ratios (OR) for colorectal cancer risk, adjusting for factors such as body mass index, physical activity, smoking, family history, hormone replacement therapy, aspirin use, and dietary intakes. 

Our findings revealed a significant inverse linear relationship between plasma 25(OH)D levels and colorectal cancer risk (P = 0.02). Among women in the highest quintile, the OR (95% confidence interval) was 0.53 (0.27-1.04), indicating a lower risk. This inverse association remained strong when analyzing women aged 60 years or older at blood collection (P = 0.006), but was not observed among younger women (P = 0.70). We also observed a benefit from higher 25(OH)D concentrations specifically for cancers located in the distal colon and rectum (P = 0.02), but not for those in the proximal colon (P = 0.81). In contrast, we did not find an association between 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and colorectal cancer. However, among women in the highest quintile of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels who were also in the lower half of the 25(OH)D distribution, the risk of colorectal cancer was elevated (OR, 2.52; 95% confidence interval, 1.04-6.11). 

Based on these results and supporting evidence from previous studies, we conclude that higher plasma levels of 25(OH)D are associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer in older women, particularly for cancers located in the distal colon and rectum.

title: DNA Deamination Mediates Innate Immunity to Retroviral Infection
text: CEM15/APOBEC3G is a cellular protein that plays a crucial role in defending against infection by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) strains lacking the virion infectivity factor (Vif). In this study, we utilized a system based on murine leukemia virus (MLV) to demonstrate that CEM15/APOBEC3G functions as a DNA deaminase. During viral production, this protein becomes incorporated into virions and subsequently induces extensive deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine within the retroviral minus (first)-strand cDNA. This process serves as a likely trigger for the destruction of the virus. Additionally, HIV Vif has the ability to shield MLV from the restriction imposed by CEM15/APOBEC3G. These findings suggest that targeted DNA deamination is a significant mechanism employed by the innate immune system to combat retroviruses, and it is also likely to contribute to the observed sequence variation in various viruses, including HIV.

title: Global, regional, and national disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) for 315 diseases and injuries and healthy life expectancy (HALE), 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015
text:
BACKGROUND: Healthy life expectancy (HALE) and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) are important measures of health that can provide valuable information on epidemiological patterns, health system performance, and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In this study, we aimed to update HALE and DALYs for countries worldwide and examine how disease burden changes with development.

METHODS: We used data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2015 (GBD 2015) to calculate HALE and DALYs for 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2015. DALYs were calculated by combining years of life lost (YLLs) and years lived with disability (YLDs) for each geography, age group, sex, and year. HALE was estimated using the Sullivan method, which takes into account age-specific death rates and YLDs per capita. We also compared observed levels of DALYs and HALE with expected trends calculated using the Socio-demographic Index (SDI), a composite indicator based on income per capita, average years of schooling, and total fertility rate.

FINDINGS: Overall global DALYs remained relatively stable from 1990 to 2015, with decreases in communicable, neonatal, maternal, and nutritional diseases offset by increases in non-communicable diseases (NCDs). This transition was driven by changes in population growth and aging, as well as improvements in SDI, which were strongly correlated with the increasing burden of NCDs. While total DALYs and age-standardized DALY rates for most Group 1 causes (communicable, neonatal, maternal, and nutritional diseases) significantly decreased by 2015, the burden of most NCDs increased. However, age-standardized DALY rates for NCDs declined. Nevertheless, several high-burden NCDs, such as osteoarthritis, drug use disorders, depression, diabetes, congenital birth defects, and diseases of the skin, oral cavity, and sense organs, either increased or remained unchanged, leading to their higher ranking in many regions. From 2005 to 2015, HALE at birth increased by an average of 2.9 years for men and 3.5 years for women, while HALE at age 65 improved by 0.85 years and 1.2 years, respectively. Rising SDI was associated with higher HALE and a smaller proportion of life spent with functional health loss, but it was also linked to increased total disability. Some countries in central America and eastern sub-Saharan Africa had lower disease burden rates than expected based on their SDI, while others experienced a growing gap between observed and expected DALYs due to war, violence, and various NCDs.

INTERPRETATION: While global health is improving, more populations are experiencing functional health loss, leading to an expansion of morbidity. The proportion of life spent in ill health decreases somewhat with increasing SDI, indicating a relative compression of morbidity. This highlights the importance of efforts to increase personal income, improve education, and limit fertility. Our analysis of DALYs and HALE in relation to SDI provides a solid framework for assessing health performance and SDG progress at the country level. Understanding the specific drivers of disease burden, particularly for causes with higher-than-expected DALYs, can inform financial and research investments, prevention efforts, health policies, and healthcare system improvements for all countries at different stages of development.

FUNDING: This study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: Adverse drug events: database construction and in silico prediction.
text:
Adverse drug events (ADEs) refer to the harmful effects that can occur when medications are used at normal dosages. These events are crucial considerations for a drug to be approved for clinical use or remain on the market. In many cases, ADEs are not identified during trials and only become apparent once the drug is approved, leading to negative health outcomes and even death. To date, millions of ADEs have been reported worldwide. Finding ways to prevent or minimize ADEs is a significant concern in drug discovery and development.

In this study, we present a comprehensive database called MetaADEDB, which contains over 520,000 associations between drugs and ADEs. This database includes 3059 unique compounds (including 1330 drugs) and 13,200 ADE items. The data was collected through integration of various sources and text mining techniques. Each compound and ADE in the database is annotated with commonly used concepts defined in Medical Subject Headings (MeSH).

Additionally, we developed a computational method called the phenotypic network inference model (PNIM) to predict potential ADEs using the MetaADEDB database. The accuracy of the method was evaluated using the area under the receive operating characteristic curve (AUC), which was found to be above 0.9 through 10-fold cross validation. Furthermore, an external validation set extracted from the US-FDA Adverse Events Reporting System yielded an AUC value of 0.912, indicating the reliability of our prediction capability.

MetaADEDB is freely accessible at http://www.lmmd.org/online_services/metaadedb/. This database, along with the PNIM method, provides a valuable tool for searching known side effects or predicting potential side effects associated with a specific drug or compound.

title: Genetic Tests for Ecological and Allopatric Speciation in Anoles on an Island Archipelago
text: The study of islands, as seen in Darwin's research on the Galapagos and Wallace's study of Indonesia, has played a significant role in the investigation of evolution. Radiations within archipelagos are commonly seen as evidence supporting the traditional view of allopatric speciation. Even as the scientific community shifts towards exploring other modes of speciation, island radiations, like the Lesser Antillean anoles, are considered to be prime examples of this process. Geological and molecular phylogenetic evidence reveals that the Martinique anoles in this archipelago provide multiple instances of secondary contact between island species. Four precursor island species, which had diverged up to 8 million years ago, came together when their islands merged to form the present-day Martinique. Additionally, neighboring anole populations display distinct adaptations to different habitat zones, allowing for the testing of both allopatric and ecological speciation in this system. We take advantage of this unique opportunity of replicated island merging and independent ecological adaptation to conduct an extensive study on population genetics using highly variable neutral nuclear markers. Our findings demonstrate that even after prolonged periods of spatial isolation, these presumed allospecies exhibit less reproductive isolation compared to populations of the same species in adjacent habitats, in all three cases of subsequent island merging. The level of genetic exchange indicates that while there is always a significant genetic signature of past allopatry, which can be particularly strong under certain selection regimes, there is no instance of complete allopatric speciation, despite the strong initial evidence supporting it. Importantly, there is greater genetic isolation across the xeric/rainforest ecotone than what is observed during any secondary contact. This challenges the notion that reproductive isolation develops solely through allopatric divergence, but supports the potential for ecological speciation, even though full speciation has not been achieved in this particular case. Furthermore, this explains why there are fewer anole species in the Lesser Antilles compared to the Greater Antilles.

title: Deficiency and pharmacological stabilization of mast cells reduce diet-induced obesity and diabetes in mice
text: Recent research suggests that mast cells, traditionally associated with allergic responses, also play a role in various other diseases including multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, aortic aneurysm, and cancer. This study provides evidence that mast cells are also involved in diet-induced obesity and diabetes. For instance, obese individuals and mice have been found to have more mast cells in their white adipose tissue (WAT) compared to their lean counterparts. Additionally, in mice on a Western diet, the absence of mast cells or their stabilization through medication has been shown to reduce weight gain, inflammatory markers, and proteases in the blood and WAT, while also improving glucose regulation and energy expenditure. Mechanistic investigations have revealed that mast cells contribute to angiogenesis in WAT and muscles, as well as cell apoptosis and cathepsin activity. Adoptive transfer experiments using mast cells deficient in certain cytokines have demonstrated that these cells, by producing interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma), contribute to the expression of cathepsin, apoptosis, and angiogenesis in adipose tissue, thereby promoting diet-induced obesity and glucose intolerance. The findings of this study, which show reduced obesity and diabetes in mice treated with mast cell-stabilizing agents already available in clinical practice, suggest the potential for developing new therapies for these common metabolic disorders in humans.

title: Familial aphasic episodes: another variant of partial epilepsy with simple inheritance?
text: We present a case study of a family experiencing partial epilepsy with a straightforward inheritance pattern. The individuals affected by this condition frequently experience episodes of aphasia that can progress to generalized seizures. The onset of symptoms typically occurs during either adolescence or adulthood. The response to medication among patients has shown significant variation. No neurological abnormalities or decline in cognitive abilities were observed. This case highlights a distinct form of rare familial partial epilepsy characterized by neocortical epilepsy features.

title: Endosome-ER Contacts Control Actin Nucleation and Retromer Function through VAP-Dependent Regulation of PI4P
text: VAP (VAPA and VAPB) is a protein that is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and plays a crucial role in creating connections between the ER and other membranes. These connections allow for the exchange of lipids between adjacent layers of membranes. In our study, we have discovered that VAP regulates the levels of a lipid called PI4P on endosomes. This regulation affects the process of actin nucleation, which is necessary for the formation of actin filaments, on these organelles. Additionally, VAP also influences the function of the retromer, a protein coat that is responsible for transporting materials from endosomes to the Golgi apparatus. VAP is recruited to specific sites on endosomes where the retromer is budding, and this recruitment is facilitated by an interaction with a subunit of the retromer called SNX2. Cells that lack VAP exhibit an accumulation of high levels of PI4P, actin comets, and trans-Golgi proteins on endosomes. Interestingly, these defects are also observed when a protein called OSBP, which interacts with VAP and transports PI4P, is downregulated. This suggests that OSBP is involved in the tethering of the ER to endosomes through VAP. Our findings demonstrate the importance of PI4P in the process of retromer-/WASH-dependent budding from endosomes. Overall, our data provide insights into how the ER can regulate the dynamics of budding and its association with the cytoskeleton of another membrane through direct contacts that lead to modifications in lipid composition.

title: Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome–Dependent Proteolysis of Human Cyclin a Starts at the Beginning of Mitosis and Is Not Subject to the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint
text: During the S and G2 phases, Cyclin A remains stable as a protein. However, once cells enter mitosis, it becomes destabilized and undergoes significant degradation before the transition from metaphase to anaphase. When antibodies against subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) or against human Cdc20 (fizzy) are microinjected, cells are arrested at metaphase, and both cyclins A and B1 are stabilized. In vitro experiments showed that Cdc20 or Cdh1-activated APC/C efficiently polyubiquitylates cyclin A. However, unlike cyclin B1, the degradation of cyclin A is not delayed by the spindle assembly checkpoint. Inhibition of the spindle assembly checkpoint accelerates the degradation of cyclin B1. These findings indicate that the APC/C is activated as cells enter mitosis and immediately targets cyclin A for degradation. On the other hand, the spindle assembly checkpoint delays the degradation of cyclin B1 until the transition from metaphase to anaphase. The "destruction box" (D-box) of cyclin A is longer by 10-20 residues compared to cyclin B. Overexpression of wild-type cyclin A delays the transition from metaphase to anaphase, while the expression of cyclin A mutants lacking a D-box arrests cells in anaphase.

title: Human T Cell Leukemia Virus Reactivation with Progression of Adult T-Cell Leukemia-Lymphoma
text:
The prognosis for adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma (ATLL) associated with human T-cell leukemia virus is very poor, despite trying various treatment approaches. When ATLL is diagnosed, the expression of the virus is often limited or absent, suggesting that genetic or epigenetic changes play a significant role in the development of the disease. 

In this study, we conducted a prospective investigation of combination chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy for ATLL. Between 2002 and 2006, nineteen patients were enrolled in a phase II clinical trial at five medical centers. They received infusional chemotherapy with etoposide, doxorubicin, and vincristine, daily prednisone, and bolus cyclophosphamide (EPOCH) for two to six cycles until they achieved the maximum clinical response. This was followed by antiviral therapy with daily zidovudine, lamivudine, and alpha interferon-2a for up to one year. Unfortunately, seven patients had to discontinue the study within a month due to disease progression or chemotherapy side effects. 

Of the remaining patients, eleven achieved an objective response, with a median duration of response of thirteen months. Two patients even achieved complete remission. Interestingly, during the induction chemotherapy, there was an increase in viral RNA expression (median 190-fold) and virus replication, which coincided with disease progression. 

In conclusion, EPOCH chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy is an effective treatment for adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma. However, the reactivation of the virus during chemotherapy induction may contribute to treatment failure. Therefore, there is a need for alternative therapies that can both prevent virus expression and effectively kill malignant cells in this disease.

title: Montelukast and fluticasone compared with salmeterol and fluticasone in protecting against asthma exacerbation in adults: one year, double blind, randomised, comparative trial.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness of montelukast and salmeterol when added to inhaled fluticasone propionate in patients with inadequately controlled asthma symptoms. The study was conducted over a period of 52 weeks and was double-blind and multicentre. Participants were randomly assigned to add either montelukast or salmeterol if their symptoms remained uncontrolled by inhaled corticosteroids. The primary outcome measure was the percentage of patients who experienced at least one asthma exacerbation. 

The results showed that 20.1% of patients in the montelukast and fluticasone group had an asthma exacerbation, compared to 19.1% in the salmeterol and fluticasone group. The difference between the two groups was 1% (95% confidence interval -3.1% to 5.0%). The risk ratio for montelukast and fluticasone compared to salmeterol and fluticasone was 1.05 (0.86 to 1.29), indicating that montelukast and fluticasone were non-inferior to salmeterol and fluticasone in terms of asthma exacerbation. 

Salmeterol and fluticasone were found to significantly increase forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and morning peak expiratory flow compared to montelukast and fluticasone (P < or = 0.001). However, FEV1 after using a beta agonist, improvements in asthma-specific quality of life, and nocturnal awakenings were similar between the two groups. Montelukast and fluticasone also significantly reduced peripheral blood eosinophil counts compared to salmeterol and fluticasone (P = 0.011). Both treatments were generally well tolerated. 

In conclusion, adding montelukast to inhaled fluticasone could provide equivalent clinical control to adding salmeterol in patients with uncontrolled asthma symptoms.

title: Control of assembly and function of glutamate receptors by the amino-terminal domain.
text: The amino-terminal domains (ATDs) of the ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits are an independent part of all glutamate receptors. They are located distal to the membrane and have control over a wide range of receptor functions. These functions include assembling subunits, guiding receptor movement, regulating channel opening, determining agonist strength, and influencing allosteric modulation. The various characteristics of different ionotropic glutamate receptor classes and subunits within a class may be due to the distinct regulation by the amino-terminal domains. Understanding the structure and function of these domains can potentially be used to target this region for therapeutic modulation of glutamatergic signaling. In this regard, NMDA receptor antagonists that interact with the GluN2B ATD have shown promise in animal models of ischemia, neuropathic pain, and Parkinson's disease.

title: Fission yeast and other yeasts as emergent models to unravel cellular aging in eukaryotes.
text: Over the past few years, the study of aging has greatly benefited from the research conducted on simple organisms like yeasts and worms. The pioneering studies carried out on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in particular, have been instrumental in uncovering numerous molecular mechanisms that contribute to cellular aging and identifying new genes associated with longevity. Importantly, these genes have been found to be conserved in more complex organisms. As a result, similar discovery approaches are now being applied to other yeast models such as Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Candida albicans, Kluyveromyces lactis, and Cryptococcus neoformans. In the case of fission yeast, researchers have made connections between asymmetrical cell division, nutrient signaling pathways, and the aging process. This review aims to provide an overview of the current understanding of the mechanisms that regulate both replicative and chronological aging in S. pombe and other emerging yeast models.

title: Centrifugal elutriation as a method for isolation of large numbers of functionally intact human peripheral blood monocytes.
text: Centrifugal elutriation was utilized to isolate human peripheral blood monocytes (HPBM) from mononuclear-enriched cells obtained after collecting platelet concentration samples. The elutriation process separated HPBM and lymphocytes in Ca++- and Mg++-free PBS without EDTA, using a speed of 3,500 +/- 5 rpm. HPBM were recovered in either one or two populations: total HPBM or small (SM) and large monocytes (LM). The total HPBM yielded an average of 5.05 +/- 1.50 X 10(8) cells with a purity of 95% +/- 3%. The SM and LM populations were obtained by dividing the total HPBM equally, resulting in HPBM purities of 92% +/- 3% and 93% +/- 3%, respectively, as determined by nonspecific esterase staining. The viability of the cells was not affected by the elutriation media, as confirmed by trypan blue exclusion. All three HPBM populations were purified from the lymphocyte population both histochemically (lack of reactivity to leu-1 and leu-7) and functionally (depletion of NK cell activity). The HPBM populations showed enrichment in HLA-Dr, OKM-1, OKM-5, MY-8, and leu M-3 monoclonal antibody marker staining. There were no differences in the percentage of positive cells between the SM and LM populations for any of the monocyte-specific monoclonal antibodies. All three monocyte populations exhibited antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity towards human red blood cells, with the LM population demonstrating higher levels of lysis (27.0% +/- 5%) compared to the SM population (7% +/- 3%).

title: Asthma in United States Olympic athletes who participated in the 1996 Summer Games.
text:
The prevalence of asthma seems to be increasing in the general population, and we wanted to investigate if this trend is also seen in highly competitive athletes. Our objective was to determine the number of United States Olympic athletes selected for the 1996 Summer Olympic Games who had a history of asthma, symptoms suggesting asthma, or used asthma medications. To achieve this, we analyzed responses to questions about allergic and respiratory diseases on the United States Olympic Committee (USOC) Medical History Questionnaire completed by all athletes representing the US in the 1996 Summer Olympic Games in Atlanta.

Out of the 699 athletes who completed the questionnaire, 107 (15.3%) had a previous asthma diagnosis, and 97 (13.9%) reported using asthma medication at some point in the past. A total of 117 (16.7%) athletes reported either using asthma medication, having an asthma diagnosis, or both, which we considered as the basis for diagnosing asthma. Among the athletes, 73 (10.4%) were currently taking asthma medication during their time in Atlanta or stated that they used asthma medication on a permanent or semi-permanent basis, indicating active asthma. The prevalence of being told they had asthma or using asthma medication in the past was highest among cyclists and mountain bikers (50%). The frequency of active asthma varied, with 45% of cyclists and mountain bikers having it, while none of the divers and weightlifters reported it. In the 1984 Summer Olympic Games, only about 11% of athletes were reported to have exercise-induced asthma based on less restrictive criteria. However, using these less restrictive criteria, over 20% of athletes in the 1996 Olympic Games could have been considered to have asthma.

In conclusion, asthma appeared to be more prevalent among athletes participating in the 1996 Summer Games compared to the general population or those in the 1984 Summer Games. This study also suggests that asthma may influence an athlete's choice of sport.

title: Relapse specific mutations in NT5C2 in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
text: Despite intensive retreatment, relapsed childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) has a poor prognosis due to inherent drug resistance. The mechanisms responsible for this resistance are currently unknown. In this study, we examined the transcriptome profiles of bone marrow samples from ten pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia patients at both initial diagnosis and relapse using RNA sequencing. Through transcriptome sequencing, we discovered 20 newly acquired nonsynonymous mutations that were not present at the time of diagnosis. Interestingly, two individuals had relapse-specific mutations in the NT5C2 gene, which encodes a 5'-nucleotidase. Further analysis of 61 additional relapse specimens revealed additional mutations in NT5C2 in five cases. Enzymatic analysis of mutant proteins demonstrated that these base substitutions led to increased enzymatic activity and resistance to nucleoside analog therapies. Clinically, all individuals with NT5C2 mutations experienced early relapse within 36 months of initial diagnosis (P = 0.03). These findings suggest that mutations in NT5C2 are associated with the emergence of drug-resistant clones in ALL.

title: Relationship between Sloan-Kettering virus expression and mouse follicular development
text: The Ski gene product, known as Sloan-Kettering virus gene product, is a unique pro-oncoprotein found in the nucleus. It belongs to the ski/sno proto-oncogene family. Ski has various functions in different types of cells. When expressed at high levels, it can both induce oncogenic transformation and promote terminal muscle differentiation. Ski and its counterpart SnoN are important regulators of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily. They mainly function through heterodimers. Since the TGF-β superfamily plays a crucial role in follicle development, and previous studies have shown that SnoN is vital for this process, this research aimed to investigate the relationship between Ski expression and mouse follicular development. The study used immunohistochemical and real-time PCR techniques to analyze the ovaries of neonatal and gonadotropin-induced immature mice. In postnatal mice, Ski was highly detected in the nuclei of oocytes on the first day after birth. As follicular development progressed, Ski gradually moved from the oocyte nuclei to the perinuclear space, and its overall levels decreased. During the estrous cycle, Ski expression was highest at proestrus and estrus, faint at metestrus, and highest again at diestrus. After gonadotropin injection, Ski was found mainly in the perinuclear space and weakly in the oocyte nuclei. Following the initiation of luteinization, Ski expression was observed in the corpus luteum. Real-time PCR results also showed that Ski mRNA expression was inversely related to the expression of genes associated with ovulation during cumulus expansion. As the follicles developed, Ski expression decreased. Ski exhibited a specific pattern of expression during follicle development, ovulation, and luteinization. Therefore, Ski likely plays essential roles in these processes, particularly during early follicular development.

title: Involvement of CB1 cannabinoid receptors in emotional behaviour
text: Reasoning: The CB1 cannabinoid receptors, which are affected by both internal and external cannabinoids, play a role in regulating various behavioral and neuroendocrine functions. These functions include emotional responses, as well as learning and memory processes. Recently, scientists have created mice that lack the CB1 cannabinoid receptor, providing a valuable tool for studying the neurophysiology of the body's natural cannabinoid system. The objective of this study was to determine the impact of the CB1 cannabinoid receptor on several emotional-related behaviors, such as aggression, anxiety, depression, and learning. To achieve this, the researchers observed the spontaneous responses of CB1 knockout mice and normal mice in different behavioral tests. The results showed that CB1 knockout mice displayed increased aggression in the resident-intruder test and exhibited anxiety-like behavior in the light/dark box. Additionally, these mice showed a greater susceptibility to depressive-like responses in the chronic unpredictable mild stress test, indicating a higher likelihood of developing an anhedonic state. Finally, CB1 knockout mice demonstrated improved learning and memory processes, as evidenced by their increased conditioned responses in the active avoidance model. In conclusion, these findings highlight the role of endogenous cannabinoids and CB1 receptors in regulating emotional behavior and participating in learning and memory processes.

title: Exosomal levels of miRNA-21 from cerebrospinal fluids associated with poor prognosis and tumor recurrence of glioma patients
text: Glioma is the most common type of primary brain tumor. Extracellular vesicles, specifically exosomes, play a role in cell-to-cell communication by transporting proteins and nucleic acids, including microRNAs (miRNAs). In this study, we analyzed the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with recurrent glioma to determine the levels of cancer-related miRNAs. We compared these levels with miR-21 levels in CSF, serum, and exosomes to evaluate their prognostic value. We collected samples from seventy glioma patients who had undergone surgery and compared them to samples from brain trauma patients as a control group without tumors. We found that exosomal miR-21 levels in the CSF of glioma patients were significantly higher than in the control group, but there was no difference in serum-derived exosomal miR-21 expression. The levels of CSF-derived exosomal miR-21 correlated with spinal/ventricle metastasis and recurrence with a preference for specific anatomical sites. To further validate our findings, we analyzed an additional 198 glioma tissue samples and found that miR-21 levels were associated with tumor grade at diagnosis and negatively correlated with overall patient survival time. We also used a lentiviral inhibitor to suppress miR-21 expression in U251 cells and observed an up-regulation of miR-21 target genes PTEN, RECK, and PDCD4 at the protein level. Based on these results, we concluded that exosomal miR-21 levels could serve as a promising indicator for glioma diagnosis and prognosis, particularly in predicting tumor recurrence or metastasis.

title: Age‐associated microRNA expression in human peripheral blood is associated with all‐cause mortality and age‐related traits
text: New research has shown that there is a connection between DNA methylation, protein-coding gene expression, and the aging process in humans. However, the relationship between microRNA expression, age, and age-related clinical outcomes has not been thoroughly examined. To address this, we conducted a study involving 5221 adults to investigate the association between age and microRNA expression in whole-blood samples. We discovered that 127 microRNAs exhibited differential expression with age, with most being underexpressed in older individuals. By analyzing the relationship between microRNA and mRNA expression, we identified changes in age-associated mRNA expression that may be influenced by age-associated microRNAs. We developed a linear model to predict "microRNA age" using the expression levels of 80 microRNAs. Interestingly, microRNA age showed a modest correlation with predicted age based on DNA methylation and mRNA expression, suggesting that it could complement existing models for age prediction. We also used the difference between microRNA age and chronological age as a biomarker for accelerated aging, which we referred to as Δage. We found that Δage was associated with all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, including coronary heart disease, hypertension, blood pressure, and glucose levels. In summary, our study provides insights into the potential use of age-associated microRNAs and their targets as biomarkers for detecting accelerated aging and predicting the risk of age-related diseases.

title: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
text:
AIMS: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is a complex condition with various clinical and pathological characteristics. While some cases are linked to specific genetic variations, the causes of other forms of FTLD, including non-genetic ones, are still unknown. Epigenetic factors, such as the regulation of histones by histone deacetylases (HDAC), may be involved in the dysregulation of transcriptional activity, which is believed to contribute to the neurodegenerative process.

METHODS: We conducted a study to assess the distribution and intensity of HDACs 4, 5, and 6 in different brain regions of 33 confirmed FTLD cases and 27 control subjects. Immunostained sections of the temporal cortex with hippocampus and cerebellum were analyzed.

RESULTS: Our findings revealed a significantly higher intensity of cytoplasmic immunostaining for HDAC4 and HDAC6 in the granule cells of the dentate gyrus in FTLD cases compared to controls. This difference was particularly pronounced in cases of FTLD associated with tau-Picks pathology. No significant differences were observed between different subtypes of FTLD-TDP or between genetic and non-genetic forms of FTLD. HDAC5 did not show any changes in FTLD or control cases.

CONCLUSIONS: The dysregulation of HDAC4 and/or HDAC6 may play a role in the development of FTLD associated with tau-Picks pathology. However, the lack of immunostaining in Pick bodies suggests that these changes do not directly contribute to their formation.

title: Evolution and Impact of Subclonal Mutations in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
text:
The progression and relapse of cancer are characterized by clonal evolution, which is a crucial aspect. In our research, we examined the heterogeneity within tumors of 149 individuals with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) by combining whole-exome sequencing and copy number analysis. This allowed us to determine the proportion of cancer cells carrying each specific mutation. We observed that certain mutations, such as MYD88, trisomy 12, and del(13q), were predominantly present in all cancer cells (clonal), while others, like SF3B1 and TP53, were found in only a subset of cells (subclonal), indicating their occurrence at different stages of CLL development. 

To further investigate this, we collected leukemia cells from 18 patients at two different time points. Among the CLL cases treated with chemotherapy (10 out of 12), clonal evolution was observed, with subclones carrying driver mutations (SF3B1 and TP53) expanding over time. In contrast, only one out of six untreated cases showed clonal evolution. Additionally, the presence of a subclonal driver mutation was identified as an independent risk factor for rapid disease progression. 

Our study sheds light on the patterns of clonal evolution in CLL, providing valuable insights into its stepwise transformation. Moreover, it establishes a connection between the presence of subclones and unfavorable clinical outcomes.

title: The transcriptional program of sporulation in budding yeast
text: The developmental process of sporulation in budding yeast involves diploid cells producing haploid cells. This process includes meiosis and spore morphogenesis. To study the changes in gene expression during sporulation, DNA microarrays containing almost all yeast genes were utilized. The analysis revealed at least seven distinct temporal patterns of gene induction. The transcription factor Ndt80 was found to play a crucial role in inducing a large group of genes towards the end of meiotic prophase. By analyzing the sequences of genes that were expressed in a coordinated manner, consensus sequences responsible for temporal regulation could be identified. The temporal expression patterns also provided insights into the potential functions of numerous genes that were previously uncharacterized. Some of these genes have homologs in vertebrates, suggesting their possible involvement in gametogenesis.

title: Grass plants bind, retain, uptake, and transport infectious prions.
text: Prions, which are protein-based infectious agents, are responsible for causing prion diseases. It has been suggested that environmental contamination with prions can contribute to the transmission of these diseases. In this study, we examined how infectious prion proteins (PrP(Sc)) bind to and remain in plants. Even small amounts of PrP(Sc) found in diluted brain tissue or excretory materials like urine and feces can attach to the roots and leaves of wheat grass. When wild-type hamsters consumed these prion-contaminated plants, they became infected with the disease. This interaction between prions and plants occurs regardless of the prion's origin, including chronic wasting disease. Additionally, leaves that were sprayed with a prion-containing solution retained PrP(Sc) for several weeks while still attached to the living plant. Lastly, plants can absorb prions from contaminated soil and transport them to other parts of the plant, such as the stem and leaves. These findings demonstrate that plants can effectively bind infectious prions and serve as carriers of the disease, suggesting that environmental prion contamination may play a role in the horizontal transmission of prion diseases.

title: Innate lymphoid cells mediate influenza-induced airway hyper-reactivity independently of adaptive immunity
text: Asthma, a significant public health issue, poses a high risk for severe illness in patients infected with the influenza virus. However, the exact mechanisms through which influenza A causes airway disease and asthma remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrate in a mouse model that influenza infection rapidly induces airway hyper-reactivity (AHR), a key characteristic of asthma, independently of T helper type 2 (TH2) cells and adaptive immunity. Instead, influenza infection triggers AHR through a previously unidentified pathway that relies on the interleukin 13 (IL-13)–IL-33 axis and non-T cell, non-B cell innate lymphoid cells known as 'natural helper cells'. Influenza A virus infection, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, leads to increased production of IL-33 by alveolar macrophages. This, in turn, activates natural helper cells, resulting in significant IL-13 production.

title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions
text:
The design and implementation of evidence-based practice rely on successful behavior change interventions. To achieve this, it is necessary to have a suitable method for describing interventions and connecting them to an analysis of the targeted behavior. Although there are numerous frameworks available for behavior change interventions, it is unclear how well they serve this purpose. This study evaluates existing frameworks and develops a new framework to overcome their limitations.

To identify behavior change intervention frameworks, a systematic search of electronic databases and consultation with behavior change experts was conducted. These frameworks were evaluated based on three criteria: comprehensiveness, coherence, and a clear link to an overarching behavior model. A new framework was then developed to meet these criteria. Its reliability was tested in two domains of behavior change: tobacco control and obesity.

Nineteen frameworks were identified, covering nine intervention functions and seven policy categories that could support these interventions. However, none of the reviewed frameworks covered the full range of intervention functions or policies, and only a few met the criteria of coherence or linkage to a behavior model. The proposed new framework centers around a "behavior system" consisting of three essential conditions: capability, opportunity, and motivation (referred to as the "COM-B system"). This forms the core of a "behavior change wheel" (BCW), with the nine intervention functions addressing deficits in these conditions and the seven policy categories enabling the interventions.

The BCW was reliably used to describe interventions in the English Department of Health's 2010 tobacco control strategy and the National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence's guidance on reducing obesity. In conclusion, interventions and policies for behavior change can be effectively characterized using the BCW, which includes a behavior system at its core, surrounded by intervention functions and policy categories. Further research is needed to determine the extent to which the BCW can enhance the design of efficient and effective interventions.

title: Intermittent prophylaxis with oral truvada protects macaques from rectal SHIV infection.
text:
The global spread of HIV through sexual contact remains a significant concern, despite advancements in treatment and care. Developing vaccines or microbicides to prevent transmission has proven challenging. However, a promising approach to preventing transmission is through prophylactic treatment with antiretroviral drugs before exposure to HIV. Clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate the effectiveness of daily treatment with reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or Truvada (TDF plus emtricitabine). 

To test the hypothesis that intermittent prophylactic treatment with long-acting antiviral drugs could be as effective as daily dosing in blocking early stages of viral replication and preventing mucosal transmission, we conducted experiments on macaque monkeys. We administered prophylactic Truvada to the monkeys intermittently and then exposed them rectally to simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV) once a week for 14 weeks. 

Our findings revealed that a simple regimen involving an oral dose of Truvada given 1, 3, or 7 days before exposure, followed by a second dose 2 hours after exposure, provided the same level of protection as daily drug administration. This may be due to the prolonged presence of the drugs within the cells. Additionally, a two-dose regimen initiated 2 hours before or after virus exposure was effective, and doubling the Truvada concentration in both doses resulted in complete protection. However, delaying the first dose until 24 hours after exposure did not provide any protection, highlighting the importance of blocking initial replication in the mucosa. 

Our results demonstrate that intermittent prophylactic treatment with antiviral drugs can be highly effective in preventing SHIV infection, with a significant window of protection. These findings support the potential development of practical and cost-effective strategies to prevent HIV transmission in humans.

title: RNA is favourable for analysing EGFR mutations in malignant pleural effusion of lung cancer.
text: Malignant pleural effusion (MPE) is a valuable sample for assessing EGFR status in nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, it has been found that directly sequencing genomic DNA from MPE samples is not sensitive enough for detecting EGFR mutations. To determine if analyzing EGFR from RNA is less affected by interference from nontumour cells with low or no EGFR expression, we compared three methods (sequencing RNA derived from cells versus sequencing and mass-spectrometric analysis of genomic DNA) for detecting EGFR mutations in MPE samples from 150 lung adenocarcinoma patients receiving first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). We found that sequencing RNA identified EGFR mutations more frequently than sequencing genomic DNA (67.3% versus 44.7% and 46.7% for all mutations; 61.3% versus 41.3% and 46.7% for L858R or exon 19 deletions, respectively). The higher mutation detection rate with RNA sequencing was also associated with better prediction of the clinical effectiveness of first-line TKIs. In patients with acquired resistance, RNA sequencing provided satisfactory detection of T790M (54.2%). These findings demonstrate that using RNA as a template for EGFR sequencing significantly improves the sensitivity of mutation detection in MPE samples, highlighting RNA as the preferred source for analyzing EGFR mutations in heterogeneous MPE specimens in NSCLC.

title: Pharmacological correction of a defect in PPARγ signaling ameliorates disease severity in Cftr-deficient mice
text: Mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (Cftr) gene cause cystic fibrosis, a condition characterized by thickened mucus that blocks airways and other organs. This mutation impairs the function of Cftr as a chloride channel and disrupts bicarbonate transport. In addition to mucus blockage, individuals with cystic fibrosis experience inflammation, changes in lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance in affected organs. Our research demonstrates that mice lacking Cftr exhibit a malfunction in peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-gamma, encoded by Pparg), which leads to abnormal gene expression. Analysis of colonic epithelial cells reveals a decrease in the natural PPAR-gamma ligand 15-keto-prostaglandin E(2) (15-keto-PGE(2)), contributing to this defect. Treatment of Cftr-deficient mice with the synthetic PPAR-gamma ligand rosiglitazone partially restores normal gene expression and reduces disease severity. Although rosiglitazone does not affect chloride secretion, it enhances the expression of carbonic anhydrases 4 and 2 (Car4 and Car2), promotes bicarbonate secretion, and reduces mucus retention in the colon. These findings highlight a reversible defect in PPAR-gamma signaling in Cftr-deficient cells that can be corrected with medication to alleviate the symptoms of cystic fibrosis in mice.

title: Visualization of volatile substances in different organelles with an atmospheric-pressure mass microscope.
text: We have created a powerful mass microscope that surpasses the capabilities of the naked eye in terms of spatial resolution. This microscope is equipped with an atmospheric pressure ion-source chamber for laser desorption/ionization (AP-LDI) and a quadrupole ion trap time-of-flight (QIT-TOF) analyzer. By combining an optical microscope with a mass spectrometer, we are able to accurately identify the specific tissue region before conducting imaging mass spectrometry (IMS). To achieve high spatial resolution, we utilized a tightly focused ultraviolet laser with a triplet lens. The atmospheric pressure ion-source chamber allows us to analyze fresh samples without losing any intrinsic water or volatile compounds. Through mass-microscopic AP-LDI imaging of freshly cut ginger rhizome sections, we discovered that the compounds responsible for pungency and flavor, 6-gingerol and the monoterpene, respectively, were localized in organelles containing oil droplets. To compare the signals from freshly cut ginger directly with the standard reagent, we employed AP-LDI-tandem MS/MS analyses. As a result, our atmosphere-imaging mass spectrometer enables us to assess the quality of plants at the organelle level.

title: Coding of Sweet, Bitter, and Umami Tastes Different Receptor Cells Sharing Similar Signaling Pathways
text: Mammals have the ability to detect a wide range of chemosensory stimuli. The perception of sweet, amino acids, and bitter compounds is mediated by two different families of receptors known as T1Rs and T2Rs. In this study, we have found that the absence of TRPM5, a taste TRP ion channel, or PLCbeta2, a phospholipase C that is specifically expressed in taste tissue, completely eliminates the ability to perceive sweet, amino acid, and bitter tastes. However, the ability to taste sour or salty flavors remains unaffected. This suggests that despite the use of different receptors, the transduction of sweet, amino acid, and bitter tastes involves common signaling molecules. To further investigate taste perception, we conducted experiments using animals that lacked PLCbeta2, which is responsible for taste perception. We discovered that when PLCbeta2 function was restored exclusively in cells expressing bitter receptors, the animals responded normally to bitter tastants but were unable to detect sweet or amino acid stimuli. This indicates that the perception of bitter tastes is independent of sweet and amino acid tastes, and taste receptor cells are not broadly responsive to all taste modalities.

title: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles and characterization of their inhibitory effects on AGEs formation using biophysical techniques
text: AGEs, which are advanced glycation end-products resulting from non-enzymatic glycation, are a major contributor to secondary complications in individuals with diabetes. Scientists are currently focused on identifying new compounds that can potentially inhibit AGEs without disrupting the normal structure and function of biomolecules. Various natural and synthetic compounds have been proposed as potential AGE inhibitors. In this particular study, we aimed to investigate the inhibitory effects of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) on AGE formation. AgNPs, with an average size of approximately 30.5 nm, were synthesized using Aloe Vera leaf extract. The AgNPs were characterized using several techniques including UV-Vis spectroscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), high resolution-transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and dynamic light scattering (DLS). To evaluate the inhibitory effects of AgNPs on AGE formation, we examined the reactivity of free amino groups (specifically lysine and arginine residues), protein-bound carbonyl content, carboxymethyl lysine (CML) content, and the impact on protein structure using various physicochemical techniques. The results of our study demonstrated that AgNPs effectively inhibit AGE formation in a concentration-dependent manner and also have a positive effect on protein structure. These findings strongly suggest that AgNPs may have therapeutic potential in managing complications associated with diabetes.

title: Myosin Light Chain–activating Phosphorylation Sites Are Required for Oogenesis in Drosophila
text:
The Drosophila spaghetti squash (sqh) gene is responsible for encoding the regulatory myosin light chain (RMLC) of nonmuscle myosin II. Previous biochemical studies on vertebrate nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosin II have shown that phosphorylation of specific amino acids in the RMLC significantly enhances the actin-dependent myosin ATPase and motor activity in vitro. To determine the importance of these phosphorylation sites in vivo, we created a series of transgenes with altered amino acids corresponding to serine-21 and threonine-20 in Drosophila. We examined the phenotypes of these transgenes in a null mutant background during oocyte development in female Drosophila.

Cystoblasts in the germ line that completely lack a functional sqh gene exhibit severe defects in proliferation and cytokinesis. The abnormal ring canals, which are cytoplasmic bridges connecting the oocyte to the nurse cells in the egg chamber, suggest that myosin II plays a role in their establishment or maintenance. Additionally, numerous aggregates of myosin heavy chain accumulate in the sqh null cells. The mutant sqh transgene sqh-A20, A21, in which both serine-21 and threonine-20 are replaced by alanines, behaves similarly to the null allele in most aspects, except that no heavy chain aggregates are observed. On the other hand, expression of sqh-A21, in which only the primary phosphorylation target serine-21 is altered, partially restores the functionality of germ line myosin II. This allows for cystoblast division and oocyte development, although some cytokinesis failure, defects in rapid cytoplasmic transport from nurse cells to cytoplasm during late stage oogenesis, and damaged ring canals are still present. Substituting a glutamate for serine-21 (mutant sqh-E21) enables completion of oogenesis with minimal defects, resulting in eggs that can develop normally and produce fertile adults. Flies expressing sqh-A20, in which only the secondary phosphorylation site is absent, appear to be completely normal. Overall, this genetic evidence suggests that phosphorylation at serine-21 is crucial for RMLC function in activating myosin II in vivo, although partial functionality can be provided by phosphorylation at threonine-20.

title: Stages of the pathologic process in Alzheimer disease: age categories from 1 to 100 years.
text: A total of 2,332 brains from individuals aged 1 to 100 years were examined using various techniques to detect abnormal tau and β-amyloid. Immunocytochemistry (AT8) and Gallyas silver staining were used to identify abnormal tau, while immunocytochemistry (4G8) and Campbell-Switzer staining were used to detect β-amyloid. Out of the 342 cases that tested negative for abnormal tau using Gallyas stain, only 10 were immunonegative when retested with AT8. Fifty-eight cases showed subcortical tau primarily in the locus coeruleus, but there was no abnormal tau in the cortex (subcortical Stages a-c). The presence of abnormal tau in neurites (Stage 1a) was first observed in the transentorhinal region, with 38 cases displaying this stage. In Stage 1b, 236 cases showed pretangle material in transentorhinal pyramidal cells. These pretangles gradually progressed into argyrophilic neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), following the progression of NFT Stages I to VI. Pretangles restricted to subcortical sites were mainly observed in younger individuals. Among all cases, 1,031 (44.2%) had β-amyloid plaques. The first plaques appeared in the neocortex after the onset of tauopathy in the brainstem. Plaque development was generally observed in the 40s in 4% of cases, reaching its peak in the tenth decade (75%). There was a significant correlation between β-amyloid plaques and NFTs (p < 0.0001). These findings suggest that tauopathy associated with sporadic Alzheimer's disease may start earlier than previously believed, possibly in the lower brainstem rather than the transentorhinal region.

title: Coronary bypass graft patency in patients with diabetes in the Bypass Angioplasty Revascularization Investigation (BARI).
text:
BACKGROUND
There have been limited studies comparing the long-term status of bypass grafts in patients with and without diabetes. It is uncertain whether diabetes independently predicts poor clinical outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).

METHODS AND RESULTS
In the Bypass Angioplasty Revascularization Investigation (BARI) study, 1526 patients underwent CABG as their initial revascularization procedure. Among them, 292 patients (34%) with treated diabetes mellitus (TDM) (those on insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents) and 1234 patients (38%) without TDM had follow-up angiography. The angiograms with the longest interval from the initial surgery and before any percutaneous graft intervention (mean 3.9 years) were reviewed. On average, patients with TDM had 3.0 grafts placed during the initial CABG, with 33% of them using the internal mammary artery (IMA). Patients without TDM had 2.9 grafts, with 34% using the IMA. Patients with TDM were more likely to have small (<1.5 mm) grafted distal vessels (29% versus 22%) and vessels of poor quality (9% versus 6%). On follow-up angiography, 89% of IMA grafts were free of stenoses ≥50% in patients with TDM, compared to 85% in patients without TDM (P=0.23). For vein grafts, the corresponding percentages were 71% versus 75% (P=0.40). After statistical adjustment, TDM was not associated with a higher risk of graft stenosis ≥50% (adjusted odds ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.32).

CONCLUSIONS
Despite diabetic patients having smaller distal vessels and vessels of poorer quality, diabetes does not seem to have a negative impact on the patency of IMA or vein grafts over an average follow-up period of 4 years. The previously observed differences in survival between CABG-treated patients with and without diabetes may be primarily due to varying risks of mortality from noncardiac causes.

title: A novel ATAC-seq approach reveals lineage-specific reinforcement of the open chromatin landscape via cooperation between BAF and p63
text: The BAF (SWI/SNF) complex is crucial for development and has been shown to remodel chromatin in vitro and regulate accessibility in vivo. However, it is still unclear how and where BAF controls the open chromatin landscape to regulate processes like human epidermal differentiation. In this study, we used a new method called "on-plate" ATAC-sequencing to profile open chromatin landscapes with a small number of adherent cells. Our results demonstrate that the BAF complex is necessary for maintaining 11.6% of open chromatin regions in epidermal differentiation. These BAF-dependent regions are specific to certain cell types and contain binding sites for p63, a key transcription factor in epidermal development. The DNA sequences of p63 binding sites naturally promote nucleosome formation and are inaccessible in other cell types without p63, preventing unwanted activation. In epidermal cells, BAF and p63 recruit each other to maintain 14,853 open chromatin regions. Additionally, BAF and p63 work together to position nucleosomes away from p63 binding sites and recruit transcriptional machinery, controlling tissue differentiation. Overall, BAF plays a specific role in regulating the open chromatin landscape during epidermal differentiation by collaborating with the master transcription factor p63 to maintain lineage-specific regions.

title: Aging, habitual exercise, and dynamic arterial compliance.
text:
BACKGROUND: The compliance of large cardiothoracic arteries is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease as individuals age. 

METHODS AND RESULTS: We conducted a study to investigate the impact of regular exercise on the age-related decline in central arterial compliance. We examined 151 healthy men between the ages of 18 and 77, categorizing them into three groups: sedentary, recreationally active, and endurance exercise-trained. Our findings revealed that central arterial compliance was lower in middle-aged and older men compared to younger men in all three groups. However, there were no significant differences between sedentary and recreationally active men at any age. On the other hand, endurance-trained middle-aged and older men exhibited 20% to 35% higher arterial compliance compared to the less active groups. This suggests that age-related differences in central arterial compliance were less pronounced in the endurance-trained men. 

In a separate intervention study, we examined 20 sedentary middle-aged and older men before and after a 3-month aerobic exercise program primarily focused on walking. The results showed that regular exercise significantly increased central arterial compliance to levels similar to those observed in the endurance-trained men. These improvements were not influenced by changes in body mass, adiposity, arterial blood pressure, or maximal oxygen consumption. 

CONCLUSIONS: Regular aerobic-endurance exercise can mitigate the age-related decline in central arterial compliance and restore levels in previously sedentary middle-aged and older men. This may be one of the mechanisms through which habitual exercise reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease in this population.

title: A comparison of cancer screening practices in cancer survivors and in the general population: the Korean national health and nutrition examination survey (KNHANES) 2001–2007
text: The purpose of this study was to examine the rates of cancer screening for second primary cancer among cancer survivors in Korea. Additionally, the study aimed to compare these rates with two control groups: individuals without a history of cancer but with other chronic diseases, and individuals without a history of cancer or other chronic diseases. The study analyzed data from the 2001, 2005, and 2007 Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (KNHANES), which included 15,556 adults aged 30 years and older. The researchers assessed the prevalence of breast, cervical, gastric, and colorectal cancer screening based on national guidelines and compared the rates to those of the control groups. The results showed that the screening rates among cancer survivors were 48.5% for breast cancer, 54.7% for cervical cancer, 34.7% for gastric cancer, and 28.6% for colorectal cancer. Cancer survivors had higher screening rates for all four types of cancer compared to both control groups. However, after adjusting for various factors such as gender, age, marital status, education, income, working status, health insurance, smoking and drinking habits, and self-reported health status, only the higher screening rate for breast cancer among cancer survivors was statistically significant. The study found that cancer survivors were more likely to undergo screening according to recommended guidelines compared to individuals without a history of cancer. Nevertheless, the screening rates, even among survivors, were not optimal, highlighting the need for a more systematic approach to screening and prevention of second primary cancer.

title: Negative effect of the transcriptional activator GAL4
text: GAL4, a yeast transcriptional activator, binds specific sites on DNA to activate nearby genes. The activating regions of GAL4 are rich in acidic residues and it is believed that these regions interact with other components of the transcriptional machinery, such as the TATA-binding protein or RNA polymerase II. The DNA-binding region of GAL4 helps position the activating region close to the gene. In our study, we have found that when various GAL4 derivatives are expressed at high levels in yeast, they actually inhibit the transcription of certain genes that do not have GAL4 binding sites. The strength of this inhibition is greater with more efficient activators, and interestingly, it does not rely on the DNA-binding domain. We propose that this inhibition, which we refer to as squelching, occurs because the activating region of GAL4 titrates or consumes a transcription factor.

title: The Bayh–Dole Act and university research and development
text: This paper investigates the correlation between university research and development (R&D) activities and the Bayh-Dole Act. The Bayh-Dole Act simplified the process for universities to acquire patents for research funded by the federal government, potentially influencing universities to modify their R&D activities. The Act could potentially encourage a decrease in basic research (which does not generate licensing fees) and an increase in applied research (which does generate patents and licensing fees). Furthermore, the Act may enhance industry's willingness to finance university R&D projects, as the outcomes would now be more easily patentable. This paper distinguishes itself from existing literature, which primarily relies on patent data (a measure of research output), by utilizing research and development data (a measure of inventive input) to analyze the impact of the Act.

title: The relation between past exposure to fine particulate air pollution and prevalent anxiety: observational cohort study
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the potential association between past exposure to particulate air pollution and prevalent high symptoms of anxiety. The study was conducted as an observational cohort study using data from the Nurses' Health Study, which included 71,271 women residing throughout the contiguous United States. The participants had valid estimates on exposure to particulate matter for at least one period of interest and data on anxiety symptoms.

The main outcome measure was the presence of meaningfully high symptoms of anxiety, defined as a score of 6 points or greater on the phobic anxiety subscale of the Crown-Crisp index, administered in 2004. The results showed that 15% of the eligible women had high anxiety symptoms. Exposure to particulate matter was assessed by estimating the average exposure to particulate matter with diameters of less than 2.5 μm (PM2.5) and between 2.5 and 10 μm (PM2.5-10) during various time periods prior to the assessment of anxiety symptoms. The residential distance to the nearest major road two years prior to assessment was also considered.

The findings revealed significantly increased odds of high anxiety symptoms with higher exposure to PM2.5 for multiple averaging periods. For example, the odds ratio per 10 µg/m(3) increase in the average PM2.5 during the prior one month was 1.12, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.06 to 1.19. Similar results were observed for the prior 12 month average PM2.5. Models including multiple exposure windows indicated that short-term averaging periods were more relevant than long-term averaging periods. However, there was no association between anxiety symptoms and exposure to PM2.5-10. The proximity to major roads did not show a dose-dependent relationship with anxiety symptoms.

In conclusion, this study found that exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was associated with high symptoms of anxiety, with more recent exposures potentially having a greater impact than more distant exposures. Further research is needed to evaluate whether reducing exposure to ambient PM2.5 could reduce the burden of clinically relevant anxiety symptoms at the population level.

title: A mitochondrially targeted compound delays aging in yeast through a mechanism linking mitochondrial membrane lipid metabolism to mitochondrial redox biology☆
text: A recent study has discovered a natural compound that can delay aging in yeast by affecting the redox processes in mitochondria. This compound, lithocholic bile acid, is introduced into yeast cells and primarily accumulates in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As a result, it induces a remodeling of phospholipid synthesis and movement in both mitochondrial membranes, which is associated with the aging process. This remodeling progresses as the yeast cell ages and leads to significant changes in the lipid composition of the mitochondrial membrane. These changes in phospholipid composition have a profound impact on mitochondrial abundance and shape, consequently triggering alterations in various redox processes that define longevity. These processes include mitochondrial respiration, the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential, the regulation of reactive oxygen species produced by mitochondria, and the coupling of electron transport to ATP synthesis.

title: Isolation from African Sykes' monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis) of a lentivirus related to human and simian immunodeficiency viruses.
text: An analysis was conducted on serum samples taken from 100 Sykes' monkeys in Kenya, both wild-caught and colony-born. The results showed that 59 of these monkeys had antibodies that reacted to both human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) and simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs). From the seropositive monkeys, a lentivirus called SIVsyk was isolated from five out of six asymptomatic monkeys. However, in four cases, the isolation of SIVsyk was only possible after depleting CD8+ lymphocytes and cocultivating the CD4(+)-enriched cell population with peripheral blood mononuclear cells from seronegative monkeys. SIVsyk had similar characteristics to other SIVs and HIVs, including its morphology, Mg2(+)-dependent reverse transcriptase enzyme, and ability to replicate and cause cytopathic effects in CEMx174 and Sup-T1 cells. However, SIVsyk differed significantly from other SIVs in that it could not replicate in normal human, mangabey, and macaque peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Additionally, serum from seropositive Sykes' monkeys immunoprecipitated env antigens from HIV-1, HIV-2, SIVsmm, and SIVagm. These findings indicate a high prevalence of natural infection in Sykes' monkeys in Kenya with a unique lentivirus that has a distinct host range and antigenic cross-reactivity.

title: Role of the Single-Stranded DNA–Binding Protein SsbB in Pneumococcal Transformation: Maintenance of a Reservoir for Genetic Plasticity
text: Bacteria possess a crucial protein called single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein (SSB) that is responsible for maintaining the genome. In Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, there is an alternative form of SSB called SsbB, which is only expressed during genetic transformation. However, the exact role of SsbB has remained unclear. In this study, we compared a mutant lacking SsbB (ssbB(-)) with a truncated version of SsbB (ssbBΔ7) in S. pneumoniae. We created the truncated version because the acidic tail of SSBs has been found to play a crucial role in interacting with other proteins. Our findings provide evidence that SsbB directly protects internalized ssDNA. We discovered that SsbB is present in high abundance, allowing it to bind approximately 1.15 Mb of ssDNA, which is equivalent to half of the genome. SsbB also plays a role in processing ssDNA into recombinants and is crucial for chromosomal transformation while inhibiting plasmid transformation at high DNA concentrations. This explains why plasmid transformation is inefficient in S. pneumoniae compared to chromosomal transformation. Our previous suggestion that SsbB creates a reservoir of ssDNA, enabling multiple recombination cycles, is supported by these findings. Interestingly, SsbBΔ7 still fulfills the reservoir function, indicating that the C-terminal region of SsbB is not necessary for the processing of proteins to access stored ssDNA. We propose that the evolutionary purpose of SsbB and its abundance is to maintain this reservoir, which enhances the genetic plasticity of S. pneumoniae by increasing the likelihood of multiple transformation events in a single cell.

title: Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly
text: The intricate nature of the human brain has posed challenges in studying various brain disorders in model organisms. This emphasizes the necessity for an in vitro model that mimics human brain development. In response to this, we have created cerebral organoids, a three-dimensional culture system derived from human pluripotent stem cells. These organoids develop distinct brain regions that are interconnected. One of these regions is the cerebral cortex, which contains progenitor populations responsible for organizing and producing mature cortical neuron subtypes. Additionally, the cerebral organoids exhibit features of human cortical development, such as the organization of progenitor zones and the presence of abundant outer radial glial stem cells. To further validate the usefulness of these organoids, we utilized RNA interference and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells to model microcephaly, a disorder that has been challenging to replicate in mice. Our findings reveal that patient organoids display premature neuronal differentiation, which could potentially explain the disease phenotype. Overall, these results demonstrate that three-dimensional organoids can effectively replicate both normal development and disease processes in the highly complex human brain.

title: Localization of a gene for partial epilepsy to chromosome 10q
text: There is compelling evidence supporting the genetic contribution to epilepsy. However, it is commonly believed that this genetic influence is only present in "generalized" epilepsies, while most forms of "partial" epilepsy are thought to be non-genetic. In our study, we conducted a linkage analysis on a single family with 11 affected individuals and found strong evidence suggesting the presence of a gene responsible for partial epilepsy. This gene is located on chromosome 10q, and the maximum two-point lod score for marker D10S192 is 3.99 at θ=0.0. Interestingly, all affected individuals in the family share a single haplotype for seven closely linked markers. The maximum lod score for this haplotype is 4.83 at θ=0.0. By analyzing key recombinants, we were able to narrow down the location of the susceptibility locus to a 10 centimorgan interval.

title: Metastatic colonization requires the repression of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition inducer Prrx1.
text: The process known as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is crucial during embryonic development as it allows cells to form tissues in locations far from their initial origin. However, in the case of carcinoma cells, they exploit this mechanism to spread and form tumors in other parts of the body. The role of EMT in cancer is still a topic of debate as it remains unclear how these migratory cells manage to colonize distant tissues and create macrometastases. Our research demonstrates that the homeobox factor Prrx1 is responsible for inducing EMT, granting cells migratory and invasive capabilities. Interestingly, the absence of Prrx1 is necessary for cancer cells to metastasize in vivo, causing them to revert back to their original epithelial state while simultaneously acquiring stem cell properties. Unlike the traditional EMT transcription factors, Prrx1 separates EMT from stemness and serves as a biomarker linked to patient survival and the absence of metastasis.

title: A cohort study of the risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 in relation to papillomavirus infection.
text:
BACKGROUND
The relationship between human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is still unclear, as well as the importance of specific HPV types, other sexually transmitted diseases, and other risk factors.

METHODS
We conducted a prospective study on a cohort of 241 women who sought evaluation for sexually transmitted diseases and had negative cervical cytologic tests. These women were followed every four months with cytologic and colposcopic examinations of the uterine cervix, as well as tests for HPV DNA and other sexually transmitted diseases.

RESULTS
Biopsy confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 in 28 women. According to survival analysis, the cumulative incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia at two years was 28 percent among women with a positive HPV test and 3 percent among those without detectable HPV DNA. The highest risk was observed in women infected with HPV types 16 or 18 (adjusted relative risk compared to women without HPV infection: 11; 95 percent confidence interval: 4.6 to 26; attributable risk: 52 percent). All 24 cases of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 among HPV-positive women were detected within 24 months after the first positive HPV test. After adjusting for HPV infection, the development of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia was also associated with younger age at first intercourse, presence of serum antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis, presence of serum antibodies to cytomegalovirus, and cervical infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

CONCLUSIONS
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia appears to be a common and early manifestation of HPV infection, particularly types 16 and 18. Additionally, it is associated with younger age at first intercourse, presence of serum antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis, presence of serum antibodies to cytomegalovirus, and cervical infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

title: Investigating survival prognosis of glioblastoma using evolutional properties of gene networks
text: In recent years, there has been a lot of interest and numerous publications on using graph theory techniques to construct and analyze gene networks from cancer cell line data. However, most of the current research has focused on a static representation of the network and has not explored the use of graph theory for studying the evolution of cancer. Some studies have used graph theory metrics like degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality to identify important genes in these networks, but they have not fully considered the significance of genes at different stages of the disease. Previous studies on human glioblastoma have identified four subtypes based on specific genes, and these subtypes have been associated with different survival times. For example, one study found that the most aggressive subtype had a median survival of 11.3 months, while the least aggressive subtype had a median survival of 13.1 months. In our research, we present an evolutionary graph theory study of glioblastoma using survival data categorization. We confirm the importance of genes associated with different survival times using established graph theory metrics. This work expands the application of graph theory approaches to studying the evolution of cancer cell line data.

title: Compound heterozygous ZMPSTE24 mutations reduce prelamin A processing and result in a severe progeroid phenotype.
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is an extremely rare and devastating disorder that imitates premature aging. Children with HGPS appear normal at birth but typically experience failure to thrive within the first two years of life. They also exhibit other symptoms such as hair loss, small jaw, loss of fat under the skin with visible veins, abnormal teeth, hardening of the skin, and bone deterioration in the collarbones and fingertips.
