On average, individuals with HGPS live until the age of 13, with atherosclerosis being the most common cause of death. While HGPS is mostly sporadic, recent research has found that the majority of patients have de novo heterozygous mutations in the LMNA gene. There have also been reports of a single family with autosomal recessive inheritance of homozygous LMNA mutations. The LMNA gene encodes lamins A and C, which are components of the nuclear lamina. Mutations in LMNA have been linked to several other inherited disorders, collectively known as laminopathies, which affect various tissues in the body. HGPS shares similarities with other laminopathies, such as Werner's syndrome and mandibuloacral dysplasia. These diseases are characterized by lipodystrophy, which is also a prominent feature of familial partial lipodystrophy of the Dunnigan variety. Mandibuloacral dysplasia has been further classified into two subtypes...

title: Reliability of patient responses in pay for performance schemes: analysis of national General Practitioner Patient Survey data in England
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the reliability of patient responses to a new national survey on patient experience, in order to determine if it can be used as a basis for providing financial incentives to doctors. The design of the study involved analyzing the representativeness of the respondents to the GP Patient Survey compared to the overall population and those who were sampled. Non-response bias was also examined by looking at the relationship between practice response rates and survey scores. The reliability of the survey was assessed by estimating the proportion of the variance of practice scores that could be attributed to true differences between practices.

The results showed that the overall response rate was 38.2%, which is similar to other surveys conducted in the UK using similar methods. However, certain groups such as men, young adults, and people living in deprived areas were under-represented among the respondents. Despite this, there was no consistent association between response rates and questionnaire scores for questions related to pay for performance. Two questions that determined payments to general practitioners were found to be reliable measures of practice performance, with high reliability coefficients. Only a small percentage of practices had fewer responses than required for conventional reliability levels.

A change in the payment formula in 2009 resulted in an increase in the impact of random variation in patient scores on payments to general practitioners compared to previous years. However, there is little evidence to support the concern that low response rates and selective non-response bias have led to unfairness in payments based on questionnaire scores.

This study raises important considerations regarding the validity and reliability of using patient surveys for determining payments, and provides valuable insights for the UK and other countries considering the implementation of pay for performance schemes based on patient experience.

title: Impact of low alcohol verbal descriptors on perceived strength: An experimental study
text:
The aim of this study was to examine how consumers perceive verbal descriptors of alcohol strength and their appeal. Low alcohol labels are labels that indicate a lower alcohol content in beverages. Policymakers and producers are increasingly interested in lower strength alcohol products, but there is a lack of evidence on how the general population perceives these verbal descriptors. 

The study involved participants rating the strength and appeal of 18 terms denoting low, high, and regular strengths for wine or beer, based on their drinking preference. A total of 1,600 adults from a nationally representative UK panel participated in the study.

The results showed that terms like Low, Lower, Light, Lighter, and Reduced were perceived as denoting lower strength products than Regular, but higher strength than terms like Extra Low, Super Low, Extra Light, and Super Light. Similar clustering in perceived strength was observed for the high verbal descriptors. Regular was rated as the most appealing strength descriptor, while the low and high verbal descriptors using intensifiers were rated as the least appealing.

In conclusion, the perceived strength and appeal of alcohol products decreased as the verbal descriptors implied a deviation from Regular. These findings have implications for policy regarding lower strength alcohol labeling and public health outcomes.

In summary, this study adds to the existing knowledge by showing that verbal descriptors effectively communicate reduced alcohol content in wine and beer. It also highlights the importance of considering the appeal of alcohol products when using verbal descriptors.

title: Transgenic Interleukin 10 Prevents Induction of Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
text: The use of interleukin 10 (IL-10) for treating inflammation in the central nervous system caused by autoimmune diseases is a topic of debate. Different studies on experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model system, have explored the effects of IL-10 using various administration methods, doses, and schedules, and have found that these factors can influence its ability to regulate the immune system. In order to investigate how these variables affect the role of IL-10 in EAE development, we conducted a study using transgenic mice that express a human IL-10 (hIL-10) gene controlled by a class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) promoter. These mice showed a high resistance to EAE when actively immunized, and this resistance seemed to be due to the suppression of autoreactive T cell function. Although myelin-reactive T helper 1 cells were present in the IL-10 transgenic mice, they did not cause any pathology. By depleting antibodies, we confirmed that the resistance to EAE was dependent on the presence of the transgenic IL-10. Furthermore, mice expressing the hIL-10 transgene but not the endogenous murine IL-10 gene demonstrated that IL-10 from MHC class II-expressing cells was sufficient to prevent the induction of EAE. This study highlights that IL-10 can completely prevent EAE if it is present at appropriate levels and at the right time during the development of the disease.

title: Autosomal dominant immune dysregulation syndrome in humans with CTLA4 mutations
text: The protein CTLA-4, also known as cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4, plays a crucial role in regulating immune responses. When this protein is lost, it can lead to severe autoimmune diseases in mice. In our study, we examined a large family where five individuals displayed a complex immune dysregulation syndrome characterized by low levels of antibodies, recurring infections, and multiple autoimmune symptoms. Through our research, we discovered a specific mutation in exon 1 of the CTLA4 gene, which was present in these individuals. Further screening of 71 unrelated patients with similar clinical symptoms revealed five additional families (nine individuals) with previously unknown mutations in CTLA4, affecting splice sites and causing missense mutations. It is important to note that not all individuals with the CTLA4 mutation showed symptoms, as eight out of 19 genetically confirmed carriers were considered unaffected. However, we observed a decrease in CTLA-4 protein expression in regulatory T cells (Treg cells) in both patients and carriers with CTLA4 mutations. Although Treg cells were present in higher numbers in these individuals, their suppressive function, ability to bind to CTLA-4 ligands, and transendocytosis of CD80 were impaired. Additionally, mutations in CTLA4 were associated with reduced levels of circulating B cells. In summary, mutations in CTLA4 that result in CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency or impaired ligand binding disrupt the balance of T and B cells, leading to a complex immune dysregulation syndrome.

title: Specific inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 by PD 0332991 and associated antitumor activity in human tumor xenografts.
text: PD 0332991 is a highly selective inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (Cdk4) and Cdk6, with IC50 values of 0.011 micromol/L and 0.016 micromol/L, respectively. It does not exhibit any activity against a group of 36 other protein kinases. In vitro studies have shown that PD 0332991 is a potent antiproliferative agent against retinoblastoma (Rb)-positive tumor cells, leading to a G1 arrest and a decrease in phospho-Ser780/Ser795 levels on the Rb protein. When orally administered to mice with Colo-205 human colon carcinoma, PD 0332991 induces significant tumor regression. Therapeutic doses of PD 0332991 result in the elimination of phospho-Rb and the proliferative marker Ki-67 in tumor tissue, as well as the down-regulation of genes controlled by E2F transcription. These findings suggest that inhibiting Cdk4/6 alone is enough to cause tumor regression and reduce tumor burden in certain types of tumors.

title: Neutrophils support lung colonization of metastasis-initiating breast cancer cells
text: Despite advancements in cancer drug development, treatments for metastatic tumors are often ineffective. The reliance of cancer cells on their microenvironment suggests that targeting the non-cancerous components of tumors could lead to new therapeutic approaches. However, the role of host responses in tumor growth and metastasis is not well understood, which limits the potential of this approach. In this study, we identify neutrophils as the main driver of metastasis in mouse breast cancer models within the lung microenvironment. Neutrophils play a crucial role in inflammatory responses, but their contribution to tumorigenesis is still debated. By blocking neutrophil recruitment to the pre-metastatic site, we demonstrate that neutrophils specifically support the initiation of metastasis. Furthermore, we find that neutrophil-derived leukotrienes promote the colonization of distant tissues by expanding the sub-population of highly tumorigenic cancer cells. Inhibiting the enzyme Alox5, which generates leukotrienes, either genetically or pharmacologically, reduces neutrophil pro-metastatic activity and subsequently decreases metastasis. These findings highlight the effectiveness of targeted therapy against specific components of the tumor microenvironment and suggest that inhibiting neutrophil Alox5 could limit metastatic progression.

title: Effect of Previous Miscarriage on Depressive Symptoms During Subsequent Pregnancy and Postpartum in the First Baby Study
text: The aim of our study was to investigate whether nulliparous women who had experienced a miscarriage were more likely to develop depression during late pregnancy, as well as at 1, 6, and 12 months after giving birth, compared to women who had not experienced a miscarriage. We analyzed data from the First Baby Study, a longitudinal cohort study, and compared 448 pregnant women with a history of miscarriage to 2,343 pregnant women without a history of miscarriage. We used logistic regression models to calculate odds ratios at each time point and generalized estimating equations for longitudinal analysis. After adjusting for sociodemographic factors, we found that women with a history of miscarriage were not more likely to be in the probable depression range during the third trimester or at 6 or 12 months postpartum. However, they were more likely to experience probable depression at 1 month postpartum (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.03–2.69). This suggests that women with a history of miscarriage may be more susceptible to depression during the first month after giving birth, but this increased risk does not persist beyond that time period. We believe it is important to raise awareness about this issue and recommend further research to identify risk factors that may contribute to higher depression risk in women with a history of miscarriage.

title: IL-1β, IL-4 and IL-12 control the fate of group 2 innate lymphoid cells in human airway inflammation in the lungs
text: In this study, we found that Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) release type 2 cytokines, which provide protection against parasites but can also contribute to various inflammatory airway diseases. Our findings demonstrate that interleukin 1β (IL-1β) directly activates human ILC2s, and that IL-12 triggers the transformation of these activated ILC2s into interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-producing ILC1s. This conversion is reversed by IL-4. The flexibility of ILCs is evident in the affected tissues of patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). These tissues display signatures of IL-12 or IL-4, along with an accumulation of ILC1s or ILC2s, respectively. Eosinophils are a significant source of IL-4, indicating communication between IL-5-producing ILC2s and IL-4-producing eosinophils. We propose that the functional identity of ILC2s is governed by IL-12 and IL-4, and an imbalance between these cytokines leads to the persistence of type 1 or type 2 inflammation.

title: Summary
text: The only known RNA coactivator, Steroid receptor RNA activator (SRA), enhances the activation of nuclear receptors (NRs). We have discovered that SLIRP (SRA stem-loop interacting RNA binding protein) binds to a functional part of SRA called STR7. SLIRP is present in both normal and tumor tissues, and it contains an RNA recognition motif (RRM). It suppresses NR activation in a manner that depends on both SRA and RRM, and it also enhances the effects of Tamoxifen. Additionally, SLIRP influences the association of SRC-1 with SRA. Another corepressor called SHARP, which contains RRM, also binds to STR7 and enhances repression in conjunction with SLIRP. SLIRP and another NR coregulator called SKIP (located at Chr14q24.3) are found in the same location and SLIRP reduces the NR signaling that is potentiated by SKIP. SLIRP is recruited to specific promoters (pS2 and metallothionein), with the latter recruitment being dependent on SRA. On the other hand, the recruitment of NCoR to the promoter is dependent on SLIRP. Most of the endogenous SLIRP is located in the mitochondria. Our findings demonstrate that SLIRP influences NR activation, suggest its potential role in regulating mitochondrial function, and provide a better understanding of the interactions between SRA, SLIRP, SRC-1, and NCoR.

title: Naringenin inhibits allergen-induced airway inflammation and airway responsiveness and inhibits NF-kappaB activity in a murine model of asthma.
text: We conducted a study to investigate the potential of naringenin, a flavonoid, to reduce allergen-induced airway inflammation in a mouse model of asthma. The mice were sensitized and challenged with ovalbumin, and some were given naringenin before the ovalbumin challenge. We assessed the development of airway inflammation and reactivity, as well as the levels of certain inflammatory markers. We also examined the degradation of IkappaBalpha and the expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in the lungs, as well as the activity of NF-kappaB. Additionally, we measured the mRNA levels of iNOS and chemokines CCL5 and CCL11. Our findings showed that naringenin reduced ovalbumin-induced airway inflammation and reactivity in the mice. The naringenin-treated mice had lower levels of IL4 and IL13 in their bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, as well as lower levels of serum total IgE. Furthermore, naringenin inhibited the degradation of IkappaBalpha and the DNA-binding activity of NF-kappaB. The levels of CCL5, CCL11, and iNOS were also significantly decreased. These results suggest that naringenin may have protective effects in the asthma process, possibly through the inhibition of NF-kappaB and the downregulation of its target genes.

title: The evolution of Fox genes and their role in development and disease
text: Originating in unicellular eukaryotes, the forkhead box (Fox) family of transcription factors has undergone expansion through numerous duplication events and occasional gene loss, resulting in over 40 members in mammals. These Fox genes have evolved to serve specialized functions in various crucial biological processes. Mutations in Fox genes have a significant impact on human disease, leading to a wide range of phenotypes including cancer, glaucoma, and language disorders. In this summary, we outline the key aspects of the evolution of the Fox gene family and emphasize the diverse contributions of different Fox subfamilies to developmental processes, spanning from organogenesis to the acquisition of speech.

title: Emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies by contact inhibition of locomotion
text: The function of cells in tissues can result in a wide range of structures. Significant changes in organization, such as epithelial-mesenchymal transitions or the formation of spheroidal aggregates, are often linked to tissue development or cancer progression. In this study, we investigate the organization of cell colonies using simulations of self-propelled particles with cell-like interactions. By considering the softness of cells, cell-cell adhesion, and contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL), we observe structures and collective behaviors that resemble various tissue phenotypes. These include evenly distributed cells, dynamic cell clusters, gel-like networks, migrating monolayers, and 3D aggregates. We provide analytical predictions for the transitions between noncohesive, cohesive, and 3D cell arrangements. We demonstrate how CIL creates a repulsive force that promotes cell dispersion, preventing the formation of cohesive tissues. However, in continuous monolayers, CIL facilitates collective cell movement, maintains intercellular stresses, and opposes cell extrusion. Therefore, our research emphasizes the significant role of CIL in determining the emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies.

title: Failure of cell cleavage induces senescence in tetraploid primary cells
text: Various defects in mitosis or cell cleavage can lead to tetraploidy in mammalian cells. When tetraploid cells continue to cycle with multiple centrosomes, it can result in aneuploidy. Therefore, arresting the tetraploid cell cycle is an important cellular control mechanism. Our study focuses on primary rat embryo fibroblasts (REF52) and human foreskin fibroblasts, which become senescent in the tetraploid G1 phase after drug-induced or small interfering RNA (siRNA)-induced failure of cell cleavage. However, T-antigen-transformed REF52 cells and p53+/+ HCT116 tumor cells rapidly become aneuploid by continuing to cycle after cleavage failure. Tetraploid primary cells quickly enter a quiescent state, as indicated by the absence of the Ki-67 proliferation marker and the fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator/late cell cycle marker geminin. This arrest is not caused by DNA damage, as the γ-H2AX DNA damage marker remains at normal levels after tetraploidy induction. Eventually, arrested tetraploid cells become senescent, as evidenced by SA-β-galactosidase activity. The arrest of tetraploid cells is dependent on the expression of p16INK4a, as suppressing p16INK4a with siRNA bypasses tetraploid arrest and allows primary cells to become aneuploid. In conclusion, tetraploid primary cells can enter senescence without DNA damage, and inducing senescence is crucial for tetraploidy arrest.

title: Cell death: the significance of apoptosis.
text: The classification of cell death can be determined by its appearance or biochemical markers, as well as the circumstances in which it occurs. Currently, the only definitive evidence of death is irreversible structural changes. Biochemical indicators that universally indicate cell death need to be precisely defined, as studies of cell function or reproductive capacity may not distinguish between death and dormant states that can potentially recover. It has been possible to categorize most dying cells into two distinct patterns of morphological change, which occur under different circumstances. One pattern involves swelling and rupture of plasma and organelle membranes, leading to the dissolution of organized structure, known as "coagulative necrosis." This pattern is caused by agents like toxins and ischemia, affects groups of cells rather than individual cells, and triggers inflammation when it occurs in living organisms. The other pattern involves condensation of the cell while maintaining organelle integrity, forming surface protrusions that separate as membrane-bound globules. In tissues, these globules are phagocytosed and digested by resident cells, without causing inflammation.

title: The mitochondrial RNA-binding protein GRSF1 localizes to RNA granules and is required for posttranscriptional mitochondrial gene expression.
text: At the core of regulating gene expression after transcription, RNA-binding proteins play a crucial role in coordinating the processing, storage, and management of cellular RNAs. In this study, we demonstrate that GRSF1, previously associated with binding and selectively translating influenza mRNAs, localizes to mitochondria. Within mitochondria, GRSF1 forms granules that align with regions of newly synthesized mtRNA adjacent to mitochondrial nucleoids. GRSF1 exhibits a preference for binding RNAs transcribed from three adjacent genes on the light strand of mtDNA: ND6 mRNA, as well as long noncoding RNAs for cytb and ND5. These RNAs contain multiple consensus binding sequences. By using RNA interference to reduce GRSF1 levels, we observe alterations in mitochondrial RNA stability, abnormal loading of mRNAs and lncRNAs onto the mitochondrial ribosome, and impaired ribosome assembly. Consequently, this leads to a specific defect in protein synthesis and an inability to assemble normal quantities of oxidative phosphorylation complexes. These findings strongly suggest that GRSF1 plays a critical role in regulating posttranscriptional gene expression within mitochondria.

title: Identification and purification of a 62,000-dalton protein that binds specifically to the polypyrimidine tract of introns.
text: UV cross-linking to mRNA precursors detected a protein called p62 in HeLa cell nuclear extracts. This protein, with a molecular size of 62,000 daltons, specifically binds to the polypyrimidine tract of the 3' splice site region of introns. When purified to homogeneity, p62 binds to the polypyrimidine tract of pre-mRNAs without requiring the AG dinucleotide at the 3' splice site. If alterations are made to the polypyrimidine tract that decrease p62 binding, there is a corresponding decrease in the efficiency of U2 snRNP/pre-mRNA complex formation and splicing. The p62 protein remains bound to the pre-mRNA and is retained in the spliceosome. This protein, known as polypyrimidine tract binding protein (pPTB), is believed to play a crucial role in recognizing the 3' splice site during splicing.

title: Capsule endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage: a prospective cohort study.
text:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
The evaluation of patients with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the emergency department may benefit from the use of capsule endoscopy. 

PATIENTS AND METHODS
We conducted a study at two academic centers, evaluating adults who presented with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. The patients were given a wireless video capsule to ingest, followed by nasogastric tube aspiration and later esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). We compared the effectiveness of capsule endoscopy with nasogastric tube aspiration in detecting blood, and with EGD in identifying the source of bleeding, peptic/inflammatory lesions, safety, and patient satisfaction.

RESULTS
A total of 49 patients (32 men, 17 women; mean age 58.3 ± 19 years) were enrolled in the study. However, three patients did not complete the capsule endoscopy and five patients were unable to tolerate the nasogastric tube. Capsule endoscopy detected blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract significantly more often (15/18 [83.3%]) compared to nasogastric tube aspiration (6/18 [33.3%]; P = 0.035). There was no significant difference in the identification of peptic/inflammatory lesions between capsule endoscopy (27/40 [67.5%]) and EGD (35/40 [87.5%]; P = 0.10, OR 0.39 95% CI 0.11 - 1.15). Capsule endoscopy successfully reached the duodenum in 45/46 patients (98%). Only one patient (2.2%) experienced self-limited shortness of breath, and one patient (2.2%) had coughing after ingesting the capsule.

CONCLUSIONS
In the emergency department, capsule endoscopy is a feasible and safe option for evaluating patients with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. It is more effective than nasogastric tube aspiration in detecting blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, including the duodenum, and is comparable to EGD in identifying inflammatory lesions. Capsule endoscopy may aid in patient triage and facilitate earlier endoscopy, but it should not replace EGD.

title: Electroporation of Cas9 protein/sgRNA into early pronuclear zygotes generates non-mosaic mutants in the mouse.
text: The CRISPR/Cas9 system is a powerful tool for understanding the functions of genes in various organisms, including mice. To create genetically modified embryos or mice using this method, Cas9 mRNA and sgRNA are typically introduced into zygotes through microinjection or electroporation. However, most mutants produced with this approach are genetically mosaic, meaning they consist of different types of cells with various mutations. This makes it challenging to analyze the phenotypes of founder embryos or mice. To simplify the analysis and gain insights into the roles of genes involved in developmental processes, a method for generating non-mosaic mutants is necessary. In this study, we developed a technique for producing non-mosaic mouse mutant embryos. We introduced Cas9 protein and sgRNA into in vitro fertilized (IVF) zygotes using electroporation, allowing genome editing to occur before the first replication of the mouse genome. Consequently, all cells in the mutant carried the same set of mutations. This method effectively addresses the issue of mosaicism and allele complexity in founder mutant embryos or mice generated by the CRISPR/Cas9 system.

title: Molecular Basis for Target RNA Recognition and Cleavage by Human RISC
text: The RNA-Induced Silencing Complex (RISC) is a complex made up of a single-stranded short interfering RNA (siRNA) and an active Argonaute protein. This complex has the ability to cleave mRNAs that are complementary to the siRNA. While we understand how RISC cleaves its target RNA, we still don't know how it actually finds the target RNA. In this study, we conducted experiments both in the lab and in living organisms to investigate this. We found that the accessibility of the target site directly affects how efficiently RISC can cleave the RNA. Interestingly, we discovered that RISC is unable to unfold structured RNA. During the process of recognizing the target RNA, RISC briefly contacts single-stranded RNA in a non-specific manner and helps the siRNA and target RNA bind together. Additionally, we found that the 5' part of the siRNA within RISC plays a role in determining how strongly RISC associates with the target RNA. Overall, our findings shed light on the mechanisms of RISC and target RNAs that are crucial for achieving efficiency and specificity in RNA interference.

title: Cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in tumor microenvironment.
text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a crucial component of the tumor microenvironment that promotes the growth and invasion of cancer cells through various mechanisms. CAFs exhibit a high level of heterogeneity due to their diverse origins, but researchers have identified distinct morphological features and physiological functions of CAFs. The interaction between cancer cells and CAFs is increasingly recognized as a key factor in cancer progression, and understanding this relationship could lead to targeted treatments for cancer patients. This review will explore the latest research on the role of CAFs in the development of tumors and metastasis, as well as the potential therapeutic implications of targeting CAFs.

title: Cold Exposure Promotes Atherosclerotic Plaque Growth and Instability via UCP1-Dependent Lipolysis
text: The molecular mechanisms responsible for the increased cardiovascular risk associated with cold temperatures are not yet understood. However, our study reveals that exposure to cold triggers a process called lipolysis, which leads to higher levels of small low-density lipoprotein (LDL) remnants in the bloodstream. This, in turn, accelerates the development of atherosclerotic lesions in mice, contributing to the risk of cardiovascular disease. We conducted experiments using two genetic mouse models (ApoE(-/-) and Ldlr(-/-) mice) and found that prolonged exposure to cold promotes the growth of atherosclerotic plaques by increasing the deposition of lipids. Additionally, we observed a significant increase in inflammatory cells and plaque-associated microvessels in the cold-acclimated mice, which further destabilized the plaques. Interestingly, when we deleted a key mitochondrial protein called uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in the ApoE(-/-) mice, which is involved in thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT), the mice were completely protected from cold-induced atherosclerotic lesions. Furthermore, we discovered that cold acclimation reduces the levels of a hormone called adiponectin in the bloodstream, and when we administered adiponectin systemically to the ApoE(-/-) mice, it protected them from plaque development. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms behind the increased cardiovascular risks associated with low temperatures.

title: Mild overexpression of MeCP2 causes a progressive neurological disorder in mice.
text: Rett syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders are caused by mutations in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2), which encodes a transcriptional repressor. The majority of these mutations result in loss of function, but the specific role of MeCP2 in causing these phenotypes is still unknown. To investigate this, we conducted experiments in transgenic mice that overexpressed the wild-type human protein using a large genomic clone containing the entire MECP2 locus. Our detailed studies in the MeCP2(Tg1) transgenic line, which expressed MeCP2 at approximately twice the normal levels, revealed the onset of phenotypes at around 10 weeks of age. Surprisingly, these mice exhibited improved motor and contextual learning abilities, as well as enhanced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus. However, by 20 weeks of age, they started experiencing seizures, became less active, and approximately 30% of them died by the age of 1 year. These findings highlight the importance of tightly regulating MeCP2 levels in vivo, as even a slight overexpression of this protein can have detrimental effects. Additionally, our results suggest that duplications or gain-of-function mutations in MECP2 may contribute to X-linked delayed-onset neurobehavioral disorders.

title: Alcohol Sales and Risk of Serious Assault
text:
BACKGROUND Alcohol is a known factor in unintentional injuries, including motor vehicle accidents. Previous studies on the connection between alcohol use and violent injuries were limited to survey data and only included cases from one trauma center, without proper controls. Additionally, previous researchers were unable to accurately capture the majority of alcohol sales. In Ontario, alcohol is primarily sold through government-run retail outlets, and hospitals are funded through a provincial healthcare system. We aimed to assess the risk of hospitalization due to assault in relation to retail alcohol sales across Ontario. 

METHODS AND FINDINGS We conducted a population-based case-crossover analysis of all individuals aged 13 and older who were hospitalized for assault in Ontario between April 1, 2002, and December 1, 2004. We compared the volume of alcohol sold at the store closest to the victim's home on the day before their hospitalization to the volume sold at the same store seven days prior. We used conditional logistic regression analysis to determine the relative risk (RR) of assault per 1,000 liters increase in daily alcohol sales. Out of the 3,212 individuals admitted to the hospital for assault, nearly 25% were between the ages of 13 and 20, and 83% were male. Of the assaults, 36% involved the use of a weapon, while 48% occurred during an unarmed fight. For every 1,000 liters increase in alcohol sales per store per day, the relative risk of hospitalization for assault was 1.13 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02-1.26). The risk was higher for males (1.18, 95% CI 1.05-1.33), youth aged 13 to 20 (1.21, 95% CI 0.99-1.46), and those in urban areas (1.19, 95% CI 1.06-1.35). 

CONCLUSIONS The risk of being a victim of serious assault increases with alcohol sales, particularly among young urban men. Similar to efforts to reduce impaired driving, it is important to consider innovative methods for preventing alcohol-related violence.

title: miR-375 inhibits autophagy and reduces viability of hepatocellular carcinoma cells under hypoxic conditions.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in regulating autophagy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells under hypoxic conditions. The researchers used gain- and loss-of-function methods to assess the impact of miRNAs on autophagy in HCC cell lines. Autophagy was measured using various techniques, including immunoblot, immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy analyses. The researchers also conducted a luciferase reporter assay to confirm the associations between miRNAs and their targets. The growth of HCC xenograft tumors in mice was analyzed as well. 

The results showed that miR-375 was down-regulated in HCC cells and tissues. It was found to inhibit autophagy under hypoxic conditions by suppressing the conversion of LC3I to LC3II, thereby affecting autophagic flux. The ability of miR-375 to inhibit autophagy was independent of its regulation of 3'-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase-1-AKT-mammalian target of rapamycin signaling. Instead, it involved the suppression of ATG7, an autophagy-associated gene. miR-375 directly bound to a predicted site in the 3' untranslated region of ATG7. 

Up-regulating miR-375 or down-regulating ATG7 inhibited mitochondrial autophagy of HCC cells, resulting in reduced elimination of damaged mitochondria under hypoxia. This led to increased release of mitochondrial apoptotic proteins and reduced viability of HCC cells. In mice, xenograft tumors expressing miR-375 had fewer autophagic cells, larger areas of necrosis, and slower growth compared to tumors from HCC cells with lower levels of miR-375. 

In conclusion, miR-375 inhibits autophagy by reducing the expression of ATG7 and impairs the viability of HCC cells under hypoxic conditions. The findings suggest that miRNAs that inhibit autophagy in cancer cells could potentially be developed as therapeutics.

title: Pseudouridine profiling reveals regulated mRNA pseudouridylation in yeast and human cells
text: RNA nucleosides undergo post-transcriptional modification in all living organisms. Pseudouridine, the most prevalent modified nucleoside in non-coding RNAs, enhances the function of transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA by stabilizing the structure of RNA. Initially, it was believed that messenger RNAs (mRNAs) did not contain pseudouridine. However, artificial pseudouridylation has a significant impact on mRNA function, altering the genetic code by facilitating non-standard base pairing in the ribosome decoding center. Despite this, the physiological relevance of naturally occurring mRNA pseudouridylation remained unclear. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of pseudouridylation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and human RNAs using Pseudo-seq, a method that identifies pseudouridine at the single-nucleotide level across the entire genome. Pseudo-seq accurately identifies known modification sites and uncovers numerous novel sites in non-coding RNAs, as well as hundreds of pseudouridylated sites in mRNAs. Through genetic analysis, we attribute most of the newly discovered modification sites to one of seven conserved pseudouridine synthases: Pus1-4, 6, 7, and 9. Importantly, the majority of pseudouridines in mRNA are regulated in response to environmental signals, such as nutrient deprivation in yeast and serum starvation in human cells. These findings suggest a mechanism for the rapid and controlled rewiring of the genetic code through inducible mRNA modifications. Additionally, our results uncover unexpected roles for pseudouridylation and provide a valuable resource for identifying the targets of pseudouridine synthases implicated in human diseases.

title: The descent of memory T-cell subsets
text: The immune system has undergone continuous evolution, becoming more complex over time to give the host an upper hand against infectious agents. The creation of immunological memory provides long-term protection and extends the lifespan of the host. By generating different subsets of memory T cells with unique properties, such as their ability to home in on specific locations and perform specific functions, our defensive capabilities are enhanced. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the developmental relationship between these subsets of memory T cells. Based on recent advancements, we propose that it is likely that two separate lineages make up the population of memory CD8+ T cells that are produced in response to infection.

title: Differential distribution of IL28B.rs12979860 single-nucleotide polymorphism among Egyptian healthcare workers with and without a hepatitis C virus-specific cellular immune response
text: The CC genotype of the IL-28B.rs12979860 gene has been linked to both spontaneous clearance and treatment response of hepatitis C virus (HCV). However, it is unclear how this single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) correlates with HCV-specific cell-mediated immune (CMI) responses in Egyptian healthcare workers (HCWs). To investigate this, we studied 402 HCWs who work with a patient population where HCV prevalence is approximately 85%. These HCWs were divided into four groups: group 1 (n = 258) consisted of seronegative aviremic individuals, group 2 (n = 25) consisted of seronegative viremic individuals, group 3 (n = 41) consisted of individuals who had spontaneously resolved HCV infection, and group 4 (n = 78) consisted of chronic HCV patients. All participants underwent testing for HCV-specific CMI responses using an ex-vivo interferon-gamma (IFNγ) ELISpot assay, which involved using nine HCV genotype-4a overlapping 15-mer peptide pools that corresponded to all HCV proteins. Additionally, all participants were tested for the IL28B.rs12979860 SNP using real-time PCR. We found that approximately 27% of the seronegative aviremic HCWs (group 1) exhibited an HCV-specific CMI response, indicating clearance of infection after low-level exposure to HCV. The frequency of IL28B.rs12979860 C allele homozygosity in the four groups was 49%, 48%, 49%, and 23%, respectively, while the frequency of the T allele was 14%, 16%, 12%, and 19%, respectively. This suggests that there are different distributions of IL28B.rs12979860 genotypes among individuals with different HCV statuses. Consistent with previous reports, IL28B.rs12979860 was found to predict the outcome of HCV infection (p < 0.05). However, we did not observe any relationship between IL28B genotypes and the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses in the four groups (p > 0.05). These findings demonstrate that there are differential distributions of IL28B.rs12979860 genotypes among Egyptian HCWs with different HCV statuses, but this SNP cannot predict the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses.

title: TCR ligand density and affinity determine peripheral induction of Foxp3 in vivo
text: The extrathymic differentiation of forkhead box p3(+) (Foxp3(+)) regulatory T cells requires the binding of T cell receptor (TCR). Various evidence suggests that weak stimulation of TCR promotes the induction of Foxp3 in the peripheral region. However, it is still unknown how the strength of TCR ligands affects this process. We examined the density and affinity of TCR ligands that favor the induction of Foxp3 and discovered that a small amount of a potent agonist leads to the highest induction of Foxp3 in vivo. Initially, weak agonist peptides could enhance the induction of Foxp3, but this effect could be disrupted by altering the interaction between TCR and peptide major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) or changing the peptide dosage. However, time course experiments revealed that Foxp3-positive cells induced by weak agonist stimulation are eliminated, along with their Foxp3-negative counterparts, while Foxp3-positive cells induced by low doses of the potent agonist persist. Our findings suggest that the potency, density, and duration of TCR interactions with pMHC ligands collectively determine the amount of TCR stimulation required for initial peripheral Foxp3 induction. However, in the persistence of induced Foxp3(+) T cells, the potency and density of TCR ligands are distinct factors that influence the path to peripheral tolerance.

title: Electromagnetic interference from radio frequency identification inducing potentially hazardous incidents in critical care medical equipment.
text: The use of autoidentification technologies, such as radio frequency identification (RFID), in health care has been suggested as a way to enhance patient safety and improve the tracking and tracing of medical equipment. However, there have been no reports on the electromagnetic interference (EMI) caused by RFID on medical devices. The objective of this study was to evaluate and categorize incidents of EMI caused by RFID on critical care equipment. The study was conducted in a controlled environment without a patient present, using two RFID systems (active 125 kHz and passive 868 MHz). A total of 41 medical devices from 17 categories and 22 different manufacturers were assessed at the Academic Medical Centre, University of Amsterdam, in May 2006. The assessment followed an international test protocol, and incidents of EMI were classified as hazardous, significant, or light based on a critical care adverse events scale. Out of 123 EMI tests (3 per medical device), 34 incidents of EMI were induced by RFID: 22 were classified as hazardous, 2 as significant, and 10 as light. The passive 868-MHz RFID signal caused a higher number of incidents (26 out of 41 EMI tests; 63%) compared to the active 125-kHz RFID signal (8 out of 41 EMI tests; 20%), with a difference of 44% (95% confidence interval, 27%-53%; P < .001). The passive 868-MHz RFID signal caused EMI in 26 medical devices, including 8 that were also affected by the active 125-kHz RFID signal (26 out of 41 devices; 63%). The median distance between the RFID reader and the medical device in all EMI incidents was 30 cm (range, 0.1-600 cm). In conclusion, this study found that RFID caused potentially hazardous incidents in medical devices in a controlled nonclinical setting. Therefore, the implementation of RFID in critical care settings should involve on-site EMI tests and updates to international standards.

title: Potent RNAi by short RNA triggers.
text: RNA interference (RNAi) is a mechanism that silences genes by targeting a specific mRNA for cleavage and degradation. This process involves a ribonucleoprotein complex called the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and a short-interfering RNA (siRNA) that is double-stranded (ds). In human cells, synthetic siRNA duplexes with 19-20 nucleotides (nt) and 2-nt overhangs at the 3'-end of both strands are commonly used for RNAi studies. However, our research has discovered that a shorter siRNA, specifically a 16-nt siRNA, can effectively induce RNAi in human cells. We found that a dsRNA with approximately 42 A A-form helix and 1.5 helical turns is the minimal requirement for triggering RNAi. The 16-nt siRNA demonstrated greater efficacy in reducing mRNA and protein levels compared to the 19-nt siRNA when targeting the CDK9 gene. Additionally, in vitro analysis showed that the 16-nt siRNA has a higher capacity for loading onto RISC in HeLa cells compared to the 19-nt siRNA. These findings suggest that RISC assembly and activation during RNAi can occur with a shorter siRNA duplex, and that 16-nt duplexes can be designed as more potent triggers for inducing RNAi.

title: IL-23–responsive innate lymphoid cells are increased in inflammatory bowel disease
text: The role of the IL-23/IL-17 axis in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been highlighted by experimental and genetic studies. While IL-23-driven inflammation has been primarily linked to Th17 cells, recent research has identified a new population of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) in mice that produce IL-17, IL-22, and IFN-γ in response to IL-23, leading to innate colitis. However, the significance of ILC populations in human health and disease is not well understood. This study aimed to analyze the role of IL-23-responsive ILCs in the human intestine, comparing control subjects with IBD patients. The results showed increased expression of the Th17-associated cytokine genes IL17A and IL17F in intestinal CD3⁻ cells in IBD. The expression of IL17A and IL17F was limited to CD56⁻ ILCs, while IL-23 induced IL22 and IL26 in the CD56⁺ ILC compartment. Additionally, a significant and selective increase in CD127⁺CD56⁻ ILCs was observed in the inflamed intestine of Crohn's disease (CD) patients, but not in ulcerative colitis patients. These findings suggest that IL-23-responsive ILCs are present in the human intestine and that intestinal inflammation in CD is associated with the accumulation of a distinct ILC population characterized by inflammatory cytokine expression. ILCs may contribute to intestinal inflammation through cytokine production, lymphocyte recruitment, and organization of the inflammatory tissue, making them a potential target for treating specific subtypes of IBD.

title: Scaling of Dorsal-Ventral Patterning by Embryo Size-Dependent Degradation of Spemann’s Organizer Signals
text: The Spemann's organizer is crucial in determining the dorsal-ventral (DV) pattern in amphibian embryos. It achieves this by releasing diffusible proteins like Chordin, which counteract the ventralizing effects of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). The DV pattern is so robust that even if the ventral half of an amphibian embryo is surgically removed, it can still develop into a smaller but proportionally patterned larva. Our research reveals that this robust patterning relies on the facilitated degradation of Chordin and the expression of the Chordin-proteinase inhibitor Sizzled on the opposite side. Sizzled, which remains stable and diffuses extensively along the DV axis, stabilizes Chordin and expands its distribution towards the ventral direction. This expanded distribution of Chordin, in turn, restricts the production of Sizzled that is dependent on BMPs, creating a feedback loop that shapes the activity of Chordin throughout the axis. Through bisection assays, we demonstrate that the degradation of Chordin is dynamically regulated by the accumulation of Sizzled, which is linked to the size of the embryo. We propose a scaling model that allows the DV pattern to adjust proportionally to the size of the embryonic axis.

title: Augmenting Antitumor Immune Responses with Epigenetic Modifying Agents
text: The cancer genome exhibits a remarkable characteristic known as epigenetic silencing, which occurs during the development of tumors. This phenomenon has a significant impact on the ability of tumor cells to process and present antigens, allowing them to evade detection by the immune system. Additionally, altered expression of immunosuppressive cytokines further disrupts the function of antigen-presenting cells and cytolytic T-cells within the tumor microenvironment. However, there is hope in the potential of epigenetic modulation to reverse this immunosuppression, offering a versatile and promising therapeutic approach to restore the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy tumors. Pre-clinical studies have already identified various components of the immune system that can be influenced by epigenetic mechanisms, leading to enhanced antigen presentation, improved function of T-cells, and the breakdown of suppressor mechanisms. Recent clinical studies have begun to explore the use of epigenetic therapies in combination with immune therapies, or as a precursor to them, in order to achieve better clinical outcomes.

title: Activation of proteinase-activated receptor 2 in human osteoarthritic cartilage upregulates catabolic and proinflammatory pathways capable of inducing cartilage degradation: a basic science study
text:
Proteinase-activated receptors (PARs) are a type of G protein-coupled receptors that are activated by serine-dependent cleavage, resulting in the release of an activating ligand. PAR-2 has been found to play a role in inflammatory pathways. In this study, we investigated the levels and modulation of PAR-2 in both normal and osteoarthritis (OA) cartilage and chondrocytes. Additionally, we examined the impact of PAR-2 on the synthesis of major catabolic factors in OA cartilage, including metalloproteinase (MMP)-1 and MMP-13, as well as the inflammatory mediator cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2). We also explored the signaling pathways activated by PAR-2 in OA chondrocytes. 

To determine PAR-2 expression, we used real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemistry in normal and OA cartilage. We then investigated protein modulation in OA cartilage explants treated with a specific PAR-2-activating peptide (PAR-2-AP), interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), transforming growth factor-beta-1 (TGF-β1), or inhibitors of p38, MEK1/2, and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). PAR-2 levels were assessed using immunohistochemistry. 

We analyzed signaling pathways in OA chondrocytes using Western blot with phospho-specific antibodies against extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (Erk1/2), p38, JNK (c-jun N-terminal kinase), and NF-κB in the presence or absence of PAR-2-AP and/or IL-1β. We also determined MMP and COX-2 levels in cartilage using immunohistochemistry. 

Our findings revealed that PAR-2 is produced by human chondrocytes and is significantly upregulated in OA compared to normal chondrocytes. The receptor levels were increased by IL-1β, TNF-α, and PAR-2-AP, and decreased by p38 inhibition. PAR-2 activation induced MMP-1 and COX-2 production, as well as the phosphorylation of Erk1/2 and p38. IL-1β had an additional effect on the activation of Erk1/2 and p38. 

This study provides evidence of the functional consequences of PAR-2 activation in human OA cartilage, identifies p38 as the primary signaling pathway regulating its synthesis, and suggests PAR-2 as a potential therapeutic target for OA treatment.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps enriched in oxidized mitochondrial DNA are interferogenic and contribute to lupus-like disease
text: The generation and functions of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in sterile inflammation and autoimmunity are not well understood. Ribonucleoprotein immune complexes (RNP ICs) induce NETosis and require mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) for optimal NET stimulation. Upon RNP IC stimulation, neutrophil mitochondria become hypopolarized and relocate to the cell surface. In vitro, the release of oxidized mitochondrial DNA externally triggers inflammation, and when injected into mice, it activates type I interferon (IFN) signaling through the DNA sensor STING. Mitochondrial ROS are also crucial for spontaneous NETosis in low-density granulocytes from individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus. This phenomenon is also observed in individuals with chronic granulomatous disease, who lack NADPH oxidase activity but still develop autoimmunity and type I IFN signatures. Inhibiting mitochondrial ROS in vivo reduces disease severity and type I IFN responses in a mouse model of lupus. These findings emphasize the involvement of mitochondria not only in the production of NETs but also in the generation of pro-inflammatory oxidized mitochondrial DNA in autoimmune diseases.

title: Microenvironment rigidity modulates responses to the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib via YAP and TAZ transcription factors.
text: Stiffness is a physical characteristic of the extracellular matrix that influences various cellular functions, such as proliferation, invasion, and differentiation. It can also impact the effectiveness of therapeutic treatments. However, the reasons behind the limited durability of cancer treatments, including chemotherapy and pathway-targeted drugs, are not well understood. As tumors progress, the biophysical properties of the tissue change. Therefore, we investigated whether the rigidity of the matrix affects the sensitivity or resistance of HER2-amplified breast cancer cells to the HER2-targeted kinase inhibitor lapatinib. We found that the ability of lapatinib to inhibit cell proliferation was inversely related to the elasticity of the adhesive substrata. By reducing the expression of the mechanosensitive transcription coactivators YAP and TAZ, either through siRNA or with the YAP/TEAD inhibitor verteporfin, we were able to eliminate the resistance to lapatinib that was dependent on matrix rigidity. In mice, reducing YAP expression also slowed the growth of implanted HER2-amplified tumors, indicating an increased sensitivity to lapatinib as YAP levels decreased. Therefore, we have explored the role of stiffness in resistance to and effectiveness of a HER2 pathway-targeted therapy through the mechanotransduction arm of the Hippo pathway.

title: Effective population size and patterns of molecular evolution and variation
text: The rate at which a population's composition changes due to genetic drift, which is the random sampling of genetic variants in a limited population, is determined by the effective size of the population, Ne. Ne plays a vital role in determining the level of variability within a population and the relative impact of selection compared to drift. This article examines the characteristics of Ne in various biological scenarios and explores the factors that influence it. Notably, the influence of selection causes Ne to vary throughout the genome, and recent advancements in genomic techniques are providing fresh perspectives on how selection shapes Ne.

title: Is emotional dysregulation part of the psychopathology of ADHD in adults?
text: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent condition that can persist into adulthood. This disorder is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. In addition to these symptoms, there is ongoing discussion about whether symptoms of emotional dysregulation can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the psychopathology of ADHD. Currently, neither the ICD-10 nor the DSM-IV includes emotional dysregulation as a core aspect of ADHD, but the upcoming DSM-5 also does not address this issue. However, some authors, such as Wender (1995), have proposed a more nuanced perspective on adult ADHD that takes into account the subjective experiences of the individual, including emotional symptoms. Empirical studies have shown that emotional dysregulation is a distinct and reliable dimension of adult ADHD. Both pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions have been found to be effective in alleviating these symptoms. This review emphasizes the importance of considering emotional symptoms in the overall symptomatology of ADHD and calls for further research in this area.

title: A neural basis for melanocortin-4 receptor regulated appetite
text: The arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) contains two types of neurons, namely pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons and agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons. These neurons play opposite roles in regulating homeostatic satiety, with POMC neurons stimulating satiety and AgRP neurons inhibiting it. The actions of these neurons are mediated by melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH). Despite their importance in energy balance, the neural circuitry underlying their function is not well understood. In this study, we used mice that express Cre recombinase in MC4R neurons to investigate the control of feeding by PVH(MC4R) neurons. We found that activating or inhibiting these neurons in real-time resulted in bidirectional control of feeding. Furthermore, we identified these PVH(MC4R) neurons as a functional component of hunger driven by ARC(AgRP) neurons. We also discovered that this function is mediated by a pathway from PVH(MC4R) neurons to the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN). Activation of this circuit encoded positive valence, but only in mice that were calorically depleted. Therefore, the satiating and appetitive nature of PVH(MC4R)→LPBN neurons supports the principles of drive reduction and suggests that this circuit could be a promising target for developing antiobesity drugs.

title: Lymph node T cell responses predict the efficacy of live attenuated SIV vaccines
text: The protection provided by live attenuated simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) vaccines (LAVs) in nonhuman primate models of HIV and AIDS is still not well understood, despite being the most effective vaccines available. In this study, we demonstrate that the level of protection offered by LAVs against intravenous wild-type SIVmac239 challenge is strongly linked to the strength and function of SIV-specific T cells in the lymph nodes. However, there is no correlation between the response of these T cells in the blood or other immune parameters. We also discovered that the maintenance of protective T cell responses is associated with ongoing LAV replication in the lymph nodes, specifically in follicular helper T cells. Therefore, effective LAVs preserve effector-differentiated, SIV-specific T cells in the lymphoid tissue, which can intercept and suppress early wild-type SIV replication. If these T cells are present in sufficient numbers, they can potentially control and even eliminate the infection. This finding supports the development of safe and persistent vectors that can induce and sustain such immune responses.

title: Activation of Serotonin 2C Receptors in Dopamine Neurons Inhibits Binge-like Eating in Mice
text: The identification of neural networks that regulate binge eating is still unknown, and there are limited effective treatments for this behavior. In this study, we utilized various approaches such as neuroanatomic, pharmacologic, electrophysiological, Cre-lox, and chemogenetic methods to investigate the role of the 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) 2C receptor (5-HT2CR) expressed by dopamine (DA) neurons in the regulation of binge-like eating behavior in mice. Our findings demonstrated that 5-HT stimulates DA neural activity through a mechanism mediated by the 5-HT2CR, and activation of this midbrain 5-HT→DA neural circuit effectively suppresses binge-like eating behavior in mice. Importantly, medications targeting 5-HT, including fluoxetine, d-fenfluramine, and lorcaserin (a selective 5-HT2CR agonist), exert their inhibitory effects on binge-like eating by acting on 5-HT2CRs expressed by DA neurons. In conclusion, we have identified the 5-HT2CR population in DA neurons as a potential target for anti-binge therapies, and our preclinical evidence suggests that 5-HT2CR agonists could be utilized for the treatment of binge eating.

title: Restoration of chaperone-mediated autophagy in aging liver improves cellular maintenance and hepatic function
text:
Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) is a selective process that degrades cytosolic proteins in lysosomes. It plays a crucial role in eliminating altered proteins as part of the cellular quality-control systems. Previous research has indicated that CMA activity declines in aged organisms, which may lead to the accumulation of altered proteins, disruption of cellular homeostasis, and ultimately, functional decline in aging organisms. To investigate whether maintaining efficient autophagic activity can prevent these negative effects of aging, we conducted a study to correct the CMA defect in aged rodents.

In our study, we developed a double transgenic mouse model that allows us to modulate the abundance of the lysosomal receptor for CMA, which is known to decrease with age. We examined the consequences of preventing the age-related decrease in receptor abundance at both the cellular and organ levels. Our findings demonstrate that if the decrease in receptor abundance is prevented, CMA activity can be maintained even at advanced ages. This preservation of autophagic activity is associated with reduced intracellular accumulation of damaged proteins, enhanced ability to handle protein damage, and improved organ function.

In summary, our study suggests that maintaining efficient autophagic activity, specifically CMA, until late in life can prevent the negative features of aging. By preventing the decline in receptor abundance, we observed improved cellular and organ function, highlighting the importance of autophagy in maintaining cellular quality-control systems and overall organismal health during aging.

title: The Incidence and Repetition of Hospital-Treated Deliberate Self Harm: Findings from the World's First National Registry
text:
BACKGROUND: Suicide is a major public health concern, with nearly one million people worldwide dying by suicide each year. Deliberate self-harm (DSH) is the most significant risk factor for suicide, yet reliable data on DSH is lacking in many countries. In the Republic of Ireland, we established a national DSH registry to determine the incidence of hospital-treated DSH at a national level, as well as the patterns and presentations of DSH and repetition.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: From 2003 to 2009, the Irish National Registry of Deliberate Self-Harm collected data on DSH presentations in all 40 hospital emergency departments in the country. Trained data registration officers used standardized methods to collect and define the cases. The registry recorded 75,119 DSH presentations involving 48,206 individuals. The total incidence rate decreased from 209 per 100,000 in 2003 to 184 per 100,000 in 2006, but then increased again to 209 per 100,000 in 2009. Notably, there were successive 10% increases in the male rate in 2008 and 2009. Rates varied significantly by age, with the highest rates in women aged 15-19 (620 per 100,000) and in men aged 20-24 (427 per 100,000). Repetition rates also varied significantly by age, method of self-harm, and number of previous episodes.

CONCLUSIONS: Population-based data on hospital-treated DSH provide important insights into the burden of mental illness and suicide risk in the community. The increase in DSH rates among Irish men in 2008 and 2009 coincided with the economic recession in Ireland. These findings highlight the urgent need for effective interventions to reduce DSH repetition rates, making it a key priority for health systems.

title: A Common Mechanism of Cellular Death Induced by Bactericidal Antibiotics
text: The classification of antibiotic mode-of-action is determined by the interaction between the drug and its target, as well as whether it effectively kills bacteria by inhibiting cellular function. In this study, we have discovered that the three main classes of antibiotics that kill bacteria, regardless of their interaction with the drug target, actually stimulate the production of harmful hydroxyl radicals in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, ultimately leading to cell death. On the other hand, we have found that antibiotics that only inhibit bacterial growth do not generate hydroxyl radicals. Our research demonstrates that the formation of hydroxyl radicals induced by bactericidal antibiotics is the final result of a cellular death pathway involving oxidative damage to the cell, depletion of NADH, destabilization of iron-sulfur clusters, and activation of the Fenton reaction. Based on our findings, we propose that targeting bacterial systems involved in repairing hydroxyl radical damage, such as proteins that trigger the DNA damage response (e.g., RecA), can enhance the effectiveness of all three major classes of bactericidal drugs.

title: Increased atherosclerosis in mice reconstituted with apolipoprotein E null macrophages.
text: Foam cells derived from macrophages in atherosclerotic lesions exhibit high levels of apolipoprotein E (apoE). To investigate the role of apoE secretion by macrophages in the development of atherosclerosis, researchers conducted bone marrow transplantation in C57BL/6 mice, replacing their macrophages with either apoE-deficient or wild-type macrophages. After 13 weeks on a diet that promotes atherosclerosis, mice with apoE-deficient marrow developed 10 times more atherosclerosis than control mice, despite similar levels of serum cholesterol and lipoprotein profiles. The macrophage-derived foam cells in mice with apoE-deficient marrow showed no expression of apoE, indicating that the absence of apoE expression by macrophages promotes foam cell formation. These findings suggest that apoE expression by macrophages plays a protective role in the early stages of atherosclerosis.

title: Endothelium-mediated relaxation of porcine collateral-dependent arterioles is improved by exercise training.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of exercise training on endothelium-dependent modulation of coronary tone in the collateral-dependent coronary microcirculation. A porcine model of chronic coronary occlusion and collateral development was used. The hypothesis was that exercise training would improve endothelium-mediated relaxation and increase endothelial nitric oxide synthase (ecNOS) mRNA levels in the collateral-dependent microvasculature.

Adult female miniature swine were subjected to chronic occlusion of the proximal left circumflex coronary artery (LCx) using an ameroid occluder. After 2 months, the animals were randomly assigned to either an exercise-training group (EX group) or a sedentary group (SED group). The EX group underwent a 16-week treadmill running program, while the SED group remained confined to cages. After completing the exercise or sedentary programs, coronary arterioles (approximately 100 micrometers in diameter) were isolated from the collateral-dependent LCx (distal to occlusion) and nonoccluded left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) regions of each heart. The arterioles were then studied using videomicroscopy or frozen for ecNOS mRNA analysis.

The results showed that relaxation to the endothelium-dependent vasodilator bradykinin was decreased in arterioles isolated from collateral-dependent LCx regions of the SED animals compared to nonoccluded LAD regions. However, there was no difference in bradykinin-mediated relaxation between LCx and LAD arterioles in the EX animals. Nitroprusside-induced relaxation was not affected by chronic occlusion or exercise. Importantly, ecNOS mRNA expression was significantly decreased in arterioles isolated from LCx regions of the SED animals compared to LAD regions. After exercise training, ecNOS mRNA expression was similar in both LAD and LCx arterioles.

In conclusion, exercise training improved bradykinin-mediated relaxation of collateral-dependent LCx arterioles after chronic coronary occlusion. This improvement is likely due to increased ecNOS mRNA expression and enhanced production of nitric oxide.

title: Loss of the RhoGAP SRGP-1 promotes the clearance of dead and injured cells in Caenorhabditis elegans
text: Animals with multiple cells efficiently eliminate dying cells from their bodies. Many of the pathways involved in this process have been preserved throughout evolution. In this study, we have discovered that srgp-1 acts as a negative regulator of cell clearance in both Caenorhabditis elegans and mammalian cells. When srgp-1 function is lost, the engulfment of apoptotic cells improves, while overexpression of srgp-1 inhibits the removal of apoptotic cell corpses. Our findings demonstrate that SRGP-1 plays a role in engulfing cells and acts as a GTPase activating protein (GAP) for CED-10 (Rac1). Interestingly, the loss of srgp-1 function not only enhances the clearance of already dead cells, but also eliminates cells that are on the brink of death due to sublethal apoptotic, necrotic, or cytotoxic insults. On the other hand, impaired engulfment allows damaged cells to evade clearance, leading to increased long-term survival. Based on these observations, we propose that C. elegans employs the engulfment machinery as part of a primitive, yet evolutionarily conserved, surveillance mechanism to identify and eliminate unfit cells within a tissue.

title: Abnormalities in the myeloid progenitor compartment in Down syndrome fetal liver precede acquisition of GATA1 mutations.
text: Children with Down syndrome (DS) are more likely to develop acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) during early childhood. Two genetic events, trisomy 21 (T21) and N-terminal-truncating GATA1 mutations, are necessary but not sufficient for DS-AMKL. To understand the role of T21 in DS-AMKL, we compared the development of blood cells in the second trimester of DS fetuses without GATA1 mutations to normal fetuses of the same gestational age. We found that in DS fetal livers (FLs), but not bone marrows, there was an increased frequency of megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (55.9% +/- 4% vs 17.1% +/- 3%, CD34(+)CD38(+) cells; P < .001), while common myeloid progenitors (19.6% +/- 2% vs 44.0% +/- 7%) and granulocyte-monocyte (GM) progenitors (15.8% +/- 4% vs 34.5% +/- 9%) were reduced. The clonogenicity of DS-FL CD34(+) cells was significantly higher (78% +/- 7% vs 15% +/- 3%), particularly in megakaryocyte-erythroid and GM colony-forming unit-granulocyte, erythrocyte macrophage, megakaryocyte (CFU-GEMM) progenitors. The replating efficiency of CFU-GEMM was also significantly increased. These findings suggest that T21 itself disrupts the development of blood cells in the fetal liver and provide a hypothesis to explain the increased susceptibility to GATA1 mutations in DS-AMKL and DS-associated transient myeloproliferative disorder.

title: Regulatory and metabolic rewiring during laboratory evolution of ethanol tolerance in E. coli
text:
Understanding the genetic basis of adaptation is a fundamental challenge in the field of biology. However, uncovering the molecular mechanisms that drive adaptation has proven to be difficult due to the fact that changes in fitness can arise from disruptions to multiple pathways, each of which may have a relatively small impact. To tackle this problem, we have developed a novel experimental and computational framework. Using this framework, we have investigated the genetic factors that contribute to ethanol tolerance in Escherichia coli.

To begin, we employed fitness profiling to assess the effects of perturbations to individual genetic loci in the presence of ethanol. This allowed us to measure the consequences of these perturbations on the organism's ability to tolerate ethanol. Next, we utilized a computational analysis at the module level to uncover the organization of the contributing loci within cellular processes and regulatory pathways. For example, we identified the involvement of pathways such as osmoregulation and cell-wall biogenesis, which play a significant role in determining ethanol tolerance.

Interestingly, our research revealed that a major component of adaptation to ethanol involves a rewiring of metabolic processes that enhance the breakdown and utilization of ethanol within the cell. To further investigate the pathways that naturally confer ethanol tolerance, we conducted phenotypic and metabolomic analyses on laboratory-evolved strains that had developed a high level of tolerance to ethanol. Remarkably, we found that these laboratory-evolved strains followed similar adaptive paths as those inferred from our earlier search of the fitness landscape.

In summary, our study provides valuable insights into the genetic basis of ethanol tolerance in Escherichia coli. By combining experimental and computational approaches, we have shed light on the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptation and identified key pathways involved in ethanol tolerance.

title: Familial risk of lymphoproliferative tumors in families of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia: results from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database.
text: Family and population studies suggest that genetic factors play a significant role in the development of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). However, it is unclear which other malignancies share common genetic factors with CLL and how sex and age affect familial risk. To investigate this, we analyzed data from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database, examining the cancer diagnoses of 14,336 first-degree relatives of 5,918 CLL cases and 28,876 first-degree relatives of 11,778 controls between 1958 and 1998. We compared cancer risks in relatives of cases with those in relatives of controls using marginal survival models. We found that relatives of cases had a significantly higher risk of developing CLL (relative risk [RR] = 7.52; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.63-15.56), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 1.45; 95% CI, 0.98-2.16), and Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 2.35; 95% CI, 1.08-5.08). The risk of CLL was similar in parents, siblings, and offspring of cases, as well as in male and female relatives, and was not influenced by the age at which the case was diagnosed. We did not find significant anticipation when analyzing the data using life table methods. In conclusion, our findings suggest that CLL shares a familial component with other lymphoproliferative malignancies, indicating common genetic pathways. However, due to the rarity of clinically diagnosed CLL, the absolute excess risk to relatives is small.

title: Collagen/Polypropylene composite mesh biocompatibility in abdominal wall reconstruction.
text:
The intraperitoneal placement of polypropylene mesh is known to cause extensive adhesions with the viscera, making it unsuitable for use. To improve the properties of polypropylene mesh, different coatings have been developed. Collagen, a protein with excellent biocompatibility and the ability to enhance cell ingrowth, has been used as a coating. In this study, a new collagen coating extracted using acetic acid was developed to allow direct contact between the polypropylene mesh and the viscera. The objective of the study was to assess the long-term effects of this collagen coating on surgical outcomes and biomechanical properties of the mesh, including complications, adhesions with the viscera, strength of incorporation, and microscopic inflammatory reaction.

Forty adult Wistar rats were divided into two groups: the experimental group, which received polypropylene mesh with the acetic acid extracted collagen coating, and the control group, which received polypropylene mesh without any coating. A standardized procedure for mesh implantation was performed. The animals were euthanized three months after surgery, and various parameters were analyzed, including complications, the area of the mesh covered by adhesions, the type of adhesions, the strength of incorporation, and the intensity of the inflammatory response.

The results showed that the mean adhesion area was significantly lower in the group with the polypropylene mesh coated with acetic acid extracted collagen (14.5 percent versus 69.9 percent, p < 0.001). The severity of adhesions was also reduced in the experimental group, with grades 0 and 1 being more frequent (p < 0.04 and p < 0.002, respectively) and grade 3 being less frequent (p < 0.0001). There was a correlation between the area of adhesions and their severity (p < 0.0001). However, there were no significant differences in complications, strength of incorporation, or intensity of inflammatory response between the two groups.

In conclusion, the use of acetic acid extracted collagen coating on polypropylene mesh significantly reduces visceral adhesions. This coating does not increase complications or affect the incorporation of the mesh.

title: Microvessel Density and Status of p53 Protein as Potential Prognostic Factors for Adjuvant Anthracycline Chemotherapy in Retrospective Analysis of Early Breast Cancer Patients Group
text: This retrospective study aimed to examine the impact of microvessel density (MVD) and the status of p53 protein on 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) in a group of breast cancer patients who received anthracycline-based chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting. The study also assessed the correlations between MVD, p53 status, and other clinicopathological parameters. Immunohistochemical analysis was conducted on 172 women with breast cancer in clinical stage T1-2, N1-N2, M0. Of these, 123 tumors (71.5%) had lower MVD (≤ 214.8 microvessels/mm(2)), while 49 tumors (28.5%) had higher MVD (>214.8 microvessels/mm(2)). The proportion of tumors with higher MVD was significantly higher in N2 and in tumors negative for estrogen or progesterone receptors. p53 positivity was observed in 50 cancers (29.1%) and was significantly associated with higher grade, negativity for steroid receptors, positivity for cytokeratin5/6, overexpression of topoisomerase IIα, and a higher proliferation rate. Univariate analysis showed that higher MVD and p53 negativity were significantly associated with longer DFS. In multivariate Cox regression analysis, MVD was independently associated with DFS. These findings suggest that higher MVD is a favorable prognostic factor for patients with early advanced breast cancer who receive adjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy.

title: Ranking of elimination feasibility between malaria-endemic countries
text:
The Global Malaria Eradication Program (1955-72) provided valuable insights into the factors that contributed to successful malaria elimination in certain countries. To objectively assess the feasibility of elimination, spatial data on these factors were collected for all malaria-endemic countries and combined. The analysis focused on Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax separately, and the limitations of the approach were acknowledged.

The rankings obtained from this analysis indicated that countries in the Americas and Asia were more likely to achieve malaria elimination, while countries in central and west Africa faced greater challenges. It is important to note that the rankings varied depending on whether technical or operational factors were considered, highlighting the unique obstacles faced by each country.

These results should not be seen as definitive or predictive assessments of feasibility, but rather as a demonstration of the availability of spatial information that can support evidence-based evaluations of the relative feasibility of malaria elimination on a country-by-country basis. Furthermore, this information can be regularly updated to ensure its relevance and usefulness.

title: Genetics of obesity in adult adoptees and their biological siblings.
text:
