A study was conducted to examine the genetic effects on obesity in adulthood through adoption. The study compared adoptees who were separated from their biological parents at an early age with their biological full and half siblings who were raised by their natural parents. The adoptees were divided into four groups based on their weight - thin, medium weight, overweight, and obese. Weight and height measurements were taken for 115 full siblings of 57 adoptees and 850 half siblings of 341 adoptees.

The results showed that in full siblings, the body mass index (BMI) significantly increased as the weight of the adoptees increased. In half siblings, the BMI also increased, but the increase was less pronounced across the four weight groups of adoptees. There were no significant differences based on the sex of the adoptees, siblings, or common parent (for half siblings).

Interestingly, when comparing full siblings of overweight and obese adoptees, there was a significant and noticeable increase in BMI. This finding contrasted with the results from half siblings and natural parents. It suggests that the level of obesity in adults living in the same environment is influenced by genetic factors that are independent of sex. These genetic factors may include both polygenic effects and major gene effects on obesity.

title: 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria: an American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative.
text:
The aim of this study was to develop new classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) that are more sensitive in detecting early disease. A joint working group from the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European League Against Rheumatism conducted this research in three phases. The focus was on identifying factors among patients with undifferentiated inflammatory synovitis that could distinguish those at high risk for persistent and/or erosive disease, which is the current understanding of RA. 

The new criteria for classifying RA as "definite RA" include the presence of synovitis in at least one joint, the absence of an alternative diagnosis that better explains the synovitis, and a total score of 6 or higher (out of 10) based on individual scores in four domains: number and location of affected joints (0-5), serological abnormality (0-3), elevated acute-phase response (0-1), and symptom duration (two levels; 0-1). 

This new classification system shifts the focus to earlier stages of the disease that are associated with persistent and/or erosive disease, rather than relying on late-stage features to define RA. It emphasizes the importance of early diagnosis and effective treatment to prevent or minimize the undesirable consequences of RA.

title: A role for fibroblasts in mediating the effects of tobacco-induced epithelial cell growth and invasion.
text: Little is currently understood about the mechanisms behind the development and progression of tumors caused by chronic exposure to carcinogens found in tobacco products, including cigarette smoke and smokeless tobacco extracts. In this study, we focused on the impact of smokeless tobacco extracts on human oral fibroblasts. Our findings reveal that these extracts increase the levels of reactive oxygen within cells, leading to oxidative DNA damage and DNA double-strand breaks. The longer the exposure to the extracts, the more likely fibroblasts are to enter a state of growth arrest resembling senescence, accompanied by significant changes in their secretory behavior. By conducting cocultures of smokeless tobacco extract-exposed fibroblasts and immortalized, non-tumorigenic keratinocytes, we discovered that factors secreted by the modified fibroblasts enhance the proliferation and invasiveness of partially transformed epithelial cells, while having no effect on their normal counterparts. Furthermore, fibroblasts exposed to smokeless tobacco extracts caused partially transformed keratinocytes to lose the expression of certain proteins associated with compromised epithelial function and commonly observed in malignant progression. These findings suggest that fibroblasts may indirectly contribute to tumorigenesis by promoting the aggressiveness of epithelial cells. Therefore, tobacco not only initiates mutagenic changes in epithelial cells but also fosters the growth and invasion of mutant cells by creating a stromal environment that supports carcinogenesis.

title: ImmTAC-redirected tumour cell killing induces and potentiates antigen cross-presentation by dendritic cells
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) are believed to play a crucial role in stimulating a diverse and long-lasting T cell response against cancer through antigen cross-presentation. Therefore, the effectiveness of emerging immunotherapeutic agents in eradicating tumors may rely on their ability to induce antigen cross-presentation. ImmTACs, a novel class of soluble bi-specific anti-cancer agents, combine T cell activation via a CD3-specific antibody fragment with TCR-based antigen recognition at pico-molar affinity. These ImmTACs specifically target tumor-associated antigens presented by cancer cells through human leucocyte antigen (HLA) restriction, leading to T cell redirection and a potent anti-tumor response. In this study, we used an ImmTAC designed for a HLA-A*02-restricted peptide derived from the melanoma antigen gp100 (IMCgp100) and observed that ImmTAC-induced melanoma cell death resulted in cross-presentation of melanoma antigens by DCs. These cross-presenting DCs were able to activate both melanoma-specific T cells and polyclonal T cells redirected by IMCgp100. Furthermore, the presence of IMCgp100 enhanced the activation of melanoma-specific T cells by cross-presenting DCs, increasing the likelihood of breaking tolerance in the tumor microenvironment. The mechanism of DC cross-presentation involves the rapid and direct capture of membrane fragments from dying tumor cells, a process known as "cross-dressing." The cross-presentation of gp100-peptide-HLA complexes by DCs was visualized and quantified using a fluorescently labeled soluble TCR. These findings demonstrate how ImmTACs interact with the innate and adaptive components of the immune system, improving the potential for an effective and long-lasting anti-tumor response in patients.

title: Basal keratinocyte tetrasomy in low-grade squamous intra-epithelial lesions of the cervix is restricted to high and intermediate risk HPV infection but is not type-specific
text: The presence of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is believed to be an early occurrence in the development of cervical cancer, but additional abnormalities are necessary for biological transformation. In this study, we examined 179 low-grade cervical squamous intra-epithelial lesions (SILs) and 15 normal cervices to determine the presence of HPV using in situ hybridization and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). PCR was conducted using GP5+/GP6+ primers, followed by hybridization with probes for low-risk (HPV 6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44), intermediate-risk (HPV 31, 33, 35, 39, 51, 52, 58, 59, 66, and 68), and high-risk (HPV 16, 18, 45, and 56) HPVs. We also performed interphase cytogenetic analysis using pericentromeric probes for chromosomes 1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 11, 17, 18, and X to identify numerical chromosomal abnormalities. Tetrasomy, the presence of four copies of each of the nine chromosomes, was observed in basal keratinocytes and was limited to epithelia infected with high-risk (17 out of 46) or intermediate-risk (23 out of 83) HPVs, but not specific to any HPV type. Tetrasomy was not found in epithelia infected with low-risk HPVs (n = 62), including cases with multiple infections. These results suggest that the induction of tetrasomy is a characteristic associated with high and intermediate-risk HPV types, but the factors determining which lesions develop this abnormality are still unknown. This study was conducted in 2000 by the Cancer Research Campaign.

title: “Rapid-Impact Interventions”: How a Policy of Integrated Control for Africa's Neglected Tropical Diseases Could Benefit the Poor
text: In the last 20 years, significant progress has been made in controlling several important tropical infections that affect humans [1]. These achievements include substantial reductions in the prevalence and incidence of neglected diseases like lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, guinea worm, leprosy, and trachoma (Box 1) [2]. These neglected diseases are primarily found in rural areas of low-income countries and contribute to poverty and social stigma (Box 2) [3]. They have been a burden on humanity for centuries, with mentions in ancient texts and the Bible [3]. However, aggressive regional interventions have created the possibility of eventually eliminating some neglected tropical infections in certain endemic areas [2–8]. In the case of guinea worm infection, eradication may soon be achievable [9]. Box 2. Common Characteristics of Neglected Tropical Diseases: - Ancient diseases that have plagued humanity for centuries - Contribute to poverty - Associated with social stigma - Found in rural areas of low-income countries and fragile states - Lack of commercial markets for products targeting these diseases - Interventions, when implemented, have a history of success

title: FTY720 (fingolimod) is a neuroprotective and disease-modifying agent in cellular and mouse models of Huntington disease.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether FTY720, an approved oral therapy for multiple sclerosis, could be effective in treating Huntington disease (HD). HD is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder with no current cure or way to slow down the brain changes it causes. We used preclinical target validation methods and tested the effects of chronic FTY720 administration in a mouse model of HD called R6/2. Our results showed that FTY720 improved motor function, increased survival, and reduced brain atrophy in the R6/2 mice. These positive effects were associated with enhanced neuronal activity and connectivity, reduced mutant huntingtin aggregates, and increased phosphorylation of mutant huntingtin at specific residues known to reduce protein toxicity. These findings suggest that FTY720 could be a potential alternative therapy for HD.

title: Specificity Residues Determine Binding Affinity for Two-Component Signal Transduction Systems
text: Unlabeled Two-component systems (TCS) consist of histidine kinases and their corresponding response regulators, enabling bacteria to detect and respond to various signals. Histidine kinases (HKs) phosphorylate and dephosphorylate their corresponding response regulators (RRs) in response to stimuli. Generally, these reactions are highly specific and require a proper association between the HK and RR proteins. The genome of Myxococcus xanthus contains one of the largest collections of signaling proteins in bacteria (685 open reading frames [ORFs]), including at least 127 HKs and at least 143 RRs. Among these, 27 are confirmed NtrC-family response regulators, with 21 of them encoded next to their predicted kinases. Through comprehensive profiling methods, we discovered that the HK-NtrC RR pairs exhibit a kinetic preference in both phosphotransfer and phosphatase functions, thus defining the corresponding signaling systems in M. xanthus. Isothermal titration calorimetry measurements revealed that cognate HK-RR pairs interact with dissociation constants (Kd) of approximately 1 µM, while noncognate pairs showed no measurable binding. Lastly, a chimera created from the histidine kinase, CrdS, and HK1190 demonstrated that residues responsible for phosphotransfer and phosphatase specificity determine binding affinity, establishing distinct protein-protein interactions that prevent cross talk. These findings highlight the critical role of binding affinity in maintaining signaling fidelity for bacterial signal transduction proteins. IMPORTANCE Through in vitro phosphotransfer and phosphatase profiling assays, as well as isothermal titration calorimetry, we have taken a comprehensive approach to demonstrate the specificity of a family of two-component signaling proteins in Myxococcus xanthus. Our results show that previously identified specificity residues determine binding affinity and that phosphatase specificity follows phosphotransfer specificity in cognate HK-RR pairs. These findings indicate that preferential binding affinity is the foundation for signaling fidelity in bacterial two-component systems.

title: hnRNP A1 associates with telomere ends and stimulates telomerase activity.
text: Telomerase is an enzyme complex made up of ribonucleoproteins that can reverse-transcribe a specific RNA template and add short DNA repeats to the ends of telomeres. The presence of a G-quadruplex structure in the DNA can prevent telomerase from extending the telomeres. Our research has discovered that hnRNP A1, which has previously been linked to the regulation of telomere length, can bind to both single-stranded and structured human telomeric repeats. In the case of the structured repeats, hnRNP A1 disrupts their higher-order structure. Through an in vitro telomerase assay, we observed that removing hnRNP A/B proteins from human embryonic kidney cell extracts significantly decreased telomerase activity. However, when we added purified recombinant hnRNP A1, the telomerase activity was fully restored. This suggests that hnRNP A1 plays an important role as an auxiliary, and possibly essential, factor in the telomerase holoenzyme. Additionally, using chromatin immunoprecipitation, we demonstrated that hnRNP A1 is associated with human telomeres in vivo. We propose that hnRNP A1 stimulates telomere elongation by unwinding G-quadruplex or G-G hairpin structures that form during each translocation step.

title: Rapamycin passes the torch: a new generation of mTOR inhibitors
text: Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a unique protein kinase that regulates growth and metabolism in response to nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy levels. It is commonly disrupted in cancer and metabolic disorders. Rapamycin, an allosteric inhibitor of mTOR, was initially approved as an immuno-suppressant in 1999. Recently, there has been growing interest in its potential as an anticancer medication. However, the effectiveness of rapamycin and its similar compounds (rapalogues) has been mediocre, with only occasional success in specific cancer types. This suggests that the full therapeutic benefits of targeting mTOR have not yet been fully explored. A new generation of inhibitors that directly target the mTOR catalytic site and compete with ATP have shown strong and comprehensive mTOR inhibition. These inhibitors are currently undergoing early clinical trials.

title: Dynamic capsule restructuring by the main pneumococcal autolysin LytA in response to the epithelium
text: Bacterial pathogens create intricate carbohydrate capsules to shield themselves from immune molecules that can kill them. Interestingly, the pneumococcal capsule actually makes the bacterium more susceptible to antimicrobial peptides found on epithelial surfaces. In our study, we demonstrate that when exposed to antimicrobial peptides, encapsulated pneumococci are able to survive by quickly removing the capsule from their cell surface. This process relies on the action of the suicidal amidase autolysin LytA. Unlike typical bacterial autolysis, LytA aids in bacterial survival during capsule shedding and is distributed evenly around the cell. However, both autolysis and capsule shedding require the cell wall hydrolytic activity of LytA. Capsule shedding significantly enhances the invasion of epithelial cells and serves as the primary method by which pneumococci reduce the amount of capsule bound to their surface during the early stages of acute lung infection in mice. The previously unknown role of LytA in removing the capsule to counteract antimicrobial peptides may explain why almost all clinical isolates of pneumococci retain this enzyme despite the strong selective pressure of antibiotics.

title: The mammalian Scribble polarity protein regulates epithelial cell adhesion and migration through E-cadherin
text: Scribble (Scrib) is a protein that plays a crucial role in various biological processes in Drosophila melanogaster, including synaptic function, neuroblast differentiation, and epithelial polarization. It is also known to act as a tumor suppressor. In rodents, Scrib has been associated with receptor recycling and planar polarity, but not with apical/basal polarity. Our study demonstrates that knocking down Scrib disrupts the adhesion between Madin-Darby canine kidney epithelial cells. As a result, these cells undergo changes in appearance, resembling mesenchymal cells, and exhibit increased migration with loss of directionality. Although the assembly of tight junctions is delayed, the polarized nature of confluent monolayers is maintained. These effects are not dependent on Rac activation or the binding of Scrib to βPIX. Instead, the depletion of Scrib interferes with E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion. The observed changes in cell morphology and migration are also observed when E-cadherin is knocked down. Partial restoration of adhesion is achieved by expressing a fusion protein of E-cadherin and α-catenin, but not by expressing E-cadherin fused with green fluorescent protein. These findings suggest that Scrib plays a role in stabilizing the interaction between E-cadherin and the catenins, and support the notion that Scrib may function as a tumor suppressor in mammals by regulating epithelial cell adhesion and migration.

title: Histone acetylation and DNA demethylation of T cells result in an anaplastic large cell lymphoma-like phenotype.
text: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma, despite originating from T-cells, exhibits a significant repression of the T-cell expression program. The reasons behind this down-regulation are still unknown. To investigate whether epigenetic mechanisms are responsible for the loss of the T-cell phenotype, we conducted experiments using epigenetic modifiers to induce DNA demethylation and histone acetylation in anaplastic large cell lymphoma and T-cell lymphoma/leukemia cell lines (n=4 each). We generated global gene expression data from treated and untreated cell lines, and analyzed differentially expressed genes using real-time reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis. Additionally, we examined histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation through chromatin immunoprecipitation. However, the combined treatment of DNA demethylation and histone acetylation in anaplastic large cell lymphoma cells was unable to restore their T-cell phenotype. Instead, this treatment led to an up-regulation of genes characteristic of anaplastic large cell lymphoma (e.g. ID2, LGALS1, c-JUN) in T-cells, and a near-complete loss of their T-cell phenotype, including CD3, LCK, and ZAP70. Furthermore, we observed suppressive trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 in anaplastic large cell lymphoma cells, specifically in important T-cell transcription factor genes (GATA3, LEF1, TCF1). This finding aligns with the absence of these genes in primary tumor specimens, as confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Our data suggest that epigenetically activated suppressors, such as ID2, contribute to the down-regulation of the T-cell expression program in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, which is maintained through histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation.

title: YEASTRACT: providing a programmatic access to curated transcriptional regulatory associations in Saccharomyces cerevisiae through a web services interface
text: The YEASTRACT information system (http://www.yeastract.com) was created to assist in the analysis of transcription regulatory associations in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The database, last updated in June 2010, contains over 48,200 regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes. It also includes 298 specific DNA-binding sites for 110 characterized TFs. All associations in the database have been reviewed and detailed information on the experimental evidence supporting these associations has been added. This evidence is classified as either direct or indirect. The addition of this new data, in response to user requests, allows users to narrow their queries based on the presence or absence of experimental evidence for the direct action of TFs in the promoter region of their target genes. Another new feature of this release is the availability of all data through a machine-readable web service interface. Users are no longer limited to the predefined queries provided by the web interface and can now use their own implementation of additional functionalities to query, retrieve, and utilize the YEASTRACT data. The YEASTRACT information system also offers several computational tools that facilitate the use of the curated data when addressing important biological questions. Since its initial release in 2006, YEASTRACT has been widely utilized by researchers worldwide. With the introduction of new data and services, we anticipate that the system will continue to be a valuable resource for yeast biologists and systems biology researchers.

title: Mechanisms that Specify Promoter Nucleosome Location and Identity
text: The typical structure of gene promoters in eukaryotes is characterized by a region without nucleosomes, known as a nucleosome-free region (NFR), which is surrounded by at least one H2A.Z variant nucleosome. Previous attempts to predict nucleosome positions based on the thermodynamic properties of DNA-histone interactions have had limited success. However, our research demonstrates that the RSC remodeling complex in S. cerevisiae plays a crucial role in explaining the discrepancy between theory and experiment. When RSC is depleted in cells, NFRs become smaller, causing the flanking nucleosomes to move closer to the predicted positions. Additionally, the positioning of nucleosomes at specific subsets of promoters requires the essential Myb family proteins Abf1 and Reb1, which have binding sites that are concentrated in NFRs. In contrast, the deposition of H2A.Z is not necessary for nucleosome positioning. Through the manipulation of H2A.Z deposition using a steroid-inducible protein splicing strategy, we demonstrate that the establishment of NFRs is essential for H2A.Z deposition. These findings suggest a sequential pathway for the assembly of chromatin architecture in gene promoters.

title: HIV seropositivity and tuberculosis in a large general hospital in Malawi.
text: Malawi has one of the highest rates of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) in Central Africa. To identify cases of the disease, patients admitted to the tuberculosis (TB) wards at Zomba General Hospital in Malawi were asked for consent to undergo testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies, as tuberculosis is often an initial sign of AIDS. Two additional studies were conducted: one involved testing all medically admitted patients suspected of having immune deficiency starting in September 1986, and the other involved testing all blood donors starting in April 1988 for HIV seropositivity. Of the TB patients, 75% agreed to be tested, and 32 out of 125 (26%) were found to be seropositive. In the high-risk age groups of 20-40 years, the percentage of seropositive cases increased to 32. Among the medically admitted patients suspected of immune deficiency, the rate of seropositivity sharply rose from April 1987 to October 1988. Among the blood donors tested, 20% were found to be seropositive.

title: Determinants of neonatal mortality in Indonesia
text:
BACKGROUND: Neonatal mortality is responsible for nearly 40% of deaths in children under the age of five worldwide. Understanding the factors that contribute to neonatal mortality is crucial for developing targeted and evidence-based health interventions to prevent these deaths. This study aimed to identify the determinants of neonatal mortality in Indonesia using a nationally representative sample of births from 1997 to 2002.

METHODS: The data for this analysis came from the 2002-2003 Indonesia Demographic and Health Survey, which provided survival information for 15,952 singleton live-born infants born between 1997 and 2002. Multilevel logistic regression was used to analyze the factors associated with neonatal deaths, taking into account community, socio-economic status, and proximate determinants.

RESULTS: At the community level, infants from East Java had significantly higher odds of neonatal death (OR = 5.01, p = 0.00), as did infants from North, Central, and Southeast Sulawesi and Gorontalo combined (OR = 3.17, p = 0.03), compared to the regions with the lowest neonatal mortality rates (Bali, South Sulawesi, and Jambi provinces). The odds of neonatal death decreased as the percentage of deliveries assisted by trained attendants increased. Infants born to employed parents had higher odds of neonatal death (OR = 1.84, p = 0.00), as did infants born to unemployed fathers (OR = 2.99, p = 0.02). Other factors associated with higher odds of neonatal death included higher rank infants with a short birth interval (OR = 2.82, p = 0.00), male infants (OR = 1.49, p = 0.01), smaller than average-sized infants (OR = 2.80, p = 0.00), and infants whose mothers had a history of delivery complications (OR = 1.81, p = 0.00). Infants who received postnatal care had significantly lower odds of neonatal death (OR = 0.63, p = 0.03).

CONCLUSION: Public health interventions aimed at reducing neonatal mortality in Indonesia should address factors at the community, household, and individual levels that have a significant impact on neonatal mortality. This includes addressing low birth weight and short birth interval infants, as well as improving perinatal health services such as skilled birth attendance and postnatal care utilization.

title: High density mapping of the MHC identifies a shared role for HLA-DRB1*01:03 in inflammatory bowel diseases and heterozygous advantage in ulcerative colitis
text: Genome-wide association studies have provided strong evidence linking the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) to Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic inflammatory bowel diseases. The MHC region contains numerous immunological candidates, including the classical human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules responsible for antigen presentation. Previous studies on IBD have identified multiple independent associations at both HLA and non-HLA genes, but lacked the statistical power to determine the exact nature of these associations and the causal alleles involved. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the MHC in over 32,000 individuals with IBD, using high-density SNP typing. Our findings revealed the involvement of multiple HLA alleles, with HLA-DRB1*01:03 playing a primary role in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Notably, we observed distinct differences between these diseases, with class II HLA variants playing a more prominent role and a heterozygous advantage observed specifically in ulcerative colitis. These findings suggest that the adaptive immune response in the colonic environment plays a crucial role in the development of IBD.

title: High-Threshold Mechanosensitive Ion Channels Blocked by a Novel Conopeptide Mediate Pressure-Evoked Pain
text: Our understanding of the molecular mechanisms behind somatosensory mechanotransduction in mammals is limited. To gain more insight, we conducted a study where we examined the effects of a library of peptide toxins on mechanically activated currents in cultured dorsal root ganglion neurons. Among the peptides tested, one called NMB-1 (noxious mechanosensation blocker 1) showed selective inhibition (IC50 1 µM) of sustained mechanically activated currents in a specific group of sensory neurons. Biotinylated NMB-1 maintained its activity and specifically bound to peripherin-positive nociceptive sensory neurons. Importantly, NMB-1 did not inhibit voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, acid-sensing ion channels, or TRPA1 channels, confirming its selectivity. In contrast, GsMTx-4, a tarantula toxin known to inhibit stretch-activated ion channels, had no effect on mechanically activated currents in sensory neurons. In behavioral tests, NMB-1 only inhibited responses to high intensity, painful mechanical stimulation, while having no impact on low intensity mechanical stimulation or thermosensation. Surprisingly, NMB-1 also acted as an inhibitor of rapid FM1-43 loading, a measure of mechanotransduction, in cochlear hair cells. These findings suggest that different channels respond to different types of mechanical stimuli and indicate that sustained mechanically activated currents are involved in noxious mechanosensation. NMB-1 therefore represents a valuable tool for identifying the molecular channels involved in hearing and pressure-induced pain.

title: Hyperactive Neuroendocrine Secretion Causes Size, Feeding, and Metabolic Defects of C. elegans Bardet-Biedl Syndrome Mutants
text: Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by various clinical symptoms such as extra fingers or toes (polydactyly), vision problems (retinopathy), excessive appetite (hyperphagia), obesity, short stature, cognitive impairment, and delays in development. BBS is caused by disruptions in BBS proteins, which affect the formation and function of cilia in different organisms. The multiple organ defects associated with BBS are believed to result from deficiencies in signaling pathways related to cilia. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, bbs genes are only expressed in the sixty ciliated sensory neurons, and mutants with bbs gene mutations display sensory issues, as well as abnormalities in body size, feeding, and metabolism. Our study reveals that unlike other mutants with cilia defects, C. elegans bbs mutants have increased release of dense-core vesicles and exhibit organism-wide abnormalities associated with heightened activities in insulin, neuropeptide, and biogenic amine signaling pathways. We demonstrate that the abnormal body size, feeding, and metabolic issues in bbs mutants can be restored to normal levels by reducing the excessive secretion of dense-core vesicles, without correcting the ciliary defects. These findings expand our understanding of the role of BBS proteins in regulating the release of dense-core vesicles and suggest that some aspects of Bardet-Biedl Syndrome may be caused by excessive secretion of neuroendocrine substances.

title: Fiji: an open-source platform for biological-image analysis
text: Fiji is a specialized version of the widely-used open-source software ImageJ, designed specifically for analyzing biological images. By incorporating modern software engineering techniques, Fiji seamlessly integrates robust software libraries with various scripting languages, allowing for quick experimentation with image-processing algorithms. Additionally, Fiji simplifies the process of converting novel algorithms into ImageJ plugins, which can then be easily shared with users through a built-in update system. We propose Fiji as an ideal platform for fostering productive collaboration between the computer science and biology research communities.

title: Pharmacologic characterization of a potent inhibitor of class I phosphatidylinositide 3-kinases.
text:
There is a wealth of evidence suggesting that the activation of the lipid phosphatidylinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway plays a significant role in the development and progression of various types of cancer in humans. As a result, inhibitors of PI3K have the potential to be highly effective in treating cancer at a molecular level. In this article, we provide a detailed analysis of the pharmacological properties of a prototype inhibitor belonging to a new series of class I PI3K inhibitors.

Known as PI103, this inhibitor has proven to be highly potent, with low IC50 values against several recombinant PI3K isoforms, including p110alpha (2 nmol/L), p110beta (3 nmol/L), p110delta (3 nmol/L), and p110gamma (15 nmol/L). Additionally, PI103 has demonstrated the ability to inhibit TORC1 by 83.9% at a concentration of 0.5 micromol/L and has exhibited an IC50 of 14 nmol/L against DNA-PK. Importantly, PI103 has shown a high degree of selectivity for the PI3K family, as it has not displayed any activity against a panel of 70 protein kinases.

In vitro studies have revealed that PI103 effectively inhibits the proliferation and invasion of various human cancer cells. Furthermore, it has been shown to modulate biomarkers in a manner consistent with the inhibition of PI3K signaling. Although PI103 is extensively metabolized, it rapidly distributes to tissues and tumors. This has resulted in a delay in tumor growth in eight different human cancer xenograft models, all of which exhibit abnormalities in the PI3K pathway. In U87MG gliomas, decreased phosphorylation of AKT was observed, indicating that the drug was able to reach therapeutic levels.

In addition to its anti-tumor effects, PI103 has also demonstrated the ability to inhibit invasion in orthotopic breast and ovarian cancer xenograft models. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that PI103 possesses antiangiogenic properties. Despite its rapid metabolism in vivo, PI103 remains a valuable tool compound for investigating the biological function of class I PI3K. Moreover, it serves as a promising starting point for the development of targeted molecular cancer therapeutics within this novel class.

title: Optimized CRISPR/Cas tools for efficient germline and somatic genome engineering in Drosophila.
text: We have developed a toolbox for efficient genome engineering in Drosophila melanogaster using the type II CRISPR/Cas system. This toolbox includes transgenic Cas9 lines and versatile guide RNA (gRNA) expression plasmids. Through systematic evaluation, we have identified Cas9 lines with different patterns of activity, either ubiquitous or restricted to the germ line. We have also found that the same gRNA expressed from different U6 snRNA promoters can have varying levels of activity, with the U6:3 promoter being the most effective. By combining the appropriate Cas9 line and gRNA, we can target both essential and nonessential genes with transmission rates ranging from 25-100%. Additionally, we have demonstrated that our optimized CRISPR/Cas tools can be used for mutagenesis through offset nicking. When combined with donor templates, such as oligonucleotides or long double-stranded DNA, our reagents enable precise genome editing through homology-directed repair, eliminating the need for selection markers. Furthermore, we have shown a novel application of CRISPR/Cas technology in revealing loss-of-function phenotypes in somatic cells by efficiently targeting both alleles using Cas9 expressed in a ubiquitous or tissue-restricted manner. Our CRISPR/Cas tools will greatly facilitate the evaluation of mutant phenotypes and precise genome modifications with single-nucleotide precision. Additionally, our results open up possibilities for high-throughput genetic screening using CRISPR/Cas.

title: Cost-effectiveness of 10-Year Risk Thresholds for Initiation of Statin Therapy for Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease.
text: The cholesterol treatment guidelines set by the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association have significant implications for the use of statins in adults without a history of cardiovascular disease. The objective of this study was to assess the cost-effectiveness of different 10-year cardiovascular disease risk thresholds that could be incorporated into these guidelines. The study utilized a microsimulation model with a lifetime time horizon, taking into account costs and health outcomes from a societal perspective in the United States. The model considered hypothetical individuals aged 40 to 75 who received statin treatment, experienced cardiovascular events, and died from cardiovascular or non-cardiovascular causes based on natural history and treatment parameters. Data sources included surveys, clinical trials, and meta-analyses. The main outcomes measured were the number of cardiovascular events prevented and the incremental costs per quality-adjusted life-year gained. The results showed that the current risk threshold of 7.5% or higher, which led to 48% of adults being treated with statins, had an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $37,000 per quality-adjusted life-year compared to a threshold of 10% or higher. More lenient thresholds of 4.0% or higher (61% of adults treated) and 3.0% or higher (67% of adults treated) had incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of $81,000 and $140,000 per quality-adjusted life-year, respectively. Lowering the risk threshold to 3.0% or higher was estimated to prevent an additional 161,560 cardiovascular events. The cost-effectiveness results were sensitive to factors such as the disutility associated with daily pill-taking, statin price, and the risk of statin-induced diabetes. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated that there was a greater than 93% chance that the optimal risk threshold was 5.0% or lower, using a cost-effectiveness threshold of $100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. In conclusion, this study suggests that the current risk threshold used in the cholesterol treatment guidelines is cost-effective, but more lenient thresholds would be optimal based on cost-effectiveness thresholds. The optimal risk threshold is influenced by patient preferences, changes in statin price, and the risk of statin-induced diabetes.

title: Biochemical Properties of Highly Neuroinvasive Prion Strains
text: Prion diseases are caused by infectious prions that enter the central nervous system (CNS) and lead to progressive neurodegeneration and death. However, the way prion diseases develop can vary greatly depending on the strain or variant of the abnormal protein, PrP(Sc), that is folded and aggregated. While most prion strains invade the CNS and cause disease symptoms, there are some strains that cannot enter and therefore do not cause clinical signs. The reason for this variation in pathogenesis among strains is not clear. In this study, we used mouse-adapted prion strains to investigate this variation. We found that highly neuroinvasive prion strains primarily form diffuse aggregates in the brain, are not easily stained with Congo red dye, are structurally unstable under denaturing conditions, and lead to rapid death. These neuroinvasive strains also efficiently generate PrP(Sc) in a short period of time. On the other hand, weakly neuroinvasive prion strains form large fibrillary plaques, are stable, stain with Congo red dye, and inefficiently generate PrP(Sc) over a longer period of time. Overall, our findings suggest that the most neuroinvasive prion strains are also the least stable, and support the idea that the efficient replication and unstable nature of rapidly converting prions may be linked to their ability to spread into the CNS.

title: The twin-arginine translocation (Tat) protein export pathway
text: The Tat protein export system, found in the cytoplasmic membranes of most bacteria and archaea, possesses a unique ability to transport fully folded proteins. This system must create a pathway across the membrane that is spacious enough to accommodate structured macromolecular substrates of varying sizes, while still maintaining the membrane's impermeability to ions. In Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative bacterium, this complex task is accomplished using just three small membrane proteins: TatA, TatB, and TatC. In this article, we provide an overview of the latest developments in our comprehension of the functioning of this extraordinary machinery.

title: New developments in the ATSAS program package for small-angle scattering data analysis
text:
This article discusses the latest advancements in the ATSAS program package (version 2.4) for processing and analyzing isotropic small-angle X-ray and neutron scattering data. The updates include several key features: 

(i) The introduction of multiplatform data manipulation and display tools, allowing for easier accessibility and compatibility across different operating systems. 

(ii) The addition of automated data processing programs that can calculate overall parameters, streamlining the analysis process. 

(iii) Improved utilization of high- and low-resolution models from other structural methods, enhancing the accuracy and reliability of the results. 

(iv) New algorithms that enable the construction of three-dimensional models from weakly interacting oligomeric systems and complexes, expanding the capabilities of the program. 

(v) Enhanced tools for analyzing data from mixtures and flexible systems, providing more comprehensive insights into complex samples. 

The updated ATSAS release also includes installers for major platforms such as Windows, Linux, and Mac OSX, making it easier for users to install and utilize the program. Additionally, the release offers improved indexed user documentation to assist users in navigating the program effectively. 

Furthermore, the article highlights web-related developments, including the introduction of a user discussion forum and expanded online access to run ATSAS programs. These developments aim to foster collaboration and provide users with a more interactive and accessible experience.

title: The First Myriapod Genome Sequence Reveals Conservative Arthropod Gene Content and Genome Organisation in the Centipede Strigamia maritima
text: Myriapods, such as centipedes and millipedes, have a relatively simple body plan compared to other arthropods. All members of this class are terrestrial, but they evolved to live on land independently from insects. Interestingly, Myriapoda is the only arthropod class that has not had its genome sequenced. In this study, we analyze the genome of the centipede Strigamia maritima. We find that its genome is compact and has experienced less gene loss and rearrangement compared to other sequenced arthropods. We also discover many genes that are conserved from the common ancestor of bilaterians but have been lost in insects. Our analysis reveals that many genes in S. maritima are located in similar positions as in other organisms, and we observe several instances of gene clustering on a smaller scale. We describe several cases where S. maritima has evolved different solutions to similar problems compared to insects. For example, S. maritima lacks the insect olfactory receptor gene family and likely relies on other receptor gene families for olfaction in air. Additionally, we find that S. maritima has evolved paralogues for certain genes to generate coding sequence diversity, whereas insects use alternate splicing. One notable example is the Dscam gene, which produces over 100,000 alternate splice forms in Drosophila but is encoded by over 100 paralogues in S. maritima. We also observe an interesting connection between the absence of known photosensory proteins in a blind organism and the lack of canonical circadian clock genes. By studying the phylogenetic position of myriapods, we can determine when specific molecular mechanisms and traits emerged in arthropods. For instance, we conclude that juvenile hormone signaling evolved with the development of the exoskeleton in arthropods and that cuticle proteins containing RR-1 evolved in the lineage leading to Mandibulata. We also identify the timing of various gene expansions and losses. The genome of S. maritima provides us with a unique insight into the ancestral arthropod genome while also revealing numerous adaptations to its specific life history.

title: Genetic and Functional Diversification of Small RNA Pathways in Plants
text: Small RNA molecules, measuring approximately 21-24 nucleotides, are produced by multicellular eukaryotes. These small RNAs, known as microRNA (miRNA) and short interfering RNA (siRNA), play a collective role in silencing or regulating genes, transposons, viruses, and modifying chromatin and genome structure. The production and function of these small RNAs rely on specific factors encoded by gene families, including DICER (or DICER-LIKE [DCL]) and ARGONAUTE proteins, as well as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDR) proteins in the case of certain siRNAs. Unlike animals, plants possess multiple DCL and RDR proteins. Through the use of insertion mutants in Arabidopsis thaliana, the unique functions of three DCL proteins (DCL1, DCL3, and DCL2) in the biogenesis of miRNA, endogenous siRNA, and viral siRNA were identified. Additionally, one RDR protein (RDR2) was found to be essential for the production of all endogenous siRNAs examined. The absence of endogenous siRNA in dcl3 and rdr2 mutants resulted in the loss of heterochromatic marks and increased transcript accumulation at certain loci. Furthermore, defects in siRNA generation in response to turnip crinkle virus in dcl2 mutant plants were associated with heightened susceptibility to the virus. In conclusion, the proliferation and diversification of DCL and RDR genes during plant evolution have contributed to the specialization of small RNA-directed pathways involved in development, chromatin structure, and defense.

title: Immunosuppressant FTY720 inhibits thymocyte emigration.
text: The thymus plays a crucial role in supplying mature T cells to the peripheral immune system, but the exact mechanisms involved in cellular export are not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the potential of a new immunosuppressive agent called FTY720 to hinder T cell export from the thymus. When FTY720 was administered daily at a dose of 1 mg/kg, there was a significant reduction in the number of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood. In the thymus, long-term daily administration of FTY720 led to a three- to fourfold increase in the proportion of mature medullary thymocytes (CD4(+)CD8(-) and CD4(-)CD8(+)), along with a slight decrease in the ratio of double-positive cells (CD4(+)CD8(+)). Analysis of their phenotype (TCRalpha beta, H-2K(d), CD44, CD69, and CD24) indicated that these increased subsets could potentially represent recent thymic emigrants in the periphery. The fact that these subsets expressed high levels of L-selectin further suggested that they were being prevented from leaving the thymus. By labeling cells with fluorescein isothiocyanate within the thymus, we found that only a quarter of the labeled cells could be detected in the lymph nodes and spleen of mice treated with FTY720, compared to control mice treated with saline. Overall, these findings suggest that the immunosuppressive effects of FTY720 may, at least in part, be attributed to its ability to inhibit T cell migration from the thymus to the periphery.

title: Validating a conceptual model for an inter-professional approach to shared decision making: a mixed methods study
text:
RATIONALE, AIMS, AND OBJECTIVES

In response to growing interest in involving inter-professional (IP) healthcare teams in patient decision-making, we have developed a conceptual model for an IP approach to shared decision making (SDM) in primary care. To validate this model, we conducted interviews with stakeholders in Canada. 

METHODS

We conducted 15 individual interviews and 7 group interviews, involving a total of 79 stakeholders. During these interviews, we asked stakeholders to: (1) suggest changes to the IP-SDM model; (2) identify barriers and facilitators to implementing the model in clinical practice; and (3) assess the model using a theory appraisal questionnaire. We analyzed the interview transcripts thematically and performed a descriptive analysis of the questionnaires. 

RESULTS

Stakeholders provided valuable feedback, suggesting improvements to the model. They recommended placing the patient at the center, expanding the definition of family to include significant others, clarifying outcomes, emphasizing the concept of time, consolidating the micro, meso, and macro levels into one figure, and acknowledging the influence of the environment and emotions. The most commonly identified barriers were time constraints, limited resources, and power imbalances among healthcare professionals. The most commonly identified facilitators were education and training in inter-professionalism and SDM, motivation to adopt an IP approach to SDM, and mutual understanding of disciplinary roles. Overall, stakeholders found the model to be clear, logical, testable, and relevant to inter-professional collaboration, SDM, and primary care. 

CONCLUSIONS

Stakeholders validated the new IP-SDM model for primary care settings and proposed minimal modifications. Future research should investigate whether the model effectively supports the implementation of SDM in IP clinical practice.

title: Glutaminolysis activates Rag-mTORC1 signaling.
text: The highly conserved kinase TORC1 is responsible for controlling cell growth, and amino acids play a crucial role in activating it. Among these amino acids, glutamine is particularly important for regulating cell growth and metabolism. However, the exact mechanism by which glutamine activates TORC1 is not well understood. Glutamine is metabolized through a process called glutaminolysis, which produces a compound called α-ketoglutarate. Our research demonstrates that when glutamine is combined with leucine, it enhances glutaminolysis and increases α-ketoglutarate production, thereby activating mammalian TORC1 (mTORC1). We found that inhibiting glutaminolysis prevents the loading of GTP onto RagB and the subsequent translocation of lysosomes, which are necessary for mTORC1 activation. On the other hand, when a constitutively active Rag heterodimer is present, mTORC1 can be activated even in the absence of glutaminolysis. Additionally, increasing glutaminolysis or using a cell-permeable analog of α-ketoglutarate stimulates lysosomal translocation and mTORC1 activation. Finally, we observed that glutaminolysis regulates cell growth and autophagy, two processes that are controlled by mTORC1. In conclusion, our findings suggest that mTORC1 senses and is activated by glutamine and leucine through the process of glutaminolysis and α-ketoglutarate production, which occurs upstream of Rag. This may help explain why cancer cells have a dependency on glutamine.

title: microRNA-31/factor-inhibiting hypoxia-inducible factor 1 nexus regulates keratinocyte differentiation.
text: The role of Notch in the transition from cell proliferation to cell differentiation in the epidermis and corneal epithelium is crucial. Abnormal Notch signaling is observed in diseases such as psoriasis, eczema, nonmelanoma skin cancer, and melanoma, which are characterized by impaired differentiation and proliferation. While the downstream events of Notch signaling are well understood, the factors responsible for regulating Notch receptor signaling after ligand activation are not fully known. One factor that can affect Notch is hydroxylation by factor-inhibiting hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (FIH-1), but the significance of this process is unclear. In this study, we found that FIH-1 expression is increased in diseased epidermis and corneal epithelium. Elevating FIH-1 levels in primary human epidermal keratinocytes (HEKs) and human corneal epithelial keratinocytes (HCEKs) impairs differentiation in both submerged cultures and a three-dimensional organotypic raft model of human epidermis. This impairment is partly due to a decrease in Notch signaling. On the other hand, reducing FIH-1 levels enhances keratinocyte differentiation. In vivo experiments showed that loss of FIH-1 increases Notch activity in the limbal epithelium, leading to a more differentiated phenotype. We also discovered that microRNA-31 (miR-31) is a natural inhibitor of FIH-1 expression, promoting keratinocyte differentiation through Notch activation. Introducing miR-31 into an undifferentiated corneal epithelial cell line promotes differentiation and mimics the characteristics of corneal epithelium in a three-dimensional raft culture model. Our findings reveal a previously unknown mechanism for determining the fate of keratinocytes, where the potential for Notch signaling is partly controlled by the miR-31/FIH-1 interaction.

title: Advantages of larval control for African malaria vectors: Low mobility and behavioural responsiveness of immature mosquito stages allow high effective coverage
text: The MacDonald-Ross model has been widely discussed as a means to reduce malaria transmission by targeting adult female mosquitoes with insecticides. However, these discussions have overlooked a crucial biological difference between adult mosquitoes and their immature stages. Adults have the ability to fly and avoid intervention measures, while mosquito eggs, larvae, and pupae are confined to small aquatic habitats and cannot easily escape control measures. Our hypothesis is that the control of adult mosquitoes is hindered by their ability to avoid interventions like insecticides. We have developed a simple model to demonstrate that this avoidance can significantly reduce the effectiveness of coverage and overall impact on malaria transmission. We have also examined historical evidence that shows larval control of African malaria vectors can be effective. We conclude that the limitations to effective larval control are practical rather than fundamental. Therefore, we propose that larval control strategies should be prioritized for further development, evaluation, and implementation as an integral part of Rolling Back Malaria, in addition to adult control interventions.

title: The Arabidopsis Chromatin-Modifying Nuclear siRNA Pathway Involves a Nucleolar RNA Processing Center
text: In Arabidopsis thaliana, a plant species, a pathway involving various proteins is responsible for directing cytosine methylation at endogenous DNA repeats using small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). This pathway includes two forms of nuclear RNA polymerase IV (Pol IVa and Pol IVb), RNA-DEPENDENT RNA POLYMERASE 2 (RDR2), DICER-LIKE 3 (DCL3), ARGONAUTE4 (AGO4), the chromatin remodeler DRD1, and the de novo cytosine methyltransferase DRM2. Our research demonstrates that RDR2, DCL3, AGO4, and NRPD1b (the largest subunit of Pol IVb) are found together with siRNAs in the nucleolus, while Pol IVa and DRD1 are located outside the nucleolus and are associated with endogenous repeat loci. When mutations occur in the pathway proteins, downstream proteins are mislocalized, providing insight into the order of their actions. Pol IVa is the first to act, and its localization is dependent on RNA, suggesting the presence of an RNA template. We propose that maintaining the heterochromatic state involves specific transcription by Pol IVa at certain loci, followed by siRNA production and the formation of silencing complexes containing AGO4 and NRPD1b within nucleolar processing centers.

title: Peripheral arterial disease in the elderly: The Rotterdam Study.
text: In order to determine the prevalence of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and intermittent claudication (IC) in an elderly population, we conducted a study involving 7715 individuals aged 55 years and above. The study consisted of 40% men and 60% women. We used the ankle-arm systolic blood pressure index (AAI) to identify the presence of PAD, and the World Health Organization/Rose questionnaire to identify IC. PAD was considered present if the AAI was less than 0.90 in either leg. The overall prevalence of PAD was found to be 19.1% (with a 95% confidence interval of 18.1% to 20.0%). The prevalence was 16.9% in men and 20.5% in women. IC symptoms were reported by 1.6% of the study population (with a 95% confidence interval of 1.3% to 1.9%). Among men, the prevalence of IC was 2.2%, while among women it was 1.2%. Among those with PAD, 6.3% reported symptoms of IC (8.7% in men and 4.9% in women). Additionally, an AAI below 0.90 was found in 68.9% of those with IC. Individuals with an AAI below 0.90 were more likely to be smokers, have hypertension, and have symptomatic or asymptomatic cardiovascular disease compared to those with an AAI of 0.90 or higher. In conclusion, the prevalence of PAD is high in the elderly population, while the prevalence of IC is relatively low. However, both prevalences increase significantly with age. The majority of PAD patients do not experience symptoms of IC.

title: Antioxidants attenuate the plasma cytokine response to exercise in humans.
text:
The effects of exercise on plasma levels of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 are well-known, but the specific factors that trigger the release of TNF-alpha and IL-1beta are not fully understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of oxidative stress and the potential involvement of monocytes in the production of these cytokines, particularly IL-1beta, in individuals who were previously untrained. 

Six healthy individuals who were not athletes participated in two 45-minute bicycle exercise sessions, performed at 70% of their maximum oxygen consumption (Vo(2 max)), before and after a 60-day regimen of antioxidants (vitamins E, A, and C), allopurinol for 15 days, and N-acetylcysteine for 3 days. Blood samples were collected at baseline, immediately after exercise, and 30 and 120 minutes post-exercise. Plasma cytokine levels were measured using ELISA, and the levels of intracellular cytokines in monocytes were assessed using flow cytometry. 

Prior to antioxidant treatment, exercise led to a 60% increase in TNF-alpha levels, a threefold increase in IL-1beta levels, and a sixfold increase in IL-6 levels (P < 0.05). After antioxidant treatment, IL-1beta was no longer detectable in the plasma, the TNF-alpha response to exercise was completely abolished, and the IL-6 response was significantly reduced (P < 0.05). The percentage of monocytes producing these cytokines and their mean fluorescence intensity did not increase with exercise. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that oxidative stress is a major factor in the production of exercise-induced cytokines in untrained individuals, and monocytes do not play a role in this process.

title: Relation between colonic proglucagon expression and metabolic response to oligofructose in high fat diet-fed mice.
text: There is evidence suggesting that fermentable dietary fiber may have a role in controlling obesity and related metabolic disorders. This study aimed to investigate the potential role of a non-digestible oligosaccharide called short chain fructo-oligosaccharide (OFS) in mice fed a standard diet and mice fed two different high-fat diets that induce metabolic disorders associated with obesity. In mice, we observed similar effects to those previously seen in rats fed a standard diet enriched with OFS, including an increase in caecum weight, a decrease in epididymal fat mass, and an increase in glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) levels in the colon and portal plasma. This increase in GLP-1 was positively correlated with higher levels of colonic proglucagon mRNA. Interestingly, when OFS was added at the same dose to the two different high-fat diets, it had different effects. Only when added to the high-fat, carbohydrate-free diet did OFS decrease energy intake, body weight gain, glycemia, and epididymal fat mass. In this diet, OFS also promoted colonic proglucagon expression and insulin secretion. Our findings suggest a link between increased proglucagon expression in the proximal colon and the effects of OFS on glycemia, fat mass development, and body weight gain. In conclusion, dietary oligosaccharides could be a promising type of dietary fiber that promotes endogenous GLP-1 production under certain conditions, leading to beneficial physiological effects. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings in human studies.

title: Aurora B phosphorylates spatially distinct targets to differentially regulate the kinetochore-microtubule interface.
text: The precise separation of chromosomes relies on carefully regulated interactions between kinetochores and microtubules. However, it is still unclear how flexibility is achieved to correct various attachment defects. In this study, we demonstrate that Aurora B kinase phosphorylates three distinct targets within the conserved outer kinetochore KNL1/Mis12 complex/Ndc80 complex (KMN) network, which is crucial for kinetochore-microtubule attachments. The combination of phosphorylation events in the KMN network produces different levels of microtubule-binding activity, with complete phosphorylation significantly impairing microtubule binding. Modifying the phosphorylation status of each protein leads to corresponding defects in chromosome segregation. Importantly, the spatial arrangement of these targets along the kinetochore axis results in their differential phosphorylation in response to changes in tension and attachment status. Instead of solely inducing binary changes in microtubule binding, our findings propose a mechanism for the tension-dependent fine-tuning of kinetochore-microtubule interactions.

title: Prognostic importance of 6-mercaptopurine dose intensity in acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text:
The combination of 6-Mercaptopurine (6MP) and methotrexate is widely used in the treatment of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Previous studies have shown that higher levels of certain metabolites of these drugs in the blood, specifically methotrexate polyglutamates (MTXPGs) and thioguanine nucleotides (TGNs), are associated with better outcomes. In this study, we aimed to determine if these metabolites, as well as the dose intensity of methotrexate and 6MP, could predict prognosis in a treatment protocol where all care was coordinated through a single center and methotrexate was administered parenterally on a weekly basis.

A total of 182 children who achieved remission were included in the study. They received weekly parenteral methotrexate at a dose of 40 mg/m2 and daily oral 6MP, with interruptions every 6 weeks for pulse chemotherapy during the first year. We analyzed 709 TGN, 418 MTX-PG, and 267 thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) measurements, as well as complete information on dose intensity for a total of 19,046 weeks of 6MP and methotrexate treatment.

In our univariate analyses, we found that higher dose intensity of 6MP and weekly methotrexate were significant predictors of overall event-free survival (EFS). The occurrence of neutropenia was associated with worse outcomes. In our multivariate analysis, only higher dose intensity of 6MP was a significant predictor of EFS, with lower TPMT activity tending to associate with better outcomes. Among patients with a homozygous wild-type TPMT phenotype, 6MP dose intensity was also associated with EFS. Lower 6MP dose intensity was primarily due to missed weeks of therapy rather than reductions in daily dose.

In conclusion, increasing the dose intensity of oral 6MP is an important factor in determining EFS in childhood ALL, particularly in patients with a homozygous wild-type TPMT phenotype. However, it is important to balance the intensity of therapy with the occurrence of neutropenia, as excessive intensity may hinder chemotherapy administration and have a negative impact on outcomes.

title: Orai1 and STIM1 are critical for breast tumor cell migration and metastasis.
text: The primary cause of death for cancer patients is tumor metastasis. By understanding the molecular mechanisms behind tumor metastasis, we can identify potential targets for drug treatment. In this study, we found that Orai1 and STIM1, both involved in store-operated calcium entry, are crucial for the migration of breast tumor cells in vitro and the spread of tumors in mice. When we reduced the levels of Orai1 or STIM1 using RNA interference in highly metastatic human breast cancer cells, or treated them with a drug that inhibits store-operated calcium channels, we observed a decrease in tumor metastasis in animal models. These findings highlight the importance of Orai1 and STIM1 in tumor metastasis and suggest that targeting store-operated calcium entry channels could be a potential therapeutic approach for cancer.

title: Mouse Spermatogenic Stem Cells Continually Interconvert between Equipotent Singly Isolated and Syncytial States
text: For a long time, researchers have been interested in understanding the characteristics and behavior of mouse spermatogenic stem cells. The prevailing belief is that stem cell function is limited to individual spermatogonia known as "As" cells. However, we propose an alternative hypothesis that syncytial spermatogonia, which are formed through fragmentation, also play a role in stem cell function during homeostasis. To test this hypothesis, we conducted live imaging and pulse labeling experiments to track the fate of GFRα1+ stem cells. Our findings reveal that, during normal spermatogenesis, the entire population of GFRα1+ cells forms a single stem cell pool, with cells constantly transitioning between As and syncytial states. By developing a simple biophysical model based on the rates of incomplete cell division and syncytial fragmentation, we accurately predict the stochastic outcomes of GFRα1+ cells during both steady-state spermatogenesis and post-insult regeneration. Therefore, our results present a dynamic and alternative model for understanding the function of spermatogenic stem cells in the mouse testis.

title: Pseudoknots: RNA Structures with Diverse Functions
text: RNA molecules have a wide range of biological functions in cells, including transferring genetic information and catalyzing reactions. These molecules, made up of uracil, guanine, cytosine, and adenine, can form complex three-dimensional structures. Similar to proteins, RNA molecules often adopt specific structural motifs, with one of the most common being the pseudoknot. Pseudoknots consist of two helical segments connected by single-stranded regions or loops. The H-type pseudoknot is the most well-studied, where bases in the loop of a hairpin form pairs with bases outside of the stem. This creates a second stem and loop, resulting in a pseudoknot with two stems and two loops. The loops often interact with the adjacent stems, forming hydrogen bonds and contributing to the overall structure. Pseudoknots can have varying lengths and types of interactions, making them structurally diverse. They have important roles in biology, such as serving as the catalytic core of ribozymes, self-splicing introns, and telomerase. Pseudoknots also play a critical role in altering gene expression by inducing ribosomal frameshifting in viruses.

title: An essential role for interferon gamma in resistance to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
text: Tuberculosis, a significant health issue in developing nations, has resurfaced in recent times in numerous industrialized countries. Research suggests that individuals with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to tuberculosis, and various experiments have shown that T cell-mediated immunity plays a crucial role in resistance. The lymphokine interferon gamma (IFN-gamma) is believed to be a primary agent in activating macrophages and providing resistance against intracellular pathogens. Scientists have created mice that are unable to produce IFN-gamma (referred to as gko mice) due to a deliberate disruption of the IFN-gamma gene. When infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, these gko mice develop granulomas but fail to generate reactive nitrogen intermediates, thus being unable to control the growth of the bacteria. In contrast to normal mice, gko mice experience increased tissue necrosis and succumb rapidly to tuberculosis, which can only be delayed, not prevented, by treatment with externally supplied recombinant IFN-gamma.

title: Malignancies, prothrombotic mutations, and the risk of venous thrombosis.
text: The aim of this study was to identify individuals with cancer who are at a higher risk of developing venous thrombosis. The study involved 3220 patients with a first deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, as well as 2131 control participants. The participants were evaluated for different tumor sites, the presence of distant metastases, and carrier status of prothrombotic mutations. The results showed that the overall risk of venous thrombosis was 7 times higher in patients with cancer compared to those without cancer. Hematological malignancies had the highest risk, followed by lung and gastrointestinal cancer. The risk was highest in the first few months after the cancer diagnosis. Patients with distant metastases had a higher risk compared to those without distant metastases. Carriers of the factor V Leiden and prothrombin 20210A mutations had an even higher risk. In conclusion, patients with cancer, especially in the presence of distant metastases and carriers of prothrombotic mutations, have a significantly increased risk of venous thrombosis.

title: The Hippo signaling pathway restricts the oncogenic potential of an intestinal regeneration program.
text: While the developmental role of Hippo signaling in controlling organ size is well understood, its function in tissue regeneration remains largely unknown. In this study, we investigate this issue using a model of colonic regeneration induced by dextran sodium sulfate (DSS). Our findings reveal that regenerating crypts exhibit increased levels of Yes-associated protein (YAP). When YAP is deactivated, no apparent intestinal defects are observed during normal homeostasis, but DSS-induced intestinal regeneration is severely impaired. Conversely, when YAP is hyperactivated, it leads to the early formation of polyps following DSS treatment. Therefore, precise control of the YAP oncoprotein is crucial in tissue regeneration to facilitate compensatory proliferation and prevent the inherent oncogenic potential of a tissue regeneration program.

title: The essence of SNPs.
text: SNPs, or single nucleotide polymorphisms, are a common type of genetic variation in the genome. They are different from rare variations because the least common allele must have a frequency of at least 1%. The study and use of SNPs have the potential to greatly benefit various fields in genetics. The recent increase in interest in SNPs is due to the convergence and advancement of several research areas, including large-scale genome analysis, bioinformatics and computing, genetic analysis of diseases, and global human population genetics. These fields will be propelled into new territories by ongoing efforts to discover hundreds of thousands of human SNPs in the coming years. This SNP revolution raises important questions about the most effective ways to fully utilize its potential, both experimentally and ethically.

title: Combination inhibition of PI3K and mTORC1 yields durable remissions in orthotopic patient-derived xenografts of HER2-positive breast cancer brain metastases
text: The treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer is greatly challenged by brain metastases. Our study focuses on the development of patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) that mimic HER2-expressing breast cancer brain metastases (BCBM). These PDXs were utilized to identify targeted combination therapies. By inhibiting both PI3K and mTOR, we observed significant tumor regressions in three out of five PDXs. The effectiveness of the treatment was associated with a decrease in the phosphorylation of 4EBP1, an mTORC1 effector. Interestingly, the two PDXs that did not respond to the treatment exhibited hypermutated genomes with a high number of mutations in DNA-repair genes. This suggests that genomic instability may contribute to therapeutic resistance. Based on these findings, we propose conducting a biomarker-driven clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy of a PI3K inhibitor in combination with an mTOR inhibitor for patients with HER2-positive BCBM.

title: Activation of Frontal Neocortical Areas by Vocal Production in Marmosets
text: Primates often rely on vocal communication to facilitate social interactions. While we have a good understanding of the acoustic structure of primate vocalizations and the social context in which they are typically used, our knowledge about the neocortical control of audio-vocal interactions in primates is still limited. Most of our understanding comes from studies on squirrel monkeys and macaques that have suffered brain damage. To investigate the neocortical areas involved in vocal control in a New World primate species, the common marmoset, we used a method that has been successful in other vertebrate species: analyzing the expression of a specific gene called Egr-1 in freely behaving animals. We compared the distribution of Egr-1 cells in the neocortex of three marmosets that were exposed to the playback of vocalizations from their own species and vocalized spontaneously (H/V group) with data from three other marmosets that also heard the playback but did not vocalize (H/n group). We found that the anterior cingulate cortex, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex had a higher number of Egr-1 cells in the H/V group compared to the H/n group. This suggests that the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, which is equivalent to Broca's area in humans and is involved in processing species-specific vocalizations and controlling facial movements in macaques, is active during vocal output in marmosets. Overall, our findings support the idea that the network of neocortical areas involved in vocal communication in marmosets is similar to that of Old World primates. We discuss the role of these areas in vocal production and their significance for the evolution of speech in primates.

title: Familial hiatal hernia in a large five generation family confirming true autosomal dominant inheritance.
text:
BACKGROUND
Familial hiatal hernia is a rare occurrence that has been sparsely documented. 

AIMS
The aim of this study is to describe the inheritance pattern of familial hiatal hernia within a specific family.

SUBJECTS
A total of thirty-eight members from a family pedigree spanning five generations were included in this study.

METHODS
All family members were interviewed and underwent investigation using a barium meal to detect any evidence of a hiatal hernia.

RESULTS
Out of the thirty-eight family members, twenty-three were found to have radiological evidence of a hiatal hernia. Interestingly, none of the individuals with a hiatal hernia were born to unaffected parents. Additionally, one case demonstrated direct male to male transmission.

CONCLUSIONS
This study confirms that familial inheritance of hiatal hernia does occur. The presence of direct male to male transmission suggests an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

title: An Excitatory Loop with Astrocytes Contributes to Drive Neurons to Seizure Threshold
text: The occurrence of seizures in focal epilepsies is due to a synchronized discharge of neurons that originates in specific areas of the brain and then spreads to larger regions. Despite extensive research, the exact cellular events that trigger and maintain focal seizures are still not well understood. Identifying these events is crucial for understanding the underlying mechanisms of focal epilepsies and developing new treatments for drug-resistant forms of epilepsy. Recently, there has been a suggestion that astrocytes play a significant role in the initiation of seizures. In this study, we investigated whether there is a collaboration between astrocytes and neurons that is necessary to support seizure-like events. We conducted simultaneous patch-clamp recordings and Ca2+ imaging in a new in vitro model of focal seizures induced by N-methyl-D-aspartic acid (NMDA) in rat entorhinal cortex slices. Our findings showed that an increase in Ca2+ levels in astrocytes is associated with both the initial development and the maintenance of a focal seizure-like discharge. We also observed delayed activation of astrocytes during seizure activity in other models, where the exact site of seizure generation cannot be precisely monitored. However, interictal discharges were not accompanied by changes in astrocyte Ca2+ levels. Inhibiting or stimulating astrocyte Ca2+ signaling selectively affected the occurrence of seizure-like discharges, but had no impact on interictal discharge generation. These results indicate that neurons and astrocytes engage in a recurrent excitatory loop, possibly involving gliotransmission, that promotes the initiation and sustenance of seizures. Targeting this interaction between neurons and astrocytes could be a promising approach for developing effective therapeutic strategies to control seizures.

title: Diminished performance on neuropsychological testing in late life depression is correlated with microstructural white matter abnormalities.
text:
BACKGROUND
In late life depression (LLD), traditional T2 weighted MR imaging results are not specific enough to determine the extent of underlying white matter structural abnormalities. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) offers a unique opportunity to investigate structural injury, but previous studies have only examined a subset of regions of interest (ROI) and have been limited by confounding factors common in elderly populations, such as comorbid vascular pathology. Additionally, the comprehensive correlation of DTI measurements, including axial and radial diffusivity measurements, has not been demonstrated in the LLD population.

METHODS
A total of 51 depressed and 16 non-depressed elderly subjects, matched for age and cerebrovascular risk factors, underwent traditional anatomic T1 and T2 weight imaging, as well as DTI. The DTI data were analyzed using tract based spatial statistics (TBSS), and both regional and global analyses were conducted.

RESULTS
The LLD group showed widespread structural abnormalities within white matter, even after accounting for age, gender, education, and global T2 white matter hyperintensities (T2WMH). Regional differences were most prominent in uncinate and cingulate white matter, and were characterized by an increase in radial diffusivity. Age-related changes, particularly in the cingulate bundle, were more advanced in individuals with LLD compared to controls. Regression analysis revealed significant correlations between regional fractional anisotropy and radial diffusivity with five different neuropsychological factor scores. TBSS analysis demonstrated a greater extent of white matter abnormalities in LLD patients who did not respond to treatment, compared to controls.

CONCLUSIONS
Late life depression compromises white matter integrity, primarily through increased radial diffusivity in specific regions, indicating underlying myelin injury. Chronic white matter ischemia related to intrinsic cerebrovascular disease may be a possible mechanism for this myelin injury. In certain regions, such as the cingulate bundle, white matter injury related to late life depression appears to be independent of and compounded by age-related changes. The correlations with neuropsychological testing highlight the impact of white matter injury on functional status. Lastly, the extent of white matter injury may influence response to treatment, emphasizing the importance of intact functional networks.

title: The atypical antipsychotic olanzapine causes weight gain by targeting serotonin receptor 2C.
text: The metabolic effects of atypical antipsychotics like olanzapine, such as excessive weight gain and type 2 diabetes, are not well understood.
