To investigate this, we conducted an experiment using female C57BL/6 mice to mimic olanzapine-induced hyperphagia and obesity. Our findings revealed that olanzapine treatment led to increased food intake, impaired glucose tolerance, and changes in physical activity and energy expenditure in the mice. Interestingly, mice lacking the serotonin 2C receptor (HTR2C) showed reduced hyperphagia and weight gain when treated with olanzapine. Additionally, we discovered that treatment with a specific agonist for HTR2C, called lorcaserin, suppressed olanzapine-induced hyperphagia and weight gain. Furthermore, lorcaserin treatment improved glucose tolerance in mice fed with olanzapine. Overall, our research suggests that olanzapine's negative metabolic effects may be due to its interference with HTR2C.

title: Case-control study of endogenous steroid hormones and endometrial cancer.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the risk of developing endometrial cancer in relation to hormone levels in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women. The study used data from a case-control study conducted in the United States, with incident cases diagnosed between June 1987 and May 1990. The study found that high levels of androstenedione were associated with increased risk in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women. Other hormone fractions had varying effects depending on menopausal status. Among postmenopausal women, high levels of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) were associated with reduced risk, while high levels of estrone were associated with increased risk. Adjusting for other risk factors, such as body mass index, diminished the effect of estrone. Albumin-bound estradiol (E2) remained an important risk factor even after adjusting for other factors. However, in premenopausal women, there was no association between hormone levels and increased risk. The study also found that obesity and fat distribution were independent risk factors for endometrial cancer, unaffected by hormone levels. The findings suggest that high levels of unopposed estrogen are related to increased risk of endometrial cancer, but there may be alternative endocrinologic mechanisms for the risk associated with obesity and body fat distribution. Further research is needed to explore these mechanisms and the biological relevance of the increased risk associated with androstenedione.

title: FOXO4 is necessary for neural differentiation of human embryonic stem cells.
text: Maintaining cell function is crucial for proteostasis, and the stability of the proteome may have a significant impact on the immortality of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). It is worth noting that hESC populations have a high concentration of active proteasomes, which are a vital component of the proteostasis network. In hESCs, the activity of proteasomes is regulated by FOXO4, a transcription factor that responds to insulin/IGF-1. Our research indicates that the absence of FOXO4 diminishes the ability of hESCs to differentiate into neural lineages. Consequently, FOXO4 bridges the gap between hESC function and the regulation of invertebrate longevity, transcending evolutionary boundaries.

title: Gestational protein restriction affects trophoblast differentiation.
text:
The impact of gestational protein restriction (PR) on placental development and function is still unknown. In order to investigate whether PR can affect trophoblast differentiation during mid and late pregnancy, rats were given either a 20% or a 6% protein diet from Day 1 to 14 or 18 of pregnancy. The effects of PR on trophoblast differentiation were assessed by examining changes in the expression of marker genes for trophoblast lineages. 

At Day 18 of pregnancy, PR was found to increase the expression of Esrrb, Id1, and Id2 (markers for trophoblast stem cells), while decreasing the expression of Ascl2 (a marker for spongiotrophoblast cells) and Prl2c1 (a marker for trophoblast giant cells) in the junctional zone (JZ). However, the expression of Gjb3 and Pcdh12 (markers for glycogen cells) in the JZ remained unchanged. 

In the labyrinth zone (LZ), PR did not affect the expression of Prl2b1 (a marker for trophoblast giant cells), Gcm1, and Syna (markers for syncytiotrophoblast cells), but it did decrease the expression of Ctsq (a marker for sinusoidal trophoblast giant cells). 

These findings suggest that PR disrupts the differentiation of trophoblast stem cells into spongiotrophoblast and trophoblast giant cells in the JZ, as well as the formation of sinusoidal trophoblast giant cells in the LZ.

title: In vitro characterization of the anti-PD-1 antibody nivolumab, BMS-936558, and in vivo toxicology in non-human primates.
text: The programmed death-1 (PD-1) receptor acts as a checkpoint in the immune system, preventing damage to healthy tissues and the development of autoimmune diseases during inflammatory responses. PD-1 is found on activated T cells and regulates their functions by binding to its ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, on antigen-presenting cells. In cancer patients, PD-1 expression on immune cells infiltrating tumors and its interaction with ligands on tumor and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment weaken the body's ability to fight against tumors. This is why PD-1 blockade is considered a promising approach in cancer immunotherapy. This article presents the development and characteristics of nivolumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks the PD-1 receptor. Nivolumab binds strongly and specifically to PD-1, effectively inhibiting its interaction with ligands. In laboratory tests, nivolumab was shown to enhance T-cell responses and cytokine production, without causing cell-mediated or complement-dependent cytotoxicity. When tested on cynomolgus macaques, nivolumab did not cause any adverse immune-related events, even at high concentrations. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of nivolumab's properties, which have been demonstrated in clinical trials to have antitumor activity and be safe for use in various solid tumors.

title: Combined Impact of Lifestyle-Related Factors on Total and Cause-Specific Mortality among Chinese Women: Prospective Cohort Study
text:
BACKGROUND
While cigarette smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, obesity, and other unhealthy lifestyle factors have been linked to chronic diseases and premature death, little is known about their combined impact on mortality outcomes, especially among non-Western populations like the Chinese. This study aimed to determine the overall impact of lifestyle-related factors on all-cause and cause-specific mortality in Chinese women, beyond active smoking and alcohol consumption.

METHODS AND FINDINGS
Data from the Shanghai Women's Health Study, a population-based prospective cohort study in China, were used. The study included 71,243 women aged 40 to 70 years who enrolled between 1996 and 2000 and were non-smokers and non-regular drinkers. A healthy lifestyle score was created based on five lifestyle-related factors independently associated with mortality outcomes: normal weight, lower waist-hip ratio, daily exercise, no exposure to spouse's smoking, and higher daily fruit and vegetable intake. The score ranged from zero (least healthy) to five (most healthy). During an average follow-up of 9 years, there were 2,860 deaths, including 775 from cardiovascular disease (CVD) and 1,351 from cancer. Adjusted hazard ratios for mortality decreased as the number of healthy lifestyle factors increased. Compared to women with a score of zero, those with four to five factors had hazard ratios of 0.57 for total mortality, 0.29 for CVD mortality, and 0.76 for cancer mortality. The inverse association between the healthy lifestyle score and mortality was consistent regardless of chronic disease status at baseline. The population attributable risks for not having 4-5 healthy lifestyle factors were 33% for total deaths, 59% for CVD deaths, and 19% for cancer deaths.

CONCLUSIONS
This study, the first of its kind to quantify the combined impact of lifestyle-related factors on mortality outcomes in Chinese women, found that a healthier lifestyle pattern, including normal weight, lower central adiposity, physical activity, nonexposure to spousal smoking, and higher fruit and vegetable intake, was associated with reduced total and cause-specific mortality in non-smoking and non-drinking women. These findings support the importance of overall lifestyle modification in disease prevention.

title: Aptamer-functionalized lipid nanoparticles targeting osteoblasts as a novel RNA interference–based bone anabolic strategy
text: Currently, there are significant concerns regarding the safety and effectiveness of RNA interference (RNAi)-based strategies for promoting bone growth. This is primarily due to the lack of delivery systems that can specifically target osteoblasts and deliver osteogenic siRNAs. In this study, we conducted a screening process using cell-SELEX to identify an aptamer called CH6 that specifically targets both rat and human osteoblasts. We then developed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) that were functionalized with the CH6 aptamer and encapsulated osteogenic siRNA targeting the Plekho1 gene (CH6-LNPs-siRNA). Our findings demonstrated that CH6 facilitated the selective uptake of Plekho1 siRNA by osteoblasts in vitro, primarily through macropinocytosis. Furthermore, in vivo experiments showed that CH6-LNPs-siRNA effectively silenced the Plekho1 gene specifically in osteoblasts, leading to increased bone formation, improved bone structure, enhanced bone mass, and improved mechanical properties in both osteopenic and healthy rodents. These results suggest that aptamer-functionalized LNPs specifically targeting osteoblasts could serve as a novel RNAi-based strategy for promoting bone growth. This approach represents an advancement in the targeted delivery of osteogenic siRNAs, moving from the tissue level to the cellular level.

title: High abundance of plasma cells secreting transglutaminase 2–specific IgA autoantibodies with limited somatic hypermutation in celiac disease intestinal lesions
text: Celiac disease is an immune-related condition where the body produces antibodies against the enzyme transglutaminase 2 (TG2) in response to the gluten protein. This occurs in individuals who have specific human leukocyte antigens (HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8). We conducted a thorough and unbiased analysis of the IgA anti-TG2 response by examining the antibody repertoire of intestinal antibody-secreting cells. Our findings revealed a significant increase in TG2-specific plasma cells in the duodenal mucosa of individuals with active celiac disease. These antibodies had a strong affinity for TG2 but showed minimal changes due to genetic mutations. Unlike plasmablasts induced by infections, the TG2-specific cells had not recently multiplied and were not short-lived outside the body. These observations suggest that there is a pre-existing repertoire of antibodies with a strong affinity for TG2, which may contribute to the excessive production of self-reactive B cells. Interestingly, the TG2-specific antibodies did not inhibit the enzyme's activity and instead became targets for TG2-mediated crosslinking when expressed as IgD or IgM, but not as IgA1 or IgG1. This could explain why plasma cells derived from naive IgD- and IgM-expressing B cells are preferentially recruited, leading to a primary immune response despite the chronic nature of the disease.

title: Alterations of white matter integrity in adults with major depressive disorder: a magnetic resonance imaging study.
text:
The aim of our study was to examine changes in the integrity of white matter in adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). To achieve this, we conducted diffusion tensor imaging with a 3T MRI scanner on a sample of 45 MDD patients and 45 healthy controls who were matched for age, sex, and education. Through voxel-based analysis, we measured the fractional anisotropy (FA) and compared the differences between the patient and control groups. Additionally, we explored the correlations between white matter microstructure abnormalities and symptom severity, age of illness onset, and cumulative illness duration. 

Our results revealed a significant decrease in FA in the left hemisphere, specifically in the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the inferior parietal portion of the superior longitudinal fasciculus, among MDD patients compared to healthy controls. Furthermore, we found that diffusion tensor imaging measures in the left anterior limb of the internal capsule were negatively associated with the severity of depressive symptoms, even after accounting for age and sex.

In conclusion, our findings provide novel evidence of microstructural changes in white matter among adults with non-late-onset depression. These results complement previous findings in late-life depression and support the hypothesis that disruptions in cortical-subcortical circuit integrity may play a role in the development of major depressive disorder.

title: [Clinical study on the therapeutic effect of acupuncture in the treatment of post-stroke depression].
text:
The objective of this study was to observe the therapeutic effect of "Xingnao Kaiqiao Zhenfa" (Acupuncture Technique for Restoring Consciousness) in treating post-stroke depression. A total of 256 stroke patients were divided into two groups: acupuncture group (n = 180, male 138, female 42) and medication group (n = 76, male 57 and female 19). Acupuncture treatment involved using acupoints Neiguan (PC 6), Renzhong (GV 26), Baihui (GV 20), Yintang (EX-HN 3), and Sanyinjiao (SP 6, the affected side), with needles retained for 20 minutes each time. Patients in the medication group were prescribed Amitriptyline (50 mg/d at first, 200 mg/d). Acupuncture treatment was administered twice daily, and after one month, the therapeutic effect was evaluated using the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) and Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD). 

Results showed that after treatment, 31 (17.2%) and 13 (17.1%) cases in the acupuncture and medication groups were cured, 73 (40.6%) and 18 (23.7%) had a marked improvement in their depression state, 27 (15.0%) and 12 (15.8%) had an improvement, and 49 (27.2%) and 33 (43.4%) failed, with effective rates of 72.8% and 56.6% respectively. The acupuncture group had significantly higher markedly effective and total effective rates compared to the medication group (P < 0.05). Additionally, the acupuncture group showed significantly better therapeutic effects in reducing SDS, HRSD, and severity index compared to the medication group (P < 0.05). The acupuncture group also had larger decreases in depression, pessimistic mood, and irritability compared to the medication group (P < 0.05). There was no significant difference between the two groups in the decrease in insomnia (P > 0.05). 

In conclusion, "Acupuncture Technique for Restoring Consciousness" effectively improves symptoms in depression patients, and its therapeutic effect is significantly superior to medication for post-stroke patients.

title: 30 Years of NF-κB: A Blossoming of Relevance to Human Pathobiology
text: The discovery of NF-κB occurred three decades ago, revealing its ability to quickly activate gene transcription. Over the years, it has been identified as a crucial player in various cellular responses, especially within the immune system. In this summary, we delve into the intricate regulatory pathways associated with this transcription factor and utilize recent findings in human genetic diseases to establish the significance of specific proteins in their respective medical and biological contexts.

title: Increased gene expression of brown fat uncoupling protein (UCP)1 and skeletal muscle UCP2 and UCP3 in MAC16-induced cancer cachexia.
text: The cause of weight loss in cancer cachexia can be attributed to a decrease in food intake and/or an increase in energy expenditure. In our study, we examined the roles of uncoupling proteins (UCPs) UCPI, -2, and -3 in a mouse model of cachexia called MAC16 adenocarcinoma. After 18 days of MAC16 inoculation, the weight of the mice dropped to 24% below that of the non-tumor-bearing controls (P < 0.01). This weight loss was accompanied by significant reductions in fat-pad mass (-67%; P < 0.01) and muscle mass (-20%; P < 0.01). The food intake of the MAC16 mice was 26-60% lower (P < 0.01) compared to the controls on days 17-18. We also observed that non-tumor-bearing mice, which were fed the same amount of food as the MAC16 mice, experienced less weight loss (10% below controls, P < 0.01) and smaller decreases in fat-pad mass (21% below controls, P < 0.01). The core temperature of the MAC16 mice was significantly lower (-2.4 degrees C, P < 0.01) than that of the controls, and pair-feeding had no effect on this temperature difference. We found that MAC16 mice had significantly higher levels of UCP1 mRNA in brown adipose tissue (BAT) compared to the controls (+63%, P < 0.01), and pair-feeding did not affect these levels. However, there were no significant differences in UCP2 and -3 expression in BAT between the groups. On the other hand, UCP2 mRNA levels in skeletal muscle were similarly increased in both the MAC16 and pair-fed groups (183% and 163% above controls, respectively; both P < 0.05), with no significant difference between these two groups. Similarly, UCP3 mRNA levels were significantly higher than controls in both the MAC16 (+163%, P < 0.05) and pair-fed (+253%, P < 0.01) groups, with no significant difference between the two experimental groups. The overexpression of UCP1 in BAT in MAC16-bearing mice may be a response to hypothermia induced by tumor products, and increased thermogenesis in BAT could contribute to tissue wasting by increasing total energy expenditure. The increased expression of UCP2 and -3 in muscle is likely due to reduced food intake and may play a role in lipid utilization during lipolysis in MAC16-induced cachexia.

title: In vitro Anti-Tumor Effects of Statins on Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review
text:
BACKGROUND: Statins are commonly prescribed for arteriosclerotic disease, but recent retrospective analyses have suggested that they may also have anti-cancer properties. This systematic review aims to investigate the in vitro anti-tumor effects of statins on head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive search of Cochrane, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and PubMed databases up until May 9, 2015, with no restrictions on language or time. Only in vitro studies focusing on the effect of statins on head and neck carcinoma were included.

RESULTS: Out of 153 papers identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. These studies demonstrated that statins had a significant impact on head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines, affecting cell viability, cell cycle, cell death, and protein expression levels involved in carcinogenesis pathways. This supports the potential in vitro anti-tumor effects of statins and provides insights into their biological mechanisms when used alone or in combination with traditional cancer therapies.

CONCLUSIONS: Although there is limited research on this topic, the available evidence suggests that statins have the potential to be used as adjuvant agents in chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy approaches for the management of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Further clinical assessment is warranted.

title: Circulating Mitochondrial DNA in Patients in the ICU as a Marker of Mortality: Derivation and Validation
text:
BACKGROUND: The role of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) as a biomarker in the intensive care unit (ICU) has not been studied extensively. We aimed to investigate the association between circulating cell-free mtDNA levels and mortality in ICU patients, as well as its potential as a risk predictor.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: We analyzed mtDNA levels in blood samples from two observational cohort studies of ICU patients: the Brigham and Women's Hospital Registry of Critical Illness (BWH RoCI) and the Molecular Epidemiology of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ME ARDS). Plasma mtDNA levels were measured using quantitative real-time PCR to assess the copy number of the NADH dehydrogenase 1 gene. We found that medical ICU patients with elevated mtDNA levels (≥3,200 copies/µl plasma) had a significantly higher risk of dying within 28 days of ICU admission in both the BWH RoCI and ME ARDS cohorts. However, no such association was observed in non-medical ICU patients. Furthermore, the inclusion of elevated mtDNA levels improved the prediction of 28-day mortality in medical ICU patients when added to clinical models in both cohorts. In the BWH RoCI cohort, patients with elevated mtDNA levels had an increased risk of death, even when limited to those with sepsis or acute respiratory distress syndrome. It is important to note that our study has limitations, including a lack of data on the specific pathological roles of mtDNA in these patients and limited measurements for some biomarkers.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that increased mtDNA levels are associated with ICU mortality, and the inclusion of mtDNA level improves risk prediction in medical ICU patients. Therefore, mtDNA could potentially serve as a useful plasma biomarker in this patient population.

title: Fructosamine Is a Useful Indicator of Hyperglycaemia and Glucose Control in Clinical and Epidemiological Studies – Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Experience from the AMORIS Cohort
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of fructosamine as an indicator of high blood sugar levels and glucose control in individuals with diabetes. The study analyzed data from the AMORIS cohort, including serum glucose, fructosamine, and HbA1c levels from the same examination. The participants were studied both cross-sectionally and longitudinally, with a total of 10,987 subjects (5,590 of whom were fasting overnight). The classification of prediabetes and diabetes followed the guidelines of the American Diabetes Association. Separate analyses were conducted for patients with newly diagnosed or previously diagnosed type 1 or type 2 diabetes. 

The results showed a strong correlation between all three biomarkers. The association between fructosamine and HbA1c was particularly notable, with Pearson linear correlation coefficients ranging from 0.67 to 0.75 in fasting and non-fasting subjects with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. When analyzing glucose control in fasting patients with type 2 diabetes, who had all three biomarkers measured at three separate occasions within an average of 290 days of the initial examination, similar trends over time were observed for glucose, fructosamine, and HbA1c levels. 

Fructosamine levels were found to be a good discriminator between individuals with and without diabetes, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.91 to 0.95. A fructosamine level of 2.5 mmol/L classified individuals as having diabetes with a sensitivity of 61% and a specificity of 97%. 

In conclusion, fructosamine is closely associated with HbA1c and glucose levels and may serve as a valuable biomarker for assessing hyperglycemia and glucose control in clinical and epidemiological studies.

title: Lifeact: a versatile marker to visualize F-actin
text: The visualization of the actin cytoskeleton in real-time is essential for studying various important biological processes. However, existing methods for observing actin have certain drawbacks. In this study, we introduce Lifeact, a peptide consisting of 17 amino acids. Lifeact effectively stained filamentous actin (F-actin) structures in both eukaryotic cells and tissues. Importantly, Lifeact did not disrupt actin dynamics when tested in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, the chemically modified form of Lifeact enabled the visualization of actin dynamics in cells that cannot be transfected with foreign genetic material.

title: Robustness of Random Forest-based gene selection methods
text: Gene selection plays a crucial role in the analysis of microarray data as it provides valuable information for understanding the underlying mechanisms of a studied phenomenon. However, gene selection is challenging due to the presence of noise in microarray data. Consequently, machine learning methods, such as the Random Forest method, are often employed for gene selection. In this study, four advanced Random Forest-based feature selection methods were compared in the context of gene selection. The focus of the analysis was on the stability of selection, which is often overlooked in similar studies despite its importance in determining the significance of results. The comparison of post-selection accuracy in validating Random Forest classifiers revealed that all the methods performed equally well in this context. However, there were notable differences in the number of selected genes and the stability of selection among the methods. Among the methods analyzed, the Boruta algorithm identified the highest number of potentially important genes. The commonly used measure of post-selection classifier error rate was found to be potentially misleading in assessing the quality of gene selection. When considering the number of consistently selected genes, the Boruta algorithm emerged as the top performer. Although it required more computational resources compared to other algorithms, the computational demands of the Boruta algorithm could be reduced to a comparable level by substituting the Random Forest importance measure with a similar measure from Random Ferns, a simplified classifier. Interestingly, the minimal optimal selection methods, despite their design assumptions, were found to select a significant proportion of false positives.

title: Improved variant discovery through local re-alignment of short-read next-generation sequencing data using SRMA
text: This article describes a novel approach called SRMA (short-read micro realigner) that improves the alignment of short reads to a reference genome in next-generation sequencing analysis. Currently, each read is aligned independently, but this method takes advantage of the high correlation between reads that observe the same non-reference DNA sequence. By leveraging this correlation, SRMA can more accurately model the true variation in the target genome and provide a more reliable consensus of the underlying DNA sequence.

title: Functional elements within the dynein microtubule-binding domain
text: Dynein interacts with microtubules through a linkage that is sensitive to ATP. This linkage is located in a structurally complex region of the heavy chain after the fourth P-loop motif. Currently, very little is known about how the binding affinity is established and regulated during ATP hydrolysis. To address this, we conducted a thorough analysis of the microtubule contact site using fragment expression, alanine substitution, and peptide competition techniques. Our investigation revealed three clusters of amino acids that play a crucial role in the physical interaction with microtubules. Interestingly, two of these clusters are located in a region that shares sequence homology with MAP1B, while the third cluster is found just downstream. Substituting amino acids within any of these regions can either eliminate or weaken the binding of microtubules (specifically, KK3379, 80, E3385, K3387, K3397, KK3410,11, W3414, RKK3418-20, F3426, R3464, S3466, and K3467), indicating that their activities are closely coordinated. Furthermore, we observed that a peptide capable of displacing MAP1B from microtubules also disrupts dynein binding, providing additional support for the existence of similar interaction sites. Additionally, we identified four amino acids (E3413, R3444, E3460, and C3469) whose substitutions affect the release of the motor from the microtubule. These findings suggest that the affinity, which is sensitive to nucleotides, may be locally regulated at the contact site. Overall, our study represents the first comprehensive investigation of the interactions between dynein and tubulin, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying affinity establishment and modulation.

title: The Transcription Factors Egr2 and Egr3 Are Essential for the Control of Inflammation and Antigen-Induced Proliferation of B and T Cells
text: The mechanisms that regulate optimal responses of lymphocytes against pathogens while minimizing inflammatory damage are currently unknown. In this study, we found that the deletion of both transcription factors Egr2 and Egr3 in lymphocytes led to a severe autoimmune syndrome. This syndrome was characterized by excessive levels of proinflammatory cytokines in the bloodstream, as well as impaired proliferation of B and T cells in response to antigen receptor stimulation. We observed that Egr2- and Egr3-deficient B and T cells exhibited overactive signaling pathways involving the proteins STAT1 and STAT3, while the activation of the transcription factor AP-1, which is crucial for immune responses, was severely compromised. Our investigation revealed that Egr2 and/or Egr3 directly promoted the expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling-1 (SOCS1) and SOCS3, which are inhibitors of STAT1 and STAT3. Additionally, Egr2 and Egr3 hindered the function of Batf, an inhibitor of AP-1, in B and T cells. Therefore, Egr2 and Egr3 play a vital role in regulating the function of B and T cells during adaptive immune responses and maintaining immune system balance by enhancing antigen receptor signaling and controlling inflammation.

title: Effect of hyperosmolality on alkaline phosphatase and stress-response protein 27 of MCF-7 breast cancer cells
text: MCF-7, a cell line derived from a human breast carcinoma, has very low alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity. The enzyme is resistant to heat and is inhibited by L-phenylalanine and L-phenylalanylgly-cylglycine, but not by L-homoarginine, 1-bromotetramisole, or levamisole. These findings suggest that MCF-7 produces term-placental ALP, which is an enzyme form that is abnormally expressed in various human tumors. Unlike other human cancer cells that only produce this enzyme, the ALP activity in MCF-7 cells is not significantly increased by glucocorticoids or sodium butyrate. However, exposure to hyperosmolality leads to a significant increase in enzyme activity, which is blocked by cycloheximide. The results from cell-free assays were confirmed by cytochemical and immunocytochemical assays on whole cells. Additionally, the effects of the tested agents on cell proliferation were examined, along with their impact on two stress-response proteins (srp 27 and srp 72), using specific immunocytochemical assays. These tests revealed that glucocorticoids do not affect either protein, sodium butyrate has no effect on srp 27 but alters the distribution of srp 72 within the cell, and hyperosmolality increases srp 27 without significantly affecting srp 72.

title: The Bile Acid Chenodeoxycholic Acid Increases Human Brown Adipose Tissue Activity.
text: The recent discovery of functional brown adipose tissue (BAT) in humans has sparked a renewed interest in using it as a target to combat metabolic disease. In rodents, BAT can be activated by bile acids, which stimulate type 2 iodothyronine deiodinase (D2) in BAT through the G-coupled protein receptor TGR5. This activation leads to increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure. In this study, we investigated the effects of orally supplementing the bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) on human BAT activity. The results showed that treating 12 healthy female subjects with CDCA for 2 days increased BAT activity. Additionally, whole-body energy expenditure was also elevated after CDCA treatment. In laboratory experiments using primary human brown adipocytes, treatment with CDCA or specific TGR5 agonists increased mitochondrial uncoupling and D2 expression. Interestingly, these effects were not observed in primary human white adipocytes. These findings highlight the potential of bile acids as a means to activate BAT in humans.

title: RNase H and Postreplication Repair Protect Cells from Ribonucleotides Incorporated in DNA
text: The presence of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) instead of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication poses a challenge to the chemical identity and integrity of the genome. The selectivity of DNA replicases helps limit the misincorporation of rNTPs. However, when ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) accumulate in the genome, it leads to replication stress and has toxic effects, especially in the absence of RNase H1 and RNase H2, which remove rNMPs. Our study demonstrates that two postreplication repair (PRR) pathways, namely MMS2-dependent template switch and Pol ζ-dependent bypass, play a crucial role in tolerating the presence of rNMPs in the chromosomes. In fact, we show that Pol ζ can efficiently replicate over 1-4 rNMPs. Additionally, cells lacking RNase H exhibit an accumulation of mono- and polyubiquitylated PCNA and have a constantly activated PRR. Our findings highlight the essential function of RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming the misincorporation of rNTPs during DNA replication. These findings may also have implications for understanding the development of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.

title: Selective elimination of high constitutive activity or chemokine binding in the human herpesvirus 8 encoded seven transmembrane oncogene ORF74.
text:
Human herpesvirus 8 encodes a protein called Open Reading Frame 74 (ORF74), which is a highly active receptor with seven transmembrane domains. This receptor is constantly active and is stimulated by angiogenic chemokines, such as growth-related oncogene-alpha, while being inhibited by angiostatic chemokines, like interferon-gamma-inducible protein. When transgenic mice express ORF74 under the control of the CD2 promoter, they develop tumors similar to Kaposi's sarcoma, which are highly vascularized.

Through targeted mutagenesis, we have created three different versions of ORF74. The first version has normal, high constitutive signaling through the phospholipase C pathway, but it lacks the ability to bind and respond to chemokines due to the deletion of 22 amino acids from the N-terminal extension. The second version has high constitutive activity, but it no longer responds to angiogenic chemokines due to the substitution of basic residues at the ends of two transmembrane domains. The third version lacks constitutive activity, but it can still be stimulated by agonist chemokines due to the introduction of an Asp residue on the hydrophobic face of another transmembrane domain.

In conclusion, by carefully dissecting the molecular structure of ORF74, we have been able to selectively eliminate its agonist or inverse agonist modulation, as well as its high constitutive activity. These mutant forms can potentially be used in transgenic animals to further understand the molecular mechanisms behind the transforming activity of this viral oncogene.

title: An insulin-like signaling pathway affects both longevity and reproduction in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Mutations in the daf-2 and age-1 genes have a significant impact on the lifespan and developmental process of Caenorhabditis elegans. These genes are responsible for encoding components of an insulin-like signaling pathway. Both daf-2 and age-1 play a crucial role in the genetic epistasis pathway for dauer arrest and longevity, and they regulate the activity of the daf-16 gene. Mutations in daf-16 result in a defective dauer phenotype and are epistatic to the diapause arrest and lifespan extension phenotypes observed in daf-2 and age-1 mutants. Additionally, we have discovered that mutations in this pathway also affect fertility and embryonic development. Even weak daf-2 alleles and maternally rescued age-1 alleles, which lead to lifespan extension without dauer arrest, have a negative impact on fertility and viability. Our findings indicate that age-1(hx546) exhibits reduced maternal and zygotic age-1 activity. Furthermore, daf-16 mutations suppress all the phenotypes associated with daf-2 and age-1, including dauer arrest, lifespan extension, reduced fertility, and viability defects. These results demonstrate that insulin signaling, mediated by DAF-2 through the AGE-1 phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase, regulates reproduction and embryonic development, as well as dauer diapause and lifespan, with DAF-16 serving as the mediator of these signals. The regulation of fertility, lifespan, and metabolism through an insulin-like signaling pathway bears resemblance to the endocrine regulation of metabolism and fertility observed in mammalian insulin signaling.

title: Estimating prion concentration in fluids and tissues by quantitative PMCA
text: The detection of prions, which are the infectious agents responsible for prion diseases, can be achieved with great sensitivity using protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) technology. In this study, we present a quantitative PMCA method that allows for the calculation of prion concentrations in biological samples, even at extremely low levels. By employing this procedure, we were able to determine the amounts of misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) present in the brain, spleen, blood, and urine of hamsters affected by scrapie.

title: Positional cloning of the APECED gene
text: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I (APS 1), also known as APECED, is a genetic disorder that is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner. Through linkage studies, it has been determined that APS 1 is located on human chromosome 21q22.3, specifically between markers D21S49 and D21S171. From this region, a new gene called AIRE (autoimmune regulator) has been isolated. AIRE encodes a protein that contains motifs resembling a transcription factor, including two zinc-finger (PHD-finger) motifs, a proline-rich region, and three LXXLL motifs. In Swiss and Finnish APECED patients, two mutations have been identified in this novel gene. One mutation is a C→T substitution that changes the amino acid Arg 257 (CGA) to a stop codon (TGA). The other mutation is an A→G substitution that changes the amino acid Lys 83 (AAG) to a Glu codon (GAG). The Arg257stop (R257X) mutation is the most common mutation found in Finnish APECED patients, accounting for 10 out of 12 alleles studied. These findings suggest that the AIRE gene is responsible for the development of APECED. Identifying the defective gene in APECED will aid in the genetic diagnosis and potential treatment of the disease, as well as contribute to our overall understanding of the mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases.

title: AMP-Activated Protein Kinase: An Ubiquitous Signaling Pathway With Key Roles in the Cardiovascular System
text: The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of energy within cells and the entire body. It works to restore energy balance when cellular energy levels are low. Recent research has revealed that AMPK also regulates various other cellular functions and has specific functions in cardiovascular tissues. It helps regulate cardiac metabolism and contractile function, while also promoting actions that prevent contraction, reduce inflammation, and prevent the development of atherosclerosis in blood vessels. This article explores the role of AMPK in the cardiovascular system, including how mutations in AMPK can affect cardiac function and the mechanisms by which AMPK regulates vascular function in both normal and abnormal conditions.

title: Differentiation of trophoblast stem cells into giant cells is triggered by p57/Kip2 inhibition of CDK1 activity.
text: The mechanism behind genome endoreduplication during mammalian development is not well understood, as it is a rare occurrence. This process is first observed when fibroblast growth factor 4 (FGF4) deprivation leads to the differentiation of trophoblast stem (TS) cells into nonproliferating trophoblast giant (TG) cells, which are necessary for embryo implantation. Our study demonstrates that inhibiting cyclin-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDK1) with RO3306 prompts the differentiation of TS cells into TG cells. However, when RO3306 is used on embryonic stem cells, it induces incomplete endoreduplication and apoptosis. This suggests that CDK1 inactivation only triggers endoreduplication in cells that are programmed to become polyploid. Similarly, FGF4 deprivation leads to CDK1 inhibition by increasing the expression of two CDK-specific inhibitors, p57/KIP2 and p21/CIP1. Our analysis of TS cell mutants reveals that p57 is necessary for initiating endoreduplication by inhibiting CDK1, while p21 suppresses the expression of the checkpoint protein kinase CHK1, preventing apoptosis. Additionally, our findings show that CDK2 is required for endoreduplication in CDK1-inhibited TS cells, as demonstrated by Cdk2(-/-) TS cells. In TG cells, p57 expression is limited to G-phase nuclei to enable CDK activation during S phase. Therefore, endoreduplication in TS cells is triggered by p57 inhibiting CDK1, while p21 suppresses the DNA damage response.

title: Atg5-independent autophagy regulates mitochondrial clearance and is essential for iPSC reprogramming
text: The reprogramming process to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) requires a significant change in metabolism, shifting from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis. However, the exact mechanism behind this metabolic reprogramming is still unknown. Our findings indicate that a type of autophagy, independent of Atg5, plays a role in clearing mitochondria, which is a key event in the metabolic switch. We discovered that blocking this specific autophagy, but not the traditional form, hinders mitochondrial clearance and prevents iPSC induction. Additionally, we observed that AMPK, a protein kinase, is involved in regulating this autophagic pathway and can be influenced by small molecules to modulate mitochondrial clearance during metabolic reprogramming. Our research not only highlights the importance of Atg5-independent autophagy in establishing pluripotency, but also suggests that iPSC generation and tumorigenesis share a similar metabolic shift.

title: A mutation in Orai1 causes immune deficiency by abrogating CRAC channel function
text: The activation of immune cells by antigens leads to the entry of calcium ions (Ca2+) through channels known as Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels. This process enhances the immune response against pathogens by activating a transcription factor called NFAT. Our previous research has demonstrated that individuals with a specific type of hereditary severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) syndrome have impaired Ca2+ entry and malfunctioning CRAC channels. In this study, we have identified the genetic defect responsible for this condition using two unbiased genome-wide approaches. These approaches include a modified linkage analysis using single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays and a Drosophila RNA interference screen designed to identify regulators of Ca2+ entry and NFAT nuclear import. Both methods have led us to discover a novel protein called Orai1, which consists of four potential transmembrane segments. The SCID patients in our study are homozygous for a single missense mutation in the ORAI1 gene. Furthermore, the expression of normal Orai1 in T cells from SCID patients restores Ca2+ influx and the CRAC current (ICRAC). Based on these findings, we propose that Orai1 is a crucial component or regulator of the CRAC channel complex.

title: Estimates of global prevalence of childhood underweight in 1990 and 2015.
text:
The United Nations Millennium Development goals aim to reduce the prevalence of underweight children under the age of 5 by half between 1990 and 2015. This study examines the trends in childhood underweight across different regions of the world. The prevalence of underweight is defined as a weight 2 standard deviations below the mean weight for age according to the National Center for Health Statistics and World Health Organization reference population. Data from the WHO Global Database on Child Growth and Malnutrition, which includes information from approximately 31 million children under 5 years old who participated in 419 national nutritional surveys in 139 countries from 1965 to 2002, was used to determine national prevalence rates.

The main outcome measures were estimated prevalence rates and the number of underweight children by region in 1990 and 2015, as well as the changes in these values between the two time periods. The results show that worldwide, the prevalence of underweight is projected to decrease from 26.5% in 1990 to 17.6% in 2015, a change of -34% (95% confidence interval [CI], -43% to -23%). In developed countries, the prevalence is estimated to decrease from 1.6% to 0.9%, a change of -41% (95% CI, -92% to 343%). In developing regions, the prevalence is forecasted to decline from 30.2% to 19.3%, a change of -36% (95% CI, -45% to -26%). However, in Africa, the prevalence of underweight is expected to increase from 24.0% to 26.8%, a change of 12% (95% CI, 8%-16%). In Asia, the prevalence is estimated to decrease from 35.1% to 18.5%, a change of -47% (95% CI, -58% to -34%). 

The study also projects that the number of underweight children worldwide will decrease from 163.8 million in 1990 to 113.4 million in 2015, a change of -31% (95% CI, -40% to -20%). However, the number of underweight children is expected to increase in sub-Saharan, Eastern, Middle, and Western Africa, while all other subregions are projected to experience a decrease. 

In conclusion, while there is an overall improvement in the global situation regarding childhood underweight, the Millennium Development goals are not expected to be achieved by the world as a whole or the developing regions. This is primarily due to the worsening situation in Africa, where all subregions, except Northern Africa, are predicted to fall short of meeting the goal.

title: Canonical Wnt signaling regulates organ-specific assembly and differentiation of CNS vasculature.
text:
Blood vessels are essential for supplying oxygen and nutrients to every organ in the body. However, the structure and composition of blood vessels can vary depending on the specific organ. In the central nervous system (CNS), the blood vessels have a tightly sealed endothelium that forms a protective barrier called the blood-brain barrier. In contrast, blood vessels in other organs are more permeable.

During the development of the CNS, two Wnt ligands called Wnt7a and Wnt7b are produced by the neuroepithelium. These ligands play a crucial role in the invasion of blood vessels into the CNS. Through genetic mouse models, we have discovered that these ligands directly target the endothelium of blood vessels. Additionally, the CNS utilizes the canonical Wnt signaling pathway to promote the formation and specific differentiation of its own blood vessels.

title: Bone progenitor dysfunction induces myelodysplasia and secondary leukemia
text: Mesenchymal cells play a role in the supportive tissue of both normal and cancerous tissues, and certain mesenchymal cells are involved in regulating stem cells. In this study, we investigated how mesenchymal osteolineage cells affect the production of blood cells, and found that deleting a gene called Dicer1 specifically in mouse osteoprogenitors (early bone-forming cells) disrupted the normal functioning of blood cell production. This led to a condition called myelodysplasia, and eventually acute myelogenous leukemia, which had acquired additional genetic abnormalities but still had intact Dicer1. We also observed changes in gene expression in osteoprogenitors due to the deletion of Dicer1, including reduced expression of Sbds, a gene associated with Schwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome, a condition that predisposes individuals to bone marrow failure and leukemia. Deleting Sbds in mouse osteoprogenitors also caused bone marrow dysfunction with myelodysplasia. These findings demonstrate that disrupting specific subsets of mesenchymal stromal cells can affect the differentiation, proliferation, and programmed cell death of other cells, leading to tissue imbalance. Additionally, primary dysfunction in the supportive tissue can contribute to the development of secondary cancer, supporting the idea of niche-induced oncogenesis.

title: Generating diploid embryos from Xenopus tropicalis.
text: Xenopus tropicalis offers a remarkable benefit in that diploid embryos can be easily produced throughout the year. By administering human chorionic gonadotropin, researchers can generate numerous synchronized embryos through in vitro fertilization or thousands of embryos from a mating pair. This ability to induce ovulations at will enables a wide range of experiments, including experimental embryology, molecular manipulation of gene products, and genetics.

title: Oct4-Induced Pluripotency in Adult Neural Stem Cells
text: Pluripotency can be induced in mouse and human fibroblasts by four transcription factors: Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc. In a previous study, we showed that adult mouse neural stem cells (NSCs) can be directly reprogrammed using Oct4 and either Klf4 or c-Myc. NSCs naturally express Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, along with several intermediate reprogramming markers. In this report, we present evidence that introducing the germline-specific transcription factor Oct4 alone is sufficient to generate pluripotent stem cells from adult mouse NSCs. These one-factor induced pluripotent stem cells (1F iPS) exhibit similar characteristics to embryonic stem cells both in vitro and in vivo. They can be efficiently differentiated into NSCs, cardiomyocytes, and germ cells in vitro, and also have the ability to form teratomas and transmit their genetic information to the germline in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that Oct4 is both necessary and capable of directly reprogramming NSCs to pluripotency.

title: Getting started with yeast.
text: The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is widely recognized as a model organism that represents a simple eukaryote with a genome that can be easily manipulated. Yeast shares many technical advantages with bacteria and their viruses, making it an ideal system for molecular genetics research. Some of the key features that make yeast suitable for biological studies include its rapid growth, dispersed cells, ease of replica plating and mutant isolation, well-defined genetic system, and most importantly, its highly versatile DNA transformation system. Additionally, yeast is nonpathogenic and can be handled with minimal precautions. Commercially available baker's yeast can be used as a cost-effective source for biochemical studies. The development of DNA transformation techniques has made yeast accessible for gene cloning and genetic engineering. By using plasmid libraries, it is possible to identify structural genes for any genetic trait through complementation. Plasmids can be introduced into yeast cells either as replicating molecules or by integrating them into the genome. Unlike most other organisms, yeast exclusively uses homologous recombination for integrative recombination of transforming DNA. This allows for the directed placement of cloned yeast sequences, along with foreign sequences on plasmids, to specific locations in the genome.

title: PCNA functions as a molecular platform to trigger Cdt1 destruction and prevent re-replication
text: The ubiquitin-mediated breakdown of the replication licensing factor Cdt1 in the S phase is a crucial process that limits DNA replication to one round per cell cycle in metazoans. In Xenopus egg extracts, Cdt1 is degraded on chromatin during DNA replication. Our study reveals that the degradation of Cdt1 during replication is dependent on its interaction with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a factor that enhances the activity of DNA polymerases. Cdt1 binds to PCNA through a specific motif that is present in all metazoans, and when PCNA is removed from the egg extracts, the destruction of Cdt1 is inhibited. By mutating the PCNA-binding motif, we were able to stabilize Cdt1, leading to re-replication. Additionally, the Cul4 E3 ubiquitin ligase component DDB1, which is responsible for the degradation of human Cdt1 in response to DNA damage, is also required for the replication-dependent breakdown of Cdt1. Cdt1 and DDB1 interact in the extracts, and the loading of DDB1 onto chromatin is dependent on the binding of Cdt1 to PCNA. This suggests that the docking of PCNA activates the pre-existing Cdt1-Cul4DDB1 ligase complex. Therefore, PCNA acts as a platform for the destruction of Cdt1, ensuring efficient and timely inactivation of this important cell-cycle regulator.

title: Meiosis in Drosophila: seeing is believing.
text: In recent times, significant progress has been made in comprehending Drosophila meiosis through the combination of cytological and genetic approaches. Novel methods have enabled the examination of chromosome position and spindle formation during female meiosis I. The nod and ncd genes, known to be crucial for the proper distribution of chromosomes without exchange events, have been discovered to encode kinesin-like motors. By studying the impact of mutations in these genes on the spindle and chromosomes, as well as the localization of the proteins, a model for the mechanism of female meiosis I has been developed. In male meiosis I, the specific DNA sequences responsible for homolog pairing have been identified, offering a basis for understanding the molecular foundation of meiotic pairing. The cytological techniques employed in Drosophila have also facilitated progress in comprehending the regulation of sister-chromatid segregation. Recently, the products of two genes (mei-S332 and ord) essential for sister-chromatid cohesion have been identified. Furthermore, advancements have been made in delineating a functional centromere using minichromosome derivatives and identifying several regulatory genes for the meiotic cell cycle in Drosophila.

title: Effect of physical activity on cognitive function in older adults at risk for Alzheimer disease: a randomized trial.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate whether physical activity can reduce cognitive decline in older adults at risk. The study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial in metropolitan Perth, Western Australia, between 2004 and 2007. The cognitive function assessors were unaware of the participants' group assignments. The study recruited individuals aged 50 years or older who reported memory problems but did not meet the criteria for dementia. Out of the 311 individuals screened for eligibility, 89 were deemed ineligible, and 52 refused to participate. A total of 170 participants were randomly assigned to either an education and usual care group or a 24-week home-based physical activity program. The main outcome measure was the change in Alzheimer Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog) scores over 18 months, with a possible range of 0-70. 

The results of the intent-to-treat analysis showed that participants in the intervention group improved by 0.26 points (95% confidence interval, -0.89 to 0.54) on the ADAS-Cog, while those in the usual care group deteriorated by 1.04 points (95% confidence interval, 0.32 to 1.82) at the end of the intervention. The absolute difference between the intervention and control groups was -1.3 points (95% confidence interval, -2.38 to -0.22) at the end of the intervention. After 18 months, participants in the intervention group improved by 0.73 points (95% confidence interval, -1.27 to 0.03) on the ADAS-Cog, while those in the usual care group improved by 0.04 points (95% confidence interval, -0.46 to 0.88). Other measures such as word list delayed recall and Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes also showed modest improvements, but word list total immediate recall, digit symbol coding, verbal fluency, Beck depression score, and Medical Outcomes 36-Item Short-Form physical and mental component summaries did not change significantly. 

In conclusion, this study found that a 6-month physical activity program provided a modest improvement in cognition over an 18-month follow-up period for adults with subjective memory impairment. The trial was registered with anzctr.org.au Identifier: ACTRN12605000136606.

title: Variants at 6q21 implicate PRDM1 in the etiology of therapy-induced second malignancies after Hodgkin's lymphoma
text: Children who have survived pediatric Hodgkin's lymphoma are at risk of developing second malignant neoplasms (SMNs) due to radiation therapy. Our research has identified two genetic variations on chromosome 6q21 that are associated with SMNs in survivors of Hodgkin's lymphoma who were treated with radiation therapy during childhood, but not as adults. These variations are located in a specific region that is linked to reduced expression of the PRDM1 gene, which encodes the PR domain containing 1 protein with a ZNF domain. Additionally, these variations impair the production of the PRDM1 protein after exposure to radiation. These findings suggest a new interaction between genes and exposure to radiation, potentially implicating PRDM1 in the development of radiation therapy-induced SMNs.

title: Long non-coding RNA profiling of human lymphoid progenitor cells reveals transcriptional divergence of B cell and T cell lineages
text: In order to understand how human lymphoid commitment is regulated during postnatal life, we utilized RNA sequencing to examine the long non-coding transcriptome in bone marrow and thymic progenitor cells. These cells represent the initial stages of B lymphoid and T lymphoid specification. Through this analysis, we discovered over 3,000 genes that encode previously unknown long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) within these rare cell populations. The expression patterns of these lncRNAs were highly specific to each stage of lymphoid commitment and more specific to the lymphoid lineage compared to protein-coding genes. We also found that protein-coding genes co-expressed with neighboring lncRNA genes were enriched for ontologies related to lymphoid differentiation. By examining the global expression patterns of lncRNAs, we were able to uncover new developmental relationships among the earliest progenitor cells in the human bone marrow and thymus, highlighting the remarkable specificity of these lncRNAs in different cell types.

title: The VTI family of SNARE proteins is necessary for plant viability and mediates different protein transport pathways.
text: The Arabidopsis genome contains a group of v-SNAREs known as VTI11, VTI12, and VTI13. Among these, only VTI11 and VTI12 are expressed at significant levels. Despite sharing 60% similarity, these two proteins serve different transport pathways when expressed in the yeast vti1 mutant. Recently, VTI11 was identified as the mutated gene in the zig mutant, which affects shoot gravitropism. Our study reveals that the vti11 zig mutant exhibits abnormalities in vascular patterning and auxin transport. On the other hand, the vti12 mutant, created through Arabidopsis T-DNA insertion, displays a normal phenotype under nutrient-rich conditions. However, under nutrient-poor conditions, vti12 exhibits an accelerated senescence phenotype, suggesting its involvement in the plant autophagy pathway. Furthermore, VTI11 and VTI12 can substitute for each other in their respective SNARE complexes, and a cross between zig and vti12 mutants results in embryo lethality. These findings indicate that VTI1 protein is crucial for plant survival and that these two proteins have overlapping functions to some extent.

title: CLASPs link focal adhesion-associated microtubule capture to localized exocytosis and adhesion site turnover
text: The turnover of integrin-based focal adhesions (FAs) with the extracellular matrix (ECM) is crucial for coordinated cell movement. In human keratinocytes migrating collectively, FAs form near the leading edge, grow and mature due to contractile forces, and disassemble beneath the advancing cell body. Our findings show that the clustering of CLASP1 and CLASP2 proteins, which are associated with microtubules, around FAs is temporally linked to FA turnover. CLASPs and LL5β (also known as PHLDB2), which recruits CLASPs to FAs, aid in the disassembly of FAs. Additionally, CLASPs are necessary for the degradation of ECM associated with FAs, and inhibiting matrix metalloproteases slows down FA disassembly in a similar manner to depleting CLASP or PHLDB2 (LL5β). Lastly, CLASP-mediated tethering of microtubules at FAs establishes a pathway for the directed transport, docking, and localized fusion of exocytic vesicles near FAs. We propose that CLASPs connect microtubule organization, vesicle transport, and cell-ECM interactions, creating a local secretion pathway that facilitates FA turnover by severing cell-matrix connections.

title: CHD4 Is a RanGTP-Dependent MAP that Stabilizes Microtubules and Regulates Bipolar Spindle Formation
text:
BACKGROUND: The production of the Ran GTPase in its GTP-bound form (RanGTP) around chromosomes activates nuclear localization signal (NLS)-containing proteins, leading to spindle assembly. While several NLS proteins have been identified as factors in spindle assembly, the complexity of the process prompted us to search for additional proteins with distinct roles in this process.

RESULTS: We have discovered that CHD4, a chromatin-remodeling ATPase, is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein (MAP) that is dependent on RanGTP. CHD4 binds to MTs through its NLS and chromatin-binding domains. In Xenopus egg extracts and cultured cells, CHD4 dissociates from mitotic chromosomes and localizes partially to the spindle. Depletion of CHD4 from egg extracts significantly reduces the amount of MTs produced around chromatin and prevents spindle assembly. RNAi of CHD4 in HeLa and Drosophila S2 cells leads to defects in spindle assembly and chromosome alignment in early mitosis, resulting in chromosome missegregation. Further analysis in egg extracts and HeLa cells reveals that CHD4 acts as a RanGTP-dependent MT stabilizer. Additionally, the CHD4-containing NuRD complex promotes the organization of MTs into bipolar spindles in egg extracts. Importantly, this function of CHD4 is independent of chromatin remodeling.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal a new role for CHD4 as a MAP that is necessary for MT stabilization and plays a role in generating spindle bipolarity.

title: Myocardial muscarinic receptor upregulation and normal response to isoproterenol in denervated hearts by familial amyloid polyneuropathy.
text:
Patients with familial amyloid polyneuropathy, a rare hereditary form of amyloidosis, experience progressive autonomic neuropathy. While the disease typically does not lead to heart failure, it is associated with sudden death, conduction disturbances, and an increased risk of complications during anesthesia. Although cardiac sympathetic denervation has been proven, the status of the postsynaptic cardiac autonomic nervous system remains unclear.

In this study, twenty-one patients (average age 39+/-11 years) with normal coronary arteries and left ventricular ejection fraction of 68+/-9% were examined. PET imaging with (11)C-MQNB (methylquinuclidinyl benzilate), a specific hydrophilic antagonist, was used to evaluate the density and affinity constants of myocardial muscarinic receptors. The functional efficiency of cardiac beta-receptors was assessed by measuring the heart rate (HR) response to intravenous infusion of isoproterenol (administered 5 minutes after 2 mg of atropine, with incremental doses of 5, 10, and 15 ng/kg per minute during 5 minutes per step).

The results showed that the mean muscarinic receptor density was higher in patients compared to control subjects (B'(max), 35.5+/-8.9 versus 26.1+/-6.7 pmol/mL, P=0.003), with no change in receptor affinity. Despite a similar basal HR, the increase in HR after administration of atropine and MQNB was lower in patients compared to control subjects (DeltaHR after atropine, 11+/-21% versus 62+/-17%; P<0.001), indicating parasympathetic denervation. However, incremental infusion of isoproterenol resulted in a similar increase in HR in both patients and control subjects.

In conclusion, familial amyloid polyneuropathy leads to cardiac autonomic denervation, resulting in an upregulation of myocardial muscarinic receptors but no change in cardiac beta-receptor responsiveness to catecholamines.

title: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase links oxidative PPP, lipogenesis and tumor growth by inhibiting LKB1-AMPK signaling
text: The role of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in promoting tumor growth is well-known, but the specific impact of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD), the third enzyme in this pathway, on tumorigenesis remains uncertain. Our research has revealed that suppressing 6PGD leads to a decrease in lipogenesis and RNA biosynthesis, while also increasing levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cancer cells. This, in turn, hampers cell proliferation and inhibits tumor growth. We have discovered that 6PGD-mediated production of ribulose-5-phosphate (Ru-5-P) disrupts the active LKB1 complex, thereby inhibiting AMPK activation and subsequently activating acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 and lipogenesis. Ru-5-P and NADPH are believed to serve as precursors in RNA biosynthesis and lipogenesis, respectively. Therefore, our findings establish a connection between the oxidative PPP and lipogenesis through Ru-5-P-dependent inhibition of LKB1-AMPK signaling. Additionally, we have successfully identified and developed inhibitors for 6PGD, namely physcion and its derivative S3. These inhibitors have proven to effectively hinder 6PGD activity, cancer cell proliferation, and tumor growth in nude mice xenografts without causing any noticeable toxicity. These results suggest that targeting 6PGD could be a promising approach for anticancer treatment.

title: Plant Nuclear RNA Polymerase IV Mediates siRNA and DNA Methylation-Dependent Heterochromatin Formation
text: All eukaryotes possess three nuclear DNA-dependent RNA polymerases, specifically Pol I, II, and III. It is worth noting that plants have an additional catalytic subunit for a fourth nuclear polymerase, known as Pol IV. Based on genetic and biochemical evidence, it is clear that Pol IV does not have functional overlap with Pol I, II, or III and is not essential for viability. However, when the genes for the Pol IV catalytic subunits NRPD1 or NRPD2 are disrupted, the association of heterochromatin into chromocenters is inhibited. This is accompanied by a decrease in cytosine methylation at pericentromeric 5S gene clusters and AtSN1 retroelements. The loss of CG, CNG, and CNN methylation in Pol IV mutants suggests a collaboration between Pol IV and the methyltransferase responsible for RNA-directed de novo methylation. Supporting this hypothesis, the presence of 5S gene and AtSN1 siRNAs is significantly reduced in Pol IV mutants. These findings indicate that Pol IV plays a role in generating siRNAs that target de novo cytosine methylation events necessary for the formation of facultative heterochromatin and higher-order heterochromatin associations.

title: Sema3A regulates bone-mass accrual through sensory innervations
text: Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) is a chemical signal that repels axons and plays a crucial role in guiding their growth. Previous research has shown that mice lacking Sema3A have various developmental issues due to abnormal connections between neurons. In this study, we discovered that Sema3A is also present in bone tissue and affects the differentiation of osteoblasts, the cells responsible for bone formation. As a result, mice lacking Sema3A had low bone mass due to reduced bone formation. However, when we specifically removed Sema3A from osteoblasts in mice, their bone mass remained normal despite the decreased presence of Sema3A in bone tissue. On the other hand, mice lacking Sema3A in neurons had low bone mass, similar to the mice lacking Sema3A overall. This suggests that Sema3A produced by neurons is responsible for the bone abnormalities, independent of its local effects in bone tissue. Specifically, the number of sensory nerve connections in trabecular bone was significantly reduced in mice lacking Sema3A in neurons, while sympathetic nerve connections remained unchanged. Additionally, removing sensory nerves decreased bone mass in normal mice, but did not further reduce bone mass in mice lacking Sema3A in neurons, highlighting the crucial role of the sensory nervous system in maintaining normal bone health. Furthermore, we found that the neuronal abnormalities observed in mice lacking Sema3A were also present in mice lacking Sema3A specifically in neurons, indicating that neuron-derived Sema3A contributes to the abnormal neural development seen in mice lacking Sema3A overall. This suggests that Sema3A produced by neurons regulates neural development in a self-regulating manner. Overall, this study demonstrates that Sema3A indirectly regulates bone remodeling by influencing the development of sensory nerves, rather than directly affecting osteoblasts.

title: Direct lineage reprogramming: strategies, mechanisms, and applications.
text: The use of defined factors to directly convert one specialized cell type into another has greatly altered our understanding of the epigenetic stability of differentiated cells. In recent years, there has been a significant rise in the generation of different cell types through direct conversion, making this approach a promising method for producing functional cells. In this review, we will examine the latest advancements in lineage reprogramming, such as the discovery of new reprogramming factors, the underlying molecular mechanisms, techniques for generating fully functional cells, and methods for characterizing induced cells. Additionally, we will explore the progress made in applying lineage reprogramming and the major challenges that lie ahead for this strategy.

title: Converging Intracranial Markers of Conscious Access
text: We conducted a study comparing the processing of briefly presented words that were consciously perceived versus those that were not consciously perceived. This was done using a visual masking technique while simultaneously recording intracranial electroencephalogram (iEEG) data from ten patients. We found that nonconscious processing of masked words occurred in various areas of the brain, primarily within a short time frame of less than 300 milliseconds. This was accompanied by an increase in gamma-band activity, but there was no coherent long-distance neural activity, suggesting a rapid dissipating feedforward wave. On the other hand, conscious processing of unmasked words was characterized by the convergence of four distinct neurophysiological markers. These markers included sustained changes in voltage, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, significant increases in spectral power in the gamma band, increases in long-distance phase synchrony in the beta range, and increases in long-range Granger causality. We argue that all of these measures provide different perspectives into the same distributed state of conscious processing. These findings have important implications for ongoing discussions in the field of neuroscience regarding the neural correlates of conscious access.

title: Hyperglycemia is associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased trabecular bone score in elderly Japanese men: The Fujiwara-kyo osteoporosis risk in men (FORMEN) study.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between glycemic and insulin resistance status and bone microarchitecture in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The study also examined the role of pentosidine and bone turnover markers in this association. A total of 2012 men aged 65 years and above participated in the study. Measurements of spine bone mineral density (BMD), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), serum insulin, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), osteocalcin, type I procollagen N-terminal propeptide, type I collagen C-terminal crosslinking telopeptide, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase isoenzyme 5b, pentosidine, height, weight, and past disease history were taken. Homeostasis model assessment-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was also calculated. T2DM was defined based on physician diagnosis or biochemical test results. Trabecular bone score (TBS) was calculated to evaluate bone microarchitecture. After excluding participants with a history of disease or taking medications affecting bone metabolism, 1683 men were analyzed. Men with T2DM had higher BMD compared to those without T2DM, but there was no significant difference in TBS. However, FPG, HbA1c, and HOMA-IR levels were inversely correlated with TBS after adjusting for age, BMI, and BMD. Linear regression analyses showed that glycemic indices (FPG and HbA1c) were associated with increased BMD and decreased TBS, while HOMA-IR was only associated with TBS. These associations remained even after adjusting for bone turnover markers and pentosidine levels. In conclusion, hyperglycemia and elevated insulin resistance were independently associated with low TBS, regardless of bone turnover and pentosidine levels.

title: Matrix Remodeling Promotes Pulmonary Hypertension through Feedback Mechanoactivation of the YAP/TAZ-miR-130/301 Circuit.
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a fatal vascular disease with mysterious molecular origins. Our research has revealed that early and widespread vascular extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and stiffening contribute to the development of PH. Through our study of various pulmonary vascular cell types, we discovered that ECM stiffening activates the co-transcription factors YAP and TAZ, leading to the induction of the microRNA-130/301 family. This microRNA family controls a PPAR?-APOE-LRP8 axis, which promotes collagen deposition and LOX-dependent remodeling. Additionally, it further upregulates YAP/TAZ through a mechanoactive feedback loop. The remodeling of the ECM, in turn, influences communication between pulmonary vascular cells by modulating mechanotransduction, regulating the secretion of vasoactive substances, and controlling associated microRNA pathways. In animal models, inhibiting microRNA-130/301, APOE, or LOX activity through pharmacological means improved ECM remodeling and alleviated PH. Therefore, our findings suggest that ECM remodeling, regulated by the YAP/TAZ-miR-130/301 feedback circuit, serves as an early trigger for PH and presents potential therapeutic targets for this devastating disease.

title: Exosomal transfer of stroma-derived miR21 confers paclitaxel resistance in ovarian cancer cells through targeting APAF1
text: The molecular factors that influence the growth of advanced ovarian cancer in the adipose tissue of the omentum are not well understood. In this study, we used advanced sequencing technology to examine the levels of microRNA-21 (miR21) isomiRNAs in exosomes and tissue samples from cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) and fibroblasts (CAFs), as well as ovarian cancer cells. We found that miR21 is present at significantly higher levels in CAAs and CAFs compared to ovarian cancer cells. Further investigation revealed that miR21 is transferred from CAAs or CAFs to cancer cells, where it inhibits apoptosis and promotes resistance to chemotherapy by targeting a novel gene called APAF1. These findings suggest that miR21 delivered by exosomes from neighboring stromal cells in the omental tumor microenvironment can alter the behavior of metastatic ovarian cancer cells. Inhibiting the transfer of miR21 from stromal cells may be a potential treatment approach for metastatic and recurrent ovarian cancer.

title: Age-related changes in kynurenic acid production in rat brain.
text: Two different laboratory tests were conducted to study the production of kynurenic acid (KYNA), a substance that acts as a broad spectrum excitatory amino acid receptor antagonist, in adult rats. The levels of the enzyme kynurenine aminotransferase, which is responsible for the synthesis of KYNA, were measured in five different regions of the brain. It was found that the enzyme activity steadily increased between 3 and 24 months of age in all brain regions examined, but no changes were observed in the liver. The most significant increases were observed in the cortex and striatum, where enzyme activity tripled during the study period. Additionally, the production of KYNA from its precursor molecule L-kynurenine was studied in slices of brain tissue, and it was found to be significantly higher in the cortex and hippocampus of older animals. The effects of depolarizing agents or sodium replacement were similar in tissues from both young and old rats. These findings align well with previous reports of an age-related increase in KYNA concentration in brain tissue, suggesting that there is an elevated level of KYNA in the aging brain. This, combined with the previously reported decrease in excitatory amino acid receptor densities in the brain with age, may contribute to cognitive and memory problems in older animals.

title: The polycomb group protein Suz12 is required for embryonic stem cell differentiation.
text: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins come together to form complexes known as Polycomb repressive complexes (PRCs). PRC2, one of these complexes, consists of PcG proteins EZH2, SUZ12, and EED. Its main function is to repress transcription by methylating lysine (K) 27 of histone H3 (H3). SUZ12 is crucial for the activity of PRC2, and when it is deactivated, mouse embryos die at an early stage. In this study, we successfully established and cultivated Suz12(-/-) mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells in tissue culture. These cells exhibit a widespread loss of H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and higher expression levels of genes specific to differentiation. Additionally, the Suz12(-/-) ES cells struggle with proper differentiation, resulting in the failure to repress ES cell markers and the activation of genes associated with differentiation. Furthermore, we discovered that PcG proteins are actively recruited to various genes during ES cell differentiation. However, despite an increase in H3K27me3 levels, this recruitment does not always prevent transcriptional activation. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that Suz12 is necessary for establishing specific expression programs crucial for ES cell differentiation. Moreover, we provide evidence that PcG proteins employ different mechanisms to regulate transcription during cellular differentiation.

title: The 1.9 A structure of a proteasome-11S activator complex and implications for proteasome-PAN/PA700 interactions.
text: The cylindrical structures known as proteasomes play a crucial role in various cellular processes by breaking down a wide range of proteins found in the cytosol and nucleus. To carry out this degradation, the proteasomes have axial pores that are opened by activator complexes, allowing substrate access and product release from the catalytic chamber. In our study, we present detailed structures of both normal and mutated archaeal proteasomes bound to the activator PA26, providing evidence that a specific open conformation is necessary for proteolysis.
