This conformation is achieved by displacing surrounding residues outwardly. Through our structures and accompanying biochemical experiments, we have uncovered the mechanism by which PA26 binds to the proteasomes, involving an interaction between the C terminus of PA26 and a conserved lysine. Surprisingly, our biochemical findings suggest that a similar interaction occurs with the unrelated ATP-dependent activators PAN and PA700.

title: Innate Immune and Chemically Triggered Oxidative Stress Modifies Translational Fidelity
text: Accurate transfer RNA (tRNA) aminoacylation is crucial for the proper functioning of proteins and cells. When purified, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases have a fidelity rate of one error per 10,000 to 100,000 couplings. However, the accuracy of tRNA aminoacylation in living organisms is uncertain and may be significantly lower. Our study reveals that in mammalian cells, approximately 1% of methionine (Met) residues used in protein synthesis are incorrectly attached to non-methionyl-tRNAs. Surprisingly, this misacylation of Met increases up to tenfold when cells are exposed to live or non-infectious viruses, toll-like receptor ligands, or chemically induced oxidative stress. The misacylation of Met specifically occurs with certain non-methionyl-tRNA families, and these incorrectly attached tRNAs are still used in translation. We found that an inhibitor of cellular oxidases can block Met misacylation, suggesting that reactive oxygen species (ROS) trigger this error. Among the six amino acids we tested, only Met showed misacylation of tRNA. Since Met residues are known to protect proteins from damage caused by ROS, we propose that Met misacylation serves as an adaptive mechanism to increase Met incorporation into proteins, thereby safeguarding cells against oxidative stress. By uncovering this unexpected aspect of mRNA decoding, our findings highlight the importance of considering alternative interpretations of the genetic code.

title: Yeast sirtuins and the regulation of aging.
text: The sirtuins are a family of protein deacetylases that rely on NAD(+) for their activity. This means that for every lysine side chain they deacetylate, they consume one molecule of NAD(+). Because of their dependence on NAD(+), the sirtuins can be influenced by changes in NAD(+) levels or biosynthesis intermediates, which connects them to cellular metabolism. The Sir2 protein, found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is the original member of the sirtuin family and is well-known for its role as a histone deacetylase. It is involved in silencing certain regions of DNA and has been linked to extending the lifespan of cells. Deleting SIR2 shortens the lifespan, while increasing its gene dosage extends it. Additionally, Sir2 has been implicated in mediating the positive effects of caloric restriction on lifespan, not only in yeast but also in other organisms. Although there have been disagreements and debates surrounding this concept, it has significantly advanced research on aging. S. cerevisiae has four other sirtuins, Hst1, Hst2, Hst3, and Hst4. This review focuses on the function of Sir2 and its homologs in both replicative and chronological aging, as well as how the sirtuins are regulated in response to environmental stresses like caloric restriction.

title: The effect of combination treatment with aliskiren and blockers of the renin-angiotensin system on hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury: systematic review and meta-analysis
text: The objective of this study was to assess the safety of using aliskiren in combination with agents that block the renin-angiotensin system. The study design involved a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Data was collected from various sources, including Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and two trial registries, up until May 7, 2011. The study included published and unpublished randomized controlled trials that compared combined treatment with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers to monotherapy using these agents for at least four weeks. The trials also needed to provide numerical data on the adverse event outcomes of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. A random effects model was used to calculate pooled risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals for these outcomes. The analysis included 10 randomized controlled studies with a total of 4,814 participants. The results showed that combination therapy with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers significantly increased the risk of hyperkalemia compared to monotherapy with these agents or aliskiren alone. However, there was no significant difference in the risk of acute kidney injury between the combined therapy and monotherapy groups. In conclusion, the use of aliskiren in combination with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers is associated with an increased risk of hyperkalemia. Therefore, careful monitoring of serum potassium levels is necessary when using these agents together.

title: The ins and outs of DNA transfer in bacteria.
text: Transformation and conjugation are two primary mechanisms that facilitate the movement of DNA across bacterial membranes. These processes play a crucial role in transferring genetic information between bacterial cells and even between bacterial and eukaryotic cells. Consequently, they are responsible for the dissemination of advantageous traits, such as antibiotic resistance. Typically, both transformation and conjugation involve the recognition of double-stranded DNA, followed by the transfer of single strands. Elaborate molecular machinery is responsible for facilitating the passage of large DNA molecules through the various layers of the cell surface. The components of these machinery involved in transformation and conjugation have been extensively studied and identified. In this study, we present models that elucidate the specific functions of these components in the transport of DNA.

title: Synaptic islands defined by the territory of a single astrocyte.
text: Astrocytes in the mammalian brain play a role in regulating neuronal function by synchronizing neuronal firing and coordinating synaptic networks. However, there is limited understanding of how this is achieved structurally. To investigate this, we examined the three-dimensional relationships between cortical astrocytes and neurons. By using a method to label astrocytes with enhanced green fluorescent protein, we reconstructed the astrocytes in tissue sections or live animals. Our findings revealed that cortical astrocytes have distinct territories that do not overlap, similar to what has been observed in the hippocampus. Through immunofluorescence labeling, we determined that on average, a single astrocyte wraps around four neuronal somata, with a maximum of eight. Additionally, using single-neuron dye-fills, we estimated that one astrocyte makes contact with 300-600 neuronal dendrites. Recent research has shown that glial Ca2+ signaling is limited to individual astrocytes in vivo and that this signaling leads to gliotransmission. Based on these findings, we propose the concept of functional islands of synapses, where groups of synapses within the boundaries of an astrocyte are influenced by the gliotransmitter environment controlled by that astrocyte. This description provides a new framework to understand the interactions between neurons and astrocytes in the mammalian brain, based on their structural organization.

title: Role of DNA Methylation and Epigenetic Silencing of HAND2 in Endometrial Cancer Development
text:
The incidence of endometrial cancer is increasing due to the aging population and obesity rates. The development of this cancer is influenced by environmental and lifestyle factors. Research suggests that the epigenome, which acts as a bridge between the genome and the environment, plays a role in cancer development through hypermethylation of certain genes. This study aimed to investigate the role of epigenetic factors in endometrial cancer.

The researchers conducted an analysis of methylation patterns in endometrial cancer tissue samples and control samples. They found that the HAND2 gene, which encodes a transcription factor in the endometrial stroma, was commonly hypermethylated and silenced in endometrial cancer. Further analysis revealed that HAND2 was the center of the most significant differential methylation hotspot in endometrial cancer.

These findings were validated in multiple clinical sample sets, showing that increased HAND2 methylation was present in premalignant endometrial lesions and correlated with decreased RNA and protein levels. Additionally, women with high HAND2 methylation in their premalignant lesions were less likely to respond to progesterone treatment. Analysis of endometrial secretions collected from women with postmenopausal bleeding using high vaginal swabs identified early stage endometrial cancer with high sensitivity and specificity.

In mice, the researchers found that those with a knockout of the Hand2 gene specifically in their endometrium developed precancerous lesions with age and showed a lack of PTEN expression.

In conclusion, HAND2 methylation is a common and important molecular alteration in endometrial cancer. It has the potential to be used as a biomarker for early detection and treatment response prediction. However, further validation in prospective studies is needed to determine its clinical utility.

title: Socioeconomic factors, material inequalities, and perceived control in self-rated health: cross-sectional data from seven post-communist countries.
text: This study investigated the relationship between perceived control, socioeconomic factors, and self-rated health in seven post-communist countries: Russia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic. Data was collected through questionnaire interviews, which included questions about self-rated health in the past year, education, marital status, perceived control based on nine questions, and material deprivation based on access to food, clothing, and heating. Two measures of material inequalities were available for each population: an inequality score calculated from survey data, which measured the difference between the 90th and 10th percentiles of material deprivation, and the Gini coefficient from published sources. The analysis included data from 5330 men and women aged 20-60. The prevalence of poor health (worse than average) ranged from 8% in Czechs to 19% in Hungarians. After adjusting for age and sex, the odds ratio for university education compared to primary education was 0.36. The odds ratios for a one standard deviation increase in perceived control and material deprivation were 0.58 and 1.51, respectively. The odds ratio for an increase in inequality equivalent to the difference between the most and least unequal populations was 1.49 using the material inequality score and 1.41 using the Gini coefficient. However, after controlling for individuals' deprivation or perceived control, there was no significant effect of either measure of inequality. The results suggest that, similar to Western populations, education and material deprivation are strongly associated with self-rated health. Perceived control was found to partially mediate the effects of material deprivation. The non-significant effects of both measures of inequality were eliminated when accounting for individuals' characteristics.

title: Integrin αvβ3/c-src “Oncogenic Unit” Promotes Anchorage-independence and Tumor Progression
text:
Integrins play a crucial role in regulating the growth, survival, and invasion of tumor cells through adhesion. Specifically, the expression of integrin alpha(v)beta(3) has been linked to the progression of various human tumors. However, our study uncovers a previously unknown function of integrin alpha(v)beta(3) in pancreatic cancer and other carcinomas, which is independent of adhesion.

In our research, we found that alpha(v)beta(3) expressed in carcinoma cells promotes tumor growth in the absence of anchorage in vitro and increases the spread of cancer cells to lymph nodes in vivo. These effects were dependent on the recruitment of c-Src to the beta(3) integrin cytoplasmic tail, resulting in the activation of c-Src, phosphorylation of Crk-associated substrate (CAS), and enhanced survival of tumor cells. Surprisingly, these effects were not influenced by cell adhesion or activation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK).

To further investigate this mechanism, we conducted experiments using pharmacological inhibitors to block c-Src kinase activity or decrease the expression of endogenous alpha(v)beta(3) integrin or c-Src. These interventions not only inhibited anchorage-independent tumor growth but also suppressed metastasis in vivo. However, they did not affect the migration or invasion of tumor cells.

Our findings highlight an unexpected role for integrin as a mediator of anchorage independence, suggesting that the alpha(v)beta(3)-c-Src signaling module may contribute to the aggressive behavior of tumors expressing integrin alpha(v)beta(3) in humans.

title: Genomewide Analysis of PRC1 and PRC2 Occupancy Identifies Two Classes of Bivalent Domains
text: The promoters of over 2,000 genes in embryonic stem (ES) cells are marked by bivalent chromatin domains, which contain both repressive and activating histone modifications. To understand these domains better, we conducted a study where we mapped key histone modifications and subunits of Polycomb-repressive complexes 1 and 2 (PRC1 and PRC2) in human and mouse ES cells. This was done using chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by ultra high-throughput sequencing. Our findings revealed that bivalent domains can be divided into two classes: one occupied by both PRC2 and PRC1 (PRC1-positive) and the other specifically bound by PRC2 (PRC2-only). The PRC1-positive domains were functionally distinct as they retained lysine 27 tri-methylation more efficiently during differentiation, showed strong conservation of chromatin state, and were associated with a large number of developmental regulator gene promoters. Additionally, we used computational genomics to search for sequence determinants of Polycomb binding. This analysis showed that the locations, sizes, and underlying motif contents of CpG islands largely predicted the genomewide locations of PRC2 and PRC1. We propose that large CpG islands lacking activating motifs play a role in epigenetic memory by recruiting the full range of Polycomb complexes in pluripotent cells.

title: Spatiotemporal regulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition is essential for squamous cell carcinoma metastasis.
text: The process known as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is believed to play a role in transforming stationary epithelial tumor cells into mobile mesenchymal cells during the spread of cancer. However, the role of EMT in metastasis is still a subject of debate, as human carcinoma metastases do not typically exhibit a mesenchymal phenotype. In this study, we utilized a mouse model of spontaneous squamous cell carcinoma to demonstrate that the activation of the EMT-inducing transcription factor Twist1 is sufficient to induce EMT in carcinoma cells and allow them to enter the bloodstream. Crucially, we found that turning off Twist1 in distant locations is necessary for disseminated tumor cells to revert back to their original state and form metastases. Our findings provide in vivo evidence for the importance of "reversible EMT" in tumor metastasis and may help resolve the controversy surrounding the role of EMT in carcinoma metastasis.

title: Control of Apoptosis by Asymmetric Cell Division
text: The processes of asymmetric cell division and programmed cell death (apoptosis) are crucial for the development and functioning of multicellular organisms. Our research has revealed a functional connection between these two processes. Specifically, we have discovered that in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, asymmetric cell division is regulated by a pathway involving three genes: dnj-11 MIDA1, ces-2 HLF, and ces-1 Snail. These genes directly control the enzymatic machinery responsible for apoptosis. Interestingly, similar proteins, such as GlsA in the alga Volvox carteri and Snail, Escargot, and Worniu in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, have previously been associated with asymmetric cell division. This suggests that the involvement of C. elegans dnj-11 MIDA1, ces-2 HLF, and ces-1 Snail in asymmetric cell division may be conserved across plant and animal species. Additionally, our findings suggest that this pathway also plays a direct role in determining the fate of apoptosis in C. elegans and potentially other animals.

title: CXCR2 mediates NADPH oxidase–independent neutrophil extracellular trap formation in cystic fibrosis airway inflammation
text: Neutrophils release DNA fibers decorated with antimicrobial proteins, forming neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) when activated. While NETs are beneficial for innate host defense, excessive NET formation has been associated with the development of autoinflammatory diseases. However, the mechanisms that regulate NET formation, especially during chronic inflammation, are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) CXCR2 is responsible for mediating NET formation. Further analysis revealed that CXCR2-mediated NET formation is not dependent on NADPH oxidase and involves Src family kinases. We also demonstrate the relevance of this mechanism in cystic fibrosis lung disease, which is characterized by chronic inflammation caused by neutrophils. We observed an abundance of NETs in the airway fluids of individuals with cystic fibrosis and in a mouse model of cystic fibrosis lung disease. The amount of NETs correlated with impaired lung function. By blocking CXCR2 in the lungs using small-molecule antagonists, we were able to inhibit NET formation and improve lung function without affecting neutrophil recruitment, proteolytic activity, or antibacterial defense. These findings establish CXCR2 as a receptor that mediates NADPH oxidase–independent NET formation and suggest that targeting this GPCR pathway could be a potential therapeutic strategy for cystic fibrosis lung disease.

title: Modelling the Impact of Artemisinin Combination Therapy and Long-Acting Treatments on Malaria Transmission Intensity
text:
BACKGROUND
Artemisinin derivatives, which are used in combination therapies for malaria, have the potential to reduce the transmission of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. As malaria elimination becomes a priority, it is important to understand the impact of different antimalarial drugs on transmission. This study aims to estimate the reduction in transmission that can be achieved by introducing different types of treatment for symptomatic P. falciparum malaria in endemic areas.

METHODS AND FINDINGS
A mathematical model was developed to predict the potential impact of introducing artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) as the first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria in six areas of varying transmission intensity in Tanzania. The study also estimated the impact of antimalarials with different efficacy, prophylactic time, and gametocytocidal effects. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 5,667 individuals conducted prior to the policy change from sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine to ACT were used to estimate rates of treatment, asymptomatic infection, and symptomatic infection in the six study areas. The effects of ACT and other drug types on gametocytaemia and infectiousness to mosquitoes were estimated using clinical trial data. 

The study found that the percentage reductions in infection prevalence and clinical episodes achieved by ACT were highest in areas with low initial transmission. In the area with the lowest baseline slide-prevalence of parasitaemia (3.7%), switching 100% of current treatment to ACT resulted in a 53% reduction in infection prevalence, compared to an 11% reduction in the highest-transmission setting (baseline slide prevalence = 57.1%). The percentage reductions in clinical episode incidence were similar. However, the absolute impact on public health was greater in the highest-transmission area, with 54 clinical episodes per 100 persons per year averted compared to five per 100 persons per year in the lowest-transmission area. High coverage of treatment was crucial for achieving these reductions. 

The study also found that reducing presumptive treatment through improved diagnosis reduced the number of treatment courses required per clinical episode averted in lower-transmission settings, although there was some loss of overall impact on transmission. In the highest-transmission setting, an antimalarial regimen with no specific gametocytocidal properties but a long prophylactic time was estimated to be more effective at reducing transmission than a short-acting ACT.

CONCLUSIONS
The results suggest that ACTs have the potential to achieve transmission reductions similar to those achieved by insecticide-treated nets in lower-transmission settings. In higher-transmission settings, ACT partner drugs and nonartemisinin regimens with longer prophylactic times could have a larger impact, although their long-term benefits must be evaluated in relation to the risk of parasite resistance development.

title: Systems metabolic engineering of Escherichia coli for L-threonine production
text: In the past, amino-acid producers have been created through random mutagenesis due to the challenges in designing the complex and tightly regulated metabolic network. However, we have now developed a genetically defined Escherichia coli strain that overproduces L-threonine using systems metabolic engineering. We achieved this by removing feedback inhibitions of aspartokinase I and III (encoded by thrA and lysC) and transcriptional attenuation regulations located in thrL. Additionally, we deleted pathways for Thr degradation by eliminating tdh and mutating ilvA. To increase the availability of precursors for Thr biosynthesis, we deleted the metA and lysA genes. Through transcriptome profiling and in silico flux response analysis, we identified target genes for further engineering and manipulated their expression levels accordingly. The final engineered E. coli strain was capable of producing Thr with a high yield of 0.393 g per gram of glucose and achieved a Thr concentration of 82.4 g/l through fed-batch culture. This systems metabolic engineering approach can be widely applied to develop genetically defined organisms for efficient production of various bioproducts.

title: Association Between ADHD and Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obesity/overweight. Previous research has shown that impulsivity and inattention, which are symptoms of ADHD, may lead to increased food intake and weight gain. However, the findings on the association between ADHD and obesity/overweight have been inconsistent. Therefore, the authors conducted a meta-analysis to estimate this association.

The researchers searched a wide range of databases and obtained unpublished studies up until August 31, 2014. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and random-effects models were used for the analysis.

A total of 42 studies, involving 728,136 individuals (48,161 with ADHD and 679,975 without ADHD), were included in the analysis. The results showed a significant association between obesity and ADHD in both children and adults. The odds ratio for obesity in children with ADHD compared to those without ADHD was 1.20 (95% CI=1.05-1.37), and for adults, it was 1.55 (95% CI=1.32-1.81). The prevalence of obesity was found to be approximately 70% higher in adults with ADHD (28.2%, 95% CI=22.8-34.4) compared to those without ADHD (16.4%, 95% CI=13.4-19.9). In children, the prevalence of obesity was approximately 40% higher in those with ADHD (10.3%, 95% CI=7.9-13.3) compared to those without ADHD (7.4%, 95% CI=5.4-10.1).

The significant association between ADHD and obesity remained even when the analysis was limited to studies that adjusted for confounding factors, diagnosed ADHD through direct interviews, and used directly measured height and weight. The association was not influenced by gender, study setting, study country, or study quality. Additionally, ADHD was also found to be significantly associated with overweight. However, individuals who were medicated for ADHD did not have a higher risk of obesity.

In conclusion, this meta-analysis provides evidence for a significant association between ADHD and obesity/overweight. Further research is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms and the long-term effects of ADHD treatments on weight in individuals with both ADHD and obesity.

title: Amyloid-DNA Composites of Bacterial Biofilms Stimulate Autoimmunity.
text: Research on the human microbiome has revealed that both helpful and harmful bacteria can impact obesity, cancer, and autoimmunity, although the specific mechanisms are not fully understood. Our study discovered that a component of bacterial biofilms, called curli, forms irreversible fibers with bacterial DNA during biofilm formation. This interaction speeds up the formation of amyloid proteins and creates powerful immunogenic complexes that activate immune cells, including dendritic cells. These activated cells produce cytokines like type I interferons, which can contribute to the development of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disease. When administered systemically, curli-DNA composites triggered immune activation and the production of autoantibodies in both lupus-prone and normal mice. Additionally, we observed that infection with curli-producing bacteria led to higher levels of autoantibodies in lupus-prone mice compared to infection with curli-deficient bacteria. These findings provide insight into how the microbiome and biofilm-producing enteric infections may contribute to the progression of SLE, and suggest a potential target for treating autoimmune conditions.

title: Comprehensive genomic characterization defines human glioblastoma genes and core pathways
text: Human cancer cells typically contain multiple abnormalities in their chromosomes, nucleotides, and epigenetic modifications, which contribute to their transformation into malignant cells. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pilot project aims to evaluate the significance of analyzing these molecular characteristics on a large scale and provide the resulting data quickly to the research community. In this study, we present an interim analysis of 206 glioblastomas, the most common type of primary brain cancer in adults. We examined DNA copy number, gene expression, DNA methylation abnormalities, and nucleotide sequence abnormalities in 91 of these glioblastomas. Our analysis reveals new insights into the roles of ERBB2, NF1, and TP53 genes, identifies frequent mutations in the PIK3R1 gene, which regulates the phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase, and provides a comprehensive view of the pathways involved in the development of glioblastoma. Additionally, by integrating mutation, DNA methylation, and clinical treatment data, we discovered a connection between MGMT promoter methylation and a hypermutator phenotype caused by mismatch repair deficiency in treated glioblastomas. This observation has potential clinical implications. Overall, these findings demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of the TCGA project in rapidly expanding our understanding of the molecular basis of cancer.

title: LY2405319, an Engineered FGF21 Variant, Improves the Metabolic Status of Diabetic Monkeys
text: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a new regulator of metabolism that shows promise as a treatment for various metabolic diseases. When diabetic animals are given recombinant wild type FGF21, their blood sugar levels improve dramatically and their overall metabolic health improves. In this study, we examine the effects of a recently developed FGF21 analogue called LY2405319 (LY) on non-human primates. Diabetic rhesus monkeys were given LY injections under the skin once a day for seven weeks. The doses of LY used were 3, 9, and 50 mg/kg, with measurements taken at 2, 4, 6, and 8 weeks after the last dose. LY therapy resulted in significant and rapid improvements in several important metabolic parameters, including blood sugar, body weight, insulin, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, at all doses tested. We also observed positive changes in the levels of adipokines in the blood, with increased adiponectin and decreased leptin, indicating that FGF21 directly affects adipose tissue. Importantly, this study demonstrates for the first time that FGF21-based therapy is effective in an animal with advanced diabetes. Although the blood sugar-lowering effect of LY was somewhat reduced in this animal, its ability to lower lipid levels was fully preserved. This suggests that FGF21 may be a viable treatment option even for patients with advanced disease progression. These findings support further investigation of the FGF21 pathway for the treatment of metabolic diseases.

title: Epigenetic Control of Stem Cell Potential during Homeostasis, Aging, and Disease.
text: The decline of stem cells plays a crucial role in the aging process and the development of age-related diseases in various tissues. The regulation of gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms is essential for maintaining the function of stem cells. Recent evidence suggests that when epigenetic regulation is disrupted, it contributes to the decline in the potential of stem cells during aging. Unlike mature cells, epigenetic dysregulation in stem cells can have long-lasting effects beyond the individual cell. These alterations can be passed down to the offspring of differentiated cells and can also be amplified within the stem cell population through self-renewal divisions. This article reviews recent research on how epigenetic regulation affects tissue-specific stem cells in normal conditions, aging, and age-related diseases.

title: Host–Parasite Interactions and the Evolution of Gene Expression
text: The interaction between hosts and parasites is a constant source of selection that drives the evolution of various characteristics in both species. In this study, we utilize a mathematically explicit model to investigate how gene expression patterns evolve at specific genetic locations responsible for host resistance and parasite infection. Our findings reveal a remarkable yet logical conclusion: gene expression evolves differently in the two species involved. Specifically, genes responsible for host resistance tend to evolve to co-express multiple alleles, while genes responsible for parasite infection tend to express only a single allele. This outcome occurs because hosts that co-express resistance alleles are capable of recognizing and eliminating a wider range of parasite genotypes. Similarly, parasites that co-express antigen or elicitor alleles are more likely to be recognized and eliminated by the host, thus favoring the expression of a single allele. Our model generates testable predictions that can aid in the interpretation of accumulating data on gene expression levels relevant to host-parasite interactions.

title: A crucial role for interleukin (IL)-1 in the induction of IL-17–producing T cells that mediate autoimmune encephalomyelitis
text: Recent research has shown that a specific type of T cells called interleukin (IL)-23–driven IL-17–producing (ThIL-17) T cells play a role in causing inflammation in certain autoimmune diseases. In our study, we found that the production of antigen-specific ThIL-17 cells, but not other types of T helper cells (Th1 or Th2), was disrupted in mice lacking the IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1RI−/−) when they were immunized with antigens and adjuvants. Additionally, the occurrence of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) was significantly lower in IL-1RI−/− mice compared to normal mice, and this was due to the failure to induce autoantigen-specific ThIL-17 cells. However, when we transferred autoantigen-specific cells from normal mice with EAE to IL-1RI−/− mice, EAE was induced. We also found that IL-23 alone did not stimulate IL-17 production in T cells from IL-1RI−/− mice, but the presence of IL-1α or IL-1β greatly enhanced IL-23-induced IL-17 production, even without T cell receptor stimulation. Our study revealed that phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, nuclear factor κB, and novel protein kinase C isoforms are essential for IL-1 and IL-23 to stimulate IL-17 production. Additionally, tumor necrosis factor α worked together with IL-23 to increase IL-17 production, and this process was dependent on IL-1. Overall, our findings demonstrate that IL-1 plays a crucial role in promoting the development of pathogenic ThIL-17 cells in EAE, acting upstream of IL-17.

title: Aberrant luminal progenitors as the candidate target population for basal tumor development in BRCA1 mutation carriers
text: Women with mutations in the BRCA1 gene, which codes for the tumor suppressor protein BRCA1, are believed to develop basal-like breast cancers from mammary stem cells. In order to investigate the early cellular changes in BRCA1 mutation carriers, we have isolated different epithelial subpopulations from normal mammary tissue and preneoplastic samples from individuals with a BRCA1 mutation. We have identified three subsets of epithelial cells: basal stem/progenitor cells, luminal progenitor cells, and mature luminal cells. Surprisingly, we have discovered that breast tissue from BRCA1 mutation carriers contains an expanded population of luminal progenitor cells that can grow independently of external factors in vitro. Additionally, gene expression analysis has shown that breast tissue with a BRCA1 mutation and basal breast tumors are more similar to normal luminal progenitor cells than any other subset, including the stem cell-enriched population. The c-KIT tyrosine kinase receptor, encoded by the KIT gene, has emerged as a significant marker for luminal progenitor cells and is expressed at higher levels in BRCA1-associated preneoplastic tissue and tumors. Our findings suggest that an abnormal population of luminal progenitor cells is a target for transformation in BRCA1-associated basal tumors.

title: Getting to the site of inflammation: the leukocyte adhesion cascade updated
text: Adhesion and transmigration through blood-vessel walls are essential for neutrophil recruitment, lymphocyte recirculation, and monocyte trafficking. The traditional three steps of rolling, activation, and firm adhesion have recently been expanded and refined. Additional steps, including slow rolling, adhesion strengthening, intraluminal crawling, and paracellular and transcellular migration, are now recognized as separate processes. In neutrophils, a second activation pathway has been discovered that does not rely on signalling through G-protein-coupled receptors, and the signalling steps leading to integrin activation are starting to be understood. This Review focuses on the latest developments in one of the central concepts of inflammation and immunity — the leukocyte adhesion cascade.

title: Genome-wide loss of 5-hmC is a novel epigenetic feature of Huntington's disease.
text: The presence of 5-Hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) may indicate a new type of cytosine epigenetic modification. Although there have been recent reports on the changes in 5-hmC levels during neurodevelopment, little is known about its distribution and functions in neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's disease (HD). In this study, we observed a significant decrease in the 5-hmC signal in the brain tissues of YAC128 HD mice (mice with a yeast artificial chromosome transgene containing 128 CAG repeats) compared to age-matched wild-type (WT) mice. This suggests a deficiency in the reconstruction of 5-hmC in HD brains during postnatal development. Further analysis of the genome-wide distribution of 5-hmC confirmed the reduction of the 5-hmC signal in the striatum and cortex of YAC128 HD mice. The general genomic features of 5-hmC remained highly conserved and were not affected by the disease or brain regions. Interestingly, we identified disease-specific differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) between YAC128 and WT mice. We found that the acquisition of DhMRs in gene bodies positively regulated gene expression. Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) of genotype-specific DhMR-annotated genes revealed that alterations in several canonical pathways related to neuronal development/differentiation (Wnt/β-catenin/Sox pathway, axonal guidance signaling pathway) and neuronal function/survival (glutamate receptor/calcium/CREB, GABA receptor signaling, dopamine-DARPP32 feedback pathway, etc.) could be important for the onset of HD. Our results suggest that the loss of the 5-hmC marker is a novel epigenetic characteristic in HD and that this abnormal epigenetic regulation may impair neurogenesis, neuronal function, and survival in the HD brain. Additionally, our study provides a new approach for HD treatment, as re-establishing the native 5-hmC landscape may have the potential to slow down or halt the progression of HD.

title: Planning for Postdisaster Resiliency
text: This article focuses on the importance of planning for resiliency after a catastrophe. The authors first explain their understanding of planning for resiliency as a goal for communities in the recovery process, and highlight the advantages of planning in creating more resilient places. They then delve into the major challenges associated with planning for post-disaster recovery, such as the obstacles imposed by federal and state governments, the potential benefits and drawbacks of compact urban form models for guiding rebuilding efforts, and the failure to involve citizens in disaster planning. Lastly, they draw insights from previous research to address these issues and provide policy recommendations that promote pre-disaster recovery planning for resilient communities.

title: Increased stress-induced inflammatory responses in male patients with major depression and increased early life stress.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the activation of the innate immune system in patients with major depression and a history of early life stress following psychosocial stress. The researchers compared plasma interleukin (IL)-6 levels, lymphocyte subsets, and DNA binding of nuclear factor (NF)-kB in peripheral blood mononuclear cells between medically healthy male subjects with current major depression and early life stress (N=14) and nondepressed male comparison subjects (N=14) before and after completing the Trier Social Stress Test. The results showed that the Trier Social Stress Test led to greater increases in IL-6 and NF-kappaB DNA-binding in major depression patients with early life stress, and these increases were independently associated with the severity of depression. However, there was no correlation between early life stress and these immune system markers. The percentage of natural killer (NK) cells also increased following stress, but there were no differences between the two groups and no correlation between NK cell percentage and stress-induced NF-kappaB DNA-binding or IL-6 levels. In conclusion, male patients with major depression and early life stress demonstrate heightened inflammatory response to psychosocial stress, suggesting a potential link between major depression, early life stress, and negative health outcomes associated with inflammation.

title: KIF3A/B: a heterodimeric kinesin superfamily protein that works as a microtubule plus end-directed motor for membrane organelle transport
text: We successfully cloned a new member of the murine brain kinesin superfamily, known as KIF3B. Upon analysis, we discovered that the amino acid sequence of KIF3B is highly similar to, but not identical to, KIF3A, which we had previously cloned and named KIF3 (with a 47% similarity). KIF3B is present in various organ tissues and developing neurons of mice, and it accumulates with membranous organelles that move in an anterograde direction after nerve axon ligation. Through an immunoprecipitation assay of the brain, we determined that KIF3B forms a complex with KIF3A and three other high molecular weight polypeptides, collectively referred to as the kinesin superfamily-associated protein 3 (KAP3). In vitro experiments using baculovirus expression systems demonstrated that KIF3A and KIF3B directly bind to each other even in the absence of KAP3. The recombinant KIF3A/B complex, which consists of a 50-nm rod with two globular heads and a single globular tail, exhibited microtubule sliding activity in the plus end-directed direction. Furthermore, we discovered that KIF3B itself possesses motor activity in vitro when combined with a chimeric motor protein (KIF3B head and KIF3A rod tail). Subcellular fractionation of mouse brain homogenates revealed that a significant portion of the native KIF3 complex is associated with membrane fractions other than synaptic vesicles. Immunoprecipitation using anti-KIF3B antibody-conjugated beads, along with electron microscopic analysis, confirmed the association of KIF3 with membranous organelles. Additionally, we observed that the composition of KAP3 differs between the brain and testis. Based on our findings, we propose that KIF3B forms a heterodimer with KIF3A and acts as a new microtubule-based anterograde translocator for membranous organelles. Furthermore, we suggest that the functional diversity of the KIF3 complex in different cell types in vivo may be determined by KAP3.

title: A genetic screen identifies an LKB1–MARK signalling axis controlling the Hippo–YAP pathway
text: The Hippo-YAP pathway is a newly discovered signaling pathway that plays a role in controlling the activity of stem cells and the size of organs. In order to understand this pathway better, we conducted a study using RNA interference to screen the kinome in human cells. This screening process helped us identify several kinases that were not previously known to be involved in Hippo signaling, but are actually responsible for controlling various cellular processes. One of the kinases we discovered, LKB1, is a well-known tumor suppressor, although its exact mechanism of action is not fully understood. Our research shows that LKB1 works through its substrates from the microtubule affinity-regulating kinase family to regulate the localization of Scribble, a polarity determinant, and the activity of the core Hippo kinases. Furthermore, our findings suggest that YAP, a protein involved in the Hippo-YAP pathway, is crucial for the tumor-suppressing effects of LKB1. This discovery establishes a connection between YAP activation and LKB1 mutations, which has important implications for the treatment of LKB1-mutant cancers in humans. Additionally, our study provides valuable insights into the upstream signals that regulate the Hippo-YAP signaling cascade.

title: Beyond melanoma: inhibiting the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in solid tumors.
text: The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors has been recognized as a groundbreaking treatment for melanoma due to its remarkable response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. This breakthrough is expected to have a significant impact on various other types of cancer, as numerous clinical trials are currently underway or proposed to explore this promising therapy. While the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors has been extensively studied in melanoma and more recently in lung cancer, there is limited knowledge regarding their use in other types of cancer. This review will concentrate on the immune microenvironment of tumors, the expression of PD-1/PD-L1, and the impact of immune modulation through PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors in patients with head and neck, prostate, urothelial, renal, breast, gastrointestinal, and lung cancers.

title: Partitioning the symptoms of hypoglycaemia using multi-sample confirmatory factor analysis
text:
The categorization of hypoglycemic symptoms into autonomous or neuroglycopenic groups is typically done without sufficient scientific evidence. To address the need for clear symptom markers of hypoglycemia, we conducted two large-scale studies that provide substantial evidence for a three-factor model of hypoglycemic symptomatology. These studies analyzed the reported symptoms of diabetic patients.

In Study 1, we examined 295 outpatients who were receiving insulin treatment. We identified 11 key hypoglycemic symptoms that could be grouped into three distinct factors: autonomous symptoms (sweating, palpitation, shaking, and hunger), neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, odd behavior, speech difficulty, and incoordination), and malaise symptoms (nausea and headache). We then validated these three factors using a separate group of 303 insulin-treated diabetic outpatients.

Confirmatory factor analyses were conducted to determine the best model for explaining the covariance of symptoms within each group. The results consistently supported the three-factor model as the optimal explanation. Furthermore, a multi-sample confirmatory factor analysis confirmed that the relative loadings of symptoms on factors were equal across groups, and the residual variance for each symptom was identical across groups. This replication of the three-factor model in detail across both samples strengthens the validity of the findings.

Based on these results, we propose that these symptom groupings can be used in future research and clinical practice as reliable indicators of hypoglycemia.

title: Extracellular vesicles from human cardiac progenitor cells inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improve cardiac function after myocardial infarction.
text:
New evidence suggests that cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) may have a positive impact on cardiac function following injury. However, the specific mechanisms by which they achieve this are not yet fully understood. One possibility is that extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes and other secreted membrane vesicles, act as mediators of paracrine signaling. In this study, we demonstrate that EVs secreted by human CPCs play a crucial role in protecting the heart. 

To conduct our research, we derived CPCs from atrial appendage explants taken from patients who had undergone heart valve surgery. We found that CPC-conditioned medium (CM) inhibited apoptosis in mouse HL-1 cardiomyocytic cells and promoted tube formation in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Importantly, these effects were only observed when CM contained EVs, as depleting EVs from CM abolished these benefits. Furthermore, we discovered that EVs secreted by CPCs, but not those secreted by human dermal fibroblasts, were able to reproduce these effects. 

Using transmission electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis, we determined that the majority of EVs were between 30-90 nm in diameter, similar to the size of exosomes. However, we also observed smaller and larger vesicles. We identified several microRNAs that were highly enriched in EVs secreted by CPCs compared to fibroblasts, including miR-210, miR-132, and miR-146a-3p. Notably, miR-210 was found to down-regulate ephrin A3 and PTP1b, known targets involved in apoptosis inhibition in cardiomyocytic cells. On the other hand, miR-132 down-regulated RasGAP-p120, a target that enhanced tube formation in endothelial cells. 

To assess the therapeutic potential of EVs, we injected them into infarcted hearts and compared the results to hearts injected with EVs from fibroblasts or control medium. We found that hearts injected with CPC-derived EVs exhibited reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, increased angiogenesis, and improved left ventricular ejection fraction compared to the control group. 

In conclusion, our findings indicate that EVs are the active component responsible for the cardioprotective effects of human CPCs. This cell-free approach using EVs could potentially overcome the limitations associated with cell transplantation.

title: Increased Adipocyte O2 Consumption Triggers HIF-1α, Causing Inflammation and Insulin Resistance in Obesity
text: Obesity-induced insulin resistance has been linked to hypoxia and inflammation in adipose tissue. In this study, we found that early in the development of obesity from a high-fat diet, adipocyte respiration becomes uncoupled, causing increased oxygen consumption and a state of relative hypoxia in adipocytes. These changes trigger the induction of HIF-1α, which leads to the chronic inflammatory response seen in obesity. At a molecular level, saturated fatty acids stimulate a protein called adenine nucleotide translocase 2 (ANT2) in the inner mitochondrial membrane, resulting in the uncoupled respiratory state. By inhibiting either ANT2 or HIF-1α through genetic or pharmacologic means, we were able to prevent or reverse these pathological events, restoring insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. These findings provide insight into the sequence of events that contribute to inflammation and insulin resistance in obesity.

title: Lpcat3-dependent production of arachidonoyl phospholipids is a key determinant of triglyceride secretion
text: The assessment of the role of specific phospholipids (PLs) in lipid transport has been challenging due to the inability to selectively manipulate membrane composition in living organisms. However, our study reveals that the enzyme lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 3 (Lpcat3) plays a crucial role in triglyceride (TG) secretion by incorporating arachidonate into membranes. In mice lacking Lpcat3 in the intestine, we observed failure to thrive during weaning, accumulation of lipids in enterocytes, and reduced levels of TGs in the bloodstream. Similarly, mice lacking Lpcat3 in the liver exhibited reduced plasma TGs, hepatosteatosis, and the secretion of lipid-poor very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) lacking arachidonoyl PLs. Our mechanistic studies suggest that Lpcat3 activity affects the mobility of membrane lipids in living cells, providing a biophysical explanation for the necessity of arachidonoyl PLs in the lipidation of lipoprotein particles. These findings highlight the significance of Lpcat3 in lipoprotein production and demonstrate how manipulating membrane composition can serve as a regulatory mechanism for controlling metabolic pathways.

title: Characterization of a single-stranded DNA-binding protein from Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1.
text: The role of Single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) in DNA metabolism, including DNA replication, repair, and recombination, is crucial for the survival of cells. We conducted a study to examine the binding properties of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 SSB (PaSSB) to single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) using fluorescence quenching measurements and electrophoretic mobility shift analysis (EMSA). Through gel filtration chromatography, we determined that purified PaSSB forms a stable tetramer in solution. In fluorescence titrations, PaSSB was found to bind 22-32 nucleotides (nt) per tetramer, depending on the salt concentration. By utilizing EMSA, we investigated the stoichiometry of PaSSB complexed with various ssDNA homopolymers and determined that the size of the binding site is approximately 29 ± 1 nt. Additionally, EMSA results indicated that the dissociation constants of PaSSB for the first tetramer were lower than those for the second tetramer. Based on these biophysical analyses, we anticipate that the ssDNA binding mode of PaSSB is noncooperative.

title: Primary cilia and coordination of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signalling.
text: This review provides an overview of primary cilia, which are sensory organelles made of microtubules. These cilia play a crucial role in coordinating various cellular processes such as cell-cycle control, migration, and differentiation, which are essential for development and tissue homeostasis. When there are problems with the assembly or function of primary cilia, it can result in a range of developmental disorders and pathological conditions known as ciliopathies. The review also focuses on the current understanding of how primary cilia coordinate receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signalling pathways. Additionally, it explores potential mechanisms of signalling crosstalk and networking within the primary cilium and discusses the connection between defects in ciliary RTK signalling and human diseases and disorders.

title: Detecting and targeting tumor relapse by its resistance to innate effectors at early recurrence
text: Tumor recurrence poses a significant challenge in clinical practice. Our findings indicate that recurrent tumors that emerge later on exhibit a completely different phenotype compared to their original primary tumors. This altered phenotype enables them to evade the innate immune response triggered by the transition from minimal residual disease (MRD) to actively growing recurrence. Through screening for this innate response, we were able to accurately predict the occurrence of recurrence in mice. Moreover, initiating recurrence prematurely made MRD susceptible to the primary therapy once again, suggesting a potential shift in the clinical approach to dormant disease. Instead of adopting a passive approach, active efforts to detect MRD before the development of the escape phenotype could be more effective. By combining screening with second-line treatments that target innate insensitivity, we achieved a cure rate of up to 100% in mice that would have otherwise experienced a relapse. These findings have the potential to revolutionize early detection and precise timing of treatment for tumor recurrence, regardless of the tumor type or initial treatment received.

title: Forces in Tissue Morphogenesis and Patterning
text: Mechanical forces play a crucial role in the development of organisms, as they can cause various changes in cells such as size, shape, number, position, and gene expression. These forces are essential for any processes involved in shaping the body. Two self-organizing phenomena, namely force generation by actin-myosin networks and force transmission through adhesive complexes, drive the morphogenesis of tissues. By coordinating and integrating forces, cells within tissues can produce significant changes in the overall shape of the tissue. Additionally, external mechanical forces also influence the patterning of tissues by regulating the fate specification and differentiation of cells. Therefore, the interaction between tissue mechanics and biochemical signaling is responsible for orchestrating the development of tissues and their patterns.

title: CD169+ MACROPHAGES PRESENT LIPID ANTIGENS TO MEDIATE EARLY ACTIVATION OF INVARIANT NKT CELLS IN LYMPH NODES
text: Invariant natural killer T cells (iNKT cells) play a crucial role in defending the host against microbial infections. However, the exact mechanism and location of their antigen encounter in vivo have yet to be fully understood. To address this, we utilized multiphoton microscopy to observe the behavior and activation of iNKT cells in lymph nodes. Our findings revealed that following antigen administration, iNKT cells became restricted in their movement in a CD1d-dependent manner, positioning themselves near subcapsular sinus CD169(+) macrophages. These macrophages not only retained and internalized lipid antigens but also presented them, thereby facilitating the activation, cytokine production, and expansion of iNKT cells. Consequently, CD169(+) macrophages serve as genuine antigen-presenting cells, playing a crucial role in regulating early iNKT cell activation and promoting the rapid initiation of immune responses.

title: Oxygen Metabolism Causes Chromosome Breaks and Is Associated with the Neuronal Apoptosis Observed in DNA Double-Strand Break Repair Mutants
text: Cells lacking a key pathway for repairing DNA double-strand breaks (known as nonhomologous DNA end joining or NHEJ) experience an increase in spontaneous chromosome breaks. However, the origin of these chromosome breaks has remained unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that the observed spontaneous chromosome breaks can be partially reduced by lowering the oxygen levels within the cells. Conversely, when the level of reactive oxygen species is increased by overexpressing the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) in a transgenic mouse, chromosome breakage is enhanced. The impact of SOD1 can also be influenced by the oxygen levels within the cells. The increased chromosome breakage is histologically associated with a significant rise in neuronal cell death in Ku86(-/-) SOD1 transgenic embryos compared to Ku86(-/-) embryos. Therefore, oxygen metabolism is a major contributor to the genomic instability observed in cells deficient in NHEJ and likely in all cells.

title: Insertional mutagenesis in gene therapy and stem cell biology.
text: The purpose of this review is to discuss the potential risks associated with the insertion of transgenes into the DNA of hematopoietic cells, as well as the recent advancements in understanding the underlying mechanisms and improving gene vector biosafety. Previous studies have shown that the random insertion of transgenes can lead to clonal competition and potentially trigger leukemia or sarcoma. This has raised concerns among researchers developing hematopoietic cell therapies. However, recent findings have shed light on the characteristic insertion patterns of retroviral gene vectors, which can be attributed to the properties of the viral integrase and cellular cofactors. Cell culture assays and animal models have also been developed to study the contributions of vector features and systemic factors to clonal imbalance. Additionally, databases summarizing vector insertion sites in dominant hematopoietic clones are being developed as tools to identify genes that regulate clonal homeostasis. By studying the mechanisms of insertional mutagenesis, researchers hope to improve the safety of advanced hematopoietic cell therapy. Furthermore, these studies are generating valuable insights into gene networks that regulate cell fitness, which have implications for the fields of hematology, oncology, and regenerative medicine.

title: Markets, voucher subsidies and free nets combine to achieve high bed net coverage in rural Tanzania
text:
Tanzania has a well-established network of commercial retailers that sell insecticide-treated nets (ITNs). In 2004, the government implemented a voucher subsidy program for pregnant women, and in mid-2005, they distributed free nets to children under the age of five in select districts, including Rufiji on the southern coast, as part of a child health campaign. This study aims to assess the impact of these different net delivery strategies on coverage in a poor rural community.

To conduct the study, a cross-sectional household survey was carried out in 31 rural villages of the Demographic Surveillance System in Rufiji district, Southern Tanzania. A total of 6,331 individuals from 1,752 randomly selected households participated in the survey. Each consenting respondent was asked about their net use, treatment status, and how they obtained the nets.

The findings of the study revealed that overall net use was 62.7%. Among infants (0 to 1 year), net use was 87.2%, while among young children (>1 to 5 years) it was 81.8%. For older children (6 to 15 years) and adults (>15 years), net use was 54.5% and 59.6% respectively. Approximately 30.2% of all nets had been treated six months prior to the survey.

The main source of nets for infants was the private sector, with a voucher subsidy covering the cost of the nets for 41.8% of users. Half of the nets used by young children (50.0%) and over a third of those used by older children (37.2%) were obtained for free through the vaccination campaign. Among the overall population, the majority of nets (45.1%) were purchased commercially, and this was also the primary means of obtaining nets for adults (60.2%).

It was observed that all delivery mechanisms, including the sale of nets at full market price, did not adequately serve the poorest individuals. However, there was no difference in equity between voucher-subsidized and freely distributed nets. 

In conclusion, all three net delivery strategies were successful in achieving high coverage in a poor rural community, providing both personal and community-level protection. Each strategy effectively reached its target group, and the distribution of free nets did not negatively impact the net market. These findings suggest that these approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive in this setting.

title: Human chorionic gonadotropin levels in maternal blood in late pregnancy: relation to birthweight, sex and condition of the infant at birth.
text: We collected a total of 527 blood samples from a diverse group of women who were between 36 and 40 weeks pregnant. We used a specific radioimmunoassay to measure the levels of serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), specifically targeting the beta 1-subunit of hCG. We found that serum hCG levels were elevated in women who were pregnant for the first time (primigravidae) and in those carrying female fetuses. Additionally, we observed a correlation between serum hCG levels and the birthweight of the child, as well as the occurrence of fetal distress.

title: Brain-Specific Phosphorylation of MeCP2 Regulates Activity-Dependent Bdnf Transcription, Dendritic Growth, and Spine Maturation
text:
Rett and Rett-like syndromes are neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by mental retardation, motor dysfunction, and autistic behaviors. They are caused by mutations or duplications in the MECP2 gene. MECP2 is expressed in various tissues in mammals and acts as a global repressor of transcription. However, the exact molecular mechanisms through which MECP2 dysfunction leads to the specific neural phenotypes of Rett syndrome (RTT) are not well understood.

In this study, we demonstrate that the phosphorylation of MECP2 at serine 421 (S421) is triggered by neuronal activity and calcium influx, and this process is dependent on CaMKII. Importantly, S421 phosphorylation occurs selectively in the brain in response to physiological stimuli. Our results reveal that S421 phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating dendritic patterning, spine morphogenesis, and the activity-dependent induction of Bdnf transcription by MECP2. These findings suggest that neuronal activity, by inducing MECP2 phosphorylation, controls a gene expression program that is essential for the maturation of the nervous system. Disruption of this process in individuals with MECP2 mutations may contribute to the specific neural pathology observed in RTT.

title: A Candidate Gene Approach Identifies the TRAF1/C5 Region as a Risk Factor for Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
Correction for: Kurreeman FAS, Padyukov L, Marques RB, Schrodi SJ, Seddighzadeh M, et al. (2007) Identification of the TRAF1/C5 Region as a Risk Factor for Rheumatoid Arthritis Using a Candidate Gene Approach. PLoS Med 4(9): e278. doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.0040278

title: Potential use of γ-secretase modulators in the treatment of Alzheimer disease.
text: Despite the considerable advancements made in comprehending the causes of Alzheimer's disease over the last two decades, we have not yet discovered any treatments that can significantly change the progression of this common neurodegenerative condition. In this brief analysis, we will explore two approaches currently undergoing clinical trials (γ-secretase inhibition and γ-secretase modulation) and highlight the notable distinctions between these therapeutic methods. Additionally, we will delve into specific genetic and biomarker-based strategies in translational research and clinical trials that could aid in the development of an effective treatment.

title: Rational design of a flavivirus vaccine by abolishing viral RNA 2'-O methylation.
text: Viruses that reproduce in the cytoplasm are unable to access the host nuclear capping machinery. These viruses have developed viral methyltransferase(s) to methylate the N-7 and 2'-O cap of their RNA. Alternatively, they "steal" the host mRNA cap to create the 5' end of viral RNA. The purpose of 2'-O methylation of the viral RNA cap is to imitate cellular mRNA and avoid detection by the host's innate immune system. A cytoplasmic virus lacking 2'-O methylation can still replicate, but its viral RNA lacks this methylation and is recognized and eliminated by the host's immune response. This type of mutant virus could be intentionally designed as a weakened live vaccine. In this study, we used Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a significant mosquito-borne flavivirus, to demonstrate this innovative vaccine concept. We discovered that JEV methyltransferase is responsible for both N-7 and 2'-O cap methylations, as well as evasion of the host's innate immune response. The recombinant virus lacking 2'-O methylation remained stable in cell culture for over 30 days. In mice, the mutant virus was weakened, triggered strong immune responses, and maintained the engineered mutation in vivo. A single immunization provided complete protection against lethal JEV strains in mice. Mechanistically, the weakened phenotype was due to the mutant virus being more susceptible to the antiviral effects of interferon and IFIT proteins. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of using a virus lacking 2'-O methylation as a vaccine strategy. This approach could be applied to other flaviviruses and nonflaviviruses that possess their own viral 2'-O methyltransferases.

title: Fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes: results from three prospective longitudinal cohort studies
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if different fruits are associated with varying risks of type 2 diabetes. The study was a prospective longitudinal cohort study conducted among health professionals in the United States. The participants included 66,105 women from the Nurses' Health Study (1984-2008), 85,104 women from the Nurses' Health Study II (1991-2009), and 36,173 men from the Health Professionals Follow-up Study (1986-2008) who were initially free of major chronic diseases. The main outcome measure was the occurrence of type 2 diabetes, which was identified through self-report and confirmed by supplementary questionnaires.

The results showed that during the follow-up period of 3,464,641 person years, 12,198 participants developed type 2 diabetes. After adjusting for personal, lifestyle, and dietary risk factors, the hazard ratio for type 2 diabetes for every three servings per week of total whole fruit consumption was 0.98. When considering individual fruits, the hazard ratios for type 2 diabetes for every three servings per week were 0.74 for blueberries, 0.88 for grapes and raisins, 0.89 for prunes, 0.93 for apples and pears, 0.95 for bananas, 0.95 for grapefruit, 0.97 for peaches, plums, and apricots, 0.99 for oranges, 1.03 for strawberries, and 1.10 for cantaloupe. The hazard ratio for the same increase in fruit juice consumption was 1.08. The associations between fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes varied significantly among different fruits.

In conclusion, this study suggests that there is heterogeneity in the associations between individual fruit consumption and the risk of type 2 diabetes. Consuming specific whole fruits, such as blueberries, grapes, and apples, is associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes, while consuming fruit juice is associated with a higher risk.

title: OncomiR-196 promotes an invasive phenotype in oral cancer through the NME4-JNK-TIMP1-MMP signaling pathway
text:
BACKGROUND: The expression of microRNA-196 (miR-196) has been found to be significantly increased in oral cancer cells and various other cancers. However, the role of miR-196 in oral cancer has not been thoroughly investigated.

METHODS: We examined the effects of miR-196 modulation on cellular functions such as cell growth, migration, invasion, and radio/chemosensitivity. Algorithm-based studies were used to identify the target gene regulated by miR-196. The target gene and downstream molecular mechanisms were confirmed through various analyses including RT-qPCR, western blot, luciferase reporter, and confocal microscopy. We also analyzed the expression of miR-196 in paired cancer and adjacent normal tissues from oral cancer patients.

RESULTS: Both miR-196a and miR-196b were found to be highly over-expressed in cancer tissues and were correlated with lymph node metastasis. Functionally, miR-196 promoted cell migration and invasion without affecting cell growth. Mechanistically, miR-196 achieved its function by inhibiting NME4 expression and activating p-JNK, suppressing TIMP1, and enhancing MMP1/9 expression.

CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that miR-196 plays a role in promoting cell migration and invasion in oral cancer. Clinically, miR-196a/b were significantly over-expressed in cancer tissues and correlated with lymph node metastasis. Therefore, miR-196 may serve as a promising marker for improved management of oral cancer.

title: Reverse engineering of TLX oncogenic transcriptional networks identifies RUNX1 as tumor suppressor in T-ALL
text: TLX1 and TLX3, two oncogenes, play a crucial role in the development of T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). In this study, we utilized reverse engineering of global transcriptional networks to unravel the oncogenic regulatory circuit governed by TLX1 and TLX3. Through this systems biology analysis, we identified T cell leukemia homeobox 1 (TLX1) and TLX3 as the master regulators of an oncogenic transcriptional circuit that controls T-ALL. Interestingly, a network structure analysis of this hierarchical network revealed that RUNX1 acts as a vital mediator in TLX1 and TLX3-induced T-ALL, and it was predicted to have a tumor-suppressor role in T cell transformation. Supporting these findings, we discovered recurrent somatic loss-of-function mutations in RUNX1 in human T-ALL. Overall, our findings position TLX1 and TLX3 as the key components of an oncogenic transcriptional network that governs leukemia development. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of network analyses in identifying crucial elements in the regulatory circuits of human cancer and identifies RUNX1 as a tumor-suppressor gene in T-ALL.

title: The Impact of the New WHO Antiretroviral Treatment Guidelines on HIV Epidemic Dynamics and Cost in South Africa
text:
In November 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that adults with HIV should begin antiretroviral therapy (ART) when their CD4+ cell counts are at or below 350 cells/µl, rather than the previous threshold of 200 cells/µl. However, South Africa decided to only adopt this strategy for pregnant women and patients co-infected with tuberculosis (TB). In this study, we aimed to assess the impact and costs of fully implementing the new WHO guidelines on the HIV epidemic in South Africa.

To do this, we used a well-established model that simulates the transmission and control of HIV within specific sexual networks and healthcare settings. We focused on the Hlabisa subdistrict in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and used the model to predict the dynamics of the HIV epidemic, the number of patients on ART, and the associated costs under the new guidelines compared to treating patients at or below 200 cells/µl over the next 30 years.

Our findings showed that in the first five years of implementing the new WHO guidelines, there would be an additional 7% annual investment required, but 28% more patients would receive treatment. Additionally, there would be a significant impact on HIV incidence, leading to lower annual costs after seven years. On average, it would take about 16 years to reach a break-even point in terms of cumulative net costs.

Based on our study, we support the WHO recommendation of initiating ART at or below 350 cells/µl for all HIV-infected patients. In addition to the benefits of saving more lives, our findings suggest that there would be net savings within a relatively short time frame by frontloading the investment. These results hold true even when considering alternative assumptions and potential changes in ART prices and effectiveness.

Therefore, we recommend that South Africa rapidly expands its healthcare infrastructure to fully embrace the new WHO guidelines. This would not only improve the health outcomes for HIV-infected individuals but also lead to cost savings in the long run.

title: ER-associated mitochondrial division links the distribution of mitochondria and mitochondrial DNA in yeast
text: The division of mitochondria plays a crucial role in their distribution and function. Recent studies have shown that the sites where mitochondria divide are marked by contacts between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria. However, the molecular basis and functions of these contacts are not yet fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that in yeast, a complex called ERMES, which tethers the ER to mitochondria, and a highly conserved protein called Gem1, which is a GTPase, are both involved in ER-associated mitochondrial division. Gem1 acts as a negative regulator of the contacts between the ER and mitochondria, which is necessary for the proper spatial resolution and distribution of newly formed mitochondrial tips after division. Previous research has shown that ERMES localizes with a specific subset of actively replicating mitochondrial nucleoids. We also show that mitochondrial division is spatially linked to these nucleoids, and that most of them segregate before division, resulting in their distribution into the newly formed tips of the mitochondrial network. Therefore, we propose that ER-associated division serves to connect the distribution of mitochondria and mitochondrial nucleoids within cells.

title: BMI-1 Autoantibody as a New Potential Biomarker for Cervical Carcinoma
text: BMI-1 is found to be overexpressed in various types of cancers, which can trigger an immune response resulting in the production of autoantibodies. However, the use of BMI-1 autoantibodies as a biomarker has been rarely studied, except in the case of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. It remains unclear whether BMI-1 autoantibodies can serve as a biomarker for cervical carcinoma. In this study, we isolated BMI-1 proteins from a T7 phage cDNA library obtained from a mixture of cervical carcinoma tissues. We examined the levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies in serum samples from 67 cervical carcinoma patients and 65 controls using ELISA and immunoblot techniques. We observed that BMI-1 mRNA or protein levels were elevated in cervical carcinoma cell lines. Immunoblot results revealed higher levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies in patient sera compared to normal sera. Furthermore, antibody affinity assay results showed no difference in BMI-1 autoantibody levels between cervical polyps and normal sera, but a significant increase was observed in patient sera compared to normal controls (patient 0.827±0.043 and normal 0.445±0.023; P<0.001). Additionally, the levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies significantly increased at stage I (0.672±0.019) compared to normal sera (P<0.001), and gradually increased during tumor progression (stage I 0.672±0.019; stage II 0.775 ±0.019; stage III 0.890 ±0.027; stage IV 1.043±0.041), showing a significant correlation with the progression of cervical cancer (P<0.001). Statistical analyses using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curves indicated that the BMI-1 autoantibody level can be used as a biomarker for cervical carcinoma (sensitivity 0.78 and specificity 0.76; AUC = 0.922). In conclusion, measuring BMI-1 autoantibody levels in cervical cancer patients could have clinical prognostic value and serve as a non-tissue specific biomarker for cancers that express BMI-1.

title: MicroRNAs can generate thresholds in target gene expression
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNA molecules that do not code for proteins and are highly conserved. They play a role in repressing gene expression in a manner that depends on the sequence. To study this regulation, we used quantitative fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry to measure protein expression of a target gene in individual cells, both with and without miRNA regulation. Our findings indicate that while the overall repression level is moderate, as previously observed in population-based studies, there is significant variation in repression among individual cells. Specifically, we demonstrate that miRNA regulation sets a threshold level of target mRNA, below which protein production is greatly repressed. Close to this threshold, protein expression is highly responsive to changes in target mRNA levels, which aligns with a mathematical model of molecular titration. These results highlight the dual role of miRNAs in gene expression, acting as both a switch and a fine-tuner.

title: Oncogenic mTOR signaling recruits myeloid-derived suppressor cells to promote tumor initiation
text: The role of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in the progression of primary and metastatic cancer is crucial. However, the regulation of MDSCs varies greatly among patients with the same type of cancer, and the reasons for this heterogeneity are largely unknown. In this study, we used human tumor genomics and syngeneic mammary tumor models to investigate the mechanisms behind this variability. We found that the mTOR signaling pathway in cancer cells determines the tumor's ability to stimulate the accumulation of MDSCs by regulating G-CSF. By inhibiting this pathway or its activators, such as FGFR, we were able to impair tumor progression. However, this impairment was partially reversed when MDSCs or G-CSF were restored. We also discovered that tumor-initiating cells (TICs) have higher levels of G-CSF. MDSCs, in turn, increase the frequency of TICs by activating Notch in tumor cells, creating a feedforward loop. Our analysis of primary breast cancers and patient-derived xenografts confirmed these mechanisms in patients. These findings reveal a non-traditional oncogenic role of mTOR signaling in recruiting pro-tumorigenic MDSCs and demonstrate how specific subsets of cancer can evolve to promote and rely on a distinct immune microenvironment.

title: Management of women who have a genetic predisposition for breast cancer.
text: Careful planning is necessary for managing women with a genetic predisposition for breast cancer. Those with BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 mutations face a higher risk of breast cancer and other cancers, particularly ovarian cancer. The management of these patients often involves screening, prophylactic surgery, and chemoprevention, and women may opt for multiple strategies. However, there have been no randomized prospective trials evaluating the specific impact of these strategies on mutation carriers. It is important to inform all patients that while screening, prophylactic surgery, and chemoprevention offer potential benefits, they also carry the risk of harm.

title: Astrocytes from Familial and Sporadic ALS Patients are Toxic to Motor Neurons
text:
