Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal disease that affects motor neurons, and astrocytes are believed to play a significant role in the death of motor neurons in familial ALS (FALS). However, the understanding of astrocytes' involvement in ALS is mainly based on studies conducted on rodent models of FALS, which only represent a small percentage of all ALS cases. The role of astrocytes in sporadic ALS (SALS), which accounts for over 90% of ALS cases, is still unknown. 

To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a study using astrocytes derived from postmortem tissue of both FALS and SALS patients. Our findings reveal that astrocytes from both patient groups have a similar toxic effect on motor neurons. Additionally, we discovered that suppressing the superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) gene, which is associated with ALS, significantly reduces astrocyte-induced toxicity towards motor neurons. 

These results emphasize the importance of astrocytes as a non-cell autonomous factor in SALS and provide a valuable in vitro model for investigating common disease mechanisms and potential therapies for both SALS and FALS.

title: High-intensity functional exercise program and protein-enriched energy supplement for older persons dependent in activities of daily living: a randomised controlled trial.
text: The purpose of this study was to determine whether a high-intensity functional exercise program can improve balance, gait ability, and lower-limb strength in older individuals who are dependent on activities of daily living. Additionally, the study aimed to investigate whether consuming a protein-enriched energy supplement immediately after the exercises enhances the effects of the training. A total of 191 older individuals living in residential care facilities, with a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 10 or below, participated in the randomized controlled trial. They were randomly assigned to either the high-intensity functional exercise program or a control activity, which consisted of 29 sessions over a period of 3 months. Participants were also assigned to receive either a protein-enriched energy supplement or a placebo. The Berg Balance Scale, self-paced and maximum gait speed, and one-repetition maximum in lower-limb strength were assessed at three and six months. The data was analyzed using a 2 x 2 factorial ANCOVA, following the intention-to-treat principle. After three months, the exercise group showed a significant improvement in self-paced gait speed compared to the control group (mean difference 0.04 m/s, p = 0.02). At six months, the exercise group demonstrated significant improvements in the Berg Balance Scale (1.9 points, p = 0.05), self-paced gait speed (0.05 m/s, p = 0.009), and lower-limb strength (10.8 kg, p = 0.03). There were no significant interaction effects between the exercise and nutrition interventions. In conclusion, a high-intensity functional exercise program has long-term positive effects on balance, gait ability, and lower-limb strength in older individuals who are dependent on activities of daily living. Consuming a protein-enriched energy supplement immediately after the exercises does not appear to enhance the effects of the training.

title: Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation modulates immunosuppressive functions of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and enhances cancer therapies
text: The growth of tumors is promoted by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) through the inhibition of T-cell immunity and the promotion of malignant cell proliferation and migration. However, the therapeutic potential of blocking MDSC in tumors has been limited due to their heterogeneity, plasticity, and resistance to different chemotherapy agents. Recent studies have focused on the role of energy metabolic pathways in the differentiation and function of immune cells, but the metabolic characteristics that regulate MDSC are still unclear. Our objective was to determine the energy metabolic pathway(s) utilized by MDSC, understand its impact on their immunosuppressive function, and investigate whether inhibiting this pathway could block MDSC and enhance antitumor therapies. Through experiments using various murine tumor models, we discovered that tumor-infiltrating MDSC (T-MDSC) increased their uptake of fatty acids and activated fatty acid oxidation (FAO). This was accompanied by an increase in mitochondrial mass, upregulation of key FAO enzymes, and an increase in oxygen consumption rate. By pharmacologically inhibiting FAO, we were able to block immune inhibitory pathways and functions in T-MDSC, leading to a decrease in their production of inhibitory cytokines. Inhibiting FAO alone significantly delayed tumor growth in a T-cell-dependent manner and enhanced the effectiveness of adoptive T-cell therapy in fighting tumors. Additionally, when combined with low-dose chemotherapy, FAO inhibition completely eliminated the immunosuppressive effects of T-MDSC and induced a significant antitumor response. Interestingly, we also observed a similar increase in fatty acid uptake and expression of FAO-related enzymes in human MDSC found in both peripheral blood and tumors. These findings suggest that inhibiting FAO could be a promising approach to block MDSC and enhance various cancer therapies.

title: Predicting mortality of patients hospitalized for acutely exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to determine the factors that influence the short-term prognosis of patients with acutely exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

METHODS: A total of 590 patients with COPD as their primary disease, who were admitted to the pneumology unit of a university hospital between 1981 and 1990, were included in this study. All patients received standardized treatment for acutely exacerbated COPD. Two observers retrospectively analyzed the patient records and collected 23 clinical and laboratory variables that defined the patient's condition upon admission. Age and arterial gas data were also considered, and the mortality outcome was recorded. Interobserver reproducibility was assessed using the kappa coefficient for dichotomous variables and Spearman's rho for continuous variables. The relationship between clinical and laboratory factors and the outcome was initially analyzed using univariate analysis, followed by logistic regression analysis to determine the independent predictive role of variables that were found to be correlated with mortality in the univariate analysis.

RESULTS: The mortality rate among the patients was 14.4%. The logistic regression analysis identified four independent predictors of death: age (odds ratio [OR] 1.07; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04 to 1.11), alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient greater than 41 mm Hg (OR 2.33; 95% CI 1.39 to 3.90), ventricular arrhythmias (OR 1.91; 95% CI 1.10 to 3.31), and atrial fibrillation (OR 2.27; 95% CI 1.14 to 4.51).

CONCLUSIONS: Patients with acutely exacerbated COPD who are at high risk of death can be identified upon admission. Variables indicating heart dysfunction play a significant role in determining this risk. Among pulmonary function data, only the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient contributes to the predictive model.

title: Clathrin is required for the function of the mitotic spindle
text: Clathrin plays a crucial role in facilitating the movement of membrane and proteins within the cell by generating vesicles. In non-dividing cells, clathrin-coated vesicles are continuously formed, but this process is halted during mitosis, when clathrin concentrates at the spindle apparatus. Our study reveals that clathrin also plays a role in stabilizing the fibres of the mitotic spindle, aiding in the proper alignment of chromosomes. Specifically, clathrin binds directly to the spindle through its amino-terminal domain. When clathrin heavy chain is depleted using RNA interference, mitosis is prolonged, and the fibres that attach to the chromosomes (kinetochore fibres) become destabilized. This leads to defective alignment of chromosomes and persistent activation of the spindle checkpoint. However, normal mitosis can be restored by introducing clathrin triskelia, but not the N-terminal domain of clathrin heavy chain alone. This suggests that the unique structure of clathrin is necessary for stabilizing kinetochore fibres. Understanding the importance of clathrin in normal mitosis may have implications for studying human cancers that involve gene fusions of clathrin heavy chain.

title: The origin and neuronal function of in vivo nonsynaptic glutamate.
text: The concentration of basal extracellular glutamate outside the synaptic cleft is found to be in micromolar levels, but its origin and function remain unknown. This study demonstrates that blocking glutamate release from the cystine-glutamate antiporter leads to a significant decrease (60%) in extrasynaptic glutamate levels in the rat striatum. On the other hand, blocking voltage-dependent Na+ and Ca2+ channels only causes minimal changes (0-30%). These findings suggest that nonvesicular glutamate release by the cystine-glutamate antiporter is the main source of extrasynaptic glutamate in the striatum. The activity of the cystine-glutamate antiporter is negatively regulated by group II metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/3) through a cAMP-dependent protein kinase mechanism, similar to vesicular release. Glutamate derived from the antiporter also regulates extracellular levels of glutamate and dopamine. Blocking the antiporter increases extracellular glutamate levels, but this effect is prevented by prior blockade of the antiporter. This indicates that glutamate released from the antiporter acts as an endogenous modulator of mGluR2/3. Blocking the antiporter also leads to an increase in extracellular dopamine, which can be reversed by infusing an mGluR2/3 agonist. This suggests that antiporter-derived glutamate can modulate dopamine transmission through mGluR2/3 heteroreceptors. Overall, these findings highlight the cystine-glutamate antiporter as the primary source of in vivo extracellular glutamate and its role in modulating both glutamate and dopamine transmission.

title: Disease-associated functions of IL-33: the new kid in the IL-1 family
text: Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is a recently discovered member of the IL-1 family. It is produced by various cell types in response to pro-inflammatory stimulation and is believed to be released upon cell lysis. The IL-33 receptor, composed of ST2 and IL-1 receptor accessory protein, is widely expressed, particularly in T helper 2 (TH2) cells and mast cells. IL-33 plays a protective role against helminth infection and reduces the development of atherosclerosis by promoting TH2-type immune responses. However, IL-33 can also contribute to the development of asthma by increasing the number of TH2 cells and can trigger joint inflammation, atopic dermatitis, and anaphylaxis through mast cell activation. Therefore, IL-33 presents itself as a potential target for therapeutic intervention in various diseases.

title: Interferon alpha therapy for hepatitis C: treatment completion and response rates among patients with substance use disorders
text: The aim of this study was to examine the completion and response rates of interferon alpha therapy (IFN) among patients with hepatitis C viral infection (HCV) who also had a history of substance use disorders (SUDs). The study used medical records from 307,437 veterans seen in the Veterans Integrated Service Network 20 (VISN 20) between 1998 and 2003. The results showed that patients with SUDs were just as likely to complete IFN therapy and achieve treatment responses as patients without SUDs. These findings suggest that individuals with both SUDs and HCV can successfully undergo antiviral therapy. Further research is needed to inform treatment strategies and guidelines for this population.

title: Association between infection with Helicobacter pylori and risk of gastric cancer: evidence from a prospective investigation.
text: AIM To examine the link between gastric cancer and prior infection with Helicobacter pylori. METHOD A case-control study was conducted to compare the prevalence of IgG antibodies to H pylori in blood samples collected before the diagnosis of gastric cancer in the cases. The presence of H pylori antibody (greater than 10 micrograms IgG/ml) was determined using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). PARTICIPANTS The study included 29 men who were later diagnosed with gastric cancer and 116 age-matched controls. The controls were selected from a pool of over 22,000 middle-aged men who had participated in two ongoing cohort studies (the British United Provident Association study and the Caerphilly collaborative heart disease study) and had provided blood samples between 1975 and 1982. RESULTS Out of the 29 cases, 20 (69%) tested positive for H pylori-specific antibody, compared to 54 out of 116 (47%) controls. The median specific IgG concentration was significantly higher in the cases than in the controls (90 micrograms/ml vs 3.6 micrograms/ml, p < 0.01). The estimated odds ratio for the risk of gastric cancer in individuals with a history of H pylori infection was 2.77 (95% confidence interval 1.04 to 7.97, p = 0.039). CONCLUSION H pylori infection may play a significant role in the development of gastric cancer, with approximately 35% to 55% of cases potentially associated with this infection.

title: Oncostatin M and leukemia inhibitory factor do not use the same functional receptor in mice.
text:
Oncostatin M (OSM) and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) belong to the interleukin-6 (IL-6) subfamily of cytokines and utilize a common signal transducer called gp130. Human OSM (hOSM) and LIF share a high-affinity receptor composed of gp130 and LIF receptor beta subunit (LIFRbeta). Recently, a second high-affinity receptor for hOSM was discovered, consisting of gp130 and the hOSM receptor beta subunit. However, the characteristics of murine OSM (mOSM) and its receptors have remained unknown. To investigate this, we generated recombinant mOSM using the recently cloned mOSM cDNA and examined its biological activity and receptor structure. 

We found that murine hematopoietic cell lines M1 and DA1.a, an embryonic stem cell line CCE, and Ba/F3 transfectants expressing gp130 and LIFRbeta responded equally well to murine LIF (mLIF) and hOSM. However, these cells only responded to mOSM at concentrations 30 to 100 times higher than mLIF and hOSM. In contrast, NIH3T3 cells responded to mOSM but not to mLIF and hOSM. Scatchard plot analyses revealed that mOSM bound to gp130 with low-affinity (kd = 2.8 to 4.2 nmol/L) and that the binding affinity did not increase in the presence of LIFRbeta. However, mOSM bound to NIH3T3 cells with high-affinity (kd = 660 pmol/L), while mLIF did not bind to NIH3T3 cells at all. These findings suggest that unlike hOSM, mOSM and mLIF do not share the same functional receptor, and mOSM only transmits signals through its specific receptor complex. Further investigations in mice will elucidate the physiological roles of OSM.

title: Multifunctional in vivo vascular imaging using near-infrared II fluorescence
text: We use single-walled carbon nanotubes as fluorophores to perform real-time epifluorescence imaging of mouse hind limb vasculatures in the second near-infrared region (NIR-II). This technique achieves high spatial resolution of approximately 30 μm and temporal resolution of less than 200 ms per frame for imaging small blood vessels at depths of 1-3 mm in the hind limb. The NIR-II optical window provides deep anatomical penetration and low scattering, enabling this level of resolution. Traditional NIR imaging (NIR-I) and microscopic computed tomography cannot achieve this spatial resolution, and scanning microscopic imaging techniques fall short in terms of temporal resolution. By using a dynamic contrast-enhanced NIR-II imaging technique, we can clearly differentiate arterial and venous vessels based on their distinct hemodynamics. Additionally, the deep tissue penetration and high spatial and temporal resolution of NIR-II imaging allow us to accurately quantify blood velocity in both normal and ischemic femoral arteries, a capability that ultrasonography lacks at lower blood velocities.

title: Colorectal cancer survival in socioeconomic groups in England: variation is mainly in the short term after diagnosis.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the disparities in cancer survival rates among different socioeconomic groups in England, focusing on short-term survival rates. The study identified individuals who were diagnosed with colorectal cancer between 1996 and 2004 using cancer registry records. The researchers calculated the five-year cumulative relative survival rates and excess death rates. 

The findings revealed a significantly higher excess death rate in the first month of follow-up for colon cancer, particularly among socioeconomically disadvantaged groups. In subsequent periods, the excess mortality rates were lower and there was less variation based on socioeconomic status. The pattern of excess death rates was similar for rectal cancer, but the socioeconomic difference in death rates persisted for several years longer. 

If the excess death rates for the entire colorectal cancer patient population were the same as those observed in the most affluent socioeconomic group, there would be a reduction of 360 deaths in colon cancer patients and 336 deaths in rectal cancer patients annually. These deaths primarily occurred within the first month and year after diagnosis. 

In conclusion, recent advancements in the national cancer control agenda have placed greater emphasis on outcome measures, with short-term cancer survival rates serving as an operational measure of progress and variation in cancer control. The results of this study provide strong support for this strategy by shedding light on the survival differences among socioeconomic groups.

title: Cardiac myocyte remodeling mediated by N-cadherin-dependent mechanosensing.
text: The maintenance of the structural and functional integrity of cardiac cells relies heavily on cell-to-cell adhesions. However, there is limited knowledge regarding the sensitivity and transmission of mechanical forces in these interactions. Previous studies have primarily focused on the interactions between cardiac cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM). This research aims to investigate the direct impact of intercellular adhesion, specifically N-cadherin-mediated mechanotransduction, on the internal organization and morphology of neonatal ventricular cardiac myocytes. The findings demonstrate that cadherin-mediated cell attachments can induce a response in the cytoskeletal network similar to that of integrin-mediated force response and transmission. This response affects the organization of myofibrils, the shape of myocytes, and the stiffness of the cell cortex. The traction forces mediated by N-cadherin were found to be comparable to those exerted by the ECM. The changes in traction forces, based on the applied loads (gel stiffness), provide further evidence that N-cadherin is a mechanoresponsive adhesion receptor. Interestingly, the measured cell-spread area in response to the imposed load (adhesive substrate rigidity) was consistently higher for N-cadherin-coated surfaces compared to ECM protein-coated surfaces, indicating a greater mechanical sensitivity response. Additionally, the cytoskeletal structure of myocytes on an N-cadherin adhesive microenvironment differed from that on an ECM environment, suggesting that these two cell adhesion systems may have both independent and complementary roles in the spatial organization of myocyte cytoskeleton. These findings highlight the involvement of cell-to-cell-mediated force perception and transmission in the development and organization of cardiac structure and function.

title: NEAT1: A novel cancer‐related long non‐coding RNA
text: The abnormal increase in the expression of the long non-coding RNA NEAT1 (nuclear paraspeckle assembly transcript 1) has been observed in various solid tumors, including lung cancer, esophageal cancer, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma. In these tumors, high levels of NEAT1 are linked to a poor prognosis. However, NEAT1 is found to be suppressed in acute promyelocytic leukemia, where it aids in the differentiation of white blood cells. This review aims to provide an overview of the current evidence on the oncogenic role of NEAT1 and its potential clinical applications. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms that lead to NEAT1 overexpression.

title: The Function and Therapeutic Potential of Long Non-coding RNAs in Cardiovascular Development and Disease
text: Advancements in genome-wide analyses and RNA sequencing have led to the discovery that a significant portion of the human genome, although transcribed, does not encode proteins. These non-coding regions, known as long non-coding RNAs, play a crucial role in regulating gene expression in both normal and disease conditions. By studying long non-coding RNAs expressed in the heart and conducting gene association studies, researchers have found that these molecules are involved in cardiovascular development and disease. Some long non-coding RNAs have been linked to cardiac pathophysiology and could potentially be targeted for therapeutic purposes. In this review, we provide an overview of the current understanding of the function of long non-coding RNAs in the cardiovascular system, with a focus on their role in hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, ischemia, and heart failure. We also discuss the potential therapeutic implications of targeting long non-coding RNAs and the challenges associated with this area of research, along with suggestions for future studies and translational applications.

title: Oct4 links multiple epigenetic pathways to the pluripotency network
text: Oct4 is a widely recognized transcription factor that plays crucial roles in the renewal of stem cells, their ability to become any type of cell (pluripotency), and the reprogramming of somatic cells. However, there is limited information available about the protein complexes associated with Oct4 and the interactions between these proteins that determine Oct4's important regulatory functions. In this study, we used an improved method of purifying Oct4 protein complexes in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and analyzed them using mass spectrometry. Through this approach, we discovered numerous new partners of Oct4 that are essential for the self-renewal and pluripotency of mESCs. Notably, we found that Oct4 is associated with multiple complexes that modify chromatin, which have been previously documented to have functional significance in maintaining stem cells and reprogramming somatic cells. Our research establishes a strong biochemical foundation for understanding the genetic and epigenetic regulation of stem cell pluripotency and provides a framework for exploring alternative reprogramming strategies based on other factors.

title: Tet1 is dispensable for maintaining pluripotency and its loss is compatible with embryonic and postnatal development.
text: The enzymes known as Tet1/2/3 are responsible for converting 5-methylcytosine (5mC) into 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC). In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), Tet1 is highly expressed and leads to an increased level of 5hmC. While Tet1 has been linked to the maintenance of ESCs and the determination of cell lineages in vitro, its exact role in development is not well understood. To investigate the function of Tet1 in pluripotency and development, we created mutant mESCs and mice lacking Tet1. These Tet1(-/-) ESCs showed lower levels of 5hmC and minor changes in overall gene expression. However, they remained pluripotent and were able to support the development of live-born mice in tetraploid complementation assays. In vitro, the mutant ESCs displayed a bias towards trophectoderm differentiation. The Tet1 mutant mice were viable, fertile, and generally appeared normal, although some had a slightly smaller body size at birth. Our findings indicate that a partial reduction in 5hmC levels due to Tet1 loss does not impact pluripotency in ESCs and is compatible with both embryonic and postnatal development.

title: LDL-cholesterol concentrations: a genome-wide association study
text: The role of LDL cholesterol in the development of cardiovascular disease has been well-established. To gain a better understanding of the biological processes involved in the metabolism and regulation of LDL cholesterol, we conducted a genome-wide association study. Our study included data from 11,685 participants across five studies, with a focus on 293,461 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that met our quality control criteria. Additionally, we analyzed data from a second genome-wide array in 4,337 participants from three of the five studies, with a focus on 290,140 SNPs. Replication studies were also conducted in two independent populations, consisting of 4,979 participants. Through statistical analysis and meta-analysis, we identified two SNPs (rs599839 and rs4970834) in the chromosomal locus 1p13.3 that showed significant association with LDL cholesterol. A third SNP (rs646776) at the same locus was also found to be statistically associated. Meta-analysis of all the data confirmed the association of rs599839 and rs646776 with LDL cholesterol concentrations. These SNPs explained approximately 1% of the variation in LDL cholesterol levels and were associated with a 15% change in LDL cholesterol per allele. Our findings suggest a novel locus for LDL cholesterol on chromosome 1p13.3, which could provide valuable insights into the regulation of LDL cholesterol and aid in the discovery of new therapeutic targets for cardiovascular disease.

title: Population Density, Water Supply, and the Risk of Dengue Fever in Vietnam: Cohort Study and Spatial Analysis
text:
In this study, we examined the relationship between human population density and lack of tap water as factors contributing to dengue fever outbreaks. Aedes aegypti, the main carrier of dengue viruses, often breeds in water storage containers used by households without access to tap water, even in densely populated urban areas. Our goal was to identify areas at highest risk for dengue outbreaks.

To conduct our study, we analyzed data from a population of 75,000 households in Vietnam, using geo-referencing to track their locations. We focused on two epidemics and looked specifically at dengue hospital admissions, totaling 3,013 cases. We used space-time scan statistics and mathematical models to validate our findings.

Surprisingly, we discovered that there is a narrow range of human population densities, between approximately 3,000 to 7,000 people per square kilometer, that are most susceptible to dengue outbreaks. In our study area, this density was typically found in villages and some peri-urban areas. Interestingly, areas with higher population densities or access to adequate water supply did not experience severe outbreaks. The risk of dengue was higher in rural areas compared to urban areas, primarily due to the lack of piped water supply, and in areas with population densities falling within the critical range. Our mathematical modeling suggests that the occurrence of outbreaks can be explained by simple assumptions about the ratio of vectors to hosts in a given area.

In conclusion, our study highlights the significant contribution of rural areas to the spread of dengue fever, on par with cities. Improving water supply and implementing effective vector control measures in areas with critical population densities for dengue transmission could greatly enhance control efforts.

title: Helicobacter pylori induces AGS cell motility and elongation via independent signaling pathways.
text: In gastric epithelial cells, Helicobacter pylori triggers both motogenic and cytoskeletal responses. Our findings reveal that these responses can be activated through separate signaling pathways, which often occur simultaneously. Interestingly, the cag pathogenicity island seems to be unnecessary for inducing motility, while the elongation phenotype relies on the translocation and phosphorylation of CagA.

title: The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools
text: The SAM format is a versatile alignment format used to store read alignments against reference sequences. It supports both short and long reads from different sequencing platforms, with a maximum size of 128 Mbp. The format is flexible, compact, and allows for efficient random access. It is also the format used for releasing alignments from the 1000 Genomes Project. SAMtools is a software that offers various utilities for post-processing SAM alignments, including indexing, variant calling, and alignment viewing. It provides universal tools for processing read alignments. SAMtools can be accessed at http://samtools.sourceforge.net.

title: Characterization of two classes of small molecule inhibitors of Arp2/3 complex
text: The actin-related protein (Arp)2/3 complex plays a crucial role in the polymerization of actin filaments, supporting various cellular movements. However, there are still uncertainties regarding the extent to which the Arp2/3 complex contributes compared to other mechanisms of actin filament nucleation in processes like path finding by neuronal growth cones. This uncertainty arises due to the lack of simple methods to reversibly inhibit the Arp2/3 complex in living cells. In this study, we present two categories of small molecules that bind to different sites on the Arp2/3 complex, effectively inhibiting its ability to nucleate actin filaments. One of these molecules, CK-0944636, binds between Arp2 and Arp3, obstructing the movement of Arp2 and Arp3 into their active conformation. The other molecule, CK-0993548, inserts into the hydrophobic core of Arp3, causing a change in its conformation. Both classes of compounds effectively hinder the formation of actin filament comet tails by Listeria and podosomes by monocytes. By utilizing inhibitors with distinct mechanisms of action, we have established a powerful approach for studying the Arp2/3 complex in living cells.

title: Stresses at the cell-to-substrate interface during locomotion of fibroblasts
text: Recent advancements in the elastic substrate technique have allowed for the production of precise measurements of the forces exerted by individual moving cells. In this research, we utilized these advancements to create maps of the forces exerted by 3T3 fibroblasts during steady movement. The resulting images have a spatial resolution of approximately 5 micrometers and a maximum intensity of around 10(2) kdyn/cm2 (10(4) pN/micrometers2). Our findings reveal that the propulsive force for fibroblast locomotion, approximately 0.2 dyn, is primarily concentrated within 15 micrometers of the leading edge. These observations demonstrate the remarkable ability of the fibroblast's lamellipodium to generate significant traction stress. The cell body and posterior, on the other hand, appear to be passive structures that are solely pulled forward by this force.

title: Cancer-associated adipocytes exhibit an activated phenotype and contribute to breast cancer invasion.
text:
The role of mature adipocytes in the progression of breast cancer is not well understood, particularly in the early stages of tumor invasion. In our study, we used a unique two-dimensional coculture system to investigate the interaction between cancer cells and adipocytes. We found that when murine and human tumor cells were cocultivated with mature adipocytes, they exhibited increased invasive capabilities both in vitro and in vivo.

Furthermore, we observed that adipocytes cultivated with cancer cells also underwent changes in their phenotype. These changes included a reduction in lipid content and a decrease in adipocyte markers, indicating an activated state. These modified adipocytes also showed increased expression of proteases, such as matrix metalloproteinase-11, and proinflammatory cytokines like interleukin-6 and interleukin-1β.

We specifically investigated the role of interleukin-6 and found that it played a crucial role in promoting the proinvasive effect of tumor cells. Additionally, we confirmed the presence of these modified adipocytes in human breast tumors using immunohistochemistry and quantitative PCR. Interestingly, we observed that tumors of larger size and/or with lymph node involvement had higher levels of interleukin-6 in the surrounding adipocytes.

Overall, our findings provide compelling evidence that invasive cancer cells have a significant impact on surrounding adipocytes. These peritumoral adipocytes undergo phenotypic changes and acquire specific biological features, leading us to refer to them as cancer-associated adipocytes (CAA). Importantly, these CAAs also modify the characteristics and behavior of cancer cells, making them more aggressive.

Our results support the novel concept that adipocytes participate in a complex cycle driven by cancer cells to promote tumor progression. This cycle may be particularly amplified in obese patients.

title: Prevalence of cardiovascular disease risk factor in the Chinese population: the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study.
text: The aim of this study was to analyze the prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors and non-fatal cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) in the Chinese population. Data was collected from the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study. A nationally representative sample of 46,239 adults aged 20 years and older was randomly recruited. Lifestyle factors, CVD diagnosis, stroke, diabetes, and family history were collected, and glucose tolerance tests were performed. The subjects reported various non-fatal CVDs. Statistical analyses were conducted using SUDAAN software, with a significance level of P < 0.05. The prevalence of coronary heart disease, stroke, and CVDs in males was 0.74%, 1.07%, and 1.78%, respectively. In females, the prevalence was 0.51%, 0.60%, and 1.10%, respectively. CVD prevalence increased with age in both genders. The prevalence of overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia in males was 36.67%, 30.09%, 67.43%, and 26.69%, respectively. In females, the prevalence was 29.77%, 24.79%, 63.98%, and 23.62%, respectively. Among the total sample, 31.17% had one risk factor, 27.38% had two, 17.76% had three, and 10.19% had four or more of the defined risk factors (smoking, overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia). After adjusting for gender and age, the odds ratios for CVDs in individuals with one, two, three, or four or more risk factors were 2.36, 4.24, 4.88, and 7.22, respectively, compared to those with no risk factors. The prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors was high in the Chinese population, with individuals often having multiple risk factors. Effective prevention strategies should be developed to address the increasing burden of cardiovascular morbidity.

title: Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes
text: Diabetes is a collection of chronic diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels. Modern medical care utilizes various lifestyle changes and medications to prevent and control high blood sugar. The goal of diabetes treatment is not only to ensure that the body receives enough glucose, but also to minimize the damage caused by high blood sugar. Protecting the body from high blood sugar is crucial, as it is the main cause of illness and death in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The harmful effects of high blood sugar are typically divided into two categories: macrovascular complications (such as coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, and stroke) and microvascular complications (including diabetic nephropathy, neuropathy, and retinopathy). It is important for doctors to understand the connection between diabetes and vascular disease, as the prevalence of diabetes is increasing in the United States and there are expanding options for preventing and treating these complications. ### Diabetic retinopathy  Diabetic retinopathy is perhaps the most common microvascular complication of diabetes. It leads to approximately 10,000 new cases of blindness each year in the United States alone. The risk of developing diabetic retinopathy or other microvascular complications depends on both the duration and severity of high blood sugar. The UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) found that the development of diabetic retinopathy in patients with type 2 diabetes is linked to both the severity of high blood sugar and the presence of hypertension. Additionally, most patients with type 1 diabetes show signs of retinopathy within 20 years of diagnosis. In some cases, retinopathy may begin to develop as early as 7 years before the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. There are several proposed mechanisms by which diabetes may contribute to the development of retinopathy...

title: Involvement of S-nitrosylation of actin in inhibition of neurotransmitter release by nitric oxide
text: The role of nitric oxide (NO) as a diffusible messenger in pain regulation is still a subject of debate, with conflicting views on whether it is pro-nociceptive or anti-nociceptive. One important mechanism by which NO acts as a signaling molecule is through the reversible post-translational modification of specific cysteine residues in proteins, known as S-nitrosylation. However, the occurrence of S-nitrosylation in the spinal cord and its potential impact on pain transmission are still not well understood. In this study, we used the "biotin-switch" method and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry to identify proteins that undergo S-nitrosylation. Our results reveal that actin, a major protein in the spinal cord, is S-nitrosylated by the NO donor S-nitroso-N-acetyl-DL-penicillamine (SNAP). Interestingly, we found that actin was more S-nitrosylated in the S2 fraction compared to the P2 fraction of the spinal homogenate. Furthermore, treatment of PC12 cells with SNAP led to rapid S-nitrosylation of actin and inhibited dopamine release from these cells. Similar to cytochalasin B, which disrupts actin filaments, SNAP reduced the amount of filamentous actin cytoskeleton just beneath the cell membrane. Importantly, the inhibition of dopamine release was not affected by inhibitors of soluble guanylyl cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase. Overall, our study demonstrates that actin is a major protein undergoing S-nitrosylation in the spinal cord and suggests that NO directly regulates neurotransmitter release through S-nitrosylation, in addition to the well-known phosphorylation by cGMP-dependent protein kinase.

title: Independent Association of Lobular Involution and Mammographic Breast Density With Breast Cancer Risk
text:
In this study, we investigated the relationship between lobular involution, mammographic breast density (MBD), and breast cancer risk in women with benign breast disease. A total of 2666 women with benign breast disease diagnosed at Mayo Clinic between January 1, 1985, and December 31, 1991 were included in the study. We categorized lobular involution as none, partial, or complete, and classified parenchymal pattern using the Wolfe classification as N1 (nondense), P1, P2 (ductal prominence occupying <25%, or >25% of the breast, respectively), or DY (extremely dense). The women were followed up for an average of 13.3 years to track any incidence of breast cancer.

After adjusting for MBD, we found that women with no or partial lobular involution had a higher risk of breast cancer compared to those with complete involution. Specifically, the hazard ratio (HR) for breast cancer incidence was 2.62 for women with no involution and 1.61 for women with partial involution. Similarly, after adjusting for involution, we observed that women with dense breasts had a higher risk of breast cancer compared to those with nondense breasts. The HR for breast cancer incidence was 1.67 for women with extremely dense breasts, 1.96 for women with P2 density, and 1.23 for women with P1 density. Additionally, we found that women with both no involution and dense breasts had a significantly higher risk of breast cancer compared to those with complete involution and nondense breasts (HR = 4.08).

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that both lobular involution and MBD are independently associated with breast cancer incidence. Furthermore, the combination of no involution and dense breasts is associated with an even greater risk for breast cancer.

title: Pleiotropy as a mechanism to stabilize cooperation
text:
Pleiotropy, the phenomenon where most genes affect multiple traits, poses a significant constraint on evolution. This is because making adaptive changes in one trait may compromise other traits that are influenced by the same genes. However, our research reveals an unexpected twist to pleiotropy, showing that it can actually benefit one of the most mysterious adaptations - cooperation.

In the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, a remarkable act of cooperation takes place. Some cells sacrifice themselves to form a stalk, which supports the other cells as reproductive spores. We have identified a gene called dimA in D. discoideum that has two contrasting effects. On one hand, it is necessary for receiving a signaling molecule called DIF-1, which triggers the differentiation into prestalk cells. On the other hand, ignoring DIF-1 and not becoming prestalk cells would allow cells to cheat by avoiding the formation of the stalk.

However, our findings show that in aggregations containing wild-type cells, the absence of the dimA gene leads to exclusion from spore formation. This pleiotropic connection between stalk and spore formation limits the potential for cheating in D. discoideum. Defecting on prestalk cell production not only results in a reduction in spores but also leads to an even greater decrease. Therefore, we propose that the evolution of pleiotropic links between cheating and personal costs can actually stabilize cooperative adaptations.

title: The homeobox gene goosecoid controls cell migration in Xenopus embryos.
text: Goosecoid (gsc), a gene that belongs to the homeobox family, is specifically expressed in the dorsal blastopore lip of the Xenopus gastrula. It is believed to play a significant role in Spemann's organizer phenomenon. To track the destiny of embryonic cells that were injected with gsc mRNA, lineage tracing and time-lapse microscopy techniques were employed. The injection of gsc mRNA had effects that extended beyond the injected cells, as it caused neighboring cells to join in the formation of a duplicated dorsal axis. When gsc mRNA was expressed in ventral blastomeres or overexpressed in dorsal blastomeres, the cells moved towards the anterior of the embryo. These findings indicate that gsc is involved in controlling the movements of groups of cells during gastrulation, but not in individual cells. Moreover, they demonstrate that a homeobox gene in vertebrates can regulate the migration of cells in specific regions.

title: Epigenetic switch involved in activation of pioneer factor FOXA1-dependent enhancers.
text: Transcription factors (TFs) specifically bind to specific regions of mammalian genomes known as cis-regulatory elements. These elements include enhancers, which play a crucial role in regulating gene expression during development and differentiation. While the importance of chromatin in controlling TF functions is recognized, there is still much to learn about the chromatin structure of enhancers and how it is established. In this study, we examined enhancers that recruit FOXA1, a pioneer transcription factor that activates transcriptional competency of these cis-regulatory sites, on a genomic scale. Importantly, we discovered that FOXA1 binds to genomic regions with local DNA hypomethylation, and its recruitment to chromatin is dependent on the differential DNA methylation levels of its binding sites in specific cell types. Using neural differentiation as a model, we demonstrated that the induction of FOXA1 expression and its subsequent recruitment to enhancers is associated with DNA demethylation. Additionally, histone H3 lysine 4 methylation is induced at these enhancers. These epigenetic changes both stabilize FOXA1 binding and enable the recruitment of transcriptional regulatory effectors. Interestingly, when these FOXA1-dependent enhancers were cloned into reporter constructs, they were able to reproduce their cell type specificity. However, their activities were hindered by DNA methylation. Therefore, these enhancers are intrinsic cell-type-specific regulatory regions that require FOXA1 to activate an epigenetic switch, including DNA demethylation, to potentiate their activities.

title: Leptin treatment ameliorates anxiety in ob/ob obese mice.
text: We conducted a study to determine the impact of administered leptin on anxiety-like behavior in ob/ob mice. Leptin was administered intraperitoneally for 5 consecutive days. Anxiety levels were assessed using the standard elevated plus maze, while body weight was measured daily. The repeated administration of leptin resulted in a significant increase in the percentage of entries in the open arms and the total number of entries. Additionally, the mice experienced a significant reduction in body weight by 13.2% after the treatment. Notably, leptin treatment not only improved obesity but also alleviated anxiety in ob/ob mice. These findings suggest that addressing obesity may contribute to resolving psychological issues.

title: Predicting new molecular targets for known drugs
text: Although drugs are designed to target specific physiological processes, some drugs can bind to multiple targets, which can explain both their side effects and effectiveness. With numerous drug-target combinations available, it would be beneficial to explore potential interactions using computational methods. In this study, we examined 3,665 drugs approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as well as investigational drugs against hundreds of targets. Each target was defined by its ligands. By analyzing chemical similarities between drugs and ligand sets, we were able to predict thousands of unexpected associations. Thirty of these associations were tested experimentally, including the discovery that the transporter inhibitor Prozac can antagonize the beta(1) receptor, the ion channel drug Vadilex can inhibit the 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) transporter, and the enzyme inhibitor Rescriptor can antagonize the histamine H(4) receptor. Overall, we confirmed 23 new associations between drugs and targets, five of which exhibited potent effects at concentrations below 100 nM. The physiological relevance of one association, involving the drug N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and serotonergic receptors, was confirmed in a knockout mouse model. Our systematic and comprehensive approach based on chemical similarity can provide insights into potential side effects and new indications for many drugs.

title: Bone loss and vascular calcification: A bi-directional interplay?
text: Vascular calcification (VC) is a well-known predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Previously thought to be a passive and degenerative process, VC is now recognized as an active process similar to bone formation. It shares many similarities with bone development and metabolism, including histopathological features, mineral composition, and initiation mechanisms. Oxidative stress and inflammation play important roles in both VC and osteoporosis (OP). Biochemical factors that regulate healthy bone metabolism also have an impact on VC. These biomarkers include vitamin D, osteoprotegerin, osteopontin, matrix Gla protein, cathepsin K, fibroblast growth factor-23, and fetuin-A. Understanding the complex regulatory network involved in these processes, which includes multiple feedback loops and communication between organs, may help reduce the increasing prevalence of calcific vasculopathy and OP in the aging population. It may also lead to the development of common preventive and therapeutic interventions for both conditions.

title: Immobilized chemokine fields and soluble chemokine gradients cooperatively shape migration patterns of dendritic cells.
text: Chemokines play a crucial role in regulating the movement of immune cells by inducing either directed or random migration and promoting cell adhesion through integrin activation. Our study focused on dendritic cell (DC) migration and found that the specific cellular responses were influenced by how chemokines were presented in tissues. When the chemokine CCL21, which is anchored to heparan sulfate, was immobilized on the cell surface, it caused DCs to randomly move within the confined area of the chemokine-presenting surface due to integrin-mediated adhesion. However, when DCs came into direct contact with CCL21, they cleaved the anchoring residues of the chemokine, releasing it from the solid phase. This soluble form of CCL21 functionally resembled another CCR7 ligand, CCL19, which lacks anchoring residues and forms soluble gradients. Both soluble CCR7 ligands induced chemotactic movement of DCs, but did not promote surface adhesion. The combination of adhesive random migration and directed steering resulted in dynamic yet spatially restricted locomotion patterns that closely resembled the cellular dynamics observed in secondary lymphoid organs.

title: Local proliferation dominates lesional macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis
text: In the process of atherogenesis, where inflammation occurs, macrophages gradually accumulate in the expanding arterial wall. It has been observed that circulating monocytes give rise to these macrophages, emphasizing the role of monocyte infiltration in macrophage buildup. However, recent research suggests that in certain inflammatory situations, macrophage accumulation does not rely on monocyte recruitment. Therefore, we decided to investigate the mechanism behind macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis. In our study on atherosclerotic lesions in mice, we discovered that macrophages have a rapid turnover rate, occurring after 4 weeks. The replenishment of macrophages in these experimental atheromata is primarily dependent on local macrophage proliferation rather than the influx of monocytes. The microenvironment plays a crucial role in orchestrating macrophage proliferation through the involvement of scavenger receptor A (SR-A). Our findings highlight macrophage proliferation as a significant event in atherosclerosis and identify macrophage self-renewal as a potential target for therapeutic interventions in cardiovascular disease.

title: Enzymatically active lysosomal proteases are associated with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer brain.
text: The development of beta-amyloid in the brains of individuals with Alzheimer's disease is dependent on the breakdown of a protein found in the cell membrane. The specific enzymes responsible for this process have not yet been identified. Cathepsins are typically enzymes found inside cells that break down proteins in lysosomes. However, when sections of Alzheimer's brains were examined using antibodies for cathepsin D and cathepsin B, high levels of these enzymes were also found in senile plaques. No cathepsin activity was observed in control brains from individuals without neurological diseases or in patients with Huntington's or Parkinson's disease. Further analysis using synthetic peptides and protein substrates revealed that senile plaques contained the highest levels of active cathepsin enzymes. At the microscopic level, cathepsin activity in senile plaques was mainly found in lysosomal dense bodies and lipofuscin granules, which are located outside of cells. Similar structures were also present in degenerating neurons of the Alzheimer's neocortex, and some senile plaques contained disintegrating neurons filled with cathepsins. The presence of abnormally high levels of active lysosomal proteases in senile plaques suggests that these enzymes may play a role in the formation of amyloid. We propose that amyloid precursor protein within senile plaques is broken down by lysosomal proteases primarily released from degenerating neurons. The escape of cathepsins from their normal intracellular environment may lead to abnormal breakdown of accumulating amyloid precursor protein.

title: Gastric juice miR-129 as a potential biomarker for screening gastric cancer
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play vital roles in the development and progression of gastric cancer. However, conventional serological tests for screening gastric cancer have limitations in terms of sensitivity and specificity. Although several miRNAs in peripheral blood have been used as biomarkers for gastric cancer, many of these miRNAs are also found in other types of cancer. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using miR-129-1/2, which are specifically expressed in gastric juice and aberrantly expressed in gastric cancer, as a screening tool for gastric cancer. We collected a total of 141 gastric juice samples from patients with gastric cancer, gastric ulcer, atrophic gastritis, minimal gastritis, or normal mucosa using gastroscopy. The levels of miR-129-1/2 in gastric juice were measured using quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. We constructed a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve to differentiate patients with gastric cancer from those with benign gastric diseases. Our findings revealed that patients with gastric cancer had significantly lower levels of gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p compared to patients with benign gastric diseases. The areas under the ROC curve (AUC) for miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p were 0.639 and 0.651, respectively. When we combined the two miRNAs in parallel, the AUC increased to 0.656. In conclusion, our results suggest that gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p have the potential to serve as biomarkers for screening gastric cancer. Furthermore, the detection of gastric juice miRNAs offers a convenient and non-invasive method for diagnosing gastric cancer.

title: Epidemiological expansion, structural studies, and clinical challenges of new β-lactamases from gram-negative bacteria.
text: The evolution of β-Lactamase poses a significant challenge for the infectious disease community when it comes to treating infections caused by gram-negative bacteria that are resistant to multiple drugs. With over 1,000 naturally occurring β-Lactamases, it has become increasingly difficult to establish a correlation between their structure and function. While new enzymes in the extended-spectrum β-Lactamase (ESBL) families are frequently discovered, the older CTX-M-14 and CTX-M-15 enzymes have become the most common ESBLs in global surveillance. The emergence of carbapenemases, which utilize either serine-based or zinc-facilitated hydrolysis mechanisms, is causing some of the most critical problems. KPC serine carbapenemases and metallo-β-Lactamases VIM, IMP, and NDM-1 are now reported in most geographical regions, despite NDM-1 being a recent discovery. The rapid emergence of these newer enzymes, often found in a single organism, makes it even more challenging to develop new β-Lactamase inhibitors or β-Lactams that are resistant to β-Lactamase activity. Combination therapy will likely be necessary to combat the ongoing evolution of these dangerous enzymes in multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Robust synchronization of coupled circadian and cell cycle oscillators in single mammalian cells
text: The synchronization of circadian cycles and cell cycles, which both have a period of approximately 1 day, is a significant phenomenon. To understand the interactions between these two oscillators, we conducted a study using time-lapse imaging of individual mammalian NIH3T3 fibroblasts over several days. Our analysis of numerous circadian cycles in dividing cells revealed that both oscillators operate in a 1:1 mode-locked state, with cell divisions consistently occurring 5 hours before the peak in circadian Rev-Erbα-YFP reporter expression. This synchrony can be attributed to either unidirectional or bidirectional coupling. While previous research has focused on the circadian cycle influencing cell division, our data, combined with stochastic modeling, unequivocally demonstrate that the reverse coupling is the primary mechanism in NIH3T3 cells. Furthermore, we found that temperature, genetic, and pharmacological perturbations do not significantly disrupt the synchronized state of these two interacting cellular oscillators, indicating a high level of robustness across a wide range of parameters. These findings have important implications for understanding circadian function in tissues that undergo proliferation, such as the epidermis, immune cells, and cancer cells.

title: Identification of a Brainstem Circuit Controlling Feeding
text: The feeling of hunger, which occurs when there is an imbalance in energy, triggers the desire to find and consume food. While certain neurons in the hypothalamus play a role in this response, the specific cell types in other areas of the brain are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), which contain transporters for GABA or glutamate (referred to as DRNVgat and DRNVGLUT3 neurons), are activated in response to changes in energy balance. Interestingly, manipulating the activity of these neurons has opposite effects on feeding - DRNVgat neurons increase food intake, while DRNVGLUT3 neurons suppress it. Additionally, when we modulated these neurons in obese mice, it resulted in reduced food intake, weight loss, and normalized activity levels. Through molecular profiling, we also identified potential targets in these neurons that can be targeted by drugs. Furthermore, we found that infusing specific receptor agonists directly into these neurons had significant effects on feeding. These findings highlight the importance of the DRN in regulating energy balance.

title: Infection-induced NETosis is a dynamic process involving neutrophil multitasking in vivo
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are released when neutrophils die in a laboratory setting, which takes several hours. This creates a time gap that invasive microbes can take advantage of. It has not been observed that neutrophils are capable of migrating and phagocytosis while undergoing NETosis. However, during Gram-positive skin infections, we were able to directly observe live polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs) rapidly releasing NETs in real-time. This prevented the spread of bacteria throughout the body. The process of NETosis occurred while the PMNs were crawling, resulting in the formation of large areas of NETs. The PMNs undergoing NETosis had diffuse decondensed nuclei and eventually lost their DNA. These cells with abnormal nuclei displayed unusual crawling behavior, characterized by erratic pseudopods and hyperpolarization, suggesting that the nucleus played a role in their movement. The release of NETs was tightly regulated by both Toll-like receptor 2 and complement-mediated opsonization. Furthermore, when live human PMNs were injected into mouse skin, they also developed decondensed nuclei and formed NETs in vivo. In Gram-positive human abscesses, intact neutrophils without nuclei were abundant. Therefore, early in an infection, NETosis involves neutrophils that do not undergo cell death and can still perform multiple tasks.

title: Swim training suppresses tumor growth in mice.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of physical training on the growth of cancer induced by injecting Ehrlich tumor cells into mice. Male Swiss mice were divided into two groups: one group underwent a swim training program (5 days a week for 6 weeks, with 1 hour of swimming at 50% of their maximum capacity), while the other group remained sedentary in their cages. At the end of the fourth week, the mice were injected with Ehrlich tumor cells, and after 6 weeks of training, they were euthanized. The weights of the heart and solid tumors were measured, and tumor volumes were calculated. Some portions of the tumors were used to assess the accumulation of macrophages and neutrophils, while others were fixed in neutral 10% buffered formalin for histological analysis. The sedentary mice had tumor volumes and weights approximately 270% and 280% higher, respectively, than the trained mice. The trained mice also had significantly lower levels of macrophage infiltration in the tumor tissue (0.65 +/- 0.16 macrophages x 10(3) compared to 1.78 +/- 0.43 macrophages x 10(3) in the sedentary group). Additionally, exercise training slightly reduced neutrophil accumulation in the tumors and decreased the number of tumor cells in the trained mice. The trained mice showed a significant increase in exercise capacity, with a 440% longer exercise time at 50% of their maximum capacity. In conclusion, swim training delayed the growth of Ehrlich tumors in mice, accompanied by a decrease in macrophage infiltration and neutrophil accumulation. These findings support the idea that controlled physical activity may be an important therapeutic approach to prevent cancer progression and improve the effectiveness of cancer treatment.

title: Lung dendritic cells imprint T cell lung homing and promote lung immunity through the chemokine receptor CCR4
text: The mechanisms behind T cell lung homing, which is crucial for lung immunity, are not well understood. However, our research demonstrates that lung dendritic cells (DCs) play a role in imprinting T cell lung homing. We found that T cells activated by lung DCs are more efficient in trafficking into the lung in response to inhaled antigen, both during homeostasis and in comparison to T cells activated by DCs from other tissues. As a result, T cells imprinted by lung DCs provide better protection against influenza compared to T cells imprinted by gut and skin DCs. We also discovered that lung DCs induce the expression of CCR4 on T cells, and CCR4 is involved in T cell lung imprinting. T cells lacking CCR4, activated by lung DCs, do not traffic into the lung as effectively and are less effective in protecting against influenza compared to T cells with sufficient CCR4 levels that are activated by lung DCs. In conclusion, lung DCs play a role in imprinting T cell lung homing and contribute to lung immunity, partly through the involvement of CCR4.

title: microRNAs: A Safeguard against Turmoil?
text: New evidence indicates that microRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in various stress responses, in addition to their well-known involvement in development. Interestingly, miRNAs, which typically inhibit the expression of target transcripts, can actually promote expression under stressful conditions. This unexpected phenomenon could be partially attributed to novel interactions between miRNA/Argonaute complexes and RNA-binding proteins that undergo relocation from distinct subcellular compartments during stress.

title: Vascular smooth muscle cell calcification is mediated by regulated exosome secretion.
text:
The purpose of this study is to investigate the regulation and role of matrix vesicle (MV) biogenesis in vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) calcification. MVs, which are secreted by VSMCs, serve as the initial site for mineralization, and fetuin-A, a potent inhibitor of calcification, is specifically loaded into MVs. However, the mechanisms involved in fetuin-A intracellular trafficking and MV biogenesis are not well understood.

In this study, Alexa488-labeled fetuin-A was taken up by human VSMCs, transported through the endosomal system, and released from multivesicular bodies via exosome release. VSMC-derived exosomes were found to contain the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81, and their release was regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3. Comparative proteomics revealed that VSMC-derived exosomes had a similar composition to exosomes from other cell sources, but also shared components with MVs derived from osteoblasts, including calcium-binding and extracellular matrix proteins.

Elevated extracellular calcium levels were found to induce the expression of sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 and the secretion of calcifying exosomes from VSMCs in vitro. Inhibition of sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 prevented VSMC calcification. In vessels from chronic kidney disease patients on dialysis, multivesicular bodies containing exosomes were observed, and CD63 was found to colocalize with calcification. Additionally, factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α and platelet-derived growth factor-BB were found to increase exosome production, leading to increased VSMC calcification under calcifying conditions.

In conclusion, this study identifies MVs as exosomes and demonstrates that factors that increase exosome release can promote vascular calcification in response to environmental calcium stress. Modulating the exosome release pathway may be a potential therapeutic target for prevention.

title: Vaccines against malaria
text:
There is currently no licensed vaccine available for any human parasitic disease, including Plasmodium falciparum malaria, which is a leading cause of infectious mortality. Developing a vaccine for this disease has proven to be a significant challenge for researchers. However, progress has been made in exploring various approaches to design and develop a malaria vaccine, thanks to the availability of a safe model for testing vaccine candidates' efficacy on a small scale.

Malaria vaccine development has been at the forefront of evaluating new vaccine technologies, such as innovative adjuvants, prime-boost regimens using vectors, and the concept of community vaccination to prevent malaria transmission. Most of the current vaccine candidates focus on targeting a specific stage of the parasite's life cycle, with the most successful results seen in vaccines targeting the early pre-erythrocytic stages. One promising vaccine is a protein in adjuvant vaccine that stimulates the production of antibodies against sporozoites, while another approach involves viral vector vaccines that trigger cellular immunity against the intracellular liver-stage parasite. These vaccines have shown partial efficacy in human trials, and the anti-sporozoite vaccine is currently undergoing phase III trials.

However, to achieve a more effective malaria vaccine that can be widely and cost-effectively deployed, it is likely that a multi-component vaccine targeting multiple stages of the parasite's life cycle will be necessary. The most promising approach in the near future is to combine existing partially effective pre-erythrocytic vaccine candidates to create a comprehensive product.

title: MicroRNA-21 is Induced by Rapamycin in a Model of Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC) and Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
text: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a disease that affects women and involves the excessive growth of smooth muscle-like cells in the lungs, leading to the formation of cysts and lung damage. Women with LAM may also develop renal angiomyolipomas. The cause of LAM is mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, which results in overactive signaling of the mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR). Treatment with the mTOR inhibitor, Rapamycin, can stabilize lung function and reduce the size of renal angiomyolipomas in LAM patients. However, when treatment is stopped, lung function declines and angiomyolipomas grow back, suggesting that factors induced by mTORC1 inhibition may support the survival of TSC2-deficient cells. The role of microRNA (miRNA) signaling in the response of LAM to mTORC1 inhibition is not yet understood. In this study, we conducted two separate screens to identify Rapamycin-dependent miRNA in cells derived from angiomyolipomas of LAM patients. The first screen focused on 132 miRNA known to be important in tumor biology, and we found that 48 miRNA were upregulated and 4 were downregulated by Rapamycin. In the second screen, which included 946 miRNA, 18 were upregulated and 8 were downregulated. Among the miRNA that were consistently upregulated in both screens were miR-29b, miR-21, miR-24, miR-221, miR-106a, and miR-199a, which we classified as "RapamiRs." Further validation using qRT-PCR confirmed the increased expression of these miRNA. Notably, miR-21, a miRNA associated with cell survival, showed the most significant increase in response to mTOR inhibition. The regulation of miR-21 by Rapamycin was found to be independent of cell type. Overall, our findings demonstrate that Rapamycin treatment leads to the upregulation of multiple miRNA, including those involved in cell survival, in cells derived from LAM patients with TSC2 mutations. The induction of these miRNA may play a role in the response of LAM and TSC patients to Rapamycin therapy.

title: Reduced NF1 expression confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in lung cancer.
text: Mutations in the EGF receptor (EGFR) can make certain drugs, like erlotinib and gefitinib, effective in treating lung cancer. However, resistance to these drugs can develop, often due to a second EGFR mutation called T790M. Our research involved studying a human lung cancer cell line and mouse models of lung adenocarcinoma with mutant EGFR. We discovered that reduced expression of neurofibromin, a protein encoded by the NF1 gene that regulates RAS activity, was associated with resistance to erlotinib. When neurofibromin levels were low, erlotinib was unable to fully inhibit RAS-ERK signaling. However, when we treated neurofibromin-deficient lung cancers with a MEK inhibitor, sensitivity to erlotinib was restored. We also found that low levels of NF1 expression were linked to both primary and acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitors in lung adenocarcinoma patients. These findings suggest that a subgroup of patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma may benefit from combination therapy using both EGFR and MEK inhibitors.

title: Human IRGM induces autophagy to eliminate intracellular mycobacteria.
text: The role of immunity-related p47 guanosine triphosphatases (IRG) in defending against intracellular pathogens has been discovered. Our research has shown that the murine Irgm1 (LRG-47) guanosine triphosphatase induces autophagy, leading to the formation of large autolysosomal organelles. This mechanism effectively eliminates intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Additionally, we have identified a similar function for a human IRG protein in controlling intracellular pathogens. Our findings indicate that the human Irgm1 ortholog, IRGM, is involved in autophagy and reducing the burden of intracellular bacilli.

title: Implementation of a Clinical Pharmacy Education Program in a Teaching Hospital: Resident Oriented Documentation and Intervention
text: The objective of this study was to establish a clinical pharmacy education program at Masih Daneshvari hospital, a Tehran-based hospital affiliated with a university in Iran. To achieve this, the most common interventions involving pharmacists and potential areas for education of pharmacy students and residents were identified. From January 2006 to January 2007, clinical pharmacy interventions and drug information forms were completed. The study yielded a total of 772 interventions during the year. Among all interventions, drug information accounted for the highest percentage at 22.30%, followed by dose adjustment and therapeutic reduction or addition. On average, each patient had 8.62 ± 7.54 medications. In conclusion, although the pharmacy profession in our country is still in its early stages compared to developed nations, this study demonstrates a significant demand for this service among healthcare providers.

title: The surgical anatomy of the conduction tissues.
text: Based on our collective experience, we have examined the arrangement of the cardiac conduction tissues as they may be observed by surgeons in both normal and abnormal hearts. The sinus node is located beneath the outer layer of the heart in the terminal sulcus. Due to its varying blood supply, the entire upper junction where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium poses a potential risk. There are no distinct pathways that extend through the atrial tissues between the sinus and atrioventricular nodes. The atrioventricular node, which is the atrial portion of the atrioventricular conduction axis, is exclusively contained within the triangle of Koch. This axis passes through the central fibrous body and branches on the muscular septum of the ventricle, just below the interventricular part of the membranous septum. The landmarks for these structures are described as they would appear when viewed through the right atrium, left atrium, and aorta. We then explore the surgical anatomy of abnormal muscular connections between the atria and ventricles, which are associated with ventricular pre-excitation syndromes. Finally, we establish guidelines for accurately predicting the arrangement of conduction tissues in hearts with congenital malformations, considering both normal and abnormal chamber connections. The most significant factors in this regard are the alignment between the septal structures of the atria and ventricles, as well as the pattern of ventricular architecture.

title: Agreement between an online dietary assessment tool (myfood24) and an interviewer-administered 24-h dietary recall in British adolescents aged 11-18 years.
text: myfood24 is an online tool that allows British adolescents and adults to assess their dietary intake 24 hours a day. However, there is limited information on the accuracy of using this technology to assess nutritional intake among adolescents. To address this, a study was conducted to compare myfood24 with a face-to-face interviewer-administered 24-hour recall among seventy-five British adolescents aged 11-18 years. The participants were asked to complete both myfood24 and the interviewer-administered recall on two separate days at school. The data collected from both methods were compared in terms of energy intake and nutrients using various statistical measures. The results showed strong agreement between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered recall for energy, macronutrients, and other reported nutrients. The mean difference in energy intake between the two methods was not significant, indicating no bias. The agreement between the two methods in classifying adolescents into tertiles of energy intake was also good. Additionally, the reliability of myfood24 was demonstrated by the consistent results obtained on day 1 and day 2. Overall, myfood24 has the potential to collect dietary data of similar quality to that obtained through an interviewer-administered recall.

title: Modulation of cancer chemotherapy by green tea.
text: The use of biochemical modulation has been crucial in the advancement of cancer chemotherapy. Our focus has been on studying the impact of common beverages, specifically green tea and its components, on the effectiveness of doxorubicin in fighting tumors. To investigate this, we conducted a combined treatment of doxorubicin and green tea on mice with Ehrlich ascites carcinoma tumors. The oral administration of green tea resulted in a 2.5-fold increase in the inhibitory effects of doxorubicin on tumor growth. Additionally, the combination of green tea with doxorubicin increased the concentration of doxorubicin in the tumor, while no such increase was observed in normal tissues. Furthermore, we observed that green tea enhanced the antitumor activity of doxorubicin even in M5076 ovarian sarcoma, which typically has low sensitivity to the drug. These findings suggest that consuming green tea can support cancer chemotherapy and potentially improve the quality of life for patients undergoing treatment.

title: Histone deacetylase 5 interacts with Krüppel-like factor 2 and inhibits its transcriptional activity in endothelium.
text: Atherosclerosis is characterized by vascular endothelial dysfunction and inflammation. The transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays a crucial role in the anti-inflammatory and anti-atherosclerotic properties of the endothelium. However, the mechanisms regulating the activation of KLF2 transcription are not well understood. In this study, we discovered that histone deacetylase 5 (HDAC5) interacts with KLF2 and inhibits its transcriptional activation. HDAC5 was found to be present in the nuclei of human umbilical cord vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) along with KLF2. Under steady laminar flow conditions, HDAC5's association with KLF2 was reduced due to HDAC5 phosphorylation-dependent nuclear export in HUVECs. We also identified the specific regions of KLF2 and HDAC5 that interact with each other. Chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase reporter assays demonstrated that HDAC5 directly suppresses KLF2 transcriptional activation. Overexpression of HDAC5 inhibited the activity of the endothelial nitric oxide synthesis (eNOS) promoter, as well as gene expression in HUVECs and bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs) that depend on KLF2. Conversely, silencing HDAC5 enhanced KLF2 transcription and subsequently increased eNOS expression in HUVECs. Furthermore, we observed that HDAC5 knockout mice had higher levels of eNOS protein and lower expression of the pro-inflammatory vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 in the thoracic aorta compared to wild-type mice. In conclusion, our study uncovers a new role for HDAC5 in regulating KLF2 transcriptional activation and eNOS expression. These findings suggest that HDAC5, as a binding partner and modulator of KLF2, could be a potential therapeutic target for preventing vascular endothelial dysfunction associated with cardiovascular diseases.

title: N348I in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase can counteract the nevirapine-mediated bias toward RNase H cleavage during plus-strand initiation.
text: Mutations in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) that lead to drug resistance can impact the balance between the enzyme's polymerase and ribonuclease H (RNase H) activities. Our recent research has shown that the N348I mutation in the connection domain causes selective dissociation from RNase H-competent complexes, while the polymerase-competent complex remains mostly unaffected. N348I has been linked to resistance against the non-nucleoside RT inhibitor (NNRTI), nevirapine, but the mechanism connecting changes in RNase H activity to changes in NNRTI susceptibility is still unknown. To address this issue, we have considered recent findings suggesting that NNRTIs may alter the orientation of RT on its nucleic acid substrate and increase RNase H activity. Our study demonstrates that NNRTIs indeed enhance RNase H-mediated primer removal, but the N348I mutant enzyme is able to counteract this effect. Efavirenz, a potent inhibitor, limits the impact of the mutation. These findings provide compelling evidence that N348I can overcome the inhibitory effects of nevirapine during the initiation of (+)-strand DNA synthesis, offering a new resistance mechanism. The data align with clinical observations, which show a stronger impact of N348I on nevirapine susceptibility compared to efavirenz.
