title: Cancer survivorship research: the challenge of recruiting adult long term cancer survivors from a cooperative clinical trials group
text:
As the number of adult cancer survivors continues to rise, there is a growing need for information that connects potential long-term effects with specific treatment plans. While only a small percentage of adult cancer patients participate in clinical trials, those who have previously been enrolled in these trials can provide valuable insights into treatment-related late effects. 

In this study, we focused on survivors of colorectal cancer and utilized a database from five phase III randomized clinical trials conducted by the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast & Bowel Project (NSABP) to recruit and enroll long-term survivors. We encountered various challenges in recruiting patients who had undergone treatment 5-20 years ago. 

We invited sixty-five NSABP treatment sites to participate in the study, and sixty agreed, giving us the potential to recruit 2,408 patients. However, we only received registration forms for 976 patients (41%), of whom 744 (76%) expressed interest in participating. Ultimately, 708 patients completed interviews, accounting for 95% of those who had expressed interest and 29% of the total potential sample. The recruitment process was hindered by difficulties in locating patients, lack of commitment from institutions, and lack of patient interest. 

It is crucial to recognize that patients treated on clinical trials offer a valuable opportunity to examine the long-term effects of cancer treatments. However, retrospective recruitment has its limitations. In the future, it is important to establish mechanisms for prospective long-term follow-up to identify and understand the frequency and nature of late effects associated with cancer treatments. 

For cancer survivors, it is increasingly important to gather insights from participants in clinical trials to determine whether specific treatment plans are associated with any significant late effects. As patients live longer, this knowledge will be crucial in improving their quality of life and overall well-being.

title: Arylsulfatase B Improves Locomotor Function after Mouse Spinal Cord Injury
text:
We conducted a study to investigate the potential of the mammalian enzyme arylsulfatase B (ARSB) in enhancing recovery after spinal cord injury in mice. Previously, bacterial chondroitinase ABC (ChaseABC) has been used to remove inhibitory chondroitin sulfate chains from chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans to improve regeneration after spinal cord injury in rodents. However, we believed that ARSB could be a more attractive alternative to ChaseABC due to its greater chemical stability and reduced immunogenicity.

In our experiment, we administered a one-time injection of human ARSB into the injured spinal cord of mice. Within five days, the injection successfully eliminated immunoreactivity for chondroitin sulfates, and this effect persisted for up to 9 weeks after the injury. We then assessed the locomotor recovery of the mice using the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) and found that, after a moderate spinal cord injury, the ARSB-treated mice showed improved recovery compared to the control group that received a buffer treatment. This improvement was observed at 6 weeks after the injection.

Furthermore, in mice with severe spinal cord injuries, both the ARSB and ChaseABC treated groups showed similar improvements in locomotor recovery, which were significantly greater than those observed in the control group. Additionally, the presence of serotonin and tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive axons was more extensive in the spinal cords of mice treated with ARSB or ChaseABC compared to the control group. Moreover, these immunoreactive axons penetrated further beyond the injury site in the ARSB or ChaseABC treated mice.

These findings suggest that mammalian ARSB can enhance functional recovery after central nervous system (CNS) injury. However, the specific structural and molecular mechanisms underlying this improvement remain to be elucidated.

title: The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population.
text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) is a self-report screening scale for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It was developed alongside the revision of the WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI). In this report, we present data on the agreement between the ASRS and a shorter version of the ASRS screener with blind clinical diagnoses in a community sample.

The ASRS consists of 18 questions that assess the frequency of recent symptoms of adult ADHD according to the DSM-IV criteria. The ASRS screener is a shorter version of the scale, consisting of six questions that were selected using stepwise logistic regression to optimize agreement with clinical diagnoses. We compared the responses on the ASRS to blind clinical ratings of adult ADHD based on DSM-IV criteria in a sample of 154 respondents who had previously participated in the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (NCS-R). We oversampled individuals who reported childhood ADHD and adult persistence.

We found that each symptom measure on the ASRS was significantly related to the corresponding clinical symptom rating. However, there was substantial variation in agreement between the two measures, with Cohen's kappa ranging from 0.16 to 0.81. The optimal scoring method to predict clinical syndrome classifications was to sum the unweighted dichotomous responses across all 18 ASRS questions. However, due to the wide variation in agreement at the symptom level, the unweighted six-question ASRS screener performed better than the unweighted 18-question ASRS in terms of sensitivity (68.7% vs. 56.3%), specificity (99.5% vs. 98.3%), total classification accuracy (97.9% vs. 96.2%), and kappa (0.76 vs. 0.58).

In conclusion, larger samples and further clinical calibration might reveal that a weighted version of the 18-question ASRS performs better than the six-question ASRS screener. However, until that time, it is recommended to use the unweighted screener instead of the full ASRS in community surveys, clinical outreach, and case-finding initiatives.

title: Human milk proresolving mediators stimulate resolution of acute inflammation
text: We conducted a study to examine the properties of human milk and its impact on resolving inflammation. We used human milk lipid mediator isolates (HLMIs) to investigate their effects on resolution programs in both live subjects and human macrophages. The HLMIs reduced the number of neutrophils and shortened the time it took for resolution to occur compared to peritonitis. Through rigorous analysis, we found that human milk contains specialized proresolving mediators (LM-SPMs) at bioactive levels that enhance the function of human macrophages and help contain bacterial infections. These SPMs include resolvins, protectins, maresins, and lipoxins. Specifically, we identified D-series resolvins, PD1, MaR1, E-series resolvins, and LXs in human milk. When administered individually, RvD2 and MaR1 significantly shortened the resolution time. Milk from mastitis, however, had higher levels of leukotriene B4 and prostanoids and lower levels of SPMs. Overall, our findings suggest that human milk has proresolving properties through the presence of LM-SPMs, which may play a role in maternal-infant biochemical imprinting.

title: Cerebral perfusion and stroke.
text: Stroke is a diverse condition caused by various disease mechanisms, all of which lead to a disturbance in the flow of blood to the brain and subsequent harm to the tissue. This article examines the mechanisms that regulate the normal circulation of blood in the brain and how they are affected in cases of illness. A key idea in the treatment of patients with sudden blockage of blood supply to the brain is the presence of an area of potentially recoverable tissue known as the "ischaemic penumbra." The evidence supporting the existence of this penumbra in humans is thoroughly explored.

title: Epigenetic regulation of miR-184 by MBD1 governs neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
text: The gene expression in adult neural stem/progenitor cells (aNSCs) is regulated by Methyl-CpG binding protein 1 (MBD1) through a DNA methylation-mediated epigenetic mechanism. Our previous research showed that a deficiency in MBD1 impairs the differentiation and neurogenesis of aNSCs, but the exact mechanism behind this was unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that MBD1 controls the expression of multiple microRNAs in aNSCs, particularly repressing miR-184. High levels of miR-184 promote cell proliferation but inhibit differentiation of aNSCs, while inhibiting miR-184 rescues the phenotypes associated with MBD1 deficiency. Additionally, we discovered that miR-184 regulates the expression of Numblike (Numbl), a known regulator of brain development, by binding to the 3'-UTR of Numbl mRNA and affecting its translation. Introducing exogenous Numbl can rescue the defects in aNSCs caused by either miR-184 overexpression or MBD1 deficiency. Therefore, MBD1, miR-184, and Numbl together form a regulatory network that helps maintain the balance between proliferation and differentiation in aNSCs.

title: Landscape of genetic lesions in 944 patients with myelodysplastic syndromes
text: The use of high-throughput DNA sequencing has made a significant impact on the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). Our study aimed to determine the biological and prognostic importance of genetic abnormalities in MDS. We screened a total of 944 patients with different subtypes of MDS for known or potential mutations or deletions in 104 genes using targeted deep sequencing and array-based genomic hybridization. Out of the 944 patients, 845 (89.5%) had at least one mutation, with a median of 3 mutations per patient (range, 0-12). We found that 47 genes were significantly mutated, with TET2, SF3B1, ASXL1, SRSF2, DNMT3A, and RUNX1 being the most commonly mutated genes, occurring in more than 10% of cases. Many of these mutations were associated with higher risk groups and increased blast levels. We also investigated the survival of 875 patients and found that 25 out of the 48 genes tested (including PRPF8) had an impact on survival (P<0.05) in univariate analysis. By combining the status of 14 genes with conventional factors, we developed a novel prognostic model ('Model-1') that divided patients into four risk groups ('low', 'intermediate', 'high', 'very high risk') with 3-year survival rates of 95.2%, 69.3%, 32.8%, and 5.3% respectively (P<0.001). We then constructed a 'gene-only model' ('Model-2') based on the 14 genes, which also resulted in four significant risk groups (P<0.001). Both models were validated in a separate cohort of 175 patients (P<0.001 each). In conclusion, the comprehensive genetic and molecular profiling of multiple target genes is essential for the classification and prognosis of MDS patients.

title: Integrated molecular genetic profiling of pediatric high-grade gliomas reveals key differences with the adult disease.
text:
The purpose of this study was to identify the copy number alterations and gene expression signatures associated with pediatric high-grade glioma (HGG). The researchers analyzed genomic imbalances in 78 pediatric HGGs, including seven diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, and 10 HGGs in children who had previously received cranial irradiation for cancer. They used single nucleotide polymorphism microarray analysis to examine copy number alterations and gene expression microarrays to analyze gene expression in 53 tumors. The results were compared to data from adult tumors.

The study found significant differences in copy number alterations between childhood and adult glioblastoma. Focal amplification of the PDGFRA gene was the most common alteration in childhood HGG, including diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas. Gene expression analysis supported the role of deregulated PDGFRalpha signaling in pediatric HGG. No IDH1 hotspot mutations were found in pediatric tumors, highlighting differences from adult secondary glioblastoma. Pediatric and adult glioblastomas were distinguished by frequent gain of chromosome 1q and lower frequency of chromosome 7 gain and 10q loss. PDGFRA amplification and 1q gain were more common in irradiation-induced tumors, suggesting they are initiating events in childhood gliomagenesis. Some pediatric HGGs showed minimal copy number changes.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated significant differences in the molecular features of pediatric and adult HGG. The findings suggest that findings in adult tumors cannot be directly applied to younger patients. PDGFRalpha may be a promising target for pediatric HGG, including diffuse pontine gliomas.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis: a knowledge-based approach for interpreting genome-wide expression profiles.
text: Although the analysis of RNA expression across the entire genome has become a common practice in biomedical research, it remains a significant challenge to extract meaningful biological information from such data. In this article, we present a highly effective analytical approach known as Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) for interpreting gene expression data. This method harnesses its strength by focusing on gene sets, which are groups of genes that share common biological function, chromosomal location, or regulation. We demonstrate the capabilities of GSEA by providing insights into various cancer-related data sets, including leukemia and lung cancer. Notably, while traditional single-gene analysis fails to identify similarities between two independent studies on patient survival in lung cancer, GSEA uncovers numerous shared biological pathways. The GSEA method is available as a freely accessible software package, accompanied by an initial database of 1,325 gene sets with well-defined biological functions.

title: The evolution of RNAs with multiple functions.
text: The discovery of transcripts that carry both protein-coding and regulatory information challenges our understanding of genes. This raises questions about how common this phenomenon is in the genome and why it has evolved in eukaryotic organisms. To explore this, we look at the evolution of genes in early life forms on Earth, where it is believed that proteins evolved from RNA-based cellular machinery. This led to the prevalence of protein-coding genes in microorganisms, but RNA likely retained its other functions, as seen in riboswitches and UTRs. We propose that mRNAs have undergone secondary selection to acquire regulatory capabilities alongside their protein-coding functions. Some protein-coding loci may have lost their original function and gained more sophisticated regulatory functions through gene duplication. Many transcripts have undergone secondary processing to produce different products, and new proteins have emerged from loci that previously functioned as regulatory RNAs. Recent studies on complex eukaryotes support the idea that there is a dynamic interplay between different types of informational RNAs, both in evolution and in real time. This challenges the notion that certain loci only express transcripts with a single function. In conclusion, we suggest that many eukaryotic loci have evolved the ability to perform multiple overlapping and potentially independent functions as both regulatory and protein-coding RNAs.

title: In Vitro–expanded Antigen-specific Regulatory T Cells Suppress Autoimmune Diabetes
text: The scarcity of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), their inactive characteristics, and their varied antigen specificity pose significant obstacles in utilizing this powerful tolerogenic population for the treatment of autoimmunity and transplant rejection. In this research, we present a strong technique for expanding antigen-specific Tregs from nonobese diabetic mice prone to autoimmune diseases. Through the use of anti-CD3, anti-CD28, and interleukin 2, purified CD4+ CD25+ Tregs were expanded by up to 200 times in less than two weeks in a laboratory setting. These expanded Tregs exhibit a typical cell surface phenotype and effectively suppress effector T cell functions both in vitro and in vivo. Most notably, even small quantities of antigen-specific Tregs can reverse diabetes after the onset of the disease, indicating a promising new approach to cellular immunotherapy for autoimmunity.

title: Stathmin overexpression identifies high-risk patients and lymph node metastasis in endometrial cancer.
text: The purpose of this study was to validate the prognostic value of Stathmin expression in endometrial carcinoma and its potential as a predictor of lymph node metastasis. A total of 1,076 endometrial cancer patients from 10 centers were recruited for this study. Stathmin immunohistochemical staining was performed on 477 hysterectomy and 818 curettage specimens. The results showed that 37% of the curettage specimens and 18% of the hysterectomy specimens had overexpression of Stathmin. Stathmin overexpression was significantly associated with nonendometrioid histology, high grade, and aneuploidy. Additionally, Stathmin expression in preoperative curettage samples was found to be a significant predictor of lymph node metastases. High Stathmin expression was also associated with poor disease-specific survival. In conclusion, Stathmin immunohistochemical staining can identify endometrial carcinomas with lymph node metastases and poor survival. However, further research is needed to determine its value as a predictive marker for response to PI3Kinase inhibition and as a tool for stratifying patients for lymph node sampling in endometrial carcinomas.

title: Statin prophylaxis and inflammatory mediators following cardiopulmonary bypass: a systematic review
text:
INTRODUCTION
The induction of an inflammatory response is believed to play a significant role in the complications that occur after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Statin drugs are increasingly recognized for their potent anti-inflammatory effects and their potential to impact an important mechanism of injury in CPB. However, there is currently no confirmation that this is indeed the case. The objective of this study was to systematically review whether pre-operative prophylactic statin therapy, compared to placebo or standard care, can reduce the inflammatory response in individuals undergoing heart surgery with CPB.

METHODS
A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of open heart surgery with CPB in adults or children who received prophylactic statin treatment prior to CPB. The studies had to report outcomes that included markers of inflammation. Two authors independently identified eligible studies, extracted data, and assessed study quality using standardized instruments. The primary summary statistic was the weighted mean difference (WMD), and data were pooled using a random effects model. Descriptive analysis was used when data could not be pooled.

RESULTS
The review included eight RCTs, with a limited number of trials for each inflammatory outcome. Pooled data showed that statin use was beneficial in attenuating the post-CPB increase in interleukins 6 and 8 (IL-6, IL-8), peak high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) (WMD [95% CI] -23.5 pg/ml [-36.6 to -10.5]; -23.4 pg/ml [-35.8 to -11.0]; -15.3 mg/L [CI -26.9 to -3.7]; -2.10 pg/ml [-3.83 to -0.37], respectively). Limited RCT evidence also suggests that prophylactic statin therapy may decrease adhesion molecules following CPB, including neutrophil CD11b and soluble P (sP)-selectin.

CONCLUSIONS
Although the RCT evidence suggests a reduction in post-CPB inflammation with statin therapy, the evidence is not definitive due to significant limitations. Several of the trials were not methodologically rigorous, and the statin intervention varied greatly in this small number of studies. This systematic review highlights a significant gap in the current literature regarding the potential anti-inflammatory effect of statin therapy prior to CPB.

title: Array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization for Genome-Wide Screening of DNA Copy Number in Bladder Tumors
text: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) was used to analyze the genome-wide copy number profiles of 41 primary bladder tumors. The study revealed alterations in both large chromosomal regions and small genomic regions, some of which had high-level amplifications or homozygous deletions. The most frequent high-level amplifications were found at 6p22.3 (E2F3), 8p12 (FGFR1), 8q22.2 (CMYC), 11q13 (CCND1, EMS1, INT2), and 19q13.1 (CCNE). Homozygous deletions were detected in 51 genomic clones, with four clones showing deletions in multiple cases: two clones at 9p21.3 (CDKN2A/p16) in nine cases, one at 8p23.1 in three cases, and one at 11p13 in two cases. The study also found significant correlations between the gain of clones containing CCNE1 and the gain of ERBB2, as well as between the gain of CCND1 and the deletion of TP53. Additionally, a significant complementary association was observed between the gain of CCND1 and the gain of E2F3. Although no significant relationship was found between copy number changes and tumor stage or grade, the interconnected behavior among genomic loci suggests that array CGH will play an increasingly important role in understanding the critical pathways involved in bladder tumor biology.

title: Tet2 is required to resolve inflammation by recruiting Hdac2 to specifically repress IL-6
text: Epigenetic modifiers play crucial roles in determining the unique characteristics of cells by controlling the specific chromatin and methylation patterns associated with different lineages. One such modification, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), is catalyzed by members of the ten eleven translocation (Tet) methylcytosine dioxygenase family. It has been gradually discovered that Tet proteins not only regulate DNA methylation but also have independent roles in modulating chromatin structure and gene transcription. However, the extent to which Tet proteins regulate immunity and inflammation, apart from their involvement in DNA methylation, remains largely unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that Tet2 specifically represses the transcription of interleukin-6 (IL-6) during the resolution of inflammation in innate myeloid cells, including dendritic cells and macrophages. Loss of Tet2 leads to the upregulation of various inflammatory mediators, including IL-6, during the later stages of the response to lipopolysaccharide challenge. Tet2-deficient mice exhibit increased susceptibility to endotoxin shock and dextran-sulfate-sodium-induced colitis, displaying a more severe inflammatory phenotype and higher IL-6 production compared to wild-type mice. We also found that IκBζ, a transcription factor specific to IL-6, facilitates the targeting of Tet2 to the Il6 promoter, indicating opposing regulatory roles of IκBζ during the initial and resolution phases of inflammation. In terms of the repression mechanism, Tet2 recruits Hdac2 and represses the transcription of Il6 through histone deacetylation, independent of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation. Our findings provide mechanistic evidence for the gene-specific transcriptional repression activity of Tet2 through histone deacetylation and its role in preventing constant transcription activation at the chromatin level to resolve inflammation.

title: Control of immunity by the TNFR-related molecule OX40 (CD134).
text: The TNFR/TNF superfamily members have the ability to regulate various aspects of immune function. Recent research has focused on the significant interaction between OX40 (CD134) and its partner OX40L (CD252) within this family. These molecules play a crucial role in controlling conventional CD4 and CD8 T cells, and emerging data suggests their involvement in modulating NKT cell and NK cell function. They also facilitate communication with professional antigen-presenting cells and various cell types such as mast cells, smooth muscle cells, and endothelial cells. Furthermore, OX40-OX40L interactions impact the differentiation and activity of regulatory T cells. In animal models of autoimmune and inflammatory disease, blocking OX40L has shown promising therapeutic effects. Looking ahead, stimulating OX40 signaling has potential as an adjuvant for vaccination and cancer treatment.

title: The Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor binds cholesterol and regulates cholesterol homeostasis.
text: Maintaining normal cellular function and preventing the harmful effects of high cholesterol levels requires cholesterol homeostasis. Our research demonstrates that the Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor binds to cholesterol and plays a crucial role in coordinating the transcriptional response of genes involved in cholesterol uptake, trafficking, and storage. Mutations in DHR96 result in death when exposed to low cholesterol levels and an accumulation of excess cholesterol when on a high-cholesterol diet. This accumulation is caused by the misregulation of npc1b, an ortholog of the mammalian gene NPC1L1, which is responsible for dietary cholesterol uptake. These findings establish DHR96 as a key regulator of cholesterol homeostasis.

title: A neuroimaging investigation of the association between aerobic fitness, hippocampal volume, and memory performance in preadolescent children.
text: Understanding the cognitive benefits of an active lifestyle in childhood is crucial due to the increasing prevalence of overweight, unhealthy, and unfit children. Animal studies have shown that aerobic exercise promotes cell growth and survival in the hippocampus, leading to improved learning and memory. Recent research has also suggested that older adults with high aerobic fitness levels have larger hippocampal volumes and better memory performance. This study aimed to investigate whether the link between fitness, hippocampal volume, and memory extends to preadolescent children. Magnetic resonance imaging was used to compare the hippocampal volumes of higher- and lower-fit 9- and 10-year-old children and assess their performance on a memory task. The hippocampus plays a crucial role in relational memory. As predicted, the higher-fit children had larger bilateral hippocampal volumes and performed better on the relational memory task compared to the lower-fit children. The study also found a positive association between hippocampal volume and relational memory performance. Additionally, the bilateral hippocampal volume was found to mediate the relationship between fitness level and relational memory. No relationship was found between aerobic fitness, nucleus accumbens volume, and memory, further supporting the specific impact of fitness on the hippocampus. These findings suggest that aerobic fitness may influence the structure and function of the preadolescent human brain.

title: Association between maternal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level and pregnancy and neonatal outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
text: The objective of this study was to examine the impact of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) levels on pregnancy outcomes and birth variables. The researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, gathering data from various sources including Medline, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, the Cochrane database of systematic reviews, and the Cochrane database of registered clinical trials. They selected studies that reported on the association between serum 25-OHD levels during pregnancy and outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, bacterial vaginosis, caesarean section, small for gestational age infants, birth weight, birth length, and head circumference. Data was extracted from original research articles by two authors, and indicators of study quality were considered. The most adjusted odds ratios and weighted mean differences were pooled, and associations were analyzed in subgroups based on patient characteristics and study quality. After reviewing 3357 studies, 31 eligible studies were included in the final analysis. The results showed that insufficient serum levels of 25-OHD were linked to an increased risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and small for gestational age infants. Pregnant women with low 25-OHD levels also had a higher risk of bacterial vaginosis and lower birth weight infants, but not caesarean section deliveries. In conclusion, vitamin D insufficiency during pregnancy is associated with an elevated risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and small for gestational age infants. Additionally, pregnant women with low 25-OHD levels are more likely to experience bacterial vaginosis and have infants with lower birth weights, but not an increased likelihood of caesarean section deliveries.

title: β-Adrenergic receptor antagonism prevents anxiety-like behavior and microglial reactivity induced by repeated social defeat.
text: Psychosocial stress is linked to changes in immune function and the development of psychological disorders such as anxiety and depression. Our study demonstrates that repeated social defeat in mice leads to increased activity in brain regions associated with fear and threat assessment, as well as the promotion of anxiety-like behavior through a mechanism involving β-adrenergic receptors. Additionally, social defeat increases the number of specific immune cells, known as macrophages, that migrate to the brain. We also observed increased levels of inflammatory markers on the surface of microglia and macrophages after social defeat. Furthermore, social defeat leads to the presence of a specific type of microglia in certain brain regions. Analysis of microglia mRNA revealed elevated levels of interleukin-1β and reduced levels of genes responsive to glucocorticoids, which are stress hormones. These changes in microglia and macrophages were prevented by a drug called propranolol, which blocks β-adrenergic receptors. When microglia from socially defeated mice were cultured and stimulated with lipopolysaccharide, they produced higher levels of certain inflammatory molecules compared to microglia from control mice. Interestingly, mice lacking functional IL-1 receptors did not exhibit anxiety-like behavior or microglia activation in response to social defeat, suggesting that the effects are dependent on the activation of both β-adrenergic and IL-1 receptors. Overall, our findings highlight the role of these receptors in mediating anxiety-like behavior and microglia reactivity induced by repeated social defeat.

title: In vitro differentiation of transplantable neural precursors from human embryonic stem cells
text: We present here a description of the potential of human embryonic stem (ES) cells to develop into various cell types for transplantation therapies. Specifically, we focus on the differentiation, enrichment, and transplantation of neural precursor cells derived from human ES cells in vitro. By forming embryoid bodies, the differentiating ES cells were able to generate numerous structures resembling the neural tube when exposed to fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2). Through selective enzymatic digestion and differential adhesion, neural precursors within these structures were isolated and further purified. Upon removal of FGF-2, these precursors differentiated into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. When transplanted into the brains of neonatal mice, the neural precursors derived from human ES cells integrated into various regions of the brain and further differentiated into neurons and astrocytes. Importantly, no formation of teratomas was observed in the recipients of these transplants. These findings highlight the potential of human ES cells as a viable source of transplantable neural precursors for potential repair of the nervous system.

title: Characterization of prostaglandin E2 production by Candida albicans.
text: Using mass spectrometry, it has been shown that Candida albicans produces lipid metabolites that have similar functions to prostaglandins found in the host. The production of authentic prostaglandin E(2) (PGE(2)) from arachidonic acid by C. albicans has been confirmed in these studies. The highest production of PGE(2) occurs at 37 degrees Celsius in the supernatants of stationary-phase cultures and in cell-free lysates derived from stationary-phase cells. Interestingly, the production of PGE(2) is inhibited by non-specific inhibitors of cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase, but not by inhibitors specific to the cyclooxygenase 2 isoenzyme. Although the C. albicans genome does not contain a cyclooxygenase homolog, several genes that may be involved in prostaglandin production were investigated. It was discovered that a C. albicans fatty acid desaturase homolog (Ole2) and a multicopper oxidase homolog (Fet3) play roles in prostaglandin production, as mutant strains lacking these genes (ole2/ole2 and fet3/fet3) exhibited lower levels of PGE(2) compared to the parent strains. This research demonstrates that the synthesis of PGE(2) in C. albicans occurs through unique pathways.

title: A global role for KLF1 in erythropoiesis revealed by ChIP-seq in primary erythroid cells.
text:
KLF1 plays a crucial role in guiding the development of erythroid cells from bipotent progenitors by regulating a diverse set of genes. In order to understand the specific regulatory contexts and transcription factor networks in which KLF1 operates, we conducted KLF1 ChIP-seq experiments in mice. Our findings revealed that endogenous KLF1 occupies at least 945 sites in the genome of E14.5 fetal liver erythroid cells. While some of these sites are located in the promoters of erythroid genes like Hbb-b1, the majority are situated far away from any known gene.

Based on our data, it appears that KLF1 directly controls various aspects of terminal erythroid differentiation. This includes the production of alpha- and beta-globin protein chains, heme biosynthesis, coordination of proliferation and anti-apoptotic pathways, as well as the construction of the red cell membrane and cytoskeleton. KLF1 primarily functions as a transcriptional activator in these processes.

Furthermore, our findings suggest novel mechanisms through which KLF1 collaborates with other transcription factors, particularly the erythroid transcription factor GATA1, to maintain homeostasis in the erythroid compartment.

title: KOBAS 2.0: a web server for annotation and identification of enriched pathways and diseases
text: We have developed a web server called KOBAS 2.0 that aims to assist in the identification of biological pathways and diseases associated with a set of genes. With the use of high-throughput experimental technologies, numerous genes can be identified that are either related to or altered in a biological or pathological process. KOBAS 2.0 utilizes known gene annotations to annotate an input set of genes, providing information on potential pathways and disease relationships. It offers the ability to map gene IDs and compare sequence similarities across different species. Additionally, KOBAS 2.0 conducts statistical tests to determine significantly enriched pathways and diseases. The server incorporates knowledge from 1327 species across five pathway databases (KEGG PATHWAY, PID, BioCyc, Reactome, and Panther) and five human disease databases (OMIM, KEGG DISEASE, FunDO, GAD, and NHGRI GWAS Catalog). To access KOBAS 2.0, please visit http://kobas.cbi.pku.edu.cn.

title: Translocation of sickle cell erythrocyte microRNAs into Plasmodium falciparum inhibits parasite translation and contributes to malaria resistance.
text: The molecular basis of the resistance of erythrocytes carrying a variant hemoglobin allele (HbS) to the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, which causes sickle cell disease, is not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the dysregulated composition of microRNAs (miRNAs) in HbAS or HbSS erythrocytes contributes to their resistance against P. falciparum. During the life cycle of the parasite, a specific group of erythrocyte miRNAs move into the parasite. Two miRNAs, miR-451 and let-7i, were found to be highly abundant in HbAS and HbSS erythrocytes, and these miRNAs, along with miR-223, negatively affected parasite growth. Surprisingly, we discovered that miR-451 and let-7i integrated into crucial parasite messenger RNAs and inhibited translation by impairing ribosomal loading. Therefore, sickle cell erythrocytes possess an inherent resistance to malaria, partly due to an unconventional miRNA activity, which may serve as a unique defense mechanism against complex eukaryotic pathogens.

title: CD28 and ITK signals regulate autoreactive T cell trafficking
text: Autoimmune organ destruction occurs when self-reactive T cells are activated and migrate to target tissues. In mice lacking the co-inhibitory receptor CTLA-4, this leads to fatal autoimmunity characterized by lymphocytic infiltration into nonlymphoid tissues. Our study reveals that the CD28 co-stimulatory pathway controls the movement of self-reactive Ctla4(-/-) T cells to tissues. Although the spontaneous activation of T cells is not blocked by the simultaneous removal of the CD28-activated Tec family kinase ITK, it does cause the accumulation of self-reactive Ctla4(-/-) T cells in secondary lymphoid organs. Despite excessive activation and proliferation of T cells in lymphoid organs, Itk(-/-); Ctla4(-/-) mice remain healthy, mount antiviral immune responses, and have a long lifespan. We propose that ITK specifically permits autoreactive T cells to enter tissues and initiate destructive immune responses. Importantly, ITK inhibitors replicate the effects of the null mutant and also prevent the infiltration of diabetogenic T cells into pancreatic islets in mouse models of type 1 diabetes. This highlights their potential as a treatment for human autoimmune disorders.

title: Delayed and Accelerated Aging Share Common Longevity Assurance Mechanisms
text: Mutant dwarf and calorie-restricted mice experience the benefits of healthy aging and live unusually long lives. On the other hand, mice with DNA repair-deficient progeroid syndromes age quickly and die prematurely. To understand the mechanisms that control mammalian longevity, we compared the liver gene expression profiles of these two groups of mice. Surprisingly, we discovered significant associations in gene expression between the progeroid and long-lived mice across the entire genome. Further analysis revealed that both delayed and premature aging were characterized by the suppression of endocrine and energy pathways, along with increased stress responses. To determine if these processes were relevant to natural aging, we compared the gene expression profiles of the liver, lung, kidney, and spleen throughout the entire lifespan of mice. We confirmed that these findings held true in an independent aging cohort. Most genes exhibited similar changes in expression across all four organs, indicating a systemic transcriptional response to aging. This response included the same biological processes observed in progeroid and long-lived mice. However, when considering the entire genome, the gene expression profiles of naturally aged mice were more closely associated with progeroid mice rather than long-lived mice. This suggests that endocrine and metabolic changes are adaptive responses to genotoxic stress or starvation, while genome-wide associations in gene expression with natural aging reflect biological age. These findings may help distinguish between pro- and anti-aging effects of treatments aimed at extending health-span.

title: Arginine depletion as a mechanism for the immune privilege of corneal allografts
text: The cornea, a tissue with immune privilege, was examined for the presence of arginase and its role in immune privilege using a mouse transplant model. It was discovered that both the endothelium and epithelium of mouse corneas express functional arginase I, which can suppress T-cell proliferation in a laboratory culture. When recipient mice were given the arginase inhibitor N-hydroxy-nor-L-Arg, the rejection of allogeneic C57BL/6 corneal grafts was accelerated. However, blocking arginase activity in vivo had no effect on the rejection of primary skin grafts that have little to no arginase. Furthermore, inhibiting arginase did not impact systemic T-cell proliferation. These findings demonstrate that arginase plays a functional role in the cornea's immune privilege and contributes to graft survival.

title: Once-a-day Concerta methylphenidate versus three-times-daily methylphenidate in laboratory and natural settings.
text:
The objective of this study was to test the effectiveness and duration of action of an extended-release formulation of methylphenidate (MPH), a commonly prescribed drug for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The short half-life of MPH requires multiple daily doses, which can be problematic for medication administration during school and after-school hours. Previous long-acting stimulants have shown similar effects to twice-daily dosing of MPH. 

In this study, sixty-eight children with ADHD, aged 6 to 12 years old, participated in a double-blind comparison of placebo, immediate-release (IR) MPH three times a day (tid), and Concerta, a once-daily MPH formulation. Three different dosing levels were used, based on each child's previous MPH dosing. The doses of Concerta were 20% higher than the equivalent tid regimen of IR MPH to ensure continuous coverage. Each medication condition was administered for 7 days in both natural and laboratory settings.

Parents received behavioral parent training and teachers implemented a school-home daily report card (DRC) to monitor the child's progress. The DRC consisted of individual target behaviors that represented the child's areas of impairment, with daily goals set by teachers and rewards provided by parents. The DRC, along with weekly standardized ratings, was used to measure medication response. In the laboratory setting, measures of classroom behavior, academic productivity/accuracy, and social behavior were taken.

Both drug conditions (Concerta and tid MPH) showed significant improvement compared to placebo on various measures in all settings. In regular school settings, both medications improved behavior as reported by teachers and measured by the DRC. In the laboratory setting, Concerta had equivalent effects to tid MPH and lasted at least 12 hours after dosing. Concerta was preferred by more parents and showed superiority on certain parent rating scores. Side effects on sleep and appetite were similar for both medications.

In the laboratory setting, both medications improved productivity, accuracy, and behavior in academic and social settings. The primary effect of medication was to prevent deterioration of behavior as the day progressed. The results support the use of background behavioral treatment in clinical trials of stimulant medication and highlight the usefulness of the DRC as an objective measure of medication response.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the efficacy of Concerta, a long-acting formulation of MPH, for parents seeking medication benefits throughout the day and early evening for their child with ADHD.

title: Leaderless genes in bacteria: clue to the evolution of translation initiation mechanisms in prokaryotes
text:
The Shine-Dalgarno (SD) signal has long been considered the primary translation initiation signal in prokaryotes. However, recent studies have shown that leaderless genes, which lack 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTR) on their mRNAs, are abundant in archaea. Unfortunately, current large-scale analyses on initiation mechanisms in bacteria focus mainly on the SD-led initiation pathway and neglect the leaderless one. This lack of research on leaderless genes in bacteria has led to an uncertain understanding of translation initiation mechanisms in prokaryotes.

In this study, we examined the signals in the translation initiation regions of all genes in 953 bacterial and 72 archaeal genomes. Our goal was to construct an evolutionary scenario for leaderless genes in bacteria. Using a specially designed algorithm, we classified genes into three categories: SD-led, TA-led, and atypical genes, based on the most probable signal in their upstream sequences. We found that the presence of TA-like signals approximately 10 base pairs upstream of the translation initiation site (TIS) in bacteria most likely indicates the presence of leaderless genes.

Our analysis revealed that leaderless genes are widespread, although not dominant, in various bacteria. In particular, Actinobacteria and Deinococcus-Thermus have more than twenty percent of their genes classified as leaderless. When analyzing closely related bacterial genomes, we observed that the change in translation initiation mechanisms, occurring between genes derived from a common ancestor, is linearly dependent on the phylogenetic relationship. Furthermore, our analysis of the macroevolution of leaderless genes showed a decreasing trend in the proportion of leaderless genes in bacteria over time.

title: Neuronal Sirt1 deficiency increases insulin sensitivity in both brain and peripheral tissues.
text: Sirt1 is an enzyme that relies on NAD(+) and belongs to class III deacetylases. It acts as a sensor for cellular energy. Recent evidence suggests that Sirt1 activity in neurons plays a role in regulating energy balance and glucose metabolism in the central nervous system. To investigate this further, we created mice with a specific knockout of Sirt1 in neurons, known as SINKO mice. These mice showed increased insulin sensitivity compared to mice with intact Sirt1 (Sirt1(f/f)) when fed a standard diet or a high-fat diet. As a result, SINKO mice had lower fasting insulin levels, improved glucose tolerance and insulin tolerance, and enhanced overall insulin sensitivity during hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp studies. Furthermore, SINKO mice exhibited increased insulin sensitivity in the hypothalamus, as evidenced by the activation of PI3K, phosphorylation of Akt and FoxO1 following systemic insulin injection. When insulin was injected directly into the brain ventricles, SINKO mice showed a greater improvement in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity compared to control mice. In line with these findings, inhibiting Sirt1 in a cultured hypothalamic cell line enhanced insulin-induced AKT and FoxO1 phosphorylation. This effect was attributed to a reduced ability of Sirt1 to deacetylate and suppress the function of IRS-1. The enhanced insulin signaling in the hypothalamus of SINKO mice was accompanied by increased insulin receptor signal transduction in the liver, muscle, and adipose tissue. In conclusion, our study suggests that neuronal Sirt1 negatively regulates insulin signaling in the hypothalamus, leading to systemic insulin resistance. Interventions that reduce neuronal Sirt1 activity have the potential to improve overall insulin action and limit weight gain on a diet that promotes obesity.

title: Candidate Causal Regulatory Effects by Integration of Expression QTLs with Complex Trait Genetic Associations
text: The recent success of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has led to the challenge of understanding how the reported susceptibility variants contribute to complex traits and diseases. Expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) have been implicated in disease associations by overlapping with GWAS signals. However, the abundance of eQTLs and the strong correlation structure in the genome make it likely that some of these overlaps are coincidental and not driven by the same functional variants. In this study, we propose a method called Regulatory Trait Concordance (RTC) that takes into account local correlation structure and combines eQTLs and GWAS results to identify the subset of association signals that are due to cis eQTLs. We use simulated genomic regions with different correlation patterns and causal variants to demonstrate that our method performs better than SNP correlation metrics. Based on the observation of a significant number of regulatory signals among published GWAS loci, we apply our method to prioritize relevant genes for complex traits. We identify several potential disease-causing regulatory effects, particularly in immunity-related conditions, which is consistent with the cell line used in the study. Additionally, we extend our method to analyze trans effects, where we investigate the downstream effects of disease variants on the entire genome to gain insights into their unknown primary biological effects. We conclude that integrating cellular phenotype associations with organismal complex traits will enhance our understanding of the genetic effects on these traits.

title: Gender-dependent differences in outcome after the treatment of infection in hospitalized patients.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the impact of gender on hospitalized patients being treated for infection. The study was conducted over a 26-month period from December 1996 to January 1999 in a university-affiliated hospital. A total of 892 patients in the surgical units of the hospital were included, with 1470 consecutive infectious episodes (782 in men and 688 in women). The main objective was to measure mortality rates during hospitalization based on gender for overall infection episodes and specific infectious sites.

The results showed that there was no significant difference in mortality based on gender for all infections (men: 11.1% vs women: 14.2%; P = .07). After conducting logistic regression analysis, factors independently associated with mortality included higher APACHE II score, older age, malignancy, blood transfusion, and diagnosis of infection more than 7 days after admission. However, gender was not found to be a significant factor (female odds ratio [OR] for death: 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.90-1.94; P = .16). Mortality rates were higher in women for lung (men: 18% vs women: 34%; P = .002) and soft tissue (men: 2% vs women: 10%; P < or = .05) infections. For other infectious sites, mortality did not differ based on gender. Logistic regression analysis for pneumonia-related mortality revealed that higher APACHE II score, malignancy, diabetes mellitus, diagnosis of infection more than 7 days after admission, older age, transplantation, and female gender were associated with mortality (OR for death: 2.25; 95% CI: 1.17-4.32; P = .02).

In conclusion, while gender may not be a predictor of mortality for all infections, women seem to be at a higher risk of death from hospital-acquired pneumonia, even after considering other comorbidities.

title: Comparative Safety of Targeted Therapies for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer between Elderly and Younger Patients: a Study Using the International Pharmacovigilance Database
text: The use of targeted therapies for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is becoming more common. However, there is limited research on the safety of these drugs, especially in older patients. This study aimed to compare the adverse drug reactions (ADRs) of targeted therapies used for mCRC in real-life settings, specifically looking at the differences between older and younger patients. The researchers analyzed data from VigiBase, which contains individual case safety reports (ICSRs) from the World Health Organization. They considered ADR reports for aflibercept, bevacizumab, cetuximab, panitumumab, and regorafenib used in CRC. They used chi-square tests to compare the frequencies of serious ADRs between patients aged 75 and older and those under 75. They also estimated the drug-ADR association for selected ADRs and each drug using the proportional reporting ratio (PRR) in both age groups. The study included 21,565 ICSRs, with 74% of them being serious and 11% fatal. The median age of patients was 64 years, and 15% were aged 75 and older. The majority of patients were male. Serious ADRs accounted for 47,292 ADRs. Neutropenia was not more commonly reported in older patients for any of the drugs, but diarrhea was more commonly reported in older patients for panitumumab. Cardiac disorders, particularly heart failure, were more commonly reported in older patients for bevacizumab, cetuximab, and regorafenib, as were respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders. Most of the PRRs were not different between the two age groups, except for encephalopathies, which were significantly associated with bevacizumab in older patients only. The ADRs related to targeted therapies used for mCRC treatment varied across age groups, but they were not consistently more reported or worse in older patients. Therefore, selected older patients could potentially be treated with these targeted therapies.

title: CpG island methylation in premalignant stages of gastric carcinoma.
text: There have been limited studies on the methylation analysis of premalignant lesions in gastric carcinoma. This is surprising considering that gastric carcinoma is known to have a high frequency of CpG island hypermethylation. To understand the frequency and timing of hypermethylation during the development of gastric carcinoma, we analyzed non-neoplastic gastric mucosa (n = 118), adenomas (n = 61), and carcinomas (n = 64) for methylation status of p16, human Mut L homologue 1 (hMLH1), death-associated protein (DAP)-kinase, thromobospondin-1 (THBS1), and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 3 (TIMP-3) using methylation-specific PCR. We found three different patterns of methylation in the five genes tested. DAP-kinase showed similar methylation frequency in all stages, while hMLH1 and p16 were more frequently methylated in cancer samples (20.3% and 42.2%, respectively) compared to intestinal metaplasia (6.3% and 2.1%, respectively) or adenomas (9.8% and 11.5%, respectively). However, hMLH1 and p16 were not methylated in chronic gastritis. THBS1 and TIMP-3 were methylated in all stages, but the frequency of hypermethylation significantly increased from chronic gastritis (10.1% and 14.5%, respectively) to intestinal metaplasia (34.7% and 36.7%, respectively; P < 0.05), and from adenomas (28.3% and 26.7%, respectively) to carcinomas (48.4% and 57.4%, respectively; P < 0.05). The hypermethylation frequencies of hMLH1, THBS1, and TIMP-3 were similar in both intestinal metaplasia and adenomas, but the hypermethylation frequency of p16 tended to be higher in adenomas (11.5%) compared to intestinal metaplasia (2.1%; P = 0.073). The average number of methylated genes per sample was 0.6, 1.1, 1.1, and 2.0 in chronic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, adenomas, and carcinomas, respectively. This indicates a significant increase in methylated genes from non-metaplastic mucosa to intestinal metaplasia (P = 0.001), as well as from premalignant lesions to carcinomas (P = 0.002). These findings suggest that CpG island hypermethylation occurs early in the development of gastric carcinoma and tends to accumulate throughout the progression of the disease.

title: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy: current and emerging treatment options for transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis
text: Transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR-FAP) is a deadly clinical condition characterized by the accumulation of abnormal fibrils derived from misfolded transthyretin (TTR) molecules outside of cells. This disease is primarily caused by a single genetic mutation in the TTR gene, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. More than 100 mutations have been identified, leading to destabilization of the normal TTR tetramer structure. Consequently, individual TTR monomers have a tendency to undergo spontaneous conformational changes and aggregate together. The main clinical feature of TTR-FAP is the progressive deterioration of sensory and motor nerves. Initially, this polyneuropathy primarily affects small unmyelinated nerve fibers, resulting in a disproportionate loss of pain and temperature sensation. Autonomic neuropathy, which often accompanies sensory deficits, manifests early in the disease progression. Symptoms include orthostatic hypotension, alternating constipation and diarrhea, erectile dysfunction, lack of sweating, and urinary retention or incontinence. As the disease advances, motor fibers become involved, leading to rapid weakness and difficulties with walking. In addition to the peripheral nervous system, the heart and gastrointestinal tract are frequently affected. The onset of symptoms occurs in two distinct peaks: one at around 33 years of age (early onset) and another in the sixth decade of life (late onset). TTR-FAP follows a uniformly progressive and fatal course. On average, Portuguese patients survive for 10.8 years after symptom onset, while late-onset Japanese patients survive for 7.3 years. Common causes of death include cachexia, heart failure, arrhythmia, and secondary infections. Liver transplantation is the standard treatment for patients who are in a suitable clinical condition to undergo the procedure, as it halts the progression of neuropathy by removing the main source of mutant TTR. Recently, an orally administered medication called tafamidis meglumine has been approved by European authorities for the treatment of FAP. This substance has been shown to stabilize the TTR tetramer, thereby improving the prognosis for patients with TTR-FAP. Various other strategies, such as gene therapy, immunization, dissolution of TTR aggregates, and the use of free radical scavengers, have been studied in laboratory settings to prevent TTR amyloidosis. However, none of these approaches are currently ready for clinical use.

title: Invariant natural killer T cells: bridging innate and adaptive immunity
text: Cells of the innate immune system interact with pathogens using conserved pattern-recognition receptors, while cells of the adaptive immune system recognize pathogens through diverse, antigen-specific receptors generated by somatic DNA rearrangement. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are a subset of lymphocytes that act as a bridge between the innate and adaptive immune systems. Although iNKT cells express T cell receptors generated by somatic DNA rearrangement, these receptors are semi-invariant and only interact with a limited range of lipid and glycolipid antigens, similar to the pattern-recognition receptors of the innate immune system. Functionally, iNKT cells closely resemble cells of the innate immune system as they quickly initiate their effector functions upon activation and do not develop immunological memory. iNKT cells can be activated by various stimuli and play a role in regulating different immune responses. When activated, iNKT cells produce cytokines that can stimulate and modulate an adaptive immune response. Several glycolipid antigens have been identified that can selectively induce specific effector functions in iNKT cells. These antigens have been used to investigate the potential therapeutic applications of iNKT cells in human diseases. In this review, we discuss the innate-like properties and functions of iNKT cells and their interactions with other immune cell types.

title: Olmesartan-based therapies: an effective way to improve blood pressure control and cardiovascular protection.
text: The primary goal of treating hypertension is to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. Among the various classes of first-line antihypertensive drugs, angiotensin-receptor blockers are known for their effectiveness and tolerability. Additionally, blocking the renin-angiotensin cascade has several benefits in protecting target organs and preventing cardiovascular issues. One specific angiotensin-receptor blocker, olmesartan, has been studied in trials focused on organ protection. These studies have shown improvements in markers of disease, such as reduced inflammation, regression of plaque volume and vascular hypertrophy, and prevention of microalbuminuria. Olmesartan has also been extensively studied in combination with hydrochlorothiazide or amlodipine, as well as in a single-pill triple combination. These combinations have demonstrated improved effectiveness in lowering blood pressure without significant effects on tolerability. This treatment strategy, utilizing a drug with these characteristics and the availability of different combination options, may be an effective approach for achieving blood pressure control in the majority of hypertensive patients and could also contribute to better prevention of cardiovascular disease.

title: Manslaughter by Fake Artesunate in Asia—Will Africa Be Next?
text: Falciparum malaria is a deadly disease, especially affecting those living in rural areas who are already impoverished. To combat this, artemisinin derivatives like artesunate play a crucial role in treating and controlling Plasmodium falciparum malaria, especially as drug resistance continues to rise worldwide. Unfortunately, since 1998, there has been a growing epidemic of counterfeit "artesunate" tablets in mainland Southeast Asia, as shown in Figure S1. Shockingly, in some countries, the majority of available artesunate is actually fake [1-5]. Artemisinin derivatives are known for their rapid and effective antimalarial properties, and they are generally well-tolerated. Consequently, these medications are highly sought after wherever they are accessible. However, due to their relatively high cost, there is a demand for cheaper alternatives among the most impoverished and vulnerable populations. Exploiting this demand, counterfeiters have targeted these individuals, resulting in tragic and fatal consequences.

title: Workshop: endothelial cell dysfunction leading to diabetic nephropathy : focus on nitric oxide.
text: This review examines the clinical signs of diabetic nephropathy, which are a result of diabetic microangiopathy. We revisit the Steno hypothesis and propose our own hypothesis that the development of endothelial cell dysfunction is a common pathway for diabetic complications. Specifically, we suggest that the ability of glucose to scavenge nitric oxide is the initial stage of endothelial dysfunction. As the disease progresses, there is a gradual buildup of advanced glycated end products and the induction of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1. This leads to a decrease in the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase and a reduction in the production of nitric oxide, which are crucial factors in the maintenance of endothelial dysfunction. By shifting our focus to the role of endothelial dysfunction in diabetic complications, we may be able to develop new strategies for prevention.

title: A nuclear Argonaute promotes multi-generational epigenetic inheritance and germline immortality
text: Epigenetic information is often erased at the beginning of each new generation, but there are cases where it can be passed down from parent to offspring, known as multigenerational epigenetic inheritance. One example of this is the double-stranded RNA-mediated gene silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans. This RNA interference (RNAi) can be inherited for more than five generations. To better understand this process, we conducted a genetic screen to identify nematodes that are unable to transmit RNAi silencing signals to future generations. Through this screen, we discovered the heritable RNAi defective 1 (hrde-1) gene. The hrde-1 gene encodes an Argonaute protein that binds to small interfering RNAs in the germ cells of offspring exposed to double-stranded RNA. In the nuclei of these germ cells, HRDE-1 activates the nuclear RNAi defective pathway, leading to the trimethylation of histone H3 at Lys 9 (H3K9me3) at RNAi-targeted genomic sites and promoting RNAi inheritance. Under normal conditions, HRDE-1 interacts with naturally produced short interfering RNAs, which silence genes in germ cells. In animals lacking hrde-1 or nuclear RNAi, germline silencing diminishes over time. Additionally, these animals experience worsening defects in gamete formation and function, eventually leading to sterility. These findings demonstrate that the Argonaute protein HRDE-1 plays a crucial role in gene silencing within germ-cell nuclei, driving multigenerational RNAi inheritance and ensuring the immortality of the germ-cell lineage. We propose that C. elegans utilizes the RNAi inheritance machinery to transmit epigenetic information accumulated by previous generations to regulate important biological processes in future generations.

title: Autophagic programmed cell death by selective catalase degradation.
text: Autophagy plays a crucial role in regulating vital cellular functions, including cell survival during periods of starvation and the control of infectious pathogens. Recent studies have demonstrated that autophagy can also trigger cell death, but the exact mechanism behind this autophagic cell death program remains unclear. Our research now reveals that inhibiting caspases, which leads to cell death through autophagy, involves the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), oxidation of membrane lipids, and disruption of the plasma membrane. By using chemical compounds or reducing the expression of key autophagy proteins like ATG7, ATG8, and receptor interacting protein (RIP), we were able to block ROS accumulation and prevent cell death. The abnormal buildup of ROS is caused by the selective degradation of catalase, a major enzyme responsible for scavenging ROS, through autophagy. Inhibiting caspases directly leads to the degradation of catalase and the accumulation of ROS, but this can be prevented by autophagy inhibitors. These findings shed light on the molecular mechanism underlying the role of autophagy in cell death and provide valuable insights into the intricate relationship between ROS and nonapoptotic programmed cell death.

title: Human epidermal stem cell function is regulated by circadian oscillations.
text: The impact of circadian rhythms on the function of human epidermal stem cells is not well understood, despite the fact that human skin is constantly exposed to harmful environmental factors that follow a circadian pattern. In this study, we demonstrate that core clock genes in human epidermal stem cells and their differentiated counterparts peak at different times throughout the day, creating distinct temporal intervals. Each of these peaks is associated with the expression of specific subsets of transcripts that regulate the response of epidermal stem cells to cues controlling their proliferation or differentiation, such as TGFβ and calcium. Disruption of circadian rhythms significantly impairs stem cell function both in laboratory cultures and in living organisms. We propose that this intricate mechanism ensures the maintenance of homeostasis by providing epidermal stem cells with relevant temporal cues throughout the day, and that its disruption may contribute to aging and the development of cancer.

title: Engraftment of engineered ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes but not BM cells restores contractile function to the infarcted myocardium
text:
Cellular cardiomyoplasty is a promising treatment option for severe heart failure. However, there is still uncertainty and controversy surrounding the most effective cell source. To address this, we conducted a study to investigate the fate and functional impact of bone marrow (BM) cells and embryonic stem cell (ES cell)-derived cardiomyocytes when transplanted into the infarcted mouse heart. This was particularly challenging for ES cells, as their transformation into cardiomyocytes and their long-term engraftment and potential for tumor formation are not well understood.

To overcome these challenges, we created transgenic ES cells that expressed puromycin resistance and enhanced green fluorescent protein under the control of a cardiac-specific promoter. By using puromycin selection, we were able to obtain a highly purified (>99%) population of cardiomyocytes, and the yield of cardiomyocytes increased significantly due to induction of proliferation during purification. We observed long-term engraftment (4-5 months) when we co-transplanted selected ES cell-derived cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts into the injured hearts of syngeneic mice. Importantly, we did not observe any teratoma formation in this group of mice (n=60).

While transplantation of ES cell-derived cardiomyocytes improved heart function, BM cells did not have any positive effects. Additionally, we did not detect any contribution of BM cells to the generation of cardiac, endothelial, or smooth muscle cells. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that ES-based cell therapy holds promise for treating impaired myocardial function and yields better results compared to BM-derived cells.

title: Hyaluronan impairs vascular function and drug delivery in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the potential of targeting the extracellular matrix component hyaluronan (HA) as a therapeutic strategy for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA). PDA is characterized by stromal desmoplasia and vascular dysfunction, which hinder the delivery of drugs to the tumor. The authors used a genetically engineered mouse model of PDA to deplete HA using a clinically formulated hyaluronidase called PEGPH20. They then assessed the effects of HA depletion on tumor perfusion, vascular permeability, and drug delivery. The results showed that PEGPH20 effectively reduced HA levels, leading to the re-expansion of blood vessels in the tumor and increased delivery of chemotherapeutic agents. PEGPH20 also induced fenestrations and gaps in the tumor endothelia, enhancing macromolecular permeability. Combination therapy with PEGPH20 and gemcitabine resulted in inhibited tumor growth and improved survival compared to gemcitabine alone. The authors conclude that targeting HA could enhance drug delivery and response in patients with pancreatic cancer.

title: Ribose 2′-O-methylation provides a molecular signature for the distinction of self and non-self mRNA dependent on the RNA sensor Mda5
text: The ribose 2'-O-methylation is present in the 5' cap structures of mRNA in higher eukaryotes. Similarly, viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes have developed 2'-O-methyltransferases to independently modify their own mRNA. However, the specific biological function of mRNA 2'-O-methylation remains unclear. In this study, we reveal that the 2'-O-methylation of viral mRNA plays a crucial role in evading the activation of type I interferon. We demonstrate that mutant forms of human and mouse coronaviruses lacking 2'-O-methyltransferase activity exhibit increased expression of type I interferon and are highly susceptible to its effects. Importantly, the induction of type I interferon by viruses lacking 2'-O-methyltransferase relies on the cytoplasmic RNA sensor Mda5. This connection between Mda5-mediated detection of viral RNA and mRNA 2'-O-methylation suggests that RNA modifications, such as 2'-O-methylation, serve as a molecular signature for distinguishing self from non-self mRNA.

title: Relationship between activity levels, aerobic fitness, and body fat in 8- to 10-yr-old children.
text: The connection between children's activity, aerobic fitness, and fatness is not clear. Estimations of activity using heart rate and recall may not reveal any associations. This study aimed to examine these relationships using the Tritrac-R3D, a pedometer, and heart rate. A total of 34 children aged 8-10 years participated in the study. The Tritrac and pedometer were worn for a maximum of 6 days, while heart rate was measured for 1 day. Activity measured by the Tritrac or pedometer showed a positive correlation with fitness in the entire group (Tritrac, r = 0.66; pedometer, r = 0.59; P < 0.01), as well as in boys and girls separately (P < 0.05). It also showed a negative correlation with fatness in the entire group (r = -0.42, P < 0.05). On the other hand, heart rate did not significantly correlate with fitness, and a heart rate above 139 beats/min correlated positively with fatness in girls (r = 0.64, P < 0.05). This suggests that heart rate is not a reliable measure of activity. The study supports a positive relationship between activity and fitness, and indicates a negative relationship between fatness and activity.

title: Junctional actin assembly is mediated by Formin-like 2 downstream of Rac1
text: The maintenance of epithelial integrity is of utmost importance, as any disruption can lead to the development of early stage cancer. The process of forming connections between individual epithelial cells, known as adherens junctions (AJ), relies on coordinated actin dynamics. However, the specific mechanisms that regulate actin polymerization for the initiation of cell-cell adhesion are not well understood. In this study, we investigated the real-time assembly of actin during the formation of daughter cell-cell adhesions in human breast epithelial cells within a three-dimensional environment. Our findings reveal that a protein called formin-like 2 (FMNL2) plays a crucial role in actin assembly and turnover at newly formed cell-cell contacts, as well as in the formation of the epithelial lumen. FMNL2 interacts with components of the AJ complex, including Rac1 activity and the FMNL2 C terminus. By using optogenetic techniques to control Rac1 activity in living cells, we were able to rapidly direct FMNL2 to the zones of cell-cell contact in epithelial cells. Furthermore, we discovered that Rac1-induced actin assembly and subsequent AJ formation critically depend on FMNL2. These results highlight the importance of FMNL2 as a key driver of AJ formation in human epithelial cells downstream of Rac1.

title: Inhibition of HDM2 and activation of p53 by ribosomal protein L23.
text: The significance of coordinating cell growth with proliferation has been acknowledged for a considerable period. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly comprehended. In this study, we demonstrate that the ribosomal protein L23 interacts with HDM2. This interaction involves the central acidic domain of HDM2 and an N-terminal domain of L23. Interestingly, both L23 and L11, another ribosomal protein that interacts with HDM2, can simultaneously interact with HDM2 to form a ternary complex, albeit in distinct ways. Our findings reveal that overexpression of L23 hampers HDM2-induced p53 polyubiquitination and degradation, leading to a p53-dependent cell cycle arrest. Conversely, depletion of L23 induces nucleolar stress, prompting the translocation of B23 from the nucleolus to the nucleoplasm. This translocation results in the stabilization and activation of p53. Based on our data, it is plausible to suggest that cells maintain a constant level of L23 during normal growth. However, altering the levels of L23 in response to changing growth conditions could disrupt the integrity of the nucleolus and impact the HDM2-p53 pathway.

title: Association of Blood Monocyte and Platelet Markers with Carotid Artery Characteristics: The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Carotid MRI Study
text:
Background: Atherosclerosis is characterized by the infiltration of inflammatory cells from the bloodstream, which could potentially contribute to the formation of plaques. 

Methods: In this study, we examined the correlation between markers of blood cell activation and quantitative measurements of carotid wall components in 1,546 participants from the ARIC Carotid MRI Study. Carotid imaging was conducted using gadolinium contrast-enhanced MRI, and cellular phenotyping was performed using flow cytometry. 

Results: Our findings revealed that Monocyte Toll-like receptor (TLR)-2 is linked to larger plaques, while CD14, myeloperoxidase, and TLR-4 are associated with smaller plaques. Additionally, Platelet CD40L is connected to smaller plaques and thinner caps, while P-selectin is related to smaller core size. 

Conclusions: The activation of blood cells is significantly correlated with atherosclerotic changes in the carotid wall.

title: Vascular endothelial cadherin controls VEGFR-2 internalization and signaling from intracellular compartments
text: The process of receptor endocytosis plays a crucial role in regulating the intensity, duration, and nature of cellular signaling events. When endothelial cells are densely packed and in contact with each other, they exhibit inhibited growth and show a weak response to the signals that promote vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling. In a previous study conducted by Lampugnani et al. (2003), it was discovered that the interaction between vascular endothelial cadherin (VEC) and VEGF receptor (VEGFR) type 2 contributes to the inhibition of growth that is dependent on cell density. In our current study, we aim to elucidate the mechanism by which VEC reduces VEGFR-2 signaling. Our findings indicate that VEGF triggers the internalization of VEGFR-2 through a process that relies on clathrin. In the absence of VEC or when VEC is not engaged at cell junctions, VEGFR-2 is internalized at a faster rate and remains in endosomal compartments for a longer duration. This internalization does not terminate the signaling of VEGFR-2; instead, the internalized receptor undergoes phosphorylation, co-localizes with active phospholipase C-γ, and activates the phosphorylation of p44/42 mitogen-activated protein kinase, leading to cell proliferation. By inhibiting the internalization of VEGFR-2, we are able to restore the contact inhibition of cell growth. Additionally, silencing the junction-associated density-enhanced phosphatase-1/CD148 phosphatase restores the internalization and signaling of VEGFR-2. Therefore, VEC acts as a regulator of cell proliferation by retaining VEGFR-2 at the cell membrane and preventing its internalization into signaling compartments.

title: Diversification in the HIV-1 Envelope Hyper-variable Domains V2, V4, and V5 and Higher Probability of Transmitted/Founder Envelope Glycosylation Favor the Development of Heterologous Neutralization Breadth
text:
A recent study conducted at nine International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) sites examined the breadth of plasma neutralization in individuals infected with HIV-1. The study found that viral load, HLA-A*03 genotype, and subtype C infection were strongly linked to the development of neutralization breadth. In this study, we further analyze the impact of the transmitted/founder (T/F) envelope (Env), early Env diversification, and autologous neutralization on the development of plasma neutralization breadth in 21 participants who were recently infected at two of those sites: Kigali, Rwanda (n = 9) and Lusaka, Zambia (n = 12). 

Through single-genome analysis of full-length T/F Env sequences, we discovered that all 21 individuals were infected with a highly homogeneous population of viral variants, categorized as subtype C (n = 12), A1 (n = 7), or recombinant AC (n = 2). By extensively analyzing the amino acid sequences of variable loop lengths and glycosylation patterns in the T/F Envs, we found that a lower ratio of NXS to NXT-encoded glycan motifs correlated with neutralization breadth.
