Further analysis comparing amino acid sequence changes, insertions/deletions, and glycan motif alterations between the T/F Env and autologous early Env variants revealed that extensive diversification primarily occurred in the V2, V4, and V5 regions of gp120. This diversification, accompanied by viral escape, significantly favored the development of neutralization breadth. These findings suggest that more efficient glycosylation of subtype A and C T/F Envs, achieved through fewer NXS-encoded glycan sites, is more likely to elicit antibodies capable of transitioning from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity following exposure to gp120 diversification. 

This process initiates an Env-antibody co-evolution cycle that increases neutralization breadth, which is further enhanced over time by additional viral and host factors. These findings highlight the importance of understanding how variations in site-specific glycosylation efficiency influence the elicitation and targeting of neutralizing antibodies. This knowledge could advance the design of immunogens aimed at inducing antibodies capable of transitioning from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity.

title: Glycolytic oligodendrocytes maintain myelin and long-term axonal integrity
text:
Oligodendrocytes, which are glial cells responsible for forming myelin in the central nervous system, play a crucial role in maintaining the long-term integrity of axons. However, the specific mechanisms underlying this support are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the metabolic aspect of the interaction between axons and glial cells by creating mutant mice with a conditional Cox10 gene (protoheme IX farnesyltransferase) mutation. This mutation prevented the assembly of stable mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (COX), also known as mitochondrial complex IV, in both oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells.

In the peripheral nervous system, the Cox10 mutant mice exhibited severe neuropathy, characterized by abnormal Remak bundles, dysmyelination, muscle atrophy, and paralysis. Interestingly, disrupting mitochondrial respiration did not lead to the death of glial cells. In the adult central nervous system, we did not observe any signs of demyelination, axonal degeneration, or secondary inflammation. Unlike cultured oligodendrocytes, which are sensitive to COX inhibitors, post-myelination oligodendrocytes were able to survive without COX activity. Importantly, our in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy analysis revealed increased brain lactate concentrations in the mutant mice compared to controls, but only when the mice were exposed to volatile anesthetics. This suggests that the products of aerobic glycolysis derived from oligodendrocytes are rapidly metabolized within the white matter tracts. Given that myelinated axons can utilize lactate as an energy source when deprived of energy, our findings propose a model in which the metabolic coupling between axons and glial cells serves a physiological function.

title: Siglec-1 Is a Novel Dendritic Cell Receptor That Mediates HIV-1 Trans-Infection Through Recognition of Viral Membrane Gangliosides
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in presenting antigens to initiate immune responses against pathogens. However, clusters of DCs and CD4(+) T cells can promote the spread of HIV-1. Uninfected DCs can capture HIV-1 and transfer it to neighboring CD4(+) T cells through a process called trans-infection. Initially, it was discovered that the C-type lectin DC-SIGN is responsible for binding HIV-1 to DCs by interacting with the viral envelope glycoproteins. However, as DCs mature, DC-SIGN is down-regulated, but HIV-1 capture and trans-infection are significantly increased through a glycoprotein-independent pathway that recognizes sialyllactose-containing membrane gangliosides. In this study, we demonstrate that the sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin 1 (Siglec-1, CD169), which is highly expressed on mature DCs, specifically binds to HIV-1 and vesicles containing sialyllactose. Moreover, Siglec-1 is crucial for trans-infection by mature DCs. These findings highlight the importance of Siglec-1 in the spread of HIV-1 through infectious DC/T-cell synapses, revealing a novel mechanism that facilitates HIV-1 dissemination in activated tissues.

title: The composition of the gut microbiota throughout life, with an emphasis on early life
text: The role of the intestinal microbiota in human health has become increasingly important. It is closely linked to the development of the immune system and plays a crucial role in the functioning and regulation of the intestines. Recent evidence suggests that the seeding of the human intestinal microbiota begins before birth, with the maternal microbiota being the initial source of microbial colonization. After birth, the diversity of microbes in the intestines increases and gradually becomes similar to that of adults by the age of 3-5 years. Various factors during the perinatal period, such as the method of delivery, diet, genetics, and intestinal mucin glycosylation, all contribute to the establishment of the microbial community. Once established, the composition of the gut microbiota remains relatively stable throughout adulthood, but can be altered by factors such as bacterial infections, antibiotic use, lifestyle changes, surgery, and long-term dietary changes. Disruptions in this complex microbial system have been linked to an increased risk of disease. Therefore, it is important to establish and maintain a healthy microbiota throughout life to reduce the risk of disease in both early and late stages. This review examines recent studies on early colonization and the factors that influence this process, which ultimately impact overall health.

title: Intrauterine protein restriction combined with early postnatal overfeeding was not associated with adult-onset obesity but produced glucose intolerance by pancreatic dysfunction
text:
We conducted a study to determine whether a combination of protein restriction during pregnancy and overfeeding during lactation would lead to adult-onset obesity and metabolic disorders. After birth, we divided the litters from dams into two groups: one group was fed a control diet with 17% protein (CO and CC groups), and the other group was fed a low protein diet with 6% protein (LO and LC groups). The litter sizes were adjusted to four pups for the CO and LO groups, and eight pups for the CC and LC groups. All offspring were fed a diet with 12% protein from weaning until they reached 90 days old.

Compared to the CC and LC groups, the CO and LO groups had higher food intake, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production. They also had lower weight and lipid content in their brown adipose tissue, but higher weight gain and white adipose tissue weight and lipid content. On the other hand, the LC and LO rats had higher food intake, brown adipose tissue weight and lipid content, but lower oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and spontaneous activity compared to the CO and CC rats. They also had higher relative weight of retroperitoneal adipose tissue, but no significant difference in absolute white adipose tissue weight and lipid content. Fasting serum glucose levels were similar among all groups, but the area under the glucose curve was higher in the LO and CO rats compared to the LC and CC rats. The LO group had lower basal insulin levels and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) compared to the other groups. The total area under the insulin curve for the LO rats was similar to the CC rats, and both were lower than the CO and LC rats. Kitt (a measure of insulin sensitivity) was higher in the LO, LC, and CO groups compared to the CC group.

In conclusion, our study found that intrauterine protein restriction followed by overfeeding during lactation did not lead to obesity. However, it did result in glucose intolerance by impairing pancreatic function in adulthood.

title: Somatic coding mutations in human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Transcription factors that are specifically defined have the ability to reprogram adult mammalian cells into induced pluripotent stem cells through epigenetic changes. However, it is currently unclear whether the genome remains unaltered at the level of individual nucleotides. In this study, we examined 22 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines that were reprogrammed using five different methods. We discovered that each cell line contained an average of five point mutations in protein-coding regions, with an estimated six mutations per exome. The majority of these mutations were non-synonymous, nonsense, or splice variants, and were found to be enriched in genes that are known to be mutated or have causative effects in cancer. Interestingly, at least half of these mutations were already present in the fibroblast progenitors at low frequencies, while the remaining mutations occurred during or after the reprogramming process. This suggests that induced pluripotent stem cells not only undergo epigenetic modifications but also acquire genetic alterations. As a result, it is crucial to conduct thorough genetic screening as a standard procedure to ensure the safety of induced pluripotent stem cells before their clinical use.

title: Cell cycle, CDKs and cancer: a changing paradigm
text: Defects in the cell cycle that are associated with tumors are often caused by changes in the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). When CDKs are not properly regulated, they can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and instability in the genetic and chromosomal makeup. Current understanding suggests that CDKs are crucial for driving each phase of the cell cycle in mammals, making it difficult to target tumor cells specifically by blocking CDK activity. However, recent genetic research has shown that while CDK1 is necessary for the cell cycle, interphase CDKs are only essential for the proliferation of specialized cells. There is emerging evidence that tumor cells may also rely on specific interphase CDKs for their growth. Therefore, selectively inhibiting CDKs could potentially be a beneficial therapeutic approach for certain types of human tumors.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome.
text: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) remains the leading cause of death for infants aged between 1 month and 1 year in developed countries, despite a decrease in prevalence over the past two decades. Epidemiological studies have identified several behavioral risk factors, including placing infants in prone or side positions for sleep, exposure to smoke, using soft bedding and sleep surfaces, and overheating. However, evidence suggests that using pacifiers during sleep and sharing a room without bed sharing can decrease the risk of SIDS. The exact cause of SIDS is still unknown, but factors such as immature cardiorespiratory autonomic control and a failure to respond to arousal from sleep play a significant role. Certain gene polymorphisms related to serotonin transport and autonomic nervous system development may also make infants more susceptible to SIDS. Campaigns promoting risk reduction have successfully reduced SIDS incidence by 50-90%. However, further efforts are needed to reduce prenatal smoke exposure and implement recommended infant care practices in order to further decrease the incidence of SIDS. Ongoing research is necessary to better understand the underlying pathophysiology of SIDS.

title: Regulation of heterochromatic silencing and histone H3 lysine-9 methylation by RNAi.
text: Eukaryotic heterochromatin is characterized by a dense concentration of repeats and transposons, along with modified histones. This type of chromatin has a significant impact on both gene expression and chromosome segregation. In our study, we focused on the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe and specifically deleted the argonaute, dicer, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene homologs. These genes are responsible for the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery. The deletion of these genes resulted in an abnormal accumulation of complementary transcripts from centromeric heterochromatic repeats. Additionally, we observed the transcriptional de-repression of transgenes integrated at the centromere, a loss of histone H3 lysine-9 methylation, and impairment of centromere function. Based on our findings, we propose that double-stranded RNA originating from centromeric repeats plays a crucial role in the formation and maintenance of heterochromatin through RNAi.

title: Conformational Changes during Pore Formation by the Perforin-Related Protein Pleurotolysin
text: The largest group of proteins responsible for forming pores in cell membranes, known as membrane attack complex/perforin-like (MACPF) proteins, play important roles in immunity and disease development. However, the structural and mechanistic details of how these proteins assemble into transmembrane pores are still not fully understood. In this study, we present a high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a fungal toxin called Pleurotolysin (Ply), which consists of two parts. We also provide crystal structures of both components of Ply: the lipid binding protein PlyA and the pore-forming MACPF component PlyB. Our findings reveal a pore that is 13 times larger than previously known, with a diameter of 80 Å and a height of 100 Å. Each subunit of the pore is made up of a PlyB molecule on top of a PlyA dimer that is bound to the cell membrane. By analyzing the cryo-EM map and conducting biophysical and computational experiments, we were able to identify different subdomains within the MACPF pore assembly. The main structural changes in PlyB involve a ∼70° opening of the central β-sheet of the MACPF domain, along with the extrusion and refolding of two α-helical regions into transmembrane β-hairpins (TMH1 and TMH2). We also determined the structures of three different prepore intermediates that were trapped by disulphide bonds. By using molecular modeling and flexible fitting techniques, we were able to propose a potential pathway for the unbending of the β-sheet. Our results suggest that the conformational changes in MACPF proteins are triggered by the disruption of the interface between a conserved helix-turn-helix motif and the top of TMH2. Once released, the transmembrane regions assemble into β-hairpins by forming hydrogen bonds, resulting in the formation of a β-barrel structure within the cell membrane. The intermediate structures observed during the refolding of the MACPF domain into the β-barrel pore provide a structural framework for understanding the transition from soluble monomers to functional pores, which may be applicable to the entire superfamily of MACPF proteins. The TMH2 region is crucial for the release of both TMH clusters, which explains why this region is targeted by natural inhibitors of MACPF function.

title: The widespread regulation of microRNA biogenesis, function and decay
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short RNA molecules that play a crucial role in regulating gene expression in eukaryotic organisms. They are approximately 21 nucleotides long and are involved in controlling various developmental and cellular processes. Over the past decade, extensive research has been conducted to understand the biogenesis of miRNAs and their fundamental functions. However, recent studies have revealed that the regulation of miRNAs themselves is highly complex. Multiple reports have highlighted the intricate control of miRNA metabolism and function through various protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions. This regulatory mechanism is essential for the context-specific roles of miRNAs.

title: The cytidine deaminase CEM15 induces hypermutation in newly synthesized HIV-1 DNA
text: The genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations is primarily caused by a high frequency of mutations during reverse transcription. This process plays a crucial role in the development of drug resistance and evasion of immune surveillance. G to A hypermutation is a common characteristic of primate lentiviruses and other retroviruses during replication in both living organisms and cell cultures. However, the specific molecular mechanisms behind this phenomenon are still not fully understood. In this study, we provide evidence that CEM15, also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G (APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication, acts as a cytidine deaminase and can induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA. The HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif) is able to counteract this effect. It appears that this viral DNA mutator serves as a defense mechanism in host cells, potentially leading to either lethal hypermutation or instability of the newly formed viral reverse transcripts. This could explain the Vif-defective phenotype. Importantly, the accumulation of non-lethal hypermutation mediated by CEM15 in the replicating viral genome significantly contributes to the genetic variation observed in primate lentiviral populations.

title: Variants in the Toll-interacting protein gene are associated with susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between variants in Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathway genes and their negative regulator genes with susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population. A total of 378 patients with severe sepsis and 390 healthy control subjects were enrolled in the study. Five genes (TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, MyD88, and TOLLIP) were examined for their association with sepsis susceptibility using a tag single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) strategy. Twelve tag SNPs were selected and genotyped by direct sequencing. The mRNA expression levels of TOLLIP were determined using real-time quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and concentrations of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). 

The results showed that the minor C-allele of rs5743867 in TOLLIP was significantly associated with a decreased risk of sepsis. A 3-SNP haplotype block containing rs5743867 also displayed a strong association with sepsis. Haplotype GTC was found to have a protective role against sepsis, while haplotype GCT increased the risk for sepsis. After exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), TOLLIP mRNA expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from homozygotes for the rs5743867C allele were significantly higher than in heterozygotes and homozygotes for the rs5743867T allele. Additionally, the concentrations of TNF-α and IL-6 in culture supernatants were significantly lower in subjects with the rs5743867CC genotype compared to CT and TT genotype subjects. 

In conclusion, the findings of this study suggest that variants in TOLLIP are significantly associated with sepsis susceptibility in the Chinese Han population.

title: Children's estimates of food portion size: the development and evaluation of three portion size assessment tools for use with children.
text: Several methods have been developed to help individuals estimate portion sizes, but their effectiveness in improving portion size estimation by children has not been thoroughly investigated. The objective of this study was to create portion size assessment tools specifically designed for children and to evaluate the accuracy of children's estimates using these tools. The tools used in the study included food photographs, food models, and an interactive portion size assessment system (IPSAS). A total of 201 children between the ages of 4 and 16 were provided with known quantities of food to consume at school. The remaining food was weighed, and 24 hours later, the children estimated the amount of each food using each tool. The portion sizes represented in the tools were based on portion sizes consumed by children in a national survey. The study found significant differences in the accuracy of estimates using the three tools. Children of all ages performed well when using the IPSAS and food photographs, but the accuracy and precision of estimates made using the food models were poor. In general, estimates of the amount of food served were more accurate than estimates of the amount consumed, highlighting the need for further research on reporting leftover food and its impact on estimates of actual consumption. The IPSAS showed promise as a tool for assessing dietary intake in children, but before it can be practically applied, it should be expanded to cover a wider range of foods and validated in real-life situations.

title: A 3D Map of the Yeast Kinetochore Reveals the Presence of Core and Accessory Centromere-Specific Histone
text: The length of the budding yeast kinetochore is approximately 68 nm, slightly larger in diameter than a 25 nm microtubule. These kinetochores, found on the 16 chromosomes, are arranged in a stereotypical cluster that surrounds the central spindle microtubules. When analyzing the inner kinetochore cluster (consisting of Cse4 and COMA), certain structural characteristics become apparent that are not visible in individually attached kinetochores. The cluster of kinetochores containing Cse4 is physically larger in a direction perpendicular to the spindle axis compared to the cluster of Ndc80 molecules. If each microtubule plus end had a single Cse4 molecule or nucleosome attached to its kinetochore, the cluster of Cse4 would appear identical to Ndc80 in terms of its geometric shape. Therefore, the structure of the inner kinetochore on the surface of the chromosomes remains unresolved. To determine the two-dimensional average position of representative components of the yeast kinetochore relative to the mitotic spindle in metaphase, we utilized point fluorescence microscopy and statistical probability maps. By comparing the experimental images to three-dimensional models generated through mathematical convolution, we discovered a group of Cse4 molecules that are displaced radially from the Cse4 at the kinetochore and kinetochore microtubule plus ends. This pool of displaced Cse4 can be experimentally depleted in mutants lacking mRNA processing pat1Δ or xrn1Δ. The peripheral Cse4 molecules do not serve as templates for outer kinetochore components. This study suggests the presence of an inner kinetochore plate at the interface between the centromere and microtubules in budding yeast and provides information regarding the number of Ndc80 molecules at the microtubule attachment site.

title: American Society of Clinical Oncology policy statement: the role of the oncologist in cancer prevention and risk assessment.
text: Oncologists have a crucial chance to use risk assessment and cancer prevention strategies to disrupt the development or progression of cancer in cancer survivors and individuals at high risk of developing cancer. By expanding their knowledge about the natural history and prognosis of cancers, oncologists can advise patients on the risk of second malignancies and treatment-related cancers. They are also well-positioned to participate in community-based cancer prevention activities as experts in the full range of cancer care. However, economic barriers such as inadequate insurance coverage can hinder patient access to these services. Additionally, insufficient reimbursement for interventions may discourage patients from seeking them. The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), a medical society representing cancer specialists involved in patient care and clinical research, is dedicated to supporting oncologists in their involvement in cancer prevention. This statement on risk assessment and prevention counseling outlines the current role of oncologists in risk assessment and prevention, provides examples of activities that should be offered by oncologists, suggests opportunities for collaboration between oncologists and primary care physicians in prevention education and coordination of care for cancer survivors, describes ASCO's efforts in educating and training oncologists in prevention, and proposes improvements in the payment environment to promote patient access to these services.

title: The BLM helicase contributes to telomere maintenance through processing of late-replicating intermediate structures
text: Werner's syndrome (WS) and Bloom's syndrome (BS) are disorders that increase the risk of cancer due to the loss of function of the RecQ helicases WRN or BLM, respectively. Both WS and BS are characterized by problems with DNA replication, excessive recombination events, and abnormalities in chromosomes, which are all indicators of cancer. In WS cells, the inefficient replication of the G-rich telomeric strand leads to chromosome abnormalities, establishing a connection between WRN, telomeres, and the stability of the genome. In this study, we present evidence that BLM also plays a role in maintaining the ends of chromosomes. Cells lacking BLM exhibit a higher frequency of telomere defects (TDs), similar to cells lacking functional WRN helicase. When both helicases are lost, TDs and chromosome abnormalities worsen, suggesting that BLM and WRN function independently in telomere maintenance. The localization of BLM, especially its recruitment to telomeres, changes in response to replication problems, such as in WRN-deficient cells or after treatment with aphidicolin. When faced with replication challenges, there is an increase in structures called decatenated deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and late-replicating intermediates (LRIs), which can be seen as ultra-fine bridges (UFBs) covered by BLM during anaphase. Some of these UFBs originate from telomeric DNA, and their frequency is correlated with telomere replication issues. We propose that the BLM complex contributes to telomere maintenance by resolving LRIs.

title: Formation of a thymus from rat ES cells in xenogeneic nude mouse↔rat ES chimeras.
text: Extensive research is currently being conducted to identify the optimal conditions for differentiating embryonic stem (ES) cells or induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells into specific cell lines. However, the challenge lies in successfully generating a functional organ with a three-dimensional structure using ES or iPS cells in a laboratory setting. In this study, we present the successful creation of a rat ES cell line that expresses green fluorescent protein, as well as the production of a mouse↔rat ES chimera by injecting rat ES cells into mouse blastocysts. Remarkably, the rat ES cells contributed to the development of various organs in the chimera, including germ cells. Furthermore, when we injected ES cells into blastocysts of nu/nu mice that lack a thymus, the resulting chimeras exhibited the presence of a rat ES cell-derived thymus in their bodies. These chimeric animals hold great potential for the derivation of diverse organs from ES or iPS cells.

title: Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is required for CNS, but not non-CNS, angiogenesis.
text: The molecular mechanisms that control the formation of blood vessels in the central nervous system (CNS) and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) are not well understood. In this study, we investigate the involvement of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in the development of CNS blood vessels. Using TOP-Gal Wnt reporter mice, we find that this signaling pathway is specifically activated in CNS blood vessels during development, but not in non-CNS blood vessels. The activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is associated with the expression of different Wnt ligands by neural progenitor cells in various regions of the CNS. For example, Wnt7a and Wnt7b are expressed in ventral regions, while Wnt1, Wnt3, Wnt3a, and Wnt4 are expressed in dorsal regions. When we block Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in vivo, we observe specific disruptions in CNS angiogenesis, including a decrease in the number of blood vessels, loss of capillary beds, and the formation of abnormal blood vessels that are attached to the meninges and prone to bleeding. Additionally, we show that Wnt/beta-catenin signaling controls the expression of a glucose transporter called glut-1, which is specific to the BBB. Overall, our findings demonstrate the crucial role of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in driving the formation of blood vessels in the CNS and provide molecular evidence of a connection between angiogenesis and BBB formation.

title: Cyanidin-3-rutinoside, a natural polyphenol antioxidant, selectively kills leukemic cells by induction of oxidative stress.
text: Anthocyanins, a group of phenolic compounds found in fruits and vegetables, have various biological activities, including antioxidant properties that contribute to their anti-mutagenic and anti-carcinogenic effects. In our study, we focused on cyanidin-3-rutinoside, the most common type of anthocyanin, and its impact on leukemia and lymphoma cell lines. Our findings revealed that cyanidin-3-rutinoside, extracted and purified from the black raspberry cultivar Jewel, induced apoptosis in HL-60 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner. Surprisingly, this compound also caused the accumulation of peroxides, which are known to trigger apoptosis in HL-60 cells. Furthermore, treatment with cyanidin-3-rutinoside led to the activation of p38 MAPK and JNK, both dependent on reactive oxygen species (ROS), which ultimately resulted in cell death through the mitochondrial pathway mediated by Bim. Apoptosis was significantly inhibited when Bim was down-regulated or when Bcl-2 or Bcl-x(L) were overexpressed. Importantly, cyanidin-3-rutinoside did not increase ROS levels in normal human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and did not exhibit cytotoxic effects on these cells. These findings suggest that cyanidin-3-rutinoside holds promise as a potential therapy for leukemia due to its wide availability and selective action against tumors.

title: Gout-associated uric acid crystals activate the NALP3 inflammasome
text: The development of gout and pseudogout, which are acute and chronic inflammatory responses, respectively, is associated with the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in joints and surrounding tissues. While MSU crystals were identified as the cause of gout in the 18th century and more recently as a signal released from dying cells, little is known about the molecular mechanisms that lead to inflammation induced by MSU or CPPD. In this study, we demonstrate that both MSU and CPPD activate the caspase-1-activating NALP3 (also known as cryopyrin) inflammasome, resulting in the production of active interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18. Macrophages lacking various components of the inflammasome, such as caspase-1, ASC, and NALP3, show impaired activation of IL-1β in response to crystal stimulation. Additionally, in an in vivo model of crystal-induced peritonitis, inflammasome-deficient mice or mice lacking the IL-1β receptor (IL-1R) exhibit reduced neutrophil influx. These findings shed light on the molecular processes involved in the inflammatory conditions of gout and pseudogout and further support the crucial role of the inflammasome in various autoinflammatory diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell quiescence promotes error-prone DNA repair and mutagenesis.
text: Adult stem cells, such as hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), are typically in a state of rest or quiescence within the body. This state of quiescence is widely recognized as a protective mechanism for stem cells, as it reduces the stress caused by cellular respiration and DNA replication. However, our research reveals that HSC quiescence can also have negative consequences. We have discovered that HSCs possess unique internal mechanisms that enable their survival when exposed to ionizing irradiation (IR). These mechanisms involve increased expression of genes that promote cell survival and the activation of a strong DNA damage response mediated by the p53 protein. Interestingly, we have found that both quiescent and actively dividing HSCs are equally protected against radiation, but they employ different methods of DNA repair. Specifically, quiescent HSCs rely on a process called nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) for DNA repair, which can lead to the acquisition of genomic rearrangements. These rearrangements can persist within the body and contribute to abnormalities in the hematopoietic system. Our findings demonstrate that quiescence is a double-edged sword for HSCs, making them inherently susceptible to mutagenesis following DNA damage.

title: Recruitment of Nck by CD3ϵ Reveals a Ligand-Induced Conformational Change Essential for T Cell Receptor Signaling and Synapse Formation
text: The process by which membrane receptors initiate signal transduction upon binding to a ligand is currently under intense investigation. In particular, the T cell receptor complex (TCR-CD3) consists of ligand binding subunits (TCR alpha/beta) and signal transduction subunits (CD3). While it has been hypothesized that TCR-CD3 undergoes a conformational change upon ligand binding, there is still a lack of confirmation. However, we have compelling evidence that ligand engagement of TCR-CD3 indeed induces a conformational change, exposing a proline-rich sequence in CD3 epsilon and leading to the recruitment of the adaptor protein Nck. Importantly, this conformational change occurs prior to and independently of tyrosine kinase activation. Furthermore, through our in vivo experiments, we demonstrate that interfering with the association between Nck and CD3 epsilon in TCR-CD3 is crucial for the maturation of the immune synapse and activation of T cells.

title: Pseudo-Seq: Genome-Wide Detection of Pseudouridine Modifications in RNA.
text:
RNA molecules contain a wide range of chemically diverse bases that undergo posttranscriptional modifications. Among these modifications, pseudouridine (Ψ) is the most abundant modified base found in cellular RNAs. Recent studies have identified hundreds of pseudouridylated sites in mRNAs, many of which are dynamically regulated. However, the pseudouridine landscape has only been explored in a limited number of cell types and growth conditions, suggesting that there are still many undiscovered pseudouridylated sites. 

To address this, we introduce Pseudo-seq, a technique that enables the genome-wide identification of pseudouridylation sites with single-nucleotide precision. In this chapter, we provide a comprehensive description of Pseudo-seq, including detailed protocols for RNA isolation from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Pseudo-seq library preparation, and data analysis. This includes the processing and mapping of sequencing reads, computational identification of pseudouridylation sites, and assignment of these sites to specific pseudouridine synthases. 

Importantly, the Pseudo-seq approach can be easily adapted to any cell or tissue type, as long as high-quality mRNA can be isolated. The identification of novel pseudouridylation sites is a crucial initial step in understanding the regulation and functions of these modifications.

title: The Mammalian Epigenome
text: The modification of DNA and histone proteins creates a complex system that controls the structure of chromatin and the functioning of the genome. The epigenome encompasses all the heritable changes in the genome, and its composition in a specific cell is influenced by genetic factors, lineage, and the environment. Now that the human genome has been sequenced, researchers are focused on understanding the extensive range of epigenetic changes that determine how genetic information is expressed in different developmental stages, tissues, and disease conditions. In this review, we discuss ongoing research efforts, particularly large-scale studies, new technologies, and the obstacles that lie ahead.

title: Microtubule-associated histone deacetylase 6 supports the calcium store sensor STIM1 in mediating malignant cell behaviors.
text: The protein STIM1 plays a role in promoting cell growth, migration, and angiogenesis in breast and cervical cancers by sensing calcium levels in the endoplasmic reticulum. In this study, we found that the protein HDAC6, which is associated with microtubules, regulates the activation of STIM1-mediated calcium entry differently in cervical cancer cells compared to normal cervical epithelial cells. Using confocal microscopy, we observed that microtubule integrity is necessary for STIM1 to move to the cell membrane and interact with Orai1, a key component of calcium entry. Cancer cells had higher levels of both STIM1 and Orai1 compared to normal cells. We also found that cancer cells had lower levels of acetylated α-tubulin, a protein associated with microtubules, which was accompanied by increased levels of HDAC6. When we inhibited HDAC6 using a specific inhibitor called Tubastatin-A, STIM1 was unable to move to the cell membrane and calcium entry was blocked in cancer cells but not in normal cells. Inhibiting HDAC6 also did not affect the interaction between STIM1 and another protein called EB1. Analysis of cervical cancer tissue samples confirmed that STIM1 and Orai1 were overexpressed in most cases, along with decreased levels of acetylated α-tubulin. Overall, our findings suggest that targeting HDAC6 could be a potential strategy to disrupt STIM1-mediated calcium entry and inhibit malignant cell behavior.

title: The tumor necrosis factor family receptors RANK and CD40 cooperatively establish the thymic medullary microenvironment and self-tolerance.
text: The expression of autoimmune regulator (Aire) and peripheral tissue-specific self-antigens by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) is responsible for establishing T cell self-tolerance. However, the signals that regulate mTEC development are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that receptor activator of NF-kappaB (RANK) and CD40 signals play a crucial role in mTEC development. While RANK signaling is essential for mTEC development during embryogenesis, cooperation between CD40 and RANK signals is required in postnatal mice to establish the medullary microenvironment. In vitro experiments with fetal thymic stroma showed that ligation of RANK or CD40 induced mTEC development in a manner dependent on tumor necrosis factor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), NF-kappaB inducing kinase (NIK), and IkappaB kinase beta (IKKbeta). These findings highlight the importance of developmental-stage-dependent cooperation between RANK and CD40 in promoting mTEC development and establishing self-tolerance.

title: Rare and common variants: twenty arguments
text: Our comprehension of the genetic factors contributing to disease risk has significantly advanced due to genome-wide association studies. However, the limited identification of specific causal loci has sparked debate regarding whether the majority of the variance is concealed within numerous rare variants with significant impact or common variants with minimal effect. In this review, I examine 20 arguments supporting and opposing each model of the genetic basis for complex traits, ultimately concluding that both types of effects can be easily reconciled.

title: DNA methylation status predicts cell type-specific enhancer activity.
text: The binding of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) to specific regions of chromatin is associated with the regulation of specific cell types. These regions can either exist naturally in the chromatin or be created by the receptor itself. However, the mechanisms behind the creation and maintenance of these sites are not well understood. We have observed that pre-programmed elements, which are already present in the chromatin, have a higher density of CpG sites. The demethylation of these CpG sites is important for maintaining an open chromatin structure in a tissue-specific manner. On the other hand, sites that are opened by the GR receptor (de novo) have a lower density of CpG sites and form a unique class of enhancers that are not affected by the suppressive effects of methyl-cytosines. Additionally, treatment with glucocorticoids leads to rapid changes in methylation levels at specific CpG sites within de novo sites. Finally, we have identified GR-binding elements that have CpG sites at critical positions and have shown that methylation can impact the interactions between GR and DNA in laboratory experiments. These findings demonstrate a connection between tissue-specific chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and the binding of transcription factors. They also highlight the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation by nuclear receptors.

title: BLM helicase facilitates telomere replication during leading strand synthesis of telomeres
text: The helicase BLM, which is associated with Bloom syndrome, is believed to play a role in telomere replication by assisting the progression of replication forks through G-rich telomeric DNA. To determine the impact of BLM helicase on telomere replication, researchers used a technique called single molecule analysis of replicated DNA (SMARD). In cells lacking BLM, replication forks originating from telomeric origins, which copy the G-rich strand through leading strand synthesis, moved slower through the telomere compared to the neighboring subtelomere. The presence of a G4 stabilizer further impeded fork progression through the telomere. By using a G4-specific antibody, the researchers discovered that deficiency of BLM or another G4-unwinding helicase called WRN, associated with Werner syndrome, led to an increase in G4 structures in cells. Importantly, the deficiency of either helicase resulted in a greater increase in G4 DNA specifically detected in the telomere, compared to G4 structures observed throughout the entire genome. Overall, these findings support the idea that BLM helicase aids telomere replication by resolving G4 structures that form during the copying of the G-rich strand through leading strand synthesis.

title: Reflecting on 25 years with MYC
text: Approximately 25 years ago, scientists discovered MYC, a human gene similar to a retrovirus that causes cancer. Since then, extensive research has been conducted on MYC, leading to remarkable progress. It is remarkable to see how each small discovery about the regulation and function of MYC has influenced various fields of biology, particularly our comprehension of molecular cancer development. In this article, we will highlight the significant breakthroughs in our understanding of MYC biology and provide a glimpse into the future of MYC research.

title: Protective effects of exercise and phosphoinositide 3-kinase(p110alpha) signaling in dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
text: Physical activity has a protective effect against cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise leads to physiological cardiac hypertrophy, which is beneficial, unlike pathological hypertrophy associated with disease. The p110alpha isoform of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) plays a crucial role in exercise-induced hypertrophy. However, it is unclear whether PI3K(p110alpha) or other genes activated in the athlete's heart have an impact on cardiac function and survival in heart failure. To investigate this, we conducted experiments using two models of heart disease: a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and acute pressure overload (ascending aortic constriction) in PI3K(p110alpha) transgenics. We examined lifespan, cardiac function, and molecular markers of pathological hypertrophy. The results showed that exercise training and increased cardiac PI3K(p110alpha) activity extended survival in the DCM model by 15-20%. Conversely, reduced PI3K(p110alpha) activity significantly reduced lifespan by approximately 50%. Increased PI3K(p110alpha) activity had a positive effect on cardiac function and fibrosis in the pressure-overload model, reducing pathological growth. PI3K(p110alpha) signaling negatively regulated G protein-coupled receptor stimulated extracellular responsive kinase and Akt (via PI3K, p110gamma) activation in isolated cardiomyocytes. These findings suggest that exercise and enhanced PI3K(p110alpha) activity can delay or prevent the progression of heart disease. Additionally, identifying genes crucial for hypertrophy in the athlete's heart could lead to new strategies for treating heart failure.

title: The effect of cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption and fruit and vegetable consumption on IVF outcomes: a review and presentation of original data
text:
BACKGROUND Lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol consumption, and dietary habits, have a significant impact on health, well-being, and the risk of chronic diseases. In the context of in-vitro fertilization (IVF) and pregnancy, these lifestyle factors can influence the production of eggs, fertilization rates, pregnancy outcomes, and the risk of pregnancy loss. Additionally, chronic, low-grade oxidative stress may contribute to poor outcomes in some IVF cases.

METHODS In this review, we examine the current literature and present previously unpublished data obtained from couples who sought treatment at the PIVET Medical Centre in Western Australia. During the study, 80% of female participants and 70% of male partners completed a 1-week diary documenting their smoking habits, alcohol consumption, and fruit and vegetable intake. The clinical outcomes of their IVF treatment, including the number of eggs collected, fertilization rates, pregnancy rates, and pregnancy loss, were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to explore the relationship between patients, treatment, and lifestyle factors. 

RESULTS The findings revealed that male smoking was associated with an increased risk of pregnancy loss (p = 0.029), while female smoking had a negative impact on ovarian reserve. Furthermore, both alcohol consumption (β = 0.074, p < 0.001) and fruit and vegetable intake (β = 0.034, p < 0.001) had positive effects on fertilization rates.

CONCLUSION Based on our results and the existing literature, it is clear that lifestyle factors significantly influence the clinical outcomes of IVF. While there are conflicting findings regarding other lifestyle factors, such as dietary habits and alcohol consumption, it is evident that chronic oxidative stress caused by lifestyle factors and poor nutrition is associated with a lower success rate in IVF.

title: Efficient Mitochondrial Genome Editing by CRISPR/Cas9
text: The CRISPR/Cas9 system, known for its ability to edit nuclear DNA, has not been tested for its potential to edit mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), despite its versatility. Originally identified as a bacterial defense mechanism against viruses, it remains unclear if CRISPR/Cas9 can be targeted to mitochondria for mtDNA editing. However, our study demonstrates that regular FLAG-Cas9 can indeed localize to mitochondria and edit mtDNA using specific guide RNAs (sgRNAs) that target specific loci in the mitochondrial genome, such as Cox1 and Cox3. By expressing FLAG-Cas9 and the corresponding gRNAs, we were able to cleave the targeted mtDNA loci. Additionally, we observed disruptions in mitochondrial protein homeostasis when mtDNA was truncated or cleaved by CRISPR/Cas9. To address the issue of nonspecific distribution of FLAG-Cas9, we developed a mitochondria-targeted version called mitoCas9. This modified Cas9 variant exclusively localizes to mitochondria, allowing for specific cleavage of mtDNA when combined with gRNA expression vectors. The reduction of mtDNA and its transcription induced by mitoCas9 resulted in disruptions in mitochondrial membrane potential and inhibited cell growth. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of mtDNA editing using CRISPR/Cas9 and the potential of mitoCas9 for targeted editing of the mitochondrial genome.

title: Histone Variant H2A.Z Marks the 5′ Ends of Both Active and Inactive Genes in Euchromatin
text: In the yeast species S. cerevisiae, the histone variant H2A.Z is placed in euchromatin regions surrounding silent heterochromatin to prevent its unintended spread. Our research demonstrates that H2A.Z nucleosomes are present in the promoter regions of almost all genes in euchromatin. These nucleosomes typically occur in pairs, flanking a region without nucleosomes known as a nucleosome-free region (NFR), which contains the transcription start site. Surprisingly, we found that enrichment of H2A.Z at the 5' ends is not only observed in actively transcribed genes but also in inactive loci. By mutating a typical promoter, we discovered that a 22 base pair segment of DNA is sufficient to create a NFR surrounded by two H2A.Z nucleosomes. This segment includes a binding site for the Myb-related protein Reb1 and an adjacent dT:dA tract. The efficient placement of H2A.Z is further facilitated by a specific pattern of acetylation on the histone H3 and H4 tails, as well as the presence of the bromodomain protein Bdf1, which is part of the Swr1 remodeling complex responsible for depositing H2A.Z.

title: Exercise and respiratory training improve exercise capacity and quality of life in patients with severe chronic pulmonary hypertension.
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of exercise and respiratory training on patients with severe symptomatic pulmonary hypertension (PH). This was the first prospective randomized study conducted on this topic. Thirty patients with PH were randomly assigned to either a control group or a primary training group. The primary end points of the study were changes in the distance walked in 6 minutes and scores on the Short Form Health Survey quality-of-life questionnaire. Other factors such as WHO functional class, Borg scale, and echocardiography and gas exchange parameters were also assessed. 

After 15 weeks, patients in the primary training group showed improvement in the 6-minute walking distance compared to the control group. Exercise training was well tolerated and resulted in improved quality of life, WHO functional class, peak oxygen consumption, oxygen consumption at the anaerobic threshold, and achieved workload. Systolic pulmonary artery pressure values at rest did not significantly change within the training group. 

In conclusion, this study suggests that respiratory and physical training could be a beneficial addition to medical treatment for severe PH. These effects complement the positive outcomes of modern medical treatment.

title: HIV-1 regulation of latency in the monocyte-macrophage lineage and in CD4+ T lymphocytes.
text: The introduction of HAART in 1996 brought hope for the eradication of HIV-1. However, the discovery of hidden HIV-1 reservoirs in CD4+ T cells and the monocyte-macrophage lineage showed that this optimism was premature. These long-lasting reservoirs pose a significant obstacle to eliminating HIV-1. In this review, we focus on how HIV-1 latency is established and maintained in the two main targets: CD4+ T cells and the monocyte-macrophage lineage. Understanding the molecular mechanisms behind latency in these reservoirs is crucial for effective treatment. Clinicians strive for complete viral eradication, and strategic interventions that target both latent and productive infected cells may be the key. We propose that combining different proviral activators could greatly reduce the size of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in patients on HAART.

title: Effects of Electro-Acupuncture Therapy on Post-Stroke Depression in Patients with Different Degrees of Motor Function Impairments: a Pilot Study
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the potential of electro-acupuncture therapy in reducing post-stroke depression (PSD) and whether the therapy's effects are influenced by motor function impairments. A total of twenty-eight PSD patients were evaluated and divided into two groups based on their motor grade: good or poor. The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS), and Manual Muscle Test (MMT) were administered during the screening and initial phases of the study, as well as at the 4th, 8th, 12th, and 16th week of daily electro-acupuncture treatment. The results showed that electro-acupuncture treatment effectively reduced PSD, as indicated by improvements in BDI and HDRS scores. Notably, the good motor function group experienced significantly greater reductions in depression compared to the poor motor function group. However, there were no changes in motor function impairment observed in either group throughout the study. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that electro-acupuncture therapy can effectively alleviate PSD and that the treatment's efficacy may vary depending on the severity of motor function impairments.

title: T cell receptor ligation induces the formation of dynamically regulated signaling assemblies
text: We investigated the process of signaling complex formation in live Jurkat leukemic T cells by examining the kinetics and mechanics. To do this, we used fluorescently tagged signaling proteins with enhanced GFP variants (EGFP). When the T cell antigen receptor (TCR) was stimulated by contacting coverslips coated with antibodies, we observed the rapid development of small clusters in the T cells. These clusters were dynamically regulated and contained various signaling proteins such as TCR, phosphotyrosine, ZAP-70, LAT, Grb2, Gads, and SLP-76. Importantly, these clusters excluded the lipid raft marker enhanced yellow fluorescent protein-GPI and were capable of inducing calcium elevations. LAT, Grb2, and Gads were only transiently associated with the TCR, while ZAP-70-containing clusters persisted for more than 20 minutes. However, photobleaching studies revealed that ZAP-70 continuously dissociated from and returned to these complexes. Interestingly, SLP-76 translocated to a perinuclear structure after clustering with the TCR. Our findings highlight the dynamic nature of signaling complexes and demonstrate that these complexes can form within seconds of TCR engagement, even in the absence of lipid raft aggregation or the formation of a central TCR-rich cluster.

title: Developmental heterogeneity of cardiac fibroblasts does not predict pathological proliferation and activation.
text:
RATIONALE: Fibrosis in the heart is partly caused by fibroblasts that deposit extracellular matrix. However, the functional consequences of the heterogeneity of these cells, which have multiple embryonic origins, are unknown.

OBJECTIVE: Our objective was to validate a set of surface markers that can be used to identify cardiac fibroblasts. We aimed to determine the developmental origins of these fibroblasts and characterize their phenotypes. Additionally, we wanted to assess the proliferation rates of different subsets of fibroblasts after pressure overload injury.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We found that the majority of cardiac fibroblasts can be identified by the surface markers Thy1(+), CD45(-), CD31(-), CD11b(-), and Ter119(-). We used various techniques including flow cytometry, microscopy, and transcriptional profiling to characterize these cells. Through lineage tracing, transplantation studies, and parabiosis, we discovered that most adult cardiac fibroblasts come from the epicardium, while a smaller portion originates from endothelial cells and Pax3-expressing cells. We did not observe the generation of cardiac fibroblasts from bone marrow or circulating cells. Interestingly, all subsets of fibroblasts showed identical proliferation rates after injury, and the relative abundance of each lineage remained the same. The anatomic distribution of fibroblast lineages also remained unchanged after pressure overload. Furthermore, gene expression analysis revealed that fibroblasts derived from Tie2 and Tbx18 within each group exhibited similar profiles.

CONCLUSIONS: The expansion of cardiac fibroblasts after transaortic constriction surgery was not limited to any specific developmental subset. The parallel proliferation and activation of a heterogeneous population of fibroblasts in response to pressure overload suggests that common signaling mechanisms drive their pathological response.

title: Pre-eclampsia: connecting angiogenic and metabolic pathways.
text: This article focuses on recent advancements in pre-eclampsia research concerning angiogenesis and metabolism. Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive condition during pregnancy that affects 5-8% of women worldwide. The main topic discussed is the "angiogenic imbalance" theory, which suggests that pre-eclampsia occurs due to an imbalance of factors that either promote or hinder angiogenesis. These factors include soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase (sFlt1), 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME), and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). Additionally, the association between pre-eclampsia and abnormal metabolism of homocysteine and placental glycogen is examined. By shedding light on the connections between angiogenesis and metabolism in pre-eclampsia, it is hoped that outdated models of pathogenesis can be updated or reconsidered.

title: Protein Lysine Acetylated/Deacetylated Enzymes and the Metabolism-Related Diseases
text: Lysine acetylation is a reversible modification that occurs after protein synthesis, known as a posttranslational modification. It is considered an epigenetic phenomenon, involving the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl CoA to the lysine e-amino group of a specific protein. This process is regulated by enzymes called acetyltransferases (histone/lysine acetyltransferases, HATs/KATs) and deacetylases (histone/lysine deacetylases, HDACs/KDACs). Lysine acetylation plays a crucial role in regulating various metabolic processes, including fatty acid oxidation, the Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and angiogenesis. Consequently, disruptions in lysine acetylation have been associated with metabolic complications such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Furthermore, recent research has shown that lysine acetylation also influences cell immune status and is implicated in degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease. This review aims to provide an overview of current studies on lysine acetylation's role in modulating metabolism and its involvement in metabolism-related diseases, specifically cardiovascular disease and disorders of fat metabolism.

title: Differential Specificity of Endocrine FGF19 and FGF21 to FGFR1 and FGFR4 in Complex with KLB
text:
Recent research suggests that betaKlotho (KLB) and endocrine FGF19 and FGF21 play a role in regulating metabolic homeostasis and suppressing obesity and diabetes. However, it is still unclear which metabolic tissue contains the main FGFR-KLB receptor that mediates the different effects of FGF19 and FGF21 on metabolism. 

To address this, we conducted a study comparing the receptor and tissue specificity of FGF21 to FGF19. We used sensitive and quantitative binding kinetics, as well as downstream signal transduction and expression of early response genes in mice after administering FGF19 and FGF21. 

Our findings show that FGF21 binds to FGFR1 with much higher affinity than FGFR4 in the presence of KLB. On the other hand, FGF19 binds to both FGFR1 and FGFR4 in the presence of KLB with similar affinity. The interaction between FGF21 and FGFR4-KLB is very weak, even at high concentrations, and may be negligible at physiological levels. Both FGF19 and FGF21, but not FGF1, have binding affinity to KLB. The binding of FGF1 depends on the presence of FGFRs. FGF19 and FGF21 cannot displace the binding of FGF1, and vice versa. These results indicate that KLB is necessary for the binding of FGF19 and FGF21 to FGFRs, but not for FGF1. 

While FGF19 primarily activates responses in the liver and to a lesser extent in adipose tissue, FGF21 mainly targets adipose tissue and adipocytes. Among various metabolic and endocrine tissues, the response of adipose tissue to FGF21 is the most significant and can be reduced by the removal of KLB or FGFR1. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that FGF21 has a lower affinity for the FGFR4-KLB complex compared to FGFR1-KLB, making it less likely to directly target the liver where FGFR4-KLB is predominantly found. However, both FGF21 and FGF19 have the potential to activate responses in adipose tissue, where FGFR1-KLB is present.

title: Therapeutic efficacy of a multi-epitope vaccine against Helicobacter pylori infection in BALB/c mice model.
text: The use of epitope vaccines shows promise as a therapeutic option for combating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection. In this research, we developed a multi-epitope vaccine consisting of five epitopes and the mucosal adjuvant E. coli heat-labile enterotoxin B subunit (LTB), which we named HUepi-LTB. We then assessed the effectiveness of HUepi-LTB in treating H. pylori infection using a mouse model. HUepi-LTB was created by incorporating three Th epitopes from UreB and two B cell epitopes from UreB and HpaA, and it was successfully expressed in E. coli. Through oral therapeutic immunization with HUepi-LTB, we observed a significant reduction in H. pylori colonization compared to oral immunization with PBS. This protection was associated with the activation of antigen-specific CD4+ T cells and the production of IgG and mucosal IgA antibodies. These findings suggest that this multi-epitope vaccine holds promise as a potential candidate for controlling H. pylori infection.

title: DNA fragments in the blood plasma of cancer patients: quantitations and evidence for their origin from apoptotic and necrotic cells.
text: Elevated levels of DNA fragments are often discovered in the blood plasma of individuals with cancer. Previous research indicates that only a portion of the DNA in blood plasma originates from cancer cells. However, it remains uncertain how much of the circulating DNA comes from cancerous or noncancerous cells. Through quantitative methylation-specific PCR of the CDKN2A tumor suppressor gene's promoter region, we were able to measure the proportion of plasma DNA derived from tumor cells. In a sample of 30 cancer patients, we detected tumor DNA quantities ranging from 3% to as high as 93% of the total circulating DNA. We also explored potential sources of non-tumor DNA in the plasma and found that T-cell DNA contributed in only a few cases. To investigate whether plasma DNA originates from apoptotic or necrotic cells, we conducted experiments using apoptotic (staurosporine) and necrotic (staurosporine plus oligomycin) cells in vitro, as well as mice with induced apoptotic (anti-CD95) or necrotic (acetaminophen) liver injuries. Increasing amounts of DNA were released in the supernatants of cells and blood plasma samples from treated animals. Gel electrophoresis allowed for clear differentiation between apoptotic and necrotic plasma DNA. The same distinct patterns of DNA fragments were observed in plasma derived from various cancer patients. These findings support the hypothesis that apoptotic and necrotic cells are significant sources of plasma DNA in individuals with cancer.

title: Pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of eptifibatide in patients with acute coronary syndromes: prospective analysis from PURSUIT.
text:
The pathogenesis of ischemic complications in acute coronary syndromes (ACS) is closely linked to platelet deposition and aggregation. While the pharmacodynamic effects of the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonist eptifibatide have been studied in healthy individuals, its effects in ACS patients remain unclear. In this study, we aimed to assess the impact of eptifibatide on platelet aggregation in ACS patients enrolled in the Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa in Unstable angina: Receptor Suppression Using Integrilin (eptifibatide) Therapy (PURSUIT) trial.

A total of 98 patients were randomly assigned to receive either an intravenous bolus (180 microgram/kg) and a 72-hour infusion of eptifibatide (2.0 microgram/kg per minute, n=48) or a placebo (n=50). We analyzed the correlation between plasma eptifibatide levels and receptor occupancy, as well as the inhibition of ex vivo platelet aggregation at various time points during and after treatment.

Blood samples were collected using buffered citrate and D-phenylalanyl-L-prolyl-L-arginine chloromethylketone anticoagulants. Our findings revealed that eptifibatide effectively inhibited platelet aggregation during therapy, but there was a partial recovery observed within 4 hours after the bolus. Furthermore, the inhibition of platelet aggregation was more pronounced when stimulated with a thrombin receptor agonist peptide compared to ADP stimulation. Additionally, the anticoagulant used influenced the degree of platelet aggregation inhibition, with citrate showing greater efficacy than D-phenylalanyl-L-prolyl-L-arginine chloromethylketone (PPACK). Interestingly, plasma eptifibatide levels were significantly correlated with receptor occupancy but not with the inhibition of platelet aggregation.

In conclusion, the administration of eptifibatide through a bolus and infusion effectively inhibits platelet aggregation in ACS patients, although there is a brief period of partial recovery. These findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between the pharmacodynamic and clinical effects of eptifibatide in ACS patients and may have important implications for its use in percutaneous interventions.

title: Proinflammatory cytokines underlying the inflammation of Crohn's disease.
text:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: The purpose of this review is to summarize our current knowledge of the proinflammatory cytokines involved in the inflammation associated with Crohn's disease and explore the potential for developing therapies that target these cytokines.

RECENT FINDINGS: Recent research has provided new insights into the role of T helper cell (Th)1 and Th17 responses in the development of Crohn's disease. Early studies suggested that interleukin-12-driven Th1 response was responsible for the inflammation in Crohn's disease, with interferon-gamma being the main mediator. However, more recent studies, primarily conducted in animal models, have shown that a Th17 response, characterized by the production of interleukin-17, is the primary cause of inflammation in Crohn's disease. A more balanced perspective is now emerging, suggesting that interferon-gamma may still play a significant role in Crohn's disease, but it may be produced by both Th1 and Th17 responses at different stages of the inflammatory process.

SUMMARY: The latest findings support the notion that anti-interleukin-12p40, an antibody that inhibits both Th1 and Th17 responses, is the most effective anticytokine therapy for treating Crohn's disease.

title: STATISTICAL METHODS FOR ASSESSING AGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO METHODS OF CLINICAL MEASUREMENT
text: When evaluating a new measurement technique in clinical settings, it is common to compare it with an established one to determine if they agree enough for the new technique to replace the old. Unfortunately, these comparisons are often analyzed incorrectly, particularly when using correlation coefficients. The use of correlation can be misleading. Instead, a different approach that involves graphical techniques and simple calculations is recommended. This alternative analysis method is also related to the assessment of repeatability.

title: The multidrug ABC transporter BmrC/BmrD of Bacillus subtilis is regulated via a ribosome-mediated transcriptional attenuation mechanism
text: The expression of specific drug transporters in response to antibiotics is a crucial factor in the development of bacterial resistance to multiple drugs, which poses a significant threat to human health. In order to gain a better understanding of the underlying regulatory mechanisms, we have studied the activation of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter BmrC/BmrD in the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis, which serves as a model organism. Through the use of promoter-GFP fusions and live cell array technology, we have observed that the transcriptional activation of the bmrCD genes is controlled in a time-dependent manner in response to antibiotics that target protein synthesis. Interestingly, the expression of bmrCD only occurs during the late-exponential and stationary growth phases, regardless of when the antibiotic challenge is administered. We have determined that this tight control of transcription is mediated by the transition state regulator AbrB. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the bmrCD genes are transcribed together with bmrB (yheJ), a small open reading frame located immediately upstream of bmrC, which contains three alternative stem-loop structures. These stem-loops appear to play a crucial role in the antibiotic-induced transcription of bmrCD. Importantly, we have discovered that the expression of bmrCD in response to antibiotics requires the translation of bmrB, suggesting that BmrB acts as a regulatory leader peptide. Overall, our study provides the first evidence that a ribosome-mediated transcriptional attenuation mechanism can regulate the expression of a multidrug ABC transporter.

title: The neural crest is a source of mesenchymal stem cells with specialized hematopoietic stem cell niche function
text: The role of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and osteolineage cells in the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow of long bones is not well understood. This study aims to clarify their developmental relationships. Our findings show that different populations of MSCs in the developing bone marrow have unique functions. MSCs derived from proliferative mesoderm, which do not express nestin, contribute to fetal skeletogenesis but lose their MSC activity shortly after birth. On the other hand, quiescent MSCs derived from neural crest cells, which express nestin, maintain their MSC activity but do not generate fetal chondrocytes. Instead, they differentiate into MSCs that form the HSC niche by secreting Cxcl12. The migration of these cells to the bone marrow is dependent on the ErbB3 receptor. Additionally, the population of Nestin-GFP(+) Pdgfrα(-) cells in neonates also includes Schwann cell precursors but not mature Schwann cells. Therefore, in the developing bone marrow, MSCs that form the HSC niche have a common origin with sympathetic peripheral neurons and glial cells. Furthermore, MSCs with distinct origins have different roles in endochondrogenesis and HSC niche formation.

title: Hotspots of aberrant epigenomic reprogramming in human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: The potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) in regenerative medicine and the study of diseases and development is vast. By reprogramming somatic cells, iPSCs acquire characteristics similar to embryonic stem (ES) cells through epigenomic reconfiguration. However, the extent to which ES-cell-like DNA methylation patterns are fully reestablished throughout the genome remains unknown. In this study, we present the first comprehensive profiles of DNA methylation at the single-base level in five human iPSC lines, as well as the methylomes of ES cells, somatic cells, and differentiated iPSCs and ES cells. Our findings reveal significant variability in the reprogramming process of iPSCs, including the retention of somatic memory and abnormal reprogramming of DNA methylation. We also observe shared regions of differential methylation near centromeres and telomeres in iPSCs, indicating incomplete reprogramming of non-CG methylation, as well as differences in CG methylation and histone modifications. Lastly, when iPSCs are differentiated into trophoblast cells, we observe a high frequency of errors in reprogramming CG methylation, suggesting the presence of an iPSC reprogramming signature that persists even after differentiation.

title: Inheritance of coronary artery disease in men: an analysis of the role of the Y chromosome
text:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery disease affects men more than women. We investigated the role of the Y chromosome in this gender disparity.

METHODS: We studied 3233 unrelated British men from three cohorts and genotyped 11 markers of the male-specific region of the Y chromosome. We categorized the Y chromosomes into 13 ancient lineages called haplogroups. We then analyzed the association between common Y chromosome haplogroups and the risk of coronary artery disease in two cross-sectional and one prospective study. Additionally, we examined the effects of the Y chromosome on the transcriptome of monocytes and macrophages.

FINDINGS: Among the identified haplogroups, two (R1b1b2 and I) accounted for 90% of the Y chromosome variants in British men. Men with haplogroup I had a 50% higher risk of coronary artery disease compared to men with other Y chromosome lineages. This association was consistent across all populations and independent of traditional risk factors. Analysis of the macrophage transcriptome revealed several molecular pathways related to inflammation and immunity that were differentially expressed in men with haplogroup I, suggesting a potential link to atherosclerosis.

INTERPRETATION: The Y chromosome is associated with the risk of coronary artery disease in men of European ancestry, possibly through interactions with immunity and inflammation.

FUNDING: This study was supported by the British Heart Foundation, UK National Institute for Health Research, LEW Carty Charitable Fund, National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia, European Union 6th Framework Programme, and Wellcome Trust.

title: Cytoscape 2.8: new features for data integration and network visualization
text: Cytoscape, a widely used bioinformatics package for visualizing biological networks and integrating data, has introduced two new powerful features in Version 2.8. These features, Custom Node Graphics and Attribute Equations, can be used together to significantly enhance Cytoscape's capabilities in data integration and visualization. With Custom Node Graphics, users can project images onto nodes, including dynamically generated or remotely located images. Attribute Equations provide spreadsheet-like functionality, allowing attributes to be computed dynamically based on other attributes and network properties. Cytoscape is a desktop Java application that is released under the Library Gnu Public License (LGPL). Users can download binary install bundles and source code for Cytoscape 2.8 from http://cytoscape.org.

title: Detection of Histone Modifications at Specific Gene Loci in Single Cells in Histological Sections
text: The use of chromatin immunoprecipitation assays has greatly enhanced our understanding of how histone modifications regulate gene activity. However, these assays are limited in their ability to analyze individual cells, making it difficult to study cell populations with diverse characteristics. In this study, we introduce a new method that allows us to visualize histone modifications at specific locations in the genome with single-cell precision, using formaldehyde-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections. This technique combines in situ hybridization and proximity ligation assays. Our results demonstrate that the dimethylation of lysine 4 on histone H3 (H3K4me2) at the MYH11 locus is only present in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in both human and mouse tissue sections. Furthermore, this modification persists even in phenotypically altered SMCs found in atherosclerotic lesions, which do not express typical SMC marker genes. This innovative methodology holds great potential for studying epigenetic mechanisms in complex multicellular tissues during development and disease.

title: Mechanistic characterization of the sulfur-relay system for eukaryotic 2-thiouridine biogenesis at tRNA wobble positions
text: In eukaryotes, the modification known as the wobble modification in tRNAs, specifically 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl-2-thiouridine (mcm(5)s(2)U), is crucial for accurately decoding NNR codons. This modification is achieved through the presence of a 2-thio group, which imparts conformational rigidity to mcm(5)s(2)U by stabilizing the C3'-endo ribose puckering. As a result, stable and precise codon-anticodon pairing is ensured. Our research has identified five genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, namely YIL008w (URM1), YHR111w (UBA4), YOR251c (TUM1), YNL119w (NCS2), and YGL211w (NCS6), that play a crucial role in the 2-thiolation of mcm(5)s(2)U. Through an in vitro sulfur transfer experiment, we discovered that Tum1p stimulates the cysteine desulfurase of Nfs1p and accepts persulfide sulfurs from Nfs1p. URM1 is a modifier related to ubiquitin, while UBA4 is an enzyme similar to E1 that is involved in protein urmylation. The carboxy-terminus of Urm1p is activated as an acyl-adenylate (-COAMP) and subsequently thiocarboxylated (-COSH) by Uba4p. This activated thiocarboxylate is then utilized in subsequent reactions for the formation of 2-thiouridine, which is mediated by Ncs2p/Ncs6p. Through the use of recombinant proteins, we were able to successfully reconstitute the formation of 2-thiouridine in vitro. Our study has revealed that the formation of 2-thiouridine shares a pathway and chemical reactions with protein urmylation. Furthermore, the sulfur-flow involved in eukaryotic 2-thiouridine formation is distinct from the bacterial sulfur-relay system, which relies on persulfide chemistry.

title: High prevalence of asthma in cross country skiers.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the prevalence of asthma symptoms and bronchial hyperresponsiveness in Swedish cross country skiers compared to non-skiers, as well as to monitor any changes in symptoms and hyperresponsiveness throughout the year. The study design involved a cross-sectional approach during both the winter ski season and the summer. The study took place in six ski clubs for elite skiers, with a total of 47 participants, located in two different areas of Sweden. The subjects included 42 elite cross country skiers and 29 non-skiing individuals for comparison. The main outcome measures were bronchial responsiveness, asthma symptoms, and lung function. The results showed that bronchial responsiveness was significantly higher and asthma symptoms were more prevalent in the skiers compared to the non-skiers. There was no difference in bronchial responsiveness within either group between the winter and summer seasons. Out of the 42 skiers, 15 used antiasthmatic drugs regularly, and 23 had a combination of asthma symptoms and hyperresponsive airways or physician-diagnosed asthma, or both. In total, 33 skiers exhibited symptoms of asthma or bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Only one of the non-skiers had symptoms of asthma and bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and none of them used antiasthmatic drugs regularly. In conclusion, asthma, asthma-like symptoms, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness are much more common in cross country skiers compared to the general population and non-skiers. The most likely explanation for persistent asthma in skiers is the strenuous exercise at low temperatures, which involves breathing in large volumes of cold air.

title: Characterization of biochemical properties of Bacillus subtilis RecQ helicase.
text: The RecQ family helicases play a crucial role in safeguarding the integrity of the genome. In contrast to Escherichia coli, the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis possesses two RecQ-like homologues, RecQ[Bs] and RecS, which are essential for repairing DNA double-strand breaks. RecQ[Bs] also has the ability to bind to forked DNA, ensuring a smooth progression of the cell cycle. In this study, we present the first biochemical analysis of recombinant RecQ[Bs].
