Our findings reveal that RecQ[Bs] has a weak binding affinity for single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and blunt-ended double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), but a strong affinity for forked dsDNA. The protein exhibits ATPase activity that is stimulated by DNA, as well as ATP- and Mg(2+)-dependent DNA helicase activity with a 3' → 5' polarity. Molecular modeling demonstrates that RecQ[Bs] shares significant sequence and structural similarity with E. coli RecQ. Surprisingly, RecQ[Bs] displays more similarities to the truncated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Sgs1 and human RecQ helicases in terms of its enzymatic activities, rather than RecQ[Ec]. Specifically, RecQ[Bs] is capable of unwinding forked dsDNA and DNA duplexes with a 3'-overhang, but it is inactive on blunt-ended dsDNA and 5'-overhung duplexes. Interestingly, RecQ[Bs] can unwind blunt-ended DNA with various structural features, including nicks, gaps, 5'-flaps, Kappa joints, synthetic replication forks, and Holliday junctions. We discuss these findings in relation to the potential functions of RecQ[Bs] in maintaining genomic stability.

title: SOD1 Integrates Signals from Oxygen and Glucose to Repress Respiration
text: The enzyme Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) is widely known for its role in regulating antioxidant defense. In our study using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we have discovered that SOD1 also plays a crucial role in transmitting signals from oxygen and glucose to suppress respiration. This mechanism involves SOD1 stabilizing two homologs of casein kinase 1-gamma (CK1γ), namely Yck1p and Yck2p, which are essential for repressing respiration. We have identified a C-terminal degron in Yck1p/Yck2p that binds to SOD1, and this interaction promotes the stability of the kinases by converting superoxide to peroxide. We have also observed similar effects on CK1γ stability with mammalian SOD1 and CK1γ, as well as in a human cell line. Therefore, through the SOD1/CK1γ signaling pathway, oxygen, glucose, and reactive oxygen species can collectively suppress respiration. Our findings shed light on the mechanistic understanding of how rapidly dividing cells and many cancers utilize glucose-mediated repression of respiration in favor of aerobic glycolysis.

title: The prognostic impact of the platelet distribution width-to-platelet count ratio in patients with breast cancer
text: The growth, angiogenesis, and invasion of tumor cells are promoted by activated platelets. Platelet volume indices (PVIs) can be used to infer platelet activity, including platelet distribution width (PDW), mean platelet volume (MPV), platelet distribution width-to-platelet count ratio (PDW/P), and mean platelet volume-to-platelet count ratio. In patients with breast cancer, platelets and platelet-related markers, such as the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, have been identified as significant prognostic factors. However, the role of PVIs in predicting survival in breast cancer is still unknown. Therefore, we conducted a retrospective analysis of 275 breast cancer patients to investigate this. We compared PVIs with clinicopathological variables and used the Cox proportional hazards model to identify independent indicators associated with disease-free survival (DFS). We found that an elevated PDW/P was significantly correlated with age and HER2 status. Univariate analysis showed that elevated PDW, MPV, and PDW/P, as well as tumor size, nuclear grade, and lymph node involvement, were significantly associated with lower DFS rates. On multivariate analysis, a large tumor size and elevated PDW/P were identified as significant prognostic factors for DFS, with hazard ratios of 3.24 and 2.99, respectively. Our study is the first to demonstrate that an elevated PDW/P significantly reduces DFS in breast carcinoma patients. Measuring PDW/P is a simple, relatively inexpensive, and widely available method using routine blood counts, making it an attractive biomarker for improved risk assessment.

title: Persistent LCMV infection is controlled by blockade of type I interferon signaling.
text: In cases of long-lasting viral infections, the progression of the disease is associated with ongoing immune activation, increased expression of negative immune regulators, an elevated interferon signature, and damage to lymphoid tissue. Our study showed that by blocking the signaling of type I interferon (IFN-I) using an antibody that neutralizes the IFN-I receptor, we were able to reduce immune system activation, decrease the expression of negative immune regulatory molecules, and restore the structure of lymphoid tissue in mice with persistent lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection. Blocking IFN-I both before and after the establishment of persistent virus infection improved the clearance of the virus, and this effect was dependent on CD4 T cells. Therefore, we have established a direct cause-and-effect relationship between IFN-I signaling, immune activation, expression of negative immune regulators, disorganization of lymphoid tissue, and virus persistence. Based on our findings, targeting IFN-I with therapies may be a potential approach to control persistent virus infections.

title: Lam6 Regulates the Extent of Contacts between Organelles
text: Effective communication between organelles is essential for eukaryotic cells to function harmoniously. One crucial method of communication is through membrane contact sites, where two organelles come close together, enabling the exchange of lipids and small solutes. These contact sites are not static, but rather can change in size in response to various environmental or cellular cues. However, the regulation of this process has remained unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that Saccharomyces cerevisiae Lam6 is present in multiple key contact sites: ERMES, vCLAMP, and NVJ. We further establish that Lam6 is capable of expanding contact sites under normal physiological conditions and is necessary for coordinating their size. As Lam6 belongs to a large protein family and is conserved in vertebrates, our findings provide a foundation for exploring the fundamental principles of organelle communication.

title: Endocrine regulation of human fetal growth: the role of the mother, placenta, and fetus.
text: The development of the fetus is heavily dependent on its environment, which plays a crucial role in its survival and long-term well-being. The regulation of normal human fetal growth involves complex interactions between the mother, placenta, and fetus. The mother provides essential nutrients and oxygen to the fetus through the placenta. In turn, the fetus influences the availability of maternal nutrients by producing hormones that regulate the mother's metabolism through the placenta. The placenta acts as the interface between the mother and fetus, controlling fetal growth by producing and metabolizing growth-regulating hormones like IGFs and glucocorticoids. Adequate invasion of trophoblasts in early pregnancy and increased blood flow to the uterus and placenta ensure proper growth of these structures as well as the fetus. The placenta can respond to fetal endocrine signals by enhancing the transport of maternal nutrients through placental growth, activation of transport systems, and production of hormones that affect the mother's physiology and behavior. Poor fetal growth has short-term and long-term consequences, including increased mortality and morbidity. The endocrine regulation of fetal growth involves intricate interactions between the mother, placenta, and fetus, and these effects can have long-lasting effects on the physiology of the individual.

title: Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition contributes to cardiac fibrosis
text: Excessive deposition of extracellular matrix, leading to cardiac fibrosis, is caused by the recruitment of fibroblasts and is associated with a decrease in microvasculature and disruption of normal myocardial structures. The origin of these fibroblasts is uncertain, and there are currently no specific therapies available to treat fibrosis. However, our research reveals that cardiac fibrosis is linked to the emergence of fibroblasts derived from endothelial cells, suggesting an endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) similar to the process that occurs during the formation of the atrioventricular cushion in the embryonic heart. We found that transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) induces EndMT in endothelial cells, while bone morphogenic protein 7 (BMP-7) preserves the endothelial phenotype. By administering recombinant human BMP-7 (rhBMP-7) systemically, we were able to significantly inhibit EndMT and the progression of cardiac fibrosis in mouse models of pressure overload and chronic allograft rejection. These findings demonstrate the contribution of EndMT to the advancement of cardiac fibrosis and suggest that rhBMP-7 can be utilized to suppress EndMT and intervene in the progression of chronic heart disease associated with fibrosis.

title: Coupled local translation and degradation regulate growth cone collapse
text: The response of axons to guidance cues like Semaphorin3A (Sema3A) is mediated by local translation. However, only a specific subset of proteins is synthesized locally, while most proteins are transported from the cell body. The reason behind this selective protein synthesis is still unknown. Our study reveals a connection between local protein synthesis and degradation in growth cones. We observed high levels of ubiquitination in growth cones, and local signaling pathways trigger the ubiquitination and degradation of RhoA, a protein involved in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse. By inhibiting RhoA degradation, we were able to eliminate the requirement for protein synthesis in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse. Furthermore, we found that the ubiquitin-proteasome system primarily targets locally translated proteins in growth cones. Therefore, local protein degradation is a significant characteristic of growth cones and necessitates local translation to replenish the proteins required for maintaining growth cone responses.

title: Cdk11 is a RanGTP-dependent microtubule stabilization factor that regulates spindle assembly rate
text: The presence of Ran-guanosine triphosphate (GTP) near chromosomes triggers the formation and reinforcement of microtubules (MTs) in the vicinity. The nuclear protein TPX2 is necessary for MT nucleation, which is dependent on RanGTP. To identify the MT stabilizer, we isolated proteins containing a nuclear localization signal (NLS) from Xenopus laevis egg extracts. This fraction of NLS proteins possesses MT stabilization properties. Through further purification, we utilized mass spectrometry to identify proteins in the active fractions, including cyclin-dependent kinase 11 (Cdk11). In Xenopus culture cells and egg extracts, Cdk11 is found on spindle poles and MTs. Recombinant Cdk11 exhibits RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization activity, while a kinase-dead mutant does not. When Cdk11 is deactivated in egg extracts, RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization is hindered, resulting in a significant decrease in the rate of spindle assembly. Additionally, simultaneous depletion of TPX2 completely prevents centrosome-dependent spindle assembly. Our findings suggest that Cdk11 is responsible for the RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization around chromosomes, which is crucial for normal rates of spindle assembly and proper spindle function.

title: Population dynamics of a pathogen: the conundrum of vivax malaria
text: Developing a mathematical model to understand how pathogens interact with their host's population involves considering factors similar to those in ecology, as pathogens can prey on cells within the host. However, within a multicellular host, the types of cells that are attacked are integrated with other cellular systems, which in turn play a role in the infection. For instance, the immune system attempts to detect and eliminate or contain pathogens, while homeostatic mechanisms try to compensate for cell loss. This article focuses on modeling techniques applied to malarias, which are diseases caused by single-cell eukaryote parasites that infect red blood cells. Specifically, it examines vivax malaria, a disease that is often considered benign (although sometimes incapacitating) because the parasite only attacks a small proportion of the youngest red blood cells. Nevertheless, through mathematical modeling, I will argue that depleting this pool of red blood cells can have disastrous consequences for the host if the growth of the parasite is not effectively controlled by the host's immune responses. Additionally, modeling can shed light on new field observations that suggest vivax malaria is more dangerous than previously believed. For more information, please refer to the electronic supplementary material available to authorized users on the online version of this article (doi:10.1007/s12551-010-0034-3).

title: Identification and analysis of ribonuclease P and MRP RNA in a broad range of eukaryotes
text: RNases P and MRP are complexes of ribonucleoproteins that participate in the processing of tRNA and rRNA, respectively. The RNA components of these enzymes share a structural similarity and play a crucial role in their enzymatic activity. Both RNAs possess a conserved helical region called P4, which is essential for the catalytic reaction. To investigate these enzymes, we employed a bioinformatics approach that utilized conserved elements to analyze genomic sequences of various eukaryotic organisms. As a result, we discovered a significant number of previously unknown nuclear genes encoding RNase P and MRP RNA. In the case of MRP RNA, our investigation tripled the number of known sequences. We have also developed secondary structure models for many of the predicted RNAs. While all sequences can adopt the consensus secondary structure of P and MRP RNAs, there is a remarkable variation in size, ranging from a 160 nt MRP RNA in Nosema locustae to much larger RNAs, such as a 696 nt P RNA in Plasmodium knowlesi. Interestingly, in some protists, the P and MRP RNA genes are found in tandem, further highlighting the close evolutionary relationship between these RNAs.

title: Calcium absorption varies within the reference range for serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
text:
BACKGROUND: The absorption of calcium is commonly believed to be hindered when there is a deficiency of vitamin D. However, the exact level of vitamin D that fully restores absorption in humans is unknown.

OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to measure calcium absorption at two different levels of vitamin D repletion using pharmacokinetic methods and commercially available calcium supplements.

DESIGN: Two experiments were conducted in the spring, one year apart. In the first experiment, participants were given pretreatment with 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD), resulting in an average serum concentration of 86.5 nmol/L. In the second experiment, participants received no pretreatment, resulting in an average serum concentration of 50.2 nmol/L. All participants were given a 500 mg oral calcium load as part of a low calcium breakfast, followed by a low calcium lunch. Blood samples were taken while fasting and at regular intervals for 10 to 12 hours.

METHODS: The relative calcium absorption at the two different 25OHD concentrations was estimated by calculating the area under the curve (AUC) for the increase in serum total calcium caused by the calcium load.

RESULTS: The AUC(9) (+/- SEM) was 3.63 mg hr/dL +/- 0.234 in participants who were pretreated with 25OHD, and 2.20 +/- 0.240 in those who received no pretreatment (P < 0.001). In summary, absorption was 65% higher at an average serum 25OHD level of 86.5 nmol/L compared to an average level of 50 nmol/L (both values within the normal reference range for this analyte).

CONCLUSIONS: Despite the fact that the mean serum 25OHD level in the experiment without supplementation fell within the current reference range, calcium absorption at 50 nmol/L was significantly lower compared to an average 25OHD level of 86 nmol/L. Therefore, individuals with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels at the lower end of the current reference range may not be fully benefiting from their calcium intake. We conclude that the lower end of the current reference range is set too low.

title: Evolution of virulence in opportunistic pathogens: generalism, plasticity, and control
text: The prevailing theory on the evolution of virulence assumes that virulence factors are kept because they help parasites exploit their hosts, leading to increased growth and transmission. However, recent studies have shown that many opportunistic pathogens (OPs) do not follow these assumptions. Instead, they maintain virulence factors because of advantages in non-parasitic situations. In this article, we examine the theory of virulence evolution in relation to OPs and emphasize the importance of considering environments beyond the main site of virulence. We demonstrate that the selection of virulence is limited by connections between these external environments and the main site, and we identify factors that drive these environmental correlations, particularly focusing on generalist strategies and phenotypic flexibility. Finally, we summarize the main theoretical and empirical challenges that need to be addressed for a more comprehensive understanding of OPs.

title: Genome-Wide Profiling of H3K56 Acetylation and Transcription Factor Binding Sites in Human Adipocytes
text: A better understanding of adipocyte biology is crucial in addressing the growing epidemic of obesity and metabolic diseases. The regulation of transcription in adipocytes is particularly important as it is targeted by various therapeutic approaches. Transcriptional outcomes are influenced by histone modifications and transcription factor binding. However, there is a lack of data on the epigenetic states and binding sites of important transcription factors in human adipocytes, unlike in the mouse 3T3-L1 cell line. In this study, we identified H3K56 acetylation sites in human adipocytes derived from mesenchymal stem cells. H3K56 is acetylated by CBP and p300, and deacetylated by SIRT1, all of which play important roles in diabetes and insulin signaling. We observed that almost half of the genome shows signs of H3K56 acetylation, with the highest levels associated with transcription factors and proteins in the adipokine signaling and Type II Diabetes pathways. To identify the transcription factors that recruit acetyltransferases and deacetylases to H3K56 acetylation sites, we analyzed DNA sequences near these regions and found an enrichment of the E2F recognition sequence. Through chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by high-throughput sequencing, we confirmed that genes bound by E2F4, HSF-1, and C/EBPα have higher levels of H3K56 acetylation than expected. We also found that the binding sites of these transcription factors and acetylation sites are often adjacent but rarely overlap. Additionally, we discovered significant differences in the bound targets of C/EBPα between 3T3-L1 and human adipocytes, emphasizing the need for species-specific epigenetic and transcription factor binding site maps. This study provides the first genome-wide profile of H3K56 acetylation, E2F4, C/EBPα, and HSF-1 binding in human adipocytes, serving as a valuable resource for understanding adipocyte transcriptional regulation.

title: Detecting and characterizing circular RNAs
text: The discovery of circular RNA transcripts dates back to the early 1990s, but our understanding of these species has been limited due to the challenges of studying them using traditional RNA analysis methods. However, recent advancements in bioinformatics, coupled with biochemical enrichment strategies and deep sequencing, have enabled comprehensive studies of circular RNA species. These studies have unveiled thousands of naturally occurring circular RNAs in mammalian cells, some of which are abundant and conserved across evolution. It is now becoming evident that certain circRNAs may play a role in regulating the function of microRNAs (miRNAs), and there are also indications of their involvement in transcriptional control. Consequently, exploring this class of noncoding RNAs holds potential implications for therapeutic and research applications. Moving forward, the primary challenge for the field will be to unravel the regulation and function of these unique molecules.

title: A classification of unstable angina revisited.
text: Unstable angina is a critical stage of coronary heart disease that presents with a wide range of symptoms and outcomes. A decade ago, a classification system based on clinical symptoms was introduced to categorize unstable angina. This system was validated through clinical studies, which showed a correlation between the classification and prognosis, as well as angiographic and histological findings. Since then, this classification has been used in numerous large clinical trials. In recent years, the role of platelet activation and inflammation in unstable angina has been better understood. As a result, improved markers of myocardial injury, acute-phase proteins, and hemostatic markers have been identified, which may be associated with clinical outcomes. Specifically, cardiac-specific troponin T and troponin I have been found to be the most reliable predictors of early risk in patients with angina at rest. Therefore, it is suggested that the original classification be expanded to include a subclassification for patients with angina at rest within the past 48 hours (class IIIB), distinguishing between troponin-positive (T(pos)) and troponin-negative (T(neg)) patients. The 30-day risk of death and myocardial infarction is estimated to be up to 20% in class IIIB-T(pos) patients, but less than 2% in class IIIB-T(neg) patients. Initial findings indicate that troponins can serve as surrogate markers for thrombus formation and effectively guide therapy with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonists or low-molecular-weight heparins. These findings support the inclusion of troponin measurement in the clinical classification and introduce a new approach to treating these high-risk patients.

title: Alcohol Intake and Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review Implementing a Mendelian Randomization Approach
text:
The relationship between alcohol consumption and hypertension has been widely studied, but there are limitations to the existing research. Observational studies can be influenced by other factors, while clinical trials are difficult to conduct and have limited follow-up time. To address these challenges, researchers have used a method called Mendelian randomization, which involves studying a specific genetic variant as a proxy for alcohol consumption. In this study, the researchers focused on a polymorphism in the ALDH2 gene, which is involved in alcohol metabolism. Individuals with the null variant of this gene experience adverse symptoms when drinking alcohol and therefore consume less alcohol than those without the variant. The researchers hypothesized that this genetic variant may influence the risk of hypertension by affecting alcohol drinking behavior. 

To test their hypothesis, the researchers conducted a meta-analysis of several studies that examined the relationship between the ALDH2 genotype and blood pressure. They found that in males, those with the *1*1 genotype (wild-type homozygotes) had a higher risk of hypertension compared to those with the *2*2 genotype (null variant homozygotes). Heterozygotes (surrogate for moderate drinkers) also had a higher risk of hypertension compared to *2*2 homozygotes. Additionally, systolic blood pressure was higher in *1*1 homozygotes and heterozygotes compared to *2*2 homozygotes. 

In conclusion, these findings provide strong evidence that alcohol intake has a significant impact on blood pressure and the risk of hypertension.

title: Rapid and Sensitive RT-QuIC Detection of Human Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease Using Cerebrospinal Fluid
text: An improved method for diagnosing Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) has been developed, allowing for faster and more accurate detection of the disease. The current method, known as real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC), takes 2.5 to 5 days and has a detection rate of 77% to 89%. The new assay, however, can identify positive samples within 4 to 14 hours and has a detection rate of 95.8%. This second-generation RT-QuIC assay greatly improves the speed and sensitivity of diagnosing CJD, a deadly and transmissible disease. The findings also have implications for other neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, as the improved method could be used to detect misfolded protein aggregates associated with these conditions.

title: Wortmannin, a phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor, selectively enhances cytotoxicity of receptor-directed-toxin chimeras in vitro and in vivo.
text:
BACKGROUND

The resistance of certain neoplastic cell lines to treatment with ligand-toxin chimeras is believed to be due to an accelerated rate of lysosomal uptake and degradation after endocytosis of the chimera-receptor complex. We hypothesized that co-exposing cells to the Pl 3-kinase inhibitor, wortmannin, could enhance the cytotoxicity of these chimeras, as Pl 3-kinase activity is known to play a role in intracellular trafficking.

METHODS

We examined the cytotoxicity of five receptor-directed toxin chimeras (bFGF-SAP, bFGF-PE, aFGF-PE, HBEGF-SAP, bFGF-gelonin) and an immunotoxin (11A8-SAP) in the presence or absence of the Pl 3-kinase inhibitor against a panel of human neoplastic cell lines: SK-MEL-5 (melanoma), PA-1 (ovarian teratocarcinoma), DU145 (prostatic carcinoma), and MCF-7 (breast carcinoma). In vivo, we evaluated the antitumor activity of a treatment regimen combining wortmannin and bFGF-SAP compared to each agent alone in mice implanted with the FSallC murine fibrosarcoma.

RESULTS

At concentrations higher than the reported Ki for Pl 3-kinase inhibition, wortmannin enhanced cytotoxicity when combined with saporin or gelonin chimeras, but had a subadditive effect when combined with Pseudomonas exotoxin chimeras. At low nanomolar concentrations selective for Pl 3-kinase inhibition, wortmannin significantly increased bFGF-SAP cytotoxicity in three out of four cell lines. However, another Pl 3-kinase inhibitor, LY294002, did not potentiate bFGF-SAP. In mice, the combination of wortmannin and bFGF-SAP resulted in a significant decrease in tumor volumes compared to controls, which was not observed with either agent alone.

CONCLUSIONS

These findings suggest that while wortmannin can enhance the cytotoxicity of certain receptor-directed chimeras, this potentiation may occur through an alternative pathway unrelated to Pl 3-kinase inhibition.

title: Chronic stress, glucocorticoid receptor resistance, inflammation, and disease risk.
text:
We propose a model that suggests chronic stress leads to resistance in glucocorticoid receptors (GCR), which in turn prevents the down-regulation of inflammatory response. To test this model, we conducted two viral-challenge studies. In study 1, we examined stressful life events, GCR, and various control variables (such as baseline antibody to the challenge virus, age, body mass index (BMI), season, race, sex, education, and virus type) in 276 healthy adult volunteers. These volunteers were then quarantined, exposed to one of two rhinoviruses, and monitored for 5 days with nasal washes to isolate the virus and assess signs/symptoms of a common cold. In study 2, we assessed the same control variables and GCR in 79 subjects who were subsequently exposed to a rhinovirus. We monitored them at baseline and for 5 days after viral challenge to measure the production of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6) in nasal secretions. 

Study 1: After accounting for the control variables, we found that individuals who had recently experienced a long-term threatening stressful event showed GCR. Furthermore, those with GCR were at a higher risk of developing a cold later on.

Study 2: Using the same control variables as in study 1, we observed that greater GCR predicted the production of more local proinflammatory cytokines among infected subjects.

These findings support our model, suggesting that prolonged stressors lead to GCR, which then disrupts the proper regulation of inflammation. Since inflammation plays a crucial role in the development and progression of various diseases, this model may have significant implications for understanding the impact of stress on overall health.

title: Pituitary Adenylate Cyclase-Activating Polypeptide (PACAP), a Neuron-Derived Peptide Regulating Glial Glutamate Transport and Metabolism
text: Glutamatergic neurotransmission in the brain is primarily terminated by the rapid uptake of released glutamate into astrocytes through specific transporters. This glutamate is then converted into glutamine by an enzyme called glutamine synthetase. Various factors have been found to modify the uptake of glutamate by these transporters. The only known condition that affects the expression of these transporters is when glia are cultured with neurons. Our study shows that neurons regulate the turnover of glutamate in glia through a substance called pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP). In the cerebral cortex, PACAP is produced by neurons and acts on a specific group of astroglia involved in glutamate turnover. When astroglia are exposed to PACAP, the uptake of glutamate is increased, and the expression of the transporters GLT-1, GLAST, and glutamine synthetase is promoted. We also found that the effects of neuron-conditioned medium on transporter expression were reduced when PACAP was blocked. Another substance called vasoactive intestinal peptide had similar effects, but at higher concentrations. This suggests that PACAP acts on glial glutamate turnover through specific receptors. The expression of GLAST was promoted by the activation of a protein called protein kinase A (PKA) by PAC1 receptors, while the expression of GLT-1 required the activation of both PKA and protein kinase C (PKC). Since there are different forms of PAC1 receptors that activate PKA and PKC to different extents, this indicates a complex mechanism by which PACAP regulates glutamate transport and metabolism in glia. Disruptions in these regulatory mechanisms could be a major cause of neurological and psychiatric disorders associated with glutamate.

title: Factors influencing B lymphopoiesis after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation.
text: The correlation between the counts of marrow B-cell precursors on days 80 and 365 and circulating B cells was observed in 93 allograft recipients, indicating that the deficiency of B cells after transplantation is partly due to inadequate B lymphopoiesis. Various factors that could impact B lymphopoiesis were examined. Patients with grade 2 to 4 acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) had at least a 4-fold decrease in the number of marrow B-cell precursors on days 30 and 80 compared to patients with grade 0 to 1 acute GVHD. Furthermore, patients with extensive chronic GVHD had an 18-fold decrease in B-cell precursors on day 365 compared to those with no or limited chronic GVHD. The number of B-cell precursors was not influenced by CD34 cell dose, type of transplant (marrow versus blood stem cells), donor age, or patient age. In conclusion, the deficiency of B cells after transplantation is partly caused by the inhibition of B lymphopoiesis due to GVHD and/or its treatment.

title: Genetic variants rs1994016 and rs3825807 in ADAMTS7 affect its mRNA expression in atherosclerotic occlusive peripheral arterial disease
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between ADAMTS7 expression and peripheral artery disease (PAD) in Turkish patients. The study also aimed to evaluate the association between matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) levels and PAD development. The researchers used various methods, including reverse transcription quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blot, to determine ADAMTS7 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). They also analyzed the frequency of ADAMTS7 rs1994016 and rs3825807 polymorphisms using real-time PCR. Additionally, plasma levels of nine MMPs were measured using a multiplex immunoassay system. 

The results showed that ADAMTS7 mRNA levels were significantly higher in PAD patients compared to healthy controls. However, there was no significant difference in the frequencies of the rs1994016 and rs3825807 variants between the two groups. In PAD patients, ADAMTS7 mRNA levels were significantly increased for specific genotypes of rs1994016 and rs3825807. Furthermore, plasma levels of several MMPs were significantly higher in PAD patients compared to controls. 

In conclusion, this study provides the first evidence of a relationship between ADAMTS7 expression and PAD, as well as the impact of specific genetic variants on PAD development. The findings suggest that ADAMTS7 may play a role in the development of PAD.

title: Distinct Parietal and Temporal Pathways to the Homologues of Broca's Area in the Monkey
text: The homologous counterparts of the two distinct architectonic areas 44 and 45, which make up the anterior language zone (known as Broca's region) in the ventrolateral frontal lobe of humans, have recently been identified in macaque monkeys. While we know that the inferior parietal lobule and the lateral temporal cortical region project to the ventrolateral frontal cortex, it is unclear which specific cortical areas in those regions project to the homologues of Broca's region in macaque monkeys, and through which white matter pathways. To investigate this, we utilized the autoradiographic method, which allows us to determine the cortical area where axons originate (injection site), the precise path they take in the white matter, and where they terminate within specific cortical areas. We examined the connections between the parietal and temporal regions with area 44 and the two subdivisions of area 45 (45A and 45B). Our results revealed a ventral temporo-frontal pathway consisting of fibers originating from various auditory, multisensory, and visual association cortical areas in the intermediate superolateral temporal region. These axons travel through the extreme capsule and primarily target area 45, with a lesser termination in area 44. In contrast, a dorsal pathway of axons originating from different cortical areas in the inferior parietal lobule and the adjacent caudal superior temporal sulcus was found to target both areas 44 and 45. These axons travel through the superior longitudinal fasciculus, with some axons originating from the ventral inferior parietal lobule and the adjacent superior temporal sulcus forming a simple arcuate fasciculus. The cortex in the most anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule is specifically connected to the ventral premotor cortex (ventral area 6), which controls the orofacial musculature. The cortex in the intermediate part of the inferior parietal lobule is connected to both areas 44 and 45. These findings provide insight into the posterior parietal and temporal connections of the ventrolateral frontal areas, which in the left hemisphere of the human brain are involved in various aspects of language production. These precursor circuits, present in nonlinguistic, nonhuman primate brains, also exist in the human brain. We discuss possible reasons why these areas have been adapted for language use in the human brain. These results shed new light on the prelinguistic precursor circuitry of Broca's region and enhance our understanding of the functional interactions between Broca's ventrolateral frontal region and the posterior parietal and temporal association areas.

title: MIRA-seq for DNA methylation analysis of CpG islands
text:
Objective: Our aim is to develop a dependable technique for analyzing DNA methylation across the entire genome.

Materials and Methods: The analysis of DNA methylation on a genome-wide scale involves various approaches, including the use of methyl-CpG-binding proteins for enrichment. One such method, called the methylated-CpG island recovery assay (MIRA), relies on the strong affinity of the MBD2b-MBD3L1 complex for CpG-methylated DNA. In this study, we provide a comprehensive description of the MIRA technique and combine it with next-generation sequencing platforms (MIRA-seq).

Results: We evaluated the performance of MIRA-seq and compared the obtained data with whole genome bisulfite sequencing.

Conclusion: MIRA-seq proves to be a reliable platform for analyzing DNA methylation on a genome-wide scale, particularly in CpG-rich genomic regions. This method is not constrained by primer or probe design and is cost-effective.

title: How many images are in an auditory scene?
text: The auditory system's ability to process sound sources in a spatially separated auditory scene was investigated in a series of experiments. Experiment I focused on localizing speech sources on the azimuth plane. Participants were presented with different words played from multiple loudspeakers and were asked to report the total number of sound sources and their individual locations. In Experiment II, the accuracy of localizing one speech source in a mixture of multiple speech sources was examined. An extra sound source was introduced, and participants had to identify its location. Experiment III replicated the setup and task of Experiment I, but with tones instead of speech sounds. The results revealed that listeners could perceive a maximum of approximately four spatially separated speech signals and three tonal signals. As the total number of sound sources increased, localization errors also increased. When there were already four or more speech sources present, participants struggled to accurately localize an additional source, performing at chance levels.

title: Mobilization of intracellular copper stores by the ctr2 vacuolar copper transporter.
text: Copper plays a crucial role in various processes, such as signaling to transcription and protein trafficking machinery, oxidative phosphorylation, iron mobilization, neuropeptide maturation, and normal development. While we have a good understanding of how cells mobilize ions like calcium within the cell, there is limited information on how eukaryotic cells mobilize their intracellular copper stores. In this study, we present a mechanism by which the Ctr2 protein in Saccharomyces cerevisiae facilitates the release of bioavailable copper from intracellular stores. Although Ctr2 shares structural similarities with the Ctr1 plasma membrane copper importer, our microscopic and biochemical fractionation studies reveal that Ctr2 is localized to the vacuole membrane. We demonstrate that Ctr2 mobilizes copper stored in the vacuole, and this process relies on specific amino acid residues that are conserved in both the Ctr1 and Ctr2 copper transport family. Mutants lacking Ctr2 (ctr2 Delta mutants) accumulate excessive amounts of copper in the vacuole. Additionally, we find that a mutant form of Ctr2, which is mislocalized to the plasma membrane, enhances the uptake of copper from the extracellular environment, providing further evidence for the direct involvement of Ctr2 in copper transport across membranes. These findings uncover a new mechanism for copper mobilization and suggest that organisms utilize intracellular vesicular stores to cope with copper deprivation.

title: Peroxisomes Are Signaling Platforms for Antiviral Innate Immunity
text: The role of peroxisomes in regulating metabolic activities in mammalian cells has long been recognized. These organelles work together with mitochondria to control the metabolism of lipids and reactive oxygen species. However, while mitochondria have been identified as a key player in antiviral signal transduction, the involvement of peroxisomes in immune defense remains unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) adaptor protein MAVS is present on both peroxisomes and mitochondria. Our findings reveal that peroxisomal and mitochondrial MAVS function sequentially to establish an antiviral state in cells. Upon viral infection, peroxisomal MAVS triggers the rapid expression of defense factors, providing short-term protection. Subsequently, mitochondrial MAVS activates a signaling pathway that is dependent on interferon, with a delayed response, to enhance and stabilize the antiviral defense. The interferon regulatory factor IRF1 plays a critical role in regulating MAVS-dependent signaling from peroxisomes. These results highlight the significance of peroxisomes as a crucial site for antiviral signal transduction.

title: Two-sided confidence intervals for the single proportion: comparison of seven methods. Stat. Med
text:
The current methods for estimating proportions using simple intervals have been found to have poor coverage and can result in intervals that are clearly inappropriate. When evaluating different methods, it is important to consider certain criteria. These criteria include how close the achieved coverage probability is to its expected value, whether the intervals are too close or too far from the middle of the scale, the expected width of the intervals, avoiding any abnormalities such as limits outside the range of 0 to 1 or intervals with zero width, and the ease of use, whether through tables, software, or formulas.

To assess these criteria, seven methods for estimating a single proportion were evaluated using 96,000 different parameter space points. Based on the evaluation, it is recommended to use intervals that are based on tail areas and the simpler score methods. In both cases, there are methods available that aim to align either the minimum or the mean coverage with the expected value of 1 - alpha.

title: Nuclear accumulation of HDAC4 in ATM deficiency promotes neurodegeneration in ataxia-telangiectasia
text: The mutation of the Atm gene causes a neurodegenerative disease known as ataxia telangiectasia. Our study reveals that the deficiency of ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) leads to the accumulation of histone deacetylase 4 (HDAC4) in the nucleus of neurons, resulting in neurodegeneration. Nuclear HDAC4 binds to chromatin, as well as myocyte enhancer factor 2A (MEF2A) and cAMP-responsive element binding protein (CREB), causing histone deacetylation and changes in neuronal gene expression. By inhibiting HDAC4 activity or preventing its nuclear accumulation, we can mitigate these neurodegenerative effects and alleviate various behavioral abnormalities in ATM-deficient mice. However, complete rescue of neurodegeneration requires the presence of HDAC4 in the cytoplasm, indicating that the ataxia telangiectasia phenotype arises from both the loss of cytoplasmic HDAC4 and its nuclear accumulation. To remain in the cytoplasm, HDAC4 must undergo phosphorylation. The phosphorylation of HDAC4 is regulated by protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), which is downregulated by ATM-mediated phosphorylation. In ATM deficiency, increased PP2A activity leads to the dephosphorylation of HDAC4 and its subsequent accumulation in the nucleus. Our findings highlight the critical role of HDAC4's cellular localization in the development of ataxia telangiectasia neurodegeneration.

title: Regulation and function of the E-cadherin/catenin complex in cells of the monocyte-macrophage lineage and DCs.
text: E-cadherin is primarily known as a protein found in adherens junctions, which helps maintain the integrity of the epithelial barrier. Within epithelial cells, the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin forms a complex with catenins and plays a role in various intracellular signaling pathways, such as Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, Rho GTPase, and NF-κB signaling. Recent advancements have revealed a new and crucial function of this adhesion molecule in mononuclear phagocyte activities. E-cadherin controls the maturation and movement of Langerhans cells, and its binding prevents bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DCs) from entering a tolerogenic state. In this regard, the activity of β-catenin may play a key role in determining the balance between the immunogenic and tolerogenic properties of DCs both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. The fusion of alternatively activated macrophages and osteoclasts also relies on E-cadherin. Furthermore, the ligands CD103 and KLRG1, which bind to E-cadherin, are expressed on subsets of DCs, T cells, and NK cells, and contribute to their interaction with DCs and macrophages that express E-cadherin. In this article, we will discuss the regulation, function, and implications of E-cadherin expression in these crucial regulators of the immune system.

title: Polymorphism and ligand dependent changes in human glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) function: allosteric rescue of loss of function mutation.
text:
The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) is an important regulator of insulin secretion and a major target for treating type II diabetes. However, the regulation of GLP-1R function is complex, involving various endogenous peptides that interact with the receptor. These peptides include full-length (1-37) and truncated (7-37) forms of GLP-1, which can exist in an amidated form (GLP-1(1-36)NH₂ and GLP-1(7-36)NH₂), as well as the related peptide oxyntomodulin. Additionally, the GLP-1R can be activated by exogenous agonists like exendin-4 and the allosteric modulator compound 2 (6,7-dichloro-2-methylsulfonyl-3-tert-butylaminoquinoxaline). The complexity of this ligand-receptor system is further complicated by the presence of several single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across the receptor.

In this study, we investigated 10 GLP-1R SNPs and characterized their effects on three physiologically relevant signaling pathways: cAMP accumulation, extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 phosphorylation, and intracellular Ca²⁺ mobilization. We also examined ligand binding and cell surface receptor expression. Our findings revealed both ligand- and pathway-specific effects for multiple SNPs, with the most significant impact observed in the Met¹⁴⁹ receptor variant. At this variant, there was a selective loss of peptide-induced responses across all pathways tested, but the response to compound 2 remained intact. In contrast, at the Cys³³³ variant, peptide responses were preserved, but the response to compound 2 was attenuated. Interestingly, we discovered that the loss of peptide function in the Met¹⁴⁹ receptor variant could be rescued by compound 2 through allosteric modulation. This provides proof-of-principle evidence that allosteric drugs could potentially be used to treat patients with this loss of function variant.

title: Neuronal circuitry mechanism regulating adult quiescent neural stem cell fate decision
text: Adult neurogenesis originates from neural stem cells located in specialized niches. The process of adult neurogenesis, including neural progenitor proliferation, new neuron maturation, synaptic integration, and survival, is regulated by neuronal activity and experience within these niches. However, it is currently unclear whether local neuronal circuitry directly affects adult neural stem cells. In this study, we demonstrate that nestin-expressing radial glia-like quiescent neural stem cells (RGLs) in the adult mouse hippocampus respond to the neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) through γ2-subunit-containing GABAA receptors. By analyzing individual RGLs, we observed that conditional deletion of γ2 leads to a rapid exit from quiescence and increased symmetrical self-renewal. RGLs are located near terminals expressing 67-kDa glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67) of parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons and respond to GABA released from these neurons. Functionally, controlling the activity of dentate PV+ interneurons using optogenetics determines whether RGLs remain quiescent or become activated. Interestingly, activation of PV+ interneurons restores RGL quiescence after social isolation, an experience that typically activates RGLs and induces symmetrical division. This study uncovers a trio of niche cells, signals, and receptors, as well as a local circuitry mechanism, that govern the activation and self-renewal of quiescent adult neural stem cells in response to neuronal activity and experience.

title: Global vitamin D levels in relation to age, gender, skin pigmentation and latitude: an ecologic meta-regression analysis
text: We conducted a comprehensive analysis of cross-sectional studies from around the world to examine the status of serum 25(OH)D. On average, the levels of serum 25(OH)D were found to be 54 nmol/l. Interestingly, women had slightly higher levels than men, and Caucasians had higher levels than non-Caucasians. Surprisingly, there was no clear trend in serum 25(OH)D levels with latitude. Vitamin D deficiency was found to be prevalent globally. Our study focused on assessing the vitamin D status, specifically measured as serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D [25(OH)D], in individuals from various regions. We conducted a meta-analysis and meta-regression using data from studies retrieved from Pubmed, Embase, and Web of Science. The search terms used were "serum," "25-hydroxy-vitamin D," "cholecalciferol," and "human." A total of 394 studies were included in our analysis. The mean level of 25(OH)D was determined to be 54 nmol/l (95% CI: 52–57 nmol/l). We observed that women had slightly higher levels of 25(OH)D compared to men, and Caucasians had higher levels compared to non-Caucasians. Additionally, individuals aged over 15 years had higher levels of 25(OH)D compared to younger individuals. When considering latitude, we found that there was no significant decrease in 25(OH)D levels. However, when analyzing Caucasians separately, we observed a significant decline in 25(OH)D levels with increasing latitude. This decline was not observed in non-Caucasians. After adjusting for age, gender, and ethnicity, we found no overall correlation between 25(OH)D levels and latitude. In conclusion, our findings suggest that there is no overall influence of latitude on 25(OH)D levels. However, when considering different ethnic groups separately, we observed a decrease in 25(OH)D levels with latitude in Caucasians but not in non-Caucasians. Furthermore, our study highlights the widespread presence of vitamin D insufficiency globally, which is below the proposed threshold levels.

title: Identification and characterization of a novel monocyte/macrophage differentiation-dependent gene that is responsive to lipopolysaccharide, ceramide, and lysophosphatidylcholine.
text: We have discovered a novel cDNA called DIF-2 that is dependent on differentiation. It was isolated from human mononuclear phagocytes using differential display. The full-length cDNA was cloned and its sequence determined. DIF-2 is made up of 156 amino acids and is predicted to have an isoelectric point of 8.84. The mRNA for DIF-2 is expressed in freshly isolated monocytes but is significantly reduced when monocytes undergo differentiation. We also observed a similar decrease in mRNA expression in normal hepatocytes compared to undifferentiated HepG2 cells. The expression of DIF-2 in monocytes is influenced by lipopolysaccharide and ceramide, both of which greatly increase DIF-2 transcription. Lysophosphatidylcholine, on the other hand, only slightly upregulates DIF-2 expression. We previously found a similar gene to DIF-2 in mouse fibroblasts, which was shown to be an immediate early gene induced by serum growth factors. Our findings suggest that DIF-2 is a gene that is regulated during differentiation processes and is highly responsive to lipopolysaccharide, ceramide, and lysophosphatidylcholine.

title: A Novel 3-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase That Regulates Reproductive Development and Longevity
text: Animal longevity can be influenced by endogenous small molecule metabolites, which are now being recognized as a novel approach to improve health and extend lifespan. In the nematode C. elegans, a group of bile acid-like steroids called dafachronic acids (DAs) play a crucial role in regulating developmental timing and longevity. This regulation is mediated by a nuclear hormone receptor called DAF-12, which is similar to sterol-regulated receptors LXR and FXR found in mammals. By employing metabolic genetics, mass spectrometry, and biochemical techniques, we have discovered new aspects of DA biosynthesis and identified a conserved enzyme called DHS-16, which acts as a 3-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. DHS-16 controls the production of DAs, thereby influencing DAF-12 activity and ultimately determining longevity in response to signals from the gonad. Our investigation into the bile acid biosynthetic pathways in C. elegans not only uncovers the potential for new ligands, but also highlights the remarkable biochemical similarities to other animals. This knowledge could pave the way for the development of innovative strategies to manipulate longevity in various organisms.

title: An Argonaute transports siRNAs from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
text: Ribonucleoprotein complexes composed of proteins similar to Argonaute and small regulatory RNAs play a crucial role in various biological processes. It is predicted that many of these small regulatory RNAs function within the nucleus. To investigate the factors essential for RNA interference (RNAi) in the nuclei of Caenorhabditis elegans, we conducted a genetic screen and identified the Argonaute protein NRDE-3. In the absence of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), NRDE-3 is located in the cytoplasm. However, when siRNAs are produced by RNA-dependent RNA polymerases from messenger RNA templates in the cytoplasm, NRDE-3 binds to them and relocates to the nucleus. This relocation to the nucleus is dependent on a functional nuclear localization signal and is crucial for nuclear RNAi. As a result, NRDE-3 associates with nascent transcripts localized in the nucleus. Therefore, specific Argonaute proteins have the ability to transport specific types of small regulatory RNAs to different cellular compartments in order to regulate gene expression.

title: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-Bisphosphate Functions as a Second Messenger that Regulates Cytoskeleton–Plasma Membrane Adhesion
text: The interaction between the plasma membrane and the cytoskeleton plays a crucial role in determining various cell functions, including cell shape, formation of cell processes, cell movement, and endocytosis. In this study, we utilized optical tweezers tether force measurements to investigate the role of plasma membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) as a second messenger in regulating the adhesion energy between the cytoskeleton and the plasma membrane. We found that receptor stimuli that hydrolyze PIP2 resulted in a decrease in adhesion energy. This effect could be replicated by expressing PH domains that sequester PIP2 or by targeting a 5'-PIP2-phosphatase to the plasma membrane to selectively reduce plasma membrane PIP2 concentration. Our findings suggest that plasma membrane PIP2 plays a crucial role in controlling dynamic membrane functions and cell shape by modulating the adhesion between the actin-based cortical cytoskeleton and the plasma membrane at a local level.

title: Tissue-resident memory T cells: local specialists in immune defence
text: The role of T cells in defending against infection and cancer is crucial. The ability of memory T cells to move throughout the body is essential for providing immune protection. However, research has shown that certain memory T cells specialize in specific tissues, which enhances regional immunity. In recent years, there has been significant progress in understanding the development and function of tissue-resident T cells. This knowledge has the potential to impact the design of vaccines for improved protective immunity. This review explores the advancements and emerging concepts in this field, summarizing what is currently known about the differentiation and protective functions of tissue-resident memory T cells in various body tissues. Additionally, it highlights important unanswered questions.

title: Defective replication stress response inhibits lymphomagenesis and impairs lymphocyte reconstitution
text:
Cancer is known to be caused by DNA replication stress, which leads to genome instability. However, the role of the replication stress response in the development of cancer is still not fully understood. One protein involved in this response, called SMARCAL1, helps stabilize DNA replication forks and prevents them from collapsing, which can cause DNA breaks and cell death. Although the functions of SMARCAL1 in fork regression and remodeling have been studied, its exact role in replication stress and cancer in living organisms is unclear.

To investigate this further, we conducted a study using a mouse model of T-cell lymphoma induced by gamma radiation (IR)-induced replication stress. We found that mice lacking one or both alleles of the Smarcal1 gene had a significant reduction in the development of lymphomas. Interestingly, a quarter of the Smarcal1-deficient mice did not develop tumors at all. Furthermore, we observed that hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) and developing thymocytes in these mice had increased DNA damage and cell death during the period of rapid cell proliferation following IR exposure. Additionally, the ability of these cells to repopulate the thymus after IR was impaired. Moreover, when challenged with other replication stress stimuli, mice lacking Smarcal1 showed significant defects in HSPC function.

Based on these findings, we conclude that the DNA replication stress response, particularly the role of Smarcal1, is crucial for the survival of hematopoietic cells and the development of tumors. Our results also shed light on the immunodeficiency observed in individuals with mutations in the SMARCAL1 gene, suggesting that it may be due to a defect in HSPCs.

title: Human DNA methylomes at base resolution show widespread epigenomic differences
text:
The modification of DNA cytosine methylation is a crucial epigenetic process that plays a vital role in various cellular functions, such as genome regulation, development, and disease. In this study, we present the first comprehensive maps of methylated cytosines in a mammalian genome, with high resolution at the single-base level. These maps were generated using human embryonic stem cells and fetal fibroblasts. Additionally, we conducted a comparative analysis of messenger RNA and small RNA components of the transcriptome, various histone modifications, and DNA-protein interaction sites for key regulatory factors.

Our findings revealed significant differences in the composition and patterns of cytosine methylation between the two genomes. Interestingly, we discovered that nearly one-quarter of all methylation observed in embryonic stem cells occurred in a non-CG context. This suggests that embryonic stem cells may employ distinct methylation mechanisms to regulate gene expression. Furthermore, we observed that non-CG methylation was predominantly located within gene bodies, while being scarce in protein binding sites and enhancers. Upon induced differentiation of embryonic stem cells, non-CG methylation disappeared, but it was restored in induced pluripotent stem cells.

Moreover, we identified numerous regions with differential methylation near genes involved in pluripotency and differentiation. Additionally, we observed widespread reduction in methylation levels in fibroblasts, which correlated with lower transcriptional activity. These reference epigenomes serve as a valuable resource for future investigations into the role of this crucial epigenetic modification in human development and disease.

title: Laparoscopic adhesiolysis in patients with chronic abdominal pain: a blinded randomised controlled multi-centre trial.
text:
The effectiveness of laparoscopic adhesiolysis for chronic abdominal pain is a topic of debate and lacks evidence-based support. Our objective was to test the hypothesis that laparoscopic adhesiolysis provides significant pain relief and improves the quality of life for patients with adhesions and chronic abdominal pain. 

Patients who experienced chronic abdominal pain attributed to adhesions underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, ruling out other potential causes for their pain. If adhesions were confirmed during the procedure, patients were randomly assigned to either receive laparoscopic adhesiolysis or no treatment. The treatment allocation was concealed from patients, and assessors were unaware of the patients' treatment and outcomes. Pain levels were assessed for one year using visual analogue score (VAS), pain change score, analgesic usage, and quality of life score. The analysis was conducted based on the intention to treat. 

Out of the 116 patients enrolled for diagnostic laparoscopy, 100 were randomly assigned to either laparoscopic adhesiolysis (52) or no treatment (48). Both groups experienced substantial pain relief and a significant improvement in quality of life. However, there was no significant difference between the two groups (mean change from baseline of VAS score at 12 months: difference of 3 points, p=0.53; 95% CI -7 to 13). 

In conclusion, although laparoscopic adhesiolysis provides relief for chronic abdominal pain, it does not offer any additional benefits compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. Therefore, laparoscopic adhesiolysis cannot be recommended as a treatment for adhesions in patients with chronic abdominal pain.

title: Insulin Signaling and Dietary Restriction Differentially Influence the Decline of Learning and Memory with Age
text: Memory loss is a devastating consequence of aging. Although there are known factors that can increase lifespan, their impact on learning and memory remains uncertain. In this study, we investigated the effects of a mutant gene called daf-2, which is associated with the Insulin/IGF-1 receptor in the worm species C. elegans. Surprisingly, we found that daf-2 mutants showed improved memory performance in early adulthood and maintained their ability to learn better as they aged. However, there was no extension in long-term memory with age. On the other hand, eat-2 mutants, which are a model of Dietary Restriction (DR), had impaired long-term memory in young adulthood but maintained this level of memory for a longer period as they aged. We also discovered that a gene called crh-1, which is similar to the CREB transcription factor in C. elegans, is necessary for long-term associative memory but not for learning or short-term memory. The expression of crh-1 decreased with age and differed in the longevity mutants. Additionally, the expression and activity of CREB were correlated with memory performance. These findings suggest that specific treatments for increasing lifespan have both immediate and long-term effects on cognitive functions that decline with age, by regulating genes that are crucial for learning and memory.

title: Unique response pathways are established by allosteric interactions among nuclear hormone receptors
text: Eukaryotic transcription factors often form heterodimers, where the 9-cis retinoic acid receptor (RXR) is a common partner for various nuclear receptors such as the thyroid hormone receptor (T3R) and retinoic acid receptor (RAR). This raises the question of whether these complexes have dual hormonal responsiveness. To investigate this, we developed a method to study the transcriptional properties of each receptor individually or when bound to a heterodimeric partner. Our results show that the binding properties of RXR are hidden in T3R-RXR and RAR-RXR heterodimers. However, RXR acts as an active cofactor without binding to DNA when paired with the NGFI-B/Nurr1 orphan receptors. The heterodimerization of RXR with constitutively active NGFI-B/Nurr1 forms a new hormone-dependent complex. These findings suggest that allosteric interactions between heterodimers create complexes with distinct characteristics. We propose that allostery plays a crucial role in generating diversity in hormone response networks.

title: Midlife and Late‐Life Vascular Risk Factors and White Matter Microstructural Integrity: The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study
text:
BACKGROUND: Diffusion tensor imaging is a method used to measure the integrity of white matter in the brain. It has been found that this method can detect white matter injury earlier than the presence of white matter hyperintensities. However, the factors that contribute to poor white matter integrity have not been established. In this study, we aimed to quantify the association between vascular risk factors in midlife and late life with measures of late-life white matter integrity.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We analyzed data from 1851 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study (ARIC) who underwent 3-T magnetic resonance imaging, including diffusion tensor imaging. These participants were part of the ARIC Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). We examined the association between lipids, glucose, and blood pressure measured during the baseline ARIC visit (1987-1989, ages 44-65, midlife) and visit 5 of ARIC (2011-2013, ages 67-90, late life, concurrent with ARIC-NCS) with measures of white matter integrity obtained at visit 5. We also investigated whether these associations were influenced by the presence of white matter hyperintensities. Our findings revealed that elevated blood pressure in both midlife and late life, as well as elevated glucose in midlife (but not late life), were associated with worse white matter integrity in late life. These associations were independent of the degree of white matter hyperintensity, and the association between glucose and white matter integrity appeared to be stronger in individuals with less white matter hyperintensity. However, there was limited evidence supporting an adverse association between lipids and white matter integrity.

CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that hypertension in both midlife and late life, as well as elevated glucose in midlife, are related to poorer white matter integrity in late life. These findings highlight the importance of managing vascular risk factors to preserve white matter integrity in older adults.

title: KRAS gene amplification and overexpression but not mutation associates with aggressive and metastatic endometrial cancer
text:
BACKGROUND: The majority of endometrial carcinomas are treated early on, but a significant percentage of patients experience recurrence with limited response to systemic therapies. While KRAS mutations have been implicated in tumorigenesis for various human cancers, their clinical relevance in endometrial carcinomas remains poorly understood.

METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive analysis of genome-wide expression, focusing on KRAS mutations and copy-number alterations, in primary and metastatic endometrial carcinoma lesions. This analysis was correlated with clinical and histopathological data. Two sets of samples were used: a primary investigation set consisting of 414 primary tumors, and a clinical validation set consisting of 61 metastatic lesions.

RESULTS: We found that amplification and gain of KRAS were present in 3% of primary lesions and 18% of metastatic lesions, and were significantly associated with poor outcomes, advanced disease stage, non-endometrioid subtype, high grade, aneuploidy, receptor loss, and high levels of KRAS mRNA. These alterations were also associated with an aggressive phenotype. In contrast, KRAS mutations were present in 14.7% of primary lesions but did not increase in metastatic lesions. KRAS mutations did not influence outcome but were significantly associated with the endometrioid subtype, low grade, and obesity.

CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that KRAS amplification and KRAS mRNA expression, both of which increase from primary to metastatic lesions, play a role in the progression of endometrial carcinoma.

title: Hyperhomocysteinemia and atherosclerotic vascular disease: pathophysiology, screening, and treatment. off.
text: Recent research has identified hyperhomocysteinemia as a significant risk factor for atherosclerotic vascular disease. This article aims to provide an overview of homocysteine metabolism, the causes of hyperhomocysteinemia, the pathophysiological findings associated with this disorder, and the results of epidemiological studies on homocysteine and vascular disease. It is recommended that individuals at high risk for vascular disease or those with abnormalities in homocysteine metabolism should undergo screening for hyperhomocysteinemia. For primary prevention of vascular disease, treatment should be considered for patients with homocysteine levels of 14 micromol/L or higher. For secondary prevention, treatment should be considered for patients with homocysteine levels of 11 micromol/L or higher. The most convenient form of treatment is a folic acid supplement (400-1000 microg) along with a high-potency multivitamin containing at least 400 microg of folate. Some patients may require higher doses of folic acid and cyanocobalamin supplements. While awaiting prospective clinical trial data, these conservative recommendations offer a safe, effective, and evidence-based approach to diagnosing, evaluating, and managing patients with hyperhomocysteinemia.

title: Best--worst scaling: What it can do for health care research and how to do it.
text: Comparisons of utility parameters from a traditional discrete choice experiment (DCE) cannot provide support or refutation for statements like "quality of care is more highly valued than waiting time." To address this limitation, best-worst scaling is employed as it presents respondents with a different choice task. However, despite a general understanding of the best-worst task, there are several design and analysis issues in conducting a best-worst choice experiment that need further explanation. This paper showcases the aggregation and analysis of such data and, through a quality of life pilot study, demonstrates how best-worst tasks can provide deeper insights.

title: Genetic variants and non-genetic factors predict circulating vitamin D levels in Hispanic and non-Hispanic White women: the Breast Cancer Health Disparities Study.
text:
In European populations, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified common genetic variations in or near the GC, CYP2R1, CYP24A1, and NADSYN1/DHCR7 genes that are linked to levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] in the bloodstream. To validate these findings, we investigated six specific genetic variations from these regions and their correlation with 25(OH)D levels in 1,605 Hispanic women (629 U.S. Hispanics and 976 Mexicans) and 354 non-Hispanic White (NHW) women. We also examined the potential interactions between these variations and established non-genetic predictors of 25(OH)D levels, such as body mass index (BMI), sunlight exposure, and vitamin D intake from diet and supplements. 

In both Hispanic and NHW women, the minor alleles of two GC variations (rs7041 and rs2282679) were significantly associated with lower 25(OH)D levels. The CYP2R1 variation, rs2060793, also showed a significant association with 25(OH)D levels in both groups. However, we did not find any significant associations for the variations in the CYP24A1 gene. Among Hispanic controls, 25(OH)D levels were significantly linked to the rs12785878T and rs1790349G haplotype in the NADSYN1/DHCR7 region. We observed significant interactions between the GC rs2282679 variation and BMI, as well as between rs12785878 and time spent in outdoor activities. 

These findings provide additional evidence for the role of common genetic variations in determining individual differences in circulating 25(OH)D levels. The interactions between these variations and non-genetic factors should be further investigated for confirmation.

title: Generation and characterization of methyl-lysine histone antibodies.
text: This chapter provides a summary of the creation and characterization of rabbit polyclonal antibodies called histone, which target the methylated H3-K9 position. It includes protocols for designing peptides, immunizing rabbits, and conducting quality controls for methyl-lysine histone antibodies. The antibodies are then used to study inter- and metaphase chromatin in wild-type and mutant mouse cells lacking the Suv39h histone methyltransferases. Histone amino-termini, which extend from the nucleosome core, undergo various post-translational modifications such as acetylation, phosphorylation, methylation, ubiquitination, and ADP-ribosylation. In addition to their structural roles, histones also play a crucial role in gene expression regulation by controlling access to the nucleosomal template. The development of high-quality methyl-lysine histone antibodies can serve as valuable tools for deciphering epigenetic information encoded by specific methylation patterns on lysine residues in histone amino-termini. A comparative analysis reveals significant variations in the specificity and affinity of available methyl-lysine histone antibodies, emphasizing the importance of thorough quality controls to ensure accurate interpretation of experimental data despite the intricate nature of histone lysine methylation.

title: The Hallmarks of Aging
text: The process of aging is characterized by a gradual decline in the body's ability to function properly, making individuals more susceptible to illness and death. This deterioration is the main factor contributing to major diseases such as cancer, diabetes, heart problems, and neurodegenerative disorders. In recent years, there has been significant progress in aging research, particularly in understanding that genetic pathways and biochemical processes play a role in determining the rate at which we age. This review identifies nine common characteristics of aging, known as hallmarks, which are observed in various organisms, with a focus on mammals. These hallmarks include genomic instability, telomere attrition, changes in gene expression patterns, disruption of protein balance, impaired nutrient sensing, malfunctioning mitochondria, cellular senescence, depletion of stem cells, and altered communication between cells. The challenge now is to understand how these hallmarks are interconnected and their individual contributions to the aging process. The ultimate goal is to identify potential targets for pharmaceutical interventions that can improve human health during aging, while minimizing any negative side effects.

title: A sensitive mass spectrometry platform identifies metabolic changes of life history traits in C. elegans
text: The aging process is characterized by abnormal nutrient metabolism, and researchers are rapidly uncovering the genetic and nutritional factors involved, using the model organism C. elegans. However, the specific metabolic effects of changes in the life history of C. elegans are still not fully understood. To address this, we developed and validated a highly sensitive mass spectrometry platform for identifying major classes of metabolites in worms. Using this platform, we detected over 600 metabolites in a sample of 2500 worms and observed significant changes in fatty acids, amino acids, and phospholipids throughout the life cycle of the worms, independent of their germ-line. We also found that worms experienced a significant shift in lipid metabolism after reaching adulthood, which was partially controlled by the metabolic regulator AAK-2/AMPK. Most amino acids peaked during development, except for aspartic acid and glycine, which accumulated in aged worms. Additionally, dietary interventions had a specific impact on the metabolite profiles of the worms, depending on the class of metabolite. Overall, these mass spectrometry-based methods provide powerful tools for studying the metabolomics of aging and metabolism in C. elegans.

title: Characterisation of antibiotic prescriptions for acute respiratory tract infections in Danish general practice: a retrospective registry based cohort study
text:
The inappropriate use of antibiotics is contributing to the increasing rates of antimicrobial resistance. In an effort to promote rational prescribing of antibiotics for acute respiratory tract infections in general practice, several Danish guidelines have been issued. However, it is unclear if these recommendations are being followed. To gain a better understanding of the pattern of antibiotic prescriptions for patients with acute respiratory tract infections, we analyzed electronic prescriptions from Danish general practice that were labeled with clinical indications.

Between July 2012 and June 2013, there were 456,532 antibiotic prescriptions issued for acute respiratory tract infections. The most common indication was pneumonia, accounting for 39% of prescriptions, followed by acute tonsillitis (21%) and acute otitis media (19%). Penicillin V was the most commonly prescribed antibiotic, making up 58% of all prescriptions, followed by macrolides (18%) and amoxicillin (15%). As age increased, the use of second-line agents also increased for all indications, with these agents comprising over 40% of prescriptions for patients over 75 years old. Additionally, women were more likely to be prescribed antibiotics regardless of clinical indication.

This study is the first in Denmark to analyze antibiotic prescription patterns for acute respiratory tract infections using data linkage of clinical indications. The findings confirm that penicillin V is the most commonly prescribed antibiotic for these infections in Danish general practice. However, there is an overuse of second-line agents such as macrolides and amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid. Strategies to improve the quality of antibiotic prescribing, particularly for pneumonia, acute otitis media, and acute rhinosinusitis, are necessary.

It is crucial to adhere to guidelines for prescribing antibiotics for different respiratory tract infections in Danish general practice. The overuse of antibiotics, especially second-line agents like amoxicillin, contributes to resistance and may lead to a scenario where antibiotics are no longer effective. The extent of overuse for different infections is not clear and further analysis of prescriptions from out-of-hours clinics is needed.

title: Lack of Skeletal Muscle IL-6 Affects Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Activity at Rest and during Prolonged Exercise
text: The role of Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) in regulating the use of substrates in skeletal muscle is crucial. During exercise, IL-6 is produced in skeletal muscle in a duration-dependent manner. It has been observed that IL-6 increases the oxidation of fatty acids in the whole body, enhances glucose uptake in muscle, and decreases PDHa activity in fed mice. This study aimed to investigate whether IL-6 in muscle contributes to the regulation of PDH during exercise. Skeletal muscle-specific IL-6 knockout (IL-6 MKO) mice and control mice completed a single session of treadmill exercise for 10, 60, or 120 minutes, with rested mice of each genotype serving as controls. The respiratory exchange ratio (RER) was higher in IL-6 MKO mice compared to control mice during the 120 minutes of exercise. However, RER decreased during exercise regardless of genotype.
