title: Cholesteryl Ester Transfer Protein (CETP) Polymorphisms Affect mRNA Splicing, HDL Levels, and Sex-Dependent Cardiovascular Risk
text: Polymorphisms in and around the CETP gene have been linked to HDL levels, risk for coronary artery disease (CAD), and response to treatment. However, the exact mechanism of action of these polymorphisms is still unknown. To investigate this, we analyzed mRNA allelic expression and splice isoform measurements in human liver tissues. We found that certain genetic variants located upstream of the transcription start site were strongly associated with CETP mRNA expression ratios in 56 human livers. Additionally, we discovered a common CETP isoform that lacked exon 9 (Δ9) and inhibited CETP secretion in a dominant-negative manner. The expression of this isoform varied among individuals, ranging from 10 to 48% of total CETP mRNA in 94 livers. The increased formation of this isoform was specifically linked to an exon 9 polymorphism (rs5883-C>T) and an intron 8 polymorphism (rs9930761-T>C). These polymorphisms altered key splicing elements and were found to have significant effects in two clinical studies. In the Whitehall II study, both rs247616 and rs5883T/rs9930761C were independently associated with higher HDL-C levels in males. Similarly, in the INVEST-GENE study, rs5883T/rs9930761C were associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality in males. However, these associations were not observed in females. Our findings suggest that CETP splicing effects on cardiovascular risk may be influenced by genetic factors and sex, independent of circulating HDL-C levels.

title: 6-Sulphated Chondroitins Have a Positive Influence on Axonal Regeneration
text: The presence of chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) in the glial scar inhibits the regeneration of axons due to their sulphated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). Following an injury, the upregulation of chondroitin 6-sulphotransferase-1 (C6ST-1) leads to an increase in 6-sulphated GAG. This study aims to determine whether this increase in 6-sulphated GAG is responsible for the heightened inhibition within the glial scar or if it represents a partial return to the permissive embryonic state dominated by 6-sulphated GAGs. To investigate this, we utilized knockout mice lacking C6ST-1 (KO) and examined the changes in chondroitin sulphotransferase (CSST) expression post-injury, as well as the impact of chondroitin 6-sulphates on both central and peripheral axon regeneration. In the central nervous system (CNS), wild-type animals (WT) exhibited an increase in C6ST-1, C6ST-2, and C4ST-1 mRNA after injury, whereas KO did not upregulate any CSSTs. In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), WT upregulated C6ST-1, while KO showed an upregulation of C6ST-2. We specifically examined the regeneration of nigrostriatal axons, which demonstrated mild spontaneous regeneration in WT. However, KO exhibited significantly fewer regenerating axons and more axonal retraction compared to WT. Interestingly, in the PNS, the repair of median and ulnar nerves resulted in similar and normal levels of axon regeneration in both WT and KO. Functional tests assessing plasticity after the repair also revealed no evidence of enhanced plasticity in KO. Our findings suggest that the upregulation of 6-sulphated GAGs following injury creates a more permissive extracellular matrix for axon regeneration. Additionally, the balance of different CSs in the microenvironment surrounding the injury site plays a crucial role in determining the outcome of nervous system injury.

title: Tissue Mechanics Orchestrate Wnt-Dependent Human Embryonic Stem Cell Differentiation.
text: The field of regenerative medicine relies on understanding how development is regulated and using this knowledge to control the fate of stem cells. During embryogenesis, the interactions between cells and their surrounding matrix play a crucial role, but it is not clear how these physical cues affect stem cells in a laboratory setting. To investigate this, we conducted experiments using human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) to determine if the mechanical properties of the extracellular environment could influence the development of mesoderm, a specific type of tissue. Our findings revealed that when hESCs were grown on a compliant hydrogel matrix, they accumulated a protein called β-catenin at the points where cells connect to each other, leading to enhanced mesoderm differentiation that depended on a signaling pathway called Wnt. We also discovered the mechanism behind this process: a protein called Src drives the modification of another protein called E-cadherin, which then releases a protein called P120-catenin. This release facilitates the activity of β-catenin, which is responsible for initiating and reinforcing mesoderm differentiation. In contrast, when hESCs were grown on a stiff hydrogel matrix, they exhibited increased activity of two proteins, GSK3 and Src, which are involved in the degradation of β-catenin and the inhibition of differentiation. Therefore, our study demonstrates that the mechanical properties of the matrix in the microenvironment can influence the differentiation of hESCs into specific types of tissues by altering how cells respond to signaling molecules.

title: Predictive performance of the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score as a screening tool for sepsis, mortality, and intensive care unit admission in patients with febrile neutropenia
text: The purpose of this study was to assess the effectiveness of the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score in identifying patients with febrile neutropenia (FN) who may have poor outcomes. We also aimed to compare the qSOFA score with the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria and Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) score for FN. We analyzed data from a registry of adult FN patients, calculating the qSOFA and SIRS scores retrospectively. The primary outcome was the development of sepsis, while secondary outcomes included ICU admission and 28-day mortality. Out of the 615 patients, 100 developed sepsis, 20 died, and 38 were admitted to ICUs. Multivariate analysis revealed that qSOFA was an independent predictor of sepsis and ICU admission. However, the qSOFA score had a lower area under the receiver operating curve compared to the MASCC score. The qSOFA score demonstrated low sensitivity (0.14, 0.2, and 0.23) but high specificity (0.98, 0.97, and 0.97) in predicting sepsis, 28-day mortality, and ICU admission. Overall, the qSOFA score performed less effectively than the MASCC score, suggesting that the existing risk stratification tool is more reliable for predicting outcomes in FN patients.

title: LIN28 Regulates Stem Cell Metabolism and Conversion to Primed Pluripotency.
text: The roles of the RNA-binding proteins LIN28A and LIN28B in embryonic development, tumorigenesis, and pluripotency are crucial but not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that LIN28B, like LIN28A, can effectively work with NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 in reprogramming cells to pluripotency. We also found that reactivating both the LIN28A and LIN28B genes is necessary for achieving maximum reprogramming efficiency. In human fibroblasts, LIN28B is activated early in the reprogramming process, while LIN28A is activated later when the cells transition to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). In mouse cells, LIN28A and LIN28B aid in the conversion from naive to primed pluripotency. Through proteomic and metabolomic analysis, we discovered that LIN28 is involved in maintaining low mitochondrial function associated with primed pluripotency and in regulating one-carbon metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, and histone methylation. LIN28 also binds to mRNAs of proteins important for oxidative phosphorylation and influences their abundance. Therefore, LIN28A and LIN28B work together to regulate reprogramming, naive/primed pluripotency, and stem cell metabolism.

title: Genetic Drift Can Compromise Mitochondrial Replacement by Nuclear Transfer in Human Oocytes.
text: Recently, the technique of replacing mitochondria through nuclear transfer between oocytes of two different women has emerged as a strategy to prevent the inheritance of mtDNA diseases. While experiments in human oocytes have shown successful replacement, the potential consequences of small amounts of mtDNA carryover have not been adequately studied. In our study using human mitochondrial replacement stem cell lines, we demonstrate that although the introduction of low levels of heteroplasmy into human oocytes through mitochondrial carryover during nuclear transfer often disappears, it can sometimes lead to mtDNA genotypic drift and a return to the original genotype. By comparing cells with identical nuclear DNA derived from oocytes but different mtDNA, we found that both mtDNA genotypes are compatible with the nucleus and that drift occurs independently of mitochondrial function. Therefore, while it is possible to functionally replace the mitochondrial genome, even small levels of heteroplasmy can impact the stability of the mtDNA genotype and compromise the effectiveness of mitochondrial replacement.

title: TAL effectors are remote controls for gene activation.
text: TAL effectors are a unique group of DNA-binding proteins that can be predicted for their specificity. These proteins are utilized by Xanthomonas, a type of Gram-negative bacteria that infects plants, to inject various effector proteins into plant cells through a type III secretion system. This injection of TAL effectors plays a crucial role in the bacteria's ability to cause disease in plants. Once inside the plant cell, TAL effectors localize to the nucleus, where they bind to specific regions of DNA called promoters and activate the expression of plant genes. The specificity of TAL effectors' DNA binding is determined by a central domain that contains repeated sequences. Each repeat is responsible for recognizing a specific base pair in the DNA. By rearranging these repeat modules, scientists can design TAL effectors with desired DNA-binding specificities. In this article, we provide an overview of how TAL specificity is encoded, including structural data and information on site-specific TAL nucleases.

title: Vascular heterogeneity and specialization in development and disease
text: Blood and lymphatic vessels are present throughout the body and play important roles in both normal physiology and disease. These vessels are lined with a layer of endothelial cells, which are specialized based on the specific needs of the tissue they serve. While the general mechanisms of blood and lymphatic vessel development are being studied in detail, our understanding of endothelial specialization is still limited to descriptive observations. However, recent studies using genetic animal models have shed light on how endothelial cells interact with each other and their surrounding tissue, offering insights into how different types of vessels and organs develop unique endothelial characteristics. Unraveling these underlying principles is crucial for comprehending tissue development and maintenance, as well as the development of abnormal function in disease.

title: Association of Intracerebral Hemorrhage Among Patients Taking Non–Vitamin K Antagonist vs Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Anticoagulants With In-Hospital Mortality
text: The use of non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) to prevent thromboembolic disease is becoming more common. However, there is limited information on the relationship between NOACs and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). This study aimed to examine the connection between prior use of oral anticoagulants (warfarin, NOACs, or no anticoagulants) and in-hospital mortality among patients with ICH. The study involved a retrospective cohort of 141,311 patients admitted to 1662 Get With The Guidelines–Stroke hospitals between October 2013 and December 2016. The main outcome measured was in-hospital mortality. The results showed that among the patients with ICH, 10.6% were taking warfarin and 3.5% were taking NOACs prior to the event. Additionally, 28.0% were taking single antiplatelet agents and 4.1% were taking dual antiplatelet agents. Patients who had previously used warfarin or NOACs were older and had a higher prevalence of atrial fibrillation and prior stroke. The severity of acute ICH stroke was similar across the three groups. The unadjusted in-hospital mortality rates were 32.6% for warfarin, 26.5% for NOACs, and 22.5% for no anticoagulants. Compared to patients without prior use of anticoagulants, those with prior use of warfarin had a higher risk of in-hospital mortality, as did those with prior use of NOACs. However, patients with prior use of NOACs had a lower risk of in-hospital mortality compared to those with prior use of warfarin. The difference in mortality between NOAC-treated patients and warfarin-treated patients was more pronounced among patients who had previously used dual antiplatelet agents. In conclusion, among patients with ICH, prior use of NOACs or warfarin was associated with higher in-hospital mortality compared to no anticoagulants. However, prior use of NOACs was linked to a lower risk of in-hospital mortality compared to warfarin.

title: Elevated red blood cell distribution width contributes to poor prognosis in patients undergoing resection for nonmetastatic rectal cancer
text: Multiple studies have indicated that increased red blood cell distribution width (RDW) is linked to a negative prognosis for various types of cancers. The objective of this study was to examine the prognostic significance of RDW in patients who underwent surgery to remove nonmetastatic rectal cancer. We conducted a retrospective analysis of a database containing information on 625 consecutive patients who had curative surgery for nonmetastatic rectal cancer at our institution between January 2009 and December 2014. The cutoff value for RDW was determined using a receiver-operating characteristic curve. The findings revealed that patients in the high RDW-cv group had lower overall survival (OS) rates (P = .018) and disease-free survival (DFS) rates (P = .004). Additionally, we observed that patients in the high RDW-sd group had significantly lower OS rates (P = .033), although there was no significant difference in DFS rates (P = .179). In the multivariate analysis, we discovered that elevated RDW-cv was associated with poor DFS (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.56, P = .010), and RDW-sd could predict worse OS (HR = 1.70, P = .009). These findings confirm that elevated RDW can independently serve as a prognostic factor in patients who undergo surgery for nonmetastatic rectal cancer. Therefore, in the future, it may be necessary to provide more intervention or surveillance for patients with nonmetastatic rectal cancer and elevated RDW values.

title: Health workers cohort study: methods and study design.
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to investigate the various health outcomes associated with specific lifestyle and genetic factors.

Materials and methods: Between March 2004 and April 2006, a sample of individuals, including employees from three different health and academic institutions, as well as their family members, were enrolled in the study after providing informed consent. At the beginning of the study and during the follow-up period from 2010 to 2013, participants completed a self-administered questionnaire, underwent a physical examination, and provided blood samples.

Results: A total of 10,729 participants, ranging in age from 6 to 94 years, were recruited at the start of the study. Among these participants, 70% were females, and 50% were affiliated with the Mexican Social Security Institute. The findings revealed that approximately 42% of the adults in the sample were overweight, while 20% were classified as obese.

Conclusion: This study has the potential to provide valuable insights into disease mechanisms and prevention by analyzing risk factor information in a large sample of Mexicans.

title: Aberrant pro-atrial natriuretic peptide/corin/natriuretic peptide receptor signaling is present in maternal vascular endothelium in preeclampsia.
text:
GOAL: This study aimed to investigate whether there is abnormal signaling of pro-ANP/corin/NPR in the maternal vascular system in preeclampsia.

METHOD: Blood samples were collected from 197 pregnant women (84 normotensive, 16 with chronic hypertension, 11 with mild preeclampsia, and 86 with severe preeclampsia). The concentrations of corin and pro-ANP in plasma were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Additionally, subcutaneous fat tissue samples were obtained from 12 pregnant women who underwent cesarean section delivery (6 normotensive and 6 with preeclampsia). Immunostaining was performed on paraffin-embedded sections of the subcutaneous fat tissue to examine the expression of ANP and its receptors NPR-A, NPR-B, and NPR-C.

RESULTS: The concentrations of corin were significantly higher in mild (2.78 ± 0.67 ng/ml, p < .05) and severe (2.53 ± 0.18 ng/ml, p < .01) preeclampsia compared to the normotensive (1.58 ± 0.08 ng/ml) and chronic hypertension (1.55 ± 0.20 ng/ml) groups. Pro-ANP concentrations were significantly higher in chronic hypertension (1.59 ± 0.53 ng/ml, p < .05) and severe preeclampsia (1.42 ± 0.24 ng/ml, p < .01) compared to the normotensive (0.48 ± 0.06 ng/ml) and mild preeclampsia (0.52 ± 0.09 ng/ml) groups. The expression of ANP and NPR-B was not detected in maternal vessels from normotensive and preeclamptic pregnancies. However, reduced expression of NPR-A and increased expression of NPR-C were observed in the endothelium of maternal vessels in preeclampsia.

CONCLUSIONS: ANP acts as a vasodilator, while NPR-C functions as a clearance receptor for ANP. The upregulation of NPR-C expression suggests an increase in the clearance or degradation of circulating ANP in preeclampsia. These findings also indicate that the pro-ANP/corin/NPR signaling pathway is dominant in the vascular system in preeclampsia.

title: Optimising Strategies for Plasmodium falciparum Malaria Elimination in Cambodia: Primaquine, Mass Drug Administration and Artemisinin Resistance
text:
In order to eliminate malaria, different approaches need to be tailored to specific transmission settings. A recent study conducted in a region of South West Cambodia with low seasonal transmission showed significant reductions in malaria parasite prevalence through mass drug administration (MDA) and high treatment coverage of symptomatic patients using artemisinin-piperaquine plus primaquine. However, it was unclear how each strategy contributed to the reduction in malaria. 

To address this, a mathematical model was developed using the trial results to assess the impact of the interventions, design optimal elimination strategies, and explore their interactions with artemisinin resistance, which has been detected in Western Cambodia. The model revealed that the initial reduction in P. falciparum malaria was primarily due to MDA with artemisinin-piperaquine. The subsequent decline and near elimination of malaria were mainly attributed to high treatment coverage with artemisinin-piperaquine, which was further enhanced by the addition of primaquine. 

Although MDA with artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) increased the proportion of artemisinin resistant infections, the increase was much lower compared to treating symptomatic cases with ACT, and the addition of primaquine slowed down this increase. The effectiveness of interventions using ACT was reduced in areas with high prevalence of artemisinin resistance. These findings remained consistent even when considering different assumptions about primaquine action and immunity. 

The key messages from these modeling results for policy makers are as follows: high coverage with ACT treatment can lead to long-term reduction in malaria, while the impact of MDA is generally short-term; primaquine enhances the effectiveness of ACT in eliminating malaria and reduces the proportion of artemisinin resistant infections; parasite prevalence is a better measure for surveillance in elimination programs compared to the number of symptomatic cases; and combinations of interventions are most effective, emphasizing the importance of sustained efforts for successful elimination.

title: Role of the Parasite-Derived Prostaglandin D2 in the Inhibition of Epidermal Langerhans Cell Migration during Schistosomiasis Infection
text: The role of epidermal Langerhans cells (LCs) in immune defense mechanisms and immunological disorders is significant. This study demonstrates that when C57BL/6 mice are percutaneously infected with the helminth parasite Schistosoma mansoni, LCs are activated but remain in the epidermis, which is surprising. Additionally, using a tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α induced experimental model of LC migration, it is shown that the parasites transiently hinder the departure of LCs from the epidermis and their subsequent accumulation as dendritic cells in the draining lymph nodes. This inhibitory effect is caused by lipophilic factors released by the parasites, rather than host-derived anti-inflammatory cytokines like interleukin-10. The study finds that prostaglandin (PG)D2, specifically through the adenylate cyclase-coupled PGD2 receptor (DP receptor), impedes the migration of LCs triggered by TNF-α. Furthermore, the DP receptor antagonist BW A868C restores LC migration in infected mice. Lastly, in a model of contact allergen-induced LC migration, it is shown that activation of the DP receptor not only inhibits LC emigration but also significantly reduces the contact hypersensitivity responses after challenge. Overall, this suggests that the inhibition of LC migration may be a strategy used by schistosomes to evade the host immune system, and that PGD2 may play a crucial role in controlling cutaneous immune responses.

title: Axicabtagene Ciloleucel CAR T‐Cell Therapy in Refractory Large B‐Cell Lymphoma
text:
Background: A phase 1 trial demonstrated the effectiveness of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), a personalized anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, in patients with refractory large B-cell lymphoma after conventional treatment failure.

Methods: In this phase 2 trial conducted at multiple centers, 111 patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma, or transformed follicular lymphoma, who had refractory disease despite prior recommended therapy, were enrolled. Patients received a targeted dose of 2×106 anti-CD19 CAR T cells per kilogram of body weight after a conditioning regimen of low-dose cyclophosphamide and fludarabine. The primary objective was to determine the rate of objective response, which included complete response and partial response. Secondary objectives included overall survival, safety, and biomarker assessments.

Results: Out of the 111 enrolled patients, axi-cel was successfully manufactured for 110 (99%) and administered to 101 (91%). The objective response rate was 82%, with a complete response rate of 54%. After a median follow-up of 15.4 months, 42% of patients maintained a response, with 40% still in complete remission. The overall survival rate at 18 months was 52%. The most common grade 3 or higher adverse events during treatment were neutropenia (78% of patients), anemia (43%), and thrombocytopenia (38%). Grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome and neurologic events occurred in 13% and 28% of patients, respectively. Three patients died during treatment. Higher levels of CAR T-cells in the blood were associated with a better response.

Conclusions: This multicenter study demonstrated that CAR T-cell therapy with axi-cel resulted in high and durable response rates in patients with refractory large B-cell lymphoma. The safety profile included myelosuppression, cytokine release syndrome, and neurologic events. (Funded by Kite Pharma and the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society Therapy Acceleration Program; ZUMA-1 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02348216.)

title: Beta adrenergic blockade decreases the immunomodulatory effects of social disruption stress
text:
The immune system is regulated by catecholamines produced by the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) during physiological or psychological stress. Previous research has shown that the activation of β-adrenergic receptors (βARs) plays a role in the actions of catecholamines, leading to increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in various cell types. However, the impact of SNS on the immune modulation of social defeat has not been investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to determine whether SNS activation during social disruption stress (SDR) affects anxiety-like behavior, as well as the activation, priming, and glucocorticoid resistance of splenocytes after social stress.

To conduct the study, CD-1 mice were exposed to one, three, or six cycles of SDR. Analysis of plasma and spleen samples using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) revealed an increase in catecholamines after six cycles of SDR. The open field test was then used to measure anxiety-like behaviors, and it was found that the increase in anxiety-like behavior induced by social defeat was blocked by pre-treatment with the β-adrenergic antagonist propranolol. However, pre-treatment with propranolol did not significantly affect corticosterone levels, indicating no difference in the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

In addition to anxiety-like behavior, SDR also caused splenomegaly and an increase in plasma levels of IL-6, TNFα, and MCP-1. These effects were reversed by pre-treatment with propranolol. Furthermore, flow cytometric analysis of cells from propranolol-pretreated mice showed a reduction in the percentage of CD11b(+) splenic macrophages induced by SDR, as well as a significant decrease in the expression of TLR2, TLR4, and CD86 on the surface of these cells. Additionally, supernatants from ex vivo cultures of splenocytes from propranolol-treated SDR mice contained lower levels of IL-6 after 18 hours of LPS stimulation. Similarly, propranolol pre-treatment prevented the glucocorticoid insensitivity of CD11b(+) cells ex vivo compared to splenocytes from SDR vehicle-treated mice.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the immune activation and priming effects of SDR are partly a result of SNS activation.

title: Stereotactic radiosurgery plus whole-brain radiation therapy vs stereotactic radiosurgery alone for treatment of brain metastases: a randomized controlled trial.
text: In patients with brain metastases, it is unclear whether adding whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) to stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) has any beneficial effects on mortality or neurologic function compared to SRS alone. The objective of this study was to determine if combining WBRT with SRS improves survival, brain tumor control, functional preservation rate, and frequency of neurologic death. The study was a randomized controlled trial involving 132 patients with 1 to 4 brain metastases, each less than 3 cm in diameter, enrolled at 11 hospitals in Japan between October 1999 and December 2003. The patients were randomly assigned to receive either WBRT plus SRS or SRS alone. The primary outcome measure was overall survival, while secondary outcome measures included brain tumor recurrence, salvage brain treatment, functional preservation, toxic effects of radiation, and cause of death. The results showed that the median survival time and the 1-year actuarial survival rate were similar between the two groups. However, the 12-month brain tumor recurrence rate was significantly lower in the WBRT + SRS group compared to the SRS alone group. Salvage brain treatment was also less frequently required in the WBRT + SRS group. There were no significant differences in systemic and neurologic functional preservation and toxic effects of radiation. In conclusion, the use of WBRT plus SRS did not improve survival for patients with 1 to 4 brain metastases compared to SRS alone. However, intracranial relapse occurred more frequently in those who did not receive WBRT, leading to the need for salvage treatment.

title: RANK signals from CD4+3− inducer cells regulate development of Aire-expressing epithelial cells in the thymic medulla
text: The expression of Aire by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) is crucial in preventing autoimmunity. These cells express tissue-restricted antigens to eliminate self-reactive T cell receptors. In this study, we uncover a new function for a population of CD4+3− inducer cells, which have previously been associated with the development of secondary lymphoid structures and the maintenance of T cell memory. These CD4+3− cells are closely linked to mTECs in the adult thymus, and their appearance in the fetal thymus coincides with the emergence of Aire+ mTECs. We demonstrate that signals from these cells, specifically RANKL signals, promote the maturation of mTEC progenitors into mature mTECs that express both CD80 and Aire. Furthermore, when RANK-deficient thymic stroma is transplanted into immunodeficient hosts, it leads to the development of autoimmunity. Overall, our findings shed light on the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in the generation of Aire+ mTECs and reveal a previously unknown role for CD4+3−RANKL+ inducer cells in maintaining self-tolerance within the thymus.

title: Proteomic approach to characterize biochemistry of meat quality defects.
text: Proteomics has the potential to analyze and identify quality issues in various types of meat, such as pale, soft, and exudative (PSE) meat in pork and poultry, woody broiler breast meat, reddish catfish fillets, meat toughness, and beef myoglobin oxidation. In the case of PSE broiler meat, 15 proteins were found to have different levels compared to normal broiler breast meat, while eight proteins showed differential expression in woody breast meat. Only hemoglobin exhibited differential expression between red and normal catfish fillets. However, subjecting catfish fillets to low oxygen and/or heat stress did not result in the production of red fillets. The proteomic data provided valuable insights into the protein variations associated with meat quality defects. Nevertheless, it is crucial to consider other factors such as genetics, nutrition, the animal's environment, muscle-to-meat conversion, meat quality analysis, sensory attributes, and their interplay with the proteomic findings to fully comprehend the causes of these defects, identify protein biomarkers, and ultimately prevent quality issues.

title: Phosphorylation of Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) links energy sensing to anti-inflammatory signaling
text: AMPK, or adenosine 5′-monophosphate–activated protein kinase, is a crucial regulator of metabolism at both the cellular and organismal levels. It also plays a role in suppressing inflammation. Our research has shown that when AMPK is pharmacologically activated, it quickly inhibits the Janus kinase (JAK)–signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway in various types of cells. Through in vitro kinase assays, we discovered that AMPK directly phosphorylates two specific residues (Ser515 and Ser518) within the Src homology 2 domain of JAK1. Activation of AMPK also enhances the interaction between JAK1 and 14-3-3 proteins in cultured vascular endothelial cells and fibroblasts. This effect is dependent on the presence of Ser515 and Ser518 and is not observed in cells lacking AMPK catalytic subunits. When Ser515 and Ser518 are mutated, the AMPK-mediated inhibition of JAK-STAT signaling is abolished, regardless of whether it is stimulated by the sIL-6Rα/IL-6 complex or the expression of a constitutively active V658F-mutant JAK1 in human fibrosarcoma cells. Additionally, clinically used AMPK activators such as metformin and salicylate enhance the inhibitory phosphorylation of endogenous JAK1 and inhibit STAT3 phosphorylation in primary vascular endothelial cells. These findings provide insight into the mechanism by which JAK1 function and inflammatory signaling can be suppressed in response to metabolic stress. They also offer a rationale for investigating AMPK activators in various diseases associated with increased activation of the JAK-STAT pathway.

title: IAP antagonists induce anti-tumor immunity in multiple myeloma
text: The amplification of cellular inhibitors of apoptosis (cIAP) 1 and 2 has been found in approximately 3% of cancers and has been identified as a potential target for therapy in various malignancies due to its role in evading apoptosis. As a result, small-molecule IAP antagonists like LCL161 have been tested in clinical trials for their ability to induce tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells. However, in multiple myeloma (MM), cIAP1 and cIAP2 are frequently homozygously deleted, leading to the constant activation of the noncanonical nuclear factor (NF)-κB pathway. Surprisingly, we observed significant anti-myeloma activity of LCL161 in a transgenic myeloma mouse model and in patients with relapsed-refractory MM. When combined with cyclophosphamide, LCL161 resulted in a median progression-free survival of 10 months. This effect was not due to direct induction of tumor cell death, but rather the upregulation of tumor-cell-autonomous type I interferon (IFN) signaling and a strong inflammatory response. This led to the activation of macrophages and dendritic cells, resulting in the phagocytosis of tumor cells. In a MM mouse model, treatment with LCL161 provided long-term protection against tumors and induced regression in some mice. Notably, when combined with the immune-checkpoint inhibitor anti-PD1, LCL161 was able to cure all treated mice.

title: Psychobiological Protective Factors Modifying the Association Between Age and Sexual Health in Men: Findings From the Men’s Health 40+ Study
text: As individuals age, their sexual health tends to decline. Among men over the age of 40, the most common sexual disorder is erectile dysfunction (ED). While risk factors for ED have been identified, protective factors have yet to be determined. Previous studies have not examined the impact of endocrine and psychosocial factors on the age-related increase in ED simultaneously. In this study, 271 healthy men between the ages of 40 and 75 provided data on sexual function and potential psychosocial protective factors. Saliva samples were also collected to analyze hormone levels and proinflammatory markers. Approximately 35% of participants reported experiencing at least mild ED. The study found that perceived general health, emotional support, relationship quality, and intimacy motivation were directly associated with ED, while hormone levels and proinflammatory markers were not. Further analysis revealed that testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), perceived general health, emotional support, intimacy motivation, and interleukin-6 all had moderating effects on the association between age and ED. Older men with ED differed from those without ED in terms of hormone levels and psychometric measures such as perceived general health, emotional support, satisfaction with life, and intimacy motivation. Both psychosocial and endocrine factors played a role in the relationship between age and sexual health. Perceived general health, emotional support, intimacy motivation, and relationship quality were identified as protective factors against ED, while higher levels of testosterone and DHEA and lower levels of interleukin-6 buffered against the age-related increase in ED.

title: Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells in cancer research and precision oncology
text: Advancements in human tissue processing, bioengineering, xenotransplantation, and genome editing have opened up new possibilities for studying human cancer. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are at the forefront of these developments. In this article, we explore the advantages and limitations of iPSC modeling and how it relates to other patient-derived cancer models like organoids, organs-on-chips, and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs). We emphasize the unique opportunities iPSC models offer beyond existing systems and animal models, as well as the current challenges and areas for improvement to encourage wider adoption of this technology.

title: Structural basis for sequence-specific recognition of DNA by TAL effectors.
text: Phytopathogenic bacteria secrete TAL (transcription activator-like) effectors that can identify specific sequences in host DNA. These effectors have a central domain made up of repeated segments, each consisting of 33 to 35 amino acids. Two hypervariable residues, known as repeat variable diresidues (RVDs), at positions 12 and 13, enable the recognition of a particular base pair. In this study, we present the crystal structures of a TAL effector with 11.5 repeats, both in the absence and presence of DNA. Each repeat of the TAL effector consists of two helices connected by a short loop containing the RVDs. The 11.5 repeats form a right-handed, superhelical structure that follows the sense strand of the DNA duplex, with the RVDs interacting with the major groove. The 12th residue stabilizes the loop containing the RVDs, while the 13th residue establishes a specific contact with the DNA base. This understanding of how TAL effectors recognize DNA could aid in the development of DNA-binding proteins for various biotechnological applications.

title: Caveolin-1 deletion exacerbates cardiac interstitial fibrosis by promoting M2 macrophage activation in mice after myocardial infarction.
text: The imbalanced resolution of inflammation is responsible for adverse remodeling after a heart attack, leading to heart failure. Macrophages play a crucial role in post-heart attack inflammation, with different subtypes promoting either inflammation and injury (M1 phenotype) or scar formation (M2 phenotype). Previous research has shown that the absence of a protein called caveolin-1 (Cav1) is associated with negative changes in heart structure in mice, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet understood. In this study, we investigate the role of Cav1 in macrophage activation using two groups of mice: wild type mice (WT) and mice lacking Cav1 (Cav1(-/-)). At 3 days after a heart attack, cardiac function was similar between the two groups. However, the absence of Cav1 resulted in a surprisingly higher percentage of M2 macrophages (identified by the presence of arginase-1) in the area affected by the heart attack. Conversely, restoring Cav1 function in WT mice after a heart attack reduced the activation of M2 macrophages. Additionally, when Cav1 null macrophages were transferred into WT mice on day 3 after a heart attack, adverse changes in heart structure were exacerbated by day 14. In laboratory studies, Cav1 null macrophages showed a more pronounced activation of the M2 profile in response to IL-4 stimulation. In summary, the deletion of Cav1 promotes various maladaptive repair processes after a heart attack, including increased signaling of TGF-β, increased infiltration of M2 macrophages, and dysregulation of the balance between M1 and M2 macrophages. Our findings suggest that therapeutic interventions targeting Cav1 function during the inflammatory response phase could improve cardiac remodeling.

title: Lipid hydroperoxide measurement by oxidation of Fe2+ in the presence of xylenol orange. Comparison with the TBA assay and an iodometric method
text: To study the role of hydroperoxides and lipid peroxidation in disease, it is necessary to have simple and sensitive methods for directly measuring hydroperoxides. In this report, we present a technique that measures hydroperoxide levels by utilizing the rapid oxidation of Fe2+ in acidic conditions. Fe3+ then forms a chromophore with xylenol orange, resulting in strong absorption at 560 nm. This yields an apparent E560 (for H2O2, butyl hydroperoxide, and cumene hydroperoxide) of 4.3×104 M−1 cm−1. We validated this assay by studying liposomal lipid peroxidation and found that the results were comparable to those obtained using an iodometric method or by measuring conjugated dienes. In contrast, the assay involving thiobarbituric acid underestimates lipid peroxidation and does not specifically measure hydroperoxides.

title: Roles of exosomes in cardioprotection.
text: Exosomes, which are vesicles originating from endosomes, play a crucial role in intercellular communication. Various types of cardiac cells, such as cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, release exosomes that regulate cellular functions. Specifically, exosomes released by human cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) have shown to be cardioprotective and improve cardiac function after a heart attack, similar to the effects of the parent cells. These CPC-derived exosomes contain an abundance of cardioprotective microRNAs, particularly miR-146a-3p. Additionally, circulating exosomes have been found to mediate remote ischaemic preconditioning and are currently being studied as potential diagnostic markers. The discovery that extracellular signaling organelles derived from cells can mediate the paracrine effects of stem cells suggests that cell-free strategies could replace cell transplantation. This review focuses on the emerging roles of exosomes in cardiovascular physiology, specifically highlighting the cardioprotective activities of CPC-derived exosomes.

title: The rate of change in declining steroid hormones: a new parameter of healthy aging in men?
text:
Recent research on healthy aging in men has increasingly focused on the impact of age-related hormonal changes. While there has been significant investigation into the decline of testosterone (T), other sex steroids such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), estradiol (E2), and progesterone (P) have been largely overlooked. As a result, there is still a need to identify a comprehensive hormone parameter that reflects the aging process in men. 

To address this gap, a study was conducted involving 271 self-reporting healthy men aged between 40 and 75. These participants provided both psychometric data and saliva samples for hormone analysis. Correlation analysis between age and sex steroids revealed negative associations for all four sex steroids (T, DHEA, E2, and P). 

To further explore these findings, a principal component analysis was conducted, which included ten salivary analytes. This analysis identified a principal component that primarily captured the variance of the four sex steroid hormones. Subsequent principal component analysis specifically focusing on the four sex steroids extracted the principal component of declining steroid hormones (DSH). 

Further analysis was conducted to examine the association between age and DSH, revealing significant moderation effects for psychosocial factors such as depression, chronic stress, and perceived general health. This suggests that psychosocial factors can influence the relationship between age and DSH. 

In conclusion, these findings provide additional evidence that sex steroids decline in aging men. The integrated hormone parameter DSH, along with its rate of change, can serve as biomarkers for healthy aging in men. Additionally, the negative association between age and DSH is influenced by psychosocial factors.

title: Development of a novel helper-dependent adenovirus-Epstein-Barr virus hybrid system for the stable transformation of mammalian cells.
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) episomes are effectively maintained in cell lines that are capable of proliferation due to the replication and segregation mediated by the EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA-1) protein. Previous research has shown that EBV episomes have the ability to provide long-term expression of transgenes and correct genetic defects in cells that are deficient. In order to achieve precise delivery of EBV episomes both in vitro and in vivo, we have developed a hybrid system called binary helper-dependent adenovirus (HDA)-EBV. This system consists of two HDA vectors - one for the expression of Cre recombinase and the other containing all the necessary sequences for the EBV episome, flanked by loxP sites. When these vectors are coinfected into cells, the Cre expressed from the first vector recombines the loxP sites on the second vector. This results in the formation of circular EBV episomes that express the desired transgene and contain the EBV-derived family of repeats, an EBNA-1 expression cassette, and 19 kb of human DNA that serves as a replication origin in mammalian cells. The HDA-EBV hybrid system successfully transformed 40% of cultured cells. Transgene expression was observed in proliferating cells for more than 20 weeks under conditions that favored transgene expression. In the absence of selection, the EBV episomes were lost at a rate of 8 to 10% per cell division. We also demonstrated the successful delivery of EBV episomes in vivo in the liver of transgenic mice that expressed Cre from the albumin promoter. This innovative gene transfer system has the potential to provide long-term episomal transgene expression, allowing for the correction of genetic defects with reduced toxicity associated with the vector and without the risk of insertional mutagenesis.

title: Spliceosome assembly pathways for different types of alternative splicing converge during commitment to splice site pairing in the A complex.
text: Alternative splicing patterns, which generate multiple mRNA isoforms, are established through the pairing of differential splice sites. This crucial process is facilitated by the spliceosome, which undergoes sequential structural rearrangements involving its five core snRNPs. To investigate the timing of splice site pairing, we conducted kinetic trap experiments using pre-mRNAs that exhibit alternative 5' splice site selection or alternative exon inclusion. Our findings demonstrate that splice site pairing occurs during the formation of the A complex, characterized by the ATP-dependent association of the U2 snRNP with the branch point. Notably, the timing of splice site pairing is not influenced by the intron or exon definition modes of splice site recognition. By utilizing the ATP analog ATPgammaS, we established that ATP hydrolysis is essential for splice site pairing, independent of U2 snRNP binding to the pre-mRNA. These results highlight the A complex as the specific step in spliceosomal assembly dedicated to splice site pairing and suggest that ATP hydrolysis secures splice sites into a splicing pattern following stable U2 snRNP association with the branch point.

title: Transcripts of the MHM region on the chicken Z chromosome accumulate as non-coding RNA in the nucleus of female cells adjacent to the DMRT1 locus
text: The MHM region, found on the short arm of the Z chromosome in male chickens, is made up of around 210 repeats of a 2.2-kb sequence unit called BamHI. The cytosines in the CpG dinucleotides of this region are heavily methylated on both Z chromosomes in males, but less methylated on the single Z chromosome in females. The methylation state of the MHM region is established shortly after fertilization, around the 1-day embryonic stage. In females, the MHM region is transcribed from a specific strand into non-coding RNA, which is accumulated at the site of transcription next to the DMRT1 locus in the nucleus. However, in males, the MHM region is transcriptionally silent, most likely due to CpG methylation. When male embryonic fibroblasts are treated with 5-azacytidine, the region becomes hypo-methylated and actively transcribed. In ZZW triploid chickens, the MHM regions are hypomethylated and transcribed on both Z chromosomes, while in ZZZ triploid chickens, the MHM regions are hypermethylated and transcriptionally inactive on all three Z chromosomes. This suggests that the W chromosome may play a role in the state of the MHM region.

title: Macropinocytosis of protein is an amino acid supply route in Ras-transformed cells
text: Macropinocytosis is a well-preserved process in cells where extracellular fluid and its contents are taken in through large, diverse vesicles called macropinosomes. It has been observed that oncogenic Ras proteins can stimulate macropinocytosis, but its role in the transformed phenotype is still unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that cells transformed by Ras utilize macropinocytosis to internalize extracellular protein. This protein is then broken down through proteolysis, producing amino acids like glutamine that can enter central carbon metabolism. Consequently, the reliance of Ras-transformed cells on free extracellular glutamine for growth can be diminished by the macropinocytic uptake of protein. This suggests that macropinocytosis plays a crucial role in nutrient uptake for tumor cells, as inhibiting it pharmacologically impairs the growth of Ras-transformed pancreatic tumor xenografts. These findings highlight macropinocytosis as a mechanism through which cancer cells meet their unique metabolic demands and suggest its potential use in developing anticancer therapies.

title: Linking Splicing to Pol II Transcription Stabilizes Pre-mRNAs and Influences Splicing Patterns
text: RNA processing occurs in close proximity to the site of transcription, indicating a regulatory connection between transcription and pre-mRNA splicing. Through an in vitro transcription/splicing experiment, we establish that the association of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) transcription and pre-mRNA splicing is crucial for efficient gene expression. RNAs synthesized by Pol II that contain functional splice sites are shielded from nuclear degradation, likely due to the high concentration of the splicing machinery in the vicinity, which ensures its interaction with the RNA rather than with nucleases. Additionally, the process of transcription influences the alternative splicing of newly formed pre-mRNAs. This link between transcription and RNA processing is specific to RNA Pol II, as other RNA polymerases do not offer the same protection from nucleases and their RNA products exhibit modified splicing patterns. We propose that the connection between Pol II transcription and pre-mRNA splicing guarantees the prolonged stability and proper processing of nascent pre-mRNAs.

title: The emerging role of skeletal muscle extracellular matrix remodelling in obesity and exercise.
text: The remodelling of the extracellular matrix in skeletal muscle has been proposed as a new characteristic associated with obesity and metabolic dysfunction. Exercise training has been shown to improve muscle function in obese individuals, potentially through its regulatory effects on the muscle extracellular matrix. This review aimed to examine the existing literature on the remodelling of the extracellular matrix in skeletal muscle during obesity and the impact of exercise. A non-systematic review of publications from 1970 to 2015 was conducted on PubMed, resulting in the inclusion of 37 studies involving humans and animals. These studies consistently reported increases in the expression of various types of collagen, growth factors, and enzymatic regulators of the skeletal muscle extracellular matrix in obesity. Only two studies investigated the effects of exercise on the extracellular matrix in skeletal muscle during obesity, both of which suggested a regulatory effect of exercise. The effects of exercise on the muscle extracellular matrix appear to be influenced by the duration and type of exercise training, with varying effects observed between a single session and longer durations of exercise. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying the remodelling of the extracellular matrix in skeletal muscle during obesity and the effects of exercise.

title: Effect of specific exercise strategy on need for surgery in patients with subacromial impingement syndrome: randomised controlled study
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if a targeted exercise strategy, focusing on the rotator cuff and scapula stabilizers, could improve shoulder function and reduce pain in patients with subacromial impingement syndrome. The study was a randomized, controlled trial conducted at a Swedish university hospital. A total of 102 patients with long-standing subacromial impingement syndrome, who had previously failed conservative treatment, were recruited through orthopedic specialists. 

The intervention group followed a specific exercise strategy, which included eccentric exercises for the rotator cuff and concentric/eccentric exercises for the scapula stabilizers, along with manual mobilization. The control group followed an unspecific exercise program for the neck and shoulder. Both groups received five to six guided treatment sessions over 12 weeks, and performed home exercises once or twice a day. 

The primary outcome measure was the Constant-Murley shoulder assessment score, which evaluated shoulder function and pain. Secondary outcomes included patients' global impression of change due to treatment and their decision regarding surgery. 

The results showed that the specific exercise group had a significantly greater improvement in the Constant-Murley score compared to the control group. Additionally, a higher proportion of patients in the specific exercise group reported a successful outcome in the patients' global assessment of change due to treatment. Furthermore, fewer patients in the specific exercise group chose to undergo surgery compared to the control group. 

In conclusion, a targeted exercise strategy focusing on eccentric exercises for the rotator cuff and concentric/eccentric exercises for the scapula stabilizers is effective in reducing pain and improving shoulder function in patients with persistent subacromial impingement syndrome. This exercise strategy also reduces the need for arthroscopic subacromial decompression within a three-month timeframe. The trial was registered under Clinical trials NCT01037673.

title: Nucleotide sequence of an avian sarcoma virus oncogene (src) and proposed amino acid sequence for gene product
text: The molecular cloning of viral DNA has allowed for the isolation of the transforming gene (src) of avian sarcoma virus (ASV) and the adjacent regions of the viral genome. The nucleotide sequence of these regions includes the entire src gene and a portion of the env gene that codes for gp 37, one of the two glycoproteins present in the viral envelope. Src encodes a single hydrophobic protein that possesses structural characteristics consistent with previous descriptions of the gene product (pp60src). It appears that a single viral protein is responsible for both initiating and maintaining neoplastic transformation caused by avian sarcoma virus. Neither src nor its product exhibit any apparent structural similarities to various other viral oncogenes and their corresponding proteins. Src is surrounded by a repeated nucleotide sequence that may facilitate frequent removal of the gene from the viral genome.

title: Issues in design and interpretation of MDR-TB clinical trials: report of the first Global MDR-TB Clinical Trials Landscape Meeting
text: In December 2014, the Global MDR-TB Clinical Trials Landscape Meeting took place to address the shortcomings of the current MDR-TB regimen and the need for new treatment options. This disease affects millions of people worldwide each year. Sixty international experts on multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) gathered in Washington D.C. and Cape Town, South Africa to discuss important trial-related issues. These included the standardization of definitions, building clinical trial capacity, and developing treatment regimens that promote compliance, prevent resistance, and are relevant for special populations such as children and those co-infected with HIV. The ultimate goal was to generate enough evidence to support regulatory approval and improve guidelines. During the meeting, participants examined ongoing Phase 2B and Phase 3 trials, as well as potential new regimens and combinations that could be evaluated in the near future. This included regimens specifically designed to enable shorter treatment duration and all-oral treatment, aiming to maximize treatment completion. The hope is that by clearly defining these challenges, solutions can be identified to accelerate progress towards effective and non-toxic treatments that can be implemented on a larger scale.

title: Para-aortic splanchnopleura from early mouse embryos contains B1a cell progenitors
text: Birds have stem cells that give rise to definitive erythropoiesis. These stem cells emerge in the splanchnopleural mesoderm near the embryonic aorta. In mammals, it is commonly believed that the yolk sac is the main source of haematopoietic stem cells during development. However, there may be an alternative source of stem cells within the mouse fetus. To investigate this, we transplanted splanchnopleura from 10- to 18-somite mouse embryos into adult immunodeficient SCID mice. We observed significant levels of donor-derived serum IgM, normal numbers of IgM-secreting plasma cells, and the Bla (IgMa brightB220dullCD5+) cell subset fully reconstituted by donor progenitors 3 to 6 months after transplantation. This suggests that there is a previously unknown site for haematogenic capacity in the embryo, which is present 12 hours before fetal liver colonization.

title: Establishment in culture of pluripotential cells from mouse embryos
text: Pluripotent cells can be found in a mouse embryo until at least the early post-implantation stage. This is evident from their involvement in the creation of chimaeric animals and the development of teratocarcinomas. Until now, it has been challenging to cultivate these cells in vitro, with cell lines only being obtained through teratocarcinoma formation in vivo. However, we have successfully established pluripotent cell lines directly from in vitro cultures of mouse blastocysts. These cells have the ability to differentiate both in vitro and in vivo, forming tumors when injected into a mouse. Additionally, they possess a normal karyotype.

title: MHC class II interaction with CD4 mediated by a region analogous to the MHC class I binding site for CD8
text: The interactions between major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules and the CD4 or CD8 coreceptors play a significant role in the selection of T-cells within the thymus. On mature T-cells, these two glycoproteins are associated with a specific preference for recognizing MHC molecules by the T-cell receptor. CD4+ T-cells respond to antigens in conjunction with MHC class II molecules, while CD8+ T-cells respond to antigens in conjunction with MHC class I molecules. Previous studies have shown that there is a physical interaction between CD4/MHC class II molecules and CD8/MHC class I molecules, as demonstrated by cell adhesion assays. Additionally, a binding site for CD8 on class I molecules has been identified. In this study, we demonstrate that a specific region of the MHC class IIβ-chain β2 domain, which is structurally similar to the CD8-binding loop in the MHC class I α3 domain, is crucial for the function of both mouse and human CD4.

title: Instability and decay of the primary structure of DNA
text: DNA, despite being the carrier of genetic information, possesses limited chemical stability. Within living organisms, hydrolysis, oxidation, and nonenzymatic methylation of DNA take place at notable rates, but they are counteracted by specific DNA repair mechanisms. The natural deterioration of DNA is expected to play a significant role in mutagenesis, carcinogenesis, and aging, while also imposing constraints on the retrieval of DNA fragments from fossils.

title: Single-cell proteomic analysis of S. cerevisiae reveals the architecture of biological noise
text: The main objective of biology is to quantitatively describe the behavior of cells. However, this task has been hindered by the challenge of measuring protein levels and their fluctuations. In this study, we propose a method that combines high-throughput flow cytometry with a library of GFP-tagged yeast strains to accurately monitor protein levels at the resolution of individual cells. By measuring the abundance of over 2,500 proteins in different growth media, we gain a comprehensive understanding of how cells respond to different conditions, uncovering changes that are not detected by DNA microarray analyses. Our data suggests that the variability in protein expression is primarily influenced by the random production and degradation of messenger RNAs. Additionally, we observe significant differences in noise levels among specific proteins, which are strongly associated with their transcriptional regulation and function. For instance, proteins that respond to environmental changes exhibit higher levels of noise, while those involved in protein synthesis are more stable. These findings demonstrate a fascinating pattern in biological noise and imply that the levels of protein variability have evolved to balance the costs and potential benefits of such variation.

title: Direct conversion of fibroblasts to functional neurons by defined factors
text:
During development, cellular differentiation and lineage commitment are typically considered as robust and irreversible processes. However, recent research has demonstrated that both mouse and human fibroblasts can be reprogrammed into a pluripotent state by utilizing a combination of four transcription factors. This discovery has led to the question of whether transcription factors can directly induce specific somatic cell fates, rather than just an undifferentiated state.

To explore this possibility, we conducted a study aiming to convert fibroblasts into neurons by expressing neural-lineage-specific transcription factors. Out of a pool of nineteen candidate genes, we identified a combination of only three factors - Ascl1, Brn2 (also known as Pou3f2), and Myt1l - that proved to be sufficient in rapidly and effectively converting mouse embryonic and postnatal fibroblasts into functional neurons in vitro.

These induced neuronal (iN) cells not only expressed multiple neuron-specific proteins but also exhibited the ability to generate action potentials and form functional synapses. The generation of iN cells from non-neural lineages could have significant implications for the study of neural development, modeling neurological diseases, and advancing regenerative medicine.

title: Inflammasome-mediated dysbiosis regulates progression of NAFLD and obesity
text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a liver condition that occurs as a result of metabolic syndrome and is the primary cause of chronic liver disease in the Western world. Approximately 20% of individuals with NAFLD develop a more severe form called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which is associated with cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and liver cancer. However, the reasons why some individuals progress from NAFLD to NASH are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the NLRP6 and NLRP3 inflammasomes, along with the protein IL-18, play a negative role in the progression of NAFLD/NASH and various aspects of metabolic syndrome by influencing the gut microbiota. Through different mouse models, we found that deficiencies in the inflammasomes led to changes in the composition of the gut microbiota, which in turn worsened liver fat accumulation and inflammation. This was due to the increased presence of TLR4 and TLR9 agonists in the portal circulation, resulting in elevated levels of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α in the liver and promoting NASH progression. Additionally, when inflammasome-deficient mice were housed with normal mice, there was a worsening of liver fat accumulation and obesity. These findings suggest that the altered interactions between the gut microbiota and the host, caused by defective NLRP3 and NLRP6 inflammasome sensing, may influence the rate of progression of various metabolic syndrome-related abnormalities. This highlights the significant role of the microbiota in the development of seemingly unrelated systemic auto-inflammatory and metabolic disorders.

title: Chromatin remodelling at promoters suppresses antisense transcription
text: Chromatin plays a crucial role in efficiently packaging DNA within eukaryotic cells. To gain insights into the control of chromatin structure in the Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome, we conducted a study on the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex Isw2 and its role in nucleosome positioning. Our findings indicate that Isw2 operates near promoter regions, where it relocates nucleosomes at the boundary between genic and intergenic sequences. This repositioning of nucleosomes by Isw2 is directional and leads to an increased presence of nucleosomes in the intergenic region. When Isw2 activity is lost, transcription becomes inappropriate, resulting in the production of both coding and noncoding transcripts. Our research demonstrates that Isw2 repositions nucleosomes to establish transcription directionality by preventing initiation from hidden sites. Through our analyses, we have gained insights into the global organization of chromatin and enhanced our understanding of transcription regulation.

title: The Human Mitochondrial DEAD-Box Protein DDX28 Resides in RNA Granules and Functions in Mitoribosome Assembly.
text: The synthesis of 13 proteins, crucial for the oxidative phosphorylation system, is a specialized function of human mitochondrial ribosomes. Despite this, the process of mitoribosome biogenesis, including compartmentalization and factors involved, remains largely unknown. In this study, we have discovered that the DEAD-box protein DDX28 is a vital component of RNA granules, necessary for the formation of the mitoribosome large subunit (mt-LSU). DDX28 interacts with both the 16S rRNA and the mt-LSU. Silencing DDX28 through RNA interference in HEK293T cells does not impact the stability of mitochondrial mRNA or the processing or modification of 16S rRNA. However, it does result in decreased levels of 16S rRNA and mt-LSU proteins, impaired mt-LSU assembly, significantly reduced mitochondrial protein synthesis, and subsequent failure to assemble oxidative phosphorylation complexes. Our findings highlight the essential role of DDX28 in the early stages of mitoribosome mt-LSU biogenesis, which primarily occurs near the mitochondrial nucleoids within the compartment defined by RNA granules.

title: Conversion of Adult Pancreatic α-cells to β-cells After Extreme β-cell Loss
text: Pancreatic beta-cells, responsible for producing insulin, typically have a long lifespan and do not replicate much in healthy conditions. However, they do exhibit increased replication when there is a higher metabolic demand or after injury, such as beta-cell loss. It is currently unknown whether adult mammals can generate new beta-cells after complete loss, as seen in diabetes. This would suggest that beta-cells can differentiate from precursor cells or from a different source. In our study, we demonstrate beta-cell regeneration in a transgenic model where acute selective near-total beta-cell loss is induced by diphtheria toxin. When given insulin, the mice survived and their beta-cell mass increased over time. By tracing the lineage of glucagon-producing alpha-cells before beta-cell loss, we found that a significant portion of regenerated beta-cells actually originated from alpha-cells. This discovery highlights the previously overlooked plasticity of pancreatic cells. Harnessing this spontaneous conversion of adult cells between different endocrine types could potentially be used to produce beta-cells for diabetes therapies, either through differentiation in vitro or induced regeneration.

title: Driver mutations in histone H3.3 and chromatin remodelling genes in paediatric glioblastoma
text: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a deadly brain tumor that affects both adults and children. However, there are differences in DNA copy number and gene expression signatures between adult and pediatric cases. To investigate the genetic events that contribute to this distinction, we analyzed the exomes of 48 pediatric GBM samples. We found somatic mutations in the H3.3-ATRX-DAXX chromatin remodeling pathway in 44% of the tumors (21 out of 48). Recurrent mutations in H3F3A, which is responsible for encoding the replication-independent histone 3 variant H3.3, were observed in 31% of the tumors. These mutations resulted in amino acid substitutions at two critical positions within the histone tail (K27M, G34R/G34V) that are involved in important regulatory post-translational modifications. Mutations in ATRX and DAXX, which encode two subunits of a chromatin remodeling complex required for H3.3 incorporation at pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres, were identified in 31% of all samples and in 100% of tumors with a G34R or G34V H3.3 mutation. Somatic TP53 mutations were found in 54% of all cases and in 86% of samples with H3F3A and/or ATRX mutations. Screening a large group of gliomas with different grades and histologies (784 in total) revealed that H3F3A mutations were specific to GBM and highly prevalent in children and young adults. Additionally, the presence of H3F3A/ATRX-DAXX/TP53 mutations was strongly associated with alternative lengthening of telomeres and specific gene expression profiles. This study is the first to report recurrent mutations in a regulatory histone in humans, and our findings suggest that defects in chromatin architecture contribute to the development of pediatric and young adult GBM.

title: Translational control of intron splicing in eukaryotes
text: The majority of eukaryotic genes have non-coding introns that need to be accurately removed from pre-messenger RNAs in order to produce translatable mRNAs. Splicing is guided by short conserved sequences, but genes usually have multiple potential splice sites and the mechanisms that determine the correct sites are not well understood. In most organisms, it is difficult to predict short introns recognized by the intron definition mechanism solely based on sequence motifs. In multicellular eukaryotes, long introns are recognized through exon definition and many genes produce different mRNA variants through alternative splicing. The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway may further influence the variants by selectively breaking down those with premature termination codons, which are common in mammals. Our study shows that the small introns of the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia are strongly selected to cause premature termination of mRNA translation if the introns are retained, and the same bias is seen in the short introns of plants, fungi, and animals. By reducing the expression of the two P. tetraurelia genes that encode UPF1, a crucial protein in NMD, we demonstrate that the efficiency of splicing varies greatly among introns and NMD can significantly decrease the amount of unspliced mRNAs. These findings suggest that, regardless of alternative splicing, species with many introns rely on NMD to compensate for inefficient and inaccurate splicing.

title: Alternatively activated macrophages produce catecholamines to sustain adaptive thermogenesis
text:
All warm-blooded animals use a process called thermogenesis to maintain their internal body temperature, allowing their cells and bodily functions to continue working in cold environments. According to the current understanding, when the hypothalamus detects cold temperatures, it triggers the release of noradrenaline in both brown and white adipose tissue through sympathetic discharge. Noradrenaline acts on β(3)-adrenergic receptors, causing lipolysis in white fat cells and activating the expression of thermogenic genes, such as PPAR-γ coactivator 1a (Ppargc1a), uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1), and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 1 (Acsl1), in brown fat cells. However, the specific cell types involved in this process are not fully understood. 

In this study, we unexpectedly found that the interleukin-4 (IL-4)-stimulated program of alternative macrophage activation is necessary for adaptive thermogenesis in mice. When exposed to cold temperatures, adipose tissue macrophages undergo alternative activation and release catecholamines, which stimulate the expression of thermogenic genes in brown fat tissue and promote lipolysis in white fat tissue. When alternatively activated macrophages were absent, the mice were unable to adapt metabolically to the cold. However, when IL-4 was administered, thermogenic gene expression, fatty acid mobilization, and energy expenditure increased, all in a macrophage-dependent manner. This discovery reveals the role of alternatively activated macrophages in coordinating an important response to cold stress in mammals.

title: Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres Mediated by Mitotic DNA Synthesis Engages Break-Induced Replication Processes.
text: ALT, or alternative lengthening of telomeres, is a mechanism for maintaining telomeres in certain cancers that does not rely on telomerase. Our analysis of telomerase-positive cells and ALT human cell lines derived from human TERC knockout cells reveals that ALT cells have more fragile telomeres, indicating problems with telomere replication. These replication issues in ALT cells trigger a process called mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) at telomeres, which is dependent on the protein RAD52 but not RAD51. Telomeric MiDAS is a conservative process of DNA synthesis that may be mediated by break-induced replication, similar to a type of ALT survival mechanism seen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Replication stresses caused by the abnormal expression of cyclin E, the formation of G-quadruplexes, or the formation of R-loops promote the ALT pathway and lead to the clustering of telomeres, a characteristic feature of ALT cancers. The TIMELESS/TIPIN complex suppresses telomere clustering and telomeric MiDAS, while the SMC5/6 complex promotes them. In summary, ALT cells have more replication defects in their telomeres, which leads to persistent DNA damage responses and the activation of telomeric MiDAS, a process of spontaneous DNA synthesis during mitosis. This MiDAS is triggered by DNA replication stress and may contribute to genomic duplications in cancer.

title: Light acts directly on organs and cells in culture to set the vertebrate circadian clock.
text: Clock genes are widely expressed in vertebrates and not limited to traditional clock structures. In zebrafish, the Clock gene exhibits a strong circadian oscillation in various tissues both in vivo and in culture, indicating the presence of internal oscillators in peripheral organs. One characteristic of circadian clocks is their ability to synchronize with local time, typically through the light-dark cycle in the environment. A crucial question is whether peripheral oscillators are entrained to local time by signals from central pacemakers, such as the eyes, or if they directly respond to light. Our findings demonstrate that the peripheral organ clocks in zebrafish are indeed regulated by light-dark cycles in culture. Additionally, we have discovered that a cell line derived from zebrafish possesses a circadian oscillator that is directly entrained by light.

title: Small molecule inhibition of the KRAS–PDEδ interaction impairs oncogenic KRAS signalling
text: The KRAS oncogene product is a significant focus in the search for anticancer drugs. However, attempts to directly interfere with KRAS signaling have not yet resulted in effective clinical drugs. The proper localization and signaling of farnesylated KRAS is regulated by the prenyl-binding protein PDEδ, which helps maintain the spatial organization of KRAS by aiding its movement in the cytoplasm. In this study, we demonstrate that disrupting the binding between mammalian PDEδ and KRAS using small molecules presents a new opportunity to inhibit oncogenic RAS signaling by altering its localization to endomembranes. Through biochemical screening and subsequent optimization based on the structure, we have developed inhibitors that selectively bind to the prenyl-binding pocket of PDEδ with high affinity, effectively inhibiting oncogenic RAS signaling. These inhibitors also suppress the growth of human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells that rely on oncogenic KRAS, both in vitro and in vivo. Our findings provide inspiration for future drug discovery efforts aimed at developing drugs that target oncogenic RAS.

title: Evolution of novel cooperative swarming in the bacterium Myxococcus xanthus
text: For evolutionary transitions to higher levels of biological organization, cooperation among individuals is essential. During these transitions, groups of individuals at one level, such as single cells, work together to form selective units at a higher level, like multicellular organisms. While observing the evolution of cooperation directly in higher eukaryotes is challenging, microorganisms provide an opportunity for such observations. In this study, we present the evolution of a new cooperative behavior in experimental lineages of the bacterium Myxococcus xanthus. The wild-type strains of M. xanthus exhibit socially dependent swarming on soft surfaces through a mechanism called 'S-motility,' which requires the presence of extracellular type IV pili. However, in lineages of M. xanthus that cannot produce pili, a new mechanism for cooperative swarming has evolved. This evolved swarming is facilitated, at least partially, by an increased production of an extracellular fibril matrix that binds cells together, serving their evolutionary interests. Although fibril production is costly to individuals, it significantly enhances population expansion in interconnected cell groups. These findings demonstrate that bacteria can readily undergo fundamental transitions towards primitive cooperation.

title: Exon duplication and divergence in the human preproglucagon gene
text: Glucagon is a hormone produced in the pancreas that opposes the blood glucose-lowering effects of insulin. It does this by stimulating the breakdown of glycogen in the liver and the production of new glucose. Recently, scientists have determined the structure of the glucagon precursor in hamsters by analyzing its cloned cDNA. This precursor is a protein made up of 180 amino acids and contains five functional regions: a signal peptide, an NH2-terminal peptide (also known as glicentin-related pancreatic peptide or GRPP), glucagon, and two carboxy-terminal glucagon-like peptides (GLP-1 and GLP-2). The structure of the glucagon precursor in anglerfish, which is not identical to the hamster protein, has also been studied. The anglerfish precursors lack the polypeptide segment corresponding to hamster GLP-2. The presence of three regions with internal homology (glucagon, GLP-1, and GLP-2) in the proglucagon protein, and the absence of GLP-2 in the anglerfish precursors, suggest that the structure of the preproglucagon gene could provide insights into the evolution of this polyprotein. The researchers have also isolated and sequenced the human preproglucagon gene and found that its organization is identical to the hamster protein.
