Importantly, the majority of these human iN cells were capable of generating action potentials and many matured to establish synaptic connections when co-cultured with primary mouse cortical neurons. Our results highlight the ability of lineage-determining transcription factors to directly convert non-neural human somatic cells, as well as pluripotent stem cells, into neurons. These methods have the potential to greatly facilitate the generation of patient-specific human neurons for disease modeling in vitro or for future applications in regenerative medicine.

title: PAAR-repeat proteins sharpen and diversify the Type VI secretion system spike
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a complex machine found in many Gram-negative bacteria that plays a crucial role in their ecological interactions. It enables these bacteria to kill both prokaryotic and eukaryotic prey cells by translocating a variety of toxic molecules. Similar to the tails of bacteriophages, the T6SS organelle is believed to penetrate cells using a trimeric protein complex called the VgrG spike. However, the exact composition of the T6SS organelle and the mechanisms of effector selection and delivery remain unknown. In this study, we discovered that proteins from the PAAR repeat superfamily form a conical extension on the VgrG spike, which helps attach effector domains to the spike. By examining the crystal structures of two PAAR-repeat proteins bound to VgrG-like partners, we observed that these proteins sharpen the tip of the T6SS spike complex. We also demonstrated that PAAR proteins are crucial for the secretion and killing of target cells by Vibrio cholerae and Acinetobacter baylyi using the T6SS. Our findings propose a new model for the T6SS organelle, suggesting that the VgrG-PAAR spike complex is adorned with multiple effectors that are simultaneously delivered into target cells through a single contraction-driven translocation event.

title: Replication stress activates DNA repair synthesis in mitosis
text: The presence of oncogenes can cause DNA replication stress, which is believed to contribute to the development of tumors. In human cancers, certain regions of the genome known as common fragile sites (CFSs) are responsible for many chromosomal rearrangements. These CFSs are difficult to replicate and can result in gaps or breaks on chromosomes when cells are exposed to replicative stress. The MUS81-EME1 endonuclease is responsible for creating these gaps or breaks at CFSs after replicative stress occurs. Our research shows that when cells enter mitotic prophase, MUS81 is recruited to CFSs. The nuclease activity of MUS81 then promotes DNA synthesis at CFSs, which is dependent on the POLD3 protein. This DNA synthesis helps prevent errors in chromosome segregation and non-disjunction. We propose that the attempt to condense incompletely duplicated regions in early mitosis triggers the completion of DNA replication at CFSs in human cells. This process of mitotic DNA synthesis, which relies on POLD3, is more active in aneuploid cancer cells that have high levels of chromosomal instability and replicative stress. Therefore, targeting this pathway could be a promising therapeutic approach.

title: A specific amyloid-β protein assembly in the brain impairs memory
text:
As people age, their memory function often declines. This decline is believed to be initially caused by changes in synaptic function rather than the loss of neurons. In some cases, individuals may go on to develop Alzheimer's disease, which involves neurodegeneration. To better understand the cause of memory decline without neurodegeneration or amyloid-β protein amyloidosis, we conducted a study using Tg2576 mice. These mice express a human amyloid-β precursor protein variant associated with Alzheimer's disease.

We observed that young Tg2576 mice (less than 6 months old) had normal memory and no signs of neuropathology. However, middle-aged mice (6-14 months old) developed memory deficits without any loss of neurons. As the mice aged further (over 14 months old), they formed abundant neuritic plaques containing amyloid-β.

Our research revealed that the memory deficits in middle-aged Tg2576 mice were caused by the accumulation of a 56-kDa soluble amyloid-β assembly, which we refer to as Aβ*56 (Aβ star 56). When we purified Aβ*56 from the brains of impaired Tg2576 mice and administered it to young rats, it disrupted their memory.

Based on these findings, we propose that Aβ*56 impairs memory independently of plaques or neuronal loss. It may play a role in the cognitive deficits associated with Alzheimer's disease.

title: Cleavage of GSDMD by inflammatory caspases determines pyroptotic cell death
text: Innate defenses rely on the activation of inflammatory caspases (caspase-1, -4, -5, and -11). Caspase-1 is triggered by various inflammasome ligands, while caspase-4, -5, and -11 directly recognize bacterial lipopolysaccharide, leading to pyroptosis. However, the mechanism behind pyroptosis induction by inflammatory caspases remains unknown. In this study, we used CRISPR-Cas9 nuclease screens to identify gasdermin D (Gsdmd) as a key player in caspase-11- and caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis in mouse bone marrow macrophages. Cells lacking GSDMD showed resistance to pyroptosis induced by cytosolic lipopolysaccharide and canonical inflammasome ligands. Additionally, the release of interleukin-1β was reduced in Gsdmd−/− cells, despite intact caspase-1 processing. Caspase-1 and caspase-4/5/11 specifically cleaved the linker between the gasdermin-N and gasdermin-C domains in GSDMD, which was necessary and sufficient for pyroptosis. This cleavage removed the intramolecular inhibition on the gasdermin-N domain, revealing its intrinsic pyroptosis-inducing activity. Other members of the gasdermin family were not cleaved by inflammatory caspases but shared autoinhibition. Gain-of-function mutations in Gsdma3, associated with alopecia and skin defects, disrupted the autoinhibition, allowing the gasdermin-N domain to trigger pyroptosis. These findings provide insights into inflammasome-mediated immunity and diseases, while also expanding our understanding of pyroptosis and programmed necrosis.

title: Role of corin in trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodelling in pregnancy
text:
During pregnancy, it is crucial for trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodelling to occur in order to reduce maternal vascular resistance and increase blood flow to the uterus and placenta. However, the exact mechanisms behind these processes have remained unclear, despite the long-standing association between impaired spiral artery remodelling and pre-eclampsia, a serious pregnancy complication. 

Recently, it has been discovered that corin, also known as atrial natriuretic peptide-converting enzyme, which is a protease found in the heart, is expressed in the pregnant uterus. This finding led to the identification of a new role for corin and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) in promoting trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodelling. 

To investigate further, experiments were conducted using pregnant mice that lacked corin or ANP. These mice developed high blood pressure and proteinuria, which are characteristic symptoms of pre-eclampsia. Additionally, their trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodelling were significantly impaired. In contrast, when human trophoblasts were exposed to ANP, they exhibited enhanced invasion capabilities in Matrigels. 

Further analysis was conducted on patients with pre-eclampsia, revealing significantly lower levels of uterine Corin messenger RNA and protein compared to normal pregnancies. Furthermore, mutations in the Corin gene were identified in pre-eclamptic patients, resulting in decreased corin activity in processing pro-ANP. 

These findings suggest that corin and ANP play essential roles in the physiological changes that occur at the maternal-fetal interface during pregnancy. Defects in corin and ANP function may contribute to the development of pre-eclampsia.

title: Metabolic rescue in pluripotent cells from patients with mtDNA disease
text:
The role of mitochondria in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation is crucial, and it relies on the expression of important genes encoded by mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Mutations in mtDNA can lead to severe disorders that are often fatal and have limited treatment options. The symptoms experienced by patients vary depending on the type of mutation and the levels of mutant and wild-type mtDNA within each cell, known as heteroplasmy.

In this study, we successfully created pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) that were genetically corrected from patients with mtDNA disease. We derived multiple induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines from patients with common heteroplasmic mutations, such as 3243A>G, which causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), and 8993T>G and 13513G>A, which are associated with Leigh syndrome.

To create isogenic MELAS and Leigh syndrome iPS cell lines, we allowed heteroplasmic mtDNA to spontaneously segregate in proliferating fibroblasts, resulting in cell lines that exclusively contained either wild-type or mutant mtDNA. Additionally, we used somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) to replace mutant mtDNA in homoplasmic 8993T>G fibroblasts, generating corrected Leigh-NT1 PSCs.

Although Leigh-NT1 PSCs contained wild-type mtDNA from donor oocytes (human haplotype D4a), which differed from the mtDNA haplotype (F1a) of the Leigh syndrome patients at 47 nucleotide sites, the Leigh-NT1 cells exhibited transcriptomic profiles similar to those of embryo-derived PSCs carrying wild-type mtDNA. This suggests that normal interactions between the nucleus and mitochondria were occurring.

Furthermore, the genetically rescued patient PSCs demonstrated normal metabolic function, in contrast to the impaired oxygen consumption and ATP production observed in mutant cells.

In conclusion, both reprogramming approaches used in this study offer complementary strategies for deriving PSCs that exclusively contain wild-type mtDNA. This can be achieved either through the spontaneous segregation of heteroplasmic mtDNA in individual iPS cell lines or through mitochondrial replacement via SCNT in diseases caused by homoplasmic mtDNA.

title: The yeast Pif1p helicase removes telomerase from telomeric DNA
text: Telomeres, which are found at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes, play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genetic material. Previous genetic studies have revealed that a DNA helicase called Pif1p in baker's yeast acts as a negative regulator of telomerase, an enzyme responsible for maintaining telomeric DNA. However, the exact mechanism behind this inhibition was not understood. In this study, we demonstrate that Pif1p reduces the efficiency of telomerase and releases it from telomeric oligonucleotides in laboratory conditions. Interestingly, the released telomerase remains enzymatically active and is capable of elongating a challenger oligonucleotide. In living organisms, overexpression of Pif1p leads to a decrease in telomerase association with telomeres, while depletion of Pif1p results in increased levels of Est1p, a telomerase subunit that is present on the telomere during telomerase activity. Based on these findings, we propose that the helicase activity of Pif1p limits the action of telomerase both in laboratory settings and within living organisms by displacing active telomerase from the ends of DNA.

title: Small regulatory RNAs inhibit RNA Polymerase II during the elongation phase of transcription
text: Eukaryotic cells have a wide range of small regulatory RNAs that play a role in various processes such as heterochromatin formation, developmental timing, defense against parasitic nucleic acids, and genome rearrangement. Many of these small regulatory RNAs are believed to function within the nuclei. For example, in plants and fungi, short interfering RNA (siRNAs) bind to newly formed transcripts and control chromatin and/or DNA modifications. To gain a better understanding of the biological functions of small regulatory RNAs, we conducted a genetic study to identify the factors necessary for RNA interference (RNAi) in the nuclei of Caenorhabditis elegans. Our findings reveal that a gene called nuclear RNAi defective-2 (nrde-2) encodes a conserved protein that is essential for siRNA-mediated silencing within the nuclei. NRDE-2 interacts with the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 within the nuclei and is recruited by NRDE-3/siRNA complexes to newly formed transcripts targeted by RNAi. We discovered that siRNAs localized within the nuclei direct NRDE-2-dependent silencing of pre-messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) downstream of RNAi sites. This process also leads to an accumulation of RNA polymerase (RNAP) II at genomic regions targeted by RNAi, as well as a decrease in RNAP II occupancy and transcriptional activity downstream of RNAi sites, both of which are dependent on NRDE-2. These findings establish NRDE-2 as a crucial component of the nuclear RNAi machinery and demonstrate that metazoan siRNAs can silence RNAs within the nucleus during transcription. Furthermore, our results reveal a novel mechanism of RNAP II regulation, where siRNAs recruit NRDE factors that inhibit RNAP II during the elongation phase of transcription.

title: Cdk1 is sufficient to drive the mammalian cell cycle
text: Yeasts, which are unicellular organisms, rely on a single cyclin-dependent kinase called Cdk1 to facilitate cell division. On the other hand, it is believed that mammalian cells require the sequential activation of four different cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) during interphase, as well as Cdk1 during mitosis, to drive cell progression. However, recent genetic evidence challenges this model, as mice have been found to survive without individual interphase Cdks. Additionally, many types of mouse cells can proliferate even in the absence of two or three interphase Cdks. Similar results have been observed when certain activating subunits of Cdks, such as D-type and E-type cyclins, are removed. In this study, we demonstrate that mouse embryos lacking all interphase Cdks (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) are still able to undergo organogenesis and develop until midgestation. In these embryos, Cdk1 binds to all cyclins, leading to the phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein pRb and the activation of genes regulated by E2F transcription factors. Mouse embryonic fibroblasts derived from these embryos can proliferate in vitro, although their cell cycle is prolonged due to inefficient inactivation of Rb proteins. However, with continuous passage, these cells become immortal. Furthermore, we found that embryos fail to progress beyond the morula and blastocyst stages in the absence of Cdk1. These findings suggest that Cdk1 is the sole essential cell cycle Cdk and can carry out all the necessary processes for cell division even in the absence of interphase Cdks.

title: Calorie restriction extends Saccharomyces cerevisiae lifespan by increasing respiration
text: Calorie restriction (CR) is a method that has been proven to increase the lifespan of various organisms and is currently the only known regimen that can extend the lifespan of mammals. To better understand the effects of CR, we conducted a study using budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model. By limiting glucose or reducing the activity of the glucose-sensing cyclic-AMP-dependent kinase (PKA), we were able to extend the lifespan of the yeast. However, in order to achieve lifespan extension in a mutant with reduced PKA activity, the presence of Sir2 and NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) was necessary. Our research aimed to investigate the mechanism through which CR activates Sir2 to extend lifespan. Our findings indicate that redirecting carbon metabolism towards the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle and the subsequent increase in respiration play a crucial role in this process. We also discuss the potential application of this metabolic strategy to CR in animals.

title: Mosaic PPM1D mutations are associated with predisposition to breast and ovarian cancer
text: The advancement of sequencing technologies has opened up unprecedented opportunities for studying the impact of rare genetic variations on common diseases. However, there are significant challenges in terms of study design, data analysis, and replication. In this study, we utilized pooled next-generation sequencing to analyze 507 genes involved in DNA repair in 1,150 samples. Our analytical approach focused on protein-truncating variants (PTVs), and we conducted a large-scale sequencing case-control replication experiment involving 13,642 individuals. Our findings reveal that rare PTVs in the p53-inducible protein phosphatase PPM1D are associated with an increased risk of breast cancer and ovarian cancer. We observed PPM1D PTV mutations in 25 out of 7,781 cases compared to only 1 out of 5,861 controls (P = 1.12 × 10−5). Specifically, we identified 18 mutations in 6,912 individuals with breast cancer (P = 2.42 × 10−4) and 12 mutations in 1,121 individuals with ovarian cancer (P = 3.10 × 10−9). Notably, all of the identified PPM1D PTVs were mosaic in lymphocyte DNA and clustered within a 370-base-pair region in the final exon of the gene, located after the phosphatase catalytic domain. Functional studies demonstrated that these mutations led to an enhanced suppression of p53 in response to ionizing radiation exposure, suggesting that the mutant alleles encode hyperactive PPM1D isoforms. Therefore, while the mutations result in premature protein truncation, they do not simply cause a loss-of-function effect typically associated with this type of variant. Instead, they likely have a gain-of-function effect. Our findings have important implications for the detection and management of breast and ovarian cancer risk. Moreover, they provide valuable insights into the role of rare and mosaic genetic variants in common conditions, as well as the use of sequencing in their identification.

title: Immunogenicity of induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have great potential for regenerative medicine as a source of autologous cells. However, it has been assumed that these autologous cells would be immune-tolerated by the recipient, but their immunogenicity has not been thoroughly examined. Our study demonstrates that while embryonic stem cells (ESCs) derived from inbred C57BL/6 (B6) mice can form teratomas without immune rejection, allogeneic ESCs from 129/SvJ mice are rapidly rejected by B6 mice. We reprogrammed B6 mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) into iPSCs using either a retroviral approach (ViPSCs) or a novel episomal approach (EiPSCs) that does not integrate into the genome. Unlike B6 ESCs, teratomas formed by B6 ViPSCs were mostly rejected by B6 recipients. Additionally, the majority of teratomas formed by B6 EiPSCs were immunogenic in B6 mice, with T cell infiltration and tissue damage observed in some cases. Gene expression analysis revealed overexpression of certain genes in teratomas derived from B6 EiPSCs, and some of these gene products directly contributed to the immunogenicity of the B6 EiPSC-derived cells in B6 mice. These findings suggest that abnormal gene expression in certain cells differentiated from iPSCs can trigger a T-cell-dependent immune response in syngeneic recipients. Therefore, the immunogenicity of therapeutically valuable cells derived from patient-specific iPSCs should be evaluated before clinical application.

title: Direct conversion of human fibroblasts to multilineage blood progenitors
text: Our understanding of lineage specification limits the application of reprogrammed human induced pluripotent stem cells, similar to embryo-derived stem cells. However, we have successfully generated progenitors and mature cells of the haematopoietic fate directly from human dermal fibroblasts without establishing pluripotency. By activating haematopoietic transcription factors through ectopic expression of OCT4 (also known as POU5F1) and treating with specific cytokines, we were able to generate cells expressing the pan-leukocyte marker CD45. These unique fibroblast-derived cells gave rise to various lineages, including granulocytic, monocytic, megakaryocytic, and erythroid, and demonstrated the ability to engraft in vivo. It is important to note that adult haematopoietic programs were activated, indicating that we bypassed the pluripotent state to generate blood fate, which is different from haematopoiesis involving pluripotent stem cells where embryonic programs are activated. These findings highlight the restoration of multipotency from human fibroblasts and propose an alternative approach to cellular reprogramming for autologous cell-replacement therapies that avoids complications associated with the use of human pluripotent stem cells.

title: Mical links semaphorins to F-actin disassembly
text: The precise effects of instructive cues on the actin cytoskeleton, which are present on the cell surface, are not well understood. Semaphorins are a large family of these cues and have been extensively studied for their impact on cell movement, navigation, angiogenesis, immunology, and cancer. While semaphorins/collapsins have been known to significantly alter actin cytoskeletal dynamics in neuronal processes, the molecules that connect them to the precise control of cytoskeletal elements remain unknown, despite progress in identifying semaphorin receptors and their signaling pathways. Recently, a group of unusual proteins called Mical enzymes have been discovered to associate with the cytoplasmic part of plexins, which are large semaphorin receptors on the cell surface. These Mical enzymes play a role in axon guidance, synaptogenesis, dendritic pruning, and other changes in cell morphology. Mical enzymes perform enzymatic reactions involving reduction-oxidation (redox) and also contain domains found in proteins that regulate cell shape. However, the role of Mical or its redox activity in mediating morphological changes is not yet understood. In this study, we demonstrate that Mical directly connects semaphorins and their plexin receptors to the precise control of actin filament dynamics. We show that Mical is essential and sufficient for semaphorin-plexin-mediated reorganization of actin filaments in living organisms. Additionally, we purified Mical protein and discovered that it directly binds to and disassembles both individual and bundled actin filaments. Furthermore, we found that Mical utilizes its redox activity to modify actin filament dynamics in living organisms and in laboratory settings, revealing a previously unknown role for specific redox signaling events in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Therefore, Mical is a novel factor that disassembles actin filaments and serves as a molecular pathway through which actin reorganization, a key feature of cell morphological changes such as axon navigation, can be precisely achieved in response to semaphorins.

title: Novel Foxo1-dependent transcriptional programs control Treg cell function
text: Regulatory T (Treg) cells, which are identified by the presence of the transcription factor forkhead box P3 (Foxp3), play a crucial role in maintaining a balanced immune system by suppressing harmful immune responses. Foxp3 functions as a late-acting factor that regulates the homeostasis and function of Treg cells. On the other hand, the early commitment of Treg cell lineage is controlled by the Akt kinase and the forkhead box O (Foxo) family of transcription factors. However, it is not well understood whether Foxo proteins continue to regulate Treg cell homeostasis and function beyond the commitment stage. In this study, we demonstrate that Foxo1 is a key regulator of Treg cell function. Treg cells express high levels of Foxo1 and show reduced activation of Akt, phosphorylation of Foxo1, and exclusion of Foxo1 from the nucleus upon stimulation of the T-cell receptor. Mice with specific deletion of Foxo1 in Treg cells develop a severe inflammatory disorder similar to that observed in mice lacking Foxp3, but without a loss of Treg cells. Through a comprehensive analysis of Foxo1 binding sites across the genome, we identify approximately 300 target genes that are bound by Foxo1, including the pro-inflammatory cytokine Ifng, which does not appear to be directly regulated by Foxp3. These findings highlight the importance of the Akt-Foxo1 signaling pathway in controlling a unique genetic program that is essential for Treg cell function.

title: Functional screening identifies miRNAs inducing cardiac regeneration
text: The enlargement of the heart in mammals during embryonic development primarily relies on an increase in the number of cardiomyocytes. However, after birth, cardiomyocytes cease to proliferate, and further growth of the myocardium occurs through the hypertrophic enlargement of existing myocytes. Due to the limited renewal of cardiomyocytes in adult life, the ability to repair cardiac damage through myocardial regeneration is greatly restricted. In this study, we demonstrate that the administration of specific microRNAs (miRNAs) can significantly stimulate cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhance cardiac repair. We conducted a comprehensive screening using high-content microscopy and high-throughput techniques to identify human miRNAs that promote neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation, utilizing a whole-genome miRNA library. We discovered that forty miRNAs greatly increased DNA synthesis and cytokinesis in neonatal mouse and rat cardiomyocytes. From these, we selected two miRNAs (hsa-miR-590 and hsa-miR-199a) for further testing, which were found to induce cell cycle re-entry in adult cardiomyocytes ex vivo and promote cardiomyocyte proliferation in both neonatal and adult animals. Following myocardial infarction in mice, these miRNAs stimulated significant cardiac regeneration and nearly complete recovery of cardiac functional parameters. The identified miRNAs show immense potential for the treatment of cardiac pathologies resulting from cardiomyocyte loss.

title: Specificity of sensory–motor connections encoded by Sema3e–Plxnd1 recognition
text: Synaptic connections between sensory afferents and motor neurons are responsible for spinal reflexes. These circuits have different levels of specificity. Only certain types of proprioceptive sensory neurons directly connect with motor neurons, following rules of motor pool specificity. They form strong connections with motor neurons that supply the same muscle, while avoiding those that supply antagonistic muscles. This connectivity pattern is initially accurate and remains unchanged even without activity, suggesting that wiring specificity depends on recognition molecules on the surface of sensory and motor neurons. However, the factors that determine fine synaptic specificity in these circuits, as well as in other parts of the central nervous system, are still unknown. To investigate the origins of synaptic specificity, we used molecular genetic techniques to manipulate recognition proteins expressed by subsets of sensory and motor neurons. Our study reveals that a recognition system involving the expression of the class 3 semaphorin Sema3e by specific motor neuron pools, and its high-affinity receptor plexin D1 (Plxnd1) by proprioceptive sensory neurons, plays a crucial role in determining synaptic specificity in sensory-motor circuits in mice. Altering the Sema3e-Plxnd1 signaling in sensory or motor neurons leads to functional and anatomical rewiring of monosynaptic connections, but does not affect motor pool specificity. These findings suggest that the patterns of monosynaptic connectivity in this central nervous system circuit are established through a recognition program based on repellent signaling.

title: A chromatin remodelling complex involved in transcription and DNA processing.
text: Chromatin, the packaging of the eukaryotic genome, creates obstacles that prevent enzymes from accessing and processing DNA. To overcome these obstacles, cells possess various ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes, each containing an ATPase subunit from the SNF2/SWI2 superfamily. These complexes, known as chromatin remodeling complexes, enhance the mobility of nucleosomes and play a clear role in transcription. In this study, we examined SNF2/SWI2- and ISWI-related proteins to identify remodeling complexes that potentially assist in other DNA processes. We successfully isolated a complex from Saccharomyces cerevisiae that contains the Ino80 ATPase. The INO80 complex consists of approximately 12 polypeptides, including two proteins similar to the bacterial RuvB DNA helicase, which is responsible for the migration of Holliday junctions. The purified complex is capable of remodeling chromatin, facilitating transcription in vitro, and exhibiting 3' to 5' DNA helicase activity. Mutations in the ino80 gene result in increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and transcriptional defects. These findings suggest that chromatin remodeling, driven by the Ino80 ATPase, may be involved in both transcription and DNA damage repair.

title: Oncogenic pathway signatures in human cancers as a guide to targeted therapies
text: The process of developing an oncogenic state is complex and involves the accumulation of multiple mutations that disrupt cell signaling pathways responsible for controlling cell growth and fate. DNA microarray-based gene expression signatures have been used in various studies to identify cancer subtypes, predict disease recurrence, and determine response to specific therapies. These studies have also shown the potential of gene expression profiles in analyzing oncogenic pathways. Our research demonstrates that gene expression signatures can indicate the activation status of multiple oncogenic pathways. When applied to large collections of human cancers, these signatures reveal patterns of pathway deregulation and clinically relevant associations with disease outcomes. By combining predictions from multiple pathways, we can identify coordinated patterns of pathway deregulation that distinguish between different cancers and tumor subtypes. Clustering tumors based on pathway signatures further helps define prognosis in specific patient groups, highlighting the role of oncogenic pathway deregulation in the development of the oncogenic phenotype and the biology and outcome of specific cancers. Additionally, our findings show that predictions of pathway deregulation in cancer cell lines can predict sensitivity to therapeutic agents targeting components of the pathway. This connection between pathway deregulation and therapeutic sensitivity provides an opportunity to use these oncogenic pathway signatures to guide the use of targeted therapies.

title: CTCF mediates methylation-sensitive enhancer-blocking activity at the H19/Igf2 locus.
text: The genes Igf2 and H19 are imprinted, meaning that the maternal and paternal alleles are silenced, respectively. This silencing is dependent on an imprinted-control region located two kilobases upstream of H19. On the paternal chromosome, this region is methylated and necessary for the silencing of H19. On the maternal chromosome, the region is unmethylated and required for silencing of the Igf2 gene, which is located 90 kilobases upstream. Our hypothesis is that the unmethylated imprinted-control region acts as a chromatin boundary, preventing the interaction between Igf2 and enhancers located 3' of H19. When the region becomes methylated, this enhancer-blocking activity is lost, allowing for the expression of Igf2 paternally. In this study, we demonstrate through the use of transgenic mice and tissue culture that the unmethylated imprinted-control regions from mouse and human H19 possess enhancer-blocking activity. Additionally, we find that CTCF, a zinc finger protein involved in vertebrate boundary function, binds to several sites within the unmethylated imprinted-control region that are crucial for enhancer blocking. Consistent with our model, DNA methylation abolishes CTCF binding. This represents the first known instance of a regulated chromatin boundary in vertebrates.

title: Broad and potent neutralization of HIV-1 by a gp41-specific human antibody
text:
The characterization of human monoclonal antibodies is providing valuable insights into the mechanisms of broad HIV-1 neutralization. In this study, we present a specific antibody called 10E8 that targets the HIV-1 gp41 membrane-proximal external region (MPER) and is capable of neutralizing approximately 98% of tested viruses. Our analysis of sera from 78 healthy HIV-1-infected individuals revealed that 27% of them contained MPER-specific antibodies, while 8% contained antibodies with similar specificities to 10E8.

Unlike other MPER antibodies with neutralizing properties, 10E8 does not bind to phospholipids, does not exhibit autoreactivity, and binds to the envelope on the surface of cells. By examining the structure of 10E8 in complex with the complete MPER, we identified a vulnerable site consisting of a narrow stretch of highly conserved hydrophobic residues in gp41, along with a critical arginine or lysine just before the transmembrane region. Our analysis of HIV-1 variants that are resistant to neutralization further confirmed the significance of these residues.

The MPER, which is highly conserved, represents a target for potent neutralizing antibodies that do not react with self-components. This suggests that HIV-1 vaccines should focus on inducing antibodies against this specific region of the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein.

title: Disruption of the Hepcidin/Ferroportin Regulatory System Causes Pulmonary Iron Overload and Restrictive Lung Disease
text: New evidence suggests that the accumulation of iron in the lungs is linked to various chronic lung diseases. However, we still do not know the exact mechanism(s) behind how iron is deposited in the lungs and its role in the development of these diseases in living organisms. In this study, we demonstrate that a specific mutation in the ferroportin gene in mice, known as hereditary hemochromatosis type 4 (Slc40a1C326S), leads to increased levels of iron in alveolar macrophages, epithelial cells that line the airways, lung tissue, and vascular smooth muscle cells. This excessive iron in the lungs is associated with oxidative stress and results in a restrictive lung disease characterized by reduced lung capacity and lower blood oxygen saturation in mice with the homozygous Slc40a1C326S/C326S mutation compared to normal mice. These findings suggest that iron plays a role in lung diseases, which is not traditionally considered an iron-related disorder.

title: Genome-wide genetic analysis of polyploidy in yeast
text: Polyploidy, the increase in the number of chromosome sets, occurs during various processes such as development, cellular stress, disease, and evolution. Despite its common occurrence, there is limited knowledge about the physiological changes that accompany polyploidy. In a previous study, we observed a phenomenon called 'ploidy-specific lethality', where the deletion of a gene that is not lethal in haploid or diploid budding yeast leads to lethality in triploids or tetraploids. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis to identify functions that are specifically lethal in different ploidy levels. Out of the 3,740 mutations screened, only 39 exhibited ploidy-specific lethality. These mutations primarily affected genomic stability by impairing processes such as homologous recombination, sister chromatid cohesion, and mitotic spindle function. Through our analysis, we also discovered defects in wild-type tetraploids that were predicted by the screening, and we identified mechanisms through which tetraploidization impacts genomic stability. Specifically, we found that tetraploids have a higher occurrence of syntelic/monopolar kinetochore attachments to the spindle pole. We propose that this defect may be attributed to discrepancies in the ability to scale the size of the spindle pole body, spindle, and kinetochores. Therefore, geometric constraints can have significant effects on genome stability, and this phenomenon may have implications in various biological contexts, including disease states like cancer.

title: Diverse and heritable lineage imprinting of early haematopoietic progenitors
text: The production of blood cells by haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their progenitors is a topic of debate due to the lack of precise understanding of the process. One proposed model suggests that lymphoid and myeloid production diverge after the lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitor (LMPP), with both branches eventually producing dendritic cells. However, this model is primarily based on laboratory experiments and population-based tracking, which may overlook the complexity of single-cell behavior in vivo. To address these limitations, we utilized a new quantitative technique called 'cellular barcoding' to track the fate of hundreds of LMPPs and HSCs at the individual cell level. Our findings reveal that LMPPs exhibit significant heterogeneity in the types of cells they produce, with some biased towards lymphoid, myeloid, or dendritic cell production. On the other hand, while certain HSCs display a lineage bias, the majority of cellular output originates from a small number of HSCs that generate all cell types. Importantly, our analysis of sibling cells derived from single LMPPs demonstrates that they often share a similar fate, suggesting that the fate of these progenitors is predetermined. Additionally, we observe similar imprinting in dendritic cell-biased LMPPs, indicating that dendritic cells may be considered a distinct lineage based on their separate ancestry. These findings support a 'graded commitment' model of haematopoiesis, where diverse lineage imprinting occurs earlier than previously believed.

title: Crowding induces live cell extrusion to maintain homeostatic cell numbers in epithelia
text: In order for an epithelium to act as a protective barrier, it must maintain a balance between cell division and cell death to regulate cell numbers. While dying cells can trigger compensatory cell division, it is unclear how cell death helps alleviate overcrowding caused by cell proliferation. When apoptosis is induced in epithelial cells, dying cells are expelled to maintain the functionality of the barrier. This expulsion occurs when dying cells signal surrounding epithelial cells to contract an actomyosin ring, which pushes the dying cell out. However, the factors driving cell death during normal homeostasis are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that overcrowding resulting from cell proliferation and migration leads to the expulsion of live cells, thus controlling the number of epithelial cells. Live cell expulsion occurs at sites with the highest overcrowding in vivo and can be induced by artificially overcrowding cell monolayers in vitro. Similar to apoptotic cell expulsion, live cell expulsion due to overcrowding also relies on sphingosine 1-phosphate signaling and Rho-kinase-dependent myosin contraction, but is distinguished by signaling through stretch-activated channels. Additionally, disrupting a stretch-activated channel called Piezo1 in zebrafish prevents cell expulsion and leads to the formation of masses of epithelial cells. Our findings reveal that during normal turnover, growth, and division of epithelial cells on a confined surface leads to overcrowding, which in turn triggers cell expulsion and subsequent cell death due to the loss of survival factors. These results suggest that live cell expulsion could be a mechanism that suppresses tumor growth by preventing the accumulation of excess epithelial cells.

title: Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells
text: In adaptive immunity, the activation of T cells is a crucial process that occurs when their T-cell receptors interact with antigenic peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs). To better understand T-cell sensitivity and the formation of an immunological synapse in individual cells, we utilized three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy. Our study focused on visualizing peptide-I-Ek class II MHC complexes, which were labeled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin. Our findings demonstrate that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen exhibit transient calcium signaling in response to even a single agonist peptide-MHC ligand. Additionally, when approximately ten agonists are present, the organization of molecules in the contact zone between the T cell and APC resembles that of an immunological synapse. Notably, the sensitivity of this response is heavily reliant on CD4, as blocking this molecule with antibodies prevents T cells from detecting fewer than approximately 30 ligands.

title: Crypt stem cells as the cells-of-origin of intestinal cancer
text: Mutations in genes like adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) activate the Wnt pathway and initiate intestinal cancer. However, the cell of origin for this type of cancer has been difficult to identify. In a mouse model called Lgr5 knockin, where a tamoxifen-inducible Cre recombinase is expressed in long-lived intestinal stem cells, we discovered that deleting Apc in these stem cells leads to their transformation in just a few days. These transformed stem cells remain at the bottom of the crypts and contribute to the growth of microadenomas. These microadenomas grow without any hindrance and develop into visible adenomas within 3-5 weeks. The presence of Lgr5+ cells within these adenomas suggests that a hierarchy of stem cells and progenitor cells is maintained in the early stages of neoplastic lesions. On the other hand, when Apc is deleted in short-lived transit-amplifying cells using a different cre mouse, the growth of microadenomas is quickly halted. Even after 30 weeks, large adenomas are extremely rare in these mice. In conclusion, the specific loss of Apc in stem cells leads to the progressive growth of neoplasia.

title: Microbial engineering for the production of advanced biofuels
text: Microorganisms can produce advanced biofuels that possess comparable properties to petroleum-based fuels and can seamlessly integrate into the current transportation infrastructure. However, achieving sufficient yields of these biofuels for practical use necessitates the manipulation of the microorganisms' metabolism. This engineering process is not limited to a single feedstock or host organism, as it can be tailored using data-driven and synthetic biology techniques to enhance both the host and pathways, thereby maximizing fuel production. Although there have been some achievements, there are still obstacles to overcome in order to advance the commercialization of these biofuels and effectively compete with traditional fuel sources.

title: Sperm chromatin proteomics identifies evolutionarily conserved fertility factors
text: Male infertility is a longstanding mystery that is of great concern in the medical field. The condition of sperm chromatin is an important indicator of male fertility and the potential for in vitro fertilization. Reproductive failure has been found to be correlated with chromosome abnormalities and damage to the DNA in sperm. By identifying proteins that play a crucial role in the structure and packaging of sperm chromatin, we can uncover universal causes of infertility. In this study, we used a combination of proteomics, cytology, and functional analysis in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans to identify proteins associated with chromatin in sperm that are essential for fertility. Our approach involved several steps, including purifying chromatin from comparable cell types undergoing spermatogenesis or oogenesis, analyzing the proteins using multidimensional protein identification technology, prioritizing proteins based on abundance, and eliminating common proteins to focus on those specific to sperm chromatin. Through this process, we narrowed down the list of proteins co-purified with spermatogenic chromatin from 1,099 to 132 for further analysis. By using RNA interference to reduce gene function and studying protein localization, we discovered conserved proteins that are crucial for DNA compaction, chromosome segregation, and fertility in spermatogenesis. Surprisingly, we also found that some proteins involved in other processes play unexpected roles in spermatogenesis. Our strategy successfully identified fertility factors that are conserved from C. elegans to mammals, as evidenced by the fact that 37% of mouse gene knockouts corresponding to nematode proteins resulted in male sterility. This comprehensive list of proteins provides a significant opportunity to uncover the causes of male infertility and develop targets for male contraceptives.

title: Nanog safeguards pluripotency and mediates germline development
text: Nanog is a protein that is present in pluripotent cells and developing germ cells in mammals. If Nanog is deleted, it leads to the death of the embryo at an early stage. On the other hand, if Nanog is constantly expressed, it allows embryonic stem cells to renew themselves independently. Nanog is considered to be a crucial component of the transcriptional network that maintains pluripotency. However, our study reveals that Nanog levels fluctuate in mouse embryonic stem cells. When Nanog is temporarily reduced, it seems to make the cells more likely to differentiate, but it does not indicate commitment to a specific cell type. Through genetic deletion, we demonstrate that embryonic stem cells can continue to self-renew indefinitely even without Nanog, although they are more prone to differentiation. Nanog-deficient cells can populate the embryonic germ layers and undergo differentiation into multiple cell lineages in both fetal and adult chimeras. While these cells can also migrate to the germ line, primordial germ cells lacking Nanog are unable to mature when they reach the genital ridge. However, this defect can be corrected by repairing the mutant allele. Therefore, Nanog is not essential for maintaining somatic pluripotency, but it plays a specific role in the development of germ cells. Nanog primarily functions in the formation of the inner cell mass and germ cell states, rather than in the general machinery that maintains pluripotency. We propose that Nanog helps to stabilize embryonic stem cells in culture by preventing or reversing alternative gene expression patterns.

title: Succinate is an inflammatory signal that induces IL-1β through HIF-1α
text: The core metabolism of macrophages is altered when activated by lipopolysaccharide, a product of Gram-negative bacteria. Specifically, their metabolism shifts from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis. In our study, we found that inhibiting glycolysis with 2-deoxyglucose effectively reduces lipopolysaccharide-induced interleukin-1β production in mouse macrophages, but not tumour-necrosis factor-α. By creating a comprehensive metabolic map of lipopolysaccharide-activated macrophages, we observed an increase in glycolytic gene expression and a decrease in mitochondrial gene expression, which directly correlates with changes in metabolite levels. One notable metabolite that significantly increases upon lipopolysaccharide stimulation is succinate, an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle. We discovered that succinate is primarily derived from glutamine-dependent anerplerosis, although the "GABA shunt" pathway also plays a role. The presence of lipopolysaccharide stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α through succinate, and this effect is inhibited by 2-deoxyglucose. Interleukin-1β is an important target of this succinate-mediated effect. Additionally, lipopolysaccharide leads to increased succinylation of various proteins. In conclusion, we have identified succinate as a metabolite involved in innate immune signaling, specifically enhancing interleukin-1β production during inflammation.

title: Planar cell polarity signalling couples cell division and morphogenesis during neurulation
text:
Neural tube closure defects (NTDs) occur in approximately 1 out of every 1,000 births due to environmental and genetic abnormalities. Previous studies using mouse and frog models have suggested that Van Gogh-like 2 (Vangl2) and other components of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling may play a role in controlling neurulation by promoting the convergence of neural progenitors towards the midline. In this study, we investigate the involvement of PCP signaling in zebrafish during neurulation and uncover a new function for this pathway.

Our findings demonstrate that non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling is responsible for polarizing neural progenitors along the anteroposterior axis. This polarization is temporarily lost during cell division in the neural keel but is re-established as daughter cells reintegrate into the neuroepithelium. We observe that the loss of zebrafish Vangl2 (in trilobite mutants) disrupts the polarization of neural keel cells, impairs the re-integration of daughter cells into the neuroepithelium, and leads to abnormal accumulations of neural progenitors and NTDs.

Interestingly, we also find that blocking cell division rescues the morphogenesis of the trilobite neural tube, despite persistent defects in convergence and extension. These results highlight the role of PCP signaling in coordinating cell division and morphogenesis during neurulation and suggest a previously unknown mechanism that may contribute to the development of NTDs.

title: The challenge of new drug discovery for tuberculosis
text: Tuberculosis (TB) is currently more widespread than ever before in human history. The pathogen responsible for TB, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, employs various tactics to survive in different host lesions and avoid detection by the immune system. A crucial question is how effective our methods are in finding new TB drugs, and what can be done to expedite the lengthy and complicated process of developing these drugs. The rise of multi-drug-resistant strains of M. tuberculosis has made it imperative to prioritize the discovery of new molecular structures, and in some cases, modify and reposition existing drug families to achieve effective control. Regardless of the approach taken, success will heavily rely on our comprehensive understanding of the intricate interactions between the pathogen and its human host. This article explores advancements in TB drug discovery and evolving strategies to expedite the delivery of newer treatments to patients.

title: Subunit Arrangement and Phenylethanolamine Binding in GluN1/GluN2B NMDA Receptors
text: Since the discovery of the neuroprotective activity of the anti-hypertensive agent ifenprodil on NMDA receptors, there has been a determined effort to understand its mechanism of action and develop better therapeutic compounds based on this knowledge. NMDA receptors play a crucial role in brain development and function by mediating neurotransmission. These receptors are composed of heteromeric ion channels that are activated when glycine and glutamate bind to the GluN1 and GluN2 subunits, respectively. A unique characteristic of NMDA receptors is that their ion-channel activity is regulated by the binding of small compounds to the amino-terminal domain (ATD) in a subtype-specific manner. Ifenprodil and similar compounds that specifically inhibit GluN1 and GluN2B NMDA receptors have been extensively studied for their potential use in treating neurological disorders like depression, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. However, the understanding of how phenylethanolamines and ATD-mediated allosteric inhibition are recognized is limited due to a lack of structural information. In this study, we present the crystal structure of the heterodimer formed by the GluN1 and GluN2B ATDs, revealing that phenylethanolamine binds at the interface between GluN1 and GluN2B rather than within the GluN2B cleft. This structure differs from the arrangements observed in non-NMDA receptors and provides insights into the molecular basis of phenylethanolamine binding. By restricting the movement of the GluN2B ATD domain through the introduction of an inter-subunit disulphide bond, we observed a significant decrease in sensitivity to ifenprodil, indicating that conformational freedom in the GluN2B ATD is crucial for its allosteric inhibition by ifenprodil. These findings open up possibilities for designing subtype-specific compounds with therapeutic potential for neurological disorders and diseases.

title: Association of NOD2 leucine-rich repeat variants with susceptibility to Crohn's disease.
text: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are two types of chronic inflammatory bowel disease that have unknown causes. Researchers have identified a specific region on chromosome 16 that is associated with susceptibility to Crohn's disease. Through a strategy called positional cloning, which involves analyzing genetic linkages and disequilibrium, three separate associations for Crohn's disease have been discovered. These associations involve variations in the NOD2 gene, which is responsible for producing a protein involved in regulating cell death. The NOD2 variants affect either the structure of the protein's leucine-rich repeat domain or the adjacent region. NOD2 activates a protein called nuclear factor NF-kB, and this activation is controlled by the carboxy-terminal leucine-rich repeat domain, which also acts as a receptor for certain microbial pathogens. These findings suggest that the NOD2 gene variants increase susceptibility to Crohn's disease by altering the recognition of these pathogens and/or by over-activating NF-kB in monocytes. This provides a molecular model for understanding the mechanisms behind Crohn's disease, which can now be further explored.

title: Human cardiovascular progenitor cells develop from a KDR+ embryonic-stem-cell-derived population
text: The functional heart is made up of different types of cells derived from the mesoderm, including cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Research on mouse embryos and mouse embryonic stem cells has shown that these three cell types develop from a common cardiovascular progenitor called Flk-1+ (also known as Kdr), which is an early stage in the specification of mesoderm to cardiovascular lineages. To determine if a similar progenitor exists during human heart development, we studied the development of cardiovascular cells in human embryonic stem cell cultures. Our findings show that when human embryonic stem cells are induced with activin A, bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF or FGF2), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF or VEGFA), and dickkopf homolog 1 (DKK1) in a serum-free environment, they generate a population of cells that are KDRlow/C-KIT(CD117)neg. These cells have the potential to become cardiac, endothelial, and vascular smooth muscle cells in vitro and in vivo after transplantation. When these cells are cultured in a monolayer, they differentiate into more than 50% contracting cardiomyocytes. When plated in methylcellulose cultures, the KDRlow/C-KITneg cells give rise to colonies containing all three cell types. Further studies using limiting dilution and cell-mixing experiments confirm that these colonies are clones and develop from a cardiovascular colony-forming cell. These findings reveal the existence of a human cardiovascular progenitor that represents one of the earliest stages of human heart development.

title: Cancer-related inflammation
text: The mediators and cellular effectors of inflammation play a crucial role in the local environment of tumors. In certain types of cancer, inflammatory conditions are present even before the onset of malignancy. On the other hand, in some types of cancer, an oncogenic change triggers an inflammatory microenvironment that facilitates tumor growth. Regardless of its origin, persistent inflammation within the tumor microenvironment has numerous tumor-promoting effects. It supports the proliferation and survival of cancerous cells, stimulates the formation of new blood vessels and the spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body, undermines the body's immune responses, and alters the way hormones and chemotherapy drugs affect the tumor. Scientists are currently unraveling the molecular pathways involved in this inflammation associated with cancer, which has led to the discovery of new molecules that could serve as targets for improved diagnosis and treatment.

title: ESCRT-III recognition by VPS4 ATPases
text: The ESCRT pathway is crucial for various important biological processes, such as the formation of intraluminal vesicles in endosomes, HIV budding, and cytokinesis. VPS4 ATPases play a vital role in this pathway by identifying ESCRT-III assemblies associated with the membrane and catalyzing their disassembly, potentially in conjunction with membrane fission. Our research demonstrates that the microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domains of human VPS4A and VPS4B bind to conserved sequence motifs located at the carboxy termini of the CHMP1–3 class of ESCRT-III proteins. Through the structures of VPS4A MIT–CHMP1A and VPS4B MIT–CHMP2B complexes, we have discovered that the C-terminal CHMP motif forms an amphipathic helix that binds in a groove between the last two helices of the tetratricopeptide-like repeat (TPR) of the VPS4 MIT domain. However, it binds in the opposite orientation compared to a typical TPR interaction. The MIT domain contains distinct pockets that bind three conserved leucine residues of the CHMP motif. Mutations that disrupt these interactions prevent VPS4 recruitment, hinder endosomal protein sorting, and alleviate the inhibitory effects of dominant-negative VPS4 on HIV budding. Therefore, our findings shed light on how VPS4 ATPases recognize their CHMP substrates, enabling the membrane fission events necessary for the release of viruses, endosomal vesicles, and daughter cells.

title: Pif1 family helicases suppress genome instability at G-quadruplex motifs
text: The Pif1 DNA helicase family, of which the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase is the prototypical member, is found in various organisms ranging from bacteria to humans. Our study reveals that the ability to unwind G-quadruplex structures is a shared characteristic among Pif1 helicases. Additionally, Pif1 helicases from organisms that have diverged over billions of years of evolution were found to protect against DNA damage at G-quadruplex motifs in yeast. The absence of Pif1 helicases resulted in the formation of G-quadruplex-induced damage, leading to novel genetic and epigenetic alterations. Moreover, when introduced into yeast, the human PIF1 helicase effectively prevented both G-quadruplex-associated DNA damage and telomere elongation.

title: Lysyl oxidase is essential for hypoxia-induced metastasis
text: Metastasis, the process responsible for the majority of cancer deaths, is influenced by both the immediate microenvironment (interactions between cells or between cells and the surrounding matrix) and the extended tumor microenvironment (such as vascularization). Hypoxia, or low oxygen levels, is clinically linked to metastasis and poor patient outcomes, although the exact underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. Studies using microarrays have revealed increased expression of lysyl oxidase (LOX) in hypoxic human tumor cells. Interestingly, LOX expression is associated with both tumor suppression and tumor progression, and its role in cancer development appears to depend on the location of the cells, the cell type, and their transformation status. In this study, we demonstrate that LOX expression is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and is correlated with hypoxia in breast and head and neck tumors in humans. Patients with tumors that express high levels of LOX have lower rates of distant metastasis-free survival and overall survival. Inhibiting LOX effectively prevents metastasis in mice with orthotopically grown breast cancer tumors. Mechanistically, LOX secreted by hypoxic cancer cells promotes invasiveness through the activation of focal adhesion kinase and cell-to-matrix adhesion. Additionally, LOX may play a crucial role in creating a favorable environment for metastatic growth. Our findings highlight the essential role of LOX in hypoxia-induced metastasis and suggest that it could be a promising therapeutic target for preventing and treating metastases.

title: Identification of human brain tumour initiating cells
text: The hypothesis of cancer stem cells (CSCs) suggests that a small fraction of cells with stem cell properties exclusively maintain neoplastic clones. While CSCs have been found in human leukemia, there is limited evidence for their presence in solid tumors, except for breast cancer. Recently, we isolated a subpopulation of CD133+ cells from human brain tumors that displayed stem cell properties in laboratory settings. However, the true indicators of CSCs are their ability to self-renew and faithfully recreate the original tumor. In this study, we present the development of a xenograft assay that identified human brain tumor initiating cells capable of initiating tumors in living organisms. Only the CD133+ fraction of brain tumor cells contained cells that could initiate tumors in the brains of NOD-SCID (non-obese diabetic, severe combined immunodeficient) mice. Injecting as few as 100 CD133+ cells resulted in a tumor that could be transplanted repeatedly and closely resembled the patient's original tumor. On the other hand, injecting 105 CD133- cells successfully engrafted but did not cause tumor formation. Therefore, the discovery of brain tumor initiating cells sheds light on the pathogenesis of human brain tumors, providing strong support for the CSC hypothesis as the foundation for many solid tumors. Additionally, it establishes a previously unknown cellular target for more effective cancer treatments.

title: Anthropometric reference data for international use: recommendations from a World Health Organization Expert Committee.
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) organized a panel of experts to reassess the use of anthropometry for evaluating health, nutrition, and social wellbeing at different stages of life. The panel's responsibilities included identifying appropriate reference data for anthropometric measurements and providing guidelines on their usage. For fetal growth, the panel recommended using an existing sex-specific multiracial reference. However, due to significant technical limitations and its inability to assess the growth of breast-fed infants, the panel suggested creating a new reference for weight and length/height measurements in infants and children, which would be a complex and expensive endeavor. To accurately interpret midupper arm circumference in preschoolers, age-specific reference data is necessary. When evaluating height-for-age in adolescents, the panel recommended using the current NCHS/WHO reference. The use of NCHS body mass index (BMI) data, with their high upper percentiles and skewness, is not recommended for setting health goals. However, these data were provisionally suggested for defining obesity based on a combination of elevated BMI and high subcutaneous fat. The NCHS values were also provisionally recommended as reference data for subscapular and triceps skinfold thicknesses. Guidelines were provided for adjusting anthropometric comparisons in adolescents based on their maturational status. Currently, there is no need for reference data for BMI in adults, and interpretation should be based on practical BMI cutoffs. Lastly, the panel noted the lack of normative anthropometric data for the elderly, particularly those over 80 years old. Defining health status, function, and biological age for this group is still an ongoing development.

title: Diverse interventions that extend mouse lifespan suppress shared age-associated epigenetic changes at critical gene regulatory regions
text:
The background of this study focuses on age-related changes in epigenetics, specifically DNA methylation, which is known to be a reliable biomarker of aging. However, the impact of genetic, dietary, and drug interventions on the epigenome is not well understood. To address this gap in knowledge, the researchers examined age-related DNA methylation changes in the liver of mice at the whole-genome, single-nucleotide level. They also investigated the effects of interventions known to promote longevity, including the Ames dwarf Prop1 df/df mutation, calorie restriction, and rapamycin.

The results showed that in wild-type mice on a normal diet, age-related hypomethylation was found in super-enhancers associated with highly expressed genes important for liver function. These hypomethylated enhancers were also linked to genes that change their expression with age. On the other hand, hypermethylation was observed at CpG islands marked with both activating and repressing histone modifications, resembling the hypermethylation patterns seen in liver cancer. The study found that age-related methylation changes were suppressed in Ames dwarf and calorie-restricted mice, and to a lesser extent in rapamycin-treated mice.

In conclusion, age-related changes in DNA methylation occur at specific regulatory regions of the genome. Different interventions known to promote longevity, such as genetic, dietary, and drug interventions, can suppress some of these age-related methylation changes. This suggests that these interventions may exert their beneficial effects, at least in part, by modulating the epigenome. This study provides a foundation for understanding the role of epigenetics in healthy aging and longevity, as well as the underlying mechanisms of the DNA methylation clock.

title: Extracellular vesicles for drug delivery.
text: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane vesicles derived from cells and serve as a natural means of communication between cells. The discovery that EVs can transfer biological information has sparked significant interest in their potential use as vehicles for delivering drugs. EVs offer several advantages over existing drug delivery methods, including their ability to bypass natural barriers, their inherent ability to target specific cells, and their stability in the bloodstream. However, the therapeutic applications of EVs as drug delivery systems have been limited by the lack of scalable methods for isolating EVs and efficiently loading them with drugs. Additionally, in order to achieve targeted drug delivery, the cell targeting properties of EVs need to be engineered. In this review, we examine recent progress and the challenges that remain in the development of EVs as drug delivery vehicles.

title: Effects of soy isoflavones and phytate on homocysteine, C-reactive protein, and iron status in postmenopausal women.
text:
BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to investigate the potential protective effects of soy protein or its components against risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) in postmenopausal women. These risk factors include total homocysteine (tHcy), C-reactive protein (CRP), and excess body iron, which tend to increase during menopause.

OBJECTIVE: The primary objective of this study was to determine the independent effects of the soy protein components isoflavones and phytate on CVD risk factors in postmenopausal women. The secondary objective was to identify factors such as blood lipids, oxidative stress indexes, serum ferritin, plasma folate, plasma vitamin B-12, and body mass index (BMI) that contribute to tHcy and CRP concentrations.

DESIGN: In a double-blind, 6-week study, 55 postmenopausal women aged 47-72 years were randomly assigned to one of four soy protein isolate treatments: native phytate and native isoflavone, native phytate and low isoflavone, low phytate and native isoflavone, or low phytate and low isoflavone. The participants' iron indexes, tHcy, CRP, and BMI were measured.

RESULTS: The results showed that soy protein with native phytate significantly reduced tHcy, transferrin saturation, and ferritin levels. However, soy protein with native isoflavones had no effect on any of the variables. At baseline, BMI was strongly correlated with tHcy and CRP, while HDL cholesterol was correlated with CRP. Multiple regression analysis revealed that LDL cholesterol and BMI significantly contributed to the overall variance in tHcy.

CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that consuming phytate-rich foods and maintaining a healthy weight may help reduce the risk factors for atherosclerotic CVD in postmenopausal women.

title: Replication Fork Stability Confers Chemoresistance in BRCA-deficient Cells
text: Cells lacking the Brca1 and Brca2 genes have a decreased ability to repair DNA double-strand breaks through homologous recombination. As a result, they are highly sensitive to substances that damage DNA, such as cisplatin and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Our study demonstrates that the absence of the MLL3/4 complex protein, PTIP, actually shields Brca1/2-deficient cells from DNA damage and saves the lives of Brca2-deficient embryonic stem cells. However, PTIP deficiency does not restore the ability to perform homologous recombination at double-strand breaks. Instead, its absence prevents the recruitment of the MRE11 nuclease to stalled replication forks, which in turn safeguards newly formed DNA strands from extensive degradation. In a broader sense, resistance to PARP inhibitors and cisplatin is linked to the protection of replication forks in Brca2-deficient tumor cells that do not undergo Brca2 reversion mutations. The disruption of various proteins, including PARP1 and CHD4, leads to the same outcome of replication fork protection, underscoring the intricate ways in which tumor cells evade chemotherapy and develop drug resistance.

title: Plasma Corin as a Predictor of Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure.
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the prognostic significance of plasma corin in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF). In recent years, there has been growing evidence suggesting that corin plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure and cardiac function. To investigate this further, we conducted a prospective cohort study involving 1,148 consecutive CHF patients. We used multivariate Cox regression analysis to examine the relationship between plasma corin levels and clinical prognosis. 

Our findings revealed that patients with low corin levels (<458 pg/ml) were more likely to be women and have hypertension. Low corin levels were associated with higher New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, as well as lower left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Multivariate Cox regression analysis indicated that log corin was an independent predictor of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) (hazard ratio: 0.62; 95% confidence interval: 0.39 to 0.95), along with age, diabetes, NYHA functional class, LVEF, eGFR, and log NT-proBNP. Furthermore, log corin was also a significant predictor for cardiovascular death (p = 0.041) and heart failure rehospitalization (p = 0.015) after adjusting for clinical variables and established biomarkers of adverse prognosis. Kaplan-Meier survival curves demonstrated that low corin was a significant predictor of MACE in patients with NT-proBNP levels above and below the median. 

In conclusion, our study highlights the value of plasma corin as a prognostic marker for MACE in CHF patients, independent of established conventional risk factors.

title: Cryo-EM structures of Tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease brain
text: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, and currently, there are no therapies that target the underlying mechanisms of the disease. The defining features of Alzheimer's disease are the presence of abundant neurofibrillary lesions and neuritic plaques in the cerebral cortex. Neurofibrillary lesions consist of paired helical and straight tau filaments, which distinguish them from other neurodegenerative diseases that exhibit tau filaments with different shapes. Unfortunately, there is a lack of detailed structures of tau filaments available for study. However, in this study, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps with a resolution of 3.4-3.5 Å and corresponding atomic models of paired helical and straight filaments obtained from the brain of an individual with Alzheimer's disease. These filaments are composed of two identical protofilaments that encompass residues 306-378 of the tau protein. They adopt a unique cross-β/β-helix structure, which serves as the foundation for tau aggregation. Interestingly, the paired helical and straight filaments exhibit distinct arrangements between the protofilaments, indicating that they are different structural forms. These findings highlight the power of cryo-EM in providing atomic-level details of amyloid filaments derived from patients, and open up possibilities for investigating various neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Modulation of the proteoglycan receptor PTPσ promotes recovery after spinal cord injury
text: Contusive spinal cord injury results in various disabilities due to limited neuronal regeneration and functional plasticity. It is widely known that an increase in glial-derived chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) within the glial scar and perineuronal net creates a barrier to the regrowth and sprouting of axons. Recently, protein tyrosine phosphatase σ (PTPσ), along with its sister phosphatase leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR) and the nogo receptors 1 and 3 (NgR), have been identified as receptors for the inhibitory glycosylated side chains of CSPGs. In our study with rats, we discovered that PTPσ plays a crucial role in converting growth cones into a dystrophic state by firmly stabilizing them within CSPG-rich substrates. To counteract the inhibitory effects of CSPGs, we developed a peptide mimetic of the PTPσ wedge domain that can penetrate cell membranes and bind to PTPσ, thereby relieving CSPG-mediated inhibition. By administering this peptide systemically over several weeks, we were able to restore significant serotonergic innervation to the spinal cord below the injury site and facilitate the recovery of locomotor and urinary functions. These findings enhance our understanding of the pivotal role of PTPσ in mediating the growth-inhibited state of neurons caused by CSPGs in the injured adult spinal cord.

title: A gp130–Src–YAP module links inflammation to epithelial regeneration
text: The mechanisms by which inflammation promotes the regeneration of injured tissues are not well understood. However, some of these mechanisms involve interleukin (IL)-6 family members, which are elevated in various diseases such as inflammatory bowel diseases and colorectal cancer. In this study, we demonstrate that gp130, a co-receptor for IL-6 cytokines, activates YAP and Notch, which are transcriptional regulators responsible for controlling tissue growth and regeneration. Interestingly, this activation occurs independently of the gp130 effector STAT3. Through YAP and Notch, gp130 signaling in the intestines stimulates the proliferation of epithelial cells, leading to abnormal differentiation and providing resistance against mucosal erosion. Additionally, gp130 associates with the tyrosine kinases Src and Yes, which become activated upon receptor engagement. These kinases phosphorylate YAP, resulting in its stabilization and translocation into the nucleus. This signaling module is highly activated during mucosal injury to facilitate healing and maintain the integrity of the barrier function.

title: Hemoglobin concentration in white, black, and Oriental children: is there a need for separate criteria in screening for anemia?
text: In several large surveys, it was discovered that the concentration of hemoglobin in blacks was consistently 0.5 to 1.0 g/dl lower than that of income-matched whites. This disparity could be attributed to racial characteristics of blacks, a higher prevalence of genetic traits like thalassemia minor and hemoglobinopathies, or environmental factors such as iron deficiency. To differentiate between these possibilities, we examined data from multiphasic examinations conducted between 1973 and 1975 on 1718 white, 741 black, and 315 Oriental healthy, nonindigent children aged 5 to 14 years. Across the entire population, the median hemoglobin concentration in blacks was consistently 0.5 g/dl lower than in whites of both genders (t test, P < 0.001). Even after excluding individuals with abnormal hemoglobin by electrophoresis (Hgb S and C) and those with mean corpuscular volume more than 5% below the normal mean for their age (to exclude iron deficiency or thalassemia minor), the differences still averaged 0.5 g/dl (P < 0.001). These findings reinforce the notion that blacks typically have a hemoglobin concentration approximately 0.5 g/dl lower than that of whites. Consequently, if the same standards are applied, around 10% of healthy blacks may be mistakenly classified as anemic.

title: Divergent reprogramming routes lead to alternative stem-cell states
text: Pluripotency refers to a cell's ability to differentiate into all three embryonic germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Pluripotent cells can be obtained through the derivation of embryonic stem cells or through somatic cell reprogramming. Somatic cells can be induced to become pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by expressing specific transcription factors. In mice, these iPSCs can generate fully iPSC-derived embryos and mice, demonstrating their pluripotent nature. However, it is unclear if there are other types of pluripotent cells or the full range of reprogrammed cell phenotypes. In this study, we investigate different outcomes of somatic reprogramming by thoroughly characterizing reprogrammed cells without preconceived definitions of iPSC states. We show that by maintaining high levels of reprogramming factors, mouse embryonic fibroblasts undergo unique epigenetic changes to reach a stable, Nanog-positive, alternative pluripotent state. This demonstrates that the pluripotent spectrum can include multiple distinct cell states.

title: Autophagy mediates degradation of nuclear lamina
text: Autophagy, also known as macroautophagy, is a process in which cellular components are broken down and associated with various human diseases. While much research has focused on the breakdown of cytoplasmic materials, little is known about how autophagy degrades nuclear components. In this study, we discovered that the autophagy machinery is responsible for breaking down nuclear lamina components in mammals. The protein LC3/Atg8, which is involved in autophagy, is found in the nucleus and directly interacts with the nuclear lamina protein lamin B1. It also binds to specific regions on chromatin that are associated with lamin B1. Interestingly, this interaction does not decrease the levels of lamin B1 during periods of starvation, but it does facilitate its degradation when cells are exposed to oncogenic insults, such as activated RAS.
