In conclusion, oral acetylcysteine effectively protects patients with moderate chronic renal insufficiency from contrast-induced deterioration in renal function after coronary angiographic procedures. This treatment is safe, cost-effective, and has minimal adverse effects.

title: DNA Methylation in the Human Cerebral Cortex Is Dynamically Regulated throughout the Life Span and Involves Differentiated Neurons
text:
The exact role of DNA cytosine methylation, which is an epigenetic regulator of chromatin structure and function, in normal and pathological brain development and aging is still not clear. In this study, we used MethyLight PCR to examine the DNA methylation status at 50 specific locations, primarily 5′ CpG islands of genes related to central nervous system growth and development, in the temporal neocortex of 125 individuals ranging in age from 17 weeks of gestation to 104 years old. We included two groups of individuals with psychiatric diseases - one with chronic neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's) and one without (schizophrenia). 

We observed a consistent and gradual increase in DNA methylation levels throughout the lifespan for 8 out of the 50 locations (GABRA2, GAD1, HOXA1, NEUROD1, NEUROD2, PGR, STK11, SYK), which was typically accompanied by a decrease in the corresponding mRNA levels. Another 16 locations showed a sharp increase in DNA methylation levels within the first few months or years after birth. Disease-related changes were only observed in 2 out of the 50 locations in the Alzheimer's group, suggesting that these changes may be an accelerated version of the normal age-related changes in the brain. 

Furthermore, our analysis of methylation in sorted nuclei provided evidence for bidirectional methylation events in cortical neurons during the transition from childhood to old age, with significant increases at 3 locations and a decrease at 1 location out of the 10 examined. Additionally, we found that the DNMT3a de novo DNA methyl-transferase was expressed at all ages, including in a subset of neurons in layers III and V of the mature cortex. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that DNA methylation is dynamically regulated in the human cerebral cortex throughout life, involving differentiated neurons, and affecting a significant number of genes primarily through an age-related increase.

title: Mulberry leaves (Morus alba L.) ameliorate obesity-induced hepatic lipogenesis, fibrosis, and oxidative stress in high-fat diet-fed mice
text: Obesity is linked to chronic illnesses like fatty liver, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and severe metabolic syndrome. It leads to metabolic dysfunction, causing excessive lipid buildup and fibrosis in the liver tissue, as well as an increase in oxidative stress. To study the impact of mulberry leaf extract (MLE) on obesity-induced oxidative stress, lipogenesis, and fibrosis in the liver, obese mice induced by a high-fat diet (HFD) were given MLE orally for 12 weeks. The MLE treatment significantly improved lipogenesis regulated by LXRα and reduced hepatic fibrosis markers like α-smooth muscle actin. Additionally, MLE increased lipolysis-associated markers such as lipoprotein lipase in the HFD-fed mice. Furthermore, MLE restored the activity of antioxidant enzymes like heme oxygenase-1 and glutathione peroxidase, in line with the protein levels of 4-hydroxynonenal in the HFD-fed mice. MLE has positive effects on obesity-related fatty liver disease by regulating hepatic lipid metabolism, fibrosis, and the antioxidant defense system. Supplementation with MLE could be a potential therapeutic approach for obesity-related diseases, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

title: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and the risk of hip fractures in elderly patients.
text: A recent study conducted on animals has shown that statins, which are lipid-lowering drugs, can significantly increase bone formation. However, it is still unclear whether statin use in humans can lead to meaningful bone formation or a decrease in the risk of osteoporotic fractures. In order to determine this, a case-control study was conducted involving 6,110 New Jersey residents aged 65 years or older who were enrolled in Medicare and either Medicaid or the Pharmacy Assistance for the Aged and Disabled program. The study found that the use of statins was associated with a reduced risk of hip fractures. The odds ratio of hip fracture was adjusted for demographic and clinical characteristics, as well as healthcare utilization. The results showed that statin use in the prior 180 days or prior 3 years was linked to a significant reduction in hip fracture risk. This association remained even after controlling for variables such as race, insurance status, psychoactive medications, estrogen and thiazide use, ischemic heart disease, cancer, and diabetes mellitus. On the other hand, the use of nonstatin lipid-lowering agents did not show any significant relationship with hip fracture risk. The extent of statin use was found to be directly related to the degree of reduction in hip fracture risk. Even after adjusting for the extent of statin use in the prior 3 years, current use was associated with a 71% reduction in risk. The relationship between statin use and hip fracture risk remained consistent even after controlling for variables such as the number of medications, comorbidity index score, and recent hospitalization or nursing home stay. The study concluded that statin use in elderly patients is associated with a reduced risk of hip fracture, but further controlled trials are needed to rule out any potential confounding factors.

title: The quality of modern cross-sectional ecologic studies: a bibliometric review.
text: Despite its limitations, the ecologic study design is widely used by epidemiologists. However, the extent to which researchers effectively address the challenges associated with this design in epidemiologic research remains unknown. This bibliometric review aimed to critically assess the characteristics, statistical methods, and reporting of results in modern cross-sectional ecologic papers. A comprehensive search of six major epidemiology journals was conducted to identify all cross-sectional ecologic studies published since January 1, 2000. A total of 125 articles that met the inclusion criteria were evaluated using common evaluative criteria. The findings revealed that a significant number of cross-sectional ecologic studies employed unreliable methods or exhibited statistical oversights. Improper adjustment of outcomes for age or sex was observed in the majority of cases (64%), and 20% of regression models raised concerns regarding statistical validity. Simple linear regression was the most frequently used analytic approach (31%). Many authors failed to provide important information regarding the ecologic nature of their study (31%), the choice of study design (58%), and the susceptibility of their research to the ecological fallacy (49%). These results highlight the need for international guidelines that standardize reporting on ecologic studies. Furthermore, greater attention should be given to the relevant biostatistical literature.

title: Efficacy of Beta1 Integrin and EGFR Targeting in Sphere-Forming Human Head and Neck Cancer Cells
text:
Resistance to radiotherapy remains a significant obstacle in the treatment of cancer, particularly head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Previous studies have shown that targeting both β1 integrin and EGFR simultaneously has a greater potential to sensitize HNSCC cancer models to radiation compared to targeting either one alone. Tumor-initiating cells (TIC), which are believed to contribute to therapy resistance and recurrence, can be enriched under certain conditions. This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of targeting β1 integrin/EGFR with and without X-ray irradiation on sphere-forming cells (SFC), which are thought to represent TIC. 

To conduct the study, HNSCC cell lines (UTSCC15, UTSCC5, Cal33, SAS) were injected into nude mice to establish tumors, and then plated under non-adhesive conditions to promote primary and secondary sphere formation, which is indicative of SFC enrichment and self-renewal capacity. Treatment involved the use of inhibitory antibodies for β1 integrin (AIIB2) and EGFR (Cetuximab), as well as X-ray irradiation at various doses. The researchers also employed flow cytometry to assess TIC marker expression and cell cycling, and Western blotting to analyze DNA repair protein expression and phosphorylation. 

The results showed that SAS cells had a higher capacity for primary and secondary sphere formation compared to the other HNSCC cell lines, which correlated with the tumor up-take rates of SAS versus UTSCC15 cells. However, the administration of AIIB2 and Cetuximab had minimal cytotoxic effects and did not sensitize SFC to radiation. Interestingly, secondary SAS spheres, which represented the surviving fraction of SFC after passaging, exhibited significantly increased radiosensitivity compared to primary spheres. Surprisingly, neither AIIB2 nor Cetuximab had a significant impact on the basal sphere-forming capacity or radiosensitivity. While an increased accumulation of G0/G1 phase cells was observed in secondary SAS spheres, there was no difference in DNA double strand break repair based on ATM and Chk2 dephosphorylation after irradiation. 

In conclusion, the study found that sphere-forming conditions selected for cells that were resistant to both anti-β1 integrin and anti-EGFR inhibitory antibodies in the HNSCC model. The data also suggested that primary and secondary SFC fractions employ distinct survival strategies independent of β1 integrin and EGFR, highlighting the need for further research to better understand SFC survival and enrichment before and after treatment. This will help identify new targets for therapeutic intervention in SFC.

title: Anxiety
text:
AIMS To investigate the impact of regularly administering psychiatric questionnaires on the identification, treatment, and outcome of psychiatric disorders in non-psychiatric environments. 

SOURCES OF DATA We conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials that examined the use of psychiatric screening and outcome questionnaires in non-psychiatric settings. We searched databases such as Embase, Medline, PsycLIT, Cinahl, Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, and also manually searched key journals. 

METHODS We analyzed the design features and outcomes of relevant studies and performed a quantitative synthesis of comparable studies using random effects models. 

MAIN OUTCOMES We assessed the impact of questionnaire feedback on the identification of psychiatric disorders, interventions for these disorders, and the overall outcome of psychiatric disorders. 

RESULTS We identified nine randomized studies that investigated the use of common psychiatric instruments in primary care and general hospital settings. These studies compared the administration of these instruments followed by feedback to clinicians, with administration without feedback. Meta-analysis was possible for four of these studies (2457 participants), which focused on the impact of feedback on the identification of depressive disorders. The routine administration and feedback of scores for all patients did not significantly increase the overall rate of identifying mental disorders such as anxiety and depression. However, two studies showed that routine administration followed by selective feedback for high scorers did increase the rate of identifying depression. Unfortunately, this increased recognition did not lead to a higher rate of intervention. Overall, studies on the routine administration of psychiatric measures did not demonstrate an effect on patient outcomes. 

CONCLUSIONS Regularly measuring outcomes in psychiatric disorders is a costly endeavor. There is limited evidence to suggest that it improves psychosocial outcomes for individuals with psychiatric disorders managed in non-psychiatric settings.

title: The challenges of overcoming antibiotic resistance: Plant extracts as potential sources of antimicrobial and resistance modifying agents
text: The issue of antibiotic resistance has led to a decrease in the effectiveness of inexpensive and older antibiotics, thus creating a need for the ongoing exploration of new antimicrobial substances. To address this problem, it is crucial to comprehend the mechanisms behind resistance in order to develop effective strategies. Pathogenic bacteria acquire or develop intrinsic resistance to antibiotics through various strategies, including active efflux of drugs, alteration of target sites, and enzymatic degradation. Multi-drug resistance (MDR) pumps have been identified in numerous gram positive and gram negative pathogens, such as Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, and more recently, mycobacteria. These pumps have the ability to recognize and expel a wide range of structurally unrelated compounds from bacterial cells, thereby conferring resistance to various antibiotics. In vitro studies have shown that certain chemical compounds, known as MDR inhibitors or resistance modifying agents, can modify the resistance phenotype in bacteria by working synergistically with antibiotics. The search for such compounds, which can be combined with antibiotics to treat drug-resistant infections, offers a potential solution to the problem of resistance in bacteria. Crude extracts from medicinal plants have emerged as promising sources of potential resistance modifying agents, and the diverse plant species found in the African biosphere hold particular promise in this regard.

title: The effect of N-acetylcysteine in the nucleus accumbens on neurotransmission and relapse to cocaine.
text:
In this study, we investigated the impact of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) on relapse to cocaine seeking and neurotransmission in the nucleus accumbens core (NAcore). Previous research has shown that low levels of glutamate in the NAcore contribute to relapse, and NAC has been found to restore glutamate balance and reduce relapse. We aimed to determine the effects of NAC directly applied to the NAcore and the involvement of metabotropic glutamate receptors 2/3 (mGluR2/3) and 5 (mGluR5).

To conduct our study, rats were trained to self-administer cocaine for two weeks and then underwent extinction training. Following extinction, the rats received either intra-accumbens NAC or systemic NAC 30 or 120 minutes before reinstatement was induced using a conditioned cue or a combination of cue and cocaine injection. We also conducted in vitro whole cell recordings in acute slices to measure postsynaptic currents and assessed cystine and glutamate uptake in primary glial cultures.

Our findings revealed that NAC microinjection into the NAcore inhibited the reinstatement of cocaine seeking. In the slices, a low concentration of NAC decreased the amplitude of evoked glutamatergic synaptic currents in the NAcore in an mGluR2/3-dependent manner, while high doses of NAC increased the amplitude in an mGluR5-dependent manner. Both effects were dependent on NAC uptake through cysteine transporters and the activity of the cysteine/glutamate exchanger. Additionally, we discovered that blocking mGluR5 potentiated the inhibition of cocaine seeking by NAC.

In conclusion, the effectiveness of NAC in preventing relapse to cocaine seeking depends on the balance between stimulating mGluR2/3 and mGluR5 in the NAcore. Furthermore, our study suggests that the efficacy of NAC can be enhanced by simultaneously inhibiting mGluR5.

title: A phospholipid transfer function of ER-mitochondria encounter structure revealed in vitro
text: The proper distribution of specific phospholipids to different cellular membranes is a crucial issue for maintaining the composition of organelle-specific phospholipids. While it has been suggested that the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) facilitates phospholipid transfer between the ER and mitochondria, this role of ERMES is still debated and requires experimental evidence. In this study, we developed a new in vitro assay system using isolated yeast membrane fractions to observe phospholipid exchange between the ER and mitochondria. Using this system, we discovered that phospholipid transport between the ER and mitochondria depends on the integrity of the membranes, rather than energy sources like ATP, GTP, or the membrane potential across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Additionally, we found that the absence of the ERMES component hinders the transport of phosphatidylserine from the ER to mitochondria, but not the transport of phosphatidylethanolamine from mitochondria to the ER. This in vitro assay system provides a valuable tool for studying non-vesicular phospholipid transport between the ER and mitochondria.

title: An integrin β3–KRAS–RalB complex drives tumour stemness and resistance to EGFR inhibition
text: Tumor cells that possess stem-like characteristics are highly aggressive and often exhibit resistance to drugs. We have discovered that integrin αvβ3 can be used as a marker for breast, lung, and pancreatic carcinomas that have stem-like properties and are highly resistant to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors like erlotinib. This observation was made in laboratory settings as well as in mice that had been implanted with tumor cells derived from patients, and in clinical samples from lung cancer patients who had not responded to erlotinib treatment. The mechanism behind this phenomenon involves αvβ3, when not bound to a ligand, recruiting KRAS and RalB to the tumor cell membrane. This leads to the activation of TBK1 and NF-κB. In fact, the expression of αvβ3 and the resulting KRAS-RalB-NF-κB pathway were both necessary and sufficient for tumor initiation, the ability of the tumor cells to grow without anchorage, self-renewal, and resistance to erlotinib. By targeting this pathway with bortezomib, we were able to reverse both the stem-like properties of the tumor cells and their resistance to erlotinib. These findings not only identify αvβ3 as a marker and driver of carcinoma stemness, but also provide a potential therapeutic strategy to make such tumors more sensitive to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibition.

title: Gain of toxic Apolipoprotein E4 effects in Human iPSC-Derived Neurons Is Ameliorated by a Small-Molecule Structure Corrector
text: Efforts to develop drugs for Alzheimer's disease (AD) have shown promise in animal studies, but have ultimately failed in human trials. This highlights the urgent need to study AD using human model systems. In our study, we utilized human neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells that expressed apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4), a variant of the APOE gene product and the primary genetic risk factor for AD. Our findings revealed that ApoE4-expressing neurons exhibited higher levels of tau phosphorylation, which was unrelated to their increased production of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides. Additionally, these neurons displayed degeneration in GABAergic neurons. Interestingly, ApoE4 increased Aβ production in human neurons, but not in mouse neurons. By using gene editing to convert ApoE4 to ApoE3, we were able to rescue these phenotypes, indicating the specific effects of ApoE4. Neurons lacking APOE behaved similarly to those expressing ApoE3, and the introduction of ApoE4 expression replicated the pathological phenotypes, suggesting that ApoE4 has toxic effects. However, we discovered that treating ApoE4-expressing neurons with a small-molecule structure corrector alleviated the detrimental effects. This demonstrates that correcting the pathogenic conformation of ApoE4 is a viable therapeutic approach for ApoE4-related AD.

title: LncRNA NEAT1/let-7a-5p axis regulates the cisplatin resistance in nasopharyngeal carcinoma by targeting Rsf-1 and modulating the Ras-MAPK pathway.
text: The role of the long non-coding RNA nuclear paraspeckle assembly transcript 1 (NEAT1) in drug resistance of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is not well understood. This study aimed to investigate the involvement of NEAT1 and its underlying mechanisms in NPC drug resistance. The expression levels of NEAT1, let-7a-5p, and Rsf-1 mRNA were measured using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The effects of NEAT1 and let-7a-5p on cell proliferation and cisplatin resistance were assessed using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) and 5-ethynyl-20-deoxyuridine (EdU) assays. Western blot analysis was conducted to determine the protein levels of Rsf-1, Ras, p-Raf1, Raf1, p-MEK1, MEK1, p-ERK1/2, and ERK1/2. Xenograft tumor assay was performed to investigate the role of NEAT1 in NPC tumor growth in vivo. The results showed that NEAT1 was upregulated and let-7a-5p was downregulated in NPC tissues and cell lines. Inhibition of NEAT1 significantly reduced cisplatin resistance in NPC cells. NEAT1 was found to interact with let-7a-5p, and a negative correlation between NEAT1 and let-7a-5p expression was observed in NPC tissues. Rsf-1 was identified as a target of let-7a-5p. NEAT1 reversed the inhibitory effect of let-7a-5p on cisplatin resistance in NPC cells. Furthermore, NEAT1 knockdown inhibited the Ras-MAPK pathway in NPC cells and suppressed tumor growth in the presence of cisplatin in vivo. These findings suggest that the NEAT1/let-7a-5p axis regulates cisplatin resistance in NPC by targeting Rsf-1 and modulating the Ras-MAPK signaling pathway.

title: Antibacterial peptide microcin J25 inhibits transcription by binding within and obstructing the RNA polymerase secondary channel.
text: The antibacterial peptide microcin J25 (MccJ25) hinders the process of transcription in bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP). Biochemical findings suggest that this hindrance occurs either at the stage of NTP uptake or NTP binding by RNAP. Genetic findings indicate that the hindrance of transcription necessitates a substantial determinant, consisting of over 50 amino acid residues, located within the RNAP secondary channel, also referred to as the "NTP-uptake channel" or "pore". Biophysical findings demonstrate that the hindrance of transcription involves the attachment of MccJ25 within the RNAP secondary channel. Molecular modeling reveals that the attachment of MccJ25 within the RNAP secondary channel obstructs it. Consequently, we can conclude that MccJ25 inhibits transcription by attaching to and obstructing the RNAP secondary channel, effectively acting as a "cork in a bottle". The obstruction of the RNAP secondary channel presents an appealing target for drug discovery.

title: Exploring and exploiting the systemic effects of deregulated replication licensing.
text:
The proper maintenance and accurate transmission of genetic material are crucial for the healthy development and overall well-being of an organism. To ensure precise replication, the replication licensing machinery plays a vital role by allowing replication to occur only once per cell cycle. It is essential to tightly regulate the expression of the components that make up this machinery to prevent re-replication, which can lead to genomic instability, a characteristic feature of cancer.

In this review, we delve into the underlying mechanisms of deregulation in replication licensing, which can have systemic effects. This deregulation has been implicated in the development of cancer and various genetic syndromes. Furthermore, recent discoveries have shed light on the fact that the replication licensing factor Cdc6 can act as a global regulator of transcription when it surpasses a certain threshold, opening up new avenues for exploration.

We also explore the role of the replication licensing factor ChlR1/DDX11, which is mutated in the Warsaw Breakage Syndrome, in the context of cancer. Lastly, we discuss future perspectives that focus on the potential therapeutic benefits of targeting replication licensing factors, particularly Cdc6.

title: Regulatory principles of pluripotency: from the ground state up.
text: Pluripotency is the extraordinary ability of a single cell to give rise to all the specialized cell types found in an adult organism. This unique characteristic can be preserved indefinitely by creating self-renewing embryonic stem cells (ESCs), which serve as a valuable tool for studying cell fate decisions and diseases. Recent advancements have shown that manipulating specific signaling cues can bring ESCs to a uniform "ground state" of pluripotency, closely resembling the pluripotent naive epiblast. In this discussion, we explore the external and internal regulatory principles that define the nature of pluripotency and examine the emerging range of pluripotent states.

title: Neonatal Mortality Levels for 193 Countries in 2009 with Trends since 1990: A Systematic Analysis of Progress, Projections, and Priorities
text:
In the past, studies on childhood mortality have primarily focused on infant and under-five mortality rates. However, neonatal mortality (deaths within the first 28 days of life) has not received much attention, despite accounting for approximately 41% of all child deaths. To better understand the progress in this area, we have developed annual estimates for neonatal mortality rates (NMRs) and neonatal deaths for 193 countries from 1990 to 2009, with projections for the future.

To gather data, we compiled a database of mortality in neonates and children under five years old, which included information from 3,551 country-years. Reliable civil registration data was available for 38 countries between 1990 and 2009. For the remaining 155 countries, including 17 with no national data, we developed a statistical model to estimate NMRs. We also consulted with countries to gather data inputs and review our estimates.

In 2009, it was estimated that 3.3 million babies died within the first month of life, compared to 4.6 million neonatal deaths in 1990. More than half of all neonatal deaths occurred in five countries: India (27.8%), Nigeria (7.2%), Pakistan (6.9%), China (6.4%), and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (4.6%). These five countries accounted for 44% of global livebirths. Between 1990 and 2009, the global NMR decreased by 28%, from 33.2 deaths per 1,000 livebirths to 23.9. The proportion of child deaths that occur during the neonatal period has increased in all regions of the world and now stands at 41% globally. While some regions have seen a halving of NMRs, Africa's NMR only dropped by 17.6% (from 43.6 to 35.9).

In conclusion, neonatal mortality rates have decreased in all regions of the world, but progress has been slowest in regions with high NMRs. To achieve Millennium Development Goal 4, which aims for a two-thirds reduction in child mortality, global health programs need to address neonatal deaths more effectively.

title: Neuroprotective Effects of Four Phenylethanoid Glycosides on H2O2-Induced Apoptosis on PC12 Cells via the Nrf2/ARE Pathway
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the neuroprotective effect and molecular mechanism of phenylethanoid glycosides (PhGs), including salidroside, acteoside, isoacteoside, and echinacoside. These PhGs have been found to exhibit antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. The study found that pretreatment with PhGs significantly reduced cytotoxicity induced by H₂O₂ in PC12 cells. This effect was achieved by promoting the nuclear translocation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and reversing the downregulation of certain proteins, including heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate cysteine ligase-catalytic subunit (GCLC), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM). The neuroprotective effect was diminished when Nrf2 was silenced using siRNA or when the HO-1 inhibitor zinc protoporphyrin (ZnPP) was used. The study also suggested that PhGs may interact with the Nrf2 binding site in Kelch-like ECH-association protein 1 (Keap1), supporting the hypothesis that PhGs activate Nrf2. Furthermore, the study found that PhGs with higher glycoside content had stronger effects, indicating a potential dose-dependent relationship.

title: Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies have estimated premature deaths caused by heat or cold in specific countries, but none have conducted a comprehensive assessment across different climates. Our objective was to determine the overall mortality burden associated with non-optimum ambient temperature, including contributions from heat, cold, moderate temperatures, and extreme temperatures.

METHODS: We collected data from 384 locations in Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Taiwan, Thailand, UK, and USA. Using a standard time-series Poisson model, we controlled for trends and day of the week. We used a distributed lag non-linear model with a 21-day lag to estimate temperature-mortality associations, and then pooled the results in a multivariate metaregression that included country indicators, temperature average, and range. We calculated attributable deaths for heat and cold, defined as temperatures above and below the optimum temperature, which corresponded to the point of minimum mortality. We also calculated attributable deaths for moderate and extreme temperatures, using cutoffs at the 2.5th and 97.5th temperature percentiles.

FINDINGS: We analyzed 74,225,200 deaths between 1985 and 2012. Overall, 7.71% (95% empirical CI 7.43-7.91) of mortality was attributed to non-optimum temperature in the selected countries during the study period. There were significant differences between countries, with Thailand having the lowest percentage at 3.37% (3.06-3.63) and China having the highest at 11.00% (9.29-12.47). The temperature percentile at which minimum mortality occurred varied from approximately the 60th percentile in tropical areas to the 80-90th percentile in temperate regions. Cold temperatures accounted for more temperature-attributable deaths (7.29%, 7.02-7.49) than heat (0.42%, 0.39-0.44). Extreme cold and hot temperatures were responsible for 0.86% (0.84-0.87) of total mortality.

INTERPRETATION: The majority of temperature-related mortality was attributed to cold temperatures. The impact of extreme temperature days was significantly less than that of milder but non-optimum weather. This evidence has important implications for public health interventions aimed at minimizing the health effects of adverse temperatures, as well as predictions of future climate change scenarios.

FUNDING: This study was funded by the UK Medical Research Council.

title: Survivin is not required for the endomitotic cell cycle of megakaryocytes.
text: Survivin, a component of the chromosome passenger complex, plays a crucial role in the alignment, separation, and cytokinesis of chromosomes. While survivin is essential for the growth and survival of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, its role in the endomitosis of megakaryocytes is still a subject of debate. To investigate the necessity of survivin in polyploidization, we examined mice with a specific deletion of survivin in megakaryocytes. These mice, known as PF4-Cre/survivin(fl/fl) mice, had normal platelet counts and megakaryocytes that achieved ploidy levels similar to those of control littermates. The CD41(+) cells in these mice showed minimal excision but increased annexin V staining, suggesting that survivin is crucial for the survival of megakaryocyte progenitors in vivo. In contrast, when survivin was excised from megakaryocytes in an ex vivo setting, there was significant excision and an enhanced level of polyploidization. These findings indicate that survivin is necessary for the survival of megakaryocyte progenitors but not essential for the polyploidization of committed megakaryocytes.

title: β1 integrin mediates an alternative survival pathway in breast cancer cells resistant to lapatinib
text:
Introduction: The overexpression of human epidermal growth factor receptor (HER)-2 in 20% of breast cancers is associated with aggressive growth and has led to the use of HER2-targeted therapies like trastuzumab (T) and lapatinib (L). However, these drugs have limited efficacy in patients with resistance to treatment. The β1 integrin plays a role in breast tumor progression, including proliferation and survival. 

Methods: We developed HER2-overexpressing cell lines resistant to L, T, and the LT combination through long-term exposure and validated these models in 3D culture. We treated the cells with HER2 and β1 integrin inhibitors in 3D and monitored colony number for 12 days. We also stained the cells for Ki-67 and Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) or harvested them for protein analysis. Statistical testing was performed using analysis of variance and linear contrasts.

Results: Using multiple cell lines, we found that in L and LT resistance, where phosphorylation of EGFR/HER1, HER2, and HER3 is inhibited, kinases downstream of β1 integrin, such as focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and Src, are up-regulated. Blocking β1 with the antibody AIIB2 inhibited this up-regulation and significantly inhibited growth of L and LT resistant cells in 3D, without affecting parental cells. Inhibiting β1 with siRNA or FAK inhibitors had the same growth inhibitory effect. Trastuzumab-resistant cells, which have high levels of phosphorylated EGFR/HER1, HER2, and HER3, were only modestly growth-inhibited by AIIB2.

Conclusions: Our data suggest that HER2 activity determines whether β1 mediates an alternative pathway driving resistance in L resistance. These findings support further clinical studies on inhibiting β1 or its downstream signaling to overcome acquired L and LT resistance.

title: Incidence and Trends of Sepsis in US Hospitals Using Clinical vs Claims Data, 2009-2014
text: Claims-based analyses suggest that sepsis incidence is increasing while mortality rates are decreasing. However, these estimates may lack accuracy due to changes in diagnosis and coding practices over time. This study aimed to estimate the national incidence of sepsis in the US using detailed clinical data from electronic health records (EHR) of various hospitals. The study included adult patients admitted to 409 academic, community, and federal hospitals from 2009-2014. Sepsis was identified using clinical indicators of presumed infection and concurrent acute organ dysfunction, based on the Sepsis-3 criteria. The main outcomes measured were sepsis incidence, outcomes, and trends. The results showed that in 2014, there were 173,690 sepsis cases among 2,901,019 adults admitted to study hospitals, resulting in a 6.0% incidence rate. Of these cases, 15.0% died in the hospital and 6.2% were discharged to hospice. From 2009-2014, sepsis incidence using clinical criteria remained stable, while incidence per claims increased. In-hospital mortality using clinical criteria declined, but there was no significant change in the combined outcome of death or discharge to hospice. In contrast, mortality using claims declined significantly, as did death or discharge to hospice. Clinical criteria were more sensitive in identifying sepsis than claims, with comparable positive predictive value. The study concludes that sepsis was present in 6% of adult hospitalizations, and neither the incidence of sepsis nor the combined outcome of death or discharge to hospice changed significantly between 2009-2014. The findings also suggest that EHR-based clinical data provide more accurate estimates for sepsis surveillance compared to claims-based data.

title: Body-mass index and risk of 22 specific cancers: a population-based cohort study of 5·24 million UK adults
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies have shown that high body-mass index (BMI) increases the risk of certain types of cancer. However, there has not been a large-scale analysis that examines the patterns of risk across all common cancers while accounting for potential confounding factors. The aim of this study was to investigate the links between BMI and the most common site-specific cancers.

METHODS: We analyzed primary care data from individuals in the Clinical Practice Research Datalink who had BMI data available. Cox models were used to examine the associations between BMI and 22 of the most common cancers, while adjusting for potential confounders. Linear and non-linear models were fitted, and effect modification by sex, menopausal status, smoking, and age was investigated. Population effects were also calculated.

FINDINGS: A total of 5.24 million individuals were included in the study, of which 166,955 developed cancers of interest. BMI was found to be associated with 17 out of the 22 cancers, although the effects varied depending on the site. Each 5 kg/m(2) increase in BMI was linearly associated with an increased risk of cancers of the uterus, gallbladder, kidney, cervix, thyroid, and leukaemia. BMI was also positively associated with liver, colon, ovarian, and postmenopausal breast cancers overall, but the effects varied depending on BMI or individual-level characteristics. Inverse associations were observed with prostate and premenopausal breast cancer risk, both overall and in never-smokers. However, no association was found for lung and oral cavity cancer in never smokers. The inverse associations observed overall were likely due to residual confounding by smoking amount. Assuming causality, excess weight could be responsible for 41% of uterine and 10% or more of gallbladder, kidney, liver, and colon cancers. We estimated that a 1 kg/m(2) increase in BMI across the population would result in 3790 additional annual UK patients developing one of the ten cancers positively associated with BMI.

INTERPRETATION: BMI is associated with cancer risk, and the effects vary depending on the cancer site and patient subgroup. These findings have important implications at the population level. The study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research, Wellcome Trust, and Medical Research Council.

title: Cryo-EM structure of a herpesvirus capsid at 3.1 Å
text:
Human herpesviruses are among the largest and most complex viruses in terms of their structure and genetics. Through the use of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and an optimized image reconstruction strategy, we have successfully determined the structure of the herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) capsid at a resolution of 3.1 angstroms. This capsid is composed of approximately 3000 proteins, which are organized into three types of hexons (central, peripentonal, and edge), pentons, and triplexes.

The major capsid protein, VP5, is present in both hexons and pentons, while hexons also contain a smaller capsid protein called VP26. Triplexes are made up of VP23 and VP19C. VP5 proteins play a crucial role as core organizers, forming extensive intermolecular networks through numerous disulfide bonds (approximately 1500 in total) and noncovalent interactions with VP26 proteins and triplexes. These interactions are essential for maintaining the stability and assembly of the capsid.

The microenvironments surrounding these proteins induce conformational changes, resulting in the formation of 46 different conformers. These conformers come together to create a massive quasisymmetric shell, showcasing the intricate structural and functional complexity of HSV.

title: Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models.
text: Mediation hypotheses are frequently seen in the behavioral sciences. Mediation occurs when a predictor indirectly influences a dependent variable through one or more intervening variables, known as mediators. Despite the clear need, there has been limited attention given to methods for assessing mediation involving multiple mediators simultaneously in the methodological literature. In this paper, we offer an overview of both simple and multiple mediation and explore three approaches that can be employed to investigate indirect processes. Additionally, we discuss methods for comparing two or more mediators within a single model. To illustrate these concepts, we present a practical example where we assess and compare potential mediators in the relationship between the helpfulness of socialization agents and job satisfaction. Furthermore, we provide SAS and SPSS macros, as well as Mplus and LISREL syntax, to facilitate the application of these methods.

title: Distinct Metabolomic Signatures Are Associated with Longevity in Humans
text: The impact of changes in metabolism on lifespan has been extensively studied in experimental models, but there is a lack of data in humans. In this study, we utilized liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to measure 217 plasma metabolites and investigate their correlation with longevity in a large group of men and women who were followed for up to 20 years. Our results indicate that higher levels of isocitrate, an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, and taurocholate, a bile acid, are associated with a decreased likelihood of reaching 80 years of age, which we define as longevity. Additionally, elevated levels of isocitrate, but not taurocholate, are linked to poorer cardiovascular health at the beginning of the study, as well as an increased risk of future cardiovascular disease and mortality. However, we did not find any association between the identified metabolites and the risk of cancer. These findings suggest that certain metabolic pathways related to human longevity are connected to the risk of common causes of death, although not all pathways are involved.

title: The expanding problem of adipose depot remodeling and postnatal adipocyte progenitor recruitment.
text: Understanding all aspects of adipose tissue biology has become increasingly urgent due to the rising incidence of obesity and associated metabolic diseases. This includes gaining knowledge about the function of adipocytes, how adipose tissue expands during obesity, and the impact of expanded adipose tissues on physiology in adults. In this article, we emphasize the growing recognition of the significance of de novo adipocyte differentiation in the expansion of adipose tissue in adult humans and animals. We provide a comprehensive overview of recent research efforts aimed at identifying adipose precursor populations that contribute to the natural recruitment of white, brown, and beige adipocytes in mice after birth. Additionally, we summarize new findings that shed light on the intricate process of adipose tissue development in vivo.

title: Clonal competition in BcrAbl-driven leukemia: how transplantations can accelerate clonal conversion
text:
The process of clonal competition in cancer occurs when the offspring of a cell clone outperforms or succumbs to other competing clones due to differences in their functional characteristics, primarily caused by acquired mutations. Although the mutations themselves are well-studied in many tumors, the dynamic process of clonal selection is not well-understood. 

In this study, we investigated the dynamics of clonal competition in a BcrAbl-induced leukemia using a γ-retroviral vector library that encoded the oncogene along with genetic barcodes. We examined the growth dynamics of transduced cells at the clonal level both in vitro and in vivo in transplanted mice. 

Our results showed that while there were some changes in clonal abundances in vitro, we observed monoclonal leukemias in 6 out of 30 mice after transplantation. Interestingly, these monoclonal leukemias were caused by only two different BcrAbl clones. To understand the success of these clones, we used a mathematical model of hematopoietic tissue maintenance, which suggested that the differential engraftment capacity of these two dominant clones could explain our observations. These findings were further supported by additional transplantation experiments and increased BcrAbl transcript levels in both clones. 

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that clonal competition in cancer is not solely determined by mutations, but is highly influenced by selection mechanisms in a specific environmental context.

title: Open Babel: An open chemical toolbox
text:
The problem of converting chemical structures between different formats is a common issue in computational modeling. Although there are standard interchange formats like Chemical Markup Language and de facto standards like SMILES format, the need to convert between formats remains a challenge due to the diverse application areas for chemistry data, variations in the data stored by different formats (such as 0D versus 3D), and competition between software programs without a neutral format.

In this study, we introduce Open Babel, an open-source chemical toolbox that can handle various types of chemical data. The latest version, Open Babel 2.3, is capable of converting over 110 formats. To accommodate the wide range of chemical and molecular data, the library implements various cheminformatics algorithms, including partial charge assignment, aromaticity detection, bond order perception, and canonicalization. We provide a detailed explanation of the implementation of Open Babel, highlight the key advancements in the 2.3 release, and discuss its applications in software products and scientific research, which go beyond simple format conversion.

Open Babel offers a solution to the problem of multiple chemical file formats. Additionally, it provides useful utilities such as conformer searching, 2D depiction, filtering, batch conversion, and substructure and similarity searching. Developers can use it as a programming library to handle chemical data in fields like organic chemistry, drug design, materials science, and computational chemistry. Open Babel is freely available under an open-source license at http://openbabel.org.

title: Young adolescents' nutrition assessment on computer (YANA-C)
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and acceptability of the computerized 24-hour recall tool called "Young Adolescent's Nutrition Assessment on Computer (YANA-C)".

Design: The food and nutrient intake data collected using YANA-C were compared with data from food records (study 1) and 24-hour dietary recall interviews (study 2).

Main outcome measures: The study assessed the intake of various food groups (fruit, fruit juice, vegetables, potatoes, bread, cereals, milk, cheese, other milk products, soft drinks, diet soft drinks, sugar/sweets, pastry/cookies, savory snacks, butter/sauces, eggs, fish, meat) and nutrients (energy, carbohydrates, protein, fat, fiber, calcium, vitamin C, and iron).

Subjects and setting: The study included 237 pupils aged 11-14 years from two primary and four secondary schools in Belgium-Flanders (study 1: n=136; study 2: n=101).

Results: YANA-C demonstrated good agreement with the standard methods in categorizing subjects as consumers or nonconsumers (κstudy 1=0.48-0.92; κstudy 2=0.38-0.90). Spearman's correlations for energy and nutrient intakes ranged from 0.44 to 0.79 for study 1 and from 0.44 to 0.86 for study 2. Overall, nutrient and energy intakes were higher in YANA-C compared to the food record (except for calcium), but not significantly different from the interview (except for fiber). The statistical analysis showed fair to moderate agreement between YANA-C and the other methods in ranking portion sizes for most food groups (weighted κ study 1=0.11-0.55; study 2=0.04-0.73). The portion sizes in YANA-C were significantly lower than the standards for cereals, and significantly higher than the food record for milk, soft drinks, sugar/sweets, and savory snacks, as well as higher than the interview for potatoes. Only a small number of pupils had negative evaluations of the program.

Conclusion: YANA-C is a promising tool for collecting detailed dietary information from young adolescents, requiring relatively low staff resources. It can be useful in various nutrition research applications.

title: Antiretroviral Therapy for Prevention of Tuberculosis in Adults with HIV: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text: The prevalence of tuberculosis (TB) has been on the rise, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, due to the high number of people living with HIV. In 2010 alone, there were approximately 1.1 million new cases of TB among the 34 million individuals with HIV worldwide. However, antiretroviral therapy (ART) has shown promise in preventing HIV-associated TB. To further explore this, we conducted a systematic review of studies analyzing the impact of ART on TB incidence in HIV-infected adults. We searched various databases and included randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, and retrospective cohort studies that compared TB incidence in HIV-infected adults receiving ART versus those not receiving ART for at least 6 months in developing countries. We categorized the studies based on CD4 counts at ART initiation and found that ART was strongly associated with a reduction in TB incidence across all CD4 count categories. This reduction was observed in individuals with CD4 counts less than 200 cells/µl, 200 to 350 cells/µl, greater than 350 cells/µl, and any CD4 count. There was no evidence of a difference in the reduction of TB incidence based on CD4 count category. In conclusion, ART is highly effective in reducing TB incidence in individuals with HIV, regardless of their CD4 count. Initiating ART earlier may be crucial in controlling the HIV-associated TB syndemic on a global and national scale.

title: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and breast cancer: a review of the current evidence.
text: The incidence of breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome has risen in recent decades due to the obesity epidemic, particularly in developed countries. Diabetes-related factors such as insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and changes in hormone signaling have been linked to the risk of breast cancer. In this review, we examined epidemiological studies investigating the association between type 2 diabetes and breast cancer risk, as well as the role of hormonal mediators in this relationship. The available evidence suggests a modest association between type 2 diabetes and breast cancer risk, which appears to be more prominent in postmenopausal women compared to premenopausal women. However, the exact mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear, as both diseases share common risk factors such as obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and potentially high intake of saturated fat and refined carbohydrates, which may confound the results. Additionally, while the metabolic syndrome is closely linked to diabetes and includes components that could potentially influence breast cancer risk, its specific role in breast carcinogenesis has not been studied and therefore remains unknown.

title: Loss of TDP43 inhibits progression of triple-negative breast cancer in coordination with SRSF3
text: Abnormal alternative splicing has emerged as a potential characteristic of cancer. In this study, we have identified TDP43 (TAR DNA-binding protein 43) as a crucial regulator of splicing, responsible for the distinct splicing pattern observed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Clinical data reveals that TDP43 is highly expressed in TNBC patients with a poor prognosis. Silencing TDP43 hampers tumor progression, including both proliferation and metastasis, while overexpression of TDP43 enhances the proliferation and malignancy of mammary epithelial cells. Through deep sequencing analysis and functional experiments, we have determined that TDP43 primarily influences splicing events in conjunction with the splicing factor SRSF3 (serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3), thereby regulating the progression of TNBC. The TDP43/SRSF3 complex specifically controls certain splicing events, such as those involving the downstream genes PAR3 and NUMB. The reduction in metastasis and proliferation observed upon TDP43 or SRSF3 knockdown is mediated by the splicing regulation of PAR3 and NUMB exon 12, respectively. Consequently, the TDP43/SRSF3 complex and the resulting PAR3 isoform represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention in TNBC.

title: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture--pathologic basis of plaque stability and instability.
text: Primary review time is 27 days. Atherosclerosis remains a significant topic in pathology research due to its complex pathogenesis and clinical consequences [1]. Many diseases, including myocardial infarction, stroke, abdominal aneurysms, and lower limb ischemia, are related to atherosclerosis and contribute to morbidity and mortality in Western populations. Despite the range of clinical manifestations, most acute events in atherosclerosis share a common feature: the rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque [2–4]. Plaque ruptures can vary in severity, from small fissures or erosions on the plaque surface to deep tears that extend into the lipid core, resulting in thrombus formation [5, 6]. The abdominal aorta is particularly susceptible to plaque formation and complications. In this large vessel, plaque disruption and thrombosis can lead to extensive ulcerations on the aortic wall, as seen in autopsies of older individuals. While atherosclerosis plays a clear role in abdominal aneurysm formation [7], the rate of clinically significant complications from mural thrombosis is surprisingly low in these patients, although cholesterol emboli are often found in their kidneys and skin postmortem. The impact of biologically active mediators released from eroded aortic surfaces on the human body remains unclear. In contrast, in smaller vessels like coronary arteries, occlusive thrombosis is a common and often fatal complication of plaque formation. For correspondence, please contact the author at +31-20-5665-633 or a.c.vanderwal@amc.uva.nl.

title: Pioneer factor Pax7 deploys a stable enhancer repertoire for specification of cell fate
text: Pioneer transcription factors play a crucial role in establishing new cell-fate capabilities by initiating changes in chromatin structure. However, there are still many aspects of pioneer action that are not well understood, such as their speed and stability. In this study, we demonstrate that Pax7 is essential and efficient in determining the fate of a specific pituitary lineage by activating a distinct set of enhancers. Pax7 quickly binds to its targeted enhancers, but the process of chromatin remodeling and gene activation is slower. The enhancers opened by Pax7 undergo changes in DNA methylation and acquire a stable epigenetic memory, as evidenced by the binding of nonpioneer factors even after Pax7 is no longer present. This research highlights that a temporary expression of Pax7 is enough to establish a stable cell identity. By analyzing the dynamics of Pax7 during pituitary lineage specification, we observe that Pax7 rapidly binds to pioneer sites marked with unique heterochromatin and initiates chromatin opening that remains stable even after Pax7 is withdrawn. This results in a loss of DNA hypermethylation at the enhancers that were pioneered by Pax7.

title: Human cancer cells utilize mitotic DNA synthesis to resist replication stress at telomeres regardless of their telomere maintenance mechanism
text: Telomeres and common fragile sites (CFSs) share similarities in terms of being difficult to replicate and exhibiting fragility during mitosis when faced with DNA replication stress. At CFSs, this fragility causes a delay in DNA replication completion until early mitosis, where cells switch to a RAD52-dependent form of break-induced replication. Our study reveals that this process, known as mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS), also occurs at human telomeres. Telomeric MiDAS is not limited to telomeres that show obvious fragility and is observed in various cell lines regardless of whether their telomeres are maintained by telomerase or the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) mechanism. MiDAS at telomeres relies on RAD52 and operates similarly to CFS-associated MiDAS, except that it does not require the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease. We propose a model in which replication stress triggers a RAD52-dependent form of break-induced replication that bypasses the need for MUS81-EME1 to complete DNA synthesis during mitosis.

title: Low drug levels and thrombotic complications in high‐risk atrial fibrillation patients treated with direct oral anticoagulants
text: Currently, laboratory monitoring is not required for Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs). However, a study was conducted to evaluate the relationship between DOAC C-trough anticoagulant levels and thromboembolic events in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). The study included 565 consecutive naive patients with AF and DOAC-specific measurements were performed at steady state within 15-25 days after starting treatment. The patients were divided into four equal classes based on their C-trough levels, and thromboembolic events occurring during 1 year of follow-up were recorded. The results showed that thromboembolic events occurred in 10 patients with the lowest baseline C-trough levels, while no events occurred in the remaining groups. These patients also had a higher mean CHA2 DS2 -VASc score compared to the total patient population. The study concludes that larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Consensus guidelines for the detection of immunogenic cell death.
text: Apoptotic cells have traditionally been thought of as non-immunogenic, meaning they do not elicit specific immune responses to dead cell-associated antigens. However, certain stimuli can trigger a unique type of apoptotic cell death that is recognized by the adaptive immune system. This phenomenon, known as "immunogenic cell death" (ICD), is characterized by the release of immunostimulatory molecules called damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) in a specific spatiotemporal pattern. Some commonly used anticancer treatments, such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy, can induce ICD. Additionally, deficiencies in the immune system's ability to recognize cell death as immunogenic can negatively impact the outcome of cancer patients treated with ICD inducers. Therefore, ICD has significant clinical and therapeutic implications. Unfortunately, the current method for detecting ICD involves vaccination experiments using mice and cancer cells, which is not feasible for large-scale screening. In this article, we present strategies for identifying surrogate markers of ICD in vitro and screening large chemical libraries for potential ICD inducers. These strategies are based on a recently developed high-content, high-throughput platform that allows for the detection of multiple DAMPs, such as cell surface-exposed calreticulin, extracellular ATP, and high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), as well as the processes that lead to their release, such as endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and necrotic plasma membrane permeabilization. We believe that this technology will facilitate the development of next-generation anticancer treatments that not only kill cancer cells but also convert them into a cancer-specific therapeutic vaccine.

title: Long-Term ERK Inhibition in KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Cancer Is Associated with MYC Degradation and Senescence-like Growth Suppression.
text: The effectiveness of Raf and MEK inhibitors in RAS-mutant cancers has been limited due to the induction of compensatory mechanisms and reactivation of ERK. Our study found that directly inhibiting ERK with pharmacologic agents suppressed the growth of a specific subset of pancreatic cancer cell lines with KRAS mutations. Furthermore, when combined with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition, it resulted in synergistic cell death. We also discovered other combinations that enhanced the action of ERK inhibitors. Surprisingly, long-term treatment of sensitive cell lines led to senescence, which was partly mediated by MYC degradation and reactivation of p16. We observed that enhanced basal PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling was associated with resistance to ERK inhibitors, as well as other protein kinases identified through kinome-wide siRNA screening and a genetic gain-of-function screen. Our findings highlight the distinct consequences of inhibiting the ERK kinase cascade.

title: TRF2 Recruits RTEL1 to Telomeres in S Phase to Promote T-Loop Unwinding
text: To maintain the integrity of telomeres in vertebrates, the helicase RTEL1 plays a crucial role in unwinding t-loops and preventing telomere fragility. However, the mechanism by which RTEL1 interacts with telomeres to promote t-loop unwinding remains unclear. In this study, we have discovered that the shelterin protein TRF2 is responsible for recruiting RTEL1 to telomeres during the S phase. This recruitment is essential to prevent catastrophic t-loop processing by structure-specific nucleases. We have also identified that the interaction between TRF2 and RTEL1 is facilitated by a metal-coordinating C4C4 motif in RTEL1. Interestingly, this motif is compromised by the RTEL1(R1264H) mutation, which is associated with Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS). Conversely, we have found that a substitution mutation (TRF2(I124D)) within the TRFH domain of TRF2 eliminates RTEL1 binding and mimics the effects of the RTEL1(R1264H) mutation. This leads to abnormal t-loop excision, telomere length heterogeneity, and loss of the telomere as a circle. These findings suggest that TRF2 plays a crucial role in recruiting RTEL1 to facilitate t-loop disassembly at telomeres during the S phase.

title: Macrophages Facilitate Electrical Conduction in the Heart
text: The specific functions of tissue-resident macrophages in the heart during normal conditions are not yet known. However, our study reveals that these macrophages play a role in facilitating electrical conduction in the distal atrioventricular node of the heart. In this region, conducting cells are closely intertwined with elongated macrophages that express connexin 43. Through connexin-43-containing gap junctions, the cardiac macrophages are able to connect with spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes. Interestingly, the macrophages have a negative resting membrane potential and depolarize in sync with the cardiomyocytes. On the other hand, the macrophages cause the resting membrane potential of the cardiomyocytes to become more positive, which, according to computational modeling, speeds up their repolarization process. When channelrhodopsin-2-expressing macrophages are stimulated with light, it improves atrioventricular conduction. Conversely, when connexin 43 is deleted in macrophages or when there is a congenital lack of macrophages, atrioventricular conduction is delayed. In a mouse model where macrophages are ablated using Cd11bDTR, there is a progressive atrioventricular block. These findings suggest that macrophages are involved in both normal and abnormal cardiac conduction.

title: A Tunable Diffusion‐Consumption Mechanism of Cytokine Propagation Enables Plasticity in Cell‐to‐Cell Communication in the Immune System
text: The communication between immune cells through the exchange of cytokines is crucial for an appropriate immune response. However, the extent of this communication is not well understood. In this study, we used theoretical models and experimental approaches to determine the spatial range of cytokine communication in dense tissues. We discovered that the competition between cytokine diffusion and consumption leads to the formation of localized areas with high cytokine concentrations and distinct boundaries. The size of these areas depends on the density of cells that consume cytokines, a parameter that is regulated during immune responses. In vivo experiments revealed interactions occurring within a range of 80-120 &mgr;m, resulting in significant variability in cytokine exposure between cells. This variability, often overlooked in single-cell studies, is a non-genetic source of cell-to-cell variability. Our findings provide insights into the role of diffusible factors in shaping the patterns of immune responses.

title: Cardiac neural crest contributes to cardiomyogenesis in zebrafish.
text: The presence of cardiac neural crest is crucial for heart development and the formation of conotruncal cushions and outflow tract septation in birds and mammals. However, it was uncertain whether zebrafish, with their unseparated outflow tract, possess cardiac neural crest. This study utilized three different methods to label and track lineage, revealing the existence of cardiac neural crest cells in zebrafish. These cells were found to have the ability to generate muscle cells in the myocardium of the major chambers during development, as indicated by the presence of MF20-positive cells. Fate-mapping experiments showed that zebrafish cardiac neural crest cells originate from neural tube regions similar to those in birds, as well as from a novel region located in front of the otic vesicle. Unlike other vertebrates, the cardiac neural crest in zebrafish invades the myocardium in all segments of the heart, including the outflow tract, atrium, atrioventricular junction, and ventricle. Along the rostrocaudal axis, three distinct groups of premigratory neural crest cells exhibit different tendencies to contribute to specific segments in the heart, and these groups are characterized by unique combinations of gene expression patterns. Zebrafish can serve as an excellent model organism for studying the interactions between cardiac neural crest cells and cardiovascular development.

title: Sodium Hydroxide Production from Seawater Desalination Brine: Process Design and Energy Efficiency.
text: The ability to raise pH levels is crucial for desalination pretreatment, particularly in reverse osmosis, as well as for various industries. However, the processes currently used to increase pH often result in significant emissions and the use of nonrenewable resources. An alternative approach involves utilizing waste brine from desalination to produce sodium hydroxide, which can be achieved through appropriate concentration and purification steps before inputting it into the chlor-alkali process. This study focuses on developing and modeling an efficient process for sodium hydroxide production from seawater desalination brine using membrane chlor-alkali electrolysis. The integrated system includes nanofiltration, concentration through evaporation or mechanical vapor compression, chemical softening, further ion-exchange softening, dechlorination, and membrane electrolysis. The study highlights the productivity of the system, performance of its components, and energy consumption of the sodium hydroxide production process. It also investigates the dependencies of these factors on the outlet conditions of the electrolyzer and the recirculation of the brine. The analysis of the process includes assessing the energy efficiency of major components, estimating the operating expenses of the system, and comparing it with similar processes. The brine-to-caustic process is found to be technically feasible and offers several advantages, such as reducing the environmental impact of desalination by minimizing brine discharge and increasing the overall water recovery ratio of the reverse osmosis facility. Furthermore, the study provides optimal conditions for producing caustic soda not only for internal use but also for potential revenue generation.

title: High-Throughput Genetic Screens Identify a Large and Diverse Collection of New Sporulation Genes in Bacillus subtilis
text: The process of Bacillus subtilis bacteria transforming into dormant spores is well-studied in biology. Through genetic screens conducted over the past 50 years, numerous factors involved in each stage of this process have been identified. Recent transcriptional profiling has revealed additional genes that are activated during sporulation and are necessary for successful spore development. In this study, we utilized transposon-sequencing (Tn-seq) to determine if there were any undiscovered sporulation genes. Our screening identified 133 out of the 148 known genes with sporulation defects. Surprisingly, we also discovered 24 new genes that had not previously been associated with spore formation. To investigate their roles, we used fluorescence microscopy to observe the development of null mutants from the B. subtilis knockout collection at different stages of differentiation. This analysis revealed mutants that experienced delays in sporulation initiation, defects in membrane remodeling, and impairments in spore maturation. Some mutants displayed unique sporulation phenotypes. We conducted a detailed examination of two newly identified factors involved in cell-cell signaling pathways during sporulation. One factor, SpoIIT, activates σE in the mother cell, while the other, SpoIIIL, is necessary for σG activity in the forespore. Our analysis also demonstrated that up to 36 sporulation-induced genes, which had not previously been associated with mutant phenotypes, are required for timely spore maturation. Additionally, we discovered a significant number of transposon insertions that triggered premature initiation of sporulation. These findings highlight the effectiveness of Tn-seq in discovering new genes and pathways involved in sporulation. Furthermore, with the completion of the null mutant collection, this approach can be applied to other less well-understood processes.

title: Psychobiological mechanisms underlying the social buffering of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis: a review of animal models and human studies across development.
text: The discovery of how social relationships can help reduce stress has been a significant finding in the field of psychobiology over the past century. However, our understanding of the underlying neurobiological and psychological mechanisms behind this stress reduction is still in its early stages. One important area of research focuses on the neurocircuitry that can regulate the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis. This review aims to bring together animal models and human studies to explore how social interactions can influence the HPA axis from infancy to adulthood, specifically looking at a process known as social buffering. Social buffering refers to the phenomenon observed in various species where the presence or assistance of a fellow member dampens the stress response of the HPA axis when faced with a threat or challenge. We discuss the relevant neurobiology when sufficient information is available and highlight the gaps in our understanding across all areas of research that we aim to integrate. We propose a working conceptual model that focuses on the role of oxytocinergic systems and prefrontal neural networks as potential biological mediators of this process. Additionally, we suggest that early experiences play a critical role in shaping the long-term effects of social buffering. This synthesis points towards future directions for research and specific experiments that need to be conducted in order to develop a more comprehensive model of the HPA social buffering effect throughout the lifespan, incorporating multiple levels of analysis including neuroendocrine, behavioral, and social aspects.

title: Elevation of circulating branched-chain amino acids is an early event in human pancreatic adenocarcinoma development
text: The majority of patients diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) have advanced disease and a survival rate of less than 12 months. PDAC has been linked to obesity and glucose intolerance, but it is unclear whether changes in circulating metabolites are associated with early cancer progression. In order to gain a better understanding of metabolic abnormalities related to early-stage PDAC, we analyzed metabolites in the plasma of individuals with pancreatic cancer (cases) and matched controls from four prospective cohort studies. Our findings reveal that elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) in the plasma are associated with a more than twofold increased risk of future pancreatic cancer diagnosis. This increased risk is independent of known predisposing factors, and the strongest association is observed in subjects whose samples were collected 2 to 5 years before diagnosis, suggesting the presence of occult disease. We also demonstrate that plasma BCAAs are elevated in mice with early-stage pancreatic cancers driven by mutant Kras expression, but not in mice with Kras-driven tumors in other tissues. Furthermore, we show that the increase in plasma BCAAs accompanying early-stage disease is due to the breakdown of tissue protein. These findings suggest that increased whole-body protein breakdown is an early event in the development of PDAC.

title: Effective Use of PI3K and MEK Inhibitors to Treat Mutant K-Ras G12D and PIK3CA H1047R Murine Lung Cancers
text:
Mutations in the p110-alpha catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), encoded by PIK3CA, have been found to activate the enzyme. These mutations are commonly observed in two specific regions: the helical domain (E545K and E542K) and the kinase domain (H1047R). While these p110-alpha mutants have been shown to transform cells in laboratory settings, their oncogenic potential has not been evaluated in genetically modified mouse models. Additionally, clinical trials using PI3K inhibitors have recently begun, but it is unclear if these drugs will only be effective in specific types of cancer with defined genetic mutations. 

To address these questions, we created a mouse model of lung adenocarcinomas that were initiated and sustained by the expression of the p110-alpha H1047R mutation. Treatment of these tumors with NVP-BEZ235, a clinical inhibitor that targets both PI3K and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), resulted in significant tumor regression as confirmed by positron emission tomography-computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and microscopic examination. In contrast, lung cancers in mice driven by mutant Kras did not show a substantial response to NVP-BEZ235 alone. However, when NVP-BEZ235 was combined with a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) inhibitor called ARRY-142886, there was a synergistic effect in reducing the size of these Kras-mutant cancers. 

These findings from our in vivo studies suggest that inhibitors targeting the PI3K-mTOR pathway may be effective in treating cancers with PIK3CA mutations. Furthermore, when combined with MEK inhibitors, they may also be a promising approach for treating lung cancers with KRAS mutations.

title: Transdifferentiation of glioblastoma cells into vascular endothelial cells.
text: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive type of brain tumor and is highly resistant to intensive combination therapies and anti-VEGF therapies. In order to understand why GBMs are resistant to anti-VEGF therapy, we studied the blood vessels in GBM tumors that were induced in mice with specific genetic modifications. Surprisingly, we found that the blood vessels contained cells that originated from the tumor itself. These tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) did not result from the fusion of normal blood vessel cells with tumor cells. Further experiments showed that hypoxia, a condition of low oxygen, played a role in the differentiation of tumor cells into endothelial cells, and this process was independent of VEGF. Importantly, TDECs were not only resistant to an inhibitor of VEGF receptors, but their presence actually increased in response to the treatment. We also observed the presence of TDECs in human GBM samples. Based on these findings, we propose that TDECs play a crucial role in the resistance to anti-VEGF therapy and could be a potential target for GBM treatment.

title: Ribosomal DNA copy loss and repeat instability in ATRX-mutated cancers
text: ATRX, a gene associated with alpha thalassemia/mental retardation X-linked syndrome, forms complexes with DAXX to facilitate the deposition of histone variant H3.3 into repetitive heterochromatin regions. Recent studies using genome sequencing techniques have identified mutations in ATRX in various cancers, which are linked to the activation of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). In this study, we demonstrate that depletion of ATRX in mouse embryonic stem cells results in a specific decrease in the number of ribosomal RNA gene (rDNA) copies. Consistent with this finding, human ALT-positive tumors with ATRX mutations also exhibit significantly lower rDNA copy numbers compared to ALT-negative tumors. Further investigation reveals that the loss of rDNA copies and instability of repetitive sequences are caused by a disruption in the deposition of H3.3 and subsequent failure in heterochromatin formation at rDNA repeats in the absence of ATRX. Additionally, ATRX-depleted cells exhibit reduced ribosomal RNA transcription output and increased sensitivity to CX5461, an inhibitor of RNA polymerase I (Pol I) transcription. Interestingly, human ALT-positive cancer cell lines also display heightened sensitivity to CX5461 treatment. Our findings shed light on the role of ATRX loss in tumorigenesis through the destabilization of rDNA and suggest the potential therapeutic value of targeting Pol I transcription in ALT-positive cancers.

title: Combining indoor residual spraying and insecticide-treated nets for malaria control in Africa: a review of possible outcomes and an outline of suggestions for the future
text: The preferred methods of controlling malaria-carrying mosquitoes are insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS). These methods are often used together in households to reduce transmission in areas with high malaria prevalence. However, there is limited evidence to suggest that using both methods together provides greater protection than using either method alone. This article proposes that the effectiveness of combining ITNs and IRS depends on how the active ingredients affect mosquitoes that enter or attempt to enter houses. It suggests that combining highly deterrent IRS compounds with highly toxic ITNs could enhance household protection. To avoid insecticide resistance, it is recommended to use ITNs and IRS products with different insecticide classes, such as pyrethroid-based nets with organophosphate or carbamate-based IRS. The overall effectiveness of these interventions also depends on factors like the coverage of the population and the behavior of the mosquito species. The article concludes by highlighting the importance of research, including mathematical modeling, to evaluate the effectiveness of combining IRS and ITNs compared to using them individually.

title: Membrane estrogen receptor-α levels in MCF-7 breast cancer cells predict cAMP and proliferation responses
text:
The complete understanding of the conditions and signaling pathways involved in the rapid induction of cAMP production by 17β-estradiol (E2) and its consequent effects on breast cancer cells is still lacking. To address this, we conducted a study comparing the mechanistic responses of cAMP in MCF-7 cell lines with low (mERlow) and high (mERhigh) expression of the membrane form of estrogen receptor (mER)-α. This allowed us to determine the specific receptor subform involved in cAMP signaling.
