We isolated MCF-7 cells and sorted them into mERhigh (mER-α-enriched) and mERlow (mER-α-depleted) populations using immunopanning and fluorescence activated cell sorting. We discovered that incubation conditions at 4°C, which had not been previously reported, were optimal for demonstrating E2-induced cAMP production. We examined the time-dependent and dose-dependent effects of E2 on cAMP production in both cell subpopulations.

To assess the effects of E2-induced cell proliferation, we conducted the crystal violet assay and evaluated the impact of forskolin, 8-CPT cAMP, protein kinase A inhibitor (H-89), and adenylyl cyclase inhibitor (SQ 22,536). We observed a rapid and transient increase in cAMP levels after stimulation with 1 pmol/l E2 in mERhigh cells. Interestingly, these responses were more reliable and robust at 4°C compared to the commonly used condition of 37°C. The decrease in cAMP at 37°C was not due to export. The presence of 3-Isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX; 1 mmol/l) only partially preserved cAMP, suggesting the involvement of multiple phosphodiesterases in modulating its levels. The accumulated cAMP was consistently higher in mERhigh cells compared to mERlow cells, indicating the involvement of mER-α levels in the process. The response induced by E2 was blocked by ICI172,780, and 17α-estradiol did not elicit a similar response, further suggesting the activity through an estrogen receptor. The dose-dependent cAMP production in response to E2 was biphasic in both cell types, but mERhigh cells were responsive to 50-fold higher E2 concentrations. The proliferation of mERlow cells was stimulated across the entire range of E2 concentrations, while the number of mERhigh cells decreased significantly at concentrations above 1 nmol/l, indicating that excessive estrogen stimulation can lead to cell death, as previously reported, and that mER-α is involved. We also demonstrated the involvement of adenylyl cyclase activation and downstream participation of protein kinase A in these responses. The rapid nongenomic signaling cascades mediated by mER-α generate cAMP and downstream signaling events, contributing to the regulation of breast cancer cell number.

title: The embryonic cell lineage of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: The complete cell lineage of Caenorhabditis elegans, from zygote to newly hatched larva, has been successfully traced, revealing a total of 671 cells generated during embryogenesis. In the hermaphrodite, 113 of these cells undergo programmed death, while the remaining cells either differentiate terminally or become postembryonic blast cells. The embryonic lineage is remarkably consistent, with the fate of each cell being predetermined. However, the correlation between cell ancestry and cell fate does not follow a clear pattern. For instance, although most neurons originate from the embryonic ectoderm, some are produced by the mesoderm, and a few are related to muscles. Additionally, the boundaries of cell lineages do not always align with functional boundaries. Nonetheless, experiments involving cell ablation and isolation demonstrate that certain sections of embryogenesis exhibit significant cell autonomy. This suggests that the intricate cell lineage itself plays a crucial role in determining cell fate. In this study, we delve into the origin of repeat units in the body wall, the generation of different orders of symmetry, the analysis of sublineages within the lineage, and the evolutionary implications of these findings.

title: Self-Reactive B Cells in the Germinal Center Reaction.
text: In order to maintain immunological self-tolerance, it is necessary to prevent lymphocytes with self-reactive antigen receptors from causing harmful or inflammatory responses. Traditionally, self-tolerance has been understood as the removal, editing, or silencing of B and T cells that develop self-reactive antigen receptors early on. However, B cells that are activated by foreign antigens can enter germinal centers (GCs), where they modify their antigen receptors through somatic hypermutation (SHM) of their immunoglobulin genes. The presence of activated, self-reactive GC B cells poses a unique challenge to self-tolerance, which must be quickly addressed to prevent the production of autoantibodies. In this discussion, we explore the current understanding of the mechanisms that enforce B cell self-tolerance, with a specific focus on controlling self-reactive GC B cells. We also examine how these cells can either escape self-tolerance and initiate autoantibody production or be salvaged through SHM and contribute to productive antibody responses.

title: Chronic inflammation (inflammaging) and its potential contribution to age-associated diseases.
text: The process of human aging is characterized by a persistent, mild inflammation known as "inflammaging." This condition poses a significant risk to the health and well-being of elderly individuals, as many age-related diseases are linked to inflammation. However, the exact cause of inflammaging and its impact on adverse health outcomes are still not fully understood. Therefore, it is crucial to identify the pathways that regulate age-related inflammation in various systems to determine if treatments targeting inflammaging could benefit older people. A session on inflammation was conducted during the Advances in Gerosciences meeting at the National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging in Bethesda on October 30 and 31, 2013, with the aim of addressing these important unanswered questions about inflammaging. This article presents the key findings from that session.

title: Cryptochromes Enabling Plants and Animals to Determine Circadian Time
text: Cryptochromes, which are blue light photoreceptors containing flavin, are closely related to photolyases. They can be found in plants, animals, and have recently been discovered in bacteria. In plants, cryptochromes have diverse functions, including regulating circadian rhythms. Similarly, in Drosophila and mammals, cryptochromes play a crucial role in the circadian clock, serving as an essential component.

title: Neural crest-derived stem cells migrate and differentiate into cardiomyocytes after myocardial infarction.
text:
Our objective was to investigate the migration and differentiation potential of primitive neural crest-derived (NC) cells in the context of myocardial infarction (MI). Previous research has shown that these cells migrate from the cardiac neural crest during embryonic development and remain in the heart as dormant stem cells, capable of differentiating into various cell types, including cardiomyocytes. 

To conduct our study, we generated double-transgenic mice by crossing protein-0 promoter-Cre mice with Floxed-enhanced green fluorescent protein mice, allowing us to visualize the NC cells expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein. In the neonatal heart, we found that NC stem cells (NCSCs) were primarily located in the outflow tract, but were also distributed throughout the ventricular myocardium in a gradient from base to apex. Through time-lapse video analysis, we observed that the NCSCs were migratory. Some NCSCs persisted in the adult heart. 

During MI, we observed that NCSCs accumulated at the ischemic border zone area (BZA), which is known to express monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Experiments using ex vivo cell migration assays confirmed that MCP-1 induced NCSC migration, and this effect was significantly reduced by an anti-MCP-1 antibody. Additionally, we observed the appearance of small NC cardiomyocytes in the BZA 2 weeks post-MI, with their numbers gradually increasing over time. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that NCSCs migrate into the BZA through MCP-1/CCR2 signaling and contribute to the generation of cardiomyocytes for cardiac regeneration following MI.

title: Mitochondria as sensors and regulators of calcium signalling
text: Over the last twenty years, the accumulation of calcium (Ca2+) in energized mitochondria has become recognized as a highly significant biological process. It has been demonstrated that the uptake of Ca2+ by mitochondria plays a crucial role in controlling intracellular Ca2+ signaling, cell metabolism, cell survival, and other functions specific to different cell types. This is achieved by maintaining appropriate levels of cytosolic Ca2+ and regulating mitochondrial effectors. Excitingly, the discovery of the specific transporters responsible for mitochondrial Ca2+ transport has provided new opportunities for further research and potential molecular interventions.

title: Caspase-11 promotes the fusion of phagosomes harboring pathogenic bacteria with lysosomes by modulating actin polymerization.
text: Inflammasomes are complexes made up of multiple proteins, including members of the NLR family and caspase-1. When bacterial molecules are detected in macrophages, the inflammasome is formed, leading to the activation of caspase-1. Caspase-11 is responsible for activating caspase-1 in response to lipopolysaccharide and bacterial toxins, but its role in bacterial infection is not yet understood. Our study showed that caspase-11 is not necessary for caspase-1 activation when Legionella, Salmonella, Francisella, and Listeria are present. However, we found that active caspase-11 in mice is crucial for limiting L. pneumophila infection. Similarly, human caspase-4 and caspase-5, which are similar to mouse caspase-11, work together to restrict L. pneumophila infection in human macrophages. Caspase-11 promotes the merging of the L. pneumophila vacuole with lysosomes by influencing actin polymerization through cofilin. However, caspase-11 is not necessary for the fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes containing nonpathogenic bacteria, revealing a fundamental difference in the movement of phagosomes based on their contents.

title: Adipocyte inflammation is essential for healthy adipose tissue expansion and remodeling.
text: The connection between obesity and its physiological consequences is largely due to chronic inflammation. Contrary to popular belief that inflammatory signals have a negative impact on metabolism, our research demonstrates that proinflammatory signaling in fat cells is actually necessary for proper remodeling and expansion of adipose tissue. We conducted experiments using three mouse models with reduced proinflammatory potential specifically in adipose tissue. These mice showed a decreased ability to generate new fat cells in vivo, but their ability to differentiate in vitro remained unchanged. When exposed to a high-fat diet, the expansion of visceral fat tissue was significantly affected. This was accompanied by a decline in intestinal barrier function, an increase in liver fat accumulation, and metabolic dysfunction. A weakened proinflammatory response in fat cells resulted in the accumulation of fat in abnormal locations, glucose intolerance, and systemic inflammation. Therefore, inflammation in adipose tissue is an adaptive response that allows for safe storage of excess nutrients and contributes to a protective barrier against gut-derived toxins.

title: Chronic variable stress activates hematopoietic stem cells
text:
Exposure to psychosocial stress is a known risk factor for various diseases, including atherosclerosis. Although the exact mechanisms are not fully understood, there is evidence suggesting that the interaction between the mind and the immune system plays a role in the development and progression of stress-related diseases. This interaction involves different pathways, such as the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis, which regulate the production of stress hormones and catecholamines.

However, it is still unclear whether chronic stress affects the activity of hematopoietic stem cells, which are responsible for producing various types of blood cells. In this study, we aimed to investigate the impact of stress on hematopoietic stem cell activity. Our findings demonstrate that stress increases the proliferation of these primitive cells, leading to higher levels of disease-promoting inflammatory leukocytes.

We observed that chronic stress induced an increase in the number of monocytes and neutrophils in humans. Further investigation in mice revealed that stress activates hematopoietic stem cells, which are located upstream in the blood cell production process. This activation is mediated by the release of surplus noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve fibers, which then signals bone marrow niche cells to decrease the levels of a specific molecule called CXCL12 through a receptor called β3-adrenergic receptor. As a result, hematopoietic stem cell proliferation is enhanced, leading to an increased production of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes.

To assess the impact of chronic stress on atherosclerosis, we subjected atherosclerosis-prone mice to chronic stress. The accelerated hematopoiesis caused by stress promoted the development of plaque features associated with vulnerable lesions, which are known to cause heart attacks and strokes in humans.

In summary, our study provides evidence that chronic stress can alter hematopoietic stem cell activity, leading to an increased production of disease-promoting inflammatory cells. This finding sheds light on the potential mechanisms linking stress and the development of diseases like atherosclerosis.

title: CNTF reverses obesity-induced insulin resistance by activating skeletal muscle AMPK
text: In both humans and rodents, Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) has been found to promote weight loss and improve glucose tolerance. It is believed that CNTF acts centrally by stimulating the growth of new neurons in the hypothalamus, which helps regulate food intake. Additionally, CNTF also affects gene expression in the liver, similar to how leptin functions. Our study reveals that CNTF activates the CNTFRα–IL-6R–gp130β receptor complex, leading to increased fatty-acid oxidation and reduced insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. This activation occurs through the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), independent of brain signaling. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that the anti-obesity effects of CNTF in the peripheral tissues are a result of direct actions on skeletal muscle. Importantly, these effects are not hindered by obesity induced by diet or genetics, making CNTF a promising therapeutic option for obesity-related diseases.

title: The Global Spread of Hepatitis C Virus 1a and 1b: A Phylodynamic and Phylogeographic Analysis
text:
BACKGROUND
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is estimated to affect 130-180 million people worldwide. The origin of HCV is unknown, but evidence suggests that HCV genotype 1 likely originated from West Africa. Previous studies have attempted to estimate the spread of the virus, suggesting that HCV transmission began in 1900 and grew steadily until the late 1980s. However, new data suggests that the expansion of HCV may have occurred after World War II. The aim of our study was to determine the timeline and route of global HCV spread.

METHODS AND FINDINGS
We used a rarely sequenced region of HCV (E2P7NS2) that is more informative for molecular epidemiology studies than the commonly used NS5B region. We analyzed a large set of new E2P7NS2 and NS5B sequences, along with existing global HCV sequences, to estimate the spread of the most prevalent HCV subtypes, 1a and 1b. Our analysis revealed that transmission of subtypes 1a and 1b increased significantly between 1940 and 1980, with subtype 1b spreading before subtype 1a by at least 16 years. Phylogeographic analysis of NS5B sequences suggested that HCV subtypes 1a and 1b spread from developed countries to developing countries.

CONCLUSIONS
Our study found that the evolutionary rate of HCV is faster than previously thought. The global spread of HCV coincided with the use of transfused blood and blood products, as well as the expansion of intravenous drug use. However, the spread slowed before the implementation of anti-HCV screening. The different transmission routes associated with subtypes 1a and 1b explain the earlier expansion of subtype 1b. Our data supports the hypothesis that HCV spread from developed countries to the developing world.

title: Pharmacological interventions for smoking cessation: an overview and network meta-analysis.
text:
Smoking is a major cause of preventable illness and premature death worldwide. There are several medications available to help people quit smoking, including nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, and varenicline. Cytisine, a treatment similar to varenicline, is also used in Russia and some former socialist countries. Other therapies, such as nortriptyline, have also been tested. 

The objective of this study is to compare the effectiveness of NRT, bupropion, and varenicline in achieving long-term abstinence, both compared to a placebo and to each other. The study also aims to compare the remaining treatments to a placebo in achieving long-term abstinence. Additionally, the study examines the risks of adverse events associated with each treatment and whether the benefits outweigh the harms. 

The study focuses on Cochrane reviews, which include randomized trials. The participants in these trials are typically adult smokers, excluding pregnant women and specific disease groups. The treatments covered in the study include NRT, bupropion, nortriptyline, varenicline, cytisine, anxiolytics, rimonabant, clonidine, lobeline, dianicline, mecamylamine, Nicobrevin, opioid antagonists, nicotine vaccines, and silver acetate. The desired outcome is continuous or prolonged abstinence for at least six months after starting treatment. The study also examines the incidence of serious adverse events associated with each treatment. 

The researchers searched the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews for relevant reviews, with the last search conducted in November 2012. The methodological quality of the reviews was assessed using a revised version of the AMSTAR scale. Network meta-analyses were conducted for NRT, bupropion, and varenicline, comparing each treatment to the others and to a placebo for effectiveness. The risks of serious adverse events were compared between varenicline and bupropion. 

The study identified 12 treatment-specific reviews, covering 267 studies and 101,804 participants. Both NRT and bupropion were found to be more effective than a placebo. Varenicline increased the odds of quitting compared to a placebo. When comparing bupropion and NRT, they were found to have equal efficacy. Varenicline was superior to single forms of NRT and to bupropion. It was also more effective than nicotine patch, nicotine gum, and other forms of NRT, but not more effective than combination NRT. Combination NRT outperformed single formulations. Cytisine showed positive results without significant adverse events. 

The study found a lower than expected rate of seizures associated with bupropion. The analysis of serious adverse events for bupropion and varenicline did not show any excess compared to a placebo. Nortriptyline was found to increase the chances of quitting, but neither nortriptyline nor bupropion enhanced the effect of NRT. Clonidine increased the chances of quitting but also led to more adverse events. The evidence regarding mecamylamine in combination with NRT was inconclusive. Other treatments did not show a benefit compared to a placebo. Nicotine vaccines are not yet licensed for smoking cessation. Nicobrevin's license has been revoked, and the development and testing of rimonabant, taranabant, and dianicline have been discontinued. 

In conclusion, NRT, bupropion, varenicline, and cytisine have been shown to improve the chances of quitting smoking. Combination NRT and varenicline are equally effective. Nortriptyline also improves the chances of quitting. Based on current evidence, none of the treatments have a significant incidence of adverse events that would discourage their use. Further research is needed to examine the safety of varenicline and the potential of cytisine as an effective and affordable treatment. However, additional research on the efficacy and safety of NRT is not necessary.

title: A library of yeast transcription factor motifs reveals a widespread function for Rsc3 in targeting nucleosome exclusion at promoters.
text: The primary way in which cells identify genomic features is through the specific binding of DNA-binding proteins to DNA sequences. In this study, we have systematically determined the DNA-binding specificities of transcription factors in yeast. We have obtained specific binding patterns for 112 DNA-binding proteins, which belong to 19 different structural classes. Interestingly, one-third of these binding patterns have not been previously documented. Some of the identified binding sequences have notable distributions in the genome, particularly in relation to transcription start sites. This suggests that these sequences are biologically significant and may play a role in the organization of promoters. For instance, we have observed that binding sequences for the Rsc3 protein, which contain the core CGCG, are predominantly located approximately 100 base pairs upstream of transcription start sites. When the RSC3 gene is mutated, we have observed a significant increase in the presence of nucleosomes in hundreds of nearby promoters that contain a Rsc3 binding element. However, this mutation has little effect on promoters that lack Rsc3 binding sequences. These findings indicate that Rsc3 has a broad role in targeting the exclusion of nucleosomes at yeast promoters.

title: EphA3 maintains tumorigenicity and is a therapeutic target in glioblastoma multiforme.
text: Considerable effort has been dedicated to identifying effective therapeutic targets in glioblastoma (GBM) in order to impede the growth of this aggressive cancer. Our research demonstrates that the receptor tyrosine kinase EphA3 is frequently overexpressed in GBM, particularly in the highly aggressive mesenchymal subtype. Significantly, EphA3 is abundantly expressed in the population of tumor-initiating cells in glioma and plays a crucial role in maintaining the less differentiated state of tumor cells by modulating mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling. Knocking down EphA3 or depleting EphA3-positive tumor cells resulted in a reduction of tumorigenic potential comparable to treatment with a therapeutic radiolabelled EphA3-specific monoclonal antibody. These findings establish EphA3 as a functional receptor that can be targeted in the treatment of GBM.

title: Chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells for acute lymphoid leukemia.
text: The use of chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells that target CD19 has shown promise in treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). However, it is still uncertain whether these chimeric antigen receptor T cells have clinical effectiveness in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Two children with relapsed and refractory pre-B-cell ALL were given infusions of T cells that were genetically modified to express an anti-CD19 antibody and a T-cell signaling molecule (known as CTL019 chimeric antigen receptor T cells). The dose administered ranged from 1.4×10(6) to 1.2×10(7) CTL019 cells per kilogram of body weight. In both patients, the CTL019 T cells expanded significantly, reaching levels over 1000 times higher than the initial engraftment level, and were detected in the bone marrow. Furthermore, the chimeric antigen receptor T cells were found in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and remained at high levels for at least 6 months. Eight severe adverse events were observed, including cytokine-release syndrome and B-cell aplasia in both patients. One child experienced a severe cytokine-release syndrome, which was successfully reversed with the use of etanercept and tocilizumab, without affecting the expansion of chimeric antigen receptor T cells or reducing their effectiveness against leukemia. Both patients achieved complete remission, with one patient still in remission 11 months after treatment. However, the other patient experienced a relapse approximately 2 months after treatment, with blast cells that no longer expressed CD19. This suggests that additional molecules, in addition to CD19, need to be targeted in some ALL patients. Overall, chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells have demonstrated the ability to effectively eliminate aggressive and treatment-resistant acute leukemia cells in vivo.

title: Extended-connectivity fingerprints.
text: Extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs) are a new type of topological fingerprints used for molecular characterization. In the past, topological fingerprints were mainly developed for substructure and similarity searching. However, ECFPs were specifically designed for structure-activity modeling. These circular fingerprints possess several advantageous qualities. Firstly, they can be computed rapidly. Secondly, they are not predetermined and can represent an almost infinite number of diverse molecular features, including stereochemical information. Additionally, their features indicate the presence of specific substructures, making it easier to interpret analysis results. Moreover, the ECFP algorithm can be customized to generate various types of circular fingerprints, optimized for different purposes. Despite the widespread adoption and validation of ECFPs, their implementation has not been previously described in the literature.

title: Suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 inhibits antiviral IFN-beta signaling to enhance HIV-1 replication in macrophages.
text: HIV-1 replication in macrophages of the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to cognitive and motor impairment, which is referred to as HIV-associated dementia (HAD) in its most severe form. During early CNS infection, IFN-beta can suppress viral replication in these cells, but its effect is temporary. Eventually, HIV-1 finds a way to overcome this innate immune response and resumes replication through an unknown mechanism, initiating the progression towards HAD. In this article, we present evidence suggesting that Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling (SOCS)3, a molecule that inhibits IFN signaling, may enable HIV-1 to evade innate immunity within the CNS. Our research shows that SOCS3 levels are elevated in an in vivo SIV/macaque model of HAD, and this pattern of expression correlates with the recurrence of viral replication and the onset of CNS disease. In laboratory experiments, we found that the HIV-1 regulatory protein transactivator of transcription induces SOCS3 in human and murine macrophages through a NF-kappaB-dependent mechanism. The expression of SOCS3 weakens the response of macrophages to IFN-beta at early stages of pathway activation and downstream antiviral gene expression, thereby overcoming the inhibitory effect of IFN-beta on HIV-1 replication. These findings suggest that the expression of SOCS3, triggered by factors present in the HIV-1-infected brain, such as transactivator of transcription, hampers the antiviral signaling of IFN-beta, leading to enhanced HIV-1 replication in macrophages. This consequence of SOCS3 expression in laboratory settings, supported by its correlation with increased viral load and the onset of CNS disease in live subjects, indicates that SOCS3 may enable HIV-1 to evade the protective innate immune response within the CNS, allowing viral replication to recur and ultimately promoting the progression towards HAD.

title: Molecular model of the human 26S proteasome.
text: The 26S proteasome is crucial for maintaining balance in eukaryotic organisms by carefully breaking down various proteins, including important regulators of cell-cycle progression and apoptosis. In this study, we utilized cryo-electron microscopy and single-particle analysis to determine the structure of the human 26S proteasome. By identifying secondary structure elements in both the 20S proteolytic core region and the 19S regulatory particle, we were able to construct a comprehensive molecular model of the entire 26S proteasome. This model provides a detailed description of the 20S core and redefines the arrangement of subunits in the 19S regulatory particle. With this information, we have laid a solid foundation for understanding the mechanisms behind the 26S proteasome's function.

title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and early reproductive health outcomes among women undergoing IVF.
text:
RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the concentration of urinary bisphenol A (BPA) in women undergoing IVF have an impact on ovarian response and early reproductive outcomes, such as oocyte maturation, fertilization, embryo quality, and blastocyst formation?

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS: Higher levels of urinary BPA were associated with decreased ovarian response, fewer fertilized oocytes, and reduced blastocyst formation.

BACKGROUND: Previous studies on animals and in vitro experiments have shown a link between BPA exposure and negative reproductive outcomes. Our previous research also found a connection between urinary BPA and decreased ovarian response in women undergoing IVF. However, there is limited data on the impact of BPA on fertilization and embryo development in humans.

STUDY DESIGN: This was a prospective preconception cohort study involving 174 women aged 18-45 who underwent 237 IVF cycles at the Massachusetts General Hospital Fertility Center between November 2004 and August 2010. The study followed these women until they either had a live birth or discontinued treatment. Cryothaw and donor egg cycles were not included in the analysis.

PARTICIPANTS AND METHODS: Urinary BPA concentrations were measured using solid-phase extraction-high-performance liquid chromatography-isotope dilution-tandem mass spectrometry. Various statistical models were used to evaluate the association between cycle-specific urinary BPA concentrations and measures of ovarian response, oocyte maturation, fertilization, embryo quality, and cleavage rate. The study accounted for the correlation among multiple IVF cycles in the same woman.

MAIN RESULTS: The geometric mean for urinary BPA concentrations was 1.50 µg/l. After adjusting for age and other potential confounders, there was a significant linear dose-response relationship between increased urinary BPA concentrations and decreased number of oocytes, decreased number of normally fertilized oocytes, and decreased E(2) levels. Women with higher urinary BPA levels had a 24-27% decrease in the number of oocytes and normally fertilized oocytes compared to those with lower levels. There was also a suggestive association between BPA concentrations and decreased blastocyst formation.

LIMITATIONS: Potential limitations include exposure misclassification due to the short half-life and variability of BPA, uncertainty about the generalizability of the results to women conceiving naturally, and a limited sample size.

IMPLICATIONS: This study, using IVF as a model, suggests that there is a negative association between urinary BPA concentrations and serum peak E(2) levels and oocyte yield. It also indicates a decrease in metaphase II oocyte count, number of normally fertilizing oocytes, and a potential impact on blastocyst formation. These findings suggest that BPA may affect reproductive function in susceptible women undergoing IVF.

FUNDING AND COMPETING INTERESTS: The study was supported by grants from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. The authors declare no competing financial interests.

DISCLAIMER: The findings and conclusions of this report are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Cost-effectiveness of options for the diagnosis of high blood pressure in primary care: a modelling study.
text:
The traditional method of diagnosing hypertension has been through blood-pressure measurements in a clinic setting. However, research has shown that home and ambulatory measurements are more accurate in predicting cardiovascular outcomes. In this study, we aimed to compare the cost-effectiveness of different diagnostic strategies for hypertension.

Using a Markov model-based probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis, we focused on a hypothetical primary-care population aged 40 years or older with a screening blood-pressure measurement greater than 140/90 mm Hg. We compared three diagnostic strategies: further blood pressure measurement in the clinic, at home, and with an ambulatory monitor. Our evaluation criteria included lifetime costs, quality-adjusted life years, and cost-effectiveness.

The findings of our study revealed that ambulatory monitoring was the most cost-effective strategy for diagnosing hypertension in both men and women of all ages. It not only resulted in cost savings for all groups but also led to more quality-adjusted life years for individuals older than 50 years. The cost savings ranged from -£56 to -£323 for different age and gender groups. This conclusion remained robust even when subjected to various sensitivity analyses.

In conclusion, ambulatory monitoring as a diagnostic strategy for hypertension, following an initial raised reading in the clinic, can reduce misdiagnosis and save costs. The additional costs associated with ambulatory monitoring are offset by the cost savings resulting from more targeted treatment. Therefore, we recommend ambulatory monitoring for most patients before initiating antihypertensive drugs. This study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence.

title: Folic acid improves endothelial function in coronary artery disease via mechanisms largely independent of homocysteine lowering.
text:
The background information states that homocysteine is a risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD), but it is not yet proven to have a causal relationship. However, it is important to determine causality because folic acid can safely and inexpensively reduce plasma homocysteine levels by 25%. The maximum reduction is achieved with a daily dose of 0.4 mg. High-dose folic acid (5 mg) has been shown to improve endothelial function in CAD, although the mechanism is still debated. Some suggest that the improvement occurs through a reduction in total or free homocysteine. The study aimed to investigate the effects of folic acid on endothelial function before any changes in homocysteine levels in CAD patients.

The methods and results of the study involved a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of folic acid (5 mg) for 6 weeks in 33 patients. Endothelial function was assessed using flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) before the first dose of folic acid, at 2 and 4 hours after the first dose, and after 6 weeks of treatment. Plasma folate levels significantly increased within 1 hour of taking folic acid. FMD showed improvement at 2 hours and was mostly complete by 4 hours. Acute changes in total homocysteine levels were not significant, and free homocysteine levels were slightly reduced at 4 hours. The improvement in FMD did not correlate with reductions in either free or total homocysteine at any time.

In conclusion, the data suggests that folic acid improves endothelial function in CAD patients acutely, and this improvement is largely independent of homocysteine levels.

title: Focal adhesion kinase links mechanical force to skin fibrosis via inflammatory signaling
text: The cause of exuberant fibroproliferation after injury is not well understood. However, one aspect of wound repair that is often overlooked is the role of mechanical force. Mechanical force controls cell-matrix interactions through focal adhesion components, such as focal adhesion kinase (FAK). In our study, we found that FAK is activated after cutaneous injury and that mechanical loading enhances this process. When we used mice with fibroblast-specific FAK knockout, we observed significantly less inflammation and fibrosis compared to control mice in a model of hypertrophic scar formation. Our research also revealed that FAK triggers the secretion of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), a potent chemokine associated with human fibrotic disorders, through extracellular-related kinase (ERK). Similarly, when we used MCP-1 knockout mice, we observed minimal scar formation, indicating that the FAK mechanotransduction-induced fibrosis is mediated through inflammatory chemokine pathways. In human cells, inhibiting FAK with small molecules blocked these effects and reduced scar formation in vivo by attenuating MCP-1 signaling and inflammatory cell recruitment. These findings suggest that physical force regulates fibrosis through inflammatory FAK-ERK-MCP-1 pathways and that targeting FAK with molecular strategies can effectively prevent pathologic scar formation by uncoupling mechanical force.

title: Prognostic Accuracy of the SOFA Score, SIRS Criteria, and qSOFA Score for In-Hospital Mortality Among Adults With Suspected Infection Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit
text: The Sepsis-3 Criteria highlighted the importance of a change of 2 or more points in the Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, introduced quick SOFA (qSOFA), and removed the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria from the sepsis definition. The objective of this study was to externally validate and assess the discriminatory capacities of an increase in SOFA score by 2 or more points, 2 or more SIRS criteria, or a qSOFA score of 2 or more points for outcomes among critically ill patients with suspected infection. The study involved a retrospective cohort analysis of 184,875 patients in Australian and New Zealand intensive care units (ICUs) from 2000 to 2015. The primary outcome measured was in-hospital mortality, while a composite secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality or ICU length of stay (LOS) of 3 days or more. The discriminatory abilities of the scoring systems were evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Adjusted analyses were conducted using a model of baseline risk determined by variables independent of the scoring systems. The results showed that among the patients, 18.7% died in the hospital, and 55.7% died or experienced an ICU LOS of 3 days or more. SOFA score increased by 2 or more points in 90.1% of patients, 86.7% had 2 or more SIRS criteria, and 54.4% had a qSOFA score of 2 or more points. SOFA demonstrated significantly better discrimination for in-hospital mortality compared to SIRS criteria or qSOFA. SOFA also outperformed the other scores for the secondary outcome. The findings suggest that an increase in SOFA score of 2 or more points is a more accurate predictor of in-hospital mortality than SIRS criteria or the qSOFA score in critically ill patients with suspected infection. Therefore, SIRS criteria and qSOFA may have limited usefulness in predicting mortality in an ICU setting.

title: Predictors of mammographic density: insights gained from a novel regression analysis of a twin study.
text: Understanding the factors that influence mammographically dense and nondense areas is crucial because the percentage of mammographic density, adjusted for age, is a significant risk factor for breast cancer. This is especially true when considering weight or body mass index. In our study, we utilized computer-assisted methods to measure mammographically dense areas in 571 monozygotic and 380 dizygotic twin pairs from Australia and North America, aged between 40 and 70 years. We employed a unique regression modeling approach, where we regressed each twin's measurement of dense and nondense area against their own covariates, as well as those of their co-twin. By doing so, we could assess the consistency of changes in regression estimates with the inclusion of these covariates, in relation to causal and other models. When adjusting for an individual's weight, we observed that the associations between weight and mammographic measures were weakened in the co-twin, suggesting a causal effect of weight on these measures. Interestingly, this effect was three times stronger for nondense areas compared to dense areas, when measured in absolute log cm(2)/kg. However, after adjusting for weight, we found that later age at menarche and greater height were associated with greater dense areas and lesser nondense areas, in a manner inconsistent with causality. On the other hand, the associations between parity and mammographic density measures were consistent with a causal effect and/or within-person confounding. Additionally, the associations between mammographic density measures and height were consistent with shared early life environmental factors that predispose individuals to both height and percentage of mammographic density, and potentially breast cancer risk.

title: Shaping the landscape of the Escherichia coli chromosome: replication-transcription encounters in cells with an ectopic replication origin
text: Unwinding millions of DNA base pairs is necessary for each cell division to enable chromosome duplication and gene transcription. Since DNA replication and transcription use the same template, conflicts between these processes are inevitable and direct collisions are particularly troublesome. Surprisingly, a recent study discovered that Escherichia coli cells with an ectopic replication origin, where highly transcribed rrn operons were forced to replicate in the opposite direction, exhibited uninterrupted cell cycle progression. To investigate further, we recreated a similar strain and observed that the doubling time was twice as long as normal cells. Analysis of the replication profiles in this strain revealed significant deviations compared to wild-type profiles, especially in regions with high transcription activity and the termination area. These deviations were mitigated by mutations that either deactivated the termination area or destabilized RNA polymerase complexes, allowing replication forks to displace them more easily. Our findings demonstrate that conflicts between head-on replication and transcription are highly problematic. Interestingly, when examining the replication profile of the previously published E. coli construct, we identified a chromosomal rearrangement that remarkably resolves replication-transcription conflicts in a simple manner. These results support the notion that avoiding head-on collisions has played a significant role in shaping the unique architecture of bacterial chromosomes.

title: Epithelial–mesenchymal transitions in tumour progression
text: If epithelial-mesenchymal transitions did not occur, where polarized epithelial cells transform into motile cells, multicellular organisms would not be able to advance beyond the blastula stage of embryonic development. Nevertheless, this crucial developmental process also plays a darker role in the advancement of tumors. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition offers a fresh perspective on comprehending how carcinoma progresses towards dedifferentiated and increasingly malignant conditions.

title: Platelets at the interface of thrombosis, inflammation, and cancer.
text: While the platelet was once primarily known for its roles in hemostasis and thrombosis, it is now increasingly recognized as a versatile cell with various functions. Circulating platelets have the ability to impact a wide range of seemingly unrelated pathophysiologic events, including inflammation. This connection between platelets and inflammation highlights their origin from a lower vertebrate cell type that serves both hemostatic and immunologic purposes. Additionally, platelets play a significant role in cancer biology, influencing the multistep development of tumors by aligning with the hallmarks of cancer. The involvement of platelets in the interplay between hemostasis, thrombosis, inflammation, and cancer is complex but crucial in each disease process. Animal models of platelet dysfunction and existing antiplatelet therapies offer valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying various pathophysiologic events. Therefore, researchers studying platelet function should expand their focus beyond traditional hemostasis and thrombosis paradigms, while hematologists must recognize the relevance of platelets in a wide range of disease processes.

title: Cellular roles of DNA topoisomerases: a molecular perspective
text: From a molecular perspective, this review explores the cellular functions of DNA topoisomerases, which can be considered as the illusionists of the DNA realm. These remarkable enzymes possess the ability to untangle DNA strands or double helices, effectively resolving all topological obstacles encountered during DNA replication, transcription, and other essential cellular processes. Through extensive biochemical and structural investigations spanning the last thirty years, scientists have developed molecular models that elucidate how different subfamilies of DNA topoisomerases manipulate DNA.

title: MicroRNA sponges: progress and possibilities.
text: The method known as the microRNA (miRNA) "sponge" was introduced three years ago as a way to continuously disrupt the function of miRNAs in cell lines and transgenic organisms. Sponge RNAs are created with binding sites that are complementary to a specific miRNA of interest, and they are produced within cells from transgenes. Similar to other miRNA target genes, the binding sites of a sponge are specific to the miRNA seed region, allowing them to block an entire family of related miRNAs. This transgenic approach has proven to be a valuable tool for investigating the functions of miRNAs in various experimental systems. In this discussion, we will explore the ways in which sponge and related constructs can be optimized, and we will also review recent applications of this method, focusing particularly on its stable expression in cancer studies and transgenic animals.

title: Wip1 phosphatase regulates p53-dependent apoptosis of stem cells and tumorigenesis in the mouse intestine.
text: Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths. To better understand how this cancer develops, we studied the role of Wip1 phosphatase in a mouse model of APC(Min)-driven polyposis. Wip1 is highly expressed in intestinal stem cells. Our research showed that removing Wip1 extended the lifespan of APC(Min) mice by significantly reducing the formation of polyps. This protection relied on the p53 tumor suppressor, which is involved in regulating the apoptosis of intestinal stem cells. When the Wnt pathway was constantly activated, apoptosis increased in Wip1-deficient mice's stem cells but not in wild-type APC(Min) mice. Therefore, we suggest that Wip1 phosphatase maintains the balance of intestinal stem cells. Consequently, the loss of Wip1 suppresses APC(Min)-driven polyposis by making p53-dependent apoptosis of stem cells more likely, thus preventing their transformation into tumor-initiating stem cells.

title: The shunt problem: control of functional shunting in normal and tumour vasculature
text: The networks of blood vessels in both normal and tumor tissues have diverse structures, with varying lengths of blood flow pathways. In order to ensure efficient distribution of blood flow, mechanisms that adjust the diameters of vessels must prevent the formation of functional shunts, where short pathways enlarge and bypass longer pathways. This adaptation relies on the transmission of information about the metabolic state of the tissue to the feeding vessels through conducted responses. Our proposal is that the impaired communication within tumor microvascular networks, which leads to functional shunting, is the main cause of dysfunctional microcirculation and local oxygen deprivation in cancer. We suggest that treating tumors with anti-angiogenic therapies may restore vascular communication and consequently enhance or normalize the distribution of blood flow in tumor vasculature.

title: Pharmacological Blockade of ASCT2-dependent Glutamine Transport Leads To Anti-tumor Efficacy in Preclinical Models
text: In the era of precision medicine, there are promising opportunities for drug discovery in cancer treatment due to the unique metabolic needs of cancer cells. However, despite efforts to target cancer metabolism therapeutically, there have been limited advancements in the development of new drugs. Glutamine, an amino acid, plays a crucial role in various metabolic processes utilized by cancer cells, such as biosynthesis, cell signaling, and protection against oxidative stress. In this study, we present the preclinical development of V-9302, a small molecule antagonist that competes with glutamine transport and specifically targets the amino acid transporter ASCT2. By blocking ASCT2 with V-9302, we observed a reduction in cancer cell growth and proliferation, an increase in cell death, and elevated oxidative stress. These effects collectively contributed to antitumor responses both in laboratory experiments and in live subjects. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate the effectiveness of a pharmacological inhibitor of glutamine transport in oncology. It represents a novel approach to targeted therapy and establishes a foundation for groundbreaking treatments that focus on cancer cell metabolism.

title: An Antidepressant Decreases CSF Aβ Production in Healthy Individuals and in Transgenic AD Mice
text:
The suppression of amyloid-β (Aβ) generation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) can be achieved through serotonin signaling, both in vitro and in animal models. Our research focused on an aged transgenic AD mouse model (APP/PS1 plaque-bearing mice) and found that the antidepressant citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, reduced Aβ levels in the brain interstitial fluid in a dose-dependent manner. We also investigated the impact of chronic citalopram administration on the growth of individual amyloid plaques in plaque-bearing mice. The results showed that citalopram halted the growth of existing plaques and significantly reduced the formation of new plaques by 78%. 

To further explore the effects of citalopram on Aβ production and concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), we conducted a study involving healthy human volunteers. We used stable isotope labeling kinetics to measure Aβ production and CSF sampling during acute citalopram dosing. The findings revealed a 37% decrease in Aβ production in CSF in the citalopram group compared to the placebo group. Additionally, the drug-treated group exhibited a 38% reduction in total CSF Aβ concentrations. These results suggest that citalopram has the potential to safely lower Aβ levels, which could be an important preventive strategy for AD. This study provides valuable insights for future AD prevention trials by demonstrating effective target engagement.

title: Variations in the quality and sustainability of long-term glycaemic control with continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the changes in HbA1c levels in individuals with Type 1 diabetes who were managed with long-term continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion. The researchers analyzed computerized clinic records of 35 adults with Type 1 diabetes who had high HbA1c levels (≥ 64 mmol/mol, 8.0%) while on multiple daily insulin injections. These individuals were then switched to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion for a minimum of 5 years.

The results of the study revealed three subgroups with similar baseline HbA1c levels but different responses to pump therapy over the long term. Group A consisted of individuals who initially showed improvement but later experienced deterioration (57% of the participants). Group B included individuals who experienced sustained improvement throughout the 5-year period (31% of the participants). Group C consisted of individuals whose HbA1c levels did not significantly change from the baseline (12% of the participants). It was observed that the patients in group C had a higher BMI compared to those in groups A and B (31.0 ± 5.2 vs. 25.9 ± 3.3 vs. 25.2 ± 3.1 kg/m², respectively; P = 0.02).

In conclusion, this study found that 88% of individuals with Type 1 diabetes were able to maintain improved glycemic control with continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion over a 5-year period. However, there were variations in the long-term effectiveness of this therapy, with some individuals experiencing both improvement and worsening, while others maintained strict control. Additionally, a small number of individuals did not respond well to subcutaneous insulin infusion.

title: Historical review: megakaryopoiesis and thrombopoiesis.
text:
The study of thrombopoiesis has undergone significant advancements since the time when platelets were referred to as "the dust of the blood," which was only about a century ago. Throughout this period, researchers have made important discoveries, such as identifying megakaryocytes as the source of blood platelets, defining and purifying marrow-derived megakaryocytic progenitor cells, and cloning and characterizing thrombopoietin, the primary regulator of the process. Additionally, therapeutic thrombopoietic agents have been developed.

During this journey, scientists have also learned that the physiological mechanisms driving proplatelet formation can be replicated in cell-free systems, allowing for the evaluation of their biochemistry. Furthermore, there has been an increasing understanding of the molecular basis of endomitosis, as well as the definition of intracellular signals triggered by the engagement of numerous surface receptors on megakaryocytes. Moreover, several transcription factors responsible for determining the fate of megakaryocytes have been identified and experimentally manipulated.

Although some of these biological processes resemble those observed in other cell types, megakaryocytes and platelets possess distinct developmental characteristics. Therefore, it is highly likely that continued research on thrombopoiesis will lead to numerous clinical and scientific insights for many decades to come.

title: Obesity and Its Metabolic Complications: The Role of Adipokines and the Relationship between Obesity, Inflammation, Insulin Resistance, Dyslipidemia and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
text: There is growing evidence suggesting that obesity is closely linked to an increased risk of metabolic diseases such as insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. The root cause of obesity is an imbalance between the amount of food consumed and the energy expended, resulting in an excessive buildup of fat tissue. It is now understood that fat tissue not only serves as a storage site for excess energy but also functions as an endocrine organ. The expansion of fat tissue leads to the production of various bioactive substances called adipocytokines or adipokines, which trigger chronic low-grade inflammation and interact with different processes in various organs. Although the exact mechanisms are still not fully understood, the abnormal production or secretion of these adipokines due to excess fat tissue and dysfunction can contribute to the development of metabolic diseases associated with obesity. This review focuses on the role of several adipokines associated with obesity and their potential impact on metabolic diseases. Multiple lines of evidence provide valuable insights into the involvement of adipokines in the development of obesity and its associated metabolic complications. However, further research is needed to fully comprehend the mechanisms underlying the metabolic effects of recently discovered adipokines.

title: Combating trastuzumab resistance by targeting SRC, a common node downstream of multiple resistance pathways
text: Trastuzumab, a therapy specifically designed to target ERBB2, has been successful. However, approximately half of individuals with ERBB2-overexpressing breast cancer do not respond to trastuzumab-based treatments due to various resistance mechanisms. Currently, there are no clinically applicable treatment plans available to overcome trastuzumab resistance caused by different mechanisms. Our research demonstrates that the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase c-SRC (SRC) plays a crucial role in determining the response to trastuzumab and acts as a common factor in multiple trastuzumab resistance pathways. We have discovered that SRC is activated in both acquired and newly developed trastuzumab-resistant cells and have identified a novel mechanism of SRC regulation involving dephosphorylation by PTEN. Increased activation of SRC leads to significant trastuzumab resistance in breast cancer cells and is correlated with resistance in patients. By targeting SRC in combination with trastuzumab, we have successfully sensitized multiple lines of trastuzumab-resistant cells to the treatment and eliminated trastuzumab-resistant tumors in vivo. These findings suggest that this strategy has the potential for clinical application in overcoming trastuzumab resistance.

title: MicroRNAs: new tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma?
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small noncoding RNAs that are highly conserved throughout evolution. They play a crucial role in regulating gene expression and protein translation. During embryogenesis, miRNAs are involved in driving the differentiation of organs and tissues. They also fine-tune important biological processes like proliferation and apoptosis. Recent studies have shown that deregulation of miRNAs is closely linked to the development and progression of cancer, where they can act as either oncogenes or oncosuppressors. This review focuses on the role of miRNAs in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and examines the potential mechanisms by which they contribute to the development of this type of cancer. Additionally, we discuss the potential use of circulating miRNAs as biomarkers for HCC, an area that requires further improvement in clinical surveillance. Finally, we explore the exciting possibility of using miRNAs as therapeutic targets or even as drugs themselves.

title: A vertebrate gene, ticrr, is an essential checkpoint and replication regulator.
text: Eukaryotes have multiple pathways to safeguard the accuracy of their genetic material during normal cell division and in response to DNA damage. In our study on zebrafish, we discovered a previously uncharacterized gene called ticrr (TopBP1-interacting, checkpoint, and replication regulator) that is crucial for preventing entry into mitosis after exposure to ionizing radiation. When ticrr is deficient, it leads to embryonic death in the absence of external DNA damage because it is necessary for the proper progression of the cell cycle. Specifically, the absence of ticrr hampers DNA replication and disrupts the S/M checkpoint, resulting in premature entry into mitosis and catastrophic consequences. Our research also reveals that the human counterpart of TICRR interacts with TopBP1, a well-known checkpoint protein and a core component of the preinitiation complex (pre-IC) responsible for DNA replication. This interaction between TICRR and TopBP1 remains stable even without chromatin and relies on BRCT motifs that are essential for TopBP1's replication and checkpoint functions. Importantly, we found that ticrr deficiency disrupts the binding of pre-IC components to chromatin, but not the prereplication complex. Overall, our findings demonstrate that TICRR collaborates with TopBP1 and plays a vital role in the formation of the pre-IC. Further investigation is needed to determine whether Ticrr is the vertebrate equivalent of the yeast pre-IC component Sld3 or a previously unknown regulator of replication and checkpoints in multicellular organisms.

title: A maternally methylated CpG island in KvLQT1 is associated with an antisense paternal transcript and loss of imprinting in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
text: Loss of imprinting at IGF2, often independent of H19, is linked to a significant number of individuals with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), a condition characterized by overgrowth and increased cancer susceptibility. The KvLQT1 locus is believed to contain imprinting control elements, as several BWS-related chromosomal rearrangements disrupt this gene. Our research has identified a conserved CpG island (KvDMR1) within an intron of the KvLQT1 gene that is methylated by the mother. Among 12 BWS cases with normal H19 methylation, 5 exhibited demethylation of KvDMR1 in their fibroblast or lymphocyte DNA. Conversely, in 4 BWS cases with H19 hypermethylation, KvDMR1 methylation was normal. Therefore, H19 inactivation and hypomethylation at KvDMR1 (or a related phenomenon) are distinct epigenetic abnormalities associated with biallelic expression of IGF2. Analysis of the human and syntenic mouse loci using reverse transcription-PCR revealed the presence of a KvDMR1-associated RNA transcribed exclusively from the paternal allele and in the opposite orientation to the maternally expressed KvLQT1 gene. We propose that KvDMR1 and/or its associated antisense RNA (KvLQT1-AS) serve as an additional imprinting control element or center in the imprinted domains of human 11p15.5 and mouse distal 7.

title: Alarming levels of drug-resistant tuberculosis in Belarus: results of a survey in Minsk
text: Resistance to anti-tuberculosis (TB) medications poses a significant public health risk in most countries of the former Soviet Union. In Belarus, there was a lack of reliable information on the extent of this problem, so a survey was conducted in the capital city of Minsk. From November 2009 to December 2010, a total of 156 newly diagnosed TB patients and 68 previously treated patients with positive TB cultures, all residing in Minsk, were included in the survey. Each patient's Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates were collected and tested for susceptibility to first- and second-line anti-TB drugs. The survey revealed that 35.3% (95% CI 27.7-42.8) of new patients and 76.5% (95% CI 66.1-86.8) of previously treated patients had multidrug-resistant (MDR)-TB. Overall, almost half of the patients enrolled in the survey had MDR-TB. Additionally, 15 out of the 107 MDR-TB patients (14.0%, 95% CI 7.3-20.7) were found to have extensively drug-resistant TB. Patients under the age of 35 had twice the odds ratio of developing multidrug-resistant TB compared to those over 35. These findings from the survey conducted in Minsk are concerning and represent the highest recorded proportions of MDR-TB worldwide. This study provides valuable insights into the burden of drug-resistant TB in urban areas of Belarus.

title: Partitioning regulatory mechanisms of within-host malaria dynamics using the effective propagation number.
text: The peaks and troughs of malaria parasitemia, which impact disease severity and transmission, are influenced by immune clearance and resource limitation (specifically, red blood cell depletion). However, quantitatively determining the relative contributions of these factors over time is challenging. To address this, we utilized data from rodent malaria to estimate the effective propagation number. This number reflects the varying importance of different control mechanisms within the host and is influenced by the initial parasite dose. Our analysis revealed that the innate immune response's ability to restrict parasite growth becomes saturated as the parasite dose increases. Additionally, we found that experimentally enhanced innate immunity can indirectly affect parasite density by depleting resources. This statistical approach provides a valuable tool for improving the targeting of drugs or vaccines for human therapy. It allows us to uncover the dynamics and interactions of regulatory mechanisms within the host.

title: Life is sweet: candy consumption and longevity.
text: Society's puritanical view on pleasure is evident in our perception of candy. We often believe that if something tastes good, it must be unhealthy. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that candy, including sugar confectionery and chocolate, is detrimental to our health. In fact, the consumption of candy has been a part of human history for centuries. Ancient civilizations such as the Arabs, Chinese, and Egyptians enjoyed candied fruits and nuts in honey, while the Aztecs indulged in a chocolate drink made from cacao beans. Even today, Americans consume an average of 5.4 kg of sugar candy and 6.5 kg of chocolate per person annually. Given the long-standing existence of candy, we questioned its overall impact on health and longevity. To investigate this, we conducted a study using data from the Harvard alumni health study, which focuses on men who entered Harvard University as undergraduates between 1916 and 1950. Our sample included 7841 men who were free of cardiovascular disease and cancer and had responded to a health survey...

title: Inter-individual variability and genetic influences on cytokine responses to bacteria and fungi
text: Our understanding of the variation in cytokine responses to different pathogens in healthy individuals is limited. In order to gain a systematic understanding of cytokine responses and the impact of genetic variation on cytokine production, we conducted a study on 197 individuals of European origin from the 200 Functional Genomics (200FG) cohort in the Human Functional Genomics Project. Over the course of three years, we analyzed cytokines produced by peripheral blood mononuclear cells. By comparing cytokine profiles induced by bacteria and fungi, we discovered that the majority of cytokine responses were specific to certain pathogens rather than being associated with a particular immune pathway or cytokine. Additionally, we examined the correlation between genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotypes and cytokine levels, leading to the identification of six cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs). Notably, one of these QTLs at the NAA35-GOLM1 locus significantly influenced interleukin (IL)-6 production in response to multiple pathogens and was linked to susceptibility to candidemia. Furthermore, the cytokine QTLs we identified were found to be enriched among SNPs previously associated with infectious diseases and heart diseases. These findings shed light on the variability in cytokine production by human immune cells in response to pathogens and provide initial insights into the underlying mechanisms.

title: Integrins promote cytokinesis through the RSK signaling axis.
text: The final stage of cell division is known as cytokinesis, but the exact mechanisms by which integrins regulate this process are not fully understood. In this study, we have found that integrin-regulated signaling pathways involving ERK and RSK play a crucial role in promoting successful cytokinesis. By inhibiting the activation of ERK and RSK in CHO cells through a mutation in the integrin β1 cytoplasmic tail or with pharmacological inhibitors, we observed an accumulation of cells with midbodies and the formation of binucleated cells. However, when we activated ERK and RSK signaling through the expression of constitutively active RAF1, the mutant phenotype was suppressed in a RSK-dependent manner. Additionally, constitutively active RSK2 was able to restore cytokinesis that was inhibited by the mutant integrin. Importantly, we found that the regulatory role of the RSK pathway is not limited to CHO cells, as MCF-10A human mammary epithelial cells and HPNE human pancreatic ductal epithelial cells also rely on RSK for successful cytokinesis. Furthermore, when mitotic MCF10A cells were deprived of integrin-mediated adhesion by being incubated in suspension, we observed a suppression of ERK and RSK activation and a failure of cytokinesis. Similarly, inhibiting RSK or integrins within the 3D context of a developing salivary gland organ explant resulted in an accumulation of epithelial cells with midbodies, indicating a defect in cytokinesis. Interestingly, we found that neither ERK nor RSK regulates cytokinesis in human fibroblasts, suggesting that this process is cell-type specific. Overall, our findings highlight the integrin-RSK signaling axis as a crucial regulator of cytokinesis in epithelial cells. We propose that the proper interaction between cells and their microenvironment through integrins is essential for maintaining genomic stability by ensuring the successful completion of cytokinesis.

title: Sympathetic neural mechanisms in normal and hypertensive pregnancy in humans.
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies have shown that there is an increased sympathetic drive in pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) and preeclampsia (PE) based on direct recordings from peripheral sympathetic nerves. However, it is unclear whether sympathetic drive is altered in normal pregnancy, where arterial blood pressure can be normal or relatively low. The objective of this study was to measure and compare peripheral sympathetic discharge, its vasoconstrictor effect, and its baroreceptor control during pregnancy and postpartum in women with normal pregnancy (NP) and PIH, as well as in normotensive nonpregnant (NN) women.

METHODS AND RESULTS: A total of 21 women with NP, 18 women with PIH, and 21 NN women participated in the study. Muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) was assessed using multiunit discharges, and single units with defined vasoconstrictor properties (s-MSNA) were also measured. The s-MSNA in NP women (38+/-6.6 impulses/100 beats) was significantly higher (P<0.05) than in NN women (19+/-1.8 impulses/100 beats), but lower than in PIH women (P<0.001) (146+/-23.5 impulses/100 beats). MSNA followed a similar pattern. Cardiac baroreceptor reflex sensitivity (BRS) was impaired in both NP and PIH women compared to NN women. After delivery, sympathetic activity decreased to levels similar to those observed in NN women, and there was an increase in BRS. In NP women, the decrease in sympathetic output occurred despite a negligible change in blood pressure.

CONCLUSIONS: Central sympathetic output was increased in women with normal pregnancy and even higher in the hypertensive pregnant group. These findings suggest that the moderate sympathetic hyperactivity during the later stages of normal pregnancy may contribute to returning arterial pressure to nonpregnant levels. However, excessive increase in sympathetic activity may lead to hypertension.

title: Barriers to recruiting urban African American women into research studies in community settings.
text: In this qualitative research, obstacles to the involvement of African American women in a behavioral intervention trial aimed at promoting mammography screening in the community were identified. Through focus group discussions with community agency providers and research team members, four key themes were identified: (1) engaging with gatekeepers, (2) understanding the cultural context, (3) considering the importance of location, and (4) addressing protocols, policies, and opportunities. Additionally, a checklist of recommended actions for nurse researchers to enhance the participation of African American women in community trials is included.

title: Geographical access to healthcare in Northern England and post-mortem diagnosis of cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous research suggests that limited access to healthcare may contribute to the diagnosis of cancer at the time of death, as indicated by death certificate records. 

METHODS: The Northern and Yorkshire Cancer Registry provided data on patients diagnosed with breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian, or prostate cancer between 1994 and 2002. Additional information on travel time to general practitioner and hospital services, as well as social deprivation, was included. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with a diagnosis at the time of death. 

RESULTS: There was no significant association between access to primary care and the likelihood of a diagnosis at the time of death. However, for all cancer types except breast cancer, individuals living in areas with longer travel times to hospitals had higher odds of being diagnosed at the time of death. This association was statistically significant for colorectal and ovarian tumors. Furthermore, individuals residing in the most deprived areas and those with the longest travel times to hospitals were 2.6 times more likely to have a diagnosis at the time of death compared to those in more affluent and closer areas. 

CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that limited access to tertiary care, particularly when combined with social disadvantages, may increase the likelihood of a diagnosis at the time of death.

title: Enhanced monocyte Fc phagocytosis by a homologue of interleukin-10 encoded by human cytomegalovirus.
text: The human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) has several counterparts of human interleukin 10 (hIL-10) that possess immunomodulatory properties. These counterparts can potentially enhance viral infection by altering the function of myeloid cells. We conducted a study to investigate the characteristics and phagocytic capability of human monocytes when exposed to hIL-10, an HCMV-encoded hIL-10 counterpart expressed during the active phase of infection (cmvIL-10), and a differentially spliced form of cmvIL-10 expressed during both latent and active phases of infection (LAcmvIL-10). Within 24 hours, both hIL-10 and cmvIL-10 increased the expression of Fcgamma receptors, stimulated the phagocytosis of IgG-opsonized erythrocytes, and reduced the expression of MHC class II (HLA-DR) on purified monocytes. However, LAcmvIL-10 only decreased HLA-DR expression at later time points (48 hours and 72 hours) and did not enhance Fcgamma receptor expression. Our findings suggest that cmvIL-10 promotes the differentiation of monocytes into a pro-phagocytic phenotype, while LAcmvIL-10 affects monocytes through a different mechanism. The implications of these properties in the pathogenesis of cytomegalovirus are discussed.

title: 3D Chromosome Regulatory Landscape of Human Pluripotent Cells.
text: This study presents an analysis of the 3D regulatory landscape of human naive and primed embryonic stem cells. To create this map, we identified transcriptional enhancers and insulators in these cells and integrated them with cohesin-associated CTCF-CTCF loops using cohesin ChIA-PET data. The CTCF-CTCF loops we discovered form a chromosomal framework of insulated neighborhoods, which then form topologically associating domains (TADs) that remain largely unchanged during the transition between the naive and primed states. During this cell state transition, regulatory changes in enhancer-promoter interactions occur within these insulated neighborhoods. The CTCF anchor regions we identified are conserved across different species, have an impact on gene expression, and are frequently mutated in cancer cells, highlighting their crucial role in cellular regulation. These 3D regulatory maps of human pluripotent cells serve as a basis for future investigations into the connections between chromosome structure and gene control in development and disease.

title: Functional analysis via standardized whole-blood stimulation systems defines the boundaries of a healthy immune response to complex stimuli.
text: The standardization of immunophenotyping procedures is now a top priority. We have created a range of assay systems that use whole-blood samples and syringes, allowing for consistent evaluation of induced innate or adaptive immune responses. By eliminating errors in the preanalytical stage of immune monitoring, we have identified the protein signatures that are triggered by (1) medically significant bacteria, fungi, and viruses; (2) specific agonists for known host sensors; (3) cytokines commonly used in clinical settings; and (4) activators of T cell immunity. Our findings offer an initial assessment of reference values for induced cytokines and chemokines in healthy donors, and we have discovered that the failure to release interleukin-1α is a common immunological trait. The naturally occurring variation in immune responses that we have observed may help explain why individuals have different susceptibilities to diseases or respond differently to therapeutic treatments. By implementing a comprehensive solution for evaluating functional immune responses, we can promote the standardization of clinical studies and facilitate the sharing of data.

title: SATB1 Expression Governs Epigenetic Repression of PD‐1 in Tumor‐Reactive T Cells
text: Despite the fact that the mechanisms regulating the expression of programmed cell death‐1 (PD‐1) are not well understood, it plays a crucial role in inhibiting T cell effector activity. Our research has found that a chromatin organizer called special AT‐rich sequence‐binding protein‐1 (Satb1) restricts the expression of PD‐1 induced by T cell activation. Satb1 achieves this by recruiting a nucleosome remodeling deacetylase (NuRD) complex to the regulatory regions of the Pdcd1 gene. When Satb1 is deficient in T cells, there is a significant increase in PD‐1 expression, up to 40 times higher. Tumor‐derived transforming growth factor &bgr; (Tgf‐&bgr;) reduces the expression of Satb1 by binding to the Satb1 promoter through Smad proteins. These Smad proteins also compete with the Satb1‐NuRD complex for binding to the enhancers of Pdcd1, resulting in the release of Pdcd1 expression from Satb1-mediated repression. Satb1-deficient tumor-reactive T cells lose their effector activity more quickly than wild-type lymphocytes when exposed to tumor beds expressing PD-1 ligand (CD274). However, this difference can be eliminated by blocking CD274 continuously. Our findings suggest that Satb1 plays a crucial role in preventing premature T cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of Pdcd1 upon T cell activation. Dysregulation of this pathway in tumor-infiltrating T cells leads to reduced anti-tumor immunity. In summary, our study demonstrates that Satb1 controls the expression of PD-1 upon T cell activation by recruiting a de-acetylase complex to the regulatory regions of the Pdcd1 gene. Tumor-derived TGF-β disrupts this pathway, resulting in increased PD-1 expression in tumor-infiltrating T cells and decreased anti-tumor immunity.

title: Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in dendritic cells induces IL-1β–dependent adaptive immunity against tumors
text: The effectiveness of anticancer chemotherapies may rely on dendritic cells (DCs), which present antigens from dying cancer cells to activate tumor-specific interferon-γ (IFN-γ)–producing T lymphocytes. Our study demonstrates that dying tumor cells release ATP, which then interacts with DCs' P2X7 purinergic receptors, triggering the activation of the NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing-3 protein (NLRP3)-dependent caspase-1 activation complex ('inflammasome'). This leads to the secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β). Without a functional IL-1 receptor 1 or in mice lacking Nlpr3 or caspase-1, the priming of IFN-γ–producing CD8+ T cells by dying tumor cells fails, unless exogenous IL-1β is provided. Consequently, anticancer chemotherapy is ineffective against tumors in purinergic receptor P2rx7−/− or Nlrp3−/− or Casp1−/− hosts. Individuals with breast cancer who carry a loss-of-function allele of P2RX7 and are treated with anthracycline experience faster development of metastatic disease compared to those with the normal allele.
