These findings suggest that the NLRP3 inflammasome connects the innate and adaptive immune responses against dying tumor cells.

title: Mfge8 promotes obesity by mediating the uptake of dietary fats and serum fatty acids
text: Fatty acids play crucial roles in storing energy, forming membranes, and signaling within cells. However, the processes involved in the uptake of fatty acids are not fully understood. In individuals with obesity and mice on a high-fat diet, the expression of Mfge8, a protein that interacts with integrins, is increased. Despite this, the specific role of Mfge8 in obesity has not been determined. Our study reveals that Mfge8 facilitates the absorption of dietary triglycerides and the uptake of fatty acids into cells. Interestingly, mice lacking Mfge8 (Mfge8−/−) are protected against diet-induced obesity, steatohepatitis, and insulin resistance. We have also discovered that Mfge8 coordinates fatty acid uptake by activating the αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrins, which in turn phosphorylate Akt through phosphatidylinositide-3 kinase and mTOR complex 2. This phosphorylation event leads to the translocation of Cd36 and Fatp1 from vesicles within the cell to the cell surface. Overall, our findings suggest that Mfge8 plays a crucial role in regulating the absorption and storage of dietary fats, as well as in the development of obesity and its associated complications.

title: RAD52 Facilitates Mitotic DNA Synthesis Following Replication Stress.
text: The process of homologous recombination (HR) is essential for addressing DNA replication stress. Common fragile site (CFS) loci are particularly vulnerable to replication stress and can experience abnormal rearrangements in tumors. In these loci, replication stress often triggers DNA repair synthesis during mitosis. This synthesis, known as MiDAS, relies on the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease and a non-catalytic subunit of the Pol-delta complex called POLD3. In this study, we investigate the role of HR factors in promoting MiDAS in human cells. Our findings reveal that RAD51 and BRCA2 are not necessary for MiDAS but are crucial for countering replication stress at CFS loci during S-phase. On the other hand, MiDAS relies on RAD52, which is required for the timely recruitment of MUS81 and POLD3 to CFSs in early mitosis. These results shed light on the mechanisms of MiDAS and highlight a specific function of human RAD52. Additionally, inhibiting MiDAS selectively could be a potential therapeutic approach to sensitize cancer cells experiencing replicative stress.

title: Excitotoxic brain injury in adult zebrafish stimulates neurogenesis and long-distance neuronal integration.
text: Zebrafish possess a greater ability than mammals to repair their central nervous system following injury. By studying the differences in regenerative responses among various vertebrate species, we can gain insights into mechanisms that could enhance repair in humans. In research on Huntington's disease and stroke, quinolinic acid, an excitotoxin, has been used to induce brain injury in rodents. When injected into the striatum of adult rodents, this toxin promotes the generation of new neurons from the subventricular zone and their migration to the site of injury. However, most of these newly formed neurons do not survive, resulting in minimal repair of the lesion. To investigate the reparative processes, we employed quinolinic acid to induce injury in the telencephalon of adult zebrafish. Additionally, we utilized conditional transgenic lineage mapping of adult radial glial stem cells to examine the survival and integration of neurons generated after the injury. The injection of quinolinic acid, and to a lesser extent, the injection of a control substance, led to cell death, infiltration of microglial cells, increased cell proliferation, and enhanced neurogenesis in the injured hemisphere. Compared to the control injection, the quinolinic acid injection resulted in more complete repair of the lesion. By mapping the fate of her4-expressing radial glia, we observed an expansion of these stem cells in response to the injury. These stem cells gave rise to neurons that migrated to the site of injury, survived for at least 8 weeks, and formed long-distance connections that crossed the anterior commissure and synapsed in the opposite hemisphere. These findings indicate that quinolinic acid-induced injury in the zebrafish brain stimulates adult neural stem cells to generate robust regeneration with the integration of new neurons over long distances. This model holds promise for elucidating reparative mechanisms that can be applied to restorative therapies for brain injuries in mammals.

title: Germinal Center T Follicular Helper Cells Are Highly Permissive to HIV-1 and Alter Their Phenotype during Virus Replication.
text: During asymptomatic HIV-1 infection, the replication of the virus is mainly concentrated in CD4(+) T cells within B cell follicles of secondary lymphoid tissues. Previous studies have suggested that a specific subset of T follicular helper cells (TFH) within germinal centers (GC) is highly susceptible to HIV-1. However, it is still unclear whether these GC TFH cells are the primary producers of the virus in vivo. In this study, we aimed to investigate the permissivity of TFH cells to HIV-1 ex vivo by exposing tonsil cells to HIV-1 GFP reporter viruses through spinoculation and culturing. Using flow cytometry, we observed higher percentages of GFP-positive cells among GC TFH (CXCR5(high)PD-1(high)) and CXCR5(+)programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)(low) cells compared to non-GC TFH (CXCR5(+)PD-1(intermediate)) or extrafollicular (EF) (CXCR5(-)) cells. However, when we sorted the cells before spinoculation, we found that GC TFH cells were significantly more permissive to HIV-1 compared to CXCR5(+)PD-1(low) or EF cells, suggesting that many GC TFH cells transition to a CXCR5(+)PD-1(low) phenotype during productive infection. In situ hybridization of lymph node sections from untreated HIV-1-infected individuals without AIDS revealed higher frequencies of HIV-1 RNA-positive cells in GC regions compared to non-GC regions of the follicle or EF regions. Additionally, superinfection of lymph node cells from HIV-1-infected individuals with GFP reporter virus confirmed the permissivity of follicular cells to HIV-1 ex vivo. Immunostaining of lymph nodes showed that 96% of CXCR5(+)CD4(+) cells were located in follicles. Furthermore, analysis of sorted lymph node cells from four HIV-infected individuals revealed that CXCR5(+) subsets harbored 11-66-fold more HIV-1 RNA than CXCR5(-) subsets, as determined by RT PCR. These findings suggest that GC TFH cells are highly susceptible to HIV-1 infection, but downregulate PD-1 and, to a lesser extent, CXCR5 during the replication of the virus. Overall, these results provide further evidence implicating GC TFH cells as the primary producers of HIV-1 during chronic asymptomatic infection.

title: Risk of death with atypical antipsychotic drug treatment for dementia: meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the evidence regarding the increased risk of mortality associated with the use of atypical antipsychotic medications in individuals with dementia. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of various databases and sources to identify relevant clinical trials. They selected published and unpublished randomized placebo-controlled trials that focused on atypical antipsychotic drugs used to treat Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Data extraction and synthesis were performed, and statistical analyses were conducted to assess the outcomes.

A total of 15 trials, including both published and unpublished studies, met the criteria for inclusion in the analysis. These trials involved a total of 3353 patients who were randomized to receive the study drug or placebo. The duration of the trials ranged from 10 to 12 weeks. The atypical antipsychotic drugs assessed in the trials included aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone.

The results of the analysis showed that there were no significant differences in dropouts between the treatment and placebo groups. However, the incidence of death was higher among patients who received the atypical antipsychotic drugs compared to those who received placebo. The meta-analysis revealed an odds ratio of 1.54, indicating a small but significant increased risk of death associated with the use of these medications. Sensitivity analyses did not indicate any differential risks for specific drugs, severity of dementia, sample selection, or diagnosis.

In conclusion, the findings suggest that atypical antipsychotic drugs may be associated with a slightly higher risk of mortality compared to placebo in individuals with dementia. However, it is important to consider this risk in the context of the medical need for these drugs, the evidence of their efficacy, the presence of medical comorbidities, and the availability of alternative treatment options. Further research, including individual patient analyses, is needed to better understand the survival outcomes and causes of death associated with these medications.

title: PI3K in cancer: divergent roles of isoforms, modes of activation and therapeutic targeting
text: In response to external signals, Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI3Ks) play a vital role in coordinating intracellular signaling. The excessive activation of PI3K signaling pathways is a prevalent occurrence in human cancers. This article examines the latest developments in understanding the functions of specific PI3K isoforms in both normal and cancer-related signaling. It also explores various mechanisms through which PI3K can be overactivated and discusses the present status and future prospects of targeting this pathway in clinical settings.

title: Amphiregulin enhances regulatory T cell-suppressive function via the epidermal growth factor receptor.
text: The Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) plays a crucial role in tissue development, maintaining balance within the body, and the development of cancer. In this study, we have discovered that regulatory T (Treg) cells, specifically those expressing Foxp3, also express EGFR during inflammatory conditions. Furthermore, we found that when Treg cells were stimulated with Amphiregulin (AREG), a growth factor similar to EGF, their function was significantly enhanced in laboratory settings. We also demonstrated the importance of AREG in Treg cell function in vivo using a colitis and tumor vaccination model. Additionally, we discovered that AREG derived from mast cells fully restored optimal Treg cell function. These findings highlight the role of EGFR in regulating local immune responses and establish a connection between mast cells and Treg cells. By targeting this immune regulatory mechanism, we may contribute to the success of EGFR-targeting treatments in cancer patients.

title: Gonadotrope-specific deletion of Dicer results in severely suppressed gonadotropins and fertility defects.
text: Pituitary gonadotropins, specifically follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone, are glycoproteins expressed in gonadotropes. Their role is to promote the development and functions of the gonads, including steroidogenesis and gametogenesis. While the transcriptional regulation of gonadotropin subunits has been extensively studied, the post-transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. To investigate whether microRNAs play a role in regulating hormone-specific gonadotropin β subunits in vivo, we utilized a genetic approach to delete Dicer in gonadotropes. Our findings indicate that several DICER-dependent microRNAs, which were predicted to bind to gonadotropin β subunit mRNAs, were suppressed in purified gonadotropes of mutant mice. This suppression led to a significant decrease in gonadotropin-β subunit proteins and subsequently, a reduction in the secretion of heterodimeric hormones. Interestingly, in addition to the suppression of basal levels, the rise in pituitary gonadotropin synthesis and secretion following gonadectomy was completely abolished in the mutants, suggesting a defective gonadal negative feedback control. Furthermore, the mutants lacking Dicer in gonadotropes exhibited severely reduced fertility, which was rescued by the administration of exogenous hormones, confirming that the fertility defects were a result of suppressed gonadotropins. Our research demonstrates that DICER-dependent microRNAs play a crucial role in maintaining gonadotropin homeostasis and fertility in mice. Additionally, our findings suggest that microRNAs are involved in the gonadal feedback control of gonadotropin synthesis and secretion. Therefore, DICER-dependent microRNAs provide an additional layer of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation in gonadotropes, contributing to the orchestration of the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis physiology.

title: Sequential histone-modifying activities determine the robustness of transdifferentiation
text: Species ranging from jellyfish to mice have shown natural interconversions between different types of somatic cells. Exploring the efficiency and reproducibility of these reprogramming events can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms that ensure successful cell conversion. In our study, we discovered that a conserved demethylase called JMJD-3.1, which removes H3K27me3/me2 marks, and the Set1 complex, a methyltransferase responsible for adding H3K4 marks, work together to guarantee consistent transdifferentiation of postmitotic hindgut cells into motor neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans. Through single-cell analysis, we found that this robust conversion relies on stepwise histone-modifying activities, which are divided into distinct phases of transdifferentiation. These phases involve the degradation of JMJD-3.1 and specific interactions with transcription factors that play important roles in cell plasticity and terminal fate determination. Our findings establish a connection between the epigenetic mechanisms that drive robust transdifferentiation in nature and the efficient reprogramming of cells in vitro.

title: Normal and leukemic stem cell niches: insights and therapeutic opportunities.
text: The bone marrow (BM) niche plays a crucial role in regulating the behavior of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which are responsible for producing blood cells. These HSCs rely on signals from the BM niche to stay dormant and adjust blood production according to the body's requirements. However, in blood malignancies, the BM niche undergoes changes that disrupt its normal function and directly impact the behavior of leukemic stem cells (LSCs) that initiate the disease. In this review, we examine recent discoveries about the cellular and molecular factors that determine the normal HSC niche. We also explore how genetic alterations in stromal cells and the remodeling of the BM niche caused by leukemia contribute to the development of blood malignancies. Additionally, we discuss how these findings can be utilized to develop therapies that target the LSC niche, even if they do not directly affect the cancer cells themselves.

title: Role of common hypnotics on the phenotypic causes of obstructive sleep apnoea: paradoxical effects of zolpidem.
text:
The use of hypnotics in individuals with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is not recommended due to concerns about relaxation of the muscles in the throat and delayed awakening, which can worsen low oxygen levels. However, there is a lack of human data on this topic. This study aimed to investigate the effects of three commonly used hypnotics on the threshold for awakening from sleep, the responsiveness of the genioglossus muscle (a muscle in the tongue), and the collapsibility of the upper airway during sleep. 

A total of 21 individuals with and without OSA, aged 18-65 years, participated in the study. They underwent 84 detailed sleep studies after receiving temazepam (10 mg), zolpidem (10 mg), zopiclone (7.5 mg), or a placebo on four separate occasions. The study followed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design (ACTRN12612001004853).

The results showed that the threshold for awakening from sleep increased with zolpidem and zopiclone compared to the placebo. The mean arousal threshold was -18.3±10 and -19.1±9 cmH2O with zolpidem and zopiclone, respectively, compared to -14.6±7 cmH2O with the placebo (p=0.02 and p<0.001). However, there was no significant change in the arousal threshold with temazepam (-16.8±9 cmH2O; p=0.17). The activity of the genioglossus muscle during stable non-REM sleep and its responsiveness during airway narrowing were not significantly different with temazepam and zopiclone compared to the placebo. Surprisingly, zolpidem increased the median muscle responsiveness three-fold during airway narrowing (median -0.15 (interquartile range -1.01 to -0.04) versus -0.05 (-0.29 to -0.03)% maximum EMG per cmH2O epiglottic pressure; p=0.03). The critical closing pressure of the upper airway did not change with any of the hypnotics. 

In conclusion, these commonly used doses of hypnotics have different effects on the threshold for awakening from sleep, but they do not reduce the activity of upper airway muscles or alter the collapsibility of the airway during sleep. In fact, zolpidem increases muscle activity during airway narrowing.

title: Clinical human papillomavirus detection forecasts cervical cancer risk in women over 18 years of follow-up.
text:
The purpose of this study is to examine the long-term benefits of clinical human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing in predicting the risk of cervical precancer and cancer. The researchers collected cervicovaginal lavages from 19,512 women attending a health maintenance program and retrospectively tested them for HPV using a clinical test. HPV-positive samples were further tested for HPV16 and HPV18 using a research test. Abnormal Pap results, classified as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) or more severe, were considered. The women were followed up prospectively with routine annual Pap testing for up to 18 years. The study calculated the cumulative incidence rates (CIRs) of grade 3 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN3+) or cancer based on the enrollment test results. 

The results showed that a negative HPV test at baseline provided greater reassurance against CIN3+ over the 18-year follow-up compared to a normal Pap test (CIR, 0.90% vs 1.27%). While both baseline Pap and HPV tests predicted the development of CIN3+ within the first 2 years of follow-up, only HPV testing predicted the development of CIN3+ 10 to 18 years later (P = .004). Women who tested positive for HPV16 and HPV18 but had a normal Pap were at a higher risk of CIN3+ compared to other HPV-positive women with a normal Pap and had a similar risk of CIN3+ compared to women with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial Pap. 

In conclusion, the study suggests that HPV testing followed by Pap testing, and potentially combined with the detection of HPV16 and HPV18 among HPV-positive individuals, would be an efficient algorithm for cervical cancer screening, particularly in women aged 30 years or older.

title: MG53 nucleates assembly of cell membrane repair machinery
text: The process of dynamic membrane repair and remodeling is crucial for maintaining the integrity of cells and ensuring efficient cellular function. In this study, we have discovered that MG53, a protein belonging to the muscle-specific tripartite motif family (TRIM72), plays a vital role in the repair mechanism of the sarcolemmal membrane. MG53 interacts with phosphatidylserine and associates with intracellular vesicles that travel to the sarcolemmal membranes and fuse with them. Mice lacking MG53 exhibit progressive myopathy and reduced exercise capability due to a defective membrane repair capacity. When the sarcolemmal membrane is injured, the extracellular oxidative environment enters and causes MG53 to form oligomers, which then recruit vesicles containing MG53 to the site of injury. Once the vesicles have been transported, the entry of extracellular calcium enables their fusion, effectively sealing the damaged membrane. Our findings suggest that the translocation of intracellular vesicles and the calcium-dependent fusion of membranes are distinct steps involved in the repair of membrane damage. Furthermore, MG53 may play a crucial role in initiating the assembly of the membrane repair machinery in an oxidation-dependent manner.

title: A large-scale replication study identifies TNIP1, PRDM1, JAZF1, UHRF1BP1 and IL10 as risk loci for systemic lupus erythematosus
text: Recent genome-wide association studies have discovered 15 susceptibility loci for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). To validate these findings and identify additional risk loci, we selected SNPs from 2,466 regions that showed potential association with SLE (P < 0.05) in a comprehensive genome-wide study. These SNPs were then genotyped in an independent sample of 1,963 cases and 4,329 controls. Through this replication effort, we identified five new SLE susceptibility loci (P < 5 × 10−8): TNIP1 (odds ratio (OR) = 1.27), PRDM1 (OR = 1.20), JAZF1 (OR = 1.20), UHRF1BP1 (OR = 1.17), and IL10 (OR = 1.19). Additionally, we discovered 21 more potential candidate loci with P≤ 1 × 10−5. By screening alleles previously associated with other autoimmune diseases, we found five loci (P < 1 × 10−3) that may contribute to SLE: IFIH1, CFB, CLEC16A, IL12B, and SH2B3. These findings expand our understanding of confirmed and potential SLE susceptibility loci and highlight the involvement of key immunologic pathways in SLE pathogenesis.

title: ARID1A-mutated ovarian cancers depend on HDAC6 activity
text: ARID1A is a gene that encodes a component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex and is commonly mutated in various types of human cancers. Interestingly, ARID1A mutations and TP53 mutations are typically found in separate cases and not together. However, the potential therapeutic approaches that can be derived from this genetic characteristic have yet to be explored. In this study, we demonstrate that the activity of HDAC6, a protein involved in cellular processes, is crucial in ovarian cancers with ARID1A mutations. By inhibiting HDAC6 activity using a small-molecule inhibitor that can be used in clinical settings, we observed a significant improvement in the survival of mice with ARID1A-mutated tumors. This improvement was accompanied by a decrease in tumor growth and spread specifically in ARID1A-mutated tumors, but not in tumors with the wild-type ARID1A gene. The reliance on HDAC6 activity in ARID1A-mutated cells was found to be linked to the direct suppression of HDAC6 by ARID1A at the transcriptional level. Furthermore, the inhibition of HDAC6 selectively induced apoptosis, or programmed cell death, in ARID1A-mutated cells. HDAC6 was also found to directly remove a specific chemical modification on p53, a protein involved in promoting apoptosis, thereby reducing its pro-apoptotic function. Consequently, the mutation of ARID1A leads to the inactivation of p53's ability to induce apoptosis by upregulating HDAC6. Taken together, these findings suggest that targeting HDAC6 through pharmacological inhibition could be a promising therapeutic strategy for cancers with ARID1A mutations.

title: Solution NMR structure of the TatA component of the twin-arginine protein transport system from gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis.
text: The Tat system, found in bacteria and plants, is responsible for transporting folded proteins across the cytoplasmic or chloroplast thylakoid membrane. In Gram-positive bacteria, the Tat system consists of two essential components: TatA and TatC proteins. TatA is a multifunctional subunit that can form a protein-conducting channel and participate in substrate recognition. However, the exact mechanism of protein translocation is still unknown. In this study, we used NMR spectroscopy to determine the solution structure of TatA(d) protein from Bacillus subtilis, providing the first atomic resolution structure of the Tat system. TatA(d) has an L-shaped structure, with a transmembrane helix and an amphipathic helix, while the C-terminal tail is unstructured. Our findings support the proposed topology of TatA(d), with the transmembrane helix inserted into the lipid bilayer and the amphipathic helix at the membrane-water interface. Additionally, the structure of TatA(d) highlights the importance of conserved residues in the hinge region, offering new insights into the protein transport mechanism of the Tat system.

title: Autoimmunity due to molecular mimicry as a cause of neurological disease
text: One theory that connects infection with autoimmune disease is known as molecular mimicry. Molecular mimicry occurs when the immune system responds to a foreign substance in the environment that resembles a component of the body, leading to the development of disease. This theory has been suggested as a possible explanation for the development of diabetes, lupus, and multiple sclerosis (MS). However, there is limited direct evidence linking specific causative agents to the immune reactions that cause these diseases. Our research aims to establish a clear connection between viral infection, autoimmunity, and neurological disease in humans. To study molecular mimicry, we focused on patients with a condition called human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), which shares similarities with MS (references 5, 6, 7). HAM/TSP patients produce antibodies that target neurons. We hypothesized that these antibodies would identify an autoantigen in the central nervous system (CNS). Through our investigation, we discovered that immunoglobulin G isolated from HAM/TSP patients recognized a protein called heterogeneous nuclear ribonuclear protein-A1 (hnRNP-A1) as the autoantigen. These antibodies also cross-reacted with HTLV-1-tax, which is associated with the immune response in HAM/TSP (references 5, 9). Furthermore, we found that the autoantibodies specifically stained human Betz cells, which are susceptible to damage. When these autoantibodies were infused into brain sections, they inhibited neuronal firing, indicating their pathogenic nature. These findings highlight the significance of molecular mimicry between an infecting agent and hnRNP-A1 in autoimmune diseases affecting the CNS.

title: Altered recognition of antigen is a mechanism of CD8+ T cell tolerance in cancer
text: The evasion of tumors through antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell tolerance, which is induced by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), is a significant mechanism. Our study using in vivo models demonstrates that MDSCs directly interfere with the binding of specific peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) dimers to CD8-expressing T cells by nitration of tyrosines in the T-cell receptor (TCR)-CD8 complex. This disruption prevents CD8-expressing T cells from binding pMHC and responding to the specific peptide, while still maintaining their ability to respond to nonspecific stimulation. The nitration of TCR-CD8 is triggered by MDSCs through the excessive production of reactive oxygen species and peroxynitrite during direct cell-cell contact. Molecular modeling suggests specific sites of nitration that may impact the flexibility of TCR-CD8's conformation and its interaction with pMHC. These findings unveil a previously unidentified mechanism of T-cell tolerance in cancer that is relevant to various pathological conditions associated with the accumulation of MDSCs.

title: A new genetic subgroup of chronic granulomatous disease with autosomal recessive mutations in p40 phox and selective defects in neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity.
text:
Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a condition characterized by recurrent pyogenic infections and granulomatous inflammation. It occurs due to recessive mutations in one of four genes that encode subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, which is responsible for superoxide production. These genes include gp91(phox), p22(phox), p47(phox), and p67(phox). Another subunit, p40(phox), plays a crucial role in the production of superoxide during phagocytosis by binding to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns(3)P) through its phox homology (PX) domain. 

In this study, we present the first case of autosomal recessive mutations in the NCF4 gene, which encodes p40(phox), in a boy with granulomatous colitis. The boy's neutrophils exhibited a significant defect in intracellular superoxide production during phagocytosis, while the release of superoxide outside the cells in response to phorbol ester or formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine (fMLF) was unaffected. Genetic analysis revealed compound heterozygosity for a frameshift mutation with a premature stop codon and a missense mutation predicting a R105Q substitution in the PX domain of p40(phox). The boy's parents and sibling were healthy carriers of these mutations.

Further investigation showed that p40(phox)R105Q was unable to bind to PtdIns(3)P and failed to restore oxidase activity during phagocytosis in granulocytes lacking p40(phox). Additionally, p40(phox)R105Q was prematurely lost from phagosomes. These findings highlight the essential role of p40(phox) binding to PtdIns(3)P in the production of oxidants during phagocytosis in human neutrophils and suggest that its absence can contribute to the development of CGD.

title: Birth weight and mammographic density among postmenopausal women in Sweden.
text: The weight at birth is a significant indicator of the likelihood of developing breast cancer later in life, and the size of the mammary glands may play a role in this process. We conducted a study to examine the relationship between birth size measurements and mammographic density, which is a marker of mammary gland mass. We collected data from 893 postmenopausal women in Sweden who had not previously had cancer. We obtained information on birth size from birth records and their most recent mammograms. The mammograms were digitized and analyzed using computer-assisted software to determine mammographic density. We used statistical models to control for potential confounding factors. We found that the average percentage of mammographic density increased when comparing the highest and lowest categories of birth weight (from 15.6% to 18.6%) and head circumference (from 15.5% to 20.4%). These trends were statistically significant (p values 0.02 and 0.007, respectively). The associations were particularly strong when the cutoff for high mammographic density was set at 50%. Women with birth weights over 4000g were nearly three times more likely to have high mammographic density compared to women weighing 3001-3500 grams at birth (odds ratio: 2.9, 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 7.9). We did not find any association between birth length and mammographic density, although birth length is known to be less accurately measured. These findings suggest that adult breast density, which is a strong predictor of breast cancer risk, has its origins in the womb, as indicated by birth size.

title: Oral ciclopirox olamine displays biological activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies.
text:
We have developed an oral version of the antimycotic drug ciclopirox olamine, which is known to chelate intracellular iron and has shown anticancer activity in laboratory and animal studies. In order to evaluate its safety and effectiveness in humans, we conducted a phase I clinical trial with patients who had relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies. The trial was registered under the ID NCT00990587.

During the trial, patients were given oral ciclopirox olamine once daily for five days in 21-day treatment cycles, with doses ranging from 5 to 80 mg/m². A subset of patients also underwent additional studies to analyze the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. After determining the half-life of ciclopirox olamine, we enrolled another group of patients who were treated with a higher dose of 80 mg/m² four times daily.

Throughout the trial, we closely monitored adverse events and clinical response. A total of 23 patients received the study treatment. We found that ciclopirox olamine was quickly absorbed and eliminated from the body, with a short half-life. Interestingly, the levels of an inactive metabolite called ciclopirox glucuronide were higher in the plasma compared to ciclopirox itself.

Furthermore, we observed a decrease in the expression of survivin, a protein associated with cancer cell survival, in peripheral blood cells from patients who received daily doses of ciclopirox olamine greater than 10 mg/m². This indicates that the drug has biological activity.

However, we did observe dose-limiting gastrointestinal side effects in patients who received the highest dose of 80 mg/m² four times daily. No dose-limiting toxicity was observed at a dose of 40 mg/m² once daily. Additionally, two patients showed improvement in their hematologic condition.

Overall, the once-daily dosing of oral ciclopirox olamine was well tolerated in patients with relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies. Further optimization of dosing regimens is necessary for this specific patient population.

title: Cancer cell–autonomous contribution of type I interferon signaling to the efficacy of chemotherapy
text: The induction of innate and T cell-mediated anticancer immune responses is responsible for some of the anti-neoplastic effects of anthracyclines in mice. In our study, we have found that anthracyclines stimulate the rapid production of type I interferons (IFNs) by malignant cells. This production is triggered by the activation of Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3), an endosomal pattern recognition receptor. The type I IFNs then bind to IFN-α and IFN-β receptors (IFNARs) on neoplastic cells, leading to the release of chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 10 (CXCL10) through autocrine and paracrine circuitries. Tumors that lack Tlr3 or Ifnar do not respond to chemotherapy unless type I IFN or Cxcl10, respectively, is artificially supplied. Additionally, we have found that a type I IFN-related signature can predict clinical responses to anthracycline-based chemotherapy in patients with breast carcinoma who have a poor prognosis. Our findings suggest that anthracycline-mediated immune responses resemble those induced by viral pathogens. We believe that this "viral mimicry" is a key characteristic of successful chemotherapy.

title: alphaE-catenin controls cerebral cortical size by regulating the hedgehog signaling pathway.
text: In the process of development, cells carefully regulate their rates of growth to create organs of specific sizes. Our study reveals that when the essential adherens junction gene, alphaE-catenin, is deleted specifically in the central nervous system, it leads to abnormal activation of the hedgehog pathway. This abnormal activation causes the cell cycle to shorten, reduces apoptosis, and results in an increase in the size of the cortical region of the brain (cortical hyperplasia). We propose that alphaE-catenin serves as a link between cell-density-dependent adherens junctions and the developmental hedgehog pathway. This connection may establish a negative feedback loop that controls the size of the developing cerebral cortex.

title: Molecular regulation of effector and memory T cell differentiation
text: The understanding of T lymphocyte subsets that provide protection from infection has advanced, shedding light on the factors that regulate their gene regulation and differentiation. We have also gained insights into tissue-resident memory lymphocytes and the origins of the heterogeneity in activated T cells. These findings show progress in understanding T cell responses, but also highlight gaps in knowledge and challenges in applying this knowledge to vaccination and immunotherapy.

title: Liver-resident macrophage necroptosis orchestrates type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type-2-mediated tissue repair during bacterial infection.
text: Kupffer cells, which are fetal-origin phagocytes that line the liver sinusoids, play a crucial role in defending against enteroinvasive bacteria. In our study, we discovered that infection with Listeria monocytogenes caused the early death of Kupffer cells through necroptosis. This was followed by the recruitment of monocytes and the initiation of an anti-bacterial inflammatory response of type 1. Additionally, the death of Kupffer cells triggered a type 2 response involving the release of interleukin-33 (IL-33) from hepatocytes and interleukin-4 (IL-4) from basophils. This led to the activation of monocyte-derived macrophages, which replaced the lost Kupffer cells and restored liver homeostasis. Therefore, the death of Kupffer cells serves as a crucial signal that coordinates both type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type 2-mediated liver repair during infection. This suggests that, in the context of a bacterial infection, type 1 and type 2 responses can develop sequentially and work together to orchestrate liver immune responses and restore homeostasis.

title: Gene regulation in the immune system by long noncoding RNAs
text: The immune system is regulated by long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), which play a crucial role in controlling gene expression. These lncRNAs are expressed in a specific manner and have the ability to influence the differentiation and function of various cell types in the immune system. This article focuses on the mechanisms through which lncRNAs regulate genes involved in the immune response. These mechanisms include direct interactions with chromatin, RNA, and proteins. Additionally, the article explores new areas of lncRNA biology, such as the functions of enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and chemical modifications to RNA in cellular processes. The authors highlight the gaps in our understanding of lncRNAs and discuss future prospects for their roles in the immune system and autoimmune disease.

title: The Ly49Q receptor plays a crucial role in neutrophil polarization and migration by regulating raft trafficking.
text: Neutrophils exhibit rapid polarization and directional movement to penetrate infection and inflammation sites. Our study reveals the essential role of an inhibitory MHC I receptor, Ly49Q, in facilitating the swift polarization and tissue infiltration of neutrophils. Under normal conditions, Ly49Q hinders neutrophil adhesion by preventing the formation of focal complexes, likely by inhibiting Src and PI3 kinases. However, in the presence of inflammatory stimuli, Ly49Q promotes rapid neutrophil polarization and tissue infiltration in a manner dependent on its ITIM domain. These opposing functions are mediated by distinct utilization of effector phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2. The regulation of membrane raft functions by Ly49Q influences its impact on neutrophil polarization and migration. We propose that Ly49Q plays a crucial role in facilitating the transition of neutrophils to their polarized morphology and rapid migration during inflammation, through its spatiotemporal control of membrane rafts and associated signaling molecules.

title: Prevalence of Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus infection in homosexual men at beginning of and during the HIV epidemic.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) infection in homosexual men in San Francisco at the start of the HIV epidemic in 1978 and 1979, and to analyze changes in KSHV prevalence from 1978 to 1996 in relation to changes in sexual behavior. The study analyzed a clinic-based sample of 398 individuals from the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort, as well as population-based samples from the San Francisco Men's Health Study (MHS) and the San Francisco Young Men's Health Study (YMHS). The main outcome measures were KSHV and HIV antibodies, as well as sexual behaviors. 

The results showed that the prevalence of KSHV infection in 1978 and 1979 was 26.5% overall, compared to 6.9% for HIV in the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort sample. The prevalence of KSHV infection remained relatively stable between the MHS sample in 1984 and 1985 (29.6%) and the YMHS sample in 1995 and 1996 (26.4%), while HIV prevalence decreased from 49.5% in 1984 and 1985 to 17.6% in 1992 and 1993. The proportion of men engaging in unprotected receptive anal intercourse with one or more partners decreased from 54% to 11% during the 1984 to 1993 period, while the prevalence of unprotected oral intercourse ranged from 60% to 90% between 1984 and 1996. 

In conclusion, KSHV infection was already highly prevalent in homosexual men when the HIV epidemic began in San Francisco, and its prevalence has remained relatively constant. The decline in Kaposi sarcoma incidence does not appear to be due to a decrease in KSHV transmission.

title: Nortriptyline for smoking cessation: a review.
text: This article examines the effectiveness of nortriptyline in helping people quit smoking, using a meta-analysis of studies from the Cochrane Library. The analysis found that nortriptyline, at doses of 75-100 mg, doubled the rates of successful quitting (OR = 2.1) compared to a placebo. However, between 4% and 12% of participants dropped out due to adverse events, although no serious adverse events were reported. Interestingly, the effectiveness of nortriptyline did not seem to be related to its antidepressant properties. Overall, nortriptyline was found to be a helpful aid for smoking cessation, with a similar level of effectiveness as bupropion and nicotine replacement therapies. However, it is still unclear whether nortriptyline may cause serious side effects in healthy, nondepressed smokers, as it has only been tested on a small group of 500 smokers. The fact that nortriptyline and bupropion were effective for smoking cessation, while selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors were not, suggests that dopaminergic or adrenergic activity, rather than serotonergic activity, is crucial for successful quitting. Until further research can confirm a low occurrence of significant adverse events, nortriptyline should be considered a second-line treatment option for smoking cessation.

title: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
text: The authors of this study explore the complex issue of emotion regulation in individuals with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Despite the recognition of this connection, there is no consensus on how to approach this clinically challenging area. The authors conducted a comprehensive analysis of existing literature using both quantitative and qualitative methods, leading to three key findings. Firstly, emotion dysregulation is prevalent in individuals with ADHD across their lifespan and significantly contributes to impairment. Secondly, deficits in orienting attention, recognizing emotions, and allocating attention to emotional stimuli may underlie emotion dysregulation in ADHD. These deficits suggest dysfunction within a specific brain network. Lastly, while current treatments for ADHD often improve emotion dysregulation, focusing on this combination of symptoms could lead to new therapeutic approaches. The authors also propose three models to explain the overlap between emotion dysregulation and ADHD: they are correlated but distinct dimensions, emotion dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, or the combination represents a separate diagnostic entity. Each model offers different predictions that can guide future research on individuals with ADHD and emotion dysregulation, a population that has been largely overlooked.

title: Use of serum C reactive protein and procalcitonin concentrations in addition to symptoms and signs to predict pneumonia in patients presenting to primary care with acute cough: diagnostic study
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the accuracy of certain inflammatory markers, along with symptoms and signs, in predicting pneumonia and to develop a diagnostic tool. The study was conducted between 2007 and 2010 in primary care centers across 12 European countries. Participants were adults with acute cough who underwent a history assessment, physical examination, and measurement of C reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin in their blood. Chest radiography was also performed within seven days. The main outcome measure was pneumonia, as determined by radiologists who were unaware of other information. 

Out of 3106 eligible patients, 286 were excluded due to missing or inadequate chest radiographs, leaving 2820 patients (mean age 50, 40% men), of whom 140 (5%) had pneumonia. A subset of 1675 chest radiographs were re-assessed, showing agreement in 94%. Six published "symptoms and signs models" had varying discrimination, with the area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (ROC) ranging from 0.55 to 0.71. 

The optimal combination of clinical prediction items derived from the study patients included the absence of a runny nose and the presence of breathlessness, crackles, and diminished breath sounds on auscultation, tachycardia, and fever. This combination had an ROC area of 0.70. Adding CRP at a cut-off of >30 mg/L increased the ROC area to 0.77 and improved diagnostic classification. In patients classified as "low risk" for pneumonia based on symptoms, signs, and CRP >30 mg/L, the prevalence of pneumonia was 2%. In those classified as "high risk," the prevalence was 31%. The positive likelihood ratio for low, intermediate, and high risk for pneumonia was 0.4, 1.2, and 8.6, respectively. Procalcitonin measurement did not provide additional diagnostic information. 

A simplified diagnostic score based on symptoms, signs, and CRP >30 mg/L resulted in proportions of pneumonia of 0.7%, 3.8%, and 18.2% in the low, intermediate, and high-risk groups, respectively. In conclusion, a clinical rule based on symptoms and signs performed best in patients with mild or severe clinical presentation. Adding CRP concentration improved diagnostic information, but procalcitonin measurement did not provide clinically relevant information in this group.

title: Somatic Mutations of the Immunoglobulin Framework Are Generally Required for Broad and Potent HIV-1 Neutralization
text:
The prevention of HIV-1 infection is crucial in the development of an effective HIV-1 vaccine, and one way to achieve this is through the use of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs). These bNAbs are particularly important because they can prevent infection. Interestingly, bNAbs are highly mutated and are produced by a small fraction of individuals who have been infected with HIV-1 for several years.

Typically, antibodies accumulate mutations in the complementarity determining region (CDR) loops, which are responsible for contacting the antigen. These CDR loops are supported by framework regions (FWRs) that are resistant to and less tolerant of mutations. However, our research shows that unlike most antibodies, including those with limited HIV-1 neutralizing activity, bNAbs actually require somatic mutations in their FWRs.

Through structural and functional analyses, we have discovered that somatic mutations in FWR residues actually enhance the breadth and potency of bNAbs. These mutations provide increased flexibility and/or direct contact with the antigen. This means that FWRs play a crucial role in bNAbs beyond just supporting the CDR loops. Therefore, when designing an HIV-1 vaccine, it is important to consider the unique contribution of FWRs to the potency and breadth of bNAbs.

title: Etiology of type 1 diabetes.
text: Recent studies in genetic mapping and gene-phenotype analysis have provided valuable insights into the genetic makeup of type 1 diabetes. At least ten genes have been identified as strong candidates that play a significant role in causing this disease. The functions of these genes shed light on the primary pathways that contribute to the development of type 1 diabetes. These pathways include the binding of HLA class II and I molecules to preproinsulin peptides and T cell receptors, activation of T and B cells, responses to viral pathogens, signaling through chemokines and cytokines, as well as the functions of T regulatory cells and antigen-presenting cells. This review focuses on the research conducted in the field of type 1 diabetes, specifically on the use of genetic approaches to identify the underlying mechanisms of the disease. It is important to note that the expression and functions of these pathways, and consequently the susceptibility to the disease, can be influenced by epigenetic and environmental factors. Furthermore, certain inherited immune phenotypes may serve as early indicators of type 1 diabetes and could potentially be utilized in future clinical trials.

title: Plasticity of epithelial stem cells in tissue regeneration
text: Stem cells play a crucial role in maintaining the balance and repairing tissues. Recent studies have revealed that the behavior and potential of epithelial stem cells can vary depending on their location within the tissue, their response to normal tissue maintenance, their involvement in wound healing, or their transplantation for tissue regeneration. This review explores the remarkable ability of different populations of lineage-restricted stem cells and committed progenitors to exhibit plasticity and regain their capacity for long-term self-renewal and differentiation into multiple cell types under physiological and regenerative conditions. Additionally, we discuss the implications of cellular plasticity in the fields of regenerative medicine and cancer research.

title: Atm-deficient mice exhibit increased sensitivity to dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis characterized by elevated DNA damage and persistent immune activation.
text: The role of the DNA double-strand break recognition and response protein, ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), in inflammation and inflammatory diseases remains unclear. Previous studies have demonstrated that intestinal inflammation induces high levels of systemic DNA damage in normal mice. To investigate the impact of Atm deficiency on inflammation, we induced experimental colitis in Atm(-/-), Atm(+/-), and wild-type mice using dextran sulfate sodium (DSS). The Atm(-/-) mice exhibited higher disease activity indices and mortality rates compared to the heterozygous and wild-type mice. We analyzed systemic DNA damage and immune response in peripheral blood during and after three cycles of treatment. Atm(-/-) mice displayed increased sensitivity to DNA strand breaks in peripheral leukocytes and micronucleus formation in erythroblasts, particularly during remission periods and after treatment completion. Markers of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species-mediated damage, such as 8-oxoguanine and nitrotyrosine, were detected in the distal colon and peripheral leukocytes, with Atm(-/-) mice exhibiting higher levels of 8-oxoguanine formation than wild-type mice. Throughout the treatment, Atm(-/-) mice showed greater upregulation of inflammatory cytokines and significantly higher percentages of activated CD69+ and CD44+ T cells in the peripheral blood. These findings suggest that ATM may play a crucial role in regulating the detrimental effects of chronic DSS-induced inflammation, contributing to systemic genomic stability and maintaining gut epithelial barrier homeostasis.

title: Activin–like kinase–3 activity is important for kidney regeneration and reversal of fibrosis
text: Molecules belonging to the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) superfamily, such as bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) and TGF-β, play a crucial role in regulating inflammation, apoptosis, and cellular transitions. In this study, we demonstrate that the BMP receptor activin-like kinase 3 (Alk3) is upregulated early in diseased kidneys following injury. Furthermore, we discovered that deleting Alk3 in the tubular epithelium leads to increased TGF-β1-Smad family member 3 (Smad3) signaling, resulting in epithelial damage and fibrosis. This suggests that Alk3-mediated signaling has a protective function in the kidney. By conducting a structure-function analysis of the BMP-Alk3-BMP receptor, type 2 (BMPR2) ligand-receptor complex and utilizing synthetic organic chemistry, we developed a library of small peptide agonists that activate BMP signaling through the Alk3 receptor. One of these peptide agonists, THR-123, effectively suppressed inflammation, apoptosis, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program. It also reversed established fibrosis in five mouse models of acute and chronic renal injury. Importantly, THR-123 specifically acts through Alk3 signaling, as mice with a targeted deletion of Alk3 in their tubular epithelium did not respond to therapy with THR-123. Additionally, combining THR-123 with the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor captopril had an additive therapeutic effect in controlling renal fibrosis. Our findings highlight the potential of BMP signaling agonists as a novel class of therapeutic agents for inducing regeneration, repair, and reversing established fibrosis in clinical settings.

title: COHCAP: an integrative genomic pipeline for single-nucleotide resolution DNA methylation analysis
text:
The City of Hope CpG Island Analysis Pipeline (COHCAP) is an algorithm designed to analyze DNA methylation data at the single-nucleotide level. This data can be generated from either an Illumina methylation array or targeted bisulfite sequencing. The main objective of the COHCAP algorithm is to identify CpG islands that exhibit a consistent pattern of methylation across CpG sites. 

What sets COHCAP apart is its unique ability to integrate gene expression data, allowing for the identification of a subset of CpG islands that are likely involved in regulating downstream gene expression. Additionally, COHCAP can generate lists of differentially methylated CpG islands that align with gene expression data, achieving approximately 50% concordance. This has been demonstrated in both cell line data and data from diverse patient populations, such as breast cancer biomarkers like the estrogen receptor, where a negative correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression has been observed.

COHCAP also offers visualization tools for quality control metrics, regions of differential methylation, and the correlation between methylation and gene expression. This software is freely available for use at https://sourceforge.net/projects/cohcap/.

title: Subgrouping of patients with neuropathic pain according to pain-related sensory abnormalities: a first step to a stratified treatment approach.
text:
BACKGROUND: Patients experiencing neuropathic pain exhibit various sensory abnormalities related to pain. These sensory features create unique patterns or mosaics, known as sensory profiles, in each patient. One theory suggests that specific pathophysiological mechanisms of pain generation result in distinct sensory abnormalities, leading to the development of sensory profiles. Although several controlled trials of promising new drugs have yielded negative results, it is possible that the heterogeneity of the patient population influenced these findings. By subgrouping patients based on their individual sensory profiles, this heterogeneity could be reduced, thereby improving trial design.

RECENT DEVELOPMENTS: A statistical analysis of patients with neuropathic pain has revealed the existence of subgroups with distinct sensory profiles, who perceive their pain differently, across various neuropathic disorders. Additionally, some disorder-specific profiles have also been identified. Initial clinical trials that employed the subgroup approach at baseline have shown a potential superior effect of the study drugs in specific subgroups, rather than in the entire patient cohort.

WHERE NEXT?: A new classification of neuropathic pain should consider the presence of subgroups with different sensory profiles. Sensory phenotyping has the potential to enhance clinical trial design by including potential treatment responders in the study population. This approach may lead to a stratified treatment strategy and ultimately personalized treatment.

title: The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3).
text:
The definitions of sepsis and septic shock were last revised in 2001, but significant advancements have been made since then in understanding the pathobiology, management, and epidemiology of these conditions. Therefore, there is a need to reexamine and update these definitions. 

The objective of this study was to evaluate and update the definitions for sepsis and septic shock. A task force consisting of 19 experts in sepsis pathobiology, clinical trials, and epidemiology was convened by the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine. The task force used various methods such as meetings, Delphi processes, analysis of electronic health record databases, and voting to generate definitions and clinical criteria. These were then circulated to international professional societies for peer review and endorsement.

The evidence synthesis revealed limitations in the previous definitions, including an excessive focus on inflammation, a misleading model of sepsis progression, and inadequate specificity and sensitivity of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria. The use of multiple definitions and terminologies for sepsis, septic shock, and organ dysfunction has led to discrepancies in reported incidence and mortality rates.

Based on their findings, the task force concluded that the term "severe sepsis" was redundant. They recommended defining sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Organ dysfunction can be represented by an increase in the Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 10%. Septic shock should be defined as a subset of sepsis characterized by profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities that carry a higher risk of mortality than sepsis alone. Patients with septic shock can be identified by the need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mm Hg or greater and a serum lactate level greater than 2 mmol/L (>18 mg/dL) in the absence of hypovolemia. This combination is associated with mortality rates greater than 40%.

In settings such as out-of-hospital, emergency departments, or general hospital wards, adult patients with suspected infection can be quickly identified as having poor outcomes typical of sepsis if they meet at least 2 of the following clinical criteria: respiratory rate of 22/min or greater, altered mentation, or systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or less. This new bedside clinical score is called quickSOFA (qSOFA).

In conclusion, these updated definitions and clinical criteria should replace previous definitions, providing greater consistency for epidemiologic studies and clinical trials. They will also help in the earlier recognition and timely management of patients with sepsis or those at risk of developing sepsis.

title: Stem cell transplantation in patients with autonomic neuropathy due to primary (AL) amyloidosis.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the outcomes of patients with autonomic neuropathy (AN) during and after autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) for AL amyloidosis. A case-control study was conducted, comparing patients with AN to a matched cohort without AN who also underwent ASCT. 

Thirteen patients with AN who underwent ASCT were identified, along with a control group of 95 patients without AN. Patients with AN had a higher number of organs involved and a lower conditioning dose of melphalan compared to the control group. The duration of hospitalization and engraftment kinetics were similar for both groups. Atrial fibrillation occurred in all patients with AN but only one control patient. The median overall survival (OS) for patients with AN was 29 months, while it was over 60 months for controls. 

Univariate analysis showed that cardiac involvement, AN, glomerular filtration rate, number of organs involved, and NT-pro-BNP all had an impact on OS. On multivariate analysis, AN remained an independent adverse factor for OS. 

In conclusion, patients with autonomic neuropathy secondary to AL amyloidosis can undergo ASCT with relative safety. However, autonomic neuropathy is an independent, adverse determinant of survival in these patients.

title: MicroRNA-148a regulates LDL receptor and ABCA1 expression to control circulating lipoprotein levels
text: The pathway of the hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) is crucial for removing LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) from the bloodstream. While we have a good understanding of how LDLR is regulated at the transcriptional level, we are only just starting to uncover the post-transcriptional mechanisms that control LDLR expression. In this study, we have developed a high-throughput screening assay to identify microRNAs (miRNAs) that play a role in regulating LDLR activity in human hepatic cells. Through this screening, we have discovered that miR-148a acts as a negative regulator of LDLR expression and activity. We have also identified a pathway, mediated by sterol regulatory element–binding protein 1 (SREBP1), through which miR-148a controls the uptake of LDL-C. In mice, inhibiting miR-148a led to increased LDLR expression in the liver and decreased levels of LDL-C in the blood. Additionally, we have found that miR-148a also regulates the expression of ATP-binding cassette, subfamily A, member 1 (ABCA1) in the liver and affects circulating levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). These findings highlight the role of miR-148a as a key regulator of hepatic LDL-C clearance by directly modulating LDLR expression. They also demonstrate the potential of inhibiting miR-148a as a therapeutic approach to improve the LDL-C/HDL-C ratio, a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

title: BRACHYURY and CDX2 Mediate BMP-Induced Differentiation of Human and Mouse Pluripotent Stem Cells into Embryonic and Extraembryonic Lineages
text: The role of BMP in inducing differentiation of hESCs towards various lineages, including mesoderm and trophoblast, has been a subject of debate in stem cell biology. In this study, we aimed to revisit the function of BMP in hESCs and mouse epiblast-derived cells. Our findings reveal that BMP4, in collaboration with FGF2 through the ERK pathway, promotes mesoderm formation while inhibiting endoderm differentiation. Under these conditions, cells exhibited high levels of BRACHYURY (BRA) and coexpressed CDX2. Notably, BRA expression preceded CDX2 expression, and both genes were crucial for the activation of not only mesodermal genes but also trophoblast-associated genes. Interestingly, the absence of FGF resulted in maximal expression of trophoblast-associated genes; however, these cells also coexpressed mesodermal genes and displayed distinct cell surface and epigenetic characteristics compared to placental trophoblast. In conclusion, our study suggests that BMP primarily induces the formation of mesoderm rather than trophoblast in human and mouse pluripotent stem cells, with BRA and CDX2 playing essential roles in this process.

title: Degradation of Cellular miR-27 by a Novel, Highly Abundant Viral Transcript Is Important for Efficient Virus Replication In Vivo
text: During lytic infection, cytomegaloviruses produce a large number of viral miRNAs. However, these miRNAs only have a modest impact on the cellular miRNA profile. The most notable change observed during lytic murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection is the rapid degradation of cellular miR-27a and miR-27b. Our study reveals that this degradation is controlled by the highly abundant MCMV m169 transcript, which is approximately 1.7 kb in length and undergoes splicing. The specificity for miR-27a/b is achieved through a single, well-optimized miRNA binding site located in the 3'-UTR of the transcript. This binding site can be easily and effectively retargeted to other cellular and viral miRNAs by replacing the target site. Expression of the 3'-UTR of m169 using an adenoviral vector is sufficient to carry out its function, indicating that no other viral factors are necessary for this process. Degradation of miR-27a/b is accompanied by 3'-tailing and -trimming. Despite the significant impact on miRNA stability, we found that this interaction is mutual, suggesting potential regulation of m169 by miR-27a/b. Interestingly, three mutant viruses that are unable to target miR-27a/b, either due to disruption of the miRNA target site or replacement of the target site, showed significant attenuation in multiple organs as early as 4 days after infection. This indicates that degradation of miR-27a/b is crucial for efficient MCMV replication in vivo.

title: Social and geographical factors affecting access to treatment of colorectal cancer: a cancer registry study
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the impact of deprivation on cancer outcomes, specifically in terms of stage at diagnosis and receipt of treatment. The researchers analyzed data from a Cancer Registry Database, which included information on stage and treatment for the first 6 months after diagnosis. They also considered the socioeconomic status of the patients' immediate area of residence and the travel time from home to the hospital. The study was conducted on a population-based sample of patients residing in a large area in the north of England. A total of 39,619 patients with colorectal cancer diagnosed between 1994 and 2002 were included in the analysis. The main outcomes measured were the stage of diagnosis and receipt of treatment, in relation to deprivation and distance from the hospital.

The results showed that patients in the most deprived quartile were significantly more likely to be diagnosed at stage 4 for rectal cancer, but this association was less pronounced for colonic cancer. There was also a trend for patients in the most deprived quartile to be less likely to receive chemotherapy for stage 4 disease, regardless of the cancer site. Patients with colonic cancer from areas other than the most affluent were significantly less likely to receive any treatment. This effect was more pronounced as the level of deprivation increased. However, the distance from the hospital did not have a significant impact on treatment receipt. The findings suggest that residing in a deprived area is associated with higher stage at diagnosis and reduced receipt of treatment, particularly for colonic cancer. These findings are consistent with previous research and highlight the need for further investigation into access to diagnosis.

title: Development of candidate genomic markers to select breast cancer patients for dasatinib therapy.
text: The selection of patients is crucial for targeted therapies, but phase I/II trials often lack sufficient power to develop predictors of drug response. This study aimed to identify genomic predictors for dasatinib that could be tested in early-phase clinical trials. The researchers compared gene expression profiles of dasatinib-sensitive and dasatinib-resistant cell lines (n = 23) to create a modified DS index, which measures dasatinib sensitivity. They also developed a revised Src index, which measures Src pathway activity, and a dasatinib target index, which combines the affinity of 19 kinases for dasatinib. The performance of these prediction models was evaluated in independent cell lines with known dasatinib sensitivity. The researchers also assessed the feasibility of applying these genomic tests to 133 biopsies of primary breast cancers. The modified DS index accurately predicted dasatinib sensitivity in independent breast cancer cell lines (n = 12), and the target index, but not the revised Src index signature, also distinguished between dasatinib-sensitive and dasatinib-resistant cells. The genomic predictors showed acceptable reproducibility in replicate cell line and human gene expression data. When all three predictors were applied to the same 133 patient samples, they identified different subsets of patients as potentially sensitive to dasatinib. The researchers identified three distinct potential predictors of dasatinib response that were reproducible across cell lines and human data. These candidate markers are currently being tested in a clinical trial to determine their usefulness.

title: BEDTools: a flexible suite of utilities for comparing genomic features
text:
MOTIVATION
In genomics research, it is essential to test for correlations between different sets of genomic features. However, the current web-based methods for searching for overlaps between features are complicated due to the large datasets produced by current sequencing technologies. To efficiently ask complex questions of this data, there is a need for fast and flexible tools.

RESULTS
This article presents a new software suite that allows for the comparison, manipulation, and annotation of genomic features in Browser Extensible Data (BED) and General Feature Format (GFF) format. Additionally, the software supports the comparison of sequence alignments in BAM format to both BED and GFF features. These tools are highly efficient and enable users to compare large datasets, such as next-generation sequencing data, with both public and custom genome annotation tracks. BEDTools can be combined with other tools and standard UNIX commands, making it easier to perform routine genomics tasks and quickly answer complex questions about large genomic datasets.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION
BEDTools was developed using C++. The source code and a comprehensive user manual are freely available at http://code.google.com/p/bedtools.

CONTACT
For further information, please contact aaronquinlan@gmail.com or imh4y@virginia.edu.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
Supplementary data can be accessed at Bioinformatics online.

title: Vegetarian diet improves insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers more than conventional diet in subjects with Type 2 diabetes
text:
The purpose of this study was to compare the effects of calorie-restricted vegetarian and conventional diabetic diets, both alone and in combination with exercise, on insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress markers in individuals with Type 2 diabetes. 

A 24-week randomized, open, parallel design was utilized, with seventy-four patients with Type 2 diabetes randomly assigned to either the experimental group (n = 37), which followed a vegetarian diet, or the control group (n = 37), which followed a conventional diabetic diet. Both diets were isocaloric and calorie-restricted (-500 kcal/day), and all meals were provided throughout the study. In the second 12 weeks of the diet, aerobic exercise was added. Participants were assessed at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks. 

The primary outcomes measured were insulin sensitivity, volume of visceral and subcutaneous fat, and oxidative stress. The intention-to-treat analysis was conducted. 

Results showed that 43% of participants in the experimental group and 5% in the control group were able to reduce their diabetes medication (P < 0.001). The experimental group also experienced a greater decrease in body weight compared to the control group [-6.2 kg (95% CI -6.6 to -5.3) vs. -3.2 kg (95% CI -3.7 to -2.5); interaction group × time P = 0.001]. Additionally, the experimental group demonstrated a significantly greater increase in insulin sensitivity [30% (95% CI 24.5-39) vs. 20% (95% CI 14-25), P = 0.04]. The reduction in both visceral and subcutaneous fat was also greater in the experimental group (P = 0.007 and P = 0.02, respectively). Plasma adiponectin increased (P = 0.02) and leptin decreased (P = 0.02) in the experimental group, with no change observed in the control group. Furthermore, the experimental group showed increases in vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione (P = 0.002, P < 0.001, and P = 0.02, respectively). The differences between groups were more pronounced after the addition of exercise training. Changes in insulin sensitivity and enzymatic oxidative stress markers correlated with changes in visceral fat. 

In conclusion, a calorie-restricted vegetarian diet demonstrated a greater ability to improve insulin sensitivity compared to a conventional diabetic diet over a 24-week period. The greater reduction in visceral fat and improvements in plasma concentrations of adipokines and oxidative stress markers with the vegetarian diet may be responsible for the decrease in insulin resistance. The addition of exercise training further enhanced the positive outcomes associated with the vegetarian diet.

title: Antidepressant use and risk of adverse outcomes in older people: population based cohort study
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the potential adverse outcomes associated with antidepressant treatment in older individuals with depression. The study also aimed to examine the risks based on the class of antidepressant, duration of use, and dosage. The study design involved a cohort of individuals aged 65 and over who were diagnosed with depression. Data was collected from 570 general practices in the United Kingdom that contributed to the QResearch primary care database. The participants included 60,746 patients who were diagnosed with a new episode of depression between the ages of 65 and 100 years from January 1, 1996, to December 31, 2007. They were followed up until December 31, 2008. The main outcome measures were hazard ratios associated with antidepressant use for various adverse outcomes, such as mortality, attempted suicide/self-harm, myocardial infarction, stroke/transient ischemic attack, falls, fractures, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, epilepsy/seizures, road traffic accidents, adverse drug reactions, and hyponatremia. The hazard ratios were adjusted for potential confounding variables. The study calculated hazard ratios for different antidepressant classes (tricyclic and related antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, other antidepressants), dosage, duration of use, and commonly prescribed individual drugs. The results showed that 89.0% of patients received at least one prescription for an antidepressant during the follow-up period. A total of 1,398,359 antidepressant prescriptions were issued, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors being the most commonly prescribed (54.7%), followed by tricyclic antidepressants (31.6%), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (0.2%), and other antidepressants (13.5%). The associations between antidepressant classes and adverse outcomes differed significantly for seven outcomes. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors had the highest adjusted hazard ratios for falls and hyponatremia compared to when antidepressants were not being used. Other antidepressants had the highest adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality, attempted suicide/self-harm, stroke/transient ischemic attack, fracture, and epilepsy/seizures compared to when antidepressants were not being used. Tricyclic antidepressants did not have the highest hazard ratio for any of the outcomes. There were also significant differences in associations between individual drugs for the same seven outcomes. Trazodone (tricyclic antidepressant), mirtazapine, and venlafaxine (both in the group of other antidepressants) had the highest rates for some of these outcomes. The absolute risks over one year for all-cause mortality were 7.04% for patients not taking antidepressants, 8.12% for those taking tricyclic antidepressants, 10.61% for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and 11.43% for other antidepressants. In conclusion, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and other antidepressants were associated with an increased risk of several adverse outcomes compared to tricyclic antidepressants. Among individual drugs, trazodone, mirtazapine, and venlafaxine had the highest risks for some outcomes. However, as this was an observational study, there may be confounding factors that could account for some of the associations between the drugs and adverse outcomes. Further research is needed to confirm these findings, but the risks and benefits of different antidepressants should be carefully evaluated when prescribing them to older individuals.

title: The benefits of statins in people without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
The aim of this study was to determine whether statins can reduce the risk of all cause mortality and major coronary and cerebrovascular events in individuals without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors. The study also aimed to investigate whether these effects are consistent across different populations, including men and women, younger and older individuals (over 65 years), and those with diabetes mellitus. 

The researchers conducted a meta-analysis of randomized trials and gathered data from the Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline. They identified studies that compared the clinical effects of statins with a placebo or control group, with a follow-up period of at least one year. The studies also had to include at least 80% of participants without established cardiovascular disease and provide outcome data on mortality and major cardiovascular disease events. 

A total of 10 trials involving 70,388 participants were included in the analysis. Of these, 23,681 (34%) were women and 16,078 (23%) had diabetes mellitus. The average follow-up period was 4.1 years. The results showed that treatment with statins significantly reduced the risk of all cause mortality, major coronary events, and major cerebrovascular events. There was no evidence of an increased risk of cancer. The researchers found no significant differences in the treatment effect among different clinical subgroups. 

In conclusion, the use of statins in individuals without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors was associated with improved survival and substantial reductions in the risk of major cardiovascular events.

title: Mechanical coupling between transsynaptic N-cadherin adhesions and actin flow stabilizes dendritic spines
text: The shape of neuronal dendritic spines plays a crucial role in synaptic function and is influenced by various factors, such as the actin/myosin cytoskeleton and N-cadherin adhesions. To investigate the mechanical relationship between these components, we conducted live-imaging experiments on primary hippocampal neurons. Our findings revealed that dendritic spines have lower actin turnover and structural motility compared to immature filopodia. However, when a nonadhesive N-cadherin mutant was expressed, both actin turnover and motility increased, resulting in an inverse correlation between spine motility and actin enrichment. Additionally, we observed that pharmacological stimulation of myosin II caused actin structures in spines to move backwards, indicating that myosin II applies tension to the actin network.
