Interestingly, we observed the formation of stable, spine-like structures enriched in actin when dendritic filopodia made contact with N-cadherin-coated beads or micropatterns. Furthermore, computer simulations of actin dynamics replicated various experimental conditions, highlighting the importance of actin flow rate in controlling actin enrichment in dendritic spines. Overall, these findings demonstrate that a clutch-like mechanism involving N-cadherin adhesions and actin flow is responsible for stabilizing dendritic filopodia into mature spines. This mechanism may have significant implications in synapse initiation, maturation, and plasticity during brain development.

title: Phosphate and R2D2 restrict the substrate specificity of Dicer-2, an ATP-driven ribonuclease.
text: Drosophila Dicer-2 is responsible for producing small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) from long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), while Dicer-1 generates microRNAs (miRNAs) from pre-miRNA. The question arises as to what makes these two Dicers specific to their respective biological substrates. Our research reveals that purified Dicer-2 is capable of efficiently cleaving pre-miRNA. However, we observed that the presence of inorganic phosphate and the Dicer-2 partner protein R2D2 inhibits the cleavage of pre-miRNA. Dicer-2 consists of C-terminal RNase III domains that facilitate RNA cleavage, as well as an N-terminal helicase motif whose function remains unclear. Our findings demonstrate that Dicer-2 acts as a dsRNA-stimulated ATPase, catalyzing the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP. This ATP hydrolysis is essential for Dicer-2 to process long dsRNA, but not pre-miRNA. Interestingly, wild-type Dicer-2, but not a mutant lacking ATP hydrolysis activity, is capable of generating siRNAs at a faster rate than it dissociates from a long dsRNA substrate. Based on these observations, we propose that the helicase domain of Dicer-2 utilizes ATP to generate multiple siRNAs from a single molecule of dsRNA before detaching from its substrate.

title: Therapeutic potential of mood stabilizers lithium and valproic acid: beyond bipolar disorder.
text: The traditional use of lithium and valproic acid (VPA) as mood stabilizers for bipolar disorder (BD) is well-known. BD is a complex mental illness caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors that affect cellular plasticity and resilience. However, there is growing support for the therapeutic potential of these drugs in other central nervous system diseases. This article examines the mechanisms of action of lithium and VPA in various neurologic, neurodegenerative, and neuropsychiatric disorders using cellular and animal models. Clinical evidence is also considered, although the limitations of these treatments are acknowledged. The review begins by explaining how lithium and VPA target glycogen synthase kinase-3 and histone deacetylases, respectively, to promote the transcription and expression of proteins that support neurotrophic, angiogenic, and neuroprotective functions. Additionally, these drugs may activate cell survival signaling pathways, counteract oxidative stress, and regulate protein quality control mechanisms. The review also explores the potential of combining these drugs with other treatments to enhance neuroprotection and improve stem cell function. Furthermore, microRNAs are identified as promising therapeutic targets. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that these drugs have neuroprotective effects by promoting anti-inflammation, angiogenesis, neurogenesis, maintaining blood-brain barrier integrity, and providing disease-specific neuroprotection. By comparing these mechanisms with the dysregulated mechanisms in specific diseases, it may be possible to identify core cellular and molecular disturbances using specific risk biomarkers. Future clinical research is needed to fully understand the therapeutic potential of lithium and VPA in a range of central nervous system diseases, with a focus on personalized medicine approaches for treatment.

title: The feasibility of malaria elimination in South Africa
text:
BACKGROUND
After the major malaria epidemic in 2000, South Africa has seen a significant decline in malaria cases. This progress has led to South Africa meeting the World Health Organization's threshold for malaria elimination. With the goal of reversing the spread of malaria by 2015, there is now a push for South Africa to adopt an elimination agenda. This study aimed to assess the feasibility of implementing a malaria elimination program in present-day South Africa.

METHODS
The study assessed the progress made by South Africa in implementing an integrated malaria control program across the three provinces where malaria is endemic. Data on vector control and case management from 2000 to 2011 were analyzed.

RESULTS
Since 2000, both malaria-related morbidity and mortality have significantly decreased in all three malaria-endemic provinces. The most significant decline was seen in KwaZulu-Natal, where cases decreased from 42,276 in 2000 to 380 in 2010, and deaths dropped from 122 to six. Although there has been a 49.2% decrease in reported malaria cases in Limpopo Province, it currently contributes the most to the malaria incidence in South Africa. Despite high insecticide spray coverage in both Mpumalanga and Limpopo, malaria incidence remains above the elimination threshold. Locally transmitted cases have decreased in all three provinces, but imported cases have been increasing. The study also identified knowledge gaps in vector distribution, insecticide resistance status, and drug usage.

CONCLUSIONS
Malaria elimination in South Africa is possible if certain criteria are met. Firstly, continued support for existing malaria control programs is crucial to sustain the progress made. Secondly, cross-border malaria control initiatives with neighboring countries must be encouraged and supported to reduce malaria in the region and prevent its importation into South Africa. Thirdly, urgent operational research is needed on vector distribution and insecticide resistance status. Lastly, surveillance systems must be improved to collect the necessary information for an elimination agenda.

title: The epidemiology of sexually transmitted co-infections in HIV-positive and HIV-negative African-Caribbean women in Toronto
text:
The frequency and distribution of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among African-Caribbean women in Canada, particularly those with HIV, have not been previously examined. To address this gap, we conducted a study in Toronto, recruiting women from a community health center based on their HIV status. Participants completed a socio-behavioral questionnaire using Audio Computer Assisted Self-Interview (ACASI) and provided samples for various STI tests.

A total of 126 HIV-positive and 291 HIV-negative women were recruited, with median ages of 40 and 31 years, respectively. We found that HIV-positive women had higher rates of active hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and lifetime exposure to HBV compared to HIV-negative women. They also reported a higher history of HBV vaccination. Classical STIs were rare in both groups, and the prevalence of bacterial vaginosis (BV) did not differ significantly between HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. However, HSV-2 infection was much more common in HIV-positive women compared to HIV-negative women. Vaginal HPV infection, particularly with high-risk oncogenic types, was also more prevalent in HIV-positive women.

In conclusion, classical STIs were uncommon among African-Caribbean women in this clinic-based population in Toronto. However, HSV-2 infection was more prevalent than previously reported in the general Canadian population and was strongly associated with HIV infection. Hepatitis B and HPV infections were also more common in HIV-positive women.

title: Characterization of Programmed Death-1 Homologue-1 (PD-1H) Expression and Function in Normal and HIV Infected Individuals
text: Persistent immune activation despite anti-retroviral therapy (ART) is the most significant indicator of disease progression in HIV infection. In individuals with HIV, monocyte/macrophages have been observed to spontaneously release cytokines, but the underlying mechanism and molecules involved remain unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that the excessive expression of a recently identified co-stimulatory molecule called PD1 homologue (PD-1H) in human monocyte/macrophages is enough to trigger the spontaneous release of multiple cytokines. This process relies on signaling through PD-1H, as deleting the cytoplasmic domain prevents cytokine secretion. We have observed this overexpression of PD-1H, along with spontaneous cytokine expression, in monocytes from individuals with chronic HIV infection. This phenomenon is associated with immune activation and a decrease in CD4 cells, but not viral load. Additionally, when PD-1H-overexpressing monocytes present antigens, it leads to an increased secretion of cytokines by HIV-specific T cells. These findings suggest that PD-1H may have a crucial role in regulating immune activation and the immune response in HIV infection.

title: A conserved mechanism for centromeric nucleosome recognition by centromere protein CENP-C.
text: The process of chromosome segregation during mitosis necessitates the formation of the kinetochore complex at the centromere. The assembly of the kinetochore relies on the specific recognition of the histone variant CENP-A in the centromeric nucleosome by centromere protein C (CENP-C). We have identified the factors that determine this recognition mechanism and have uncovered that CENP-C attaches to a hydrophobic region in the CENP-A tail and attaches to the acidic patch of histone H2A and H2B. Additionally, we have discovered that the more widely conserved CENP-C motif employs the same mechanism for recognizing the CENP-A nucleosome. Our findings demonstrate a conserved mechanism for recruiting proteins to centromeres and a mode of histone recognition in which an unordered peptide binds to the histone tail through hydrophobic interactions facilitated by nucleosome docking.

title: Chemical tools for biomolecular imaging.
text: Cell biology is being revolutionized by the ability to visualize biologically relevant molecules and activities within living cells. This transformation is turning cell biology into a truly quantitative science. However, despite remarkable achievements in certain areas, the majority of cellular processes remain hidden from view, even with our most powerful laser beams. To make further progress, we need not only better instrumentation but also the development of new fluorophores and fluorescent sensors that can specifically target these activities. In this review, we discuss recent strategies for creating such sensors, the techniques for attaching them to specific biomolecules, and their applications in solving various biological problems.

title: Reactive oxygen species, DNA damage, and error-prone repair: a model for genomic instability with progression in myeloid leukemia?
text: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a diverse group of disorders characterized by ineffective blood cell production and an increased risk of developing acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). The underlying molecular causes of MDS progression are not fully understood, but one important factor is the loss of genetic material (genomic instability). In our study, we used a two-step mouse model to investigate the progression of myeloid leukemia. By overexpressing mutant NRAS and BCL2 genes in mice, we observed a gradual increase in DNA damage, particularly in the form of double-strand breaks (DSB), and a higher frequency of error-prone repair through a process called nonhomologous end-joining. We also found that reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels increased as the disease progressed in these transgenic mice. Interestingly, we discovered that RAC1, a crucial component of the ROS-producing NADPH oxidase, is downstream of RAS and plays a role in ROS production in NRAS/BCL2 mice. To further investigate this, we treated the mice with an antioxidant called N-acetyl cysteine, which reduced or reversed DNA damage and error-prone repair in vivo. Our findings establish a connection between gene abnormalities, ongoing DNA damage, and increased errors in DNA repair during MDS progression. This provides a potential mechanism for the higher error rate in DNA repair observed in MDS patients. Based on these results, targeting the RAS/RAC pathways and reducing ROS production may be promising treatment strategies for MDS/AML in humans.

title: A link between inflammation and metastasis: serum amyloid A1 and A3 induce metastasis, and are targets of metastasis-inducing S100A4
text: The role of S100A4 in metastasis and chronic inflammation is not fully understood. However, our research has established a connection between inflammation and the progression of metastatic tumors that is dependent on S100A4. We have discovered that S100A4 regulates the transcription of serum amyloid A (SAA) proteins 1 and 3, which are acute-phase response proteins, through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB signaling. These SAA proteins then stimulate the transcription of RANTES, G-CSF, MMP2, MMP3, MMP9, and MMP13. Additionally, we have found that SAA proteins can stimulate their own transcription as well as the transcription of proinflammatory S100A8 and S100A9 proteins. Furthermore, SAA proteins enhance tumor cell adhesion to fibronectin and promote the migration and invasion of both human and mouse tumor cells. When S100A4 protein is injected intravenously, it induces the expression of SAA proteins and cytokines in a specific organ-dependent manner. In an animal model of breast cancer, the ectopic expression of SAA1 or SAA3 in tumor cells leads to widespread formation of metastases and a significant infiltration of immune cells. Moreover, the coordinated expression of S100A4 and SAA in tumor samples from colorectal carcinoma patients is associated with reduced overall survival. These findings demonstrate that SAA proteins play a crucial role in the metastasis-promoting functions of S100A4 and serve as a connection between inflammation and tumor progression.

title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and acetyl group accumulation during exercise after different diets.
text:
The study investigated the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDHa) and the accumulation of acetyl groups in human skeletal muscle during rest and exercise, following different diets. Five male participants cycled at 75% of their maximum oxygen uptake (VO2 max) until exhaustion. This was done after consuming a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD) for 3 days, and then again 1-2 weeks later after consuming a high-carbohydrate diet (HCD) for the same duration. 

The results showed that resting PDHa was lower after the LCD (0.20 +/- 0.04 mmol.min-1.kg wet wt-1) compared to the HCD (0.69 +/- 0.05 mmol.min-1.kg wet wt-1; P < 0.05). This decrease in PDHa coincided with higher levels of intramuscular acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, acetyl-CoA content, and acetylcarnitine content. During exercise, PDHa increased in both diet conditions, but at a slower rate in the LCD condition compared to the HCD condition (1.46 +/- 0.25 vs. 2.65 +/- 0.23 mmol.min-1.kg wet wt-1 at 16 minutes and 1.88 +/- 0.20 vs. 3.11 +/- 0.14 at the end of exercise; P < 0.05). 

During exercise, the levels of muscle acetyl-CoA and acetylcarnitine content, as well as the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, decreased in the LCD condition but increased in the HCD condition. The study found that under resting conditions, PDHa was influenced by the availability of fat or carbohydrate fuels, which affected the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio. However, during exercise, the activation of PDHa occurred independently of changes in the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, suggesting that other factors play a more significant role.

title: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential and its distinction from myelodysplastic syndromes.
text: Recent genetic studies on large populations have shown that as people age, they commonly acquire somatic mutations in their hematopoietic cells, leading to clonal expansion. This clonally restricted hematopoiesis is associated with a higher risk of developing myeloid or lymphoid neoplasia and increased mortality overall. However, it is important to note that not everyone who acquires clonal hematopoiesis will develop myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), which are characterized by low blood cell counts, abnormal cell morphology, and clonal hematopoiesis. In cases where somatic mutations drive clonal expansion without causing cytopenias or dysplastic hematopoiesis, it is referred to as clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP). This is similar to precursor states like monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, which are usually benign and do not progress to hematologic neoplasms. However, the presence of an MDS-associated somatic mutation in a patient with low blood cell counts but no other signs of MDS can create diagnostic uncertainty. In this article, we will discuss the nature and prevalence of CHIP, how it differs from MDS, and the current challenges in establishing diagnostic criteria for myeloid malignancies.

title: DNA Methylation mediated down-regulating of MicroRNA-33b and its role in gastric cancer
text: The discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs) has provided a valuable new tool for studying the mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment of human cancers. It is now recognized that the down-regulation of tumor suppressive miRNAs through CpG island hypermethylation is a common characteristic of cancer. In this study, we have found that the down-regulation of miR-33b is associated with the pM stage of gastric cancer (GC) patients. By introducing miR-33b into HGC-27 and MGC-803 cells, we observed a significant inhibition of cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, which may be attributed to miR-33b's targeting of the oncogene c-Myc. Additionally, we confirmed an increased level of methylation in the CpG island upstream of miR-33b in GC patients with down-regulated miR-33b using methylation-specific PCR (MSP) amplification. Furthermore, the reintroduction of miR-33b effectively suppressed tumorigenesis in GC cells in nude mice. In conclusion, miR-33b functions as a tumor suppressor, and the hypermethylation of the CpG island upstream of miR-33b is responsible for its down-regulation in gastric cancer.

title: Modulation of glucose metabolism in macrophages by products of nitric oxide synthase.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the impact of nitric oxide (NO) synthase (NOS) activity on glucose metabolism in rat resident peritoneal macrophages. The researchers examined the effects of NOS activity on glucose pathways in macrophages at rest and after stimulation with zymosan. They manipulated NOS activity by adjusting the L-arginine concentration in the culture media and using a specific inhibitor called NG-monomethyl-L-arginine. The researchers measured NOS activity using radiolabeled L-arginine.

The results showed that NOS activity was associated with increased glucose disappearance, glycolysis, and hexose monophosphate shunt activity. This aligns with the known inhibition of oxidative metabolism caused by NO production. NOS activity also led to a decrease in the flux of glucose and butyrate carbon through the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Furthermore, treatments that suppressed NOS activity enhanced the relative increase in glucose utilization following zymosan stimulation.

Overall, these findings indicate that NOS products significantly influence the characteristics of glucose metabolism in macrophages.

title: SOCS1/JAB is a negative regulator of LPS-induced macrophage activation.
text: The innate immune responses triggered by bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) through Toll-like receptor (TLR) 4 are regulated by the suppressor of cytokine-signaling-1 (SOCS1/JAB). In our study, we observed that LPS rapidly induces the expression of SOCS1, which in turn negatively regulates LPS signaling. We found that mice with reduced or absent SOCS1 expression, either with or without interferon-gamma (IFNgamma) deficiency, were more susceptible to the lethal effects of LPS compared to their wild-type counterparts. Macrophages lacking SOCS1 showed increased synthesis of NO(2)(-) and production of TNFalpha in response to LPS. Additionally, SOCS1-deficient cells exhibited a significant reduction in LPS tolerance, a protective mechanism against endotoxin shock. We also observed that SOCS1-deficient macrophages displayed enhanced I-kappaB and p38 phosphorylation upon LPS stimulation, while forced expression of SOCS1 suppressed NF-kappaB activation induced by LPS. These findings suggest that SOCS1 directly suppresses TLR4 signaling and modulates innate immunity.

title: Bacteria-triggered CD4+ T Regulatory Cells Suppress Helicobacter hepaticus–induced Colitis
text: Previous studies have shown that mice lacking interleukin (IL)-10, known as IL-10 knockout (KO) mice, develop colitis after being infected with Helicobacter hepaticus. In this study, we demonstrate that recombination activating gene (RAG) KO mice develop intestinal inflammation after receiving CD4+ T cells from IL-10 KO mice. Interestingly, transferring CD4+ T cells from H. hepaticus-infected wild-type (WT) mice, but not uninfected WT mice, prevents colitis in the RAG KO mice. The protective CD4+ cells are found in the CD45RBlow fraction and are present in both the CD25+ and CD25- subpopulations, with a higher frequency in the latter. The mechanism by which these CD45RBlow CD4+ cells prevent colitis involves IL-10, not transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, as blocking IL-10 with anti-IL-10R monoclonal antibody abolishes their protective effect. In vitro experiments show that CD45RBlow CD4+ cells from infected WT mice produce IL-10 and suppress interferon-γ production by IL-10 KO CD4+ cells in an H. hepaticus antigen-specific manner. These findings support the idea that H. hepaticus infection induces regulatory T cells in WT mice that protect against bacteria-induced colitis. This induction of regulatory T cells in response to gut flora may be a mechanism that safeguards healthy individuals from developing inflammatory bowel disease.

title: The NLRP12 Sensor Negatively Regulates Autoinflammatory Disease by Modulating Interleukin-4 Production in T Cells.
text: Mutations in the Nlrp12 gene, which belongs to the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor pyrin domain containing family, have been linked to periodic fever syndromes and atopic dermatitis in humans. In this study, we have demonstrated that NLRP12 plays a crucial role in suppressing pathogenic T cell responses. When Nlrp12(-/-) mice were immunized with antigens, they exhibited hyperinflammatory T cell responses. Additionally, transferring CD4(+)CD45RB(hi)Nlrp12(-/-) T cells into immunodeficient mice resulted in more severe colitis and atopic dermatitis. Interestingly, NLRP12 deficiency did not lead to worsened ascending paralysis in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), but instead, Nlrp12(-/-) mice developed atypical neuroinflammatory symptoms such as ataxia and loss of balance. The enhanced production of interleukin-4 (IL-4) by T cells promoted the development of atypical EAE disease in Nlrp12(-/-) mice. These findings reveal an unexpected role for NLRP12 as a negative regulator of T-cell-mediated immunity and highlight altered NF-κB regulation and IL-4 production as important factors in NLRP12-associated diseases.

title: Shc coordinates signals from intercellular junctions and integrins to regulate flow-induced inflammation
text: Atherosclerotic plaques form in areas of blood vessels linked to chronic inflammation caused by disrupted flow patterns. The process of endothelial phenotype modulation by flow involves multiple mechanotransduction pathways, but its exact mechanism remains unclear. Our study reveals that the adaptor protein Shc becomes activated and associates with both cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions in response to flow. This activation of Shc relies on the tyrosine kinases vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and Src. The association between Shc activation and vascular endothelial cadherin (VE-cadherin) is not influenced by the extracellular matrix. However, Shc binding to integrins requires VE-cadherin and is limited to specific matrices. Silencing Shc leads to a decrease in both matrix-independent and matrix-dependent signals. Additionally, Shc plays a role in regulating flow-induced inflammatory signaling by activating nuclear factor kappaB-dependent signals that contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. In vivo, Shc is activated in regions of arteries prone to atherosclerosis, and its activation correlates with the presence of atherosclerotic plaques. Our findings support a model in which Shc coordinates signals from both cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions to initiate flow-induced inflammatory signaling.

title: SIRT1 Redistribution on Chromatin Promotes Genomic Stability but Alters Gene Expression during Aging
text: Eukaryotic aging is characterized by genomic instability and changes in gene expression. In yeast, the histone deacetylase Sir2 plays a role in silencing transcription and stabilizing repetitive DNA. However, as yeast ages or in response to DNA damage, the Sir complex relocates to areas of genomic instability. This leads to the activation of genes that cause sterility, a hallmark of yeast aging. Our research using embryonic stem cells demonstrates that the mammalian counterpart of Sir2, SIRT1, also represses repetitive DNA and a diverse set of genes throughout the mouse genome. When DNA damage occurs, SIRT1 dissociates from these regions and moves to the sites of DNA breaks to facilitate repair. This results in changes in gene expression that resemble those observed in the aging mouse brain. Increased expression of SIRT1 promotes survival in a mouse model with genomic instability and suppresses age-related changes in gene expression. Therefore, the redistribution of SIRT1 and other chromatin-modifying proteins in response to DNA damage may be a conserved mechanism of aging in eukaryotes.

title: Bariatric Surgery in the United Kingdom: A Cohort Study of Weight Loss and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Clinical Care.
text:
The prevalence of bariatric surgery as a treatment for obesity is increasing. However, there is a lack of comprehensive evidence regarding the long-term effects of contemporary surgery on various clinical outcomes in large populations treated in routine clinical practice. This study aimed to examine the association between bariatric surgery, weight, body mass index (BMI), and obesity-related co-morbidities. 

The study utilized data from the United Kingdom Clinical Practice Research Datalink and included 3,882 patients who underwent bariatric surgery on or before December 31, 2014. These patients were matched by propensity score to 3,882 obese patients without surgery. The main outcome measures included changes in weight and BMI over a 4-year period, incident diagnoses of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, fractures, obstructive sleep apnea, and cancer, as well as mortality and resolution of hypertension and T2DM. 

Weight measurements were available for different time intervals post-procedure, with the first four months showing rapid weight loss at a rate of 4.98 kg/month. Slower weight loss was sustained throughout the 4-year period. Gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy were associated with greater initial weight reduction compared to gastric banding. 

Bariatric surgery demonstrated protective effects for incident T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnea. Strong associations were found between bariatric surgery and the resolution of T2DM and hypertension. However, no association was found between bariatric surgery and fractures, cancer, or stroke. The study did not find a protective association between bariatric surgery and mortality. 

It is important to note that the data used in this study were recorded for primary care management and may be subject to inaccuracies, potentially leading to underestimates of the true effects. 

In conclusion, bariatric surgery as performed in the UK healthcare system leads to significant and sustained weight loss over a 4-year period. This weight loss is accompanied by substantial improvements in pre-existing T2DM and hypertension, as well as a reduced risk of incident T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnea. Expanding access to bariatric surgery could have significant health benefits for individuals with morbid obesity.

title: Notch signalling acts in postmitotic avian myogenic cells to control MyoD activation.
text: During the process of muscle differentiation in Drosophila, Notch signalling plays a role at various stages. In vertebrates, it has been observed that Notch activation inhibits the activation of MyoD and muscle differentiation in vitro, indicating that this pathway may be involved in maintaining cells in a proliferative state without differentiation. This study focuses on investigating the role of Notch signalling in chick myogenesis in vivo. The researchers first establish that the Notch1 receptor is expressed in postmitotic cells of the myotome, while the Notch ligands Delta1 and Serrate2 are found in specific subsets of differentiating myogenic cells, suggesting that they can signal to Notch1 during myogenic differentiation. The expression of MyoD and Myf5 during avian myogenesis is also reexamined, and it is observed that Myf5 is expressed earlier than MyoD, consistent with previous findings in mice. The researchers then demonstrate that introducing the Notch ligand Delta1 during early myogenesis using a retroviral system does not affect the expression of early myogenic markers Pax3 and Myf5, but significantly reduces the expression of MyoD in infected somites. Although the overexpression of Delta1 leads to the absence of differentiated muscles, further examination of the infected embryos reveals that the initial formation of a myotome is not hindered, indicating that the exit from the cell cycle has not been blocked. These findings suggest that Notch signalling plays a role in controlling a crucial step of muscle differentiation in postmitotic myogenic cells.

title: Hepatitis C virus infection in a large cohort of homosexually active men: independent associations with HIV-1 infection and injecting drug use but not sexual behaviour.
text: The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence and risk factors for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in a group of homosexually active men, with a focus on assessing sexual transmission. The study design involved testing for HCV antibody in stored sera from a cohort of men between 1984 and 1989, and analyzing risk factors using questionnaire data from both HCV positive and negative subjects. The study included 1038 homosexually active men who were part of a larger study on identifying risk factors for AIDS. These men were recruited from primary care and sexually transmissible disease services in central Sydney. The main outcome measures were the prevalence of HCV antibody and its association with HIV-1 infection, other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), number of sexual partners, sexual practices, and recreational drug use. The results showed that 7.6% of the subjects tested were seropositive for HCV antibody. In univariate analysis, HCV infection was significantly associated with injecting drug use (IDU), HIV infection, and a self-reported history of syphilis, anogenital herpes, gonorrhea, and hepatitis B. In case control analysis, similar sexual behaviors were reported by HCV positive and negative subjects, except that HCV negative subjects more frequently reported engaging in certain unprotected sexual practices. Multiple logistic regression analyses showed that only HIV-1 infection and recent IDU were significantly associated with the presence of HCV antibody. The study concluded that IDU was the main behavioral risk factor for HCV infection, and if sexual transmission did occur, it may have been facilitated by concurrent HIV-1 infection.

title: Analysis of human cytomegalovirus-encoded microRNA activity during infection.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are present in a wide range of organisms, including plants and animals, and play a crucial role in regulating gene expression after transcription. Virally encoded miRNAs are unique because they have the potential to target both viral and host genes. Our previous research has shown that a miRNA called miR-UL112, encoded by the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), can decrease the expression of a host immune gene called MICB. Interestingly, this same miRNA also reduces the expression of immediate-early viral genes, leading to decreased viral replication and titers when it is overexpressed. The specific targets and functions of most viral miRNAs are still unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that miR-UL112 also targets a gene called UL114, and we provide evidence that the reduction of UL114 by miR-UL112 decreases its activity as uracil DNA glycosylase, but has only a minimal impact on virus growth. Additionally, we show that two other HCMV-encoded miRNAs, miR-US25-1 and miR-US25-2, not only reduce the replication and DNA synthesis of HCMV, but also of other viruses. This suggests that these two miRNAs target cellular genes that are essential for virus growth. Therefore, we propose that in addition to miR-UL112, these two additional HCMV miRNAs also play a role in controlling the virus's life cycle.

title: Anti-obesity drugs: past, present and future
text: The perfect drug for combating obesity would result in long-term weight loss with minimal side effects. However, the complex nature of energy regulation, which overlaps with various physiological functions and is influenced by social, hedonic, and psychological factors, has made it difficult to develop effective pharmacological interventions. Many attempts to discover anti-obesity drugs have been unsuccessful, with some even being withdrawn due to unforeseen adverse effects. While targeting metabolic tissues like adipocytes, liver, and skeletal muscle has shown promise in preclinical studies, no drugs in this category have made it to clinical development. Recent advancements in understanding the signaling of hunger and satiety from the gastrointestinal tract, as well as the homeostatic mechanisms related to leptin and its pathways in the hypothalamus, have opened up new possibilities. However, it remains uncertain whether these drugs will meet the strict regulatory requirements for anti-obesity drug approval. GLP-1 receptor agonists have already proven successful in treating diabetes and may pave the way for other anti-obesity agents due to their ability to lower body weight in humans. To achieve the same level of weight control as surgical interventions, a new approach is needed. In other therapeutic areas like diabetes and hypertension, combining lower doses of multiple agents that target different pathways often yields better results than focusing on a single pathway. Some combination approaches using peptides and small molecules are currently being tested in clinical trials, but significant challenges remain. In the future, this polytherapeutic strategy could potentially rival surgery in terms of effectiveness, safety, and sustainability of weight loss.

title: Cytochemical Analysis of Pollen Development in Wild-Type Arabidopsis and a Male-Sterile Mutant.
text: The process of microsporogenesis was analyzed in both wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana and the nuclear male-sterile mutant BM3 using cytochemical staining. The mutant BM3 lacks adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme involved in the purine salvage pathway that converts adenine to AMP. In the mutant, pollen development started to deviate from the wild type right after meiosis, when the tetrads of microspores were released from their callose walls. The first sign of abnormal pollen development in the mutant was a darker staining of the microspore wall, indicating incomplete synthesis of the intine. Vacuole formation in the mutant was delayed and irregular, and most of the mutant microspores failed to undergo mitotic divisions. The activities of alcohol dehydrogenase and esterases decreased in the mutant shortly after meiosis and were undetectable in mature pollen grains. RNA accumulation was also reduced. These findings are discussed in relation to the potential role(s) of adenine salvage in pollen development.

title: Prevalence, risk factors, and uptake of interventions for sexually transmitted infections in Britain: findings from the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
text:
The aim of this study was to gather population-based data on the prevalence, risk distribution, and intervention uptake for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in Britain. The study, known as the third National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-3), was conducted between September 6, 2010, and August 31, 2012. A total of 15,162 men and women aged 16-74 years were included in the survey, which involved face-to-face and self-completion questionnaires. Urine samples were collected from a subset of participants aged 16-44 years who reported having at least one sexual partner in their lifetime. The samples were tested for Chlamydia trachomatis, type-specific human papillomavirus (HPV), Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV antibody. The study examined the prevalence of these infections, as well as the uptake of interventions, and compared the findings to previous surveys conducted in 1990-91 (Natsal-1) and 1999-2001 (Natsal-2). 

Out of the 8,047 participants invited to provide a urine sample, 4,828 (60%) agreed. After excluding 278 samples, the final analysis included 4,550 (94%) participants with STI test results. The prevalence of Chlamydia was 1.5% in women and 1.1% in men. Among individuals aged 16-24 years, the prevalence was higher, with 3.1% in women and 2.3% in men. Risk factors for Chlamydia included area-level deprivation and having a higher number of partners, particularly without using condoms. Surprisingly, a significant proportion of Chlamydia cases (60.4% in women and 43.3% in men) occurred in individuals who had only one partner in the past year. Among sexually active 16-24-year-olds, 54.2% of women and 34.6% of men reported testing for Chlamydia in the past year, with higher testing rates among those with more partners. The prevalence of high-risk HPV was 15.9% in women, similar to the findings in Natsal-2. The coverage of HPV catch-up vaccination was 61.5%. The prevalence of HPV types 16 and 18 in women aged 18-20 years was lower in Natsal-3 compared to Natsal-2. Gonorrhoea and HIV were uncommon, with less than 0.1% prevalence in women and men for gonorrhoea, and 0.1% prevalence in women and 0.2% in men for HIV. These infections were limited to participants with recognized high-risk factors. Since Natsal-2, there has been a significant increase in attendance at sexual health clinics and HIV testing in the past 5 years. However, STIs continue to persist in individuals who do not access these services. The findings of this study provide valuable information for future sexual health interventions and services. The study was funded by grants from the UK Medical Research Council and the Wellcome Trust, with support from the Economic and Social Research Council and the Department of Health.

title: Cancer Pharmacogenomics and Pharmacoepidemiology: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation
text: Advancements in genomic research have recently revealed the significant role of genomic factors in predicting how individuals respond to cancer treatments. Scientists in the fields of cancer pharmacogenomics and pharmacoepidemiology aim to understand the reasons behind the varying responses to drug therapy, including both adverse effects and treatment effectiveness. To determine the research priorities and necessary resources and infrastructure to advance these fields, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) organized a workshop called "Cancer Pharmacogenomics: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation" on July 21, 2009, in Bethesda, MD. In this article, we summarize and discuss five science-based recommendations and four infrastructure-based recommendations that emerged from the discussions during this workshop. Key recommendations include: 1) supporting the regular collection of germline and tumor biospecimens in NCI-sponsored clinical trials and certain observational and population-based studies; 2) integrating pharmacogenomic markers into clinical trials; 3) addressing the ethical, legal, social, and biospecimen- and data-sharing implications of pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic research; and 4) establishing collaborations between NCI, other federal agencies, and industry. These recommendations will facilitate the discovery and validation of clinical, sociodemographic, lifestyle, and genomic markers associated with cancer treatment response and adverse events. Furthermore, they will enhance the speed and efficiency with which new pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic information is translated into clinical practice.

title: Differential transcription of the orphan receptor RORbeta in nuclear extracts derived from Neuro2A and HeLa cells.
text:
The superfamily of nuclear receptors is a crucial model system for studying the process of productive transcription. These receptors primarily function as ligand-controlled transcription factors. However, there are several "orphan" nuclear receptors that have been discovered without any identified ligands. The regulation of transcription by these orphan receptors remains largely unknown. 

In this study, we have examined the biochemical and transcriptional properties of the orphan nuclear receptor RORbeta (NR1F2), which is expressed in neurons. We compared these properties with the retinoic acid receptor heterodimer RXRalpha-RARalpha (NR2B1-NR1B1) and Gal-VP16 in vitro. While RORbeta binds to its DNA-binding sites with relatively low affinity, it effectively directs transcription in nuclear extracts derived from a neuronal cell line called Neuro2A. However, it does not have the same transcriptional activity in nuclear extracts from non-neuronal HeLa cells. 

On the other hand, RXRalpha-RARalpha and the acidic transcription factor Gal-VP16 support transcription equally efficiently in both Neuro2A and HeLa nuclear extracts. These findings suggest that members of the NR1 subfamily of nuclear receptors require different (co)factors for transactivation.

title: Estrogens, progestogens, normal breast cell proliferation, and breast cancer risk.
text: Epidemiological studies indicate that ovarian hormones play a role in the development of breast cancer at all stages. The risk of breast cancer is reduced by early menopause and premenopausal obesity, while postmenopausal obesity and menopausal estrogen replacement therapy increase the risk. However, combined oral contraceptives and Depo-Provera do not lower the risk. It seems that estrogens and progestogens work together with proto-oncogenes and growth factors to influence breast cell proliferation and the development of breast cancer. Animal studies suggest that estrogen causes division of interlobular ductal cells, while progesterone leads to increased division of terminal duct lobular unit cells during the luteal phase. Most breast carcinomas originate from these terminal duct lobular unit cells, which multiply during pregnancy and the luteal phase. However, there is significant variation among individuals. Although no studies have compared breast cell division rates with serum hormone concentrations, the peak of mitosis occurs approximately three days before cell death in the late luteal and early follicular phases. Other research suggests a link between breast stem cell proliferation and breast cancer development. Endocrine therapy reduces mitotic activity, indicating the presence of estrogen and progesterone receptors in breast cancers. All estrogen-dependent breast cancer cell lines are also progesterone-dependent, and progesterone can block the estrogen-dependent cell lines that resemble endometrial cells. The findings from various studies on breast cell proliferation and breast cancer are not clear, and further research is needed to identify a molecular explanation that can help us understand these different findings.

title: Analysis of the interaction of primate retroviruses with the human RNA interference machinery.
text: The issue of whether retroviruses, such as HIV-1, interact with the cellular RNA interference system has been a subject of debate. In this study, we provide evidence that both HIV-1 and HTLV-1 do not produce significant levels of small interfering RNAs or microRNAs in persistently infected T cells. Additionally, we show that the retroviral nuclear transcription factors HIV-1 Tat and HTLV-1 Tax, as well as the Tas transactivator from primate foamy virus, do not inhibit RNA interference in human cells. Furthermore, the presence of HIV-1 Tat at physiological levels does not globally suppress microRNA production or expression in infected human cells. These findings suggest that HIV-1 and HTLV-1 do not induce the production of viral small interfering RNAs or microRNAs, nor do they suppress the cellular RNA interference system in infected cells.

title: Impact of diabetes on long-term prognosis in patients with unstable angina and non-Q-wave myocardial infarction: results of the OASIS (Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes) Registry.
text:
BACKGROUND
Unstable coronary artery disease is the primary cause of admission to a coronary care unit, but the long-term prognosis for patients with this condition is unknown. This is particularly true for patients with diabetes mellitus, who have a high risk of complications and death following an acute myocardial infarction.

METHODS AND RESULTS
Data from the Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes (OASIS) registry, collected from six different countries, were analyzed to determine the two-year prognosis of diabetic and nondiabetic patients hospitalized with unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction. Out of 8,013 registry patients, 1,718 (21%) had diabetes. Diabetic patients had a higher rate of coronary bypass surgery compared to nondiabetic patients (23% versus 20%, P:<0.001), but similar rates of catheterization and angioplasty. Diabetes was an independent predictor of mortality (relative risk [RR], 1.57; 95% CI, 1.38 to 1.81; P:<0.001), as well as cardiovascular death, new myocardial infarction, stroke, and new congestive heart failure. Additionally, women had a significantly higher risk than men (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.60 to 2.44; and RR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.56, respectively), compared to their nondiabetic counterparts. Interestingly, diabetic patients without prior cardiovascular disease had the same event rates for all outcomes as nondiabetic patients with previous vascular disease.

CONCLUSIONS
Hospitalization for unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction is associated with a high two-year risk of complications and death, especially for patients with diabetes. Diabetic patients without previous cardiovascular disease have the same long-term risk as nondiabetic patients with established cardiovascular disease after being hospitalized for unstable coronary artery disease.

title: Strain improvement by metabolic engineering: lysine production as a case study for systems biology.
text: The main objective of systems biology is to understand cell function and physiology by integrating genomic and physiological data. This approach has been widely used in the past and is crucial for analyzing metabolic flux, controlling pathways, and advancing metabolic engineering. For example, researchers have applied these tools to enhance the production of lysine in Corynebacterium glutamicum strains. By systematically studying the organism's physiology, they were able to identify specific metabolic targets and significantly improve product yield and productivity. This case study can serve as a blueprint for developing systems biology tools to effectively utilize extensive transcriptional and physiological data at a cellular and genome-wide level.

title: Cognitive behavioral therapy vs zopiclone for treatment of chronic primary insomnia in older adults: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Insomnia is a common problem among older adults and can have negative effects on their health, social life, and mental well-being. Previous studies have shown that both psychological therapy and medication can be helpful in treating insomnia, but there is a lack of research comparing the effectiveness of these treatments in a controlled manner. 

The objective of this study was to investigate the short- and long-term effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication in older adults with chronic primary insomnia. The study was conducted between January 2004 and December 2005 at a university-based outpatient clinic in Norway. 

A total of 46 adults (mean age 60.8 years, 22 women) with chronic primary insomnia participated in the study. They were randomly assigned to receive either CBT (which included various techniques such as sleep hygiene, sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, and relaxation), sleep medication (7.5-mg zopiclone each night), or a placebo medication. The treatment duration for all groups was 6 weeks, and the effects of the active treatments were assessed again after 6 months. 

The main outcome measures were determined using ambulant clinical polysomnographic data and sleep diaries. These measures included total wake time, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and slow-wave sleep (which was only assessed using polysomnography). 

The results showed that CBT led to better short- and long-term outcomes compared to zopiclone on 3 out of 4 outcome measures. Zopiclone did not differ significantly from the placebo for most outcomes. Participants who received CBT improved their sleep efficiency from 81.4% before treatment to 90.1% at the 6-month follow-up, while the zopiclone group saw a decrease from 82.3% to 81.9%. The CBT group also spent more time in slow-wave sleep and less time awake during the night compared to the other groups. Total sleep time was similar in all three groups, but at the 6-month mark, patients who received CBT had better sleep efficiency according to polysomnography compared to those taking zopiclone. 

In conclusion, these findings suggest that CBT-based interventions are more effective than zopiclone treatment for managing insomnia in older adults, both in the short- and long-term. The study was registered on clinicaltrials.gov with the identifier NCT00295386.

title: Local changes in lipid environment of TCR microclusters regulate membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain
text: The T cell receptor's CD3ε and ζ cytoplasmic domains bind to the inner layer of the plasma membrane (PM). A previous nuclear magnetic resonance structure revealed that both tyrosines of the CD3ε immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif are present in the bilayer. It has been previously demonstrated that electrostatic interactions between acidic phospholipids and clusters of basic CD3ε residues are crucial for the binding of CD3ε and ζ to the membrane. Phosphatidylserine (PS), the most abundant negatively charged lipid on the inner layer of the PM, significantly contributes to the membrane binding of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain. In this study, we demonstrate that the triggering of the T cell receptor by peptide-MHC complexes leads to the detachment of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain from the plasma membrane. This detachment is accompanied by a significant decrease in negative charge and available PS in TCR microclusters. Interestingly, these changes in lipid composition within TCR microclusters occur even when TCR signaling is blocked with a Src kinase inhibitor. Consequently, local alterations in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters allow for accessibility of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain during the early stages of T cell activation.

title: Humans and great apes share a large frontal cortex
text: The exceptional cognitive abilities of humans are often believed to be a result of the human frontal lobe undergoing a significant enlargement throughout evolution. This belief is primarily based on comparing the brains of humans with other primates, while excluding most great apes. To investigate this further, we conducted a study using magnetic resonance imaging to compare the size of the frontal cortices in various primate species, including all living hominoids. Surprisingly, we found that the frontal cortices of humans were not disproportionately larger than those of the great apes. Instead, we propose that the unique cognitive abilities associated with a frontal advantage may be attributed to differences in specific cortical areas and a more intricate interconnectivity. These factors do not necessitate an increase in the overall relative size of the frontal lobe during the evolution of hominids.

title: Virus-Plus-Susceptibility Gene Interaction Determines Crohn's Disease Gene Atg16L1 Phenotypes in Intestine
text: The reason why only a small number of individuals with common risk alleles for disease susceptibility genes develop the disease is not clear. However, our study shows that a specific virus infection, combined with a mutation in the Crohn's disease susceptibility gene Atg16L1, can cause intestinal problems in mice. This interaction between the virus and susceptibility gene leads to abnormalities in granule packaging and unique gene expression patterns in Paneth cells. Additionally, the response to injury caused by a harmful substance called dextran sodium sulfate is altered in a way that resembles aspects of Crohn's disease. These disease-like symptoms triggered by the virus-susceptibility gene interaction rely on the presence of TNFalpha and IFNgamma, and can be prevented by treatment with broad spectrum antibiotics. Therefore, we present a specific example of how a combination of a virus, susceptibility gene, environmental factors, and commensal bacteria can determine the characteristics of individuals with common risk alleles for inflammatory diseases.

title: CaMKII Triggers the Diffusional Trapping of Surface AMPARs through Phosphorylation of Stargazin
text: The synaptic recruitment of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) during development and plasticity is critically dependent on the Ca(2+)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII). However, the specific mechanism behind this process remains unknown. Our study utilized single-particle tracking of AMPARs to investigate this mechanism. We discovered that the activation of CaMKII and its translocation to the postsynaptic region lead to the trapping of diffusing AMPARs at the synapse. This immobilization of AMPARs requires the phosphorylation of the auxiliary subunit Stargazin and its binding to PDZ domain scaffolds. It is not influenced by the PDZ binding domain of the GluA1 AMPAR subunit or its phosphorylation at Ser831. Furthermore, the CaMKII-dependent immobilization of AMPARs plays a role in regulating short-term plasticity. Therefore, the NMDA-dependent influx of Ca(2+) in the postsynaptic region triggers a decrease in the diffusional exchange of AMPARs at synapses, which is dependent on CaMKII and Stargazin, ultimately controlling synaptic function.

title: Epigenetics in diabetic nephropathy, immunity and metabolism
text:
The epigenome is a complex realm that can be both enlightening and perplexing. By navigating this delicate balance, we can uncover a captivating layer of transcription control. While the genetic code serves as the foundation for encoding information into proteins, there exists another set of rules governing the interpretation of chemical information above the genome level. These epigenetic modifications reveal a diverse and regulated aspect of the genetic code, capable of transiently altering genetic transcription in various ways, from short-term to long-term changes.

Although this complexity grants us exquisite control, it also presents a formidable challenge when attempting to decipher the mechanisms behind complex diseases. Fortunately, recent advancements in technology and computation have allowed for unbiased acquisition of epigenomic patterns, enhancing our understanding of the intricate chromatin landscape. To unravel the distinct chromatin signatures associated with diabetic complications, it is crucial to identify the true physiological targets of regulatory proteins. These proteins include reader proteins that recognize specific chemical moieties, writer proteins that deposit them, and eraser proteins that remove them.

But how do this diverse group of proteins regulate the epigenomic landscape in the context of diabetes? Drawing from a vast array of experimental and clinical studies, this review provides an overview of the current understanding and explores the chromatin-dependent mechanisms implicated in diabetic complications, with a particular focus on diabetic nephropathy. We propose the existence of a codified signature within the diabetic epigenome and highlight potential candidates for chemical modification. Additionally, we delve into future strategies for pharmacologically controlling epigenetic marks, aiming to expedite and refine the search for clinically relevant discoveries. Finally, we address the challenges associated with therapeutic approaches targeting epigenetic pathways.

title: Drinking pattern and mortality: the Italian Risk Factor and Life Expectancy pooling project.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to investigate the correlation between drinking patterns (specifically, drinking with or without meals) and the risk of all-cause and specific-cause mortality.

METHODS: This study utilized data from the Risk Factors and Life Expectancy Study, which is a compilation of various epidemiological studies conducted in Italy. The study included 8,647 men and 6,521 women between the ages of 30 and 59 who were free of cardiovascular disease at the start of the study. Participants were followed for an average of 7 years to track mortality rates from all causes, cardiovascular diseases, and noncardiovascular diseases.

RESULTS: The findings revealed that individuals who consumed wine outside of meals had higher death rates from all causes, noncardiovascular diseases, and cancer compared to those who consumed wine with meals. This association remained significant even after accounting for baseline cardiovascular disease risk factors and the amount of alcohol consumed. Additionally, this relationship appeared to be stronger in women than in men.

CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that drinking patterns play a crucial role in determining health outcomes, and therefore, it is important to consider this aspect of alcohol use. Previous studies on the relationship between alcohol consumption and disease have had limitations, primarily due to the lack of comprehensive information on alcohol consumption. This study aimed to address this limitation by focusing on one aspect of drinking pattern (drinking wine outside meals) and its impact on mortality in a large cohort of men and women.

title: Pointing in the right direction: new developments in the field of planar cell polarity
text: Planar cell polarity (PCP) is evident in various developmental processes that entail the coordinated movement of cells and the organization of tissues. Disruption of PCP can result in significant developmental abnormalities. Recent research conducted on flies and vertebrates has uncovered novel roles and signaling components associated with PCP, leading to the proposal of new mechanistic models. Nevertheless, despite these advancements, the quest for simplified principles of comprehension persists, as there are still significant uncertainties regarding the underlying mechanisms, presenting formidable challenges.

title: ADAR1 Forms a Complex with Dicer to Promote MicroRNA Processing and RNA-Induced Gene Silencing
text: The focus of this study was to examine the relationship between RNA editing and RNA interference (RNAi) in the context of Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs). ADARs are enzymes that convert adenosine residues to inosine in double-stranded RNAs. Our findings reveal that ADAR1 interacts with Dicer, a key component of the RNAi machinery, through direct protein-protein interaction. This interaction has significant implications, as ADAR1 enhances the rate at which pre-microRNA (miRNA) is cleaved by Dicer (referred to as Vmax) and facilitates the loading of miRNA onto RNA-induced silencing complexes. These findings highlight a novel role for ADAR1 in miRNA processing and RNAi mechanisms. ADAR1 distinguishes its functions in RNA editing and RNAi by forming either ADAR1/ADAR1 homodimer or Dicer/ADAR1 heterodimer complexes, respectively. As expected, the absence of ADAR1 in mouse embryos (ADAR1(-/-)) leads to a global inhibition of miRNA expression. Consequently, this alteration in miRNA expression affects the regulation of target genes and potentially contributes to the lethal phenotype observed in these embryos.

title: Interchangeability of Biosimilars: A European Perspective
text: In the EU, many popular biological medicinal products, known as 'blockbusters', are facing competition from similar products called biosimilars. Biosimilars are based on the concept of comparability, which has been successfully used for many years to ensure that a biological product remains similar before and after manufacturing changes. The past decade has shown that even complex biotechnology-derived proteins can be successfully replicated as biosimilars. Since most top-selling biologicals are used for long-term treatment, there has been a lot of discussion about whether a biosimilar can be used interchangeably with its reference product, with concerns about potential immune reactions. In this article, we examine the theoretical basis for the perceived risks of switching between a biosimilar and its reference product, as well as the available data on such switches. Our conclusion is that switching between comparable versions of the same active substance, approved in accordance with EU regulations, is not expected to cause or worsen immune reactions. Based on current knowledge, it is unlikely and challenging to prove that two products, comparable at a population level, would have different safety or effectiveness in individual patients when switching between them. Therefore, we conclude that biosimilars licensed in the EU are interchangeable.

title: Exome sequencing identifies somatic gain-of-function PPM1D mutations in brainstem gliomas
text: Brainstem and thalamic gliomas are highly destructive tumors that present significant challenges for surgical removal. In order to gain insight into the genetic and epigenetic characteristics of these tumors, we conducted exomic sequencing on 14 brainstem gliomas (BSGs) and 12 thalamic gliomas. Additionally, we performed targeted mutational analysis on an additional 24 tumors of this nature, as well as genome-wide methylation profiling on 45 gliomas. Through this comprehensive study, we made a significant discovery: 37.5% of the BSGs with hallmark H3F3A mutations, which encode p. Lys27Met substitutions, exhibited tumor-specific mutations in PPM1D. PPM1D encodes wild-type p53-induced protein phosphatase 1D (WIP1). Notably, these PPM1D mutations were found to be mutually exclusive with TP53 mutations in BSG and were shown to attenuate p53 activation in vitro. The PPM1D mutations observed were truncating alterations in exon 6, which enhanced the ability of PPM1D to suppress the activation of CHK2, a DNA damage response checkpoint protein. These findings establish PPM1D as a frequently targeted gene for somatic mutation and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target in brainstem gliomas.

title: Crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing the variant histone H2A.Z
text: The presence of the essential histone variant H2A.Z in nucleosomes has been linked to the activation of transcription in chromatin. H2A.Z, along with other histone variants, may create distinct chromosomal domains, but the exact molecular mechanism of their function remains largely unknown. In this study, we present the crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing H2A.Z at a resolution of 2.6 Å. The overall structure is similar to a previously reported nucleosome structure containing major histone proteins, but there are localized changes that subtly destabilize the interaction between the (H2A.Z-H2B) dimer and the (H3-H4)2 tetramer. Additionally, H2A.Z nucleosomes exhibit an altered surface that includes a metal ion. This modified surface could potentially lead to changes in higher order chromatin structure and/or facilitate the binding of specific nuclear proteins to H2A.Z. Lastly, the incorporation of both H2A.Z and H2A within the same nucleosome is unlikely due to significant alterations in the interface between the two H2A.Z-H2B dimers.

title: Dendritic Cell KLF2 Expression Regulates T Cell Activation and Proatherogenic Immune Responses.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in regulating inflammation in various diseases, including atherosclerosis. However, we still have limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms through which DCs either mitigate or promote inflammatory pathogenesis. Previous research has shown that the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) has an important anti-inflammatory function in regulating the activation of different cell types involved in the development of atherosclerotic lesions, such as endothelial cells, macrophages, and T cells. To investigate the role of KLF2 in DC activation, function, and inflammation control in the context of hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis, we used a mouse model with a gene knockout of KLF2 specifically in CD11c-expressing DCs. Our findings revealed that the absence of KLF2 led to increased expression of costimulatory molecules CD40 and CD86 on the surface of DCs, resulting in enhanced T cell proliferation and apoptosis. Furthermore, when we transplanted bone marrow from mice with KLF2-deficient DCs into Ldlr-/- mice, we observed aggravated atherosclerosis compared to control mice. This aggravation was likely due to heightened vascular inflammation, as evidenced by increased presence of DCs within lesions, enhanced T cell activation and cytokine production, and increased cell death in atherosclerotic lesions. In summary, our data suggest that KLF2 regulates the level of DC activation, thereby influencing the intensity of proatherogenic T cell responses.

title: Targeting tumor-necrosis factor receptor pathways for tumor immunotherapy
text: The field of tumor immunotherapy is rapidly expanding due to the success of ipilimumab and the potential of programmed death-1 pathway-targeted agents. New targets for clinical development in this field include certain members of the tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) family. By using agonist antibodies to these co-stimulatory molecules, both T and B cells can be targeted, leading to the modulation of T-cell activation and the enhancement of immune responses. Preclinical data conducted in vitro and in vivo have provided a foundation for the ongoing development of 4-1BB, OX40, glucocorticoid-induced TNFR-related gene, herpes virus entry mediator, and CD27 as potential therapies for cancer patients. This review aims to summarize the immune response to tumors, examine preclinical and early clinical data on specific TNFR family members, address potential challenges in translation, and propose combination therapies that could induce long-lasting antitumor responses.

title: Plasma soluble corin in patients with heart failure.
text:
BACKGROUND: Corin, a transmembrane protease responsible for processing natriuretic peptides in the heart, is shed from the cell surface like many other membrane proteins.

METHODS AND RESULTS: In this study, we collected plasma samples from healthy individuals and patients with heart failure (HF) and acute myocardial infarction. We used an ELISA method to measure soluble corin levels in the plasma. Among the healthy adults (n=198), the average plasma corin level was 690 pg/mL (SD, 260 pg/mL), and there were no significant differences in corin levels among different age groups. However, in patients with HF (n=291), the plasma corin levels were significantly lower compared to healthy controls (365 pg/mL [SD, 259]; P<0.001). The reduction in plasma corin levels appeared to be correlated with the severity of HF. Among patients in New York Heart Association classes II, III, and IV, the plasma corin levels were 450 pg/mL (SD, 281 pg/mL; n=69), 377 pg/mL (SD, 270 pg/mL; n=132), and 282 pg/mL (SD, 194 pg/mL; n=90), respectively (P<0.001 class II vs class IV; P<0.05 class III vs class IV). On the other hand, the plasma corin levels in patients with acute myocardial infarction (n=73) were similar to those of healthy controls (678 pg/mL [SD, 285 pg/mL]; P>0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Soluble corin was found in human plasma, and its levels were significantly reduced in patients with HF but not in those with acute myocardial infarction. These findings suggest that corin deficiency may play a role in the development of HF and that plasma corin could potentially be used as a biomarker for diagnosing HF.

title: The NLRP3 inflammasome functions as a driver of the myelodysplastic syndrome phenotype.
text: Despite the presence of genetic diversity, myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) exhibit common characteristics such as abnormal cell development and ineffective blood cell production. Our study reveals that the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome is a defining feature of MDSs, leading to the expansion of abnormal cells and cell death through pyroptosis. Regardless of the specific genetic makeup, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in MDSs show increased expression of inflammasome proteins and the presence of activated NLRP3 complexes, which trigger the activation of caspase-1, the production of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18, and ultimately pyroptotic cell death. The mechanism behind pyroptosis involves the alarmin S100A9, which is found in excessive amounts in MDS HSPCs and bone marrow plasma. Similar to somatic gene mutations, the signaling induced by S100A9 activates NADPH oxidase (NOX), leading to an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels that initiate cell swelling, cation influx, and the activation of β-catenin. Importantly, we found that suppressing pyroptosis, ROS generation, and nuclear β-catenin through the knockdown of NLRP3 or caspase-1, neutralization of S100A9, or pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3 or NOX can restore effective blood cell production in MDSs. Therefore, the presence of alarmins and founder gene mutations in MDSs establishes a common inflammasome circuit that is sensitive to redox changes, providing potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Structural Brain Correlates Associated with Professional Handball Playing
text: The importance of good bimanual performance in skilled handball playing cannot be overstated. Efficient catching and throwing require control of both hands, making the non-dominant hand particularly challenging to master. In this study, we aimed to examine the structural neuroplasticity induced by training in professional handball players. We utilized various structural neuroimaging techniques and analytic approaches to investigate these adaptations and also reviewed existing literature on sport-induced structural neuroplastic changes. We anticipated structural brain adaptations in areas involved in motor and somatosensory processing, such as the grey matter of the primary/secondary motor and somatosensory cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum, as well as the white matter of the corticospinal tract and corpus callosum. We expected these adaptations to be more pronounced in brain regions controlling the non-dominant left hand. Our results revealed increased grey matter volume in handball players compared to control subjects in the right primary/secondary motor cortex, bilateral supplementary motor area/cingulate motor area, and left intraparietal sulcus. Additionally, fractional anisotropy and axial diffusivity were higher within the right corticospinal tract in handball players compared to control women. The age at which handball training began was inversely correlated with grey matter volume in the right and left primary/secondary motor cortex, while years of handball training experience were inversely correlated with radial diffusivity in the right corticospinal tract. Subcortical structures also tended to be larger in handball players. The anatomical measures of brain regions associated with handball playing were positively correlated in handball players but not in control women. These findings suggest that training induces structural alterations in the somatosensory-motor network of handball players, with greater effects observed in the right hemisphere controlling the non-dominant left hand. The correlations between handball training-related measures and anatomical differences imply neuroplastic adaptations rather than a genetic predisposition for ball playing affinity. Studying neuroplasticity specifically in athletes can contribute to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying expertise in general.

title: The role of epigenetics in aging and age-related diseases
text: Understanding the impact of epigenetics on aging and age-related diseases is crucial in the fields of molecular physiology and medicine. This is because certain epigenetic factors are believed to play a role in connecting the genome with the environment. For epigenetics to actively contribute to aging, two conditions must be met: there must be specific epigenetic changes that occur during the aging process, and these changes must be functionally linked to the characteristics associated with aging. Additionally, it is important to determine whether these specific epigenetic modifications are influenced by genetic, environmental, or random factors, and whether they can be passed down from one generation to the next. In this discussion, we will explore the current understanding of these topics and outline future research directions in this field.

title: Effects of a high-fat diet exposure in utero on the metabolic syndrome-like phenomenon in mouse offspring through epigenetic changes in adipocytokine gene expression.
text: The exact connections between obesity in parents and their children, as well as the influence of genes and a shared environment, are not fully understood. Adipocytokines, such as leptin and adiponectin, play important roles in the metabolism of glucose and lipids. Therefore, we investigated whether offspring from mothers who were exposed to a high-fat diet during pregnancy (referred to as OH mice) developed hypertension, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia, and if there were any epigenetic changes in the expression of adipocytokine genes. From 14 weeks of age, OH mice were significantly heavier than the offspring of mothers who were exposed to a control diet during pregnancy (referred to as OC mice), after consuming more calories from 8 weeks. At 24 weeks, OH mice had higher blood pressure and poorer glucose tolerance compared to OC mice. At 12 weeks of age, OH mice had significantly higher levels of total triglycerides and leptin, and significantly lower levels of adiponectin, compared to OC mice. This was accompanied by alterations in the expression of leptin and adiponectin in white adipose tissue. In the adipose tissues of OH mice, there were lower levels of acetylation and higher levels of methylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 in the promoter of adiponectin at 2, 12, and 24 weeks of age, compared to OC mice. On the other hand, methylation of histone 4 at lysine 20 in the leptin promoter was significantly higher in OH mice compared to OC mice. Therefore, exposure to a high-fat diet during pregnancy may lead to a metabolic syndrome-like condition through epigenetic modifications in the expression of adipocytokines, specifically adiponectin and leptin genes.

title: Highly efficient miRNA-mediated reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells to pluripotency.
text: Cellular reprogramming using transcription factors has been a promising method for converting somatic cells into a pluripotent state. However, this approach has faced limitations due to the need for transcription factors and the inefficiency of the process. In this study, we demonstrate that the expression of the miR302/367 cluster can rapidly and effectively reprogram mouse and human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) without the need for exogenous transcription factors. Compared to the standard Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-mediated methods, this miRNA-based reprogramming approach is significantly more efficient, with a two orders of magnitude improvement. The resulting miR302/367 iPSCs in both mouse and human cells exhibit similar characteristics to Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-iPSCs, including the expression of pluripotency markers, the ability to form teratomas, and, in the case of mouse cells, contribution to chimeras and germline. Our findings indicate that miR367 expression is crucial for miR302/367-mediated reprogramming as it activates Oct4 gene expression, and the suppression of Hdac2 is also necessary. Therefore, our data demonstrate that miRNA and Hdac-mediated pathways can synergistically reprogram somatic cells into a pluripotent state.

title: Unmet needs and depression among carers of people newly diagnosed with cancer.
text:
The purpose of this analysis was to investigate the levels of unmet needs and depression among caregivers of individuals recently diagnosed with cancer. Additionally, the study aimed to identify any groups that may be at a higher risk by examining their demographic characteristics. 

To conduct the analysis, a total of 150 pairs of individuals newly diagnosed with cancer and their caregivers, who were 18 years or older, were recruited from four hospitals in Australia. Eligible participants were those receiving adjuvant cancer treatment with curative intent. The caregivers completed the Supportive Care Needs Survey-Partners & Caregivers (SCNS-P&C45), while both caregivers and patients completed the Centre of Epidemiologic-Depression Scale (CES-D). 

The results showed that 57% of caregivers reported having at least one unmet need, with 37% reporting at least three, 31% reporting at least five, and 15% reporting at least ten unmet needs. The most commonly reported unmet needs were related to information and healthcare services. Additionally, 30% of caregivers and 36% of patients were at risk of clinical depression. There was a weak to moderate positive relationship between unmet needs and caregiver depression. 

The analysis also revealed that caregiver levels of unmet needs were significantly associated with caregiver age, hospital type, treatment type, cancer type, living situation, and relationship status.
