In this article, we will discuss the latest advancements in our understanding of the mechanisms that regulate the production of astrocytes from NSCs, focusing specifically on the developing forebrain in mammals.

title: Regulation of the latent-lytic switch in Epstein-Barr virus.
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is known to play a role in the development of various types of cancer in humans, such as Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Being a herpesvirus, EBV can either establish a dormant or active infection in cells. Tumors that are EBV-positive primarily consist of cells with dormant EBV infection. Researchers are currently exploring methods to trigger active EBV infection in tumor cells as a potential treatment for EBV-positive tumors. This article examines the mechanisms by which cellular and viral proteins control the transition between dormant and active EBV infection in infected B cells and epithelial cells, and explores the therapeutic potential of inducing active viral reactivation.

title: Efficacy of HPV DNA testing with cytology triage and/or repeat HPV DNA testing in primary cervical cancer screening.
text:
The effectiveness of primary cervical screening using human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing and cytological examination of cervical cells with a Pap test has been studied in randomized clinical trials. It has been found that screening strategies that use HPV DNA testing as the primary screening test may be more effective, as the majority of women with positive cytology are also HPV DNA positive. 

In this study, the researchers used data from a population-based randomized trial to evaluate the efficacy of 11 different cervical screening strategies. These strategies were based on HPV DNA testing alone, cytology alone, and HPV DNA testing combined with cytology. The study focused on women aged 32-38 years. The main outcome measures were the sensitivity for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 or worse (CIN3+) within 6 months of enrollment or at colposcopy for women with a persistent type-specific HPV infection, as well as the number of screening tests and positive predictive value (PPV) for each strategy. 

The results showed that double testing with cytology and HPV DNA testing for type-specific HPV persistence increased the sensitivity to detect CIN3+ by 35%, without a significant reduction in PPV. However, this strategy required more than twice as many screening tests. Strategies that incorporated screening for high-risk HPV subtypes resulted in reduced PPV compared to cytology. 

On the other hand, primary screening with HPV DNA testing followed by cytological triage and repeat HPV DNA testing of HPV DNA-positive women with normal cytology increased the CIN3+ sensitivity by 30%, maintained a high PPV, and only resulted in a 12% increase in the number of screening tests. 

In conclusion, the most feasible cervical screening strategy appears to be primary HPV DNA-based screening with cytology triage and repeat HPV DNA testing of cytology-negative women.

title: Extrasynaptic Glutamate Spillover in the Hippocampus: Dependence on Temperature and the Role of Active Glutamate Uptake
text: Excitatory synapses on CA1 pyramidal cells in the hippocampus detect a higher amount of quantal content through N-methyl-D-aspartic acid receptors (NMDARs) compared to alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs). A new explanation for this difference is that glutamate released from presynaptic terminals of one cell can diffuse and activate NMDARs on a neighboring cell, but not AMPARs. If this occurs in the brain, it challenges the notion that glutamatergic synapses serve as exclusive communication channels between neurons. Our study demonstrates that the difference in quantal content mediated by these two receptors is significantly reduced at physiological temperature, as opposed to conventional recording conditions. This temperature effect is not caused by changes in release probability or the exposure of latent AMPARs. However, it is partially reversed by the glutamate uptake inhibitor dihydrokainate. These findings suggest that glutamate transporters play a crucial role in limiting the diffusion of glutamate outside the synapse, thereby minimizing communication between neighboring excitatory synapses.

title: Molecular mechanisms of hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury and preconditioning.
text: Ischemia-reperfusion injury contributes to the morbidity associated with liver surgery under total vascular exclusion or after liver transplantation. The pathophysiology of hepatic ischemia-reperfusion involves several mechanisms that contribute to varying degrees of overall injury. This review discusses cellular mechanisms of injury, the formation of pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators, the expression of adhesion molecules, and the role of oxidant stress during the inflammatory response. Additionally, the review examines the roles of nitric oxide in preventing microcirculatory disturbances and as a substrate for peroxynitrite formation. It also explores emerging mechanisms of protection through ischemic preconditioning. Based on current knowledge, preconditioning or pharmacological interventions that mimic these effects have the potential to improve clinical outcomes in liver surgery involving ischemic stress and reperfusion.

title: Characterization of a FGF19 Variant with Altered Receptor Specificity Revealed a Central Role for FGFR1c in the Regulation of Glucose Metabolism
text: Diabetes and related metabolic conditions have become a global pandemic, highlighting the urgent need for new therapies that are effective and safe. FGF19 and FGF21, two unique members of the FGF family, act as hormones in the body. They have powerful effects on normalizing glucose, lipid, and energy balance, making them promising candidates for next-generation treatments against the rising rates of type 2 diabetes and obesity. However, the exact mechanism behind these impressive metabolic effects is still unknown. Although both FGF19 and FGF21 can activate FGFRs 1c, 2c, and 3c in the presence of co-receptor βKlotho in laboratory settings, it remains unclear which receptor is responsible for the observed metabolic activities in living organisms. To address this, we have developed a modified version of FGF19 called FGF19-7, which has a stronger preference for FGFR1c. Our findings demonstrate that FGF19-7 is just as effective as the original FGF19 in regulating glucose, lipid, and energy metabolism in mouse models of diet-induced obesity and leptin deficiency. These results provide the first direct evidence of the crucial role played by the βKlotho/FGFR1c receptor complex in glucose and lipid regulation. Furthermore, they strongly suggest that activation of this receptor complex alone may be sufficient to achieve all the metabolic functions of endocrine FGF molecules.

title: Empirical verification of evolutionary theories of aging
text: We have recently discovered 3 mutant strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae that have a longer lifespan due to exposure to lithocholic acid. These mutant strains can maintain their extended lifespan even without lithocholic acid. In our study, we used these long-lived yeast mutants to test evolutionary theories of aging. Our findings provide evidence that the genetic trait responsible for longevity in these mutants does not affect important early-life fitness characteristics such as growth rate, post-growth effectiveness, and reproductive ability. However, it does enhance their ability to withstand chronic external stresses and resist programmed cell death. These results support the idea that aging is a programmed process. Additionally, we found that under laboratory conditions that simulate natural selection, each of these long-lived mutants is outcompeted by the shorter-lived wild-type strain. This suggests that yeast cells have mechanisms in place to limit their lifespan once they reach a certain age. These mechanisms drive the evolution of yeast longevity to maintain a finite lifespan within ecosystems.

title: Differential regulation of actin microfilaments by human MICAL proteins.
text: The MICAL protein in Drosophila melanogaster is vital for the functioning of the neuronal growth cone machinery, which operates through axonal signaling mediated by plexin and semaphorin. Additionally, Drosophila MICAL plays a role in regulating myofilament organization and synaptic structures, and acts as a factor for disassembling actin downstream of plexin-induced axonal repulsion. In mammalian cells, there are three known isoforms of MICAL (MICAL1, MICAL2, and MICAL3), as well as MICAL-like proteins (MICAL-L1 and MICAL-L2). However, little is known about their function, and the available information mainly comes from neural cells. In this study, we demonstrate that human MICALs are necessary for normal actin organization in non-neural cells, and all three MICALs regulate actin stress fibers. Furthermore, we present evidence that the production of reactive oxygen species by MICAL proteins is crucial for their role in regulating actin. However, while MICAL1 is inhibited by its C-terminal coiled-coil region, MICAL2 remains active and affects stress fibers. These findings suggest that MICAL1 and MICAL2 have distinct yet complementary functions in regulating actin microfilaments.

title: Suppression of inflammatory and neuropathic pain by uncoupling CRMP-2 from the presynaptic Ca2+ channel complex
text: The treatment of pain using N-type voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.2) blockers is limited due to various physiological side effects. However, we have discovered a potential solution. Our findings indicate that by inhibiting the binding of collapsin response mediator protein 2 (CRMP-2) to CaV2.2, and subsequently reducing channel function, we can effectively suppress inflammatory and neuropathic hypersensitivity. We achieved this by utilizing a peptide of CRMP-2 fused to the HIV transactivator of transcription (TAT) protein, known as TAT-CBD3. This innovative approach resulted in a decrease in neuropeptide release from sensory neurons, as well as a reduction in excitatory synaptic transmission in dorsal horn neurons. Additionally, TAT-CBD3 demonstrated the ability to reduce meningeal blood flow, alleviate nocifensive behavior caused by formalin injection or corneal capsaicin application, and reverse neuropathic hypersensitivity induced by an antiretroviral drug. Notably, TAT-CBD3 exhibited mild anxiolytic effects without impacting memory retrieval, sensorimotor function, or depression. It is important to note that at doses ten times higher than the required amount to alleviate hypersensitivity in vivo, TAT-CBD3 did cause a temporary episode of tail kinking and body contortion. By preventing CRMP-2-mediated enhancement of CaV2.2 function, TAT-CBD3 effectively alleviated inflammatory and neuropathic hypersensitivity. This approach holds promise for managing chronic pain.

title: Identification and characterization of a common set of complex I assembly intermediates in mitochondria from patients with complex I deficiency.
text: Complex I deficiency, caused by deficiencies in the activity of complex I (NADH: ubiquinone oxidoreductase), is a significant contributor to human mitochondrial disease. Complex I is made up of at least 46 structural subunits that are encoded in both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. Deficiency in the enzyme can occur due to impaired catalytic efficiency or an inability to assemble the complete holoenzyme complex. However, the process of assembly is not well understood. To investigate complex I assembly in muscle mitochondria from four patients with complex I deficiency caused by mitochondrial or nuclear gene defects, we utilized two-dimensional Blue-Native/SDS gel electrophoresis and a panel of 11 antibodies targeting structural subunits of the enzyme. Through immunoblot analyses of denaturing gels in the second dimension, we identified seven distinct complex I subcomplexes in the patients studied, five of which were also detectable in the first dimension of nondenaturing gels. While the abundance of these intermediates varied among the patients, a common set of subcomplexes was observed in all cases. A similar profile of subcomplexes was also found in a human/mouse hybrid fibroblast cell line with a severe complex I deficiency, where the holoenzyme complex was almost completely absent. The fact that different causes of complex I deficiency result in a similar pattern of complex I subcomplexes suggests that these subcomplexes are intermediates in the assembly of the complete holoenzyme complex. We propose a potential assembly pathway for the complex, which differs significantly from the current model for complex I assembly in Neurospora.

title: Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship.
text:
The 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommended that individuals engage in a minimum of 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity or 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week for optimal health benefits. It was also suggested that additional benefits could be obtained by exceeding this amount. However, the upper limit of physical activity that provides longevity benefits or potential harm is not clear. 

The objective of this study was to determine the relationship between leisure time physical activity and mortality, and to identify the upper limit of benefit or harm associated with increased levels of physical activity. Data from 6 studies in the National Cancer Institute Cohort Consortium were analyzed, including a total of 661,137 men and women with a median age of 62 years. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with a median follow-up time of 14.2 years. 

The main outcome measured was the upper limit of mortality benefit from high levels of leisure time physical activity. The results showed that compared to individuals who reported no leisure time physical activity, those who engaged in less than the recommended minimum had a 20% lower mortality risk. This risk decreased further to 31% and 37% lower at 1-2 times and 2-3 times the recommended minimum, respectively. The upper threshold for mortality benefit was observed at 3-5 times the physical activity recommendation, with a 39% additional benefit compared to the recommended minimum. No evidence of harm was found at 10 or more times the recommended minimum. Similar results were observed for mortality due to cardiovascular disease and cancer. 

In conclusion, meeting the minimum physical activity guidelines was associated with nearly the maximum longevity benefit. There was a benefit threshold at approximately 3-5 times the recommended minimum, with no excess risk at higher activity levels. Therefore, healthcare professionals should encourage inactive adults to engage in leisure time physical activity and should not discourage those who already participate in high levels of activity.

title: Green tea polyphenol causes differential oxidative environments in tumor versus normal epithelial cells.
text: Green tea polyphenols (GTPPs) have been recognized for their potential health benefits, particularly as agents that can prevent the development of cancer. Recent studies have found that high concentrations of the most abundant GTPP, (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) in tumor cells and certain normal cell cultures. However, if EGCG also triggers the production of ROS in normal epithelial cells, it may limit the use of EGCG in higher doses for topical applications. To investigate this further, the present study examined the oxidative status of normal epithelial cells, normal salivary gland cells, and oral carcinoma cells treated with EGCG. This was done by measuring ROS levels and conducting catalase and superoxide dismutase activity assays. The results showed that high concentrations of EGCG only induced oxidative stress in tumor cells, while reducing ROS levels in normal cells to their baseline levels. Additionally, the study compared the effects of EGCG on two oral carcinoma cell lines using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide assay and 5-bromodeoxyuridine incorporation data. These findings suggest that the difference in endogenous catalase activity levels may play a crucial role in reducing oxidative stress caused by EGCG in tumor cells. In conclusion, the pathways activated by GTPPs or EGCG in normal epithelial cells versus tumor cells create distinct oxidative environments, which either support the survival of normal cells or lead to the destruction of tumor cells. This discovery may pave the way for utilizing naturally occurring polyphenols to enhance the effectiveness of chemo/radiation therapy, promoting the death of cancer cells while safeguarding normal cells.

title: Protein acetylation affects acetate metabolism, motility and acid stress response in Escherichia coli
text: Protein acetylation is a widely observed phenomenon, but its specific regulatory functions are not well understood. To gain a better understanding of its functionality, we studied the acetylome in Escherichia coli knockout mutants of cobB, the only known sirtuin-like deacetylase, and patZ, the most well-known protein acetyltransferase. We identified and quantified over 2,000 unique acetylated peptides belonging to 809 proteins under four different growth conditions. The majority of these proteins (about 65%) are involved in metabolism. The activity of CobB plays a significant role in the deacetylation of numerous substrates and has a major impact on the physiology of the cell. In addition to regulating acetyl-CoA synthetase, we discovered that CobB-controlled acetylation of isocitrate lyase helps fine-tune the glyoxylate shunt. Acetylation of the transcription factor RcsB prevents it from binding to DNA, leading to the activation of flagella biosynthesis and motility, as well as increased susceptibility to acid stress. Surprisingly, deleting patZ resulted in increased acetylation in acetate cultures, suggesting that it regulates the levels of acetylating agents. These findings provide new insights into the functional roles of protein acetylation in metabolic fitness and overall cellular regulation.

title: Ribosome biogenesis: Achilles heel of cancer?
text: The distinction between cancer and non-cancer cells based on their nucleolar morphologies has been known for a long time. In the 19th century, it was observed that cancer cells have larger and more irregularly shaped nucleoli. Pathologists have since used nucleolar morphology to predict clinical outcomes. The alteration of nucleolar morphology is caused by the up-regulation of ribosomal gene transcription. Ribosomal genes are transcribed by RNA polymerase I within nucleoli. The resulting pre-ribosomal RNA transcripts are modified and processed into mature rRNAs. Another type of rRNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase III in the nucleoplasm. These rRNAs, along with ribosomal proteins, are imported into the nucleolus where ribosomal subunits are assembled before being exported to the cytoplasm. Oncogenes like c-Myc can upregulate rDNA transcription, while tumor suppressors like p53 and Rb suppress ribosome biogenesis. Mutations in these genes not only disrupt cell cycle control but also lead to increased ribosome biogenesis. The nucleolus also plays a role in p53 activation and serves as a cellular stress sensor. The higher translational capacity of cancer cells allows them to maintain higher proliferation rates. This addiction to ribosome biogenesis provides new therapeutic opportunities. Many chemotherapeutic drugs used in cancer treatment already inhibit ribosome biogenesis. A recent survey showed that 20 out of 36 drugs in clinical use have this effect. However, these drugs also cause toxicity in normal highly proliferating tissues. For example, ActinomycinD (AMD) preferentially inhibits RNA polymerase I transcription due to the GC-richness of rDNA and its open chromatin conformation. Other drugs like cisplatin, oxaliplatin, and camptothecin also inhibit pol I transcription. The extent to which inhibition of ribosome biogenesis contributes to the efficacy of these drugs is unclear. This raises the question of whether targeting ribosome biogenesis without causing DNA damage could be a viable therapeutic approach. Two drugs, CX-5461 and BMH-21, have shown promise in inhibiting ribosome biogenesis by targeting pol I transcription of rDNA. CX-5461 activates p53 via nucleolar stress and induces autophagy, senescence, and apoptosis in cancer cells. BMH-21, like AMD, is a DNA intercalator that specifically inhibits rDNA transcription and induces nucleolar reorganization. It causes nucleolar stress, leading to decreased proliferation and cell death. P53 is activated in BMH-21 treated cells, but its anti-proliferative effects do not depend on p53. Cancer cells with high demands for ribosome biogenesis are selectively targeted by BMH-21. A recent study has ruled out the involvement of DNA damage signaling and repair pathways in the response to BMH-21. This study highlights the importance of ribosome biogenesis addiction in cancer cells and provides a potential target for therapy.

title: Cell and molecular mechanisms of insulin-induced angiogenesis
text:
Angiogenesis, the process of forming new blood vessels from existing ones, plays a crucial role in the creation of granulation tissue during wound healing. The proper development, maturation, and differentiation of these new blood vessels are essential for the establishment of functional neovasculature in wounds. To investigate the effects of insulin on angiogenesis and understand the signaling mechanisms involved, we conducted in vivo studies and utilized various cellular and molecular techniques in vitro.

Our experiments involved injecting insulin into the skin of mice, which resulted in the growth of longer vessels with more branches. Additionally, there was an increase in the number of alpha-smooth muscle actin-expressing cells associated with these vessels, indicating their appropriate differentiation and maturation. Furthermore, we discovered that insulin promotes the migration and formation of tubes in human microvascular endothelial cells. Interestingly, these effects were not mediated by VEGF/VEGFR signaling but were dependent on the insulin receptor itself.

We also investigated the downstream signaling pathways involved in insulin-induced angiogenesis. Our findings revealed the involvement of PI3K, Akt, sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP-1), and Rac1. Inhibition of these pathways resulted in the elimination of endothelial cell migration and tube formation, as well as a significant decrease in microvessel development.

Based on our results, we propose that insulin could be a promising treatment option for conditions characterized by impaired blood vessel development, such as ischaemic wounds.

title: Inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin potentiates thrombin-induced intercellular adhesion molecule-1 expression by accelerating and stabilizing NF-kappa B activation in endothelial cells.
text: We investigated the regulatory function of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) in the mechanism of thrombin-induced ICAM-1 gene expression in endothelial cells. When HUVECs were pretreated with rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR, the expression of thrombin-induced ICAM-1 was enhanced. On the other hand, over-expression of mTOR inhibited the transcriptional activity of NF-kappaB, an essential regulator of ICAM-1 transcription. Further analysis of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway revealed that mTOR inhibition promoted the activation of IkappaB kinase, leading to the phosphorylation of IkappaBalpha on Ser32 and Ser36. This phosphorylation is necessary for the degradation of IkappaBalpha. Consistent with these findings, we observed that mTOR inhibition resulted in a more efficient and stable nuclear localization of RelA/p65 and increased DNA binding activity of NF-kappaB in response to thrombin. These results demonstrate a new role of mTOR in down-regulating thrombin-induced ICAM-1 expression in endothelial cells by controlling a delayed and transient activation of NF-kappaB.

title: Homologous recombination resolution defect in werner syndrome.
text: We conducted a study on Werner syndrome (WRN), a rare genetic disorder that causes premature aging, genetic instability, and an increased risk of cancer. Through three different experimental approaches, we demonstrated that the cellular characteristics of WRN, including limited cell division potential, sensitivity to DNA damage, and impaired homologous recombination (HR), are interconnected. We found that the expression of wild-type WRN protein or a bacterial resolvase protein called RusA could rescue WRN cells, allowing them to survive and produce viable offspring through mitotic recombination. Additionally, we showed that the cellular phenotypes of WRN are dependent on RAD51-dependent HR pathways. By using a dominant-negative RAD51 protein to inhibit mitotic recombination in both WRN and control cells, we observed a significant improvement in the survival of WRN cells after DNA damage. These findings highlight the important role of the WRN RecQ helicase protein in RAD51-dependent HR and establish a mechanistic connection between defective recombination resolution, limited cell division potential, DNA damage sensitivity, and genetic instability in human somatic cells.

title: Risk factors at medical school for subsequent professional misconduct: multicentre retrospective case-control study
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to investigate whether certain factors during a doctor's time at medical school are associated with professional misconduct later on.

DESIGN: This study utilized a matched case-control design. Data was collected from records of medical schools and the General Medical Council (GMC).

PARTICIPANTS: The study included 59 doctors who graduated from eight medical schools in the United Kingdom between 1958 and 1997 and were found guilty of serious professional misconduct in GMC proceedings between 1999 and 2004 (cases). For each case, four controls were selected from the same graduation cohorts using systematic sampling. The GMC revealed the case-control status after data entry was completed.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The main outcome measure was the odds ratios for being a "case," determined through multivariable conditional logistic regression. Potential risk factors, including pre-admission characteristics and progress during the course, were analyzed using anonymized copies of the students' progress files from their original medical schools.

RESULTS: Univariate conditional logistic regression analysis revealed that cases were more likely to be male, have a lower estimated social class, and experience academic difficulties during their medical course, particularly in the early years. Multivariable analysis showed that male sex (odds ratio 9.80, 95% confidence interval 2.43 to 39.44, P=0.001), lower social class (4.28, 1.52 to 12.09, P=0.006), and failure of early or preclinical examinations (5.47, 2.17 to 13.79, P<0.001) were independently associated with being a case.

CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that being male, having a lower socioeconomic background, and experiencing academic difficulties early on in medical school may be risk factors for professional misconduct in the future. However, these findings are preliminary and should be interpreted with caution. It is important to note that most doctors with these risk factors will not face disciplinary action from the GMC.

title: MiD49 and MiD51, new components of the mitochondrial fission machinery.
text: The process of fission and fusion allows mitochondria to create complex networks. In this study, we have identified two proteins, MiD49 and MiD51, which are found in the outer membrane of mitochondria. These proteins form structures similar to dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), which is involved in fission. MiD49/51 directly recruit Drp1 to the surface of mitochondria. When MiD49/51 are reduced, Drp1 association is also reduced, resulting in uncontrolled fusion. On the other hand, overexpression of MiD49/51 prevents Drp1 from functioning properly at mitochondria, causing fused tubules to interact with actin. Therefore, MiD49/51 play a role in mitochondrial division by affecting the action of Drp1 at mitochondria.

title: Maximal activation of transcription by statl and stat3 requires both tyrosine and serine phosphorylation
text: Initially, Stat1 and Stat3, which are latent transcriptional factors, are activated through phosphorylation on single tyrosine residues induced by the occupation of cell surface receptors by cytokines and growth factors. However, our findings demonstrate that phosphorylation on a single serine residue (727) in each protein is also necessary for optimal transcriptional activity. Both cytokines and growth factors have the ability to induce serine phosphorylation of Stat1 and Stat3. These experiments reveal that gene activation by Stat1 and Stat3, which requires tyrosine phosphorylation to become active, also relies on one or more serine kinases for maximum activation.

title: Protein restriction during pregnancy affects maternal liver lipid metabolism and fetal brain lipid composition in the rat.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of protein restriction during pregnancy on maternal liver lipid metabolism and fetal brain development. Two groups of mothers, one with a normal diet and one with a restricted protein diet, were examined. At 19 days of gestation, blood samples and tissues from the mothers and fetuses were collected. Insulin and leptin levels were measured in the mothers' blood, and lipid levels were quantified in the maternal and fetal livers and brains. Fatty acids in the maternal liver and fetal brain were analyzed using gas chromatography. The results showed that the restricted protein diet led to lower fat composition in the mothers' bodies, including their livers. The restricted group also had higher fasting insulin levels and higher serum leptin levels compared to the control group. Gene expression related to lipid metabolism was reduced in the maternal liver of the restricted group, as well as the concentration of certain fatty acids. The fetuses from the restricted group had lower body weight and reduced levels of liver and brain lipids, including a decrease in the content of a specific fatty acid in the brain. These findings suggest that protein restriction during pregnancy can have negative effects on fetal brain development through changes in maternal lipid metabolism.

title: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans mediate internalization and propagation of specific proteopathic seeds.
text: New experimental findings indicate that the progression of neurodegenerative diseases may be driven by the transmission of fibrillar protein aggregates between cells, resembling the behavior of prions. This phenomenon has been extensively studied in cell and animal models, revealing that protein aggregates are released into the extracellular space and then taken up by neighboring cells, promoting further fibril formation. However, the exact mechanism by which aggregated proteins like tau and α-synuclein bind to and enter cells to trigger intracellular fibril formation remains unknown. Previous research has suggested that prion protein aggregates bind to heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) on the cell surface to propagate pathological processes. In this study, we have discovered that tau fibrils are also taken up by cells through binding to HSPGs. This uptake process can be inhibited in cultured cells and primary neurons by substances like heparin, chlorate, heparinase, and by reducing the expression of a key enzyme involved in HSPG synthesis, Ext1. Preventing tau binding to HSPGs effectively stops recombinant tau fibrils from inducing intracellular aggregation and halts the transmission of aggregates between cells. In vivo experiments using a heparin-like compound called F6 demonstrate that it can block the uptake of tau fibrils when injected into specific regions of the brain. Furthermore, we have observed that α-synuclein fibrils, but not huntingtin fibrils, also utilize the same mechanism as tau for uptake and propagation. These findings suggest a common mechanism for the uptake and spread of tauopathy and synucleinopathy, providing a potential target for therapeutic interventions.

title: Effects of Bifidobacterium animalis administered during lactation on allergic and autoimmune responses in rodents.
text: Probiotics are widely promoted for their health benefits and their positive impact on the immune system. These benefits are believed to be due to various mechanisms, including the stimulation of T helper 1 (Th1) immunity. To investigate the effects of the probiotic Bifidobacterium animalis on Th1- and Th2-mediated immune responses, two different animal models were used: a rat model for experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) representing Th1 responses, and a mouse model for respiratory allergy induced by ovalbumin (OVA) representing Th2 responses. The administration of B. animalis began when the mice or rats were 2 weeks old, and the respiratory allergy or EAE was induced when the animals were 6-7 weeks old. In the allergy model, B. animalis showed a modest reduction in the number of eosinophils and lymphocytes in the lungs, but did not affect allergen-specific serum immunoglobulin E levels. Analysis of cytokine profiles after culturing spleen cells with the mitogen concanvalin A (ConA) revealed that B. animalis shifted the Th1/Th2 balance towards Th1 in females. However, B. animalis did not affect allergen-induced cytokine production in females. In males, B. animalis significantly decreased interleukin-13 levels induced by ConA and showed a trend towards lower levels of Th2 cytokines induced by OVA. In the EAE model, B. animalis significantly reduced the duration of clinical symptoms by nearly 2 days in males and improved body weight gain compared to the control group. These findings demonstrate that B. animalis has a positive impact on various immune parameters in both the allergy and autoimmunity models.

title: Planar Cell Polarity Signaling Pathway in Congenital Heart Diseases
text: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a prevalent cardiac disorder in humans. Despite significant progress in comprehending CHD and identifying numerous related genes, the underlying cause for most cases remains uncertain. The planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling pathway, which governs tissue polarity in Drosophila and influences gastrulation movements and cardiogenesis in vertebrates, has been found to have various roles in cardiac differentiation and development. The impaired function of PCP signaling has been linked to certain CHDs. In this summary, we present our current knowledge regarding the impact of PCP factors on the development of CHD.

title: Cost-effectiveness of human papillomavirus vaccination and screening in Spain.
text: In Spain, there is a free-of-charge prophylactic vaccination program against human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 for girls aged 11-14. However, screening for cervical cancer is opportunistic and contributes to social and geographical disparities. To assess the impact of adding HPV vaccination to cervical cancer screening, a multi-HPV-type microsimulation model was calibrated using epidemiologic data from Spain. Different strategies were evaluated, including screening alone for women over 25 with varying frequency and test type, and HPV vaccination combined with screening for 11-year-old girls. The outcomes measured included lifetime cancer risk, life expectancy, lifetime costs, number of clinical procedures, and cost-effectiveness ratios. The results showed that after the introduction of HPV vaccination, screening would still be necessary, and strategies that incorporated HPV testing were more effective and cost-effective than those using cytology alone. For vaccinated girls, a 5-year organized cytology screening with HPV testing as triage from ages 30 to 65 cost 24,350€ per year of life saved (YLS), assuming lifelong vaccine immunity with 90% coverage. Unvaccinated girls would benefit from organized cytology screening with HPV testing as triage, with a cost of 16,060€/YLS for 5-year screening from ages 30 to 65 and 38,250€/YLS for 4-year screening from ages 30 to 85. The cost-effectiveness of these interventions would depend on the cost-effectiveness threshold and the vaccine price. In conclusion, in Spain, the current screening programs are inefficient due to inequitable coverage and overuse of cytology. Achieving high vaccination coverage among pre-adolescent girls and implementing organized cytology screening with HPV triage starting at ages 30 to at least 65 every 4-5 years would provide the best balance between costs and benefits.

title: Dosimetry and risk estimates of radioiodine therapy for large, multinodular goiters.
text:
In patients with a large, multinodular goiter weighing over 100 grams, we estimated the radiation absorbed doses in the thyroid, surrounding tissues, and the rest of the body after administering therapeutic doses of 131I (3.7 MBq or 100 microCi/g of thyroid tissue retained at 24 hours). 

To measure these doses, we used thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLD) on 23 patients, including 12 euthyroid and 11 hyperthyroid individuals, with an average thyroid weight of 222 +/- 72 grams and an average dose of 2.1 +/- 0.9 GBq of 131I. We placed the TLDs on the skin over the thyroid, submandibular gland, and parotid gland. Additionally, we measured thyroid radioactivity daily in 6 euthyroid and 6 hyperthyroid patients, with an average thyroid weight of 204 +/- 69 grams and an average dose of 1.9 +/- 0.9 GBq of 131I. 

Using an iodine biokinetic model and the MIRD methodology, we estimated the absorbed doses in various organs. We also calculated the cancer risks based on ICRP Publication 60. 

The results showed that the cumulated absorbed doses on the skin were 4.2 +/- 1.4 Gy for the thyroid, 1.2 +/- 0.6 Gy for the submandibular gland, and 0.4 +/- 0.2 Gy for the parotid gland. These values were significantly correlated with the amount of radioiodine retained in the thyroid at 24 hours, regardless of whether the patient was euthyroid or hyperthyroid. 

We calculated absorbed doses in the thyroid to be 94 +/- 25 Gy for euthyroid patients and 93 +/- 17 Gy for hyperthyroid patients, based on thyroid radioactivity measurements. The extrathyroidal absorbed doses (averages of 12 patients) were 0.88 Gy in the urinary bladder, 0.57 Gy in the small intestine, 0.38 Gy in the stomach, and ranged from 0.05 to 0.30 Gy in other organs. There was no significant difference between euthyroid and hyperthyroid patients in terms of extrathyroidal absorbed doses. 

Based on our calculations, there is a 1.6% lifetime risk of developing cancer outside the thyroid gland. When considering individuals aged 65 years and older, the estimated risk is approximately 0.5%. 

In conclusion, these findings can assist in determining the appropriate treatment approach for patients with a large, multinodular goiter who require treatment for hyperthyroidism or compressive problems. Surgery may be preferred for younger patients, while noninvasive radioiodine treatment may be more beneficial for elderly patients and those with cardiopulmonary disease, despite the lifetime risk associated with this therapy.

title: RBM3 regulates temperature sensitive miR-142–5p and miR-143 (thermomiRs), which target immune genes and control fever
text: Fever is a common tool for diagnosing diseases and is consistently linked to higher mortality rates in critically ill patients. However, we have limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control elevated body temperature. Our research has uncovered that the expression of RNA-binding motif protein 3 (RBM3), which is known to respond to cold stress and regulate microRNA (miRNA) expression, is reduced in 30 fever patients and in THP-1-derived macrophages maintained at a fever-like temperature of 40 °C. Interestingly, this reduction in RBM3 expression occurs during fever regardless of whether an infection is present or not. The decrease in RBM3 expression leads to an increase in the expression of temperature-sensitive miRNAs that are targeted by RBM3, which we have named thermomiRs. These thermomiRs, such as miR-142-5p and miR-143, then target endogenous pyrogens including IL-6, IL6ST, TLR2, PGE2, and TNF to establish a negative feedback mechanism that may be crucial in preventing pathological hyperthermia. To further support our findings, we conducted experiments using normal PBMCs that were exposed to a fever-like temperature of 40 °C, which showed a consistent trend of decreased RBM3 levels being associated with increased levels of miR-142-5p and miR-143, and vice versa, over a 24-hour period. Overall, our results suggest the presence of a negative feedback loop that regulates fever through reduced RBM3 levels and increased expression of miR-142-5p and miR-143.

title: Patient preferences and expectations for care: determinants in patients with lumbar intervertebral disc herniation.
text:
RESEARCH DESIGN
This study utilized a prospective observational cohort design to examine the baseline characteristics of patients diagnosed with intervertebral disc herniation who had different treatment preferences. The aim was to explore the relationship between specific expectations and treatment preferences.

BACKGROUND
Data for this study were collected from the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT) observational cohort. Patients in this cohort met the same eligibility criteria as those in the randomized cohort but chose their preferred treatment instead of being randomly assigned.

METHODS
Baseline preference and expectation data were collected at the time of patient enrollment, prior to the informed consent process. Univariate analyses were conducted using t-tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Multivariate analyses were also performed using ANCOVA for continuous variables and logistic regression for categorical variables. Multiple logistic regression models were developed in a stepwise manner using blocks of variables.

RESULTS
The majority of patients (67%) preferred operative care, while 28% preferred nonoperative treatment, and 6% were unsure. Among those who preferred surgery, 53% had a definite preference, compared to only 18% of those who preferred nonoperative care. Patients who preferred surgery were younger, had lower levels of education, and higher levels of unemployment/disability. They also reported higher levels of pain, worse physical and mental functioning, more back pain-related disability, longer symptom duration, and greater use of opiates. Gender, race, comorbidities, and use of other therapies did not significantly differ across preference groups. Patients' expectations regarding improvement with nonoperative care were the strongest predictor of treatment preference.

CONCLUSION
The primary factor influencing surgery preference among patients with lumbar intervertebral disc herniation is their expectations, particularly regarding the benefits of nonoperative treatment. Demographic factors, functional status, and prior treatment experience were also associated with patients' expectations and preferences.

title: Cord factor and peptidoglycan recapitulate the Th17-promoting adjuvant activity of mycobacteria through mincle/CARD9 signaling and the inflammasome.
text: The mechanisms by which heat-killed mycobacteria in CFA promote Th17 CD4(+) T cell responses were investigated in this study. It was found that IL-17 secretion by CD4(+) T cells following CFA immunization requires MyD88 and IL-1β/IL-1R signaling. Th17 differentiation, rather than just IL-17 production, is controlled by MyD88-dependent signaling. The inflammasome, specifically caspase-1, ASC, and NLRP3, is involved in CFA-induced Th17 differentiation, with peptidoglycan being the main component responsible for inflammasome activation. Caspase activation and recruitment domain 9 (CARD9) signaling plays a major role in triggering pro-IL-1β expression in the injection site skin of CFA-immunized mice. The C-type lectin receptor mincle recognizes the mycobacterial glycolipid trehalose dimycolate (cord factor), partially explaining the requirement for CARD9. Purified peptidoglycan and cord factor administered in mineral oil synergize to replicate the Th17-promoting activity of CFA, and this response is diminished in caspase-1- and CARD9-deficient mice. These findings suggest a strategy for designing Th17-skewing adjuvants by combining agonists of the CARD9 pathway with inflammasome activators.

title: OPA1 gene therapy prevents retinal ganglion cell loss in a Dominant Optic Atrophy mouse model
text: Dominant optic atrophy (DOA) is a rare disease that causes progressive and irreversible blindness. It is one of the most common forms of hereditary optic neuropathy. DOA is primarily caused by a dominant mutation in the OPA1 gene, which encodes a large mitochondrial GTPase that plays a crucial role in membrane dynamics and cell survival. Hereditary optic neuropathies are characterized by the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells, leading to optic nerve atrophy and a gradual loss of visual acuity. Despite advancements in understanding the disease's mechanisms, DOA remains difficult to treat. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of gene therapy using a genetically-modified mouse model that mimics DOA-related vision loss. We administered intravitreal injections of an Adeno-Associated Virus carrying the human OPA1 cDNA, controlled by the cytomegalovirus promoter. Our findings demonstrate that gene therapy is successful in alleviating retinal ganglion cell degeneration, a key feature of DOA, by restoring normal OPA1 expression. These results are promising for the treatment of Dominant Optic Atrophy and encourage further research towards clinical trials in patients.

title: Multiple degradation pathways regulate versatile CIP/KIP CDK inhibitors.
text: The CIP/KIP family of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors (CKIs) in mammals consists of three proteins: p21(Cip1/WAF1), p27(Kip1), and p57(Kip2). These proteins bind to and inhibit cyclin-CDK complexes, which play a crucial role in regulating the cell cycle. However, the CIP/KIP CKIs also have other independent functions in controlling transcription, apoptosis, and actin cytoskeletal dynamics. Interestingly, these functions are carried out in different parts of the cell and contribute to the conflicting observation that the CKIs can both suppress and promote cancer. To add to the complexity, multiple ubiquitin ligases (E3s) are responsible for targeting p21, p27, and p57 for degradation by the proteasome. In this review, we will examine recent data that shed light on how specific E3 pathways regulate subsets of the CKIs to govern their diverse functions.

title: Dislocation of a type I membrane protein requires interactions between membrane-spanning segments within the lipid bilayer.
text: The gene product US11 from the human cytomegalovirus is responsible for the rapid degradation of class I major histocompatibility complex (MHCI) heavy chains. It achieves this by causing the dislocation of the heavy chains from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and subsequent degradation by the proteasome. This process is similar to the natural cellular quality control pathway that eliminates misfolded or unassembled proteins from the ER. Our research demonstrates that the transmembrane domain (TMD) of US11 is necessary for the dislocation of MHCI heavy chains, but not for their binding. A specific Gln residue at position 192 in the US11 TMD plays a crucial role in the ubiquitination and degradation of MHCI heavy chains. Cells expressing US11 TMD mutants still allow the formation of MHCI-beta2m complexes, but the rate at which they exit the ER is significantly reduced. Additional mutagenesis experiments support the presence of an alpha-helical structure in the US11 TMD that is essential for the dislocation of MHCI heavy chains. Interestingly, the inability of US11 TMD mutants to catalyze dislocation is a unique case where a polar residue in the TMD of a type I membrane protein is necessary for its function. The targeting of MHCI heavy chains for dislocation by US11 therefore relies on the formation of interhelical hydrogen bonds within the ER membrane.

title: Prostate cancer-associated gene expression alterations determined from needle biopsies.
text:
The purpose of this study was to accurately identify gene expression changes that distinguish cancerous prostate cells from normal cells. The researchers aimed to avoid contamination from other cellular components and to account for gene expression changes caused by tumor devascularization and resulting ischemia. 

To conduct the experiment, approximately 3,000 cancerous and benign prostate cells were isolated using laser capture microdissection from frozen biopsy specimens provided by 31 patients who later participated in a clinical trial of preoperative chemotherapy. The researchers then synthesized cDNA from amplified total RNA and hybridized it to custom-made microarrays containing 6,200 clones from the Prostate Expression Database. They also verified expression differences for selected genes using quantitative reverse transcription-PCR. 

The results of the comparative analyses revealed 954 transcript alterations associated with cancer, including 149 genes with unknown functional roles. Importantly, the researchers found no gene expression changes related to ischemia or surgical removal of the prostate gland. Genes up-regulated in prostate cancer were primarily involved in cellular metabolism, energy use, signal transduction, and molecular transport. On the other hand, genes down-regulated in prostate cancer were primarily related to immune response, cellular responses to pathogens, and apoptosis. The researchers also observed a varied pattern of androgen receptor expression changes. 

In further analysis, the researchers found that down-regulation of the androgen receptor was associated with a lower likelihood of cancer relapse after neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical prostatectomy. 

In conclusion, the researchers suggest that assessments of tumor phenotypes based on gene expression, for the purpose of treatment stratification and targeting oncogenic alterations, may be best achieved through biopsy-based analyses that avoid the confounding effects of ischemia.

title: Circulating trimethylamine N‐oxide and the risk of cardiovascular diseases: a systematic review and meta‐analysis of 11 prospective cohort studies
text: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the relationship between circulating trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) and the risk of cardiovascular events. TMAO is a metabolite produced by gut flora and has been linked to cardiovascular disorders. However, the quantitative evaluation of the association between circulating TMAO and cardiovascular events has not been done before. We searched the Embase and PubMed databases for relevant cohort studies and extracted hazard ratios for cardiovascular events and mortality. We assessed heterogeneity among the studies using Cochran's Q Test and I2 statistics and used random-effect or fixed-effect models depending on the heterogeneity. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Out of the 11 eligible studies, three reported both cardiovascular events and mortality, one reported only cardiovascular events, and the remaining seven provided mortality data only. Our analysis showed that higher levels of circulating TMAO were associated with a 23% increased risk of cardiovascular events and a 55% increased risk of all-cause mortality. However, the latter association may be influenced by publication bias, although sensitivity analysis did not significantly alter the results. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression did not find any significant impact of study location, follow-up duration, publication year, population characteristics, or TMAO sample types on the results. In conclusion, elevated levels of circulating TMAO may independently predict the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality.

title: PDGF-BB secreted by preosteoclasts induces angiogenesis during coupling with osteogenesis
text: Angiogenesis is closely linked to osteogenesis during bone modeling and remodeling. A recent study discovered a specific type of blood vessel, characterized by high levels of CD31 and endomucin (CD31hiEmcnhi), that plays a crucial role in coupling angiogenesis and osteogenesis. The study also found that platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB), secreted by preosteoclasts, promotes the formation of CD31hiEmcnhi vessels during bone modeling and remodeling. Mice with depleted PDGF-BB in the tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-positive cell lineage exhibited lower levels of trabecular and cortical bone mass, as well as reduced concentrations of PDGF-BB in the serum and bone marrow. Additionally, they had fewer CD31hiEmcnhi vessels compared to wild-type mice. In an osteoporotic mouse model induced by ovariectomy (OVX), both serum and bone marrow levels of PDGF-BB, as well as the number of CD31hiEmcnhi vessels, were significantly lower compared to sham-operated controls. However, treatment with exogenous PDGF-BB or inhibition of cathepsin K, which increases the number of preosteoclasts and consequently the levels of PDGF-BB, led to an increase in CD31hiEmcnhi vessel number and stimulated bone formation in OVX mice. Therefore, targeting pharmacotherapies that enhance PDGF-BB secretion from preosteoclasts could be a promising approach for treating osteoporosis by promoting angiogenesis and bone formation.

title: Discovery of endothelial to mesenchymal transition as a source for carcinoma-associated fibroblasts.
text: Activated fibroblasts are commonly found in various types of tumors. These include myofibroblasts, activated fibroblasts, and perivascular mesenchymal cells like pericytes, all of which contribute to the progression of cancer. Numerous studies have indicated that myofibroblasts promote tumor growth and cancer advancement. However, the source of myofibroblasts and other activated fibroblasts within tumors is still a subject of debate. While one possible source is the activation of dormant fibroblasts into alpha-smooth muscle actin (alpha SMA)-positive myofibroblasts, other mechanisms such as epithelial to mesenchymal transition and recruitment from the bone marrow are also emerging as potential explanations for the presence of a diverse population of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts. In this study, we demonstrate that transforming growth factor-beta1 can induce proliferating endothelial cells to transform into fibroblast-like cells, a process known as endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT). This transition is characterized by the emergence of the mesenchymal marker fibroblast-specific protein-1 (FSP1) and the down-regulation of CD31/PECAM. Furthermore, we observe EndMT in tumors using the B16F10 melanoma model and the Rip-Tag2 spontaneous pancreatic carcinoma model. By crossing Tie2-Cre mice with R26Rosa-lox-Stop-lox-LacZ mice, we are able to permanently label endothelial cells. Our findings provide clear evidence of EndMT at the invasive front of tumors in these transgenic mice. Overall, our results demonstrate that EndMT is a unique mechanism for the accumulation of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts and suggest that antiangiogenic treatment of tumors may directly reduce the presence of activated fibroblasts, which are known to facilitate cancer progression.

title: ERCC1 and MUS81–EME1 promote sister chromatid separation by processing late replication intermediates at common fragile sites during mitosis
text: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is a key characteristic of the initiation and progression of tumors. Certain regions of the genome, known as common fragile sites (CFSs), are particularly susceptible to instability when faced with replication stress. The rearrangements of these CFSs in tumor cells contribute to the development of cancer. Recent research has revealed that the Fanconi anemia (FANC) pathway plays a role in preventing defective chromosome segregation and CIN when replication stress occurs. Interestingly, FANCD2 is recruited to the regions of metaphase chromosomes that contain CFSs. In order to understand the mechanisms that protect CFSs during the G2/M phase, we conducted a search for proteins that co-localize with FANCD2 on mitotic chromosomes. This led to the identification of two structure-specific endonucleases, XPF-ERCC1 and MUS81-EME1. Our findings demonstrate that the depletion of either ERCC1 or MUS81-EME1 disrupts the accurate processing of replication intermediates or under-replicated DNA that persists at CFSs until mitosis. Depletion of these endonucleases also results in an increased frequency of chromosome bridges during anaphase, which subsequently promotes the accumulation of DNA damage in the subsequent G1 phase.

title: Engineered RNA viral synthesis of microRNAs.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNA molecules that do not code for proteins but play a role in silencing genes and regulating gene expression. While hundreds of cellular miRNAs have been identified, miRNAs derived from viruses have also been discovered. These viral miRNAs have been found to influence both the life cycle of the virus and the expression of genes in the host cell. However, it has been observed that RNA viruses have not been able to produce miRNAs like DNA viruses. This is believed to be due to the limitations imposed by the processing of a genomic hairpin by an enzyme called RNase III. To investigate whether RNA viruses can produce miRNAs, we conducted a study using the influenza A virus. We modified the virus to express a specific cellular miRNA called miR-124. By inserting the miR-124 hairpin into a specific region of the viral genome, we were able to achieve the production of functional miR-124. Importantly, this modification did not negatively impact the replication of the virus or result in the targeting of the viral genome by the miRNA. Our findings demonstrate that RNA viruses can indeed produce functional miRNAs, suggesting that this type of gene regulation may not be limited to DNA viruses.

title: The developmental potential of iPSCs is greatly influenced by reprogramming factor selection.
text: The transduction of Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Myc (OSKM) into cells is a common method for generating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, iPSCs often vary in terms of quality, which can be measured in mice through chimera contribution and tetraploid complementation. In order to use iPSCs for future therapeutic applications, it is important to have consistently high-quality cells. In this study, we found that the combination of reprogramming factors used is a major factor in determining iPSC quality. Using tetraploid complementation, we discovered that ectopic expression of Sall4, Nanog, Esrrb, and Lin28 (SNEL) in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) generated high-quality iPSCs more efficiently than other combinations of factors, including OSKM. While high- and low-quality iPSCs had similar characteristics such as differentially methylated regions, transcript numbers of master regulators, establishment of specific superenhancers, and global aneuploidy, there were distinguishing features that could potentially be applicable to humans as well. These features included aberrant gene expression, trisomy of chromosome 8, and abnormal H2A.X deposition.

title: GiardiaDB and TrichDB: integrated genomic resources for the eukaryotic protist pathogens Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis
text: GiardiaDB and TrichDB are the genome databases for Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis, respectively. They are the newest additions to the EuPathDB family of functional genomic databases, which also includes CryptoDB, PlasmoDB, and ToxoDB. Like the other EuPathDB sites, GiardiaDB and TrichDB use the same framework and offer fully integrated and searchable databases. Users can access genomic-scale data through these resources by conducting BLAST searches, searching for annotation keywords and gene IDs, exploring GO terms, sequence motifs, and other protein characteristics. Additionally, users can perform functional queries based on transcript and protein expression data from various platforms. The databases also allow users to investigate phylogenetic relationships. The ability to combine results from different queries and save queries and results for future use enables comprehensive, genome-wide analysis of functional genomic data.

title: A coding-independent function of gene and pseudogene mRNAs regulates tumour biology
text: The primary function of messenger RNA (mRNA) is to transport information for protein synthesis. However, we have theorized that RNAs may have a regulatory role by competing for microRNA binding, regardless of their protein-coding function. To illustrate this non-protein-coding role of RNAs, we examine the relationship between the mRNAs produced by the PTEN tumor suppressor gene and its pseudogene PTENP1, and the significant consequences of this interaction. Our research shows that PTENP1 is biologically active, capable of regulating PTEN levels and suppressing growth. Additionally, we observe that the PTENP1 locus is specifically lost in human cancer. Expanding our investigation to other cancer-related genes with pseudogenes, such as oncogenic KRAS, we also demonstrate the functional activity of protein-coding gene transcripts like PTEN. These findings highlight a new biological function for expressed pseudogenes, as regulators of coding gene expression, and unveil a non-coding role for mRNAs.

title: Identification of a Multicomponent Complex Required for Outer Membrane Biogenesis in Escherichia coli
text: The outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria serves as a protective barrier against harmful substances like antibiotics and detergents. This OM is made up of a lopsided bilayer consisting of phospholipids, glycolipids, and proteins. The assembly of this crucial structure takes place outside the cytoplasm, in an environment devoid of obvious energy sources like ATP. Unfortunately, the mechanisms involved in this process are not well understood. In this study, we present the discovery of a complex made up of multiple proteins that is necessary for the assembly of proteins in the OM of Escherichia coli. Additionally, we demonstrate that there are genetic interactions between the genes responsible for the components of this protein assembly complex and imp, a gene involved in the assembly of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in the OM. These genetic interactions suggest that YfgL, one of the lipoprotein components of the protein assembly complex, plays a role in a homeostatic control mechanism that coordinates the overall assembly of the OM.

title: Transtheoretical model-based multiple behavior intervention for weight management: effectiveness on a population basis.
text:
The increasing prevalence of overweight and obesity highlights the need for effective interventions for weight management that can be easily implemented on a large scale. The Transtheoretical Model (TTM) offers a promising framework for interventions targeting multiple behaviors related to weight management. 

In this study, a group of overweight or obese adults (BMI 25-39.9; n=1277) were randomly assigned to either a control group or a home-based intervention that focused on multiple behaviors related to weight management. The interventions were tailored to each individual's stage of change and were delivered at 0, 3, 6, and 9 months. All participants were reassessed at 6, 12, and 24 months. 

The results showed significant improvements in healthy eating, exercise, managing emotional distress, and fruit and vegetable intake among those in the intervention group compared to the control group. These improvements were sustained at the 24-month follow-up. The intervention group also experienced greater weight loss compared to the control group. 

Interestingly, individuals in the intervention group who made progress in one behavior were more likely to make progress in another behavior. This co-variation of behavior change was more pronounced in the intervention group and had a greater impact compared to interventions targeting a single behavior. 

Overall, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of TTM-based tailored feedback in improving multiple behaviors related to weight management on a population level. The intervention had a significant impact and sets a benchmark for future interventions targeting multiple behaviors.

title: Autoinduction and signal transduction in the regulation of staphylococcal virulence.
text: The complex regulatory network of Staphylococcus aureus controls various accessory genes, including those involved in causing disease. This network consists of at least four two-component systems, one of which is called agr and acts as a quorum sensor. Additionally, there is an alternative sigma factor and a group of transcription factors, including two superantigen genes called tst and seb. These regulatory genes are believed to work together in a time- and population density-dependent manner. They receive signals from the external environment and integrate them with the cell's internal metabolic processes. This integration allows the organism to produce specific subsets of accessory/virulence factors when and in the appropriate quantities needed for survival in different locations within the host organism. The regulatory agenda is likely tailored to specific sites in the host organism that are targeted for infection. To test this hypothesis, it is crucial to thoroughly understand the intricate regulatory interactions among the organism's various controlling systems. This review aims to consolidate a vast amount of data and develop a preliminary model that can guide future research towards a comprehensive examination of this topic.

title: Macrophages in the Pathogenesis of Atherosclerosis
text: The buildup of apolipoprotein B-lipoproteins beneath the layer of endothelial cells in blood vessels is responsible for the development of atherosclerosis. This accumulation leads to the activation of monocytes, which are immune cells that give rise to macrophages and dendritic cells. The macrophages derived from these monocytes contribute to an inflammatory response that is not beneficial and does not resolve, causing the expansion of the subendothelial layer due to the accumulation of cells, lipids, and matrix. Over time, some of these lesions develop a necrotic core, which can trigger acute thrombotic vascular diseases such as myocardial infarction, stroke, and sudden cardiac death. This article focuses on the significant roles played by macrophages in each stage of the disease's progression.

title: Three-dimensional superresolution colocalization of intracellular protein superstructures and the cell surface in live Caulobacter crescentus.
text:
In recent times, advancements in single-molecule imaging and photocontrol have made it possible to surpass the limitations of Abbe's diffraction and achieve superresolution optical microscopy of cellular structures. This has expanded the possibilities of noninvasive imaging within living cells. However, the challenge of imaging three-dimensional (3D) structures in relation to their biological context, such as the cellular membrane, has hindered live-cell superresolution imaging. 

To address this challenge, we have developed a technique called superresolution by power-dependent active intermittency and points accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography (SPRAIPAINT). This technique combines the imaging of intracellular enhanced YFP (eYFP) fusions (SPRAI) with stochastic localization of the cell surface (PAINT). It allows for the sequential imaging of two different fluorophores using only one laser. The technique relies on the simple light-induced blinking of eYFP and the collisional flux onto the cell surface by Nile red to achieve single-molecule localizations. Importantly, this technique does not require any antibody labeling, cell membrane permeabilization, or thiol-oxygen scavenger systems.

In this study, we demonstrate the application of our technique for live-cell 3D superresolution imaging. Specifically, we image Crescentin-eYFP, a cytoskeletal fluorescent protein fusion, colocalized with the surface of the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus using a double-helix point spread function microscope. By achieving three-dimensional colocalization of intracellular protein structures and the cell surface, our superresolution optical microscopy technique enables the analysis of protein interactions in living cells with exceptional precision (20-40 nm in 3D) and a wide field of view (12x12 μm).

title: Overweight prevalence among youth in the United States: Why so many different numbers?
text: There have been multiple recent publications that have provided varying estimates for the number of overweight young people in the United States. Despite all of these publications using the same data from the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III), the prevalence estimates range from 11% to 24%. This paper aims to discuss the different estimates for overweight prevalence and how they have evolved over time. It also considers the issues surrounding the definition, measurements, criteria selection, and comparison groups used in these estimates. Furthermore, the implications of these variations in estimating the prevalence of overweight among young people are explored. Additionally, this paper compares the reference percentiles for body mass index (BMI) from various publications and explains the differences in the published estimates derived from NHANES III.

title: Senescence and aging: the critical roles of p53
text: p53 serves as a transcription factor that plays a role in controlling the cell cycle, repairing DNA, inducing apoptosis, and responding to cellular stress. In addition to its ability to halt cell growth and trigger cell death, p53 activation also influences cellular senescence and the aging process in organisms. Senescence is a permanent halt in the cell cycle that plays a critical role in both aging and as a strong natural defense against tumors, countering cancer-causing damage. Therefore, by regulating senescence, p53 contributes to suppressing tumor growth, but this is contingent upon its expression and the specific cellular environment. This review focuses on recent advancements in understanding p53's involvement in cellular senescence and its implications for cancer treatment, as well as its impact on the lifespan of animals. Furthermore, we explore how p53 regulates various physiological pathways that may mediate its role in both senescence and aging.

title: Asymmetric cryo-EM reconstruction of phage MS2 reveals genome structure in situ
text: The assembly of virus capsids and the packaging of the genome are closely linked processes in single-stranded ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses. By using cryo-electron microscopy and single particle analysis, we were able to determine the structure of the bacteriophage MS2 virion, which is asymmetrical. This structure consists of 178 copies of the coat protein, a single copy of the A-protein, and the RNA genome. Our findings reveal that the viral RNA genome can adopt a specific conformation within the virion. The RNA forms a network of stem-loops that are mainly located near the inner surface of the capsid. These stem-loops predominantly bind to coat protein dimers that are found in one-half of the capsid. This suggests that the genomic RNA plays a significant role in both genome packaging and the assembly of the virion.

title: Harnessing transposons for cancer gene discovery
text: In recent times, there has been a breakthrough in mobilizing the Tc1/mariner transposon, known as Sleeping Beauty (SB), in mouse somatic cells. This mobilization occurs at frequencies that are high enough to trigger cancer development. The formation of tumors is a result of SB insertional mutagenesis of cancer genes. This process has proven to be beneficial in identifying the specific genes and signaling pathways that contribute to tumor formation. Additionally, a conditional SB transposition system has been created, allowing for control over where SB mutagenesis takes place. This system offers the opportunity to selectively model various types of human cancer. Through SB mutagenesis, a significant number of known cancer genes have already been identified, along with numerous potential candidate cancer genes and targets for drug development.

title: MicroRNA-Containing T-Regulatory-Cell-Derived Exosomes Suppress Pathogenic T Helper 1 Cells
text: The complete understanding of how Foxp3(+) T regulatory (Treg) cells prevent inflammatory disease is still lacking. However, recent research has shown that gene silencing through RNA interference can play a role in regulating cells both autonomously and non-autonomously. In this study, we provide evidence that non-autonomous gene silencing, facilitated by miRNA-containing exosomes, is a mechanism utilized by Treg cells to suppress T-cell-mediated disease. Treg cells transfer microRNAs (miRNA) to various immune cells, such as T helper 1 (Th1) cells, effectively inhibiting their proliferation and secretion of cytokines. By using Treg cells deficient in Dicer or double-deficient in Rab27a and Rab27b, which disrupt miRNA production or the exosomal pathway respectively, we were able to establish the importance of miRNAs and exosomes in Treg-cell-mediated suppression. Through transcriptional analysis and miRNA inhibitor studies, we discovered that the transfer of Let-7d from Treg cells to Th1 cells via exosomes contributes to the suppression and prevention of systemic disease. These findings shed light on a novel mechanism by which Treg cells exert their suppressive effects through miRNA-containing exosomes.

title: Estimating risk curves for first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer’s disease: The REVEAL study
text:
The purpose of the REVEAL study is to examine the psychological and behavioral effects of disclosing APOE information in a risk assessment protocol for first degree relatives of Alzheimer's disease patients. The risk information is presented in the form of cumulative incidence curves. This article explains how these curves were calculated. 

To estimate the curves, Bayes' rule was used to compute the posterior survival curves, taking into account the APOE information. 

The results were obtained by combining survival data from the MIRAGE study with gender- and age-specific APOE odds ratios. This allowed the creation of risk curves for males and females within each of the 6 APOE genotypes. 

In conclusion, by utilizing comparative genotype relative risk information and survival data from family studies, it is possible to generate estimates of gender-, age-, and genotype-specific risk. These estimates can be used in a research study that involves disclosing genotype information for risk assessment purposes.

title: Up-regulation of endothelial nitric-oxide synthase by endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor involves mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase C signaling pathways.
text: The proposed role of Cytochrome P450 (P450)-dependent metabolites of arachidonic acid, known as epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), as endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors (EDHF) that affect vascular tone is not well understood in relation to endothelial-derived nitric oxide biosynthesis. In this study, we aimed to investigate the regulation of endothelial nitric-oxide synthase (eNOS) by EDHF and explore the relevant signaling pathways involved. To do this, we transfected cultured bovine aortic endothelial cells with P450 epoxygenases CYP102 F87V mutant, CYP2C11-CYPOR, and CYP2J2, and assessed the effects of endogenously formed or exogenously applied EETs on eNOS expression and activity. The transfection of P450 epoxygenases resulted in increased eNOS protein expression, which was reduced when cotreated with the P450 inhibitor 17-ODYA. Northern analysis revealed that P450 transfection also led to increased eNOS mRNA levels, indicating an effect at the pretranslational level. Furthermore, P450 epoxygenase transfection increased eNOS activity, as evidenced by the conversion of L-arginine to L-citrulline. Additionally, the addition of synthetic EETs to the culture media increased eNOS expression and activity. The inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), MAPK kinase, and protein kinase C signaling pathways using apigenin, PD98059, and H-7, respectively, significantly attenuated the effects of P450 transfection on eNOS expression. Overexpression of P450 epoxygenases in rats also resulted in increased aortic eNOS expression, providing direct evidence of the influence of EDHF on vascular eNOS levels in vivo. Based on these findings, we conclude that EDHF up-regulates eNOS through the activation of MAPK and protein kinase C signaling pathways.

title: Prostaglandin E2 promotes intestinal tumor growth via DNA methylation
text: The mechanisms responsible for DNA methylation changes in cancer are still not fully understood, despite aberrant DNA methylation being recognized as a significant factor in the silencing of tumor-suppressor and DNA-repair genes during tumor development and advancement. In this study, we demonstrate that prostaglandin E(2) (PGE(2)) plays a role in promoting tumor growth by silencing specific tumor-suppressor and DNA-repair genes through DNA methylation. These findings reveal a previously unknown function of PGE(2) in facilitating tumor progression.

title: Nef is physically recruited into the immunological synapse and potentiates T cell activation early after TCR engagement.
text: In vivo, the HIV-1 protein Nef enhances the severity of the virus and speeds up the progression of the disease. It achieves this by enhancing T cell activation through an unknown mechanism, likely by optimizing the internal conditions for HIV replication. Through the use of a new T cell reporter system, we have discovered that Nef more than doubles the number of cells expressing the transcription factors NF-kappaB and NFAT after TCR stimulation. This priming of TCR signaling pathways by Nef occurs independently of calcium signaling and involves an initial step before protein kinase C activation. When the TCR is engaged by MHC-bound Ag, it triggers the formation of the immunological synapse by recruiting lipid rafts, which are detergent-resistant membrane microdomains. Around 5-10% of Nef is localized within these lipid rafts. Through confocal and real-time microscopy, we observed that Nef in lipid rafts is recruited into the immunological synapse within minutes after the TCR/CD3 and CD28 receptors are engaged by antibodies.
