This recruitment relies on the N-terminal domain of Nef, which includes its myristoylation. Nef does not increase the number of lipid rafts or immunological synapses on the cell surface. Recent studies have shown that Nef specifically interacts with an active subpopulation of p21-activated kinase-2 found only in lipid rafts. Therefore, the simultaneous recruitment of Nef and key cellular partners, such as activated p21-activated kinase-2, into the immunological synapse may explain the increased frequency of cells expressing transcriptionally active forms of NF-kappaB and NFAT, as well as the resulting changes in T cell activation.

title: Microenvironmental regulation of tumor progression and metastasis
text: Cancer develops in complex tissue environments, relying on them for growth, invasion, and spread. Unlike tumor cells, the stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) are genetically stable and therefore make an appealing target for therapy with lower risk of resistance and tumor recurrence. However, disrupting the pro-cancer TME is a difficult task because it can have both positive and negative effects on tumor development. Additionally, research has shown that the microenvironment can actually normalize tumor cells, suggesting that re-educating stromal cells may be a more effective approach to treating cancer than directly targeting them. In this article, we explore the contradictory roles of the TME in different stages of cancer progression and metastasis, as well as recent efforts to re-educate stromal cells in the TME to have anti-cancer effects.

title: Bezafibrate in men with lower extremity arterial disease: randomised controlled trial.
text: The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of bezafibrate on the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke in men with lower extremity arterial disease. The study design was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial conducted in 85 general practices and nine hospital vascular clinics. A total of 1568 men, with a mean age of 68.2 years (ranging from 35 to 92), were recruited for the study. The participants were divided into two groups: one group received bezafibrate 400 mg daily (783 men) and the other group received a placebo (785 men). The main outcome measures were the combination of coronary heart disease and stroke. The study found that bezafibrate did not reduce the incidence of coronary heart disease and stroke. There were 150 events in the bezafibrate group and 160 events in the placebo group (relative risk 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.76 to 1.21). However, there was a reduction in non-fatal coronary events in the bezafibrate group, particularly in men aged <65 years at entry (relative risk 0.38, 95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.72). There were no significant effects observed in older men. The study also found no significant difference in the incidence of strokes between the two groups (relative risk 1.34, 95% confidence interval 0.80 to 2.01). In terms of mortality, there were 204 deaths in the bezafibrate group and 195 deaths in the placebo group (relative risk 1.03, 95% confidence interval 0.83 to 1.26). However, bezafibrate did show a reduction in the severity of intermittent claudication for up to three years. In conclusion, bezafibrate does not have an effect on the incidence of coronary heart disease and stroke combined, but it may reduce the incidence of non-fatal coronary events, particularly in men aged <65 years at entry.

title: The modulation of human natural killer cell activity by prostaglandins.
text: Prostaglandins (PGs) have been suggested to play a role in regulating tumor growth in both mice and humans. As natural killer cells (NK) are crucial for immune surveillance against cancer, it is worth investigating whether tumors produce enough PGs to suppress NK activity. Therefore, we studied the impact of different PGs on the NK activity of human peripheral mononuclear cells. We measured the percentage of cytotoxicity by monitoring the release of Cr51 from labeled K562 and other target cells. At very high concentrations of PG (10(-6) M), we observed suppression with PGE2, PGD2, PGA2, and PGF2 alpha. However, at physiologically relevant concentrations of PG (10(-8) M), significant suppression was only seen with PGE2 and PGD2. The percentage of suppression with PGE2 ranged from 77% to 9.5% across concentrations from 10(-5) to 10(-9) M (45% at 10(-8) M). We observed significant suppression at 10(-8) M PGE2 with four different targets and at effector:target ratios ranging from 50:1 to 12.5:1. To determine whether the suppressive effect of PGE2 was directed at the effector or target cell, we pretreated K562 cells or effector cells with PGE2. We found significant suppression with effector cell pretreatment but not with target cell pretreatment. Finally, we examined the suppressive effects of supernatants obtained from tumor cell lines (specifically, the polyoma virus-transformed murine fibroblast cell line, PY3T3). The strong suppressive effect of the supernatant could be attributed to its PGE content. Therefore, it seems that the production of PGE by tumor cells may play a significant role in modulating human NK activity.

title: Association analysis between anterior-pharynx defective-1 genes polymorphisms and Alzheimer's disease.
text: Recent biological research has highlighted the significance of anterior-pharynx defective-1 (APH-1) proteins in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). To investigate further, we examined APH-1 genes for any sequence variations using denaturing high performance liquid chromatography. We then analyzed the distribution of these variations in a group of 113 AD patients and 132 controls from Italy. Our findings revealed the presence of six different polymorphisms, with three of them occurring exclusively in APH-1b and resulting in amino acid substitutions (T27I, V199L, and F217L). The remaining polymorphisms were either silent or located in non-coding regions. However, none of these variations showed a significant association with the disease. When we stratified the data based on the carrier status of the apolipoprotein E epsilon4 allele, we observed a trend suggesting a coexistence between the transversion c+651T>G (F217L) and the epsilon4 allele. Overall, our data indicate that polymorphisms in the coding regions of APH-1a/b are not strongly linked to an increased risk of sporadic AD in our Italian population sample.

title: Dynamic epigenetic regulation of glioblastoma tumorigenicity through LSD1 modulation of MYC expression.
text: The evidence available indicates that the deadliness of glioblastoma is caused by small groups of cells that have the ability to renew themselves and form tumors. It is still not clear whether this ability to form tumors is a fixed characteristic of a few cells or if it can be acquired dynamically. To investigate this, we conducted experiments using tumor-sphere and xenograft formation as tests for tumor-forming ability. We studied subclones taken from established and primary glioblastoma cell lines. Our findings suggest that the ability to form tumors in glioblastoma is mostly predetermined, but it can also be acquired spontaneously at low frequencies. Additionally, these dynamic transitions are controlled by changes in the epigenetic programming of cells through a protein called lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1). When LSD1 is depleted, there is an increase in a specific modification of a protein called histone 3 at a gene called MYC, which leads to higher expression of MYC. MYC, in turn, regulates the activity of three important transcription factors - oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factor 2 (OLIG2), SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 2 (SOX2), and POU class 3 homeobox 2 (POU3F2). These transcription factors are essential for reprogramming glioblastoma cells into a stem-like state. Our model proposes that the epigenetic regulation of these key transcription factors controls the transitions between different tumor-forming states in glioblastoma. This understanding provides a framework for the development of therapeutic approaches for glioblastoma.

title: Auditory Cortex Tracks Both Auditory and Visual Stimulus Dynamics Using Low-Frequency Neuronal Phase Modulation
text: The integration of information from different senses to create a unified understanding of multi-sensory signals is a crucial aspect of perception in ecological settings. A thought-provoking hypothesis based on neurophysiology suggests that there is an early and direct modulation of phases between different sensory modalities. Through our study using magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings of participants watching audiovisual movies, we have found evidence that low-frequency neuronal activity is essential for coordinating information between auditory and visual streams. Specifically, the phase of delta and theta band responses in the 2-7 Hz range contains reliable information about the temporal structure of stimuli in both sensory modalities, even on a single trial basis. These experiments are the first to demonstrate in humans that a specific cortical mechanism, involving the modulation of delta-theta phase in early sensory areas, actively tracks naturalistic audio-visual streams, conveying dynamic multi-sensory information and reflecting real-time cross-sensory interaction.

title: The diagnosis and management of gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants.
text: During the first few months of life, it is common for infants to experience gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). Gastro-oesophageal reflux can be a primary issue with the gastrointestinal motility, or it can be a secondary condition caused by factors like cow's milk protein allergy. Diagnosing this condition objectively can be challenging because there may not always be a clear correlation between the patient's history, pH monitoring results, and histology. Interestingly, severe GORD can sometimes present with minor symptoms, while minor GOR can cause severe symptoms. Fortunately, there are various therapeutic interventions available. For instance, using thickened formula can help reduce regurgitation, and alginates and proton pump inhibitors can be used to decrease acid GOR, depending on the severity of the GORD. However, the efficacy of prokinetic drugs is either lacking or disappointing. One particular drug of interest in terms of side-effects is cisapride, although other medications have similar effects. It is important to note that the long-term consequences of therapeutic management, especially with acid-reducing medications, have not been sufficiently studied, particularly in relation to nutritional effects.

title: Increased sensitivity of antigen-experienced T cells through the enrichment of oligomeric T cell receptor complexes.
text: The molecular basis for the increased sensitivity of memory T cells compared to naive T cells is not yet fully understood. However, our previous research has shown that the T cell receptor (TCR) exists in different-sized groups on the surface of resting T cells, with larger groups being preferentially activated by low levels of antigen. Using biochemistry and electron microscopy, we have now discovered that previously stimulated and memory T cells have more and larger TCR groups on their cell surface compared to naive T cells. By introducing a point mutant of the CD3ζ subunit, which impairs TCR group formation, into cells and mice, we were able to demonstrate that the larger size of TCR groups directly contributes to the increased sensitivity of antigen-experienced T cells. Therefore, we propose that a mechanism called "avidity maturation" is responsible for T cell antigenic memory.

title: G*Power 3: a flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences.
text: G*Power, developed by Erdfelder, Faul, and Buchner in 1996, is a comprehensive power analysis program specifically designed for social and behavioral research. The latest version, G*Power 3, represents a significant upgrade from its predecessors, offering enhanced functionality and improved performance. It is compatible with popular computer platforms such as Windows XP, Windows Vista, and Mac OS X 10.4. G*Power 3 covers a wide range of statistical tests commonly used in research, including t-tests, F-tests, and chi-square tests. Additionally, it provides power analyses for z-tests and certain exact tests. The software incorporates advanced effect size calculators and graphical options, accommodating both distribution-based and design-based input modes. It caters to the diverse needs of users by offering various types of power analyses. Similar to its previous versions, G*Power 3 is available for free.

title: Dynamic interactions of cortactin and membrane type 1 matrix metalloproteinase at invadopodia: defining the stages of invadopodia formation and function.
text: Metastatic tumor cells that migrate and invade surrounding tissues rely on invadopodia, which are membrane protrusions that contain enzymes necessary for breaking down the extracellular matrix (ECM). However, there is limited knowledge about how invadopodia are formed, their function, and how they are regulated. In this study, we demonstrate that invadopodia have two distinct roles: (a) they provide a structural framework for organizing the actin cytoskeleton and forming membrane protrusions, and (b) they use proteolytic enzymes to degrade the ECM. By using small interfering RNA (siRNA) to inhibit invadopodia formation, we found that cortactin is necessary for the structural organization of invadopodia. Additionally, through protease inhibitor studies, we identified membrane type 1 matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP) as the key enzyme responsible for degrading the gelatin matrix in breast carcinoma cells. When cortactin was depleted, invadopodia formation was blocked, resulting in a failure to degrade the matrix. Inhibition or depletion of MT1-MMP moderately decreased invadopodia formation, but those that did form were unable to degrade the matrix. Through further examination and live-cell imaging, we observed four distinct stages of invadopodia: cortactin aggregation at the membrane, MT1-MMP accumulation at the site of cortactin accumulation, matrix degradation, and subsequent dissociation of cortactin from the area where MT1-MMP continued to accumulate. Based on these findings, we propose a stepwise model for the formation and function of invadopodia.

title: PEP-FOLD: an updated de novo structure prediction server for both linear and disulfide bonded cyclic peptides
text:
In light of the growing interest in peptides as therapeutic agents, it is crucial to have an online resource that can predict the 3D structure of peptides with well-defined structures in aqueous solution. We are pleased to introduce an updated version of PEP-FOLD, which now has the capability to handle both linear and cyclic peptides with 9-36 amino acids, including those with disulphide bonds. This server allows biologists to define disulphide bonds and determine the proximity between different residues. 

To assess the accuracy of PEP-FOLD, we conducted benchmark tests using 34 cyclic peptides with one, two, and three disulphide bonds. The best PEP-FOLD models showed an average root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 2.75 Å from the full NMR structures. Additionally, we tested 37 linear peptides, and PEP-FOLD successfully identified the lowest-energy conformations with an RMSD of 3 Å from the NMR rigid cores. 

The evolution of PEP-FOLD represents a significant improvement over the previous server and now serves as a new online service. To access the server, please visit: http://bioserv.rpbs.univ-paris-diderot.fr/PEP-FOLD.

title: Discrimination of speech stimuli based on neuronal response phase patterns depends on acoustics but not comprehension.
text: The neural activity in the listener, triggered by speech stimuli, can be observed as waveforms using magnetoencephalography. While these waveforms can vary significantly from trial to trial due to unrelated activity, it has been shown that spoken sentences can be distinguished based on the theta-band phase patterns in the response waveforms. Additionally, when the speech signal envelope and fine structure are manipulated to reduce intelligibility, there is a corresponding decrease in discrimination performance, suggesting a connection between theta-band phase patterns and speech comprehension. This study aims to investigate this relationship and proposes that theta-band phase patterns primarily reflect the cortical processing of low-frequency modulations (<40 Hz) present in the acoustic signal, which are necessary for intelligibility, rather than processing solely related to comprehension (such as lexical, syntactic, or semantic processing). By using stimuli that are similar to normal spoken sentences in terms of low-frequency modulation characteristics but are unintelligible (i.e., their time-inverted counterparts), the study finds that discrimination performance based on theta-band phase patterns is the same for both types of stimuli. Consistent with previous findings, it is also observed that theta-band phase patterns differ across stimuli, while power patterns do not. To further understand these results, a simulation model of the single-trial response to spoken sentence stimuli is used, demonstrating that phase-locked responses to low-frequency modulations of the acoustic signal can explain both the phase and power results. This simulation provides insights into the interpretation of the empirical results in relation to phase-resetting and power-enhancement models of the evoked response.

title: Breathing more with weaker respiratory muscles in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
text: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension often experience exertional fatigue and dyspnea, which limits their daily activities. These symptoms are typically attributed to the right ventricle's inability to adequately supply oxygen to the lungs and meet the body's oxygen demands. As a result, patients with pulmonary hypertension often exhibit reduced peak oxygen uptake, anaerobic threshold, oxygen pulse, ventilatory efficiency, and 6-minute walk distance. This profile is similar to that of congestive heart failure, further supporting the idea that impaired cardiac output adaptation is the primary cause of decreased exercise capacity. However, the correlation between ergospirometric variables, walk distances, and haemodynamic function is stronger with functional class and prognosis rather than with the specific cardiac function. Additionally, studies have shown that skeletal muscle function is impaired in heart failure, leading to a "muscle hypothesis" that suggests dyspnea and fatigue symptoms are related to reflexes in the skeletal muscles. This hypothesis suggests that there is persistent activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which has been observed in both heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. However, until now, there have been no studies on skeletal muscle function in pulmonary arterial hypertension. In a recent study published in the European Respiratory Journal, Meyer et al. found that respiratory muscle strength is decreased in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension. They measured significant decreases in maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures, as well as an increased mouth occlusion pressure within the first 0.1 seconds of inspiration, suggesting inadequate muscle function.

title: Acetic Acid Activates the AMP-Activated Protein Kinase Signaling Pathway to Regulate Lipid Metabolism in Bovine Hepatocytes
text: The impact of acetic acid on the metabolism of liver lipids differs greatly between ruminants and monogastric animals. Therefore, the objective of this research was to examine how acetic acid regulates the metabolism of liver lipids in dairy cows. The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling pathway plays a crucial role in regulating the metabolism of liver lipids. In this study, bovine hepatocytes were cultured in vitro and treated with varying concentrations of sodium acetate (neutralized acetic acid) and BML-275 (an inhibitor of AMPKα). Acetic acid consumed a significant amount of ATP, leading to an increase in the phosphorylation of AMPKα. This increase in phosphorylation of AMPKα enhanced the expression and activity of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α, which in turn upregulated the expression of genes involved in lipid oxidation, thereby promoting lipid oxidation in bovine hepatocytes. Additionally, the heightened phosphorylation of AMPKα reduced the expression and activity of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1c and carbohydrate responsive element-binding protein, resulting in a decrease in the expression of genes involved in lipogenesis, thus reducing lipid biosynthesis in bovine hepatocytes. Furthermore, the activated AMPKα inhibited the activity of acetyl-CoA carboxylase. As a result, the triglyceride content in the hepatocytes treated with acetate was significantly reduced. These findings suggest that acetic acid activates the AMPKα signaling pathway, leading to an increase in lipid oxidation and a decrease in lipid synthesis in bovine hepatocytes, ultimately reducing the accumulation of fat in the liver of dairy cows.

title: Unawareness of hypoglycaemia and inadequate hypoglycaemic counterregulation: no causal relation with diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
text: The objective of this study was to investigate the traditional belief that unawareness of hypoglycemia and insufficient hypoglycemic counterregulation in individuals with insulin dependent diabetes mellitus are symptoms of autonomic neuropathy. The study involved assessing the unawareness of hypoglycemia and autonomic neuropathy in patients with insulin dependent diabetes, based on the adequacy of their hypoglycemic counterregulation. The study took place in a routine diabetic unit at a university teaching hospital. The participants included 23 patients aged 21-52 with insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, 10 controls without a personal or family history of diabetes, and similar age distribution. The main outcome measures included the presence of autonomic neuropathy, adequacy of hypoglycemic glucose counterregulation, history of unawareness of hypoglycemia, and response of plasma pancreatic polypeptide during hypoglycemia. The results showed that there was little evidence of autonomic neuropathy in patients with a history of unawareness of hypoglycemia or inadequate hypoglycemic counterregulation. However, patients with clear evidence of autonomic neuropathy did not have a history of unawareness of hypoglycemia and had adequate hypoglycemic counterregulation. Unawareness of hypoglycemia and inadequate hypoglycemic counterregulation were significantly associated. The response of plasma pancreatic polypeptide in patients with adequate counterregulation but without autonomic neuropathy was similar to that of the controls. Patients with autonomic neuropathy had a negligible plasma pancreatic polypeptide response, but this response was also blunted in patients with inadequate hypoglycemic counterregulation compared to the controls. In conclusion, unawareness of hypoglycemia and inadequate glucose counterregulation are related but not caused by autonomic neuropathy. The blunted plasma pancreatic polypeptide responses in patients with inadequate counterregulation may be due to reduced responsiveness of a central glucoregulatory center, rather than classical autonomic neuropathy.

title: Genetic Abnormalities in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: Where We Are and Where We Go
text: Chromosomal abnormalities are found in up to 80% of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). These abnormalities, including deletions of 11q, 13q, 17p, and trisomy 12, have a known prognostic value and play a significant role in the development and progression of CLL. They determine the outcome of patients and guide therapeutic approaches. Conventional G-banding cytogenetics (CGC) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) are the standard methods used to identify these genomic aberrations. While FISH is considered the gold standard, CGC can detect chromosomal translocations and complex karyotypes, which are associated with a poor prognosis. Genomic arrays have a higher resolution and can detect hidden abnormalities, but they are not widely used in routine laboratories. In recent years, next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods have identified various gene mutations (e.g., TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, and BIRC3), which have enhanced our understanding of CLL development. This has allowed us to refine prognostic subgroups and develop better therapeutic strategies. Clonal evolution, which integrates cytogenetic alterations and mutations, has also emerged as a crucial aspect of CLL, providing insights into its clinical course and relapse.

title: Epidermal growth factor receptor expression identifies functionally and molecularly distinct tumor-initiating cells in human glioblastoma multiforme and is required for gliomagenesis.
text: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a well-known diagnostic marker for human glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), although its prognostic significance remains controversial. However, the functional role and biological importance of EGFR in GBM are still not fully understood. In this study, we have successfully isolated multiple subpopulations of GBM cells from patient specimens and cancer stem cell (CSC) lines based on their expression of EGFR and other potential CSC markers. These subpopulations are distinct at both molecular and functional levels, and all possess tumorigenic properties, with EGFR expression being crucial for promoting tumor growth in experimental models. Among these subpopulations, the tumor-initiating cells (TICs) that express EGFR exhibit the most aggressive molecular and functional characteristics. Manipulating EGFR expression using gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches in GBM CSC lines enhances or reduces their tumorigenic potential, respectively, indicating that EGFR plays a fundamental role in the development of gliomas. These findings suggest the existence of functionally diverse EGFR-positive and EGFR-negative TIC subpopulations within the same tumor, which may impact the clinical response to treatment. Consequently, these results provide new insights into potential therapeutic strategies for GBM, considering the presence of functionally heterogeneous EGFR-positive and EGFR-negative TIC subpopulations within the tumor.

title: Stress-induced apoptosis associated with null mutation of ADAR1 RNA editing deaminase gene.
text: RNA editing can involve the conversion of adenosine residues to inosine in double-stranded RNA. This process is carried out by adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR). A-to-I RNA editing in the coding sequence can lead to the production of proteins that are not directly encoded in the genome. ADAR also edits non-coding sequences of target RNAs, such as introns and 3'-untranslated regions, which can impact splicing, translation, and mRNA stability. Three members of the ADAR gene family (ADAR1-3) have been identified in mammals. In this study, we examined the characteristics of mice with a homozygous ADAR1 null mutation. While ADAR1-/- embryos with normal appearance were observed until E11.5, widespread apoptosis was found in many tissues. Fibroblasts derived from ADAR1-/- embryos were also susceptible to apoptosis triggered by serum deprivation. Our findings highlight the crucial role of ADAR1 in embryogenesis and suggest that it promotes the survival of various tissues by editing one or more double-stranded RNAs necessary for protection against stress-induced apoptosis.

title: Outcome of multipair donor kidney exchange by a web-based algorithm.
text: Donor kidney exchange is a well-established method for addressing the incompatibility of donor-recipient pairs (DRP). In order to facilitate this process, a computerized algorithm was developed and tested across multiple transplant centers. The algorithm, created based on consensus among participating centers, enables the exploration of all possible exchange combinations, not only between two incompatible DRP, but also in circular arrangements involving three DRP. It then selects the most optimal set of exchange combinations, taking into account various factors that can impact the success of the transplant. The algorithm was implemented as a web-based program and underwent five rounds of matching. A total of 53 DRP were enrolled from five transplant centers. The number of DRP enrolled in each matching round were as follows: 38 (25 carryover, 13 newcomers), 39 (34 carryover, 5 newcomers), 33 (31 carryover, 2 newcomers), 32 (28 carryover, 4 newcomers), and 34 (30 carryover, 4 newcomers). The number of generated exchange combinations were 4 two-pair exchanges and 11 three-pair exchanges, 3 two-pair exchanges and 17 three-pair exchanges, 2 two-pair exchanges and 12 three-pair exchanges, 2 two-pair exchanges and 3 three-pair exchanges, and 2 two-pair exchanges and 3 three-pair exchanges, respectively. The number of DRP included in the selected exchange combinations were six, twelve, six, five, and four for each matching round. Among the selected exchange combinations, there were five DRP with blood type O recipients and one with an AB donor. Six DRP from the two-pair exchange combinations and six DRP from the three-pair exchange combinations underwent successful transplantation. This study demonstrates the potential of the computerized algorithm for donor kidney exchange, particularly in improving outcomes for disadvantaged DRP with blood type O recipients or AB donors.

title: Light Activation of Channelrhodopsin-2 in Excitable Cells of Caenorhabditis elegans Triggers Rapid Behavioral Responses
text: To study the function of specific neurons in their natural circuitry, it is necessary to have precise control over their activity. However, this can be challenging in live animals, particularly small model organisms, as it often requires dissection to accurately stimulate the neurons electrically or apply neurotransmitters. In our research, we utilized channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), a cation channel found in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, to manipulate the behavior of excitable cells in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans simply by using light. Channelrhodopsins are proteins with seven transmembrane helices that are similar to bacteriorhodopsin, a light-driven proton pump. However, instead of pumping protons, channelrhodopsins use the chromophore all-trans retinal to open a cation pore. When ChR2 was activated by light in muscle cells, it caused strong and simultaneous contractions. These contractions were reduced when L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) and ryanodine receptors (RyRs) were mutated. Electrophysiological analysis showed rapid inward currents that lasted as long as the illumination. When ChR2 was expressed in mechanosensory neurons, light stimulation triggered withdrawal behaviors that are typically induced by mechanical stimulation. Additionally, ChR2 allowed these neurons to be active in mutants lacking the MEC-4/MEC-10 mechanosensory ion channel. Therefore, by expressing ChR2 in specific neurons or muscles, we were able to quickly and reversibly activate them using light in live animals that were behaving or dissected.

title: Neuronal activity regulates remyelination via glutamate signalling to oligodendrocyte progenitors
text: The mechanisms and causes of frequent failure in myelin regeneration in demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis (MS) are not fully understood. In this study, we used an in-vivo remyelination model to demonstrate that demyelinated axons are electrically active and form new synapses with recruited oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs). These OPCs sense neuronal activity early after the lesion is induced by expressing AMPA/kainate receptors. When neuronal activity, axonal vesicular release, or AMPA receptors are blocked in demyelinated lesions, remyelination is reduced. In the absence of neuronal activity, the number of OPCs within the lesions increases approximately six-fold, while the proportion of differentiated oligodendrocytes decreases. These findings indicate that neuronal activity and glutamate release instruct OPCs to differentiate into new myelinating oligodendrocytes, leading to the recovery of lost function. The co-localization of OPCs with the presynaptic protein VGluT2 in MS lesions suggests that targeting this mechanism could enhance remyelination therapeutically.

title: The threshold for polyglutamine-expansion protein aggregation and cellular toxicity is dynamic and influenced by aging in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Research on the mutant gene in Huntington's disease and related neurodegenerative disorders has revealed that polyglutamine (polyQ) expansions are responsible for cellular toxicity. This discovery has led to a hypothesis that protein aggregation and cellular dysfunction occur when there are approximately 40 glutamine residues. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment where we expressed fluorescently tagged polyQ proteins (Q29, Q33, Q35, Q40, and Q44) in the muscle cells of Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that young adults showed a clear boundary at 35-40 glutamines, which was associated with the formation of protein aggregates and loss of motility. Surprisingly, animals with genetically identical backgrounds but near-threshold polyQ repeats exhibited varying degrees of protein aggregates and cellular toxicity, depending on the length of the repeat and worsening with age. To investigate the role of genetically determined aging pathways in the progression of age-dependent polyQ-mediated aggregation and cellular toxicity, we expressed Q82 in age-1 mutant animals that have an extended lifespan. We observed a significant delay in polyQ toxicity and the appearance of protein aggregates. These findings provide experimental evidence supporting the threshold hypothesis of polyQ-mediated toxicity in an experimental organism and highlight the significance of the threshold as a point where genetic modifiers and aging impact the biochemical environment and protein homeostasis in cells.

title: Inflammation meets cancer, with NF-κB as the matchmaker
text: Inflammation is a crucial defense mechanism that can sometimes malfunction and contribute significantly to the development of various chronic diseases, such as cancer. This article examines the evolutionary connection and contrasting roles of the transcription factor NF-κB in both inflammation and cancer. While NF-κB appears to predominantly promote tumor growth in many cancer types, its role in certain tumors remains perplexing. Gaining a comprehensive understanding of NF-κB's activity and function in the context of tumor formation is vital for effectively controlling it, presenting a significant challenge in modern cancer research.

title: IgBLAST: an immunoglobulin variable domain sequence analysis tool
text: Multiple genes, including the variable (V) gene, the diversity (D) gene, and the joining (J) gene, encode the variable domain of an immunoglobulin (IG) sequence. Analyzing IG sequences involves identifying each gene and comparing sequence variations within specific regions. However, general tools like the BLAST program have limited utility for these tasks due to the rearranged nature of IG sequences and the variable length of each gene. Consequently, multiple rounds of BLAST searches are required for a single IG sequence. Moreover, manually assembling different genes is challenging and prone to errors. To address these issues and facilitate common tasks in IG sequence analysis, we have developed a sequence analysis tool called IgBLAST (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/igblast/). IgBLAST allows users to view matches to the germline V, D, and J genes, details at rearrangement junctions, and the delineation of IG V domain framework regions and complementarity determining regions. It can analyze both nucleotide and protein sequences and process sequences in batches. Additionally, IgBLAST enables simultaneous searches against germline gene databases and other sequence databases to minimize the risk of missing the best matching germline V gene.

title: Evidence into practice. Application of psychological models of change in evidence-based implementation.
text: For many years, psychiatrists have acknowledged the importance of incorporating external evidence into their everyday clinical practice (Lewis, 1958). In fact, psychiatric researchers were pioneers in utilizing multi-center randomized controlled trials to showcase the efficacy of antipsychotics. Similarly, psychologists were among the early adopters in the healthcare field to develop meta-analysis techniques. Social workers also highlight their historical involvement, as evidenced by the publication of one of the earliest controlled trials (Lehrman, 1949).

title: Wnt signaling establishes anteroposterior neuronal polarity and requires retromer in C. elegans.
text: The regulation of neural connectivity is influenced by secreted Wnt proteins, which control axon guidance, dendritic morphogenesis, and synapse formation. Our study reveals a novel function of Wnt and Frizzled proteins in determining the anteroposterior polarity of mechanosensory neurons ALM and PLM in C. elegans. Disruption of Wnt signaling results in a complete reversal of ALM and PLM polarity, with the anterior process acquiring the characteristics of the wild-type posterior process, and vice versa. Different sets of Wnt proteins, with some overlap, govern neuronal polarity in distinct body regions. Wnts directly interact with PLM through the Frizzled LIN-17 receptor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Wnts are crucial for axon branching and anterior-directed axon growth. Additionally, we identify the retromer, a conserved protein complex involved in transcytosis and endosome-to-Golgi protein trafficking, as a key player in Wnt signaling. Deletion mutations of retromer subunits lead to defects in ALM and PLM polarity, as well as other Wnt-related abnormalities. Our findings highlight the requirement of the retromer protein VPS-35 in Wnt-expressing cells and propose that retromer activity is essential for generating a fully functional Wnt signal.

title: Adjustable gastric banding and conventional therapy for type 2 diabetes: a randomized controlled trial.
text: The purpose of this study was to determine if surgically induced weight loss is more effective in controlling glycemic levels and reducing the need for diabetes medications compared to conventional approaches to weight loss and diabetes control. The study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial at the University Obesity Research Center in Australia, with participants recruited from the general community. The participants were 60 obese patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes. The interventions included conventional diabetes therapy with a focus on lifestyle changes for weight loss, and laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding with conventional diabetes care. The main outcome measures were the remission of type 2 diabetes, weight loss, and components of the metabolic syndrome. The results showed that 73% of the surgical group achieved remission of type 2 diabetes, compared to only 13% in the conventional-therapy group. The surgical group also experienced a significantly greater weight loss compared to the conventional-therapy group. The remission of type 2 diabetes was found to be related to weight loss and lower baseline HbA1c levels. No serious complications were reported in either group. The study concludes that surgical therapy may be more effective in achieving remission of type 2 diabetes through greater weight loss. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings in a larger and more diverse population, as well as to assess the long-term efficacy of surgical therapy. The trial was registered under the identifier ACTRN012605000159651.

title: Integration of antiretroviral therapy with tuberculosis treatment.
text:
In a previous report, we found that combining antiretroviral therapy (ART) with tuberculosis treatment reduces mortality. However, the optimal timing for starting ART during tuberculosis treatment is still uncertain. To address this, we conducted a randomized controlled trial in South Africa involving 642 ambulatory patients with confirmed tuberculosis, HIV infection, and a CD4+ T-cell count below 500 per cubic millimeter. In this study, we present the findings from the group that initiated ART within 4 weeks of starting tuberculosis treatment (214 patients) and the group that initiated ART during the first 4 weeks of the continuation phase of tuberculosis treatment (215 patients). 

At the beginning of the study, both groups had a median CD4+ T-cell count of 150 per cubic millimeter and a median viral load of 161,000 copies per milliliter, with no significant differences between them. The incidence rate of AIDS or death was 6.9 cases per 100 person-years in the earlier-ART group (18 cases) and 7.8 per 100 person-years in the later-ART group (19 cases), showing no significant difference (incidence-rate ratio, 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.44 to 1.79; P=0.73). However, among patients with CD4+ T-cell counts below 50 per cubic millimeter, the incidence rates of AIDS or death were 8.5 and 26.3 cases per 100 person-years, respectively (incidence-rate ratio, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.07 to 1.13; P=0.06). The incidence rates of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) were 20.1 and 7.7 cases per 100 person-years, respectively (incidence-rate ratio, 2.62; 95% CI, 1.48 to 4.82; P<0.001). Adverse events requiring a change in antiretroviral drugs occurred in 10 patients in the earlier-ART group and 1 patient in the later-ART group (P=0.006). 

In conclusion, initiating ART early in patients with CD4+ T-cell counts below 50 per cubic millimeter increased the likelihood of AIDS-free survival. Delaying the initiation of ART until the first 4 weeks of the continuation phase of tuberculosis therapy in patients with higher CD4+ T-cell counts reduced the risks of IRIS and other adverse events related to ART without increasing the risk of AIDS or death. This study was funded by the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief and others, and its clinical trial number is NCT00398996.

title: From bloodjournal.hematologylibrary.org at PENN STATE UNIVERSITY on February 23, 2013. For personal use only.
text: Megakaryocytes (MK) are naturally polyploid cells that give rise to platelets. Polyploidization occurs through a process called endomitosis, which was previously believed to be an incomplete mitosis halted in anaphase. In this study, we utilized time-lapse confocal video microscopy to observe the endomitotic process in primary human megakaryocytes. Our findings indicate that the transition from mitosis to endomitosis occurs due to a late failure of cytokinesis, accompanied by a backward movement of the two daughter cells. No abnormalities were detected in the central spindle of endomitotic MKs. Although a furrow formation was present, the contractile ring was abnormal due to a lack of nonmuscle myosin IIA accumulation. Furthermore, dipolar endomitotic MKs exhibited a defect in cell elongation during telophase. RhoA and F-actin were partially concentrated at the furrowing site. Inhibition of the Rho/Rock pathway resulted in the disappearance of F-actin at the midzone and an increase in MK ploidy level. This inhibition also led to a more pronounced defect in furrow formation and spindle elongation. Based on our results, we propose that the late failure of cytokinesis responsible for the endomitotic process is associated with a partial defect in the activation of the Rho/Rock pathway.

title: Key role for IL-21 in experimental autoimmune uveitis.
text: IL-21 is a versatile type 1 cytokine that shares the γ-chain receptor, γ(c), with IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, and IL-15. Among these cytokines, IL-21 is most similar to IL-2. Although these cytokines are encoded by neighboring genes, they have distinct functions. While IL-2 promotes the growth of regulatory T cells and offers protection against autoimmune diseases, IL-21 encourages the differentiation of Th17 cells and is associated with various autoimmune conditions, including type 1 diabetes and systemic lupus erythematosus. However, the roles of IL-21 and IL-2 in central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases like multiple sclerosis and uveitis have been a subject of debate. In this study, we created Il21-mCherry/Il2-emGFP dual-reporter transgenic mice and demonstrated that the development of experimental autoimmune uveitis (EAU) was linked to the presence of T cells expressing both IL-21 and IL-2 in the retina. Additionally, we found that Il21r(-/-) mice were more resistant to EAU development compared to wild-type mice, and the transfer of Il21r(-/-) T cells resulted in less severe EAU, highlighting the importance of IL-21 in the progression of this disease. These findings suggest that targeting IL-21/γ(c)-signaling pathways could potentially be a strategy for managing CNS auto-inflammatory diseases.

title: Nicotinamide Phosphoribosyltransferase/Visfatin Does Not Catalyze Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Formation in Blood Plasma
text: Nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in the synthesis of NAD in mammals. It converts nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) from nicotinamide (Nam) and 5-phosphoribosyl 1-pyrophosphate (PRPP). NAMPT is also known as visfatin, an adipocytokine with various functions, although its physiological significance is still unclear. It has been suggested that visfatin may act by forming NMN outside of cells. However, our highly specific and sensitive liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry did not detect NMN in mouse blood plasma. Additionally, there is little or no ATP, which activates NAMPT, in extracellular spaces. This led us to question whether visfatin can catalyze the formation of NMN in such extracellular environments. To investigate this, we determined the K(m) values for Nam and PRPP in the NAMPT reaction with or without ATP, using a recombinant human enzyme. We found that 1 mM ATP significantly reduces the K(m) values for the substrates, particularly PRPP, to levels found inside cells. Consistent with these kinetic data, NAMPT efficiently catalyzed NMN formation only when ATP was present at millimolar concentrations, matching the intracellular substrate concentrations. However, the much lower concentrations of Nam and the almost complete absence of PRPP and ATP in blood plasma suggest that NAMPT is not efficient in catalyzing its reaction outside of cells. Indeed, we did not observe NMN formation by NAMPT in blood plasma. Based on our enzyme kinetics and quantitative analysis of substrates, activators, and products, we conclude that visfatin does not contribute to NMN formation in extracellular environments. Furthermore, the absence of NMN in blood plasma does not support the concept of "NAMPT-mediated systemic NAD biosynthesis." Our study enhances our understanding of visfatin physiology.

title: Hepatitis B virus replication is regulated by the acetylation status of hepatitis B virus cccDNA-bound H3 and H4 histones.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between viral replication and the assembly, transcription, and interaction of HBV chromatin with viral and cellular regulatory proteins. To achieve this, a quantitative chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) technique was coupled with a method that allows the amplification of HBV genomes after transfection of linear HBV DNA into human hepatoma cells. The ChIP technique was also used to study HBV minichromosome transcriptional regulation in liver tissue from HBV-infected patients.

The results showed that the acetylation status of the histones bound to the HBV chromatin plays a role in regulating HBV replication. Inhibitors of histone deacetylases, which are enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histones, increased the acetylation of the histones bound to the HBV chromatin and also increased HBV replication. Additionally, liver tissue from hepatitis B patients showed low levels of HBV viremia, which correlated with hypoacetylation of histones and recruitment of histone deacetylase 1 onto the HBV chromatin.

In conclusion, this study developed a ChIP-based assay to analyze the transcriptional regulation of HBV chromatin. The results provide new insights into the regulation of HBV replication and identify the enzymatic activities that modulate the acetylation of histones bound to the HBV chromatin as potential targets for anti-HBV drugs.

title: Visualization of cell cycle in mouse embryos with Fucci2 reporter directed by Rosa26 promoter.
text: Fucci technology enables the differentiation of live cells in the G(1) and S/G(2)/M phases through dual-color imaging. This technology relies on ubiquitylation-mediated proteolysis, and transgenic mice expressing Fucci serve as a valuable model system for studying the coordination of the cell cycle and development. Initially, the mice were created using the CAG promoter, with separate lines expressing the G(1) and S/G(2)/M phase probes emitting orange (mKO2) and green (mAG) fluorescence, respectively. However, due to the varying strength of the CAG promoter in different cell types and the positional effects of random transgenesis, there was some variability in Fucci expression levels. To ensure more reliable control over the expression of cell cycle probes, we employed different genetic approaches to generate two types of reporter mouse lines with Fucci2 and Rosa26 transcriptional machinery. Fucci2 is a recently developed derivative that emits red (mCherry) and green (mVenus) fluorescence, providing better color contrast than Fucci. The new transgenic line, R26p-Fucci2, utilizes the Rosa26 promoter and contains both G(1) and S/G(2)/M phase probes in a single transgene to maintain their co-inheritance. In the other approach, R26R-Fucci2, the two probes are conditionally incorporated into the Rosa26 locus. The Cre-mediated loxP recombination technique allows researchers to design cell-type-specific Fucci2 expression. By conducting time-lapse imaging experiments using R26p-Fucci2 and R26-Fucci2, where R26R-Fucci2 had undergone germline loxP recombination, we demonstrated the immense potential of these mouse reporters for studying cell cycle behavior in vivo.

title: Tit-for-Tat: Type VI Secretion System Counterattack during Bacterial Cell-Cell Interactions
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a dynamic structure used by bacteria to target and inhibit other cells by transporting effector proteins. Time-lapse fluorescence microscopy has observed the fascinating movement of opposing T6SS structures in neighboring cells of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which has been referred to as "T6SS dueling." This phenomenon likely represents a biological process driven by T6SS antibacterial attack. Our study demonstrates that T6SS dueling significantly impacts the ability of P. aeruginosa to prey on different bacterial species. Specifically, we found that T6SS-mediated killing of Vibrio cholerae or Acinetobacter baylyi is greatly enhanced when these prey species possess active T6SS. Our findings suggest that in P. aeruginosa, the assembly and counterattack of T6SS structures are regulated by a signal triggered by the T6SS apparatus of a second aggressive T6SS-positive bacterial cell.

title: The effects of LY2405319, an FGF21 analog, in obese human subjects with type 2 diabetes.
text: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a newly discovered regulator of metabolism. Animal studies have shown that introducing FGF21 externally can have positive effects on metabolism. However, it is unclear if these findings can be applied to humans. To investigate this, we conducted a trial using LY2405319 (LY), a variant of FGF21, in patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes. The trial was randomized, placebo-controlled, and double-blind. Patients were given either a placebo or daily doses of LY at 3, 10, or 20 mg for 28 days. The results showed that LY treatment led to significant improvements in dyslipidemia, including reductions in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides, and increases in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. There was also a shift towards a potentially less harmful apolipoprotein concentration profile. Positive effects on body weight, fasting insulin, and adiponectin levels were observed as well. However, there was only a slight improvement in glucose levels. These findings demonstrate that FGF21 is active in humans and suggest that therapies based on FGF21 may be effective in treating certain metabolic disorders.

title: Visualization of recombination intermediates produced by RAD52-mediated single-strand annealing.
text: DSBs occur frequently during DNA replication and can also be caused by ionizing radiation, chemical damage, or as part of programmed events in meiosis. In yeast, RAD52 is a crucial protein for repairing DSBs through homologous recombination. In this study, we investigate the role of human RAD52 protein in a model system for single-strand annealing (SSA) using tailed duplex DNA molecules that have undergone exonuclease resection. The purified human RAD52 protein binds to resected DSBs and facilitates the association between complementary DNA termini. Through electron microscopy, we observe heteroduplex intermediates in these recombination reactions, showing the specific binding of multiple RAD52 rings to the resected termini. Additionally, we observe the formation of large protein complexes at heteroduplex joints, which are formed by RAD52-mediated annealing.

title: Crucial Role of Interferon Consensus Sequence Binding Protein, but neither of Interferon Regulatory Factor 1 nor of Nitric Oxide Synthesis for Protection Against Murine Listeriosis
text:
Listeria monocytogenes is commonly used as a model to study immune responses against bacteria that reside within cells. Previous research has demonstrated that neutrophils and macrophages play a crucial role in limiting bacterial replication during the early stages of infection in mice. The cytokines interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) have been identified as essential for protection. However, the specific signaling pathways and mechanisms involved in this process are not well understood. 

This study aimed to investigate the impact of deficiencies in IFN-dependent transcription factors, including interferon consensus sequence binding protein (ICSBP), interferon regulatory factor (IRF)1, and IRF2, on the ability to eliminate Listeria both in vivo and in vitro. The study also examined the production of reactive nitrogen intermediates (RNI) and reactive oxygen intermediates (ROI) in macrophages. 

The results showed that mice lacking ICSBP were highly susceptible to Listeria infection, while IRF2-deficient mice were also susceptible, albeit to a lesser extent. This susceptibility was associated with impaired elimination of Listeria from infected peritoneal macrophage (PEM) cultures when stimulated with IFN-γ in vitro. Additionally, these cultures exhibited reduced and delayed oxidative burst upon IFN-γ stimulation, while nitric oxide production remained normal. 

In contrast, mice deficient in IRF1 were unable to produce nitric oxide, but they effectively controlled Listeria both in vivo and in vitro. These findings suggest that the ICSBP/IRF2 complex is crucial for IFN-γ-mediated protection against Listeria, and that ROI, along with other unidentified effector mechanisms, may be responsible for the anti-Listeria activity of macrophages. Furthermore, the study indicates that IRF1-induced RNI are not a limiting factor in this process.

title: Neuronal replacement from endogenous precursors in the adult brain after stroke
text: New neurons are continuously produced in certain areas of the adult brain, but it is unclear whether these neurons can replace those that are lost due to damage or disease. Our study demonstrates that stroke in adult rats leads to a significant increase in cell growth in a specific region of the brain. These newly generated neurons, along with neuroblasts that were likely already present before the stroke, migrate to the severely damaged area of the brain and exhibit characteristics of developing and mature neurons. This suggests that stroke prompts the differentiation of new neurons into the same type of neurons that were destroyed by the stroke. Our findings indicate that the adult brain has the ability to repair itself after experiencing significant neuronal loss. If these new neurons are functional and their production can be stimulated, it may be possible to develop a new therapeutic approach for stroke in humans.

title: Overexpression of the circadian clock gene Bmal1 increases sensitivity to oxaliplatin in colorectal cancer.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of the circadian clock gene Bmal1 on the sensitivity of colorectal cancer cells to oxaliplatin and its clinical significance. Three colorectal cancer cell lines were used for in vitro and in vivo experiments. The effects of Bmal1 overexpression on cell proliferation, oxaliplatin sensitivity, cell-cycle distribution, and apoptosis rate were examined. The downstream proteins expressed upon Bmal1 overexpression were determined, and Bmal1 expression in colorectal cancer tumors from patients treated with oxaliplatin-based regimens was analyzed. The results showed that Bmal1 overexpression inhibited colorectal cancer cell proliferation and increased sensitivity to oxaliplatin. Patients with high Bmal1 levels in their tumors had significantly longer overall survival and progression-free survival compared to those with low Bmal1 levels. Mechanistically, Bmal1 regulated G2-M arrest by activating the ATM pathway. These findings suggest that Bmal1 could serve as a prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target in colorectal cancer.

title: Evolution of an HIV glycan–dependent broadly neutralizing antibody epitope through immune escape
text: Neutralizing antibodies are expected to have a crucial role in a preventive HIV-1 vaccine. Although attempts to generate broadly cross-neutralizing (BCN) antibodies through vaccination have been unsuccessful, a small number of individuals naturally produce these antibodies after many years of infection. The process by which these antibodies develop and the influence of viral evolution on their formation are still unknown. In this study, we present evidence from two HIV-1-infected individuals who developed BCN antibodies that target a specific glycan at position 332 on the gp120 envelope. Interestingly, this glycan was not present on the initial infecting virus but evolved within 6 months due to immune escape from earlier strain-specific antibodies. This escape resulted in a shift of a glycan to position 332. The viruses that lacked the glycan at amino acid 332 were resistant to the BCN monoclonal antibody PGT128, which depends on the presence of this glycan. However, the escaped variants that acquired this glycan became sensitive to PGT128. Analysis of large sequence and neutralization data sets revealed that the 332 glycan was significantly less common in transmitted subtype C viruses compared to chronic viruses. The absence of this glycan corresponded with resistance to PGT128. These findings demonstrate the dynamic interaction between early antibodies and viral escape in driving the evolution of conserved BCN antibody epitopes.

title: Sir2-Independent Life Span Extension by Calorie Restriction in Yeast
text: The process of calorie restriction has been shown to slow down the aging process and increase the lifespan of various organisms. In yeast, it has been suggested that this occurs through the activation of Sir2. However, we have now discovered another pathway, independent of Sir2, that is responsible for the majority of the longevity benefits associated with calorie restriction. Previous studies have shown that deleting FOB1 and overexpressing SIR2 can increase lifespan by reducing the levels of harmful rDNA circles in older mother cells. Our research demonstrates that combining calorie restriction with either of these genetic interventions significantly enhances longevity, resulting in the longest-lived yeast strain ever reported. Interestingly, we also found that calorie restriction has a greater effect on lifespan extension in cells lacking both Sir2 and Fob1 compared to cells where Sir2 is present. These findings suggest that Sir2 and calorie restriction work in separate pathways to promote longevity in yeast and potentially in higher organisms as well.

title: The Effect of Submaximal Exercise Preceded by Single Whole-Body Cryotherapy on the Markers of Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in Blood of Volleyball Players
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of a single whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) session before submaximal exercise on the activity of antioxidant enzymes, the concentration of lipid peroxidation products, total oxidative status, and the level of cytokines in the blood of volleyball players. The study included 18 male professional volleyball players who were exposed to extremely cold air (-130°C) before exercising on a cycloergometer. Blood samples were collected five times: before WBC, after WBC treatment, after exercise following cryotherapy (WBC exercise), and before and after exercise without cryotherapy (control exercise). The activity of catalase significantly increased after the control exercise. Additionally, the activity of catalase and superoxide dismutase was lower after WBC exercise compared to the control exercise (P < 0.001). After WBC exercise, the levels of IL-6 and IL-1β were also lower (P < 0.001) than after the control exercise. These findings suggest that cryotherapy before exercise may possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. The relationship between the levels of oxidative stress and inflammatory markers indicates the involvement of reactive oxygen species in the release of cytokines into the bloodstream in response to exercise and WBC.

title: Incidence of childhood distal forearm fractures over 30 years: a population-based study.
text: The occurrence of distal forearm fractures in children is highest during the pubertal growth spurt, potentially because physical activity increases during a period of reduced cortical bone mass caused by the heightened calcium demand during peak skeletal growth. Therefore, alterations in physical activity or diet may impact the risk of forearm fractures. The objective of this study was to determine if there has been a change in the incidence of distal forearm fractures in children in recent years. The study was conducted among residents of Rochester, Minn, under the age of 35 with distal forearm fractures in four different time periods: 1969-1971, 1979-1981, 1989-1991, and 1999-2001. The main outcome measure was the estimated incidence of distal forearm fractures in each time period. The results showed that the age- and sex-adjusted annual incidence rates per 100,000 increased from 263.3 in 1969-1971 to 322.3 in 1979-1981 and further to 399.8 in 1989-1991 before stabilizing at 372.9 in 1999-2001. When comparing 1999-2001 to 1969-1971, the age-adjusted incidence rates per 100,000 were 32% higher among males (409.4 vs 309.4) and 56% higher among females (334.3 vs 214.6). The peak incidence and greatest increase occurred between ages 11 and 14 in boys and 8 and 11 in girls. In conclusion, there has been a statistically significant increase in the incidence of distal forearm fractures in children and adolescents. However, the exact cause of this increase, whether it is due to changing patterns of physical activity, decreased bone acquisition from inadequate calcium intake, or a combination of both, remains unclear. Further research is necessary to determine the cause(s) of this rise, considering the substantial number of childhood fractures.

title: Tolerance of whole-genome doubling propagates chromosomal instability and accelerates cancer genome evolution.
text: The impact of whole-genome doubling on chromosomal instability (CIN) and tumor development is not well understood. To investigate how a genome-doubling event affects genome stability over time, we conducted a long-term culture of isogenic tetraploid cells derived from a stable diploid colon cancer progenitor. We found that rare cells that survived genome doubling showed increased tolerance to chromosome aberrations. However, tetraploid cells did not exhibit higher frequencies of structural or numerical CIN per chromosome. Despite this, the tolerant phenotype in tetraploid cells, combined with a doubling of chromosome aberrations per cell, allowed for the specific evolution of chromosome abnormalities in tetraploids, mirroring the chromosomal changes observed in genomically complex colorectal tumors. Additionally, we discovered that a genome-doubling event independently predicted poor relapse-free survival in early-stage disease in two separate cohorts through multivariate analyses [discovery data: hazard ratio (HR), 4.70, 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.04-21.37; validation data: HR, 1.59, 95% CI, 1.05-2.42]. These findings emphasize the significant role of genome doubling tolerance in driving the evolution of cancer genomes. Our study sheds light on the importance of whole-genome doubling events in the evolution of colorectal cancer. We demonstrate that tetraploid cells undergo rapid genomic changes and mirror the genetic alterations observed in chromosomally unstable tumors. Furthermore, we establish that a genome-doubling event is a prognostic factor for poor relapse-free survival in this type of cancer.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Risk Gene CD33 Inhibits Microglial Uptake of Amyloid Beta
text: The protein CD33, which is found in the cell membrane, is a lectin that binds to sialic acid and plays a role in regulating innate immunity. However, its functions in the brain are not yet known. Previous research has shown that the CD33 gene is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). In this study, we observed that CD33 expression is increased in microglial cells in the brains of individuals with AD. The minor allele of a specific CD33 genetic variant, known as rs3865444, provides protection against AD and is associated with lower levels of CD33 expression and insoluble amyloid beta 42 (Aβ42) in the AD brain. Additionally, the number of microglia that show CD33 activity is positively correlated with the levels of insoluble Aβ42 and the amount of amyloid plaques in the AD brain. In laboratory cell cultures, CD33 inhibits the uptake and clearance of Aβ42 by microglial cells. Furthermore, mice that lack the CD33 gene show significantly reduced levels of insoluble Aβ42 and amyloid plaque burden in the brain. Therefore, inactivating CD33 can alleviate Aβ pathology, suggesting that inhibiting CD33 could be a promising therapeutic approach for treating AD.

title: Aluminum fluoride stimulates surface protrusions in cells overexpressing the ARF6 GTPase
text: In order to examine the function of the ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF) 6 GTP-binding protein, we introduced wild-type, epitope-tagged ARF6 into HeLa cells through transfection. Previous studies have shown that ARF6 indirectly activates the ARF1 GTPase. When ARF6-transfected cells were treated with aluminum fluoride (AIF), both ARF6 and actin were redistributed to specific locations on the plasma membrane, which gradually became more protrusive over time. These effects caused by AIF were reversible and specific to cells transfected with wild-type ARF6. Furthermore, they resembled the cellular protrusions observed in cells expressing a mutant form of ARF6 that is defective in GTPase activity. Importantly, the protrusions seen in ARF6-transfected cells were different from the enhanced stress fibers and membrane ruffles observed in cells transfected with RhoA and Rac1, respectively. In cells forming protrusions, there appeared to be an increase in macropinocytosis and membrane recycling within these protrusive structures. However, there was no disruption in transferrin uptake or changes in the distribution of clathrin AP-2 complexes in these cells. The formation of protrusive structures induced by AIF and dependent on ARF6 was inhibited by cytochalasin D and inhibitors of the lipoxygenase pathway. These findings suggest a new role for the ARF6 GTPase in shaping the plasma membrane and the underlying cytoskeleton.

title: A longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging study assessing white matter fiber tracts after sports-related concussion.
text: The severity of structural damage in concussions caused by sports is crucial in determining the recovery process, long-term effects, and the decision to resume playing. In this study, we utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to evaluate the integrity of white matter (WM) fiber tracts within 2 days, 2 weeks, and 2 months after the concussion. The participants were right-handed male varsity athletes involved in contact sports (average age of 20.2±1.0 years) who had been medically diagnosed with a concussion but did not lose consciousness. They were compared to right-handed male varsity athletes participating in non-contact sports, who served as the control group (average age of 19.9±1.7 years). Our findings revealed a significant increase in radial diffusivity (RD) in concussed athletes (n=12) at the 2-day mark, compared to the 2-week post-injury time point (paired t-test, tract-based spatial statistics; p<0.025). This increase was observed in a cluster of voxels in the right hemisphere, spanning the posterior limb of the internal capsule (IC), the retrolenticular part of the IC, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (sagittal stratum), and the anterior thalamic radiation. Further analysis of the cluster using post-hoc, univariate, between-group (controls vs. concussed), mixed-effects analysis showed significantly higher RD at 2 days (p=0.002) compared to the controls, with a trend in the same direction at 2 months (p=0.11). The results for fractional anisotropy (FA) in the same cluster exhibited a similar pattern, but in the opposite direction; FA was decreased at 2 days and at 2 months post-injury, compared to the healthy controls. At 2 weeks post-injury, there were no statistical differences between concussed and control athletes in terms of RD or FA. These findings support the hypothesis that RD increases and FA decreases within 72 hours after the injury, followed by a recovery period that may extend beyond 2 weeks. RD appears to be a sensitive measure of concussive injury.

title: HIV–1 Infects Multipotent Progenitor Cells Causing Cell Death and Establishing Latent Cellular Reservoirs
text: HIV is responsible for a long-lasting infection that leads to a decrease in CD4(+) T lymphocytes and the occurrence of opportunistic infections. Despite the existence of drugs that hinder the spread of the virus, finding a cure for HIV has proven challenging due to unidentified reservoirs of infected cells that are resistant to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and the immune system's response. In this study, we utilized CD34(+) cells obtained from infected individuals and conducted laboratory experiments using wild-type HIV to demonstrate the infection and destruction of CD34(+) multipotent hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs). We also identified latent infection in certain HPCs, which remained stable in cell culture until the activation of viral gene expression by differentiation factors. By employing a unique reporter HIV that directly detects latently infected cells in vitro, we confirmed the presence of distinct populations of active and latently infected HPCs. These findings hold significant implications for comprehending the bone marrow pathology caused by HIV and the mechanisms underlying persistent infection.

title: The human long non-coding RNA-RoR is a p53 repressor in response to DNA damage
text: The elevated level of the tumor suppressor p53 is widely known to occur during times of stress. However, despite extensive research, we still do not fully understand the underlying mechanism that regulates p53 in response to stress. In this study, we provide evidence that a human lincRNA called RoR acts as a strong inhibitor of p53. Unlike MDM2, which degrades p53 through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, RoR suppresses p53 by directly interacting with a protein called hnRNP I. We found that a specific 28-base sequence in RoR, which contains hnRNP I binding motifs, is crucial for repressing p53. Additionally, we discovered that RoR prevents p53 from carrying out its functions in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Furthermore, we observed a feedback loop where p53 actually induces the expression of RoR. These findings suggest that the RoR-hnRNP I-p53 axis may serve as an additional surveillance system in cells to effectively respond to various stresses.

title: Experimental and clinical studies on lactate and pyruvate as indicators of the severity of acute circulatory failure (shock).
text: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between lactate (L) and pyruvate (P) levels in arterial blood during shock states and their role in measuring oxygen deficit and irreversible injury. The researchers used a standardized method to induce hemorrhagic shock in Wistar rats. Over a 4-hour bleeding period, the rat's oxygen consumption decreased to approximately 40% of the control value, pH levels dropped from 7.39 to 7.08, and there was a simultaneous increase in L from 0.80 to 6.06 mm and in P from 0.07 to 0.18 mm. The cumulative oxygen debt showed a correlation with log L (r = 0.50; P < 0.0005) and both were significantly associated with survival. However, the correlation between cumulative oxygen debt and survival, as well as with P and computed values of the lactate pyruvate ratio (L/P) and excess lactate (XL), did not yield higher magnitudes. Partial correlation analysis revealed that measuring P or calculating L/P or XL did not improve predictability.

title: Virtual microdissection identifies distinct tumor- and stroma-specific subtypes of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal disease, with only a 4% 5-year survival rate. One of the challenges in studying PDAC is the extensive involvement of the surrounding stroma, which makes it difficult to obtain precise molecular information specific to the tumor. However, we have successfully addressed this issue by utilizing blind source separation on a diverse collection of PDAC gene expression microarray data, including samples from primary tumors, metastatic sites, and normal tissues. Through this approach, we have been able to digitally separate the gene expression profiles of the tumor, stroma, and normal tissues. As a result, we have identified and validated two distinct tumor subtypes, one of which is a 'basal-like' subtype that exhibits a worse prognosis and shares molecular similarities with basal tumors found in bladder and breast cancers. Additionally, we have defined 'normal' and 'activated' stromal subtypes, both of which have independent prognostic value. These findings offer valuable insights into the molecular makeup of PDAC, which could potentially be utilized to personalize treatment strategies or provide decision support in a clinical setting where the timing and selection of therapies are crucial.

title: Inducible nitric oxide synthase in pulmonary alveolar macrophages from patients with tuberculosis
text: The production of nitric oxide through the high-output pathway is beneficial in protecting mice from various pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. However, there is controversy surrounding whether human mononuclear phagocytes can produce the corresponding inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS; NOS2), as studies on blood-cultured cells have yielded conflicting results. This study aimed to investigate alveolar macrophages obtained directly after bronchopulmonary lavage. The findings revealed that 65% of macrophages from 11 untreated patients with culture-positive pulmonary tuberculosis expressed human NOS2, as confirmed by an antibody specific to NOS2. In contrast, only 10% of bronchoalveolar lavage cells from five clinically normal individuals tested positive. The macrophages of tuberculosis patients also exhibited diaphorase activity in the same proportion as NOS2 staining, indicating a strict dependence on NOS2 expression. Additionally, NOS2 mRNA was detected in bronchoalveolar lavage specimens. Therefore, it can be concluded that macrophages in the lungs of individuals with clinically active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection often express functional NOS2.

title: The use of mouse models to understand and improve cognitive deficits in Down syndrome
text: Significant progress has been achieved in the field of therapeutics for cognitive impairment in individuals with Down syndrome (DS) through the utilization of mouse models. This article provides a concise overview of the characteristics of mouse models that serve as benchmarks for drug testing, the cognitive assessment methods employed to evaluate impairments, and the established mechanisms of action of various drugs currently undergoing preclinical investigations or expected to be tested in clinical trials. The identification of common targets and pathways affected by these diverse drugs in the trisomic brain indicates promising directions for future DS research and the development of effective medications.

title: position-specific gap penalties
text:
The progressive multiple sequence alignment method commonly used for aligning divergent protein sequences has undergone significant improvements in sensitivity. These improvements are achieved through several modifications. 

Firstly, individual weights are assigned to each sequence in a partial alignment. This allows for the down-weighting of near-duplicate sequences and the up-weighting of the most divergent ones. 

Secondly, the amino acid substitution matrices are varied at different stages of the alignment process, depending on the divergence of the sequences being aligned. 

Thirdly, specific penalties for gaps in residues and locally reduced penalties for gaps in hydrophilic regions are implemented. This encourages the creation of new gaps in potential loop regions rather than in regular secondary structures. 

Lastly, positions in early alignments where gaps have been opened receive locally reduced gap penalties. This encourages the creation of new gaps at these positions. 

All of these modifications have been incorporated into a new program called CLUSTAL W, which is freely available for use.

title: Pedestrian Detection via Periodic Motion Analysis
text:
We present algorithms that can detect pedestrians in videos captured by infrared and color sensors. We propose two different approaches based on gait. The first approach utilizes computationally efficient periodicity measurements. Unlike other methods, it estimates the frequency of periodic motion by employing two cascading hypothesis testing steps to filter out non-cyclic pixels.
