This approach works effectively for both radial and lateral walking directions. The extraction of the period is efficient and robust, even in the presence of sensor noise and cluttered backgrounds. 

In the second approach, we integrate shape and motion by converting the cyclic pattern into a binary sequence using Maximal Principal Gait Angle (MPGA) fitting. This method does not require alignment and continuously estimates the period using a Phase-locked Loop. 

We evaluate both methods through experimental results, measuring their performance in terms of size, movement direction, frame rate, and sequence length.

title: Seroepidemiological survey of feline retrovirus infections in cats in Taiwan in 1993 and 1994.
text: To investigate the occurrence of three feline retroviruses (feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), feline leukemia virus (FeLV), and feline syncytial virus (FSV)) in Taiwan, we collected a total of 75 blood samples from cats in veterinary hospitals, a breeding cattery, and a homeless shelter during 1993 and 1994. We utilized indirect immunofluorescence and/or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays to detect the presence of anti-FIV and FSV antibodies, as well as FeLV-p27 antigen in these samples. All FIV-positive serum samples were obtained from homeless cats, resulting in an overall FIV positive rate of 4%. The overall positive rates for FSV and FeLV were 28% and 1.3% respectively. These findings, combined with previous seroepidemiological studies conducted by others, indicate that the prevalence of FIV and FeLV infections in Taiwan appears to be lower compared to the United States or Japan. However, the prevalence of FSV infection in Taiwan is similar to that in Japan.

title: Notch targets and their regulation.
text: Activation of the Notch receptor triggers proteolytic cleavages that result in the release of a fragment called Notch intracellular domain. This fragment then enters the nucleus and activates the transcription of specific targets. The transcriptional changes are a significant outcome of this pathway. However, it is evident that the Notch outputs vary across different cell types. In this review, we explore the current knowledge regarding Notch targets, the mechanisms governing their transcriptional regulation, and the factors that may contribute to the activation of distinct sets of targets in different cell types.

title: Extraction and Analysis of Multiple Periodic Motions in Video Sequences
text: The examination of recurring or repetitive movements has various practical applications, including the identification and categorization of human and animal activities. Current techniques for analyzing periodic motions typically involve extracting motion paths using spatial data and then determining their periodicity. However, these methods often rely on feature matching or spatial correlation, which can be impractical, unreliable, or computationally intensive. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that involves analyzing the video sequence as a whole using time-frequency analysis. This allows us to extract multiple periodic trajectories and estimate their periods simultaneously. We also utilize spatial domain information to identify objects that exhibit periodic movement. Through experiments with both synthetic and real sequences, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

title: MicroRNA-21 is up-regulated in allergic airway inflammation and regulates IL-12p35 expression.
text: The role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in allergic airway inflammation has not been reported yet, despite the significant changes in gene and protein expression that occur in this process. Using a highly sensitive microarray-based approach, we discovered 21 miRNAs with different levels of expression between doxycycline-induced lung-specific IL-13 transgenic mice (with allergic airway inflammation) and control mice. Specifically, we found that miR-21 was overexpressed and miR-1 was underexpressed in the induced IL-13 transgenic mice compared to the control mice. These findings were confirmed in two other models of allergen-induced allergic airway inflammation and in IL-4 lung transgenic mice. While IL-13-induced miR-21 expression depended on IL-13Ralpha1, allergen-induced miR-21 expression was mainly independent of IL-13Ralpha1 and STAT6. Interestingly, predictive algorithms identified potential direct targets of miR-21 among IL-13-regulated lung transcripts, including IL-12p35 mRNA, which was decreased in IL-13 transgenic mice. Introducing pre-miR-21 inhibited the expression of a reporter vector containing the 3'-untranslated region of IL-12p35 in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, mutating the miR-21 binding sites in the IL-12p35 3'-untranslated region prevented miR-21-mediated repression. In conclusion, we have identified a miRNA signature in allergic airway inflammation, which includes miR-21 that regulates IL-12, a molecule important for Th cell polarization.

title: COPD: epidemiology, prevalence, morbidity and mortality, and disease heterogeneity.
text: COPD remains a significant burden on both the health and economy of the United States and the world. The known risk factors for COPD include smoking, exposure to certain occupations, air pollution, airway hyperresponsiveness, asthma, and specific genetic variations. However, there are still many unanswered questions, such as why less than 20% of smokers develop severe airway obstruction. The definition of COPD varies and relies on an accurate diagnosis from a physician, which can greatly impact estimates of the condition in the population. Additionally, it is becoming evident that COPD encompasses various disease processes that may require different interventions. In most parts of the world, the prevalence and mortality of COPD are still increasing, especially among women and adolescents due to increased smoking rates. To combat this significant cause of illness and death, resources should be directed towards smoking cessation and prevention, COPD education and early detection, and improved treatment.

title: Changing geographic ranges of ticks and tick-borne pathogens: drivers, mechanisms and consequences for pathogen diversity
text: Due to global and local environmental changes, the geographic ranges of ticks and tick-borne pathogens are undergoing alterations. In this review, we delve into the current understanding of the factors driving these changes, focusing on their impact on the basic reproduction number (R 0) and the mechanisms of dispersal that enable ticks and tick-borne pathogens to colonize new habitats. By examining the expanding distribution of Lyme disease vectors and agents, we then explore the potential implications for the diversity of tick-borne pathogens during the range expansion process, comparing it to the current observations. Additionally, we investigate how historical population and range expansions and contractions may be reflected in the phylogeography of ticks and tick-borne pathogens in recent years. Ultimately, we propose that a combined study of the changing ranges and diversity of ticks and tick-borne pathogens, along with phylogeographic analysis, could enhance our ability to predict future patterns of invasion and diversity.

title: Mutant KRAS is a druggable target for pancreatic cancer.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is a challenging disease to treat. The mutated KRAS oncogene, which drives PDA, has been considered difficult to target with drugs. However, we propose a new approach using RNA interference to effectively target KRAS in patients. To accomplish this, we have developed a system called Local Drug EluteR (LODER) that delivers siRNA against the mutated KRAS (siG12D LODER) directly to the tumor site. We tested the siG12D LODER in vitro and in vivo to assess its structure, release, and delivery properties. We also evaluated its impact on tumor growth in mouse models, as well as its effect on the KRAS signaling pathway. The siG12D LODER remained stable and active in vivo for 155 days. Treatment with siG12D LODER significantly reduced KRAS levels in PDA cells, leading to inhibition of proliferation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In vivo, siG12D LODER slowed the growth of human pancreatic tumor cells and increased mouse survival. Our study demonstrates a reliable and safe delivery platform using a biodegradable polymeric matrix for controlled and prolonged siRNA release. This technology offers several advantages, including protection of siRNA from degradation, local and sustained release within the tumor, and a therapeutic effect that confirms the druggability of mutated KRAS.

title: Trimmomatic: a flexible trimmer for Illumina sequence data
text:
We were unable to find any existing next-generation sequencing (NGS) read preprocessing tools that met our requirements for flexibility, accurate handling of paired-end data, and high performance. As a result, we developed Trimmomatic, a more flexible and efficient preprocessing tool that can properly handle paired-end data. 

In our study, we demonstrate the importance of NGS read preprocessing for both reference-based and reference-free tasks. Trimmomatic consistently produces output that is at least comparable to, and often superior to, that of other tools in all tested scenarios. 

Trimmomatic is licensed under GPL V3 and is available for use on any platform that supports Java 1.5+. It can be accessed at http://www.usadellab.org/cms/index.php?page=trimmomatic. For further inquiries, please contact usadel@bio1.rwth-aachen.de. 

Supplementary data can be found at Bioinformatics online.

title: Basics of PD-1 in self-tolerance, infection, and cancer immunity
text: Understanding the immune response of the host against tumor cells is crucial for successful cancer treatment. PD-1 is a receptor belonging to the CD28 superfamily, acting as an immune activation "checkpoint." It plays a role in maintaining immune self-tolerance to prevent autoimmunity and regulates T-cell response during infection to avoid excessive tissue damage. Tumor cells, originating from normal tissue, acquire mutations that can be targeted by lymphocytes. However, evidence suggests that tumor cells evade the host immune system by expressing PD-1 ligands and activating PD-1 on lymphocytes. Researchers have shown that administering monoclonal antibodies that inhibit the binding of PD-1 to its ligands can reactivate T cells and enhance the immune response against cancer. This review provides an overview of T-cell biology, the regulation of T cells by PD-1, and explores the current understanding and unanswered questions surrounding this complex molecule.

title: Dissociation of β1- and β2-adrenergic receptor subtypes in the retrieval of cocaine-associated memory.
text: The maintenance of drug-seeking behavior is influenced by encounters with cues associated with drug use. Disrupting the retrieval of these drug-cue associations can reduce the risk of relapse. The retrieval of memories associated with cocaine use relies on the activation of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs), and blocking these receptors leads to a persistent deficit in retrieval. However, it is still unclear whether a specific subtype of β-AR is responsible for the retrieval of cocaine-associated memories. To investigate this, we conducted a study using a cocaine conditioned place preference (CPP) procedure. We aimed to determine whether the retrieval of a cocaine CPP memory is collectively mediated by both β1- and β2-ARs or by one subtype alone. Our results showed that blocking both β1- and β2-ARs together eliminated the expression of CPP during drug-free tests, leading to a long-lasting deficit in retrieval that prevented subsequent cocaine-induced reinstatement. To further understand the necessity of either β1- or β2-ARs alone, we administered subtype-specific antagonists before retrieval. The administration of a β1-AR antagonist before the initial CPP trial dose-dependently reduced the expression of CPP compared to vehicle administration. On the other hand, the administration of a β2-AR antagonist had no effect on the initial expression of CPP, although the highest dose reduced subsequent CPP expression. Importantly, blocking either β1- or β2-ARs before an initial retrieval trial prevented subsequent cocaine-induced reinstatement. Our findings suggest that the β1-AR subtype is responsible for the retrieval of a cocaine CPP, and blocking either β1- or β2-ARs can effectively prevent cocaine-induced reinstatement. Therefore, β-AR antagonists, particularly β1-AR antagonists, could be used as adjuncts in addiction therapies to prevent the retrieval of drug-associated memories and provide protection against relapse.

title: Podoplanin-Rich Stromal Networks Induce Dendritic Cell Motility via Activation of the C-type Lectin Receptor CLEC-2
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) initiate adaptive immunity by moving from parenchymal tissues to lymphoid organs. They do this by migrating along stromal scaffolds that display a glycoprotein called podoplanin (PDPN). PDPN is expressed by lymphatic endothelial and fibroblastic reticular cells and plays a role in separating blood and lymph during development. It does this by activating a receptor called CLEC-2 on platelets. In this study, we explore the role of CLEC-2 in the behavior and movement of DCs. We found that DCs lacking CLEC-2 had difficulty entering lymphatics and moving within lymph nodes, which resulted in reduced T cell priming. Engagement of PDPN by CLEC-2 was necessary for DCs to spread and migrate along stromal surfaces. It was also sufficient to induce membrane protrusions. Activation of CLEC-2 triggered cell spreading by reducing RhoA activity and myosin light-chain phosphorylation. It also triggered the formation of F-actin-rich protrusions through Vav signaling and Rac1 activation. In summary, activation of CLEC-2 by PDPN rearranges the actin cytoskeleton in DCs, promoting efficient movement along stromal surfaces.

title: The Public Health Responsibility Deal: brokering a deal for public health, but on whose terms?
text:
Coalitions of multinational food and drink businesses have made a commitment to reformulate their products and promote responsible marketing. However, there are concerns about the credibility of these voluntary initiatives, which are primarily led and regulated by the industry itself. In contrast, the Public Health Responsibility Deal in England is a government-led voluntary initiative. This raises the question of whether public leadership can lead to meaningful results for public health through voluntary actions. 

The research focuses on the calorie reduction initiative of the Responsibility Deal. The information for the study was primarily obtained through Freedom of Information requests in the UK. It includes previously unpublished documents from the Department of Health, which relate to meetings held in 2011 and 2012. 

The results show that the Responsibility Deal involves the food industry in determining the measures for calorie reduction, such as reformulation and portion control. However, this approach compromises public health objectives and hinders proper monitoring and evaluation. 

In conclusion, the Responsibility Deal approach is flawed because it expects the industry to prioritize public health over its own interests through voluntary actions. Being government-led is not enough without enforcement measures to ensure compliance. Instead, this initiative allows private interests to influence public health policies and strategies that impact their products in their favor.

title: Role of endothelial shear stress in the natural history of coronary atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling: molecular, cellular, and vascular behavior.
text: Although the entire coronary tree is exposed to the harmful effects of systemic risk factors, atherosclerotic lesions tend to form in specific areas of the arteries where there is low and irregular endothelial shear stress (ESS). Low ESS affects the expression of genes in the endothelial cells through complex mechanoreception and mechanotransduction processes, leading to the development of an atherogenic endothelial phenotype and the formation of early atherosclerotic plaques. Each early plaque has its own unique progression, regression, or stabilization pattern, which depends not only on the development and advancement of atherosclerosis but also on the response of the blood vessels to remodeling. Although we do not fully understand the mechanisms involved in the remodeling of the atherosclerotic wall, it is likely that the dynamic interaction between the local hemodynamic environment, particularly low ESS, and the biology of the arterial wall plays a significant role. In this review, we delve into the molecular, cellular, and vascular processes that support the role of low ESS in the natural progression of coronary atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling. We also discuss potential mechanisms that explain the different progression patterns of individual coronary lesions. Atherosclerotic plaques that undergo excessive expansive remodeling become high-risk plaques because the conditions of low ESS persist, leading to continued accumulation of lipids, inflammation, oxidative stress, breakdown of the extracellular matrix, and ultimately further progression and excessive expansive remodeling of the plaque. By gaining a better understanding of the pathological processes responsible for atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling, we may be able to identify high-risk coronary plaques at an early stage, which could pave the way for innovative diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for the management of coronary patients and the prevention of acute coronary syndromes.

title: Schistosoma mansoni worms induce anergy of T cells via selective up-regulation of programmed death ligand 1 on macrophages.
text: The survival of infectious pathogens within humans can be facilitated by selectively stimulating the activation or suppression of T cells. In this study, we have discovered that the trematode parasite Schistosoma mansoni has developed two distinct mechanisms to suppress T cell activation. During the initial 4- to 12-week acute stages of a worm infection, both CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells become anergized. However, infection with male and female worms induces T cell anergy at 4 weeks, which is then replaced by T cell suppression via a known NO-dependent mechanism after egg laying. This suppression can be detected for up to 40 weeks after infection. The anergy induced by the worms is mediated by splenic F4/80(+) macrophages (Mphi) through a mechanism that is independent of IL-4, IL-13, IL-10, TGF-beta, and NO, but dependent on cell contact. In vitro experiments have shown that F4/80(+) Mphi isolated from worm-infected mice can induce anergy in naive T cells. Additionally, naive Mphi exposed to live worms in vitro also induce anergy in naive T cells. Flow cytometry analysis of worm-modulated Mphi, both in vivo and in vitro, has revealed that only programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) among the B7 costimulatory molecules is selectively up-regulated. Blocking PD-L1 with inhibitory antibodies, but not PD-L2, completely prevents the ability of worm-modulated Mphi to induce T cell anergy. These findings demonstrate a novel mechanism by which S. mansoni worms exploit PD-L1 to reduce T cell activation during the early acute stages of infection, before the emergence of egg-induced T cell suppression in the chronic stages of infection.

title: Thawing Frozen Robust Multi-array Analysis (fRMA)
text:
INTRODUCTION
A new method called Frozen Robust Multi-array Analysis (fRMA) has been developed for microarray preprocessing. This method offers the advantage of multi-array preprocessing while allowing individual array preprocessing. However, the generation of frozen parameter estimates required by this algorithm is time-consuming and relies on a large database of publicly available arrays. As a result, fRMA has only been implemented on widely used Affymetrix platforms.

RESULTS
We have developed an R package called frmaTools, which enables users to quickly create their own frozen parameter vectors. In this study, we explain how this package fits into a preprocessing workflow and investigate the necessary size of the training dataset to generate reliable frozen parameter estimates. Additionally, we discuss specific scenarios where users may prefer to create their own fRMA implementation. We demonstrate that fRMA performs well in certain situations, even when a large database of arrays is not available.

CONCLUSIONS
The frmaTools package significantly enhances the applicability of the fRMA algorithm by allowing users to easily create their own fRMA implementation. This package is freely accessible as part of the Bioconductor project.

title: Transcriptional repressor Blimp-1 is essential for T cell homeostasis and self-tolerance
text: Maintaining T cell balance is crucial for a properly functioning immune system. When regulatory T cells are lacking or the ability to control immune responses is compromised, an excess of T cells can accumulate, leading to inflammation and autoimmune disorders. In our study, we discovered that Blimp-1, a transcriptional repressor known as a 'master regulator' of B cell maturation, is also expressed in a specific subset of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that have encountered antigens before. By using fetal liver stem cells that expressed a mutated form of Blimp-1 lacking the DNA-binding domain, we observed that mice developed a severe inflammatory disease affecting multiple organs. This was caused by an excessive buildup of effector and memory T cells. These findings highlight the critical role of Blimp-1 in maintaining T cell balance and suggest that it plays a role in regulating both B cell and T cell maturation.

title: Nuclear repositioning of the VSG promoter during developmental silencing in Trypanosoma brucei
text: The positioning of chromosomes within the nucleus during interphase has been linked to the epigenetic control of RNA polymerase (pol) II transcription. However, there is limited knowledge regarding the regulation of RNA pol I-transcribed loci based on nuclear position. To address this question, the parasite Trypanosoma brucei serves as an ideal model system. This is because its two primary surface protein genes, procyclin and variant surface glycoprotein (VSG), are transcribed by pol I and undergo distinct activation or downregulation events during developmental differentiation. While the VSG locus, which is expressed from a single allele, is exclusively found in an extranucleolar body in the bloodstream form, our study reveals that the procyclin genes, which are not mutually exclusive, are located at the periphery of the nucleolus. Interestingly, the loci responsible for ribosomal DNA and pol I transcription activity are also found in similar positions near the nucleolus. However, when transcription is downregulated during development, the active VSG promoter rapidly and dramatically relocates to the nuclear envelope. Subsequently, the VSG promoter region undergoes chromatin condensation. We propose a model in which the pol I promoter of the VSG expression site is selectively targeted for temporal nuclear repositioning during developmental silencing.

title: An administrative claims measure suitable for profiling hospital performance on the basis of 30-day all-cause readmission rates among patients with heart failure.
text:
BACKGROUND: Hospital readmission shortly after discharge is a costly and avoidable occurrence for patients with heart failure. We present a model, approved by the National Quality Forum, that allows for public reporting of hospital-level readmission rates by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We developed a hierarchical logistic regression model to calculate risk-standardized 30-day all-cause readmission rates for patients hospitalized with heart failure. The model was created using Medicare claims data from a 2004 cohort and validated using claims and medical record data. The unadjusted readmission rate was 23.6%. The final model included 37 variables and had a discrimination range of 15% to 37% for observed 30-day readmission rates. The model's c statistic was 0.60. The risk-standardized readmission rates across 4669 hospitals ranged from 23.1% to 24.0% for the 25th and 75th percentiles, and from 22.2% to 25.1% for the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively. The odds of all-cause readmission for a hospital 1 standard deviation above average was 1.30 times that of a hospital 1 standard deviation below average. State-level adjusted readmission rates, developed using the claims model, were similar to rates produced using a medical record model for the same cohort (correlation, 0.97; median difference, 0.06 percentage points).

CONCLUSIONS: This claims-based model for hospital risk-standardized readmission rates in heart failure patients provides estimates that can be used as substitutes for those derived from a medical record model.

title: Queueing up for enzymatic processing: correlated signaling through coupled degradation
text: The advancement of high-throughput technologies has resulted in the creation of intricate wiring diagrams that depict the interactions between various cellular species. While these diagrams are valuable for studying biological systems on a large scale, it is crucial to have a detailed comprehension of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the observed network connections in order to further develop systems and synthetic biology. In this study, we utilize queueing theory to explore how "waiting lines" can cause correlations between protein "customers" that are only connected through a downstream group of enzymatic "servers". By using the E. coli ClpXP degradation machine as a model system, we discover significant communication between two networks that are indirectly linked through a shared set of processors. Additionally, we demonstrate the implications of enzymatic queueing through a synthetic biology application, where two independent synthetic networks exhibit synchronized behavior when the common ClpXP machinery is overwhelmed. Our findings highlight that such post-translational processes can establish dynamic connections in cellular networks and potentially offer a mechanistic explanation for existing yet unexplained links.

title: The histone demethylases Jhdm1a/1b enhance somatic cell reprogramming in a vitamin-C-dependent manner.
text: The epigenome can be reset to an embryonic-like state by reprogramming somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). The reprogramming process can be enhanced by vitamin C, although the mechanisms behind this are not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the histone demethylases Jhdm1a/1b play a crucial role in somatic cell reprogramming following vitamin C treatment. Initially, we observed that vitamin C induces demethylation of H3K36me2/3 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts both in culture and during reprogramming. Subsequently, through gain- and loss-of-function experiments, we identified Jhdm1a/1b as potent regulators of reprogramming. Additionally, we discovered that Jhdm1b promotes cell cycle progression and inhibits cell senescence during reprogramming by suppressing the Ink4/Arf locus. Furthermore, Jhdm1b collaborates with Oct4 to activate the microRNA cluster 302/367, which is essential for maintaining pluripotency. These findings highlight the significance of H3K36me2/3 in determining cell fate and establish a connection between histone demethylases and vitamin C-induced reprogramming.

title: Preexisting helminth infection induces inhibition of innate pulmonary anti-tuberculosis defense by engaging the IL-4 receptor pathway
text: The coexistence of tuberculosis and helminthic infections is common in many parts of the world. However, the impact of helminth-induced Th2 responses on the host's ability to control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection has not been fully investigated. Our study demonstrates that mice infected with the intestinal helminth Nippostrongylus brasiliensis (Nb) experience a temporary decrease in resistance to airborne Mtb infection. Additionally, a second Nb infection significantly increases the bacterial burden in the lungs of co-infected mice. Interestingly, the Th2 response in these co-infected animals does not hinder the initiation and development of protective Mtb-specific Th1 cellular immune responses. However, the helminth-induced Th2 environment leads to the accumulation of alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) in the lungs. Co-infected mice lacking interleukin (IL) 4Rα exhibit an improved ability to control Mtb infection, accompanied by a significant reduction in AAM accumulation. Furthermore, IL-4Rα(-/-) mice that receive wild-type macrophages through adoptive transfer have a higher Mtb load in their lungs compared to those receiving IL-4Rα(-/-) macrophages, suggesting that the IL-4R pathway directly contributes to the increased susceptibility of co-infected animals. Therefore, the Th2 response can enhance the intracellular persistence of Mtb by promoting the alternative activation of macrophages through the IL-4Rα signaling pathway.

title: Archaea in biogeochemical cycles.
text: Archaea make up a significant portion of the microbial biomass found on Earth. Similar to Bacteria, they have developed various ways to obtain energy by using organic and/or inorganic substances as electron donors and acceptors. Additionally, many Archaea are capable of extracting carbon from inorganic sources. As a result, Archaea play vital roles in the Earth's global geochemical cycles and have an impact on greenhouse gas emissions. Methanogenesis and anaerobic methane oxidation are crucial steps in the carbon cycle, and both are exclusively carried out by anaerobic Archaea. Thaumarchaeota are responsible for the oxidation of ammonia to nitrite and are the only group of Archaea that exist in large numbers in aerobic terrestrial and marine environments worldwide. Sulfur-dependent Archaea are mainly found in hot environments, but acidophiles that leach metals and anaerobic, nonthermophilic methane oxidizers that reduce sulfate have the potential to affect the environment. The metabolic processes of numerous Archaea, especially those dominant in the subsurface, are still waiting to be explored.

title: Novel proteinaceous infectious particles cause scrapie.
text: After being infected and going through a long period of incubation, the scrapie agent triggers a degenerative disease in the central nervous system of sheep and goats. There are six lines of evidence, including sensitivity to proteases, that indicate this agent contains a necessary protein for infectivity. While alkali can permanently deactivate the scrapie agent, five procedures aimed at modifying nucleic acids failed to achieve the same result. The agent displays heterogeneity in size, likely due to its hydrophobic nature, with the smallest form potentially weighing 50,000 or less. Given that the scrapie agent possesses unique characteristics that differentiate it from viruses, plasmids, and viroids, a new term "prion" is suggested to describe this small proteinaceous infectious particle that is resistant to most nucleic acid-modifying procedures. Understanding the structure of the scrapie agent could hold significance in comprehending the causes of various degenerative diseases.

title: Viral Carcinogenesis.
text: Cancer has been acknowledged for millennia. The ancient Egyptians believed that cancer was caused by the gods. Hippocrates, on the other hand, believed that an imbalance of the four humors - blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile - led to human diseases, with cancer being a result of excess black bile. The humoral theory was later replaced by the lymph theory of cancer, which was then replaced by the blastema theory. Rudolph Virchow was the first to realize that cancer cells, like all cells, originated from other cells, and he believed that chronic irritation was the cause of cancer. At the same time, there was a belief that trauma could cause cancer, but this theory did not progress after numerous experiments inducing trauma. The field of virology was born in 1892 when Dimitri Ivanofsky demonstrated that diseased tobacco plants remained infectious even after their sap was filtered to trap bacteria. Martinus Beijerinck named the tiny infectious agent a virus, and both Ivanofsky and Beijerinck are considered the fathers of virology. Shortly after, in 1911, Payton Rous discovered a transmittable sarcoma in chickens, which later became known as Rous sarcoma virus or RSV, founding the field of tumor virology. The first identified human tumor virus was the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), named after Tony Epstein and Yvonne Barr, who visualized the virus particles in Burkitt's lymphoma cells using electron microscopy in 1965. Since then, many viruses have been linked to carcinogenesis, including the well-studied human papilloma virus, which is associated with cervical carcinoma, anogenital carcinomas, and oropharyngeal carcinoma. The World Health Organization estimates that approximately 22% of worldwide cancers are caused by infectious agents, with viral etiologies accounting for 15-20% of these cases. The field of tumor virology/viral carcinogenesis has not only identified viruses as causes of human cancers but has also provided molecular insights into all types of human cancers, including the activation of oncogenes and the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes.

title: Monitoring spatiotemporal biogenesis of macromolecular assemblies by pulse-chase epitope labeling.
text:
Understanding how multiprotein complexes form is a crucial question in cell biology, as many cellular proteins carry out their functions within these assemblies. To address this, we have developed a translation-controlled pulse-chase system that enables us to isolate newly forming multiprotein complexes at specific time points. This system allows us to obtain sufficient quantities of these complexes for biochemical and cell biological analysis. 

In our approach, we initiate the "pulse" by using an unnatural amino acid that triggers immediate translation of a specific mRNA encoding the protein of interest. This mRNA is designed with a built-in tag for easy detection and purification. Subsequently, we induce the "chase" phase by halting the translation of the bait protein using a riboswitch in the corresponding mRNA. 

During the validation of our method, we made an interesting discovery. We observed a distinct time-resolved assembly step in the biogenesis of nuclear pore complexes (NPCs). Additionally, we were able to directly monitor the spatiotemporal maturation of preribosomes by using immunofluorescence detection and purification of a pulse-labeled ribosomal protein. 

Overall, our innovative strategy provides a valuable tool for studying the dynamic assembly of proteins within cellular networks.

title: Statins in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
text:
The use of statins to lower the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) is well-established and supported by evidence. While they are widely used for secondary prevention in individuals with CVD, there are concerns about their expanding use in primary prevention for those without documented CVD. 

Firstly, research suggests that statins significantly reduce the occurrence of CVD in primary prevention, but their impact on reducing CVD mortality is only moderate. Secondly, there is a possibility of adverse effects, such as the development of diabetes mellitus, with long-term use of statins. 

Additionally, the cost-effectiveness of using statins for primary prevention is uncertain, and the potential risk of overmedicating the general population needs to be considered. However, data clearly support the use of statins for primary prevention in high-risk individuals, where the benefits outweigh the risks and it is cost-effective. 

The effectiveness of primary prevention in individuals at low or moderate risk is still uncertain. Therefore, the decision to prescribe statins for primary prevention should be based on individual clinical judgment, especially for those at low risk. 

In appropriately selected individuals, statins should also be considered for primary prevention of ischaemic stroke and transient ischaemic attack.

title: Acetylation of apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1 regulates Helicobacter pylori-mediated gastric epithelial cell apoptosis.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of Helicobacter pylori infection and acetylation of Apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1 (APE-1) on gastric epithelial cell (GEC) apoptosis. It is known that H. pylori-induced GEC apoptosis involves activation of the tumor suppressor p53, as well as bax transcription and cytochrome c release from mitochondria. APE-1 regulates the transcriptional activity of p53, and H. pylori infection induces APE-1 expression in human GECs. Additionally, H. pylori infection increases intracellular calcium ion concentration ([Ca2+]i) in GECs, which leads to APE-1 acetylation. 

To investigate these effects, AGS cells (with or without suppressed APE-1), KATO III cells, and cells isolated from gastric biopsy specimens were infected with H. pylori. Various assays were performed, including immunoblotting, real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence microscopy, chromatin immunoprecipitation, mobility shift, DNA binding, and luciferase assays. 

The results showed that H. pylori infection increased [Ca2+]i and acetylation of APE-1 in GECs. However, the acetylation status of APE-1 did not affect the transcriptional activity of p53. In GECs, expression of a non-acetylatable form of APE-1 increased levels of Bax, both total and mitochondrial, and induced release of cytochrome c and DNA fragmentation. On the other hand, expression of wild-type APE-1 reduced these apoptotic events. 

Furthermore, a negative calcium response element was identified in the human bax promoter, and it was found that poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase 1 recruited the acetylated APE-1/histone deacetylase-1 repressor complex to this element. 

In conclusion, H. pylori-mediated acetylation of APE-1 suppresses Bax expression, thereby preventing p53-mediated apoptosis in H. pylori-infected GECs.

title: A beginning of the end: new insights into the functional organization of telomeres
text: Researchers have been fascinated by telomeres ever since they were first discovered to have a repetitive sequence and a unique replication pathway. Over the years, we have learned a great deal about how telomeres function in protecting the ends of chromosomes. We now know that telomeres are made up of a complex of proteins and DNA called shelterin, and that the formation of t-loops helps to shield them from damage. T-loops are created when the 3' overhang of telomeric repeats is inserted into the sequence with the help of a protein called TRF2. Recent studies have revealed new types of chromosome end-structures that suggest telomere organization may play a role in cellular processes beyond just protecting telomeres. One such structure, which we have named interstitial telomere loops (ITLs), forms in a TRF2-dependent manner at interstitial telomere repeat sequences. These ITLs also rely on the presence of lamin A/C, a protein that is part of the nucleoskeleton and is associated with various human diseases, including progeroid syndromes. Our research suggests a connection between cellular aging (caused by telomere shortening) and organismal aging (represented by Hutchinson Gilford Progeria Syndrome) through the formation of ITLs. In this article, we speculate on other potential effects of ITL formation, such as its impact on gene expression, genome stability, and chromosome structure.

title: Biochemical analysis of TssK, a core component of the bacterial Type VI secretion system, reveals distinct oligomeric states of TssK and identifies a TssK–TssFG subcomplex
text: The Type VI secretion system (T6SS) is utilized by Gram-negative bacteria to inject toxic proteins into rival bacteria or eukaryotic cells. However, there is still much to learn about how the T6SS functions. In this study, we focused on TssK, a conserved component of the T6SS, using the antibacterial T6SS of Serratia marcescens as a model. We confirmed that TssK is necessary for effector secretion by the T6SS. Although TssK is not an integral membrane protein, it was found to localize to the inner membrane, suggesting its presence within a membrane-anchored assembly. We purified recombinant TssK from S. marcescens and discovered that it exists in various stable oligomeric forms, including trimers, hexamers, and higher-order species. Through native-level purification of TssK, we identified TssF and TssG as interacting proteins. While TssF and TssG are conserved T6SS components with unknown functions, we found that they are necessary for T6SS activity but not for the proper localization of TssK. We subsequently purified a complex containing TssK, TssF, and TssG in vitro, confirming that these three proteins form a new subcomplex within the T6SS. Based on our findings, we propose a model in which TssK recruits TssFG into the membrane-associated T6SS complex, and the different oligomeric states of TssK may contribute to the dynamic mechanism of the system.

title: Involvement of ER Stress in Dysmyelination of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease with PLP1 Missense Mutations Shown by iPSC-Derived Oligodendrocytes
text: The disease known as Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is a type of X-linked leukodystrophy that arises from mutations in the proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1) gene. While it has been observed that PLP1 proteins with missense mutations tend to accumulate in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in animal models and cell lines transfected with mutant PLP1 genes, the precise mechanism behind the development of PMD has not been fully understood until now. This study aimed to shed light on this matter by creating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from two PMD patients who carried the missense mutation and then differentiating these cells into oligodendrocytes in a laboratory setting. The researchers discovered that in the PMD iPSC-derived oligodendrocytes, the mutant PLP1 proteins were mislocalized to the ER. They also observed a connection between an increased susceptibility to ER stress and a higher number of apoptotic oligodendrocytes. Additionally, electron microscopy revealed a significant reduction in myelin formation accompanied by abnormal ER morphology. Consequently, this study provides evidence that ER stress plays a role in the pathogenic dysmyelination observed in the oligodendrocytes of PMD patients with the PLP1 missense mutation.

title: Using Routine Surveillance Data to Estimate the Epidemic Potential of Emerging Zoonoses: Application to the Emergence of US Swine Origin Influenza A H3N2v Virus
text:
BACKGROUND
Before zoonotic diseases like SARS appear in human populations, they occasionally infect individuals who have been exposed to reservoir species. The risk of widespread epidemics in humans can be determined by monitoring the reproduction number R, which is the average number of people infected by each human case. However, estimating R has traditionally required detailed investigations of human clusters, which can be resource-intensive and may not always be feasible. Additionally, existing methods do not account for important biases in selection and under-ascertainment. In this study, we present simple estimation methods that address these limitations.

METHODS AND FINDINGS
Our approach is based on a simple mathematical model of disease transmission and only requires data collected through routine surveillance and standard case investigations. We apply this approach to assess the transmissibility of swine-origin influenza A H3N2v-M virus in the US, Nipah virus in Malaysia and Bangladesh, and also provide a non-zoonotic example with cholera in the Dominican Republic. Estimation is based on two summary statistics: the proportion of detected cases that were infected by the natural reservoir (G), and the proportion of the first detected cases in each cluster that were infected (F). If the detection of one case does not affect the detection of other cases in the same cluster, we find that R can be estimated by 1-G. If the case detection rate is low, R can be estimated by 1-F. In more complex cases, we can still derive bounds on R.

CONCLUSIONS
We have developed a simple approach that requires minimal data and allows for robust assessment of the risks posed by emerging zoonotic diseases. We demonstrate this by estimating the transmissibility of the H3N2v-M virus, which is an important step in evaluating its potential as a pandemic threat. Please refer to the Editors' Summary for more information.

title: Independently Evolving Species in Asexual Bdelloid Rotifers
text: Asexual individuals provide a valuable opportunity to examine the reasons behind the existence of different species. If asexual groups showed the same distinct variations as sexual groups, it would challenge the traditional belief that sexual reproduction is necessary for species diversification. However, previous evidence has been insufficient, as all potential examples involved organisms that had recently or currently engaged in recombination. Additionally, these examples relied on visual interpretation of genetic and physical variations, rather than formal tests of alternative evolutionary scenarios. In this study, we present evidence that a well-known asexual group, the bdelloid rotifers, has indeed diversified into separate evolutionary species. Through extensive sampling of the Rotaria genus, we discovered distinct genetic clusters that indicate independent evolution. Furthermore, by combining genetic and physical analyses, we observed divergent selection in feeding morphology, suggesting niche divergence. Some of these distinct morphological groups, which experienced divergent selection, contained multiple genetic clusters, similar to the discovery of hidden species in sexual organisms. Our findings demonstrate that the primary factors driving speciation in sexual organisms, such as population isolation and divergent selection, have similar effects in asexual groups. Moreover, this study highlights how a combination of molecular and physical analyses can provide new insights into the evolutionary nature of species.

title: The Ribosome Biogenesis Factor Nol11 Is Required for Optimal rDNA Transcription and Craniofacial Development in Xenopus
text: The production of ribosomes is essential for all living organisms, which makes it surprising that defects in ribosome biogenesis are responsible for a growing number of inherited disorders known as ribosomopathies. In previous research, we discovered that a protein called NOL11 plays a crucial role in the transcription and processing of ribosomal RNA in human tissue culture cells. However, we still don't know how NOL11 contributes to the development of multicellular organisms. In this study, we uncover an important function of NOL11 in the formation of ribosomes and the development of the craniofacial region in vertebrates. We observe high levels of Nol11 expression in the developing cranial neural crest of amphibians and mammals. When we reduce the levels of Nol11 in Xenopus frogs, we observe impaired ribosomal RNA transcription and processing, increased cell death, and abnormal development of the craniofacial cartilages. Interestingly, inhibiting a protein called p53 rescues the skeletal abnormalities but not the underlying ribosome biogenesis defect. This suggests that there is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that eliminates craniofacial cells with impaired ribosomes. However, excessive activation of this mechanism hinders craniofacial development. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of Nol11 in craniofacial development, provide a new frog model for studying ribosomopathies, and offer insights into the relationship between ribosome biogenesis proteins and the survival of craniofacial cells, which has clinical implications.

title: Genomic Nucleosome Organization Reconstituted with Pure Proteins
text: The regulation of genes by chromatin remodelers, which organize nucleosomes around promoters, is a complex process that is difficult to understand due to factors such as redundancy and indirect effects in the in vivo environment. To overcome this problem, it is crucial to reconstruct the organization of promoter nucleosomes using purified proteins on a genome-wide scale. In this study, we successfully reconstituted four stages of nucleosome architecture using purified components, including yeast genomic DNA, histones, sequence-specific Abf1/Reb1, and remodelers RSC, ISW2, INO80, and ISW1a. Through this reconstitution, we were able to identify direct, specific, and sufficient contributions that were validated by in vivo observations. Firstly, RSC was found to clear promoters by removing nucleosomes in a directional manner through the translation of poly(dA:dT). Secondly, we observed partial redundancy, where INO80 alone or ISW2 at Abf1/Reb1 sites positioned +1 nucleosomes. Thirdly, both INO80 and ISW2 were found to align downstream nucleosomal arrays. Lastly, ISW1a was responsible for tightening the spacing between nucleosomes to canonical repeat lengths. These findings demonstrate that a minimal set of rules and proteins can establish the core mechanisms by which promoter chromatin architecture is formed through a combination of redundancy and specialization.

title: Identification of splenic reservoir monocytes and their deployment to inflammatory sites.
text: According to the current belief, monocytes freely circulate and patrol blood vessels, but once they enter tissues, they irreversibly differentiate into dendritic cells (DCs) or macrophages. However, our research reveals that undifferentiated monocytes actually reside in the spleen and outnumber those found in circulation. These monocytes form clusters in the cords of the subcapsular red pulp and are distinct from macrophages and DCs. When there is ischemic myocardial injury, the motility of splenic monocytes increases. They then leave the spleen in large numbers, accumulate in the injured tissue, and contribute to the healing process. These findings demonstrate that the spleen serves as a storage site for monocytes and allows for their rapid deployment. Additionally, splenic monocytes are identified as a valuable resource that the body utilizes to regulate inflammation.

title: Prox1 Is Required for Granule Cell Maturation and Intermediate Progenitor Maintenance During Brain Neurogenesis
text: The dentate gyrus plays a crucial role in the process of learning and memory. It has been suggested that adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus may contribute to the formation of new memories. During embryonic development and adult neurogenesis, the homeobox gene Prox1 is expressed in the dentate gyrus. Our study reveals that Prox1 is essential for the development of granule cells in the dentate gyrus and the maintenance of intermediate progenitors during adult neurogenesis. Additionally, we have discovered that Prox1-expressing intermediate progenitors are necessary for the self-maintenance of adult neural stem cells in the subgranular zone. This finding uncovers a previously unknown regulatory feedback mechanism that controls adult neurogenesis in this specific region of the mammalian brain. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the premature differentiation of neural stem cells can be induced by the ectopic expression of Prox1.

title: The abbreviated pluripotent cell cycle.
text: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells have a rapid and symmetrical cell division process, resulting in identical progeny cells. On the other hand, lineage committed cells have a longer and symmetrical cell cycle, where one progeny cell remains a progenitor while the other differentiates. The pluripotent cell cycle can be understood in three main contexts: temporal, regulatory, and structural. In the temporal context, the self-renewal cell cycle of hESCs has a short G1 period without reducing the time allocated to S phase, G2, and mitosis. The rules governing proliferation in hESCs are not fully understood, but evidence suggests that the naïve transcriptome of hESCs plays a crucial role in regulating the cell cycle. This allows pluripotent cells to self-propagate while suppressing the expression of genes related to lineage commitment and tissue specificity. Additionally, the architectural organization and assembly of regulatory machinery in nuclear microenvironments play a unique role in defining pluripotency parameters. Understanding the control of the abbreviated ESC cycle can have both biological and clinical implications, such as coordinating proliferation and differentiation in wound healing, tissue engineering, and cell-based therapy to address developmental abnormalities.

title: Senescent growth arrest in mesenchymal stem cells is bypassed by Wip1-mediated downregulation of intrinsic stress signaling pathways.
text: The growth arrest of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) cultured in vitro has been a major obstacle in studying these cells for cell therapy. This growth arrest, also known as "premature senescence," hampers the ability to genetically modify the cells for desired tissue differentiation. The molecular mechanisms behind this phenomenon are not fully understood, except for a few studies that have shown the involvement of p16INK4a induction. In our study, we observed that the premature growth arrest in hMSCs is accompanied by the induction of p16INK4a, which occurs when inhibitory phosphorylation of retinoblastoma protein is disrupted. This stress response is also associated with increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROSs) from mitochondria and increased activity of p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK). By introducing Wip1, a stress modulator, we were able to reduce p16INK4a expression and deactivate p38 MAPK, thereby extending the lifespan of hMSCs and maintaining their ability to differentiate into multiple cell types. These findings suggest that the senescent growth arrest in hMSCs may be caused by activation of stress signaling pathways and subsequent stress responses, partly due to ROS production during prolonged in vitro culture.

title: Understanding the Odd Science of Aging
text: The concept of evolution implies that aging is not a result of intentional gene programming, but rather a consequence of inherent limitations in the maintenance of our bodies, leading to the accumulation of damage over time. Various ecological factors, such as the likelihood of encountering dangers and the availability of food, play a role in determining the balance between investing in growth, reproduction, and the preservation of our bodies. This explains why different species have evolved different lifespans and why the rate of aging can sometimes be influenced, for instance, through dietary restrictions. To comprehend the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying aging means to unravel the multitude of processes that contribute to the accumulation of damage, as well as the intricate network of systems that work to counteract this damage.

title: Fate mapping reveals origins and dynamics of monocytes and tissue macrophages under homeostasis.
text: Mononuclear phagocytes, such as monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, play a crucial role in maintaining tissue integrity and defending against both innate and adaptive immune threats. Recent research suggests that manipulating these cells could have therapeutic potential. However, the specific development of each population and the overall organization of this cellular network are not well understood. In this study, we used a fate-mapping approach to investigate the monocyte and macrophage compartment in mice. By utilizing the CX(3)CR1 promoter-driven Cre recombinase expression, we found that major tissue-resident macrophage populations, including liver Kupffer cells and lung alveolar, splenic, and peritoneal macrophages, are established before birth and persist throughout adulthood without being replenished by blood monocytes. Additionally, we discovered that short-lived Ly6C(+) monocytes are essential precursors for blood-resident Ly6C(-) cells, and the abundance of Ly6C(+) blood monocytes directly influences the lifespan of their progeny in circulation.

title: Dealing with substantial heterogeneity in Cochrane reviews. Cross-sectional study
text:
The issue of dealing with heterogeneity in meta-analyses can be challenging, and there is limited guidance available for authors on how to address it. In this study, we aimed to examine how authors handled different levels of heterogeneity, specifically whether they used a fixed effect model, which assumes that all included studies estimate the same true effect, or a random effects model where this assumption is not made. 

To conduct our investigation, we randomly selected 60 Cochrane reviews from 2008 that had significant heterogeneity (I2 greater than 50%, indicating that more than 50% of the variation is due to heterogeneity rather than chance). We collected data on the choice of statistical model, how authors dealt with the heterogeneity, and assessed the methodological quality of the reviews in relation to these factors. 

Our findings showed that the distribution of heterogeneity was fairly consistent across the entire I2 range of 50-100%. Out of the 60 reviews, 33 (55%) used a fixed effect model, but there was no correlation between the level of heterogeneity and the choice of model (P = 0.79). We identified major issues in 20 reviews (33%), with 16 of them using a fixed effect model. The most common problems included the use of a fixed effect model without providing a rationale for this choice, lack of discussion on even severe heterogeneity, and failure to provide explanations for its likely causes. Additionally, the problematic reviews had significantly fewer included trials compared to other reviews (4.3 vs. 8.0, P = 0.024). However, we observed that these problems became less prominent over time, as more recently updated reviews tended to use a random effects model more frequently. 

In conclusion, our study revealed that one-third of Cochrane reviews with significant heterogeneity had major issues in their handling of heterogeneity. It is crucial to pay more attention to this issue, as the problems we identified can greatly impact the conclusions drawn from these reviews.

title: Antagonistic Controls of Autophagy and Glycogen Accumulation by Snf1p, the Yeast Homolog of AMP-Activated Protein Kinase, and the Cyclin-Dependent
text: Glycogen serves as a carbohydrate reserve in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae when nutrients are scarce. When the SNF1 gene, which encodes a protein kinase necessary for glucose derepression, is mutated in yeast, glycogen accumulation decreases and glycogen synthase becomes inactive. Restoring synthesis in an snf1 strain only leads to temporary glycogen accumulation, suggesting that other SNF1-dependent mechanisms control glycogen storage. A genetic analysis revealed that SNF1 may regulate two autophagy-related genes, APG1 and APG13. Wild-type cells entering the stationary phase showed increased autophagic activity, but this was impaired in snf1 strains. Mutants lacking autophagy were able to synthesize glycogen as they approached the stationary phase, but were unable to maintain their glycogen stores due to impaired synthesis and enhanced degradation by phosphorylase Gph1p. Deleting GPH1 partially reversed the loss of glycogen accumulation in autophagy mutants. Additionally, loss of the vacuolar glucosidase SGA1 protected glycogen stores, but only in the late stationary phase. Gph1p and Sga1p may degrade different pools of glycogen. Pho85p, a cyclin-dependent protein kinase, opposes SNF1's control of glycogen synthesis. Autophagy induction in pho85 mutants entering the stationary phase was exaggerated compared to wild-type cells, but was blocked in apg1 pho85 mutants. We propose that Snf1p and Pho85p act as positive and negative regulators of autophagy, potentially through Apg1 and/or Apg13. Defective glycogen storage in snf1 cells can be attributed to both impaired synthesis upon entering the stationary phase and the lack of autophagy, which impairs glycogen maintenance.

title: Preferential binding of a kinesin-1 motor to GTP-tubulin–rich microtubules underlies polarized vesicle transport
text: The polarization of transport in neurons is crucial for the development of neuronal circuitry. A truncated form of KIF5, a kinesin-1 protein that contains a motor domain, is responsible for recognizing and accumulating at the tips of axons, which are enriched in binding sites for EB1. However, it is still unknown what specific signal KIF5 responds to in order to achieve this selective accumulation. Our research has shown that axonal microtubules, which are preferentially stained by the anti-GTP-tubulin antibody hMB11, are the sites where KIF5 attaches. By using super-resolution microscopy and EM immunocytochemistry, we have observed that hMB11 is localized at these attachment sites. Furthermore, EB1, which has a preference for binding to microtubules containing guanylyl-methylene-diphosphate (GMPCPP) in vitro, also recognizes the binding sites of hMB11 on axonal microtubules. When we expressed the hMB11 antibody in neurons, it disrupted the selective accumulation of truncated KIF5 at the tips of axons. In vitro studies have shown that the motor head of KIF5 binds approximately three times stronger to GMPCPP microtubules compared to GDP microtubules. Based on these findings, we propose that the presence of GTP-tubulin in axonal microtubules may be responsible for the selective localization of KIF5 and the polarized transport of vesicles in axons.

title: Developmental biology of the pancreas.
text:
The pancreas is a vital organ that consists of two distinct groups of cells: exocrine cells, which release enzymes into the digestive tract, and endocrine cells, which release hormones into the bloodstream. It develops from the endoderm as a dorsal and ventral bud that eventually merge to form a single organ. Mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians have similar pancreatic histology and developmental processes. However, in some fish, the islet cells are segregated as Brockmann bodies. Invertebrates lack a pancreas, but comparable endocrine cells can be found in the gut or brain.

During early development, the pancreatic bud expresses the homeobox gene IPF-1 (also known as IDX-1, STF-1, or PDX). Mutations in this gene result in the complete absence of the pancreas. The presence of heterotopic pancreas in embryos and the metaplasias observed in regenerating adult pancreas suggest that only a few gene products differentiate pancreatic cells from the surrounding tissues of the duodenum, gall bladder, and liver.

In the developing pancreatic buds, endocrine cells differentiate before exocrine cells, and it is common to observe the co-expression of different hormones by the same cell at early stages. Although pancreatic endocrine cells produce gene products characteristic of neurons, evidence from in vitro cultures and grafts shows that they originate from the endoderm, not the neural crest.

Observational studies strongly suggest that both endocrine and exocrine cells arise from the same endodermal rudiment. The development of the pancreas during embryonic life requires a trophic stimulus from the associated mesenchyme. In postnatal life, all cell types in the pancreas continue to grow. If acinar tissue is destroyed through duct ligation or ethionine treatment, rapid regeneration occurs. Surgical removal of parts of the pancreas leads to moderate but incomplete regeneration of both acini and islets. Poisoning with alloxan or streptozotocin can result in permanent depletion of beta cells.

Although the cell kinetics of the pancreas are not fully understood, it is likely that there is a continuous slow turnover of cells, supported by a population of stem cells in the ducts. The production rate of each cell type is controlled locally rather than systemically.

title: Long term pharmacotherapy for obesity and overweight: updated meta-analysis.
text:
The objective of this study was to summarize the long-term effectiveness of anti-obesity drugs in reducing weight and improving health status. The study design involved an updated meta-analysis of randomized trials. The data sources included Medline, Embase, the Cochrane controlled trials register, the Current Science meta-register of controlled trials, and reference lists of identified articles. The search covered the period from December 2002 to December 2006. The study reviewed double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials of approved anti-obesity drugs used in adults aged over 18 for one year or longer.

The results of the study showed that 30 trials met the inclusion criteria, with durations ranging from one to four years. These trials included 16 trials of orlistat (with 10,631 participants), 10 trials of sibutramine (with 2,623 participants), and four trials of rimonabant (with 6,365 participants). Out of these trials, 14 were new and 16 had been previously identified. The attrition rates averaged 30-40%.

Compared to placebo, orlistat reduced weight by 2.9 kg, sibutramine by 4.2 kg, and rimonabant by 4.7 kg. Patients receiving active drug treatment were significantly more likely to achieve 5% and 10% weight loss thresholds. Orlistat also reduced the incidence of diabetes and improved concentrations of total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, blood pressure, and glycaemic control in patients with diabetes. However, it increased rates of gastrointestinal side effects and slightly lowered concentrations of high-density lipoprotein. Sibutramine improved concentrations of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides. Rimonabant improved concentrations of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides, blood pressure, and glycaemic control in patients with diabetes, but it increased the risk of mood disorders.

In conclusion, orlistat, sibutramine, and rimonabant have modest effects on weight reduction and have differing effects on cardiovascular risk profiles. They also have specific adverse effects.

title: The centrosome cycle: Centriole biogenesis, duplication and inherent asymmetries
text: Animal cells have centrosomes, which are responsible for organizing microtubules. They play a role in shaping the microtubule cytoskeleton, act as a base for the primary cilium, and serve as a hub for important signaling pathways. The centrosome consists of two cylindrical structures called centrioles, which recruit pericentriolar material. Each cell starts the cell cycle with one centrosome, and the duplication of centrioles only occurs once per cell cycle at a specific location in the cell. This duplication process results in two centrioles of different ages and maturity, leading to different functions. For instance, the older centriole can initiate the formation of a ciliary axoneme. We explore the spatial aspects of centrosome duplication, the assembly mechanism of centrioles, and the potential consequences of the inherent asymmetry of centrioles and centrosomes.

title: Osteoclasts control reactivation of dormant myeloma cells by remodelling the endosteal niche
text: Despite the development of therapies targeting myeloma cell-intrinsic pathways, multiple myeloma remains largely incurable. Disease relapse is believed to stem from dormant myeloma cells residing in specialized niches, which are resistant to treatment and repopulate the tumor. However, there is limited knowledge about these niches and how they control myeloma cell dormancy and reactivation. This study utilizes intravital imaging to track individual myeloma cells as they establish themselves in the endosteal niche, enter a dormant state, and subsequently become activated to form colonies. The findings reveal that dormancy is a reversible state triggered by interactions with bone-lining cells or osteoblasts, and reversed by osteoclasts remodeling the endosteal niche. Dormant myeloma cells exhibit resistance to chemotherapy targeting dividing cells. The study underscores the crucial role of the endosteal niche in controlling myeloma cell dormancy, highlighting the potential of targeting cell-extrinsic mechanisms to overcome cell-intrinsic drug resistance and prevent disease relapse.

title: Human embryonic stem cells with biological and epigenetic characteristics similar to those of mouse ESCs.
text: Human and mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are derived from blastocyst-stage embryos but have distinct biological properties. Molecular analyses suggest that the pluripotent state of human ESCs corresponds to that of mouse-derived epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). In this study, we aimed to reprogram conventional human ESCs into a more immature state that closely resembles pluripotent mouse ESCs. To achieve this, we induced the expression of Oct4, Klf4, and Klf2 factors, along with LIF and inhibitors of GSK3beta and ERK1/2 pathways. Forskolin, a protein kinase A pathway agonist, temporarily substituted the need for ectopic transgene expression by inducing Klf4 and Klf2 expression. These epigenetically converted cells exhibited growth properties, X-chromosome activation state (XaXa), gene expression profile, and signaling pathway dependence similar to mouse ESCs. Furthermore, the same growth conditions allowed the derivation of human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells with properties resembling mouse iPS cells. The generation of validated "naïve" human ESCs will enable the study of a previously undefined pluripotent state in humans and may facilitate patient-specific, disease-relevant research.

title: IDEAL in meshes for prolapse, urinary incontinence, and hernia repair.
text: The purpose of this study is to analyze the incidence and prevention of adverse events after mesh implantation, as mesh surgeries are commonly performed but there is no systematic analysis on this topic. The researchers followed the recommendations of IDEAL and developed an in vitro test system to assess the biocompatibility of surgical meshes. They also developed coating strategies to optimize biocompatibility. The native and modified materials were tested in an animal model over a period of 2 years. The results showed that the thickness of inflammatory tissue, connective tissue, and macrophage infiltration were comparable at different time points after explantation. The in vivo performance of the meshes in a sheep model was predictable based on the in vitro test system. Coating the meshes with autologous plasma prior to implantation had a positive effect on biocompatibility. Overall, this study provides a ranking of currently available meshes and has the potential to optimize future meshes.

title: Heterotopic of bone marrow. Analysis of precursor cells for osteogenic and hematopoietic tissues.
text: Chromosome markers (T6) and reverse transplantation into the initial donor line were used to determine the origin of osteogenic and hematopoietic cells in semisyngeneic heterotopic bone marrow transplants. When bone marrow was grafted under the renal capsule in syngeneic and semisyngeneic cases, both bone and bone marrow were formed. However, in allogeneic grafts, only bone was formed and later resorbed. In 14-month semisyngeneic transplants, the bone marrow consisted of recipient cells, including the proliferating pool and hematopoietic tissue stem cells. On the other hand, the osteogenic precursor cells and bone tissue in these transplants were of donor origin. The relationship between determinated osteogenic precursor cells (preosteoblasts) and hematopoietic stem cells (or their descendants) in which osteogenesis can be induced is also discussed.

title: TRPM7 is required for breast tumor cell metastasis.
text: TRPM7 is responsible for encoding a cation channel that allows the passage of calcium ions and possesses kinase activity. While TRPM7 has been linked to the regulation of cell adhesion and migration, its role in cancer progression remains uncertain. In this study, we present evidence that high levels of TRPM7 expression are an independent predictor of unfavorable outcomes in breast cancer patients. Additionally, we demonstrate that TRPM7 is essential for the development of metastasis in a mouse model of human breast cancer. Through further investigation, we discovered that TRPM7 controls cellular tension based on myosin II, leading to alterations in focal adhesion number, cell-cell adhesion, and polarized cell movement. Consequently, our findings propose that TRPM7 is a component of a mechanosensory complex utilized by cancer cells to facilitate the formation of metastasis.

title: Frailty Syndrome: A Transitional State in a Dynamic Process
text: Frailty has long been associated with disability and comorbidity, commonly observed in older individuals and linked to a higher risk of falls, hospitalization, and mortality. However, there is growing recognition that frailty may actually be a distinct clinical syndrome with a biological foundation. It is seen as a transitional state in the dynamic progression from robustness to functional decline. During this process, the body's overall physiological reserves decrease and become insufficient for maintaining and repairing the aging body. The clinical concept of frailty emphasizes that it is not defined by a single altered system, but rather involves multiple systems. Consensus among clinicians regarding the characteristics of frailty includes wasting (loss of muscle mass, strength, and weight), decreased endurance, impaired balance and mobility, slowed performance, relative inactivity, and potentially decreased cognitive function. Frailty is easily identifiable by clinicians, presenting with various manifestations, and no single symptom is sufficient or essential for its diagnosis. These manifestations include physical appearance (whether consistent with age or not), nutritional status (thinness, weight loss), subjective health rating, performance (cognition, fatigue), sensory/physical impairments (vision, hearing, strength), and current care (medication, hospitalization). While the early stages of frailty may not exhibit noticeable clinical signs, once depleted reserves reach a critical threshold, the syndrome becomes detectable through clinical, functional, behavioral, and biological markers. Therefore, gaining a better understanding of these clinical changes and their underlying mechanisms, starting from the pre-frail state, may confirm the belief held by many geriatricians that increasing frailty is distinct from normal aging and potentially reversible. This article provides an update on the pathophysiology, clinical characteristics, and biological aspects of the frailty process, as well as speculating on potential preventive approaches.

title: Progression of preclinical diastolic dysfunction to the development of symptoms.
text: The objective of this study was to determine the clinical characteristics and progression to heart failure (HF) in a group of patients with normal systolic function and moderate or severe diastolic dysfunction, as determined by Doppler criteria, but without any clinical diagnosis of HF or symptoms of HF at the time of echocardiography. The authors reviewed the medical charts of 82 patients who met the inclusion criteria. The mean age of the patients was 69 years, with a majority being female. The presence of hypertension, coronary artery disease, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and renal dysfunction was observed in a significant portion of the cohort. The 2-year cumulative probability of developing HF according to the Framingham criteria was low at 1.9%, but the probability of developing any symptoms was 31.1%. The probability of cardiac hospitalization within 2 years was 21.2%. Peripheral vascular disease and hypertension were independently associated with an increased likelihood of developing symptoms. The study suggests that hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and renal dysfunction are common in patients with preclinical diastolic dysfunction. Although the progression to clinical HF was low, there was a moderate degree of progression to symptoms and cardiac hospitalizations. The authors speculate that ventricular-arterial interaction may play a role in the progression of diastolic dysfunction to symptoms.

title: Aspirin in the chemoprevention of colorectal neoplasia: an overview.
text: There is substantial evidence supporting the effectiveness of aspirin in preventing colorectal cancer (CRC) and vascular disease. Numerous epidemiologic studies have consistently found a negative correlation between aspirin use and the risk of CRC. A recent analysis of four randomized trials on cardiovascular disease prevention, involving nearly 14,000 patients, revealed that daily aspirin treatment for approximately five years resulted in a 34% decrease in CRC mortality over a 20-year period. Another meta-analysis of four randomized adenoma prevention trials, with almost 3,000 patients who had a history of colorectal adenoma or cancer, demonstrated that aspirin reduced the occurrence of advanced adenomas by 28% and any adenoma by 17%. In a clinical trial involving patients with Lynch syndrome, a hereditary CRC syndrome, aspirin treatment for at least two years led to a 50% or greater reduction in CRC risk starting five years after randomization, even after discontinuing aspirin. Some observational studies have also shown improved survival rates among CRC patients who use aspirin. These findings collectively support the consideration of long-term aspirin use for CRC prevention. However, despite the compelling data, there is still no consensus on the balance of risks and benefits associated with long-term aspirin use, particularly in low-risk populations. Further investigation is needed to determine the optimal dosage for cancer prevention and the precise mechanism by which aspirin exerts its anticancer effects.

title: Chemokine receptor trio: CXCR3, CXCR4 and CXCR7 crosstalk via CXCL11 and CXCL12.
text:
The role of chemokines in immunity and endothelial cell activation and proliferation is well established. However, there is a growing body of literature suggesting that the chemokine receptors CXCR3, CXCR4, and CXCR7 play a critical role in the development and progression of solid tumors. These receptors interact with shared ligands, namely I-TAC (CXCL11) and SDF-1 (CXCL12), to mediate the effect on tumorigenesis. CXCR4, in particular, has been extensively studied and found to be overexpressed in most human solid tumors, making it a target for understanding its role in cancer metastasis.

To expand the range of anti-cancer agents available, inhibitors of the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis have emerged as potential options for neo-adjuvant treatments. Some of these inhibitors are currently in preclinical and clinical stages of development.
