However, the discovery of CXCR7 as another receptor for CXCL12, with a high binding affinity, and recent reports suggesting its involvement in cancer progression, have raised questions about the effectiveness of selectively blocking CXCR4 as a cancer treatment. Interestingly, CXCR7 can also bind CXCL11, which is a known ligand for CXCR3. Recent studies have shown that CXCR3 and its ligands are overexpressed in various solid tumors and play a role in regulating tumor growth and metastasis. Therefore, it is important to consider the interactions and crosstalk between these three chemokine receptors and their ligands in order to develop effective anti-cancer therapies.

Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that these receptors are expressed differently in tumor endothelial cells and cancer stem cells, indicating their direct involvement in regulating tumor angiogenesis and metastasis. This review will focus on the signals mediated by this trio of receptors through their shared ligands and their role in tumor growth and progression.

title: Human Cyclin a Is Required for Mitosis until Mid Prophase
text: We utilized microinjection and time-lapse video microscopy to examine the function of cyclin A in the process of mitosis. Specifically, we injected purified, active cyclin A/cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) into synchronized cells at specific stages of the cell cycle and assessed its impact on cell division. Our findings indicate that cyclin A/CDK2 induces G2 phase cells to enter mitosis within 30 minutes of microinjection, which is up to 4 hours earlier than control cells. However, this premature mitosis often exhibits abnormalities, such as incomplete chromosome condensation and fusion of daughter cells. Interestingly, microinjecting cyclin A/CDK2 into S phase cells does not affect their progression through subsequent G2 phase or mitosis. In complementary experiments, we introduced the amino terminus of p21Cip1/Waf1/Sdi1 (p21N) into cells via microinjection to inhibit cyclin A/CDK2 activity. Our results demonstrate that p21N prevents S phase or G2 phase cells from entering mitosis and causes early prophase cells to revert back to interphase. These findings suggest that cyclin A/CDK2 is a crucial component that regulates entry into mitosis and progression through mitosis until late prophase. Additionally, they propose that cyclin A/CDK2 may be the target of the recently identified prophase checkpoint.

title: Brief, four-session group CBT reduces binge eating behaviors among bariatric surgery candidates.
text:
This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of a short, 4-session cognitive behavioral group therapy for binge eating in individuals seeking bariatric surgery at an academic medical center. Binge eating behaviors have been associated with poorer outcomes in bariatric surgery patients, and some surgery programs require preoperative treatment for binge eating disorder. However, no previous research has investigated whether a preoperative intervention can effectively reduce binge eating in severely obese individuals seeking bariatric surgery. 

A total of 243 bariatric surgery candidates participated in a brief cognitive behavioral group treatment for binge eating and completed the Binge Eating Scale. They reported the number of weekly binge eating episodes during the initial psychological evaluation and again after the group sessions. The study utilized a pre-post intervention design. 

The findings indicated significant reductions in both binge eating behaviors and thoughts, as well as the number of binge eating episodes following the group intervention. The intervention's effectiveness was consistent across genders and ethnicities (black and white). 

In conclusion, a brief cognitive behavioral intervention can effectively reduce binge eating behaviors in individuals seeking bariatric surgery. Considering the potential impact of binge eating on surgical outcomes, bariatric surgery programs could benefit from addressing binge eating prior to surgery.

title: Influence of smoking cessation after diagnosis of early stage lung cancer on prognosis: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the impact of smoking cessation after diagnosis of a primary lung tumor on prognosis.

DESIGN: This study utilized a systematic review with meta-analysis methodology.

DATA SOURCES: The data sources for this study included CINAHL (from 1981), Embase (from 1980), Medline (from 1966), Web of Science (from 1966), CENTRAL (from 1977) up until December 2008, as well as reference lists of included studies.

STUDY SELECTION: The study included randomized controlled trials or observational longitudinal studies that measured the effect of quitting smoking after diagnosis of lung cancer on prognostic outcomes, regardless of stage at presentation or tumor histology.

DATA EXTRACTION: Two researchers independently identified studies for inclusion and extracted data. Estimates were combined using a random effects model, and the I(2) statistic was used to assess heterogeneity. Life tables were used to model five-year survival for early stage non-small cell lung cancer and limited stage small cell lung cancer, using death rates for continuing smokers and quitters obtained from this review.

RESULTS: Out of the 10 studies included, 9 focused on patients diagnosed with an early stage lung tumor. Continued smoking was found to be significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality and recurrence in early stage non-small cell lung cancer, as well as all-cause mortality, development of a second primary tumor, and recurrence in limited stage small cell lung cancer. However, no study provided data on the effect of quitting smoking on cancer-specific mortality or development of a second primary tumor in non-small cell lung cancer. Life table modeling based on these findings estimated a 33% five-year survival rate for 65-year-old patients with early stage non-small cell lung cancer who continued to smoke, compared to 70% for those who quit smoking. In limited stage small cell lung cancer, the estimated five-year survival rate was 29% for continuing smokers and 63% for quitters.

CONCLUSIONS: This review suggests that smoking cessation after diagnosis of early stage lung cancer can improve prognostic outcomes. The estimated number of deaths prevented is higher than expected from the reduction of cardiorespiratory deaths after smoking cessation, indicating that most of the mortality gain is likely due to reduced cancer progression. These findings suggest that offering smoking cessation treatment to patients with early stage lung cancer may be beneficial.

title: Epigenetic reprogramming and induced pluripotency.
text: The cloning of animals using adult cells has shown that adult cells can be transformed into embryonic cells through unknown factors found in the oocyte. Recently, scientists have discovered transcription factors that can induce pluripotency in somatic cells without the need for oocytes, resulting in induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. These iPS cells offer a valuable tool for studying the molecular processes involved in epigenetic reprogramming. Additionally, iPS cells can provide insights into normal development and disease, and potentially enable personalized cell therapy for patients.

title: Sex differences in mortality following acute coronary syndromes.
text:
There is conflicting information regarding whether sex differences affect short-term mortality after acute coronary syndromes (ACS). The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between sex and 30-day mortality in ACS, and to determine if this relationship was influenced by clinical syndrome or coronary anatomy. The study used a large database from 11 independent ACS clinical trials conducted between 1993 and 2006. The sample included 136,247 patients, with 38,048 (28%) being women. Of these, 102,004 (26% women) had ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), 14,466 (29% women) had non-STEMI (NSTEMI), and 19,777 (40% women) had unstable angina.

The main outcome measure was 30-day mortality following ACS. The results showed that 30-day mortality was 9.6% in women and 5.3% in men, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.91. However, after adjusting for potential confounding clinical factors, there was no significant difference in mortality between women and men (adjusted OR, 1.06). There was a significant interaction between sex and type of ACS (P < .001). In STEMI, 30-day mortality was higher among women (adjusted OR, 1.15), while in NSTEMI and unstable angina, mortality was lower among women (adjusted OR, 0.77 and 0.55, respectively).

Among the subset of patients with angiographic data (35,128 patients), women were more likely to have nonobstructive coronary disease and less likely to have 2-vessel and 3-vessel disease, regardless of ACS type. After adjusting for angiographic disease severity, there was no significant difference in 30-day mortality between women and men, regardless of ACS type. The relationship between sex and 30-day mortality was consistent across different levels of angiographic disease severity.

In conclusion, there are sex-based differences in 30-day mortality among ACS patients, which vary depending on the clinical presentation. However, these differences can largely be explained by clinical differences at presentation and the severity of angiographically documented disease.

title: Membrane topology of the 60-kDa Oxa1p homologue from Escherichia coli.
text: We have examined the structure of a 60-kDa protein found in the inner membrane of Escherichia coli. This protein is similar to the recently discovered Oxa1p protein in Saccharomyces cerevisiae mitochondria, which is involved in assembling proteins in the mitochondrial inner membrane. Through hydrophobicity and alkaline phosphatase fusion analyses, we have determined that this protein has six transmembrane segments. Interestingly, it also contains an N-terminal signal-anchor sequence that is not found in the mitochondrial Oxa1p protein. Unlike partial N-terminal fusion protein constructs, the full-length protein adopts a conformation that is resistant to protease digestion. This suggests that important folding elements are located in the C-terminal region of the protein.

title: Identifying and Characterizing Interplay between Hepatitis B Virus X Protein and Smc5/6
text: The role of Hepatitis B X protein (HBx) in the replication cycle of the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) has long been a mystery. However, recent findings have shed light on its function. It has been discovered that the structural maintenance of chromosome 5/6 complex (Smc5/6) inhibits transcription from the HBV genome, known as covalently-closed circular DNA (cccDNA). Additionally, it has been found that HBx plays a crucial role in redirecting the DNA-damage binding protein 1 (DDB1) E3 ubiquitin ligase to target and degrade the Smc5/6 complex. This action by HBx relieves the transcriptional repression caused by Smc5/6 and enhances HBV gene expression. In this review, we delve into the identification and characterization of the interaction between HBx and Smc5/6. We also explore the repression of cccDNA transcription by Smc5/6, the timing of HBx expression, and the potential involvement of HBx in the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

title: Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Vertical Transmission in 12-Month-Old Infants Born to HCV-Infected Women and Assessment of Maternal Risk Factors
text:
The prevalence of pediatric liver disease caused by Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is often underestimated, especially when acquired through vertical transmission (VT) from mother to child. Current guidelines recommend screening infants for HCV RNA at 1-2 months, but these recommendations were based on outdated testing methods. Previous studies have shown VT rates of 4%-15% and a correlation with high maternal viral load. In this study conducted in Cairo, Egypt, we aimed to evaluate HCV RNA in infants with HCV VT and identify maternal risk factors. 

Between December 2012 and March 2014, pregnant women were screened for HCV. Among the 2514 women screened, 54 were found to be viremic (2.1%) and delivered 56 infants. At 12 months of age, 51 infants from 49 women were tested for HCV RNA using real-time PCR. Only 7 infants tested positive, resulting in an HCV VT rate of 14.3% (7 out of 49). The median HCV RNA level in the infants was 2100 IU/mL. None of the maternal risk factors analyzed, including HCV RNA levels, mode of delivery, and maternal IL28B genotype, were found to be associated with transmission. 

In conclusion, our study in Egypt, where HCV is highly prevalent, revealed a 12-month HCV VT rate of 14.3%. Further research should focus on identifying pregnant women who are more likely to transmit HCV vertically and implementing earlier testing of infants to identify those at risk of developing chronic infection.

title: Long-term follow-up of cervical disease in women screened by cytology and HPV testing: results from the HART study
text:
BACKGROUND Numerous studies have demonstrated that testing for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types is more sensitive in detecting CIN2+ compared to cytology, although it may have slightly lower specificity. 

METHODS We collected follow-up data, including at least one smear test after participating in the HART study, which compared HPV testing (HC-II) with cytology as the primary screening method. 

RESULTS After a median follow-up of 6 years, we identified an additional 42 cases of CIN2+. Women who tested positive for HPV at baseline were more likely to develop CIN2+ compared to those who tested negative (hazard ratio (HR) 17.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) (9.3-31.6)). The risk of developing CIN2+ increased with higher viral load. Compared to HPV-negative women (relative light unit (RLU) <1), the HR (95% CI) was 5.4 (1.6, 18.2) for 1-10 RLU and 25.5 (13.6, 47.9) for RLU ≥ 10. Positive cytology (borderline or worse compared to negative) also predicted the development of CIN2, although to a lesser extent (HR 8.7; 95% CI (4.5-17.1)). Only one case of CIN3 and three cases of CIN2 were found in women who had positive cytology but were HPV negative at baseline. 

CONCLUSION After 5 years of follow-up, the occurrence of CIN2+ was 0.23% in women who were HPV negative at baseline, compared to 0.48% in women with a negative cytology result. This suggests that HPV testing provides a longer interval of low risk for CIN2+ compared to cytology.

title: The Burden of Trachoma in Ayod County of Southern Sudan
text:
The prevalence of trachoma-induced blindness in Southern Sudan is a significant issue that can be prevented through various interventions, including surgery, antibiotics, facial hygiene, and environmental improvements (SAFE). To assess the need for intervention activities in Ayod County, Jonglei State, we conducted a survey. 

In November 2006, a cross-sectional two-stage cluster random survey was conducted. All residents of selected households underwent clinical assessments for trachoma using the World Health Organization's simplified grading scheme. A total of 2,335 individuals from 392 households were examined, with 1,107 being over 14 years old. 

The prevalence of active trachoma signs in children aged 1-9 years was as follows: trachomatous inflammation follicular (TF) = 80.1%, trachomatous inflammation intense (TI) = 60.7%, and TF and/or TI (active trachoma) = 88.3%. Among adults over 14 years old, the prevalence of trachomatous trichiasis (TT) was 14.6%, while in children aged 1-14 years, it was 2.9%. Overall, the prevalence of TT was 8.4%. Among individuals with TT, 6.4% had corneal opacity. There was no significant difference in trachoma signs between genders. 

Trachoma affected almost all households surveyed, with 98.0% having at least one person with active trachoma and 33.2% having at least one person with trichiasis. 

In conclusion, trachoma is a significant public health problem in Ayod. The high prevalence of active trachoma and trichiasis highlights the severe burden of blinding trachoma in other post-conflict areas of Southern Sudan. Based on WHO recommendations, all aspects of the SAFE strategy are necessary to eliminate blinding trachoma in Ayod.

title: A Century of Cholesterol and Coronaries: From Plaques to Genes to Statins
text: Coronary heart disease is responsible for a significant portion of deaths in developed nations, accounting for one-fourth of all fatalities. Extensive research spanning a century has identified the primary culprit behind this disease: low-density lipoprotein (LDL), which carries cholesterol. The liver plays a crucial role in regulating LDL through specific receptors known as LDLRs, which remove it from the bloodstream. Mutations that result in the absence of LDLRs lead to elevated LDL levels and early-onset heart attacks, while mutations that increase the presence of LDLRs reduce LDL levels and decrease the likelihood of heart attacks. To effectively combat coronary disease, the primary objective should be to lower LDL. Fortunately, there are currently available methods to achieve this goal. However, determining who should receive treatment, when treatment should commence, and how long it should be administered remain key questions that need to be addressed.

title: Perinatal mortality in rural China: retrospective cohort study.
text:
GOALS: To examine the utilization of local civil registration data in evaluating perinatal mortality in a typical rural county in a less developed province in China during the years 1999-2000.

METHOD: A retrospective cohort study was conducted, tracking pregnancies in a group of women from the time of pregnancy registration until seven days after the birth of the infant. The study took place in 20 rural townships in eastern China, using routine family planning records.

PARTICIPANTS: A total of 3,697 pregnancies were registered by the local family planning system in 1999.

OUTCOMES: The main outcome measures included abortions, stillbirths, early neonatal mortality, and perinatal mortality.

RESULTS: Only three cases were lost during the follow-up period. The average age of the women at the time of pregnancy was 25.9 years. Out of the 3,697 pregnancies, 312 ended in abortion and 240 resulted in miscarriage, making a total of 552 cases (15%). The perinatal mortality rate was 69 per 1,000 births, with a stillbirth rate of 24 per 1,000 births and an early neonatal mortality rate of 46 per 1,000 live births. The early neonatal mortality rate was 29 per 1,000 live births for boys and 69 per 1,000 live births for girls. The perinatal mortality rate showed a significant increase with parity and was higher in townships with lower income per capita.

CONCLUSIONS: The local family planning system proves to be a valuable source of data for studying perinatal mortality in rural China. The perinatal mortality rate in the study county was higher than previously reported rates for both rural and urban areas in China. The findings regarding parity and infant sex raise concerns about the impact of the one-child policy.

title: Genetic disruption of aurora B uncovers an essential role for aurora C during early mammalian development.
text: Multiple kinases control mitosis, driving cell cycle progression and preventing chromosome mis-segregation. The chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), consisting of Aurora kinase B, survivin, borealin, and incenp, regulates microtubule-kinetochore attachments and cytokinesis. While the absence of survivin, borealin, or incenp leads to early lethality at the morula stage, our study demonstrates that Aurora B is not necessary for CPC function during early cell divisions, and Aurora B-null embryos implant normally. This is because Aurora C plays a crucial role in these early embryonic cycles. However, Aurora C expression decreases during late blastocyst stages, resulting in post-implantation defects in Aurora B-null embryos. These defects are associated with an abundance of prometaphase figures and apoptotic cell death in the inner cell mass lacking Aurora B. Conditional deletion of Aurora B in somatic cells that do not express Aurora C leads to chromosomal misalignment and a lack of chromosome segregation. Restoring wild-type Aurora C, but not a kinase-dead version, rescues this defect, indicating functional overlap between these two kinases. Lastly, Aurora B-null cells partially arrest in the presence of nocodazole, suggesting that this kinase is not essential for the spindle assembly checkpoint.

title: NuSAP is essential for chromatin-induced spindle formation during early embryogenesis.
text: The process of mitotic spindle assembly involves two pathways: one involving the centrosome and the other involving the chromosomes. The latter pathway is regulated by RanGTP, which releases inhibitory complexes from microtubule-associated proteins. NuSAP, a protein that binds to microtubules and DNA, is targeted by RanGTP and promotes the formation of microtubules near the chromosomes. However, the role of NuSAP in cell proliferation in living organisms is not yet understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the expression of NuSAP is closely linked to cell proliferation during both embryonic development and adult life, making it a reliable marker for cells that are actively dividing. Furthermore, we found that mice lacking NuSAP experience early embryonic death. In these mice, spindle assembly is highly inefficient and the chromosomes remain scattered throughout the cytoplasm during mitosis. As a result, the cells are unable to progress through mitosis due to sustained spindle checkpoint activity, ultimately leading to the activation of caspases and apoptotic cell death. These findings highlight the essential role of NuSAP in the proliferation of embryonic cells and emphasize the importance of chromatin-induced spindle assembly.

title: E2F-6: a novel member of the E2F family is an inhibitor of E2F-dependent transcription
text: The E2F family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in regulating genes necessary for proper cell cycle progression. Previous studies have identified five members of this family, known as E2F1-5. These five members are essential for controlling the expression of vital genes and can be categorized into two functional groups: those that promote S-phase progression in dormant cells (E2Fs 1-3) and those that do not (E2Fs 4-5). In this study, we introduce a new member of the E2F family, referred to as E2F-6. E2F-6 shares significant similarities with E2Fs 1-5, particularly in the DNA binding, heterodimerization, and marked box domains. However, unlike E2Fs 1-5, E2F-6 lacks a transactivation and pocket protein binding domain, making it a distinct third group within the E2F family. E2F-6 is a nuclear protein that can form heterodimers with DP proteins (DP-1 and DP-2) both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. Our findings demonstrate that the complex formed by E2F-6 and DP proteins exhibits strong DNA binding activity, with a preference for a TTTCCCGC E2F recognition site, which slightly differs from the E2F consensus site derived from the E2 promoter (TTTCGCGC). In contrast to other E2F family members, overexpression of E2F-6 represses transcription from promoters containing E2F recognition sites instead of activating it. Additionally, elevated levels of E2F-6 suppress the transactivational effects of co-expressed E2F-1 and DP-1. The inhibitory effect of E2F-6 relies on its DNA binding activity and its ability to form heterodimers with the DPs. Interestingly, ectopic expression of E2F-6 leads to an accumulation of cells in S-phase. Our data suggest that E2F-6 expression delays the exit from S-phase rather than inducing it, highlighting the functional distinction between E2F-6 and previously known E2F family members.

title: Enhancement of hippocampal pyramidal cell excitability by the novel selective slow-afterhyperpolarization channel blocker 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077).
text:
The role of the slow afterhyperpolarization (sAHP) in hippocampal neurons and its impact on learning and memory have been studied. However, there are two main reasons why its precise role in cell excitability and central nervous system function has not been fully understood. Firstly, there are currently no selective inhibitors available that effectively reduce the underlying current in living organisms or intact tissue preparations. Secondly, although it is known that a small conductance K(+) channel is responsible for the sAHP, the exact molecular identity of this channel remains unknown. 

In this study, we introduce a new compound called 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077), which effectively suppressed the sAHP in hippocampal neurons in both cultured cells (IC(50) = 0.5 microM) and slice preparations (IC(50) approximately 10 microM). UCL2077 demonstrated selectivity by having minimal effects on Ca(2+) channels, action potentials, input resistance, and the medium afterhyperpolarization. Additionally, UCL2077 had little impact on small conductance Ca(2+)-activated K(+) (SK) channels that were artificially expressed. 

Furthermore, the effects of UCL2077 and apamin, a selective SK channel blocker, on spike firing in hippocampal neurons were found to be different, suggesting that SK channels are unlikely to be responsible for the sAHP. These findings provide further evidence regarding the role of SK channels in the sAHP. 

Overall, this study demonstrates that UCL2077 is the most potent and selective sAHP blocker discovered thus far. It serves as a valuable pharmacological tool for investigating the role of sAHP channels in regulating cell excitability in intact tissue preparations and potentially in living organisms.

title: Lessons from sudden coronary death: a comprehensive morphological classification scheme for atherosclerotic lesions.
text: This review aims to reassess the existing understanding of the critical final stages in the development of atherosclerotic lesions. The current paradigm, which originated from observations of autopsy tissues by Davies and colleagues, suggests that the rupture of an advanced atherosclerotic lesion is the cause of death in atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. While this assumption may hold some truth, recent autopsy studies indicate that it is not entirely accurate. To challenge this paradigm, we have reevaluated the morphological classification system for lesions proposed by the American Heart Association (AHA). However, this system presents two challenges. Firstly, it utilizes a lengthy list of roman numerals with letter codes that are difficult to remember. Secondly, it implies a linear and orderly progression of lesions, which can be ambiguous as it is unclear if there is a single sequence of events for all lesions. Therefore, we have attempted to develop a simpler classification system that aligns with the AHA categories but is more user-friendly, capable of accommodating various morphological variations, and not burdened by excessive mechanistic implications. The current paradigm is based on the belief that type IV lesions, also known as "atheromas," as described by the AHA, are stable due to the presence of a fibrous cap rich in smooth muscle cells that contains the fatty, necrotic core. However, Virchow's analysis in 1858 highlighted that historically, the term "atheroma" referred to a dermal cyst called "Grutzbalg," which was fatty in nature...

title: Loss of allergen 1 confers a hypervirulent phenotype that resembles mucoid switch variants of Cryptococcus neoformans.
text: The ability of a pathogen to survive in a host often relies on its capacity to undergo changes that help it evade the host's defense mechanisms. The fungus Cryptococcus neoformans, which is harmful to humans, undergoes a process called phenotypic switching within the body to ensure its persistence in tissue. Through the use of microarray and real-time PCR analyses, researchers discovered that the allergen 1 gene (ALL1) is downregulated in the hypervirulent mucoid switch variant of the fungus. This downregulation occurs during both logarithmic growth and intracellular growth in macrophages. The ALL1 gene is responsible for encoding a small cytoplasmic protein involved in the formation of the fungus's protective capsule. Interestingly, the growth of a mutant lacking the all1Delta gene appeared normal. However, similar to cells of the mucoid switch variant, the all1Delta cells produced a larger capsule made of polysaccharides compared to the smooth parent cells. This enlarged capsule hindered the ability of macrophages to engulf the fungus through phagocytosis. The mutant also showed a slight deficiency in capsule induction compared to other variants. In animal models, the all1Delta mutant displayed a phenotype similar to the hypervirulent mucoid switch variant, which is characterized by reduced host survival and increased pressure within the brain. The decreased survival is likely due to both an ineffective immune response and impaired phagocytosis by macrophages. Therefore, the researchers concluded that unlike most virulence-associated genes, the loss of the ALL1 gene actually enhances the fungus's virulence by altering the interaction between the host and the pathogen, thereby hindering clearance. This study identified the first cryptococcal gene associated with elevated intracranial pressure and supports the hypothesis that an opportunistic pathogen in the environment can modify its virulence within the host by epigenetically downregulating gene function.

title: Lessons from more than 80 structures of the GluA2 ligand-binding domain in complex with agonists, antagonists and allosteric modulators.
text:
Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) are a group of ion channels that are crucial for facilitating rapid communication between neurons in the central nervous system. These receptors play a vital role in the development and functioning of the nervous system, as well as in processes such as learning and memory. However, iGluRs have also been implicated in various brain disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia. The connection between iGluRs and these neurological conditions has sparked significant interest in understanding their structure and function.

Since the initial discovery in 1998 of the structure of a recombinant soluble protein containing the ligand-binding domain of GluA2, extensive research has yielded numerous crystal structures of both normal and mutated proteins, as well as different ligands. The combination of structural information and functional data has allowed scientists to develop models explaining how these receptors are activated and desensitized by agonists, inhibited by antagonists, and prevented from desensitizing by positive allosteric modulators. Additionally, these studies have provided a solid foundation for the design of new, targeted compounds that selectively interact with iGluRs.

title: Diaphragm Atrophy and Contractile Dysfunction in a Murine Model of Pulmonary Hypertension
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) leads to weight loss and dysfunction of the inspiratory (diaphragm) muscles. To understand the causes of PH, researchers have extensively used a mouse model induced by the drug monocrotaline (MCT). However, it remains unclear whether this mouse model accurately reproduces the weight loss and diaphragm muscle dysfunction observed in patients. This is an important factor to consider before using mice to study the mechanisms of cachexia and diaphragm abnormalities in PH. Therefore, we conducted a study where we measured body weight, soleus muscle weight, food intake, and diaphragm contractile properties in mice after 6-8 weeks of saline (control) or MCT (600 mg/kg) injections. We found that body weight progressively decreased in mice with PH, while food intake was similar in both groups. PH also resulted in a decrease in diaphragm maximal isometric specific force, maximal shortening velocity, and peak power (P<0.05). However, the levels of protein carbonyls in whole-diaphragm lysates and the abundance of select myofibrillar proteins were unchanged by PH. Our findings demonstrate that the murine model of PH induced by MCT exhibits abnormalities in diaphragm isometric and isotonic contractile function. Overall, this mouse model accurately mimics the weight loss and diaphragm muscle weakness observed in PH patients.

title: Identification of an anti-inflammatory protein from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a commensal bacterium deficient in Crohn's disease.
text:
BACKGROUND: Dysbiosis associated with Crohn's disease (CD) is characterized by a decrease in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which produces an anti-inflammatory effect. However, the specific compounds responsible for this effect have not been identified. 

METHODS: Mass spectrometry was used to analyze the peptides present in F. prausnitzii supernatant. The anti-inflammatory effects of these peptides were tested in vitro on intestinal epithelial cell lines and on cell lines transfected with a plasmid encoding the candidate protein. In vivo, the candidate protein's cDNA was delivered to the gut using recombinant lactic acid bacteria to prevent DNBS-colitis in mice. 

RESULTS: Seven peptides were identified in the F. prausnitzii culture supernatant, all derived from a 15 kDa microbial anti-inflammatory molecule (MAM) composed of 53% non-polar residues. The non-polar nature of the peptides made it difficult to directly characterize their anti-inflammatory activity. Transfection of epithelial cells with MAM cDNA resulted in a significant decrease in activation of the NF-κB pathway, with a dose-dependent effect. Additionally, the use of Lactococcus lactis, a food-grade bacterium delivering a plasmid encoding MAM, was able to alleviate DNBS-induced colitis in mice. 

CONCLUSIONS: F. prausnitzii produces a 15 kDa protein with anti-inflammatory properties, which inhibits the NF-κB pathway in intestinal epithelial cells and prevents colitis in an animal model. This protein may play a role in the pathogenesis of CD.

title: Calcium store sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1-dependent signaling plays an important role in cervical cancer growth, migration, and angiogenesis.
text: Store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) is the primary mechanism for Ca(2+) entry in nonexcitable cells. Stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) is a sensor for Ca(2+) in the endoplasmic reticulum that triggers the activation of SOCE. However, the role of STIM1 in regulating cancer progression is still debated and its clinical significance is unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that STIM1-dependent signaling is crucial for the proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis of cervical cancer cells. We observed overexpression of STIM1 in tumor tissue in 71% of early-stage cervical cancer cases. The level of STIM1 expression in tumor tissues is significantly associated with the risk of metastasis and survival. The migration of cancer cells stimulated by EGF requires the expression of STIM1, and EGF enhances the interaction between STIM1 and Orai1 in specific areas near the cell membrane, leading to an influx of Ca(2+). STIM1 is involved in the activation of the Ca(2+)-regulated protease calpain and the Ca(2+)-regulated cytoplasmic kinase Pyk2, which regulate the dynamics of focal adhesions in migratory cervical cancer cells. Silencing STIM1 in cervical cancer cells significantly inhibits cell proliferation by arresting the cell cycle at the S and G2/M phases, likely due to increased levels of p21 protein and decreased levels of Cdc25C protein. STIM1 also regulates the production of VEGF in cervical cancer cells. Interfering with STIM1 expression or blocking SOCE activity inhibits tumor angiogenesis and growth in animal models, confirming the critical role of STIM1-mediated Ca(2+) influx in promoting tumor development in vivo. These findings suggest that targeting STIM1-dependent signaling could be a promising strategy for therapeutic intervention.

title: A feasibility study for a randomised controlled trial of the Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention, a novel supportive technique for recurrent miscarriage
text:
The aim of this study is to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of a self-administered supportive technique called the Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention (PRCI) in improving the quality of life for women who have experienced recurrent miscarriage (RM) during the waiting period of a subsequent pregnancy. Currently, there is limited support and therapy available for these women, leaving many to cope alone. The PRCI has been shown to be effective in patients undergoing in vitro fertilisation treatment. 

This study will consist of a randomised controlled trial (RCT) feasibility study to determine if a larger multicentre RCT can be conducted to definitively test the effects of the PRCI on the psychological well-being of women with previous RM. In addition, a qualitative process evaluation will explore the initial experience of pregnancy following repeated miscarriages. 

Participants (n=50) will be randomly assigned to either the PRCI intervention group or the non-intervention group. The intervention group will receive the PRCI card and weekly questionnaires to assess their psychological well-being during the waiting period of their new pregnancy. The non-intervention group will complete the same weekly questionnaires. 

Ethics approval has been obtained and participating centers have given National Health Service R&D approval. The study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, national and international conferences, and lay user groups. The trial has been registered with the ISRCTN and recruitment of participants began in February 2014.

title: Report of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Workshop on Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Disease: recent advances and future directions.
text: Approximately 37% of individuals in the US who are considered to be at high risk for developing coronary artery disease (CAD), according to the National Cholesterol Education Program guidelines, have elevated levels of plasma lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. In contrast, only 14% of those at low risk have increased Lp(a) levels. This highlights the need to better understand the role of Lp(a) in CAD and other vascular diseases, as well as the underlying mechanisms. However, the complex structure and size variability of Lp(a) have made it challenging to develop accurate immunoassays for measuring Lp(a) concentrations in plasma. The significant variation in Lp(a) values obtained through different methods has made it difficult to compare data from various clinical studies and establish a consistent interpretation of clinical findings. To address these issues, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recently organized a workshop. The workshop aimed to assess our current knowledge of Lp(a) as a risk factor for atherosclerotic disorders, determine how future studies can provide a clearer understanding of the extent and mechanisms of Lp(a) involvement in these processes, and present the outcomes of the NHLBI-supported program for evaluating and standardizing Lp(a) immunoassays. This report includes the latest data presented by workshop participants, along with practical and research recommendations that emerged from the discussions.

title: Classification, functions, and clinical relevance of extracellular vesicles.
text: Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells have the ability to release small vesicles enclosed by phospholipids into their surroundings. The purpose of this vesicle release is to eliminate outdated cellular molecules, as initially observed in eukaryotic cells. While this process benefits the cell, it can also pose a risk to the environment, particularly in the case of blood where vesicles can support coagulation. Recent evidence suggests that vesicles serve as cargo containers for eukaryotic cells to exchange biomolecules, such as transmembrane receptors and genetic information. Additionally, bacteria also utilize extracellular vesicles for intercellular communication, indicating that this mode of information exchange is conserved throughout evolution. Consequently, vesicles are likely to be an efficient, robust, and cost-effective means of communication between cells. Moreover, vesicles play a role in protecting cells from waste accumulation and drugs, contribute to both physiology and pathology, and have numerous potential clinical applications, ranging from biomarkers to anticancer therapy. Due to their ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, vesicles can even be considered naturally occurring liposomes. Unfortunately, tumors and infectious diseases exploit the pathways of vesicle release and vesicles themselves to facilitate spreading and evade immune surveillance. This review will delve into the various types, nomenclature, functions, and clinical significance of vesicles.

title: Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range
text:
Researchers often combine the results of sample mean and standard deviation from similar clinical trials in systematic reviews and meta-analysis. However, some trials report the study using different measures such as the median, minimum and maximum values, and first and third quartiles. Therefore, in order to combine the results, it may be necessary to estimate the sample mean and standard deviation for these trials. 

This paper aims to enhance the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, we highlight the limitations of the sample standard deviation estimation method proposed by Hozo et al. (2005) and demonstrate its practical inadequacy. Building on this, we propose a new estimation method that incorporates the sample size, which yields more satisfactory results. 

Secondly, we systematically investigate the problem of estimating the sample mean and standard deviation under more general circumstances where the first and third quartiles are also available for the trials. Through simulation studies, we illustrate that our proposed methods significantly improve upon existing approaches and contribute to the existing body of literature. 

Finally, we conclude our work by presenting a summary table that provides comprehensive guidance for conducting meta-analysis in various scenarios.

title: Fascin protein is critical for transforming growth factor β protein-induced invasion and filopodia formation in spindle-shaped tumor cells.
text: Fascin, a protein that bundles actin and is found in high levels in all types of carcinomas, has been linked to a poor prognosis, shorter survival, and increased metastatic diseases. It is believed that fascin aids in the spread of tumors by promoting the formation of invasive membrane protrusions. However, the exact mechanisms behind the overexpression of fascin in tumors are not yet understood. TGFβ, a cytokine secreted by tumor and mesenchymal cells, has been shown to promote metastasis in late-stage tumors, but the specific ways in which it does so are not fully known. In this study, we demonstrated that TGFβ induces the expression of fascin in spindle-shaped tumor cells through the canonical Smad-dependent pathway. Fascin is crucial for TGFβ-induced formation of filopodia, as well as migration and invasion in these tumor cells. Importantly, we found a significant correlation between the expression of fascin and the levels of TGFβ1 and TGFβ receptor I in a group of primary breast tumor samples. These findings suggest that the elevated levels of TGFβ in the tumor microenvironment may be responsible for the overexpression of fascin in certain metastatic tumors. Furthermore, our data indicate that fascin may play a central role in TGFβ-induced tumor metastasis.

title: DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
text: The ability to accurately predict age using DNA methylation levels across various human tissues and cell types, as well as the biological significance of such predictions, is still unknown. In this study, I have developed a predictor that can estimate the DNA methylation age of most tissues and cell types. This predictor, which is freely available, was created using 8,000 samples from 82 Illumina DNA methylation array datasets, covering 51 healthy tissues and cell types. I have discovered several properties of DNA methylation age: it is close to zero in embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells, it correlates with cell passage number, it produces a highly heritable measure of age acceleration, and it is applicable to chimpanzee tissues. Additionally, analysis of 6,000 cancer samples from 32 datasets revealed that all 20 cancer types examined exhibit significant age acceleration, with an average of 36 years. Cancer tissues with low age acceleration are associated with a high number of somatic mutations and TP53 mutations, while mutations in steroid receptors greatly accelerate DNA methylation age in breast cancer. Finally, I have characterized the 353 CpG sites that form an aging clock in terms of chromatin states and tissue variance. In conclusion, I propose that DNA methylation age reflects the cumulative impact of an epigenetic maintenance system. This innovative epigenetic clock can be utilized to address various questions in developmental biology, cancer, and aging research.

title: Whole-body MR vascular screening detects unsuspected concomitant vascular disease in coronary heart disease patients
text:
We conducted a study to determine how often whole-body MR imaging can detect other arterial pathologies in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD), and how often these pathologies were unknown to the patients. Out of the 4,814 participants in the Heinz Nixdorf Recall Study, 327 reported CHD and 160 of them (with a mean age of 66.4 years) underwent MR imaging of the brain, heart (excluding the coronary arteries), and whole-body MR angiography. We assessed the prevalence of each vascular pathology, compared them to the patients' medical histories, and correlated them with each other. 

Among the 160 CHD patients, 16 (10%) showed signs of stroke on the MR imaging, and 77 (48.1%) had a stenosis of more than 50% in at least one extracerebral peripheral artery (excluding the coronaries). This included 28 (17.5%) with relevant renal artery stenoses and 20 (12.5%) with relevant extracerebral internal carotid artery stenoses. We found that 12 out of 81 cases with myocardial infarctions and 11 out of 16 cases with cerebrovascular infarctions had false negative histories. 

This whole-body MR screening program for atherosclerosis allows us to detect previously unknown concomitant vascular diseases in patients with coronary heart disease. Further studies should be conducted to assess its prospective value.

title: Key role of Ubc5 and lysine-63 polyubiquitination in viral activation of IRF3.
text: The protein known as MAVS, or mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein, is crucial for the innate immune response against RNA viruses. It transmits signals from cytosolic receptors called RIG-I-like receptors, which bind to viral RNAs. However, the mechanism by which MAVS activates transcription factors like IRF3 to induce type-I interferons is not well understood. To investigate this, we developed a cell-free system where mitochondria from virus-infected cells activate IRF3 in the cytosol. By fractionating the cytosol, we identified Ubc5 as a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) that is necessary for IRF3 activation. Through an inducible RNAi approach, we demonstrated that Ubc5, with its catalytic activity, is required for IRF3 activation during viral infection. Additionally, the activation of IRF3 relies on two ubiquitin-binding domains of NEMO. Moreover, we found that replacing the natural ubiquitin with a mutant form (K63R) eliminates the viral activation of IRF3, highlighting the crucial role of K63 polyubiquitination in IRF3 activation.

title: Profiling of residual breast cancers after neoadjuvant chemotherapy identifies DUSP4 deficiency as a mechanism of drug resistance
text:
We conducted a study to investigate the effects of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) on patients with breast cancer. We found that approximately 30% of patients achieved a complete response to the treatment. However, a significant number of patients still had residual cancer after chemotherapy, which increased their risk of metastatic recurrence and led to poorer outcomes compared to those who achieved a complete response.

To understand the underlying mechanisms of drug resistance, we performed molecular profiling of tumors after NAC. Using digital transcript counting, we analyzed surgically resected breast cancers. Our findings revealed that low levels of dual specificity protein phosphatase 4 (DUSP4), an ERK phosphatase, were associated with increased tumor cell proliferation after NAC. Additionally, these low levels of DUSP4 were more prevalent in basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) cases.

Further analysis showed that BLBC tumors had higher levels of DUSP4 promoter methylation and gene expression patterns associated with activation of the Ras-ERK pathway compared to other breast cancer subtypes. We also observed that overexpression of DUSP4 enhanced chemotherapy-induced apoptosis, while depletion of DUSP4 reduced the response to chemotherapy.

Moreover, we found that reduced DUSP4 expression in primary tumors after NAC was linked to treatment-refractory high Ki-67 scores and shorter recurrence-free survival. Finally, we discovered that inhibiting mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) in combination with docetaxel treatment had a synergistic effect in BLBC xenografts.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that downregulation of DUSP4 activates the Ras-ERK pathway in BLBC, leading to a diminished response to anti-cancer chemotherapy. These findings highlight the importance of understanding the molecular mechanisms of drug resistance in breast cancer and suggest potential therapeutic strategies for improving treatment outcomes.

title: Age-related behaviors have distinct transcriptional profiles in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: There has been significant interest in finding potential biomarkers of aging. These biomarkers would be helpful in predicting vulnerabilities in individuals that may occur earlier than expected due to varying rates of aging. Previous attempts to identify biomarkers of aging have often involved comparing long-lived animals to a control group. However, interventions in model systems that extend lifespan can be challenging to interpret because they can have unintended effects on physiology unrelated to aging. Therefore, finding reliable biomarkers of aging is difficult, but it would be valuable to have metrics that can predict either physiological or chronological age. One method that has been used to identify biomarkers for various diseases is gene expression profiling. In this study, we examined the gene expression profiles of individual wild-type Caenorhabditis elegans throughout their entire lifespan. We assessed age-related behaviors and survival in these nematodes and correlated them with their gene expression profiles. This allowed us to identify transcriptional profiles that were strongly associated with either physiological or chronological age. Overall, our approach provides a model for finding potential biomarkers of aging in higher organisms that can be sampled repeatedly throughout their lifespan.

title: Synchronization of Diffusively-Connected Nonlinear Systems: Results Based on Contractions with Respect to General Norms
text: The theory of contraction offers a sophisticated method for analyzing the behavior of specific nonlinear dynamical systems. This study focuses on the application of contraction to achieve synchronization among interconnected components described by nonlinear differential equations. We present estimations of the convergence of state differences between components in various scenarios, including line, complete, and star graphs, as well as their Cartesian products. Our approach is based on contraction theory, utilizing matrix measures derived from norms that are not induced by inner products. These norms are particularly suitable for numerous applications; however, proofs cannot rely on Lyapunov-like linear matrix inequalities. Instead, alternative techniques, such as the utilization of the Perron-Frobenius Theorem for L1 or L∞ norms, must be introduced.

title: GeneTrack--a genomic data processing and visualization framework.
text: In order to overcome the informatics challenges faced by research groups with limited computational support, we have developed a software platform called GeneTrack. This platform is designed to store, analyze, and visualize large data sets generated by high-throughput 'ChIP-chip' and 'ChIP-seq' methodologies. GeneTrack automates various steps of the data processing pipeline, such as smoothing and peak detection, and also enables easy sharing of results through the web. Our software can be accessed for free through the Google Project Hosting environment at http://genetrack.googlecode.com.

title: Multisite optical recording of excitability in the enteric nervous system.
text: We used a multisite optical recording technique that involved an array of 464 photodiodes to measure changes in transmembrane potentials (Vm) of guinea-pig and mouse enteric neurones. These neurones were stained with the voltage-sensitive dye Di-8-ANEPPS. By using this technique, we were able to observe Vm changes in enteric neurones that were evoked by depolarizing current pulses or synaptic activation. These changes in Vm were consistent with the intracellular measurements taken from the same neurone. The fluorescence of action potentials showed a fractional change of -0.09 +/- 0.06% and the peak to peak noise level was 20 +/- 14% of the action potential amplitude. When we stimulated interganglionic nerve strands electrically, we observed slow EPSPs, nicotinergic supra- and subthreshold fast EPSPs, as well as the propagation of action potentials along interganglionic strands. Additionally, when we applied acetylcholine locally onto a single ganglion, we consistently induced action potential discharge in a dose-dependent manner. This demonstrated the feasibility of conducting neuropharmacological studies using this technique. The optical mapping allowed us to simultaneously record action potentials in a large number of neurones with high spatiotemporal resolution, which cannot be achieved with conventional techniques. This technique is a powerful tool for studying the spread of excitability within enteric circuits and assessing the differential activation of enteric populations in response to various stimuli that directly modulate neuronal activity or act through synaptic mechanisms.

title: Telomere-bound TRF1 and TRF2 stall the replication fork at telomeric repeats.
text: Vertebrate telomeres are made up of repeated sequences of T2AG3 and associated proteins, including TRF1 and TRF2, which are DNA-binding proteins specific to telomeres. It has been proposed that telomeres can exist in two different states: an open state that allows interaction with various factors, and a closed state that prevents such interactions. TRF1 and TRF2 are thought to promote the closed state. However, little is known about how these states affect DNA replication. To investigate this, we conducted experiments both in vitro and in vivo. In our in vitro replication system using linear SV40 DNA, we observed that telomeric repeats are not efficiently replicated. Additionally, the presence of recombinant TRF1 and TRF2 significantly hindered the progression of the replication fork at telomeric repeats. In HeLa cells overexpressing TRF1, we observed an accumulation of cells with 4N DNA content. Furthermore, cytological analyses showed that the replication focus coincided with telomere signals at a much higher frequency in TRF1-overexpressing cells compared to control cells. These findings suggest that TRF1 and TRF2 have inhibitory effects on the progression of the replication fork.

title: Margination of white blood cells in microcapillary flow.
text: In order for white blood cells (WBCs) to effectively stick to the walls of blood vessels, they must first move towards them. To understand this process, we used a two-dimensional model of blood flow to simulate how WBCs interact with the vessel walls. We also considered the collective behavior and ability of the WBCs to change shape. Our findings show that the best conditions for WBCs to move towards the vessel walls occur when the volume of red blood cells (RBCs) and the flow rate are within certain intermediate ranges. Outside of these ranges, the movement of WBCs towards the walls is significantly reduced. We also discovered that when RBCs clump together, it enhances the movement of WBCs towards the walls, while the ability of WBCs to change shape reduces this movement. We have created state diagrams that illustrate the conditions under which WBCs move towards the vessel walls for a wide range of flow and cell suspension conditions.

title: Lung cancer treatment waiting times and tumour growth.
text:
We conducted a study at a single center, prospectively auditing 29 lung cancer patients who were awaiting potentially curative radiotherapy. These patients were assessed by one consultant in 1999 and deemed suitable for radical treatment. At the time of assessment, they had recently been diagnosed and staged using a chest computed tomographic (CT) scan. Prior to starting treatment, they underwent another CT scan for radiation field planning. 

In our study, we measured the size of the tumors on the diagnostic scans and compared them to the size on the planning scans. We also documented the time delay between the diagnostic and planning CT scans, as well as the total time between the patients' first hospital visit and the start of treatment. 

During the waiting period, two patients experienced progression of symptoms, rendering them unfit for radical treatment. Additionally, four patients had tumor progression on the planning CT scan, resulting in their tumors being too large for radical treatment. Therefore, 21% of patients who were initially considered potentially curable became incurable while on the waiting list. 

The delay between the diagnostic and planning CT scans ranged from 18 to 131 days, with an average delay of 54 days. During this time, the cross-sectional tumor size increased by up to 373%. The delay between the first hospital visit and the start of treatment ranged from 35 to 187 days, with an average delay of 94 days. The delay between the date of the radiotherapy request and the start of treatment ranged from 23 to 61 days, with an average delay of 44 days. 

This study highlights that limited access to specialists is often cited as the reason for the UK's poor performance in treating lung cancer. However, even for the small group of patients who receive specialist referral and are deemed suitable for potentially curative treatment, waiting times can lead to tumor progression and negatively impact outcomes.

title: Functional coupling of RNAP II transcription to spliceosome assembly.
text: In higher eukaryotes, the process of gene expression involves a complex network of interactions between different components at each step. In this study, we have developed an effective in vitro system to investigate the connection between RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) transcription and pre-mRNA splicing. Surprisingly, our findings demonstrate that newly synthesized pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) by RNAP II is immediately and completely directed towards the spliceosome assembly pathway. On the other hand, pre-mRNA produced by T7 RNA polymerase is assembled into the nonspecific H complex, which consists of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) proteins and inhibits spliceosome assembly. As a result, RNAP II transcription significantly enhances both the speed and overall production of spliced mRNA compared to T7 transcription. In conclusion, RNAP II facilitates the functional connection between transcription and splicing by guiding the nascent pre-mRNA into spliceosome assembly, thus bypassing the inhibitory hnRNP proteins.

title: Calicum microdomains form within neutrophils at the neutrophil–tumor cell synapse: role in antibody-dependent target cell apoptosis
text: Cellular signal transduction relies heavily on Ca2+ messages. In immune cells, Ca2+ signaling is a crucial step in various forms of activation. One such form is neutrophil-mediated antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), which plays a significant role in killing tumor cells both in vitro and in patient care. Through the use of fluorescence methodologies, we have discovered that neutrophils exhibit Ca2+ signals during ADCC against breast fibrosarcoma cells. These signals are particularly localized to Ca2+ microdomains at the interface between neutrophils and tumor cells, where they exhibit dynamic features like movement, fusion, and fission. We have also found that these signals can be blocked by the intracellular Ca2+ buffer BAPTA. At the synapse between neutrophils and tumor cells, we observed an enrichment of STIM1, a crucial mediator of Ca2+ signaling, in the neutrophil's cytoplasm. However, the Ca2+-binding proteins calbindin and parvalbumin were unaffected. Based on our findings, we propose that these Ca2+ microdomains are a result of an active signaling process. Furthermore, as Ca2+ signals within neutrophils are necessary for specific tumor cell apoptosis, it suggests that microdomains play a central role in leukocyte-mediated tumor cell destruction.

title: Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors reduce mortality in diabetic patients with non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndromes.
text:
Diabetes mellitus is a significant risk factor for negative outcomes following acute coronary syndromes (ACS). Due to the potential association between this disease and increased platelet aggregation, we conducted a study to determine if diabetic patients with ACS experience specific benefits from platelet glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa receptor inhibition. 

Our study involved a meta-analysis of diabetic populations from six large-scale platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor ACS trials: PRISM, PRISM-PLUS, PARAGON A, PARAGON B, PURSUIT, and GUSTO IV. Among the 6,458 diabetic patients included in the analysis, platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibition was found to significantly reduce mortality at 30 days, from 6.2% to 4.6% (OR 0.74; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.92; P=0.007). In contrast, the 23,072 nondiabetic patients did not experience any survival benefit (3.0% versus 3.0%). The interaction between platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibition and diabetic status was statistically significant (P=0.036). 

Among the 1,279 diabetic patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) during their hospitalization, the use of these agents was associated with a mortality reduction at 30 days from 4.0% to 1.2% (OR 0.30; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.69; P=0.002). 

In conclusion, our meta-analysis, which includes data from large-scale trials on intravenous platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors for the medical management of non-ST-segment-elevation ACS, demonstrates that these agents may significantly reduce mortality at 30 days in diabetic patients. Although our findings are not based on a randomized assessment, the survival benefit appears to be more pronounced in patients undergoing PCI. Therefore, the use of platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors should be strongly considered for diabetic patients with ACS.

title: Glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and alterations in mitogen-activated protein kinase activation are mediated by oxidative stress in multidrug-resistant human breast carcinoma cells.
text: In our previous study, we observed that depriving multidrug-resistant human breast carcinoma cells (MCF-7/ADR) of glucose led to cell death. To further investigate this phenomenon, we aimed to determine if metabolic oxidative stress was the underlying cause or at least the link between the causative processes behind the cell toxicity. In the experiments described here, we found that mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) was activated within 3 minutes of being in a glucose-free environment and remained active for 3 hours. Depriving the cells of glucose for 2-4 hours also resulted in oxidative stress, as indicated by a three-fold increase in the concentration of oxidized glutathione and a three-fold rise in pro-oxidant production. However, when the cells were treated with glucose and glutamate, MAPK activation was rapidly suppressed, and the cells were rescued from cytotoxicity. Additionally, the use of glutamate and the peroxide scavenger, pyruvate, not only saved the cells from cell death but also reduced pro-oxidant production. Furthermore, the thiol antioxidant, N-acetyl-L-cysteine, protected the cells from glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and suppressed MAPK activation. These findings suggest that oxidative stress mediated by glucose deprivation plays a role in the cytotoxicity and alterations in MAPK signal transduction in MCF-7/ADR cells. Moreover, these results support the hypothesis that metabolic oxidative stress may be a common mechanism underlying glucose deprivation-induced cell toxicity in mammalian cells.

title: A structural basis for kinetochore recruitment of the Ndc80 complex via two distinct centromere receptors.
text: The Ndc80 complex plays a crucial role in binding microtubules to the kinetochore. While the interaction between Ndc80-Nuf2 heads and microtubules is well understood, little is known about how the Spc24-25 heterodimer connects to centromeric chromatin. In this study, we present the molecular details of the Spc24-25 complex with the histone-fold protein Cnn1/CENP-T, which reveals how this connection links microtubules to chromosomes. The conserved Ndc80 receptor motif of Cnn1 binds as an α helix in a hydrophobic cleft between Spc24 and Spc25. Mutations that disrupt the Ndc80-Cnn1 interaction also prevent binding to the Mtw1 complex and are lethal in yeast. We also identify a Cnn1-related motif in the Dsn1 subunit of the Mtw1 complex, which is necessary for Ndc80 binding and essential for yeast growth. When the Cnn1 peptide replaces this region, yeast viability is restored, demonstrating the functionality of the Ndc80-binding module in different molecular contexts. Additionally, phosphorylation of the Cnn1 N-terminus coordinates the binding of the two competing Ndc80 interaction partners. Overall, our findings provide structural insights into how the Ndc80 complex binds to its centromere recruiters in a modular manner.

title: Feedback Circuit among INK4 Tumor Suppressors Constrains Human Glioblastoma Development
text: We have created a novel algorithm called the nonheuristic genome topography scan (GTS) algorithm to analyze the genomic alterations in human glioblastoma (GBM). Through this algorithm, we have identified a common occurrence of p18(INK4C) and p16(INK4A) codeletion. When we reintroduced p18(INK4C) into GBM cells lacking both p16(INK4A) and p18(INK4C), we observed a disruption in cell-cycle progression and a decrease in tumorigenic potential. Conversely, when we used RNAi to deplete p18(INK4C) in primary astrocytes deficient in p16(INK4A) or established GBM cells, we observed an increase in tumorigenicity both in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, we found that suppressing p16(INK4A) in primary astrocytes led to a simultaneous increase in p18(INK4C). These findings reveal a feedback regulatory circuit in the astrocytic lineage and demonstrate that p18(INK4C) acts as a genuine tumor suppressor in human GBM. It works in collaboration with other INK4 family members to restrict inappropriate cell proliferation.

title: The SMC5/6 complex maintains telomere length in ALT cancer cells through SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins
text:
Telomerase activation is a common strategy used by cancer cells to extend their telomeres and achieve unlimited replicative potential. However, some cancer cells are unable to activate telomerase and instead rely on a mechanism called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), which involves telomere homologous recombination (HR). One characteristic of ALT cells is the recruitment of telomeres to PML bodies, also known as APBs.

In this study, we demonstrate that the SMC5/6 complex localizes to APBs in ALT cells and plays a crucial role in directing telomeres to these structures. Specifically, the MMS21 SUMO ligase, a component of the SMC5/6 complex, modifies several telomere-binding proteins, including TRF1 and TRF2, through a process called SUMOylation. When the SUMOylation of TRF1 or TRF2 is inhibited, APB formation is prevented.

Furthermore, when the SMC5/6 subunits are depleted using RNA interference, telomere HR is impaired, leading to telomere shortening and senescence in ALT cells. This suggests that the SMC5/6 complex is essential for facilitating telomere HR and elongation in ALT cells by promoting APB formation through the SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins.

title: Dynein pulls microtubules without rotating its stalk.
text: Dynein, a motor protein found in cilia and flagella, is responsible for their movement. It has been suggested that the sliding of doublet microtubules is caused by a conformational change in the motor domain, which in turn moves a microtubule attached to the end of an extension called the stalk. The prevailing theory proposes that the head domain, along with its stalk, rotates towards the plus end of the microtubule. However, observing stalks bound to microtubules has proven challenging. In this study, we present the clearest images to date of stalks in action using a new method called "cryo-positive stain" electron microscopy. By studying sea urchin outer arm dynein molecules bound to microtubules, we confirmed their activity in in vitro motility assays. Analysis of the electron micrographs revealed that the angles between the stalks and microtubules remained relatively constant in different states of the dynein molecule. However, the heads, along with their stalks, shifted in relation to their attachment to the A-tubule. These findings contradict models that propose the stalk acts as a lever arm to amplify structural changes. Instead, our observations suggest a new mechanism in which dynein utilizes its stalk as a grappling hook, latching onto a tubulin subunit located 8 nm ahead and exerting force by retracting a portion of the tail (linker).

title: The INO80 chromatin remodeling complex in transcription, replication and repair.
text: The Ino80 ATPase is part of the SNF2 family of ATPases and plays a crucial role in a complex that remodels chromatin using ATP. While INO80 complexes in yeast and higher eukaryotes have similar core subunits, they have evolved differently and gained new subunits with functions specific to each species. Recent research has demonstrated that the INO80 complex is involved in various nuclear processes that rely on chromatin, such as transcription, DNA repair, and DNA replication.

title: VEX1 controls the allelic exclusion required for antigenic variation in trypanosomes.
text: The exclusion of alleles is crucial for the variation of antigens and the evasion of the immune system in African trypanosomes. These parasites in the bloodstream utilize RNA polymerase-I (pol-I) to transcribe only one telomeric variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) gene at a time, resulting in an abundance of switchable VSG coats. Through a genetic screening, we have identified a trypanosome VSG exclusion-1 (VEX1) that is involved in the exclusive expression of telomeres. VEX1 is sequestered by the active VSG, and when VEX1 is either ectopically expressed or depleted, the silencing of other VSGs is affected, indicating positive and negative regulation, respectively. Positive regulation impacts both VSGs and non-telomeric pol-I-transcribed genes, while negative regulation primarily affects VSGs. Additionally, negative regulation by VEX1 also influences telomeric pol-I-transcribed reporter constructs, but only when they contain sequences that share homology with a pol-I-transcribed locus. In conclusion, the combination of restricted positive regulation through VEX1 sequestration and VEX1-dependent, possibly homology-dependent silencing, drives a mechanism of allelic exclusion where the "winner-takes-all".

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates monocyte differentiation and functions in mBSA and IL-1β-induced arthritis.
text: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays a crucial role in regulating various immune cells, including monocytes. Our previous research has demonstrated that KLF2 inhibits the activation of monocytes that leads to inflammation. However, the impact of KLF2 on arthritis has not been investigated yet. In our current study, we have discovered that KLF2 hemizygous mice exhibit a significant increase in the recruitment of an inflammatory subset of monocytes (CD11b(+)F4/80(+)Ly6C+) to sites of inflammation compared to wild type littermate controls. Additionally, we found that bone marrow-derived monocytes from KLF2 hemizygous mice showed a significant up-regulation of inflammatory mediators such as MCP-1, Cox-2, and PAI-1, in comparison to wild-type controls. Furthermore, KLF2 hemizygous mice displayed more severe arthritis when induced with methylated-BSA and IL-1β, compared to their wild type littermate controls. This increased severity of arthritis was associated with an elevated number of matured and differentiated monocytes towards the osteoclastic lineage in KLF2 hemizygous mice, potentially contributing to the damage of cartilage and bone in arthritic mice. Moreover, arthritic KLF2 hemizygous mice exhibited higher expression levels of proteins such as HSP60, HSP90, and MMP13, along with reduced levels of pPTEN, p21, p38, and HSP25/27 molecules in bone marrow cells, compared to wild type controls. These findings provide valuable insights and evidence regarding the role of KLF2 in the transcriptional regulation of arthritis through the modulation of monocyte differentiation and function.

title: Relationship of collegiate football experience and concussion with hippocampal volume and cognitive outcomes.
text:
The importance of concussion and subconcussive impacts in collegiate athletes has been well-documented in terms of short-term cognitive performance. However, there is limited data on the long-term effects on brain structure and cognitive function. This study aimed to assess the relationship between concussion history, years of football experience, hippocampal volume, and cognitive performance in collegiate football athletes.

The study was conducted between June 2011 and August 2013 at a US psychiatric research institute specializing in neuroimaging. The participants included collegiate football players with a history of clinician-diagnosed concussion, collegiate football players without a history of concussion, and non-football-playing healthy controls matched for age, sex, and education.

The main outcomes measured were brain volumes using high-resolution anatomical magnetic resonance imaging and cognitive assessment using a computerized concussion-related cognitive battery.

The results showed that both players with and without a history of concussion had smaller hippocampal volumes compared to healthy controls. Additionally, players with a history of concussion had smaller hippocampal volumes than players without concussion. There was also a significant inverse relationship between left hippocampal volume and the number of years of football played in both athlete groups.

Behavioral testing did not show any differences in cognitive measures between athletes with and without a concussion history. However, there was a correlation between years of playing football and slower reaction time.

In conclusion, this study highlights the inverse relationship between concussion history, years of football played, and hippocampal volume in collegiate football athletes. It also suggests that years of football experience may be associated with slower reaction time. Further research is needed to understand the temporal relationships of these findings.

title: STING and the innate immune response to nucleic acids in the cytosol
text: Detecting pathogen-derived nucleic acids in the cytosol is crucial for activating the innate immune defense against various types of pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and eukaryotes. However, an inappropriate response to cytosolic nucleic acids can lead to severe autoimmune diseases. The protein STING has been identified as a key signaling molecule in the innate immune response to cytosolic nucleic acids. It plays a particularly important role in responding to cytosolic DNA and a unique type of bacterial nucleic acids known as "cyclic dinucleotides". In this article, we will discuss the latest advancements in understanding STING and highlight the unresolved questions in this field.

title: Global Assessment of Genomic Regions Required for Growth in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
text: Understanding the fundamental physiology of bacterial pathogens relies on identifying the essential genomic elements for their viability. Recent advancements in high-density mutagenesis and deep sequencing have enabled the discovery of necessary and conditionally necessary genes in various bacteria. However, genes represent only a fraction of the intricate genomes of significant bacterial pathogens. In this study, we employ an unbiased approach to comprehensively identify genomic regions, encompassing genes, domains, and intergenic elements, crucial for the optimal growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a major global health threat. Our findings reveal that certain proteins possess both essential growth-required domains and dispensable domains. Furthermore, numerous non-coding regions, such as regulatory elements and non-coding RNAs, play a critical role in mycobacterial growth. This analysis demonstrates that the genetic prerequisites for growth are more intricate than what can be discerned through a gene-focused investigation.

title: Cyclooxygenase-Dependent Tumor Growth through Evasion of Immunity
text: The exact ways in which melanoma and other cancer cells avoid being targeted by the immune system are not fully understood. However, our research reveals that the growth of tumors formed by mutant Braf(V600E) mouse melanoma cells in a host with a fully functioning immune system relies on the production of prostaglandin E2 by the cancer cells. This prostaglandin E2 suppresses the immune response and promotes inflammation that supports tumor growth. By eliminating cyclooxygenases (COX) or prostaglandin E synthases in Braf(V600E) mouse melanoma cells, as well as in Nras(G12D) melanoma or breast or colorectal cancer cells, we found that these cancer cells become vulnerable to immune control and trigger a shift in the tumor's inflammatory profile towards anti-cancer immune pathways. This COX-dependent inflammatory signature observed in mice is also present in human cutaneous melanoma biopsies, suggesting that COX activity plays a role in immune suppression across different species.
