Our pre-clinical data demonstrates that combining COX inhibitors with anti-PD-1 blockade effectively eliminates tumors, indicating that COX inhibitors could be beneficial in combination with immune-based therapies for cancer patients.

title: Anti-alphav integrin monoclonal antibody intetumumab enhances the efficacy of radiation therapy and reduces metastasis of human cancer xenografts in nude rats.
text:
In a previous study, we found that intetumumab, a fully human anti-αv integrin monoclonal antibody, can enhance the effects of radiation therapy in mice with xenograft tumors. However, since intetumumab does not react with mouse integrins but does react with rat integrins, we decided to investigate the combined use of radiation therapy and intetumumab in human cancer xenograft models in nude rats. Our goal was to assess the impact on both tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment.

We conducted experiments on nude rats that had human head and neck cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) xenografts. These rats were treated with intetumumab and fractionated local tumor radiotherapy. We examined the effects on tumor growth, metastasis, blood perfusion, oxygenation, and gastrointestinal toxicity.

When intetumumab was used alone, it had a moderate effect on tumor growth. However, when combined with fractionated radiation therapy, intetumumab significantly inhibited tumor growth and produced a better tumor response rate compared to radiation therapy alone. Additionally, intetumumab treatment significantly reduced lung metastasis in the NSCLC xenograft model.

We also observed that intetumumab treatment led to increased oxygenation and blood perfusion in the xenograft tumors, as measured by microbubble-enhanced ultrasound imaging. Furthermore, the combined use of intetumumab and radiation therapy reduced the density of microvessels and increased apoptosis in both tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment.

Toxicity studies revealed that intetumumab treatment did not cause any histopathologic changes in the lungs and did not sensitize the sensitive gastrointestinal epithelium to the effects of radiation therapy.

Overall, our findings suggest that intetumumab can enhance the effectiveness of fractionated radiation therapy in human cancer xenograft tumors in nude rats without increasing toxicity.

title: Methylomic trajectories across human fetal brain development.
text: During development, epigenetic processes play a crucial role in regulating gene expression. The significance of DNA methylation in the development of the fetal brain is evident through the dynamic expression of de novo DNA methyltransferases and the presence of neurodevelopmental deficits in individuals with mutations in the MECP2 gene, which is involved in binding methyl-CpG. However, our understanding of how the epigenome changes over time during fetal brain development has been limited. To address this, we analyzed DNA methylation patterns at approximately 400,000 sites in 179 human fetal brain samples (100 male, 79 female) ranging from 23 to 184 days post-conception. Our analysis revealed significant changes in DNA methylation across fetal brain development at more than 7% of the sites, with a higher occurrence of hypomethylation as the fetus ages. These changes were found to be less frequent in promoter regulatory regions but more frequent in regions surrounding CpG islands (shores and shelves) and gene bodies. Additionally, we observed significant differences in DNA methylation between males and females at several autosomal sites, with a few regions exhibiting sex-specific DNA methylation patterns during brain development. Through weighted gene comethylation network analysis (WGCNA), we identified distinct modules of co-methylated sites associated with fetal age, which were enriched for genes involved in neurodevelopmental processes. This study represents the most comprehensive investigation of DNA methylation during human fetal brain development to date, highlighting the significant epigenomic plasticity that occurs during the prenatal period.

title: Synaptic Determinants of Rett Syndrome
text: There is increasing evidence indicating that both human patients and animal models of neurological and psychiatric diseases experience changes in the structure and molecular organization of synaptic connections. As a result of these experimental findings, the concept of synapsopathies has been introduced to describe brain disorders that affect synaptic function and plasticity. The relationship between neurological diseases and synaptic abnormalities is particularly significant in syndromes that also involve mental retardation, such as Rett syndrome (RS). RS is a dominant X-linked neurological disorder that is primarily caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) gene. This article will focus on the current understanding of the synaptic changes caused by MeCP2 mutations in mouse models of RS and will discuss potential experimental therapies that are currently being used. Various experimental approaches have revealed that RS may result from an imbalance in synaptic transmission homeostasis in specific brain regions. In fact, the absence of MeCP2 leads to impaired forms of experience-induced neuronal plasticity. Based on the findings presented in this article, it is reasonable to suggest that we are getting closer to understanding how diseases like RS affect the brain. This knowledge will help us identify the neurobiological foundations of human cognition.

title: Depressive symptoms and physical decline in community-dwelling older persons.
text: The older community-dwelling population commonly experiences significant symptoms of depression. However, it is unclear whether these depressive symptoms contribute to a decline in physical function. This study aimed to determine if depressive symptoms in older individuals increase the risk of subsequent decline in physical function, as measured by objective performance-based tests. The study was a 4-year prospective cohort study conducted in the communities of Iowa and Washington counties, Iowa. A total of 1286 individuals aged 71 years and older completed a short battery of physical performance tests in 1988 and again 4 years later. Baseline depressive symptoms were assessed using the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale. Physical performance tests included an assessment of standing balance, a timed 2.4-m (8-ft) walk, and a timed test of 5 repetitions of rising from a chair and sitting down. The results showed that, after adjusting for baseline performance score, health status, and sociodemographic factors, increasing levels of depressive symptoms predicted greater decline in physical performance over 4 years. The odds ratio for decline in those with depressed mood compared to those without was 1.55, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.02-2.34. Even among those who reported no disability and were at the high end of the functional spectrum, the severity of depressive symptoms predicted subsequent decline in physical performance. The odds ratio for decline in this group was 1.03, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.00-1.08. In conclusion, this study provides evidence that older individuals who report depressive symptoms are at a higher risk of subsequent physical decline. These findings suggest that preventing or reducing depressed mood could potentially reduce functional decline in older individuals.

title: Foxk proteins repress the initiation of starvation-induced atrophy and autophagy programs
text: Autophagy, the main process that breaks down molecules in response to starvation, is regulated not only in the cytosolic compartment but also in the nucleus. However, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of how specific transcription factors control the expression of genes necessary for autophagy. In this study, we have discovered that Foxk proteins (Foxk1 and Foxk2) act as transcriptional repressors of autophagy in muscle cells and fibroblasts. Interestingly, Foxk1/2 counteract another forkhead transcription factor, Foxo3, which activates a similar set of autophagic and atrophic targets in muscle. Foxk1/2 recruit Sin3A-HDAC complexes to prevent the acetylation of histone H4 and the expression of crucial autophagy genes. Surprisingly, mTOR enhances the transcriptional activity of Foxk1 by facilitating its entry into the nucleus, specifically limiting the basal levels of autophagy in nutrient-rich conditions. Our study reveals a conserved mechanism, dating back to ancient times, in which mTOR interprets the nutritional status to restrict autophagy by repressing essential autophagy genes through Foxk-Sin3-mediated transcriptional control.

title: PRRSV receptors and their roles in virus infection
text: The Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) has a limited ability to infect certain types of cells, specifically those that are well-differentiated and belong to the monocyte/macrophage lineage. These include pulmonary alveolar macrophages and cell lines such as MA-104 (derived from African green monkey kidney), Marc-145, Vero, and CL-2621. The infection of host cells by PRRSV is a process called receptor-mediated endocytosis and replication. The presence or absence of specific cellular receptors determines whether a cell line is susceptible or resistant to PRRSV infection. Some cell lines that are normally resistant to PRRSV, such as BHK-21, PK-15, and CHO-K1, can become sensitive to the virus when recombinant receptor proteins are expressed. Several important PRRSV receptors have been identified, including heparin sulfate, sialoadhesin, CD163, CD151, and vimentin. These receptors play a role in virus attachment, internalization, and uncoating. Each receptor has a specific distribution in different cells, functions at different stages of virus infection, and interacts with viral proteins or genes in a unique way. Recently, there has been increased interest in studying the combined effects of these receptors due to their specific functions. PRRSV receptors are now being targeted for the development of new antiviral agents and recombinant cell lines that can be used to isolate the virus or create more effective vaccines. This is because the receptor sequences are more conserved compared to the genetic variation of the virus. This paper reviews the role of PRRSV receptors and the molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction between the virus and these receptors.

title: Kinetic Analysis Reveals the Fate of a MicroRNA following Target Regulation in Mammalian Cells
text:
Considerable progress has been made in understanding the biogenesis and regulation of microRNA (miRNA). However, there is still limited knowledge about what happens to miRNA after it regulates its target. To gain a better understanding of this process, we conducted a kinetic analysis of miRNA turnover. We specifically looked at the decay of miRNA after its biogenesis and during the regulation of a target that is not subject to Ago2-mediated cleavage.

Through our analysis, we discovered that each miRNA molecule is capable of regulating at least two target transcripts. This finding provides in vivo evidence that miRNA is not permanently bound to its target and that the non-slicing pathway of miRNA regulation involves multiple turnovers. Using deep sequencing, we also found that miRNA recycling is restricted by target regulation. This regulation leads to posttranscriptional modifications at the 3' end of the miRNA and accelerates its decay rate.

These findings shed new light on the efficiency of miRNA regulation and help explain how a single miRNA can regulate a large number of transcripts. Additionally, our research identifies one of the mechanisms that contribute to the specificity of miRNA decay in mammalian cells.

title: Estimation of nuclear DNA content in plants using flow cytometry
text: Flow cytometry (FCM) is currently the most widely used method for measuring nuclear DNA content in plants, thanks to its use of DNA-selective fluorochromes. Compared to other methods like Feulgen densitometry, FCM offers advantages such as easier sample preparation and higher sample throughput, making it more suitable for estimating genome size, generative polyploidy levels, nuclear replication state, and endopolyploidy (polysomaty). In this article, we present four protocols for preparing samples (intact cell nuclei suspensions) and describe the analysis of nuclear DNA amounts using FCM. We discuss the necessary chemicals and equipment, the measurement process, data analysis, and common issues encountered with plant material, such as interference from secondary metabolites. We also delve into the importance and requirements of internal and external standardization. Additionally, we emphasize the significance of using accurate terminology for DNA amounts and genome size, and provide an explanation of its fundamental principles.

title: Predictive value of bone resorption and formation markers in cancer patients with bone metastases receiving the bisphosphonate zoledronic acid.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the correlation between bone metabolism and clinical outcomes in patients receiving bisphosphonate therapy for bone metastases. Three large randomized trials have shown that zoledronic acid reduces the risk of skeletal-related events. In this study, urinary measurements of N-telopeptide (Ntx) and serum bone alkaline phosphatase (BAP) were obtained from 1,824 bisphosphonate-treated patients. Of these patients, 1,462 were treated with zoledronic acid and 362 were treated with pamidronate. The patients were grouped based on their baseline and most recent levels of Ntx and BAP. The results showed that patients with high and moderate Ntx levels had a significantly higher risk of skeletal complications and disease progression compared to patients with low Ntx levels. High Ntx levels were also associated with a higher risk of death on study. The study concluded that Ntx is a valuable marker for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with bone metastases receiving bisphosphonates.

title: Role of CD28-B7 interactions in generation and maintenance of CD8 T cell memory.
text: While the activation of naive T cells through CD28-B7 interaction is well understood, its role in the formation and preservation of T cell memory remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the significance of CD28-B7 interactions in primary T cell activation and immune memory. The researchers compared the CD8 T cell responses to a lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection in wild-type (+/+) mice and CD28-deficient (CD28(-/-)) mice. During the primary response, both +/+ and CD28(-/-) mice experienced a significant activation and expansion of LCMV-specific CD8 T cells. However, the magnitude of the primary CD8 T cell response to dominant and subdominant LCMV CTL epitopes was approximately 2- to 3-fold lower in CD28(-/-) mice compared to +/+ mice. Interestingly, the absence of CD28-mediated costimulation did not result in preferential suppression of CD8 T cell responses to the weaker subdominant epitopes. Similarly, blocking B7-mediated costimulation with CTLA4-Ig treatment in +/+ mice also led to a 2-fold reduction in anti-LCMV CD8 T cell responses. However, the loss of CD28/B7 interactions did not significantly impact the generation and maintenance of CD8 T cell memory. The magnitude of CD8 T cell memory was approximately 2-fold lower in CD28(-/-) mice compared to +/+ mice. Nevertheless, LCMV-specific memory CD8 T cells in CD28(-/-) mice exhibited normal homeostatic proliferation in vivo and provided protective immunity. Therefore, CD28 signaling is not essential for the proliferative renewal and maintenance of memory CD8 T cells.

title: Systematic reviews from astronomy to zoology: myths and misconceptions.
text:
Systematic literature reviews are widely utilized to support evidence-based decision making. They are particularly valuable in assessing the effectiveness of healthcare interventions through reviews of randomized controlled trials. However, the prominence of systematic reviews in evidence-based medicine has led to misconceptions about their purpose and methods. One common misconception is that systematic reviews are only applicable to randomized controlled trials and cannot handle other types of evidence, such as non-randomized studies or qualitative research. In reality, systematic literature reviews involve locating, evaluating, and synthesizing evidence from various sources.

The importance of regularly updating systematic reviews to assess the effectiveness of healthcare interventions was demonstrated by Antman and colleagues, who found that review articles failed to mention advancements in treatment identified by an updated systematic review. The term "meta-analysis," referring to the quantitative synthesis of primary study results, was coined by Gene Glass almost 25 years ago. However, the need to minimize bias in literature reviews has been emphasized by social scientists since the 1960s.

In recent years, systematic reviews have gained significance in health services research, and the growing interest in evidence-based decision making suggests that their use will continue to rise. Despite this, not everyone agrees on the necessity or desirability of systematic reviews. As one moves further away from clinical applications, skepticism about their usefulness tends to increase. Common arguments against a broader role for systematic reviews often stem from misconceptions about their history, purpose, methods, and applications. In this article, I will address eight common myths surrounding systematic reviews.

title: Acellular pertussis vaccines protect against disease but fail to prevent infection and transmission in a nonhuman primate model.
text:
Pertussis, caused by the bacterial pathogen Bordetella pertussis, is a highly contagious respiratory illness. In recent years, the United States has seen an increase in pertussis rates, reaching a 50-year high of 42,000 cases in 2012. The reasons behind this resurgence are not fully understood, but we believe that the current acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines may not effectively prevent colonization and transmission of the bacteria.

To test this hypothesis, we conducted a study using infant baboons. These baboons were vaccinated with either aP or whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccines at 2, 4, and 6 months of age. At 7 months, they were then exposed to B. pertussis. We monitored the infection by measuring colonization in nasopharyngeal washes and observing leukocytosis and symptoms.

The results showed that baboons vaccinated with aP were protected from severe pertussis symptoms but not from colonization. They did not clear the infection faster than unvaccinated animals and were able to transmit B. pertussis to unvaccinated contacts. On the other hand, vaccination with wP led to a quicker clearance of the infection compared to unvaccinated and aP-vaccinated animals. Interestingly, previously infected animals did not get colonized upon secondary infection.

Although all vaccinated and previously infected animals showed strong serum antibody responses, there were notable differences in T-cell immunity. Previously infected and wP-vaccinated animals had robust B. pertussis-specific T helper 17 (Th17) memory and Th1 memory. In contrast, aP vaccination induced a Th1/Th2 response instead.

These findings suggest that aP, which induces an immune response that does not match the natural infection, fails to prevent colonization and transmission of pertussis. This provides a plausible explanation for the resurgence of pertussis and highlights the need for improved vaccines to effectively control the disease.

title: Specific and cooperative binding of E. coli single-stranded DNA binding protein to mRNA.
text: The protein responsible for binding to single-stranded DNA in E. coli was examined using fluorometric titration with different RNAs. The results revealed that the protein binds specifically and cooperatively to its own mRNA. This binding had an inhibitory effect on the expression of ssb and bla in vitro, but not nusA. Interestingly, this inhibition occurred at a concentration of SSB that is typically found in the body. The implications of this protein's role in gene regulation are further explored and discussed.

title: ACAM2000™: The new smallpox vaccine for United States Strategic National Stockpile
text: Smallpox, a disease that was eradicated over 30 years ago, has once again become a concern due to increased fears of bioterrorism. The previous smallpox vaccine in the United States, Dryvax, was effective but not enough to vaccinate the entire population. However, Dryvax had safety concerns as it consisted of various strains of the vaccinia virus and was grown on calf skin, which posed a risk of contamination. To address this, the US government supported the development of a new and improved smallpox vaccine called ACAM2000. ACAM2000 is a purified derivative of Dryvax, grown in cell culture to eliminate contamination risks. Trials conducted in 2008 showed that ACAM2000 had similar effectiveness and adverse events as Dryvax. However, both vaccines were found to have a higher than expected rate of myocarditis and pericarditis, as determined through cardiac screening. ACAM2000 received FDA approval in August 2007 and replaced Dryvax for smallpox vaccinations in February 2008. Currently, there are over 200 million doses of ACAM2000 available in the US Strategic National Stockpile. This review provides an overview of the production, characterization, clinical trials, and adverse events associated with ACAM2000.

title: Risk of malignant neoplasms in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis.
text:
The association between sarcoidosis and malignancy, specifically lymphoma and lung cancer, has been a topic of debate for more than 20 years. The concern has been primarily focused on misclassification. This study aimed to examine the occurrence of malignancies in a group of sarcoidosis patients by linking them to a nationwide cancer register.

The cohort consisted of 254 patients who were followed for a median of 25 years until their death, emigration, or December 31, 1992, whichever came first. The expected number of cancer cases was determined using the annual age and sex-specific cancer rates from the Danish Cancer Registry.

Out of the registered 36 cancers, three were initially misclassified as sarcoidosis, resulting in 33 confirmed cases compared to the expected 23 (standardized incidence ratio (SIR) = 1.4; 95% CI 0.99 to 2.0). Five cases of lung cancer were observed, exceeding the expected 2.5 cases, resulting in an SIR of 2.0 (95% CI 0.7 to 4.7). No instances of lymphoma were found, with only one case of leukemia. Notably, there was a significant excess of pharyngeal cancers based on two cases (SIR = 15.4; 95% CI 1.7 to 56).

In conclusion, this study does not support the theory of a connection between sarcoidosis and malignancy. Previous studies suggesting such an association are likely influenced by selection bias and misclassification.

title: Rps14 haploinsufficiency causes a block in erythroid differentiation mediated by S100A8 and S100A9
text: The impaired production of red blood cells in the deletion 5q subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) has been associated with the deletion of RPS14, a gene that codes for a small subunit of ribosomal protein. To investigate this further, we conducted experiments on mice with Rps14 inactivation and found that they exhibited a defect in the maturation of red blood cells, specifically during the transition from polychromatic to orthochromatic erythroblasts. This defect led to progressive anemia, abnormal development of megakaryocytes, and loss of quiescence in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) as the mice aged. Through quantitative proteomics analysis, we discovered that the mutant erythroblasts expressed higher levels of proteins involved in innate immune signaling, particularly the S100a8 and S100a9 proteins, which are calcium-binding proteins. The increased expression of S100a8 was observed not only in mutant erythroblasts but also in monocytes and macrophages. We determined that S100a8 plays a functional role in the erythroid defect caused by Rps14 deletion, as the addition of recombinant S100a8 was sufficient to induce a differentiation defect in normal erythroid cells. Furthermore, when we genetically deactivated S100a8 expression, we were able to rescue the erythroid differentiation defect in HSCs with Rps14 haploinsufficiency. Our findings establish a connection between Rps14 haploinsufficiency in del(5q) MDS and the activation of the innate immune system, leading to the induction of S100A8-S100A9 expression and ultimately resulting in a p53-dependent defect in the maturation of red blood cells.

title: A Microtubule Interactome: Complexes with Roles in Cell Cycle and Mitosis
text: The microtubule (MT) cytoskeleton plays a crucial role in various cellular functions, such as intracellular material transport, cell polarity maintenance, and mitosis regulation. MT-associated proteins (MAPs) are responsible for coordinating these functions by binding to and modifying the properties of MTs. In this study, we utilized a combination of MT cosedimentation assay, 1D and 2D PAGE, and mass spectrometry to identify more than 250 MAPs in early Drosophila embryos. To understand the cellular function of these newly discovered MAPs, we employed two complementary approaches. Firstly, we conducted an RNA interference (RNAi) screen, which led to the identification of 21 previously uncharacterized genes involved in MT organization. Secondly, we performed a bioinformatics analysis using binary protein interaction data to construct potential interaction networks of MAPs. By integrating both approaches, we successfully identified and validated MAP complexes that likely play significant roles in cell cycle regulation and mitosis. This study highlights the effectiveness of a multidisciplinary approach in obtaining biologically relevant data and reveals novel MAPs, many of which are crucial in cell division.

title: Structure of the Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factor Sec7 Domain of Human Arno and Analysis of the Interaction with ARF GTPase
text: The initiation of vesicle budding from the Golgi membrane surface is facilitated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that are related to Sec7. These GEFs convert the GTPase ARF into a GTP-bound form that is associated with the membrane. In this study, we present the crystal structure of the catalytic Sec7 homology domain of Arno, which is a human GEF for ARF1. The structure was determined at a resolution of 2.2 angstroms. The Sec7 domain is a protein composed of helices and has a unique hydrophobic groove that is conserved across different species. Through mutagenesis experiments based on the structure, we have identified the groove and an adjacent conserved loop as the surface that interacts with ARF. Further experiments using protein footprinting have mapped the sites of interaction between the Sec7 domain and ARF1 to the switch 1 and switch 2 regions of the GTPase. This provides a model for understanding the interaction between ARF GTPases and Sec7 domain exchange factors.

title: Brief Communication Repeated Cocaine Administration Increases Voltage-Sensitive Calcium Currents in Response to Membrane Depolarization in Medial Prefrontal Cortex Pyramidal Neurons
text: The role of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in cocaine addiction is crucial, but there is still incomplete evidence on how it functions in this addiction. Recent studies have shown that repeated cocaine use leads to changes in pyramidal mPFC neurons, including a decrease in voltage-gated K+ currents (VGKCs) and a possible increase in voltage-sensitive Ca2+ currents (I(Ca)). To investigate these changes further, we conducted current-clamp and voltage-clamp recordings in brain slices and dissociated cells to determine if I(Ca) is altered in mPFC pyramidal neurons after chronic cocaine use with short or long-term withdrawal. We also studied the role of VGKCs in regulating the generation of Ca2+ plateau potentials in mPFC neurons. After a 3-day withdrawal, repeated cocaine use significantly prolonged the duration of evoked Ca2+ plateau potentials and increased whole-cell I(Ca) in mPFC neurons. Blocking L-type Ca2+ channels with nifedipine not only increased the threshold but also reduced the duration and amplitude of Ca2+ plateau potentials in both saline- and cocaine-withdrawn mPFC neurons. However, there was no significant difference in the changes observed between saline- and cocaine-withdrawn neurons after blocking L-type Ca2+ channels. Additionally, after 2-3 weeks of withdrawal, an increase in amplitude was observed, while the prolonged duration of Ca2+ potentials persisted. These findings suggest that chronic cocaine use enhances the responsiveness of I(Ca), particularly through activated L-type Ca2+ channels, to excitatory stimuli in rat mPFC pyramidal neurons.

title: Rational Extension of the Ribosome Biogenesis Pathway Using Network-Guided Genetics
text: The process of ribosome biogenesis is crucial for all eukaryotic cells and involves over 170 genes that are responsible for assembling, modifying, and transporting ribosome components across various cellular compartments. Despite extensive research, it is likely that there are still many more genes involved in this pathway. In this study, we used a network-guided genetics approach, which utilizes recent advancements in functional genomics and proteomics, to computationally identify additional genes involved in ribosomal biogenesis. We conducted experiments on over 100 candidate genes in yeast and confirmed the involvement of at least 15 new genes, including some that were previously unknown (YDL063C, YIL091C, YOR287C, YOR006C/TSR3, YOL022C/TSR4). We linked these new genes to specific aspects of ribosomal subunit maturation, ribosomal particle association, and ribosomal subunit nuclear export. Additionally, we identified genes that are specifically required for the processing of 5S, 7S, 20S, 27S, and 35S rRNAs. These findings reveal new connections between ribosome biogenesis and mRNA splicing and expand the biogenesis pathway by more than 10%, with many of the newly identified genes having human counterparts. This significantly enhances our understanding of this universally conserved process in eukaryotes.

title: Quantifying Transmission Investment in Malaria Parasites
text: Microparasites often infect new hosts by developing specialized life stages, which requires a portion of the parasite population to stop reproducing and instead transform into transmission forms. The production of these transmission stages affects how easily the parasite can infect hosts, exploit them, and respond to medical interventions such as drug treatment. To predict how parasites will react to public health efforts in both the short and long term, it is crucial to understand their transmission strategies. However, directly observing these strategies is rare, and they are usually inferred from infection patterns. In this study, we use malaria as a case study to evaluate previously proposed methods for inferring transmission stage investment. We generate simulated data using a model of infection dynamics within a host, where the true transmission investment is known. Our results demonstrate that the existing methods are inadequate and potentially misleading. The main challenge lies in distinguishing transmission stages produced by different generations of parasites. To address this issue, we develop a new approach that performs significantly better on simulated data. Applying this new approach to real data from mice infected with a single strain of Plasmodium chabaudi, we estimate that transmission investment ranges from zero to 20%. We also find evidence of variable investment over time in some hosts but not others. These findings suggest that even in controlled experimental infections, where host genetics and environmental factors are regulated, parasites can exhibit diverse patterns of transmission investment.

title: Roles of induced expression of MAPK phosphatase-2 in tumor development in RET-MEN2A transgenic mice
text: Mutations in the RET tyrosine kinase gene are responsible for the development of multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A and 2B (MEN2A and MEN2B). However, the mechanisms underlying the mutant RET-mediated signaling are not well understood. In this study, we observed elevated levels of mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase-2 (MKP-2) in carcinomas developed in transgenic mice carrying the MEN2A mutation (RET-MEN2A). Interestingly, MKP-2 expression was not only induced by RET-MEN2A or RET-MEN2B mutant proteins, but also by the activation of endogenous RET by its ligand, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). We also observed MKP-2 expression in the MKK-f cell line, derived from a mammary tumor in a RET-MEN2A transgenic mouse. Inhibition of MKP-2 reduced the in vitro and in vivo proliferation of MKK-f cells, which was associated with decreased expression of cyclin B1. Additionally, we found high levels of MKP-2 in medullary thyroid carcinomas from MEN2A patients. These findings suggest that increased MKP-2 expression may play a critical role in oncogenic signaling downstream of mutant RET, leading to dysregulation of the cell cycle.

title: Effects of repeated social stress on leukocyte distribution in bone marrow, peripheral blood and spleen
text: The movement of white blood cells between different parts of the body serves an important purpose in monitoring for foreign substances and allowing the immune system to respond quickly and effectively. When male mice living in groups were repeatedly subjected to aggressive encounters with another mouse, it significantly changed the movement of white blood cells and caused a gradual redistribution of immune cells in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and spleen. Exposure to this stressor for 2, 4, or 6 consecutive days resulted in the mobilization of cells and increased production of certain types of white blood cells in the bone marrow. This was accompanied by an accumulation of neutrophils and monocytes in the bloodstream and spleen. The number of B cells in the bone marrow and blood decreased significantly, while there was an increase in B cells in the spleen, suggesting a redirection of this cell type. On the other hand, T cells were greatly reduced in these immune compartments. The recruitment of specific types of white blood cells from the bone marrow to the spleen, such as monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils, may play a crucial role in the development of glucocorticoid resistance in the spleen, as previously observed in mice subjected to repeated social defeat.

title: Lentivirally transduced dendritic cells as a tool for cancer immunotherapy.
text:
BACKGROUND: Dendritic cells (DC) are specialized immune cells that play a crucial role in cancer immunotherapy by presenting antigens to T cells. In this study, we investigated the influence of different elements (cPPT, trip, WPRE, SIN) on the efficiency of transducing human DC. We also examined the effects of transduction on the phenotype and function of both human and murine DC. Additionally, we tested the ability of transduced DC to present antigens and stimulate immune responses.

METHODS: Lentiviruses encoding tNGFR were used to transduce human and murine DC. We assessed the transduction efficiency by comparing different lentiviral vectors containing various elements. We also evaluated the stability of gene expression, viability, phenotype, and function of transduced DC. To test antigen presentation, human DC were transduced with lentiviruses encoding huIi80MAGE-A3, while murine DC were transduced with huIi80tOVA.

RESULTS: The lentiviral vector containing the trip element and a self-inactivating (SIN) design was the most efficient in transducing human DC. At a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 15, this vector achieved stable gene expression in up to 94.6% of murine DC and 88.2% of human DC, without affecting their viability, phenotype, or function. Human DC transduced with huIi80MAGE-A3 were able to stimulate MAGE-A3-specific CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cell clones and prime both types of T cells in vitro. Murine DC transduced with huIi80tOVA were capable of presenting OVA peptides in the context of MHC class I and class II in vitro. Furthermore, these transduced DC induced a strong OVA-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte response in vivo, which provided protection against subsequent challenge with OVA-expressing tumor cells.

CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that lentiviral vectors can efficiently transfer genes into human and murine DC, enabling these cells to elicit antigen-specific immune responses both in vitro and in vivo. The choice of transfer vector composition significantly affects the transduction efficiency.

title: Global Reorganization of Replication Domains During Embryonic Stem Cell Differentiation
text: The regulation of DNA replication in mammals involves the coordinated firing of replicon clusters, which duplicate large chromosome segments during a specific phase of cell division. Previous studies have shown that these replicon clusters form subchromosomal units that persist through multiple cell generations, but the exact boundaries of these units have not been determined. Additionally, the relationship between changes in replication timing and transcription changes during cell differentiation has not been thoroughly investigated. In this study, we have generated detailed replication-timing profiles in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation into neural precursor cells. Our findings reveal that chromosomes can be divided into large domains of coordinated replication, referred to as "replication domains," which are separated by transition regions that lack origins of replication. Interestingly, the boundaries of these replication domains are highly conserved across different ESC lines and induced pluripotent stem cells, despite their distant relationship. Surprisingly, during ESC differentiation, smaller replication domains merge into larger units that replicate at similar times, which are more closely associated with the GC content and density of LINE-1 transposable elements, rather than gene density. Changes in replication timing are more closely coordinated with changes in transcription for weak promoters compared to strong promoters, and are accompanied by changes in subnuclear positioning. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that replication profiles are specific to cell types, and changes in these profiles reveal chromosome segments that undergo significant reorganization during differentiation. Furthermore, the presence of smaller replication domains and a higher density of timing transition regions that disrupt isochore replication timing are unique characteristics of the pluripotent state.

title: Molecular characterization of the yeast meiotic regulatory gene RIM1.
text:
Genetic studies in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae indicate that the RIM1 gene plays a crucial role as a positive regulator of meiosis. Mutations in the rim1 gene result in reduced expression of IME1, which is necessary for the expression of various meiotic genes. Consequently, these mutations lead to a partial defect in meiosis and spore formation. In this study, we present the sequence of the RIM1 gene and conduct a functional analysis of its coding region.

The RIM1 gene product, known as RIM1, consists of three regions that bear resemblance to C2H2 zinc fingers. When serine replaces cysteine in each of these putative zinc fingers, RIM1 loses its function. The carboxyl-terminus of RIM1 is rich in acidic amino acids and is essential for its full activity. Additionally, RIM1 contains two potential phosphorylation sites for cAMP-dependent protein kinase (cAPK). Substituting serine with alanine at one site has no effect on RIM1 activity, while substitution at the other site impairs its function. Based on this analysis, it is suggested that RIM1 may act as a transcriptional activator.

To further investigate the role of RIM1, we generated a complete deletion of the RIM1 gene using cloning techniques. This null allele, similar to previously identified rim1 mutations, causes a partial defect in meiosis. In addition to RIM1, optimal expression of IME1 requires the gene products of MCK1 and IME4. Defects in the expression of a meiotic reporter gene (ime2-lacZ) and sporulation associated with rim1, mck1, and ime4 mutations are cumulative. These findings indicate that RIM1 functions independently of MCK1 and IME4 to enhance IME1 expression.

title: Butyrate greatly enhances derivation of human induced pluripotent stem cells by promoting epigenetic remodeling and the expression of pluripotency-associated genes.
text: In this report, we present findings that demonstrate the significant enhancement of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell derivation from human adult or fetal fibroblasts through the use of butyrate, a naturally occurring fatty acid commonly used as a nutritional supplement and differentiation agent. The efficiency of iPS cell derivation is greatly increased (15- to 51-fold) after a short butyrate treatment, regardless of whether retroviral or piggyBac transposon vectors expressing 4 to 5 reprogramming genes are used. Notably, the effect of butyrate stimulation is even more pronounced (>100- to 200-fold) when either the KLF4 or MYC transgene is absent. Importantly, butyrate treatment does not have a negative impact on the properties of established iPS cell lines generated using either 3 or 4 retroviral vectors or a single piggyBac DNA transposon vector. These characterized iPS cell lines, including those derived from an adult patient with sickle cell disease using either the piggyBac or retroviral vectors, exhibit normal karyotypes and pluripotency. To gain a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying butyrate stimulation, we conducted comprehensive analyses, including genome-wide gene expression and promoter DNA methylation microarrays, as well as other epigenetic analyses, on established iPS cells and cells from intermediate stages of the reprogramming process. Our results show that butyrate treatment enhances histone H3 acetylation, promoter DNA demethylation, and the expression of endogenous pluripotency-associated genes, such as DPPA2, which partially substitutes for butyrate stimulation. Therefore, butyrate, as a cell permeable small molecule, offers a simple tool for further investigation into the molecular mechanisms of cellular reprogramming. Additionally, butyrate stimulation provides an efficient method for reprogramming various human adult somatic cells, including those from patients that are typically more difficult to reprogram.

title: Nanoparticle conjugation of CpG enhances adjuvancy for cellular immunity and memory recall at low dose.
text: We have discovered a way to improve the effectiveness of subunit vaccines by targeting the adjuvant to the lymph node using ultrasmall polymeric nanoparticles. These nanoparticles quickly travel to the lymph node after being injected into the skin, resulting in a significant enhancement of adjuvant efficacy even at low doses. By attaching CpG-B or CpG-C oligonucleotides to the nanoparticles, we were able to better target both the adjuvant and antigen to cross-presenting dendritic cells, compared to using free adjuvant. This led to increased maturation of dendritic cells and secretion of T helper 1 (Th1)-cytokines, ultimately resulting in stronger activation of effector CD8(+) T-cells with improved cytolytic profiles and enhanced memory recall. Remarkably, even with just 4 μg of CpG, the nanoparticle-bound CpG-B was able to provide substantial protection against syngeneic tumor challenge in mice, even after 4 months of vaccination, whereas free CpG-B did not. These findings demonstrate that nanocarriers can significantly enhance the efficacy of vaccines by using a low dose of adjuvant to induce potent and long-lasting cellular immunity.

title: Induction of pluripotent stem cells by defined factors is greatly improved by small-molecule compounds
text: The reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells can be accomplished by introducing transcription factors in an abnormal location, although the success rate is typically low. However, we have discovered that the efficiency of reprogramming can be significantly enhanced by utilizing inhibitors of DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase (HDAC). Specifically, valproic acid (VPA), an HDAC inhibitor, has been found to enhance reprogramming efficiency by over 100 times when utilizing Oct4-GFP as a reporter. Additionally, VPA allows for the successful generation of pluripotent stem cells without the need to introduce the oncogene c-Myc.

title: Noninvasive ventilation for treatment of acute respiratory failure in patients undergoing solid organ transplantation: a randomized trial.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare noninvasive ventilation (NIV) with standard treatment using supplemental oxygen administration in recipients of solid organ transplantation with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. The study was conducted at a university hospital's general intensive care unit. Out of 238 patients who underwent solid organ transplantation, 51 were treated for acute respiratory failure, and 40 were eligible for the study. The patients were randomly assigned to either the NIV group or the standard treatment group. The main outcome measures were the need for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, complications, duration of ventilatory assistance, length of hospital stay, and intensive care unit mortality. 

The results showed that within the first hour of treatment, a higher percentage of patients in the NIV group showed improvement in their PaO2 to FIO2 ratio compared to the standard treatment group. Over time, a sustained improvement in PaO2 to FIO2 was observed in a higher percentage of patients in the NIV group. The use of NIV was associated with a significant reduction in the rate of endotracheal intubation, rate of fatal complications, length of stay in the intensive care unit, and intensive care unit mortality. However, there was no difference in hospital mortality between the two groups. 

In conclusion, these findings suggest that NIV should be considered as a treatment option for selected recipients of transplantation with acute respiratory failure.

title: BIOINFORMATICS APPLICATIONS NOTE
text: MADE4, also known as microarray ade4, is a software tool designed to simplify the analysis of microarray gene-expression data using multivariate techniques. It is compatible with various gene-expression data formats and utilizes the comprehensive statistical and graphical functions available in the R package ade4. MADE4 expands upon these functions to specifically cater to microarray data analysis. Furthermore, it introduces novel graphical and visualization tools that assist in the interpretation of multivariate analysis results for microarray data.

title: Dual and opposing roles of primary cilia in medulloblastoma development
text: New research has demonstrated that primary cilia play a crucial role in Hedgehog (Hh) signaling during the development of mammals. It is also known that abnormal Hh signaling can lead to cancer, but the significance of primary cilia in the development of cancer is still unclear. Medulloblastomas, which are the most common malignant brain tumors in children, can arise from cerebellar granule neuron precursors (GNPs). The proliferation of GNPs relies on the presence of the primary cilium and Hh signaling. To investigate whether primary cilia in GNPs contribute to the growth of medulloblastomas in mice, we genetically removed primary cilia. The results showed that the formation of medulloblastomas was halted when the tumor was driven by a constantly active Smoothened protein (Smo), an activator of Hh signaling. On the other hand, the removal of cilia was necessary for the growth of medulloblastomas caused by a constantly active glioma-associated oncogene family zinc finger-2 (GLI2), a transcription factor downstream of Hh signaling. Therefore, depending on the specific oncogenic event that triggers it, primary cilia either promote or inhibit the formation of medulloblastomas. Interestingly, the presence or absence of cilia was associated with specific variations of human medulloblastomas. Primary cilia were found in medulloblastomas with activation in HH or WNT signaling, but not in most medulloblastomas belonging to other distinct molecular subgroups. This suggests that primary cilia could potentially serve as a diagnostic tool and offer new insights into the mechanisms of tumorigenesis.

title: RAS genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: signal transduction in search of a pathway.
text: Initially, it was believed that Ras proteins in budding yeasts played a role in controlling the start of the cell cycle based on the availability of nutrients. However, recent studies have shed light on the mechanism of Ras-mediated signal transmission, challenging our understanding of the signal Ras conveys. Presently, it is hypothesized that Ras aids in coordinating cellular metabolism and the accumulation of mass, but the specific stimuli that Ras responds to remain uncertain.

title: Use of synthetic peptides to locate novel integrin alpha2beta1-binding motifs in human collagen III.
text: We utilized a collection of 57 artificial peptides that cover the entire triplehelical region of human collagen III to identify the specific sites where the collagen-binding integrin alpha(2)beta(1) binds. We investigated the ability of these peptides to facilitate the binding of various integrin preparations in the presence of Mg(2+). We tested different types of integrins, including wild-type integrins (recombinant alpha(2) I-domain, alpha(2)beta(1) purified from platelet membranes, and recombinant soluble alpha(2)beta(1) expressed as an alpha(2)-Fos/beta(1)-Jun heterodimer), and found that they bound well to only three peptides. These peptides contained GXX'GER motifs (GROGER and GMOGER, where O represents hydroxyproline) and one peptide contained two adjacent GXX'GEN motifs (GLKGEN and GLOGEN). We also examined two mutant alpha(2) I-domains: the inactive T221A mutant, which did not recognize any peptides, and the constitutively active E318W mutant, which bound to a larger subset of peptides. We observed that activated human platelets adhered more strongly to peptides containing the GER motif compared to resting platelets, and HT1080 cells bound well to a greater number of peptides compared to platelets. The binding of cells and recombinant proteins was completely abolished by the anti-alpha(2) monoclonal antibody 6F1 and by removing Mg(2+). We have identified two new integrin-binding motifs with high affinity in human collagen III (GROGER and GLOGEN), as well as a third motif (GLKGEN) that displayed intermediate activity. We confirmed the presence of each motif using shorter synthetic peptides.

title: Locations of cerebral infarctions in tuberculous meningitis
text: The study examined the locations of cerebral infarctions in 14 patients with tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and 173 patients with noninflammatory ischemic stroke (IS). Among TBM patients, 75% of infarctions were found in the "TB zone," which is supplied by the medial striate and thalamoperforating arteries. Only 11% occurred in the "IS zone," supplied by the lateral striate, anterior choroidal, and thalamogeniculate arteries. In IS patients, 29% of infarctions occurred in the IS zone, 29% in the subcortical white matter, and 24% in (or affecting) the cerebral cortex. Only 11% occurred in the TB zone. Bilaterally symmetrical infarctions of the TB zone were common in TBM patients (71%), but rare in IS patients (5%).

title: TRP channels of intracellular membranes.
text: Ion channels are traditionally known for controlling the movement of ions across the plasma membrane in response to various external and internal signals. They also serve important functions within intracellular membranes. These channels can be temporarily located in intracellular membranes during their production or transport to their final destination. They may also be present in endocytic pathways, where they are either recycled back to the plasma membrane or directed to the lysosome for degradation. Some intracellular membrane channels are involved in intracellular signal transmission, with the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP(3)R) in the endoplasmic reticulum being a well-known example. Certain organellar intracellular membrane channels are necessary for maintaining the ionic balance within their respective organelles. Recently discovered intracellular membrane calcium (Ca(2+)) channels also play active roles in membrane trafficking. Transient receptor potential (TRP) proteins, a superfamily consisting of 28 members in mammals, are Ca(2+)-permeable channels with diverse tissue distribution, subcellular localization, and physiological functions. Most mammalian TRP channels, including the ancestral yeast TRP channel (TRPY1) found in the vacuole compartment, are not only located in the plasma membrane but also in intracellular membranes. Accumulating evidence suggests that intracellularly-localized TRP channels actively contribute to the regulation of membrane traffic, signal transmission, and vesicular ion balance. This review aims to provide a summary of recent research in this area, including a discussion on the fundamental membrane and electrical properties of the compartments where TRP channels are found.

title: the Development of Autoimmune Myocarditis in Mice by an
text: The role of IL-12 in promoting inflammation and T-helper 1 responses is well-known. In this study, we investigated the impact of IL-12 receptor signaling on the development of experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) in mice. We found that mice lacking IL-12Rbeta1 or STAT4 were resistant to myocarditis induction, while treatment with IL-12 worsened the disease. Surprisingly, we discovered that IFN-gamma, which is produced as a result of IL-12 activation, actually suppressed EAM. Depletion of IFN-gamma or genetic deficiency exacerbated myocarditis, leading to increased cellularity and cytokine production in the spleens of mice. Conversely, treatment with recombinant IFN-gamma inhibited the development of myocarditis. In conclusion, IL-12/IL-12R/STAT4 signaling promotes EAM, while IFN-gamma has a protective role, potentially by controlling the expansion of activated T lymphocytes.

title: The Viral and Cellular MicroRNA Targetome in Lymphoblastoid Cell Lines
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a common herpesvirus in humans that has been linked to various B cell cancers and lymphoproliferative disorders. During a latent infection, EBV produces 25 viral pre-microRNAs (miRNAs) and triggers the expression of specific host miRNAs, such as miR-155 and miR-21, which may contribute to the development of viral-induced cancers. However, the exact role of EBV miRNAs in viral pathogenesis and lymphomagenesis is not well understood due to limited knowledge about their targets. In this study, we utilized a technique called photoactivatable ribonucleoside-enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (PAR-CLIP) along with deep sequencing and computational analysis to comprehensively investigate the interactions between viral and cellular miRNAs in EBV-infected lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) using the B95-8 strain of EBV. Our analysis identified 7,827 sites where miRNAs interacted with cellular 3'UTRs, with 531 of these sites containing matches to viral miRNAs. We confirmed 24 of these interactions using reporter assays. Our findings demonstrate that during latent infection, EBV miRNAs primarily target cellular transcripts, allowing the virus to manipulate the host environment. Additionally, the targets of EBV miRNAs are involved in various cellular processes that are directly relevant to viral infection, including innate immunity, cell survival, and cell proliferation. We also provide evidence that host miRNAs from the miR-17/92 cluster, which are regulated by the myc gene, can regulate the expression of latent viral genes. This comprehensive analysis of the miRNA targetome in EBV-infected B cells is a crucial step towards understanding the functions of EBV-encoded miRNAs and potentially identifying new therapeutic targets for EBV-associated malignancies.

title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Leads to Nuclear Genome Instability via an Iron-Sulfur Cluster Defect
text: Multiple human diseases are caused by mutations and deletions in the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) and instability of the nuclear genome. In this study, we demonstrate that in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the loss of mtDNA leads to instability in the nuclear genome. This instability occurs due to a cellular crisis, characterized by cell-cycle arrest and selection. Interestingly, this crisis is not caused by the absence of respiration, but rather by a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential. Further analysis revealed that cells experiencing this crisis have a defect in iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) biogenesis, which is dependent on normal mitochondrial function. We also discovered that reducing the production of nonmitochondrial ISC proteins is enough to induce genomic instability in cells with intact mitochondrial function. These findings suggest that mitochondrial dysfunction triggers nuclear genome instability by inhibiting the production of ISC-containing proteins, which are crucial for maintaining the integrity of the nuclear genome. To watch a video summary of this study, please refer to the PaperFlick file available in the online Supplemental Data.

title: Replisome stall events have shaped the distribution of replication origins in the genomes of yeasts
text: In S phase, it is crucial to duplicate the entire genome accurately, leaving no sections of DNA unreplicated. In this study, we have developed a simple mathematical model to explain the likelihood of replication failure caused by the irreversible stalling of replication forks. Our findings demonstrate that the probability of complete genome replication is highest when replication origins are evenly distributed, the largest distances between origins are minimized, and the origins closest to the ends of chromosomes are positioned nearby. We have observed that the positions of origins in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome adhere to all three predictions, thus maximizing the probability of successful replication in the event of replication fork stalling. Additionally, we have found that the positions of origins in four other yeasts - Kluyveromyces lactis, Lachancea kluyveri, Lachancea waltii, and Schizosaccharomyces pombe - also align with these predictions. By comparing failure rates at chromosome ends to those in the interior regions, we have determined a mean rate of ∼5 × 10(-8) per nucleotide for replication fork stalling, which is consistent with experimental estimates. Utilizing this value in our theoretical predictions, we have calculated replication failure rates that align with data obtained from replication origin knockout experiments. Furthermore, our theory predicts that larger genomes, such as those found in mammals, will have a significantly higher probability of genome-wide replication failure and will likely require additional compensatory mechanisms.

title: Regulation of chromatin by histone modifications
text: Chromatin is not a passive structure, but rather an active DNA scaffold that can respond to external signals to control the various functions of DNA. One crucial element of chromatin that plays a vital role in this control is the modification of histones. There is a continuously expanding list of these modifications, and we are only just beginning to understand the complexity of their effects. However, it is evident that histone modifications are essential in most biological processes that involve the manipulation and expression of DNA. In this article, we will outline the known histone modifications, identify their genomic locations, and discuss some of their functional consequences, with a focus on transcription, which has been extensively studied.

title: Single-Cell Expression Analyses during Cellular Reprogramming Reveal an Early Stochastic and a Late Hierarchic Phase
text: During the process of cellular reprogramming, only a small portion of cells are able to transform into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Previous studies on gene expression during reprogramming have focused on analyzing groups of cells, making it difficult to identify reprogramming events at the single-cell level. To overcome this limitation, we employed two gene expression technologies to examine the expression of 48 genes in individual cells at different stages of the reprogramming process. Our analysis of early stages revealed significant variation in gene expression among cells, whereas late stages showed more consistent patterns. We found that the expression of Esrrb, Utf1, Lin28, and Dppa2 is a more reliable indicator of cells progressing into iPSCs compared to the previously suggested reprogramming markers Fbxo15, Fgf4, and Oct4. Early in reprogramming, gene expression appears to be stochastic, but as the process advances, a hierarchical phase emerges with Sox2 acting as the upstream factor in a gene expression hierarchy. Finally, downstream factors from the late phase, excluding Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc, and Nanog, can activate the pluripotency circuitry.

title: Scaffold-based three-dimensional human fibroblast culture provides a structural matrix that supports angiogenesis in infarcted heart tissue.
text:
CONTEXT Our team has developed a method to implant angiogenic patches onto the outer layer of the heart in order to promote the growth of new blood vessels in areas of damaged heart tissue. These patches are made using a 3D culture of human dermal fibroblasts, which contain cells that release substances that stimulate blood vessel growth. We wanted to test whether these patches, when made with viable cells, could stimulate the growth of new blood vessels in areas of heart tissue that had been damaged by a heart attack.

METHODS AND RESULTS We conducted experiments on mice with severe combined immunodeficiency. We induced a blockage in one of the arteries that supplies blood to the heart, causing a heart attack. We then implanted the 3D fibroblast patches, with or without viable cells, onto the outer layer of the heart at the site of the damaged tissue. We compared the results to a group of mice that underwent the same heart attack procedure but did not receive any patches. Fourteen and 30 days after the surgery, we examined the hearts and took tissue samples for analysis. We found that the damaged heart tissue that received the patches with viable cells showed a significantly greater growth of new blood vessels (including small arteries, veins, and capillaries) compared to the groups that did not receive patches or received patches without viable cells.

CONCLUSIONS Based on our animal model, we have found that the 3D fibroblast patches with viable cells can stimulate the growth of new blood vessels in areas of heart tissue that have been damaged by a heart attack. This suggests that these patches could potentially be used to repair damaged heart tissue caused by a heart attack.

title: Global tuberculosis control: lessons learnt and future prospects
text: Tuberculosis (TB) is an ancient illness that continues to persist in the present. Although it was no longer a concern in the 1960s and 1970s, TB resurfaced in the early 1990s due to factors such as the HIV/AIDS epidemic and the rise of drug-resistant strains. Despite the discovery of the tubercle bacillus by Robert Koch over a century ago, the global status of TB control remains uncertain. In this article, we examine the progression of worldwide TB control policies, including DOTS (directly observed therapy, short course) and the Stop TB Strategy. We also evaluate the challenges and barriers faced by the global public health community in developing and implementing these strategies, and explore how these experiences can inform future efforts towards eliminating TB.

title: Global prevalence of glaucoma and projections of glaucoma burden through 2040: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The purpose of this study was to provide updated information on the global prevalence of glaucoma, as previous estimates were outdated and focused primarily on European populations. The researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 50 population-based studies to determine the prevalence of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG). They also projected the number of affected individuals in 2020 and 2040. The study found that the global prevalence of glaucoma among individuals aged 40-80 years is 3.54%. The prevalence of POAG is highest in Africa (4.20%), while the prevalence of PACG is highest in Asia (1.09%). In 2013, it was estimated that there were 64.3 million people worldwide with glaucoma, a number that is projected to increase to 76.0 million in 2020 and 111.8 million in 2040. The researchers also identified factors associated with glaucoma, such as gender, ancestry, and urbanization. Men were found to be more likely to have POAG than women, and individuals of African ancestry were more likely to have POAG than those of European ancestry. Additionally, people living in urban areas had a higher likelihood of having POAG compared to those in rural areas. These findings highlight the need for effective glaucoma screening, treatment, and public health strategies, particularly in Asia and Africa where the burden of glaucoma is expected to be highest in the coming years.

title: Gastrointestinal tract as a major site of CD4+ T cell depletion and viral replication in SIV infection.
text: HIV and SIV, which are viruses that affect humans and monkeys, replicate most effectively in activated memory CD4(+) T cells. These cells are abundant in the intestine. When rhesus monkeys were infected with SIV, there was a significant and specific reduction in CD4+ T cells in the intestine shortly after infection. This occurred before any similar changes were observed in other lymphoid tissues. The decrease in CD4+ T cells in the intestine happened at the same time as a productive infection of a large number of mononuclear cells in that area. It seems that the intestine is a primary target for SIV replication and the main location for CD4+ T cell loss during the early stages of SIV infection.

title: Interaction of streptavidin-based peptide-MHC oligomers (tetramers) with cell-surface TCRs.
text: The interaction between oligomeric peptide-MHC (pMHC) complexes and T cell receptors (TCR) on the cell surface can be considered as a representation of TCR-pMHC interactions at cell-cell interfaces. In this study, we examined the binding and dissociation kinetics of streptavidin-based pMHC oligomers (tetramers) from CD8(pos) T cells derived from 2C-TCR transgenic mice and T cell hybridomas expressing either the 2C TCR or a high-affinity mutant (m33) of this TCR. Our findings indicate that the tetramers did not fully saturate the cell-surface TCR, contrary to the assumption made when determining affinity values (K(D)). This is partly due to dissociative losses from tetramer-stained cells. Using a kinetic model, we observed that the dissociation rate and equilibrium constants of the oligomers depended not only on monovalent association and dissociation rates (k(off) and k(on)), but also on a multivalent association rate (μ) and TCR cell-surface density. Our results suggest that dissociation rates may explain the unexpectedly high frequency of tetramer-negative, functionally competent T cells observed in certain T cell responses.

title: Human monocyte characteristics are altered in hypercholesterolaemia.
text: During the development of atherosclerosis, peripheral blood monocytes play a role in adhering to the endothelium, migrating into the subendothelial space, and taking up lipoproteins to become macrophage/foam cells. We conducted a study to determine if the characteristics of peripheral blood monocytes are altered in individuals with hyperlipidemia, comparing age, sex, and smoking status matched pairs of patients and controls. Monocytes from hypercholesterolemic patients were found to be more responsive to stimulation by the agonist N-formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine compared to the controls. Specifically, they exhibited increased chemokinesis, chemotaxis, and adhesion to porcine aortic endothelial monolayers. The patients' monocytes also showed an increase in the total surface expression of the adhesion glycoprotein CD11b/CD18, but not CD11c/CD18. However, the monocytes in hyperlipidemia were larger in size, resulting in no change in the surface density of CD11b/CD18. These findings suggest that circulating monocytes in hypercholesterolemia have functional differences, which may contribute to their increased involvement in atherosclerosis associated with hypercholesterolemia.

title: Adult Mammalian Neural Stem Cells and Neurogenesis: Five Decades Later.
text: The maintenance of balanced tissue regeneration and increased adaptability in different organs is attributed to adult somatic stem cells. The study of adult neurogenesis and neural stem cells, which began fifty years ago, has evolved into a well-established field that has greatly impacted neuroscience, developmental biology, and regenerative medicine. In this review, we highlight recent advancements and address inquiries concerning adult mammalian neural stem cells, which can also be applied to other somatic stem cells. Additionally, we explore emerging subjects that are shaping the field's direction towards a deeper comprehension of adult neural stem cells and their potential for enhancing human well-being.

title: Relationship of ambulatory blood pressure and the heart rate profile with renal function parameters in hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease.
text: The management of hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) requires strict control of blood pressure (BP). This cross-sectional study aimed to explore the relationship between ambulatory BP, heart rate (HR) profile, central hemodynamics, arterial stiffness, and renal function parameters in 25 hospitalized hypertensive patients with CKD. The study found significant positive associations between urine albumin excretion rate (UACR) and 24-hour, daytime, and nighttime ambulatory systolic BP. Additionally, UACR showed significant negative associations with 24-hour and daytime HR variability. B-type natriuretic peptide level and hemoglobin A1c were also positively related to UACR. Regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), 24-hour and nighttime HR variability were positively associated with eGFR, while circulating pentosidine and nighttime HR had a negative relationship with eGFR. Central hemodynamics and arterial stiffness did not show any significant associations with renal function parameters. These findings suggest that renal function deterioration influences ambulatory BP and the HR profile. Further research is needed to investigate the causal relationship between ambulatory BP, HR profile, and renal function parameters in hypertensive patients with CKD.

title: The frequency and immunodominance of islet-specific CD8+ T-cell responses change after type 1 diabetes diagnosis and treatment.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the changes in islet-reactive CD8(+) T-cell responses in type 1 diabetic patients after clinical diagnosis and insulin treatment. A validated islet-specific CD8(+) T-cell assay was used to measure responses against specific epitopes in 15 adult type 1 diabetic patients at two time points: close to diagnosis and 7-16 months later. The results showed that CD8(+) T-cell reactivities were less frequent at the second time point compared to diagnosis. While autoantibody titers remained unchanged in most cases, the fraction of patients responding to certain epitopes decreased significantly. Additionally, previously subdominant epitopes became the immunodominant ones. These findings suggest that changes in CD8(+) T-cell responses occur more rapidly than changes in autoantibody titers, indicating potential clinical applications for T-cell and autoantibody measurements.

title: A Protein Inventory of Human Ribosome Biogenesis Reveals an Essential Function of Exportin 5 in 60S Subunit Export
text: The process of assembling ribosomal subunits in eukaryotes is intricate and involves multiple steps. Most of the research on this topic has been conducted in yeast, specifically S. cerevisiae. In yeast, over 200 factors, including ribosomal proteins and trans-acting factors, are necessary for the organized assembly of 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits. So far, only a small number of human counterparts to these yeast ribosome synthesis factors have been studied. In this study, we utilized a systematic RNA interference (RNAi) method to examine the role of 464 candidate factors in ribosomal subunit formation in human cells. Our approach involved using inducible, fluorescent ribosomal proteins as indicators, which were then analyzed using computer-based image analysis and supervised machine-learning techniques. Through this analysis, we found evidence suggesting that 153 human proteins are functionally linked to ribosome synthesis. Our findings demonstrate that key aspects of ribosome assembly are conserved between yeast and humans, although there are some differences, particularly in the export of 60S subunits. Surprisingly, our RNAi screen revealed that the export receptor Exportin 5 (Exp5) is required for the nuclear export of 60S subunits in human cells. We also discovered that Exp5, similar to the known 60S exportin Crm1, binds to pre-60S particles in a RanGTP-dependent manner. Inhibiting the function of either Exp5 or Crm1 prevents 60S export in both human cells and frog oocytes, while only Crm1 inhibition affects 40S export. Therefore, the export of 60S subunits in vertebrate cells relies on at least two RanGTP-binding exportins.

title: Binding of the winged-helix transcription factor HNF3 to a linker histone site on the nucleosome.
text: The transcription factor HNF3 and linker histones H1 and H5 both have winged-helix DNA-binding domains. However, HNF3 and other fork head-related proteins activate genes during development, while linker histones compact DNA in chromatin and repress gene expression. We conducted a comparison of how these two classes of factors interact with chromatin templates and discovered that HNF3 binds DNA at the side of nucleosome cores, similar to linker histone. At the albumin transcriptional enhancer, a nucleosome structural binding site for HNF3 is present in active and potentially active chromatin, but not in inactive chromatin in vivo. Although the wild-type HNF3 protein does not compact DNA extending from the nucleosome like linker histone does, site-directed mutants of HNF3 can compact nucleosomal DNA if they contain basic amino acids at positions previously shown to be crucial for nucleosomal DNA compaction by linker histones. These findings demonstrate that transcription factors can possess unique nucleosome-binding activities that cannot be predicted solely from studies of factor interactions with free DNA.

title: Rapid recent growth and divergence of rice nuclear genomes.
text:
Using the nuclear DNA of the African rice Oryza glaberrima as a reference genome, we were able to identify the timing, nature, mechanisms, and specificities of recent sequence evolution in the indica and japonica subspecies of Oryza sativa. Our data shows that both indica and japonica have experienced significant increases in genome size, with indica increasing by over 2% and japonica by over 6%, since their divergence from a common ancestor. This increase is primarily due to the amplification of LTR-retrotransposons. However, the growth of the rice genome has been attenuated by the loss of all classes of DNA sequence through unequal homologous recombination and illegitimate recombination. Small deletions have been particularly common throughout the genome. 

In our analysis of over 1 Mb of orthologous regions, we did not find any cases of complete gene acquisition or loss in either indica or japonica, nor did we find any examples of precise transposon excision. However, we did observe a high rate of divergence between genes, indicating a molecular clock for transposable elements that is at least 2-fold faster than synonymous base substitutions within genes. We also found that regions prone to frequent insertions and deletions have higher levels of point mutation. These findings suggest that the rice genome is highly dynamic, with competing processes for the generation and removal of genetic variation.

title: Detection of an autoreactive T-cell population within the polyclonal repertoire that undergoes distinct autoimmune regulator (Aire)-mediated selection.
text: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) plays a crucial role in central tolerance by facilitating the presentation of tissue-specific antigens in the thymus. To investigate the impact of Aire on thymic selection in a natural environment, we utilized tetramer reagents to identify autoreactive T cells that target the Aire-dependent tissue-specific antigen interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP) within the diverse T-cell repertoire. We designed two class II tetramer reagents to specifically detect T cells that recognize two distinct peptide epitopes of IRBP. Analysis of the T-cell repertoire revealed a significant presence of activated T cells specific for both IRBP tetramers in Aire(-/-) mice, but not in Aire(+/+) mice. Interestingly, while one population of tetramer-binding T cells was effectively eliminated in an Aire-dependent manner within the thymus, the second population of tetramer-binding T cells remained unaffected and could be detected in both Aire(-/-) and Aire(+/+) T-cell repertoires. Our findings indicate that Aire-dependent thymic deletion of IRBP-specific T cells relies on the transfer of IRBP between thymic stroma and antigen-presenting cells derived from the bone marrow. Additionally, our data suggest that Aire-mediated deletion is not solely dependent on thymic expression of IRBP, but also on the proper processing and presentation of IRBP by thymic antigen-presenting cells.

title: Spatial and temporal heterogeneity of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum transmission along the Kenyan coast.
text: Over the course of one year, we conducted a study on the seasonal patterns and geographical distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum parasites in 30 villages located in Malindi, Kilifi, and Kwale Districts along the coast of Kenya. We collected Anopheline mosquitoes from inside houses at each site every two months, and at the end of the study, we determined the prevalence of malaria parasites in local school children. In total, we collected 5,476 Anopheles gambiae s.l. and 3,461 An. funestus mosquitoes.
