Through polymerase chain reaction analysis, we identified the species within the An. gambiae complex, which consisted of 81.9% An. gambiae s.s., 12.8% An. arabiensis, and 5.3% An. merus. Anopheles gambiae s.s. was found to be the primary transmitter of P. falciparum along the coast, while An. funestus accounted for over 50% of transmission in Kwale District. We observed significant spatial variations in transmission intensity, ranging from less than 1 to 120 infective mosquito bites per person per year, which corresponded to significant variations in parasite prevalence (ranging from 38% to 83%). Surprisingly, 32% of the sites with malaria prevalence rates between 38% and 70% had annual entomologic inoculation rates (EIR) of less than five infective mosquito bites per person per year. Rainfall did not significantly influence the densities of Anopheles gambiae s.l. and An. funestus in Kwale District, but in Malindi and Kilifi Districts, the mosquito densities were positively correlated with rainfall from one to three months prior. These unexpected variations in the relationship between mosquito populations and rainfall suggest environmental heterogeneity in the aquatic habitats in each district. One important finding is that the relationship between EIRs and prevalence is highly non-linear, indicating that the consistent high prevalence of malaria may be due to substantial variations in transmission intensity as measured by entomologic surveys. Therefore, the field-based estimation of entomologic parameters at the district level may not accurately reflect transmission intensity in this study.

title: Myelodysplasia and leukemia of Fanconi anemia are associated with a specific pattern of genomic abnormalities that includes cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions.
text:
Our study focused on Fanconi anemia (FA), a genetic condition that is associated with bone marrow (BM) failure, myelodysplasia (MDS), and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). We examined 57 FA patients who had either hypoplastic or aplastic anemia (n = 20), MDS (n = 18), AML (n = 11), or no BM abnormalities (n = 8). We analyzed BM samples using karyotype analysis, high-density DNA arrays in comparison to paired fibroblasts, and selected oncogene sequencing.

In patients with MDS/AML, we identified a specific pattern of chromosomal abnormalities, including 1q+ (44.8%), 3q+ (41.4%), -7/7q (17.2%), and 11q- (13.8%). Additionally, we observed cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions (translocations, deletions, or mutations) for the first time in FA (20.7%). We also found rare mutations of NRAS, FLT3-ITD, MLL-PTD, ERG amplification, and ZFP36L2-PRDM16 translocation, but no mutations in TP53, TET2, CBL, NPM1, and CEBPα. Homozygosity regions were more likely due to consanguinity rather than somatic copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, suggesting that homologous recombination is not a common mechanism in FA progression.

Importantly, we found that the RUNX1 and other chromosomal/genomic lesions were present at the MDS/AML stages, except for 1q+, which was found at all stages. These findings have implications for staging and therapeutic management of FA patients, as well as for understanding the mechanisms of clonal evolution and oncogenesis in the context of genomic instability and BM failure.

title: Molecular and Cellular Approaches for Diversifying and Extending Optogenetics
text: The use of light to control biological processes in specific cells in living organisms, known as optogenetic technologies, can be enhanced by applying molecular trafficking principles. This allows for several advancements in optogenetic control. Firstly, subcellular and transcellular trafficking strategies enable optical regulation across the entire visible spectrum, including the far-red/infrared border. Secondly, optical inhibition can be increased without requiring more light power, thanks to nanoampere-scale chloride-mediated photocurrents that maintain the light sensitivity and reversible, step-like kinetic stability of previous tools. Lastly, targeting cells based on their morphology and tissue topology is now possible, in addition to genetic identity. This allows for versatile targeting in cases where promoters are unknown or in organisms that are difficult to genetically manipulate. These findings demonstrate the application of cell-biological principles to expand the capabilities of fast and versatile optogenetic technologies, which are useful for studying intact-systems biology and behavior.

title: An analysis of the Caenorhabditis elegans lipid raft proteome using geLC-MS/MS.
text: Lipid rafts are small regions within the phospholipid bilayer that are believed to form stable "islands" serving as a platform for various cellular processes. These rafts contain important proteins involved in signaling and are anchored by glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins. Previous studies on lipid rafts have primarily focused on mammalian cell lines and single-cell organisms. However, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a well-studied model organism with a defined developmental profile, offers an ideal system to investigate this subcellular region within a complex developmental context. In this study, we examined the lipid raft proteome of C. elegans. Through geLC-MS/MS analysis, we identified a total of 44 proteins in the lipid raft fraction, with 40 of them likely being raft proteins based on their predicted functions. Additionally, we predicted that 21 of these proteins may be modified by GPI-anchoring, and experimental confirmation confirmed two of them to be GPI-anchored. This study represents the first investigation of the lipid raft proteome in C. elegans. Our findings suggest that raft proteins, including numerous GPI-anchored proteins, may play diverse and important roles in the nematode, making C. elegans a valuable model for studying lipid rafts.

title: Geographic distribution of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus soft tissue infections.
text:
The purpose of this study is to examine the growth patterns of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections in our local area and determine if certain geographic areas are at higher risk. 

To conduct the study, a retrospective chart review was performed on 614 patients who underwent incision and drainage of an abscess by a single pediatric surgical practice from January 2004 to December 2008. Additionally, previously published data from 195 patients who underwent the same procedure from January 2000 to December 2003 were also reviewed. 

The results showed that the most commonly cultured organism in the pediatric population undergoing incision and drainage was S aureus, with 388 cases identified. Out of these, 258 (66%) were methicillin resistant, indicating a 21% increase in MRSA cultures compared to the previous time period. 

Using geographic information system space-time analysis, a cluster of 14 MRSA cases was found within a 1.44-km radius between 2000 and 2003. Furthermore, geographic information system spatial analysis identified 5 separate clusters of more than 20 MRSA infection cases each in 3 different cities over the 8-year period (P value = .001). 

In conclusion, methicillin-resistant S aureus has become the most prevalent organism isolated from cultures of community-acquired abscesses requiring incision and drainage in the pediatric population in our local area. There is also a significant clustering of MRSA infections in various cities within our geographic region.

title: The right place at the right time: chaperoning core histone variants.
text: The regulation of chromatin structure and epigenetic signaling is dynamically controlled by histone proteins in order to maintain cell homeostasis. To achieve this, histones are deposited and removed from chromatin in a spatially and temporally controlled manner by specific chaperones. As histone variants have evolved, a network of chaperones with specific functions has emerged. However, the molecular details regarding how chaperones specifically interact with different histone variants are still being uncovered at a slow pace. A comprehensive understanding of these processes is crucial to gain insight into the true biological roles of histone variants, their chaperones, and their impact on chromatin dynamics.

title: Phosphorylation site mutations in heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) reduce or eliminate silencing activity.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of HP1 phosphorylation on its biological activity and biochemical properties. HP1 is a crucial protein associated with heterochromatin in Drosophila. It plays a role in silencing euchromatic genes that are mistakenly located in heterochromatin and is also necessary for the normal expression of heterochromatic genes. In vivo, HP1 undergoes multiple phosphorylation events, and hyperphosphorylation of HP1 is linked to the assembly of heterochromatin during development.

To determine the impact of phosphorylation on HP1, we expressed Drosophila HP1 in lepidopteran cultured cells using a recombinant baculovirus vector. By using matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization/time of flight mass spectroscopy, we identified phosphopeptides containing target sites for casein kinase II, protein tyrosine kinase, and PIM-1 kinase. We found that purified HP1 from bacterial cells (unphosphorylated) and lepidopteran cells (phosphorylated) had similar secondary structures.

However, phosphorylation did affect the DNA binding properties of HP1 without altering its ability to self-associate. This suggests that phosphorylation may regulate the interactions that HP1 has with other molecules in a differential manner. To further investigate the functional consequences of phosphorylation, we introduced serine-to-alanine and serine-to-glutamate substitutions at consensus protein kinase motifs in HP1. These mutant forms of HP1 showed reduced or complete loss of silencing activity in transgenic flies.

These findings indicate that the dynamic process of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating the activity of HP1 in heterochromatic silencing.

title: Elimination of paternal mitochondria in mouse embryos occurs through autophagic degradation dependent on PARKIN and MUL1
text: Mitochondria are known for their maternal mode of inheritance, but the cellular mechanism responsible for eliminating paternal mitochondria from early mammalian embryos is not well understood. While autophagy has been suggested as a mechanism in nematodes, its conservation in mammals has been debated. In this study, we demonstrate that both cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos utilize a common pathway for eliminating mitochondria. This pathway involves mitophagy, where autophagosomes sequester mitochondria and deliver them to lysosomes for degradation. The E3 ubiquitin ligases PARKIN and MUL1 have redundant roles in eliminating paternal mitochondria. This process is associated with the depolarization of paternal mitochondria and requires the involvement of the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and the PINK1 kinase. Our findings suggest that the strict maternal transmission of mitochondria relies on mitophagy and reveal a collaboration between MUL1 and PARKIN in this process.

title: Ribosome Profiling Provides Evidence that Large Noncoding RNAs Do Not Encode Proteins
text: Large noncoding RNAs are becoming increasingly recognized as a crucial element in cellular regulation. Extensive evidence suggests that these RNA transcripts directly function as functional RNAs, rather than producing proteins through encoding. However, a recent study on ribosome occupancy revealed that many large intergenic ncRNAs (lincRNAs) are bound by ribosomes, raising the possibility that they may be translated into proteins. In this study, we demonstrate that classical noncoding RNAs and 5' UTRs exhibit the same ribosome occupancy as lincRNAs, indicating that ribosome occupancy alone cannot determine whether a transcript is coding or noncoding. Instead, we propose a metric based on the well-known property of translation, where ribosomes are released upon encountering a genuine stop codon. We show that this metric effectively distinguishes between protein-coding transcripts and all known noncoding transcript classes, including lincRNAs. Collectively, these findings strongly suggest that the majority of lincRNAs do not function through encoded proteins.

title: Isolation of a Fusion Transcript, AMLl IETO, With Similarity to
text:
We have successfully created a map that shows the specific location of the chromosome 21 breakpoint region involved in t(8;21)(q22;q22.3) acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). Furthermore, we have managed to isolate a clone that contains genetic material from both chromosome 8 and 21. By using probes from these regions, we have identified rearrangements in all nine cases of t(8;21) AML that we examined. Additionally, we have obtained cDNA clones from a t(8;21) AML cDNA library that contain fused sequences from both chromosome 8 and 21.

The chromosome 8 component, known as ETO (eight twenty-one), is encoded over a large genomic region, as indicated by our analysis of corresponding yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs). The DNA sequence of the chromosome 21 portion of the fusion transcript is derived from the normal AML1 gene. Interestingly, we discovered a significant similarity between AML1 and the Drosophila segmentation gene, runt, with a 67% identity over 387 base pairs and a corresponding 69% amino acid identity.

The most crucial consequence of this translocation is the positioning of 5' sequences of AML1 next to 3' sequences of ETO on the der(8) chromosome, with the orientation being from the telomere to the centromere.

title: Treatment of spondyloarthropathy with 5-aminosalicylic acid (mesalazine): an open trial.
text:
The objective of this study was to determine the efficacy of 5-acetylsalicylic acid (5-ASA) in the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and spondyloarthropathy (SpA). These inflammatory diseases have unknown causes and are influenced by various factors. Sulfasalazine (SSZ) is commonly used as a disease modifying drug for AS and SpA, but it is unclear whether 5-ASA or sulfapyridine (SP) is the effective component of SSZ. Since the bowel, colon, and ileum are important in the development of AS and SpA, it is possible that 5-ASA acts similarly to its use in treating inflammatory bowel disease. To investigate this, an open pilot study was conducted with two groups of patients with SpA. 

The study included twenty patients who were switched from SSZ to 5-ASA (Pentasa), and nineteen patients who were treated with 5-ASA without prior SSZ administration. The results showed that 85% of patients in the first group responded positively to the physician's assessment compared to their previous SSZ treatment. Additionally, the second group showed a statistically significant improvement in erythrocyte sedimentation rate. 

Based on these findings, it can be concluded that 5-ASA may be the active component of SSZ in the treatment of SpA.

title: Relationship of physical activity and television watching with body weight and level of fatness among children: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
text: The relationship between physical inactivity and weight gain in adults is well-known, but it is not clear if this relationship holds true for children of different ethnic backgrounds. The objective of this study was to examine the participation in vigorous activity and television watching habits of US children and their impact on body weight and fatness. The study was conducted through a nationally representative cross-sectional survey, which included in-person interviews and medical examinations. The participants were 4063 children aged 8 to 16 years, examined as part of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III between 1988 and 1994. Mexican Americans and non-Hispanic blacks were oversampled to ensure reliable estimates for these groups. The main outcome measures were the frequency of weekly vigorous activity, daily hours of television watched, and their relationship to body mass index and body fatness. The results showed that 80% of US children reported engaging in 3 or more bouts of vigorous activity per week. However, this rate was lower among non-Hispanic black and Mexican American girls, with only 69% and 73% respectively reporting the same level of activity. On the other hand, 20% of US children participated in 2 or fewer bouts of vigorous activity per week, and this rate was higher among girls (26%) compared to boys (17%). In terms of television watching habits, 26% of US children watched 4 or more hours per day, while 67% watched at least 2 hours per day. Non-Hispanic black children had the highest rates of watching 4 or more hours of television per day (42%). The study also found that boys and girls who watched 4 or more hours of television each day had higher body fat and body mass index compared to those who watched less than 2 hours per day. In conclusion, a significant number of US children watch excessive amounts of television and do not engage in enough vigorous activity. Girls, non-Hispanic blacks, and Mexican Americans have the lowest levels of vigorous activity. Intervention strategies are needed to promote lifelong physical activity among US children and prevent the negative health consequences of inactivity.

title: Vascular Calcification in Chronic Kidney Disease is Induced by Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 via a Mechanism Involving the Wnt/β-Catenin Pathway
text:
Background: Vascular calcification (VC) is a risk factor for accelerated atherosclerosis in chronic kidney disease (CKD). This occurs when vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) transform into osteoblast-like cells. Phosphate is known to regulate VC. 

Methods: We examined the expression of different markers for smooth muscle cells and osteogenesis in rat VSMCs exposed to high levels of phosphate or exogenous bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP-2). We used qRT-PCR and western blotting to analyze the expression, and radioimmunoassay to measure osteocalcin secretion. We also assessed VSMC differentiation and calcification using alkaline phosphatase activity assay and Alizarin staining. To investigate the involvement of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in VSMC calcification and osteoblastic differentiation induced by high phosphate or BMP-2, we used short hairpin RNA-mediated silencing of β-catenin. Apoptosis was determined using TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence imaging.

Results: CKD patients had significantly higher levels of BMP-2 in their serum compared to controls. High phosphate levels and BMP-2 induced VSMC apoptosis and upregulated the expression of β-catenin, Msx2, Runx2, and the phosphate cotransporter Pit1. However, these effects were reversed when a BMP-2 neutralization antibody was used. Knockdown of β-catenin eliminated the effects of high phosphate and BMP-2 on VSMC apoptosis and calcification.

Conclusions: BMP-2 plays a critical role in calcium deposition in VSMCs and VC in CKD patients through the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.

title: Advances in brain tumor surgery.
text: The medical community is increasingly optimistic about the possibility of treating intrinsic brain tumors, thanks to advancements in molecular and translational research, oncology, and surgery. With the help of intraoperative imaging and brain mapping, surgeons can now operate near sensitive areas of the brain with greater confidence and safety, allowing for more extensive tumor removal. However, it is important to note that surgical intervention cannot completely eradicate the infiltrating edge of a tumor or microscopic satellite lesions that are located far from the main tumor site. Therefore, the key to effectively managing this primary cause of treatment failure lies in ongoing research focused on developing a chemobiologic agent that can deliver successful results.

title: Systematic review of controlled clinical trials of gastric lavage in acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.
text:
The issue of organophosphorus pesticide (OP) self-poisoning is a significant problem in rural areas of developing countries. However, there is a lack of clinical trial data to guide treatment, making it difficult to determine the best approach. Despite the known adverse effects, gastric lavage is commonly performed in Asia. Our objective was to find studies that evaluate the effectiveness of this procedure.

We conducted a systematic search of the literature to find controlled clinical studies that examined the impact of gastric lavage on OP pesticide self-poisoning. We found a total of 56 studies, all of which were from China. These studies reported positive outcomes from the interventions studied, which included multiple gastric lavages, the use of norepinephrine or pralidoxime in the lavage fluid, concurrent treatment with naloxone or scopolamine, insertion of the gastric tube through a laparotomy incision, and lavage performed more than 12 hours after ingestion. However, only 23 of these studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and none of them provided sufficient methodology to assess their quality. The patient population and treatment protocols were not clearly defined, and there was significant variation in the control arm's case fatality rates (ranging from 4.5% to 93%), indicating substantial differences between studies and likely between study groups. No study compared the intervention to a control group that did not receive gastric lavage, nor did they provide any data on the removal of a significant amount of poison.

In conclusion, despite the widespread use of multiple gastric lavages for OP pesticide poisoning in Asia, there is currently no high-quality evidence to support its clinical effectiveness. Further research is needed to determine which patients and for how long gastric lavage can effectively remove significant amounts of poison. Following these studies, large-scale clinical trials will be necessary to assess the effectiveness and safety of gastric lavage (whether single or multiple) in cases of acute OP pesticide poisoning.

title: Integrin activation by Fam38A uses a novel mechanism of R-Ras targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: The integrin family, which consists of heterodimeric cell-surface receptors, plays a crucial role in cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion. Alterations in either the affinity between integrins and their ligands or the expression of integrin genes are key factors in various disease processes, including inflammation, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. During our search for new substances that activate integrin-ligand affinity, we discovered a previously unknown protein called Fam38A. Fam38A is located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and has multiple transmembrane domains. When we used siRNA to knock down Fam38A in epithelial cells, it resulted in the deactivation of endogenous beta1 integrin and a decrease in cell adhesion. Fam38A facilitates integrin activation by recruiting the small GTPase R-Ras to the ER. This, in turn, activates the calcium-activated protease calpain by increasing the release of Ca(2+) from cytoplasmic stores. The activation of integrin by Fam38A can be blocked by inhibiting either R-Ras or calpain activity, or by using siRNA to knock down talin, a well-known calpain substrate. This discovery sheds light on a new mechanism by which Fam38A activates integrins, utilizing calpain and R-Ras signaling from the ER. These findings provide the first description of a spatial regulator for R-Ras, an alternative pathway for suppressing integrin activation through the direct relocation of R-Ras to the ER, and a mechanism that links R-Ras and calpain signaling from the ER to the modulation of integrin-ligand affinity.

title: Convergence of 9-cis retinoic acid and peroxisome proliferator signalling pathways through heterodimer formation of their receptors
text: Peroxisomes are organelles found in the cytoplasm that play a crucial role in maintaining lipid balance in mammals. They are involved in the metabolism of long-chain fatty acids and the conversion of cholesterol to bile salts. Studies have shown that certain compounds, like clofibric acid, can be used as hypolipidemic agents in humans and can stimulate the growth of peroxisomes in rodents. These compounds, known as peroxisome proliferators, along with all-trans retinoic acid, activate genes that are responsible for the breakdown of fatty acids through peroxisomal-mediated β-oxidation. In this study, we demonstrate that the receptor activated by peroxisome proliferators and the retinoid X receptor-α form a complex that triggers the expression of the acyl-CoA oxidase gene in response to either clofibric acid or the retinoid X receptor-α ligand, 9-cis retinoic acid, a metabolite of all-trans retinoic acid. Furthermore, when both activators are present simultaneously, there is a synergistic increase in gene expression. These findings highlight the interconnectedness of the peroxisome proliferator and retinoid signaling pathways and provide evidence for the role of 9-cis retinoic acid in regulating lipid metabolism.

title: The Utilization of Extracellular Proteins as Nutrients Is Suppressed by mTORC1
text: Although mammalian cells are surrounded by a variety of nutrients, they have a preference for metabolizing glucose and free amino acids. Recently, it has been discovered that Ras-induced macropinocytosis of extracellular proteins can reduce the dependence of transformed cells on extracellular glutamine. In addition to this, we have found that protein macropinocytosis can also serve as a crucial source of essential amino acids. The degradation of extracellular proteins in lysosomes can sustain cell survival and activate mTORC1, but it does not lead to significant cell accumulation. Interestingly, we have observed that mTORC1 activation, which promotes growth under normal amino acid conditions, actually suppresses proliferation when cells rely on extracellular proteins as their amino acid source. By inhibiting mTORC1, we have seen an increase in the breakdown of endocytosed proteins and enhanced cell proliferation in nutrient-depleted conditions in vitro and within tumors that have compromised blood supply in vivo. Therefore, mTORC1 links cell growth to the availability of free amino acids by preventing the consumption of extracellular proteins. These findings could have important implications for the use of mTOR inhibitors as therapeutic agents.

title: A general model to explore complex dominance patterns in plant sporophytic self-incompatibility systems.
text:
We have developed a comprehensive model of self-incompatibility in plants, specifically focusing on the sporophytic type. This model takes into account negative frequency-dependent selection and allows for complex patterns of dominance among alleles. By applying this model deterministically, we were able to investigate how various factors affect the equilibrium frequencies of different alleles.

We examined the impact of the number of dominance classes, the number of alleles within each dominance class, the asymmetry in dominance expression between pollen and pistil, and whether selection acts solely on male fitness or on both male and female fitness. Our findings demonstrate that the "recessive effect" occurs in a wide range of scenarios.

Furthermore, we discovered interesting properties in finite population models with multiple alleles per dominance class. Specifically, we observed that more dominant classes tend to maintain a higher number of alleles, and the number of dominance classes itself can evolve over time. Additionally, we explored the occurrence of homozygous genotypes and found that the most recessive alleles can make up a significant proportion of these genotypes.

To validate our model, we applied it to two species with complex dominance patterns and compared the predicted allelic frequencies to those observed in natural populations. Our results suggest that our model can be used to explicitly test for additional, allele-specific selective forces.

In summary, our developed model provides a valuable tool for studying self-incompatibility and can be utilized to investigate various aspects of allele frequencies and selective forces in natural populations.

title: Metabolic Reprograming in Macrophage Polarization
text: In recent years, there has been a focus on studying the metabolism of immune cells, which has highlighted the strong connection between their metabolic state and phenotype. Macrophages serve as a prime example of this relationship. The way in which macrophages obtain their energy, either through glycolysis or oxidative metabolism, can lead to different phenotypes. Classically activated or M1 macrophages play a crucial role in the initial defense against bacterial infections and rely on glycolysis for energy. On the other hand, alternatively activated or M2 macrophages are involved in tissue repair and wound healing, utilizing oxidative metabolism for their long-term functions. It is important to note that metabolic intermediates not only serve as an energy source but also directly influence macrophage phenotype. In M1 macrophages, the intermediate succinate in the Krebs cycle regulates HIF1α, which is responsible for sustaining the production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL1β. In M2 macrophages, the sedoheptulose kinase carbohydrate kinase-like protein plays a critical role in regulating the pentose phosphate pathway. The ability to target these events and potentially impact disease outcomes is an exciting prospect.

title: Characterization of constitutive CTCF/cohesin loci: a possible role in establishing topological domains in mammalian genomes
text:
Recent research has indicated that the human/mammalian genomes are divided into distinct domains that serve as units of chromosome organization. CTCF, a protein known as CCCTC binding factor, has various functions in genome regulation, including controlling gene expression, establishing boundaries between chromosomal regions, facilitating DNA replication, and packaging chromatin. However, it is still unclear whether a specific subset of CTCF binding sites is responsible for establishing and maintaining these chromatin domains.

To gain more insight into this matter, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenetic characteristics of CTCF binding sites in 56 different human cell lines from the ENCODE project. Our investigation identified approximately 24,000 CTCF sites, which we refer to as constitutive sites, as they were present in over 90% of the cell lines examined. 

Our analysis revealed several key findings: 
1) Constitutive CTCF sites were predominantly located in regions of open chromatin and often co-localized with cohesin loci, which are known to play a role in chromosome organization.
2) Most constitutive CTCF sites were found at a distance from transcription start sites and lacked CpG islands, but they exhibited a high abundance of CTCF motifs, including a recently discovered 33/34-mer motif and two potentially novel motifs (22/26-mer).
3) Importantly, the majority of constitutive CTCF sites were involved in chromatin interactions mediated by CTCF, as detected by a technique called ChIA-PET. These interactions primarily occurred within topological domains identified by Hi-C, a method used to map chromatin interactions, rather than between different domains.

Based on our findings, we propose that constitutive CTCF sites may have a crucial role in organizing and maintaining the recently identified topological domains that are shared across most human cells.

title: Regulation of Bcl-2 expression by HuR in HL60 leukemia cells and A431 carcinoma cells.
text: The overexpression of the proto-oncogene bcl-2 hinders apoptosis and promotes abnormal cell survival. The stability of bcl-2 mRNA, which determines its expression, is regulated by various mechanisms. The 3'-untranslated region of bcl-2 mRNA contains elements that play a role in controlling its stability. Previous studies have shown that the RNA binding proteins nucleolin and Ebp1 contribute to stabilizing bcl-2 mRNA in HL60 cells. In this study, we have identified HuR as another component of bcl-2 messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes. Through RNA coimmunoprecipitation assays, we have confirmed that HuR binds to bcl-2 mRNA in living cells. Additionally, we have observed that HuR and nucleolin co-precipitate with RNA, suggesting their presence in common mRNP complexes. Furthermore, both nucleolin and HuR bind to bcl-2 AU-rich element (ARE) RNA separately in vitro, indicating distinct binding sites for these proteins on bcl-2 mRNA. Knocking down HuR in A431 cells results in the down-regulation of bcl-2 mRNA and protein levels. The decreased ratio of bcl-2 mRNA to heterogeneous nuclear RNA in HuR knockdown cells confirms the positive role of HuR in regulating bcl-2 stability. Recombinant HuR also slows down the decay of bcl-2 ARE RNA mediated by exosomes in HL60 cell extracts. This finding supports the involvement of HuR in regulating bcl-2 mRNA stability in both HL60 and A431 cells. Furthermore, the addition of nucleolin and HuR to HL60 cell extracts has a synergistic protective effect on the decay of bcl-2 ARE RNA. HuR knockdown also leads to the redistribution of bcl-2 mRNA from polysomes to monosomes. Therefore, HuR appears to play a positive role in both the regulation of bcl-2 mRNA translation and mRNA stability.

title: The Worldwide Variation in Avian Clutch Size across Species and Space
text: The number of eggs in a clutch can vary greatly among different species and environments. Typically, this has been studied either by comparing species or by examining geographic patterns. In our research, we analyzed clutch size in 5,290 bird species worldwide, excluding species that lay their eggs in other birds' nests or live in the open ocean. We developed a model that combines various factors, such as physical characteristics, behavior, environment, and evolutionary relationships, to predict 68% of the variation in clutch size between species. We then used this model to predict average clutch size in 2,521 bird communities around the world and found that it accurately explains the observed patterns. We discovered that species that nest in cavities and those that live in seasonal environments tend to have the largest clutches. This suggests that both the survival of offspring and adult mortality play a role in determining clutch size, and these factors are influenced by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Our findings bridge the gap between large-scale ecological patterns and comparative biology, providing a comprehensive understanding of the variation in clutch size across species and environments.

title: Diastolic heart failure--abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness of the left ventricle.
text:
BACKGROUND
Patients who exhibit symptoms of heart failure but have a normal left ventricular ejection fraction are diagnosed with diastolic heart failure. It has long been believed that the underlying cause of heart failure in these patients is an abnormality in the diastolic properties of the left ventricle. However, this hypothesis lacks substantial evidence.

METHODS
We conducted a prospective study involving 47 patients who met the diagnostic criteria for definite diastolic heart failure. All patients displayed signs and symptoms of heart failure, had a normal ejection fraction, and exhibited increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. A control group of ten patients without cardiovascular disease was also included. Left ventricular diastolic function was evaluated using cardiac catheterization and echocardiography.

RESULTS
Patients with diastolic heart failure demonstrated abnormal left ventricular relaxation and increased left ventricular chamber stiffness. The mean time constant for isovolumic-pressure decline (tau) was significantly longer in the diastolic heart failure group compared to the control group (59+/-14 msec vs. 35+/-10 msec, P=0.01). The diastolic pressure-volume relation was shifted upwards and to the left in patients with diastolic heart failure compared to the controls. The corrected left ventricular passive-stiffness constant was significantly higher in the diastolic heart failure group compared to the control group (0.03+/-0.01 vs. 0.01+/-0.01, P<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS
Patients with heart failure and a normal ejection fraction exhibit significant abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness. In these patients, the underlying cause of elevated diastolic pressures and heart failure is abnormal diastolic function.

title: The lncRNAs PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not implicated in castration resistant prostate cancer
text: The role of long noncoding RNAs (IncRNAs) in cancer biology, particularly in relation to essential functions of cancer cells such as proliferation, invasion, and metastasis, is increasingly recognized. In prostate cancer, certain lncRNAs have been identified as potentially critical players in the development of the disease. Specifically, the expression of PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 has been suggested to contribute to disease progression by influencing androgen receptor (AR) signaling (Yang et al., Nature 2013, see ref. [1]). However, doubts have been raised regarding the reliability of these findings. Therefore, we conducted a study to investigate the association between PCGEM1, PRNCR1, and prostate cancer. By analyzing RNA-sequencing data (RNA-seq) in a comprehensive manner, we found evidence supporting the association of PCGEM1 with prostate cancer, but not PRNCR1. To strengthen our findings, we examined a large group of over 230 high-risk prostate cancer patients with long-term outcome data. Contrary to previous reports, we found that neither PCGEM1 nor PRNCR1 were associated with poor patient outcomes. Additionally, we observed no evidence of interaction between PCGEM1, PRNCR1, and AR, indicating that these lncRNAs are not involved in AR signaling. Therefore, our study conclusively demonstrates that PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not prognostic lncRNAs in prostate cancer and refutes the suggestion that these lncRNAs interact with AR signaling.

title: p38MAPK controls expression of multiple cell cycle inhibitors and islet proliferation with advancing age.
text: The process of aging is intricate and influenced by genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors. Research suggests that various inhibitors of the cell cycle play a role in mammalian aging, but we have limited knowledge about the signals that trigger their expression. In this study, we investigate the impact of p38MAPK by creating a dominant-negative allele (p38(AF)) that alters the activating phosphorylation sites Thr180 and Tyr182. Heterozygous p38(AF) mice exhibit a significant reduction in p38-dependent signaling and the age-related expression of multiple cell cycle inhibitors in various organs, including pancreatic islets. Consequently, aged p38(AF/+) mice experience heightened proliferation and regeneration of islets compared to their wild-type counterparts. Additionally, we observe a decline in the expression of the p38-specific phosphatase Wip1 as mice age. Wip1-deficient mice demonstrate decreased islet proliferation, while overexpressing Wip1 rescues the decline in proliferation and regenerative capacity associated with aging. Based on these findings, we propose that manipulating p38MAPK activity could offer new therapeutic approaches for certain age-related degenerative diseases.

title: ACTA PSYCHIATRICA
text:
GOAL: Our objective was to examine the personal experiences associated with olanzapine, risperidone, and older antipsychotics. 

METHOD: We conducted a thorough analysis of comments about prescribed medications from an online database. 

RESULTS: We analyzed a total of 223 comments about risperidone, 170 comments about olanzapine, and 46 comments about three older antipsychotics. The most common subjective effects reported for all drugs were sedation, cognitive impairment, and emotional flattening or indifference. We observed a connection between these effects and Parkinsonian-like symptoms with the older antipsychotics, sexual impairment with risperidone, and metabolic effects with olanzapine. Many individuals also reported experiencing akathisia, which was frequently associated with suicidal thoughts. Some respondents mentioned that the subjective effects of the drugs helped alleviate symptoms of mania, psychosis, and anxiety. 

CONCLUSION: While the generalizability of internet data is uncertain, our findings suggest that adverse subjective effects are a significant aspect of the antipsychotic drug experience and may be linked to the desired therapeutic benefits.

title: White matter hyperintensities are a core feature of Alzheimer's disease: Evidence from the dominantly inherited Alzheimer network.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the presence and severity of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) in individuals genetically predisposed to develop Alzheimer's disease (AD). WMHs are areas of increased signal on MRI scans that are commonly associated with small vessel cerebrovascular disease. It is known that increased WMH volume is linked to the risk and progression of AD. However, it is unclear whether these abnormalities are merely additive factors contributing to symptom presentation or if they are core features of the disease. 

The study included 299 participants from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network, consisting of individuals with a mutation that leads to AD (61.5%) and first-degree relatives who served as noncarrier controls (38.5%). The estimated years from expected symptom onset (EYO) were calculated by subtracting the affected parent's symptom onset age from the participant's age. Baseline MRI data were analyzed to assess total and regional WMH. 

The results showed that mutation carriers had greater total WMH volumes, with an increase observed approximately 6 years before expected symptom onset. The effects were most pronounced in the parietal and occipital lobes, where divergent effects were seen as early as 22 years before estimated onset. 

These findings suggest that autosomal-dominant AD is associated with increased WMH well before expected symptom onset. This indicates that WMHs may be a core feature of AD and should be considered as a potential therapeutic target. Additionally, these results highlight the importance of integrating WMHs into pathogenic models of the disease.

title: Maternal and child undernutrition: consequences for adult health and human capital
text:
This paper examines the connections between maternal and child undernutrition and their impact on human capital and the risk of adult diseases in low-income and middle-income countries. We conducted an analysis using data from five long-term prospective cohort studies conducted in Brazil, Guatemala, India, the Philippines, and South Africa. Our findings revealed that various indicators of maternal and child undernutrition, such as maternal height, birthweight, intrauterine growth restriction, and weight, height, and body-mass index at 2 years according to the new WHO growth standards, were associated with adult outcomes including height, schooling, income or assets, offspring birthweight, body-mass index, glucose concentrations, and blood pressure.

To further investigate these outcomes, we conducted systematic reviews of studies from low-income and middle-income countries, focusing on indicators related to blood lipids, cardiovascular disease, lung and immune function, cancers, osteoporosis, and mental illness. The results showed a strong association between undernutrition and shorter adult height, less schooling, reduced economic productivity, and lower offspring birthweight for women. However, the associations with adult disease indicators were not as clear-cut.

We found that increased size at birth and during childhood were positively associated with adult body-mass index and, to a lesser extent, blood pressure values, but not with blood glucose concentrations. In our new analyses and in previously published work, lower birthweight and undernutrition in childhood were identified as risk factors for high glucose concentrations, blood pressure, and harmful lipid profiles, after adjusting for adult body-mass index and height. This suggests that rapid postnatal weight gain, particularly after infancy, is linked to these conditions.

The review of published works also revealed a lack of sufficient information regarding long-term changes in immune function, blood lipids, or osteoporosis indicators. However, birthweight was found to be positively associated with lung function and the incidence of certain cancers, while undernutrition could potentially be associated with mental illness.

We observed that height-for-age at 2 years was the most accurate predictor of human capital, and undernutrition was consistently associated with lower human capital. In conclusion, the damage experienced during early life can lead to permanent impairment and may also impact future generations. Preventing undernutrition is likely to result in significant health, educational, and economic benefits. It is important to note that undernourished children who experience rapid weight gain after infancy are particularly susceptible to chronic diseases.

title: Ubiquitin-dependent intramembrane rhomboid protease promotes ERAD of membrane proteins.
text: The ERAD pathway is a crucial defense mechanism in cells, responsible for directing misfolded and unassembled proteins from the ER to the proteasome. However, there is still limited knowledge regarding the specific components involved in the ERAD of membrane proteins. In this study, we present evidence that the highly conserved protein RHBDL4, belonging to the rhomboid family, acts as a ubiquitin-dependent protease located within the ER membrane. RHBDL4 is upregulated in response to ER stress and is capable of cleaving both single-spanning and polytopic membrane proteins with unstable transmembrane helices. This cleavage leads to the degradation of these proteins through the canonical ERAD machinery. Furthermore, RHBDL4 exhibits a specific interaction with the AAA+-ATPase p97, suggesting a functional link between proteolytic processing and dislocation into the cytosol. The relationship between rhomboids and the ERAD factor derlin, as observed in their phylogenetic relationship, implies that the recruitment of substrates for intramembrane proteolysis and protein dislocation occurs through a shared mechanism.

title: Detection and function of nitric oxide during the hypersensitive response in Arabidopsis thaliana: where there's a will there's a way.
text: Around 20 years ago, researchers identified nitric oxide (NO) as a significant factor in plant defense responses. Since then, a substantial amount of evidence has been gathered, supporting its role as a signaling molecule. However, there are several inconsistencies in current methods of detecting NO, and the specific enzymatic pathways responsible for its synthesis remain unknown. These uncertainties have sparked intense debates regarding the function of NO in plants, with some even questioning its existence within plants. In this study, we present data collected from the Arabidopsis/Pseudomonas model pathosystem, which confirms the production of NO during the hypersensitive response. This data also supports the notion that NO acts as a trigger for hypersensitive cell death and plays a role in the expression of defense genes. Additionally, we explore potential sources of NO synthesis, with a particular focus on the role of nitrite as a major substrate for NO production during incompatible interactions.

title: The Cytosolic Chaperonin CCT/TRiC and Cancer Cell Proliferation
text: The molecular chaperone CCT/TRiC plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of proteins within cells by assisting in the folding of important cytoskeletal proteins such as tubulins and actins. It is also involved in folding various proteins related to cancer, including cyclin E, the Von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein, cyclin B, and p21(ras), suggesting its involvement in cell proliferation and the development of tumors. To investigate the role of CCT/TRiC in tumor development, we measured its expression levels and activity in 18 cancer cell lines, one non-cancerous human cell line, and a non-cancerous human liver. Our findings demonstrate that the expression levels of CCT/TRiC are higher in cancer cell lines compared to normal cells. However, the activity of CCT/TRiC does not always correlate with its expression levels. Therefore, we also examined the expression levels of proteins that regulate and interact with CCT/TRiC, including PhLP3, Hop/P60, prefoldin, and Hsc/Hsp70. Our analysis reveals a functional relationship between molecular chaperones, which may contribute to the precise control of CCT/TRiC activity in cell proliferation through changes in the levels of prefoldin, Hsc/p70, and the availability of CCT/TRiC client proteins. These findings provide new insights into the role of CCT/TRiC-mediated protein folding machinery in the development of cancer cells.

title: RBP2 Belongs to a Family of Demethylases, Specific for Tri-and Dimethylated Lysine 4 on Histone 3
text: The stable modification of histones known as methylation has long been considered a key aspect of the cell's epigenetic program, controlling both chromatin structure and transcription. However, recent discoveries of histone demethylases have raised questions about the stability of histone methylation. In this study, we present evidence that the JARID1 proteins RBP2, PLU1, and SMCX are specific demethylases for di- and trimethylated histone 3 lysine 4 (H3K4). Our findings support the idea that the JARID1 Drosophila homolog Lid, which regulates the expression of homeotic genes during development, plays a role in displacing RBP2 from Hox genes during embryonic stem (ES) cell differentiation. This displacement is associated with an increase in H3K4me3 levels and gene expression. Additionally, we demonstrate that mutation or depletion of the C. elegans JARID1 homolog rbr-2 leads to elevated levels of H3K4me3 during larval development and defects in vulva formation. Overall, these results suggest that demethylation of H3K4me3/me2 by the JARID1 family is crucial for proper development.

title: Mitochondria: Dynamic Organelles in Disease, Aging, and Development
text: Most eukaryotic cells rely on mitochondria as their main energy source. These organelles also play a role in intermediary metabolism, calcium signaling, and apoptosis. One might assume that mitochondrial dysfunction would lead to a consistent set of defects in all tissues, given these well-known functions. However, in multicellular organisms, mitochondrial dysfunction has diverse effects. There is still much to learn about the fundamental biology of mitochondria. In this discussion, we explore recent research indicating that the dynamics of these organelles, specifically fusion and fission, are crucial in both development and disease.

title: Persistence of HIV-1 Receptor-Positive Cells after HSV-2 Reactivation: A Potential Mechanism for Increased HIV-1 Acquisition
text: In order to investigate how herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infection is connected to the acquisition of HIV-1, we conducted a study analyzing the cellular infiltrate from sequential biopsies of HSV-2 lesions in patients both on and off antiviral therapy. We found that CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, as well as a mixed population of plasmacytoid and myeloid dendritic cells (DCs), including cells expressing the C-type lectin receptor DC-SIGN, remained present at sites of HSV-2 reactivation for several months even with daily antiviral therapy. The CD4(+) T cells that persisted reacted to HSV-2 antigen, had a higher expression of the chemokine receptor CCR5, and were in close proximity to DCs expressing the interleukin-3 receptor CD123 or DC-SIGN. When these cells were infected with a CCR5-tropic strain of HIV-1 in a laboratory setting, we observed higher concentrations of integrated HIV-1 DNA in cells derived from healed genital lesion biopsies compared to cells from control skin biopsies. The persistence and enrichment of inflammatory cells that are receptive to HIV in the genital area help to explain why anti-HSV-2 therapy is unable to reduce the acquisition of HIV.

title: Chronic daily headache in Taipei, Taiwan: prevalence, follow-up and outcome predictors.
text: In Taipei, Taiwan, we conducted a survey on headaches among individuals aged 15 and older. We used a two-stage population-based approach to identify subjects with chronic daily headache (CDH) in the past year. These individuals were interviewed and followed-up. CDH was defined as experiencing headaches more than 15 days per month, lasting for more than 4 hours each day. Out of the 3377 participants, 108 (3.2%) met the criteria for CDH, with a higher prevalence in women (4.3%) compared to men (1.9%). The most common subtype of CDH was tension-type migraine (TM), accounting for 55% of cases, followed by chronic tension-type headache (CTTH) at 44%. Additionally, 34% of CDH subjects were found to overuse analgesics. After a 2-year follow-up, 35% of CDH subjects still experienced CDH. Factors that significantly predicted persistent CDH at follow-up included being older (40 years or older) (RR = 2.4), experiencing CDH onset after the age of 32 (RR = 1.8), having CDH for 6 years or longer (RR = 2.0), medication overuse (RR = 1.8), and having a "daily" headache (RR = 2.1). Our findings indicate that CDH is not uncommon in the community and its prevalence is similar across different populations. Older individuals and those who overuse medication may experience a more prolonged course of illness.

title: In vivo microtubules are copolymers of available beta-tubulin isotypes: localization of each of six vertebrate beta-tubulin isotypes using polyclonal antibodies elicited by synthetic peptide antigens
text:
The genomes of higher animals contain a small multigene family that encodes beta-Tubulin. This family consists of approximately seven functional genes. These genes produce a group of closely related polypeptide isotypes that are distinct from each other. The main distinguishing factor between these isotypes is the sequence within the carboxy-terminal amino acid residues, which is approximately 15 in length. 

To create antibodies specific to each of the six distinct isotypes, rabbits were immunized with chemically synthesized peptides that correspond to the variable domain sequences. The specificity of each antiserum has been clearly demonstrated by the binding of antibodies to bacterially produced, cloned proteins that represent each isotype. Additionally, the binding of antibodies can be inhibited by preincubating the antiserum with the immunizing peptide, but not with other unrelated peptides. 

Protein blotting techniques have allowed for the accurate measurement of the quantity of each beta-Tubulin isotype present in soluble and polymer forms in different cells. However, no bias for preferential assembly of any isotype has been observed. 

Through indirect immunofluorescence, the localization of each isotype has been determined in three different cell types. This technique has shown that in vivo, each class of microtubules, distinguishable by light microscopy, is assembled as copolymers of all isotypes expressed in a single cell.

title: Topiramate for smoking cessation: a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study.
text:
INTRODUCTION
Topiramate (TOP) has the ability to block glutamate receptors and enhance GABA neurotransmission, which may aid in smoking cessation. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of behavioral counseling combined with (a) TOP, (b) TOP/nicotine patch (TOP/NIC), or (c) placebo (PLC) for quitting smoking.

METHODS
A 10-week randomized trial was conducted, with subjects and research personnel being unaware of whether participants received TOP or PLC, but aware of the TOP/NIC patch condition. In the TOP groups, the medication dosage was gradually increased to a maximum of 200 mg/day. The quit date was set after 2 weeks of medication treatment, and subjects in the TOP/NIC group started using a 21 mg nicotine patch on the quit date. The primary outcome measure was the end-of-treatment, 4-week continuous abstinence rate (CAR), which was confirmed through biochemical testing.

RESULTS
Fifty-seven subjects were randomly assigned to treatment. The 4-week CAR was 5% in the PLC group, 26% in the TOP group, and 37% in the TOP/NIC group (p = .056). Pairwise comparisons revealed a significant difference between TOP/NIC and PLC (p = .042), but the difference between TOP and PLC was not statistically significant (p = .18). The PLC group experienced a weight gain of 0.37 lb/week, while the TOP group lost 0.41 lb/week and the TOP/NIC group lost 0.07 lb/week (p = .004). Pairwise comparisons showed a significant difference between TOP and PLC (p < .001) and between TOP/NIC and PLC groups (p = .035). Paresthesia was more common in subjects taking TOP compared to PLC (p = .011).

CONCLUSIONS
TOP, either alone or in combination with NIC, showed a higher quit rate than PLC and also resulted in weight loss. However, further research with a larger, placebo-controlled trial is necessary to confirm these findings.

title: Break-induced DNA replication.
text: Break-induced replication (BIR), also known as recombination-dependent DNA replication, was initially proposed to explain recombination events in bacteriophage. However, it has recently been recognized as a crucial mechanism for repairing double-strand chromosome breaks in eukaryotes. This mechanism plays a critical role in restarting stalled and broken replication forks and maintaining the integrity of eroded telomeres. While BIR helps preserve genome integrity during replication, it also contributes to genome instability by causing loss of heterozygosity, nonreciprocal translocations, and complex chromosomal rearrangements.

title: The state of US health, 1990-2010: burden of diseases, injuries, and risk factors.
text:
Understanding the major health issues in the United States and how they are changing over time is crucial for informing national health policies. The objectives of this study were to assess the prevalence of diseases, injuries, and leading risk factors in the United States from 1990 to 2010 and compare these findings with those of the 34 countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). 

To achieve these objectives, we conducted a systematic analysis of descriptive epidemiology, examining 291 diseases and injuries, 1160 sequelae, and 67 risk factors or clusters of risk factors. This analysis was based on data from the Global Burden of Disease 2010 Study, which covered 187 countries. We calculated years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLLs) by multiplying the number of deaths at each age by a reference life expectancy. Years lived with disability (YLDs) were determined by multiplying prevalence by disability weight for each sequela. Disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) were estimated as the sum of YLDs and YLLs. Deaths and DALYs related to risk factors were based on systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Healthy life expectancy (HALE) was used to summarize overall population health, considering both length of life and levels of ill health experienced at different ages. 

The results showed that life expectancy in the United States increased from 75.2 years in 1990 to 78.2 years in 2010, while HALE increased from 65.8 years to 68.1 years during the same period. The leading causes of years of life lost in 2010 were ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and road injuries. Age-standardized rates of years of life lost increased for Alzheimer's disease, drug use disorders, chronic kidney disease, kidney cancer, and falls. The diseases with the highest number of years lived with disability in 2010 were low back pain, major depressive disorder, other musculoskeletal disorders, neck pain, and anxiety disorders. As the US population has aged, years lived with disability have become a larger proportion of DALYs compared to years of life lost. The main risk factors contributing to DALYs were dietary risks, tobacco smoking, high body mass index, high blood pressure, high fasting plasma glucose, physical inactivity, and alcohol use. 

When comparing the United States to the 34 OECD countries between 1990 and 2010, the US rank for age-standardized death rate decreased from 18th to 27th, age-standardized years of life lost rate decreased from 23rd to 28th, age-standardized years lived with disability rate increased from 5th to 6th, life expectancy at birth decreased from 20th to 27th, and HALE decreased from 14th to 26th. 

In conclusion, the United States has made significant progress in improving health from 1990 to 2010, with increases in life expectancy and HALE, and decreases in all-cause death rates. However, morbidity and chronic disability now account for a significant portion of the health burden in the US, and the country's population health improvements have not kept pace with those of other wealthy nations.

title: Malaria risk perception, knowledge and prophylaxis practices among travellers of African ethnicity living in Paris and visiting their country of origin in sub-Saharan Africa.
text: A study was conducted to assess the perception of malaria risk, knowledge, and prophylaxis practices among individuals of African ethnicity living in Paris and traveling to their country of origin to visit friends or relatives (VFR). The study compared two groups of VFR who had sought advice from either a travel clinic (TC) or a travel agency (TA) before their departure. Out of the VFR participants, 47% expressed concern about malaria as a health issue, and 75% of them were aware that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes and that bed nets are an effective preventive measure. The perception of high malaria risk was higher in the TA group (33%) compared to the TC group (7%). Approximately 35% of the VFR mentioned the availability of a malaria vaccine, but there was often confusion between the yellow fever vaccine and malaria prevention. Only 29% of the participants took adequate chemoprophylaxis with complete adherence, and this percentage was higher among the TC group (41%) compared to the TA group (12%). The effective measures used for protection against mosquitoes included bed nets (16%), wearing long clothes at night (14%), and using air conditioning (8%). There were no significant differences between the study groups, except for the use of impregnated bed nets, which was reported by 11% of the TC group and none of the TA group. To reduce the high rate of inadequate malaria prophylaxis among VFR, it is recommended to improve media coverage, provide reimbursement for malaria chemoprophylaxis, and adapt preventive messages to the cultural context.

title: Effect modification by population dietary folate on the association between MTHFR genotype, homocysteine, and stroke risk: a meta-analysis of genetic studies and randomised trials
text:
BACKGROUND: The MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism has been linked to increased homocysteine levels and a higher risk of stroke. Previous research suggested that the effects were more pronounced in regions with low dietary folate intake, but it was challenging to differentiate between the impact of folate and small-study bias. A meta-analysis of randomized trials on homocysteine-lowering interventions found no reduction in coronary heart disease events or stroke, but these trials were mostly conducted in populations with high folate consumption. Our objective was to minimize small-study bias and investigate whether folate status modifies the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke through a genetic analysis and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

METHODS: We formed a collaboration of genetic studies comprising 237 datasets with data from 59,995 individuals on homocysteine and 20,885 stroke events. We compared the genetic findings with a meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials on homocysteine-lowering treatments and stroke risk, involving 45,549 individuals, 2314 stroke events, and 269 transient ischemic attacks.

FINDINGS: The impact of the MTHFR 677C→T variant on homocysteine levels was more significant in regions with low folate intake (Asia; difference between individuals with TT versus CC genotype: 3.12 μmol/L, 95% CI 2.23 to 4.01) compared to areas with folate fortification (America, Australia, and New Zealand, high; 0.13 μmol/L, -0.85 to 1.11). The odds ratio (OR) for stroke was also higher in Asia (1.68, 95% CI 1.44 to 1.97) than in America, Australia, and New Zealand, high (1.03, 0.84 to 1.25). Most randomized trials were conducted in regions with high or increasing population folate levels. The summary relative risk (RR) of stroke in trials of homocysteine-lowering interventions (0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.04) was similar to the predicted RR for the same degree of homocysteine reduction in large genetic studies involving populations with similar folate status (predicted RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.11). Although the predicted effect of homocysteine reduction from large genetic studies in low folate regions (Asia) was greater (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.90), no trial has specifically evaluated the effect of homocysteine reduction on stroke risk in a low folate region.

INTERPRETATION: In regions with increasing or established population folate supplementation, evidence from genetic studies and randomized trials suggests that lowering homocysteine does not provide any benefit for stroke prevention. Further large-scale genetic studies are needed to determine if folate modifies the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke in low folate settings, and to distinguish this from small-study bias. If future randomized trials on homocysteine-lowering interventions for stroke prevention are conducted, they should be carried out in regions with low folate consumption.

FUNDING: Full funding sources listed at the end of the paper (see Acknowledgments).

title: Porcine circovirus type 2 DNA influences cytoskeleton rearrangements in plasmacytoid and monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
text: The disruption of dendritic cells (DC) is a key strategy used by viral pathogens to avoid the host's immune defenses. Porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2), a single-stranded DNA virus, hinders the activation of plasmacytoid DC (pDC) and conventional DC by certain viruses or Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands. This inhibitory effect is linked to the viral DNA, but it does not impact all signaling pathways. When small chemical molecules bind to TLR7, interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α secretion are still induced, but interferon-α or IL-12 are not. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms behind this silencing. The use of PP2, a potent inhibitor of the Lyn and Hck kinases, resulted in a similar profile to PCV2 DNA interference, inhibiting the activation of cells through TLR9 but not TLR7. Confocal microscopy and cytometry analysis strongly suggested that PCV2 DNA impairs actin polymerization in pDC and endocytosis in monocyte-derived DC. Overall, this study provides insight into the specific molecular mechanisms involved in PCV2's interference with DC's ability to recognize danger, which may explain the virus-induced immunosuppression observed in infected pigs.

title: Sympathetic neural and cardiovascular responses during static handgrip exercise in women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy
text: Women who have experienced hypertensive pregnancy are at a higher risk for future cardiovascular events, but the reasons for this increased risk are not known. Research suggests that exercise can reveal hidden hypertensive tendencies, helping to identify those who are most at risk for developing cardiovascular disease. This study aimed to investigate whether women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy have an exaggerated response to exercise. The study included normotensive women who had experienced a healthy pregnancy (CON; n = 9) and those who had experienced hypertensive pregnancy (HP+; n = 12). The participants were tested during the mid-luteal phase of their menstrual cycle. Measurements of heart rate (HR), systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP, DBP), and muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) were taken during a cold pressor test (CPT), as well as during static handgrip to fatigue (SHG) and post-exercise circulatory arrest (PECA) after a sufficient recovery period. The results showed that the response of SBP to SHG and PECA was similar between the two groups, but DBP and HR were significantly higher in the HP+ group (both p < 0.05). The frequency of MSNA bursts tended to be higher in the HP+ group during the stressor (peak Δ from baseline 31 ± 13 vs. 23 ± 13 bursts/min; p for group = 0.06), although there were no differences in burst incidence or total activity. Despite not showing any clinical signs of cardiovascular disease or hypertension, women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy exhibited a heightened cardiovascular response to exercise compared to those with a history of healthy pregnancy. This response may indicate impaired cardiovascular control that precedes the development of hypertension or cardiovascular events.

title: Exercise and the immune system: regulation, integration, and adaptation.
text: Extensive research has been conducted on stress-induced immunological reactions to exercise, leading to advancements in stress immunology and neuroimmunology. It has been proposed that exercise can serve as a model for temporary immunosuppression following intense physical stress. This exercise-stress model allows for easy experimental manipulation and facilitates the study of interactions between the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems. This review focuses on the underlying mechanisms behind exercise-induced immune changes, including neuroendocrinological factors such as catecholamines, growth hormone, cortisol, beta-endorphin, and sex steroids. Additionally, the review explores the connection between skeletal muscles and the lymphoid system, highlighting the metabolic link. The mechanisms of exercise-related muscle damage and the initiation of the inflammatory cytokine cascade are also discussed. Considering that exercise has the ability to modulate the immune system in healthy individuals, it is crucial to consider the clinical implications of exercise in preventing diseases involving the immune system. Therefore, this review draws upon experimental, clinical, and epidemiological literature to examine the interactions between exercise and infectious diseases, as well as exercise and neoplasia, in the context of aging and nutrition.

title: Positive feedback between PU.1 and the cell cycle controls myeloid differentiation.
text: The control of stem cell differentiation is governed by regulatory gene circuits that involve positive-feedback loops. However, there are multiple mechanisms that contribute to this positive feedback. In this study, we investigate the feedback mechanisms through which the transcription factor PU.1 regulates lymphoid and myeloid differentiation. By using quantitative live-cell imaging, we discovered that developing B cells decrease PU.1 levels by reducing PU.1 transcription. On the other hand, developing macrophages increase PU.1 levels by lengthening their cell cycles, resulting in stable PU.1 accumulation. When exogenous PU.1 is expressed in progenitor cells, it increases endogenous PU.1 levels by inducing cell cycle lengthening, suggesting a positive feedback loop between the regulatory factor and the cell cycle. Through mathematical modeling, we demonstrate that this feedback architecture, coupled with the cell cycle, effectively stabilizes a slow-dividing differentiated state. These findings highlight the role of cell cycle duration as an essential component of a positive autoregulatory circuit that controls cell fate.

title: Peripheral B cell subsets.
text: Our knowledge of the origins and biological functions of different peripheral B cell subsets is constantly evolving. While we have gained some understanding of the interplay between BCR-derived signals and other receptors and signaling pathways that drive the development of follicular, marginal zone, and B-1 B cells, this remains a complex and poorly understood topic. Recent findings have shed light on the origins of B-1 and B-2 B cells, the capacity of follicular B cells to mature in both the bone marrow and spleen, the existence of a definable precursor for MZ B cells, and the ability of follicular B cells to occupy two distinct niches. These advancements are discussed in detail in this review.

title: Human IL-10 is produced by both type 1 helper (Th1) and type 2 helper (Th2) T cell clones and inhibits their antigen-specific proliferation and cytokine production.
text: The expression of IL-10 gene and production of IL-10 protein were examined in CD4+ human T cell clones of both Th1 and Th2 types using polymerase chain reaction and ELISA, respectively. While Th2 clones showed higher levels of IL-10 mRNA, Th1 clones also consistently expressed IL-10 mRNA. Similarly, measurable levels of IL-10 were detected in the supernatants of both Th1 and Th2 clones. The impact of human IL-10 (h-IL-10) and viral IL-10 (v-IL-10) on the proliferation and cytokine production of Th1 and Th2 clones was also investigated. The addition of h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 in culture significantly reduced the proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones in response to specific antigens and PHA, but had no inhibitory effect on the proliferative response to IL-2. h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 also inhibited the production of gamma-interferon (IFN-gamma) by Th1 clones and the production of IL-4 and IL-5 by Th2 clones in response to antigens, but had no effect on cytokine synthesis when the same clones were stimulated with PMA plus anti-CD3 antibody. Preincubation of antigen-presenting cells (APC), but not clonal T blasts, with h-IL-10 resulted in the inhibition of antigen-induced proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones, suggesting that h-IL-10 primarily affects APC. These findings demonstrate that, unlike in mice where IL-10 is produced by Th2 cells and mainly down-regulates the Th1 response, in humans, IL-10 is produced by and down-regulates the function of both Th1 and Th2 cells.

title: Evaluating strategies for improving ovarian response of the poor responder undergoing assisted reproductive techniques.
text:
AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness of different controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) methods in patients with a history of poor response to standard COH regimens, who are preparing for assisted reproductive techniques.

METHOD: A review of English-language literature was conducted.

PATIENTS: Candidates for assisted reproductive techniques who had previously shown suboptimal response to standard COH regimens.

INTERVENTIONS: Various COH regimens were examined, including increased doses of gonadotropins, different types of gonadotropins, growth hormone (GH) supplementation, initiation of long GnRH agonist (GnRH-a) in the luteal phase, initiation of flare GnRH-a in the early follicular phase, initiation of ultrashort GnRH-a in the low-dose luteal phase, progestin pretreatment, and initiation of microdose flare GnRH-a.

OUTCOME MEASURES: The study assessed maximal serum E(2) levels, follicular development, dose and duration of gonadotropin therapy, cycle cancellation rates, number of oocytes retrieved, number of embryos transferred, and clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates.

RESULTS: The lack of consistent definition for poor responders and limited prospective randomized trials made data interpretation challenging. Among the various strategies proposed, microdose GnRH-a flare and late luteal phase initiation of a short course of low-dose GnRH-a before COH appeared to be more consistently beneficial.

CONCLUSIONS: There is no one-size-fits-all regimen for poor responders. It is crucial to establish uniform definitions and conduct large-scale prospective randomized trials. The development of a reliable precycle screening method will enable effective differentiation between normal responders, poor responders, and those who are unlikely to conceive with their own oocytes.

title: Identification and Functional Characterization of N-Terminally Acetylated Proteins in Drosophila melanogaster
text: Protein modifications play a crucial role in the various biological processes of living organisms. A common modification found in all forms of life is the acetylation of the amino-terminal of proteins. This occurs when the nascent polypeptide chain is being synthesized, usually after the removal of the initiating methionine residue. Although the enzymes and protein complexes involved in this process have been extensively studied, little is known about the biological function of these N-terminal modifications. To gain insight into the principles of N-terminal acetylation, we examined the amino-terminal peptides of proteins extracted from Drosophila Kc167 cells. Our analysis revealed over 1,200 mature protein N-termini, demonstrating that N-terminal acetylation occurs in insects at a similar frequency as in humans. We discovered that the (X)PX rule is the sole determinant for N-terminal acetylation, indicating that acetylation is prevented under all circumstances. By genetically engineering a protein, we were able to investigate the biological significance of the presence or absence of an acetyl group, creating a versatile assay to explore the functional importance of N-terminal acetylation. We applied this assay by expressing mutated proteins as transgenes in cell lines and flies. In this study, we present a straightforward strategy to systematically examine the functional relevance of N-terminal acetylations in both cells and whole organisms. Given that the (X)PX rule appears to be universally applicable across different species, we propose that it can be utilized to investigate the function of N-terminal acetylation in all organisms.

title: Bax translocation and mitochondrial fragmentation induced by Helicobacter pylori.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of mitochondria in programmed cell death induced by Helicobacter pylori infection. Previous studies have shown a link between H. pylori infection and apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells, but the exact mechanisms involved are not fully understood. In this study, we examined whether Bax translocation and mitochondrial fragmentation occur in gastric epithelial cells exposed to H. pylori, leading to cell death. We conducted experiments using human gastric adenocarcinoma cells, cells transfected with the HPV-E6 gene (which inactivates p53 function), mouse embryonic fibroblasts, and p19(ARF) null MEFs. After incubating the cells with a cag positive H. pylori strain for up to 24 hours, we analyzed cytoplasmic and mitochondrial membrane fractions for Bax translocation using western blot. Our results showed that Bax translocation occurred in AGS, AGS-neo, and normal MEF cells after three hours of exposure to H. pylori, but not in ARF(-/-) MEFs cells.
