Bax translocation was also observed in AGS-E6 cells, although to a lesser extent than in AGS-neo cells. Additionally, we used confocal microscopy to assess mitochondrial morphology in living cells infected with H. pylori. We found that mitochondrial fragmentation was detectable after 10 hours of H. pylori incubation in AGS cells and after seven hours in MEF cells. Wild-type MEFs showed significantly higher mitochondrial fragmentation compared to ARF null MEFs. Furthermore, mitochondrial depolarization and caspase-3 activity were initiated within four hours in cells incubated with H. pylori, and these events were inhibited by forced expression of Bcl-2. In conclusion, our findings suggest that Bax translocates to the mitochondria during H. pylori-induced apoptosis, leading to mitochondrial depolarization and fragmentation. Functional ARF and p53 proteins may play a crucial role in H. pylori-induced mitochondrial modification.

title: Cancer chemoprevention: a rapidly evolving field
text: The prevention of cancer, known as cancer chemoprevention, involves the long-term use of synthetic, natural, or biological substances to reduce or delay the occurrence of malignant tumors. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through trials conducted on breast, prostate, and colon cancer. Over the past decade, the process of developing new chemopreventive agents has undergone significant changes. It now includes thorough preclinical evaluation of these agents to understand their mechanisms of action before initiating clinical trials. Additionally, there is a focus on identifying biomarkers that can indicate the effectiveness of these agents early on. This review aims to provide an overview of the current state of cancer chemoprevention and highlight potential advancements in the field.

title: Dengue is still an imported disease in China: a case study in Guangzhou.
text:
Approximately 390 million people worldwide are infected with the Dengue virus and its four serotypes (DENV 1-4) each year, with the majority of cases occurring in tropical and subtropical regions. Due to the repeated introduction of DENV from epidemic regions and favorable weather conditions, many areas have transitioned from having low levels of the virus to high levels in recent decades. It is crucial to understand the current situation of Dengue in China, as the country has experienced outbreaks since 1978. This understanding is essential for implementing effective control and prevention strategies. 

A study was conducted to determine whether Dengue in China is endemic or not. The study utilized data from the disease notification system, as well as phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses. The results showed that all four serotypes of the virus have been detected in Guangzhou, China, with DENV 1-2 being the most prevalent. The analysis of the Maximum Likelihood tree revealed that the viruses detected in Guangzhou belonged to different clades, except for those from 2002 and 2003, which clustered together. The study also found evidence of mutual introductions between Guangzhou and Southeast Asia. Most of the viruses were imported from Southeast Asia, with outbreaks in Guangzhou originating mainly from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines. 

Overall, the study suggests that Dengue in China is still primarily an imported disease, but there is a possibility of localization.

title: The UNAIDS Estimation and Projection Package: a software package to estimate and project national HIV epidemics.
text: In this paper, the Estimation and Projection Package (EPP) is presented as a tool for estimating and projecting HIV prevalence levels in countries with generalised epidemics. The paper provides an overview of the software and its interface, explaining how it can be used to define and model a national epidemic by considering locally relevant sub-epidemics. It also outlines the four epidemiological parameters that are utilized to generate prevalence trends in the epidemic through curve fitting. Additionally, the paper includes a case study demonstrating the application of EPP in a country with a generalised epidemic. Furthermore, the strengths and weaknesses of the software are discussed, along with its potential future developments.

title: Oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24 Inhibits the growth of breast cancer in vitro and in vivo
text:
Background: Interleukin-24 (IL-24) is a cytokine belonging to the IL-10 family. It has the ability to selectively induce apoptosis in cancer cells, making it a potential strategy for cancer gene therapy.

Methods: In this study, we constructed a recombinant type five adenovirus containing the IL-24 gene (designated CNHK600-IL24). This virus only replicates in tumor cells. We assessed the replication of CNHK600-IL24 in breast tumor cells and fibroblasts using TCID50 and MTT assays. The secretion of IL-24 was measured using ELISA and western blotting. We also investigated the in vivo anti-tumor effect of CNHK600-IL24 in nude mice with orthotopic or metastatic breast tumors.

Results: Our findings showed that CNHK600-IL24 efficiently replicated and resulted in high levels of IL-24 expression and cell death in human breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231), but not in normal fibroblast cells (MRC-5). Furthermore, administration of CNHK600-IL24 significantly suppressed orthotopic breast tumor growth in the nude mice model. In the metastatic model generated by tail vein injection, CNHK600-IL24 virotherapy improved survival compared to the same virus expressing EGFP. A similar phenomenon was observed in the metastatic model achieved by left ventricular injection, as indicated by in vivo luminescence imaging of tumor growth.

Conclusion: Our study suggests that the oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24, which demonstrated enhanced anti-tumor activity and improved survival, holds promise as a virotherapy candidate for breast cancer.

title: Brain stem and cerebellar hyperintense lesions in migraine.
text:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE Migraine sufferers have a higher risk of experiencing cerebellar infarcts and white matter lesions in the upper part of the brain. However, little is known about the prevalence, frequency, and distribution of hyperintense lesions in the lower part of the brain in migraine patients. 

METHODS We conducted an MRI evaluation on a group of adults aged 30 to 60, including individuals with migraine with aura (n=161), migraine without aura (n=134), and a control group (n=140) from a population-based sample. 

RESULTS We discovered hyperintense lesions in the lower part of the brain (infratentorial) in 13 out of 295 (4.4%) migraine patients, compared to only 1 out of 140 (0.7%) individuals in the control group (P=0.04). These lesions were mostly found bilaterally in the dorsal basis pontis. Additionally, those with infratentorial hyperintensities were more likely to have white matter lesions in the upper part of the brain (supratentorial). 

CONCLUSIONS Our findings reveal a higher prevalence of hyperintense lesions in the lower part of the brain, specifically the pontine region, in migraine patients from the general population. This expands our understanding of the vulnerable brain regions and types of lesions present in migraine patients. It is likely that these lesions are caused by a hemodynamic ischemic process, but further research is necessary to confirm this.

title: NDRG1 promotes growth of hepatocellular carcinoma cells by directly interacting with GSK-3β and Nur77 to prevent β-catenin degradation
text: The N-myc downstream regulated gene 1 (NDRG1) is strongly associated with advanced tumor stages and poor survival in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), suggesting its potential as a target for HCC treatment. Our goal is to gain a deeper understanding of its biological roles in hepatocarcinogenesis in order to exploit it for therapeutic purposes. Through screening with ProtoArray® Human Protein Microarrays, we have identified glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK-3β) and the orphan nuclear receptor (Nur77) as potential interaction partners of NDRG1. These interactions were confirmed in vitro using co-immunoprecipitation in HCC cell lines, and the co-localization of NDRG1 with GSK-3β and Nur77 was observed through immunofluorescence staining. Furthermore, we found that high levels of NDRG1 competitively bind to GSK-3β and Nur77, preventing the degradation of β-catenin and leading to increased levels of downstream oncogenic genes. In vivo, we consistently observed that suppressing NDRG1 in HCC xenografts reduced β-catenin levels and its downstream target Cyclin D1, resulting in inhibited tumor growth. Clinically, we found that the over-expression of NDRG1 in HCC patient samples is positively correlated with the expressions of GSK-3β-9ser, Nur77, and β-catenin. In conclusion, we have identified GSK-3β and Nur77 as new interaction partners of NDRG1. These protein-protein interactions regulate the turnover of β-catenin and subsequent signaling in HCC cells, providing potential targets for future therapeutic interventions.

title: A tutorial on statistical methods for population association studies
text: Despite the existence of genetic association studies for a considerable period, there remains a lack of agreement on the most suitable statistical methods, even for basic analyses. In this article, I aim to provide an overview of statistical approaches for population association studies. This includes initial analyses such as testing for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, inferring phase and handling missing data, as well as SNP tagging. Additionally, I will discuss single-SNP and multipoint tests for association. The objective is to outline the main methods while briefly addressing challenges such as population structure and multiple testing. Furthermore, I will explore potential solutions and highlight ongoing advancements in the field.

title: Identification and Characterization of Multiple TRIM Proteins That Inhibit Hepatitis B Virus Transcription
text: The family of tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins consists of more than 100 members that share conserved tripartite motifs and have various biological functions. Some TRIM proteins have been found to restrict viral infections and regulate the innate immune responses of host cells. To identify TRIM proteins that affect the infection of hepatitis B virus (HBV), we conducted tests on 38 human TRIMs to observe their impact on HBV gene expression, capsid assembly, and DNA synthesis in human hepatoma cells (HepG2). The results of the study showed that the introduction of 8 TRIM proteins into HepG2 cells significantly reduced the levels of secreted HBV surface and e antigens, as well as intracellular capsid and capsid DNA. Further analysis revealed that these 8 TRIMs not only decreased the expression of HBV mRNAs, but also inhibited the activities of HBV enhancer I and enhancer II. Specifically, the investigation of TRIM41 demonstrated that a specific segment of HBV DNA, spanning from nucleotide 1638 to nucleotide 1763, was crucial for TRIM41-mediated inhibition of HBV enhancer II activity. This inhibitory effect relied on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of TRIM41 and the intactness of TRIM41's C-terminal domain. Additionally, when endogenous TRIM41 was suppressed in a stable cell line derived from HepG2, the level of HBV preC/C RNA significantly increased, resulting in elevated viral core protein, capsid, and capsid DNA. Therefore, our research has identified eight TRIM proteins that can impede HBV transcription and provided compelling evidence suggesting the intrinsic role of TRIM41 in regulating HBV transcription in human hepatoma cells.

title: A mouse Mecp2-null mutation causes neurological symptoms that mimic Rett syndrome
text: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare genetic disorder that affects females and occurs in approximately 10,000-15,000 births. Initially, affected females develop normally for about 6-18 months, but then experience a loss of voluntary movements, including speech and hand skills. The majority of RTT patients have mutations in the MECP2 gene, which is located on the X chromosome and is responsible for a protein that helps regulate gene activity. Previous studies using embryonic stem cells lacking the MECP2 gene have shown its importance in mouse development. In this study, we used a technique called Cre-loxP technology to create mice that lacked the MECP2 gene. Both the mice lacking MECP2 and those in which MECP2 was specifically deleted in the brain exhibited severe neurological symptoms at around six weeks of age. There was no evidence of compensation by another protein called MeCP1 in other tissues, as observed in genetic and biochemical tests. Additionally, after several months, female mice with only one copy of the MECP2 gene also displayed behavioral symptoms. The fact that both humans and mice experience a similar delay in symptom onset, despite their different rates of development, suggests that the absence of MeCP2 may compromise the stability of brain function rather than brain development itself.

title: The p38/MK2-Driven Exchange between Tristetraprolin and HuR Regulates AU–Rich Element–Dependent Translation
text: The expression of TNF in macrophages is tightly controlled at the translational level. This control is dependent on the p38 MAPK/MK2 pathway and the AU-rich element (ARE) present in the TNF mRNA. In this study, we aim to understand the molecular mechanism behind the regulation of TNF translation through phosphorylation. Our findings reveal that the translation of TNF precursor at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) requires the presence of human antigen R (HuR), a factor that binds and stabilizes the ARE. Additionally, either the activation of the p38 MAPK/MK2 pathway or the absence of tristetraprolin (TTP), a factor that binds and destabilizes the ARE, is necessary for efficient translation. We demonstrate that phosphorylation of TTP by MK2 reduces its affinity for the ARE, impairs its ability to replace HuR, and allows HuR to initiate the translation of TNF mRNA. This mechanism also regulates the translation of TTP's own mRNA, creating an intrinsic feedback control for the inflammatory response. The phosphorylation-regulated exchange of TTP and HuR at target mRNAs serves as a reversible switch, determining whether the mRNA is unstable and non-translatable or stable and efficiently translated.

title: miR-205 hinders the malignant interplay between prostate cancer cells and associated fibroblasts.
text:
The tumor microenvironment plays a crucial role in determining the metastatic potential of cancer cells. Our recent research has shown that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) induce a redox-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in prostate cancer (PCa) cells. This process is driven by the cycloxygenase-2/hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)/nuclear factor-κB pathway, leading to increased tumor aggressiveness. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in the interaction between tumors and the surrounding stroma, with the goal of identifying potential strategies to counteract oxidative stress and metastasis.

Our results revealed that miR-205 is the most downregulated miRNA in PCa cells when stimulated by CAFs. This downregulation is a result of direct transcriptional repression by HIF-1, a well-known transcription factor sensitive to redox signaling. To confirm the role of miR-205, we conducted rescue experiments by overexpressing miR-205 in PCa cells. The results showed that ectopic miR-205 expression counteracted CAF-induced EMT, thereby inhibiting cell invasion, stem cell-like characteristics, tumorigenicity, and metastasis. Additionally, miR-205 prevented the activation of surrounding fibroblasts by reducing the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Overall, our findings suggest that miR-205 acts as a suppressor of PCa metastasis by interrupting the communication between tumor cells and associated fibroblasts. This interruption disrupts the pro-oxidant and pro-inflammatory pathways activated by reactive stroma. In conclusion, the replacement of miR-205 in PCa cells not only prevents but also reverses the oxidative/pro-inflammatory axis leading to CAF-induced EMT. These findings provide a rationale for the development of miRNA-based approaches to prevent and treat metastatic disease.

title: The prevention of type 2 diabetes
text: More than 7% of adults in the US are affected by Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which causes significant personal and economic burden. In individuals with prediabetic conditions, insulin secretion and action, which are potential targets for preventive measures, are impaired. Studies have shown that lifestyle modifications, such as weight loss and exercise, are effective in preventing the onset of T2DM in high-risk groups, with weight loss having the greatest impact. Additionally, various medications like metformin, thiazolidinediones, and acarbose can also delay or prevent T2DM. It is currently unknown whether these diabetes-prevention strategies can also prevent the development of diabetic vascular complications, but they do have a positive impact on cardiovascular risk factors. Preventive strategies that can be easily implemented in routine clinical settings have been developed and evaluated. However, their widespread application has been hindered by local financial considerations, despite the potential cost-effectiveness at the population level.

title: The transcriptional landscape of the mammalian genome.
text: In this study, we conducted a thorough examination of transcription start and termination sites, as well as an analysis of previously unknown full-length complementary DNAs derived from the mouse genome. Our findings include the identification of the boundaries of 181,047 transcripts, which exhibit significant variation due to alternative promoter usage, splicing, and polyadenylation. Among these transcripts, we discovered 16,247 new mouse protein-coding transcripts, including 5154 that encode proteins not previously identified. By mapping the transcriptome onto the genome, we observed transcriptional forests characterized by overlapping transcription on both strands, interspersed with deserts where few transcripts are present. These data provide a comprehensive foundation for studying and comparing transcriptional regulation in mammalian differentiation and development.

title: The Protein Data Bank
text: The Protein Data Bank (PDB) is a global repository of primary structural data for biological macromolecules. Numerous secondary sources of information rely on PDB data, making it a crucial resource for studies in structural bioinformatics. This article outlines the objectives of the PDB, the procedures for depositing and accessing data, ways to obtain additional information, and future plans for resource development. By the end of this article, readers will have a comprehensive understanding of the PDB's scope and the valuable resources it offers.

title: Cell-State-Specific Metabolic Dependency in Hematopoiesis and Leukemogenesis
text: Maintaining a proper balance between oxidative and nonoxidative glucose metabolism is crucial for various pathological processes. To investigate the impact of modulating glucose metabolism on hematopoietic and leukemic cell populations, we conducted experiments by eliminating enzymes that influence aerobic glycolysis to different extents. Our results demonstrate that a deficiency in the M2 pyruvate kinase isoform (PKM2) leads to a decrease in the levels of metabolic intermediates necessary for biosynthesis, impairing progenitor function without affecting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). On the other hand, deletion of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) significantly hampers the function of both HSCs and progenitors during hematopoiesis. Interestingly, when it comes to leukemia initiation caused by transforming alleles that potentially impact HSCs or progenitors, the absence of either PKM2 or LDHA inhibits the process. This suggests that the specific responses to metabolic manipulation in hematopoiesis do not necessarily apply to the development of leukemia. Consequently, this finding implies that adjusting the level of glycolysis could be a potential therapeutic approach for treating leukemia while preserving HSC function.

title: A transition in brain state during propofol-induced unconsciousness.
text: During active behavior, sleep, and general anesthesia, cortical dynamics are influenced by rhythmic oscillations. Although cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling is a significant characteristic of cortical oscillations, its role in organizing conscious and unconscious brain states remains unclear. By utilizing high-density EEG and intracranial electrocorticography, we investigated the effects of gradual induction of propofol general anesthesia in humans. Our findings revealed a rapid transition induced by the drug, leading to distinct states with contrasting phase-amplitude coupling and cortical source distributions. One state corresponds to unconsciousness and bears similarities to sleep slow oscillations, while the other state occurs during the loss or recovery of consciousness and resembles an enhanced slow cortical potential. These results establish objective electrophysiological markers for different unconscious brain states and have the potential to enhance EEG-based monitoring for general anesthesia.

title: Cohesins and condensins orchestrate the 4D dynamics of yeast chromosomes during the cell cycle
text: The process of duplicating and separating chromosomes involves rearranging their internal structure with the help of specific proteins. These proteins, known as structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes, include cohesin and condensin. Despite ongoing research on the functions of these proteins, we still lack a complete understanding of how chromosome architecture changes during cell division on a genome-wide scale. In this study, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the three-dimensional organization of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome throughout the cell cycle. We also investigate how SMC complexes control these structural changes. During replication, the establishment of cohesion leads to the formation of many long-range contacts within chromosomes, which ultimately results in the individualization of chromosomes during metaphase. In anaphase, the mechanical forces exerted by the mitotic spindle cause a sudden reorganization of the chromosomes. Additionally, we observe the formation of a loop, facilitated by condensin, that connects the centromere cluster with the rDNA loci. This suggests that condensin-mediated forces may play a direct role in chromosome segregation. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how chromosome dynamics change throughout the cell cycle in a single-celled organism. It also reveals new insights into the structural reorganization of chromosomes during key stages of cell division that are conserved across different organisms.

title: Genome-wide patterns of divergence and gene flow across a butterfly radiation.
text: The Heliconius butterflies are a diverse group that has recently undergone significant evolutionary changes, resulting in multiple levels of divergence. Despite this divergence, there is still ongoing gene flow between different species within the group. By sequencing the genome of Heliconius melpomene, we were able to study the genomic evolution of this group using a technique called dense RAD marker sequencing. Through phylogenetic analysis of 54 individuals, we found strong evidence supporting the idea that H. melpomene and Heliconius cydno are distinct species, refuting previous hypotheses that suggested H. melpomene may be closely related to H. cydno. We also discovered that Heliconius timareta forms a separate but closely related clade to H. cydno, with Heliconius heurippa falling within this clade. Our research also revealed evidence of genetic admixture between populations of H. melpomene and H. cydno/timareta that live in the same geographic area. This admixture is particularly prevalent between H. cydno and H. melpomene in Central America, as well as between H. timareta and H. melpomene in the eastern slopes of the Andes. When it comes to the divergence between different races within the group, we found that it is primarily driven by isolation due to geographic distance. Interestingly, we did not detect any significant genetic population structure between races that live in adjacent but not overlapping geographic areas. This suggests that hybrid zones between races are not areas where different races come into contact with each other. Our findings also support previous research indicating that certain genetic loci responsible for color patterns are shared between populations and species that have similar color patterns. This pattern is unique to these specific genomic regions, as only a small number of other loci show significant similarity between populations and species with similar color patterns.

title: Randomized, double-blind study of the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of tafenoquine versus mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis in nonimmune subjects.
text: This study is the first phase III trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and effectiveness of tafenoquine as a malaria prophylaxis. Australian soldiers participating in a peacekeeping mission in East Timor were randomly assigned to receive either 200 mg tafenoquine (492 subjects) or 250 mg mefloquine (162 subjects) on a weekly basis for 6 months. Upon returning to Australia, the tafenoquine group received a placebo while the mefloquine group received 30 mg primaquine daily for 14 days. There were no significant differences in hematological and biochemical parameters between the two treatment groups. The occurrence of treatment-related adverse events was similar in both groups (13.4% for tafenoquine and 11.7% for mefloquine). Only three subjects (0.6%) in the tafenoquine group discontinued prophylaxis due to possible drug-related adverse events, while none in the mefloquine group did so. No cases of malaria were diagnosed during the deployment period for either group. However, after discontinuation of medication, there were 4 cases (0.9%) of Plasmodium vivax infection in the tafenoquine group and 1 case (0.7%) in the mefloquine group, occurring up to 20 weeks later. In a subset of subjects who underwent detailed safety assessments, 93% (69 out of 74) of those in the tafenoquine group exhibited mild vortex keratopathy, while none of the 21 mefloquine subjects did. This keratopathy did not affect visual acuity and resolved completely in all subjects within one year. Overall, tafenoquine appears to be a safe and well-tolerated drug for malaria prophylaxis. Although this study could not definitively establish the volunteers' exact exposure to malaria, tafenoquine seems to be highly effective in preventing the disease.

title: Domain-wide regulation of DNA replication timing during mammalian development
text: Research on replication timing offers insight into previously inaccessible levels of chromosome organization and their flexibility during development. While the mechanisms governing replication timing remain unclear, recent comprehensive studies have shed light on the extent to which it is regulated during early cell fate transitions in mammals. These studies have revealed coordinated changes in specific chromosomal segments spanning 400-800 kb, affecting at least half of the genome. Additionally, alterations in replication timing are associated with changes in sub-nuclear organization and genome-wide transcriptional potential. Notably, replication timing profiles specific to different tissues are conserved between mice and humans, suggesting developmental significance. Consequently, these studies have established a strong foundation for understanding the relationship between megabase-level chromosome structure and function, highlighting the central role of replication in domain-level genome organization.

title: PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R is crucial for leukemia stem cell potential induced by MOZ-TIF2
text: The presence of self-renewing stem cells in leukemias and other cancers plays a crucial role in maintaining the disease. Therefore, eliminating these cancer stem cells is believed to be essential for effective anticancer treatment. In our study, we used a model of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) induced by the fusion protein MOZ-TIF2, which is associated with monocytic leukemia. We demonstrate that AML can be cured by eradicating leukemia stem cells. The fusion proteins MOZ-TIF2 and MOZ-CBP interact with the transcription factor PU.1 to stimulate the expression of the macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor (CSF1R), also known as M-CSFR, c-FMS, or CD115. Our experiments using PU.1-deficient mice reveal that PU.1 is necessary for MOZ-TIF2 to establish and maintain AML stem cells. Cells expressing high levels of CSF1R (CSF1Rhigh cells) exhibit potent leukemia-initiating activity, while those expressing low levels of CSF1R (CSF1Rlow cells) do not. By utilizing transgenic mice expressing a drug-inducible suicide gene controlled by the CSF1R promoter, we successfully cured AML by eliminating CSF1Rhigh cells. Additionally, AML induction was suppressed in CSF1R-deficient mice, and CSF1R inhibitors slowed the progression of MOZ-TIF2-induced leukemia. Therefore, in this particular subtype of AML, leukemia stem cells are found within the CSF1Rhigh cell population, suggesting that targeting the PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R expression could be a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: Pharmacological blockage of fibro/adipogenic progenitor expansion and suppression of regenerative fibrogenesis is associated with impaired skeletal muscle regeneration.
text: The expansion of fibro/adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) and the temporary deposition of extracellular matrix are triggered by acute skeletal muscle injury. If this phase continues, it can result in permanent tissue scarring, but the effects of suppressing it have not been studied. In our study using a model of acute muscle damage, we discovered that inhibiting FAP expansion with Nilotinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor known for its antifibrotic properties, has a negative impact on myogenesis during regeneration. We observed that Nilotinib prevents the injury-induced expansion of satellite cells in vivo, but it does not affect their proliferation in vitro, suggesting that its effect is not cell-autonomous. Nilotinib hinders the regenerative fibrogenesis process by impeding the expansion and differentiation of resident CD45(-):CD31(-):α7integrin(-):Sca1(+) mesenchymal FAPs triggered by the injury. Our findings support the idea that the expansion of FAPs and the temporary fibrogenesis observed during regeneration play a crucial role in supporting tissue-specific stem cells.

title: Deregulation of Scribble Promotes Mammary Tumorigenesis and Reveals a Role for Cell Polarity in Carcinoma
text: The absence of cell polarity proteins like Scribble leads to the development of tumors in Drosophila by encouraging uncontrolled cell growth. However, the role of polarity proteins in tumorigenesis in mammals is not well understood. In this study, we show that the depletion of Scribble in mammary epithelial cells disrupts cell polarity, hinders the formation of three-dimensional structures, prevents cell death, and ultimately leads to the development of abnormal tissue growth that progresses into tumors over time. The loss of Scribble collaborates with oncogenes like c-myc to transform epithelial cells and induce tumors in vivo by blocking the activation of a pathway that triggers cell death. Interestingly, both reduced levels and misplacement of Scribble from cell-cell junctions are observed in spontaneous mammary tumors in mice and humans. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that Scribble inhibits the formation of breast cancer and that the disruption of polarity pathways promotes abnormal tissue growth and tumor formation in mammals by interfering with the formation of structures and inhibiting cell death.

title: The Polymeal: a more natural, safer, and probably tastier (than the Polypill) strategy to reduce cardiovascular disease by more than 75%.
text: The aim of this study was to find a better and safer alternative to the Polypill, known as the Polymeal. While the Polypill has potential benefits for managing cardiovascular risk, its costs and adverse effects are major drawbacks. To create the Polymeal, we gathered data on its ingredients from various sources, including wine, fish, dark chocolate, fruits, vegetables, garlic, and almonds. Using data from the Framingham heart study and the Framingham offspring study, we constructed life tables to model the benefits of the Polymeal in the general population starting at age 50. By combining these ingredients, we found that the Polymeal could reduce cardiovascular disease events by 76%. For men, consuming the Polymeal daily would increase total life expectancy by 6.6 years, increase life expectancy without cardiovascular disease by 9.0 years, and decrease life expectancy with cardiovascular disease by 2.4 years. The corresponding differences for women were 4.8, 8.1, and 3.3 years, respectively. In conclusion, the Polymeal shows promise as an effective, non-pharmacological, safe, affordable, and delicious alternative to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and increase life expectancy in the general population.

title: Islet-Like Clusters Derived from Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Wharton's Jelly of the Human Umbilical Cord for Transplantation to Control Type 1 Diabetes
text:
The development of renewable sources of islet-replacement tissue for type I diabetes mellitus has generated significant interest. Human mesenchymal cells derived from the Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord (HUMSCs) possess stem cell properties and can be easily obtained and processed compared to other types of stem cells. These HUMSCs have the potential to be a valuable source for generating islets. 

In this study, we induced HUMSCs to transform into islet-like cell clusters in vitro by culturing them in neuron-conditioned medium. To evaluate the functionality of these cell clusters in vivo, we transplanted them into the livers of diabetic rats. After 12 weeks, we measured glucose tolerance and conducted immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy analysis. The islet-like cell clusters were found to contain human C-peptide and release human insulin in response to normal glucose levels. Real-time RT-PCR also detected the expression of insulin and other pancreatic beta-cell-related genes in these cell clusters. 

Furthermore, the transplantation of these islet-like cell clusters significantly alleviated hyperglycemia and glucose intolerance in the diabetic rats, without the need for immunosuppressants. We also observed the presence of fused liver cells in addition to the islet-like cell clusters in the liver. These fused liver cells exhibited positive staining for human insulin and nuclei, as well as secretory granules. 

In conclusion, we successfully differentiated HUMSCs into mature islet-like cell clusters that possess insulin-producing ability both in vitro and in vivo. HUMSCs derived from the Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord appear to be a favorable source of stem cells for converting into insulin-producing cells due to their large donor pool, easy availability, minimal discomfort for the donor, and low risk of rejection.

title: Use of perioperative hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% in elective joint arthroplasty and association with adverse outcomes: a retrospective population based analysis
text: The objective of this study was to determine if the use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% during elective joint arthroplasties increases the risk of perioperative complications. The study design was a retrospective cohort study using population-based data from 2006 to 2013. The data was collected from 510 different hospitals in the United States that participated in the Premier Perspective database. The participants included 1,051,441 patients who underwent elective total hip and knee arthroplasties. The exposures studied were perioperative fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch 6%, albumin 5%, or neither. The main outcome measures were acute renal failure and complications such as thromboembolic, cardiac, and pulmonary issues. The results showed that compared to patients who did not receive either colloid, those who received hydroxyethyl starch 6% or albumin 5% had a higher risk of acute renal failure and most other complications. The use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% has decreased recently, while the use of albumin 5% has increased. In conclusion, this study found that the use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% during elective joint arthroplasties is associated with an increased risk of complications, similar to studies in critically ill patients. These findings raise concerns about the widespread use of these colloids in elective joint arthroplasty procedures.

title: BMAL1 and CLOCK, Two Essential Components of the Circadian Clock, Are Involved in Glucose Homeostasis
text: The molecular clock, a unique series of autoregulatory interactions, is responsible for generating circadian timing. The behavioral rhythms that are influenced by the molecular clock are well understood. Our study reveals that Bmal1 and Clock play a role in regulating glucose homeostasis. When the clock components Bmal1 and Clock are deactivated, the daily fluctuations in glucose and triglycerides are suppressed. Deletion of Bmal1 eliminates gluconeogenesis, while Clock mutants experience a decrease in gluconeogenesis. However, the response of corticosterone and glucagon to insulin-induced hypoglycemia remains intact. Additionally, a high-fat diet affects carbohydrate metabolism by intensifying the circadian variation in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity. Mutation of Clock restores the normal phenotype seen in mice fed a regular diet. Bmal1 and Clock, which are genes involved in the core molecular clock, have significant control over recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycemia. Furthermore, dietary cues that are out of sync with the internal clock may impact glucose homeostasis by interacting with peripheral molecular clocks.

title: Mechanisms of progression and regression of renal lesions of chronic nephropathies and diabetes.
text: The prevalence of chronic kidney diseases is on the rise globally, posing a significant public health concern. While genetic factors play a role in the susceptibility and progression of renal disease, proteinuria has been identified as an independent predictor of the outcome. By using various medications and adopting a low-protein diet, urinary protein levels can be reduced, thereby limiting the decline in renal function for individuals with both diabetic and nondiabetic nephropathies. In fact, experimental studies on animals and even humans have shown that disease remission and regression of renal lesions can occur. In animal models, the reversal of glomerular structural changes is linked to the remodeling of the glomerular architecture. This discovery was made possible through 3D reconstruction studies of the glomerular capillary tuft, which allowed for the measurement of reduced sclerosis volume and the regeneration of capillaries following treatment. The regeneration of capillary segments may be attributed to resident cells, but progenitor cells from within or outside the kidney may also play a role. This review provides an overview of recent advancements in our understanding of the mechanisms and mediators involved in the repair of renal tissue, ultimately leading to the regression of renal injury.

title: Contemporary type 1 diabetes pregnancy outcomes: impact of obesity and glycaemic control.
text:
The objective of this study was to compare pregnancy outcomes in women with and without type 1 diabetes, and to examine the effects of obesity and glycaemic control on these outcomes. The study was conducted as a historical cohort study in a specialist diabetes and maternity network in Victoria. The participants included all singleton births (at least 20 weeks' gestation) from 2010 to 2013, with 107 pregnancies to women with type 1 diabetes and 27,075 pregnancies to women without diabetes. Women with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes were excluded. Data were extracted from the Birthing Outcomes System database, and associations between type 1 diabetes and pregnancy outcomes were analyzed using multivariable regression. The main outcome measures were mode of birth, maternal and neonatal outcomes.

The results showed that women with type 1 diabetes had a higher mean body mass index compared to women without diabetes. The median gestation period for their babies was shorter, and they were more likely to have babies that were large for gestational age. Women with type 1 diabetes were also more likely to have had labor induced, a caesarean delivery, or a pre-term birth. Their babies were more likely to have shoulder dystocia, hypoglycemia, jaundice, respiratory distress, or to suffer perinatal death. In women with type 1 diabetes, greater obesity was associated with increased odds for a large for gestational age baby or congenital malformation, and increased HbA1c levels were associated with pre-term birth and perinatal death.

In conclusion, women with type 1 diabetes, even when managed in a specialist setting, still experience adverse obstetric and neonatal outcomes. Poor glycaemic control is not solely responsible for these outcomes, highlighting the importance of other risk factors such as obesity and weight gain.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Vitamin D Action
text: The hormone metabolite of vitamin D, known as 1α,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25D), triggers biological responses by binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR). When 1,25D occupies the VDR, it interacts with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) to form a heterodimer. This heterodimer then binds to vitamin D responsive elements in the genes that are directly controlled by 1,25D. By recruiting complexes of coactivators or corepressors, the ligand-activated VDR-RXR modulates the transcription of genes that encode proteins responsible for the traditional functions of vitamin D. These functions include signaling intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption to maintain skeletal and calcium homeostasis. Therefore, the action of vitamin D in a specific cell depends on the production or delivery of sufficient concentrations of the 1,25D ligand, the expression of adequate VDR and RXR coreceptor proteins, and the cell-specific programming of transcriptional responses to regulate select genes that encode proteins involved in mediating the effects of vitamin D. For instance, 1,25D induces the expression of RANKL, SPP1 (osteopontin), and BGP (osteocalcin) to control bone mineral remodeling; TRPV6, CaBP9k, and claudin 2 to enhance intestinal calcium absorption; and TRPV5, klotho, and Npt2c to regulate renal calcium and phosphate reabsorption. It seems that VDR also functions without being bound by 1,25D in keratinocytes, where it drives mammalian hair cycling by regulating genes such as CASP14, S100A8, SOSTDC1, and others that affect Wnt signaling. Additionally, there have been reports of alternative, low-affinity, non-vitamin D VDR ligands, such as lithocholic acid, docosahexaenoic acid, and curcumin. The combined use of these alternative VDR ligands and 1,25D/VDR control of gene expression may potentially delay chronic disorders associated with aging, such as osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

title: Quantitative Temporal Viromics: An Approach to Investigate Host-Pathogen Interaction
text:
We have developed a proteomic technique called "quantitative temporal viromics" (QTV) that allows for a systematic quantitative analysis of changes in host and viral proteins during a productive infection. This approach provides dynamic insights into the interaction between the virus and its host. Using multiplexed tandem-mass-tag-based mass spectrometry, we applied QTV to study human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), an important pathogen known for its ability to evade the immune system.

Through QTV, we were able to uncover how HCMV manipulates signaling pathways and counteracts the host's intrinsic, innate, and adaptive immune defenses. We identified over 8,000 cellular proteins, including 1,200 cell-surface proteins, that are orchestrated by HCMV. Additionally, QTV predicted potential therapeutic targets, such as natural killer and T cell ligands, as well as 29 viral proteins present at the cell surface.

Furthermore, we defined the temporal profiles of more than 80% of HCMV canonical genes and 14 noncanonical HCMV open reading frames using QTV. This comprehensive analysis provides valuable information about the progression of viral infection.

QTV is a powerful method that can be applied to study any virus with a robust in vitro model. It offers important insights into viral infection dynamics and has the potential to contribute to the development of effective antiviral strategies.

title: Interactions between sleep, circadian function, and glucose metabolism: implications for risk and severity of diabetes.
text: This review aims to provide an update on the current understanding of the relationship between sleep disturbances, circadian dysfunction, and glucose metabolism. Sleep disturbances, such as insufficient sleep and fragmented sleep, have been found to be associated with abnormal glucose metabolism and an increased risk of diabetes. Laboratory studies have shed light on the underlying mechanisms, while large prospective studies have further supported the link between sleep disturbances and incident diabetes. Obstructive sleep apnea, a condition characterized by both sleep fragmentation and low oxygen levels, is a significant risk factor for insulin resistance and potentially diabetes. However, there is still debate about whether treating sleep apnea can improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes. In recent years, there has been growing attention to sleep disturbances during pregnancy and their potential impact on gestational diabetes and hyperglycemia, which can have adverse effects on both the mother and the fetus. Animal studies have also suggested that disruption of the circadian system may contribute to negative metabolic outcomes. This review discusses experimental, prospective, and interventional studies to provide a comprehensive overview of the current knowledge on the topic.

title: Antibody-Based HIV-1 Vaccines: Recent Developments and Future Directions
text: In May 2007, the Global HIV Vaccine Enterprise organized a two-day workshop to discuss the immune responses to HIV and strategies for developing vaccines that can generate protective antibody responses against the virus. The workshop aimed to address scientific issues, gaps, and opportunities that have emerged since the publication of the Enterprise Strategic Plan in 2005 [1], and to provide recommendations for planning new activities. Effective viral vaccines typically work by producing antibodies that can neutralize or deactivate the invading virus. It is widely believed that an effective HIV-1 vaccine should be able to elicit potent antiviral neutralizing antibodies. However, HIV-1 is unique because it replicates chronically in the host and evades the antibody response. This immune evasion, combined with the genetic diversity of HIV-1 strains worldwide, has presented significant challenges for vaccine development. Current HIV vaccine candidates do not generate neutralizing antibodies against most circulating virus strains, making the induction of a protective antibody response a top priority for HIV-1 vaccine research. The effectiveness of an antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine is typically assessed through in vitro tests that measure the ability of vaccine-induced antibodies to neutralize a wide range of viral isolates representing different genetic subtypes of HIV-1 [2]. While the level and breadth of neutralization needed to predict protection in vaccine recipients is still unknown, it is clear that current vaccine candidates only neutralize a small fraction of circulating isolates. Therefore, significant progress needs to be made in this area. Additionally, while virus neutralization is an important benchmark for an HIV-1 vaccine, it may not be the only factor that determines the success of antibody-based vaccine candidates. The primary targets for neutralizing antibodies against HIV-1 are the gp120 and gp41 envelope glycoproteins (Env) on the virus surface, which facilitate the binding to receptors and the fusion with host cells [3]. Antibodies neutralize the virus by binding to these viral spikes and preventing the virus from entering susceptible cells, such as CD4+ T cells [4,5]. To evade antibody recognition, the virus employs various mechanisms, including a dense outer coating of sugar molecules and the strategic positioning of specific structures on the gp120 molecule [6–8]. Although these shielding mechanisms are highly effective, they also have vulnerabilities due to fitness constraints. Understanding the precise location and molecular structure of these vulnerable regions could be valuable for designing improved vaccine candidates. During the workshop, participants identified four areas that, if given sufficient attention, could provide crucial information to advance the development of an effective antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine: (1) using structural information to design better vaccine candidates, (2) understanding the role of Fc receptors and complement in the immune response, (3) standardizing and validating assays, and (4) studying the regulation of B cell responses in the immune system.

title: Targeted therapy for cancer stem cells: the patched pathway and ABC transporters
text: Evidence from certain types of leukemia, brain cancer, and breast cancer suggests the existence of a small group of tumor cells that possess characteristics similar to stem cells and the ability to self-renew. These self-renewing cells, referred to as "cancer stem cells," make up a small percentage, as low as 1%, of the total cells within a tumor, making them challenging to identify and study. Similar to normal stem cells, cancer stem cells possess several properties that enable them to withstand traditional cancer treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy. These properties include the expression of high levels of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) drug transporters, which contribute to their resistance, a relatively inactive state, increased DNA repair capabilities, and a reduced ability to undergo apoptosis. By targeting both the cancer stem cells and the non-stem cells, combined cancer therapies may be developed to enhance effectiveness. This article will discuss efforts to target the Hedgehog/Patched pathway, which plays a critical role in embryonic growth and differentiation, as well as the ABCG2 drug efflux transporter.

title: Increased in vivo amyloid-β42 production, exchange, and loss in presenilin mutation carriers.
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is believed to be caused by either an excessive production or a decreased clearance of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide. Autosomal dominant AD (ADAD), which is caused by mutations in the presenilin (PSEN) gene, is thought to result from an increased production of Aβ42 compared to Aβ40 in the central nervous system (CNS). While this has been observed in animal models of ADAD, it has not been confirmed in humans with these mutations. To investigate the effects of PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutations on the production and turnover of Aβ isoforms, we conducted compartmental modeling studies using stable isotope labeling kinetic (SILK) in human carriers of PSEN mutations and noncarriers. We compared these results based on mutation status and the amount of fibrillar amyloid deposition, as measured by positron emission tomography (PET) using the amyloid tracer Pittsburgh compound B (PIB). We found that CNS Aβ42 to Aβ40 production rates were 24% higher in mutation carriers compared to noncarriers, regardless of the amount of amyloid deposits detected by PET PIB imaging. The turnover rate of soluble Aβ42 relative to Aβ40 was 65% faster in mutation carriers and correlated with amyloid deposition, indicating an increased deposition of Aβ42 into plaques, which led to a reduced recovery of Aβ42 in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). We also observed reversible exchange of Aβ42 peptides with preexisting unlabeled peptide in the presence of plaques. These findings support the theory that Aβ42 is overproduced in the CNS of individuals with PSEN mutations that cause AD, and demonstrate that the turnover and exchange processes of soluble Aβ42 are altered in the presence of amyloid plaques, resulting in lower concentrations of Aβ42 in the CSF.

title: Basic residues in the T-cell receptor ζ cytoplasmic domain mediate membrane association and modulate signaling.
text: The T-cell receptor (TCR) is composed of different protein complexes, including a TCRαβ heterodimer, a TCRζ homodimer, and CD3γε and CD3δε heterodimers. However, the exact process by which T-cell activation occurs after TCR binds to its ligand is still not fully understood. Previous research has suggested that the cytoplasmic tail of CD3ε binds to the plasma membrane through a stretch of basic residues and proposed that detachment from the membrane is necessary for its phosphorylation. In this study, we demonstrate that similar basic residue-rich stretches (BRS) within the cytoplasmic tail of TCRζ are responsible for its association with the plasma membrane, and TCR engagement leads to the dissociation of TCRζ from the membrane. This dissociation is dependent on the phosphorylation of specific tyrosine-based activation motifs on TCRζ by a protein called lymphocyte cell-specific protein tyrosine kinase (Lck), but not by ζ-chain-associated protein kinase 70 binding. Mutations in the BRS motifs of TCRζ that disrupt its association with the membrane weaken both the immediate and downstream responses triggered by TCR engagement. These mutations also seem to affect the positioning of TCRζ in relation to Lck and the mobility of the TCR complex. This study reveals that the phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of TCRζ plays a crucial role in its interaction with the plasma membrane and emphasizes the functional significance of TCRζ BRS motifs.

title: Policies for alcohol restriction and their association with interpersonal violence: a time-series analysis of homicides in Cali, Colombia.
text:
In Cali, Colombia, there is a significant problem with interpersonal violence resulting in deaths. To address this issue, various alcohol control policies have been implemented. The purpose of this study was to examine whether these policies had any impact on the incidence rate of homicides. 

The study was conducted from 2004 to 2008 using a time-series design. The policies varied in terms of the hours during which alcohol sales and consumption were restricted. The most restrictive policies prohibited alcohol between 2 a.m. and 10 a.m. for a total of 446 non-consecutive days. Moderately restrictive policies prohibited alcohol between 3 a.m. and 10 a.m. for 1277 non-consecutive days. Lax policies allowed alcohol until 4 a.m. and restricted it until 10 a.m. for 104 non-consecutive days. 

Using conditional autoregressive negative binomial regressions, the rates of homicides and unintentional injury deaths (excluding traffic events) were compared during different periods when different policies were in effect. 

The results showed that there was a higher risk of homicides during periods when the moderately restrictive policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect. The incidence rate ratio (IRR) was 1.15, with a 90% confidence interval (CI) of 1.05-1.26, and a p-value of 0.012. Furthermore, there was an even higher risk of homicides during periods when the lax policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect. The IRR was 1.42, with a 90% CI of 1.26-1.61, and a p-value of less than 0.001. 

On the other hand, less restrictive policies did not show an increased risk of unintentional injury deaths. 

In conclusion, the study found that extended hours of alcohol sales and consumption were associated with an increased risk of homicides. Therefore, implementing strong restrictions on alcohol availability could potentially reduce the incidence of interpersonal violence in communities with high homicide rates.

title: Effects of SNF1 on Maltose Metabolism and Leavening Ability of Baker's Yeast in Lean Dough.
text: Glucose repression negatively affects the metabolism of maltose in baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) in lean dough, leading to a delay in dough fermentation. To improve maltose metabolism and leavening ability, it is necessary to alleviate glucose repression. The Snf1 protein kinase plays a crucial role in responding to glucose repression and is required for the transcription of glucose-repressed genes, including the maltose-utilization genes (MAL). In this study, we constructed and characterized industrial baker's yeast strains with SNF1 overexpression and deletion. We examined their maltose utilization, growth and fermentation characteristics, mRNA levels of MAL genes (MAL62 encoding maltase and MAL61 encoding maltose permease), and maltase and maltose permease activities. Our findings indicate that SNF1 overexpression effectively derepressed glucose, resulting in increased expression levels of MAL genes and enhanced activities of maltase and maltose permease enzymes. These improvements led to an 18% increase in maltose metabolism in industrial baker's yeast in LSMLD medium (a low sugar model liquid dough fermentation medium) containing glucose and maltose, as well as a 15% increase in leavening ability in lean dough. These results provide valuable insights for breeding industrial baker's yeast strains that can undergo rapid fermentation.

title: Review article
text: Ribosomopathies refer to a group of disorders where genetic abnormalities result in impaired ribosome biogenesis and function, leading to distinct clinical phenotypes. Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a disorder characterized by hypoplastic, macrocytic anemia caused by congenital mutations in RPS19 and other genes that encode ribosomal proteins. Other rare congenital syndromes such as Schwachman-Diamond syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, cartilage hair hypoplasia, and Treacher Collins syndrome have also been linked to mutations in genes necessary for normal ribosome biogenesis. The 5q- syndrome, a subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome, is caused by the acquired deletion of chromosome 5q, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the ribosomal protein RPS14 and a similar erythroid phenotype to Diamond-Blackfan anemia. Abnormalities in ribosome function have also been associated with various human malignancies. Defects in ribosome biogenesis activate the p53 pathway, which plays a crucial role in protein translation surveillance and genome integrity. This pathway appears to be a key mediator of the clinical features observed in ribosomopathies. Understanding the mechanisms by which specific abnormalities in ribosome biogenesis lead to distinct clinical syndromes holds promise for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

title: PD-L1 expression in human cancers and its association with clinical outcomes
text:
PD-L1 is a molecule that inhibits the immune response by suppressing the activation of T cells, which can contribute to the progression of tumors. High levels of PD-L1 expression in certain cancers, including gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer, ovarian cancer, and bladder cancer, are associated with poor clinical outcomes. However, in breast cancer and merkel cell carcinoma, PD-L1 expression is actually linked to better clinical outcomes. The role of PD-L1 expression as a prognostic factor in lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and melanoma is still debated.

Blocking antibodies that target PD-1 and PD-L1 have shown impressive response rates in cancer patients with PD-L1-overexpressing tumors. However, relying solely on PD-L1 as a predictive biomarker for cancer immunotherapy is questionable due to the limited accuracy of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry staining. Several factors can influence the accuracy of PD-L1 staining, including variations in antibody sensitivity across different studies, differences in the cut-off value for determining PD-L1 positivity, and the non-uniform expression of PD-L1 in tumors. Additionally, the timing and location of tissue sampling can impact the results of PD-L1 staining.

To improve the identification of patients who will benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade therapy, it is crucial to gain a better understanding of the tumor microenvironment and utilize other biomarkers, such as gene markers and combined indices.

title: Primate cytomegaloviruses encode and express an IL-10-like protein.
text: A homologous open reading frame (ORF) to interleukin-10 (IL-10) has been discovered in rhesus cytomegalovirus (RhCMV). This IL-10-like protein is produced from a multispliced, polyadenylated early gene transcript that includes a portion of the corresponding UL111A ORF found in human CMV (HCMV). Immunological analyses have confirmed the expression of the IL-10-like protein in both tissue culture and in rhesus macaques infected with RhCMV. Conserved ORFs have also been identified in CMV from humans, baboons, and African green monkeys. Additionally, a fully processed transcript has been mapped in fibroblasts infected with the Towne strain of HCMV. The conservation of this previously unknown ORF suggests that the protein may have a crucial role in the persistence and pathogenesis of primate CMV.

title: Genome Sequencing and Analysis of the Tasmanian Devil and Its Transmissible Cancer
text: The Tasmanian devil, known as Sarcophilus harrisii, is the largest carnivorous marsupial and is currently at risk of extinction due to a contagious facial cancer that is transmitted through biting. In this study, we present the complete sequencing, assembly, and annotation of the Tasmanian devil genome, as well as the whole-genome sequences of two different subclones of the cancer that were found in geographically distant locations. Through genomic analysis, we have determined that the cancer originated from a female Tasmanian devil and has since undergone genetic divergence as it spread throughout Tasmania. The devil cancer genome contains over 17,000 somatic base substitution mutations and exhibits a unique mutational process. By genotyping somatic mutations in 104 Tasmanian devil tumors that were distributed across different regions and time periods, we have been able to track the evolution and spread of this parasitic clonal lineage. Our findings indicate a selective sweep in one specific area, as well as the persistence of parallel lineages in other populations.

title: A Temporarily Distinct Subpopulation of Slow-Cycling Melanoma Cells Is Required for Continuous Tumor Growth
text: The significance of the different subpopulations within highly heterogeneous melanomas is not well understood. We have identified a small group of slow-cycling melanoma cells that express the H3K4 demethylase JARID1B. These cells have a longer doubling time of more than four weeks compared to the rapidly proliferating majority. When isolated, JARID1B-positive melanoma cells give rise to a highly proliferative offspring. Knocking down JARID1B initially accelerates tumor growth, but eventually leads to exhaustion, indicating that the JARID1B-positive subpopulation is crucial for continuous tumor growth. The expression of JARID1B is dynamically regulated and does not follow a hierarchical cancer stem cell model, as JARID1B-negative cells can become positive and even single melanoma cells, regardless of selection, are capable of forming tumors. These findings suggest a new perspective on melanoma heterogeneity, where tumor maintenance is a dynamic process mediated by a temporarily distinct subpopulation.

title: A map of human circular RNAs in clinically relevant tissues
text: Cellular circular RNAs (circRNAs) are produced through head-to-tail splicing and are present in all multicellular organisms that have been studied thus far. Recently, circRNAs have emerged as a significant group of RNA molecules that can act as regulators in post-transcriptional processes. It has also been observed that many circRNAs are specifically expressed in certain tissues and developmental stages. Furthermore, the unique stability and expression specificity of circRNAs make them promising candidates for clinical biomarker research. In this study, we present a comprehensive resource of circRNA expression in 20 human tissues that are highly relevant to disease-related research. These tissues include vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), human umbilical vein cells (HUVECs), artery endothelial cells (HUAECs), atrium, vena cava, neutrophils, platelets, cerebral cortex, placenta, and samples from mesenchymal stem cell differentiation. Through analysis of eight samples from a single donor, we discovered highly tissue-specific circRNA expression. Additionally, we found that many circRNAs were expressed at higher levels than their linear host transcripts, as indicated by circular-to-linear RNA ratios. Among the 71 circRNAs that were validated, we identified potential biomarkers. In samples from patients with adenosine deaminase-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA-SCID) and Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS), we observed differential circRNA expression of genes that play a role in the molecular pathogenesis of both conditions. These findings highlight the importance of studying circRNAs in the mechanisms of human diseases. KEY MESSAGES: We have created a catalog of circRNAs in 20 clinically relevant tissues. CircRNA expression is highly specific to different tissues. CircRNA transcripts are often more abundant than their linear host RNAs. CircRNAs can exhibit differential expression in genes associated with diseases.

title: Arp2/3 complex inhibition radically alters lamellipodial actin architecture, suspended cell shape, and the cell spreading process
text: Recent research has focused on studying the dendritic actin cytoskeleton in the lamellipodial (LP) region of the cell edge. This was done by experimentally reducing the activity of the Arp2/3 complex, which is responsible for nucleating and branching actin filaments. In this study, we expand on these findings by using pharmacological methods to inhibit the Arp2/3 complex in sea urchin coelomocytes. These cells have a particularly wide LP region and exhibit strong centripetal flow. Through light and electron microscopy, we observed that inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex with the drug CK666 significantly changed the structure of the LP actin, slowed down centripetal flow, caused suspended cells to transition from a lamellipodial to a filopodial shape, and induced a new organization of actin during cell spreading. One common characteristic of the CK666-treated coelomocytes was the presence of transverse actin arcs, which were found to be dependent on formin activity. Additionally, we found that CK666 treatment also resulted in actin arcs in other cells with wide LP regions, such as fish keratocytes and Drosophila S2 cells. We propose that the actin arcs observed in coelomocytes following Arp2/3 complex inhibition may represent an exaggerated form of elongated mother filaments, which could potentially serve as a scaffold for the formation of the dendritic actin network.

title: Synergistic Activation of HIV-1 Expression by Deacetylase Inhibitors and Prostratin: Implications for Treatment of Latent Infection
text: The presence of HIV-1 reservoirs that are transcriptionally silent but still capable of replication in individuals undergoing Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) poses a significant obstacle to eradicating the virus. To address this issue, researchers have proposed using a combination of HIV-1 gene activation and effective HAART as an additional therapy to reduce the number of latent viral reservoirs. In this study, we demonstrated a strong synergistic activation of HIV-1 production by combining clinically used histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACIs) with prostratin, a nuclear factor (NF)-kappaB inducer that does not promote tumor growth. Using latently-infected U1 monocytic cell lines and J-Lat T-cell clones, we found that this synergism was partially due to the recruitment of unresponsive cells into the population of expressing cells. Through transient transfection reporter assays, we showed that the combination of prostratin+HDACI synergistically activated the 5' Long Terminal Repeat (5'LTR) from HIV-1 Major group subtypes, which are the most prevalent viral genetic forms. Mechanistically, HDACIs increased the DNA-binding activity of nuclear NF-kappaB and the degradation of cytoplasmic NF-kappaB inhibitor, IkappaBalpha, induced by prostratin. Furthermore, the combined treatment of prostratin+HDACI caused more significant nucleosomal remodeling in the U1 viral promoter region compared to treatment with either compound alone. This enhanced remodeling correlated with a synergistic reactivation of HIV-1 transcription following the combined treatment, as evidenced by the recruitment of RNA polymerase II to the 5'LTR and the production of initiated and elongated transcripts. The physiological relevance of the prostratin+HDACI synergism was demonstrated in CD8(+)-depleted peripheral blood mononuclear cells from HAART-treated patients with undetectable viral load. Additionally, this combined treatment reactivated viral replication in resting CD4(+) T cells isolated from similar patients. Our findings suggest that using combinations of different proviral activators may have significant implications for reducing the size of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in HAART-treated patients.

title: Centrosome aberrations: cause or consequence of cancer progression?
text: Centrosome abnormalities are frequently observed in various human tumors, suggesting a disruption in the normal structure, duplication, or segregation of centrosomes. These centrosomes play a crucial role in organizing microtubule arrays throughout the cell cycle, influencing tissue architecture and the precise segregation of chromosomes. However, the origins of these centrosomal abnormalities in tumors and their impact on the development of invasive, genetically imbalanced cells during cancer progression remain unclear.

title: Autonomic neuropathy, QT interval lengthening, and unexpected deaths in male diabetic patients
text:
In a study involving 13 normal male subjects, 13 male diabetic subjects without autonomic neuropathy, and 13 male diabetic subjects with autonomic neuropathy, the researchers measured QT intervals over RR intervals ranging from 500 ms to 1000 ms. They found a strong linear relationship between QT and RR intervals in all subjects. Interestingly, the autonomic neuropathy group had a significantly steeper slope in the regression line compared to the normal group.

Furthermore, the researchers conducted a follow-up study with 32 male diabetic subjects who had varying degrees of autonomic dysfunction. These subjects had repeat QT measurements taken 3 years later, with a range of 2 to 6 years between recordings. The results showed a significant lengthening of QT and QTC intervals during the second visit, which was not related to age or time between recordings. However, these changes in QT length were correlated with changes in autonomic function.

Additionally, out of 71 male diabetic subjects under 60 years who were followed for 3 years, 13 had died unexpectedly, with 8 of them having autonomic neuropathy. Interestingly, those with autonomic neuropathy who subsequently died had significantly longer QT and QTC intervals compared to those who did not, despite similar ages and duration of diabetes.

In conclusion, this study suggests that the relationship between QT and RR intervals is altered in diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Furthermore, changes in QT length over time seem to parallel changes in autonomic function. There may also be a potential association between QT interval prolongation and the risk of unexpected death in individuals with diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

title: Incidence of cancer after immunosuppressive treatment for heart transplantation.
text: The occurrence of cancer is more common in individuals who undergo prolonged or intense immunosuppressive therapy following organ transplantation. However, there are notable variations in the frequency of cancer between heart and heart-lung transplant recipients compared to renal transplant patients. The most significant disparity is seen in the occurrence of lymphomas, which is higher in cardiac patients than in renal patients. Additionally, cardiac recipients experience a twofold increase in all types of neoplasms, with a nearly sixfold increase in tumors affecting internal organs. Various factors contribute to these discrepancies. Cardiac allograft recipients often require intense immunosuppression to combat acute rejection, and a large number of cardiac transplants were performed during a time when polypharmacy, typically involving triple therapy, was prevalent.

title: Nucleating actin for invasion
text: Metastasis, the primary cause of cancer-related deaths, begins with the invasion of cancer cells into the surrounding tissue. This invasion is a crucial initial step that necessitates the formation of specific structures like invadopodia and pseudopodia. These structures rely on the assembly of actin, which is regulated by specialized actin nucleation factors. Human cells possess a diverse range of actin nucleators, including formins, spire, and Arp2/3-regulating proteins, with the potential for further expansion. By studying the mechanisms of these various actin nucleation factors involved in cancer cell function, we may uncover novel treatments for invasive and metastatic diseases.

title: GFI1 and GFI1B control the loss of endothelial identity of hemogenic endothelium during hematopoietic commitment.
text: New research has shown that hematopoietic progenitors and stem cells are produced from hemogenic endothelium precursors through a process called endothelial to hematopoietic transition (EHT) during embryonic development. The transcription factor RUNX1 is crucial for this process, but its main downstream effects are not well understood. In this study, we have identified Gfi1 and Gfi1b as direct targets of RUNX1 and important regulators of EHT. GFI1 and GFI1B can induce the down-regulation of endothelial markers and the formation of round cells, which is a characteristic change during EHT, even in the absence of RUNX1. On the other hand, blood progenitors in embryos lacking Gfi1 and Gfi1b continue to express endothelial genes. Additionally, these cells are not released from the yolk sac and do not spread to other embryonic tissues. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the GFI1 transcription factors play a critical and specific role in the initial stages of generating hematopoietic progenitors from hemogenic endothelium.

title: An RNA-directed nuclease mediates post-transcriptional gene silencing in Drosophila cells.
text: In a diverse group of organisms, including Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, planaria, hydra, trypanosomes, fungi, and plants, the introduction of double-stranded RNAs can inhibit gene expression in a specific way. This process, known as RNA interference or post-transcriptional gene silencing, has various functions such as providing defense against viruses, regulating gene expression, and modulating transposition. To understand the mechanisms behind this genetic phenomenon, we have taken a biochemical approach. Our research demonstrates that by introducing specific double-stranded RNAs into cultured Drosophila cells, we can create 'loss-of-function' phenotypes. This is accompanied by a significant decrease in the levels of corresponding cellular messenger RNAs. We have also discovered that extracts from transfected cells contain a nuclease activity that specifically degrades external transcripts that are similar to the transfected double-stranded RNA. This nuclease enzyme contains an essential RNA component. After partially purifying the enzyme, we found that the sequence-specific nuclease co-fractionates with a distinct RNA species of approximately 25 nucleotides. This RNA species may contribute to the enzyme's specificity by having homology to the substrate mRNAs.

title: Expression of basal cell keratin 15 and keratin 19 in oral squamous neoplasms represents diverse pathophysiologies.
text: The human epithelium contains keratin, which is expressed during the process of differentiation. Different types of keratin are expressed depending on the specific cell type, and changes in these keratins appear to indicate changes in cell properties. In the oral epithelium, the basal cells express keratin 5 (K5), K14, K15, and K19, but it is unclear how these keratins are altered in tumors. To address this question and explore potential diagnostic applications, we studied the expression of these keratins in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and squamous intraepithelial neoplasm (SIN). We used cDNA microarray analysis to examine 43 OSCC samples and found a slight increase in KRT14 expression, a decrease in KRT15 and KRT19 expression, and no change in KRT5 expression. There were significant variations in KRT15 and KRT19 expression among the different cancers. Well-differentiated OSCC tended to have higher levels of KRT15 and lower levels of KRT19 compared to moderately or poorly differentiated OSCC. KRT15 expression was positively correlated with the expression of the differentiation-related keratin, KRT13. We further investigated these findings using immunohistochemical examination. We found that K5 and K14 were expressed in all 50 OSCC and 50 SIN samples. K15 and K19 were generally downregulated, but were still present in about half of the cases and showed different patterns of expression. Cancers that were positive for K15 tended to have a well-differentiated phenotype, while those positive for K19 tended to have more invasive tumor fronts. Most K19-positive cancers appeared to develop without associated SIN. K19 was consistently downregulated in SIN, while K15 was mainly downregulated in high-grade SIN. In summary, K15 and K19, unlike K5 or K14, are expressed variably in both SIN and OSCC, reflecting differences in their development and behavior. This suggests that they could be used as markers to classify OSCC and SIN.

title: Exosomes in Plasma of Patients with Ovarian Carcinoma: Potential Biomarkers of Tumor Progression and Response to Therapy.
text: This study investigates the relationship between the presence and protein content of exosomes in the plasma of patients with Ovarian Cancer (OvCa) and their disease outcome, response to standard therapy, and resistance to treatments. The study includes patients who were studied at diagnosis and also during and after therapy.
