Exosomes were isolated from the plasma of OvCa patients (n=22), patients with benign tumors (n=10), and healthy controls (n=10) using ultracentrifugation. The exosomes were visualized using scanning electron microscopy, and their protein content was measured. The presence of MAGE 3/6 and TGF-β1 in the exosomes was evaluated using Western blots. The results showed that OvCa patients' plasma had higher levels of exosomal proteins compared to patients with benign tumors or healthy controls. The exosomes isolated from OvCa patients' plasma carried TGF-β1 and MAGE3/6, which distinguished them from patients with benign tumors and healthy controls. The protein levels of exosomes were higher in newly diagnosed patients compared to advanced stages of OvCa. The levels of exosomes varied during and after chemotherapy, and there were correlations between the changes in exosomal protein levels and clinical data, suggesting that the protein content of exosomes could be useful in predicting responses to therapy and prognosis in OvCa patients. In conclusion, analyzing the levels of plasma exosomes provides a new approach to diagnosing and monitoring the response to therapies in OvCa patients.

title: Insecticide impregnated curtains to control domestic transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Venezuela: cluster randomised trial.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the impact of using insecticide-impregnated curtains on the transmission of leishmaniasis. The study design involved a cluster randomised controlled trial, which included a household interview survey, an observational study of people's behaviour, and an entomological study using light traps to capture sandflies inside houses. The study was conducted in 14 urban sectors in Trujillo, Venezuela, with a total of 2913 participants from 569 houses.

The intervention involved pairing sectors based on their 12-month cumulative incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis. One sector in each pair was randomly assigned to receive polyester curtains impregnated with lambdacyhalothrin (intervention group), while the other sector received curtains without insecticide or no curtains (control groups). After 12 months, a follow-up household survey was conducted to assess the outcomes.

The main outcome measures were the reduction in the abundance of sandflies indoors and the 12-month incidence of clinical cases of cutaneous leishmaniasis. The results showed that transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis mainly occurred in the domestic setting, with an incidence of 4% over 12 months. The average number of sandflies captured per trap per night was 16.

After the follow-up period, the 12-month incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis was 0% in the intervention group, compared to 8% in the control group that received unimpregnated curtains (mean difference 8, 95% confidence interval 4.22 to 11.78; P=0.001). Additionally, there were significantly fewer sandflies in the intervention group (2 vs 15, mean difference 13 sandflies per trap; 9 to 17; P<0.001).

In conclusion, the use of insecticide-impregnated curtains provides a high level of protection against indoor transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

title: Chronic pancreatitis is essential for induction of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by K-Ras oncogenes in adult mice.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), one of the most lethal forms of cancer in humans, often involves the activation of K-Ras oncogenes. Our study reveals that when an endogenous K-Ras(G12V) oncogene is selectively expressed in embryonic cells of the acinar/centroacinar lineage, it leads to the development of pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) and invasive PDA. This suggests that PDA may originate from the differentiation of acinar/centroacinar cells or their precursors into ductal-like cells. Interestingly, adult mice become resistant to K-Ras(G12V)-induced PanINs and PDA. However, when these mice are exposed to a mild form of chronic pancreatitis, they exhibit the full range of PanINs and invasive PDA. These findings indicate that, in adulthood, PDA arises from a combination of genetic factors (such as somatic K-Ras mutations) and non-genetic factors (such as tissue damage).

title: Relative roles of direct regeneration versus paracrine effects of human cardiosphere-derived cells transplanted into infarcted mice.
text:
RATIONALE: The efficacy of cardiac cell therapy is influenced by multiple biological mechanisms. The most significant of these mechanisms include the direct regeneration of heart muscle and blood vessels by transplanted cells, as well as the enhancement of tissue preservation and recruitment of the body's own repair mechanisms through paracrine effects.

OBJECTIVE: This study aims to investigate the paracrine effects of cardiac progenitor cells, specifically those cultured as cardiospheres (CSps) or as CSp-derived cells (CDCs), and determine their relative importance compared to the direct differentiation of transplanted cells in cardiac regeneration.

METHODS AND RESULTS: In vitro experiments revealed the presence of numerous growth factors in the media conditioned by human adult CSps and CDCs. CDC-conditioned media demonstrated antiapoptotic effects on neonatal rat ventricular myocytes and proangiogenic effects on human umbilical vein endothelial cells. In vivo experiments using a SCID mouse model of acute myocardial infarction showed that transplanted human CDCs secreted vascular endothelial growth factor, hepatocyte growth factor, and insulin-like growth factor 1, which improved cardiac function and promoted tissue regeneration. Injection of CDCs in the peri-infarct zone resulted in increased expression of Akt, decreased apoptotic rate and caspase 3 level, and increased capillary density, indicating improved tissue resilience. Quantitative analysis revealed that direct differentiation accounted for 20% to 50% of the observed effects, based on the number of human-specific cells relative to the overall increase in capillary density and myocardial viability.

CONCLUSIONS: Transplanted CDCs not only differentiate into cardiac and angiogenic cells but also serve as "role models" by recruiting the body's own regenerative mechanisms and enhancing tissue resistance to ischemic stress. The contribution of the role model effect is comparable to or even greater than that of direct regeneration.

title: The IC(50) of anti-Pfs25 antibody in membrane-feeding assay varies among species.
text: Plasmodium falciparum surface protein 25 (Pfs25) is being considered as a potential component for transmission-blocking vaccines (TBVs). The presence of Anti-Pfs25 antibodies has been found to impede the growth of oocysts in membrane-feeding experiments, and we have observed that the effectiveness of these antibodies is directly related to their concentration. In this investigation, we isolated Pfs25-specific IgGs to quantify antibody concentration in micrograms per milliliter and determined the minimum amount of antibody needed to inhibit 50% of oocyst development (IC(50)). The IC(50) values were found to be 15.9, 4.2, 41.2, and 85.6 microg/mL for mouse, rabbit, monkey, and human, respectively, and the variations between species were statistically significant. The competition patterns of Anti-Pfs25 sera from rabbit, monkey, and human against six mouse monoclonal antibodies differed, and the strength of antibody binding varied among the four species as well. These findings suggest that information obtained from animal studies evaluating the effectiveness of TBV candidates may not easily translate to human immunization.

title: Single-Cell RNA-Seq Reveals Dynamic, Random Monoallelic Gene Expression in Mammalian Cells
text: Analyses of diploid cell populations typically show expression from both alleles, but there is a lack of studies examining allelic expression patterns at the single-cell level. In this study, we conducted global analyses of allelic expression in individual cells of mouse preimplantation embryos with a mixed background (CAST/EiJ × C57BL/6J). Our findings revealed a significant amount (12 to 24%) of monoallelic expression of autosomal genes, with the two alleles being expressed independently. This monoallelic expression appeared to be random and dynamic, as there was considerable variation among closely related embryonic cells. Similar patterns of monoallelic expression were also observed in mature cells. Additionally, our analysis showed that the paternal X chromosome undergoes de novo inactivation. In conclusion, our study suggests that independent and stochastic allelic transcription leads to abundant random monoallelic expression in mammalian cells.

title: Lipopolysaccharide-dependent prostaglandin E(2) production is regulated by the glutathione-dependent prostaglandin E(2) synthase gene induced by the Toll-like receptor 4/MyD88/NF-IL6 pathway.
text: During inflammation, macrophages produce a significant amount of PGE(2). This lipid mediator plays a role in regulating various immune responses. Specifically, PGE(2) acts on macrophages and inhibits the production of cytokines like TNF-alpha and IL-12. The enzyme responsible for synthesizing PGE(2), known as membrane-bound glutathione-dependent PGE(2) synthase (mPGES), has been identified as a terminal enzyme in the cyclooxygenase-2-mediated PGE(2) biosynthesis. In this study, we discovered that mPGES is induced by LPS in macrophages. However, the expression of mPGES was not induced by LPS in mice lacking Toll-like receptor 4 or MyD88. Additionally, mice deficient in NF-IL6 did not show any induction of mPGES or biosynthesis of PGE(2) in response to LPS. This suggests that mPGES expression in response to LPS is regulated by a Toll-like receptor 4/MyD88/NF-IL6-dependent signaling pathway. To further investigate the role of mPGES, we generated mice that lacked this enzyme and studied their response in vivo. Interestingly, these mice did not show an increase in PGE(2) production when exposed to LPS. However, they did not exhibit any impairment in the production of inflammatory cytokines or in their response to LPS-induced shock. Therefore, while mPGES is crucial for the biosynthesis of LPS-induced PGE(2), it is not necessary for modulating inflammatory responses.

title: A microRNA feedback loop regulates global microRNA abundance during aging.
text: The levels of many microRNAs (miRNAs) change as organisms and tissues age, with a global decline observed. However, the reasons behind this change and its biological significance are not well understood. To investigate this, we studied the network of genes that control miRNA production and processing during the aging process in C. elegans. Our findings revealed that genes involved in miRNA production are closely connected to transcription factors and miRNAs associated with aging. Specifically, miR-71, which is known to affect lifespan and is up-regulated during aging, suppresses the expression of alg-1/Argonaute after transcription during the aging process. In mutants lacking mir-71, there was an increase in the abundance of ALG-1, leading to a global increase in miRNA expression. Interestingly, these mutants showed widespread dysregulation of mRNA expression and reduced variability in both gene expression and overall lifespan. Therefore, the gradual decline in molecular function often attributed to accumulated damage throughout an organism's life may be partially explained by a miRNA-directed mechanism of age-related decline.

title: Early lymphocyte expansion is severely impaired in interleukin 7 receptor-deficient mice
text: The high affinity receptor for Interleukin 7 (IL-7), known as IL-7R, plays a crucial role in stimulating the growth of B cell progenitors, thymocytes, and mature T cells. To better understand the impact of IL-7 and its receptor on B and T cell development, we conducted experiments using mice that were genetically deficient in IL-7R. These mutant mice exhibited a significant decrease in the number of cells in the thymus and peripheral lymphoid tissues. By analyzing the different stages of lymphoid progenitor populations in IL-7R-deficient mice, we were able to pinpoint the specific developmental stages affected by the mutation. Our findings highlight the essential role of IL-7R in early lymphoid development. Importantly, our studies demonstrate that the expansion of thymocytes before T cell receptor gene rearrangement is heavily reliant on the high affinity receptor for IL-7.

title: Immune Activation with HIV Vaccines
text: Developing a safe and effective HIV vaccine is the most crucial and difficult objective in HIV-AIDS research. Recent advancements using a poxvirus vector prime and envelope protein boost strategy have shown a moderate yet statistically significant level of effectiveness, proving that a vaccine could potentially prevent HIV infection (1). Efforts are currently underway to enhance the durability and efficacy of this approach (2). However, the outcomes of two vaccine concepts utilizing recombinant adenovirus serotype-5 (rAd5) (3–5) have raised concerns about a potential major issue: these vaccines may actually increase susceptibility to HIV infection. This has also prompted the question of whether this problem extends to other recombinant adenovirus vectors currently being developed or to other vector-based vaccines.

title: Distribution of dystrophin- and utrophin-associated protein complexes during activation of human neutrophils.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the expression and distribution of dystrophins, utrophins, and their associated proteins in neutrophils. Previous research has focused on their roles in nonmuscle tissues, but their presence in neutrophils has not been explored. We used immunoblot and confocal microscopy analysis to examine resting and activated human neutrophils. Immunoprecipitation assays were also conducted to confirm the presence of protein complexes. Our findings revealed two dystrophin-associated protein complexes in both resting and activated neutrophils. The first complex consisted of Dp71d/Dp71Delta(110)(m) and dystrophin-associated proteins (beta-dystroglycan, alpha-syntrophin, alpha-dystrobrevin-1, and -2). The second complex contained Up400 instead of Dp71d/Dp71Delta(110)(m) as a central component. Confocal analysis showed that Dp71d/Dp71Delta(110)(m) and Up400 were redistributed in F-actin-based structures during activation with fMLP. These findings suggest that these protein complexes play a dynamic role in the chemotaxis process.

title: Global and regional burden of hospital admissions for severe acute lower respiratory infections in young children in 2010: a systematic analysis
text:
The global incidence of hospital admissions and in-hospital deaths due to severe acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in young children is not known. Our objective was to estimate the number of admissions and deaths for these infections in children under 5 years old in 2010. 

To achieve this, we analyzed data from a systematic review of studies published between January 1, 1990, and March 31, 2012, as well as data from 28 unpublished population-based studies. We calculated the incidence of severe and very severe ALRI admissions in children under 5, categorized by age and region. Using population estimates for 2010, we determined the global and regional burden of severe ALRI admissions in children for that year. 

We also estimated in-hospital mortality rates for severe and very severe ALRI by combining incidence estimates with case fatality ratios from hospital-based studies. 

Our findings indicate that in 2010, there were approximately 11.9 million (95% CI 10.3-13.9 million) cases of severe ALRI resulting in hospital admissions in young children worldwide, as well as 3.0 million (2.1-4.2 million) cases of very severe ALRI. Incidence rates were higher in boys compared to girls, with the greatest disparity observed in South Asian studies. 

Based on data from 37 hospital studies reporting case fatality ratios for severe ALRI, we estimated that around 265,000 (95% CI 160,000-450,000) in-hospital deaths occurred in young children, with 99% of these deaths occurring in developing countries. Interestingly, our data suggests that while 62% of children with severe ALRI receive treatment in hospitals, 81% of deaths occur outside of hospitals. 

In conclusion, severe ALRI poses a significant burden on global health services and is a major cause of hospital referrals and admissions in young children. Improving access to hospitals and reducing disparities, such as those related to gender and rural status, could significantly reduce mortality rates associated with these infections. Implementing community-based management strategies for severe ALRI could also be an important approach to reducing pneumonia mortality and health inequities. 

This study was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO).

title: Identification of a novel p53 functional domain that is necessary for mediating apoptosis.
text: The ability of p53 to trigger apoptosis relies on its ability to bind to specific DNA sequences. However, even when the transactivation ability of p53(Gln22-Ser23) is impaired, it can still induce apoptosis. Previous research has shown that the region between residues 23 and 97 in p53 is crucial for this activity. To pinpoint the exact domain within the N terminus that is necessary for apoptosis, we discovered that removing the first 23 amino acids compromises p53's ability to induce apoptosis, but does not eliminate it entirely. Surprisingly, p53(Delta1-42), which lacks the first 42 amino acids and the previously identified activation domain, actually induces apoptosis at an even higher level than the normal p53. However, when the deletion is extended to eliminate the first 63 amino acids, p53 becomes completely inactive in mediating apoptosis. Additionally, we found that both p53(Delta1-42) and p53(Gln22-Ser23) can activate a subset of cellular p53 targets. Furthermore, we demonstrated that residues 53 and 54 are crucial for the apoptotic and transcriptional activities of both p53(Delta1-42) and p53(Gln22-Ser23). Based on these findings, we propose that an apoptotic domain, as well as another transcriptional activation domain, exist within residues 43-63. Therefore, we hypothesize that the apoptotic activity in p53(Gln22-Ser23) and p53(Delta1-42) still relies on transcription.

title: Risk of breast cancer in relation to blood lipids: a prospective study of 31,209 Norwegian women
text: This prospective study aimed to investigate the relationship between blood lipids and the risk of breast cancer. The study included 31,209 Norwegian women aged 20 to 54 who participated in a health screening conducted by the Norwegian National Health Screening Services between 1977 and 1983. The screening involved a questionnaire, measurements of body size, and nonfasting blood samples to analyze total serum cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), and high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. Low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol was calculated using Friedewald's formula. Over a period of seven to 13 years, 302 cases of breast cancer were identified through linkage with the Norwegian Cancer Registry. After adjusting for known risk factors of breast cancer, the relative risk of women in the highest quartile of TC compared to those in the lowest quartile was 0.87 (95% confidence interval [CI]=0.61–1.23). Similarly, the relative risks and CIs for TG, HDL, and LDL were 0.82 (CI=0.58–1.16), 1.02 (CI=0.73–1.42), and 0.93 (CI=0.67–1.29) respectively. No significant association between blood lipids and breast cancer risk was observed in the overall population or when the data was analyzed separately for women diagnosed before or after the age of 50, which serves as a dividing line between pre- and postmenopausal diagnosis.

title: Involvement of lysosomal dysfunction in autophagosome accumulation and early pathologies in adipose tissue of obese mice
text: The debate surrounding whether obesity accelerates or suppresses autophagy in adipose tissue remains unresolved. In order to gain a better understanding of the dysregulation of autophagy and its role in the pathologies of obese adipose tissue, our study focused on examining lysosomal function, protease maturation, and activity both in vivo and in vitro. Our findings revealed that autophagosome formation was accelerated, but autophagic clearance was impaired in obese adipose tissue. Additionally, we observed that the protein and activity levels of CTSL (cathepsin L) were suppressed, while the activity of CTSB (cathepsin B) was significantly enhanced in obese adipose tissue. Furthermore, we observed the activation of cellular senescence and inflammasomes in obese adipose tissue. In our experiments with 3T3L1 adipocytes, we found that downregulation of CTSL worsened autophagic clearance, increased expression of CTSB, promoted cellular senescence, and activated inflammasomes. Conversely, upregulation of CTSB further activated the inflammasomes. Therefore, our study suggests that the observed lysosomal dysfunction in obese adipose tissue leads to reduced autophagic clearance, resulting in the accumulation of autophagosomes. Additionally, the lysosomal abnormalities, including impaired CTSL function and compensatory activation of CTSB, contribute to cellular senescence and inflammasome activation. These findings strongly support the involvement of lysosomal dysfunction in the early pathologies of obese adipose tissue.

title: ARNO regulates VEGF-dependent tissue responses by stabilizing endothelial VEGFR-2 surface expression.
text:
The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is responsible for stimulating angiogenesis, which involves the permeability, proliferation, and migration of endothelial cells. This process is crucial in ischaemic diseases. The ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF) nucleotide-binding site opener (ARNO), also known as cytohesin-2, is a guanine exchange factor that plays a significant role in cellular signalling through ARF GTPases. However, the involvement of ARNO in VEGF-dependent endothelial processes has not been documented. Therefore, our study aimed to investigate the role of ARNO in the activation of endothelial cells and vessel permeability in response to VEGF.

To assess ARNO expression, we conducted various experiments both in vitro and ex vivo. We used RT-PCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence to observe ARNO expression in endothelial cells in vitro. Additionally, we performed immunohistochemical staining of mouse aorta to confirm ARNO expression ex vivo. Inhibition of cytohesin using the inhibitor SecinH3 or ARNO siRNA prevented VEGF-induced Akt activation and endothelial cell proliferation in vitro. We measured endothelial cell proliferation using methylthiazoletetrazolium (MTT) reduction. Furthermore, suppression of ARNO reduced VEGF-induced vessel permeability in the mouse cremaster muscle in vivo. We measured vessel permeability by assessing the extravasation of fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-dextran. Additionally, ARNO knock-down accelerated the reduction of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR-2) surface expression, internalization, and degradation in response to ligand stimulation. We assessed these changes using flow cytometry and western blotting.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that ARNO plays a crucial and previously unknown role in VEGF-dependent angiogenesis. It regulates VEGFR-2 internalization in endothelial cells, leading to the activation of the Akt pathway, vessel permeability, and ultimately endothelial proliferation. Therefore, ARNO may be an essential component of endothelial signalling and angiogenesis.

title: Effects of Hypoxia and Oxidative Stress on Expression of Neprilysin in Human Neuroblastoma Cells and Rat Cortical Neurones and Astrocytes
text: Recent research has linked the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD) to vascular disorders like ischemia and stroke. AD is characterized by the buildup of β-amyloid peptide (Aβ) deposits in the brain. Aβ is produced in the brain from amyloid precursor protein (APP) through the action of β- and γ-secretases. Certain forms of Aβ are harmful to neurons. The brain has a natural mechanism for removing Aβ through proteolytic degradation, with the zinc metalloproteinase neprilysin (NEP) playing a crucial role in regulating Aβ levels. Decreased NEP activity may increase the risk of developing AD. Our study compared the effects of hypoxia and oxidative stress on NEP expression and activity in human neuroblastoma NB7 cells and rat primary cortical neurons. We found that hypoxia reduced NEP expression at both the protein and mRNA levels, as well as its activity. However, in astrocytes, hypoxia actually increased NEP mRNA expression.

title: Genetics and Beyond – The Transcriptome of Human Monocytes and Disease Susceptibility
text:
The variability of gene expression in humans may connect variations in gene sequences and phenotypes. However, non-genetic variations, either alone or in combination with genetics, can also impact expression traits and play a crucial role in physiological and disease processes.

To gain a better understanding of the overall variability of gene expression, we examined the transcriptome of circulating monocytes in 1,490 unrelated individuals. Monocytes are a key cell involved in immunity-related diseases and atherosclerosis. We also investigated the association between gene expression and over 675,000 SNPs and 10 common cardiovascular risk factors.

Out of the 12,808 expressed genes, we detected 2,745 expression quantitative trait loci (P<5.78x10(-12)), with the majority (90%) being cis-modulated. Extensive analysis revealed that the associations identified by genome-wide association studies of lipids, body mass index, or blood pressure were rarely influenced by monocyte expression levels at the locus.

At a study-wide level (P<3.9x10(-7)), we found that 1,662 expression traits (13.0%) were significantly associated with at least one risk factor. Genome-wide interaction analyses indicated that genetic variability and risk factors mostly had an additive effect on gene expression. Due to the correlation structure among expression traits, the variability of risk factors could be characterized by a limited set of independent gene expressions, which may have biological and clinical significance. For instance, expression traits associated with cigarette smoking were more strongly linked to carotid atherosclerosis than smoking itself.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the monocyte transcriptome serves as a powerful integrator of genetic and non-genetic influences that are relevant for disease pathophysiology and risk assessment.

title: Molecular mechanisms of (-)-epicatechin and chlorogenic acid on the regulation of the apoptotic and survival/proliferation pathways in a human hepatoma cell line.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of (-)-epicatechin (EC) and chlorogenic acid (CGA) on the regulation of cell death and cell survival/proliferation pathways in a human liver cancer cell line (HepG2). Previous research has suggested that dietary polyphenols may reduce the risk of chronic diseases, but the specific molecular mechanisms of this protection are not well understood. 

After treating the cells with EC or CGA for 18 hours, it was found that there was a slight decrease in cell viability and a reduction in the formation of reactive oxygen species. EC alone promoted cell proliferation, while CGA increased the levels of glutathione, an antioxidant. However, neither EC nor CGA induced the caspase cascade, a process involved in cell death, and there was no effect on the expression levels of Bcl-xL or Bax, proteins involved in regulating cell survival and death.

Interestingly, EC treatment resulted in a sustained activation of the major survival signals AKT/PI-3-kinase and ERK, while CGA did not have the same effect. This suggests that EC and CGA do not directly impact cell death, but instead enhance the cell's ability to tolerate oxidative stress by activating survival/proliferation pathways or increasing antioxidant potential in HepG2 cells.

title: Wnt5a mediates nerve growth factor-dependent axonal branching and growth in developing sympathetic neurons.
text:
The role of nerve growth factor (NGF) in promoting survival and growth of neurons in the peripheral nervous system has been extensively studied. However, the specific mechanisms by which NGF influences axonal growth and target innervation are still being understood. In this study, we have identified Wnt5a, a member of the Wnt family of growth factors, as a crucial mediator of axonal branching and growth in developing sympathetic neurons, downstream of NGF.

We observed that Wnt5a is highly expressed in sympathetic neurons when their axons are innervating targets that produce NGF. The signaling between NGF and its receptor TrkA enhances the expression of Wnt5a in neurons. Wnt5a has a rapid effect on inducing axon branching, while it also has a long-term impact on promoting axon extension.

To further investigate the role of Wnt5a, we conducted experiments where Wnt5a function was disrupted. We found that Wnt5a is necessary for NGF-dependent axonal branching and growth, but not for neuronal survival, in laboratory settings. Additionally, mice lacking Wnt5a showed reduced innervation of tissues that produce NGF, leading to increased neuronal apoptosis in living organisms.

In developing sympathetic neurons, Wnt5a functions by activating protein kinase C locally in axons. This discovery establishes a new regulatory pathway in which Wnt5a, expressed in response to NGF from target tissues, controls the innervation of peripheral targets by sympathetic neurons.

title: The Snf1 kinase controls glucose repression in yeast by modulating interactions between the Mig1 repressor and the Cyc8-Tup1 co-repressor.
text: Glucose repression, a widely observed mechanism in lower eukaryotes, regulates carbon catabolism. The pathway involves key components such as the Snf1 kinase, the Mig1 DNA-binding repressor, and the Mig1-interacting co-repressor complex Cyc8(Ssn6)-Tup1. Previous studies suggested that the translocation of Mig1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, triggered by its phosphorylation by Snf1, is the crucial step in releasing glucose repression. However, our report re-evaluates this model and presents new findings. We confirm the coordinated repressive action of Mig1 and Cyc8-Tup1 on GAL1 transcription, but we discover that Cyc8-Tup1 is not bound to the promoter DNA by Mig1. Our experiments demonstrate that both negative regulators continuously occupy GAL1, regardless of repression or activation conditions, although most of the Mig1 redistributes to the cytoplasm upon activation. We also show that Snf1-dependent phosphorylation of Mig1 disrupts its interaction with Cyc8-Tup1. Based on these findings, we propose that the regulation of this interaction, rather than the cytoplasmic localization of Mig1, serves as the molecular switch controlling transcriptional repression and de-repression.

title: ARID1A mutations in endometriosis-associated ovarian carcinomas.
text:
BACKGROUND: The molecular events involved in the transformation of ovarian clear-cell and endometrioid carcinomas from endometriosis have not been described. 

METHODS: We conducted whole transcriptome sequencing on 18 ovarian clear-cell carcinomas and 1 ovarian clear-cell carcinoma cell line. Somatic mutations in the ARID1A gene were found in 6 of the samples. ARID1A encodes BAF250a, a key component of the SWI-SNF chromatin remodeling complex. We further sequenced ARID1A in an additional 210 ovarian carcinomas and a second ovarian clear-cell carcinoma cell line. BAF250a expression was measured through immunohistochemical analysis in an additional 455 ovarian carcinomas. 

RESULTS: ARID1A mutations were observed in 55 out of 119 ovarian clear-cell carcinomas (46%), 10 out of 33 endometrioid carcinomas (30%), and none of the 76 high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas. Seventeen carcinomas had two somatic mutations each. Loss of BAF250a protein strongly correlated with ovarian clear-cell carcinoma and endometrioid carcinoma subtypes, as well as the presence of ARID1A mutations. In two patients, ARID1A mutations and loss of BAF250a expression were present in the tumor and contiguous atypical endometriosis, but not in distant endometriotic lesions. 

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that ARID1A is a frequently disrupted tumor-suppressor gene in ovarian clear-cell and endometrioid carcinomas. The presence of ARID1A mutation and loss of BAF250a in preneoplastic lesions suggests that this is an early event in the transformation of endometriosis into cancer. (Funded by the British Columbia Cancer Foundation and the Vancouver General Hospital-University of British Columbia Hospital Foundation.)

title: The ALS-associated proteins FUS and TDP-43 function together to affect Drosophila locomotion and life span.
text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a fatal motor neuron disease in adults, shares similarities with frontotemporal dementia (FTD), an early-onset neurodegenerative disorder. Recent studies have linked the RNA/DNA-binding proteins fused in sarcoma (FUS; also known as TLS) and TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) to familial forms of ALS and FTD. However, it remains unclear whether the disruption of these proteins leads to disease independently of their normal function or through the disturbance of critical molecular processes. In this study, we investigated the effects of disrupting the homolog of FUS in Drosophila and found that it resulted in decreased adult viability, reduced locomotor speed, and shortened lifespan compared to control flies. These phenotypes were fully restored when wild-type human FUS was introduced, but not when ALS-associated mutant FUS proteins were used. Similarly, a mutant of the Drosophila homolog of TDP-43 exhibited similar, but more severe deficits. Through further analysis, we discovered that FUS and TDP-43 acted together in a common genetic pathway in neurons, with FUS functioning downstream of TDP-43. Additionally, we observed that these proteins formed an RNA-dependent complex. Our findings demonstrate that FUS and TDP-43 work together in vivo and suggest that disruptions in molecular pathways requiring the combined activities of these proteins may contribute to the development of ALS and FTD.

title: Non-canonical PI3K-Cdc42-Pak-Mek-Erk Signaling Promotes Immune-Complex-Induced Apoptosis in Human Neutrophils
text: Neutrophils are a type of white blood cell found in the bloodstream that play a crucial role in defending against bacterial and fungal infections. They are also involved in triggering the inflammatory response. Various receptors on the surface of neutrophils regulate important cellular processes by activating specific enzymes called PI3Ks. Our research reveals a previously unknown, PI3K-dependent, non-traditional pathway that leads to programmed cell death (apoptosis) in human neutrophils when they are activated by insoluble immune complexes. This pathway involves the activation of FcγR-PI3Kβ/δ-Cdc42-Pak-Mek-Erk, which is distinct from the typical Ras/Raf-dependent activation of Erk and the PI3K-mediated activation of Cdc42. Furthermore, comparing the signaling pathways triggered by immune complexes and another stimulus called fMLF reveals significant differences between human and mouse neutrophils. The non-traditional pathway we have discovered in this study may have implications for resolving inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases that rely on immune complex-induced activation of neutrophils.

title: Inflammation-induced tumorigenesis in the colon is regulated by caspase-1 and NLRC4.
text: The exact mechanism behind the association between chronic inflammation and tumorigenesis is currently unknown. However, recent studies have shown that the inflammasome, a complex formed by certain proteins in the NOD-like receptor (NLR) family, plays a role in coordinating immune responses. Despite this, little research has been done on its potential involvement in inflammation-induced cancer. In this study, we used a colorectal cancer model to investigate the role of caspase-1, a protein involved in the inflammasome, in tumor formation. Surprisingly, we found that mice lacking caspase-1 had an increased risk of developing tumors. Interestingly, this was not due to the regulation of colonic inflammation, but rather to the regulation of cell proliferation and apoptosis in the colon. Specifically, caspase-1-deficient mice showed increased cell proliferation in the early stages of tumor formation and reduced apoptosis in advanced tumors. Based on these findings, we propose a model in which the NLRC4 inflammasome plays a central role in inflammation-induced tumor formation by regulating the response of epithelial cells to injury.

title: The nuclear receptors SF1 and LRH1 are expressed in endometrial cancer cells and regulate steroidogenic gene transcription by cooperating with AP-1 factors.
text: The primary risk factor for endometrial cancer is excessive exposure to estradiol. The abnormally high levels of estradiol in the endometrium of women with endometrial cancer are likely caused by the tumor itself, which overproduces the hormone. The genes responsible for synthesizing estradiol are expressed in endometrial cancer cells. Our study utilized RT-PCR and Western blot techniques to demonstrate that the nuclear receptors SF1 and LRH1, which are well-known regulators of steroidogenic gene expression in gonadal and adrenal cells, are also present in endometrial cancer cell lines. Through transient transfections, we discovered that SF1 and LRH1, but not the related nuclear receptor NUR77, can activate the promoters of three human steroidogenic genes: STAR, HSD3B2, and CYP19A1 PII. Similarly, forskolin, but not PMA, was able to activate all three promoters. Furthermore, we observed that both SF1 and LRH1 can work together with the AP-1 family members c-JUN and c-FOS, which are known to enhance the proliferation of endometrial carcinoma cells, to further enhance the activation of the STAR, HSD3B2, and CYP19A1 PII promoters. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of steroidogenic gene expression in endometrial cancer cells and the regulation of estradiol production by tumor cells.

title: Dietary factors in chronic inflammation: food tolerances and intolerances of a New Zealand Caucasian Crohn's disease population.
text: The role of diet in the symptoms of Crohn's disease (CD), an inflammatory bowel disease, is well-known. While there is no one-size-fits-all diet for all individuals with CD, most patients are aware of foods that have either negative or positive effects on their symptoms. This study aims to categorize foods based on their impact on CD symptoms in a New Zealand Caucasian population. A total of 446 subjects from two different centers in New Zealand participated in the study. They completed a comprehensive dietary questionnaire that included 257 food items grouped into 15 categories, reporting their dietary tolerances and intolerances. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in responses to foods within each food group. A two-dimensional graphical summary was used to classify foods as either beneficial or detrimental based on the probability of their effects. A few foods were consistently considered beneficial, such as white fish, salmon, tuna, gluten-free products, oatmeal, bananas, boiled potatoes, sweet potatoes (kumara), pumpkin, soya milk, goat's milk, and yogurt. On the other hand, foods typically considered detrimental included grapefruit, chili or chili sauce, corn and corn products, peanuts, cream, salami, curried foods, cola drinks, high energy drinks, beer, and red wine. Interestingly, some foods were beneficial for one group of subjects but detrimental for others, such as soya milk, goat's milk, yogurt, oatmeal, kiwifruit, prunes, apple, broccoli, cauliflower, linseed, pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, ginger and ginger products, beef, lamb, liver, and oily fish. It was not possible to identify a specific group of foods that should be avoided by all CD patients. The wide range of detrimental items suggests that maintaining remission through diet is likely to be challenging and may require excluding a significant number of foods. Personalized diets may be particularly important for individuals with CD.

title: Age as a risk factor for thrombocytopenia and anaemia in children treated for acute uncomplicated falciparum malaria.
text:
BACKGROUND & OBJECTIVES
The occurrence of anaemia in children with malaria is well-known, but there is inconsistency in reports regarding abnormalities in leucocyte and platelet counts associated with malaria. This study aimed to investigate the impact of age, gender, parasite density, and temperature on haematological parameters in children with acute uncomplicated malaria.

METHODS
Haematological parameters were assessed in children with acute uncomplicated malaria and their correlation with age, sex, temperature, and parasite density was examined. Statistical analysis was conducted using SAS 9.1.

RESULTS
A total of 695 children with acute uncomplicated malaria participated in the study. The average age was 51.7 months +/- 33.8. At the time of presentation, 43.8% of the patients had anaemia, and children under the age of five had significantly lower haematocrit levels (28.4% +/- 4.8) compared to older children (32.8% +/- 4.8) (p <0.001). However, there was no significant difference in haematocrit levels on days 14 and 28. There was no difference observed between males and females. Leucocytosis was more prevalent than leucopenia (9.5% vs 3%). Thrombocytopenia was found in 59.3% of the enrolled patients, and more than half of those with thrombocytopenia had recovered by Day 28. Baseline platelet count was correlated with Day 14 (r = 0.6, p < 0.0001) and Day 28 (r = 0.2, p = 0.0015), as well as haematocrit on Day 28 (r = 0.12, p = 0.00197). Platelet count did not show any correlation with temperature, parasite density, or leucocyte count. Haematocrit levels were correlated with age (r = 0.4, p < 0.0001), but not with parasite density or temperature. Leucocyte count did not show any correlation with age or parasite density.

CONCLUSION
Thrombocytopenia was the most common haematological finding and may be diagnostically significant. However, anaemia and leucocytosis were more prevalent in children under the age of five.

title: Discovery of endogenous catecholamines in lymphocytes and evidence for catecholamine regulation of lymphocyte function via an autocrine loop.
text: New evidence has been gathered indicating that catecholamines and their byproducts can be found in individual lymphocytes and extracts of T- and B-cell clones using capillary electrophoresis with electrochemical detection. When tyrosine hydroxylase is pharmacologically inhibited, the observed levels of catecholamines decrease, suggesting that lymphocytes are capable of synthesizing these substances. Additionally, it has been observed that intracellular dopamine levels increase when exposed to extracellular dopamine, indicating a mechanism of cellular uptake. Moreover, when lymphocytes are incubated with either dopamine or L-dihydroxyphenylalanine, a dopamine precursor, there is a dose-dependent inhibition of lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation. These findings collectively suggest the existence of an autocrine loop in which lymphocytes regulate their own activity.

title: Structure-based drug design identifies polythiophenes as antiprion compounds
text: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, caused by prions, currently have no treatment available. Prions are made up of a misfolded and clumped form of the cellular prion protein (PrPC). In our study, we investigated the ability of luminescent conjugated polythiophenes (LCPs) to counteract prions by binding to and stabilizing protein aggregates. Through the use of osmotic minipumps, we administered a variety of structurally diverse LCPs to the brains of prion-infected mice. Our findings revealed that effective antiprion activity required LCPs with at least five thiophene rings that had regularly spaced carboxyl side groups. By conducting solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance analyses and molecular dynamics simulations, we discovered that the anionic side chains of the LCPs interacted with the cationic amyloid residues of model prions in a complementary and regularly spaced manner. This allowed us to establish structural guidelines for the interaction between LCPs and protein aggregates, which we utilized to design a new set of LCPs with enhanced binding capabilities. The new LCPs demonstrated strong preventive and therapeutic effects in prion-infected mice, with the lead compound extending survival by over 80% and exhibiting efficacy against both mouse and hamster prions. Furthermore, the LCPs proved effective when administered intraperitoneally in mice. These results highlight the potential of targeted chemical design to develop compounds that could be valuable in the treatment of diseases characterized by abnormal protein aggregation, such as prion disease.

title: Comparisons of patient and physician expectations for cancer survivorship care.
text:
The purpose of this study was to compare the expectations for cancer survivorship care between patients and their physicians, as well as between primary care providers (PCPs) and oncologists. The researchers surveyed survivors and their physicians to evaluate their expectations regarding physician involvement in primary cancer follow-up, screening for other cancers, general preventive health, and management of comorbidities. 

Out of the 992 eligible survivors and 607 physicians surveyed, 535 survivors (54%) and 378 physicians (62%) were included in the analysis. Among the physician respondents, 255 (67%) were PCPs and 123 (33%) were oncologists. 

The results showed that there were significant discrepancies in expectations between patients and their oncologists, particularly when it came to screening for cancers other than the index one. Only 29% of patients and oncologists had agreement on this aspect, with patients expecting more involvement from their oncologists. 

Similarly, expectations between patients and their PCPs were most incongruent when it came to primary cancer follow-up, with only a 35% agreement rate. PCPs believed they should have a greater role in this aspect of care. Overall, expectations between patients and their PCPs were more aligned compared to expectations between patients and their oncologists. 

There were also high discordances between PCPs and oncologists in their perceptions of their own roles for primary cancer follow-up, cancer screening, and general preventive health. Agreement rates for these aspects were 3%, 44%, and 51% respectively. Both PCPs and oncologists believed they should have substantial responsibility for primary cancer follow-up. 

In conclusion, this study highlights the discordant expectations between patients and physicians regarding the roles of PCPs and oncologists in cancer survivorship care. These uncertainties can lead to deficiencies in care, emphasizing the importance of incorporating survivorship care planning as a standard component in cancer management.

title: MHC class I antigen presentation: learning from viral evasion strategies
text: The presentation of peptides by MHC class I molecules on the surface of cells to lymphocytes is a crucial defense mechanism for the host against invading pathogens. Nevertheless, viruses have developed sophisticated tactics to hinder different steps of the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway and hinder the display of viral peptides. This article emphasizes the significance of uncovering the mechanisms behind viral immune evasion in order to enhance our comprehension of interactions between viruses and hosts. Additionally, it can contribute to our understanding of the MHC class I presentation pathway and other cellular pathways.

title: T cell receptor-proximal signals are sustained in peripheral microclusters and terminated in the central supramolecular activation cluster.
text: The initiation and continuation of T cell receptor (TCR) signaling occurs in microclusters. However, it is unclear whether signaling also takes place in the central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC), which is rich in TCR. Our research demonstrates that the cSMAC, formed by the merging of microclusters, contains a higher concentration of CD45 compared to microclusters. Additionally, it is enriched with lysobisphosphatidic acid, a lipid involved in the sorting of ubiquitinated membrane proteins for degradation. The blockade of calcium signaling through TCR was observed within 2 minutes when treated with anti-MHCp, and within 1 minute when treated with latrunculin-A. Interestingly, TCR-MHCp interactions within the cSMAC remained intact despite these disruptions for a duration of 10 minutes, indicating that they were insufficient to sustain signaling. Furthermore, the microclusters of TCR were resistant to disruption caused by anti-MHCp and latrunculin-A treatments. Based on our findings, we propose that TCR signaling is maintained by stabilized microclusters and terminated within the cSMAC, where TCR molecules are sorted for degradation. This study also highlights the involvement of F-actin in TCR signaling, extending beyond its role in microcluster formation.

title: The role of red cell distribution width in the prognosis of patients with gastric cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND
Previous studies have shown that the red cell distribution width (RDW) can be used as a reliable predictor of prognosis in various types of cancer. However, the prognostic value of RDW in gastric carcinoma has not yet been investigated.

OBJECTIVE
The aim of this study was to examine the role of red cell distribution width (RDW) in predicting prognosis in patients with gastric cancer.

METHODS
We evaluated a total of 172 gastric cancer patients who underwent curative surgery over a five-year period. The patients' demographics, preoperative RDW levels, tumor characteristics (early stage: I and II, advanced stage: IIIA-B-C), disease-free survival (DFS), and overall survival (OS) were retrospectively reviewed. The patients were divided into two groups based on their RDW levels: high RDW group (RDW ≥ 16, n= 62) and low RDW group (RDW < 16, n= 110).

RESULTS
The overall mortality rate was 55%, and the postoperative 60-day mortality rate was 14% in both groups. We observed a borderline significant association between RDW and mortality (p= 0.063). Patients with short-term mortality had significantly higher preoperative RDW levels compared to those without short-term mortality (17.9 ± 4.3 vs. 16 ± 3.2, p= 0.015). In the high RDW group, there was a significantly higher incidence of advanced gastric cancer (75% vs. 51%, p= 0.002), as well as lower DFS (p= 0.035) and OS (p= 0.04).

CONCLUSION
Patients with high RDW values had a higher frequency of advanced gastric cancer. High RDW values were strongly associated with short-term mortality, although only a borderline relationship with overall survival was observed.

title: Vascular responsiveness in isolated perfused kidneys of diabetic hypertensive rats.
text: The objective of this study was to examine the combined effects of diabetes and hypertension on the responses to vasoconstrictor and vasodilator agents in isolated perfused kidneys from diabetic Wistar-Kyoto (WKY) rats and diabetic spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR). The rats were administered streptozotocin (STZ) to induce diabetes and the kidneys were isolated and perfused with a salt solution. The results showed that both diabetes and hypertension led to an increase in kidney weight. The responses to vasoconstrictor agents were similar in diabetic WKY rats and normoglycemic WKY rats, while the responses were enhanced in kidneys from SHR compared to their normotensive controls. However, the presence of diabetes impaired this enhancement. The vasodilator responses were not affected by either hypertension or diabetes. In conclusion, the study found that diabetes did not influence vasoconstriction, but impaired the enhanced vascular reactivity seen in hypertension. Vasodilation was not affected by either condition.

title: DNA replication is required To elicit cellular responses to psoralen-induced DNA interstrand cross-links.
text: After the introduction of DNA interstrand cross-links (ICLs), mammalian cells exhibit either chromosome breakage or a delay in the cell cycle, resulting in a 4N DNA content. To gain a deeper understanding of this delay, previously referred to as a G(2)/M arrest, we developed a protocol to create ICLs at specific stages of the cell cycle. We treated synchronized populations of G(1), S, and G(2) cells with photoactivated 4'-hydroxymethyl-4,5',8-trimethylpsoralen (HMT) and observed their progression into mitosis. Unlike the findings with ionizing radiation, the introduction of ICLs during G(2) did not lead to a G(2)/M arrest, mitotic arrest, or chromosome breakage. Instead, it was necessary for the cells to pass through S phase in order to trigger both chromosome breakage and arrest in the subsequent cell cycle. Similarly, ICLs introduced during G(1) did not cause a G(1)/S arrest. We conclude that DNA replication is essential for the cellular responses of cell cycle arrest and genomic instability following psoralen-induced ICLs. In primary human fibroblasts, the 4N DNA content cell cycle arrest induced by ICLs was long-lasting but reversible. Kinetic analysis indicated that these cells could eliminate approximately 2,500 ICLs/genome at an average rate of 11 ICLs/genome/h.

title: DNA methylation and healthy human aging
text: The aging process leads to various changes at the cellular and molecular levels, including senescence, telomere shortening, and alterations in gene expression. Epigenetic patterns also undergo changes over time, suggesting that they play a significant role in aging. One of the most extensively studied epigenetic marks is DNA methylation, which involves the presence of methyl groups at specific locations in the DNA sequence called CpG dinucleotides. These dinucleotides are often found near gene promoters and are associated with gene expression levels. Initial studies indicated that global DNA methylation levels increase during the first few years of life and then decrease in late adulthood. However, recent advancements in technology have revealed that DNA methylation variability increases with age, and specific patterns at certain sites have been identified. Moreover, certain CpG sites are strongly linked to age, to the extent that a small number of these sites can accurately predict a person's chronological age. These findings suggest the existence of two phenomena contributing to age-related DNA methylation changes: epigenetic drift and the epigenetic clock. This review focuses on the process of healthy human aging throughout life, discussing the dynamics of DNA methylation and how interactions between the genome, environment, and epigenome influence the rate of aging. Additionally, the impact of determining "epigenetic age" on human health is explored, along with important considerations for current and future studies.

title: Parathyroid hormone-induced E4BP4/NFIL3 down-regulates transcription in osteoblasts.
text: The parathyroid hormone (PTH) is a key regulator of bone metabolism. It activates the PTHR1 receptor on the osteoblast plasma membrane, triggering signaling and the transcription of primary response genes. These primary genes then regulate the expression of downstream PTH targets. In our research, we have discovered that the adenovirus E4 promoter-binding protein/nuclear factor regulated by IL-3 (E4bp4) is one of these primary genes induced by PTH in osteoblasts. E4BP4 is a transcription factor known as a basic leucine zipper (bZIP) that can either repress or activate transcription in cells other than osteoblasts. Our findings show that PTH rapidly and temporarily increases the production of E4bp4 mRNA in osteoblastic cells, and this increase does not require protein synthesis. PTH also stimulates the synthesis of E4BP4 protein and its binding to a specific response element (EBPRE), but not to a mutated version of this element. When E4BP4 is overexpressed, it inhibits the activity of a promoter-reporter construct containing the EBPRE. Additionally, PTH treatment reduces the activity of the same construct in primary mouse osteoblasts. Finally, E4BP4 overexpression also inhibits PTH-induced activity of a promoter-reporter construct for cyclooxygenase-2. Based on our data, we propose that E4BP4 plays a role in attenuating the transcription of PTH target genes in osteoblasts.

title: Molecular basis of synaptic vesicle cargo recognition by the endocytic sorting adaptor stonin 2
text: The recycling of synaptic vesicles (SVs) in synaptic transmission relies on clathrin-mediated processes. However, the specific targeting of certain SV proteins for internalization has remained unclear. Stonins are adaptors that have been conserved throughout evolution and are responsible for the sorting of the SV protein synaptotagmin during endocytosis. Our research has identified the key factors involved in the recognition of synaptotagmin by stonin 2 or its equivalent in Caenorhabditis elegans, UNC-41B. This interaction occurs through the direct association of clusters of basic residues on the cytoplasmic domain of synaptotagmin 1 and a beta strand within the mu-homology domain of stonin 2. When specific mutations (K783, Y784, and E785) are made to alanine within this beta strand of stonin 2, the mutant stonin protein fails to associate with synaptotagmin, accumulate at synapses, and facilitate synaptotagmin internalization. Similarly, when UNC-41B, which is unable to bind to synaptotagmin, is introduced into stonin mutant animals in C. elegans, it is unable to rescue paralysis. These findings suggest that the mechanism of stonin-mediated recognition of SV cargo is conserved from worms to mammals.

title: Size separation of circulatory DNA in maternal plasma permits ready detection of fetal DNA polymorphisms.
text:
BACKGROUND Recently, a new method for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis called analysis of fetal DNA in maternal plasma has been introduced. This method is particularly useful for analyzing fetal genetic traits that are not present in the maternal genome, such as RHD or Y-chromosome-specific sequences. However, analyzing other fetal genetic traits has been challenging due to the abundance of maternal DNA sequences in the circulation. In this study, we aimed to determine if there are differences in the biochemical properties of fetal and maternal circulatory DNA.

METHODS We examined plasma DNA using agarose gel electrophoresis. We then used real-time PCR to measure the fractions of fetal and maternal DNA in size-fractionated fragments. To determine paternally and maternally inherited fetal genetic traits, we used highly polymorphic chromosome-21-specific microsatellite markers.

RESULTS Our analysis of circulatory DNA showed that the majority of cell-free fetal DNA had a molecular size of less than 0.3 kb, while maternally derived sequences were generally larger than 1 kb. By analyzing size-fractionated DNA (less than or equal to 0.3 kb) from maternal plasma samples, we were able to easily detect both paternally and maternally inherited microsatellite markers.

CONCLUSIONS By selectively enriching circulatory fetal DNA through size selection of fragments smaller than approximately 0.3 kb, we can more easily analyze both paternally and maternally inherited DNA polymorphisms.

title: The intravascular volume effect of Ringer's lactate is below 20%: a prospective study in humans
text:
INTRODUCTION

Perioperative fluid management relies heavily on isotonic crystalloids. While isotonic colloids like human albumin or hydroxyethyl starch are often used to compensate for acute blood losses, recent data suggests that crystalloids may have a comparable intravascular volume effect. However, general physiological knowledge and clinical experience suggest otherwise.

METHODS

In a prospective study, we conducted double-tracer blood volume measurements on ten female adults before and after intended normovolemic hemodilution. During this process, we substituted the three-fold amount of withdrawn blood with Ringer's lactate. Any deficits were then substituted with half the volume of 20% human albumin, followed by another blood volume assessment. We used repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) and paired t-tests to assess significance between measurements. A significance level of P < 0.05 was used.

RESULTS

A total of 1,097 ± 285 ml of whole blood were withdrawn (641 ± 155 ml/m(2) body surface area) and replaced with 3,430 ± 806 ml of Ringer's lactate. Hemodilution resulted in a significant decrease in blood volume (-459 ± 185 ml; P < 0.05) without relevant hemodynamic changes, and a significant increase in interstitial water content (+2,157 ± 606 ml; P < 0.05). The volume effect of Ringer's lactate was 17 ± 10%. Infusing 245 ± 64 ml of 20% human albumin restored blood volume back to baseline values, with a volume effect of 184 ± 63%.

CONCLUSIONS

Substituting isolated intravascular deficits with three-fold Ringer's lactate impairs maintenance of intravascular normovolemia in cardiopulmonary healthy adults. The main side effect is interstitial fluid accumulation, which can be partially restored by intravenous infusion of 20% human albumin. We recommend using a five-fold amount of crystalloids or an isooncotic preparation in patients with acute bleeding to prevent edema.

title: Fibroblast Growth Factor 21 Prevents Atherosclerosis by Suppression of Hepatic Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein-2 and Induction of Adiponectin in Mice
text: The role of fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) in the cardiovascular system is not well understood. FGF21 is a metabolic hormone that affects glucose and lipid metabolism, as well as insulin sensitivity. It is regulated by peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α and γ, which are used to lower lipids and increase insulin sensitivity. In this study, the impact of FGF21 deficiency and replenishment with recombinant FGF21 on atherosclerosis was investigated in mice lacking apolipoprotein E (apoE). The results showed that FGF21 deficiency led to increased plaque formation and premature death in apoE-deficient mice, along with low levels of adiponectin and high cholesterol. Replenishing FGF21 protected against atherosclerosis in these mice through two mechanisms: increasing adiponectin production in adipocytes, which then acted on blood vessels to inhibit plaque formation and inflammation, and reducing cholesterol synthesis in the liver by suppressing the expression of sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2. Treatment with adiponectin partially reversed atherosclerosis without affecting cholesterol levels in FGF21-deficient mice, while the cholesterol-lowering effects of FGF21 were diminished when sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2 was expressed in the liver. These findings suggest that FGF21 plays a role in protecting against atherosclerosis by regulating communication between the liver, adipose tissue, and blood vessels.

title: VARNA: Interactive drawing and editing of the RNA secondary structure
text:
VARNA is a software tool that automates the drawing, visualization, and annotation of RNA secondary structures. It is specifically designed to be used alongside web servers and databases. 

Some of the key features of VARNA include four drawing algorithms, support for input/output using formats such as dbn, ct, bpseq, and RNAML, and the ability to export drawings in five different picture formats, including JPEG, PNG, SVG, EPS, and XFIG. 

Additionally, VARNA allows for manual modification and structural annotation of the resulting drawings. This can be done through an interactive point and click approach within a web server or via command-line arguments. 

VARNA is freely available software, released under the GPLv3.0 license. It can be accessed at http://varna.lri.fr. Supplementary data for VARNA can be found at Bioinformatics online.

title: C-reactive protein decreases interleukin-10 secretion in activated human monocyte-derived macrophages via inhibition of cyclic AMP production.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of C-Reactive Protein (CRP) in atherosclerosis, a cardiovascular disease. It was found that atherosclerotic plaques express CRP and interleukin (IL)-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine. The absence of IL-10 led to increased plaque formation, while the delivery of IL-10 reduced plaque formation. The effect of CRP on IL-10 secretion was tested in human monocyte-derived macrophages (HMDMs) stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The results showed that CRP decreased IL-10 mRNA and protein levels induced by LPS, and also destabilized IL-10 mRNA. Additionally, CRP increased the secretion of IL-8, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor from HMDMs, and did not inhibit the secretion of these cytokines induced by LPS. The inhibition of CRP-mediated IL-10 was reversed by Fc gamma receptor I antibodies. CRP also decreased intracellular cAMP, phospho-cAMP response element binding protein (pCREB), and adenyl cyclase activity. The inhibition of IL-10 by CRP was reversed by cAMP agonists. Overexpression of wild-type and constitutively active CREB in THP-1 cells attenuated the inhibitory effect of CRP on LPS-induced IL-10 levels. CRP also inhibited IL-10 and heme oxygenase-1 induced by hemoglobin:haptoglobin. Furthermore, administration of human CRP to rats decreased IL-10 levels. In conclusion, this study suggests that CRP alters the balance between anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory factors by decreasing IL-10, thereby promoting inflammation, which is important in the development of atherosclerosis.

title: The DNA polymerase activity of Pol ε holoenzyme is required for rapid and efficient chromosomal DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts
text: DNA polymerase ε (Pol ε) is involved in various processes in eukaryotic cells, including DNA replication, repair, and cell-cycle checkpoint control. While the roles of replicative Pol α and Pol δ in chromosomal DNA replication are well understood, the specific role of Pol ε in this process remains unclear. To shed light on this, researchers used a Xenopus egg extract DNA replication system. Previous studies have shown that when Pol ε is depleted from these extracts, the initiation timing and elongation of chromosomal DNA replication are significantly impaired, resulting in reduced accumulation of replicative intermediates and products. However, the researchers found that normal replication can be restored by adding Pol ε holoenzyme back to the depleted extracts. Importantly, this restoration does not occur when polymerase-deficient forms of Pol ε, such as polymerase point or deletion mutants or incomplete enzyme complexes, are added. The study also provides evidence that Pol ε holoenzyme directly interacts with GINS, Cdc45p, and Cut5p, which are all involved in the initiation of chromosomal DNA replication in eukaryotic cells. These findings indicate that the DNA polymerase activity of Pol ε holoenzyme is crucial for normal chromosomal DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts. Notably, these are the first biochemical data to demonstrate the essential role of Pol ε holoenzyme's DNA polymerase activity in chromosomal DNA replication in higher eukaryotes, unlike in yeasts.

title: DAF-16/FOXO employs the chromatin remodeller SWI/SNF to promote stress resistance and longevity
text: Organisms face constant challenges from stress and deprivation, requiring adaptive responses for survival. The transcription factor DAF-16/FOXO, also known as forkhead box O, plays a central role in these responses. However, little is known about how it regulates its target genes. By using proteomic techniques to identify DAF-16/FOXO-binding partners in Caenorhabditis elegans and evaluating their functions through RNA interference, we discovered several potential cofactors for DAF-16/FOXO, with the chromatin remodeller SWI/SNF being the most notable. DAF-16/FOXO and SWI/SNF form a complex and co-localize at the target promoters of DAF-16/FOXO. Our research demonstrates that, specifically for gene activation, DAF-16/FOXO relies on SWI/SNF to recruit it to target promoters and activate transcription by remodeling the local chromatin. This dependence on SWI/SNF is crucial for DAF-16/FOXO-mediated processes in animals, including dauer formation, stress resistance, and longevity promotion. Therefore, our findings shed light on the mechanisms of DAF-16/FOXO-mediated transcriptional regulation and establish a vital connection between ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling and lifespan regulation.

title: Association of type and location of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations with risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
text: The importance of understanding the relationship between specific mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 and cancer risk is limited. The objective of this study was to identify the specific cancer risks associated with different mutations in BRCA1/2. The study involved women who were identified between 1937 and 2011 and found to carry disease-associated BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. The international sample included 19,581 carriers of BRCA1 mutations and 11,900 carriers of BRCA2 mutations from 55 centers in 33 countries. The researchers estimated the hazard ratios for breast and ovarian cancer based on the type, function, and position of the mutations. They also calculated the ratio of breast to ovarian cancer hazard ratios. A value greater than 1 indicated an elevated risk of breast cancer, while a value less than 1 indicated an elevated risk of ovarian cancer. The main exposures in the study were mutations of BRCA1 or BRCA2, and the main outcomes were breast and ovarian cancer risks. The results showed that among BRCA1 mutation carriers, 46% were diagnosed with breast cancer, 12% with ovarian cancer, 5% with both breast and ovarian cancer, and 37% without cancer. Among BRCA2 mutation carriers, 52% were diagnosed with breast cancer, 6% with ovarian cancer, 2% with both breast and ovarian cancer, and 40% without cancer. The researchers identified specific regions in BRCA1 and BRCA2 that were associated with increased breast or ovarian cancer risks. They also found that mutations causing nonsense-mediated decay were linked to different risks of breast or ovarian cancer and an earlier age of breast cancer diagnosis for both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers. The study concluded that breast and ovarian cancer risks vary depending on the type and location of BRCA1/2 mutations. These findings could potentially be used for risk assessment and decision making regarding cancer prevention for individuals with BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.

title: Endogenous bone marrow MSCs are dynamic, fate-restricted participants in bone maintenance and regeneration.
text: The function of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) in their natural environment is not well understood, despite their widespread use in clinical applications. In this study, we conducted genetic pulse-chase experiments to investigate the role of osteoblastic cells, which are short-lived and nonreplicative, in the presence of bone-marrow-derived, Mx1(+) stromal cells with "MSC" characteristics. These Mx1(+) cells respond to tissue stress and migrate to injured areas, where they provide new osteoblasts during the healing of fractures. Through single cell transplantation, we found that these cells not only maintain their progenitor function but also differentiate into osteoblasts, contributing to the formation of new bone. They have the ability to move locally and systemically, and can be transplanted multiple times. Although these cells meet the current in vitro definition of MSCs, they are limited to the osteolineage in vivo, both in growing and adult animals. Therefore, bone-marrow-derived MSCs may consist of a diverse population, with the Mx1(+) population representing a highly dynamic and stress-responsive group of stem/progenitor cells with restricted potential, which fulfills the high demand for cell replacement in the adult skeleton.

title: Dscam and DSCAM: complex genes in simple animals, complex animals yet simple genes.
text: Cadherins and immunoglobulin (Ig) proteins are responsible for creating a wide range of surface receptors. These receptors serve as both cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) and signal-transducing receptors. These functions are closely connected and rely on specific binding between similar molecules as well as interactions between different molecules. The Drosophila receptor Dscam is an exceptional example of specific binding between similar molecules and is involved in important biological processes like neural wiring and innate immunity. By using different combinations of alternatively spliced Ig-domains, approximately 18,000 isoform-specific receptor pairs with similar binding properties can be generated. While the isoform diversity of Dscam is unique to arthropods, recent genetic analysis of vertebrate DSCAM (Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule) genes has shown that the molecular functions underlying neural wiring are conserved. This review explores the various functions of Dscam in different species, highlighting its remarkable versatility and its conserved basic functions in neural development. We also discuss how arthropods have utilized an unprecedented expansion of complex alternative splicing to create diverse surface receptors that are crucial for cell-cell communication, self-recognition in neurons, and innate immune defenses. Finally, we propose a speculative hypothesis that explains the significant differences in the structures of Dscam and DSCAM genes while still accounting for their conserved functions in molecular recognition during neural circuit formation.

title: Differential innate immune response programs in neuronal subtypes determine susceptibility to infection in the brain by positive stranded RNA viruses
text: The vulnerability of neurons in the brain to microbial infection is a crucial factor in determining the clinical outcome. However, there is limited knowledge regarding the molecular factors that govern this susceptibility. In this study, we demonstrate that two types of neurons from different regions of the brain exhibit varying levels of permissiveness to the replication of positive-stranded RNA viruses. Specifically, granule cell neurons in the cerebellum and cortical neurons in the cerebral cortex possess distinct innate immune programs that confer different susceptibilities to viral infection both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. Through the introduction of genes that are more highly expressed in granule cell neurons into cortical neurons, we have identified three interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs; Ifi27, Irg1, and Rsad2, also known as Viperin) that play a role in the antiviral response against various neurotropic viruses. Additionally, we have observed that the epigenetic state and microRNA-mediated regulation of these ISGs are associated with an enhanced antiviral response in granule cell neurons. Consequently, neurons originating from distinct brain regions possess unique innate immune signatures that likely contribute to their varying susceptibility to infection.

title: Small-airway obstruction and emphysema in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between small-airway obstruction and emphysematous destruction in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). We utilized multidetector computed tomography (CT) to compare the number of airways measuring 2.0 to 2.5 mm in diameter in 78 patients with varying stages of COPD, as determined by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) scale. We also examined isolated lungs from COPD patients who underwent lung transplantation, as well as donor lungs, using microCT to measure the extent of emphysema, the number of terminal bronchioles per milliliter of lung volume, and the dimensions of terminal bronchioles.

Our findings from multidetector CT scans revealed a reduction in the number of airways measuring 2.0 to 2.5 mm in diameter in COPD patients compared to control samples. This reduction was observed in patients with GOLD stage 1 disease, GOLD stage 2 disease, and GOLD stage 3 or 4 disease. MicroCT analysis of isolated lungs from patients with GOLD stage 4 disease showed a significant decrease in the total cross-sectional area and number of terminal bronchioles. These reductions were substantial, ranging from 81 to 99.7% in cross-sectional area and 72 to 89% in the number of terminal bronchioles.

Furthermore, our comparison of terminal bronchioles and dimensions at different levels of emphysematous destruction revealed that the narrowing and loss of terminal bronchioles occurred prior to the onset of emphysematous destruction in COPD. This suggests that the narrowing and disappearance of small conducting airways contribute to the increased peripheral airway resistance observed in COPD.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the narrowing and disappearance of small conducting airways precede emphysematous destruction in COPD. These findings provide insight into the mechanisms underlying increased peripheral airway resistance in COPD. This research was supported by funding from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and other sources.

title: Stepwise Histone Replacement by SWR1 Requires Dual Activation with Histone H2A.Z and Canonical Nucleosome
text: Most eukaryotic promoters contain nucleosomes that incorporate a histone variant called H2A.Z. This incorporation is facilitated by a complex called SWR1, which replaces the standard histone H2A with H2A.Z in nucleosomes using ATP. In this study, we found that nucleosomes near promoters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae exhibit a high degree of heterogeneity in terms of H2A.Z content, with some nucleosomes containing one, two, or zero H2A.Z molecules. In vitro experiments showed that SWR1 catalyzes the replacement of H2A with H2A.Z in a stepwise and one-directional manner, adding one H2A.Z-H2B dimer at a time. This process produces intermediate nucleosomes with mixed histone composition and eventually results in nucleosomes composed solely of H2A.Z. Interestingly, the ATPase activity of SWR1 is specifically stimulated by nucleosomes containing H2A, without causing eviction of histone H2A. Surprisingly, the addition of free H2A.Z-H2B dimer further enhances the ATPase activity, leading to eviction of nucleosomal H2A-H2B and deposition of H2A.Z-H2B. These findings suggest that the interplay between H2A-containing nucleosomes and free H2A.Z-H2B dimer, acting as both an effector and a substrate for SWR1, determines the specificity and outcome of the replacement reaction.

title: Logic of the yeast metabolic cycle: temporal compartmentalization of cellular processes.
text: Under continuous, nutrient-limited circumstances, budding yeast display strong, regular cycles in the form of respiratory bursts. Research using microarrays shows that more than half of the yeast genome is periodically expressed during these metabolic cycles.
