Genes that encode proteins with similar functions have similar patterns of temporal expression, and genes related to energy and metabolism are particularly expressed with great regularity. Crucial cellular and metabolic events happen in coordination with the metabolic cycle, indicating that important processes in a basic eukaryotic cell are organized in time.

title: Molecular pathways: induction of polyploidy as a novel differentiation therapy for leukemia.
text:
Differentiation therapy has emerged as a potent method for targeting specific blood cancers. A notable example is the use of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which has greatly improved outcomes for patients with this particular type of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In exploring the potential of differentiation therapy in other forms of AML, we hypothesized that compounds capable of inducing terminal differentiation of megakaryocytes could be effective treatments for acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AMKL), a subtype of AML. Additionally, we speculated that these agents could also impact the differentiation of megakaryocytes in myelodysplastic syndromes and reduce the presence of abnormal blood cells in primary myelofibrosis.

Through a high-throughput chemical screening approach, we identified small molecules that facilitated various aspects of terminal megakaryocyte differentiation, including the induction of polyploidization. Polyploidization is a process in which cells accumulate DNA to 32N or greater, and once cells enter this state, they no longer divide. This irreversible process could effectively reduce the tumor burden. Clinical studies involving polyploidy inducers, such as aurora kinase A inhibitors, are currently underway for a wide range of malignancies. Trials specifically targeting AMKL and primary myelofibrosis are also in development. This innovative form of differentiation therapy may become available for clinical use in the near future.

title: Dual mutations in the AML1 and FLT3 genes are associated with leukemogenesis in acute myeloblastic leukemia of the M0 subtype
text: Mutations in the transcription factor AML1 are linked to the development of acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML). The most common genetic alterations in AML are internal tandem duplications (ITDs) in the juxtamembrane domain and mutations in the second tyrosine kinase domain of the FLT3 gene. However, these mutations alone do not seem to be enough to cause leukemia. To determine if both AML1 and FLT3 mutations contribute to leukemogenesis, we studied mutations in these genes in patients with the AML M0 subtype, where AML1 mutations were predominantly found. Out of 51 patients, eight had a mutation in the Runt domain of the AML1 gene: one had a heterozygous missense mutation with normal function, five had heterozygous frameshift mutations, and two had biallelic nonsense or frameshift mutations, resulting in reduced or complete loss of AML1 activity. On the other hand, out of 49 patients examined, 10 had the FLT3 mutation. We found the FLT3 mutation in five out of eight (63%) patients with AML1 mutation, while only five out of 41 (12%) patients without AML1 mutation had the FLT3 mutation (P=0.0055). These findings suggest that decreased AML1 activity makes cells more susceptible to acquiring the activating FLT3 mutation as a secondary event, leading to full transformation in AML M0.

title: Unravelling mechanisms of p53-mediated tumour suppression
text: p53 plays a critical role in suppressing tumors by responding to various stress signals and coordinating specific cellular reactions. These reactions include temporarily halting the cell cycle, inducing cellular senescence, and promoting apoptosis, all of which contribute to tumor suppression. However, recent research has questioned the significance of these traditional cellular responses in p53-mediated tumor suppression. Instead, studies have highlighted p53's involvement in regulating other cellular processes such as metabolism, stem cell maintenance, invasion, metastasis, and communication within the tumor microenvironment. In this Opinion article, we explore the roles of both classical p53 functions and emerging p53-regulated processes in tumor suppression.

title: Stem cell-related "self-renewal" signature and high epidermal growth factor receptor expression associated with resistance to concomitant chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma.
text: The purpose of this study was to identify molecular profiles that are specific to treatment resistance in glioblastomas, which are known for their resistance to therapy. This resistance has been attributed to DNA-repair proficiency, deregulated molecular pathways, and the behavior of tumor stem-like cells. The study analyzed gene expression profiles of 80 glioblastomas to determine their association with resistance to therapy. The patients in the study were treated with concomitant chemoradiotherapy using the alkylating agent temozolomide. The results showed that an expression signature dominated by HOX genes, including Prominin-1 (CD133), was a predictor for poor survival in patients treated with concomitant chemoradiotherapy. This association was validated in an independent data set. The HOX cluster was similar to a "self-renewal" signature recently identified in a mouse leukemia model. The HOX signature and EGFR expression were independent prognostic factors, even when adjusted for other factors such as the O-6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) methylation status and age. The study also found that better outcomes were associated with gene clusters related to tumor-host interaction, tumor vascularization, cell adhesion, and innate immune response. This study provides clinical evidence for the involvement of a "glioma stem cell" or "self-renewal" phenotype in treatment resistance of glioblastoma. The biologic mechanisms identified in this study can guide future targeted therapies and the development of markers for individualized treatment and patient selection.

title: Heterogeneity Underlies the Emergence of EGFRT790 Wild-Type Clones Following Treatment of T790M-Positive Cancers with a Third-Generation EGFR Inhibitor.
text: The text describes the findings of a study on the resistance mechanisms of rociletinib, a third-generation EGFR inhibitor used in lung cancers with the T790M mutation. The researchers biopsied patients who had progressed on rociletinib to investigate the resistance mechanisms. Out of the 12 patients with T790M-positive cancers at the start of rociletinib treatment, six had rociletinib-resistant biopsies with the T790 wild-type mutation. Two of these cancers transformed into small cell lung cancer, while three acquired EGFR amplification. The researchers also observed the coexistence of T790 wild-type and T790M-positive clones in a single biopsy taken before rociletinib treatment. The fraction of T790M-positive cells before treatment affected the response to rociletinib. Longitudinal analysis of circulating tumor DNA revealed an increase in plasma EGFR-activating mutation, with T790M indicating rociletinib resistance in some patients, while in others, the activating mutation increased but T790M remained suppressed. These findings highlight the importance of tumor heterogeneity when targeting a single resistance mechanism and suggest the need for combination regimens that target both T790 wild-type and T790M clones to improve outcomes. The study also demonstrates that plasma ctDNA analysis can sometimes predict emerging resistance mechanisms.

title: Extrathymic Generation of Regulatory T Cells in Placental Mammals Mitigates Maternal-Fetal Conflict
text: Regulatory T (Treg) cells, which rely on the X chromosome-encoded transcription factor Foxp3 for their differentiation and function, are produced in the thymus (tTreg) and outside of it (peripheral, pTreg). The absence of these cells leads to severe autoimmune diseases. In this study, we present evidence that a specific enhancer of Foxp3, known as conserved noncoding sequence 1 (CNS1), is crucial for the generation of pTreg cells but not necessary for tTreg cell development. Interestingly, CNS1 is only found in placental mammals. It consists mainly of mammalian-wide interspersed repeats (MIR) that have undergone retrotransposition during the early stages of mammalian evolution. During pregnancy, pTreg cells that recognize a paternal alloantigen were produced in a CNS1-dependent manner and accumulated in the placenta. Moreover, when CNS1-deficient females were mated with males from a different genetic background (allogeneic), they experienced increased fetal resorption, along with heightened infiltration of immune cells and impaired remodeling of spiral arteries. These findings suggest that, throughout evolution, placental animals have developed a CNS1-dependent mechanism for the extrathymic differentiation of Treg cells, which plays a crucial role in maintaining maternal-fetal tolerance.

title: Acquired EGFR C797S mutation mediates resistance to AZD9291 in non–small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR T790M
text:
In this study, we examined cell-free plasma DNA (cfDNA) from individuals with advanced lung cancer who had developed resistance to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) AZD9291. Initially, we conducted next-generation sequencing on cfDNA samples from seven participants and identified an acquired EGFR C797S mutation in one individual. To confirm the role of this mutant EGFR in resistance, we introduced it into a cell line and observed that it rendered the cells resistant to AZD9291. 

Subsequently, we analyzed serial cfDNA samples from 15 individuals undergoing AZD9291 treatment using droplet digital PCR. Prior to treatment, all participants tested positive for the T790M mutation. However, upon developing resistance to AZD9291, we observed three distinct molecular subtypes: six cases acquired the C797S mutation, five cases maintained the T790M mutation without acquiring the C797S mutation, and four cases lost the T790M mutation despite having the underlying EGFR activating mutation. 

Our findings shed light on the various mechanisms by which tumors develop resistance to AZD9291 and emphasize the importance of developing therapies that can overcome resistance mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation.

title: The Translation Initiation Factor 3f (eIF3f) Exhibits a Deubiquitinase Activity Regulating Notch Activation
text: The activation of the mammalian Notch receptor following ligand binding involves a series of events, including metalloprotease-cleavage, endocytosis, monoubiquitination, and subsequent processing by the gamma-secretase. This process leads to the formation of a soluble, transcriptionally active molecule. Previous studies have suggested that the Notch1 receptor undergoes monoubiquitination prior to gamma-secretase cleavage, with the specific lysine residue located in its submembrane domain. To gain a better understanding of the regulation of this step by a deubiquitinase (DUB) activity, we conducted an immunofluorescence-based screening of an shRNA library. Through this screening, we identified eIF3f, a subunit of the translation initiation factor eIF3, as a DUB that targets the activated Notch receptor. Our findings demonstrate that eIF3f possesses intrinsic DUB activity. Knocking down eIF3f resulted in an accumulation of monoubiquitinated forms of activated Notch, which was counteracted by murine WT eIF3f but not by a catalytically inactive mutant. Additionally, we observed that eIF3f is recruited to activated Notch on endocytic vesicles by the putative E3 ubiquitin ligase Deltex1, acting as a bridging factor. Furthermore, both catalytically inactive forms of eIF3f and shRNAs targeting eIF3f suppressed Notch activation in a coculture assay, indicating that eIF3f serves as a positive regulator of the Notch pathway. Our results support two significant conclusions: (1) The activated form of Notch must undergo deubiquitination before being processed by gamma-secretase and entering the nucleus to fulfill its transcriptional function. (2) The enzyme responsible for this deubiquitinase activity is eIF3f, which was previously known solely as a translation initiation factor. These findings enhance our understanding of Notch signaling and also open up new avenues of research on the Zomes family and translation initiation factors.

title: Focal contacts as mechanosensors: externally applied local mechanical force induces growth of focal contacts by an mDia1-dependent and ROCKindependent mechanism
text: The process of transitioning from small focal complexes to elongated focal contacts in cell-matrix adhesions is dependent on the activity of the GTPase Rho. Specifically, the activation of Rho-associated kinase (ROCK), a target of Rho, is crucial for the formation of focal contacts through myosin II-driven contractility. To understand how Rho induces focal contacts and the role of cell contractility, we applied mechanical force to vinculin-containing adhesions at the cell edge using a micropipette. This localized pulling resulted in the assembly and elongation of these adhesions, transforming them into streak-like focal contacts. We observed this transformation through the dynamics of green fluorescent protein-tagged vinculin or paxillin and interference reflection microscopy. When Rho activity was inhibited by C3 transferase, the force-induced formation of focal contacts was suppressed. However, when cells treated with C3 transferase were exposed to constitutively active mutants of mDia1, another target of Rho, the formation of force-induced focal contacts was restored. Interestingly, the formation of focal contacts in response to external tension force still occurred even when myosin II and ROCK were inhibited, as long as mDia1 remained active. This suggests that integrin-containing focal complexes act as individual mechanosensors, assembling in a specific direction in response to local force.

title: Maternal Protein Restriction Affects Postnatal Growth and the Expression of Key Proteins Involved in Lifespan Regulation in Mice
text: In a previous study, we found that restricting protein intake in rodents during pregnancy affected their growth rate in early life and ultimately influenced their lifespan. We discovered that rodents with low birth weight due to protein restriction followed by catch-up growth had shorter lifespans, while those with protein restriction and slow growth during lactation had longer lifespans. Our goal is to understand the underlying mechanisms behind these differences. In this study, we examined the effects of maternal diet on organ growth, metabolic parameters, and the expression of insulin/IGF1 signaling proteins and Sirt1 in the muscle of male mice at weaning. We found that mice with protein restriction during lactation had lower fasting glucose and insulin levels, indicating improved insulin sensitivity. These mice also had higher relative weights of the brain and thymus compared to controls, suggesting that the enhanced functional capacity of these tissues is beneficial for longevity. Additionally, they showed increased expression of insulin receptor substrate 1 and protein kinase C zeta. On the other hand, mice with catch-up growth expressed decreased levels of several insulin signaling proteins, which may make them more prone to insulin resistance. The expression of Sirt1 protein was also reduced in these mice. These findings suggest that maternal protein restriction can affect important metabolic pathways involved in lifespan regulation at a young age, which may explain the impact of maternal diet on longevity.

title: ‘Short stature in children - a questionnaire for parents’: a new instrument for growth disorder-specific psychosocial adaptation in children
text: New research studies have found that children with a growth disorder have similar psychosocial adaptation compared to those without a growth disorder. However, this may be because there is a lack of sensitive and specific techniques for analyzing and comparing their quality of life. In this study, we introduce a new questionnaire for parents of children with short stature. Our approach includes both qualitative and quantitative methods to gather specific information about the level of individual stress factors and sources of support. The questionnaire was completed by the parents of 442 children with growth retardation caused by various factors. Through a principal component analysis, we identified four dimensions of psychosocial adaptation: suffering, future anxieties, behavioral problems, and coping efforts. The reliability of the scales was found to be sufficient. When comparing two specific growth disorder groups (achondroplasia and growth hormone deficiency), we discovered that they had different profiles of psychosocial adaptation, but not significantly so. The qualitative analysis revealed that achondroplasia had more physical restrictions as a stress factor. These findings demonstrate the specificity and validity of our new instrument. Therefore, we can conclude that this questionnaire is a valuable tool for obtaining growth disorder-specific information about individual stress factors, resources, and psychosocial adaptation.

title: Alphavirus-derived small RNAs modulate pathogenesis in disease vector mosquitoes.
text: Mosquito-borne viruses cause significant illness and death in humans and domesticated animals. To survive in nature, these viruses rely on a transmission cycle involving replication in both a susceptible vertebrate and mosquito host. While vertebrate infections are often associated with disease, the continued transmission of these viruses depends on the establishment of a nonpathogenic infection in the mosquito vector. In flies, an antiviral RNAi response has been shown to limit the replication of RNA viruses. However, it is unclear how important the RNAi pathway is as an antiviral defense in mammals. The differences in immune responses between mammals and mosquitoes may explain why these viruses do not typically cause harm to the mosquito hosts. In our study, we discovered small interfering RNAs (viRNAs) derived from the virus in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with the mosquito-borne virus Sindbis (SINV). These viRNAs were 21 nucleotides long and were distributed asymmetrically across the SINV genome. To understand the role of viRNAs in controlling the virus's pathogenic potential, we infected mosquitoes with recombinant alphaviruses that expressed suppressors of RNA silencing. We observed decreased survival in mosquitoes where the accumulation of viRNAs was suppressed. These findings suggest that an exogenous siRNA pathway is crucial for the survival of mosquitoes infected with alphaviruses and, therefore, for the maintenance of these viruses in nature.

title: Nuclear RNAi maintains heritable gene silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: In Caenorhabditis elegans, RNA interference (RNAi) can be passed down from one generation to the next. When C. elegans is exposed to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), its offspring inherit the ability to silence specific genes targeted by RNAi in the previous generation. In this study, we aim to understand how this inheritance of RNAi occurs in C. elegans. Our findings reveal that when animals are exposed to dsRNA, they pass on small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and specific chemical modifications called histone 3 lysine 9 methylation (H3K9me) marks to their progeny. Interestingly, siRNAs are detected before the appearance of H3K9me marks, suggesting that the marks are not directly inherited but rather reestablished in the offspring. Furthermore, the H3K9me marks are more prominent in the progeny than in animals directly exposed to dsRNA, indicating that the transmission of silencing signals through the germ line may enhance the efficiency of siRNA-directed H3K9me. Finally, we demonstrate that a pathway called nuclear RNAi (Nrde) is responsible for maintaining heritable RNAi silencing in C. elegans. The protein Argonaute (Ago) NRDE-3 associates with heritable siRNAs and, together with other nuclear RNAi factors (NRDE-1, NRDE-2, and NRDE-4), promotes siRNA expression in the offspring. These findings establish that siRNA expression can be inherited in C. elegans and define a pathway that ensures the maintenance of RNAi silencing and siRNA expression in the progeny of animals exposed to dsRNA.

title: Cancer survivors in the United States: prevalence across the survivorship trajectory and implications for care.
text:
BACKGROUND: The population of cancer survivors is growing and diverse in their needs for medical care, psychosocial support, and practical assistance. This manuscript aims to provide information on the prevalent population of cancer survivors, including overall numbers and prevalence based on cancer site and time since diagnosis. 

METHODS: Data on incidence and survival from 1975-2007 were obtained from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program, while population projections were obtained from the United States Census Bureau. The Prevalence Incidence Approach Model was used to estimate cancer prevalence for 2012 and beyond, assuming constant future incidence and survival trends but dynamic projections of the U.S. population. 

RESULTS: As of January 1, 2012, there were approximately 13.7 million cancer survivors in the United States, with prevalence projected to reach 18 million by 2022. Among this population, 64% have survived 5 years or more, 40% have survived 10 years or more, and 15% have survived 20 years or more since diagnosis. Over the next decade, the number of people who have lived 5 years or more after their cancer diagnosis is expected to increase by approximately 37% to 11.9 million. 

CONCLUSIONS: A coordinated research and practice agenda is necessary to address the long-term medical, psychosocial, and practical needs of cancer survivors throughout their survivorship journey. 

IMPACT: The prevalence estimates for cancer survivors across the survivorship trajectory will inform the national research agenda and help project the health service needs of this population in the future.

title: Human aneuploidy: mechanisms and new insights into an age-old problem
text: At least 10% of human pregnancies are affected by trisomic and monosomic (aneuploid) embryos. For women who are nearing the end of their reproductive lifespan, this percentage may even exceed 50%. The errors that cause aneuploidy primarily occur in the oocyte, but despite extensive research, the exact molecular reasons behind these errors remain unknown. Recent studies on both humans and model organisms have provided new insights into the complexity of meiotic defects. These studies suggest that the increase in errors in older women is not solely due to one factor, but rather a combination of unique characteristics of oogenesis and various internal and external factors.

title: The Drosophila hindgut lacks constitutively active adult stem cells but proliferates in response to tissue damage.
text: Recent research has challenged the notion that the adult Drosophila hindgut contains active stem cells that replenish the tissue, similar to those found in the midgut. Contrary to this belief, our studies using clonal marking and BrdU incorporation techniques revealed no active stem cells and minimal cell turnover in adult hindgut tissue. Additionally, we found no evidence to support the idea that anterior stem cells generate the adult hindgut during larval/pupal development. However, we did observe that severe tissue damage in the hindgut triggers cell proliferation in a ring of potentially dormant stem cells located at the anterior of the pylorus. Therefore, the hindgut does not serve as a model for tissue maintenance through constantly active stem cells, but it does offer valuable insights into the mechanisms of stress-induced tissue repair.

title: Vitamin d deficiency in postmenopausal women - biological correlates.
text:
INTRODUCTION
Low levels of vitamin D (VD) are linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism, which can have negative effects such as reduced bone mineral density (BMD), increased risk of fractures, and falls.

OBJECTIVE
The objective of this study was to examine the VD status and related factors in a group of postmenopausal women.

MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a study on 123 postmenopausal women who were evaluated at the C.I.Parhon National Institute of Endocrinology, specifically in the Pituitary and Neuroendocrine Diseases department. All participants were referred by their general practitioners for BMD evaluation. The evaluation included measuring serum levels of total and ionized calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), 25-hydroxy vitamin D (25OHD), parathyroid hormone (PTH), osteocalcin, and betacrosslaps. Central DXA osteodensitometry was also performed.

RESULTS
Among the cases, 91.9% had 25OHD serum levels below 30 ng/ml, with 74.8% having VD deficiency and 17.1% having VD insufficiency. Only 8.1% had sufficient VD levels. A history of fragility fractures was found in 45.83% of osteoporotic patients, 27.27% of osteopenic patients, and 15.15% of women with normal BMD. Of the participants, 32 women (26%) were taking VD supplementation at the time of evaluation. Among these individuals, those with prior fragility fractures had significantly higher 25OHD levels (p=0.018), as did those with osteoporosis (p=0.008). The concentration of 25OHD was negatively correlated with PTH, ALP, and osteocalcin. The bone markers evaluated showed a significant inverse correlation with radius BMD, T scores, and Z scores (p=0.004). Among the cases with VD deficiency, 27.17% had secondary hyperparathyroidism, and their 25OHD concentration was significantly lower (p=0.000).

CONCLUSIONS
VD insufficiency is highly prevalent but often goes unrecognized and untreated, potentially leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Compliance with VD supplementation is lower in individuals without osteoporosis or fragility fractures. It is important to implement primary prevention measures more actively.

title: CD44v6 is a marker of constitutive and reprogrammed cancer stem cells driving colon cancer metastasis.
text: The mechanism by which cancer stem cells (CSCs) develop metastatic traits is not well understood. However, our research demonstrates that all colorectal cancer stem cells (CR-CSCs) express CD44v6, which is crucial for their ability to migrate and generate metastatic tumors. While CD44v6 expression is low in primary tumors, it is present in clonogenic CR-CSC populations. We have found that certain cytokines, such as hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), osteopontin (OPN), and stromal-derived factor 1α (SDF-1), secreted by tumor-associated cells, can increase CD44v6 expression in CR-CSCs. This occurs through the activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, which promotes migration and metastasis. Progenitor cells lacking CD44v6 do not give rise to metastatic lesions. However, when exposed to cytokines, these cells acquire CD44v6 expression and gain metastatic capacity. Importantly, inhibiting phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) selectively kills CD44v6 CR-CSCs and reduces metastatic growth. In patient cohorts, low levels of CD44v6 are associated with a higher probability of survival. Therefore, the initiation of the metastatic process in colorectal cancer is driven by CSCs through the expression of CD44v6. This molecule serves as both a functional biomarker and a potential therapeutic target.

title: Senescent Cells, Tumor Suppression, and Organismal Aging: Good Citizens, Bad Neighbors
text: Various stressors, such as dysfunctional telomeres, DNA damage, strong mitogenic signals, and disrupted chromatin, can cause cells from organisms with renewable tissues to permanently exit the cell cycle. This process, known as cellular senescence, is regulated by the p53 and RB tumor suppressor proteins and serves as a powerful defense against cancer. However, senescent cells undergo phenotypic changes that may contribute to aging and certain age-related diseases, including late-life cancer. Consequently, while the senescence response initially promotes early-life survival by preventing cancer development, it eventually hampers longevity as dysfunctional senescent cells accumulate.

title: Advances in high-resolution imaging--techniques for three-dimensional imaging of cellular structures.
text: The primary objective in biology is to understand the connection between cellular organization and function. To accomplish this, a deeper comprehension of the composition and structure of organelles is necessary. While fluorescence and electron microscopy have become common tools for cell biologists to visualize cellular organelles, recent advancements have allowed for a more precise depiction of the cell. Advanced light-microscopy techniques have achieved resolutions below the diffraction limit, and electron microscopy tomography provides high-resolution three-dimensional images of cellular structures. The ability to perform both fluorescence and electron microscopy on the same sample, known as correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM), enables the identification of the location of a fluorescently labeled protein in relation to organelle structures visualized by electron microscopy. In this review, we will discuss the current state of 3D biological imaging techniques, with a particular focus on recent advancements in electron microscopy and fluorescence super-resolution techniques.

title: Quercetin attenuates vascular calcification by inhibiting oxidative stress and mitochondrial fission.
text: The present study aimed to investigate the impact of quercetin on vascular calcification caused by oxidative stress and abnormal mitochondrial dynamics. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments were conducted to assess the effects. The study found that vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) treated with inorganic phosphate (Pi) experienced mitochondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by decreased mitochondrial potential and ATP production. Additionally, a rat model of adenine-induced aortic calcification showed disruption of mitochondrial structural integrity. Pi-treated VSMCs also exhibited increased production of reactive oxygen species, enhanced expression and phosphorylation of Drp1 (a protein involved in mitochondrial fission), and excessive mitochondrial fragmentation. These effects were accompanied by mitochondria-dependent apoptotic events, such as the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria into the cytosol and subsequent activation of caspase-3. However, quercetin was found to inhibit Pi-induced apoptosis and calcification of VSMCs by reducing oxidative stress and decreasing mitochondrial fission through the inhibition of Drp1 expression and phosphorylation. Furthermore, quercetin significantly improved adenine-induced aortic calcification in rats. In conclusion, the study suggests that quercetin can attenuate calcification by reducing VSMC apoptosis through the inhibition of oxidative stress and mitochondrial fission.

title: The M/GP5 Glycoprotein Complex of Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome Virus Binds the Sialoadhesin Receptor in a Sialic Acid-Dependent Manner
text: The porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) poses a significant global threat to swine health and is currently the most important viral disease in the swine industry. Previous research has identified several crucial receptors and entry mediators involved in the virus's ability to enter host cells. However, the viral counterparts for these molecules have remained elusive, preventing the development of effective new vaccines. This study aimed to identify the viral counterparts for sialoadhesin, a vital PRRSV receptor found on macrophages. To achieve this, a soluble form of sialoadhesin was created and validated. The soluble sialoadhesin was able to bind to PRRSV in a sialic acid-dependent manner and neutralize PRRSV infection in macrophages, confirming the role of sialoadhesin as an essential PRRSV receptor. While sialic acids are present on the envelope glycoproteins GP(3), GP(4), and GP(5), only the M/GP(5) glycoprotein complex of PRRSV was identified as a ligand for sialoadhesin. This interaction relied on the sialic acid binding capacity of sialoadhesin and the presence of sialic acids on GP(5). These findings not only enhance our understanding of PRRSV biology but also provide valuable knowledge and tools for the development of new PRRSV vaccines.

title: A versatile zero background T-vector system for gene cloning and functional genomics.
text: The demand for high-throughput and cost-efficient systems for gene cloning and functional analysis has increased with the availability of complete genomic sequences of many organisms. While site-specific recombination-based cloning systems like Gateway cloning technology are useful for transferring DNA fragments into multiple destination vectors, the two-step cloning process is time-consuming and expensive. In this study, we present a zero background TA cloning system that allows for simple and efficient direct cloning of PCR-amplified DNA fragments with minimal self-ligation. Our improved T-vector system utilizes the restriction enzyme XcmI to generate a T-overhang after digestion and the negative selection marker gene ccdB to eliminate self-ligation background after transformation. We demonstrate the versatility of this technology by developing a range of transient and stable transformation vectors for various applications in plants, including constitutive gene expression, gene silencing, protein tagging, protein subcellular localization detection, and promoter fragment activity analysis. This system can be easily adapted for developing specialized expression vectors for other organisms, making zero background TA a cost-efficient and high-throughput platform that complements the Gateway cloning system for gene cloning and functional genomics.

title: GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-Cortactin Pathway Frequently Used in Cancer Invasion Is Activated by VEGFR2 to Promote Angiogenesis
text: Cancer malignancy is greatly influenced by angiogenesis and cancer invasiveness. In breast cancer, the overexpression of Arf6 and its effector, AMAP1, plays a significant role in promoting invasion and metastasis. The activation of Arf6 in this pathway is facilitated by EGFR through GEP100. Arf6 is also highly expressed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and is involved in angiogenesis. Our research reveals that AMAP1 is also highly expressed in HUVECs and that vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR2) recruits GEP100 to activate Arf6. AMAP1 functions by binding to cortactin, which contributes to cancer invasion and metastasis. We have demonstrated that the GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway is crucial for angiogenesis activities, such as cell migration, tubular formation, cell permeability enhancement, and VE-cadherin endocytosis in VEGF-stimulated HUVECs. The components of this pathway are highly expressed in pathological angiogenesis, and blocking this pathway effectively inhibits VEGF- or tumor-induced angiogenesis and choroidal neovascularization. The GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway, activated by receptor tyrosine kinases, appears to be a common mechanism in both angiogenesis and cancer invasion and metastasis, making it a promising target for therapeutic interventions.

title: Dynamics of Cryptococcus neoformans-Macrophage Interactions Reveal that Fungal Background Influences Outcome during Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis in Humans
text: Cryptococcosis, an infection caused by the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans, is a complex disease with varying clinical presentations and outcomes. The differences in these outcomes are often attributed to host factors. In order to investigate whether the diversity of clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans influences their interaction with host cells and clinical outcomes, we developed and validated new quantitative assays using flow cytometry and J774 macrophages. We analyzed 54 clinical isolates recovered from cerebrospinal fluids of unrelated patients and determined their interactions with macrophages based on phagocytic index and intracellular proliferation indexes at 2 hours and 48 hours. The phenotypes of these interactions varied greatly. Isolates with low phagocytic index and intracellular proliferation indexes were associated with failure to clear the infection from cerebrospinal fluid at week 2, while isolates with high indexes were associated with death at month 3. We also found that a subset of 9 isolates with different phenotypes exhibited variable virulence in mice and had varying levels of gene expression within macrophages, which correlated with intracellular proliferation. These results indicate that the expression of virulence factors in Cryptococcus neoformans depends not only on experimental conditions, but also on the fungal background. Therefore, in addition to host factors, the outcome of cryptococcosis may be influenced by fungal determinants. Understanding the molecular events involved in the fate of Cryptococcus neoformans inside host cells is crucial for understanding the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis. Cryptococcus neoformans is a dangerous fungal pathogen that causes approximately 1 million cases of meningitis each year, primarily in HIV-infected individuals. The diversity of infecting isolates and the importance of host factors are well known. The interaction between the fungus and macrophages is a critical step in the development of cryptococcosis. However, the impact of the diversity of clinical isolates on macrophage interactions and the outcome of cryptococcosis in humans is still unclear. Using our new assays, we discovered that the interactions between yeast and macrophages varied greatly among clinical isolates, and we identified specific behaviors that were associated with different outcomes of cryptococcosis. Additionally, we found a correlation between the expression of certain virulence factors and intracellular proliferation. While previous studies have shown that virulence factors can be expressed differently depending on experimental conditions, our study demonstrates that clinical isolates behave differently even under the same conditions. This diversity may contribute to the variable outcomes of infection in humans.

title: Angiopoietin-2 at high concentration can enhance endothelial cell survival through the phosphatidylinositol 3′-kinase/Akt signal transduction pathway
text: The angiopoietin-Tie2 system plays a crucial role in regulating vasculogenesis and maintaining vascular integrity in endothelial cells. During tumorigenesis, there is an increase in the levels of angiopoietin-2 (Ang2) mRNA, indicating its involvement in vascular activation. While Ang2 is known to counteract the effects of angiopoietin-1 (Ang1) in vivo, its specific function remains unclear. In this study, we discovered that a high concentration of Ang2 (800 ng/ml) acts as a survival factor for endothelial cells during apoptosis induced by serum deprivation. However, this survival effect was blocked when the cells were pre-treated with soluble Tie2 receptor or specific inhibitors of PI 3′-kinase, such as wortmannin and LY294002. Furthermore, the high concentration of Ang2 (800 ng/ml) led to the phosphorylation of Tie2, the p85 subunit of PI 3′-kinase, and Akt at Ser473 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. On the other hand, lower concentrations of Ang2 (50–400 ng/ml) did not have significant effects. These findings suggest that, similar to Ang1, Ang2 can promote the survival of endothelial cells during apoptosis by activating the Tie2 receptor, PI 3′-kinase, and Akt. Consequently, Ang2 may serve as a positive regulator of tumor angiogenesis.

title: Lipoxin a4 analogs attenuate induction of intestinal epithelial proinflammatory gene expression and reduce the severity of dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis.
text: The eicosanoid lipoxin A(4) (LXA(4)), its derivative aspirin-triggered 15-epi-LXA(4), and similar compounds have been found to decrease the secretion of IL-8 and the recruitment of neutrophils by intestinal epithelial cells. To understand how these lipid mediators affect proinflammatory processes in cells, we used cDNA microarrays to analyze global gene expression in epithelial cells. We found that the LXA(4) derivative alone did not significantly alter the expression of any of the >7000 genes we examined. However, pretreatment with the LXA(4) derivative reduced the induction of approximately 50% of the 125 genes that were up-regulated in response to the pathogen Salmonella typhimurium, which causes gastroenteritis. Many of the genes whose induction was reduced by the LXA(4) derivative are regulated by a transcription factor called NF-kappaB, suggesting that the LXA(4) derivative affects the activity of this factor. We found that nanomolar concentrations of the LXA(4) derivative decreased NF-kappaB-mediated transcriptional activation in a manner that depended on the LXA(4) receptor, and also inhibited the degradation of IkappaBalpha, a protein involved in NF-kappaB signaling. The LXA(4) derivative did not affect earlier signaling events that lead to IkappaBalpha degradation, such as calcium mobilization or phosphorylation of IkappaBalpha. To determine if these findings are relevant in vivo, we tested whether LXA(4) derivatives could affect intestinal inflammation using a mouse model of DSS-induced inflammatory colitis. We found that oral administration of the LXA(4) derivative (15-epi-16-para-fluoro-phenoxy-LXA(4), 10 microg/day) significantly reduced weight loss, bleeding, and mortality associated with DSS colitis. Therefore, the down-regulation of proinflammatory gene expression by the LXA(4) derivative through inhibition of the NF-kappaB pathway could be a therapeutic approach for diseases characterized by inflammation of the mucosal lining.

title: Serum plant and other noncholesterol sterols, cholesterol metabolism and 22-year mortality among middle-aged men.
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the long-term prognostic impact of serum noncholesterol sterols, including plant sterols, in middle-aged men with a high risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), who were not taking statins at the beginning of the study. The study included 232 men with an average age of 60 years, who were considered to be at high risk of CVD between 1985 and 1986. Most of the participants had high cholesterol levels, 29 had a history of CVD or cancer, 6 had diabetes, and 46 had metabolic syndrome (MS). The noncholesterol sterols that were measured included lathosterol and desmosterol (which reflect cholesterol synthesis), as well as plant sterols (campesterol and sitosterol) and cholestanol (which reflect cholesterol absorption). The main outcome measure was total mortality. 

At the beginning of the study, the markers of cholesterol synthesis and absorption showed the expected inverse associations. During the 22-year follow-up period, 101 men (43%) died. At the beginning of the study, the men who did not survive were more likely to smoke, exercise less, and have more components of MS (although they did not meet strict criteria for MS). However, there were no significant differences in traditional risk factors for CVD between the survivors and non-survivors. Among the noncholesterol sterols, only sitosterol was significantly higher in survivors compared to non-survivors. In multivariable analyses, the highest tertile of sitosterol-to-cholesterol ratio was associated with a significantly lower risk of mortality (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30-0.87) compared to the lowest tertile. Other associations were not significant, although an overall index of cholesterol metabolism (desmosterol-to-sitosterol ratio) suggested that higher cholesterol synthesis and lower absorption were associated with higher total and CVD mortality. 

In conclusion, higher levels of serum plant sterols in middle-aged men were found to predict a lower long-term risk of mortality, possibly indicating an association between higher cholesterol synthesis/lower absorption and mortality.

title: Intracoronary autologous cardiac progenitor cell transfer in patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome: the TICAP prospective phase 1 controlled trial.
text:
RATIONALE: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a congenital cardiac defect that is known to be fatal. Recent studies have suggested that injecting autologous cardiosphere-derived cells (CDCs) directly into the coronary arteries may improve the function of the ventricles. 

OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to determine if delivering CDCs through the coronary arteries is both safe and feasible for patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome. 

METHODS AND RESULTS: Between January 5, 2011, and January 16, 2012, a total of 14 patients (with an average age of 1.8±1.5 years) were chosen to receive an intracoronary infusion of autologous CDCs. This was done 33.4±8.1 days after undergoing staged procedures. An additional 7 patients were assigned as controls and received standard palliative care alone. The primary goal of the study was to assess the safety of the procedure, while the secondary goal was to determine if there were any improvements in right ventricular ejection fraction between the baseline and the 3-month follow-up. The manufacturing and delivery of CDCs were found to be feasible, and no serious adverse events were reported during the 18-month follow-up period. The patients who received CDCs showed an improvement in right ventricular ejection fraction from baseline to the 3-month follow-up (46.9%±4.6% to 52.1%±2.4%; P=0.008). When compared to the control group at the 18-month mark, the CDC-treated patients had a higher right ventricular ejection fraction (31.5%±6.8% versus 40.4%±7.6%; P=0.049), improved somatic growth (P=0.0005), reduced heart failure status (P=0.003), and a lower incidence of coil occlusion for collaterals (P=0.007). 

CONCLUSIONS: The intracoronary infusion of autologous CDCs appears to be both safe and feasible for children with hypoplastic left heart syndrome after undergoing staged surgery. Further large-scale phase 2 trials are necessary to examine the potential effects of cardiac function improvements and the long-term benefits on clinical outcomes. 

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered at http://www.clinicaltrials.gov with the unique identifier NCT01273857.

title: A Whole Brain Staining, Embedding, and Clearing Pipeline for Adult Zebrafish to Visualize Cell Proliferation and Morphology in 3-Dimensions
text:
The field of macro-imaging has experienced significant growth due to the development of innovative clearing methods and confocal microscopes with lasers that can penetrate deeper into tissues. This advancement has allowed researchers to visualize and model the growth of entire organs as they develop, or in response to manipulation, disease, or injury. This new approach provides fresh insights into development, tissue-wide signaling, and cell-to-cell interactions.

The zebrafish (Danio rerio) has transitioned from being primarily used as a developmental model to becoming a leading model for studying tissue regeneration in adults. The mature central nervous system of the zebrafish, in particular, has attracted much attention due to its unmatched neurogenic and regenerative capabilities. However, there is a lack of tools available to study the adult brain.

Currently, there are no straightforward methods for visualizing changes in the entire adult brain in three dimensions (3-D) to examine patterns of cell proliferation or specific cell populations of interest under normal, injured, or diseased conditions. The method presented here is the first of its kind to provide a step-by-step pipeline for labeling the entire brain using intraperitoneal injections of a proliferative marker called 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU). This method also allows for the visualization of GFP-reporter lines and cell-specific antibodies in the presence or absence of EdU. The small size of the adult zebrafish brain, the consistent labeling achieved with EdU, and the use of basic clearing agents make this method accessible to most laboratories interested in studying the vertebrate central nervous system.

After imaging the adult zebrafish brains injected with EdU using optical projection tomography (OPT), post-processing with software such as IMARIS and/or FIJI/IMAGEJ allows for the observation and analysis of proliferative patterns. This protocol will be a valuable tool for gaining a deeper understanding of systemic patterns in cell proliferation in both healthy and injured brains, brain-wide cellular interactions, stem cell niche development, and changes in brain morphology.

title: Single-Construct Polycistronic Doxycycline-Inducible Vectors Improve Direct Cardiac Reprogramming and Can Be Used to Identify the Critical Timing of Transgene Expression
text: Direct reprogramming is a promising approach in the field of regenerative medicine. By overexpressing specific cardiac transcription factors, such as Gata4, Mef2c, and Tbx5 (GMT), or GMT in combination with Hand2 (GHMT), fibroblasts can be directly transformed into cardiomyocyte-like cells (iCMs). However, the exact timing of transgene expression and the molecular mechanisms involved in cardiac reprogramming are still not fully understood. The conventional doxycycline (Dox)-inducible temporal transgene expression systems require the simultaneous transduction of two vectors (pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-cDNA) containing the reverse tetracycline transactivator (rtTA) and the tetracycline response element (TRE)-controlled transgene, respectively. This method has proven to be inefficient in achieving cardiac reprogramming. To address this issue, we have developed a single-construct-based polycistronic Dox-inducible vector (pDox-cDNA) that expresses both the rtTA and TRE-controlled transgenes. Through fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) analyses, quantitative RT-PCR, and immunostaining, we have discovered that pDox-GMT increases cardiac reprogramming three-fold compared to the conventional pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-GMT system. After four weeks, the iCMs induced by pDox-GMT express multiple cardiac genes, form sarcomeric structures, and exhibit spontaneous beating. Furthermore, co-transduction of pDox-Hand2 with retroviral pMX-GMT increases cardiac reprogramming three-fold compared to pMX-GMT alone. Temporal administration of Dox has revealed that the expression of the Hand2 transgene is crucial during the initial two weeks of cardiac reprogramming. Microarray analyses have also shown that Hand2 represses genes that promote cell cycle progression while enhancing cardiac reprogramming. In conclusion, we have developed an efficient temporal transgene expression system that could greatly contribute to the study of cardiac reprogramming.

title: Increasing microtubule acetylation rescues axonal transport and locomotor deficits caused by LRRK2 Roc-COR domain mutations
text:
Mutations in Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are the most common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. LRRK2 is a protein that affects various cellular processes and has been found to bind microtubules. It is believed that defective axonal transport, which relies on microtubules, may contribute to Parkinson's disease, but it is unclear whether LRRK2 mutations play a role in this process. 

In this study, we discovered that LRRK2 mutations in the Roc-COR domain (R1441C, Y1699C) specifically interact with deacetylated microtubules, leading to inhibition of axonal transport in primary neurons and Drosophila models. This inhibition results in locomotor deficits in vivo. 

Furthermore, we found that increasing microtubule acetylation using deacetylase inhibitors or the tubulin acetylase αTAT1 prevents the association of mutant LRRK2 with microtubules. Additionally, the deacetylase inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA) restores axonal transport in vitro. 

To validate these findings in a living organism, we knocked down the deacetylases HDAC6 and Sirt2 in vivo, or administered TSA, which successfully rescued both axonal transport and locomotor behavior. 

Overall, this study uncovers a potential mechanism for the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease and suggests a potential intervention by targeting microtubule acetylation.

title: G1 arrest and differentiation can occur independently of Rb family function
text: Understanding the mechanisms behind cell cycle exit is crucial for proper embryonic development and maintaining balance in the body. However, there is still much to learn about this process. In this study, we investigated the role of the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein and its family members, p107 and p130, in G0/G1 arrest and differentiation in mammalian cells. Surprisingly, we discovered that mouse embryos lacking all three Rb family members could survive until days 9-11 of gestation. Furthermore, some of these cells, particularly in epithelial and neural lineages, were able to exit the cell cycle in G0/G1 and differentiate both in teratomas and in culture. This ability of the triple knockout cells to arrest in G0/G1 was linked to the suppression of important E2F target genes. Therefore, G1 arrest does not always rely on Rb family members, highlighting the resilience of cell cycle regulatory networks during differentiation. Additionally, this finding opens up possibilities for identifying potential pathways to hinder the growth of cancer cells with mutations in the Rb pathway.

title: Induction of ectopic eyes by targeted expression of the eyeless gene in Drosophila.
text: The gene eyeless (ey) in Drosophila encodes a transcription factor that possesses both a paired domain and a homeodomain. It shares similarities with the Small eye (Pax-6) gene in mice and the Aniridia gene in humans. These genes exhibit significant sequence identity, conserve the position of three intron splice sites, and display similar expression patterns in the developing nervous system and the eye during morphogenesis. Loss-of-function mutations in both insect and mammalian genes have been observed to result in a reduction or absence of eye structures, indicating the involvement of ey in eye morphogenesis. Through targeted expression of the ey complementary DNA in various imaginal disc primordia of Drosophila, abnormal eye structures were induced on the wings, legs, and antennae. These ectopic eyes displayed normal morphology and consisted of fully differentiated ommatidia containing a complete set of photoreceptor cells. These findings provide evidence supporting the notion that ey serves as the master control gene for eye morphogenesis. Given the presence of homologous genes in vertebrates, ascidians, insects, cephalopods, and nemerteans, it is plausible that ey functions as a master control gene across the metazoa.

title: mir-1-mediated paracrine effect of cancer-associated fibroblasts on lung cancer cell proliferation and chemoresistance.
text: Lung cancer is the primary cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide in humans. Additionally, the survival rate after five years is only 15%. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for nearly 80% of all lung cancer cases. Within NSCLCs, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) have been identified in a significant number of cases. CAFs have been proven to play a role in promoting tumor progression, metastasis, and resistance to therapy through paracrine effects in various solid tumors. In this study, we first isolated CAFs from patient tissues and demonstrated their ability to enhance cell proliferation and resistance to cisplatin in lung cancer cell lines A549 and 95D through paracrine signaling. Secondly, using ELISA and quantitative PCR, we observed a higher presence of stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1) in CAFs compared to normal fibroblasts (NFs). Thirdly, we discovered that SDF-1 facilitated lung cancer cell proliferation and drug resistance by activating the CXCR4-mediated signaling pathway, involving NF-κB and Bcl-xL. Furthermore, we confirmed that the expression of SDF-1 in CAFs was negatively regulated by microRNA mir-1 through overexpression and quantitative PCR. Overall, our findings provide insight into the impact of CAFs on lung cancer cells and suggest CAFs as a potential target for therapeutic interventions in tumor treatment.

title: Genome-wide association analyses in East Asians identify new susceptibility loci for colorectal cancer
text:
In order to discover new genetic factors associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), we conducted a comprehensive study on the genomes of individuals of east Asian descent. By analyzing the genetic data of 2,098 CRC cases and 5,749 controls, we identified 64 potential SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) that showed promise for further investigation. These SNPs were then replicated in an independent set of samples, consisting of up to 5,358 cases and 5,922 controls. 

Through this process, we were able to identify four SNPs that displayed significant associations with CRC, with P values ranging from 8.58 × 10(-7) to 3.77 × 10(-10) in the combined analysis of all east Asian samples. To validate our findings, we conducted a separate study involving 26,060 individuals of European descent. In this study, three of the four SNPs were replicated, with combined P values of 1.22 × 10(-10) for rs647161 (located at 5q31.1), 6.64 × 10(-9) for rs2423279 (located at 20p12.3), and 3.06 × 10(-8) for rs10774214 (located at 12p13.32 near the CCND2 gene). These results were obtained through a meta-analysis of data from both east Asian and European-ancestry populations.

Overall, this study has successfully identified three new susceptibility loci for CRC and has provided valuable insights into the genetics and biology of this disease.

title: Long non-coding RNAs as novel players in β cell function and type 1 diabetes
text:
Background: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a subset of non-coding RNAs that play a crucial role in regulating gene expression in various disease conditions. These lncRNAs interact with RNA, DNA, or proteins to carry out their functions. Numerous studies have shown the involvement of lncRNAs in autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including type 1 diabetes (T1D). This review focuses on the emerging roles of lncRNAs in immune and islet β cell function, as well as the challenges and opportunities in understanding the development of T1D and its complications.

Conclusion: We emphasize that lncRNAs located within T1D-loci regions, along with regulatory variants and enhancer clusters, play a significant role in remodeling the chromatin structure in β cells. This, in turn, acts as a determinant for the regulation of islet cell transcriptional programs, both locally (cis) and distantly (trans).

title: Costs of the COPD. Differences between intensive care unit and respiratory intermediate care unit.
text: The aim of this study was to determine whether respiratory intermediate care units (RICUs) are a cost-effective alternative to intensive care units (ICUs) for patients with exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The study was conducted in 15 ICUs and 6 RICUs, using a multi-centre, prospective, bottom-up cost analysis. Patients with COPD who stayed in the hospital for more than 48 hours were included in the study, while those who came from other ICUs/RICUs, had immune-deficiency or stroke were excluded. After standardizing the ICU sample to match the RICU distribution of reasons for admission and use of vasoactive drugs upon admission, a total of 60 ICU patients and 65 RICU patients were included in the analysis, out of the original 164 recruited. Clinical data on admission and discharge, as well as daily information on resource consumption and costs, were recorded for each patient. The results showed that the total cost per patient was significantly lower in RICUs compared to ICUs (754 vs. 1507 Euro; P < 0.0001). Except for drugs and nutrition, all other cost items were significantly lower in RICUs. It was observed that deceased patients in ICUs had more severe disease compared to those in RICUs, while there was no significant difference in disease severity among surviving patients. In conclusion, this study suggests that RICUs may be a successful and cost-effective option for treating less severe COPD patients with pure respiratory failure.

title: eRNAs are required for p53-dependent enhancer activity and gene transcription.
text: The p53 tumor suppressor gene is able to regulate the transcription and cell-cycle progression of target genes involved in cell proliferation and survival by binding to them or nearby. Through genome-wide chromatin-binding profiles, we have discovered that p53 also binds to regions that are far away from any known p53 target gene. Interestingly, these regions contain conserved p53-binding sites and exhibit all the characteristics of enhancer regions. We have demonstrated that these p53-bound enhancer regions (p53BERs) indeed have enhancer activity and interact with multiple neighboring genes within the same chromosome to regulate transcription over long distances in a p53-dependent manner. Additionally, p53BERs produce enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) in a p53-dependent manner, which are necessary for efficient transcriptional enhancement of the interacting target genes and the induction of a p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest. Therefore, our findings reveal that p53 has the ability to enhance transcription and regulate multiple genes from a single genomic binding site. Furthermore, the production of eRNAs from p53BERs is crucial for the efficient enhancement of p53 transcription.

title: Induction of pluripotent stem cells from mouse embryonic fibroblasts by Oct4 and Klf4 with small-molecule compounds.
text: The combination of four transcription factors, Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/c-Myc or Oct4/Sox2/Nanog/LIN28, can induce somatic cells to become pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). This is a useful method for obtaining patient-specific cells for therapeutic and research purposes. However, there are still challenges to overcome in order for this approach to be applicable in therapy, mainly due to issues with efficiency and viral genome integration. Recent research has shown that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) can be reprogrammed into iPSCs by transducing them with Oct4/Klf4. Interestingly, NPCs naturally express Sox2, which may aid in the reprogramming process without the need for exogenous Sox2. In this study, we have discovered a combination of small molecules, BIX-01294 and BayK8644, that can enable the reprogramming of Oct4/Klf4-transduced mouse embryonic fibroblasts. These fibroblasts do not naturally express the factors necessary for reprogramming. Our findings demonstrate that small molecules identified through a phenotypic screen can compensate for the viral transduction of critical factors, such as Sox2, and enhance the efficiency of reprogramming.

title: Vps22/EAP30 in ESCRT-II mediates endosomal sorting of growth factor and chemokine receptors destined for lysosomal degradation.
text: In this study, we examined the involvement of the protein Hrs, which binds to ubiquitin, and the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT)-I and ESCRT-III in the sorting of receptors that have been endocytosed and ubiquitinated. Their role is to direct these receptors to lysosomes for degradation, thereby efficiently terminating signaling. Specifically, we investigated the function of the ESCRT-II subunit Vps22/EAP30 in the sorting of ubiquitinated receptors for degradation. We found that Vps22 was present in endosomes that contained epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFRs) that had been endocytosed, as well as Hrs, ESCRT-I, and ESCRT-III. When Vps22 was depleted using small interfering RNA, along with a decrease in other ESCRT-II subunits, the degradation of EGFR, its ligand EGF, and the chemokine receptor CXCR4 was greatly reduced. In cells lacking Vps22, EGFR accumulated on the membranes of early endosomes and formed abnormally small multivesicular bodies. Depletion of Hrs or the ESCRT-I subunit Tsg101 resulted in sustained phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of extracellular-signal-regulated kinase1/2 downstream of the EGF-activated receptor. However, this was not observed when Vps22 was depleted. These findings highlight the important role of Vps22 in the turnover of EGFR and CXCR4 induced by ligands, and suggest that termination of EGF signaling occurs before ESCRT-II is engaged.

title: XPG stabilizes TFIIH, allowing transactivation of nuclear receptors: implications for Cockayne syndrome in XP-G/CS patients.
text: Inherited photosensitive disorder, xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) associated with Cockayne syndrome (XP-G/CS), is caused by mutations in the human XPG gene. The clinical features of CS in XP-G/CS patients are challenging to understand based solely on a defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER). Our research has revealed that XPG forms a stable complex with TFIIH, which is involved in transcription and NER. Mutations in XPG found in XP-G/CS patient cells disrupt the association with TFIIH, leading to the dissociation of CAK and XPD from the core TFIIH. Consequently, the phosphorylation and transactivation of nuclear receptors are disrupted in XP-G/CS and xpg(-/-) MEF cells, but can be restored by introducing wild-type XPG. These findings shed light on the role of XPG in stabilizing TFIIH and regulating gene expression, providing an explanation for some of the clinical features observed in XP-G/CS.

title: Metabolic cycling in single yeast cells from unsynchronized steady-state populations limited on glucose or phosphate.
text: The "metabolic cycle," which is typically observed in prestarved, continuous cultures of yeast, is associated with oscillations in the expression patterns of a significant portion of yeast genes. To investigate whether these oscillations occur in single cells taken from unsynchronized cultures that are exponentially growing in chemostats, we conducted FISH experiments on mRNA in individual cells. By utilizing gene-expression data from synchronized cultures, we were able to predict the simultaneous appearance of mRNAs from pairs of genes in the unsynchronized cells. Our quantitative analysis of the FISH results confirms that individual unsynchronized cells, which are growing slowly due to glucose or phosphate limitation, exhibit the predicted oscillations. Therefore, we can conclude that the yeast metabolic cycle is an inherent characteristic of yeast metabolism and is not reliant on either synchronization or external limitations imposed by the carbon source.

title: in polyploid species
text: The Yeast Gene Order Browser (YGOB; http://wolfe.gen.tcd.ie/ygob) was created to simplify the visual comparison and computational analysis of synteny relationships in yeasts. The data available in YGOB currently covers seven species and is derived from meticulously curated sets of homologous genes. These genes were selected based on both sequence similarity and genomic context (synteny). We have successfully merged various lists of paralogous gene pairs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae resulting from genome duplication (known as ohnologs). Additionally, we provide comprehensive lists of ohnolog pairs that are retained in S. cerevisiae (551 pairs, including 22 previously unidentified), Saccharomyces castellii (599 pairs), and Candida glabrata (404 pairs).

title: Immune complex relay by subcapsular sinus macrophages and non-cognate B cells drives antibody affinity maturation
text: The properties of subcapsular sinus (SCS) macrophages, which play a role in capturing antigens from lymph and presenting them to B cells, are not well understood. In this study, we found that the development of SCS macrophages relies on lymphotoxin-alpha1beta2. These cells have low expression of lysosomal enzymes and keep opsonized antigens on their surface. Through intravital imaging, we observed immune complexes being transported by macrophage processes into the follicle. Additionally, we discovered that noncognate B cells can transfer antigen opsonized by newly produced antibodies from the subcapsular region to the germinal center. Disruption of this transport process impairs affinity maturation. Overall, our findings characterize SCS macrophages as specialized antigen-presenting cells that function at the top of an antigen transport chain, promoting humoral immunity.

title: Promoter decoding of transcription factor dynamics involves a trade-off between noise and control of gene expression
text: The activation of transcription factors (TFs) contains valuable information about upstream signals, but how downstream genes interpret this information is not well understood. To address this, we used microfluidics to control the movement of the budding yeast TF Msn2 between the nucleus and cytoplasm. Through our experiments, we uncovered the principles that govern how different gene promoters convert the dynamic input of Msn2 into gene expression output in individual cells. By combining modeling and experiments, we categorized promoters based on their signal-processing behavior and discovered that the dynamics of Msn2 can encode multiple distinct gene expression programs. We found that both oscillatory TF dynamics and slow promoter kinetics result in higher noise in gene expression. Additionally, we observed a relationship between the timescale of promoter activation and nucleosome remodeling. Our findings suggest a fundamental trade-off: while the cell can utilize different types of promoters to control gene expression using TF dynamics, the amount of information that can be encoded in the dynamics of a single TF and reliably interpreted by promoters is limited by gene expression noise.

title: GaAs nanopillar-array solar cells employing in situ surface passivation
text:
Arrays of III-V direct-bandgap semiconductor nanopillars are a promising option for photovoltaic applications. This is due to their high optical absorption coefficients, which minimize reflection through light trapping. Additionally, they allow for efficient charge collection in the radial direction and can be synthesized on low-cost platforms.

However, the increased surface area of these nanopillar arrays leads to the presence of surface states that hinder the power conversion efficiency. In this study, we present the first demonstration of GaAs nanopillar-array photovoltaics using epitaxial passivation. This passivation technique involves the growth of high-bandgap epitaxial InGaP shells in situ, which cap the radial p-n junctions and alleviate the effects of surface states.

When exposed to light, these photovoltaic devices exhibit open-circuit voltages of 0.44 V, short-circuit current densities of 24.3 mA cm(-2), and fill factors of 62%. Moreover, they demonstrate high external quantum efficiencies exceeding 70% across the spectral range of interest.

To further enhance their performance, we utilize a novel transparent ohmic anode made from a titanium/indium tin oxide annealed alloy. This anode allows for efficient electrical contact while maintaining transparency.

Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of GaAs nanopillar-array photovoltaics with epitaxial passivation as a viable option for high-efficiency solar energy conversion.

title: Roles of histone acetylation and chromatin remodeling factor in a meiotic recombination hotspot.
text: Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling factors (ADCRs) play a role in selectively regulating genes by modifying the local chromatin configuration. In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the activation of the recombination hotspot ade6-M26 is mediated by a cAMP responsive element (CRE)-like sequence called M26, and a heterodimeric ATF/CREB transcription factor known as Atf1.Pcr1. During meiosis, chromatin remodeling occurs around M26. To understand the involvement of HATs and ADCRs in this process, we investigated their roles in chromatin remodeling around M26. We found that histones H3 and H4 around M26 were hyperacetylated early in meiosis in an M26- and Atf1-dependent manner. The S. pombe homolog of Gcn5p, called SpGcn5, was primarily responsible for histone H3 acetylation around M26 in vivo. Deleting gcn5+ caused a significant delay in chromatin remodeling, but only a partial reduction in M26 meiotic recombination frequency. However, when the snf22+ gene (a homologue of Swi2/Snf2-ADCR) was deleted, along with gcn5+, chromatin remodeling was completely abolished, and there was a significant reduction in meiotic recombination around M26. These findings suggest that HATs and ADCRs work together to modify the local chromatin structure, similar to selective transcription activation, to activate meiotic recombination at M26 in a specific location.

title: The Somatic Genomic Landscape of Glioblastoma
text: We present a comprehensive analysis of over 500 glioblastoma tumors, revealing the landscape of somatic genomic alterations. Our study uncovers new mutated genes and complex rearrangements in key receptors like EGFR and PDGFRA. We also find that TERT promoter mutations are associated with increased mRNA expression, suggesting a role in telomerase reactivation. Additionally, our analysis confirms that the proneural subtype's survival advantage is linked to the G-CIMP phenotype, while MGMT DNA methylation may only predict treatment response in classical subtype GBM. Furthermore, our integrative analysis of genomic and proteomic profiles challenges the idea of targeting a pathway instead of the specific target itself. These findings will aid in identifying potential therapeutic and diagnostic targets, validating research and clinical observations, and generating new hypotheses to enhance our understanding of this deadly cancer.

title: Radioiodine treatment of multinodular non-toxic goitre.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the long-term effects of radioactive iodine on thyroid function and size in patients with non-toxic multinodular goitre. The study design involved selecting consecutive patients with multinodular non-toxic goitre for radioactive iodine treatment and following them for a minimum of 12 months (median 48 months) after receiving an intended dose of 3.7 MBq/g thyroid tissue corrected to a 100% uptake of iodine-131 in 24 hours.

The study included 69 patients with a growing multinodular non-toxic goitre that caused local compression symptoms or cosmetic inconveniences. The treatment was chosen for patients with a high operative risk, previous thyroidectomy, or those who refused surgery. The main outcome measurements included standard thyroid function variables and ultrasonically determined thyroid volume before treatment, as well as at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months after treatment, and then once a year.

The results showed that 56 patients were treated with a single dose of 131I, 12 with two doses, and one with four doses. Among the 45 patients treated with one dose who remained euthyroid, the median thyroid volume decreased from 73 ml (interquartile range 50-106 ml) to 29 ml (23-48 ml) at 24 months in the 39 patients in whom this was measured during follow-up. The median reduction was 40 ml (22-48 ml), representing a 60% reduction (p < 0.0001), with half of the reduction occurring within three months. Patients treated with two doses, as well as those who developed hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, also experienced a significant reduction in thyroid volume. Eleven patients developed hypothyroidism, with a cumulative five-year risk of 22% (95% confidence interval 4.8% to 38.4%). Side effects were minimal, with three cases of hyperthyroidism and two cases of radiation thyroiditis. Only one patient expressed dissatisfaction with the results and was referred for surgery six months after treatment.

In conclusion, the study found that radioactive iodine treatment resulted in a substantial reduction in thyroid volume, accompanied by a low incidence of hypothyroidism and minimal side effects. This makes radioactive iodine a promising alternative to surgery for selected cases of non-toxic multinodular goitre.

title: Alterations in microRNA-124 and AMPA receptors contribute to social behavioral deficits in frontotemporal dementia
text: The causes of behavioral deficits in neurodegenerative diseases like frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are not well understood. In this study, we examined the effects of a mutant CHMP2B gene associated with FTD when expressed specifically in the forebrain of mice. We found that this expression led to various age-dependent neurodegenerative symptoms, including impairments in social behavior. These social deficits were accompanied by changes in the composition of AMPA receptors (AMPARs), which are involved in calcium signaling. Specifically, there was an imbalance between AMPARs that allow calcium to enter the cell (Ca(2+)-permeable) and those that do not (Ca(2+)-impermeable). The expression of most AMPAR subunits was regulated by a brain-specific microRNA called miR-124, which was significantly reduced in the superficial layers of the cerebral cortex in mice expressing the mutant CHMP2B gene. We observed similar changes in miR-124 and AMPAR levels in the frontal cortex and neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of individuals with behavioral variant FTD. Additionally, when we artificially increased miR-124 expression in the medial prefrontal cortex of mutant mice, AMPAR levels decreased and some behavioral deficits were partially rescued. Knocking down the AMPAR subunit Gria2 also improved social impairments. These findings reveal a previously unknown mechanism involving miR-124 and AMPARs in the regulation of social behavior in FTD, suggesting a potential therapeutic approach.

title: Activated AMPK boosts the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling axis—A role for the unfolded protein response
text: We conducted a study to explore the interaction between nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and AMP-activated kinase (AMPK), which are key regulators of cellular redox and energy balance. Using xanthohumol (XN) as an activator of both AMPK and Nrf2 signaling pathways, we found that AMPK positively influences Nrf2/heme oxygenase (HO)-1 signaling in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. When we genetically removed or pharmacologically inhibited AMPK, the expression of Nrf2-dependent HO-1 was reduced by XN at the mRNA level. XN activates AMPK by affecting mitochondrial function and activating liver kinase B1 as an upstream AMPK kinase. The subsequent enhancement of the Nrf2/HO-1 response by AMPK does not rely on inhibiting the mammalian target of rapamycin, inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase 3β, or altering the abundance of Nrf2. However, we did observe a decrease in endoplasmic reticulum stress, which contributes to the AMPK-augmented Nrf2/HO-1 response. Overall, our findings provide further insight into the previously unclear interaction between the LKB1/AMPK and Nrf2/HO-1 pathways, highlighting the involvement of the unfolded protein response as an additional factor and suggesting close cooperation between signaling pathways that control cellular redox, energy, and protein homeostasis.

title: The IDEAL recommendations and urological innovation
text: Urology, like other surgical branches, has faced significant challenges in aligning the research processes for evaluating new interventions with the principles of Evidence-Based Medicine.
