This article discusses the IDEAL framework and recommendations, and how they can impact the assessment of controversial urological procedures. From an insider's perspective, we provide an overview of the efforts made by the IDEAL Working Group, with a focus on Urology. There are notable differences between drugs and interventions when it comes to the evolution of innovations. The traditional framework for conducting trials of new treatments is primarily based on drugs, which can lead to significant issues when evaluating surgical innovations using the same approach. The difficulties in conducting randomized controlled trials for surgical techniques and the continued reliance on case series in scientific literature have been the most contentious aspects of this mismatch between research subject and methodology. The IDEAL framework offers a comprehensive description of the innovation and development process for surgical trials, along with recommendations for alternative study designs that address the specific challenges of new techniques. IDEAL presents a fresh framework for surgical innovation, developed with input from the surgical community, and is expected to revolutionize the way urologists conduct clinical research.

title: Prolonged conservative care versus early surgery in patients with sciatica caused by lumbar disc herniation: two year results of a randomised controlled trial.
text: AIMS To assess the impact of early lumbar disc surgery compared to prolonged conservative care on patients with sciatica over a two-year period. DESIGN A randomized controlled trial. LOCATION Nine hospitals in the Netherlands. PARTICIPANTS 283 patients experiencing sciatica for 6-12 weeks. INTERVENTIONS Early surgery or conservative treatment for six months, with the option of delayed surgery if necessary. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Scores from the Roland disability questionnaire for sciatica, visual analogue scale for leg pain, and Likert self-rating scale of global perceived recovery. RESULTS Out of the 141 patients assigned to early surgery, 125 (89%) underwent microdiscectomy. Among the 142 patients assigned to conservative treatment, 62 (44%) eventually required surgery, with seven undergoing surgery in the second year of follow-up. There was no significant difference in disability scores between the two treatment groups over the first two years (P=0.25). Patients randomized to early surgery experienced faster improvement in leg pain, with a significant difference in "areas under the curves" over two years (P=0.05). However, this short-term benefit of early surgery was no longer significant after six months and continued to decrease between six months and 24 months. Patient satisfaction slightly decreased for both groups between one and two years. At the two-year mark, 20% of all patients reported an unsatisfactory outcome. CONCLUSIONS Early surgery provided quicker relief for sciatica compared to conservative care, but outcomes were similar after one year and remained consistent in the second year. TRIAL REGISTRY ISRCT No 26872154.

title: Human papillomavirus testing for the detection of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancer: final results of the POBASCAM randomised controlled trial.
text: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of HPV DNA testing in the first round of cervical screening on the detection of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 3 or worse, CIN grade 2 or worse, and cervical cancer in the second round of screening. The study was conducted in the Netherlands from January 1999 to September 2002, and women aged 29-56 years participating in the cervical screening program were randomly assigned to receive HPV DNA and cytology co-testing or cytology testing alone. The primary endpoint was the number of CIN grade 3 or worse detected. The results showed that HPV DNA testing in the first round led to a decrease in the detection of CIN grade 3 or worse and cervical cancer in the second round. Additionally, the detection of CIN grade 2 or worse was higher in the intervention group compared to the control group. The study supports the use of HPV DNA testing for all women aged 29 years and older in cervical screening programs. The study was funded by the Netherlands Organisation for Health Research and Development.

title: Epigenetic therapy activates type I interferon signaling in murine ovarian cancer to reduce immunosuppression and tumor burden.
text: Ovarian cancer, the most deadly among gynecological cancers, necessitates the development of new treatments. Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is characterized by a microenvironment that suppresses the immune system, and the response to immune therapies for ovarian cancer has been disappointing thus far. However, in a mouse model of EOC, we have discovered that clinically relevant doses of DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors (DNMTi and HDACi) can reduce the immune suppressive microenvironment through type I IFN signaling, leading to an improved response to immune checkpoint therapy. These findings demonstrate that the DNMTi 5-azacytidine (AZA) requires a type I IFN response to effectively combat tumors in vivo. By activating type I IFN signaling, AZA increases the presence of CD45+ immune cells and the percentage of active CD8+ T and natural killer (NK) cells in the tumor microenvironment, while simultaneously reducing tumor size and extending survival. AZA also enhances the expression of viral defense genes in both tumor and immune cells, and decreases the percentage of macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells in the tumor microenvironment. When combined with an HDACi, AZA further enhances the modulation of the immune microenvironment, particularly by increasing T and NK cell activation and reducing macrophages compared to AZA treatment alone, resulting in even greater survival rates for the mice. Finally, a triple combination of DNMTi/HDACi and the immune checkpoint inhibitor α-PD-1 demonstrates the most effective antitumor effect and longest overall survival, making it a promising candidate for future clinical trials in ovarian cancer.

title: IGF2 is parentally imprinted during human embryogenesis and in the Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome
text: Parental imprinting is a phenomenon where a specific parental allele of certain genes on chromosomes is preferentially expressed. This phenomenon has only been observed in mice until now. In this study, we demonstrate that the allele of the human insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene inherited from the father is the only one active in embryonic and extra-embryonic cells during the first trimester of pregnancy. Furthermore, we found that only the paternal allele is expressed in tissues from a patient with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. These findings suggest that the parental imprinting of IGF2 is conserved from mice to humans and has implications for the development of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

title: Safety and reliability of Radio Frequency Identification Devices in Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Computed Tomography
text: In this study, the researchers aimed to assess the safety and reliability of RFID devices worn on the skin during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scanning in hospitals. They tested sixty RFID tags of two types, I-Code SLI, with different antenna sizes. The tests included evaluating signal loss, movement of the devices, and heat generation in MRI systems with different strengths. Additionally, the data integrity of the tags was tested during CT scanning. The results showed that there was no memory loss or data alteration in the RFID tags after the scanning procedures. The heating and movement of the devices were within acceptable limits. However, there was some signal loss, which affected the interpretability of MR images when assessing superficial structures. In conclusion, patients wearing RFID wristbands are safe during MRI and CT scanning in specific conditions, using the tested RFID tags.

title: LXR-Dependent Gene Expression Is Important for Macrophage Survival and the Innate Immune Response
text: The liver X receptors (LXRs) are nuclear receptors that have established functions in controlling lipid metabolism. Our research reveals that LXR signaling not only regulates the metabolism of cholesterol in macrophages but also affects their ability to fight against microbial infections. Mice lacking LXRs are highly vulnerable to infection by the intracellular bacteria Listeria monocytogenes (LM). Through bone marrow transplant experiments, we have determined that the susceptibility is primarily due to altered macrophage function. When challenged with LM, LXR-deficient macrophages undergo accelerated apoptosis and struggle to clear the bacteria in vivo. These deficiencies are, at least in part, caused by the loss of regulation of the antiapoptotic factor SPalpha, which is directly controlled by LXRalpha. The expression of LXRalpha or SPalpha in macrophages inhibits apoptosis during LM infection. Our findings demonstrate that LXR-dependent gene expression unexpectedly plays a role in innate immunity and suggest that common nuclear receptor pathways are involved in macrophage responses to modified lipoproteins and intracellular pathogens.

title: Alterations on peripheral B cell subsets following an acute uncomplicated clinical malaria infection in children
text: The impact of Plasmodium falciparum on B-cell balance has not been thoroughly studied. This research aimed to determine if acute malaria in young children leads to changes in the peripheral B cell characteristics. By using flow-cytofluorimetric analysis, the B cell phenotypes in the peripheral blood of children aged 2-5 years were examined during an episode of acute uncomplicated clinical malaria, four weeks after recovery, and in healthy age-matched controls. The results showed a significant decrease in CD19+ B lymphocytes during acute malaria. Additionally, the analysis of CD19+ B cell subsets based on IgD and CD38 expression revealed a decrease in naive 1 CD38-IgD+ B cells and an increase in CD38+IgD- memory 3 B cells during acute malaria. Further examination of the peripheral B cell characteristics also identified an expansion of transitional CD10+CD19+ B cells in children after an episode of acute malaria, with this subset accounting for up to 25% of the total CD19+ B cell pool. In conclusion, children with acute uncomplicated clinical malaria experience significant disruptions in B cell balance.

title: SETD2: an epigenetic modifier with tumor suppressor functionality
text: Over the past decade, significant advancements have been made in our understanding of the epigenetic regulatory machinery. It is now evident that genetic abnormalities in multiple epigenetic modifier proteins are linked to various forms of cancer. Additionally, targeting the epigenome has emerged as a promising approach for treating cancer patients. Recently, the development of drugs that specifically target SETD2-negative tumors has been reported. In this review, we delve into the research surrounding Set domain containing 2 (SETD2), a histone modifier that has only recently been associated with cancer formation. Our review begins by examining the structural characteristics of SETD2 and expands to its function by analyzing studies conducted on SETD2 in yeast, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, mice, and humans. SETD2 is now recognized as the sole human gene responsible for the trimethylation of lysine 36 of Histone H3 (H3K36). The impact of this histone modification is determined by H3K36me3 readers, which recruit protein complexes to carry out specific processes such as transcription elongation, RNA processing, and DNA repair. Lastly, we discuss the prevalence of SETD2-inactivating mutations in cancer, with clear cell Renal Cell Cancer exhibiting the highest frequency, and explore how SETD2 inactivation may contribute to tumor development.

title: Updated energy budgets for neural computation in the neocortex and cerebellum.
text: The brain's ability to process information and produce functional imaging signals is determined by its energy supply. Previous estimates of energy usage in the neural information processing of the grey matter in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex need to be reevaluated. Recent research has shown that action potentials in mammalian neurons are more energy efficient than previously believed. This paper presents revised estimates for the energy expenditure in neural computation, using a simple model for the cerebral cortex and a detailed model of the cerebellar cortex. In the cerebral cortex, the majority of energy (50%) is used by postsynaptic glutamate receptors, followed by 21% for action potentials, 20% for resting potentials, 5% for presynaptic transmitter release, and 4% for transmitter recycling. In the cerebellar cortex, excitatory neurons use 75% of the energy, while inhibitory neurons use 25%. Non-principal neurons, particularly Purkinje cells, consume only 15% of the energy for information processing. The majority of energy in the cerebellar cortex is used for maintaining resting potentials (54%) and postsynaptic receptors (22%), with action potentials accounting for only 17% of the energy usage.

title: Plasma homocysteine is a risk factor for recurrent vascular events in young patients with an ischaemic stroke or TIA
text:
Patients who are young and have experienced an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) often do not have any vascular risk factors. While hyperhomocysteinaemia is a known risk factor for stroke in elderly patients, it is unclear whether it also plays a significant role in the prognosis of young patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA. To investigate this, we conducted a study to examine the potential impact of plasma homocysteine levels on the risk of recurrent vascular events in patients aged 18 to 45 years. 

Our study included 161 consecutive patients who had recently suffered a cerebral infarction or TIA. We collected data on the primary event and homocysteine levels retrospectively from hospital records. We also contacted general practitioners and patients by telephone to gather information on vascular events and the medications used during the follow-up period. Vascular events considered in the study included cerebral infarction, TIA, pulmonary embolism, venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and peripheral arterial disease. 

Analysis of the data revealed a dose-effect relationship between the length of event-free survival and tertiles of homocysteine levels, as shown by a Kaplan-Meier curve (Log rank statistic 5.91; p = 0.05). After adjusting for homocysteine lowering treatment, the Cox hazard ratio was 1.7 (95% CI, 1.1 to 2.8) for any vascular outcome event, 1.9 (95% CI, 1.1 to 3.0) for arterial outcome events, and 1.8 (95% CI, 1.1 to 2.9) for cerebral outcome events. Despite the limited number of outcome events, we found a significant association at the 95% confidence level between homocysteine levels and the risk of recurrent vascular events in young patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA. This association is comparable in magnitude to that observed in elderly individuals.

title: LDL inhibits the mediation of cholesterol efflux from macrophage foam cells by apoA-I-containing lipoproteins. A putative mechanism for foam cell formation.
text: Although the build-up of cholesterol in macrophages is believed to be an initial step in the development of atherosclerosis, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), a major risk factor for the disease, does not directly contribute to cholesterol accumulation in macrophages. Conversely, lipoproteins containing apolipoprotein (apo) A-I have the ability to remove cholesterol from cholesterol-loaded macrophages (known as foam cells) and prevent further cholesterol accumulation. We conducted a study to investigate the impact of LDL on cholesterol removal by two types of apoA-I-containing lipoproteins: one containing only apoA-I (LpA-I) and the other containing both apoA-I and apoA-II (LpA-I/A-II). When foam cells were exposed to LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II, the amount of cellular cholesterol decreased. However, when LDL was introduced, the cholesterol-reducing abilities of these lipoproteins were progressively inhibited in a dose-dependent manner. In the presence of LDL, LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II primarily removed free cholesterol from LDL rather than from the plasma membrane of foam cells. Additionally, a significant portion of cellular cholesterol was directly transferred to LDL instead of LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II. However, the cholesterol that moved to LDL was fully compensated by the influx of cholesterol from LDL to foam cells. Consequently, the net cholesterol efflux (a combination of influx and efflux) from foam cells was hindered by LDL. These findings suggest that LDL may accelerate the formation of foam cells by impeding cholesterol removal from these cells. Moreover, elevated levels of LDL in the bloodstream may pose a risk for atherosclerosis by impairing the function of LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II at the cellular level.

title: Sugar-sweetened beverages, weight gain, and incidence of type 2 diabetes in young and middle-aged women.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the link between the consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and weight gain and the risk of type 2 diabetes in women. The study was conducted from 1991 to 1999 among women in the Nurses' Health Study II. The analysis included 91,249 women who were free of diabetes and other major chronic diseases at the start of the study. The weight change analysis included 51,603 women who had complete dietary information and body weight measurements in 1991, 1995, and 1999. During the follow-up period, 741 cases of confirmed type 2 diabetes were identified.

The results showed that women who increased their consumption of sugar-sweetened soft drinks from 1 or fewer drinks per week to 1 or more drinks per day had the highest weight gain over a 4-year period. On the other hand, women who decreased their intake had the smallest weight gain. Similar findings were observed for fruit punch consumption. After adjusting for lifestyle and dietary factors, women who consumed 1 or more sugar-sweetened soft drinks per day had a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to those who consumed less than 1 of these beverages per month. The same trend was observed for fruit punch consumption.

In conclusion, higher consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with greater weight gain and an increased risk of type 2 diabetes in women. This may be due to the excessive calories and large amounts of rapidly absorbable sugars present in these beverages.

title: Pancreatic stellate cells: partners in crime with pancreatic cancer cells.
text:
The role of pancreatic stellate cells (PSC) in pancreatic cancer progression is not fully understood. To investigate this, we conducted experiments using an orthotopic model of pancreatic cancer and cultured human PSCs (hPSC) along with human pancreatic cancer cell lines MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1. Athymic mice were injected with saline, hPSCs, MiaPaCa-2 cells, or hPSCs + MiaPaCa-2 into the pancreas. After 7 weeks, we assessed tumor size, metastases, and tumor histology. In vitro studies were also conducted to examine the effects of cancer cell secretions on PSC migration and the effects of hPSC secretions on cancer cell proliferation, apoptosis, and migration. We also investigated potential mediators of the effects of hPSC secretions on cancer cell proliferation using neutralizing antibodies. 

Compared to mice receiving MiaPaCa-2 cells alone, mice injected with hPSCs + MiaPaCa-2 showed increased tumor size, regional and distant metastasis, fibrotic bands (desmoplasia) containing activated PSCs within tumors, and increased tumor cell numbers. In vitro studies revealed that PSC migration was significantly increased in the presence of pancreatic cancer cells. Additionally, hPSC secretions induced the proliferation and migration of MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1 cells, while inhibiting apoptosis. The proliferative effect of hPSC secretions on pancreatic cancer cells was inhibited when a neutralizing antibody to platelet-derived growth factor was present. 

Our findings suggest a significant interaction between pancreatic cancer cells and stromal cells (PSCs), indicating that pancreatic cancer cells recruit stromal cells to create an environment that promotes cancer progression.

title: Preoperative statin treatment reduces systemic inflammatory response and myocardial damage in cardiac surgery.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate whether taking statins before cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) can reduce systemic inflammatory response (SIR) and markers of myocardial damage. A prospective cohort of 138 patients who underwent coronary and valvular surgery with CPB were included in the study. The patients were divided into two groups: group A consisted of 72 patients who took statins, and group B consisted of 66 patients who did not take statins. Blood samples were collected before surgery and at various time points after surgery to measure levels of pro-inflammatory interleukins (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-2R), creatine phosphokinase (CPK), CPK-MB, and troponin I. 

The results showed that there were no significant differences in baseline characteristics, operative outcomes, and postoperative morbidity and mortality between the two groups. However, group A had significantly lower levels of IL-6 at 6h, 24h, and before hospital discharge compared to group B. Group A also had lower average IL-6 levels in the first 24h after surgery. Additionally, the group treated with statins had lower levels of CPK-MB at 24h and troponin I levels at the end of the surgery and at 24h compared to the group not taking statins. 

In conclusion, preoperative treatment with statins is associated with lower levels of SIR and myocardial damage markers following cardiac surgery with CPB, regardless of whether it is coronary bypass grafting (CABG) or valvular surgery.

title: MEGA7: Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis Version 7.0 for Bigger Datasets.
text:
Introducing the latest edition of Mega, the Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis software. This upgraded version offers a wide range of advanced methods and tools for phylogenomics and phylomedicine. Notably, Mega has been optimized for 64-bit computing systems, enabling the analysis of larger datasets. Researchers can now explore and analyze tens of thousands of sequences using Mega. 

Additionally, this new version includes a sophisticated wizard for constructing timetrees and a novel feature that automatically predicts gene duplication events in gene family trees. The 64-bit Mega is accessible through two interfaces: graphical and command line. The graphical user interface (GUI) is a native application for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X. Meanwhile, the command line Mega is available as native applications for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X. These versions are specifically designed for high-throughput and scripted analysis. 

Both the graphical and command line versions of Mega can be downloaded free of charge from www.megasoftware.net.

title: DNA replication fidelity
text: The accuracy of DNA replication plays a crucial role in maintaining the stability of the genome and is essential for the evolution of species and the development of human diseases. In this review, we examine our current knowledge of replication accuracy, focusing on the structural and biochemical investigations of DNA polymerases. These studies have provided valuable insights into the significance of hydrogen bonding, base pair geometry, and conformational changes induced by substrates in maintaining accuracy. Additionally, they have uncovered the interactions between polymerases and the DNA minor groove, both at and before the active site, which influence the selection of nucleotides, the efficiency of proofreading, and the occurrence of errors due to misalignments. We highlight the common features that contribute to the accuracy of any DNA synthesis process and explore the reasons behind variations in fidelity based on the enzymes, errors, and local sequence environment.

title: Viable neutrophils release mitochondrial DNA to form neutrophil extracellular traps
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are structures outside of cells that can bind and kill microorganisms. It is believed that they are created when neutrophils die, allowing these dying or dead cells to eliminate microbes. Our research demonstrates that when neutrophils are exposed to granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and then stimulated with toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) or complement factor 5a (C5a) receptors for a short period of time, they can produce NETs while still being alive. Surprisingly, the NETs formed by living cells contain mitochondrial DNA but not nuclear DNA. By using drugs or genetic methods to prevent the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), we found that NET formation relies on ROS. Additionally, neutrophils stimulated with GM-CSF and C5a had better survival rates compared to resting neutrophils that did not produce NETs. In conclusion, the release of mitochondrial DNA by neutrophils and the formation of NETs do not require neutrophil death and do not shorten the lifespan of these cells.

title: ATP-driven exchange of histone H2AZ variant catalyzed by SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex.
text: The important role of the conserved histone variant H2AZ in gene expression regulation and the prevention of silent heterochromatin spread is well-established. However, the process of incorporating histone variants like H2AZ into nucleosomes has remained unclear. Our research has revealed that Swr1, a Swi2/Snf2-related adenosine triphosphatase, serves as the catalytic core of a multisubunit histone-variant exchanger. This exchanger efficiently replaces conventional histone H2A with H2AZ in nucleosome arrays. In vivo, Swr1 is essential for depositing H2AZ at specific chromosome locations, and both Swr1 and H2AZ play a role in regulating a subset of yeast genes. These findings shed light on a previously unknown function of the adenosine triphosphate-dependent chromatin remodeling machinery.

title: FACT Disrupts Nucleosome Structure by Binding H2A-H2B with Conserved Peptide Motifs.
text: The essential histone chaperone FACT is composed of Spt16 and Pob3, forming a heterodimer. Our study demonstrates that the binding activity between H2A-H2B, which is crucial for FACT's function, is located in short acidic regions near the C termini of each subunit. Mutations in these regions have an impact on binding and result in correlated phenotypes that can range from mild to lethal. Surprisingly, the most significant contributions to binding come from an aromatic residue and a nearby carboxylate residue within each domain. Spt16 and Pob3 bind to overlapping sites on H2A-H2B, and the Spt16-Pob3 heterodimers simultaneously bind to two H2A-H2B dimers, which is the same stoichiometry as the components of a nucleosome. By analyzing the crystal structure of Spt16 in complex with H2A-H2B, we are able to explain the biochemical and genetic data, propose a model for Pob3 binding, and suggest a mechanism for FACT reorganization, which we have confirmed through biochemical experiments. Additionally, we have discovered unexpected similarities between the binding of ANP32E and Swr1 with H2A.Z-H2B, indicating that various H2A-H2B chaperones utilize common mechanisms to bind histones and regulate nucleosome functions.

title: Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in mechanism of metformin action.
text:
Metformin is a commonly used medication for managing type 2 diabetes, but its exact cellular mechanism of action is not well understood. It works by reducing the production of glucose in the liver and increasing its utilization in the body, leading to lower blood sugar levels. Additionally, metformin has been found to have positive effects on lipid levels, particularly in reducing fatty liver. This is believed to be due to its activation of a protein called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which plays a major role in regulating both lipid and glucose metabolism.

In our study, we discovered that metformin activates AMPK in liver cells, resulting in a decrease in the activity of an enzyme called acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC). This leads to an increase in the oxidation of fatty acids and a suppression of the expression of enzymes involved in lipogenesis (the production of lipids). Furthermore, metformin's activation of AMPK also inhibits the expression of a key transcription factor called SREBP-1, which is involved in lipogenesis.

In rats treated with metformin, we observed a reduction in the expression of SREBP-1 and other lipogenic genes, as well as a decrease in the activity of ACC, which is a target of AMPK. To confirm the role of AMPK in metformin's effects, we used a new inhibitor of AMPK and found that its activation is necessary for metformin to inhibit glucose production in liver cells.

We also investigated the effects of metformin on glucose uptake in isolated rat skeletal muscles and found that it stimulates glucose uptake when AMPK is activated.

Overall, our findings suggest that the activation of AMPK is responsible for the various beneficial effects of metformin. This knowledge opens up possibilities for developing alternative methods of modulating AMPK for the treatment of metabolic disorders.

title: Interferon alfa therapy for chronic hepatitis B in children: a multinational randomized controlled trial.
text:
The purpose of this study was to assess the safety and effectiveness of interferon alfa (IFN-alpha) in children with chronic hepatitis B and elevated transaminase levels. The study involved administering IFN-alpha2b to some children while others received no treatment. After 24 weeks of therapy and 48 weeks of observation in the control group, the clearance of viral replication markers was evaluated. 

Out of the 149 children enrolled, 144 were included in the analysis (70 treated and 74 controls). It was found that 26% of treated children and 11% of controls had negative serum hepatitis B e antigen and viral DNA (P < 0.05). Responders also experienced normalized aminotransferase levels and improved liver histology. Additionally, 10% of treated patients and 1% of controls had undetectable hepatitis B surface antigen. The only significant predictors of response were female gender and interferon treatment, while factors such as ethnic origin, baseline aminotransferase level, initial DNA levels, and histology did not correlate with response. 

Most adverse reactions were mild or moderate, and the dose had to be reduced in 24% of children. In conclusion, IFN-alpha promotes the elimination of viral replication markers and surface antigen, as well as improves aminotransferases and histology in children with chronic hepatitis B.

title: ImmTACs for targeted cancer therapy: Why, what, how, and which.
text:
Overcoming immunosuppression and activating a cytotoxic T cell response has the potential to stop the progression of cancer and, in certain cases, eliminate it completely. However, developing therapeutic interventions that achieve this goal has proven to be quite challenging. Fortunately, there is now a better understanding of the complexities of immune responses, which is starting to yield some significant breakthroughs.

One such breakthrough is the development of ImmTACs (immune-mobilising monoclonal TCRs against cancer), which belong to a new class of bispecific reagents. These reagents are based on soluble monoclonal T cell receptors that have been engineered to have an extremely high affinity for the specific tumor antigen. This overcomes the issue of low affinity tumor-specific T cells that are limited by thymic selection. ImmTACs also provide access to a wide range of antigens presented as peptide-HLA complexes.

When ImmTACs bind to tumor cells, the anti-CD3 effector end of the ImmTAC recruits polyclonal T cells to the tumor site. This leads to a powerful redirected T cell response and the destruction of tumor cells. Extensive testing in the lab, along with promising early clinical data, has provided a better understanding of how ImmTACs function in the body. It also suggests their potential therapeutic benefits, including a long-lasting response and ultimately the ability to break T cell tolerance.

This review introduces ImmTACs in the context of immunotherapy. It explains their design, construction, and mechanism of action. It also examines target selection and aspects of preclinical safety testing.

title: Angiopoietin-like protein 3 supports the activity of hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow niche.
text: The specific functions of angiopoietin-like proteins (Angptls) in the hematopoietic system are still not understood. However, our research reveals that Angptl3-null mice have a reduced number of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) that are also less active. When HSCs from Angptl3-null mice were transplanted into recipient mice without Angptl3, their ability to repopulate was impaired. We observed that bone marrow sinusoidal endothelial cells, which are located near HSCs, express high levels of Angptl3. Interestingly, when Angptl3 was lacking in bone marrow stromal cells or endothelium, their ability to support the expansion of repopulating HSCs was significantly reduced. We also found that Angptl3 suppresses the expression of a transcription factor called Ikaros. When Ikaros is overexpressed without regulation, it diminishes the repopulation activity of HSCs. Therefore, Angptl3, acting as an external factor, plays a crucial role in maintaining the stemness of HSCs within the bone marrow environment.

title: Subsequent chemotherapy reverses acquired tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and restores response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer
text:
BACKGROUND
Patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may develop acquired resistance to the tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) erlotinib and gefitinib, which target the epidermal growth factor receptor. In this report, we present two cases of advanced NSCLC where alternating chemotherapy and TKIs were successfully used to treat patients who had developed resistance to TKI therapy.

CASE PRESENTATION
Two patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC received palliative chemotherapy followed by erlotinib/gefitinib treatment. When TKI therapy proved ineffective, two cycles of chemotherapy were administered, followed by re-challenge with erlotinib or gefitinib.

CONCLUSION
It is important to aggressively manage NSCLC patients who develop acquired resistance to TKIs. Subsequent chemotherapy and targeted treatment can be a reasonable option for those who initially responded well to erlotinib/gefitinib treatment. Further research is needed to confirm the effectiveness of erlotinib/gefitinib treatment in NSCLC patients with acquired TKI resistance.

title: Epigenetic Therapy Ties MYC Depletion to Reversing Immune Evasion and Treating Lung Cancer
text: The combination of DNA-demethylating agents (DNMTis) and histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) shows promise in improving cancer immune therapy. In this study, we investigate the pharmacologic and isoform specificity of HDACis to determine their suitability for combining with DNMTis. This allows us to develop a new, low-dose, sequential treatment plan that effectively fights non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). By treating NSCLC cell lines in the lab, we uncover a transcriptional program driven by interferon α/β, which leads to increased expression of antigen presentation machinery. This effect is partly mediated by the induction of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Additionally, we observe a decrease in MYC signaling and an increase in the T cell chemoattractant CCL5. When we apply this combination treatment to mouse models of NSCLC, we observe a reversal of tumor immune evasion and a shift in T cell exhaustion towards memory and effector T cell phenotypes. These findings provide important insights for an upcoming clinical trial that aims to enhance immune checkpoint therapy for NSCLC.

title: The Role of PPARγ in Advanced Glycation End Products-Induced Inflammatory Response in Human Chondrocytes
text: The objective of this study was to investigate the role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors gamma (PPARγ) in the inflammatory response induced by advanced glycation end products (AGEs) in human chondrocytes. Primary human chondrocytes were treated with AGEs in the presence or absence of a neutralizing antibody against the receptor for AGEs (RAGE), specific inhibitors of MAPK signaling pathways, and a PPARγ agonist called pioglitazone. The expression of inflammatory markers (IL-1, MMP-13, TNF-α), PPARγ, nuclear NF-κB p65, and cytosol IκBα was measured using western blotting and real-time PCR. The results showed that AGEs increased the expression of IL-1, TNF-α, and MMP-13, while decreasing the level of PPARγ in a time- and dose-dependent manner. However, this effect was reversed by the anti-RAGE antibody, SB203580 (a P38 MAPK inhibitor), and SP600125 (a JNK inhibitor). Treatment with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone inhibited the inflammatory response induced by AGEs and prevented the down-regulation of PPARγ. Additionally, AGEs caused degradation of cytosol IκBα and increased the level of nuclear NF-κB p65 in human chondrocytes, which was counteracted by pioglitazone. In conclusion, AGEs down-regulate PPARγ expression and increase inflammatory mediators in human chondrocytes, but these effects can be reversed by pioglitazone. The activation of RAGE by AGEs triggers a signaling cascade involving MAPK JNK/p38, PPARγ, and NF-κB. Therefore, PPARγ could be a potential target for pharmacological intervention in the treatment of osteoarthritis.

title: Surgical versus medical treatment with cyclooxygenase inhibitors for symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants.
text:
The background of this study is focused on patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants, which can lead to increased morbidity and mortality. The two main treatment options for closing the PDA are pharmacological intervention with cyclooxygenase inhibitors or surgical ligation. Both methods have been proven effective, but it is unclear which treatment is preferred as the initial approach for symptomatic PDA in preterm infants.

The objective of this study is to compare the outcomes of surgical ligation versus medical treatment with cyclooxygenase inhibitors (indomethacin, ibuprofen, or mefenamic acid) as the initial treatment for symptomatic PDA in preterm infants, specifically focusing on neonatal mortality. The researchers conducted a thorough search of relevant databases and included trials that met specific criteria, such as randomized or quasi-randomized patient allocation, preterm infants or low-birth-weight infants with symptomatic PDA, and a comparison between surgical ligation and medical treatment with cyclooxygenase inhibitors.

Only one eligible study was found, which compared surgical ligation with indomethacin treatment as the primary approach. No other trials comparing surgery to other cyclooxygenase inhibitors were identified. The study included 154 infants and found no significant difference in mortality during hospital stay, chronic lung disease, bleeding, necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, creatinine level, or intraventricular hemorrhage between the surgical and indomethacin groups. However, the surgical group had a higher incidence of pneumothorax and retinopathy of prematurity stage III and IV compared to the indomethacin group. The surgical group also had a lower failure rate of ductal closure compared to the indomethacin group.

Based on these findings, the authors concluded that there is insufficient data to determine whether surgical ligation or medical treatment with indomethacin is the preferred initial approach for symptomatic PDA in preterm infants. It is worth noting that recent observational studies have suggested increased risks associated with PDA ligation, such as chronic lung disease, retinopathy of prematurity, and neurosensory impairment. Factors such as waiting time for surgery and transportation to a facility with surgical capabilities, as well as perioperative care, may impact outcomes.

title: The Effect of Collinearity on Parameter Estimates in Nonlinear Mixed Effect Models
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate how correlations among predictor variables in a population pharmacokinetic model can impact the identification of relevant covariates for inclusion in the structural pharmacokinetic model. To achieve this, Monte Carlo simulation was employed to generate multiple-dose concentration-time data resembling that observed in a Phase III clinical trial. The pharmacokinetics of the drugs under investigation were influenced by two covariates. Five different data sets were simulated, each with an increasing correlation between the two covariates. All data sets were analyzed using NONMEM, both with and without the inclusion of the covariates in the structural pharmacokinetic model. Summary measures for ill-conditioning and sensitivity analysis were utilized to assess the impact of increasing correlation among covariates on the accuracy and precision of the parameter estimates. 

The results of the study revealed that when the covariates were included in the structural pharmacokinetic model and the correlation between them increased, the standard error of the parameter estimates also increased, and the parameter estimates themselves became increasingly biased. Specifically, when the correlation between predictor variables reached 0.75, the standard errors of the parameter estimates were too large to establish statistical significance. 

In conclusion, researchers should be cautious when encountering correlations among predictor variables greater than 0.5 when simultaneously entering them into the model. This is because such correlations can lead to biased parameter estimates and inflated precision of the estimates due to ill-conditioning.

title: An analysis of age and gender influences on the relative risk for suicide and psychotropic drug self-poisoning.
text: Psychiatric illness poses a significant risk for both attempted and completed suicide, with psychotropic medications accounting for 80% of all prescription drug overdoses. Clinicians face the challenge of balancing the benefits of treatment with the risk of drug overdose. This study aimed to compare the age and gender distribution of patients prescribed psychotropic drugs with those who attempted or completed suicide using these drugs. Data was gathered from the Australian census, studies on general practitioner prescribing, and patients who presented with self-poisoning or committed suicide within a specific geographic area. The characteristics of these populations were analyzed to calculate odds ratios for suicide attempts or completions with psychotropic drugs, both before and after adjusting for prescription rates, in different age and gender groups. The odds ratios for self-poisoning were higher among individuals under 45 years old, despite this group being the least likely to be prescribed psychotropic drugs. Men had a higher rate of completed suicide using more lethal methods. After adjusting for prescription rates, the odds ratios for self-poisoning and suicide with psychotropic drugs were 11.1 and 1.7, respectively, for individuals aged 15 to 24 years. Those aged 25 to 44 years had odds ratios of 4.9 and 4.3, while individuals over 75 years had odds ratios of 0.03 and 0. Women were slightly more likely to self-poison with psychotropic drugs, but this reversed after adjusting for prescription rates. It is concluded that caution should be exercised when prescribing for individuals under 45 years old due to their higher risk of drug overdose, and less toxic compounds should be used. The risk among the elderly may have been exaggerated, potentially leading to some patients being denied adequate treatment.

title: Cell death and immune privilege.
text: The body's reaction to pathogens involves intricate inflammatory responses and immune reactions. While these are crucial for defending the body and eliminating infections, they often result in damage to nearby tissues. Most organ systems can withstand these responses without lasting harm. However, there are certain areas that restrict the spread of inflammation due to the potential harm it poses to organ function. Notably, the eye, brain, and reproductive organs (testis, ovary) fall into this category, where even minor instances of inflammation can have lasting consequences for the organism's survival. In these organs, immune responses either do not occur or occur differently compared to other areas, earning them the term "immunologically privileged." Surprisingly, in these organs, a properly functioning immune response can actually be the cause of disease.

title: Niche-Independent Symmetrical Self-Renewal of a Mammalian Tissue Stem Cell
text:
Pluripotent mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells have the ability to multiply through symmetrical divisions in a simple monoculture. However, in their natural environment (in vivo), stem cells are believed to rely on specialized cellular microenvironments and undergo mostly asymmetric divisions. The expansion of pure populations of tissue stem cells outside of the body has been challenging. Neural progenitor cells, for example, are grown together with differentiating progeny in floating clusters called neurospheres. However, the proportion of stem cells in neurospheres is low and they cannot be directly observed or studied.

In this study, we show that the complex neurosphere environment is not necessary for the maintenance of stem cells. We demonstrate that a combination of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2) and epidermal growth factor (EGF) is sufficient to derive and continuously expand pure cultures of neural stem (NS) cells through symmetrical division. Initially, NS cells were derived from mouse ES cells and then induced to differentiate into neural lineage. Growth factors were added to the culture media. In the presence of only EGF and FGF-2, the resulting NS cells proliferated continuously, maintained their diploid state, and were capable of forming colonies. After prolonged expansion, these cells retained their ability to efficiently differentiate into neurons and astrocytes both in vitro and when transplanted into the adult brain. When a single NS cell was grown into a colony, all the cells in the colony produced neurons when the growth factors were withdrawn. The NS cells exhibited morphological, cell biological, and molecular characteristics of radial glia, which are developmental precursors of neurons and glia. Adherent NS cell lines could also be established from fetal mouse brain, indicating the consistency of this profile. Similar NS cells could be generated from human ES cells and human fetal brain.

The extrinsic factors EGF and FGF-2 were found to be sufficient to sustain pure symmetrical self-renewing divisions of NS cells. These cultures represent the first example of tissue-specific stem cells that can be propagated without accompanying differentiation. The homogenous nature of these cultures will allow for the study of molecular mechanisms that define tissue-specific stem cells and enable direct comparison with pluripotent ES cells.

title: A Bivalent Chromatin Structure Marks Key Developmental Genes in Embryonic Stem Cells
text: The presence of highly conserved noncoding elements (HCNEs) in mammalian genomes suggests that these regions, which are rich in genes encoding important transcription factors (TFs) involved in development, may play a crucial role in regulatory controls during development. To investigate this, we examined histone methylation patterns in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells across 56 large HCNE-rich loci. Our analysis revealed a distinct modification pattern known as "bivalent domains," characterized by extensive H3 lysine 27 methylation with smaller regions of H3 lysine 4 methylation. These bivalent domains were often associated with TF genes expressed at low levels. We propose that these bivalent domains serve to silence developmental genes in ES cells while keeping them primed for activation. Additionally, we observed a strong correlation between genome sequence and histone methylation in ES cells, which became less pronounced in differentiated cells. These findings underscore the significance of DNA sequence in shaping the initial epigenetic landscape and suggest a novel mechanism based on chromatin for maintaining pluripotency.

title: Ovarian Surface Epithelium in Patients with Severe Ovarian Infertility: A Potential Source of Cells Expressing Markers of Pluripotent/Multipotent Stem Cells
text: The objective of this study was to validate the existence of stem cells in the ovarian surface epithelium of patients diagnosed with premature ovarian failure and lacking mature follicles and oocytes. Following the scraping of the ovarian surface epithelium, small round cells expressing the pluripotency marker SOX-2 were observed among the epithelial cells. These cells were found to be an integral part of the ovarian surface epithelium. Subsequently, when these scraped cells were cultured in a medium supplemented with follicular fluid to mimic the ovarian environment, primitive oocyte-like cells and clusters of round-shaped cells were developed. These cells exhibited positive staining for alkaline phosphatase, as well as markers of pluripotency such as SOX-2 and SSEA-4. The expression of these markers was observed early on and throughout the culture period. Additionally, single oocyte-like cells expressed genes OCT4A, SOX-2, NANOG, NANOS, STELLA, CD9, LIN28, KLF4, GDF3, and MYC, which are characteristic of pluripotent stem cells. The findings of this study confirmed the presence of potential stem cells in the ovarian surface epithelium of these patients, laying the groundwork for the future establishment of a stem cell line.

title: Structural Homeostasis: Compensatory Adjustments of Dendritic Arbor Geometry in Response to Variations of Synaptic Input
text:
During the development of the nervous system, there is a natural variation in the connections formed between differentiating neurons. However, despite this variability, functional and resilient neural circuits are established. Neurons have a way of dealing with the variability in their inputs by making compensatory changes in their electrical properties. In addition to this, our research shows that neurons also make compensatory adjustments to their structure.

To investigate this further, we studied the development of dendrites on a specific central neuron (aCC) in the late Drosophila embryo. This was done at the stage when the neuron receives its first connections and becomes electrically active. Simultaneously, we examined the distribution of presynaptic sites on the developing postsynaptic arbor. By manipulating the genes of the presynaptic partners, we discovered that the postsynaptic dendritic arbor adjusts its growth to compensate for changes in the activity and density of synaptic sites.

When the synthesis or release of presynaptic neurotransmitter was blocked, we observed a greater extension of the dendritic arbor. Conversely, an increase in the density of presynaptic release sites led to a reduction in the size of the dendritic arbor. These growth adjustments occurred locally in the arbor and were a result of the promotion or inhibition of neurite growth near the presynaptic sites.

Our findings also suggest that the activity state of protein kinase A in the postsynaptic neuron plays a role in mediating these structural adjustments. This protein kinase A modifies dendritic growth in response to synaptic activity. Overall, our research indicates that the dendritic arbor acts as a homeostatic device during early stages of connectivity. It adjusts its size and geometry to match the level and distribution of input received. This ensures that an appropriate level of input is achieved, counterbalancing natural variations in synaptic density and activity.

title: Nutrition and physical activity guidelines for cancer survivors.
text: Cancer survivors often have a strong desire to gather information about their food choices, physical activity, and dietary supplements in order to improve their treatment outcomes, quality of life, and overall survival. To address these concerns, the American Cancer Society (ACS) brought together a panel of experts in nutrition, physical activity, and cancer survivorship. Their goal was to evaluate the scientific evidence and best clinical practices regarding optimal nutrition and physical activity after a cancer diagnosis. This report summarizes their findings and aims to provide healthcare providers with the most reliable information to assist cancer survivors and their families in making informed decisions about nutrition and physical activity. The report covers nutrition and physical activity guidelines throughout the cancer care process, briefly touching on important issues during cancer treatment and for patients with advanced cancer. However, the main focus is on the needs of individuals who are either disease-free or have stable disease after recovering from treatment. It also addresses specific nutrition and physical activity concerns such as body weight, food choices, food safety, and dietary supplements. Additionally, it discusses issues related to different types of cancer and addresses common questions about diet, physical activity, and cancer survivorship.

title: The role of protein clearance mechanisms in organismal ageing and age-related diseases.
text: As individuals age, their ability to maintain a functional proteome, known as proteostasis, diminishes. This decline leads to the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, which in turn impairs the functioning of cells and disrupts tissue homeostasis. The buildup of these damaged proteins is a contributing factor to various age-related diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease. To counteract this, the body relies on the ubiquitin-proteasome system and autophagy-lysosome pathway, both of which are crucial components of the proteostasis network, to degrade these damaged proteins. By modulating the activity of either the proteasome or autophagic-lysosomal system, it is possible to extend lifespan and protect organisms from the symptoms associated with proteostasis disorders. This suggests a direct link between protein clearance mechanisms and the process of aging, as well as age-related diseases.

title: A distinctive DNA damage response in human hematopoietic stem cells reveals an apoptosis-independent role for p53 in self-renewal.
text: Effective DNA damage responses (DDR) are crucial for highly regenerative tissues like blood, as they need to balance long-term regeneration with protection against leukemogenesis. Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for lifelong blood production, but their response to DNA damage is not well understood. In our study, we found that human HSCs have a delayed ability to repair DNA double-strand breaks, resulting in persistent gammaH2AX foci. Additionally, they exhibit enhanced apoptosis through p53- and ASPP1-dependent pathways after exposure to gamma radiation, compared to progenitor cells. By inactivating p53 or overexpressing Bcl-2, we were able to reduce radiation-induced apoptosis and preserve the in vivo repopulating function of HSCs. However, only the HSCs overexpressing Bcl-2 showed higher self-renewal capacity, indicating that intact p53 positively regulates self-renewal independently of apoptosis. The reduced self-renewal observed in HSCs with inactivated p53 was associated with an increase in spontaneous gammaH2AX foci in secondary transplants of HSCs. Our findings highlight the distinct physiological roles of p53 in ensuring optimal HSC function, including the regulation of apoptosis and prevention of gammaH2AX foci accumulation during HSC self-renewal.

title: Behavioral characterization of neuropeptide Y knockout mice.
text:
We conducted a thorough analysis of the behavior of mice that lack the neuropeptide Y (NPY) gene. This included observing their response to fasting for 24 and 48 hours, as well as exposing them to small molecule antagonists of NPY receptors (specifically Y1 and Y5 receptors) that are known to affect feeding behavior. We also compared the behavior of these mice to wildtype (WT) mice and NPY knockout (KO) mice in various tests, such as locomotor monitors, elevated plus maze, inhibitory avoidance, acoustic startle, prepulse inhibition, and hot plate assays.

One of the main findings of our study was that the NPY KO mice consumed less food compared to the WT controls when subjected to fasting. Additionally, based on the results of our behavioral tests, it is possible that the NPY KO mice exhibit anxiety-like behavior and show reduced sensitivity to pain in the hot plate test. These findings provide further support for the involvement of NPY in regulating energy balance, anxiety, and potentially nociception.

title: Epigenetic-induced repression of microRNA-205 is associated with MED1 activation and a poorer prognosis in localized prostate cancer
text: The deregulation of microRNA (miRNA) expression can play a crucial role in the development of cancer. In this study, we have observed that the transcription of miRNA-205 (miR-205) is commonly suppressed and the MIR-205 gene is hypermethylated in prostate cancer. Additionally, the function of LOC642587, the host gene for MIR-205, is also deactivated. Our findings demonstrate that miR-205 is responsible for silencing the transcription of mediator 1 (MED1), also known as TRAP220 and PPARBP, in normal prostate cells. This leads to a decrease in MED1 mRNA levels, as well as in the total and active phospho-MED1 protein. Overexpression of miR-205 in prostate cancer cells negatively impacts cell viability, indicating its role as a tumor suppressor. We have also discovered a strong correlation between hypermethylation of the MIR-205 gene and a decrease in miR-205 expression, as well as an increase in MED1 expression, in primary tumor samples (n=14) compared to matched normal prostate samples (n=7). Further analysis of a larger patient group (tumor n=149, matched normal n=30) revealed significant MIR-205 DNA methylation in tumors compared to normal tissue. Moreover, MIR-205 hypermethylation is significantly associated with biochemical recurrence (hazard ratio=2.005, 95% confidence interval (1.109, 3.625), P=0.02) in patients with low preoperative prostate specific antigen levels. In conclusion, our findings suggest that miR-205 acts as an epigenetically regulated tumor suppressor by targeting MED1, and it may serve as a potential biomarker for managing prostate cancer.

title: Th2 cytokine response in Major Depressive Disorder patients before treatment
text: We examined the interaction between the neuroendocrine and immune systems in individuals with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Our study compared the balance of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines (Th1/Th2) in MDD patients and a control group without depression. The MDD patients exhibited higher levels of cortisol and TNF-alpha, increased percentages of CD3+CD8+ and natural killer (NK) cells, decreased B cell counts, and no significant changes in CD3+CD4+ lymphocytes. Additionally, the MDD group showed elevated levels of IL-4 and IL-13 (Th2 cytokines) and significantly lower levels of IL-2 and IFN-gamma (Th1 cytokines). These findings suggest that these alterations may be linked to the elevated cortisol levels observed in MDD patients. Further research is needed to investigate these results and their potential implications for future therapeutic approaches in MDD patients.

title: CDD: conserved domains and protein three-dimensional structure
text: CDD, also known as the Conserved Domain Database, is a component of NCBI's Entrez system for querying and retrieving information. It can be accessed through the website http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Structure/cdd/cdd.shtml. The main purpose of CDD is to provide annotations for protein sequences by identifying conserved domain footprints and functional sites based on these footprints. Users can access pre-computed annotations through Entrez, and the interactive search services allow for single protein or nucleotide queries, as well as batch submissions of protein sequences for rapid identification of potential matches using RPS-BLAST. CDD includes various collections of protein domains and full-length protein models, and it is actively curated to provide detailed classifications for well-known protein domain families, supported by available protein three-dimensional (3D) structures and published literature. Currently, the majority of protein 3D structures are represented by models tracked by CDD, and the curators are continuously characterizing new families that are discovered through protein structure determination efforts.

title: Extensive diversity of Ig-superfamily proteins in the immune system of insects.
text: The vast array of immune receptors found in higher vertebrates is a distinguishing characteristic. However, it remains unclear whether molecular diversity plays a role in immune protection for invertebrates. Our research provides evidence that immune-competent cells in Drosophila have the ability to produce over 18,000 variations of the immunoglobulin (Ig)-superfamily receptor known as Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule (Dscam). We observed that different forms of Dscam were present in the hemolymph, and when Dscam was specifically lost in hemocytes, the ability to efficiently engulf bacteria was impaired, potentially due to reduced bacterial binding. Significantly, the molecular diversity of Dscam transcripts, which is generated through alternative splicing, is remarkably consistent across major insect groups. This suggests an unexpected level of molecular complexity in the innate immune system of insects.

title: Preparing the outbreak assistance laboratory network in the Netherlands for the detection of the influenza virus A(H1N1) variant.
text:
In late April 2009, there was an emergence of human infection with a variant influenza virus A(H1N1)v in the Northern Americas. This virus posed a potential threat of becoming the next pandemic influenza virus. The objective of this study was to prepare laboratories in the Netherlands for an increase in patients suspected of A(H1N1)v infection by enhancing their molecular diagnosis capacity. 

The study design involved distributing a panel of 10 blinded specimens to outbreak assistance laboratories (OAL). These specimens contained seasonal A(H1N1) or A(H3N2) influenza virus, A/Netherlands/602/2009(H1N1)v influenza virus, or a negative control. Along with the specimens, the OAL received specific primers and probes for influenza virus A (M-gene), swine influenza virus A (NP-gene), and influenza virus A(H1N1)v (H1v-gene), as well as a protocol from the CDC in Atlanta, USA. The laboratories were then asked to implement and test this protocol. 

The results showed that all OAL were able to detect A(H1N1)v using the CDC M-gene reagents, with most laboratories achieving similar sensitivity to their in-house M-gene based assays. The routine diagnostic RT-PCRs used in the OAL, which were specifically designed to detect H1, H3, or NS1 from seasonal influenza A viruses, did not cross-react or showed very low levels of cross-reactivity with A(H1N1)v. The CDC swine NP-gene and H1v-gene RT-PCRs had slightly reduced sensitivity compared to the CDC and in-house M-gene RT-PCRs. However, the in-house developed A(H1N1)v specific H1v-gene and N1v-gene RT-PCRs showed equal sensitivity to the CDC and in-house M-gene RT-PCRs. 

In conclusion, the Dutch OAL are prepared to detect and specifically identify A(H1N1)v, although there was some level of cross-reactivity observed with seasonal influenza viruses. It is recommended to use M-gene based generic influenza A virus detection in routine settings to be able to detect emerging influenza A viruses.

title: Averting Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes in India through Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Taxation: An Economic-Epidemiologic Modeling Study
text:
BACKGROUND: The proposal to tax sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) in high-income countries as a means to reduce obesity and type 2 diabetes has gained traction. In this study, we aimed to estimate the potential health effects of implementing such a fiscal strategy in India, a middle-income country with varying levels of SSB consumption, substitution patterns between SSBs and other beverages, and significant differences in chronic disease risk within the population.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: Using data on consumption and price variations from a nationally representative survey of 100,855 Indian households, we first calculated how changes in SSB prices would impact per capita consumption of SSBs and substitution with other beverages. We then incorporated SSB sales trends, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes incidence data stratified by age, sex, income, and urban/rural residence into a validated microsimulation model. This model estimated the effects of a 20% SSB excise tax on caloric consumption, glycemic load, overweight/obesity prevalence, and type 2 diabetes incidence among different subpopulations in India. The results showed that the 20% SSB tax could potentially reduce overweight and obesity prevalence by 3.0% (95% CI 1.6%-5.9%) and type 2 diabetes incidence by 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%-1.9%) among various Indian subpopulations from 2014-2023, assuming SSB consumption continued to increase linearly based on secular trends. However, if SSB consumption trends accelerated in line with industry marketing models, the impact of taxation would be greater, with a potential reduction of 4.2% (95% CI 2.5-10.0%) in prevalent overweight/obesity and 2.5% (95% CI 1.0-2.8%) in incident type 2 diabetes from 2014-2023. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, the largest relative effect of SSB taxation would be expected among young rural men, rather than urban populations. It is important to note that this estimation approach has limitations, including the assumption that consumer expenditure behavior from previous years will reflect future behavior and potential underreporting of consumption in dietary recall data.

CONCLUSION: Implementing a sustained high tax rate on SSBs could help mitigate the rising rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes in India, benefiting both urban and rural subpopulations.

title: Acute myopericarditis after multiple vaccinations in an adolescent: case report and review of the literature.
text: In this report, we present a case of acute myopericarditis occurring after vaccination in an adolescent. The patient experienced sudden chest pain, widespread ST-segment elevation, and increased levels of cardiac enzymes. Cardiac MRI confirmed the diagnosis of acute myocarditis. Fortunately, the patient responded well to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory treatment and recovered within a few days. At the 10-week follow-up, the patient remained stable, with improved MRI results. Additionally, we review other cases of myopericarditis reported in the pediatric literature following vaccination.

title: Cardiovascular protection with antihypertensive drugs in dialysis patients: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Epidemiological studies have shown that dialysis patients with lower blood pressure and a decline in blood pressure over time have a higher risk of mortality. However, randomized controlled trials do not have enough evidence to support the benefits of antihypertensive therapy. This meta-analysis focused on long-term dialysis patients who participated in randomized controlled trials and received antihypertensive drug therapy. The study assessed the hazard ratio of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in the treated group compared to the control group. Out of the 1202 patients identified in 5 studies, the overall benefit of antihypertensive therapy compared to the control or placebo group had a combined hazard ratio for cardiovascular events of 0.69 (95% CI: 0.56 to 0.84) using a fixed-effects model and 0.62 (95% CI: 0.45 to 0.86) using a random-effects model. In a sensitivity analysis, it was found that the hypertensive group had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.49 (95% CI: 0.35 to 0.67), but when normotensives were included in the trial, there was less cardiovascular protection (pooled hazard ratio of 0.86 [95% CI: 0.67 to 1.12]). The test for heterogeneity between the hypertensive and "normotensive-included" groups was significant (P<0.006). Similar results were observed for the risk ratio of death and cardiovascular events. There was evidence of publication bias based on Egger's test and funnel plot. Randomized trials indicated a potential benefit of antihypertensive therapy for hemodialysis patients. However, more adequately powered randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings, particularly among those with hypertension.

title: Protoplasmic astrocytes in CA1 stratum radiatum occupy separate anatomical domains.
text:
There is growing evidence that protoplasmic astrocytes play a significant role in interacting with neuronal elements in the brain and influencing their activity. Recent studies suggest that there may be different forms of these cells in the central nervous system (CNS), both physiologically and functionally. However, our current understanding of the form and distribution of astrocytes is mainly based on studies that used the astrocytic marker glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and metal-impregnation techniques. These methods have limitations in visualizing the interactions among these complex cells.

In this study, we used intracellular injection combined with immunohistochemistry for GFAP to investigate the volume of astrocytes delineated by GFAP. We found that GFAP only represents approximately 15% of the total volume of the astrocyte. This means that previous images based on GFAP have led to incorrect conclusions about the interactions between neighboring astrocytes. To further examine these interactions, we injected adjacent protoplasmic astrocytes in the CA1 stratum radiatum with fluorescent intracellular tracers of different wavelengths. We then analyzed these cells using three-dimensional (3D) confocal analysis and electron microscopy.

Our findings reveal that protoplasmic astrocytes primarily establish exclusive territories. Understanding how the complex morphology of these astrocytes affects their relationships with other astrocytes, oligodendroglia, neurons, and the brain's vasculature is crucial for our comprehension of nervous system function.

title: Leptin-receptor-expressing mesenchymal stromal cells represent the main source of bone formed by adult bone marrow.
text: The lack of markers that allow for the identification and tracking of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in vivo has hindered studies on their identity and physiological function. However, we have discovered that the Leptin Receptor (LepR) serves as a highly effective marker for enriching bone marrow MSCs. Approximately 0.3% of bone marrow cells were found to be LepR(+), and among these, 10% were CFU-Fs, accounting for 94% of all bone marrow CFU-Fs. In both culture and transplantation experiments, LepR(+) cells demonstrated the ability to form bone, cartilage, and adipocytes. These cells also exhibited the markers Scf-GFP(+), Cxcl12-DsRed(high), and Nestin-GFP(low), which were also highly enriched in CFU-Fs. However, they were negative for Nestin-CreER and NG2-CreER, markers that were unlikely to be present in CFU-Fs. Through fate-mapping, we determined that LepR(+) cells originate after birth and give rise to the majority of bone and adipocytes found in adult bone marrow, including those regenerated after irradiation or fracture. While LepR(+) cells are typically quiescent, they do undergo proliferation in response to injury. Therefore, LepR(+) cells serve as the primary source of bone and adipocytes in adult bone marrow.

title: High-resolution sperm typing of meiotic recombination in the mouse MHC Ebeta gene.
text:
Pedigree analysis in mice has revealed the presence of hotspots for meiotic crossovers in the MHC cluster. To further investigate these hotspots, we conducted a high-resolution analysis of sperm crossovers in the class II E(beta) gene. Our findings confirm the existence of a highly localized hotspot within the second intron of E(beta), spanning 1.0-1.6 kb. Interestingly, this hotspot is surrounded by DNA that is largely unresponsive to recombination. 

When mice heterozygous for haplotype s and another MHC haplotype were examined, we observed significant variation in crossover rates depending on the haplotype. However, regardless of the haplotype, the same hotspot was consistently utilized, even in crosses involving the highly diverged p haplotype. 

Although crossovers occurred at similar rates in reciprocal orientations, their distribution within the hotspot differed. Specifically, the center points of crossovers in the two orientations were shifted by an average of 400 bp. This asymmetry resulted in biased gene conversion, favoring hotspot markers from the non-initiating haplotype. These findings support the double-strand break repair model of recombination, with haplotype s being the most efficient initiator of crossovers. 

Remarkably, the behavior of the E(beta) hotspot closely resembles that of human hotspots, including highly localized recombination initiation.

title: Long-term survival of beta thalassemia major patients treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation compared with survival with conventional treatment.
text:
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) remains a challenge in the treatment of thalassemia. We conducted a case-control study at a single center, involving a large group of 516 children and adult patients. These patients were treated with either HSCT or received blood transfusion support and iron chelation therapy. Out of the total cohort, 258 patients (with a median age of 12, ranging from 1 to 45) underwent HSCT, either from a sibling (67%) or an unrelated donor (33%). Additionally, 97 patients were adults (16 years of age or older). The median follow-up period after HSCT was 11 years, ranging from 1 to 30 years. The conditioning regimen used was either busulfan (80.6%) or treosulfan-based (19.4%). We randomly selected a group of 258 conventionally treated (CT) patients who were age and sex matched with the transplanted patients. 

In the transplanted patients, the 30-year overall survival (OS) rate was 82.6% ± 2.7%, and the thalassemia-free survival (TFS) rate was 77.8% ± 2.9%. These rates were compared to the OS rate of 85.3% ± 2.7% in the CT patients, and the difference was not statistically significant (P = NS). The incidence of grade II-IV acute and chronic graft versus host disease (GvHD) was 23.6% and 12.9%, respectively. The probability of rejection was 6.9%. The transplant-related mortality (TRM) rate was 13.8%, which was similar to the probability of dying from cardiovascular events in the CT patients (12.2%). A high-risk Pesaro score (class 3) was associated with lower OS (OR = 1.99, 95% C.I.=1.31-3.03) and TFS (OR = 1.54, 95% C.I.=1.12-2.12). 

In adult patients, the 23-year OS rate and TFS rate after HSCT were 70% ± 5% and 67.3% ± 5%, respectively, compared to an OS rate of 71.2% ± 5% in the CT patients, and the difference was not statistically significant (P = NS). Finally, treosulfan was associated with a lower risk of acute GvHD (P = .004; OR = 0.28, 95% C.I.=0.12-0.67). 

In conclusion, the 30-year survival rate of patients who underwent HSCT for thalassemia was similar to that expected in CT thalassemia patients. The majority of HSCT survivors were cured of thalassemia.

title: Global analysis of ATM polymorphism reveals significant functional constraint.
text:
Currently, the gene associated with ataxia-telangiectasia, known as ATM, is linked to cerebellar degeneration, abnormal growth of small blood vessels, and cancer. These significant clinical manifestations have sparked interest in understanding the variations in the sequence of the ATM gene. To achieve this, we conducted a thorough examination of sequence variation in ATM across diverse human populations. We analyzed the protein-encoding exons of the gene (9,168 bp), as well as the adjacent intron and untranslated sequences (14,661 bp), in 93 individuals from seven major human populations. Additionally, we analyzed the coding sequence in one chimpanzee, one gorilla, one orangutan, and one Old World monkey. 

Through denaturing high-performance liquid chromatography, we discovered 88 variant sites in human ATM, with a sensitivity of 96%-100% for detecting DNA sequence variation. We compared ATM to 14 other autosomal genes in terms of nucleotide diversity. While the noncoding regions of ATM exhibited diversity values similar to other genes, the coding regions displayed very low diversity, particularly in the final 29% of the protein sequence. 

To test the neutral evolution hypothesis, we utilized the Hudson/Kreitman/Aguadé statistic. The results revealed that this specific region of the human ATM gene was significantly constrained compared to that of the orangutan, Old World monkey, and mouse, but not in comparison to the chimpanzee or gorilla. ATM exhibited extensive linkage disequilibrium, indicating the suppression of meiotic recombination at this locus. 

We defined seven haplotypes, with two haplotypes accounting for 82% of all analyzed chromosomes across major populations. Interestingly, two other haplotypes carrying the same D126E missense polymorphism accounted for 33% of chromosomes in Africa but were absent outside of Africa. The high frequency of this polymorphism may be attributed to either a population expansion within Africa or selective pressure.

title: Ablation and regeneration of tolerance-inducing medullary thymic epithelial cells after cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone treatment.
text: Immunosuppressive drugs and cytotoxic chemotherapy agents are specifically designed to eliminate or suppress T cells that are autoreactive, alloaggressive, or hyperinflammatory, as well as to combat disseminated malignancies. However, these medications also have significant immunological side effects, ranging from disruption of thymopoiesis and general immunodeficiency to the unexpected development of autoimmunity. In line with the communication between thymocytes and stromal cells, our research demonstrates that these commonly used therapeutic agents have a profound impact on murine thymic epithelial cells (TEC), which are crucial for rebuilding immunity after treatment. We have discovered that the immunosuppressant cyclosporine A, which has been associated with a thymus-dependent autoimmune syndrome in certain patients, leads to extensive loss of autoimmune regulator (Aire(+)) tolerance-inducing MHC class II(high) medullary TEC (mTEC(high)). However, Aire expression is restored within 7 days after cyclosporine A administration.
