The intervention group also had a higher relative contribution of folate intake from fruits, vegetables, and wholegrain bread. The increased intake of folate from wholegrain bread was associated with a decrease in plasma total homocysteine levels.

In conclusion, the dietary intervention successfully increased the intake of vegetables, fruits, and wholegrain bread, resulting in a higher folate intake from these foods. The reduction in plasma total homocysteine levels was specifically linked to the increased folate intake from wholegrain bread.

title: Beta interferon controls West Nile virus infection and pathogenesis in mice.
text: Research conducted on mice lacking the common plasma membrane receptor for type I interferon (IFN-αβR(-)(/)(-)) has provided insights into the role of IFN signaling in limiting the spread and severity of infections caused by West Nile virus (WNV) and other pathogenic viruses. However, the specific functions of individual IFN subtypes remain unclear. In this study, we focused on understanding the antiviral and immunomodulatory effects of IFN-β by using IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice. We found that these mice were more susceptible to WNV infection compared to wild-type mice, with a faster progression of the disease and higher overall mortality, although the severity of the phenotype was less pronounced than in IFN-αβR(-)(/)(-) mice. The increased vulnerability of IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice was accompanied by higher levels of viral replication in various tissues. This suggests that IFN-β plays a direct role in controlling WNV replication, as demonstrated by higher viral titers in macrophages, dendritic cells, fibroblasts, and cerebellar granule cell neurons from IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice compared to wild-type cells. Interestingly, cortical neurons did not show the same increase in viral replication. While detailed analysis of the immune response did not reveal major deficiencies in WNV-specific antibodies or CD8(+) T cells, we did observe an altered response in CD4(+) CD25(+) FoxP3(+) regulatory T cells, with higher numbers after infection. These findings suggest that IFN-β plays a crucial role in controlling WNV pathogenesis by limiting infection in specific cell types and modulating T cell regulatory networks.

title: Frontrunners of T cell activation: Initial, localized Ca2+ signals mediated by NAADP and the type 1 ryanodine receptor
text:
T cell activation serves as the primary trigger for the adaptive immune system. The activation process relies heavily on Ca2+ signaling, which initially manifests as brief, localized Ca2+ signals. Upon T cell activation, the second messenger NAADP rapidly forms and stimulates early Ca2+ signaling. To better understand these early signaling events and investigate the channels responsible for NAADP-dependent Ca2+ signals, we developed a high-resolution imaging technique that utilizes multiple fluorescent Ca2+ indicator dyes. 

In our experiments, we observed that within the first few seconds of activating primary murine T cells or human Jurkat cells using CD3-coated beads, we detected Ca2+ signals that were extremely small in diameter and located near the activation site on the plasma membrane. However, when we knocked down the ryanodine receptor (RyR) in Jurkat cells or used primary T cells from RyR1−/− mice, we either failed to detect these early Ca2+ signals or observed a significant reduction in their number. Additionally, local Ca2+ signals triggered by microinjection of NAADP into Jurkat cells were also sensitive to RyR knockdown. Interestingly, the transient receptor potential channel subtype melastatin 2 (TRPM2), a potential target channel for NAADP, was not necessary for the formation of initial Ca2+ signals in primary T cells. 

In summary, our high-resolution imaging method allowed us to characterize the early release of Ca2+ in T cells and provided evidence supporting the involvement of RyR and NAADP in these signals.

title: A missense LAMB2 mutation causes congenital nephrotic syndrome by impairing laminin secretion.
text: Laminin β2 is a crucial part of laminin-521, which plays a significant role in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). When laminin β2 (LAMB2) experiences null mutations, it leads to Pierson syndrome, a severe congenital nephrotic syndrome accompanied by ocular and neurologic abnormalities. On the other hand, patients with LAMB2 missense mutations, like R246Q, may have less severe extrarenal defects but still exhibit congenital nephrotic syndrome. To investigate how these missense mutations in LAMB2 cause proteinuria, we conducted an experiment using three transgenic lines of mice. In these mice, the R246Q-mutant rat laminin β2 replaced the wild-type mouse laminin β2 in the GBM. Interestingly, these transgenic mice developed significantly less severe proteinuria compared to their nontransgenic Lamb2-deficient littermates. The level of proteinuria was found to be inversely correlated with the expression of R246Q-LAMB2. At the onset of proteinuria, the expression and localization of proteins associated with the slit diaphragm and foot processes were normal, and there were no noticeable structural abnormalities. However, low expressors of the transgene developed heavy proteinuria, foot process effacement, GBM thickening, and renal failure within 3 months. On the other hand, high expressors only experienced mild proteinuria after 9 months. In vitro studies revealed that the R246Q mutation impairs the secretion of laminin. Overall, these findings suggest that the R246Q mutation causes nephrotic syndrome by hindering the secretion of laminin-521 from podocytes into the GBM. However, increased expression of the mutant protein can overcome this secretion defect and improve glomerular permselectivity.

title: Interleukin-33 prevents apoptosis and improves survival after experimental myocardial infarction through ST2 signaling.
text:
Background: ST2 is a member of the interleukin (IL)-1 receptor family and exists in two forms: membrane-bound (ST2L) and soluble (sST2). The presence of sST2 is associated with poor outcomes in patients with myocardial infarction (MI). IL-33, a recently discovered ligand for ST2, activates nuclear factor kappaB and may regulate apoptotic cell death. We aimed to investigate whether IL-33 has a cardioprotective effect after MI through ST2 signaling.

Methods and Results: In our study, we found that IL-33 protected cultured cardiomyocytes from apoptosis induced by hypoxia. However, this cardioprotective effect was partially inhibited by sST2. IL-33 also increased the expression of antiapoptotic factors XIAP, cIAP1, and survivin. To further understand the role of IL-33 in vivo, we conducted a blinded and randomized study using rats with ischemia/reperfusion. The results showed that IL-33 reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, suppressed caspase-3 activity, and increased the expression of IAP family member proteins. Additionally, IL-33 decreased both infarct and fibrosis volumes at 15 days. Echocardiographic and hemodynamic studies revealed that IL-33 improved ventricular function. To determine if the cardioprotective effect of IL-33 is mediated through ST2 signaling, we conducted a randomized and blinded study using ST2(-/-) mice and wild-type littermate mice subjected to MI. After 4 weeks, IL-33 reduced ventricular dilation and improved contractile function in wild-type mice but not in ST2(-/-) mice. Furthermore, IL-33 improved survival after MI in wild-type mice but not in ST2(-/-) mice.

Conclusions: Our findings suggest that IL-33 prevents cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improves cardiac function and survival after MI through ST2 signaling.

title: The impact of open versus closed format ICU admission practices on the outcome of high risk surgical patients: a cohort analysis
text:
In the year 2000, the ICU at the Zaandam Medical Centre (ZMC) changed its organizational structure from an open format to a closed format. The purpose of this study was to assess the impact of this change on the outcomes of high-risk surgical patients. 

To conduct the study, the medical records of high-risk surgical patients admitted to the ICU between 1996 and 1998 (open format) and between 2003 and 2005 (closed format) were examined. High-risk patients were identified based on the Identification of Risk in Surgical patients (IRIS) score. The parameters analyzed included mortality, morbidity, ICU length of stay (LOS), and hospital LOS. 

The results showed that the mortality rate among ICU patients was 25.7% in the open format group and 15.8% in the closed format group (p = 0.01). Morbidity decreased slightly from 48.6% to 46.1% (p = 0.6). The average hospital stay was 17 days in the open format group and 21 days in the closed format group (p = 0.03). 

In conclusion, high-risk surgical patients in the ICU require specialized treatment and close monitoring to ensure their safety and optimal care. Our findings suggest that a closed format ICU is more advantageous than an open format in minimizing the negative effects of high-risk surgery and achieving favorable outcomes for this patient population.

title: Induction therapy with autologous mesenchymal stem cells in living-related kidney transplants: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the use of autologous mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) as a replacement for antibody induction therapy in patients with end-stage renal disease who undergo kidney transplants from a living-related donor. The study included 159 patients and took place at a single site from February 2008 to May 2009.

During the study, patients were given autologous MSCs derived from their own bone marrow at the time of kidney reperfusion and two weeks later. Some patients also received standard-dose or low-dose calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs), while others received anti-IL-2 receptor antibody plus standard-dose CNIs. The primary outcomes measured were the incidence of acute rejection and renal function, while secondary outcomes included patient and graft survival and adverse events.

The results showed that patient and graft survival rates were similar across all groups. However, after 6 months, the incidence of biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was lower in the autologous MSC groups compared to the control group. None of the patients in the MSC groups experienced glucocorticoid-resistant rejection, while some patients in the control group did. Additionally, renal function improved more quickly in the MSC groups compared to the control group.

Furthermore, during the 1-year follow-up, the combined analysis of the MSC-treated groups showed a decreased risk of opportunistic infections compared to the control group.

In conclusion, the use of autologous MSCs as a replacement for anti-IL-2 receptor antibody induction therapy in renal transplant patients resulted in a lower incidence of acute rejection, decreased risk of opportunistic infection, and improved renal function at 1 year.

title: Cerebral cortex assembly: generating and reprogramming projection neuron diversity
text: The mammalian cerebral cortex is responsible for the highest levels of associative, cognitive, and motor functions. Within the central nervous system (CNS), the cortex serves as a prime example of extreme neuronal diversity. This diversity can be broadly classified into two categories: excitatory projection neurons (PNs) and inhibitory interneurons (INs). In this review, we will discuss recent advancements in understanding the strategies and mechanisms that contribute to the diversity of PNs during embryogenesis. Furthermore, we will explore how PN classes may be maintained throughout the organism's life after birth. Additionally, we will consider the intriguing possibility that PNs could potentially undergo directed reprogramming to enhance cortical plasticity in adult individuals.

title: Mechanical modulation of receptor-ligand interactions at cell-cell interfaces.
text:
Extensive research has been conducted on cell surface receptors due to their role in initiating and regulating signal transduction cascades, which ultimately lead to various functional outcomes within cells. However, there is still limited understanding of a specific class of immune receptors, such as T-cell antigen receptors, whose ligands are attached to the surfaces of other cells. The process by which ligand binding triggers receptor phosphorylation, known as "receptor triggering," is a topic of controversy.

Recent studies have shown that the lifetimes of receptor-ligand complexes at the interface between cells are shorter than those in a three-dimensional solution. However, the underlying mechanism behind this observation remains unknown. At the cell-cell interface, the distance between the receptor-ligand complex and long surface molecules (LSMs), including phosphatases like CD45, is relatively short (15 nm). These LSMs are responsible for dephosphorylating the receptor. It has been suggested that the size-based segregation of LSMs from the receptor-ligand complex may be a mechanism for receptor triggering. However, it is unclear whether the mechanical and chemical processes support such small-scale segregation.

In this study, we present a mathematical model at the nanometer scale that combines membrane elasticity with the compressional stiffness and lateral mobility of LSMs. Our model demonstrates a robust segregation of LSMs from a single receptor-ligand complex, which occurs in a supradiffusive manner. According to our model, the redistribution of LSMs over time creates tension on the complex, leading to a decrease in its two-dimensional lifetime. Interestingly, our model also predicts a nonlinear relationship between the three- and two-dimensional lifetimes, which can enhance the receptors' ability to distinguish between similar ligands.

title: High-performance neuroprosthetic control by an individual with tetraplegia.
text:
BACKGROUND: The loss of hand orientation and the ability to grasp, manipulate, and carry objects due to paralysis or amputation of an arm can greatly impact daily activities. Brain-machine interfaces offer a potential solution for restoring these functions. In this study, we aimed to determine if a person with tetraplegia could regain control of a high-performance prosthetic limb using this type of interface.

METHODS: We surgically implanted two 96-channel intracortical microelectrodes in the motor cortex of a 52-year-old individual with tetraplegia. Over a period of 13 weeks, the participant underwent training to learn how to control an anthropomorphic prosthetic limb with seven degrees of freedom. Clinical measures of upper limb function were used to assess the participant's ability to control the prosthetic limb. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01364480.

FINDINGS: On the second day of training, the participant was able to freely move the prosthetic limb within a three-dimensional workspace. After 13 weeks, the participant consistently performed complex movements with the prosthetic limb. The success rate on target-based reaching tasks was significantly higher than chance levels. The participant also showed improvements in completion time and path efficiency. Additionally, the participant was able to perform skilled and coordinated reach and grasp movements, resulting in clinically significant gains in upper limb function. No adverse events were reported.

INTERPRETATION: With further development of neuroprosthetic limbs, individuals with long-term paralysis could regain natural and intuitive control over hand placement, orientation, and reaching, enabling them to perform daily activities. This research was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, National Institutes of Health, Department of Veterans Affairs, and UPMC Rehabilitation Institute.

title: Phase locking and multiple oscillating attractors for the coupled mammalian clock and cell cycle.
text: Many species exhibit daily synchronous rhythms of cell division at the tissue or organism level, indicating a coupling between the circadian clock and cell cycle oscillators. However, the biological relevance of this coupling and its effect on clock and cell cycle progression in mammals remains unclear. Specifically, we lack understanding of how the temporal organization of cell division at the single-cell level contributes to the daily rhythm observed at the tissue level. To address this question, we utilized multispectral imaging of single live cells, computational methods, and mathematical modeling in proliferating mouse fibroblasts. Our findings demonstrate that in unsynchronized cells, the cell cycle and circadian clock are robustly phase locked in a 1:1 fashion. This synchronization allows the two oscillators to oscillate in a coordinated manner with a common frequency in an expanding cell population. Synchronization induced by dexamethasone reveals additional clock states, including distinct coexisting states with a significantly higher period clock. These states are transitioned to after dexamethasone synchronization. The temporal coordination of cell division through phase locking to the clock at the single-cell level has significant implications, as disrupted circadian function has been increasingly associated with the development of various diseases, including cancer.

title: Moderate effect of artemisinin-based combination therapy on transmission of Plasmodium falciparum.
text:
Background: The objective of this study was to investigate the impact of different malaria treatments on submicroscopic gametocytemia and infectiousness. Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) has been effective in reducing microscopically confirmed gametocytemia and mosquito infection. However, recent molecular techniques have revealed high prevalences of submicroscopic gametocytemia. 

Methods: A total of 528 Kenyan children aged 6 months to 10 years were randomly assigned to four treatment groups. Gametocytemia was assessed using both microscopy and Pfs25 RNA-based quantitative nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (Pfs25 QT-NASBA). Transmission was determined through membrane-feeding assays. 

Results: At enrollment, the prevalence of gametocytemia, as determined by Pfs25 QT-NASBA, was 89.4% (219/245). After treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) plus artesunate (AS), SP plus amodiaquine (AQ), and artemether-lumefantrine (AL; Coartem), the prevalence decreased. Membrane-feeding assays conducted on a randomly selected group of children showed that the proportion of infectious children was up to four times higher than expected based on microscopy. ACT did not significantly reduce the proportion of infectious children but did reduce the proportion of infected mosquitoes. 

Conclusions: Submicroscopic gametocytemia is common after treatment and significantly contributes to mosquito infection. However, the impact of ACT on malaria transmission appears to be moderate and limited to the duration of gametocyte carriage and the proportion of infected mosquitoes. It is important to consider the transmission intensity when interpreting these findings.

title: Lip movements entrain the observers’ low-frequency brain oscillations to facilitate speech intelligibility
text: In this study, we examined how lip movements during speech can aid in the processing of speech. We used MEG to directly investigate the interaction between these visual signals and the rhythmic brain activity of participants who were both listening to and watching the speaker. Initially, we looked at the coherence between the oscillatory brain activity and the speaker's lip movements, and found a significant synchronization in the visual cortex. To isolate the effects of the visual speech, we used partial coherence to remove the contributions of the auditory speech signal. By comparing the synchronization under different attention conditions, we discovered that focusing on visual speech enhances the coherence between the visual cortex and the speaker's lips. Additionally, we found a significant partial coherence between the left motor cortex and lip movements, which directly correlated with comprehension accuracy. These findings highlight the importance of visually entrained and attention-modulated rhythmic brain activity in improving audiovisual speech processing.

title: Loss of DExD/H box RNA helicase LGP2 manifests disparate antiviral responses.
text: The DExD/H box RNA helicase retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and the melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) are important receptors within cells that detect virus infections and stimulate the production of type I IFN. Another helicase gene, Lgp2, is similar to Rig-I and Mda5 but lacks a caspase activation and recruitment domain. We conducted experiments using mice that lacked Lgp2 and found that the absence of this gene made cells highly sensitive to the induction of type I IFN by cytosolic polyinosinic/polycytidylic acid. However, we also discovered that the negative feedback inhibition of IFN-beta transcription remained normal in the absence of LGP2, suggesting that LGP2 is not the primary regulator of type I IFN production. Our findings also revealed that Lgp2-deficient mice were resistant to lethal vesicular stomatitis virus infection, which is recognized by RIG-I to trigger type I IFN production. However, these mice did show a deficiency in type I IFN production when infected with encephalomyocarditis virus, which activates MDA5-dependent innate immune responses. Overall, our data demonstrate that LGP2 plays a distinct regulatory role in the activation of innate immune signaling pathways during RNA virus infections.

title: Three-dimensional, single-molecule fluorescence imaging beyond the diffraction limit by using a double-helix point spread function.
text:
We present a novel technique for achieving single-molecule fluorescence imaging in three dimensions, surpassing the limitations imposed by optical diffraction. This is accomplished using a wide-field microscope equipped with a double-helix point spread function (DH-PSF). The DH-PSF design offers exceptional and consistent Fisher information, featuring two prominent lobes in the image plane. The angular orientation of these lobes varies with the axial (z) position of the emitter.

In our experiments, we successfully localized individual fluorescent molecules within a thick polymer sample. This localization was achieved through single 500-ms acquisitions, with a remarkable precision of 10-20 nm, over a large depth of field (2 microm). The localization process involved identifying the center of the two DH-PSF lobes.

To further enhance our imaging capabilities, we employed a photoactivatable fluorophore. By repeatedly imaging sparse subsets of molecules using the DH-PSF microscope, we achieved superresolution imaging of high concentrations of molecules in all three dimensions. This breakthrough was made possible by the combination of the optical PSF design and digital postprocessing techniques, facilitated by the photoactivatable fluorophores. Consequently, our approach opens up new possibilities for improving the resolution of 3D imaging beyond the limitations imposed by the Rayleigh diffraction limit.

title: A unique cell division machinery in the Archaea.
text: Unlike bacteria, euryarchaea, and eukaryotes, the second main archaeal phylum, Crenarchaeota, lacks identified division components. However, our study reveals that a three-gene operon, cdv, in the crenarchaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius, plays a crucial role in cell division. This operon is activated during genome segregation and division, and the resulting Cdv proteins form a polymer structure between segregating nucleoids that persists throughout cell division, gradually shrinking during constriction. Interestingly, the cdv operon is significantly down-regulated after UV irradiation, indicating a response to DNA damage that inhibits division, similar to eukaryotic checkpoint systems. The phylogenetic range of the cdv genes complements the FtsZ-based archaeal division systems, suggesting that one or the other system is present in most archaeal lineages. Notably, two of the Cdv proteins, CdvB and CdvC, share homology with components of the eukaryotic ESCRT-III sorting complex involved in vesicle budding and HIV-1 virion release, suggesting mechanistic similarities and a common evolutionary origin.

title: Modelling and rescuing neurodevelopmental defect of Down syndrome using induced pluripotent stem cells from monozygotic twins discordant for trisomy 21
text: The most common viable chromosomal disorder with intellectual impairment and other developmental abnormalities is Down syndrome, also known as trisomy 21. In this study, we generated and studied induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from monozygotic twins who had different levels of trisomy 21. This allowed us to eliminate the effects of genomic background variability. By analyzing the genetic alterations in the iPSCs and early development, we were able to identify the transcriptional signature of Down syndrome. We also observed abnormal neural differentiation in the Down syndrome iPSCs when they formed teratomas in mice and when they were differentiated into neuroprogenitors and neurons in vitro. These defects were associated with changes in the structure and density of neurons, astroglial and oligodendroglial cells, as well as misexpression of genes involved in neurogenesis and differentiation. Additionally, we discovered that a gene called dual-specificity tyrosine-(Y)-phosphorylation regulated kinase 1A (DYRK1A) on chromosome 21 likely contributes to these defects. Importantly, we found that targeting DYRK1A either pharmacologically or using shRNA resulted in significant correction of these defects.

title: Programmed death-1–induced interleukin-10 production by monocytes impairs CD4+ T cell activation during HIV infection
text: During HIV infection, the replication of viruses and the movement of microbes from the gut to the bloodstream result in excessive immune activation, which contributes to the decrease in CD4+ T cell numbers. In this process, the expression of Programmed death-1 (PD-1) and interleukin-10 (IL-10) is increased. In animal models of chronic viral infections, blocking the interactions between PD-1 and programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1), as well as between IL-10 and IL-10 receptor (IL-10R), leads to the elimination of viruses and improvement in T cell function. Our study reveals that individuals with HIV infection have elevated levels of microbial products and inflammatory cytokines in their blood, which leads to an increase in PD-1 expression on monocytes. This increase in PD-1 expression is correlated with high concentrations of IL-10 in the blood. When PD-1 on monocytes is triggered by PD-L1 on various cell types, it induces the production of IL-10 and causes reversible dysfunction in CD4+ T cells. We have discovered a new role for PD-1, where microbial products inhibit the expansion and function of T cells by upregulating PD-1 levels and IL-10 production by monocytes after PD-1 binds to PD-L1.

title: A general role for splicing enhancers in exon definition.
text: ESEs play a crucial role in exon definition by aiding in the recruitment of splicing factors to the neighboring intron. In our study, we have shown that suboptimal 5' and 3' splice sites can be independently activated by ESEs when they are present on different exons. However, when these weak splice sites are located within a single exon, a single ESE can simultaneously activate both the 5' and 3' splice sites. These findings highlight the ability of a single ESE to facilitate the recognition of both exon/intron junctions in a single step during exon definition. Our results suggest that ESEs recruit a complex comprising essential components of the splicing machinery required for the selection of 5' and 3' splice sites.

title: SecDFyajC is not required for the maintenance of the proton motive force.
text: The role of SecDFyajC in protein export in Escherichia coli is not well understood. To investigate its function, we examined its potential involvement in maintaining the proton motive force. Previous studies have shown that inner membrane vesicles lacking SecDFyajC have difficulty generating a stable proton motive force when energized with succinate. However, this issue does not arise when NADH is used as an electron donor. Interestingly, the proton motive force in SecDFyajC-depleted vesicles still promotes protein translocation to the same extent as in vesicles containing SecDFyajC. Further analysis revealed that the reduced proton motive force in SecDFyajC-lacking vesicles is due to a decrease in the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase. The expression of this enzyme complex is suppressed when cells are grown on glucose media, which is the condition used to deplete SecDFyajC. These findings indicate that SecDFyajC is not necessary for proton motive force-driven protein translocation.

title: The serine protease inhibitor SerpinA3N attenuates neuropathic pain by inhibiting T cell-derived leukocyte elastase
text: Neuropathic pain is a significant and challenging clinical issue, and its underlying mechanisms are not well understood. While recent studies on gene expression profiling have identified potential targets for pain treatment, traditional research methods often yield unclear results due to the varying expression of numerous genes between control and nerve-injured groups. This makes validation, especially regarding the specificity of pain modulation, difficult. To address this, we conducted experiments using two genetically similar strains of rats that were selectively bred to exhibit contrasting levels of neuropathic pain sensitivity. We discovered that SerpinA3N, a serine protease inhibitor, was upregulated in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) following nerve injury. This finding was further confirmed in mice, as their homologous gene also showed increased expression. Mice lacking SerpinA3N displayed heightened neuropathic mechanical allodynia compared to wild-type mice, while the introduction of SerpinA3N reduced mechanical allodynia in wild-type mice. Additionally, T lymphocytes infiltrated the DRG after nerve injury and released leukocyte elastase (LE), which was inhibited by SerpinA3N produced by DRG neurons. The genetic absence of LE or the application of a LE inhibitor (Sivelastat) in wild-type mice reduced neuropathic mechanical allodynia. In summary, our study uncovers a novel and clinically significant role for a member of the serpin superfamily and leukocyte elastase, as well as the interaction between neurons and T cells in the modulation of neuropathic pain.

title: Tissue Transglutaminase Is an Integrin-Binding Adhesion Coreceptor for Fibronectin
text: The enzyme tissue transglutaminase, which is responsible for protein cross-linking, has a strong affinity for fibronectin through its 42-kD gelatin-binding domain. Our study reveals that transglutaminase on the cell surface facilitates cell adhesion and spreading on the 42-kD fibronectin fragment, even though it lacks integrin-binding motifs. When tissue transglutaminase is overexpressed, it increases its presence on the cell surface, leading to enhanced adhesion and spreading on both fibronectin and its 42-kD fragment. Additionally, it enlarges focal adhesions and intensifies the phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase, which is dependent on adhesion. These effects are specific to tissue transglutaminase and are not observed with its functional counterpart, the catalytic subunit of factor XIII. The adhesive function of tissue transglutaminase does not rely on its cross-linking activity but rather on its stable noncovalent association with integrins. Transglutaminase directly interacts with multiple integrins from the β1 and β3 subfamilies, but not with β2 integrins. The formation of complexes between transglutaminase and integrins occurs during biosynthesis inside the cell and accumulates on the cell surface and in focal adhesions. Overall, our findings demonstrate that tissue transglutaminase acts as an integrin-associated coreceptor, facilitating the interaction between integrins and fibronectin to promote cell adhesion and spreading.

title: Imaging the expression of transfected genes in vivo.
text: For the first time, successful gene transduction has been observed in vivo through the use of an appropriate combination of a "marker gene" and a "marker substrate" in an experimental animal model. In this study, the herpes simplex virus 1 thymidine kinase (HSV1-tk) gene was chosen as the marker gene, and the recombinant STK retrovirus containing HSV1-tk was utilized to transduce RG2 glioma cells both in vitro and in vivo. The RG2TK+ cell lines, which expressed the HSV1-tk gene, were evaluated along with three potential marker substrates for the HSV1-TK enzyme. It was found that radiolabeled 5-iodo-2'-fluoro-2'deoxy-1-beta-D-arabinofuranosyluracil (FIAU) was a significantly superior marker substrate compared to 5-iodo-2'-deoxyuridine or ganciclovir. The level of FIAU accumulation in different RG2TK+ clones correlated with their sensitivity to ganciclovir and the amount of HSV1-tk mRNA expression. The expression of HSV1-tk in transduced RG2 tumor cells was successfully visualized in animals using quantitative autoradiography. The accumulation of 2-[14C]FIAU was found to be high in RG2TK+ brain tumors in one hemisphere, while it was very low in nontransduced RG2 tumors in the opposite hemisphere. The transduction of RG2 tumor cells with the HSV-tk gene in vivo resulted in tumors that accumulated FIAU to high levels and produced clear images. Based on the level of FIAU accumulation in the transduced tumors, it is likely that a clinically applicable method for imaging HSV1-tk gene expression can be developed using existing clinical imaging techniques.

title: Engulfment of apoptotic cells: signals for a good meal
text: Phagocytes play a crucial role in removing apoptotic cells from the body, which is essential for maintaining a healthy immune system. Any abnormalities in this process can have serious consequences for self tolerance and the development of autoimmune diseases. Recent studies have shed light on how phagocytes locate and consume apoptotic cells, as well as how they maintain cellular balance after engulfing them. New factors that regulate this process have been discovered, while the roles of previously known factors need to be reevaluated. This review examines these recent findings and aims to address important unanswered questions in this field.

title: Related IgA1 and IgG producing cells in blood and diseased mucosa in ulcerative colitis.
text:
BACKGROUND
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by the infiltration of plasma cells producing IgG autoantibodies in the colonic mucosa. It is unclear whether this is a local mucosal response that has switched to IgG or a peripheral response initiated by antigens that have reached the colonic mucosa. The distribution of IgG secreting cells and isotype switched variants in UC is unknown. The aim of this study was to investigate the distribution of mucosal IgG clones in UC and to search for related IgG and IgA secreting cells in normal and diseased mucosa and blood. Additionally, we aimed to identify characteristics that may differentiate between the mucosal and peripheral repertoire in both normal mucosa and UC.

PATIENTS
We studied blood samples, as well as normal and diseased mucosa, from two patients with UC.

METHODS
We used immunoglobulin gene analysis and clone specific polymerase chain reaction to study the distribution and characteristics of IgG and related IgA in the mucosa and blood of UC patients.

RESULTS
The mucosal IgG response in UC patients consisted of widespread clones of cells that were present in both the diseased mucosa and blood, but were scarce in normal mucosa. Clonally related IgA class switch variants, specifically IgA1, were also detected in the diseased mucosa and blood. This suggests that these clones preferentially home to the diseased mucosa. We found that J(H)1 usage was characteristic of the peripheral repertoire, and observed examples of J(H)1 usage in mucosal IgG in UC.

CONCLUSIONS
Overall, these findings support a model of UC in which a peripheral response is expressed and expanded in the colonic mucosa.

title: Geovisual analytics to enhance spatial scan statistic interpretation: an analysis of U.S. cervical cancer mortality
text:
The spatial scan statistic developed by Kulldorff and its software implementation, SaTScan, are widely used for detecting and evaluating geographic clusters. However, there are two challenges in using the method and interpreting its results. Firstly, the method lacks cartographic support to understand the clusters in a geographic context. Secondly, the results are sensitive to parameter choices related to cluster scaling, but the system does not provide direct support for making these choices. To address these issues and enhance the interpretation of SaTScan results, we employ established and novel geovisual analytics methods. We demonstrate our approach through a case study analysis of cervical cancer mortality in the U.S.

To address the first issue, we provide an interactive visual interface to support the interpretation of SaTScan results. For the second issue, we conducted multiple SaTScan runs with systematically selected parameters to investigate cluster result stability. The results show that no single spatial scan scaling value is optimal for identifying clusters at different scales. Instead, multiple scans with varying parameters are necessary. We introduce a novel method to measure and visualize reliability, which helps identify stable homogeneous clusters across analysis scales. Finally, we propose a logical approach to analyze SaTScan results.

Our geovisual analytics approach facilitates the interpretation of spatial cluster detection methods by providing cartographic representation of SaTScan results and visualization methods to support parameter selection. Our methods distinguish between heterogeneous and homogeneous clusters and assess the stability of clusters across different scales of analysis. We analyzed cervical cancer mortality data for the U.S. aggregated by county between 2000 and 2004. We ran SaTScan fifty times with different parameter choices and used our visual analytic platform to interactively explore and compare the results. We visualized the Standardized Mortality Ratio and reliability scores for all counties to identify stable, homogeneous clusters. We evaluated our analysis by comparing it to results produced by other independent techniques. Our geovisual analytics approach is implemented in our Java-based Visual Inquiry Toolkit.

title: Neurological development of 5-year-old children receiving a low-saturated fat, low-cholesterol diet since infancy: A randomized controlled trial.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of parental counseling on children's diets, specifically focusing on reducing saturated fat and cholesterol intake, on neurodevelopment during the first five years of life. The study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial between February 1990 and November 1996 at an outpatient clinic in Turku, Finland. A total of 1062 seven-month-old infants and their parents were recruited from well-baby clinics between 1990 and 1992. At age five, 496 children still living in Turku participated in neurodevelopmental testing. 

Participants were randomly assigned to receive individualized counseling aimed at limiting the child's fat intake to 30% to 35% of daily energy, with a saturated:monounsaturated:polyunsaturated fatty acid ratio of 1:1:1 and a cholesterol intake of less than 200 mg/d (intervention group) or usual health education (control group). The main outcome measures were nutrient intake, serum lipid concentrations, and neurological development at age five. 

Results showed that children in the intervention group had significantly lower intakes of fat, saturated fatty acids, and cholesterol compared to the control group. The mean percentages of daily energy from fat and saturated fat were lower in the intervention group. Additionally, serum cholesterol concentrations were consistently lower in children in the intervention group. However, there were no significant differences in neurological development between the intervention and control groups. 

In conclusion, the study suggests that providing repeated dietary counseling to parents during the first five years of a child's life can help reduce age-related increases in serum cholesterol without negatively impacting neurological development.

title: Vasodilator responses of coronary resistance arteries of exercise-trained pigs.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether exercise training increases the vasodilator responses of porcine coronary resistance arteries. Yucatan miniature swine were divided into two groups: exercise-trained (ET) and sedentary (SED) control pigs. The ET pigs underwent a progressive treadmill training program for 16 to 20 weeks, while the SED pigs remained inactive during the same period. Coronary resistance arteries with diameters ranging from 64 to 157 microns were isolated for in vitro evaluation of their relaxation responses to different dilators. The dilators tested were sodium nitroprusside, adenosine, and bradykinin. The results showed that exercise training did not alter the relaxation responses to adenosine and sodium nitroprusside. However, the endothelium-dependent relaxation to bradykinin was enhanced in the coronary resistance arteries of ET pigs compared to SED pigs. To determine the mechanisms involved in this enhancement, the responses to bradykinin were examined in the presence of indomethacin and nitro-monomethyl L-arginine (L-NMMA). Both indomethacin and L-NMMA significantly inhibited the bradykinin-induced relaxation in both groups. Despite the decreased relaxation after indomethacin, the bradykinin-induced vasodilation was still enhanced in the ET group. L-NMMA caused greater inhibition of the bradykinin-induced relaxation in the coronary resistance arteries of ET pigs compared to SED pigs and eliminated the training-induced enhancement of the bradykinin responses. In conclusion, these findings suggest that exercise training enhances bradykinin-induced vasodilation by increasing the production of endothelium-derived relaxing factor/nitric oxide through the L-arginine/nitric oxide synthase pathway.

title: Modulation of mitochondrial function and morphology by interaction of Omi/HtrA2 with the mitochondrial fusion factor OPA1.
text: Loss of Omi/HtrA2 function in mouse models leads to the loss of nerve cells and has been associated with neurodegeneration in Parkinson's and Huntington's disease. Omi/HtrA2 is a serine protease that is released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol as a pro-apoptotic factor. While its involvement in protecting against cellular stress is believed to occur under normal conditions, the exact cytological and molecular mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Omi/HtrA2 deficiency results in an accumulation of reactive oxygen species and a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential. Live cell imaging of Omi/HtrA2 knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts, as well as Omi/HtrA2 silenced human HeLa cells and Drosophila S2R+ cells, revealed elongated mitochondria. Electron microscopy confirmed these alterations in mitochondrial morphology and showed abnormal cristae structure. Analysis of proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion revealed a selective increase in the soluble OPA1 protein. Restoring wild-type Omi/HtrA2 in knockout cells reversed the mitochondrial elongation phenotype and OPA1 alterations, while the protease mutant [S306A]Omi/HtrA2 did not have the same effect. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated a direct interaction between Omi/HtrA2 and endogenous OPA1. This study provides the first evidence of the direct impact of Omi/HtrA2 loss on mitochondrial morphology and reveals a novel role of this mitochondrial serine protease in modulating OPA1. These findings highlight the crucial role of impaired mitochondrial dynamics in neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Four prognostic groups predict long-term survival from prostate cancer following radiotherapy alone on Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trials.
text:
The purpose of this analysis is to determine the prognostic subgroups that correlate with disease-specific survival (DSS) in men with prostate cancer who were treated with external beam radiotherapy (XRT). The factors considered in this analysis are the Gleason score (GS), T stage, and pathologic lymph node status, which have been identified as independent predictors of death from prostate cancer. 

For this study, a total of 1557 men who participated in one of four Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) Phase III randomized trials between 1975 and 1992 were selected. The inclusion criteria were that the patients were evaluable and eligible for the trial, did not receive hormonal therapy as part of their initial treatment, and had available follow-up data. A DSS event was declared if the patient's death was certified as due to prostate cancer, complications of treatment, or unknown causes with active malignancy. The median follow-up for patients treated on early and late RTOG studies exceeded 11 and 6 years, respectively.

Based on the pretreatment GS, T stage, and lymph node status, the patients were grouped into four subgroups with similar risk of dying from prostate cancer. Group 1 consisted of patients with a GS of 2-6 and T1-2Nx; Group 2 included patients with a GS of 2-6 and T3Nx, or GS of 2-6 and N+, or GS of 7 and T1-2Nx; Group 3 comprised patients with T3Nx and GS of 7, or N+ and GS of 7, or T1-2Nx and GS of 8-10; and Group 4 consisted of patients with T3Nx and GS of 8-10, or N+ and GS of 8-10.

The DSS rates at 5, 10, and 15 years were as follows: 96%, 86%, and 72% for Group 1; 94%, 75%, and 61% for Group 2; 83%, 62%, and 39% for Group 3; and 64%, 34%, and 27% for Group 4.

In conclusion, identifying these four risk groups allows for estimating the long-term DSS in men treated with XRT alone and can aid in the design of future prospective randomized trials.

title: The pathogenesis of bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice.
text: Pulmonary fibrosis was induced in mice by administering 0.5 mg of bleomycin twice a week for a period of 4 weeks. The initial damage occurred in the intima of pulmonary arteries and veins, where endothelial cells became swollen and separated from the underlying basement membrane due to large blebs. These lesions appeared after 2 weeks and were accompanied by the infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells into the perivascular spaces. After 4 weeks, capillary endothelial cells started to form blebs and interstitial edema was observed. At this stage, type 1 alveolar epithelial cells experienced multifocal necrosis, leading to the exudation of fibrin into the alveoli. The repair process involved the proliferation and transformation of type 2 epithelial cells, the organization of alveolar fibrin by fibroblasts, and the development of fibrosis in the interstitium within 8 to 12 weeks. These consistent changes, similar to those seen in diffuse pulmonary fibrosis or fibrosing alveolitis in humans, suggest that bleomycin-induced injury could serve as a suitable model for studying this group of diseases, which are currently poorly defined.

title: The DNA damage response during mitosis.
text: Cells possess an intrinsic signaling network known as the DNA damage response (DDR), which detects DNA damage and triggers various pathways to halt the cell cycle and repair the damaged DNA. Alternatively, the DDR can eliminate irreparable cells through apoptosis or senescence. The DDR can be activated at any stage of the cell cycle in response to DNA damage, although the extent of signaling differs in each phase. Notably, the response to DNA double strand breaks is minimal during mitosis. Early studies revealed that cells exposed to radiation during mitosis continued dividing without repairing their broken chromosomes. These findings suggested a reduced DNA repair capacity and absence of an immediate cell cycle arrest due to DNA damage. Recently, researchers have shed light on the mechanisms that rewire DDR signaling during mitosis. Specific signaling pathways within the DDR network are deactivated in mitotic cells, but the cells still mark their damaged DNA for repair after exiting mitosis. Understanding how cancer cells handle DNA damage during interphase versus mitosis is crucial, as cancer treatments often involve agents that induce DNA damage and inhibit mitotic progression. This review explores the molecular intricacies of DDR signaling during mitosis and the implications of encountering DNA damage in mitotic cells.

title: Model-based Geostatistics
text: The field of geostatistics focuses on solving estimation and prediction problems for phenomena that are continuous in space, using data collected from a limited number of specific locations. Model-based geostatistics involves applying statistical principles of modeling and inference to address geostatistical problems. This book is the first comprehensive treatment of model-based geostatistics.

title: Placebo-Controlled Trials and Active-Control Trials in the Evaluation of New Treatments. Part 1: Ethical and Scientific Issues
text: Placebo-controlled trials are commonly used in the development of new pharmaceuticals. However, there is ongoing debate about their ethical implications when patients could be treated with existing therapies. The Declaration of Helsinki, an international document that outlines ethical principles for clinical investigation, is often cited in this discussion. Some argue that placebo controls are unethical when effective treatment options are available. However, this interpretation is flawed for several reasons. Firstly, it would also prohibit active-control and historically controlled trials, not just placebo-controlled trials. Secondly, not all failures to use known effective therapy should be considered equivalent. In cases where the treatment does not affect long-term health, it is not reasonable to deem placebo-controlled trials unethical. For example, using placebos in short-term studies for conditions like allergic rhinitis or insomnia may not be unethical if patients are fully informed. Additionally, the phrase in the Declaration that is often cited to support the argument against placebo controls was added in 1975 and was not intended to discourage such trials. The American Medical Association, the World Health Organization, and the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences have all rejected the notion that the Declaration universally prohibits placebo-controlled trials when proven therapy is available. Informed consent is crucial in placebo-controlled trials, and patients must be fully informed about their alternatives. While concerns about the validity of informed consent are valid, they apply to all types of clinical trials, not just placebo-controlled ones. It is concluded that placebo-controlled trials can be ethically conducted even when effective therapy exists, as long as patients are not harmed and are fully informed. However, determining the effectiveness of new treatments through active-control trials can be challenging. Active-control equivalence trials, which aim to show that a new drug is equivalent or noninferior to a known effective treatment, have limitations. These trials require the assumption that the active control had an effect in the study, which cannot be tested within the trial itself. Assay sensitivity, the ability of a study to distinguish between active and inactive treatments, is crucial in determining the effectiveness of a new drug. In many cases, this assumption cannot be made, and external information from past placebo-controlled studies is needed to interpret the results. Therefore, active-control trials often cannot replace placebo-controlled trials in evaluating the effectiveness of new treatments.

title: Breath-methane in patients with cancer of the large bowel.
text: Out of the 30 patients diagnosed with cancer of the large bowel, 24 individuals (80%) exhibited measurable levels of methane in their breath. In comparison, only 25 patients (39%) out of the 64 individuals with non-malignant large-bowel disease and 83 subjects (40%) out of the 208 individuals without large-bowel disease had detectable levels of methane. These findings indicate a potential variance in the anaerobic intestinal flora between patients with cancer of the large bowel and those without the disease. This distinction could either precede the development of the tumor or be a consequence of it.

title: Immune cells contribute to the maintenance of neurogenesis and spatial learning abilities in adulthood
text: The adult brain is known to undergo neurogenesis. This study highlights the significance of T lymphocytes and microglia in maintaining hippocampal neurogenesis and spatial learning abilities in adulthood. The presence of T cells and activation of microglia were observed during hippocampal neurogenesis induced by an enriched environment. However, in mice with compromised immune systems, hippocampal neurogenesis was severely impaired and could not be improved through environmental enrichment. Nevertheless, when T cells recognizing a specific CNS antigen were introduced, hippocampal neurogenesis was restored and enhanced. Additionally, CNS-specific T cells were found to be essential for spatial learning, memory, and the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in the dentate gyrus. These findings suggest that a shared immune-related mechanism plays a role in various aspects of hippocampal plasticity and cell renewal in the adult brain.

title: Sperm cross-over activity in regions of the human genome showing extreme breakdown of marker association.
text: Recent population diversity data have yielded significant insights into meiotic recombination in the human genome. These data have revealed a landscape dominated by numerous cross-over hotspots, although only a small fraction of these hotspots have been directly studied for cross-over activity. In this study, we present a search for highly active hotspots by utilizing a marker association breakdown as a guide for high-resolution analysis of sperm cross-over. This approach has allowed us to identify the most active cross-over hotspots known to date. These hotspots exhibit similar characteristics in terms of morphology, sequence attributes, and cross-over processes compared to less active hotspots. However, their activity in sperm cannot be accurately predicted based on population diversity information. Some of these hotspots also displayed evidence of biased gene conversion accompanying cross-over, and in certain cases, there was variation in cross-over activity between individuals, with two hotspots showing complete presence/absence polymorphism in different individuals. While polymorphism is common in less active hotspots, it was not observed in any of the most active hotspots. This contradicts the expectation that extreme hotspots would be more susceptible to attenuation by meiotic drive, favoring mutations that suppress recombination. Consequently, these extreme hotspots offer a valuable resource for studying meiotic recombination processes and pathways in humans.

title: An efficient nonviral method to generate integration-free human-induced pluripotent stem cells from cord blood and peripheral blood cells.
text: The ability to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient-specific somatic cells, such as blood cells, is a valuable tool for disease modeling and drug discovery. In order to facilitate research using these cells, it is important to develop methods that are less invasive and use easily accessible tissues. Our recent study demonstrated the successful generation of human iPSCs from adult fibroblasts using a combination of plasmids encoding specific factors. In this report, we present a modified protocol that allows for efficient iPSC induction from CD34+ cord blood cells and peripheral blood obtained from healthy donors using the same plasmid vectors. While the original plasmid mixture was able to induce iPSCs, the efficiency was low. However, by introducing an additional plasmid encoding EBNA1, a crucial factor for episomal amplification of the vectors, we significantly improved the efficiency of iPSC induction, particularly when using αβT cells. With this enhancement, we were able to successfully generate blood-derived iPSCs from seven healthy donors, ranging in age from their 20s to their 60s. This induction method has the potential to be a valuable tool for generating patient-specific iPSCs without the need for integration and could also be adapted for the production of clinical-grade iPSCs in the future.

title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
text: The synthesis of new proteins is necessary for various types of long-lasting behavioral and synaptic plasticity. For instance, long-term potentiation (LTP) that lasts for more than an hour requires both transcription and translation. However, the mechanisms that connect synaptic events to protein translation during long-lasting synaptic plasticity are not well understood. One signaling pathway that is activated by growth factors and leads to the translation of specific mRNAs involves the rapamycin-sensitive kinase mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR, also known as FRAP and RAFT-1). Western blot analysis has shown that several components of this translational signaling pathway, including mTOR, eukaryotic initiation factor-4E-binding proteins 1 and 2, and eukaryotic initiation factor-4E, are present in the rat hippocampus. Immunostaining studies have also revealed the presence of these proteins in the cell bodies and dendrites of hippocampal slices. In cultured hippocampal neurons, these proteins are found in dendrites and often near the presynaptic protein, synapsin I. They completely overlap with a postsynaptic protein, PSD-95, at synaptic sites, suggesting their postsynaptic localization. Inhibiting mTOR signaling with rapamycin reduces the expression of late-phase LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation, while the early phase of LTP remains unaffected. Rapamycin also blocks the synaptic potentiation induced by brain-derived neurotrophic factor in hippocampal slices. These findings demonstrate the crucial role of rapamycin-sensitive signaling in the expression of two forms of synaptic plasticity that require new protein synthesis. The localization of this translational signaling pathway at postsynaptic sites may serve as a mechanism for regulating local protein synthesis at potentiated synapses.

title: The FASEB Journal express article 10.1096/fj.00-0815fje. Published online June 27, 2001. Essential role for cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration
text:
SPECIFIC AIMS
The aim of this study is to investigate the relationship between lipid metabolism and amyloid beta protein (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease. Specifically, we will examine the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration using adult rat hippocampal slice technology, limited cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolic labeling, extracellular recording of CA1 field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), and immunofluorescence.

PRINCIPAL FINDINGS
Our previous research suggested that the connection between lipid metabolism and Aβ is a crucial piece of the puzzle in understanding Alzheimer's disease. In this current study, we focused on the impact of cholesterol on synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration. We used a combination of techniques including adult rat hippocampal slice technology, limited cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolic labeling, extracellular recording of CA1 field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), and immunofluorescence.

Our main findings indicate that increased cholesterol efflux negatively affects both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity. Synaptic plasticity is a vital characteristic of the central nervous system (CNS) that allows synapses to retain previous activity and adapt to current synaptic action. We investigated whether an increased cholesterol efflux, induced ex vivo by normal human CSF-HDL3 and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD), could impact synaptic plasticity.

title: Functional inhibition of osteoblastic cells in an in vivo mouse model of myeloid leukemia.
text: The cause of morbidity in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is often attributed to pancytopenia, although the exact reason behind it remains unclear. Previous studies have shown that normal osteoblastic cells play a role in supporting hematopoiesis. In order to understand how leukemia affects osteoblastic cells, we conducted experiments using a mouse model of AML that had a functioning immune system. The results showed that leukemic mice experienced a decrease in osteoblastic cells, as evidenced by lower levels of the bone formation marker osteocalcin in their serum. Additionally, there was a reduction in osteoprogenitor cells and osteopontin(+) cells lining the endosteum, and a decrease in osteocalcin mRNA in CD45(-) marrow cells. As a result, there was a significant loss of mineralized bone. Although osteoclasts were temporarily increased, there was no significant increase in bone resorption, and inhibiting their activity only partially prevented leukemia-induced bone loss. In vitro experiments suggested that a secreted factor derived from leukemia cells inhibited osteoblastic cells. Given that the chemokine CCL-3 has been reported to inhibit osteoblastic function in myeloma, we investigated its expression in our model and in AML patients. Consistent with its potential role in leukemic-induced bone loss, we found a significant increase in CCL-3 mRNA in malignant marrow cells from leukemic mice and in samples from AML patients. Based on these findings, we propose that targeting the disruption of osteoblastic and osteoclastic cell interactions caused by leukemia could be a novel therapeutic approach to promote normal hematopoiesis in patients with myeloid neoplasms.

title: Fibroblast heterogeneity in the cancer wound
text: Fibroblasts play a crucial role in maintaining the structure and function of healthy tissues. They also contribute to tissue repair after acute inflammation, but can become overactive during chronic inflammatory conditions like cancer. These cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) have the ability to influence the tumor microenvironment and impact the behavior of cancer cells, either promoting or inhibiting tumor growth. The diverse functions of fibroblasts demonstrate their adaptability and offer potential opportunities for understanding and treating cancer. In this discussion, we explore the emerging concepts in CAF biology in relation to tumor development and therapy.

title: Cohort profile: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS).
text: The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) is a comprehensive survey that focuses on individuals in China who are 45 years of age or older, as well as their spouses. It aims to assess the social, economic, and health conditions of community residents. CHARLS specifically examines how the population in China is adapting to the challenges of rapid aging. The initial national survey for CHARLS took place from June 2011 to March 2012 and involved 17,708 participants. These respondents are then followed up every 2 years through face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviews (CAPI). Physical measurements are taken during each follow-up, and blood samples are collected once every two follow-up periods. In 2008, a pilot survey was conducted in two provinces of China, involving 2,685 individuals who were then resurveyed in 2012. To ensure the use of best practices and facilitate international comparisons, CHARLS was aligned with the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) model, a leading international research study. For collaboration inquiries, please contact Dr. Yaohui Zhao at yhzhao@nsd.edu.cn. All CHARLS data is stored at the National School of Development of Peking University and will be accessible to researchers worldwide through the study's website. The pilot data from 2008 can be found at: http://charls.ccer.edu.cn/charls/. The national baseline data for the study is expected to be released in January 2013.

title: Central role of Th2/Tc2 lymphocytes in pattern II multiple sclerosis lesions
text:
AIM The aim of this study was to identify, isolate, and characterize brain-infiltrating clonally expanded T cells in pattern II multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions. 

METHODS Next-generation sequencing was used to identify clonally expanded T cells in demyelinating pattern II brain autopsy lesions. These T-cell clones were then isolated from autologous cerebrospinal fluid and functionally characterized. 

RESULTS Clonally expanded CD8(+) and CD4(+) T cells were identified in demyelinating pattern II lesions. For the first time, these T cells were successfully isolated as live T-cell clones. Functional characterization revealed that the T-cell infiltrate in pattern II brain lesions was dominated by T cells releasing Th2 cytokines and providing B cell help. 

CONCLUSION This study provides the first functional evidence for a potential role of Th2/Tc2 cells in pattern II MS, challenging the commonly ascribed protective role of Th2 cells. These findings have important implications for future treatments of pattern II MS patients.

title: Coordinated oscillations in cortical actin and Ca2+ correlate with cycles of vesicle secretion
text: The role of the actin cortex in the exocytosis of secretory granules is both supportive and inhibitory. However, the mechanism by which cells reconcile these conflicting functions has not been well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that antigen activation of mast cells triggers oscillations in the levels of calcium ions (Ca2+) and PtdIns(4,5)P(2) lipids, which in turn leads to cyclic recruitment of N-WASP and oscillations in cortical actin levels. Through experimental and computational analysis, we propose that the fusion of vesicles is correlated with the observed oscillations in actin and Ca2+ levels. The process of vesicle secretion follows a cycle, beginning with the capture of vesicles by actin when cortical F-actin levels are high. Subsequently, the vesicles pass through the cortex when F-actin levels are low, and finally fuse with the plasma membrane when Ca2+ levels increase. This suggests that cells utilize fluctuating levels of Ca2+, PtdIns(4,5)P(2), and cortical F-actin to enhance the efficiency of secretion, thereby explaining how the actin cortex can serve as both a carrier and a barrier for vesicle secretion.

title: WK175, a novel antitumor agent, decreases the intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide concentration and induces the apoptotic cascade in human leukemia cells.
text: We have recently developed a new class of antitumor agents that effectively inhibit the growth of various tumor cells when cultured in a laboratory setting. Among these agents, WK175 has demonstrated strong efficacy in vitro and was chosen as a representative compound for further study. WK175 works by disrupting the normal levels of NAD(+) within the cells, leading to a decrease in cellular NAD(+) concentration. Interestingly, WK175 induces cell death through apoptosis without causing any damage to the DNA. To understand the mechanism behind this apoptotic pathway, we conducted detailed experiments using THP-1 cells, a human monocytic leukemia cell line. We observed changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, release of cytochrome c, activation of caspase 3, cleavage of caspase 3 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, and the appearance of a sub-G(1) cell cycle population over time. After 24 hours of treatment with 10 nM WK175, we observed activation of this cascade. Importantly, we found that the induction of apoptosis could be prevented by inhibitors of the mitochondrial permeability transition and caspase 3 and 9, such as bongkrekic acid, Z-Asp-Glu-Val-Asp-fluoromethylketone, and Z-Leu-Glu-His-Asp-fluoromethylketone, respectively. However, a specific inhibitor of caspase 1, Ac-Tyr-Val-Ala-Asp-CHO, did not prevent apoptosis, suggesting that the permeability transition pore, caspase 3, and caspase 9 are involved in the apoptotic cascade induced by WK175. These findings indicate that the decrease in NAD(+) concentration triggers the apoptotic cascade, leading to the antitumor effects of WK175.

title: Husbands' involvement in delivery care utilization in rural Bangladesh: A qualitative study
text:
The lack of access to professional delivery care is a major contributor to the high maternal mortality rate in Bangladesh. To better understand women's access to and utilization of maternal health services, it is crucial to examine the role of the family, particularly the husband, during pregnancy and childbirth. This qualitative study focuses on husbands' involvement during childbirth and their utilization of professional delivery care in a rural sub-district of Netrokona district, Bangladesh.

To conduct this study, ten households that utilized a skilled attendant during the birth of their youngest child were selected and matched with ten households that utilized an untrained traditional birth attendant, known as a dhatri. The selection of households was based on specific criteria, such as household income, ethnicity, and proximity to the nearest hospital. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with the husbands of these households in June 2010, and the interviews were transcribed, translated into English, and analyzed using NVivo 9.0.

By purposefully selecting households that differed in the type of provider used during delivery, we were able to eliminate common barriers such as high costs, poor transportation, and long distances to health facilities as factors influencing the utilization of professional delivery care. Instead, we identified divergent themes related to husbands' social support and perceived social norms as underlying factors associated with delivery care utilization. Husbands whose wives utilized professional delivery care provided emotional, instrumental, and informational support during delivery and believed in the necessity of medical intervention. On the other hand, husbands whose wives utilized an untrained dhatri at home were uninvolved during delivery and adhered to the local tradition of childbirth taking place at home.

These findings provide valuable insights into male involvement during childbirth in rural Bangladesh. Program planners should consider culturally sensitive approaches to involve husbands in maternal health interventions and evaluate the effectiveness of educational strategies targeted at husbands.

title: Mapping Meiotic Single-Strand DNA Reveals a New Landscape of DNA Double-Strand Breaks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: Meiotic recombination is initiated by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) caused by the Spo11 protein. Previous studies on DSB mapping have used rad50S or sae2Δ mutants, which have defects in break processing, to accumulate Spo11-linked DSBs. These studies have reported the presence of large "DSB-hot" regions (≥ 50 kb) that are separated by "DSB-cold" domains of similar size. However, it has been observed that substantial recombination occurs in some of these DSB-cold regions, suggesting abnormal DSB patterns in rad50S or sae2Δ mutants. To address this, a new method was developed to map genome-wide, single-strand DNA (ssDNA)-associated DSBs that accumulate in dmc1Δ and dmc1Δ rad51Δ mutants, which are capable of processing but unable to repair DSBs. The results showed the presence of DSBs not only in known hot spots but also in most previously identified DSB-cold regions, including those near centromeres and telomeres. While approximately 40% of the genome is DSB-cold in rad50S mutants, analysis of meiotic ssDNA from dmc1Δ mutants revealed significant DSB activity in most of these regions. Southern blot assays of DSBs in selected regions in dmc1Δ, rad50S, and wild-type cells confirmed these findings. Therefore, it was concluded that DSBs are distributed more uniformly than previously believed. Comparisons of DSB signals in different mutant strains identified Dmc1 as a critical factor for strand-exchange activity throughout the genome and confirmed that Spo11-induced lesions initiate all meiotic recombination.

title: Alterations in liver ATP homeostasis in human nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a pilot study.
text: The exact mechanisms that lead to the progression from fatty liver to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis are not known. However, studies on obese mice with fatty livers have shown that they are susceptible to liver adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion and necrosis, indicating that altered hepatic energy balance may play a role. The objective of this study was to determine if patients with fatty liver disease have impaired recovery from hepatic ATP depletion. The study involved analyzing liver ATP levels using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy before and after inducing transient hepatic ATP depletion through fructose injection. The study was conducted between July 15 and August 30, 1998, at a university hospital. The participants included eight adults with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and seven healthy controls matched for age and sex. The main outcome measure was the level of ATP one hour after fructose infusion in patients compared to controls. The results showed that patients had increased serum aminotransferase levels compared to controls (P = .02). However, albumin and bilirubin values were normal, and there was no clinical evidence of portal hypertension in either group. Two patients had moderate fibrosis, and one had cirrhosis on liver biopsy. The mean serum glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels were similar between the two groups, but patients weighed significantly more than controls (P = .02). Liver ATP levels were similar in both groups before fructose infusion and decreased similarly in both groups after fructose infusion (P = .01 compared to initial ATP levels). However, controls were able to replenish their hepatic ATP stores during the one-hour follow-up period (P<.02 compared to minimum ATP), while patients were not. As a result, patients had lower hepatic ATP levels than controls at the end of the study (P = .04). Body mass index (BMI) was inversely correlated with ATP recovery, even in controls (R = -0.768; P = .07). Although BMI was higher in patients than controls (P = .02) and strongly correlated with fatty liver and serum aminotransferase elevations, neither of these parameters nor the severity of fibrosis on histology strongly predicted hepatic ATP recovery. In conclusion, these findings suggest that as body mass increases, the ability to recover from hepatic ATP depletion becomes progressively less efficient in healthy individuals and is severely impaired in patients with obesity-related nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

title: Blockade of class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase ameliorates obesity-induced inflammation and insulin resistance.
text: The key features of metabolic syndrome, namely obesity and insulin resistance, are closely linked to a state of chronic, low-grade inflammation characterized by abnormal infiltration of macrophages into adipose tissues. While it has been observed that chemokines activate class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3Kγ) to promote leukocyte migration during inflammatory states, little is known about the role of PI3Kγ in the infiltration of macrophages into tissues, systemic inflammation, and the development of insulin resistance in obesity. In this study, we utilized murine models of both diet-induced and genetically induced obesity to investigate the involvement of PI3Kγ in the accumulation of tissue macrophages and the development of obesity-induced insulin resistance. Mice lacking the catalytic subunit of PI3Kγ (Pik3cg(-/-)) demonstrated improved systemic insulin sensitivity with enhanced insulin signaling in the tissues of obese animals. In obese Pik3cg(-/-) mice, the numbers of proinflammatory macrophages infiltrating adipose tissues and livers were significantly reduced, resulting in the suppression of inflammatory reactions in these tissues. Additionally, the deletion of PI3Kγ specifically in bone marrow cells and the pharmacological blockade of PI3Kγ also improved macrophage infiltration and insulin resistance induced by obesity. These findings suggest that PI3Kγ plays a critical role in the development of both obesity-induced inflammation and systemic insulin resistance, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes.

title: Identifying common impairments in frail and dependent older people: validation of the COPE assessment for non-specialised health workers in low resource primary health care settings
text:
In resource-poor settings, frail and dependent older individuals often do not receive adequate care from health systems that lack outreach capabilities. To address this issue, the COPE (Caring for Older PEople) multidimensional assessment tool was developed to assist community health workers (CHWs) in identifying significant impairments and providing evidence-based interventions. 

In this study, 150 older individuals identified as frail or dependent by CHWs were assessed at home using the structured COPE assessment tool. This assessment provided information on impairments related to nutrition, mobility, vision, hearing, continence, cognition, mood, and behavior. The older individuals were then reassessed by local physicians who made clinical judgments regarding the presence or absence of the same impairments using the EASY-Care assessment tool.

The results showed that the COPE tool was easy to administer and empowered CHWs to understand and address the needs of older individuals. However, there was only modest agreement between the COPE assessment by CHWs and the assessments made by clinicians (ranging from 45.8% to 91.3%) for most impairments. Clinicians generally reported higher prevalence of impairments, particularly for visual impairment (98.7% vs. 45.8%), cognitive impairment (78.4% vs. 38.2%), and depression (82.0% vs. 59.9%). 

Most cases identified by the WHO-COPE tool were confirmed by clinicians (positive predictive values ranging from 72.2% to 98.5%), and the levels of disability and care needs among those identified by COPE were higher than those identified solely by clinicians. 

In conclusion, the COPE assessment tool is feasible for identifying specific impairments in frail and dependent older individuals in the community. The impairments identified by COPE are likely to be confirmed as clinically relevant by clinicians, and the tool may be particularly effective in targeting those with the greatest unmet needs.

title: The carboxyl terminus of human cytomegalovirus-encoded 7 transmembrane receptor US28 camouflages agonism by mediating constitutive endocytosis.
text: US28, a chemokine receptor encoded by human cytomegalovirus, is one of four 7 transmembrane (7TM) receptors.
