It has been observed to exhibit both ligand-independent signaling and endocytosis in a constitutively active manner. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between the constitutive activity and constitutive endocytosis of US28. To do so, we generated various chimeric and mutant US28 proteins that had alterations in either their constitutive endocytic or signaling properties. Our findings indicate that the cytoplasmic tail domain of US28 plays a crucial role in regulating receptor endocytosis, independent of the signaling ability of the core domain. Furthermore, we discovered that the constitutive endocytic property of US28 can be transferred to other 7TM receptors, such as the herpes virus 8-encoded ORF74 and the tachykinin NK1 receptor. When the C terminus of US28 was deleted, we observed a decrease in constitutive endocytosis and an increase in signaling capacity for all tested receptors. This was determined through various assays measuring inositol phosphate turnover, NF-kappa B, and cAMP-responsive element-binding protein transcription. Additionally, we found that the constitutive endocytic property of US28 influences the activity of its chemokine ligand fractalkine/CX3CL1. In the absence of the US28 C terminus, fractalkine/CX3CL1 acts as an agonist on US28. This study provides novel insights into how the endocytic properties of a 7TM receptor can mask the agonist properties of a ligand.

title: Geometry, epistasis, and developmental patterning.
text: Developmental signaling networks in embryos are made up of numerous components, making it challenging to measure their interactions. However, geometric reasoning allows for the creation of a discrete hierarchy of phenotypic models using a few composite variables, which can be defined using in vivo data. The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans provides a classic model for studying the integration of two signaling pathways in vulval development: EGF induction and Notch lateral signaling. By analyzing existing data on the probabilities of different terminal cell types in various genetic backgrounds, as well as timed ablation of the inductive signal, a geometric model can be constructed and most of its parameters can be determined. This dynamic model encompasses both signaling and commitment, and can predict the correlated cell fate probabilities when crossing different backgrounds or conditions. The two signaling pathways are combined additively, without any interactions, and epistasis only occurs due to the nonlinear flow in the landscape defined by the geometric model. Consequently, the model can accurately explain genetic experiments that suggest mutual pathway repression. Additionally, the model can quantify the contributions of external and internal sources of noise in the penetrance of mutant phenotypes in signaling hypomorphs, and can account for available experiments without requiring any additional parameters. The parameters necessary to define Notch autocrine signaling can be determined using data from anchor cell ablation.

title: Table of Contents
text: The development of the C. elegans embryo is primarily influenced by the growth of the epidermis, also known as the hypodermis, which forms a single layer around the animal. The morphogenesis of the epidermis involves interactions between cells and internal tissues, such as the developing nervous system and musculature. Through genetic analysis of mutants with abnormal epidermal structure, multiple stages in epidermal morphogenesis have been identified. In a normal embryo, epidermal cells are produced on the upper side of the embryo from four early embryonic blastomeres. The fate of becoming epidermal cells is controlled by a hierarchy of transcription factors. Once specified, the dorsal epidermal cells rearrange through a process called dorsal intercalation. Most epidermal cells merge together to form multinucleate syncytia. The epidermal sheet located on the upper side of the embryo then undergoes epiboly to enclose the rest of the embryo, known as ventral enclosure. This movement requires both an intact epidermal layer and substrate neuroblasts. Different regions of the epidermis exhibit three distinct types of cellular behavior during the enclosure process. After enclosure, the epidermis elongates as a result of coordinated changes in cell shape. Elongation is influenced by various components, including actin microfilaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments, and body wall muscles. The final shape of the epidermis is maintained by the collagenous exoskeleton, which is secreted by the upper surface of the epidermis.

title: High-throughput sequencing reveals extensive variation in human-specific L1 content in individual human genomes.
text: We developed a method using high-throughput sequencing to identify the insertion sites of nearly all members of the human-specific L1 retrotransposon family in any human genome. By using specific nucleotides as markers, we successfully located around 800 copies of L1Hs that belong to the pre-Ta, Ta-0, and Ta-1 L1Hs subfamilies. More than 90% of the sequenced reads corresponded to human-specific elements. Our analysis revealed that, on average, two individual genomes differ at approximately 285 sites in terms of the presence or absence of L1 insertions. In our study, we examined a total of 25 individuals, including 15 unrelated individuals, at 1139 sites. Among these sites, 772 were shared with the reference genome, while 367 were nonreference L1 insertions. We observed that the L1Hs profiles accurately reflected genetic ancestry and allowed us to determine the distribution of these elements across chromosomes. Based on our findings, we estimate that the rate of L1 retrotransposition in humans ranges from 1 in 95 to 1 in 270 births. Additionally, we identified between 3000 and 10,000 dimorphic L1 elements in the human population with gene frequencies greater than 0.05.

title: Nationwide trends in incidence, treatment and survival of colorectal cancer patients with synchronous metastases
text:
The objective of this study was to analyze the incidence, treatment, and survival rates of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients with synchronous metastases (Stage IV) in the Netherlands. A population-based study was conducted, including 160,278 patients diagnosed with CRC between 1996 and 2011. The study examined changes in stage distribution, location of synchronous metastases, and treatment over four consecutive periods. Statistical tests were used to determine trends, and Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to calculate median survival in months. 

The proportion of Stage IV CRC patients (n = 33,421) increased from 19% in the period 1996-1999 to 23% in the period 2008-2011 (p < 0.001). This increase was primarily due to a significant rise in the incidence of lung metastases, which went from affecting 1.7% to 5.0% of all CRC patients. Throughout the study period, the resection of the primary tumor occurred less frequently in Stage IV patients, decreasing from 65% to 46%. Conversely, the use of systemic treatment increased from 29% to 60%. Additionally, there was an increase in metastasectomy among patients with only one metastatic site, particularly in those with liver-only disease, which rose from 5% to 18% (p < 0.001). 

The median survival of all Stage IV CRC patients increased from 7 to 12 months. Notably, patients with metastases confined to the liver or lungs experienced a significant improvement in survival, with median survival rates of 9 to 16 months and 12 to 24 months, respectively (both p < 0.001). Over the past two decades, there has been an increase in the detection of lung metastases, as well as a higher proportion of Stage IV CRC patients receiving systemic therapy and/or metastasectomy. Consequently, patient survival has significantly improved. However, the prognosis for Stage IV patients has become increasingly diverse.

title: The curious case of the tumour virus: 50 years of Burkitt's lymphoma
text: The discovery of Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) occurred half a century ago, coinciding with the identification of the first human tumour virus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), in BL tumours. Over time, the involvement of EBV in BL development has become increasingly puzzling. Recently, however, we have made significant progress in comprehending the intricate and fascinating interaction between EBV and B cells, which contributes to the susceptibility to BL. In this article, we explore the intertwined histories of EBV and BL, as well as their connection to the contributing factors in BL pathogenesis, namely malaria and the MYC translocation.

title: Nanotoxicology: An Emerging Discipline Evolving from Studies of Ultrafine Particles
text: The exposure of humans to airborne nanosized particles (NSPs; < 100 nm) has increased significantly in the past century due to human activities, in addition to the exposure that has occurred throughout our evolutionary history. The field of nanotechnology, which is rapidly advancing, is expected to contribute to this exposure through inhalation, ingestion, skin contact, and injection of engineered nanomaterials. It is crucial to gather information about the safety and potential hazards associated with this exposure. The expanding field of nanotoxicology, which involves evaluating the safety of engineered nanostructures and nanodevices, can draw upon the findings of older studies on NSPs and more recent studies on airborne ultrafine particles. These studies provide the basis for understanding some key concepts in nanotoxicology. When NSPs are inhaled, they can efficiently deposit in all parts of the respiratory tract through diffusional mechanisms. Their small size allows them to enter cells and move across epithelial and endothelial cells into the bloodstream and lymphatic system, potentially reaching sensitive areas such as the bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, and heart. There is also evidence that NSPs can access the central nervous system and ganglia by traveling along axons and dendrites of neurons. NSPs that penetrate the skin can be distributed through the lymphatic channels. The process of endocytosis and the biokinetics of NSPs depend largely on their surface chemistry and any modifications they undergo in vivo. NSPs have a larger surface area per mass compared to larger particles of the same chemistry, making them more biologically active. This activity can include both inflammatory and pro-oxidant effects, as well as antioxidant activity, which may explain the mixed findings regarding the toxicity of NSPs to species in the environment. The presence of NSPs in mitochondria and the induction of oxidative stress suggest the need for further research on their interactions with subcellular structures. When assessing the safety of engineered NSPs, it is important to carefully select appropriate doses/concentrations and consider the potential for increased effects in compromised organisms, as well as the potential benefits of desirable effects. Nanotoxicology research requires an interdisciplinary approach, involving fields such as toxicology, materials science, medicine, molecular biology, and bioinformatics, to ensure appropriate risk assessment.

title: ADHD medications and risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults.
text: More than 1.5 million adults in the US use stimulants and other medications to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, there are concerns about the cardiovascular safety of these drugs, as they can increase heart rate and blood pressure. The objective of this study was to investigate whether the current use of ADHD medications is associated with a higher risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults. The study was conducted using electronic health care records from four different sites, starting in 1986 and ending in 2005, with additional data from a 2007 survey. The participants were adults aged 25 to 64 years who had been prescribed methylphenidate, amphetamine, or atomoxetine. Each medication user was matched with two non-users based on study site, birth year, sex, and calendar year. The main outcome measures were serious cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death, and stroke. The results showed that during the follow-up period, there were 1357 cases of myocardial infarction, 296 cases of sudden cardiac death, and 575 cases of stroke. The incidence rates per 1000 person-years for these events were 1.34, 0.30, and 0.56, respectively, among current users. The rate ratio for serious cardiovascular events in current users compared to non-users was 0.83. Among new users, the rate ratio was 0.77. The rate ratio for current users compared to remote users was 1.03, and for new users compared to remote users, it was 1.02. These findings suggest that there is no increased risk of serious cardiovascular events associated with the current or new use of ADHD medications in young and middle-aged adults. The apparent protective associations observed may be due to healthy-user bias.

title: The Rho GEFs LARG and GEF-H1 regulate the mechanical response to force on integrins
text: Biologists are highly interested in understanding how individual cells respond to mechanical forces, as these forces have a significant impact on various aspects of cell behavior. When force is applied to integrins, it initiates rearrangements in the cytoskeleton and promotes growth of the adhesion complex, leading to an increase in cellular stiffness, also known as reinforcement. However, the specific molecular mechanisms that regulate the activity of RhoA, a protein involved in reinforcement, remain unknown. Through a combination of biochemical and biophysical approaches, we have identified two key molecules, LARG and GEF-H1, as guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that play a crucial role in regulating cellular adaptation to force. Our research demonstrates that when integrins are stimulated with tensional force, it activates LARG and GEF-H1, causing them to be recruited to adhesion complexes. Interestingly, the activation of LARG and GEF-H1 involves distinct signaling pathways. We have discovered that LARG is activated by the Src family tyrosine kinase Fyn, while the catalytic activity of GEF-H1 is enhanced by ERK, which is downstream of a signaling cascade involving FAK and Ras.

title: Cell death from antibiotics without the involvement of reactive oxygen species.
text: Recent observations indicate that classic antibiotics may kill bacteria by promoting the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). If this is true, it could lead to new strategies for enhancing the effectiveness of antibiotics. In this study, we directly examined this hypothesis. Surprisingly, antibiotic treatment did not accelerate the production of hydrogen peroxide in Escherichia coli and did not increase the levels of intracellular free iron, which is necessary for the generation of lethal damage. Furthermore, the lethality of the antibiotics persisted even in the absence of oxygen, and mutants lacking DNA repair mechanisms did not show increased sensitivity, challenging the idea that the toxicity was caused by oxidative DNA damage. Based on these findings, we conclude that the antibiotics tested in this study did not generate ROS, and instead, their lethality likely resulted from directly inhibiting cell-wall assembly, protein synthesis, and DNA replication.

title: Pioneer Transcription Factors Target Partial DNA Motifs on Nucleosomes to Initiate Reprogramming
text: Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) have the ability to access silent chromatin and initiate changes in cell fate by utilizing various types of DNA binding domains (DBDs). The prototypical pioneer TF, FoxA, possesses a winged helix DBD that resembles linker histone, allowing it to bind to target sites on nucleosomes and compacted chromatin. In this study, we compare the nucleosome and chromatin targeting activities of Oct4 (POU DBD), Sox2 (HMG box DBD), Klf4 (zinc finger DBD), and c-Myc (bHLH DBD), which collectively reprogram somatic cells to pluripotency. In vitro experiments demonstrate that purified Oct4, Sox2, and Klf4 proteins can bind to nucleosomes, and in vivo, they exhibit a preference for targeting silent sites that are enriched with nucleosomes. The pioneer activity is primarily determined by the ability of a specific DBD to recognize partial motifs present on the surface of the nucleosome. This recognition can occur through coordinated binding between multiple factors. Our findings shed light on the mechanisms by which pioneer factors are able to target naive chromatin sites.

title: Experimental Evolution of an RNA Virus in Wild Birds: Evidence for Host-Dependent Impacts on Population Structure and Competitive Fitness
text: RNA viruses within hosts form genetically and phenotypically complex populations. The heterogeneity in their genomes is caused by error-prone replication, which is partially reduced by stochastic and selective mechanisms that are not fully understood. Understanding how natural selection shapes these virus populations is crucial for informing treatment strategies and improving control efforts. To investigate this, we allowed West Nile virus (WNV) to replicate in wild-caught American crows, house sparrows, and American robins, which differ in their susceptibility to virus-induced mortality. After five passages in each bird species, we examined the phenotype and population diversity of WNV using fitness competition assays and next-generation sequencing. Our findings show that fitness gains occur in a species-specific manner, with the highest replicative fitness gains in robin-passaged WNV and the lowest in crow-passaged WNV. Sequencing data revealed that the WNV populations within hosts were strongly influenced by purifying selection, and the overall complexity of the viral populations was similar across different hosts. However, the selective pressures that control WNV populations appear to be dependent on the bird species. Crow-passaged WNV populations had the highest number of unique mutations (about 1.7 times more than sparrows and 3.4 times more than robins) and defective genomes (about 1.4 times more than sparrows and 2.7 times more than robins), but the lowest average mutation frequency (similar to sparrows and 2.6 times lower than robins). Therefore, our data suggest that WNV replication in the most disease-susceptible bird species is positively associated with virus mutational tolerance, likely through complementation, and negatively associated with the strength of selection. These differences in genetic composition are likely to have distinct phenotypic consequences for the virus populations. Overall, these results provide valuable insights into how different hosts may contribute to the emergence of RNA viruses.

title: sasCIF: an extension of core Crystallographic Information File for SAS
text: Various small angle scattering facilities have created their own data acquisition packages, resulting in different formats for storing both raw and processed data. In order to promote data sharing among laboratories, the small angle scattering community has agreed upon using an ASCII format for one-dimensional data. This format includes a header that provides essential details about the sample and instrumental conditions, followed by the raw or reduced data presented in a tabular form. To achieve this, a format called sasCIF was developed as an extension of the core CIF (Crystallographic Information File) dictionary.

title: Migratory dendritic cells transfer antigen to a lymph node-resident dendritic cell population for efficient CTL priming.
text: Skin dendritic cells (DCs) are believed to play a crucial role in initiating local T cell immunity. Our study demonstrates that, following skin infection with herpes simplex virus (HSV), the activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) relies on MHC class I-restricted presentation by nonmigratory CD8(+) DCs rather than DCs derived from the skin. Surprisingly, even though migratory DCs do not directly present antigens, blocking their exit from infected skin significantly impairs class I-restricted presentation and the generation of HSV-specific CTL responses. These findings support the notion that antigens are initially transported by migrating DCs and then transferred to lymphoid-resident DCs for presentation and CTL priming. Furthermore, our results suggest that the transfer of antigens between DCs serves to amplify presentation across a larger network of lymphoid-resident DCs, leading to efficient T cell activation. Notably, we observed robust CTL responses with only a small number of DCs that had emigrated from the skin, indicating the importance of inter-DC antigen transfer in facilitating presentation by a broader population of lymphoid-resident DCs.

title: Thrombopoietin-induced Polyploidization of Bone Marrow Megakaryocytes Is Due to a Unique Regulatory Mechanism in Late Mitosis
text: The process of polyploidization in megakaryocytes is still not fully understood. It has been suggested that this occurs because mitosis is skipped after each round of DNA replication. However, our immunohistochemical studies on mouse bone marrow megakaryocytes undergoing polyploidization induced by thrombopoietin revealed a different mechanism. We observed that these megakaryocytes do enter mitosis and progress through the stages of prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, and anaphase A, but not anaphase B, telophase, or cytokinesis. Interestingly, multiple spindle poles were formed as the polyploid megakaryocytes entered mitosis, the nuclear membrane broke down during prophase, and the sister chromatids aligned on a multifaced plate at metaphase. Additionally, the centrosomes were symmetrically located on either side of each face of the plate. During anaphase A, a set of sister chromatids moved into the multiple centrosomes. We also observed that the pair of spindle poles in anaphase were located close to each other, likely due to the absence of outward movement during anaphase B. Consequently, the reassembling nuclear envelope may enclose all the sister chromatids in a single nucleus at anaphase, bypassing telophase and cytokinesis. These findings indicate that polyploidization in megakaryocytes is not solely a result of skipping mitosis, but rather involves a unique regulatory mechanism in anaphase. Factors regulating anaphase, such as microtubule motor proteins, may play a role in this polyploidization process.

title: Unifying Viral Genetics and Human Transportation Data to Predict the Global Transmission Dynamics of Human Influenza H3N2
text:
Spatial epidemiological models rely on information about global human movement patterns to predict the behavior of infectious diseases such as influenza. However, it is challenging to determine which modes of dispersal drive the spread of pathogens at different geographic scales using standard epidemiological data alone. Evolutionary analyses of pathogen genome sequences have provided some insights into the spatial dynamics of influenza viruses, but they have largely overlooked the valuable information on human mobility due to the lack of a statistical framework that combines viral gene sequences and empirical data on host movement.

To address this issue, we have applied a phylogeographic approach to study the global spread of human influenza subtype H3N2 and evaluate its ability to predict the spatial spread of human influenza A viruses worldwide. Our framework estimates the migration history of human influenza while simultaneously testing and quantifying various potential predictive variables of spatial spread. Our findings reveal that the global dynamics of influenza H3N2 are primarily driven by air passenger flows, while at more local scales, spread is also influenced by factors correlated with geographic distance. Our analyses also confirm the significant role of mainland China and Southeast Asia in maintaining a source population for global influenza diversity.

By comparing our model's output with the known pandemic expansion of H1N1 in 2009, we demonstrate that predictions of influenza spatial spread are most accurate when integrating data on human mobility and viral evolution. In conclusion, the global dynamics of influenza viruses can be best explained by combining information on human mobility with the spatial characteristics inherent in sampled viral genomes. This integrated approach has great potential for enhancing epidemiological surveillance through phylogeographic reconstructions and improving predictive models for disease control.

title: Microtubule sliding activity of a kinesin-8 promotes spindle assembly and spindle length control
text: Molecular motors play crucial roles in the creation of mitotic spindles, either by controlling the stability of individual microtubules or by connecting and moving arrays of microtubules. Kinesin-8 motors are primarily known for their regulatory functions in managing microtubule dynamics. They possess activities that destabilize microtubules and limit the length of spindles in various cell types and organisms. In this study, we present evidence of an opposing activity of the budding yeast kinesin-8, Kip3, which slides antiparallel microtubules. The significance of this sliding activity was determined by identifying specific Kip3 mutants that separate the sliding and microtubule-destabilizing activities. Working together with Cin8, a member of the kinesin-5 family, the sliding activity of Kip3 facilitates the assembly of bipolar spindles and the maintenance of genome stability. We propose a model where the sliding and destabilizing activities of Kip3 are balanced during pre-anaphase, enabling normal spindle assembly. However, in late anaphase, the destabilizing activity of Kip3 becomes dominant, inhibiting spindle elongation and ultimately leading to spindle disassembly.

title: A Pharmacological Map of the PI3-K Family Defines a Role for p110α in Insulin Signaling
text: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3-Ks) are a class of drug targets that are gaining importance, but the specific roles of PI3-K isoforms are not well understood. In this study, we present a method to investigate the PI3-K family using pharmacological approaches. We synthesized a diverse range of PI3-K inhibitors and examined their selectivity towards different targets through biochemical analysis. Surprisingly, we discovered hidden similarities among targets and chemical types. By studying the crystal structures of three inhibitors bound to p110gamma, we identified a flexible region that is exploited by selective compounds. Using this chemical panel, we determined which PI3-K isoforms are involved in insulin signaling. Our findings indicate that p110alpha is the primary PI3-K responsible for insulin response in cultured cells, while p110beta is not essential but sets a threshold for p110alpha activity. In vivo experiments showed that compounds targeting p110alpha block the immediate effects of insulin treatment, whereas a p110beta inhibitor has no impact. These results demonstrate the systematic validation of targets using a range of inhibitors that cover an entire protein family.

title: Identification of Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen 1 protein domains that direct interactions at a distance between DNA-bound proteins.
text: The EBNA1 protein from Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) activates DNA replication from the EBV latent origin of replication, oriP, by binding to it. This binding occurs through a direct interaction with two separate parts of oriP. The EBNA1 molecules that are bound to these parts of oriP efficiently interact with each other through a DNA looping mechanism. In previous research, we identified a specific region of EBNA1, known as the looping region, which is necessary for facilitating the interaction between EBNA1 molecules bound to oriP. In our latest study, we demonstrate that two fragments of this looping region, which mainly consist of an eight amino acid repeat, can also facilitate interactions when transferred to another DNA-binding protein. These protein interactions mediated by the EBNA1 looping region seem to rely on DNA binding, as they were only observed between forms of the proteins that were bound to DNA.

title: Primary prevention of hypertension: clinical and public health advisory from The National High Blood Pressure Education Program.
text: In 1993, the National High Blood Pressure Education Program Coordinating Committee released its initial statement on preventing hypertension. This article provides an update to the 1993 report, incorporating new evidence from scientific literature. The current recommendations for preventing hypertension involve two strategies: a population-based approach and a targeted strategy for individuals at high risk. These strategies work together and highlight six proven approaches for preventing hypertension: engaging in moderate physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol consumption, reducing sodium intake, ensuring adequate potassium intake, and following a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy products, and low in saturated and total fat. Implementing these approaches in public health and clinical practice can effectively prevent an increase in blood pressure and reduce elevated levels for those with high normal blood pressure or hypertension.

title: Formins: intermediates in signal-transduction cascades that affect cytoskeletal reorganization.
text: The growth and polarity of cells rely on a dynamic actin cytoskeleton that can reorganize in response to developmental and environmental cues. In animals and fungi, formins are one of the four main classes of poly-L-proline-containing (PLP) proteins that play a role in the signal-transduction cascade leading to actin cytoskeleton rearrangement. The analysis of the Arabidopsis genome sequence suggests that, unlike animals and fungi, formins are the only conserved PLP proteins that bind to profilin in plants. Additionally, plant formins exhibit significant structural differences compared to their counterparts in animals and fungi, suggesting that they may be regulated by unique mechanisms or have distinct functions in plants.

title: Genetic variability in GLP-1 receptor is associated with inter-individual differences in weight lowering potential of liraglutide in obese women with PCOS: a pilot study
text: The weight reduction potential of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) varies between individuals and is not predictable in a clinical setting. The impact of genetic variations in the GLP-1R gene on weight loss response to GLP-1 RAs in obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has not been studied. A group of 57 obese women with PCOS (average age 30.7 ± 7.0, BMI 38.6 ± 5.3 kg/m2) were given liraglutide 1.2 mg once daily subcutaneously for 12 weeks. They were classified as strong responders if they lost 5% or more of their initial body weight. The participants were genotyped for two common GLP-1R single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) - rs6923761 and rs10305420. Changes in measures of obesity were assessed before and after the treatment. Out of the 57 subjects, 20 were strong responders and lost an average of 7.38 ± 1.74 kg, while poor responders lost only 2.11 ± 2.17 kg. Individuals carrying at least one polymorphic rs10305420 allele had a poorer response to the treatment compared to those with two wild type alleles (OR = 0.27, 95% CI = 0.09–0.85, P = 0.025). Carriers of at least one polymorphic rs6923761 allele tended to have a stronger response to the treatment compared to carriers of two wild type alleles (OR = 3.06, 95% CI = 0.96–9.74, P = 0.058). Fasting glucose and glucose levels after an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) decreased similarly in both groups compared to baseline, while no differences were observed in androgen levels within the treatment. Gastrointestinal side effects were similar in both strong and poor responders. The presence of the GLP-1R rs10305420 polymorphism explained some of the differences in weight loss response to liraglutide in obese women with PCOS.

title: Cost-effectiveness of aromatase inhibitor co-treatment for controlled ovarian stimulation.
text: The aim of this study was to compare the clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness of using the aromatase inhibitor, letrozole, in combination with FSH versus FSH alone for controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in patients undergoing intrauterine insemination (IUI) for various indications. A total of 432 patients who underwent 872 IUI cycles were included in the study. The patients were divided into two groups: Group I received letrozole and FSH for indications such as anovulation, male factor infertility, unexplained infertility, endometriosis, and combined indications, while Group II received FSH only for indications such as ovarian factor infertility, male factor infertility, unexplained infertility, endometriosis, and other indications. The main outcome measures included the number of mature follicles, FSH dose per cycle, clinical pregnancy rate, and cost-effectiveness ratio per pregnancy. The results showed that the FSH dose required for ovarian stimulation was significantly lower in the letrozole group. Although Group II had a higher number of mature follicles and endometrial thickness, the pregnancy rates were similar between the two groups. The letrozole group had a lower IUI cancellation rate and a significantly lower cost per cycle compared to the FSH-only group. The cost-effectiveness ratio was also lower in the letrozole group. In conclusion, a combination of letrozole and FSH may be an effective and cost-effective protocol for ovarian stimulation in IUI cycles. Further research is needed to confirm these findings through a randomized controlled trial.

title: The cost effectiveness of stereotactic radiosurgery versus surgical resection in the treatment of solitary metastatic brain tumors.
text: Neurosurgeons commonly encounter solitary metastatic brain tumors, which are the most prevalent type of intracranial neoplasms. When compared to whole brain radiotherapy (WBR) alone, surgical resection of brain metastasis significantly improves survival rates. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SR) also shows promising results similar to surgical resection. To assess the economic efficiency of these treatments, we analyzed data from medical literature published between 1974 and 1994. Our inclusion criteria consisted of studies where at least 75% of patients received WBR, the study dates were in the computed tomography era (after 1975), operative morbidity, mortality, and median survival were reported, the study dates were not included in a more recent update or review, tumor histologies were reported, and the cobalt-60 gamma unit was used for SR. We identified three surgical resection studies and one SR study that met all the requirements. We used two prospective, randomized trials to establish the WBR baseline for incremental cost effectiveness analysis. Our model considered typical resource usage for uncomplicated procedures, reported complications, and subsequent craniotomies for both treatment options. Costs were estimated from the societal perspective using the 1992 Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, with average cost:charge ratios for surgery and WBR. Radiosurgery costs were determined through a survey of capital and operating costs from five sites. Our analysis revealed that radiosurgery had a lower cost for uncomplicated procedures ($20,209 versus $27,587), a lower average cost per case for complications ($2,534 versus $2,874), and a lower total cost per procedure ($22,743 versus $30,461). Additionally, radiosurgery was more cost effective ($24,811 versus $32,149 per life year) and had a better incremental cost effectiveness ($40,648 versus $52,384 per life year) compared to surgical resection. Sensitivity analysis showed that significant changes in key assumptions would be necessary to alter the analysis outcome. To equalize the incremental cost effectiveness of the two treatments, one of the following would be required: 1) a 38.7% reduction in SR annual case volume, 2) a 34.7% increase in SR procedure cost, 3) an 18.8% reduction in surgical resection procedure cost, 4) a 240.5% increase in SR morbidity cost, 5) a 12.7% reduction in SR median survival, or 6) a 16.8% increase in surgical resection median survival. Even if all surgical resection morbidity costs were eliminated, radiosurgery would still demonstrate superior incremental cost effectiveness.

title: Trans-ancestry mutational landscape of hepatocellular carcinoma genomes
text: Different populations have varying rates of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) due to diverse epidemiological factors. However, the specific genetic changes in HCC genomes that are influenced by different ancestral backgrounds are still not well understood. To address this, a study analyzed data from 503 liver cancer genomes from various populations and identified 30 potential driver genes and 11 core pathway modules. Additionally, a collaboration between two large-scale cancer genome projects compared the substitution signatures in 608 liver cancer cases across different ancestries and discovered unique mutational patterns that are more prevalent in Asian cases. This research sheds light on previously unexplored ancestral mutational processes in HCC development. The study also found that a combination of TERT promoter mutation, TERT focal amplification, and viral genome integration is present in over 68% of cases, suggesting that TERT plays a central role in hepatocarcinogenesis regardless of ancestry. Furthermore, new alterations in genes responsible for metabolic enzymes, chromatin remodelers, and a significant number of mTOR pathway activations were identified, presenting potential opportunities for therapeutic and diagnostic advancements.

title: Organization of the mitotic chromosome.
text: For more than a century, the internal organization of mitotic chromosomes has remained largely unresolved, despite being one of the most recognizable structures in the cell. To address this, we utilized chromosome conformation capture methods, specifically 5C and Hi-C, throughout the cell cycle. Our findings revealed two distinct three-dimensional folding states of the human genome. Interestingly, the highly compartmentalized and cell type-specific organization previously observed in nonsynchronous cells was found to be limited to interphase. In metaphase, we discovered a uniform folding state that is independent of specific loci, consistent across all chromosomes, and shared among different cell types. This suggests the existence of a general principle governing metaphase chromosome organization. Through polymer simulations, we determined that the metaphase Hi-C data does not align with traditional hierarchical models. Instead, it is best explained by a linearly organized longitudinally compressed array of consecutive chromatin loops.

title: Compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome.
text: The term 'Compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome' (CARS) was introduced by Roger Bone in 1997 to describe the consequences of counter-regulatory mechanisms that are activated to control excessive inflammation in patients with sepsis or systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), whether caused by infection or non-infectious factors. One significant outcome of CARS is the alteration of the immune system, which can increase the vulnerability of intensive care patients to hospital-acquired infections. Animal models have shown that after an initial insult, there is an increased susceptibility to infection. However, this observation is influenced by the specific experimental procedure used. In sepsis and SIRS patients, as well as in animal models, various functions of circulating white blood cells are affected. However, this is more of a reprogramming of these cells rather than a global impairment of their immune functions. Additionally, within tissues, white blood cells are more likely to be primed or activated rather than suppressed. Therefore, CARS can be seen as a localized response aimed at suppressing certain genes responsible for acute inflammation while maintaining the expression of genes involved in fighting infections.

title: Quantum dots spectrally distinguish multiple species within the tumor milieu in vivo
text: In order to understand the pathophysiology of solid tumors, it is crucial to be able to distinguish and monitor the different components involved. However, traditional fluorophores make it difficult to simultaneously image these components in dynamic studies. To overcome this limitation, we utilized multiphoton microscopy techniques and transgenic mice expressing green fluorescent protein, along with quantum dot preparations. By customizing these fluorescent semiconductor nanocrystals, we were able to image and differentiate tumor vessels from the surrounding perivascular cells and extracellular matrix. Additionally, we used quantum dots to assess the ability of particles of varying sizes to penetrate the tumor. Furthermore, we successfully tracked the recruitment of bone marrow-derived precursor cells labeled with quantum dots to the tumor vasculature. These examples demonstrate the versatility of quantum dots in studying tumor pathophysiology and opening up new possibilities for treatment.

title: Arginase I: a limiting factor for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis by activated macrophages?
text: The potential of arginase to regulate nitric oxide (NO) and polyamine synthesis arises from its ability to hydrolyze arginine, producing ornithine and urea. To investigate whether the expression of the cytosolic isoform of arginase (arginase I) limits NO or polyamine production in activated RAW 264.7 macrophage cells, we conducted experiments. We treated RAW 264.7 cells, which were stably transfected to overexpress either arginase I or beta-galactosidase, with interferon-gamma to induce type 2 NO synthase, or with lipopolysaccharide or 8-bromo-cAMP (8-BrcAMP) to induce ornithine decarboxylase. Surprisingly, overexpression of arginase I had no impact on NO synthesis. However, cells overexpressing arginase I produced twice as much putrescine after activation compared to cells expressing beta-galactosidase. Furthermore, cells overexpressing arginase I produced more spermidine after treatment with 8-BrcAMP than cells expressing beta-galactosidase. These findings suggest that endogenous levels of arginase I limit polyamine synthesis but not NO synthesis in activated macrophage cells. Importantly, this study demonstrates that altering arginase I levels can significantly affect polyamine synthesis without affecting induced NO synthesis.

title: Opposing Effects of PKCθ and WASp on Symmetry Breaking and Relocation of the Immunological Synapse
text: The immunological synapse (IS) is a connection between the T cell and antigen-presenting cell, consisting of supramolecular activation clusters (SMACs). Currently, there is a lack of research on the dynamics of the IS in naive T cells. In this study, we discovered that the formation of the IS during antigen recognition involves a series of stable IS formations and independent migration of naive T cells. The migration phase is influenced by PKCtheta, which is concentrated in the F-actin-dependent peripheral (p)SMAC. In vitro and in vivo experiments showed that PKCtheta(-/-) T cells formed excessively stable IS, similar to WT cells, and exhibited rapid oscillations in the distal SMAC. However, they displayed reduced slow oscillations in pSMAC integrity. On the other hand, the reformation of the IS is controlled by the Wiscott Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASp). WASp(-/-) T cells showed normal IS formation but were unable to reform the IS after migration unless PKCtheta was inhibited. Therefore, the opposing effects of PKCtheta and WASp regulate the stability of the IS by breaking the symmetry of pSMAC and facilitating reformation.

title: Integrins regulate microtubule nucleating activity of centrosome through mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MEK/ERK) signaling.
text: The formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton relies on the crucial step of microtubule nucleation. Our recent findings demonstrate that androgen and Src play a role in promoting microtubule nucleation and the accumulation of γ-tubulin at the centrosome. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms through which androgen and Src regulate these processes and examine the potential involvement of integrins. To disrupt integrin function, we introduce a mutation in the integrin β1 tail, specifically in the membrane-proximal NPIY motif, replacing tyrosine with alanine. Our results show that this mutant significantly reduces microtubule nucleation and γ-tubulin accumulation at the centrosome. Given that androgen stimulation enhances the interaction between the androgen receptor and Src, leading to PI3K/AKT and MEK/ERK signaling, we investigate whether these pathways are affected by the mutant integrin and whether they influence microtubule nucleation. Our findings indicate that the formation of the androgen receptor-Src complex and the activation of downstream pathways are greatly inhibited when cells adhere to the mutant integrin. Inhibitor studies reveal that microtubule nucleation relies on MEK/ERK signaling but not PI3K/AKT signaling. Importantly, the expression of activated RAF-1 rescues microtubule nucleation impaired by the mutant integrin by promoting the accumulation of γ-tubulin at the centrosome. Our data establish a novel understanding of integrin signaling, where integrins regulate microtubule nucleation by facilitating the formation of androgen receptor-Src signaling complexes to activate the MEK/ERK signaling pathway.

title: Consumption of added sugars from liquid but not solid sources predicts impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance among youth at risk of obesity.
text: We have limited knowledge about the relationship between consuming added sugars (both solid and liquid sources) and glucose-insulin balance over time in young individuals. In this study, we recruited Caucasian children aged 8-10 years who had at least one obese biological parent from the QUébec Adipose and Lifestyle InvesTigation in Youth (QUALITY) cohort. We followed up with them after 2 years. We assessed their added sugar intake through three 24-hour dietary recalls at the beginning of the study. Using multivariate linear regression models, we analyzed the changes in various factors over the two-year period, taking into account baseline levels, age, sex, Tanner stage, energy intake, fat mass, and physical activity. We found that consuming added sugars from either liquid or solid sources did not have a significant impact on measures of adiposity (such as fat mass, body mass index, or waist circumference). However, consuming higher amounts of added sugars from liquid sources (10g per day) was associated with slightly higher fasting glucose levels, higher fasting insulin levels, increased insulin resistance, and decreased insulin sensitivity in all participants. These associations were not observed with added sugars from solid sources. We also found that overweight or obese children at the beginning of the study experienced greater increases in adiposity indicators, fasting insulin levels, and insulin resistance, as well as decreases in insulin sensitivity, compared to normal-weight children over the two-year period. In conclusion, consuming added sugars from liquid or solid sources did not lead to changes in adiposity, but consuming liquid added sugars was a risk factor for the development of impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance over a two-year period in young individuals at risk of obesity.

title: Towards an improved investment approach for an effective response to HIV/AIDS.
text: To achieve long-term benefits, significant changes are necessary in the approach to investing in the response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic. Currently, resources are allocated based on a commodity approach that promotes the expansion of various strategies simultaneously, regardless of their effectiveness. We propose a strategic investment framework that aims to improve the management of national and international HIV/AIDS responses compared to the existing system. Our framework includes community mobilization, synergy between program elements, and the use of antiretroviral therapy for HIV transmission prevention to achieve major efficiency gains. It suggests three categories of investment, comprising six fundamental programmatic activities, interventions to create an enabling environment for maximum effectiveness, and programmatic efforts in other health and development sectors related to HIV/AIDS. The estimated annual cost of achieving universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support by 2015 is at least $22 billion. By implementing the new investment framework, we can prevent 12.2 million new HIV infections and 7.4 million AIDS-related deaths between 2011 and 2020, compared to continuing with current approaches. This would result in a gain of 29.4 million life-years. The framework is cost-effective, with a cost of $1060 per life-year gained, and the additional investment required can be largely offset by savings in treatment costs alone.

title: Pivotal Roles of T-Helper 17-Related Cytokines, IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23, in Inflammatory Diseases
text: Th17 cells, also known as T-helper 17 cells, produce interleukin-17 (IL-17, also called IL-17A), IL-17F, IL-21, and IL-22, and potentially TNF-α and IL-6 when stimulated. The development of Th17 cells is promoted by IL-23, and the IL-17 and IL-22 produced by these cells play crucial roles in various inflammatory diseases, including experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, colitis, and Concanavalin A-induced hepatitis. This review focuses on summarizing the functional role of Th17 cells, particularly their cytokines IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23, in both mouse models and human inflammatory diseases.

title: LXRS and FXR: the yin and yang of cholesterol and fat metabolism.
text: Liver X receptors (LXRs) and farnesoid X receptor (FXR) are nuclear receptors that act as internal detectors for sterols and bile acids, respectively. When activated by their respective ligands, these receptors trigger transcriptional responses that ensure a well-regulated balance of cholesterol and bile acid metabolism. LXRs also facilitate the efficient storage of energy derived from carbohydrates and fats, while FXR activation leads to a decrease in triglyceride levels and modulation of glucose metabolism. The intricate interplay between these two receptor systems suggests that they evolved together to form a highly sensitive and effective mechanism for maintaining optimal levels of body fat and cholesterol. Recent evidence indicates that the specific actions of these receptors in different tissues are crucial for the proper functioning of the cardiovascular, immune, reproductive, endocrine pancreas, renal, and central nervous systems. Consequently, LXRs and FXR hold promise as potential targets for therapeutic interventions aimed at treating and preventing various metabolic and lipid-related disorders.

title: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus/human herpesvirus type 8-positive solid lymphomas: a tissue-based variant of primary effusion lymphoma.
text: We have identified four cases of Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) in solid lymphomas. These cases occurred in AIDS patients (cases 1 to 3) and in an HIV-negative individual (case 4). The patients presented with masses in the abdomen (cases 1, 3, and 4) or skin (case 2), as well as nodal involvement and Kaposi's sarcoma (case 3). Two patients had gastrointestinal tract involvement (cases 1 and 3), but none developed a lymphomatous effusion. KSHV was detected in the tumor cells of all cases using immunohistochemistry and polymerase chain reaction. Epstein-Barr virus was found in two of the HIV-related cases. All KSHV-positive solid lymphomas exhibited a cell morphology similar to primary effusion lymphoma (PEL). To further understand the relationship between these disorders and PEL, we tested the KSHV-positive solid lymphomas for the expression of a set of genes previously associated with PEL tumor cells. The results showed that the expression of these genes in KSHV-positive lymphomas is similar to PEL but distinct from KSHV-negative AIDS-associated diffuse large cell lymphomas. Based on the similarities in pathobiological features, we suggest that KSHV-positive solid lymphomas should be considered a tissue-based variant of classical PEL, regardless of HIV status.

title: STAR: ultrafast universal RNA-seq aligner.
text:
The accurate alignment of high-throughput RNA-seq data is a complex problem that has yet to be fully solved. This is due to the non-contiguous structure of transcripts, the relatively short length of reads, and the constantly increasing throughput of sequencing technologies. Currently available RNA-seq aligners have limitations such as high mapping error rates, slow mapping speed, read length restrictions, and mapping biases.

To address these challenges, we have developed a software called Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR). This software utilizes a novel RNA-seq alignment algorithm that involves sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching procedures. Our software outperforms other aligners by more than 50 times in terms of mapping speed. It can align 550 million 2 × 76 bp paired-end reads per hour on a modest 12-core server, while also improving alignment sensitivity and precision.

In addition to accurately detecting canonical junctions, STAR can also identify non-canonical splices and chimeric (fusion) transcripts. It is even capable of mapping full-length RNA sequences. We have experimentally validated 1960 novel intergenic splice junctions with an 80-90% success rate using Roche 454 sequencing of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction amplicons, which confirms the high precision of our mapping strategy.

STAR is implemented as a standalone C++ code and is available as free open source software under the GPLv3 license. It can be downloaded from http://code.google.com/p/rna-star/.

title: Effect of alendronate on risk of fracture in women with low bone density but without vertebral fractures: results from the Fracture Intervention Trial.
text:
The study aimed to investigate whether alendronate sodium could reduce the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women with low bone mineral density (BMD) but no vertebral fractures. The trial was a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study conducted at eleven community-based clinical research centers. The participants were women aged 54 to 81 years with a femoral neck BMD of 0.68 g/cm2 or less but no vertebral fractures. Out of the 4432 women randomized, 4272 (96%) completed the outcome measurements at the final visit, which occurred on average 4.2 years later. 

During the trial, participants reporting calcium intakes of 1000 mg/d or less received a calcium and cholecalciferol supplement. They were then randomly assigned to either placebo or alendronate sodium, with the latter group receiving 5 mg/d for 2 years followed by 10 mg/d for the rest of the trial. The main outcome measures were clinical fractures confirmed by x-ray reports, new vertebral deformities detected by radiographs, and BMD measured by dual x-ray absorptiometry.

The results showed that alendronate increased BMD at all sites studied and reduced the number of clinical fractures, although not significantly (14% reduction; relative hazard [RH], 0.86; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73-1.01). However, among women with baseline osteoporosis at the femoral neck, alendronate reduced clinical fractures by 36% (RH, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.50-0.82; treatment-control difference, 6.5%; number needed to treat [NNT], 15). There was no significant reduction in clinical fractures among those with higher BMD (RH, 1.08; 95% CI, 0.87-1.35). Alendronate decreased the risk of radiographic vertebral fractures by 44% overall (relative risk, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.39-0.80; treatment-control difference, 1.7%; NNT, 60). The use of alendronate did not increase the risk of gastrointestinal or other adverse effects.

In conclusion, the study found that in women with low BMD but without vertebral fractures, alendronate safely increased BMD and decreased the risk of first vertebral deformity. Alendronate significantly reduced the risk of clinical fractures among women with osteoporosis but not among women with higher BMD.

title: AP-1/sigma1B-adaptin mediates endosomal synaptic vesicle recycling, learning and memory.
text: The recycling of synaptic vesicles involves the process of AP-2/clathrin-mediated endocytosis. However, it is currently unknown whether the endosomal pathway is also necessary for this process. In mice that lack the tissue-specific AP-1-sigma1B complex, there is a noticeable impairment in the recycling of synaptic vesicles specifically in hippocampal synapses. On the other hand, the ubiquitously expressed AP-1-sigma1A complex is responsible for sorting proteins between the trans-Golgi network and early endosomes. In vertebrates, there are three isoforms of the sigma1 subunit: A, B, and C. The expression levels of sigma1A and sigma1B are particularly high in the brain. When neurons cultured from sigma1B-deficient mice are stimulated, there is a reduction in synaptic vesicle reformation, and there is an accumulation of large endosomal intermediates. These mice also exhibit reduced motor coordination and severe impairment in long-term spatial memory. These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanism underlying a severe form of human X-chromosome-linked mental retardation.

title: Update of the FANTOM web resource: high resolution transcriptome of diverse cell types in mammals
text: We have recently released the fifth version of the Functional Annotation of Mammalian Genomes collaborative project, known as FANTOM5. To assist researchers in studying transcriptional regulation and cellular states, we have consolidated a range of primary data and database systems into the FANTOM web resource (http://fantom.gsc.riken.jp). Throughout our collaboration, we have expanded the primary data and analysis results, as well as improved the functionalities of the database systems. We firmly believe that our data and web systems are invaluable resources that will greatly benefit the scientific community. With this latest update, researchers can deepen their understanding of mammalian cellular organization. In this article, we will provide an overview of the contents of FANTOM5, discuss recent updates to the web resource, and present future perspectives.

title: Adverse Events Associated With the Treatment of Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is an increasing public health issue. The use of multiple second-line drugs and the lengthy duration of therapy make adverse drug events (ADEs) a major concern for patients undergoing anti-MDR-TB treatment. This study aimed to assess the frequency and type of treatment-related ADEs associated with MDR-TB therapy. The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE databases were searched from their inception until October 1, 2012, and the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease was manually searched. Studies reporting ADEs in MDR-TB patients treated with regimens including second-line drugs were included. Pooled estimations of ADE incidence were calculated using a random-effects model, with 95% confidence intervals. Out of the 5346 patients included in the analysis, 2602 (57.3%) experienced at least one ADE. The most common ADEs were gastrointestinal disorders (32.1%), ototoxicity (14.6%), and psychiatric disorders (13.2%). Subgroup analyses based on study population, previous tuberculosis treatment, human immunodeficiency virus prevalence, and length of treatment did not reveal any significant differences between groups. Among the 1519 patients with available data on the impact of ADEs on MDR-TB therapy, 70.4% required a change in their treatment. ADEs were common in MDR-TB cases, affecting more than half of the patients, with over two-thirds requiring a change in their anti-MDR-TB treatment. Close monitoring and aggressive management of side effects, particularly ototoxicity and psychiatric disorders, are crucial for MDR-TB patients undergoing therapy.

title: Presynaptically Localized Cyclic GMP-Dependent Protein Kinase 1 Is a Key Determinant of Spinal Synaptic Potentiation and Pain Hypersensitivity
text: The role of synaptic long-term potentiation (LTP) in spinal neurons that transmit pain-specific signals from the body to the brain has been suggested as a trigger for increased sensitivity to pain in pathological conditions. Previous research has implicated the NMDA receptor-NO pathway and the second messenger cGMP in these processes. However, the specific targets of cGMP, their mechanisms of action, and their location in the spinal circuitry are still unclear. In this study, we discovered that Protein Kinase G1 (PKG-I) plays a crucial role in the expression of spinal LTP. We used genetically modified mice to selectively remove PKG-I from the presynaptic terminals of nociceptors in the spinal cord. Our findings showed that the activity-induced LTP between nociceptors and spinal neurons projecting to the periaqueductal grey (PAG) was completely abolished in these mice, while basal synaptic transmission remained unaffected. Further analysis revealed that presynaptic PKG-I regulates the probability of neurotransmitter release by phosphorylating Inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor 1 and myosin light chain kinase in nociceptive neurons. Additionally, behavioral experiments demonstrated significant impairments in nociceptive hypersensitivity in the genetically modified mice, and pharmacological studies confirmed the contribution of PKG-I in spinal terminals of nociceptors. These findings suggest that presynaptic mechanisms involving an increase in release probability from nociceptors are involved in the expression of synaptic LTP in spinal-PAG projection neurons, and that PKG-I in presynaptic nociceptor terminals plays a crucial role in regulating pain sensitivity.

title: A Sleeping Beauty mutagenesis screen reveals a tumor suppressor role for Ncoa2/Src-2 in liver cancer.
text: The SB transposon mutagenesis system, known as the Sleeping Beauty, is a valuable tool for identifying mutations that speed up the development of tumors. In this research, our aim was to find mutations that work together with MYC, a gene commonly associated with human cancer. To do this, we conducted a genetic screen using mice with MYC-induced liver cancer and the SB mutagenesis system. By analyzing the insertions in 63 liver tumor nodules, we discovered at least 16 genes/loci that contribute to the accelerated growth of tumors. To further confirm our findings, we used RNAi to knock down three of these genes, Ncoa2/Src-2, Zfx, and Dtnb, in a liver progenitor cell line, and found that they act as tumor suppressors in liver cancer. Additionally, we observed that deleting Ncoa2/Src-2 in mice makes them more susceptible to liver tumorigenesis induced by diethylnitrosamine. These results uncover genes and pathways that restrain MYC-mediated liver tumorigenesis, potentially offering targets for cancer treatment.

title: Protein-Protein Interaction Inhibition (2P2I)-Oriented Chemical Library Accelerates Hit Discovery.
text: Therapeutic intervention can greatly benefit from protein-protein interactions (PPIs). Recently, we and others have identified key rules that can aid in the identification of innovative drugs to target this challenging class of proteins in the next decade. Using these rules, we created a chemical library consisting of diverse "PPI-like" modulators with privileged structures found in therapeutics. We purchased 1664 structurally diverse compounds based on this library and evaluated them using homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) technology on various protein-protein interfaces with different potential for drug targeting. For certain PPI classes, the hit rates were significantly higher compared to non-oriented chemical libraries, indicating a correlation with the druggability of the targets. We focused on selectivity profiles, three-dimensional molecular modes of action determined by X-ray crystallography, and the biological activities of identified hits that targeted the well-defined druggable bromodomains of the bromo and extraterminal (BET) family as a proof-of-concept. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning-based oriented chemical libraries in accelerating the discovery of hits that target PPIs. By applying this method to a larger set of compounds, we can expedite the discovery of original and potent probes for this challenging class of proteins.

title: Molecular characterization of endometrial cancer: a correlative study assessing microsatellite instability, MLH1 hypermethylation, DNA mismatch repair protein expression, and PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF mutation analysis.
text: The purpose of this research was to examine a group of endometrial cancers using various molecular genetic and immunohistochemical techniques. The study found that endometrial cancer is linked to chromosomal abnormalities, microsatellite instability, and changes in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes. The researchers analyzed 96 cases and looked for genomic alterations, including MSI, MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, p53 and mismatch repair protein expression, and PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF mutations. They discovered that PTEN alterations were the most common abnormality, occurring in 48 out of 87 specimens tested. PIK3CA alterations were found in 16 specimens. Additionally, 29 out of 94 tumors tested for MSI exhibited an MSI-H phenotype, with 24 of those cases showing methylation of the MLH1 promoter region. Immunohistochemistry results revealed that 23 out of 28 MSI-H cases had loss of expression of MLH1/PMS2, MSH2/MSH6, or MSH6 only. Of the 19 MSI-H cases with loss of MLH1/PMS2, 18 were positive for MLH1 promoter hypermethylation. KRAS mutations were found in 12 out of 94 cases, while no BRAF V600E mutations were identified. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of commonly studied targets in a large group of endometrial cancers.

title: Identification of indole-3-carboxylic acid as mediator of priming against Plectosphaerella cucumerina.
text: The combination of various hormonal-controlled signalling pathways is responsible for plant resistance against the necrotrophic pathogen Plectosphaerella cucumerina. The priming agent β-aminobutyric acid (BABA) effectively induces resistance against this pathogen by promoting the deposition of callose-rich cell walls. This study demonstrates that BABA-Induced Resistance (BABA-IR) in Arabidopsis against P. cucumerina involves additional components, such as the activation of defences mediated by indolic derivatives. To detect and characterize metabolites enhanced by BABA, a chromatographic approach was developed, which only showed results when the pathogen was present. Metabolites that meet this criteria are considered to be primed by BABA. The analytical procedure combines liquid chromatography (LC) with a triple quadrupole (TQD) detector in a precursor ion scanning mode. Using this system, a signal at 160 m/z in negative electro-spray mode was found to be primed by BABA in infected plants. Further analysis using a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer confirmed that this ion was the indole-derivative metabolite indole-3-carboxylic acid (I3CA). The identity of indole-3-carboxilic acid was definitively confirmed by comparing its retention time and fragmentation spectra with a commercial standard. Quantification of I3CA in primed plants revealed that this indolic metabolite is specifically primed by BABA during P. cucumerina infection, while other indolic compounds like IAA and camalexin are not. These findings, along with the known role of callose in priming against this pathogen, suggest that priming is not a single mechanism but rather a multi-component defence.

title: Evaluation of networks of randomized trials.
text: Randomized trials can be approached in two ways: as individual experiments or in relation to other relevant evidence. The availability and complexity of randomized evidence differ across various topics. Systematic reviews are helpful in identifying gaps in existing randomized evidence, highlighting discrepancies between trials, and planning future trials. A debated but promising extension of systematic reviews, known as mixed treatment comparison (MTC) meta-analysis, has gained popularity recently. MTC meta-analysis allows for the interpretation of randomized evidence from networks of trials and can rank multiple treatments, surpassing simple pairwise comparisons. However, evaluating networks poses challenges and considerations. This article provides a review of the statistical methodology for MTC meta-analysis. It explores the concept of inconsistency and proposed methods for its evaluation, as well as remaining methodological gaps. The article introduces the concepts of network geometry and asymmetry, proposing metrics for assessing asymmetry. Lastly, it discusses how inconsistency, network geometry, and asymmetry inform the planning of future trials.

title: Metabolic regulation by the mitochondrial phosphatase PTPMT1 is required for hematopoietic stem cell differentiation.
text: The complete understanding of how mitochondrial metabolism is regulated and coordinated with the self-renewal and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) is still lacking. In this study, we present findings that demonstrate the depletion of PTPMT1, a mitochondrial phosphatase similar to PTEN, in mice with inducible or hematopoietic-cell-specific knockout resulted in hematopoietic failure. This failure was attributed to changes in the cell cycle and a block in the differentiation of HSCs. Surprisingly, the knockout mice exhibited a significant increase in the HSC pool, approximately 40-fold. However, the reintroduction of wild-type PTPMT1, not catalytically deficient or truncated PTPMT1 lacking mitochondrial localization, restored the differentiation capabilities of the knockout HSCs. Further investigation revealed that PTPMT1 deficiency altered mitochondrial metabolism and that phosphatidylinositol phosphate substrates of PTPMT1 directly enhanced the activation of mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2 induced by fatty acids. Interestingly, the depletion of PTPMT1 from myeloid, T lymphoid, or B lymphoid progenitors did not result in any defects in lineage-specific knockout mice. This study highlights the crucial role of PTPMT1 in the metabolic regulation of HSC function.

title: GSK-3-mediated phosphorylation enhances Maf-transforming activity.
text: The Maf oncoproteins belong to the AP-1 superfamily and function as b-Zip transcription factors. They play crucial roles in various processes including development, metabolism, and tumorigenesis. In human multiple myelomas, approximately 50% of cases exhibit overexpression of Maf proteins. Our study reveals that the oncogenic activity of Maf is regulated by phosphorylation mediated by GSK-3. Interestingly, phosphorylation by GSK-3 can enhance the oncogenic potential of Maf. Through microarray analysis, we have identified a specific gene-expression subprogram that is controlled by GSK-3-mediated phosphorylation of Maf. This subprogram is involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and has implications for cancer progression. Additionally, we have demonstrated that GSK-3 triggers sequential phosphorylation of MafA at specific residues (S61, T57, T53, and S49), leading to its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Surprisingly, this phosphorylation actually increases the transcriptional activity of MafA by facilitating the recruitment of the coactivator P/CAF. Furthermore, our findings indicate that P/CAF protects MafA from ubiquitination and degradation. This suggests that once the coactivator complex is released, MafA undergoes polyubiquitination and degradation, allowing for the termination of its response.

title: NETs are a source of citrullinated autoantigens and stimulate inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis.
text: The exact early events that lead to the development of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are not yet fully understood. However, the formation of autoantibodies to citrullinated protein antigens (ACPAs) is believed to be a significant factor in the disease. Neutrophils taken from patients with various autoimmune diseases have been found to exhibit increased neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, which exposes autoantigens in the presence of immunostimulatory molecules. We conducted a study to determine if abnormal NETosis occurs in RA, identify its triggers, and examine its harmful inflammatory effects. We discovered that enhanced NETosis was present in both circulating neutrophils and synovial fluid neutrophils in RA patients, compared to neutrophils from healthy individuals and patients with osteoarthritis (OA). Additionally, neutrophils that formed NETs were found in RA synovial tissue, rheumatoid nodules, and skin. The occurrence of NETosis was correlated with the presence and levels of ACPAs, as well as systemic inflammatory markers. We also found that sera from RA patients and immunoglobulin fractions from patients with high levels of ACPAs and/or rheumatoid factor significantly increased NETosis, and the NETs induced by these autoantibodies contained distinct proteins. During NETosis, neutrophils released the citrullinated autoantigens associated with RA pathogenesis, and anti-citrullinated vimentin antibodies strongly induced NET formation. Furthermore, the inflammatory cytokines interleukin-17A (IL-17A) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) triggered NETosis in neutrophils from RA patients. In turn, NETs significantly amplified inflammatory responses in synovial fibroblasts from both RA and OA patients, including the production of IL-6, IL-8, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. These findings suggest that accelerated NETosis plays a role in the development of RA by exposing citrullinated autoantigens and immunostimulatory molecules, which may contribute to abnormal immune responses in the joints and throughout the body, perpetuating the disease's pathogenic mechanisms.

title: Is autoimmunity the Achilles' heel of cancer immunotherapy?
text: Integrating immuno-oncology into the treatment of metastatic cancer alongside chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted small-molecule compounds is crucial for its success. It is equally important to understand the limitations and toxicities of immunotherapy. Initially, immunotherapy was seen as a less toxic option compared to other therapies, but as its use becomes more common, immunotoxicity and autoimmunity are emerging as significant challenges. In this Perspective, we examine the evidence that suggests immunotoxicity can be beneficial for patients and explore the mechanisms that may contribute to the development of autoimmunity. We also discuss strategies to minimize immunotoxicity and highlight the need for further research and reporting to address this issue.

title: Trophoblast differentiation defect in human embryonic stem cells lacking PIG-A and GPI-anchored cell-surface proteins.
text:
Pluripotent hES cells have the ability to develop into different cell types from the three embryonic germ layers and extraembryonic tissues like trophoblasts. However, the mechanisms that control the lineage choices of hES cells are not well understood. In this study, we present our findings on two hES cell clones that lack a group of cell surface molecules called GPI-APs (glycosyl-phosphatidyl-inositol-anchored proteins). This deficiency is caused by a lack of gene expression of PIG-A (phosphatidyl-inositol-glycan class A), which is necessary for the first step of GPI synthesis. 

Although the GPI-AP-deficient hES cells were able to form embryoid bodies and initiate differentiation into the three embryonic germ layers, they were unable to form trophoblasts. This inability was observed both when the cells were induced to differentiate through embryoid body formation and when exogenous BMP4 was added. The reason for this defect in trophoblast formation was the absence of GPI-anchored BMP coreceptors, which resulted in impaired activation of BMP4 signaling in the GPI-AP-deficient hES cells. 

These findings demonstrate that GPI-APs play a crucial role in the full activation of BMP signaling, which is necessary for the formation of human trophoblasts.

title: CRISPR Interference Limits Horizontal Gene Transfer in Staphylococci by Targeting DNA
text: Bacteria and archaea can transfer genes horizontally through phage transduction, transformation, or conjugation. Among these methods, conjugation is particularly significant in the dissemination of antibiotic resistance. The presence of Clustered, regularly interspaced, short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) loci provides a defense mechanism against phages by conferring sequence-directed immunity. In a clinical isolate of Staphylococcus epidermidis, a CRISPR spacer is found to match the nickase gene found in almost all staphylococcal conjugative plasmids. Our study demonstrates that CRISPR interference effectively prevents conjugation and plasmid transformation in S. epidermidis. Interestingly, when a self-splicing intron is inserted into the nickase gene, interference is blocked despite the reconstitution of the target sequence in the spliced mRNA. This suggests that the interference machinery directly targets DNA. In conclusion, CRISPR loci play a crucial role in countering various mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer and can restrict the spread of antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria.

title: Development of leukemia in donor cells after allogeneic stem cell transplantation--a survey of the European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT).
text: Donor cell leukemia (DCL), a rare but serious complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT), lacks clear definitions regarding its incidence, potential causes, treatment options, and patient outcomes. To address this, a questionnaire survey was conducted among European Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group (EBMT) centers. The survey included 91 centers and covered 10,489 allogeneic SCTs performed between December 1982 and September 2003. Out of these, 14 cases of DCL were identified, with most cases exhibiting a myeloid phenotype (7 cases of acute myeloid leukemia, 3 cases of acute lymphocytic leukemia, and 1 case of chronic myeloid leukemia). Molecular analysis of chimerism was used to confirm the donor cell origin in most cases. The type of DCL and cytogenetic alterations were found to be independent of the original disease. The median time between transplantation and DCL diagnosis was 17 months (ranging from 4 to 164 months). No specific conditioning, donor, graft manipulation, graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis, or subsequent complications were identified as risk factors for DCL.
