Chemotherapy was effective in inducing remission in DCL, and two out of five patients remained in remission after a second transplant. Importantly, none of the stem cell donors developed hematologic malignancies during a median follow-up period of 9 years (ranging from 6 to 30 years). DCL is an extremely rare complication of allogeneic SCT, and treatment with chemotherapy and a second SCT is justified. Furthermore, stem cell donors do not have an increased risk of developing hematologic malignancies.

title: Lack of evidence of transfusion transmission of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in a US surveillance study.
text: In 2004, concerns were raised about the possibility of nonvariant or classic forms of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) being transmitted through blood transfusions, following reported cases of variant CJD transmissions in the United Kingdom. To investigate this, patients diagnosed with CJD who had a history of blood donation were identified and their blood recipients were traced through blood distribution and hospital records. The vital status and cause of death of the recipients were determined by matching their personal identifiers with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Death Index database. The study included 36 blood donors who later developed CJD and 436 recipients. By 2006, 91 recipients were still alive, 329 had passed away, and 16 were lost to follow-up. The three groups had collectively survived for 2096.0 person-years after transfusion. Out of the 144 recipients who survived for 5 years or longer after transfusion, 68 had received blood donated within 60 months before the onset of CJD in the donor. No cases of CJD were identified among the recipients. These findings from the ongoing study provide strong evidence that the risk, if any, of transfusion transmission of CJD from donors is significantly lower than the risk from variant CJD donors.

title: Large-scale hypomethylated blocks associated with Epstein-Barr virus-induced B-cell immortalization.
text: Altered DNA methylation is a common occurrence in human cancer, starting from the earliest detectable stages. To better understand how and when this alteration happens, it is helpful to analyze it within the context of carcinogenesis caused by a specific agent. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a herpesvirus known to cause lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in humans, and it is also commonly used in laboratories to immortalize human B-cells in culture. In this study, we conducted whole-genome bisulfite sequencing on normal B-cells, activated B-cells, and EBV-immortalized B-cells from the same three individuals. The goal was to identify the impact of transformation on the methylome. Surprisingly, we found that EBV immortalization induced large-scale hypomethylated blocks, covering two-thirds of the genome, whereas B-cell activation alone did not have the same effect. These hypomethylated blocks were similar to those observed in human cancer and were associated with gene-expression variability, resembling the patterns seen in human cancer. This suggests that epigenomic changes, caused by methylation disruption, play a crucial role in promoting tumor cell heterogeneity. Additionally, we observed small-scale changes in DNA methylation near CpG islands. Overall, these findings indicate that methylation disruption is an early and critical step in the development of malignant transformation.

title: Stem cell self-renewal specified by JAK-STAT activation in response to a support cell cue.
text: Throughout adulthood, stem cells play a crucial role in generating various types of short-lived cells, including blood, skin, and sperm. These stem cells possess the ability to divide and produce daughter cells that can either renew themselves or differentiate into specialized cells. While the surrounding microenvironment, known as the niche, influences the fate of stem cells, there is limited knowledge about the signals from the niche that promote self-renewal. In our study, we have discovered that the apical hub cells in the Drosophila testis serve as a cellular niche, supporting the self-renewal of stem cells. These hub cells express a ligand called Unpaired (Upd), which activates the Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway in neighboring germ cells. This activation is crucial for specifying self-renewal and ensuring the continuous maintenance of the germ line stem cell population.

title: Effects of interventions in pregnancy on maternal weight and obstetric outcomes: meta-analysis of randomised evidence
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the impact of dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy on the weight of both the mother and the fetus, as well as to determine the effects of these interventions on obstetric outcomes. The study design involved a systematic review and meta-analysis. Data was collected from major databases from the beginning of the databases until January 2012, with no language restrictions. The study included randomized controlled trials that evaluated any dietary or lifestyle interventions that had the potential to affect maternal weight during pregnancy and the outcomes of the pregnancy. The results were analyzed and presented as relative risks for dichotomous data and mean differences for continuous data. 

A total of 44 relevant randomized controlled trials, involving 7278 women, were identified. These trials evaluated three categories of interventions: diet, physical activity, and a combination of both. Overall, the interventions resulted in a reduction of 1.42 kg (95% confidence interval 0.95 to 1.89 kg) in gestational weight gain compared to the control group. When all interventions were combined, there were no significant differences in birth weight (mean difference -50 g, -100 to 0 g) or the incidence of large or small for gestational age babies between the groups. However, physical activity alone was associated with a reduced birth weight (mean difference -60 g, -120 to -10 g). The interventions were also found to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia (0.74, 0.60 to 0.92) and shoulder dystocia (0.39, 0.22 to 0.70), but had no significant effect on other important outcomes. Dietary intervention resulted in the largest reduction in maternal gestational weight gain (3.84 kg, 2.45 to 5.22 kg) and improved pregnancy outcomes compared to other interventions. The overall evidence rating for important outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and preterm delivery was low to very low. 

In conclusion, dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy can reduce maternal gestational weight gain and improve outcomes for both the mother and the baby. Among the interventions, those based on diet are the most effective and are associated with reductions in maternal gestational weight gain and improved obstetric outcomes.

title: Tetraspanin 3 Is Required for the Development and Propagation of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia.
text: Acute Myelogenous Leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer that affects both adults and children and is often resistant to treatment. Therefore, it is crucial to identify the signals necessary for AML development in order to find new ways to treat this disease. In this study, we discovered that Tetraspanin 3 is a target of the RNA binding protein Musashi 2, which plays a critical role in AML. By creating mice without the Tspan3 gene, we found that they were born without any obvious defects. However, the absence of Tspan3 impaired the ability of leukemia stem cells to renew themselves and propagate the disease, resulting in significantly improved survival rates in mouse models of AML. Furthermore, inhibiting Tspan3 prevented the growth of AML samples from patients, indicating its importance in human disease as well. We also found that Tspan3 deficiency disrupted the response to CXCL12/SDF-1 and caused problems with the localization of AML within the niche. These findings demonstrate that Tspan3 is a crucial regulator of aggressive leukemias and suggest that it plays a role in the development of cancer.

title: Reorganization of enhancer patterns in transition from naive to primed pluripotency.
text: Distinct signaling requirements, transcriptomes, and developmental properties characterize naive and primed pluripotency. However, both cellular states share key transcriptional regulators, namely Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. In this study, we demonstrate that the transition between these two pluripotent states is associated with a widespread relocation of Oct4, accompanied by a global rearrangement of enhancer chromatin landscapes. Through genomic and biochemical analyses, we have identified potential mediators of primed state-specific Oct4 binding, including Otx2 and Zic2/3. Interestingly, even in the absence of differentiation cues, premature overexpression of Otx2 is sufficient to exit the naive state, induce transcription of a significant subset of genes associated with primed pluripotency, and redirect Oct4 to previously inaccessible enhancer sites. However, the ability of Otx2 to engage with new enhancer regions is influenced by its levels, intrinsic properties of the sites, and the signaling environment. These findings shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying pluripotency and suggest that the ability of transcription factors like Otx2 and Oct4 to pioneer new enhancer sites is highly dependent on the specific context.

title: Topoisomerase II plays an essential role as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.
text:
We investigated the impact of topoisomerases I and II on the replication of SV40 DNA using a purified protein system called the monopolymerase system. In the presence of both topoisomerases, two distinct nascent DNAs were observed. One product, resulting from the replication of the leading template strand, was approximately half the size of the template DNA. The other product, derived from the lagging template strand, consisted of short DNAs. These products were synthesized from both SV40 naked DNA and SV40 chromosomes.

When replicating SV40 naked DNA, either topoisomerase I or II facilitated replication fork movement and supported complete leading strand synthesis. However, when replicating SV40 chromosomes with the same proteins, reactions containing only topoisomerase I produced shorter leading strands. On the other hand, reactions supplemented with topoisomerase II, as well as reactions containing only topoisomerase II, accumulated mature size DNA products.

In the presence of crude extracts of HeLa cells, the specific inhibitor of topoisomerase II, VP-16, hindered elongation of the nascent DNA during SV40 chromosome replication. These findings suggest that topoisomerase II plays a crucial role as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.

title: Bromodomain Proteins Contribute to Maintenance of Bloodstream Form Stage Identity in the African Trypanosome
text: The tsetse fly transmits Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite responsible for African sleeping sickness, to its mammalian host. In the fly, the parasite's surface is covered with invariant procyclin, while in the mammal, it resides outside the cells in its bloodstream form (BF) and is densely covered with highly immunogenic Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG). The parasite varies this VSG surface using around 2500 distinct VSG genes. Recent studies in mammals suggest that bromodomain proteins, which recognize histone acetyl-lysine, play a role in maintaining stem cell fate. This led us to hypothesize that bromodomain proteins may also maintain the BF cell fate in trypanosomes. To test this, we used small-molecule inhibitors and genetic mutants for individual bromodomain proteins. RNA-seq experiments showed changes in the transcriptome similar to those observed during differentiation from the BF to the insect stage. This was confirmed at the protein level by the appearance of insect-stage proteins on the cell surface. Additionally, bromodomain inhibition disrupted two major BF-specific immune evasion mechanisms used by trypanosomes to avoid mammalian host antibody responses. First, it disrupted the monoallelic expression of the antigenically varied VSG. Second, it blocked the rapid internalization of antibodies bound to VSG on the trypanosome surface. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that trypanosome bromodomain proteins play a role in maintaining the identity of the bloodstream stage and in immune evasion. Importantly, inhibiting bromodomain proteins reduced virulence in a mouse model of infection, suggesting that these proteins could be potential therapeutic targets for trypanosomiasis. Our crystal structure analysis at a resolution of 1.25Å of a trypanosome bromodomain in complex with I-BET151 revealed a unique binding mode of the inhibitor, providing a promising starting point for rational drug design.

title: Timing requirements for insulin/IGF-1 signaling in C. elegans.
text: The insulin/IGF-1 signaling pathway, which includes insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), plays a significant role in the lifespan, reproduction, and diapause of various organisms. Given its crucial role in animal physiology, we aimed to determine the specific stage of an animal's life when this pathway is necessary for regulating these processes. Our study focused on Caenorhabditis elegans and revealed that the pathway primarily influences aging during adulthood, even at advanced ages. However, it primarily regulates diapause during the developmental stage. Furthermore, we discovered that longevity and reproduction are controlled independently by this pathway. These findings demonstrate that the regulation of lifespan can occur at different times than phenotypes that may initially appear to diminish the overall quality of life.

title: Predominance of Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Rectal Mucosa of Patients With Non-Celiac Wheat Sensitivity: Reversal After a Wheat-Free Diet
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the inflammatory response in the rectal mucosa of patients with non-celiac wheat sensitivity (NCWS), a condition characterized by a reaction to wheat ingestion after ruling out celiac disease and wheat allergy. We conducted a prospective study involving 22 patients with symptoms resembling irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), who were diagnosed with NCWS through a double-blind placebo-controlled challenge. As controls, we included eight IBS patients who did not show improvement on a wheat-free diet. After administering an oral challenge of 80 grams of wheat daily, we isolated cells from rectal biopsies and analyzed them using fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Our findings revealed that rectal biopsies from wheat-challenged NCWS patients exhibited a significant infiltration of CD45(+) cells, consisting of both CD3(+) and CD3(-) lymphocytes. Interestingly, the CD3(-) lymphocytes produced higher levels of interferon (IFN)-γ compared to the IBS controls. Further analysis revealed that approximately 30% of the IFN-γ-producing CD45(+) cells were T-bet(+), CD56(-), NKP44(-), and CD117(-), indicating that they were type-1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1). Notably, the number of IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells significantly decreased in 10 patients who resumed a wheat-free diet after two weeks. These findings suggest that in patients with active NCWS, IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells infiltrate the rectal mucosa, highlighting the potential role of this innate lymphoid cell population in the pathogenesis of NCWS.

title: Folding and Self-Assembly of the TatA Translocation Pore Based on a Charge Zipper Mechanism
text: We present a novel idea for the folding and self-assembly of the TatA complex, which forms pores in the Twin-arginine translocase, as well as other membrane proteins. This concept is based on electrostatic "charge zippers." Each TatA subunit consists of a transmembrane segment, an amphiphilic helix (APH), and a densely charged region (DCR) at the C-terminal. The charges in the DCR are complementary to the charge pattern on the APH, suggesting that the protein can be assembled by forming a ladder of seven salt bridges. The resulting hairpin structure matches the thickness of the lipid bilayer, allowing for the spontaneous formation of a transmembrane pore through intra- and intermolecular salt bridges. Molecular dynamics simulations support the feasibility of this steric arrangement, and experimental evidence is provided by studying the equilibrium between monomers and oligomers of specific charge mutants. We propose similar "charge zippers" for other membrane-associated proteins, such as the biofilm-inducing peptide TisB, the human antimicrobial peptide dermcidin, and the pestiviral E(RNS) protein.

title: Molecular mechanisms of ribosomal protein gene coregulation.
text: The gene coregulation of the 137 ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) in Saccharomyces serves as a useful model. We conducted a detailed analysis of the regulators (Rap1, Fhl1, Ifh1, Sfp1, and Hmo1), the transcription machinery (TFIIB, TFIID, and RNA polymerase II), and chromatin organization at a near-base-pair resolution using ChIP-exo. This was done because RPGs undergo coordinated reprogramming. We observed that when Hmo1 was present in high amounts, Fhl1, Ifh1, Sfp1, and Hmo1 were broadly linked to the promoter DNA in a manner specific to RPGs. This was marked by a widening of the general minor groove. Importantly, Hmo1 extended 20-50 base pairs downstream from Fhl1. When RPGs were repressed, Fhl1 remained in place while Hmo1 dissociated. This dissociation was accompanied by an upstream shift of the +1 nucleosome, as indicated by the extension of Hmo1 and the core promoter region. Fhl1 and Hmo1 may act as two distinct barriers that can be regulated, and chromatin remodelers position the +1 nucleosome into either an activating or repressive state against these barriers. Our findings are consistent with previous in vitro studies and show that specific subunits of TFIID, in addition to binding at the core promoter, also make precise connections at Rap1 sites. This suggests that these connections reflect native interactions between Rap1 and TFIID. Our results provide insights into how sequence-specific DNA binding influences nucleosome positioning and the assembly of transcription complexes over a distance of more than 300 base pairs. Additionally, our findings shed light on how coregulation has coevolved with coding sequences.

title: Lipoatrophy and severe metabolic disturbance in mice with fat-specific deletion of PPARγ.
text: Adipose tissue plays a crucial role in metabolism, and when it malfunctions, it can lead to obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is known as the main regulator of adipocyte differentiation and function. While its role in adipogenesis has been proven in cell culture, previous studies on mice with fat-specific PPARγ gene knockouts did not show significant effects in vivo. However, in this study, we used Adipoq-Cre mice to specifically target adipose tissue and found a unique PPARγ knockout mouse model (PPARγ FKO) that had very little visible brown and white adipose tissue at 3 months old. As a result, these PPARγ FKO mice had enlarged pancreatic islets, fatty livers, and extremely high levels of blood glucose and serum insulin, indicating severe insulin resistance. Additionally, these mice experienced delayed hair coat formation due to the absence of dermal fat, disrupted mammary gland development resulting in the loss of mammary fat pads, and increased bone mass with loss of bone marrow fat. These findings highlight the crucial role of adipose PPARγ in adipose tissue formation, overall metabolic balance, and normal development of fat-containing tissues.

title: Fluconazole prophylaxis: can we eliminate invasive Candida infections in the neonatal ICU?
text: The prevention of invasive Candida infections in extremely preterm infants is crucial due to the high mortality, risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, and end-organ involvement associated with fungal infections in this population. Recent studies have shown that even with prompt or empiric treatment, mortality and neurodevelopmental impairment rates remain high in infants weighing less than 1000 g. However, fluconazole prophylaxis has been proven effective and safe in multiple studies, including a recent multicenter randomized controlled trial. These studies have consistently demonstrated a significant decrease in the incidence of invasive Candida infections in high-risk infants weighing less than 1000 g by 91% and in all infants weighing less than 1500 g by 85%. Additionally, the mortality rate from all causes was found to be 25% lower with fluconazole prophylaxis. Furthermore, targeting fluconazole prophylaxis specifically to infants weighing less than 1000 g has been shown to completely eliminate Candida-related mortality in entire neonatal ICUs. In summary, implementing fluconazole prophylaxis in infants weighing less than 1000 g or born at or before 27 weeks gestation is a highly effective, safe, and cost-effective strategy that can eliminate invasive Candida infections as a cause of neurodevelopmental impairment and mortality.

title: Fumarase deficiency in dichorionic diamniotic twins.
text: Fumarase deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that affects the Krebs Tricarboxylic Acid cycle. This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Fumarase deficiency can cause severe neurological problems, such as microcephaly, dystonia, developmental delay, seizures, and even death in infancy. Additionally, individuals who are carriers of this condition have an increased risk of developing hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma. In this case, we present a family who are not closely related, but had a twin pregnancy resulting in twin boys with fumarase deficiency. This diagnosis was confirmed through biochemical, enzymatic, and molecular testing. The twins also showed signs of liver involvement. We identified a new mutation in the fumarate hydratase gene in this family.

title: Angiopoietin-2 is increased in sepsis and inversely associated with nitric oxide-dependent microvascular reactivity
text:
The introduction discusses the role of angiopoietin-2 (ang-2) in endothelial activation and vascular permeability. It mentions that ang-2 levels are elevated in severe sepsis but the reasons for this are unknown. The text also highlights the role of nitric oxide (NO) in inhibiting the release of ang-2 and how its availability is decreased in sepsis. The hypothesis is that endothelial NO availability is inversely correlated with ang-2 levels in sepsis. 

To test this hypothesis, the study assessed plasma ang-2, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and endothelial-active cytokines in 83 patients with early sepsis and 41 hospital controls. These measurements were then related to reactive hyperaemia-peripheral arterial tonometry (RH-PAT), which is a measure of endothelial NO availability. 

The results showed that plasma ang-2 levels were elevated in sepsis, with higher levels in severe sepsis compared to sepsis without organ failure and controls. Ang-2 levels were inversely correlated with RH-PAT and positively correlated with IL-6 levels and the degree of organ failure. The correlation between ang-2 and RH-PAT remained significant even after controlling for sepsis severity. 

In a longitudinal analysis, it was found that recovery of RH-PAT over time was associated with a decline in ang-2 levels. 

The conclusion of the study is that ang-2 levels increase with sepsis severity and are inversely correlated with NO-dependent microvascular reactivity. Impaired endothelial NO availability may contribute to the release of ang-2, endothelial activation, and capillary leak. The study suggests that interventions aimed at increasing endothelial NO availability or inhibiting ang-2 activity may have therapeutic potential in sepsis.

title: Ecologic versus individual-level sources of bias in ecologic estimates of contextual health effects.
text: Several authors have made efforts to defend aggregate studies in ecology by arguing that the purpose of these studies is to estimate contextual or group-level effects rather than individual-level effects. However, critics of these arguments point out that despite disclaimers, ecologic effect estimates are inevitably used as estimates of individual effects. Another issue is that the variation in individual effects within an ecological setting can bias the estimates of contextual effects. This bias is likely to occur in studies that examine the relationship between ecosocial factors and health outcomes, as social context is not randomly distributed across typical analysis units such as administrative regions. Ecologic data only provide limited observations on the joint distribution of individually defined confounders and outcomes, and therefore cannot identify contextual or individual-level effects. While ecologic studies can still be valuable with appropriate cautionary notes, their limitations can be better addressed through multilevel study designs that incorporate both individual and group-level data. However, it is worth noting that these multilevel studies often encounter similar issues as ecologic studies, including problems related to inappropriate aggregation and temporal changes in covariate distributions.

title: Left–right asymmetry in the vertebrate embryo: from early information to higher-level integration
text: While vertebrates may appear to have bilateral symmetry on the outside, there are actually various internal asymmetries in the arrangement and positioning of internal organs. These asymmetries are formed during embryonic development through intricate epigenetic and genetic processes. Recent research on different model organisms has made significant advancements in understanding how this information about laterality is generated and transmitted to different parts of the embryo. Similarities and differences have been observed in the mechanisms used by various vertebrates to specify the left-right axis. Additionally, recent evidence suggests interesting connections between the establishment of left-right asymmetries and the symmetrical elongation of the anterior-posterior axis.

title: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cancer: the insulin and IGF connection.
text: Research on the relationship between obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D), and cancer suggests a positive correlation, indicating an increased risk of cancer and cancer-related mortality. Various factors, including insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, elevated levels of IGF, steroid and peptide hormones, as well as inflammatory markers, contribute to the link between these diseases. The medications commonly prescribed for T2D management, such as metformin and exogenous insulin, may impact the likelihood of developing cancer and cancer-related mortality. In the field of cancer treatment, novel therapies are being developed to target the insulin and IGF1 systems.

title: Non-coding RNAs: Functions and applications in endocrine-related cancer.
text: A significant portion of the human genome is transcribed into non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). This transcriptome challenges the traditional understanding of gene expression regulation and plays a crucial role in transcriptional and post-transcriptional processes. Notably, dysregulation of several ncRNAs has been observed in cancer, leading to ongoing research on the potential use of these ncRNAs as cancer biomarkers and targets for anti-cancer drugs. This is particularly important in endocrine-related cancers, where survival rates are often low. In this review, we aim to summarize the roles and clinical implications of recently discovered ncRNAs, such as long ncRNAs, PIWI-interacting RNAs, tRNA- and Y RNA-derived ncRNAs, and small nucleolar RNAs, in endocrine-related cancers affecting both males and females. Our focus is on recent studies that shed light on the biology and expression of ncRNAs in cancer, and we conclude with a discussion on the challenges and future directions, including potential clinical applications. While ncRNAs hold great promise as diagnostic tools and therapeutic targets, further research is needed to fully harness the potential of these unconventional transcripts.

title: NMR structural and kinetic characterization of a homeodomain diffusing and hopping on nonspecific DNA.
text: Protein-DNA interactions that are not specific are inherently dynamic and involve the diffusion of the protein along the DNA as well as the hopping of the protein from one DNA molecule or segment to another. Understanding the structure and dynamics of how gene regulatory proteins interact with DNA in a nonspecific manner is challenging because the experimental observations are an average of many rapidly exchanging states. To tackle this challenge, we have utilized various NMR spectroscopic techniques, such as relaxation analysis, paramagnetic relaxation enhancement, and residual dipolar couplings. Through these techniques, we have examined the structural and kinetic aspects of the interaction between the HoxD9 homeodomain and a nonspecific 24-bp DNA duplex. In this system, the protein is not restricted to any specific site. Our data demonstrate that HoxD9 binds to nonspecific DNA in the same manner and orientation as it does in the specific complex. However, the mobility of Arg side-chains that come into contact with the DNA is increased in the nonspecific complex compared to the specific one. Additionally, we have analyzed the kinetics of intermolecular translocation between two different nonspecific DNA molecules. Our findings reveal that at high DNA concentrations, such as those found in living organisms, direct transfer from one nonspecific complex to another nonspecific DNA molecule occurs without the need for free protein as an intermediary. This discovery provides a straightforward mechanism for accelerating the search for the specific site in a sea of nonspecific sites in vivo. It allows for more efficient sampling of available DNA sites as the protein jumps from one segment to another.

title: MHC Haplotype Matching for Unrelated Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
text: The current criteria for selecting unrelated donors for hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) involve matching the alleles of each human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). However, even after finding HLA-identical unrelated donors, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a significant and potentially life-threatening complication. The MHC contains over 400 genes, and the total number of transplantation antigens is still unknown. To identify genes that affect transplantation outcomes, it would be helpful to define the extended MHC haplotypes of the unrelated donor and recipient using linkage disequilibrium (LD)-mapping approaches.

title: The SIR2/3/4 complex and SIR2 alone promote longevity in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by two different mechanisms. Genes Dev 13
text: The SIR genes play a crucial role in determining the life span of yeast mother cells. Our study demonstrates that the regulation of life span by the Sir proteins is not dependent on their involvement in nonhomologous end joining. The reduced life span observed in sir3 or sir4 mutants is a result of the simultaneous expression of both a and alpha mating-type information. This leads to an indirect increase in rDNA recombination and the production of extrachromosomal rDNA circles. Similarly, the shortened life span of sir2 mutants is directly linked to their inability to suppress recombination caused by the Fob1p-mediated replication block in the rDNA. Sir2p is a critical factor in promoting longevity in yeast, and increasing its gene dosage extends the life span of wild-type cells. We also discuss the potential role of the conserved SIR2 gene in mammalian aging.

title: Meta-analysis identifies common variants associated with body mass index in East Asians
text: Genome-wide association studies have primarily focused on populations of European ancestry to identify genetic loci associated with obesity or body mass index (BMI). However, in this study, we conducted a meta-analysis on approximately 2.4 million SNPs in 27,715 east Asians. This was followed by replication studies in an additional 37,691 and 17,642 east Asians. Through this analysis, we discovered ten BMI-associated loci that reached genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 × 10(-8)). Among these loci, seven were previously identified (FTO, SEC16B, MC4R, GIPR-QPCTL, ADCY3-DNAJC27, BDNF, and MAP2K5), while three were novel (CDKAL1, PCSK1, and GP2). Additionally, three other loci, including two previously identified (GNPDA2 and TFAP2B) and one newly identified near PAX6, nearly reached the genome-wide significance threshold with P < 5.0 × 10(-7). These findings not only provide insights into new pathways involved in obesity but also highlight the importance of including non-European populations in genetic studies.

title: Phosphorylation of histone H3(T118) alters nucleosome dynamics and remodeling
text: Nucleosomes, which are the basic building blocks of chromatin structure, play a crucial role in regulating and hindering transcription, replication, and repair processes. The modification of histone proteins within nucleosomes, known as post-translational modifications (PTMs), controls these DNA processes. One specific PTM, phosphorylation of Histone H3 at site T118 (H3(T118ph)), is involved in the regulation of transcription and DNA repair. To investigate its impact on nucleosome dynamics, we produced H3(T118ph) using expressed protein ligation and examined its effects. Our findings reveal that H3(T118ph) weakens the binding between DNA and histones by 2 kcal/mol, significantly enhances nucleosome mobility by 28-fold, and increases DNA accessibility near the central region by 6-fold. Additionally, H3(T118ph) accelerates the disassembly of nucleosomes by the hMSH2-hMSH6 complex and enables nucleosome disassembly by the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler. These studies suggest that H3(T118ph) directly enhances and potentially alters chromatin remodeling reactions.

title: Mechanosignaling through YAP and TAZ drives fibroblast activation and fibrosis.
text: The development of pathological fibrosis is influenced by a continuous cycle in which the fibrotic extracellular matrix both triggers and is a result of fibroblast activation. However, the specific molecular mechanisms involved in this process are not well understood. In this study, we have discovered that yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ), which are transcriptional effectors of the Hippo pathway, play a crucial role in regulating fibroblast activation and matrix synthesis in response to changes in matrix stiffness. YAP and TAZ are highly expressed in fibrotic lung tissue, particularly in spindle-shaped fibroblastic cells. When fibroblasts are grown on pathologically stiff matrices, YAP and TAZ accumulate in the nuclei, whereas this does not occur on physiologically compliant matrices. In vitro experiments have shown that knocking down YAP and TAZ together significantly reduces important fibroblast functions, such as matrix synthesis, contraction, and proliferation, but only on pathologically stiff matrices. The profibrotic effects of YAP and TAZ are partially mediated through their regulation of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, which is influenced by matrix stiffness independently of transforming growth factor-β signaling. Furthermore, when immortalized fibroblasts expressing active YAP or TAZ mutant proteins are transferred to the lungs of mice, they are able to overcome the growth limitations imposed by soft matrices and promote fibrosis, highlighting the ability of fibroblast YAP/TAZ activation to drive a profibrotic response in vivo. Overall, these findings demonstrate that YAP and TAZ act as coordinators of the matrix-driven feedback loop that amplifies and sustains fibrosis in a mechanosensitive manner.

title: Control of cellular cholesterol efflux by the nuclear oxysterol receptor LXR alpha.
text: LXR alpha, a nuclear receptor, has previously been found to regulate the conversion of cholesterol to bile acids. In this study, we investigate its role in controlling the removal of cellular cholesterol. We conducted experiments using retroviral expression of LXR alpha in NIH 3T3 fibroblasts and RAW264.7 macrophages, as well as treating these cells with oxysterol ligands of LXR. Our results show that this leads to a significant increase (7- to 30-fold) in the mRNA encoding the potential cholesterol/phospholipid transporter ATP-binding cassette (ABC)A1. However, when cells express dominant-negative forms of LXR alpha or LXR beta lacking the AF2 transcriptional activation domain, the induction of ABCA1 mRNA in response to oxysterols is reduced. Additionally, we demonstrate that the expression of LXR alpha in NIH 3T3 fibroblasts and treatment with oxysterols is enough to stimulate cholesterol removal to extracellular apolipoprotein AI. Interestingly, the ability of oxysterol ligands of LXR to stimulate removal is significantly diminished in Tangier fibroblasts, which have a mutation in the ABCA1 gene. These findings suggest that cellular cholesterol removal is regulated, at least partially, at the transcriptional level through a nuclear receptor-signaling pathway. We propose a model in which activation of LXRs by oxysterols, in response to cellular sterol accumulation, leads to the induction of the ABCA1 transporter and the promotion of lipid removal to extracellular acceptors. These results have important implications for understanding cholesterol homeostasis in mammals and offer potential opportunities for pharmacological regulation of cellular lipid metabolism.

title: Circadian regulation of intracellular G-protein signalling mediates intercellular synchrony and rhythmicity in the suprachiasmatic nucleus
text: The circadian center, known as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), relies on synchronized oscillations of numerous cellular clocks. These clocks are coordinated through cell-cell communication, although the exact mechanism remains largely unknown. Our study reveals that a protein called RGS16, which is responsible for deactivating Gαi, increases at specific times during the circadian cycle. This increase allows for the time-dependent activation of intracellular cyclic AMP signaling within the SCN. When the Rgs16 gene is removed, the production of cAMP becomes disrupted, resulting in a lengthened circadian period for behavioral rhythms. The precise regulation of the cAMP signal by clock-controlled RGS16 is crucial for maintaining the proper phase relationship between different regions of the SCN. Ultimately, this temporal regulation of intracellular G protein signaling by RGS16 ensures the synchronization of SCN pacemaker neurons and defines the 24-hour behavioral rhythm.

title: MDC1 collaborates with TopBP1 in DNA replication checkpoint control
text: The control of the DNA replication checkpoint is greatly influenced by Human TopBP1. In this study, we have discovered that MDC1, a crucial protein involved in the cellular response to DNA double-strand breaks, is associated with TopBP1. The interaction between TopBP1 and MDC1 is specifically mediated by the fifth BRCT domain of TopBP1 and the Ser-Asp-Thr (SDT) repeats of MDC1. Additionally, we have shown that the H2AX/MDC1 signaling cascade promotes the accumulation of TopBP1 at stalled replication forks. Furthermore, MDC1 plays a significant role in the activation of ATR-dependent Chk1 in response to replication stress. Overall, our findings indicate that MDC1 facilitates several important processes in both the cellular DNA damage response and the DNA replication checkpoint.

title: Deregulated DNA polymerase β strengthens ionizing radiation-induced nucleotidic and chromosomal instabilities
text: DNA polymerase β (Pol β) is an enzyme that is prone to errors and has been found to be excessively expressed in various human tumors. In this study, we utilized two recombinant CHO cells that only differed in the expression of Pol β to demonstrate that cells with an overexpression of Pol β are significantly more susceptible to treatments involving ionizing radiation (IR), leading to an increase in apoptosis. Additionally, we observed that the surviving cells exhibited a hypermutator phenotype, which could be attributed to various pathways involving Pol β. These pathways include an enhanced ability to incorporate the mutagenic dGTP analog, 8-oxo-dGTP, into DNA. This analog is one of the most prevalent purine-derived nucleotides exposed to γ-irradiation. Furthermore, the induction of DNA breaks by IR and the accumulation of radiation-induced chromosome aberrations also contribute to the hypermutator phenotype. Consequently, alterations in Pol β expression in irradiated cells appear to reinforce both cell death and genetic changes associated with a malignant phenotype. These findings offer novel insights into the cellular response to radiation and the resulting carcinogenic consequences.

title: Chromosome 7 gain and DNA hypermethylation at the HOXA10 locus are associated with expression of a stem cell related HOX-signature in glioblastoma
text:
The HOX genes are a group of developmental genes that are not normally expressed in the developing forebrain or in the healthy brain. However, in glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, there is abnormal expression of a HOX-gene dominated stem-cell signature. This abnormal expression has been linked to increased resistance to chemo-radiotherapy and sustained proliferation of cancer cells. In this study, we investigate the epigenetic and genetic changes associated with the expression of this signature in glioblastoma.

Our results show that there is significant hypermethylation of the HOXA locus 7p15.2 in glioblastoma compared to non-cancerous brain tissue. This hypermethylation is associated with a gain of chromosome 7, which is a characteristic feature of glioblastoma. It is possible that this hypermethylation compensates for the increased gene dosage caused by the tumor, preventing excessive gene expression. We also identify a specific region of the HOXA10 gene that escapes hypermethylation in glioblastoma with high levels of HOX gene expression. The combination of gene copy gain at 7p15.2 and DNA methylation at specific regulatory sites in HOXA10 is strongly associated with the expression of the HOX gene signature.

Furthermore, we find that the methylation status of these regulatory sites corresponds to the presence of active or inactive chromatin marks in glioblastoma-derived spheres with high or low levels of HOX gene expression, respectively.

Based on these findings, we propose that there is a co-evolution and interaction between gene copy gain, associated with the gain of chromosome 7, and additional epigenetic changes that trigger an inappropriate HOX gene transcriptional program in glioblastoma.

title: Probing the phenomenon of trained immunity in invertebrates during a transgenerational study, using brine shrimp Artemia as a model system
text:
The innate immune system of the invertebrate was found to exhibit adaptive features known as trained immunity. However, the specifics of how the innate immune system retains memory and the underlying mechanisms are still unclear. To investigate this, we conducted a study using the invertebrate model Artemia. Our aim was to determine whether trained immunity is possible or not, by examining whether enduring memory against homologous and heterologous antigens (Vibrio spp.) exists during a transgenerational study. Additionally, we sought to uncover the mechanisms behind this phenomenon. 

Our findings revealed that Artemia's immune system possesses memory and partial discrimination. This was demonstrated by the increased resistance of three successive generations of Vibrio-exposed ancestors to a homologous bacterial strain, as opposed to a heterologous strain. The enhanced resistance phenotype was associated with elevated levels of signaling molecules hsp70 and hmgb1, as well as changes in the expression of key genes related to innate immunity. 

Furthermore, our results showed a stochastic pattern in the acetylation and methylation levels of histones H4 and H3K4me3, respectively, in the progenies of challenged ancestors. These findings suggest that innate immune responses in invertebrates can be trained, and that epigenetic reprogramming of selected innate immune effectors likely plays a central role in the mechanisms underlying trained immunity.

title: Using Structural Information to Change the Phosphotransfer Specificity of a Two-Component Chemotaxis Signalling Complex
text: Histidine protein kinases (HPKs) and their response regulators (RRs) are widely utilized in two-component signal transduction pathways to regulate bacterial responses to environmental challenges. Numerous bacteria possess more than 150 different two-component pathways, and the phosphotransfer reactions within these systems are tightly controlled to prevent unwanted crosstalk. Among these pathways, the chemotaxis pathway is one of the most well-understood. In this study, we present the crystal structure of the histidine-containing phosphotransfer domain of the chemotaxis HPK, CheA(3), in complex with its corresponding RR, CheY(6), at a resolution of 1.40 A. We discovered that a methionine finger on CheY(6) plays a crucial role in the interaction, fitting snugly into a hydrophobic pocket in CheA(3). Interestingly, this methionine finger is only present in the cognate RRs of CheA(3), CheY(6), and CheB(2). Through site-directed mutagenesis, we demonstrated that mutating this methionine, along with two adjacent residues, completely abolished binding and phosphotransfer from CheA(3)-P to CheY(6), as confirmed by surface plasmon resonance studies. Furthermore, by introducing this methionine and an adjacent alanine residue into various noncognate CheYs, we observed a significant change in their specificity, enabling protein interaction and rapid phosphotransfer from CheA(3)-P. The structural insights provided by this study allowed us to identify the determinants of specificity in the CheA-CheY interaction and successfully reengineer phosphotransfer signaling. Overall, our findings offer valuable understanding of how cells achieve specificity in one of the most prevalent signaling pathways in biology, two-component signal transduction.

title: Combination varenicline and bupropion SR for tobacco-dependence treatment in cigarette smokers: a randomized trial.
text: The importance of combining pharmacotherapies for tobacco-dependence treatment in increasing smoking abstinence was investigated in a randomized clinical trial. The objective was to determine the efficacy and safety of varenicline and bupropion sustained-release (SR) as combination therapy compared to varenicline alone (monotherapy) in cigarette smokers. The trial took place between October 2009 and April 2013 at three midwestern clinical research sites, with 506 adult smokers participating. The participants were randomly assigned to receive either varenicline and bupropion SR or varenicline and a placebo for a 12-week treatment period, followed by a follow-up period up to week 52. The primary outcomes measured were abstinence rates at week 12, defined as prolonged abstinence (no smoking from 2 weeks after the target quit date) and 7-day point-prevalence abstinence (no smoking in the past 7 days). Secondary outcomes included abstinence rates at weeks 26 and 52. The results showed that at 12 weeks, the combination therapy group had higher rates of prolonged and 7-day point-prevalence abstinence compared to the varenicline monotherapy group. At 26 weeks, the combination therapy group still had higher rates of abstinence. However, at 52 weeks, there was no significant difference between the two groups. Participants receiving combination therapy reported more anxiety and depressive symptoms. In conclusion, the combined use of varenicline and bupropion increased prolonged abstinence but not 7-day point prevalence at 12 and 26 weeks. Further research is needed to determine the role of combination therapy in smoking cessation.

title: Effect of a C/EBP gene replacement on mitochondrial biogenesis in fat cells.
text: CCAAT/enhancer-binding proteins, C/EBPalpha and C/EBPbeta, play a crucial role in the differentiation and maturation of fat cells. Previous research has demonstrated that when C/EBPalpha is replaced with C/EBPbeta, resulting in the beta/beta alleles in the mouse genome, the accumulation of lipids in white adipose tissue (WAT) is prevented. This study aimed to investigate the impact of the beta/beta alleles on the lifespan and energy expenditure of mice, compared to their control littermates. The results showed that beta/beta mice had a longer lifespan and higher energy expenditure, primarily due to increased oxidation of energy in WAT. The WAT of beta/beta mice exhibited a higher concentration of metabolically active and thermogenic mitochondria, which are known for their ability to burn energy. The effect of the beta/beta allele was mediated by the upregulation of the G protein alpha stimulatory subunit (Galphas) in WAT. Overexpression of Galphas in fat-laden 3T3-L1 cells resulted in enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis, similar to what was observed in the WAT of beta/beta mice, and effectively reduced the stored lipid pool.

title: Variable breakpoints target PAX5 in patients with dicentric chromosomes: a model for the basis of unbalanced translocations in cancer.
text: The search for target genes involved in unbalanced acquired chromosomal abnormalities has not been successful due to the variability of breakpoints in these rearrangements. However, we present the example of dicentric chromosomes in B cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia to demonstrate that single genes are targeted through various mechanisms, despite this heterogeneity. Through FISH analysis, we observed that breakpoints on 9p led to the partial or complete deletion of PAX5, although they were heterogeneous. Molecular copy number counting allowed us to further identify the breakpoints and clone them using long-distance inverse PCR. This approach enabled us to identify 5 fusion gene partners with PAX5: LOC392027 (7p12.1), SLCO1B3 (12p12), ASXL1 (20q11.1), KIF3B (20q11.21), and C20orf112 (20q11.1). In each fusion protein, the DNA-binding paired domain of PAX5 was present. Using quantitative PCR, we demonstrated that both the deletion and gene fusion events resulted in the underexpression of PAX5, which also affected the expression of PAX5 target genes, including EBF1, ALDH1A1, ATP9A, and FLT3. Further molecular analysis revealed the deletion and mutation of the homologous PAX5 allele, providing additional evidence for the crucial role of PAX5. Our findings suggest that specific gene loci can be targeted by heterogeneous translocation breakpoints in human cancer, operating through various mechanisms. This approach has implications for identifying cancer genes in solid tumors, where unbalanced chromosomal rearrangements are common and few genes have been identified. It is likely that this strategy will uncover similar mechanisms in cancer pathogenesis overall.

title: Copyright � 1996, American Society for Microbiology Endotoxin-Induced Enhancement of Glucose Influx into
text: Hypoglycemia, a harmful metabolic disorder caused by endotoxemia, is a significant concern. In animal experiments using lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to induce endotoxemia, there is a noticeable increase in glucose consumption in organs rich in macrophages. However, the direct impact of LPS on glucose uptake by macrophages is not fully understood. Therefore, this study aimed to provide insight into this matter. By using 2-deoxy-D-[3H]glucose, the consumption and uptake of glucose by murine peritoneal exudate macrophages in culture were found to be two to three times faster when stimulated with 3 ng of LPS per ml. The rate of glucose uptake reached a plateau after 20 minutes of stimulation and remained at its maximum as long as LPS was present. Analysis using cDNA probes for five known isoforms of glucose transporter (GLUT) through Northern (RNA) blot revealed that during LPS stimulation, macrophages only expressed the GLUT1 isoform, and the amount of GLUT1 mRNA increased due to the stimulation. These findings suggest that macrophages respond to LPS by rapidly and consistently taking in glucose through GLUT1, which contributes to the development of systemic hypoglycemia during prolonged endotoxemia.

title: Factors associated with American Board of Medical Specialties member board certification among US medical school graduates.
text: The certification by an American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) member board is becoming increasingly important in assessing the quality of physicians. The objective of this study was to identify the demographic and educational factors that are associated with ABMS member board certification among graduates of US medical schools. The study was conducted retrospectively on a national cohort of graduates from 1997 to 2000, who were categorized based on their specialty choice at graduation and followed up until March 2, 2009. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify the factors associated with ABMS member board certification in each specialty category. The main outcome measure was ABMS member board certification. Out of the 42,440 graduates included in the study, 87.3% were board certified. Graduates in all specialty categories who achieved high scores on the US Medical Licensing Examination Step 2 Clinical Knowledge were more likely to be board certified. The odds ratios varied by specialty, with the lowest odds observed in emergency medicine and the highest odds in radiology. Except for family medicine, graduates who identified as underrepresented racial/ethnic minorities were less likely to be board certified in each specialty category. Additionally, an increase in debt was associated with a lower likelihood of board certification in obstetrics/gynecology, while it was associated with a higher likelihood in family medicine. In conclusion, demographic and educational factors were found to be associated with board certification among US medical school graduates in all specialty categories, although the specific findings varied.

title: Body-mass index and mortality in Korean men and women.
text:
BACKGROUND: The relationship between body weight and the risk of death is a topic of debate, despite the known health risks associated with obesity.

METHODS: We conducted a 12-year prospective cohort study involving 1,213,829 Koreans aged 30 to 95 years. We analyzed data on 82,372 deaths from any cause and 48,731 deaths from specific diseases, including cancer, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disease. Body-mass index (BMI) was used to assess body weight, calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters.

RESULTS: Both men and women had an average baseline BMI of 23.2. The rate of death from any cause showed a J-shaped association with BMI, regardless of smoking history. The lowest risk of death from any cause was observed among individuals with a BMI of 23.0 to 24.9. The risk of death from respiratory causes was higher among those with a lower BMI, while the risk of death from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or cancer was higher among those with a higher BMI. The association between BMI and death risk decreased with age.

CONCLUSIONS: Men and women who were underweight, overweight, or obese had higher death rates compared to those with normal weight. The relationship between BMI and death risk varied depending on the cause of death and was influenced by age, sex, and smoking history.

title: Human iPSC-based modeling of late-onset disease via progerin-induced aging.
text: In this study, we present a method for introducing aging-related traits into human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived lineages, specifically for modeling Parkinson's disease (PD). Reprogramming somatic cells to iPSCs resets their identity to an embryonic state, which poses a challenge for studying late-onset disorders. To overcome this hurdle, we utilized progerin, a truncated form of lamin A associated with premature aging. By expressing progerin in iPSC-derived fibroblasts and neurons, we observed the induction of various aging-related markers and characteristics, including the accumulation of neuromelanin, a dopamine-specific phenotype. By inducing aging in PD iPSC-derived dopamine neurons, we were able to observe disease phenotypes that require both aging and genetic susceptibility, such as dendrite degeneration, progressive loss of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, and the presence of enlarged mitochondria or Lewy-body-precursor inclusions. Therefore, our study suggests that progerin-induced aging can be utilized to uncover age-related disease features in hiPSC-based disease models.

title: SNAREs — engines for membrane fusion
text: SNARE proteins were first discovered in the late 1980s and have since been acknowledged as crucial elements of protein complexes responsible for membrane fusion. Despite significant differences in their sequences, SNARE proteins have a conserved mechanism that can be adjusted to facilitate various fusion reactions, including those involved in cell growth, membrane repair, cytokinesis, and synaptic transmission. A captivating understanding of these resilient nanomachines is gradually unfolding.

title: Maintaining the norm: T-cell homeostasis
text: Immunologists have long been intrigued by the endurance of naive and memory T cells, yet the factors that impact the survival and balance of these subsets have remained unclear. However, recent findings have revealed that the equilibrium of both naive and memory T-cell populations is constantly changing and carefully controlled by internal signals, such as cytokines and self-peptide-MHC ligands that bind to the T-cell receptor. These mechanisms of homeostasis could play a crucial role in determining the T-cell pool's ability to effectively respond to both foreign and self-antigens.

title: Cell type of origin influences the molecular and functional properties of mouse induced pluripotent stem cells
text: The ectopic expression of defined factors has allowed for the creation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from various somatic cell populations. However, it is still unclear whether iPSCs derived from different cell types are similar in terms of their molecular and functional characteristics. In this study, we have found that iPSCs obtained from mouse fibroblasts, hematopoietic cells, and myogenic cells display distinct patterns in terms of gene expression and epigenetics. Additionally, we have discovered that the cellular origin of iPSCs influences their ability to differentiate into embryoid bodies and different types of hematopoietic cells in vitro. Interestingly, these differences are largely diminished with continuous passaging of iPSCs. Our findings suggest that early-passage iPSCs retain a temporary epigenetic memory of their original somatic cells, which results in differential gene expression and altered differentiation potential. These findings have implications for the use of iPSCs in disease modeling and could be utilized to enhance the differentiation of iPSCs into desired cell lineages in potential therapeutic applications.

title: Spatiotemporal control of mitosis by the conserved spindle matrix protein Megator
text: The existence and functionality of a putative spindle matrix, which is believed to mediate chromosome motion, has been a subject of controversy. However, our report provides evidence that Megator (Mtor), the equivalent protein of the human nuclear pore complex protein translocated promoter region (Tpr) in Drosophila melanogaster, forms a conserved complex with the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) protein Mad2. This complex localizes to a nuclear derived spindle matrix in living cells. Through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments, we have observed that Mtor remains around spindle microtubules and exhibits distinct dynamic properties. Mtor/Tpr is responsible for recruiting Mad2 and Mps1, but not Mad1, to unattached kinetochores (KTs), thereby regulating normal mitotic duration and SAC response. During anaphase, Mtor also plays a role in spindle elongation, affecting proper chromosome movement. Our proposal suggests that Mtor/Tpr acts as a spatial regulator of the SAC, ensuring efficient recruitment of Mad2 to unattached KTs at the beginning of mitosis and facilitating proper spindle maturation. Additionally, the enrichment of Mad2 in a spindle matrix helps confine the effects of a diffusible "wait anaphase" signal to the vicinity of the spindle.

title: Randomized trial of folic acid supplementation and serum homocysteine levels.
text:
BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of folic acid supplementation on serum homocysteine levels and mortality from ischemic heart disease. While it is known that a dosage of 1 mg/d of folic acid can effectively reduce homocysteine levels, the effect of lower doses, which are relevant to food fortification, remains uncertain.

METHODS: A total of 151 patients with ischemic heart disease were randomly assigned to receive one of five dosages of folic acid (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 mg/d) or a placebo. Fasting blood samples were collected at the beginning of the study, after 3 months of supplementation, and 3 months after discontinuing folic acid use for analysis of serum homocysteine and serum folate levels.

RESULTS: The median serum homocysteine level decreased as the dosage of folic acid increased, reaching its maximum reduction at 0.8 mg/d, with a homocysteine reduction (adjusted for placebo) of 2.7 micromol/L (23%). This reduction was similar to the known effect of folic acid dosages of 1 mg/d and above. The response to folic acid was greater in individuals with higher initial serum homocysteine levels, but statistically significant reductions were observed regardless of the initial level. Serum folate levels increased linearly with folic acid dosage (5.5 nmol/L for every 0.1 mg of folic acid). Fluctuations in serum homocysteine levels over time, as observed in the placebo group, were larger than the effect of folic acid, making individual monitoring impractical.

CONCLUSIONS: A dosage of 0.8 mg/d of folic acid is necessary to achieve the maximum reduction in serum homocysteine levels across the population. The current levels of folic acid fortification in the US will only lead to a small reduction in homocysteine levels.

title: Adherens junctions in Drosophila retinal morphogenesis.
text: Animal morphogenesis is greatly influenced by adherens junctions and their core molecular components, known as classic cadherins. While the importance of cadherins in development is widely acknowledged, the precise mechanisms that regulate adherens junction function during morphogenesis are still being extensively studied. Adherens junctions play a crucial role in organizing simple cellular patterns, as well as facilitating more intricate cell shape changes and cell movements, which rely on the dynamic modulation of adherens junctions.

title: Multiple roles of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in skeletal development, growth, and repair.
text: This chapter explores the role of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in skeletal morphogenesis, discusses potential future research directions in this area, and highlights some challenges in the field. VEGF plays a crucial role in regulating osteoclastic differentiation, migration, and activity, making it a key player in the entire process. It is essential for osteoclastic activity during the establishment of the primary ossification center and later stages of bone growth. Numerous studies have identified VEGF as a critical factor for the survival of chondrocytes. Additionally, several factors involved in bone formation also induce the expression of VEGF in osteoblasts. These factors include prostaglandins E1 and E2, BMP-4, BMP-6, BMP-7, FGF-2, TGF-β, endothelin-1, IGF-1, and vitamin D3, which activate various signaling pathways to stimulate VEGF expression. Bone fractures can heal through two distinct processes, similar to the formation of bone during embryonic development. Stabilized fractures heal through intramembranous ossification, while unstable fractures undergo endochondral ossification. The resemblance between embryonic bone development and the repair of fractured bones, along with the presence of VEGF at fracture sites, suggests that VEGF is involved in bone repair, just as it is in bone development.

title: Effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after stroke (CLOTS trial 1): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial
text: The effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings (GCS) in reducing deep vein thrombosis (DVT) after stroke was assessed in a randomised controlled trial. A total of 2518 immobile patients admitted to hospital within 1 week of an acute stroke were enrolled from 64 centres in the UK, Italy, and Australia. They were randomly allocated to receive routine care plus thigh-length GCS or routine care without GCS. Compression Doppler ultrasound was performed on both legs at around 7-10 days and, when possible, again at 25-30 days after enrolment. The primary outcome was the occurrence of symptomatic or asymptomatic DVT in the popliteal or femoral veins. The study found that the use of thigh-length GCS did not significantly reduce the risk of DVT compared to avoiding their use. However, patients allocated to GCS had a higher incidence of skin breaks, ulcers, blisters, and skin necrosis. These findings suggest that the use of thigh-length GCS in patients with acute stroke admitted to hospital may not be beneficial. It is recommended that national stroke guidelines be reconsidered based on these results. The study was funded by the Medical Research Council (UK), Chief Scientist Office of Scottish Government, Chest Heart and Stroke Scotland, Tyco Healthcare (Covidien) USA, and UK Stroke Research Network.

title: Streptococcus pneumoniae early response genes to human lung epithelial cells
text:
The colonization of the host respiratory tract by Streptococcus pneumoniae infection involves interaction with host respiratory tract epithelial cells. In order to study the pneumococcal genes involved in the initial stage of interaction with host epithelial cells, we used TIGR (JCVI) microarray technology to investigate the transcriptional responses of an encapsulated pathogenic pneumococcal strain TIGR4 when exposed to human lung epithelial cells A549 for 0.5 hours and 1 hour. The gene expression changes were confirmed using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis.

Our findings revealed different transcriptional profiles at the two incubation time periods. Most gene expressions were down-regulated at 0.5 hours, but up-regulated at 1 hour. Genes associated with ribonucleotide biosynthesis were down-regulated at both time points, while genes associated with cell envelope, energy metabolism, transport, and protein synthesis were mostly up-regulated at 1 hour. We also compared these profiles to the transcriptomes of a TIGR4-derived strain exposed to human macrophages for the same time periods. We identified a set of genes that exhibited similar expression changes in response to both types of host cells, including cell envelope-associated genes bgaA (SP0648) and nanA (SP1693), as well as uncharacterized gene clusters such as SP1677-SP1680 and SP1688-SP1690.

In conclusion, our data suggests that during the early stage of interaction with host epithelial cells, there is a complex regulation and expression change in bacteria. Some of these genes may play a crucial role in pathogen-host interactions and the establishment of infection.

title: Proteomic identification of a novel isoform of collapsin response mediator protein-2 in spinal nerves peripheral to dorsal root ganglia.
text: We conducted a proteomic study to determine the polarity of primary afferent fibers, which originate from sensory cells in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and transmit external stimuli from the skin to the spinal cord. We dissected lumbar spinal nerve segments from 5-week-old Wistar rats and analyzed the lysates using large-sized 2-DE at pH 5-6. Out of approximately 800 protein spots detected in the central and peripheral fractions, we identified a unique spot in the peripheral fraction with a molecular weight of 60 kDa and an isoelectric point of 5.6. This spot was confirmed to be an isoform of collapsin response mediator protein-2 (CRMP-2) using MALDI-TOF MS and Western blots with anti-CRMP-2 antibodies. Specifically, the antibodies recognized residues 1-17 and 486-528 of CRMP-2. We named this novel spot periCRMP-2 because it was only detected in the peripheral fraction and not in the central fraction, DRG, or other brain regions. MS analyses did not detect the C-terminal fragment of CRMP-2 in periCRMP-2. Furthermore, the expression of periCRMP-2 decreased after sciatic nerve injury. These findings suggest that periCRMP-2 is a C-terminal truncated isoform that is polarized in the peripheral side of spinal nerves and may play a role in nerve degeneration and regeneration.

title: Empirical statistical estimates for sequence similarity searches
text: The FASTA package, a set of programs for comparing sequences, has been updated to accurately estimate statistical measures for local sequence similarity scores that include gaps. These estimates are obtained by using the extreme value distribution, which takes into account the average and variance of local similarity scores from unrelated sequences. Additionally, the scores are adjusted for the expected impact of the length of the library sequence. This approach allows for precise calculations of similarity scores for protein/protein, DNA/DNA, and protein/translated-DNA comparisons in both FASTA and Smith-Waterman algorithms. The accuracy of these statistical estimates has been evaluated for 54 protein families using FASTA and Smith-Waterman scores. The probability estimates derived from the distribution of similarity scores tend to be conservative, as do the probabilities calculated using the Altschul-Gish lambda, kappa, and eta parameters. To assess the effectiveness of different methods for correcting similarity scores based on library-sequence length, 54 protein superfamilies from the PIR39 database and 110 protein families from the Prosite/SwissProt rel. 34 database were examined. Both regression-scaled and Altschul-Gish scaled scores outperform unscaled Smith-Waterman or FASTA similarity scores. When using the Prosite/SwissProt test set, regression-scaled scores show slightly better performance, while Altschul-Gish scaled scores perform best with the PIR database. Consequently, length-corrected similarity scores enhance the sensitivity of database searches. Statistical parameters derived from the distribution of similarity scores from numerous unrelated sequences commonly encountered in a database search provide accurate estimates of statistical significance, enabling the inference of sequence homology.

title: Steroid hormone signalling links reproduction to lifespan in dietary-restricted Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Restricting one's diet has been found to increase the length of a healthy lifespan in various species, including primates. However, it is often accompanied by a decline in reproductive function. It is still unclear whether signals from the reproductive system play a role in the effects of dietary restriction on lifespan. In this study, we discovered that the expression of a specific enzyme called cytochrome P450 DAF-9/CYP450 and the production of a steroid hormone called Δ(7)-dafachronic acid (DA) are elevated in C. elegans worms that are subjected to dietary restriction. The hormone DA activates a non-traditional nuclear hormone receptor called NHR-8/NHR and a nutrient-responsive kinase called let-363/mTOR, both of which are crucial for the increased lifespan observed during dietary restriction. Additionally, steroid hormone signaling also affects the adaptability of the reproductive system in response to limited nutrients, and this adaptability is necessary for the extension of lifespan. These findings demonstrate that steroid hormone signaling connects the physiology of the reproductive system to lifespan when nutrients are scarce, and they establish a central role for let-363/mTOR in integrating signals from nutrients and steroid hormones.

title: Regulation and effects of hypothalamic galanin: relation to dietary fat, alcohol ingestion, circulating lipids and energy homeostasis.
text: Galanin (GAL) is a peptide that is known to stimulate feeding behavior. It has distinct properties and functions compared to other feeding stimulants like neuropeptide Y and agouti-related protein. GAL in the hypothalamus does not respond significantly to food deprivation, changes in corticosterone, glucose utilization, dietary carbohydrate, or leptin. This suggests that GAL is not essential when food is scarce or when low-energy, high-carbohydrate diets are consumed. However, recent evidence indicates that GAL in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) plays a role in relation to dietary fat and alcohol. Specifically, it mediates functions that help animals adapt to conditions of positive energy balance involving excessive consumption of these nutrients. GAL in the PVN is stimulated by a high-fat diet and alcohol. It is also stimulated by an increase in circulating lipids caused by consuming a fat-rich meal or alcohol. GAL levels rise during the middle of the active feeding cycle, when fat consumption and triglycerides naturally increase. When GAL is injected into the PVN, it increases the consumption of food and alcohol. Additionally, it produces a significantly stronger feeding response in rats maintained on a fat-rich diet, which also promotes alcohol intake. This evidence supports the existence of non-homeostatic, positive feedback circuits between GAL and both dietary fat and alcohol. These circuits are believed to contribute to larger meal sizes, excessive alcohol consumption, and obesity that are commonly associated with fat-rich foods.

title: Evidence-based interventions for improvement of maternal and child nutrition: what can be done and at what cost?
text:
Maternal malnutrition is a significant factor in the deaths of 800,000 newborns each year due to babies being born small for their gestational age. Additionally, nearly 3.1 million child deaths annually are attributed to stunting, wasting, and deficiencies in essential nutrients. However, progress has been made in implementing interventions on a large scale, and the evidence supporting the effectiveness of nutrition interventions and delivery strategies has grown since The Lancet Series on Maternal and Child Undernutrition in 2008.

To provide an updated assessment of interventions addressing undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies in women and children, we conducted a comprehensive analysis using standard methods to evaluate emerging evidence for delivery platforms. We also modeled the impact on lives saved and the cost of these interventions in the 34 countries where 90% of the world's children with stunted growth reside. Additionally, we examined the effects of different delivery platforms and options, including the use of community health workers to engage impoverished populations and promote behavior change, as well as access and uptake of interventions.

Our analysis indicates that by ensuring populations have access to ten evidence-based nutrition interventions with 90% coverage, the current number of deaths in children under five years old can be reduced by 15%. Furthermore, providing access to and increasing the use of iodized salt can alleviate iodine deficiency and improve health outcomes. By improving access in this manner, it is possible to avert approximately one-fifth of the existing burden of stunting. The estimated additional annual cost for scaling up access to these ten direct nutrition interventions in the 34 focus countries is Int$9.6 billion.

Continued investment in nutrition-specific interventions, focusing on community engagement and delivery strategies that reach the most vulnerable segments of the population, can have a significant impact on averting maternal and child undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies. Furthermore, linking improved access to nutrition-sensitive approaches such as women's empowerment, agriculture, food systems, education, employment, social protection, and safety nets can greatly accelerate progress in countries with the highest burden of maternal and child undernutrition and mortality.

title: FGF regulates TGF-β signaling and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition via control of let-7 miRNA expression.
text:
The regulation of normal endothelial function is not well understood, but it is crucial for various aspects of blood vessel function. In this study, we demonstrate that when the baseline fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling to the endothelium is disrupted, there is a significant decrease in let-7 miRNA levels. This decrease in let-7 miRNA levels leads to an increase in the expression of transforming growth factor (TGF)-β ligands and receptors, as well as the activation of TGF-β signaling. Consequently, this leads to a process called endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Endo-MT). 

Furthermore, we have discovered that Endo-MT plays a significant role in the formation of neointima in a murine transplant arteriopathy model and in the rejection of human transplant lesions. The decrease in FGF signaling input in endothelial cells is a result of the development of an FGF resistance state. This state is characterized by a reduction in the expression and activation of key components of the FGF signaling cascade, which is dependent on inflammation.

These findings highlight the critical role of FGF signaling in maintaining endothelial homeostasis and reveal an unexpected involvement of Endo-MT in vascular pathology.

title: Nuclear Receptors, RXR, and the Big Bang
text: The isolation of genes that encode receptors for steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and thyroid hormone, along with their analysis of structure and function, has revealed a template for nuclear hormone receptors that is conserved throughout evolution. This groundbreaking discovery led to the identification of numerous genes that encode related proteins, known as orphan receptors. The study of these orphan receptors, particularly the retinoid X receptor (RXR), has placed nuclear receptors at the forefront of molecular endocrinology. In this review, we offer a personal perspective on nuclear receptors and delve into their interconnected and coordinated signaling networks, which are crucial for the existence of multicellular life. We specifically focus on the RXR heterodimer, its associated ligands, and its transcriptional mechanism.

title: A genome-wide short hairpin RNA screening of jurkat T-cells for human proteins contributing to productive HIV-1 replication.
