text: The use of short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to inhibit the replication of HIV-1 has faced challenges due to a high mutation rate in targeted viral sequences and cytotoxicity when cellular genes are suppressed. In order to identify cellular proteins that play a role in HIV-1 replication and can be silenced without causing significant harm, we utilized a shRNA library that targets 54,509 human transcripts. This library was used to generate a diverse population of Jurkat T-cell clones, each expressing a specific shRNA. These Jurkat clones were then infected with HIV-1. The clones that survived the viral infection were considered to have silenced a human mRNA necessary for virus replication, without causing cytotoxicity. In total, we identified 252 individual Jurkat mRNAs that fit this criteria. Out of these, 22 mRNAs were further confirmed for their contributions to HIV-1 replication. We focused on five specific mRNAs, NRF1, STXBP2, NCOA3, PRDM2, and EXOSC5, and studied their impact on different stages of the HIV-1 life cycle. We also compared our findings from the shRNA-based screening in Jurkat T-cells with results from other researchers who used siRNA-based screenings in HeLa or 293T cells, discussing the similarities and differences between the two approaches.

title: UNR facilitates the interaction of MLE with the lncRNA roX2 during Drosophila dosage compensation.
text: The process of dosage compensation ensures a balanced expression of X-chromosomal genes in males (XY) and females (XX). In Drosophila, this process involves non-coding RNAs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) with unknown functions. Our study reveals that the Drosophila RBP UNR plays a role in directing the activating male-specific-lethal complex to the X-chromosome. UNR facilitates the interaction between two important subunits, the RNA helicase MLE and the long non-coding RNA roX2.

title: BMP/SMAD1 signaling sets a threshold for the left/right pathway in lateral plate mesoderm and limits availability of SMAD4.
text: Bistability in developmental pathways refers to the ability to produce either of two distinct outcomes from inputs that vary in intensity or consistency. The establishment of signaling thresholds is crucial for achieving bistability. In the development of the left/right (LR) axis in vertebrate embryos, the expression of a transforming growth factor beta (TGFbeta) member called NODAL in the left lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) is regulated by complex feed-forward and feedback loops, resulting in a bistable pattern. In this study, we present evidence that the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)/SMAD1 signaling pathway establishes a repressive threshold in the LPM, which is necessary for the proper functioning of LR signaling. When Smad1, a key component of the BMP/SMAD1 pathway, was conditionally deleted in the LPM, the LR pathway was prematurely and bilaterally activated. This bilateral activation was attributed to the expression of NODAL from both the left and right sides of the node, indicating that the mutant LPM was sensitive to noisy input from the LR system. In vitro experiments demonstrated that BMP signaling inhibits the activation of the NODAL pathway and the formation of the SMAD2/4-FOXH1 transcriptional complex downstream of NODAL. However, the inhibitory effect of BMP signaling was reversed by overexpression of SMAD4. In embryos, elevated levels of SMAD4 in the right LPM strongly activated LR gene expression, but this effect was counteracted by superactivated BMP signaling. In conclusion, our findings suggest that BMP/SMAD1 signaling establishes a bilateral, repressive threshold for NODAL-dependent activation in the LPM, thereby limiting the availability of SMAD4. This repressive threshold is essential for achieving the bistable output of the LR system.

title: Human Macrophages Infected with a High Burden of ESAT-6-Expressing M. tuberculosis Undergo Caspase-1- and Cathepsin B-Independent Necrosis
text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infects lung macrophages, which instead of killing the pathogen, can be influenced by the bacteria to create an environment suitable for replication and spreading to nearby cells. The impact of host cell death during Mtb infection is a topic of debate because the bacteria have been shown to have both anti-apoptotic properties, keeping the host cell alive to avoid the antimicrobial effects of apoptosis, and pro-necrotic properties, killing the host macrophage to facilitate infection of neighboring cells. Since mycobacteria activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, we investigated whether Mtb could induce two types of cell death modes, pyroptosis and pyronecrosis, which are linked to the inflammasome. These cell death modes are mediated through caspase-1 and cathepsin-B, respectively. We infected human monocyte-derived macrophages with virulent Mtb (H37Rv) at different levels of infection. A higher level of infection resulted in a significantly increased release of IL-1β, while a lower level of infection did not trigger an IL-1β response. We collected the infected macrophages and assessed their cell viability by examining the integrity of DNA, mitochondria, and the plasma membrane. We discovered that infection with H37Rv at a high level of infection, but not at a low level, over a period of two days led to extensive DNA fragmentation, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, loss of plasma membrane integrity, and release of HMGB1. Although we observed plasma membrane permeabilization and IL-1β release from infected cells, the cell death induced by Mtb was not reliant on caspase-1 or cathepsin B. However, it did depend on the mycobacterial expression of ESAT-6. In conclusion, when virulent Mtb reaches a certain number of bacteria inside the human macrophage, ESAT-6-dependent necrosis occurs, activating caspase-1 in the process.

title: Differentiation of Human Induced-Pluripotent Stem Cells into Smooth-Muscle Cells: Two Novel Protocols
text: The current methods for differentiating human induced-pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into smooth-muscle cells (SMCs) are not very effective and often do not produce cells with the desired SMC phenotype (either contractile or synthetic SMCs). In this study, we introduce two new protocols for differentiating hiPSCs into SMCs, one that primarily yields contractile SMCs and another that primarily yields synthetic SMCs. Flow cytometry analysis showed that approximately 45% of the cells obtained using each protocol exhibited an SMC phenotype, and these populations could be further purified to about 95% using metabolic selection. Examination of cellular mRNA and protein levels revealed that the expression of smooth-muscle actin (SMA), myosin heavy chain II, collagen 1, calponin, transgelin, connexin 43, and vimentin in the SMCs generated using the Contractile SMC protocol and the traditional protocol were similar. However, SMCs produced using the Synthetic SMC protocol showed lower levels of calponin, higher levels of collagen 1, and higher levels of connexin 43. Functional assessments of the two SMC populations also revealed differences: Contractile SMCs exhibited a greater decline in two-dimensional surface area (to 12% of the original size) in response to carbachol treatment, while Synthetic SMCs showed increased cell migration and proliferation. Overall, these findings demonstrate that our new differentiation protocols can effectively generate SMCs from hiPSCs.

title: Conserved Histone Variant H2A.Z Protects Euchromatin from the Ectopic Spread of Silent Heterochromatin
text: Boundary elements impede the propagation of heterochromatin, although these locations do not fully explain the preservation of neighboring euchromatin. The histone variant H2A.Z (known as Htz1 in yeast) replaces conventional H2A in numerous nucleosomes. Analysis using microarrays demonstrated that genes activated by HTZ1 tend to cluster near telomeres. The decreased expression of most of these genes in htz1Delta cells was reversed when SIR2 (sir2Delta) was deleted, suggesting that H2A.Z counteracts telomeric silencing. Other genes activated by Htz1 are situated adjacent to the silent HMR mating-type locus. Their dependence on Htz1 can be bypassed by sir2Delta or by deleting the silencing initiation sites in HMR. In htz1Delta cells, Sir2 and Sir3 extend into neighboring euchromatic regions, resulting in alterations in histone H4 acetylation and H3 4-methylation, which indicate the formation of ectopic heterochromatin. Htz1 is concentrated in these euchromatic regions and collaborates with a boundary element to prevent the spread of heterochromatin. Therefore, both euchromatin and heterochromatin possess components that counteract the transition to the opposite chromatin state.

title: COMMD proteins, a novel family of structural and functional homologs of MURR1.
text:
We have made an exciting discovery regarding a protein called MURR1. MURR1 is a versatile protein that has the ability to inhibit a transcription factor called nuclear factor kappaB (NF-kappaB). NF-kappaB is involved in various important processes such as innate and adaptive immunity, apoptosis, cell cycle regulation, and oncogenesis. 

In our research, we have identified a new group of proteins that share similarities with MURR1. These proteins form complexes made up of multiple units and were found through a biochemical screening process looking for factors associated with MURR1. 

This group of proteins is characterized by a unique and conserved motif called the COMM (copper metabolism gene MURR1) domain. This domain serves as a platform for interactions between proteins. Similar to MURR1, some of these proteins also have the ability to associate with and inhibit NF-kappaB. 

These proteins, known as COMMD or COMM domain containing 1-10, are highly conserved in multicellular eukaryotic organisms. They represent a new family of proteins that share both structural and functional similarities with MURR1. 

The prototype of this protein family, MURR1/COMMD1, suppresses NF-kappaB activity not by affecting its movement into the nucleus or its binding to specific DNA sequences. Instead, it operates within the nucleus by influencing the interaction between NF-kappaB and chromatin.

title: Occurrence of chromosome 9 and p53 alterations in multifocal dysplasia and carcinoma in situ of human urinary bladder
text: The aim of this study was to examine the genetic alterations in flat urothelial lesions, specifically carcinoma in situ (CIS) and moderate dysplasias (DII), in the two chromosomal regions most commonly affected in bladder cancer. A total of 33 CIS and 16 DII samples from 21 patients were analyzed using microdissection of the urothelium. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was performed using gene locus probes for 9q22 (FACC), 9p21 (CDK), 17p13 (p53), and centromeric probes on interphase nuclei. Additionally, DNA from these samples was used for loss of heterozygosity (LOH) analysis and sequencing of exons 5-9 of p53. The results showed similar deletion frequencies for chromosomes 9 and 17 in CIS (chromosome 9, 86%; p53, 84%). DII had a lower deletion rate compared to CIS (chromosome 9, 75%; p53, 53%). There was a strong correlation between the results of FISH and LOH analyses. p53 mutations were found in 12 out of 15 patients (CIS, 72%; DII, 67%). In three out of 16 patients with multifocal tumors, LOH analysis identified oligoclonal lesions, which was supported by p53 sequencing revealing two different p53 deletions in two cases. In conclusion, the findings suggest that chromosome 9 deletions are not specific to papillary growth, as they are present in both types of flat urothelial lesions associated with papillary tumors and those that are not. The similar distribution and lower number of genetic changes in DII suggest that DII may be a precursor lesion of CIS.

title: Fresh meat and further processing characteristics of ham muscles from finishing pigs fed ractopamine hydrochloride.
text: Ractopamine hydrochloride (RAC) has consistently been found to improve the cutting yields of finishing pigs' carcasses and is commonly used as a feed additive in US finishing pig diets. However, there is limited knowledge about the impact of RAC on the characteristics of further processed products. Some studies have shown that pigs fed RAC have higher ultimate pH levels in their LM, which could potentially affect the characteristics of processed hams, such as protein interaction and texture. The aim of this study was to investigate whether RAC-fed pigs produce hams with higher ultimate pH levels and, if so, whether this advantage improves the texture and water retention of the processed hams. Two hundred hams from barrows and gilts that were fed either RAC or control diets were selected based on their HCW. The hams were divided into 5 separate pieces to determine cutting yields, and the ultimate pH of 6 different muscles was evaluated. The hams were then processed to make cured and smoked hams. The results showed that Ractopamine increased the cutting yields of the whole ham, inside, outside, and knuckle when expressed as a percentage of the chilled side weight (P < 0.0001, P < 0.01, P < 0.01, and P < 0.01, respectively). The ultimate pH levels of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and semitendinosus muscles were all 0.06 pH units higher (P < 0.05), the biceps femoris was 0.04 pH units higher (P = 0.02), and the semimembranosus and adductor muscles were 0.03 pH units higher in pigs fed 7.4 mg/kg of RAC compared to control pigs. The cured hams from RAC-fed pigs were heavier at all stages of production. However, there were no differences in binding strengths (P = 0.88) or protein fat-free values (P = 0.13) between RAC and control hams. In conclusion, Ractopamine increased cutting yields, the total weight of cured hams, and the ultimate pH of the muscles. It can be used in pig diets to achieve growth advantages and cutting yields without affecting the characteristics of further processed hams.

title: Translocated LPS Might Cause Endotoxin Tolerance in Circulating Monocytes of Cystic Fibrosis Patients
text: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a hereditary disease with multiple effects that occur due to abnormalities in the gene codes of a chloride channel. CF patients often have chronic lung infections caused by various pathogens, but cases of bacteraemia are rare in this condition. Additionally, CF patients' circulating monocytes exhibit a clear state of Endotoxin Tolerance (ET), as they show a significant decrease in the inflammatory response to bacterial stimuli. Despite previous research on this phenomenon, the exact cause of ET in CF patients remains unknown. In this study, we investigated the potential role of microbial/endotoxin translocation from a localized infection to the bloodstream as a possible cause of ET induction in CF patients. Analysis of plasma from fourteen CF patients revealed high levels of LPS compared to healthy volunteers and patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. In vitro experiments demonstrated that the concentrations of endotoxin found in CF patients' plasma were sufficient to induce an ET phenotype in monocytes from healthy individuals. Consistent with clinical data, we did not detect bacterial DNA in CF plasma. Our findings suggest that soluble endotoxin present in the bloodstream of CF patients leads to endotoxin tolerance in their circulating monocytes.

title: Effect of mammographic screening from age 40 years on breast cancer mortality in the UK Age trial at 17 years' follow-up: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
The effectiveness and timing of mammographic screening for different age groups is a topic of debate. The UK Age trial aimed to compare the impact of annual mammographic screening starting at age 40 versus age 50 on breast cancer mortality. The initial results after 10 years of follow-up showed no significant difference in mortality between the two groups. In this study, we present the findings after 17 years of follow-up.

Women aged 39-41 from 23 UK NHS Breast Screening Programme units were randomly assigned to either the intervention group (offered annual screening until their 48th birthday) or the control group (usual medical care with screening starting at age 50 and every 3 years thereafter). Both groups were categorized by general practice. We analyzed breast cancer incidence and mortality based on the time since randomization. The study included all women who could be traced with the National Health Service Central Register and who were alive and residing in the country at the time of entry. The primary outcomes measured were breast cancer mortality (deaths with breast cancer as the underlying cause) and breast cancer incidence (including in-situ, invasive, and total cases). We also examined the timing of the mortality effect by analyzing the results in different follow-up periods. The trial is registered under the number ISRCTN24647151.

Between October 14, 1990, and September 25, 1997, a total of 160,921 participants were randomly assigned, with 53,883 women in the intervention group and 106,953 in the control group included in this analysis. After a median follow-up of 17 years, the rate ratio for breast cancer mortality was 0.88 (95% CI 0.74-1.04) for tumors diagnosed during the intervention phase. We observed a significant reduction in breast cancer mortality in the intervention group compared to the control group during the first 10 years after diagnosis (RR 0.75, 0.58-0.97), but no significant difference thereafter (RR 1.02, 0.80-1.30) for tumors diagnosed during the intervention phase. The overall breast cancer incidence during the 17-year follow-up was similar between the intervention and control groups (RR 0.98, 0.93-1.04).

Our findings support the early reduction in breast cancer mortality with annual mammography screening for women aged 40-49. However, further data is needed to fully understand the long-term effects. Cumulative incidence figures suggest a small possibility of overdiagnosis. This study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research Health Technology Assessment program and the American Cancer Society, with past funding received from the Medical Research Council, Cancer Research UK, the UK Department of Health, and the US National Cancer Institute.

title: Concordance, disease progression, and heritability of coeliac disease in Italian twins.
text:
The aim of this study was to use the twin method to determine the genetic and environmental factors contributing to susceptibility to coeliac disease (CD). The researchers recruited 23 monozygotic (MZ) and 50 dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs, with at least one twin affected by CD, from the Italian Twin Registry and the Italian Coeliac Disease Association. Zygosity was determined using DNA fingerprinting, and HLA-DQ and DR alleles were genotyped. Disease status was confirmed through antibody testing and bowel biopsy. 

The results showed a higher concordance rate for CD in MZ twin pairs (83.3% probandwise, 71.4% pairwise) compared to DZ twin pairs (16.7% probandwise, 9.1% pairwise). The concordance rate was not influenced by the sex or HLA genotype of the co-twin, but being MZ was significantly associated with the occurrence of CD. In 90% of concordant pairs, the time of discordance was within two years. Within five years, MZ co-twins had a 70% cumulative probability of having symptomatic CD, while DZ co-twins had a 9% probability. Using ACE models, the heritability estimates for CD were 87% and 57% for populations with prevalences of 1/91 and 1/1000, respectively. 

In conclusion, MZ twin pairs have a high likelihood of being concordant for CD, regardless of sex or HLA genotype. Most affected co-twins receive a diagnosis within two years. Genetic factors account for a significant proportion of the phenotypic variance in CD.

title: A literature review of the safety of medical body area network devices in magnetic resonance imaging
text: Modern life includes the presence of electro-magnetic fields and wireless technology. In healthcare, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) machines are increasingly used to examine internal human structures and functions. As wireless devices continue to rapidly develop and become smaller, they are also being used as clinical tools, creating an expanding intersection between these technologies. While safety standards for devices in MRI machines have been previously established, it is uncertain whether newer wireless technologies, particularly those used in Medical Body Area Networks (MBAN), have undergone rigorous testing or disclosure. To investigate this issue, we conducted a review of the clinical scientific literature and the adverse events database of the United States Food and Drug Administration. Our findings indicate that there are currently no published studies specifically addressing the safety of wireless devices potentially used in MBAN within MRI machines. Therefore, we propose the inclusion of a research track to assess the safety of MBAN devices in MRI machines. By designing MBAN components, devices, and systems with informed knowledge, we can prevent potential adverse events for patients resulting from the unintended consequences of using these technologies concurrently in MRI machines.

title: Synaptic glutamate release by ventromedial hypothalamic neurons is part of the neurocircuitry that prevents hypoglycemia.
text: The significance of neuropeptides in the hypothalamus has been established through experimental research. However, the roles of the fast-acting neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA are largely unknown due to difficulties in assessing their function in living organisms. The transporters responsible for vesicular uptake and release of neurotransmitters, VGLUTs for glutamate and VGAT for GABA, play a crucial role in this process. Glutamatergic neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) primarily express VGLUT2. To investigate the impact of glutamate release from VMH neurons, we created mice that lack VGLUT2 specifically in SF1 neurons, a major subset of VMH neurons. These mice experience hypoglycemia during fasting because their ability to increase the glucose-raising pancreatic hormone glucagon and induce the production of PGC-1alpha and gluconeogenic enzymes PEPCK and G6Pase in the liver is impaired. Additionally, these mice exhibit defective counterregulatory responses to insulin-induced hypoglycemia and 2-deoxyglucose, an antimetabolite. Therefore, glutamate release from VMH neurons plays a crucial role in the neurocircuitry that prevents hypoglycemia.

title: c-Src and cooperating partners in human cancer.
text: The c-src proto-oncogene is not commonly mutated in human cancers, and when it is overexpressed in normal cells, it has little or weak cancer-causing effects. These findings have led to doubts about the role of c-src in the development of human tumors. However, recent research has demonstrated that c-Src, a type of non-receptor tyrosine kinase, has increased levels and activity in various types of human cancers. Additionally, it has been discovered that c-Src plays a crucial role in multiple signaling pathways that control cell growth, survival, spread, and the formation of new blood vessels. Due to its significant involvement in these cancer-promoting processes, c-Src represents a promising target for therapeutic intervention.

title: Type 1 diabetes-associated IL2RA variation lowers IL-2 signaling and contributes to diminished CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cell function.
text: Multiple studies have shown that individuals with various autoimmune diseases, including type 1 diabetes, have CD4(+)CD25(+) regulatory T cells (Tregs) that are deficient in their ability to control proinflammatory responses compared to healthy individuals. This Treg dysfunction could be a primary cause or a result of immune system disturbances during disease development. Polymorphisms in genes related to Treg function, such as IL2RA, increase the risk of autoimmune disease. However, the connection between IL2RA gene polymorphisms and Treg function has not been investigated. To address this, we examined the impact of an IL2RA haplotype associated with type 1 diabetes on Treg fitness and suppressive function. Our studies were conducted using healthy individuals to avoid any effects of disease. We found that the presence of an autoimmune disease-associated IL2RA haplotype is linked to reduced IL-2 responsiveness in CD4(+) T cells that have encountered antigens, as indicated by decreased phosphorylation of STAT5a. Additionally, this haplotype is associated with lower levels of FOXP3 expression in Tregs and a decrease in their ability to suppress the proliferation of autologous effector T cells. These findings provide insight into the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which polymorphisms in the IL-2RA gene impact immune regulation and susceptibility to autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cells and other hematopoietic cells show broad resistance to chemotherapeutic agents in vivo when overexpressing bcl-2.
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to investigate the impact of bcl-2 overexpression on resistance to chemotherapeutic agents in a transgenic mouse system, allowing for the examination of various cell populations, including rare hematopoietic stem cells (HSC). 

Methods: H2K-bcl-2 transgenic mice and wild-type (WT) mice were treated with different chemotherapeutic agents (5-fluoruracil, cyclophosphamide, and busulfan) to assess the influence of increased bcl-2 levels on their response. Flow cytometry was used to enumerate the populations of cells. HSC were further analyzed through FACS purification and in vivo reconstitution assays, while resistance was confirmed through short-term proliferation assays with varying concentrations of chemotherapeutic agents in vitro. 

Results: Overexpression of bcl-2 provided protection to multiple cell types, although the level of protection varied among different populations and agents. However, even the sensitive populations in transgenic mice returned to their pre-treatment levels faster. Additionally, bcl-2 overexpression prevented significant changes in HSC following 5-FU treatment, such as downregulation of c-kit, upregulation of Lin, and less efficient long-term reconstitution. In vitro studies directly demonstrated increased resistance of bcl-2 overexpressing HSC to chemotherapeutic agents. 

Conclusions: Increased expression of bcl-2 in HSC and their progeny conferred broad resistance to chemotherapeutic agents. The ability to differentially regulate the sensitivity to apoptosis of bystander and tumor cells has significant clinical implications.

title: Direct sensing of systemic and nutritional signals by hematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila
text:
The Drosophila lymph gland is an organ responsible for producing blood cells. It contains progenitor cells that are similar to the common myeloid progenitor found in mammals. These progenitor cells multiply and develop into three types of mature cells: plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and lamellocytes. These mature cells have functions that resemble mammalian myeloid cells. 

During the early stages of larval development, the lymph gland only contains progenitor cells. However, in the later stages, the gland has a medial region called the medullary zone where the progenitor cells are located. The maturing blood cells are found in a peripheral region known as the cortical zone. Additionally, there is a group of cells called the posterior signalling centre that acts as a niche for blood cell production. 

Similar to mammalian myeloid cells, Drosophila blood cells respond to various stresses such as hypoxia, infection, and oxidative stress. However, the mechanisms by which myeloid progenitors sense systemic signals to determine their fate have not been well understood. 

In this study, we demonstrate that the haematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila are directly influenced by systemic signals, such as insulin, and nutritional signals, such as essential amino acids. These signals help maintain the progenitor cells by promoting Wingless signaling (WNT signaling in mammals). We anticipate that this research will encourage further investigation into the direct signal sensing mechanisms of mammalian myeloid progenitors.

title: Regulation of autophagy by cytoplasmic p53
text: Autophagy can be triggered by various cellular stressors, such as the activation of the tumor suppressor p53. In this study, we demonstrate that the removal, reduction, or inhibition of p53 can induce autophagy in human, mouse, and nematode cells that have undergone knockout, knockdown, or pharmacological inhibition of p53. This enhanced autophagy promotes the survival of p53-deficient cancer cells in conditions of low oxygen and nutrient scarcity, enabling them to maintain high levels of ATP. Interestingly, autophagy was observed in cells lacking a nucleus, and it was found that cytoplasmic p53, rather than nuclear p53, can suppress the heightened autophagy in p53-deficient cells. Additionally, various autophagy inducers, such as starvation, rapamycin, and toxins affecting the endoplasmic reticulum, were found to promote the degradation of p53 through the proteasome pathway, which relies on the E3 ubiquitin ligase HDM2. Preventing the degradation of p53 inhibited the activation of autophagy in multiple cell lines in response to different stimuli. These findings provide evidence of a crucial signaling pathway that connects autophagy to the dysregulation of p53, which is commonly associated with cancer.

title: The Neurobiology of Sleep: Genetics, cellular physiology and subcortical networks
text: In order to understand the neural basis of sleep, it is crucial to examine this common behavior in mammals from various biological perspectives. At the molecular level, the circadian rhythm of sleep involves a complex interplay of positive and negative feedback mechanisms among circadian genes and their protein products in cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus. These cells are influenced by light and adjust accordingly to the surrounding conditions. The circadian information is then combined with information about the body's sleep needs in the nuclei of the anterior hypothalamus. These nuclei interact with arousal systems in the posterior hypothalamus, basal forebrain, and brainstem to regulate the onset of sleep. Once asleep, a rhythmic oscillator in the mesopontine junction controls the alternating patterns of rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM sleep. Throughout the sleep cycles, various neuromodulatory influences on forebrain structures impact behavior, consciousness, and cognition.

title: Suppression of intestinal neoplasia by deletion of Dnmt3b
text: Abnormal gene silencing, accompanied by DNA methylation, is linked to the progression of tumors that also exhibit a widespread loss of DNA methylation. By deactivating the de novo methyltransferase Dnmt3b in Apc(Min/+) mice under specific conditions, we have demonstrated that the absence of Dnmt3b does not affect the formation of microadenomas, which are considered the earliest stage of intestinal tumor development. However, we did observe a significant reduction in the formation of visible colonic adenomas. Interestingly, several large adenomas displayed regions where Dnmt3b was deactivated, indicating that Dnmt3b is necessary for the initial growth of visible adenomas but not for their maintenance. These findings support the idea that Dnmt3b plays a role in the transition phase between microadenoma formation and the growth of visible colonic tumors. Furthermore, our results suggest that Dnmt3b, and consequently de novo methylation, is not essential for sustaining tumor growth once this transition phase has occurred.

title: Epithelium-intrinsic NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome drives infected enterocyte expulsion to restrict Salmonella replication in the intestinal mucosa.
text: The gut lining separates the host from the microbiota, but certain harmful bacteria like Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm) can invade and break through this barrier. We still don't fully understand how the body defends against these sudden attacks. To investigate this, we used a mouse model of Salmonella enterocolitis to study how the body limits the amount of bacteria in the gut lining during early infection. Initially, the invading S.Tm bacteria replicate within the gut lining, but they are eventually expelled into the gut lumen by infected cells. This expulsion mechanism is compromised when certain components of the inflammasome (NAIP1-6, NLRC4, caspase-1/-11) are deleted or specifically removed from the gut lining. As a result, the amount of bacteria within the gut lining increases by about 100 times, and the bacteria spread to the lymph nodes more quickly. Interestingly, the cytokines interleukin (IL)-1α/β and IL-18, which are produced when the inflammasome is activated, do not seem to play a role in restricting early infection within the gut lining. These findings show that the inflammasome within the gut lining is responsible for expelling infected cells and limiting the bacteria's growth within the gut lining. This mechanism may be a general defense against infections in the gut.

title: GEMC1 is a TopBP1 interacting protein required for chromosomal DNA replication
text: Unicellular eukaryotes have provided valuable insights into the factors necessary for chromosomal DNA replication. However, our understanding of this process in multicellular organisms remains limited. In this study, we introduce a newly discovered protein called GEMC1 (geminin coiled-coil containing protein 1), which is essential for chromosomal DNA replication in vertebrates. GEMC1 is highly conserved among vertebrates and is predominantly expressed in actively dividing cells. Through experiments using Xenopus laevis egg extract, we demonstrate that Xenopus GEMC1 (xGEMC1) interacts with the checkpoint and replication factor TopBP1, facilitating the binding of xGEMC1 to chromatin during the formation of pre-replication complexes (pre-RCs). We also show that xGEMC1 directly interacts with replication factors such as Cdc45 and the kinase Cdk2-CyclinE, resulting in extensive phosphorylation of xGEMC1. Phosphorylated xGEMC1 promotes the initiation of DNA replication, while depletion of GEMC1 prevents the onset of DNA replication by hindering the loading of Cdc45 onto chromatin. Furthermore, inhibiting GEMC1 expression using morpholino and siRNA oligos prevents DNA replication in both embryonic and somatic vertebrate cells. These findings suggest that GEMC1 plays a crucial role in initiating chromosomal DNA replication in multicellular organisms by facilitating the recruitment of Cdc45 onto replication origins through interactions with TopBP1 and Cdk2.

title: Does an arthroscopic suture bridge technique maintain repair integrity?: a serial evaluation by ultrasonography.
text: The suture bridge technique has been shown in biomechanical studies to improve contact area, strength, and pressure on the rotator cuff tendon footprint. Based on these findings, we aimed to investigate several aspects: (1) the success rate of the suture bridge technique in maintaining cuff integrity after surgery, (2) changes in the repaired cuff over time, (3) whether preoperative factors could predict postoperative cuff integrity, and (4) the impact of retears on pain, function, range of motion, and muscle strength compared to intact repairs. We conducted a prospective study on 78 patients who underwent arthroscopic repairs using the suture bridge technique. The integrity of the rotator cuff repair was assessed using ultrasonography at 4.5 and 12 months post-surgery. At 4.5 months, 91% of patients had intact cuffs, and this was maintained at the 12-month follow-up. Failure rates varied depending on tear size, with massive tears having the highest rate at 17.6%. Preoperative fatty degeneration of the supraspinatus muscle was found to strongly predict cuff integrity. There was no significant correlation between cuff integrity and clinical outcomes, except for a temporary decrease in abduction strength at 6 months. In conclusion, arthroscopic repair using the suture bridge technique can achieve a low retear rate in rotator cuff tears, and the occurrence of retear does not impact the overall outcome. This study is classified as Level IV evidence according to the Guidelines for Authors.

title: Widespread and tissue specific age-related DNA methylation changes in mice.
text: Abnormal methylation of promoter CpG islands in cancer is linked to the suppression of tumor-suppressor genes. Additionally, age-related hypermethylation in seemingly normal mucosa may increase the risk of colon cancer in humans. However, it remains unclear whether this age-related DNA methylation phenomenon is exclusive to human tissues. To investigate this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of DNA methylation in the promoter regions of aging mouse intestines using methylated CpG island amplification and microarray analysis. By comparing 3-month-old and 35-month-old C57BL/6 mice, we identified 774 (21%) genes that exhibited increased methylation and 466 (13%) genes that showed decreased methylation. To validate these findings, we employed pyrosequencing and confirmed linear age-related methylation changes in all 12 genomic regions examined. Subsequently, we assessed age-related methylation in 11 genomic loci in other tissues. Among these loci, three out of 11 displayed similar changes in the lung, seven out of 11 changed in the liver, and six out of 11 changed in the spleen, albeit to a lesser extent than in the colon. Notably, there was partial conservation between age-related hypermethylation in human and mouse intestines, and the hypermethylated genes were enriched with Polycomb targets in embryonic stem cells. Our findings reveal a surprisingly high occurrence of hyper- and hypomethylation in normal mouse small intestine tissues as a result of aging, with a strong tissue-specificity to the process. Consequently, we conclude that epigenetic deregulation is a common characteristic of aging in mammals.

title: Environmental and economic costs of soil erosion and conservation benefits.
text: Soil erosion poses a significant risk to the long-term viability and productivity of agriculture, thereby endangering the environment. Over the past four decades, approximately 30% of the world's arable land has been lost due to erosion, and this trend persists with an annual loss of over 10 million hectares. Moreover, as the global population grows by a quarter of a million individuals daily, the demand for food is escalating, while the per capita food productivity is starting to decline.

title: Association between influenza vaccination and cardiovascular outcomes in high-risk patients: a meta-analysis.
text:
IMPORTANCE Recent influenza-like infections have been linked to fatal and nonfatal cardiovascular events, making it important to investigate whether influenza vaccination can prevent such events. 

OBJECTIVES This study aimed to determine the association between influenza vaccination and prevention of cardiovascular events. 

DATA SOURCES AND STUDY SELECTION The researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials comparing influenza vaccine to placebo or control in high-risk cardiovascular disease patients. They searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library Central Register of Controlled Trials for relevant studies. 

DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS Two investigators independently extracted data on trial design, patient characteristics, outcomes, and safety events from published manuscripts and unpublished supplemental data. High-quality studies were defined as those with appropriate randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and follow-up. 

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The researchers calculated risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using random-effects Mantel-Haenszel analysis for composite cardiovascular events, cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and individual cardiovascular events. They also conducted subgroup analyses based on patients with and without a history of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) within the past year. 

RESULTS The study included five published and one unpublished randomized clinical trials involving 6735 patients. The mean age of the patients was 67 years, with 51.3% women and 36.2% with a cardiac history. The mean follow-up time was 7.9 months. Influenza vaccine was associated with a lower risk of composite cardiovascular events (2.9% vs 4.7%; RR, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.48-0.86], P = .003) in the published trials. A treatment interaction was observed between patients with recent ACS (RR, 0.45 [95% CI, 0.32-0.63]) and those without (RR, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.55-1.61]) (P for interaction = .02). The results remained consistent when unpublished data were included. 

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE This meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials found that influenza vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. The greatest benefit was observed in high-risk patients with active coronary disease. Further large-scale trials are needed to confirm these findings and assess specific cardiovascular endpoints.

title: Baby hands that move to the rhythm of language: hearing babies acquiring sign languages babble silently on the hands
text: The sound "ba, ba, ba" that babies make around 7 months old has caught the attention of scientists because it helps us understand how language is acquired and its evolutionary origins. However, the main question remains: what is the biological basis of babbling? One hypothesis suggests that it is a motor activity driven by the baby's control over their mouth and jaw, while another suggests that it is a linguistic activity reflecting the baby's sensitivity to specific phonetic-syllabic patterns. To investigate this, two groups of hearing babies were studied at different ages (6, 10, and 12 months). These groups were similar in all aspects of development except for the type of language input they received: one group learned spoken language (group 1: "speech-exposed"), and the other group learned sign language only (group 2: "sign-exposed"). Despite the sign-exposed group's exposure to sign language, the motor activity hypothesis would predict similar hand activity to that seen in the speech-exposed group because sign language does not involve the mouth. Using innovative technology called Optotrak 3-D motion-tracking, which was used for the first time in studying infant language acquisition, we measured the physical movements of the hands, similar to a speech spectrogram but for the hands. We found that the rhythmic frequencies of the hands in the sign-exposed group differed depending on whether they were producing linguistic or non-linguistic activity. Linguistic activity was produced at a low frequency of approximately 1 Hz, while non-linguistic activity was produced at a higher frequency of approximately 2.5 Hz, which was the same as the speech-exposed group. Surprisingly, the sign-exposed babies babbled systematically on their hands, even without the use of their mouth. From this, we conclude that babbling is fundamentally a linguistic activity and explain that the differentiation between linguistic and non-linguistic hand activity in a single manual modality (distinct from the mouth) could only occur if all babies are born with a sensitivity to specific rhythmic patterns that are essential to human language and have the ability to use them.

title: The Ten-Eleven Translocation-2 (TET2) gene in hematopoiesis and hematopoietic diseases
text: Loss-of-function mutations, deletions, and IDH1/2 gene mutations commonly lead to the inactivation of the Ten-Eleven Translocation-2 (TET2) gene in myeloid and lymphoid malignancies. Interestingly, similar TET2 gene mutations can also accumulate with age in healthy individuals with clonal hematopoiesis. TET2 is one of the three proteins in the TET family, which are enzymes that play a crucial role in DNA demethylation by converting 5-methyl-cytosine (5-mC) to 5-hydroxymethyl-cytosine (5-hmC). These enzymes require 2-oxoglutarate, oxygen, and Fe(II) for their activity, and their function is enhanced in the presence of ascorbic acid. TET2 is the most abundant TET gene expressed in hematopoietic tissue, particularly in hematopoietic stem cells. In addition to its role as a hydroxylase, TET2 also recruits the O-linked β-D-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) enzyme to chromatin, facilitating post-transcriptional modifications of histones and promoting gene expression. The level of TET2 is regulated by its interaction with IDAX, a protein derived from TET2 gene fission during evolution, and by the microRNA miR-22. TET2 plays various roles in hematopoiesis, including stem-cell self-renewal, lineage commitment, and terminal differentiation of monocytes. Studies on Tet2 knockout mice, which are viable and fertile, have shown that Tet2 acts as a tumor suppressor, and its haploinsufficiency can initiate myeloid and lymphoid transformations. This review provides an overview of the recently discovered physiological and pathological functions of TET2 and discusses how this knowledge can impact therapeutic approaches in hematological malignancies and potentially other types of tumors.

title: Impaired Awareness of Hypoglycemia in a Population-Based Sample of Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes
text: The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence and clinical associations of impaired awareness of hypoglycemia in a population-based sample of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. A validated questionnaire was given to 656 patients with type 1 diabetes over a 6-month period to assess their hypoglycemia awareness status. The study found that 29% of patients had impaired awareness of hypoglycemia. These patients had an earlier onset of diabetes, were younger, and had lower mean levels of A1C since diabetes onset and at their last visit. The rate of severe hypoglycemia in the preceding year was 24.5 episodes per 100 patient-years. Patients with impaired awareness of hypoglycemia had a higher rate of severe hypoglycemia compared to those without impaired awareness. Among patients aged <6 years, 59% of care providers reported impaired awareness of hypoglycemia, and the rate of severe hypoglycemia was significantly higher in those reporting impaired awareness. Patients with recurrent hypoglycemia were more likely to have impaired awareness of hypoglycemia. The study concludes that screening for impaired awareness is important in routine diabetes care as it can help identify patients at increased risk of severe hypoglycemic events.

title: Enhancing circadian clock function in cancer cells inhibits tumor growth
text:
The circadian clock plays a crucial role in regulating cell cycle factors, and disruptions to this clock have been linked to the development of cancer. In order to investigate whether improving circadian rhythmicity in tumor cells can impact cell cycle progression and reduce proliferation, we conducted a study comparing the growth and cell cycle events of B16 melanoma cells and tumors with either a functional or dysfunctional clock.

Our findings revealed that clock genes were suppressed in both B16 cells and tumors. However, when we treated these cells and tumors with substances that induce circadian rhythmicity, such as dexamethasone, forskolin, and heat shock, we observed a restoration of rhythmic clock and cell cycle gene expression. This resulted in a decrease in the number of cells in the S phase and an increase in the number of cells in the G1 phase. Consequently, the proliferation of B16 cells in vitro and the growth of tumors in vivo were significantly slowed down. We also observed similar effects in human colon carcinoma HCT-116 cells.

Importantly, we determined that the effects of dexamethasone were not due to an increase in apoptosis or an enhancement of immune cell recruitment to the tumor. To further investigate the role of the circadian clock in these effects, we knocked down the essential clock gene Bmal1 in B16 tumors. This prevented the effects of dexamethasone on tumor growth and cell cycle events.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the effects of dexamethasone on cell cycle progression and tumor growth are mediated by the tumor's intrinsic circadian clock. This suggests that enhancing circadian clock function could be a promising strategy for controlling the progression of cancer.

title: Distinct functions of nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites in the four AAA modules of cytoplasmic dynein.
text:
Cytoplasmic dynein is a motor protein found in cells that is responsible for transporting materials in a backward direction along microtubule filaments. The motor domain of dynein consists of six AAA modules, which are associated with various cellular activities and are linked together. The first four modules, known as P1-P4, contain sites where nucleotide binding and hydrolysis are predicted to occur. To understand the functions of these nucleotide-binding sites, we conducted experiments using purified motor domains of Dictyostelium dynein with mutations that blocked nucleotide binding at each of the four AAA modules. We then examined the biochemical properties of these mutant proteins.

The P1 mutant protein was found to be stuck in a state where it strongly binds to ATP, even in the presence of ATP, and it lost its ability to move. The P3 mutant protein also had a high affinity for microtubules in the presence of ATP, but it lost most of its ATPase activity that is activated by microtubules. However, it still retained the ability to slide along microtubules, although at a much slower speed compared to the wild type protein. On the other hand, mutations in the P2 or P4 sites did not affect the binding affinity of the mutant protein to microtubules in the presence of ATP, but it did reduce both ATPase activity and microtubule sliding activity.

These findings suggest that ATP binding and hydrolysis specifically at the P1 site are crucial for the motor activities of cytoplasmic dynein. The other nucleotide-binding sites, P2 and P4, seem to regulate the motor activities by affecting ATPase and microtubule sliding activities. Nucleotide binding at the P3 site is not essential but plays a critical role in the microtubule-activated ATPase and motile activities of cytoplasmic dynein.

title: Over-expression of RCAN1 causes Down syndrome-like hippocampal deficits that alter learning and memory.
text: Abnormal brain structure is observed in individuals with Down syndrome (DS), along with disruptions in neurotransmission and signaling pathways that regulate brain function. Due to the simultaneous expression of numerous genes at abnormal levels in DS, it is challenging to identify which gene(s) are responsible for specific abnormalities and determine the key molecular pathways involved. To address this, we created RCAN1-TG mice to investigate the effects of RCAN1 over-expression and its contribution to the brain phenotype of DS. These mice exhibit structural brain abnormalities in areas affected by DS, including a reduction in the volume and number of neurons in the hippocampus, which is associated with impaired adult neurogenesis. Additionally, the density of dendritic spines on RCAN1-TG hippocampal pyramidal neurons is decreased. Deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning, short- and long-term memory, and the inability to maintain long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal slices are also observed. In response to LTP induction, we observed diminished calcium transients and decreased phosphorylation of CaMKII and ERK1/2 proteins, which are crucial for LTP maintenance and memory formation. These findings strongly suggest that RCAN1 plays a significant role in normal brain development and function, and its up-regulation likely contributes to the neural deficits associated with DS.

title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of prostate and total cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial.
text:
Many people take vitamins in the hopes of preventing chronic diseases like cancer, and vitamins E and C are among the most commonly used individual supplements. A large-scale randomized trial suggested that vitamin E may lower the risk of prostate cancer, but there haven't been many trials that have been able to fully investigate this relationship. No previous trial in men at average risk has looked at the effects of vitamin C alone in preventing cancer. 

The objective of this study was to determine whether long-term supplementation of vitamin E or C can decrease the risk of prostate and total cancer events in men. The study, called the Physicians' Health Study II, was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial that started in 1997 and ended in 2007. It involved 14,641 male physicians in the United States who were initially aged 50 years or older, including 1307 men with a history of prior cancer at the time of enrollment. 

The participants were given individual supplements of 400 IU of vitamin E every other day and 500 mg of vitamin C daily. The main outcome measures were prostate and total cancer. 

After an average follow-up of 8.0 years, there were 1008 confirmed cases of prostate cancer and 1943 cases of total cancer. The results showed that vitamin E had no effect on the incidence of prostate cancer or total cancer compared to the placebo group. Similarly, vitamin C had no significant effect on total cancer or prostate cancer. Neither vitamin E nor vitamin C had a significant effect on colorectal, lung, or other site-specific cancers. 

Adjustment for adherence to the supplement regimen and exclusion of the first 4 or 6 years of follow-up did not change the results. Stratification by various cancer risk factors also showed no significant modification of the effect of vitamin E on prostate cancer risk or either supplement on total cancer risk. 

In conclusion, this large and long-term trial involving male physicians found that neither vitamin E nor C supplementation reduced the risk of prostate or total cancer. These findings do not support the use of these supplements for cancer prevention in middle-aged and older men. The trial was registered under clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00270647.

title: Micromanagers of gene expression: the potentially widespread influence of metazoan microRNAs
text: We suggest that the microRNA environment, which is unique to each type of cell, effectively reduces the expression of numerous mRNAs and plays a crucial role in the development of all metazoan mRNA sequences. When it comes to genes that should not be active in a specific cell type, the production of proteins is significantly decreased. For other genes, the amount of protein produced is adjusted to allow for customized expression in various cell types, while maintaining a more consistent level within each cell type. In this manner, microRNAs contribute an extensive layer of gene regulation that works alongside transcriptional and other regulatory processes to enhance the complexity of metazoan gene expression.

title: The Kinase Regulator Mob1 Acts as a Patterning Protein for Stentor Morphogenesis
text:
Morphogenesis and pattern formation are crucial processes in all organisms, regardless of whether they are unicellular or multicellular. However, while we have a good understanding of these processes in plants and animals, the mechanisms behind morphogenesis and pattern formation in single cells are still largely unknown. Although all cells develop patterns, ciliates, such as the giant ciliate Stentor coeruleus, exhibit these patterns most prominently. Therefore, we have chosen Stentor as a classical model system for studying unicellular organisms.

In our research, we have discovered that the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery is conserved in Stentor. By utilizing RNAi, we have identified a protein called Mob1, which acts as a kinase coactivator and plays a role in cell division and morphogenesis in various organisms, from plants to humans. Interestingly, Mob1 is asymmetrically localized and serves as a patterning protein that is essential for global patterning during both development and regeneration in Stentor. These findings have opened up new possibilities for using Stentor as a model system to study regeneration processes.

title: Measurement and clinical monitoring of human lymphocyte clonality by massively parallel VDJ pyrosequencing.
text: We demonstrate that the vast array of immune receptors produced by B and T cells allows for the recognition of various threats to the host organism. Our study focuses on the use of massively parallel DNA sequencing to directly detect and track immune diversity and expanded clonal lymphocyte populations in both normal and pathological situations. We extracted DNA from blood and tissue samples and utilized a set of redundant primers to amplify different DNA rearrangements. The resulting mixtures of barcoded amplicons were then sequenced using long-read ultra deep sequencing. By analyzing the DNA segments that were joined to create a functional or nonfunctional immune effector, we were able to characterize individual DNA molecules. Our experimental setup can handle up to 150 samples in a single sequence run, and the depth of sequencing allows us to identify stable and dynamic aspects of the immune repertoire in both healthy individuals and those with diseases. These findings provide a detailed understanding of the immune profiles in normal individuals and patients with hematological malignancies. Specifically, they shed light on the initial behavior of clonal tumor populations and the subsequent suppression or re-emergence of these populations following treatment.

title: Can we apply the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel definition of the metabolic syndrome to Asians?
text:
The aim of this study was to address the lack of information regarding the metabolic syndrome in Asians and the appropriateness of using waist circumference as a measure of central obesity in this population. The study also aimed to estimate the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in an Asian population.

To achieve these objectives, data from the 1998 Singapore National Health Survey were analyzed. The survey included 4,723 men and women of Chinese, Malay, and Asian-Indian ethnicity aged 18-69 years. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was conducted to determine the optimal waist circumference for diagnosing central obesity in Asians. The results suggested that a waist circumference greater than 80 cm in women and greater than 90 cm in men was a more suitable definition of central obesity in this population.

Using the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III) criteria, the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome was then calculated with and without the modified waist circumference criteria. The findings showed that decreasing waist circumference increased the crude prevalence of the metabolic syndrome from 12.2% to 17.9% in Asians. When the modified Asian criteria were applied, the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome increased from 2.9% in those aged 18-30 years to 31.0% in those aged 60-69 years. It was also found to be more common in men (20.9% prevalence in men compared to 15.5% in women) and Asian Indians (28.8% prevalence in Asian-Indians, 24.2% in Malays, and 14.8% in Chinese).

In conclusion, applying the NCEP ATP III criteria to an Asian population underestimates the population at risk for the metabolic syndrome. By using a lower waist circumference cutoff, the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in Asians is comparable to that in Western populations. It is important to recognize that ethnic differences likely exist between populations across Asia.

title: Serotonin and fluoxetine levels in plasma and platelets after fluoxetine treatment in depressive patients.
text: Depression is a mood disorder characterized by changes in neurotransmitters like serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Specifically, there is strong evidence of abnormalities in serotonin neurotransmission. To understand these biochemical changes related to depression, researchers have examined peripheral markers of serotonin transmission, such as the levels of serotonin in plasma and platelets. These markers have also been used to study how antidepressant drugs like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work. This particular study aimed to investigate the relationship between plasma and platelet levels of fluoxetine (an SSRI) and serotonin after administering fluoxetine to depressed patients. Twelve patients diagnosed with major depression according to the DSM-IV criteria were given a single oral dose of fluoxetine in the morning. The dosage started at 5 mg for the first 5 days, increased to 10 mg from day 6 to day 10, and then to 20 mg from day 11 to day 40. Blood samples were taken at 0, 7, 10, and 24 hours after drug administration on the first day of 5 mg fluoxetine, as well as on the 1st and 30th day of 20 mg fluoxetine (day 11 and day 40 of treatment, respectively). The results showed that plasma levels of fluoxetine and serotonin increased after drug administration, with the highest levels observed on the 30th day of 20 mg fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was also detected in platelets, and its levels varied similarly to those in plasma. However, platelet serotonin levels decreased after drug administration, reaching their lowest point on the 30th day of 20 mg fluoxetine.

title: The histone acetyltransferase MOF is a key regulator of the embryonic stem cell core transcriptional network.
text: The regulation of pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ESCs) involves their ability to self-renew and respond quickly to differentiation signals. These features are controlled by epigenetic mechanisms. In this study, we investigate the role of the histone acetyltransferase Mof in maintaining ESC self-renewal and pluripotency. When Mof is deleted in ESCs, they lose their typical appearance, alkaline phosphatase staining, and ability to differentiate. Additionally, the core transcription factors Nanog, Oct4, and Sox2 are expressed abnormally in these Mof-deficient ESCs. Interestingly, overexpression of Nanog partially rescues the phenotypes of Mof-null ESCs, suggesting that Mof acts as an upstream regulator of Nanog in ESCs. Through genome-wide ChIP-sequencing and transcriptome analyses, we demonstrate that Mof is an essential component of the core transcriptional network in ESCs and prepares genes for various developmental programs. Furthermore, Mof is necessary for the recruitment of Wdr5 and H3K4 methylation at important regulatory sites, highlighting the intricate and interconnected nature of chromatin regulators in ESCs.

title: Role of the CXCR4/SDF-1 chemokine axis in circulating neutrophil homeostasis.
text:
The bone marrow is where neutrophils are primarily produced and released into the bloodstream. The interaction between hematopoietic stem cells, lymphocytes, and developing neutrophils in the marrow is influenced by the CXC chemokine receptor-4/stromal derived factor-1 (CXCR4/SDF-1) axis. We wanted to investigate if there are reciprocal mechanisms involving CXCR4 that play a role in the release of neutrophils from the marrow and their subsequent return after circulating in the body.

By using a neutralizing antibody to CXCR4, we observed a significant reduction in the retention of infused neutrophils in the marrow (from 45.7% +/- 0.5% to 6.9% +/- 0.5%). Additionally, the antibody was able to mobilize neutrophils from the marrow (34.4% +/- 4.4%). As neutrophils mature and become activated, their expression of CXCR4 decreases, along with a decrease in SDF-1-induced calcium flux. These changes correspond to a decrease in the ability of neutrophils to home to the marrow in vivo.

When we infused the inflammatory mediator and CXCR2 ligand KC, we observed mobilization of neutrophils from the marrow. This effect was further enhanced by low doses of a CXCR4-blocking antibody, which on its own had no mobilizing effect. Further examination revealed that KC may cause heterologous desensitization to SDF-1, contributing to its mobilizing effect.

These findings suggest that the CXCR4/SDF-1 axis is crucial for maintaining neutrophil homeostasis in the bloodstream. It also appears to play a role in the rapid release of neutrophils from the marrow during inflammation, possibly through an interaction with inflammatory CXC chemokines.

title: Vitamin D and prevention of colorectal cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Insufficient photosynthesis or inadequate oral intake of Vitamin D has been linked to a higher incidence of colorectal cancer. However, the relationship between dosage and response has not been thoroughly examined.

METHODS: We analyzed observational studies on Vitamin D intake and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels to establish dose-response gradients. By plotting trend lines, we identified the point on each line where the odds ratio reached 0.50. This point represented the Vitamin D intake or 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration associated with a 50% lower risk compared to those with less than 100IU/day of Vitamin D or less than 13ng/ml of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. We determined the medians of these values.

RESULTS: Overall, individuals who consumed 1000IU/day or more of oral Vitamin D (p<0.0001) or had serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of 33ng/ml or higher (p<0.01) had a 50% lower incidence of colorectal cancer compared to the reference values.

CONCLUSIONS: An intake of 1000IU/day of Vitamin D, which is half the safe upper intake limit established by the National Academy of Sciences, was associated with a 50% lower risk of colorectal cancer. Similarly, a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 33ng/ml, known to be safe, was also linked to a 50% lower risk. Urgent public health measures are necessary to promote a daily intake of 1000IU of Vitamin D(3) and encourage moderate sunlight exposure to increase 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels.

title: Repeat expansion in the budding yeast ribosomal DNA can occur independently of the canonical homologous recombination machinery
text: The ribosomal DNA (rDNA) is a major component of eukaryotic genomes and consists of repeated sequences with specific copy numbers. The maintenance of these copy numbers is regulated by recombination processes. Although we have identified mechanisms that initiate rDNA recombination, none of them are directional and cannot explain how the precise number of repeats is controlled. In this study, we discovered that yeast cells lacking the histone chaperone Asf1 undergo reproducible expansions of rDNA repeats. These expansions do not rely on the protein Fob1, which is known to be involved in rDNA expansion, suggesting the existence of a regulated pathway for gaining rDNA repeats that is constitutively active in asf1Δ mutants. Cells lacking ASF1 accumulate rDNA repeats with high accuracy over multiple cell divisions. Surprisingly, this repeat gain mechanism does not require the homologous recombination proteins Rad52, Rad51, and Rad59, although it depends on highly repetitive sequences. Mutations that decrease the processivity of DNA replication compromise the expansion mechanism, leading to a gradual loss of rDNA repeats. Our findings suggest the occurrence of a novel form of break-induced replication in repetitive DNA that relies on high homology but does not necessitate the conventional homologous recombination machinery.

title: cDNA and genomic cloning of lacritin, a novel secretion enhancing factor from the human lacrimal gland.
text: The differentiation factors that promote the development of secretory pathways in exocrine secretory cells are not well understood, especially those that are specific to certain organs. In this study, we have identified a new glycoprotein called lacritin, which is secreted and enhances exocrine secretion in lacrimal acinar cells. These cells typically lose their secretory function in overnight cultures, but lacritin is able to restore it. Lacritin is highly expressed in the lacrimal gland, moderately expressed in major and minor salivary glands, and slightly expressed in the thyroid. It is not found in any other human tissues that have been examined. Lacritin shares some similarities with brain-specific neuroglycan C and fibulin-2, and it primarily localizes to secretory granules and secretory fluid. The lacritin gene has five exons, does not undergo alternative splicing, and is located on chromosome 12q13. Recombinant lacritin enhances unstimulated secretion in acinar cells, promotes ductal cell proliferation, and stimulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation and release of calcium. It binds to collagen IV, laminin-1, entactin/nidogen-1, fibronectin, and vitronectin, but not collagen I, heparin, or EGF. Lacritin acts as an autocrine/paracrine enhancer of the constitutive secretory pathway in the lacrimal gland, a mitogen for ductal cells, and a stimulator of corneal epithelial cells. It may play a crucial role in the function of the lacrimal gland-corneal axis.

title: The structure of informal care: are there differences by race?
text: The purpose of this study was to examine if there are any variations in the structure of informal caregiving networks based on race. The researchers analyzed data from the 1989 National Long-Term Care Survey, which included information on 3,793 individuals aged 65 and above who had functional impairments. The study found that there were no racial differences in the size of the overall caregiver network or the unpaid network. However, disabled older blacks were more likely to have non-immediate family members as unpaid caregivers. These findings raise questions about whether disparities in nursing home usage and paid long-term care services, as observed in previous studies, can be attributed to differences in caregiving arrangements.

title: Proteomic and genomic approaches reveal critical functions of H3K9 methylation and Heterochromatin Protein-1γ in reprogramming to pluripotency
text: The process of reprogramming somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) involves a significant rearrangement of chromatin. In order to identify changes in histone modifications that occur during this process, we utilized a quantitative mass-spectrometry-based method. Our results showed that iPSCs have higher levels of histone modifications associated with active chromatin compared to the starting fibroblasts and a late reprogramming intermediate called pre-iPSCs. Additionally, iPSCs have lower levels of histone modifications related to transcriptional elongation and certain repressive modifications like H3K9me2/me3. By studying the role of H3K9 methylation in reprogramming, we discovered that the H3K9 methyltransferases Ehmt1, Ehmt2, and Setdb1 regulate global levels of H3K9me2/me3 and that their depletion enhances iPSC formation from both fibroblasts and pre-iPSCs. Similarly, inhibiting heterochromatin protein-1γ (Cbx3), which recognizes H3K9 methylation, also promotes reprogramming. Through genome-wide location analysis, we found that Cbx3 primarily binds to active genes in both pre-iPSCs and pluripotent cells, but with a distinct distribution. In pre-iPSCs, Cbx3 associates with active transcriptional start sites, suggesting a developmentally regulated role in transcriptional activation. Despite their different functions and association with active transcription, both the H3K9 methyltransferases and Cbx3 inhibit reprogramming by repressing the pluripotency factor Nanog. Overall, our findings demonstrate that Cbx3 and H3K9 methylation impede late reprogramming events and indicate that a significant change in global chromatin structure acts as an epigenetic barrier for reprogramming.

title: Tissue exit: a novel control point in the accumulation of antigen-specific CD8 T cells in the influenza a virus-infected lung.
text:
Memory and effector T cells have the ability to efficiently move into tissues outside of the lymph nodes and areas of infection. This allows them to provide immunosurveillance and act as a first line of defense against invading pathogens. However, the process of T cell egress from infected tissues is not well understood, even though it has the potential to regulate the size, quality, and duration of the immune response in the tissue.

To investigate this, we used a mouse model of influenza A virus infection. Our findings showed that effector CD8 T cells leave the infected lung in a manner that depends on the protein CCR7. However, after recognizing the antigen, the egress of effector CD8 T cells decreased and the function of CCR7 was reduced both in vivo and in vitro. This suggests that the exit of CD8 T cells from infected tissues is tightly controlled.

Based on our data, we propose that the regulation of T cell egress is a mechanism to keep antigen-specific effector T cells at the site of infection. This promotes the clearance of the virus while reducing the number of bystander T cells and preventing excessive inflammation.

title: The relation between dietary flavonol intake and coronary heart disease mortality: a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between dietary flavonol intake and the subsequent risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) mortality.

Design: This study conducted a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies that were published prior to September 2001. The studies were identified through searches of MEDLINE and EMBASE databases, as well as by reviewing relevant reference lists. The researchers extracted various information from the published reports, including the size of the cohort, mean age, mean duration of follow-up, number of fatal CHD events, mean flavonol intake, main sources of flavonol intake, degree of adjustment for potential confounders, and the association between CHD mortality and dietary flavonol intake measured at baseline.

Results: A total of seven prospective cohorts, consisting of both men and women, were included in the analysis, with a combined total of 2087 fatal CHD events. After adjusting for known CHD risk factors and other dietary components, individuals in the top third of dietary flavonol intake had a risk ratio of 0.80 (95% CI 0.69–0.93) compared to those in the bottom third.

Conclusion: This meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies suggests that a high dietary intake of flavonols, obtained from a small number of fruits and vegetables, tea, and red wine, may be associated with a reduced risk of CHD mortality in free-living populations.

Sponsorship: This study was sponsored by the Institute for International Health at the University of Sydney.

title: MRI in the diagnosis of MS: a prospective study with comparison of clinical evaluation, evoked potentials, oligoclonal banding, and CT.
text:
In a prospective evaluation of 200 patients suspected of having multiple sclerosis (MS), we compared the diagnostic capabilities of MRI, CT, evoked potentials (EP), and CSF oligoclonal banding analysis. Our findings showed that MRI was the most effective method for demonstrating dissemination in space. In cases of monosymptomatic disease, an abnormal EP result was typically supported by MRI and CSF analysis, indicating a predictive value for MS as a clinical diagnosis. However, a normal EP study was not sufficient as MRI and CSF analysis often did not support a non-MS diagnosis. When three of these paraclinical studies agreed, the diagnosis of MS was likely to be definitive. 

For research purposes, we were able to diagnose laboratory-supported definite MS (LSDMS) in 85 out of the total 200 patients (42.5%). Among patients with optic neuritis (ON), LSDMS was diagnosed in 19 out of 38 (50%) cases, and in 24 out of 52 (46%) cases of chronic progressive myelopathy (CPM). MRI successfully identified all patients who qualified for LSDMS in the ON and CPM groups. 

During a short follow-up period of less than 1 year, 19 out of 200 patients (10%) progressed to develop clinically definite MS (CDMS), and MRI accurately predicted this diagnosis in 18 out of 19 cases (95%). However, only long-term follow-up will determine the true predictive value of these studies and the LSDMS category in relation to the development of CDMS. It is important to note that the clinical diagnosis of MS (CDMS), despite being 95% accurate, remains the gold standard.

title: Osteoclasts promote the formation of hematopoietic stem cell niches in the bone marrow
text: The development of the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow (BM) is closely linked to endochondral ossification, but the specific mechanisms involved are not well understood. To investigate this, we utilized the oc/oc mouse model, which has impaired endochondral ossification due to a lack of osteoclast (OCL) activity. Our aim was to examine the role of osteoblasts (OBLs) and OCLs in the formation of the HSC niche. The absence of OCL activity resulted in a defective HSC niche characterized by an increased number of mesenchymal progenitors but reduced osteoblastic differentiation. As a result, the homing of HSCs to the BM was impaired. However, when OCL activity was restored, the defect in HSC niche formation was reversed. These findings highlight the importance of OBLs in establishing HSC niches and demonstrate that OCLs play a role in inducing osteoblastic development. By expanding our understanding of HSC niche formation, these findings contribute to our knowledge of normal and abnormal hematopoiesis.

title: A prospective study of plasma homocyst(e)ine and risk of myocardial infarction in US physicians.
text:
The objective of this study was to prospectively assess the risk of coronary heart disease in individuals with elevated plasma levels of homocyst(e)ine. The study design involved a nested case-control approach using blood samples collected from participants in the Physicians' Health Study. A total of 14,916 male physicians, aged 40 to 84 years, with no prior history of myocardial infarction or stroke provided plasma samples at baseline and were followed up for 5 years. Plasma samples from 271 men who later developed myocardial infarction were analyzed for homocyst(e)ine levels, along with paired controls matched by age and smoking status. The main outcome measure was acute myocardial infarction or death due to coronary disease. 

The results showed that levels of homocyst(e)ine were higher in cases compared to controls (11.1 +/- 4.0 [SD] vs 10.5 +/- 2.8 nmol/mL; P = .03). This difference was primarily due to an excess of high values among men who later experienced myocardial infarction. The relative risk for individuals in the highest 5% of homocyst(e)ine levels compared to the bottom 90% was 3.1 (95% confidence interval, 1.4 to 6.9; P = .005). After adjusting for additional factors such as diabetes, hypertension, aspirin assignment, Quetelet's Index, and total/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, the relative risk increased to 3.4 (95% confidence interval, 1.3 to 8.8) (P = .01). Thirteen controls and 31 cases (11%) had homocyst(e)ine values above the 95th percentile of the controls. 

In conclusion, moderately high levels of plasma homocyst(e)ine are associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction independent of other coronary risk factors.
