METHODS AND RESULTS: We conducted experiments using human umbilical vein endothelial cells and found that knockdown of Dicer, an enzyme involved in miRNA processing, increased the levels of KLF2 mRNA, suggesting that KLF2 is regulated by miRNAs. In silico analysis predicted that miR-92a could bind to the 3' untranslated region of KLF2 mRNA. Overexpression of miR-92a resulted in decreased expression of KLF2, as well as its downstream targets endothelial nitric oxide synthase and thrombomodulin, at both the mRNA and protein levels. Conversely, inhibition of miR-92a increased the expression of KLF2, endothelial nitric oxide synthase, and thrombomodulin. Further investigations revealed that atheroprotective laminar flow downregulated the levels of miR-92a precursor, leading to increased KLF2 expression. Additionally, the level of flow-induced KLF2 was reduced by miR-92a precursor. Moreover, miR-92a levels were lower in human umbilical vein endothelial cells exposed to atheroprotective pulsatile shear flow compared to atheroprone oscillatory shear flow. Anti-Ago1/2 immunoprecipitation coupled with real-time polymerase chain reaction demonstrated that pulsatile shear flow decreased the functional targeting of miR-92a precursor/KLF2 mRNA in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Consistent with these findings, mouse carotid arteries receiving miR-92a precursor exhibited impaired vasodilatory response to flow.

CONCLUSIONS: Atheroprotective flow patterns decrease the levels of miR-92a, which in turn increases KLF2 expression to maintain endothelial homeostasis.

title: Effectiveness of a diabetes education and self management programme (DESMOND) for people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus: three year follow-up of a cluster randomised controlled trial in primary care
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if the benefits of a structured education and self-management program for individuals with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus were maintained after three years. The study design involved a three-year follow-up of a randomized controlled trial conducted in primary care settings, with randomization at the practice level. The study took place in 207 general practices across 13 primary care sites in the United Kingdom. Out of the 824 participants included in the original trial, 731 were eligible for follow-up. Biomedical data was collected for 604 participants (82.6%), and questionnaire data was collected for 513 participants (70.1%). 

The intervention consisted of a six-hour structured group education program delivered in the community by two trained healthcare professionals, compared to usual care. The primary outcome measure was glycated hemoglobin (HbA(1c)) levels, and secondary outcomes included blood pressure, weight, blood lipid levels, smoking status, physical activity, quality of life, beliefs about illness, depression, emotional impact of diabetes, and drug use at three years. 

The results showed that HbA(1c) levels had decreased in both groups after three years, but the difference was not statistically significant after adjusting for baseline and cluster (difference -0.02, 95% confidence interval -0.22 to 0.17). There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of other biomedical and lifestyle outcomes and drug use. However, the intervention group did show sustained improvements in some illness beliefs, with significant benefits observed in four out of five health beliefs at 12 months (P<0.01). Depression scores and quality of life did not differ at three years. 

In conclusion, a single program for individuals with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus did not result in significant differences in biomedical or lifestyle outcomes after three years, although there were sustained improvements in some illness beliefs. The trial was registered with Current Controlled Trials (ISRCTN17844016).

title: Acetylation of Histone H3 Lysine 56 Regulates Replication-Coupled Nucleosome Assembly
text: Chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF-1) and Rtt106 are involved in the formation of nucleosomes by depositing newly synthesized histones onto replicating DNA. This process is crucial for maintaining genome stability and passing on specialized chromatin structures in cells that are actively dividing. However, the exact role of acetylation of newly synthesized histones in this pathway of nucleosome assembly during DNA replication is still unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that a specific acetylation of histone H3 at lysine 56 (H3K56Ac) is incorporated into replicating DNA. By increasing the affinity of CAF-1 and Rtt106 for histone H3, H3K56Ac enhances the ability of these histone chaperones to assemble DNA into nucleosomes. Our genetic analysis suggests that H3K56Ac functions independently from the acetylation of the N-terminal residues of H3 and H4 in nucleosome assembly. These findings provide insights into how H3K56Ac regulates replication-coupled nucleosome assembly, which is mediated by CAF-1 and Rtt106.

title: Selective inhibition of Ras-dependent cell growth by farnesylthiosalisylic acid.
text: S-trans,trans-Farnesylthiosalicylic acid (FTS) is a new derivative of farnesylated rigid carboxylic acid. It acts as a strong competitive inhibitor (Ki = 2.6 microM) of prenylated protein methyltransferase (PPMTase) in cell-free systems. PPMTase is responsible for methylating the carboxyl-terminal S-prenylcysteine in various prenylated proteins, including Ras. FTS inhibits Ras methylation but not Ras farnesylation in these systems. Inhibition of PPMTase by FTS is also observed in homogenates or membranes of different tissues and cell lines, as evidenced by the blockage of methylation in exogenously added substrates like N-acetyl-S-trans,trans-farnesyl-L-cysteine, and endogenous substrates like small GTP-binding proteins. FTS can also inhibit methylation of these proteins in intact cells, such as Rat-1 fibroblasts, Ras-transformed Rat-1, and B16 melanoma cells. However, higher concentrations of FTS (50-100 microM) are required for partial blocking (10-40%) of protein methylation in intact cells. Therefore, FTS is a weak inhibitor of methylation in intact cells. Since methylation is the final step in the processing of Ras and related proteins, FTS is unlikely to affect preceding steps like protein prenylation. This may explain why the growth and morphology of various cultured cell types are unaffected by FTS concentrations up to 25 microM, and why FTS does not induce cytotoxicity. However, FTS does reduce the levels of Ras in cell membranes and can inhibit Ras-dependent cell growth in vitro, independent of methylation. It inhibits the growth of Ha-ras-transformed cells (EJ cells) and reverses their transformed morphology in a dose-dependent manner (0.1-10 microM). FTS does not interfere with the growth of cells transformed by v-Raf or T-antigen, but it inhibits the growth of ErbB2-transformed cells and blocks the mitogenic effects of epidermal and basic fibroblast growth factors. This suggests that FTS selectively targets Ras growth signaling, possibly by modulating Ras-Raf communication. Overall, these findings suggest that FTS may specifically disrupt the interaction between Ras and a farnesylcysteine recognition domain in the cell membrane.

title: NADPH oxidase controls phagosomal pH and antigen cross-presentation in human dendritic cells.
text: The phagocyte NADPH oxidase (NOX2) is crucial for the bactericidal function of phagocytic cells and plays a significant role in innate immunity. Our recent study demonstrated that NOX2 activity in mouse dendritic cells (DCs) prevents the acidification of phagosomes, thereby promoting antigen cross-presentation. To investigate the impact of NOX2 on the regulation of phagosomal pH in human DCs, we examined the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the pH of phagosomes/endosomes in monocyte-derived DCs and macrophages (M(diameter)s) from healthy individuals and patients with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). As expected, human M(diameter)s acidify their phagosomes more effectively than human DCs. This is consistent with the higher expression of the vacuolar proton ATPase (V-H(+)-ATPase) in M(diameter)s compared to DCs. However, phagosomal ROS production is also higher in M(diameter)s due to elevated levels of gp91phox expression and recruitment to phagosomes. In contrast, in the absence of active NOX2, the pH of phagosomes and endosomes decreases. Both the presence of a NOX2 inhibitor and DCs derived from CGD patients impair the cross-presentation of two model tumor antigens. In conclusion, NOX2 activity is involved in the regulation of phagosomal and endosomal pH in human DCs and is necessary for efficient antigen cross-presentation.

title: Activation of fast skeletal muscle troponin as a potential therapeutic approach for treating neuromuscular diseases
text: Muscle weakness in neuromuscular disease occurs due to limited neural input, which leads to a decrease in muscle innervation density, neuromuscular junction activation rate, or synaptic transmission efficiency. To address this issue, we have developed a fast-skeletal-troponin activator called CK-2017357. This small-molecule compound aims to enhance muscle strength by amplifying the muscle's response when neural input is reduced due to neuromuscular disease. CK-2017357 selectively binds to the fast-skeletal-troponin complex, resulting in a slower release of calcium from troponin C and increased muscle sensitivity to calcium. Consequently, the force-calcium relationship of muscle fibers and the force-frequency relationship of nerve-muscle pairs shift to the left. This means that CK-2017357 enhances muscle force production during sub-maximal nerve stimulation rates. Importantly, our research demonstrates that the sensitization of the fast-skeletal-troponin complex to calcium immediately improves muscle force and grip strength after administering single doses of CK-2017357 in a model of myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular disease. Troponin activation could potentially offer a novel therapeutic approach to enhance physical activity in conditions where neuromuscular function is compromised.

title: Cortactin regulates cofilin and N-WASp activities to control the stages of invadopodium assembly and maturation
text: Invadopodia, which are protrusions on the membrane of invasive carcinoma cells that degrade the extracellular matrix, have unclear mechanisms for their assembly and maturation. However, we have conducted a thorough analysis of the different stages involved in invadopodium assembly and maturation. Our research reveals that cortactin phosphorylation plays a crucial role as a master switch during these processes. Specifically, we have discovered that cortactin phosphorylation regulates actin polymerization, which is dependent on cofilin and the Arp2/3 complex. By directly binding to cofilin, cortactin inhibits its ability to sever actin filaments. However, cortactin phosphorylation is necessary to release this inhibition, allowing cofilin to sever actin filaments and create barbed ends at invadopodia, which support Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization. Once barbed ends are formed, cortactin is dephosphorylated, preventing cofilin from severing actin filaments and thereby stabilizing invadopodia. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of actin polymerization in the invadopodia of metastatic carcinoma cells. Additionally, we have identified four distinct stages of invadopodium assembly and maturation: invadopodium precursor formation, actin polymerization, stabilization, and matrix degradation.

title: Calreticulin exposure dictates the immunogenicity of cancer cell death
text: Tumor cells treated with anthracyclins are highly effective in triggering an immune response against cancer, unlike other DNA-damaging agents like etoposide and mitomycin C which do not cause immunogenic cell death. Our study demonstrates that anthracyclins cause calreticulin (CRT) to rapidly move to the surface of the cell before apoptosis occurs. When CRT is blocked or reduced, dendritic cells are unable to engulf anthracyclin-treated tumor cells, and their ability to stimulate an immune response in mice is eliminated. The translocation of CRT induced by anthracyclins can be replicated by inhibiting the protein phosphatase 1/GADD34 complex. By administering recombinant CRT or inhibitors of protein phosphatase 1/GADD34, we were able to restore the immunogenicity of cell death caused by etoposide and mitomycin C, and enhance their effectiveness against tumors in vivo. These findings highlight the importance of CRT in determining immune responses against cancer and suggest a potential strategy for immunogenic chemotherapy.

title: In vivo disruption of Xenopus U3 snRNA affects ribosomal RNA processing.
text: We injected a DNA oligonucleotide that complements sequences in the 5' third of U3 snRNA into the nuclei of Xenopus oocytes. This injection was done to disrupt the natural U3 snRNA present in the oocytes. We then examined the impact of this disruption on the processing of rRNA. Our findings revealed that certain toads have only one pathway for rRNA processing, while others have the ability to have two pathways coexist within a single oocyte. When U3 snRNA was disrupted in toads with the single rRNA processing pathway, there was a decrease in the levels of 20S and '32S' pre-rRNA. On the other hand, in toads with two rRNA processing pathways, there was an increase in the levels of '36S' pre-rRNA from the second pathway. This experiment provides the first in vivo evidence that U3 snRNA plays a role in the processing of rRNA. We also discovered that cleavage site #3, which is located at the boundary of ITS 1 and 5.8S, is responsible for linking all the affected rRNA intermediates. In the first pathway, cleavage at site #3 produces the 20S and '32S' products, while in the second pathway, the '36S' pre-rRNA serves as the substrate for cleavage at site #3. Based on these findings, we propose that U3 snRNP assists in folding pre-rRNA into a specific conformation that ensures proper cleavage at processing site #3.

title: A genome-wide siRNA screen reveals diverse cellular processes and pathways that mediate genome stability.
text:
The maintenance of genome stability is crucial for the proper functioning of cells and is associated with various diseases, including cancer. To better understand this process, we conducted a comprehensive study using a genome-wide siRNA screen. Our aim was to identify additional genes that play a role in genome stabilization by monitoring the phosphorylation of a specific histone variant called H2AX, which is an early indicator of DNA damage. Through this screen, we discovered numerous genes whose downregulation resulted in increased levels of H2AX phosphorylation (known as gammaH2AX). These genes are associated with cellular complexes and have functions that are not yet classified.

Our research also revealed the significant involvement of mRNA-processing factors in preventing DNA damage. In some cases, this damage is caused by abnormal RNA-DNA structures. Additionally, we found a connection between elevated gammaH2AX levels and a neurological disorder called Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) syndrome. Furthermore, we identified several CMT proteins that play a role in the response to DNA damage.

These findings highlight the fact that the preservation of genome stability involves a larger network of biological processes than previously recognized.

title: Alphavbeta6-Fyn signaling promotes oral cancer progression.
text: Previous research has demonstrated that the integrin beta6 is newly expressed in invasive oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and is associated with the advancement of oral tumors. However, the precise mechanism by which integrin beta6 contributes to the progression of oral tumors remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether integrin beta6 signaling triggers the activation of Fyn, thereby facilitating the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma. We examined the integrin beta6 signaling complex and explored the role of these signaling molecules in oral SCC cells. Our findings revealed that when the integrin beta6 binds to fibronectin, it forms a complex with Fyn and activates it. The activation of Fyn then recruited and activated focal adhesion kinase within this complex. This complex was crucial for the activation of Shc and for connecting beta6 signaling to the Raf-ERK/MAPK pathway. This pathway, in turn, transcriptionally activated the matrix metalloproteinase-3 gene, promoting the proliferation of oral SCC cells and facilitating experimental metastasis in vivo. These results suggest that integrin beta6 signaling triggers the activation of Fyn, thereby promoting the progression of oral cancer.

title: miRNA-dependent gene silencing involving Ago2-mediated cleavage of a circular antisense RNA.
text: In human cells, microRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that are approximately 22 nucleotides long. They typically bind to the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of target messenger RNAs (mRNAs) in the cytoplasm. This binding leads to destabilization of the mRNA and repression of translation. However, our research reveals that miRNAs can also regulate gene expression by targeting non-coding antisense transcripts. Specifically, we have discovered that miR-671 is responsible for cleaving a circular antisense transcript of the Cerebellar Degeneration-Related protein 1 (CDR1) locus. This cleavage occurs in a manner that depends on the Ago2-slicer protein. As a result, the circular antisense transcript is downregulated, leading to a decrease in CDR1 mRNA levels. Importantly, this downregulation occurs independently of heterochromatin formation. This study provides the first evidence that non-coding antisense transcripts can be functional targets of miRNAs. It also uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism that involves a positive correlation between mRNA and antisense circular RNA levels.

title: Regulation of Serum Amyloid A3 (SAA3) in Mouse Colonic Epithelium and Adipose Tissue by the Intestinal Microbiota
text: The gut microbiota is believed to be an environmental factor that influences the development of metabolic and inflammatory diseases in mammals. Recent studies have shown that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) derived from gut bacteria can trigger obesity and insulin resistance in mice. However, the specific molecular interactions responsible for the microbial regulation of host metabolism and inflammation have not been thoroughly investigated. Hepatic serum amyloid A (SAA) proteins are markers and potential mediators of inflammation that are found in higher levels in the serum of insulin-resistant mice. SAA3, derived from adipose tissue, has been shown to have chemotactic activity for monocytes and may contribute to metabolic inflammation associated with obesity and insulin resistance. To explore the potential link between the gut microbiota and the induction of proinflammatory factors, we conducted molecular analyses using germ-free, conventionally raised, and genetically modified Myd88-/- mouse models. We found that the presence of intestinal microbes significantly increased SAA3 expression in adipose tissue (9.9+/-1.9-fold; P<0.001) and colonic tissue (7.0+/-2.3-fold; P<0.05). In the colon, we discovered that SAA3 is partially regulated through the Toll-like receptor (TLR)/MyD88/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. We identified epithelial cells and macrophages as the cellular sources of SAA3 in the colon and observed that colonic epithelial expression of SAA3 may be a response to LPS from gut bacteria that is dependent on NF-kappaB. In vitro experiments demonstrated that LPS treatment induced SAA3 expression in both epithelial cells and macrophages (27.1+/-2.5-fold vs. 1.6+/-0.1-fold, respectively). Our findings suggest that LPS, as well as other products of the gut microbiota, may increase cytokine expression in tissues and contribute to the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in obesity.

title: Reversing the tide — diagnosis and prevention of T2DM in populations of African descent
text: Summary | Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a significant health issue for populations of African descent worldwide. The problem is worsened by late diagnosis, leading to preventable complications. Early detection is crucial for reducing undiagnosed cases, improving data accuracy, resource allocation, and overall health outcomes. One overlooked factor contributing to undiagnosed T2DM in these populations is the suboptimal performance of screening tests for hyperglycemia, such as fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c. To address this issue, combining tests or incorporating glycated albumin as a nonfasting marker of glycaemia may be beneficial. However, due to various factors like diet, exercise, BMI, environment, gene-environment interactions, and the prevalence of sickle cell trait, diagnostic tests and interventions may not have uniform effectiveness in individuals of African, Caribbean, or African-American descent. Intensive lifestyle interventions have shown promise in preventing T2DM in African-Americans but not in secondary prevention. Customized lifestyle interventions tailored to the specific needs of African and Caribbean populations, considering their low health literacy and poor glycaemic control, may be effective in both primary and secondary prevention. In conclusion, innovative strategies that acknowledge the diversity within populations of African descent are necessary for the diagnosis and prevention of T2DM.

title: Biofeedback and relaxation in the treatment of migraine headaches: comparative effectiveness and physiological correlates.
text: A total of 27 individuals suffering from migraine headaches were divided into three groups of equal size. Each group received a different form of treatment: thermal biofeedback, frontalis EMG biofeedback, or relaxation training. The training sessions were conducted intensively, with nine sessions per week, consisting of 18 training sessions and six test-generalisation sessions. Although all groups showed improvements in their headaches, the group that received thermal biofeedback experienced the most significant improvements. By the end of the training, this group nearly eliminated their migraine attacks and maintained this progress for up to six months afterward. Additionally, analyzing the changes in skin temperature and EMG patterns throughout the training period suggests a correlation between controlling skin temperature and reducing migraine symptoms. This finding indicates the need for further investigation into this relationship.

title: Fine-scale chromatin interaction maps reveal the cis-regulatory landscape of human lincRNA genes
text: Advancements in our understanding of the three-dimensional (3D) structure of genomes have been made possible by high-throughput methods based on chromosome conformation capture. However, these methods have limitations in resolution due to their reliance on restriction enzymes. In this study, we introduce a new method called DNase Hi-C, which utilizes DNase I for chromatin fragmentation. This approach significantly enhances efficiency and resolution compared to traditional Hi-C. By combining DNase Hi-C with DNA-capture technology, we have developed a high-throughput method for accurately mapping fine-scale chromatin architecture. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we applied targeted DNase Hi-C to analyze the 3D organization of 998 large intergenic noncoding RNA (lincRNA) promoters in two human cell lines. Our findings reveal that the expression of lincRNAs is intricately regulated by a combination of super-enhancers and the Polycomb repressive complex. This study provides valuable insights into the cell type-specific 3D organization of lincRNA genes.

title: BASOPHILS AND THE T HELPER 2 ENVIRONMENT CAN PROMOTE THE DEVELOPMENT OF LUPUS NEPHRITIS
text: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the kidneys can be targeted by self-reactive antibodies, resulting in kidney failure and potential mortality. Our findings indicate that autoreactive IgE can activate basophils, causing them to migrate to lymph nodes. This promotes the differentiation of T helper type 2 (T(H)2) cells and increases the production of self-reactive antibodies, which contribute to lupus-like nephritis in mice lacking the Lyn protein tyrosine kinase. Individuals with SLE also exhibit elevated levels of serum IgE, self-reactive IgEs, and activated basophils expressing CD62 ligand (CD62L) and the human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR) molecule, which are associated with increased disease activity and active lupus nephritis. Basophils are also present in the lymph nodes and spleen of SLE patients. Therefore, in Lyn(-/-) mice, basophils and IgE autoantibodies amplify the production of autoantibodies that lead to lupus nephritis. Similarly, in individuals with SLE, IgE autoantibodies and activated basophils are factors associated with disease activity and nephritis.

title: Behavioral treatment of obesity in patients encountered in primary care settings: a systematic review.
text: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) approved intensive behavioral weight loss counseling for obese patients in primary care settings in 2011. The objective of this study was to review the effectiveness of behavioral counseling for overweight and obese patients in primary care, delivered by primary care practitioners or trained interventionists. A systematic review was conducted, searching for randomized controlled trials that recruited overweight and obese patients from primary care and provided behavioral counseling for at least 3 months. Twelve trials involving 3893 participants met the criteria. No studies were found where primary care practitioners followed the CMS guidelines. Weight loss in the intervention groups ranged from 0.3 kg to 6.6 kg at 6 months, while the control group had a change ranging from a gain of 0.9 kg to a loss of 2.0 kg. Weight loss generally decreased with longer follow-up. Interventions that included reduced energy intake, increased physical activity, and behavioral therapy produced larger weight loss. More treatment sessions, delivered in person or by telephone by trained interventionists, were associated with greater weight loss. In conclusion, intensive behavioral counseling can lead to significant weight loss, but there is limited research on primary care practitioners providing this care. Trained interventionists could be considered for treating overweight or obesity in primary care settings.

title: Guanylate binding protein 1 is a novel effector of EGFR-driven invasion in glioblastoma
text: The function of GBP1 (guanylate binding protein 1) remains largely unknown, despite being one of the first interferon-inducible proteins discovered. Genetic abnormalities involving the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) through amplification or mutation are common in various human tumors, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). GBM is characterized by invasive growth into normal brain tissue, rapid growth, necrosis, and angiogenesis. Our study demonstrates that EGFR activation stimulates the expression of GBP1 in GBM cell lines through a signaling pathway involving Src and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase. Additionally, we have identified YY1 (Yin Yang 1) as the downstream transcriptional regulator responsible for regulating EGFR-driven GBP1 expression. GBP1 is essential for EGFR-mediated MMP1 (matrix metalloproteinase 1) expression and the invasion of glioma cells in vitro. While deregulation of GBP1 expression does not affect glioma cell proliferation, overexpression of GBP1 enhances glioma cell invasion by inducing MMP1 expression. This process is dependent on the C-terminal helical domain of GBP1 and is unrelated to its GTPase activity. Furthermore, reducing GBP1 levels through RNA interference significantly inhibits the ability of invasive GBM cells to infiltrate the brain tissue in mice. In human GBM tumors and cell lines, particularly those of the neural subtype, GBP1 expression is high and positively correlated with EGFR expression. These findings establish GBP1 as a previously unknown connection between EGFR activity and MMP1 expression, suggesting it as a potential therapeutic target for inhibiting GBM invasion.

title: ATP binding to PAN or the 26S ATPases causes association with the 20S proteasome, gate opening, and translocation of unfolded proteins.
text: The archaeal ATPase complex PAN, which is similar to the eukaryotic 26S proteasome-regulatory ATPases, has been observed to temporarily associate with the 20S proteasome when ATP or ATPgammaS is bound, but not when ADP is present. Using electron microscopy (EM), PAN appears as a two-ring structure that covers the 20S and resembles two densities in the 19S complex. The N termini of the archaeal 20S alpha subunits act as a gate, preventing the entry of seven-residue peptides but allowing tetrapeptides to pass through. When PAN binds to the 20S particle, it stimulates the opening of the gate. While the degradation of globular proteins requires ATP hydrolysis, the PAN-20S complex with ATPgammaS is able to transport and break down unfolded and denatured proteins. Similarly, rabbit 26S proteasomes can degrade these unfolded proteins upon ATP binding, without hydrolysis. Therefore, although the process of unfolding requires energy from ATP hydrolysis, the binding of ATP alone supports the association of ATPase-20S, the opening of the gate, and the translocation of unfolded substrates into the proteasome. This translocation can occur through facilitated diffusion facilitated by the ATPase.

title: Cytokines and anti-cytokine biologicals in autoimmunity: present and future.
text: The growing understanding of cytokines' role in autoimmunity, along with the recognition that tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) plays a central role in the inflammatory and destructive processes seen in various human autoimmune diseases, has led to the emergence of a new generation of therapeutics known as TNFalpha blocking agents. This article provides an overview of the current knowledge regarding cytokines' involvement in autoimmunity, as revealed through laboratory and clinical studies. Additionally, it explores potential future prospects for anti-TNFalpha therapy, including the possibility of combining it with other anti-cytokine or anti-T cell biologicals, or utilizing small chemicals that target molecules involved in TNFalpha production, such as NF-kappaB and p38 MAPK. The future advancements in anti-TNFalpha and anti-cytokine therapy as a whole hold great interest.

title: Vegetarian dietary patterns and mortality in Adventist Health Study 2.
text: The importance of vegetarian dietary patterns in reducing mortality is not well established. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the association between vegetarian diets and mortality. The study was conducted on a large cohort of Seventh-day Adventist men and women recruited between 2002 and 2007. After exclusions, a total of 73,308 participants were included in the analysis. Diet was assessed at baseline using a food frequency questionnaire and categorized into five dietary patterns: nonvegetarian, semi-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, and vegan. The main outcome measured was the relationship between vegetarian diets and all-cause and cause-specific mortality. Deaths were identified from the National Death Index. During a mean follow-up time of 5.79 years, there were 2570 deaths among the participants. The mortality rate was 6.05 deaths per 1000 person-years. After adjusting for important demographic and lifestyle factors, the hazard ratio for all-cause mortality in all vegetarians combined compared to nonvegetarians was 0.88. The hazard ratio for all-cause mortality in vegans was 0.85, in lacto-ovo-vegetarians was 0.91, in pesco-vegetarians was 0.81, and in semi-vegetarians was 0.92, all compared to nonvegetarians. Significant associations with vegetarian diets were found for cardiovascular mortality, noncardiovascular noncancer mortality, renal mortality, and endocrine mortality. These associations were more pronounced in men than in women. In conclusion, vegetarian diets are associated with lower all-cause mortality and some reductions in cause-specific mortality, particularly in males. These findings should be carefully considered by those providing dietary guidance.

title: TEAD mediates YAP-dependent gene induction and growth control.
text: The YAP transcription coactivator has been linked to cancer and is amplified in human tumors. Recent research has shown that the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway phosphorylates and inhibits YAP. Our study demonstrates that the TEAD family of transcription factors is crucial for YAP-dependent gene expression. TEAD is also necessary for YAP-induced cell growth, oncogenic transformation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. We have identified CTGF as a direct target gene of YAP that is important for cell growth. Additionally, the relationship between YAP and TEAD is conserved in Drosophila, with Yki (the YAP homolog) and Scalloped (the TEAD homolog) playing similar roles. Our findings reveal TEAD as a new component of the Hippo pathway, playing essential roles in mediating the biological functions of YAP.

title: Direct isolation of human central nervous system stem cells.
text: Stem cells possess the ability to replace or repair damaged tissue due to their clonogenic nature, self-renewal capabilities, and ability to differentiate into multiple cell types. In our study, we successfully isolated clonogenic stem cells from fresh human fetal brain tissue, specifically the central nervous system (hCNS-SC). This isolation was achieved by utilizing antibodies that target cell surface markers and a technique called fluorescence-activated cell sorting. The hCNS-SC we obtained displayed a distinct phenotype, being positive for 5F3 (CD133) and 5E12 markers, while negative for CD34, CD45, and CD24 markers. By sorting and culturing single cells that were positive for CD133, but negative for CD34 and CD45, we were able to generate neurosphere cultures. These clonogenic cells within the neurospheres had the ability to differentiate into both neurons and glial cells. Furthermore, we demonstrated the self-renewal potential of this highly enriched population by replating single cells from the neurosphere cultures, which successfully reestablished neurosphere cultures. To assess the functionality of these hCNS-SC, we transplanted them into the brains of immunodeficient neonatal mice. The sorted and expanded hCNS-SC exhibited robust engraftment, proliferation, migration, and neural differentiation within the mouse brains.

title: p53 mutation in breast cancer. Correlation with cell kinetics and cell of origin.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare p53 mutations with various phenotypic and differentiation markers in breast cancer. The expression of cytokeratins, vimentin, EGFR, ER, and PgR was investigated in previous studies, but no study has directly compared these markers with p53 mutations in the same case. Therefore, this study aimed to provide this information. 

The methods involved evaluating the expression of p53 and bcl-2 proteins using immunohistochemistry in 37 cases of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and 27 cases of infiltrating ductal carcinoma (IDC) of the breast. Additionally, p53 gene mutation was examined using polymerase chain reaction single strand conformation polymorphism analysis (SSCP). 

The results showed that some cases exhibited a stem cell phenotype, characterized by expression of CK8, CK14, CK18, vimentin, and EGFR. Other cases exhibited a luminal cell phenotype, characterized by expression of CK8 and CK1, weak or negative expression of CK18, and negative expression of vimentin and EGFR. The stem cell phenotype cases were ER/PgR negative and intermediately or poorly differentiated, while the luminal cell phenotype cases were ER/PgR positive and well or intermediately differentiated. The stem cell phenotype cases also showed higher proliferative activity compared to the luminal cell phenotype cases. 

Furthermore, the stem cell phenotype cases were p53 positive and bcl-2 negative, while the luminal cell phenotype cases were p53 negative and bcl-2 positive. In IDC, p53 expression was associated with a reduction in both mitotic index and apoptotic index compared to DCIS. The more differentiated luminal phenotype cases showed increased cell kinetic parameters from DCIS to IDC. 

These findings suggest that there are subsets of DCIS and IDC that may originate from different subpopulations of normal breast cells with distinct control mechanisms of cell proliferation and neoplastic progression. However, it is also possible that p53 mutants occur by chance during neoplastic transformation. 

In conclusion, these results support the hypothesis that the phenotype of the cell of origin influences both tumor phenotype and the choice of genetic events. However, the possibility of p53 mutants occurring randomly during neoplastic transformation cannot be ruled out.

title: Cardiorespiratory fitness and body mass index as predictors of cardiovascular disease mortality among men with diabetes.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether higher levels of cardiorespiratory fitness are linked to a lower risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in overweight and obese individuals with diabetes. The study used data from the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study, including 2316 men with diabetes who had no history of stroke or myocardial infarction. The participants underwent a medical examination and a maximal exercise test between 1970 and 1997, with mortality surveillance until December 31, 1998. The main outcome measure was CVD mortality, and the results showed that men with a low fitness level had a significantly higher risk of mortality compared to those with a high fitness level, regardless of their weight category. In conclusion, low fitness level was associated with an increased risk of CVD mortality in men with diabetes, regardless of their weight.

title: Effect of screening on cervical cancer mortality in England and Wales: analysis of trends with an age period cohort model.
text: In 1997, the number of women who died from cervical cancer was 7% lower compared to 1996. Furthermore, there has been a significant decrease of over 25% since 1992. This rapid decline can be attributed, at least in part, to cervical screening. However, it is important to note that previous fluctuations in cervical mortality have been influenced by strong cohort effects. To estimate the positive impact of cervical screening, we conducted a study using mortality data. This involved considering age and year of birth, as well as identifying trends within four age groups over time. The mortality data was obtained from death registrations in England and Wales, categorized into 5-year age bands, and rates were calculated using mid-year population estimates. To account for changes in the classification of cause of death, mortality rates since 1993 were adjusted upwards by 4%. Our analysis assumed that age-specific mortality is influenced by a smoothly varying age effect, birth cohort effect, and age-dependent factors.

title: The regulation of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors by Src kinase.
text: SFKs, known as Src family kinases, play crucial roles in controlling various cellular functions through growth factors, G-protein-coupled receptors, and ligand-gated ion channels. Recent research has revealed that SFKs act as a convergence point for multiple signaling pathways that regulate N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in the central nervous system. Key SFK molecules like Src and Fyn closely interact with NMDA receptors, employing both direct and indirect binding mechanisms. The SFK signaling complex associated with the NMDA receptor consists of SFKs, the SFK-activating phosphatase protein tyrosine phosphatase α, and the SFK-inactivating kinase C-terminal Src kinase. Early studies have shown that intramolecular interactions involving the SH2 or SH3 domain keep SFKs in a closed conformation. Disrupting these interdomain interactions can activate SFKs, triggering multiple signaling pathways involved in the regulation of this process. The enzyme activity of SFKs exhibits a graded pattern, with different levels corresponding to their activation states. Additionally, it has been suggested that the SH2 and SH3 domains may enhance the catalytic activity of protein tyrosine kinases like Abl. Recent findings indicate that the enzyme activity of neuronal Src protein is linked to its stability, and the interactions between the SH2 and SH3 domains not only restrict the activation of neuronal Src but also regulate its enzyme activity when it is active. Overall, these discoveries unveil new mechanisms that govern the regulation of SFKs.

title: The art and design of genetic screens: RNA interference
text: The incredible RNAi gene knockdown technique has revolutionized genetic screening in both model organisms and human cells, presenting thrilling opportunities. In this article, we will discuss the current advancements in RNAi screening and emphasize the significance of meticulously designed assays and analytical methods for conducting extensive screening experiments. These experiments range from simplified homogenous assays in high-throughput screens to more complex microscopy and whole-animal experiments. Similar to traditional genetic screens, the triumph of large-scale RNAi surveys relies on the thoughtful creation of phenotypic assays and their interpretation within a biologically relevant framework.

title: Computer assisted learning in undergraduate medical education.
text:
The use of computer assisted learning is increasingly recognized as a valuable tool in the education of undergraduate medical students. The availability of various online options can make learning more engaging, effective, and memorable. However, it is important to note that this assumption is not always true. 

Box 1: Reasons to invest in computer assisted learning:

1. Inevitability: Many lecturers and departments are already incorporating computer based applications into their teaching methods. However, a planned and coordinated approach is preferable to haphazard expansion.

2. Convenience and flexibility: Courses supported by computer assisted learning can reduce the need for in-person lectures and seminars, allowing for greater flexibility in terms of time and location. This is particularly beneficial for students in peripheral hospitals or primary care centers.

3. Enhanced presentation: Computer presentations are well-suited for visually intensive subjects that are difficult to grasp, such as complex biochemical processes or microscopic images. Additionally, virtual cases can reduce the reliance on animal or human tissue for learning purposes.

4. Personalized learning: Each student can progress at their own pace, with the ability to repeat, pause, and resume as needed. This can be especially advantageous for weaker students.

5. Economies of scale: Once a computer application is set up, the cost of offering it to additional students is relatively low.

6. Competitive advantage: The quality of information technology can be a deciding factor for potential medical school applicants. A technologically advanced virtual campus is likely to attract high-caliber students.

7. Achieving the goal of higher education: The ultimate aim is to connect individuals within learning communities. Computer applications, particularly the internet and world wide web, provide an efficient means of achieving this.

8. Expanding pedagogical horizons: The use of computer assisted learning opens up new possibilities for teaching methods and approaches.

Overall, while computer assisted learning has numerous potential benefits, it is important to approach its implementation with careful planning and consideration.

title: Combined Impact of Health Behaviours and Mortality in Men and Women: The EPIC-Norfolk Prospective Population Study
text:
The evidence supporting the influence of behavioral factors on health is overwhelming, but their collective impact on the general population is not well-documented. Our objective was to quantify the potential combined effect of four health behaviors on mortality in men and women living in the general community. 

In this study, we examined the relationship between lifestyle and mortality in a population study of 20,244 individuals aged 45-79 years with no known cardiovascular disease or cancer at the start of the study in 1993-1997. These participants were living in the United Kingdom and were followed up until 2006. 

Each participant was assigned a score based on four health behaviors: non-smoking, physical activity, moderate alcohol intake (1-14 units per week), and adequate fruit and vegetable intake (at least five servings per day). The total score ranged from zero to four. 

After an average follow-up of 11 years, we found that individuals with fewer health behaviors had a higher risk of all-cause mortality. The relative risks for all-cause mortality, adjusted for age, sex, body mass, and social class, were 1.39, 1.95, 2.52, and 4.04 for individuals with three, two, one, and zero health behaviors, respectively, compared to those with four health behaviors. These relationships held true across different subgroups, including sex, age, body mass index, and social class. The trends were particularly strong for cardiovascular causes of death. 

The mortality risk for individuals with four health behaviors was equivalent to being 14 years younger in chronological age compared to those with zero health behaviors. 

In conclusion, the combination of four health behaviors predicts a four-fold difference in total mortality in both men and women, with an estimated impact equivalent to being 14 years younger.

title: Increased Cell Bond Tension Governs Cell Sorting at the Drosophila Anteroposterior Compartment Boundary
text:
The subdivision of proliferating tissues into compartments is a strategy of animal development that has been conserved throughout evolution [1-6]. Communication between these compartments through signals can lead to the organization and growth of tissues through the expression of secreted proteins [1-6]. It is crucial to have distinct and defined boundaries between these compartments in order to stabilize the position of these organizers and ensure precise implementation of body plans. However, the mechanisms that maintain these boundaries in proliferating tissues are not well understood. 

In this study, we examined the cell morphology and response to laser ablation of cell bonds near the anteroposterior compartment boundary in developing Drosophila wings. We discovered that there is approximately a 2.5-fold increase in mechanical tension on cell bonds along this boundary compared to the rest of the tissue. This tension is reduced in the presence of Y-27632, an inhibitor of Rho-kinase, which is known to affect Myosin II, the main effector of Rho-kinase [8]. 

Using simulations with a vertex model [9], we demonstrated that a 2.5-fold increase in local cell bond tension is sufficient to guide the rearrangement of cells after cell division and maintain compartment boundaries. Our findings provide a physical mechanism in which the increase in Myosin II-dependent cell bond tension directs cell sorting at compartment boundaries.

title: Plant products as antimicrobial agents.
text:
In recent years, there has been a significant increase in the use and search for drugs and dietary supplements derived from plants. Experts in ethnopharmacology, botany, microbiology, and natural-products chemistry are actively exploring the Earth in search of phytochemicals and potential treatments for infectious diseases. Although 25 to 50% of current pharmaceuticals are derived from plants, none are currently used as antimicrobials. However, traditional healers have long relied on plants to prevent or cure infectious conditions, and Western medicine is now attempting to replicate their successes.

Plants are a valuable source of various secondary metabolites, including tannins, terpenoids, alkaloids, and flavonoids, which have demonstrated antimicrobial properties in laboratory studies. This review aims to provide an overview of ongoing botanical screening efforts and in vivo studies evaluating their effectiveness and toxicity. Additionally, the structure and antimicrobial properties of phytochemicals are discussed.

It is important for clinicians to consider the implications of patients self-medicating with unregulated botanical preparations, as many of these compounds are readily available and their use by the public is rapidly increasing. Therefore, understanding the potential consequences of such self-medication is crucial.

title: Nature, Nurture, or Chance: Stochastic Gene Expression and Its Consequences
text: The process of gene expression is inherently random, resulting in differences in mRNA and protein levels between cells. This variability is observed in various organisms, from small microbes to complex metazoans, and is influenced by both the physical properties of gene expression and the structure of gene networks. The stochastic nature of gene expression has significant implications for cellular function, with both positive and negative effects. Examples of these effects can be seen in the stress response, metabolism, development, the cell cycle, circadian rhythms, and aging.

title: Nuclear Hormone Receptor NHR-49 Controls Fat Consumption and Fatty Acid Composition in C. elegans
text: The control of energy metabolism in mammals is precisely regulated by nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs) such as liver X receptor, farnesoid X receptor, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs). These receptors are important targets for treating metabolic diseases like diabetes and obesity. However, our understanding of NHR fat regulatory networks has been limited due to a lack of genetically tractable experimental systems. In this study, we demonstrate that deleting the NHR gene nhr-49 in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans resulted in worms with increased fat content and a shorter lifespan. Through a quantitative RT-PCR screen, we identified 13 genes involved in energy metabolism that were influenced by nhr-49. Specifically, nhr-49 played a crucial role in regulating fat usage by modulating pathways that control fat consumption and maintain a normal balance of fatty acid saturation. We discovered that the two phenotypes observed in the nhr-49 knockout worms were linked to distinct pathways and could be separated: the high-fat phenotype was caused by reduced expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, while the shortened lifespan was a result of impaired expression of a stearoyl-CoA desaturase. Despite its sequence similarity to the mammalian hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 receptor, nhr-49 exhibited biological activities most similar to those of mammalian PPARs, suggesting a conserved role for NHRs in regulating fat consumption and composition. Our findings in C. elegans provide new insights into the coordination of NHR regulatory networks in governing fat metabolism.

title: Folate and vitamin B6 from diet and supplements in relation to risk of coronary heart disease among women.
text:
CONTEXT: Hyperhomocysteinemia is a condition caused by genetic and lifestyle factors, such as low intake of folate and vitamin B6. However, there is a lack of prospective data on the relationship between the intake of these vitamins and the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the intake of folate and vitamin B6 in relation to the incidence of nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI) and fatal CHD.

DESIGN: The study was a prospective cohort study.

SETTING AND PATIENTS: In 1980, a total of 80,082 women from the Nurses' Health Study, who had no previous history of cardiovascular disease, cancer, hypercholesterolemia, or diabetes, completed a detailed food frequency questionnaire. The researchers derived the usual intake of folate and vitamin B6 from this questionnaire.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The main outcome measures were nonfatal MI and fatal CHD, confirmed using World Health Organization criteria.

RESULTS: Over a 14-year follow-up period, the researchers documented 658 incident cases of nonfatal MI and 281 cases of fatal CHD. After adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors, including smoking, hypertension, alcohol intake, fiber, vitamin E, and saturated, polyunsaturated, and trans fat, the relative risks (RRs) of CHD between the highest and lowest quintiles were 0.69 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.55-0.87) for folate (median intake, 696 microg/d vs 158 microg/d) and 0.67 (95% CI, 0.53-0.85) for vitamin B6 (median intake, 4.6 mg/d vs 1.1 mg/d). When controlling for the same variables, the RR was 0.55 (95% CI, 0.41-0.74) among women in the highest quintile of both folate and vitamin B6 intake compared to the lowest quintile. The risk of CHD was also reduced among women who regularly used multiple vitamins (RR=0.76; 95% CI, 0.65-0.90), which are the main source of folate and vitamin B6. Additionally, excluding multiple vitamin users, those with higher dietary intakes of folate and vitamin B6 also had a lower risk of CHD. In a subgroup analysis, the inverse association between a high-folate diet and CHD was strongest among women who consumed up to 1 alcoholic beverage per day (RR=0.69; 95% CI, 0.49-0.97) or more than 1 drink per day (RR=0.27; 95% CI, 0.13-0.58).

CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that consuming folate and vitamin B6 above the recommended dietary allowance may play a crucial role in the primary prevention of CHD among women.

title: Control of oocyte meiotic maturation and fertilization.
text: Meiosis is crucial for sexual reproduction as it produces haploid gamete nuclei, which combine during fertilization to create a diploid zygote. In most animal species, oocytes pause during meiotic prophase and complete meiosis when they receive signals from neighboring cells, a process known as meiotic maturation. This maturation involves the transition from diakinesis to metaphase of meiosis I, accompanied by the breakdown of the nuclear envelope, rearrangement of the cortical cytoskeleton, and assembly of the meiotic spindle. Therefore, meiotic maturation is vital for meiosis and prepares the oocyte for fertilization. In C. elegans, meiotic maturation, ovulation, and fertilization are synchronized: sperm use a hormone called major sperm protein to trigger oocyte meiotic maturation, and in response, the maturing oocyte signals its own ovulation, facilitating fertilization. This chapter focuses on recent advancements in understanding the signaling of meiotic maturation and the interactions between gametes necessary for successful fertilization.

title: From Cell Differentiation to Cell Collectives: Bacillus subtilis Uses Division of Labor to Migrate
text: Collective properties can arise from the organization of cells through cell-cell interactions. These properties become advantageous when cells work together to overcome environmental challenges that they cannot handle individually. Migration is a significant challenge for microorganisms, and in this research, we demonstrate how flagellum-independent migration occurs through the division of labor between two cell types in Bacillus subtilis sliding motility. Cell collectives form tightly aligned chains known as "van Gogh bundles," which create filamentous loops at the edge of the colony. Through time-course microscopy, we observe that these loops migrate by pushing themselves away from the colony. The formation of van Gogh bundles relies on the synergistic interaction between surfactin-producing and matrix-producing cells. Surfactin-producing cells reduce friction between cells and their substrate, enabling matrix-producing cells to form bundles. The folding properties of these bundles determine the rate at which the colony expands. Our study highlights how the simple organization of cells within a community can provide a significant ecological advantage, which is a crucial factor in the development of multicellularity.

title: Tissue-resident macrophages self-maintain locally throughout adult life with minimal contribution from circulating monocytes.
text: Despite accumulating evidence suggesting that tissue macrophages are self-maintained locally in the steady state, the prevailing belief is that tissue macrophages originate from monocytes. Through the use of parabiosis and fate-mapping techniques, we have confirmed that monocytes do not significantly contribute to tissue macrophages in the steady state. Additionally, we have discovered that when lung macrophages are depleted, the majority of repopulation occurs through stochastic cellular proliferation in situ, dependent on macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-Csf) and granulocyte macrophage (GM)-CSF, but independent of interleukin-4. Furthermore, our findings indicate that host macrophages retain the ability to expand even when the development of donor macrophages is compromised after bone marrow transplantation. This expansion of host macrophages is functional and prevents the development of alveolar proteinosis in mice with GM-Csf-receptor-deficient progenitors. In conclusion, these results suggest that tissue-resident macrophages and circulating monocytes should be classified as separate mononuclear phagocyte lineages that are independently maintained in the steady state.

title: Registration and real-time visualization of transcranial magnetic stimulation with 3-D MR images
text: This paper presents a technique for registering and visualizing the outcomes of transcranial magnetic stimulations (TMS) in real-time on corresponding anatomical locations in MR images of the brain. The method consists of three main steps. Initially, the patient's scalp is digitized in physical space using a magnetic-field digitizer, following a specific digitization pattern. Next, a registration process is employed to minimize the mean square distance between these points and a segmented scalp surface extracted from the magnetic resonance image. Once this registration is complete, the physician can track the change in coil position in real-time through the visualization interface and adjust it to the desired anatomical location. Lastly, the amplitude of motor evoked potentials can be projected onto the segmented brain to generate functional brain maps. In a study using simulated data, the registration achieved subpixel accuracy, while in a study involving 24 subjects, the point to surface root-mean-square error was found to be 1.17 ± 0.38 mm.

title: Enzymatic targeting of the stroma ablates physical barriers to treatment of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAs) exhibit a strong fibroinflammatory response. Our research demonstrates that this reaction leads to extremely high interstitial fluid pressures (IFPs), surpassing previous measurements for solid tumors. Additionally, it causes vascular collapse and creates significant obstacles for the delivery of small molecule therapeutics through perfusion, diffusion, and convection. We have identified hyaluronan, also known as hyaluronic acid (HA), as the main factor responsible for these barriers. By administering an enzymatic agent systemically, we can remove stromal HA from autochthonous murine PDA, normalize IFP, and restore the microvasculature. When combined with the standard chemotherapy drug gemcitabine, this treatment permanently alters the tumor microenvironment and consistently leads to positive tumor responses, resulting in a nearly twofold increase in overall survival.

title: Circulating adiponectin, leptin and adiponectin-leptin ratio and endometrial cancer risk: Evidence from a meta-analysis of epidemiologic studies.
text: We conducted a meta-analysis of epidemiological studies to examine the links between circulating adiponectin, leptin, and the adiponectin-leptin (A/L) ratio and the risk of endometrial cancer. We identified relevant articles by searching the PubMed and ISI Web of Science databases, as well as by manually searching the references cited in the retrieved articles. We used random-effects models to estimate the summary odds ratio (SOR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for these associations. Our analysis included 14 articles with a total of 13 studies (five nested case-control and eight case-control studies), involving 1,963 endometrial cancer cases and 3,503 noncases. Overall, comparing individuals with high circulating concentrations of adiponectin, leptin, and A/L ratio (top tertile) to those with low concentrations of these biomarkers (bottom tertile) yielded SORs of 0.47 (95% CI: 0.34-0.65; I(2) = 63.7%; n = 13), 2.19 (95% CI: 1.44-3.31; I(2) = 64.2%; n = 7), and 0.45 (95% CI: 0.24-0.86; I(2) = 90.1%; n = 5), respectively. Notably, there was an 18% reduction in risk for each 5 μg/mL increase in circulating adiponectin concentrations (SOR = 0.82; 95% CI: 0.74-0.90; I(2) = 49%; n = 8). When stratifying the analysis by study characteristics and whether potential confounders were considered or adjusted for, the findings remained consistent for circulating adiponectin and leptin. We did not find any evidence of publication bias. In conclusion, our meta-analysis suggests that higher circulating adiponectin and A/L ratio or lower leptin concentrations are associated with a reduced risk of endometrial cancer. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: CDE-1 Affects Chromosome Segregation through Uridylation of CSR-1-Bound siRNAs
text: Our research focused on understanding the role of a protein called CDE-1 in RNAi and chromosome segregation in C. elegans. We discovered that CDE-1 localizes specifically to mitotic chromosomes in embryos. This localization is dependent on the presence of the RdRP EGO-1, which physically interacts with CDE-1, and the Argonaute protein CSR-1. We also found that CDE-1 is necessary for the uridylation of CSR-1 bound siRNAs. In the absence of CDE-1, these siRNAs accumulate to abnormal levels, leading to defects in both meiotic and mitotic chromosome segregation. The increased levels of siRNAs are associated with incorrect gene silencing, likely due to the inappropriate loading of CSR-1 siRNAs into other Argonaute proteins. Based on our findings, we propose a model in which CDE-1 specifically directs EGO-1-generated siRNAs to the CSR-1 mediated RNAi pathway that is associated with chromosomes, thereby separating it from other endogenous RNAi pathways. The fact that CDE-1 is conserved suggests that similar sorting mechanisms may exist in other animals, including mammals.

title: Localized diacylglycerol drives the polarization of the microtubule-organizing center in T cells
text: The movement of the T cell microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) towards the antigen-presenting cell allows for the targeted release of cytokines and lytic factors. Through the activation of the T cell antigen receptor in individual cells, we have discovered that the polarization of the MTOC is driven by the localized buildup of diacylglycerol (DAG). The reorientation of the MTOC is preceded by the production of DAG and the recruitment of the microtubule motor protein dynein. When DAG production is blocked or the localization of DAG is disrupted, the recruitment of the MTOC is impaired. The accumulation of DAG in specific areas is also necessary for the cytotoxic T cell's ability to kill. Additionally, the activation of DAG alone is enough to cause temporary polarization. Our findings reveal a pathway that relies on DAG and dynein to regulate microtubule polarity in T cells.

title: Dual roles of plcA in Listeria monocytogenes pathogenesis.
text: The Listeria monocytogenes plcA gene codes for a phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (Pl-PLC) that is secreted. Recent research has demonstrated that mutations caused by transposons in plcA lead to the loss of virulence in mice and have various effects when studied in tissue-culture models of infection. Genetic analysis has revealed that many of these effects are a result of the transposon insertions preventing readthrough transcription from plcA into the downstream prfA gene. The prfA gene is responsible for encoding a crucial transcription factor for numerous virulence genes in L. monocytogenes. When an in-frame deletion was made in plcA, it did not impact the expression of prfA, allowing for a direct understanding of the role of Pl-PLC in pathogenesis. Pl-PLC was found to play a significant part in facilitating the escape of L. monocytogenes from phagosomes in primary murine macrophages. Interestingly, this defect was observed in the liver but not in the spleen of infected mice.

title: Fine-tuning in regulation of Clp protein content in Bacillus subtilis.
text: Clp-controlled proteolysis in Bacillus subtilis appears to have a significant role, especially during stressful conditions. To estimate the approximate number of Clp molecules in a single cell, calibrated Western blot analyses were conducted. These analyses suggest that the various Clp ATPases do not compete for the proteolytic subunit ClpP. Coimmunoprecipitation experiments confirmed the predicted specific interactions between ClpX-ClpP, ClpC-ClpP, and ClpE-ClpP. In wild-type cells experiencing continuous heat stress, ClpE and ClpX are rapidly degraded, but in a clpP mutant, they remain relatively stable, indicating ClpP-dependent degradation. Notably, ClpCP seems to be involved in the degradation of the short-lived ClpE ATPase, suggesting a negative "autoregulatory" circuit for this specific Clp ATPase at the posttranslational level. Analysis of the half-life of stress-inducible clp mRNAs during exponential growth and heat shock revealed precise regulation of the synthesis of each Clp protein at the posttranscriptional level, ensuring the requirements of B. subtilis are met.

title: A C-Type Lectin Collaborates with a CD45 Phosphatase Homolog to Facilitate West Nile Virus Infection of Mosquitoes
text: The United States is commonly affected by West Nile virus (WNV), a flavivirus transmitted by arthropods. However, the specific ligands responsible for infection are still unknown. Our research reveals that a C-type lectin called mosGCTL-1, found in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, is induced by WNV. It interacts with the virus in a calcium-dependent manner and facilitates infection both in vivo and in vitro. Another protein, mosPTP-1, which is similar to human CD45, recruits mosGCTL-1 to enable viral attachment to cells and enhance viral entry. In experiments conducted on mosquitoes, we found that mosGCTL-1 and mosPTP-1 are part of the same pathway and are crucial for WNV infection. This phenomenon was also observed in Culex quinquefasciatus, a natural WNV vector, further confirming the involvement of these genes in WNV infection. Additionally, when mosGCTL-1 antibodies were used during mosquito blood-feeding, WNV infection was blocked in vivo. Understanding the interactions between flaviviruses and arthropods at a molecular level could potentially lead to strategies for controlling the spread of these viruses in nature.

title: Use of human embryonic stem cells to model pediatric gliomas with H3.3K27M histone mutation
text: More than 70% of aggressive brainstem tumors in pediatric patients, known as diffuse intrinsic pediatric gliomas, have a specific genetic mutation. This mutation causes a substitution of an amino acid called lysine with methionine at position 27 in the tail of a protein called histone H3.3. The exact role of this mutation, known as H3.3K27M, in the development of these tumors is not fully understood. To gain insight into this, researchers used a system involving human embryonic stem cells to model the tumor. They discovered that the expression of H3.3K27M, along with the loss of a tumor suppressor gene called p53 and the activation of a gene called PDGFRA, led to the transformation of neural progenitor cells derived from human embryonic stem cells into cancerous cells. Further analysis revealed that these transformed cells reverted to a more primitive stem cell state, with significant changes in the chemical modifications of histones at key regulatory genes. Through drug screening experiments, the researchers identified a compound that targets a protein called menin, which was found to inhibit the growth of tumor cells both in laboratory tests and in mice.

title: Basis for avid homologous DNA strand exchange by human Rad51 and RPA.
text: The ability of Human Rad51 (hRad51), a member of a conserved family of general recombinases, to create DNA joints between similar DNA molecules and facilitate efficient DNA strand exchange of these paired molecules over a distance of at least 5.4 kilobase pairs is demonstrated in this study. Additionally, it is found that the maximum efficiency of homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange relies heavily on the heterotrimeric single-stranded DNA binding factor hRPA. These processes require specific conditions that reduce interactions between the homologous duplex and the hRad51-single-stranded DNA nucleoprotein filament. This system of homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange can be utilized to investigate the mechanism of action of hRad51 and understand its functional interactions with other recombination factors.

title: A multiple indicators multiple causes model of late-life depression in Latin American countries
text:
The Euro-D depression scale is a tool used to assess symptoms of depression in older adults. However, there is still a need for further investigation to determine how demographic and cognitive characteristics may be related to different symptom clusters. Additionally, it is important to understand the impact of measurement bias on the conclusions drawn from the scale.

To address these issues, a study was conducted with a sample of 10,405 older adults living in six Latin American countries. A Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) model was used to simultaneously examine measurement bias and the relationship between Euro-D symptom clusters and background variables.

The results consistently supported the two-dimensional structure of the Euro-D scale, with symptom clusters related to affective suffering and motivation disturbance. While complete measurement invariance could not be assumed across countries, the level of measurement bias was minimal. Both symptom clusters were not associated with age, but were related to gender and impairment in memory and verbal fluency. Gender differences were more pronounced for affective suffering, while verbal fluency impairment was more strongly related to motivation disturbance.

There were some limitations to the study. The analysis only examined invariance at the level of indicator thresholds, and the generalizability of the findings to clinical populations needs to be explored. Additionally, a wider range of cognitive tests should be used in future research. The study did not investigate the factors that may have contributed to the variation in Euro-D scores across countries, as this was not the focus of the paper.

In conclusion, this study provides further support for the validity of the Euro-D scale and suggests that different symptom clusters may be associated with gender and verbal fluency in older adults. Understanding the heterogeneity of depression in late-life can have important implications for diagnosis and treatment in older individuals.

title: Microvesicles derived from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells stimulated by hypoxia promote angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo.
text: Despite the increasing use of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to treat various diseases, the specific mechanisms by which they work are still not well understood. In this study, we focused on MSCs derived from human umbilical cords (UC) and investigated their response to hypoxia. We collected membrane microvesicles (MVs) from the supernatants of these MSCs using ultracentrifugation, examined them under an electron microscope, and used flow cytometry to determine their origin. Our findings revealed that when exposed to hypoxia, MSCs released a significant amount of MVs measuring approximately 100 nm in diameter. These MVs exhibited similar characteristics to the parent MSCs, except for a majority of them lacking the receptor for platelet-derived growth factor. Through a DiI-labeling assay, we discovered that MSC-MVs could be taken up by human UC endothelial cells (UC-ECs) within 8 hours of being added to the culture medium. Additionally, using the carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester-labeling technique and MTT test, we found that MSC-MVs promoted the proliferation of UC-ECs in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, the MVs were able to enhance the formation of capillary networks in UC-ECs when cultured in a Matrigel matrix. In a rat hindlimb ischemia model, both MSCs and MSC-MVs significantly improved blood flow recovery compared to the control medium, as assessed by laser Doppler imaging analysis (P<0.0001). These results suggest that the release of MVs is a major mechanism through which MSC therapy promotes angiogenesis.

title: Evaluation of oxidative status and depression-like responses in Brown Norway rats with acute myeloid leukemia
text: Research has shown that oxidative stress levels increase when individuals with leukemia also experience depression. This suggests that oxidative stress may play a role in the development of depression in cancer patients. The objective of this study was to determine if Brown Norway rats with acute myeloid leukemia, which is accompanied by oxidative stress, exhibit behavioral and receptor changes similar to those seen in rat models of depression. The rats were divided into two groups: leukemic rats and healthy control rats. Leukemia was induced by injecting promyelocytic leukemia cells into the rats' peritoneal cavity. Depression-like behavior was assessed using the forced swim test 30 or 34 days after the leukemia cell injection. After the assessment, the rats were euthanized and their spleens, brain cortex, and hippocampus were removed. The red-ox state of the tissues was evaluated by measuring the levels of total glutathione (GSH), the ferric ion reducing ability of plasma (FRAP), the expression of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), biliverdin reductase (BvR), and ferritin mRNA, as well as the activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and the concentration of malondialdehyde (MDA). Radioligand binding assays were used to assess the effect of leukemia on cortical receptors. Leukemic cells were identified using the RM-124 antibody and FACS Calibur flow cytometry. The results showed that leukemia affected the rats' locomotory activity and forced swim test behavior throughout the 34-day experiment. Signs of oxidative stress were observed in the leukemic rats at every stage of leukemia development. The FRAP values and glutathione contents were significantly lower, while HO-1 mRNA expression and malondialdehyde concentrations were significantly higher in the spleen and brain structures of the leukemic rats compared to the healthy controls. Additionally, there was a significant increase in the potency of glycine to displace [(3)H]L-689,560 from the strychnine-insensitive glycine site of the N-methyl-D-aspartic (NMDA) receptor complex in the cortical homogenates of the leukemic rats in both the 30- and 34-day experimental series compared to the control group. Upregulation of 5-HT(2A) receptors was observed in the rat cortex after 30 days of leukemia development, but not in the 34-day series, compared to the control group. In conclusion, disturbances in the antioxidant system in the brain cortex were accompanied by an activation of glycine sites of the NMDA receptor complex, regardless of the stage of leukemia development, which are characteristic of depression models. The findings of this study demonstrate a connection between glutamatergic activity, oxidative stress, and leukemia.

title: Distinct roles for DNA-PK, ATM and ATR in RPA phosphorylation and checkpoint activation in response to replication stress
text: The risk of destabilizing the genome and potentially causing cancer is posed by DNA damage that occurs during DNA replication. When damage occurs, checkpoint systems are activated, leading to cell cycle arrest, repair promotion, and programmed cell death if the damage is severe. These checkpoints are crucial components of the DNA damage response network, which helps suppress cancer. Replication stress, caused by DNA damage and disruption of the replication machinery, results in the accumulation of single-stranded DNA bound by replication protein A (RPA). This accumulation triggers the activation of ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3 related (ATR) and the phosphorylation of RPA32, a subunit of RPA. This phosphorylation leads to the activation of Chk1 and cell cycle arrest. DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs), which is related to ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and ATR, is well-known for its role in repairing DNA double-strand breaks but its role in RPA phosphorylation induced by replication stress is not well understood. Our study demonstrates that cells with mutant DNA-PKcs are unable to arrest replication after experiencing stress. Additionally, mutations in the RPA32 phosphorylation sites targeted by DNA-PKcs increase the number of cells in mitosis, impair ATR signaling to Chk1, and result in a defect in G2/M arrest. Inhibition of ATR and DNA-PK (but not ATM) produces similar defects to those observed in cells expressing mutant RPA32. Cells expressing mutant RPA32 or DNA-PKcs exhibit sustained H2AX phosphorylation in response to replication stress, which persists as the cells enter mitosis. This indicates inappropriate entry into mitosis without repairing the damage.

title: The essential Schizosaccharomyces pombe Pfh1 DNA helicase promotes fork movement past G-quadruplex motifs to prevent DNA damage
text:
G-quadruplexes (G4s) are unique DNA structures made up of four guanines held together by hydrogen bonds. These structures, known as G4 motifs, are present in both bacterial and eukaryotic genomes. In particular, the Pif1 DNA helicase found in budding yeast and certain bacterial helicases are capable of unwinding G4 structures and preventing G4-induced DNA damage in yeast cells.

To further understand the relationship between G4 motifs and the Pfh1 helicase in fission yeast, we examined the distribution and conservation of G4 motifs in four different species. Through chromatin immunoprecipitation and deep sequencing, we discovered that many G4 motifs in the genome of S. pombe were associated with Pfh1. When Pfh1 was depleted, we observed increased fork pausing and DNA damage near G4 motifs, as evidenced by high DNA polymerase occupancy and phosphorylated histone H2A. Interestingly, G4 motifs were generally less common in genes. However, we found that Pfh1-associated G4 motifs were more frequently located on the transcribed strand of highly transcribed genes, suggesting that Pfh1 plays a role in replication or transcription at these sites.
