Overall, our findings indicate that the absence of functional Pfh1 leads to unresolved G4 structures, which in turn cause fork pausing and DNA damage similar to that seen in human tumors.

title: Wnt7a signaling promotes dendritic spine growth and synaptic strength through Ca²⁺/Calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II.
text: Maintaining a proper balance between excitatory and inhibitory synapses is essential for the normal functioning of the brain. The presence of Wnt proteins has been found to promote the formation of synapses by enhancing their assembly. However, it remains unclear whether Wnt signaling affects the formation of excitatory and inhibitory synapses differently. In this study, we provide evidence that Wnt7a specifically stimulates the formation and functioning of excitatory synapses. In experiments conducted on hippocampal neurons, Wnt7a was observed to increase the number of excitatory synapses while having no effect on inhibitory synapses. Additionally, the introduction of Wnt7a or the expression of Dishevelled-1 (Dvl1), a core component of Wnt signaling, in the postsynaptic region resulted in an increase in the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs), but not miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs). Wnt7a was also found to enhance the density and maturity of dendritic spines. Conversely, mice lacking Wnt7a and Dvl1 exhibited abnormalities in spine morphogenesis and mossy fiber-CA3 synaptic transmission in the hippocampus. By utilizing a postsynaptic reporter for Ca(2+)/Calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) activity, we demonstrated that Wnt7a rapidly activates CaMKII in spines. Importantly, inhibiting CaMKII activity abolished the effects of Wnt7a on spine growth and excitatory synaptic strength. These findings suggest that Wnt7a signaling plays a crucial role in regulating spine growth and synaptic strength by locally activating CaMKII at dendritic spines. Consequently, dysregulated Wnt7a signaling may contribute to neurological disorders characterized by disruptions in excitatory signaling.

title: Bitter taste receptors and α-gustducin regulate the secretion of ghrelin with functional effects on food intake and gastric emptying.
text:
The factors that control the secretion of ghrelin, a hunger hormone with properties that aid digestion, from the stomach are currently unknown. However, recent research has shown that bitter taste receptors (T2R) and certain gustatory G proteins, specifically α-gustducin (gust) and α-transducin, are present in the gut and play a role in sensing nutrients. This study aimed to investigate the effects of T2R-agonists on ghrelin release through α-gustducin and its impact on food intake and gastric emptying. 

The mouse stomach contains two types of ghrelin cells: one type contains octanoyl and desoctanoyl ghrelin, which are colocalized with α-gustducin and α-transducin, and the other type only stains for desoctanoyl ghrelin. When T2R-agonists were administered through gavage, plasma levels of octanoyl ghrelin increased in normal mice (WT), but this effect was partially reduced in mice lacking the gust protein (gust(-/-)). Intragastric administration of T2R-agonists led to increased food intake in the first 30 minutes in WT mice, but not in gust(-/-) mice or mice lacking the ghrelin receptor. This increase in food intake was accompanied by an increase in the expression of agouti-related peptide mRNA in the hypothalamus of WT mice, but not in gust(-/-) mice. However, after the initial increase, food intake decreased for the next 4 hours, which coincided with a delay in gastric emptying. This delay was partially counteracted by ghrelin and was not influenced by cholecystokinin and GLP-1, but rather by a direct inhibitory effect of T2R-agonists on gastric contractility. 

This study provides unique functional evidence that activation of bitter taste receptors stimulates the secretion of ghrelin. Modulating ghrelin levels through tastants may have potential therapeutic applications for weight and gastrointestinal motility disorders.

title: Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors regulate growth of human glioblastoma via Akt activation.
text: Accumulated evidence suggests that glioblastoma cells utilize glutamate to promote their proliferation and migration through autocrine or paracrine loops involving Ca2+-permeable AMPA-type glutamate receptors. Our study demonstrates that Ca2+ signaling, mediated by AMPA receptors, plays a crucial role in regulating the growth and motility of glioblastoma cells by activating Akt. Specifically, Ca2+ influx through Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors leads to the phosphorylation of Akt at Ser-473, facilitating cell proliferation and mobility. We observed that inhibiting Akt, using a dominant-negative form, effectively suppressed cell proliferation and migration induced by overexpression of Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors. Conversely, introducing a constitutively active form of Akt rescued tumor cells from apoptosis triggered by the conversion of Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors to Ca2+-impermeable receptors through the delivery of GluR2 cDNA. Therefore, Akt acts as a downstream effector in the Ca2+-signaling pathway mediated by AMPA receptors in glioblastoma cells. Activation of the glutamate-AMPA receptor-Akt pathway likely contributes to the highly aggressive and invasive nature of human glioblastoma. Targeting this novel pathway may offer an alternative therapeutic strategy.

title: The Extracellular Surface of the GLP-1 Receptor Is a Molecular Trigger for Biased Agonism
text: The concept of ligand-directed signal bias presents opportunities for shaping molecular events, leading to the development of improved and safer therapeutics. A crucial aspect of harnessing signal bias lies in comprehending the molecular events that connect ligand binding to intracellular signaling. The activation of class B G protein-coupled receptors is initiated by the interaction between the peptide N terminus and the receptor core. To gain insight into how this interaction drives signaling, we have employed advanced analytical techniques that allow us to distinguish between effects on pathway-specific signaling and those that alter agonist affinity. Additionally, we have mapped the functional consequences of modifying the receptor onto three-dimensional models of a receptor-ligand complex. This approach provides us with molecular insights into the initiation of receptor activation and the underlying mechanisms behind biased agonism. Our findings demonstrate that peptide agonists can engage different regions of the receptor's extracellular surface to facilitate effector coupling and biased signaling. This knowledge serves as a basis for the rational design of biased agonists.

title: A local macrophage chemokine network sustains protective tissue-resident memory CD4 T cells
text: CD8 tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells play a crucial role in controlling viral infections at the local level, but the function of CD4 TRM cells remains uncertain. In this study, we utilized parabiotic mice to demonstrate that a preexisting population of CD4 TRM cells in the genital mucosa is necessary for complete protection against a deadly herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) infection. The maintenance of vaginal CD4 TRM cells within memory lymphocyte clusters (MLCs) was facilitated by chemokines secreted by a local network of macrophages, independent of circulating memory T cells. Furthermore, CD4 TRM cells within the MLCs exhibited an enrichment of clones that expanded in response to HSV-2. These findings emphasize the importance of vaccine strategies that promote the establishment of TRM cells for safeguarding against sexually transmitted viruses and shed light on the mechanisms underlying the formation of such a protective pool.

title: Influence of smoking and plasma factors on patency of femoropopliteal vein grafts.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the impact of smoking, plasma lipids, lipoproteins, apolipoproteins, and fibrinogen on the success of saphenous vein femoropopliteal bypass grafts after one year. The study was conducted as a prospective analysis of patients who had undergone this type of bypass graft and were enrolled in a multicentre trial. The study took place in surgical wards, outpatient clinics, and through home visits coordinated by two referral centres in London and Birmingham. A total of 157 patients participated in the study, with an average age of 66.6 years. Of these patients, 113 had patent grafts after one year, while 44 had occluded grafts. The main outcome measure was the cumulative percentage of grafts that remained patent after one year.

The results of the study showed that markers for smoking, such as blood carboxyhaemoglobin concentration and plasma thiocyanate concentration, were significantly higher in patients with occluded grafts. Additionally, plasma concentrations of fibrinogen and apolipoproteins AI and (a) were also significantly higher in patients with occluded grafts. On the other hand, patients with grafts that remained patent after one year had significantly higher serum cholesterol concentrations. Analysis of the smoking markers revealed that 40 patients were not truthful about quitting smoking. Life table analysis showed that smokers had significantly lower graft patency after one year compared to non-smokers. Furthermore, patients with a plasma fibrinogen concentration below the median had significantly higher graft patency than those with a concentration above the median. Surprisingly, higher plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration was associated with improved graft patency at values above the median.

In conclusion, the study found that plasma fibrinogen concentration was the most important factor in predicting graft occlusion, followed by smoking markers. The findings suggest that a more aggressive approach is needed to help patients quit smoking, and therapeutic interventions should focus on reducing plasma fibrinogen concentration rather than serum cholesterol concentration to improve graft patency.

title: No effect of dietary fat on short-term weight gain in mice treated with atypical antipsychotic drugs
text:
Objective: This study aimed to investigate the impact of a high-fat diet on weight gain and serum lipids in female C57BL/6J mice treated with atypical antipsychotic drugs (AAD), as the effects of dietary fat in this model are currently unknown.

Methods: Female C57BL/6J mice were administered AAD for 3 weeks and divided into two groups, one receiving a low-fat diet (4.6% fat by weight) and the other a high-fat diet (15.6% fat by weight). During the treatment period, food intake, body weight, body composition, and serum lipids were measured. Energy intake and feed efficiency were also calculated. Changes between groups were analyzed using repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), and serum lipid concentrations, energy intake, and feed efficiency were compared using two-way ANOVA.

Results: After 3 weeks, the mice treated with AAD gained significantly more weight than the control group (P<0.001). Both treatment and diet had significant effects on food intake and energy intake over time (P<0.001). The AAD-treated mice had significantly higher feed efficiency than the control group (P<0.05), but there was no significant interaction between the drug and diet (P=0.65). Risperidone low-fat mice gained significantly more absolute fat mass than placebo low-fat mice (P<0.05). All treatment groups, except quetiapine low-fat and olanzapine high-fat, gained significantly more absolute lean mass than the placebo controls (P<0.05). Cholesterol levels were significantly lower in quetiapine and risperidone groups compared to the placebo group (P<0.05). Risperidone low-fat mice had significantly higher triglyceride levels than the placebo and risperidone high-fat mice (P<0.05).

Conclusion: The results of this study indicate that a high-fat diet does not increase the weight gain induced by AAD in female mice during a 3-week treatment period.

title: The role of free radicals in cold injuries.
text: Cold injury occurs when tissues are exposed to freezing temperatures or a severely cold and windy environment. When frozen tissue is warmed, blood flow is restored and free oxygen radicals are generated. This review discusses the current understanding of how free oxygen radicals contribute to cold injury during the rewarming process. During periods of reduced blood flow, energy stores decrease, leading to the accumulation of adenine nucleotides and the release of free fatty acids from lipid membranes. Upon rewarming, these free fatty acids are metabolized through cyclo-oxygenase, while adenine nucleotides are metabolized through the xanthine oxidase pathway. These metabolic processes may be the source of the free oxygen radicals. Additionally, leukocytes may also play a significant role in the development of cold injury. Although oxygen radical scavengers like superoxide dismutase and catalase can help reduce cold-induced damage, their effectiveness is limited because they cannot easily cross the plasma membrane. Lipid soluble antioxidants are likely to be more effective scavengers as they are present in membranes where peroxidative reactions can be halted.

title: SIRT1 deacetylase in SF1 neurons protects against metabolic imbalance.
text: Obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are widespread health issues caused by chronic consumption of high-calorie diets. These conditions affect millions of people worldwide, making it crucial to understand how to protect against diet-induced metabolic imbalances. In this study, we demonstrate that mice lacking SIRT1 in steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1) neurons are highly susceptible to dietary obesity due to inefficient energy expenditure. Additionally, these mutant mice are more prone to developing T2DM as a result of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. The underlying mechanisms involve impaired metabolic functions of the neuropeptide orexin-A and the hormone leptin. Conversely, mice with increased SIRT1 expression in SF1 neurons exhibit greater resistance to diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance, thanks to heightened energy expenditure and improved skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity. Our findings shed light on the crucial protective roles of SIRT1 in SF1 neurons against dietary metabolic imbalances.

title: mTOR supports long-term self-renewal and suppresses mesoderm and endoderm activities of human embryonic stem cells.
text: Although the transcriptional regulatory circuitry involving SOX2, NANOG, and OCT-4 has been recently identified, the intracellular signaling networks that govern the pluripotency of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) are still not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the serine/threonine protein kinase mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) plays a crucial role in regulating the long-term undifferentiated growth of hESCs. When mTOR is inhibited, pluripotency is impaired, cell proliferation is halted, and mesoderm and endoderm activities are enhanced in hESCs. At the molecular level, mTOR integrates signals from external factors that support pluripotency and suppresses the transcriptional activities of certain genes involved in development and growth inhibition, as revealed by genome-wide microarray analyses. The repression of these developmental genes by mTOR is essential for maintaining hESC pluripotency. These findings unveil a new signaling mechanism through which mTOR controls fate decisions in hESCs. Our discoveries may contribute to the development of effective strategies for tissue repair and regeneration.

title: Intrinsic genetic characteristics determine tumor-modifying capacity of fibroblasts: matrix metalloproteinase-3 5A/5A genotype enhances breast cancer cell invasion
text: The release of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) by stromal fibroblasts can contribute to tumor invasion. Previous studies have indicated that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in MMP genes can affect gene expression levels and may be associated with breast cancer risk and progression. This study aimed to directly examine the impact of MMP SNP genotype on the ability of host fibroblasts to promote tumor cell invasion. Primary breast fibroblasts were obtained from patients with (n = 13) or without (n = 19) breast cancer, and their ability to promote breast cancer cell invasion was assessed using in vitro invasion assays. The fibroblast invasion-promoting capacity (IPC) was analyzed in relation to donor type (tumor or non-tumor patient), MMP-1, MMP-3, and MMP-9 SNP genotype, as well as MMP activity. Statistical analysis was performed using independent samples t-tests and analysis of variance. All statistical tests were two-sided. The results showed that fibroblasts derived from tumors promoted higher levels of invasion compared to normal fibroblasts (p = 0.041). When IPC was examined in relation to genotype, tumor fibroblasts with the high-expressing MMP-3 5A/5A genotype exhibited higher levels of IPC compared to those with the 5A/6A and 6A/6A genotypes (p = 0.05 and 0.07, respectively). This was associated with increased release of MMP-3. The functional importance of MMP-3 was confirmed by enhanced invasion in the presence of recombinant MMP-3, while inhibition of MMP-3 led to a reduction in invasion. An inverse relationship was observed between fibroblast IPC and the high-expressing MMP-1 genotype (p = 0.031), but no relationship was found with MMP-9 SNP status. In contrast, normal fibroblasts did not show any variation in IPC based on MMP genotype. Fibroblasts with the MMP-3 5A/5A genotype exhibited significantly lower levels of IPC compared to their tumor-derived counterparts (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that tumor-derived fibroblasts have higher levels of IPC compared to normal fibroblasts, and that the MMP-3 5A/5A genotype contributes to this through increased MMP-3 release. However, despite having a high-expressing genotype, normal fibroblasts do not exhibit higher IPC or enhanced MMP release. This suggests that more complex changes occur in tumor-derived fibroblasts, allowing for full expression of the MMP SNP genotype, possibly through epigenetic mechanisms. Overall, the results suggest that in women with breast cancer, a high-expressing MMP-3 genotype may promote tumor progression more effectively.

title: Hallmarks of Cancer: The Next Generation
text: The hallmarks of cancer consist of six biological capabilities that are acquired during the development of human tumors. These hallmarks serve as a framework for understanding the complexities of cancer. They include the ability to sustain proliferative signaling, evade growth suppressors, resist cell death, enable replicative immortality, induce angiogenesis, and activate invasion and metastasis. These hallmarks are underpinned by genome instability, which leads to genetic diversity and facilitates their acquisition, as well as inflammation, which supports their functions. Recent advancements have identified two additional emerging hallmarks with potential generality: reprogramming of energy metabolism and evading immune destruction. In addition to cancer cells, tumors also involve a diverse range of normal cells that contribute to the development of hallmark traits by creating the "tumor microenvironment." Recognizing the broad applicability of these concepts will have a growing impact on the development of new treatments for cancer.

title: BCR/ABL oncogenic kinase promotes unfaithful repair of the reactive oxygen species-dependent DNA double-strand breaks.
text: The oncogenic BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase causes continuous DNA damage in leukemia cells that have the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph). Our research shows that BCR/ABL leads to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROSs), which in turn result in long-term oxidative DNA damage and the formation of double-strand breaks (DSBs) during the S and G(2)/M phases of the cell cycle. These breaks are repaired through BCR/ABL-induced homologous recombination repair (HRR) and nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) mechanisms. Interestingly, we observed a high rate of mutations in HRR products specifically in BCR/ABL-positive cells, while normal cells did not exhibit this mutation rate. Furthermore, we exclusively detected large deletions in NHEJ products in BCR/ABL cells. Based on our findings, we propose that the sequence of events involving BCR/ABL, ROSs, oxidative DNA damage, DSBs in dividing cells, and error-prone HRR and NHEJ repair mechanisms may contribute to the genomic instability observed in Ph-positive leukemias.

title: Cancer risks attributable to low doses of ionizing radiation: assessing what we really know.
text: Humans experience negative effects, such as cancer, when exposed to high levels of ionizing radiation. However, the consequences of low doses of radiation are not as clear. Nevertheless, the risks associated with low-dose radiation are important for society to consider in various areas, including cancer screening tests, nuclear power, occupational exposure, frequent flying, space exploration, and terrorism involving radiation. This article examines the challenges in determining the risks of low-dose radiation and addresses two specific questions. Firstly, what is the lowest dose of x- or gamma-radiation that has strong evidence of increasing cancer risks in humans? Epidemiological data suggests that it is around 10-50 mSv for acute exposure and 50-100 mSv for prolonged exposure. Secondly, how should we estimate cancer risks at even lower doses? Currently, a linear extrapolation of cancer risks from intermediate to very low doses seems to be the most appropriate approach, supported by experimental and measurable biophysical arguments. However, this assumption may not be the most cautious approach, potentially underestimating some radiation-induced cancer risks while overestimating others.

title: Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation for alleviating chronic pelvic pain: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Chronic pelvic pain is a common condition that significantly impacts a person's quality of life, work productivity, and healthcare utilization. One treatment option for patients with chronic pelvic pain is laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA), which involves the surgical interruption of nerve trunks in the uterosacral ligaments. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of LUNA in patients with chronic pelvic pain. 

The study was a randomized controlled trial involving 487 women with chronic pelvic pain lasting longer than 6 months, either with minimal or without endometriosis, adhesions, or pelvic inflammatory disease. These women were recruited by consultant gynecological surgeons from 18 hospitals in the UK between February 1998 and December 2005. Follow-up was conducted through questionnaires mailed at various intervals over a period of 5 years. 

The participants were divided into two groups: one group underwent bilateral LUNA, while the other group underwent laparoscopy without pelvic denervation (no LUNA). The participants were unaware of their treatment allocation. The primary outcome measure was pain, assessed using a visual analogue scale. The data on three types of pain (noncyclical pain, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia) were analyzed separately, as well as the worst pain level experienced from any of these three types. The secondary outcome measure was health-related quality of life, measured using a generic instrument called EuroQoL EQ-5D and EQ-VAS. 

After a median follow-up of 69 months, there were no significant differences in pain levels between the LUNA group and the no LUNA group. This was true for the worst pain, noncyclical pain, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia. Additionally, there were no differences in quality of life between the two groups. 

In conclusion, LUNA did not lead to improvements in pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, or quality of life compared to laparoscopy without pelvic denervation in women with chronic pelvic pain. The trial was registered under the identifier ISRCTN41196151.

title: Identification of bone and liver metastases from breast cancer by measurement of plasma alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activity.
text: The aim of this study was to assess the use of plasma alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activities in diagnosing and monitoring bone and liver metastases in patients with breast cancer. Out of the 50 patients with radiologically confirmed bone metastases, 42% showed an increase in bone alkaline phosphatase activity, while only 20% showed an increase in total alkaline phosphatase activity. Among the 25 patients with liver metastases, 48% had raised liver alkaline phosphatase activity. It was observed that all patients with liver metastases also had bone metastases. Furthermore, patients with symptomatic bone disease had significantly higher bone alkaline phosphatase activity. In terms of patient management, isoenzyme determination provided additional information that would have altered the course of treatment in five out of 20 patients who were monitored over time. Although less sensitive than imaging procedures, measuring alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activity can be helpful in screening for and detecting a significant number of bone and liver metastases, as well as providing objective evidence of treatment response.

title: Recommendations on how to ensure the safety and effectiveness of biosimilars in Latin America: a point of view
text: The use of biotechnology-derived medicines has significantly increased in recent decades. However, biosimilars, which are highly complex molecules, require rigorous characterization and clinical studies to ensure their safety and effectiveness. Even small changes in the purification and production process of a biosimilar can have significant implications for its safety and effectiveness. In Latin America, regulatory authorities have started establishing well-defined and standardized pathways for the commercial licensure of biosimilars. To ensure that a biosimilar performs as expected in ordinary clinical use, it is crucial to establish an intensive post-licensing monitoring system. This system is the only way to determine the true similarity between the original biologic and its biosimilar. Pharmacovigilance plays a vital role in allowing national authorities to assess a drug's performance in the market. Implementing an effective tracking and pharmacovigilance system for biological medicines involves multiple steps and processes. To assist policy makers in Latin America in addressing the challenges associated with establishing such a system, the Americas Health Foundation brought together a group of experts to discuss the topic and develop recommendations. The group focused on current challenges and gaps in pharmacovigilance in Latin America, particularly regarding traceability and pharmacovigilance of biosimilars after their approval. The recommendations developed by the group aim to help countries accurately document the safety and performance of biosimilars in real-life conditions, ultimately contributing to the successful implementation of pharmacovigilance of biosimilars across the region.

title: Coordinated regulation of sulfur and phospholipid metabolism reflects the importance of methylation in the growth of yeast
text: A yeast strain that lacks Met4p, the main regulator of the sulfur assimilation pathway, is unable to produce methionine. This seemingly simple auxotroph did not thrive in nutrient-rich media with excess methionine, resulting in small colonies on yeast extract/peptone/dextrose plates. However, when overnight cultures were plated, larger colonies that grew faster were plentiful, indicating that suppressor mutations that alleviate the growth defect occur frequently. To identify these suppressor mutations, we employed genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism analysis and standard genetic techniques. The most common suppressor mutations were found in OPI1, which encodes a transcriptional repressor involved in phospholipid metabolism. By utilizing a novel system that enables rapid and specific degradation of Met4p, we were able to investigate the dynamic expression of all genes following the loss of Met4p. Experiments conducted with and without Opi1p using this system revealed that Met4 activates genes while Opi1p represses genes that regulate the levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the primary substrate for most methyltransferase reactions. Cells lacking Met4p exhibit normal growth when SAM is added to the media or when one of the SAM synthetase genes is overexpressed. SAM is utilized as a methyl donor in three Opi1p-regulated reactions to produce the abundant membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylcholine. Our findings demonstrate that rapidly growing cells necessitate significant methylation, likely for the synthesis of phospholipids.

title: Glossary of reference terms for alternative test methods and their validation.
text: The purpose of this glossary is to serve as a technical resource for those working in the field of alternatives to animal testing. It has been created by gathering information from various existing reference documents from different sources, and its aim is to be a reliable point of reference for information on alternatives to animal testing. Due to the increasing number of alternative test methods and approaches that have been developed in recent decades, it is necessary to combine, revise, and harmonize previously published collections of terms used in the validation of these methods. The need to update previous glossary efforts arose from the recognition that new terms have emerged with the development of new approaches, while others have become outdated, and the meanings of some terms have changed over time. Through this glossary, our intention is to provide guidance on issues related to the validation of new or updated testing methods that align with current approaches. Additionally, given the continuous advancements and technologies, it is important for the glossary to be a dynamic and regularly updated document. An online version of this compilation can be accessed at http://altweb.jhsph.edu/, allowing for the inclusion of new material.

title: Combinatorial transcriptional control in blood stem/progenitor cells: genome-wide analysis of ten major transcriptional regulators.
text: The control of cellular phenotypes, including stem cell formation, maintenance, and differentiation, is governed by combinatorial interactions among transcription factors (TFs). In this study, we present a comprehensive dataset of genome-wide binding patterns and combinatorial interactions for ten key regulators of blood stem/progenitor cells: SCL/TAL1, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, MEIS1, PU.1, ERG, FLI-1, and GFI1B. This dataset represents the most extensive TF data set for any adult stem/progenitor cell type to date. Through computational analysis and functional validation, we made several important discoveries. Firstly, we identified a previously unknown combinatorial interaction among a group of seven TFs (SCL, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, ERG, and FLI-1). Secondly, we found evidence of direct protein-protein interactions between four key regulators (RUNX1, GATA2, SCL, and ERG) that contribute to the stabilization of complex binding to DNA. Lastly, we observed that mice with compound heterozygosity for Runx1(+/-) and Gata2(+/-) are not viable and exhibit severe hematopoietic defects during midgestation. Overall, this study highlights the importance of genome-wide analysis in uncovering novel insights into the transcriptional control of stem and progenitor cells.

title: Influence of CYP2D6 Polymorphisms on Serum Levels of Tamoxifen Metabolites in Spanish Women with Breast Cancer
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the effects of genetic variations in the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genes on the pharmacokinetics of tamoxifen and its metabolites in Spanish women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer tumors rely on estrogen signaling for their growth and can be treated with tamoxifen, an anti-estrogen therapy. However, certain polymorphisms in the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genes have been linked to a reduced response to tamoxifen.

Ninety women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer were included in the study. The AmpliChip CYP450 test was used to identify genetic variants in the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genes. High-performance liquid chromatography was used to measure the levels of tamoxifen and its metabolites in the participants' plasma.

The results showed that 80% of the patients had an extensive metabolizer phenotype for CYP2D6, while 12.2% were intermediate metabolizers, 2.2% were ultra-rapid metabolizers, and 5.6% were poor metabolizers. The allele frequencies were 35.0% for allele (*)1, 21.0% for *2, and 18.9% for *4. All of the poor metabolizers in the study had the *4/*4 genotype, and their levels of endoxifen and 4-hydroxy tamoxifen were 25% lower than those of the extensive metabolizers. The CYP2C19*2 allele, which has been associated with breast cancer outcomes, was found in 15.6% of the alleles analyzed.

In conclusion, the CYP2D6*4/*4 genotype was found to be inversely related to levels of 4-hydroxy tamoxifen and endoxifen. Based on these findings, it is recommended to perform CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotyping before prescribing tamoxifen therapy.

title: Role of tumor associated macrophages in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis
text: Tumor angiogenesis is a crucial process that supplies rapidly growing malignant tissues with necessary nutrients and oxygen. This process allows tumor cells to survive, grow, and spread to other parts of the body. Tumor cells recruit and reprogram monocyte-derived macrophages, which release angiogenic factors that promote angiogenesis. The tumor endothelium also releases angiopoietin-2, which attracts TIE2 receptor expressing monocytes to the tumor site. Hypoxia in avascular areas of tumors triggers tumor-associated macrophages to produce angiogenic factors like VEGFA, which stimulate the movement of endothelial cells and macrophages. In some tumors, TAMs are a major source of MMP9, which breaks down the extracellular matrix and releases bioactive VEGFA. TAMs also release other angiogenic factors like bFGF, TP, uPA, and ADM. These factors, including VEGF-A and MMP9, also support lymphangiogenesis. TAMs can express LYVE-1, a marker of lymphatic endothelium, and support tumor lymphangiogenesis by secreting pro-lymphangiogenic factors and transforming into lymphatic endothelial cells. YKL-40, a member of the CLP family, is a newly discovered pro-angiogenic factor that acts as a cytokine or growth factor. It has been found to induce angiogenesis in vitro and in animal tumor models. Blocking YKL-40 with a monoclonal antibody inhibits tumor angiogenesis and progression. The roles of YKL-39 and SI-CLP in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis are still unknown and require further investigation.

title: The HIV Treatment Gap: Estimates of the Financial Resources Needed versus Available for Scale-Up of Antiretroviral Therapy in 97 Countries from 2015 to 2020
text:
In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that all individuals diagnosed with HIV should begin antiretroviral therapy (ART), regardless of their CD4 count. However, there is limited research on the global resources needed to rapidly expand ART. As part of the Health Policy Project, we conducted modeling analyses for 97 countries to estimate the number of individuals eligible for and receiving ART from 2015 to 2020, as well as the financial resources required at the facility level. We compared these estimated financial requirements to the available funding.

Our estimates were based on country-specific epidemiological and demographic data, taking into account current coverage levels and future treatment needs. We simulated the annual number of individuals on treatment using three scenarios: (1) continuing with countries' current eligibility policies, (2) adopting aspects of the WHO 2013 eligibility guidelines universally, and (3) expanding eligibility as per the WHO 2015 guidelines and meeting the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS "90-90-90" ART targets. We also considered uncertainty in the annual resource requirements for antiretroviral drugs, laboratory tests, and facility-level personnel and overhead.

Our findings suggest that by 2020, if countries maintain their current eligibility plans and increase coverage based on historical rates, approximately 25.7 million adults and 1.57 million children could receive ART. If countries uniformly adopt aspects of the WHO 2013 guidelines, these numbers could increase to 26.5 million adults and 1.53 million children. Under the 90-90-90 scenario, 30.4 million adults and 1.68 million children could receive treatment by 2020. The facility-level financial resources needed for scaling up ART in these countries from 2015 to 2020 are estimated to be US$45.8 billion under the current scenario, US$48.7 billion under the WHO 2013 scenario, and US$52.5 billion under the 90-90-90 scenario.

After considering recent funding trends, we estimate a financing gap of US$19.8 billion to US$25.0 billion over six years, depending on the costing scenario and the contribution level of the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. The gap for ART commodities alone ranges from US$14.0 billion to US$16.8 billion. It is important to note that our study does not include above-facility and other essential costs related to ART service delivery, and the quality and availability of country-specific data may limit our findings.

In conclusion, our projections suggest that countries are unlikely to meet the 90-90-90 treatment target unless they adopt a test-and-offer approach and increase ART coverage. The future resource needs for ART scale-up are smaller than previously estimated but still pose a significant threat to the sustainability of the global HIV response. Additional resource mobilization from domestic or innovative financing sources, as well as efficiency gains, are necessary. As the world adopts the WHO 2015 guidelines, advancements in technology, such as lower-cost and highly effective antiretroviral regimens, may play a crucial role in expanding ART coverage with the available resources.

title: Distinction and relationship between elongation rate and processivity of RNA polymerase II in vivo.
text: The process of transcriptional elongation by RNA polymerase (Pol) II involves various proteins and drugs. However, the factors that control the rate of elongation (nucleotide additions per minute) and processivity (nucleotide additions per initiation event) in vivo are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that a mutation in the Rpb2 subunit of Pol II decreases both the elongation rate and processivity in vivo. On the other hand, the putative elongation factors tested do not affect the elongation rate, although mutations in the THO complex and Spt4 significantly reduce processivity. Additionally, the drugs 6-azauracil and mycophenolic acid decrease both the elongation rate and processivity, and this processivity defect is worsened by mutations in Spt4, TFIIS, and CTDK-1. Our findings suggest that, in vivo, a slower rate of Pol II elongation causes premature dissociation from the chromatin template, and that Pol II processivity can be separated from elongation rate.

title: Neurite sprouting and synapse deterioration in the aging Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system.
text: Caenorhabditis elegans is an effective model for studying the mechanisms that regulate healthy aging. While the aging nematode nervous system does not show obvious signs of neuronal death or loss of processes, we used fluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy (EM) to examine nervous system changes at a high resolution. Our findings indicate two major morphological changes in the aging C. elegans nervous system: the accumulation of new outgrowths from specific neurons and a decline in synaptic integrity. These new outgrowths, which include branching from the main dendrite or new growth from somata, are observed frequently in some aging neurons but not all. We also observed a connection between age-associated branch sites and mitochondria. Lowered insulin signaling helps maintain the structural integrity of ALM and PLM neurons in old age, and both the DAF-16/FOXO and heat shock factor transcription factor HSF-1 play a role in neuroprotection. Specifically, HSF-1 can act autonomously in this capacity. Examination of synapse-rich regions using EM revealed a significant decrease in the number of synaptic vesicles and a reduction in the size of presynaptic density. Interestingly, older animals that maintain their locomotory abilities show less decline in synaptic integrity compared to frail animals of the same age, suggesting a correlation between synaptic health and locomotory healthspan. Our findings suggest that the aging C. elegans nervous system shares similarities with the mammalian brain, indicating conserved neuronal responses to aging. By studying the mechanisms of neuronal aging in C. elegans, we may be able to develop therapies that extend brain healthspan.

title: Determinants of adolescent physical activity and inactivity patterns.
text:
OBJECTIVES: This article aims to investigate the impact of environmental and sociodemographic factors on physical activity and inactivity patterns among subpopulations of US adolescents. By examining these determinants, the goal is to identify intervention strategies that can increase physical activity and decrease inactivity among adolescents at a societal level.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY: The study population consists of nationally representative data from the 1996 National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, including 17,766 US adolescents enrolled in middle and high schools. Questionnaires were used to collect data on hours/week of inactivity and times/week of moderate to vigorous physical activity. Logistic regression models were used to analyze the relationship between physical activity/inactivity and sociodemographic and environmental factors.

RESULTS: The study found that non-Hispanic black and Hispanic adolescents had lower levels of moderate to vigorous physical activity and higher levels of inactivity. Participation in school physical education programs decreased with age for these adolescents. However, participation in daily school physical education classes and use of community recreation centers were associated with increased likelihood of engaging in high levels of physical activity. Maternal education and high family income were also associated with increased physical activity and decreased inactivity. On the other hand, high levels of serious crime in the neighborhood were associated with decreased likelihood of engaging in high levels of physical activity.

CONCLUSIONS: The results highlight the importance of modifiable environmental factors, such as participation in school physical education and community recreation programs, in influencing the activity patterns of adolescents. However, the study also revealed that only a small percentage of adolescents actually participated in school physical education programs.

title: Suicide prevention strategies: a systematic review.
text: In 2002, approximately 877,000 lives were lost globally due to suicide. Some developed countries have implemented national plans to prevent suicide, but the effectiveness of these plans is often not evaluated. The objective of this study was to examine the evidence for the effectiveness of specific interventions to prevent suicide and provide recommendations for future prevention programs and research. Relevant publications were identified through electronic searches of various databases, including MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and PsychINFO. The studies included in this review evaluated interventions in different areas, such as education and awareness for the general public and professionals, screening tools for at-risk individuals, treatment of psychiatric disorders, restricting access to lethal means, and responsible media reporting of suicide. Data were extracted on primary outcomes, such as suicidal behavior (completion, attempt, ideation), as well as intermediary or secondary outcomes, including treatment seeking, identification of at-risk individuals, antidepressant prescription/use rates, and referrals. Experts from 15 countries reviewed all the studies. The included articles reported on completed and attempted suicide, suicidal ideation, and intermediate outcomes, such as help-seeking behavior, identification of at-risk individuals, entry into treatment, and antidepressant prescription rates. Three major types of studies were included: systematic reviews and meta-analyses, quantitative studies (randomized controlled trials or cohort studies), and ecological or population-based studies. Due to the heterogeneity of the study populations and methodologies, a formal meta-analysis was not possible, so a narrative synthesis was presented instead. The data synthesis showed that educating physicians and restricting access to lethal means were effective in preventing suicide. Other methods, such as public education, screening programs, and media education, require further testing. In conclusion, educating physicians about depression recognition and treatment and restricting access to lethal methods can reduce suicide rates. However, more evidence is needed to determine the efficacy of other interventions. It is crucial to identify which components of suicide prevention programs are effective in order to make the best use of limited resources.

title: Oxidative damage of DNA confers resistance to cytosolic nuclease TREX1 degradation and potentiates STING-dependent immune sensing.
text: Detecting DNA is crucial for the immune system's response to viruses, but it can also lead to autoimmune diseases like lupus erythematosus (LE). In this study, we present evidence that a specific modification in damaged DNA plays a role in recognizing DNA in the cytosol. This modification, called 8-hydroxyguanosine (8-OHG), is a marker of oxidative damage in DNA and enhances the immune response by making it less susceptible to degradation by a protein called 3' repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1). We found that these oxidative modifications occur naturally in pathogen DNA when exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS) in lysosomes, as well as in DNA released by neutrophils during an oxidative burst. Additionally, we observed high levels of 8-OHG in skin lesions of LE patients that were exposed to UV radiation, and this marker was found to colocalize with type I interferon (IFN), a molecule involved in immune responses. When we injected oxidized DNA into the skin of mice prone to lupus, it resulted in lesions that closely resembled those seen in patients. Therefore, oxidized DNA serves as a representative marker of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and has significant implications for infection, inflammation, and autoimmune conditions.

title: IL-18 induction of osteopontin mediates cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction in mice.
text: The fibrotic process during tissue remodeling is associated with osteopontin (OPN), a crucial component of the extracellular matrix. Overexpression of OPN and the cytokine interleukin (IL)-18 has been observed in various human cardiac pathologies. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of IL-18 in the regulation of cardiac OPN expression and its impact on interstitial fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction. Our findings revealed a simultaneous increase in IL-18, OPN expression, and interstitial fibrosis in murine models of left ventricular pressure and volume overload. Administering exogenous recombinant (r)IL-18 for 2 weeks resulted in elevated cardiac OPN expression, interstitial fibrosis, and diastolic dysfunction. Stimulation of the T helper (Th)1 lymphocyte phenotype using a selective toll-like receptor (TLR)9 agonist induced cardiac IL-18 and OPN expression, leading to higher concentrations of cardiac fibrillar collagen and interstitial fibrosis, ultimately resulting in diastolic dysfunction. Additionally, rIL-18 increased OPN expression and protein levels in primary cardiac fibroblast cultures. Conditioned media from TLR9-stimulated T lymphocyte cultures induced IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac fibroblasts, while blocking the IL-18 receptor with a neutralizing antibody prevented the increase in OPN expression. Furthermore, a mutation in the transcriptional factor interferon regulatory factor (IRF)1 or IRF1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) led to decreased expression of IL-18 and OPN in cardiac fibroblasts. Under pressure overload conditions, IRF1-mutant mice exhibited downregulation of IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac tissue, reduced cardiac fibrotic development, and improved left ventricular function compared to wild type mice. These findings provide direct evidence that the induction of IL-18 regulates OPN-mediated cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell: self-renewal versus differentiation.
text: The mammalian blood system relies on a specific cell type called hematopoietic stem cell (HSC), which is responsible for the production of more than 10 different mature cell types. HSCs possess the unique ability to both differentiate into various blood cells and renew themselves. Differentiation refers to the process of becoming specialized blood cells, while self-renewal allows HSCs to generate more HSCs without differentiation. As mature blood cells have a short lifespan, HSCs continuously produce new progenitor cells while maintaining the HSC population size through a delicate balance of self-renewal and differentiation. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms behind HSC self-renewal and differentiation is crucial. This review focuses on the hierarchical structure of the hematopoietic system, the current knowledge of the microenvironment and molecular signals that regulate HSC self-renewal and differentiation in adults, and the emerging systems approaches used to study HSC biology.

title: RSEM: accurate transcript quantification from RNA-Seq data with or without a reference genome
text:
RNA-Seq is revolutionizing the measurement of transcript abundances. However, there are challenges in quantifying transcripts from RNA-Seq data, such as handling reads that map to multiple genes or isoforms. This is especially difficult when using de novo transcriptome assemblies without sequenced genomes, as it is hard to determine which transcripts belong to the same gene. Another issue is the design of RNA-Seq experiments, including the number of reads, read length, and whether reads come from one or both ends of cDNA fragments.

To address these challenges, we have developed RSEM, a user-friendly software package for quantifying gene and isoform abundances from single-end or paired-end RNA-Seq data. RSEM provides abundance estimates, 95% credibility intervals, and visualization files, and can also simulate RNA-Seq data. Unlike other tools, RSEM does not require a reference genome, making it suitable for accurate transcript quantification in species without sequenced genomes when combined with a de novo transcriptome assembler.

In comparisons with other methods using simulated and real data sets, RSEM has shown superior or comparable performance in quantification without a reference genome. By effectively utilizing ambiguously-mapping reads, RSEM can provide accurate gene-level abundance estimates with large numbers of short single-end reads. Additionally, the use of paired-end reads can improve estimates of the relative frequencies of isoforms within single genes, depending on the number of possible splice forms for each gene.

In conclusion, RSEM is an accurate and user-friendly software tool for quantifying transcript abundances from RNA-Seq data. Its ability to work without a reference genome makes it particularly valuable for quantification with de novo transcriptome assemblies. Furthermore, RSEM has provided valuable guidance for cost-efficient design of RNA-Seq quantification experiments, which can be relatively expensive.

title: A synthetic Escherichia coli predator–prey ecosystem
text: We have created a synthetic ecosystem using two populations of Escherichia coli bacteria. These populations communicate with each other through quorum sensing and control each other's gene expression and survival using engineered gene circuits. Our synthetic ecosystem resembles traditional predator-prey systems in terms of how it functions and changes over time. The predator cells kill the prey by causing them to produce a protein that is lethal to them, while the prey cells save the predators by causing them to produce a protein that counteracts the lethal effects. Depending on the conditions we set, the predator and prey populations can either die out, coexist, or exhibit oscillatory behavior. We have confirmed these possibilities through long-term culturing of the system in microchemostats. To better understand these dynamics, we have developed a simple mathematical model. By combining experiments with mathematical analysis, we can predict and explore the interactions between these populations in a reliable way.

title: Funnel trap for the capture of phlebotomine sand flies (Diptera: Psychodidae) from tree holes.
text: In order to capture adult phlebotomine sand flies, specifically Lutzomyia shannoni Dyar, on Ossabaw Island in Chatham County, Georgia, a funnel trap was utilized. This trap was designed to fit over the holes that led into hollow trees, where these insects would rest during the day. At night, as the flies exited the tree holes, they were collected by the funnel traps. The trap itself is lightweight, durable, inexpensive, waterproof, and has the ability to selectively capture the desired species. During the months of July and August in 1988, when adult flies were plentiful on the island, a single investigator was able to capture over 100 healthy L. shannoni per night using this trap.

title: Cystine/glutamate exchange regulates metabotropic glutamate receptor presynaptic inhibition of excitatory transmission and vulnerability to cocaine seeking.
text:
The reduction of extracellular glutamate levels in the nucleus accumbens during withdrawal from chronic cocaine can be attributed to a decrease in cystine/glutamate exchange (xc-). However, by activating xc- with N-acetylcysteine, the extracellular glutamate can be restored, effectively preventing cocaine-induced drug seeking. It was hypothesized that the activation of xc- prevents drug seeking by increasing the glutamatergic tone on presynaptic group II metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/3), which in turn inhibits excitatory transmission. 

To determine the capacity of glutamate derived from xc- to regulate excitatory transmission via mGluR2/3, the first experiment involved restoring physiological levels of cystine (100-300 nm) in acute tissue slices from the nucleus accumbens or prefrontal cortex. This restoration of cystine resulted in an increase in glutamate efflux and a decrease in miniature EPSC (mEPSC) and spontaneous EPSC (sEPSC) frequency, as well as evoked EPSC amplitude. These effects were found to be presynaptic, as there was no change in mEPSC or sEPSC amplitude, but an increase in the evoked EPSC paired-pulse facilitation ratio. The reduction in EPSCs caused by cystine was reversed when either xc- or mGluR2/3 was blocked.

In the second experiment, it was observed that blocking mGluR2/3 prevented the ability of N-acetylcysteine to inhibit the reinstatement of drug seeking in rats trained to self-administer cocaine. These findings indicate that nonsynaptic glutamate derived from xc- plays a role in modulating synaptic glutamate release, thereby regulating cocaine-induced drug seeking.

title: Survival analysis: time-dependent effects and time-varying risk factors.
text: In traditional Kaplan-Meier or Cox regression analysis, the relationship between a risk factor measured at the beginning and mortality is typically examined. However, during the follow-up period, there may be changes in this relationship. The effect of a fixed baseline risk factor may vary over time, resulting in either a weakening or strengthening of associations. Alternatively, the risk factor itself may change over time. This paper focuses on the distinction between short-term and long-term effects, also known as time-dependent effects, of a fixed baseline risk factor. An example is provided to illustrate that being underweight is a significant risk factor for mortality in dialysis patients, particularly in the short term. On the other hand, being overweight is a risk factor for mortality that becomes stronger in the long term compared to the short term. Additionally, the analysis demonstrates how time-varying risk factors, referred to as time-dependent risk factors, are related to mortality. It highlights the importance of avoiding the pitfall of adjusting for sequelae. The proper analysis of effects over time should be guided by a clear research question. Both types of research questions, those concerning time-dependent effects and time-dependent risk factors, can be examined using time-dependent Cox regression analysis. It will be shown that focusing on time-dependent risk factors typically involves studying short-term effects exclusively.

title: Control of interneuron dendritic growth through NRG1/erbB4-mediated kalirin-7 disinhibition
text: Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) is a trophic factor that is released and activates the erbB4 receptor tyrosine kinase in the postsynaptic region. Both NRG1 and erbB4 have been consistently linked to schizophrenia, but their specific targets downstream are not well known. ErbB4 is found in high levels in interneurons, and the activation of erbB4 by NRG1 has been shown to affect interneuron function. However, the role of NRG1-erbB4 signaling in regulating the growth of interneuron dendrites is not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that NRG1/erbB4 promote the growth of dendrites in mature interneurons through kalirin, a key regulator of dendritic Rac1-GEF. Recent research has also shown associations between the KALRN gene and schizophrenia. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation in the C terminus of kalirin-7 plays a crucial role in these effects. As reduced length of interneuron dendrites is observed in schizophrenia, understanding how NRG1-erbB4 signaling influences the morphogenesis of interneuron dendrites may provide insights into alterations in cortical circuits associated with the disease.

title: Use of gene-expression profiling to identify prognostic subclasses in adult acute myeloid leukemia.
text: The current classification system for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) does not fully capture the molecular diversity of the disease, making it challenging to determine the appropriate treatment. This is particularly true for patients with intermediate-risk AML and a normal karyotype. To address this issue, we conducted a study using complementary-DNA microarrays to analyze gene expression in peripheral-blood and bone marrow samples from 116 adults with AML, including 45 with a normal karyotype. Through unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis, we identified distinct molecular subgroups with unique gene-expression patterns. We then developed a gene-expression-based clinical-outcome predictor using a novel supervised learning algorithm. This predictor was tested on an independent validation group of 57 patients. Our analysis revealed new molecular subtypes of AML, including two subgroups that were prognostically relevant for patients with a normal karyotype. The gene-expression predictor, consisting of 133 genes, accurately predicted overall survival in the validation group, including patients with a normal karyotype. In multivariate analysis, the gene-expression predictor emerged as a strong independent prognostic factor. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that gene-expression profiling enhances the molecular classification of adult AML.

title: Perspectives on public health workforce research.
text: The Office of Workforce and Career Development at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is dedicated to building a skilled, sustainable, and diverse public health workforce. They achieve this through evidence-based training, career and leadership development, and strategic workforce planning to enhance the health outcomes of the population. This article examines past efforts in identifying research priorities for the public health workforce, which can be summarized into eight major themes. We present a strategic framework for conducting research on the public health workforce, which encompasses six functional areas: definition and standards, data, methodology, evaluation, policy, and dissemination and translation. To prioritize and conceptualize the development of an actionable research agenda, we created a matrix that outlines the key challenges in analyzing the workforce across different categories. Through extensive reviews, we have identified valuable methods, models, and approaches for studying the public health workforce. Additionally, we explore innovative tools and approaches to address priority areas in research for public health workforce and career development, and evaluate how insights from various social science disciplines can inform the advancement of research and policy in this field.

title: Gene targeting using zinc finger nucleases
text: The ability to manipulate the mammalian genome in specific locations has significant implications for both basic and applied research. Gene targeting is a process that involves replacing a specific segment of a chromosome with a introduced DNA molecule through homologous recombination. This provides a precise method for manipulating the genome. However, the efficiency of gene targeting in mammalian cells has been limited in the past. Zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs) offer a promising solution to improve the efficiency of gene targeting. ZFNs introduce double-strand breaks in target genes, which then stimulate the cell's natural homologous recombination machinery. Recent studies have demonstrated that ZFNs can achieve targeting frequencies of up to 20% in a gene responsible for human diseases. However, further research is necessary to apply these findings in vivo and determine whether ZFNs cause any unintended genomic instability.

title: relative expression results in real-time
text: Real-time reverse transcription followed by polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is the most appropriate technique for detecting and measuring mRNA levels. It offers excellent sensitivity, reproducibility, and a wide range of quantification. Nowadays, relative expression is commonly employed, where the expression of a target gene is normalized using a non-regulated reference gene. Various mathematical algorithms have been developed to calculate an expression ratio based on the efficiency of real-time PCR and the deviation in crossing points between an unknown sample and a control. However, existing equations and models only allow for determining a single transcription difference between one control and one sample. To address this limitation, a new software tool called REST (relative expression software tool) was created. REST enables the comparison of two groups, with up to 16 data points in both the sample and control groups, for reference and up to four target genes. The mathematical model employed by REST is based on PCR efficiencies and the average crossing point deviation between the sample and control groups. Furthermore, the expression ratio results of the four analyzed transcripts are assessed for significance using a randomization test. This article explains the development and application of REST and discusses the benefits of using relative expression in real-time PCR with REST. The latest version of REST software and examples for proper usage can be downloaded from http://www.wzw.tum.de/gene-quantification/.

title: Pain attacks in non-complicated and complicated gallstone disease have a characteristic pattern and are accompanied by dyspepsia in most patients: the results of a prospective study.
text: The objective of this study was to determine the typical pain pattern and extent of associated dyspepsia in patients with gallstone disease. A total of 220 patients with symptomatic gallstone disease were interviewed using detailed questionnaires. The results showed that all patients experienced pain in the right upper quadrant, with 20% localizing the pain to the right subcostal area and 14% to the upper epigastrium. The remaining 66% had more evenly distributed pain. A specific area of maximal pain could be identified in 90% of patients, with 51% experiencing it under the costal arch and 41% in the epigastrium. The pain was referred to the back in 63% of patients. The mean visual analogue scale score for pain intensity was 90 mm on a 0-100 scale. The majority of patients experienced a pattern of incipient or low-grade warning pain that would then subside. Seventy-one percent of patients had an urge to walk around during pain attacks, which typically occurred in the late evening or at night and lasted for more than one hour. Sixty-six percent of patients were intolerant to at least one type of food, with fatty foods being the most common trigger for symptoms. Symptoms of functional indigestion, such as gastroesophageal reflux, dyspepsia, or irritable bowel symptoms, were commonly seen in association with pain attacks. In conclusion, gallstone-associated pain follows a specific pattern in most patients, with a defined area of pain and referred pain. The pain typically occurs at night and lasts for more than one hour. Functional indigestion, particularly reflux or dyspepsia, is also commonly experienced by patients with gallstone disease.

title: Prevalence and cardiovascular disease correlates of low cardiorespiratory fitness in adolescents and adults.
text:
The population surveys in the United States indicate that physical activity levels are low. This lack of activity leads to low cardiorespiratory fitness, which is a known risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality. However, the prevalence of cardiorespiratory fitness in representative US population samples has not been quantified. 

The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of low fitness in the US population aged 12 through 49 years and to examine its relationship with CVD risk factors. The study used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999-2002, which included adolescents (aged 12-19 years) and adults (aged 20-49 years) without previously diagnosed CVD. Participants underwent submaximal graded exercise treadmill testing to estimate their maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max). 

The main outcome measures were low fitness, defined using percentile cut points of estimated VO2max, and various CVD risk factors measured using standard methods. The results showed that 33.6% of adolescents (approximately 7.5 million) and 13.9% of adults (approximately 8.5 million) had low fitness. The prevalence of low fitness was similar between adolescent females and males, but higher in adult females compared to males. Non-Hispanic blacks and Mexican Americans were found to be less fit than non-Hispanic whites. 

In all age-sex groups, higher body mass index and waist circumference were associated with lower fitness. The odds ratios of overweight or obesity were significantly higher in individuals with low fitness compared to those with moderate or high fitness. Participants with low fitness also had higher total cholesterol levels and systolic blood pressure, and lower levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. 

In conclusion, low fitness is common in both adolescents and adults in the US population, and it is associated with an increased prevalence of CVD risk factors.

title: In situ regulation of DC subsets and T cells mediates tumor regression in mice.
text: For patients with advanced cancer, vaccines are not very effective. This is because advanced disease requires strong and continuous activation of CD8(+) cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) to kill tumor cells and eliminate the disease. Recent studies have shown that certain types of dendritic cells (DCs) specialize in presenting antigens and producing cytokines that regulate both CTLs and T regulatory (Treg) cells, which suppress the immune response. In this study, we tested the idea that coordinated regulation of a network of DCs, particularly plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) and CD8(+) DCs, could enhance the immune response in mice. We used biomaterials that contained different combinations of an inflammatory cytokine, an immune danger signal, and tumor lysates to control the activation and location of DC populations in the body. The number of pDCs and CD8(+) DCs, as well as the production of interleukin-12, were strongly correlated with the strength of the immune response against tumors and the generation of powerful CD8(+) CTLs. By using this vaccination method, we were able to maintain local and systemic CTL responses for a long time while suppressing the activity of FoxP3 Treg cells during antigen clearance. As a result, distant and established melanoma tumors completely regressed. The effectiveness of this vaccine as a standalone treatment for large invasive tumors may be due to the local activity of pDCs and CD8(+) DCs, which are induced by persistent danger and antigen signals at the vaccine site. These findings suggest that a specific pattern of DC subsets is associated with the development of effective antitumor responses and can serve as a guide for future vaccine design.

title: VEGF inhibits tumor cell invasion and mesenchymal transition through a MET/VEGFR2 complex.
text: Blocking VEGF signaling in mouse models of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and certain GBM patients treated with bevacizumab leads to a proinvasive behavior. Our study reveals that vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) directly and negatively regulates tumor cell invasion by promoting the recruitment of protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to a MET/VEGFR2 complex. This recruitment suppresses HGF-dependent MET phosphorylation and inhibits tumor cell migration. Consequently, blocking VEGF restores and enhances MET activity in GBM cells, independent of hypoxia, and induces a program resembling epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. This is characterized by a switch from T-cadherin to N-cadherin and the acquisition of enhanced mesenchymal features. In mouse models of GBM, inhibiting MET prevents mesenchymal transition and invasion triggered by VEGF inhibition, resulting in significant improvement in survival.

title: Interaction between Oct3/4 and Cdx2 Determines Trophectoderm Differentiation
text: The first cell lineage to differentiate in mammalian embryogenesis is known as the trophectoderm (TE), which gives rise to the placenta, a unique structure in mammalian development. Although the differentiation of TE is a significant event in early mammalian development, the molecular mechanisms underlying this process are not well understood. By suppressing the POU-family transcription factor, Oct3/4, it is possible to induce embryonic stem (ES) cells to differentiate into the TE lineage. In this study, we demonstrate that this differentiation can also be achieved by overexpressing Caudal-related homeobox 2 (Cdx2), which is capable of generating trophoblast stem (TS) cells. While Cdx2 is not necessary for TE differentiation induced by Oct3/4 repression, it is crucial for the self-renewal of TS cells. In preimplantation embryos, Cdx2 and Oct3/4 are initially coexpressed and form a complex that reciprocally represses their target genes in ES cells. This suggests that the reciprocal inhibition of lineage-specific transcription factors may play a role in the initial differentiation event of mammalian development.

title: SSEA-1 is an enrichment marker for tumor-initiating cells in human glioblastoma.
text: It has been reported that CD133+ populations of human glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) cells are enriched for tumor stem cells (TSCs) or tumor-initiating cells (TICs). However, around 40% of freshly isolated GBM specimens do not contain CD133+ tumor cells, which raises the possibility that CD133 may not be a universal marker for GBM TSCs/TICs. In this study, we demonstrate that GBM cells expressing stage-specific embryonic antigen 1 (SSEA-1/LeX) fulfill the functional criteria for TSC/TIC. Firstly, SSEA-1+ cells are highly tumorigenic in vivo, unlike SSEA-1- cells. Secondly, SSEA-1+ cells can give rise to both SSEA-1+ and SSEA-1- cells, establishing a cellular hierarchy. Lastly, SSEA-1+ cells have the ability to self-renew and differentiate into multiple lineages. Almost all primary GBMs examined (n = 24) contained a distinct subpopulation of SSEA-1+ cells, with the exception of one case. Additionally, most CD133+ tumor cells were also SSEA-1+, suggesting that SSEA-1 may serve as a general marker for TSC/TIC enrichment in human GBMs.

title: Temporal regulation of topoisomerase IV activity in E. coli.
text:
We discovered a mutant form of dnaX, which encodes the tau and gamma subunits of the DNA polymerase III holoenzyme. This mutant allele causes cells to undergo extreme filamentation, but interestingly, it does not impact cell growth or DNA replication. The reason behind this phenotype is a defect in the decatenation of daughter chromosomes during rapid growth.

In these mutant cells, we observed a change in the behavior of ParC, one of the subunits of topoisomerase IV. Normally, in wild-type cells, ParC is associated with the replication factory. However, in the mutant cells, ParC was found to be distributed uniformly on the nucleoid. On the other hand, the distribution of ParE, the other subunit of topoisomerase IV, remained unaffected.

Furthermore, our experiments revealed that the majority of topoisomerase IV activity in synchronized cell populations occurred late in the cell cycle, when replication was almost complete. This suggests that the activity of topoisomerase IV in vivo might rely on the release of ParC from the replication factory.

title: Molecularly targeted therapy based on tumour molecular profiling versus conventional therapy for advanced cancer (SHIVA): a multicentre, open-label, proof-of-concept, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial.
text: The efficacy of molecularly targeted agents used off-label in patients with advanced cancer was assessed in a study conducted in France. The study included adult patients with metastatic solid tumors that were refractory to standard treatment. The molecular profile of each patient's tumor was established through biopsy and genomic testing. Patients were randomly assigned to receive a matched molecularly targeted agent or treatment of the physician's choice. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival. The study found that the use of molecularly targeted agents outside their indications did not improve progression-free survival compared to treatment at the physician's choice. The study suggests that off-label use of molecularly targeted agents should be discouraged, but enrollment in clinical trials should be encouraged to assess predictive biomarkers of efficacy.

title: CRTC2 (TORC2) contributes to the transcriptional response to fasting in the liver but is not required for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
text: The liver plays a role in maintaining glucose levels in the body by either storing or producing glucose, depending on the body's needs. The cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is a key regulator of genes involved in the liver's response to fasting, but how it activates these genes is still debated. To understand the role of a coactivator called CRTC2 in liver glucose metabolism, we created mice that lacked CRTC2. These mutant mice had reduced glucose production when exposed to glucagon, a hormone that stimulates glucose production. This decrease in glucose production was linked to a decrease in CREB binding to several genes involved in glucose production. However, despite the reduced expression of CREB target genes, such as PEPCK, G6Pase, and PGC-1alpha, the mutant mice did not experience low blood sugar levels. These findings suggest that CRTC2 plays a role in the liver's response to fasting at the genetic level, but its contribution to maintaining glucose levels is limited.

title: Ancient Hybridization and an Irish Origin for the Modern Polar Bear Matriline
text:
Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are highly vulnerable to the rapidly changing arctic climate, making their survival a global concern. However, there is limited knowledge about the evolutionary history of polar bears. Understanding their basic evolutionary information, such as when they diverged from brown bears (U. arctos) or how they responded to past environmental changes, would greatly benefit future conservation strategies. 

To address this, we used a spatially explicit phylogeographic model to analyze 242 brown bear and polar bear matrilines collected over the past 120,000 years across their current and historical geographic ranges. Our findings reveal that the distribution of these matrilines today is a result of both regional stability and long-distance dispersal from ice-age refugia. Furthermore, there is evidence of multiple instances of hybridization between polar bears and brown bears during the Late Pleistocene. 

The reconstructed matrilineal history of brown and polar bears has two notable characteristics. Firstly, it is marked by significant and distinct dispersal events driven by climate changes. Secondly, the overlapping ranges of these two species have led to opportunistic mating and a strong genetic influence. Notably, genetic exchange with extinct Irish brown bears is believed to have contributed to the origin of the modern polar bear matriline. This suggests that interspecific hybridization may be more common than previously thought and could serve as a mechanism for species to adapt to marginal habitats during periods of environmental deterioration.

title: FBW7 ubiquitin ligase: a tumour suppressor at the crossroads of cell division, growth and differentiation
text: FBW7, also known as F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7, plays a crucial role as the component responsible for recognizing substrates in the SCF (SKP1, CUL1, and F-box protein) ubiquitin ligase complex, which is evolutionarily conserved. SCFFBW7 is responsible for breaking down several proto-oncogenes involved in cellular growth and division pathways, such as MYC, cyclin E, Notch, and JUN. Additionally, FBW7 acts as a tumor suppressor, but its regulatory network is disrupted in various human malignancies. Numerous mutations associated with cancer have been found in both FBW7 and its substrates. Loss of FBW7 function leads to chromosomal instability and the development of tumors. This review focuses on the structural and functional aspects of FBW7 and its role in cancer development.

title: Hypoglycemic episodes and risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text:
The purpose of this study was to determine if severe hypoglycemic episodes requiring hospitalization are linked to an increased risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes.
