The study followed a cohort of 16,667 patients with type 2 diabetes for 27 years, from 1980 to 2007. The patients, with an average age of 65, were part of an integrated health care delivery system in northern California.

The main outcome measure was the occurrence of hypoglycemic events between 1980 and 2002, which were identified through hospital discharge and emergency department diagnoses. Patients who had no prior diagnoses of dementia, mild cognitive impairment, or general memory complaints as of January 1, 2003, were followed up until January 15, 2007, to determine if they developed dementia. The analysis used Cox proportional hazard regression models, adjusting for various factors such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, duration of diabetes, glycated hemoglobin levels, diabetes treatment, duration of insulin use, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke, transient cerebral ischemia, and end-stage renal disease.

During the follow-up period, 1,465 patients (8.8%) experienced at least one episode of hypoglycemia, while 1,822 patients (11%) were diagnosed with dementia. Among these patients, 250 had both dementia and at least one episode of hypoglycemia (16.95%). The study found that compared to patients without hypoglycemia, those with one or multiple episodes had an increased risk of dementia. The fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were as follows: for one episode (HR, 1.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.10-1.49); for two episodes (HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.37-2.36); and for three or more episodes (HR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.42-2.64). The attributable risk of dementia between individuals with and without a history of hypoglycemia was 2.39% per year (95% CI, 1.72%-3.01%). These results remained consistent even after considering medical utilization rates, length of health plan membership, or time since initial diabetes diagnosis. When examining emergency department admissions for hypoglycemia (535 episodes), the results were similar, with fully adjusted HRs of 1.42 (95% CI, 1.12-1.78) for one episode and 2.36 (95% CI, 1.57-3.55) for two or more episodes.

In conclusion, this study found that older patients with type 2 diabetes who had a history of severe hypoglycemic episodes had a higher risk of developing dementia. However, it remains unclear if minor hypoglycemic episodes also contribute to the risk of dementia.

title: Defective mast cell effector functions in mice lacking the CRACM1 pore subunit of store-operated calcium release–activated calcium channels
text: CRACM1, also known as Orai1, is responsible for forming the pore subunit of calcium channels that are activated by the release of calcium from stores. A mutation in the CRACM1 gene has been linked to severe combined immunodeficiency disease in humans. To study the effects of CRACM1 deficiency, we created mice that lacked CRACM1 and used β-galactosidase activity as a marker for CRACM1 expression. These CRACM1-deficient mice were smaller in size compared to normal mice. Mast cells derived from these mice exhibited significant defects in degranulation and cytokine secretion, and the allergic reactions observed in vivo were suppressed in the absence of CRACM1. We observed strong expression of CRACM1 in skeletal muscles and certain areas of the brain, heart, and kidney, but not in the lymphoid regions of the thymus and spleen. Conversely, CRACM2 expression was found to be higher in T cells of mice. Consistent with these findings, the influx of calcium from stores and the development and proliferation of T cells lacking CRACM1 were unaffected. Therefore, while CRACM1 plays a crucial role in mast cell function in mice, T cell calcium channels can still function properly without CRACM1.

title: MicroRNA-7: A miRNA with expanding roles in development and disease.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNA molecules that play a role in controlling gene expression after transcription. They bind to specific sequences on mRNA transcripts, leading to the degradation of the mRNA or a decrease in translation. Abnormal miRNA expression is closely linked to various human diseases, as miRNAs are involved in many aspects of normal cell development and functioning. Because of their important role in cellular processes, miRNAs have potential as therapeutics, diagnostic tools, and prognostic indicators in human health. One specific miRNA, miR-7, is highly conserved and has limited expression during development and maturity. It is generated from three different genes in humans and mice, highlighting its redundancy and significance in regulating key cellular processes. This review explores the expanding role of miR-7 in health, focusing on organ differentiation and development, as well as its involvement in various diseases of the brain, heart, endocrine pancreas, skin, and cancer. As we continue to study miR-7, we discover the complexity of its regulation and its potential applications as both a biomarker and therapeutic tool.

title: Integration-free induced pluripotent stem cells model genetic and neural developmental features of down syndrome etiology.
text: Down syndrome (DS) is the most common cause of congenital mental retardation in humans. The cognitive impairments associated with DS are a result of abnormal cellular processes during both development and in adult tissues. However, the exact mechanisms behind the development of DS are not well understood. In order to study DS and its characteristics, we created induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that accurately represent DS and normal (wild-type) cells. These iPSCs were generated using a nonviral method called episomal reprogramming. The DS iPSCs showed an overexpression of genes from chromosome 21, which is consistent with the extra copy of this chromosome in DS individuals. This overexpression led to the deregulation of thousands of genes throughout the genome. When the DS and wild-type iPSCs were converted into neural cells, they showed similar abilities in terms of lineage potency, differentiation kinetics, proliferation, and axon extension in the early stages. However, as time progressed, the DS cultures showed a preference for glial lineages, which are a type of support cell in the nervous system. Additionally, the DS neural cultures were more sensitive to oxidative stress-induced cell death compared to the wild-type cultures. This increased sensitivity could be prevented by using an antioxidant called N-acetylcysteine. Our findings highlight the complex genetic alterations caused by trisomy 21 (the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21) that contribute to the developmental abnormalities seen in DS. We also demonstrate that defective early glial development plays a central role in these abnormalities. Furthermore, the increased sensitivity to oxidative stress likely contributes to the accelerated neurodegeneration observed in DS. We provide evidence that DS iPSCs and their derivatives can be used to screen potential therapeutic interventions. The use of nonviral DS iPSCs allows for the modeling of complex human diseases in a renewable and ethically sound manner.

title: In Vivo CRISPR/Cas9 Gene Editing Corrects Retinal Dystrophy in the S334ter-3 Rat Model of Autosomal Dominant Retinitis Pigmentosa
text: The use of Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeat (CRISPR)/Cas9 for genome editing has the potential to effectively correct inherited diseases in patients. To demonstrate this, we have successfully utilized CRISPR/Cas9 in vivo to specifically eliminate the rhodopsin gene carrying the dominant S334ter mutation (Rho(S334)) in rats that serve as models for severe autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. By administering a single subretinal injection of guide RNA/Cas9 plasmid along with electroporation, we were able to disrupt the Rho(S334) allele in a targeted manner. This intervention effectively prevented retinal degeneration and resulted in improved visual function.

title: Vitamin D insufficiency and the blunted PTH response in established osteoporosis: the role of magnesium deficiency
text: Vitamin D insufficiency is a common issue, but not everyone experiences the biochemical effects of excessive parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. This is also true for patients with established osteoporosis. The reason behind the reduced PTH response is unclear, but it may be linked to a deficiency in magnesium (Mg). The objective of this study was to compare patients with established osteoporosis and varying levels of vitamin D and PTH to determine: (1) the presence of Mg deficiency using the standard Mg loading test, (2) the effects of Mg loading on the calcium-PTH endocrine axis, and (3) the effects of short-term oral Mg supplementation on the calcium-PTH endocrine axis and bone turnover. A total of 30 patients (10 women in 3 groups) were prospectively evaluated, measuring calcium, PTH, Mg retention (Mg loading test), dietary nutrient intake (calcium, vitamin D, Mg), and bone turnover markers (serum CTX & P1CP). Multivariate analysis was conducted to control for potential confounding baseline variables. In the low vitamin D and low PTH group, all subjects showed evidence of Mg depletion after the magnesium loading test [mean(SD) retention 70.3%(12.5)]. They also experienced an increase in calcium levels by 0.06(0.01) mmol/l [95% CI 0.03, 0.09, p=0.007] and a rise in PTH levels by 13.3 ng/l (4.5) [95% CI 3.2, 23.4, p=0.016] compared to baseline. Following oral supplementation, bone turnover markers increased: CTX by 0.16 (0.06) mcg/l [95%CI 0.01, 0.32 p=0.047] and P1CP by 13.1 (5.7) mcg/l [95% CI 0.29, 26.6 p=0.049]. In subjects with low vitamin D and elevated PTH levels, the mean retention of Mg was 55.9%(14.8), while in the vitamin replete group, it was 36.1%(14.4). There was little change in both acute markers of calcium homeostasis and bone turnover markers following both the loading test and oral supplementation. This study confirms that in patients with established osteoporosis, there is a distinct group with low vitamin D and blunted PTH levels, and Mg deficiency (as measured by the Mg loading test) plays a significant role.

title: Novel syndromes associated with JC virus infection of neurons and meningeal cells: no longer a gray area.
text:
The purpose of this review is to discuss the emergence of JC virus (JCV)-associated brain syndromes in patients with autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, Crohn's disease, and psoriasis. These syndromes were not previously recognized as factors for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The review focuses on three novel syndromes caused by JCV infection of neurons and meningeal cells that have been discovered in the last decade.

Recent findings have challenged the previous understanding that JCV exclusively infects oligodendrocytes and astrocytes in the white matter of the brain in immunosuppressed individuals. It is now known that JCV-infected glial cells can be found in the gray-white matter junction or solely within the gray matter, leading to demyelination in the cortex. Mutations in JCV can also cause a change in tropism, affecting other cell types like neurons and meningeal cells, resulting in distinct clinical entities. These new aspects of JCV infection pose challenges for clinicians caring for affected patients and researchers studying the virus's biology, pathogenesis, and tropism.

The hope is that increased awareness of these syndromes will lead to early diagnosis and facilitate further research to better understand JCV pathogenesis and develop effective therapies. However, it is important to remain vigilant and consider the possibility that other JC variants or unknown polyomaviruses may also be associated with neurological diseases.

title: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling pathways in tumor progression, invasion and angiogenesis.
text: The aim of this study is to explore the involvement of the PI3 kinase signalling pathway in human cancers and its potential as a target for anticancer therapy. The researchers conducted a review of recent literature on the role of PI3 kinase in tumor progression, focusing on its mechanisms of action and clinical implications. The results show that the misregulation of the PI3 kinase pathway is common in many types of cancer, either through the loss of the suppressor protein PTEN or the activation of PI3 kinase isoforms and downstream elements like AKT and mTOR. This activation not only promotes cell survival and proliferation but also enhances cytoskeletal deformability and motility, which are crucial for tumor invasion. Additionally, the PI3K pathway is involved in various aspects of angiogenesis, including the upregulation of angiogenic cytokines due to tumor hypoxia or oncogene activation and the response of endothelial cells to these cytokines. These cytokines signal through receptors such as VEGF-R, FGF-R, and Tie-2, facilitating processes necessary for neoangiogenesis, such as cell proliferation, migration, differentiation into tubules, and invasion of capillary sprouts into the extracellular matrix. In conclusion, a better understanding of the role of the PI3 kinase pathway in cancer will pave the way for the development of more potent and selective inhibitors that can complement conventional therapies by targeting key points in tumor progression, including cell survival, invasion, and angiogenesis.

title: Complementary foods for infant feeding in developing countries: their nutrient adequacy and improvement
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the energy and nutrient content of various complementary foods commonly consumed in parts of Africa, India, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and Thailand. 

Method: The energy, nutrient, and anti-nutrient (dietary fiber and phytic acid) content of twenty-three plant-based complementary foods consumed in developing countries were calculated per 100 g as eaten, per 100 kcal, and per day. This was done using food composition values based on chemical analysis for trace minerals, non-starch polysaccharides, and phytic acid, as well as information from the literature. The results were then compared to the estimated nutrient needs from complementary foods for infants aged 9-11 months, assuming a breast milk intake of average volume and composition, and three complementary feedings per day, each weighing 250 g.

Results: It was found that complementary foods should ideally provide approximately 25-50% of the total daily requirements for protein, riboflavin, and copper; 50-75% for thiamin, calcium, and manganese; and 75-100% for phosphorus, zinc, and iron. Most or all of the complementary foods appeared to meet the estimated daily nutrient needs for protein, thiamin, and copper. However, they fell short in meeting the needs for calcium, iron, and in some cases, zinc, even when assuming moderate bioavailability for iron and zinc. Additionally, some of the rice-based complementary foods were also lacking in riboflavin.

Conclusions: It was concluded that even if strategies to improve the bioavailability of iron and zinc were implemented, they would likely not be sufficient to address the deficiencies in calcium, iron, and zinc. Therefore, further research is urgently needed to explore the feasibility of fortifying plant-based complementary foods in developing countries with calcium, iron, and zinc.

Sponsorship: This study received support from the Micronutrient Initiative through the Canadian International Development Agency.

title: Early aging and age-related pathologies in mice deficient in BMAL1, the core componentof the circadian clock.
text: Mice lacking the circadian transcription factor BMAL1, which is responsible for regulating biological rhythms, exhibit disrupted circadian behavior and a loss of rhythmicity in the expression of target genes. Our study reveals that these BMAL1-deficient mice have shorter lifespans and display various signs of premature aging, such as sarcopenia, cataracts, reduced subcutaneous fat, organ shrinkage, and other symptoms. The early aging phenotype observed in these mice is associated with elevated levels of reactive oxygen species in certain tissues. These findings, combined with evidence of CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated control of stress responses, offer a potential explanation for the early onset of age-related diseases in the absence of BMAL1.

title: A self-inactivating lentiviral vector for SCID-X1 gene therapy that does not activate LMO2 expression in human T cells.
text: In order to improve the safety and effectiveness of gene therapy for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID-X1), we have assessed new self-inactivating lentiviral vectors derived from the HIV virus. The CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen vector contains the complete genomic sequence of the human common gamma chain (gamma(c)), controlled by the gamma(c) promoter. Meanwhile, the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector utilizes a promoter fragment from the eukaryotic elongation factor alpha (EF1alpha) gene to express a codon-optimized human gamma(c) cDNA. Both vectors incorporate a 400-bp insulator fragment from the chicken beta-globin locus within the self-inactivating long-terminal repeat. By transducing bone marrow cells with either of these vectors, we were able to restore the development and function of T, B, and natural killer lymphocytes in a mouse model of SCID-X1 transplantation. Furthermore, transduction of human CD34(+) bone marrow cells from SCID-X1 patients with either vector successfully reinstated T-cell development in an in vitro assay. In terms of safety, our Jurkat LMO2 activation assay revealed that only the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector did not possess the ability to activate LMO2 protein expression, whereas the CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen vector significantly activated LMO2 protein expression. Additionally, the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector did not induce any tumors in transplanted mice. Based on these preclinical demonstrations of efficacy and safety, we conclude that the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector shows promise for potential testing in a clinical trial.

title: Genetic Variants at Newly Identified Lipid Loci Are Associated with Coronary Heart Disease in a Chinese Han Population
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate whether genetic variants at newly discovered lipid-associated loci were linked to coronary heart disease (CHD) susceptibility in a Chinese Han population. We conducted a two-stage case-control study, with the first stage consisting of 1,376 CHD cases and 1,376 age and sex-matched controls. We examined five novel lipid-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) identified from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in Caucasians and their association with CHD risk in the Chinese population. We then validated significant SNPs in the second stage, which included 1,269 cases and 2,745 controls. Additionally, we tested the associations between SNPs within the five novel loci and blood lipid levels in 4,121 controls. Our findings revealed two novel SNPs (rs599839 in CELSR2-PSRC1-SORT1 and rs16996148 in NCAN-CILP2) that were significantly associated with a reduced risk of CHD in the Chinese population. The odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) in the dominant model were 0.76 (0.61-0.90; P = 0.001) and 0.67 (0.57-0.77; P = 3.4×10(-8)) for rs599839 and rs16996148, respectively. Furthermore, multiple linear regression analyses using the dominant model showed that rs599839 was associated with decreased LDL levels (P = 0.022), while rs16996148 was associated with increased LDL and HDL levels (P = 2.9×10(-4) and 0.001, respectively). In conclusion, our study identified two novel SNPs (rs599839 and rs16996148) at newly discovered lipid-associated loci that were significantly associated with CHD susceptibility in the Chinese Han population.

title: Spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress regulates glutamate excitotoxicity after partial respiratory inhibition of mitochondrial complex I with rotenone.
text: Rodents were used to study the effects of rotenone, a partial inhibitor of mitochondrial respiratory complex I, on Parkinson's disease. The hypothesis that rotenone-induced neuronal cell death is caused by oxidative stress was tested using rat cerebellar granule neurons in an acute glutamate excitotoxicity model. Even at low concentrations (5 nM), rotenone increased levels of mitochondrial superoxide and worsened glutamate-induced cytoplasmic calcium deregulation, which is the first irreversible stage of necrotic cell death. Surprisingly, the use of a cell-permeant superoxide trap did not prevent the effects of rotenone. The impact of rotenone on cellular respiration was measured by monitoring cell respiration. Glutamate activation of NMDA receptors utilized the full respiratory capacity of the mitochondria, with over 80% of the respiration increase attributed to increased cellular ATP demand. At a concentration of 20 nM, rotenone inhibited basal and stimulated cell respiration and caused respiratory failure in the presence of glutamate. Additionally, the inhibition of ATP synthase by oligomycin was toxic in the presence of glutamate. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that in the specific conditions of this study, the vulnerability of cells in the rotenone model of partial complex I deficiency is primarily determined by spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress.

title: Isolated liver perfusion for non-resectable liver tumours: a review.
text: Numerous treatments have been suggested for non-resectable primary or secondary liver cancer, but the outcomes have generally been unsatisfactory. Isolated Hepatic Perfusion (IHP) was initially attempted forty years ago, but it was only recently accepted after achieving remarkable tumor responses in isolated limb perfusion with melphalan and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) for melanomas and sarcomas. Surgical isolation of the liver is a technically challenging procedure that enables the safe administration of high doses of chemotherapy and TNF. Percutaneous techniques using balloon occlusion catheters are simpler but result in higher leakage rates from the perfusion circuit into the bloodstream. Several phase I-II trials indicate that IHP can produce high tumor response rates, even in cases of resistance to systemic chemotherapy. However, no significant improvement in overall survival has been demonstrated thus far. IHP offers unique pharmacokinetic advantages for localized chemotherapy and biotherapy. It may also facilitate gene therapy with minimal systemic exposure and toxicity. Currently, IHP remains an experimental treatment approach that should only be utilized in controlled trials.

title: Combinatorial control of exon recognition.
text: Pre-mRNA splicing is an essential process necessary for the expression of most genes in multicellular organisms. The spliceosome, responsible for this process, removes noncoding intronic sequences and assembles exons into mature mRNAs before exporting them for translation. Despite the complexity of higher eukaryotic genes and the variability of splice sites, the splicing machinery demonstrates remarkable precision in recognizing and pairing these sites. It efficiently removes introns of various sizes, ranging from less than 100 bases to as long as 100,000 bases. Additionally, a multitude of alternative splicing events occur in different cell types, during development, and in other biological processes. This extensive alternative splicing highlights the flexibility of the spliceosome in identifying and processing exons within a given pre-mRNA molecule. To achieve this flexibility, splice site selection in higher eukaryotes has evolved to depend on multiple factors, including splice site strength, the presence or absence of splicing regulators, RNA secondary structures, the organization of exons and introns, and the pre-mRNA synthesis process itself. The relative contributions of these factors determine the efficiency of splice site recognition and the removal of flanking introns.

title: High CTLA-4 expression on Th17 cells results in increased sensitivity to CTLA-4 coinhibition and resistance to belatacept.
text: Belatacept, a blocker of CD28/cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4), is known for selectively inhibiting alloreactive T cell responses. However, it has been observed that belatacept is linked to a high occurrence of acute rejection after kidney transplantation. This prompted us to investigate the causes of belatacept-resistant graft rejection. T cells have the ability to differentiate into various subsets of memory T cells, which collectively provide protection against different types of pathogens and can also react with allogeneic antigens, leading to graft rejection. Among these subsets, T helper 17 (Th17) cells are pro-inflammatory CD4+ cells that play a role in immunity against pathogens and are pathogenic in autoimmune diseases. Our research revealed that both Th1 and Th17 memory compartments had a similar frequency of divided cells after allogeneic stimulation. However, Th17 memory cells expressed significantly higher levels of the coinhibitory molecule CTLA-4 compared to Th1 cells. When stimulated in the presence of belatacept, Th1 responses were inhibited, while Th17 cells were augmented due to their greater sensitivity to coinhibition by CTLA-4. Interestingly, Th17 cells from kidney transplant recipients were resistant to ex vivo CD28/CTLA-4 blockade with belatacept, and a higher frequency of Th17 memory cells was associated with acute rejection during belatacept therapy. These findings emphasize the differences in costimulatory and coinhibitory requirements among CD4+ memory subsets and demonstrate that the heterogeneity of pathogen-derived memory has implications for strategies aimed at modulating the immune response.

title: A small molecule modulates Jumonji histone demethylase activity and selectively inhibits cancer growth
text: By inhibiting general transcriptional regulators, it is possible to impede growth by targeting multiple tumorigenic signaling pathways simultaneously. Through an innovative cell-based screening method, we have identified a distinct small molecule called JIB-04 that specifically inhibits the activity of Jumonji family histone demethylases in vitro, cancer cells, and tumors in vivo. Unlike existing inhibitors, JIB-04 does not competitively inhibit α-ketoglutarate. In cancer cells, but not in normal cells from the same patients, JIB-04 alters a subset of transcriptional pathways and hinders viability. In mice, JIB-04 reduces tumor size and extends survival. Importantly, we have discovered that breast cancer patients with overexpression of Jumonji demethylases have significantly lower survival rates. Therefore, JIB-04, a novel inhibitor of Jumonji demethylases in vitro and in vivo, represents a unique potential therapeutic and research tool against cancer. This finding also validates the use of unbiased cellular screens to uncover chemical modulators with relevance to diseases.

title: Gq protein alpha subunits Galphaq and Galpha11 are localized at postsynaptic extra-junctional membrane of cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal cells.
text: After the activation of cell surface receptors, the alpha subunit of Gq subclass of GTP-binding proteins initiates the phosphoinositide signalling pathway. In this study, we investigated the expression and distribution of Gq protein alpha subunits in the adult mouse brain using in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry. Among the four members of Gq protein alpha subunits, Galphaq and Galpha11 were predominantly transcribed in the brain. The highest level of Galphaq transcription was observed in cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs) and hippocampal pyramidal cells, while Galpha11 was mainly expressed in hippocampal pyramidal cells. The antibody targeting the C-terminal peptide common to Galphaq and Galpha11 strongly labeled the cerebellar molecular layer and hippocampal neuropil layers. In these regions, immunogold labeling specifically marked the cytoplasmic side of the postsynaptic cell membrane in PCs and pyramidal cells. The immunoparticles were distributed along the non-junctional cell membrane of spines, dendrites, and somata, but were mostly absent from the junctional membrane. Through double immunofluorescence, we found extensive colocalization of Galphaq/Galpha11 with metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR1alpha in dendritic spines of PCs and with mGluR5 in those of hippocampal pyramidal cells. Considering the concentrated localization of mGluR1alpha and mGluR5 in a peri-junctional annulus on PC and pyramidal cell synapses, our molecular-anatomical findings suggest that peri-junctional activation of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors is mediated by Galphaq and/or Galpha11, leading to the activation of the intracellular effector, phospholipase Cbeta.

title: The Bloom's syndrome gene product is homologous to RecQ helicases
text: The BLM gene, responsible for Bloom's syndrome (BS), plays a crucial role in maintaining the stability of genetic material in non-reproductive cells. To identify a potential candidate for the BLM gene, researchers directly selected a complementary DNA (cDNA) derived from a specific 250 kb segment of the genome where BLM was previously located through somatic crossover point mapping. This innovative mapping technique involved using cells from individuals with BS who had experienced recombination within the BLM gene. Through cDNA analysis, the researchers discovered a 4437 bp cDNA that codes for a 1417 amino acid peptide. This peptide showed similarities to the RecQ helicases, a subgroup of DNA and RNA helicases containing the DExH box. The confirmation that the candidate gene was indeed BLM came from the identification of chain-terminating mutations in individuals with BS.

title: Preventing obesity in children and adolescents.
text: This review focuses on the natural progression of obesity in children, effective approaches for preventing obesity in families and schools, and the challenges and opportunities associated with secondary prevention. The periods of adiposity rebound and adolescence are identified as critical stages of risk during childhood. However, caution is advised when interpreting early rebound as solely attributable to changes in body fat. To effectively prevent childhood obesity, it is crucial to target families and schools as key areas for intervention. A productive approach involves examining factors that impact energy balance and identifying more immediate influences on these factors. This approach can help narrow down strategies for preventing or treating childhood obesity. For instance, interventions targeting television viewing can address both energy intake and expenditure. Pediatricians can play a role in providing anticipatory guidance to change parental attitudes and practices related to television viewing. Similarly, school-based interventions can focus on promoting healthier food choices and reducing sedentary behavior.

title: Culture of Preimplantation Mouse Embryos Affects Fetal Development and the Expression of Imprinted Genes1
text:
The growth and differentiation of preimplantation mammalian embryos and cells can be influenced by their cultural environment. In a previous study, we found that the culture of mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in the deregulation of genomic imprinting, affecting their ability to develop into normal fetuses. In this current study, we aimed to investigate whether the culture of preimplantation mouse embryos in a chemically defined medium (M16) with or without fetal calf serum (FCS) could impact their subsequent development and the expression of imprinted genes. 

We discovered that only one third of the blastocysts cultured from two-cell embryos in M16 medium supplemented with FCS were able to develop into viable Day 14 fetuses after being transferred into recipients. These M16 + FCS fetuses had a reduced weight compared to the controls and M16 fetuses, and they exhibited decreased expression of the imprinted H19 and insulin-like growth factor 2 genes. This decrease in expression was associated with an increase in DNA methylation at an imprinting control region upstream of H19. Additionally, these fetuses showed increased expression of the imprinted gene Grb10. On the other hand, the expression of the growth factor receptor binding gene Grb7 was significantly reduced in most of the M16 + FCS fetuses. No changes were observed in the imprinted gene Mest. 

Our findings suggest that the culture of preimplantation embryos in the presence of serum can impact the regulation of multiple imprinted genes related to growth, leading to abnormal fetal growth and development.

title: Results of screening for intracranial aneurysms in patients with coarctation of the aorta.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the prevalence of intracranial aneurysms (IAs) in patients with aortic coarctation. Previous studies have shown that IAs are found in 2.3% of adults, with the mean age of detection being 52 years. However, the prevalence is less than 0.5% in young adults. Early studies have suggested that 10%-50% of patients with aortic coarctation have IAs, but screening recommendations vary.

To examine the prevalence of IAs, we conducted a screening using magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) on consecutive patients aged 16 and above with coarctation. The study included patients who underwent brain MRA between May 1999 and October 2007. MRA was performed using a 1.5T scanner with a 3D time-of-flight protocol, and simultaneous imaging of the heart and aorta was also done. The cerebral MRAs were reviewed by a neuroradiologist. Statistical analysis was performed using mean ± standard deviation and median ± range. Continuous variables were compared using Student t tests and Mann-Whitney U tests, while categorical variables were compared using the Fisher exact test.

A total of 117 MRAs were reviewed in this study. The median age of the patients was 29 ± 11 years (range, 16-59 years). IAs were found in 12 patients (10.3%), with a mean diameter of 3.9 mm (range, 2.0-8.0 mm). Patients with IAs were older (median, 37 years; range, 16-50 years) compared to those without IAs (median, 23 years; range, 16-59 years; Z = -2.01, P = .04). Hypertension was more common in patients with IAs (83% with IA versus 43% without IA, P = .01). There was no association between ascending aortopathy, bicuspid aortic valves, and IAs.

In conclusion, patients with coarctation have a higher prevalence of IAs, which occur at an earlier age compared to the general population. The appropriateness of routine screening for this group of patients remains unclear. Hypertension is likely to be an important factor in the development of IAs.

title: A new look at the heart in diabetes mellitus: from ailing to failing
text: This review examines the various mechanisms involved in diabetes that make patients more susceptible to cardiac morbidity and mortality. Studies using single photon emission computerized tomography or photon emission tomography with radioactive labeled analogues of norepinephrine have demonstrated that cardiac sympathetic dysfunction and incompetence are both early and late abnormalities in patients with Type I (insulin-dependent) and Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus. Additionally, photon emission tomography has revealed that in patients without myocardial perfusion deficits, there is a significant reduction in endothelial-dependent vasodilation in relation to cardiac sympathetic dysfunction. Furthermore, early signs of endothelial activation have been observed in patients with Type I and Type II diabetes, even before vascular disease is clinically detected. This activation, along with glycemic control, plays a crucial role in determining macrovascular mortality. However, with near normalization of glycemia, cardiac sympathetic dysfunction can be partially restored to normal levels. These findings suggest that previously unrecognized subtle changes in the heart can lead to failure, particularly after ischemia-induced remodeling, and can contribute to the instability and rupture of arteriosclerotic plaques. These changes, combined with the effects of hyperglycemia and diabetes on the endothelium of large blood vessels, such as impaired nitric oxide release or activation of protein kinase-C β, further exacerbate the situation. Therefore, meticulous glucose control early on and prompt correction of hyperglycemia in patients with acute coronary syndrome are essential components of a comprehensive approach to prevent the progression of heart failure in diabetes. [Diabetologia (2000) 43: 1455–1469]

title: Genetic and epigenetic mutations affect the DNA binding capability of human ZFP57 in transient neonatal diabetes type 1
text: In mice, ZFP57 has three classical Cys2His2 zinc finger domains (ZF) and recognizes the methylated TGC(met)CGC target sequence using the first and second ZFs. This study demonstrates that the human version of ZFP57 (hZFP57), which has six Cys2His2 ZFs, binds to the same methylated sequence using the third and fourth ZFs. The study also identifies the amino acids that are crucial for the interaction between hZFP57 and DNA. Furthermore, the study provides evidence suggesting that mutations in hZFP57 and hypomethylation of the TNDM1 ICR, both of which are associated with Transient Neonatal Diabetes Mellitus type 1, lead to the loss of hZFP57 binding to the TNDM1 locus. This loss of binding likely results in the activation of PLAGL1.

title: Physiological astrocytic calcium levels stimulate glutamate release to modulate adjacent neurons.
text: The release of glutamate by astrocytes can occur in a calcium-dependent manner, allowing them to communicate with nearby neurons. However, it is unclear whether this pathway is used during normal physiological signaling or only in abnormal conditions. One reason for this uncertainty is the limited knowledge about the specific levels of calcium required to trigger glutamate release from astrocytes and how these levels compare to the normal calcium levels in these cells. To address this, we conducted experiments using flash photolysis to increase the internal calcium levels in astrocytes. We simultaneously monitored the calcium levels in the astrocytes and the release of glutamate, which resulted in slow inward currents that were measured in single neurons grown on microislands of astrocytes. Our findings revealed that even modest changes in astrocytic calcium, ranging from 84 to 140 nM, led to significant glutamatergic currents in neighboring neurons (-391 pA). The Hill coefficient, a measure of the steepness of the response curve, ranged from 2.1 to 2.7. Importantly, our quantitative studies demonstrated that the agonists glutamate, norepinephrine, and dopamine all raised astrocytic calcium levels above 1.8 microM. This indicates that the release of glutamate from astrocytes is activated at physiological levels of internal calcium. Therefore, the calcium-dependent release of glutamate from astrocytes operates within a suitable range of astrocytic calcium levels, allowing it to function as a signaling pathway in the functional nervous system.

title: Albumin and furosemide therapy in hypoproteinemic patients with acute lung injury.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the potential benefits of diuresis and colloid replacement in hypoproteinemic patients with acute lung injury. The study was designed as a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial and was conducted in all adult intensive care units of two university hospitals. The study included thirty-seven mechanically-ventilated patients with acute lung injury and serum total protein levels of 5.0 g/dL or less.

The intervention consisted of a five-day protocolized regimen, where patients received 25 g of human serum albumin every 8 hours along with continuous infusion of furosemide. The control group received dual placebo. The primary outcomes measured were changes in weight, serum total protein, fluid balance, hemodynamics, respiratory system compliance, and oxygenation.

Baseline characteristics were similar between the treatment and control groups, with trauma being the main cause of acute lung injury. Over the course of five days, the treatment group experienced diuresis and weight loss, with a significant difference of 5.3 kg compared to the control group (p =.04). Within 24 hours, the treatment group also showed improvements in the Pao2/Fio2 ratio, increasing from 171 to 236 (p =.02). There were no significant changes in respiratory mechanics. Mean arterial pressure increased from 80 to 88 mm Hg (p =.10), and heart rate decreased from 110 to 95 beats/min (p =.008) over time in the treatment group. There was no difference in mortality, but there were favorable trends in measures of intensive care.

In conclusion, albumin and furosemide therapy improved fluid balance, oxygenation, and hemodynamics in hypoproteinemic patients with acute lung injury. However, further studies are needed to determine the impact of this therapy on cost, outcomes, and other patient populations.

title: Advances in functional and structural mr image analysis and implementation as fsl
text: The interrogation and analysis techniques used for neuroimaging data play a significant role in determining the flexibility, sensitivity, and range of neuroimaging experiments. The advancement of these methodologies has enabled researchers to address scientific questions that were previously unanswerable, making it a crucial field of study. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the research conducted by the Analysis Group at the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain (FMRIB). The primary focus of this research has been on developing novel methodologies for analyzing both structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging data. The majority of the research discussed in this paper has been implemented as freely accessible software tools within FMRIB's Software Library (FSL).

title: Metformin—mode of action and clinical implications for diabetes and cancer
text: For many years, metformin has been the primary treatment for diabetes mellitus. However, the exact mechanisms of how metformin works have not been well-defined. Recent advancements have shed light on the potential of metformin to target metabolic differences between normal and abnormal metabolic signaling, in addition to its ability to lower glucose levels. Understanding how metformin functions can aid in the development of new treatments. The main focus of metformin's action is altering the cell's energy metabolism. It achieves its glucose-lowering effect by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and counteracting the effects of glucagon. By inhibiting mitochondrial complex I, metformin disrupts cAMP and protein kinase A signaling in response to glucagon. While the activation of 5'-AMP-activated protein kinase is not necessary for metformin's glucose-lowering effect, it does enhance insulin sensitivity by regulating lipid metabolism. Metformin may also have an impact on tumorigenesis, indirectly by reducing insulin levels systemically and directly by inducing energetic stress. However, further research is needed to fully understand these effects. In this discussion, we explore the updated understanding of metformin's antigluconeogenic action in the liver and the implications of its targets for the treatment of diabetes mellitus and cancer.

title: Characteristics of the Earliest Cross-Neutralizing Antibody Response to HIV-1
text: Recent studies have shown that a significant percentage of individuals infected with HIV-1 develop broadly cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies. However, it is unclear when these antibodies first appear and whether they target specific regions of the viral envelope glycoprotein. In this study, we examined the cross-neutralizing antibody responses in plasma samples collected shortly after HIV-1 infection and up to seven years later. Our findings indicate that these antibodies typically emerge around 2.5 years after infection, although in some cases they can appear as early as 1 year after infection. If cross-neutralizing antibodies do not develop within the first 2-3 years of infection, it is unlikely that they will appear later on. We also observed a potential connection between the development of these antibodies and certain markers on T cells, as well as the level of virus in the bloodstream. The earliest cross-neutralizing antibodies primarily target the CD4-binding site and other epitopes found on the trimeric form of the viral envelope, rather than the monomeric form. In contrast, individuals who do not develop cross-neutralizing antibodies tend to have neutralizing activity against epitopes on the monomeric form of the envelope protein. This research not only enhances our understanding of how the immune system interacts with HIV, but also provides insights that could inform the development of effective vaccination strategies. Given that antibodies targeting complex epitopes on the viral envelope spike are crucial for early cross-neutralizing activity, future vaccine efforts should focus on eliciting similar antibodies.

title: Gender, age, and heart failure with preserved left ventricular systolic function.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine whether women are more likely than men to have heart failure (HF) with preserved systolic function, taking into account potential confounding factors such as age. Previous research has suggested a link between female gender and preserved left ventricular systolic function (LVSF) in HF patients, but these studies have been limited by referral biases, small sample sizes, or the inability to adjust for various confounding variables. 

For this cross-sectional study, data was collected from retrospective medical chart reviews of a national sample of Medicare beneficiaries who were hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of HF in non-governmental acute-care hospitals in the U.S. between April 1998 and March 1999. To be included in the analysis, patients had to be 65 years or older, have documentation of LVSF, and confirmation of the HF diagnosis. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with preserved LVSF, which was defined as normal function or an ejection fraction of 0.50 or higher. Stratified regressions were conducted by gender to identify any significant interactions. 

Out of the 19,710 patients included in the analysis, 6,700 (35%) had preserved LVSF, with 79% of them being women. In contrast, among the 12,956 patients with impaired LVSF, only 49% were women. Patients with preserved LVSF were, on average, 1.5 years older than those with impaired LVSF. After adjusting for age and other patient factors, female gender remained strongly associated with preserved LVSF, with a calculated risk ratio of 1.71 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.63 to 1.78. This association was consistent across all age groups and was similar in patients with or without coronary artery disease, hypertension, pulmonary disease, renal insufficiency, or atrial fibrillation. 

In conclusion, in elderly patients hospitalized with HF, preserved systolic function is primarily observed in women, regardless of important demographic and clinical characteristics.

title: YAP/TAZ-Dependent Reprogramming of Colonic Epithelium Links ECM Remodeling to Tissue Regeneration
text: The process of tissue regeneration involves cells adapting to the wound environment in a dynamic manner. However, the specific mechanisms by which this occurs at the cellular level and how severe tissue damage affects cell fate are still not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the changes in cell fate that occur during colonic regeneration in a mouse model of colitis induced by dextran sulfate sodium (DSS). Our findings reveal that the epithelium undergoes a temporary reprogramming into a more primitive state. This reprogramming is characterized by the activation of fetal markers and the suppression of markers associated with adult stem cells and differentiated cells. The orchestration of this fate change involves the remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), an increase in FAK/Src signaling, and ultimately the activation of YAP/TAZ. To further understand this process, we conducted experiments using a cell culture system that mimics the ECM remodeling observed in vivo. We found that a collagen 3D matrix supplemented with Wnt ligands is sufficient to sustain the activation of endogenous YAP/TAZ and induce a conversion in cell fate. These findings provide a simplified model for tissue regeneration, highlighting the importance of cellular reprogramming in this process.

title: Summary
text: Podocyte morphology relies on the presence of Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and podocalyxin. Our study demonstrates a functional relationship between basement membrane components (collagen IV and laminin), podocalyxin expression, and the morphology of human glomerular epithelial cells (podocytes). Specifically, we found that GBM and laminin, but not collagen IV, up-regulate the expression of podocalyxin. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that laminin induces a modified morphology of podocytes, characterized by process formation, which is more pronounced in the presence of GBM. At high magnification, podocytes appear ruffled, and raised areas are observed on the basal cell surface using transmission electron microscopy. Interestingly, the presence of anti-podocalyxin antibody enhances the adhesion and spreading of podocytes to both collagen IV and laminin, suggesting that podocalyxin inhibits cell-matrix interactions. Furthermore, when podocytes are grown under increased glucose concentration, the expression of podocalyxin is significantly suppressed, and although the cells still adhere and spread to basement membrane components, there is no increase in adhesion and spreading in the presence of anti-podocalyxin antibody, nor any ruffling of the cell edges. Additionally, in podocytes expressing podocalyxin, the presence of anti-podocalyxin antibody partially reverses the inhibition of adhesion to collagen IV caused by anti-beta1 integrin antibody, indicating that podocalyxin competes with beta1-related cell adhesion. Based on these findings, we propose that the inhibitory effect of podocalyxin on binding to the matrix contributes to the unique conformation of the basal surface of podocytes.

title: Mfold web server for nucleic acid folding and hybridization prediction
text: The 'mfold web server' is a collection of software applications found on the World Wide Web (WWW) that are used to predict the secondary structure of single stranded nucleic acids. The main goal of this web server is to provide easy access to RNA and DNA folding and hybridization software for the scientific community. To ensure compatibility, the server utilizes web GUIs (Graphical User Interfaces) that are universally accessible. The server offers detailed output, including structure plots with or without reliability information, single strand frequency plots, and 'energy dot plots' for single sequences. Additionally, there are 'bulk' servers available that provide less information but process multiple sequences in a shorter time. The mfold web server can be accessed through the URL http://www.bioinfo.rpi.edu/applications/mfold, which will be referred to as 'MFOLDROOT'.

title: Grip strength in healthy caucasian adults: reference values.
text:
The purpose of this study was to update the reference data for handgrip strength in healthy adults of both genders across a wide age range, and to analyze potential factors that may influence grip strength. The study involved 769 healthy adults (403 women and 366 men) between the ages of 20 and 95. Grip strength measurements were taken using a Baseline digital hydraulic dynamometer in a standardized manner, considering the neutral position of the arm, forearm, and wrist.

The results showed that women had approximately 41% less grip strength (29 kg right hand, 27 kg left hand) compared to men (49 kg right hand, 47 kg left hand), resulting in a slightly higher left-to-right hand ratio of approximately .95 for both genders. Grip strength developed similarly in both genders, peaking at 35 years of age and gradually decreasing thereafter. Anthropometric factors such as forearm circumference and length, hand size, and body mass were positively correlated with grip strength. However, body mass index, type of work, and hand dominance only showed a partial positive correlation or no correlation at all with grip strength.

Gender and age were found to be the most significant predictors of handgrip strength, followed by parameters representing body length and obesity. These factors were used to generate prediction equations. The study recommends adjusting measured values for intra-individual comparison, considering anthropometric characteristics, and using gender- and age-adjusted reference values. Hand dominance can be disregarded. The regression equations generated in this study may be useful for clinicians or those using normative values in software to provide more accurate predictions of strength scores for specific applications.

title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age
text: Despite the lack of evidence supporting their usefulness, biomarkers of ovarian reserve are being promoted as potential indicators of reproductive potential. The objective of this study was to examine the associations between biomarkers of ovarian reserve and reproductive potential in women of late reproductive age. The study was a prospective time-to-pregnancy cohort study conducted from 2008 to March 2016, involving 981 women aged 30 to 44 years without a history of infertility who had been trying to conceive for 3 months or less. The participants were recruited from the community in the Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina area. The study measured the early-follicular-phase serum levels of antimüllerian hormone (AMH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and inhibin B, as well as the urinary level of FSH. The primary outcomes measured were the cumulative probability of conception by 6 and 12 cycles of attempt, as well as the relative fecundability (probability of conception in a given menstrual cycle). The results showed that women with low AMH values did not have a significantly different probability of conceiving compared to women with normal values. Similarly, women with high serum FSH values or high urinary FSH values did not have a significantly different probability of conceiving compared to women with normal values. Inhibin B levels were also not associated with the probability of conceiving in a given cycle. In conclusion, among women aged 30 to 44 years without a history of infertility who had been trying to conceive for 3 months or less, biomarkers indicating diminished ovarian reserve were not associated with reduced fertility. Therefore, the use of urinary or blood follicle-stimulating hormone tests or antimüllerian hormone levels to assess natural fertility in women with these characteristics is not supported by these findings.

title: Matrix-embedded osteocytes regulate mobilization of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells.
text: The bone marrow (BM) niche consists of various cell types that regulate the movement of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) from the niche to the bloodstream. In this study, we show that osteocytes, the main cells in mature bone, play a role in controlling HSPC release. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), which is used in clinical settings to mobilize HSPCs, causes changes in the structure and gene expression of the osteocytic network before affecting osteoblasts. This rapid response is likely controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, as osteocytes express the β2-adrenergic receptor, and surgical sympathectomy prevents the response. Mice with targeted removal of osteocytes or a disrupted osteocyte network have similar numbers of HSPCs in the bone marrow but fail to mobilize HSPCs when exposed to G-CSF. These findings suggest that the interface between the BM/bone niche is crucially regulated from within the bone matrix and highlight the important role of skeletal tissues in hematopoietic function.

title: Generation of Genetically Modified Mice by Oocyte Injection of Androgenetic Haploid Embryonic Stem Cells
text: Genetic analysis can be conducted using haploid cells. Recent advancements in creating haploid embryonic stem cells (haESCs) from mice through parthenogenesis have allowed for genetic screening in mammalian cells. However, the successful generation of live animals from these haESCs, which is crucial for expanding genetic analysis to the organism level, has not yet been accomplished. In this study, we present the development of haESCs from androgenetic blastocysts. These cells, known as AG-haESCs, retain some paternal imprints, express typical pluripotency markers of embryonic stem cells, and contribute to various tissues, including the germline, when injected into diploid blastocysts. Remarkably, live mice can be produced by injecting AG-haESCs into MII oocytes, and these mice inherit genetic traits carried by the haESCs and grow into fertile adults. Additionally, gene targeting through homologous recombination is possible in the AG-haESCs. Our findings demonstrate that AG-haESCs can serve as a genetically manipulable fertilization tool for generating live animals by injecting them into oocytes.

title: The impact of hydroxyethyl starches in cardiac surgery: a meta-analysis
text:
INTRODUCTION
Recent research conducted on septic patients has suggested that the potential negative effects of hydroxyethyl starches (HESs) may outweigh their benefits, particularly in patients with severely impaired physiological haemostasis. However, it remains unclear whether this applies to patient populations that are less vulnerable. In this meta-analysis, we aimed to assess the impact of different generations of HES on safety and efficacy outcomes in patients undergoing cardiac surgery.

METHODS
We conducted a thorough search of the PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published in English or German. These trials compared the use of HES to any other colloid or crystalloid during open heart surgery.

RESULTS
Our findings indicate that older starches with mean molecular weights exceeding 200 kDa were associated with higher blood loss and transfusion requirements compared to other volume substitutes. However, this effect was not observed with the latest-generation tetrastarches (130/0.4), which performed even better when compared to albumin (blood loss of tetrastarch versus albumin: standardized mean difference (SMD), -0.34; 95% CI, -0.63, -0.05; P = 0.02; versus gelatin: SMD, -0.06; 95% CI, -0.20, 0.08; P = 0.39; versus crystalloids: SMD, -0.05; 95% CI, -0.20, 0.10; P = 0.54). Similar results were observed for transfusion needs. Additionally, patients treated with tetrastarches had significantly shorter lengths of stay in the intensive care unit and hospital compared to those treated with gelatin (intensive care unit: SMD, -0.10; 95% CI, -0.15, -0.05; P = 0.0002) and crystalloids (hospital: SMD, -0.52; 95% CI, -0.90, -0.14; P = 0.007).

CONCLUSIONS
Based on our meta-analysis of RCTs, we did not find any safety concerns associated with tetrastarches when compared to other colloid or crystalloid solutions in terms of blood loss, transfusion requirements, or hospital length of stay in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. However, the safety data on coagulation with older starches raise important questions that should be addressed in future trials.

title: Place of care in advanced cancer: a qualitative systematic literature review of patient preferences.
text: The current literature suggests that many patients desire to die at home, but there has not been a comprehensive review of the evidence regarding preferences for place of terminal care and death. The aim of this study was to conduct a systematic literature review on the preferences for place of care and death among advanced cancer patients. The researchers identified relevant studies through systematic searches of databases such as MEDLINE, PsychLit, and Bath Information Data Service. The studies were assessed and data were extracted and synthesized following the guidelines of the NHS Centre for Reviews and Dissemination. The studies included preferences from both the general population and specific groups, such as cancer patients and their caregivers. A total of eighteen studies were identified, which obtained views from patients, the general population, families, and professionals. The majority of respondents expressed a preference for dying at home, ranging from 49% to 100%. However, one study conducted in London with patients under the care of a continuing care team found that only 25% to 29% of patients desired a home death, with inpatient hospice care being the preferred option. It is important to note that the response rate for this study was unknown. Among the general public, there was a higher preference for inpatient hospice care among individuals who had recent experience with the death or dying of a close friend or relative. When comparing the views of patients, families, and professionals, there was general agreement, although patients expressed the strongest preference for dying at home. Only two of the studies provided longitudinal data, and nine of the eighteen studies had significant flaws in design or reporting. These flaws included poor or unknown response rates, unclear or unsystematic methods of eliciting preferences, and sample or measurement bias. However, when conducting a sensitivity analysis on the more robust and larger studies, the finding of a preference for home care at the end of life in over 50% of patients remained consistent. In conclusion, home care is the most common preference for advanced illness, followed by inpatient hospice care. Meeting these preferences could be important outcomes for healthcare services. Improvements in study designs in this area are necessary.

title: Linkage Disequilibrium Mapping of       CHEK2: Common Variation and Breast Cancer Risk
text:
Checkpoint kinase 2 (CHEK2) is a gene that plays a crucial role in preventing the development of cancer by promoting cell cycle arrest and activating DNA repair in cells that have genetic damage. Previous research has focused on the rare 1100delC mutation of the CHEK2 gene and its association with breast cancer. However, the impact of common variations in this gene on breast cancer risk is still unknown. In this study, we aimed to assess the significance of common CHEK2 variants in the general population's risk for breast cancer by examining a wide range of genetic diversity in the gene using haplotype tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms (tagSNPs). 

We analyzed 14 common SNPs that spanned 52 kilobases (kb) of the CHEK2 gene in a group of 92 Swedish women. Our evaluation showed that these selected SNPs effectively represented the association signals from other untyped SNPs in the same region. Six out of the 14 SNPs accurately predicted both the haplotypic and single SNP variations within the CHEK2 gene. We then genotyped these six tagSNPs in a larger group of 1,577 postmenopausal breast cancer cases and 1,513 population controls. However, we did not find any convincing association between common CHEK2 haplotypes and breast cancer risk. 

The rare 1100delC mutation was found in only a small percentage of our Swedish population, with 0.7% in cases and 0.4% in controls. The odds ratio for carriers of the mutation compared to noncarriers was 2.26 (95% confidence interval, 0.99–5.15). Based on the frequency and odds ratio of the 1100delC mutation, our sample is representative of a Northern European population.

title: Decoding Mammalian Ribosome-mRNA States by Translational GTPase Complexes
text: In eukaryotes, the accurate synthesis of proteins relies on a group of translational GTPases that work together with specific decoding factors to interpret the mRNA code on ribosomes. We have examined the structures of the mammalian ribosome in association with decoding factor⋅GTPase complexes, which represent different stages of translation elongation (aminoacyl-tRNA⋅eEF1A), termination (eRF1⋅eRF3), and ribosome rescue (Pelota⋅Hbs1l). Through comparative analysis, we have discovered that each decoding factor utilizes the flexibility of the ribosomal decoding center to modify ribosomal proteins and rRNA in distinct ways. This results in varying degrees of large-scale movements of the ribosome and suggests that different mechanisms are employed to transmit information from the decoding center to each GTPase. Furthermore, we have captured additional structural snapshots of the translation termination pathway, revealing the conformational changes that orchestrate the incorporation of decoding factors into the peptidyl transferase center. Our findings establish a structural framework for understanding how the mammalian ribosome selectively interacts with the appropriate decoding factor⋅GTPase complex to ensure accurate protein synthesis.

title: Intestinal Cgi-58 Deficiency Reduces Postprandial Lipid Absorption
text:
The protein Comparative Gene Identification-58 (CGI-58) is associated with lipid droplets (LDs) and promotes the breakdown of triglycerides (TGs) within cells. Mutations in CGI-58 in humans lead to the accumulation of TGs in various tissues, including the intestine. It was previously believed that enterocytes, which are cells in the intestine, do not store LDs rich in TGs. However, it has been observed that after consuming a fatty meal, LDs temporarily accumulate in the cytoplasm of enterocytes. These accumulated LDs are eventually cleared, suggesting the presence of a mechanism for breaking down TGs in enterocytes. However, the specific proteins responsible for this LD-TG breakdown have not been identified. 

In this study, we found that when CGI-58 is deactivated specifically in the intestine of mice, there is a significant decrease in postprandial plasma TG levels and TG hydrolase activity in the intestine. This is accompanied by a four-fold increase in TG content in the intestine and the accumulation of large LDs in the cytoplasm of absorptive enterocytes during fasting. Additionally, the mice with intestine-specific CGI-58 knockout showed a mild but significant decrease in the absorption and oxidation of fatty acids in the intestine. 

Interestingly, the inactivation of CGI-58 in the intestine led to an increase in both plasma and intestinal cholesterol levels, while reducing hepatic cholesterol levels. However, this did not affect the absorption of cholesterol in the intestine or the excretion of neutral sterols in feces. 

In summary, CGI-58 in the intestine is necessary for efficient secretion of TGs in lipoproteins after a meal and for maintaining lipid balance in the liver and plasma. Our animal model will be useful in further understanding how fat metabolism in the intestine contributes to the development of metabolic disorders like obesity and type 2 diabetes.

title: Transglutaminase 2 Undergoes a Large Conformational Change upon Activation
text: Human transglutaminase 2 (TG2) is an enzyme that belongs to a large family of enzymes responsible for protein crosslinking. It plays a crucial role in the extracellular matrix biology of various tissues and is associated with the development of celiac sprue, a condition triggered by gluten. While vertebrate transglutaminases have been extensively studied, the structurally characterized members of this enzyme family have only been observed in conformations where their active sites are inaccessible. However, we have successfully trapped human TG2 in complex with an inhibitor that mimics inflammatory gluten peptide substrates. Through X-ray crystallography, we have solved the crystal structure of TG2 at a resolution of 2-A. The inhibitor causes TG2 to adopt an extended conformation that is significantly different from previously observed transglutaminase structures. This conformation exposes the active site, revealing that catalysis occurs within a tunnel. This tunnel is bridged by two tryptophan residues, which separate the acyl-donor from the acyl-acceptor and stabilize the tetrahedral reaction intermediates. To further investigate the acyl-acceptor side of the tunnel, we conducted site-directed mutagenesis experiments. These experiments resulted in mutants that displayed a higher preference for hydrolysis over transamidation. By visualizing this activated conformation, our findings provide a foundation for understanding both the catalytic and non-catalytic roles of TG2 in biology. Additionally, this knowledge can help unravel the process by which the autoimmune response to TG2 is triggered in patients with celiac sprue.

title: Lactic acidosis in patients with diabetes treated with metformin.
text:
Dear Editor,

I am writing to bring attention to a concerning issue regarding the use of metformin in the United States. Since its introduction in May 1995, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has received reports of lactic acidosis in 66 patients who were treated with metformin until June 30, 1996. Out of these cases, 47 patients had their diagnosis of lactic acidosis confirmed based on circulating lactate values (>5 mmol per liter), following established criteria for diagnosis (Table 1).1,2 

Among the 47 patients with confirmed diagnoses, 43 of them had one or more risk factors for lactic acidosis. Specifically, 30 patients (64 percent) had preexisting cardiac disease, with 18 of them having a history of congestive heart failure. This information raises concerns about the safety of metformin use in patients with cardiac conditions. 

Thank you for considering this matter.

Sincerely,

title: The Apaf-1 apoptosome induces formation of caspase-9 homo- and heterodimers with distinct activities
text: According to established beliefs, initiator caspases are activated by coming into close proximity and forming identical pairs, but some studies suggest that during apoptosis, caspase-9 may instead join forces with the Apaf-1 apoptosome to create a complete enzyme. Through various biochemical methods, including a new technique that links specific sites together, we present the initial direct proof that procaspase-9 forms pairs within the apoptosome, significantly increasing its affinity for the complex and causing selective internal cleavage at Asp-315. Surprisingly, however, procaspase-9 could also attach to the NOD domain in Apaf-1 through its smaller subunit, resulting in the creation of a pair that more effectively activated procaspase-3. After being cleaved, the connecting part between the subunits (along with the accompanying changes in shape) in caspase-9-p35/p12 hindered its ability to form pairs, whether they were identical or not. Nevertheless, feedback cleavage by caspase-3 at Asp-330 completely removed the connecting part and partially restored the activity of caspase-9-p35/p10. Therefore, the apoptosome facilitates the formation of both caspase-9 identical pairs and non-identical pairs, both of which are affected by cleavage and contribute to its overall function.

title: Repositioning of aurora B promoted by chiasmata ensures sister chromatid mono-orientation in meiosis I.
text:
During the first stage of meiosis, known as meiosis I, the kinetochores of sister chromatids come together and fuse, resulting in a mono-orientation. On the other hand, homologous chromosomes that are paired through chiasmata, called bivalents, must undergo biorientation. In some species, including humans, there have been rare instances where sister chromatids, known as univalents, also undergo biorientation, which can lead to aneuploidy.

Our study conducted in fission yeast demonstrates that during early prometaphase I, biorientation of fused sister kinetochores is the predominant mechanism. However, in the absence of chiasmata, this undesired biorientation of univalents persists and eventually bypasses the spindle assembly checkpoint, resulting in abnormal anaphase.

We discovered that when univalents are connected either through chiasmata or an artificial tether, this incorrect attachment is converted to a monopolar attachment and becomes stable. This stability is achieved through a specific chromosome configuration that positions the kinetochores at the outer edge of the bivalent, while bringing Aurora B, a protein that destabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachment, inward.

Our findings provide insight into how chiasmata promote the biorientation of bivalents over univalents during meiosis I.

title: Biophysical Constraints Arising from Compositional Context in Synthetic Gene Networks.
text: The expression of synthetic genes is greatly influenced by the internal structure of the gene itself, such as the promoter structure, spacing regions between the promoter and coding sequences, and ribosome binding sites. However, we have limited knowledge about how the overall arrangement and orientation of genes on the DNA, known as intergenic compositional context, affects gene expression in synthetic gene networks. In this study, we compared the expression levels of induced genes that were arranged in convergent, divergent, or tandem orientations. We found that the induction of convergent genes resulted in significantly higher expression levels, increased sensitivity, and a wider dynamic range compared to divergent or tandem-oriented genes. The orientation of the genes had an impact on gene expression, regardless of whether one or both genes were induced. We propose that the interference in transcription caused by supercoiling in divergent and tandem genes can explain the differences in expression levels. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted modeling and in vitro experiments to relax the supercoiling. Treatment with gyrase, an enzyme that relaxes supercoiling, eliminated the effects of intergenic context and brought the expression levels within 30% of each other. Based on these findings, we reconstructed the toggle switch using convergent genes, leveraging the effects of supercoiling to enhance threshold detection and improve the stability of the switch.

title: Glucose repression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: Glucose serves as the main energy source for the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. While yeast cells have the ability to utilize various carbon sources, the presence of glucose inhibits the molecular processes involved in using alternative carbon sources, as well as represses respiration and gluconeogenesis. This dominant influence of glucose on yeast carbon metabolism is controlled by multiple signaling and metabolic interactions that primarily regulate transcriptional activity, but also have an impact at the post-transcriptional and post-translational levels. This article examines the effects of glucose repression on yeast carbon metabolism, focusing on the roles of the Snf3/Rgt2 glucose-sensing pathway and Snf1 signal transduction in the establishment and alleviation of glucose repression.

title: The p21 Cdk-interacting protein Cip1 is a potent inhibitor of G1 cyclin-dependent kinases.
text: The association between cyclin-dependent kinase Cdk2 and cyclins A, D, and E has been linked to the regulation of the G1 to S phase transition in mammals. In order to identify potential regulators of Cdk2, we utilized an improved two-hybrid system to isolate human genes that encode Cdk-interacting proteins (Cips). Among these proteins, CIP1 was discovered to encode a novel 21 kd protein that is present in immunoprecipitates of cyclin A, cyclin D1, cyclin E, and Cdk2. p21CIP1 is a powerful inhibitor of Cdks, forming a strong bond with them, and effectively inhibiting the phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin A-Cdk2, cyclin E-Cdk2, cyclin D1-Cdk4, and cyclin D2-Cdk4 complexes. Through cotransfection experiments, it has been observed that CIP1 and SV40 T antigen work in opposition to each other to regulate the progression of the cell cycle.

title: Exploring the temporal structure of heterochronous sequences using TempEst (formerly Path-O-Gen)
text: The analysis of gene sequences collected at different time points can provide insights into the evolutionary relationships on a natural timescale. This is possible when the sequences undergo noticeable changes over time. Such datasets are referred to as heterochronous and are increasingly used in various fields of biology, particularly in studying rapidly evolving viruses. In this study, we present TempEst, a software tool that allows for the visualization and analysis of sequence data collected at different time points. TempEst utilizes an interactive regression approach to explore the relationship between genetic divergence and sampling dates in a given molecular phylogeny. It serves two main purposes: (1) to determine if the data contains enough temporal information for phylogenetic molecular clock analysis, and (2) to identify sequences that exhibit inconsistencies between their genetic divergence and sampling dates. By examining these inconsistencies, TempEst can help identify potential issues with the data quality, such as annotation errors, sample contamination, sequence recombination, or alignment errors. We strongly recommend that users of the molecular clock models implemented in BEAST use TempEst as a preliminary step to assess their data before conducting further analysis.

title: Diabetes treatments and risk of amputation, blindness, severe kidney failure, hyperglycaemia, and hypoglycaemia: open cohort study in primary care
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the risks of various complications, such as amputation, blindness, severe kidney failure, hyperglycemia, and hypoglycemia, in patients with type 2 diabetes who were prescribed diabetes drugs, particularly newer agents like gliptins or glitazones. The study was conducted as an open cohort study in primary care, with data collected from 1243 practices contributing to the QResearch database in England. The participants included 469,688 patients with type 2 diabetes aged 25-84 years between April 1, 2007, and January 31, 2015. The study assessed the use of hypoglycemic agents (glitazones, gliptins, metformin, sulphonylureas, insulin, and others) alone and in combination. The main outcome measures were the first recorded diagnoses of amputation, blindness, severe kidney failure, hyperglycemia, and hypoglycemia, as documented in patients' primary care, mortality, or hospital records. Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios for diabetes treatments, adjusting for potential confounders. 

During the follow-up period, 4.5% of patients received prescriptions for glitazones, and 6.9% received prescriptions for gliptins. Compared to non-use, glitazones were associated with a decreased risk of blindness and an increased risk of hypoglycemia. Gliptins, on the other hand, were associated with a decreased risk of hypoglycemia. The study also found that patients prescribed gliptin monotherapy or glitazone monotherapy had significantly increased risks of severe kidney failure compared to those prescribed metformin monotherapy.
