However, patients prescribed dual therapy involving metformin with either gliptins or glitazones had significantly lower risks of hyperglycemia compared to metformin monotherapy. Patients prescribed triple therapy with metformin, sulphonylureas, and either gliptins or glitazones had higher risks of hypoglycemia compared to metformin monotherapy, but these risks were similar to those involving dual therapy with metformin and sulphonylureas. However, patients prescribed triple therapy with metformin, sulphonylureas, and glitazones had a reduced risk of blindness compared to metformin monotherapy. 

In conclusion, this study found that dual therapy involving metformin with either gliptins or glitazones was associated with lower risks of hyperglycemia compared to metformin alone. However, triple therapy with metformin, sulphonylureas, and either gliptins or glitazones was associated with an increased risk of hypoglycemia, similar to the risk for dual therapy with metformin and sulphonylureas. Additionally, triple therapy with metformin, sulphonylureas, and glitazones was associated with a reduced risk of blindness compared to metformin monotherapy. These findings, although subject to residual confounding, could have implications for the prescribing of hypoglycemic drugs.

title: Vertebrate rod photoreceptors express both BK and IK calcium-activated potassium channels, but only BK channels are involved in receptor potential regulation.
text: The Ca(2+)-activated K(+) current (I(KCa)) in salamander rods effectively maintains the dark membrane potential at its normal resting level. Through various experimental methods, including electrophysiology, pharmacology, and immunohistochemistry, we have determined that salamander rods express large-conductance Ca(2+)- and voltage-dependent potassium (BK) channels and intermediate-conductance Ca(2+)-dependent potassium (IK) channels, but not small-conductance Ca(2+)-dependent potassium (SK) channels. When 100 nM iberiotoxin or 100 nM clotrimazole was applied, the net I(KCa) was reduced to 36% and 63%, respectively, while the current remained unaffected by 1 microM apamin. Additionally, staining with anti-SK1, -SK2, and -SK3 antibodies did not show any presence in rod photoreceptors, whereas anti-BK and -SK4/IK1 antibodies heavily stained the ellipsoid region of the inner segments of the rods. Furthermore, in current-clamp experiments, it was evident that the strong clamping effect of the total I(KCa) was lost when IbTx, but not CLTZ, was applied to the bath. This suggests that only BK channels, not IK channels, are responsible for the clamping effect on the photoreceptor membrane potential.

title: Ondansetron reduces nausea and vomiting after paediatric adenotonsillectomy.
text: A multinational, multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness, safety, and resource implications of a single intravenous dose of ondansetron (0.1 mg.kg-1, maximum 4 mg) in children aged 1-12 years undergoing tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy. The study analyzed the occurrence of emesis (retching and/or vomiting) and nausea separately. The results showed that a significantly higher number of children treated with ondansetron had no episodes of emesis (127/212, 60%) compared to those in the placebo group (100/215, 47%) (P = 0.004). Similarly, a greater proportion of ondansetron-treated children experienced no postoperative nausea (135/211, 64%) compared to the placebo group (108/213, 51%) (P = 0.004) within the first 24 hours. Ondansetron also reduced the number of emetic episodes (P < 0.001), the time to the first emetic episode (P < 0.001), and overall severity of nausea (P = 0.003). Additionally, fewer children treated with ondansetron required rescue or withdrawal from the study (5% vs 10%; P = 0.042). Ondansetron also resulted in a lower need for nursing intervention (34% vs 45%; P = 0.007), with significantly shorter intervention times (4.6 vs 8.1 minutes; P = 0.001). The use of resources to manage postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) was significantly reduced with ondansetron (43% vs 57%; P = 0.014).

title: Assessing the cost effectiveness of using prognostic biomarkers with decision models: case study in prioritising patients waiting for coronary artery surgery
text:
The objective of this study was to determine the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of using information from circulating biomarkers to inform the prioritization process of patients with stable angina awaiting coronary artery bypass graft surgery. The study used a decision analytical model to compare different prioritization strategies, including those without biomarkers and those using biomarkers. The order in which patients would undergo coronary artery bypass grafting was determined by each strategy, and the mean lifetime costs and quality adjusted life years (QALYs) were compared.

The data for the study was sourced from the Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry, which included 9935 patients with stable angina awaiting coronary artery bypass grafting. These patients were followed up for cardiovascular events after the procedure for an average of 3.8 years. Meta-analyses of prognostic effects of biomarkers were also used as data sources.

The results showed that the observed risk of cardiovascular events while on the waiting list for coronary artery bypass grafting was 3 per 10,000 patients per day within the first 90 days. Using a cost effectiveness threshold of pound20,000- pound30,000 per additional QALY, the most cost effective strategy was found to be a prioritization strategy using a risk score with estimated glomerular filtration rate. This strategy had a cost per additional QALY of less than pound410 compared to the Ontario urgency score. Implementing this strategy would result in an additional 800 QALYs per 100,000 patients at an additional cost of pound 245,000 to the National Health Service.

On the other hand, the prioritization strategy using a risk score with C reactive protein was associated with lower QALYs and higher costs compared to a risk score using estimated glomerular filtration rate. Therefore, it was concluded that prioritization strategies based on the prognostic information conferred by C reactive protein, or a combination of C reactive protein and estimated glomerular filtration rate, are unlikely to be cost effective.

In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of evaluating the cost effectiveness of prognostic biomarkers, even when their effects at an individual level are small. It suggests that formal prioritization of patients awaiting coronary artery bypass grafting using a routinely assessed biomarker, such as estimated glomerular filtration rate, along with simple clinical information, is cost effective. The study also emphasizes the need to replace the widespread practice of using implicit or informal means of clinically ordering the waiting list with formal prioritization approaches.

title: Cytokine control of memory T-cell development and survival
text: There is growing evidence suggesting that cytokines play a crucial role in the development of memory T cells. In this study, we examine the journey of CD8+ T cells from their initial activation to the formation of memory cells, highlighting the specific points at which cytokines determine the fate of these cells. Among the cytokines, interleukin-7 (IL-7) and IL-15, which belong to the common cytokine-receptor γ-chain (γc)-cytokine family, play a significant role in promoting proliferation and survival at each stage of the immune response. This mechanism allows for the establishment and maintenance of a stable, protective, and long-lasting pool of memory CD8+ T cells.

title: Histone Methylation-Dependent Mechanisms Impose Ligand Dependency for Gene Activation by Nuclear Receptors
text: The conformational changes of nuclear receptors, which are necessary for corepressor-coactivator exchange, are known to be ligand-dependent. However, it is still unclear whether specific epigenetic landmarks are required to impose ligand dependency for gene activation. In this study, we present an unexpected and general strategy that relies on specific groups of inhibitory histone methyltransferases (HMTs) to enforce gene-specific gatekeeper functions. These functions prevent unliganded nuclear receptors and other regulated transcription factors from binding to their target gene promoters and causing constitutive gene activation in the absence of stimulating signals. This strategy, which is partially based on an HMT-dependent inhibitory histone code, necessitates specific histone demethylases, such as LSD1, to enable ligand- and signal-dependent activation of regulated gene expression. These findings establish a connection between the inhibitory methylation component of the histone code and a widely employed approach that prevents pathological constitutive gene induction by physiologically regulated transcription factors.

title: Human IRGM Regulates Autophagy and Its Cell-Autonomous Immunity Functions Through Mitochondria
text: An unknown mechanism allows IRGM, a human immunity-related GTPase, to provide autophagic defense against intracellular pathogens. In this study, we present a surprising discovery about how IRGM functions. IRGM displayed varying affinity for the mitochondrial lipid cardiolipin, relocated to the mitochondria, influenced mitochondrial fission, and triggered autophagy. The process of mitochondrial fission was crucial for IRGM to control intracellular mycobacteria through autophagy. IRGM also impacted mitochondrial membrane polarization and cell death. Overexpression of the IRGMd isoform, but not the IRGMb splice isoforms, led to mitochondrial depolarization and cell death that was independent of autophagy but dependent on Bax/Bak. By targeting mitochondria, IRGM can either provide autophagic protection or induce cell death, which explains its role in defending against tuberculosis and contributing to the damaging inflammation seen in Crohn's disease.

title: The Developmental Transcriptome of the Mosquito Aedes aegypti, an Invasive Species and Major Arbovirus Vector
text: Mosquitoes carry various diseases that are harmful to both humans and animals. In order to develop effective methods of controlling these disease vectors, it is crucial to have a deep understanding of mosquito biology. To achieve this, we utilized RNA-seq technology to identify new genes and gain a detailed understanding of the transcriptome during mosquito development and in response to blood feeding. Our study focused on Aedes aegypti, a mosquito species that is the primary carrier of Dengue and yellow fever, both of which are significant human diseases. We analyzed mRNA expression at 34 different time points throughout Aedes development, including various tissues in adult mosquitoes. Through polyA+ RNA-seq, we discovered 14,238 new transcribed regions corresponding to 12,597 new loci, as well as novel transcript isoforms of previously known genes. This significantly expands our knowledge of the transcribed genome in terms of long polyA+ RNAs. Additionally, we identified patterns of shared gene expression, as well as genes and exons that are expressed differently between sexes. We also examined the expression profiles of small RNAs in different tissues, leading to the discovery of 38 new Aedes-specific miRNAs and approximately 291,000 new transcribed regions of small RNAs, many of which are likely to be endogenous small-interfering RNAs and Piwi-interacting RNAs. Furthermore, we highlighted genes that could be of interest for transgene-based strategies to control mosquito populations. To make our findings accessible, we have incorporated our data into a user-friendly genome browser located at www.Aedes.caltech.edu, which includes relevant links to Vectorbase (www.vectorbase.org).

title: Gut microbial diversity is associated with lower arterial stiffness in women
text: The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between gut microbiome composition and arterial stiffness. The researchers analyzed data from 617 middle-aged women in the TwinsUK cohort, including measurements of carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV), a marker of arterial stiffness, and information on gut microbiome composition and serum metabolomics. After adjusting for covariates, they found a negative correlation between PWV and gut microbiome alpha diversity. Additionally, they identified seven specific microbial units associated with PWV, two of which belonged to the Ruminococcaceae family. These associations remained significant even after accounting for levels of gut-derived metabolites. By combining the PWV-associated gut microbiome variables, the researchers determined that microbiome factors explained 8.3% of the variance in PWV. Mediation analysis revealed that only a small proportion of the effect of the gut microbiome on PWV was mediated by metabolic syndrome and other risk factors. In conclusion, this study provides evidence that gut microbiome diversity is inversely associated with arterial stiffness in women, suggesting that targeting the microbiome could be a potential approach to treating arterial aging.

title: ALS-FUS pathology revisited: singleton FUS mutations and an unusual case with both a FUS and TARDBP mutation
text:
INTRODUCTION
Mutations in the FUS gene are a rare cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS-FUS). Although there is extensive clinical and genetic documentation, there have been limited studies on the neuropathological aspects. Recent research has suggested a potential link between pathological features, such as the presence of basophilic inclusions in neurons, and the rate of clinical decline. However, other studies have found inconsistencies between the clinical detection of upper motor neuron features and the associated pathology. This study aims to describe the pathological features associated with recently discovered FUS mutations and reexamine those with well-known mutations to establish a correlation between pathology, mutation, and clinical phenotype. The brains and spinal cords of seven ALS-FUS cases were examined neuropathologically, including cases with the newly identified p. K510E mutation and a case with both a known p. P525L mutation in the FUS gene and a truncating p. Y374X mutation in the TARDBP gene.

RESULTS
Neuropathological examination of all cases revealed the presence of basophilic and FUS inclusions in the spinal cord. The density and type of inclusions varied significantly among cases, but did not provide a clear correlation with clinical progression. Only one case exhibited significant motor cortical pathology, despite four patients showing clinical features of upper motor neuron involvement. The case with both FUS and TARDBP mutations displayed FUS-positive inclusions but no TDP-43 pathology. Instead, there were unusual p62-positive, FUS-negative neuronal and glial inclusions, as well as dot-like neurites.

CONCLUSIONS
This study confirms that ALS-FUS primarily affects lower motor neurons and demonstrates that the associated pathology does not neatly align with clinical features or genetics. Additionally, the case with both FUS and TARDBP mutations presents an intriguing pathological profile, involving a unique staining pattern for the ubiquitin-binding protein p62.

title: Coronary heart disease in south Asians overseas: a review.
text: Coronary heart disease rates among individuals from the Indian subcontinent have been reported to be unusually high in various parts of the world. It is noteworthy that high rates of coronary disease are prevalent among South Asian groups regardless of their geographical origin, religion, or language. This poses a challenge to our understanding of coronary heart disease, as the elevated rates in South Asians cannot be explained solely by factors such as high serum cholesterol, smoking, or hypertension. Instead, consistent findings indicate that South Asians living abroad exhibit low levels of plasma HDL cholesterol, high levels of plasma triglycerides, and a high prevalence of non-insulin-dependent diabetes. These findings likely reflect an underlying condition of insulin resistance. Further research is necessary to determine whether this metabolic disturbance can account for the increased rates of coronary heart disease in South Asians and to identify potential preventive measures.

title: A systematic review of parent and clinician views and perceptions that influence prescribing decisions in relation to acute childhood infections in primary care
text:
AIMS To examine the perspectives of parents, clinicians, and children regarding the decision-making process for prescribing antibiotics for acute childhood infections in primary care. 

METHODS A systematic review was conducted on qualitative studies. Meta-ethnographic methods were utilized to analyze and interpret data from the primary studies. 

RESULTS Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The literature primarily focused on concerns about over-prescription of antibiotics. Children's perspectives were not adequately represented. Clinicians prescribed antibiotics when they felt pressured by parents or external factors (e.g. employers), when there was a clear clinical indication, or when they were uncertain about clinical or social outcomes and prescribed "just in case". Parents desired antibiotics when they believed it would improve their child's current illness and when they felt pressure from daycare providers or employers. Clinicians avoided prescribing antibiotics when they were concerned about adverse reactions or drug resistance, when they were certain antibiotics were not necessary, or when there was no perceived pressure from parents. Parents also wanted to avoid the adverse effects of antibiotics and did not want them if they would not alleviate current symptoms. Some parents preferred to avoid medication altogether. During pediatric consultations, parents sought a medical evaluation and decision. Primary care clinicians aimed to satisfy parents and keep consultations brief. 

CONCLUSIONS Antibiotic prescriptions for childhood infections in primary care often occur as a precautionary measure. These findings suggest that interventions that address clinician uncertainty regarding social or clinical outcomes and provide strategies to meet parents' needs within a short consultation are most likely to reduce antibiotic prescribing.

title: Prevalent abnormal prion protein in human appendixes after bovine spongiform encephalopathy epizootic: large scale survey
text:
The aim of this study was to conduct a further investigation into the prevalence of subclinical infection with prions after the bovine spongiform encephalopathy outbreak. The study also aimed to determine if a broader birth cohort was affected and to understand the implications for the management of blood and blood products, as well as the handling of surgical instruments. 

The study design involved a large-scale survey of archived appendix samples that were irreversibly unlinked and anonymized. The samples were obtained from the pathology departments of 41 UK hospitals that participated in a previous survey, as well as additional hospitals in regions with lower participation levels. 

A total of 32,441 archived appendix samples were tested for the presence of abnormal prion protein (PrP). Out of these samples, 16 tested positive for abnormal PrP, indicating an overall prevalence of 493 per million population (95% confidence interval 282 to 801 per million). The prevalence did not significantly differ between those born in 1941-60 (733 per million) and those born between 1961 and 1985 (412 per million). The prevalence was similar across both sexes and the three geographical areas sampled. 

Genetic testing of the positive specimens revealed a high proportion of valine homozygous individuals compared to the normal population. This is in contrast to confirmed clinical cases of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD), which were all methionine homozygous. 

In conclusion, this study supports previous findings and suggests a high prevalence of infection with abnormal PrP, indicating vCJD carrier status in the population compared to the number of confirmed vCJD cases to date. These findings have important implications for the management of blood and blood products, as well as the handling of surgical instruments.

title: Involvement of cortical fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive basket cells in epilepsy.
text: The parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking basket cells subtype (PV INs), which are GABAergic interneurons, play a crucial role in regulating cortical network excitability and gamma oscillations, which are involved in signal processing and cognition. When the development or function of PV INs is impaired, it has been linked to epilepsy in various animal models and some genetic forms of epilepsy in humans. This review provides an overview of experimental data that connects dysfunction of PV INs with epilepsy, specifically focusing on disorders related to the specification, migration, maturation, synaptic function, or connectivity of PV INs. Additionally, we discuss the potential therapeutic applications of stimulating PV INs within active networks and transplanting PV INs precursors for the treatment of epilepsy and its associated conditions.

title: Dynamic Gene Regulatory Networks of Human Myeloid Differentiation.
text: Reconstructing gene regulatory networks that control cell differentiation is still a difficult task, especially when using high-throughput gene expression and chromatin data. In this study, we aimed to create dynamic gene regulatory networks for human myeloid differentiation by analyzing a 5-day time series of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. Specifically, we examined the differentiation of HL-60 promyelocytes into macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes, and monocyte-derived macrophages. Our findings revealed that certain key transcription factors and lineage markers rapidly influenced the expression of a subset of their targets at specific times. This was followed by changes in chromatin accessibility and further gene expression alterations. Interestingly, we observed differences between promyelocyte-derived and monocyte-derived macrophages at both the transcriptional and chromatin landscape levels, despite using the same differentiation stimulus. This suggests that the specific path taken by cells during differentiation determines their final cell state. Overall, our approach, which involved combining neighboring time points and replicates to increase sequencing depth, effectively allowed us to infer footprint-based regulatory networks from long series data.

title: Canonical transient receptor potential 5 channel in conjunction with Orai1 and STIM1 allows Sr2+ entry, optimal influx of Ca2+, and degranulation in a rat mast cell line.
text: The degranulation of mast cells in response to Ag or the calcium mobilizing agent, thapsigargin, relies on the release of Ca(2+) from intracellular stores and the subsequent influx of external Ca(2+), also known as store-operated calcium entry. However, it is unlikely that the calcium release-activated calcium channel is the only mechanism for Ca(2+) entry, as other divalent cations like Sr(2+) also permeate and support degranulation in stimulated mast cells. In this study, we demonstrate that the influx of Ca(2+) and Sr(2+), as well as degranulation, depend on the presence of the canonical transient receptor potential (TRPC) channel protein TRPC5, along with STIM1 and Orai1. We achieved this by using inhibitory RNAs to knock down each of these proteins in a rat mast cell (RBL-2H3) line. Overexpression of STIM1 and Orai1, which are known to be crucial components of the calcium release-activated calcium channel, allows the entry of Ca(2+) but not Sr(2+). On the other hand, overexpression of STIM1 and TRPC5 enables the entry of both Ca(2+) and Sr(2+). These findings, along with other observations, suggest that the Sr(2+)-permeable TRPC5 associates with STIM1 and Orai1 in a stoichiometric manner to enhance the entry of Ca(2+) and generate a signal for degranulation.

title: LincRNA-p21 suppresses target mRNA translation.
text: The primary role of mammalian long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) is to regulate transcription. However, our study reveals a new function for lincRNA-p21 in modulating translation. We found that lincRNA-p21 interacts with the RNA-binding protein HuR, which promotes the recruitment of let-7/Ago2 to lincRNA-p21. This interaction leads to decreased stability of lincRNA-p21. When HuR levels are reduced, lincRNA-p21 accumulates in HeLa cells, specifically binding to JUNB and CTNNB1 mRNAs and inhibiting their translation. Conversely, elevated HuR levels result in decreased lincRNA-p21 levels, which in turn enhances JunB and β-catenin translation and increases the levels of these proteins. Our study suggests that HuR regulates the translation of certain target mRNAs by influencing the levels of lincRNA-p21. These findings highlight the role of lincRNA as a posttranscriptional inhibitor of translation.

title: Large intestine-targeted nanoparticle-releasing oral vaccine to control genitorectal viral infection
text: Transmission of pathogenic microorganisms can occur through both rectal and vaginal mucosal surfaces. Animal studies have shown that vaccination through the large intestinal mucosa can provide protection for both of these sites. However, direct intracolorectal administration is not practical in a clinical setting. Oral vaccine delivery is a preferred method, but there is a risk of the vaccine being destroyed in the upper gastrointestinal tract. To address this issue, we developed a targeted oral delivery system using pH-dependent microparticles containing vaccine nanoparticles. This system successfully induced colorectal immunity in mice, offering protection against rectal and vaginal viral challenges. In contrast, when the vaccine was targeted to the small intestine, it only provided immunity in that area and did not protect the rectal or vaginal mucosa. This demonstrates the functional compartmentalization within the gut mucosal immune system. Therefore, targeting the large intestine with this oral vaccine delivery system could be a viable strategy for immune protection of the rectal and vaginal mucosa.

title: Timing of menarche and first full-term birth in relation to breast cancer risk.
text: The age at which a woman first menstruates and the age at which she has her first child are known to be risk factors for breast cancer. The time period between these two events can also impact the risk, as the breast is more vulnerable to cancer-causing factors during this time compared to after childbirth. However, there have been limited studies on this relationship. In this study, the authors used logistic regression to examine the link between the timing of reproductive events and breast cancer risk. They analyzed data from a large study involving 4,013 cases and 4,069 controls, consisting of White and African-American women in the United States between 1994 and 1998. Among White women who were premenopausal or postmenopausal and had given birth, those who had an interval of 16 years or more between the ages of menarche and first birth had a 1.5-fold and 1.4-fold increased risk of breast cancer, respectively, compared to those with an interval of 5 years or less. When adjusting for age at first birth, these risk estimates changed slightly to odds ratios of 1.5 and 1.0, respectively. These associations were stronger for lobular and hormone-receptor-positive tumors, but were not observed among premenopausal African-American women. The authors conclude that the time period between the age at menarche and the age at first birth is linked to the risk of hormonally sensitive types of breast cancer, particularly among White women.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in Cardiac Amyloidosis
text:
The impact of cardiac involvement on the prognosis and treatment of immunoglobulin light chain (AL) and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, the two main types of cardiac amyloidosis, is significant. While cardiovascular magnetic resonance with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is commonly used for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis, its potential for risk stratification is not well understood. 

In this study, 250 subjects were recruited, including 122 patients with ATTR amyloidosis, 9 asymptomatic mutation carriers, and 119 patients with AL amyloidosis. All subjects underwent LGE cardiovascular magnetic resonance and were followed up for an average of 24±13 months. LGE was performed using phase-sensitive inversion recovery (PSIR) and magnitude-only inversion recovery techniques, and extracellular volume was measured using T1 mapping. 

The results showed that PSIR was superior to magnitude-only inversion recovery LGE because it consistently nullified the tissue (blood or myocardium) with the longest T1 (least gadolinium). LGE was classified into three patterns: none, subendocardial, and transmural, which correlated with increasing amyloid burden as determined by extracellular volume. The transition from no LGE to subendocardial LGE occurred at an extracellular volume of 0.40 to 0.43 for AL amyloidosis and 0.39 to 0.40 for ATTR amyloidosis, while the transition to transmural LGE occurred at 0.48 to 0.55 for AL amyloidosis and 0.47 to 0.59 for ATTR amyloidosis. 

During the follow-up period, 67 patients (27%) died. Transmural LGE was found to be a predictor of death, even after adjusting for other prognostic factors such as N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide, ejection fraction, stroke volume index, E/E', and left ventricular mass index. 

In conclusion, there is a continuum of cardiac involvement in systemic AL and ATTR amyloidosis. Transmural LGE, reliably determined by PSIR, indicates advanced cardiac amyloidosis. The PSIR technique provides additional information on outcome, independent of known prognostic factors.

title: Global, regional, and national comparative risk assessment of 79 behavioural, environmental and occupational, and metabolic risks or clusters of risks, 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015
text:
The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2015 offers an updated synthesis of evidence on risk factor exposure and the resulting burden of disease. This study provides national and subnational assessments over the past 25 years, which can inform discussions on the importance of addressing risks in different contexts. 

To estimate the number of deaths, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and trends in exposure, we utilized the comparative risk assessment framework developed for previous iterations of the Global Burden of Disease Study. We examined 79 behavioral, environmental and occupational, and metabolic risks or clusters of risks from 1990 to 2015. We included 388 risk-outcome pairs that met World Cancer Research Fund-defined criteria for convincing or probable evidence. We gathered relative risk and exposure estimates from various sources such as randomized controlled trials, cohorts, household surveys, census data, satellite data, and more. Statistical models were used to pool data, adjust for bias, and incorporate covariates. We developed a metric called the summary exposure value, which allows for comparisons of exposure across different risk factors. By comparing the actual scenario to a theoretical minimum risk level, we estimated the proportion of deaths and DALYs that could be attributed to a specific risk. We analyzed trends in attributable burden by considering contributions from population growth, population age structure, risk exposure, and risk-deleted cause-specific DALY rates. We also characterized risk exposure in relation to a Socio-demographic Index (SDI). 

Between 1990 and 2015, global exposure to unsafe sanitation, household air pollution, childhood underweight, childhood stunting, and smoking each decreased by more than 25%. However, exposure to several occupational risks, high body-mass index (BMI), and drug use increased by more than 25% during the same period. In 2015, all risks evaluated together accounted for 57.8% of global deaths and 41.2% of DALYs. The ten largest contributors to global DALYs among Level 3 risks in 2015 were high systolic blood pressure, smoking, high fasting plasma glucose, high BMI, childhood undernutrition, ambient particulate matter, high total cholesterol, household air pollution, alcohol use, and diets high in sodium. From 1990 to 2015, attributable DALYs declined for micronutrient deficiencies, childhood undernutrition, unsafe sanitation and water, and household air pollution. These declines were driven by reductions in risk-deleted DALY rates rather than reductions in exposure. On the other hand, rising exposure contributed to notable increases in attributable DALYs from high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose, occupational carcinogens, and drug use. Environmental risks and childhood undernutrition decreased as SDI increased, while low physical activity, high BMI, and high fasting plasma glucose increased with SDI. In 119 countries, metabolic risks such as high BMI and fasting plasma glucose contributed the most attributable DALYs in 2015. Smoking remained among the leading risk factors for attributable DALYs in 109 countries, and childhood underweight and unsafe sex were primary drivers of early death and disability in much of sub-Saharan Africa. 

In conclusion, declines in certain environmental risks have led to reductions in critical infectious diseases. Some risks remain consistent regardless of SDI. Increasing risks, such as high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose, drug use, and certain occupational exposures, contribute to a growing burden of disease but also present opportunities for intervention. Despite a decline in exposure, preventable risks like smoking still contribute significantly to attributable DALYs. Public policymakers should prioritize risks that are becoming major contributors to the global burden. This study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: Human RecQ helicases in DNA repair, recombination, and replication.
text: RecQ helicases, found in both bacteria and humans, are a crucial group of proteins responsible for monitoring the genome. The five RecQ helicases in humans each have vital roles in maintaining and stabilizing the genome, earning them the nickname "guardians of the genome". The significance of these proteins in cellular balance is evident as defects in BLM, WRN, and RECQL4 are associated with distinct hereditary human diseases. Each human RecQ helicase has its own unique set of protein partners, which determine its specialized functions in genome maintenance, such as DNA repair, recombination, replication, and transcription. Additionally, human RecQ helicases interact with one another, greatly influencing their enzyme activity. Future research in this field aims to gain a deeper understanding of the specific responsibilities of each human RecQ helicase and how they collaborate and cooperate to enhance genome stability.

title: Metabolomics study of the therapeutic mechanism of Schisandra Chinensis lignans in diet-induced hyperlipidemia mice
text:
BACKGROUND: Schisandra is a plant that is distributed globally and has been used in China for the treatment of diseases such as hyperlipidemia, fatty liver, and obesity. In this study, we used rapid resolution liquid chromatography coupled with quadruple-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (RRLC-Q-TOF-MS)-based metabolomics to investigate the effects of Schisandra chinensis lignans (SCL) on hyperlipidemia in mice induced by a high-fat diet (HFD).

METHODS: Hyperlipidemia mice were given oral doses of SCL (100 mg/kg) once a day for 4 weeks. Serum biochemistry assays were conducted to measure triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c) levels to confirm the lipid regulation effects of SCL. Metabolomics analysis was performed on serum samples, and principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) were used for pattern recognition and identification of characteristic metabolites. The levels of critical regulatory factors of liver lipid metabolism, sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs), and their related gene expressions were measured using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to investigate the underlying mechanism.

RESULTS: Oral administration of SCL significantly decreased serum levels of TC, TG, and LDL-c, and increased the serum level of HDL-c in hyperlipidemia mice. No effect on blood lipid levels was observed in control mice. The PCA scores plots showed distinct clustering of serum samples from the control, HFD, and SCL groups. Thirteen biomarkers were identified, and nine of them returned to normal levels after SCL treatment. Based on Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis, the anti-hyperlipidemia mechanisms of SCL may involve tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, synthesis of ketone bodies and cholesterol, choline metabolism, and fatty acid metabolism. SCL also significantly inhibited the mRNA expression levels of hepatic lipogenesis genes such as SREBP-1c, fatty acid synthase (FAS), and acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and decreased the mRNA expression of liver X receptor α (LXRα). Additionally, SCL significantly decreased the expression levels of SREBP-2 and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) in the liver of hyperlipidemia mice.

CONCLUSION: The anti-hyperlipidemia effect of SCL was confirmed through both serum biochemistry and metabolomics analysis. The mechanism may involve the down-regulation of LXRα/SREBP-1c/FAS/ACC and SREBP2/HMGCR signaling pathways.

title: Tet1 and Tet2 regulate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine production and cell lineage specification in mouse embryonic stem cells.
text:
The enzymes belonging to the TET family are responsible for converting 5-methylcytosine (5mC) into 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in DNA. In this study, we demonstrate that Tet1 and Tet2 are enzymes regulated by Oct4, and they work together to maintain the presence of 5hmC in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Additionally, these enzymes are induced simultaneously with the appearance of 5hmC during the process of reprogramming fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells.

When Tet1 is depleted in ESCs using RNA interference (RNAi), we observe a decrease in the expression of the Nodal antagonist Lefty1. This leads to hyperactive Nodal signaling and a skewed differentiation towards the endoderm-mesoderm lineage in embryoid bodies cultured in vitro. Furthermore, in culture conditions supplemented with Fgf4 and heparin, Tet1-depleted ESCs activate the trophoblast stem cell lineage determinant Elf5 and are capable of colonizing the placenta in midgestation embryo chimeras.

Consistent with these findings, Tet1-depleted ESCs form aggressive hemorrhagic teratomas characterized by an increase in endoderm, a decrease in neuroectoderm, and the appearance of trophoblastic giant cells in ectopic locations. Therefore, we conclude that 5hmC is an epigenetic modification associated with the pluripotent state, and Tet1 plays a crucial role in regulating the potential for lineage differentiation in ESCs.

title: Polycomb Associates Genome-wide with a Specific RNA Polymerase II Variant, and Regulates Metabolic Genes in ESCs
text: Polycomb repressor complexes (PRCs) play a crucial role in modifying chromatin and are closely associated with pluripotency and cancer. However, the relationship between PRCs and RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) in the context of chromatin activity remains unclear. To address this, we conducted ChIP-seq experiments to map PRC repression markers and four different states of RNAPII in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Our findings reveal that PRC targets exhibit a diverse range of RNAPII variants. Specifically, we observed that developmental PRC targets are bound by unproductive RNAPII (S5p(+)S7p(-)S2p(-)) throughout the genome. Through sequential ChIP, depletion of Ring1B, and genome-wide correlations, we demonstrated that PRCs and RNAPII-S5p physically bind to the same chromatin and functionally synergize. Additionally, we identified a group of genes marked by both PRC and elongating RNAPII (S5p(+)S7p(+)S2p(+)). These genes are actively transcribed, resulting in the production of mRNA and protein, and their expression levels increase upon PRC1 knockdown. Importantly, we observed that this subset of PRC targets can switch between active and PRC-repressed states within the ESC population, with many of them playing roles in metabolism.

title: Chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1) and chemokine (C-C motif) receptor-like 2 (CCRL2); two multifunctional receptors with unusual properties.
text: Chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1), also known as ChemR23, and chemokine (C-C motif) receptor-like 2 (CCRL2) are receptors with seven transmembrane domains. They were cloned in the late 1990s because of their similarity to known G-protein-coupled receptors. Initially, their biological functions were unknown, but recent research has identified ligands for these receptors and shed light on their roles. One of the ligands for CMKLR1 is chemerin, a chemoattractant derived from plasma proteins. Activation of CMKLR1 with chemerin induces the movement of macrophages and dendritic cells in laboratory settings, suggesting a proinflammatory function. However, studies using mice lacking CMKLR1 indicate an anti-inflammatory role, possibly due to the recruitment of tolerogenic plasmacytoid dendritic cells. The interaction between chemerin and CMKLR1 also promotes the development of fat cells and blood vessel formation. Another ligand for CMKLR1 is resolving E1, an anti-inflammatory lipid mediator. It inhibits the infiltration of white blood cells and the expression of proinflammatory genes. These conflicting results suggest that CMKLR1 has multiple functions. CCRL2, on the other hand, is reported to bind to the chemokines CCL5 and CCL19. Similar to other receptors like Duffy antigen for chemokine receptor (DARC), D6, and CCX-CKR, CCRL2 does not transmit signals but instead recycles continuously. This recycling process may reduce the local concentration of CCL5 and CCL19, thereby dampening immune responses. Surprisingly, chemerin, which is a ligand for CMKLR1, also binds to CCRL2. CCRL2 binds to chemerin and increases its local concentration, facilitating its presentation to nearby cells expressing CMKLR1. This establishes a connection between CCRL2 and CMKLR1. Although these findings suggest an anti-inflammatory role for CCRL2, recent research using mice lacking CCRL2 indicates a proinflammatory function, suggesting that CCRL2 may also have multiple roles. Further investigations using mice lacking CMKLR1 or CCRL2 are necessary to fully understand the functions of these receptors in immune responses and other cellular processes.

title: Identification of vitronectin as an extrinsic inducer of cancer stem cell differentiation and tumor formation.
text: There is increasing evidence suggesting that tumors are initiated by a rare group of cells known as cancer stem cells (CSCs). These CSCs are typically inactive, have the ability to self-renew, form tumors in small quantities, and give rise to the diverse cell types found within a tumor. Although CSCs obtained from various tumor types can differentiate both in laboratory settings and within living organisms when cultured in serum, the specific factors responsible for their differentiation remain unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that vitronectin, a component of human serum, plays a crucial role in driving the differentiation of stem cells through a mechanism dependent on the integrin alpha V beta 3. When CSCs are cultured on vitronectin, they exhibit a decrease in the expression of stem cell genes, changes in differentiation markers, and a loss of beta-catenin nuclear localization. By blocking the integrin alpha V beta 3, we can inhibit the differentiation process and subsequently prevent tumor formation. This suggests that CSCs require one or more external signals to undergo differentiation and initiate tumor growth, thereby establishing a new avenue for potential therapies targeting both the extracellular and intracellular pathways.

title: STIM1 Is a Calcium Sensor Specialized for Digital Signaling
text: When cells are stimulated by calcium-mobilizing substances at low, natural levels, the resulting calcium signals typically manifest as repetitive regenerative discharges of stored calcium, known as calcium oscillations [1]. Biologists have long been intrigued by these intracellular calcium oscillations as a form of digitized intracellular communication. Recent research has emphasized the importance of calcium influx as a crucial component of calcium oscillations [2]. This influx occurs through a process called store-operated calcium entry, which is initiated by calcium sensor proteins, STIM1 and STIM2, located in the endoplasmic reticulum [3]. STIM2 is activated by changes in endoplasmic reticulum calcium levels close to the resting state, while STIM1 activation requires a certain level of calcium depletion [4]. Surprisingly, our findings demonstrate that it is exclusively STIM1, not STIM2, that is involved in calcium entry during calcium oscillations. This suggests that each oscillation leads to a temporary decrease in endoplasmic reticulum calcium, which is sufficient to transiently activate STIM1. In certain cells, this transient activation of STIM1 can be observed using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy. This arrangement provides a well-defined and unambiguous signaling system, converting a digital calcium release signal into calcium influx that can communicate with downstream effectors.

title: Trends in the use of complementary health approaches among adults: United States, 2002-2012.
text:
The objective of this report is to present national estimates of the use of complementary health approaches among adults in the United States at three different time points. The report compares trends in the use of selected complementary health approaches for the years 2002, 2007, and 2012, and also examines differences based on selected demographic characteristics.

For this report, data from a total of 88,962 adults aged 18 and over, collected as part of the 2002, 2007, and 2012 National Health Interview Survey, were analyzed. The sample data were weighted to produce national estimates that accurately represent the civilian noninstitutionalized U.S. adult population. Differences between percentages were assessed using two-sided significance tests at a significance level of 0.05.

The results showed that while the use of individual approaches varied across the three time points, nonvitamin, nonmineral dietary supplements remained the most popular complementary health approach used. The use of yoga, tai chi, and qi gong increased steadily over the three time points, with yoga accounting for approximately 80% of the prevalence among these three approaches. The use of any complementary health approach also differed based on selected sociodemographic characteristics. The most significant differences in use were observed based on age, Hispanic or Latino origin, and race.

title: Histone structure and nucleosome stability.
text: The transition between active and inactive chromatin states relies heavily on histone proteins, which serve crucial roles in both structure and function. While histones are highly conserved to uphold the overall structure of the nucleosomal octameric core, they have also evolved variants to fulfill various functions in gene regulation and epigenetic silencing. These histone variants, along with post-translational modifications and interactions with chromatin remodeling complexes, have a significant impact on DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination. In this review, the authors discuss recent discoveries regarding the structure of chromatin, which validate previous observations of interparticle interactions seen in crystal structures.

title: Cerebral palsy among term and postterm births.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between the timing of birth and the risk of cerebral palsy (CP). While preterm delivery is a known risk factor for CP, it only accounts for a small number of affected infants. Limited information is available on the association between CP risk and gestational age in the term range, where the majority of CP cases occur. 

To address this, a population-based follow-up study was conducted using the Medical Birth Registry of Norway. The study included 1,682,441 singleton children born between 1967 and 2001, with a gestational age between 37 and 44 weeks and no congenital anomalies. The cohort was followed up until 2005 by linking it to other national registries. 

The main outcome measures were the absolute and relative risk of CP for children who survived until at least 4 years of age. Out of the term and postterm children in the cohort, 1938 were registered with CP in the National Insurance Scheme. The lowest risk of CP was observed in infants born at 40 weeks, with a prevalence of 0.99/1000 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-1.08). The risk of CP increased with earlier or later delivery. For instance, the prevalence at 37 weeks was 1.91/1000 (95% CI, 1.58-2.25) with a relative risk (RR) of 1.9 (95% CI, 1.6-2.4). Similarly, the prevalence at 38 weeks was 1.25/1000 (95% CI, 1.07-1.42) with an RR of 1.3 (95% CI, 1.1-1.6). The prevalence at 42 weeks was 1.36/1000 (95% CI, 1.19-1.53) with an RR of 1.4 (95% CI, 1.2-1.6), and the prevalence after 42 weeks was 1.44 (95% CI, 1.15-1.72) with an RR of 1.4 (95% CI, 1.1-1.8). These associations were even stronger in a subset of participants with gestational age determined by ultrasound measurements. For example, at 37 weeks, the prevalence was 1.17/1000 (95% CI, 0.30-2.04) and the relative risk was 3.7 (95% CI, 1.5-9.1). At 42 weeks, the prevalence was 0.85/1000 (95% CI, 0.33-1.38) and the relative risk was 2.4 (95% CI, 1.1-5.3). Adjusting for factors such as infant sex, maternal age, and socioeconomic measures had minimal impact on the results. 

In conclusion, compared to delivery at 40 weeks' gestation, delivering at 37 or 38 weeks or at 42 weeks or later was associated with an increased risk of CP.

title: 53BP1 Inhibits Homologous Recombination in Brca1-Deficient Cells by Blocking Resection of DNA Breaks
text: The malfunctioning of DNA repair through homologous recombination (HR) is believed to be a significant factor in the development of tumors in individuals with Brca1 mutations. In this study, we demonstrate that in Brca1-deficient cells, DNA breaks are improperly joined together, resulting in complex chromosome rearrangements. This joining process is dependent on the nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) factors 53BP1 and DNA ligase 4. When 53BP1 is lost, the hypersensitivity of Brca1 mutant cells to PARP inhibition is reduced, and error-free repair through HR is restored. The deletion of 53BP1 promotes the ATM-dependent processing of broken DNA ends, generating single-stranded DNA that is capable of undergoing HR. On the other hand, the deficiency of Lig4 does not fix the HR defect in Brca1 mutant cells but prevents the joining of breaks in chromatids, thus preventing chromosome rearrangements. Our findings demonstrate that HR and NHEJ compete in processing DNA breaks that occur during DNA replication, and manipulating the balance between these pathways can be used to selectively protect or eliminate cells with Brca1 mutations.

title: The genetics of Mexico recapitulates Native American substructure and affects biomedical traits
text:
The cultural and ethnic diversity in Mexico is extensive, but there is still much to learn about the specific genetic variations within this region. In our study, we examined the genomic variation of over 1000 individuals from 20 indigenous and 11 mestizo populations in Mexico. What we discovered was a significant genetic stratification among the indigenous populations, which varied depending on their level of geographic isolation. In fact, some groups were found to be as genetically distinct from each other as Europeans are from East Asians. Additionally, the genetic makeup of admixed mestizo individuals across the country reflected the pre-Columbian genetic substructure. 

Furthermore, we conducted two separate studies involving Mexicans and Mexican Americans, both of which showed a strong correlation between subcontinental ancestry and lung function. This suggests that understanding the fine-scale ancestry patterns is crucial for medical and population genetic research not only within Mexico and Mexican-descent populations, but also in other populations around the world.

title: COPI Complex Is a Regulator of Lipid Homeostasis
text: Lipid droplets are organelles that store triglycerides and sterol esters, playing a crucial role in energy storage and biosynthesis. Although the process of lipid droplet formation and regulation is not well understood, it is clear that proteins from the PAT family (perilipin, adipocyte differentiation related protein, tail interacting protein of 47 kDa) coat the surface of these droplets and facilitate interactions with lipases that mobilize the stored lipids. Through RNA interference (RNAi) screening and an image segmentation-based optical read-out system, we have identified important candidate genes in Drosophila that regulate lipid droplets. We have also demonstrated that these regulatory functions are conserved in mice. One of the key regulators we discovered is the vesicle-mediated Coat Protein Complex I (COPI) transport complex, which plays a role in limiting lipid storage. Our research has shown that COPI components control the composition of PAT proteins on the surface of lipid droplets and facilitate the association of adipocyte triglyceride lipase (ATGL) with these droplets, enabling lipolysis. We have found that two compounds, Exo1 and Brefeldin A, which are known to inhibit COPI function, produce similar effects to COPI knockdowns. Additionally, when we inhibited ATGL through RNAi and simultaneously treated cells with drugs, we observed that COPI and ATGL function in the same pathway. These findings indicate that the COPI complex is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of lipid homeostasis and highlight the interaction between vesicle transport systems and lipid droplets.

title: Differentiation of effector CD4 T cell populations (*).
text: CD4 T cells play crucial roles in facilitating adaptive immunity against various pathogens. They are also implicated in autoimmunity, asthma, allergic responses, and tumor immunity. When activated by TCR in a specific cytokine environment, naive CD4 T cells can differentiate into different lineages of T helper (Th) cells, such as Th1, Th2, Th17, and iTreg. These lineages are characterized by their unique cytokine production and functions. In this review, we provide an overview of the discovery, functions, and interconnections among Th cells. We also discuss the cytokine and signaling requirements for their development, the transcription factors involved in their differentiation, the epigenetic regulation of their key cytokines and transcription factors, and the human diseases associated with impaired CD4 T cell differentiation.

title: Homocysteine and other thiols in plasma and urine: automated determination and sample stability.
text:
We have developed an enhanced version of our fully automated column-switching HPLC method for determining the total plasma homocysteine. This method is based on single-column (reversed-phase) separation. It allows for the determination of homocysteine, cysteine, and cysteinylglycine in plasma (total concentrations), acid-precipitated plasma (non-protein-bound concentrations), and urine. The process of derivatization and chromatography is carried out automatically by a sample processor.

To achieve successful separation of all thiol species within a short time frame of 15 minutes, we have accurately adjusted the pH of the mobile phase to 3.65 (for plasma) or 3.50 (for acid-precipitated plasma and urine). The maximum fluorescence yield of cysteine, cysteinylglycine, and to a lesser extent, homocysteine, depends on the optimal concentrations of EDTA and dithioerythritol during reduction (with NaBH4) and derivatization (with monobromobimane).

Our method is highly sensitive, with a detection limit of approximately 0.05 pmol, and it demonstrates a high degree of precision with a CV of less than 5%. The sample output is approximately 70 samples within a 24-hour period. Additionally, we can also analyze serum and heparin plasma.

Even hemolysis up to approximately 2.0 g/L of hemoglobin does not interfere with the accurate recovery of homocysteine or cysteine during the analytical process. However, it is crucial to standardize the collection of blood, separation of plasma from whole blood, and acid precipitation to obtain reproducible thiol results.

Through our modifications and the standardization of blood-sampling procedures, we have significantly improved the method and expanded its applications.

title: Induced pluripotent stem cells in Alzheimer’s disease: applications for disease modeling and cell-replacement therapy
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in individuals aged 65 and older. Despite identifying several disease-causing genes and risk factors, the exact underlying mechanisms of AD remain unclear. This is primarily due to the inability to test theoretical hypotheses on non-postmortem and patient-specific research systems. However, the use of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), a recently developed and optimized technology, shows promise in creating reliable models for better understanding the etiopathological process of AD and for efficient screening of anti-AD drugs. Additionally, iPSCs derived from human sources may serve as a valuable tool for cell-replacement therapy against AD. Although significant progress has been made, there are still key challenges that need to be addressed in iPSCs research, such as identifying robust disease phenotypes in AD modeling and making iPSCs-based cell-replacement therapy clinically available for humans. This review focuses on the recent advancements in iPSCs research and discusses the challenges of using AD patients-derived iPSCs for disease modeling and cell-replacement therapy.

title: Nitrite protects against morbidity and mortality associated with TNF- or LPS-induced shock in a soluble guanylate cyclase–dependent manner
text: Nitrite (NO2-), previously considered to be a metabolite and biomarker of the vasodilator NO, is now recognized as an important reservoir of NO in the body. It plays a role in hypoxic signaling, vasodilation, and protection against damage caused by ischemia-reperfusion injury in blood vessels and tissues. Nitrite can be converted to NO through enzymatic processes involving deoxyhemoglobin, deoxymyoglobin, xanthine oxidase, mitochondrial complexes, or NO synthase (NOS) under conditions of low pH and oxygen tension. In our study, we found that treatment with nitrite significantly reduced hypothermia, mitochondrial damage, oxidative stress, tissue infarction, and mortality in a mouse model of shock induced by a lethal tumor necrosis factor challenge. This protective effect of nitrite was in stark contrast to the detrimental effects of NOS inhibition. The mechanism of nitrite-dependent protection did not involve inhibition of mitochondrial complex I activity, as previously observed in ischemia-reperfusion, but rather relied on the presence of the soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) alpha1 subunit, which is a key receptor and signal transducer for NO within the cardiovascular system. Nitrite also showed potential for protecting against toxicity induced by Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide, although higher doses were needed. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that nitrite can provide protection against toxicity in shock through sGC-dependent signaling, which may involve hypoxic vasodilation to maintain microcirculation and organ function, as well as cardioprotection.

title: Mammographic density and the risk and detection of breast cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Extensive mammographic density is linked to a higher risk of breast cancer and makes it challenging to detect cancer through mammography. However, the impact of density on risk based on the method of cancer detection is not known.

METHODS: We conducted three nested case-control studies in screened populations, involving 1112 matched case-control pairs. We analyzed the association between the measured percentage of density in the initial mammogram and the risk of breast cancer, considering the method of cancer detection, time since screening initiation, and age.

RESULTS: Women with density in 75% or more of the mammogram had a significantly increased risk of breast cancer compared to those with density in less than 10% (odds ratio, 4.7; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.0 to 7.4). This increased risk was observed whether the cancer was detected through screening (odds ratio, 3.5; 95% CI, 2.0 to 6.2) or within 12 months after a negative screening examination (odds ratio, 17.8; 95% CI, 4.8 to 65.9). The elevated risk of breast cancer, regardless of the detection method, persisted for at least 8 years after study entry and was higher in younger women compared to older women. Among women younger than the median age of 56 years, 26% of all breast cancers and 50% of cancers detected within 12 months after a negative screening test were attributed to density in 50% or more of the mammogram.

CONCLUSIONS: Extensive mammographic density is strongly associated with the risk of breast cancer detected through screening or between screening tests. A significant proportion of breast cancers can be attributed to this risk factor.

title: Pooled analysis of prospective cohort studies on height, weight, and breast cancer risk.
text:
The researchers examined the connection between anthropometric measurements and the likelihood of developing breast cancer by analyzing data from seven different prospective cohort studies. These studies included a total of 337,819 women, among whom there were 4,385 cases of invasive breast cancer. After adjusting for various reproductive, dietary, and other risk factors, the analysis revealed that for every 5 cm increase in height, the relative risk (RR) of breast cancer was 1.02 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.96, 1.10) in premenopausal women and 1.07 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.12) in postmenopausal women.

The study also found that body mass index (BMI) had different associations with breast cancer depending on menopausal status. Among premenopausal women, there was a significant inverse relationship between BMI and breast cancer, while among postmenopausal women, there was a positive association. These associations were found to be nonlinear. For premenopausal women with a BMI below 21 kg/m2, the risk of breast cancer was reduced, with a relative risk of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.34, 0.85). In postmenopausal women, the risk did not increase further when BMI exceeded 28 kg/m2, and the relative risk for these women was 1.26 (95% CI: 1.09, 1.46).

The researchers did not find much evidence of interaction between these anthropometric indices and other risk factors for breast cancer. However, their data did suggest that height is an independent risk factor for postmenopausal breast cancer, while the relationship is less clear for premenopausal women. The association between BMI and breast cancer also varied depending on menopausal status. The findings suggest that maintaining a healthy weight may help reduce the risk of breast cancer among postmenopausal women.

title: Cost effectiveness of ward based non-invasive ventilation for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: economic analysis of randomised controlled trial.
text: The objective of this study was to assess the cost effectiveness of standard treatment with and without the addition of ward based non-invasive ventilation for patients admitted to the hospital with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The study involved a randomised controlled trial conducted in 14 hospitals in the United Kingdom. The participants were 236 patients with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and mild to moderate acidosis. The economic analysis compared the treatment costs for these patients after randomisation. The main outcome measure was the incremental cost per in-hospital death. The results showed that 24 out of 118 patients died in the group receiving standard treatment, while 12 out of 118 patients died in the group receiving non-invasive ventilation. Allocation to the non-invasive ventilation group resulted in a cost reduction of £49,362, mainly due to reduced use of intensive care units. The incremental cost effectiveness ratio was -£645 per death avoided, indicating that non-invasive ventilation was a dominant strategy (more effective and less costly). Modelling of the data suggested that a typical UK hospital providing non-invasive ventilation could prevent six deaths and three to nine admissions to intensive care units per year, resulting in a cost reduction of £12,000-£53,000 per year. In conclusion, non-invasive ventilation is a highly cost effective treatment that reduces costs and improves mortality in hospital.

title: Persistent human papillomavirus infection and cervical neoplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the reliability of using persistent cervical carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA as a marker for cervical cancer risk in clinical trials. They searched MEDLINE and Current Contents databases up until January 30, 2006, and identified 41 eligible studies for inclusion in the meta-analysis. The analysis included over 22,500 women and evaluated the association between persistent HPV DNA and high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2-3), high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), and invasive cervical cancer (CIN2-3/HSIL+). The relative risks (RRs) were stratified based on the HPV comparison group. The RRs ranged from 1.3 to 813.0 for CIN2-3/HSIL+ versus HPV-negative reference group. The results consistently showed a strong association between HPV persistence and CIN2-3/HSIL+, regardless of variations in definitions and study methods. Longer duration of persistence, wider testing intervals, CIN2-3/HSIL+, and use of an HPV-negative reference group were consistently associated with higher RRs. These findings highlight the importance of precise definition and standardization of HPV testing, sampling procedure, and test interval for reliable clinical testing. Overall, the study validates HPV persistence as a clinical marker and endpoint for assessing cervical cancer risk.

title: Post-transcriptional Wnt Signaling Governs Epididymal Sperm Maturation
text: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway plays a crucial role in both development and disease. However, there is a growing interest in understanding whether the upstream cascade of this pathway has other important functions beyond its involvement in β-catenin-mediated transcription. Unfortunately, studying these roles has been challenging due to the widespread influence of β-catenin. In this study, we demonstrate that spermatozoa, which are typically transcriptionally silent, respond to Wnt signals released from the epididymis. Additionally, we found that mice with a mutation in the Wnt regulator Cyclin Y-like 1 are unable to produce viable sperm due to their immotility and abnormal structure. We discovered that post-transcriptional Wnt signaling affects spermatozoa through GSK3 in three ways: (1) by reducing the overall poly-ubiquitination of proteins to maintain protein balance, (2) by inhibiting the phosphorylation of septin 4 to create a barrier in the sperm tail membrane, and (3) by inhibiting protein phosphatase 1 to initiate sperm motility. These findings suggest that Wnt signaling plays a crucial role in the post-transcriptional maturation of sperm and also raise the possibility of reevaluating the role of transcription-independent Wnt signaling in other types of cells.

title: CD28 Costimulation: From Mechanism to Therapy.
text: Activation of naive T cells requires both ligation of the T cell receptor (TCR) and the CD28 receptor. In this article, we explore the expression, structure, and biochemistry of CD28 and its ligands. CD28 signaling is crucial for various T cell processes, such as cytokine production, cytoskeletal remodeling, survival, and differentiation. Unlike TCR ligation alone, CD28 ligation induces distinct epigenetic, transcriptional, and post-translational changes in T cells. We delve into the roles of CD28 and its ligands in effector and regulatory T cells. CD28 is essential for the survival of regulatory T cells and the maintenance of immune balance. Additionally, we examine the involvement of CD28 and its family members in human diseases and evaluate the effectiveness of drugs targeting CD28 ligands. Despite the importance of CD28 and its ligands in immune function, many aspects of CD28 biology remain unclear. The translation of our understanding of CD28 function into immunomodulatory therapies has yielded mixed results, likely due to complex interactions between CD28 family members, disparities between mouse and human CD28 families, and cell-specific functions of CD28 family members.

title: Recommended diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis: guidelines from the International Panel on the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.
text: The International Panel on MS Diagnosis has released updated diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis (MS). The main focus remains on objectively demonstrating the presence of lesions in both time and space. Magnetic resonance imaging is now combined with clinical and other diagnostic methods. These revised criteria make it easier to diagnose MS in patients with various presentations, including those with symptoms that suggest MS, those with a typical pattern of relapses and remissions, and those with a gradual progression of the disease without clear attacks and remissions. The terms "clinically definite" and "probable MS" that were previously used are no longer recommended. The outcome of a diagnostic evaluation is now categorized as either MS, "possible MS" (for those at risk for MS but with inconclusive diagnostic results), or "not MS."

title: Regulation of radial glial survival by signals from the meninges.
text: Radial glial cells (RGCs) in the developing cerebral cortex play a crucial role as progenitors for neurons and glia, while also providing guidance for migrating neurons. However, it has remained unclear whether the processes of RGCs also have a direct influence on the function of RGCs themselves. In this study, we present evidence that the absence of beta1 integrins in RGCs leads to a decrease in the number of RGCs and the size of the cortex in mice. Through TUNEL stainings and time-lapse video recordings, we observed that RGCs lacking beta1 integrins detach from the meningeal basement membrane (BM) and subsequently undergo apoptotic cell death. Additionally, surgical removal of the meninges also induced apoptosis. Furthermore, mice deficient in the BM components laminin alpha2 and alpha4 exhibited defects in the attachment of RGC processes to the meninges, a reduction in cortical size, and an increase in apoptosis of RGC cells. These findings highlight the importance of the attachment of RGC processes to the meninges for the survival of RGCs and the regulation of cortical size.

title: The sterol regulatory element binding proteins are essential for the metabolic programming of effector T cells and adaptive immunity
text: The metabolic reprogramming of newly activated CD8(+) T cells is crucial for their clonal expansion, but the specific signals responsible for this reprogramming are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs) play a vital role in the acquisition of effector-cell metabolism. When SREBP signaling was disrupted, CD8(+) T cells were unable to undergo blastogenesis, leading to reduced clonal expansion during viral infection. Further investigation revealed that SREBPs were necessary to meet the increased lipid demands for membrane synthesis during blastogenesis. Interestingly, SREBPs were not required for homeostatic proliferation, suggesting that their role is specific to effector responses. These findings shed light on the molecular signals involved in the metabolic reprogramming of CD8(+) T cells as they transition from a quiescent state to activation.

title: Human contribution to the European heatwave of 2003
text: The summer of 2003 in Europe was likely the hottest since at least 1500 AD, and there were a significant number of deaths caused by the extreme heat in France, Germany, and Italy. It is difficult to determine whether the 2003 heatwave was solely caused by changes in external factors affecting the climate, such as the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere. This is because any weather event could potentially occur by chance in an unaltered climate. However, it is possible to estimate the extent to which human activities have heightened the likelihood of such a heatwave occurring. In this study, we utilize this conceptual framework to calculate the contribution of human-induced increases in greenhouse gas and pollutant concentrations in the atmosphere to the risk of unusually high average summer temperatures across a large area of continental Europe. By establishing a threshold for average summer temperature that was surpassed only in 2003, and not in any other year since 1851, when instrumental records began, we estimate with a high level of confidence (>90%) that human influence has at least doubled the risk of a heatwave surpassing this threshold magnitude.

title: Do Antidepressants Cure or Create Abnormal Brain States?
text:
The term antidepressant is used to describe a medication that helps to correct specific biological abnormalities that cause the symptoms of depression. This aligns with the "disease-centred" model of how psychotropic drugs work. This model is based on the approach used in general medicine, where drugs like insulin for diabetes or antibiotics for infections target the underlying pathology of the disease. In contrast, we propose an alternative "drug-centred" model that better explains the observed effects of drugs in psychiatric conditions.

According to the drug-centred model, instead of correcting a biochemical abnormality, drugs themselves create abnormal states that coincidentally relieve psychiatric symptoms. For example, alcohol's disinhibiting effects may alleviate symptoms of social phobia, but it doesn't mean that alcohol corrects the chemical imbalance causing social phobia. Sedation can reduce high arousal in acute psychiatric situations, while drugs like neuroleptics or opiates that induce indifference may help alleviate distress from acute psychotic symptoms. Low-dose stimulants can improve attention and concentration in the short term.

The disease-centred model in psychiatry leads researchers to infer antidepressant effects based on patients' scores on symptom rating scales, assuming that these scales assess the manifestations of the disease. On the other hand, the drug-centred model suggests that the physiological and subjective effects of drugs should be examined independently. These effects include sedation, stimulation, and various biopsychological states. Depending on individual factors and the context, such as a person's emotional state when taking the drug, some drugs can produce euphoria or mood elevation. However, these euphoric effects diminish with long-term use due to tolerance.

If antidepressants or other psychotropic drugs could be proven to have long-term mood-elevating effects that are not diminished by being in a depressed emotional state, it would distinguish them from drugs that cause euphoria. This could make them uniquely beneficial for depressed patients.

title: Cancer exosomes trigger fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation.
text: There is a growing interest in understanding how cancer cells communicate with each other through secreted vesicles called exosomes. In this study, we investigated whether exosomes produced by cancer cells could transmit information to normal stromal fibroblasts and cause a cellular response. We discovered that certain exosomes derived from cancer cells could induce increased expression of α-smooth muscle actin and other changes that are consistent with the process of fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts. We also found that TGF-β, a protein involved in cell signaling, is present on the surface of exosomes in association with a transmembrane proteoglycan called betaglycan. Although this complex is initially inactive, it becomes fully functional in triggering SMAD-dependent signaling. When we inhibited either the signaling pathway or the expression of betaglycan, the differentiation process was attenuated. While the timing and overall extent of the cellular response were similar to those achieved with soluble TGF-β, we observed important qualitative differences specific to the exosomal delivery of TGF-β. For instance, there was a significant increase in the production of fibroblast FGF2, a growth factor, when TGF-β was delivered through exosomes. This previously unknown mechanism of inducing cellular differentiation has significant implications for understanding the mechanisms involved in cancer-associated stroma, fibrotic diseases, and wound healing responses.

title: A model of multiple myeloma: culture of 5T33 murine myeloma cells and evaluation of tumorigenicity in the C57BL/KaLwRij mouse.
text: This study focuses on the 5T33 multiple myeloma, which is a type of cancer that spontaneously develops in C57BL/KaLwRij mice. The aim of this research is to establish and characterize the 5T33 murine myeloma as a cultured cell line. The study examines its morphology, growth rate, expression of paraprotein (IgG2b), and its ability to form tumors in syngeneic animals. The 5T33 cell line has been successfully cultured for over 10 months and has undergone more than 34 passages. In culture, the 5T33 myeloma cells grow either as individual cells or in small clusters that are loosely attached to a stromal cell layer. The cells have a maximum doubling time of approximately 25 hours, and more than 90% of them express cytoplasmic IgG2b paraprotein. When injected into C57BL/KaLwRij mice, as few as 500 5T33 cells can induce paralysis and lead to death by day 36. The rate of tumor development and the detection of IgG2b paraprotein depend on the dosage of cells injected. Two weeks after injecting 5 x 10(5) cultured 5T33 myeloma cells intravenously, tumor cells were easily identified in the bone marrow. By week 3, the 5T33 myeloma cells had spread to various tissues in the animal.
