Further studies are currently being conducted to determine the sensitivity of this cell line to different therapeutic approaches.

title: HIV Treatment as Prevention: Systematic Comparison of Mathematical Models of the Potential Impact of Antiretroviral Therapy on HIV Incidence in South Africa
text: The aim of this study was to compare the predictions of different mathematical models that simulate the impact of expanding access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) on new HIV infections. The challenge in comparing these models is that they address different questions and use different outcome metrics. In this study, twelve independent models evaluated standardized ART intervention scenarios in South Africa and reported a common set of results. These scenarios varied the CD4 count threshold for treatment eligibility, access to treatment, and program retention. The models projected that HIV incidence would be 35% to 54% lower eight years after the introduction of ART compared to a scenario without ART. However, there was more variation in the long-term reductions in incidence over 38 years. The impact of optimistic interventions, such as immediate ART initiation, varied widely across models, leading to uncertainty about the potential for eliminating HIV using ART alone in the next four decades. The number of person-years of ART per infection averted ranged from 5.8 to 18.7 over eight years. When considering the actual scale-up of ART in South Africa, seven models estimated that current HIV incidence is 17% to 32% lower than it would have been without ART. Differences in model assumptions about CD4 decline and HIV transmissibility explained only a small portion of the variation in results. In conclusion, while mathematical models differ in structure and parameter choices, they all suggest that ART, with high levels of access and adherence, can significantly reduce new HIV infections. There is agreement on the short-term impact of ambitious treatment scale-up, but more variation in longer-term projections and the efficiency of treatment in reducing new infections. Differences in model predictions cannot be explained by differences in model structure or parameterization that were thought to affect intervention impact.

title: Self-harm in prisons in England and Wales: an epidemiological study of prevalence, risk factors, clustering, and subsequent suicide
text:
BACKGROUND: The prevalence and characteristics of self-harm and suicide in prisoners are not well understood. This study aimed to gather information on the extent of self-harm in the prison population, identify associated risk factors, examine clustering effects, and assess the risk of subsequent suicide after self-harm.

METHODS: Data on self-harm incidents in all prisons in England and Wales were collected between January 2004 and December 2009. A case-control comparison was conducted between prisoners who self-harmed and those who did not between January 2006 and December 2009. A Bayesian approach was used to analyze clustering of self-harm incidents. Prisoners who self-harmed and later died by suicide were compared to other inmates who self-harmed.

FINDINGS: Between 2004 and 2009, there were 139,195 recorded self-harm incidents involving 26,510 individual prisoners. Each year, 5-6% of male prisoners and 20-24% of female inmates engaged in self-harm. Self-harm rates were over ten times higher in female prisoners compared to male prisoners. Repetition of self-harm was common, particularly among women and teenage girls. A subgroup of 102 prisoners accounted for 17,307 episodes. Self-harm was associated with younger age, white ethnic origin, prison type, and a life sentence or being unsentenced. In female inmates, committing a violent offense against an individual was also a contributing factor. Clustering of self-harm incidents in time and location was observed. There were 109 subsequent suicides in individuals who had self-harmed, with a higher risk compared to the general prison population. More than half of these deaths occurred within a month of self-harm. Risk factors for suicide after self-harm included older age and a previous self-harm incident of high or moderate lethality in male prisoners, and a history of more than five self-harm incidents within a year in female inmates.

INTERPRETATION: Self-harm is a significant issue in the prison population, particularly among women. Self-harm is associated with an increased risk of subsequent suicide in this setting. Preventing and treating self-harm in prisoners is crucial for suicide prevention in prisons.

FUNDING: This study was supported by the Wellcome Trust, National Institute for Health Research, National Offender Management Service, and Department of Health.

title: Elimination of HIV in South Africa through Expanded Access to Antiretroviral Therapy: A Model Comparison Study
text: The objective of our study was to examine the impact of different model structures and assumptions on the long-term effects of universal test and treat (UTT) for HIV in South Africa. We developed nine different mathematical models of the HIV epidemic in South Africa, ranging from simple to complex. The simplest model was similar to the initial model that suggested HIV elimination within 7 years, while the most comprehensive model included sexual networks and different stages of HIV infection. UTT was defined as annual screening and immediate antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all HIV-infected adults, starting at 13% coverage in January 2012 and increasing to 90% coverage by January 2019. All models predicted HIV elimination, but the more complex models predicted elimination at a later time, around 20 to 25 years. The most comprehensive model also showed that the current ART treatment policy in South Africa, which treats individuals with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/µl, could also lead to elimination, albeit 10 years later than UTT. Despite the delay in elimination, UTT was still cost-effective and would save many additional life-years. However, it was not as cost-effective as previously predicted, as the current ART treatment policy alone could already drive HIV into elimination. It is important to note that our study had limitations, such as defining elimination as incidence below 1/1,000 person-years rather than 0% prevalence, and not modeling drug resistance. In conclusion, our results confirm that UTT can eliminate the HIV epidemic in South Africa, but it is likely to occur later than initially suggested. UTT is still a cost-effective intervention, but not as cost-effective as previously thought, as the current ART treatment policy could also lead to elimination.

title: Bile acid receptor TGR5 agonism induces NO production and reduces monocyte adhesion in vascular endothelial cells.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the role of TGR5, a G-protein-coupled receptor for bile acids, in vascular endothelial cells. The researchers conducted experiments using bovine aortic endothelial cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells to examine the effects of a bile acid called taurolithocholic acid (TLCA) on nitric oxide (NO) production.

The results showed that treatment with TLCA significantly increased NO production in bovine aortic endothelial cells. This effect was found to be dependent on the presence of TGR5, as depletion of TGR5 using small interfering RNA abolished the increase in NO production. Similar results were observed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells, where TLCA also increased intracellular cGMP accumulation and phosphorylation of endothelial NO synthase (ser1177). This response was accompanied by increased phosphorylation of Akt (ser473) and intracellular calcium levels. Inhibition of these signaling pathways significantly reduced TLCA-induced NO production.

The researchers also investigated the impact of TGR5-mediated NO production on inflammatory responses in endothelial cells. They found that TLCA significantly reduced the adhesion of monocytes, expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, and activation of nuclear factor-κB in human umbilical vein endothelial cells stimulated with tumor necrosis factor-α. TLCA also inhibited monocyte adhesion to mesenteric venules in response to lipopolysaccharide in vivo. These inhibitory effects of TLCA were dependent on NO synthase activity.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that TGR5 activation induces NO production in vascular endothelial cells through Akt activation and intracellular calcium increase. This function of TGR5 inhibits monocyte adhesion in response to inflammatory stimuli.

title: Structural insights into calicivirus attachment and uncoating.
text: The Caliciviridae family consists of positive-sense RNA viruses that are of importance in both medical and veterinary fields. In humans, caliciviruses are a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis, while in animals they are known to cause respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, stomatitis, and hemorrhagic disease. However, the study of virus-host interactions is hindered by the lack of culture systems for many viruses within this family. Fortunately, Feline calicivirus (FCV), which belongs to the Vesivirus genus, serves as a suitable model as it can be grown in cell culture. Recently, Feline junctional adhesion molecule 1 (fJAM-1) has been identified as a functional receptor for FCV. To gain a better understanding of this virus-receptor interaction, we utilized cryo-electron microscopy and three-dimensional image reconstruction techniques, along with fitting of high-resolution coordinates obtained from homology modeling. Our findings reveal that domain 1 of fJAM-1 binds to the outer surface of the P2 domain of the FCV capsid protein VP1, leading to structural changes in the viral capsid. This study provides the first-ever structural insight into a native calicivirus-protein receptor complex, shedding light on the mechanisms of virus attachment and uncoating.

title: Human SNP Links Differential Outcomes in Inflammatory and Infectious Disease to a FOXO3-Regulated Pathway
text: The prognosis of complex diseases can vary greatly among individuals, but this variability is not well understood. To gain insight into the role of genetics in prognosis, we analyzed existing genome-wide association study data. Our findings reveal a noncoding variation in the FOXO3A gene (rs12212067: T > G) that is associated with a milder course of Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis, but an increased risk of severe malaria. Interestingly, this variation does not affect disease susceptibility. We discovered that individuals carrying the minor (G) allele have reduced inflammatory responses in monocytes due to a pathway driven by FOXO3. This pathway, mediated by TGFβ1, decreases the production of proinflammatory cytokines like TNFα and increases the production of anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10. Therefore, we have identified a shared genetic factor that influences prognosis in different diseases by modulating inflammatory responses through the FOXO3-driven pathway.

title: Patient Outcomes with Teaching Versus Nonteaching Healthcare: A Systematic Review
text:
There is ongoing debate in the healthcare community regarding whether the quality of medical care at teaching hospitals is better or worse than that at non-teaching hospitals. Therefore, our objective was to systematically evaluate the evidence on this topic. 

To accomplish this, we conducted a review of all studies that compared patient outcomes, including mortality, between teaching and non-teaching healthcare facilities, regardless of the health condition being treated. We gathered these studies from PubMed, expert contacts, and cross-referencing of relevant literature. We extracted data on various factors such as the setting, patients, data sources, author affiliations, definition of compared groups, types of diagnoses considered, adjusting covariates, and estimates of effect for mortality and other outcomes. 

In total, we identified 132 eligible studies, with 93 focusing on mortality and 61 on other outcomes (22 studies addressed both). When we synthesized the adjusted estimates on mortality, we found a summary relative risk of 0.96 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.93–1.00) for teaching hospitals compared to non-teaching hospitals, and 1.04 (95% CI, 0.99–1.10) for minor teaching hospitals compared to non-teaching ones. There was significant heterogeneity between the studies (I2 = 72% for the main analysis). These results were consistent across studies that used clinical or administrative databases. 

In the 14 studies that fully adjusted for volume/experience, severity, and comorbidity, there were no significant differences in patient outcomes (relative risk 1.01). The results of smaller studies did not differ from those of larger studies. Some variations were observed for specific diagnoses, such as better survival rates for breast cancer and cerebrovascular accidents in teaching hospitals, and better survival rates for cholecystectomy in non-teaching hospitals. However, these differences were generally small. Other outcomes varied, but teaching hospitals typically did not perform better than non-teaching hospitals. 

In conclusion, the available data have limitations due to their nonrandomized design. However, overall, they do not indicate that a healthcare facility's teaching status significantly improves or worsens patient outcomes. Small differences for specific diseases cannot be ruled out, but are likely to be minimal.

title: DNA damage and Repair Modify DNA methylation and Chromatin Domain of the Targeted Locus: Mechanism of allele methylation polymorphism
text: We examine the modifications in chromatin structure, DNA methylation, and transcription during and after the process of homologous DNA repair (HR). Our findings reveal that HR brings about changes in the DNA methylation pattern of the repaired segment. Additionally, HR also impacts local histone H3 methylation and alters chromatin structure by initiating DNA-chromatin loops that connect the 5' and 3' ends of the repaired gene. Over a two-week period following repair, demethylation associated with transcription, facilitated by Base Excision Repair enzymes, further modifies the methylation of the repaired DNA. Consequently, the repaired genes exhibit stable yet diverse methylation profiles, which govern the expression levels in each clone. Based on our data, we propose that DNA methylation and chromatin remodeling induced by HR could serve as a potential source of permanent variation in gene expression within somatic cells.

title: DNA repair factor APLF is a histone chaperone.
text: Poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation plays a significant role in the repair of DNA by regulating the relaxation of chromatin, a crucial step in the repair process. However, the precise molecular mechanism through which poly(ADP-ribose) affects chromatin remains poorly understood. In this study, we have identified a protein called APLF, which is regulated by poly(ADP-ribose) and acts as a histone chaperone specific to DNA damage. APLF binds preferentially to the histone H3/H4 tetramer using its C-terminal acidic motif, which is similar to the motif found in histone chaperones of the NAP1L family (NAP1L motif). We have also demonstrated that APLF exhibits histone chaperone activities, dependent on its acidic domain, and that the NAP1L motif is crucial for APLF's ability to repair DNA in living organisms. Additionally, we have discovered similar proteins in lower eukaryotes that can bind to histones and localize to sites where poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation is induced by DNA damage. These findings collectively establish the involvement of histone chaperones in poly(ADP-ribose)-regulated DNA repair reactions.

title: Regulation of sympathetic nerve activity during the cold pressor test in normotensive pregnant and nonpregnant women.
text:
During normotensive pregnancy, there is a decrease in baseline neurovascular transduction. However, there is limited knowledge about the changes in neurovascular transduction during periods of heightened sympathetic activation. To investigate this, we conducted a study comparing pregnant women to nonpregnant controls.

We hypothesized that despite pregnant women experiencing an intensified response in muscle sympathetic nerve activity when exposed to cold pressor stimulation, the blunting of neurovascular transduction in these women would lead to similar changes in vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure compared to nonpregnant controls.

Our findings revealed that baseline neurovascular transduction was indeed reduced in pregnant women compared to controls. This was evident when considering both total resistance and mean arterial pressure, as well as sympathetic burst frequency. The differences were statistically significant (P<0.001 and P=0.001, respectively).

Furthermore, pregnant women exhibited greater sympathetic activation throughout the entire 3-minute cold pressor stimulation compared to nonpregnant controls. Peak sympathoexcitation was also higher in pregnant women, regardless of how it was measured (sympathetic burst frequency, burst incidence, or total activity). These differences were also statistically significant (P=0.049, P=0.03, and P=0.04, respectively).

However, despite the heightened sympathetic activation, neurovascular transduction during peak cold pressor-induced sympathoexcitation remained blunted in pregnant women. The differences in neurovascular transduction were statistically significant (P<0.001 and P=0.006, respectively).

Interestingly, mean arterial pressure and total peripheral resistance were not significantly different between pregnant and nonpregnant women during peak sympathoexcitation. This suggests that the dissociation of sympathetic outflow from hemodynamic outcomes occurs in the third trimester of normotensive pregnancy.

In conclusion, our data indicate that normotensive pregnancy in the third trimester is associated with reductions in neurovascular transduction. This leads to a disconnect between sympathetic outflow and hemodynamic responses, even during cold pressor-induced sympathoexcitation.

title: The Germ Cell Determinant Blimp1 Is Not Required for Derivation of Pluripotent Stem Cells
text: Blimp1 (Prdm1) is a crucial factor in determining the fate of primordial germ cells (PGCs) and works in conjunction with Prdm14 during the specification of PGCs from postimplantation epiblast cells. Together, they initiate epigenetic reprogramming in early germ cells, leading them towards a pluripotent state similar to embryonic stem cells (ESCs). While Prdm14 alone can drive reprogramming and is vital for maintaining pluripotency, it remains unclear whether Blimp1 plays a similar role. Through genetic experiments, we have found that Blimp1 is not necessary for the derivation and maintenance of ESCs and postimplantation epiblast stem cells (epiSCs). Interestingly, Blimp1 is also not required for reprogramming epiSCs back into ESCs. Therefore, while Blimp1 is essential for PGC specification, it is not needed for the reversal of epiSCs to ESCs or for their subsequent maintenance. This study suggests that reprogramming, including the conversion of somatic cells to ESCs, may not necessarily involve passing through a Blimp1-positive PGC-like state.

title: A Nexus for Gene Expression—Molecular Mechanisms of Spt5 and NusG in the Three Domains of Life
text: RNA polymerases (RNAPs), which consist of multiple subunits, are responsible for transcribing the genomes of all living organisms. While the core subunits of RNAPs are conserved across all three domains of life, indicating a common evolutionary ancestry, this is only true for one specific transcription factor called Spt5 (also known as NusG in bacteria). Other factors that assist RNAP during the transcription process are specific to each domain or are only conserved between archaea and eukaryotes. Spt5 and its bacterial counterpart NusG play a role in regulating gene expression in various ways. They can influence the speed and efficiency of transcription, control the coupling of transcription with RNA processing or translation, and recruit termination factors to silence laterally transferred DNA and protect the genome from double-stranded DNA damage. Recent discoveries have highlighted the importance of Spt5-like factors as evolutionarily conserved components that regulate and coordinate the machineries responsible for processing information within cells. This review explores these findings in detail.

title: Haplotype estimation using sequencing reads.
text: The current methods for inferring haplotypes from genotype data do not routinely utilize phase information that can be obtained from high-throughput sequencing technologies. These technologies generate short sequence reads that may contain phase information if they cover multiple heterozygote genotypes. In order to improve the accuracy of haplotype phasing, we have enhanced the SHAPEIT2 method by incorporating phase-informative sequencing reads. Our approach involves incorporating the read information into a probabilistic model using base quality scores within each read. This method is primarily designed for high-coverage sequence data or datasets with pre-called genotypes. It has important applications in medical sequencing and rare disease studies, particularly for phasing single samples sequenced at high coverage. Additionally, our method can also utilize existing panels of reference haplotypes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted tests using a mother-father-child trio that was sequenced at high coverage by Illumina, along with low-coverage sequence data from the 1000 Genomes Project. The results showed that the use of phase-informative reads increased the average distance between switch errors by 22%, from 274.4 kb to 328.6 kb. Furthermore, we simulated sequencing reads with varying insert size, read length, and base error rate using male chromosome X haplotypes from the 1000 Genomes Project samples. When using short 100 bp paired-end reads, we found that using mixtures of insert sizes yielded the best results. On the other hand, when using longer reads with high error rates (5-20 kb read with 4%-15% error per base), the phasing performance was significantly improved.

title: Time and Money: The True Costs of Health Care Utilization for Patients Receiving "Free" HIV/Tuberculosis Care and Treatment in Rural KwaZulu-Natal.
text:
In many sub-Saharan African countries, HIV and tuberculosis (TB) services are provided free of charge. However, patients still have to bear certain costs. To investigate this issue, patient-exit interviews were conducted in primary health care clinics in rural South Africa. The study included 200 HIV-infected patients enrolled in a pre-antiretroviral treatment (pre-ART) program, 300 patients receiving antiretroviral treatment (ART), and 300 patients receiving TB treatment. The researchers calculated health expenditures, travel time, and how patients financed their spending for each group. Multivariate regression models were used to assess the associations between patient group and costs.

The results showed that the total monthly health expenditures were ZAR 171 for pre-ART patients, ZAR 164 for ART patients, and ZAR 122 for TB patients. The total monthly time costs were 3.4 hours for pre-ART patients, 5.0 hours for ART patients, and 3.2 hours for TB patients. Although overall patient costs were similar across groups, pre-ART patients spent more on traditional healers and chemists/private doctors compared to ART patients. On the other hand, ART patients spent more on transport to clinics than pre-ART patients. A significant percentage of patients (31% of pre-ART, 39% of ART, and 41% of TB patients) had to borrow money or sell assets to finance their health care.

In conclusion, patients receiving free care for HIV/TB still face significant private costs, which often lead to financial distress. The study suggests that providing subsidized transport, reducing clinic visits, and establishing drug pick-up points closer to patients' homes could help reduce costs for ART patients, potentially improving retention and adherence. The findings also indicate that transitioning patients to ART earlier may not substantially increase their financial burden, as suggested by HIV treatment-as-prevention policies.

title: A new system for naming ribosomal proteins.
text: The authors present a system for naming ribosomal proteins, which they plan to implement in the future. They strongly encourage others to adopt this system in order to address the confusion arising from assigning identical names to ribosomal proteins from unrelated species with different structures and functions. Under this proposed system, ribosomal proteins that are homologous will be given the same name, regardless of the species. The system is designed to ensure that the new names are easily recognizable by their similarity to the old names, while also clearly indicating that they belong to the 'new system'.

title: COSMIC: mining complete cancer genomes in the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer
text: COSMIC is a website that collects and organizes information about somatic mutations in human cancer. The latest release, v48 (July 2010), includes data on over 136,000 coding mutations found in nearly 542,000 tumor samples. Out of the 18,490 genes documented, 26% (4803) have at least one mutation. The website provides comprehensive scientific literature curations on 83 major cancer genes and 49 fusion gene pairs, with 19 new cancer genes and 30 new fusion pairs added this year. One of the key genes included is TP53, which is now accessible through a collaboration with the IARC p53 database. In addition to data from the Cancer Genome Project (CGP) at the Sanger Institute in the UK and The Cancer Genome Atlas project (TCGA), COSMIC also curates information from large systematic screens. The website has undergone major upgrades, making the data more easily searchable with new selection filters and graphics. A Biomart feature is now available for automated data mining and integration with other biological databases. COSMIC has also focused on annotating genomic features and has started curating full-genome resequencing experiments, developing new web pages, export formats, and graphics styles. All genomic information has been updated to GRCh37, and COSMIC is working on closer integration with Ensembl and other data resources.

title: Quantitative imaging assay for NF-κB nuclear translocation in primary human macrophages
text: The measurement of NF-kappaB nuclear translocation is a crucial tool in cellular immunology research. However, current methodologies have limitations such as poor sensitivity, high cost, or reliance on specific cell lines. New imaging techniques have been developed to measure the translocation of active NF-kappaB components, but they require specialized equipment and image analysis software. In this study, we propose a method for quantitatively detecting NF-kappaB rel A nuclear translocation using immunofluorescence microscopy and the freely available image analysis software ImageJ. This method is easily applicable to cellular immunology research, does not require specialized image analysis expertise, and is cost-effective. To validate our method, we demonstrate the time course and dose response of NF-kappaB nuclear translocation in primary human macrophages stimulated with LPS, and compare the results with those obtained from a commercial NF-kappaB activation reporter cell line.

title: An RNA-sequencing transcriptome and splicing database of glia, neurons, and vascular cells of the cerebral cortex.
text: The brain consists of different cell classes that vary in their developmental processes, metabolism, signaling, and function. In order to gain a better understanding of these cell types and how they interact, we isolated specific populations of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, newly formed oligodendrocytes, myelinating oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and pericytes from the mouse cerebral cortex. Through RNA sequencing, we created a transcriptome database for these eight cell types and used an algorithm to detect alternative splicing events in each cell type. By analyzing the data, we discovered numerous new genes and splicing isoforms that are specific to each cell type. These findings will serve as valuable markers for identifying cells, tools for genetic manipulation, and insights into brain biology. For instance, we found that neurons and astrocytes differ in their ability to regulate glycolytic flux and lactate generation due to unique splicing of the PKM2 gene, which encodes the glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase. This dataset will be a valuable resource for studying brain development and function. To ensure easy access to these datasets, we have created a user-friendly website (http://web.stanford.edu/group/barres_lab/brain_rnaseq.html) where researchers can analyze and compare transcription and alternative splicing profiles of different cell classes in the brain.

title: C9orf72 repeat expansions cause neurodegeneration in Drosophila through arginine-rich proteins
text: The most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is an expanded GGGGCC repeat in C9orf72. A crucial question is whether the toxicity is caused by the repeat RNA itself or by dipeptide repeat proteins that are produced through non-ATG translation associated with the repeat. To investigate this, we created models in vitro and in vivo to examine the toxicity of repeat RNA and dipeptide repeat proteins. In Drosophila, the expression of pure repeats, but not stop codon-interrupted "RNA-only" repeats, led to neurodegeneration in adult-onset. Therefore, the expansion of repeats promoted neurodegeneration through dipeptide repeat proteins. Furthermore, when individual dipeptide repeat proteins with a non-GGGGCC RNA sequence were expressed, both poly-(glycine-arginine) and poly-(proline-arginine) proteins caused neurodegeneration. These findings support a dual mechanism of toxicity, where both arginine-rich proteins and repeat RNA contribute to C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration.

title: Targeted nanoparticles containing the proresolving peptide Ac2-26 protect against advanced atherosclerosis in hypercholesterolemic mice
text: Chronic inflammation that does not resolve is a crucial factor in the clinical progression of advanced atherosclerotic lesions. Annexin A1, a protein regulated by glucocorticoids, is among the agonists that mediate resolution in the normal inflammatory response. Annexin A1 exerts its proresolving effects through its receptor N-formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2/ALX), and these effects can be replicated by a peptide consisting of amino acids 2-26 (Ac2-26). We evaluated nanoparticles (NPs) targeted to collagen IV (Col IV) and containing Ac2-26 for their therapeutic impact on chronic, advanced atherosclerosis in mice lacking the Ldlr gene (fat-fed Ldlr−/− mice). When administered to mice with existing lesions, the Col IV–Ac2-26 NPs specifically targeted the lesions and significantly improved key properties of advanced plaques. These improvements included an increase in the protective collagen layer above the lesions (accompanied by a decrease in collagenase activity within the lesions), suppression of oxidative stress, and a reduction in plaque necrosis. However, in mice lacking FPR2/ALX in their myeloid cells, these improvements were not observed. Therefore, administering a peptide that promotes resolution within targeted NPs activates its receptor on myeloid cells, leading to the stabilization of advanced atherosclerotic lesions. These findings support the idea that impaired resolution of inflammation contributes to advanced atherosclerosis and suggest a novel therapeutic approach.

title: Interleukin-2 gene variation impairs regulatory T cell function and causes autoimmunity
text: Imbalances in normal immune physiology and regulation are believed to be the cause of autoimmune diseases. Our study reveals a correlation between autoimmune disease susceptibility and resistance alleles on mouse chromosome 3 (Idd3) and the expression of the immunoregulatory cytokine interleukin-2 (IL-2). To directly test the hypothesis that a twofold reduction in IL-2 is responsible for the destabilization of immune homeostasis linked to Idd3, we engineered a decrease in Il2 gene expression. This engineered haplodeficiency not only resulted in a twofold reduction in T cell IL-2 production, but also replicated the autoimmune dysregulatory effects observed with naturally occurring susceptibility alleles of Il2. The reduced IL-2 production, achieved through either genetic mechanism, was associated with decreased function of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining immune homeostasis.

title: GRSF1 Regulates RNA Processing in Mitochondrial RNA Granules
text: The cytosol and nucleus have been extensively studied in terms of specialized domains, but there is limited knowledge about compartmentalization within the mitochondrial matrix. Previously, GRSF1 (G-rich sequence factor 1), an RNA binding protein, was reported to localize in the cytosol. However, our research has discovered that a specific form of GRSF1 accumulates in distinct clusters within the mitochondrial matrix. These clusters consist of newly formed mitochondrial RNA and also contain RNase P, an enzyme involved in mitochondrial RNA processing. We have observed that GRSF1 interacts with RNase P and is essential for the processing of both classical and tRNA-less RNA precursors. In the absence of GRSF1, the cleavage of primary RNA transcripts becomes abnormal, resulting in reduced expression of mitochondrially encoded proteins and impaired mitochondrial function. Based on our findings, we propose that these clusters, which contain GRSF1 and RNase P, serve as convergence points for primary RNA transcripts to undergo processing. We have named these large ribonucleoprotein structures "mitochondrial RNA granules."

title: Midlife Serum Cholesterol and Increased Risk of Alzheimer’s and Vascular Dementia Three Decades Later
text:
Objective: This study aimed to examine the relationship between midlife cholesterol levels and the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD) in a large group of men and women from diverse ethnic backgrounds.

Methods: The database for this study was obtained from the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Medical Group, a healthcare delivery organization. A total of 9,844 participants underwent comprehensive health evaluations between 1964 and 1973 when they were between the ages of 40 and 45. These participants remained members of the health plan until 1994. Medical records were used to identify cases of AD and VaD between January 1, 1994, and June 1, 2007. Cox proportional hazards models were used to analyze the data, adjusting for various factors including age, education, race/ethnicity, sex, midlife diabetes, hypertension, BMI, and late-life stroke.

Results: Out of the total participants, 469 were diagnosed with AD and 127 with VaD. Compared to individuals with desirable cholesterol levels (<200 mg/dl), those with borderline cholesterol levels (200-239 mg/dl) had a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.23 (95% CI: 0.97-1.55) for AD, while those with high cholesterol levels (≥240 mg/dl) had an HR of 1.57 (95% CI: 1.23-2.01). For VaD, the HR was 1.50 (95% CI: 1.01-2.23) for borderline cholesterol and 1.26 (95% CI: 0.82-1.96) for high cholesterol. Further analysis for AD, using cholesterol quartiles with the first quartile as the reference, revealed that cholesterol levels above 220 mg/dl were a significant risk factor. The HRs were 1.31 (95% CI: 1.01-1.71) for the third quartile (221-248 mg/dl) and 1.58 (95% CI: 1.22-2.06) for the fourth quartile (249-500 mg/dl).

Conclusion: This study found that midlife serum total cholesterol levels were associated with an increased risk of developing AD and VaD. Even moderately elevated cholesterol levels were found to increase the risk of dementia. These findings highlight the importance of addressing dementia risk factors early in midlife, before the onset of underlying diseases or symptoms.

title: "The contribution of chronic diseases to the prevalence of dependence among older people in Latin America, China and India: a 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based survey"
text:
BACKGROUND
The global population of older individuals is projected to significantly increase in the coming years. This demographic shift is expected to lead to a rise in age-related chronic diseases, which are major contributors to disability and future dependence. However, the study of dependence has received less attention, despite its intrinsic connection to disability. Our research aimed to examine the prevalence and factors associated with dependence among older individuals in middle-income countries.

METHODS
We conducted a one-phase cross-sectional survey at 11 sites in seven countries, including urban areas in Cuba, Venezuela, and the Dominican Republic, as well as urban and rural areas in Peru, Mexico, China, and India. All individuals aged 65 years and older residing in specific geographic regions were eligible to participate. A total of 15,022 interviews were completed, with an informant interview conducted for each participant. We utilized the comprehensive 10/66 Dementia Research Group survey protocol, which included assessments for depression, dementia, physical impairments, and self-reported diagnoses. Dependence was determined by interviewers based on responses from key informants regarding the participant's care needs. We calculated the prevalence of dependence and the independent contribution of underlying health conditions. Site-specific prevalence ratios were meta-analyzed, and population attributable prevalence fractions (PAPF) were calculated.

RESULTS
The prevalence of dependence increased with age across all sites, with a tendency for lower prevalence in men compared to women. When standardized for age, the prevalence of dependence was lower in all sites compared to the United States. Apart from rural China, dementia was found to be the largest independent contributor to dependence, with a median PAPF of 34% (range 23%-59%). Other significant contributors included limb impairment (9%, 1%-46%), stroke (8%, 2%-17%), and depression (8%, 1%-27%).

CONCLUSION
The ongoing demographic and health transitions will result in a substantial and rapid increase in the number of dependent older individuals, particularly in middle-income countries. It is crucial to prioritize the prevention and management of chronic neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases, as well as the development of long-term care policies and plans.

title: An actomyosin-based barrier inhibits cell mixing at compartmental boundaries in Drosophila embryos
text: Partitioning tissues into separate compartments is crucial for the proper development of animal embryos and organs. Various hypotheses have been suggested to explain how cells are sorted into compartments, such as differential adhesion, regulation of the cytoskeleton, or cell proliferation. However, the specific molecular and cellular mechanisms that prevent cells from mixing at boundaries are still not fully understood. In this study, we present evidence from early Drosophila melanogaster embryos that barriers composed of actomyosin prevent cells from invading neighboring compartments. Our analysis reveals that cells can briefly invade neighboring compartments, particularly during cell division, but are then pushed back into their original compartment. Actomyosin cytoskeletal components are concentrated at compartment boundaries, forming cable-like structures when the outer layer of the embryo is actively dividing. When the function of MyoII (a type of non-muscle myosin II) is inhibited, including specifically at the cable using chromophore-assisted laser inactivation (CALI) in live embryos, dividing cells are no longer pushed back, resulting in mixing of cells between compartments. Based on these findings, we propose that local regulation of actomyosin contractility, rather than differential adhesion, is the primary mechanism responsible for sorting cells at compartment boundaries.

title: Clinical algorithms for malaria diagnosis lack utility among people of different age groups.
text:
We conducted a study in Kilifi District, Kenya, to determine the usefulness of clinical algorithms in diagnosing malaria among people living in an area with moderate malaria transmission. A total of 1602 individuals of all age groups participated in the study. We collected smears and recorded clinical signs and symptoms of all individuals who visited the study clinic with a history of fever, whether prompted or spontaneous. A malaria case was defined as a person who presented to the clinic with a history of fever and concurrent parasitaemia. 

We selected a set of clinical signs and symptoms (algorithms) that had the highest sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing a malaria case in different age groups: </=5 years, 6-14 years, and >/=15 years. These age-optimized algorithms were able to identify approximately 66% of the cases among individuals under 15 years of age, but only 23% of cases among adults. 

If these algorithms were used as a basis for treatment decisions at the clinic, approximately 16% of children aged </=5 years, 44% of those aged 6-14 years, and 66% of adults with a history of fever and parasitaemia >/=5000 parasites/microl of blood would be sent home without treatment. 

Therefore, clinical algorithms do not appear to be very useful in diagnosing malaria, especially among older age groups. This is concerning because avoiding unnecessary use of anti-malarials in these age groups would make more drugs available for the vulnerable population of children under 5 years of age who truly need them.

title: Large-scale genetic fine mapping and genotype-phenotype associations implicate polymorphism in the IL2RA region in type 1 diabetes
text:
Genome-wide association studies have made significant progress in identifying chromosome regions associated with diseases. However, to pinpoint the specific variant(s) responsible for the disease, further steps such as resequencing, genotyping, and statistical analyses in large sample sets are necessary. These steps ultimately lead to targeted functional studies.

In our study, we successfully localized the association between type 1 diabetes (T1D) and the interleukin 2 receptor alpha (IL2RA) gene region. We found that this association is present in two independent groups of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which span overlapping regions of 14 and 40 kilobases. These regions include IL2RA intron 1 and the 5′ regions of IL2RA and RBM17. The odds ratio for this association is 2.04, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.70-2.45. The p-value is 1.92 × 10−28, and the control frequency is 0.635.

Additionally, we discovered that individuals with IL2RA T1D susceptibility genotypes have lower levels of the biomarker soluble IL-2RA. This finding suggests that an inherited lower immune responsiveness may predispose individuals to T1D.

title: Maternal obesity epigenetically alters visceral fat progenitor cell properties in male offspring mice.
text:
The density of adipogenic progenitor cells in offspring adipose tissue is reduced by maternal obesity. When exposed to a high-fat diet, the ability of adipose tissue in the offspring of obese mothers to expand is limited and is associated with metabolic dysfunction. Maternal obesity causes DNA demethylation in the promoter of zinc finger protein 423, which increases the adipogenic capacity of progenitor cells. This demonstrates a long-term effect of maternal obesity on the adipogenic capacity of progenitor cells in offspring adipose tissue, indicating a developmental programming effect.

In this study, the researchers aimed to investigate whether maternal obesity predisposes adipocyte progenitors in offspring fat to adipogenic differentiation and subsequent depletion, leading to a lack of plasticity in adipose tissue under positive energy balance and contributing to metabolic dysfunction. Female C57BL/6 mice were fed either a control diet or a high-fat diet before mating. Male offspring of control and obese dams were then weaned onto either a regular or obesogenic diet until 3 months of age.

At weaning, male offspring of obese dams had higher expression of Zinc finger protein 423 (zfp423), a key transcription factor in adipogenesis, and lower DNA methylation of its promoter in progenitors of epididymal fat compared to offspring of control dams. This was correlated with enhanced adipogenic differentiation. At 3 months of age, the density of progenitor cells was 30.9% lower in offspring of obese dams on the obesogenic diet compared to offspring of control dams on the same diet. Additionally, there was limited expansion of the adipocyte number in these offspring when challenged with a high-energy diet. This difference was associated with lower DNA methylation in the zfp423 promoter in the epididymal fat of offspring of obese dams, which was correlated with increased expression of macrophage chemotactic protein-1 and hypoxia-inducible factor 1α.

In conclusion, maternal obesity epigenetically restricts the expansion capacity of offspring adipose tissue, providing an explanation for the metabolic dysfunction observed in male offspring of obese mothers.

title: Quality Testing of Artemisinin-Based Antimalarial Drugs in Myanmar.
text: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are currently the primary treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. However, the presence of counterfeit and substandard artemisinin-based antimalarials in Southeast Asia has posed a significant challenge to the efforts to eliminate malaria. In order to provide an update on this issue, we conducted a study where we obtained 153 artemisinin-containing antimalarials from various private drug stores in different regions of Myanmar. We assessed the quality of these drugs by testing their artemisinin derivative content using specific dipsticks designed for this purpose, as well as high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) for a subset of the samples. Our findings revealed that over 35% of the drugs we collected were oral artesunate and artemether monotherapies. When tested with the dipsticks, all but one sample met the required standards, indicating that the detected artemisinin derivative content was consistent with the labeled contents. However, one sample of artesunate injection was found to contain no active ingredient at all, as confirmed by both the dipstick assay and subsequent HPLC analysis. The ongoing circulation of oral monotherapies and the discovery of falsified parenteral artesunate for the first time highlight the concerning issue of poor antimalarial drug quality in Myanmar during the malaria elimination phase. This situation calls for increased oversight from regulatory authorities.

title: LINE-1 Retrotransposition Activity in Human Genomes
text: The majority of retrotransposition activity in the human genome is attributed to highly active long interspersed element-1 (LINE-1 or L1) sequences, commonly referred to as "hot" L1s. However, the extent of hot L1s in the human population has not been thoroughly investigated. In this study, we employed a fosmid-based, paired-end DNA sequencing approach to identify 68 full-length L1s that are present in some individuals but not in the human genome reference sequence. Further analysis revealed that most of these L1s were highly active in a cultured cell retrotransposition assay. By genotyping 26 elements, we discovered that two L1s are exclusive to Africa and two others are absent from the H952 subset of the Human Genome Diversity Panel. These findings indicate that hot L1s are more prevalent in the human population than previously recognized, and that ongoing L1 retrotransposition remains a significant contributor to interindividual genetic variation.

title: Immune cell promotion of metastasis
text: Metastatic cancer is the leading cause of death in cancer patients, and current treatments like immunotherapy and chemotherapy have had limited success in stopping its progression. Studies using mouse models have shown that immunosuppressive cells are recruited to tumors, shielding metastatic cancer cells from killer cells and rendering immunotherapy ineffective. This process ultimately leads to the establishment of metastasis. Additionally, immune cells that infiltrate the tumor often transform into cells that facilitate each stage of the metastatic process, making them promising targets for therapy. In this article, we explore the role of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in the metastatic process and discuss potential therapeutic approaches to target these cells.

title: PICH: a DNA translocase specially adapted for processing anaphase bridge DNA.
text: The protein known as Plk1-interacting checkpoint helicase (PICH) is found in ultrafine anaphase bridges (UFBs) during mitosis, along with a group of DNA repair proteins that includes the Bloom's syndrome protein (BLM). However, there is limited knowledge regarding the role of PICH and how it is recruited to UFBs. To gain a better understanding, we conducted experiments using microfluidics, fluorescence microscopy, and optical tweezers to study PICH in an in vitro model of an anaphase bridge. Our findings reveal that PICH has a strong affinity for duplex DNA, leading to ATP-dependent protein movement and elongation of the DNA. Notably, the affinity of PICH for DNA binding increases when the DNA is stretched under tension, mimicking the effect of the mitotic spindle on a UFB. Additionally, PICH binding seems to prevent force-induced DNA melting. Based on these observations, we propose a model in which PICH recognizes and stabilizes DNA under tension during anaphase, thereby aiding in the resolution of tangled sister chromatids.

title: The Dynamics of Genome-wide DNA Methylation Reprogramming in Mouse Primordial Germ Cells
text: We conducted a study to investigate the reprogramming of DNA methylation in mouse primordial germ cells (PGCs) and preimplantation embryos. However, the specific dynamics and biological outcomes of this process are not well understood. To gain insights, we performed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (BS-Seq) and RNA-Seq at various stages from E6.5 epiblast to E16.5 PGCs. Our findings revealed a global loss of methylation during PGC expansion and migration, indicating passive demethylation. However, certain sequences that retain long-term epigenetic memory, such as imprints, CpG islands on the X chromosome, and germline-specific genes, only became demethylated when PGCs entered the gonads. Despite the overall hypomethylation, the transcriptional profile of PGCs remained tightly controlled, with transient expression of the pluripotency network. This suggests a close relationship between reprogramming and pluripotency. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the epigenetic ground state of pluripotency in the germline.

title: Major histocompatibility complex associations of ankylosing spondylitis are complex and involve further epistasis with ERAP1
text: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a prevalent, highly heritable, inflammatory arthritis. The major genetic risk factor for AS is HLA-B*27, although its exact role in the development of AS is still unclear. To gain a better understanding of the genetic basis of susceptibility in the MHC region, we analyzed 7,264 MHC SNPs in a group of 22,647 individuals of European descent, including both AS cases and controls. We used imputation to determine SNPs, classical HLA alleles, and amino-acid residues within HLA proteins, and then tested these for association with AS status. Our findings reveal that, in addition to the effects of HLA-B*27 alleles, several other HLA-B alleles also contribute to susceptibility. Furthermore, even after accounting for the associated haplotypes in HLA-B, we identified independent associations with variants in the HLA-A, HLA-DPB1, and HLA-DRB1 loci. Additionally, we discovered that the association of the ERAP1 SNP rs30187 is not limited to carriers of HLA-B*27, but is also present in carriers of HLA-B*40:01 regardless of HLA-B*27 genotype.

title: RNA sequencing identifies dysregulation of the human pancreatic islet transcriptome by the saturated fatty acid palmitate.
text: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is primarily caused by dysfunction and death of pancreatic β-cells. In individuals with a genetic predisposition, saturated fatty acids contribute to the development of diabetes by causing β-cell failure. To understand the molecular changes induced by palmitate, a saturated fatty acid, we conducted RNA sequencing on human islet preparations treated with palmitate. We identified 1,325 genes that were modified by palmitate. Palmitate triggered fatty acid metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Through functional studies, we discovered new mediators of adaptive ER stress signaling. Palmitate also modified genes involved in ubiquitin and proteasome function, autophagy, and apoptosis. Inhibition of autophagic flux and lysosome function contributed to the harmful effects of palmitate. Additionally, palmitate inhibited the activity of transcription factors that control the β-cell phenotype, such as PAX4 and GATA6. Among the genes expressed in human islets, 59 were associated with T2D, and 11 of them were modified by palmitate. Palmitate also altered the expression of 17 splicing factors and affected the alternative splicing of 3,525 transcripts. Analysis of the modified genes and transcripts confirmed that the most significant changes were related to cell death. Further analysis using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) revealed the involvement of transcription factors PAX4, GATA, and ER stress response regulators XBP1 and ATF6 in the palmitate-induced modifications. This study of the human islet transcriptome provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying β-cell dysfunction and death caused by palmitate. The findings suggest that there is a communication between metabolic stress and candidate genes at the β-cell level.

title: The Ratio of Monocytes to Lymphocytes in Peripheral Blood Correlates with Increased Susceptibility to Clinical Malaria in Kenyan Children
text:
Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to be a significant cause of illness and death in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly affecting young children. While older children and adults may experience fewer clinical attacks, they are still susceptible to asymptomatic P. falciparum infection. Understanding the host factors associated with immunity to clinical malaria and the ability to sustain asymptomatic infection is crucial for developing better disease prevention strategies.

In this study, we aimed to determine if full differential blood counts could predict susceptibility to clinical malaria in Kenyan children. We conducted five annual cross-sectional surveys and found that the ratio of monocytes to lymphocytes in peripheral blood directly correlated with the risk of clinical malaria during follow-up. This association was observed in children with asymptomatic P. falciparum infection at the time of cell count measurement, but not in those without detectable parasitemia.

Based on these findings, we suggest that the monocyte to lymphocyte ratio, which can be easily derived from routine full differential blood counts, reflects an individual's ability to mount an effective immune response to P. falciparum infection.

title: Dynamic analysis of filopodial interactions during the zippering phase of Drosophila dorsal closure.
text:
Dorsal closure is a crucial process in the development of Drosophila embryos, where two opposing sheets of epithelial cells fuse together to seal a hole in the midline. This fusion is facilitated by the presence of filopodia on the leading edge cells, which interdigitate and form adhesions. However, since the two epithelial sheets have distinct molecular patterns, there must be a mechanism to align them accurately during fusion.

To investigate this alignment mechanism, we created a genetically modified fly that expresses RFP-Moesin and GFP-Moesin in different patterns within each segment. Specifically, we used the engrailed and patched promoters to generate mutually exclusive stripes of these proteins. Through our observations, we found that the filopodia of engrailed and patched cells interact exclusively with their matching counterparts. These interactions result in the formation of tethers between the filopodia, which can then pull misaligned epithelial sheets into proper alignment.

Interestingly, we also observed similar filopodial matching during the repair of laser wounds in the ventral epithelium. This suggests that this behavior is not limited to leading edge cells during dorsal closure but is a more general phenomenon. Additionally, we studied the behavior of a patched-expressing cell within the engrailed region of segments A1-A5. Our findings provide evidence that this cell also contributes to the process of cell matching.

In summary, our research sheds light on the mechanisms involved in dorsal closure and the alignment of opposing epithelial sheets. The interactions between filopodia and the formation of tethers play a crucial role in ensuring accurate fusion and sealing of the midline hole.

title: Expression of Versican 3′-Untranslated Region Modulates Endogenous MicroRNA Functions
text:
BACKGROUND: Mature microRNAs (miRNAs) are single-stranded RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. In a previous study, we discovered that a fragment of non-coding transcript called versican 3'UTR can counteract the function of miR-199a-3p, which in turn regulates the expression of matrix proteins versican and fibronectin. This leads to increased cell-cell adhesion and organ adhesion. However, the impact of this non-coding fragment on tumorigenesis is still unknown.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: Through computational prediction and experiments conducted in vitro and in vivo, we found that the expression of versican 3'UTR not only counteracts miR-199a-3p, but also reduces its overall expression. In a mouse breast carcinoma cell line called 4T1, the expression of versican 3'UTR decreased the levels of miR-199a-3p. This decrease in miRNA activity resulted in differences in tumor growth. Computational analysis revealed that both miR-199a-3p and miR-144 target a cell cycle regulator called Rb1. Additionally, miR-144 and miR-136, which also interact with versican 3'UTR, were found to target PTEN. The expression of Rb1 and PTEN was up-regulated synergistically in vitro and in vivo, indicating that the 3'UTR binds and modulates miRNA activities, allowing for the translation of Rb1 and PTEN mRNAs. In tumor formation assays, cells transfected with the 3'UTR formed smaller tumors compared to cells transfected with a control vector.

CONCLUSION: Our results demonstrate that a 3'UTR fragment can be used to modulate miRNA functions. Furthermore, our study suggests that miRNAs in cancer cells are more susceptible to degradation due to their interaction with a non-coding 3'UTR. This non-coding component of mRNA may be used retrospectively to modulate miRNA activities.

title: Prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy of the epitope vaccine CTB-UA against Helicobacter pylori infection in a BALB/c mice model
text: The use of an epitope vaccine based on the enzyme urease of Helicobacter pylori shows promise as a preventive and therapeutic option against H. pylori infection. In a previous study, we developed a vaccine called CTB-UA, which consists of the mucosal adjuvant cholera toxin B subunit (CTB) and an epitope (UreA183–203) from the H. pylori urease A subunit (UreA). This vaccine demonstrated strong immunogenicity and immunoreactivity, generating specific neutralizing antibodies that effectively inhibited the enzymatic activity of H. pylori urease. To further evaluate its efficacy, we conducted experiments using a BALB/c mice model. The results showed that oral administration of CTB-UA as a preventive or therapeutic measure significantly reduced H. pylori colonization compared to oral administration of PBS. Additionally, the protection observed was associated with antigen-specific IgG, IgA, and mucosal secretory IgA antibody responses. These findings suggest that CTB-UA holds promise as a potential vaccine candidate for controlling H. pylori infection.

title: Spatial co-distribution of neglected tropical diseases in the east African great lakes region: revisiting the justification for integrated control.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the spatial distribution of co-endemicity of schistosomiasis mansoni and soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) in the Great Lakes region of East Africa. This information would be used to plan integrated neglected tropical disease programs in the region. 

Parasitological surveys were conducted in Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, and Burundi, involving 28,213 children from 404 schools. Bayesian geostatistical models were used to estimate the prevalence of these infections across the study area. The prevalence maps were then overlaid to identify areas of co-endemicity. 

The results showed that in the Great Lakes region, the prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni was 18.1%, hookworm was 50.0%, Ascaris lumbricoides was 6.8%, and Trichuris trichiura was 6.8%. Hookworm infection was found throughout the region, while S. mansoni, A. lumbricoides, and T. trichiura were more localized. Most areas had a high prevalence (greater than or equal to 10%) or were hyperendemic (greater than or equal to 50%) for one or more STHs. However, schistosomiasis mansoni was only endemic in areas near large perennial water bodies. 

Based on these findings, it is recommended that treatment programs for STHs be implemented throughout the region due to the widespread presence of hookworm. However, for efficient control of schistosomiasis, interventions should be targeted at specific high-risk areas. Therefore, integration of schistosomiasis control with STH control is only necessary in limited areas of East Africa.

title: Direct conversion of patient fibroblasts demonstrates non-cell autonomous toxicity of astrocytes to motor neurons in familial and sporadic ALS.
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease that leads to the degeneration of motor neurons, resulting in paralysis and ultimately death. It is crucial to accurately model the disease, identify its mechanisms, and develop effective treatments. In our previous study, we discovered that astrocytes derived from the spinal cords of deceased ALS patients exhibited toxicity towards motor neurons. However, obtaining these cells is only possible after death, and their growth is limited. 

Now, we present a fast and highly reliable method to convert fibroblasts from living ALS patients into induced neuronal progenitor cells, which can then be differentiated into astrocytes (referred to as i-astrocytes). When these i-astrocytes from familial ALS patients with mutations in the superoxide dismutase gene or hexanucleotide expansion in C9orf72 (located on chromosome 9) - the two most common causes of ALS - were co-cultured with motor neurons, we observed non-cell autonomous toxicity. Surprisingly, i-astrocytes from sporadic ALS patients exhibited the same level of toxicity as those with known causative mutations, suggesting a shared mechanism.

The ease of producing and expanding i-astrocytes now allows for rapid disease modeling and efficient screening of potential drugs to alleviate astrocyte-induced toxicity.

title: Combined Single-Cell Functional and Gene Expression Analysis Resolves Heterogeneity within Stem Cell Populations
text: The durability of adult hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in self-renewal varies due to their heterogeneity, which poses a challenge in understanding the molecular framework governing HSC function. Previous gene expression studies have been hindered by the presence of different HSC subtypes and non-HSC contaminants in bulk HSC populations. To gain a deeper understanding of the gene expression program of murine HSCs, we employed single-cell functional assays, flow cytometric index sorting, and single-cell gene expression assays. By integrating these datasets using bioinformatics, we developed an unbiased sorting strategy that effectively separates non-HSCs from HSCs. We then conducted single-cell transplantation experiments using the enriched HSC population and combined the results with RNA-seq data to identify key molecules associated with long-term durable self-renewal. This approach generated a single-cell molecular dataset that is directly linked to functional stem cell activity. Furthermore, we demonstrated the broader applicability of this approach by successfully linking key molecules to defined cellular functions in another stem cell system.

title: Acids: Structures, Properties, and Functions (University Science Books, Sausalito, CA, 2000).
text: Defective expression of the transcription factor AIRE (autoimmune regulator) in humans leads to the development of autoimmune diseases affecting multiple organs. To investigate the role of this transcription factor in regulating autoimmunity, we conducted experiments using mice lacking the aire gene. Our hypothesis was that AIRE promotes the ectopic expression of tissue-specific antigens in medullary epithelial cells of the thymus, thereby influencing autoimmunity. Our hypothesis was confirmed as the mutant mice displayed a distinct profile of autoimmune diseases, which was directly linked to the absence of aire in thymic stromal cells. Notably, the aire-deficient thymic medullary epithelial cells exhibited a specific decrease in the abnormal transcription of genes responsible for encoding peripheral antigens. These findings emphasize the significance of "central" tolerance imposed by the thymus in controlling autoimmunity.

title: Directed Actin Polymerization Is the Driving Force for Epithelial Cell–Cell Adhesion
text: We have made an interesting discovery regarding the behavior of epithelial cells in their process of intercellular adhesion mediated by cadherin. Surprisingly, this process involves the utilization of calcium and actin polymerization in unique ways. Calcium serves to stimulate the formation of filopodia, which are able to penetrate and embed into neighboring cells. At the tips of these filopodia, E-cadherin complexes cluster together, creating a two-rowed zipper-like structure of embedded puncta. Desmosomes clamp the opposing surfaces of the cells, while vinculin, zyxin, VASP, and Mena are recruited to these adhesion zippers through a mechanism that requires alpha-catenin. Actin undergoes reorganization and polymerization, causing the puncta to merge into a single row and effectively seal the borders between cells. However, in keratinocytes lacking alpha-catenin or with impaired VASP/Mena function, filopodia are still able to embed into neighboring cells, but the reorganization and polymerization of actin are prevented, resulting in the inability of the cell membranes to seal. In summary, we have uncovered a dynamic mechanism for intercellular adhesion that involves the activation of calcium-induced filopodia penetration and the VASP/Mena-dependent reorganization and polymerization of actin.

title: Ribosomal DNA copy number loss and sequence variation in cancer
text:
The copy number of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) is highly variable in the human genome. However, we have limited knowledge about the factors that control its copy number, stability, and sequence in mammals due to mapping and analysis challenges. To address this, we utilized computational and droplet digital PCR techniques to measure rDNA copy number in normal and cancerous states of both human and mouse genomes. Our findings reveal that copy number and sequence can indeed change in cancer genomes.

Interestingly, human cancer genomes exhibit a reduction in rDNA copies, accompanied by a global co-variation in copy number. Additionally, the sequence of rDNA can be more variable in cancer genomes. We observed that cancer genomes with lower rDNA copies display mutational evidence of mTOR hyperactivity. The mTOR kinase pathway is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor PTEN phosphatase, which is crucial for genome stability. Surprisingly, our observations in human cancer genomes align with those in a mouse model of leukemia, where hematopoietic cancer stem cells lacking the Pten gene also exhibit lower rDNA copy number despite increased proliferation, rRNA production, and protein synthesis. The loss of rDNA copies occurs early in cancer development and is associated with heightened sensitivity to DNA damage.

Therefore, the loss of rDNA copies is a recurring characteristic in cancers linked to mTOR activation. Consequently, rDNA copy number could serve as a straightforward and valuable indicator to determine whether a cancer will respond to DNA damaging treatments.

title: The association of Red cell distribution width and in-hospital mortality in older adults admitted to the emergency department
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate whether higher red cell distribution width (RDW) levels upon admission to the emergency department (ED) increase the risk of mortality in older patients. A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients admitted to the ED between May 2013 and October 2013. The study included patients over the age of 65 who presented with any medical issues. RDW values were measured upon admission, and the primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Multivariate logistic analysis was performed. 

A total of 1,990 patients were included in the study, with a mean age of 75 years. Of these patients, 936 were male. The in-hospital mortality rate was 3.76%, with higher RDW values observed in non-survivors compared to survivors (15.9 ± 2.5 vs. 13.8 ± 1.7, p < 0.001). Multivariate logistic analysis revealed that RDW was associated with all-cause in-hospital mortality, even after adjusting for other factors. 

The study concludes that RDW levels upon admission are an independent predictor of all-cause in-hospital mortality in patients over the age of 65. For each 1% increase in RDW, the all-cause in-hospital mortality rate increased by 21.8% after adjusting for confounding variables. However, the authors caution against using these findings in clinical decision-making until they are validated externally.

title: Gene regulation by the act of long non-coding RNA transcription
text: The largest class of transcripts in the mouse and human transcriptomes is believed to be long non-protein-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). There are two important questions regarding lncRNAs: whether they all have a function and how they exert their function. While some lncRNAs have been shown to function through their product, there are other possible modes of action. This review focuses on the role of lncRNA transcription, independent of the lncRNA product, in regulating the activity of protein-coding genes in cis. We discuss examples where lncRNA transcription leads to gene silencing or activation, and we describe strategies to determine whether the regulatory effect is caused by the lncRNA product or its transcription.

title: Life and death of cardiac stem cells: a paradigm shift in cardiac biology.
text:
The understanding that myocyte mitosis occurs in the fetal, neonatal, adult, and hypertrophied heart, and that there is a pool of undifferentiated cells in the myocardium, has presented a new perspective on the biology of the heart. This new paradigm suggests that myocyte formation continues throughout postnatal life, even in adulthood and old age, indicating that the heart has a remarkable capacity for growth throughout an organism's lifespan. This article examines a significant amount of recent information that supports the idea that the mammalian heart has the inherent ability to continuously replace its parenchymal cells, and that this unexpected characteristic has important implications for understanding myocardial homeostasis, cardiac aging, and tissue repair. 

For the past three decades, the prevailing belief in cardiology has been that the heart is a postmitotic organ that cannot regenerate parenchymal cells. This belief has greatly influenced both basic and clinical research in the field. According to this paradigm, cardiomyocytes can undergo cellular hypertrophy but cannot be replaced by either a subpopulation of nonterminally differentiated myocytes entering the cell cycle or a pool of primitive cells that commit to the myocyte lineage. The only response of cardiomyocytes to stress is hypertrophy or death. As a result, extensive efforts have been made to identify the molecular mechanisms and genetic control of myocyte hypertrophy. Significant progress has been made in understanding the various signaling pathways involved, and our knowledge of hypertrophic myocyte growth has greatly advanced. New technologies have also been introduced, leading to a scientific revolution in terms of the questions asked, approaches taken, and interpretation of experimental results. However, despite this progress in understanding the basic mechanisms of hypertrophy, there is still a lack of understanding about the potential for myocyte replacement in the heart.

title: Paraneoplastic thrombocytosis: the secrets of tumor self-promotion.
text: Many solid tumors are linked to paraneoplastic thrombocytosis, which is often linked to lower survival rates. Recent research indicates that there may be a harmful cycle between platelets and tumor cells, where tumor growth and metastasis interact with thrombocytosis and platelet activation. Certain molecular pathways have been discovered, showing how tumors can stimulate platelet production and activation, and how activated platelets can further promote tumor growth and metastasis. These discoveries offer promising targets for potential therapeutic interventions.

title: Perceived age as clinically useful biomarker of ageing: cohort study.
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if perceived age is related to survival and important age-related characteristics. The study involved a follow-up of twins, with survival data collected until January 2008, at which point 37% of the twins had died. The study took place in Denmark and included 20 nurses, 10 young men, and 11 older women as assessors, along with 1826 twins aged 70 or older. The main measures included the assessors' perception of the twins' age based on photographs, as well as physical and cognitive tests and a molecular biomarker of aging called leucocyte telomere length for the twins.

The results showed that perceived age was significantly associated with survival for all three groups of assessors, even after adjusting for chronological age, sex, and rearing environment. This association remained significant even after further adjustment for physical and cognitive functioning. The study also found that the older-looking twin in a pair was more likely to die first if there was a larger difference in perceived age within the pair. Twin analyses suggested that there are common genetic factors that influence both perceived age and survival. Additionally, perceived age, when controlled for chronological age and sex, was found to correlate significantly with physical and cognitive functioning, as well as leucocyte telomere length.

In conclusion, perceived age is a reliable biomarker of aging that can predict survival in individuals aged 70 or older. It also correlates with important functional and molecular aging characteristics. This finding is significant as perceived age is commonly used by clinicians as an indicator of a patient's overall health.

title: Inflammatory Reaction as Determinant of Foreign Body Reaction Is an Early and Susceptible Event after Mesh Implantation
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine and compare the short-term and long-term effects of various factors on foreign body reaction in an animal model, in order to predict the biocompatibility of meshes. Three different types of meshes (TVT, UltraPro, and PVDF) were implanted in sheep. These meshes were either native or coated with plasma, and were placed in different locations within the sheep: (a) interaperitoneally, (b) as a fascia onlay, and (c) as a muscle onlay (fascia sublay). The meshes were removed at various time intervals (5 min, 20 min, 60 min, and 120 min) and examined for signs of inflammation, macrophage infiltration, vessel formation, myofibroblast invasion, and connective tissue accumulation. The results were then compared to long-term values over a period of 24 months. 

The findings showed that macrophage invasion was highest in the short-term, reaching up to 60%, but decreased to about 30% within 24 months. Inflammatory infiltrate increased within the first 2 hours and remained stable throughout the long-term follow-up period, with varying levels and rankings among the different meshes. No activity was observed for myofibroblasts, connective tissue, and CD31+ cells within the first 120 minutes. 

In conclusion, the local inflammatory reaction is an early and sensitive event following mesh implantation. It is not affected by prior plasma coating and is independent of the location of implantation.

title: Riesz pyramids for fast phase-based video magnification
text: Introducing the Riesz pyramid, a novel compact image pyramid representation designed for real-time phase-based motion magnification. Unlike the smallest two orientation, octave-bandwidth complex steerable pyramid, our new representation is less overcomplete. It can be implemented using compact and efficient linear filters in the spatial domain. The motion-magnified videos generated using this new representation exhibit similar quality to those produced with the complex steerable pyramid. When combined with phase-based video magnification, the Riesz pyramid selectively phase-shifts image features along their dominant orientation only, as opposed to every orientation as done by the complex steerable pyramid.

title: Alpha-Synuclein Induces Lysosomal Rupture and Cathepsin Dependent Reactive Oxygen Species Following Endocytosis
text: The dysregulation of α-synuclein is a crucial factor in the development of Parkinson's disease. Recent research has shown that α-synuclein aggregates are harmful to cells in culture and can be transmitted between cells. However, the specific mechanisms behind this toxicity and transmission are not well understood. In studies of viruses and bacteria, which enter the cytoplasm by rupturing intracellular vesicles, galectin proteins have been used to measure vesicle rupture. Using this method, we have found that α-synuclein aggregates can cause the rupture of lysosomes after being taken up by neuronal cell lines. This rupture can occur when α-synuclein aggregates are directly added to cells or transferred between cells. We have also observed that lysosomal rupture caused by α-synuclein leads to an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in target cells, which is dependent on the presence of cathepsin B. Additionally, α-synuclein aggregates can activate the inflammasome in THP-1 cells.
