Lysosomal rupture is known to result in mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation, both of which are well-established factors in Parkinson's disease. This connects the pathology of α-synuclein to the progression of Parkinson's disease in cells.

title: Mechanistic Fracture Criteria For The Failure Of Human Cortical Bone
text: Understanding how fractures occur in human bone is crucial for predicting the risk of fractures associated with aging and disease. Despite extensive research, there is still a lack of knowledge regarding how the microstructure of bone contributes to its failure. While there have been models developed to explain the failure of metallic and ceramic materials at a microscopic level, there are very few models available for biological materials like bone. Additionally, there is no concrete evidence to support the widely accepted belief that bone fractures are controlled by local strain, as seen in ductile fractures of metallic materials. In this study, we aim to provide evidence for this belief through a unique set of experiments using a double-notch-bend geometry. These experiments will help us understand the critical events that lead to bone failure and how the propagating crack interacts with the bone's microstructure. By doing so, we can gain a mechanistic understanding of fractures and determine how properties vary with different orientations. Our findings reveal that fractures in human cortical bone are indeed strain-controlled, and the microstructure of the bone plays a significant role in this process. We also identify several toughening mechanisms, such as uncracked-ligament bridging, and provide estimates of their relative importance.

title: Inhibition of limb regeneration in the axolotl after treatment of the skin with actinomycin D.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of the wound epidermis on underlying tissues during limb regeneration, using actinomycin D. In this experiment, the skin was removed from the elbow to the shoulder of axolotl forelimbs. The skin from the right limbs was soaked in actinomycin D (5.0 or 10.0 μg/ml 0.6% NaCl) for three hours, while the skin from the left limbs was soaked in 0.6% NaCl as a control. Each piece of skin was then replanted in its original position, and both limbs were amputated above the treated skin, near the elbow.

After an initial healing period, the control limbs regenerated normally. The limbs with actinomycin-treated skin appeared similar to the controls, both visually and under microscopic examination, during the first week after amputation, except for a slightly lighter color. However, there was no visible evidence of regeneration in the experimental limbs, although some dedifferentiation was observed histologically. The control regenerates typically showed three to four digits before blastemas appeared on the experimental limbs. Around 35-40 days after amputation, blastemas started to form on most of the experimental limbs. These blastemas developed rapidly and reached a level of development similar to the controls in a short period of time.

The use of actinomycin D temporarily inhibited the formation of the apical epidermal cap and the subsequent aggregation of dedifferentiated cells into a blastema. However, once the effect of actinomycin D wore off, an apical cap formed and the dedifferentiated cells quickly organized into a blastema and began to differentiate.

title: Retinoic acid-related orphan receptors α and γ: key regulators of lipid/glucose metabolism, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity
text: The regulatory role of retinoic acid-related orphan receptors RORα and RORγ extends to lipid/glucose homeostasis and various immune functions. These receptors have been implicated in metabolic syndrome and several inflammatory diseases. Interestingly, mice lacking RORα are protected against age- and diet-induced obesity, hepatosteatosis, and insulin resistance. This protection against hepatosteatosis is due to reduced expression of genes involved in lipid synthesis, transport, and storage. Additionally, RORα-deficient mice show diminished adipose tissue-associated inflammation, a key factor in the development of insulin resistance. This is evident through reduced infiltration of M1 macrophages and decreased expression of proinflammatory genes. On the other hand, deficiency in RORγ also protects against diet-induced insulin resistance, but through a different mechanism than RORα deficiency. Recent studies have highlighted the role of RORs in linking the circadian clock machinery with the regulation of metabolic genes and metabolic syndrome. As ligand-dependent transcription factors, RORs present potential therapeutic targets for managing obesity and associated metabolic diseases, such as hepatosteatosis, adipose tissue-associated inflammation, and insulin resistance.

title: ERS/ESTS clinical guidelines on fitness for radical therapy in lung cancer patients (surgery and chemo-radiotherapy).
text: The European Respiratory Society (ERS) and the European Society of Thoracic Surgery (ESTS) have collaborated to bring together a group of experts from various disciplines to evaluate the functionality of lung cancer patients. Their goal is to create recommendations and guidelines for clinicians regarding the suitability of surgery and chemo-radiotherapy for these patients. The experts were divided into different topics, with each topic assigned to at least two experts. They conducted their own literature searches, without a central review of the literature. The experts then wrote draft reports on their respective topics, which were reviewed, discussed, and voted on by the entire panel. The evidence supporting each recommendation was summarized and graded according to the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network Grading Review Group. The final result was the creation of clinical practice guidelines in the form of a functional algorithm for risk stratification of candidates for lung resection. This algorithm emphasizes the evaluation of cardiological factors, forced expiratory volume in 1 second, systematic carbon monoxide lung diffusion capacity, and exercise testing. However, when it comes to chemo-radiotherapy, there is a lack of data, making it impossible to recommend any specific test, cut-off value, or algorithm. The experts strongly recommend that lung cancer patients be treated in specialized settings by multidisciplinary teams.

title: The Ran GTPase regulates mitotic spindle assembly
text: Ran is a nuclear GTPase that plays a significant role in nuclear transport during interphase. However, its involvement in mitotic regulation is not fully understood. The activity of Ran is controlled by two proteins: RanGAP1, a GTPase activating protein, and RCC1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor. Additionally, Ran interacts with RanBP1, a guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor. RanBP1 has a strong affinity for GTP-bound Ran and acts as a cofactor for RanGAP1, enhancing the rate of GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis on Ran by about ten times. The levels of RanBP1 fluctuate throughout the cell cycle, and higher concentrations of RanBP1 lead to prolonged mitosis in mammalian cells and Xenopus egg extracts. To understand the impact of increased RanBP1 concentrations on mitosis, we conducted experiments. We discovered that the addition of exogenous RanBP1 to Xenopus egg extracts in the M phase significantly disrupts spindle assembly. Our findings suggest that Ran's involvement in spindle assembly is unrelated to nuclear transport and likely occurs through alterations in microtubule dynamics.

title: A summary of the effects of antihypertensive medications on measured blood pressure.
text: The impact of antihypertensive medications on the analysis of blood pressure (BP) in family data is often problematic. This summary reviews multiple clinical trials that examined the effects of BP-lowering medications. The methods involved reviewing published clinical trials from PubMed, including 137 trials with single-drug therapies and 28 trials with combination drug therapies, totaling 11,739 participants. The antihypertensive medications were categorized into six major groups based on ethnicity: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, cardioselective beta-blockers (beta1-blockers), calcium channel blockers, thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, and loop diuretics. The results showed that, when considering all ethnic groups, monodrug therapy with ACE inhibitors reduced systolic and diastolic BP by an average of 12.5/9.5 mm Hg, alpha1-blockers by 15.5/11.7 mm Hg, beta1-blockers by 14.8/12.2 mm Hg, calcium channel blockers by 15.3/10.5 mm Hg, thiazide diuretics by 15.3/9.8 mm Hg, and loop diuretics by 15.8/8.2 mm Hg. However, ACE inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, and beta1-blockers were less effective in African Americans compared to non-African Americans, while calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and loop diuretics were more effective in African Americans. For combination therapy with all ethnic groups, the second medication reduced systolic and diastolic BP by 84% and 65%, respectively, compared to its effect as a single-drug therapy. In conclusion, the reported BP-lowering effects can be used to estimate pretreatment BP levels, enhancing the information and statistical power of epidemiologic analysis in studies where antihypertensive medication use may confound BP measurements.

title: Stem Cells and Early Lineage Development
text: The emergence of pluripotent stem cell lines from various sources, such as reprogrammed adult somatic cells, has sparked a debate regarding the developmental similarity of these distinct pluripotent states. Researchers have identified at least two distinct states: the epiblast progenitors found in the blastocyst and the pluripotent progenitors present in the later gastrulating embryo. It is crucial to comprehend the initial developmental state of these diverse pluripotent lines in order to establish the appropriate conditions for differentiating them into cell types that hold therapeutic significance.

title: Divergent clonal evolution of castration resistant neuroendocrine prostate cancer
text: Prostate cancer has been increasingly found to develop a resistance to androgen receptor (AR)-directed therapy through a mechanism called epithelial plasticity. This involves tumor cells showing low or no expression of AR and often displaying neuroendocrine features. However, the reasons behind this treatment-resistant cell state are not fully understood. To shed light on this, we examined whole-exome sequencing data from metastatic biopsies of patients and discovered significant genomic similarities between castration-resistant tumors classified as prostate adenocarcinomas (CRPC-Adeno) and neuroendocrine prostate cancer (CRPC-NE). Further analysis of biopsy samples from the same individuals over time suggested a model of divergent clonal evolution. Additionally, a genome-wide DNA methylation analysis revealed distinct epigenetic differences between CRPC-NE tumors and CRPC-Adeno, and identified some CRPC-Adeno samples with clinical features of AR independence as CRPC-NE. This suggests that epigenetic modifiers may contribute to the development and maintenance of this treatment-resistant state. Overall, our study supports the idea that an alternative, 'AR-indifferent' cell state emerges through divergent clonal evolution as a mechanism of treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer.

title: S-phase-promoting cyclin-dependent kinases prevent re-replication by inhibiting the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state
text:
The activation of kinase complexes, consisting of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks), triggers DNA replication and mitosis. It was previously believed that the association of Cdks with different types of cyclins determines whether S phase or M phase occurs. However, recent research in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has challenged this idea. It has been discovered that certain B-type cyclins (CLB1-CLB6) can play roles in both DNA replication and mitosis. 

In this study, S. cerevisiae strains lacking C1b1-C1b4 undergo DNA replication once but are unable to enter mitosis. Mutations in two genes, SIM1 and SIM2 (which is the same as SEC72), have been identified. These mutations allow cells to undergo an additional round of DNA replication without entering mitosis. The Clb5 kinase, which promotes S phase, remains active during the G2-phase arrest in the parental strain's cells. However, its activity decreases rapidly in sim mutants. Increased expression of the CLB5 gene prevents re-replication. This suggests that a cyclin B-kinase that promotes DNA replication in G1-phase cells can prevent re-replication in G2-phase cells. 

By expressing the specific C1b-Cdk1 inhibitor p40SIC1, the C1b kinases can be inactivated, leading to a prereplicative state at replication origins in cells blocked in G2/M phase by nocodazole. Reactivating the C1b-Cdk1 kinases induces a second round of DNA replication. 

Based on these findings, we propose a model in which S-phase-promoting cyclin B-Cdk complexes inhibit the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state during S, G2, and M phases. This model explains why origins only fire once per S phase and why S phase relies on the completion of the preceding M phase.

title: E-cadherin engagement stimulates proliferation via Rac1
text: The suppression of tumor growth and inhibition of cell proliferation in culture have been associated with E-cadherin. Our observations revealed that reducing the seeding density of normal rat kidney-52E (NRK-52E) or MCF-10A epithelial cells from confluence resulted in the release of cells from growth arrest. Surprisingly, further decreasing the seeding density to isolate cells from neighboring cells led to a decrease in proliferation. Experiments using microengineered substrates demonstrated that E-cadherin engagement stimulated peak proliferation at intermediate seeding densities. The proliferation arrest at high densities was not influenced by E-cadherin, but rather by a decrease in cell spreading against the underlying substrate due to crowding. Rac1 activity, induced specifically at intermediate seeding densities by E-cadherin engagement, was necessary for cadherin-stimulated proliferation. The control of Rac1 activation by E-cadherin was mediated by p120-catenin. These findings highlight the stimulatory role of E-cadherin in regulating proliferation and provide insight into how cell-cell contact can trigger or inhibit epithelial cell proliferation in different scenarios.

title: Structure of Actin-related protein 8 and its contribution to nucleosome binding
text:
The molecular functions of nuclear actin-related proteins (Arps) within chromatin remodelers are not well understood. However, we have determined the crystal structure of the ATP-bound form of Arp8, a subunit of the INO80 complex. In humans, Arp8 has certain insertions in its conserved actin fold that prevent it from polymerizing. Interestingly, one of these insertions wraps around the active site cleft, providing structural stability to the domain. Additionally, the active site features of Arp8 resemble those of actin, suggesting that its ATPase activity is controlled allosterically. 

Through quantitative binding studies, we have found that Arp8 and the Arp8-Arp4-actin-HSA sub-complex of INO80 have a strong preference for nucleosomes and H3-H4 tetramers over H2A-H2B dimers. This suggests that Arp8 acts as a module for recognizing nucleosomes. On the other hand, Arp4 shows a preference for free (H3-H4)(2) rather than nucleosomes, indicating that it may play a role in binding to (dis)assembly intermediates during the remodeling process.

title: Regulation of β-Adrenergic Receptor Signaling by S-Nitrosylation of G-Protein-Coupled Receptor Kinase 2
text: Beta-adrenergic receptors (beta-ARs) are a type of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that play a crucial role in controlling various physiological processes. GPCR kinases (GRKs) are responsible for limiting G-protein signaling and targeting receptors for internalization. The exact molecular details of how nitric oxide (NO) and/or S-nitrosothiols (SNOs) prevent the loss of beta-AR signaling in living organisms are currently unknown. However, our research in mice demonstrates that SNOs enhance beta-AR expression and prevent the downregulation of receptors stimulated by agonists. Additionally, in cell studies, SNOs reduce the phosphorylation of beta-ARs mediated by GRK2 and subsequently inhibit the recruitment of beta-arrestin to the receptor. This leads to a decrease in receptor desensitization and internalization. Both in cells and tissues, GRK2 is S-nitrosylated by SNOs and NO synthases, and this S-nitrosylation of GRK2 increases after the activation of multiple GPCRs by agonists. We have identified Cys340 of GRK2 as a primary site of inhibition through S-nitrosylation. Overall, our findings uncover a fundamental molecular mechanism that regulates GPCR signaling.

title: Electroporation enables the efficient mRNA delivery into the mouse zygotes and facilitates CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing
text: The use of the CRISPR/Cas9 system has recently made it much quicker to produce mutant mice. However, the process is still slowed down by the time-consuming microinjection step, which limits its use for high-throughput genetic analysis. In this study, we have developed a straightforward and highly effective method for editing the genome on a large scale. Instead of microinjection, we electroporated the RNAs for the CRISPR/Cas9 system into zygotes. Using this method, we successfully performed knock-in experiments in mouse embryos using single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotides (ssODNs). This new approach greatly facilitates genetic analysis in mice on a larger scale.

title: Summary
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) and restrictive dermopathy (RD) are genetic diseases caused by the buildup of farnesylated prelamin A due to defects in the lamin A maturation pathway. These diseases exhibit symptoms that resemble accelerated aging, but the exact mechanism behind this process is not fully understood. Our study provides evidence that HGPS and RD fibroblasts have persistently activated DNA damage checkpoints, leading to compromised genomic integrity. By inactivating checkpoint kinases ATM and ATR in these patient cells, we were able to partially overcome their early replication arrest. However, treating patient cells with a protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor (FTI) did not reduce DNA double-strand breaks or damage checkpoint signaling, although it did significantly reverse the abnormal shape of their nuclei. This suggests that DNA damage accumulation and abnormal nuclear morphology are independent effects resulting from prelamin A buildup in these progeroid syndromes. Given that DNA damage accumulation plays a crucial role in HGPS symptoms, our findings question the efficacy of treating HGPS solely with FTIs.

title: The Buccaneer software for automated model building. 1. Tracing protein chains.
text: This article presents a novel method for automatically tracing protein chains in electron-density maps obtained from experiments. The method utilizes a targeted function based on electron-density likelihood, which is repeatedly applied to identify probable C(alpha) positions. This function is employed to locate a small number of promising seed positions in the map and to expand these initial C(alpha) positions into longer chain fragments. The paper also discusses techniques for assembling these fragments into an initial chain trace.

title: Expression profile of genes modulated by Aloe emodin in human U87 glioblastoma cells.
text: Glioblastoma, the most aggressive and malignant form of glioma, seems to be resistant to different chemotherapy drugs. Therefore, researchers have been extensively studying ways to target specific molecular pathways involved in the development and progression of glioblastoma. Aloe emodin is believed to affect the expression of multiple genes in cancer cells. Our goal was to understand the molecular mechanisms behind the therapeutic effect of Aloe emodin on gene expression in the human U87 glioblastoma cell line using microarray technology. The analysis of gene expression showed that after 24 hours of treatment with 58.6 μg/ml, a total of 8,226 gene alterations out of 28,869 genes were detected. Out of these, 34 genes showed statistically significant changes (p<0.05), ranging from 1.07 to 1.87 fold. The results revealed that 22 genes were up-regulated and 12 genes were down-regulated in response to Aloe emodin treatment. These genes were then categorized into different clusters based on their biological functions, showing an increase in the expression of genes involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death) and tissue remodeling in U87 cells (p<0.01). Several genes with significant changes in expression levels, such as SHARPIN, BCAP31, FIS1, RAC1, and TGM2 from the apoptotic cluster, were confirmed using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). These findings can guide further research to identify molecular targets for cancer therapy using Aloe emodin treatment.

title: The miniature genome of a carnivorous plant Genlisea aurea contains a low number of genes and short non-coding sequences
text:
The carnivorous plant Genlisea aurea, belonging to the Lentibulariaceae family, has a remarkably small genome size of 63.6 Mb, making it one of the smallest genomes among higher plants. Based on data on genome sizes and the phylogeny of Genlisea, it is believed that this small genome size is a derived state within the genus. Therefore, G. aurea serves as an ideal model organism for studying the evolutionary mechanisms behind genome contraction.

In this study, we have successfully sequenced and assembled the G. aurea genome from scratch. The assembly consists of 10,687 contigs with a total length of 43.4 Mb, and it includes 17,755 complete and partial protein-coding genes. By comparing the G. aurea genome with that of Mimulus guttatus, another representative of the higher core Lamiales clade, we have discovered significant differences in gene content and the length of non-coding regions.

Our findings suggest that genome contraction is a complex process involving gene loss and reduction in the lengths of introns and intergenic regions, but not intron loss. Furthermore, we have observed that gene loss is more common in genes belonging to multigenic families, indicating that genetic redundancy plays a crucial role in reducing genome size.

title: Abnormal Spine Morphology and Enhanced LTP in LIMK-1 Knockout Mice
text: Studies conducted in a laboratory setting have suggested that the LIM kinase family plays a part in controlling the phosphorylation of cofilin and the dynamics of actin. Additionally, the abnormal expression of LIMK-1 has been linked to Williams syndrome, a mental disorder characterized by severe impairments in visuospatial cognition. However, the specific function of this group of kinases in living organisms has remained unclear. By using mice that lack the LIMK-1 gene, we have been able to demonstrate a significant role for LIMK-1 in vivo in the regulation of cofilin and the actin cytoskeleton. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these knockout mice displayed notable abnormalities in the structure of their dendritic spines and in synaptic function, including an increase in hippocampal long-term potentiation. The mice lacking LIMK-1 also exhibited altered fear responses and spatial learning abilities. These results strongly suggest that LIMK-1 plays a crucial role in the development of dendritic spines and in the functioning of the brain.

title: Wdr5 Mediates Self-Renewal and Reprogramming via the Embryonic Stem Cell Core Transcriptional Network
text: The networks responsible for maintaining the self-renewal of embryonic stem (ES) cells, including their transcriptional and chromatin-modifying processes, are crucial. However, it is still unclear whether these networks interact and, if so, what factors facilitate such interactions. In this study, we present evidence that WD repeat domain 5 (Wdr5), a core component of the mammalian Trithorax (trxG) complex, is closely associated with the undifferentiated state and plays a role in regulating ES cell self-renewal. We demonstrate that Wdr5, which acts as an "effector" of H3K4 methylation, interacts with the pluripotency transcription factor Oct4. Through genome-wide protein localization and transcriptome analyses, we reveal that Oct4 and Wdr5 have overlapping functions in regulating gene expression. The Oct4-Sox2-Nanog circuitry and trxG work together to activate the transcription of key regulators of self-renewal. Additionally, the expression of Wdr5 is necessary for the efficient generation of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. Based on these findings, we propose an integrated model that combines transcriptional and epigenetic control, facilitated by specific trxG members, to maintain ES cell self-renewal and enable somatic cell reprogramming.

title: Neurons derived from reprogrammed fibroblasts functionally integrate into the fetal brain and improve symptoms of rats with Parkinson's disease.
text: The ultimate objective of nuclear transfer or alternative reprogramming methods is to generate donor cells that are specific to each patient for transplantation therapy. This would help avoid the complications of immunorejection, which is a significant issue in current transplantation medicine. Recent studies have revealed that four transcription factors, namely Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc, can induce pluripotency in mouse fibroblasts. However, the potential of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells for neural cell replacement strategies has not been explored until now. In this study, we demonstrate that iPS cells can be effectively differentiated into neural precursor cells, which can then develop into various types of neuronal and glial cells in a laboratory setting. When transplanted into the brains of fetal mice, these cells migrate to different regions of the brain and differentiate into glia and neurons, including subtypes such as glutamatergic, GABAergic, and catecholaminergic. Through electrophysiological recordings and morphological analysis, we confirmed that the transplanted neurons exhibited mature neuronal activity and were functionally integrated into the host brain. Additionally, we successfully induced iPS cells to differentiate into midbrain dopamine neurons and observed an improvement in behavior in a rat model of Parkinson's disease after transplantation into the adult brain. To minimize the risk of tumor formation, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting to separate pluripotent cells and committed neural cells. Our findings highlight the therapeutic potential of directly reprogrammed fibroblasts for replacing neuronal cells in animal models.

title: Responses of primate frontal cortex neurons during natural vocal communication.
text: The involvement of the primate frontal cortex in vocal communication and its significance in the evolution of language have been a subject of debate. While evidence suggests that the processing of vocalizations takes place in neurons located in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, it has been proposed that vocal-motor activity is primarily subcortical and differs from the neural architecture seen in humans. Previous studies on neural activity during natural vocal communication have been limited to animals restrained in chairs. In this study, we recorded the activity of individual neurons in various regions of the prefrontal and premotor cortex in freely moving marmosets while they engaged in a natural vocal behavior called antiphonal calling. Our goal was to determine whether neurons in the marmoset frontal cortex responded during the processing of vocal signals and/or the production of vocal-motor movements in the context of active, natural communication. We observed changes in single neuron activity related to motor movements during vocal production, but the sensory responses to vocalization processing were relatively weak during this natural behavior. The vocal-motor responses occurred before and during the production of calls and were typically synchronized with the timing of each vocalization pulse. Despite the weak sensory responses, a population classifier was able to distinguish between neural activity during the presentation of vocalization stimuli that elicited an antiphonal response and those that did not. These findings suggest the role of nonhuman primate frontal cortex neurons in natural communication and provide a foundation for further investigations into the functional contributions of these neocortical areas during vocal behaviors.

title: Salt-inducible kinase 2 links transcriptional coactivator p300 phosphorylation to the prevention of ChREBP-dependent hepatic steatosis in mice.
text:
Increased lipogenesis in the liver is linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes. This leads to the accumulation of fat in liver cells, known as hepatic steatosis, which is the most common cause of liver dysfunction in the United States. Carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein (ChREBP) is a key player in the development of hepatic steatosis in mice, as it activates genes involved in glycolysis and lipogenesis. However, the specific molecular mechanisms that enhance ChREBP's activity are not well understood. 

In this study, we have identified two important regulators of ChREBP activity: the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) coactivator p300 and the serine/threonine kinase salt-inducible kinase 2 (SIK2). In cultured mouse liver cells, we found that glucose activates p300, which then acetylates ChREBP on a specific site (Lys672). This acetylation increases ChREBP's ability to bind to its target gene promoters and enhances its transcriptional activity. On the other hand, SIK2 inhibits p300's HAT activity by directly phosphorylating it on a specific site (Ser89). This phosphorylation reduces ChREBP-mediated lipogenesis in liver cells and in mice that overexpress SIK2. 

Furthermore, when we knocked down SIK2 specifically in the liver or overexpressed p300, we observed hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, and inflammation. These negative effects were reversed when we co-overexpressed SIK2 and p300. Finally, in mouse models of type 2 diabetes and obesity, we found that low SIK2 activity was associated with increased p300 HAT activity, hyperacetylation of ChREBP, and hepatic steatosis. 

Based on our findings, we propose that inhibiting p300 activity in the liver could be beneficial for treating hepatic steatosis in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Additionally, we suggest that activating SIK2 and developing specific inhibitors for p300 could be potential targets for pharmaceutical intervention.

title: A Role for NuSAP in Linking Microtubules to Mitotic Chromosomes
text: The spindle apparatus is a machinery that uses microtubules (MTs) to attach to and separate the chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis. The process of organizing the spindle around the chromatin involves assembling MTs, attaching them to the chromosomes, and arranging them into a bipolar structure. One factor that regulates the self-organization of the spindle is RanGTP. RanGTP is produced at the chromatin and activates a group of soluble spindle factors, including TPX2, NuMA, and NuSAP, which are regulated by Ran. How these spindle factors guide and attach MTs to the chromosomes remains a significant question. Recently, Nucleolar and Spindle-Associated Protein (NuSAP) was discovered as a crucial protein that stabilizes and bundles MTs. It is highly concentrated in the central part of the spindle. Through biochemical reconstitution, we demonstrate that NuSAP can effectively bind to isolated chromatin and DNA, and it can directly generate and maintain high concentrations of MTs near the chromatin or DNA. Additionally, our findings show that the interaction between NuSAP and chromatin is regulated by Ran and can be inhibited by Importin alpha (Impalpha) and Imp7. We propose that the presence of MT binding agents like NuSAP, which can directly attach to chromatin, is essential for directing MT production to vertebrate chromosomes during spindle self-organization.

title: Molecular features of cellular reprogramming and development
text: During the development process, somatic cells become more specialized in their functions. However, through experimental methods, these cells can be directed to become other types of cells, even those with the ability to develop into any cell in the body. In the past, techniques like somatic cell nuclear transfer and cell fusion presented challenges in understanding how cells maintain their identity. However, the discovery of direct reprogramming, which involves introducing a specific set of transcription factors, has provided a way to study the molecular characteristics of cell specification, differentiation, stability, and pluripotency. In this discussion, we will explore how direct reprogramming has shed light on the control and maintenance of cellular identity during developmental transitions, focusing on the role of transcriptional and epigenetic regulation.

title: Small molecule modifiers of circadian clocks
text: The circadian clocks regulate important physiological and behavioral processes that occur in a 24-hour cycle in response to daily changes in the environment. These clocks are incredibly accurate in stable conditions but can be easily influenced by signals that reset them. While the core components of the clock have been mostly identified at the molecular level, recent studies have started to investigate mechanisms and molecules that can modify the clock. Specifically, small molecules, whether they occur naturally or are introduced from outside, are proving to be valuable tools for studying the fundamental biology of the clock and potentially developing treatments for clock-related diseases. This article will focus on synthetic compounds that have the ability to alter the timing, phase, or strength of circadian clocks, with a particular emphasis on the clocks found in mammals. We will explore the potential of using these small molecule modifiers in both basic research and practical applications.

title: NVP-BEZ235, a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, prevents PI3K signaling and inhibits the growth of cancer cells with activating PI3K mutations.
text:
The deregulation of the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is a common occurrence in human cancer. This can happen through the inactivation of the tumor suppressor phosphatase and tensin homologue deleted from chromosome 10 or through activating mutations of p110-alpha. These specific mutations lead to the oncogenic activity of the enzyme and contribute to resistance against the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab. As a result, the PI3K pathway is an attractive target for cancer therapy.

Our study focused on NVP-BEZ235, a dual inhibitor of both PI3K and the downstream mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). We found that NVP-BEZ235 effectively inhibited the activation of downstream effectors such as Akt, S6 ribosomal protein, and 4EBP1 in breast cancer cells. In fact, the antiproliferative activity of NVP-BEZ235 was more potent than the allosteric selective mTOR complex inhibitor everolimus in a panel of 21 cancer cell lines with different origins and mutation statuses.

We also observed that higher doses of NVP-BEZ235 prevented the described Akt activation caused by mTOR inhibition. Furthermore, NVP-BEZ235 was able to reverse the hyperactivation of the PI3K/mTOR pathway caused by the oncogenic mutations of p110-alpha (E545K and H1047R). It also inhibited the proliferation of HER2-amplified BT474 cells that were engineered to express these mutations, which made them resistant to trastuzumab.

In a breast cancer xenograft model with trastuzumab-resistant BT474 H1047R cells, NVP-BEZ235 showed potent antitumor activity by inhibiting PI3K signaling. Additionally, in treated animals, we observed complete inhibition of PI3K signaling in the skin at pharmacologically active doses. This suggests that the skin could serve as a surrogate tissue for pharmacodynamic studies.

In conclusion, NVP-BEZ235 effectively inhibits the PI3K/mTOR axis and demonstrates antiproliferative and antitumoral activity in cancer cells with both wild-type and mutated p110-alpha.

title: Pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and pharmacogenetic determinants of osteonecrosis in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text: Osteonecrosis, a serious complication of acute lymphoblastic leukemia treatment caused by glucocorticoids, was examined in a prospective study involving 364 children. Magnetic resonance imaging of the hips and knees was conducted on all participants, regardless of symptoms. The study found that the cumulative incidence of any grade (1-4) osteonecrosis was 71.8%, while the incidence of symptomatic (grade 2-4) osteonecrosis was 17.6%. The researchers investigated various factors to determine their association with symptomatic osteonecrosis, including age, race, sex, treatment arm, body mass, serum lipids, albumin and cortisol levels, dexamethasone pharmacokinetics, and germline genetic polymorphisms. Age over 10 years and more intensive treatment were identified as risk factors and were included as covariates in all analyses. Lower albumin levels and elevated cholesterol were found to be associated with symptomatic osteonecrosis, and severe osteonecrosis was linked to poor dexamethasone clearance. After adjusting for clinical features, genetic polymorphisms of ACP1, which regulates lipid levels and osteoblast differentiation, were found to be associated with the risk of osteonecrosis, as well as lower albumin and higher cholesterol levels. In conclusion, older age, lower albumin levels, higher lipid levels, and dexamethasone exposure were all associated with osteonecrosis and may be influenced by inherited genomic variation.

title: Prevention of Rectal SHIV Transmission in Macaques by Daily or Intermittent Prophylaxis with Emtricitabine and Tenofovir
text:
In the absence of an effective vaccine, HIV continues to spread globally, highlighting the need for new strategies to limit its transmission. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with antiretroviral drugs could be an effective intervention if we can identify highly effective and cost-effective PrEP methods. To evaluate different PrEP regimens, we conducted a study using a macaque model that closely resembles human transmission.

In our study, we used a repeat-exposure macaque model where 14 weekly rectal virus challenges were administered. Three different drug treatments were given once daily to separate groups of six rhesus macaques. Group 1 received a subcutaneous dose of emtricitabine (FTC), group 2 received an oral dose of both FTC and tenofovir-disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and group 3 received a subcutaneous dose of FTC and a higher dose of tenofovir. Another group of six macaques (group 4) received an intermittent PrEP regimen similar to group 3, but only 2 hours before and 24 hours after each weekly virus challenge. We compared the results to 18 control macaques that did not receive any drug treatment.

The risk of infection in macaques treated in groups 1 and 2 was 3.8- and 7.8-fold lower, respectively, compared to untreated macaques. All six macaques in group 3 were protected from infection. Breakthrough infections had lower levels of the virus in the blood, and drug resistance was observed in two of the six animals in group 3. All six animals in group 4, which received intermittent PrEP, were also protected.

Based on our findings, it appears that single drugs used for daily PrEP can provide protection, but a combination of antiretroviral drugs may be necessary to increase the level of protection. Additionally, short but potent intermittent PrEP can offer protection comparable to daily PrEP in this macaque model. These results support the need for PrEP trials in humans for HIV prevention and identify promising PrEP methods.

title: Direct-coupling analysis of residue co-evolution captures native contacts across many protein families
text:
The similarity in the three-dimensional structures of proteins that are similar in sequence imposes strong limitations on the variability of their sequences. It has been suggested for a long time that the correlations among the amino acid compositions at different positions in the sequence can be used to infer the spatial contacts within the protein's three-dimensional structure. To achieve this, it is crucial to distinguish between direct and indirect correlations, which can be done using a method called Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA), as introduced by Weigt et al. in 2009.

In this study, we have developed a computationally efficient implementation of DCA. This allows us to assess the accuracy of contact prediction by DCA for a large number of protein domains, based solely on sequence information. We have found that DCA is able to predict a significant number of contacts correctly, accurately representing the overall structure of the contact map for most of the protein domains we examined. Additionally, our analysis reveals signals beyond contacts within the same domain, including those arising from alternative protein conformations, residue couplings mediated by ligands, and interactions between domains in protein oligomers.

Based on our findings, we propose that the contacts predicted by DCA can serve as a reliable guide for computational predictions of alternative protein conformations, protein complex formation, and even the prediction of protein domain structures from scratch. This is particularly feasible given the increasing availability of a large number of homologous sequences, thanks to advancements in genome sequencing.

title: Variation in antibiotic prescribing and its impact on recovery in patients with acute cough in primary care: prospective study in 13 countries.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the differences in antibiotic prescribing for acute cough in various European settings and how it affects recovery. The study design was a cross-sectional observational study involving clinicians from 14 primary care research networks in 13 European countries. Clinicians recorded symptoms and management, and patients were followed up for 28 days using patient diaries. The study took place in primary care settings and included adults with a new or worsening cough or symptoms suggestive of lower respiratory tract infection. The main outcome measures were the prescribing of antibiotics by clinicians and total symptom severity scores over time.

A total of 3402 patients were recruited, with clinicians completing a case report form for 99% of participants and 80% returning a symptom diary. Mean symptom severity scores at presentation varied across networks, ranging from 19 to 38 on a scale of 0 to 100. Antibiotic prescribing varied widely among networks, ranging from 20% to nearly 90% (with an overall average of 53%). There was also variation in the types of antibiotics prescribed, with amoxicillin being the most common overall but ranging from 3% to 83% among networks. Fluoroquinolones were not prescribed in three networks but were prescribed for 18% of patients in the Milan network. Even after adjusting for clinical presentation and demographics, significant differences remained in antibiotic prescribing, ranging from an odds ratio of 0.18 to 11.2 compared to the overall mean. However, the rate of recovery was similar for patients who were and were not prescribed antibiotics once clinical presentation was taken into account.

In conclusion, there is significant variation in antibiotic prescribing for acute cough in Europe, which is not explained by differences in clinical presentation. Furthermore, this variation in prescribing does not have a clinically significant impact on recovery. The trial was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov under NCT00353951.

title: Dorsomorphin, a Selective Small Molecule Inhibitor of BMP Signaling, Promotes Cardiomyogenesis in Embryonic Stem Cells
text:
Pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cells have the potential to develop into any type of tissue in the body, making them a promising source for regenerative therapy. However, we still have limited knowledge about how these cells differentiate into specific lineages, and it is challenging to generate enough of the desired cell types. Small molecules, such as those that can influence key developmental pathways like the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling cascade, offer a potential solution. These molecules can be used to study lineage specification in vitro and direct the differentiation of stem cells into specific cell types. 

In this study, we investigated the use of a small molecule inhibitor called dorsomorphin to induce myocardial differentiation in mouse ES cells. We found that dorsomorphin significantly increased the production of spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, by at least 20 times. Interestingly, dorsomorphin was more effective than the naturally occurring BMP antagonist Noggin when used during the initial 24 hours of ES cell differentiation. 

Further analysis showed that inhibiting BMP signaling with dorsomorphin during the early stages of differentiation promoted the development of cardiomyocytes, but reduced the differentiation of endothelial, smooth muscle, and hematopoietic cells. 

In conclusion, using a selective small molecule inhibitor of BMP signaling during the early stages of ES cell differentiation greatly enhances the production of cardiomyocytes, potentially at the expense of other mesodermal lineages. Small molecule modulators like dorsomorphin could be valuable tools for stem cell research and regenerative medicine.

title: Cineradiography of Monkey Lip-Smacking Reveals Putative Precursors of Speech Dynamics
text: The stereotypical 5 Hz rhythm is a significant characteristic of speech. One theory suggests that this rhythm developed from rhythmic facial movements in our primate ancestors. To explore this hypothesis, we took a comparative approach. Using cineradiography (X-ray movies), we examined and measured the internal dynamics of the macaque monkey vocal tract during lip-smacking (a rhythmic facial expression) and chewing. Previous studies on humans have shown that speech movements are faster than chewing movements, and there is a different functional coordination between vocal tract structures for each behavior. If rhythmic speech evolved from rhythmic ancestral facial movements, we would expect to see similar differences in monkey lip-smacking versus chewing. Our findings revealed that the lips, tongue, and hyoid move in a speech-like 5 Hz rhythm during lip-smacking, but not during chewing. Furthermore, the functional coordination between these structures differed for each behavior. These results provide empirical evidence supporting the notion that the rhythm of human speech evolved from the rhythmic facial expressions of our primate ancestors.

title: Interneuronal DISC1 regulates NRG1-ErbB4 signalling and excitatory-inhibitory synapse formation in the mature cortex.
text: The mechanisms that regulate the signaling of Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) and its receptor ErbB4 in the mature brain are not well understood, although they have been found to influence various neurodevelopmental processes. DISC1 is a versatile scaffold protein that plays a role in many cellular processes. In this study, we establish a functional connection between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling in mature cortical interneurons. Through targeted gene manipulation in vitro and in vivo, including using a mutant DISC1 mouse model, we demonstrate that DISC1 inhibits the activation and signaling of ErbB4 induced by NRG1. This inhibition is likely achieved through competitive interference with the binding of ErbB4 to PSD95. Additionally, we observe that DISC1 in interneurons affects the phenotypes mediated by NRG1-ErbB4 in the circuit between fast-spiking interneurons and pyramidal neurons. Previous studies on post-mortem brain tissue and genetics have reported deficits in interneurons and the involvement of DISC1, NRG1, and ErbB4 genes in schizophrenia, respectively. Our findings propose a potential mechanism by which the interaction between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling may contribute to these deficits.

title: The Proto-Oncogene c-maf Is Responsible for Tissue-Specific Expression of Interleukin-4
text: The underlying mechanism behind the unique expression of cytokines in CD4+ T helper 1 (Th1) and T helper 2 (Th2) subsets is still unknown. In this study, we reveal that the proto-oncogene c-maf, a transcription factor with a basic region/leucine zipper structure, regulates the specific expression of IL-4 in different tissues. c-Maf is only present in Th2 clones and is induced during the differentiation of precursor cells into Th2 lineage, but not Th1 lineage. c-Maf binds to a specific region called c-Maf response element (MARE) in the IL-4 promoter, which is adjacent to a site that is only recognized by extracts from Th2 clones, not Th1 clones. When c-Maf is artificially introduced into Th1 cells, B cells, and nonlymphoid cells, it activates the IL-4 promoter, and this function is associated with the MARE and the Th2-specific site. Additionally, c-Maf works together with another transcription factor called nuclear factor of activated T cells (NF-ATp) to initiate the production of IL-4 by B cells. By manipulating c-Maf, it may be possible to alter the balance of Th subsets in human diseases.

title: hClock gene expression in human colorectal carcinoma.
text: The objective of this study was to examine the changes in the expression of the human Clock (hClock) gene, which is a key component of the circadian gene family, in colorectal carcinomas (CRCs) and discuss their potential effects. Previous research has shown that disruptions in circadian rhythms are among the internal factors that contribute to the development and initiation of CRCs. However, the specific molecular changes to circadian genes associated with CRCs have not been investigated. We conducted immunofluorescence and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analyses to assess the expression of the hCLOCK protein and gene in 30 CRC cases. The hCLOCK protein was present in all specimens obtained from the CRC patients. We observed higher levels of hCLOCK expression in human CRC tissues compared to the corresponding non-cancerous tissues. Furthermore, hCLOCK expression was significantly higher in poorly differentiated or late-stage Dukes' grade tumors, as well as in 64.3% of tumor cases with lymph node metastasis. The hClock gene was expressed in all specimens, and its expression was significantly higher in human CRC cases compared to the paired non-cancerous tissues. We found a strong positive linear correlation between hClock gene expression and protein expression in human CRCs. Additionally, there was a strong positive linear correlation between hClock gene expression and the expression of ARNT, HIF-1α, and VEGF in human CRCs. However, we did not observe a significant correlation between hClock and Bak, Bax, Bid, tumor necrosis factor receptor I (TNFR I), and TNFR II. Our findings suggest that the circadian gene hClock is consistently expressed in human colorectal mucosa and plays a crucial role in regulating the expression of downstream clock-controlled genes. Moreover, hCLOCK may interact with HIF-1α/ARNT and activate VEGF to promote tumor angiogenesis and metastasis.

title: The Antiretroviral Therapy in Lower Income Countries (ART-LINC) Collaboration and ART Cohort Collaboration (ART-CC) groups Summary
text:
BACKGROUND: The expansion of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) is underway in developing nations. We conducted a comparison of baseline characteristics and outcomes during the initial year of HAART between HIV-1-infected patients in low-income and high-income settings.

METHODS: Data from 18 HAART programs in Africa, Asia, and South America (low-income settings) and 12 HIV cohort studies from Europe and North America (high-income settings) were collected. This included 4,810 treatment-naïve adult patients starting HAART in low-income settings and 22,217 in high-income settings. Survival analyses included all patients from high-income settings and 2,725 (57%) patients from low-income settings who were actively followed-up.

FINDINGS: Patients in low-income settings had lower CD4 cell counts (median 108 cells per muL vs 234 cells per muL), were more likely to be female (51% vs 25%), and more likely to start treatment with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) (70% vs 23%) compared to high-income countries. At 6 months, the median number of CD4 cells gained (106 cells per muL vs 103 cells per muL) and the percentage of patients reaching HIV-1 RNA levels lower than 500 copies/mL (76% vs 77%) were similar. Mortality rates were higher in low-income settings (124 deaths during 2,236 person-years of follow-up) compared to high-income settings (414 deaths during 20,532 person-years). The adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of mortality comparing low-income with high-income settings decreased from 4.3 (95% CI 1.6-11.8) in the first month to 1.5 (0.7-3.0) in months 7-12. The provision of free treatment in low-income settings was associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.23; 95% CI 0.08-0.61).

INTERPRETATION: Patients initiating HAART in resource-poor settings experience higher mortality rates in the initial months of therapy compared to those in developed countries. Early diagnosis, assessment of treatment eligibility, and free provision of HAART may help reduce this excess mortality.

title: A family of phosphoinositide 3-kinases in Drosophila identifies a new mediator of signal transduction
text:
The background of this study is focused on mammalian phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI 3-kinases) and their involvement in receptor-mediated signal transduction. These enzymes have been linked to processes such as transformation and mitogenesis by increasing cellular phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate levels. In addition, a PI 3-kinase activity that produces phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate has been found to be necessary for protein trafficking in yeast.

The results of this study reveal the identification of a family of three distinct PI 3-kinases in Drosophila. The researchers used a polymerase chain reaction approach to amplify a region corresponding to the conserved catalytic domain of PI 3-kinases. One of these family members, PI3K_92D, is closely related to the prototypical PI 3-kinase, p110 alpha. Another member, PI3K_59F, is similar to Vps34p. The third member, PI3K_68D, is a novel PI 3-kinase that is expressed throughout the entire life cycle of Drosophila.

The PI3K_68D gene encodes a 210 kDa protein that lacks sequences involved in linking p110 PI 3-kinases to p85 adaptor proteins. However, it contains an amino-terminal proline-rich sequence that could bind to SH3 domains, as well as a carboxy-terminal C2 domain. Biochemical analyses demonstrate that PI3K_68D has a unique substrate specificity in vitro, limited to phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate. It is unable to phosphorylate phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate, which is believed to be the in vivo substrate for p110.

In conclusion, this study describes a family of PI 3-kinases in Drosophila, including a novel class represented by PI3K_68D. This enzyme has the potential to interact with signaling molecules containing SH3 domains, lacks p85-adaptor-binding sequences, possesses a Ca(2+)-independent phospholipid-binding domain, and displays a limited in vitro substrate specificity. Therefore, it may define a new signal transduction pathway.

title: Mammalian RAD52 Functions in Break-Induced Replication Repair of Collapsed DNA Replication Forks
text: Cancer cells are characterized by the presence of DNA replication stress caused by oncogenes, which makes them reliant on repair pathways like break-induced replication (BIR) to fix damaged DNA replication forks. To gain a better understanding of BIR, we conducted a targeted siRNA screen to identify genes that hindered the progression from G1 to S phase when oncogenic cyclin E was overexpressed. Among the top hits was RAD52, a gene that is not essential for normal development in mice. In cells where fork collapse was induced by oncogenes or chemicals, the Rad52 protein was found to concentrate at sites of DNA replication stress. Depleting Rad52 through siRNA or using CRISPR/Cas9 to knockout the gene impaired the ability to restart collapsed forks and resulted in DNA damage in cells experiencing replication stress. Additionally, in mice with a predisposition to cancer due to heterozygous APC mutations, completely deleting the Rad52 gene suppressed tumor growth and extended lifespan. Therefore, we propose that RAD52 in mammals aids in repairing collapsed DNA replication forks in cancer cells.

title: Neural crest cell lineage segregation in the mouse neural tube.
text:
The origin and development of neural crest (NC) cells in the dorsal neural tube (NT) and their subsequent migration into the embryo to form various cell types is a topic of interest. One key question that remains unanswered is when and how the fate of NC cells is determined. Multiple studies suggest that NC cells have the potential to differentiate into different cell types, and their fate is determined during or after migration. Additionally, there is evidence suggesting that the NC is already divided into distinct precursor subpopulations within the NT. To address this question, we conducted research using mouse embryos.

Our findings reveal that a specific group of cells located in the most dorsomedial region of the NT express the receptor tyrosine kinase Kit (previously known as c-kit). These cells exclusively migrate into the developing dermis and subsequently express markers specific to melanocyte lineage, indicating that they are melanocyte progenitor cells. These progenitor cells are primarily generated at the midbrain-hindbrain junction and cervical trunk, with a significant number also present in the lower trunk. On the other hand, other cells within the dorsal NT do not express Kit and migrate ventrally. Starting from embryonic day 9.5, these cells express the neurotrophin receptor p75 and are likely to give rise to ventral NC derivatives such as neurons and glia. The p75+ cells are located ventrolateral to the Kit+ cells in areas of the NT where both cell types are present. These findings provide direct evidence in vivo for the segregation of NC lineages within the mouse neural tube.

title: How absolute is zero? An evaluation of historical and current definitions of malaria elimination
text: Decisions regarding the eradication of malaria from a country or a specific area are complex and made more complicated by the lack of clarity surrounding key terms such as "control" and "elimination." Without clear definitions, it is impossible to accurately predict the resources and operations needed. Even during the Global Malaria Eradication Program, there was debate over the precise meaning of "eradication." Today, there is a lack of discussion about the definitions of "elimination" and "control," despite their importance in program planning. This paper aims to contribute to the ongoing debate by providing a historical review of commonly used terms like control, elimination, and eradication, in order to provide context for the current understanding of these concepts. The review is supported by an analysis of mathematical models that describe the spread of malaria cases. The analysis highlights the need for practical definitions that can guide malaria control and elimination programs. The paper suggests new conceptual definitions to more accurately describe the goals of "control" and "elimination." It also argues for the inclusion of a third state, called "controlled non-endemic malaria," to describe the situation where endemic transmission has been interrupted, but malaria cases resulting from imported infections continue to occur at a high level. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines for developing operational definitions and metrics that can make these concepts relevant, measurable, and achievable in specific environments.

title: Fission Yeast Scm3: A CENP-A Receptor Required for Integrity of Subkinetochore Chromatin
text: The precise mechanisms responsible for the specific incorporation of CENP-A at centromeres are not well understood. However, it has been observed that Mis16 and Mis18 are essential for localizing CENP-A at centromeres. These proteins form a complex that is conserved across different organisms, from fission yeast to humans. In fission yeast sim1 mutants, which alleviate the silencing of kinetochore domains, there is a defect in Scm3(Sp), the equivalent of Scm3(Sc) in budding yeast. Scm3(Sp) relies on Mis16/18 for its localization at centromeres and, like them, is recruited to centromeres during late anaphase. Interestingly, Scm3(Sp) co-purifies with CENP-A(Cnp1) and interacts with it in vitro. However, Scm3(Sp) localizes independently of intact CENP-A(Cnp1) chromatin and is released from chromatin in a different manner. While it has been suggested that Scm3(Sc) forms a unique hexameric nucleosome with CENP-A(Cse4) and histone H4 at budding yeast point centromeres, we propose a different model. In our model, Scm3(Sp) acts as a receptor/assembly factor for CENP-A(Cnp1), working together with Mis16 and Mis18 to receive CENP-A(Cnp1) from the Sim3 escort protein and facilitate the assembly of CENP-A(Cnp1) into subkinetochore chromatin.

title: The Molecular Basis for Oat Intolerance in Patients with Celiac Disease
text:
Background: Celiac disease is a condition that affects the small intestine and causes inflammation, malabsorption, nutrient deficiency, and various clinical symptoms. It occurs when the immune system reacts inappropriately to gluten in the diet and is typically managed with a gluten-free diet. Recent studies have suggested that oats may be safe for individuals with celiac disease, leading to their inclusion in the celiac disease diet. This study aimed to investigate whether some individuals with celiac disease may still have an intolerance to oats and to understand the underlying cellular and biological processes involved.

Methods and Findings: The study included nine adults with celiac disease who had previously consumed oats. Four of these patients experienced clinical symptoms while on an oats-containing diet, and three of the four also had intestinal inflammation consistent with celiac disease at the time of oats consumption. We established specific intestinal T-cell lines from these three patients, as well as from two other patients who appeared to tolerate oats. These T-cell lines reacted to avenin, a protein found in oats, in the context of a specific genetic marker called HLA-DQ2. The avenin peptides recognized by these T-cells had sequences similar to those found in wheat gluten, with high levels of proline and glutamine residues. The formation of these avenin epitopes involved a process called deamidation, where glutamine is converted to glutamic acid by an enzyme called tissue transglutaminase.

Conclusions: In conclusion, some individuals with celiac disease have T-cells in their intestinal lining that react to avenin, leading to inflammation. This intolerance to oats may contribute to villous atrophy and inflammation in celiac disease patients who consume oats while following a strict gluten-free diet. It is recommended to closely monitor celiac disease patients who consume oats as part of their diet.

title: A comparison of continuous and bi-level positive airway pressure non-invasive ventilation in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: a meta-analysis
text: The purpose of this study was to compare the effects of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP) noninvasive ventilation in patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema. We reviewed randomized controlled studies from various databases and assessed the quality of the studies. The results showed that there were no significant differences in hospital mortality or the need for invasive ventilation between patients treated with CPAP and those treated with BiPAP. The duration of noninvasive ventilation and length of hospital stay were also similar between the two groups. However, there was a slight trend towards an increase in new onset acute myocardial infarction in patients treated with BiPAP. In conclusion, BiPAP does not offer any significant clinical benefits over CPAP in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The choice of treatment will depend on the availability of equipment until further research is conducted.

title: CaMKII induces permeability transition through Drp1 phosphorylation during chronic β-AR stimulation
text: The involvement of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) in cardiac dysfunction during chronic stimulation of β-adrenergic receptors (β-AR) is not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that continuous administration of isoproterenol (ISO) consistently raises the occurrence of mPTP openings, leading to mitochondrial damage and cardiac dysfunction. We have identified the mechanism behind this effect, which involves the phosphorylation of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a mitochondrial fission protein, by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) at a specific serine 616 (S616) site. By mutating this phosphorylation site or inhibiting Drp1 activity, we were able to prevent CaMKII- or ISO-induced mPTP opening and myocyte death in laboratory experiments, as well as rescue heart hypertrophy in animal models. Furthermore, we observed an increase in Drp1 phosphorylation at S616 in human failing hearts. These findings reveal a pathway that connects chronic β-AR stimulation to cytosolic stress signals and mitochondrial dysfunction in the heart, involving CaMKII, Drp1, and mPTP.

title: MicroRNA Response of Primary Human Macrophages to Arcobacter Butzleri Infection
text: The significance of microRNAs (miRNAs) in infectious diseases is becoming increasingly evident, and there is a growing focus on using miRNAs as a diagnostic tool and for therapeutic purposes. This study aimed to identify miRNAs involved in the immune response of macrophages to Arcobacter (A.) butzleri infection, a foodborne pathogen that causes gastroenteritis. To achieve this, primary human macrophages were isolated and infected, and the expression of miRNAs was analyzed using RNAseq. The analysis revealed the expression of several miRNAs, including miR-155, miR-125, and miR-212, which have previously been associated with bacterial infections. These miRNAs play a crucial role in Toll-like receptor signaling, where they help establish a balanced immune response. Additionally, miRNAs that have not been previously identified in bacterial infections, such as miR-3613, miR-2116, miR-671, miR-30d, and miR-629, were found to be differentially regulated in A. butzleri-infected cells. The targets of these miRNAs were found to accumulate in pathways related to apoptosis and endocytosis, which may be involved in the pathogenesis of A. butzleri. This study provides new insights into the interaction between A. butzleri and human innate immune cells, helping to enhance our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms in macrophages during infection.

title: The circadian factor Period 2 modulates p53 stability and transcriptional activity in unstressed cells
text: Human Period 2 (hPer2) is a crucial regulator in the circadian clock system, responsible for maintaining the negative feedback loop that keeps the clock running. Its significance in human disease is highlighted by its impact on various biochemical and physiological processes. When hPer2 is absent, it leads to the development of different types of cancers and increases the cell's vulnerability to genotoxic stress. Therefore, our objective was to identify a previously unknown checkpoint where circadian components integrate signals from environmental stress to the DNA-damage response. Our research revealed that hPer2 binds to the C-terminal half of human p53 (hp53) and forms a stable trimeric complex with Mdm2, a negative regulator of hp53. We discovered that hPer2's interaction with hp53 prevents Mdm2 from being ubiquitinated and targeting hp53 for degradation by the proteasome. Decreasing hPer2 expression directly affects hp53 levels, while overexpression of hPer2 influences both the stability of hp53 protein and the transcription of specific genes. In summary, our findings establish hPer2 as a central player in the hp53-mediated response, ensuring that basal levels of hp53 are present to prime the cell for a rapid transcriptional response when needed.

title: Properties of Commelina yellow mottle virus's complete DNA sequence, genomic discontinuities and transcript suggest that it is a pararetrovirus.
text: The second group of plant viruses, known as non-enveloped bacilliform viruses, have a circular double-stranded DNA genome. In this study, we have examined the viral transcript and determined the complete sequence of the genome of Commelina mellow mottle virus (CoYMV), which belongs to this group. Our analysis of the viral transcript reveals that the virus produces a single transcript that is genome-length plus 120 nucleotides. Some of these transcripts are polyadenylated, while the majority are not. The genome sequence analysis shows that the CoYMV genome is 7489 base pairs long and contains three open reading frames on the transcribed strand. These open reading frames have the potential to encode proteins of 23, 15, and 216 kilodaltons (kd). The functions of the 25 and 15 kd proteins are currently unknown. However, the 216 kd polypeptide shows similarities to the coat protein and protease/reverse transcriptase polyprotein of cauliflower mosaic virus, suggesting that it is a polyprotein that undergoes proteolytic processing to produce the virion coat protein, a protease, and replicase (reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H). The CoYMV genome has site-specific discontinuities on both strands. The locations of these discontinuities, as well as the presence of a region on the CoYMV transcript that can bind to the 3'-end of cytosolic initiator methionine tRNA, suggest that the virus replicates through reverse transcription. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that introducing a construct containing 1.3 CoYMV genomes into Commelina diffusa, the host for CoYMV, using Agrobacterium-mediated infection, results in successful infection.

title: The Glucocorticoid Receptor Inhibits
text: Glucocorticoids suppress the activation of proinflammatory genes, such as interleukin-8 (IL-8) and ICAM-1, which are mediated by NFkappaB. Our experiments indicate that the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) achieves this effect by interacting with NFkappaB through protein-protein interactions at the respective gene sites. Specifically, we demonstrate that the zinc binding region (ZBR) of GR, which includes the receptor's DNA binding and dimerization functions, directly binds to the dimerization domain of the RelA subunit of NFkappaB in laboratory tests. Additionally, we show that the ZBR alone is sufficient to associate with RelA bound at NFkappaB response elements in living organisms. Furthermore, we establish that GR does not disrupt NFkappaB's ability to bind to DNA, both in vivo and in vitro. In our transient transfection experiments, we discover that the ligand binding domain of GR is crucial for repressing NFkappaB, but not for its association with NFkappaB. We also find that GR can repress an NFkappaB variant that carries a different activation domain. To understand how the tethered GR represses NFkappaB-activated transcription, we employ chromatin immunoprecipitation assays in untransfected A549 cells. As expected, we observe that the inflammatory signal TNFalpha stimulates the assembly of preinitiation complexes (PIC) at the promoters of IL-8 and ICAM-1, and that the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (pol II) in these complexes becomes phosphorylated at serines 2 and 5 in its carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS). These modifications are necessary for transcription initiation. Interestingly, we find that under repressing conditions, GR does not inhibit PIC assembly, but instead interferes with the phosphorylation of serine 2 of the pol II CTD.

title: Regulation of myeloid cell function through the CD200 receptor.
text: Myeloid cells have significant roles in chronic inflammatory diseases due to their ability to promote inflammation, cause damage, and remodel tissues. CD200 is found on various cell types, while CD200R is specifically expressed on myeloid cells and T cells. When CD200 is deleted in vivo, it leads to dysregulation of myeloid cells and increased susceptibility to autoimmune inflammation, indicating that the interaction between CD200 and CD200R is involved in immune suppression. Our study demonstrates that CD200R agonists can suppress the function of myeloid cells from mice and humans in laboratory settings, and we have also identified a relationship between the level of receptor expression and the extent of cellular inhibition. Engagement of CD200R inhibits the secretion of cytokines stimulated by IFN-gamma and IL-17 in mouse peritoneal macrophages. However, the inhibitory effects are not universal, as responses stimulated by LPS are unaffected. Inhibition of cytokine production in U937 cells is correlated with the level of CD200R expression, and inhibition is only observed in cells with low CD200R expression when the CD200R agonists are cross-linked. CD200R agonists also inhibit the secretion of IL-5 and IL-13 in human PBMCs stimulated by tetanus toxoid. This inhibition is dependent on cross-linking the CD200R on monocytes, but not on CD4+ T cells. Overall, our findings provide direct evidence that the interaction between CD200 and CD200R controls the function of monocytes/macrophages in both mice and humans, supporting the potential use of CD200R agonists in the treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Management of hepatitis C disease among VA patients with schizophrenia and substance use disorders.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare the rates of hepatitis C (HCV) infection, testing, and treatment among different patient groups. These groups included patients with schizophrenia, a substance use disorder, or both schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and a substance use disorder, as well as a control group. The researchers obtained information from 293,445 patients in the Northwest Veterans Healthcare Administration.

The results showed that the substance use disorder group made up 13.6 percent of the sample, the schizophrenia group accounted for 1.6 percent, and the co-occurring disorders group represented 1.4 percent. These groups were respectively about four, two, and six times more likely than the control group to receive HCV testing. Additionally, they were approximately seven, two, and eight times more likely to be infected with HCV.

Interestingly, the rate of interferon (IFN) therapy was significantly lower for the substance use disorder group and the group with co-occurring disorders. However, the differences in rates were not substantial, suggesting that these high-risk groups were not excluded from IFN therapy.

title: Equity in adherence to antiretroviral therapy among economically vulnerable adolescents living with HIV in Uganda
text: Research conducted in sub-Saharan Africa has shown that children living in poverty are disproportionately affected by HIV, often contracting the virus through mother-to-child transmission. For young people living with HIV, their ability to adhere to life-saving treatment regimens is often hindered by the complex economic and social challenges faced by their families, which can also worsen their health problems. To investigate this further, we used data from the Suubi+Adherence study, funded by the National Institute of Child and Human Development (NICHD), to examine how various measures of equity influence self-reported adherence among Ugandan adolescents aged 10-16 (n = 702) living with HIV. The results revealed that adolescents from families with greater asset ownership, particularly those with seven or more tangible assets, were more likely to adhere to their treatment (OR 1.69, 95% CI: 1.00-2.85). Additionally, the distance to the nearest health clinic was found to impact adherence to antiretroviral (ARV) regimens, with those living closer to a clinic being more likely to report optimal adherence (OR 1.49, 95% CI: 0.92-2.40). Furthermore, when considering composite equity scores, we discovered that adolescents with greater economic advantages, such as owning household assets, having financial savings, and having a caregiver who is employed, had higher odds of adherence (OR 1.70, 95% CI: 1.07-2.70). These findings suggest that interventions aimed at addressing economic and social inequities could be beneficial in improving ART uptake among economically vulnerable youth, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study is one of the first to explore the relationship between equity and adherence to ART among economically vulnerable youth living with HIV.

title: High-Resolution Phenotypic Profiling Defines Genes Essential for Mycobacterial Growth and Cholesterol Catabolism
text:
The interconnected pathways of cellular metabolism have a profound impact on the functioning of individual enzymes. Therefore, traditional methods of measuring gene expression are not sufficient in predicting the effects of losing a specific function in a cell. In this study, we introduced a new approach called global phenotypic profiling to identify the genes necessary for the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). By combining high-density mutagenesis and deep-sequencing, we analyzed complex mutant libraries under different conditions. This allowed us to clearly identify the genes essential for Mtb growth in vitro, which was a significant improvement compared to previous methods. 

To further investigate the functions required for Mtb persistence in the host, we focused on the pathways involved in utilizing cholesterol as a crucial carbon source during infection. Surprisingly, only a few of the genes we discovered had been previously associated with this adaptation through transcriptional profiling. Additionally, only a fraction of these genes were located in the chromosomal region known for encoding sterol catabolic functions. However, these genes accounted for a substantial portion of the genes necessary for bacterial growth in mouse tissue, highlighting the importance of this nutritional change in adapting to the host environment. 

This study provides the most comprehensive genetic characterization of a sterol catabolic pathway to date. It also suggests potential roles for uncharacterized virulence genes and precisely maps genes that could serve as targets for drug development.

title: Tyrosine phosphorylation regulates the endocytosis and surface expression of GluN3A-containing NMDA receptors.
text:
Selective control of receptor trafficking allows for the remodeling of excitatory synapses by altering the composition of receptors.
