This process supports synaptic transmission, plasticity, and development. GluN3A, previously known as NR3A, is a unique member of the NMDA receptor subunit family. It gives NMDAR channels lower calcium permeability and reduced magnesium sensitivity compared to NMDARs that only consist of GluN1 and GluN2 subunits. Due to these distinct properties, GluN3A subunits act as a molecular brake, limiting the plasticity and maturation of excitatory synapses. Therefore, the removal of GluN3A is a crucial step in the development of neuronal circuitry. However, the specific molecular signals responsible for GluN3A endocytic removal are still unknown.

In this study, we have identified a novel endocytic motif (YWL) located within the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail of GluN3A. This motif mediates the binding of GluN3A to the clathrin adaptor AP2. By introducing alanine mutations within the GluN3A endocytic motif, we observed inhibited clathrin-dependent internalization. This led to an accumulation of GluN3A-containing NMDARs on the cell surface. Conversely, mimicking phosphorylation of the tyrosine residue promoted internalization and reduced cell-surface expression. We confirmed these findings through immunocytochemical and electrophysiological approaches in recombinant systems and rat neurons in primary culture.

Furthermore, we discovered that the tyrosine residue is phosphorylated by Src family kinases. Activation of Src limits the surface expression of GluN3A in neurons. Overall, our results reveal a new molecular signal for GluN3A internalization. This signal links the functional surface expression of GluN3A-containing receptors to the phosphorylation state of GluN3A subunits. It provides a molecular framework for regulating the composition of NMDAR subunits, which has implications for synaptic plasticity and neurodevelopment.

title: Myeloid-specific Krüppel-like factor 2 inactivation increases macrophage and neutrophil adhesion and promotes atherosclerosis.
text:
RATIONALE: Previous research has shown that a deficiency in the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) can worsen atherosclerosis in mice with high cholesterol levels. However, it is unclear which specific type of cell is responsible for this increased risk. This study aimed to investigate the impact of KLF2 inactivation in myeloid cells on atherosclerosis.

METHODS AND RESULTS: The researchers used Cre/loxP recombination to create mice with a specific knockout of KLF2 in myeloid cells. They found that macrophages from these knockout mice behaved similarly to macrophages from normal mice in terms of activation, polarization, and lipid accumulation. However, the knockout macrophages adhered more strongly to endothelial cells compared to normal macrophages. Neutrophils from the knockout mice also showed increased adhesion to endothelial cells and had a lower survival rate in culture compared to normal neutrophils. When the knockout mice were bred with mice lacking the Ldlr gene and fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet, they exhibited a significant increase in atherosclerosis compared to their normal littermates. The increased atherosclerosis in the knockout mice was associated with higher levels of neutrophils and macrophages, as well as increased presence of myeloperoxidase and markers of oxidative stress in their lesion areas.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that KLF2 expression in myeloid cells plays a role in modulating atherosclerosis. The increased accumulation of neutrophils and progression of atherosclerosis in mice with myeloid-specific KLF2 deficiency highlights the importance of neutrophils in promoting vascular oxidative stress and atherosclerosis. These findings suggest that increasing KLF2 expression may be a potential strategy for preventing and treating atherosclerosis.

title: Epidemiology of Staphylococcus aureus blood and skin and soft tissue infections in the US military health system, 2005-2010.
text: The rates of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections acquired in hospitals are reported to be decreasing, but there is less information available about rates of MRSA infections acquired in the community. The objective of this study was to examine the overall and annual incidence rates of community-onset and hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia and skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) in a national healthcare system, and to evaluate trends in the incidence rates of MRSA infections. The study analyzed data from all Department of Defense TRICARE beneficiaries from January 2005 to December 2010. Medical records were used to identify and classify all annual first-positive S. aureus blood and wound or abscess cultures as either methicillin-susceptible S. aureus or MRSA, and as community-onset or hospital-onset infections. The main outcome measures were the unadjusted incidence rates per 100,000 person-years of observation, the proportion of infections that were due to MRSA, and annual trends from 2005 to 2010. The results showed that during the study period, there were 2643 cases of MRSA bacteremia and 80,281 cases of MRSA SSTIs. The annual incidence rates for community-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased from 1.7 per 100,000 person-years in 2005 to 1.2 per 100,000 person-years in 2010. The annual incidence rates for hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia also decreased from 0.7 per 100,000 person-years in 2005 to 0.4 per 100,000 person-years in 2010. Additionally, the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA decreased from 62% in 2006 to 52% in 2010. In conclusion, the rates of both community-onset and hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased in the Department of Defense population, while the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA has also declined.

title: Potentiation of NMDA currents by pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide in neonatal rat sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
text: We conducted whole cell patch-clamp recordings on sympathetic preganglionic neurons (SPNs) in the intermediolateral cell column of thoracolumbar spinal cord slices taken from 12- to 16-day-old rats. Our aim was to investigate the impact of pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide (PACAP)-38 on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)- and kainate (KA)-induced inward currents. We found that PACAP, at concentrations of 10-30 nM, did not significantly alter holding currents but did enhance NMDA-induced currents while having no effect on KA-induced currents. When PACAP concentrations exceeded 30 nM, a sustained inward current was observed. However, this potentiating effect of PACAP was abolished when the slices were pre-incubated with the adenylate cyclase inhibitor MDL-12,330A (25 microM). Additionally, when the slices were exposed to the membrane-permeable cyclic AMP analogue N6,2'-O-dibutyryladenosine 3':5'-cyclic monophosphate (100-300 microM) in the presence of the phosphodiesterase inhibitor 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (700 microM), NMDA currents were further increased. These findings suggest that PACAP selectively enhances NMDA-receptor-mediated responses in rat SPNs, likely through a cyclic-AMP-dependent mechanism. This provides evidence that the peptide may play a role in synaptic plasticity.

title: Aberrant Expression of RCAN1 in Alzheimer’s Pathogenesis: A New Molecular Mechanism and a Novel Drug Target
text: AD, a devastating neurodegenerative disorder, is the most prevalent cause of dementia in older individuals. Patients with AD exhibit three distinct neuropathological features, including the accumulation of neuritic plaques, the formation of neurofibrillary tangles, and the loss of neurons. Emerging evidence suggests that the dysregulation of regulator of calcineurin 1 (RCAN1) plays a significant role in the development of AD. Abnormal RCAN1 expression promotes neuronal cell death and the excessive phosphorylation of Tau protein, ultimately leading to neuronal loss and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. This review aims to provide an overview of recent advancements in understanding the regulation of RCAN1 expression and its physiological functions. Additionally, it summarizes the impact of AD risk factors on RCAN1 dysregulation and its contribution to neuronal loss, impaired synaptic function, and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. Furthermore, we explore the effects of RCAN1 dysregulation on the processing of amyloid precursor protein (APP), the generation of amyloid-beta (Aβ), and the formation of neuritic plaques. We also discuss the potential underlying mechanisms and the prospects of targeting RCAN1 as a novel therapeutic approach.

title: Congruent Visual Speech Enhances Cortical Entrainment to Continuous Auditory Speech in Noise-Free Conditions.
text: The comprehension of a speaker is improved when their audio and visual cues are congruent, even in the absence of noise. However, when the auditory and visual information is incongruent, it can hinder perception and even lead to the perception of information that was not presented in either modality. Previous studies have mainly focused on discrete audiovisual syllables that are spatially and temporally congruent, with less attention given to natural, continuous speech. Recent research has shown that cortical response measures to continuous auditory speech can be easily obtained using multivariate analysis methods. In this study, we apply these methods to investigate audiovisual speech and propose a new framework for assessing multisensory integration in the context of continuous speech. Specifically, we examine how the temporal and contextual congruency of ongoing audiovisual speech influences the cortical encoding of the speech envelope in humans using electroencephalography. Our findings demonstrate that the cortical representation of the speech envelope is enhanced when congruent audiovisual speech is presented in noise-free conditions. Additionally, we identify neural generators that are not highly active during unimodal stimulation as contributing to this enhancement, particularly at the syllabic rate (2-6 Hz). Moreover, our data suggest that neural entrainment to the speech envelope is inhibited when the auditory and visual streams are incongruent both temporally and contextually. In summary, our study highlights the importance of visual cues in speech comprehension and introduces a new methodological approach using scalp recordings to investigate the brain's processing of continuous auditory and visual speech.

title: Telomere tethering at the nuclear periphery is essential for efficient DNA double strand break repair in subtelomeric region
text: In yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae without lamins, the nuclear pore complex (NPC) is believed to play a role in organizing chromatin. Through fluorescence microscopy in live cells, we demonstrate that nuclear pore proteins from the Nup84 core complex, namely Nup84p, Nup145Cp, Nup120p, and Nup133p, act as anchors for telomere XI-L at the outer edge of the nucleus. The integrity of this complex is necessary to suppress the URA3 gene inserted in the subtelomeric region of this chromosome end. Additionally, disrupting the integrity of this complex reduces the efficiency of repairing a DNA double-strand break (DSB) only when it occurs in the subtelomeric region, despite functional repair machinery. These effects are specific to the Nup84 complex. Our findings confirm and expand on the role of the NPC, specifically the Nup84 complex, in the functional organization of chromatin. They also indicate that anchoring telomeres is crucial for effective repair of DSBs in that region and for maintaining genome integrity.

title: p63 Regulates adult neural precursor and newly born neuron survival to control hippocampal-dependent Behavior.
text: The precise mechanisms that control the survival of adult neural precursor cells (NPCs) and the maintenance of adult neurogenesis are not well understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of p63, a member of the p53 family, in the functioning of adult NPCs in mice. By selectively removing p63 in adult NPCs or reducing its levels, we observed a decrease in the number of NPCs and newly generated neurons in the regions of the brain responsible for neurogenesis, such as the hippocampus, lateral ventricles, and olfactory bulb. This reduction was due to an increase in programmed cell death (apoptosis) of NPCs and newborn neurons. However, we were able to rescue these reductions by inhibiting caspase activity, p53, or a protein called PUMA, which is involved in p53-mediated apoptosis. Importantly, these cellular deficits had functional consequences, as they disrupted memory formation processes that rely on the hippocampus. Our findings suggest that p63 plays a crucial role in regulating the population of adult NPCs and newly generated neurons, as well as cognitive functions that depend on neural stem cells. This regulation occurs, at least in part, through the inhibition of p53-mediated cell death.

title: Tyrosine-Phosphorylated Caveolin-1 Blocks Bacterial Uptake by Inducing Vav2-RhoA-Mediated Cytoskeletal Rearrangements
text: Some bacterial adhesins seem to promote a pathogen's existence outside of host cells rather than its entry into them. However, we have limited knowledge about the reactions that occur during these interactions between pathogens and host cells. In this study, we discovered that Neisseria gonorrhoeae (P(+)GC), which produces type IV pili (Tfp), immediately recruits caveolin-1 (Cav1) in the host cell. This recruitment prevents bacterial internalization by triggering changes in the cell's cytoskeleton through downstream phosphotyrosine signaling. Through a comprehensive analysis, we identified a direct interaction between tyrosine-phosphorylated Cav1 and the Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav2. Both Vav2 and its substrate, the small GTPase RhoA, play a direct role in preventing bacterial uptake mediated by Cav1. Our findings, which also apply to enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, demonstrate how Tfp-producing bacteria evade host cell uptake. Additionally, our data establish a connection between Cav1 phosphorylation and pathogen-induced reorganization of the cytoskeleton, enhancing our understanding of caveolin function.

title: Effects of GC Bias in Next-Generation-Sequencing Data on De Novo Genome Assembly
text: The field of genome assembly has been revolutionized by Next-generation-sequencing (NGS) due to its higher data throughput and lower cost compared to traditional Sanger sequencing. However, NGS presents new computational challenges for de novo genome assembly. One of these challenges is the presence of GC bias in NGS data, which has been known to worsen genome assembly. However, it is not clear how much GC bias affects genome assembly in general. In this study, we have conducted a systematic analysis to determine the effects of GC bias on genome assembly. Our analysis has revealed that GC bias only reduces assembly completeness when the degree of GC bias exceeds a certain threshold. In cases of strong GC bias, the fragmentation of the assembly can be attributed to the low coverage of reads in GC-poor or GC-rich regions of the genome. This effect is observed across all the assemblers studied. Increasing the total amount of NGS data can mitigate the assembly fragmentation caused by GC bias. However, the amount of data required for a complete rescue depends on the distribution of GC contents. Both low and high coverage depths resulting from GC bias decrease the accuracy of assembly. These findings provide valuable insights for improving de novo genome assembly in the presence of GC bias.

title: Cancer inhibition through circadian reprogramming of tumor transcriptome with meal timing.
text: Disruption of the circadian rhythm speeds up the progression of cancer, while strengthening the circadian rhythm could stop it. In this study, mice with pancreatic adenocarcinoma were divided into two groups: one group was allowed to eat whenever they wanted, while the other group had specific meal times. The mice were also given either a normal or a high-fat diet. Gene expression patterns were analyzed in the tumors and liver at different times of the day. The researchers found that the group with meal timing had a 40% reduction in cancer growth compared to the group with unrestricted eating, regardless of calorie intake. The expression of clock genes remained irregular in the tumors, regardless of feeding schedule or diet. However, meal timing did affect the expression of 423 tumor genes at different times of the day. Additionally, certain genes involved in cellular stress, cell cycle, and metabolism were upregulated at one time and downregulated 12 hours later. Meal timing also significantly increased the expression of certain genes in the tumors. The levels of corticosterone and insulin-like growth factor-I did not play a role in inhibiting tumor growth. However, meal timing consistently doubled the amplitude of body temperature fluctuations, which corresponded to the peak expressions of certain genes in the tumors. Strengthening the circadian rhythm in the host induced rhythmic expression of critical genes in tumors that lacked a functioning circadian clock, resulting in the inhibition of cancer growth. This study suggests that targeting circadian clocks could be a promising approach for cancer treatment.

title: Role of chicken melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 in induction and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses to infectious bursal disease virus in cultured macrophages
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether chicken melanoma-differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) detects infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) infection and triggers an innate immune response that connects to adaptive immunity. In HD11 cells infected with IBDV, the levels of IBDV and RNA increased significantly up to 3.4 × 107 plaque-forming units (PFU)/mL and 1114 ng/µL, respectively, at 24 hours post-infection (hpi). The infection also led to a significant increase in the expression levels of chicken MDA5 (59-fold), interferon-β (IFN-β) (693-fold), dsRNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) (4-fold), 2’, 5’-oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS) (286-fold), myxovirus resistance gene (Mx) (22-fold), interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (5-fold), IL-6 (146-fold), IL-8 (4-fold), IL-10 (4-fold), inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) (15-fold), and major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) (4-fold). The production of nitric oxide in the culture supernatants also significantly increased up to 6.5 μM at 24 hpi. The expressed chMDA5 and IBDV-derived dsRNA were found in the cytoplasm of HD11 cells during IBDV infection. Knockdown of chMDA5 in HD11 cells resulted in significantly higher levels of IBDV RNA at 24 hpi, as well as lower nitric oxide production and expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-18, IL-10, iNOS, MHC class I, and CD86 at 24 hpi. On the other hand, overexpression of chMDA5 in HD11 cells led to significantly reduced IBDV levels and RNA loads, as well as increased nitric oxide production at 16 and 24 hpi. It also resulted in higher expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-10, and iNOS at 2 hpi. In conclusion, these findings suggest that chMDA5 detects IBDV infection in chicken macrophages, leading to the expression of IFN-β and initiation of an innate immune response that activates the adaptive immune response and restricts IBDV replication.

title: Age-Associated Sperm DNA Methylation Alterations: Possible Implications in Offspring Disease Susceptibility
text: New evidence suggests that the age of the father can impact the susceptibility of offspring to certain diseases. It is well known that conditions like schizophrenia, autism, trinucleotide expansion associated diseases, and some forms of cancer are more common in children of older fathers. However, the mechanisms behind these effects are not fully understood. It is believed that epigenetics, specifically changes in DNA methylation, may play a role. In this study, we examined how aging affects DNA methylation in mature human sperm. We analyzed the methylation patterns of sperm samples collected from 17 fertile donors, comparing samples taken 9-19 years apart. Our findings revealed 139 regions that consistently showed decreased methylation with age, and 8 regions that showed increased methylation. We confirmed a subset of these changes in a separate group of individuals. These alterations in methylation were associated with 117 genes, some of which have been linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. While our data does not prove a causal relationship, it suggests that age-related methylation changes in sperm may contribute to the increased risk of neuropsychiatric and other disorders in children of older fathers. However, further research is needed to determine the extent of this relationship.

title: Mutations in the nuclear bile acid receptor FXR cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
text: Neonatal cholestasis is a serious condition that requires immediate diagnosis as it can be life-threatening. While mutations in various genes can lead to progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, not all cases can be explained by known genes. In this study, we present four individuals from two unrelated families who experienced neonatal cholestasis and had mutations in the NR1H4 gene. NR1H4 encodes the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a nuclear hormone receptor that is activated by bile acids and plays a role in regulating bile acid metabolism. Severe and persistent NR1H4-related cholestasis is characterized by neonatal onset, rapid progression to end-stage liver disease, vitamin K-independent coagulopathy, low-to-normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase activity, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels, and undetectable expression of the liver bile salt export pump (ABCB11). These findings highlight the crucial role of FXR in maintaining bile acid balance and protecting the liver.

title: Phase II study of panobinostat in combination with bevacizumab for recurrent glioblastoma and anaplastic glioma.
text:
In this study, we investigated the combination of panobinostat and bevacizumab in patients with recurrent high-grade glioma (HGG). Panobinostat is a drug that inhibits histone deacetylase and has been shown to have antineoplastic and antiangiogenic effects in glioma. We conducted a multicenter phase II trial to evaluate the efficacy of this combination therapy.

Patients with recurrent HGG were given oral panobinostat at a dose of 30 mg three times per week, every other week, in combination with bevacizumab at a dose of 10 mg/kg every other week. The primary endpoint of the study was the 6-month progression-free survival (PFS6) rate for patients with recurrent glioblastoma (GBM). Patients with recurrent anaplastic glioma (AG) were also included in an exploratory arm of the study.

At the interim analysis, it was determined that the GBM arm did not meet the criteria for continued accrual, and therefore, it was closed. A total of 24 patients with GBM were enrolled before the closure. The PFS6 rate in this group was 30.4%, with a median PFS of 5 months and a median overall survival (OS) of 9 months.

On the other hand, accrual in the AG arm continued until completion, with a total of 15 patients enrolled. In this group, the PFS6 rate was 46.7%, with a median PFS of 7 months and a median OS of 17 months.

In conclusion, this phase II study showed that the combination of panobinostat and bevacizumab did not meet the criteria for continued accrual in patients with recurrent GBM. Although the treatment was well tolerated, the addition of panobinostat did not significantly improve the PFS6 compared to historical controls of bevacizumab monotherapy in either the GBM or AG cohorts.

title: Blood monocytes consist of two principal subsets with distinct migratory properties
text: Peripheral blood monocytes are a diverse group of circulating white blood cells. By using a system in mice where monocytes are transferred, we were able to study how they migrate and change in the body. We found two distinct types of monocytes in mouse blood: one subset that is attracted to inflamed tissues and another subset that is attracted to non-inflamed tissues. Both subsets have the ability to transform into dendritic cells in the body. The level of a protein called CX(3)CR1 also determines the two main types of monocytes in humans, known as CD14(+)CD16(-) and CD14(lo)CD16(+) monocytes, which have similar characteristics and migration abilities as the mouse subsets. These discoveries open up possibilities for new treatments for inflammatory diseases.

title: The Spemann Organizer Signal noggin Binds and Inactivates Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4
text: The Spemann organizer in the amphibian gastrula releases signals that can directly trigger the formation of neural tissue from ectoderm and transform ventral mesoderm into muscle through dorsalization. The polypeptide noggin, which is secreted at the appropriate time and location, imitates these actions and plays a role in the organizer's signal. However, bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) counteract neural induction and mesoderm dorsalization by promoting the development of epidermis and ventral mesoderm instead. In this study, we demonstrate that noggin protein binds strongly to BMP4 and can neutralize its effects by preventing it from binding to its corresponding cell-surface receptors. These findings suggest that noggin, secreted by the organizer, shapes the embryo by disrupting BMP signaling.

title: A Conserved MST-FOXO Signaling Pathway Mediates Oxidative-Stress Responses and Extends Life Span
text: The impact of oxidative stress on cell survival and homeostasis is not fully understood. However, our research reveals that the protein kinase MST1 is responsible for cell death caused by oxidative stress in primary mammalian neurons. This occurs through the direct activation of FOXO transcription factors. MST1 phosphorylates FOXO proteins at a specific site, disrupting their interaction with 14-3-3 proteins. This leads to the translocation of FOXO proteins into the nucleus, ultimately resulting in cell death in neurons. We have also found that this MST-FOXO signaling link extends to nematodes. In C. elegans, the knockdown of the MST1 ortholog CST-1 leads to a shortened lifespan and accelerated tissue aging. Conversely, overexpression of cst-1 promotes longevity and delays aging. The extension of lifespan induced by cst-1 is dependent on the daf-16 gene. The discovery that FOXO transcription factors are major targets of MST1, and that this relationship is evolutionarily conserved, suggests that MST kinases play crucial roles in various biological processes, including cellular responses to oxidative stress and longevity.

title: Physician Emigration from Sub-Saharan Africa to the United States: Analysis of the 2011 AMA Physician Masterfile
text: The emigration of physicians from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) to high-income countries is a significant concern. This study aimed to examine the current emigration trends of SSA physicians in the United States. The researchers analyzed physician data from the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Workforce Statistics and graduation and residency data from the 2011 American Medical Association Physician Masterfile (AMA-PM). They estimated the proportion of emigration, year of entry into the US, years of practice before emigration, and length of time in the US. According to the AMA-PM, there were 10,819 physicians from 28 SSA countries practicing in the US. Of these, 68% were trained in SSA, 20% were trained in the US, and 12% were trained outside both SSA and the US. The majority of active physicians were estimated to be under the age of 70. Migration trends among SSA-trained physicians increased from 2002 to 2011, except for South Africa, which saw a decrease in physician migration to the US. Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, and Sudan experienced significant increases in migration. Liberia was the most affected country, with 77% of its estimated physicians practicing in the US. On average, SSA-trained physicians had been in the US for 18 years, with 6.5 years of practice before emigrating. Many physicians emigrated during the implementation years of structural adjustment programs. In conclusion, physician emigration from SSA to the US is increasing, and without comprehensive policies, this trend will continue, making the US a primary destination for SSA physicians leaving their home countries.

title: Kynurenic Acid Is a Nutritional Cue that Enables Behavioral Plasticity
text: The kynurenine pathway, which is responsible for metabolizing tryptophan, has been implicated in the development of various brain diseases. However, its exact functions in the body are still not fully understood. Our study reveals that kynurenic acid, a metabolite produced in this pathway, acts as a regulator of behavioral changes related to food intake in C. elegans. When these worms experience fasting, it affects their feeding rate and other behaviors when they encounter food again. Fasting depletes the levels of kynurenic acid produced by neurons, leading to the activation of interneurons expressing NMDA receptors. This, in turn, triggers a signaling pathway similar to neuropeptide-y, which promotes increased feeding by enhancing serotonin release when the worms come into contact with food. As the worms start to eat again, the levels of kynurenic acid gradually replenish, signaling the end of the heightened feeding period. Since tryptophan is an essential amino acid, our findings suggest that kynurenic acid plays a crucial role in directly connecting metabolism to the activity of NMDA and serotonergic circuits, which regulate a wide range of behaviors and physiological processes.

title: Comprehensive Identification and Annotation of Cell Type-Specific and Ubiquitous CTCF-Binding Sites in the Human Genome
text: Chromatin insulators are DNA elements that control gene expression levels. They do this by either preventing gene silencing through maintaining boundaries between active and inactive chromatin regions, or by blocking interactions between enhancers and promoters to prevent gene activation. The protein CTCF, which is found in all cells and binds to DNA using 11 zinc fingers, is the only protein known to be involved in establishing insulators in vertebrates. However, research on CTCF has been limited to a few cell types in the human genome, so it is unclear if the differences in CTCF-binding sites between cell types have any functional significance. In this study, we identify and study cell type-specific and ubiquitous CTCF-binding sites in the human genome using data from the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) consortium, which includes information from 38 different cell types. We find that these CTCF-binding sites have unique functions in regulating gene expression and have distinct chromatin features. Additionally, we confirm that CTCF-binding acts as an insulator and also discover a new role for CTCF in DNA replication. These findings are an important step towards understanding the diverse roles of CTCF-dependent insulators in the human genome.

title: Experimental and Theoretical Approaches to Conscious Processing
text: Recent studies and models have started to tackle the challenge of establishing a causal connection between subjective conscious experience and measurable neuronal activity. This review specifically focuses on the issue of how information, whether from an external source or internal, surpasses nonconscious processing and enters conscious processing, which is characterized by a reportable subjective experience. Neuroimaging and neurophysiological data, obtained through minimal experimental comparisons between conscious and nonconscious processing, indicate objective neural indicators of conscious access. These indicators include the amplification of relevant sensory activity at a later stage, synchronization of neural activity at beta and gamma frequencies across different brain regions, and the activation of a large-scale prefronto-parietal network. We compare these findings with existing theoretical models of conscious processing, such as the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) model. According to the GNW model, conscious access occurs when incoming information becomes globally available to multiple brain systems through a network of neurons with long-range axons that are densely distributed in prefrontal, parieto-temporal, and cingulate cortices. The implications of these results for general anesthesia, coma, vegetative state, and schizophrenia are also discussed.

title: Reconstruction of the yeast Snf1 kinase regulatory network reveals its role as a global energy regulator
text: The AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) is a highly conserved regulator of carbon metabolism in eukaryotic cells. In order to understand the interactions surrounding AMPK in yeast (Snf1) and the role of its regulatory subunit Snf4, we conducted a study measuring mRNA, protein, and metabolite levels in different knockout strains. By utilizing new computational tools, including DOGMA sub-network analysis, we demonstrated the advantages of integrating three levels of omics data to uncover the broader role of Snf1 kinase in yeast. This study is the first to identify the global regulation of gene and protein expression by Snf1 and highlights its extensive involvement in energy metabolism. Furthermore, we discovered the complementary functions of Snf1 and Snf4. Our findings suggest that Snf1 serves as a checkpoint for low-energy states, similar to AMPK in humans. This research establishes yeast as a valuable model system for studying the molecular mechanisms underlying the global regulation of AMPK in mammals, which is crucial for understanding metabolic diseases.

title: Influence of Steroid Hormone Signaling on Life Span Control by Caenorhabditis elegans Insulin-Like Signaling
text: Sterol-sensing nuclear receptors and insulin-like growth factor signaling have conserved functions in regulating aging. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, dafachronic acids (DAs), which are bile acid-like steroid hormones, affect longevity by binding to and controlling the activity of the conserved nuclear receptor DAF-12. Additionally, the insulin receptor (InsR) ortholog DAF-2 regulates lifespan by inhibiting the FoxO transcription factor DAF-16. However, the interaction between the DA/DAF-12 pathway and DAF-2/InsR signaling in lifespan control is not well understood. Therefore, we specifically examined the roles of liganded and unliganded DAF-12 in lifespan control in the context of reduced DAF-2/InsR signaling. In animals with reduced daf-2/InsR activity, mutations that decrease DA production or completely eliminate DAF-12 activity result in a shorter lifespan, indicating that liganded DAF-12 promotes longevity. In animals with reduced DAF-2/InsR activity induced by daf-2/InsR RNAi, both liganded and unliganded DAF-12 contribute to lifespan extension. However, in daf-2/InsR mutants, liganded and unliganded DAF-12 have opposing effects on lifespan control. Therefore, in situations where DAF-2/InsR signaling is reduced, multiple activities of DAF-12 influence lifespan in different ways. Our findings reveal new roles for a conserved steroid signaling pathway in lifespan control and provide insights into the interactions between DA biosynthetic pathways, DAF-12, and DAF-2/InsR signaling in the aging process.

title: Asymmetric Cell Divisions Sustain Long-Term  Hematopoiesis from Single-sorted Human Fetal Liver Cells
text: It is believed that adult marrow contains hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) that originate from fetal liver precursors. In order to examine the cell kinetics involved in long-term hematopoiesis, we conducted a study on single-sorted candidate HSCs from fetal liver. These cells were cultured in the presence of a combination of stimulating cytokines. After 8-10 days, the number of cells in the primary cultures ranged from 10,000 cells. Slow-growing colonies were recloned when they reached a stage of 100-200 cells. Interestingly, the number of cells in the subclones varied greatly once again. These findings suggest that primitive hematopoietic cells undergo asymmetric divisions, resulting in uneven distribution of proliferative potential and cell cycle properties among the daughter cells. The continuous generation of functional heterogeneity among the clonal progeny of HSCs supports the idea of intrinsic control of stem cell fate. This study provides a model for understanding the long-term maintenance of hematopoiesis both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Reprogramming factor expression initiates widespread targeted chromatin remodeling.
text: Despite significant progress in understanding how transcription factors can reprogram somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), there are still many unanswered questions about the underlying mechanisms. In order to shed light on the initial stages of the reprogramming process, we conducted a systematic analysis of the changes in gene expression and epigenetic modifications that occur after the introduction of specific factors. We found that there were rapid and widespread changes in a specific histone modification called H3K4me2, which is associated with active gene expression. These changes occurred at over a thousand locations in the genome, including many gene promoters and enhancers that are important for pluripotency and development. In contrast, another histone modification called H3K27me3, which is associated with gene repression, remained largely unchanged except for specific regions where H3K4 methylation was gained. These epigenetic changes occurred before any noticeable changes in gene expression. Our findings suggest that there is an early and coordinated epigenetic response to the introduction of reprogramming factors, which helps to reset the identity of somatic cells during the reprogramming process.

title: Stroke and migraine--the spectrum of cause and effect.
text: The connection between migraine and stroke is intricate. While stroke and migraine may occur simultaneously by chance, migraine could potentially raise the likelihood of stroke in women under 45 years old and potentially in men who experience migraine with aura. Stroke can imitate migraine, but migraine syndromes may also indicate underlying cerebrovascular disorders. However, instances of stroke directly caused by migraines are uncommon. The exact mechanisms behind stroke during a migraine attack are yet to be determined, but it is likely that they involve a combination of dynamic changes in cerebral blood flow and risk factors for stroke.

title: MicroRNA Regulation of Cbx7 Mediates a Switch of Polycomb Orthologs during ESC Differentiation
text: The Polycomb Group (PcG) is responsible for regulating pluripotency and differentiation by modifying chromatin. In mammals, there are multiple versions of the Polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1) components, with five versions of the Drosophila Polycomb protein (Cbx2, Cbx4, Cbx6, Cbx7, and Cbx8). Our research has identified Cbx7 as the main Polycomb version in PRC1 complexes in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). During ESC differentiation, the expression of Cbx7 decreases, while Cbx2, Cbx4, and Cbx8 increase. Cbx7 directly represses these other versions. When Cbx7 is artificially expressed, it inhibits differentiation and X chromosome inactivation, while promoting ESC self-renewal. Conversely, when Cbx7 is reduced, differentiation occurs and lineage-specific markers are activated. In our functional screen, we discovered that the miR-125 and miR-181 families regulate Cbx7 and are induced during ESC differentiation. The ectopic expression of these miRNAs speeds up ESC differentiation by controlling Cbx7. These findings demonstrate the crucial role of Cbx7 and its regulatory miRNAs in determining pluripotency.

title: Differences in the Clinical Effects of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers: A Critical Review of the Evidence
text: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system plays a significant role in the development of hypertension and related cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. While both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor antagonists (ARBs) are equally important in treating hypertension, recent research suggests that they may have distinct cardiovascular protective effects due to their different mechanisms of action. As our understanding of these mechanisms grows, more studies will likely explore the differences between ACE inhibitors and ARBs. ACE inhibitors are a safe treatment option for hypertensive patients with a high risk of cardiovascular complications.

title: A talin-dependent LFA-1 focal zone is formed by rapidly migrating T lymphocytes
text: The coordinated movement of cells like fibroblasts and endothelial cells relies on specific integrin-containing focal adhesions and complexes. However, the organization of integrins on highly mobile T lymphocytes is not well understood. To address this, we examined the distribution, activity, and connection to the cytoskeleton of the integrin lymphocyte function associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) on human T lymphocytes migrating on endothelial cells and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) ligands. The expression of total LFA-1 varies, with low levels in the lamellipodia and high levels in the uropod. However, high affinity, clustered LFA-1 is only found in a specific mid-cell zone that remains stable over time and across different densities of ICAM-1. The presence of talin is crucial for the formation and stability of this LFA-1 zone. Disrupting the talin-integrin connection results in the loss of zone integrity and a significant decrease in migration speed on ICAM-1. We refer to this unique adhesive structure, which differs from the integrin-containing attachments seen in other cell types, as the "focal zone."

title: Tricyclic antidepressants and headaches: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and side effects of tricyclic antidepressants in treating migraine, tension-type, and mixed headaches. The study design was a meta-analysis, and the data sources included Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Trials Registry, and PsycLIT. The inclusion criteria were randomized trials of adults who received tricyclics as the sole treatment for at least four weeks. The data extracted included the frequency and intensity of headaches, as well as the headache index. 

A total of 37 studies met the inclusion criteria. Tricyclics were found to significantly reduce the number of days with tension-type headaches and the number of headache attacks in migraine compared to placebo. However, there was no significant difference between tricyclics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in terms of reducing these measures. The effectiveness of tricyclics increased with longer treatment duration. Tricyclics were also more likely to reduce headache intensity by at least 50% compared to placebo and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. 

However, tricyclics were associated with more adverse effects compared to placebo and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. These adverse effects included dry mouth, drowsiness, and weight gain. Despite this, tricyclics did not increase dropout rates compared to placebo and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. 

In conclusion, tricyclic antidepressants are effective in preventing migraine and tension-type headaches and are more effective than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. However, they also come with a higher risk of adverse effects. The effectiveness of tricyclics appears to improve over time.

title: Functional Consequences of Splicing of the Antisense Transcript COOLAIR on FLC Transcription
text: The functionality of antisense transcription in various genomes is a subject of intense debate. Our research focuses on a group of long noncoding antisense transcripts known as COOLAIR, which are produced at the Arabidopsis FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC). COOLAIR begins just after the main sense transcript's poly(A) site and can either terminate early or extend into the FLC promoter region. We have discovered that the splicing of COOLAIR plays a crucial role in its functionality. This was demonstrated by studying a hypomorphic mutation in the core spliceosome component PRP8. The prp8 mutation disrupts a feedback mechanism that connects COOLAIR processing to histone demethylation in the FLC gene body, resulting in reduced FLC transcription. To further confirm the significance of COOLAIR splicing in this repression mechanism, we disrupted COOLAIR production and mutated the COOLAIR proximal splice acceptor site. Our findings indicate that changes in the splicing of a long noncoding transcript can quantitatively regulate gene expression through cotranscriptional coupling mechanisms.

title: Nuclear Factor-�B Affects Tumor Progression in a Mouse Model of Malignant Pleural Effusion
text: We have created a new mouse model for malignant pleural effusion (MPE) by directly injecting Lewis lung cancer (LLC) cells into the pleural space of syngeneic C57B/6 mice. The pleural effusions in this model exhibit similar cellular and biochemical characteristics to human MPEs. The implantation and growth of pleural tumors trigger an inflammatory response in the host, leading to the influx of various inflammatory cells into the pleural fluid. In both in vitro and in vivo settings, LLC cells demonstrate high basal nuclear factor (NF)-κB activity. To track the pleural tumors, we utilized this NF-κB activity to drive the expression of a NF-κB-dependent fusion reporter construct consisting of green fluorescent protein and firefly luciferase. This reporter expression enabled us to trace the pleural tumors in real-time. Inhibiting NF-κB in LLC cells did not affect their viability in culture. However, when we injected LLC cells expressing a dominant NF-κB inhibitor, we observed a reduction in tumor burden, pleural effusion volume, and levels of TNF-α in the pleural effusion. These findings suggest that NF-κB plays a crucial role in tumor development and progression in this model.

title: A phase I study of PF-04449913, an oral hedgehog inhibitor, in patients with advanced solid tumors.
text:
The purpose of this study was to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of the drug PF-04449913 when used alone, and to assess its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary effectiveness in patients with advanced tumors. The study followed a 3+3 design, where patients were enrolled in an open-label, multicenter, phase I trial and the dose of PF-04449913 was escalated or de-escalated until the MTD was identified. The drug was administered orally once daily in 28-day treatment cycles, starting at a dose of 80 mg. 

A total of 23 patients were enrolled in the study, with 19 patients being evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) during the first treatment cycle. The rate of DLT during the first cycle was 33.3% at the 640 mg dose level, and the MTD was estimated to be 320 mg once daily. The recommended dose for phase II trials was not determined. PF-04449913 was generally well tolerated at doses ranging from 80 to 320 mg once daily. The most common treatment-related adverse events were mild to moderate dysgeusia, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dizziness, dehydration, and diarrhea. Grade 3 adverse events only occurred in patients receiving the highest dose of 640 mg once daily, and no grade 4 or 5 adverse events were reported. 

Pharmacokinetic analysis showed that the drug had dose-proportional kinetics with biphasic elimination, supporting once-daily dosing. PF-04449913 was found to modulate hedgehog signaling at the tested dose levels, as evidenced by more than 80% downregulation of GLI1 expression in the skin of treated patients. Eight patients (34.8%) achieved stable disease, while none had a complete or partial response. Three patients with disease progression at the start of the study experienced prolonged disease stabilization for at least 6 months. 

In conclusion, the results of this study suggest that further investigation of PF-04449913 in patients with advanced solid tumors is warranted.

title: Histone levels are regulated by phosphorylation and ubiquitylation dependent proteolysis
text: To prevent harmful consequences such as genomic instability and hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, the levels of histones, highly basic proteins, are tightly controlled when DNA replication slows down or halts. While chromosomal histones remain stable, excessive histones that are not bound to chromatin are swiftly broken down in a manner dependent on the Rad53 kinase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In this study, we demonstrate that surplus histones interact with Rad53 in living organisms and undergo modifications like tyrosine phosphorylation and polyubiquitylation before being degraded by the proteasome. We have identified the Tyr 99 residue of histone H3 as crucial for the efficient ubiquitylation and degradation of this histone. Additionally, we have identified the ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (E2) Ubc4 and Ubc5, as well as the ubiquitin ligase (E3) Tom1, as enzymes involved in the ubiquitylation of excessive histones. The regulated breakdown of histones has significant implications for maintaining epigenetic marks on chromatin, ensuring genomic stability, and packaging sperm DNA.

title: TLR-activated B cells suppress T cell-mediated autoimmunity.
text: TLR receptors detect microbial infections and regulate immune responses. Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes express TLR receptors and the signaling protein MyD88. However, the impact of TLR-activated B cells on T cell-mediated inflammation is not well understood. To investigate this, we conducted a study using mice with B cell-specific deficiencies in MyD88 or specific TLR receptors, focusing on their effect on experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), an autoimmune disease. Our findings reveal that TLR signaling in B cells inhibits inflammatory T cell responses (both Th1 and Th17) and promotes recovery from EAE. Interestingly, only certain TLR receptors on B cells are necessary for resolving EAE, while they are not required for disease initiation. This suggests that a specific group of TLR agonists triggers a suppressive function in B cells, limiting autoimmune disease. These TLR agonists responsible for regulating B cell function are found in components of Mycobacterium tuberculosis present in the adjuvant. Therefore, MyD88 signaling in B cells counteracts MyD88 signaling in other cells, which promotes the differentiation of Th17 cells and is crucial for inducing EAE. Overall, our data demonstrate that B cells connect the recognition of microbial products through TLR receptors to the suppression of T cell-mediated autoimmune diseases.

title: Successful expansion of functional and stable regulatory T cells for immunotherapy in liver transplantation
text:
Intensive research is currently focused on developing strategies to prevent organ transplant rejection and reduce the need for long-term immunosuppression. One promising approach involves the use of regulatory T cells (Tregs), which are nearing clinical application. A clinical trial called ThRIL has recently begun at King's College London, aiming to induce tolerance in liver transplant recipients through Treg cell therapy. The success of this trial could potentially revolutionize the treatment of these patients and pave the way for drug-free transplants in the future.

In this study, we report the production of clinical-grade Tregs from prospective liver transplant recipients using a CliniMACS-based GMP isolation technique. These Tregs were then expanded using anti-CD3/CD28 beads, IL-2, and rapamycin. We successfully enriched a pure and stable population of Tregs, with over 95% of the cells expressing CD4, CD25, and FOXP3 markers. We were able to generate a sufficient number of Tregs for their clinical application.

Our protocol not only facilitated the expansion of highly functional Tregs but also prevented their conversion into Th17 cells under pro-inflammatory conditions. This is a significant finding as Th17 cells are known to contribute to transplant rejection. The final Treg product was manufactured in the clinical research facility (CRF), which is a crucial step for the clinical application of these cells.

The data presented in this manuscript, along with the anticipated clinical results from ThRIL, will undoubtedly provide valuable insights for the improved management of liver transplant recipients.

title: A framework for improving microRNA prediction in non-human genomes
text:
Recently, there has been significant interest in predicting new pre-microRNA (miRNA) from genomic sequences. However, most of these studies have focused solely on the human genome. Previous research has shown that when human-trained methods are applied to other species, they maintain sensitivity (the ability to correctly detect true miRNA). However, these studies have failed to acknowledge the significant decrease in specificity (the ability to accurately reject non-miRNA sequences) in non-human genomes. This lack of specificity, coupled with the fact that the ratio of true miRNA sequences to pseudo-miRNA sequences is approximately 1:1000, hinders the application of existing tools to non-human genomes. The high number of false positives overwhelms the true predictions. 

To address this issue, we have developed a framework called SMIRP, which creates species-specific miRNA prediction systems by utilizing sequence conservation and phylogenetic distance information. When applied to three different prediction systems representing two types of classifiers (support vector machine and Random Forest) and based on three different feature sets, with both human-specific and taxon-wide training data, our framework significantly improves specificity and precision for four non-human test species. The SMIRP framework has the potential to be applied to all miRNA prediction systems, and we anticipate substantial improvements in precision and specificity while maintaining sensitivity, regardless of the chosen machine learning technique.

title: CD8 Cells of Patients with Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Display Functional Exhaustion: The Latter Is Reversed, In Vitro, by TLR2 Agonists
text: Leishmania mexicana (Lm) is responsible for causing localized (LCL) and diffuse (DCL) cutaneous leishmaniasis. DCL patients have a weakened cellular immune response, resulting in a chronic condition. While it is believed that CD8 T lymphocytes (CD8) play a crucial role in clearing the infection, the exact role of CD8 cytotoxicity in controlling the disease remains unclear. Studies have shown that DCL patients have lower levels of CD8 compared to LCL patients, and treatment for leishmaniasis helps restore CD8 levels. Given the strong response of CD8 against Leishmania parasites, we aimed to investigate potential functional differences between CD8 from LCL and DCL patients. We compared the production of IFNγ, antigen-specific proliferation, and cytotoxicity of CD8 isolated from PBMC against autologous macrophages infected with Leishmania mexicana. Additionally, we examined tissue biopsies from both patient groups to determine if there was evidence of cytotoxicity associated with apoptotic cells in the lesions. Our findings revealed that CD8 cells from DCL patients exhibited low cytotoxicity, antigen-specific proliferation, and IFNγ production when stimulated with infected macrophages, in comparison to LCL patients. Furthermore, DCL patients had significantly fewer TUNEL+ cells in their lesions, indicating similarities to the cellular "exhaustion" observed in chronic infections. To restore the functional capacity of CD8 cells in DCL patients, we preincubated them with TLR2 agonists, specifically Lm lipophosphoglycan (LPG) or Pam3Cys. This pre-stimulation resulted in the restoration of cytotoxicity against infected macrophages, antigen-specific proliferation, and IFNγ production, while reducing the expression of PD-1, a molecule associated with cellular exhaustion. Our research suggests that the CD8 response is crucial for controlling Lm infection in LCL patients, and chronic infection in DCL patients leads to a state of CD8 functional exhaustion, potentially facilitating the spread of the disease. This study is the first to demonstrate the presence of functionally exhausted CD8 T lymphocytes in DCL patients and highlights the ability of TLR2 ligands to restore the effector mechanisms of CD8 T lymphocytes from DCL patients against Leishmania mexicana-infected macrophages.

title: Enhancer Evolution across 20 Mammalian Species
text: The mammalian radiation has led to significant changes in noncoding regions of the genome, but our understanding of regulatory evolution in mammals is still incomplete. In this study, we examine the evolution of promoters and enhancers that are active in the liver across 20 mammalian species from six different orders. We do this by analyzing the genomic enrichment of H3K27 acetylation and H3K4 trimethylation. Our findings show that the rapid evolution of enhancers is a common characteristic of mammalian genomes. Interestingly, most of the recently evolved enhancers come from ancestral DNA adaptation, rather than the expansion of repeat elements specific to certain lineages. On the other hand, nearly all liver promoters are conserved either partially or fully across these species. Additionally, our data reveals that recently evolved enhancers can be linked to genes that are undergoing positive selection, highlighting the usefulness of this approach in identifying regulatory adaptations in genomic sequences. These results provide valuable insights into the functional genetics that drive mammalian regulatory evolution.

title: IDH1 mutations alter citric acid cycle metabolism and increase dependence on oxidative mitochondrial metabolism.
text: The metabolic effects of oncogenic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1/2) in various cancers are not fully understood. To address this, we conducted a study using isogenic cell lines with heterozygous IDH1/2 mutations and performed (13)C metabolic flux analysis. Our findings revealed that IDH1-mutant cells exhibited increased oxidative tricarboxylic acid metabolism and decreased reductive glutamine metabolism under hypoxic conditions, whereas IDH2-mutant cells did not show these changes. However, inhibiting the mutant IDH1 enzyme function did not reverse the defect in reductive carboxylation activity. Additionally, this metabolic reprogramming made IDH1-mutant cells more sensitive to hypoxia or electron transport chain inhibition in vitro. Moreover, when grown as subcutaneous xenografts in a hypoxic in vivo microenvironment, IDH1-mutant cells exhibited poor growth. Overall, our results suggest potential therapeutic strategies to target the specific metabolic vulnerabilities associated with IDH1 mutation.

title: The assessment of the prognostic value of tumor markers and cytokines as SCCAg, CYFRA 21.1, IL-6, VEGF and sTNF receptors in patients with squamous cell cervical cancer, particularly with early stage of the disease
text: The purpose of this study is to assess the predictive significance of tumor markers, such as squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCCAg) and cytokeratin-19 fragment (CYFRA 21.1), as well as interleukin 6 (IL-6), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor I (sTNF RI), and sTNF RII in patients diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. The study included 138 patients classified as stage I-IVA according to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) criteria. All data were collected from a single oncology center. Over a 10-year follow-up period, 56 cases of relapse and 53 deaths were recorded, with 45% of patients experiencing recurrent disease in the early stages. The serum levels of SCCAg, CYFRA 21.1, IL-6, VEGF, sTNF RI, and sTNF RII were measured in all patients prior to treatment. The log-rank test and Cox regression model were used to evaluate the probability of disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). The analysis of the ROC curve revealed that SCCAg and IL-6 had the largest area under the curve for patients with recurrence, while SCCAg and VEGF were most significant for patients who died. Cox analysis indicated that SCCAg was the only independent prognostic factor for DFS, while IL-6 and SCCAg were significant for OS. However, in patients with early-stage disease, VEGF was a prognostic factor for DFS, and IL-6 and CYFRA 21.1 were significant for OS. Therefore, the serum levels of VEGF, CYFRA 21.1, and IL-6 before treatment in patients with early-stage cervical cancer appear to be important prognostic factors.

title: Combination of platelet count and mean platelet volume (COP-MPV) predicts postoperative prognosis in both resectable early and advanced stage esophageal squamous cell cancer patients
text: The objective of this study is to identify the most influential prognostic factor in routine blood tests for patients with esophageal squamous cell cancer (ESCC). Various laboratory tests were assessed, including those that measure red blood cell parameters (hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and red blood cell distribution width), platelet morphological parameters (mean platelet volume and platelet count), blood coagulation status (D-dimer), and a tumor biomarker (CA19-9). Additionally, known inflammatory indices (NLR and PLR) were calculated. A total of 468 ESCC patients diagnosed between December 2005 and December 2008 were retrospectively analyzed. Through univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard analyses, it was discovered that platelet count and mean platelet volume were significantly associated with overall survival and disease-free survival in ESCC patients, with optimal cutoff values of 212 and 10.6, respectively. Furthermore, a combination of preoperative platelet count and mean platelet volume (referred to as COP-MPV) was calculated as follows: patients with both platelet count (≥212 × 10(9) L(-1)) and mean platelet volume (≥10.6 fL) elevation were assigned a score of 2, while patients with one or neither were assigned a score of 1 or 0. COP-MPV was identified as an independent prognostic factor for overall survival (hazard ratio 0.378, 95% confidence interval 0.241 to 0.593, P < 0.001, 0/2) and disease-free survival (hazard ratio 0.341, 95% confidence interval 0.218 to 0.534, P < 0.001, 0/2) in multivariate analyses. Subgroup analyses for early (stages I and II) and locally advanced (stage III) patients revealed that COP-MPV was significantly associated with overall survival and disease-free survival in each group (P = 0.025 and P = 0.018 for overall survival, and P = 0.029 and P = 0.002 for disease-free survival). In conclusion, COP-MPV is considered a promising predictor for postoperative survival in ESCC patients.

title: Dementia incidence and mortality in middle-income countries, and associations with indicators of cognitive reserve: a 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based cohort study
text:
BACKGROUND: Several cohort studies conducted in low- and middle-income countries have suggested a lower incidence of dementia compared to high-income countries. In this study, we aimed to assess the incidence of dementia using criteria from the 10/66 Dementia Research Group and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) IV. We also examined the impact of dementia at baseline on mortality, as well as the independent effects of age, sex, socioeconomic position, and indicators of cognitive reserve.

METHODS: We conducted a population-based cohort study involving individuals aged 65 years and older living in urban areas of Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Venezuela, as well as rural and urban areas of Peru, Mexico, and China. We identified incident cases of 10/66 and DSM-IV dementia 3-5 years after the start of the cohort. Information on age, sex, educational level, literacy, occupational attainment, and household assets was collected through questionnaires. Mortality data were obtained from all study sites, and for deceased participants, interviews were conducted with friends or relatives to determine the likelihood of dementia before death.

FINDINGS: A total of 12,887 participants were interviewed at baseline, of whom 11,718 were dementia-free. Among these, 8,137 (69%) were reinterviewed, contributing to 34,718 person-years of follow-up. The incidence of 10/66 dementia ranged from 18.2 to 30.4 per 1000 person-years, which was 1.4-2.7 times higher than the incidence of DSM-IV dementia (9.9-15.7 per 1000 person-years). Individuals with dementia at baseline had mortality hazards 1.56-5.69 times higher than those without dementia. Informant reports indicated a high incidence of dementia before death, suggesting that overall incidence could be 4-19% higher if these data were included. Incidence of 10/66 dementia was independently associated with older age, female sex, and lower education, but not with occupational attainment.

INTERPRETATION: Our findings support the cognitive reserve hypothesis, demonstrating that education, literacy, verbal fluency, and motor sequencing provide significant protection against the onset of dementia in both middle-income and high-income countries.

FUNDING: This study was funded by the Wellcome Trust Health Consequences of Population Change Programme, WHO, US Alzheimer's Association, and FONACIT/ CDCH/ UCV.

title: Regulation of immune responses by extracellular vesicles
text: Extracellular vesicles, such as exosomes, are small sacs made of membranes that come from either multivesicular bodies or the plasma membrane. Almost all cell types release these vesicles, which then enter the body's fluids. These vesicles contain a specific set of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids that come from the original cell. It is believed that extracellular vesicles play a crucial role in communication between cells, both locally and throughout the body, as they transfer their contents, including proteins, lipids, and RNAs, from one cell to another. These vesicles are involved in various physiological processes, and those from both immune and non-immune cells have important roles in regulating the immune system. Additionally, researchers are developing and testing therapies based on extracellular vesicles for the treatment of inflammatory diseases, autoimmune disorders, and cancer. Considering the immense potential of extracellular vesicles in therapy, this Review focuses on their ability to modulate immune responses and their potential applications in treatment.

title: Risk of cancer after low doses of ionising radiation: retrospective cohort study in 15 countries.
text:
AIMS
The objectives of this study were to provide accurate estimates of the risk of cancer following prolonged exposure to low doses of ionising radiation and to enhance the scientific foundation of radiation protection standards for various environmental, occupational, and medical diagnostic exposures.

METHODS
A multinational retrospective cohort study was conducted to examine cancer mortality rates. The study focused on cohorts of nuclear industry workers from 15 different countries. A total of 407,391 workers were individually monitored for external radiation, with a cumulative follow-up period of 5.2 million person-years.

OUTCOMES
The main outcome measurements were estimates of excess relative risks per sievert (Sv) of radiation dose for mortality from cancers other than leukaemia, as well as from leukaemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. These were the primary causes of death considered by radiation protection authorities.

RESULTS
The study found that the excess relative risk for cancers other than leukaemia was 0.97 per Sv, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.14 to 1.97. Analyses of causes of death related or unrelated to smoking indicated that while smoking may contribute to the increased risk, it is unlikely to account for the entire effect. The excess relative risk for leukaemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukaemia was 1.93 per Sv, ranging from less than 0 to 8.47. Based on these estimates, it is estimated that 1-2% of cancer deaths among workers in this cohort may be attributed to radiation.

CONCLUSIONS
This study, the largest ever conducted on nuclear workers, found that the risk estimates for cancer were higher than those currently used for radiation protection standards. However, the results were statistically compatible with the existing standards. The findings suggest that there is a small excess risk of cancer, even at the low doses and dose rates typically experienced by nuclear workers in this study.

title: Gamma-Secretase Represents a Therapeutic Target for the Treatment of Invasive Glioma Mediated by the p75 Neurotrophin Receptor
text: The p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75(NTR)) is a versatile signaling protein that plays a crucial role in the aggressive nature of malignant gliomas. In this study, we demonstrate that the neurotrophin-dependent regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP) of p75(NTR) is essential for glioma invasion, and we uncover a previously unidentified approach for targeted therapy against gliomas. By using cleavage-resistant versions of p75(NTR) or administering gamma-secretase inhibitors to animals with p75(NTR)-positive brain tumors, we observed a significant reduction in glioma invasion and an increase in survival time. Furthermore, we detected the proteolytic processing of p75(NTR) in patient tumor samples and brain tumor initiating cells that expressed p75(NTR). This research underscores the significance of p75(NTR) as a potential therapeutic target, suggesting that gamma-secretase inhibitors could be directly applied in clinical settings for the treatment of malignant gliomas.

title: Preliminary assessment of inhaled nitric oxide for acute vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease.
text:
The occurrence of vaso-occlusion plays a central role in the painful crises and organ damage experienced by individuals with sickle cell disease. The abnormal regulation of vascular tone, adhesion, platelet activation, and inflammation, which is dependent on nitric oxide, contributes to the development of vaso-occlusion. Nitric oxide shows potential as a treatment for vaso-occlusion by targeting the underlying mechanisms of the disease. 

The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of inhaled nitric oxide (INO) in treating vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients. The study was designed as a prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial and took place between September 1999 and October 2001 at an urban, tertiary care children's hospital in the United States. 

Twenty patients between the ages of 10 and 21, who were experiencing severe acute vaso-occlusive crisis due to sickle cell disease, participated in the study. The patients were randomly assigned to receive either INO (80 ppm with 21% final concentration of inspired oxygen) or a placebo (21% inspired oxygen) for a duration of 4 hours. 

The main outcome measure was the change in pain levels after 4 hours of inhalation compared to preinhalation pain, which was measured using a 10-cm visual analog scale (VAS). Secondary outcome measures included pain levels over 6 hours, parenteral narcotic use over 24 hours, duration of hospitalization, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and methemoglobin concentration. 

The results showed that the preinhalation VAS pain scores were similar in both the INO and placebo groups. The decrease in VAS pain scores after 4 hours was 2.0 cm in the INO group and 1.2 cm in the placebo group. Repeated-measures analysis of variance indicated that the INO group experienced a greater reduction in pain scores compared to the placebo group. Morphine use over 6 hours was significantly lower in the INO group, but there was no significant difference in morphine use over 4 hours or 24 hours. The duration of hospitalization was shorter in the INO group, although this difference was not statistically significant. No adverse effects of INO were observed. 

In conclusion, the findings of this preliminary study suggest that INO may be beneficial in treating acute vaso-occlusive crisis. Further investigation is warranted to validate these results.

title: Corresponding author:
text: Over time, cytogenetic analysis methods have evolved and become a standard part of laboratory testing, providing valuable diagnostic and prognostic information for hematologic disorders. Karyotypic abnormalities contribute to our understanding of the molecular causes of diseases and help guide the use of appropriate treatments. The majority of advancements in this field have come from metaphase cytogenetics (MC), but recently, new molecular technologies have been introduced to complement MC and overcome the limitations of traditional cytogenetics, such as the need for cell culture. Comparative genomic hybridization and single nucleotide polymorphism arrays (CGH-A; SNP-A) can be used to analyze unbalanced chromosomal defects in somatic or clonal cells. SNP-A, in particular, allows for the detection of copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, a type of genetic change that cannot be identified using MC but may have significant implications for disease development. Despite the inability to detect balanced translocations, whole genome scanning arrays have a higher success rate in identifying chromosomal defects in patients with hematologic malignancies. The discovery of new chromosomal abnormalities, including somatic uniparental disomy, may lead to more accurate prognostic schemes for various diseases.

title: Rare Variants Create Synthetic Genome-Wide Associations
text:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have discovered over 2,000 common variants that are potentially linked to common diseases or related traits. Many of these variants have been replicated and are widely accepted as markers for these conditions. It is commonly believed that these markers indicate the presence of a nearby common causal site, which is associated with the marker. As a result, extensive efforts have been made to identify these causal sites through resequencing.

However, we propose an alternative explanation. We suggest that variants that are much less common than the associated marker may create what we call "synthetic associations." These associations occur stochastically, meaning they happen by chance, and are more likely to be found in association with one allele at the common site rather than the other. While synthetic associations are a theoretical possibility, they have not been systematically explored as an explanation for GWAS findings.

To investigate this further, we conducted computer simulations to demonstrate the conditions under which synthetic associations can arise and how they can be identified. Our simulations show that synthetic associations are not only possible but also inevitable. Furthermore, under simple and reasonable genetic models, they are likely to explain or contribute to many of the signals identified in recent genome-wide association studies.

To illustrate the behavior of synthetic associations in real datasets, we examined rare causal mutations responsible for hearing loss and sickle cell anemia. We found that these mutations create genome-wide significant synthetic associations, with the latter extending over a 2.5-Mb interval and encompassing numerous associated variants.

In conclusion, uncommon or rare genetic variants can easily generate synthetic associations that are mistakenly attributed to common variants. This possibility should be carefully considered when interpreting and following up on GWAS signals.

title: Decoding of Cytoplasmic Ca2+ Oscillations through the Spatial Signature Drives Gene Expression
text: The occurrence of Ca(2+) oscillations in the cytoplasm is a widespread method of cellular communication that triggers various responses [1, 2]. These oscillations are considered the natural way in which Ca(2+) signals are transmitted because they happen even with low levels of stimulus intensity [3]. It is believed that the amplitude and frequency of Ca(2+) oscillations convey information that leads to the activation of specific targets downstream [4-6]. In this study, we demonstrate that the spatial distribution of Ca(2+) within the oscillation is crucial. When plasmalemmal Ca(2+) extrusion was inhibited, Ca(2+) oscillations in mast cells induced by different concentrations of agonists in the presence or absence of external Ca(2+) were indistinguishable. However, only oscillations accompanied by Ca(2+) entry through store-operated CRAC channels triggered gene expression. Increasing cytoplasmic Ca(2+) buffering prevented oscillations but did not affect gene activation. Therefore, it is the local influx of Ca(2+) and not the global oscillations that drives gene expression at physiological levels of stimulation. Instead of simply maintaining Ca(2+) oscillations by replenishing stores, we propose that the role of oscillations is to activate CRAC channels, ensuring the generation of spatially restricted Ca(2+) signals that drive gene activation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spatial profile of a Ca(2+) oscillation provides a new mechanism by which a versatile messenger specifically activates gene expression.

title: Effect of glucosamine on pain-related disability in patients with chronic low back pain and degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of glucosamine on patients with chronic low back pain (LBP) and degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis (OA). The study was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted at Oslo University Hospital Outpatient Clinic in Norway. A total of 250 patients over the age of 25 with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA were included in the study.

The participants were divided into two groups: one group received a daily dose of 1500 mg of oral glucosamine, while the other group received a placebo. The intervention period lasted for 6 months, and the effects were assessed at the end of the intervention period and again at 1 year (6 months post-intervention).

The primary outcome measure was pain-related disability, which was measured using the Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ). Secondary outcomes included pain ratings at rest and during activity, as well as quality of life measured using the EuroQol-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D) instrument. Data was collected at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year.

The results showed that there was no significant difference in pain-related disability between the glucosamine and placebo groups at baseline, 6 months, and 1 year. The mean RMDQ scores were similar for both groups at all time points. There were also no significant differences in pain ratings at rest and during activity, as well as quality of life, between the two groups.

Mild adverse events were reported by both groups, with no significant difference between them.
