In conclusion, the study found that 6-month treatment with oral glucosamine did not result in reduced pain-related disability in patients with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA compared to placebo. The trial was registered on clinicaltrials.gov with the identifier NCT00404079.

title: Adult cervicocerebral artery dissection: a single-center study of 301 Finnish patients.
text:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
There have been limited studies conducted on the potential risk factors, comorbidity, and prognostic factors in adult spontaneous cervicocerebral artery dissection (CAD). This retrospective, hospital-based analysis aimed to assess the prognostic factors and association of CAD with vascular risk factors in 301 consecutive Finnish patients diagnosed between 1994 and 2007.

METHODS
A retrospective analysis was conducted on 301 Finnish patients diagnosed with CAD between 1994 and 2007. The study aimed to identify prognostic factors and assess the association of CAD with vascular risk factors.

RESULTS
Out of the 301 patients, 68% were men. Women tended to be younger than men. The prevalence of migraine was higher in patients with CAD (36% of all patients), particularly those with visual aura (63% of all migraineurs), compared to the general Finnish population. Smoking was also more common in CAD patients. At the 3-month mark, 83% of patients achieved a favorable outcome. Poorer outcomes were associated with occlusion of the dissected artery, internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD), and recent infection in patients with infarction. ICAD patients were less likely to experience brain infarction, but the strokes they did have were more severe. During the follow-up period (mean 4.0 years, 1186 patient years), seven patients (2.3%) died, and six patients (2%) experienced CAD recurrence.

CONCLUSIONS
This study provides evidence supporting the association of CAD with male sex, and suggests a possible association with smoking and migraine. Occlusion of the dissected artery, ICAD, and infection appear to be linked to poorer outcomes.

title: Genetic variation and gastric cancer risk: a field synopsis and meta-analysis.
text:
The prevalence of genetic susceptibility to sporadic gastric carcinoma has been extensively studied, but there has been a lack of comprehensive and quantitative analysis. In this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the association between DNA variation and the risk of developing stomach cancer. We assessed the credibility of the results using the Venice criteria and calculated the false positive report probability (FPRP) to validate the significance of the findings. Additionally, we performed subgroup meta-analyses based on ethnicity, tumor histology, tumor site, and Helicobacter pylori infection status. 

Our literature search identified 824 relevant studies, which included a total of 2,530,706 subjects (10.3% of whom were cases). These studies investigated 2,841 polymorphisms in 952 different genes. Overall, we conducted 456 primary and subgroup meta-analyses on 156 variants in 101 genes. We found 11 variants that were significantly associated with the risk of gastric cancer and had a high level of summary evidence. These variants included MUC1 rs2070803 at 1q22 (diffuse carcinoma subgroup), MTX1 rs2075570 at 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2294008 at 8q24.2 (non-cardia), PRKAA1 rs13361707 5p13 (non-cardia), PLCE1 rs2274223 10q23 (cardia), TGFBR2 rs3087465 3p22 (Asian), PKLR rs3762272 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2976392 (intestinal), GSTP1 rs1695 11q13 (Asian), CASP8 rs3834129 2q33 (mixed), and TNF rs1799724 6p21.3 (mixed). The first nine variants had a low FPRP, indicating a high level of credibility. We also identified 110 polymorphisms with lower quality but still significant associations. 

In conclusion, we have identified several high-quality biomarkers of gastric cancer susceptibility. These findings will be used to create an annually updated online resource that will be valuable for studying the genetics of gastric carcinoma and may contribute to future screening programs.

title: Structure and function of the blood–brain barrier
text: The central nervous system (CNS) relies on precise neural signaling, which necessitates a tightly controlled microenvironment. Three crucial interfaces between the blood and the CNS, namely the blood-brain barrier (BBB), blood-CSF barrier, and arachnoid barrier, form barriers to ensure this control. Among these interfaces, the BBB, located at the level of brain microvessel endothelium, plays a major role in the exchange between blood and the CNS. The structure and function of the BBB can be summarized as follows: it consists of tight junctions formed by endothelial cells, creating a physical barrier, and membrane transporters and vesicular mechanisms, forming a transport barrier. Additionally, the roles of associated cells, such as astrocytic glial cells' endfeet, pericytes, and microglia, are outlined. The development of the BBB during embryonic stages and its changes in pathology are also described. The BBB is subject to both short-term and long-term regulation, which can be disrupted in pathological conditions. Therefore, any drug discovery or delivery program aiming to target or avoid the CNS must take into account the unique characteristics of the BBB.

title: Golli protein negatively regulates store depletion-induced calcium influx in T cells.
text: The regulation of calcium influx in T cell activation and differentiation is not fully understood. However, our study reveals that golli protein, a product of the myelin basic protein gene, plays a crucial role in this process. Golli-deficient T cells exhibited hyperproliferation and increased calcium entry upon T cell receptor stimulation. We also discovered that golli controls calcium influx by inhibiting store depletion-induced calcium entry. When the myristoylation site on golli was mutated, its association with the plasma membrane was disrupted, and its inhibitory effect on calcium influx was reversed. This suggests that golli's membrane association is necessary for its inhibitory function. Overall, our findings demonstrate that golli has a unique mechanism of action in regulating T cell activation by modulating calcium homeostasis.

title: Extracellular vesicles derived from renal cancer stem cells induce a pro-tumorigenic phenotype in mesenchymal stromal cells
text: The presence of cancer stem cells (CSCs) in renal carcinomas has been proven to contribute to tumor growth and metastasis. These CSCs release extracellular vesicles (EVs) that contain various molecules and can cause epigenetic changes in target cells. Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs) can be influenced by tumor signals and recruited to tumor sites. However, the exact role of MSCs in tumor development is still a topic of debate, as both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects have been observed. This study aimed to investigate the interaction between renal CSC-derived EVs and MSCs in tumor development. The results showed that CSC-derived EVs caused lasting changes in MSCs, leading to increased expression of genes associated with cell migration, matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and tumor growth. EV-stimulated MSCs displayed enhanced migration towards the tumor environment in vitro. Additionally, these EV-stimulated MSCs promoted the migration of renal tumor cells and induced the formation of vessel-like structures. In vivo experiments demonstrated that EV-stimulated MSCs supported tumor growth and vascularization when co-injected with renal tumor cells. In conclusion, CSC-derived EVs induce phenotypical changes in MSCs that contribute to tumor growth.

title: In vivo effect of chronic hypoxia on the neurochemical profile of the developing rat hippocampus.
text: The cognitive impairments observed in children with cyanotic congenital heart disease indicate that the developing hippocampus may be involved. It is possible that chronic postnatal hypoxia experienced during infancy plays a role in these impairments. In order to understand the biochemical mechanisms of hippocampal injury in chronic hypoxia, a study was conducted using a rat model of chronic postnatal hypoxia. The study evaluated a neurochemical profile consisting of 15 metabolite concentrations and 2 metabolite ratios in the hippocampus using in vivo 1H NMR spectroscopy at 9.4 T. Chronic hypoxia was induced by continuously exposing rats to 10% oxygen from postnatal day 3 to day 28. The concentrations of 15 metabolites were measured on postnatal day 14, day 21, and day 28 and compared to a control group of rats in a normoxic environment. The developmental trajectory of neurochemicals in chronic hypoxia was similar to that seen in the normoxic group. However, chronic hypoxia had an impact on the concentrations of several neurochemicals, including aspartate, creatine, phosphocreatine, GABA, glutamate, glutamine, glutathione, myoinositol, N-acetylaspartate (NAA), phosphorylethanolamine, and the ratios of phosphocreatine/creatine (PCr/Cr) and glutamate/glutamine (Glu/Gln). The increased PCr/Cr ratio suggests decreased brain energy consumption. Based on the known connection between excitatory neurotransmission and brain energy metabolism, it is hypothesized that elevated levels of glutamate, Glu/Gln ratio, and GABA indicate suppressed excitatory neurotransmission in an energy-limited environment. The decreased levels of NAA and phosphorylethanolamine suggest reduced neuronal integrity and phospholipid metabolism. The altered neurochemistry in the hippocampus during development may contribute to the cognitive impairments observed in infants at risk of chronic hypoxia.

title: Noncoding Transcription by RNA Polymerase Pol IVb/Pol V Mediates Transcriptional Silencing of Overlapping and Adjacent Genes
text: Nuclear transcription is not limited to genes but occurs throughout the intergenic and noncoding regions of eukaryotic genomes. The functional significance of this widespread noncoding transcription is largely unknown. Our research demonstrates that Arabidopsis RNA polymerase IVb/Pol V, a complex nuclear enzyme essential for silencing transposons and other repetitive elements through siRNA-mediated gene silencing, transcribes intergenic and noncoding sequences. This transcription process facilitates the formation of heterochromatin and the silencing of neighboring and overlapping genes. The activity of Pol IVb/Pol V transcription relies on the presence of the chromatin-remodeling protein DRD1, but it is not dependent on siRNA production. However, both Pol IVb/Pol V transcription and siRNA generation are necessary for the suppression of transposons, indicating that Pol IVb/Pol V generates RNAs or chromatin structures that act as scaffolds for siRNA-mediated heterochromatin formation. The function of Pol IVb/Pol V provides a solution to the paradox of epigenetic control, where transcription is required to silence the same genomic region.

title: Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis
text: The metabolism of choline and phosphatidylcholine by the bacteria in the intestines produces trimethylamine (TMA), which is then converted into trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), a substance that promotes the development of atherosclerosis. In this study, we show that the metabolism of dietary L-carnitine, a type of trimethylamine found in red meat, by the intestinal bacteria also leads to the production of TMAO and accelerates the progression of atherosclerosis in mice. When compared to vegans or vegetarians, omnivorous individuals produced higher levels of TMAO after consuming L-carnitine, and this was due to the presence of specific bacterial species in their feces. Furthermore, elevated levels of plasma L-carnitine in individuals undergoing cardiac evaluation were associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease and major adverse cardiac events, but only if they also had high TMAO levels. In mice, chronic supplementation of L-carnitine in the diet altered the composition of the gut microbiota, increased the synthesis of TMA and TMAO, and promoted the development of atherosclerosis. However, these effects were not observed when the intestinal bacteria were suppressed. Additionally, in mice with a normal gut microbiota, supplementation with TMAO, carnitine, or choline reduced the reverse cholesterol transport in the body. These findings suggest that the intestinal bacteria may play a role in the well-known association between high consumption of red meat and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: Hepatotoxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy in adults infected with human immunodeficiency virus and the role of hepatitis C or B virus infection.
text: The purpose of this study was to determine if the incidence of severe liver damage during antiretroviral therapy is similar for all combinations of antiretroviral drugs, and to understand the role of chronic viral hepatitis in its development. The study was conducted at a university-based urban HIV clinic and included 298 patients who were prescribed new antiretroviral therapies between January 1996 and January 1998. Of these patients, 211 received protease inhibitors as part of combination therapy and 87 received dual nucleoside analog regimens. Approximately 52% of the patients had chronic hepatitis C infection and 2.7% had chronic hepatitis B infection. The main outcome measure was severe liver damage, defined as a significant change in levels of certain enzymes in the blood. The results showed that severe liver damage occurred in 10.4% of the patients, with a higher incidence observed in those using ritonavir. However, there was no significant difference in the incidence of liver damage among the other treatment groups. While chronic viral hepatitis was associated with an increased risk of severe liver damage in patients not using ritonavir, the majority of patients with hepatitis C or B did not experience significant toxic effects. The rate of severe toxicity with any protease inhibitor in patients with hepatitis C infection was 12.2%. In multivariate analysis, only ritonavir and an increase in CD4 cell count were associated with severe liver damage. No irreversible outcomes were observed in patients with severe liver damage. In conclusion, the data suggest that the use of ritonavir may increase the risk of severe liver damage. However, the study does not support withholding protease inhibitor therapy from patients coinfected with hepatitis B or C virus.

title: Mutations in the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase pathway predict for antitumor activity of the inhibitor PX-866 whereas oncogenic Ras is a dominant predictor for resistance.
text: The effectiveness of the PI3K inhibitor PX-866 was tested on 13 different human tumor xenografts derived from cell lines of various tissue origins. It was found that the presence of mutant PI3K (PIK3CA) and loss of PTEN activity were sufficient, but not necessary, indicators of sensitivity to PX-866 in the presence of wild-type Ras. However, tumors with mutant oncogenic Ras showed resistance to the inhibitor, even when coexisting mutations in PIK3CA were present. The level of activation of PI3K signaling, as measured by tumor phosphorylated Ser(473)-Akt, was not enough to predict the response to PX-866 in vivo. Further analysis using reverse-phase protein array revealed that the downstream targets c-Myc and cyclin B, which are dependent on Ras, were elevated in cell lines that were resistant to PX-866 in vivo. Additional studies using an H-Ras construct showed that mutant Ras mediates resistance by utilizing multiple pathways for tumorigenesis, specifically Raf, RalGDS, and PI3K. Understanding the role of Ras and its downstream signaling pathways in resistance to PI3K inhibition can be valuable in selecting patients for clinical trials and developing effective combinations with other targeted agents.

title: Changing mortality patterns in East and West Germany and Poland. II: short-term trends during transition and in the 1990s.
text:
The aim of this study was to analyze the changes in life expectancy and mortality patterns in the former German Democratic Republic (GDR) and Poland during the political transition and throughout the 1990s. The researchers used a decomposition method to examine life expectancy by age and cause of death. They analyzed data from 1988/89 and 1990/91 for the GDR and Poland during the transition period, and data from 1992-97 for Germany and 1991-96 for Poland after the transition.

The results showed that male life expectancy at birth declined by almost one year during the transition in both the GDR and Poland. This decline was mainly due to increased death rates from external causes and circulatory diseases. In Poland, female life expectancy decreased by 0.3 years, primarily due to rising circulatory mortality among the elderly. In the GDR, rising death rates in children and young adults were offset by declining circulatory mortality among those over 70, resulting in a minimal change in female life expectancy.

Between 1991/92 and 1996/97, male life expectancy at birth increased by 2.4 years in the GDR, 1.2 years in the old Federal Republic of Germany, and 2.0 years in Poland. For women, the increases were 2.3, 0.9, and 1.2 years, respectively. In the GDR and Poland, the overall improvement in life expectancy was mainly driven by declining mortality among men aged 40-64, while in women, those over 65 contributed the most to the gains.

The study found that changes in mortality among men aged 15-39 accounted for a 0.4-year increase in life expectancy at birth in both the GDR and Poland, primarily due to decreases in deaths from external causes. Among those over 40, the GDR had greater contributions to changing life expectancy in both sexes, mainly due to circulatory diseases.

In Germany, there was a persistent east-west gap in life expectancy of 2.1 years in men in 1997, largely attributed to external causes, diseases of the digestive system, and circulatory diseases. The one-year gap in female life expectancy was primarily explained by higher death rates from circulatory diseases among the elderly.

In conclusion, this study highlights the health effects of political transition. Post-transition improvements in life expectancy and mortality were more significant in East Germany compared to Poland. Changes in dietary patterns and medical care may have played a role in shaping post-transition mortality trends, particularly in Germany.

title: 0021-972X/06/$15.00/0 The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 91(3):760–771 Printed in U.S.A. Copyright © 2006 by The Endocrine Society doi: 10.1210/jc.2005-1923 REVIEW: Aromatase Inhibitors for Ovulation Induction
text:
Over the past 40 years, clomiphene citrate (CC) has been the primary treatment for anovulation in infertile women. While CC is effective, it can cause side effects such as antiestrogenic effects on the endometrium and cervical mucus, which may hinder pregnancy despite successful ovulation. Additionally, there is a higher risk of multiple pregnancies with CC compared to natural cycles. To address these issues, we propose using aromatase inhibitors (AIs) as a new method of ovulation induction that can avoid the adverse effects of CC. The objective of this review is to explain the different mechanisms of action for CC and AIs and compare their efficacy in inducing ovulation. 

To gather evidence, we conducted a systematic review of published studies that compared CC and AI treatments for ovulation induction or augmentation. We included controlled and noncontrolled studies, as well as studies that combined these treatments with gonadotropins. We found that there were limited controlled studies on AIs for ovulation induction, with most studies being pilot or preliminary comparisons. However, based on these studies, it seems that AIs are just as effective as CC in inducing ovulation, but without the antiestrogenic side effects. AIs also result in lower estrogen levels and have good pregnancy rates with a lower incidence of multiple pregnancies compared to CC. When used in combination with gonadotropins for assisted reproductive technologies, AIs reduce the required dose of FSH and improve the response in poor responders. 

In conclusion, preliminary evidence suggests that AIs may replace CC in the future due to their similar efficacy and reduced side effect profile. However, there is still a lack of definitive studies in the form of randomized controlled trials comparing CC with AIs. Although the use of AIs for ovulation induction is increasing worldwide, further research is needed to establish their effectiveness.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus: lack of evidence for common treatments.
text: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is frequently diagnosed in extremely premature infants, particularly those with lung disease. Various treatments are commonly employed to close the PDA. However, despite extensive research spanning almost three decades, the question of whether the advantages of these treatments in preventing ductal patency or promoting closure outweigh the associated risks remains unresolved. The authors of this article seldom utilize treatments aimed at closing the PDA. This review examines three factors supporting this cautious approach: the rates at which the ductus arteriosus spontaneously closes, the adverse effects of persistent ductal patency, and the benefits and risks associated with treatments for closure.

title: Gene therapy of arthritis with TCR isolated from the inflamed paw.
text:
The use of biological agents has greatly advanced the treatment of autoimmune diseases in recent years. However, some of these biologics have severe side effects, such as tuberculosis and other infections. This highlights the urgent need for targeted methods of delivering these therapeutic agents that do not affect the entire body. 

In our study, we aimed to treat arthritis in a mouse model by using T cells that expressed a regulatory molecule and were specifically directed to the inflamed paw. To do this, we first identified the TCR alphabeta genes that were accumulating in the inflamed paw of mice with collagen-induced arthritis (CIA). We used a combination of single-strand chain polymorphism analysis of TCR and single-cell sorting to identify an expanded clone called B47. This clone was autoreactive but not specific to type II collagen. 

In experiments conducted in vivo, we found that TCR genes from B47-transduced T cells accumulated in the inflamed paw. When we injected cells that were cotransduced with the B47 and soluble TNFRIg genes, we observed a significant suppression of CIA. The extent of suppression was correlated with the amount of TNFRIg transcripts in the hind paw, rather than the serum concentrations of TNFRIg. 

Furthermore, we discovered that T cells cotransduced with the B47 and intracellular Foxp3 genes were able to significantly suppress CIA. This was accompanied by reductions in the expression of TNF-alpha, IL-17A, and IL-1beta, as well as a decrease in bone destruction. Additionally, T cells cotransduced with B47 and Foxp3 genes were able to suppress the progression of established CIA. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that using autoreactive TCRs for immunosuppressive therapy is a promising strategy for treating arthritis. Whether these TCRs are used to deliver soluble or intracellular suppressive molecules, they have the potential to be effective in suppressing the disease.

title: Melatonin: A Mitochondrial Targeting Molecule Involving Mitochondrial Protection and Dynamics
text: There is speculation that mitochondria are the main source of melatonin synthesis. This speculation is supported by the discovery that aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase/serotonin N-acetyltransferase (AANAT/SNAT) is found in the mitochondria of oocytes, and that isolated mitochondria can produce melatonin. It is also believed that melatonin acts as an antioxidant specifically targeting mitochondria. It accumulates in mitochondria at high concentrations, against a concentration gradient, possibly through active transportation via mitochondrial melatonin transporters. Melatonin protects mitochondria by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibiting the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), and activating uncoupling proteins (UCPs). This helps to maintain optimal mitochondrial membrane potential and preserve mitochondrial functions. Melatonin also plays a role in regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics. In most cases, it reduces mitochondrial fission and promotes fusion. Mitochondrial dynamics follow an oscillatory pattern that aligns with the circadian secretory rhythm of melatonin in pinealeocytes and possibly other cells. Recent research has shown that melatonin promotes mitophagy and improves mitochondrial homeostasis.

title: Self-reported health status and access to health services in a sample of prisoners in Italy
text: The aim of this cross-sectional study was to examine the self-reported health status, quality of life, and access to health services among male prisoners in Italy. A total of 908 prisoners were given an anonymous questionnaire covering demographic and detention characteristics, self-reported health status and quality of life, access to health services, lifestyles, and participation in preventive, social, and rehabilitation programs. Out of the 908 prisoners, 650 agreed to participate and returned the questionnaire. The results showed that 31.6% of prisoners reported a poor perceived health status, while 43.5% reported a poor quality of life. Additionally, 60% stated that their health had worsened during their time in prison. Factors such as older age, lower education, psychiatric disorders, self-reported health problems upon entry to prison, and suicide attempts within prison were significantly associated with a perceived worse health status. At the time of the survey, 30% of prisoners reported a health problem upon entry to prison, and 82% reported a health problem at the time of the survey. The most commonly reported health problems included dental issues, arthritis or joint pain, eye problems, gastrointestinal diseases, emotional problems, and high blood pressure. On average, prisoners visited general practitioners six times in the previous year, and the frequency of medical visits was significantly associated with older age, sentenced prisoners, psychiatric disorders, and self-reported health problems upon entry to prison. These findings suggest that prisoners have a perceived poor health status and that there is a lack of specific care and health promotion programs available to them. It is crucial to implement programs that address risk behavior and prevent long-term effects of incarceration on prisoners' health.

title: BH3-only Protein Noxa Is a Mediator of Hypoxic Cell Death Induced by Hypoxia-inducible Factor 1α
text: Hypoxia, a condition characterized by low oxygen levels, is a common cause of cell death and is associated with various diseases such as stroke and chronic degenerative disorders. When cells are exposed to hypoxia, they activate certain genes to adapt to the changes in metabolic demands, reduce oxygen requirements, and eliminate irreversibly damaged cells. Through a technique called polymerase chain reaction–based suppression subtractive hybridization, we have identified a protein called Noxa from the BH3-only Bcl-2 family, which is differentially expressed in hypoxia. Noxa is believed to play a role in p53-induced apoptosis, a process of programmed cell death. Our research demonstrates that the Noxa promoter is directly responsive to hypoxia through a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α. By using antisense oligonucleotides to suppress Noxa expression, we were able to rescue cells from hypoxia-induced cell death and reduce the extent of tissue damage in an animal model of ischemia. Additionally, our findings suggest that the production of reactive oxygen species and the subsequent release of cytochrome c contribute to Noxa-mediated cell death under hypoxic conditions. Overall, our study provides evidence that Noxa is induced by HIF-1α and plays a role in hypoxic cell death.

title: Neutrophil extracellular chromatin traps connect innate immune response to autoimmunity
text: Autoantibodies to DNA and histones (chromatin) are the key antigen specificity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and related musculoskeletal disorders, but the mechanisms responsible for their induction remain unknown. However, this changed rapidly with the discovery of neutrophil extracellular chromatin traps (NETs), which were observed to play a crucial role in innate immune responses to various microbial pathogens. During an infectious process, neutrophils release nuclear chromatin into the extracellular space, forming complex NETs consisting of nuclear chromatin and antimicrobial proteins. These NETs immobilize and degrade microbial pathogens. In this article, we critically assess the evidence supporting NETs as a source for nuclear antigens in autoimmunity, compared to apoptotic bodies. We also explore the possibility that NET chromatin is a vital component of immune deposits in the development of glomerulonephritis in SLE and other autoimmune immune complex diseases.

title: Bcl2 Regulation by the Melanocyte Master Regulator Mitf Modulates Lineage Survival and Melanoma Cell Viability
text: Both Kit/SCF signaling and Mitf-dependent transcription play crucial roles in the development and pigmentation of melanocytes. In order to identify the genes regulated by Mitf in primary melanocytes, microarray studies were conducted. One of the genes identified as a target of Mitf was BCL2, which is known to cause melanocyte loss when deleted in the germline and showed synergistic effects with Mitf in mice. The regulation of BCL2 by Mitf was confirmed in melanocytes, melanoma cells, and through chromatin immunoprecipitation of the BCL2 promoter. Mitf also regulates BCL2 in osteoclasts, and both Mitf(mi/mi) and Bcl2(-/-) mice exhibit severe osteopetrosis. Disruption of Mitf in melanocytes or melanoma leads to significant apoptosis, which can be rescued by overexpression of BCL2. Clinically, analysis of primary human melanoma expression microarrays revealed a strong correlation between MITF and BCL2 expression. This correlation helps to explain the crucial roles of both Mitf and Bcl2 in the melanocyte lineage and the well-known resistance of melanoma to treatment.

title: YOKO HONDA AND SHUJI HONDA 1
text: The daf-2 gene network in Caenorhabditis elegans is responsible for regulating longevity. Mutations in the daf-2 gene, which codes for a member of the insulin receptor family, result in the Age phenotype (increased lifespan) and the constitutive dauer phenotype (a specialized larval form for dispersal). The Age phenotype is further enhanced by mutations in both the daf-2 and clk-1 genes, the latter being a homologue of yeast CAT5/COQ7 that regulates ubiquinone biosynthesis. Our study also revealed that the daf-2 mutation confers an oxidative stress resistance phenotype, which is further enhanced by the clk-1 mutation. Similar to the Age phenotype, the Oxr phenotype is regulated by the genetic pathway of insulin-like signaling from daf-2 to the daf-16 gene, a homologue of the HNF-3/forkhead transcription factor. These findings prompted us to investigate whether the insulin-like signaling pathway regulates the expression of antioxidant defense enzymes. We discovered that the mRNA level of the sod-3 gene, which encodes Mn-superoxide dismutase (SOD), is significantly higher in daf-2 mutants compared to the wild type. Furthermore, the increased sod-3 gene expression is regulated by the insulin-like signaling pathway. Although the clk-1 mutant alone does not exhibit the Oxr and increased sod-3 expression phenotypes, it enhances these traits in the daf-2 mutant, suggesting that clk-1 is involved in longevity through two mechanisms: the original clk-1 longevity program and the daf-2 longevity program. These observations indicate that the daf-2 gene network controls longevity by regulating the Mn-SOD-associated antioxidant defense system, which plays a crucial role in maintaining life efficiency during the dauer stage.

title: Brown Fat and Browning for the Treatment of Obesity and Related Metabolic Disorders
text: Brown fat is a specialized type of fat that has the ability to increase energy expenditure and generate heat. The discovery of active brown fat in adult humans, as well as the identification of new transcription factors that control the development of brown fat cells, has sparked significant interest in the study of this tissue. Researchers are now actively exploring the potential benefits of expanding or activating brown fat, as it has been shown to increase energy expenditure, create a negative energy balance, and prevent weight gain in mice. Additionally, brown fat has the unique ability to utilize glucose and lipids from the bloodstream, leading to improved glucose metabolism and blood lipid levels, independent of weight loss. Cold exposure and certain medications can induce the transformation of white fat cells into brown fat cells, a process known as browning. These newly formed brown fat cells, called beige adipocytes, have a different origin and molecular signature compared to classical brown fat cells, but they share similar characteristics such as high mitochondria content, expression of UCP1 (a protein involved in thermogenesis), and thermogenic capacity when activated. Increasing the browning of white fat may also be an effective strategy to enhance overall brown fat activity. Recent studies in humans have shown promising results, suggesting that findings from mouse studies can be replicated in humans. This makes brown fat a promising candidate for the treatment of obesity and related disorders.

title: Hypoxia-induced energy stress regulates mRNA translation and cell growth.
text: The lack of oxygen, known as hypoxia, has significant impacts on the metabolism and growth of cells. One way cells adapt to low oxygen levels is by activating a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). In our study, we found that hypoxia hinders the translation of mRNA by suppressing several important regulators, including eIF2alpha, eEF2, and the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) effectors 4EBP1, p70S6K, and rpS6. Interestingly, this inhibition occurs independently of HIF. Hypoxia also leads to a shortage of energy and activates the AMPK/TSC2/Rheb/mTOR pathway. The activation of AMPK, a protein kinase, during hypoxia also inhibits eEF2. Furthermore, the effects of hypoxia on cellular energy production and mTOR inhibition become more pronounced over time. Mutations in the TSC2 tumor suppressor gene provide cells with a growth advantage by suppressing hypoxic mTOR inhibition and hypoxia-induced G1 arrest. In summary, the inhibition of eIF2alpha, eEF2, and mTOR are important mechanisms, independent of HIF, that help conserve energy and promote cell survival in low oxygen conditions.

title: The dystonia-associated protein torsinA modulates synaptic vesicle recycling.
text: Most cases of early onset autosomal dominant primary dystonia are caused by the loss of a glutamic acid residue in the AAA-ATPase torsinA, which is associated with diverse cellular activities. In this study, we discovered that snapin, a protein that binds SNAP-25 and enhances the association of the SNARE complex with synaptotagmin, interacts with both the normal and mutant forms of torsinA. Snapin was found to co-localize with torsinA on dense core granules in PC12 cells and was recruited to perinuclear inclusions containing the mutant DeltaE-torsinA in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Based on these findings, we investigated synaptic vesicle recycling using the lipophilic dye FM1-43 and an antibody targeting an intravesicular epitope of synaptotagmin I. Our results showed that overexpression of normal torsinA negatively impacts synaptic vesicle endocytosis, while overexpression of DeltaE-torsinA in neuroblastoma cells increases FM1-43 uptake. Knockdown of snapin and/or torsinA using small interfering RNAs had a similar inhibitory effect on the exo-endocytic process. Furthermore, down-regulation of torsinA leads to the persistence of synaptotagmin I on the plasma membrane, which closely resembles the effect observed with overexpression of the DeltaE-torsinA mutant. Overall, these findings suggest that torsinA, in conjunction with snapin, plays a role in regulated exocytosis and that the DeltaE-torsinA mutant exerts its pathological effects through a loss of function mechanism. This may impact the neuronal uptake of neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, and contribute to the development of dystonic movements.

title: In vivo electroporation in the embryonic mouse central nervous system
text: This protocol outlines a fundamental technique for in vivo electroporation in embryonic mice's nervous system. By delivering electric pulses after microinjecting DNA into the brain ventricle or spinal cord central canal, efficient gene transfection into the nervous system is achieved. The use of forceps-type electrodes, which grasp the uterus and/or yolk sac containing the embryo, facilitates transfection. Within a span of 30 minutes, more than ten embryos from a single pregnant mouse can be operated on. Over 90% of the operated embryos survive, and of these survivors, more than 90% appropriately express the transfected genes. Neuronal gene expression persists for an extended period, even during postnatal stages, following electroporation. Consequently, this method can be employed to investigate the functions of genes not only in embryonic development but also in higher-order nervous system processes, such as learning.

title: Hierarchical phylogenetic models for analyzing multipartite sequence data.
text:
There is ongoing debate regarding how to incorporate information from multipartite sequence data in phylogenetic analyses. Some argue for strict combined-data approaches, which involve concatenating all partitions and estimating a single evolutionary history to maximize the explanatory power of the data. On the other hand, consensus/independence approaches endorse a two-step procedure where partitions are analyzed independently, and then a consensus is determined from the multiple results. To integrate these methods, popular methods involve mixtures across the model space of a strict combined-data approach and a priori independent parameters.

In this study, we propose an alternative approach by constructing a Bayesian hierarchical phylogenetic model. Our hierarchical framework allows researchers to pool information across data partitions, improving estimate precision in individual partitions while also permitting estimation and testing of tendencies in across-partition quantities. These quantities include the distribution from which individual topologies relating the sequences within a partition are drawn. We propose standard hierarchical priors on continuous evolutionary parameters across partitions, while the structure on topologies varies depending on the research problem.

To illustrate our model, we provide three examples. Firstly, we explore the evolutionary history of the guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) using alignments of 13 mitochondrial genes. Our hierarchical model returns significantly more precise continuous parameter estimates compared to an independent parameter approach, without losing the important features of the data. Secondly, we analyze the frequency of horizontal gene transfer using 50 prokaryotic genes. We assume an unknown species-level topology and allow individual gene topologies to differ from this with a small estimable probability. By simultaneously inferring the species and individual gene topologies, we find a transfer frequency of 17%. Lastly, we examine HIV sequences longitudinally sampled from HIV+ patients. We investigate whether the posttreatment development of CCR5 coreceptor virus represents concerted evolution from middisease CXCR4 virus or reemergence of the initial infecting CCR5 virus. Our hierarchical model combines partitions from multiple unrelated patients by assuming that the topology for each patient is drawn from a multinomial distribution with unknown probabilities. Preliminary results suggest evolution rather than reemergence.

title: Up-to-date catalogues of yeast protein complexes
text:
Protein-protein interactions can be inferred and validated using gold standard datasets on protein complexes. While the Munich Information Center of Protein Sequences database has been a reliable reference for characterizing protein complexes in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, it no longer reflects the current state of knowledge. To address this, we have conducted systematic curation efforts and created two new catalogues of yeast protein complexes.

The first catalogue, known as CYC2008, consists of 408 manually curated heteromeric protein complexes. These complexes are supported by small-scale experiments reported in the current literature, making them a reliable and up-to-date reference set for biologists interested in studying protein interactions and complexes.

The second catalogue, called YHTP2008, includes 400 high-throughput complexes that have been annotated with evidence from current literature. Of these complexes, 262 partially or fully overlap with the CYC2008 complexes. For 68 complexes that do not overlap or only partially overlap with CYC2008, evidence for interacting subunits has been collected. However, no literature evidence was found for 100 complexes in this catalogue.

These partially supported and unsupported complexes may be of interest to researchers for further experimental investigation. Both catalogues, CYC2008 and YHTP2008, are freely available at the following website: http://wodaklab.org/cyc2008/.

title: Synergistic Mechanisms of DNA Demethylation during Transition to Ground-State Pluripotency
text: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) exist in various molecular states, ranging from a basic state in 2i to more advanced states such as embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). In order to understand the role of DNA methylation (5mC) in different pluripotent states, we conducted a study where we analyzed the distribution of 5mC and 5-hydroxymethycytosine (5hmC) across multiple PSCs. We found that ground-state ESCs have a different distribution of 5mC and 5hmC compared to ESCs in serum, with lower absolute levels. On the other hand, EpiSCs have increased 5mC at promoters and reduced 5hmC, which contributes to their limited developmental potential. When PSCs transition to the ground state in 2i, there is a rapid onset of gene expression specific to this state and a global decrease in DNA methylation. This demethylation process is driven by the repression of de novo methylases by PRDM14, which occurs at a slow pace. Additionally, the conversion of 5hmC by TET1/TET2 enzymes enhances the speed and extent of hypomethylation. These processes work together to establish a robust hypomethylated state during the transition to ground-state pluripotency.

title: Febrile seizures in the developing brain result in persistent modification of neuronal excitability in limbic circuits
text: Febrile seizures, which are induced by fever, impact around 3-5% of infants and young children. The connection between febrile seizures and the development of epilepsy later in life has been a subject of debate despite their high occurrence. By utilizing a new rat model of complex febrile seizures and employing patch clamp techniques, we have discovered that seizures induced by hyperthermia in immature rats result in a specific increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus. This increase persists into adulthood, indicating that the effects of febrile seizures on synaptic communication are long-lasting. These findings challenge the prevailing notion that early-life febrile convulsions are benign.

title: Identification of an allele of VAM3/SYP22 that confers a semi-dwarf phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana.
text: The Arabidopsis thaliana mutants known as short stem and midrib (ssm) exhibit both semi-dwarf stature and wavy leaves due to deficiencies in stem internode and leaf elongation. Interestingly, these abnormalities cannot be corrected by external phytohormones. Initially, ssm was identified as a recessive mutant in the Columbia (Col-0) ecotype. However, through genetic crossing experiments, it was discovered that this mutant phenotype can be restored by a gene present in the Landsberg erecta (Ler) ecotype but absent in Col-0. By employing map-based cloning techniques, researchers have identified a small deletion in the sixth intron of a gene encoding a syntaxin called VAM3/SYP22 in the ssm mutants. This syntaxin is involved in vesicle transport to the vacuole. The mutation causes an insertion of a peptide in the VAM3/SYP22 polypeptide sequence due to faulty splicing of the shortened sixth intron. Notably, a comparison between the wild-type genomes of Ler and Col-0 reveals that Col-0 has a frameshift mutation in SYP23, a gene closely related to VAM3/SYP22. These findings suggest that VAM3/SYP22 and SYP23 have overlapping functions and that vesicle transport mediated by these syntaxins plays a crucial role in shoot morphogenesis.

title: Class Ia MHC-deficient BALB/c mice generate CD8+ T cell-mediated protective immunity against Listeria monocytogenes infection.
text: This study aimed to investigate the protective capacity of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells in the context of Listeria monocytogenes infection. To do so, class Ia MHC-deficient mice with reduced levels of circulating CD8(+) T cells were used. The K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mutation was introduced into a C.B10 background, as BALB/c mice are more susceptible to Listeria infection compared to other commonly studied mouse strains. Immunizing C.B10 K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mice with a sublethal dose of L. monocytogenes resulted in full protection against subsequent lethal infection. Adoptive transfer experiments revealed that CD8(+) T cells played a major role in this protective immune response. A CD8(+) T cell line isolated from the spleen of a Listeria-infected class Ia MHC-deficient mouse demonstrated specific recognition of Listeria-infected cells in vitro, as evidenced by IFN-gamma secretion and cytotoxicity assays. Transfer of this T cell line alone provided significant protection against L. monocytogenes challenge. These findings suggest that even a small number of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells are capable of generating a rapid recall response necessary for protection against secondary L. monocytogenes infection.

title: Upregulated PD-1 Expression Is Associated with the Development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, but Not the PD-1.1 Allele of the PDCD1 Gene
text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease with a genetic component. Programmed death 1 (PD-1), a molecule that regulates T cell activity, is believed to play a role in the development of SLE. To investigate the impact of PD-1 expression on SLE, a study recruited 30 SLE patients and 30 healthy controls. The researchers measured PD-1 expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using flow cytometry and quantitative real-time-reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). They also examined the relationship between PD-1 expression levels, a specific genetic variant (SNP rs36084323), and the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI). The study found that PD-1 expression levels were significantly higher in SLE patients compared to healthy controls. Furthermore, the increased PD-1 expression levels were strongly associated with higher SLEDAI scores. However, no significant difference was observed in PD-1 expression levels and the SNP rs36084323. These findings suggest that elevated PD-1 expression may be involved in the development of SLE and could serve as a potential biomarker for diagnosis. Additionally, targeting PD-1 with inhibitors may hold promise for SLE treatment.

title: Endothelial cell membranes contain podocalyxin--the major sialoprotein of visceral glomerular epithelial cells
text: We have discovered that podocalyxin, the main sialoprotein in the glycocalyx of glomerular podocytes, can also be found outside of the glomerulus. Through our research, we used a specific antibody to locate podocalyxin in various organs, including the lung, heart, kidney, small intestine, brain, pancreas, aorta, periportal blood vessels in the liver, and central arteries of follicles in the spleen. However, we did not find podocalyxin in the endothelia that line the sinusoids of these organs. Using immunoelectron microscopy, we were able to determine that podocalyxin is located on the luminal membrane domain of endothelial cells, but in a patchy distribution. We also confirmed the presence of podocalyxin in lung tissue through immunoblotting. In conclusion, we have found that podocalyxin is a common component of endothelial plasma membranes, specifically in the luminal membrane domain, and its distribution on the endothelial cell surface is uneven.

title: Teratogen-Induced Oxidative Stress Targets Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate Dehydrogenase in the Organogenesis Stage Mouse Embryo
text: Exposure to hydroxyurea (HU) during the organogenesis stage of mouse embryo development leads to the development of curly tail and limb malformations. The toxicity of HU is attributed to oxidative stress, where reactive oxygen species (ROS) interact with polyunsaturated bilipid membranes to produce α,β-unsaturated reactive aldehydes. One of the most harmful aldehydes, 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), forms covalent adducts with proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. This study aims to investigate if HU exposure on gestation day 9 in CD1 mice results in region-specific 4-HNE-protein adducts in the embryo and to identify the targeted proteins. The formation of 4-HNE-protein adducts was found to be higher in the caudal region of control embryos, and HU exposure further increased the formation of these adducts in that area. Interestingly, three of the proteins modified by 4-HNE, namely glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase 2, and aldolase 1, A isoform, are involved in energy metabolism. The formation of 4-HNE-GAPDH adducts reduced GAPDH enzymatic activity by 20% and decreased lactate production by 40%. Additionally, HU exposure caused the translocation of GAPDH to the nucleus in the caudal region of exposed embryos. This translocation may be linked to the reactivation of oxidized proteins involved in DNA repair, such as apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1, and the stimulation of E1A-associated P300 protein/creb-binding protein (p300/CBP) activity, leading to cell death through a p53-dependent pathway. Based on these findings, it is suggested that GAPDH is a target of oxidative stress in the embryo and may play a role in the stress response during development.

title: Recurrent venous thromboembolism and bleeding complications during anticoagulant treatment in patients with cancer and venous thrombosis.
text: This study aimed to determine whether patients with cancer have a higher risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism or bleeding during anticoagulant treatment compared to those without cancer. Out of the 842 patients included in the study, 181 had cancer at the beginning. The results showed that cancer patients had a 20.7% cumulative incidence of recurrent thromboembolism within 12 months, compared to 6.8% in patients without cancer. The hazard ratio was 3.2, indicating a significantly higher risk for cancer patients. Additionally, the cumulative incidence of major bleeding was 12.4% in cancer patients and 4.9% in patients without cancer, with a hazard ratio of 2.2. Both recurrence and bleeding were more common in the first month of anticoagulant therapy and were associated with the severity of cancer. These findings suggest that cancer patients with venous thrombosis are more likely to experience recurrent complications and major bleeding during anticoagulant treatment. The current paradigms of anticoagulation may have limited effectiveness in improving these outcomes, highlighting the need for new treatment strategies.

title: Fitting multilevel models in complex survey data with design weights: Recommendations
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the performance of scaled-weighted and unweighted analyses in multilevel models (MLM) using complex survey data. Previous research has suggested that analysts should scale design weights using two methods and fit the MLM using both unweighted and scaled-weighted data. To examine this, data from the 2005-2006 National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs (NS-CSHCN) was used, which included information from children clustered within states. The study assessed the performance of scaling methods across different outcome types (categorical vs. continuous), model types (level-1, level-2, or combined), and software programs (Mplus, MLwiN, and GLLAMM). The results showed that scaled weighted estimates and standard errors were slightly different from unweighted analyses, but they were more consistent with each other than with unweighted analyses. However, these differences were minimal and did not affect the inferential conclusions. Additionally, the study found minimal differences across software programs, which increased confidence in the results and inferential conclusions regardless of the software used. In conclusion, when using design weights in MLM, analysts should scale the weights and use software that properly incorporates the scaled weights in the estimation process.

title: Functional outcomes of multi-condition collaborative care and successful ageing: results of randomised trial
text: The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of integrated care for chronic physical diseases and depression in improving quality of life and reducing disability. The study design involved a randomized controlled trial comparing multi-condition collaborative care for depression and poorly controlled diabetes and/or risk factors for coronary heart disease with usual care among middle-aged and elderly individuals. The study took place in fourteen primary care clinics in Seattle, Washington. Participants included patients with diabetes or coronary heart disease, or both, who had blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg, low density lipoprotein concentration >3.37 mmol/L, or glycated hemoglobin 8.5% or higher, and PHQ-9 depression scores of ≥ 10. The intervention consisted of a 12-month program aimed at improving depression, glycemic control, blood pressure, and lipid control by integrating a "treat to target" approach for diabetes and risk factors for coronary heart disease with collaborative care for depression. The intervention included self-management support, disease control monitoring, and pharmacotherapy for depression, hyperglycemia, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. The main outcome measures were social role disability, global quality of life rating, and disabilities in activities of daily living. Results showed that patients in the intervention group had significantly greater improvements in social role disability and global quality of life rating at six and twelve months compared to those in the usual care group. There was also a trend towards greater improvement in disabilities in activities of daily living. In conclusion, integrated care that addresses both chronic physical disease and comorbid depression can reduce social role disability and improve global quality of life. The trial was registered under Clinical Trials NCT00468676.

title: A Comparison of Cost Effectiveness Using Data from Randomized Trials or Actual Clinical Practice: Selective Cox-2 Inhibitors as an Example
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the accuracy of cost-effectiveness studies by comparing the data used in these studies, which are typically based on randomized clinical trials (RCTs), to real-world observational data. The study focused on the use of selective Cox-2 inhibitors (coxibs) as an example. 

The researchers used the UK General Practice Research Database (GPRD) to gather information on the exposure characteristics and individual probabilities of upper gastrointestinal (GI) events associated with the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or coxibs. They developed a basic cost-effectiveness model to compare the outcomes of prescribing conventional NSAIDs versus coxibs. The outcomes measured included upper GI events recorded in the GPRD and hospitalizations for upper GI events recorded in the national registry of hospitalizations (Hospital Episode Statistics) linked to the GPRD. Prescription costs were based on the number of tablets prescribed as recorded in the GPRD and the 2006 cost data from the British National Formulary. 

The study included over 1 million patients who were prescribed conventional NSAIDs or coxibs. However, only a small percentage of patients used the drugs long-term and daily, which was in contrast to the requirements of coxib RCTs that required daily use for at least 6-9 months. The cost of preventing one upper GI event, as recorded in the GPRD, ranged from US$64k to US$182k depending on the frequency of drug use, and the cost of hospitalizations was US$298k on average. The costs of events recorded in the GPRD increased over time, with an average of US$58k during 1990-1993 and US$174k during 2002-2005. When RCT data was used instead of GPRD data for event probabilities, the mean cost was significantly lower, at US$16k with the VIGOR RCT and US$20k with the CLASS RCT. 

In conclusion, the published cost-effectiveness analyses of coxibs did not accurately represent real-world patients and should not have been used to inform prescribing policies. The study highlights the importance of external validity in cost-effectiveness analyses and suggests that it should be a requirement in future studies.

title: 7α, 25-dihydroxycholesterol-mediated activation of EBI2 in immune regulation and diseases
text: EBI2, also known as GPR183, is a receptor that belongs to the G-coupled receptor family. It was initially discovered in 1993 as one of the main genes induced in the Burkitt's lymphoma cell line BL41 by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. In 2009, it was reported that this receptor plays a crucial role in regulating the migration and responses of B cells. This finding prompted us to search for its natural ligand. In 2011, our group and another research team identified 7α, 25-dihydroxyxcholesterol (7α, 25-OHC), an oxysterol, as the probable physiological ligand for EBI2. Subsequent studies shed light on how 7α, 25-OHC binds to EBI2 and how a gradient of this oxysterol can be generated in the body to regulate the migration, activation, and functions of various immune cells and astrocytes. The discovery of 7α, 25-OHC as a ligand for EBI2 unveiled a previously unknown signaling system involving oxysterols, a class of molecules with significant biological functions. It is believed that dysregulation of the synthesis or functions of these molecules contributes to various diseases, including inflammation, autoimmune diseases, cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Therefore, targeting EBI2 holds promise for therapeutic interventions in human diseases.

title: PrimPol Bypasses UV Photoproducts during Eukaryotic Chromosomal DNA Replication
text: Genomic instability can occur when DNA damage causes the DNA replication machinery to stall. To ensure genome duplication even without a pristine DNA template, various mechanisms are in place, although the identification of the enzymes involved is still incomplete. In this study, we demonstrate that Primase-Polymerase (PrimPol; CCDC111), an archaeal-eukaryotic primase (AEP) found in eukaryotic cells, plays a role in chromosomal DNA replication. PrimPol is essential for the progression of replication forks on DNA templates damaged by ultraviolet (UV) light, potentially through its ability to catalyze translesion synthesis (TLS) of these lesions. This PrimPol UV lesion bypass pathway operates independently of the Pol η-dependent pathway and provides protection against UV-induced cytotoxicity in xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) patient cells. Furthermore, we establish that PrimPol is also necessary for efficient replication fork progression during an undisturbed S phase. These findings, among others, highlight the significance of PrimPol in the advancement of replication forks in eukaryotic cells.

title: The novel immunosuppressive enzyme IL4I1 is expressed by neoplastic cells of several B-cell lymphomas and by tumor-associated macrophages
text: In our previous report, we highlighted the significant expression of the IL4I1 gene in primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL). We have now identified this gene as encoding a secreted L-phenylalanine oxidase protein, which is naturally produced by myeloid cells. This protein has been found to inhibit T-cell proliferation in laboratory settings. In this study, we examined the expression pattern of IL4I1 protein in 315 cases of human lymphoid and non-lymphoid malignancies. Apart from PMBL, IL4I1 expression was observed frequently in tumors. Tumor-associated macrophages in most tumors and neoplastic cells in follicular lymphoma, classic and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphomas, and small lymphocytic lymphoma (all germinal center derived) were found to express IL4I1. Additionally, IL4I1-positive tumor cells were detected in rare cases of solid cancers, particularly mesothelioma. The presence of enzymatic activity correlated with protein expression, indicating that IL4I1 is functional in vivo. Depending on the type of tumor, IL4I1 may have varying effects on infiltrating lymphocyte populations, which can impact tumor progression. Notably, in follicular lymphoma cells, which are susceptible to cytotoxic T-cell-mediated killing but rely on interactions with local T helper cells for survival, high levels of IL4I1 expression appear to be associated with the absence of bone marrow involvement and a more favorable outcome. These findings suggest that IL4I1 should be considered as a potential prognostic factor and warrant further investigation.

title: Poor prognosis in carcinoma is associated with a gene expression signature of aberrant PTEN tumor suppressor pathway activity.
text: The future of cancer management lies in pathway-specific therapy. In solid tumors, the oncogenic phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is frequently activated. However, there is currently no reliable test available to detect PI3K pathway activation in human tumors. To address this, we focused on the observation that loss of PTEN, the negative regulator of PI3K, leads to robust activation of this pathway. We developed and validated a microarray gene expression signature for immunohistochemistry (IHC)-detectable PTEN loss in breast cancer (BC). The most significant gene in this signature was PTEN itself, indicating that PTEN mRNA levels are the primary determinant of PTEN protein levels in BC. Some BCs that tested positive for PTEN in IHC actually exhibited the signature of PTEN loss. This was associated with moderately reduced PTEN mRNA levels, along with specific types of PIK3CA mutations and/or amplification of HER2. This demonstrates that the signature is more sensitive than PTEN IHC in identifying tumors with pathway activation. In independent data sets of breast, prostate, and bladder carcinoma, the signature accurately predicted poor patient outcomes. The signature gene STMN1, which encodes Stathmin, was an accurate IHC marker of the signature and had prognostic significance in BC. Stathmin also showed pathway-pharmacodynamic effects in vitro and in vivo. Therefore, the signature, or its components such as Stathmin, could be clinically useful tests for stratifying patients for anti-PI3K pathway therapy and monitoring treatment effectiveness. This study highlights the strong association between aberrant PI3K pathway signaling and metastasis, as well as poor survival across different types of carcinoma. It emphasizes the potential impact on patient survival that could be achieved through pathway inhibition.

title: Suppression of subtelomeric VSG switching by Trypanosoma brucei TRF requires its TTAGGG repeat-binding activity
text:
The parasite Trypanosoma brucei is responsible for causing human African trypanosomiasis. To evade the immune response of its mammalian host, the parasite regularly changes its major surface antigen, known as VSG. These VSGs are only expressed from specific regions near the ends of the chromosomes, called subtelomeric loci. Previous research has shown that two telomere proteins, TbTIF2 and TbRAP1, are important for regulating VSG switching and VSG silencing, respectively.

Now, we have made a new discovery that another telomere protein, TbTRF, also plays a crucial role in regulating VSG switching. When TbTRF is temporarily depleted, there is a significant increase in VSG switching events. We have determined the structure of the DNA-binding Myb domain of TbTRF using NMR, and it forms a typical helix-loop-helix structure that is similar to the Myb domains found in mammalian TRF proteins.

Interestingly, the TbTRF Myb domain is able to accommodate the bulky J base found in T. brucei telomere DNA without any issues. The DNA-binding affinity of TbTRF is not affected by the presence of J, both in laboratory experiments and in living organisms. Furthermore, we have discovered that specific mutations in the TbTRF Myb domain, which reduce its ability to bind to telomere DNA, also lead to a significant increase in VSG switching frequencies. This indicates that the DNA-binding activity of TbTRF is crucial for its role in regulating VSG switching.

title: CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity eliminates primary tumor cells in metastatic melanoma through high MHC class II expression and can be enhanced by inhibitory receptor blockade
text: Metastatic melanoma is a fast-progressing disease with a high mortality rate and limited treatment options. Utilizing immunotherapy to target cytotoxic T cells that attack tumors shows promise as a strategy. To aid in its development, we investigated the feasibility and effectiveness of using CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. We also examined the regulatory mechanisms that control CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Our findings revealed that CD4+ cytotoxic T cells expressing granzyme B and perforin, which occur naturally, can be found in significantly higher frequencies in metastatic melanoma patients compared to healthy individuals. These CD4+ cytotoxic T cells were capable of killing autologous tumor cells taken from metastatic melanoma, without the need for CD8+ T cells or other cell types. However, we observed several limiting factors. Firstly, the cytolytic activity of CD4+ T cells required melanoma cells to have high MHC class II expression, which was not the case in some melanomas. Secondly, the release of granzyme B and perforin by activated CD4+ cytotoxic T cells decreased after being cultured with autologous melanoma cells, characterized by low LAMP-1 expression and reduced secretion of granzyme B and perforin in the surrounding fluid. This indicated the presence of inhibitory mechanisms that suppress CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. Indeed, blocking PD-1 and CTLA-4 increased the cytolytic activity of CD4+ T cells, but only in melanomas with high MHC class II expression, not in those with low MHC class II expression. In conclusion, our study demonstrated that CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity can eliminate primary melanoma cells, but its effectiveness depends on MHC class II expression.

title: The epidemiology and iatrogenic transmission of hepatitis C virus in Egypt: a Bayesian coalescent approach.
text: The Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a major cause of liver cancer and cirrhosis, and Egypt has one of the highest rates of HCV worldwide. In this article, we have used a newly developed Bayesian inference framework to estimate how HCV spreads in Egypt based on sampled viral gene sequences, and to predict the impact it has on public health. Our findings show that the number of HCV infections in Egypt grew rapidly between 1930 and 1955. This growth was likely due to extensive antischistosomiasis injection campaigns. Although our results indicate that HCV transmission has decreased since then, we believe that HCV will continue to be a problem in Egypt for many years to come. Our analysis, which combines population genetics and epidemiology, provides detailed estimates of how HCV prevalence has changed over time in Egypt. These results also serve as an objective test of inference methods that are based on the coalescent process, as they align with a predetermined demographic scenario.

title: Improving population representation through geographic health information systems: mapping the MURDOCK study.
text:
This paper examines the use of geospatial analysis to evaluate and enhance recruitment efforts in order to ensure the representativeness of study populations. The methods discussed are applied to the Measurement to Understand Reclassification of Disease of Cabarrus/Kannapolis (MURDOCK) study, which focuses on the city of Kannapolis and Cabarrus County, NC. Despite attempts to recruit a participant registry that is representative of the entire catchment area, there is an inevitable bias in recruitment. However, the MURDOCK study provides geospatial information about participants at entry, which can be utilized to monitor and guide recruitment efforts.

To assess the representativeness of the MURDOCK participant population, chi-squared tests were conducted to compare the MURDOCK population with 2010 Census data. This comparison was done for both the entire catchment area and individual Census tracts. Additionally, a logistic regression model was used to identify Census tracts with low recruitment rates, defined as having fewer than 56 participants from that tract. The logistic regression took into account the distance to the enrollment site, with the median distance to the enrollment site used as a variable.

The analysis revealed that tracts with low recruitment rates had higher minority and younger populations, suggesting the need for targeted strategies to improve recruitment in these areas. Furthermore, it was observed that areal units farther away from the enrollment sites were underrepresented, despite being within the study area. This indicates that distance traveled to the enrollment site may act as a barrier to participation.

These findings have important implications for recruitment efforts and the generalizability of study samples, not only in the MURDOCK study but also in other population-based studies. By utilizing geospatial analysis, researchers can better understand the factors influencing recruitment and develop strategies to ensure the representativeness of study populations.

title: Haplotype-based variant detection from short-read sequencing
text: In order to detect haplotypes directly from short-read DNA sequencing data, modifications are necessary in current small-variant detection methods. In this study, we have devised a Bayesian statistical framework that can effectively model multiallelic loci in groups of individuals with varying copy numbers. Subsequently, we present our application of this framework in a variant detector called FreeBayes, which is based on haplotypes.

title: Longitudinal Genome-Wide Association of Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors in the Bogalusa Heart Study
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of death globally. Recent studies examining the entire genome have identified numerous genetic locations associated with CVD risk factors in adults. However, it remains uncertain whether these locations can predict trait levels at all ages, if they are linked to the development of traits over time, or if they can be used to screen individuals who are pre-symptomatic in order to implement preventive measures before the onset of disease. In this study, we conducted a genome-wide association study on participants from the Bogalusa Heart Study (BHS), a long-term study, to investigate the relationship between genetic factors and the development of CVD risk factors from childhood to adulthood. Our findings reveal seven significant associations between genetic factors and CVD risk factors, two of which have been previously reported. We further tested these top regions for replication in the Young Finns Study (YF) and found strong replication for two associations: rs247616 in CETP with high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and rs445925 at APOE with low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels. Our results demonstrate that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) previously identified in adult cross-sectional studies tend to have consistent effects across different ages in the BHS. Additionally, these previously identified variants were associated with trait levels in adulthood that exceeded those observed in childhood. However, we also found variants with effects that varied over time, which showed promise as predictors. This study is the first to examine the role of common genetic variants in the development of CVD risk factors in children as they progress into adulthood. It highlights the importance of longitudinal studies in identifying genetic predictors of adult traits in children.

title: Actin and serum response factor transduce physical cues from the microenvironment to regulate epidermal stem cell fate decisions
text:
The balance between stem cell renewal and differentiation is crucial for maintaining the health of the skin. This balance is regulated by signals from the extracellular matrix (ECM). To better understand the pathways involved, scientists have developed a method to create microenvironments where they can precisely control different variables. In this study, the researchers used micropatterned surfaces to investigate how restricted contact with the ECM triggers human epidermal stem cells to undergo terminal differentiation.

By placing the cells on small circular islands, the researchers observed that the cells remained rounded and differentiated more frequently compared to cells on larger islands. Interestingly, the differentiation process was not influenced by the composition or density of the ECM. Instead, it was found that the actin cytoskeleton, which provides structural support to the cells, played a role in regulating the activity of a transcription factor called serum response factor (SRF). Knocking down SRF or its co-factor MAL inhibited differentiation, while overexpressing MAL stimulated SRF activity and the expression of a protein called involucrin.

Furthermore, the researchers discovered that two other genes, FOS and JUNB, were also necessary for differentiation. The gene c-Fos was responsible for mediating the response to serum, while JunB was regulated by actin and MAL. These findings highlight how physical cues are translated into changes in gene expression, ultimately determining the fate of epidermal cells.

title: Reproducibility and automatic measurement of QT dispersion.
text:
In this study, the researchers examined the consistency of QT dispersion measurements from abnormal electrocardiograms in patients with previous myocardial infarction. They specifically looked at the agreement between two observers and two measurements, and compared the results obtained using a user-interactive system versus an automatic measurement system.

To conduct the study, standard 12-lead electrocardiograms were randomly selected from 70 patients who had experienced a myocardial infarction. These electrocardiograms were then scanned into a computer and processed using specialized software. The software allowed for user-interactive measurements, where the user could use a mouse and computer screen to make measurements, or automatic measurements using a specially designed algorithm.

The researchers found that the reproducibility of the RR interval, which measures the time between two consecutive heartbeats, was excellent for all methods. The mean absolute errors ranged from 3 to 4 milliseconds, and the relative errors ranged from 0.3 to 0.5%.

The reproducibility of the mean QT interval, which measures the time it takes for the heart to repolarize, was good. The intrasubject error, which measures the consistency of measurements within the same individual, was 6 milliseconds (1.4% relative error). The interobserver error, which measures the agreement between two observers, was 7 milliseconds (1.8% relative error). The errors between the observers and the automatic measurement system were 10 and 11 milliseconds (2.5% and 2.8% relative errors), respectively.

However, the researchers found that the measurements of QTc dispersion, which assesses the variability of QT intervals, had large errors for all methods. The intrasubject error was 12 milliseconds (17.3% relative error), the interobserver error was 15 milliseconds (22.1% relative error), and the errors between the observers and the automatic measurement system were 30 and 28 milliseconds (35.4% and 31.9% relative errors), respectively.

The measurement of QT dispersion is challenging because it relies on accurately measuring the most difficult QT intervals. This poses a problem for reproducibility. Any automatic measurement system must be able to recognize not only common T wave morphologies but also these more difficult T waves in order to be useful for measuring QT dispersion. The poor reproducibility of QT dispersion limits its usefulness as a clinical tool, particularly as a predictor of events.

title: Inhibition of LSD1 sensitizes glioblastoma cells to histone deacetylase inhibitors.
text: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor that continues to be a devastating disease. Despite advancements in GBM treatment, patient survival rates have not significantly improved in the last ten years. Enzymes that control epigenetic changes are of great interest as targets for cancer therapy due to their crucial roles in cellular processes that contribute to the development of cancer. Several inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) have been developed and tested in GBM with moderate success. Our research focused on the effects of HDAC inhibitors on GBM cells, specifically the accumulation of histone methylation, a modification that is removed by lysine specific demethylase 1 (LSD1). This led us to investigate the potential benefits of simultaneously inhibiting HDACs and LSD1 as a combination therapy. We examined the induction of apoptosis in GBM cell lines after inhibiting LSD1 and HDACs together. We achieved LSD1 inhibition through targeted short hairpin RNA or pharmacological methods, and HDAC inhibition through treatment with either vorinostat or PCI-24781. The results showed a significant increase (>2-fold) in caspase-dependent apoptosis in LSD1-knockdown GBM cells treated with HDAC inhibitors. Furthermore, when we pharmacologically inhibited LSD1 with the monoamine oxidase inhibitor tranylcypromine in combination with HDAC inhibitors, we observed a synergistic effect resulting in apoptotic cell death in GBM cells, while normal human astrocytes were unaffected.
