These findings suggest that LSD1 and HDACs work together to regulate crucial pathways of cell death in GBM cell lines, but not in normal cells. They also support the use of LSD1 and HDAC inhibitors in combination as a potential therapeutic approach for GBM.

title: Challenges for malaria elimination in Zanzibar: pyrethroid resistance in malaria vectors and poor performance of long-lasting insecticide nets
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual house spraying (IRS) in controlling malaria vectors in Zanzibar. Mosquitoes were collected from Pemba and Unguja islands and tested for susceptibility to the insecticides used in LLINs and IRS. Additionally, 150 LLINs were collected from households on Unguja and examined for durability and efficacy.

The results showed that the majority of the Anopheles gambiae complex mosquitoes were An. arabiensis, with a small number of An. gambiae s.s. and An. merus present. The mosquitoes from Pemba were found to be resistant to the pyrethroids used in LLINs and IRS, while those from Unguja were susceptible. The examination of the LLINs revealed that two-thirds of them were damaged after only three years of use. The used nets also had a significantly lower permethrin concentration compared to new ones. Furthermore, their efficacy decreased significantly after just six washes.

These findings indicate that the resistance of malaria vectors to pyrethroids and the short lifespan of LLINs pose a serious threat to the gains made in malaria control in Zanzibar. The study suggests that achieving malaria elimination with the current control measures will be challenging, even in well-resourced and manageable areas like Zanzibar.

title: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen acts as a cytoplasmic platform controlling human neutrophil survival
text: The process of neutrophil apoptosis, which is crucial for resolving inflammation, is not fully understood. This study investigates a survival pathway controlled by a nuclear factor called proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), which is involved in DNA replication and repair. The researchers found that mature neutrophils, despite being unable to proliferate, have high levels of PCNA in their cytosol. PCNA is associated with procaspases, which are proteins that prevent their activation. During apoptosis, the abundance of cytosolic PCNA decreases, but it increases when exposed to the survival factor granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). The researchers also discovered that peptides derived from a protein called p21, which compete with procaspases for binding to PCNA, trigger neutrophil apoptosis. This suggests that modifying PCNA's protein interactions affects neutrophil survival. Additionally, overexpressing PCNA makes neutrophil-differentiated PLB985 myeloid cells more resistant to apoptosis induced by certain factors. Conversely, reducing PCNA expression makes these cells more susceptible to apoptosis. Finally, a mutation in the PCNA binding site for many partners weakens its antiapoptotic effect. These findings reveal PCNA as a regulator of neutrophil lifespan and suggest it as a potential target for modulating pathological inflammation.

title: Development of the Human Infant Intestinal Microbiota
text: Immediately after birth, a new microbial ecosystem is established in a person's gastrointestinal tract. This ecosystem is an essential part of human biology, but there is still much to learn about its development, sources of microbes, variations between infants, and its impact on human health. To investigate these questions, we created a microarray to detect and measure the gene sequences of bacteria in stool samples from 14 healthy infants over their first year of life. We also analyzed samples from their mothers, fathers, and siblings to explore potential sources of the infant microbiota. The composition and patterns of microbial communities varied greatly among the babies, but each baby had distinct features that remained consistent for weeks to months. The similarities in temporal patterns between twins suggested that environmental exposures played a significant role in shaping the microbial community. By the end of the first year, the unique microbial ecosystems in each baby had started to resemble the adult gastrointestinal tract.

title: Combinatorial modulation of galP and glk gene expression for improved alternative glucose utilization
text: Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) is a crucial precursor for the anaerobic production of succinate and malate. However, when the PEP/carbohydrate phosphotransferase systems (PTS) are deactivated to increase PEP supply, the resulting strain has a low rate of glucose utilization. To enhance the anaerobic glucose utilization rate for efficient succinate and malate production, we conducted a combinatorial modulation of gene expression for galactose permease (galP) and glucokinase (glk) in an Escherichia coli strain with deactivated PTS. Initially, we constructed libraries of artificial regulatory parts, including promoters and messenger RNA stabilizing regions (mRS), in front of the β-galactosidase gene (lacZ) in the E. coli chromosome using λ-Red recombination. Most regulatory parts selected from the mRS library exhibited constitutive strengths under various cultivation conditions. We then employed a simple one-step recombination method to modulate the expression of galP and glk genes using different regulatory parts. The glucose utilization rates of strains modulated with either galP or glk increased, and the rates were positively correlated with the expression strength of both genes. Combinatorial modulation had a synergistic effect on the glucose utilization rate, with the highest rate (1.64 g/L h) being ten times higher than the PTS− strain and 39% higher than the wild-type E. coli. These modulated strains show promise for efficient anaerobic production of succinate and malate.

title: Matrix eQTL: Ultra fast eQTL analysis via large matrix operations
text: The goal of eQTL mapping is to identify specific regions of the genome that regulate gene transcription. This technique is used to study the regulatory structure of normal tissues and to investigate genetic factors involved in complex diseases like cancer, diabetes, and cystic fibrosis. Analyzing eQTL data can be computationally challenging due to the large number of SNPs and transcripts measured across numerous samples. This often leads researchers to focus on a subset of transcripts and SNPs due to the heavy computational burden. However, as larger datasets become available, there is a growing need for faster tools for eQTL analysis. We introduce a new method called Matrix eQTL, which utilizes linear models to perform fast eQTL analysis. Matrix eQTL can test for association using both linear regression and ANOVA models, and it can incorporate covariates to account for factors like population structure, gender, and clinical variables. Additionally, it supports testing of heteroscedastic models and models with correlated errors. In our experiments with large datasets, Matrix eQTL proved to be thousands of times faster than existing popular software for QTL/eQTL analysis. It is available as both Matlab and R packages, making it compatible with Windows, Mac OS, and Linux systems. The software can be accessed for free at the following website: http://www.bios.unc.edu/research/genomic_software/Matrix_eQTL.

title: The structure of DdrB from Deinococcus: a new fold for single-stranded DNA binding proteins
text: The ability of Deinococcus spp. to recover quickly from severe genomic fragmentation caused by exposure to high levels of ionizing radiation or desiccation is well-known. However, despite being studied for over 50 years, the exact mechanism behind this remarkable repair process is still not well understood. In this study, we present the 2.8 A structure of DdrB, a unique single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein found only in Deinococcus spp., which plays a crucial role in DNA damage recovery. DdrB forms a pentameric ring that can bind to ssDNA but not double-stranded DNA. Surprisingly, the crystal structure reveals that DdrB has a completely new fold, which is different from all other known single-stranded binding (SSB) proteins. The need for a specific ssDNA binding function in response to severe damage suggests that DdrB may have a distinct role, not only in protecting ssDNA but also in recruiting proteins or maintaining DNA architecture. We discuss possible mechanisms of DdrB's action in damage recovery.

title: N348I in the Connection Domain of HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Confers Zidovudine and Nevirapine Resistance
text:
The catalytically active subunit of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) reverse transcriptase (RT) is made up of DNA polymerase, connection, and ribonuclease H (RNase H) domains. Most RT inhibitor resistance mutations are found in the polymerase domain. However, the connection and RNase H domains are not commonly analyzed in clinical samples, and current genotyping assays do not sequence the entire RT coding region. The British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS (the Centre) genotypes clinical isolates up to codon 400 in RT and has identified an N348I mutation in the RT connection domain in treatment-experienced individuals. This study aims to determine the significance of this mutation in vivo and its role in drug resistance.

The prevalence of N348I in clinical isolates, the time it takes for it to emerge under selective drug pressure, and its association with changes in viral load, specific drug treatment, and known drug resistance mutations were analyzed using data from the Centre's database. The prevalence of N348I increased from less than 1% in 368 treatment-naive individuals to 12.1% in 1,009 treatment-experienced patients. N348I appeared early in therapy and was strongly associated with thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), lamivudine resistance mutations, and non-nucleoside RTI (NNRTI) resistance mutations. The association with TAMs and NNRTI resistance mutations was consistent with the selection of N348I in patients treated with regimens that included both zidovudine and nevirapine. The emergence of N348I was also associated with a significant increase in viral load. However, this analysis did not consider the simultaneous selection of other RT or protease inhibitor resistance mutations.

To further understand the role of this mutation in RT inhibitor resistance, N348I was introduced into HIV-1 molecular clones with different genetic backgrounds. N348I decreased susceptibility to zidovudine and nevirapine and significantly potentiated resistance to these drugs when combined with other mutations. Biochemical analyses of recombinant RT containing N348I supported the role of this mutation in zidovudine and NNRTI resistance and provided insight into the molecular mechanism of resistance.

In conclusion, the N348I mutation in the RT connection domain is associated with drug resistance and a significant increase in viral load. This study provides evidence for the role of this mutation in resistance to zidovudine and NNRTIs and sheds light on its molecular mechanism.

title: Dual Targeting of PDGFRα and FGFR1 Displays Synergistic Efficacy in Malignant Rhabdoid Tumors
text: A significant number of human cancers are caused by mutations in the subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex. Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are deadly pediatric cancers that lack the SWI/SNF subunit SMARCB1. In this study, we used a combination of molecular profiling and chemical biology to show that the receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) PDGFRα and FGFR1 are simultaneously activated in MRT cells. Blocking both receptors together had a synergistic effect in inhibiting tumor growth. By targeting both receptors and using the dual inhibitor ponatinib, we were able to suppress the AKT and ERK1/2 pathways, leading to cell death. MRT cells that had developed resistance to the PDGFRα inhibitor pazopanib were still susceptible to FGFR inhibitors. We also discovered that the expression of PDGFRα is regulated by SMARCB1, and analysis of clinical samples confirmed the presence of both PDGFRα and FGFR1 in rhabdoid tumor patients. These findings suggest that targeting RTK coactivation dependencies could be a promising therapeutic strategy for cancers with SWI/SNF deficiencies.

title: A nano-positioning system for macromolecular structural analysis
text: Standard structural biology methods often cannot determine the positions of flexible domains within macromolecules or macromolecular complexes. To address this issue, we have developed a method that combines single-molecule measurements with X-ray crystallography data using probabilistic data analysis. This method not only identifies the most probable position of a fluorescent dye molecule attached to the domain, but also provides a three-dimensional probability distribution that represents the experimental uncertainty. By utilizing this approach, single-pair fluorescence resonance energy transfer measurements can now serve as a quantitative tool for studying the position and dynamics of flexible domains within macromolecular complexes. We have applied this method to locate the 5′ end of the nascent RNA exiting transcription elongation complexes of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) RNA polymerase II and examined the impact of transcription factor IIB on the RNA's position.

title: Tumor-associated macrophages correlate with the clinicopathological features and poor outcomes via inducing epithelial to mesenchymal transition in oral squamous cell carcinoma
text:
BACKGROUND
The roles of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and the epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in promoting tumor progression are well-established. However, it is still unclear whether TAMs can induce EMT in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

RESULTS
In this study, we examined the expression of macrophage markers CD68 and CD163, as well as the epithelial marker E-cadherin and the mesenchymal marker vimentin, in 127 OSCC patients using semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry. Interestingly, we found that CD68 and CD163 expression was not limited to infiltrating TAMs, but was also detected in cancer cells. Moreover, a high number of CD68-positive macrophages was associated with poor overall survival. Similarly, the expression of CD163 in both macrophages and cancer cells was linked to poor overall survival and had a significant prognostic impact in OSCC. Importantly, the expression of CD163 in cancer cells was significantly correlated with E-cadherin and vimentin. Additionally, when cancer cells (HN4, HN6, and SCC9) were exposed to TAMs conditioned medium, they exhibited a fibroblast-like appearance and showed altered expression of E-cadherin and vimentin. These changes were associated with enhanced migration and invasion abilities.

CONCLUSIONS
Our findings suggest that TAMs can promote EMT in cancer cells, thereby contributing to the progression of oral cancer.

title: Geometric cues for directing the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells.
text: Considerable efforts have been dedicated to comprehending the factors that impact the commitment of stem cells to specific lineages. This study provides evidence that the shape of cells, regardless of soluble factors, significantly influences the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) derived from bone marrow. When exposed to competing signals for differentiation, cells cultured in rectangles with increasing aspect ratios and in shapes with pentagonal symmetry but varying subcellular curvature - all occupying the same area - exhibit distinct profiles of adipogenesis and osteogenesis. These findings indicate that geometric characteristics that enhance actomyosin contractility promote osteogenesis and align with the in vivo conditions of the differentiated cells' microenvironment. The disruption of the cytoskeleton through pharmacological agents modulates the trends in lineage commitment based on shape, confirming the crucial role of focal adhesion and myosin-generated contractility during differentiation. Microarray analysis and studies inhibiting specific pathways suggest that contractile cells enhance osteogenesis by activating c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and extracellular related kinase (ERK1/2) in conjunction with elevated wingless-type (Wnt) signaling. Overall, this research highlights the significance of geometric shape cues in orchestrating the mechanochemical signals and paracrine/autocrine factors that guide MSCs towards appropriate fates.

title: Amyloid accumulation is a late event in sporadic Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in nontransgenic rats
text: The amyloid cascade hypothesis suggests that the buildup of the amyloid β (Aβ) peptide in the brain is a crucial factor in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, recent evidence suggests that amyloid toxicity may not be the primary cause of sporadic AD, which is characterized by cognitive decline. In this study, we used nontransgenic OXYS rats with accelerated senescence to confirm that Aβ aggregation occurs later in the progression of AD-like pathology. We observed that the levels of Aβ₁₋₄₂ and extracellular Aβ deposits in the brains of OXYS rats increased with age, but after synaptic losses, neuronal cell death, mitochondrial structural abnormalities, and hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein. We also identified specific gene variants, such as App, Apoe4, Bace1, Psen1, Psen2, and Picalm, that are strongly associated with the risk of late-onset or early-onset AD. Interestingly, we found that nonsynonymous SNPs were only present in the Casp3 and Sorl1 genes in OXYS rats. Therefore, our findings suggest that OXYS rats could serve as a model for sporadic AD. It is possible that multiple age-related pathological processes occur before toxic amyloid accumulation, which then triggers the final stage of sporadic AD and becomes a defining characteristic of the disease.

title: Estimating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by the Friedewald equation is adequate for classifying patients on the basis of nationally recommended cutpoints.
text:
We conducted a study comparing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) values obtained using the Friedewald formula to those obtained through lipoprotein fractionation. We analyzed 4736 specimens for this comparison. The Friedewald formula calculates LDL cholesterol by subtracting high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) cholesterol (estimated as triglyceride divided by 5) from total cholesterol.

Our findings showed that when triglyceride levels were below 2.0 g/L, over 90% of the estimated LDL cholesterol values were within +/- 10% of the measured values, making them acceptable. However, at triglyceride concentrations of 2.0-4.0 g/L and 4.0-6.0 g/L, only 72% and 39% of the estimates respectively, were considered acceptable.

We also examined an alternative formula that estimated VLDL as triglycerides divided by 6. However, the LDL values derived from this formula were even less accurate.

Despite the limitations in accuracy, we found that using estimated LDL for risk classification based on the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel cutpoints of 1.30 and 1.60 g/L was still considered acceptable.

In cases where triglyceride concentrations were less than or equal to 5.0 g/L, 88% of risk classifications based on estimated LDL (using triglycerides divided by 5) were in agreement with those determined by measured LDL. Only 11% of classifications were shifted across one cutpoint, with an equal distribution between high and low classifications. Less than 1% of classifications, all involving Type III hyperlipoproteinemia, were misclassified two cutpoints higher.

We also explored refinements in the estimation model, but these did not significantly improve LDL estimation or the agreement of risk classification.

title: Conditional Kif3a ablation causes abnormal hedgehog signaling topography, growth plate dysfunction, and excessive bone and cartilage formation during mouse skeletogenesis.
text: The roles of the motor protein Kif3a and primary cilia in skeletogenesis are not well understood, despite their importance in developmental processes. In this study, we generated mice with a deficiency in Kif3a specifically in cartilage and focused on the cranial base and synchondroses. The deficiency of Kif3a resulted in impaired growth and abnormal development of the cranial base, which was evident in newborn animals through anatomical and micro-computed tomography (microCT) examination. Additionally, the deficiency of Kif3a altered the organization and function of the synchondrosis growth plate, with the severity of these changes increasing over time. By postnatal day (P)7, the mutant growth plates lacked the typical zones of chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, instead consisting of chondrocytes with an unusual phenotype characterized by high expression of the collagen II (Col2a1) gene but barely detectable expression of Indian hedgehog (Ihh), collagen X (Col10a1), Vegf (Vegfa), MMP-13 (Mmp13), and osterix (Sp7). Concurrently, unexpected developmental events occurred in the perichondrial tissues, including excessive ossification along the perichondrial border and the formation of abnormal cartilage masses. To investigate the potential causes of these processes, we examined the hedgehog signaling pathway by monitoring the expression of the hedgehog effectors Patched 1 and Gli1, as well as the cell-surface component syndecan 3, which binds to hedgehog. Compared to control mice, the hedgehog signaling was weak within the mutant growth plates as early as P0, but was actually increased and widespread in the mutant perichondrial tissues. Finally, we also studied mice deficient in Ihh in cartilage during the postnatal period, and found that their cranial base defects only minimally resembled those observed in Kif3a-deficient mice. In conclusion, Kif3a and primary cilia play unique roles in the development of the cranial base and synchondrosis growth plates. Their deficiency leads to abnormal hedgehog signaling, dysfunction of the growth plates, and abnormal responses and processes in the perichondrial tissues, including the formation of abnormal cartilage and excessive ossification.

title: Morin Attenuates Ovalbumin-Induced Airway Inflammation by Modulating Oxidative Stress-Responsive MAPK Signaling.
text:
Asthma is a common inflammatory disease that is characterized by airway hyperresponsiveness, inflammation, and remodeling. Morin, an active ingredient derived from Moraceae plants, has shown promising anti-inflammatory effects in various disorders. However, its impact on pulmonary diseases, particularly asthma, remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether morin can alleviate airway inflammation in chronic asthma, with a focus on its modulation of oxidative stress.

In this study, mice sensitized to ovalbumin (OVA) were treated with morin or dexamethasone before challenge. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissues were collected for cell counts, histological analysis, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Additionally, human bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) were exposed to tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) in vitro. The supernatant was analyzed for proinflammatory proteins, while the cells were evaluated for reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activity.

The OVA-sensitized mice exhibited severe inflammatory responses and remodeling in their airways. However, treatment with morin significantly reduced the infiltration of inflammatory cells in the BALF and inhibited their presence around the respiratory tracts and vessels. Morin also suppressed goblet cell hyperplasia and collagen deposition/fibrosis, and dose-dependently decreased the levels of IgE, TNF-α, interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-13, matrix metalloproteinase-9, and malondialdehyde induced by OVA. In human BECs challenged with TNF-α, morin consistently decreased the levels of proinflammatory proteins such as eotaxin-1, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, IL-8, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1.

Furthermore, morin inhibited intracellular ROS production and MAPK phosphorylation in TNF-α-challenged BECs, suggesting that the relief of airway inflammation is mediated through the ROS/MAPK signaling pathway. This study provides the first evidence that morin can alleviate airway inflammation in chronic asthma, potentially through its modulation of oxidative stress-responsive MAPK signaling. These findings highlight the potential of morin as a potent agent for managing asthma.

title: Spontaneous autoimmunity prevented by thymic expression of a single self-antigen
text: The presence of self-antigen in the thymus is thought to be responsible for removing autoreactive T lymphocytes, which is crucial for maintaining tolerance to self. The Autoimmune regulator (Aire) gene, which is defective in autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, has been found to enhance the expression of self-antigens in the thymus. However, there has been a lack of evidence linking specific thymic self-antigens to a particular autoimmune phenotype in this model. Our study demonstrates that autoimmune eye disease in mice lacking aire occurs due to the absence of a single eye antigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP), in the thymus. Furthermore, the lack of IRBP expression solely in the thymus, even with aire expression, is enough to trigger spontaneous autoimmunity specific to the eyes. These findings suggest that the failure of selective self-antigen expression in the thymus can be adequate to cause organ-specific autoimmune disease, even in individuals who are otherwise tolerant to self.

title: Preventing bacterial DNA release and absent in melanoma 2 inflammasome activation by a Legionella effector functioning in membrane trafficking.
text: Legionella pneumophila, the bacteria responsible for causing Legionnaires' pneumonia, resides within a specific structure known as the Legionella-containing vacuole (LCV). The LCV is resistant to fusion with lysosomes and allows for efficient replication of the bacteria in host macrophages. This replication process is facilitated by a secretion system called Dot/Icm type IVB. One of the key components of this system is a protein called SdhA, which is crucial for the intracellular growth of L. pneumophila and plays a role in preventing the death of host cells. In our study, we found that the absence of SdhA led to increased activation of caspase-1, secretion of IL-1β, and a process called macrophage pyroptosis during Legionella infection. These activation processes were not dependent on the established flagellin-NAIP5-NLRC4 pathway, but instead relied on the DNA-sensing AIM2 inflammasome. Additionally, we discovered that Legionella DNA was released into the cytosol of macrophages, and this effect was significantly enhanced in the absence of SdhA. SdhA contains a functional Golgi-targeting GRIP domain, which is necessary for preventing activation of the AIM2 inflammasome. Furthermore, when SdhA was artificially expressed, it formed a unique ring-shaped membrane structure, indicating its involvement in membrane trafficking and maintaining the integrity of the LCV membrane. Overall, our findings suggest a potential connection between the trafficking/maturation of the LCV and the suppression of host innate immune detection, mediated by the function of SdhA.

title: Cytosolic viral sensor RIG-I is a 5'-triphosphate-dependent translocase on double-stranded RNA.
text:
RIG-I, also known as retinoic acid inducible-gene I, is a protein found in the cytosol that plays a crucial role in detecting viral RNA and initiating an immune response against viruses. It consists of multiple domains, including two N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARDs) that transmit the signal, and a regulatory domain that prevents signaling in the absence of viral RNA. RIG-I is able to distinguish between pathogenic and self-RNA by recognizing two molecular patterns: 5'-triphosphate and double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). However, the exact function of the DExH box helicase domain, which is also necessary for RIG-I's activity, is not fully understood.

Through the use of single-molecule protein-induced fluorescence enhancement, researchers have discovered that RIG-I possesses a strong ability to translocate dsRNA using the energy from adenosine 5'-triphosphate. The presence of the CARDs significantly inhibits this translocation process when 5'-triphosphate is absent. However, when activated by 5'-triphosphate, RIG-I selectively translocates on dsRNA in a cis manner. This integration of two RNA molecular patterns allows RIG-I to specifically detect and counteract replicating viruses.

In summary, RIG-I is a cytosolic protein that detects viral RNA and triggers an immune response. It utilizes the CARDs to transmit signals, while the regulatory domain prevents signaling in the absence of viral RNA. By recognizing 5'-triphosphate and dsRNA, RIG-I can distinguish between pathogenic and self-RNA. The DExH box helicase domain is also involved in RIG-I's activity, although its exact role is not fully understood. The discovery of RIG-I's dsRNA translocation activity powered by adenosine 5'-triphosphate provides insights into how RIG-I can specifically sense and combat replicating viruses.

title: Human Cytomegalovirus-Encoded Interleukin-10 Homolog Inhibits Maturation of Dendritic Cells and Alters Their Functionality
text:
Our study aimed to investigate the role of interleukin-10 (IL-10) in suppressing the maturation and cytokine production of dendritic cells (DCs), which are important regulators of adaptive immunity. We also wanted to understand how human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) utilizes its viral IL-10 homolog (cmvIL-10) to attenuate DC functionality and hinder the induction of antiviral immune responses.

Through RNA and protein analyses, we found that the cmvIL-10 gene was expressed with late gene kinetics. When immature DCs (iDCs) were treated with supernatant from HCMV-infected cultures, their maturation and proinflammatory cytokine production were inhibited. These inhibitory effects were specifically mediated through the IL-10 receptor and were not observed when DCs were treated with supernatant from cells infected with a cmvIL-10-knockout mutant. Additionally, incubation of iDCs with recombinant cmvIL-10 replicated the inhibition of maturation. Furthermore, cmvIL-10 had long-term effects on mature DCs (mDCs), enhancing their migration towards lymph node homing chemokines but greatly reducing their cytokine production. The inability of mDCs to secrete IL-12 was maintained, even when they were restimulated by the activated T-cell signal CD40 ligand in the absence of cmvIL-10. Importantly, cmvIL-10 also induced endogenous cellular IL-10 expression in DCs, further enhancing its anti-inflammatory effects.

In summary, our findings demonstrate that cmvIL-10 causes long-term functional alterations at all stages of DC activation.

title: Model for unidirectional movement of axonemal and cytoplasmic dynein molecules
text:
We propose a model that explains the unidirectional movement of dynein based on structural observations and biochemical experimental results. According to this model, the binding affinity of dynein for microtubules remains constant regardless of its nucleotide state. Instead, the transition between strong and weak microtubule-binding is naturally determined by the relative orientation between the stalk and microtubule as the stalk rotates following a nucleotide-state transition. This eliminates the need for the enigmatic communication from the ATP binding site in the globular domain to the far microtubule-binding site in the tip of the stalk, as required in conventional models.

By utilizing this model, we can effectively explain previous experimental findings. These include the impact of ATP and ADP bindings on the dissociation of dynein from microtubules, the processive movement of single-headed axonemal dyneins under saturating ATP concentration, the load dependence of step size for the processive movement of two-headed cytoplasmic dyneins, and the relationship between stall force and ATP concentration.

title: The inflammasome component NLRP3 impairs antitumor vaccine by enhancing the accumulation of tumor-associated myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text:
The inflammasome is a complex that breaks down proteins and produces the active forms of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18. The activation of the inflammasome is controlled by NLR proteins, which respond to both microbial and nonmicrobial stimuli. Among these proteins, NLRP3 is able to detect a wide range of stimuli and enhance adaptive immunity. However, its role in antitumor immunity is not yet understood. Therefore, we conducted a study to investigate the function of the NLRP3 inflammasome in the immune response using dendritic cell vaccination against a melanoma cell line called B16-F10, which has low immunogenicity. 

When we vaccinated mice that lacked the Nlrp3 gene, we observed a 4-fold increase in their survival compared to the control group. This increase in survival was dependent on CD8(+) T cells and showed immune specificity and memory. The improved vaccine efficacy in the Nlrp3-deficient mice was not due to differences in dendritic cells, but rather differences in myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC). Although Nlrp3 was present in MDSCs, its absence did not affect their ability to inhibit T cells or their presence in peripheral lymphoid tissues. Instead, the absence of Nlrp3 led to a 5-fold decrease in the number of MDSCs associated with tumors in the host mice. 

Further experiments involving the transfer of MDSCs also demonstrated that Nlrp3-deficient MDSCs were less effective in reaching the tumor site. Depleting MDSCs with an anti-Gr-1 antibody increased the survival of tumor-bearing mice with normal Nlrp3 levels, but had no effect on the survival of Nlrp3-deficient mice. 

Based on these findings, we concluded that Nlrp3 plays a critical role in the accumulation of MDSCs in tumors and in the inhibition of antitumor T-cell immunity following dendritic cell vaccination. Our results reveal an unexpected role for Nlrp3 in hindering antitumor immune responses, suggesting new strategies to enhance the effectiveness of antitumor vaccines by targeting Nlrp3 signaling.

title: Natural Killer Cells for Immunotherapy – Advantages of the NK-92 Cell Line over Blood NK Cells
text: NK cells are powerful cells that can effectively kill cancer cells and potentially combat severe viral infections. However, there are difficulties in obtaining a sufficient number of functional NK cells from a patient's blood, as they only make up 10% of lymphocytes and are often dysfunctional. An alternative approach is to obtain cells from a healthy donor, but this requires removing the allogeneic T cells to prevent graft-versus-host reactions. Cell lines with cytotoxic properties have been developed from patients with clonal NK-cell lymphoma. These cells can be expanded in culture with the help of IL-2. However, out of the seven known NK cell lines, only the NK-92 cell line consistently demonstrates high antitumor cytotoxicity. Moreover, NK-92 cells can easily be genetically modified to recognize specific tumor antigens or enhance the activity of monoclonal antibodies through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Notably, NK-92 is the only cell line product that has been successfully infused into patients with advanced cancer, resulting in clinical benefits and minimal side effects.

title: Differential activation of DNA-PK based on DNA strand orientation and sequence bias
text: The complex responsible for repairing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) through non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) consists of DNA-PKcs and Ku. Ku, a protein made up of two subunits, binds to the ends of DNA and helps recruit the catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs. We conducted a study to investigate how the orientation and sequence of DNA strands affect the activation of DNA-PK. Additionally, we examined how the position and orientation of cisplatin adducts on DNA impact kinase activation. We created various DNA substrates with specific cisplatin-DNA adducts placed in three different orientations on the DNA. To direct DNA-PK binding to the unblocked ends with a specific DNA strand orientation and cisplatin-DNA adduct position, we modified the ends with biotin and blocked them with streptavidin (SA). We measured the activity of DNA-PK kinase and found that the orientation and sequence of DNA strands have a significant impact on kinase activation, with only a portion of this effect being attributed to Ku-DNA binding. Furthermore, the position of cisplatin-DNA adducts resulted in varying degrees of inhibition depending on their distance from the ends and strand orientation. These findings emphasize the importance of local variations in DNA structure, chemistry, and sequence in influencing DNA-PK activation and potentially NHEJ.

title: Regulators of Trypanosoma brucei Cell Cycle Progression and Differentiation Identified Using a Kinome-Wide RNAi Screen
text: The African trypanosome, Trypanosoma brucei, has a strong connection between cell cycle regulation and differentiation throughout its complex life cycle. Although there have been studies on changes in phosphorylation between the mammalian bloodstream form and the insect procyclic form, there is limited knowledge about the parasite's protein kinases (PKs) that control cellular proliferation and differentiation. To address this, a library of T. brucei kinome-wide RNAi cell lines was created, allowing for the individual knockdown of each of the parasite's 190 predicted protein kinases. By using a cell viability assay, screening of this library identified at least 42 PKs that are necessary for normal bloodstream form proliferation in culture. A secondary screening revealed 24 PKs that, when depleted through RNAi, caused various defects in the cell cycle, including in G1/S, kinetoplast replication/segregation, mitosis, and cytokinesis. Among these PKs, 15 were newly discovered as cell cycle regulators. Another screening identified two PKs, named repressor of differentiation kinase (RDK1 and RDK2), which, when depleted, promoted the differentiation of the bloodstream form to the procyclic form. RDK1 is a membrane-associated STE11-like PK, while RDK2 is a NEK PK that is crucial for parasite proliferation. RDK1 works together with the PTP1/PIP39 phosphatase cascade to prevent uncontrolled differentiation from the bloodstream to the procyclic form, while RDK2 is a PK that efficiently induces differentiation even without known triggers. Therefore, the RNAi kinome library is a valuable resource for studying cell signaling pathways in African trypanosomes, as well as for identifying and validating drug targets.

title: Chemotherapy options in elderly and frail patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (MRC FOCUS2): an open-label, randomised factorial trial
text: The aim of the study, FOCUS2, was to investigate the use of reduced-dose chemotherapy options and identify objective predictors of outcome in elderly and frail patients with advanced colorectal cancer. The trial was conducted in 61 UK centers and included patients who were deemed unfit for full-dose chemotherapy. Patients were randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups: intravenous fluorouracil with levofolinate, oxaliplatin and fluorouracil, capecitabine, or oxaliplatin and capecitabine. The primary outcome measures were the addition of oxaliplatin and the substitution of fluorouracil with capecitabine, assessed by progression-free survival and change in global quality of life, respectively. The study found that the addition of oxaliplatin showed some improvement in progression-free survival, but the finding was not statistically significant. The replacement of fluorouracil with capecitabine did not improve global quality of life. The risk of toxic effects was not significantly increased with oxaliplatin, but was higher with capecitabine compared to fluorouracil. The study also found that baseline symptoms, disease extent, and the use of oxaliplatin were predictive of better treatment outcomes. Overall, the study demonstrated that elderly and frail patients can participate in randomized controlled trials with appropriate design and reduced starting doses of chemotherapy. The study was funded by Cancer Research UK and the Medical Research Council.

title: Whole-genome sequencing of Oryza brachyantha reveals mechanisms underlying Oryza genome evolution
text: We present the newly assembled genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha, a wild species of the Oryza genus. This genome holds a vast collection of agriculturally significant genes that have yet to be fully explored for rice improvement. Our analysis reveals that Oryza brachyantha has a compact genome due to the low activity of long-terminal repeat retrotransposons and extensive internal deletions of ancient long-terminal repeat elements. Within this genome, we have identified 32,038 protein-coding genes, with only 70% of them found in collinear positions when compared to the rice genome. By studying the breakpoints of non-collinear genes, we have discovered that double-strand break repair through non-homologous end joining plays a crucial role in gene movement and the erosion of collinearity in Oryza genomes. Additionally, the transition from euchromatin to heterochromatin in the rice genome is accompanied by segmental and tandem duplications, which are further expanded by the insertion of transposable elements. This high-quality reference genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha serves as a valuable resource for studying the functional and evolutionary aspects of the Oryza genus.

title: Ultrasound imaging for lumbar punctures and epidural catheterisations: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The objective of this study was to determine if ultrasound imaging can decrease the likelihood of failed lumbar punctures or epidural catheterizations compared to standard palpation methods. Additionally, the study aimed to assess if ultrasound imaging can reduce the number of traumatic procedures, insertion attempts, and needle redirections. The study design involved a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Data was sourced from Ovid Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials up to May 2012, with no restrictions on language or publication status. The review included 14 studies with a total of 1334 patients, with 674 patients assigned to the ultrasound group and 660 to the control group. Five studies evaluated lumbar punctures and nine evaluated epidural catheterizations. In the ultrasound group, six out of 624 procedures failed, while in the control group, 44 out of 610 procedures failed. Ultrasound imaging significantly reduced the risk of failed procedures (risk ratio 0.21, 95% confidence interval 0.10 to 0.43, P<0.001). Subgroup analysis for lumbar punctures and epidural catheterizations showed similar risk reduction (risk ratio 0.19, P=0.002 and risk ratio 0.23, P=0.003, respectively). Ultrasound imaging also significantly reduced the risk of traumatic procedures (risk ratio 0.27, P=0.005), the number of insertion attempts (mean difference -0.44, P<0.001), and the number of needle redirections (mean difference -1.00, P<0.001). In conclusion, ultrasound imaging can decrease the risk of failed or traumatic lumbar punctures and epidural catheterizations, as well as reduce the number of needle insertions and redirections. Ultrasound may be a valuable tool for these procedures.

title: Guidance of B cells by the orphan G protein-coupled receptor EBI2 shapes humoral immune responses.
text: Both rapid and long-term antibody production against invading pathogens relies on humoral immunity. This is accomplished through the creation of separate populations of extrafollicular plasmablast and follicular germinal center (GC) B cells. However, the exact signals that direct responding B cells to these different compartments are not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the expression of the orphan G protein-coupled receptor Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 2 (EBI2, also known as GPR183) by activated B cells is necessary for their migration to extrafollicular sites and the initiation of early plasmablast responses. Conversely, when EBI2 is downregulated, B cells are able to enter the center of follicles and facilitate efficient GC formation. Therefore, EBI2 adds a previously unknown aspect to B cell migration that is vital for coordinating rapid and long-term antibody responses.

title: SIRT1 is required for long-term growth of human mesenchymal stem cells
text: The therapeutic potential of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) lies in their ability to renew themselves and transform into various tissues. However, when MSCs are cultured in a lab setting, they often undergo senescence, and the reasons behind this are not fully understood. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms behind this phenomenon and found that a protein called SIRT1, which relies on NAD for its function, is expressed differently in MSCs derived from bone marrow (B-MSCs) and adipose tissue after multiple passages in culture. By using lentiviral shRNA, the researchers were able to selectively reduce the levels of SIRT1 in early passage human MSCs, which resulted in slower cell growth and accelerated senescence. On the other hand, overexpressing SIRT1 in B-MSCs that had been cultured for a long time delayed senescence and preserved their ability to transform into adipogenic and osteogenic tissues. The researchers also discovered that the delayed accumulation of a protein called p16 played a role in the effects of SIRT1. However, the use of resveratrol, a compound known to activate SIRT1, only temporarily promoted the proliferation of B-MSCs. These findings provide insights into the role of SIRT1 in the aging of normal cells and may contribute to strategies for preventing senescence in human MSCs, which would benefit tissue engineering and therapies involving MSCs.

title: Rapid and persistent modulation of actin dynamics regulates postsynaptic reorganization underlying bidirectional plasticity
text: The synapse is a specialized cellular structure that undergoes reorganization based on the strength of input signals. However, the mechanisms behind these changes are not well understood. One potential factor in the reorganization of synapse components and structure is actin, which serves as both a cytoskeleton and a scaffold for synapses. Actin exists in a dynamic equilibrium between F-actin and G-actin, which is influenced by cellular signaling. To investigate this further, we used a new imaging technique called FRET to monitor the equilibrium between F-actin and G-actin. Our findings demonstrate that tetanic stimulation leads to a rapid and persistent shift towards F-actin in the dendritic spines of rat hippocampal neurons. This results in the enlargement of spines and an increase in postsynaptic binding capacity. On the other hand, prolonged low-frequency stimulation shifts the equilibrium towards G-actin, leading to a loss of postsynaptic actin and structure. This bidirectional regulation of actin plays an active role in protein assembly and disassembly, and provides a foundation for bidirectional synaptic plasticity.

title: Sublime Microglia: Expanding Roles for the Guardians of the CNS
text: New research challenges the idea that microglia only play a role in disease states within the central nervous system (CNS). Instead of simply responding to CNS injury, infection, or pathology, recent evidence suggests that microglia also shape the structure of the CNS, refine neuronal circuitry and network connections, and contribute to its plasticity. These normal physiological functions of microglia begin during development and continue into adulthood. In this article, we propose a new framework for understanding the functions of microglia beyond neuroinflammation. We also explore the diverse range of signaling and communication patterns in microglia that are crucial for both pathological conditions and the normal functioning of the CNS.

title: Cancer after pre-eclampsia: follow up of the Jerusalem perinatal study cohort.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare the occurrence of cancer in women with and without a history of pre-eclampsia. The study was conducted as a cohort study, using data from the Jerusalem perinatal study, which included women who gave birth in three major hospitals in West Jerusalem between 1964 and 1976. A total of 37,033 women participated in the study. The main outcome measures were age-adjusted and multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for cancer incidence in the entire cohort and in women who were first-time mothers at the start of the study.

The results showed that cancer developed in 91 women with pre-eclampsia and 2204 women without pre-eclampsia. The hazard ratio for cancer incidence was 1.27 (95% confidence interval 1.03 to 1.57), indicating an increased risk of cancer in women with a history of pre-eclampsia. The risk of specific types of cancer, such as stomach, ovary epithelium, breast, and lung or larynx cancer, was particularly elevated. In addition, primiparous women who had pre-eclampsia at the start of the study had an increased incidence of stomach, breast, ovary, kidney, and lung or larynx cancer.

In conclusion, this study found that a history of pre-eclampsia is associated with an overall increased risk of cancer and an increased incidence of cancer at several specific sites. This could be due to shared environmental and genetic factors that contribute to the development of both pre-eclampsia and cancer in this population.

title: Keeping your senescent cells under control
text: Cellular senescence is a type of cell-cycle arrest that limits the ability of premalignant cells to proliferate. It was first observed in 1961 by Hayflick and Moorhead in human fibroblasts undergoing replicative exhaustion in culture. Senescence can be triggered in various cell types in response to cellular damage or stress. Recent studies have shown that senescence acts as a failsafe mechanism against tumorigenesis and contributes to the effectiveness of certain anticancer treatments. Senescent cells have also been found in aged or damaged tissues, suggesting that senescence can affect tissue regeneration and organismal aging. However, senescence can also have positive effects on organ maintenance by limiting pathological responses to acute injuries. Senescent cells communicate with their environment by secreting cytokines and growth factors, known as the "senescence associated secretory phenotype (SASP)". The SASP can have both pro-tumorigenic and anti-tumor effects, and it may also influence tissue aging. Recent research has identified microRNAs that regulate the secretion of certain SASP components, suggesting a potential therapeutic target for modulating the SASP. Further studies are needed to fully understand the regulatory pathways controlling the SASP and its role in aging and cancer.

title: Role for insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons in control of energy homeostasis.
text: The integration of signals on food palatability and food-associated reward by dopaminergic midbrain neurons plays a crucial role in regulating energy balance. To investigate the involvement of insulin receptor (IR) signaling in this process, we disrupted IR signaling specifically in tyrosine hydroxylase (Th)-expressing cells in mice (IR(ΔTh)). This disruption led to significant increases in body weight, fat mass, and food intake. Interestingly, while insulin normally increased the firing frequency of dopaminergic VTA/SN neurons, this effect was completely abolished in IR(ΔTh) mice. Additionally, these mice displayed altered responses to cocaine when food was restricted. These findings highlight the importance of insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons for the control of food intake and energy balance in vivo.

title: [New guidelines to evaluate the response to treatment in solid tumors].
text: The investigation of the antitumor activity of anticancer agents involves assessing the extent to which they can shrink tumors. In the late 1970s, the International Union Against Cancer and the World Health Organization (WHO) established specific criteria for evaluating tumor response. In 1994, various organizations involved in clinical cancer research collaborated to review these criteria based on their expertise. After extensive discussions, new guidelines have been developed to replace the previous WHO criteria. Additionally, one of the participating groups devised a model that allows for the calculation of response rates using unidimensional measurements of tumor lesions instead of the traditional bidimensional approach. This model has been validated by the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (Recist) Group and incorporated into the current guidelines. This article provides a philosophical background to clarify the different purposes of response evaluation and proposes a model that combines the assessment of all existing lesions, including target and nontarget lesions, to determine the overall response to treatment. The methods for assessing tumor lesions have been more clearly defined, and all other aspects of response evaluation have been thoroughly discussed, reviewed, and revised as necessary.

title: Structural Rearrangements of NR1/NR2A NMDA Receptors during Allosteric Inhibition
text: The subunits of ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) have a large N-terminal domain (NTD) that comes before the agonist-binding domain (ABD) and plays a role in subunit oligomerization. In NMDA receptors (NMDARs), the NTDs of NR2A and NR2B subunits also serve as binding sites for the natural inhibitor Zn(2+) ion. While these allosteric sites have been well-studied, the molecular mechanisms through which the NTDs communicate with the rest of the receptor to promote inhibition are still unknown. In this study, we have identified the ABD dimer interface as a crucial structural element that allows for coupling between the NTDs and the channel gate. The strength of this interface also determines proton inhibition, which is another form of allosteric modulation in NMDARs. Therefore, conformational changes at the ABD dimer interface seem to be a fundamental mechanism present in all iGluR subfamilies, but they have evolved to serve different functions: rapid desensitization in AMPA and kainate receptors, and allosteric inhibition in NMDARs.

title: The role of iron in Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilm formation: the exochelin siderophore is essential in limiting iron conditions for biofilm formation but not for planktonic growth
text: Structured biofilm communities of mycobacteria can be found at liquid-air interfaces and on solid surfaces. The complete development of Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilms necessitates the addition of supplemental iron above 1 μM ferrous sulphate, although iron is not necessary for planktonic growth. Analysis of the M. smegmatis transcriptome using microarrays reveals that genes responsive to iron, particularly those involved in siderophore synthesis and iron uptake, are highly induced during biofilm formation, indicating a response to iron deprivation even when 2 μM iron is present. The acquisition of iron under these circumstances relies specifically on the exochelin synthesis and uptake pathways, as demonstrated by the significant impairment of an iron-exochelin uptake mutant in transitioning to biofilm growth. Conversely, although the expression of mycobactin and iron ABC transport operons is greatly upregulated during biofilm formation, mutants in these systems are still able to form normal biofilms under low-iron (2 μM) conditions. The close relationship between iron availability and matrix-associated fatty acids suggests a potential metabolic role in the later stages of biofilm maturation, in addition to its early regulatory function. Similarly, M. smegmatis surface motility is dependent on iron availability, requiring both supplemental iron and the exochelin pathway for acquisition.

title: Plasma lipids and prolactin in patients with breast cancer.
text: A comparative study was conducted to examine the differences in circulating plasma prolactin and lipid concentrations between pre- and postmenopausal women with benign and malignant breast disease. The results revealed several disparities. Prior to surgery, breast cancer patients had higher levels of plasma lipids, phospholipids, triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids in their blood. Additionally, these patients exhibited significantly lower levels of HDL-Cholesterol. These variations persisted even when the patient groups were further divided based on menopausal status. Furthermore, plasma prolactin concentrations were found to be elevated in cancer patients compared to non-cancer patients, with a more pronounced effect observed in premenopausal individuals. Among premenopausal patients, those with invasive or poorly differentiated disease had significantly higher levels of prolactin compared to those with non-invasive disease. However, no correlations were identified between plasma prolactin and any of the lipid fractions.

title: expression by oxidized linoleic
text: Impairments in endothelium-dependent vascular relaxations are associated with hypercholesterolemia. Surprisingly, the production of nitrogen oxides by the endothelium is increased in the early stages of hypercholesterolemia. Previous research has focused on the effects of oxidized low density lipoprotein (LDL) on the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), with lysophosphatidyl choline (LPC) being identified as a component of oxidized LDL that may modulate this effect. Another biologically active component of oxidized LDL is 13-hydroperoxyoctadecadienoic acid (13-HPODE), which is an oxidized form of linoleic acid. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of HPODE on the expression of eNOS in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs). Treatment of the endothelial cells with HPODE for 24 hours resulted in a dose-dependent increase in eNOS mRNA levels, as determined by Northern analysis. Time response studies revealed that eNOS mRNA levels were significantly elevated at 12 and 24 hours following HPODE treatment. Additionally, treatment with 20 microM HPODE led to a significant increase in eNOS protein content and enzyme activity. Nuclear run-on studies indicated that the transcription rate of the eNOS gene was significantly higher 4 hours after HPODE treatment compared to control cultures. Furthermore, actinomycin D studies demonstrated that the half-life of eNOS mRNA was extended from 6 hours to 12 hours by HPODE treatment. Therefore, the up-regulation of eNOS expression induced by HPODE is mediated by both transcriptional and posttranscriptional mechanisms. These findings suggest that endothelial cells may increase eNOS expression in the early stages of hypercholesterolemia as a compensatory response to oxidative injury.

title: Specific killing of multiple myeloma cells by (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate extracted from green tea: biologic activity and therapeutic implications.
text: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) is a polyphenol derived from green tea that acts as an antioxidant and has potential in preventing and treating cancer. We conducted a study to assess the effectiveness of EGCG in multiple myeloma (MM) by examining its impact on cell growth. Our findings revealed that EGCG can halt the growth of MM cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner, leading to cell death through apoptosis. Importantly, this effect was observed in both IL-6-dependent MM cells and primary patient cells, while having minimal impact on the growth of normal cells. Furthermore, treatment with EGCG induced apoptosis in myeloma cells grown as tumors in mice. We discovered that EGCG interacts with the 67-kDa laminin receptor 1 (LR1), which is significantly elevated in myeloma cells compared to normal cells. By inhibiting LR1, we were able to prevent EGCG-induced apoptosis in myeloma cells, suggesting that LR1 plays a crucial role in mediating EGCG's effects in MM while sparing normal cells. Additionally, our analysis of gene expression changes revealed that EGCG activates specific pathways involved in growth arrest and apoptosis in MM cells. These pathways include the expression of proteins associated with death receptor-dependent apoptosis, p53-like proteins, positive regulators of apoptosis and NF-kappaB activation, and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors. We confirmed the expression of these proteins at the protein level through Western blot analysis. Overall, our results demonstrate the potent and targeted antimyeloma activity of EGCG, supporting its potential for clinical use.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 arrests the growth of glioblastoma multiforme intracranial xenografts.
text: The activation of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (cdk4/6) is a common occurrence in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) tumors and presents a promising target for the development of small molecule inhibitors. In this study, we examined the molecular factors and response of various GBM cell lines and xenografts to PD-0332991, a specific inhibitor of cdk4/6. In vitro testing of PD-0332991 on a range of GBM cell lines showed that it effectively arrested the cell cycle at the G(1) phase and induced senescence in all 16 cell lines that had functional retinoblastoma protein (Rb), regardless of other genetic abnormalities. However, 5 cell lines with complete inactivation of Rb were resistant to the treatment. Depletion of Rb expression using short hairpin RNA also made GBM cells resistant to PD-0332991, further confirming the requirement of Rb for sensitivity to cdk4/6 inhibition. PD-0332991 was able to cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently and effectively suppressed the growth of intracranial GBM xenograft tumors, even those that had recurred after initial treatment with temozolomide. Notably, none of the mice receiving PD-0332991 died due to disease progression while on the therapy. Furthermore, the combination of PD-0332991 and radiation therapy significantly improved survival compared to either therapy alone. Overall, our findings support the need for clinical trials to evaluate PD-0332991 for both newly diagnosed and recurrent GBM, and highlight the importance of Rb status in determining the potential benefits of this treatment.

title: Choosing Haplotype-Tagging SNPS Based on Unphased Genotype Data Using a Preliminary Sample of Unrelated Subjects with an Example from the Multiethnic Cohort Study
text:
We are currently implementing a method to select haplotype-tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms (htSNPs) in two large nested case-control studies within a multiethnic cohort (MEC). These studies aim to identify associations between the risk of prostate and breast cancer and common genetic variations in candidate genes. 

To estimate haplotype frequencies, we initially genotyped a high density of SNPs selected every 3-5 kb in and around a candidate gene using a preliminary sample of 70 randomly chosen control subjects from each of the 5 ethnic groups in the MEC. We utilized a modified version of the Excoffier-Slatkin E-M algorithm. 

To assess the performance of a candidate set of htSNPs, which will be genotyped in a much larger case-control sample, we treated the estimated haplotype frequencies as known. We then conducted a formal calculation to determine the uncertainty in the number of copies of common haplotypes carried by an individual. This calculation was summarized as a coefficient of determination, R2h. 

The candidate set of htSNPs was selected to maximize the minimum value of R2h across the common haplotypes, h.

title: A model for the role of gut bacteria in the development of autoimmunity for type 1 diabetes
text: There is substantial evidence indicating that the gut microbiome plays a role in type 1 diabetes. Administering probiotics or antibiotics to rodents prone to diabetes prevents the onset of the disease. Additionally, these diabetes-prone rodents have a noticeably different gut microbiome compared to healthy rodents. Recent research conducted on children with a high genetic risk for type 1 diabetes has revealed significant differences in the gut microbiome between those who develop autoimmunity for the disease and those who remain healthy. However, it is important to note that the variations in microbiome composition between autoimmune and healthy children are not consistent across all studies due to the significant influence of environmental factors such as diet and geography. By controlling for these confounding factors, researchers have identified bacterial associations with the disease. For instance, a study conducted on a human cohort from a single Finnish city, where geography is limited, discovered a strong link between a dominant bacterial species called Bacteroides dorei and type 1 diabetes (Davis-Richardson et al. Front Microbiol 2014;5:678). Furthermore, recent DNA methylation analyses suggest that a comprehensive epigenetic analysis of the gut microbiome may be necessary. These studies propose a testable hypothesis that a diet high in fat and gluten, and low in resistant starch, may be the primary cause of gut dysbiosis. This dysbiosis may result in a lack of butyrate production by gut bacteria, which subsequently leads to the development of a permeable gut and autoimmunity. Although the bacterial community responsible for these changes in butyrate production may vary worldwide, bacteria belonging to the genus Bacteroides are believed to play a significant role.

title: METHODS AND RESULTS
text:
Cytoscape is a software project that aims to integrate biomolecular interaction networks with high-throughput expression data and other molecular states. It provides a unified conceptual framework for analyzing molecular components and interactions. While it can be used for any system, Cytoscape is particularly powerful when combined with large databases of protein-protein, protein-DNA, and genetic interactions that are increasingly available for humans and model organisms. 

Cytoscape's software Core offers basic functionality for organizing and querying the network. It also allows for visual integration of the network with expression profiles, phenotypes, and other molecular states. Additionally, it enables linking the network to databases of functional annotations. The Core can be extended through a plug-in architecture, which facilitates the rapid development of additional computational analyses and features. 

Several case studies of Cytoscape plug-ins are available, including a search for interaction pathways that correlate with changes in gene expression, a study of protein complexes involved in cellular recovery from DNA damage, the inference of a combined physical/functional interaction network for Halobacterium, and an interface to detailed stochastic/kinetic gene regulatory models.

title: Dual Regulation of miRNA Biogenesis Generates Target Specificity in Neurotrophin-Induced Protein Synthesis
text: Regulation of gene expression relies heavily on controlling translation. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays a crucial role in protein synthesis, leading to long-lasting changes in synaptic function. However, the mechanism behind BDNF's selective impact on a small fraction of expressed mRNAs remains unclear. Our findings demonstrate that BDNF rapidly boosts Dicer levels, resulting in increased mature miRNA levels and the formation of RNA processing bodies in neurons. Additionally, BDNF swiftly induces Lin28, leading to the loss of Lin28-regulated miRNAs and a corresponding increase in translation of their target mRNAs. The presence of binding sites for Lin28-regulated miRNAs is essential for conferring BDNF responsiveness to a transcript. Deficiency in Lin28 or expression of a Lin28-resistant Let-7 precursor miRNA hampers the specificity of BDNF-mediated translation and dendrite arborization dependent on BDNF. Our data establish that the specificity of BDNF-regulated translation relies on a two-part posttranscriptional control of miRNA biogenesis. This control generally enhances mRNA repression in association with GW182 while selectively derepressing and increasing translation of specific mRNAs.

title: A Viral microRNA Cluster Strongly Potentiates the Transforming Properties of a Human Herpesvirus
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a cancer-causing herpesvirus in humans, stimulates the growth of resting B lymphocytes, which serve as its reservoir in the body. While it is known that the virus's latent proteins are necessary for continuous B cell growth, it remains uncertain if they alone are sufficient. Recent research has discovered that EBV also produces microRNAs (miRNAs) that are present in infected B cells and certain EBV-related lymphomas. These miRNAs are organized into two clusters, located either next to the BHRF1 gene or within the viral BART transcripts. To investigate the role of the BHRF1 miRNA cluster, scientists created a mutant virus lacking all three miRNAs (Δ123), as well as a virus that reverted back to its original form. The results showed that the Δ123 EBV mutant had a significantly reduced ability to transform B cells, over 20 times less than the wild type or revertant viruses. B cells exposed to the knock-out virus exhibited slower growth and a two-fold decrease in the number of cells entering the cell cycle S phase. Additionally, these cells had higher levels of latent gene expression and latent protein production compared to their wild type counterparts. Therefore, the BHRF1 miRNAs accelerate B cell expansion even at lower levels of latent gene expression. This miRNA cluster not only promotes the growth of the virus reservoir but also reduces the viral antigenic load, which could aid in the virus's persistence within the infected host. Consequently, the EBV BHRF1 miRNAs may serve as potential targets for therapeutic interventions in certain EBV-related lymphomas.

title: EMSY overexpression disrupts the BRCA2/RAD51 pathway in the DNA-damage response: implications for chromosomal instability/recombination syndromes as checkpoint diseases
text:
EMSY is a protein that connects the BRCA2 pathway to sporadic breast and ovarian cancer. It produces a nuclear protein that binds to the BRCA2 N-terminal domain, which is involved in regulating chromatin and transcription. However, when EMSY is amplified or overexpressed sporadically, it inhibits the transactivation potential of BRCA2 and causes chromosomal instability. This mimics the effects of BRCA2 mutations in the development of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

In addition to its role in chromatin and transcription regulation, EMSY may also be involved in the response to DNA damage. This is suggested by its ability to localize at sites of DNA damage and repair in chromatin. This implies that overexpression of EMSY may also inhibit BRCA2 in processes such as DNA damage replication, checkpoint control, and recombination and repair. These processes require the interaction of EMSY with other proteins such as PALB2, RPA, and RAD51.

Using a well-established assay system for recombination and repair, we demonstrate that even a slight increase in EMSY levels can inhibit these processes independently of transcriptional interference. Since EMSY, RPA, and PALB2 all bind to the same region of BRCA2, these findings further support the idea that EMSY amplification may mimic BRCA2 deficiency by disrupting the BRCA2/RAD51 complex at sites of DNA damage and replication. It also suggests that BRCA2 and RAD51 coordinate these processes by utilizing EMSY, PALB2, and RPA.

We extensively discuss the molecular details of how this can occur and its implications for a new recombination mechanism that functions as a checkpoint rather than a DNA repair system for cell division, survival, death, and human diseases. This includes considering the tissue-specific predisposition to cancer and how it may impact targeted therapy and prevention strategies.

title: Original Article
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of taking dehydrated concentrates from mixed fruit and vegetable juices (Juice Plus+R) on various health markers. Previous research has shown that consuming fruits and vegetables can lower the risk of chronic diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease due to their antioxidant properties. The study recruited 60 Japanese participants who were randomly assigned to either the supplement group or the placebo group. Blood and urine samples were collected at the beginning of the study, after 14 days, and after 28 days for analysis. 

The results showed that after 28 days of supplementation, the concentration of beneficial antioxidants such as beta-carotene, lycopene, and alpha tocopherol in the blood significantly increased compared to the placebo group. Serum folate levels also increased, and this was associated with a decrease in plasma homocysteine levels. Measures of oxidative stress, such as serum lipid peroxides and urine 8OHdG, decreased compared to baseline. 

Furthermore, when the data was analyzed specifically for smokers, similar changes were observed after 28 days of supplementation. 

In conclusion, taking the fruit and vegetable juice concentrate capsules proved to be an effective way of increasing the levels of important antioxidants in the body. This was associated with a decrease in markers of oxidative stress and an improvement in folate status. These benefits were observed in both smokers and non-smokers.

title: NCBI GEO: archive for functional genomics data sets—update
text: The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) is a global public database (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) where researchers can submit high-throughput microarray and next-generation sequence functional genomic data sets. This valuable resource allows for the storage of raw data, processed data, and metadata, all of which are organized, interconnected, and searchable. Users can freely download the data in various formats. Additionally, GEO offers a range of web-based tools and strategies to aid users in querying, analyzing, and visualizing the data. This article presents the current state of GEO and highlights recent advancements, such as the introduction of GEO2R, a web application based on R that facilitates data analysis for GEO users.

title: Viral Paratransgenesis in the Malaria Vector Anopheles gambiae
text: Paratransgenesis, which involves genetically modifying the microorganisms that live inside insects, is being considered as a potential method to control diseases transmitted by vectors, such as malaria. However, the lack of suitable microorganisms for the major malaria vector, Anopheles gambiae, has hindered progress in paratransgenic malaria control. Densonucleosis viruses (DNVs) have shown promise in other systems as agents for viral paratransgenesis because they can infect important vector insects, can be genetically manipulated, and can be passed on to future generations. Unfortunately, An. gambiae has been resistant to DNV dissemination. However, we have recently discovered, cloned, and characterized the first DNV (AgDNV) that is capable of infecting and spreading in An. gambiae. We have also developed a flexible AgDNV-based expression vector that can be used to express any gene of interest in An. gambiae using a two-plasmid helper-transducer system. To demonstrate the potential of this viral paratransgenesis strategy, we used this system to introduce an exogenous gene (enhanced green fluorescent protein; EGFP) into An. gambiae mosquitoes. Both the wild-type and EGFP-transducing AgDNV virions were highly infectious to An. gambiae larvae, spread to and expressed EGFP in relevant adult tissues such as the midgut, fat body, and ovaries, and were passed on to subsequent generations of mosquitoes. These proof-of-concept results suggest that AgDNV could be used as part of a paratransgenic malaria control strategy by introducing anti-Plasmodium peptides or insect-specific toxins into Anopheles mosquitoes. Additionally, AgDNV will be a valuable tool for transient gene expression or RNAi in An. gambiae, as it is effective and easy to use in laboratory settings.

title: The polycomb group protein L3mbtl2 assembles an atypical PRC1-family complex that is essential in pluripotent stem cells and early development.
text: The biological function of L3mbtl2 has not been clearly defined, although it has been linked to transcriptional repression and chromatin compaction. In our study, we discovered that disrupting L3mbtl2 leads to embryonic lethality and failure of gastrulation. This is accompanied by impaired proliferation and abnormal differentiation of L3mbtl2(-/-) embryonic stem cells. L3mbtl2 controls gene expression by recruiting a complex similar to the E2F6-complex, which includes G9A, Hdac1, and Ring1b, and is related to the Polycomb Repressive Complex1 (PRC1). The presence of L3mbtl2 at target genes is associated with specific modifications of histones, such as H3K9 dimethylation, low histone acetylation, and H2AK119 ubiquitination. However, the latter modification is not solely dependent on L3mbtl2 and is not sufficient for gene repression. Our genome-wide analysis revealed that the L3mbtl2-dependent complex primarily regulates genes that are not bound by the canonical PRC1 and PRC2 complexes. Nevertheless, some developmental regulators are repressed by the combined activity of all three complexes. Overall, our findings highlight the crucial and selective role of an unconventional PRC1-family complex in early development and embryonic stem cells.

title: Long-term effect of aspirin on cancer risk in carriers of hereditary colorectal cancer: an analysis from the CAPP2 randomised controlled trial
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous observational studies have suggested that regular aspirin consumption may reduce the risk of colorectal cancer. However, randomized controlled trials have not yet investigated the prevention of colorectal cancer as a primary endpoint. The CAPP2 trial aimed to examine the antineoplastic effects of aspirin and resistant starch in individuals with Lynch syndrome, the most common form of hereditary colorectal cancer. In this report, we present the long-term follow-up results of participants who were randomly assigned to receive either aspirin or a placebo.

METHODS: In the CAPP2 trial, individuals with Lynch syndrome were randomly assigned to receive either 600 mg of aspirin or an aspirin placebo, as well as either 30 g of resistant starch or a starch placebo, for a period of up to 4 years. Randomization was done in blocks of 16, with the option for single-agent randomization and extended double-blind follow-up after the intervention. Both participants and investigators were unaware of the treatment allocation. The primary endpoint of the trial was the development of colorectal cancer. The analysis was conducted based on intention to treat and per protocol. The trial is registered under ISRCTN59521990.
