RESULTS: A total of 861 participants were randomly assigned to receive either aspirin or an aspirin placebo. After a mean follow-up of 55.7 months, 48 participants had developed 53 primary colorectal cancers (18 out of 427 in the aspirin group, 30 out of 434 in the placebo group). The intention-to-treat analysis of the time to first colorectal cancer showed a hazard ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.35-1.13, p=0.12). The Poisson regression analysis, which accounted for multiple primary events, yielded an incidence rate ratio of 0.56 (95% CI 0.32-0.99, p=0.05). For participants who completed 2 years of intervention (258 in the aspirin group, 250 in the placebo group), the per-protocol analysis showed a hazard ratio of 0.41 (0.19-0.86, p=0.02) and an incidence rate ratio of 0.37 (0.18-0.78, p=0.008). No adverse event data were available after the intervention, but during the intervention period, there were no significant differences in adverse events between the aspirin and placebo groups.

INTERPRETATION: The daily consumption of 600 mg of aspirin for an average of 25 months significantly reduced the incidence of cancer after 55.7 months in individuals with hereditary colorectal cancer. Further studies are needed to determine the optimal dosage and duration of aspirin treatment.

FUNDING: This study was funded by the European Union, Cancer Research UK, Bayer Corporation, National Starch and Chemical Co, UK Medical Research Council, Newcastle Hospitals trustees, Cancer Council of Victoria Australia, THRIPP South Africa, The Finnish Cancer Foundation, SIAK Switzerland, and Bayer Pharma.

title: Drosophila CPEB Orb2A Mediates Memory Independent of Its RNA-Binding Domain
text: The synthesis of new proteins at activated synapses is believed to be necessary for long-term memory and synaptic plasticity. The CPEB family of RNA binding proteins, including Drosophila Orb2, has been linked to this process. However, the exact mechanism by which these molecules control memory formation is not well understood. To investigate the role of the endogenous orb2 gene in long-term memory formation, we used gene targeting and site-specific transgenesis to modify it. Our findings reveal that both the Orb2A and Orb2B isoforms are crucial for memory formation, but they have distinct functions. Although both isoforms possess glutamine-rich and RNA-binding domains, Orb2A specifically relies on the former, while Orb2B relies on the latter. Additionally, we discovered that Orb2A induces Orb2 complexes in a manner that depends on both its glutamine-rich region and neuronal activity. Our hypothesis is that Orb2B functions as a conventional CPEB, regulating the transport and/or translation of specific mRNAs, while Orb2A operates in an unconventional manner, forming stable Orb2 complexes that are vital for memory persistence.

title: Functional hemichannels in astrocytes: a novel mechanism of glutamate release.
text: There is limited knowledge regarding the expression and potential roles of unopposed gap junction hemichannels in the brain. Recent evidence suggests that these hemichannels can function independently in astrocytes. Through various techniques such as immunocytochemistry, dye uptake, and HPLC measurements, we have demonstrated that astrocytes in a laboratory setting express functional hemichannels that facilitate the release of glutamate and aspartate. The functionality of these hemichannels was confirmed by the passage of extracellular lucifer yellow (LY) into astrocytes in a solution without divalent cations (DCFS), which could be blocked by agents that inhibit gap junctions. The release of glutamate/aspartate (or LY loading) in DCFS was hindered by multivalent cations (Ca2+, Ba2+, Sr2+, Mg2+, and La3+) and gap junction blocking agents (carbenoxolone, octanol, heptanol, flufenamic acid, and 18alpha-glycyrrhetinic acid) with similar affinities to those reported for the blockade of intercellular communication through gap junctions. Furthermore, the efflux of glutamate through hemichannels was accompanied by a significant reduction in glutamate uptake. However, the release of glutamate in DCFS was not primarily mediated by the reversal of the glutamate transporter, as it did not reach saturation and was not inhibited by glutamate transporter blockers. Control experiments in DCFS ruled out the involvement of volume-sensitive anion channels, P2X7 purinergic receptor pores, or general purinergic receptor activation in glutamate release. Inhibition of intracellular Ca2+ mobilization by BAPTA-AM or thapsigargin did not prevent glutamate release in DCFS. Additionally, the removal of divalent cations induced glutamate release from intact CNS white matter (specifically, the acutely isolated optic nerve), which could be blocked by carbenoxolone, suggesting the presence of functional hemichannels in their natural environment. Our findings indicate that astrocyte hemichannels have the potential to influence the levels of extracellular glutamate in the central nervous system, with implications for both normal brain function and pathological conditions.

title: Human Rad52 binds and wraps single-stranded DNA and mediates annealing via two hRad52–ssDNA complexes
text: The annealing of complementary DNA strands bound by replication protein A (RPA) during repair pathways is facilitated by Rad52. In this study, we utilized fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) between two fluorescent dyes incorporated into DNA substrates to investigate how human Rad52 (hRad52) interacts with and facilitates the annealing of ssDNA-hRPA complexes. We found that hRad52 can bind to ssDNA or ssDNA-hRPA complexes in two different modes, depending on its concentration. At low concentrations of hRad52, the ssDNA wraps around the protein ring, while at higher concentrations, the ssDNA is stretched between multiple hRad52 rings. The most efficient annealing by hRad52 occurs when each complementary DNA strand or each ssDNA-hRPA complex is bound by hRad52 in a wrapped configuration, indicating that homology search and annealing happen through two hRad52-ssDNA complexes. In contrast to the normal protein, mutants of hRad52 (RQK/AAA) and hRad52 (1-212) that have impaired ability to bind hRPA protein compete with hRPA for binding to ssDNA and are unable to counteract hRPA-mediated destabilization of duplexes. This highlights the significance of hRad52-hRPA interactions in promoting effective DNA annealing.

title: Mendelian Randomization Study of B-Type Natriuretic Peptide and Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence of Causal Association from Population Studies
text:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence suggesting that there is a reverse relationship between B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels in the blood and the risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the prospective association between BNP and T2D is uncertain, and it is unclear if there are any confounding factors.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: In this study, we examined the association between levels of the N-terminal fragment of pro-BNP (NT-pro-BNP) in the blood and the risk of developing T2D. We conducted a prospective case-cohort study and also genotyped a variant within the BNP locus in three T2D case-control studies. We combined our findings with existing data in a meta-analysis of 11 case-control studies. Using a Mendelian randomization approach, we compared the observed association between the variant and T2D to what was expected based on the association between NT-pro-BNP levels and T2D, as well as the difference in NT-pro-BNP levels per allele of the variant.

In our case-cohort study, we found that individuals who were free of T2D and cardiovascular disease at the start of the study had a 21% decreased risk of developing T2D for every one standard deviation increase in log-transformed NT-pro-BNP levels. This association remained significant even after adjusting for various factors. In the case-control studies, we observed a similar association between the variant and T2D as what was expected based on the pooled estimate from our study and published data. There were no significant associations between the variant and potential confounding factors.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that the BNP system may play a causal role in the development of T2D. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms underlying this association and explore potential preventive interventions.

title: brain organization
text: During a specific period of early development, estrogen receptors (ER) in the brain play a crucial role in the defeminization of reproductive function and sexual behavior. There are two main types of ER, alpha and beta, which are found in neural circuits that regulate the ovarian cycle and sexual behavior. This study used highly selective agonists for each ER isoform to demonstrate their distinct contributions to estrogen-dependent defeminization. Activation of ERalpha in female rats during the neonatal stage led to the cessation of cyclic ovarian activity and female sexual behavior in adulthood. These effects were accompanied by male-like changes in the structure of the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and sexually dimorphic nucleus of the preoptic area (SDN-POA), as well as a reduced response to estrogen-induced sexual receptivity. On the other hand, exposure to an ERbeta-selective agonist resulted in persistent estrus and a strong defeminizing effect on the AVPV, which is responsible for generating the hypothalamic gonadotropin surge. However, neonatal activation of ERbeta did not affect female sexual behavior, responsiveness to estrogens, or the morphological characteristics of the behaviorally relevant SDN-POA. Therefore, although both ER isoforms are present in various brain regions involved in female reproductive control, they convey different chemical signals during the neonatal period of sex-specific brain development, which may not act synergistically.

title: Thresholds for the cost–effectiveness of interventions: alternative approaches
text:
When evaluating health interventions, many countries rely on the cost-effectiveness thresholds recommended by the World Health Organization's Choosing Interventions that are Cost-Effective project (WHO-CHOICE). According to this project, the threshold for cost-effectiveness is determined by comparing the cost of the intervention per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted to the country's annual gross domestic product (GDP) per capita. Specifically, the cost of the intervention should be less than three times the country's annual GDP per capita to be considered cost-effective. Highly cost-effective interventions, on the other hand, are defined as those that meet a threshold of once the annual GDP per capita per DALY averted.

However, we believe that relying solely on these thresholds diminishes the value of cost-effectiveness analyses and renders them too simplistic for practical use in the field of public health. The use of these thresholds lacks solid theoretical justification, avoids the challenging task of ranking locally-applicable interventions based on their relative values, and fails to consider what is truly affordable. The WHO-CHOICE thresholds set such a low standard for cost-effectiveness that only a few interventions with proven efficacy can be excluded. Consequently, these thresholds offer little insight into the trade-offs that decision-makers must confront.

In light of these limitations, we propose alternative approaches for applying cost-effectiveness criteria to guide the allocation of healthcare resources.

title: Effect of low doses of ionising radiation in infancy on cognitive function in adulthood: Swedish population based cohort study.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate whether exposure to low levels of ionising radiation during infancy has an impact on cognitive function in adulthood. The study was conducted as a population-based cohort study in Sweden. The participants included 3094 men who had received radiation treatment for cutaneous haemangioma before the age of 18 months between 1930 and 1959. The main outcome measures were the radiation dose to the frontal and posterior parts of the brain, and the association between the dose and intellectual capacity at the age of 18 or 19 years, as determined by cognitive tests assessing learning ability, logical reasoning, spatial recognition, and high school attendance.

The results showed that the proportion of boys who attended high school decreased as the radiation dose to both the frontal and posterior parts of the brain increased. Among those not exposed to radiation, approximately 32% attended high school, whereas this percentage decreased to around 17% in those who received doses greater than 250 mGy. The multivariate odds ratio for the frontal dose was 0.47 (95% confidence interval 0.26 to 0.85, P for trend 0.0003), indicating a significant negative association between radiation dose and high school attendance. For the posterior dose, the multivariate odds ratio was 0.59 (0.23 to 1.47, 0.0005), suggesting a similar negative association, although not statistically significant. Furthermore, a negative dose-response relationship was observed for the cognitive tests assessing learning ability and logical reasoning, but not for the test of spatial recognition.

In conclusion, this study provides evidence that low levels of ionising radiation exposure to the brain during infancy can have an impact on cognitive abilities in adulthood.

title: Differential effects of charybdotoxin on the activity of retinal ganglion cells in the dark- and light-adapted mouse retina
text: We conducted patch-clamp recordings on retinal ganglion cells in the mouse retina. During dark adaptation, inhibiting BK(Ca) channels led to an increase in spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and light-induced On-EPSCs, but a decrease in light-induced Off inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs). However, during light adaptation, it resulted in a decrease in light-induced On-EPSCs, spontaneous IPSCs, and light-induced On- and Off-IPSCs. The blockage of BK(Ca) channels had a significant impact on the output of retinal ganglion cells, causing their light-induced responses to shift towards a bursting pattern and increasing the depolarization of their membrane potentials. However, it did not have a significant effect on the peak firing rates of light-induced responses.

title: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome: review of the phenotype
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a rare condition that is well-known for its distinct characteristics, including extremely short stature, low body weight, early hair loss, lipodystrophy, scleroderma, decreased joint mobility, osteolysis, and facial features resembling those of elderly individuals. Unfortunately, individuals with HGPS often experience cardiovascular issues that lead to an early death. However, their cognitive development remains normal. In this study, we present data on 10 cases from our own research and 132 cases from existing literature. The incidence of HGPS in the Netherlands in the last century was 1 in 4,000,000, with a slightly higher occurrence in males. The main initial symptoms observed were failure to thrive (55%), hair loss (40%), skin problems (28%), and lipodystrophy (20%). On average, individuals were diagnosed with HGPS at 2.9 years of age. Growth in weight was more affected than growth in height, and growth delays were evident even before birth. By the age of 13, the average height was 109.0 cm and the average weight was 14.5 kg. Osteolysis was widespread but not severe, except in the facial bones, and was limited to membranous bones. Lipodystrophy was generalized, with only intra-abdominal fat remaining. Cardiovascular problems varied greatly in terms of age of onset and nature, with stroke and coronary dysfunction being the most common. Pathological findings in the coronary arteries and aorta sometimes resembled those seen in elderly individuals, but could also be less severe. The loss of smooth muscle cells was the most significant finding. On average, individuals with HGPS lived until the age of 12.6 years. Patients with HGPS can be divided into two categories: those with classical HGPS, which follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and is often caused by spontaneous mutations, and those with non-classical progeria, who may experience less growth retardation, retain scalp hair for a longer period, have slower progression of lipodystrophy, exhibit more pronounced osteolysis except in the face, and have a higher chance of surviving into adulthood. The inheritance pattern of non-classical progeria is likely autosomal recessive. The cause of HGPS is an abnormally formed protein called Lamin A, which can result from mutations in the LMNA gene or abnormal posttranslational processing due to mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. Among the 34 LMNA mutations found in progeria patients, 26 were classical p. G608G mutations (76%). The pathogenesis of HGPS is believed to involve multiple pathways. Potential therapeutic strategies are being developed, including RNA interference techniques and inhibition of the negative effects of abnormally formed Lamin A on the polymerization of normally formed Lamin A.

title: Identification of an autoantigen demonstrates a link between interstitial lung disease and a defect in central tolerance.
text: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a common occurrence in systemic autoimmunity, characterized by the progressive inflammation or scarring of the lungs. These complications can severely impair gas exchange, leading to hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, and even death. However, there is limited understanding of the underlying causes of these diseases, including the role of specific immune tolerance defects. Additionally, it remains unclear whether autoimmune responses targeting the lung parenchyma are crucial in the development of ILD, including isolated idiopathic forms. Our study reveals that a specific defect in central tolerance, caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator gene (Aire), triggers an autoreactive T cell response to a lung antigen called vomeromodulin, resulting in the development of ILD. Through our research, we observed similar lung pathology in both a human patient and mice with Aire defects, indicating that the AIRE-deficient model of autoimmunity is a valuable system for understanding the fundamental mechanisms of ILD pathogenesis.

title: In vivo role of ER-associated peptidase activity in tailoring peptides for presentation by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules
text: The final proteolytic processing of peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules is believed to involve the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated aminopeptidase (ERAP)1. In order to assess the function of ERAP1 in vivo, we have created mice that lack this enzyme. These mice showed a significant decrease in the expression of the class Ia molecules H-2Kb and H-2Db, as well as the class Ib molecule Qa-2, on their cell surfaces. While cells from these mutant mice had a reduced ability to present certain self- and foreign antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells restricted by Kb-, Db-, or Qa-1b, the presentation of some antigens was unaffected or even improved. As a result, the mice exhibited impaired CD8+ T cell responses against antigens presented by class I molecules. These findings highlight the crucial role of ER-associated peptidase activity in shaping peptides for presentation by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules in vivo.

title: PD 0332991, a selective cyclin D kinase 4/6 inhibitor, preferentially inhibits proliferation of luminal estrogen receptor-positive human breast cancer cell lines in vitro
text:
INTRODUCTION: Cell cycle regulators have been implicated in breast cancer, and PD 0332991 is a selective inhibitor of cyclin D kinases that can block retinoblastoma phosphorylation. To determine predictors of response, we tested the sensitivity of breast cancer cell lines to PD 0332991 and analyzed gene expression data.

METHODS: We treated 47 breast cancer cell lines with PD 0332991 and determined IC50 values. We then compared these values to baseline gene expression data to identify genes associated with response.

RESULTS: Luminal estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) cell lines, including those with HER2 amplification, were most sensitive to PD 0332991. Nonluminal/basal subtypes were the most resistant. We found 450 differentially expressed genes between sensitive and resistant cells, with elevated pRb and cyclin D1 and decreased CDKN2A (p16) in the sensitive lines. Cell cycle analysis showed G0/G1 arrest in sensitive lines, and Western blot analysis confirmed that Rb phosphorylation was blocked in sensitive lines but not resistant lines. PD 0332991 also showed synergy with tamoxifen and trastuzumab in ER+ and HER2-amplified cell lines, respectively. Additionally, PD 0332991 enhanced sensitivity to tamoxifen in cell lines with resistance to ER blockade.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that CDK4/6 inhibition may be effective in certain breast cancers and provide criteria for patient selection in clinical studies of PD 0332991.

title: Identification of secreted proteins that mediate cell-cell interactions in an in vitro model of the lung cancer microenvironment.
text: The presence of somatic mutations in K-ras in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells leads to the recruitment of various cell types, collectively referred to as "stromal cells," within the tumor. These stromal cells can either promote or inhibit tumor growth, but the exact mechanisms behind their actions are not fully understood. In this study, we hypothesized that stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment alter the secretion of proteins necessary for tumor growth and spread. To test this hypothesis, we developed an in vitro model using a murine K-ras mutant lung adenocarcinoma cell line (LKR-13) and murine lung stromal cells (macrophages, endothelial cells, or fibroblasts). Co-culturing these cells resulted in enhanced migration of stromal cells, formation of endothelial tubes, increased proliferation of LKR-13 cells, and regulation of protein secretion involved in angiogenesis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Among these proteins, CXCL1 has been shown to promote NSCLC development, while the role of interleukin-18 (IL-18) remains unclear. By using genetic and pharmacological approaches to inhibit CXCL1 and IL-18, we found that stromal cell migration, LKR-13 cell proliferation, and tumorigenicity depended on one or both of these proteins. In conclusion, stromal cells enhance LKR-13 cell tumorigenicity by influencing the secretome of LKR-13 cells. Targeting tumor/stromal cell interactions could be a potential therapeutic strategy for NSCLC patients.

title: Tightrope act: autophagy in stem cell renewal, differentiation, proliferation, and aging
text: Autophagy is a process in which damaged organelles and protein aggregates are broken down through a lysosomal catabolic pathway. Stem cells possess unique characteristics such as self-renewal, pluripotency, and quiescence. Due to their long lifespan and limited ability to eliminate cellular waste and spent organelles, stem cells rely heavily on autophagy. Additionally, stem cells require remodeling in order to differentiate, further emphasizing the importance of autophagy in their biology. In this review, we examine the current literature on the role of autophagy in embryonic and adult stem cells, specifically hematopoietic, mesenchymal, and neuronal stem cells. We highlight the diverse and contrasting roles that autophagy plays in these cell types. Furthermore, we discuss the limited studies on lysosomal activity and autophagy in stem cells. To better understand the significance of autophagy in different types of stem cells, novel techniques for detecting autophagy in primary cells are necessary. These advancements will contribute to our understanding of the role of autophagy in stem cells during transplantation, a promising therapeutic approach for various diseases.

title: Variant Histone H2A.Z Is Globally Localized to the Promoters of Inactive Yeast Genes and Regulates Nucleosome Positioning
text: H2A.Z is a histone variant that is highly conserved throughout evolution and plays a role in various biological processes such as transcriptional regulation, antisilencing, silencing, and genome stability. However, the exact mechanisms by which H2A.Z carries out these functions are not well understood. This is partly due to a lack of knowledge about where H2A.Z is located on chromosomes and how it affects chromatin structure. To address this, we conducted a study in yeast where we mapped the distribution of H2A.Z across the genome with high resolution. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation and tiling microarrays, we identified 4,862 small regions, typically consisting of one or two nucleosomes, that were enriched with H2A.Z. These regions, known as "Z loci," were predominantly found within specific nucleosomes in the promoter regions of inactive genes throughout the genome. Additionally, we demonstrated that H2A.Z can influence the positioning of nucleosomes at the GAL1 promoter. In regions called HZAD domains, where H2A.Z has an antisilencing function, we observed a broader pattern of H2A.Z localization, suggesting that this histone variant regulates silencing and transcriptional activation through different mechanisms. Our findings indicate that the incorporation of H2A.Z into specific nucleosomes in promoters helps to configure chromatin structure in a way that prepares genes for transcriptional activation. We also discuss the implications of these findings for higher eukaryotes.

title: Collective trauma in northern Sri Lanka: a qualitative psychosocial-ecological study
text: The psychosocial impact of war and natural disasters extends beyond the individual, affecting families, communities, and society as a whole. Just as individuals can experience both distress and psychiatric disorders, widespread trauma and loss can lead to changes at the family, community, and societal levels. This study conducted a qualitative, ecological investigation in Northern Sri Lanka, focusing on the Tamil community and their psychosocial and community mental health programs. Data was collected through participatory observation, interviews with relief workers and officials, and focus group discussions. The study compared the effects of the chronic war situation with the pre-war and post-tsunami contexts. The findings revealed significant changes in family and community dynamics. The war had a more profound impact, leading to transformations such as single-parent families, lack of trust, changes in relationships, and child-rearing practices. Communities became more dependent, passive, mistrustful, and suspicious. Traditional structures, institutions, and social norms deteriorated. Various interventions were attempted at the community level. In conclusion, exposure to conflict, war, and disasters alters fundamental family and community dynamics, necessitating integrated multi-level approaches in relief, rehabilitation, and development programs to address collective trauma effectively.

title: Guidelines for the selection of highly effective siRNA sequences for mammalian and chick RNA interference.
text: The current study extensively examined the correlation between the sequence of short interfering RNA (siRNA) and the effectiveness of RNA interference (RNAi). This analysis involved 62 targets from four exogenous and two endogenous genes, as well as three mammalian and Drosophila cells. Our findings reveal the rules that govern the preference for siRNA sequences, which can be used to design highly effective siRNAs for systematic mammalian functional genomics. According to these rules, siRNAs that meet the following four sequence conditions are capable of inducing significant gene silencing in mammalian cells: (i) A/U at the 5' end of the antisense strand, (ii) G/C at the 5' end of the sense strand, (iii) at least five A/U residues in the 5' terminal one-third of the antisense strand, and (iv) the absence of any GC stretch longer than 9 nucleotides. Conversely, siRNAs that do not meet these conditions result in minimal or no gene silencing in mammalian cells. Interestingly, the same rules for siRNA sequence preference apply to DNA-based RNAi in mammalian cells and in ovo RNAi using chick embryos. However, in Drosophila in vivo RNAi, little preference for siRNA sequence was observed.

title: Overview of the CCP4 suite and current developments
text: The CCP4 software suite, also known as Collaborative Computational Project, Number 4, is a comprehensive collection of programs, data, and software libraries that facilitate macromolecular structure determination through X-ray crystallography. This suite offers users various methods to achieve their goals, ensuring flexibility in their approach. Although the programs are sourced from diverse origins, they are unified by a common infrastructure that utilizes standard file formats, data objects, and graphical interfaces. As the field of macromolecular crystallography moves towards automation, the CCP4 suite incorporates multiple automation pipelines. This article provides a brief overview of CCP4's evolution over the past three decades and highlights the current suite's features. While detailed descriptions can be found in accompanying articles, this piece demonstrates how each individual program contributes to a comprehensive software package.

title: Histone Demethylase Expression Enhances Human Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Efficiency and Promotes Derivation of Pluripotent Stem Cells.
text: The potential application of human embryonic stem cell (hESC) derivation using somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) is limited due to its extremely low efficiency. Only some oocyte donors are able to achieve blastocyst formation from human SCNT embryos, and even then, it occurs at a low rate. However, previous studies in mice have shown that by reducing histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) through the introduction of the H3K9me3 demethylase Kdm4d, the development of SCNT embryos can be greatly improved. In this study, we demonstrate that overexpression of a related H3K9me3 demethylase, KDM4A, also enhances human SCNT. Similar to mice, we find that H3K9me3 in the somatic cell genome of humans acts as a barrier to SCNT reprogramming. By overexpressing KDM4A, we significantly increase the rate of blastocyst formation in human SCNT embryos, enabling efficient derivation of SCNT-derived ESCs using somatic nuclei from adult Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) patients. This mechanistic insight, which is conserved across species, holds promise for improving SCNT in various contexts, including regenerative medicine.

title: Interface Contractility between Differently Fated Cells Drives Cell Elimination and Cyst Formation
text: While much research has been conducted on cellular tumor-suppression mechanisms, there is limited knowledge about the mechanisms that operate at the tissue level to prevent the occurrence of abnormal cells in epithelial tissues. Our study focuses on the expression of transcription factors that determine cell fates and how this can lead to the development of abnormal epithelial cysts in Drosophila imaginal discs. Interestingly, these cysts do not form autonomously within individual cells, but rather result from the interaction between two populations of cells with different fates. This interaction causes an increase in actomyosin at the shared interface between the two cell populations, both at adherens junctions and along basolateral interfaces. Through experimental validation and 3D vertex model simulations, we have discovered that this enhanced interface contractility can explain various morphogenetic behaviors that depend on the size of the cell clusters. These behaviors range from cyst formation in intermediate-sized clusters to the segregation of large cell populations through the formation of smooth boundaries or apical constriction in small groups of cells. Additionally, we have observed that single cells experiencing lateral interface contractility are eliminated from the tissues through apoptosis. However, when the elimination of these aberrant cells fails and they continue to proliferate, cysts that disrupt the continuity of the epithelium are formed. This suggests that increased interface contractility serves as an error correction mechanism, eliminating single aberrant cells from tissues. However, if this mechanism fails, it can lead to the formation of large cysts that may promote disease. Overall, our findings provide a new perspective on the morphogenetic mechanisms that arise from cell-fate differences within tissues and their role in maintaining or disrupting epithelial homeostasis.

title: Resonating circadian clocks enhance fitness in cyanobacteria.
text: Organisms can experience improved longevity, growth, and developmental rate when they follow a light/dark cycle that aligns optimally with their internal circadian clock. However, there is currently no evidence to suggest that reproductive fitness is enhanced by the resonance between the internal clock and the environmental cycle. To investigate the importance of circadian programming, we conducted a study comparing the relative fitness of different strains of cyanobacteria with varying circadian periods. Our findings indicate that strains with a circadian period similar to the light/dark cycle were favored in competitive environments, suggesting the influence of soft selection.

title: Stromal Fibroblasts Present in Invasive Human Breast Carcinomas Promote Tumor Growth and Angiogenesis through Elevated SDF-1/CXCL12 Secretion
text: The functional role of fibroblasts in breast carcinoma is not well understood, despite their prevalence in the stromal cells. To shed light on this, we conducted a study using a coimplantation tumor xenograft model. Our findings reveal that carcinoma-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) extracted from breast carcinomas have a significantly greater impact on the growth of breast carcinoma cells compared to normal mammary fibroblasts from the same patients. These CAFs, which exhibit myofibroblast characteristics, play a crucial role in promoting tumor cell growth by secreting stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1). Additionally, CAFs facilitate angiogenesis by attracting endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) into the carcinomas, partly through the action of SDF-1. Furthermore, CAF-secreted SDF-1 directly stimulates tumor growth by interacting with the CXCR4 receptor expressed by carcinoma cells. Our findings highlight the significant contribution of fibroblasts within invasive breast carcinomas to tumor promotion, primarily through the secretion of SDF-1.

title: Embryonic Origin of Postnatal Neural Stem Cells
text: The lateral ventricles of adult brains contain adult neural stem/progenitor (B1) cells that generate various types of neurons for the olfactory bulb (OB). The specific location of these B1 cells determines the specific types of OB neurons they produce. Our research demonstrates that the majority of B1 cell precursors in mice are generated between embryonic days (E) 13.5 and 15.5, and they remain mostly inactive until they are reactivated after birth. By using a retroviral library with over 100,000 genetic tags, we discovered that B1 cells share a common ancestor with embryonic cells of the cortex, striatum, and septum. However, this lineage connection is lost before E15.5. The regional specification of B1 cells is evident as early as E11.5 and is linked to the production of neurons that populate different regions of the forebrain. This study provides insights into the early embryonic regional specification of postnatal neural stem cells and their relationship with embryonic progenitor cells.

title: The Opa1-Dependent Mitochondrial Cristae Remodeling Pathway Controls Atrophic, Apoptotic, and Ischemic Tissue Damage
text: The occurrence of changes in the shape and structure of mitochondria during apoptosis and autophagy is not well understood in terms of their relevance to tissue response to damage in living organisms. In this study, we aim to investigate the role of a pathway called optic atrophy 1 (OPA1)-dependent cristae remodeling in living organisms and provide evidence that it regulates the response of various tissues to stimuli that cause cell death, tissue degeneration, and tissue shrinkage. By genetically inhibiting the cristae remodeling pathway in living organisms, we found that it does not affect development but offers protection against muscle wasting caused by denervation, damage to the heart and brain due to lack of blood supply, and cell death in the liver. The mechanism behind this protection involves the stabilization of mitochondrial cristae by OPA1, which enhances the efficiency of mitochondrial respiration and prevents mitochondrial dysfunction, release of cytochrome c, and production of harmful reactive oxygen species. Our findings suggest that the OPA1-dependent cristae remodeling pathway is a crucial factor in determining tissue damage in living organisms and can be targeted for therapeutic purposes.

title: First Proposal of Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine
text: Advancements in stem cell research have sparked numerous studies in regenerative medicine across various institutions and companies worldwide. However, the lack of a standardized format for experiments hinders reproducibility and data exchange among laboratories and cell banks. To address this issue and improve information flow in stem cell and derivative cell research, we propose the implementation of a minimum information standard for describing cellular assay data. This standard, known as Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine (MIACARM), builds upon the existing Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay and enables the description of advanced cellular experiments with a defined taxonomy of human cell types. By utilizing controlled terms, such as ontologies, MIACARM will establish a platform for the exchange of cellular assay data among cell banks or registries, which are currently established at over 20 sites worldwide. The significance of this proposal lies in the fact that there are currently more than 20 human cell information storage sites globally. However, the lack of a standardized format for experiments often leads to inadequate or non-existent reproducibility and data exchange among different laboratories or cell information providers. This collaborative study, involving scientists from stem cell banks and cellular information registries across the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and Japan, aims to address this issue by introducing new minimum information guidelines through MIACARM. The implementation of MIACARM is intended to promote data exchange and facilitate practical regenerative medicine.

title: The PAR proteins: fundamental players in animal cell polarization.
text: The par genes were initially discovered through genetic screenings aimed at identifying regulators of cytoplasmic partitioning in the early embryo of C. elegans. These genes encode six distinct proteins that play a crucial role in the asymmetric cell division of the worm zygote. Interestingly, certain PAR proteins exhibit asymmetrical localization and interact physically with each other to form complexes. Remarkably, these PAR proteins have been found to govern cell polarization in various animals, indicating their involvement in an ancient and fundamental mechanism for cell polarization. Although the precise functioning of PAR proteins is not fully understood, recent advancements in cell biology and biochemistry have shed light on their role in polarizing cells.

title: Prions Adhere to Soil Minerals and Remain Infectious
text: The natural transmission of prion diseases (also known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies [TSEs]) in sheep, deer, and elk is partly contributed by an unidentified environmental source of infectivity. This infectivity can enter soil environments through the shedding of prions from diseased animals and the decomposition of infected carcasses. Unfortunately, the burial of TSE-infected cattle, sheep, and deer as a means of disposal has unintentionally introduced prions into subsurface environments. To investigate the potential of soil to act as a reservoir for TSEs, we conducted a study on the interaction between the disease-associated prion protein (PrPSc) and common soil minerals. Our findings revealed significant adsorption of PrPSc to two clay minerals, quartz, and four whole soil samples. We also measured the binding capacities of each mineral for PrPSc. Additionally, we observed that PrPSc desorbed from montmorillonite clay was cleaved at a specific site and had a strong interaction with the clay, making it difficult for the protein to be released. Despite this cleavage and strong binding, the PrPSc bound to the clay remained infectious. These results indicate that PrPSc released into soil environments can be preserved in a form that is accessible to other organisms, perpetuating the spread of prion diseases and exposing other species to the infectious agent.

title: Regulated Accumulation of Desmosterol Integrates Macrophage Lipid Metabolism and Inflammatory Responses
text: The mechanisms connecting cholesterol buildup to inflammation and LXR-dependent response pathways in atherosclerotic lesions are not well understood. To investigate this, we used lipidomic and transcriptomic methods to examine how diet and LDL receptor genotype affect the formation of macrophage foam cells in the peritoneal cavities of mice. We found that foam cell formation led to significant changes in numerous lipid species and surprisingly, suppressed inflammatory gene expression instead of activating it. Our findings suggest that the controlled accumulation of desmosterol is responsible for many of the homeostatic responses observed in macrophage foam cells, including the activation of LXR target genes, inhibition of SREBP target genes, reprogramming of fatty acid metabolism, and suppression of inflammatory-response genes. These results indicate that macrophage activation in atherosclerotic lesions is caused by external proinflammatory signals within the artery wall that hinder the homeostatic and anti-inflammatory functions of desmosterol.

title: A JOURNAL OF NEUROLOGY
text:
Glial cells in the brain, which are five times more abundant than neurons, have recently gained attention for their potential involvement in epileptic seizures. Specifically, microglia and astrocytes, which are associated with inflammatory immune responses, are responsible for monitoring brain damage that often leads to seizures. This has led to the intriguing suggestion that seizures may be facilitated or even triggered by immune responses in the brain. While recent evidence strongly suggests that immune responses can lower the threshold for seizures in experimental models of epilepsy, there is currently no proof that they can independently initiate seizures in living organisms.

However, our research demonstrates that innate immune responses in the cortex alone can significantly increase brain excitability, resulting in focal seizures. We discovered that applying lipopolysaccharide, which binds to toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), to the cortex triples the amplitude of evoked field potentials and produces focal epileptiform discharges. These effects can be prevented by pre-applying interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Our findings show how the innate immune response can contribute to acute seizures by increasing neuronal excitability through the release of interleukin-1 in response to TLR4 detecting danger signals associated with central nervous system infections and brain injuries.

These results suggest that innate immunity plays an important role in the development of epilepsy and highlight the potential of inhibiting glial activity, through blocking TLR4 and the release of pro-inflammatory mediators by activated glia, in the study and treatment of seizure disorders in humans.

title: Sequential domain assembly of ribosomal protein S3 drives 40S subunit maturation.
text: The assembly of eukaryotic ribosomes involves the combination of ribosomal RNA and ribosomal proteins to form precursor particles in the nucleus. These particles then undergo a complex maturation process, guided by non-ribosomal assembly factors. In this study, we investigate the functional aspects of ribosomal protein S3 and its role in the maturation of the 40S ribosomal subunit. Our findings reveal that S3 undergoes successive structural changes that promote its maturation. Initially, S3 forms a dimer and enters the nucleus with its N-domain in a rotated conformation, accompanied by the chaperone Yar1. The C-domain of S3 interacts with the 40S precursors during the initial assembly, while the N-domain remains exposed on the surface of the 40S subunit. Yar1 is then replaced by the assembly factor Ltv1, which locks the N-domain of S3 in the rotated position, preventing its association with the 40S subunit. Finally, phosphorylation triggers the release of Ltv1 and causes the N-domain of S3 to flip into its final position, leading to the stable integration of S3. This stepwise assembly process represents a novel mechanism for the incorporation of ribosomal proteins.

title: Assaying proliferation and differentiation capacity of stem cells using disaggregated adult mouse epidermis
text: This protocol outlines the procedure for isolating keratinocytes from the adult mouse epidermis. These keratinocytes are then separated into various sub-populations based on cell surface markers. Their function is then examined in an in vivo skin reconstitution assay, where they are combined with disaggregated neonatal dermal cells. Additionally, we explain how the isolated keratinocytes can be analyzed both in vitro and in vivo through clonal analysis. Furthermore, we provide a method for enriching hair follicle-inducing dermal papilla cells in the dermal preparation. By utilizing these techniques, it becomes possible to compare the proliferative capacity and differentiation potential of different populations of adult epidermal stem cells along various epidermal lineages. The process of isolating, fractionating, and grafting cells for the skin reconstitution assay typically spans over two days. Clonal growth in culture is then assessed after 14 days, while evaluation of the grafts is conducted after 4-5 weeks.

title: Telomerase-negative immortalized human cells contain a novel type of promyelocytic leukemia (PML) body.
text: We have discovered that telomerase-negative immortalized human cells use a process called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) to maintain their telomeres. In this study, we present the identification of a new structure called ALT-associated PML body (APB) in ALT cells. APBs are large nuclear structures shaped like donuts and contain PML protein, telomeric DNA, and the telomere binding proteins human telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2. Additionally, immunostaining revealed the presence of replication factor A, RAD51, and RAD52 in APBs, which are proteins involved in DNA synthesis and recombination. Interestingly, APBs appeared simultaneously with the activation of ALT during the process of immortalization. We observed the presence of APBs in ALT tumors and cell lines, but not in mortal cell strains or telomerase-positive cell lines or tumors.

title: Prediction of coronary artery disease by a systemic atherosclerosis score index derived from whole-body MR angiography
text: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between whole-body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA) findings and the presence of significant coronary artery disease (CAD). WB-MRA has shown promise as a non-invasive method for assessing the arterial vasculature. The study involved 50 patients scheduled for cardiac catheterization, and their extra-cardiac vessel segments were evaluated and scored based on luminal narrowing. The atherosclerosis score index (ASI) was calculated by summing the scores and dividing by the number of analyzable segments. The results showed that patients with significant CAD had a higher ASI compared to those without CAD. The ASI also correlated with risk scores for coronary events. An ASI of > 1.54 was found to predict significant CAD with moderate sensitivity and high specificity. Logistic regression analysis revealed that an ASI > 1.54 was the strongest independent predictor for CAD. Additionally, the presence of extra-cardiac stenosis was more common in patients with CAD compared to those without CAD. The likelihood of extra-cardiac stenosis varied depending on the vascular territory. These findings highlight the close association between extra-cardiac and coronary atherosclerosis and suggest the potential prognostic implications of WB-MRA in screening for coronary disease in patients with extra-cardiac manifestations of atherosclerosis.

title: Analysis of re-replication from deregulated origin licensing by DNA fiber spreading
text: Ensuring that DNA replication origins do not initiate more than once, a phenomenon called re-replication, is a major challenge in each human cell-division cycle. When replication control is severely disrupted, it leads to extensive DNA damage, activation of cell-cycle checkpoints, and cell death. On the other hand, moderate disruption promotes genome instability and the development of tumors. However, it has been difficult to directly prove re-replication or determine if it occurs only during a specific phase of the cell cycle, especially when there are no noticeable increases in cellular DNA content. By using a modified version of DNA fiber spreading, we have successfully detected re-replication on individual DNA molecules from human chromosomes. Our method has shown significant re-replication within one hour of entering the S phase in cells that overproduce the replication factor, Cdt1. Additionally, comparing the HeLa cancer cell line to untransformed fibroblasts suggests that HeLa cells exhibit replication signals consistent with low-level re-replication in normal cell cycles. Standard assays cannot detect re-replication after depleting the Cdt1 inhibitor, geminin, in untransformed fibroblasts, but it can be easily quantified using DNA fiber spreading analysis. By directly examining re-replicated DNA molecules, we can gain a better understanding of the events that either promote or disrupt genome stability.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 is essential for pregnancy
text:
The successful progression of pregnancy relies on the coordination of various signals and factors from different tissues. One crucial component in this process is liver receptor homolog-1 (Lrh-1), an orphan nuclear receptor responsible for regulating metabolism and hormone synthesis. Lrh-1 is highly expressed in the granulosa cells of ovarian follicles and the corpus luteum in both rodents and humans. In mice, the elimination of the gene Nr5a2 (also known as Lrh-1), which codes for Lrh-1, during embryonic development leads to lethal consequences during gastrulation.

By depleting Lrh-1 in the ovarian follicle, it has been observed that this receptor plays a role in regulating genes necessary for steroid synthesis and ovulation. To further investigate the impact of Lrh-1 on mouse gestation, its expression was genetically disrupted in the corpus luteum, resulting in luteal insufficiency. Although hormone replacement allowed for embryo implantation, it ultimately led to gestational failure characterized by impaired endometrial decidualization, compromised placental formation, fetal growth retardation, and fetal death.

Lrh-1 is also present in the endometrium of mice and humans. In a primary culture of human endometrial stromal cells, reducing the abundance of NR5A2 transcripts through RNA interference hindered decidualization. These findings demonstrate that Lrh-1 is essential for maintaining the corpus luteum, promoting decidualization, and facilitating placental formation. Therefore, it plays multiple indispensable roles in establishing and sustaining pregnancy.

title: Transcriptional Signature and Memory Retention of Human-Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
text: The process of genetically reprogramming somatic cells into a pluripotent state, known as induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), has been successfully achieved in both mouse and human cells by over-expressing specific genes. However, there is still uncertainty regarding the similarities between human iPSCs and human Embryonic Stem Cells (hESCs). In this study, we present the transcriptional profile of human iPSCs that were generated without the use of viral vectors or genomic insertions. Our findings indicate that these cells are generally similar to hESCs, but with notable differences. To generate human iPSCs without viral vectors or genomic insertions, we introduced the pluripotent factors Oct4 and Nanog into human fetal neural progenitor cells using episomal vectors. The temporary expression of these factors, either together or with Oct4 alone, resulted in the efficient generation of human iPSCs. This reprogramming strategy not only identified a potential transcriptional signature for human iPSCs, but also preserved the gene expression of the donor cells in the reprogrammed cells, free from viral and transgene interference. Furthermore, the use of episomal vectors in the reprogramming process offers a safe approach for generating human iPSCs for both clinical applications and basic research.

title: A CXCL1 Paracrine Network Links Cancer Chemoresistance and Metastasis
text: The connection between metastasis and chemoresistance in cancer is not well understood. However, our research has revealed a network of signals between carcinoma, myeloid, and endothelial cells that drives both processes in breast cancer. Cancer cells that have an excessive expression of CXCL1 and 2, either through transcriptional hyperactivation or 4q21 amplification, are more likely to survive in metastatic sites. These CXCL1/2 molecules attract CD11b(+)Gr1(+) myeloid cells into the tumor, which then produce chemokines like S100A8/9 that enhance cancer cell survival. While chemotherapy can kill cancer cells, it also triggers a reaction in the surrounding stromal cells, leading to the production of TNF-α by endothelial and other stromal cells. TNF-α, through NF-kB, increases the expression of CXCL1/2 in cancer cells, creating a loop with S100A8/9 and causing chemoresistance. By blocking CXCR2, we can disrupt this cycle and improve the effectiveness of chemotherapy against breast tumors, especially in preventing metastasis. This network of interactions between endothelial cells, carcinoma cells, and myeloid cells provides a mechanism that explains the link between chemoresistance and metastasis, and also presents opportunities for intervention.

title: Prophylaxis of postoperative vomiting in children undergoing tonsillectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Postoperative vomiting (POV) is a common problem after tonsillectomy in children and can lead to significant complications. Many different methods of preventing POV have been studied, but there has been limited research specifically focused on children undergoing this procedure. To address this gap, a systematic search was conducted using various databases to identify double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials that investigated prophylactic anti-emetic interventions in children undergoing tonsillectomy, with or without adenoidectomy. The main outcome of interest was the occurrence of POV within the first 24 hours after surgery. The results of the identified studies were analyzed using fixed effect meta-analysis to estimate the effectiveness of each prophylactic anti-emetic strategy. Logistic regression was also used to assess dose-response effects when applicable. A total of 22 articles met the inclusion criteria. The findings provided strong evidence supporting the use of dexamethasone (odds ratio [OR] 0.23, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16-0.33) and serotinergic antagonists such as ondansetron (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.29-0.46), granisetron (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.06-0.19), tropisetron (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.06-0.35), and dolasetron (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.1-0.59) for preventing POV. Metoclopramide was also found to be effective (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.34-0.77). However, there was insufficient evidence to support the use of dimenhydrinate, perphenazine, droperidol, gastric aspiration, or acupuncture in the doses studied. In conclusion, dexamethasone and anti-serotinergic agents appear to be the most effective prophylactic treatments for preventing POV in children undergoing tonsillectomy.

title: A method of comparing the areas under receiver operating characteristic curves derived from the same cases.
text: The purpose of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves is to analyze and compare the effectiveness of diagnostic technology and algorithms. This research aims to enhance the statistical comparison of the areas under two ROC curves obtained from the same group of patients by considering the correlation between these areas, which arises due to the paired nature of the data. By utilizing the relationship between the area under an ROC curve and the Wilcoxon statistic, and assuming Gaussian distributions (binormal), a conversion table is created to determine the correlation between the paired ratings of images and the correlation between the two ROC areas. This correlation between the areas can then be utilized to decrease the uncertainty (standard error) surrounding the observed difference in areas. Similar to the paired t-test, this adjustment for pairing can significantly enhance the statistical sensitivity (power) of the comparison. In studies involving multiple readers, this method provides a means to assess a component of the sampling variation that is otherwise challenging to obtain.

title: Transient inactivation of Rb and ARF yields regenerative cells from postmitotic mammalian muscle.
text: One intriguing question in biology is why mammals have limited tissue regeneration, while urodele amphibians and teleost fish can regenerate major structures through cell cycle reentry. When the Rb gene is deactivated, postmitotic urodele skeletal muscle can proliferate, but this mechanism is absent in mammalian muscle. We hypothesized that a tumor suppressor called ARF (alternative reading frame), which is present in mammals but not in regenerative vertebrates, may suppress regeneration. By deactivating both Arf and Rb, we observed cell cycle reentry in mammalian muscle, loss of differentiation properties, and an increase in cytokinetic machinery. We isolated single postmitotic myocytes using laser micro-dissection-catapulting and temporarily suppressed Arf and Rb, resulting in myoblast colonies that could still differentiate and fuse into myofibers when transplanted in vivo. These findings demonstrate that mammalian cell differentiation can be reversed by deactivating Arf and Rb, supporting the idea that Arf evolved at the expense of regeneration.

title: CENP-B Controls Centromere Formation Depending on the Chromatin Context
text: The centromere is a region of chromatin that acts as the point of attachment for the spindle and guides the accurate inheritance of eukaryotic chromosomes during cell divisions. However, the process by which the centromere forms and stabilizes at a specific location in the genome is not well understood. To create a functional centromere on a human or mammalian artificial chromosome (HAC/MAC), the presence of alpha-satellite DNA with binding motifs for the centromeric CENP-B protein is necessary. Our research demonstrates that the assembly of a centromere on a HAC/MAC is reliant on CENP-B. Conversely, when alpha-satellite DNA is integrated into a chromosomal site in cells expressing CENP-B, centromere formation is suppressed. Interestingly, CENP-B enhances histone H3-K9 trimethylation and DNA methylation on these integration sites, promoting the formation of heterochromatin. Therefore, we propose that CENP-B has a dual role in centromere formation: facilitating the creation of a centromere on DNA without a functional centromere, while preventing the formation of excessive centromeres on chromosomes.

title: Improved tools for biological sequence comparison.
text:
We have created three computer programs that are designed for comparing protein and DNA sequences. These programs have various functionalities such as searching sequence databases, assessing similarity scores, and identifying periodic structures through local sequence similarity. 

The first program, FASTA, is an enhanced version of FASTP. It can be utilized to search protein or DNA sequence databases and can also compare a protein sequence to a DNA sequence database by translating the DNA data as it is being searched. FASTA incorporates an additional step in the calculation of the initial pairwise similarity score, which enables the combination of multiple regions of similarity to enhance the score of related sequences.

The second program, RDF2, is capable of evaluating the significance of similarity scores using a shuffling method that maintains the local sequence composition. This program provides a reliable measure of the significance of the observed similarity scores.

Lastly, the LFASTA program allows for the visualization of all regions of local similarity between two sequences with scores surpassing a specified threshold. It employs the same scoring parameters and alignment algorithm, and these local similarities can be displayed either as a "graphic matrix" plot or as individual alignments. Furthermore, these programs have been designed to accommodate the comparison of DNA or protein sequences based on a variety of alternative scoring matrices.

title: The adverse consequences of unmet need among older persons living in the community: dual-eligible versus Medicare-only beneficiaries.
text:
Our goal is to estimate and compare the prevalence of negative outcomes associated with a lack of assistance among a vulnerable subgroup of older adults who are eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid, compared to those who are only eligible for Medicare. 

Using data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a survey representative of the older Medicare population, we determined the prevalence of disability-related need for assistance with self-care, household tasks, and mobility activities, as well as the prevalence of negative outcomes resulting from unmet need, based on whether individuals were dually eligible or eligible for Medicare only. 

The results showed that over 2 million older adults living in the community experienced negative outcomes due to a lack of assistance with self-care, such as soiling their clothes. Additionally, over 2 million experienced negative outcomes due to a lack of assistance with household tasks, such as going without groceries. Furthermore, over 3 million individuals experienced at least one negative outcome due to a lack of assistance with mobility-related activities, such as being confined to bed, in the month prior to the NHATS interview. 

Dually eligible individuals had higher rates of 6 out of the 11 negative outcomes studied and were more likely to experience at least one negative outcome in all three domains compared to others. 

In conclusion, various care models are emerging to integrate medical care, behavioral health, and long-term services for the dual eligible population. Monitoring indicators of negative outcomes resulting from unmet need can help assess the quality and adequacy of these care systems.

title: Supplementary information: ‘MesoRD User’s Guide ’ and other
text: MesoRD is a stochastic simulation tool designed for chemical reactions and diffusion. It utilizes the next subvolume method, an exact approach for simulating the Markov process associated with the reaction-diffusion master equation. MesoRD is freely available as open-source software, written in C++ and licensed under the GNU General Public License (GPL). It is compatible with Linux, Mac OS X, NetBSD, Solaris, and Windows XP operating systems. To download MesoRD, visit http://mesord.sourceforge.net. For any inquiries, please contact johan.elf@icm.uu.se or johan.hattne@embl-hamburg.de. Supplementary information, including the 'MesoRD User's Guide' and other related documents, can be found at http://mesord.sourceforge.net.

title: Functional anatomy of T cell activation and synapse formation.
text: The activation and function of T cells rely on a structured interaction with antigen-presenting cells. These interactions can be categorized into two distinct dynamics observed in vivo: transient contacts known as immunological kinapses, which facilitate movement and allow T cells to recognize self-peptide-MHC (pMHC) and search for pathogen-derived pMHC; and prolonged contacts known as immunological synapses, which are formed when T cell receptors (TCRs) interact with agonist pMHC under specific conditions. Immunological synapses are associated with robust immune responses that lead to the production of effector and memory T cells. Through high-resolution imaging, it has been discovered that the synapse is highly coordinated, involving cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and a range of activating and inhibitory ligands that either promote or prevent T cell signaling. In this review, we explore the molecular components, geometry, and timing involved in kinapses and synapses. By integrating recent molecular and physiological data, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding and propose future directions in this field.

title: Modulation of Replicative Lifespan in Cryptococcus neoformans: Implications for Virulence
text: The fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans has been found to experience replicative aging, where older cells exhibit advanced generational age and phenotypic changes that make them more resistant to host and antifungal-based killing. As a result, these older cells accumulate during chronic infections. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that altering the generational age of a pathogenic yeast population would impact its vulnerability to the host and its virulence. SIR2, a well-conserved histone deacetylase and a key target for anti-aging drugs, was tested for its effect on C. neoformans' replicative lifespan (RLS). We first created a mutant strain of C. neoformans (sir2Δ) and confirmed that it had a shorter RLS, consistent with its known role in aging. RLS analysis then showed that treating C. neoformans with Sir2p-agonists significantly extended its RLS, while treatment with a Sir2p-antagonist shortened it. These effects on RLS were dependent on SIR2 and not observed in sir2Δ cells. Since SIR2 loss slightly impaired fitness, we couldn't compare the effects of genetic RLS modulation on virulence with wild type cells. Instead, we chemically modulated RLS and investigated the impact of Sir2p modulating drugs on C. neoformans cells in a Galleria mellonella infection model. Consistent with our hypothesis that altering the generational age of the infecting yeast population affects its vulnerability to host cells, we observed reduced virulence of C. neoformans in the Galleria host when RLS was extended by treatment with Sir2p agonists. Conversely, treatment with a Sir2p antagonist, which shortened RLS, increased virulence in Galleria. Additionally, combining Sir2p agonists with antifungal therapy enhanced the effectiveness of the antifungal treatment. Importantly, there was no difference in virulence observed with drug treatment when sir2Δ cells were used for infection, confirming the specificity of the target and ruling out non-specific effects of the drugs on the Galleria host. Therefore, this study suggests that RLS modulating drugs, such as Sir2p agonists, can alter the lifespan and vulnerability of the fungal population, and should be further explored as a potential class of novel antifungal drug targets that can enhance antifungal efficacy.

title: Pf4-Cre transgenic mice allow the generation of lineage-restricted gene knockouts for studying megakaryocyte and platelet function in vivo.
text: In order to create mice that specifically express Cre-recombinase in the megakaryocytic lineage, we made modifications to a mouse bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) clone using homologous recombination. We replaced the first exon of the platelet factor 4 (Pf4), also known as CXCL4, with a codon-improved Cre cDNA. We successfully obtained several strains that expressed the transgene, and one particular strain, Q3, was extensively studied. By crossing Q3 mice with the ROSA26-lacZ reporter strain, we observed that Cre-recombinase activity was limited to megakaryocytes. To further confirm these findings, we crossed the Q3 mice with a strain that contained loxP-flanked integrin beta1. At the DNA level, we observed complete excision of this conditional allele in megakaryocytes, resulting in platelets that were almost entirely lacking the integrin beta1 protein. The Pf4-Cre transgenic strain will serve as a valuable tool for investigating megakaryopoiesis, platelet formation, and platelet function.

title: LIN-44/Wnt Directs Dendrite Outgrowth through LIN-17/Frizzled in C. elegans Neurons
text: The proper development of axons and dendrites is essential for the functioning of the nervous system. While both domains play an equally important role in transmitting signals, our understanding of dendrite development is limited. In this study, we investigate the role of the Wnt ligand, LIN-44, and its receptor, LIN-17, in regulating dendrite development in the PQR oxygen sensory neuron of C. elegans. We observe that in mutants lacking lin-44 or lin-17, the PQR dendrites either fail to form, exhibit stunted growth, or are misrouted. By manipulating the expression of LIN-44 during embryogenesis and conducting cell-ablation experiments, we find that this molecule is patterned and acts as an attractive cue for dendrite emergence. The genetic interaction between lin-44 and lin-17 suggests that the LIN-44 signal is transmitted through the LIN-17 receptor, which acts autonomously in PQR. Additionally, we discover that LIN-17 interacts with another Wnt molecule, EGL-20, and functions alongside MIG-1/Frizzled in this process. Overall, our findings highlight the crucial role of Wnt and Frizzled molecules in regulating dendrite development in vivo.

title: Why do general practitioners prescribe antibiotics for upper respiratory tract infections to meet patient expectations: a mixed methods study
text: AIMS This study aims to examine the impact of patient expectations on general practitioners' (GPs) prescribing of antibiotics for upper respiratory tract infections (URTI). METHODS A mixed methods approach was used, including a cross-sectional survey and semistructured interviews. The study was conducted among primary care GPs in Australia. PARTICIPANTS A total of 584 GPs completed the survey, resulting in a response rate of 23.6%. Additionally, 32 GPs were individually interviewed. OUTCOME The main outcome measure was the prescribing of antibiotics for URTI. RESULTS The survey revealed that over half of the GPs reported prescribing antibiotics for URTI in order to meet patient expectations. The qualitative findings indicated that "patient expectations" encompassed various factors contributing to inappropriate prescribing, such as time constraints, communication issues, and diagnostic uncertainty. The study identified three role archetypes to explain GPs' behavior in relation to antibiotic prescribing for URTIs. The qualitative component also revealed that many GPs did not believe that their prescribing in primary care contributed to antibiotic resistance, as they perceived other factors, such as hospital prescribing and veterinary use, to have a greater impact. Consequently, they did not perceive any significant negative consequences from their inappropriate prescribing. CONCLUSIONS This study highlights the importance of raising awareness among GPs about the extent of antibiotic resistance and the role of primary care prescribing. It is crucial to emphasize the contribution of individual prescribing decisions to the problem of antibiotic resistance.

title: Migraine and cardiovascular disease: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between migraine and cardiovascular disease, specifically stroke, myocardial infarction, and death due to cardiovascular disease. The study design was a systematic review and meta-analysis. The researchers gathered data from electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library) and reference lists of relevant studies and reviews published up until January 2009. The selection criteria included case-control and cohort studies that investigated the association between any type of migraine or specific migraine subtypes and cardiovascular disease. The review process involved two investigators independently assessing the eligibility of the identified studies in a two-step approach, with disagreements resolved through consensus. The studies were categorized based on migraine and cardiovascular disease. Data extraction was conducted by two investigators, and pooled relative risks and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. The results showed heterogeneity in participant characteristics and the definition of cardiovascular disease across the studies. Nine studies examined the association between any migraine and ischemic stroke, with a pooled relative risk of 1.73 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.31 to 2.29. Additional analyses indicated a significantly higher risk among individuals with migraine with aura (2.16, 1.53 to 3.03) compared to those without aura (1.23, 0.90 to 1.69; meta-regression for aura status P=0.02). The results also suggested a greater risk among women (2.08, 1.13 to 3.84) compared to men (1.37, 0.89 to 2.11). Age less than 45 years, smoking, and oral contraceptive use further increased the risk. Eight studies examined the association between migraine and myocardial infarction (1.12, 0.95 to 1.32), and five studies examined the association between migraine and death due to cardiovascular disease (1.03, 0.79 to 1.34). Only one study investigated the association between women with migraine with aura and myocardial infarction and death due to cardiovascular disease, showing a twofold increased risk. In conclusion, migraine is associated with a twofold increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly among individuals with migraine with aura. The results also suggest a higher risk among women, and the risk is further amplified for individuals with migraine who are under 45 years old, smokers, and women who use oral contraceptives. There was no overall association found between any type of migraine and myocardial infarction or death due to cardiovascular disease. However, there are not enough studies available to reliably evaluate the impact of factors such as migraine aura on these associations.

title: Effect of Duration and Intermittency of Rifampin on Tuberculosis Treatment Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text: The effectiveness of treatment regimens for active tuberculosis (TB) that involve intermittent use of rifampin or only using it during the initial phase has been questioned. To address this, we conducted a systematic review of treatment regimens for active TB to determine the impact of the duration and intermittency of rifampin use on treatment outcomes. We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane CENTRAL database for clinical trials published in English, French, or Spanish between 1965 and June 2008. The selected studies used standardized treatment with rifampin-containing regimens and reported failure and/or relapse in previously untreated patients with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB. We analyzed a total of 57 trials with 312 arms and 21,472 participants. The results showed that regimens using rifampin only for the first 1-2 months had higher rates of failure, relapse, and acquired drug resistance compared to regimens using rifampin for 6 months. This was especially true when there was initial drug resistance to isoniazid, streptomycin, or both. However, there was little evidence of a difference in failure or relapse between daily or intermittent treatment schedules, although there was not enough published evidence to support the efficacy of twice-weekly rifampin administration throughout therapy. In conclusion, shorter durations of rifampin treatment and initial drug resistance to isoniazid and/or streptomycin led to worse treatment outcomes for TB. Intermittent treatment schedules showed similar outcomes, but there is not enough evidence to support twice-weekly treatment throughout therapy.

title: A novel set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments for sensitive/specific detection of bladder cancer.
text: The purpose of this study is to identify a more accurate set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments for the detection of bladder cancer. The researchers profiled 59 tumor-associated genes in bladder cancer cell lines, cancer biopsies, and urine sediments using methylation-specific PCR. They then selected 21 candidate genes for further analysis in urine sediments from 132 bladder cancer patients, as well as patients with noncancerous urinary lesions, neurologic diseases, and healthy volunteers. The results showed that 15 genes exhibited cancer-specific hypermethylation in urine sediments, confirming the diagnosis of 121 out of 132 bladder cancer cases with a sensitivity of 91.7% and an accuracy of 87%. Importantly, the test was able to detect over 75% of stage 0a and 88% of stage I bladder cancer cases, indicating its potential for early diagnosis. Interestingly, the methylation markers identified in this study were different from those used in the United States, suggesting a possible epigenetic difference between American and Chinese bladder cancer cases. In conclusion, methylation profiling of an 11-gene set in urine sediments offers a sensitive and specific method for detecting bladder cancer.

title: Posttranslational Acetylation of α-Tubulin Constrains Protofilament Number in Native Microtubules
text: In this study, we investigated the role of acetylation of MEC-12 α-tubulin in constraining the number of protofilaments in microtubules. We found that in C. elegans touch receptor neurons, the absence of α-tubulin acetyltransferase activity resulted in short microtubules with lattice defects and varying protofilament numbers. In contrast, wild-type neurons had long microtubules with a consistent 15-protofilament structure. Our molecular dynamics simulations suggest that acetylation of lysine 40 promotes the formation of salt bridges between protofilaments, which stabilizes lateral interactions and ensures the formation of structurally uniform microtubules. Overall, our findings demonstrate that acetylation of α-tubulin is crucial for maintaining the proper number of protofilaments in microtubules, and we propose a model in which this modification facilitates the formation of stable and uniform microtubule populations in vivo.

title: A KEY ROLE FOR OREXIN IN PANIC ANXIETY
