text: Panic disorder is a serious anxiety disorder characterized by recurring and debilitating panic attacks. People with this disorder often experience decreased activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the central nervous system, along with heightened autonomic and respiratory responses when given hypertonic sodium lactate intravenously. In a rat model of panic disorder, inhibiting GABA synthesis in a specific region of the hypothalamus leads to anxiety-like states and increased vulnerability to sodium lactate-induced cardioexcitatory responses. This region of the hypothalamus contains orexin (also known as hypocretin) neurons, which play a crucial role in arousal, vigilance, and central autonomic mobilization - all important factors in panic. Our study demonstrates that activating these orexin neurons is necessary for the development of a panic-prone state in rats, and blocking the gene responsible for orexin synthesis or using ORX-1 receptor antagonists effectively prevents panic responses. Additionally, we found that individuals with panic anxiety have higher levels of orexin in their cerebrospinal fluid compared to those without panic anxiety. These findings suggest that the orexin system may play a role in the pathophysiology of panic anxiety, and that ORX antagonists could be a promising new treatment approach for panic disorder.

title: Local Increases in Mechanical Tension Shape Compartment Boundaries by Biasing Cell Intercalations
text:
During the development of animals, mechanical forces play crucial roles in tissue organization. Tissues are often organized into distinct groups of cells called compartments, which do not mix with each other. The boundaries between these compartments have a straight shape and are associated with signaling centers that are important for tissue growth and patterning. Recent studies have shown that an increase in mechanical tension at the junctions between cells along compartment boundaries prevents cell mixing and maintains the straight boundaries. However, the specific cellular mechanisms behind this phenomenon are not well understood.

In this study, we used live imaging and quantitative image analysis to investigate the cellular dynamics at and near the boundaries of the Drosophila pupal abdominal epidermis. We found that cell mixing within compartments involves multiple cell intercalations, where cells move and rearrange themselves. Interestingly, the frequency and orientation of these intercalations remain unchanged along the compartment boundaries. Instead, there is an asymmetry in the shrinkage of junctions during intercalation, which leads to cell rearrangements that suppress cell mixing.

To further understand this phenomenon, we conducted simulations of tissue growth. These simulations showed that local increases in mechanical tension can explain the bias in junctional shrinkage observed during cell intercalation. Based on these findings, we conclude that local increases in mechanical tension play a crucial role in maintaining separate cell populations by influencing junctional rearrangements during cell intercalation.

title: MDA5 and PTPN2, two candidate genes for type 1 diabetes, modify pancreatic β-cell responses to the viral by-product double-stranded RNA
text: The destruction of beta-cells in type 1 diabetes (T1D) is partly due to communication between beta-cells and the immune system. This communication can be influenced by an individual's genetic background. We investigated the impact of two candidate genes for T1D, MDA5 and PTPN2, on beta-cell responses to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which is produced during viral replication. These genes were chosen based on a comparison of known T1D candidate genes and genes expressed in pancreatic beta-cells, as identified in previous array analysis. We used small interference RNAs (siRNAs) to target MDA5 or PTPN2 in INS-1E cells and purified rat beta-cells obtained through fluorescence-activated cell sorting. The cells were then exposed to synthetic dsRNA (polyinosinic-polycitidilic acid-PIC) within the cells. We used real-time RT-PCR, western blot, and viability assays to assess gene/protein expression and cell viability. We found that PIC increased MDA5 and PTPN2 mRNA expression, which was inhibited by the specific siRNAs. PIC induced apoptosis in INS-1E and primary beta-cells, and this effect was enhanced by PTPN2 knockdown. However, inhibiting MDA5 did not alter PIC-induced apoptosis. On the other hand, silencing MDA5 reduced the expression of cytokines and chemokines induced by PIC, while inhibiting PTPN2 had minimal or no effect on these inflammatory mediators. These results suggest that changes in MDA5 and PTPN2 expression can alter beta-cell responses to dsRNA. MDA5 regulates inflammatory signals, while PTPN2 may act as a defense mechanism against pro-apoptotic signals generated by dsRNA. These two candidate genes for T1D may therefore modulate beta-cell apoptosis and/or the local release of inflammatory mediators during a viral infection, at least in part, at the level of pancreatic beta-cells.

title: Tumor necrosis factor signaling mediates resistance to mycobacteria by inhibiting bacterial growth and macrophage death.
text: Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) is a crucial factor in controlling tuberculosis. It is believed to protect against the disease by promoting the formation of granulomas, which are organized clusters of immune cells including macrophages. When TNF signaling is lost, tuberculosis progresses in humans, and infected mice experience higher mortality due to disorganized necrotic granulomas. However, the specific roles of TNF signaling leading up to this outcome are still unclear. To better understand how TNF signaling operates in mycobacterial pathogenesis, we observed live zebrafish infected with transparent Mycobacterium marinum. Through a step-by-step analysis, we discovered that the loss of TNF signaling led to increased mortality, even when only innate immunity was active. Without TNF, the growth of intracellular bacteria and the formation of granulomas were accelerated, resulting in the death of overloaded macrophages and the breakdown of granulomas through necrosis. Therefore, while TNF is not necessary for the formation of tuberculous granulomas, it indirectly maintains their integrity by limiting the growth of mycobacteria within macrophages and preventing their necrosis.

title: Loss of negative regulation by Numb over Notch is relevant to human breast carcinogenesis
text: The balance between Notch and Numb, two biological factors, plays a crucial role in controlling the growth and differentiation of cells during development and maintaining stability in the body. While changes in Notch signaling have been associated with diseases like cancer in humans, the extent of Notch's involvement in tumors has been unclear. However, our research reveals that in approximately 50% of human mammary carcinomas, the control of Notch signaling by Numb is lost. This is due to a specific process called Numb ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. We have found that Numb acts as a tumor suppressor, as introducing Numb into tumor cells that lack it inhibits their proliferation. In Numb-negative tumors, there is an increase in Notch signaling, but this returns to normal levels when Numb is reintroduced. On the other hand, silencing Numb leads to increased Notch signaling in normal breast cells and Numb-positive breast tumors. Additionally, we have discovered that inhibiting Notch through pharmacological means can suppress the growth of Numb-negative breast tumors. Therefore, the antagonistic relationship between Numb and Notch is crucial for maintaining the balance in normal mammary tissue, and its disruption contributes to the development of human mammary carcinomas.

title: Cortical Dynein Controls Microtubule Dynamics to Generate Pulling Forces that Position Microtubule Asters
text: The presence of dynein at the cortex plays a role in various processes that involve the positioning of microtubules. This includes spindle positioning during embryonic cell division and centrosome positioning during fibroblast migration. In order to understand how cortical dynein interacts with the ends of microtubules to generate force and how this interaction affects positioning, we conducted experiments using microfabricated barriers to recreate the 'cortical' interaction between dynein and dynamic microtubule ends in a controlled in vitro system. Our findings reveal that dynein attached to the barriers captures microtubule ends, inhibits their growth, and triggers catastrophes, thereby controlling the length of microtubules. Furthermore, the interaction with shrinking microtubule ends generates pulling forces of several pN. Through a combination of experiments in microchambers and a theoretical model of aster mechanics, we demonstrate that dynein-mediated pulling forces result in the reliable centering of microtubule asters in simple confined spaces. These results highlight the inherent ability of cortical microtubule-dynein interactions to regulate the dynamics of microtubules and drive positioning processes within living cells.

title: Breast cancer risk factors in relation to breast density (United States)
text:
We conducted a study to evaluate the known risk factors for breast cancer in relation to breast density. Our analysis included 144,018 women from New Hampshire who had at least one mammogram recorded in a statewide mammography registry. Radiologists used the BI-RADS classification to measure mammographic breast density, and we obtained information on risk factors from patient intake forms and questionnaires.

Our initial findings revealed a strong inverse relationship between age and body mass index (BMI) and breast density. We also observed that women with a late age at menarche, late age at first birth, premenopausal women, and those currently using hormone therapy (HT) tended to have higher breast density. On the other hand, women with greater parity tended to have less dense breasts.

Further analysis, stratified by age and BMI, indicated potential interactions between these factors. To formally assess these interactions, we used a multivariable model. We found that the impact of current HT use differed across age groups. In younger women, there was an inverse association between HT use and breast density, while in older women, there was a positive association (p < 0.0001 for the interaction).

We also observed that the positive effects of age at menarche and age at first birth, as well as the inverse influence of parity, were less pronounced in women with low BMI compared to those with high BMI (p = 0.04, p < 0.0001, and p = 0.01 for the interactions, respectively). Additionally, we found stronger positive effects for age at first birth in postmenopausal women (p = 0.004 for the interaction).

Finally, our multivariable model indicated a slight positive influence of family history of breast cancer on breast density. We also noted that the influence of age at menarche and reproductive factors on breast density is less evident in women with high BMI. Furthermore, breast density is reduced in young women using HT, but increased in HT users aged 50 or older.

title: Perspective: repression of competition and the evolution of cooperation.
text: The repression of competition within groups, alongside kin selection, has played a significant role in shaping the evolution of cooperation throughout the history of life. When opportunities for competition against neighboring groups are limited within a group, individuals can only enhance their own success by improving the efficiency and productivity of the entire group. Consequently, traits that suppress competition within groups promote cooperation and contribute to the overall success of the group. This concept was initially proposed by Leigh in the context of fair meiosis, where each chromosome has an equal chance of being transmitted through gametes. The random nature of success in fair meiosis means that each part of the genome can only increase its own success by increasing the total number of offspring and thus benefiting the group as a whole. Alexander built upon this idea and applied it to his theories on the evolution of human sociality, suggesting that social structures in humans spread when they repress competition within groups and facilitate successful competition between groups. Buss introduced another example by suggesting that the success of metazoans depended on repressing competition between cellular lineages. Maynard Smith then synthesized various perspectives on the repression of competition. In this paper, I present simple mathematical models to illustrate the key processes through which the repression of competition evolves. Once the concepts are clarified, I delve into the history of this idea and conclude by summarizing recent advancements in this field and identifying promising avenues for future research.

title: Article
text: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by uncontrolled immune responses in inflamed mucosa, with an abundance of IL-17-producing cells and a deficiency of Treg cells. The objective of this study was to investigate the impact and mechanisms of RA, the ligand of RARalpha, on immune responses in colitis in both humans and mice. Colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) were cultured and treated with RA as an agonist of RARalpha or LE135 as an antagonist of RARalpha. The expressions of IL-17 and FOXP3 were examined using immunohistochemistry. In mice, colitis was induced by intrarectal administration of TNBS on Day 1. The mice were then treated with RA or LE135 daily for 7 days. Cytokine levels in the cultures of mouse lamina propria mononuclear cells (LPMCs) were measured. The expressions of FOXP3 and IL-17 in colon tissues or mesenteric lymph nodes (MLN) were detected using immunohistological analysis. Body weight and colon inflammation were assessed. RA treatment increased FOXP3 expression and decreased IL-17 expression in colon biopsies of patients and in colon tissues and MLN of mice with colitis compared to controls. LPMCs from RA-treated mice produced lower levels of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-17) but higher levels of regulatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-beta) compared to untreated mice. LE135 had the opposite effect of RA. Furthermore, RA improved TNBS-induced colitis in a dose-dependent manner, as evidenced by improved body weight and reduced colon inflammation. RA downregulates colon inflammatory responses in patients with IBD in vitro and in murine colitis in vivo, suggesting a potential therapeutic approach for IBD treatment.

title: Multiple RNA surveillance pathways limit aberrant expression of iron uptake mRNAs and prevent iron toxicity in S. cerevisiae.
text: To maintain iron balance and prevent harm from excessive iron levels, it is crucial to tightly regulate the production of mRNAs that encode proteins responsible for iron uptake. Our study reveals that in the absence of the S. cerevisiae RNase III ortholog Rnt1p or the nuclear exosome component Rrp6p, numerous mRNAs encoding iron uptake or mobilization proteins are expressed even when iron levels are sufficient. Furthermore, when Rnt1p or the 5'-->3' exonucleases Xrn1p and Rat1p are absent, these mRNAs accumulate in extended forms, indicating that multiple degradation pathways are involved in monitoring abnormal versions of these transcripts. Cells lacking RNase III exhibit heightened sensitivity to high iron concentrations, suggesting that Rnt1p-mediated RNA surveillance is necessary to prevent iron toxicity. These findings demonstrate that various ribonucleolytic pathways are involved in RNA surveillance, playing a role in maintaining iron balance in yeast and preventing the potentially harmful consequences of expressing the iron starvation response when iron levels are adequate.

title: Differential regulation of adherens junction dynamics during apical-basal polarization.
text: The turnover of adherens junctions (AJs) in epithelial cells is constantly changing to adjust adhesion properties in different physiological and developmental situations. However, it is still unclear how the regulation of AJ dynamics occurs during the apical-basal polarization of primary epithelia. In this study, we utilized new and genetically validated GFP markers for Drosophila E-cadherin (DE-cadherin, referred to as DE-Cad) and β-catenin (Armadillo, Arm) to quantitatively assess the in vivo dynamics of biosynthetic turnover and membrane redistribution using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) assays. Our findings demonstrate that the biosynthetic turnover of membrane DE-Cad and Arm in AJs of polarizing epithelial cells is much faster compared to polarized cells. The rapid turnover of membrane DE-Cad is not dependent on actin- and dynamin-based trafficking, but rather on microtubules. Additionally, Arm in AJs of polarizing cells exhibits a faster and diffusion-based membrane redistribution, which is distinct from the slower and exchange-based DE-Cad membrane distribution. This suggests that the association between Arm and DE-Cad is more dynamic in polarizing cells and becomes stable only in polarized epithelial cells. Consistent with these observations, biochemical assays reveal that the binding of Arm to DE-Cad is weaker in polarizing cells compared to polarized cells. Our results uncover a modulation of the molecular interaction between DE-Cad and Arm during apical-basal polarization, indicating a potential mechanism crucial for establishing apical-basal polarity by regulating AJ dynamics.

title: Phylogenetic analysis of mRNA polyadenylation sites reveals a role of transposable elements in evolution of the 3′-end of genes
text: mRNA polyadenylation is a crucial step in the development of most eukaryotic mRNAs. It is closely linked to the termination of transcription and helps define the 3'-end of genes. Many human and mouse genes have multiple polyadenylation sites, known as poly(A) sites, which result in mRNA variants with different 3'-untranslated regions (UTRs) and/or encode different protein sequences. In this study, we investigated the conservation and divergence of various types of alternative poly(A) sites in human, mouse, rat, and chicken. Our findings show that the poly(A) sites closest to the 3'-end of genes are more likely to be conserved compared to those located further upstream. However, poly(A) sites found upstream of the 3'-most exon, known as intronic poly(A) sites, are much less conserved. Genes with a longer evolutionary history are more prone to having alternative polyadenylation, suggesting that poly(A) sites have been gained through evolution. We also discovered that nonconserved poly(A) sites are more frequently associated with transposable elements (TEs) than conserved ones, although they are utilized less often. Different classes of TEs have distinct characteristics in their connection to poly(A) sites, as they incorporate TE sequences into polyadenylation elements. Our results establish a conservation pattern for alternative poly(A) sites in various vertebrate species and demonstrate that TEs can dynamically modify the 3'-end of genes through evolution.

title: Inter- and Intra-Host Viral Diversity in a Large Seasonal DENV2 Outbreak
text: RNA viruses are known for their high genetic diversity, both within and between hosts, due to errors in genome replication. Previous studies have focused on chronic infections in humans, but few have investigated acute viral infections transmitted by arthropods. In this study, we sequenced the complete genomes of ten DENV2 isolates from a large outbreak in Brazil using two different methods. Analysis of the consensus genomes confirmed that the 2010 epidemic had a greater extent than a previous epidemic caused by the same viruses in another city two years earlier. Within-host analysis revealed a high level of conservation, with very low intra-host genetic diversity after excluding certain regions. We found a small number of variable sites per genome population, with a frequency of over 1%. Most of these changes were non-synonymous, indicating purifying selection at the population level. Despite the error-prone nature of RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase, dengue viruses maintain low levels of intra-host variability.

title: Serum Soluble Corin Deficiency Predicts Major Disability within 3 Months after Acute Stroke
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the association between serum soluble corin and the risk of poor outcomes within 3 months after a stroke. A total of 522 stroke patients were followed for 3 months to identify major disability, death, and vascular events. Serum soluble corin levels were measured at the beginning of the study for all participants. Logistic regression was used to analyze the relationship between baseline serum soluble corin levels and stroke outcomes, taking into account various factors such as age, sex, baseline NIHSS score, time from onset to hospitalization, smoking, drinking, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, family history of stroke, and stroke subtype.

The results showed that patients with high corin levels had a significantly lower risk of major disability or death compared to patients with low corin levels. This association remained significant even after adjusting for age and baseline NIHSS score. Furthermore, after additional adjustment for other conventional factors, the association remained marginally significant. However, no association was found between serum soluble corin levels and other composite outcomes.

In conclusion, a deficiency in serum soluble corin was found to be a predictor of major disability within 3 months after a stroke, independent of baseline neurological deficits. These findings suggest that corin may play a role in stroke prognosis.

title: Altered PTEN expression; a diagnostic marker for differentiating normal, hyperplastic and neoplastic endometrium
text: The aim of this study was to examine the expression of the PTEN gene in different types of endometrial tissue. The researchers conducted an immunohistochemical evaluation of PTEN on 87 specimens from three groups: normal proliferative endometrium, hyperplastic endometrium (including simple and complex hyperplasia), and endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (EECA). They analyzed the immunostaining of cells using quantitative methods based on the area of staining and intensity of color reaction. The results showed that PTEN immunoreactivity was present in all normal proliferative endometrium, all simple hyperplasia, 75% of atypical complex hyperplasia, and 48% of EECA. The intensity of PTEN reaction was significantly higher in the group with proliferative endometrium compared to hyperplastic endometrium and EECA. In conclusion, PTEN expression was found to be significantly higher in cyclical endometrium compared to atypical hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma.

title: Care Seeking for Neonatal Illness in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review
text:
Despite recent progress in reducing child mortality, neonatal deaths remain a significant issue, accounting for 41% of all deaths in children under five worldwide. The majority of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where infections are a leading cause of death. Limited access to care for sick neonates contributes to high mortality rates. However, there is a lack of information on care-seeking behaviors in LMICs. This review aims to describe care seeking for neonatal illnesses in LMICs, with a focus on the type of care sought. 

To conduct this review, we analyzed studies that reported the proportion of caregivers seeking care for ill or suspected ill neonates in LMICs. Out of 784 studies initially identified, 22 studies provided relevant data from community household surveys, facility-based surveys, and intervention trials. The majority of these studies were conducted in South Asia, particularly in rural areas, and were published within the last four years. 

Among the 9,098 ill or suspected ill neonates included in the studies, 4,320 caregivers sought some form of care. This included seeking care from a health facility or a healthcare provider. The percentage of caregivers seeking care ranged from 10% to 100%, with a median of 59%. Care seeking from a healthcare provider showed a similar range and median, while care seeking at a health facility ranged from 1% to 100%, with a median of 20%. However, these estimates were limited by the lack of studies conducted in urban settings and regions outside of South Asia. Additionally, there was inconsistency in how illness, care-seeking, and care provider were defined across studies. 

In conclusion, there is a lack of data on newborn care-seeking behaviors, particularly in South Asia where care seeking for newborn illness, especially from health care facilities and medically trained providers, is low. It is crucial to gather representative data on care-seeking patterns in different geographic regions and to better understand how to improve care seeking during this vulnerable period.

title: Synaptic Incorporation of AMPA Receptors during LTP Is Controlled by a PKC Phosphorylation Site on GluR1
text: The inclusion of GluR1-containing AMPA receptors in synapses is crucial for various forms of neural plasticity, such as long-term potentiation (LTP). Although several signaling pathways that initiate this process have been identified, the specific modifications of GluR1 that regulate its inclusion in synapses remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that phosphorylation of GluR1 by PKC at a conserved serine 818 residue is elevated during LTP and is essential for the expression of LTP. We observed that GluR1 is phosphorylated by PKC at this site both in laboratory experiments and in living organisms. Furthermore, when GluR1 S818 is acutely phosphorylated by PKC or when a phosphomimetic mutation is introduced, the synaptic inclusion of GluR1 is enhanced. Conversely, inhibiting the phosphorylation of GluR1 S818 reduces LTP and prevents the PKC-driven synaptic inclusion of GluR1. In conclusion, we propose that the phosphorylation of GluR1 S818 by PKC is a critical event in the synaptic inclusion of AMPA receptors driven by plasticity.

title: The Bloom's syndrome helicase promotes the annealing of complementary single-stranded DNA
text: Bloom's syndrome is caused by a mutation in the BLM gene, which produces a DNA helicase known as BLM. This helicase belongs to the RecQ family, which is highly conserved. Apart from its conventional function of separating DNA strands, BLM also has the ability to disrupt non-B-form DNA structures like G-quadruplexes and facilitate the movement of Holliday junctions. In our study, we have discovered a new activity of BLM: it promotes the annealing of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). This activity does not require the presence of Mg2+ ions, but it is inhibited by ssDNA binding proteins and ATP. Furthermore, the length of the DNA molecule influences the efficiency of this annealing process. By examining different truncation mutants of BLM, we have determined that the C-terminal domain is crucial for strand annealing. Within this domain, we have identified a specific 60 amino acid segment that is important for both ssDNA binding and strand annealing. Based on our findings, we propose a model in which the ssDNA annealing activity of BLM assists in the repair of damaged replication forks by processing DNA intermediates.

title: Bayesian selection of continuous-time Markov chain evolutionary models.
text: We have developed a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo approach for estimating the posterior distribution of phylogenies using aligned DNA/RNA sequences under various hierarchical evolutionary models. By employing a proper, nontruncated, and uninformative prior, we showcase the advantages of the Bayesian approach in hypothesis testing and estimation within phylogenetics. We compare different models for infinitesimal rates of change among nucleotides, the number of rate classes, and the relationships among branch lengths to determine their relative probabilities and assess the suitability of a molecular clock using Bayes factors. Our most comprehensive model, originally proposed by Tamura and Nei, parameterizes the infinitesimal change probabilities among nucleotides (A, G, C, T/U) with six parameters. These parameters consist of three for the nucleotide stationary distribution, two for nucleotide transitions, and one for nucleotide transversions. Nested models include the Hasegawa, Kishino, and Yano model with equal transition rates, as well as the Kimura model with a uniform stationary distribution and equal transition rates. To illustrate our methodology, we analyze simulated data, 16S rRNA sequences from various contemporary organisms (eubacteria, halobacteria, eocytes, and eukaryotes), 9 primate sequences, and the complete HIV genome from 11 isolates. Our findings indicate that the Kimura model is overly restrictive, the Hasegawa, Kishino, and Yano model can be rejected for certain datasets, there is evidence for multiple rate classes and a molecular clock among similar taxa, and a molecular clock can be rejected for more distantly related taxa.

title: The intersection between aging and cardiovascular disease.
text: The average lifespan of humans is on the rise, resulting in a significant increase in the number of individuals aged 65 and older. This trend is expected to continue over the next two decades. Among this age group, cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death, and the expenses associated with its treatment are projected to rise. Aging is an unavoidable aspect of life and unfortunately poses the greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease. While numerous studies have explored the cardiovascular health of both young and elderly individuals, there are still many unanswered questions regarding how genetic pathways that regulate aging in model organisms impact cardiovascular aging. Similarly, the molecular biology of aging field has not fully examined the role of these aging pathways in cardiovascular health. However, there is progress being made in bridging this gap, as these two fields are starting to merge. In this article, we provide an overview of key genes involved in regulating lifespan and health span, such as sirtuins, AMP-activated protein kinase, mammalian target of rapamycin, and insulin-like growth factor 1, and their roles in regulating cardiovascular health. Additionally, we discuss a series of upcoming review articles that will offer a more comprehensive analysis of studies linking genes associated with aging and cardiovascular health, as well as provide insights into future directions for these interconnected fields.

title: Single-RNA counting reveals alternative modes of gene expression in yeast
text: Accurate control of timing and amplitude is crucial for the proper execution of transcriptional programs in gene expression regulation. However, the exact mechanism by which the transcription machinery achieves this task remains unknown. To investigate this, we employed an in situ hybridization method that allows us to detect single mRNA molecules. By measuring mRNA abundance and transcriptional activity in individual Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells, we discovered that the expression levels of certain genes are higher than previously reported and can vary significantly among cells. Surprisingly, the variability in expression for most genes that are constitutively expressed is quite small. Our analysis, combining single-transcript measurements with computational modeling, suggests that this low variation in expression is achieved by transcribing genes through single transcription-initiation events that are well-separated in time, rather than through transcriptional bursts. However, we observed that the gene PDR5, which is regulated by the transcription coactivator complex SAGA, is expressed through transcriptional bursts, resulting in larger variation. These findings provide direct evidence for the existence of multiple expression modes that are utilized to modulate the transcriptome.

title: A complete landscape of post-transcriptional modifications in mammalian mitochondrial tRNAs
text: Mitochondrial DNA in mammals contains 22 species of tRNAs that play vital roles in translating 13 essential subunits of respiratory chain complexes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. After transcription, nuclear-encoded tRNA-modifying enzymes modify mitochondrial tRNAs to ensure their proper functioning. Without these modifications, there can be pathological consequences. However, the available information about these modifications has been incomplete. To address this issue, we isolated all 22 species of mitochondrial tRNAs from bovine liver and used mass spectrometry to comprehensively determine the post-transcriptional modifications in each tRNA. In this study, we describe the primary structures with post-transcriptional modifications of seven previously uncharacterized species of mitochondrial tRNAs and provide revised information about base modifications in five other mitochondrial tRNAs. In the complete set of bovine mitochondrial tRNAs, we identified 15 species of modified nucleosides at 118 positions, which accounts for 7.48% of the total bases. This result offers insights into the molecular mechanisms involved in the decoding system of mammalian mitochondria and allows for the prediction of candidate tRNA-modifying enzymes responsible for each modification of mitochondrial tRNAs.

title: Preventing coronary heart disease: B vitamins and homocysteine.
text: The list of risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease that can be prevented or reversed is continuously expanding. Established risk factors include cigarette smoking, high blood pressure, physical inactivity, elevated cholesterol, lipoprotein abnormalities, lipoprotein(a), diabetes, overweight, male gender, and age. In the 1990s, there were numerous reports linking high levels of plasma homocysteine to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease. It was consistently found that dietary and supplemental folic acid can lower homocysteine levels. The article by Robinson and colleagues in this edition of Circulation provides further evidence on the significance of homocysteine and suggests that plasma folate and plasma pyridoxal-l-phosphate (vitamin B6) have protective effects. Their study was part of the European Concerted Action Project and involved 750 patients under the age of 60 with recent diagnoses of coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral vascular disease, as well as 800 healthy control subjects. The patient groups were relatively young and diverse, with nonfatal clinical events or symptoms of arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease supported by ECG, angiographic, or Doppler evidence. The study took place in 19 centers across nine European countries. Men in the highest quintile for fasting total homocysteine (tHcy) had a significantly higher relative risk of vascular disease, with a strong dose-response relationship. This risk was further amplified when combined with cigarette smoking and high blood pressure. The estimated relative risk for coronary heart disease was similar. Robinson and colleagues specifically examined the effects of three B vitamins on fasting and post-methionine-loading tHcy levels, as well as their independent effects on cardiovascular disease.

title: Relationship between serum parathyroid hormone levels, vitamin D sufficiency, and calcium intake.
text:
In recent years, there has been increased recognition of the importance of adequate vitamin D status for optimal bone health. However, the ideal intake of vitamin D is still unknown. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is commonly used as an indicator of vitamin D status, but there is no universally accepted reference level.

The objective of this study was to investigate the relative importance of high calcium intake and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for calcium homeostasis, as determined by serum intact parathyroid hormone (PTH). The study was a cross-sectional study conducted on 2310 healthy Icelandic adults, who were divided into three age groups (30-45 years, 50-65 years, or 70-85 years). The participants were recruited between February 2001 and January 2003. A semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire was used to assess their vitamin D and calcium intake. The participants were further divided into groups based on their calcium intake (<800 mg/d, 800-1200 mg/d, and >1200 mg/d) and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (<10 ng/mL, 10-18 ng/mL, and >18 ng/mL).

The main outcome measure of the study was serum intact PTH, which was determined by calcium intake and vitamin D levels. A total of 944 healthy participants completed all parts of the study. After adjusting for relevant factors, it was found that serum PTH was lowest in the group with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of more than 18 ng/mL, but highest in the group with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of less than 10 ng/mL. At the low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (<10 ng/mL), a calcium intake of less than 800 mg/d compared to more than 1200 mg/d was significantly associated with higher serum PTH. At a calcium intake of more than 1200 mg/d, there was a significant difference between the lowest and highest vitamin D groups.

In conclusion, as long as vitamin D status is ensured, calcium intake levels of more than 800 mg/d may not be necessary for maintaining calcium metabolism. In northern climates, vitamin D supplements are necessary to achieve adequate vitamin D status.

title: Sex-specific effects of the DAF-12 steroid receptor on aging in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Differences in lifespan and aging between males and females can be observed in various animal species. These differences are likely influenced by disparities in hormonal activity. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, males tend to live longer than females. In this study, we investigate whether discrepancies in insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and steroid hormones contribute to the variation in aging between the sexes. We conducted experiments using C. elegans populations in liquid culture. Our findings reveal that in hermaphrodite populations, the absence of the DAF-12 steroid receptor affects lifespan, consistent with previous studies conducted on solid plates. Mutant longevity is suppressed in a weak daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutant but enhanced in a stronger daf-2 mutant. However, in males, mutation of daf-12 has minimal impact on aging, regardless of whether they are weak or strong daf-2 mutants. Additionally, while mutation of daf-12 slightly reduces lifespan in daf-2(+) hermaphrodites, as observed in plate-cultured populations, it does not have the same effect in daf-2(+) males. These results suggest that, similar to mammals, disparities in steroid hormone activity may contribute to the differences in aging between males and females in C. elegans.

title: Nonclassical binding of formylated peptide in crystal structure of the MHC class lb molecule H2-M3
text: The mouse possesses a class Ib MHC molecule called H2-M3, which exhibits a strong preference for binding N-formylated peptides, with a 10(4)-fold selectivity. In order to understand the underlying mechanism behind this unique specificity, we conducted an experiment where we expressed and crystallized a soluble form of M3 along with a formylated nonamer peptide, fMYFINILTL. By utilizing X-ray crystallography, we were able to determine the structure of M3 at a resolution of 2.1 A. The overall structure of M3 resembles that of class la MHC molecules; however, it differs in the peptide-binding groove. The A pocket, which typically accommodates the free N-terminus of a bound peptide, is closed in this case, causing the peptide to shift by one residue. As a result, the P1 side chain becomes lodged in the B pocket. Additionally, the formyl group is coordinated by His-9 and a bound water molecule located on the floor of the groove.

title: Sequential signals toward podosome formation in NIH-src cells
text:
Podosomes, also known as invadopodia in cancer cells, are structures rich in actin that adhere to the extracellular matrix and have the ability to degrade it. These structures can develop in different types of cells and play a significant role in physiological processes. However, the exact molecular mechanism behind podosome formation remains largely unknown. In this study, we aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms involved in podosome formation.

By examining the expression of various phosphoinositide-binding domains, we discovered that podosomes in NIH3T3 cells transformed by the Src protein (NIH-src cells) are particularly enriched with a phosphoinositide called PtdIns(3,4)P2. This finding suggests that PtdIns(3,4)P2 plays an important role in the formation of podosomes. Through live-cell imaging analysis, we observed that the expression of Src protein stimulates the formation of podosomes at focal adhesions in NIH3T3 cells, following the accumulation of PtdIns(3,4)P2.

We also investigated the involvement of an adaptor protein called Tks5/FISH, which is known to be essential for podosome formation. Our findings revealed that Tks5/FISH forms a complex with Grb2 at adhesion sites, and this interaction is dependent on the presence of Src protein. Furthermore, we discovered that N-WASP, a protein involved in actin polymerization, binds to all SH3 domains of Tks5/FISH. This interaction facilitates the formation of circular podosomes.

Based on these results, we propose that the augmentation of the N-WASP-Arp2/3 signaling pathway occurs on the platform of the Tks5/FISH-Grb2 complex at focal adhesions. This complex is stabilized by the presence of PtdIns(3,4)P2.

title: Forebrain engraftment by human glial progenitor cells enhances synaptic plasticity and learning in adult mice.
text: The size and complexity of human astrocytes are greater compared to those of infraprimate mammals, suggesting that their role in neural processing has expanded over time. In order to examine the unique characteristics of human glia, we transplanted human glial progenitor cells (GPCs) into immunodeficient mice shortly after birth. As the recipient brains matured, they displayed a significant increase in the number and proportion of human glial progenitors and astrocytes. The transplanted human glia formed gap junctions with the host astroglia, but maintained the size and variability of astroglia found in hominids. Additionally, they transmitted calcium signals three times faster than the host astrocytes. The human glial chimeric mice exhibited a significant enhancement in long-term potentiation (LTP), as well as improved learning abilities in tasks such as Barnes maze navigation, object-location memory, and both contextual and tone fear conditioning. On the other hand, mice that received murine GPCs did not show any enhancement in LTP or learning. These findings demonstrate that human glia selectively enhance both activity-dependent plasticity and learning in mice.

title: Reprogramming of human fibroblasts to pluripotency with lineage specifiers.
text: Ever since it was discovered that the overexpression of OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC can induce pluripotency in somatic cells, new methodologies have been developed to replace these factors and improve our understanding of the reprogramming process. However, unlike in mice, replacing OCT4 during the reprogramming of human cells has not been successful. In this study, we present a strategy to achieve this replacement. By analyzing the transcriptome and using bioinformatics, we have identified factors that are known to specify lineages and can replace OCT4 and SOX2 in the reprogramming of human fibroblasts. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to simultaneously replace OCT4 and SOX2 with alternative lineage specifiers in the reprogramming of human cells. Furthermore, our results support the idea that opposing lineage specification networks play a crucial role in inducing pluripotency.

title: Mechanisms of endocytosis.
text: This article examines the control of lipid and protein composition in the plasma membrane through endocytic mechanisms, which play a crucial role in regulating cellular interactions with the environment. Specifically, we focus on mammalian endocytic mechanisms and the cellular proteins that govern these processes. We delve into the extensively studied clathrin-mediated endocytic mechanisms and also explore alternative pathways that operate independently of clathrin. These clathrin-independent pathways encompass the CLIC/GEEC endocytic pathway, arf6-dependent endocytosis, flotillin-dependent endocytosis, macropinocytosis, circular dorsal ruffles, phagocytosis, and trans-endocytosis. Additionally, we critically evaluate the involvement of caveolae and caveolin1 in endocytosis. We highlight the significance of lipids, proteins that modulate membrane curvature, small G proteins, actin, and dynamin in endocytic pathways. Furthermore, we discuss the functional importance of distinct endocytic pathways and underscore the necessity of studying these pathways to gain insights into human disease processes.

title: Birth Size and Breast Cancer Risk: Re-analysis of Individual Participant Data from 32 Studies
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the association between birth size and breast cancer risk. Previous studies have provided inconsistent findings, so we re-analyzed data from published and unpublished studies to obtain more precise estimates. We identified 32 studies, comprising 22,058 breast cancer cases, and used random effect models to combine the study-specific estimates.

The results showed that birth weight was positively associated with breast cancer risk in studies based on birth records and parental recall during childhood. However, there was no association found in studies based on adult self-reports or maternal recall during adulthood. There was also heterogeneity between the different data sources.

Compared to women who weighed between 3.000-3.499 kg at birth, those who weighed less than 2.500 kg had a slightly lower risk, while those who weighed 4.000 kg or more had a slightly higher risk. Birth length and head circumference were also positively associated with breast cancer risk.

When adjusting for all three birth size variables, birth length was found to be the strongest independent predictor of risk. These associations were not influenced by established breast cancer risk factors, age, or menopausal status.

Based on the study populations, the cumulative incidence of breast cancer by age 80 was estimated to be higher in women with longer birth length.

In conclusion, this analysis supports the idea that birth size, particularly birth length, is independently associated with breast cancer risk in adulthood.

title: LncRNA-GAS5 induces PTEN expression through inhibiting miR-103 in endometrial cancer cells
text:
BACKGROUND: Growth arrest-specific 5 (GAS5) has been implicated and found to be aberrantly expressed in multiple cancers. However, the expression and mechanism of action of GAS5 in endometrial carcinoma are poorly understood.

RESULTS: Through real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and flow cytometry analysis, we observed that GAS5 was down-regulated in endometrial cancer cells and stimulated apoptosis in these cells. We performed RT-PCR to investigate the expression of GAS5, PTEN, and miR-103. We found that the expression of PTEN was up-regulated when endometrial cancer cells overexpressed GAS5. Bioinformatics online predicted that GAS5 could bind to miR-103, which was further confirmed to be regulated by GAS5. Additionally, we discovered that the miR-103 mimic decreased the mRNA and protein levels of PTEN, as determined by luciferase reporter assay and western blotting. However, the regulation effect of GAS5 plasmid could reverse this effect in endometrial cancer cells.

CONCLUSION: In summary, our findings demonstrate that GAS5 acts as a tumor suppressor long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) in endometrial cancer. By inhibiting the expression of miR-103, GAS5 significantly enhances the expression of PTEN, promoting cancer cell apoptosis. Therefore, GAS5 could be an important mediator in the pathogenesis of endometrial cancer.

title: Modification of kidney barrier function by the urokinase receptor
text: Podocyte dysfunction, characterized by the loss of foot processes and the presence of protein in the urine, is often the initial stage of progressive kidney disease. Currently, there are no therapies available that target the cellular level of this disease. However, our study demonstrates that activation of the urokinase receptor (uPAR) in podocytes leads to foot process loss and protein leakage through a mechanism involving the activation of αvβ3 integrin, which is dependent on lipids. Mice lacking uPAR are protected from proteinuria caused by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), but develop the disease when a constitutively active β3 integrin is expressed. Gene transfer experiments reveal that uPAR expression in podocytes, but not in endothelial cells, is necessary for the development of LPS-induced proteinuria. Mechanistically, uPAR is essential for the activation of αvβ3 integrin in podocytes, which promotes cell movement and activates the small GTPases Cdc42 and Rac1. Blocking αvβ3 integrin reduces podocyte movement in vitro and decreases proteinuria in mice. Our findings demonstrate the physiological role of uPAR signaling in the regulation of kidney permeability.

title: Jagged1-induced Notch signaling drives proliferation of multiple myeloma cells.
text: The interaction between Notch receptors on hematopoietic stem cells and their ligands on bone marrow stromal cells plays a crucial role in determining cell fate and survival. Our recent findings have shown that Notch signaling is involved in the proliferation and survival of B cell-derived tumor cells in classic Hodgkin disease, revealing a new mechanism for the oncogenic potential of Notch. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether Notch signaling is also involved in the important interactions between neoplastic plasma cells and their bone marrow microenvironment, which are necessary for tumor cell growth in multiple myeloma (MM). Our results demonstrate that both Notch receptors and their ligand Jagged1 are highly expressed in cultured and primary MM cells, while nonneoplastic counterparts have low to undetectable levels of Notch. Functional data suggest that ligand-induced Notch signaling acts as a growth factor for MM cells and may contribute to the development of myelomagenesis in vivo.

title: An Extensive MicroRNA-Mediated Network of RNA-RNA Interactions Regulates Established Oncogenic Pathways in Glioblastoma
text: We have made a significant discovery by analyzing gene expression data in glioblastoma along with matched microRNA profiles. We have found a surprisingly large posttranscriptional regulation layer consisting of over 248,000 microRNA (miR)-mediated interactions. Among these interactions, approximately 7,000 genes act as miR "sponges" while 148 genes use alternative, nonsponge interactions. Through biochemical analyses in cell lines, we have confirmed that this network regulates well-known drivers of tumor initiation and subtype implementation, such as PTEN, PDGFRA, RB1, VEGFA, STAT3, and RUNX1. This suggests that these interactions facilitate communication between canonical oncogenic pathways. By silencing 13 miR-mediated PTEN regulators using siRNA, we observed a downregulation of PTEN in a 3'UTR-dependent manner and an increase in tumor cell growth rates. Therefore, these miR-mediated interactions offer a mechanistic explanation for the loss of PTEN expression in a large number of glioma samples with an intact PTEN locus, which has been experimentally validated.

title: Direct reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to neural progenitors.
text: The technique of induced pluripotency, although simple, has the potential to provide a wide range of differentiated cells for cell therapy and drug development. However, the process of creating the necessary cells through induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) involves reprogramming somatic cells and then redifferentiating them, which can be both difficult and time-consuming. In order to overcome this challenge, we wanted to investigate whether it was possible to directly convert somatic cells into lineage-specific stem/progenitor cells of a different germ layer, bypassing the pluripotent stage. Our research demonstrates that by temporarily inducing the four reprogramming factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc), we can effectively transdifferentiate fibroblasts into functional neural stem/progenitor cells (NPCs) with the appropriate signaling inputs. Compared to induced neurons (iN cells), which are directly converted from fibroblasts, transdifferentiated NPCs have the advantage of being able to expand in vitro and retain the ability to generate multiple types of neurons and glial cells. These findings present a new approach to iPSC-factor-based reprogramming, showing that it can be easily adapted as a general platform for transdifferentiation.

title: Tissue-Specific Knockout of the Insulin Receptor in Pancreatic β Cells Creates an Insulin Secretory Defect Similar to that in Type 2 Diabetes
text: The dysfunction of the pancreatic beta cell is a significant defect in the development of type 2 diabetes, although its exact connection to insulin resistance is not clear. To investigate whether insulin signaling plays a role in the beta cell, we utilized the Cre-loxP system to specifically deactivate the insulin receptor gene in these cells. As a result, the mice displayed a specific decrease in insulin secretion when exposed to glucose, along with a gradual decline in glucose tolerance. These findings indicate that the insulin receptor plays a crucial functional role in the beta cell's ability to sense glucose, and suggest that impairments in insulin signaling within the beta cell may contribute to the observed changes in insulin secretion seen in type 2 diabetes.

title: Social variations in access to hospital care for patients with colorectal, breast, and lung cancer between 1999 and 2006: retrospective analysis of hospital episode statistics
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between socioeconomic circumstances, age, sex, and year of admission with the type of hospital admission (emergency or elective) and surgical procedure for colorectal, breast, and lung cancer. The study used data from individual patients between April 1999 and March 2006 from the Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) dataset. A total of 564,821 patients aged 50 and over with a diagnosis of colorectal, breast, or lung cancer were included in the analysis. The main outcomes measured were the proportion of patients admitted as emergencies and the proportion receiving the recommended surgical treatment.

The results showed that patients from deprived areas, older individuals, and women were more likely to be admitted as emergencies. For instance, patients with breast cancer from the least deprived fifth of deprivation had a lower odds ratio of 0.63 (95% confidence interval 0.60 to 0.66) compared to those from the most deprived fifth. Similarly, patients with lung cancer aged 80-89 had a higher odds ratio of 3.13 (2.93 to 3.34) compared to those aged 50-59. Although there were some improvements in disparities between age groups, there was no improvement over time for patients living in deprived areas.

Furthermore, patients from deprived areas were less likely to receive the preferred surgical procedures for rectal, breast, and lung cancer, and this disparity did not improve with time. For example, only 67.4% of patients in the most deprived fifth of deprivation had anterior resection for rectal cancer compared to 75.5% of patients in the least deprived fifth. Similarly, 54.0% of patients in the most deprived fifth had breast conserving surgery compared to 63.7% of patients in the least deprived fifth. Men were also less likely than women to undergo certain surgical procedures, such as anterior resection and lung cancer resection, and older individuals were less likely to receive breast conserving surgery and lung cancer resection.

In conclusion, despite the implementation of the NHS Cancer Plan, social factors continue to strongly influence access to and provision of care for cancer patients.

title: Identification of Gene Positioning Factors Using High-Throughput Imaging Mapping
text: In the cell nucleus, genomes are not randomly arranged in 3D space. To address this, we have created HIPMap, a precise and efficient imaging pipeline using fluorescent in situ hybridization. HIPMap allows us to map the spatial location of genome regions on a large scale. By using high-throughput imaging position mapping, we were able to conduct an unbiased siRNA screen to identify factors that play a role in genome organization in human cells. Through this screen, we discovered 50 cellular factors that are necessary for the proper positioning of various genomic loci with different functions. These positioning factors consist of chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, as well as nuclear envelope and pore proteins. Notably, components of the replication and post-replication chromatin re-assembly machinery are prominently represented among these positioning factors. Additionally, our findings indicate that the timely progression of cells through replication, rather than mitosis, is crucial for correct gene positioning. Overall, our study establishes a method for mapping genome locations on a large scale and has led to the identification of a comprehensive list of cellular factors involved in spatial genome organization.

title: Astrocyte-Mediated Distributed Plasticity at Hypothalamic Glutamate Synapses
text: We have observed that afferent activity can lead to rapid and specific changes in synaptic efficacy. Through the use of electrophysiology, caged molecule photolysis, and Ca(2+) imaging, we have identified a type of plasticity where astrocytes are recruited in response to afferent activity. This recruitment causes a distributed increase in the amplitude of synaptic currents at multiple glutamate synapses on magnocellular neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus. This plasticity is primarily multiplicative, meaning that it results in a proportional increase in the strength of all synapses on the neuron. To achieve this effect, there is a metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated rise in Ca(2+) in the astrocyte processes surrounding the neuron, as well as the release of the gliotransmitter ATP. ATP then acts on postsynaptic purinergic receptors. These findings provide evidence for a type of synaptic plasticity that is distributed, feed-forward, and quickly expressed, all of which are mediated by the synaptic activation of neighboring astrocytes.

title: Effect of smoking reduction on lung cancer risk.
text: Many smokers are unable or unwilling to quit smoking completely. One proposed method of harm reduction is to decrease the number of cigarettes smoked per day. However, it is unclear whether this approach reduces the risk of tobacco-related diseases. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of smoking reduction on the incidence of lung cancer. The study was an observational population-based cohort study conducted by the Copenhagen Centre for Prospective Population Studies. The study included data from three longitudinal studies conducted in Copenhagen and suburbs. The participants were 11,151 men and 8,563 women aged 20 to 93 years. They attended two consecutive examinations with a 5- to 10-year interval between 1964 and 1988. The participants underwent physical examinations and completed self-filled questionnaires about their lifestyle habits. The study population was divided into six groups based on smoking habits: continued heavy smokers (15 or more cigarettes per day), reducers (reduced their smoking by at least 50% without quitting), continued light smokers (1-14 cigarettes per day), quitters (stopped smoking between the first and second examination), stable ex-smokers, and never smokers. The main outcome measure was the incidence of primary lung cancer cases, which was assessed by record linkage with the National Cancer Registry until December 31, 2003. During the follow-up period, there were 864 incident lung cancer cases. The results of the study showed that reducers had a 0.73 hazard ratio for lung cancer compared to persistent heavy smokers. Light smokers had a hazard ratio of 0.44, quitters had a hazard ratio of 0.50, stable ex-smokers had a hazard ratio of 0.17, and never smokers had a hazard ratio of 0.09. In conclusion, reducing smoking by 50% significantly reduces the risk of lung cancer among individuals who smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day.

title: Facilities for macromolecular crystallography at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin
text: The Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB) offers three macromolecular crystallography (MX) beamlines to the structural biology user community at regional, national, and international levels. These state-of-the-art synchrotron beamlines, BL14.1, BL14.2, and BL14.3, are situated in the low-β section of the BESSY II electron storage ring. All three beamlines are powered by a superconducting 7 T wavelength-shifter insertion device. BL14.1 and BL14.2 can be tuned to energies between 5-16 keV, while BL14.3 operates at a fixed energy of 13.8 keV. CCD detectors are installed on all three beamlines. BL14.1 and BL14.2 are regularly used by approximately 50 research groups across Europe, providing around 200 beam days and 600 user shifts per year. Initially used as a test facility, BL14.3 became fully operational for users in 2010. BL14.1 has recently been upgraded with a microdiffractometer, mini-κ goniometer, and an automated sample changer. Additional user facilities include office space near the beamlines, a sample preparation laboratory, a biology laboratory (safety level 1), and high-end computing resources. This article provides a description of the beamline instrumentation and summarizes the experimental capabilities and ancillary equipment available to the user community.

title: PHENIX: a comprehensive Python-based system for macromolecular structure solution
text: Macromolecular X-ray crystallography is commonly used to gain insights into biological processes at a molecular scale. However, it still requires a significant amount of time and effort to solve and finalize many of these structures. This is mainly due to the manual interpretation of complex numerical data using various software packages and the repeated use of interactive three-dimensional graphics. To address these challenges, PHENIX has been created as a comprehensive system for solving macromolecular crystallographic structures, with a strong focus on automating all procedures. This achievement has been made possible through the development of algorithms that minimize or eliminate subjective input, automate traditionally manual procedures, and establish a framework that enables seamless integration between these algorithms.

title: Telomeric 3′ Overhangs Derive from Resection by Exo1 and Apollo and Fill-In by POT1b-Associated CST
text: The presence of a 3' overhang is crucial for safeguarding and preserving telomeres in mammals. However, it is important to regulate its synthesis to prevent excessive removal of the 5' end, which could lead to telomere shortening. The specific mechanism by which this balance is achieved in mammals remains unresolved. In this study, we aimed to uncover the process of 3' overhang synthesis in mouse cells by examining changes in telomeric overhangs throughout the cell cycle and at leading- and lagging-end telomeres. Our findings reveal that Apollo, a nuclease associated with the shelterin subunit TRF2, initiates the formation of the 3' overhang at leading-end telomeres, but not at lagging-end telomeres. The shelterin protein POT1b prevents excessive resection by Apollo at both ends. Exo1, on the other hand, extensively removes material from both telomere ends, resulting in temporary elongated 3' overhangs during the S/G2 phase. CST/AAF, an accessory factor of DNA polα.primase, binds to POT1b and shortens the extended overhangs generated by Exo1, likely through fill-in synthesis. Overall, the formation of the 3' overhang involves multiple steps that are controlled by shelterin, ensuring the presence of functional telomeric overhangs at the ends of chromosomes.

title: Targeting BRCA1 and BRCA2 Deficiencies with G-Quadruplex-Interacting Compounds
text: G-quadruplex (G4) sequences found in the genome, such as telomeres, act as natural barriers to replication forks. When replication forks become stalled, they can be stabilized and restarted through a process called homologous recombination (HR), which also repairs DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that occur at collapsed forks. Previous studies have shown that HR plays a role in facilitating telomere replication. In this study, we demonstrate that the replication efficiency of guanine-rich telomeric repeats is significantly reduced in cells lacking HR. Treatment with a compound called pyridostatin (PDS), which stabilizes G4 structures, increases the fragility of telomeres in cells deficient in the BRCA2 protein. This suggests that the formation of G4 structures contributes to telomere instability. Interestingly, PDS also reduces the proliferation of HR-defective cells by causing an accumulation of DSBs, activating checkpoints, disrupting the progression of the cell cycle, and exacerbating the replication defect associated with HR deficiency. The toxicity of PDS extends to HR-defective cells that have developed resistance to the drug olaparib through the loss of either the 53BP1 or REV7 protein. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of G4-stabilizing drugs to selectively eliminate cells and tumors that are compromised in HR, including those that are resistant to PARP inhibition.

title: Downloaded from
text:
Physical activity triggers a mild inflammatory response in the body, which is partly caused by leukocytes. This response is characterized by increased levels of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), circulating in the blood. However, the source of these cytokines during exercise is still unknown. To address this question, we conducted a study to investigate the changes in plasma cytokine levels and their corresponding mRNA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells following exercise. 

We recruited ten healthy but untrained men with a peak oxygen uptake of 48.8 ± 6.5 (SD) ml · kg−1 · min−1 and an average age of 25 ± 5 (SD) years. These participants engaged in 3 hours of exercise, including cycling and inclined walking, at an intensity of 60-65% of their peak oxygen uptake. We observed an increase in the number of circulating leukocyte subsets during and 2 hours after exercise, but these levels returned to normal within 24 hours. Plasma concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α reached their peak at the end of exercise and remained elevated at 2 hours (IL-6) and up to 24 hours (IL-1β and TNF-α) after exercise. 

Furthermore, we analyzed the gene expression of cytokines in circulating mononuclear cells and found that the mRNA expression of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α mirrored the changes in their plasma concentrations. These findings suggest that exercise-induced inflammation involves the production of cytokines by mononuclear cells in the blood.

title: Receptor tyrosine kinases endocytosis in endothelium: biology and signaling.
text: Receptor tyrosine kinases play a crucial role in regulating important processes in endothelial biology, such as proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis. It is widely accepted that receptor tyrosine kinase signaling occurs both inside the cell and on the cell's outer membrane, although there are still many important details that need to be clarified. The process of endocytosis and subsequent intracellular trafficking play a vital role in regulating receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, while signaling endosomes serve as a platform for organizing signaling events. This article provides an overview of recent advancements in our understanding of how endothelial receptor tyrosine kinases are internalized and how they signal, using vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 as a prime example.

title: Ethnographic study of incidence and severity of intravenous drug errors.
text: AIMS To investigate the frequency and clinical significance of mistakes in the preparation and administration of intravenous medications, as well as the specific stages of the process in which these errors occur. METHODOLOGY This study employed a prospective ethnographic approach, utilizing disguised observation. PARTICIPANTS The study involved nurses responsible for the preparation and administration of intravenous drugs. LOCATION The research was conducted in 10 wards across both teaching and non-teaching hospitals in the United Kingdom. MAIN OUTCOMES The study aimed to determine the number, type, and clinical significance of errors made during the process. FINDINGS A total of 249 errors were identified. At least one error occurred in 212 out of 430 intravenous drug doses (49%, with a 95% confidence interval of 45% to 54%). Three doses (1%) had potentially severe errors, 126 (29%) had potentially moderate errors, and 83 (19%) had potentially minor errors. The majority of errors occurred during the administration of bolus doses or the preparation of drugs that required multiple steps. CONCLUSIONS The rate of intravenous drug errors was found to be high. While most errors would only result in short-term adverse effects, a few had the potential to be serious. Implementing strategies such as reducing the amount of preparation done on the ward, providing training, and utilizing technology for administering slow bolus doses would likely have the greatest impact on reducing error rates.

title: Feature Selection with the Boruta Package
text: In this article, we present the Boruta R package, which introduces a new feature selection algorithm for identifying all relevant variables. The algorithm functions as a wrapper around a Random Forest classification algorithm and employs a statistical test to iteratively eliminate features that are deemed less relevant than random probes. The Boruta package offers a user-friendly interface to this algorithm, along with a brief explanation of its workings and practical examples of its application.

title: Integrin-linked kinase expression is elevated in human cardiac hypertrophy and induces hypertrophy in transgenic mice.
text: The molecular basis of the hypertrophic response in human heart diseases is not well understood, despite knowledge of numerous signaling pathways activated in experimental cardiac hypertrophy. Integrin-linked kinase (ILK) is a protein kinase that connects beta-integrins with the actin cytoskeleton, suggesting a potential role as a mechanoreceptor. In this study, we observed a significant increase in ILK protein levels in hypertrophic ventricles of patients with congenital and acquired outflow tract obstruction. This increase in ILK was associated with the activation of Rho family guanine triphosphatases, Rac1 and Cdc42, as well as known hypertrophic signaling kinases, including extracellular signal-related kinases (ERK1/2) and p70 S6 kinase. Transgenic mice expressing a constitutively active ILK (ILK(S343D)) or wild-type ILK (ILK(WT)) specifically in the heart showed a compensated ventricular hypertrophic phenotype and exhibited an activation profile of guanine triphosphatases and downstream protein kinases similar to that observed in human hypertrophy. On the other hand, transgenic mice expressing a kinase-inactive ILK (ILK(R211A)) only in cardiomyocytes were unable to mount a compensatory hypertrophic response to angiotensin II in vivo. In conclusion, these findings suggest that ILK-regulated signaling plays a crucial role in the adaptive hypertrophic response mechanism relevant to a wide range of clinical heart diseases.

title: Functional and molecular defects of pancreatic islets in human type 2 diabetes.
text: In order to gain a better understanding of the main changes in insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes and the potential mechanisms involved, we conducted a study on the functional and molecular properties of islets taken from the pancreas of 13 individuals with type 2 diabetes and 13 non-diabetic organ donors who were matched in terms of characteristics. We found that the release of insulin in response to glucose stimulation was significantly lower in the islets from individuals with type 2 diabetes compared to the control islets. However, the release of insulin in response to arginine and glibenclamide was less affected. These defects were accompanied by a decrease in the expression of GLUT1 and -2 and glucokinase mRNA, as well as a reduction in glucose oxidation. Additionally, the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase was reduced. Furthermore, the expression of insulin was decreased, while the expression of pancreatic duodenal homeobox-1 (PDX-1) and forkhead box O1 (Foxo-1) was increased. Markers of oxidative stress, such as nitrotyrosine and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine concentrations, were significantly higher in the islets of individuals with type 2 diabetes compared to the control islets, and these markers were correlated with the degree of impairment in glucose-stimulated insulin release. Interestingly, exposure to glutathione for 24 hours resulted in a significant improvement in glucose-stimulated insulin release and a decrease in nitrotyrosine concentration, along with a partial recovery of insulin mRNA expression. These findings provide direct evidence that the defects in insulin secretion in type 2 diabetic islets are associated with various changes in islet cells. Importantly, our study demonstrates that the functional impairment of type 2 diabetic islets can be partially reversed. Therefore, it is suggested that reducing oxidative stress in islet cells could be a potential target for the treatment of type 2 diabetes in humans.

title: Induction of stem-like cells with malignant properties by chronic exposure of human lung epithelial cells to single-walled carbon nanotubes
text: This study aimed to investigate the potential health risks of carbon nanotubes (CNT) and their association with lung cancer. The researchers hypothesized that the development of cancer stem cells (CSC) may contribute to CNT-induced carcinogenesis. To test this hypothesis, non-tumorigenic lung epithelial cells were exposed to single-walled CNT for six months. The presence of CSC-like cells was evaluated using specific conditions, and their aggressive behaviors and tumor-initiating capability were assessed. The study found that CSC-like cells were present in all clones of CNT-exposed cells and exhibited characteristics associated with lung CSC, including self-renewal, aggressive cancer behaviors, and tumorigenesis. These cells also displayed abnormal stem cell markers. Restoring the expression of the tumor suppressor p53 reversed the CSC properties of these cells. Additionally, specific stem cell surface markers were identified that were associated with CNT-induced CSC formation and tumorigenesis. These findings highlight the importance of prevention strategies and exposure control for CNT and suggest that detecting CSC and related surface markers could be an effective screening tool for predicting the carcinogenic potential of CNT and similar nanoparticles.

title: Reprogramming factor stoichiometry influences the epigenetic state and biological properties of induced pluripotent stem cells.
text: We conducted a comparison between two highly defined transgenic systems to determine the factors that affect the reprogramming of somatic cells into a pluripotent state. Our findings reveal that the level and balance of reprogramming factors during the process strongly impact the resulting pluripotency of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). By combining high expression of Oct4 and Klf4 with lower expression of c-Myc and Sox2, we successfully generated iPSCs that efficiently produced "all-iPSC mice" through tetraploid (4n) complementation. These iPSCs also maintained normal imprinting at the Dlk1-Dio3 locus and did not give rise to tumors in mice. Although loss of imprinting (LOI) at the Dlk1-Dio3 locus did not consistently correlate with reduced pluripotency, it did decrease the efficiency of generating "all-iPSC mice". Our data suggest that the balance of reprogramming factors can influence the epigenetic and biological characteristics of iPSCs. This concept adds complexity to the task of defining a "generic" epigenetic state for iPSCs and embryonic stem cells (ESCs), and should be taken into account when comparing different iPSC and ESC lines.

title: Activator protein-1 (AP-1) DNA binding activity is induced by hydroxyurea in organogenesis stage mouse embryos
text: Hydroxyurea is a powerful substance that can cause birth defects. However, the effects of this substance can be reduced by using antioxidants or free radical scavengers. Activator Protein-1 (AP-1) and NF-kappaB are transcription factors that play important roles in normal development and the body's response to stress. This research aimed to investigate whether exposure to teratogenic doses of hydroxyurea leads to oxidative stress and changes in gene expression by activating these transcription factors. Pregnant mice were given either saline or hydroxyurea at doses of 400, 500, or 600 mg/kg on gestation day 9 (GD 9). They were then euthanized at different time points after treatment (GD 9, 0.5, 3, or 6 hours) to assess oxidative stress and transcription factor activities. Another group of mice were euthanized on GD 18 to evaluate fetal development. The results showed that exposure to 400 mg/kg of hydroxyurea did not have any effect on the offspring. However, exposure to 500 or 600 mg/kg resulted in a dose-dependent increase in fetal resorptions and malformations, such as curly tails, abnormal limbs (oligodactyly, hemimelia, and amelia), and short ribs. The study found that hydroxyurea did not cause oxidative stress, as indicated by the ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione, and it did not alter the DNA binding activity of NF-kappaB in the GD 9 conceptus. On the other hand, exposure to hydroxyurea at any dose increased the DNA binding activity of AP-1 in embryos and yolk sacs 0.5 or 3 hours after treatment. The activity of c-Fos heterodimers, a component of AP-1, peaked at 3 hours and remained elevated at 6 hours, while the activity of c-Jun dimers was not affected by the drug. The study also observed a significant increase in c-Fos immunoreactivity in hydroxyurea-treated embryos. The induction of AP-1 DNA binding activity by hydroxyurea serves as an early and sensitive indicator of the embryonic response to injury.

title: BCL-6 represses genes that function in lymphocyte differentiation, inflammation, and cell cycle control.
