The expression of Nanog in normal cells was also significantly higher than in normal lung tissues and benign lung lesions in cancer stem cells. Nanog was found to be highly expressed in CD44+ cells, and its expression in lung cancer stem cells was significantly higher (p<0.05). In conclusion, both group A (lung cancer) and group B (squamous cell lung carcinoma) exhibited significantly higher Nanog gene expression. The data from this study indicate that patients with stage III and IV lung cancer had higher Nanog gene expression. Additionally, lung cancer patients demonstrated higher levels of Nanog expression. Conversely, stronger Nanog gene expression was associated with a lower degree of cell differentiation in lung cancer.

title: Current knowledge and future directions of TLR and NOD signaling in sepsis
text: The prevalence of sepsis is on the rise, accompanied by an increased risk of mortality. Sepsis treatment incurs significant costs annually in the United States. The process of death from sepsis is complex, involving a disruption in normal immune functions and an overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, ultimately leading to failure of multiple organs. The Toll-like receptor (TLR) family, which includes a member initially discovered in Drosophila, plays a crucial role in identifying microbial pathogens. These pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) activate internal signaling pathways upon detecting invading microorganisms. NOD signaling also contributes to the identification of bacteria and works synergistically with the TLR family to initiate an effective immune response against invading pathogens. TLRs and NOD1/NOD2 respond to different patterns associated with pathogens (PAMPs). The modulation of both TLR and NOD signaling pathways is an area of research that has generated much excitement and debate as a potential therapeutic approach in sepsis management. Although molecules targeting TLR and NOD signaling pathways exist, unfortunately, none have demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials thus far.

title: Concentration Sensing by the Moving Nucleus in Cell Fate Determination: A Computational Analysis
text:
During the development of the vertebrate neuroepithelium, the nucleus in neural progenitor cells (NPCs) undergoes a process called interkinetic nuclear migration. This involves the nucleus moving from the apex towards the base, then returning to the apex before the cell divides. It is believed that the fate of the resulting daughter cells depends on the sampling of a spatial concentration profile of the cytoplasmic Notch intracellular domain (NICD) by the moving nucleus. However, the nucleus undergoes complex stochastic motions, including random waiting and back-and-forth movements, which can expose it to varying levels of cytoplasmic NICD. The mechanism by which nuclear position determines daughter cell fate despite the stochastic nature of nuclear migration is not well understood. 

To address this, we developed a mathematical model that incorporates the reaction, diffusion, and nuclear accumulation of NICD in NPCs during interkinetic nuclear migration. We used experimentally measured data on the probabilities of nuclear turning, waiting times, and average speeds in NPCs in the developing zebrafish retina to perform stochastic simulations. These simulations allowed us to compute the probabilities of NPC differentiation based on the trajectory of the nucleus. By comparing these results with experimentally measured NICD concentrations and probabilities of differentiation, we were able to estimate the cytoplasmic gradient of NICD. 

Our findings suggest that the spatially polarized production of NICD, rapid cytoplasmic consumption, and the time-averaging effect of nuclear import/export kinetics are sufficient to explain the observed probabilities of differentiation. These computational studies provide quantitative support for the idea that the nuclear concentration-sensing mechanism plays a role in determining the fate of NPCs in the zebrafish retina.

title: Odorant-specific adaptation pathways generate olfactory plasticity in C. elegans
text: After being exposed to a smell for a long time, C. elegans shows a reduced reaction to that smell for several hours. This adaptation to smells is specific to each smell; the animals can adapt separately to different smells detected by a single pair of olfactory neurons called the AWC neurons. The process of adapting to smells is genetically complex, as different genes are needed to adapt to different smells. Animals with a mutation in the adp-1 gene are unable to adapt to some of the smells detected by the AWC neurons; adp-1 affects a process that relies on calcium and is necessary for adaptation. Mutations in another gene, osm-9, affect the adaptation to a different but partially overlapping group of smells detected by the AWC neurons. Mutations in adp-1 and osm-9 do not affect the ability of unadapted animals to respond to smells, which suggests that sensing smells and adapting to them are separate processes.

title: Genome-wide dFOXO targets and topology of the transcriptomic response to stress and insulin signalling
text: The FoxO transcription factors, which are inhibited by insulin/insulin-like growth factor signalling (IIS), play a crucial role in various processes in organisms, including lifespan. By using genomic tools, we have discovered more than 700 direct targets of dFOXO in adult female Drosophila. In the wild-type fly, dFOXO is directly responsible for the transcription of several components of IIS and pathways that interact with it, such as TOR. The genomic locations occupied by dFOXO in adults are different from those observed in larvae or cultured cells. These locations remain unchanged when activated by stresses or reduced IIS, but the binding is increased and additional targets are activated when there is a genetic reduction in IIS. We have identified the specific part of the IIS transcriptional response that is directly controlled by dFOXO, as well as the indirect effects. We have also shown that certain parts of the transcriptional response to reduced IIS do not require dfoxo. Through promoter analyses, we have identified GATA and other forkhead factors as potential mediators of the indirect effects that are independent of dfoxo. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the targets of dFOXO are conserved across the genome between the fly and the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. These targets are enriched with a second tier of regulators, including the dHR96/daf-12 nuclear hormone receptor.

title: Stable partnership and progression to AIDS or death in HIV infected patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy: Swiss HIV cohort study.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the connection between having a stable partnership and the clinical outcomes of HIV infected patients who were receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The study design was a prospective cohort study of adults with HIV, specifically the Swiss HIV cohort study. The study took place in seven outpatient clinics across Switzerland. The participants were 3736 patients from the cohort who had started HAART before 2002. Their median age was 36 years, with 29% being female, and the median follow-up period was 3.6 years.

The main outcome measures of the study were the time it took for participants to develop AIDS or die (primary endpoint), death alone, increases in CD4 cell count of at least 50 and 100 above baseline, optimal viral suppression (having a viral load below 400 copies/ml), and viral rebound.

The results showed that during the follow-up period, 80% of participants (2985 individuals) reported having a stable partnership at least once. When they started HAART, 52% of participants (545 out of 1042) reported having a stable partnership. After five years of follow-up, this percentage decreased to 46% (190 out of 412) of participants.

In an analysis that took into account previous antiretroviral therapy and clinical stage at the start of HAART, the adjusted hazard ratio for progression to AIDS or death was 0.79 (with a 95% confidence interval of 0.63 to 0.98) for participants with a stable partnership compared to those without. The adjusted hazard ratios for other endpoints were 0.59 (0.44 to 0.79) for progression to death, 1.15 (1.06 to 1.24) for an increase in CD4 cells of 100 counts/microliter or more, and 1.06 (0.98 to 1.14) for optimal viral suppression.

In conclusion, this study found that having a stable partnership is associated with a slower rate of progression to AIDS or death in HIV infected patients who are receiving HAART.

title: Specific deficit of the ON response in visual transmission by targeted disruption of the mGIuR6 gene
text: We utilized the limited expression of metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype 6 (mGluR6) in retinal ON bipolar cells to create mice lacking mGluR6 expression. The mice with the mutated gene exhibited a loss of ON responses to light, while their OFF responses remained unaffected. There were no noticeable changes in the arrangement of retinal cells or the projection of optic fibers to the brain in the mutant mice. Additionally, the mice lacking mGluR6 displayed visual behavioral responses to light stimulation, as observed through shuttle box avoidance behavior experiments using light exposure as a conditioned stimulus. These findings highlight the crucial role of mGluR6 in synaptic transmission to the ON bipolar cell and emphasize the significance of the OFF response in transmitting visual information.

title: Common BRCA1 variants and susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer in the general population.
text: The majority of families with multiple cases of early-onset breast cancer and ovarian cancer are believed to be caused by highly penetrant mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. However, these mutations are rare in the general population and likely only account for a small percentage of all breast cancer cases. It is possible that a larger proportion of breast cancer cases are caused by common variants that confer more modest individual risks. In the BRCA1 gene, there are several common variations that result in changes to amino acids. We have studied the frequency of four of these variations (Gln356Arg, Pro871Leu, Glu1038Gly, and Ser1613Gly) in a large group of breast and ovarian cancer patients and matched controls. Due to strong genetic linkage, these four variations only produce three haplotypes with a frequency greater than 1.3%. The most common haplotypes, defined by the alleles Gln356Pro871Glu1038Ser1613 and Gln356Leu871Gly1038Gly1613, have frequencies of 0.57 and 0.32 respectively, and these frequencies do not significantly differ between the patient and control groups. Therefore, the most common variations in the BRCA1 gene do not significantly contribute to the risk of breast or ovarian cancer. However, our data suggests that the Arg356 allele may have a different distribution in breast cancer patients compared to controls (Arg356 homozygotes are more common in the control group, P = 0.01), indicating a potential protective effect against breast cancer. If this finding is confirmed, it could provide insights into the structural characteristics of the BRCA1 protein that are crucial for its function.

title: Exercise causes a tissue-specific change of NO production in the kidney and lung.
text:
Exercise leads to changes in blood flow, with an increase in systemic blood flow and a redistribution of blood flow in different tissues. This study aimed to investigate the effect of exercise on the production of nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator, in the kidneys and lungs of rats.

The rats were subjected to a 45-minute treadmill run at a speed of 25 m/min, while control rats remained at rest. After exercise, the kidneys and lungs were quickly removed for analysis. The researchers examined the expression of NO synthase (NOS) mRNA and protein, NOS activity, and the levels of nitrite/nitrate (stable end products of NO) in these organs.

The results showed that exercise had a tissue-specific effect on NO production. In the kidneys, the expression of endothelial NOS (eNOS) mRNA was significantly lower in exercise rats compared to control rats. Conversely, in the lungs, the expression of eNOS mRNA was significantly higher in exercise rats. Western blot analysis confirmed these changes in eNOS protein levels.

However, there were no differences in the expression of neuronal NOS (nNOS) mRNA and protein, or inducible NOS (iNOS) mRNA and protein between exercise and control rats in both the kidneys and lungs. NOS activity in the kidneys was significantly lower in exercise rats, while it was significantly higher in the lungs. The activity of iNOS did not differ between exercise and control rats in either organ.

Furthermore, the levels of nitrite/nitrate in the kidneys were significantly lower in exercise rats, whereas they were significantly higher in the lungs.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that exercise leads to marked and tissue-specific changes in NO production in the kidneys and lungs. These findings suggest that exercise has a differential effect on NO regulation in different organs.

title: Ballistic labeling and dynamic imaging of astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures
text: In vivo, protoplasmic astrocytes in mammalian CNS tissues have a complex 3D structure. However, when they are cultured as dissociated cells, they often take on a flattened, fibroblast-like shape with only a few simple processes. Through fluorescent labeling and confocal reconstruction, we have discovered that many astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures display a more natural and intricate cytoarchitecture. While astrocytes on the surface of the slice cultures exhibit a reactive form with thick glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-positive processes, astrocytes located deeper within the tissue slices maintain a highly complex 3D structure with numerous delicate spine- or veil-like protrusions. By using gene gun-mediated ballistic delivery of gold or tungsten particles carrying cDNAs (Biolistics), lipophilic dyes (DiOlistics), or fluorescent intracellular calcium indicators (Calistics), we are able to label dozens of astrocytes in a single slice culture. The expression of a membrane-targeted form of eGFP (Lck-GFP) is more effective than soluble eGFP in visualizing the fine processes of astrocytes. Through time-lapse confocal imaging of Lck-GFP transfected astrocytes or "calistically" labeled astrocytes, we can observe structural changes and calcium transients, respectively. This method provides an in vitro system for studying the functional structure, development, and dynamic changes of astrocytes, as well as their interactions with neurons and glia in live mammalian brain tissues.

title: A bipotential precursor population for pancreas and liver within the embryonic endoderm.
text: The pancreas develops from separate regions of the embryonic gut endoderm, known as the dorsal and ventral domains. Previous studies in mice have identified factors necessary for the development of the dorsal pancreas, but the factors responsible for initiating the ventral pancreas have remained unknown. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether the emergence of the ventral pancreas is linked to the emergence of the liver. Our findings reveal that the liver and ventral pancreas are specified simultaneously and within the same group of cells. Through experiments involving the transplantation of embryo tissues, we discovered that the default fate of the ventral foregut endoderm is to activate the genes associated with pancreas development. However, signaling from the cardiac mesoderm, specifically FGF signaling, redirects this endoderm to express genes related to liver development instead of those associated with the pancreas. We did not find any evidence suggesting that the choice between pancreas and liver cell types is influenced by growth or viability. The cardiac mesoderm or FGF induces the local expression of sonic hedgehog, which inhibits pancreas development but not liver development. The precursor cells that have the potential to become either pancreas or liver during embryonic development, as well as their fate selection by FGF, exhibit characteristics that are also observed in the adult pancreas and are reflected in the evolutionary history of these organs.

title: ErbB4-neuregulin signaling modulates synapse development and dendritic arborization through distinct mechanisms.
text: Schizophrenia has been linked to disruptions in the function of neuregulin-1 (NRG1) and ErbB4. Patients with the condition show changes in the levels of these proteins and experience reduced activity in glutamatergic synapses, as well as alterations in neuronal circuitry. However, the impact of NRG1/ErbB4 on synapse maturation and the formation of neuronal processes has not been thoroughly investigated. In this study, we reveal that ErbB4 is present in inhibitory interneurons at both excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic sites. Increasing the expression of ErbB4 after synapse formation enhances the size of presynaptic inputs, but not their number. Conversely, reducing ErbB4 levels using shRNA decreases the size of presynaptic inputs, indicating that endogenous ErbB4 plays a specific role in synapse maturation. Through the use of ErbB4 mutant constructs, we demonstrate that the extracellular domain of ErbB4 is necessary for synapse maturation, while its tyrosine kinase activity is not. Additionally, we show that depleting ErbB4 leads to a decrease in the number of primary neurites, and stimulating ErbB4 with a soluble form of NRG1 results in excessive dendritic branching through activation of the tyrosine kinase domain of ErbB4 and the phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway. These findings highlight the differential regulation of synapse maturation and dendritic morphology by NRG1/ErbB4 signaling, which involves trans-synaptic signaling and tyrosine kinase activity, respectively.

title: Dynamic Helix Interactions in Transmembrane Signaling
text: The study of how protein transmembrane domains transmit signals across membranes faces distinct challenges. In this discussion, we explore the factors that have contributed to achievements in this field and contemplate the knowledge gained from these instances. These endeavors indicate that the most intriguing characteristics of transmembrane helix interactions may be the most difficult to investigate using existing methods.

title: Association between smoking and risk of bladder cancer among men and women.
text:
The previous research suggests that tobacco smoking is responsible for 50% to 65% of bladder cancer cases in men and 20% to 30% in women. It also shows that current smokers are three times more likely to develop bladder cancer compared to those who have never smoked. Although the incidence rates of bladder cancer have remained stable in the United States over the past 30 years, changes in smoking habits and cigarette composition necessitate a reevaluation of the risks associated with smoking and bladder cancer.

The objective of this study was to examine the link between tobacco smoking and bladder cancer. The study involved a cohort of 281,394 men and 186,134 women from the National Institutes of Health-AARP (NIH-AARP) Diet and Health Study. Participants completed a lifestyle questionnaire and were followed up between October 25, 1995, and December 31, 2006. The researchers conducted a systematic review of previous cohort studies on smoking and incident bladder cancer to estimate the relative risks using fixed-effects models. The heterogeneity of the results was assessed using the I(2) statistic.

The main outcome measures were hazard ratios (HRs), population attributable risks (PARs), and number needed to harm (NNH). Over the course of 4,518,941 person-years of follow-up, there were 3,896 cases of incident bladder cancer in men (144.0 per 100,000 person-years) and 627 cases in women (34.5 per 100,000 person-years). Former smokers had a higher risk of bladder cancer (119.8 per 100,000 person-years; HR, 2.22; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.03-2.44; NNH, 1250), as did current smokers (177.3 per 100,000 person-years; HR, 4.06; 95% CI, 3.66-4.50; NNH, 727), compared to never smokers (39.8 per 100,000 person-years). In contrast, the summary risk estimate for current smoking in seven previous studies conducted between 1963 and 1987 was 2.94 (95% CI, 2.45-3.54; I(2) = 0.0%). The PAR for ever smoking in our study was 0.50 (95% CI, 0.45-0.54) in men and 0.52 (95% CI, 0.45-0.59) in women.

In conclusion, the relative risks associated with smoking in the more recent NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study cohort were higher compared to a pooled estimate of US data from cohorts initiated between 1963 and 1987. The population attributable risks for women were comparable to those for men.

title: Leptin regulates glutamate and glucose transporters in hypothalamic astrocytes.
text: Glial cells play crucial roles in modifying the metabolism and functioning of neurons, and there is growing interest in their involvement in appetite and energy regulation. Previous studies have shown that leptin, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism, can affect the structure and morphology of glial cells. In this study, we provide evidence that metabolic status and leptin also impact the specific transporters for glutamate and glucose in astrocytes, indicating that metabolic signals influence the efficiency of synaptic communication and glucose uptake, ultimately affecting neuronal function. We observed that the electrical activity of hypothalamic proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in mice, both at rest and when stimulated by glucose, was altered in the offspring of mothers who were fed a high-fat diet. Furthermore, in adulthood, increased body weight and fasting also affected the expression of glucose and glutamate transporters. These findings highlight the influence of whole-organism metabolism on the activity of glial cells in the hypothalamus and suggest that these cells may play a significant role in the development of obesity.

title: Metabolic phenotyping of human blood plasma: a powerful tool to discriminate between cancer types?
text:
BACKGROUND: Growing evidence suggests that cancer cell metabolism differs from that of normal cells. However, it remains unclear whether specific metabolite profiles can distinguish between different types of cancer. This study aims to determine whether the plasma metabolic phenotype can differentiate between lung and breast cancer.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: The proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum of plasma was divided into 110 integration regions, which represent the metabolic phenotype. These regions reflect the relative concentrations of metabolites and were used to train a classification model to distinguish between 80 female breast cancer patients and 54 female lung cancer patients, all with adenocarcinoma. The model's validity was assessed through permutation testing and by classifying an independent validation cohort consisting of 60 female breast cancer patients and 81 male lung cancer patients, all with adenocarcinoma.

RESULTS: The model correctly classified 99% of breast cancer patients and 93% of lung cancer patients, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.96. The model was validated in the independent cohort, achieving a sensitivity of 89%, specificity of 82%, and an AUC of 0.94. Decreased levels of sphingomyelin and phosphatidylcholine (phospholipids with choline head group), along with increased levels of phospholipids with long, saturated fatty acid chains, suggest that lung tumor cell membranes are more rigid and less susceptible to lipid peroxidation. Other discriminating metabolites indicate a more pronounced response to the Warburg effect in lung cancer.

CONCLUSION: Metabolic phenotyping of plasma can differentiate between lung and breast cancer, suggesting that the metabolite profile reflects more than a general cancer marker.

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT02362776.

title: Direct in vivo assessment of microcirculatory dysfunction in severe falciparum malaria.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine and quantify changes in the small blood vessels of the mucosal surfaces in patients with severe malaria. This was done by directly observing the blood vessels using a technique called orthogonal polarization spectral (OPS) imaging. The study assessed the microcirculation in the rectal mucosa of adult patients with severe malaria using OPS imaging, both upon admission and daily thereafter. Comparison groups included patients with uncomplicated falciparum malaria, patients with bacterial sepsis, and healthy individuals.

The results showed that the flow of red blood cells in the small blood vessels was significantly disrupted in patients with severe falciparum malaria, and the severity of the disruption was proportional to the severity of the disease. Blocked capillaries were found in 67% of the patients, and in 93% of those cases, adjacent blood vessels had abnormally fast blood flow. The presence of blocked capillaries was correlated with abnormal levels of base deficit and lactate in the blood. These abnormalities disappeared as the patients recovered. In contrast, no stagnant red blood cells were found in healthy individuals or in patients with uncomplicated malaria or sepsis. Patients with sepsis, however, did exhibit abnormally fast blood flow.

In conclusion, patients with severe falciparum malaria experience extensive blockage in their small blood vessels, and the severity of the blockage corresponds to the severity of the disease. This highlights the significant role that microvascular blockage plays in the development of severe malaria and demonstrates the fundamental difference between the microvascular pathophysiology of malaria and bacterial sepsis.

title: Multiple archaeal groups mediate methane oxidation in anoxic cold seep sediments.
text: No microorganism that can grow anaerobically on methane as the only source of carbon has been successfully cultivated. Therefore, information about these microorganisms has been deduced from studying field samples through geochemical and microbiological observations. By analyzing stable isotopes in lipid biomarkers and conducting rRNA gene surveys, specific microorganisms have been implicated in the anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM). In this study, we utilized a combination of fluorescent in situ hybridization and secondary ion mass spectrometry analyses to identify anaerobic methanotrophs in marine methane-seep sediments. The results provide direct evidence that at least two distinct groups of archaea (ANME-1 and ANME-2) are involved in AOM at methane seeps. While both groups of archaea were often found in physical association with bacteria, they were also observed as individual aggregations or single cells. The ANME-1 archaea were more commonly found as individual aggregations or filaments without a bacterial partner. The bacteria associated with both groups of archaea included, but were not limited to, closely related species of Desulfosarcina. Isotopic analyses suggest that both individual archaeal cells and cell aggregates were actively involved in anaerobic methanotrophy, as were consortia of multiple species. Overall, the data indicate that the microbial species and interactions involved in anaerobic methanotrophy are diverse and complex. The data also clearly demonstrate that highly structured ANME-2/Desulfosarcina consortia are not the sole entities responsible for AOM at marine methane seeps. Other microbial groups, including ANME-1 archaea, are capable of anaerobic methane consumption either as individual cells, in individual aggregations, or in consortia with multiple species.

title: N-cadherin in the spotlight of cell-cell adhesion, differentiation, embryogenesis, invasion and signalling.
text: Cell migration is a crucial process that occurs during embryonic development, throughout adulthood, and in certain pathological conditions. The neural cell adhesion molecule N-cadherin, specifically, plays a significant role in migration. During embryogenesis, N-cadherin is the primary molecule involved in gastrulation and neural crest development. N-cadherin-mediated contacts activate various pathways, such as Rho GTPases, and contribute to tyrosine kinase signaling (e.g., through the fibroblast growth factor receptor). In cancer, cadherins regulate the balance between suppressing and promoting invasion. E-cadherin acts as an invasion suppressor and is typically downregulated in most carcinomas, while N-cadherin, as an invasion promoter, is often upregulated. The expression of N-cadherin in epithelial cells induces morphological changes, leading to a fibroblastic phenotype and enhancing cell motility and invasiveness. However, in certain cancers like osteosarcoma, N-cadherin may function as a tumor suppressor. N-cadherin can have multiple functions, either promoting adhesion or inducing migration depending on the specific cellular context.

title: Role of fascin in filopodial protrusion
text: This study aimed to investigate the mechanisms of actin-bundling in filopodia. By analyzing the cellular localization of known actin cross-linking proteins in mouse melanoma B16F1 cells, it was found that fascin was specifically localized along the entire length of all filopodia, while other actin cross-linkers were not. When fascin was suppressed through RNA interference, the number of filopodia decreased, and the remaining filopodia exhibited abnormal morphology with wavy and loosely bundled actin organization. The dephosphorylation of serine 39 appeared to play a role in determining the frequency of cellular filopodia. The constitutively active fascin mutant S39A increased the number and length of filopodia, whereas the inactive fascin mutant S39E reduced the frequency of filopodia. Through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments using GFP-tagged wild-type and S39A fascin, it was observed that dephosphorylated fascin underwent rapid cycles of association and dissociation from actin filaments in filopodia, with a half-life (t1/2) of less than 10 seconds. Based on these findings, it is proposed that fascin serves as a crucial and specific actin cross-linker, providing stiffness to filopodial bundles. Furthermore, its dynamic behavior allows for efficient coordination between the elongation and bundling of filopodial actin filaments.

title: TOR Signaling in Growth and Metabolism
text: In this review, we focus on the target of rapamycin (TOR), a Ser/Thr kinase that plays a crucial role in regulating cell growth and metabolism based on environmental cues. By examining findings from studies conducted on model organisms, we delve into the mammalian TOR complexes and the signaling pathways they control. TOR is a component of two distinct multiprotein complexes: TOR complex 1 (TORC1), which is sensitive to rapamycin, and TORC2, which is not affected by rapamycin. The dysregulation of mammalian TORC1 has significant physiological implications, suggesting that inhibitors targeting mammalian TOR could potentially be beneficial in treating various conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, autoimmunity, and metabolic disorders.

title: Self-Organization of the Escherichia coli Chemotaxis Network Imaged with Super-Resolution Light Microscopy
text: The chemotaxis network in Escherichia coli serves as a model for processing biological signals. In this bacterium, transmembrane receptors responsible for signal transduction come together to form large clusters consisting of thousands of proteins. These clusters, known as sensory clusters, have been observed at the poles of the cell and at future division sites. Despite extensive research, the process of cluster formation, the factors controlling their size and density, and how their cellular location is maintained in growing and dividing cells remain unclear. To address these questions, we utilized photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM) to precisely map the cellular locations of three key proteins involved in bacterial chemotaxis: the Tar receptor, CheY, and CheW. Our findings reveal that cluster sizes follow an exponential distribution, with no specific characteristic size. Additionally, we discovered that one-third of Tar receptors are part of smaller lateral clusters rather than the larger polar clusters. By analyzing the relative cellular locations of over a million individual proteins from 326 cells, we propose that clusters form through stochastic self-assembly. The high-resolution PALM maps of E. coli receptors support the idea that stochastic self-assembly can generate and maintain approximately periodic structures in biological membranes, without the need for direct involvement of the cytoskeleton or active transport.

title: Ciliary Extracellular Vesicles: Txt Msg Organelles
text: Cilia are sensory structures that extend from the surface of cells to monitor the surrounding environment. In addition to their role in sensing, cilia also release extracellular vesicles (EVs). The release of these tiny EVs is a form of communication between cells that is found in all three kingdoms of life. These extracellular structures play important roles in both short and long-range signaling between cells, and they may coordinate responses within an organism in both normal and diseased states. The shedding of EVs from ciliated cells and their interactions with cilia are evolutionary conserved phenomena, but there is still much to learn about the relationship between cilia and EVs and the basic biology of EVs. Studies in model organisms like Chlamydomonas and Caenorhabditis elegans have started to provide insights into ciliary EVs. In Chlamydomonas, EVs are released from the tips of flagella and have biological activity. In Caenorhabditis elegans, EVs are shed and released by ciliated sensory neurons in a manner that depends on intraflagellar transport. These EVs in Caenorhabditis elegans play a role in modulating communication between animals, and their biological activity depends on the cargo they carry. Some ciliary pathologies, known as ciliopathies, are associated with abnormal shedding of EVs or abnormal interactions between cilia and EVs. Until recently, both cilia and EVs were disregarded as useless or cellular waste. However, as research interest in these organelles grows, a new field of cell biology is emerging. In this article, we propose that the cilium is a specialized organelle for the production and reception of EVs. We will also discuss possible mechanisms by which EVs exert their biological effects and explain how studying EV production and function in model organisms can provide insights into ciliopathies in humans.

title: The NOD-like receptor NLRP12 attenuates colon inflammation and tumorigenesis.
text: The physiological function of NLRP12, a member of the Nod-like receptor (NLR) family located within cells, remains unknown. However, it has been suggested that NLRP12 may play a role in reducing the production of inflammatory cytokines. To investigate this further, we conducted a study using mice lacking the Nlrp12 gene. Our findings demonstrate that these mice are highly susceptible to colon inflammation and the development of colorectal tumors. This susceptibility is linked to an increase in the production of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and factors that promote tumor growth. We also discovered that the absence of Nlrp12 leads to the failure of macrophages to suppress the activation of NF-κB and ERK, which are key signaling pathways involved in inflammation. These results highlight the crucial role of NLRP12 in maintaining the balance of the intestinal environment and protecting against the development of colorectal tumors.

title: Ionic mechanism of ouabain-induced concurrent apoptosis and necrosis in individual cultured cortical neurons
text: Energy deficiency and dysfunction of the Na+, K+-ATPase are common consequences of various pathological insults. However, the exact nature and mechanism of cell injury caused by impaired Na+, K+-ATPase are not well understood. To investigate this, we conducted experiments using cultured cortical neurons. Our hypothesis was that blocking the Na+, K+-ATPase would lead to apoptosis by depleting cellular K+ and, at the same time, induce necrotic injury in the same cells by increasing intracellular Ca2+ and Na+. We found that the Na+, K+-ATPase inhibitor ouabain caused neuronal death in a concentration-dependent manner. Ouabain initially caused transient swelling of the neuronal cells, followed by shrinkage, along with an increase in intracellular Ca2+ and Na+, and a decrease in K+. Additionally, we observed the release of cytochrome c, activation of caspase-3, and DNA laddering. Electron microscopy revealed features of both apoptosis and necrosis in individual cells. When we used the caspase inhibitor Z-Val-Ala-Asp(OMe)-fluoromethyl ketone (Z-VAD-FMK), it blocked more than 50% of ouabain-induced neuronal death. Blocking potassium channels or using a high K+ medium prevented cytochrome c release, caspase activation, and DNA damage, while blocking calcium channels did not have the same effect. Blocking potassium, calcium, or sodium channels individually, or using a high K+ medium, reduced ouabain-induced cell death. When we combined the inhibition of potassium channels with calcium or sodium channels, we observed additional protection. Furthermore, coapplication of Z-VAD-FMK and nifedipine resulted in almost complete neuroprotection. These findings suggest that neuronal death caused by Na+, K+-pump failure involves both apoptotic and necrotic components, mediated by depletion of intracellular K+ and accumulation of Ca2+ and Na+, respectively. The hybrid death induced by ouabain may represent a unique form of cell death associated with brain injury due to inadequate energy supply and disrupted ion homeostasis.

title: Potential consequences of replacing a retail alcohol monopoly with a private licence system: results from Sweden.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the potential impact of replacing the current Swedish alcohol retail system with a private licensing system on alcohol consumption and related harm. Two scenarios were analyzed: (1) replacing the current alcohol retail monopoly with privately licensed stores specializing in alcohol sales, and (2) making all alcohol available in grocery stores. A multiplicative model was used to project the effects of changes in key factors such as hours of sale, retail prices, promotion and advertising, and outlet density. The projected increase in consumption was then estimated to determine its effect on various indicators of harm. Data for the model parameters were obtained from existing research literature. 

The measurements of alcohol-related harm included alcohol-related mortality, accident mortality, suicide, homicide, assaults, drunk driving, and sickness absence. The findings showed that scenario 1 would result in a 17% increase in consumption (1.4 liters per capita), leading to an additional 770 deaths, 8,500 assaults, 2,700 drunk driving offenses, and 4.5 million sick days per year. In scenario 2, there would be a 37.4% increase in consumption (3.1 liters per capita), resulting in an additional 2,000 deaths, 20,000 assaults, 6,600 drunk driving offenses, and 11.1 million sick days annually. 

Based on the research literature, the projections indicate that privatizing the Swedish alcohol retail market would significantly increase alcohol consumption and related harm.

title: A comprehensive genomic binding map of gene and chromatin regulatory proteins in Saccharomyces.
text:
The transcription process in Saccharomyces involves numerous proteins that regulate and carry out transcription. However, there has been a lack of comprehensive investigation into their relationships. In this study, we examined the binding locations of 200 transcription-related proteins throughout the genome, both under normal conditions and during acute heat-shock. Our findings shed light on several important aspects: 

1. We discovered a greater diversity and specialization of regulation within the SAGA transcription pathway compared to the TFIID pathway. 
2. We identified new regulators that are particularly enriched at tRNA genes. 
3. We uncovered a global network of over 20,000 unique combinations of regulators, revealing extensive interconnections among genes with low expression levels. 
4. We observed that regulators of the SAGA pathway tend to be located distally from the core promoter, while regulators of the TFIID pathway are located proximally. 
5. We observed distinct mobilization patterns of regulators linked to the SAGA pathway compared to those linked to the TFIID pathway during acute heat shock.

title: Tie2/Angiopoietin-1 Signaling Regulates Hematopoietic Stem Cell Quiescence in the Bone Marrow Niche
text: The state of being inactive is believed to be a necessary characteristic for the preservation of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). The interaction between HSCs and their specific environments, known as stem cell niches, is crucial for adult hematopoiesis in the bone marrow (BM). In this study, we show that HSCs expressing the receptor tyrosine kinase Tie2 are both inactive and resistant to cell death, and make up a subset of HSCs called the side-population (SP), which attach to osteoblasts (OBs) in the BM niche. The interaction between Tie2 and its ligand Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) causes HSCs to form cobblestone-like structures in vitro and maintains their long-term repopulating activity in vivo. Additionally, Ang-1 enhances the ability of HSCs to become inactive and promotes their adhesion to bone, thereby protecting the HSC compartment from myelosuppressive stress. These findings suggest that the Tie2/Ang-1 signaling pathway plays a crucial role in maintaining HSCs in an inactive state within the BM niche.

title: Thirty-One Novel Biomarkers as Predictors for Clinically Incident Diabetes
text:
BACKGROUND: The prevalence of diabetes is increasing in developed countries, making its prevention a priority in public health. However, there is still limited understanding of the predictors of diabetes risk. In this study, we aimed to determine if 31 new biomarkers could help predict the risk of developing diabetes.

METHODS AND FINDINGS: We initially evaluated these biomarkers in the FINRISK97 cohort, which included 7,827 participants, 417 of whom developed diabetes during the follow-up period. We then replicated our findings in the Health 2000 cohort, which included 4,977 participants, 179 of whom developed diabetes. Using Cox proportional hazards models, we calculated the relative risk of diabetes for each biomarker after adjusting for traditional risk factors. We also assessed the ability of individual biomarkers to discriminate diabetes risk using receiver operating characteristic curves, C-statistics, integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and net reclassification improvement (NRI). Finally, we developed a biomarker score in the FINRISK97 cohort and validated it in the Health 2000 cohort. The biomarker score, consisting of adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, C-reactive protein, and ferritin, nearly doubled the relative risk of diabetes in the validation cohort. It also improved the discrimination and reclassification of diabetes risk. Gender-specific analyses revealed that the optimal biomarker score differed between men and women. Among men, the best results were obtained with a score including adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, ferritin, and interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Among women, the best score included adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, C-reactive protein, and insulin.

CONCLUSIONS: We identified novel biomarkers that were associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes, independent of traditional risk factors. This provides new insights into the development of diabetes and may aid in targeting prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Exploiting lymphatic transport and complement activation in nanoparticle vaccines
text:
In the field of vaccine development, researchers have been exploring ways to improve the delivery of antigens to dendritic cells and enhance their activation. In this study, we investigate the potential use of nanoparticles as a vaccine platform by specifically targeting dendritic cells residing in the lymph nodes through interstitial flow and activating these cells through complement activation.

When ultra-small nanoparticles (25 nm) were injected into the skin, they were efficiently transported through interstitial flow into lymphatic capillaries and the corresponding draining lymph nodes. These nanoparticles successfully targeted half of the dendritic cells residing in the lymph nodes. On the other hand, larger nanoparticles (100 nm) were only 10% as efficient in this process.

The surface chemistry of these nanoparticles triggered the complement cascade, leading to the generation of a danger signal in the immediate environment and effectively activating dendritic cells. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we used nanoparticles conjugated to a model antigen called ovalbumin. The results showed that the size of the nanoparticles and their ability to activate complement were crucial factors in generating both humoral and cellular immunity in mice.

In summary, our findings suggest that nanoparticles can serve as a promising vaccine platform by targeting lymph node-residing dendritic cells and activating them through complement activation. This approach holds potential for the development of more effective vaccines.

title: The sheddase ADAM10 is a potent modulator of prion disease
text: The prion protein (PrP(C)) is abundantly expressed in the nervous system and plays a crucial role in prion diseases, where it undergoes misfolding to form pathogenic PrP(Sc). Additionally, it has been proposed that PrP(C) acts as a receptor that mediates neurotoxicity in common neurodegenerative proteinopathies like Alzheimer's disease. The shedding of PrP(C) at the plasma membrane by the metalloprotease ADAM10 has been observed, but its impact on prion disease remains unclear. By using mice with a conditional knockout of ADAM10 in forebrain neurons, we demonstrate that the depletion of ADAM10 leads to an increase in posttranslational levels of PrP(C). When these mice are infected with prions, clinical, biochemical, and morphological data indicate that the absence of ADAM10 significantly shortens the incubation period and enhances the formation of PrP(Sc). However, spatiotemporal analysis suggests that the lack of shedding impairs the spread of prion pathology. Our findings support a dual role for ADAM10-mediated shedding and emphasize the importance of proteolytic processing in prion disease.

title: High-affinity zinc inhibition of NMDA NR1-NR2A receptors
text: We conducted experiments to investigate the effects of extracellular Zn2+ on NMDA receptors. We focused on the voltage-independent and voltage-dependent inhibitions, and their specificity to different subunits of the receptor. We used recombinant NMDA receptors expressed in HEK 293 cells and Xenopus oocytes to compare NR1a-NR2A and NR1a-NR2B receptors. We found that the voltage-dependent inhibition was similar in both receptor types, but the voltage-independent inhibition occurred at much lower Zn2+ concentrations in NR1a-NR2A receptors (nanomolar range) compared to NR1a-NR2B receptors (micromolar range). The high affinity of the effect observed with NR1a-NR2A receptors was mainly due to the slow dissociation of Zn2+ from its binding site. We also investigated the contributions of different subunits (NR1 and NR2) to the voltage-independent Zn2+ inhibition by analyzing various combinations (NR1a or NR1b with NR2A, NR2B, or NR2C). Our results showed that both NR1 and NR2 subunits contribute to the voltage-independent Zn2+ inhibition. Additionally, we observed that the addition of low concentrations of heavy metal chelators significantly enhanced the responses of NR1a-NR2A receptors, but not NR1a-NR2B receptors, in zero nominal Zn2+ solutions. This suggests that trace amounts of a heavy metal (likely Zn2+) contaminate standard solutions and continuously inhibit NR1a-NR2A receptors. The chelation of the contaminant metal could also explain the rapid potentiation of NR2A subunit-specific responses by reducing compounds like DTT or glutathione.

title: PrimPol, an Archaic Primase/Polymerase Operating in Human Cells
text:
We have discovered a second primase, called PrimPol, in human cells. Unlike regular primases that only use ribonucleotides, PrimPol has the unique ability to initiate DNA chains with deoxynucleotides. Additionally, PrimPol is a specialized DNA polymerase that can bypass common oxidative lesions in DNA, such as abasic sites and 8-oxoguanine.

Through subcellular fractionation and immunodetection studies, we have determined that PrimPol is present in both the nuclear and mitochondrial DNA compartments. We have also found that PrimPol activity can be detected in mitochondrial lysates from both human and mouse cells. However, this activity is absent in mitochondria derived from mice with a PRIMPOL gene knockout.

Further experiments involving gene silencing or ablation of the PRIMPOL gene in human and mouse cells have shown that mitochondrial DNA replication is impaired without the presence of PrimPol. Based on our observations of synergy with replicative DNA polymerases Polγ and Polε, we propose that PrimPol facilitates the progression of replication forks by acting as a translesion DNA polymerase or as a specific DNA primase that restarts synthesis downstream of lesions. This function is crucial for both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA replication.

title: Predictors of Attrition and Academic Success of Medical Students: A 30-Year Retrospective Study
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the attrition rates and factors that contribute to academic success among medical students at the University of Split in Croatia. The researchers analyzed the academic records of 2054 students who were enrolled between 1979 and 2008. 

The results showed that 26% (533 out of 2054) of the students did not graduate. The most common reasons for attrition were personal reasons (36.4%), transferring to another medical school (35.6%), and dismissal due to unsatisfactory academic performance (21.2%). The study also found that the grade point average (GPA) and the duration of study were significantly associated with the educational background of the students' parents. 

Out of the total number of students, 1126 successfully graduated, with 395 men and 731 women. The average GPA of the graduates was 3.67±0.53, and the average duration of study was 7.6±2.44 years. Only 6.4% (42 out of 654) of the students were able to complete the 5-year curriculum on time, while 55% (240 out of 472) were able to graduate on time after the curriculum was extended to 6 years. 

The study also identified several variables that predicted whether a student would graduate or not, including high school grades, entrance exam scores, and the year of enrollment. High school grades and entrance exam scores were significant predictors of graduation grades, while entrance exam scores also predicted the length of study. 

In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of preadmission academic qualifications and the year of enrollment in predicting academic success in medical school. The findings suggest that more attention should be given to addressing the high attrition rates among medical students.

title: Mechanical regulation of cell function with geometrically modulated elastomeric substrates
text: We have established a collection of micromolded elastomeric micropost arrays in order to manipulate the rigidity of the substrate without affecting adhesive properties or other surface characteristics of the material. Our experiments have shown that the rigidity of these microposts affects various aspects of cell behavior, including cell shape, focal adhesions, cytoskeletal contractility, and the differentiation of stem cells. Additionally, we found that alterations in cytoskeletal contractility at an early stage can predict the fate of individual stem cells at a later time.

title: THE EMBO JOURNAL
text: The extracellular portion of glutamate-gated ion channels, known as ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), consists of two clamshell-shaped segments that sense the surrounding environment. The N-terminal domain (NTD), located distally, has the potential to undergo allosteric changes in NMDA-type iGluRs, but this has not been observed in the corresponding domain of AMPA receptors (AMPARs). In this study, we present new structural data that reveal the dynamic properties of the GluA2 and GluA3 AMPAR NTDs. GluA3 exhibits a dimer interface that is partially open, allowing for unrestricted movement of the lower clamshell lobes, similar to metabotropic GluRs (mGluRs). This flexible interface enables rotations between the receptor subunits, which can affect downstream receptor segments. Analysis shows that the motion of AMPAR NTDs is primarily driven by two mechanisms: clamshell motions within each subunit and counter-rotations between subunits, with the ability to transition between AMPAR and mGluR conformations. Additionally, we observe electron density in the interlobe cleft of GluA2, suggesting the presence of a potential ligand that may induce lobe movements. These findings support the notion that AMPAR NTDs play a dynamic role, expanding the allosteric landscape of the receptor and offering a new target for ligand development.

title: A complex secretory program orchestrated by the inflammasome controls paracrine senescence
text: The suppression of tumors relies on oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), which triggers a complex pro-inflammatory response known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). The SASP not only reinforces senescence and activates immune surveillance, but also paradoxically possesses pro-tumorigenic properties. In this study, we provide evidence that the SASP can induce paracrine senescence in normal cells both in laboratory cultures and in living models of OIS in humans and mice. By utilizing quantitative proteomics and small-molecule screens, we have identified several components of the SASP that mediate paracrine senescence, including TGF-β family ligands, VEGF, CCL2, and CCL20. Among these components, TGF-β ligands play a significant role by regulating the expression of p15(INK4b) and p21(CIP1). The expression of the SASP is controlled by inflammasome-mediated IL-1 signaling. Inflammasome and IL-1 signaling are activated in senescent cells, and the expression of IL-1α can replicate SASP activation, leading to senescence. Our findings demonstrate that the SASP can induce paracrine senescence, thereby influencing tumor suppression and senescence in living organisms.

title: Prospective Study of One Million Deaths in India: Rationale, Design, and Validation Results
text: More than 75% of the estimated 9.5 million deaths that occur in India each year happen at home, and most of these deaths do not have a certified cause. It is crucial for India and other developing countries to accurately determine the causes of death. They also need more reliable evidence about the impact of physical factors (like blood pressure and obesity), behavioral factors (such as smoking, alcohol consumption, risky behavior related to HIV-1, and immunization history), and biological factors (such as blood lipids and gene variations) on the development of diseases in individuals or disease rates in populations. This report discusses the reasons, design, and implementation of the largest prospective study in the world on the causes and factors associated with mortality. The study will monitor nearly 14 million people from 2.4 million representative households in India to determine their vital status and, if deceased, the causes of death using a well-validated verbal autopsy instrument. This study aims to accurately identify the underlying causes of deaths in both children and adults, as well as important risk factors (behavioral, physical, environmental, and eventually genetic). It provides a model that can be replicated globally to estimate cause-specific mortality using verbal autopsy, and it strengthens India's main system for monitoring mortality. Despite the expected misclassification, the new data on causes of death will be significantly more reliable than previous information. [PLoS Medicine, February 2006.]

title: Genome-wide identification of genes directly regulated by the pleiotropic transcription factor Spx in Bacillus subtilis
text: The role of the transcriptional regulator Spx in maintaining redox homeostasis in Bacillus subtilis cells exposed to disulfide stress is crucial. Previous studies have shown that defects in Spx lead to differential expression of many genes, but it was difficult to distinguish between direct and indirect regulatory effects. In this study, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation of Spx to identify 283 specific chromosomal sites that could potentially be bound by the Spx-RNA polymerase (Spx-RNAP) complex. Three-quarters of these sites were found near Sigma(A)-dependent promoters. When treated with diamide, the fraction of the Spx-RNAP complex increased, along with the number and occupancy of DNA sites. By correlating Spx-RNAP-binding sites with gene differential expression in wild-type and Δspx strains exposed to diamide or not, we found that 144 transcription units, comprising 275 genes, were potentially under direct Spx regulation. Spx-controlled promoters had an extended -35 box, and the nucleotide composition at the -43/-44 positions strongly correlated with observed activation. In vitro transcription experiments confirmed that oxidized Spx activated seven newly identified promoters, one of which was also activated by reduced Spx. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive characterization of the Spx regulatory network, revealing its involvement in the basal expression of certain genes and its intricate interplay with other stress responses.

title: Expression of interleukin-18 in human atherosclerotic plaques and relation to plaque instability.
text: In this study, we investigated the presence and function of interleukin (IL)-18 in atherosclerosis. IL-18 is a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that may contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. We examined human carotid atherosclerotic plaques obtained through endarterectomy to determine the expression of IL-18 using various techniques including reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (PCR), Western blot, and immunohistochemistry. We found that IL-18 was highly expressed in the atherosclerotic plaques compared to normal arteries, and it was mainly localized in plaque macrophages. The IL-18 receptor was also upregulated in plaque macrophages and endothelial cells, indicating potential biological effects. To further understand the role of IL-18 in atherosclerosis, we analyzed the relationship between IL-18 mRNA expression and signs of plaque instability. Interestingly, we observed significantly higher levels of IL-18 mRNA in symptomatic (unstable) plaques compared to asymptomatic (stable) plaques. These findings suggest that IL-18 may play a crucial role in destabilizing atherosclerotic plaques, leading to acute ischemic syndromes.

title: US-SOMO HPLC-SAXS module: dealing with capillary fouling and extraction of pure component patterns from poorly resolved SEC-SAXS data
text: The combination of size-exclusion chromatography and SAXS (small-angle X-ray scattering), typically done with a flow-through capillary, has the potential to directly collect data from monodisperse samples. However, issues with capillary fouling and peaks that are not well-resolved can hinder its effectiveness. The HPLC-SAXS module of the UltraScan solution modeler (US-SOMO) offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing such data. This includes a simple linear baseline correction and symmetrical Gaussian decomposition tools, as described in a study by Brookes, Pérez, Cardinali, Profumo, Vachette, and Rocco (2013). Recent improvements have been made to both routines, and these enhancements include the use of advanced statistical tools to evaluate the results. The new integral baseline-correction procedure is based on the assumption that the impact of capillary fouling on scattering increases consistently with the intensity of the material within the X-ray beam. Additionally, non-symmetrical modified Gaussian functions can now accurately decompose overlapping peaks, which are often distorted due to the interaction of the sample with the column matrix. To illustrate the capabilities of this approach, the analysis of a polydisperse solution of aldolase is presented. Despite the complexity of the peaks, individual SAXS profiles of tetramers, octamers, and dodecamers can be extracted and reliably modeled.

title: Determination of Malaria Epidemiological Status in Iran’s Malarious Areas as Baseline Information for Implementation of Malaria Elimination Program in Iran
text:
BACKGROUND
In order to facilitate the elimination of malaria in Iran, the Ministry of Health decided to conduct a research study in 2007 to assess the current status of the disease and gather necessary information for the elimination program. This study serves as the foundation for the national malaria elimination program, which was initiated in 2010.

METHODS
This descriptive study analyzed data at the district level, using various variables. The focus was on the three southeastern provinces where malaria is locally transmitted. The study utilized the national malaria surveillance system to identify and analyze malaria cases.

RESULTS
The province of Sistan & Baluchestan has a higher prevalence of vivax malaria, with the number of vivax cases being approximately equal to the total number of malaria positive cases. Notably, the district of Nikshahr has the highest number of local vivax cases in this province, while the district of Sarbaz reports the highest number of falciparum cases. In Hormozgan Province, except for Bandar Jask and one case in Minab, no autochthonous falciparum cases were detected in any other district. Similarly, in Kerman Province, only Kahnoj and Ghale Ganj reported one case each in 2007.

CONCLUSION
The number of locally transmitted malaria cases in Iran has been increasing in recent years, prior to the implementation of the malaria elimination plan. This may be attributed to the return of Afghan refugees to their home country, resulting in a decrease in imported malaria cases and a clearer demonstration of local cases.

title: Local neuroinflammation and the progression of Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Immunohistochemical studies conducted after death have revealed that Alzheimer's disease is associated with chronic inflammation, which is primarily limited to specific areas of the brain affected by the disease. This inflammation involves various components, including activated microglia (brain macrophages), proteins from the classical complement cascade, pentraxins, cytokines, and chemokines. Interestingly, this inflammation does not involve the adaptive immune system or peripheral organs, but rather stems from the innate immune system, which is evolutionarily older and present in most tissues of the body. Chronic inflammation can be detrimental to the host tissue, and the brain is particularly susceptible due to the non-renewable nature of neurons.

Many of the inflammatory mediators implicated in Alzheimer's disease are produced locally and are selectively elevated in the affected regions of the brain. Similar innate immune reactions have been observed in other degenerative conditions such as atherosclerosis and heart infarction. Epidemiological and limited clinical evidence suggests that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may delay the onset and slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease. However, these drugs primarily target the peripheral aspects of the inflammatory response. It is possible that more promising outcomes could be achieved by developing drugs that specifically inhibit the activation of microglia or the complement system in the brain. Additionally, combining drugs that target different inflammatory targets may prove to be more effective than using single agents alone.

title: BLAST+: architecture and applications
text:
CONTEXT Sequence similarity searching is a crucial task in bioinformatics. Although the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) is more efficient than exact methods due to its use of heuristics, the current BLAST software's speed is not optimal for lengthy queries or database sequences. Additionally, there are some drawbacks in the user interface of the existing command-line applications.

RESULTS We present the enhancements and features of the revamped BLAST software, along with the introduction of new command-line applications. To expedite processing, lengthy query sequences are divided into smaller chunks, resulting in significantly reduced run times in certain cases. For extensive database sequences, it is now possible to retrieve only the relevant sections of the sequence, thereby decreasing CPU time and memory usage when searching short queries against contig or chromosome databases. The program can now obtain masking information for database sequences from the BLAST databases. Furthermore, a novel modular software library enables access to subject sequence data from diverse data sources. We introduce various new features, such as strategy files that enable users to save and reuse their preferred options. These strategy files can be uploaded to and downloaded from the NCBI BLAST website.

CONCLUSION The new BLAST command-line applications exhibit substantial speed enhancements for lengthy queries and chromosome-length database sequences compared to the current BLAST tools. We have also enhanced the user interface of the command-line applications.

title: Intrauterine environments and breast cancer risk: meta-analysis and systematic review
text:
INTRODUCTION
Several factors during the perinatal period, such as birth weight, birth order, maternal age, gestational age, twin status, and parental smoking, have been suggested to influence the risk of breast cancer in daughters by altering the hormonal environment of the developing mammary glands. However, previous epidemiological studies have produced conflicting results despite the biological plausibility. In this study, we conducted meta-analyses to investigate the associations between perinatal factors and subsequent breast cancer risk.

METHODS
We conducted a comprehensive review of breast cancer studies published between January 1966 and February 2007 that included data on birth weight, birth order, maternal age, gestational age, twin status, and maternal or paternal smoking. Random effect models were used to perform meta-analyses and summarize the results.

RESULTS
Our analysis revealed that higher birth weights were associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. Specifically, studies with five categories of birth weight showed odds ratios (ORs) of 1.24 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04 to 1.48) for birth weights of 4,000 g or more, and 1.15 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.26) for birth weights between 3,500 g and 3,999 g, compared to birth weights of 2,500 to 2,599 g. These findings did not support a J-shaped relationship between birth weight and risk. Additionally, studies with three birth weight categories (OR 1.15 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.31] for birth weights > or =4,000 g compared to <3,000 g) and two birth weight categories (OR 1.09 [95% CI 1.02 to 1.18] for birth weights > or =3,000 g compared to <3,000 g) also provided evidence of an association with birth weight. The results regarding older maternal age and twin status were inconsistent across studies and publication years, but suggested a slight increase in risk. However, birth order, prematurity, and maternal smoking were not found to be related to breast cancer risk.

CONCLUSION
Our findings support the hypothesis that in utero exposures reflecting higher levels of endogenous hormones may influence the risk of developing breast cancer in adulthood.

title: Epidemiologic studies on Dengue in Santiago de Cuba, 1997.
text:
In January 1997, there was a small outbreak of dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome (DHF/DSS) caused by dengue virus type 2 (DEN-2) in Santiago de Cuba, Cuba. A total of 205 cases of DHF/DSS were reported, all in individuals over the age of 15. Almost all of them had evidence of a previous dengue infection, with the only known opportunity being the islandwide epidemic of dengue virus type 1 (DEN-1) that occurred between 1977 and 1979. Comprehensive clinical and laboratory surveillance of the disease was successfully carried out. 

Between December 1997 and January 1998, a random sample of serum was collected from 1,151 individuals in 40 residential clusters in Santiago, stratified by age. These samples were tested for neutralizing antibodies against DEN-1 and DEN-2. The prevalence of DEN-2 antibodies in children aged 15 and below, who were born after the 1981 DEN-2 epidemic, was used as an indicator of the 1997 DEN-2 infection rate. This rate was slightly adjusted to account for observed cases, resulting in an estimated infection rate of 4.3%. 

The rates of dengue fever and DHF/DSS were calculated based on the estimated total number of primary and secondary DEN-2 infections. Only 3% of the 13,116 primary infections showed symptoms. The DHF/DSS attack rate for adults of all ages was calculated to be 420 per 10,000 secondary DEN-2 infections.

title: Prognostic and Predictive Value of KRAS Mutations in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
text: The clinical implications of KRAS mutations in advanced non-small cell lung cancer are still not clear. We conducted a retrospective study to assess the prognostic and predictive value of KRAS mutations in patients with advanced NSCLC. Out of 484 patients who had results for both KRAS and EGFR mutations, 39 (8%) had KRAS mutations, 182 (38%) had EGFR mutations, and two had both mutations. The median overall survival for patients with KRAS mutations, EGFR mutations, or wild types for both genes were 7.7, 38.0, and 15.0 months, respectively (P<0.001). In the multivariate analysis, the KRAS mutation was identified as an independent poor prognostic factor (hazard ratio = 2.6, 95% CI: 1.8-3.7). The response rates and progression-free survival (PFS) for the pemetrexed-based regimen were 14% and 2.1 months in the KRAS mutation group, which were lower than those (28% and 3.9 months) in the KRAS wild type group. The KRAS mutation was associated with worse treatment outcomes after gemcitabine-based chemotherapy, but there was no difference in outcomes with taxane-based regimens. While patients with KRAS wild type had better clinical outcomes with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) compared to those with KRAS mutations, there was no statistical difference in response rates and PFS when considering EGFR mutation status. Two patients with both KRAS and EGFR mutations showed a partial response to EGFR TKIs. Although the G12D mutation was more common in never smokers, there was no difference in clinical outcomes based on KRAS genotypes. These findings suggest that KRAS mutations have an independent prognostic value but a limited predictive role for EGFR TKIs or cytotoxic chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC.

title: A Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator And A Direct Test For Heteroskedasticity
text: In this paper, we introduce a parameter covariance matrix estimator that remains reliable even when the disturbances of a linear regression model exhibit heteroskedasticity. Unlike other estimators, this one does not rely on a specific model of the heteroskedasticity structure. By comparing the elements of this new estimator to those of the conventional covariance estimator, we can directly test for heteroskedasticity. If there is no heteroskedasticity, the two estimators will be approximately equal, but they will diverge in other cases. This test can be interpreted using a least squares approach, making it particularly appealing.

title: Two Subsets of Naive T Helper Cells with Distinct T Cell Receptor Excision Circle Content in Human Adult Peripheral Blood
text: As individuals age, the function of the thymus decreases, resulting in an inability to produce enough peripheral T helper (Th) cells to meet the body's needs. As a result, the maintenance of naive Th cells must rely partially on peripheral sources. This peripheral expansion of recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) during aging leads to a decrease or dilution of T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) in a subset of naive T cells. We have discovered two subsets of naive Th cells in the peripheral blood of adult humans that differ significantly in their TREC content, indicating different histories of peripheral proliferation. TRECs are abundant in peripheral naive CD45RA+ Th cells that also express CD31, while they are barely detectable in peripheral naive CD45RA+ Th cells that lack CD31 expression. Additionally, we have observed that CD31−CD45RA+ Th cells make up a larger proportion of the naive peripheral Th cell population as individuals age, but they still exhibit the characteristics of naive Th cells. Since CD31 is lost when T cell receptors (TCRs) are engaged in vitro, we propose that TCR activation is necessary for the homeostatic expansion of human naive RTEs in the periphery. In this study, we describe the identification of peripherally expanded naive Th cells in the peripheral blood of adult humans, characterized by the absence of CD31 expression and a significantly reduced TREC content.

title: A Role for the Vacuolating Cytotoxin, VacA, in Colonization and Helicobacter pylori–Induced Metaplasia in the Stomach
text: The presence of Helicobacter pylori strains that produce more active forms of VacA (s1/i1) is closely linked to gastric adenocarcinoma. We conducted a study to investigate the impact of different polymorphic forms of VacA on inflammation and metaplasia in mice, and we believe we are the first to do so. We found that bacteria producing the less active form of VacA (s2/i2) were able to colonize mice more effectively than mutants lacking VacA or strains producing more active forms of it. This provides the initial evidence of a positive role for the minimally active s2/i2 toxin. Strains that produced more active forms of the toxin induced more severe and extensive metaplasia and inflammation in the mouse stomach compared to strains producing the weakly active s2/i2 toxin. We also investigated this association in humans, while controlling for cagPAI status. In human gastric biopsy samples, we observed a strong association between the vacA i1 allele and precancerous intestinal metaplasia. Subjects infected with i2-type strains showed almost no presence of intestinal metaplasia, even in cases where there was a vacA s1, cagA(+) background.

title: Systematic review of role of bisphosphonates on skeletal morbidity in metastatic cancer.
text:
The objective of this review is to examine the evidence regarding the effectiveness of bisphosphonates in reducing skeletal complications in cancer patients with bone metastases. The data for this review was obtained from electronic databases, reference lists, consultations with experts, and pharmaceutical companies. Foreign language papers were also included. The selection criteria for the studies included in this review were randomized controlled trials involving patients with malignant disease and bone metastases who were treated with oral or intravenous bisphosphonates compared to another bisphosphonate, placebo, or standard care. The primary outcome measured in all trials was skeletal morbidity.

A total of 95 articles were identified, and after applying the inclusion criteria, 30 studies were included in this review. In studies that lasted for at least 6 months, bisphosphonates were found to significantly reduce the odds ratio for fractures (vertebral: 0.69, 95% confidence interval 0.57 to 0.84, P < 0.0001; non-vertebral: 0.65, 0.54 to 0.79, P < 0.0001; combined: 0.65, 0.55 to 0.78, P < 0.0001), radiotherapy (0.67, 0.57 to 0.79, P < 0.0001), and hypercalcemia (0.54, 0.36 to 0.81, P = 0.003). However, there was no significant reduction in orthopedic surgery (0.70, 0.46 to 1.05, P = 0.086) or spinal cord compression (0.71, 0.47 to 1.08, P = 0.113). The reduction in orthopedic surgery was only significant in studies that lasted over a year (0.59, 0.39 to 0.88, P = 0.009). Bisphosphonate use also increased the time to the first skeletal-related event but did not improve overall survival. Subanalyses indicated that intravenous aminobisphosphonates were the most effective.

In conclusion, bisphosphonates significantly reduce skeletal morbidity in individuals with metastatic bone disease, except for spinal cord compression. Treatment should be initiated upon diagnosis of bone metastases and continued until it is no longer clinically relevant.

title: Rodent Models of Depression: Neurotrophic and Neuroinflammatory Biomarkers
text: Rodent models play a crucial role in studying the causes and progression of depression. The regulation of normal brain plasticity is controlled by interconnected systems of neurotrophic factors and cytokines. When these systems are impaired, it can lead to the development of mental illnesses and other cerebral pathologies. This review focuses on various experimental rodent models of depression, which are induced by different stress factors during early life or adulthood. The emphasis is on the changes in neurotrophic factors and neuroinflammatory markers in the brain, as these parameters are closely linked to depressive symptoms and disruptions in neuronal plasticity. Furthermore, these changes are influenced by gender and genotype. The expression of neurotrophins and cytokines in the rodent brain in response to stress is specific to certain regions. Contradictory findings among different research groups may be due to variations in stress paradigms or experimental conditions. Although these stress-induced depression-like conditions are simplified versions of clinical depression, they provide valuable insights into the role of neurotrophic factors and cytokines in the disease's development, which cannot be fully understood in a clinical setting. Targeting these major regulatory systems could be beneficial for therapeutic interventions and the development of drugs to treat depression.

title: The docking domain of histone H2A is required for H1 binding and RSC-mediated nucleosome remodeling
text: The C-terminal regions of histone variants in the H2A family exhibit significant differences. In this study, we investigated the impact of these differences, specifically focusing on the docking domain of the H2A COOH-terminus, on the structural and functional properties of the nucleosome. Through a combination of biochemical methods, Atomic Force Microscopy, and Electron Cryo-Microscopy, we discovered that the H2A-docking domain plays a crucial role in the structure of the nucleosome. When this domain is deleted or replaced with the incomplete docking domain from the H2A.Bbd variant, notable structural changes occur in the nucleosome.
