These changes include increased accessibility to nucleases, unwrapping of approximately 10 base pairs of DNA from each end of the nucleosome, and alterations in the entry/exit angle of DNA ends. These structural modifications are associated with a decreased ability of the chromatin remodeler RSC to remodel and mobilize the nucleosomes. Additionally, nucleosomes containing the incomplete docking domain of H2A.Bbd are unable to bind linker histone H1. Our findings highlight the unique role of the H2A-docking domain in coordinating the structural and functional aspects of nucleosome properties. Furthermore, our data suggest that the incorporation of a 'defective' docking domain may serve as a primary structural function of H2A.Bbd in chromatin.

title: Regulation of poly(A) site choice of several yeast mRNAs
text: Multiple transcripts with different 3'-ends are produced by several yeast genes. Among these genes, CBP1, AEP2/ATP13, RNA14, and SIR1 are known to produce truncated transcripts that end within the coding sequence of longer transcripts. It has been observed that the level of the truncated CBP1 transcript increases during the transition to respiratory growth, while the level of the full-length transcript decreases. To investigate if this phenomenon is specific to CBP1, northern analysis was conducted to determine if the levels of other truncated transcripts are similarly regulated by the carbon source. The levels of the shortest transcripts of AEP2/ATP13 and RNA14 increased during respiration, while the shortest SIR1 transcript remained constant. However, two longer SIR1 transcripts were reciprocally regulated by the carbon source. Sequencing partial cDNA clones allowed mapping of the 3'-ends of each transcript, revealing multiple 3'-ends for each transcript. Analysis of the sequences surrounding the 3'-ends of the induced transcripts did not identify a consensus sequence, but weak putative 3'-end formation signals were found in all transcripts. Similarly, no consensus sequence was found when comparing the sequences surrounding the 3'-ends of the longest transcripts, but weak putative 3'-end formation signals were identified. These findings suggest that carbon source may regulate alternative poly(A) site choice in yeast.

title: Circular RNA and miR-7 in cancer.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNA) have crucial roles in regulating gene expression and are frequently disrupted in cancer. The discovery of competing endogenous RNA and circular RNA (circRNA) as significant regulators of miRNA function highlights the growing complexity of non-coding RNA-mediated regulatory networks. In particular, the recently identified circRNA, ciRS-7, which acts as a specific inhibitor/sponge for miR-7, has fundamentally changed our understanding of miRNA networks. Since miR-7 controls the expression of multiple oncogenes, unraveling the regulation of miR-7 activity is likely to enhance our understanding of various cancer causes. In this review, we summarize the current knowledge regarding the ciRS-7/miR-7 axis in cancer-related pathways and propose potential models to explain the importance of coexpressing miR-7 alongside a circRNA inhibitor.

title: Angiotensin II Evokes Angiogenic Signals within Skeletal Muscle through Co-ordinated Effects on Skeletal Myocytes and Endothelial Cells
text:
The expression of angiogenic factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-2, is induced by skeletal muscle overload, resulting in the growth of new capillaries. Our study found that the increase in angiogenesis caused by overload, as well as the increase in VEGF, MMP-2, and MT1-MMP transcripts, was prevented in muscle VEGF knockout mice. This highlights the crucial role of VEGF derived from myocytes in controlling this process. However, the specific upstream mediators that contribute to the overload-induced expression of VEGF have not yet been determined.

We also discovered that muscle overload leads to an increase in the expression of angiotensinogen, a precursor of angiotensin (Ang) II. Ang II signaling was found to play a significant role in the basal production of VEGF in C2C12 cells. Additionally, VEGF released from myoblasts bound to the extracellular matrix induced the activation of endothelial cells, as indicated by elevated levels of phosphorylated p38 in these cells. Furthermore, we observed that exogenous Ang II increases the expression of VEGF and MMP-2 transcripts in C2C12 myotubes. Interestingly, these responses were also observed in skeletal muscle endothelial cells when treated with Ang II, suggesting that these cells can directly respond to the stimulus.

To assess the involvement of Ang II in overload-induced angiogenesis, we examined the effects of blocking AT1R-dependent Ang II signaling using losartan. Surprisingly, we found that losartan did not attenuate capillary growth. In fact, increased levels of VEGF protein were detected in overloaded muscle from losartan-treated rats. Similarly, cultured endothelial cells treated with losartan alone or in combination with Ang II showed elevated VEGF production. These findings conclusively demonstrate the necessity of muscle-derived VEGF in overload-induced angiogenesis and highlight the role of Ang II in the basal production of VEGF in skeletal muscle. However, while Ang II signaling is activated during overload and contributes to muscle VEGF production, inhibiting this pathway alone is not enough to stop overload-induced angiogenesis. This suggests that AT1-independent signals are responsible for maintaining VEGF production in losartan-treated muscle.

title: A specific loop in human DNA polymerase mu allows switching between creative and DNA-instructed synthesis
text: Human DNA polymerase mu (Polμ) is a member of family X and possesses terminal transferase activity. Despite an unconventional selection of template information, Polμ exhibits its highest catalytic efficiency in DNA-templated reactions. Polμ, similar to terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), contains a specific loop (loop1) that contributes to its terminal transferase activity. Deletion of loop1 in human Polμ eliminates TdT activity but enhances DNA-binding and DNA template-dependent polymerization. Interestingly, when loop1 from TdT is inserted into Polμ, replacing its original loop1, the resulting chimaera gains TdT activity, with a preference for inserting dGTP residues, but experiences a significant reduction in template-dependent polymerization activity. Thus, a specialized loop in Polμ, capable of adopting different conformations, appears to provide the enzyme with a dual capacity: (i) the ability to generate new DNA information independently of a template, with loop1 acting as a "pseudotemplate"; and (ii) template-dependent polymerization, where loop1 facilitates binding to the template strand. Recent in vivo and in vitro evidence suggests that this dual capacity may be advantageous in resolving microhomology-mediated end-joining reactions.

title: Dnmt1-Independent CG Methylation Contributes to Nucleosome Positioning in Diverse Eukaryotes
text:
In many eukaryotes, Dnmt1 is responsible for propagating symmetrical CG methylation through epigenetic mechanisms. These organisms typically have a low abundance of CG dinucleotides due to imperfect repair of methylcytosines that have undergone deamination. However, our extensive survey of various species lacking Dnmt1 has revealed a surprising finding: symmetrical CG methylation is still frequently observed and catalyzed by a different family of DNA methyltransferases called Dnmt5. 

We have discovered that numerous organisms containing Dnmt5, which diverged over a billion years ago, exhibit clustered methylation specifically in nucleosome linkers. This clustered methylation occurs at unprecedented densities and directly affects the positioning of nucleosomes, contributing to the arrangement of nucleosomes between the clusters. The dense methylation is made possible by a genomic sequence evolution that increases the abundance of CG dinucleotides, resulting in the highest CG frequencies ever recorded. 

Species with linker methylation have small nuclei that are transcriptionally active and approach the physical limits of chromatin compaction. This unique genome architecture, characterized by dense methylation influencing nucleosome positions, likely facilitates nuclear processes under extreme spatial constraints. These findings shed light on a previously unrecognized aspect of genome organization and its impact on nuclear function.

title: The Immunogenicity and Safety of the Live-attenuated SA 14-14-2 Japanese Encephalitis Vaccine Given with a Two-dose Primary Schedule in Children
text: Vaccination is a crucial method for preventing Japanese encephalitis (JE) in areas where it is prevalent. The SA 14-14-2 JE vaccine (LAJEV), which is a live attenuated vaccine, has been widely used but there is limited data on its effectiveness in Korea. To address this, we conducted a prospective cohort study to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of LAJEV. A total of ninety participants were enrolled and received LAJEV in two doses, with a twelve-month interval between them. We measured neutralizing antibody levels before and after each vaccination and closely monitored any adverse events. After the first dose, 91.1% of participants had seroprotection, with a geometric mean titer (GMT) of 40.9. Following the second dose, the seroprotection rate increased to 97%, and the GMT showed a 6.5-fold increase. Most adverse events were mild and resolved on their own, and no serious adverse events were reported within 42 days of each dose. Overall, the two-dose administration of LAJEV in the primary immunization schedule was found to be highly effective and safe.

title: Centrosome-dependent asymmetric inheritance of the midbody ring in Drosophila germline stem cell division
text:
Stem cells, such as Drosophila germline stem cells (GSCs), often divide in an asymmetric manner. This means that when they divide, they produce one stem cell and one daughter cell that starts to differentiate. The process of cytokinesis, which is the final stage of cell division, is also often asymmetric. This means that only one of the daughter cells inherits a structure called the midbody ring (MR) when the cell division is complete, even if the division appeared to be symmetrical. However, it is not well understood whether this asymmetry in cytokinesis is related to the fate of the cells or if it has any functional significance.

In this study, we investigated the asymmetry of MR segregation during GSC divisions and found that it depends on the age of the centrosome. Centrosomes are structures that help organize the cell division process. Male GSCs, which inherit the centrosome from their mother cell, do not inherit the MR. On the other hand, female GSCs, which inherit the centrosome from their daughter cell, do inherit the MR. We also discovered that the way the MR is inherited is linked to the identity of the stem cells. Our findings suggest that the MR itself does not determine the identity of stem cells, but its asymmetrical inheritance is controlled by the stemness of the cells. This inheritance pattern may also provide a platform for the asymmetric segregation of certain factors.

title: Penile Curvature Incidence in Hypospadias: Can It Be Determined?
text: The objective of this study was to determine the actual occurrence of congenital penile curvature in different types of hypospadias, in order to guide the assessment and correction of curvature during surgery. We examined 842 patients with hypospadias who underwent surgery between 2003 and 2010, and divided them into two groups. The first group underwent routine intraoperative assessment for curvature, while the second group had curvature assessed mainly in cases of severe hypospadias. We analyzed the results using Fisher's and chi-square tests. Overall, we confirmed 238 cases (28.3%) of associated curvature. Curvature was significantly more common in the first group, both for hypospadias in general (P < 0.01) and for distal (P < 0.05) and midshaft forms (P < 0.01). Penile curvature is a frequent occurrence in hypospadias, including distal types. Intraoperative assessment for associated curvature should be considered as a routine procedure during hypospadias repair.

title: Home birth and barriers to referring women with obstetric complications to hospitals: a mixed-methods study in Zahedan, southeastern Iran
text:
The delayed use of Emergency Obstetric-Care (EmOC) facilities is a contributing factor to high maternal mortality in developing countries. This study aimed to identify the barriers that prevent midwives and parturient women from seeking hospital care when complications occur during home births in Sistan and Baluchestan province, Iran. In this province, 23% of deliveries occur outside of hospitals. 

A mixed-methods approach was used for data collection and analysis. The quantitative phase involved comparing health-sector data with World Health Organization (WHO) standards for EmOC services. The qualitative phase included interviews with midwives, traditional birth attendants, and mothers. The data collected in this phase were analyzed using qualitative data analysis principles. 

The findings revealed three main factors that contribute to indecisiveness and delay in seeking EmOC services. Socio-cultural and familial reasons lead some women to choose home births and hesitate to seek professional emergency care for complications. Midwives may be reluctant to refer patients to hospitals due to concerns about being insulted by physicians, protecting their professional integrity, and an inability to persuade their patients. Additionally, the low quality and cost of EmOC services, as well as the lack of health insurance among mothers, contribute to delays in referral. 

To increase the utilization of available hospitals, it is important to train midwives and educate mothers and their decision-makers about the importance of timely referral in life-threatening situations. Hospitals should provide safe, comfortable, and culturally sensitive environments for childbirth. Proper management of financial and insurance-related issues can also help midwives and mothers make informed decisions when complications arise.

title: ATPase-Dependent Control of the Mms21 SUMO Ligase during DNA Repair
text: The modification of proteins by SUMO is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the genome. During the replication of DNA, the Mms21-branch of the SUMO pathway counteracts recombination intermediates at damaged replication forks, which helps in separating sister chromatids. The Mms21 SUMO ligase attaches to the arm region of the Smc5 protein in the Smc5/6 complex, and together they work during DNA repair through recombination. However, we still don't know how the activity of the SUMO ligase is regulated. In this study, we demonstrate that the SUMO ligase and the chromosome separation functions of Mms21 rely on its attachment to an intact and active Smc5/6 complex, indicating that the Smc5/6-Mms21 complex functions as a large SUMO ligase in living organisms. Despite the physical distance between the E3 and nucleotide-binding domains in Smc5/6, the sumoylation process dependent on Mms21 requires ATP binding to Smc5, which is a step in the ligase mechanism that assists Ubc9 function. This communication is made possible by a conserved disruption in the coiled coil domain of Smc5, suggesting potential conformational changes for activating the SUMO ligase. Supporting this, scanning force microscopy of the Smc5-Mms21 heterodimer reveals that the molecule undergoes physical remodeling in an ATP-dependent manner. Our findings demonstrate that the ATP-binding activity of the Smc5/6 complex is coordinated with its SUMO ligase through the coiled coil domain of Smc5 and the physical remodeling of the molecule, promoting sumoylation and chromosome separation during DNA repair.

title: Cadherins in brain morphogenesis and wiring.
text: Cadherins, which are molecules responsible for cell-cell adhesion and are dependent on calcium ions, play crucial roles in the development of animals. Additionally, various cadherin-related molecules have been discovered, exhibiting diverse functions beyond regulating cell adhesion. These molecules also contribute to cell proliferation and planar cell polarity. Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the roles of these molecules in the nervous system. They are not only important for the development of the nervous system but also for its functioning, ultimately impacting neural disorders. This review focuses on discussing the roles of cadherins and related molecules in the development and functioning of the vertebrate brain.

title: Autocrine WNT signaling contributes to breast cancer cell proliferation via the canonical WNT pathway and EGFR transactivation
text: Mutations in APC and Axin, proteins that target β-catenin for destruction, have been associated with various types of human cancer by deregulating the wingless and integration site growth factor (WNT) signaling pathway. Interestingly, these genetic alterations are rarely observed in breast tumors. However, there is evidence suggesting that WNT signaling may still be disrupted in breast cancer. Most breast tumors exhibit hypermethylation of the promoter region of secreted Frizzled-related protein 1 (sFRP1), a negative regulator of the WNT pathway, resulting in decreased expression. Consequently, WNT signaling is enhanced and may contribute to the proliferation of breast tumor cells. Previous studies have shown that WNT signaling not only activates the canonical WNT/β-catenin pathway but also triggers the extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) pathway in mouse mammary epithelial cells through epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) transactivation. In this study, we aimed to interfere with autocrine WNT signaling at the ligand-receptor level using the WNT modulator sFRP1 and short interfering RNA-mediated Dishevelled (DVL) knockdown. We assessed the impact on proliferation, β-catenin, EGFR, ERK1/2 activation, and PARP cleavages in human breast cancer cell lines through various assays and techniques. Our results showed that interfering with this autocrine WNT signaling loop reduced active β-catenin levels, suppressed ERK1/2 activity, inhibited proliferation, and induced apoptosis in multiple breast cancer cell lines. Phospho-DVL and stabilized β-catenin were detected in many breast tumor cell lines, indicating the presence of autocrine WNT signaling activity. We also found that the effects of WNT signaling were partly mediated by EGFR transactivation in human breast cancer cells, dependent on metalloprotease and Src. Additionally, Wnt1 rescued estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer cells from the anti-proliferative effects of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-HT), and this rescue could be blocked by an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Overall, our findings demonstrate that interfering with autocrine WNT signaling in human breast cancer cells reduces proliferation and survival, and rescues ER+ tumor cells from 4-HT through activation of the canonical WNT pathway and EGFR transactivation. These results suggest that combining interference with WNT signaling at the ligand-receptor level with other targeted therapies may enhance the effectiveness of breast cancer treatments.

title: Alternative Markers of Hyperglycemia and Risk of Diabetes
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between fructosamine, glycated albumin, and 1,5-anhydroglucitol (1,5-AG) and the risk of developing diabetes in patients with no prior history of the disease. The study used Cox proportional hazards models to analyze data from 1,299 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study. Incident diabetes cases were self-reported during annual telephone calls.

During a median follow-up period of 3.3 years, there were 119 new cases of diabetes. The fourth quartiles of fructosamine and glycated albumin were found to be significantly associated with an increased risk of diabetes (hazard ratio [HR] 3.99 [95% CI 1.93-8.28] and 5.22 [2.49-10.94], respectively), compared to the lowest quartile. Conversely, the fourth quartile of 1,5-AG was associated with a significantly lower risk of diabetes (0.27 [0.14-0.55]). These associations remained significant even after adjusting for hemoglobin A(1c) (A1C) or fasting glucose.

In conclusion, fructosamine, glycated albumin, and 1,5-AG were found to be independently associated with the development of diabetes, regardless of baseline A1C and fasting glucose levels. These alternative biomarkers may be valuable in identifying individuals at risk for diabetes.

title: ROR-γ drives androgen receptor expression and represents a therapeutic target in castration-resistant prostate cancer
text: The androgen receptor (AR) is excessively expressed and hyperactivated in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) in humans. However, the factors that contribute to AR overexpression in CRPC are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that retinoic acid receptor-related orphan receptor γ (ROR-γ) is both overexpressed and amplified in metastatic CRPC tumors. Furthermore, ROR-γ is responsible for driving AR expression in these tumors. ROR-γ recruits nuclear receptor coactivator 1 and 3 (NCOA1 and NCOA3, also known as SRC-1 and SRC-3) to an AR-ROR response element (RORE), which stimulates the transcription of the AR gene. By using ROR-γ antagonists, we were able to suppress the expression of both AR and its variant AR-V7 in prostate cancer (PCa) cell lines and tumors. Additionally, these antagonists significantly reduced AR binding throughout the genome, decreased the abundance of H3K27ac (a histone modification associated with active gene expression), and lowered the expression of genes within the AR target network. Finally, ROR-γ antagonists inhibited tumor growth in various xenograft PCa models that expressed AR, but not in models lacking AR expression. Furthermore, these antagonists effectively enhanced the sensitivity of CRPC tumors to enzalutamide (a commonly used drug for CRPC treatment) without causing any noticeable toxicity in mice. In conclusion, our findings establish ROR-γ as a crucial factor in CRPC, acting upstream of AR, and suggest that it could be a potential therapeutic target for advanced PCa.

title: affy--analysis of Affymetrix GeneChip data at the probe level.
text:
Motivation: Recently, data analysts have been focusing on the processing of Affymetrix GeneChip data. Various alternatives to the original procedure have been proposed, and some of these new methods have gained widespread usage.

Results: The affy package, an R package consisting of functions and classes, is designed for the analysis of oligonucleotide arrays produced by Affymetrix. Currently in its second release, affy offers users great flexibility in conducting analyses and enables access to and manipulation of probe intensity data. This paper presents the key classes and functions within the package and showcases their application in processing probe-level data. Additionally, we emphasize the significance of probe-level analysis when utilizing the Affymetrix GeneChip platform.

title: Inducible caspase-9 suicide gene controls adverse effects from alloreplete T cells after haploidentical stem cell transplantation.
text:
In order to determine if manipulating a single T-cell can eliminate alloreactivity without affecting antiviral and antitumor T cells, we conducted a study where 12 haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients were infused with increasing numbers of alloreplete haploidentical T cells expressing the inducible caspase 9 suicide gene (iC9-T cells). Our goal was to assess if the iC9-T cells could lead to immune reconstitution and if any graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) could be controlled by using a chemical inducer of dimerization (CID; AP1903/Rimiducid). 

We found that all patients who received more than 10(4) alloreplete iC9-T lymphocytes per kilogram experienced rapid immune response reconstitution towards 5 major pathogenic viruses and were able to control active infections. Four patients were given a single dose of AP1903. The infusion of CID resulted in the elimination of 85% to 95% of circulating CD3(+)CD19(+) T cells within 30 minutes, with no recurrence of GVHD within 90 days. In one patient, symptoms and signs of GVHD-associated cytokine release syndrome (CRS-hyperpyrexia, high levels of proinflammatory cytokines, and rash) resolved within 2 hours of AP1903 infusion. Another patient with varicella zoster virus meningitis and acute GVHD had iC9-T cells present in the cerebrospinal fluid, which were reduced by more than 90% after CID treatment. Importantly, virus-specific T cells were still present even after AP1903 administration and continued to protect against infection. 

In conclusion, alloreplete iC9-T cells can successfully reconstitute immunity after transplantation, and the administration of CID can effectively eliminate them from both peripheral blood and the central nervous system (CNS), leading to rapid resolution of GVHD and CRS. This approach shows promise for the quick and effective treatment of toxicities associated with the infusion of engineered T lymphocytes. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT01494103.

title: Clonal analysis of epiblast fate during germ layer formation in the mouse embryo.
text:
The study focused on the fate of cells in the epiblast during the prestreak and early primitive streak stages. To investigate this, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) was injected into single cells within 6.7-day mouse embryos, and the labeled descendants were identified after one day of culture, specifically at the midstreak to neural plate stages. 

The findings revealed that the ectoderm consisted of descendants of epiblast progenitors located in the anterior region of the embryonic axis, prior to the primitive streak. Embryonic mesoderm, on the other hand, originated from all areas of the epiblast except the distal tip and the adjacent anterior region. The most anterior mesoderm cells originated posteriorly and passed through the primitive streak early. Labeled cells in the posterior part of the streak during the neural plate stage were derived from extreme anterior axial and paraxial epiblast progenitors. Head process cells were derived from the epiblast near or at the anterior end of the primitive streak. 

Endoderm descendants were primarily derived from a region that extended beyond the region producing the head process. Epiblast descendants were present in the endoderm by the midstreak stage and continued to be present in later stages. Yolk sac and amnion mesoderm developed from the posterolateral and posterior epiblast. 

The resulting fate map demonstrated similarities to those of chick and urodele, indicating that despite geometric differences, the topological fate relationships are conserved among these vertebrates. It was also observed that clonal descendants were not limited to a single germ layer or extraembryonic mesoderm, suggesting that these lineages are not separated at the beginning of gastrulation. 

During the neural plate stage, the embryonic axis lengthened through the elongation of the primitive streak, incorporating the expanding lateral and initially more anterior regions of the epiblast. Additionally, the region of epiblast immediately cranial to the anterior end of the primitive streak expanded. 

The population doubling time of labeled cells was determined to be 7.5 hours, with approximately 43% having completed or being in their fourth cell cycle. No significant regional differences in the number of descendants were found. 

Furthermore, the clonal analysis revealed that growth in the epiblast was noncoherent and predominantly directed towards the primitive streak, with anisotropic characteristics in most regions. The midline did not act as a barrier to clonal spread, both in the epiblast in the anterior half of the axis and in the primitive streak. 

Overall, these findings suggest that while individual cells in the epiblast behave independently, the morphogenetic movement during germ layer formation is coordinated within the population as a whole.

title: Effects of a High-Intensity Functional Exercise Program on Dependence in Activities of Daily Living and Balance in Older Adults with Dementia
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the impact of a high-intensity functional exercise program on independence in daily activities and balance in older individuals with dementia, and to determine if the effects of exercise varied depending on the type of dementia. The study was a cluster-randomized controlled trial called the Umeå Dementia and Exercise (UMDEX) study, conducted in residential care facilities in Umeå, Sweden. The participants included individuals aged 65 and older with a dementia diagnosis, a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 10 or higher, and dependence in daily activities (N=186). 

The intervention consisted of a high-intensity functional exercise program, which included exercises to improve lower limb strength and balance. Ninety-three participants were assigned to the exercise program, while the remaining 93 were assigned to a seated control activity. Blinded assessors measured the participants' independence in daily activities using the Functional Independence Measure (FIM) and Barthel Index (BI), as well as their balance using the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) at baseline, 4 months (immediately after completing the intervention), and 7 months. 

The results from linear mixed models showed no significant difference in independence in daily activities between the exercise group and the control group at 4 months (FIM=1.3, 95% confidence interval (CI)=-1.6-4.3; BI=0.6, 95% CI=-0.2-1.4) or 7 months (FIM=0.8, 95% CI=-2.2-3.8; BI=0.6, 95% CI=-0.3-1.4). However, there was a significant difference in balance favoring the exercise group at 4 months (BBS=4.2, 95% CI=1.8-6.6). 

In further analysis, it was found that the effects of exercise varied significantly depending on the type of dementia. Positive exercise effects were observed in participants with non-Alzheimer's dementia in terms of independence in daily activities at 7 months, as well as in terms of both the BI and BBS at 4 and 7 months. 

In conclusion, a 4-month high-intensity functional exercise program appears to slow the decline in independence in daily activities and improve balance in older individuals with mild to moderate dementia living in residential care facilities. However, these effects were only observed in participants with non-Alzheimer's dementia.

title: Effect of Health Literacy on Quality of Life amongst Patients with Ischaemic Heart Disease in Australian General Practice
text:
BACKGROUND

Having a proper understanding of health information is crucial for patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD) as it helps in managing risk factors and improving their quality of life. 

OBJECTIVES

The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between health literacy and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in patients with ischaemic heart disease (IHD), while also considering sociodemographic and clinical variables as potential confounders. 

METHODS

This cross-sectional study involved patients with IHD who were recruited from a stratified sample of general practices in Queensland and South Australia between 2007 and 2009. Health literacy was assessed using a validated questionnaire and categorized as inadequate, marginal, or adequate. The physical and mental components of HRQoL were evaluated using the Medical Outcomes Study Short Form (SF12) questionnaire. Multiple linear regression was used to adjust for confounders such as sociodemographic variables, clinical history of IHD, number of CVD comorbidities, and CVD risk factors. 

RESULTS

A total of 587 patients with IHD were included in the study, with a mean age of 72.0±8.4 years. The majority of participants were male (76.8%), retired or pensioners (84.2%), and had up to a secondary educational level (51.4%). The mean health literacy score was 39.6±6.7 points, with 14.3% (95%CI 11.8-17.3) classified as having inadequate health literacy. The scores for the physical component of HRQoL were 39.6 (95%CI 37.1-42.1), 42.1 (95%CI 40.8-43.3), and 44.8 (95%CI 43.3-46.2) for inadequate, marginal, and adequate health literacy, respectively (p-value for trend = 0.001). This association remained significant even after adjusting for confounders. However, there was no significant association between health literacy and the mental component of HRQoL (p-value = 0.482). Advanced age, lower educational level, disadvantaged socioeconomic position, and a higher number of CVD comorbidities were found to have a negative impact on both health literacy and HRQoL. 

CONCLUSION

Inadequate health literacy contributes to poor physical functioning in patients with IHD. Improving health literacy may enhance HRQoL and reduce the impact of IHD in patients with this chronic CVD.

title: in
text: The enzyme Transglutaminase 2 (TGase 2) is dependent on calcium ions (Ca+2) and is responsible for catalyzing cross-linking reactions both inside and outside cells through the transamidation of specific glutamine residues. TGase 2 plays a role in the events that occur in the cell membrane and are necessary for the release of insulin from pancreatic beta cells in response to glucose stimulation. Our research demonstrates that disrupting TGase 2 impairs the secretion of insulin in response to glucose stimulation. Mice lacking TGase 2 (TGase 2-/-) exhibit glucose intolerance after receiving glucose through intraperitoneal injection. These mice also display a tendency to experience low blood sugar levels (hypoglycemia) after receiving exogenous insulin due to increased phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate 2 (IRS-2). We propose that the heightened sensitivity to insulin in the peripheral tissues partially compensates for the impaired insulin secretion in this animal model. The phenotype of TGase 2-/- mice resembles that of patients with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). During our investigation of the TGase 2 gene in Italian individuals exhibiting clinical features of MODY, we identified a missense mutation (N333S) in the active site of the enzyme. These findings collectively suggest that TGase 2 may be a potential candidate gene involved in type 2 diabetes.

title: Chromatin structure and gene expression programs of human embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells.
text: Understanding the chromatin structure and gene expression patterns of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is crucial in determining their pluripotent states. Recent research suggests that ESCs and iPSCs exhibit distinct pluripotent states with significant differences in gene expression profiles. In this study, we compare the global chromatin structure and gene expression data of a range of human ESCs and iPSCs. Our findings reveal that there is minimal disparity between ESCs and iPSCs in terms of nucleosome maps with histone H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 modifications. Additionally, gene expression profiles demonstrate that the transcriptional programs of ESCs and iPSCs exhibit few consistent differences. Although some variations in chromatin structure and gene expression were observed, these discrepancies were insufficient to distinguish between ESCs and iPSCs.

title: Myeloid Cells Expressing VEGF and Arginase-1 Following Uptake of Damaged Retinal Pigment Epithelium Suggests Potential Mechanism That Drives the Onset of Choroidal Angiogenesis in Mice
text: Although data acknowledges the accumulation of myeloid cells and complement activation in choroidal neovascularisation (CNV), there is no clear explanation for the angiogenic drive that promotes pathological angiogenesis. One possible explanation is the early conditioning and activation of the myeloid cell infiltrate. In a murine model of laser-induced CNV, we observed that the disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and Bruch's membrane led to the early recruitment of macrophages derived from monocytes and microglia, before angiogenesis and at the same time as complement activation in the lesion. The early recruited CD11b(+) cells expressed a specific gene signature of inflammatory mediators, particularly Arg-1. Macrophages from the retina and peripheral blood were activated at the site of injury, showing increased expression of VEGF, even before the RPE or the earliest stages of angiogenesis. These initial events, including the presence of VEGF (+) Arg-1(+) myeloid cells, subsided once CNV was established and RPE-VEGF expression was at its highest. Depletion of inflammatory CCR2-positive monocytes confirmed that infiltrating monocytes were responsible for the expression of Arg-1, as the Arg-1 signal was lost and CNV was suppressed after depletion. Furthermore, our in vitro data supported the idea that myeloid cells take up damaged RPE or its derivatives, leading to the generation of the VEGF (+) Arg-1(+) phenotype in vivo. Our results suggest that an early driver of angiogenesis is the myeloid-derived VEGF drive following the uptake of damaged RPE, providing an explanation for why CNV develops at any stage of macular degeneration. This finding could be further explored for therapeutic purposes.

title: Monitoring Tumorigenesis and Senescence In Vivo with a p16INK4a-Luciferase Model
text: Monitoring cancer and aging in living organisms is a challenging task in experimental research. In this study, we introduce a mouse model (p16(LUC)) that has been genetically modified to express a protein called p16(INK4a), which serves as both a tumor suppressor and an aging biomarker. By observing the luminescence produced by the p16(+/LUC) mice throughout their entire lifespan, we discovered that the intensity of the luminescence increased exponentially as the mice aged. However, this increase varied greatly among a group of genetically identical mice that were housed together. Surprisingly, the expression of p16(INK4a) with aging did not accurately predict the development of cancer, suggesting that the accumulation of senescent cells is not the primary factor leading to cancer-related death. Interestingly, in all 14 tested tumor models, the p16(LUC) gene was activated in specific regions by early neoplastic events, allowing us to visualize tumors with greater sensitivity compared to other imaging techniques. The activation of p16(INK4a) was observed not only in the emerging tumor cells but also in the surrounding stromal cells. These findings indicate that the activation of p16(INK4a) is a common characteristic of all developing cancers, making the p16(LUC) allele a highly sensitive and unbiased indicator of neoplastic transformation.

title: The Bacteroides sp. 3_1_23 Pif1 protein is a multifunctional helicase
text: The ScPif1 DNA helicase is a well-known member of a helicase superfamily that operates in a 5'-to-3' direction. This superfamily is conserved across various organisms, from bacteria to humans, and plays a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability. While extensive research has been conducted on eukaryotic Pif1 helicases, such as those found in yeast and humans, the functions and biochemical properties of prokaryotic Pif1 helicases remain largely unexplored. In this study, we present our findings on the expression, purification, and biochemical analysis of the Pif1 helicase from Bacteroides sp. 3_1_23 (BsPif1). Our results demonstrate that BsPif1 has a broad range of DNA substrates it can bind to, including partial duplex DNAs with 5'-overhangs, fork-like substrates, D-loop and flap-like substrates. This suggests that BsPif1 may play a role in resolving stalled DNA replication forks and enhancing Okazaki fragment maturation. Similar to its eukaryotic counterparts, BsPif1 is also capable of resolving R-loop structures and unwinding DNA-RNA hybrids. Additionally, BsPif1 exhibits efficient unfolding of G-quadruplexes and disruption of nucleoprotein complexes. These findings indicate that prokaryotic Pif1 helicases may play a crucial role in resolving common issues that arise during DNA transactions. Interestingly, we observed that BsPif1 differs from yeast Pif1 but shares more similarities with human Pif1 in terms of substrate specificity, helicase activity, and mode of action. These findings shed light on the potential functions of prokaryotic Pif1 helicases in vivo and are discussed in detail.

title: Netting neutrophils in autoimmune small-vessel vasculitis
text: Chronic autoinflammatory condition known as small-vessel vasculitis (SVV) is associated with antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies (ANCAs). Our study reveals that ANCA-stimulated neutrophils release chromatin fibers called neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which contain the targeted autoantigens proteinase-3 (PR3) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). The presence of NETs in inflamed kidneys and circulating MPO-DNA complexes suggests that NET formation triggers vasculitis and fosters the autoimmune response against neutrophil components in individuals with SVV.

title: Control of Nutrient Stress-Induced Metabolic Reprogramming by PKCζ in Tumorigenesis
text: The energetic and anabolic needs of tumor cells are well-known, as they have the ability to adapt their metabolism in order to survive and continue to grow even when faced with nutrient stress. Our research reveals that a deficiency in PKCζ actually promotes the flexibility required for cancer cells to reprogram their metabolism and utilize glutamine through the serine biosynthetic pathway, even in the absence of glucose. PKCζ plays a role in suppressing the expression of two important enzymes in this pathway, namely PHGDH and PSAT1. Additionally, it phosphorylates PHGDH at specific sites, inhibiting its enzymatic activity. Interestingly, when PKCζ is lost in mice, it leads to an increase in intestinal tumorigenesis and higher levels of these two metabolic enzymes. Similarly, patients with low levels of PKCζ tend to have a poor prognosis. Moreover, we have observed a correlation between the activities of PKCζ and caspase-3 and the levels of PHGDH in human intestinal tumors. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that PKCζ is a crucial metabolic tumor suppressor in both mouse and human cancer.

title: XRCC4's interaction with XLF is required for coding (but not signal) end joining
text: The proteins XRCC4 and XLF are closely related in structure and play an important role in the function of DNA Ligase IV. XRCC4 forms a strong bond with DNA Ligase IV, while XLF directly interacts with XRCC4. Both XRCC4 and XLF can form pairs of identical molecules, known as homodimers, which can come together to form filaments that are different from DNA Ligase IV. Recent studies have shown that XRCC4 and XLF work together to create a filamentous structure that helps connect DNA molecules. In this study, we demonstrate that disrupting the interaction between XRCC4 and XLF leads to problems in DNA repair, specifically affecting the coding of VDJ sequences but not the joining of signal ends. These findings support the idea that XRCC4/XLF complexes play a crucial role in bringing DNA ends together, which is essential for coding end joining but not necessary for signal end joining. Additionally, we found that phosphorylation of XRCC4/XLF complexes by DNA-PK interferes with DNA bridging in laboratory experiments, suggesting that DNA-PK's phosphorylation of XRCC4/XLF complexes may have a regulatory function.

title: Loss of imprinting in colorectal cancer linked to hypomethylation of H19 and IGF2.
text: Epigenetic changes in human cancers involve various modifications, such as reduced overall DNA methylation, decreased methylation of specific genes, increased methylation of gene promoters, and loss of imprinting (LOI) of the insulin-like growth factor-II gene (IGF2). LOI has been previously explained by hypermethylation of a differentially methylated region (DMR) located before the H19 gene, which allows activation of the usually inactive maternal allele of IGF2. However, our research demonstrates that this mechanism does not apply to colorectal cancers. Instead, both colorectal cancers and normal mucosa from the same patients, as well as cell lines with DNA methyltransferases DNMT1 and DNMT3B knocked out, exhibit hypomethylation of the H19 DMR and a DMR before exon 3 of IGF2. These findings suggest that hypomethylation is a mechanism for LOI, the widely accepted IGF2-H19 enhancer competition model for IGF2 imprinting is not applicable to the human colon, and an alternative model for LOI would involve a transcriptional repressor acting on the usually inactive maternal allele of IGF2.

title: Management of patients with sore throats in relation to guidelines: An interview study in Sweden
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate how a group of Swedish general practitioners (GPs) handle patients with a sore throat in relation to current guidelines, as expressed in interviews. The researchers used qualitative content analysis to analyze semi-structured interviews. The study took place in Swedish primary care and involved a strategic sample of 25 GPs. The main focus was on the GPs' perceived management of sore throat patients.

The results showed that out of the 25 GPs interviewed, nine adhered to the current guidelines for sore throat management, while 16 did not. The two groups differed in terms of their knowledge of the guidelines. Adherent GPs shared their knowledge within the team, while non-adherent GPs had idiosyncratic knowledge. Adherent GPs had little or no concerns about bacterial infections and differential diagnosis, whereas non-adherent GPs believed that any bacterial infection in patients with a sore throat should be identified and treated with antibiotics. Adherent GPs primarily relied on patient history and examination, while non-adherent GPs often considered these to be redundant. Non-adherent GPs reported difficulties in convincing patients to abstain from antibiotics, whereas adherent GPs did not encounter such problems.

In conclusion, this interview study of sore throat management among a strategically sampled group of Swedish GPs revealed that two-thirds of the GPs were non-adherent to the guidelines and had a liberal attitude towards antibiotics. On the other hand, one-third of the GPs adhered to the guidelines and had a more restricted view on antibiotics. Non-adherent GPs demonstrated significant knowledge gaps, while adherent GPs had discussed the guidelines within their primary care team. Therefore, it appeared that guideline implementation was facilitated by knowledge shared in team discussions.

title: Catch and release: how do kinetochores hook the right microtubules during mitosis?
text: In the world of sport fishing, anglers use tension on their lines to prevent fish from escaping once they are hooked. A similar principle can be observed at the molecular level during mitosis, where a process called biorientation is crucial for accuracy. During mitosis, the mitotic spindle randomly attaches to chromosomes, but it is the tension exerted by opposing microtubules that stabilizes the correct attachments. If the attachments lack tension, they become unstable and quickly release, providing another opportunity for biorientation. This tension-based stabilization also occurs in various other physiological contexts, including cell adhesion, motility, hemostasis, and tissue morphogenesis. In this review, we explore different models that explain how kinetochore attachments are stabilized, and we also consider emerging models for other systems that are activated by force. While the mitosis field has primarily focused on a kinase-based mechanism, it is possible that multiple mechanisms work together to stabilize properly bioriented kinetochores. Additionally, some principles governing tension-sensitive systems in other contexts may also apply to kinetochores.

title: Label-free in vivo imaging of myelinated axons in health and disease with spectral confocal reflectance microscopy
text: We present a novel technique for high-resolution imaging of myelinated axons in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerve without the need for fluorescent labeling. This method, called spectral confocal reflectance microscopy (SCoRe), utilizes a conventional laser-scanning confocal system to merge reflected signals from multiple lasers of different wavelengths, resulting in vivid color patterns specific to each myelinated fiber. These patterns aid in tracing the fibers in densely packed axonal regions and highlight important structures such as nodes of Ranvier and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures, enabling the detection of various myelin pathologies. With SCoRe, we successfully conducted long-term imaging of the mouse cortical axons in vivo, capturing the process of de novo myelination up to a depth of 400 μm. Furthermore, we demonstrated the feasibility of imaging myelinated axons in the human cerebral cortex. SCoRe is a valuable addition to the expanding toolkit for non-invasive myelination imaging in both animal models and potentially in humans.

title: Applicability of current staging/categorization of α-synuclein pathology and their clinical relevance
text: The presence of alpha-synuclein (alphaS) pathology in Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is known to have a consistent distribution pattern. Currently, there are two staging/categorization systems, Braak's and McKeith's, used to assess alphaS pathology. These systems aim to not only determine the stage/severity of the pathology but also evaluate the likelihood of related clinical symptoms such as dementia and extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). In this study, we examined the applicability of these staging/categorization systems and the frequency of dementia and EPS in a group of 226 individuals who tested positive for alphaS. These individuals were selected from a larger sample of autopsies (n = 1,720) based on the presence of alphaS-immunoreactivity (IR) in vulnerable nuclei, including the dorsal motor nucleus of vagus, substantia nigra, and basal forebrain. The frequency of alphaS-IR lesions in this larger sample was 14% (248 out of 1,720). For the 226 subjects with all necessary data, we assigned a neuropathological stage/category of PD/DLB using the staging/categorization systems and analyzed the neuropathological data in relation to dementia and EPS. We found that 83% of subjects had a distribution pattern of alphaS-IR that aligned with the current staging/categorization systems. Interestingly, approximately 55% of subjects with widespread alphaS pathology (Braak's PD stages 5-6) did not exhibit clinical signs of dementia or EPS. Similarly, among subjects who met the McKeith criteria for the diffuse neocortical category and had only mild Alzheimer's disease-related pathology, only 48% were demented and 54% displayed EPS. Notably, 17% of subjects deviated from the suggested caudo-rostral propagation, suggesting alternative progression routes possibly influenced by other diseases and genetic factors. In conclusion, our findings confirm that the current staging/categorization systems can be applied to most individuals with alphaS pathology. However, the fact that approximately half of those with significant alphaS pathology remain neurologically intact raises questions about whether we are accurately assessing the disease process.

title: Batf is important for IL-4 expression in T follicular helper cells
text: T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, in addition to T helper (Th)-2 cells, are a significant group of T cells that produce IL-4 and are crucial for regulating type 2 humoral immunity. However, the mechanisms controlling IL-4 production in Tfh cells are not well understood. Our study reveals that the transcription factor ATF-like, Batf, plays a key role in IL-4 expression specifically in Tfh cells, rather than in canonical Th2 cells. Functionally, Batf, in collaboration with interferon regulatory factor (IRF) 4, Stat3, and Stat6, triggers IL-4 production in Tfh cells by directly binding to and activating the CNS2 region in the IL-4 gene. Furthermore, the Batf-to-c-Maf signaling pathway is an important factor in determining IL-4 expression in Tfh cells. Deficiency in Batf impairs the generation of IL-4-producing Tfh cells, resulting in protection against allergic asthma. Our findings highlight the positive contribution of Batf in promoting the development of pro-allergic IL-4-producing Tfh cells.

title: Autocrine VEGF Signaling Synergizes with EGFR in Tumor Cells to Promote Epithelial Cancer Development
text: The role of tumor cell-derived VEGF in promoting angiogenesis and tumor growth has been well established. However, our study focuses on K5-SOS-dependent mouse skin tumors and reveals that autocrine VEGF is crucial for tumor cell proliferation in a manner that is independent of angiogenesis. We observed an upregulation of VEGF in SOS-expressing tumors, and deleting VEGF in epidermal cells resulted in a delay in tumorigenesis by suppressing both angiogenesis and tumor cell proliferation. Additionally, deleting Flt1 specifically in the epidermis also impaired tumorigenesis and proliferation. Interestingly, we found that complete tumor inhibition occurred even in the absence of VEGF in EGFR mutant mice, indicating a synergistic effect between VEGFR and EGFR in promoting tumor growth in neoplastic cells. Mechanistically, K5-SOS upregulated VEGF, Flt1, and Neuropilin-1 in an Erk-dependent manner, activating an autocrine proliferation loop, while EGFR prevented tumor cells from undergoing apoptosis. Furthermore, we observed an upregulation of Flt1 in human SCC, and inhibiting Flt1 in SCC cells impaired proliferation. Therefore, in addition to its role in regulating angiogenesis, VEGF should be recognized as a potent growth factor for epidermal tumors.

title: Discovery and development of the Polo-like kinase inhibitor volasertib in cancer therapy
text: The Polo-like kinase (Plk) family, specifically Plk1, has become a promising target for cancer treatment due to its crucial role in regulating the cell cycle. Over the years, several inhibitors of Plk1 have been developed, and some have shown promising results in early clinical trials. This article focuses on volasertib (BI 6727), an investigational drug that specifically inhibits Plk. Volasertib has demonstrated significant activity in various cancer cell lines and animal models of human cancer. Clinical trials conducted so far indicate that volasertib is effective in treating different types of cancer, with particularly encouraging outcomes in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Notably, recent phase II data has shown that combining volasertib with low-dose cytarabine (LDAC) leads to higher response rates and improved event-free survival compared to LDAC alone in previously untreated AML patients. Based on these findings, as well as its manageable safety profile, volasertib is currently undergoing phase III development as a potential treatment for AML patients who cannot undergo intensive remission induction therapy. This is a significant unmet need, as many AML patients are older and frail. In this review, we discuss the scientific rationale behind Plk1 inhibitors in cancer treatment, the progress of volasertib in clinical trials for solid tumors and AML, and the future identification of biomarkers that could predict response to volasertib and help determine its role in clinical practice.

title: Babies driving robots: self-generated mobility in very young infants
text:
The cognitive, social, and motor development of young infants greatly benefit from self-generated mobility through locomotion. However, some children with special needs can only achieve self-generated mobility with the help of assistive technology like a power wheelchair. Previously, infants under 24 months old were not considered suitable for power mobility training. However, recent research conducted in our labs and others suggests that even younger infants can learn power mobility by utilizing their reaching and grasping abilities. This interdisciplinary study combines our previous work on motor development and learning in infants with special needs, along with the use of robot technology for rehabilitation. The aim is to determine whether young infants, without any structured training, can drive a mobile robot and how their driving skills evolve over multiple sessions.

In this pilot study, we focused on two infants who participated in the most sessions. Both infants showed improvements in their total session time, the percentage of time spent driving, and the total distance covered. These findings indicate that young infants can independently move themselves using a mobile robot, even without any formal training. These results lay the groundwork for future training studies aimed at enhancing self-generated mobility in young infants with special needs. Our upcoming research will explore various training methods and technology combinations to overcome barriers to exploration through self-generated mobility, ultimately promoting the overall development of infants with special needs.

title: Effects of Abciximab on the architecture of platelet-rich clots in patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing primary coronary intervention.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether the effectiveness of abciximab in improving reperfusion in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is related to changes in clot architecture. A total of 23 AMI patients participating in the ADMIRAL trial were included in the study. They were randomly assigned to receive either abciximab or placebo before primary stenting. The mechanical (G') and morphological (mean platelet aggregate surface area [SAG]) properties of ex vivo platelet-rich clots (PRC) were assessed before and after the administration of abciximab or placebo. The results showed that abciximab significantly reduced both G' and SAG, indicating a decrease in platelet aggregate size and an increase in fibrin accessibility. These changes may contribute to the improved coronary artery patency observed with abciximab. These effects were observed in all patients, regardless of previous heparin administration. In conclusion, abciximab has a significant impact on clot architecture in AMI patients, potentially leading to better reperfusion outcomes.

title: Natural Mutagenesis of Human Genomes by Endogenous Retrotransposons
text: The continuous generation of new retrotransposon insertions in human genomes is primarily attributed to two classes of mobile elements, namely Alu and L1 elements. It is estimated that these elements have produced millions of new germline insertions in individual human genomes worldwide. However, the current technologies available are unable to detect most of these recent insertions, making it challenging to fully understand the extent of germline mutagenesis caused by endogenous human retrotransposons. In this study, we present novel technologies that enable the detection of these young retrotransposon insertions and provide evidence that such insertions are indeed prevalent in human populations. Additionally, our research reveals that new somatic L1 insertions occur frequently in the genomes of human lung cancer patients. Through genome-wide analysis, we propose that altered DNA methylation may be responsible for the heightened levels of L1 mobilization observed in these tumors. Our findings strongly suggest that transposon-mediated mutagenesis is widespread in human genomes and is likely to have a significant impact on human biology and the development of diseases.

title: Knowledge of young African American adults about heart disease: a cross-sectional survey
text:
BACKGROUND: African Americans have higher rates of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality compared to other ethnic groups. Interventions targeting young adults are crucial in preventing and reducing disease risk. This study aimed to assess the level of knowledge regarding lifestyle risk factors for CVD among young African American adults in Phoenix. The findings will inform the development of CVD outreach programs specifically tailored to this population. The Health Belief Model served as the conceptual framework for this study.

METHODS: A convenience sample of 172 African American men and women aged 18-26 years completed a questionnaire adapted from national surveys conducted by the American Heart Association. Descriptive statistics were analyzed based on age, gender, education level, and health status variables such as BMI, smoking status, and physical activity.

RESULTS: Young adult African Americans demonstrated good knowledge of certain aspects of heart disease. However, knowledge regarding other important risk factors (such as menopause) and preventive behaviors (such as reducing animal product consumption) varied among respondents. Education level had a greater impact on knowledge of individual variables compared to gender. Predictors of a summary CVD knowledge score included higher education, female gender, and high self-efficacy (adjusted R2 = 0.158, p < .001). Predictors of self-efficacy in changing CVD risk were higher education and perceived low risk of CVD (adjusted R2 = 0.064, p < .001), but these factors only explained 6% of the variance.

CONCLUSIONS: Evaluating baseline knowledge of CVD is crucial in designing effective health promotion programs. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses in knowledge can help tailor programs to be more impactful. Further research is needed to identify additional characteristics that influence knowledge and risk perception.

title: Recent insights into the role of Notch signaling in tumorigenesis
text: The Notch family of transmembrane receptors plays a crucial role in determining the fate of cells. In recent years, it has become clear that Notch is involved in the development of both hematologic and solid malignancies. Notch signaling affects various cellular functions and environmental cues related to tumor formation, such as cell proliferation, cell death, cell adhesion, the transition from epithelial to mesenchymal cells, and the growth of new blood vessels. It is now evident that Notch signaling can have both oncogenic and tumor-suppressing effects. This review focuses on recent discoveries about the molecular and functional aspects of Notch-mediated transformation in cancer. Additionally, the review explores potential cellular mechanisms that may explain the complex role of Notch in tumor formation.

title: BRIEFINGS IN FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS AND PROTEOMICS. VOL 5. NO 3. 209^221 doi:10.1093/bfgp/ell028 Histone acetylation in gene regulation
text: Chromatin, a dynamic nucleoprotein structure, contains genetic information. Key proteins undergo post-translational modifications to regulate various biological processes. Among these modifications, acetylation of lysine residues at the N-terminal histone tails is extensively studied for its impact on gene regulation in eukaryotic cells. This review highlights the significance of enzymes that control acetylation levels in both histone and non-histone proteins within cells, with a specific focus on their implications in cancer.

title: Efficacy of monthly tafenoquine for prophylaxis of Plasmodium vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria.
text: We conducted a study to evaluate the effectiveness of monthly doses of tafenoquine in preventing Plasmodium vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria. The study involved 205 Thai soldiers who were randomly assigned to receive either a loading dose of tafenoquine 400 mg (base) daily for 3 days, followed by monthly 400-mg doses (n = 104), or a placebo (n = 101), for a maximum of 5 consecutive months. Among the participants who completed the follow-up (96 tafenoquine recipients and 91 placebo recipients), there were 22 cases of P. vivax, 8 cases of P. falciparum, and 1 case of mixed infection. All infections, except for 1 case of P. vivax, occurred in the placebo group. This indicates that tafenoquine had a protective efficacy of 97% for all types of malaria (95% confidence interval [CI], 82%-99%), 96% for P. vivax malaria (95% CI, 76%-99%), and 100% for P. falciparum malaria (95% CI, 60%-100%). Monthly tafenoquine was found to be safe, well tolerated, and highly effective in preventing P. vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria in Thai soldiers over a period of 6 months.

title: Headache, migraine, and structural brain lesions and function: population based Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing-MRI study
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between overall and specific headaches and the volume of white matter hyperintensities, brain infarcts, and cognition. The study was conducted as a population-based, cross-sectional study in Nantes, France, as part of the Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing study. A total of 780 participants, with a mean age of 69 and 58.5% women, underwent detailed headache assessments. The main outcome measures included brain scans to evaluate the volume of white matter hyperintensities (using fully automated imaging processing) and the classification of infarcts (using visual reading with a standardized assessment grid). Cognitive function was assessed using a battery of tests, including the mini-mental state examination.

The results showed that 20.9% of participants reported a history of severe headache, and 116 had migraines, with 14.7% of them reporting aura symptoms. There was a significant association between any history of severe headache and an increasing volume of white matter hyperintensities. Participants with any history of severe headache had a 2.0 times higher odds of being in the highest third for total volume of white matter hyperintensities compared to those without severe headache in the lowest third. This association was consistent across all headache types. Migraine with aura was the only headache type strongly associated with volume of deep white matter hyperintensities and brain infarcts. The odds ratio for being in the highest third for volume of deep white matter hyperintensities was 12.4 for participants with migraine with aura compared to those without, and the odds ratio for brain infarcts was 3.4. The location of infarcts was mainly outside the cerebellum and brain stem. However, there was no evidence of cognitive impairment associated with any headache type, with or without brain lesions.

In conclusion, this population-based study found that any history of severe headache was associated with an increased volume of white matter hyperintensities. Migraine with aura was the only headache type associated with brain infarcts. However, there was no evidence to suggest that any type of headache, either alone or in combination with brain lesions, was associated with cognitive impairment.

title: Characterization of adipocytes derived from fibro/adipogenic progenitors resident in human skeletal muscle
text: Recently, researchers discovered a group of fibro/adipogenic progenitors situated between skeletal muscle fibers. The objective of this study was to investigate the extent to which these progenitors develop into fully functional adipocytes. Understanding the characteristics of adipocytes derived from muscle progenitors is crucial in comprehending muscle homeostasis, as they are believed to be the source of intermuscular adipose tissue that forms in various pathophysiological conditions. In this study, fibro/adipogenic progenitors were isolated from 15 human muscle biopsies based on the specific cell-surface immunophenotype CD15+/PDGFRα+CD56-. This allowed researchers to examine their differentiation into adipocytes and the functions of fully differentiated adipocytes. The regulation of adipogenic differentiation in these progenitors was found to be similar to that of progenitors derived from white subcutaneous adipose tissue. Likewise, basic adipocyte functions, such as triglyceride synthesis and lipolysis, occurred at comparable levels to those observed in adipocytes derived from subcutaneous adipose tissue progenitors. However, muscle progenitor-derived adipocytes were discovered to be unresponsive to insulin-induced glucose uptake, which was associated with the impairment of phosphorylation of key insulin-signaling effectors. These findings suggest that muscle adipogenic progenitors generate genuine white adipocytes that possess the unexpected characteristic of being insulin-resistant.

title: Membrane lipids in invadopodia and podosomes: Key structures for cancer invasion and metastasis
text: Invadopodia are protrusions formed by cancer cells that degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM). Podosomes are similar structures found in transformed fibroblasts and certain cells derived from monocytes, such as macrophages and osteoclasts. These structures are believed to play crucial roles in remodeling the ECM during cancer invasion and metastasis. Identifying the molecular components and regulators of invadopodia/podosomes has been a major focus in the search for therapeutic targets against malignant cancers. However, the process of assembling these components into invadopodia/podosomes and the spatial and temporal regulation of this assembly remain largely unknown. This review will provide an overview of recent advancements in understanding the molecular mechanisms behind invadopodia/podosome formation, with particular emphasis on the involvement of lipid rafts and phosphoinositides.

title: CCR2 and CXCR4 regulate peripheral blood monocyte pharmacodynamics and link to efficacy in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis
text: The role of CCR2 in regulating monocyte trafficking to sites of inflammation has attracted significant interest as a potential target for inflammatory diseases. In this study, we investigated the effects of blocking CCR2 with a potent small molecule antagonist on the peripheral blood monocyte compartment during acute and chronic inflammatory processes. Our results showed that CCR2 antagonism led to a rapid decrease in the number of circulating Ly6Chi monocytes. This decrease was primarily due to the sequestration of these cells in the bone marrow, which was dependent on CXCR4. These findings provide pharmacological evidence for the regulation of monocyte dynamics in vivo. Additionally, CCR2 antagonism resulted in increased levels of circulating CCL2 and CCL7, suggesting a role for CCR2 in regulating the levels of its ligands under normal conditions. Furthermore, chronic dosing of the CCR2 antagonist in a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis demonstrated significant reductions in disease severity, characterized by decreased accumulation of monocytes and other cells in the central nervous system. Overall, our study highlights the tractable pharmacodynamic effects of CCR2 antagonism in vivo, which can be utilized to align target engagement with the biological effects on disease activity.

title: Displacement of a DNA binding protein by Dda helicase
text: Recent studies have shown that the monomeric form of Bacteriophage T4 Dda helicase is capable of unwinding short duplex oligonucleotides and displacing streptavidin from 3'-biotinylated oligonucleotides. However, it has been observed that the activity of Dda helicase for streptavidin displacement and DNA unwinding increases as the number of Dda molecules bound to the substrate molecule increases. To investigate the ability of Dda to displace DNA binding proteins, a substrate was designed with a DNA binding site for the Escherichia coli trp repressor introduced into an oligonucleotide substrate for Dda helicase, which also contained a single-stranded overhang. Our findings demonstrate that a single Dda monomer is insufficient to displace the E.coli trp repressor from dsDNA under single turnover conditions. However, when the single-stranded overhang is long enough to accommodate two Dda molecules, the substrate is unwound and the repressor is displaced. Furthermore, the quantity of product formed increases when the substrate can accommodate more than two Dda molecules. These results suggest that multiple Dda molecules work together to displace DNA binding proteins, and this cooperative activity is correlated with the DNA unwinding and streptavidin displacement activities. We propose a cooperative inchworm model to explain the activities of Dda helicase.

title: Control of Developmental Regulators by Polycomb in Human Embryonic Stem Cells
text:
The role of Polycomb group proteins in human development is not well understood, although they are known to be crucial for early development in metazoans. In this study, we focused on the subunit SUZ12 of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) and its distribution in human embryonic stem (ES) cells. By mapping SUZ12 across the nonrepeat portion of the genome, we discovered its presence in a significant number of genes that encode key regulators of development. These genes are characterized by nucleosomes that are trimethylated at histone H3K27, indicating transcriptional repression. Additionally, these genes contain highly conserved noncoding elements in the genome. 

Furthermore, we observed that during ES cell differentiation, the PRC2 target genes are preferentially activated. Interestingly, we also found that the ES cell regulators OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG coexist in a significant subset of these genes. These findings suggest that PRC2 occupies a specific group of developmental genes in ES cells that need to be repressed to maintain pluripotency. However, these genes are also poised for activation during ES cell differentiation.

title: PAD4 is essential for antibacterial innate immunity mediated by neutrophil extracellular traps
text: The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) is crucial for neutrophils to trap and kill bacteria. These traps are highly decondensed chromatin structures. Previous research has shown that histone hypercitrullination, which is catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4), is associated with chromatin decondensation during NET formation. However, the specific role of PAD4 in NET-mediated bacterial trapping and killing has not been investigated. In this study, we used mice that lacked PAD4 to demonstrate that PAD4 is essential for the antibacterial function of NETs. Unlike neutrophils with normal PAD4 levels, neutrophils lacking PAD4 were unable to form NETs when stimulated with chemokines or exposed to bacteria. As a result, they were deficient in their ability to kill bacteria through NETs. In a mouse model of necrotizing fasciitis, PAD4-deficient mice were more susceptible to bacterial infection compared to mice with normal PAD4 levels, primarily due to their inability to form NETs. Additionally, we discovered that citrullination reduced the bacterial killing activity of histones and nucleosomes, indicating that PAD4 primarily contributes to chromatin decondensation for NET formation rather than enhancing histone-mediated bacterial killing. These findings highlight the importance of histone hypercitrullination in the innate immune response during bacterial infections.

title: Human ‘brite / beige’ adipocytes develop from capillary networks and their implantation improves metabolic homeostasis in mice
text: The expression of Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) is high in brown adipose tissue, where it generates heat by separating electron transport from ATP production. UCP1 is also present in adipocytes outside of traditional brown adipose tissue depots, known as 'brite' or 'beige' adipocytes. In humans, the presence of brite/beige adipocytes is associated with a lean and metabolically healthy phenotype, but it is unclear if there is a causal relationship. Our study reveals that human brite/beige adipocyte progenitors multiply when exposed to pro-angiogenic factors, along with the expansion of capillary networks. Adipocytes derived from these progenitors undergo a transformation in response to adenylate cyclase activation, changing from UCP1 negative to UCP1 positive, which is a key characteristic of the beige/brite phenotype. These transformed adipocytes exhibit uncoupled respiration. When implanted into mice that are fed a normal chow diet or a high-fat diet and have glucose intolerance, the activated brite/beige adipocytes from in vitro experiments improve systemic glucose tolerance. These adipocytes also express neuroendocrine and secreted factors, including the pro-protein convertase PCSK1, which is strongly linked to human obesity. Therefore, pro-angiogenic conditions stimulate the proliferation of human beige/brite adipocyte progenitors, and activated beige/brite adipocytes can impact systemic glucose regulation, potentially through a neuroendocrine mechanism.

title: Mindfulness meditation and improvement in sleep quality and daytime impairment among older adults with sleep disturbances: a randomized clinical trial.
text: Sleep disturbances are common among older adults and often go untreated. There is a need for accessible programs that can help improve sleep quality. The objective of this study was to determine if mindfulness meditation, a mind-body medicine intervention, could promote sleep quality in older adults with moderate sleep disturbances. The study was conducted as a randomized clinical trial with two groups, and participants were older adults with moderate sleep disturbances. They were assigned to either a mindfulness meditation intervention or a sleep hygiene education intervention. The main outcome measured was moderate sleep disturbance, and secondary outcomes included insomnia symptoms, depression, anxiety, stress, fatigue, and inflammatory signaling. The results showed that the mindfulness meditation group had significant improvement in sleep quality compared to the sleep hygiene education group. The mindfulness meditation group also showed improvement in secondary health outcomes such as insomnia symptoms, depression symptoms, and fatigue. There were no significant differences in anxiety, stress, or inflammatory signaling between the two groups. The study concluded that the use of a community-accessible mindfulness meditation intervention can improve sleep quality in older adults, which has implications for their quality of life.

title: THE ORIGIN AND DIFFERENTIATION OF MICROGLIAL CELLS DURING DEVELOPMENT
text: There is debate among authors regarding the origin of microglia, with some claiming they come from the neuroepithelium. However, most now believe that microglial cells are actually derived from mesoderm and are part of the monocyte/macrophage cell line. These cells must enter the developing central nervous system (CNS) either from the bloodstream, the ventricular space, or the meninges. Once inside, microglial cells are distributed throughout the nervous parenchyma in a relatively uniform manner. During development, there are recognized patterns of migration, with long-distance tangential migration occurring before radial migration of individual cells. As microglial cells move through the nervous parenchyma, they take on an ameboid shape, but eventually differentiate into ramified microglia once they reach their final location. This is supported by the presence of cells that exhibit features intermediate between ameboid and ramified microglia.
