The factors that control the invasion of the nervous parenchyma, migration within the developing CNS, and differentiation of microglial cells are not well understood. It appears that these processes depend on environmental factors such as soluble or cell-surface bound molecules and components of the extracellular matrix. Microglial cells within the developing CNS play a role in clearing cell debris and removing misdirected or temporary axons. They also likely support cell survival and the growth of neurites.

title: Integrin αvβ8-Mediated TGF-β Activation by Effector Regulatory T Cells Is Essential for Suppression of T-Cell-Mediated Inflammation
text: The role of Regulatory T (Treg) cells in suppressing harmful T cell responses is well-known, but how they achieve this suppression to maintain immune balance and limit responses during inflammation is not fully understood. In this study, we discovered that effector Treg cells possess high levels of a protein called integrin αvβ8, which allows them to activate latent transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β). When we specifically deleted integrin αvβ8 in Treg cells, there was no spontaneous inflammation observed, indicating that this pathway is not crucial for maintaining immune balance. However, Treg cells lacking integrin αvβ8 expression were unable to suppress harmful T cell responses during active inflammation. Therefore, our findings reveal a mechanism through which Treg cells control excessive immune responses, emphasizing the importance of effector Treg cell-mediated activation of latent TGF-β in suppressing harmful T cell responses during inflammation.

title: Effects of treatment for intestinal helminth infection on growth and cognitive performance in children: systematic review of randomised trials.
text:
The objective of this study was to summarize the effects of anthelmintic drug treatment on the growth and cognitive performance of children. The data sources included electronic databases such as Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group controlled trial register, Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline. Citations of all identified trials were also considered, and contact was made with the World Health Organization and field researchers.

The review methods involved a systematic review of randomized controlled trials in children aged 1-16, comparing anthelmintic treatment with placebo or no treatment. The assessment of validity and data abstraction was conducted independently by two reviewers. The main outcome measures were growth and cognitive performance.

A total of thirty randomized controlled trials involving more than 15,000 children were identified. The effects on mean weight were not significant, and there was heterogeneity in the results. However, some positive effects on mean weight change were observed in trials reporting this outcome. After a single dose of any anthelmintic, the pooled estimates were 0.24 kg (95% confidence interval 0.15 kg to 0.32 kg) using a fixed effects model and 0.38 kg (0.01 kg to 0.77 kg) using a random effects model. Results from trials with multiple doses showed mean weight change of 0.10 kg (0.04 kg to 0.17 kg) using a fixed effects model and 0.15 kg (0.00 to 0.30) using a random effects model in up to one year of follow-up. At more than one year of follow-up, mean weight change was 0.12 kg (-0.02 kg to 0.26 kg) using a fixed effects model and 0.43 (-0.61 to 1.47) using a random effects model. The results from studies on cognitive performance were inconclusive.

In conclusion, there is limited evidence suggesting that routine treatment of children in areas with common helminth infections may have some effects on weight gain, although this is not consistent across trials. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether this intervention improves cognitive performance.

title: Choosing appropriate substitution models for the phylogenetic analysis of protein-coding sequences.
text: While protein-coding sequences are widely studied in phylogenetic inference, there is a lack of incorporation of evolutionary models that consider the genetic code. This issue is further compounded by the exclusion of codon-based models from commonly used model selection techniques, likely due to the computational burden associated with codon models. To address this, we explored an efficient alternative to traditional nucleotide substitution models by incorporating codon position (CP) into the model. We assessed the most suitable model for alignments of 177 RNA virus genes and 106 yeast genes, considering 11 substitution models, including one codon model and four CP models. Our findings indicate that the majority of gene alignments are better described by CP substitution models rather than standard nucleotide models, and this can be achieved without the computational expense of full codon models. These results have significant implications for phylogenetic inference of coding sequences, as they demonstrate that substitution models incorporating CPs not only offer a computationally feasible alternative to standard models but may also frequently provide superior statistical performance.

title: Polycomb Proteins Remain Bound to Chromatin and DNA during DNA Replication In Vitro
text: During development, the transcriptional status of a gene can be preserved through multiple rounds of cell division. This phenomenon, known as an epigenetic effect, is believed to be a result of heritable changes in the folding of chromatin and modifications or variants of histones at specific genes. However, little is currently understood about how these chromatin features are inherited during cell division. One particular challenge in maintaining transcriptional states is DNA replication, which can disrupt or dilute the proteins and modifications associated with chromatin. Polycomb group protein complexes of the PRC1 class are crucial for development and are thought to silence transcription in a heritable manner by altering chromatin folding and histone modifications. It remains unclear whether these complexes and their effects are maintained during DNA replication or if they are re-established afterwards. Our research has discovered that when chromatin or DNA bound by PRC1-class Polycomb complexes is replicated in vitro, these complexes remain bound to the replicated templates. This retention of Polycomb proteins throughout DNA replication may contribute to the preservation of transcriptional silencing during cell division.

title: Control of CNS Cell-Fate Decisions by SHP-2 and Its Dysregulation in Noonan Syndrome
text: In the developing mammalian central nervous system (CNS), growth factors play a crucial role in guiding multipotent precursors to differentiate into neurons or glia. Any disruption in this process can lead to neural dysfunction. Noonan Syndrome (NS) is a condition associated with learning disabilities and mental retardation, caused by genetic mutations that result in the constant activation of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2. In our study, we have shown that reducing the expression of SHP-2 in cultured cortical precursors or in the embryonic cortex inhibits the production of neurons and promotes the early formation of astrocytes. On the other hand, expressing a mutant form of SHP-2 associated with NS promotes the generation of neurons and inhibits the formation of astrocytes. We have also observed similar disruptions in neural cell fate decisions in a mouse model that mimics NS in humans. Therefore, SHP-2 plays a crucial role in instructing precursors to become neurons rather than astrocytes during the period of neurogenesis. The imbalances in the proportions of these two cell types caused by the constant activation of SHP-2 may contribute to the cognitive impairments observed in NS patients.

title: Global Regulation of H2A.Z Localization by the INO80 Chromatin-Remodeling Enzyme Is Essential for Genome Integrity
text: INO80 is a chromatin-remodeling enzyme that is conserved throughout evolution and relies on ATP for its function. It plays important roles in transcription, DNA repair, and replication. Our study reveals that yeast INO80 contributes to these processes by regulating the distribution of a specific histone variant called H2A.Z across the entire genome. When INO80 is absent, H2A.Z nucleosomes are not properly positioned, and the levels of H2A.Z at gene promoters do not respond effectively to changes in transcription. This suggests that INO80 is responsible for controlling the dynamics of H2A.Z. Furthermore, we demonstrate that INO80 has the ability to exchange histones, specifically replacing nucleosomal H2A.Z/H2B with free H2A/H2B dimers. The genetic interactions observed between ino80 and htz1 support a model in which INO80 removes unacetylated H2A.Z from chromatin, thereby promoting genome stability.

title: Rho GTPase signalling in cell migration
text: The manner in which cells move varies depending on their surroundings, such as the composition of the extracellular matrix, interactions with neighboring cells, and chemical signals. Rho GTPases are crucial in all forms of cell migration, although their specific impact differs based on the environment and cell type. This article examines recent advancements in our comprehension of how Rho GTPases contribute to various migration types, specifically comparing lamellipodium-driven and bleb-driven modes. Additionally, the text explores the process of cell migration across the endothelium. Apart from the well-known regulators of migration, Rho, Rac, and Cdc42, the roles of other members of the Rho family that are less extensively studied are also discussed.

title: A Novel Adaptor Protein Orchestrates Receptor Patterning and Cytoskeletal Polarity in T-Cell Contacts
text: The recognition of antigens by T cells necessitates the creation of a specialized connection between the T cell and the antigen-presenting cell. This connection is formed through the recruitment and exclusion of specific proteins in the area of contact. The mechanisms that govern these processes are currently unknown. In our study, we provide evidence that the engagement of the adhesion molecule CD2 by its ligand triggers a series of events including protein segregation, CD2 clustering, and cytoskeletal polarization. Interestingly, while protein segregation did not rely on the cytoplasmic domain of CD2, CD2 clustering and cytoskeletal polarization required an interaction between the CD2 cytoplasmic domain and a newly discovered SH3-containing protein called CD2AP. CD2AP is likely to play a role in organizing receptors in the contact area by connecting specific adhesion receptors to the cytoskeleton.

title: Operable non-small cell lung cancer diagnosed by transpleural techniques : do they affect relapse and prognosis?
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of transpleural methods, such as needle aspiration or tumor excision, on relapse and prognosis in patients with peripheral lung cancer.

DESIGN: This was a retrospective study conducted at a national referral hospital.

PATIENTS: A total of 239 patients who underwent surgery between 1990 and 1998 for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with a maximum diameter of < 3 cm were included in the study. All patients had complete resection of the tumor. The follow-up period ranged from 12 to 105 months, with a median of 45 months.

INTERVENTIONS: The transbronchial method, which involved the use of a bronchoscope, was compared to the transpleural method, which involved needle aspiration cytology or tumor excision. Variables analyzed included gender, histologic type of carcinoma, pathologic stage, and whether the diagnostic method was the first-line transbronchial or second-line transpleural.

RESULTS: NSCLC was diagnosed using the transpleural technique in 45 patients and the transbronchial technique in 194 patients. There were no significant differences in age, gender, histologic type, pathologic stage, or tumor size between the two groups. The number of relapses was 7 in the transpleural group and 35 in the transbronchial group (p = 0.90). In the transpleural group, there were 4 cases of distant metastasis and 3 cases of local relapse, while in the transbronchial group, there were 20 cases of distant metastasis and 15 cases of local relapse (p = 0.99). Pleural carcinomatosis occurred in none of the patients in the transpleural group and in 1 case (0.5%) in the transbronchial group (p = 0.99). The 5-year survival rate was statistically better in the transpleural group compared to the transbronchial group (79.4% vs 60.3%, p = 0.04). This finding was also confirmed in a multivariate analysis as an independent prognostic factor.

CONCLUSIONS: Based on our study, transpleural methods appear to be a suitable approach for diagnosing operable lung cancer that is difficult to diagnose using bronchoscopy. These methods did not have a negative impact on relapse and prognosis in our patient population.

title: Characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage in vivo
text: The proliferation and differentiation of precursor cells lead to the formation of mature adipocytes. Previous research has identified a specific group of cells, known as Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(+) (CD24(+)) cells, in white adipose tissue (WAT) that have the ability to generate functional WAT. In this study, we used various mouse models with Cre recombinase to determine the lineage of adipocytes in vivo. While it has been suggested that white adipocytes come from endothelial and hematopoietic lineages, our findings indicate that neither of these lineages label white adipocytes. However, the platelet-derived growth factor receptor α (PdgfRα)-Cre trace labels all white adipocytes. By analyzing WAT from PdgfRα-Cre reporter mice, we identified CD24(+) and Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(-) (CD24(-)) cells as adipocyte precursors. We demonstrated that CD24(+) cells give rise to the CD24(-) population in vivo, and the CD24(-) cells express late markers of adipogenesis. Based on these findings, we propose a model in which CD24(+) adipocyte progenitors become more committed to the adipocyte lineage as CD24 expression is lost, resulting in the generation of CD24(-) preadipocytes. This characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage will aid in the study of the mechanisms that regulate WAT formation and WAT mass expansion in obesity.

title: Reducing Plasmodium falciparum Malaria Transmission in Africa: A Model-Based Evaluation of Intervention Strategies
text:
In the past ten years, efforts have been made to increase malaria intervention coverage in Africa. However, it is still uncertain how much transmission reduction can be achieved with the tools currently available. 

To address this, we developed a simulation model for Plasmodium falciparum transmission in Africa, taking into account the three main vector species (Anopheles gambiae s.s., An. arabiensis, and An. funestus). We used data from 34 transmission settings across Africa to determine the parameters for the model. We also considered the impact of the switch to artemisinin-combination therapy (ACT) and the increasing use of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLINs) since 2000.

We then examined the effects of various interventions in six representative settings with different levels of transmission intensity, vector species, and patterns of seasonality. These interventions included the continued distribution of LLINs, additional rounds of indoor residual spraying (IRS), mass screening and treatment (MSAT), and the potential future use of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine. We set a realistic target of 80% coverage for all interventions.

In settings with low transmission, LLINs have the potential to reduce malaria transmission to very low levels (<1% parasite prevalence in all age groups) if they are used consistently and at high levels. In two of the moderate transmission settings, additional rounds of IRS with DDT combined with MSAT could bring parasite prevalence below the 1% threshold. However, in the third moderate transmission setting where An. arabiensis is the dominant vector, these interventions alone are not enough to reach the threshold. In high transmission settings, achieving the 1% threshold would require either unrealistically high coverage levels (>90%) or the development of new tools and significant social improvements. However, even with existing tools and realistic coverage levels, significant reductions in prevalence can still be achieved.

In conclusion, current interventions can lead to significant reductions in P. falciparum malaria transmission and the associated disease burden in Africa. In low to moderate transmission settings with primarily indoor-resting vectors, comprehensive and sustained intervention programs can bring prevalence below the 1% threshold. However, in high transmission settings and those with mainly outdoor-resting vectors, additional tools targeting outdoor-biting and outdoor-resting mosquitoes, as well as partly zoophagic mosquitoes, will be necessary.

title: Golgi Export of the Kir2.1 Channel Is Driven by a Trafficking Signal Located within Its Tertiary Structure
text: The mechanisms responsible for sorting newly synthesized proteins from the Golgi to the cell surface are not well understood. In this study, we discovered that the potassium channel Kir2.1, which is associated with Andersen-Tawil syndrome when mutated, is selected as cargo for Golgi export carriers in a unique signal-dependent manner. Unlike typical trafficking signals, which consist of short linear peptide sequences, the Golgi exit of Kir2.1 is determined by specific residues located within the confluence of two separate domains. This signal patch acts as a recognition site for interaction with the AP1 adaptor complex, marking Kir2.1 for inclusion into clathrin-coated vesicles at the trans-Golgi. By identifying a trafficking signal within the tertiary structure of Kir2.1, we have uncovered a quality control step that links protein conformation to Golgi export. This finding provides molecular insight into how mutations in Kir2.1 lead to the retention of channels at the Golgi.

title: Characteristics of Body Fat, Body Fat Percentage and Other Body Composition for Koreans from KNHANES IV
text:
As the prevalence of obesity continues to rise, accurately measuring fat mass has become increasingly important. In this study, we examined the fat and muscle mass of Koreans using data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey IV (KNHANES IV). A total of 10,456 subjects, including 4,476 men and 5,980 women aged 20 to 85 years, were included in the analysis. Fat and muscle mass were measured using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, and reference values for body composition were obtained using the LMS method.

We found that the fat mass index (FMI), which is calculated as body fat mass divided by height squared (kg/m²), did not correlate with age in Korean men (P = 0.452), but it did in Korean women (P < 0.001). Additionally, the ratio of fat percentage in the trunk and legs increased with age in both genders. In terms of muscle mass, the appendicular lean mass divided by height squared (kg/m²) was negatively associated with age in Korean men (P < 0.001), while it increased with age in Korean women (P < 0.001).

When we classified obesity based on FMI, the prevalence rates were 6.1% (FMI > 9 kg/m²) in men and 2.7% (FMI > 13 kg/m²) in women. These findings suggest that muscle mass decreases and obesity increases with age in Korean men, whereas both fat mass and obesity increase with age in Korean women.

title: The Evolution of Dominance in Sporophytic Self-Incompatibility Systems. II. Mate Availability and Recombination
text: Sporophytic self-incompatibility (SSI) is a mechanism in plants that promotes cross-pollination by recognizing and rejecting self-pollen. This recognition process is controlled by a complex locus consisting of five separate genes that determine the specificity of both the pollen and the stigma. Experimental studies have shown that S-alleles, which are responsible for self-recognition, can exhibit dominant, recessive, or codominant behavior, and the dominance level can vary depending on whether it is the pollen or the stigma specificity being examined. In this study and its companion paper by Llaurens and colleagues, the researchers investigate the evolution of dominance in a single-locus SSI system using numerical models and simulations. They specifically focus on factors that can cause differences in S-allele dominance between the pollen and the stigma. The researchers also examine the impact of recombination between the S-locus and a modifier locus. The models predict that the evolution of S-allele dominance in the stigma requires a limitation in the number of compatible mates, whereas this limitation is not necessary for the evolution of dominance in the pollen. Additionally, when the S-locus and modifier locus are tightly linked, it promotes the development of dominance hierarchies among S-alleles. The results of the models are interpreted in relation to existing knowledge about the molecular basis of dominance in SSI systems and the reported dominance relationships of S-alleles in various species. These studies reveal that dominant S-alleles are more prevalent in the pollen than in the stigma, suggesting that mate limitation may be relatively uncommon in natural populations with SSI.

title: Neurological outcomes of animal models of uterine artery ligation and relevance to human intrauterine growth restriction: a systematic review
text:
The aim of this review is to examine the molecular, neurological, and behavioral effects observed in animal models of uterine artery ligation. We will assess the relevance of this model to the pathological and functional characteristics associated with cerebral palsy and its developmental comorbidities in humans. 

To conduct this review, we performed a literature search on the PubMed database for studies utilizing the uterine artery ligation model published between 1990 and 2013. We then summarized any relevant neuroanatomical and behavioral deficits reported in each study for further analysis. 

Our review included 25 papers that met the criteria, and we summarized several outcomes from these studies. Fetal growth restriction was found to result in a gradient of reduced body weight, with the brain mass being relatively spared. The size of the somatosensory cortex, hippocampus, and corpus callosum were significantly reduced, while the motor cortex appeared to be unaffected. Apoptotic proteins were upregulated, while those important for neuronal survival, growth, and differentiation were downregulated. Neuronal apoptosis and astrogliosis were observed throughout various brain regions. White matter injury involved a halt in oligodendrocyte precursor maturation, hypomyelination, and abnormal organization of existing myelin. Animals with growth restriction exhibited deficits in gait, memory, object recognition, and spatial processing. 

In conclusion, this review demonstrates that uterine artery ligation in animal models leads to neuronal death, white matter injury, motor abnormalities, and cognitive deficits. These findings closely resemble the deficits observed in human cerebral palsy, making this model clinically relevant.

title: The fidelity of the ligation step determines how ends are resolved during Nonhomologous end joining
text: The resolution of chromosome breaks through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) is effective, even when dealing with different end structures. However, it remains unclear how the specific steps involved in this resolution process are determined. To address this question, we conducted an analysis of cellular NHEJ using ends that had systematically mispaired and damaged termini. Our findings demonstrate that NHEJ has a unique ability to bypass subtle terminal mispairs and radiomimetic damage through direct ligation. However, the ability to bypass varies greatly, with more severe mispairs resulting in a gradual reduction of bypass products from 85% to 6%. To compensate for this, there is an increase in end-processing by nucleases and polymerases, although pathways with the fewest steps to generate a suitable substrate for ligation are favored. Therefore, both the frequency and nature of end processing are tailored to meet the requirements of the ligation step. We propose a model in which the ligase coordinates all the steps involved in NHEJ within the stable paired-end complex to limit end processing and associated errors.

title: Laminin-based cell adhesion anchors microtubule plus ends to the epithelial cell basal cortex through LL5α/β
text: In this study, researchers have discovered that LL5beta, a factor that anchors microtubules, is responsible for attaching microtubule plus ends to the cell cortex. LL5beta and its homologue LL5alpha (LL5s) were found to colocalize with autocrine laminin-5 and its receptors, integrins alpha3beta1 and alpha6beta4, at the basal side of fully polarized epithelial sheets. When both laminin receptor integrins were depleted, the cortical localization of LL5s was abolished. Additionally, LL5 depletion resulted in a decrease in the amount of integrin alpha3 at the basal cell cortex. The activation of integrin alpha3 alone was enough to initiate LL5 accumulation at the cell cortex. LL5s were found to form a complex with the cytoplasmic tails of these integrins, although their interaction may be indirect. By visualizing EB1-GFP in epithelial sheets and using RNA interference, researchers discovered that LL5s are necessary to maintain the density of growing microtubules specifically at the basal cortex. These findings demonstrate that signaling from laminin-integrin associations is responsible for attaching microtubule plus ends to the epithelial basal cell cortex.

title: DNA topoisomerases: structure, function, and mechanism.
text: DNA topoisomerases play a crucial role in resolving the topological challenges associated with DNA replication, transcription, recombination, and chromatin remodeling. They achieve this by creating temporary breaks in the DNA strands, either single or double. Additionally, these enzymes regulate the level of DNA supercoiling to ensure optimal protein interactions with the DNA and prevent excessive supercoiling, which can be harmful. Recent advancements have allowed for the determination of crystal structures of various topoisomerase fragments, representing almost all known classes of these enzymes. These structures have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms of topoisomerases, complementing previous findings from biochemical analyses. Interestingly, despite lacking significant sequence similarity, both type IA and type IIA topoisomerases from prokaryotes, as well as type IIA enzymes from eukaryotes, share similar structural folds that likely correspond to functional motifs within critical regions of the enzymes. On the other hand, type IB topoisomerases exhibit distinct structural characteristics compared to other known topoisomerases but bear resemblance to a group of enzymes known as tyrosine recombinases. Common structural features among all topoisomerases include hinged clamps that open and close to bind DNA, DNA binding cavities for temporary storage of DNA segments, and the coupling of protein conformational changes to DNA rotation or movement. In the case of type II topoisomerases, the binding and hydrolysis of ATP further regulate conformational changes in the enzymes, ultimately leading to alterations in DNA topology.

title: Pilot testing of dipsticks as point-of-care assays for rapid diagnosis of poor-quality artemisinin drugs in endemic settings
text:
BACKGROUND: The effective management of malaria cases is hindered by the increasing prevalence of poor-quality artemisinin drugs in many endemic countries. Therefore, it is crucial to have access to good-quality artemisinin drugs for malaria treatment.

METHODS: In order to address this issue in resource-limited areas, we developed a point-of-care assay using specific monoclonal antibodies against artesunate and artemether. We created prototypes of lateral flow dipstick assays for rapid identification of counterfeit and substandard artemisinin drugs. The feasibility of these dipsticks was evaluated in different endemic settings, and their performance was assessed when used by untrained personnel.

RESULTS: The results of the pilot test demonstrated that the dipstick tests can be successfully conducted by various investigators, following the provided instruction sheet. None of the artemether and artesunate drugs obtained from public pharmacies in different endemic countries failed the test.

CONCLUSION: With further optimization of test conditions and sensitivity, the simple dipstick assays have the potential to be used as a qualitative and semi-quantitative assay for rapid screening of counterfeit artemisinin drugs in endemic settings.

title: Increased Microerythrocyte Count in Homozygous α+-Thalassaemia Contributes to Protection against Severe Malarial Anaemia
text:
The heritable blood disorder alpha(+)-thalassaemia is caused by a decrease in the production of alpha-globin chains, which are a part of normal adult hemoglobin (Hb). Individuals with alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygosity have smaller red blood cells and a higher red blood cell count. This condition provides significant protection against severe malaria, including severe malarial anemia (SMA) where Hb concentration is less than 50 g/l, but it does not affect the number of parasites. We conducted a study to test the hypothesis that the red blood cell indices associated with alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygosity offer a hematological advantage during acute malaria.

We reanalyzed data from children in Papua New Guinea who participated in a case-control study on the protective effects of alpha(+)-thalassaemia against severe malaria. The aim was to assess the genotype-specific reduction in red blood cell count and Hb levels during acute malarial disease. We found that all children with acute falciparum malaria had a median reduction in red blood cell count of approximately 1.5 x 10(12)/l compared to community children (p < 0.001). We developed a simple mathematical model to understand the relationship between Hb concentration and red blood cell count. According to this model, children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassaemia experience less Hb loss than children with a normal genotype when the red blood cell count decreases by more than 1.1 x 10(12)/l due to the lower mean cell Hb in alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygotes. Additionally, children with alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygosity require a 10% greater reduction in red blood cell count than children with a normal genotype (p = 0.02) for Hb concentration to drop to 50 g/l, the cutoff for SMA. We estimated that the hematological profile in children with alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygosity reduces the risk of SMA during acute malaria compared to children with a normal genotype (relative risk 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24-1.12, p = 0.09).

In conclusion, the increased red blood cell count and microcytosis in children with alpha(+)-thalassaemia homozygosity may significantly contribute to their protection against SMA. Having a lower Hb concentration per red blood cell and a larger population of red blood cells may be a biologically advantageous strategy against the substantial decrease in red blood cell count that occurs during acute infection with the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. This hematological profile may also reduce the risk of anemia caused by other Plasmodium species and other causes of anemia. Other host polymorphisms that increase red blood cell count and microcytosis may provide a similar advantage.

title: Construction of Escherichia coli K-12 in-frame, single-gene knockout mutants: the Keio collection
text: We have systematically created a comprehensive set of precise and well-defined deletions for all nonessential genes in Escherichia coli K-12. The coding regions of open-reading frames were replaced with a kanamycin cassette that was flanked by FLP recognition target sites. This was achieved using a one-step method to inactivate chromosomal genes, along with primers designed to create deletions that maintain the reading frame upon removal of the resistance cassette. Out of the 4288 targeted genes, we successfully obtained mutants for 3985 of them. To address potential issues encountered in high-throughput studies, we saved two independent mutants for each deleted gene. These mutants, known as the "Keio collection," serve as a valuable resource for not only systematic analyses of unknown gene functions and gene regulatory networks but also for conducting genome-wide tests to assess the effects of mutations in a common strain background, E. coli K-12 BW25113. Unfortunately, we were unable to disrupt 303 genes, including 37 with unknown functions, which are potential candidates for essential genes. The distribution of these resources is being managed through GenoBase (http://ecoli.aist-nara.ac.jp/).

title: Validated RealTime reverse transcriptase PCR methods for the diagnosis and pathotyping of Eurasian H7 avian influenza viruses
text:
BACKGROUND: Avian influenza (AI) caused by H7 AI viruses (AIVs) of both low pathogenicity (LP) and high pathogenicity (HP) are diseases that must be reported in poultry.

OBJECTIVES: The aim is to design and validate two RealTime reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (RRT PCRs) for detecting and determining the pathotype of Eurasian H7 AIVs.

METHODS: The H7 RRT PCRs targeted two regions of the haemagglutinin gene: (i) HA2 and (ii) cleavage site CS. Validation was done using 65 H7 AIVs, 57 non-H7 AIVs, and 259 poultry swabs, comparing the results to M gene (AI generic) RRT PCR and virus isolation (VI). An additional 38 swabs and 20 tissue specimens were used for extended validation against M gene RRT PCR.

RESULTS: Both H7 RRT PCRs successfully amplified all 61 Eurasian lineage H7 AIVs and none of the 57 non-H7 AIVs. Sensitivity and specificity were determined using 297 poultry swabs compared to M gene RRT PCR. The HA2 RRT PCR had a sensitivity of 95.4% and specificity of 97.9%, while the CS RRT PCR had a sensitivity of 64.6% and specificity of 99.6%. The HA2 RRT PCR was more sensitive than virus isolation. The CS RRT PCR correctly determined the pathotype of all 61 Eurasian lineage H7 AIVs tested.

CONCLUSIONS: The highly sensitive HA2 RRT PCR is suitable for poultry surveillance and disease diagnosis. The CS RRT PCR allows for rapid determination of the pathotype of H7 AIVs.

title: Interleukin-6 receptor pathways in coronary heart disease: a collaborative meta-analysis of 82 studies
text:
The role of persistent inflammation in the development of cardiovascular disease has been suggested. Interleukin-6 receptor (IL6R) signalling is known to contribute to inflammation. To investigate the potential causal relationship between IL6R and coronary heart disease, we examined a genetic variant, Asp358Ala (rs2228145), which affects IL6R signalling. 

In a collaborative meta-analysis, we analyzed the presence of Asp358Ala in IL6R in 125,222 participants and compared it to conventional risk factors and inflammation biomarkers. We also compared the frequency of Asp358Ala in 51,441 patients with coronary heart disease and 136,226 controls. Additionally, we assessed the relationship between Asp358Ala and gene expression as well as interleukin 6 production.

The minor allele frequency of Asp358Ala was found to be 39%. There was no association between Asp358Ala and lipid concentrations, blood pressure, adiposity, dysglycaemia, or smoking. However, for each copy of 358Ala inherited, there was a significant increase in IL6R and interleukin 6 concentrations, as well as a decrease in C-reactive protein and fibrinogen concentrations. Furthermore, the risk of coronary heart disease decreased by 3.4% for each copy of 358Ala inherited. There was no correlation between Asp358Ala and IL6R mRNA levels or interleukin-6 production in monocytes.

Based on our findings from large-scale genetic and biomarker data, there appears to be a causal association between IL6R-related pathways and coronary heart disease. This research was funded by the British Heart Foundation, UK Medical Research Council, UK National Institute of Health Research, Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre, and the BUPA Foundation.

title: Plasma exosomes can deliver exogenous short interfering RNA to monocytes and lymphocytes
text: Before RNA interference (RNAi) can be effectively used in cancer therapy, several technical challenges need to be addressed. The main obstacle lies in delivering nucleic acids across the cell's plasma membrane. However, a recent study has shown that exosome vesicles derived from humans have the ability to transport short interfering RNA (siRNA) to human mononuclear blood cells. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that originate from endocytic processes and play a role in cell-to-cell communication, including antigen presentation, tolerance development, and RNA transportation (primarily mRNA and microRNA). After testing various methods, researchers found that electroporation was the most effective technique to introduce siRNA into exosomes from different sources. These exosomes, obtained from peripheral blood, were then used as gene delivery vectors (GDVs) to transport exogenous siRNA to human blood cells. The vesicles successfully delivered the siRNA to monocytes and lymphocytes, resulting in the selective silencing of mitogen-activated protein kinase 1. These findings indicate that human exosomes can serve as GDVs to deliver therapeutic siRNAs and other foreign nucleic acids to cells.

title: Quantitative analysis of tumor-derived methylated p16INK4a sequences in plasma, serum, and blood cells of hepatocellular carcinoma patients.
text:
The purpose of this study was to use real-time quantitative methylation-specific PCR (RTQ-MSP) to measure methylated p16INK4a sequences and determine the concentration of circulating tumor DNA in plasma, serum, and peripheral blood cells from patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). A total of 49 patients were included in the study, and samples were collected before, during, and after surgery.

The results showed that RTQ-MSP was able to detect as few as 10 genome-equivalents of methylated p16INK4a sequences. The data were expressed as the methylation index, which represented the percentage of methylated p16INK4a sequences out of all bisulfite converted unmethylated and methylated p16INK4a sequences. Methylated p16INK4a sequences were found in the peripheral circulation of 80% of HCC patients (23 out of 29). There was no significant difference in the detectability and concentrations of methylated p16INK4a sequences between preoperative plasma and serum samples.

The methylation indices of p16INK4a ranged from 0.2% to 100% in plasma samples and from 0.012% to 0.075% in buffy coat samples collected before surgery. After surgical resection, the median methylation indices in plasma and buffy coat samples decreased by 12- and 15-fold, respectively. These findings demonstrate the clinical usefulness of RTQ-MSP in detecting and monitoring HCC after treatment. Intraoperative plasma samples showed no methylation of p16INK4a, and only two intraoperative buffy coat samples were positive for p16INK4a methylation.

In conclusion, quantifying epigenetic changes in peripheral blood using RTQ-MSP is a valuable method for detecting and monitoring HCC.

title: Dynamic control of excitatory synapse development by a Rac1 GEF/GAP regulatory complex.
text: The actin-dependent remodeling necessary for various cellular processes, including synapse development, is orchestrated by the small GTPase Rac1. However, the precise regulation of Rac1 is not well understood, particularly regarding the mechanisms that allow Rac1 activators (GEFs) and inhibitors (GAPs) to work together in controlling Rac1 signaling. In this study, we have identified a regulatory complex consisting of a Rac-GEF (Tiam1) and a Rac-GAP (Bcr) that collaborate to regulate excitatory synapse development. Disruption of Bcr's function within this complex leads to increased Rac1 activity and remodeling of dendritic spines, resulting in excessive synaptic growth. However, this excessive growth can be rescued by inhibiting Tiam1. Interestingly, the Tiam1-Bcr complex is utilized by EphB receptors to control synaptogenesis. Upon activation of EphB receptors, Tiam1 promotes Rac1-dependent spine formation, while Bcr prevents Rac1-mediated internalization of the receptors, thereby promoting spine growth instead of retraction. This discovery highlights the importance of a Rac-specific GEF/GAP complex in maintaining optimal levels of Rac1 signaling and provides valuable insights into the regulation of small GTPases.

title: 4-1BB Costimulation Ameliorates T Cell Exhaustion Induced by Tonic Signaling of Chimeric Antigen Receptors
text: CARs targeting CD19 have shown significant success in treating hematologic malignancies, while CARs targeting other antigens have had limited tumor regression. It is unclear whether the effectiveness of CD19 CARs is due to the susceptibility of hematologic malignancies to CAR therapies or the superior functionality of the CD19 CAR itself. Our research demonstrates that the continuous activation of CAR T cells through antigen-independent clustering of CAR single-chain variable fragments leads to early exhaustion, reducing the efficacy of CAR therapies. This activation is present in all CARs except the highly effective CD19 CAR. Additionally, we found that CD28 costimulation enhances exhaustion induced by persistent CAR signaling, while 4-1BB costimulation reduces exhaustion. These findings explain the antitumor effects of CD19 CARs and the observation that CD19 CAR T cells with the 4-1BB costimulatory domain are more persistent in clinical trials compared to those with CD28.

title: Ultrafast Evolution and Loss of CRISPRs Following a Host Shift in a Novel Wildlife Pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum
text: The rates at which genomes evolve in bacterial pathogens in the wild, especially during and after switching hosts, are not well understood. Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG) is a pathogenic bacterium that primarily affects poultry but has recently spread to wild house finches, a common North American songbird. In this study, we examine the genome of MG in house finch isolates for the first time and measure the rates of genome evolution. We also compare these rates to those in poultry strains. By analyzing the whole-genome sequences of 12 house finch isolates collected over a 13-year period, as well as four newly sequenced poultry strains, we find that the nucleotide diversity in house finch isolates is only about 2% of that in ancestral poultry strains. Additionally, the nucleotide substitution rate is estimated to be 0.8-1.2×10(-5) per site per year, which is exceptionally fast and comparable to some of the highest estimates reported for bacteria. We also observe that the CRISPR arrays in poultry MG strains show high diversity and complete turnover before the switch to the house finch host. However, after the invasion of house finches, there is a progressive loss of CRISPR repeat diversity, and the recruitment of new CRISPR repeats stops. The house finch MG strains from 2007 retain only about 50% of the CRISPR repertoire found in the founding strains from 1994-95, and they have lost the CRISPR-associated genes necessary for CRISPR function. These findings suggest that genome evolution in bacterial pathogens of wild birds can occur at an extremely rapid pace and may be accompanied by the functional loss of CRISPRs.

title: Inducing Tumor Immunity through the Selective Engagement of Activating Fcγ Receptors on Dendritic Cells
text: Efficient activation of tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells relies on dendritic cells (DCs) effectively capturing and presenting tumor antigens. To transition from antigen capture to T cell stimulation, a maturation signal is necessary; without it, tolerance rather than immunity may develop. Although immune complexes (ICs) can enhance antigen capture, they are not very effective at inducing DC maturation, naive T cell activation, and protective immunity. However, we have discovered that by interfering with the inhibitory signal delivered by FcγRIIB on DCs, ICs can be transformed into potent maturation agents that result in T cell activation. By applying this approach to immunization using DCs pulsed ex-vivo with ICs, we have successfully generated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in vivo and achieved efficient protective immunity in a murine melanoma model. These findings suggest that ICs typically function to maintain tolerance by binding to inhibitory FcγRs on DCs, but they can be converted into powerful immunogenic stimuli by selectively engaging activating FcγRs. This mechanism presents a promising new strategy for the development of tumor vaccines.

title: Homocysteine and the risk of ischemic stroke in a triethnic cohort: the NOrthern MAnhattan Study.
text:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: The association between mild to moderate fasting total homocysteine (tHcy) levels and the incidence of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular death has not been fully understood, especially in elderly minority subjects. Therefore, we conducted a multiethnic prospective study to investigate this association.

METHODS: A population-based cohort was followed to track vascular events such as stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular death. At baseline, tHcy and methylmalonic acid levels were measured in 2939 subjects, with a mean age of 69+/-10. Among the subjects, 61% were women, 53% were Hispanics, 24% were blacks, and 20% were whites. Cox proportional models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for different tHcy categories, after adjusting for various factors including age, race, education, renal insufficiency, B12 deficiency, and other risk factors.

RESULTS: After adjusting for the aforementioned factors, the highest adjusted HR was observed for a tHcy level > or =15 micromol/L compared to <10 micromol/L, with the greatest risk for vascular death (HR=6.04; 95% CI, 3.44 to 10.60). This was followed by combined vascular events (HR=2.27; 95% CI, 1.51 to 3.43), ischemic stroke (HR=2.01; 95% CI, 1.00 to 4.05), and nonvascular death (HR=2.02; 95% CI, 1.31 to 3.14). Mild to moderate elevations of tHcy levels between 10 to 15 micromol/L were not significantly predictive of ischemic stroke, but did increase the risk of vascular death (HR=2.27; 95% CI, 1.44 to 3.60) and combined vascular events (HR=1.42; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.88). The impact of tHcy levels was stronger among whites and Hispanics, but it was not a significant risk factor for blacks.

CONCLUSIONS: Elevations in total homocysteine levels above 15 micromol/L independently increase the risk of ischemic stroke, while mild elevations of tHcy levels between 10 to 15 micromol/L are less predictive. The vascular effects of tHcy are more pronounced in whites and Hispanics, but less significant in blacks.

title: Expression and purification of recombinant methylated HBHA in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
text: The Heparin-Binding Haemagglutinin (HBHA) is a protein found in Mycobacterium tuberculosis that plays a role in spreading the bacteria from the initial infection site. It is also being considered as a potential component for a new tuberculosis vaccine. Methylation, a process that adds a methyl group to the protein, has been found to affect the protein's immunological properties. We wanted to investigate if we could produce methylated HBHA in fast-growing mycobacteria for further study in immunology and biochemistry. We cloned the complete coding sequence of HBHA into a plasmid called pMV206, using a strong promoter (hsp60) or its own promoter. We then introduced these constructs into Mycobacterium smegmatis and checked for the presence of HBHA protein using specific antibodies. Our findings showed that producing large amounts of intact protein was harmful to the mycobacteria. We were only able to obtain methylated HBHA in M. smegmatis when using a weaker promoter than hsp60, and the complete gene sequence was necessary for successful methylation. We successfully created a recombinant M. smegmatis strain (pMV3-38) that expressed a histidine-tagged methylated HBHA, which could be easily purified. Using fast-growing M. smegmatis strains to produce significant quantities of purified HBHA protein in a short period of time could be an effective approach for evaluating a new HBHA-based tuberculosis vaccine candidate.

title: Detection of alternative lengthening of telomeres by telomere quantitative PCR
text: One of the two known mechanisms for maintaining the length of telomeres, called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), is crucial for the unlimited growth potential of cancer cells. However, current methods for detecting ALT in tumors are time-consuming and require a significant amount of tumor material, making it challenging to study the prevalence and prognostic importance of ALT in large groups of tumors. In this study, we propose a new approach that utilizes telomere quantitative PCR to diagnose ALT. This protocol is faster than traditional methods and examines two distinct characteristics of ALT cells simultaneously: long telomeres and the presence of C-circles (partially double-stranded circles of telomeric C-strand DNA). By only requiring 30 ng of genomic DNA, this protocol will enable extensive investigations of ALT in tumors and can be easily implemented by clinical laboratories.

title: Noise and interlocking signaling pathways promote distinct transcription factor dynamics in response to different stresses
text: Elaborate stress-sensing networks enable all cells to perceive and react to environmental stresses. In yeast cells, stress is detected through various signaling pathways that ultimately converge on the transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4. These transcription factors respond by initiating rapid and unique cycles of movement into and out of the nucleus. To comprehend the significance of the dynamics of Msn2/4 nuclear localization, we conducted time-lapse studies of Msn2-GFP localization in living cells and employed computational modeling of stress-sensing signaling networks. Our findings reveal that multiple signaling pathways, such as Ras/protein kinase A, AMP-activated kinase, the high-osmolarity response mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and protein phosphatase 1, regulate the activation of Msn2 in distinct manners in response to different stresses. Furthermore, we discovered that bursts of nuclear localization elicit a more robust transcriptional response compared to sustained nuclear localization. Through stochastic modeling, we were able to replicate the responses of Msn2 to various stresses in a virtual environment. This modeling demonstrated that bursts of localization arise from noise in the signaling pathways, which is amplified by the limited number of Msn2 molecules present in the cell. This noise contributes to diverse behaviors in genetically identical cells, enabling cell populations to adapt to an uncertain future and strike a balance between growth and survival in an unpredictable environment.

title: Long-term financing needs for HIV control in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015-2050: a modelling study.
text: The objectives of this study were to estimate the funding needed for HIV treatment and prevention in nine sub-Saharan African countries, analyze the gaps between current expenditures and funding obligations, and discuss the policy implications of future financing needs. The researchers used the Goals module from Spectrum and the most up-to-date cost and coverage data to provide estimates for future financing obligations under different scenarios of intervention scale-up. The results showed that the resources required for HIV prevention and treatment ranged from US$98 billion to US$261 billion, depending on the scale-up scenario. The study also found that investing upfront in scale-up of HIV services would reduce HIV incidence and future treatment expenditures. However, the financial obligations were too substantial for most countries to be met from domestic sources alone, highlighting the need for new sources of funding. Debt sustainability for sustained HIV response was identified as an urgent imperative for affected countries and donors.

title: Cell-mediated immunity and antibody responses elicited by attenuated Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi strains used as live oral vaccines in humans.
text: Improving typhoid vaccines is a crucial global public health priority. However, progress has been hindered by a lack of knowledge about the specific factors that contribute to protective immunity against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) infection in humans. While antibodies to S. Typhi O, H, and Vi seem to play a role in protection, it is unclear whether these antibodies alone provide protection, work in conjunction with other immune responses, or simply indicate the presence of other more dominant protective immune responses (such as cell-mediated immunity [CMI]). Immunization with attenuated S. Typhi oral vaccines triggers CMI responses in individuals, including lymphoproliferation, production of type 1 cytokines (such as interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha), and both classical major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class Ia-restricted and novel nonclassical MHC class Ib (human leukocyte antigen [HLA]-E)-restricted CD8(+) cytotoxic T cell responses. Overall, human immunity to S. Typhi following immunization is unexpectedly diverse and intricate. However, the specific immune markers of protection are still largely unknown.

title: Extensive Promoter-Centered Chromatin Interactions Provide a Topological Basis for Transcription Regulation
text: Our understanding of how higher-order chromosomal organization regulates transcription in eukaryotes is limited. To address this, we utilized ChIA-PET, a genome-wide Chromatin Interaction Analysis with Paired-End-Tag sequencing, to map long-range chromatin interactions associated with RNA polymerase II in human cells. Through this analysis, we discovered a wide range of interactions occurring within and between promoters, genes, and regions outside of genes. These interactions formed higher-order clusters, connecting genes that were both close and distant from each other through promoter-promoter interactions. Interestingly, most genes involved in promoter-promoter interactions were actively transcribed in a cooperative manner, suggesting a complex interplay of transcriptional controls. By comparing different cell lines, we observed that cell-specific chromatin interactions played a role in structuring cell-specific transcription, with enhancer-promoter interactions being particularly enriched in cell-specific functions. Additionally, we found that disease-associated noncoding elements were spatially engaged with their corresponding genes through long-range interactions. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the role of three-dimensional chromatin interactions in transcription regulation for both essential and cell-specific genes in human cells.

title: Resazurin microtiter assay plate: simple and inexpensive method for detection of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
text: This article presents a technique for identifying multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis by utilizing a resazurin reduction. A total of eighty clinical isolates were examined for their susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin. The results obtained after 7 days were compared to those obtained through the proportion method. The method demonstrated exceptional specificity and sensitivity. Moreover, it is a straightforward, cost-effective, and swift approach that could potentially be employed for testing other antituberculosis medications.

title: The pervasiveness and plasticity of circadian oscillations: the coupled circadian-oscillators framework.
text:
The role of circadian oscillations in coordinating the homeostasis and behavior of biological systems has been observed in various organisms such as animals, plants, fungi, and cyanobacteria. These oscillations are regulated by genetically encoded molecular clocks present in almost every cell. These clocks rely on negative transcription/translation feedback loops and a small number of genes to maintain the oscillations. However, recent gene expression experiments have shown that a larger fraction of transcripts in a typical tissue oscillate with the day-night cycle, and the specific species that oscillate vary depending on the tissue type. This suggests that a larger fraction of transcripts, and possibly other molecular species, may have the potential for circadian oscillations.

To better understand the pervasiveness and flexibility of circadian oscillations, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of 18 circadian transcriptomic studies and 10 circadian metabolomic studies in mice. These studies were conducted using different tissues and under different conditions. Our findings reveal that more than half of the protein coding genes in a cell can produce circadian transcripts under at least one set of conditions, as can measured metabolites. Genetic or environmental changes can disrupt existing oscillations by altering their amplitudes and phases, suppressing them, or even giving rise to new circadian oscillations. The specific species that oscillate and their patterns provide a unique signature of the physiological state of the corresponding cell or tissue. Molecular networks consist of multiple oscillator loops that have evolved over countless day-night cycles to have an intrinsic circadian frequency. These oscillating loops are interconnected through shared nodes in a large network of coupled circadian oscillators, with the clock genes playing a major role. Cells have the ability to program and re-program their circadian repertoire through epigenetic and other mechanisms.

High-resolution circadian data and tissue/condition-specific networks can be accessed at http://circadiomics.igb.uci.edu. For further information, please contact pfbaldi@ics.uci.edu. Supplementary data can be found online at Bioinformatics.

title: Gene–environment interactions in 7610 women with breast cancer: prospective evidence from the Million Women Study
text:
There is limited information available regarding the combined effects of low-penetrance genetic susceptibility polymorphisms and environmental factors on breast cancer incidence. In order to investigate gene-environment interactions, we conducted a large prospective study in the UK, comparing genotypic relative risks for breast cancer across various risk factors. 

Our study included 7610 women who developed breast cancer and 10,196 controls without the disease. We examined the effects of 12 different polymorphisms in relation to ten established environmental risk factors, such as age at menarche, parity, breastfeeding, and alcohol consumption. 

After considering multiple testing, we did not find any significant evidence of a gene-environment interaction among the 120 comparisons. Contrary to previous suggestions, the genotypic relative risks were not significantly affected by the use of hormone replacement therapy, either overall or for oestrogen-receptor-positive disease. 

Out of the 12 polymorphisms, only one was found to be correlated with any of the ten other risk factors. Carriers of the high-risk C allele of MAP3K1-rs889312 were found to be significantly shorter than non-carriers. 

In conclusion, the risks of breast cancer associated with low-penetrance susceptibility polymorphisms do not vary significantly with the ten established environmental risk factors examined in our study. 

This research was funded by Cancer Research UK and the UK Medical Research Council.

title: Thrombocytopenia as an Indicator of Malaria in Adult Population
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to assess the predictive value of thrombocytopenia in malaria.
Patients and Methods: This study was conducted as a prospective observational study on febrile patients with thrombocytopenia who presented to the Medical Unit of Hayat Abad Medical Complex between November 2008 and November 2010.
Results: Out of the 228 patients with fever and thrombocytopenia, 121 patients (53%) were diagnosed with malaria. Among these, 82 patients (68%) had falciparum malaria and 39 patients (32%) had vivax infection. The platelet counts in these 121 patients ranged from 25,000 to 150,000/dL, with a mean value of 101,000/dL (SD ± 47,500) and a median of 75,000/dL. Among the 107 patients who did not have malaria, the platelet counts ranged from 10,000 to 150,000/dL, with a mean value of 58,000/dL (SD ± 54,000) and a median of 50,000/dL.
Conclusions: Thrombocytopenia may serve as a predictor of malaria in the adult population.

title: AMPA receptor ligand binding domain mobility revealed by functional cross linking.
text:
Glutamate receptors play a crucial role in transmitting excitatory signals in the central nervous system (CNS). Among these receptors, the AMPA-subtype exhibits rapid kinetics, with activation, deactivation, and desensitization occurring within milliseconds or even faster. Through crystallographic, biochemical, and functional studies, it has been suggested that GluR2 Cys mutants, which form intermolecular disulfide cross-links between the lower D2 lobes of the ligand binding cores, can be trapped in a conformation representing the desensitized state. To investigate this further, we utilized multi-channel rapid perfusion techniques to examine the state dependence of cross-linking in these mutants.

Under reducing conditions, both the wild-type GluR2 and the G725C and S729C mutants displayed normal activation and desensitization kinetics. However, the Cys mutants could be efficiently trapped in nonconducting states when oxidized. In contrast, the I664C mutant only experienced partial inactivation under oxidizing conditions. For the S729C mutant, disulfide cross-links formed rapidly when the receptors were desensitized in the presence of glutamate. Interestingly, receptors also became trapped at rest, in the absence of agonist. We evaluated this spontaneous trapping under various conditions, including the presence of CNQX, a competitive antagonist, kainate, a weak partial agonist, or when desensitization was blocked by the L483Y mutation, which stabilizes the D1 dimer interface.

These experiments revealed that trapping in the absence of glutamate is attributed to two motions: the spontaneous breaking of the D1 dimer interface and the hyperextension of the lower lobes of the ligand binding core. These findings demonstrate that the glutamate binding domains exhibit surprising mobility in the absence of ligand, potentially influencing receptor activity in the brain.

title: Ncf1 (p47phox) Is Essential for Direct Regulatory T Cell Mediated Suppression of CD4+ Effector T Cells
text:
BACKGROUND
Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain how CD4+FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress CD4+ effector T cells (Teffs), but none fully account for this suppression. Previous research suggests that Tregs may influence the redox state of the microenvironment. Given the sensitivity of T cells to redox changes, we investigated whether oxidants could directly mediate the suppression of Teffs by Tregs.

METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS
We isolated Tregs and Teffs from the spleens of wild type (WT) C57BL/6 mice or Ncf1(p47phox)-deficient C57BL/6 mice, which lack NADPH oxidase function. Teffs were labeled with CFSE and co-cultured with unlabeled Tregs at different Treg:Teff ratios in the presence of anti-CD3/CD28 coated beads for 3 days in suppression assays. We quantified Treg-mediated suppression by analyzing CFSE dilution in Teffs using flow cytometry. The presence of antioxidants such as n-acetylcysteine (NAC) or 2-mercaptoethanol, or inhibitors of NADPH oxidase (diphenyleneiodonium and VAS-2870), led to reduced suppression mediated by WT Tregs. This suppression was partially dependent on TGFβ, as it was partially blocked by neutralizing antibodies. The suppression of Teff proliferation induced by exogenous TGFβ treatment could be overcome with NAC. Ncf1-deficient Teffs were slightly but significantly less sensitive to suppression by exogenous TGFβ compared to WT Teffs. Ncf1-deficient Tregs poorly suppressed Ncf1-deficient Teffs compared to WT controls. In assays with WT Tregs and Ncf1-deficient Teffs, there was partial but incomplete reconstitution of suppression.

CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE
Our findings suggest that ROS derived from NADPH oxidase play a role in the direct suppression of CD4+ effector T cells by Tregs. This process can be blocked by thiol-containing antioxidants, NADPH oxidase inhibitors, or a lack of Ncf1 expression in Tregs and Teffs. Oxidants may represent a potential new target for therapeutic modulation of Treg function.

title: Oxidative damage targets complexes containing DNA methyltransferases, SIRT1, and polycomb members to promoter CpG Islands.
text: Cancer cells exhibit both widespread losses and gains in DNA methylation. Our study reveals that when cellular oxidative stress is induced through hydrogen peroxide treatment, DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) is recruited to damaged chromatin. DNMT1 then becomes part of a complex that includes DNMT3B and members of the polycomb repressive complex 4. As a result of hydrogen peroxide treatment, these proteins relocate from non-GC-rich regions to GC-rich areas. In an in vivo colitis model, key components of this complex are also found to be enriched at gene promoters. While high-expression genes that are enriched for complex members show changes in histone marks and nascent transcription, low-expression genes containing CpG islands experience an increase in promoter DNA methylation. Therefore, oxidative damage triggers the formation and relocation of a silencing complex, which may contribute to the cancer-specific abnormal DNA methylation and transcriptional silencing.

title: Expression profiles during dedifferentiation in newt lens regeneration revealed by expressed sequence tags
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the process of lens regeneration in adult newts by examining the dedifferentiation of pigmented epithelial cells (PECs) in the dorsal iris. To achieve this, the researchers purified mRNA from the iris during dedifferentiation and created a cDNA library. They then sequenced and analyzed 10,449 clones from the library. The results showed that 780 contigs and 1,666 singlets were annotated from the reads. Interestingly, the presence of cancer- and apoptosis-related genes during newt dedifferentiation was discovered, suggesting their potential role in the process. Additionally, several candidate genes that may be involved in reprogramming during dedifferentiation were identified. These findings suggest that the expression of cancer- and apoptosis-related genes could serve as markers during dedifferentiation. The sequence information obtained from this study is available in GenBank with accession numbers FS290155-FS300559, providing a valuable resource for future research on newt dedifferentiation.

title: In vivo proliferation and cell cycle kinetics of long-term self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), which are rare, need to undergo a significant expansion in order to produce mature blood cells. By isolating HSC from mice, we have the opportunity to directly determine their proliferation kinetics. In our study, we examined the proliferation and cell cycle kinetics of long-term self-renewing HSC (LT-HSC) in normal adult mice. We found that at any given time, around 5% of LT-HSC were in the S/G2/M phases of the cell cycle, while another 20% were in the G1 phase. To determine the rate at which different groups of HSC entered the cell cycle over time, we used BrdUrd incorporation. We discovered that approximately 50% of LT-HSC incorporated BrdUrd within 6 days, and over 90% incorporated it within 30 days. By 6 months, 99% of LT-HSC had incorporated BrdUrd. Based on our calculations, we estimated that about 8% of LT-HSC entered the cell cycle asynchronously each day. Through nested reverse transcription-PCR analysis, we observed a high expression of cyclin D2 in a significant proportion of LT-HSC. Although approximately 75% of LT-HSC were in a quiescent state (G0) at any given time, all HSC were regularly recruited into the cell cycle, resulting in 99% of LT-HSC dividing on average every 57 days.

title: The role of the tissue omega-6/omega-3 fatty acid ratio in regulating tumor angiogenesis
text: Angiogenesis plays a crucial role in the growth and spread of tumors. It is widely known that omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids, which are essential nutrients obtained from the diet and cannot be produced by mammals, have different effects on cellular processes. Omega-6 fatty acid-derived metabolites promote angiogenesis by increasing the expression of growth factors, while omega-3 fatty acids have properties that inhibit angiogenesis and tumor growth. However, most studies have overlooked the importance of the ratio between omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids in angiogenesis, instead focusing solely on their absolute levels. This article emphasizes the biochemical interactions between omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids and highlights how the ratio between these two types of fatty acids in tissues affects tumor angiogenesis. We propose that future research should consider the omega-6/omega-3 fatty acid ratio as a critical factor in experimental design and analysis. Additionally, we recommend that clinical interventions aim to both decrease omega-6 metabolites and increase omega-3 fatty acid intake.

title: The Natural Statistics of Audiovisual Speech
text: Humans, like other animals, are constantly exposed to a variety of signals that are dynamic, multimodal, extended, and constantly changing. These signals need to be processed and transmitted by our sensory systems to the brain, where they help us choose appropriate actions. To simplify this complex process, it has been proposed that the brain takes advantage of statistical patterns in the stimuli. However, most studies on this topic have focused on single-mode signals and natural scenes, leaving a gap in our understanding of the statistical properties of human speech, which is a type of multisensory signal. We don't know which signals our brain actively combines from an audiovisual speech stream to form a perception, and which signals are already present in the structure of the stream itself. In this study, we identified several important statistical features of audiovisual speech. Firstly, we found strong correlations and temporal alignment between the mouth opening and the acoustic envelope. Secondly, we discovered that the mouth opening is most strongly correlated with vocal tract resonances. Thirdly, we observed that both the mouth opening and the voice envelope are modulated in the frequency range of 2-7 Hz. Finally, we consistently observed that the timing of mouth movements relative to the voice onset falls between 100 and 300 ms. These findings are consistent with recent neural theories of speech, which propose that speech communication is a reciprocal and multisensory process, where the signals produced by the speaker are matched to the neural processes of the listener.

title: Establishment of human iPSC-based models for the study and targeting of glioma initiating cells
text: The transformation of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) can give rise to glioma tumour-initiating cells (GTICs). Previous studies on GTICs have mainly focused on primary tumours and the use of human embryonic material. However, recent research has provided insights into the somatic genomic landscape of human gliomas. It has been found that dysregulation of RTK (receptor tyrosine kinase) and p53 signalling occurs in approximately 90% and 86% of primary tumours, respectively. In this study, we explore the use of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) to model gliomagenesis. By inducing dysregulation of RTK and p53 signalling in hiPSC-derived NPCs (iNPCs), we are able to replicate GTIC properties in vitro. Furthermore, transplantation of transformed iNPCs into animals leads to the formation of highly aggressive tumours containing both undifferentiated stem cells and their differentiated derivatives. We also discover that metabolic modulation can compromise the viability of GTICs. Additionally, through screening 101 anti-cancer compounds, we identify three molecules that specifically target transformed iNPCs and primary GTICs. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of hiPSCs as a valuable tool for studying human tumourigenesis.

title: Thyroid Hormone Receptor Repression Linked to Type I Pneumocyte Associated Respiratory Distress Syndrome
text: The formation of type I pneumocytes, which are responsible for gas exchange in the lungs, is not well understood. However, it is known that the glucocorticoid receptor and its ligand can promote the maturation of type II pneumocytes. Glucocorticoids are often given to infants with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) to reduce its severity. In this study, we found that mice with mutations in the nuclear co-repressor SMRT develop a previously unknown form of RDS due to premature development of type I pneumocytes. Interestingly, these mice do not respond to glucocorticoids, but treatment with anti-thyroid hormone drugs rescues the RDS. This suggests that the thyroid hormone receptor (TR) plays an important role in lung development that was previously unrecognized. We discovered that TR and SMRT control the differentiation of type I pneumocytes through a protein called Klf2, which activates the genes responsible for type I pneumocyte development. Additionally, mice without Klf2 in their lungs do not have mature type I pneumocytes and die shortly after birth, similar to the SMRT mutant mice. These findings reveal TR as a second nuclear receptor involved in lung development, specifically in the differentiation of type I pneumocytes. They also suggest a potential new treatment option for RDS that does not respond to glucocorticoids.

title: Assessing the ceRNA hypothesis with quantitative measurements of miRNA and target abundance.
text: Recent research has shown that competitive endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) can act as sponges for microRNAs (miRNAs) by binding to their binding sites. It has also been found that changes in the abundance of ceRNAs from specific genes can influence the activity of miRNAs. To better understand this hypothesis, it is important to determine the quantitative relationship between a miRNA and its endogenous target sites. In this study, we manipulated the abundance of target sites within cells by expressing a miR-122 target in hepatocytes and livers. We then examined the impact on miR-122 target genes. We observed that repression of the target was released in a threshold-like manner when target site abundance was high (≥1.5 × 10(5) added target sites per cell). Interestingly, this threshold was not affected by the levels of the miRNA. Additionally, in liver disease models that caused extreme metabolic changes, the overall abundance of target sites in hepatocytes did not change enough to significantly impact miRNA-mediated repression. Therefore, it is unlikely that modulation of miRNA target abundance through ceRNA effects will have significant effects on gene expression and metabolism.

title: Immunological mechanisms for desensitization and tolerance in food allergy
text: Food allergy is a significant concern for public health in developed countries, with an estimated prevalence of 5% in children and 3-4% in adults. Currently, allergen-specific immunotherapy for food allergy is being actively studied, but it is still considered experimental. The most effective approach, including the method of administering the food, the appropriate maintenance dose, and the duration of maintenance therapy, as well as the ideal candidates for these procedures, are still being determined. The mechanisms that lead to successful food desensitization are also not fully understood, partly due to the lack of a standardized immunotherapy protocol. However, potential mechanisms may involve the suppression of mast cells and basophils, the production of food-specific IgG4 antibodies, a decrease in the ratio of food-specific IgE/IgG4, the increase and expansion of natural or inducible regulatory T cells, a shift from a Th2 to a Th1 immune response, and the induction of anergy or deletion in antigen-specific cells. Further research is necessary to uncover and comprehend these mechanisms, which could potentially identify valuable biomarkers for evaluating and monitoring food allergic patients undergoing immunotherapy.

title: Prodromal non-motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease
text: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor symptoms such as bradykinesia, muscular rigidity, and tremor. These symptoms occur due to the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Recent studies have shown that Lewy bodies, which are intraneuronal markers of PD, accumulate in various types of neurons throughout the brain. This suggests that PD is not solely a disease that affects dopaminergic neurons in the mesencephalon, but rather a severe multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder. Furthermore, the neuropathological changes outside the substantia nigra are closely associated with the non-motor symptoms of PD. This has led to increased interest in identifying prodromal non-motor symptoms of PD. Autonomic disturbances, olfactory dysfunctions, depression, and sleep disorders, particularly REM-sleep behavior disorder, have been suggested as potential prodromal non-motor symptoms of PD based on literature findings. Various tests are available to detect most of these symptoms. Identifying prodromal non-motor symptoms could contribute to early diagnosis of PD and may be useful in testing the effectiveness of neuroprotective treatments in the future.

title: Erythroid Krüppel-Like Factor Directly Activates the Basic Krüppel-Like Factor Gene in Erythroid Cells �
text: The Sp/Krüppel-like factor (Sp/Klf) family consists of approximately 25 zinc finger transcription factors that recognize CACCC boxes and GC-rich elements. We have investigated the basic Krüppel-like factor (Bklf/Klf3) and have found that its expression in erythroid tissues is highly dependent on another family member, erythroid Krüppel-like factor (Eklf/Klf1). We have observed a significant reduction in Bklf mRNA in erythroid tissues from Eklf-null murine embryos. Our findings indicate that Bklf is primarily regulated by two promoters: a GC-rich upstream promoter, 1a, which is active in all cell types, and an erythroid downstream promoter, 1b. Both promoters produce transcripts that encode identical proteins. Interestingly, both the ubiquitous and erythroid promoters are dependent on Eklf in erythroid cells. In transient assays, Eklf activates both promoters. Experiments using an inducible form of Eklf have shown that the endogenous Bklf gene is activated even in the presence of a protein synthesis inhibitor.
