title: Fibrillar Collagen Inhibits Arterial Smooth Muscle Proliferation through Regulation of Cdk2 Inhibitors
text: Smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the arteries are halted in the G1 phase of the cell cycle when they come into contact with polymerized type I collagen fibrils. However, when SMCs are exposed to monomer collagen, their proliferation is supported. On polymerized collagen, the phosphorylation of cyclin E-associated kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (cdk2) is inhibited, and the levels of the cdk2 inhibitors p27Kip1 and p21Cip1/Waf1 are increased compared to SMCs on monomer collagen. In SMCs on polymerized collagen, p27Kip1 binds to the cyclin E-cdk2-p21Cip1/Waf1 complex. Blocking antibodies to alpha2 integrins, which are responsible for adhesion to both forms of collagen, produce similar effects on monomer collagen. Additionally, polymerized collagen quickly suppresses p70 S6 kinase, which may regulate p27Kip1. Therefore, fibrillar collagen specifically controls early integrin signaling, which could result in the up-regulation of cdk2 inhibitors and the inhibition of SMC proliferation.

title: Memory CD4+ T cells induce innate responses independently of pathogen
text: We investigated whether the adaptive immune system can influence the nature and strength of innate inflammatory responses. Specifically, we examined the impact of memory and naive CD4+ T cells on the production of multiple innate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (IICs) in the lung. Our findings revealed that memory CD4+ T cells, but not naive cells, significantly enhance the production of IICs during influenza infection, leading to early control of the virus. This effect is dependent on the recognition of specific antigens by memory cells and is most effective when these cells are polarized towards T helper type 1 (TH1) or TH17. Interestingly, this response is not reliant on interferon-γ (IFN-γ) or tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) production, nor does it require the activation of conserved pathogen recognition pathways. This discovery unveils a novel mechanism by which memory CD4+ T cells stimulate an early innate response, thereby bolstering immune protection against pathogens.

title: Direct Upregulation of STAT3 by MicroRNA-551b-3p Deregulates Growth and Metastasis of Ovarian Cancer.
text: The amplification of 3q26.2 in high-grade serous ovarian cancer results in an increase in the expression of mature microRNA miR551b-3p, which is linked to a negative clinical outcome. It is noteworthy that miR551b-3p contributes to resistance against apoptosis and promotes the survival and proliferation of cancer cells both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. miR551b-3p enhances the levels of STAT3 protein, and the presence of STAT3 is necessary for the effects of miR551b-3p on cell proliferation. Contrary to expectations, instead of reducing the levels of target mRNA, our research demonstrates that miR551b-3p binds to a complementary sequence on the STAT3 promoter, attracting RNA polymerase II and the TWIST1 transcription factor to activate STAT3 transcription, thereby directly increasing STAT3 expression. Additionally, the inhibition of miR551b-3p reduced STAT3 expression in ovarian cancer cells in laboratory settings and in living organisms, leading to a decrease in ovarian cancer growth. Collectively, our findings highlight the involvement of miR551b-3p in transcriptional activation. Consequently, miR551b-3p emerges as a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target for ovarian cancer.

title: Human albumin administration in critically ill patients: systematic review of randomised controlled trials.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to assess the impact of administering human albumin or plasma protein fraction on mortality rates in critically ill patients.

DESIGN: This study involved a systematic review of randomized controlled trials that compared the administration of albumin or plasma protein fraction with no administration or the administration of crystalloid solution in critically ill patients with hypovolemia, burns, or hypoalbuminemia.

SUBJECTS: A total of 30 randomized controlled trials, including 1419 patients, were included in the analysis.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The main outcome measure was the mortality rate from all causes at the end of the follow-up period for each trial.

RESULTS: The results showed that the risk of death was higher in the albumin-treated group compared to the comparison group for each patient category. The relative risk of death after albumin administration was 1.46 (95% confidence interval 0.97 to 2.22) for hypovolemia, 2.40 (1.11 to 5.19) for burns, and 1.69 (1.07 to 2.67) for hypoalbuminemia. The pooled relative risk of death with albumin administration was 1.68 (1.26 to 2.23). The pooled difference in the risk of death with albumin was 6% (95% confidence interval 3% to 9%) using a fixed effects model. These findings suggest that for every 17 critically ill patients treated with albumin, there is one additional death.

CONCLUSIONS: The study concludes that there is no evidence to support the use of albumin administration in reducing mortality rates in critically ill patients with hypovolemia, burns, or hypoalbuminemia. In fact, there is a strong suggestion that it may increase mortality. Therefore, the use of human albumin in critically ill patients should be urgently reviewed and limited to rigorously conducted, randomized controlled trials.

title: A fine-scale map of recombination rates and hotspots across the human genome.
text: Genetic maps are crucial tools for genetic analyses as they provide information on the variation of recombination rates across a genome. In this study, we present a highly detailed genetic map of the human genome. By analyzing genetic variation data, we have identified over 25,000 recombination hotspots. Additionally, we have discovered specific motifs and sequence contexts that influence hotspot activity. Our findings indicate that recombination rates behave differently on large (megabase) and small (kilobase) scales. Based on this observation, we propose a two-stage model for recombination. According to this model, hotspots are random occurrences within a framework where large-scale rates are regulated.

title: Mental Health Support Provided Throughout the Bariatric Surgery Clinical Pathway in French Specialized Care Centers for Obesity
text: International guidelines recommend that bariatric surgery candidates undergo pre-operative psychological assessment. Therefore, it is recommended that bariatric patient care teams include at least one mental health provider, such as a psychologist or psychiatrist. The aim of this study was to assess the availability and practices of psychology and psychiatry resources in the 37 specialized obesity centers (CSOs) established by the French Ministry of Health. CSO coordinators were contacted via email to gather general information about the centers, including the number of bariatric operations performed. Additionally, psychologists and psychiatrists from each center completed an anonymous questionnaire to evaluate their professional practices and organization of care pathways. The survey received responses from the majority of CSO coordinators (81%, n = 26/32). The results revealed significant differences and deficiencies in terms of available psychology/psychiatry resources. Most psychologists (n = 26/31) and psychiatrists (n = 10/10) reported that they only meet new patients before surgery (56%) or both before and after the operation (30%). However, a small percentage of psychologists and psychiatrists (14%) do not consistently meet with all patients (before and/or after surgery). Nevertheless, all professionals provide psychology assessments, and approximately 75% of them offer psychological follow-up, indicating similarities in the practices of psychologists and psychiatrists. The findings highlight the importance of psychological/psychiatric evaluations in French CSOs and underscore the lack of mental health providers in several of these services. Post-operative psychological follow-up is typically not provided, suggesting the need for clear recommendations regarding long-term psychological or psychiatric follow-up after surgery.

title: Calcium: Regulation of cell death: the calcium–apoptosis link
text: The question of whether to live or die is of utmost importance, as it beautifully captures the dual nature of Ca2+ in living beings - a factor essential for survival or a merciless destroyer. For a long time, it has been understood that Ca2+ signals play a crucial role in numerous vital functions of cells, thus being indispensable for their survival. However, it has now become evident that an excessive accumulation of Ca2+ within cells or disruption of its proper distribution can lead to cellular toxicity, resulting in either programmed cell death (apoptosis) or uncontrolled cell death (necrosis).

title: Breaking the code of DNA binding specificity of TAL-type III effectors.
text: The ability of many bacteria to cause disease relies on their ability to inject effector proteins into eukaryotic cells through type III secretion. This injection allows the bacteria to manipulate cellular processes. TAL (transcription activator-like) effectors, found in plant pathogenic Xanthomonas, are crucial virulence factors that function as transcriptional activators in the nucleus of plant cells. They achieve this by directly binding to DNA using a central domain made up of repeated sequences. In this study, we demonstrate how the TAL effectors achieve specificity in binding to target DNA. Each repeat contains two highly variable amino acid residues that recognize a single base pair in the target DNA. We were able to predict and confirm the recognition sequences of TAL effectors through experiments. The modular structure of these proteins also allowed us to create artificial effectors with new specificities. Our research sheds light on the functionality of a unique DNA binding domain and provides a framework for designing DNA binding domains for biotechnological applications.

title: Interferon-Gamma at the Crossroads of Tumor Immune Surveillance or Evasion
text: Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) is a versatile molecule that has various effects on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and tumor growth. It is often considered a key player in the immune response and has been used to treat several diseases, despite its negative side effects. Although there is strong evidence linking IFN-γ to tumor immune surveillance, clinical trials using IFN-γ-based therapies have had limited success. Recent reports suggest that IFN-γ may actually promote tumor growth by making cells less responsive to its signaling, reducing the expression of important immune molecules, and increasing the activity of proteins that inhibit cell death. However, IFN-γ-mediated responses have been shown to improve patient survival in certain cancers. Therefore, it is crucial to conduct further research to understand how IFN-γ works in the tumor microenvironment and its complex effects on the immune system. This review explores the current understanding of IFN-γ's pro- and anti-tumor effects, emphasizing the importance of identifying patients who will respond well to IFN-γ-based therapies for better treatment outcomes.

title: Role of antioxidants in paraquat toxicity.
text: Paraquat, a herbicide containing quarternary nitrogen, is an extremely toxic compound that poses a significant threat to both humans and animals. Numerous cases of acute poisoning and fatalities have been reported in recent decades. The toxicity of paraquat operates through two main mechanisms. Firstly, it generates the superoxide anion, which can further produce highly toxic reactive oxygen species like hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radical. Secondly, it oxidizes the cellular NADPH, which is crucial for reducing paraquat within cells. This oxidation disrupts important biochemical processes that rely on NADPH. The primary cause of death in paraquat poisoning is respiratory failure, resulting from oxidative damage to the alveolar epithelium and subsequent fibrosis. The management of paraquat poisoning has primarily focused on supportive care and modifying the toxicokinetics of the poison. Unfortunately, there are currently no effective pharmacological antagonists or chelating agents capable of binding paraquat in the bloodstream or tissues. However, recognizing that paraquat exerts its toxic effects through oxidative stress-mediated mechanisms, efforts have been made to explore the use of antioxidants in managing paraquat poisoning. This review presents the current status of antioxidants in alleviating or treating the toxic effects induced by paraquat.

title: Nucleation of nuclear bodies by RNA
text: The mechanisms behind the development of various functional compartments within the nucleus of mammalian cells are not well understood. Specifically, the initial step in the formation of nuclear bodies is still largely unknown. In this study, we present evidence that RNA can serve as both a structural component and a catalyst for the formation of nuclear bodies. We have discovered that different types of coding and noncoding RNAs are capable of assembling histone locus bodies (alongside Cajal bodies), nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and nuclear stress bodies from scratch, and are naturally abundant in these structures. The formation of nuclear bodies is facilitated by the recruitment and accumulation of proteins that are already present in these structures, triggered by the presence of nucleating RNA. These findings highlight the crucial role of transcription in the formation of nuclear bodies and demonstrate that RNA transcripts can act as a framework for the development of major nuclear structures. Overall, our data suggest that the biogenesis of nuclear bodies is a fundamental principle of nuclear organization, with RNA playing a key role in this process.

title: Evaluation of human papillomavirus testing in primary screening for cervical abnormalities: comparison of sensitivity, specificity, and frequency of referral.
text:
The clinical usefulness of human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing in women with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) detected through Papanicolaou (Pap) smears has been established. However, the effectiveness of HPV DNA testing alone as a primary screening method is still uncertain. This study aimed to determine the accuracy of HPV DNA testing in detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 3 or cancer, which is considered the gold standard. 

Between December 1997 and October 2000, a total of 4075 women attending Planned Parenthood clinics in Washington State were simultaneously screened using thin-layer Pap and HPV DNA testing. Two different methods, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and liquid-based RNA-DNA hybridization capture with signal amplification assay (signal amplification), were used for HPV DNA testing. Women who tested positive for high-risk HPV types or had Pap results of ASCUS or higher were considered to have positive screening results and were referred for colposcopy and biopsy. A random sample of women with negative screening results was also referred for colposcopy. 

Based on the results of the thin-layer Pap, HPV PCR, and HPV signal amplification tests from the screening and colposcopy visits, seven colposcopy triage strategies were defined and evaluated. The main outcome measures were the sensitivity and specificity of each triage strategy in detecting CIN 3 or higher. 

The estimated prevalence of CIN 3 or higher was 3.2%. The sensitivity of thin-layer Pap (with a result of ≥ ASCUS) in identifying women with CIN 3 or higher was only 61.3%, compared to 88.2% for HPV testing by PCR and 90.8% for signal amplification. Differences in specificities were also observed: 82.4% for thin-layer Pap (with a result of ≥ ASCUS), 78.8% for PCR, and 72.6% for signal amplification. 

Compared to referring all women with ASCUS or higher for colposcopy, using signal amplification testing for women with ASCUS and referring those with a positive result had similar sensitivity (61.3% vs 60.3%) and significantly higher specificity (82.4% vs 88.9%). The strategy of requiring repeat positive PCR tests on two visits had a sensitivity of 84.2% and a specificity of 86.2%. All tests were more specific and less sensitive in women aged 30 years or older compared to younger women. 

In conclusion, HPV testing has higher sensitivity but lower specificity compared to thin-layer Pap screening. In certain settings, especially where screening intervals are irregular or infrequent, HPV DNA testing may be a reasonable alternative to cytology-based screening for women of reproductive age.

title: Breaking the chains: structure and function of the deubiquitinases
text: Ubiquitylation, a reversible protein modification, plays a crucial role in various cellular functions. Recent advancements have significantly contributed to understanding a group of isopeptidases called deubiquitinases (DUBs), which remove ubiquitin. These enzymes exhibit diverse mechanistic features, indicating a lack of uniformity in structure and function. Despite the relatively small number of DUBs (<100), their selectivity is not compromised as they are regulated by multiple layers of control that influence both their activity and specificity. Given their significant involvement in essential regulatory processes, these enzymes hold potential as novel therapeutic targets.

title: Replication protein A: a heterotrimeric, single-stranded DNA-binding protein required for eukaryotic DNA metabolism.
text: Replication protein A (RPA), also known as replication factor A (RFA) and human single-stranded DNA-binding protein, is an essential protein involved in various processes of eukaryotic DNA metabolism. These processes include DNA replication, DNA repair, and recombination. RPA homologues have been found in all eukaryotic organisms studied so far. They are abundant heterotrimeric proteins consisting of subunits weighing approximately 70, 30, and 14 kDa. This protein family binds to single-stranded DNA in a non-specific manner and interacts with multiple proteins, either modifying their activities or forming interactions with them. When RPA is bound to single-stranded DNA, it can be phosphorylated by DNA-dependent protein kinase, particularly during the S phase and after DNA damage. This phosphorylation event may play a crucial role in coordinating DNA metabolism within the cell. Additionally, RPA might also have a role in regulating gene expression.

title: Internal fixation versus nonoperative treatment of displaced 3-part proximal humeral fractures in elderly patients: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the outcomes of elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus who were randomly assigned to either treatment with a locking plate or nonoperative treatment over a 2-year period. A total of 60 patients, with a mean age of 74 years (ranging from 56 to 92), were included in the study, with 81% of them being women. The main measures used to assess the outcomes were the Constant and Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) scores, as well as the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) based on the EQ-5D.

After the final 2-year follow-up, the results showed that the locking plate group had better range of motion (ROM), function, and HRQoL compared to the nonoperative group. The mean flexion in the locking plate group was 120°, while it was 111° in the nonoperative group (P = .36). Similarly, the mean abduction was 114° in the locking plate group compared to 106° in the nonoperative group (P = .28). The Constant score was 61 in the locking plate group versus 58 in the nonoperative group (P = .64), and the DASH score was 26 versus 35 (P = .19). The mean EQ-5D (index) score was 0.70 in the locking plate group compared to 0.59 in the nonoperative group (P = .26).

Despite achieving good primary reduction in 86% of the fractures in the locking plate group, 13% of the patients required a major reoperation due to fracture complications, and 17% underwent a minor reoperation. In conclusion, our study suggests that treatment with a locking plate leads to better functional outcomes and HRQoL in elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus, although it comes with the drawback of additional surgery in 30% of the patients.

title: Good and bad consequences of altered fatty acid metabolism in heart failure: evidence from mouse models.
text: The preference for using glucose instead of fatty acid oxidation (FAO) in heart failure has traditionally been seen as a way to conserve oxygen. As a result, inhibiting FAO has become an accepted method for treating heart failure. However, recent evidence suggests that relying more on glucose may actually harm the failing heart rather than help it. This article explores new findings on metabolic adaptations in heart failure, with a specific focus on studies using mouse models to manipulate cardiac FA metabolism at different stages of the FA metabolic pathway. We also examine how these manipulations affect cardiac function in both ischemic and non-ischemic heart failure, and whether they offer any protection against heart failure.

title: Pericytes of human skeletal muscle are myogenic precursors distinct from satellite cells
text: Cells derived from blood vessels in human skeletal muscle have the ability to regenerate skeletal muscle, similar to embryonic mesoangioblasts. However, these adult cells do not express endothelial markers. Instead, they express markers of pericytes, such as NG2 proteoglycan and alkaline phosphatase (ALP). These cells can be isolated from freshly dissociated ALP+ cells. Unlike satellite cells, which are canonical myogenic precursors, pericyte-derived cells only express myogenic markers when they differentiate into myotubes. They have a high efficiency in spontaneously forming myotubes. When these cells are transplanted into mice with severe combined immune deficiency-X-linked muscular dystrophy (scid-mdx), they colonize the host muscle and generate numerous fibers that express human dystrophin. Similar cells isolated from patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and engineered to express human mini-dystrophin, also give rise to many fibers that are positive for dystrophin in vivo. These findings suggest that myogenic precursors, which are distinct from satellite cells, are associated with the walls of microvessels in human skeletal muscle. They may be a correlate of embryonic mesoangioblasts that are present after birth and could be a promising candidate for future cell therapy protocols in patients.

title: Ten years' experience with alendronate for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women.
text:
In this study, we investigated the long-term effects of alendronate, an antiresorptive agent commonly used to treat osteoporosis, in postmenopausal women. The study was conducted over a period of 10 years and involved a multinational, randomized, double-blind design.

During the initial three-year phase of the study, we compared three different daily doses of alendronate with a placebo. Women who initially received the placebo were later given alendronate in years 4 and 5 before being discharged from the study. On the other hand, women who were initially in the active-treatment groups continued to receive alendronate during the first extension (years 4 and 5). In the subsequent extensions (years 6 and 7, and 8 through 10), women who received either 5 mg or 10 mg of alendronate daily continued with the same treatment. Women in the discontinuation group were given 20 mg of alendronate daily for two years, followed by 5 mg daily in years 3, 4, and 5, and then five years of placebo. Throughout the entire 10-year period, the randomization and blinding of the groups were maintained.

We analyzed the results for the 247 women who participated in all four phases of the study. The findings showed that treatment with 10 mg of alendronate daily for 10 years led to significant increases in bone mineral density at various sites, including the lumbar spine, trochanter, femoral neck, and total proximal femur. The gains were even smaller in the group given 5 mg daily. When alendronate was discontinued, there was a gradual loss of its effects on bone density and biochemical markers of bone remodeling. However, the safety data, including fractures and stature, did not indicate any loss of benefit from prolonged treatment.

In conclusion, our study demonstrated that alendronate had sustained therapeutic effects and was well tolerated over a 10-year period. Discontinuation of the drug resulted in a gradual loss of its effects.

title: UCP1-independent signaling involving SERCA2b-mediated calcium cycling regulates beige fat thermogenesis and systemic glucose homeostasis
text: The role of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat is well-established, but its role in beige fat is still unclear. However, we have discovered a strong thermogenic mechanism in beige fat that does not rely on UCP1. This mechanism involves an increased ATP-dependent cycling of calcium ions by sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase 2b (SERCA2b) and ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2). When SERCA2b is inhibited, UCP1-independent thermogenesis in beige fat is impaired in humans, mice, and even pigs, which do not have a functional UCP1 protein. On the other hand, activating α1- and/or β3-adrenergic receptors or the SERCA2b-RyR2 pathway enhances calcium cycling and stimulates UCP1-independent thermogenesis in beige adipocytes. In the absence of UCP1, beige fat efficiently utilizes glucose through increased glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid metabolism, and pyruvate dehydrogenase activity for ATP-dependent thermogenesis via the SERCA2b pathway. This means that beige fat acts as a "glucose sink" and improves glucose tolerance independently of weight loss. Our study reveals a unique thermogenic mechanism in beige fat that regulates overall energy balance through calcium cycling.

title: Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) mediates 3′-end maturation of the telomerase RNA component
text: The PARN gene, responsible for encoding poly(A)-specific ribonuclease, is known to cause telomere diseases such as familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and dyskeratosis congenita. However, the exact way in which PARN deficiency affects telomere maintenance remains unclear. In this study, we utilized somatic cells and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from dyskeratosis congenita patients with PARN mutations to investigate the role of PARN in telomerase RNA component (TERC) maturation. Our findings reveal that PARN is essential for the 3'-end maturation of TERC. Cells derived from patients with PARN mutations, as well as immortalized cells with disrupted PARN, exhibit reduced levels of TERC. Through deep sequencing of TERC RNA 3' termini, we discovered that PARN is necessary for the removal of oligo(A) tails acquired post-transcriptionally, which target nuclear RNAs for degradation. Restoring PARN, which is limited in TERC maturation, normalizes the diminished TERC levels and increased proportion of oligo(A) forms of TERC. These results not only uncover a novel role for PARN in TERC biogenesis but also provide a mechanism that links PARN mutations to telomere diseases.

title: Folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake, and risk of preeclampsia
text:
Background/Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate whether folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake before and during pregnancy can reduce the risk of preeclampsia. Previous epidemiologic studies have provided inconclusive results on this topic.

Subjects/Methods: A birth cohort study was conducted at the Gansu Provincial Maternity & Child Care Hospital in Lanzhou, China, between 2010 and 2012. A total of 10,041 pregnant women without chronic hypertension or gestational hypertension were included in the study.

Results: The results showed that pregnant women who used folic acid supplements had a lower risk of preeclampsia compared to nonusers (OR=0.61, 95% CI: 0.43–0.87). Among women who only used folic acid supplements during pregnancy, there was a significant dose-response relationship with the duration of use (P-trend=0.007). The reduced risk associated with folic acid supplementation was consistent for both mild and severe preeclampsia, as well as for early- and late-onset preeclampsia. However, statistically significant associations were only observed for mild (OR=0.50, 95% CI: 0.30–0.81) and late-onset (OR=0.60, 95% CI: 0.42–0.86) preeclampsia. In terms of dietary folate intake during pregnancy, a reduced risk was only seen for severe preeclampsia (OR=0.52, 95% CI: 0.31–0.87) in the highest quartile of intake compared to the lowest.

Conclusions: Based on our study findings, it can be concluded that folic acid supplementation and higher dietary folate intake during pregnancy can help reduce the risk of preeclampsia. However, further research is needed to confirm these associations.

title: Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS)
text: Introducing MACS, a Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq data, designed specifically for analyzing data produced by short read sequencers like Solexa's Genome Analyzer. MACS employs an empirical approach to accurately estimate the shift size of ChIP-Seq tags, enhancing the precision of predicted binding sites. Additionally, MACS utilizes a dynamic Poisson distribution to effectively account for local biases in the genome, resulting in more reliable predictions. In comparison to other peak-finding algorithms for ChIP-Seq, MACS demonstrates superior performance and is readily accessible at no cost.

title: Familial obesity and leanness.
text:
We conducted a study using the Princeton School District Family Study cohort to determine the prevalence of suspected familial obesity and leanness. Our goal was to provide risk estimates for the proportion of first-degree relatives who were affected and to assess the contributions of diseases, drugs, and caloric intake to relative obesity and leanness. We analyzed data from 379 probands, including 125 white and 52 black individuals from a random recall group, as well as 147 white and 55 black individuals from a hyperlipidemic recall group.

We identified suspected familial obesity and leanness in kindreds where at least two first-degree relatives had the same Quetelet index decile as the proband, either in the top or bottom decile. Among white individuals in the random recall group, 2.4% had suspected familial obesity and 6% had suspected familial leanness. In the hyperlipidemic recall group, these percentages were 2.4% for obesity and 1.4% for leanness. Among randomly recalled black individuals, 3.8% had suspected familial leanness.

We found that white first-degree relatives of probands in the top decile of the Quetelet index were approximately twice as likely to also have a top decile index. Similarly, first-degree relatives of probands in the bottom decile were approximately three times as likely to have a bottom decile index. In families with top decile index white probands, 19% and 31% had at least two other first-degree relatives who were similarly obese in the random and hyperlipidemic recall groups, respectively. For white probands with bottom decile indices, 18% and 20% had suspected familial leanness in the random and hyperlipidemic recall groups, respectively.

Most individuals with familial obesity or leanness did not have any obvious metabolic or pharmacological explanations for their body habitus. We observed a common clustering of hypertension within families with suspected familial obesity, while this clustering was absent in families with suspected familial leanness. This clustering of obesity and leanness within families can be diagnostically useful. For effective therapeutic intervention to reduce obesity, it should be implemented at a family-wide level in the many families that share familial obesity.

title: In-hospital switching of oral P2Y12 inhibitor treatment in patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention: prevalence, predictors and short-term outcome.
text:
The availability of prasugrel and ticagrelor, in addition to clopidogrel, has led to the practice of switching P2Y12 inhibitors in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). In the GReek AntiPlatelet REgistry (GRAPE), we examined the prevalence, factors predicting switching, and short-term outcomes of in-hospital P2Y12 inhibitor switching in 1794 ACS patients undergoing PCI. 

We found that switching occurred in 636 (35.5%) patients, with most switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent. Factors such as presentation to a non PCI-capable hospital, use of bivalirudin, age ≥75 years (inverse predictor), and regional trends influenced the decision to switch to a novel agent. 

When comparing outcomes, we found no differences in major adverse cardiovascular events or bleeding events between switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent and constant administration of a novel agent. However, there were more bleeding events and fewer major adverse cardiovascular events when switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent compared to only using clopidogrel. 

In conclusion, switching P2Y12 inhibitors during hospitalization is a common practice in ACS patients undergoing PCI. Clinical factors and regional differences play a role in the choice to switch, and switching to a novel agent may increase the risk of bleeding.

title: Structural basis of allosteric and synergistic activation of AMPK by furan-2-phosphonic derivative C2 binding.
text: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses metabolic stress, plays a crucial role in regulating metabolism based on energy supply and demand. The activation of AMPK through drugs could potentially be beneficial in treating metabolic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes. By studying the crystal structure of AMPK in conjunction with its activator 5-(5-hydroxyl-isoxazol-3-yl)-furan-2-phosphonic acid (C2), we have discovered two distinct C2-binding sites in the γ-subunit, separate from nucleotide sites. C2, when combined with the drug A769662, synergistically activates AMPK α1-containing complexes without the need for upstream kinases. These findings suggest that utilizing dual drug therapies could be an effective approach to target AMPK and treat metabolic diseases.

title: Validity of age at menarche self-reported in adulthood.
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the accuracy of self-reported age at menarche in adulthood and determine if factors such as socioeconomic position, education, gynecological events, and psychological symptoms affect the reliability of recall. The study was conducted as a prospective birth cohort study in England, Scotland, and Wales, involving 1050 women from the Medical Research Council National Survey of Health and Development. The women provided two measures of age at menarche, one recorded during adolescence and the other self-reported at age 48.

The results of the study, determined through the calculation of limits of agreement, kappa statistic, and Pearson's correlation coefficients, revealed that the validity of self-reported age at menarche in middle age compared to the recorded age in adolescence was moderate (kappa = 0.35, r = 0.66, n = 1050). However, when age at menarche was categorized into three groups (early, normal, and late), the validity improved (kappa = 0.43). The agreement between the two measures was influenced by educational level and the experience of stillbirth or miscarriage.

Based on these findings, it is questionable whether self-reported age at menarche in middle age can be considered reliable. The potential for error and bias exists, and researchers should exercise caution when using such measures. It is important to be aware of these limitations and consider alternative approaches when studying age at menarche.

title: Seroepidemiologic survey of captive Old-World primates for antibodies to human and simian retroviruses, and isolation of a lentivirus from sooty mangabeys (Cercocebus atys).
text: A total of 526 Old-World monkeys and apes, belonging to 50 different species and 20 genera, and residing in zoos and vivaria in the US, were examined for antibodies to HTLV-I, HTLV-III/LAV, and simian-AIDS retrovirus, type I (SRV-I). Initially, the sera were screened using ELISA, and both ELISA-positive and ELISA-negative sera from cage contacts were further tested using Western blotting. The study revealed a significant number of false-positive results and a small number of false-negative results from the ELISA screening. While most true positive reactions were specific to a single retrovirus, a few individuals from four species tested positive for more than one retrovirus. Among the animals tested, 39 out of 526 (7%) from 15 species showed specific seroreactivity to HTLV-I. True positive reactions to SRV-I were found in 21 out of 516 (4%) animals, including talapoins and two species of macaques. Specific serologic reactions to HTLV-III/LAV were detected in 23 out of 526 (4%) monkeys. The majority of HTLV-III/LAV seropositive animals were from a mixed-species zoo exhibit that housed sooty mangabeys, mandrills, Kolb's guenons, and talapoins. A type D virus was isolated from the blood of 3 out of 10 SRV-I antibody-positive Tonkeana macaques, but none from the 11 seropositive talapoins. A lentivirus was isolated from the blood of 4 out of 7 HTLV-III/LAV seropositive sooty mangabeys, but not from the seropositive talapoins in the same exhibit or the 2 seropositive colobus monkeys from another zoo. The sooty mangabey lentivirus caused generalized lymphadenopathy, leukopenia, and decreased levels of T4 lymphocytes in two rhesus macaques that were experimentally infected.

title: Coronary plaque disruption.
text: Coronary atherosclerosis is the most common cause of ischemic heart disease, leading to acute coronary syndromes such as unstable angina, myocardial infarction, and sudden death. The key question is not why atherosclerosis develops, but rather why it suddenly becomes complicated by life-threatening thrombosis after years of slow growth. The composition and vulnerability of the plaque, rather than its size or the severity of stenosis, are the main factors determining the risk of thrombus-mediated acute coronary syndromes. Lipid-rich and soft plaques are more dangerous because they are unstable and prone to rupture, making them highly thrombogenic. This review will explore the mechanisms behind the transformation of a stable atherosclerotic plaque into an unstable and life-threatening atherothrombotic lesion, known as plaque fissuring, rupture, or disruption. Atherosclerosis is a complex process involving inflammation, endothelial activation, smooth muscle cell proliferation, lipid accumulation, necrosis, calcification, and thrombosis. Thrombosis typically occurs as a complication of mature plaques, rather than being an inherent part of atherosclerosis.

title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin.
text: The gene p16INK4A, which regulates the cell cycle and inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, is believed to play a significant role in cellular aging and premature senescence. While there is evidence of increased p16INK4A expression in human fibroblast senescence in laboratory settings, there is currently no data on the age-related changes of p16INK4A in living organisms. To investigate whether p16INK4A expression in human skin is linked to donor age, we conducted immunohistochemistry analysis of p16INK4A expression, as well as the expression of the p16INK4A repressor BMI1. We selected samples from three age groups: 0-20, 21-70, and 71-95 years, from a collection of healthy human skin. Our findings reveal that the number of cells expressing p16INK4A is significantly higher in older individuals compared to younger age groups. This increase in p16INK4A positive cells was observed in both the epidermis and dermis, which are compartments with different rates of cell proliferation. Additionally, we observed a down-regulation of BMI1 gene expression with increasing donor age, while no significant age differences were found for Ki67 expression. Co-expression studies using immunofluorescence showed that cells positive for Ki67 did not express p16INK4A, and cells expressing BMI1 were also negative for Ki67. In conclusion, our study provides the first evidence that p16INK4A expression directly correlates with chronological aging of human skin in living organisms. Therefore, p16INK4A can serve as a biomarker for human aging in vivo. These findings suggest a model for changes in gene expression regulation that drive aging in human skin.

title: hPrimpol1/CCDC111 is a human DNA primase-polymerase required for the maintenance of genome integrity.
text: Prim-pol is a newly discovered member of the archaeao-eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily, functioning as a DNA primase-polymerase. In this study, we investigate a previously unidentified prim-pol in human cells, which we refer to as hPrimpol1 (human primase-polymerase 1). Through in vitro experiments, we demonstrate that hPrimpol1 possesses both primase and DNA polymerase activities. Additionally, we observe that hPrimpol1 directly interacts with RPA1 and is recruited to sites of DNA damage and stalled replication forks in an RPA1-dependent manner. Depletion of hPrimpol1 in cells leads to an increase in spontaneous DNA damage and impairments in the restart of stalled replication forks. Notably, both RPA1 binding and the primase activity of hPrimpol1 are essential for its role in DNA replication. Our findings highlight hPrimpol1 as a novel component involved in the cellular response to DNA replication stress.

title: Functional proteomics identifies miRNAs to target a p27/Myc/phospho-Rb signature in breast and ovarian cancer
text: The myc oncogene is found to be overexpressed in nearly half of breast and ovarian cancers, but efforts to develop effective treatments against myc have proven to be difficult. Myc plays a role in regulating various biological processes, including the cell cycle, and is associated with cell proliferation and the progression of tumors. We have discovered a protein signature that is indicative of high myc levels, low p27 levels, and high phospho-Rb levels, which is significantly linked to poor patient survival in breast and ovarian cancers. Through screening a miRNA library using functional proteomics in multiple cell lines and analyzing data from patient tumors, we have identified a group of five microRNAs (miRNAs) (miR-124, miR-365, miR-34b*, miR-18a, and miR-506) that have the potential to act as tumor suppressors and reverse the protein signature of p27/myc/phospho-Rb. Further investigation has revealed that miR-124 has an RNA-activation function, leading to the direct increase of p27 protein levels by binding to and inducing transcription in the p27 promoter region, resulting in a G1 arrest. Moreover, in vivo studies using a xenograft model have demonstrated that delivering miR-124 through nanoparticles can reduce tumor growth and enhance the sensitivity of cells to etoposide, suggesting that miRNAs could be used as therapeutics to target the functional impact of myc on tumor growth in a clinical setting.

title: The potential role of miRNAs 21 and 199-a in early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
BACKGROUND
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is considered one of the most common types of cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. The urgent need is to identify sensitive markers for early detection of HCC. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a group of small non-coding RNAs that can regulate gene expression through endogenous RNA interference. This study aimed to detect the levels of miR-21 and miR-199-a in serum and tissue samples as potential early detection markers for HCC.

METHODS
A total of 40 serum and tissue samples were collected, including 17 samples from patients with chronic hepatitis and 23 samples from HCC patients. The levels of miR-21 and miR-199-a were measured using real-time quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR (RT-qPCR) in both serum and tissue samples. The relationship between miR-21 and miR-199-a levels and clinical and pathological factors was also investigated.

RESULTS
The expression of serum miR-21 was significantly higher in HCC patients compared to those with chronic hepatitis (P<0.001). On the other hand, miR-199-a levels were significantly lower in HCC patients compared to those with chronic hepatitis (P<0.001). In tissue samples, the median level of miR-21 was higher in malignant tissues compared to adjacent non-malignant tissues, although the difference was not statistically significant (P=0.191). However, miR-199-a levels were significantly lower in malignant tissues compared to adjacent non-malignant tissues (P<0.001). ROC analysis suggested that miR-21 and miR-199-a could be potential biomarkers for HCC.

CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, the expression of miR-21 was significantly up-regulated and miR-199-a was significantly down-regulated in the serum of HCC patients. Due to their reasonable sensitivity and specificity in disease progression, miR-21 and miR-199-a could serve as potential circulating biomarkers for HCC.

title: Tex10 Coordinates Epigenetic Control of Super-Enhancer Activity in Pluripotency and Reprogramming.
text: Super-enhancers (SEs) are large clusters of enhancers that are occupied by multiple transcription factors specific to a particular cell lineage. These transcription factors drive the expression of genes that define the identity of the cell. In embryonic stem cells (ESCs), SEs are particularly enriched with the core pluripotency factors Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. The aim of this study was to understand the molecular mechanisms that control SE activity in pluripotency and reprogramming. By focusing on the protein interaction network surrounding Sox2, we discovered that Tex10 is a crucial pluripotency factor that plays a significant role in ESC self-renewal, early embryo development, and reprogramming. Tex10 is found in high levels at SEs, and its presence is dependent on Sox2. Tex10 coordinates the processes of histone acetylation and DNA demethylation at SEs. Tex10's activity is also important for pluripotency and reprogramming in human cells. This study highlights Tex10 as a fundamental component of the pluripotency network and provides insights into its role in the epigenetic control of SE activity, which ultimately determines cell fate.

title: Value of whole brain re-irradiation for brain metastases--single centre experience.
text:
The purpose of our study was to examine the practice of re-irradiation for patients with progressive or recurrent brain metastatic disease after initial whole brain radiation therapy (WBRT) at Princess Margaret Hospital. We used a computerized database to identify patients who received more than one course of WBRT between 1997 and 2003. A total of 72 patients were treated with WBRT for brain metastases and later retreated with WBRT. We reviewed the records of these patients.

The median age of the patients was 56.5 years, with the most common primary sites being lung (51 patients) and breast (17 patients). The majority of patients received an initial radiotherapy dose of 20 Gy/5 fractions. For re-irradiation, the most common doses were 25 Gy/10 fractions, 20 Gy/10 fractions, 15 Gy/5 fractions, and 20 Gy/8 fractions. After re-irradiation, 31% of patients experienced a partial clinical response, 27% remained stable, and 32% deteriorated. Patients with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1 at the time of retreatment had longer survival.

In responders, the average duration of response was 5.1 months, and the median survival after re-irradiation was 4.1 months. One patient experienced memory impairment and pituitary insufficiency after 5 months of progression-free survival. Based on our findings, repeat radiotherapy may be beneficial for carefully selected patients. As survival rates improve and more systemic treatment options become available for metastatic disease, more patients may be eligible for repeat WBRT. However, further prospective studies are necessary to better understand the outcomes of this approach.

title: Bisphosphonates in oncology: rising stars or fallen heroes.
text: The introduction of bisphosphonates in the field of oncology has had a profound impact on the management of patients with metastatic bone disease. In this manuscript, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the existing body of clinical trials that support the utilization of bisphosphonates in this particular context. Furthermore, we provide an overview of both new and ongoing research in this area. Additionally, we summarize the available data that demonstrates the advantages of using bisphosphonates in preventing treatment-induced bone loss. Moreover, we discuss the emerging and intriguing evidence regarding the potential antitumor effects of certain bisphosphonates when employed in the adjuvant setting. Lastly, we emphasize the importance of carefully considering the potential benefits of bisphosphonate therapy, while also acknowledging the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw, a recently identified late-toxicity associated with their use.

title: IL-33, a recently identified interleukin-1 gene family member, is expressed in human adipocytes.
text: We investigated whether IL-33, a newly discovered member of the IL-1 gene family, and its associated receptors are present in human adipocytes, specifically in adipose tissue affected by obesity. Our findings revealed that IL-33, IL-1RL1, and IL-1RAP gene expression was detected in human visceral white fat, as well as in preadipocytes and adipocytes (SGBS cells). When treated with TNFalpha for 24 hours, both preadipocytes and adipocytes exhibited a significant 6-fold increase in IL-33 mRNA levels. Further analysis with adipocytes demonstrated that the peak increase in IL-33 mRNA occurred at 12 hours, reaching a remarkable >55-fold increase. Interestingly, the response to TNFalpha differed greatly when compared to IL-1beta (which peaked at 2 hours with a 5.4-fold increase) and IL-18 (which peaked at 6 hours with a >1500-fold increase). Additionally, exposure to hypoxia (1% O(2), 24 hours) did not affect IL-33 mRNA levels in adipocytes, but preadipocytes experienced a 3-fold increase. In conclusion, our study confirms the presence of IL-33 in human adipocytes and preadipocytes, while highlighting the distinct responsiveness of various IL-1 family members to TNFalpha.

title: Imaging techniques for assaying lymphocyte activation in action
text: Advancements in imaging techniques have significantly enhanced our comprehension of lymphocyte activation. The development of improved spatial and temporal resolution, along with the introduction of new labelling tools, has allowed researchers to directly observe the activation process. Consequently, the utilization of imaging approaches in studying lymphocyte activation has expanded, offering an unparalleled level of cellular and molecular insight in the field. This has led to the verification of certain models of lymphocyte activation, the revision of others, and the introduction of new concepts. In this article, we provide an overview of the current imaging techniques employed to assess lymphocyte activation in various contexts, ranging from whole animals to individual molecules. Additionally, we discuss the advantages and potential limitations associated with these methods.

title: Extending healthy life span--from yeast to humans.
text: When organisms like yeast and rodents consume less food (dietary restriction), they tend to live longer compared to those on a normal diet. This same effect can be observed when the activity of nutrient-sensing pathways is reduced through mutations or chemical inhibitors. In rodents, both dietary restriction and decreased nutrient-sensing pathway activity can decrease the occurrence of age-related functional decline and diseases, including tumors and neurodegeneration. Dietary restriction has also been found to extend lifespan and provide protection against diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease in rhesus monkeys. In humans, it induces changes that safeguard against these age-related ailments. Humans with mutations in the growth hormone receptor also exhibit a lower incidence of tumors and diabetes, while genetic variations in nutrient-sensing pathways are linked to increased human lifespan. Therefore, it appears that dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing pathway activity may slow down aging through similar mechanisms that have been preserved throughout evolution. We explore these discoveries and their potential application in preventing age-related diseases and promoting healthy aging in humans, while also acknowledging the challenge of potential negative side effects.

title: Hospital and 1-year survival of patients admitted to intensive care units with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the outcomes and identify the factors associated with hospital and 1-year survival for patients admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The study was a prospective, multicenter, inception cohort study conducted in 42 ICUs at 40 US hospitals. A total of 362 admissions for COPD exacerbation were selected from the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) III database, which included a total of 17,440 ICU admissions.

The results showed that the hospital mortality rate for the 362 admissions was 24%. Among the 167 patients aged 65 years or older, the mortality rate was 30% at hospital discharge, 41% at 90 days, 47% at 180 days, and 59% at 1 year. The median survival for all patients was 224 days, and for those who died within 1 year, the median survival was 30.5 days.

Multiple regression analysis revealed that variables such as age, severity of respiratory and nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction, and hospital length of stay before ICU admission were associated with hospital mortality. The development of nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction was found to be the major predictor of hospital mortality (60% of total explanatory power) and 180-day outcomes (54% of explanatory power). Respiratory physiological variables indicative of advanced dysfunction, such as respiratory rate, serum pH, PaCO2, PaO2, and alveolar-arterial difference in partial pressure of oxygen (PAO2-PaO2), were more strongly associated with 180-day mortality rates (22% of explanatory power) than hospital death rates (4% of explanatory power). Interestingly, after controlling for severity of illness, mechanical ventilation at ICU admission did not have an impact on either hospital mortality or subsequent survival.

In conclusion, patients with COPD admitted to an ICU for an acute exacerbation have a significant hospital mortality rate of 24%. For patients aged 65 years or older, the mortality rate doubles within 1 year from 30% to 59%. The development of nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction is closely linked to hospital and longer-term mortality, while the severity of underlying respiratory function greatly influences mortality after hospital discharge. The need for mechanical ventilation at ICU admission does not affect short- or long-term outcomes. Physicians should consider these findings when making treatment decisions or evaluating new therapies.

title: Kindlin-3 is essential for integrin activation and platelet aggregation
text: The adhesion and aggregation of platelets through integrins play a crucial role in sealing damaged blood vessels and preventing blood loss. However, excessive platelet aggregation can lead to arterial thrombosis, which can cause heart attacks and strokes. To ensure that platelets only aggregate at sites of injury, integrins on circulating platelets are initially in a low-affinity state. They then transition to a high-affinity state, known as integrin activation or priming, upon contact with a wounded vessel. This transition is facilitated by the binding of the cytoskeletal protein Talin to the β subunit cytoplasmic tail. Our research demonstrates that platelets lacking the adhesion plaque protein Kindlin-3 are unable to activate integrins, despite normal Talin expression. Consequently, the absence of Kindlin-3 leads to severe bleeding and resistance to arterial thrombosis. Mechanistically, Kindlin-3 directly binds to specific regions of β-integrin tails, distinct from those bound by Talin, triggering integrin activation. Therefore, we have identified Kindlin-3 as a novel and essential component for platelet integrin activation in both hemostasis and thrombosis.

title: Opening of compacted chromatin by early developmental transcription factors HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4.
text: The earliest known transcription factors, HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4, have been found to bind the enhancer of the albumin gene in liver precursor cells during embryonic development. In order to understand how they access these sites in silent chromatin, we conducted experiments using nucleosome arrays that contained albumin enhancer sequences. These arrays were then compacted with linker histone. Interestingly, HNF3 and GATA-4 were able to bind their respective sites in the compacted chromatin and open up the surrounding nucleosomal domain. This was observed even in the absence of ATP-dependent enzymes. On the other hand, NF-1, C/EBP, and GAL4-AH were unable to bind their sites in the compacted chromatin. The ability of HNF3 to open up the chromatin is facilitated by a high affinity DNA binding site and the C-terminal domain of the protein, which interacts with histones H3 and H4. These findings suggest that transcription factors involved in development have the inherent capability to initiate chromatin opening events.

title: N- and E-cadherins in Xenopus are specifically required in the neural and non-neural ectoderm, respectively, for F-actin assembly and morphogenetic movements.
text: Calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion molecules known as transmembrane cadherins have recently been discovered to serve as sites for actin assembly during the formation of adhesive contacts. However, the precise roles of actin assembly on transmembrane cadherins during development remain unclear. In this study, we utilized the developing ectoderm of the Xenopus embryo as a model to demonstrate that F-actin assembly is a crucial function of both N-cadherin in the neural ectoderm and E-cadherin in the non-neural (epidermal) ectoderm. Furthermore, we found that each cadherin is indispensable for the characteristic morphogenetic movements of these two tissues. Interestingly, despite depleting N-cadherin and E-cadherin, dissociation did not occur in these tissues at the neurula stage, likely due to the presence of C-cadherin expression in each tissue. Notably, the depletion of each cadherin could not be rescued by the other or by the expression of C-cadherin, which is expressed in both tissues. This observation suggests that each cadherin is expressed in a distinct domain of the cell membrane. These findings highlight the combinatorial nature of cadherin function, emphasizing that N- and E-cadherin not only play primary roles in F-actin assembly but also contribute to cell adhesion, with each cadherin exhibiting specific functions. Additionally, these results demonstrate how cell adhesion and motility can synergistically drive morphogenetic tissue movements, ultimately shaping the form and structure of embryonic organs.

title: Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency.
text: We present a case study on two siblings who were born to first cousin parents and were diagnosed with fumarase deficiency, an inborn error of the tricarboxylic acid cycle. The siblings exhibited symptoms such as progressive encephalopathy, dystonia, leucopenia, and neutropenia. Further investigation revealed elevated lactate levels in the cerebrospinal fluid and increased fumarate excretion in the urine. This prompted us to examine the activities of the respiratory chain and the Krebs cycle, ultimately leading to the identification of fumarase deficiency in these children. The deficiency was severe and affected both the cytosolic and mitochondrial fumarase isoenzymes equally in all tissues examined. Analysis of fumarase cDNA revealed that both patients had a homozygous missense mutation, specifically a G-955-->C transversion, resulting in a Glu-319-->Gln substitution. This substitution occurred in a highly conserved region of the fumarase cDNA. The parents, on the other hand, had half the expected fumarase activity in their lymphocytes and were found to be heterozygous for this substitution. This study represents the first molecular characterization of tricarboxylic acid deficiency, a rare inherited metabolic disorder in childhood.

title: Adult Neurogenesis Is Sustained by Symmetric Self-Renewal and Differentiation.
text: Multiple adult tissues have been found to contain somatic stem cells. Understanding whether self-renewal occurs symmetrically or asymmetrically is crucial for comprehending how stem cells are maintained long-term and how progeny for cell replacement are generated. In the adult mouse brain, neural stem cells (NSCs) known as B1 cells are located in the walls of the lateral ventricles, specifically in the ventricular-subventricular zone (V-SVZ). However, the mechanism behind the retention of B1 cells into adulthood for lifelong neurogenesis remains unknown. Through the use of various clonal labeling techniques, our research demonstrates that the majority of B1 cells divide symmetrically. Approximately 20%-30% of these cells undergo symmetric self-renewal and can persist in the niche for several months before producing neurons. On the other hand, 70%-80% of B1 cells undergo consuming divisions, generating progeny and leading to the gradual depletion of B1 cells over time. This cellular mechanism separates self-renewal from the generation of progeny. The observed levels of neurogenesis throughout life can be explained by limited rounds of symmetric self-renewal and consuming symmetric differentiation divisions.

title: A common missense variant in NUDT15 confers susceptibility to thiopurine-induced leukopenia
text: The use of Thiopurine therapy, which is commonly prescribed for autoimmune conditions, can be complicated by a potentially life-threatening condition called leukopenia. This condition is linked to genetic variations in TPMT, which is responsible for encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase. Interestingly, despite Asians having a lower frequency of TPMT mutations, they have a higher incidence of thiopurine-induced leukopenia compared to individuals of European descent. To further investigate this, we conducted a two-stage association study using Immunochip technology on 978 Korean subjects with Crohn's disease who were being treated with thiopurines. Our study revealed a significant association between a specific genetic variation in NUDT15 (encoding p. Arg139Cys) and early leukopenia caused by thiopurine therapy. The odds ratio for this association was 35.6, with a combined p-value of 4.88 × 10−94. In Koreans, this genetic variant demonstrated a sensitivity of 89.4% and specificity of 93.2% for predicting thiopurine-induced early leukopenia, compared to 12.1% and 97.6% for TPMT variants. Additionally, although rare, this SNP was also strongly associated with thiopurine-induced leukopenia in individuals of European descent with inflammatory bowel disease (odds ratio = 9.50; p-value = 4.64 × 10−4). Therefore, NUDT15 is a significant pharmacogenetic factor in determining the risk of thiopurine-induced leukopenia in diverse populations.

title: Induction of cell cycle entry eliminates human leukemia stem cells in a mouse model of AML
text: Cancer stem cells are believed to play a crucial role in the development, persistence, and recurrence of various types of cancer, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In a previous study, we found that CD34+CD38− AML stem cells, located in the endosteal region of the bone marrow, exhibit a higher resistance to chemotherapy. In our current research using a NOD/SCID/IL2rγnull mouse model of human AML, we have discovered that these AML stem cells in the endosteal region are in a state of cell cycle dormancy. However, we have also found that treatment with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) can stimulate these stem cells to enter the cell cycle. When combined with chemotherapy that targets actively dividing cells, G-CSF treatment significantly increases the rate of cell death and elimination of AML stem cells in vivo. This combination therapy has shown to greatly improve the survival rate of secondary recipients who receive a transplantation of leukemia cells, compared to chemotherapy alone.

title: Reconstitution of the immune system after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in humans
text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation leads to a significant weakening of the immune system, leaving the patient highly susceptible to infections. The innate immune response, which includes epithelial barriers, monocytes, granulocytes, and NK cells, typically recovers within a few weeks after the transplantation. However, the recovery of adaptive immunity is much slower. While B- and T-cell counts return to normal levels within the initial months following the transplantation, T-cell immunity, in particular, may remain impaired for an extended period, even years. Fortunately, in the past decade, researchers have made significant progress in understanding the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon. These findings offer hope for the development of novel therapies that can expedite the recovery process.

title: Vision tests in the mouse: Functional phenotyping with electroretinography.
text: Electroretinography (ERG) is a well-established diagnostic technique used in clinical ophthalmology to objectively assess retinal function. It is also widely employed in basic research, particularly in studying hereditary retinopathies using animal models. These models have greatly enhanced our understanding of ERG responses and how retinal degenerative diseases affect retinal function. By genetically engineering transgenic mice to mimic human mutations that cause retinal diseases, researchers can effectively compare electrophysiological assessments with clinical data. Additionally, limitations that exist when examining human patients, such as the duration of measurements and range of light intensity, are less of a concern when assessing mice. To accurately measure and analyze retinal responses, several important factors must be taken into account. This paper focuses on these factors and presents exemplary ERG data obtained from normal wild-type mice, as well as transgenic mice with specific functional properties, namely Rho-/- (rod opsin knockout, cone function only) and Cnga3-/- (cone CNG channel deficient, rod function only). These examples illustrate the contributions of the rod and cone systems to ERG responses.

title: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 is essential for meiosis but not for mitotic cell division in mice
text: We used homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells to target the locus that encodes cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2). Embryonic fibroblasts that lack CDK2 are able to proliferate normally and become immortal after continuous passage in culture. When a conditional Cdk2 allele is eliminated in these immortal cells, it does not significantly affect their proliferation. Cdk2−/− mice are viable and can survive for up to two years, indicating that CDK2 is not necessary for the proliferation and survival of most cell types. However, CDK2 plays a crucial role in the completion of prophase I during meiotic cell division in male and female germ cells, which was an unexpected function for this cell cycle kinase.

title: Capsaicin-sensitive sensory nerve fibers contribute to the generation and maintenance of skeletal fracture pain.
text: Although skeletal pain can greatly affect a patient's ability to function and their overall quality of life, there is limited knowledge about the specific types of peripheral nerve fibers that contribute to non-malignant bone pain. In this study, young adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were given capsaicin or a control substance, and then their femurs were fractured. The capsaicin treatment resulted in a significant decrease in the density of calcitonin-gene related peptide positive (CGRP(+)) sensory nerve fibers in the periosteum, which is a thin tissue that covers the outer surface of most bones. However, there was no change in the density of 200 kDa neurofilament H positive (NF200(+)) sensory nerve fibers. The periosteum appears to play a crucial role in causing fracture pain. Rats treated with capsaicin showed a 50% reduction in the severity of fracture-induced skeletal pain-related behaviors, such as flinching, guarding, and weight bearing, but there was no change in the duration of these behaviors. This suggests that both capsaicin-sensitive (primarily CGRP(+) C-fibers) and capsaicin-insensitive (primarily NF200(+) A-delta fibers) sensory nerve fibers contribute to skeletal fracture pain. Skeletal pain can significantly hinder recovery after trauma-induced fractures, fractures caused by osteoporosis, and orthopedic surgeries like knee and hip replacements. By understanding which specific types of sensory nerve fibers are involved in generating and maintaining skeletal pain, it may be possible to develop more targeted therapies that effectively reduce acute and chronic skeletal pain.

title: Surgical therapy for dystonia.
text: Surgical treatments for dystonia have been available since the early 20th century, but advancements in technology and a better understanding of the role of the basal ganglia have improved their effectiveness. Dystonia refers to involuntary movements that can occur due to various conditions. It can affect specific body regions or be more widespread. It is important to determine whether the dystonia is primary (genetic or idiopathic) or secondary (resulting from structural, metabolic, or neurodegenerative disorders). Secondary dystonias are more common than primary dystonias. Primary dystonias respond well to pallidotomy or deep brain stimulation of the internal segment of the globus pallidum, while secondary dystonias have limited response. The thalamus shows promise as a target for treating secondary dystonias, but further studies are needed. Although bilateral targets can be used with current technology, they are not widely utilized due to surgical risks and costs. This article provides an overview of the surgical treatment of dystonia, focusing on outcomes for primary versus secondary dystonias and generalized versus cervical dystonia.

title: MEG3 imprinted gene contribution in tumorigenesis.
text: Maternally expressed gene 3 (MEG3) is an imprinted gene that is primarily expressed by the mother. It is a large noncoding RNA that also hosts microRNAs (miRNAs) and small nucleolar RNAs. MEG3 has the ability to interact with cyclic AMP, p53, murine double minute 2 (MDM2), and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), which are all involved in controlling cell proliferation. The expression of MEG3 is regulated by epigenetic factors, and abnormal CpG methylation has been observed in various types of cancer. Additionally, loss of gene copies has been identified as another mechanism associated with the development of tumors. Deletion of MEG3 appears to increase the expression of genes that are primarily expressed by the father, while simultaneously decreasing the expression of genes and tumor suppressor miRNAs that are primarily expressed by the mother. However, there is conflicting data on this topic. MEG3 is believed to be a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 14q32, and its association with tumorigenesis is continuously growing.

title: Uptake of rosuvastatin by isolated rat hepatocytes: comparison with pravastatin.
text:
1. The liver is the desired target organ for the lipid-regulating effect of rosuvastatin, a new inhibitor of the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase. It is important for this drug to have selective uptake in the liver. To investigate the uptake kinetics of rosuvastatin, it was compared to pravastatin using isolated rat hepatocytes.

2. Both drugs were found to be taken up through a combination of active transport and passive diffusion processes. The uptake rate of rosuvastatin had a Michaelis constant (K(m)) of 9.17 micro M, which was approximately half that of pravastatin (16.5 micro M). However, the maximum uptake rate (V(max)) and carrier-mediated uptake clearance (V(max)/K(m)) of rosuvastatin were significantly higher than those of pravastatin (p < 0.01). Rosuvastatin also had a larger contribution of carrier-mediated uptake clearance to total uptake clearance compared to pravastatin.

3. The uptake of both rosuvastatin and pravastatin was not significantly influenced by sodium and chloride ions. However, depletion of cellular ATP and the presence of organic anions like bromosulfophthalein inhibited the uptake of both drugs.

4. Rosuvastatin competitively inhibited the uptake of pravastatin, with an inhibition constant (K(i)) of 2.75 micro M, which was relatively similar to its K(m).

5. The results indicate that an organic anion transport protein is the main mediator of the hepatic uptake of both rosuvastatin and pravastatin, and this uptake is dependent on ATP. Our findings suggest that rosuvastatin is taken up by hepatocytes through the same transport systems as pravastatin, but with a higher affinity and efficiency.

title: Junctophilin-4, a component of the endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane junctions, regulates Ca2+ dynamics in T cells.
text: Orai1 and STIM1 are responsible for store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) in immune cells. STIM1, a sensor for Ca(2+) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), detects when the stores are depleted and interacts with Orai1 channels on the plasma membrane (PM) at the ER-PM junctions. However, the specific components of these junctions in T cells are not well understood. In this study, we discovered that junctophilin-4 (JP4), a protein found in excitable cells, is expressed in T cells and localized at the ER-PM junctions to regulate Ca(2+) signaling. When JP4 was silenced or genetically manipulated, the ER Ca(2+) content and SOCE in T cells decreased. This led to impaired activation of the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) and extracellular signaling-related kinase (ERK) signaling pathways, as well as reduced expression of activation markers and cytokines. Mechanistically, JP4 directly interacted with STIM1 through its cytoplasmic domain and helped recruit it into the junctions. Consequently, the expression of this cytoplasmic fragment of JP4 inhibited SOCE. Additionally, JP4 formed a complex with junctate, a Ca(2+)-sensing protein found in the ER, which has previously been shown to mediate STIM1 recruitment into the junctions. Based on our findings, we propose that the junctate-JP4 complex at the junctions cooperatively interacts with STIM1 to maintain ER Ca(2+) homeostasis and facilitate SOCE in T cells.

title: The PI3K inhibitor arsenal: choose your weapon!
text: The therapeutic potential of inhibitors of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway has gained significant attention due to their widespread activation in inflammation and cancer. This has led to a growing interest in compounds with suitable pharmacological profiles, primarily targeting PI3K itself. However, since class I PI3Ks are also crucial for normal physiological processes, inhibiting them broadly could lead to poor tolerance. In recent years, there have been patents describing a new generation of PI3K inhibitors, focusing on developing compounds with enhanced isoform selectivity for use in anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory therapies. Nevertheless, there are still challenges to overcome in successfully targeting this enzyme family pharmacologically.

title: Infralimbic BDNF/TrkB enhancement of GluN2B currents facilitates extinction of a cocaine-conditioned place preference.
text: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays a crucial role in regulating synaptic activity and behavioral flexibility. Reduced levels of BDNF are strongly linked to psychiatric disorders and cognitive dysfunction. While restoring BDNF-dependent activity could potentially alleviate these impairments, its clinical usefulness is limited due to its pharmacokinetics. In this study, we demonstrate that activating the tropomyosin-related kinase B (TrkB) receptor, a primary target of BDNF, enhances the strength and duration of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) currents in male rat infralimbic prefrontal pyramidal neurons. These effects were found to be dependent on NMDARs containing the GluN2B subunit. Our findings reveal that this signaling pathway plays a bidirectional role in regulating the extinction of a cocaine-induced conditioned place preference (CPP), a task that requires behavioral flexibility. Blocking the TrkB receptors or GluN2B-containing NMDARs in the infralimbic region disrupted the consolidation of CPP extinction. Conversely, enhancing TrkB receptor activity through BDNF infusions or injections of a newly synthesized TrkB receptor agonist called 7,8 dihydroxyflavone (7,8DHF) strengthened the extinction process. However, this enhancement was prevented by blocking GluN2B-containing NMDARs. Overall, our results suggest that activating TrkB receptors in the infralimbic region strengthens GluN2B-containing NMDAR currents, facilitating extinction learning. Therefore, TrkB receptor agonists could serve as valuable adjuncts in extinction-based therapies for psychiatric disorders associated with reduced BDNF activity.

title: Compaction of chromatin by diverse Polycomb group proteins requires localized regions of high charge.
text: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins play a crucial role in maintaining developmental genes in a silent state through epigenetic mechanisms. Within the PcG, the Polycomb-repressive complex 1 (PRC1) class of proteins is highly conserved from flies to humans and is responsible for inhibiting transcription. One proposed mechanism for PRC1 is its ability to compact chromatin, as evidenced by electron microscopy experiments demonstrating nucleosomal array compaction in Drosophila PRC1. Our study reveals that this compaction function is conserved in both Drosophila and mouse PRC1 complexes and requires a region rich in basic amino acids. Interestingly, while this active region is found in the Posterior Sex Combs (PSC) subunit in Drosophila, it is unexpectedly located in a different PRC1 subunit, a Polycomb homolog known as M33, in mice. To further support the significance of a charged region, we predict the compacting capability of PcG proteins from species other than Drosophila and mice and validate our predictions through solution assays and microscopy.
