This is true even when there is a complete and irreversible interruption of long descending supraspinal pathways in mice. Our findings demonstrate that significant functional recovery can occur after severe SCI without the need for the maintenance or regeneration of direct projections from the brain beyond the lesion. Instead, it can be achieved through the reorganization of descending and propriospinal connections. By focusing on interventions that enhance the remodeling of relay connections, we may develop new therapeutic strategies to bypass lesions and restore function after SCI, as well as in other conditions like stroke and multiple sclerosis.

title: "Grazing": a high-risk behavior.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the eating patterns of gastric bypass patients before and after surgery. Previous research has shown that patients with disturbed eating patterns, such as binge eating, are more likely to continue these patterns after surgery, leading to poorer outcomes. While "grazing" behavior has not been extensively studied, it is also considered a high-risk pattern. This study is a descriptive analysis of postoperative eating patterns in a group of patients.

Before surgery, patients completed self-report questionnaires and underwent a mental health evaluation to assess their eating patterns. Patients with high-risk patterns, including binge eating and "grazing," were identified and invited to participate in a post-surgery therapy group. They were also given follow-up questionnaires to assess their eating patterns after surgery.

The results of the study were consistent with previous research, showing that many high-risk patients experienced recurrent loss of control over eating and, in some cases, weight gain after surgery. While they were no longer able to eat large amounts, "grazing" became a more common pattern, typically occurring six months or more after surgery.

In conclusion, it is important to assess different forms of overeating in gastric bypass patients, focusing on the subjective loss of control rather than the quantity consumed. Both binge eaters and "grazers" are at high risk for postoperative complications. Interventions should be developed to support these at-risk patients.

title: Molecular strategies in biological evolution of antimicrobial peptides.
text: The skin of hylid and ranin frogs is safeguarded against harmful microorganisms by gene-encoded antimicrobial peptides. These peptides are derived from a unique group of precursor polypeptides that possess a distinct arrangement of conserved and variable regions, unlike conventional secreted peptides. Within this family, known as preprodermaseptin, the N-terminal preproregion remains highly conserved across species, while the C-terminal domain, responsible for antimicrobial peptides, exhibits significant variation in terms of length, sequence, charge, and antimicrobial properties. Each frog species possesses its own set of 10-20 antimicrobial peptides, resulting in an estimated 100,000 different peptide antibiotics among the 5000 ranids and hylids. This remarkable diversity is achieved through repeated duplications of an ancestral gene that dates back 150 million years, focal hypermutation of the antimicrobial peptide domain (possibly involving a mutagenic DNA polymerase similar to Escherichia coli Pol V), and subsequent positive (diversifying) selection. The extensive divergence of skin antimicrobial peptides can be seen as the successful evolution of a multi-drug defense system, offering frogs maximum protection against rapidly evolving microbial populations while minimizing the risk of microorganisms developing resistance to individual peptides. The wide range of frog skin antimicrobial peptide expressions presents an opportunity to discover new molecules and structural motifs that specifically target microorganisms for which effective treatments are currently limited.

title: Microbiome-driven allergic lung inflammation is ameliorated by short-chain fatty acids
text: The gastrointestinal tract of mammals contains a community of microorganisms that play a crucial role in maintaining the health of the host. These microorganisms produce metabolites that can influence the functions of immune cells. When mice are treated with vancomycin, their microbiome and metabolite profile are altered, leading to increased T helper type 2 cell (Th2) responses and heightened susceptibility to allergic lung inflammation. However, we have discovered that supplementing the diet with short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) can alleviate this increased susceptibility to asthma by affecting the activity of T cells and dendritic cells (DCs). Mice with dysbiosis who receive SCFAs have fewer CD4+ T cells producing interleukin-4 (IL4) and lower levels of circulating immunoglobulin E (IgE). Furthermore, DCs exposed to SCFAs exhibit reduced activation of T cells, decreased mobility in response to CCL19 in laboratory settings, and a weakened ability to transport inhaled allergens to the lymph nodes in the lungs. Our findings demonstrate that gut dysbiosis can worsen allergic lung inflammation through mechanisms involving both T cells and DCs, and that these mechanisms can be inhibited by SCFAs.

title: Promiscuous gene expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells mirrors the peripheral self
text: The expression of antigens in the thymus that are found in other parts of the body has been linked to T cell tolerance and autoimmune diseases. In our study, we have identified a specific type of cell called medullary thymic epithelial cells that express a wide range of antigens specific to different tissues. We discovered that this diverse gene expression is a characteristic of these cells and is maintained throughout the production of T cells in the thymus. This may help in the development of tolerance towards self-antigens that are normally isolated from the immune system in terms of time or location. However, the selection of self-antigens that are promiscuously expressed appears to be random rather than specific, and is not limited to isolated self-antigens.

title: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 is a transcriptional factor regulating the gene expression of SALL4.
text: The pluripotent and self-renewal state of embryonic stem cells relies on the presence of both signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and SALL4. Our hypothesis was that STAT3, a latent transcriptional factor, may control the gene expression of SALL4. Supporting this idea, our analysis of the DNA sequence of the SALL4 gene promoter revealed four potential STAT3-binding sites. Through a SALL4-luciferase reporter gene assay, we observed that manipulating STAT3 activity significantly increased luciferase activity. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation, we identified the segment of the SALL4 promoter with the highest affinity for STAT3, which was located from -366 to -163. Within this segment, there was only one potential STAT3 binding site starting at -199. By mutating all four potential STAT3-binding sites in the SALL4 promoter, we found that its responsiveness to STAT3 was significantly reduced, with the most notable effect observed at the binding site starting at -199. To further investigate the relationship between STAT3 and SALL4, we utilized MDA-MB-231, a breast cell line with constitutive SALL4 expression and STAT3 activity. Inhibiting STAT3 activity using a dominant-negative construct led to a significant decrease in SALL4 expression. In conclusion, our findings suggest that STAT3 and SALL4 likely work together in both normal and abnormal conditions.

title: GATA3 transcription factor abrogates Smad4 transcription factor-mediated fascin overexpression, invadopodium formation, and breast cancer cell invasion.
text: The regulation of tumor progression is influenced by transforming growth factor β (TGFβ), which is a powerful and context-dependent factor. TGFβ specifically promotes the spread of basal-like breast cancer to the lungs, but not luminal-like breast cancer. In our study, we have discovered that fascin, a protein that bundles actin and promotes metastasis, is directly affected by the canonical TGFβ-Smad4 signaling pathway in basal-like breast cancer cells. TGFβ and Smad4 cause an increase in fascin production by binding directly to a specific element on the fascin promoter. Additionally, we have identified GATA3, a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in the development of mammary glands and luminal differentiation, as a negative regulator of TGFβ- and Smad4-induced fascin overexpression. When GATA-3 is introduced into basal-like breast cancer cells, it prevents the overexpression of fascin and other genes that respond to TGFβ, as well as inhibiting invadopodium formation, cell migration, and invasion. This suggests that GATA3 suppresses the canonical TGFβ-Smad signaling pathway. Mechanistically, GATA3 achieves this by disrupting the interactions between Smad4 and its DNA binding elements, possibly through physical interactions between the N-terminal of GATA3 and Smad3/4 proteins. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of how TGFβ influences cell motility and invasiveness in breast cancer, and how these processes are regulated differently depending on the subtype of breast cancer.

title: The American Rheumatism Association 1987 revised criteria for the classification of rheumatoid arthritis.
text: The revised criteria for classifying rheumatoid arthritis (RA) were developed by analyzing data from 262 patients with RA and 262 control subjects with other rheumatic diseases (non-RA). The new criteria include the following: 1) experiencing morning stiffness in and around joints for at least 1 hour before improvement; 2) a physician observing soft tissue swelling (arthritis) in 3 or more joint areas; 3) swelling (arthritis) in the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal, or wrist joints; 4) symmetric swelling (arthritis); 5) presence of rheumatoid nodules; 6) presence of rheumatoid factor; and 7) radiographic erosions and/or periarticular osteopenia in hand and/or wrist joints. Criteria 1 to 4 must be present for at least 6 weeks. A diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis requires the presence of 4 or more criteria, without any additional qualifications or exclusions. Additionally, a "classification tree" schema is presented, which performs equally well as the traditional format of requiring 4 out of 7 criteria. The new criteria showed a sensitivity of 91-94% and specificity of 89% for identifying RA compared to control subjects with non-RA rheumatic diseases.

title: A new look at the origin, function, and "stem-cell" status of muscle satellite cells.
text: Muscle satellite cells have long been recognized as a distinct myogenic lineage responsible for the growth, repair, and maintenance of skeletal muscle after birth. However, recent studies in mice have shown that highly purified hematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow can also contribute to muscle regeneration. Additionally, a group of stem cells isolated directly from skeletal muscle has been found to efficiently restore the hematopoietic system and participate in muscle regeneration when injected intravenously in mice. This discovery has raised important questions about the relationship between muscle-derived stem cells and skeletal muscle satellite cells. Moreover, the ability of hematopoietic cells to undergo myogenesis has led to investigations into the embryonic origin of satellite cells. Recent developmental studies suggest that a subset of satellite cells originates from progenitors in the embryonic vasculature. Collectively, these findings provide the initial evidence that adult skeletal muscle contains pluripotential stem cells. Tissue-specific stem cells, including satellite cells, may share a common embryonic origin and possess the ability to activate various genetic programs in response to environmental cues. Manipulating these tissue-specific stem cells could potentially revolutionize therapies for degenerative diseases, such as muscular dystrophy.

title: Involving family members in cancer care: focus group considerations of patients and oncological providers.
text: The involvement of family members is crucial in a patient's cancer care, starting from the moment they receive the diagnosis until the end of treatment. Family members bring with them a range of emotions, interpersonal dynamics, and expectations for the patient's care. This research is part of a larger project involving multiple institutions, aiming to enhance the cancer care process. The study involved 19 focus groups, consisting of 11 patients and 8 healthcare providers, who discussed issues related to doctor-patient communication in eight cancer centers across the United States. The conversations were analyzed, and several themes emerged, highlighting both the strengths and challenges associated with family involvement. The comments from the focus groups emphasize the importance of open discussions among healthcare professionals, patients, and their loved ones to address and negotiate the expectations and needs of each team member. The findings have implications for clinical practice and provide strategies for effectively working with family members.

title: Improving Adherence to Antiretroviral Therapy With Triggered Real-time Text Message Reminders: The China Adherence Through Technology Study.
text:
In this study, we examined the impact of cell phone reminders and counseling on antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence among HIV-infected patients in China. We provided patients with a medication device equipped with cellular technology to monitor their adherence electronically. After 3 months, we divided the patients into two groups based on their adherence levels and randomized them into intervention and control arms. From months 4 to 9, the intervention group received personalized reminders triggered by late dose taking and counseling based on the data generated by the device. The control group did not receive any reminders or data-informed counseling. We compared the proportions of patients achieving optimal adherence, the average adherence, and clinical outcomes after the intervention. 

Out of the 120 patients enrolled, 116 (96.7%) completed the trial. Before the intervention, the proportions of patients with optimal adherence were similar in both the intervention and control groups (63.5% vs. 58.9%, respectively; P = 0.60). However, in the last month of the intervention, 87.3% of the intervention group achieved optimal adherence compared to 51.8% in the control group [risk ratio (RR): 1.7, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.3 to 2.2]. The average adherence was also higher in the intervention group (96.2% vs. 89.1%, P = 0.003). Among patients with suboptimal adherence before the intervention, 78.3% in the intervention group achieved optimal adherence compared to 33.3% in the control group (RR: 2.4, CI: 1.2 to 4.5). The average adherence was 93.3% in the intervention group and 84.7% in the control group (P = 0.039). Among patients with optimal adherence before the intervention, 92.5% in the intervention group and 62.9% in the control group achieved optimal adherence (RR: 1.5, CI: 1.1 to 1.9). The average adherence was 97.8% in the intervention group and 91.7% in the control group (P = 0.028). However, there were no significant differences in clinical outcomes after the intervention. 

In conclusion, real-time reminders significantly improved ART adherence in this population. This approach shows promise for managing HIV and other chronic diseases and should be further investigated and adapted in other settings.

title: Origin and T cell receptor diversity of Foxp3+CD4+CD25+ T cells.
text: The differentiation of Foxp3(+)CD4(+)CD25(+) regulatory T cells from Foxp3(-)CD4(+) medullary thymocytes and Foxp3(-)CD4(+) naive T cells is not well understood in terms of its impact on the size and composition of the peripheral repertoire of regulatory T cells. In this study, we investigated the fate of individual Foxp3(+)CD4(+)CD25(+) thymocytes and T cells in T cell receptor (TCR) transgenic mice that have a limited but diverse repertoire of TCRs. Using high-throughput single-cell analysis, we found that Foxp3(+)CD4(+) peripheral T cells originated from thymic precursors with different TCRs compared to Foxp3(-)CD4(+) medullary thymocytes and Foxp3(-)CD4(+) T cells. Additionally, the diversity of TCRs on Foxp3(+)CD4(+) regulatory T cells was greater than that on Foxp3(-)CD4(+) naive T cells, even in mice lacking tissue-specific antigens. These findings suggest that the higher TCR diversity on Foxp3(+) regulatory T cells enables them to match the specificities of autoreactive and naive T cells.

title: Reproducibility of the diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia: a Gynecologic Oncology Group study.
text:
The effectiveness of hormonal therapy for atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) is often determined by gynecologists based on the current classification provided by the International Society of Gynecologic Pathologists (ISGP) and the World Health Organization (WHO). However, there have been concerns about the reliability of this classification. To address this issue, the Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) conducted a study to assess the reproducibility of AEH diagnoses made by different pathologists.

In the first phase of the study (Part A), 306 women with a diagnosis of AEH from their referring institution's pathologist were included. The available slides were independently evaluated and interpreted by a panel of three gynecologic pathologists using the ISGP/WHO criteria. The majority diagnosis was determined based on agreement between at least two of the three panelists.

The results showed that the referring institution's pathologist's diagnosis of AEH was supported by the majority of the panel in only 38% of cases. The overall agreement among the panelists for the diagnosis of AEH was low, with a kappa value of 0.28. In 29% of cases, the majority diagnosis was adenocarcinoma, while 7% were diagnosed as cycling endometrium, and 18% as nonatypical hyperplasia. Unanimous agreement among all three panelists for any diagnosis was reached in 40% of cases. The paired kappa values for any diagnosis ranged from 0.34 to 0.43, with an overall kappa value of 0.40.

In conclusion, the reproducibility of AEH diagnoses made by referring institution's pathologists is poor when assessed by a panel of gynecologic pathologists. Both underestimation and overestimation of the severity of the lesion are common. The level of agreement among subspecialist panel members for the diagnosis of AEH in these specimens is also low. To improve the reproducibility of this diagnosis, better criteria and sampling methods are needed, especially when making clinical decisions.

title: Replication Fork Slowing and Reversal upon DNA Damage Require PCNA Polyubiquitination and ZRANB3 DNA Translocase Activity
text: The process of DNA damage tolerance during replication in eukaryotes is controlled by the ubiquitination of PCNA. When PCNA is monoubiquitinated, it activates a mutagenic pathway called translesion synthesis. On the other hand, polyubiquitination of PCNA activates an error-free pathway that allows for damage bypass through template switching. In laboratory settings, fork reversal has been observed and is driven by various enzymes, including ZRANB3, a DNA translocase that binds to polyubiquitinated PCNA. However, it was unclear whether this interaction promotes fork remodeling and template switching in living organisms. Our study reveals that in mammalian cells, damage-induced fork reversal relies on PCNA ubiquitination, UBC13, and K63-linked polyubiquitin chains, which have previously been associated with error-free damage tolerance. Additionally, fork reversal in living organisms also depends on the translocase activity of ZRANB3 and its interaction with polyubiquitinated PCNA. This highlights ZRANB3 as a crucial factor in error-free DNA damage tolerance. Mutations that affect fork reversal also lead to uncontrolled fork progression and chromosomal breakage, suggesting that fork remodeling serves as a mechanism to slow down and protect forks on a global scale. Targeting these systems that protect forks could be a promising approach to enhance the effectiveness of cancer chemotherapy.

title: Bed sharing when parents do not smoke: is there a risk of SIDS? An individual level analysis of five major case–control studies
text:
The objective of this study was to determine the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) associated with bed sharing when neither parent smokes and the baby is breastfed. The study compared the frequency of bed sharing during the last sleep between infants who died of SIDS and living control infants. Data from five large SIDS case-control datasets were combined, and missing data were imputed. The analysis used random effects logistic regression to control for confounding factors.

The study examined the sleeping arrangements of infants in 19 studies across the UK, Europe, and Australasia. The participants included 1472 SIDS cases and 4679 controls. Each study included all cases based on standard criteria, and controls were randomly selected normal infants of similar age, time, and place.

The results showed that in the combined dataset, 22.2% of SIDS cases and 9.6% of controls were bed sharing. The adjusted odds ratio (AOR) for bed sharing versus room sharing for all ages was 2.7, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.4 to 5.3. The risk of bed sharing decreased with increasing infant age. However, when neither parent smoked, the baby was less than 3 months old, breastfed, and had no other risk factors, the AOR for bed sharing versus room sharing was 5.1, with a CI of 2.3 to 11.4. The estimated absolute risk for room sharing infants in this group was very low (0.08 per 1000 live-births), but it increased to 0.23 per 1000 live-births when bed sharing.

The study also found that smoking and alcohol use significantly increased the risk of bed sharing. The conclusions of the study were that bed sharing for sleep increases the risk of SIDS, especially when combined with parental smoking, maternal alcohol consumption, and/or drug use. The study suggests that a substantial reduction in SIDS rates could be achieved if parents avoided bed sharing.

title: Decoupling activation and exhaustion of B cells in spontaneous controllers of HIV infection.
text: The objective of this study was to determine how chronic viremia and immune activation impact B-cell exhaustion in HIV infection. In progressive HIV infection, B-cell anergy and exhaustion occur alongside hypergammaglobulinemia. While CD95 upregulation and CD21 loss have been used as markers of infection-related B-cell dysfunction, little is known about the specific profiles of dysfunctional B cells and the role of persistent viral replication and immune activation in driving B-cell dysfunction. Multiparameter flow cytometry was used to define the profile of dysfunctional B cells, tracking changes in CD21 and CD95 expression on B-cell subpopulations in patients with different levels of viral replication control. The results showed that while exhausted, CD21 tissue-like memory B cells emerged similarly in progressors and controllers, the frequency of CD21 activated memory B cells was lower in spontaneous controllers. These findings suggest that the loss of CD21 and the upregulation of CD95 occur as separate events during the development of B-cell dysfunction. CD21 loss indicates B-cell exhaustion in the absence of significant viral replication, while CD95 upregulation is closely linked to persistent viral replication and immune activation. Therefore, these dysfunctional profiles may represent two distinct states within the B-cell compartment.

title: Label-free DNA imaging in vivo with stimulated Raman scattering microscopy.
text: In biology and medicine, there is a strong need for label-free DNA imaging techniques that can visualize cell nuclei without affecting cell function and provide instant histological examination of tissues during surgical procedures. In this study, we present a label-free DNA imaging method using stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy. This method allows for the visualization of cell nuclei in live animals and intact fresh human tissues with subcellular resolution. By leveraging the unique Raman spectral features of carbon-hydrogen bonds in DNA, we are able to distinguish DNA distribution from the background of proteins and lipids. This is achieved through a linear decomposition of SRS images at three carefully selected Raman shifts. By monitoring changes in DNA condensation within the nucleus, we were able to observe chromosome dynamics during cell division both in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, we used this technique to track the proliferation of mouse skin cells induced by drug treatment by counting the mitotic rate in vivo. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our label-free histology method for diagnosing human skin cancer provides comparable results to conventional tissue staining methods such as H&E. Our approach offers higher sensitivity compared to SRS imaging of DNA in the fingerprint spectral region. Moreover, it is three orders of magnitude faster than spontaneous Raman imaging of DNA, enabling real-time studies of chromatin dynamics and label-free optical histology.

title: A common variant in BRCA2 is associated with both breast cancer risk and prenatal viability
text: Mutations in the BRCA2 gene are known to increase the risk of early onset breast cancer, but they are responsible for less than 2% of cases in East Anglia. It is believed that the majority of inherited susceptibility to breast cancer is due to low penetrance alleles, with polymorphic variants in genes like BRCA2 being potential candidates. BRCA2 is involved in repairing DNA double strand breaks and mice with truncated Brca2 often do not survive to birth. Those that do survive are usually male, smaller than their normal littermates, and have a high incidence of cancer. Our study reveals that a common human polymorphism (N372H) in exon 10 of BRCA2 increases the risk of breast cancer. Homozygotes with the HH genotype have a 1.31-fold greater risk compared to those with the NN genotype. Additionally, we observed a significant deficiency of homozygotes in normal female controls of all ages, which deviates from the expected distribution according to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. In contrast, there is an excess of homozygotes in males, with the HH group having a fitness estimate of 0.82 in females and 1.38 in males. Therefore, this particular variant of BRCA2 also appears to impact fetal survival in a sex-dependent manner.

title: Pathophysiology of obstructive nephropathy in the newborn.
text: Congenital obstructive nephropathy is a condition where abnormal development of the urinary tract leads to impaired growth and injury of the kidneys. In our study, we examined how the kidneys of neonatal rodents (guinea pigs, rats, and mice) respond to unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO). Unlike in adults, UUO in neonates hinders the development of nephrons, glomeruli, and tubular cells, while promoting compensatory growth of the unaffected kidney. This impaired growth and tubular damage is likely caused, at least in part, by increased renal tubular cell death. This may be due to a loss of cell polarity, reduced levels of the oncoprotein bcl-2 and epidermal growth factor (EGF), and increased expression of the fibrogenic cytokine transforming growth factor-beta1 (TGF-beta1). Infusing EGF promotes cell growth, prevents cell death, and reduces tubular damage and fibrosis. TGF-beta1 is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, which is highly activated by UUO in neonates. The consequences of obstructive nephropathy in early development include increased filtration by the remaining nephrons, followed by a gradual decline in glomerular filtration rate that may only become apparent later in life. To improve the management of congenital urinary tract obstruction, we need a better understanding of the cellular mechanisms involved. This knowledge may lead to targeted treatments using gene therapy or substances that promote renal growth and development.

title: Lipid homeostasis, lipotoxicity and the metabolic syndrome.
text:
In the 20th century, developed countries have experienced an unprecedented rise in obesity. The United States, in particular, has become the epicenter of this epidemic, with over two-thirds of the population being overweight and one in six Americans diagnosed with metabolic syndrome. While genetics play a role in determining susceptibility to environmental factors, it is clear that the main cause of this epidemic is the increased consumption of calorie-dense, highly fatty foods, combined with a significant decrease in physical activity due to modern technology. If this lifestyle continues, severe consequences are almost certain, including the development of type II diabetes and a group of related disorders known as "the metabolic syndrome," typically occurring in middle age.

Before middle age, the negative effects of excessive calorie intake are somewhat mitigated by the body's ability to store these calories as fat in specialized cells called adipocytes. Leptin, a hormone, has been suggested as the primary regulator of this calorie storage process. However, there are multiple factors that can influence the capacity of fat tissue to store calories, and when this capacity is exceeded, fat begins to accumulate in other organs, a condition known as ectopic lipid deposition. The organs most affected by metabolic syndrome include skeletal muscle, liver, heart, and pancreas, all of which have been found to contain abnormal levels of triglycerides. While neutral fat may not be harmful, it serves as an indicator of excessive ectopic lipid accumulation. Derivatives of fatty acids can interfere with cell function and ultimately lead to cell death through a process called lipoapoptosis, resulting in gradual organ failure.

title: A twin-study of genetic contributions to morningness-eveningness and depression.
text: The preference for sleep-wake timing, also known as morningness-eveningness (ME), is associated with circadian rhythms. Both ME and circadian rhythms are influenced by genetic factors. Research has shown a connection between eveningness and depression. This study aims to explore the heritability of ME and whether there are shared genetic influences between ME and depression. The study included 1237 participants from the Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging, a longitudinal study focused on aging in midlife. As part of a comprehensive neurocognitive and psychosocial assessment, participants completed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) and the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CES-D) Scale. The correlations between MEQ scores for members of twin pairs were 0.41 for monozygotic (MZ) twins and 0.28 for dizygotic (DZ) twins. For CES-D scores, the correlations were 0.38 for MZ twins and 0.24 for DZ twins. The study found that greater eveningness (lower MEQ scores) was significantly associated with more depression symptoms. The heritability estimates were 0.42 for MEQ and 0.37 for CES-D. A significant genetic correlation of -0.21 indicated that ME and depression share a considerable amount of their genetic variance. The genetic covariance between ME and depression accounted for 59.1% of the phenotypic correlation. Among the CES-D sub-scales, Depressed Mood and Interpersonal Difficulties were significantly heritable, while only Well-Being had a significant genetic correlation with ME. These findings suggest that both ME and depression have a genetic component (ME 0.42, depression 0.37) and share common genetic factors, indicating a potential overlap in their causes and the importance of circadian rhythms in depression. Further investigation of this relationship may provide insights into the causes of depression and potential treatment targets.

title: The Transcription Factor T-bet Regulates Intestinal Inflammation Mediated by Interleukin-7 Receptor+ Innate Lymphoid Cells
text: Mice that lack the transcription factor T-bet in their innate immune system develop colitis that is dependent on the microbiota. In our study, we found that interleukin-17A (IL-17A)-producing innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) that express IL-7Rα were strong promoters of disease in mice with ulcerative colitis. Dendritic cells that do not express CD103 but express CD11b produced TNF-α, which worked together with IL-23 to stimulate the production of IL-17A by ILCs. This revealed a previously unknown interaction between dendritic cells and ILCs. We also discovered that Helicobacter typhlonius plays a crucial role in triggering the disease by causing excessive TNF-α production and promoting colitis in these mice. Importantly, T-bet also suppressed the expression of IL-7R, a molecule that plays a key role in regulating the balance of ILCs in the intestine. We demonstrated the significance of IL-7R signaling in the development of colitis in these mice by observing a significant reduction in intestinal ILCs and a decrease in colitis severity when IL-7R was blocked. Overall, our findings provide insight into how T-bet controls the intricate interactions between mucosal dendritic cells, ILCs, and the intestinal microbiota.

title: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-Redirected Regulatory T Cells Suppress Experimental Allergic Airway Inflammation, a Model of Asthma
text: Cellular therapy using cytotoxic T cells that have been redirected with chimeric antigen receptors (CAR) has shown impressive effectiveness in treating blood cancers. In our study, we investigated the use of regulatory T cells (Treg) as a therapy for allergic airway inflammation, which serves as a model for asthma. Asthma is characterized by hyper-reactivity in the airways and a chronic immune response dominated by T helper-2 (Th2) cells in response to allergens. To restore immune balance in the lungs, we redirected Tregs using CARs specifically designed for lung epithelial cells in mice with experimentally induced allergic asthma, closely resembling the clinical scenario. The CAR Tregs that were transferred into the mice accumulated in the lungs and tracheobronchial lymph nodes, resulting in reduced airway hyper-reactivity and decreased inflammation characterized by lower cell numbers in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and reduced cell infiltrates in the lungs. Additionally, the CAR Tregs prevented excessive production of mucus in the lungs, as well as the increase in allergen-specific IgE and Th2 cytokine levels in the exposed animals. Compared to non-modified Tregs, the CAR Tregs were more effective in controlling asthma, highlighting the importance of activating specific Treg cells in the affected organ. These findings demonstrate that CAR Tregs targeted to the lungs can improve key aspects of experimental airway inflammation, opening up possibilities for cell therapy in severe allergic asthma.

title: α-Catenin as a tension transducer that induces adherens junction development
text: The mechanism by which adherens junctions (AJs) maintain tissue integrity is not fully understood at the molecular level. However, it is believed that AJs, which are formed by adhesion proteins and the actin cytoskeleton, can sense pulling forces from neighboring cells and adjust opposing forces. Previously, it was thought that α-catenin, a protein involved in AJ formation and function, did not directly link the membrane to the actin cytoskeleton. However, our research demonstrates that α-catenin can recruit vinculin, another important actin-binding protein of AJs, through changes in its conformation that are dependent on force. By introducing mutant α-catenin into cells and conducting in vitro binding assays, we identified specific regions in the α-catenin molecule that are necessary for its force-dependent interaction with vinculin. Additionally, our findings from fluorescence recovery after photobleaching analysis, as well as the detection of an antibody that recognizes α-catenin in a force-dependent manner, provide further evidence that α-catenin acts as a tension transducer. It is capable of converting mechanical stimuli into a chemical response, ultimately contributing to the development of AJs.

title: A population-based cohort study to elucidate temporal relationship between schizophrenia and metabolic syndrome (KCIS no. PSY3).
text:
The relationship between metabolic syndrome (MetS) and schizophrenia (SCZ) is important for the treatment of both conditions, but the causal effects have not been fully understood. This study aimed to investigate the impact of MetS on the development of SCZ, as well as the reverse relationship, using a population-based cohort sample. 

A total of 76,545 subjects who participated in a community-based health screening program between 1999 and 2004 were included in the study. Participants with existing MetS or SCZ at the start of the study were excluded, and two separate cohorts were followed over time to determine the incidence of SCZ and MetS. The hazard ratios for each predictor were calculated, taking into account potential confounding factors. 

The overall incidence rate of SCZ was 61.15 per 100,000 person-years. The incidence rate was lower in patients with MetS compared to those without (44.24 versus 64.20), indicating that MetS did not increase the risk of developing SCZ. However, participants with abnormal waist circumference (WC) were twice as likely to develop SCZ compared to those with normal WC. 

In the reverse direction, the incidence of MetS was higher in patients with SCZ compared to those without (11.25% versus 7.94%), suggesting that SCZ increased the risk of developing MetS. 

In conclusion, this large-scale study confirmed that central obesity, a component of MetS, is an independent predictor for the development of SCZ. Patients with SCZ are also at a higher risk of developing MetS. These findings suggest a reciprocal interaction between SCZ and central obesity.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF A MEASURE OF EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
Cholesterol glucosylation promotes immune evasion by Helicobacter pylori
text: Infection with Helicobacter pylori leads to gastric issues like ulcers and carcinoma. Since H. pylori cannot produce its own cholesterol, we investigated how it assimilates cholesterol during infection. Our findings reveal that H. pylori follows a cholesterol gradient and extracts lipids from the plasma membranes of epithelial cells, which are then converted into glucose. When there is an excess of cholesterol, antigen-presenting cells like macrophages and dendritic cells are more likely to phagocytose H. pylori, leading to enhanced T cell responses. Interestingly, a diet rich in cholesterol during bacterial challenge reduces the H. pylori burden in the stomach through T cell-mediated mechanisms. However, when cholesterol is intrinsically glucosylated, phagocytosis of H. pylori and subsequent T cell activation are prevented. We have identified the gene hp0421, which encodes the enzyme cholesterol-α-glucosyltransferase responsible for cholesterol glucosylation. By generating knockout mutants lacking hp0421, we have confirmed the crucial role of cholesteryl glucosides in evading phagocytosis, activating T cells, and clearing the bacteria in vivo. Therefore, we propose a mechanism that regulates the interaction between the host and pathogen, where glucosylation of a lipid determines whether the immune system evades or responds to the infection.

title: Regulation of in situ to invasive breast carcinoma transition.
text: Understanding the transition from ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to invasive carcinoma is a crucial aspect of breast tumor progression that remains poorly understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of myoepithelial cells and fibroblasts in the progression of in situ carcinomas using a model of human DCIS and primary breast tumors. Our findings revealed that fibroblasts played a promoting role in the transition to invasion, while normal myoepithelial cells inhibited this process. Through analyzing the molecular profiles of isolated luminal epithelial and myoepithelial cells, we identified a complex interaction network involving TGFbeta, Hedgehog, cell adhesion, and p63. These factors were found to be crucial for myoepithelial cell differentiation, and their elimination led to the loss of myoepithelial cells and subsequent progression to invasion.

title: Health and access to care: perspectives of homeless youth in Baltimore City, U.S.A.
text:
Little is known about the perceptions and context of health issues among homeless youth, despite their high rates of health problems. To address this gap, a study was conducted using a combination of qualitative techniques from participatory rural appraisal and rapid assessment procedures. The aim was to investigate the health needs as perceived by shelter-based youth in Baltimore, MD, USA.

The study found that the most common health problems identified by the youth included STDs, HIV/AIDS, pregnancy, depression, drug use, and injuries. These findings aligned with objective health status data for the same group of youth. The youth also expressed concerns about environmental safety, particularly violence and victimization by adults, as well as experiences of racism and sexism in their lives.

Interestingly, the youth highlighted the importance of trusted adult figures, such as grandmothers, as sources of health advice. Despite being homeless and coming from less than ideal family situations, many of these youth maintained contact with and sought advice from their parents and other family members.

The study emphasizes the need for health interventions targeting urban street youth to recognize the significance of the social context in which these youth live. It also underscores the reality of violence as a daily health threat for this population.

title: Differential requirement for CARMA1 in agonist-selected T-cell development.
text: Caspase recruitment domain-containing membrane-associated guanylate kinase protein-1 (CARMA1) plays a crucial role in the NF-kappaB signaling pathway activated by TCR engagement. TCR signaling is not only important for the activation of naïve T cells, but also for the development of specific T-cell subsets such as Treg, NKT cells, and CD8-alpha alpha T cells. However, the role of CARMA1 in the development of these subsets is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the impact of CARMA1 deficiency on the populations of agonist-selected T cells. Our findings demonstrate that CARMA1-deficient mice (CARMA1(-/-)) exhibit altered populations of specific T-cell subsets. Specifically, CARMA1(-/-) mice show impaired development of natural and adaptive Treg cells, while NKT cell numbers remain unaffected compared to wild-type mice. Interestingly, CD8-alpha alpha T cells, which may develop through a different selection pathway, are more abundant in the gut of CARMA1(-/-) mice. On the other hand, memory-phenotype CD4(+) T cells (CD62L(low)/CD44(high)) are reduced in number in the periphery. These results indicate that CARMA1 is crucial for Treg cell development, but not essential for the development of other agonist-selected T-cell subsets. Overall, our findings highlight the differential role of CARMA1-mediated TCR signaling in T-cell development.

title: Simian immunodeficiency viruses of diverse origin can use CXCR4 as a coreceptor for entry into human cells.
text: We examined primary simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) isolated from different primate species, including sooty mangabey (SIVsm [n = 6]), stumptail (SIVstm [n = 1]), mandrill (SIVmnd [n = 1]), and African green (SIVagm [n = 1]), to determine their ability to infect human cells and their coreceptor requirements. All isolates were able to infect human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a CCR5(+/+) donor, and seven out of eight isolates also infected CCR5(-/-) PBMCs. Using GHOST and U87 cell lines, we analyzed the coreceptor utilization and found that all tested isolates used CCR5 and the orphan receptors STRL33 and GPR15. Some primary SIV isolates also utilized coreceptors such as CCR2b, CCR3, CCR8, and CX3CR1. Importantly, we discovered that SIVstm, SIVagm, and four SIVsm isolates used CXCR4 as a coreceptor in GHOST and U87 cells. These findings suggest that primary SIV isolates from various primate species can utilize CXCR4 for viral entry, similar to human immunodeficiency viruses.

title: Cloning of rat uncoupling protein-3 and uncoupling protein-2 cDNAs: their gene expression in rats fed high-fat diet.
text: To investigate the energy balance in skeletal muscle, we successfully cloned the cDNA of a homologue of uncoupling protein (UCP) from rat skeletal muscle. Additionally, we cloned rat UCP-2 cDNA from rat brown adipose tissue (BAT). The UCP cloned from rat skeletal muscle exhibited 57% and 72% similarity to rat UCP-1 and UCP-2, respectively. The mRNA expression of this UCP was abundant in skeletal muscle, moderate in BAT, and low in white adipose tissue (WAT). It appeared as a major band at 2.5 kb and a minor band at 2.8 kb. On the other hand, the UCP-2 gene expression was detected throughout the body, with significant levels in WAT and slight levels in skeletal muscle and BAT. Our rat UCP shared 86% identity with the recently cloned human UCP-3, which was also abundantly expressed in skeletal muscle with a signal of 2.4 kb. Therefore, we concluded that our rat UCP was equivalent to rat UCP-3. In rats fed a high-fat diet, the expression of UCP-3 gene in skeletal muscle was doubled, while UCP-2 mRNA levels significantly increased (1.6-fold) in epididymal WAT. This upregulation of UCPs may serve as a defense mechanism against high-fat induced obesity and glucose metabolism impairment.

title: A two-step mechanism for epigenetic specification of centromere identity and function
text: The centromere, which is the key factor in chromosome inheritance, is determined by an epigenetic mark in many eukaryotes. Through the use of gene targeting in human cells and fission yeast, it has been demonstrated that the epigenetic mark responsible for identifying, maintaining, and propagating centromere function is the chromatin containing the centromere-specific histone H3 variant known as CENP-A. This mark operates through a two-step process. Initially, the centromere position is replicated and preserved by chromatin that incorporates the centromere-targeting domain (CATD) of CENP-A in place of H3. Subsequently, it is shown that the nucleation of kinetochore assembly onto the CATD-containing chromatin requires either the amino- or carboxy-terminal tail of CENP-A. These tails are responsible for recruiting inner kinetochore proteins, such as CENP-B, which stabilizes binding to human centromeres, or CENP-C, which is directly recruited.

title: Cancer stem cell theory in gastrointestinal malignancies: recent progress and upcoming challenges
text: There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that malignant tumors are not uniform, but rather consist of various subpopulations of cells with distinct characteristics. These cells have the ability to initiate tumor growth and spread to other parts of the body, a process known as metastasis. This phenomenon can be explained by the cancer stem cell (CSC) theory. Recent advancements in technology have allowed for a better understanding and characterization of CSCs. While applying this theory to blood cancers and solid tumors shows promise for new cancer treatments, there are also doubts. It is important to explore effective therapeutic approaches that target the CSC population in order to overcome treatment failures and improve patient outcomes. This review will focus on the regulation of CSCs, both from within the cells themselves and from external factors, as well as the development of therapeutic strategies specifically targeting CSCs, with a particular emphasis on gastrointestinal cancers.

title: In vitro splicing pathways of pre-mRNAs containing multiple intervening sequences?
text: We examined the splicing pathways of three pre-mRNAs with multiple intervening sequences (IVS) in vitro. The pre-mRNAs analyzed were human beta-globin, which has two IVSs; rat alpha-lactalbumin, which has three IVSs; and murine interleukin-3, which has four IVSs. Our findings revealed that there are specific and preferred pathways for IVS removal from these multi-IVS pre-mRNAs in vitro. In the case of rat alpha-lactalbumin, the three IVSs were sequentially excised from 5' to 3', with IVS1 being removed first, followed by IVS2, and finally IVS3 in most molecules. The splicing pathway of interleukin-3 pre-mRNA was more intricate. Although there was a preferred temporal order for the excision of the four IVSs, it was not strictly sequential or directional. In most molecules, IVS1 and IVS4 were removed first, either simultaneously or in rapid succession. Subsequently, IVS2 was excised, followed by IVS3. These observed splicing pathways seemed to be influenced by differences in lag times and maximum excision rates of the various IVSs. Importantly, we did not detect any exon skipping during the splicing of these transcripts in vitro. These findings have implications for proposed models of splice site selection.

title: Automated genome sequence analysis and annotation.
text:
The motivation behind this study is the increasing number of sequences generated by large-scale genome projects, most of which are not yet characterized biochemically. Bioinformatics research aims to develop computational methods for characterizing these sequences. However, the installation and application of these methods can be time-consuming and require experience. 

In this study, we introduce an automatic system for preliminary functional annotation of protein sequences. This system has been used to analyze sets of sequences from complete genomes, improving overall performance and making new discoveries comparable to those made by human experts. The GeneQuiz system includes a web-based browser that allows users to examine the evidence behind the automatic annotation, providing additional information, result views, and links to biological databases that complement the automatic analysis. 

We provide detailed information on the structure and operating principles of the system, including the use of multiple sequence databases, underlying sequence analysis tools, lexical analyses of database annotations, and decision criteria for functional assignments. The system also assesses the quality of results based on prior experience with the sequence analysis tools, with estimated error rates of 2.5-5% for cases annotated with the highest reliability. We discuss potential sources of over-interpretation of results and propose improvements. 

We present a conservative definition for reporting "new findings" that considers the maturity of the database, along with examples of possible discoveries made by the system, such as new functions, families, and superfamilies. We analyze the system's performance in relation to sequence database coverage, dynamics, and search methods, highlighting the advantages of an integrated automatic approach that uses multiple databases and search methods in an objective and repeatable manner. 

The GeneQuiz system is publicly available for protein sequence analysis through a web server at http://www.sander.ebi.ac.uk/gqsrv/submit.

title: GAPDH Mediates Nitrosylation of Nuclear Proteins
text: Nitric oxide plays a significant role in cell signaling through the process of S-nitrosylation, which involves the attachment of nitric oxide to proteins. This process regulates various proteins, including nuclear proteins like HDAC2 and PARP1. The reactivity of nitric oxide with protein thiols and its selective nature within cells suggest the presence of targeting mechanisms. Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) binds to target proteins, either directly or through scaffolding proteins like PSD-95 and CAPON, to achieve specificity in nitric oxide signaling. However, since the main isoforms of NOS are non-nuclear, the mechanisms behind the selective nitrosylation of nuclear proteins have been unclear. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) is naturally nitrosylated at its Cys 150 residue. Nitrosylated GAPDH (SNO-GAPDH) binds to Siah1, which has a nuclear localization signal, and is transported to the nucleus. In our study, we demonstrate that SNO-GAPDH physiologically transfers nitric oxide to nuclear proteins, including SIRT1, HDAC2, and DNA-PK. These findings uncover a new mechanism for targeted nitrosylation of nuclear proteins and suggest that protein-protein transfer of nitric oxide groups may be a common mechanism in cellular signal transduction.

title: The transcription factor c-Maf controls the production of interleukin-4 but not other Th2 cytokines.
text: The promotion of naive CD4+ T cells into IL-4-producing T helper 2 (Th2) cells is facilitated by IL-4. Previous research suggested, but did not definitively prove, that the transcription factor c-Maf controlled the tissue-specific expression of IL-4. It was unclear whether c-Maf also regulated the transcription of other Th2 cytokine genes. To gain a better understanding of c-Maf's role, we investigated cytokine production in mice lacking c-Maf (c-maf(-/-)). We observed a significant deficiency in IL-4 production in CD4+ T cells and NK T cells from c-maf(-/-) mice. However, these mice still produced normal levels of IL-13 and IgE. Additionally, when c-maf(-/-) T cells were differentiated in the presence of exogenous IL-4, they produced approximately normal levels of other Th2 cytokines. Based on these findings, we conclude that c-Maf plays a critical and selective role in the transcription of the IL-4 gene in vivo.

title: Genome-wide association of IL28B with response to pegylated interferon-α and ribavirin therapy for chronic hepatitis C
text: The standard treatment for patients with chronic hepatitis C, which involves using pegylated interferon-α (PEG-IFN-α) along with ribavirin (RBV), does not guarantee a sustained virologic response (SVR) for all patients. In this study, we conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to investigate the lack of virological response (NVR) in the treatment of patients with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1 within the Japanese population. Our findings revealed that two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near the IL28B gene on chromosome 19 were strongly linked to NVR (rs12980275, P = 1.93 × 10−13, and rs8099917, 3.11 × 10−15). We were able to replicate these associations in an independent cohort, with combined P values of 2.84 × 10−27 (OR = 17.7; 95% CI = 10.0–31.3) and 2.68 × 10−32 (OR = 27.1; 95% CI = 14.6–50.3), respectively. Additionally, these SNPs were also found to be associated with SVR when compared to NVR (rs12980275, P = 3.99 × 10−24, and rs8099917, P = 1.11 × 10−27). Further analysis of the IL28B region through fine mapping identified seven SNPs (rs8105790, rs11881222, rs8103142, rs28416813, rs4803219, rs8099917, and rs7248668) that displayed the most significant associations (P = 5.52 × 10−28–2.68 × 10−32; OR = 22.3–27.1). Moreover, real-time quantitative PCR assays conducted on peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed lower expression levels of IL28B in individuals carrying the minor alleles (P = 0.015).

title: The WUSCHEL-related homeobox gene WOX11 is required to activate shoot-borne crown root development in rice.
text: The shoot-borne crown roots, which are the main type of roots in rice (Oryza sativa), are formed at the lower stem nodes as part of normal plant growth. However, we have limited understanding of the regulatory mechanism behind crown root development. In this study, we demonstrate that a gene called WOX11, which is related to WUSCHEL and belongs to the Homeobox family, plays a role in activating the emergence and growth of crown roots. We observed that WOX11 is expressed in newly emerging crown roots and later in regions of the root meristem where cell division occurs. The expression of WOX11 can be induced by the application of auxin or cytokinin. When the WOX11 gene was mutated or downregulated, the number and growth rate of crown roots decreased. Conversely, overexpression of the gene led to premature growth of crown roots and a significant increase in root biomass, with crown roots forming at the upper stem nodes and the base of florets. The overexpression and RNA interference of WOX11 also affected the expression of genes that respond to auxin and cytokinin. Further investigation revealed that WOX11 directly represses the expression of RR2, a gene that regulates cytokinin response and is expressed in crown root primordia. These findings suggest that WOX11 may act as a mediator between auxin and cytokinin signaling pathways, influencing cell proliferation during crown root development.

title: Inducible depletion of satellite cells in adult, sedentary mice impairs muscle regenerative capacity without affecting sarcopenia
text: Sarcopenia, the age-related decline in skeletal muscle mass and strength, is a significant factor in geriatric frailty. While the exact cause of sarcopenia is still unknown, there is a correlation between the decrease in activity of satellite cells (muscle stem cells) and impaired muscle regeneration during aging. This correlation has led to the hypothesis that the loss of satellite cell activity is a contributing factor to sarcopenia. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment on sedentary male mice, depleting their satellite cells to a level that would hinder regeneration for the rest of their lives. Through a detailed analysis of multiple muscles at different stages of aging, we found that the muscles remained normal in size despite reduced regenerative capacity, but did show increased fibrosis. These findings suggest that the lifelong reduction of satellite cells did not worsen sarcopenia or affect muscle size and fiber composition during aging. However, the loss of satellite cells may contribute to age-related muscle fibrosis.

title: Reproductive clonality in protozoan pathogens--truth or artefact?
text: The discussion regarding the frequency and significance of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa has been ongoing for several decades. Recently, there have been claims suggesting that the population structures of various crucial protozoan pathogens can be explained by predominant clonal evolution. However, we present an alternative viewpoint. We propose that the apparent clonality observed may be a result of insufficient sampling and flawed study designs. To support this argument, we review current research to understand why it is challenging to detect sexual reproduction in protozoan parasite populations. In doing so, we compare laboratory models of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa with natural patterns of genetic diversity and assess the advantages of sexual reproduction at different evolutionary levels. We explore strategies to enhance the accuracy of efforts to study genetic exchange in the field. Additionally, we analyze the implications of the initial population genomic studies on the debate surrounding sex and clonality in parasitic protozoa, while also discussing potential limitations for future research.

title: The ACF1 complex is required for DNA double-strand break repair in human cells.
text: The repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is a complex process that involves nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR). However, the specific cellular mechanisms involved in this repair process are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that two ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling factors, ACF1 and SNF2H, rapidly accumulate at DSBs and are essential for DSB repair in human cells. Suppression of ACF1 or SNF2H expression renders cells highly sensitive to X-rays and chemical treatments that cause DSBs, resulting in unrepaired DSBs. ACF1 directly interacts with KU70 and is necessary for the recruitment of KU proteins to DSBs. Following DSB-inducing treatments, the KU70/80 complex becomes more closely associated with the chromatin-remodeling factors of the CHRAC complex, which includes ACF1, SNF2H, CHRAC15, and CHRAC17. Additionally, the frequency of NHEJ and HR, both of which are induced by DSBs in chromosomal DNA, is significantly reduced in cells lacking these factors. These findings highlight the crucial roles of ACF1 and its complexes in the repair of DSBs.

title: Findings to date from the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS).
text:
There is ongoing debate in the United States regarding the appropriate evaluation and management of low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) and equivocal cervical cytologic interpretations (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASCUS, now ASC-US]). To address this issue, the National Cancer Institute initiated the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS), a randomized clinical trial conducted at multiple centers. The purpose of ALTS was to assess three different methods of management: immediate colposcopy, cytologic follow-up, and triage using human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing. This article provides a summary of the major findings from ALTS that have been published thus far.

Between November 1996 and December 1998, a total of 3,488 patients with ASCUS and 1,572 patients with LSIL were randomly assigned to different research arms and followed for a period of two years. The primary outcome of interest was the presence of histologic cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 or cancer. The prevalence of oncogenic HPV was found to be too high to effectively triage LSIL using HPV DNA testing with Hybrid Capture 2. However, for women referred with a cytologic interpretation of ASCUS, HPV triage was found to be useful. It demonstrated sensitivity equivalent to immediate colposcopy and resulted in a significant reduction in the number of colposcopic referrals. Among older women with ASCUS, HPV testing remained sensitive in detecting CIN 3 and cancer, but the referral rate was considerably lower compared to younger women.

ALTS also provided valuable insights into the performance of cytology and histopathology. Experienced pathologists showed significant differences in their interpretations of cervical abnormalities, particularly in cases of histologic CIN 1 and cytologic ASCUS. Nevertheless, it was possible to identify a relatively rare type of ASCUS that was equivocal for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. This type of ASCUS had a high positive predictive value for detecting underlying high-grade CIN. Additional analyses from ALTS are currently underway.

title: Marine organisms as a source of new anticancer agents.
text: Plants and microorganisms found on land have provided a variety of active anticancer substances. Four decades ago, the discovery of C-nucleosides in the Caribbean sponge, Cryptotheca crypta, laid the foundation for the development of cytarabine, the first marine-derived anticancer drug used in clinical practice. Cytarabine is currently employed in the standard treatment of leukemia and lymphoma patients. Additionally, gemcitabine, a fluorinated derivative of cytarabine, has been approved for treating pancreatic, breast, bladder, and non-small-cell lung cancer. In recent years, numerous new experimental anticancer drugs derived from marine sources have entered preclinical and clinical trials. This field has expanded significantly due to advancements in deep-sea collection technology, extraction methods, and large-scale production through aquaculture and synthesis. This article briefly discusses examples of marine-derived experimental drugs currently undergoing preclinical and early clinical evaluation. Furthermore, it provides a summary of available information on the outcomes of phase I and II trials for drugs like aplidine, ecteinascidin-734 (ET-734), dolastatin 10, and bryostatin 1.

title: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of diindolylmethane for breast cancer biomarker modulation in patients taking tamoxifen
text: A study was conducted to investigate the effects and safety of using BioResponse DIM® (BR-DIM) in combination with tamoxifen for breast cancer prevention. Diindolylmethane (DIM), a compound found in cruciferous vegetables, has been suggested to have cancer-preventing properties. However, there is limited evidence on its effectiveness and long-term safety. The study involved 130 women who were prescribed tamoxifen and randomly assigned to receive either oral BR-DIM at a dose of 150 mg twice daily or a placebo for 12 months. The primary goal of the study was to assess changes in the urinary 2/16α-hydroxyestrone (2/16α-OHE1) ratio, which is an indicator of estrogen metabolism. Other factors such as serum estrogens, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), breast density, and tamoxifen metabolites were also evaluated. Ninety-eight women completed the intervention, with high compliance rates. The results showed that BR-DIM increased the 2/16α-OHE1 ratio compared to the placebo group. Serum SHBG levels were also higher in the BR-DIM group. However, there were no significant changes in breast density. The levels of tamoxifen metabolites were reduced in women receiving BR-DIM. Adverse events were minimal and similar in both groups. The study suggests that daily BR-DIM may have positive effects on estrogen metabolism and SHBG levels in breast cancer patients taking tamoxifen. Further research is needed to determine if the reduction in tamoxifen metabolites affects the clinical benefits of tamoxifen.

title: Intracellular coenzymes as natural biomarkers for metabolic activities and mitochondrial anomalies.
text: Mitochondria have a crucial role in energy metabolism, programmed cell death, and oxidative stress. When mitochondrial DNA is mutated in diseased cells, it compromises the structure of important enzyme complexes and impairs mitochondrial function. This can lead to various health conditions such as cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and aging. Detecting mitochondrial and metabolic abnormalities early on is vital for effective diagnosis and treatment. Reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) play significant roles in a wide range of cellular oxidation-reduction reactions. Notably, NADH and FAD exhibit natural fluorescence, enabling noninvasive imaging of metabolic activities in living cells and tissues. Additionally, NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be excited using different wavelengths for complementary imaging techniques and are sensitive to protein binding and local environment. This article focuses on recent advancements in using intracellular NADH and FAD as potential biomarkers for assessing metabolic and mitochondrial activities.

title: Biochemical differences in the alphabeta T cell receptor.CD3 surface complex between CD8+ and CD4+ human mature T lymphocytes.
text: We have documented variations in the biochemical and structural characteristics of the alphabeta T cell receptor (TCR) complex between CD4(+) and CD8(+) CD3gamma-deficient (gamma(-)) mature T cells. In this study, we have expanded our knowledge and extended our findings to primary T lymphocytes from normal (gamma(+)) individuals. The surface TCR.CD3 components, excluding CD3gamma, in CD4(+) gamma(-) T cells were detectable and similar in size to CD4(+) gamma(+) controls. The native TCR.CD3 complex in CD4(+) gamma(-) T cells was also similar to CD4(+) gamma(+) controls, except for a difference in stoichiometry, with an alphabeta(deltaepsilon)(2)zeta(2) configuration instead of an alphabetagammaepsilondeltaepsilonzeta(2) configuration. On the other hand, the surface TCRalpha, TCRbeta, and CD3delta chains in CD8(+) gamma(-) T cells did not exhibit their usual sizes. Through confocal immunofluorescence, TCRalpha was barely detectable in CD8(+) gamma(-) T cells. Blue native gels (BN-PAGE) revealed the presence of a diverse population of TCR.CD3 in these cells. Using primary peripheral blood T lymphocytes from normal (gamma(+)) donors, we conducted an extensive analysis of epitopes. Unlike other monoclonal antibodies specific to TCR.CD3, RW2-8C8 showed stronger staining in CD8(+) T cells compared to CD4(+) T cells, and this difference was dependent on the glycosylation of the TCR.CD3 complex but independent of T cell activation or differentiation. The staining of CD8(+) T cells with RW2-8C8 was found to be more reliant on the integrity of lipid rafts compared to CD4(+) T cells. Lastly, immunoprecipitation studies on purified primary CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells revealed differences in TCR glycosylation between the two cell types. Overall, these findings support the presence of lineage-specific variations in the conformation or topology of the TCR.CD3 complex in CD4(+) and CD8(+) wild type T cells. These differences may have implications for cis interactions during antigen recognition and signal transduction.

title: Circulating mitochondrial DNA in serum of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
text: Neutrophils play a crucial role in the development of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a disease characterized by inflammation of blood vessels. Recently, researchers have discovered the presence of neutrophil extracellular traps in this condition, which also release mitochondrial DNA. To investigate further, we conducted a study measuring the levels of circulating cell-free mitochondrial and genomic DNA in the serum of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. We enrolled 14 patients in the active stage of the disease, 11 in remission, and 10 healthy individuals as controls. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), we measured fragments of mitochondrial DNA (79 base pairs and 230 base pairs) and quantified Alu repeats to assess the abundance of nuclear DNA in the serum, with the presence of a plasmid control. We found that both fragments of mitochondrial DNA, as well as genomic DNA, were significantly elevated in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis compared to the control group. Specifically, the shorter 79 base pair fragment of mitochondrial DNA correlated with the active stage of the disease and clinical symptoms. This suggests that the release of mitochondrial DNA into the extracellular space is a mechanism associated with the active stage of granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Furthermore, the levels of circulating mitochondrial DNA were exceptionally high in untreated patients, indicating that mitochondrial DNA could serve as a useful biomarker for monitoring treatment effectiveness.

title: Estrogen receptor-alpha promotes alternative macrophage activation during cutaneous repair.
text: Efficient recruitment of local monocytes/macrophages is crucial for the repair of tissues. When macrophages are recruited, they can be polarized towards either a proinflammatory or prohealing activation state in response to cytokines. It is important for this polarization to be tightly regulated in order to facilitate efficient wound healing. Estrogen has been found to act as a powerful anti-inflammatory regulator in the healing of skin. However, there is currently a lack of understanding regarding the contribution of estrogen and its receptor (ER) to macrophage polarization and the subsequent effects on wound healing. In this study, we have discovered a previously unreported role of estrogen receptor α (ERα) in preferentially polarizing macrophages from various sources towards an alternative phenotype. Our experiments involving the removal of ER specifically in inflammatory cells confirm that ERα, but not ERβ, plays a role in poor healing characterized by an altered cytokine profile and a decrease in alternatively activated macrophages. Additionally, we have observed intrinsic changes in ERα-deficient macrophages, which are unable to respond to signals that induce alternative activation in vitro. Overall, our findings demonstrate that ERα expressed in inflammatory cells promotes the polarization of macrophages towards an alternative phenotype, which is beneficial for timely wound healing. Considering the diverse roles of ERs in various physiological processes, these findings are likely to be relevant to many conditions involving excessive inflammation.

title: Disturbance in cerebral spinal fluid sphingolipid content is associated with memory impairment in subjects infected with the human immunodeficiency virus
text: Despite the widespread use of antiretroviral therapies to control the replication of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), approximately 50% of those infected still experience cognitive dysfunctions known as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). Currently, there is no biomarker available to identify HIV-infected individuals who are at risk of developing HAND. Previous studies have identified specific sphingolipid species that are dysregulated in HAND, but the relationship between these biochemical findings and neurocognitive function is not yet understood. To address this question, we conducted a study comparing the levels of sphingomyelin, ceramide, and sterol species in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with performance on standard neurological tests that assess cognitive and motor function in HIV-infected individuals. Our findings revealed that the sphingomyelin:ceramide ratios for acyl chain lengths of C16:0, C18:0, C22:0, and C24:0 were associated with poorer performance on various memory tests. Particularly, the acyl chain length of C18:0 consistently correlated with performance on multiple memory tests. These results suggest that the sphingomyelin:ceramide ratio for C18:0 may serve as a reliable surrogate marker for memory dysfunction in HIV-infected individuals.

title: An observational study fluid balance and patient outcomes in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level of Replacement Therapy trial.
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between mean daily fluid balance during enrollment in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level (RENAL) replacement therapy study and clinical outcomes in intensive care unit patients. The study design involved a statistical analysis of data from multicenter, randomized, controlled trials. The study took place in thirty-five intensive care units in Australia and New Zealand, with a cohort of 1453 patients enrolled in the RENAL study. The interventions included analyzing the association between daily fluid balance and clinical outcomes using various statistical models.

The main results showed that survivors had a mean daily fluid balance of -234 mL/day, while nonsurvivors had a mean daily fluid balance of +560 mL/day. The cumulative fluid balance over the same period was -1941 mL for survivors and +1755 mL for nonsurvivors. A negative mean daily fluid balance during the study treatment was independently associated with a lower risk of death at 90 days and increased survival time. It was also associated with more renal replacement-free days, intensive care unit-free days, and hospital-free days. These findings remained consistent across different statistical models.

In conclusion, this study found that a negative mean daily fluid balance was consistently linked to improved clinical outcomes in the RENAL study. Manipulating fluid balance may be a potential target for future interventional trials involving critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy.

title: Prison health care: a review of the literature.
text: The number of people in prison is on the rise, and the health problems faced by inmates are significant. Prisons are designed to punish, correct, and rehabilitate individuals, which can sometimes conflict with the goals of providing healthcare. A review of existing literature has identified mental health, substance abuse, and communicable diseases as the main concerns in prison healthcare. Female and elderly prisoners have unique needs that differ from those of other inmates. It is important for prison healthcare to prioritize health promotion and the well-being of the community beyond prison walls. Delivering effective healthcare to prisoners requires a partnership between healthcare and prison services, and telemedicine offers a potential solution for this.

title: A Brief History of Long-Term Potentiation
text: Since its discovery in 1973, long-term potentiation (LTP) has been the subject of numerous research papers, exploring its fascinating role as a cellular model for learning and memory. Despite facing challenges along the way, LTP has now reached a significant milestone in its development. In this review, we delve into the extensive history of LTP, highlighting the current era of exciting advancements and the remarkable speed at which new discoveries are being made.

title: Tumor-Induced IL-6 Reprograms Host Metabolism to Suppress Anti-tumor Immunity
text: Cachexia, a wasting syndrome commonly found in cancer patients, is linked to a deficiency in calories. This deficiency leads to changes in the body's metabolic response, which in turn suppresses the immune system within the tumor. In our study, we focused on mice with colorectal cancer or pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) that were in the pre-cachectic stage. We discovered that IL-6, a protein produced by the tumor, inhibits the liver's ability to produce ketones by suppressing PPARalpha, a key regulator of ketogenesis. When these mice were subjected to a calorie-deficient diet, their ketone levels dropped significantly, causing a rise in glucocorticoid levels as a stress response. This hormonal stress response suppressed multiple immune pathways within the tumor. Additionally, when we administered corticosterone to elevate glucocorticoid levels to a level lower than that seen in cachectic mice, the response of mouse PDA to an immunotherapy that was being tested in clinical trials was completely abolished. Therefore, IL-6 produced by the tumor impairs the body's ability to produce ketones in response to reduced calorie intake, leading to a systemic metabolic stress response that hinders the effectiveness of anti-cancer immunotherapy.

title: Chaperoning stem cells: a role for heat shock proteins in the modulation of stem cell self-renewal and differentiation?
text: The processes of self-renewal and differentiation in stem cells are tightly controlled and influenced by both internal and external signals. Molecular chaperones and co-chaperones, particularly heat shock proteins (Hsp), are molecules found throughout the body that play a role in shaping the structure and interactions of proteins. While the function of Hsp is well understood in specialized cells, their role in stem cells is still not fully understood. It seems that embryonic stem cells have a higher tolerance to stress and express higher levels of chaperones. This article critically examines research on stem cells from the perspective of molecular chaperones. Additionally, we propose a model that suggests chaperones play a role in regulating self-renewal in mouse embryonic stem cells.

title: How much alcohol and how often? Population based case-control study of alcohol consumption and risk of a major coronary event.
text:
GOAL: To assess the impact of the amount and frequency of alcohol consumption on the likelihood of experiencing acute myocardial infarction and coronary death.
