METHOD: This study utilized a case-control design and was conducted in the Lower Hunter region of New South Wales, Australia, from 1983 to 1994. The participants included men and women aged 35-69 years. The primary outcome measure was the occurrence of acute myocardial infarction or coronary death.

RESULTS: The study compared the alcohol consumption patterns of 11,511 individuals who experienced acute myocardial infarction or coronary death with 6,077 randomly selected controls from the same study population. After adjusting for age, smoking, and medical history, it was observed that men and women who consumed one or two alcoholic drinks on five or six days per week had a reduced risk of major coronary events compared to non-drinkers (odds ratios: men 0.31 (95% confidence interval 0.22 to 0.45); women 0.33 (0.18 to 0.59)). This risk reduction remained consistent even after excluding non-drinkers who were previously moderate to heavy drinkers. Additionally, individuals who regularly consumed one or two drinks within 24 hours before experiencing symptoms also exhibited a protective effect (odds ratios: men 0.74 (0.51 to 1.09); women 0.43 (0.20 to 0.95)).

CONCLUSIONS: The frequency and quantity of alcohol consumption play a significant role in determining the risk of major coronary events. Men who consume one to four drinks daily on five or six days per week, as well as women who consume one or two drinks daily on five or six days per week, have the lowest risk.

title: Tracking adipogenesis during white adipose tissue development, expansion and regeneration
text: White adipose tissue exhibits a high level of flexibility. We have created a system called the AdipoChaser mouse, which allows us to label mature adipocytes in a way that is both inducible and permanent. Using this system, we have been able to track the process of adipogenesis during different stages, such as development, high-fat diet feeding, and exposure to cold temperatures. When subcutaneous fat undergoes a process known as 'browning' due to cold exposure, the majority of beige adipocytes are formed from newly differentiated adipocytes. On the other hand, during high-fat diet feeding, adipogenesis begins in the epididymal fat after 4 weeks, while subcutaneous fat experiences hypertrophy for up to 12 weeks. Gonadal fat develops after birth, while subcutaneous fat develops between embryonic days 14 and 18. These findings emphasize the significant variations in the potential for adipogenesis in different fat depots.

title: Blockade of adrenoreceptors inhibits the splenic response to stroke.
text: Recent research has emphasized the role of the peripheral immune system in the delayed degeneration of cells following a stroke. In a stroke model called permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), the spleen undergoes a decrease in size due to the release of immune cells from the organ. However, when human umbilical cord blood cells (HUCBC) are administered systemically 24 hours after the stroke, the reduction in spleen size is prevented and there is a significant decrease in the volume of tissue damage. Additionally, removing the spleen two weeks before the stroke also reduces tissue damage, further illustrating the harmful impact of this organ on stroke-induced neurodegeneration. After MCAO, the sympathetic nervous system becomes activated, leading to increased levels of catecholamines in both the spleen and the systemic circulation when released from the adrenal medulla. These catecholamines bind to alpha and beta adrenoreceptors in the spleen. This study investigates whether catecholamines play a role in regulating the spleen's response to stroke. Male Sprague-Dawley rats either underwent denervation of the spleen two weeks before MCAO or were treated with carvedilol (a pan adrenergic receptor blocker), prazosin (an alpha1 receptor blocker), or propranolol (a beta receptor blocker). The denervation was confirmed by observing reduced expression of tyrosine hydroxylase in the spleen. Denervation prior to MCAO did not affect tissue damage or spleen size. Treatment with propranolol also had no impact on these outcomes. However, treatment with either prazosin or carvedilol prevented the reduction in spleen size, with only carvedilol significantly reducing tissue damage (p < 0.05). These findings demonstrate that circulating catecholamines in the blood regulate the spleen's response to stroke by activating both alpha and beta adrenergic receptors.

title: Effects of Thiazolidinediones on Stroke Recovery: A Case-Matched Controlled Study
text: The use of anti-inflammatory therapy has been shown to reduce the size of a heart attack and improve recovery from a stroke. Thiazolidinedione peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)gamma agonists are a type of medication that have strong anti-inflammatory properties and can also help with insulin sensitivity and diabetes management. In a study, thirty stroke patients with type 2 diabetes who were admitted for acute inpatient stroke rehabilitation were given either pioglitazone or rosiglitazone, while another group of thirty stroke patients with type 2 diabetes did not receive these medications. The two groups were matched for age, sex, initial FIMTM score (a measure of functional independence), and time since the stroke. The researchers compared various outcome measures between the two groups. The results showed that the group receiving thiazolidinediones had a significantly greater improvement in their FIMTM score compared to the control group (25.6 ± 10.2 SD vs. 19.8 ± 10.5, respectively, P = 0.015). However, there was no significant difference in the length of their stay in the rehabilitation hospital (24.2 ± 7.6 vs. 25.1 ± 7.4 days, P = 0.657) or their final discharge destination (home/institution, 19/11 versus 17/13, P = 0.792). Overall, the use of thiazolidinediones was associated with better functional recovery in stroke patients with type 2 diabetes.

title: Crosstalk between tumor and endothelial cells promotes tumor angiogenesis by MAPK activation of Notch signaling.
text: Although progress has been made in understanding how secreted angiogenic factors induce tumor vasculature, there is limited knowledge about the signals that promote tumor angiogenesis through direct contact. In this study, we discovered that the growth factors stimulate the production of the Notch ligand Jagged1 in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cells via the mitogen-activating protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. This induced the activation of Notch in neighboring endothelial cells (ECs) and facilitated the formation of capillary-like sprouts. HNSCC cells expressing Jagged1 significantly increased neovascularization and tumor growth in vivo. Furthermore, the level of Jagged1 was strongly associated with the presence of tumor blood vessels and correlated with the development of HNSCC. Our findings reveal a new mechanism in which the interaction between tumor cells and ECs directly promotes angiogenesis through the MAPK and Notch signaling pathways.

title: A Sequential splicing mechanism promotes selection of an optimal exon by repositioning a downstream 5' splice site in preprotachykinin pre-mRNA.
text: In order to investigate the underlying structure of alternative splicing, we conducted an analysis on the splicing of pre-mRNAs that contain an optional exon, E4, from the preprotachykinin gene. This particular gene is responsible for encoding substance P and related tachykinin peptides through alternative splicing of a shared pre-mRNA. Our findings demonstrate that alternative splicing of preprotachykinin pre-mRNA occurs primarily by skipping the optional E4 exon. The mechanism that competes with this skipping process and incorporates E4 into the final spliced RNA is limited by an initial block in the splicing of the immediate upstream intervening sequence (IVS), known as IVS3. However, this block is relieved through sequential splicing, where the immediate downstream IVS4 is removed first. The initial splicing event causes a structural change that directly activates IVS3 splicing. This structural rearrangement replaces IVS4 sequences with E5 and its adjacent IVS5 sequences. To understand how this structural change promotes IVS3 splicing, we investigated what structural changes would restore the activity of IVS3 splicing-defective mutants. The most significant effect was observed when a 2-nucleotide substitution converted the 5' splice site of E4 to an exact consensus match, GUAAGU. Exon 5 sequences alone did not promote splicing when present in one or multiple copies. However, when a 15-nucleotide segment of IVS5 containing GUAAGU was inserted downstream of the hybrid exon segment E4E5 in a splicing-defective mutant, splicing activity was recovered. Interestingly, the 72-nucleotide L2 exon of adenovirus, without its associated 5' splice site, activated splicing when placed next to E4. Various models for the activation of splicing through an RNA structural change are discussed.

title: Melatonin and the circadian regulation of sleep initiation, consolidation, structure, and the sleep EEG.
text: The natural internal rhythm of melatonin, which is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, is closely linked to the natural internal rhythm of sleepiness and the variations in brain wave activity during sleep, such as sleep spindles and slow waves. This connection remains even when the sleep-wake cycle is not in sync with the melatonin rhythm. Taking melatonin during the day increases the likelihood of daytime sleep, as shown by both the time it takes to fall asleep and the quality of sleep. The brain wave activity during daytime sleep after taking melatonin is similar to that during nighttime sleep, with more sleep spindles and less slow-wave sleep and activity, as measured by EEG analysis. Taking higher doses of melatonin (5 mg or more) before nighttime sleep leads to more rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. These findings demonstrate that melatonin affects key aspects of human sleep, including the time it takes to fall asleep, the quality of sleep, brain wave activity, sleep spindles, and REM sleep. Further research is needed using appropriate doses and delivery methods that produce natural melatonin levels in the blood in order to fully understand the role of the natural melatonin rhythm in regulating sleep.

title: Long-term survival, quality of life, and quality-adjusted life-years among critically ill elderly patients.
text: AIMS To evaluate the mortality, quality of life (QOL), and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) of critically ill elderly patients. DESIGN A survey conducted in a ten-bed medical-surgical intensive care unit (ICU) at a tertiary care university hospital. PARTICIPANTS The study included 882 elderly patients (aged ≥65 years) and 1,827 controls (aged <65 years) treated between 1995 and 2000. INTERVENTION None. MEASUREMENTS AND RESULTS Mortality rates were assessed during the ICU and hospital stays, as well as at 12, 24, and 36 months after ICU discharge. The cumulative 3-year mortality rate among the elderly (57%) was significantly higher (p < .05) than that among the controls (40%). The majority (66%) of elderly patients who did not survive passed away within 1 month after leaving the ICU. All elderly patients with a day-1 Sequential Organ Failure (SOFA) score >15 died during their ICU stay. QOL was evaluated using EQ-5D and RAND-36 measures from 10 months to 7 years after discharge. The majority (88%) of elderly survivors rated their current health state as good or satisfactory; 66% reported it to be similar or better than 12 months prior, and 48% reported it to be similar or better than their preadmission state. RAND-36 QOL measures showed that aging had the greatest impact on physical functioning, physical role limitations, and vitality, but the elderly had better mental health values compared to the controls. However, the QALYs of elderly respondents were 21% to 35% lower than the mean QALY minus 2 standard deviation units of the age- and gender-adjusted general population. CONCLUSIONS Advanced age alone should not be a determining factor in denying intensive care, but the perceived benefits of intensive care appear to diminish with age when measured as QALYs. Nevertheless, 97% of elderly survivors were able to live at home, and 88% of them considered their QOL to be satisfactory or good after being discharged from the hospital. Therefore, more accurate information on outcomes for the elderly is necessary.

title: Recent developments and complexities in neutrophil transmigration.
text:
The purpose of this review is to provide an overview of recent research on the migration of neutrophils from blood to inflamed tissues. This process is crucial for innate immunity and plays a significant role in the development of inflammatory disorders. The review will focus on the mechanisms involved in neutrophil transmigration, an area that has seen significant advancements.

The review will cover various aspects related to neutrophil migration through venular walls. This includes leukocyte luminal crawling, as well as cellular and molecular changes in leukocytes and endothelial cells that facilitate transendothelial cell migration. The review will also discuss the advances in both paracellular and transcellular neutrophil migration through endothelial cells, highlighting the roles and regulation of endothelial cell adhesion molecules.

Additionally, the review will touch upon migration through the vascular pericyte coverage and basement membrane. These aspects are important in understanding the complete process of neutrophil migration.

In summary, the significant role of neutrophils in inflammatory conditions emphasizes the need for a better understanding of the specific mechanisms involved in their migration. By gaining this knowledge, it may be possible to identify new pathways that can be targeted for the development of more targeted anti-inflammatory interventions.

title: Exploring the epidemiological characteristics of cancers of unknown primary site in an Australian population: implications for research and clinical care.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the incidence, mortality, and survival rates of cancer of unknown primary site (CUP) and consider its clinical implications. The researchers used data from the South Australian Cancer Registry to calculate age-standardized incidence and mortality rates from 1977 to 2004. They also investigated disease-specific survival rates and identified socio-demographic, histological, and secular predictors of CUP using multivariable logistic regression.

The results showed that the incidence and mortality rates of CUP increased by approximately 60% between 1977-80 and 1981-84, with rates peaking in 1993-96. The male to female incidence and mortality rate ratios were around 1.3:1. Incidence and mortality rates also increased with age. The odds of having an unspecified histological type, compared to more common adenocarcinomas, were higher for males, non-metropolitan residents, those from low socio-economic areas, and for the period between 1977-88. CUP represented a higher proportion of cancers in Indigenous patients. The case survival rate at 10 years from diagnosis was only 7%. Factors associated with lower case survival included older age, male sex, Indigenous status, lower socio-economic status, and unspecified histology type.

In conclusion, the study revealed poor outcomes for CUP, although there was a slight improvement in survival rates. The researchers identified socio-demographic groups at higher risk of CUP and worse treatment outcomes, highlighting the need for increased research and clinical attention in these areas.

title: Alkylating agent melphalan augments the efficacy of adoptive immunotherapy using tumor-specific CD4+ T cells.
text: The immune-boosting effects of certain commonly used chemotherapy drugs have gained recognition in recent years. This has led to the idea of combining traditional chemotherapy with immunotherapy strategies to achieve long-lasting therapeutic benefits. Previous research has suggested that melphalan, an alkylating agent commonly used to treat multiple myeloma, has immunomodulatory effects, but the specific mechanisms behind this are not well understood. In this study, we investigated how melphalan affects the immune cells in the body and tumor-specific CD4(+) T cells that are transferred into mice with tumors. We found that melphalan treatment caused a rapid increase in inflammatory cytokines and chemokines as the body's cells recovered from the effects of melphalan-induced myelodepletion and leukodepletion. After melphalan treatment, the tumor cells displayed characteristics of immunogenic cell death, such as the movement of calreticulin from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell membrane and the release of high-mobility group box 1 into the extracellular space. Additionally, dendritic cells in the lymph nodes near the tumor showed increased uptake of tumor antigens. These immunomodulatory effects of melphalan led to the activation of CD8(+) T cells in the body and, more importantly, promoted the expansion and differentiation of the transferred tumor-specific CD4(+) T cells. Importantly, combining melphalan with CD4(+) T cell adoptive cell therapy was more effective than either treatment alone in prolonging the survival of mice with advanced B cell lymphomas or colorectal tumors. These findings shed light on the mechanisms behind melphalan's immune-stimulating effects and demonstrate the potential of combining melphalan with adoptive cell therapy using antitumor CD4(+) T cells for treatment.

title: Influence of cigarette smoking on inhaled corticosteroid treatment in mild asthma.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of cigarette smoking on the effectiveness of inhaled corticosteroid treatment in patients with mild asthma. Previous research on this topic has primarily focused on non-smokers, leaving a gap in knowledge regarding the effects of smoking on asthma treatment. 

To address this gap, a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study was conducted. The study included 38 adult asthmatic patients, 21 of whom were non-smokers. These patients were previously not treated with corticosteroids. They were divided into two groups, with one group receiving inhaled fluticasone propionate (1000 microg daily) and the other group receiving a placebo for a period of three weeks. 

The effectiveness of the treatment was assessed using various measures, including morning and evening peak expiratory flow (PEF) readings, spirometric parameters, bronchial hyperreactivity, and sputum eosinophil counts. The responses to treatment were compared between non-smokers and smokers with asthma. 

The results showed that non-smokers experienced a significantly greater increase in mean morning PEF compared to smokers after receiving inhaled fluticasone (27 l/min vs -5 l/min). Non-smokers also had significant improvements in mean morning PEF (27 l/min), forced expiratory volume in 1 second (0.17 l), and geometric mean PC20 (2.6 doubling doses), as well as a significant decrease in the proportion of sputum eosinophils (-1.75%) after receiving fluticasone compared to the placebo. However, no significant changes were observed in the smoking asthmatic patients for any of these parameters. 

In conclusion, active cigarette smoking hinders the effectiveness of short-term inhaled corticosteroid treatment in patients with mild asthma. This finding has important implications for the management of mild asthma in patients who smoke.

title: Hitting the target: emerging technologies in the search for kinase substrates.
text: Protein kinases have the ability to modify the activity, location, protein interactions, and stability of their targets through a process called phosphorylation. However, the identification of specific substrates for protein kinases has been a slow process, despite its significance in understanding cell biology. Traditional techniques like genetics, yeast two-hybrid screens, and biochemical purification have proven to be time-consuming and unreliable in identifying true kinase substrates. Fortunately, new methods have emerged and have been successful in identifying genuine substrates in vivo. These methods include screening for protein phosphorylation using phage expression libraries, analyzing peptide libraries to determine preferred motifs for specific kinases, utilizing phospho-motif antibodies, and employing structurally modified kinases along with allele-specific adenosine triphosphate analogs and kinase inhibitors. In this article, we will discuss these approaches, their usefulness, and the limitations they may have.

title: Histone phosphorylation: a chromatin modification involved in diverse nuclear events.
text: Histone posttranslational modifications are essential components of various processes that regulate the structure of chromatin. These modifications serve as signals during different chromatin-related events and serve as platforms for the recruitment, assembly, or retention of factors associated with chromatin. The most well-known function of histone phosphorylation occurs during the cellular response to DNA damage, where phosphorylated histone H2A(X) marks large chromatin domains surrounding the site of DNA breakage. However, numerous studies have also demonstrated that histone phosphorylation plays critical roles in chromatin remodeling associated with other nuclear processes. In this review, we provide an overview of the current understanding of histone phosphorylation and discuss the numerous kinases and phosphatases that regulate it. We explore the significant roles played by this histone modification in DNA repair, transcription, and chromatin compaction during cell division and apoptosis. Furthermore, we describe the intricate interplay between phosphorylation and other histone modifications, which enables precise control over chromatin remodeling processes.

title: Neurodevelopmental Outcome After a Single Course of Antenatal Steroids in Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text:
The objective of this study was to review and analyze data on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of children who received a single course of antenatal corticosteroids for threatened preterm labor. The data sources included MEDLINE, Scopus, CENTRAL, and www.clinicaltrials.gov from inception to August 2014. The search terms used were "prenatal," "antenatal," "cortico*," "*steroid*," "betamethasone," "dexamethasone," "neurodevelopment*," "*development*," and "follow-up." The references of the retrieved articles were also examined. 

The study included randomized and nonrandomized trials that reported on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of children whose mothers received a single course of betamethasone or dexamethasone antenatally for threatened preterm birth, compared to placebo or no treatment. The data was tabulated and integrated, and summary risk ratios (RR) were calculated for dichotomous data. Standardized mean difference was calculated for trials that measured the same outcome using different methods. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I statistic. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were planned based on study design, specific steroid used, and mean gestational age at birth. 

The results showed that a single course of antenatal corticosteroids was associated with a reduced risk of cerebral palsy, psychomotor development index less than 70, and severe disability. Steroid treatment also increased the rates of intact survival. Betamethasone was found to significantly decrease the risk of severe disability and increase the rate of intact survival. Dexamethasone increased the rate of intact survival, but there was limited data available for dexamethasone and other planned subgroup analyses. The limitations of the study included the inclusion of nonrandomized studies and limited data on finer neurodevelopmental outcomes. 

In conclusion, a single course of antenatal corticosteroids in women at high risk for preterm birth appears to improve most neurodevelopmental outcomes in offspring born before 34 weeks of gestation.

title: Prognostic impact of minimal pleural effusion in non-small-cell lung cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the clinical relevance of minimal pleural effusion (PE) in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and its impact on survival. The study also aimed to explore possible accumulation mechanisms. A total of 2,061 patients were classified into three groups based on their PE status: no PE, minimal PE, and malignant PE. The researchers analyzed 21 variables associated with patient, stage migration, tumor, and treatment factors to determine their correlation with survival. 

The results showed that 13.2% of patients had minimal PE. The distribution of stages among the patients was as follows: 5.2% stage I, 10.9% stage II, 13.2% stage IIIA, 23.8% stage IIIB, and 13.9% stage IV. Minimal PE was found to be significantly associated with shorter survival compared to no PE (median survival time of 7.7 months vs. 17.7 months; log-rank P < .001). This association remained significant even after adjusting for all variables (adjusted hazard ratio of 1.40; 95% CI, 1.21 to 1.62). The prognostic impact of minimal PE was higher in early-stage disease compared to advanced stages (Pinteraction = .001). In 87.8% of patients with minimal PE, pleural invasion or attachment was observed as a direct mechanism, which was independently associated with worse survival (P = .03). 

In conclusion, minimal PE is a common concern in the staging of NSCLCs. Its presence is an important prognostic factor for worse survival, particularly in early-stage disease.

title: Fusion proteins for versatile antigen targeting to cell surface receptors reveal differential capacity to prime immune responses.
text: Targeting proteins to antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is a promising approach to stimulate adaptive immune responses. However, the relationship between the choice of the targeted receptor and the quality and quantity of these responses is not well understood. In this study, we present a method for expressing antigens (Ags), including hydrophobic proteins, as soluble fusion proteins. These fusion proteins are designed to be efficiently presented by the proteasome-dependent MHC class I pathway and form stable complexes with various targeting antibodies. When administered through subcutaneous immunization, these complexes were initially taken up by CD169+ macrophages in the lymph node subcapsular sinus. In an experimental model using ovalbumin (OVA), the receptor-targeted antigenic complexes effectively stimulated specific T and B cell responses both in vitro and in vivo, at least 100 times more efficiently than Ag alone. By comparing 10 different targeting receptors, we were able to establish a ranking based on their ability to prime CD8+ T cell responses. We also observed significant differences in the efficacy of priming CD8+ and CD4+ T cell subsets, as well as B cells, among the different receptors. These fusion proteins provide a valuable tool for developing optimized strategies for targeted delivery of protein Ags in the context of tolerization or vaccination.

title: A sequential model for peptide binding and transport by the transporters associated with antigen processing.
text: The transportation of antigenic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum is facilitated by the TAP proteins. However, studying the specificity of this process has been challenging due to the presence of TAP-independent factors that affect the accumulation of peptides in the ER during transport assays. To overcome this, we have created an overexpression system that allows us to measure the binding of peptides to the TAP substrate-binding site and their transport separately. We have observed that the efficiency of peptide accumulation in the ER is directly related to the affinity for the TAP substrate-binding site. However, this accumulation can be influenced by interactions with the glycosylation system within the ER and possibly by peptide efflux. Interestingly, random peptide mixtures consisting of 9-16 amino acids exhibit a significantly higher affinity for the binding site compared to mixtures of shorter or longer peptides. We have also discovered that peptides bind to TAP heteromers even in the absence of ATP, and are released upon ATP binding. This finding provides a potential model for understanding the function of TAP.

title: Outcome of repeated radiosurgery for recurrent metastatic brain tumors.
text:
Our objective was to examine the outcomes of repeated gamma knife radiosurgery (GKS) for patients who experienced local or remote recurrence after their initial radiosurgery. We conducted a retrospective review of 204 patients who underwent GKS treatment. Among them, 43 patients (21%) received GKS more than once. The second GKS was administered for recurrence at previously treated sites in 16 patients, new lesions at remote sites in 13 patients, and both local recurrence and new lesions in 14 patients. 

The median survival from the first GKS was 36 (7-190) weeks for all patients and 68 (16-156) weeks for the 43 patients who underwent repeated GKS. The median time from the first GKS to the second was 37 weeks. The median survival from the second radiosurgical intervention was 32 (7-132) weeks. The local control rate at 6 months after salvage GKS was 90.7%. The dominant prognostic factor for both initial and salvage GKS was the RPA class. 

In conclusion, recurrence is common among patients with metastatic brain tumors after their initial radiosurgery. The local control and survival time after salvage treatment are comparable to those after initial radiosurgery. GKS as a salvage treatment may offer additional survival benefits for selected patients.

title: Human CYP3A4 and murine Cyp3A11 are regulated by equol and genistein via the pregnane X receptor in a species-specific manner.
text:
Pregnane X receptor (PXR) plays a crucial role in the body's defense system by eliminating harmful substances. It can be activated by both natural and synthetic chemicals, such as steroids, antibiotics, bile acids, and herbal compounds, leading to increased drug metabolism. Our study aimed to investigate the activation of human and mouse PXR by isoflavones genistein, daidzein, and its metabolite equol, both in vitro and in vivo.

Using cell-based experiments and primary hepatocytes, we examined the ability of genistein, daidzein, and equol to activate PXR. In transient transfection assays, genistein and daidzein were able to activate the full-length, wild-type mouse PXR, but not a mutant form. Among the isoflavones, genistein showed the highest potency. On the other hand, equol was a more potent activator of human PXR compared to genistein and daidzein. In a mammalian 2-hybrid assay, isoflavones were found to recruit the coactivator steroid receptor coactivator 1 to PXR.

Furthermore, we tested the effects of equol on the native human Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) promoter. Equol demonstrated stronger activation compared to genistein and daidzein, leading to increased mRNA and protein expression of CYP3A4 in human hepatocytes. In mouse hepatocytes, genistein and daidzein induced the expression of Cytochrome P450 3A11 (Cyp3A11) mRNA in wild-type mice, but not in PXR(-/-) mice. Additionally, feeding mice a soy protein-containing diet resulted in the induction of Cyp3A11 mRNA in vivo.

In summary, our findings highlight species-specific differences in the activation of PXR by isoflavones and equol. Genistein and daidzein were more effective in activating mouse PXR, while equol showed stronger activation of human PXR. These results provide valuable insights into the role of isoflavones and equol in drug metabolism and their potential impact on human health.

title: Metabolism of glucose, glutamine, long-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies by murine macrophages.
text: The study focused on the maximum activities of key enzymes involved in metabolism in macrophages and lymphocytes. In macrophages, the activity of hexokinase was found to be exceptionally high, surpassing that of phosphorylase or 6-phosphofructokinase. This suggests that glucose is a more important source of fuel than glycogen in these cells, and that the pentose phosphate pathway is also significant. This suggestion is supported by the high activities of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. However, when macrophages were incubated in vitro, the rate of glucose utilization was found to be less than 10% of the activity of 6-phosphofructokinase. This indicates that glycolysis is greatly increased during phagocytosis or heightened secretory activity. Macrophages also exhibited higher activities of citrate synthase and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase compared to lymphocytes, suggesting that the tricarboxylic acid cycle may play a crucial role in energy generation in these cells. The activity of 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase was higher in macrophages, while that of 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase was significantly lower than in lymphocytes. Additionally, macrophages had higher levels of carnitine palmitoyltransferase, indicating that fatty acids, along with acetoacetate, could serve as substrates for the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Resting macrophages did not show any detectable rate of acetoacetate or 3-hydroxybutyrate utilization during incubation, but oleate utilization was observed at a rate of 1.0 nmol/h per mg of protein, which accounted for approximately 2.2% of the activity of palmitoyltransferase. The activity of glutaminase was approximately four times higher in macrophages compared to lymphocytes, suggesting a potentially high rate of glutamine utilization. However, the rate of glutamine utilization by resting incubated macrophages was similar to that reported for rat lymphocytes, but considerably lower than the activity of glutaminase.

title: TGF-beta inhibition of endothelial cell proliferation: alteration of EGF binding and EGF-induced growth-regulatory (competence) gene expression.
text: TGF-beta, a growth inhibitor, hinders the growth of endothelial cells from different sources, including human umbilical vein, bovine aorta, and rat heart. When rat heart endothelial cells are exposed to TGF-beta for a long period, they undergo significant morphological changes that resemble senescent cells. These changes are accompanied by a reduction in the number of high-affinity receptors for epidermal growth factor (EGF), while the total receptor count remains mostly unchanged. Moreover, the expression of specific competence genes (c-myc, JE, KC) induced by EGF is decreased, whereas the induction of c-fos gene expression by EGF remains unaffected by TGF-beta treatment. These findings suggest that growth inhibitors like TGF-beta may modify the cell's response to growth-stimulatory factors.

title: Human NK cells in acute myeloid leukaemia patients: analysis of NK cell-activating receptors and their ligands
text: The activation of natural killer (NK) cells is carefully regulated to protect healthy cells while identifying and eliminating tumor-transformed or virus-infected cells. NK cells possess a wide range of receptors on their surface to carry out this selective killing. The interaction between inhibitory and activating receptors and their ligands determines whether the NK cell becomes activated and targets the cell for destruction. In this study, we observed a decrease in the expression of activating receptors NKp46, NKp30, DNAM-1, CD244, and CD94/NKG2C on NK cells from patients with acute myeloid leukemia. This reduction may be caused by prolonged exposure to ligands on leukemia cells. Analysis of the ligands for NK cell-activating receptors revealed that the majority of leukemia cells express these ligands. DNAM-1 ligands are frequently present on leukemia cells, while the NKG2D ligand MICA/B is found in half of the patients, and CD48, a ligand for CD244, is present in only one-fourth of the patients. The decreased expression of NK cell-activating receptors and/or the variable expression of ligands on leukemia cells can compromise the ability of NK cells to effectively surveil and target tumors. Understanding the repertoire of activating receptors on NK cells and their potential ligands on leukemia cells, as well as the ability to modulate their expression, could open up new avenues for utilizing NK cells in immunotherapy against leukemia.

title: Production of interleukin-6 in contracting human skeletal muscles can account for the exercise-induced increase in plasma interleukin-6.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine if the production of interleukin (IL)-6 by contracting skeletal muscle is significant enough to account for the increase in IL-6 concentration in the blood during exercise. Six healthy males participated in the study and performed one-legged dynamic knee extensor exercise for 5 hours at 25 W, which was 40% of their peak power output. Arterial-femoral venous differences were measured before and every hour during the exercise, and leg blood flow was measured using ultrasound Doppler. IL-6 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). 

The results showed that arterial plasma concentrations of IL-6 increased 19-fold compared to rest. The difference in IL-6 levels between the arterial and femoral venous blood over the exercising leg followed the same pattern as the net IL-6 release. There was no significant difference or net IL-6 release over the resting leg. The contracting muscles produced 2.5 kg of active muscle, resulting in a median IL-6 production of 6.8 ng min-1 (kg active muscle)-1 during the last 2 hours of exercise. 

The net IL-6 release from the muscle during the last 2 hours of exercise was 17-fold higher than the increase in arterial IL-6 concentration. After 5 hours of exercise, the net release of IL-6 during 1 minute was half of the IL-6 content in the plasma. This suggests a high turnover of IL-6 during muscular exercise. The study proposes that IL-6 produced by contracting skeletal muscle plays a role in maintaining glucose homeostasis during prolonged exercise.

title: Symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with IDDM.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with insulin-dependent diabetes, as perceived by both the children and their parents. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the symptom reporting of diabetic children with that of adult diabetic patients. 

A total of 100 parents and 43 children were interviewed for this research. The structured interviews documented the frequency and intensity of hypoglycemia symptoms, which were then categorized into groups using Principal Components Analysis (PCA). 

The results revealed a strong agreement between diabetic children and their parents regarding the frequency and intensity of reported symptoms. The PCA analysis showed that both children and parents identified the same distinct subgroups of hypoglycemia-related symptoms, namely behavioral disturbance and autonomic-neuroglycopenic subgroups. 

In conclusion, the symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with diabetes differ significantly from those experienced by insulin-treated adults. Notably, behavioral changes were identified as primary features of low blood glucose in children. These findings have important implications for educating parents about hypoglycemia.

title: Comparative Protein Structure Modeling Using MODELLER.
text: Comparative protein structure modeling is a method used to predict the three-dimensional structure of a specific protein sequence (referred to as the target) by comparing it to one or more proteins with known structures (referred to as templates). This prediction process involves several steps, including fold assignment, target-template alignment, model building, and model evaluation. This section provides instructions on how to calculate comparative models using the MODELLER program and how to access the ModBase database, which contains these models. It also covers all four steps of comparative modeling, common errors that are often encountered, and various applications of this technique. To illustrate the process, the modeling of lactate dehydrogenase from Trichomonas vaginalis (TvLDH) is presented as an example. Additionally, the section includes a guide on how to download and install the MODELLER software. This content is copyrighted by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. in 2016.

title: IL-6 as a keystone cytokine in health and disease
text: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) has a wide-ranging impact on both immune and non-immune cells, often exhibiting hormone-like characteristics that influence processes related to maintaining internal stability. IL-6 possesses both pro- and anti-inflammatory properties, which vary depending on the context, making it a significant target for clinical intervention. However, the signaling mechanism that regulates IL-6 activity is complex, and different strategies can impede this pathway. The use of IL-6 antagonists in clinical practice has prompted new inquiries into the optimal timing and approach for blocking this cytokine to enhance disease outcomes and patient well-being. In this discussion, we explore IL-6's effects on innate and adaptive immunity, examine the potential benefits of various IL-6 antagonists, and consider how understanding the immunobiology of IL-6 can guide clinical decision-making.

title: Chaperoning 5S RNA assembly.
text: In eukaryotes, three out of the four ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are derived from a single pre-rRNA transcript and assembled into ribosomes. These three rRNAs are known as 5.8S, 18S, and 25S/28S rRNAs. The fourth rRNA, called 5S rRNA, is transcribed separately by RNA polymerase III and then combined with ribosomal proteins Rpl5/uL18 and Rpl11/uL5 to form the 5S ribonucleoprotein particle (RNP). This 5S RNP plays a crucial role in regulating the tumor suppressor p53 in mammals. The localization of the 5S RNP in the nucleolus and its assembly into preribosomes are facilitated by a specialized complex consisting of Rpf2 and Rrs1 in yeast, and Bxdc1 and hRrs1 in humans. In this study, we present the structural and functional analysis of the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex both alone, in association with the 5S RNA, and within pre-60S ribosomes. Our findings reveal that the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex contains a unique module that binds to the E-loop of the 5S RNA, interacts with the Rpl5 protein, and also contacts the ribosome assembly factor Rsa4 and the 25S RNA. Based on our observations, we propose that the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex establishes a network of interactions that guide the incorporation of the 5S RNP into preribosomes, assuming its initial conformation before undergoing rotation to form the central protuberance observed in the mature large ribosomal subunit.

title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and neutrophil infiltration: role of cigarette smoke and cyclooxygenase products.
text: Cigarette smoke is the primary cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which leads to inflammation in the airways. PGE(2), a substance produced in the human airways, has both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory properties. We measured the levels of PGE(2) in sputum samples from different groups of individuals and compared them to the presence of neutrophils and the expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). To assess the impact of smoking on COX-2 and PGE(2) receptor expression, as well as PGE(2) release in neutrophils and alveolar macrophages (AM), we used cigarette smoke extract (CSE) on cells obtained from non-smokers. We also examined the effects of PGE(2) and PGE receptor agonists and antagonists on the adhesion of neutrophils to a human bronchial epithelial cell line (16HBE). We found that PGE(2) levels, COX-2 expression, and neutrophil infiltration were significantly higher in both normal smokers and COPD smokers compared to controls and COPD former smokers. The sputum samples from COPD smokers caused increased neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE, which was reduced by PGE(2) immunoprecipitation. In laboratory experiments, we confirmed that CSE increased PGE(2) release and COX-2 and PGE(2) receptor expression in neutrophils and AM. PGE(2) also enhanced neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE, and this effect was diminished by a specific E-prostanoid 4 (EP(4)) receptor antagonist. These findings suggest that CSE promotes the induction of COX-2 and contributes to the pro-inflammatory effects of PGE(2) in the airways of individuals with COPD.

title: Non-receptor tyrosine kinase Etk is involved in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer cells.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of epithelial and endothelial tyrosine kinase (Etk), also known as Bmx, in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) cells. The study also aimed to determine if there was a correlation between Etk expression and the levels of apoptosis-associated proteins such as Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53. A total of 171 lung cancer specimens, including 71 SCLCs and 100 non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs), were immunostained for Etk, Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53. The researchers used the SCLC H446 cell line and a subline (H446-Etk) that overexpressed Etk to study the role of Etk in apoptosis induced by doxorubicin. The results showed that Etk was highly expressed in 74.6% of SCLC cases compared to only 40% of NSCLC cases. There was also a significant difference in the expression levels of Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53 between Etk-positive and Etk-negative SCLC cases. Additionally, the levels of Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L) increased significantly in H446-Etk cells after doxorubicin treatment and were positively associated with Etk expression. However, p53 did not correspond with Etk expression, although its expression decreased greatly with apoptosis in both H446-Etk and H446 cells. Furthermore, the cell viability was significantly higher in H446-Etk cells compared to parental H446 cells after doxorubicin treatment. Downregulation of Etk by Etk siRNA sensitized H446 cells to doxorubicin. These findings suggest that the upregulation of Etk may be a new mechanism involved in protecting SCLC cells from apoptosis. Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L), but not p53, may contribute to doxorubicin-induced apoptosis through the Etk pathway.

title: No Pasaran! Role of the axon initial segment in the regulation of protein transport and the maintenance of axonal identity.
text: The transmission of information in the brain relies on the specialized structure of neurons. Various cellular transport processes support this organization, including active targeting of proteins and passive movement between compartments. The axon initial segment (AIS), which separates the somatodendritic and axonal compartments, plays a crucial role in neuronal function, serving as the site where action potentials are initiated and controlling the growth of axons. Over time, scientists have made progress in understanding the main components of the AIS and how they interact, as well as their role in its formation and upkeep. Two mechanisms have been identified that regulate protein transport at the AIS: a barrier on the surface that restricts diffusion and a filter within the cell that controls traffic. However, there is still much to learn about the molecular details of these processes. By studying the structure of the AIS cytoskeleton, recent findings have shed light on how a deeper understanding of its architecture can enhance our knowledge of its role in protein transport regulation and the maintenance of axonal identity.

title: The effectiveness of right heart catheterization in the initial care of critically ill patients. SUPPORT Investigators.
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the use of right heart catheterization (RHC) within the first 24 hours of care in the intensive care unit (ICU) and subsequent survival, length of stay, intensity of care, and cost of care. The study was conducted as a prospective cohort study in five US teaching hospitals between 1989 and 1994. The subjects of the study were 5735 critically ill adult patients who were receiving care in an ICU for one of nine specific disease categories. The main outcome measures included survival time, cost of care, intensity of care, and length of stay in the ICU and hospital. A propensity score for RHC was created using multivariable logistic regression. Case-matching and multivariable regression modeling techniques were used to estimate the association between RHC and specific outcomes, while adjusting for treatment selection using the propensity score. Sensitivity analysis was also conducted to assess the potential impact of any unidentified or missing covariate on the results. 

The results of the study showed that patients who underwent RHC had a higher 30-day mortality rate compared to those who did not (odds ratio, 1.24; 95% confidence interval, 1.03-1.49). The mean cost per hospital stay was also higher for patients who underwent RHC compared to those who did not. Similarly, the mean length of stay in the ICU was longer for patients who underwent RHC. These findings were consistent across different analysis techniques. Subgroup analysis did not identify any patient group or site where RHC was associated with improved outcomes. Patients with a higher baseline probability of surviving 2 months had the highest relative risk of death following RHC. Sensitivity analysis indicated that a missing covariate would have to significantly increase the risk of death and the risk of RHC for a true beneficial effect of RHC to be misrepresented as harmful. 

In conclusion, this observational study found that, after adjusting for treatment selection bias, RHC was associated with increased mortality and increased utilization of resources in critically ill patients. The reasons for this lack of benefit are unclear. The results of this study should be validated in other observational studies. These findings suggest the need for a randomized controlled trial of RHC and may help guide patient selection for such a study.

title: Natural history of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and approaches to therapy
text: After being transmitted from cell to cell, HTLV-I increases its viral genome through new infections and the proliferation of infected cells. This proliferation of infected cells is both clonal and persistent within the body. During the carrier state, the host's immune system, as well as the genetic and epigenetic environment of proviral integration sites, and other factors, select infected cells within the body. In leukemic cells, the expression of the tax gene is often hindered by genetic and epigenetic mechanisms. This loss of Tax expression allows ATL cells to evade the host's immune system. However, ATL cells develop the ability to proliferate without Tax through intracellular genetic and epigenetic changes. Despite advancements in support and the development of new treatment options, the prognosis for ATLL remains poor. Nevertheless, certain therapies, such as interferon-α plus zidovudine (possibly after 1-2 cycles of CHOP), intensive chemotherapy like LSG-15 with G-CSF support, and Allo-SCT (which offers potential for a cure), have shown promise in improving prognosis compared to CHOP (VEPA). Other emerging approaches include HDAC inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, and proteasome inhibitors. However, comparing different treatment approaches is challenging due to variations in the natural history of ATLL, differences in patient recruitment (naïve-to-therapy, refractory, or relapsed), and inconsistencies in outcome reporting that often exclude difficult-to-evaluate patients. Furthermore, the results from relatively small proof-of-principle studies have not been validated through randomized, controlled trials. Consequently, there is currently no clear evidence supporting the superiority of any specific treatment approach. To minimize unnecessary patient suffering and identify the most effective therapy as quickly as possible, large-scale randomized, controlled trials involving collaborations between multiple centers and international partners will be necessary.

title: Hierarchical organization of the plasma membrane: investigations by single-molecule tracking vs. fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
text: The use of single-molecule tracking and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) has provided valuable insights into the behavior of the plasma membrane in living cells. These techniques have revealed previously unknown information about molecular diffusion, interaction, and signal transduction within the plasma membrane. It is now evident that the plasma membrane is not a uniform structure, but rather a complex and diverse entity consisting of various nano-meso-scale structures (ranging from 2 to 200 nm) with different lifetimes. Certain molecules within the membrane form temporary associations, while molecular interactions take place within the time-dependent and non-uniform two-dimensional liquid environment of the plasma membrane. This understanding of the plasma membrane's heterogeneity and dynamics is crucial for comprehending its functions.

title: Stability of the antimalarial drug dihydroartemisinin under physiologically relevant conditions: implications for clinical treatment and pharmacokinetic and in vitro assays.
text: Artemisinins are powerful antimalarial drugs, but they are highly chemically unstable. They break down when exposed to ferrous iron, Fe(II)-heme, or other biological reductants. However, it is not well-documented how this instability affects their chemical stability and antimalarial activity under different conditions in laboratory testing and clinical situations. In this study, we focused on dihydroartemisinin (DHA), which is both an antimalarial drug on its own and the main metabolite of other artemisinins. We examined how DHA behaves in phosphate-buffered saline, plasma, and erythrocyte lysate at different temperatures and pH levels. We evaluated the antimalarial activity of the remaining drug using a chemosensitivity assay on Plasmodium falciparum, and we measured the extent of DHA decomposition using high-performance liquid chromatography with electrochemical detection analysis. We also investigated the role of Fe(II)-heme by blocking its reactivity with carbon monoxide (CO). We found that the antimalarial activity of DHA significantly decreased after incubation in plasma, and to a lesser extent in erythrocyte lysate. After 3 hours, the activity was reduced by half, and after 24 hours, it was almost completely abolished. DHA activity was also affected by serum-enriched media. These effects were dependent on temperature and pH, and they correlated with the increased rate of DHA decomposition at pH levels above 7 and in plasma. These findings suggest that caution should be exercised when conducting and interpreting in vitro studies, as their results can be influenced by experimental conditions and how the drug is stored. Disorders such as fever, hemolysis, or acidosis, which are associated with severe malaria, may contribute to the instability of artemisinins and reduce their effectiveness in clinical settings.

title: Modulation of anxiety through blockade of anandamide hydrolysis
text: The active component of cannabis, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, affects humans through CB1 cannabinoid receptors, suggesting that natural cannabinoids may play a role in regulating emotions. However, the varying effects of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol make it difficult to interpret these findings and limit the potential of direct cannabinoid agonists for therapy. An alternative strategy could involve developing drugs that enhance the effects of natural cannabinoids by preventing their breakdown. In this study, we present a group of potent, selective, and systemically active inhibitors of fatty acid amide hydrolase, an enzyme responsible for breaking down the natural cannabinoid anandamide. Similar to anti-anxiety medications, these inhibitors exhibit benzodiazepine-like properties in rats, as demonstrated by their effects in the elevated zero-maze test and suppression of vocalizations caused by isolation. These effects are accompanied by increased levels of anandamide in the brain and can be blocked by CB1 receptor blockade. Our findings suggest that anandamide plays a role in regulating emotional states and highlight fatty acid amide hydrolase inhibition as a novel approach to treating anxiety.

title: Familial clustering of reflux symptoms
text:
Objective: This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of reflux symptoms and medication use among relatives of patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in order to determine the importance of familial factors in the disease.

Methods: A postal questionnaire was conducted among the first degree relatives of six groups of matched patients. These groups included patients with: 1) no dyspeptic symptoms; 2) reflux symptoms and a normal pH study; 3) reflux symptoms, an abnormal pH study, and a lower esophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure greater than 10 mm Hg; 4) reflux symptoms, an abnormal pH study, and a LOS pressure less than 10 mm Hg; 5) Barrett's esophagus; and 6) peptic stricture.

Results: A total of 418 subjects responded to the questionnaire, resulting in a 78% response rate. Infrequent reflux symptoms were equally common among all groups of relatives. However, frequent reflux symptoms were more prevalent among relatives of patients with an abnormal pH study and normal (26%, p= 0.007) or low LOS pressure (27%, p= 0.01), as well as among relatives of patients with Barrett's esophagus (30%, p= 0.003), compared to relatives of patients without dyspeptic symptoms (9%). Relatives of patients with a normal pH study (16%) or peptic stricture (18%) did not show a higher prevalence of frequent reflux symptoms. The use of reflux medication followed a similar pattern.

Conclusions: This study demonstrates a familial clustering of reflux symptoms in relatives of patients with reflux symptoms and increased esophageal acid exposure, as well as in relatives of patients with Barrett's esophagus.

title: Histone chaperones: 30 years from isolation to elucidation of the mechanisms of nucleosome assembly and disassembly
text: It has been over thirty years since the discovery of nucleosomes in 1974 and the first identification of a histone chaperone in 1978. Although various types of histone chaperones have been found and studied, the fundamental processes of nucleosome assembly and disassembly have not been fully understood. Recently, scientists have determined the three-dimensional structure of a complex made up of the histone chaperone CIA/ASF1 and the histone H3-H4 dimer. This complex is believed to be an intermediate step in the assembly and disassembly of nucleosomes. Additionally, CIA alone has been shown to separate the histone (H3-H4)2 tetramer into two histone H3-H4 dimers. This activity suggests that CIA plays a role in regulating the replication of nucleosomes. In this article, we provide an overview of important histone chaperones and aim to uncover the mechanisms that preserve and modify epigenetic information. We also discuss the processes involved in nucleosome assembly and disassembly.

title: Specificity of the dRP/AP lyase of Ku promotes nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) fidelity at damaged ends.
text: Efficient repair of chromosome breaks relies on Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ). However, the ligation step of NHEJ is often hindered by nucleotide damage associated with the breaks, such as base loss (abasic site or 5'-dRP/AP sites). To prepare the ends for ligation, Ku, a 5'-dRP/AP lyase, can remove this damage. Our study demonstrates that this activity is most effective when the abasic site is located within a short 5' overhang, and it is necessary and sufficient to prepare the termini for ligation. Conversely, Ku is less active near 3' strand termini, as excision in this region would result in a ligation-blocking α,β-unsaturated aldehyde. Additionally, the Ku AP lyase activity is significantly inhibited by as few as two paired bases located 5' of the abasic site. Importantly, in vitro experiments on end joining reveal that abasic sites embedded within double-stranded DNA do not impede the NHEJ ligation step. Therefore, suppression of Ku's excision activity in this context is not crucial for ligation and actually aids NHEJ in preserving terminal sequence in junctions. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the DNA between the 5' terminus and the abasic site can also be retained in junctions formed by cellular NHEJ, suggesting that these sites are partially resistant to other abasic site-cleaving activities. Consequently, the 5'-dRP/AP lyase activity of Ku is highly specific to substrates where excision of an abasic site is necessary for ligation, promoting more accurate joining.

title: Gut-expressed gustducin and taste receptors regulate secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1.
text: The mechanism behind the oral ingestion of glucose inducing the secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) from gut endocrine L cells is currently unknown. However, our research has shown that human duodenal L cells possess sweet taste receptors, the taste G protein gustducin, and other taste transduction elements. Similarly, mouse intestinal L cells also express alpha-gustducin. When glucose was ingested by mice lacking alpha-gustducin, deficiencies in GLP-1 secretion and the regulation of plasma insulin and glucose were observed. Additionally, isolated small bowel and intestinal villi from these mice displayed significantly impaired GLP-1 secretion in response to glucose. The human L cell line NCI-H716, which expresses alpha-gustducin, taste receptors, and other taste signaling elements, demonstrated that GLP-1 release was stimulated by sugars and the noncaloric sweetener sucralose, but inhibited by the sweet receptor antagonist lactisole or siRNA for alpha-gustducin. Based on these findings, we conclude that L cells in the gut "taste" glucose using the same mechanisms as taste cells in the tongue. Manipulating GLP-1 secretion in gut "taste cells" could potentially offer a valuable treatment for obesity, diabetes, and abnormal gut motility.

title: Apoptosis in breast cancer: relationship with other pathological parameters.
text: Apoptosis, a common occurrence in breast cancer, can be observed through light microscopy in traditional histopathological sections or through specialized staining techniques. The apoptotic index (AI) is used to describe the percentage of apoptotic cells in relation to the total number of cells or the number of apoptotic cells per square millimeter of neoplastic tissue. Interestingly, the AI in breast cancer is not associated with tumor size, axillary lymph node metastasis, or distant metastasis upon diagnosis. However, it is higher in invasive ductal carcinomas compared to other histological types. Additionally, a high AI is correlated with high histological and nuclear grades, comedo-type necrosis, absence of tubule formation, and dense infiltration of lymphocytes within the tumor. Tumors lacking sex steroid receptors tend to have higher AIs than those with positive receptors. Aneuploid breast cancers with high S-phase fractions (SPFs) also exhibit elevated AI values compared to diploid tumors with low SPFs. Breast cancers that are p53-positive demonstrate high AIs, while those that are Bcl-2 positive have low AIs. The AI strongly correlates with various indicators of cell proliferation, such as the mitotic index and Ki67 immunolabeling. Univariate survival analyses indicate that a high AI is associated with unfavorable disease outcomes in both axillary lymph node-negative and -positive breast cancer cases. However, multivariate analyses suggest that AI is not an independent prognostic factor. In conclusion, a high AI in breast cancer is linked to malignant cellular characteristics, invasiveness, and indicators of cell proliferation.

title: Dietary flavonoids: bioavailability, metabolic effects, and safety.
text: Flavonoids are the most common type of plant polyphenols and contribute to the taste and color of fruits and vegetables. There are over 5000 different types of flavonoids. The main subclasses of flavonoids are flavones (such as apigenin and luteolin), flavonols (such as quercetin and myricetin), flavanones (such as naringenin and hesperidin), catechins or flavanols (such as epicatechin and gallocatechin), anthocyanidins (such as cyanidin and pelargonidin), and isoflavones (such as genistein and daidzein). Most flavonoids in plants are attached to sugars, although sometimes they are found without sugars. Flavonoids have gained interest for their antioxidant and free-radical scavenging properties observed in lab studies. Recent human feeding studies have shown that specific flavonoids are more easily absorbed and available in the body than previously thought. However, research on the role of flavonoids in human health through epidemiological studies has yielded inconclusive results. Some studies suggest that consuming flavonoids may have a protective effect against cardiovascular disease and cancer, while others show no effect or even potential harm. Since flavonoids have various biological activities that can be beneficial or harmful depending on the circumstances, further studies in both lab settings and with populations are needed.

title: Virus-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocyte responses select for amino-acid variation in simian immunodeficiency virus Env and Nef
text: Early after infection, cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) responses to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) occur but are ultimately ineffective in preventing the progression to AIDS. HIV has the ability to evade the CTL response by accumulating amino-acid replacements within CTL epitopes. To investigate this phenomenon, we examined 10 CTL epitopes throughout the course of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) disease progression in three related macaques. In all 10 epitopes, amino-acid replacements accumulated and demonstrated signs of positive selection by the time the macaques succumbed to the disease. Many of these amino-acid replacements within the epitopes resulted in a decrease or elimination of major histocompatibility complex class I binding and/or CTL recognition. These findings provide strong evidence in support of the CTL 'escape' hypothesis.

title: TRICHOME BIREFRINGENCE and its homolog AT5G01360 encode plant-specific DUF231 proteins required for cellulose biosynthesis in Arabidopsis.
text: The TBR mutant in Arabidopsis, which has a significant decrease in crystalline cellulose in trichomes, had an unknown molecular identity. Through our research, we discovered that TBR belongs to the plant-specific DUF231 domain gene family, which consists of 46 members with unknown functions in Arabidopsis. These genes also possess a plant-specific domain called the TBL domain, which contains a conserved GDSL motif found in esterases/lipases. TBR and TBR-like3 (TBL3) are coordinated with primary and secondary CELLULOSE SYNTHASE (CESA) genes, respectively. The tbr and tbl3 mutants exhibit lower levels of crystalline cellulose and have altered pectin composition in trichomes and stems, respectively. These tissues are typically associated with secondary wall crystalline cellulose. However, the levels of primary wall cellulose remain unchanged in both mutants, as observed in etiolated tbr and tbl3 hypocotyls. In this tissue, the amount of esterified pectins is reduced, and pectin methylesterase activity is increased. Additionally, etiolated tbr hypocotyls display reduced length and swollen epidermal cells, which is a characteristic phenotype of primary cesa mutants or the wild type treated with cellulose synthesis inhibitors. In summary, our findings demonstrate that two TBL genes play a role in the synthesis and deposition of secondary wall cellulose, potentially by influencing the esterification state of pectic polymers.

title: Genetic predictors of taxane-induced neurotoxicity in a SWOG phase III intergroup adjuvant breast cancer treatment trial (S0221)
text: Taxanes have been shown to improve survival rates for breast cancer patients, but they often come with the side effect of neurological toxicities. It would be beneficial to identify biomarkers that are related to these toxicities in order to determine the most appropriate treatment plan. In this study, we examined single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the Fanconi Anemia (FA)/BRCA pathway to see if they were associated with grade 3/4 neurotoxicities in breast cancer patients who participated in the SWOG0221 trial. This trial involved four different dose/schedules of cyclophosphamide (C), doxorubicin (A), and paclitaxel (T). We also looked at the correlation between significant FANCD2 SNPs and the corresponding gene expression in a separate group of patients. Our findings showed that out of the 20 SNPs in FANCD2 that were tested, four of them were significantly linked to a nearly two-fold increased risk of toxicity. Additionally, two FANCD2 haplotypes were associated with neurological toxicity, with odds ratios (OR) of 1.8 and 1.7 in the overall population. Although the sample size was small, we found that a specific haplotype in African-Americans was associated with a nearly three-fold increase in the risk of neurologic toxicity. Further analysis revealed that the significant FANCD2 SNPs were also linked to higher levels of FANCD2 expression. On the other hand, we did not find any associations between SNPs in BRCA1 and neurotoxicities. In conclusion, our study suggests that in breast cancer patients receiving CA+T treatment, SNPs in FANCD2, but not in BRCA1, are associated with a 70-80% higher odds of grade 3/4 neurological toxicities and increased expression of the gene. If these findings are replicated, it would be important to closely monitor women with these genotypes for toxicities and consider alternative therapeutic approaches or preventive measures.

title: Preoperative C-reactive protein predicts mid-term outcome after cardiac surgery.
text:
BACKGROUND
C-reactive protein (CRP) is a well-known risk factor for cardiovascular events in both healthy individuals and patients with coronary artery disease. While high CRP levels before cardiac surgery have been linked to worse short-term outcomes, its impact after discharge home is still unclear. This study aimed to assess the effect of CRP on short-term and mid-term outcomes following cardiac surgery.

METHODS
Between August 2000 and May 2004, preoperative CRP values were available for 597 patients undergoing cardiac operations. The cohort was divided into two groups based on CRP levels: a low inflammatory status (LHS) group consisting of 354 patients with CRP levels below 0.5 mg/dL, and a high inflammatory status (HIS) group consisting of 243 patients with CRP levels of 0.5 mg/dL or higher. Follow-up lasted a maximum of 3 years (median, 1.8 +/- 1.5 years) and had a completion rate of 92.6%.

RESULTS
In-hospital mortality was 8.2% in the HIS group compared to 3.4% in the LHS group (odds ratio [OR], 2.61; p = 0.02). The incidence of postoperative infections was 16.5% in the HIS group and 5.1% in the LHS group (OR, 3.25; p = 0.0001). Sternal wound infections were also more common in the HIS group (10.7% versus 2.8%; OR, 3.43; p = 0.002). During the follow-up period, the HIS group had lower survival rates (88.5% +/- 2.9% versus 91.9% +/- 2.5%; OR, 1.93; p = 0.05) and a higher need for hospitalization due to cardiac-related causes (73.6% +/- 6% versus 86.5% +/- 3.2%; OR, 1.82; p = 0.05).

CONCLUSIONS
Patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CRP levels of 0.5 mg/dL or higher face an increased risk of in-hospital mortality and postoperative infections. Despite surgical correction of cardiac disease, a high preoperative CRP value remains an independent risk factor for mid-term survival and hospitalization due to cardiac causes.

title: Inhibition of Hedgehog signaling enhances delivery of chemotherapy in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is one of the deadliest forms of cancer in humans, mainly due to its resistance to many chemotherapy drugs. By studying a mouse model of PDA that does not respond well to the commonly used drug gemcitabine, we discovered that the tumors in this model had poor blood flow and a lack of blood vessels, which are also characteristics of human PDA. To improve the delivery and effectiveness of gemcitabine in these mice, we tested a combination therapy with IPI-926, a drug that reduces the stromal tissue surrounding the tumor by inhibiting the Hedgehog cellular signaling pathway. This combination therapy temporarily increased the density of blood vessels within the tumor and the concentration of gemcitabine, resulting in a temporary stabilization of the disease. Therefore, the inefficient delivery of drugs may play a significant role in the resistance to chemotherapy in pancreatic cancer.

title: Mutant SOD1 inhibits ER-Golgi transport in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
text: The misfolding of Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase in familial and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is not fully understood in terms of how it triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress or other pathological processes. In this study, we demonstrate that mutant SOD1 is primarily located in the cytoplasm of neuronal cells. Additionally, we observe that mutant SOD1 hinders the transport of secretory proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. This disruption of endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transport is associated with endoplasmic reticulum stress, Golgi fragmentation, and axonal transport impairment. Furthermore, we find that the inhibition of endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking occurs before the onset of endoplasmic reticulum stress, Golgi fragmentation, protein aggregation, and cell death in cells expressing mutant SOD1. By restoring endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transport through the overexpression of the coatomer coat protein II subunit Sar1, we are able to protect against inclusion formation and cell death, thus establishing a connection between dysfunction in endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transport and cellular pathology. These findings provide insight into the early cellular events that occur in cells expressing mutant SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

title: High spatial resolution mapping of malaria transmission risk in the Gambia, west Africa, using LANDSAT TM satellite imagery.
text: When designing intervention or vaccine trials, it is crucial to understand the local variability in malaria transmission risk. To achieve this, we utilized field data, satellite image analysis, and GIS modeling to create a detailed map of malaria entomological inoculation rates (EIR) in The Gambia, West Africa. Our analysis was based on the differences in exposure to malaria parasites observed in 48 villages in 1996 and 21 villages in 1997. The EIR ranged from 0 to 166 infective bites per person per rainy season. Through comprehensive field surveys, we were able to identify the main breeding habitats of the Anopheles gambiae s.l. mosquito species. These habitats were accurately mapped using a LANDSAT TM satellite image, with an overall accuracy of 85%. By examining the size and proximity of these breeding areas, we observed a decrease in village EIRs following a power function. Leveraging this relationship and the identified breeding habitats, we were able to map the variation in EIR across the entire 2500-km(2) study area.

title: Functional analysis of repressor binding sites in the iab-2 regulatory region of the abdominal-A homeotic gene.
text: The spatial boundaries of homeotic gene expression are established and sustained by two groups of transcriptional repressors: the products of the gap genes and the Polycomb group proteins. Previously, it was discovered that the Hunchback (HB) protein plays a role in determining the anterior limit of expression for the UBX homeotic protein in parasegment 6. In this study, we investigate the DNA elements and trans-acting repressors that regulate the spatial expression of the Abdominal-A (ABD-A) homeotic protein. Through analysis of a 1.7-kb enhancer element called iab-2(1.7) from the iab-2 regulatory region, we find that both HB and Krüppel (KR) are necessary to establish the anterior boundary of ABD-A in parasegment 7. DNase I footprinting and site-directed mutagenesis experiments reveal that HB and KR directly regulate this iab-2 enhancer. Interestingly, the KR site can be relocated 100 bp away from its original position and still maintain its repressive activity, but relocation by 300 bp completely abolishes its function. These findings suggest that KR repression operates through a local quenching mechanism. Additionally, we demonstrate that the gap repressor Giant (GT) initially sets the posterior limit of expression at parasegment 9, which then shifts posteriorly after the blastoderm stage. Finally, we discover that the iab-2 enhancer contains multiple binding sites for the Polycomb group protein Pleiohomeotic (PHO). These PHO sites are essential in vivo for the repression of a mini-white reporter gene that is dependent on chromosome pairing. However, the PHO sites alone are insufficient to maintain repression of a homeotic reporter gene anterior to parasegment 7. Complete repression at later stages of embryonic development requires additional sequences adjacent to the iab-2(1.7) enhancer.

title: Apolipoprotein E: high-avidity binding to beta-amyloid and increased frequency of type 4 allele in late-onset familial Alzheimer disease.
text: Apolipoprotein E is found in the senile plaques, vascular amyloid, and neurofibrillary tangles associated with Alzheimer's disease. In laboratory tests, apolipoprotein E in cerebrospinal fluid strongly binds to synthetic beta A4 peptide, which is a major component of the senile plaque. Specifically, amino acids 12-28 of the beta A4 peptide are necessary for this binding. The gene responsible for producing apolipoprotein E is located on chromosome 19q13.2, a region previously linked to late-onset familial Alzheimer's disease. When comparing individuals with Alzheimer's disease to healthy controls, it was discovered that there is a significant association between the apolipoprotein E type 4 allele (APOE-epsilon 4) and late-onset familial Alzheimer's disease. The frequency of the APOE-epsilon 4 allele in 30 affected patients from different Alzheimer's disease families was 0.50 +/- 0.06, while the frequency in 91 unrelated controls of the same age group was 0.16 +/- 0.03 (Z = 2.44, P = 0.014). These findings suggest that the apolipoprotein E-E4 isoform may play a functional role in the development of late-onset familial Alzheimer's disease.

title: Unmarked gene deletion and host–vector system for the hyperthermophilic crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus
text: Sulfolobus islandicus is currently being utilized as a model organism for the study of archaeal biology, geo-biology, and evolution. However, there is currently no available genetic system for this particular organism. In order to create a mutant of S. islandicus that is suitable for genetic analysis, we conducted a screening process to identify colonies with a spontaneous pyrEF mutation.
