Eventually, we obtained one mutant that contained only 233 bp of the original pyrE sequence in its mutant allele. This mutant was then used as a host to delete the β-glycosidase (lacS) gene. We employed two different methods for unmarked gene deletion: plasmid integration and segregation, as well as marker replacement and looping out. By using each method, we were able to obtain unmarked lacS mutants. However, the latter method revealed a new alternative recombination mechanism called marker circularization and integration, which did not result in the intended deletion mutation. Following this, we constructed Sulfolobus-E. coli plasmid shuttle vectors that genetically complemented the ΔpyrEFΔlacS mutation after transformation. As a result, we successfully established a comprehensive set of genetic tools for S. islandicus, utilizing pyrEF and lacS as genetic markers.

title: ADAM13 disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains bind to the second heparin-binding domain of fibronectin.
text: ADAM13, a protein belonging to the disintegrin and metalloprotease family, is crucial for the migration of cranial neural crest cells. It acts as an active protease, capable of cleaving fibronectin in laboratory settings and remodeling a fibronectin substrate in living organisms. Through the use of a recombinant secreted protein containing the disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains of ADAM13, it has been demonstrated that the "adhesive" region of the protein directly binds to fibronectin. By utilizing fibronectin fusion proteins representing different functional domains, the second heparin-binding domain has been identified as the binding site for ADAM13. The mutation of the syndecan-binding site within this domain eliminates the binding of the recombinant disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains of ADAM13. Additionally, it has been observed that the adhesive disintegrin and cysteine-rich domain of ADAM13 can facilitate cell adhesion through beta(1) integrins. This adhesion process requires integrin activation and can be hindered by antibodies targeting the cysteine-rich domain of ADAM13 and beta(1) integrin. Furthermore, the wild type form of ADAM13, but not the E/A mutant of its metalloprotease domain, can be shed from the cell surface, releasing the metalloprotease domain associated with the disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains. This suggests that ADAM13 shedding may involve its own metalloprotease activity and that the released protease may interact with both integrins and extracellular matrix proteins.

title: Clinical epidemiology of heart failure.
text: The objective of this paper is to examine the clinical epidemiology of heart failure. The most recent comprehensive study on the epidemiology of heart failure in Heart was published in 2000. Although there has been a rise in research papers discussing the epidemiological aspects of heart failure since the 1990s, there is still a requirement for further information, as highlighted by several editorials.

title: Toll-like receptor 7 agonist GS-9620 induces prolonged inhibition of HBV via a type I interferon-dependent mechanism.
text:
GS-9620 is an oral drug that is currently being developed for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Previous studies have shown that GS-9620 can effectively suppress the hepatitis B virus (HBV) in animal models, but the exact mechanisms behind its antiviral effects were not fully understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms that contribute to the antiviral response to GS-9620 using in vitro models of HBV infection.

To conduct our study, we infected cryopreserved primary human hepatocytes (PHH) and differentiated HepaRG (dHepaRG) cells with HBV and treated them with GS-9620, conditioned media from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells treated with GS-9620 (GS-9620-CM), or other innate immune stimuli. We then examined the antiviral and transcriptional response to these agents.

Our results showed that GS-9620 had no direct antiviral activity in HBV-infected PHH, which was consistent with the low level of toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) mRNA expression in human hepatocytes. However, GS-9620-CM induced a prolonged reduction in HBV DNA, RNA, and antigen levels in both PHH and dHepaRG cells through a type I interferon (IFN)-dependent mechanism. Interestingly, GS-9620-CM did not reduce the levels of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is the stable form of the HBV genome. Transcriptional profiling revealed that GS-9620-CM strongly induced various HBV restriction factors, but not APOBEC3A or the Smc5/6 complex. Additionally, our findings indicated that established HBV infection did not modulate innate immune sensing or signaling in cryopreserved PHH. GS-9620-CM also increased the expression of immunoproteasome subunits and enhanced the presentation of an immunodominant viral peptide in HBV-infected PHH.

In conclusion, our study demonstrated that GS-9620 can durably suppress HBV in human hepatocytes through the induction of type I IFN, without reducing cccDNA levels. Furthermore, our findings suggested that other components of the TLR7-induced immune response, such as the activation of immune cells that kill infected cells, may also play a significant role in the antiviral response to GS-9620.

title: Depletion of glutathione induces 4-hydroxynonenal protein adducts and hydroxyurea teratogenicity in the organogenesis stage mouse embryo.
text: During the stage of organogenesis, maintaining a balance of glutathione (GSH) is crucial. To understand the effects of GSH depletion on oxidative stress and the teratogenicity of drugs during this stage, we administered l-buthionine-S,R-sulfoximine (BSO) to pregnant CD-1 mice before exposing them to a model teratogen, hydroxyurea (HU) [400 mg/kg (HU-400) or 600 mg/kg (HU-600)]. The administration of BSO or HU alone, or BSO combined with HU-400, did not affect the ratio of glutathione disulfide/GSH in the embryos. However, the combination of BSO and HU-600 did increase this ratio at 0.5 and 3 hours after exposure to HU, indicating the induction of oxidative stress in the embryos. We observed the presence of 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) protein adducts, a product of lipid peroxidation, in embryos treated with saline. The intensity and nuclear localization of 4-HNE protein adduct immunoreactivity in specific regions of the embryo significantly increased when exposed to BSO alone or BSO combined with either dose of HU. BSO pretreatment also increased the occurrence and variety of external and skeletal malformations (such as curly tail, hind limb malformations, hydrocephaly, exencephaly, open eye, spina bifida, and gastroschisis) induced by HU-400 and HU-600. However, BSO exposure did not affect the effects of HU on fetal mortality or fetal weights, nor did it affect HU's induction of c-Fos heterodimer-dependent activator protein 1 DNA binding activity. The formation of 4-HNE protein adducts in teratogen-exposed embryos was localized to regions highly susceptible to damage, namely the somites and caudal neural tube. This correlation suggests that the presence of 4-HNE adducts disrupts pattern formation during organogenesis.

title: Nonproductive human immunodeficiency virus type 1 infection in nucleoside-treated G0 lymphocytes.
text: The activation of target cells is necessary for productive infection by human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1). When HIV-1 infects quiescent peripheral CD4 lymphocytes, the reverse transcription process is incomplete and unstable. Our previous research identified G1b as the cell cycle stage required for optimal completion of reverse transcription in T lymphocytes. However, the mechanism(s) responsible for blocking reverse transcription remains unknown. In this study, we investigated whether nucleotide levels affect viral reverse transcription in G0 cells. To do this, we bypassed the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase by adding external deoxyribonucleosides to purified T cells in the G0 or G1a phase of the cell cycle. Our findings demonstrated a significant improvement in the efficiency of reverse transcription after the addition of deoxyribonucleosides. To assess the stability and functionality of these complete reverse transcripts, we utilized an HIV-1 reporter virus that expresses the murine heat-stable antigen on infected cell surfaces. Despite activating infected quiescent cells treated with external nucleosides, we did not observe an increased rescue of productive infection. Therefore, in addition to the failure to complete reverse transcription, there was an irreversible blockage of productive infection in quiescent T cells. These experiments have important implications in the field of gene therapy, particularly in enhancing the ability of lentivirus vectors to enter metabolically inactive cells like hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Imported malaria in children: a national surveillance in the Netherlands and a review of European studies.
text:
Falciparum malaria, also known as malaria tropica, is a major cause of childhood mortality worldwide. The majority of malaria-related deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where approximately 365 million clinical cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria are reported each year. In Europe, cases of imported malaria are primarily due to travelers returning from or immigrants originating from African countries. Children are particularly vulnerable to this disease. The aim of this study was to identify high-risk groups for imported childhood malaria in Europe in order to develop effective strategies for prevention, early detection, and management. 

To achieve this objective, we reviewed all cases of pediatric malaria reported to the Dutch Paediatric Surveillance System (Nederland Signalerings Centrum Kindergeneeskunde, NSCK) between May 2003 and January 2005, as well as relevant literature on imported malaria in children in Europe published from 1996 to 2006. 

Our findings revealed that malaria primarily affected children of long-term (47%) and new (25%) immigrants, with the majority of cases acquired in sub-Saharan Africa. The most common species of malaria was P. falciparum. Shockingly, only a quarter of the children had received adequate malaria chemoprophylaxis. Complications occurred in 31% of cases. Additionally, we conducted a literature review and identified 6082 reported cases of imported malaria among children in Europe. Out of these cases, four resulted in death and only one was reported to have developed neurological complications. 

In conclusion, imported malaria in children remains a significant problem and is unlikely to decrease unless the issue of inadequate prophylaxis is addressed.

title: Respiratory and cardiovascular responses to walking down a traffic-polluted road compared with walking in a traffic-free area in participants aged 60 years and older with chronic lung or heart disease and age-matched healthy controls: a randomised, crossover study
text: The aim of this study was to examine the effects of walking in a highly polluted area compared to a less polluted area on respiratory and cardiovascular responses in older adults. Participants included individuals with stable ischaemic heart disease or COPD, as well as healthy volunteers. Measurements of pollution levels were taken during each walk session. The study found that walking on a busy street with high pollution levels led to increased respiratory symptoms in individuals with COPD. Additionally, walking in the less polluted area resulted in improved lung function and decreased pulse wave velocity and augmentation index, while these benefits were diminished after walking on the busy street. The study suggests that short-term exposure to traffic pollution can negate the positive effects of walking in individuals with COPD and ischaemic heart disease. Medication use may help mitigate the adverse effects of air pollution in individuals with ischaemic heart disease. The study concludes that efforts should be made to control air pollution levels in busy areas to protect public health. The study was funded by the British Heart Foundation.

title: Overall and cancer related mortality among patients with ocular inflammation treated with immunosuppressive drugs: retrospective cohort study.
text:
CONTEXT: The impact of immunosuppressive treatment on survival is uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: To determine if immunosuppressive drugs contribute to higher mortality rates.
DESIGN: A retrospective cohort study examining overall and cancer mortality in relation to immunosuppressive drug use among patients with ocular inflammatory diseases. Data on demographics, clinical information, and treatment were collected from medical records, and mortality data were obtained from the United States National Death Index. The cohort's mortality risk was compared to US vital statistics using standardized mortality ratios. Survival analysis was conducted to assess overall and cancer mortality in relation to immunosuppressive drug use within the cohort.
SETTING: Five tertiary ocular inflammation clinics.
PATIENTS: A total of 7,957 US residents with non-infectious ocular inflammation, of whom 2,340 received immunosuppressive drugs during follow-up.
EXPOSURES: Use of antimetabolites, T cell inhibitors, alkylating agents, and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Overall mortality and cancer mortality.
RESULTS: Over a span of 66,802 person-years (17,316 after exposure to immunosuppressive drugs), 936 patients died (1.4/100 person-years), with 230 (24.6%) deaths attributed to cancer. The risks of overall mortality (standardized mortality ratio 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.94 to 1.11) and cancer mortality (1.10, 0.93 to 1.29) for patients not exposed to immunosuppressive treatment were similar to those of the general US population. Patients who used azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, systemic corticosteroids, or dapsone had overall and cancer mortality rates comparable to those who never took immunosuppressive drugs. Among patients who used cyclophosphamide, overall mortality was not increased, and cancer mortality showed a non-significant increase. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors were associated with higher overall (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.99, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.98) and cancer mortality (adjusted HR 3.83, 1.13 to 13.01).
CONCLUSIONS: The majority of commonly used immunosuppressive drugs do not appear to increase overall or cancer mortality. However, our findings regarding the potential increase in mortality with tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are less conclusive and require further evidence.

title: Ephrin B1–mediated repulsion and signaling control germinal center T cell territoriality and function
text: The role of follicular T helper (TFH) cells in coordinating the germinal center (GC) reaction is not well understood. In this study, we discovered that a protein called ephrin B1 (EFNB1), which is expressed in the GC, inhibits the adhesion of T cells to B cells and the retention of TFH cells in the GC. This inhibition occurs through signaling between EFNB1 and the EPHB6 receptor on TFH cells. However, EFNB1 also promotes the production of interleukin-21 from GC TFH cells by signaling primarily through EPHB4. As a result, GCs lacking EFNB1 had impaired production of plasma cells, despite having an excess of TFH cells. In a competitive GC reaction, B cells lacking EFNB1 interacted more efficiently with TFH cells and produced more plasma cells in the bone marrow, likely due to increased contact-dependent help. These findings demonstrate the existence of a contact-dependent repulsive guidance system that regulates the dynamics and functions of GC TFH cells locally.

title: Molecular profiling and predictive value of circulating tumor cells in patients with metastatic breast cancer: an option for monitoring response to breast cancer related therapies
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the presence of circulating tumor cells (CTC) in the blood of patients with metastatic breast cancer and determine if this method could predict the response to therapy. The AdnaTest BreastCancer was used to analyze CTC for the presence of EpCAM, MUC1, and HER2 transcripts, as well as the expression of estrogen (ER) and progesterone (PR) receptors using RT-PCR. 

The results showed that CTC were detected in 52% of patients, with 86% expressing EpCAM and MUC1, 32% expressing HER2, 35% expressing ER, and 12% expressing PR. Interestingly, 45% of patients with steroid receptor-positive tumors had CTC that were negative for ER, 78% had CTC that were negative for PR, and 60% had CTC that were negative for HER2. Additionally, 29% of patients with HER2-negative tumors had HER2-positive CTC. 

The test was able to predict therapy response in 78% of cases. Furthermore, the persistence of CTC was found to be significantly associated with shorter overall survival. 

In conclusion, the molecular profiling of CTC may provide valuable prognostic information for assessing the risk of recurrence and predicting the effectiveness of different therapeutic regimens.

title: Alternate-day wheel access: effects on feeding, body weight, and running.
text:
The impact of having access to a running wheel on rats is that it significantly reduces their desire to eat, but only for a short period of time. The reasons behind this feeding suppression and why it is temporary are not yet clear. To investigate the effects of having access to the wheel every other day, a study was conducted using 25 male Sprague-Dawley rats. These rats were divided into three groups: one group had no access to the wheel, another group had continuous access to the wheel, and the last group had access to the wheel every other day. 

The results showed that when the rats had access to the wheel every other day, their food intake was reduced on the days they had access to the wheel, but increased on the days they did not have access to the wheel. This pattern continued throughout the entire 32-day experiment. Additionally, the rats' body weight decreased on the days they had access to the wheel, but showed a significant increase on the days they did not have access to the wheel. 

The study also found that the rats in both wheel groups showed similar levels of running activity, which reached a plateau after a certain number of days. However, when the rats in the alternate-day wheel group were reintroduced to the wheel after a period of no access, their running activity was higher compared to the rats in the continuous-access group, but only for the first few hours. 

These findings suggest that the feeding suppression caused by the wheel is not solely due to the novelty of the wheel, and that this suppression can be prolonged by providing periods of no access to the wheel. The temporary nature of the feeding suppression in conditions of chronic access may be attributed to longer-term motivational changes.

title: Evaluation of the association between the first observation and the longitudinal change in C-reactive protein, and all-cause mortality.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between vascular inflammation, as indicated by subacute C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, and all-cause mortality. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the association between changes in CRP status and all-cause mortality. The researchers utilized probabilistic record linkage to match hospital episode data, laboratory reports, and mortality statistics in a large urban population. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to evaluate survival.

The results showed that among the 22,962 patients with their first CRP measurement in the subacute range (1-10 mg/l), each additional unit increase in CRP across this range was associated with a 7.3% increase in the hazard ratio of death over a 4-year period, after accounting for confounding factors (p<0.001). Furthermore, among the 5,811 subjects with repeated CRP observations around 1 year apart, patients whose CRP changed from normal (≤3 mg/l) to elevated (>3 mg/l) had a 6.7-fold increase in the hazard ratio compared to those whose CRP remained normal (p<0.001). Conversely, among subjects whose CRP decreased from elevated to normal, the hazard ratio decreased by half to 3.5 (p=0.018). A similar pattern of risk was observed in the analysis of time to cardiovascular events, although the analysis was underpowered.

In conclusion, CRP levels were found to be predictive of all-cause mortality, with the inclusion of prior changes in CRP levels and current CRP levels enhancing this prediction. Increasing vascular inflammation, as indicated by CRP, was associated with a higher likelihood of death.

title: Research Priorities in Sudden Unexpected Infant Death: An International Consensus.
text: Despite the progress made in safe sleep campaigns and understanding risk factors, the rate of decline in sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) cases has slowed down. SIDS remains a leading cause of postneonatal mortality in many developed countries. To address this issue, it is crucial to determine the most effective approach for the sudden infant death research community. The Global Action and Prioritization of Sudden Infant Death Project aimed to define and guide future research by investigating the priorities of experts and members of the sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) community worldwide. This project involved scientific researchers, clinicians, counselors, educators, and SUID parents from 25 countries who participated in online surveys. Subsequently, workshops were conducted in the United Kingdom, United States, and Australia to establish consensus on 10 priority areas for research. The identified priorities revolved around three main themes: gaining a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying SUID, ensuring best practices in data collection, management, and sharing, and improving understanding of target populations and effectively communicating risks. By providing a shared list of research priorities, this project equips the international SUID community to work more effectively in explaining and reducing the number of sudden infant deaths worldwide.

title: Modification of the Constant-Murley shoulder score-introduction of the individual relative Constant score Individual shoulder assessment.
text: The Constant-Murley shoulder assessment score has proven to be a valuable tool for diagnosis. However, its clinical accuracy can vary when comparing patients in larger, diverse patient groups. To address this issue, the "relative Constant score" (CS(rel)) uses reference parameters from healthy individuals of the same age and gender. In this study, the authors aimed to demonstrate that using the functional performance of the uninjured shoulder of the same person as a reference, known as the "individual relative Constant score" (CS(indiv)), is even more accurate. They compared CS(indiv) and CS(rel) in 125 patients with shoulder disorders and a control group of 125 healthy volunteers. The non-parametric comparison of the receiver operating characteristics showed that CS(indiv) had a higher ability to distinguish between patients and healthy volunteers (p=0.004). This suggests that the individual relative Constant score provides a more accurate assessment of functional outcomes for shoulder disorders. It is expected to be more reliable in larger and diverse patient populations, as it eliminates interindividual differences in age, gender, constitution, and other physiological parameters.

title: Celiac disease screening by immunochromatographic visual assays: results of a multicenter study.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of two immunochromatographic visual stick assays for screening celiac disease (CD). The first assay, called the antitissue transglutaminase antibodies (AtTGA) stick, detects IgA/G antibodies to tissue transglutaminase (tTG). The second assay, called the AtTGA/antigliadin antibodies (AGA) stick, detects IgA antibodies for tTG and/or gliadins.

The study involved four pediatric gastroenterology units in Spain and two in Latin America. A total of 72 control children with normal small bowel mucosa and 113 untreated patients with CD were enrolled. The results were evaluated by gastroenterologists and two independent observers at the coordination center, and there was very little variation between their assessments.

The AtTGA stick had a sensitivity of 96.5% and a specificity of 98.6%. The AtTGA/AGA stick had a sensitivity of 94.5% and a specificity of 98.6% for AtTGA, and a sensitivity of 63.1% and a specificity of 95.2% for AGA. The AtTGA stick had the highest efficiency and positive likelihood ratio, surpassing the IgA AtTGA by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. An additional advantage of the AtTGA stick was that it eliminated the need for previous investigation of total serum IgA levels.

The IgA AtTGA/AGA stick had an efficiency of 95.1%, compared to 89.2% when the results of the two enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays were combined. This made it an excellent diagnostic tool for infants without IgA deficiency.

In conclusion, these two assays are highly effective for screening CD. They combine high diagnostic accuracy with the simplicity and speed of visual methods.

title: Down-regulation of keratin 4 and keratin 13 expression in oral squamous cell carcinoma and epithelial dysplasia: a clue for histopathogenesis.
text: The objective of this study was to identify relevant keratin subtypes that may be associated with the development of oral epithelial neoplasms. To achieve this, the expression of all keratin subtypes was analyzed using cDNA microarray analysis in 43 cases of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Additionally, immunohistochemical expression of major keratins was examined in 100 cases of OSCC and oral epithelial dysplasia (OED). The study revealed numerous changes in keratin expression, with a consistent down-regulation of keratin 4 (K4) and K13 expression. The abnormal expression of K4 and K13 was found to be linked to morphological changes in the affected oral epithelium. Further experiments using cell cultures transfected with different keratin subtypes suggested that alterations in keratin subtype expression can lead to changes in cell shape and movement. In conclusion, the aberrant expression of K4 and K13, which are the primary keratins associated with differentiation in oral keratinocytes, indicates a disruption in epithelial differentiation in OSCC and OED. These keratins, particularly K4, could potentially be used for pathological diagnosis. The study proposes that the abnormal expression of K4 and K13, along with the simultaneous up-regulation of other keratins, may be one of the contributing factors to the morphological changes observed in the affected epithelium.

title: Identification of short-lived long non-coding RNAs as surrogate indicators for chemical stress response.
text: Changes in environmental factors can cause stress in human cells, both abiotic and biotic. This stress triggers a complex molecular response that involves the regulation of gene expression, and it is crucial for maintaining homeostasis, ecological balance, and evolutionary processes. While research has mainly focused on signaling pathways and protein networks, there is growing evidence that long non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) play a role in cellular stress responses. In our study, we discovered six new short-lived long ncRNAs (MIR22HG, GABPB-AS1, LINC00152, IDI2-AS1, SNHG15, and FLJ33630) that are responsive to chemical stressors such as cisplatin, cycloheximide, and mercury (II) oxide in HeLa Tet-off cells. Our findings suggest that these short-lived long ncRNAs are sensitive to both general and specific chemical stressors. The expression levels of these ncRNAs increased due to prolonged decay rates caused by the stressors and disruption of RNA degradation pathways. Based on these observations, we propose that these long ncRNAs could serve as reliable indicators of cellular stress responses.

title: Isolation of a gene encoding a functional zinc finger protein homologous to erythroid Krüppel-like factor: identification of a new multigene family.
text: We have discovered and characterized a new zinc finger transcription factor gene called lung Krüppel-like factor (LKLF). LKLF was found using the zinc finger domain of erythroid Krüppel-like factor (ELKF) as a hybridization probe and is closely related to this gene specific to erythroid cells. LKLF is primarily expressed in the lungs and spleen, with limited expression in other tissues. The gene's expression is regulated during development, with initial expression in the 7-day embryo, followed by down-regulation at 11 days and subsequent reactivation. The zinc finger regions of LKLF and EKLF show a high degree of similarity, but their sequences differ significantly beyond this domain. However, both LKLF and EKLF have proline-rich regions as putative transactivation domains. In the DNA-binding domain, the three zinc finger motifs are conserved to such an extent that the predicted DNA contact sites are identical, suggesting that both proteins may bind to the same core sequence. This hypothesis was supported by transactivation assays, where mouse fibroblasts were transfected with a human beta-globin reporter gene in the presence or absence of an LKLF cDNA construct. The expression of the LKLF gene activated the human beta-globin promoter, which contains the CACCC sequence known to be a binding site for EKLF. Mutating this potential binding site significantly reduced the expression of the reporter gene. Therefore, LKLF and EKLF can be classified as members of a distinct family of transcription factors that exhibit specific expression patterns in different tissues and recognize the same DNA-binding site.

title: A small molecule restores function to TRPML1 mutant isoforms responsible for mucolipidosis type IV.
text: Mucolipidosis type IV (MLIV) is a lysosomal storage disorder that is often characterized by severe neurodevelopmental abnormalities and neuro-retinal degeneration. MLIV is caused by mutations in the TRPML1 gene, which is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. In our study, we employed lead optimization strategies to identify potential small-molecule activators that could restore the function of the mutant TRPML1 channel. To test the efficacy of these activators, we conducted experiments using fibroblasts from MLIV patients. By utilizing the whole-lysosome planar patch-clamp technique, we observed a significant reduction in the activation of MLIV mutant isoforms by the endogenous ligand PI(3,5)P2. However, we found that synthetic ligands could increase the activity of these mutant isoforms. Additionally, we discovered that the F465L mutation made TRPML1 pH insensitive, while the F408Δ mutation affected the binding of synthetic ligands. Furthermore, we observed that the small molecule treatment could rescue trafficking defects and the accumulation of zinc in lysosomes of MLIV mutant fibroblasts. Overall, our findings demonstrate that small molecules have the potential to restore channel function and alleviate disease-associated abnormalities in patient cells expressing specific MLIV point mutations.

title: Characterization of a murine monoclonal antibody to Cryptococcus neoformans polysaccharide that is a candidate for human therapeutic studies.
text: The murine monoclonal antibody (MAb) 18B7, which is an immunoglobulin G1(kappa), is currently being developed for the treatment of Cryptococcus neoformans infections. In order to prepare for its potential use in humans, we conducted a thorough analysis of the serological and biological properties of MAb 18B7. By comparing its structure to the protective MAb 2H1, we found that the antigen binding site is conserved despite some amino acid differences. Through immunofluorescence and agglutination studies, we determined that MAb 18B7 can bind to all four serotypes of C. neoformans, opsonize serotypes A and D, enhance antifungal activity in human and mouse effector cells, and activate the complement pathway, resulting in the deposition of complement component 3 (C3) on the cryptococcal capsule. When administered to mice, MAb 18B7 effectively cleared serum cryptococcal antigen and deposited it in the liver and spleen. Immunohistochemical studies further revealed that MAb 18B7 specifically bound to capsular glucuronoxylomannan in infected mouse tissues, with no reactivity observed in normal human, rat, or mouse tissues. These findings demonstrate that both the variable and constant regions of MAb 18B7 are biologically functional, supporting its potential use in human therapeutic trials.

title: Treatment with cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors enables repeated administration of vaccinia virus for control of ovarian cancer.
text: Metastatic ovarian cancer is the primary cause of death for women with gynecologic malignancies in the United States. Due to the lack of effective treatment options for advanced ovarian cancer, there is a need for the development of innovative therapies. Utilizing oncolytic viruses for cancer therapy shows promise in controlling tumors. Vaccinia virus has demonstrated a preference for infecting tumor cells while sparing normal tissue. However, the use of recombinant viruses in oncolytic therapy is limited by viral clearance caused by the production of neutralizing antibodies. In our recent study, we discovered that circumventing this limitation is possible by using cyclooxygenase-2 (Cox-2) inhibitors, which allow for repeated administration of vaccinia virus without losing infectivity. We measured the antivaccinia antibody response through enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and neutralization assays, demonstrating that Cox-2 inhibitors hindered the production of neutralizing antibodies. Additionally, we observed that combining Cox-2 inhibitors with vaccinia virus treatment was more effective in treating MOSEC/luc tumor-bearing mice compared to either treatment alone. Therefore, the combination of Cox-2 inhibitors and vaccinia virus presents a potential innovative approach for controlling ovarian tumors.

title: Ser-752-->Pro mutation in the cytoplasmic domain of integrin beta 3 subunit and defective activation of platelet integrin alpha IIb beta 3 (glycoprotein IIb-IIIa) in a variant of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
text:
Integrins play a crucial role in cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion by acting as membrane receptors. Specifically, integrin alpha IIb beta 3, also known as glycoprotein IIb-IIIa, functions as a receptor for fibrinogen on platelets, facilitating platelet aggregation. The process of platelet activation is necessary for alpha IIb beta 3 to transition from an inactive state to a state capable of binding soluble fibrinogen. However, the exact steps involved in this transition are not well understood.

To gain further insight, we conducted a study on a variant of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a congenital bleeding disorder characterized by the absence of platelet aggregation and fibrinogen binding. Interestingly, the patient's platelets contained alpha IIb beta 3 but failed to bind fibrinogen after activation by ADP or thrombin. Nonetheless, when we isolated alpha IIb beta 3, it was able to bind to an affinity column containing the Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser peptide. Additionally, we observed that the binding of soluble fibrinogen to the patient's platelets could be triggered by modulators that affect the conformation of alpha IIb beta 3, such as the Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser peptide and alpha-chymotrypsin.

Based on these findings, we concluded that a functional Arg-Gly-Asp binding site was present within alpha IIb beta 3 and that the patient's defect was not due to a blockade of alpha IIb beta 3 in an inactive conformation. Instead, it suggested a potential issue with the coupling between platelet activation and the up-regulation of alpha IIb beta 3. To investigate this further, we sequenced the cytoplasmic domain of beta 3 using platelet RNA obtained through polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Our analysis revealed a T-->C mutation at nucleotide 2259, resulting in a Ser-752-->Pro substitution. This mutation is likely responsible for the uncoupling of alpha IIb beta 3 from cellular activation because it is not a common genetic variation, it is the only mutation found in the entire alpha IIb beta 3 sequence, and genetic analysis of the patient's family confirmed that the absence of the Pro-752 beta 3 allele was associated with a normal phenotype.

In summary, our data highlight the importance of the C-terminal portion of the cytoplasmic domain of beta 3 in the coupling between alpha IIb beta 3 and platelet activation.

title: Crossover and noncrossover pathways in mouse meiosis.
text: Recombination during meiosis generates crossover (CR) and noncrossover (NCR) products between homologous chromosomes. CRs establish connections between homologs, while intermediates leading to NCRs may participate in homologous pairing. However, the differentiation and regulation of these events are still unknown. To address this, we have developed a method to detect, quantify, and map NCRs alongside CRs at the Psmb9 meiotic recombination hot spot in male and female mouse germ lines. Our findings provide direct molecular evidence for distinct CR and NCR pathways of DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair in mouse meiosis. We observed that both CRs and NCRs require Spo11, but NCR products have shorter conversion tracts compared to CRs. Additionally, only CRs require the MutL homolog Mlh1. Our results indicate that both CR and NCR products are formed during the middle to late pachytene of meiotic prophase. Furthermore, we present evidence for an Mlh1-independent CR pathway, where mismatch repair does not rely on Mlh1.

title: IAP regulation of metastasis.
text: The role of Inhibitor-of-Apoptosis (IAP) proteins in tumor progression is not fully understood. However, our study reveals that the cooperation between XIAP and survivin promotes tumor cell invasion and metastasis. Surprisingly, this pathway does not involve the inhibition of cell death by IAP. Instead, a complex formed by survivin and XIAP activates NF-kappaB, which subsequently increases the expression of the fibronectin gene. This leads to signaling by beta1 integrins and the activation of cell motility kinases FAK and Src. Consequently, IAPs can be considered as direct metastasis genes, and targeting them could potentially serve as an antimetastatic therapy for cancer patients.

title: 15-Hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase is down-regulated in colorectal cancer.
text: The modulation of various pathways involved in tumor progression, such as proliferation, angiogenesis, cell migration, invasion, and apoptosis, can be stimulated by Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). While the levels of PGE2 in tissues are determined by the balance between biosynthesis and breakdown, most studies have focused solely on the formation of this bioactive lipid through cyclooxygenase-dependent mechanisms. However, the degradation of PGE2 is facilitated by an enzyme called NAD+-dependent 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (15-PGDH). In this study, we investigated the expression of 15-PGDH in normal tissues of humans and mice and found that it is highly expressed in the large intestine. Conversely, the expression of 15-PGDH is reduced in colorectal carcinoma cell lines, as well as in other human malignancies like breast and lung carcinomas. This decrease in expression is also observed in ApcMin+/- mouse adenomas. The activity of 15-PGDH is directly correlated with its expression levels, and the genetic disruption of 15-PGDH completely inhibits the production of the urinary PGE2 metabolite. Furthermore, the expression and activity of 15-PGDH are significantly down-regulated in human colorectal carcinomas compared to normal tissue. Overall, these findings suggest that the loss of 15-PGDH expression plays a novel role in suppressing tumor growth during colorectal tumor progression.

title: Stimulation of CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells through GITR breaks immunological self-tolerance
text: In normal animals, CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells are responsible for maintaining immunological self-tolerance. Our research demonstrates that glucocorticoid-induced tumor necrosis factor receptor family–related gene (GITR, also known as TNFRSF18) is primarily expressed on CD25+CD4+ T cells and CD25+CD4+CD8− thymocytes in normal naïve mice. When GITR is stimulated, it disrupts the suppression mediated by CD25+CD4+ T cells. Furthermore, eliminating GITR-expressing T cells or administering a monoclonal antibody to GITR leads to organ-specific autoimmune disease in otherwise healthy mice. This highlights the crucial role of GITR in maintaining dominant immunological self-tolerance through CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells, making it a potential target for preventing or treating autoimmune disease.

title: The missing cases of tuberculosis in Malawi: the contribution from cross-border registrations.
text: The low detection rates of new smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients worldwide are a cause for concern. This study aimed to determine the number and percentage of TB patients registered in Malawi who lived in a neighboring country, as well as the registration, recording, and reporting practices for these patients. All 44 non-private hospitals in the public health sector in Malawi, which register and treat TB patients, were visited. In 2001, 23% of hospitals maintained a separate register for cross-border TB cases, and this number increased to 32% in 2002. However, patients recorded in these registers were not officially reported to the Malawi National TB Programme (NTP), the neighboring country's NTP, or the World Health Organization (WHO). Therefore, these patients are considered missing cases. In Malawi, there were 77 cross-border new smear-positive PTB cases in 2001 and 91 cases in 2002, accounting for approximately 3% of missing smear-positive cases in hospitals with cross-border registers and about 1% of missing cases nationwide.

title: Parathyroid hormone induces E4bp4 messenger ribonucleic acid expression primarily through cyclic adenosine 3',5'-monophosphate signaling in osteoblasts.
text: The binding of PTH to its receptor activates protein kinase A (PKA), protein kinase C (PKC), and calcium signaling, which in turn induces the transcription of primary response genes in osteoblasts. One of these primary response genes is E4BP4/NFIL3, a transcriptional repressor, which is induced by PTH in primary mouse osteoblasts (MOBs). In this study, we aim to investigate the signaling pathway(s) that lead to the induction of E4bp4 mRNA expression by PTH. We found that both 10 and 100 nm PTH resulted in maximum expression of E4bp4 in MOBs. Additionally, forskolin (FSK), an inducer of adenylate cyclase, 8-bromo-cAMP, a cAMP analog, and phorbol myristate acetate, an activator of PKC, increased the levels of E4bp4 mRNA. However, ionomycin, a calcium ionophore, had no effect on E4bp4 expression. Furthermore, pretreatment of cells with H89, a PKA inhibitor, strongly inhibited the induction of E4bp4 expression by PTH and FSK. On the other hand, pretreatment with phorbol myristate acetate to down-regulate PKC signaling did not alter the effects of PTH and FSK. Interestingly, PTH (3-34), which does not activate cAMP signaling, did not increase E4bp4 expression. Prostaglandin E(2), which signals through cAMP, increased E4bp4 mRNA at all doses, while prostaglandin F(2alpha), which primarily activates PKC and calcium signaling, induced E4bp4 only at high doses. Fluprostenol, which only activates PKC and calcium signaling, had no effect on E4bp4 expression. Finally, an intraperitoneal injection of 80 microg/kg PTH (1-34) induced E4bp4 mRNA expression at 1 hour in mice, whereas 80 microg/kg PTH (3-34) had no effect. Based on our findings, we propose that PTH-induced E4bp4 mRNA expression is primarily mediated through cAMP-PKA signaling both in vitro and in vivo. Together with our previous report, we hypothesize that E4bp4 attenuates the transcription of osteoblastic genes that possess E4bp4 promoter binding sites.

title: Managing finances of shipping living donor kidneys for donor exchanges.
text: Kidney donor exchanges allow recipients who have donors that are not immunologically compatible to receive compatible living donor grafts. However, the financial management of these exchanges, especially when an organ needs to be shipped, is complex and could hinder the wider implementation of donor exchange programs. To address this issue, representatives from transplant centers that use the National Kidney Registry database to facilitate donor exchange transplants have developed a financial model that can be applied to paired donor exchanges and donor chain transplants. The first principle of this model is to ensure that the donor does not bear any financial liability. The model also takes into account the costs of donor evaluation, donor nephrectomy hospital expenses, donor nephrectomy physician fees, organ transportation, donor complications, and recipient inpatient services. Instead of using charges, billing between hospitals is based on the costs defined in Medicare cost reports. We believe that this model is in line with current federal regulations and accurately captures the costs of donor and recipient services. It could serve as a financial framework for the United Network for Organ Sharing managed donor exchange program.

title: Human herpesvirus 8 infection and Kaposi's sarcoma among human immunodeficiency virus-infected and -uninfected women.
text:
Limited information is available regarding the prevalence and characteristics of human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) infections in women. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted to investigate HHV-8 infection rates among women who were either infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or at high risk of HIV infection. The study involved 2483 participants from multiple locations, and serological tests were used to detect HHV-8 infection using both latent and lytic antigens.

The results showed that 4.1% of women tested positive for HHV-8 infection using the latent antigen, while 12.0% tested positive using the induced antigen. Interestingly, seven out of eight women who reported having Kaposi's sarcoma also had HHV-8 antibodies. Among HIV-positive women, HHV-8 infection was found to be associated with the use of crack, cocaine, or heroin (76% vs. 65%; P<.001), a history of syphilis (29% vs. 20%; P<.001), having a male sex partner who injects drugs (61% vs. 53%; P=.014), being of black race (P=.010), and the specific enrollment site (P=.015).

Further analysis using multivariate analysis revealed that HHV-8 infection was independently associated with HIV infection, older age, a history of syphilis, being of black race, and the enrollment site. Overall, this study demonstrated that in this particular cohort of North American women, HHV-8 infection was linked to HIV infection, drug use, and engaging in risky sexual behavior.

title: Cloning of three novel neuronal Cdk5 activator binding proteins.
text: The neuronal Cdc2-like kinase (Nclk) plays a role in regulating neuronal differentiation and the dynamics of the neuro-cytoskeleton. It is composed of a catalytic subunit called Cdk5 and a 25 kDa activator protein (p25nck5a) derived from a 35 kDa protein specific to neurons (p35nck5a). In a previous study, we discovered that neurofilament proteins are associated with p35nck5a. In this study, we have identified three other proteins associated with p35nck5a using the yeast two-hybrid screen. These proteins, named C42, C48, and C53, have molecular masses of 66, 24, and 57 kDa, respectively. Northern analysis revealed that these proteins are expressed in various human tissues, including the heart, brain, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, liver, kidney, and pancreas. When expressed as fusion proteins with glutathione S-transferase (GST) in bacteria, these three proteins were able to co-precipitate p35nck5a complexed with Cdk5 from insect cell lysate. Only C48 and C53 were found to be phosphorylated by Nclk, suggesting that they may be substrates of this kinase. Sequence homology searches showed that C48 is somewhat related to restin protein, while the function of the C42 protein's homologues in Caenorhabditis elegans and Arabidopsis thaliana is unknown.

title: The Artemis:DNA-PKcs endonuclease cleaves DNA loops, flaps, and gaps.
text: NHEJ, a major repair pathway for DSBs in eukaryotic cells, involves the collaboration of Artemis and DNA-PKcs, a 469kDa protein kinase. Together, they act as a crucial nuclease in vertebrate organisms. The activation of Artemis' structure-specific endonucleolytic activity is achieved through its binding to and phosphorylation by DNA-PKcs. To gain insight into the recognition of DNA structures by the Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex, we conducted experiments using various DNA structures. Our findings reveal that the complex can cleave all tested substrates containing single-to-double-strand transitions near the transition region. These substrates include heterologous loops, stem-loops, flaps, and gapped substrates. This versatile activity in single-/double-strand transition regions is significant for understanding how reconstituted NHEJ systems lacking DNA polymerases can join incompatible DNA ends while preserving 3' overhangs. Moreover, the flexibility of the Artemis:DNA-PKcs nuclease may play a crucial role in removing secondary structures that impede the processing of DNA ends during NHEJ.

title: A promoter derived from taro bacilliform badnavirus drives strong expression in transgenic banana and tobacco plants
text:
The Taro bacilliform virus (TaBV) is a type of pararetrovirus belonging to the Badnavirus genus. It specifically infects taro, a monocotyledonous plant known as Colocasia esculenta. To study its genetic makeup, a specific region of the TaBV genome was examined. This region, spanning nucleotides 6,281 to 12, includes the 3′ end of open reading frame 3 (ORF 3) and the intergenic region leading to the tRNAmet-binding site. Additionally, four different 5′ deletion fragments (T600, T500, T250, and T100) were also analyzed for their promoter activity.

In transient assays, it was discovered that only the T1200, T600, and T500 fragments exhibited promoter activity in various cells such as taro leaf, banana suspension cells, and tobacco callus. Further experiments were conducted by evaluating these three promoters in stably transformed banana and tobacco plants grown in vitro. The results showed that all three promoters led to near-constant expression of either the green fluorescent protein or the β-glucuronidase (GUS) reporter gene in the stem, leaves, and roots of the transgenic plants. The highest expression was observed in the vascular tissue.

Comparing the promoters, the T600 promoter in transgenic banana leaves demonstrated four times greater GUS activity compared to the T1200, T500, and maize polyubiquitin-1 promoters. In transgenic tobacco leaves, the levels of GUS expression directed by the three promoters were between four and ten times lower than that of the double Cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter.

These findings suggest that the promoters derived from TaBV could be valuable for achieving high-level, constant expression of transgenes in both monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous species.

title: Age of ovary determines remaining life expectancy in old ovariectomized mice.
text:
We conducted a study to examine the potential of young ovaries, transplanted into older ovariectomized CBA mice, to extend the lifespan of the recipients. The donor females were sexually mature 2-month-olds, while the recipients were prepubertally ovariectomized at 3 weeks and received transplants at 5, 8, or 11 months of age. 

Compared to ovariectomized control females, the life expectancy at 11 months was increased by 60% in 11-month recipient females and by 40% compared to intact control females. Only 20% of the 11-month transplant females died within the 300-day period following ovarian transplantation, whereas nearly 65% of the ovariectomized control females died during the same period. 

The 11-month-old recipient females resumed their estrous cycles and continued to cycle for several months beyond the age at which control females typically experience reproductive senescence. The increase in life expectancy observed in the recipient mice was directly proportional to the relative youth of the transplanted ovary across all recipient age groups. 

These findings align with recent discoveries regarding the impact of gonadal function on aging in Caenorhabditis elegans and may provide insights into how the mammalian gonad, including that of humans, could influence the aging process and determine longevity.

title: Use of macrolides in mother and child and risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: nationwide cohort study
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between the use of macrolide antibiotics in mothers and infants, from pregnancy until 120 days after birth, and infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS). The study was conducted as a nationwide register-based cohort study in Denmark from 1996 to 2011. The participants included 999,378 liveborn singletons, and individual-level information was collected on macrolide prescriptions, surgery for IHPS, and potential confounding factors. The main outcome measures were surgery for IHPS in three categories of macrolide use: during pregnancy in mothers, after birth in mothers, and after birth in infants. 

The results showed that 880 infants developed IHPS, with a rate of 0.9 cases per 1000 births. Compared to infants who did not use macrolides, the adjusted rate ratio for IHPS in infants who used macrolides during days 0 to 13 after birth was 29.8 (95% confidence interval 16.4 to 54.1), and during days 14 to 120 was 3.24 (1.20 to 8.74). The corresponding absolute risk differences were 24.4 (95% confidence interval 13.0 to 44.1) and 0.65 (0.06 to 2.21) cases per 1000 infants exposed to macrolides, respectively. The rate ratio for maternal use of macrolides during days 0 to 13 after birth was 3.49 (1.92 to 6.34), and for days 14 to 120 was 0.70 (0.26 to 1.90). The corresponding absolute risk differences were 2.15 (0.82 to 4.64) and -0.11 (-0.26 to 0.31). The rate ratios for maternal use of macrolides during pregnancy were 1.02 (0.65 to 1.59) for weeks 0 to 27 and 1.77 (0.95 to 3.31) for weeks 28 to birth. The corresponding absolute risk differences were 0.01 (-0.31 to 0.50) and 0.67 (-0.06 to 2.02). 

In conclusion, the use of macrolide antibiotics in young infants was strongly associated with IHPS, and therefore, should only be administered if the potential treatment benefits outweigh the risk. Maternal use of macrolides during the first two weeks after birth was also associated with an increased risk of IHPS. There was also a possible association found with use during late pregnancy.

title: The psychiatric manifestations of mitochondrial disorders: a case and review of the literature.
text: The objective of this study is to highlight the underdiagnosis of mitochondrial disorders in psychiatric patients. Mitochondrial disorders are caused by gene mutations in mitochondrial or nuclear DNA and primarily affect energy-dependent organs like the brain. However, there is limited literature on this topic. Therefore, this article presents a case study of a patient with borderline personality disorder and treatment-resistant depression who was eventually diagnosed with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS). Additionally, the authors conducted a literature search for case reports of patients with mitochondrial disorders presenting with psychiatric symptoms. They identified fifty cases and extracted information about the psychiatric presentation. The most common psychiatric manifestations in mitochondrial disorders were mood disorder, cognitive deterioration, psychosis, and anxiety. The most common diagnosis was a MELAS mutation, followed by other genetic mitochondrial diagnoses. The study concludes that psychiatrists should be aware of the clinical features indicative of a mitochondrial disorder, investigate patients with suggestive presentations, and understand the treatment implications of the diagnosis.

title: Polo kinase and Asp are needed to promote the mitotic organizing activity of centrosomes
text: Disrupting the function of polo-like kinases can result in the development of monopolar spindles. These kinases also play a role in regulating the initiation of mitosis, activation of the anaphase-promoting complex, and the necessary conditions for cytokinesis. The similarities observed between the Drosophila mutants asp and polo suggest a shared role in spindle pole function. The asp mutants exhibit abnormal bipolar spindles with disorganized broad poles that display an abnormal distribution of γ-tubulin. Additionally, the interaction between polo1 and aspE3 double mutants suggests a potential involvement of these genes in a common process. Asp, a microtubule-associated protein with a molecular weight of 220,000, is located at the centrosome and interacts with spindle microtubules. In purified centrosomes, Asp works in conjunction with γ-tubulin to organize microtubule asters. Our study reveals that Asp is a substrate of Polo kinase, with a molecular weight of 220,000. Polo kinase phosphorylates Asp in vitro, resulting in the conversion of Asp into an MPM2 epitope. Immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that Polo and Asp proteins interact and form a complex of 25-38S. Extracts from embryos derived from polo mutants are unable to restore the ability of salt-stripped centrosomes to initiate the formation of microtubule asters. However, this defect can be rescued by the addition of phosphorylated Asp or active Polo kinase.

title: How long will long-term potentiation last?
text: The main characteristic of long-term potentiation (LTP) as a memory mechanism is its ability to persist over time. While the basic understanding of LTP persistence was established three decades ago, recent insights have shed light on the extent of this persistence and how it is regulated by activity and experience. It is now clear that LTP in the dentate gyrus can either decrease over time, lasting from hours to weeks, or remain stable for months or even longer. The induction of LTP plays a role in regulating its persistence, but the maintenance of LTP is also influenced by activity patterns after its induction, whether induced experimentally or through experience. These new discoveries make dentate gyrus LTP a valuable model for studying the mechanisms that govern the induction, maintenance, and interference with long-term memory, including memories that last for months or longer. The next challenge is to investigate LTP persistence in other areas of the brain and determine if the properties and regulation of LTP maintenance are related to the properties of the information stored in those regions.

title: An IL-13 inhibitor blocks the development of hepatic fibrosis during a T-helper type 2-dominated inflammatory response.
text: Chronic parasite egg-induced granuloma formation in schistosomiasis can cause tissue destruction and fibrosis, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. In this study, we highlight the importance of IL-13 in the development of schistosomiasis and present the potential therapeutic efficacy of an IL-13 inhibitor, sIL-13Ralpha2-Fc, in controlling hepatic fibrosis. Previous research focused on T-helper type 2 (Th2) cytokines in mice infected with Schistosoma mansoni, but the specific roles of IL-13 and IL-4 in fibrosis development were not explored. Our findings reveal that both cytokines contribute to granuloma formation, explaining why IL-4-deficient mice can still form granulomas around eggs. However, IL-13 emerges as the dominant Th2-type cytokine regulating fibrosis. IL-13 stimulates collagen production in fibroblasts, and the expression of procollagen I and procollagen III mRNA is reduced in mice treated with sIL-13Ralpha2-Fc. Furthermore, the reduction in fibrosis observed in IL-4-deficient mice is less significant compared to sIL-13Ralpha2-Fc-treated animals. Fibrosis is a major pathological feature in various allergic, autoimmune, and infectious diseases. Therefore, our findings suggest that IL-13 inhibitors could have broad therapeutic benefits in preventing tissue fibrosis caused by Th2-dominated inflammatory responses.

title: Validity and reliability of observational methods for studying medication administration errors.
text: A study was conducted to examine the reliability and validity of observational methods in identifying medication administration errors (MAEs). Two pharmacists observed nurses during drug administration rounds on two wards in a U.K. hospital between January and June 1998. They recorded all identified MAEs and intervened in cases of potentially harmful errors. The study analyzed MAE records to determine the percentage of omitted doses with documented reasons during observation and non-observation periods. Error rates for each drug administration round were also analyzed based on the nurse's first, second, third, and subsequent observed rounds. The study calculated error rates before and after the first intervention with nurses who received an intervention. Observer reliability was assessed by comparing the rates of errors identified by the two observers. The study found no difference in the percentage of omitted doses with documented reasons between observation and non-observation periods. Additionally, there was no change in error rates with repeated observations. The study also found no difference in error rates before and after the first intervention for each nurse. Furthermore, there was no difference in error detection between the two observers, and no change in error detection with increasing duration of observation. The study concluded that observing nurses during drug administration and tactful interventions by observers did not significantly affect the MAE rate. Observer reliability was found to be high. Therefore, concerns about the validity and reliability of observational methods for identifying MAEs may be unfounded.

title: Directly reprogrammed fibroblasts show global epigenetic remodeling and widespread tissue contribution.
text: The ectopic expression of four transcription factors, Oct4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, can transform the fibroblast genome into induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, which possess a pluripotent state. However, it is unclear whether this nuclear reprogramming process can reset the epigenetic differences between differentiated and pluripotent cells on a global scale. To investigate this, we used innovative selection methods to generate iPS cells from fibroblasts and examine their epigenetic state. In female iPS cells, we observed the reactivation of a silenced X chromosome and random X inactivation during differentiation. Through a genome-wide analysis of two crucial histone modifications, we found that iPS cells closely resemble embryonic stem (ES) cells. Furthermore, these iPS cells were able to produce viable chimeras with a high degree of contribution to the germline, supporting our observations. These findings demonstrate that reprogramming induced by transcription factors can effectively revert the somatic epigenome to an ES-like state on a global scale. Consequently, our results establish a model for studying the epigenetic modifications associated with nuclear reprogramming and suggest that abnormal epigenetic reprogramming does not hinder the potential therapeutic applications of iPS cells.

title: Exocrine ontogenies: on the development of pancreatic acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells.
text: In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the current knowledge regarding the development of the exocrine pancreas. Specifically, we focus on the formation of acinar, ductal, and centroacinar cells. We delve into the role of transcription factors in driving the differentiation process, starting from multipotent progenitor cells and culminating in fully differentiated acinar and ductal cells. During embryonic pancreas development, multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells undergo a gradual restriction, either to a central "trunk" domain that gives rise to the islet and ductal lineages, or to a peripheral "tip" domain that gives rise to acinar cells. We also explore the influence of soluble morphogens and signaling pathways on these developmental events. Additionally, we investigate the enigmatic nature of centroacinar cells, a pancreatic cell type whose lineage remains uncertain, and whose potential as progenitor cells is still being investigated.

title: The history of SIVS and AIDS: epidemiology, phylogeny and biology of isolates from naturally SIV infected non-human primates (NHP) in Africa.
text:
SIV, or simian immunodeficiency virus, naturally infects non-human primates in Africa. Currently, there have been 40 different SIVs identified in both natural hosts and other species. These viruses are highly diverse and can be categorized into six distinct phylogenetic lineages. Some SIVs are considered recombinant viruses, as they exhibit different clustering patterns in various genomic regions. There are three known types of SIV genomes based on the number of accessory genes they contain: vpr-containing genomes, vpr-vpx containing genomes, and vpr-vpu-containing genomes. The vpx gene is a duplication of the vpr gene that is found in SIVs infecting the Papionini tribe of monkeys and HIV-2 in humans. The vpu gene is characteristic of SIVcpz and HIV-1 and may have originated from a recombination involving SIVs from cercopitecini monkeys.

In most natural hosts, SIV does not cause disease despite high levels of viral replication. This is likely due to virus-host adaptation, where the incubation period of the disease is longer than the lifespan of the African primate host. SIVs also have a high likelihood of being transmitted between different species. The outcome of infection in the new host can range from no apparent symptoms to highly pathogenic, with African monkeys experiencing the former and macaques and humans experiencing the latter. The high diversity of SIVs is a result of a high mutation rate, low fidelity of the reverse-transcriptase enzyme, active viral and host cell turnover, host-dependent evolution, and recombination. While cross-species transmission is not uncommon, most transmissions occur through preferential host switching.

Many SIVs have been found to grow in human cells in vitro, leading to concerns that SIV could infect humans in Central Africa and cause AIDS. However, while it is widely accepted that HIV has a simian origin, there is no evidence to suggest that AIDS is acquired as a zoonosis. SIV may undergo adaptation in a new human host in order to spread within the general population. Studying SIV in its natural hosts is crucial for understanding the potential threat to human populations and the mechanisms behind long-term viral infections without clinical consequences for the host.

title: The association between common physical impairments and dementia in low and middle income countries, and, among people with dementia, their association with cognitive function and disability. A 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based study.
text:
AIM: Our objective was to investigate the prevalence of chronic physical comorbidity in dementia and its impact on cognitive function and disability in low and middle income countries. These countries often have high rates of chronic diseases and untreated impairments, making it crucial to establish good practice guidelines for addressing these issues.

METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey in 11 catchment areas in China, India, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Mexico, and Peru. The study included all residents over the age of 65 (n = 15,022). We assessed the prevalence of pain, incontinence, hearing and visual impairments, mobility impairment, and undernutrition in relation to the presence and severity of dementia. Additionally, we examined the independent contribution of these impairments to cognitive function and disability, while controlling for age, gender, education, and dementia severity.

RESULTS: Incontinence, hearing impairment, mobility impairment, and undernutrition were consistently associated with the presence and severity of dementia across all regions. Among individuals with dementia, incontinence, hearing impairment, and mobility impairment were independently associated with disability in all regions. However, the contributions of pain, visual impairment, and undernutrition varied. Only hearing impairment significantly contributed to cognitive impairment.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the urgent need for clinical trials to assess the feasibility, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of regular physical health checks and interventions for identified pathologies. Given the high prevalence of comorbidity in our population-based studies and the strong evidence of its independent impact on functioning, it is crucial to establish guidelines for addressing these issues effectively.

title: Serum biomarkers as predictors of lung function decline in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
Recent studies have shown that individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) experience low-grade systemic inflammation, and that higher levels of plasma fibrinogen and neutrophil counts are associated with faster declines in lung function. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between serum biomarkers and the decline of lung function in COPD patients. 

We measured the baseline levels of nine serum biomarkers (TIMP-1, alpha1-antitrypsin, MMP-9, TNF-alpha, TGF-beta, IL-6, IL-8, neutrophil elastase, and CRP), as well as fibrinogen and white blood cell counts, in 96 COPD patients. Lung function was assessed at the time of blood sampling and every 3-6 months over a median observation period of 25.0 months. 

Our results showed that 20 patients experienced rapid declines in lung function, while 53 patients did not show any decline. Neutrophil counts, serum CRP, and MMP-9 were significantly higher in the rapid decliners. Furthermore, the annual change in % predicted FEV(1) (forced expiratory volume in one second) was inversely correlated with MMP-9 and CRP levels. These correlations remained significant even after adjusting for factors such as age, sex, cardiovascular disease, smoking history, and baseline % predicted FEV(1). 

However, we did not find any significant correlations between the remaining biomarkers and the annual change in % predicted FEV(1). 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that serum CRP and MMP-9 levels are associated with the decline in FEV(1) in COPD patients. These biomarkers may serve as potential predictors for rapid declines in lung function. Further studies with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are needed to fully understand the roles of these biomarkers in COPD.

title: Phosphorylation of ATM by Cdk5 mediates DNA damage signaling and regulates neuronal death
text: The enzyme ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated), which is similar to phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase, plays a crucial role in coordinating various responses to DNA damage, such as controlling cell-cycle checkpoints, repairing DNA, and inducing apoptosis. Mutations in ATM can lead to a range of defects, from neurodegeneration to an increased risk of cancer. However, the exact mechanism by which DNA damage activates ATM is not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that DNA damage activates the enzyme Cdk5 (cyclin-dependent kinase 5), which directly phosphorylates ATM at a specific site called Ser 794 in neurons that have stopped dividing. This phosphorylation event occurs before and is necessary for ATM to autophosphorylate at another site called Ser 1981, which then activates ATM's kinase activity. The Cdk5-ATM signal also controls the phosphorylation and function of two proteins, p53 and H2AX, which are targets of ATM. Disrupting the Cdk5-ATM pathway prevents DNA-damage-induced re-entry of neurons into the cell cycle and the expression of two proteins, PUMA and Bax, which are regulated by p53. This interruption ultimately protects neurons from death. Therefore, the activation of Cdk5 by DNA damage acts as a crucial signal to initiate the ATM response and regulate various cellular processes that depend on ATM.

title: Nerve-induced release of nitric oxide in the rabbit gastrointestinal tract as measured by in vivo microdialysis.
text:
The aim of this study was to measure the formation of nitric oxide (NO) in the gastrointestinal tract, as it has been suggested to act as a neurotransmitter in the gut. In order to do this, the researchers measured the production of nitrite and nitrate, which are oxidation products of nitric oxide, during stimulation of the vagal nerve in rabbits under anesthesia. Microdialysis probes were inserted into the stomach and colon walls, and the levels of nitrite and nitrate in the dialysate were measured using capillary electrophoresis. 

The results showed that during stimulation of both vagal nerves, there was an increase in the formation of nitrite and nitrate in the stomach, and nitrite in the colon. This increase was inhibited when the rabbits were given an intravenous dose of the NO synthase inhibitor N omega-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME 30 mg kg-1). Additionally, L-NAME significantly increased the contractions of the stomach and colon induced by nerve stimulation, as well as spontaneous contractions in the colon. 

In conclusion, this study presents a new method for quantifying small changes in nitric oxide formation in the gastrointestinal tract in vivo. The findings provide evidence that nitric oxide is released in the walls of the stomach and colon during vagal nerve activity, and at concentrations that are capable of inhibiting smooth muscle contractions in vivo.

title: Screening for concomitant diseases in peripheral vascular patients. Results of a systematic approach.
text:
BACKGROUND
Patients undergoing arterial surgery often have multiple coexisting diseases, including cardiac, vascular, and other conditions, which can impact their surgical risk and survival. To address this, we developed a systematic approach to identify these coexisting diseases in our vascular surgical patients, primarily using non-invasive diagnostic techniques.

METHODS
We conducted a study involving 200 consecutive patients admitted to the vascular surgery department of an academic teaching hospital. Our goal was to determine the overall incidence of relevant coexisting disorders, assess the extent to which our screening process revealed previously unknown diagnostic information, and evaluate the impact on short-term (one-year) survival.

RESULTS
We found that 46% of the patients had coronary artery disease, with 22% experiencing active ischemia, which was newly diagnosed in 5.5% of cases. Impaired cardiac function was present in 37% of patients, with severe impairment newly diagnosed in 27% of cases. Carotid artery disease was found in 32% of patients, with critical stenoses identified in 9% and new diagnoses made in 29.9% of cases. Aortic aneurysms were present in 7% of patients, with 5% being newly diagnosed. Severe renal artery stenosis was found in 5% of patients, with 3.5% being newly diagnosed. Additionally, 16% of patients had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, with 3.5% being newly diagnosed. Unexpected disorders were discovered in 4.5% of patients, all of which were new diagnoses. Overall, new diagnoses were made in 64.5% of the population, leading to immediate changes in therapeutic strategy for 21% of patients. The presence of coronary artery disease and cardiac failure were strongly associated with one-year survival.

CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, our systematic screening strategy, primarily utilizing non-invasive techniques, effectively detects the presence of coexisting diseases in vascular surgical patients. The identification of newly diagnosed diseases is particularly important, as it alters surgical management in one out of every five patients and has significant implications for patient prognosis.

title: Archetypal trajectories of social, psychological, and spiritual wellbeing and distress in family care givers of patients with lung cancer: secondary analysis of serial qualitative interviews
text:
The aim of this study was to examine whether family caregivers of lung cancer patients experience similar patterns of social, psychological, and spiritual well-being and distress as the patients themselves, from the time of diagnosis until death. The research involved analyzing qualitative interviews conducted every three months for up to a year or until the caregiver experienced bereavement. The study took place in South East Scotland and included 19 lung cancer patients and their respective caregivers, resulting in a total of 88 interviews (42 with patients and 46 with caregivers).

The findings revealed that caregivers followed distinct patterns of social, psychological, and spiritual well-being and distress that mirrored the experiences of the patients they were caring for. Some caregivers also experienced a decline in physical health, which affected their ability to provide care. Psychological and spiritual distress were particularly dynamic and commonly experienced by caregivers. Witnessing the suffering of the patient triggered personal reflections on the meaning and purpose of life, in addition to the common response of "Why us?". Certain stages of the illness, such as diagnosis, initial treatment at home, recurrence, and the terminal stage, were particularly challenging for both caregivers and patients.

In conclusion, family caregivers witness and share much of the illness experience of the dying patient. The multidimensional distress experienced by lung cancer patients was reflected in the suffering of their caregivers in the social, psychological, and spiritual aspects, with psychological and spiritual distress being the most prominent. Caregivers may require support throughout the entire duration of the illness, rather than just during the terminal phase and bereavement, as is currently the norm.

title: HER-2/neu induces p53 ubiquitination via Akt-mediated MDM2 phosphorylation
text: Amplification or overexpression of HER-2/neu can cause cancer cells to become resistant to apoptosis and promote their growth. The p53 gene plays a crucial role in regulating cell growth and apoptosis, but it is often mutated or deleted in various types of tumors. Interestingly, even in tumors with a normal p53 gene, its function is often suppressed by certain oncogenic signals. In this study, we demonstrate that HER-2/neu-mediated resistance to DNA-damaging drugs relies on the activation of Akt, which enhances the degradation of p53 through MDM2-mediated ubiquitination. Akt physically interacts with MDM2 and phosphorylates it at Ser166 and Ser186. This phosphorylation leads to increased nuclear localization of MDM2 and its interaction with p300, while inhibiting its interaction with p19ARF. Consequently, p53 degradation is increased. Our findings suggest that inhibiting the Akt pathway activated by HER-2/neu could enhance the effectiveness of DNA-damaging drugs in tumor cells with a normal p53 gene.

title: T cell memory.
