text: Recent advancements in technology have improved our understanding of the processes involved in generating and maintaining T cell memory. T cell memory, whether induced by prior infection or vaccination, offers enhanced protection against subsequent microbial infections. The development of memory T cells is initiated by signals from antigen-loaded, activated antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and inflammatory mediators produced by the innate immune response. As the immune response subsides and returns to homeostasis, additional signals are triggered, although their exact nature remains unclear. Cytokines play a crucial role in regulating the persistence of resting memory T cells. This chapter explores recent discoveries regarding the development of memory T cells and their ability to provide long-term protective immunity.

title: The impact of organisational change on outcome in an intensive care unit in the United Kingdom
text:
Aim: To examine the impact of implementing a team of resident medical staff and transitioning from an "open" to a "closed" organizational structure on patient outcomes in an intensive care unit.

Method: This study involved reviewing a database of prospectively collected data. The research was conducted in the intensive care unit of a postgraduate teaching hospital. The study included 1134 admissions to the intensive care unit over a period of three years, with 476 (42%) of these admissions following elective surgery.

Primary Outcome Measure: The main outcome measure was hospital mortality, adjusted for illness severity using the APACHE II scoring system.

Results: The crude hospital mortality rate decreased from 28% prior to the changes to 20% afterwards (P=0.01). After accounting for case-mix factors, the likelihood of death following the changes was reduced by nearly half (OR 0.51; CI 0.32, 0.82, P=0.005).

Conclusion: Implementing a "closed" organizational format for delivering care in intensive care units may lead to improved outcomes for patients.

title: Monitoring effectiveness and safety of Tafamidis in transthyretin amyloidosis in Italy: a longitudinal multicenter study in a non-endemic area
text: Tafamidis is a medication that helps stabilize transthyretin (TTR) and prevent the dissociation of TTR tetramers. Previous studies have shown promising results for Tafamidis in treating early-onset inherited transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) caused by the Val30Met mutation. However, there is limited information on its effectiveness in later stages of the disease and in patients with non-Val30Met mutations. To address this, we conducted a multi-center observational study on symptomatic ATTR patients who were prescribed Tafamidis. These patients were followed up according to a standardized protocol, which included medical, cardiological, and neurological assessments at the beginning of the study and every 6 months for up to 3 years. A total of 61 patients (42 males) were enrolled in the study. Only 28% of the participants had the Val30Met mutation, and the average age of onset was relatively late at 59 years. Additionally, 18% of the patients were in an advanced stage of the disease at the start of the study. Tafamidis was found to be safe and well-tolerated by the patients. Over the course of 36 months, one-third of the patients did not experience significant disease progression, regardless of their mutation type or disease stage. Neurological function worsened, particularly in the first 6 months, but the rate of progression slowed significantly thereafter. Autonomic function remained stable in 33% of the patients, worsened in 56%, and improved in 10%. Fifteen percent of the patients showed progression of cardiac disease, and 30% developed new-onset cardiomyopathy. Overall, Tafamidis was not able to prevent functional progression of the disease in 23 (43%) of the subjects, including 16 patients who experienced a decline in their walking ability and 12 patients who had a higher NYHA score during the follow-up period. However, patients with a higher baseline body mass index (BMI) had better preservation of neurological function. In conclusion, neuropathy and cardiomyopathy continued to progress in a significant proportion of patients despite treatment with Tafamidis. However, the rate of neurological function decline slowed after the first 6 months, and patients with more advanced neuropathy and those with non-Val30Met mutations still benefited from the treatment. Preserving body weight is an important factor for a favorable prognosis.

title: The Spliceosome: Design Principles of a Dynamic RNP Machine
text: Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) play a crucial role in various cellular functions, including gene expression and its regulation. While most RNP enzymes remain stable in their composition and contain preformed active sites, the spliceosome operates differently. The spliceosome is responsible for removing noncoding introns from precursor messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) and employs distinct strategies. It combines accuracy in recognizing reactive splice sites in the pre-mRNA with flexibility in choosing splice sites during alternative splicing. This is achieved through exceptional compositional and structural dynamics, which are utilized during substrate-dependent complex assembly, catalytic activation, and active site remodeling.

title: Blimp-1 attenuates Th1 differentiation by repression of ifng, tbx21, and bcl6 gene expression.
text: The deletion of Blimp-1 specifically in T cells leads to abnormal T cell balance and function, resulting in spontaneous and fatal colitis in mice. In this study, we investigate the role of Blimp-1 in the differentiation of Th1 and Th2 cells. We find that both the mRNA and protein levels of Blimp-1 are higher in Th2 cells compared to Th1 cells. Additionally, Blimp-1 suppresses the production of IFN-gamma in CD4 cells activated under nonpolarizing conditions. While Blimp-1-deficient T cells can still differentiate into Th2 cytokines in vitro, Blimp-1 is necessary in vivo for normal Th2 immune responses to NP-KLH immunization. The absence of Blimp-1 in CD4 T cells leads to increased levels of IFN-gamma, T-bet, and Bcl-6 mRNA. Through chromatin immunoprecipitation, we demonstrate that Blimp-1 directly binds to a distal regulatory region in the ifng gene, as well as multiple sites in the tbx21 and bcl6 genes. Our findings provide evidence that Blimp-1 plays a role in reinforcing Th2 differentiation by repressing critical Th1 genes in Th2 cells.

title: CX3CR1 is required for airway inflammation by promoting T helper cell survival and maintenance in inflamed lung
text: Allergic asthma is a lung disease that is primarily influenced by T helper type 2 (T(H)2) cells. In individuals with asthma, a portion of CD4(+) T cells express the CX3CL1 receptor, known as CX3CR1. When exposed to allergens, the expression of CX3CL1 is increased in the airway smooth muscle, lung endothelium, and epithelium. Our research has shown that mice lacking CX3CR1 or mice treated with CX3CR1-blocking substances experience reduced lung disease after being sensitized and challenged with allergens. Additionally, when we transferred CD4(+) T cells from normal mice into CX3CR1-deficient mice, the characteristic symptoms of asthma returned. However, when CX3CR1-deficient recipients were injected with T(H)2 cells from normal mice and treated with CX3CR1-blocking substances, airway inflammation was prevented. We also discovered that CX3CR1 signaling promotes the survival of T(H)2 cells in inflamed lungs, and when we injected CX3CR1-deficient T(H)2 cells that were transduced with B cell leukemia/lymphoma-2 protein (BCl-2) into CX3CR1-deficient mice, asthma was restored. This survival effect was also observed in T(H)1 cells during airway inflammation, but not in normal conditions or during peripheral inflammation. Therefore, targeting CX3CR1 and CX3CL1 could be promising therapeutic strategies for asthma.

title: TRPC6 is a glomerular slit diaphragm-associated channel required for normal renal function
text: Progressive kidney failure encompasses a diverse range of disorders that are both genetically and clinically heterogeneous. The podocyte foot processes and the glomerular slit diaphragm, which are crucial components of the kidney's permeability barrier, play a vital role in this condition. When genes responsible for the structural proteins of the podocyte undergo mutations, it leads to the development of proteinuria, ultimately resulting in progressive kidney failure and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Our study reveals that the canonical transient receptor potential 6 (TRPC6) ion channel is expressed in podocytes and forms part of the glomerular slit diaphragm. Through our investigation, we have identified five families with autosomal dominant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, where the disease is linked to mutations in the TRPC6 gene located on chromosome 11q. Notably, two of the TRPC6 mutants exhibited increased current amplitudes. These findings highlight the crucial role of TRPC6 channel activity at the slit diaphragm in maintaining the proper regulation of podocyte structure and function.

title: Usefulness of high mobility group box 1 protein as a plasma biomarker in patient with peripheral artery disease.
text: Chronic vascular inflammation is often linked to the development of atherosclerosis. The protein known as high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) has multiple functions, acting not only as a regulator of gene expression in the nucleus but also as a mediator of inflammation. Previous research has suggested that fibrinogen, a protein involved in blood clotting, is an important factor in the progression of atherosclerosis. In this study, we aimed to investigate the levels of HMGB1 protein in the plasma of patients with atherosclerosis. We examined 24 patients with atherosclerosis and peripheral artery disease (PAD), as well as 10 healthy individuals as controls. Our findings revealed that the concentrations of HMGB1 were elevated in the plasma of patients with atherosclerosis, and there were significant associations between plasma HMGB1 levels and fibrinogen levels. These results suggest that plasma HMGB1 may play a crucial role in the development of both clinical and experimental atherosclerosis.

title: Functional specialization of Piwi proteins in Paramecium tetraurelia from post-transcriptional gene silencing to genome remodelling
text: The Argonaute family consists of proteins that carry small RNA molecules and guide regulatory complexes to their targets. This family is divided into two main subgroups. The Ago subclade, found in most eukaryotic phyla, binds various types of small RNAs and regulates gene expression at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. The Piwi subclade, on the other hand, seems to have been lost in plants and fungi and has mainly been studied in metazoa. In metazoa, Piwi proteins bind piRNAs and play crucial roles in sexual reproduction. The presence of Piwi proteins in ciliates, which are single-celled organisms that have both germline micronuclei and somatic macronuclei, provides an interesting perspective on the evolution of their functions. In this study, we conducted phylogenetic and functional analyses of the 15 Piwi genes from Paramecium tetraurelia. Our findings reveal that four proteins are consistently expressed and are involved in siRNA pathways that regulate gene silencing throughout the organism's life cycle. Two other proteins, which are specifically expressed during meiosis, are necessary for the accumulation of scnRNAs during sexual reproduction and for programmed genome rearrangements during the development of the somatic macronucleus. Our results demonstrate that Paramecium Piwi proteins have evolved to perform both vegetative and sexual functions, employing mechanisms that range from cleaving mRNA molecules to epigenetically regulating genome rearrangements.

title: A parasomnia overlap disorder involving sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and REM sleep behavior disorder in 33 polysomnographically confirmed cases.
text:
Over an 8-year period, a group of 33 patients with a combination of sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, known as "parasomnia overlap disorder," were studied. The patients underwent clinical and polysomnographic evaluations. The average age of the patients was 34 years, with a standard deviation of 14 years. The average age of onset for the parasomnia was 15 years, ranging from 1 to 66 years. Of the patients, 70% (n = 23) were male. 

Within the group, there were two subgroups. The first subgroup, consisting of 22 patients, had an idiopathic form of the disorder, with an earlier average age of onset at 9 years. The second subgroup, consisting of 11 patients, had a symptomatic form of the disorder, with an average age of onset at 27 years. The symptomatic subgroup had various underlying causes for their parasomnia, including neurologic disorders, nocturnal paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, posttraumatic stress disorder/major depression, chronic ethanol/amphetamine abuse and withdrawal, and mixed disorders. 

The rate of psychiatric disorders according to the DSM-III-R was not higher than expected in the group, and the group's scores on psychometric tests were also not elevated. Forty-five percent of the patients had previously received psychological or psychiatric therapy for their parasomnia, but without success. 

Treatment outcomes were available for 20 patients, and 90% of them achieved significant control over their parasomnia with bedtime clonazepam, alprazolam and/or carbamazepine, or self-hypnosis. This suggests that "parasomnia overlap disorder" is a treatable condition that can occur in different clinical settings and can be understood within the current knowledge on parasomnias and motor control during sleep.

title: How can health care organizations be reliably compared?: Lessons from a national survey of patient experience.
text:
The use of patient experience to evaluate organizational performance is becoming more common, particularly in public reporting and pay-for-performance programs. However, the conventional methods of using 95% confidence intervals to determine survey sample sizes or report performance may not provide reliable comparisons between organizations. 

To address this issue, we analyzed data from 2.2 million patients who participated in the 2009 General Practice Patient Survey in England. The survey included 45 questions about patient experience across six different care domains. We calculated organization-level reliability and intraclass correlation coefficients for each question, both unadjusted and adjusted for age, sex, and ethnicity.

The mean number of responses per organization varied greatly, ranging from 23 to 256 for primary care practices and from 1454 to 2758 for out-of-hours care organizations. Adjusted and unadjusted reliability values were similar. We found that 26 questions had excellent reliability, while seven nurse communication questions had very good reliability. However, three anticipatory care planning questions had lower reliability.

Questions with fewer than 100 mean responses per practice typically had reliability below 0.70, indicating that only a subset of patients were eligible to answer them. Nine questions had both excellent reliability and high intraclass correlation coefficients, suggesting both reliable measurement and significant performance variability.

In conclusion, high reliability is crucial for comparing healthcare organizations. Using the General Practice Patient Survey as an example, we demonstrate how reliability and intraclass correlation coefficients can be used to select measures that support robust organizational comparisons and design surveys that provide high-quality measurement while optimizing costs.

title: Conservation of methylation reprogramming in mammalian development: aberrant reprogramming in cloned embryos.
text: During early preimplantation development, mouse embryos experience genome-wide methylation reprogramming through demethylation, followed by remethylation. This phenomenon is observed in various mammalian species, but its occurrence in embryos cloned using highly methylated somatic donor nuclei remains uncertain. Our investigation focused on bovine, rat, and pig zygotes, which displayed demethylated paternal genomes, indicating active demethylation. In bovine embryos, methylation levels decreased further during cleavage until the eight-cell stage, followed by de novo methylation by the 16-cell stage. Cloned one-cell embryos exhibited a reduction in methylation, suggesting active demethylation, but no additional demethylation occurred subsequently. Instead, many cloned embryos underwent premature de novo methylation and nuclear reorganization of methylation patterns resembling those found in differentiated cells. Notably, only cloned morulae displayed highly methylated nuclei in all blastomeres, resembling the fibroblast donor cells. Our study highlights the aberrant epigenetic reprogramming in most cloned embryos, suggesting that incomplete reprogramming may contribute to the low efficiency of cloning.

title: Intracellular transport of fat-soluble vitamins A and E.
text: Vitamins play a crucial role in the normal growth, reproduction, and functioning of the human body. Out of the 13 known vitamins, vitamins A, D, E, and K are considered fat-soluble because they dissolve in fat. Due to their fat-solubility, these vitamins rely on carrier proteins within cells to be transported and exert their effects. Vitamin A and its derivatives, known as retinoids, are transported by proteins such as cellular retinol-binding protein (CRBP), cellular retinoic acid-binding protein (CRABP), and cellular retinal-binding protein (CRALBP). These proteins act as chaperones, regulating the metabolism, signaling, and transport of retinoids. The intracellular transport of retinoids mediated by CRALBP is crucial for human vision. α-Tocopherol, the primary form of vitamin E in the body, is transported by α-tocopherol transfer protein (α-TTP) in liver cells. Defects in α-TTP can lead to vitamin E deficiency and neurological disorders in humans. Recent research has shown that the interaction between α-TTP and phosphoinositides plays a vital role in the intracellular transport of α-tocopherol and is associated with familial vitamin E deficiency. This review provides an overview of the mechanisms and biological importance of the intracellular transport of vitamins A and E.

title: Reduced Cytokine Release in Ex Vivo Response to Cilengitide and Cetuximab Is a Marker for Improved Survival of Head and Neck Cancer Patients
text: Cilengitide, a drug that targets αVβ3 and αVβ5 integrins, has shown potential in reducing the growth of solid tumors, including head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Preclinical studies have indicated that cilengitide may have increased effectiveness when used in combination with other treatment methods. The only published trial in HNSCC, known as ADVANTAGE, examined the use of cisplatin, 5-fluorouracil, and cetuximab (PFE) alone or in combination with once (PFE+CIL1W) or twice weekly cilengitide (PFE+CIL2W) for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC. The ADVANTAGE trial demonstrated that the cilengitide arms were well-tolerated and had fewer adverse events compared to PFE. However, the overall survival benefit expected based on preclinical data was not observed. Our findings from the FLAVINO assay, a short-term ex vivo test for predicting chemosensitivity, revealed that only a specific subgroup of HNSCC patients exhibited an enhanced suppressive effect of cilengitide-containing combination therapies on the formation of epithelial cell colonies (CFec) and the release of pro-angiogenic and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Other HNSCC patients did not respond to this treatment. The response to cilengitide's targeting of αVβ3 and αVβ5 integrins can help classify HNSCC patients based on their expected outcomes. Based on our FLAVINO data, we propose further development of cilengitide in combination with cetuximab for the treatment of a specific subgroup of HNSCC patients who can potentially be identified using the FLAVINO assay and a set of biomarkers for response evaluation.

title: Genes required for mycobacterial growth defined by high density mutagenesis.
text: Despite more than a century of research, tuberculosis continues to be a major cause of infectious deaths worldwide. With the emergence of drug-resistant strains, it is crucial to identify the genes necessary for the growth of this organism in order to develop new antimycobacterial agents. In this study, we utilized transposon site hybridization (TraSH) to comprehensively identify the genes essential for optimal growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis. These genes include both those involved in essential pathways and those with unknown functions. Interestingly, the genes crucial for M. tuberculosis growth are mostly conserved in the degenerate genome of Mycobacterium leprae, the bacterium responsible for leprosy. This suggests that non-essential functions have been lost in M. leprae since its divergence from other mycobacteria. On the other hand, a significant proportion of these genes do not have identifiable counterparts in other bacteria, indicating that the minimal gene set required for survival varies greatly among organisms with different evolutionary histories.

title: Production of de novo cardiomyocytes: human pluripotent stem cell differentiation and direct reprogramming.
text: Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death globally. Due to the limited ability of heart tissue to regenerate, there have been advancements in methods for creating new cardiomyocytes, both in laboratory settings and within the body. In addition to their use in cell replacement therapy, patient-specific cardiomyocytes could have various applications in drug testing, drug discovery, and disease modeling. Recently, there have been developments in generating cardiomyocytes from three main sources: human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) derived from adult hearts, and reprogrammed fibroblasts. In this discussion, we will explore the latest techniques for generating new cardiomyocytes from hPSCs and reprogrammed fibroblasts, while also highlighting potential uses and future challenges.

title: Within the hemopoietic system, LAR phosphatase is a T cell lineage-specific adhesion receptor-like protein whose phosphatase activity appears dispensable for T cell development, repertoire selection and function.
text: The expression of the receptor-type tyrosine phosphatase LAR was examined in cells of the murine hemopoietic system. The gene is active in all cells of the T cell lineage, but not in cells of any other hemopoietic lineage. The level of LAR expression in T cells is regulated during development. Early thymic immigrants (CD4(-)8(-)44(+)) and mature thymocytes and T cells (CD4(+)8(-)/CD4(-)8(+)) have low levels of LAR expression, while immature thymocytes (CD4(-)8(-)44(-) and CD4(+)8(+)) have high levels. Among bone marrow cells, only uncommitted c-kit(+)B220(+)CD19(-) precursors express low levels of LAR, while B cell lineage committed c-kit(+)B220(+)CD19(+) precursors do not. Interestingly, pre-BI cells from PAX-5-deficient mice express LAR, suggesting that PAX-5-mediated commitment to the B cell lineage suppresses LAR expression. During differentiation of PAX-5-deficient pre-BI cells into non-T cell lineages, LAR expression is turned off, but it is up-regulated during differentiation into thymocytes. Therefore, LAR appears to be a receptor-type phosphatase specific to the T cell lineage within the hemopoietic system. Surprisingly, truncation of its phosphatase domains does not have an obvious effect on T cell development, repertoire selection, or function.

title: Competition and the evolution of reproductive restraint in malaria parasites.
text: All living organisms must make choices about how to allocate their resources in order to survive and reproduce. Malaria parasites, for example, reproduce asexually within their host but need to produce sexual stages in order to spread to new hosts. This means that they have to divide their resources between these different life processes, which is a challenge for natural selection to solve. Despite the importance of understanding their reproductive strategies for medical and economic reasons, we still have limited knowledge and their strategies often seem counterintuitive. In this study, we tested a recent theory that suggests competition within the host influences how parasites allocate their resources between replication within the host and transmission to new hosts. We found that Plasmodium chabaudi parasites, across different genotypes, are able to detect the presence of competing genotypes and adjust their investment in sexual stages accordingly, in order to maximize their competitive ability. Additionally, we observed that the parasites adjust their allocation to sexual stages based on the availability of red blood cell resources that can be exploited. These findings align with evolutionary theory that explains trade-offs in resource allocation in other multicellular organisms and suggest that the reason why only a few transmission stages are produced in most natural infections is because heavy investment in reproduction may compromise the parasite's survival within the host.

title: [Neutrophils and macrophages related to the pathogenesis and disease development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease by the inflammatory reaction].
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term respiratory disorder characterized by a persistent limitation of airflow that cannot be fully reversed with treatment. Inflammatory changes in the smaller airways, specifically those with a diameter less than 2mm (known as small airway disease), are believed to be the initial stages of COPD. It is important to note that neutrophils and macrophages play a crucial role in the development of these lesions. Research using bronchoalveolar lavage has shown an increase in the number of neutrophils and the presence of the neutrophil chemoattractant interleukin-8. Recent studies have also revealed that neutrophils and macrophages are elevated and contain various proteases, which contribute to cell infiltration and activation. Further investigations using genetically modified animals and anti-cytokine treatments will aid in gaining a better understanding of the role of neutrophils and macrophages, leading to potential new therapies.

title: Piezo1 Is as a Novel Trefoil Factor Family 1 Binding Protein that Promotes Gastric Cancer Cell Mobility In Vitro
text: The TFF1 protein, a member of the TFF-domain peptide family, plays a role in the healing of epithelial tissue and cell movement. In our study, we investigated the possibility of Piezo1 protein binding to TFF1. Our goal was to confirm this interaction and understand its impact on the mobility of gastric cancer cells. Through co-immunoprecipitation and co-localization experiments in GES-1 cells, we confirmed the interaction between TFF1 and Piezo1. To further explore this interaction, we used stable RNA interference to reduce Piezo1 protein levels and then reintroduced TFF1 in gastric cancer cell lines SGC-7901 and BGC-823. We evaluated cell mobility using invasion and migration assays in vitro. Additionally, we examined the expression levels of integrin subunits β1, β5, α1, as well as β-catenin and E-cadherin using Western blot analysis. Our findings showed that TFF1 specifically binds to and co-localizes with Piezo1 in the cytoplasm, but not with TFF2 or TFF3. The interaction occurs with the C-terminal portion of the Piezo1 protein. Wound healing and trans-well assays revealed that the reintroduction of TFF1 enhanced cell mobility in gastric cancer cells, and this effect was diminished when Piezo1 was knocked down. Western blot analysis also demonstrated reduced expression of integrin β1 in Piezo1-knockdown cells. Our data suggest that Piezo1 is a new binding partner for TFF1 and plays a crucial role in TFF1-mediated cell migration. This interaction may serve as a potential therapeutic target for inhibiting invasion and metastasis in gastric cancer.

title: A conditionally lethal yeast mutant blocked at the first step in glycosyl phosphatidylinositol anchor synthesis.
text: Glycosyl phosphatidylinositols (GPIs) play a crucial role in anchoring numerous proteins to the surface of eukaryotic cells. Additionally, they can act as sorting signals on proteins and participate in signal transduction. Through a colony screen aimed at identifying cells with impaired [3H]inositol incorporation into protein, we successfully identified a Saccharomyces cerevisiae mutant known as gpi1. This mutant exhibits a deficiency in vitro in the production of N-acetylglucosaminyl phosphatidylinositol, which is the initial intermediate in GPI synthesis. Furthermore, the gpi1 mutant displays temperature sensitivity in terms of growth. Consequently, the completion of the first step in GPI assembly is essential for the growth of the unicellular eukaryote S. cerevisiae. Exploiting GPI synthesis as a target for antifungal or antiparasitic agents could therefore be a viable approach.

title: Beyond pattern recognition: five immune checkpoints for scaling the microbial threat
text: The innate immune system has the ability to recognize patterns and detect microorganisms. However, the process of evaluating the level of microbial threat, which is important for triggering appropriate antimicrobial responses without causing excessive tissue inflammation, is not well understood. Recent evidence suggests that the immune system can detect certain characteristics of microbial viability, leading to strong responses that are not necessary for dead microorganisms. In this proposal, we introduce five immune checkpoints that collectively determine the severity of microbial encounters.

title: Macrophages induce COX-2 expression in breast cancer cells: role of IL-1β autoamplification.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between tumor-associated macrophages, cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) levels, and prognosis in breast cancer patients. We wanted to determine if macrophages have an impact on COX-2 expression in breast cancer cells. To do this, we conducted experiments using THP-1 cells and HCC1954 breast cancer cells. The results showed that coculturing these cells led to an increase in COX-2 expression in the HCC1954 cells and higher levels of prostaglandin E(2) in the conditioned media. Similar findings were observed when THP-1 cells were incubated with HCC1937 breast cancer cells or when human monocyte-derived macrophages were cocultured with HCC1954 cells. The coculture also triggered the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the HCC1954 cells. We found that COX-2 induction was blocked when cells were preincubated with a reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase inhibitor or when p67PHOX, a subunit of NADPH oxidase, was silenced. The production of ROS activated Src and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs). Blocking Src or MAPK activities, or antagonizing the activator protein-1 (AP-1) transcription factor, reduced COX-2 induction in HCC1954 cells. The coculture also resulted in the rapid induction of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) in both breast cancer cells and macrophages. Increased IL-1β expression was inhibited by an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), indicating autocrine and paracrine effects. Importantly, blocking IL-1β using IL-1Ra or anti-IL-1β IgG prevented macrophage-induced COX-2 expression in HCC1954 cells. These findings suggest that macrophage-mediated induction of COX-2 in breast cancer cells is a result of IL-1β-mediated stimulation of ROS→Src→MAPK→AP-1 signaling. The IL-1β-dependent induction of COX-2 in breast cancer cells provides insight into how macrophages contribute to tumor progression and identifies potential therapeutic targets in breast cancer.

title: A graphene-based platform for induced pluripotent stem cells culture and differentiation.
text: The culture, maintenance of pluripotency, and induction of differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) pose challenges in the field of regenerative medicine. On the other hand, graphene (G) and graphene oxide (GO) have gained significant attention in materials science, physics, chemistry, and nanotechnology. In this study, we present findings that demonstrate the ability of G and GO to support the culture of mouse iPSCs and facilitate spontaneous differentiation. Interestingly, the surfaces of G and GO exhibited distinct effects on cell proliferation and differentiation. When compared to a glass surface, iPSCs cultured on G showed similar levels of cell adhesion and proliferation, while iPSCs on GO adhered and proliferated at a faster rate. Additionally, G effectively maintained iPSCs in an undifferentiated state, while GO expedited their differentiation. Both G and GO surfaces allowed iPSCs to spontaneously differentiate into ectodermal and mesodermal lineages without significant differences. However, G suppressed the differentiation of iPSCs towards the endodermal lineage, while GO enhanced endodermal differentiation. These findings collectively demonstrate that the unique surface properties of G and GO influence the behavior of iPSCs, suggesting the potential of graphene-based materials as a platform for iPSCs culture and various applications.

title: Aerobic capacity in black adolescent girls.
text: The aim of our study was to determine the aerobic capacities (VO2max) of a group of black female adolescents aged between 11.4 and 15.8 years. We randomly selected 91 girls from a single urban school. Out of these, 64 girls participated in an incremental treadmill running test until they reached exhaustion, and their VO2max was measured using expired gas measures. We also collected data on their height (in meters), weight (in kilograms), and calf and triceps skinfolds (to estimate body fat percentage). Additionally, we asked the girls whether they had experienced menarche. On average, the girls' VO2max was 37.3 +/- 6.2 ml.kg-1 x min-1. We found significant correlations between VO2max and height (-.32, p < .01), body mass index (-.63, p < .001), and body fat percentage (-.65, p < .001), but not with age (-.16, p > .10). Postmenarchal girls were significantly taller and older than premenarchal girls. Surprisingly, contrary to previous studies, we did not find a relationship between the girls' VO2max values and their biological age. Our subjects' aerobic capacity values were, on average, 14% lower than those reported in the literature for nonblack U.S. female adolescents. This difference in VO2max was primarily due to differences in body weight. These findings suggest that overweight in adult black women may have its origins in early adolescence or even earlier. Future longitudinal studies should be conducted to investigate the impact of aerobic fitness on reducing cardiovascular risk factors in black adolescent girls.

title: Acetylation controls Notch3 stability and function in T-cell leukemia
text: The functional role of post-translational modifications of Notch3 in T-cell leukemia, particularly in cases of Notch3 overexpression, is not well understood. In this study, we have discovered a new characteristic of Notch3, which involves its acetylation and deacetylation at lysines 1692 and 1731 by p300 and HDAC1, respectively. This balance is disrupted by HDAC inhibitors (HDACi), leading to increased acetylation. Through the use of HDACi and a mutated form of Notch3 that cannot be acetylated (Notch3-K/R1692−1731), we have demonstrated that acetylation of Notch3 primes it for ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the proteasome. Consequently, the expression of Notch3 protein and its transcriptional activity are reduced both in vitro and in vivo in transgenic mice overexpressing Notch3, resulting in impaired downstream signaling of target genes. Furthermore, HDACi inhibits Notch3-induced T-cell proliferation, while the non-acetylatable Notch3-K/R1692−1731 mutant enhances it. Finally, HDACi-induced hyperacetylation of Notch3 prevents the growth of T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in transgenic mice. Overall, our findings suggest that the acetylation/deacetylation process of Notch3 serves as a crucial regulatory switch in Notch signaling, making it a potential target for therapeutic intervention in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

title: Hypoglycemia: incidence and clinical predictors in a large population-based sample of children and adolescents with IDDM.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the frequency of moderate and severe hypoglycemia in a large population of children and adolescents with IDDM, and to identify any clinical predictors associated with its occurrence. A total of 657 patients, with an average age of 12.1 years, were included in the study, providing data for a total of 1,449 patient-years. Over a period of three years, the occurrence of severe hypoglycemia (resulting in a seizure or coma) and moderate hypoglycemia (requiring assistance from another person, excluding severe episodes) was prospectively assessed. Patients and caregivers reported episodes of significant hypoglycemia at each three-month clinic visit, along with HbA1c levels. The data was analyzed using generalized estimating equation models with the exchange correlation structure. 

The results showed that the overall incidence of severe hypoglycemic events was 4.8 per 100 patient-years, while the incidence of moderate events was 13.1 per 100 patient-years. Over the course of three years, severe events occurred in 8.5% of children and moderate events occurred in 26.9%. Notably, significant hypoglycemia was rare in the first year after diagnosis. The rates of hypoglycemia were higher in children under six years of age compared to those over six years (40.9 vs. 16.6 per 100 patient-years, respectively, p < 0.001). Rates of hypoglycemia doubled when HbA1c levels fell below 8%, and children with HbA1c levels below 7% had a threefold increase in both moderate and severe hypoglycemia (e.g., severe episodes occurred at a rate of 14.9 per 100 patient-years for HbA1c ≤ 7% compared to 4.1 per 100 patient-years for HbA1c > 7%, p < 0.001). Most severe events were seizures, with 75% of them occurring at night. The majority of events were related to missed meals or increased activity, although in 38% of cases, no predisposing factor was evident. 

In conclusion, newly diagnosed children with IDDM appear to be protected from severe hypoglycemia. However, rates of hypoglycemia increase with lower glycated hemoglobin levels, particularly when mean HbA1c is below 8.0%. Younger children, who may be more vulnerable to the adverse effects of neuroglycopenia, are at a higher risk of significant hypoglycemia.

title: Efficacy of a 6-month versus 9-month intermittent treatment regimen in HIV-infected patients with tuberculosis: a randomized clinical trial.
text:
RATIONALE: The effectiveness of intermittent thrice-weekly antituberculosis treatment of varying durations in HIV-associated tuberculosis is not clear. 

OBJECTIVES: To compare the effectiveness of a 6-month intermittent regimen (Reg6M) with a 9-month regimen (Reg9M) in HIV/tuberculosis (TB) patients. 

METHODS: HIV-infected patients with newly diagnosed pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB were randomly assigned to either Reg6M or Reg9M. They were monitored for 36 months to assess clinical, immunological, and bacteriological parameters. Primary outcomes included favorable responses at the end of treatment and recurrences during follow-up, while the secondary outcome was death. 

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Of the patients, 70% had culture-positive pulmonary TB, with a median viral load of 155,000 copies/ml and a CD4(+) cell count of 160 cells/mm(3). The favorable response to antituberculosis treatment was similar in both groups. Bacteriological recurrences occurred more frequently in the Reg6M group, although overall recurrences were not significantly different. By 36 months, the mortality rate was similar in both groups. All patients who failed treatment developed acquired rifamycin resistance, with baseline isoniazid resistance being the main risk factor. 

CONCLUSIONS: Among antiretroviral treatment-naive HIV-infected patients with TB, a 9-month regimen resulted in a similar outcome at the end of treatment but a lower bacteriological recurrence rate compared to a 6-month thrice-weekly regimen. Acquired rifamycin resistance was high with these intermittent regimens, and the lengthening of TB treatment did not affect mortality or acquired rifamycin resistance. 

Clinical Trials Registry Information: ID# NCT00376012 registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov.

title: High prevalence of evolutionarily conserved and species-specific genomic aberrations in mouse pluripotent stem cells.
text: Mouse pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) are extensively studied and considered the benchmark for comparing human PSCs. However, the genomic integrity of mouse PSCs has not been thoroughly evaluated, unlike human PSCs which have received significant attention. The stability of PSCs' genomes is crucial as it impacts their ability to differentiate, maintain pluripotency, and their potential to form tumors. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of 325 mouse PSC samples, including 127 induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) samples. Our findings revealed frequent genomic abnormalities in mouse embryonic stem cells from different mouse strains, as well as in mouse iPSCs derived from various cell sources and techniques. We identified four specific regions prone to chromosomal aberrations: full trisomy 11 (with a recurrent gain in 11qE2), full trisomy 8, and deletions in chromosomes 10qB and 14qC-14qE. Interestingly, the most common aberration in mouse PSCs, gain 11qE2, was found to be syntenic with the common aberration 17q25 in human PSCs, while other recurrent aberrations were species-specific. Additionally, our analysis of 74 rhesus macaque PSC samples revealed a gain in chromosome 16q, which is syntenic to the hotspot in human 17q. These shared aberrations have significant implications as they can confound the interpretation of previous studies comparing PSCs, where unintentional comparisons were made between normal and aberrant cells. Therefore, our work underscores the importance of closely monitoring the genomic integrity of PSCs from all species to ensure their appropriate use in biomedical research.

title: Inhibition of cell proliferation and induction of apoptosis by ExFABP gene targeting.
text: Ex-FABP, a lipocalin that binds fatty acids outside of cells, is naturally produced by differentiating chicken chondrocytes and myoblasts. Its production is increased after cells are exposed to inflammatory substances and decreased by anti-inflammatory agents, indicating that it functions as an acute phase protein. When chicken liver fragments are cultured and treated with bacterial endotoxins, the expression of Ex-FABP is enhanced. To investigate the role of Ex-FABP, we introduced an expression vector containing antisense Ex-FABP cDNA into growing chondrocytes. This resulted in a significant decrease in cell viability and a strong inhibition of cell growth and differentiation. Additionally, when chondrocytes were transfected with the antisense Ex-FABP cDNA, there was an increase in the number of apoptotic cells. Similarly, myoblasts transfected with the same expression vector experienced extensive cell death and impaired formation of myotubes. These findings suggest that Ex-FABP plays a crucial role in cell survival and that its expression and activation are essential for protecting chondrocytes from cell death.

title: Profile of the Navrongo Health and Demographic Surveillance System.
text: The Navrongo health and demographic surveillance system (NHDSS) is situated in the Kassena-Nankana districts in the northern region of Ghana. It was established in 1992 by the Navrongo health research centre (NHRC), which is one of the three research centres of the Ghana health service. This article describes the activities and potential of the NHDSS for collaborative research. The main purpose of the NHDSS is to monitor the health and demographic trends in the two districts and assess the impact of health and social interventions on morbidity and mortality. Currently, the NHDSS covers a population of 152,000 individuals residing in 32,000 households. The system routinely tracks various events such as pregnancies, births, illnesses, deaths, migration, marriages, and vaccination coverage. Trained fieldworkers update the data every four months. In addition to surveillance, the NHRC conducts biomedical and socio-economic studies. The NHDSS also incorporates a community key informant system, where volunteers report important events like births and deaths in their localities. Furthermore, the system utilizes a verbal autopsy (VA) approach to determine the likely causes of deaths that occur within the community. Data collected by the NHDSS is shared with funders, collaborators, and partners in the INDEPTH Network. The Director of the NHDSS serves as the main contact person for potential collaborations and data usage.

title: The impact of COPD on lung health worldwide: epidemiology and incidence.
text: Data on the prevalence of COPD was gathered from various sources including vital statistics, health interview surveys, hospital charge records, national publications, and the World Health Organization (WHO). These findings indicate that COPD is a widespread disease that has significant implications for global health. In the United States, COPD is responsible for 4% of morbidity, making it the fourth leading cause of death, surpassed only by heart attacks, cancer, and stroke. Internationally, there is considerable variation in death rates, which may be influenced by factors such as smoking habits, tobacco type and processing, pollution, climate, respiratory management, and genetic factors. To address this growing burden, the Global Obstructive Lung Disease Initiative was launched by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and the WHO. The initiative aims to raise awareness about COPD, reduce morbidity and mortality rates, encourage further research on the condition, and implement preventive programs.

title: TLR activation triggers the rapid differentiation of monocytes into macrophages and dendritic cells
text: Leprosy provides an opportunity to study how the innate immune system contributes to protecting the host against infection. In one form of the disease, the infection progresses, while in the other form, it is limited. Our findings show that when Toll-like receptors (TLRs) on human monocytes are activated, they quickly differentiate into two distinct subsets: DC-SIGN+ CD16+ macrophages and CD1b+ DC-SIGN− dendritic cells. The activation of TLRs leads to an increase in interleukin (IL)-15 and IL-15 receptor, which expands the population of phagocytic macrophages. Similarly, TLR activation increases granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and its receptor, promoting the expansion of CD1b+ dendritic cells. These dendritic cells activate T cells and secrete proinflammatory cytokines. We observed that DC-SIGN+ macrophages were present in lesions and after TLR activation in all leprosy patients. However, CD1b+ dendritic cells were not found in lesions or after TLR activation of peripheral monocytes in individuals with the progressive lepromatous form, except during reversal reactions when the bacteria were cleared by T helper type 1 (TH1) responses. In tuberculoid lepromatous lesions, DC-SIGN+ cells expressed macrophage markers but not dendritic cell markers. Therefore, the TLR-induced differentiation of monocytes into either macrophages or dendritic cells appears to play a crucial role in effective host defenses against human infectious diseases.

title: Mismatch repair status and clinical outcome in endometrial cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
The relationship between the lack of mismatch repair (MMR) genes and prognosis in women with endometrial cancer is not clear. In this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate this association. 

To identify relevant studies, we searched literature databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane) from 1980 to December 2011. These studies evaluated the connection between MMR status and clinical outcomes in endometrial cancer. The main outcome measures were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). 

A total of 23 studies met the inclusion criteria. The median sample size of the studies was 112, with 74% being retrospective case-series. Additionally, 70% of the studies performed microsatellite instability (MSI) analysis to assess the MMR status. However, only 22% of the studies used the recommended panel of five microsatellite markers by the National Cancer Institute. Immunohistochemistry was used in seven studies to define MMR deficiency, but only two of them examined the expression of all four MMR proteins. 

Overall, 32% of the studies showed significant associations between MMR and outcome. However, there was significant heterogeneity among the studies regarding estimates of OS and DFS. The pooled analysis did not reveal any significant association between MMR deficiency and worse OS (six studies, hazard ratio [HR] 2.0, p=0.11) or DFS (four studies, HR ratio 1.31, p=0.66). 

In conclusion, there is currently no definitive evidence supporting a significant association between MMR status and detrimental survival in endometrial cancer.

title: p53 induces formation of NEAT1 lncRNA-containing paraspeckles that modulate replication stress response and chemosensitivity
text: We have discovered a long noncoding RNA called NEAT1 that plays a role in the p53 tumor suppressor pathway. This pathway is responsible for various cellular responses, some of which can be contradictory. NEAT1 is an important component of paraspeckle nuclear bodies, but its significance in disease is not well understood. When p53 is activated, either through drugs or replication stress caused by oncogenes, paraspeckles are formed in both mouse and human cells. By silencing the expression of Neat1 in mice, we observed that the absence of paraspeckles made preneoplastic cells more susceptible to cell death caused by DNA damage and hindered the development of skin tumors. Our research suggests that NEAT1 promotes ATR signaling in response to replication stress, creating a negative feedback loop that reduces the activation of p53 by oncogenes. Targeting NEAT1 in established human cancer cell lines resulted in synthetic lethality when combined with genotoxic chemotherapeutics, such as PARP inhibitors, and non-genotoxic activation of p53. This study establishes a crucial genetic connection between NEAT1 paraspeckles, p53 biology, and tumorigenesis, and identifies NEAT1 as a promising target to increase the sensitivity of cancer cells to both chemotherapy and p53 reactivation therapy.

title: Regulation of innate immunity by NADPH oxidase.
text: NADPH oxidase is an essential regulator of both the body's defense against microbes and the inflammatory response. When activated by microbes or their byproducts, the NADPH oxidase in phagocytes quickly assembles and produces reactive oxidant intermediates (ROIs) to combat the infection. Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an inherited disorder of the NADPH oxidase, which leads to recurrent and severe bacterial and fungal infections, as well as excessive inflammation-related complications. Research on CGD patients and mouse models has shown that NADPH oxidase not only fights infections but also plays a crucial role in controlling inflammation and preventing tissue damage. Understanding the mechanisms by which NADPH oxidase kills pathogens and regulates inflammation is vital for comprehending normal immune responses and conditions like acute lung injury, bacterial infections, and fungal infections.

title: Protection from olanzapine-induced metabolic toxicity in mice by acetaminophen and tetrahydroindenoindole
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of the analgesic acetaminophen (APAP) and the antioxidant tetrahydroindenoindole (THII) in preventing metabolic changes induced by the second-generation antipsychotic drug olanzapine (OLZ) in mice.

Design and Measurement: C57BL/6J mice were divided into groups and fed either a normal diet or a high-fat (HF) diet. They were then treated with OLZ alone or in combination with APAP or THII for a period of 10 weeks. Various parameters related to body composition, metabolism, glucose and insulin homeostasis, and oxidative stress were measured.

Results: Treatment with OLZ resulted in significant weight gain and increased body fat in mice on the HF diet. However, these effects were partially prevented by both APAP and THII, without affecting food consumption. THII treatment was associated with improved whole body and mitochondrial respiration. OLZ also worsened glucose tolerance and insulin resistance induced by the HF diet, but these effects were prevented by both APAP and THII. Additionally, OLZ increased oxidative stress in white adipose tissue, as evidenced by increased lipid peroxidation, NADPH-dependent O2 uptake, and H2O2 production. However, APAP, THII, and a NADPH oxidase inhibitor were able to abolish oxidative stress in white adipose tissue.

Conclusions: In conclusion, both APAP and THII were found to be effective in preventing obesity and metabolic complications associated with OLZ treatment. These findings suggest that these interventions may be beneficial in mitigating the adverse effects of OLZ on metabolism.

title: Detection of prions in blood
text: Prion diseases arise from an unconventional infectious agent known as prion, primarily composed of the misfolded prion protein (PrPSc). To prevent the disease from spreading, it is crucial to develop highly sensitive assays for detecting PrPSc in blood. In this study, we demonstrate the automation and optimization of the protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) technology to efficiently amplify PrPSc. By performing 140 PMCA cycles, we achieved a remarkable 6,600-fold increase in sensitivity compared to standard detection methods. Furthermore, two consecutive rounds of PMCA cycles resulted in a staggering 10 million-fold increase in sensitivity, enabling the detection of as few as 8,000 equivalent molecules of PrPSc. Notably, through serial PMCA, we successfully detected PrPSc in blood samples from hamsters affected by scrapie with 89% sensitivity and 100% specificity. These groundbreaking findings mark the first instance of biochemical detection of PrPSc in blood, offering promising prospects for the development of a noninvasive method for early diagnosis of prion diseases.

title: Genetic alterations and their relationship in the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Akt pathway in thyroid cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the occurrence and relationship of genetic alterations in the PI3K/Akt pathway in thyroid tumors and determine if this pathway could be a potential therapeutic target for thyroid cancer. The researchers examined the major genetic alterations in this pathway, including PIK3CA copy number gain and mutation, Ras mutation, and PTEN mutation, in a large group of primary thyroid tumors. 

The results showed that these genetic alterations were present in a significant number of benign thyroid adenoma (BTA), follicular thyroid cancer (FTC), papillary thyroid cancer (PTC), and anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) cases. FTC and ATC had the highest frequency of these genetic alterations. The researchers also found that PIK3CA copy gain was associated with increased PIK3CA protein expression. 

In BTA, FTC, and PTC, the genetic alterations appeared to have independent roles in tumorigenesis through the PI3K/Akt pathway. However, as the tumors progressed to ATC, there was an increasing coexistence of these genetic alterations. The coexistence of these genetic alterations with BRAF mutation was also common in PTC and ATC. 

Based on these findings, the researchers concluded that aberrant activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway plays a significant role in thyroid tumorigenesis, particularly in FTC and ATC. The accumulation of genetic alterations in this pathway promotes the progression of BTA to FTC and ATC. Additionally, the coexistence of PI3K/Akt pathway-related genetic alterations and BRAF mutation may facilitate the progression of PTC to ATC. Therefore, the PI3K/Akt pathway could be a major therapeutic target for thyroid cancers.

title: Vitamin D and obesity: current perspectives and future directions.
text:
In recent years, new roles for vitamin D have been discovered, going beyond its traditional role in calcium balance and bone health. These new roles have linked this fat-soluble vitamin to various non-communicable diseases. Low levels of vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) < 25-30 nmol/l) and sub-optimal levels (25(OH)D < 50-100 nmol/l) are increasingly associated with unfavorable metabolic conditions such as insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. These conditions are also commonly associated with overweight and obesity.

Early studies showed that morbidly obese individuals often had poor vitamin D levels. More recently, it has been observed that there is a relationship between vitamin D levels and body mass index (BMI), or specifically, body fat, in the general population. There are several hypotheses to explain how obesity affects the vitamin D system. One possibility is that vitamin D gets stored in adipose tissue, or that increased body size dilutes the concentration of vitamin D. Another hypothesis is that heavier individuals may have less sun exposure due to less outdoor activity or covering up with clothing, which limits the production of vitamin D in the skin.

Furthermore, some studies have shown that BMI and body fat are negatively associated with changes in vitamin D levels after supplementation. This raises the question of whether body size and adiposity should be considered when determining the dietary requirements for vitamin D. This review will examine the current evidence linking vitamin D levels and supplementation to overweight and obesity, and discuss the implications for setting dietary recommendations.

title: Transcriptional regulation by p53 through intrinsic DNA/chromatin binding and site-directed cofactor recruitment.
text: The protein p53, which suppresses tumor growth, plays a crucial role in how cells respond to stress signals by controlling genes involved in stopping cell division and inducing cell death. It is believed that p53 cannot bind to DNA unless its C terminus is modified or changed in structure. However, our research demonstrates that unmodified p53 can indeed bind to two specific sites within the p21 promoter, located at -1.4 and -2.3 kilobases, when assembled in chromatin. This binding process requires both the C terminus of p53 and a protein called p300, which is responsible for adding acetyl groups to histones. Surprisingly, the acetylation of the C terminus by p300 is not necessary for p53 to bind to the promoter or activate it. Instead, p300 acetylates the nucleosomes that are bound to p53 in the p21 promoter, causing the acetylation to spread towards the TATA box. This suggests that p53 is an active protein that can bind to both DNA and chromatin, and it may selectively control its target genes by recruiting specific cofactors to distinct binding sites with unique structures.

title: Pleiotropic effects of statins.
text: Statins are powerful inhibitors of cholesterol production in the body. In clinical trials, they have been found to be effective in preventing both primary and secondary coronary heart disease. However, the benefits of statins seem to go beyond just lowering cholesterol levels. Recent studies suggest that statins have additional effects on the body, such as improving the function of blood vessels, stabilizing plaque build-up in arteries, reducing oxidative stress and inflammation, and preventing blood clot formation. Moreover, statins have positive effects on the immune system, central nervous system, and bone health. These extra benefits are believed to be due to the inhibition of isoprenoids, which are molecules that play a role in cell signaling. Specifically, statins inhibit the activity of small GTP-binding proteins, such as Rho, Ras, and Rac, which rely on isoprenylation for proper function. This inhibition may be crucial in mediating the various positive effects of statins.

title: Increasing the efficiency of precise genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9 by inhibition of nonhomologous end joining
text: By introducing targeted double-strand breaks (DSBs) into DNA, we can enhance the accuracy of genome editing. This is achieved by increasing the incorporation rate of externally supplied DNA fragments into the genome through homologous recombination. However, the effectiveness of these methods is hindered by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), an alternative DNA repair pathway that competes with homology-directed repair (HDR). To address this issue, we focused on DNA ligase IV, a crucial enzyme in the NHEJ pathway, and utilized the inhibitor Scr7 to target it. Treatment with Scr7 resulted in a significant improvement in the efficiency of HDR-mediated genome editing. This approach was successfully applied to mammalian cell lines and mice, resulting in up to a 19-fold increase in editing efficiency for all four genes examined. Furthermore, this strategy can be extended to other customizable endonucleases, such as zinc finger nucleases and transcription activator-like effector nucleases, as well as nonmammalian cells with similar NHEJ and HDR mechanisms.

title: Molecular mechanism of BST2/tetherin downregulation by K5/MIR2 of Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus.
text: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) has two viral proteins, K3/MIR1 and K5/MIR2, which belong to the membrane-associated RING-CH (MARCH) ubiquitin ligase family. These proteins play a role in evading the immune system by attaching ubiquitin to immunostimulatory transmembrane proteins. In a previous study, we found that K5 and the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein VPU both decrease the levels of bone marrow stromal cell antigen 2 (BST2), also known as CD317 or tetherin, suggesting that BST2 may be a target of K5 and VPU. Recent research has shown that in the absence of VPU, HIV-1 particles are stuck to the cell membrane in BST2-expressing HeLa cells. By targeting BST2, K5 may also overcome the host's innate antiviral defense mechanism. In this study, we confirm that despite BST2's structure as a type II transmembrane protein with a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, it is indeed targeted by K5 and is downregulated during primary KSHV infection and reactivation. After leaving the endoplasmic reticulum, K5 attaches ubiquitin to lysines in the short amino-terminal domain of BST2, leading to rapid degradation of the protein. This degradation depends on the ubiquitination of BST2, as BST2 lacking cytosolic lysines is resistant to K5, and inhibiting the proteasome to deplete ubiquitin restores BST2 surface expression. Therefore, BST2 is the first type II transmembrane protein targeted by K5 and the first example of a protein that is both ubiquitinated and GPI linked. Additionally, we show that KSHV release is reduced when K5 is absent, in a BST2-dependent manner, suggesting that K5 helps the virus evade intracellular antiviral defense mechanisms.

title: Regulation of beta catenin signaling and parathyroid hormone anabolic effects in bone by the matricellular protein periostin.
text: Periostin (Postn) is a protein found in the extracellular matrix that is primarily produced by osteocytes and periosteal osteoblasts in response to mechanical stimulation and parathyroid hormone (PTH). However, the impact of periostin expression on bone growth is still not fully understood. To investigate this, we studied the skeletal response of adult mice with and without the Postn gene to intermittent PTH treatment. We found that mice lacking the Postn gene had lower bone mass, cortical bone volume, and strength compared to mice with the gene when treated with PTH. The bone-forming indicators stimulated by PTH were significantly lower in mice without the Postn gene, especially at the periosteum. Additionally, we observed that PTH-induced activation of Wnt-β-catenin signaling, as assessed in TOPGAL reporter mice, was inhibited in the absence of periostin. In vitro experiments showed that PTH stimulated periostin production and suppressed the expression of MEF2C and sclerostin (Sost) in bone and osteoblasts. Recombinant periostin also inhibited Sost expression, which was mediated through the integrin αVβ3 receptor, while blocking periostin with an antibody prevented the inhibition of MEF2C and Sost by PTH. Furthermore, administering an antibody that blocks Sost partially restored the PTH-induced increase in bone mass in mice without the Postn gene. Additionally, primary osteoblasts from mice without the Postn gene exhibited lower proliferation, mineralization, and migration, both spontaneously and in response to PTH. Gene expression analysis confirmed a defect in osteoblast differentiation in mice without the Postn gene, both with and without PTH treatment, as well as increased osteoblast apoptosis in the absence of periostin. These findings shed light on the intricate role of periostin in bone growth, involving the regulation of Sost, Wnt-β-catenin signaling, and osteoblast differentiation.

title: Lipoprotein(a) concentration and the risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, and nonvascular mortality.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) concentration and the risk of major vascular and nonvascular outcomes, such as coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke. The researchers conducted a review of long-term prospective studies published between January 1970 and March 2009 that recorded Lp(a) concentration and subsequent major vascular morbidity and/or cause-specific mortality. They analyzed individual records from 126,634 participants in 36 studies and found that Lp(a) concentration was weakly correlated with conventional vascular risk factors and remained consistent within individuals over time. The associations between Lp(a) and CHD risk were continuous, with higher baseline Lp(a) concentrations associated with increased rates of CHD. After adjusting for age, sex, lipids, and other risk factors, the researchers found that higher Lp(a) concentrations were still associated with a modestly increased risk of CHD and ischemic stroke. However, there was no significant association between Lp(a) concentration and nonvascular outcomes, such as cancer deaths. In conclusion, this study suggests that Lp(a) concentration is independently and modestly associated with the risk of CHD and stroke, but not with nonvascular outcomes.

title: The biphasic behavior of incoherent feed-forward loops in biomolecular regulatory networks.
text: The incoherent feed-forward loop (FFL) is a common pattern in biomolecular regulatory networks. It was previously believed that the purpose of this FFL is to generate a temporary response characterized by fast activation and delayed inhibition. However, we have discovered that there are two distinct types of dynamics exhibited by incoherent FFLs: time-dependent biphasic responses and dose-dependent biphasic responses. This raises the question of why structurally identical incoherent FFLs can have such different roles in the system. Through computational studies, we have determined that the dynamics of these two types of incoherent FFLs are mutually exclusive. Based on further computational results and experimental observations, we propose that incoherent FFLs have been optimally designed to fulfill specific biological functions in different cellular contexts. For more information, please refer to the online version of the article, which includes additional supporting information.

title: Antipsychotic prescribing patterns in Germany: a retrospective analysis using a large outpatient prescription database.
text: The prescribing practices for antipsychotics are a topic of great interest when it comes to the quality of care. Therefore, we conducted an analysis of all prescriptions filled at pharmacies in Southern Germany between July 1999 and December 2001, which were covered by the statutory health insurance. This database includes prescriptions for approximately 25 million individuals. During the study period, up to 6% of the population were prescribed an antipsychotic at least once. The majority of these prescriptions were for conventional antipsychotics and were written by non-specialist physicians. Patients who received second generation antipsychotics were more likely to receive continuous antipsychotic therapy. A significant number of patients were also observed to be taking multiple antipsychotics at the same time, as well as additional medications for physical illnesses. In particular, medications for cardiovascular and metabolic disorders were frequently prescribed alongside antipsychotics. Physicians should take into account the cardiovascular and metabolic risk profile of patients when making treatment decisions. The data suggests that the majority of antipsychotics are being used to treat conditions other than schizophrenia. It is crucial to educate non-specialist physicians about the indications, effectiveness, and side effects of antipsychotics, as they are responsible for the majority of prescriptions.

title: Structural basis for the activation of microtubule assembly by the EB1 and p150Glued complex.
text: The regulation of microtubule dynamics is carried out by proteins known as plus-end tracking proteins, including EB1 and the dynein/dynactin complex. These proteins are believed to stabilize microtubules by forming a complex at the growing ends of the microtubules, although the exact mechanisms are not well understood. In this study, we present the crystal structure of two components of this complex: the carboxy-terminal dimerization domain of EB1 and the microtubule binding (CAP-Gly) domain of the dynactin subunit p150Glued. The EB1 dimer consists of two helices that form a conserved four-helix bundle, and it also contains binding sites for p150Glued in its flexible tail region. Through a combination of crystallography, NMR, and mutational analyses, we have identified the crucial elements of both EB1 and p150Glued that interact with each other, and we have found that mutations in these elements affect the polymerization activity of microtubules. Additionally, we have discovered that removing the flexible tail from EB1 activates microtubule assembly by EB1 alone, suggesting that the flexible tail acts as a negative regulator of EB1 activity. Based on these findings, we propose that EB1 adopts an auto-inhibited conformation, which is relieved by p150Glued acting as an allosteric activator.

title: Epigenetic regulation of NANOG by miR-302 cluster-MBD2 completes induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming.
text: The molecular mechanisms necessary for achieving full reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells are currently unknown, as most cells undergoing reprogramming only reach partially reprogrammed stages. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play a role in reprogramming by fine-tuning mRNA translation, but the specific miRNA targets that are crucial for complete iPS cell reprogramming have not been identified. In our research, we have discovered that methyl-DNA binding domain protein 2 (MBD2) acts as an epigenetic suppressor, preventing full reprogramming of somatic cells to iPS cells by directly binding to NANOG promoter elements and inhibiting transcriptional activation. However, when we overexpressed the miR-302 cluster, we observed a significant increase in the conversion of partially reprogrammed cells to fully reprogrammed iPS cells by suppressing MBD2 expression and increasing NANOG expression. Therefore, by introducing the exogenous miR-302 cluster (excluding miR-367), we can efficiently achieve a fully reprogrammed iPS state in partially reprogrammed cells by relieving the inhibition of NANOG expression caused by MBD2. These findings provide a direct molecular mechanism for generating complete human iPS cell reprogramming, which can be utilized for studying disease pathogenesis, drug screening, and potential cell-based therapies.

title: Complex physiology and compound stress responses during fermentation of alkali-pretreated corn stover hydrolysate by an Escherichia coli ethanologen.
text: The physiology of ethanologenic Escherichia coli grown without oxygen in plant hydrolysates that have been treated with alkali is not well understood and is quite complex. In order to gain a better understanding of how E. coli responds to these hydrolysates, we conducted a study using E. coli K-12 ethanologen that was fermenting a hydrolysate made from corn stover that had been pretreated with ammonia fiber expansion. Despite the hydrolysate having a high sugar content (approximately 6% glucose and 3% xylose) and being relatively non-toxic, the growth of E. coli stopped long before all the glucose was used up. However, the cells remained active metabolically and continued to convert glucose into ethanol until all the glucose was consumed. Through gene expression profiling, we discovered that there were complex and changing patterns of metabolic physiology and cellular stress responses during different phases of growth - the exponential growth phase, the transition phase, and the stationary phase when glycolysis was still active. During the exponential and transition phases, the costs of cell maintenance and stress responses were reduced to some extent by the presence of free amino acids in the hydrolysate. However, once the majority of amino acids were depleted, the cells entered the stationary phase and all the ATP derived from glucose fermentation was used up solely for cell maintenance in the hydrolysate. By comparing gene expression profiling and metabolic modeling of the ethanologen, we concluded that the high energy cost of dealing with osmotic stress, lignotoxin stress, and ethanol stress collectively limits the growth, sugar utilization rates, and ethanol yields in alkali-pretreated lignocellulosic hydrolysates.

title: Systemic arterial hypertension in children following renal transplantation: prevalence and risk factors.
text: The purpose of this study was to examine blood pressure control in children following renal transplantation and identify factors associated with hypertension in this population. Data was collected from pediatric kidney transplant patients in the UK at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 5 years post-transplantation. The prevalence of hypertension (systolic and/or diastolic blood pressure > 95th percentile) was determined, and the use of anti-hypertensive medication was assessed. The study found that approximately 25% of patients remained hypertensive 5 years after transplantation. Factors associated with systolic hypertension included receiving a deceased donor kidney, having a lower height z-score, and being on anti-hypertensive medication. There was also significant variation in hypertension rates between different centers, suggesting differences in the management of hypertension. Overall, blood pressure control in pediatric kidney transplant patients in the UK was found to be sub-optimal.

title: Coupling cAMP signaling to transcription in the liver: pivotal role of CREB and CREM.
text: The basic domain-leucine zipper superfamily consists of transcriptional factors that bind to cAMP-responsive elements (CREs) in gene promoters. In mammals, this superfamily is composed of three genes: CREB, CREM, and ATF-1. Posttranscriptional events, particularly alternative splicing, generate a large number of CREB, CREM, and ATF-1 proteins, which act as activators or repressors to regulate gene expression. Activation occurs when a key acceptor site (Ser133 in CREB) is phosphorylated by various kinases, including PKA, CamKIV, and Rsk-2. Phosphorylation is necessary for the interaction between CREB and CBP (CREB-binding protein), a co-activator with histone acetyltransferase activity. Repression, on the other hand, involves the dephosphorylation of activators, leading to decreased association with CBP. Another pathway of transcriptional repression on CRE sites involves ICER (inducible cAMP early repressor), a product of the CREM gene. ICER is an inducible repressor involved in autoregulatory feedback loops that down-regulate early response genes like c-fos. The liver is a significant physiological setting where cAMP-responsive signaling plays a major role. Partial hepatectomy triggers a finely tuned program of gene expression, allowing coordinated tissue regeneration through specific checkpoints. The temporal kinetics of transcriptional activation after hepatectomy show early induction patterns for several genes, some of which are controlled by CREB/CREM transcription factors. The robust induction of ICER after partial hepatectomy suggests an important role for CREM in liver physiology. The delay in tissue regeneration observed in CREM-deficient mice confirms the crucial function of this factor in regulating hepatocyte proliferation. As gene induction is accompanied by critical changes in chromatin organization, understanding the specific modification codes that histones display during liver regeneration and physiology will provide valuable insights into the dynamics of chromatin architecture.

title: Comparison of dietary assessment methods in a Southern French population: use of weighed records, estimated-diet records and a food-frequency questionnaire
text:
Objective: The main goal of this study was to develop suitable dietary assessment tools for the French Mediterranean region and validate their accuracy. 

Subjects and Methods: A sample of 150 male and female volunteers participated in the study. Out of these, 98 completed the protocol, which included a 4-day weighed dietary record (PETRA), a 7-day estimated-diet record (S7) based on a checklist and a set of photographs, and a semi-quantitative food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ) that also collected socio-demographic and anthropometric data. The PETRA and S7 records were completed once in each season of the year, while the FFQ was completed only once. 

Results: The validation of the assessment methods was based on nutrients and foods. The energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between S4 and PETRA ranged from 0.32 for vitamin E to 0.81 for vitamin C, with a mean of 0.65 for 21 nutrients. There was minimal misclassification in opposite extreme quartiles. The Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.63 for fish and seafood to 0.90 for wine, with a mean of 0.76 for 16 food groups. Again, there was minimal misclassification in opposite extreme quartiles.
