The de-attenuated energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between the FFQ and S7 ranged from 0.22 for proteins and monounsaturated fatty acids to 0.80 for iron, with a mean of 0.45. Less than 10% of subjects were misclassified in opposite extreme quartiles, except for vitamin C (12%). The Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.25 for green-yellow-red raw vegetables to 0.76 for wine, with a mean of 0.42. Less than 8% of subjects were misclassified in opposite extreme quartiles, except for citrus fruit (11%). 

Conclusions: The use of the set of photographs for portion estimation was validated by the correlation between S4 and PETRA for both nutrients and foods. The FFQ provided a reasonably reliable measure of macronutrient intake and a good measure of micronutrient intake when compared to existing literature. However, it performed less well for food intake. Better results can be achieved for the FFQ by using the set of photographs instead of standard portions and by including additional questions on foods that are not adequately covered. 

Sponsorship: This study was financially supported by INSERM contract 91-1006 and the Ardèche and Hérault Committees of the ‘Ligue contre le cancer’.

title: Substrate fate in activated macrophages: a comparison between innate, classic, and alternative activation.
text: Macrophages have a significant role in both innate and adaptive immunity, depending on the stimuli they receive. From an analytical and functional perspective, macrophage stimulation can be categorized into three main pathways: innate, classic, and alternative. These different pathways lead to the activation of specific sets of genes that release either pro- or anti-inflammatory stimuli. In this study, we investigated whether specific metabolic patterns are dependent on the activated signaling pathway. We used a metabolomics approach with a [1,2-(13)C(2)]glucose tracer to analyze the metabolic flux distributions in macrophages stimulated through the classic, innate, and alternative pathways. By combining this methodology with mass isotopomer distribution analysis of newly formed metabolites, we found that activated macrophages primarily rely on glycolysis as their main metabolic pathway. There is a clear distinction between the classic/innate activation and the alternative pathway. Interestingly, macrophage activation through LPS/IFN-gamma or TLR-2, -3, -4, and -9 leads to similar flux distribution patterns regardless of the pathway activated. However, stimulation through the alternative pathway has minimal metabolic effects. The molecular basis for these differences involves a switch in the expression of 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK2) from the liver type-PFK2 to the more active ubiquitous PFK2 isoenzyme. This switch is triggered by Hif-1alpha activation, which increases the concentration of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and enhances glycolytic flux. Interestingly, even when Hif-1alpha is targeted in macrophages, the switch of PFK2 isoenzymes still occurs in LPS/IFN-gamma-activated macrophages, suggesting that this pathway regulates ubiquitous PFK2 expression through mechanisms independent of Hif-1alpha.

title: The effect of folic acid supplementation on plasma homocysteine in an elderly population.
text:
BACKGROUND: Elevated levels of homocysteine in the blood have been linked to various cardiovascular conditions such as coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and venous thrombosis. Folic acid has been found to be the most effective treatment for reducing homocysteine levels. However, it is unclear what the optimal dosage of folic acid is, especially for the elderly population who are most at risk for these conditions.

AIM: This study aimed to investigate the effects of different daily doses of folic acid supplementation (ranging from 0 to 600 microg) on plasma homocysteine levels in elderly individuals.

DESIGN: The study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.

METHODS: A total of 368 participants aged 65-75 years were randomly assigned to receive one of the six treatment options for a duration of 6 weeks. Plasma homocysteine levels were measured after 3 weeks and 6 weeks of supplementation.

RESULTS: Only the groups receiving 400 microg and 600 microg of folic acid showed significant reductions in homocysteine levels compared to the placebo group (p=0.038 and p<0.001, respectively). Using multiple linear regression analysis and considering both dietary and supplemental folic acid intake, it was estimated that a total daily intake of 926 microg of folic acid would be necessary to ensure that 95% of the elderly population is not at risk for cardiovascular issues related to folate deficiency.

DISCUSSION: Achieving a daily folic acid intake of 926 microg through diet alone is unlikely. Individual supplementation or fortification of food with folic acid will be necessary to meet this target.

title: Central obesity and hyperinsulinaemia in women are associated with polymorphism in the 5' flanking region of the human insulin gene.
text:
Obesity is a complex disease influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. The heterogeneity of obesity is evident in the distribution of body fat, such as upper body (central) and lower body (gluteal) obesity. Interestingly, the distribution of fat is more strongly influenced by genetics compared to overall body fat. Central obesity, characterized by high insulin levels and insulin resistance, shares similarities with conditions like non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atherosclerosis.

To investigate the genetic basis of central obesity, we conducted a study involving 56 severely obese young non-diabetic women of British Caucasian descent. We examined the association between candidate genes, including the insulin receptor, insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, and insulin, with various measurements related to body size, insulin secretion, and insulin resistance. Our findings revealed a significant association between the class 3 allele of the hypervariable region in the 5' flanking region of the insulin gene and upper body obesity (P = 0.005). Additionally, this allele was also linked to fasting hyperinsulinemia (P = 0.01), stimulated insulin secretion (P = 0.01), and insulin resistance as determined by the homeostatic model of assessment (HOMA; P = 0.008). No similar associations were observed with the other candidate genes investigated. These results suggest that genetic variations in the 5' flanking region of the insulin gene may influence its expression and subsequently impact insulin production in severely obese women.

title: Population density profiles of nasopharyngeal carriage of 5 bacterial species in pre-school children measured using quantitative PCR offer potential insights into the dynamics of transmission.
text: Bacterial vaccines have the potential to decrease the number of individuals carrying bacteria. Typically, colonization is seen as a yes or no outcome. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a method that can measure the amount of bacterial DNA in mucosal samples across a wide range. In our study, we used culture and single-gene species-specific qPCRs for Streptococcus pneumoniae (lytA), Streptococcus pyogenes (ntpC), Moraxella catarrhalis (ompJ), Haemophilus influenzae (hdp), and Staphylococcus aureus (nuc). By comparing the results to log-phase reference strain broth cultures, we were able to determine the frequency and peak density of bacterial carriage in nasopharyngeal swabs from 161 healthy children aged 2-4 years. The swabs were collected into STGG broth. Overall, the results from qPCR and culture were consistent. However, there were some discrepancies, particularly at lower detection thresholds for both methods. The PCR assays for S. pyogenes and S. aureus were found to be less sensitive. The density of bacteria varied greatly across the five species, spanning 5-7 orders of magnitude. The more abundant species tended to have higher values (modes: S. pneumoniae log3-4, M. catarrhalis & H. influenzae log4-5 CFU/ml broth). The wide range of bacterial DNA concentrations in healthy children carrying these bacteria suggests that different individuals may vary greatly in terms of infectiousness at different times. By understanding the factors that influence colonization density, such as the host, microbial, and environmental determinants, we can better predict the effectiveness of vaccines.

title: Circadian mechanisms in murine and human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells following dexamethasone exposure.
text: A group of regulatory factors controls circadian rhythms in mammalian cells. While the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain acts as the central circadian oscillator, circadian clocks also exist in peripheral tissues and cells. Recent evidence has shown that more than 20% of expressed mRNAs in bone and adipose tissues oscillate in a circadian manner. This study presents evidence of the core circadian transcriptional apparatus in primary cultures of murine and human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). When confluent, quiescent BMSCs were exposed to dexamethasone, the expression of mRNAs encoding albumin D binding protein (dbp), brain-muscle arnt-like 1 (bmal1), period 3 (per3), rev-erb alpha (Rev A), and rev-erb beta (Rev B) became synchronized in their oscillation. These genes exhibited an average oscillatory period of 22.2 to 24.3 hours. The peak expression of mRNAs encoding "positive" (bmal1) and "negative" (per3) components of the circadian regulatory apparatus were out of phase with each other by approximately 8-12 hours, consistent with observations in vivo. In vivo, the phosphorylation of per3 and components of the core circadian regulatory apparatus by glycogen synthase kinase 3beta (GSK3beta) regulates their turnover. In vitro, the addition of lithium chloride, a GSK3beta inhibitor, caused a significant shift in the peak expression time of all genes by 4.2-4.7 hours in BMSCs. However, only male murine BMSCs showed a significant increase in the length of the oscillation period. Based on these findings, we conclude that human and murine BMSCs are a valid in vitro model for studying circadian mechanisms in bone metabolism and stem cell biology.

title: Herpesvirus-encoded GPCRs: neglected players in inflammatory and proliferative diseases?
text: The viral genomes of herpesviruses contain G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that are located in the cell membrane and have a similar structure to chemokine receptors. These GPCRs exploit the cellular signaling networks of the host to ensure their own survival, replication, and ability to cause disease. Specifically, the chemokine receptors ORF74, BILF1, and US28, which are produced by the herpesvirus and found in areas of inflammation and tumor cells, are important targets for therapies aimed at combating the virus. Considering the high potential for GPCRs to be targeted by drugs in general, these viral GPCRs show promise as targets for antiviral medications.

title: Midbody accumulation through evasion of autophagy contributes to cellular reprogramming and tumorigenicity
text: The midbody, which is a single organelle formed between daughter cells during cytokinesis and necessary for their final separation, remains present in cells long after division as midbody derivatives (MBds). However, it is unclear what happens to these MBds. In this study, we demonstrate that MBds are inherited unevenly by the daughter cell with the older centrosome. They tend to accumulate specifically in stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and potential cancer "stem cells" both in vivo and in vitro. As stem cells differentiate, they lose MBds, which occurs through autophagic degradation facilitated by the binding of the autophagic receptor NBR1 to the midbody protein CEP55. Differentiating cells and normal dividing cells do not accumulate MBds and exhibit high autophagic activity. On the other hand, stem cells and cancer cells evade autophagosome encapsulation, leading to the accumulation of MBds and displaying low autophagic activity. The enrichment of MBds enhances the reprogramming process to induced pluripotent stem cells and increases the tumorigenicity of cancer cells in vitro. These findings reveal unexpected roles for MBds in stem cells and cancer "stem cells".

title: Integrated genomic analysis identifies clinically relevant subtypes of glioblastoma characterized by abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR, and NF1.
text: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network has recently documented recurring genetic abnormalities in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). In this study, we present a robust classification of GBM based on gene expression, dividing it into four subtypes: Proneural, Neural, Classical, and Mesenchymal. We also integrate various genomic data to identify patterns of somatic mutations and DNA copy number alterations. The aberrations and gene expression of EGFR, NF1, and PDGFRA/IDH1 specifically define the Classical, Mesenchymal, and Proneural subtypes, respectively. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between subtypes and different neural lineages based on gene signatures of normal brain cell types. Importantly, the response to aggressive therapy varies depending on the subtype, with the Classical subtype showing the greatest benefit and the Proneural subtype showing no benefit. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework that combines transcriptomic and genomic dimensions to stratify GBM at a molecular level, which has significant implications for future research in this field.

title: Chronic Hepatitis B Infection: A Review
text:
The global prevalence of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is alarmingly high, affecting over 240 million individuals. If left untreated, a significant percentage of these individuals (15% to 40%) may develop cirrhosis, which can lead to liver failure and liver cancer. However, there are treatment options available that can suppress HBV replication, improve liver inflammation and fibrosis, and reduce the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Pegylated interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues (such as lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide) have shown effectiveness in suppressing HBV DNA replication and improving liver health. Cohort studies have demonstrated that long-term viral suppression can lead to regression of liver fibrosis and a decreased risk of liver cancer.

Unfortunately, the cure rates after treatment remain relatively low, ranging from 3% to 7% with pegylated interferon and 1% to 12% with nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy. Pegylated interferon therapy, although not associated with drug resistance, has limitations due to poor tolerability and adverse effects such as bone marrow suppression and exacerbation of neuropsychiatric symptoms like depression. Newer agents like entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide have shown promise in reducing the risk of drug resistance and should be considered as the first-line treatment.

In conclusion, patients with chronic HBV infection and liver inflammation should be offered antiviral treatment with either pegylated interferon or a nucleos(t)ide analogue. Nucleos(t)ide analogues, in particular, should be considered as the initial therapy. However, it is important to note that due to the low cure rates, most patients will require long-term therapy indefinitely to manage the disease and prevent its progression.

title: CD64 expression distinguishes monocyte-derived and conventional dendritic cells and reveals their distinct role during intramuscular immunization.
text: Although the majority of vaccines are administered intramuscularly (i.m.), there is limited knowledge about the dendritic cells (DCs) present in skeletal muscles. This article aims to address this gap by demonstrating that the expression of CD64, the high-affinity IgG receptor FcγRI, can distinguish conventional DCs from monocyte-derived DCs (Mo-DCs). By utilizing this distinguishing marker, we have identified the distinct subsets of DCs residing in skeletal muscles and their migratory counterparts in draining lymph nodes (LNs). This capability has allowed us to analyze the functional specialization of muscle DCs. Following i.m. administration of Ag adsorbed to alum, we have observed that alum-injected muscles contain a significant number of conventional DCs belonging to the CD8α(+)- and CD11b(+)-type DCs. Both types of conventional DCs are capable of capturing Ag and migrating to draining LNs, where they efficiently activate naive T cells. In alum-injected muscles, Mo-DCs are equally abundant as conventional DCs, but only a small fraction migrates to draining LNs. Consequently, alum alone does not induce significant migration of Mo-DCs to draining LNs. However, we have demonstrated that the addition of small amounts of LPS to alum enhances Mo-DC migration. Notably, migratory Mo-DCs have a higher capacity, per cell, to induce IFN-γ-producing T cells compared to conventional DCs. Therefore, the addition of LPS to alum enhances the overall immunogenicity of Ags presented by muscle-derived DCs. This study highlights the heterogeneous migratory and functional behavior of muscle DCs and Mo-DCs, which should be considered for a comprehensive understanding of the role of adjuvants in i.m. vaccination.

title: T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse
text: The field of T-cell-antigen recognition has seen significant advancements in the past five years, with much focus on the immunological synapse. This intricate cellular structure forms at the junction between a T cell and a cell that displays the necessary peptide-MHC complexes. Recent advancements in imaging technologies have allowed us to gain insights into the function of cell-surface molecules and their associated signaling modules in the realm of cell-to-cell communication. The pace of progress has been so remarkable that T-cell-antigen recognition may become the first system where we fully comprehend the molecular mechanisms underlying cell-cell recognition.

title: Key interactions by conserved polar amino acids located at the transmembrane helical boundaries in Class B GPCRs modulate activation, effector specificity and biased signalling in the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor.
text:
The GLP-1 receptor, a key therapeutic target for diabetes and obesity, is a Class B GPCR that can activate multiple signalling effectors and exhibit biased agonism when stimulated by ligands. In a previous study, we identified important polar amino acids in the transmembrane (TM) domain of the GLP-1 receptor. In this current study, we used mutagenesis, pharmacological characterisation, mathematical and computational molecular modelling to identify additional conserved polar residues in Class B GPCRs that play a role in GLP-1 receptor stability, signalling specificity, and biased agonism.

Our findings revealed three positively charged residues (R3.30227, K4.64288, R5.40310) located at the extracellular boundaries of TMs 3, 4, and 5. These residues were predicted to stabilize extracellular loop 2, which is crucial for ligand affinity and receptor activation. Additionally, we discovered a hydrogen bond network between residues in TMs 2 (R2.46176), 6 (R6.37348), and 7 (N7.61406 and E7.63408) at the cytoplasmic face of the receptor. This network plays a role in stabilizing the inactive receptor and directing signalling specificity. Furthermore, we identified residues at the bottom of TM 5 (R5.56326) and TM6 (K6.35346 and K6.40351) that are essential for receptor activation and downstream signalling. Lastly, we found that residues involved in stabilizing TM4 (N2.52182 and Y3.52250) also influence cell signalling.

Overall, this study enhances our understanding of how the GLP-1 receptor mediates peptide-induced signalling.

title: Influence of lifestyle modification on arterial stiffness and wave reflections.
text: Arterial stiffness and wave reflections have numerous negative effects on cardiovascular function and increase the risk of disease. They are also linked to higher mortality rates in patients with end-stage renal failure and essential hypertension. Therefore, it is crucial to prioritize the prevention and treatment of arterial stiffness. Recognizing arterial stiffening as a crucial precursor to cardiovascular disease, it is important to comprehend the impact of lifestyle changes in preventing and reversing this condition. Existing evidence suggests that lifestyle modifications, particularly aerobic exercise and reducing sodium intake, are effective therapeutic interventions for preventing and treating arterial stiffness. Consequently, there is enough evidence to recommend lifestyle modifications as a primary approach to managing arterial stiffening. However, further research is necessary to fully understand and optimize the use of lifestyle modifications in this context.

title: Effect of exercise-induced ischemia on QT interval dispersion.
text: This study aimed to investigate the impact of exercise on QT dispersion in individuals with ischemic heart disease (IHD), as an increased spatial dispersion of ventricular repolarization duration (QT dispersion) is associated with a higher vulnerability to arrhythmias. Fourteen members of a control group, 17 patients with IHD, and 14 patients with IHD who were taking beta-blockers (IHD-B) were included in the study. All participants underwent a standard Bruce protocol exercise test, and QT intervals were measured at rest and peak exercise using a digitizing tablet connected to a personal computer. The study found that QT dispersion at rest was significantly higher in the IHD group compared to the control and IHD-B groups (74 +/- 7, 40 +/- 4, 49 +/- 5 milliseconds, respectively; p < 0.03). Moreover, the corrected QT dispersion at peak exercise was greater in the IHD group compared to the control group (57 +/- 5 vs 26 +/- 3 msec, p < 0.03). The percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise was significantly higher in the IHD group (52% +/- 5%) compared to both the control group (28% +/- 4%, p < 0.002) and the IHD-B group (30% +/- 3%, p < 0.01). These findings suggest that the IHD group is more susceptible to arrhythmias due to a larger mean QT dispersion at peak exercise and an increased percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise. The protective effect of beta-blockers may be attributed to their ability to attenuate exercise-induced changes in QT dispersion.

title: Effects of powered mobility on self-initiated behaviors of very young children with locomotor disability.
text: In this study, the impact of powered mobility on the self-initiated behavior of six children with different disabilities is examined. These children, aged between 23 and 38 months, were able to learn how to use motorized wheelchairs in less than three weeks. The researchers used a multiple baseline design and recorded two-hour observation periods at 10-day intervals before and after the children achieved independent mobility. The frequency of self-initiated interaction with objects, spatial exploration, and communication with caregivers was analyzed. The results showed that three children increased all three types of behavior, one child increased in two types but decreased in interaction with objects, and two children only increased in spatial exploration.

title: BCR/ABL modifies the kinetics and fidelity of DNA double-strand breaks repair in hematopoietic cells.
text: The oncogenic BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase aids in the restoration of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Our research reveals that leukemia cells with BCR/ABL-positive mutations accumulate more DSBs after gamma-irradiation compared to normal cells. These damages are effectively repaired over time through BCR/ABL-induced non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and subsequent homologous recombination repair (HRR) mechanisms. However, we observed mutations in HRR products and significant deletions in NHEJ products within BCR/ABL-positive leukemia cells. We propose that inaccurate repair of DSBs may contribute to the genetic instability seen in Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemias.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein signaling in nephron progenitor cells
text: The role of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling is crucial in various aspects of kidney development and significantly influences the outcome of kidney injury. Additionally, BMP treatment is a vital element in protocols aimed at differentiating nephron progenitors from pluripotent stem cells. This review examines the significance of BMP signaling in nephron progenitor cells within these specific contexts.

title: Computational analysis of 3'-ends of ESTs shows four classes of alternative polyadenylation in human, mouse, and rat.
text: Many organisms use alternative initiation, splicing, and polyadenylation as mechanisms to create diversity among mature mRNA transcripts from the same transcription unit. Previous computational analyses have mainly focused on polyadenylation activities within or downstream of the normal 3'-terminal exons. However, we have conducted the first genome-wide analysis of alternative polyadenylation patterns in the human, mouse, and rat genomes, covering the entire transcribed regions of mRNAs. We aligned 3'-ESTs with poly(A) tails to genomic sequences to obtain these results. Our analysis reveals four distinct classes of alternative polyadenylation patterns: tandem poly(A) sites, composite exons, hidden exons, and truncated exons. We estimate that at least 49% (human), 31% (mouse), and 28% (rat) of polyadenylated transcription units exhibit alternative polyadenylation. Some of these alternative polyadenylation events lead to the production of new protein isoforms.

title: Epigenetic instability in ES cells and cloned mice.
text: Cloning through nuclear transfer (NT) is an inefficient procedure where the majority of clones perish before birth, and those that do survive often exhibit growth abnormalities. To investigate the relationship between gene expression, survival, and excessive fetal growth, we have analyzed the expression of imprinted genes in both mice cloned through nuclear transfer and the embryonic stem (ES) cell donor populations they originated from. The epigenetic condition of the ES cell genome was discovered to be highly unstable. Likewise, there was observed variation in imprinted gene expression in most cloned mice, even among those derived from ES cells of the same subclone. Despite widespread gene dysregulation, many of these animals managed to reach adulthood, suggesting that mammalian development may possess a certain level of tolerance towards epigenetic abnormalities in the genome. These findings suggest that even seemingly normal cloned animals may exhibit subtle irregularities in gene expression.

title: Successful three-way kidney paired donation with cross-country live donor allograft transport.
text: The use of kidney paired donation (KPD) to provide transplantation opportunities for patients with incompatible live donors is considered a crucial strategy for addressing the shortage of organs. It has been estimated that implementing a national KPD program in the United States could result in an additional 1000-2000 transplants per year. While most of these transplants could be arranged within local or regional areas, patients with difficult-to-match blood types or broad HLA sensitization would benefit from matching across larger geographic regions. In such cases, either the patients or the organs would need to travel in order to fully utilize the benefits of a national program. In this study, we present a case where a triple KPD facilitated the successful transplantation of a well-matched kidney from a live donor on the opposite coast for a highly sensitized patient (PRA 96%). The kidney was removed in San Francisco and transported to Baltimore, where it was reperfused after 8 hours. The patient experienced immediate kidney function and, one year later, has a serum creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dl. This case serves as a model for addressing the complexities associated with implementing a national KPD program in a large country like the United States.

title: Role of PACAP and VIP in astroglial functions.
text: Astrocytes make up at least half of the volume of the human brain and play a crucial role in supporting its functions. They are not only involved in various supportive functions but also contribute to the regulation of stem cell proliferation, synaptic plasticity, and neuroprotection. Additionally, astrocytes have an impact on neuronal physiology by responding to neurotransmitters and neuropeptides and releasing regulatory factors known as gliotransmitters. Specifically, during development and/or in adulthood, astrocytes express receptors such as PAC1-R for PACAP, as well as VPAC1-R and VPAC2-R for PACAP/VIP. Recent evidence confirms that PACAP and VIP have the ability to modulate several astrocyte activities, including proliferation, plasticity, glycogen production, and the synthesis of neurotrophic factors and gliotransmitters.

title: A subset of 26S proteasomes is activated at critically low ATP concentrations and contributes to myocardial injury during cold ischemia.
text: The molecular mechanisms that cause damage to the heart during warm or cold ischemia are not well understood. While it is believed that proteasomes play a role in the injury that occurs when blood flow is restored to the heart after a period of ischemia, their specific functions during the ischemic period are still unknown. Since donor hearts are often subjected to prolonged periods of cold ischemia before transplantation, we investigated the role and regulation of proteasomes during the storage of rat hearts in a cold solution, taking into account the levels of ATP in the heart tissue. We found that as ATP levels decreased during cold ischemic storage for up to 48 hours, the activity of cardiac proteasomes increased by 225%. However, when we added a specific proteasome inhibitor called epoxomicin to the storage solution, proteasome activity in the heart extracts was reduced, leading to less swelling and preserving the structural integrity of the heart muscle cells. Through experiments using purified proteasome enzymes, we discovered that this activation of proteasomes is caused by a subset of proteasomes that remain stable even at very low levels of ATP, and that ATP actually inhibits their activity. The proteasomes are most active when ATP levels are in the low micromolar range. These findings suggest that proteasome activation is a relevant mechanism of injury to the heart during cold ischemia. A specific subset of proteasomes appears to be responsible for damaging the heart cells as ATP levels decrease. By inhibiting proteasomes during cold ischemia, we can protect the structural integrity of the heart muscle cells.

title: Coping and satisfaction with growth hormone treatment among short-stature children.
text: This study examines how children with a chronic medical condition that requires long-term treatment are able to cope, and how this affects their quality of life and that of their parents. It also serves as an indicator of the effectiveness of the treatment. Specifically, the study focuses on children who have a stature two or more standard deviations below the average for their age and gender. The study included 96 patients, 53 of whom were male, who had been receiving growth hormone (GH) treatment for at least one year. Of these patients, 65 had no underlying disease, 15 had classical GH deficiency, and 16 had Turner syndrome or renal disease. All patients received daily injections at home for a period ranging from 12 to 66 months. The researchers used a self-administered questionnaire to assess the patients' ability to cope, as well as their level of satisfaction and compliance with the treatment. The results showed no significant differences based on gender, the presence of an underlying disease, the age at which treatment started, or the duration of treatment. Despite the fact that the impact of GH treatment on final height is still uncertain, the patients reported high levels of satisfaction and compliance.

title: Risk for breast cancer development determined by mammographic parenchymal pattern.
text: A risk classification system for breast cancer development has been created based solely on the appearance of the breast tissue as seen on mammograms. The study involved analyzing mammograms of women over the age of 30 who had been examined at Hutzel Hospital in Detroit over a five-year period. On average, the follow-up period was around 2 1/2 years. Four distinct groups were identified, with incidences of breast cancer development ranging from 0.1 to 2.2. The characteristics of these breast tissue patterns are explained, along with the criteria for identifying them.

title: Accurate coarse-grained modeling of red blood cells.
text: A systematic coarse-graining procedure is developed in this study to model red blood cells (RBCs) using mean-field theory arguments. The model considers the bending energy, in-plane shear energy, and constraints of fixed surface area and fixed enclosed volume in a three-dimensional RBC membrane. This coarse-graining procedure is applicable to any level of coarse-graining and does not require the use of fitting parameters. The sensitivity of the coarse-grained model is examined, and its performance is validated against experimental data and dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations of RBCs in capillary and shear flows.

title: Mice deficient in CD4 T cells have only transiently diminished levels of IFN-gamma, yet succumb to tuberculosis.
text: CD4 T cells play a crucial role in the immune response against tuberculosis. To understand how these cells contribute to protection against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, two mouse models lacking CD4 T cells were used. The first model involved mice deficient in MHC class II, while the second model involved mice deficient in CD4 molecules. Both models showed increased susceptibility to M. tuberculosis compared to wild-type mice. Interestingly, the MHC class II-deficient mice were more susceptible than the CD4-deficient mice, as evidenced by their survival rates after M. tuberculosis challenge. However, the increased resistance observed in CD4-deficient mice did not seem to be due to higher numbers of CD4-8- (double-negative) T cells. Analysis of IFN-gamma production in the lungs of infected mice revealed that both mutant mouse strains had a temporary impairment in their ability to produce IFN-gamma following infection. At 2 weeks post-infection, the mutant mice showed a more than 50% reduction in IFN-gamma production compared to wild-type mice, as measured by RT-PCR and intracellular cytokine staining. However, by 4 weeks post-infection, both mutant and wild-type mice had similar levels of IFN-gamma mRNA and protein production. In CD4 T cell-deficient mice, IFN-gamma production was attributed to CD8 T cells. This suggests that the early production of IFN-gamma by CD4 T cells is crucial in the course of M. tuberculosis infection, supporting the hypothesis that early events play a significant role in determining the outcome of the infection.

title: Treatment and management of graft-versus-host disease: improving response and survival.
text: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a major cause of illness and death after allogenic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. As a result, it has been the subject of extensive research. Although we have made significant progress in understanding the causes, diagnosis, and risk factors for both acute and chronic forms of the disease, there is still no standardized treatment strategy. Corticosteroid therapy has shown to be effective in treating both acute and chronic GVHD initially. However, the best approach for treating steroid-refractory disease is still debated, as current practices vary among different institutions and are based on smaller studies. Early diagnosis, collaboration among different medical disciplines, and proper supportive care, including infection prevention, are crucial in improving patient response and survival. It is hoped that future research strategies and the discovery of new therapeutic targets will further enhance outcomes. This review aims to discuss the available options for treating and managing acute and chronic GVHD.

title: The value of self-report assessment of adherence, rhinitis and smoking in relation to asthma control.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the usefulness of self-report measures in assessing adherence to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), the severity of rhinitis, and smoking status, and how these factors relate to asthma control. The study involved patients with asthma who were prescribed ICS from 85 practices in the UK. Participants were given validated questionnaires to assess their level of control (Asthma Control Questionnaire; ACQ) and adherence to medication (Medication Adherence Report Scale), as well as a two-item questionnaire to determine their smoking status and a single-item questionnaire to assess the severity of their rhinitis symptoms. 

The results showed that complete and anonymous questionnaires were obtained from 3916 participants. It was found that poor asthma control (ACQ >1.5) was associated with self-reported rhinitis (OR = 4.62; 95% CI: 3.71-5.77), smoking (OR = 4.33; 95% CI: 3.58-5.23), and low adherence to ICS (OR = 1.35; 95% CI: 1.18-1.55). The severity of rhinitis was found to be significant, with participants reporting severe rhinitis experiencing the worst asthma control, followed by those with mild rhinitis and those without any rhinitis symptoms (F(2, 3913)=128.7, p<.001). Additionally, there was a correlation between the number of cigarettes smoked per day and asthma control (F(5,655)=6.08, p<.001). 

In conclusion, poor asthma control is linked to self-reported rhinitis, smoking, and low adherence to medication. These factors, which can be identified through a brief self-report questionnaire, are potentially modifiable and should be routinely assessed during asthma reviews.

title: Development of a syngeneic mouse model for events related to ovarian cancer.
text: We obtained Mouse ovarian surface epithelial cells (MOSEC) from mature, virgin mice using a mild trypsinization method and cultured them in vitro. In the early passages (<20 passages), the cells displayed a cobblestone morphology and showed contact inhibition of growth. However, after approximately 20 passages, the cobblestone morphology and contact inhibition of growth were lost. To determine the tumor-forming potential, we injected early and late passage MOSEC into athymic and syngeneic C57BL6 mice subcutaneously (s.c.) and intraperitoneally (i.p.). Subcutaneous tumors formed only at the injection site after around 4 months. In contrast, intraperitoneal injection of late passage MOSEC into athymic and syngeneic mice resulted in the growth of tumor implants throughout the abdominal cavity and the production of hemorrhagic ascitic fluid. Early passage MOSEC did not form tumors in vivo. Histopathologic analysis of the tumors revealed a highly malignant neoplasm containing both carcinomatous and sarcomatous components. Late passage MOSEC expressed cytokeratin and did not produce ovarian steroids when stimulated with gonadotropins in vitro. We established ten clonal lines from late passage MOSEC, and each clone formed multiple peritoneal tumors and ascitic fluid after i.p. injection into C57BL6 mice. Cytogenetic analysis of three cell lines showed that they were polyploid with near-tetraploid modal chromosome numbers. Common clonal chromosome gains and losses included +5, +15, +19, -X, -3, and -4. One cell line had a clonal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 18, while another had a small marker chromosome. We did not observe any common structural abnormalities. These findings demonstrate the development of a mouse model for studying ovarian cancer in humans. The ability of MOSEC to form extensive tumors within the peritoneal cavity, similar to those observed in women with Stage III and IV cancer, and its ability to produce tumors in mice with intact immune systems make this model unique for investigating molecular and immune interactions in ovarian cancer development.

title: Hypoxia in cancer: significance and impact on clinical outcome
text: Hypoxia, a common feature of advanced solid tumors, has become a crucial factor in understanding tumor progression and resistance to treatment. It has a dual nature in tumor biology, as it can both inhibit and promote tumor growth and development. Regardless of traditional prognostic factors, hypoxia has been identified as a negative prognostic factor for patient outcomes. Studies have shown that patients with hypoxic cervical cancers or soft tissue sarcomas have worse disease-free survival rates. In head and neck cancers, hypoxia has been linked to survival and local control. Due to technical limitations, surrogate markers such as hypoxia-related proteins or bioreductive drugs are often used to assess tumor hypoxia. While endogenous markers have shown prognostic significance in some studies, the relevance of exogenous markers appears to be limited. Noninvasive imaging techniques like PET, SPECT, or MRI can be used to assess hypoxia, but their clinical application and impact on patient prognosis are still limited. The lack of standardized treatment protocols, inconsistencies in defining oxygenation status, and methodological differences in staining procedures may affect the reliability of prognostic parameters used in clinical studies.

title: Knowledge and Practice of Standard Precautions and Awareness Regarding Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for HIV among Interns of a Medical College in West Bengal, India.
text:
GOALS: The aim of this study was to evaluate the interns' understanding of standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, and to identify any discrepancies between their knowledge and actual practice. Additionally, the study aimed to determine the barriers that interns perceive as hindrances to adhering to standard precautions.

METHODS: The study was conducted on 130 interns from the 2010-11 batch of a government medical college in Kolkata, India. Each participant completed a self-administered questionnaire that covered the fundamental aspects of standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV. The questionnaire also included open-ended questions regarding the reasons for non-compliance with standard precautions, allowing participants to provide specific comments if desired.

RESULTS: The findings revealed that interns had a good understanding of the correct practices for using personal protective equipment, hand washing, and safe handling and disposal of needles and sharp objects. However, poor adherence to these practices was observed. The main reasons cited for non-compliance included difficulties in handling needles, discomfort when wearing gloves or aprons, impracticality of regular hand-washing, and lack of availability of equipment. While the majority of respondents (84.6%) were aware of the importance of washing injured sites with soap and water, approximately 32.3% were unaware that antiseptics could potentially cause more harm. Furthermore, only 63.8% of participants expressed awareness of the need to report any incidents of occupational exposure, and overall knowledge of post-exposure prophylaxis regimens was found to be lacking.

CONCLUSION: The significant gap between interns' knowledge and their actual practice of standard precautions, as well as their inadequate understanding of post-exposure prophylaxis, highlights the necessity for continuous on-site training, supportive supervision, and monitoring of interns' activities.

title: Viruses and microRNAs
text: The discovery of RNA interference and cellular microRNAs (miRNAs) has not only revolutionized biological research methods but has also unveiled a previously unknown level of post-transcriptional gene regulation. In this discussion, I explore the potential roles of miRNAs encoded by pathogenic human viruses and propose that cellular miRNAs may have significantly influenced viral evolution and continue to impact the tissue tropism of viruses in vivo. As our understanding of the importance and function of virally encoded miRNAs grows, it is likely to provide valuable insights into how viruses that establish latent infections, such as herpesviruses, evade elimination by the host's innate or adaptive immune system. Furthermore, studying the function of viral miRNAs may suggest novel approaches for treating diseases caused by viral infections.

title: Economic impact of primary open-angle glaucoma in Australia.
text:
BACKGROUND: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide and presents significant concerns for public health and the economy.

DESIGN: This study is a review of published randomized trials and population-based studies conducted since 1985.

METHODS: We examined the economic impact of primary open-angle glaucoma and modeled the potential effects of changes in detection rates and management strategies.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The cost-effectiveness of various interventions aimed at preventing vision loss from primary open-angle glaucoma was assessed in terms of financial cost (in Australian dollars) and disability-adjusted life years.

RESULTS: The prevalence of glaucoma in Australia is projected to rise from 208,000 cases in 2005 to 379,000 cases in 2025 due to the aging population. Health system costs during the same period are estimated to increase from $AU355 million to $AU784 million. Overall costs, including health system costs, indirect costs, and costs associated with loss of well-being, are expected to increase from $AU1.9 billion to $AU4.3 billion in Australia.

CONCLUSION: Primary open-angle glaucoma imposes a significant economic burden, which is anticipated to grow substantially by 2025. This dynamic model serves as a valuable tool for ongoing policy development and assessing the economic impact of interventions aimed at preventing visual impairment and blindness caused by glaucoma.

title: The LIM domain-containing homeo box gene Xlim-1 is expressed specifically in the organizer region of Xenopus gastrula embryos.
text: A unique motif rich in cysteine, known as LIM, has been discovered in the lin-11, Isl-1, and mec-3 homeo box genes, which are responsible for determining cell lineages in Caenorhabditis elegans. We have isolated LIM class homeo box genes from Xenopus laevis that bear a close resemblance to lin-11 and mec-3 in terms of the LIM and homeo domains. This study focuses on one of these genes, Xlim-1. The Xlim-1 mRNA is initially found in low quantities in the unfertilized egg, but experiences a significant increase during the gastrula stage, followed by a decrease and subsequent rise during the tadpole stage. Among adult tissues, the brain exhibits the highest abundance of Xlim-1 mRNA by a large margin. The expression patterns of the Xlim-1 gene, both maternal and late, suggest that it serves multiple functions at different stages of the Xenopus life cycle. In the gastrula embryo, Xlim-1 mRNA is specifically localized in the dorsal lip and the dorsal mesoderm, which corresponds to the region of Spemann's organizer. Experiments involving explants have demonstrated that Xlim-1 mRNA is induced by the mesoderm-inducer activin A and retinoic acid, which, although not a mesoderm inducer, affects patterning during Xenopus embryogenesis. Interestingly, the combined application of activin A and retinoic acid results in a synergistic induction. The structure, inducibility, and localized expression of the Xlim-1 gene in the organizer strongly suggest its involvement in establishing body pattern during gastrulation.

title: Signal transduction proteins that associate with the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptor mediate the PDGF-induced release of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase from permeabilized cells.
text:
The study conducted by Stanton et al. (1991) investigated the rapid release of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) in permeabilized rat kidney cells upon stimulation with peptide growth factors. Two cell lines, one transfected with wild type platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptors (PDGFR) and the other with mutant PDGFR, were used to evaluate the signal transduction pathways involved in G6PD release. Two permeabilization protocols were employed, and G6PD release was assessed through enzyme activity and Western blot analysis.

The results showed that PDGF induced a significant increase in G6PD release within 1 minute in cells transfected with wild type PDGFR. However, PDGF did not stimulate G6PD release in cells transfected with tyrosine kinase-deficient PDGFR. Similarly, cells transfected with partially autophosphorylation-deficient PDGFR, where four known signaling proteins failed to associate with the PDGFR, did not exhibit PDGF-induced G6PD release. Interestingly, the PDGF-stimulated release of G6PD was partially restored in PDGFR mutants that allowed either phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase or phospholipase C gamma 1 to associate with the PDGFR. Notably, there was no basal or PDGF-stimulated phosphorylation of G6PD observed.

In conclusion, the release of G6PD is dependent on the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of PDGFR, requires PDGFR autophosphorylation, and is mediated by signaling proteins that associate with the PDGFR. Furthermore, the release of G6PD is not directly mediated by its phosphorylation.

title: Microarrays for the study of viral gene expression during human cytomegalovirus latent infection.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a large DNA virus that is widely distributed in the human population. After the initial infection, it establishes a lifelong latent infection in certain cells of the immune system, such as monocytes and their precursor cells. While most adults with HCMV infection do not experience any symptoms, it can cause neurological problems in infants and remains a significant cause of illness and death in individuals with weakened immune systems. Microarray-based studies have provided valuable insights into the genes that are active during both the active and latent phases of HCMV infection. This chapter outlines the methods for studying these genes using microarrays and two specific cell types: human foreskin fibroblasts infected with the virus and primary human myeloid progenitor cells that are latently infected.

title: Physiological implications of hydrogen sulfide: a whiff exploration that blossomed.
text: Hydrogen sulfide (H(2)S) plays a crucial role in supporting life, starting from bacteria and extending to plants, invertebrates, vertebrates, and mammals. However, for many centuries, H(2)S was only recognized for its toxicity and environmental dangers. It was only in the past decade that the physiological significance of H(2)S began to be appreciated. This understanding emerged with the discovery of H(2)S production within mammalian cells and further research that identified various physiological functions of this gasotransmitter. The enzymes responsible for catalyzing H(2)S are expressed differently in multiple systems, including cardiovascular, neuronal, immune, renal, respiratory, gastrointestinal, reproductive, liver, and endocrine systems. These enzymes influence the functions of these systems through the production of H(2)S. The physiological effects of H(2)S are mediated by various molecular targets, such as ion channels and signaling proteins. Disruptions in H(2)S metabolism can lead to a range of pathological disturbances, including hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart failure, diabetes, cirrhosis, inflammation, sepsis, neurodegenerative diseases, erectile dysfunction, and asthma. To aid in the therapeutic intervention of diseases related to abnormal H(2)S metabolism, new technologies have been developed to detect endogenous H(2)S production, and novel compounds for delivering H(2)S have been invented. Although there are challenges ahead, research on H(2)S physiology and medicine is currently experiencing a period of exponential exploration.

title: TatC is a specificity determinant for protein secretion via the twin-arginine translocation pathway.
text: The recent identification of a widespread translocation pathway, specifically necessary for proteins with a twin-arginine motif in their signal peptide, has drawn attention to its membrane-bound components, one of which is called TatC. Unlike most organisms whose genomes have been fully sequenced, the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis has two tatC-like genes known as tatCd and tatCy. The corresponding TatCd and TatCy proteins have the potential to participate in the translocation of 27 proteins with potential twin-arginine signal peptides, of which approximately 6-14 are likely to be secreted into the growth medium. Through a proteomic approach, we demonstrate that PhoD of B. subtilis, a phosphodiesterase belonging to a novel protein family whose members are all synthesized with typical twin-arginine signal peptides, is secreted via the twin-arginine translocation pathway. Interestingly, TatCd plays a crucial role in the secretion of PhoD, while TatCy is not necessary for this process. Therefore, TatC seems to determine the specificity of protein secretion through the Tat pathway. Based on our findings, we propose that the TatC-mediated pathway specificity relies on specific interactions between TatC-like proteins and other pathway components, such as TatA, of which B. subtilis has three paralogues.

title: Function and regulation of SUMO proteases
text: The attachment of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) to proteins through covalent bonds is highly dynamic, and the process of both attaching and removing SUMO from proteins can be regulated. The removal of SUMO from proteins is carried out by enzymes called SUMO proteases, which play a role in controlling various cellular mechanisms such as transcription, cell division, and ribosome biogenesis. Recent advancements in this field include the identification of two new classes of SUMO proteases, a better understanding of the specificity of these enzymes, and the discovery of previously unknown functions of SUMO proteases in important cellular pathways. Additionally, the connection between SUMO proteases and a newly discovered group of enzymes called SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligases (STUbLs) has opened up exciting opportunities for further research in this area.

title: Review article: prebiotics in the gastrointestinal tract.
text:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are short-chain carbohydrates that have a positive impact on the gut microbiota. They are expected to improve health similar to probiotics, but at a lower cost and with less risk and easier incorporation into the diet.

AIM: This review aims to examine the existing evidence on the effects of prebiotics on gut function and human health.

METHODS: We conducted a search using the Science Citation Index with keywords related to prebiotics, gut bacteria, gut microbiota, large intestine, mucosa, bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, pouchitis, calcium, and cancer. We focused on studies conducted in humans and reports published in English. No clinical studies or meta-analyses on this topic were found in the Cochrane Library.

RESULTS: Three prebiotics, namely oligofructose, galacto-oligosaccharides, and lactulose, have been shown to alter the balance of the large bowel microbiota by increasing the numbers of bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus. These carbohydrates are fermented and produce short-chain fatty acids and intestinal gas. However, their effects on bowel habits are relatively minor. There are limited randomized-controlled trials examining their effects in a clinical setting, but animal studies have shown anti-inflammatory effects in inflammatory bowel disease and increased calcium absorption.

CONCLUSIONS: Prebiotics are still in the early stages of research, but they have the potential to modify the balance of gut microbiota and provide direct health benefits in a cost-effective and safe manner.

title: Pain catastrophizing and general health status in a large Dutch community sample.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between pain catastrophizing and overall health status in a sample of adults from the Netherlands. The study also aimed to replicate previous research on the factor structure, reliability, and validity of the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS). The results showed that regardless of the specific type of musculoskeletal pain, catastrophizing was a significant predictor of various aspects of general health status, even after accounting for pain intensity, age, gender, and chronicity. The strongest associations were found between catastrophizing and mental health, general health perception, social functioning, and vitality. Additionally, the association between catastrophizing and general health status was not influenced by the duration of the pain. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a three-factor model of the PCS, which was consistent across different subgroups of individuals with musculoskeletal pain. The correlations between the factors were high, and the three-factor model only slightly improved the explanatory power compared to a one-factor model. This suggests that a one-factor model may be justifiable, particularly in the general population. The reliability of the PCS total and subscales was satisfactory across various pain subgroups, and there was additional evidence supporting the concurrent validity of the PCS.

title: Variability in risk of gastrointestinal complications with individual non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: results of a collaborative meta-analysis.
text:
AIM: To compare the risks of severe gastrointestinal complications associated with different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

METHODS: A systematic review was conducted on controlled epidemiological studies that examined the relationship between NSAID use and hospital admissions for hemorrhage or perforation. The studies included both hospital and community-based case-control and cohort studies.

OUTCOMES: The study aimed to determine the estimated relative risks of gastrointestinal complications for each individual drug, using ibuprofen as the reference. Additionally, a ranking system was developed to summarize the sequence of relative risks observed in the studies.

RESULTS: Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, with 11 providing comparative data on ibuprofen and other drugs. In 10 out of the 11 studies, ibuprofen had the lowest or equal lowest risk. Pooled relative risks, calculated using ibuprofen as the reference, were all significantly greater than 1.0 (ranging from 1.6 to 9.2). Overall, ibuprofen had the lowest relative risk, followed by diclofenac. Azapropazone, tolmetin, ketoprofen, and piroxicam had the highest risk, while indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac, and aspirin fell in intermediate positions. Higher doses of ibuprofen were associated with similar risks to naproxen and indomethacin.

CONCLUSIONS: The low risk of serious gastrointestinal complications with ibuprofen can be attributed to the low doses commonly used in clinical practice. However, at higher doses, ibuprofen carries a similar risk to other NSAIDs. Therefore, using low-risk drugs at low dosages as the first line of treatment could significantly reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with serious gastrointestinal toxicity from these drugs.

title: Accuracy of weighed dietary records in studies of diet and health.
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of seven day weighed dietary records in assessing habitual dietary intake for research on the relationship between diet and health. The subjects were selected from a previous study in Northern Ireland using stratified random sampling to represent a range of energy intakes. The study included 31 free living adults, 16 men and 15 women. The main outcome measures were energy intake recorded through the dietary records and total energy expenditure estimated using the doubly labelled water technique. 

The results showed that the average recorded energy intakes were significantly lower than the measured expenditure for the overall group. The mean ratio of intake to expenditure was close to 1.0 for those in the upper third of energy intakes, indicating accurate records. However, for those in the middle and lower thirds, the ratios were much lower, suggesting underreporting of energy intake. 

These findings highlight a serious bias in reporting habitual energy intake, which could have significant implications for the interpretation of nutritional studies.

title: A novel family of sequence-specific endoribonucleases associated with the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.
text: The molecular mechanisms by which Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPRs) and associated CAS proteins protect microbial cells from foreign genetic elements are currently unknown. However, all CRISPR systems contain proteins from the CAS2 family, indicating their significant involvement in this process. In this study, we demonstrate that CAS2 proteins are a newly discovered family of endoribonucleases. Through experimentation with six purified CAS2 proteins from various organisms, we found that they preferentially cleave single-stranded RNAs within regions rich in uracil (U). Specifically, the CAS2 enzyme SSO1404 from Sulfolobus solfataricus was able to cleave the phosphodiester linkage on the 3'-side, resulting in the generation of oligonucleotides with a 5'-phosphate and a 3'-hydroxyl terminus. By solving the crystal structure of SSO1404 at a resolution of 1.6A, we discovered that it possesses a ribonuclease with a ferredoxin-like fold, a first of its kind. Through mutagenesis experiments, we identified six crucial residues (Tyr-9, Asp-10, Arg-17, Arg-19, Arg-31, and Phe-37) in SSO1404 that are essential for its enzymatic activity. Notably, Asp-10 was identified as the potential principal catalytic residue. Based on these findings, we propose that CAS2 proteins function as sequence-specific endoribonucleases and may play a role in degrading phage or cellular mRNAs as part of the CRISPR-mediated defense against phages.

title: Menstrual and reproductive factors in relation to mammographic density: the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN)
text: The relationship between menstrual and reproductive factors and breast cancer risk may be influenced by increased mammographic density. We conducted a study to determine if known or suspected menstrual and reproductive risk factors for breast cancer were associated with mammographic density. We measured the area of radiographic density and total breast area on mammograms from 801 participants in the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN), which included pre- and early perimenopausal women from various ethnic backgrounds. Using multivariable linear regression, we found that the following menstrual or reproductive factors were independently associated with percent mammographic density (area of dense breast/breast area): older age at menarche (β = 10.3, P < 0.01, for >13 vs. <12 years), premenstrual cravings and bloating (β = −3.36, P = 0.02), younger age at first full-term birth (β = −8.12, P < 0.01 for ≤23 years versus no births), greater number of births (β = −6.80, P < 0.01 for ≥3 births versus no births), and premenopausal status (β = 3.78, P < 0.01 versus early perimenopausal). After adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, study site, body mass index (BMI), and smoking, only the number of births remained associated with percent density. Furthermore, when we analyzed the data by BMI tertile, we found that the association with number of births was only significant in women with the lowest BMI (β = −12.2, P < 0.01 for ≥3 births versus no births). Our findings suggest that parity and breast cancer risk may be influenced by mammographic density in pre- and early perimenopausal women, and this relationship may be modified by body size.

title: Genetic and environmental determinants of 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in Hispanic and African Americans.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between three vitamin D-related genes and levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)2D] in Hispanics (HAs) and African Americans (AAs). The study was conducted as a cross-sectional analysis within the Insulin Resistance Atherosclerosis Family Study, which recruited participants from Los Angeles, California (AAs), San Luis Valley (SLV), Colorado (HAs), and San Antonio (SA), Texas (HAs). The main outcome measures were plasma levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D. 

The results showed that SLV-HAs had the highest levels of 25(OH)D, followed by SA-HAs, and AAs had the lowest levels. Levels of 1,25(OH)2D were similar in AAs and SLV-HAs, but higher in SA-HAs. After adjusting for gender and age, two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the vitamin D binding protein gene (DBP), rs4588 and rs7041, were found to be associated with 25(OH)D, and one SNP in the DBP, rs4588, was associated with 1,25(OH)2D at all three study centers. 

In conclusion, SNPs in the DBP gene are linked to levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D in HA and AA participants in the Insulin Resistance Atherosclerosis Family Study.

title: Changes in the levels of inositol phosphates after agonist-dependent hydrolysis of membrane phosphoinositides.
text: The study examined the production of inositol phosphates in response to agonists in brain slices, parotid gland fragments, and insect salivary glands. To incorporate the phosphoinositides, the tissues were initially incubated with [3H]inositol. Anion-exchange and high-resolution anion-exchange chromatography, high-voltage paper ionophoresis, and paper chromatography were used to identify glycerophosphoinositol, inositol 1-phosphate, inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate in all the tissues. However, there was no evidence of inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate. A simple anion-exchange chromatographic method was developed to separate these inositol phosphates for quantitative analysis. Stimulation did not affect the levels of glycerophosphoinositol in any of the tissues. The most significant change was observed in inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, which increased significantly in the insect salivary gland and parotid gland after stimulation with 5-hydroxytryptamine and carbachol, respectively. Carbachol also induced a substantial increase in the level of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate in the parotid gland. Brain slices stimulated with carbachol showed a modest increase in bis- and tris-phosphate. In all the tissues, there was a notable agonist-dependent increase in the level of inositol 1-phosphate. This increase may be derived from inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, as homogenates of the insect salivary gland contained a bisphosphatase in addition to a trisphosphatase. These findings suggest that the initial step in the stimulus-response pathway involves the hydrolysis of polyphosphoinositides by a phosphodiesterase, resulting in the production of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, which are then further hydrolyzed to inositol 1-phosphate and inositol. The absence of inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate could indicate that, shortly after stimulation, phosphatidylinositol is not broken down by its specific phosphodiesterase or that any cyclic derivative released is rapidly hydrolyzed by inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate 2-phosphohydrolase.

title: RNA editing in brain controls a determinant of ion flow in glutamate-gated channels.
text: L-glutamate, which is the main transmitter responsible for excitatory signals in the brain, controls the ion channels that facilitate rapid neurotransmission. Through cDNA cloning, we have identified the subunit components of two related types of glutamate receptor channels. These subunits have been found to contain either an arginine or a glutamine residue in a specific position of their channel-forming segment. The presence of an arginine residue in this segment significantly affects the properties of ion flow, as observed in one of the channel classes. Surprisingly, we have discovered that the genomic DNA sequences encoding this particular channel segment in all subunits actually contain a glutamine codon (CAG), despite the fact that the mRNAs of three subunits contain an arginine codon (CGG). We have ruled out the possibility of multiple genes or alternative exons being responsible for the arginine codon, leading us to propose that RNA editing is responsible for altering the transcripts of these three subunits. This process of RNA editing appears to affect the subunit transcripts of the two glutamate receptor classes with varying efficiency and selectivity.

title: Post-translational modifications of the beta-1 subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase affect enzyme activity and cellular localization.
text: The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a protein kinase found in mammals that plays a crucial role in helping cells adapt to metabolic stress. This enzyme is made up of three subunits: a catalytic alpha subunit, and regulatory beta and gamma subunits. Each of these subunits belongs to a larger isoform family. AMPK is regulated by AMP and by phosphorylation of the alpha subunit through allosteric mechanisms. The beta subunit undergoes post-translational modifications, including myristoylation and multi-site phosphorylation. In this study, we investigated how these modifications to the beta-1 subunit affect enzyme activity, assembly of the heterotrimer, and its location within the cell. We used site-directed mutagenesis and expressed the subunits in mammalian cells to examine these effects. When we removed the myristoylation site (G2A mutant), the enzyme became 4 times more active and the beta subunit relocated from a concentrated area outside the nucleus to a more evenly distributed location within the cell. On the other hand, mutating the serine-108 phosphorylation site to alanine inhibited the enzyme, but did not affect its cellular location. In contrast, mutations in the phosphorylation sites SS24, 25AA, and S182A did not impact enzyme activity, but caused the subunit to redistribute within the nucleus. Overall, these findings demonstrate that both myristoylation and phosphorylation of the beta subunit of AMPK play a role in regulating enzyme activity and its location within the cell, adding complexity to the regulation of AMPK.

title: Caloric restriction delays age-related methylation drift
text: The extended lifespan observed in mammals under caloric restriction is consistently linked to changes in DNA methylation, a form of epigenetic information. This DNA methylation is normally tightly regulated, but as mammals age, there is a noticeable shift in methylation patterns, with some sites gaining methylation and others losing it. In this study, the researchers found that this epigenetic drift is not only present in multiple species, but also correlates with lifespan. They conducted experiments on rhesus monkeys and mice, subjecting them to caloric restriction, and observed that the age-related methylation drift was reduced in these animals compared to the control group. In fact, the blood methylation age of the caloric-restricted monkeys appeared 7 years younger than their actual age. The effects were even more pronounced in the mice, with a 40% caloric restriction resulting in a significant reduction in age-related methylation drift. These changes in DNA methylation were consistent across different tissues and were also associated with changes in gene expression. Based on these findings, the researchers propose that epigenetic drift plays a role in determining lifespan in mammals.

title: Structural analysis of multiprotein complexes by cross-linking, mass spectrometry, and database searching.
text: The structural analysis of most protein complexes is challenging due to their inaccessibility to high resolution techniques. In this study, we present a novel approach that combines cross-linking, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics to investigate two human complexes, namely the NDEL1 homodimer and the NDC80 heterotetramer, which contain large coiled-coil segments. One major drawback of the cross-linking method has been the difficulty in identifying cross-linked peptides from fragmentation spectra. However, our innovative approach overcomes this limitation by developing a specialized database that matches spectra with cross-linked peptides. Additionally, we have devised a scoring system to assess the accuracy of our identifications and estimate false positive rates. Through our analysis, we have gained valuable insights into crucial structural parameters such as the directionality of the NDEL1 homodimeric coiled coil, the alignment of the NDC80 complex's heterodimeric coiled coils, and the arrangement of a tetramerization region within the NDC80 complex. Our approach is particularly valuable for studying complexes that are challenging to analyze using conventional structural methods.

title: The long non-coding RNA H19-derived miR-675 modulates human gastric cancer cell proliferation by targeting tumor suppressor RUNX1.
text: Recent research has shown that the lncRNA H19 is upregulated and plays a significant role in the development of gastric cancer. However, the exact molecular mechanism of H19 and its mature product miR-675 in the formation of gastric cancer is still unclear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between miR-675 and H19 in promoting the growth of gastric cancer cells. Our findings revealed a positive correlation between miR-675 and H19, suggesting that miR-675 acts as a crucial mediator in H19-induced gastric cancer cell growth. Further experiments confirmed that the tumor suppressor RUNX1 is a direct target of miR-675, as demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays and Western blotting analyses. Rescue assays also indicated that RUNX1 is involved in the phenotypic changes induced by H19/miR-675 in gastric cancer cells. Additionally, the expression of RUNX1 was found to be inversely related to H19/miR-675 in both gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. Overall, our study highlights the H19/miR-675/RUNX1 pathway as a novel regulator of gastric cancer development and suggests its potential as a therapeutic target for gastric cancer treatment.

title: Methylphenidate-induced erections in a prepubertal child.
text: Methylphenidate is commonly prescribed to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. In this case, we present the situation of a young child who experienced unintended erections upon starting a modified dosage of sustained release methylphenidate. Although priapism is an uncommon side effect of methylphenidate, it is crucial for physicians and parents to be informed about its potential for significant long-term complications.

title: Mechanism of NO-mediated oxidative and nitrative DNA damage in hamsters infected with Opisthorchis viverrini: a model of inflammation-mediated carcinogenesis.
text: Infection-induced inflammation plays a significant role in the development of cancer. Opisthorchis viverrini (OV) infection is a known risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma (CHCA), likely due to chronic inflammation. To investigate this further, we examined the formation of 8-nitroguanine and 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-oxodG), as well as the expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), in the livers of hamsters infected with OV. We successfully generated a specific anti-8-nitroguanine antibody that did not cross-react with other substances. Through double immunofluorescence staining, we observed that 8-oxodG and 8-nitroguanine were predominantly formed in the same inflammatory cells and epithelium of bile ducts starting from day 7, with the strongest immunoreactivity observed on days 21 and 30, respectively. Interestingly, even on day 180, when alanine aminotransferase activity had returned to normal levels, 8-oxodG and 8-nitroguanine were still present in the epithelium of bile ducts. The expression of iNOS correlated with the time course of 8-nitroguanine formation. Additionally, our study revealed that HO-1 expression and subsequent iron accumulation may contribute to the increased oxidative DNA damage in the epithelium of small bile ducts. In conclusion, the presence of nitrative and oxidative DNA damage, mediated by iNOS expression in hamsters infected with OV, may play a role in the development of CHCA.

title: Monte Carlo tests for associations between disease and alleles at highly polymorphic loci.
text: When comparing allele frequencies at a highly polymorphic locus between cases and controls in an association analysis, there is a potential issue with the conventional chi-squared test. This test may not be valid for a large, sparse contingency table. However, there is no longer a need to rely on statistics with known asymptotic distribution. Monte Carlo simulations can now be used to estimate the significance level of any test statistic. We have developed a Monte Carlo method for four 'chi-squared' test statistics, three of which involve combining alleles. We evaluated the performance of these statistics using real data. Combining rare alleles to avoid small expected cell counts and testing each allele against the rest reduced the power to detect a genuine association when there were a large number of alleles. To preserve the evidence for an association, we should either not combine alleles at all or combine them in a way that maintains the evidence.

title: KLF4-dependent phenotypic modulation of smooth muscle cells has a key role in atherosclerotic plaque pathogenesis
text: Previous studies on the role of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and macrophages in the development of atherosclerosis have yielded conflicting results due to unreliable methods for accurately identifying these cell types. In this study, we used Myh11-CreERT2 ROSA floxed STOP eYFP Apoe−/− mice to trace the lineage of SMCs. Surprisingly, traditional methods of detecting SMCs through immunostaining for SMC markers failed to identify more than 80% of SMC-derived cells within advanced atherosclerotic lesions. These unidentified SMC-derived cells exhibited characteristics of other cell lineages, such as macrophages and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). By specifically knocking out Krüppel-like factor 4 (Klf4) in SMCs, we observed a decrease in the number of SMC-derived MSC- and macrophage-like cells, a significant reduction in lesion size, and improvements in various indicators of plaque stability, including an increase in fibrous cap thickness compared to wild-type controls. Through in vivo KLF4 chromatin immunoprecipitation–sequencing (ChIP-seq) analyses and experiments with cholesterol-treated cultured SMCs, we identified over 800 KLF4 target genes, many of which regulate the pro-inflammatory responses of SMCs. Our findings suggest that the contribution of SMCs to atherosclerotic plaques has been greatly underestimated and that KLF4-dependent transitions in SMC phenotype play a critical role in the development of these lesions.
