The objective of this study was to use immunohistochemistry to compare the distribution of 6 matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, and 13) and 2 proinflammatory cytokines (interleukin-1beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha) in osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage with normal, age-matched articular cartilage. The researchers obtained articular cartilage samples from OA knees removed during arthroplasty and from normal, nonarthritic knees obtained at autopsy. The samples were fixed, processed, embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and examined using immunohistochemistry to detect MMP and cytokine production. Additionally, human articular chondrocytes (HAC) were treated in vitro with interleukin-1beta, tumor necrosis factor alpha, or phorbol myristate acetate to determine their ability to produce each MMP using Western blotting and gelatin zymography. 

The results showed that collagenases (MMPs 1, 8, and 13) and stromelysin 1 (MMP-3) were present in a proportion of chondrocytes in the superficial zone of most OA specimens with degenerative matrix changes. The gelatinases (MMPs 2 and 9) were also detected, but to a lesser extent. Chondrocytes positive for interleukin-1beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha were observed in the superficial zones of OA specimens. In contrast, normal cartilage specimens showed minimal immunostaining for these MMPs and cytokines. The deep zone of all OA specimens, where the cartilage matrix and chondrocyte morphology appeared normal, had much less immunostaining for MMPs and cytokines. The researchers confirmed that chondrocytes can produce these 6 MMPs using HAC cultures treated with interleukin-1beta, tumor necrosis factor alpha, or phorbol myristate acetate; the conditioned medium from activated HAC contained all the MMPs detected by immunohistochemistry. Dual immunolocalization studies of OA cartilage specimens showed that interleukin-1 coexpressed with MMP-8 in individual chondrocytes. 

In conclusion, the superficial zone of OA cartilage specimens, characterized by fibrillations, chondrocyte clusters, and degenerative matrix changes, contains a variable proportion of cells that immunostain for interleukin-1beta, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and 6 different MMPs. These findings support the idea that cytokine-MMP associations reflect a modified chondrocyte phenotype and an intrinsic process of cartilage degradation in OA.

title: β-catenin-independent WNT signaling in basal-like breast cancer and brain metastasis.
text: The role of WNT signaling in primary breast cancers of the basal-like subtype and its potential as a predictor of brain metastasis has been discussed. However, the specific WNT ligand responsible for this process has not been identified. To gain further insight into this matter, we conducted a comparative study involving 22 human breast cancer brain metastases, as well as the highly invasive human breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-231 and the less motile MCF-7 cell line, which serve as models for the basal-like and luminal A subtypes, respectively. Our analysis revealed that WNT5A and WNT5B were overexpressed in MDA-MB-231 cells compared to MCF-7 cells. Consequently, the invasiveness of MDA-MB-231 cells was reduced when treated with WNT inhibitors, whereas the invasion of MCF-7 cells was enhanced by recombinant WNT5B and inhibited by WNT and Jun-N-terminal kinase antagonists. The expression and subcellular distribution of β-catenin, a key component of the WNT signaling pathway, remained unaffected. Interestingly, β-catenin was not found in the nuclei of brain metastases, but strong nuclear c-Jun staining was observed. Similar to MDA-MB-231 cells, the metastases exhibited expression of WNT5A/B and the alternative WNT receptors ROR1 and ROR2. These findings were further validated using external gene expression datasets from different breast cancer subtypes and brain metastases. Hierarchical cluster analysis revealed a close relationship between basal-like cancers and brain metastases. Gene set enrichment analyses confirmed the enrichment of the WNT pathway not only in basal-like primary tumors but also in cerebral metastases of all subtypes. In conclusion, WNT signaling appears to be highly relevant for basal-like and other subtypes of breast cancers that metastasize to the brain. β-catenin-independent WNT signaling, likely mediated through ROR1 and ROR2, plays a significant role in this context.

title: Retinal attenuates inflammatory arthritis by reciprocal regulation of IL-17-producing T cells and Foxp3(+) regulatory T cells and the inhibition of osteoclastogenesis.
text: The purpose of this research was to investigate whether a derivative of vitamin A called retinal can reduce inflammation and joint damage in mice with collagen-induced arthritis. The study found that mice treated with retinal had lower arthritis scores and incidence compared to those treated with cottonseed oil. The mice treated with retinal also had less joint damage and fewer immune cells infiltrating their joints. Additionally, the expression of proinflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress proteins, and osteoclast markers was reduced in mice treated with retinal. In laboratory experiments, retinal increased the expression of a protein called Foxp3, which is associated with regulatory T cells, and inhibited the development of Th17 cells, which are involved in inflammation. The proportion of regulatory T cells was increased in the spleens of mice treated with retinal, while the proportion of Th17 cells was reduced. In both mice and a human culture system, retinal reduced the number of cells associated with bone destruction. The expression of markers for osteoclast differentiation was also decreased with the addition of retinal. This study is the first to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of retinal in an autoimmune arthritis model by regulating Th17 and regulatory T cells and protecting against osteoclast activation. Overall, these findings suggest that retinal has significant immunoregulatory effects and could be a valuable treatment for autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

title: NRAGE promotes the malignant phenotype of hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a deadly disease due to the lack of effective therapies for advanced or recurrent stages. To improve patient prognosis, it is crucial to find a biomarker for HCC progression and a molecular target for treatment. Neurotrophin receptor-interacting melanoma antigen-encoding protein (NRAGE) is a protein that plays a role in apoptosis and cell death by interacting with various proteins. Its function in HCC is unknown, so this study aimed to uncover its role in HCC tumorigenesis. Tumor and non-cancerous liver tissues from 151 HCC patients, as well as HCC cell lines, were analyzed using polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemical techniques to measure NRAGE expression levels and the levels of genes encoding interacting proteins. The study found that NRAGE mRNA levels were significantly correlated with apoptosis-antagonizing transcription factor (AATF) levels and were higher in HCC tissues compared to non-cancerous liver tissues unaffected by cirrhosis. The expression patterns of NRAGE protein and mRNA were consistent in representative specimen pairs. Additionally, increased NRAGE expression in HCC patients was associated with a shorter disease-specific survival time and was identified as an independent prognostic factor. These findings suggest that increased NRAGE expression contributes to HCC progression through its interaction with AATF and may serve as a new biomarker and therapeutic target for HCC treatment.

title: Regulation of ISW2 by concerted action of histone H4 tail and extranucleosomal DNA.
text: DNA footprinting and photoaffinity labeling experiments using recombinant histone octamers have demonstrated that the stable interaction between ISW2 and nucleosomal DNA occurs approximately 20 base pairs away from the dyad. This interaction specifically requires the presence of the histone H4 N-terminal tail. Efficient remodeling by ISW2 also relies on the H4 N-terminal tail, although its absence can be partially compensated for by increasing the incubation time or concentration of ISW2. Additionally, the length of extranucleosomal DNA has an impact on the stable interaction between ISW2 and the internal nucleosomal site, with the optimal length being between 70 and 85 base pairs. These findings suggest that the histone H4 tail, in conjunction with an appropriate length of extranucleosomal DNA, plays a role in recruiting and properly orienting ISW2 onto the nucleosome, thereby facilitating efficient nucleosome remodeling. This property of ISW2 is likely responsible for its observed nucleosome spacing activity.

title: Embryonic Stem Cells for Severe Heart Failure: Why and How?
text: The knowledge gained from cardiac cell therapy suggests that it is unlikely to achieve regeneration of extensively damaged areas of the heart solely through the paracrine effects of the transplanted cells. Instead, it is necessary for these cells to be converted into cardiomyocytes that can replace the irreversibly lost ones. Using human pluripotent embryonic stem cells in this context is highly justified. Encouraging experimental results have been obtained in animal models of heart attacks. However, before clinical applications can be implemented, several critical issues need to be addressed. These include optimizing the cardiac specification of the embryonic stem cells, purifying the resulting progenitor cells to ensure a contamination-free population that does not carry the risk of tumor formation, and finding clinically acceptable methods to prevent rejection of the transplanted cells by the recipient's immune system. Solving these problems is essential for the success of this approach. Additionally, the therapeutic success will also depend on efficiently delivering the cells to the target tissue, ensuring their survival after transplantation, and enabling their spatial organization in a way that allows them to contribute to the heart's contractile function.

title: A comparison of letrozole to gonadotropins for ovulation induction, in subjects who failed to conceive with clomiphene citrate.
text:
AIM To compare the pregnancy rates (PR) of letrozole and gonadotropins in individuals who were unsuccessful in conceiving with clomiphene citrate (CC). 

METHODS This study was conducted as a retrospective cohort study at a university reproductive center. The participants included individuals who were treated with letrozole or gonadotropins after failing to conceive with CC. The interventions involved controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH), transvaginal ultrasound, ovulation induction, and intrauterine insemination (IUI). 

OUTCOME MEASURES The main outcome measure was the pregnancy rates per cycle. 

RESULTS Among patients who were unable to conceive after at least three cycles of CC, gonadotropins had a higher pregnancy rate per cycle compared to letrozole. However, among individuals who failed to conceive after less than three cycles of CC and had their medications changed due to a thin uterine lining or intolerable side effects, the average pregnancy rates per cycle for letrozole and gonadotropin treatments were similar. All patients achieved conception within three stimulation cycles using either gonadotropins or letrozole. 

CONCLUSIONS In patients who were unsuccessful in conceiving with CC, gonadotropins have a higher pregnancy rate for ovulation induction compared to letrozole. However, the pregnancy rates with letrozole were still high enough to justify its use in this specific patient population. It is recommended that letrozole and gonadotropins should not be used for more than three cycles without achieving conception.

title: Epigenetic mechanisms in neurological disease
text: New and groundbreaking discoveries are being made in the field of brain epigenomes, which encompass different forms of DNA methylation and covalent histone modifications. These findings are shedding light on the intricate processes involved in neural development, neurological diseases, and aging. In the past, defects in chromatin within the brain were believed to be fixed abnormalities occurring during early development and associated with rare genetic syndromes. However, it is now evident that mutations and dysfunctions in the epigenetic machinery span a broader spectrum, including adult-onset neurodegenerative diseases. In this article, we will explore how recent advancements in neuroepigenetics have enhanced our understanding of developmental and degenerative brain disorders. Additionally, we will discuss the potential impact of these discoveries on the development of future therapies for these conditions.

title: Reversal of the cellular phenotype in the premature aging disease Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a disease that causes premature aging in children. It is caused by a spontaneous mutation in a gene called lamin A, which is an important part of the nucleus in mammalian cells. This mutation leads to the production of a shortened version of lamin A and a decrease in the normal lamin A protein. Cells from individuals with HGPS have abnormal structures in the nucleus. However, our research shows that this disease can be reversed in these cells. Introducing the normal lamin A protein does not fix the symptoms of the disease. Instead, we can eliminate the mutant lamin A protein by correcting the abnormal splicing of the LMNA gene using a modified oligonucleotide. When the splicing is corrected, the cells from individuals with HGPS return to a normal nuclear structure. The abnormal distribution and levels of certain proteins associated with the nucleus are also fixed, as well as defects in specific modifications of histones, which are proteins involved in gene regulation. Additionally, the expression of several genes that were misregulated in HGPS is restored to normal. These findings demonstrate that it is possible to correct the premature aging symptoms in individuals with HGPS.

title: Agouti-related peptide–expressing neurons are mandatory for feeding
text: The expression of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus is regulated by multiple hormones involved in energy balance. Surprisingly, when the genes responsible for producing NPY and/or AgRP are deactivated in mice, it does not affect their food intake. However, our study reveals that specifically targeting and eliminating AgRP-expressing neurons in adult mice leads to an immediate decrease in feeding. This provides direct evidence that these neurons play a crucial role in regulating energy balance.

title: Predictors of survival after acute paraquat poisoning.
text: Acute paraquat poisoning is frequently fatal, and although various treatment methods have been studied, there is currently no standard treatment available. This study aimed to identify the factors that predict survival in 602 patients who experienced acute paraquat poisoning. The level of paraquat exposure was determined by the amount ingested and a semi-quantitative measurement of paraquat in the urine. Upon arrival at the emergency room, initial clinical parameters such as vital signs, hemoglobin levels, white blood cell count, pH levels, PaCO2, PaO2, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, amylase, and glucose were recorded. The outcomes of acute paraquat poisoning were divided into two categories: survivors and non-survivors. Multiple logistic regression analysis was used to identify the predictors of survival. Among patients who ingested paraquat orally, 55.5% survived, while all those exposed through percutaneous or inhalational routes survived. The average amount of paraquat ingested was 45.6 +/- 74.1 mL (mean +/- standard deviation), with a concentration of 24.5% of 1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridium dichloride. In addition to the level of paraquat exposure, survival after acute paraquat poisoning was associated with age, respiratory rate, pH levels, PaCO2, hemoglobin levels, white blood cell count, blood urea nitrogen, amylase levels, and the number of failed organs, as determined by multiple logistic regression analysis. In conclusion, younger age, exposure through percutaneous or inhalational routes, lower levels of paraquat exposure, and lesser degrees of leukocytosis, acidosis, and renal, hepatic, and pancreatic failures upon admission are positive prognostic factors for survival after acute paraquat poisoning.

title: Decreased neurogenesis after cholinergic forebrain lesion in the adult rat.
text: The regulation of adult neurogenesis is influenced by various external signals, such as hormones, growth factors, and neurotransmitters. The cholinergic system in the basal forebrain is an important transmitter system for learning and memory. Since adult neurogenesis is linked to cognitive performance, this study aims to determine the role of cholinergic input in adult neurogenesis using an immunotoxic lesion method. Cholinergic neurons in the cholinergic basal forebrain (CBF), which connect to the two main regions of adult neurogenesis (the dentate gyrus and the olfactory bulb), were selectively damaged by infusing the immunotoxin 192IgG-saporin into the lateral ventricle of adult rats. Five weeks after the lesion, there was a significant decrease in neurogenesis, as indicated by a reduction in the number of cells that expressed both bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) and the neuronal nuclei marker NeuN in the granule cell layers of the dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb. Additionally, the immunotoxic lesion to the CBF resulted in an increased number of apoptotic cells specifically in the subgranular zone (the progenitor region of the dentate gyrus) and the periglomerular layer of the olfactory bulb. We propose that the cholinergic system promotes the survival of neuronal progenitors and immature neurons in regions of adult neurogenesis, similar to its effects during brain development. As a working hypothesis, the loss of neurons in the CBF system not only leads to cognitive deficits but also affects the functionality of the dentate gyrus at a cellular level, potentially exacerbating cognitive impairments.

title: DNA Methylation in Major Depressive Disorder.
text: The regulation of gene expression is controlled by epigenetic mechanisms, which have an impact on protein levels and ultimately shape characteristics throughout life. However, both random variations in epigenetics and environmental influences on the epigenome can affect neurodevelopment and aging, potentially contributing to the development of mental health issues. Understanding the role of epigenetic mechanisms is difficult due to the need to consider changes that are specific to genotype, tissue, and cell type, while the complex nature of mental disorders also presents challenges in linking them to biological factors. In this chapter, we provide a summary of the current evidence suggesting that DNA methylation plays a significant role as an epigenetic mechanism in major depressive disorder.

title: Consensus structural features of purified bacterial TatABC complexes.
text:
We conducted a study on the twin-arginine translocation (Tat) system, which is responsible for transporting folded proteins across bacterial plasma membranes and the chloroplast thylakoid membrane. Our investigation focused on the composition and structural organization of three purified Tat complexes from Escherichia coli, Salmonella typhimurium, and Agrobacterium tumefaciens.

To begin, we confirmed the functional activity of these Tat systems in vivo. By expressing the tatABC operons from S. typhimurium or A. tumefaciens in an E. coli tat null mutant strain, we observed efficient Tat-dependent export of an E. coli cofactor-containing substrate called TMAO reductase. This demonstrated that the Tat systems from these bacterial species were fully functional.

The three Tat complexes we isolated were tagged with an affinity tag and consisted of TatA, TatB, and TatC subunits. This indicated a strong interaction between these three subunits. Using single-particle electron microscopy, we examined the structure of all three complexes. We observed oval-shaped, asymmetric particles with maximum dimensions of up to 13 nm. A notable feature was the presence of stain-excluding densities surrounding central pools of stain, suggesting the presence of protein-lined pores or cavities.

The size variation among the particles suggested a modular form of assembly and/or the recruitment of varying numbers of TatBC/TatA units. Despite having low levels of sequence homology, our combined data indicated both structural and functional conservation in the Tat systems of these three bacterial species.

title: Advances in graft-versus-host disease biology and therapy
text: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is utilized for the treatment of various disorders, but its effectiveness is hindered by the occurrence of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in comprehending the role of stimulating and inhibitory components of the adaptive and innate immune systems in both the donor and the host, contributing to the development of GVHD. Fresh insights from fundamental immunology, preclinical models, and clinical studies have paved the way for innovative strategies in prevention and treatment. This article highlights recent advancements in understanding the pathophysiology of GVHD and its management, with a particular emphasis on immune system manipulations that can be applied in a clinical setting.

title: Ly6Chi monocytes direct alternatively activated profibrotic macrophage regulation of lung fibrosis.
text:
RATIONALE: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating disease with no benefit from anti-inflammatory therapies, such as corticosteroids. The role of monocytes and macrophages in IPF is controversial.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to determine the role of monocytes and macrophages in lung fibrogenesis and resolution, as well as investigate the phenotype of these cells.

METHODS: Multiple in vivo depletional strategies were used, along with adoptive transfer techniques. Samples from IPF patients were also analyzed.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Depletion of lung macrophages during fibrogenesis resulted in reduced pulmonary fibrosis, as indicated by measurements of lung collagen, fibrosis score, and quantitative polymerase chain reaction for fibrosis markers. There was also a decrease in markers of the profibrotic alternative macrophage activation phenotype. The alternative macrophage marker CD163 was expressed on lung macrophages from IPF patients. Depletion of circulating monocytes reduced pulmonary fibrosis and the number of alternatively activated lung macrophages. However, adoptive transfer of these monocytes during fibrogenesis exacerbated fibrosis, although they were not found in the recipient's lungs.

CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the importance of circulating monocytes and lung macrophages in pulmonary fibrosis, particularly the alternatively activated macrophage phenotype. It also suggests that Ly6Chi monocytes contribute to the progression of fibrosis but do not engraft into the lungs. Additionally, empirical data suggests that macrophages may play a role in resolving bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis during the reversible phase.

title: A single RNA-dependent RNA polymerase assembles with mutually exclusive nucleotidyl transferase subunits to direct different pathways of small RNA biogenesis.
text: The conserved family of eukaryotic RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (Rdrs) play a role in the synthesis of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) intermediates in various pathways of small RNA (sRNA) biogenesis and RNA-mediated silencing. However, the Rdr-dependent pathways and the Rdr enzymes themselves are not well understood compared to their viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase counterparts. In a previous study, we demonstrated a connection between the Tetrahymena thermophila Rdr, Rdr1, and a Dicer enzyme, Dcr2, in the production of approximately 24-nucleotide (nt) sRNA in vitro. In this study, we investigate the endogenous complexes that contain Rdr1, known as RDRCs. RDRCs consist of different combinations of Rdr1 and four associated proteins. Two of these proteins, Rdn1 and Rdn2, have unique ribonucleotidyl transferase motifs. Our findings show that Rdn1 and Rdn2 are uridine-specific polymerases in separate RDRCs. Two other RDRC subunits, Rdf1 and Rdf2, are only present in RDRCs that contain Rdn1. We found that the catalytic activity of Rdr1 is still present in RDRCs purified from cell extracts that lack nonessential RDRC subunits (Rdn2, Rdf1, Rdf2) or if the RDRC contains an inactive Rdn. However, disrupting each RDRC has distinct consequences at the cellular level and affects the accumulation of specific 23-24-nt sRNA sequences in vivo. Our study reveals a previously unknown complexity of Rdr-dependent sRNA biogenesis in vivo, both in terms of its biochemical and biological aspects.

title: Identification of T6SS-dependent effector and immunity proteins by Tn-seq in Vibrio cholerae.
text: The Type VI protein secretion system (T6SS) plays a crucial role in bacterial competition by killing neighboring competitors through direct contact. T6SS delivers specific proteins, known as effectors, to nearby cells, while corresponding antagonistic proteins provide immunity against these effectors when delivered by sister cells. Despite being present in over 100 gram-negative bacteria, including many human pathogens, the specific effector and immunity proteins involved in T6SS have not been extensively studied. In this study, we utilized a high-throughput approach called transposon mutagenesis and deep sequencing (Tn-seq) to identify T6SS immunity proteins in Vibrio cholerae. We performed saturating transposon mutagenesis in both the wild type and a T6SS null mutant. Genes encoding immunity proteins were predicted to be essential in the wild type but dispensable in the T6SS mutant. By comparing the abundance of each transposon mutant in the mutant library using deep sequencing, we successfully identified three immunity proteins that provide protection against killing by T6SS predatory cells. Additionally, we discovered three corresponding T6SS-secreted effectors and demonstrated their importance not only in antibacterial and antieukaryotic activities but also in the assembly of the T6SS apparatus. The identification of lipase and muramidase T6SS effectors in this study highlights the diverse range of T6SS-secreted substances and the distinct mechanisms involved in their secretion by the dynamic T6SS organelle.

title: Immunotherapy of metastatic kidney cancer.
text: Between April 1986 and September 2000, a total of 122 patients with MRCC were treated using monthly intralymphatic injections. These injections contained an average of 573 IL-2 U and 26 x 10(6) LAK cells. Additionally, patients received i.m. administration of IFN and TF. Out of these patients, 71 also underwent a 3-day cycle of monthly IL-2 inhalations, with an average of 998 daily U. For comparison, 89 MRCC cases were not treated with immunotherapy and served as historical controls. The treatment had minimal adverse side effects. Out of the 122 patients, 11 achieved complete remission (CR) and 13 achieved partial remission (PR), resulting in a total of 24 responding patients. Among these responders, 17 experienced disease progression again, while 7 remained in remission for a period ranging from 11 to 69 months. The median survival of treated patients was 28 months, which was 3.5 times higher than the median survival of the historical controls (7.5 months). A Kaplan-Meier curve demonstrated a 25% survival rate 11 years after the initiation of immunotherapy. It appears that the addition of IL-2 inhalation improved survival rates. This immunotherapy protocol has shown to be effective, safe, and without significant adverse side effects. It is also more cost-effective compared to other treatments and provides a good quality of life for MRCC patients. If confirmed in a multicenter trial, this protocol could serve as the foundation for developing low-dose immunomodulatory treatments.

title: Autoimmune T cell responses in the central nervous system
text: The role of autoreactive T cell responses in diseases of the central nervous system (CNS), such as multiple sclerosis, is crucial. Recent evidence suggests that CNS autoimmunity can be caused by two distinct types of CD4+ T cells, which produce either interferon-γ or interleukin-17. The activity of these CD4+ T cell subsets within the CNS affects the development and progression of the disease. Additionally, new animal models have shown that myelin-specific CD8+ T cells can also contribute to CNS autoimmunity. This review focuses on recent advancements in understanding the mechanisms, regulation, and interaction between these different T cell subsets in CNS autoimmunity.

title: Effects of FXR in foam-cell formation and atherosclerosis development.
text:
The Farnesoid X receptor (FXR) is a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily that is activated by bile acids. It plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of bile acids, cholesterol, and triglycerides in the body. When the FXR gene is disrupted in mice, it leads to an unhealthy lipid profile with increased levels of cholesterol and triglycerides, which can contribute to the development of atherosclerosis.

However, the specific role of FXR in foam-cell formation and the progression of atherosclerosis is not well understood. In a recent study, researchers found that macrophages isolated from mice lacking the FXR gene took up less oxidized LDL-cholesterol (oxLDL-C), a key factor in foam-cell formation. This decrease in oxLDL-C uptake was accompanied by a significant reduction in CD36 expression, a protein involved in lipid uptake, in these macrophages. Interestingly, FXR was not detected in these macrophages, suggesting that the effect is independent of FXR.

To further investigate the impact of FXR on atherosclerosis development, the researchers generated mice lacking both FXR and ApoE, another protein involved in lipid metabolism. Female mice were used for the analysis of atherosclerosis. Surprisingly, the FXR/ApoE double-null mice had smaller atherosclerotic lesions in their aortas compared to mice lacking only ApoE, despite having even higher levels of cholesterol and triglycerides in their blood. These findings suggest that disruption of the FXR gene may actually attenuate the progression of atherosclerosis, possibly due to the reduced uptake of oxLDL-C by macrophages.

Overall, this study highlights the importance of considering factors beyond serum lipid levels when evaluating the effectiveness of FXR modulators in treating hyperlipidemia. The findings suggest that targeting FXR may have potential therapeutic benefits in preventing or slowing down the development of atherosclerosis.

title: Purkinje cell compartments in the reeler mutant mouse as revealed by Zebrin II and 90-acetylated glycolipid antigen expression
text: The cerebellum is divided into bands that are aligned in a parasagittal manner. These bands can be seen through histological staining of Purkinje cell sets using specific antibodies. In this study, we compared the staining patterns of normal mice using these antibodies and an antibody to calbindin, with those of reeler mutants. Reeler mutants have impaired Purkinje cell migration beneath the cerebellar white matter. The results showed that despite their abnormal location in subcortical masses, Purkinje cells in reeler mutants still exhibited a tendency to distribute into alternating zones that either stained for Zebrin II or for P-path. There were also transition zones with mixed labeling. However, the number of zones in the mutants was lower compared to normal mice. The mutants had around 7-9 zones per side, while wild type mice had 14 major divisions. These findings suggest that neurons expressing these markers may be segregated during their migration, and the final phase of migration into the cortex may involve further splitting or interdigitation between cell sets expressing the two antigens.

title: Awake craniotomy with brain mapping as the routine surgical approach to treating patients with supratentorial intraaxial tumors: a prospective trial of 200 cases.
text: In a prospective trial conducted at a single institution, awake craniotomy was used as the standard surgical approach for supratentorial intraaxial tumors, regardless of involvement of eloquent cortex. The study included 200 patients who were all treated by the same surgeon. Patient presentations, comorbid conditions, tumor locations, and histological characteristics were documented. Brain mapping was successfully performed in 195 out of 200 patients (97.5%). The overall complication rate was 16.5%, with a total of 33 patients experiencing complications. The mortality rate was 1%, with two deaths occurring in the series. New postoperative neurological deficits were observed in 13% of patients, but only 4.5% of these deficits were permanent. Patients with gliomas or preoperative neurological deficits, as well as those who had undergone prior radiation therapy or surgery, had higher complication rates. However, no patient who entered the operating room without neurological deficits sustained a permanent deficit postoperatively. Among the most recent 50 patients treated, three (6%) required intensive care unit stays, and the median total hospital stay was one day. In conclusion, awake craniotomy is a practical and effective surgical approach for supratentorial tumors, with a low complication rate. It offers an excellent alternative to craniotomy under general anesthesia, as it allows for brain mapping and avoids the need for general anesthesia. Additionally, the use of awake craniotomy can significantly reduce resource utilization by minimizing intensive care time and total hospital stay.

title: Reactive Oxygen Species Localization Programs Inflammation to Clear Microbes of Different Size
text: The mechanism by which the number of immune cells recruited to infection sites is determined and adjusted based on the differences in cellular composition between the host and pathogen remains unknown. In this study, we have discovered that reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a role as sensors of microbe size. By detecting the varying distribution of ROS produced in response to microbes of different sizes, neutrophils regulate their interleukin (IL)-1β expression through the selective oxidation of NF-κB, enabling the implementation of distinct inflammatory responses. When encountering small microbes, ROS are generated within the neutrophils, suppressing IL-1β expression to limit the recruitment of neutrophils, as each phagocyte is capable of eliminating multiple pathogens. Conversely, when encountering large microbes, ROS are generated outside the neutrophils, leading to an amplification of IL-1β expression and the recruitment of numerous neutrophils, forming cooperative clusters. Impairments in the ability to sense microbe size through ROS-mediated mechanisms result in excessive neutrophil infiltration and clustering in response to small microbes, contributing to inflammatory diseases. These findings emphasize the importance of ROS localization in signal transduction.

title: Helicobacter pylori infection triggers aberrant expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase in gastric epithelium
text: Infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) increases the risk of developing gastric cancer. Our study demonstrates that when gastric epithelial cells are infected with cag pathogenicity island (cagPAI)-positive H. pylori, it leads to abnormal expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID). AID belongs to the cytidine-deaminase family and functions as an enzyme for editing DNA and RNA. This abnormal expression of AID is induced through the IκB kinase–dependent nuclear factor-κB activation pathway. Consequently, H. pylori infection causes an increase in AID levels, resulting in the accumulation of genetic alterations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene in gastric cells in laboratory settings. These findings suggest that the abnormal expression of AID caused by H. pylori infection may contribute to the accumulation of mutations in the gastric mucosa during the development of H. pylori–associated gastric cancer.

title: The role of the immune response during SIVagm infection of the African green monkey natural host.
text: The African green monkey (AGM) is one of several African species that are naturally infected with simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV). Unlike other hosts, AGMs do not develop AIDS, making it crucial to understand why they are resistant to disease progression. Initially, our group focused on identifying immune mechanisms that could potentially control the virus, but we did not find any clear candidates. This assumption was proven wrong when we discovered that SIVagm replicates in AGMs just as vigorously as HIV-1 does in humans. Consequently, our attention shifted towards identifying immunopathologic features present in susceptible hosts but absent in AGMs. The remarkable immune tolerance of AGMs to the SIVagm core protein led us to hypothesize that anti-Gag antibodies may form immune complexes, trapping the virus in lymph nodes and causing immune dysfunction. However, testing this hypothesis in vivo has proven challenging. Therefore, our current research focuses on the possibility that T-cell tolerance to Gag plays a crucial role in preventing the devastating immune system collapse seen in heterologous primate hosts infected with immunodeficiency viruses.

title: The S-LANSS score for identifying pain of predominantly neuropathic origin: validation for use in clinical and postal research.
text: This article presents the development and validation of the S-LANSS score, which is a self-report version of the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs pain scale. The purpose of the S-LANSS is to identify neuropathic pain, as opposed to nociceptive pain, without the need for a clinical examination. Two hundred patients with chronic pain were asked to complete the S-LANSS on their own. Afterwards, a researcher administered the S-LANSS scale and the Neuropathic Pain Scale (NPS) through interviews. An independent clinician determined the type of pain (neuropathic or nociceptive) and rated their certainty of the diagnosis. The S-LANSS scale was also included in a chronic pain questionnaire that was sent to 160 community patients and 150 newly referred patients waiting for pain clinic assessment. The self-completed S-LANSS correctly identified 75% of pain types, while the interview format identified 80%. The sensitivity of self-completed S-LANSS scores ranged from 74% to 78%, depending on the cutoff score. There were significant associations between NPS items and total score with S-LANSS score. In the postal survey, 57% of patients (n = 174) returned completed questionnaires. The internal consistency and convergent validity of the survey S-LANSS scores were confirmed. These findings support the validity and reliability of the S-LANSS scale as a self-report tool for identifying neuropathic pain, and it is also suitable for use in postal survey research. Having valid measures of symptoms and signs in neuropathic pain will enable standardized comparisons with other investigative measures, potentially leading to new insights into the relationship between pathophysiologic mechanisms and clinical manifestations of pain.

title: Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test.
text: The aim of this study was to determine whether a test of asymmetry of funnel plots can predict discrepancies between meta-analyses and large trials, and to assess the prevalence of bias in published meta-analyses. The researchers conducted a Medline search to find pairs consisting of a meta-analysis and a single large trial. They analyzed funnel plots from 37 meta-analyses found in four general medicine journals from 1993-1996, as well as 38 meta-analyses from the second 1996 issue of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. The main outcome measure was the degree of funnel plot asymmetry. The results showed that out of the eight pairs of meta-analysis and large trial identified, four were concordant and four were discordant. Discordance was due to meta-analyses showing larger effects. Funnel plot asymmetry was present in three out of four discordant pairs, but none of the concordant pairs. In 38% of journal meta-analyses and 13% of Cochrane reviews, funnel plot asymmetry indicated bias. In conclusion, analyzing funnel plots can be a useful tool for detecting bias in meta-analyses, but caution should be exercised when interpreting results from meta-analyses based on a limited number of small trials.

title: Exploring Metabolic Configurations of Single Cells within Complex Tissue Microenvironments.
text: In recent years, there has been a growing body of evidence showing the importance of metabolism in various cellular functions and how changes in metabolism can affect cell differentiation and fate. In this study, we introduce a method to examine the metabolic state of individual cells in their natural tissue environment. This is achieved by visualizing and quantifying multiple enzymatic activities under optimal substrate conditions, followed by identifying the specific cell types. To validate this approach and showcase its potential, we investigated the metabolic profiles of different immune cell populations in both healthy and tumor colon tissue. Additionally, we explored the metabolic interactions between cancer cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts in a breast cancer tissue array. Our findings highlight the usefulness of assessing metabolic configurations in single cells as a valuable tool for researchers studying metabolic networks in their native context.

title: Twenty-four hour and early morning blood pressure control of olmesartan vs. ramipril in elderly hypertensive patients: pooled individual data analysis of two randomized, double-blind, parallel-group studies.
text:
The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness of olmesartan medoxomil and ramipril in reducing 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure (ABP) in elderly hypertensive patients. The study analyzed pooled data from two studies with identical designs, one conducted in Italy and one in Europe.

A total of 1453 elderly hypertensive patients (aged 65-89 years) with sitting office diastolic blood pressure (DBP) between 90-109 mmHg and/or sitting office systolic blood pressure (SBP) between 140-179 mmHg underwent a 2-week placebo wash-out period. After the wash-out period, the patients were randomly assigned to receive a 12-week double-blind treatment with either olmesartan medoxomil 10 mg or ramipril 2.5 mg once daily. The dosage was increased to 20 and 40 mg for olmesartan medoxomil and 5 and 10 mg for ramipril after 2 and 6 weeks, respectively, for patients whose office blood pressure had not normalized. 24-hour ABP was measured at the beginning of the study and after 12 weeks of treatment.

The results showed that in 715 patients with valid baseline and end-of-treatment recordings, olmesartan medoxomil resulted in greater reductions in 24-hour SBP and DBP compared to ramipril. The differences between the two treatments were statistically significant [SBP: 2.2 (3.8, 0.6), P = 0.006; DBP: 1.3 (2.2, 0.3), P = 0.009]. Olmesartan medoxomil also showed greater reductions in blood pressure during the last 6 hours of the dosing interval and had higher smoothness indices compared to ramipril. Additionally, olmesartan medoxomil reduced the morning rise in SBP, while ramipril did not. Among the 582 patients with sustained hypertension, olmesartan medoxomil still showed a greater antihypertensive effect compared to ramipril [SBP: 2.1 (3.9, 0.4), P = 0.019; DBP: 1.2 (2.3, 0.1), P = 0.032].

In conclusion, olmesartan medoxomil is more effective in controlling 24-hour blood pressure in elderly hypertensive patients compared to ramipril, especially during the hours furthest from the last intake of medication.

title: Abi1 is essential for the formation and activation of a WAVE2 signalling complex
text: WAVE2 is a protein that plays a role in rearranging actin by transmitting signals from Rac to the Arp2/3 complex, which leads to the formation of lamellipodia protrusions. In laboratory settings, WAVE2 has been found to have the ability to initiate actin nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex, but it does not directly bind to Rac. Instead, it forms larger complexes that have been reported to have both positive and negative regulatory effects. However, the process of assembling, localizing, and activating these complexes in living organisms is still not fully understood. In this study, we utilized tandem mass spectrometry to identify a complex based on Abi1, which includes WAVE2, Nap1, and PIR121. Abi1 directly interacts with the WHD domain of WAVE2, enhancing its actin polymerization activity and facilitating the formation of a WAVE2–Abi1–Nap1–PIR121 complex. This complex, along with the WAVE2–Abi1 sub-complex, is equally effective in stimulating the Arp2/3 complex. Upon Rac activation, the WAVE2–Abi1–Nap1–PIR121 complex is relocated to the leading edge of ruffles in living organisms. Consistently, when Abi1 is inhibited through RNA interference, Rac-dependent lamellipodia protrusion is disrupted. Therefore, Abi1 plays a crucial role in orchestrating the proper assembly and activation of the WAVE2 complex at the leading edge in living organisms.

title: The dendritic cell lineage: ontogeny and function of dendritic cells and their subsets in the steady state and the inflamed setting.
text: The formation of dendritic cells (DCs) creates an extraordinary cellular network that influences adaptive immune responses based on external signals. Extensive research over the past forty years has revealed that DCs originate from a separate hematopoietic lineage, setting them apart from other types of white blood cells and establishing the DC system as a distinct branch of hematopoiesis. Recent studies have further demonstrated that DCs in different tissues consist of unique subsets that have distinct roles in regulating the function of T lymphocytes. This article explores significant progress in our comprehension of how DC lineage commitment, differentiation, diversification, and function are regulated within their natural environment.

title: IL-15 Receptor Deletion Results in Circadian Changes of Locomotor and Metabolic Activity
text: The cytokine Interleukin-15 (IL-15) is produced in the normal brain and interacts with its specific receptor IL-15Rα, as well as co-receptors IL-2Rβ and IL-2Rγ, in neuronal cells. However, the exact functions of the IL-15 system in the brain are still unclear. In order to investigate the hypothesis that IL-15Rα plays a role in regulating metabolic activity and body temperature, we examined the specific metabolic characteristics of mice lacking IL-15Rα. These mice appeared normal but were leaner and had lower levels of body fat. Throughout the day, the knockout mice exhibited significantly higher levels of locomotor activity and heat dissipation. During the light phase, they also showed increased food intake, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production. This difference between the light and dark phases suggests that IL-15Rα is involved in regulating circadian rhythms. The higher oxygen consumption during the light phase indicates that the knockout mice undergo adaptive thermogenesis. Furthermore, the body temperature of the receptor knockout mice was significantly higher than that of the control mice during the light phase, particularly between 0600 and 0900 h. In addition to conducting metabolic chamber studies and circadian rhythm analyses, we also performed qPCR on hypothalamic homogenates, which revealed higher mRNA expression of orexin and transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 cation channels. This suggests that IL-15Rα has a direct impact on the hypothalamus. Indeed, when we treated wild-type mice with IL-15, we observed increased c-Fos expression in the preoptic area, indicating activation of hypothalamic neurons. In conclusion, our findings suggest that IL-15 activation of hypothalamic neurons in mice contributes to thermoregulation and modifies the metabolic characteristics of the animals.

title: Vaginal progesterone, cerclage or cervical pessary for preventing preterm birth in asymptomatic singleton pregnant women with a history of preterm birth and a sonographic short cervix.
text: The aim of this study was to compare the outcomes of pregnancy in women with a history of preterm birth and a short cervix who were managed with different treatment protocols: cerclage, vaginal progesterone, or cervical pessary. The study included 142 women treated with cerclage in the USA, 59 women treated with vaginal progesterone in the UK, and 42 women treated with cervical pessary in Spain. Perinatal outcomes were compared among the three groups. The results showed no significant differences in perinatal losses, neonatal morbidity, and preterm births between the three groups, except for a higher rate of preterm birth before 34 weeks' gestation in the vaginal progesterone group compared to the cervical pessary group. However, when comparing only the subgroups of women with a cervical length less than 25 mm, regardless of gestational age, the difference between these two groups was not statistically significant. In conclusion, cerclage, vaginal progesterone, and cervical pessary appear to be equally effective management strategies for women with a singleton pregnancy, previous spontaneous preterm birth, and a short cervix. Further randomized comparisons of these strategies, or combinations thereof, are needed to determine the optimal management approach.

title: The oxytocinase subfamily of M1 aminopeptidases.
text: The placental leucine aminopeptidase (P-LAP), adipocyte-derived leucine aminopeptidase (A-LAP), and leukocyte-derived aminopeptidase (L-RAP) are part of a distinct group within the M1 family of aminopeptidases, known as the "Oxytocinase subfamily". These enzymes share HEXXH(X)18E Zn-binding and GAMEN motifs that are crucial for their enzymatic activities. A defining characteristic of this subfamily is their intracellular localization. P-LAP is transported from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane in response to stimuli, while both A-LAP and L-RAP remain in the endoplasmic reticulum. These enzymes possess specific sequences that enable their precise localization within the cell. It is becoming increasingly clear that the members of this subfamily play vital roles in maintaining homeostasis, including the regulation of normal pregnancy, memory retention, blood pressure, and antigen presentation. This review provides an overview of the current understanding of this newly identified subfamily.

title: Myc represses primitive endoderm differentiation in pluripotent stem cells.
text: The use of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offers a new approach to studying the mechanisms that govern stem cell pluripotency and self-renewal. Previous research has highlighted the importance of Myc in maintaining murine embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and promoting the reprogramming of fibroblasts by influencing gene expression. However, the specific way in which Myc regulates pluripotency is still unknown. In this study, we discovered that deleting both c- and N-MYC in iPSCs and ESCs leads to their spontaneous differentiation into primitive endoderm. Our research reveals that Myc maintains pluripotency by suppressing the master regulator GATA6, which controls primitive endoderm development. Additionally, Myc plays a role in cell cycle regulation through its influence on the mir-17-92 miRNA cluster. These findings demonstrate that c- or N-myc is essential for pluripotency beyond its role in controlling cell proliferation and metabolism.

title: [Vitamin D and latitude as environmental factors in multiple sclerosis].
text: The prevalence of multiple sclerosis (MS) significantly rises as latitudes increase, whether it be north or south of the equator. One possible explanation for this difference in prevalence is the role of vitamin D. As latitude increases, the intensity of ultraviolet light, necessary for vitamin D synthesis, decreases. Vitamin D is known to have immunomodulatory properties and can suppress MS in animal models. Additionally, genes related to vitamin D are believed to be crucial susceptibility genes for MS. Therefore, a comprehensive investigation into the relationship between vitamin D and MS is required, considering both environmental and genetic factors.

title: Type 2 cytokines: mechanisms and therapeutic strategies
text: Type 2 immune responses are characterized by the presence of certain cytokines, namely interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-5, IL-9, and IL-13. These cytokines can have either a protective effect for the host or contribute to the development of diseases. Type 2 immunity plays a role in defending against parasitic infections, suppressing autoimmune diseases driven by type 1 responses, neutralizing toxins, maintaining metabolic balance, and regulating the healing and regeneration of tissues after infection or injury. However, when type 2 responses are not properly regulated, they can become significant drivers of disease. The inflammatory response induced by type 2 immunity involves various components such as eosinophils, mast cells, basophils, type 2 innate lymphoid cells, IL-4 and/or IL-13-conditioned macrophages, and T helper 2 (TH2) cells. These components are crucial in the development of allergic and fibrotic disorders. As chronic type 2 immune responses contribute to disease progression, it is important to understand the mechanisms that regulate their maintenance, as they can serve as key factors in modifying disease outcomes. This review explores the various natural mechanisms that act as negative regulators of type 2 immunity and discusses the development of therapies targeting these pathways to treat diseases mediated by type 2 immune responses.

title: Implanted microvessels progress through distinct neovascularization phenotypes.
text:
Our previous research has shown that implanted microvessels can form a new microcirculation with minimal involvement from the host's vessels. In this study, our goal was to identify the different vascular phenotypes that occur during neovascularization in these implants and to understand the events that take place after angiogenesis. Through morphological, functional, and transcriptional assessments, we identified three distinct vascular phenotypes: sprouting angiogenesis, neovascular remodeling, and network maturation.

The first phenotype observed was sprouting angiogenesis, which was characterized by high levels of cell proliferation and low coverage of mural cells. This was followed by a neovascular remodeling phenotype, where a poorly organized neovascular network with blood flow was present, along with reduced proliferation and re-associated mural cells. The final phenotype consisted of a well-organized vascular network with a stereotypical tree structure, containing vessels with normal perivascular cell associations. In this phase, proliferation was low and limited to the walls of larger microvessels.

The transition from angiogenesis to neovascular remodeling coincided with the appearance of blood flow in the implant neovasculature. Analysis of gene expression revealed that the neovascular remodeling phenotype had distinct transcriptional characteristics compared to the other two phenotypes. This suggests that this phenotype is not simply a transitional phase, but a unique vascular phenotype involving specific cellular and vascular processes.

Furthermore, we propose that this neovascular remodeling phase may be a normal part of the overall neovascularization process. Therefore, the presence of similar dysfunctional microvasculatures in compromised or diseased tissues may not necessarily indicate a failure to progress through a normally occurring neovascularization phenotype.

title: Characterization of a highly variable eutherian microRNA gene.
text: The miRNAs miR-290-miR295, found in mice, are believed to play a crucial role in embryonic stem cells and preimplantation embryos. Our research provides evidence that a primary transcript, which is spliced, capped, and polyadenylated, encompasses the entire Early Embryonic microRNA Cluster (EEmiRC). During processing, Drosha produces additional large nuclear RNA intermediates. The transcription of EEmiRC is directed by a conserved promoter element that contains a TATA-box. Sequence analysis reveals that the EEmiRC transcription unit is highly variable and can only be identified through bioinformatics in placental mammals. EEmiRC is specifically expressed in trophoblastic stem cells, indicating its function in eutherian development. When studying the evolutionary and functional relationships, it is important to consider the organization of the entire miRNA loci, not just the mature miRNA sequences. Based on this concept, we propose that EEmiRC is a recently acquired gene that evolves rapidly and plays a crucial role in eutherian development.

title: The function of follicular helper T cells is regulated by the strength of T cell antigen receptor binding
text: Understanding how follicular helper T cells (TFH cells) differentiate to regulate B cell immunity is crucial for effective protein vaccination. In this study, we identify three subsets of antigen-specific effector helper T cells that express the transcription factor T-bet. These subsets have distinct functions, migratory properties, and developmental programming in vivo. By examining the expression of the transcriptional repressor Blimp-1, we distinguish T zone 'lymphoid' effector helper T cells (CD62LhiCCR7hi) from CXCR5lo 'emigrant' effector helper T cells and CXCR5hi 'resident' TFH cells that express the transcriptional repressor Bcl-6 (CD62LloCCR7lo). Through adoptive transfer and intact polyclonal responses, we demonstrate that helper T cells with the highest specific binding of peptide–major histocompatibility complex class II and the most restricted T cell antigen receptor junctional diversity preferentially develop into the antigen-specific effector TFH compartment. Our findings highlight the importance of differences in the binding strength of the T cell antigen receptor in programming specialized effector TFH function in vivo.

title: Disruption of tumor necrosis factor-alpha gene diminishes the development of atherosclerosis in ApoE-deficient mice.
text: The role of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) in the development of atherosclerosis is still not fully understood, although it is known to be involved in the inflammatory process. To investigate the impact of TNF-alpha on atherosclerosis, we created mice that lacked both apolipoprotein E (apoE) and TNF-alpha (apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/-) and compared them to mice that only lacked apoE (apoE-/-). While both apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- and apoE-/- mice had significantly higher levels of total cholesterol in their blood compared to normal mice, there were no differences between the two groups. However, the size of atherosclerotic plaques on the inner surface of the aorta was significantly smaller in apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice (3.1+/-0.4%) compared to apoE-/- mice (4.7+/-0.4%, p<0.001), despite similar cholesterol levels. Similarly, the size of atherosclerotic lesions in the aortic sinus was also significantly smaller in apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice (5.1+/-0.3 x 10(5)microm(2)) compared to apoE-/- mice (7.0+/-0.3 x 10(5)microm(2), p<0.0001). Analysis of gene expression showed that the levels of intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) were significantly higher in apoE-/- mice compared to apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice. Macrophages from apoE-/- mice also had higher uptake of oxidized LDL and increased expression of scavenger receptor class A (SRA) compared to macrophages from apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice. These findings suggest that TNF-alpha promotes atherosclerosis by increasing the expression of ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and MCP-1 in the blood vessels, and by inducing SRA expression and uptake of oxidized LDL in macrophages.

title: Differential expression of bcl-2 and susceptibility to anti-Fas-mediated cell death in peripheral blood lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils.
text: The Fas antigen (Ag), recently discovered, is a molecule found on the surface of cells that can trigger apoptosis. The cytoplasmic product of the proto-oncogene bcl-2 has been found to inhibit apoptosis and prolong cellular survival. To understand the importance of both molecules, we examined their expression on different types of blood leukocytes and assessed their sensitivity to anti-Fas antibody-induced cell death. While Fas Ag was present on a fraction of lymphocytes, both neutrophils and monocytes consistently expressed Fas Ag. However, there was a significant difference in bcl-2 expression among these leukocytes. Lymphocytes showed strong bcl-2 expression, while monocytes had weaker expression, and neutrophils had virtually no expression. Corresponding to the lack of bcl-2 expression, neutrophils were more prone to undergoing apoptotic cell death in vitro compared to monocytes and lymphocytes. We demonstrated that anti-Fas antibody effectively accelerated apoptotic cell death in neutrophils. However, the antibody had minimal effect on inducing apoptosis in monocytes, and lymphocytes were resistant to its effects. These findings suggest that the susceptibility to anti-Fas-mediated cell death may be influenced by the expression of bcl-2 in Fas+ lymphoid and hematopoietic cells.

title: Foxp2 and Foxp1 cooperatively regulate lung and esophagus development.
text: The lungs develop their airways through a repetitive process of branching morphogenesis, which creates the complex and extensive surface area needed for breathing after birth. The transcription factors Foxp2 and Foxp1 are expressed in various tissues derived from the foregut, including the lungs and intestines. In this study, we demonstrate that the absence of Foxp2 in mice leads to impaired lung alveolarization after birth, contributing to their death shortly after. Through laboratory experiments and observations in living organisms, we establish that T1alpha, a gene specific to type 1 alveolar epithelial cells in the lungs, is directly regulated by Foxp2 and Foxp1. Interestingly, when one allele of Foxp1 is lost in addition to complete loss of Foxp2, the severity of morphological defects in the lungs worsens, resulting in the death of all Foxp2(-/-);Foxp1(+/-) mice shortly after birth. The expression of N-myc and Hop, which are critical regulators of lung development, is also compromised in these mutant mice. Furthermore, the development of esophageal muscles is disrupted in Foxp2(-/-);Foxp1(+/-) embryos, a tissue where both Foxp2 and Foxp1 are present. These findings highlight the importance of Foxp2 and Foxp1 in regulating lung and esophageal development, emphasizing their essential role in the development of tissues derived from the front part of the digestive tract. Additionally, this study demonstrates the functional cooperation between members of the Foxp1/2/4 family in tissues where they are co-expressed.

title: Crystal structure of the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal subunit in complex with initiation factor 6.
text: Ribosomes are responsible for catalyzing protein synthesis in all organisms. However, eukaryotic ribosomes, compared to their prokaryotic counterparts, are significantly larger and undergo more complex regulation. The larger ribosomal subunit (60S) plays a crucial role in forming peptide bonds and contains the exit tunnel for nascent polypeptides. In this study, we present the structure of the 60S ribosomal subunit from Tetrahymena thermophila, which is in complex with eukaryotic initiation factor 6 (eIF6) and co-crystallized with the antibiotic cycloheximide. Cycloheximide is a specific inhibitor of protein synthesis in eukaryotes. The resolution of the structure is 3.5 angstroms. Our findings reveal the intricate functional architecture of the eukaryotic 60S subunit, highlighting the complex network of interactions between eukaryotic-specific ribosomal protein features and RNA expansion segments. Additionally, we uncover the roles of eukaryotic ribosomal protein elements in stabilizing the active site and the extent of eukaryotic-specific differences in other functional regions of the subunit. Furthermore, our study elucidates the molecular basis of the interaction between the 60S subunit and eIF6, providing a structural framework for further investigations into ribosome-associated diseases and the role of the 60S subunit in protein synthesis initiation.

title: Hedgehog signaling regulates brain tumor-initiating cell proliferation and portends shorter survival for patients with PTEN-coexpressing glioblastomas.
text: The discovery of brain tumor stem-like cells (BTSCs) has revealed the importance of biological self-renewal processes in the development and spread of clinical brain tumors. However, the specific molecular mechanisms that drive the tumor-forming abilities of BTSCs are still unknown. In this study, we have analyzed the gene expression profiles of BTSCs to identify molecular signatures associated with glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), a type of brain tumor. We have found that both Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling-dependent and -independent BTSCs exist, and we have also examined surgical specimens from patients with glioblastoma. Through experiments conducted in vitro and in mice with intracranial tumors, we have demonstrated that the proliferation of BTSCs can be inhibited by targeting specific pathways. Both SHH-dependent and -independent brain tumor growth were found to rely on the phosphoinositide 3-kinase-mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway. Furthermore, in human GBMs, the expression levels of SHH and PTCH1 were significantly higher in tumors that expressed PTEN compared to tumors that lacked PTEN. We have also observed that hyperactive SHH-GLI signaling in PTEN-coexpressing human GBM is associated with shorter survival time. These findings suggest that different signaling pathways may drive the proliferation of BTSCs in glioblastoma. By understanding these mechanisms, we may be able to develop personalized treatments for glioblastoma.

title: Stress and host immunity amplify Mycobacterium tuberculosis phenotypic heterogeneity and induce nongrowing metabolically active forms.
text: The involvement of nonreplicating and metabolically inactive bacteria in latent tuberculosis infections and relapses after "sterilizing" chemotherapy is well-known. However, there is limited evidence connecting bacterial dormancy and persistence in living organisms. In this study, we used quantitative time-lapse microscopy and a reporter of ribosomal RNA gene expression to measure the replication and ribosomal activity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis at the single-cell level. We found that the dynamics of individual cells varied under normal growth conditions, and this variability was further amplified under stressful conditions such as nutrient limitation, stationary phase, intracellular replication, and growth in the lungs of mice. Moreover, we discovered that chronically infected mice had a subpopulation of bacteria in their lungs that were not actively growing but still metabolically active. These bacteria were not present in mice lacking interferon-γ, a cytokine crucial for antituberculosis immunity. Interestingly, these hidden forms of bacteria were more prevalent in mice treated with the antituberculosis drug isoniazid, suggesting a potential role in relapses after chemotherapy. Therefore, the amplification of bacterial phenotypic heterogeneity in response to host immunity and drug pressure may contribute to the persistence of tuberculosis.

title: Proteomic analysis reveals Warburg effect and anomalous metabolism of glutamine in pancreatic cancer cells.
text: In this study, we examined the proteomes of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell line PANC-1 and normal pancreatic duct cells using mass spectrometry with LTQ-Orbitrap. We successfully identified over 1700 proteins in each sample. By utilizing a spectra count label-free quantification approach, we discovered numerous metabolic enzymes and proteins involved in various cellular processes such as cytoskeleton organization, cell adhesion, transport, transcription, translation, and cell proliferation. Our findings indicate that metabolic pathways are disrupted in PANC-1, consistent with the Warburg effect. Furthermore, our comparative MS analysis revealed abnormal metabolism of glutamine, suggesting that glutamine is predominantly utilized as a nitrogen donor for nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis in PANC-1. This comprehensive analysis provides valuable insights into the metabolism of PANC-1 and may contribute to the development of new diagnostic and treatment strategies for PDAC.

title: Prevalence of attempting weight loss and strategies for controlling weight.
text: The prevalence of overweight and obesity is on the rise in the United States. It is important for individuals to make changes in their diet and physical activity in order to control their weight. The objective of this study was to examine the prevalence of weight loss or weight maintenance attempts and describe the strategies used for weight control among US adults. The study utilized the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, a random-digit telephone survey conducted in 1996 by state health departments. The survey included participants from 49 states and the District of Columbia. The participants were adults aged 18 years and older, totaling 107,804 individuals. The main outcome measures included reported current weights and goal weights, prevalence of weight loss or maintenance attempts, and the strategies used to control weight, such as eating fewer calories, eating less fat, or engaging in physical activity. The results showed that 28.8% of men and 43.6% of women attempted to lose weight, while 35.1% of men and 34.4% of women attempted to maintain their weight. Among those trying to lose weight, a common strategy was to consume less fat without reducing calorie intake. Only a small percentage of men (21.5%) and women (19.4%) reported using the recommended combination of eating fewer calories and engaging in at least 150 minutes of leisure-time physical activity per week. The median weight for men trying to lose weight was 90.4 kg with a goal weight of 81.4 kg, while for women, the median weight was 70.3 kg with a goal weight of 59.0 kg. In conclusion, weight loss and weight maintenance are common concerns for both men and women in the United States. However, most individuals attempting to lose weight are not following the recommended combination of reducing calorie intake and engaging in regular physical activity.

title: Antibodies specific for Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen-1 cross-react with human heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L.
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been linked to multiple sclerosis (MS), and MS patients consistently show elevated levels of antibodies to the EBV nuclear antigen-1 (EBNA-1). This study aims to explore the possibility that anti-EBNA-1 antibodies in MS patients react with a self antigen. To do so, we isolated anti-EBNA-1 antibodies from human plasma, used them to extract antigens from the human brain, and identified the bound antigens using mass spectrometry. We found that anti-EBNA-1 antibodies consistently bound to a protein called heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L (HNRNPL). We expressed both the long and short isoforms of HNRNPL and confirmed through Western blots and ELISA that the long isoform cross-reacts with EBNA-1. Immunohistochemistry revealed that anti-EBNA-1 antibodies bound to an antigen in the nucleus of cultured rat central nervous system cells. ELISA tests showed the presence of antibodies to HNRNPL in the plasma of both healthy controls and MS patients, but the levels of anti-HNRNPL antibodies were not elevated in MS patients. In conclusion, we have discovered that HNRNPL is an autoantigen that cross-reacts with EBNA-1. Further investigation is needed to determine the significance of this autoantigen in MS and other autoimmune diseases.

title: Roles of chromatin remodellers in DNA double strand break repair.
text: Now that we have a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms involved in repairing DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) and the signaling of damage caused by DSBs, there is a growing focus on the changes required in the chromatin environment to facilitate efficient DSB repair. Mutations in chromatin remodeling complexes have been found in cancer, highlighting the importance of assessing their impact on genomic stability. Our current knowledge of DSB repair pathways suggests that each pathway has specific requirements for chromatin remodeling. Additionally, limiting the extent of chromatin modifications may play a significant role in determining which pathway is utilized. In this review, we assess the distinct DSB repair pathways and their potential reliance on chromatin remodeling, as well as examine the roles of ATP-driven chromatin remodelers in these pathways.

title: Epstein-Barr virus and virus human protein interaction maps.
text: A thorough analysis of the interactions between Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proteins and human proteins can offer valuable insights into the replication and persistence strategies employed by EBV. To achieve this, we utilized a rigorous high-throughput yeast two-hybrid system to examine the interactions between EBV proteins and both each other and human proteins. Through this approach, we identified a total of 43 interactions between EBV proteins and 173 interactions between EBV and human proteins. These interaction maps, or "interactomes," provided a foundation for generating hypotheses regarding protein function. For instance, we discovered that LF2, an EBV protein with an unknown function, interacts with the EBV immediate early R transactivator (Rta) and inhibits Rta transactivation. Taking a broader perspective, we classified EBV genes into two evolutionary categories: "core" genes, which are conserved across all herpesviruses, and "noncore" genes, which are specific to the subfamily. Notably, our EBV-EBV interactome map exhibited a higher prevalence of interactions among proteins within the same evolutionary class. Additionally, we observed that EBV proteins tend to target highly connected or "hub" proteins and those with shorter paths to other proteins in the human interactome network. This suggests that EBV may efficiently reorganize cellular processes by targeting these central proteins.

title: Relation between Medicare screening reimbursement and stage at diagnosis for older patients with colon cancer.
text: The reimbursement policy for Medicare was altered in 1998 to include coverage for screening colonoscopies for patients at high risk of colon cancer. In 2001, the policy was expanded to cover screening colonoscopies for all individuals. The objective of this study was to determine whether these changes in Medicare reimbursement were associated with an increase in colonoscopy use or early stage colon cancer diagnosis. The study analyzed data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Medicare linked database, focusing on patients aged 67 and older with a primary diagnosis of colon cancer between 1992 and 2002. The study also included a group of Medicare beneficiaries without cancer who resided in the same areas. The main outcome measures were trends in colonoscopy and sigmoidoscopy use among Medicare beneficiaries without cancer, and the stage of colon cancer diagnosis among patients with cancer. The study found that colonoscopy use significantly increased after the reimbursement policy changes, with rates rising from 285/100,000 per quarter in the period without coverage to 889 and 1919/100,000 per quarter in the periods with limited and universal coverage, respectively. The proportion of patients diagnosed at an early stage also increased during the study period. The changes in Medicare coverage had a strong association with early stage diagnosis for patients with proximal colon lesions, but a weak or no association for patients with distal colon lesions. In conclusion, the expansion of Medicare reimbursement for colon cancer screening led to increased colonoscopy use among beneficiaries and an increased likelihood of early stage diagnosis for those with colon cancer. The findings suggest that the coverage change had a selective effect on proximal colon lesions, indicating the importance of whole-colon screening methods like colonoscopy.

title: Direct visualization of the endomitotic cell cycle in living megakaryocytes: differential patterns in low and high ploidy cells.
text: The process of endomitosis in megakaryocytes (MKs) involves the repeated replication of DNA without cytokinesis, and it plays a crucial role in MK development. However, the dynamics of chromosomes during this process have never been observed in living MKs. To address this, we have created a new transgenic mouse model in which human histone H2B fused with green fluorescent protein is specifically expressed in MKs. Through ex vivo time-lapse microscopy analysis, we have discovered that chromosomal condensation occurs during early mitosis in all MKs. In MKs with high ploidy (greater than or equal to 8N), late anaphase is characterized by a ring-like alignment of chromosomes, with multiple territories formed between them. On the other hand, in MKs with low ploidy, mitotic chromosomes segregate to form two distinct groups, separated by a clear space, before rejoining into one cluster. This study is the first to document the patterns of chromosomal segregation during endomitosis ex vivo, and it suggests that these patterns may be regulated differently in cells with low and high ploidy.

title: Aberrant expression and altered cellular localization of desmosomal and hemidesmosomal proteins are associated with aggressive clinicopathological features of oral squamous cell carcinoma
text: Cell adhesion disruption plays a crucial role in the dedifferentiation, invasion, and spread of various cancers. The desmosome and hemidesmosome are types of anchoring junctions that regulate cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion, respectively. To better understand their impact on the biological characteristics of oral cancer, we conducted immunohistochemical analysis on 51 cases of oral squamous cell carcinoma. We examined the expression of desmoglein 1 (DSG1), DSG2, DSG3, desmocollin 2 (DSC2), integrin beta 4 (ITGB4), laminin gamma chain 2 (LAMC2), and collagen type 17 alpha 1 (COL17A1). In normal oral epithelial cells, DSG1, DSG3, DSC2, and COL17A1 were found on the plasma membrane, while ITGB4 and mature LAMC2 were located at the basement membrane. However, in cancer cells, the expression of DSG1, DSG3, DSC2, and COL17A1 decreased and moved to the cytoplasm.
