On the other hand, DSG2, ITGB4, and LAMC2 were expressed in the cytoplasm of cancer cells facing the stroma. We evaluated the immunohistochemical expression and correlated it with clinicopathological parameters such as histologic differentiation, invasion pattern, and presence of lymph node metastasis. The decrease in DSG3 and DSC2 expression was associated with a more aggressive cancer phenotype, characterized by less differentiation, increased invasion, and a higher incidence of nodal metastasis. Lower COL17A1 expression and higher LAMC2 expression were also linked to a more aggressive phenotype. This study highlights the abnormal expression and altered cellular localization of desmosomal and hemidesmosomal proteins in relation to aggressive clinicopathological features of oral cancer. It further supports the idea that disruption of keratin-associated anchoring junctions contributes to the aggressive behavior of cancer cells.

title: Histone/protein deacetylase inhibitors increase suppressive functions of human FOXP3+ Tregs.
text: Histone/protein deacetylases (HDACs) are responsible for reducing the acetylation of histones and proteins, which typically results in the suppression of gene transcription and the modulation of various protein functions. Our research has revealed significant differences in the expression of HDACs before and after stimulating human T regulatory (Treg) and T effector cells. This suggests that there is potential for selectively targeting Tregs with HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) in the future. By using different small molecules that inhibit HDACs, we were able to enhance the suppressive functions of both freshly isolated and expanded human Tregs by up to 4.5-fold (with an average increase of 2-fold). These findings align with our previous studies conducted on mice. The use of HDACi also led to an increase in Treg expression of CTLA-4, a crucial negative regulator of the immune response. We discovered a direct and significant correlation between the expression of CTLA-4 and Treg suppression. Therefore, HDACi compounds show promise as pharmacological tools to enhance Treg suppressive functions. This action could potentially benefit patients with autoimmunity or those who have undergone transplantation.

title: Enhanced pathological angiogenesis in mice lacking β3 integrin or β3 and β5 integrins
text: The suppression of neovascularization and tumor growth has been linked to the inhibition of αvβ3 or αvβ5 integrin function, suggesting that these integrins play a crucial role in angiogenesis. However, our findings reveal that mice lacking β3 integrins or both β3 and β5 integrins not only support tumorigenesis but also experience enhanced tumor growth. Additionally, the tumors in these integrin-deficient mice exhibit increased angiogenesis, indicating that neither β3 nor β5 integrins are necessary for neovascularization. Furthermore, we observed that the absence of β3 integrins significantly amplifies the angiogenic responses to hypoxia and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Although we found no evidence of altered expression or functions of other integrins due to β3 deficiency, we did observe elevated levels of VEGF receptor-2 (also known as Flk-1) in β3-null endothelial cells. These findings suggest that αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrins are not essential for vascular development or pathological angiogenesis, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the mechanisms of action of αv-integrin antagonists in anti-angiogenic therapies.

title: A lineage of myeloid cells independent of Myb and hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in cellular immunity and are believed to originate and regenerate from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). However, it has been observed that certain macrophages develop in the embryo before the definitive HSCs appear. Therefore, we decided to reexamine the process of macrophage development. Our investigation revealed that the transcription factor Myb is essential for the development of HSCs, as well as all CD11b(high) monocytes and macrophages. However, Myb is not necessary for the formation of yolk sac (YS) macrophages or the development of YS-derived F4/80(bright) macrophages in various tissues, including liver Kupffer cells, epidermal Langerhans cells, and microglia. These cell populations can persist in adult mice independently of HSCs. Consequently, our findings establish a distinct lineage of tissue macrophages that originate from the YS and are genetically different from HSC progeny.

title: Heterogenic Loss of the Wild-Type BRCA Allele in Human Breast Tumorigenesis
text: Individuals who have inherited a mutated BRCA allele, which predisposes them to breast and ovarian cancer, typically require the loss of the normal allele for the initiation and progression of cancer. However, there is evidence suggesting that the effects on phenotype may be due to BRCA haploinsufficiency. We examined tissue samples from women with harmful mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2. We identified areas of normal breast tissue, atypical ductal hyperplasia, ductal carcinoma-in-situ, and invasive ductal carcinoma in breast cancer cases linked to BRCA1 and BRCA2. We also studied prophylactic mastectomy samples from BRCA carriers and invasive ovarian carcinomas. Using laser catapult microdissection, we isolated cells from the different pathological lesions and corresponding normal tissues. We then used real-time polymerase chain reaction assays to determine the proportion of wild-type to mutant BRCA alleles in each sample. Our analysis revealed significant heterogeneity in loss of heterozygosity within and between preinvasive lesions and invasive cancers in individuals with breast cancer and BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. However, all BRCA-associated ovarian cancers showed complete loss of the wild-type BRCA allele. These findings suggest that the loss of the wild-type BRCA allele is not necessary for the development of BRCA-related breast tumors. This has important implications for understanding the genetic mechanism of BRCA tumor suppression and for the clinical management of individuals in this patient population.

title: Targeted therapies in urothelial carcinoma.
text:
The purpose of this review is to gain a better understanding of the biology and genetics of urothelial carcinoma in order to identify and define the molecules and pathways that are suitable for novel-targeted therapies. In this review, we will discuss the targeted therapies that have been reported or are currently being tested in clinical trials for urothelial carcinoma. We will also highlight the molecular targets that have been characterized in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Recent findings have shown that trials in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer are examining the role of immunotherapy and agents that target vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) or fibroblast growth factor receptor-3. In muscle-invasive bladder cancer, neoadjuvant studies have focused on combining VEGF agents with chemotherapy, while adjuvant studies are testing vaccines and agents that target the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, p53, and Hsp27. In the first-line treatment of metastatic urothelial carcinoma, novel targets in clinical trials include tubulin, cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4, Hsp27, and p53. The majority of targeted agents studied in urothelial carcinoma are in the second-line setting, with new targets including CD105, polo-like kinase-1, phosphatidylinositide 3-kinases (PI3K), transforming growth factor β receptor/activin receptor-like kinase β, estrogen receptor, and the hepatocyte growth factor receptor (HGFR or MET).

In summary, the development of targeted therapies for urothelial carcinoma is still in its early stages, and there have been no major therapeutic breakthroughs thus far. However, the increased understanding of urothelial carcinoma and solid tumor biology has led to a surge in clinical trials, which could potentially result in significant advancements in treatment strategies.

title: H2S and HS− donor NaHS releases nitric oxide from nitrosothiols, metal nitrosyl complex, brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells
text: The relaxation of norepinephrine precontracted rat aortic rings was significantly increased by Nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) at a concentration of 500 nmol/l. This effect was further enhanced by the H2S- and HS−-donor NaHS at a pH of 7.5, but not at a pH of 6.3. To investigate the molecular mechanism behind this effect, we examined whether NaHS could release NO from NO donors. Using an electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy method and measuring the nitrite oxidation product through the Griess reaction, we found that NaHS released NO from nitrosothiols such as GSNO, S-nitroso-N-acetyl-dl-penicillamine (SNAP), metal nitrosyl complex nitroprusside (SNP), as well as from rat brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells. The release of NO was more pronounced at a pH of 8.0 compared to a pH of 6.0, suggesting that HS−, rather than H2S, is responsible for the NO-releasing effect. Since H2S and HS− are naturally produced in mammals, we propose that their ability to release NO from nitrosothiols and metal nitrosyl complexes contributes to their biological activities, potentially playing a role in S-nitrosothiol-signalling reactions.

title: Amitriptyline is effective in chronic but not in episodic tension-type headache: pathogenetic implications.
text: Amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, is a highly effective medication for treating chronic tension-type headaches and other chronic pain conditions. It has also shown effectiveness in preventing episodic headaches like migraines. However, its effectiveness in treating episodic tension-type headaches is still unclear. In an open-label study, we compared the effectiveness of a daily dose of 25 mg of amitriptyline in 82 nondepressed patients with either chronic or episodic tension-type headaches. The results showed that amitriptyline significantly reduced the frequency and duration of headaches, as well as the use of pain relievers, in patients with chronic tension-type headaches. However, it did not have the same effect on patients with episodic tension-type headaches. Further placebo-controlled trials, potentially using higher doses of amitriptyline, may help determine if the varying response to the medication can be attributed to differences in central nociception and peripheral myofascial factors between chronic and episodic tension-type headaches.

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 is required for trafficking but not quiescence in postactivated T cells.
text: The function of the transcription factor Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) in postactivated T cells is not well understood, although it has been suggested to regulate genes involved in cell cycle entry and T cell trafficking. Previous studies have shown that the cytokines IL-2 and IL-15 can influence the re-expression of KLF2 in postactivation T cells and also affect the differentiation of effector and memory T cells. To investigate the specific role of KLF2 expression in activated CD8(+) T cells cultured with these cytokines, we used conditional and inducible KLF2-knockout model systems. Our findings revealed that KLF2 is necessary for the effective transcription of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1P(1)) and CD62L in postactivation T cells. However, while different cytokines had a significant impact on the expression of cell-cycle-related genes, the absence of endogenous KLF2 had minimal effects. Interestingly, KLF2-deficient T cells exhibited dysregulated trafficking but did not show any changes in proliferative characteristics following in vivo responses to Ag. These results provide insights into the KLF2-dependent and -independent aspects of activated CD8(+) T cell differentiation and suggest that KLF2 may not play a physiological role in cell cycle regulation.

title: Hypoalbuminemia in acute illness: is there a rationale for intervention? A meta-analysis of cohort studies and controlled trials.
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if hypoalbuminemia is an independent risk factor for poor outcomes in acutely ill patients and to assess the potential benefits of administering exogenous albumin to improve outcomes in hypoalbuminemic patients. Previous research has shown that hypoalbuminemia is associated with negative outcomes in acutely ill patients, but it is unclear if this association is causal. Trials investigating the use of albumin therapy to correct hypoalbuminemia have yielded inconclusive results. 

To address these questions, a meta-analysis was conducted, including 90 cohort studies with a total of 291,433 patients to evaluate hypoalbuminemia as a predictor of outcomes using multivariate analysis. Additionally, nine prospective controlled trials with a total of 535 patients were analyzed to assess the effects of correcting hypoalbuminemia. 

The results showed that hypoalbuminemia is a strong and dose-dependent independent predictor of poor outcomes. Each 10-g/L decrease in serum albumin concentration significantly increased the odds of mortality by 137%, morbidity by 89%, prolonged intensive care unit and hospital stays by 28% and 71% respectively, and increased resource utilization by 66%. This association between hypoalbuminemia and poor outcomes appeared to be independent of nutritional status and inflammation. 

Analysis of the controlled trials on albumin therapy suggested that complication rates may be reduced when the serum albumin level reaches or exceeds 30 g/L during administration. 

In conclusion, hypoalbuminemia is strongly associated with negative clinical outcomes. Further well-designed trials are needed to fully understand the effects of albumin therapy in hypoalbuminemic patients. In the meantime, there is no compelling reason to withhold albumin therapy if it is deemed clinically appropriate.

title: Methionine restriction decreases visceral fat mass and preserves insulin action in aging male Fischer 344 rats independent of energy restriction.
text:
Male Fischer 344 rats that consume a reduced methionine diet (0.17% methionine, MR) and practice calorie restriction (CR) experience a longer lifespan. The reasons behind this are not fully understood, but both regimens result in lower body weight and decreased adiposity. In the case of CR, reduced fat deposition is associated with the preservation of insulin responsiveness in older animals. This study aims to investigate the connection between insulin responsiveness and visceral fat in MR rats and determine if the decrease in visceral fat and preservation of insulin sensitivity observed in MR rats is not solely due to CR.

To achieve this, rats were pair-fed (pf) a control diet (0.86% methionine, CF) to match the food intake of MR rats for 80 weeks. The pf rats exhibited insulin, glucose, and leptin levels similar to control-fed animals and had comparable amounts of visceral fat. In contrast, MR rats had significantly reduced visceral fat compared to CF and PF rats, along with lower basal insulin, glucose, and leptin levels, and higher adiponectin and triiodothyronine levels. Additionally, the daily energy expenditure of MR rats was significantly higher than that of PF and CF rats. In a separate group, older MR rats showed similar insulin responses to oral glucose challenges as young animals. Long-term assessments of MR and CF rats up to 112 weeks of age revealed that MR prevented age-related increases in serum lipids. By 16 weeks, MR rats had a 40% reduction in insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels, which remained consistent throughout their lifespan. In contrast, CF rats experienced a decline in IGF-1 levels starting at 112 weeks. Overall, these findings suggest that MR reduces visceral fat and preserves insulin activity in aging rats independently of energy restriction.

title: Generation of T cell receptor–retrogenic mice: improved retroviral-mediated stem cell gene transfer
text: The use of retrogenic mice provides a fast and adaptable method for creating T cell receptor (TCR)-transgenic mice. By introducing a retrovirus that carries a specific TCR-α/β subunit into bone marrow progenitor cells, TCR-retrogenic mice can be generated in just 4-6 weeks, whereas traditional TCR transgenics can take 6 months or more. In this updated procedure, we have enhanced the efficiency of bone marrow transduction and reconstitution compared to our previous method. The main change from the previous protocol involves using spin transduction with the viral supernatant instead of coculturing with the viral producer cell line. These modifications improve bone marrow viability, enhance consistency in bone marrow transduction and engraftment, and reduce the number of bone marrow donor mice needed compared to bone marrow recipients.

title: Transient delivery of modified mRNA encoding TERT rapidly extends telomeres in human cells.
text: The extension of telomeres has been suggested as a way to enhance cell culture, tissue engineering, and disease treatment. However, current methods of telomere extension that do not involve viruses or integration are not very effective. In this study, we demonstrate that delivering modified mRNA encoding TERT to human fibroblasts and myoblasts temporarily increases telomerase activity (for 24-48 hours) and rapidly extends telomeres. However, after this initial extension, telomeres begin to shorten again. By performing three consecutive transfections over a four-day period, we were able to extend telomeres by up to 0.9 kb in fibroblasts and myoblasts, resulting in an additional 28 ± 1.5 and 3.4 ± 0.4 population doublings, respectively. The increase in proliferative capacity was dose-dependent. Interestingly, the second and third transfections had less of an impact on proliferative capacity compared to the first, indicating a temporary refractory period. However, this refractory period was short-lived, as a fourth transfection later on increased fibroblast proliferative capacity by an additional 15.2 ± 1.1 population doublings, similar to the first transfection. Overall, these treatments led to a more than 10(12)-fold increase in absolute cell number. Importantly, unlike immortalized cells, all treated cell populations eventually ceased to increase in number and exhibited senescence markers to the same extent as untreated cells. This rapid method of telomere extension and increased cell proliferative capacity, without the risk of insertional mutagenesis, holds great potential for disease modeling, drug screening, and regenerative medicine.

title: The death receptor CD95 activates adult neural stem cells for working memory formation and brain repair.
text: Ongoing neurogenesis in the subventricular zone and dentate gyrus of adults can be triggered by central nervous system injury. However, the impact of newly formed neurons on neuronal networks is limited. Our study reveals that stimulating the "death receptor" CD95 in neural stem cells does not cause cell death as expected, but instead promotes stem cell survival and the development of neurons. This unexpected effect is achieved through the activation of the Src/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which ultimately leads to an overall increase in protein production. We confirmed that CD95 induces neurogenesis in the ischemic CA1 region, the naive dentate gyrus, and when CD95L is artificially expressed in the adult subventricular zone. When CD95 is absent in the hippocampus, neurogenesis is reduced and working memory is impaired. However, CD95-mediated brain repair after global ischemia successfully restores normal behavior. Therefore, we have identified the CD95/CD95L system as a crucial signal for both ongoing and injury-induced neurogenesis.

title: Umbilical Cord Blood Therapy Potentiated with Erythropoietin for Children with Cerebral Palsy: A Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial
text: The therapeutic potential of allogeneic umbilical cord blood (UCB) for cerebral palsy (CP) can be enhanced by the concomitant administration of recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO), which has neurotrophic effects. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of allogeneic UCB potentiated with rhEPO in children with CP. The children were randomly assigned to one of three groups: the pUCB group, which received allogeneic UCB with rhEPO; the EPO group, which received rhEPO with placebo UCB; and the Control group, which received placebo UCB and placebo rhEPO. All participants underwent rehabilitation therapy. The main outcomes measured were changes in scores on the gross motor performance measure (GMPM), gross motor function measure, and Bayley scales of infant development-II (BSID-II) Mental and Motor scales during the 6-month treatment period. Baseline and follow-up F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18F-FDG-PET/CT) and diffusion tensor images (DTI) were obtained to detect changes in the brain. A total of 96 subjects completed the study. The pUCB group had significantly higher scores on the GMPM and BSID-II Mental and Motor scales at 6 months compared to the EPO and Control groups. DTI showed significant correlations between the GMPM improvement and changes in fractional anisotropy in the pUCB group. 18F-FDG-PET/CT revealed different activation and deactivation patterns among the three groups. The incidence of serious adverse events did not differ between the groups. In conclusion, UCB treatment improved motor and cognitive dysfunction in children with CP undergoing active rehabilitation, accompanied by structural and metabolic changes in the brain.

title: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)) enhances N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor function and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression via RACK1.
text:
We have recently discovered a new way to control the phosphorylation and function of the N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor using a protein called RACK1. Our research has shown that RACK1 binds to both the NR2B subunit of the NMDA receptor and a protein-tyrosine kinase called Fyn. By doing so, RACK1 prevents Fyn from phosphorylating NR2B and reduces the currents produced by the NMDA receptor in CA1 hippocampal slices (Yaka et al., 2002).

In our latest study, we have identified the signaling pathway that leads to the release of RACK1 from the NMDA receptor complex and the consequences of this dissociation. We have found that activating the cAMP/protein kinase A pathway in hippocampal slices causes RACK1 to detach from NR2B and Fyn. This, in turn, leads to the phosphorylation of NR2B and an increase in NMDA receptor activity through Fyn. Additionally, we have discovered that a neuropeptide called pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)) can induce the phosphorylation of NR2B and enhance NMDA receptor potentials.

Furthermore, our research has revealed that activating the cAMP/protein kinase A pathway causes RACK1 to move to the nuclear compartment in isolated hippocampal neurons. In the nucleus, RACK1 regulates the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is induced by PACAP(1-38). Overall, our findings suggest that PACAP(1-38) activates adenylate cyclase, leading to the release of RACK1 from the NMDA receptor and Fyn. This, in turn, results in the phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor, increased activity mediated by Fyn, and the induction of brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression by RACK1.

title: MUC1 oncoprotein activates the IκB kinase β complex and constitutive NF-κB signalling
text: The activation of Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) in various human malignancies is not well understood. Most human carcinomas exhibit abnormal overexpression of the MUC1 oncoprotein, which, like NF-κB, inhibits apoptosis and promotes transformation. This study reveals that the overexpression of MUC1 in human carcinoma cells leads to the constant activation of NF-κB p65. We demonstrate that MUC1 interacts with the high-molecular-weight IκB kinase (IKK) complex in living organisms, and the cytoplasmic domain of MUC1 directly binds to IKKβ and IKKγ. The interaction between MUC1 and both IKKβ and IKKγ is crucial for the activation of IKKβ, resulting in the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα. Research on non-malignant epithelial cells shows that MUC1 is recruited to the TNF-R1 complex and interacts with IKKβ–IKKγ upon TNFα stimulation. The recruitment of MUC1 induced by TNFα depends on TRADD and TRAF2, but not RIP1, the death-domain kinase. Furthermore, the activation of IKKβ mediated by MUC1 relies on TAK1 and TAB2. These findings indicate that MUC1 plays a significant role in the physiological activation of IKKβ and that the excessive expression of MUC1, as observed in human cancers, leads to sustained activation of the IKKβ–NF-κB p65 pathway.

title: Lipoxins: novel series of biologically active compounds formed from arachidonic acid in human leukocytes.
text: Recently, a unique group of oxygenated derivatives called trihydroxytetraenes was discovered in human leukocytes. These compounds are formed from arachidonic acid. The main compound in this series, known as 5,6,15L-trihydroxy-7,9,11,13-icosatetraenoic acid, has been structurally identified. In addition, a second member of this series, called 5D,14,15L-trihydroxy-6,8,10,12-icosatetraenoic acid, has also been characterized. When introduced to human neutrophils, 5,6,15L-trihydroxy-7,9,11,13-icosatetraenoic acid was found to stimulate the generation of superoxide anions and degranulation at low concentrations, without causing significant aggregation. In terms of superoxide anion generation, this compound exhibited similar potency to leukotriene B4. However, it was much less potent than either leukotriene B4 or fMet-Leu-Phe in inducing degranulation. These findings suggest that the interaction between the 5- and 15-lipoxygenase pathways in human leukocytes leads to the production of a new series of oxygenated derivatives of arachidonic acid, which may play a role in regulating specific cellular responses. The proposed names for these new compounds are lipoxin A (5,6,15L-trihydroxy-7,9,11,13-icosatetraenoic acid) and lipoxin B (5D,14,15L-trihydroxy-6,8,10,12-icosatetraenoic acid).

title: Nitric oxide synthase generates superoxide and nitric oxide in arginine-depleted cells leading to peroxynitrite-mediated cellular injury.
text: In addition to producing nitric oxide (NO), purified neuronal NO synthase (nNOS) can also generate superoxide (.O2-) at lower concentrations of L-Arginine (L-Arg). We used electron paramagnetic resonance spin-trapping techniques to observe the formation of NO and .O2- in human kidney 293 cells transfected with nNOS. In cells transfected with a control, the Ca2+ ionophore A23187 triggered the production of NO but not .O2-. However, when the cells were placed in a medium without L-Arg, we observed an increase in .O2- formation as the levels of cytosolic L-Arg decreased, while the generation of NO decreased. The formation of .O2- was almost completely stopped by the specific NOS blocker, N-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME). In cells depleted of L-Arg, we found an accumulation of nitrotyrosine, a specific product of peroxynitrite nitration, but this was not observed in control cells. Activation by A23187 was toxic to L-Arg-depleted cells, but not to control cells, as indicated by significant release of lactate dehydrogenase. This cytotoxicity was largely prevented by either superoxide dismutase or L-NAME. Therefore, when L-Arg availability is reduced, NOS induces cytotoxicity by generating .O2- and NO, which combine to form the powerful oxidant peroxynitrite. Regulating arginine levels may offer a therapeutic approach to disorders involving cellular injury mediated by .O2-/NO.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome and unclassified sudden infant deaths: a definitional and diagnostic approach.
text: The original definition of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) was established in 1969 and underwent modifications two decades later. Over the next 15 years, a significant amount of additional information became available, necessitating further refinement of the SIDS definition to include epidemiologic features, risk factors, pathologic features, and ancillary test findings. A group of experts, including pediatric and forensic pathologists and pediatricians, carefully considered these factors and developed a new comprehensive definition of SIDS for administrative and vital statistics purposes. This new definition was then categorized to facilitate research on sudden infant death. Additionally, a separate category called unclassified sudden infant deaths was introduced for cases that did not meet the criteria for a SIDS diagnosis and where alternative diagnoses of natural or unnatural conditions were uncertain. It is expected that these definitions will be revised in the future as our understanding of SIDS and sudden infant death continues to evolve.

title: Inter-viral conflicts that exploit host CRISPR immune systems of Sulfolobus.
text: The host CRISPR immune system in Sulfolobus islandicus REY15A was not triggered to acquire spacers when infected with a mixture of different Sulfolobus viruses, including STSV2. However, when coinfected with the tailed fusiform viruses SMV1 and STSV2, the host exhibited hyperactive spacer acquisition in both CRISPR loci, exclusively from STSV2. This resulted in the loss of STSV2 but not SMV1. Interestingly, SMV1 was found to activate adaptation while being resistant to CRISPR-mediated adaptation and DNA interference. In a particular clone S-1 obtained from an SMV1 + STSV2-infected culture, which had lost STSV2 but not SMV1, spacers from SMV1 were acquired. This phenomenon was reproducible when wild-type host cells were reinfected with a variant SMV1 isolated from the S-1 culture. The SMV1 variant lacked a virion protein ORF114, which was found to bind DNA. Additionally, this study revealed that there are limits to the maximum sizes of CRISPR loci, spacer uptake significantly slows down the growth of infected cultures, protospacer selection is essentially random and non-directional, and the uptake of spacers from STSV2 and SMV1 is reversible. A hypothesis is proposed to explain the conflicting interactions between SMV1 and the host CRISPR immune system.

title: Lung Carcinogenesis by Diesel Exhaust Particles and the Carcinogenic Mechanism Via Active Oxygens.
text: In a study investigating the role of oxygen radicals in the development of lung cancer caused by diesel exhaust particles (DEP), we discovered a strong correlation between lung tumor growth and the presence of 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) in the DNA of mice exposed to DEP through repeated intratracheal instillation. This exposure to DEP also led to an increase in the activity of cytochrome P-450 reductase, an enzyme associated with the production of superoxide, as well as two types of nitric oxide (NO) synthase, cNOS and iNOS, in the lungs. Conversely, the activity of antioxidant enzymes CuZn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and Mn-SOD was reduced following DEP instillation. These findings suggest that the production of superoxide, hydroxyI radicals, and nitric oxide is heightened in the epithelial cells of the airways, and that the increased levels of superoxide and nitric oxide readily combine to form peroxynitrite (ONOO(-)). Peroxynitrite, in turn, generates hydroxyI radicals, which may play a significant role in the development of cancer caused by DEP.

title: Prion-induced amyloid heart disease with high blood infectivity in transgenic mice.
text: We conducted a study on scrapie-infected transgenic mice that expressed prion protein without the glycophosphatydylinositol membrane anchor. We examined extraneural manifestations in the brain, blood, and heart. Through immunoblot analysis and inoculation into nontransgenic recipients, we were able to easily detect abnormal protease-resistant prion protein (PrPres) and prion infectivity in these organs. The concentration of infectious scrapie in the blood plasma was found to be higher than 10(7) 50% infectious doses per milliliter. Additionally, we observed the presence of PrPres-positive amyloid deposits in the hearts of these transgenic mice, which resulted in myocardial stiffness and cardiac disease.

title: Circulating plasma microRNAs as a screening method for detection of colorectal adenomas.
text:
BACKGROUND: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNA molecules that do not code for proteins. Changes in the levels of specific miRNAs have been observed in colon and other cancers, suggesting their involvement in cancer development. In the UK, the Bowel Cancer Screening Programme relies on the detection of colorectal polyps. However, the national uptake of screening remains low, at less than 60%. Our goal was to investigate whether circulating plasma miRNAs could be used to screen for patients with colorectal polyps, adenomas, or both.

METHODS: We collected blood samples from patients participating in the Bowel Cancer Screening Programme who tested positive for fecal occult blood (indicating the presence of blood in the stool). We extracted plasma RNA and identified target miRNAs using pooled case miRNA assay cards. We quantified the miRNA fraction using a quantitative RT-PCR assay. We compared the results with endoscopy reports and histology findings of any identified and removed polyps. Data analysis was performed using Excel (2011) and SPSS (version 20) software.

FINDINGS: Our study included 210 patients, consisting of 117 with polyps, 12 with cancer, and 81 healthy controls who tested positive for fecal occult blood. The miRNA panel showed significant differences in expression between patients and controls for those with polyps, cancer, or both. We also observed significant differences in expression for patients with polyps, adenomas, multiple adenomas, and right-sided adenomas. Receiver operating characteristic analysis indicated that the miRNA panel had a sensitivity of 60% or more and a specificity of 86% or more for various patient groups.

INTERPRETATION: The identified target miRNAs exhibited significant differences in expression levels between patients with polyps or adenomas and controls. This panel of miRNAs has the potential to be used as a screening test.

FUNDING: This study was supported by the Bowel Disease Research Foundation.

title: Short term persistence of human papillomavirus and risk of cervical precancer and cancer: population based cohort study
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the occurrence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia II or worse (grade II+) or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade III+ after a short period of persistent detection of carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV). The study was conducted as a population-based cohort study in Guanacaste, Costa Rica. A total of 2282 sexually active women were actively followed after enrollment. The primary endpoints were the three-year and five-year cumulative incidence of histologically confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade II+ (n=70). Cervical specimens collected at each visit were tested for more than 40 HPV genotypes, with HPV 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, and 82 considered as the primary carcinogenic genotypes. 

The results showed that women who tested positive for a carcinogenic HPV at enrollment and after approximately one year had a three-year cumulative incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade II+ of 17.0%. Those who tested negative/positive, positive/negative, and negative/negative were at a significantly lower risk, with cumulative incidences of 3.4%, 1.2%, and 0.5% respectively. There was little difference in the cumulative incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade II+ between testing positive twice for any carcinogenic HPV genotype (same or different genotypes) versus testing positive twice for the same carcinogenic genotype (17.0% vs 21.3% respectively). Short-term persistence of HPV 16 strongly predicted cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade II+, with a three-year cumulative incidence of 40.8%. Similar patterns were observed for the five-year cumulative incidence of grade II+ and for the three-year and five-year cumulative incidence of grade III+. 

In conclusion, short-term persistence of a prevalently detected carcinogenic HPV infection, particularly HPV 16, strongly indicates a subsequent diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia II+ over the next few years.

title: Nature and anisotropy of cortical forces orienting Drosophila tissue morphogenesis
text: The ability of cells to change their connections with neighboring cells is crucial for the development of embryos and organs. In order to understand this process, we used quantitative modeling and laser nano-dissection to investigate the mechanics of a specific morphogenetic process in Drosophila melanogaster embryos - the elongation of the tissue due to polarized cell neighbor exchanges. Our findings demonstrate that the anisotropy of cortical tension at the apical cell junctions is enough to drive tissue elongation. We determined the value of this tension by comparing computer simulations with real-life data using various tissue descriptors. By dissecting the actomyosin network at a nano-scale level, we discovered that tension is distributed in an anisotropic manner and relies on the accumulation of myosin II. Furthermore, the relaxation of junctions after nano-dissection suggests that cortical elastic forces play a dominant role in this process. Interestingly, we observed that fluctuations in the position of vertices, where three or more cells meet, facilitate neighbor exchanges. We also identified the contribution of subcellular tensile activity in polarizing junction remodeling, as well as the permissive role of vertex fluctuations during tissue elongation.

title: The influence of some metabolic inhibitors on phagocytic activity of mouse macrophages in vitro.
text: The study examined how various metabolic inhibitors affected the process of phagocytosis in macrophages from mouse peritoneal exudate cultured in vitro. The researchers tested several inhibitors, including sodium iodoacetate, sodium fluoride, sodium fluoroacetate, sodium malonate, 2-4-dinitrophenol, sodium azide, ouabain, and cycloheximide, all at a concentration of 10(-3) M. The results showed that iodoacetate strongly inhibited phagocytosis, confirming that glycolysis is the primary energy source for this process. In contrast, fluoride, despite being an effective inhibitor of glycolysis, had no effect. This discrepancy may be due to the fact that sodium fluoride only blocks anaerobic glycolysis in vitro at an unnatural temperature of 0 degrees C. Fluoroacetate and malonate, which interfere with the Krebs cycle, did not inhibit phagocytosis, likely because macrophages have limited Krebs cycle activity. Sodium azide and 2-4-dinitrophenol, inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation, only affected phagocytosis after 3 hours of contact with the cell cultures. Ouabain, which blocks Na+ and K+ transport across the plasma membrane, likely inhibited phagocytosis by interfering with cell membrane movements. The mode of action of cycloheximide on phagocytosis remains uncertain, as this compound inhibits protein synthesis and may prevent cell membrane renewal.

title: Two-tiered coupling between flowing actin and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes in neuronal growth cones.
text: The mechanisms by which neuronal growth cones move forward by connecting actin-based motility to substrate adhesion are not fully understood at the molecular level. To investigate this, we conducted experiments where we cultured primary neurons on micropatterned substrates coated with N-cadherin. Using single particle tracking combined with photoactivated localization microscopy (sptPALM), we observed the interactions between adhesion and cytoskeletal proteins at the ventral surface of growth cones. We found that there were transient interactions between flowing actin filaments and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes, resulting in a local reduction of actin retrograde flow. However, the normal actin flow on micropatterns was restored when we expressed a dominant negative N-cadherin construct that competed with the coupling between actin and endogenous N-cadherin. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments confirmed the different kinetics of actin and N-cadherin, and also revealed that 20% of the actin population was confined at N-cadherin micropatterns, contributing to local actin accumulation. We used computer simulations with relevant kinetic parameters to model N-cadherin and actin turnover, which validated this mechanism. This combination of short- and long-lived interactions between the motile actin network and spatially restricted adhesive complexes represents a two-tiered clutch mechanism that likely enables dynamic environment sensing and provides the necessary force for growth cone migration.

title: Cloning of factors related to HIV-inducible LBP proteins that regulate steroidogenic factor-1-independent human placental transcription of the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc.
text: The enzyme cytochrome P450scc, known as the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, is responsible for initiating the production of all steroid hormones. The process of gene transcription for P450scc in the adrenal and gonadal glands is essentially the same and relies on the orphan nuclear receptor steroidogenic factor-1. However, in the placenta, a different approach is taken for the transcription of P450scc, using specific elements that are not utilized in the adrenal strategy and do not depend on steroidogenic factor-1. Since the expression of P450scc in the placenta is crucial for human pregnancy, we aimed to identify factors that bind to the -155/-131 region of the human P450scc promoter, which is involved in placental transcription but not in the adrenal or gonadal glands. Through a yeast one-hybrid screen of cDNA clones from human placental JEG-3 cells, we discovered two unique clones. One of them is the previously known transcription factor LBP-1b, which is induced by HIV type I infection of lymphocytes, and the other is a newly identified factor called LBP-9, sharing 83% amino acid sequence similarity with LBP-1b. When these factors were expressed in transfected yeast, they specifically bound to the -155/-131 DNA region. Antisera to LBP proteins caused a shift in the LBP-9.DNA complex and inhibited the formation of the LBP-1b.DNA complex. Reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction analysis detected LBP-1b in various human cells, including placental JEG-3, adrenal NCI-H295A, liver HepG2, cervical HeLa, and monkey kidney COS-1 cells. However, LBP-9 was only detected in JEG-3 cells. When the -155/-131 fragment was linked to a minimal promoter, co-expression of LBP-1b increased transcription by 21-fold in a dose-dependent manner. On the other hand, the addition of LBP-9 suppressed the stimulatory effect of LBP-1b. The roles of LBP transcription factors in normal human physiology have been unclear. However, their involvement in placental P450scc transcription, but not adrenal transcription, highlights the distinct strategies employed by the placenta for the regulation of steroidogenic enzyme genes.

title: Functional reprogramming of polyploidization in megakaryocytes.
text: Polyploidization, a natural process often seen alongside differentiation, is associated with genomic instability and cancer when it becomes deregulated. However, the reasons why cells choose different polyploidization mechanisms remain unknown. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive genetic analysis of endomitosis, a process where megakaryocytes become polyploid by entering mitosis but stopping before anaphase. We found that removing the APC/C cofactor Cdc20 leads to mitotic arrest and severe thrombocytopenia, while the absence of the kinases Aurora-B, Cdk1, or Cdk2 does not affect megakaryocyte polyploidization or platelet levels. When Cdk1 is removed, endocycles without mitosis take over, and polyploidization occurs in the absence of both Cdk1 and Cdk2, accompanied by abnormal re-replication events. Importantly, removing these kinases rescues the defects in Cdc20 null megakaryocytes. These findings suggest that alternative polyploidization mechanisms can replace endomitosis in vivo and provide a cellular basis for therapeutic strategies that distinguish between mitotic and polyploid cells.

title: Histone methyltransferase activity associated with a human multiprotein complex containing the Enhancer of Zeste protein.
text: Enhancer of Zeste [E(z)] is a member of the SET domain-containing protein family and functions as a Polycomb-group transcriptional repressor. While many SET-domain proteins have histone methyltransferase (HMT) activity, recombinant E(z) protein was found to be inactive in an HMT assay. In this study, we have discovered a multiprotein complex containing E(z), extra sex combs, suppressor of zeste-12 [Su(z)12], and the histone binding proteins RbAp46/RbAp48. This complex, named Polycomb repressive complex (PRC) 2, exhibits HMT activity specifically targeting Lys 9 (K9) and Lys 27 (K27) of histone H3. The HMT activity of PRC2 relies on the intact SET domain within the E(z) protein. We propose that the E(z) protein mediates transcriptional repression through methylation-dependent recruitment of PRC1. The presence of Su(z)12, a potent suppressor of position effect variegation, in PRC2 suggests that PRC2 may have a broad role in heterochromatin-mediated silencing.

title: Simvastatin reduces platelet-endocardium adhesion in atrial fibrillation.
text:
OBJECTIVES: The objectives of this study were to examine the relationship between the CD40/CD40L system and increased thrombogenesis in atrial fibrillation (AF), and to investigate the effects of simvastatin treatment.

METHODS: This in vitro study utilized human tissue obtained from a tertiary referral center, specifically right atrial segments collected before the initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass. The experiments were conducted in the presence or absence of 5 microM simvastatin. Two groups of patients, one with chronic atrial fibrillation and the other with sinus rhythm at the time of cardiac surgery, were included. The study evaluated the endocardial expression of CD40, the release of CD40L, and the adhesion of platelets to the endocardium. Additionally, the thickness of platelet aggregates and the distribution of platelets on the endocardium were assessed.

RESULTS: Atrial fibrillation was found to be associated with a significant increase in endocardial CD40 expression (293.1+/-55.1 pg/ml vs. 230.9+/-53.3 pg/ml, p<0.01), as well as platelet-endocardial adhesion compared to sinus rhythm atria (10.8+/-2.2 vs. 5.2+/-1.3 platelet CD41 AU, p<0.01). Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that approximately 62% of fibrillating endocardium was covered by platelets, compared to only 12% in non-sinus rhythm atria. The addition of simvastatin significantly reduced CD40 expression and platelet adhesion to fibrillating atria, and this effect was not reversed by the addition of mevalonic acid.

CONCLUSIONS: Chronic atrial fibrillation acutely upregulates CD40 expression and platelet adhesion to the endocardium. Simvastatin effectively modulates this expression, suggesting its potential to reduce the risk of intra-atrial thrombus formation.

title: Transmission of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease by blood transfusion: risk factor or possible biases.
text:
The recent occurrence of transfusion transmissions of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) cases has brought attention to the potential risk posed by other forms of CJD. In this study, we examined patients with a definite or probable diagnosis of CJD (sporadic CJD, n = 741; genetic CJD, n = 175) and patients without CJD but with a definite alternative diagnosis (n = 482) who had a documented history of blood transfusion. We assessed the risk of exposure to blood transfusion occurring more than 10 years before the onset of disease, taking into account potential confounding factors. We calculated crude odds ratios (ORs) and conducted multivariate logistic regression analyses to evaluate the significance of the findings. 

The results of the univariate analysis showed that blood transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset was 4.1 times more common in sporadic CJD patients compared to those with other neurologic disorders. However, this significance was lost when the 10-year lag time was not considered. In the multivariate analysis, adjusting for possible confounding factors, the risk of developing sporadic CJD after transfusion increased (OR, 5.05). Interestingly, no significant risk factors associated with transfusion were found in patients with genetic CJD. 

In conclusion, this case-control study provides evidence of a significant risk of transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset in sporadic CJD patients. It is unclear whether these findings are biologically plausible or the result of study design biases. Nonetheless, they challenge previous epidemiologic reports that may have overestimated the safety of blood transfusion in sporadic CJD.

title: Advantages and pitfalls of fructosamine and glycated albumin in the diagnosis and treatment of diabetes.
text:
Efficiently diagnosing and accurately monitoring diabetic patients is crucial for reducing the risk of complications. Currently, the main diagnostic and prognostic strategies for diabetes rely on two tests: plasma (or capillary) glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). However, these measures are not foolproof and can be influenced by various clinical and analytical factors. To address this, introducing other indicators of glucose homeostasis, such as fructosamine and glycated albumin (GA), may be an appealing alternative. This is particularly true for patients who may have biased or unreliable HbA1c measurements, such as those with rapid changes in glucose levels, larger glycemic excursions, red blood cell disorders, or renal disease.

Based on available evidence, GA appears to have superior diagnostic efficiency compared to fructosamine across a wide range of clinical settings. Additionally, the method for measuring GA is better standardized and less susceptible to preanalytical variables than the methods used for assessing fructosamine. GA also offers advantages over HbA1c, including lower reagent costs and the ability to automate the analysis on conventional laboratory instruments.

While further research is necessary to definitively establish GA as a complement or potential replacement for conventional measures of glycemic control like HbA1c, it has the potential to aid in the clinical management of diabetic patients for whom HbA1c values may be unreliable.

title: Catalytic-Independent Functions of PARP-1 Determine Sox2 Pioneer Activity at Intractable Genomic Loci.
text: Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) act as the first responders in the genome, binding to inaccessible areas of chromatin to promote the formation of enhancers. How these pioneer TFs gain access to chromatin is still an unanswered question. In this study, we demonstrate that PARP-1, a protein that binds to nucleosomes, works together with the inherent properties of the pioneer TF Sox2 to facilitate its binding to difficult genomic sites in embryonic stem cells. These actions of PARP-1 are independent of its poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferase activity. The sites where PARP-1-dependent Sox2 binding occurs are located in euchromatic regions of the genome with high nucleosome occupancy and low co-occupancy by other transcription factors. PARP-1 enhances the stability of Sox2 binding to nucleosomes at suboptimal sites through cooperative interactions on DNA. Our findings identify both intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics that determine the pioneer activity of Sox2. The conditional pioneer activity observed with Sox2 at a subset of binding sites may also be a crucial feature of other pioneer TFs that operate at challenging genomic locations.

title: Steroid regulation of C. elegans diapause, developmental timing, and longevity.
text: Hormones have a crucial function in facilitating significant stage changes and developmental timing events in various species. In the nematode C. elegans, the receptor for steroid hormones, known as DAF-12, operates at the intersection of pathways that control developmental timing, stage determination, and lifespan. DAF-12 connects environmental and physiological signals to the regulation of life history, and it is integrated within a complex framework that governs a wide range of processes. In this article, we emphasize the molecular understanding, intricate circuitry, and signaling pathways that govern stage transitions in the worm, and how they have provided fundamental insights into the role of steroids in biological timing.

title: A core subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 1 is broadly conserved in function but not primary sequence.
text: Polycomb Group (PcG) proteins are responsible for heritable gene silencing by modifying the structure of chromatin. One crucial PcG complex, known as PRC1, compacts chromatin and prevents chromatin remodeling. In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the intrinsically disordered C-terminal region of a protein called PSC (PSC-CTR) is responsible for these noncovalent effects on chromatin and is essential for the organism's survival. However, because the sequence of PSC-CTR is not well conserved, it was unclear whether its effects on chromatin were significant outside of Drosophila. Additionally, the absence of folded domains in PSC-CTR made it difficult to understand how its sequence encoded its function. To investigate the mechanistic basis and extent of conservation of PSC-CTR activity, researchers identified 17 PSC-CTRs from various organisms ranging from chordates to arthropods. They examined the sequence features and biochemical properties of these PSC-CTRs. Although the PSC-CTR sequences were not highly conserved, they all exhibited high levels of charge and structural disorder. The researchers discovered that active PSC-CTRs, which tightly bind to DNA and efficiently inhibit chromatin remodeling, lacked extended negatively charged stretches. They also found that dispersing the negative charge of PSC-CTR increased its activity, confirming the importance of this property. By using the sequence properties that were identified as important for PSC-CTR activity, the researchers predicted the presence of active PSC-CTRs in other diverse genomes. This analysis revealed that PSC-CTR activity is broadly conserved across different metazoans, a conclusion that could not have been reached through sequence alignments alone. The researchers also discovered that plants lacking active PSC-CTRs possess a functionally similar PcG protein called EMF1. Therefore, this study suggests that a disordered domain with dispersed negative charges is responsible for PRC1 activity and is conserved across both metazoans and plants.

title: Dietary status of trained female cyclists.
text: The dietary status of eight highly trained female cyclists was assessed. Each cyclist maintained a 3-day record of their food intake, which was then analyzed for nutrient content using computer software. Blood samples were also collected and examined for hemoglobin, hematocrit, and albumin levels. The findings revealed that the cyclists' diets were deficient in energy (85% of the recommended daily allowance) and carbohydrates (4.4 grams per kilogram of body weight per day), which is not ideal for an athletic group. The average daily intake of folacin, magnesium, iron, and zinc fell well below the recommended daily allowances (76%, 81%, 59%, and 48% respectively). Furthermore, more than one-third of the cyclists failed to consume 67% of the recommended daily allowance for several micronutrients, including pyridoxine, folacin, cobalamin, vitamin E, magnesium, iron, and zinc. Although the hemoglobin (135 grams per liter), hematocrit (0.39), and albumin (45 grams per liter) values were within the normal range, most hemoglobin values were on the lower end. The diets of most athletes lacked foods such as meats, poultry, fish, beans, peas, and nuts. By incorporating more of these foods, the dietary quality of this group of female cyclists could have been significantly improved. Therefore, it is recommended that these athletes receive nutrition education and diet counseling to optimize their performance.

title: Regulation of Pax-3 expression in the dermomyotome and its role in muscle development.
text: The segmented mesoderm in vertebrates gives rise to various cell types in the embryo, including the axial skeleton and muscle. During embryogenesis, several transcription factors with a paired domain (known as Pax proteins) are expressed in the segmented mesoderm. Among these factors are Pax-3 and a closely related gene, Pax-7, both of which are expressed in the segmental plate and dermomyotome. This study demonstrates that signals from the notochord influence the expression of Pax-3, Pax-7, and Pax-9 in somites, as well as the subsequent differentiation of cell types originating from the somitic mesoderm. The role of the Pax-3 gene in the differentiation of cell types derived from the dermomyotome is directly examined by analyzing muscle development in splotch mouse embryos, which lack a functional Pax-3 gene. In homozygous splotch embryos, a population of Pax-3-expressing cells derived from the dermomyotome, which normally migrate into the limb, is absent, resulting in the loss of limb muscles. However, no abnormalities are observed in the trunk musculature of splotch embryos, indicating that Pax-3 is necessary for limb muscle development but not trunk muscle development.

title: Angiopoietin 2 is a partial agonist/antagonist of Tie2 signaling in the endothelium.
text: Angiopoietin 2 (Ang2) was initially discovered to compete with Ang1 as an antagonist for the receptor tyrosine kinase Tie2 in endothelial cells (ECs). However, there have been conflicting reports on whether Ang2 acts as an agonist or antagonist of Tie2. In this study, we demonstrate that Ang2 acts as an agonist in the absence of Ang1, but as a dose-dependent antagonist when Ang1 is present. When introduced externally, Ang2 activates Tie2 and the PI3K/Akt pathway, which promotes cell migration and survival in ECs. However, its potency and affinity are lower compared to Ang1. ECs naturally produce Ang2 but not Ang1. This endogenous Ang2 maintains Tie2, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, and Akt activities, and supports EC survival, migration, and tube formation. Nevertheless, when ECs are exposed to both Ang1 and Ang2, Ang2 inhibits Ang1-induced Tie2 phosphorylation, Akt activation, and EC survival in a dose-dependent manner. In conclusion, Ang2 can function as both an agonist and antagonist of Tie2. Despite being a weaker agonist than Ang1, endogenous Ang2 plays a crucial role in maintaining Tie2 activation, which is essential for various EC functions. These findings help reconcile conflicting reports on the effects of Ang2 on Tie2, enhance our understanding of endogenous receptor tyrosine kinase signaling mechanisms, and have implications for targeting Ang2 and Tie2 in conditions like sepsis and cancer.

title: Bacteremia caused by a strain of Desulfovibrio related to the provisionally named Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis.
text: Over a period of 5 years, a total of eight Desulfovibrio spp. isolates were obtained from abdominal or brain abscesses or blood samples. Out of these isolates, seven were found to be part of a mixed flora. However, one particular strain was isolated in pure culture from the blood of a patient with peritonitis originating from the appendix. Based on the analysis of the 16S rRNA gene sequences, this strain was found to be closely related to Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis. This report focuses on the fourth isolate of this recently identified species, which was found to be either isolated in pure culture or as the predominant part of the flora, and was associated with infectious processes. These findings suggest that D. fairfieldensis may possess a higher potential for causing disease compared to other Desulfovibrio species.

title: Vitamin D: The "sunshine" vitamin.
text: Vitamin D insufficiency affects nearly half of the global population. Approximately 1 billion people worldwide, spanning all ethnicities and age groups, suffer from a deficiency in vitamin D (VDD). This widespread issue of low vitamin D levels can primarily be attributed to lifestyle factors such as reduced outdoor activities and environmental factors like air pollution, which limit exposure to sunlight. Sunlight is necessary for the production of vitamin D in the skin through ultraviolet-B (UVB) rays. The high prevalence of vitamin D insufficiency is a significant public health concern because it is an independent risk factor for overall mortality in the general population. Recent studies suggest that the recommended daily intake of vitamin D may need to be increased to prevent chronic diseases. As the number of individuals with VDD continues to rise, research is increasingly focused on understanding the role of this hormone in overall health and the prevention of chronic illnesses. VDD is prevalent across all age groups, and since only a few foods naturally contain vitamin D, guidelines recommend supplementation at suggested daily intake and tolerable upper limit levels. It is also recommended to measure the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level as the initial diagnostic test for individuals at risk of deficiency. Treatment for deficient patients typically involves supplementation with either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3. A meta-analysis conducted in 2007 demonstrated that vitamin D supplementation was associated with a significant reduction in mortality. This review aims to summarize the presumed mechanisms underlying the relationship between vitamin D, explore its biology, and discuss its clinical implications.

title: Cyclin D1 activation in B-cell malignancy: association with changes in histone acetylation, DNA methylation, and RNA polymerase II binding to both promoter and distal sequences.
text: Chromosome translocation in mantle cell lymphoma and a subset of multiple myeloma leads to the deregulation of Cyclin D1 expression. The exact molecular mechanisms responsible for long-distance gene deregulation are not well understood, but changes in acetylated histones and methylated CpG dinucleotides may play a significant role. To investigate this further, we examined the patterns of DNA methylation and histone acetylation at the Cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11q13 in B-cell malignancies. We found that the Cyclin D1 promoter was hypomethylated and hyperacetylated in cell lines and patient samples that expressed Cyclin D1, while it was methylated and hypoacetylated in cell lines that did not express Cyclin D1. Interestingly, we observed domains of hyperacetylated histones and hypomethylated DNA extending over 120 kb upstream of the Cyclin D1 gene. These patterns were also present at the Cyclin D1 promoter, but not at the upstream major translocation cluster region, in nonexpressing B and T cells that were not tumorigenic. Furthermore, we found that RNA polymerase II binding occurred at both the Cyclin D1 promoter and the 3' immunoglobulin heavy-chain regulatory regions only in malignant B-cell lines with deregulated Cyclin D1 expression. Based on these findings, we propose a model where RNA polymerase II bound at IgH regulatory sequences can activate the Cyclin D1 promoter through either long-range polymerase transfer or tracking.

title: The physiological regulation of toll-like receptor expression and function in humans.
text:
To date, eleven mammalian toll-like receptors (TLRs 1-11) have been identified and are known to play a crucial role in regulating immune responses. However, the factors that control TLR expression and function in living organisms are not well understood. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to investigate how TLR expression and function are regulated in humans under normal physiological conditions.

To examine the impact of daily rhythms on TLR expression and function, we collected peripheral venous blood samples from eight healthy volunteers at different times corresponding to the peak and lowest levels of naturally circulating cortisol. We found no evidence of daily rhythmicity in the expression of TLRs 1, 2, 4, or 9. However, when we activated CD14(+) monocytes with specific TLR ligands, we observed a greater upregulation of costimulatory molecules (CD80 and CD86) and antigen-presenting molecules (MHC class II) in samples obtained in the evening compared to the morning (P < 0.05).

Next, we investigated the influence of physical stress on TLR expression and function. We collected peripheral venous blood samples from eleven healthy volunteers at rest and after 1.5 hours of intense exercise in a hot environment (34 degrees C). We found that strenuous exercise led to a decrease (P < 0.005) in the expression of TLRs 1, 2, and 4 on CD14(+) monocytes. Additionally, the upregulation of CD80, CD86, MHC class II, and interleukin-6 by CD14(+) monocytes following activation with specific TLR ligands was reduced (P < 0.05) in samples obtained after exercise compared to samples obtained at rest.

These findings demonstrate that TLR function can be modulated under normal physiological conditions in living organisms. They also provide evidence for the involvement of immunomodulatory hormones in regulating TLR function.

title: A review of psychosocial needs of breast-cancer patients and their relatives.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to identify the psychosocial needs of breast cancer patients and their relatives, as well as the factors that affect these needs. Additionally, we aimed to develop a preliminary model to guide further research and need assessments in clinical practice.

BACKGROUND: Women diagnosed with breast cancer face the challenge of dealing with a life-threatening illness. The treatment and recovery process can be physically and emotionally demanding for both patients and their relatives. Conducting a need assessment can help clinicians focus on providing appropriate support.

DESIGN: This study involved a literature review.

METHOD: We conducted a search using electronic databases and specific research terms. A total of 20 articles were identified and analyzed.

RESULTS: The needs identified by patients included treatment-related physical and social impairments, such as fatigue, menopausal symptoms, and changes in body image. Patients also experienced emotional distress, including fear of recurrence, anxiety, and depression. Partners of patients required assistance in protecting themselves and the patient from various threats. Women with breast cancer needed information to maintain control and manage their illness, while partners desired information about the patient's condition and prognosis. However, there is a lack of knowledge regarding the needs of relatives. The interaction between patients and their partners can be influenced by mutual familial support, the health of both individuals, and emotional distress.

CONCLUSIONS: We propose a preliminary family-based model to guide further research and clinical support. Additional research is necessary to determine the specific psychosocial factors that may impact the fulfillment of patients' and relatives' needs.

RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: The proposed model can serve as a framework for healthcare professionals to assess the met and unmet needs of patients and their relatives, as well as the actual demand for assistance. This model can guide care planning, counseling, and education.

title: Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase 1 Represses Liver X Receptor-mediated ABCA1 Expression and Cholesterol Efflux in Macrophages.
text: Liver X receptors (LXR) are nuclear receptors that are activated by oxysterols. They play a crucial role in reverse cholesterol transport by increasing the expression of ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABCA1 and ABCG1), which facilitate the removal of cholesterol from cells. Activation of LXRs has been shown to reduce atherosclerosis and promote the regression of existing plaques in mouse models. However, the factors that regulate LXR-dependent gene activation in macrophages are still not fully understood. To identify new regulators of LXR activity, we used affinity purification and mass spectrometry to analyze LXRα complexes in the nucleus. Through this analysis, we discovered that poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) is associated with LXRs. In fact, PARP-1 interacts with both LXRα and LXRβ. Depletion or inhibition of PARP-1 activity increased the expression of ABCA1 in macrophages, but had no effect on the expression of other LXR target genes such as ABCG1 and SREBP-1c. Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments confirmed that PARP-1 is recruited to the LXR response element in the promoter of the ABCA1 gene. Furthermore, we found that PARP-1 poly(ADP-ribosyl)ates LXR, suggesting that this modification may influence LXR function. Importantly, treatment with a PARP inhibitor called 3-aminobenzamide enhanced cholesterol efflux mediated by ABCA1 in macrophages. These findings highlight the significant role of PARP-1 in regulating lipid homeostasis through LXR. Understanding the interaction between PARP-1 and LXR could potentially lead to the development of new therapeutics for the treatment of atherosclerosis.

title: Emergency contraception: advance provision in a young, high-risk clinic population.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine if providing emergency contraception in advance would increase its usage and if it would have any impact on regular contraceptive use. The study involved a controlled trial with female clients aged 16-24 who visited a publicly funded family planning clinic. The participants were randomly assigned to either receive advance provision of emergency contraception and education (treatment group) or education only (control group). Out of the 263 participants enrolled, 213 completed the follow-up (111 in the treatment group, 102 in the control group). The main outcomes measured were emergency contraception knowledge and usage, frequency of unprotected sex, and contraceptive use patterns in the past 4 months. 

The results showed that participants were aware of emergency contraception during the follow-up, but the treatment group was three times more likely to use it compared to the control group. Although the treatment group did not report higher frequencies of unprotected sex, a higher percentage of women in the treatment group (28%) reported using less effective contraception at follow-up compared to enrollment, compared to the control group (17%). Both groups showed an increase in consistent pill use from enrollment to follow-up, but the control group (58%) was more likely to report consistent pill use compared to the treatment group (32%) at follow-up. 

In conclusion, providing advance provision of emergency contraception increased its usage, while education alone did not have the same effect. However, there were potentially negative effects observed, such as changes to less effective contraceptive methods and patterns of pill use, which need to be further explored in relation to the observed benefits.

title: Immunophenotypic analysis of AIDS-related diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and clinical implications in patients from AIDS malignancies consortium clinical trials 010 and 034
text: The purpose of this study was to determine if immunohistochemical analyses of biopsies from patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and HIV infection are relevant for prognosis. The study examined 81 DLBCLs from patients with AIDS and compared the immunophenotype with survival data, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) positivity, and CD4 counts. The results showed that the different subtypes of DLBCL did not significantly differ in overall survival or CD4 count at cancer presentation. EBV was found in both subtypes but did not affect survival. The expression of certain markers (FOXP1, Blimp-1/PRDM1, or BCL-2) was not correlated with outcome in patients with AIDS-related DLBCL. The only marker that showed predictive value was Ki-67, with higher proliferation rates associated with better survival and a better response to therapy. These findings suggest that commonly used immunohistochemical markers may not be clinically relevant in HIV-infected patients with DLBCL, given current treatment strategies for lymphoma and control of HIV infection.

title: Prion-like activity of Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase: implications for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
text:
Neurodegenerative diseases are part of a larger group of disorders called proteinopathies, which involve the misfolding of proteins. There is growing evidence suggesting that prion-like mechanisms play a role in many common neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, tauopathies, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). These diseases are characterized by the abnormal misfolding and aggregation of specific proteins. The prion paradigm offers an explanation for how a mutant or wild-type protein can drive the progression of disease by initiating the self-propagation of protein misfolding.

ALS, a fatal disease that causes the progressive degeneration of motor neurons, is considered a classic proteinopathy. It is characterized by the formation of protein aggregates within and around motor neurons, which can contribute to neurotoxicity. It is well-known that misfolded or oxidized SOD1 protein is highly toxic to motor neurons and plays a significant role in the pathology of ALS. Recent research has discovered that both mutant and wild-type SOD1 can propagate protein misfolding, which may explain the observed spread of the disease throughout the nervous system.

In this review, we will explore the current understanding of the prion-like properties of SOD1 and discuss the proposed mechanisms of intercellular transmission.

title: Analysis of Epstein-Barr virus-regulated host gene expression changes through primary B-cell outgrowth reveals delayed kinetics of latent membrane protein 1-mediated NF-κB activation.
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a type of human herpesvirus that has the ability to alter the expression of genes in host cells, leading to the immortalization of primary B cells. In this research, we examined the changes in gene expression that occur in host cells following infection with EBV, both during the initial stage of cell proliferation and as the cells transform into lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs). While most of the genes regulated by EBV were altered during the transition from resting, uninfected B cells to the initial stage of cell proliferation, a significant number of genes changed specifically during the transition from early proliferation to LCL outgrowth. We identified biological processes, protein classes, and targets of specific transcription factors that were consistently and dynamically regulated by EBV. Shortly after infection, genes associated with cell proliferation, stress responses, and the p53 pathway were highly affected. However, as the cells transitioned from early to long-term outgrowth, genes involved in inhibiting apoptosis, regulating the actin cytoskeleton, and activating NF-κB became more prominent. It was previously believed that a viral protein called latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) was responsible for activating NF-κB and that its expression occurred within 2 days after infection. However, our data showed that while this is true, high levels of LMP1 expression and NF-κB activity were not observed until 3 weeks after the initial B-cell infection. Additionally, we found that activating NF-κB during the first week after infection increased the efficiency of cell transformation, while inhibiting NF-κB had no effect on transformation. In fact, inhibiting NF-κB did not harm EBV-infected cells until LMP1 levels and NF-κB activity were high. These findings demonstrate the dynamic nature of gene expression regulated by EBV and support the idea that early EBV-infected proliferating B cells have a fundamentally different growth and survival phenotype compared to LCLs.

title: Clinical and laboratory features of adult T-cell leukaemia lymphoma in Barbados.
text: We present a study on 23 Afro-Caribbean patients diagnosed with adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Barbados over a period of five years. Of the patients, 9 were male and 14 were female, with a median age of 38 years (ranging from 14 to 84). Among them, 12 had acute leukaemia, 10 had lymphoma (including 4 with solitary extra nodal lesions), and 1 had the smouldering subtype. Two patients had a previous history of tropical spastic paraparesis/HTLV I associated myelopathy (TSP/HAM). The prognosis was unfavorable, as only 3 patients achieved complete responses to chemotherapy (CHOP), which lasted between 9 and 36 months. In conclusion, our findings suggest that ATLL in Barbados shares similarities with the disease in other Caribbean islands and Japan, although the age of onset in Barbados is approximately ten years younger than in Japan.

title: Acoustic landmarks drive delta-theta oscillations to enable speech comprehension by facilitating perceptual parsing.
text: Recent research indicates that slow oscillations in the auditory cortex, occurring at frequencies below 10 Hz, may be involved in processing complex auditory signals such as speech. Specifically, studies have found that these oscillations align with the temporal envelopes of critical-band frequencies, which are important acoustic features. However, the exact role of this alignment in speech intelligibility remains unclear. In this study, we propose that the "sharpness" of temporal fluctuations in the critical band envelope serves as a cue for the syllabic rate of speech, leading to the synchronization of delta-theta rhythms and enhancing intelligibility. Our findings suggest that these sharp events in the stimulus cause cortical rhythms to realign and segment the stimulus into syllable-sized chunks, aiding in further decoding. Through magnetoencephalographic recordings, we demonstrate that removing temporal fluctuations at the syllabic rate reduces envelope-tracking activity, while reintroducing these fluctuations restores the activity. Moreover, the changes in tracking correlate with the intelligibility of the stimulus. Overall, our results indicate that the sharpness of fluctuations in the stimulus, as reflected in the cochlear output, drives oscillatory activity to synchronize with and track the stimulus at its syllabic rate. This process likely facilitates the segmentation of the stimulus into meaningful chunks, improving perception and intelligibility.

title: Crystal structures of complexes of the small ribosomal subunit with tetracycline, edeine and IF3.
text: We utilized X-ray crystallography to examine the structures of three distinct complexes involving the small ribosomal subunit of Thermus thermophilus. These complexes included the A-site inhibitor tetracycline, the universal initiation inhibitor edeine, and the C-terminal domain of the translation initiation factor IF3. Through crystal structure analysis, we discovered the crucial site responsible for blocking the A-site in the tetracycline complex.
