Additionally, we identified five other tetracycline sites that resolved previous conflicting biochemical data regarding its location. The interaction between edeine and the small subunit revealed its role in inhibiting initiation and its connection to P-site tRNA. Furthermore, the positioning of the C-terminal domain of IF3 on the solvent side of the platform provided insights into the formation of the initiation complex. This positioning also suggested that the anti-association activity of IF3 stems from its influence on the conformational dynamics of the small ribosomal subunit.

title: Plasmid-encoded proinsulin preserves C-peptide while specifically reducing proinsulin-specific CD8⁺ T cells in type 1 diabetes.
text: In individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D), there is a strong inflammatory response that destroys the β cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, which are responsible for producing and releasing insulin. Researchers have long been searching for a therapy that specifically targets the autoimmune response in T1D without affecting the rest of the immune system. One major target of the immune response in T1D is proinsulin. We hypothesized that a modified DNA plasmid called BHT-3021, which contains the genetic information for proinsulin, could help preserve β cell function in T1D patients by reducing the number of insulin-specific CD8⁺ T cells. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a study with 80 subjects over the age of 18 who had been diagnosed with T1D within the past 5 years. The subjects were randomly assigned to receive either intramuscular injections of BHT-3021 or a placebo (BHT-placebo) on a weekly basis for 12 weeks. We then monitored the subjects in a blinded manner to assess safety and immune responses. Four different doses of BHT-3021 were tested: 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, and 6.0 mg. We used C-peptide as both an exploratory measure of efficacy and a safety measure. We also assessed the frequency of islet-specific CD8⁺ T cells using multimers of monomeric human leukocyte antigen class I molecules loaded with peptides from pancreatic and unrelated antigens. No serious adverse events related to BHT-3021 were observed. C-peptide levels improved compared to the placebo at all doses, with the 1 mg dose showing the most significant improvement at the 15-week mark (+19.5% BHT-3021 versus -8.8% BHT-placebo, P < 0.026). The number of proinsulin-reactive CD8⁺ T cells decreased in the BHT-3021 group (P < 0.006), while there were no significant changes in T cells targeting unrelated islet or foreign molecules. There were also no notable changes in the production of interferon-γ, interleukin-4 (IL-4), or IL-10 in CD4 T cells. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that a modified DNA plasmid encoding proinsulin can reduce the frequency of CD8⁺ T cells that react to proinsulin while preserving C-peptide levels during the course of treatment.

title: Dexamethasone and risk of nausea and vomiting and postoperative bleeding after tonsillectomy in children: a randomized trial.
text: The objective of this study was to determine if different doses of dexamethasone can reduce the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in pediatric tonsillectomy patients. The study was a randomized placebo-controlled trial conducted on 215 children undergoing elective tonsillectomy at a major public teaching hospital in Switzerland from February 2005 to December 2007. The children were randomly assigned to receive either dexamethasone (at doses of 0.05, 0.15, or 0.5 mg/kg) or a placebo intravenously after anesthesia induction. Postoperative pain relief was provided with acetaminophen-codeine and ibuprofen. Follow-up continued until the 10th postoperative day. The primary outcome measure was the prevention of PONV at 24 hours, while secondary outcome measures included the decrease in the need for ibuprofen at 24 hours and the evaluation of adverse effects. The results showed that at 24 hours, a higher percentage of participants who received the placebo experienced PONV compared to those who received dexamethasone at different doses. The children who received dexamethasone also required less ibuprofen. However, there were more postoperative bleeding episodes in the dexamethasone group, with the highest risk observed in those who received a dose of 0.5 mg/kg. Eight children had to undergo emergency reoperation due to bleeding, all of whom had received dexamethasone. The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns. In conclusion, dexamethasone reduced the risk of PONV in pediatric tonsillectomy patients, but it was associated with an increased risk of postoperative bleeding. The trial was registered under clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00403806.

title: Detection of sweet and umami taste in the absence of taste receptor T1r3.
text: It is believed that the ability to detect the tastes of sugars (sweet) and glutamate (umami) is attributed to the T1r receptors found in taste cells. Through molecular genetics and heterologous expression, it has been determined that T1r2 combined with T1r3 functions as a receptor for sweetness, while T1r1 combined with T1r3, along with a truncated version of the type 4 metabotropic glutamate receptor (known as taste-mGluR4), serves as receptors for umami. In our study, we observed that mice lacking T1r3 did not exhibit a preference for artificial sweeteners and displayed reduced, but not completely eliminated, behavioral and nerve responses to sugars and umami compounds. These findings suggest that there are other receptors and/or pathways in taste cells that are independent of T1r3 and are responsible for detecting sweet and umami tastes.

title: Cyclin A1 is required for meiosis in the male mouse
text: The mammalian A-type cyclin family comprises of two members, namely cyclin A1 (encoded by Ccna1) and cyclin A2 (encoded by Ccna2). Cyclin A2 plays a crucial role in promoting both G1/S and G2/M transitions, and when Ccna2 is deleted in mice, it leads to embryonic death. In mice, cyclin A1 is exclusively expressed in the germ cell lineage, while in humans, it is predominantly found in the testis and certain myeloid leukemia cells. To explore the function of cyclin A1 and the potential overlap with other cyclins in vivo, we created mice with a Ccna1 null mutation. Male mice lacking Ccna1 (Ccna1-/-) were infertile due to a blockage in spermatogenesis before the initial meiotic division, whereas female mice were unaffected. The arrest of meiosis in Ccna1–/– males was associated with an increase in germ cell apoptosis, abnormalities in desynapsis, and a decrease in Cdc2 kinase activation at the end of meiotic prophase. Therefore, cyclin A1 is indispensable for the progression of spermatocytes into the first meiotic division in male mice, and this function cannot be compensated by the concurrently expressed B-type cyclins.

title: Metabolic effects of isoenergetic nutrient exchange over 24 hours in relation to obesity in women.
text: A study was conducted using twenty-four hour whole body indirect calorimetry to examine the effects of feeding isoenergetic diets with varying fat and carbohydrate content during a sedentary test day. The study included three groups of women: lean, obese, and post-obese after weight loss. The results showed that energy expenditure was higher in absolute terms in the obese women. When fasting, the twenty-four hour energy expenditure was only 3-7 percent lower compared to when fed to achieve energy balance. There were no significant differences in energy expenditure between the two diets or between the groups. However, the thermogenic effect of the high carbohydrate diet was significantly greater than that of the high fat diet. The post-obese group tended to have lower energy expenditure per kilogram of fat-free mass compared to the controls when fasting and when fed a high-fat diet. This pattern was not observed in the obese group. The post-obese group also had particularly low energy expenditure during sleep when fed a high-fat diet. Diurnal variations in respiratory quotient (RQ) showed a more pronounced increase in morning RQ from the nocturnal minimum in the obese and post-obese groups, suggesting a potential energy-saving mechanism through increased availability of stored dietary carbohydrate.

title: Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease: an integrated clinical syndrome.
text: The previous belief that survivors of acute kidney injury (AKI) tend to fully recover renal function is now being questioned. It is now understood that AKI can directly lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and increase the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) or worsening existing CKD. The severity, duration, and frequency of AKI also play a role in predicting poor patient outcomes. CKD itself is a significant risk factor for the occurrence and detection of AKI. Experimental data supports the observations that AKI and CKD have a bidirectional relationship. Factors such as reduced renal mass, insufficient blood flow to the kidneys, disruption of cell cycles, and ineffective repair mechanisms contribute to disease progression in patients with or without CKD. The distinction between AKI and CKD may not be clear-cut. Instead, it is important to consider the integrated clinical syndrome of reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR) with acute and chronic stages, where the disease's progression and outcome are influenced by various factors, including the balance between adaptive and maladaptive repair mechanisms over time. Physicians should provide long-term follow-up to patients who experience their first episode of AKI, even if their renal function appears normal.

title: Fatty acids as modulators of the immune response.
text: There is a wealth of research on the role of fatty acids in inflammation and immune responses. Specifically, omega-3 fatty acids have been extensively studied and have shown strong anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects in various diseases in animal studies, such as autoimmunity, arthritis, and infection. However, the evidence from human trials is not as clear-cut. This review aims to provide a historical context for understanding how fatty acids may impact the immune system. Additionally, it highlights two recent important reports from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which critically evaluate the evidence from human clinical trials on omega-3 fatty acids and their effects on rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, and other immune-mediated diseases. Furthermore, the review examines data from human clinical trials investigating the influence of different bioactive fatty acids on immune response both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. The limitations of experimental design and commonly used immune assays are also discussed. The lack of consistency between expectations and evidence in this field has been disappointing. The review concludes with recommendations for improving both animal-based and human studies in order to enhance our understanding of the role of fatty acids in inflammation and immune responses.

title: Common and rare variants in multifactorial susceptibility to common diseases
text: In this article, we provide a historical overview of the search for genetic variations that impact an individual's susceptibility to chronic diseases. We start with RA Fisher's groundbreaking work and then move on to the current excitement surrounding whole-genome association studies (WGAS). Additionally, we explore the concepts behind identifying common variations as causal factors for diseases and compare them to the fundamental ideas underlying the rare variant hypothesis. The identification of rare variations involves carefully selecting candidate genes for examination, utilizing highly efficient resequencing techniques, and accurately assessing the functional consequences of the implicated variation. We believe that this approach can currently be successfully applied to uncover the role of rare variations in the complex inheritance of common diseases. Ultimately, this could lead to the implementation of much-needed preventative screening programs.

title: Cell-cell adhesion and signalling.
text: Recently, researchers have discovered signalling pathways that are triggered by Rho small GTPases. These pathways play a crucial role in coordinating the assembly, stability, and function of junctions, as well as the interactions between adhesive complexes and the cortical cytoskeleton beneath them. One particularly fascinating aspect is the interaction between adherens junctions, the activation of Rho proteins, and the dynamic behavior of microtubules, actin, and intermediate filaments. This interaction holds significant implications for regulating the functionality of cell-cell adhesion and suggests a more comprehensive understanding of signalling processes.

title: Fibroblast growth factor 21 as an emerging metabolic regulator: clinical perspectives.
text: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a hormone primarily produced by the liver, but it is also found in adipocytes and the pancreas. It plays a crucial role in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism in these tissues as well as in the brain. In mice, fasting triggers the liver to increase the expression of FGF21 through PPAR-α, which then stimulates processes like gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and ketogenesis as a response to fasting and starvation. In a fed state, FGF21 acts as an autocrine factor in adipocytes, influencing the activity of PPAR-γ through a feed-forward loop mechanism. Studies have shown that administering recombinant FGF21 to obese mice and diabetic monkeys can provide various metabolic benefits, such as improved insulin sensitivity, blood glucose levels, lipid profile, and body weight, without any negative side effects. These findings suggest that FGF21 could be a potential therapeutic agent for obesity-related medical conditions. However, in human studies, high levels of circulating FGF21 have been observed in obesity and related cardiometabolic disorders, including metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and coronary artery disease. This may indicate the presence of FGF21 resistance or compensatory responses to metabolic stress, suggesting that higher doses of FGF21 may be needed to achieve therapeutic effectiveness. On the other hand, serum FGF21 has been identified as a potential biomarker for early detection of these cardiometabolic disorders. This review provides an overview of recent advancements in understanding FGF21 from both physiological and clinical perspectives.

title: Assessment of the cerebral circulation in adults with coarctation of the aorta.
text: The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence and identify high-risk features of intracranial aneurysm (IA) in adults with coarctation of the aorta (CoA). Current guidelines recommend computed tomography angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance imaging for evaluation, but this recommendation is not universally accepted. From January 2008 to February 2011, a screening program was conducted where adults with CoA underwent CTA of the intracranial vessels. Forty-three patients completed the screening, and 11% were found to have IA. The patients with IA were older than those without. There were no significant differences in other variables measured. The study concluded that screening adults with CoA is justified, particularly in the fourth and fifth decades of life. Further research is needed to understand the development, natural history, and treatment of IA.

title: Bioenergetic aspects of apoptosis, necrosis and mitoptosis
text:
This review examines the relationship between bioenergetic processes and programmed cell death, specifically apoptosis, necrosis, and mitoptosis. The following conclusions are drawn: 

1. ATP and mitochondrial hyperpolarization (an increase in membrane potential) are necessary for certain stages of apoptosis and necrosis. 
2. Apoptosis initially leads to an increase in ATP and hyperpolarization, but eventually results in a collapse of membrane potential and a decrease in ATP levels. 
3. Moderate reduction in ATP levels (around three-fold) for short and long durations induces apoptosis and necrosis, respectively. 
4. In certain types of apoptosis and necrosis, cell death is triggered by an excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by Complex I and Complex III of the respiratory chain, which is dependent on membrane potential. 
5. ROS-induced mitoptosis is proposed as a mechanism to eliminate mitochondria that overproduce ROS. 
6. Extensive mitoptosis can lead to cell death by releasing cell death proteins that are normally concealed in the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol.

title: Embryonic stem cells require Wnt proteins to prevent differentiation to epiblast stem cells
text:
Pluripotent stem cells can exist in two different states: naive and primed. This can be seen in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), respectively. In the naive state, ESCs have a unique open conformation of the genome and possess minimal repressive epigenetic marks. On the other hand, EpiSCs have activated the epigenetic machinery that supports differentiation into various embryonic cell types. The transition from naive to primed pluripotency is a crucial step in cellular differentiation, but the signals that control this process are still not fully understood.

Our study reveals that both paracrine and autocrine Wnt signals play a vital role in maintaining the self-renewal of ESCs. These signals are necessary to prevent ESCs from differentiating into EpiSCs. Additionally, we have found that a combination of Wnt proteins and the cytokine LIF is sufficient to support ESC self-renewal even in the absence of any other undefined factors. This discovery has allowed us to derive new ESC lines, including ones from mouse strains that were previously considered non-permissive.

Our findings not only demonstrate the regulatory role of Wnt signals in the transition from naive to primed pluripotency, but also highlight the importance of Wnt as a critical factor for ESC self-renewal.

title: CLIP identifies Nova-regulated RNA networks in the brain.
text: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia (POMA) is an autoimmune neurologic disease characterized by abnormal motor inhibition, which targets neuron-specific antigens known as Nova proteins. These proteins play a crucial role in regulating neuronal pre-messenger RNA splicing by directly binding to RNA. In order to identify the specific RNA targets of Nova proteins, a method was developed to purify protein-RNA complexes from mouse brain using ultraviolet cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP). Through this technique, thirty-four transcripts were repeatedly identified as Nova CLIP targets. Among these, three-quarters were found to encode proteins that function at the neuronal synapse, while one-third were involved in neuronal inhibition. Further investigation in Nova-/- mice confirmed that Nova proteins regulate the splicing of important targets such as c-Jun N-terminal kinase 2, neogenin, and gephyrin. Gephyrin, in particular, encodes a protein responsible for clustering inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine receptors, both of which have been previously identified as Nova splicing targets. This discovery suggests that Nova proteins coordinately regulate a biologically coherent set of RNAs that encode multiple components of the inhibitory synapse. This finding may provide insights into the underlying cause of abnormal motor inhibition in POMA.

title: Anti-Angiogenic Activity of Selected Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors, PD166285 and PD173074: Implications for Combination Treatment with Photodynamic Therapy
text: Angiogenesis, the process of forming new blood vessels from existing ones, is necessary for the growth of tumors. It involves communication between endothelial and tumor cells through signaling from angiogenic growth factors. Disrupting these events can suppress tumor growth. In this study, the anti-angiogenic activity and anti-tumor effectiveness of two inhibitors, PD166285 and PD173074, were evaluated in combination with photodynamic therapy (PDT). Various assays and studies were conducted to assess the effects of these compounds on blood vessel formation and tumor growth. PD166285 inhibited several receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), including PDGFR-β, EGFR, FGFR1TK, and c-src TK, at concentrations between 7−85nM. PD173074 specifically inhibited FGFR1TK at 26nM. PD173074 showed selective growth inhibition of human umbilical vein endothelial cells compared to a panel of tumor cell lines. Both PD166285 and PD173074 inhibited the formation of microcapillaries on Matrigel-coated plastic at a concentration of 10nM. In vivo studies in mice demonstrated that oral administration of PD166285 (1−25 mg/kg) or PD173074 (25−100 mg/kg) dose-dependently inhibited angiogenesis. When combined with PDT, daily oral doses of PD166285 (5−10 mg/kg) or PD173074 (30−60 mg/kg) significantly prolonged tumor regression in a murine mammary 16c tumor compared to PDT alone (p<0.001). The combination treatment also resulted in many long-term survivors. PD166285 and PD173074 exhibited strong anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor effects and extended the duration of the anti-tumor response to PDT. Inhibiting specific RTKs, such as FGFR1TK, could lead to the development of new chemotherapeutic agents that limit tumor angiogenesis and regrowth after cytoreductive treatments like PDT.

title: The VirB type IV secretion system of Bartonella henselae mediates invasion, proinflammatory activation and antiapoptotic protection of endothelial cells.
text: Bartonella henselae is a pathogen that is transmitted by arthropods and can cause infection in both cats and humans. In cats, it leads to a blood infection, while in humans, it can cause a variety of clinical symptoms. Interestingly, B. henselae has the ability to specifically infect the cells lining blood vessels in humans, causing inflammation and the formation of abnormal blood vessel growths. To study this interaction, researchers have used cultured human cells that mimic the lining of blood vessels. However, there is still much to learn about the specific factors that make B. henselae pathogenic. Recently, scientists discovered that a protein called VirB, which is part of a secretion system in the bacteria, is crucial for causing infection in the animal host. In this study, the researchers demonstrate that VirB is also responsible for many of the harmful effects of B. henselae on human endothelial cells. These effects include rearrangement of the cell's internal structure, activation of inflammatory pathways, and prevention of cell death. Additionally, the researchers found that high levels of bacteria can have toxic effects on the cells, which can interfere with their normal growth. Overall, the VirB protein is a key factor in the ability of B. henselae to infect and manipulate human endothelial cells, which contributes to its ability to cause disease in the blood vessels.

title: Serum Cystatin C Is Related to Pulse Wave Velocity Even in Subjects with Normal Serum Creatinine
text: Our hypothesis was that serum cystatin C may be a more reliable indicator of arterial stiffness compared to serum creatinine and creatinine-based glomerular filtration rate (GFR). The objective of this study was to assess the relationship between serum cystatin C and arterial stiffness, independent of serum creatinine, in individuals with normal serum creatinine levels. A total of 2,018 participants (1,120 males, 898 females) were included in the study. Mean brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) was used as a measure of arterial stiffness, and separate analyses were conducted for males and females. In males, a positive correlation was observed between baPWV and serum cystatin C (Y=1109.0548+329.9102X, r2=0.056, p<0.001). Stepwise multivariate regression analysis in males revealed that age, waist circumference, heart rate, cystatin C level, triglyceride level, and fasting glucose were independent predictors of baPWV. Similarly, in females, a positive relationship was found between baPWV and serum cystatin C (Y=1035.7828+402.2970X, r2=0.090, p<0.001). Stepwise multivariate regression analysis in females showed that age, heart rate, cystatin C level, fasting glucose, and insulin level were independent predictors of baPWV. Age, heart rate, fasting glucose, and serum cystatin C were significant variables in both genders that contributed to baPWV. In conclusion, this study confirmed that serum cystatin C was associated with pulse wave velocity even in individuals with normal serum creatinine levels. These findings suggest that cystatin C may be a more reliable marker of arterial stiffness compared to serum creatinine and creatinine-based GFR.

title: Screening for inhibition of Vibrio cholerae VipA-VipB interaction identifies small-molecule compounds active against type VI secretion.
text: The most common bacterial secretion system, known as the type VI secretion system (T6SS), is crucial for the virulence of Gram-negative bacteria. It is used to either attack eukaryotic cells or combat other microbes. While the components of this system vary, two homologues called VipA and VipB have been found in all T6SSs studied so far, specifically in Vibrio cholerae. The secretion process relies on the binding of a specific region of VipA to VipB. If this binding does not occur, both components are quickly degraded and secretion stops. The purpose of this study was to investigate whether this interaction could be blocked, with the hypothesis that such inhibition would halt T6SS activity. A collection of 9,600 small-molecule compounds was screened to determine their ability to prevent the binding of VipA and VipB in a bacterial two-hybrid system (B2H). After eliminating compounds that were toxic to eukaryotic cells, inhibited Vibrio growth, or interfered with an unrelated B2H interaction, 34 compounds were further examined for their impact on T6SS-dependent secretion of hemolysin-coregulated protein (Hcp) or phospholipase A1 activity. Two compounds, KS100 and KS200, demonstrated significant effects in both assays. Similar compounds were obtained, and those with potent inhibitory effects in the assays and favorable physicochemical properties as predicted by computer analysis were identified. Since these compounds specifically target a virulence mechanism without affecting bacterial replication, they have the potential to reduce virulence with minimal risk of resistance development.

title: Early life compartmentalization of human T cell differentiation and regulatory function in mucosal and lymphoid tissues
text: The mechanism by which the immune response is appropriately stimulated in early life to provide protection while avoiding excessive activation due to new antigens is not well understood. T cells play a crucial role in adaptive immunity, and studies in mice have shown that the localization of different subsets of T cells in tissues is important for both protective immunity and immune regulation. However, the early development and function of T cells in tissues in humans have not been thoroughly investigated. In this study, we analyzed T cells derived from lymphoid and mucosal tissues of pediatric organ donors in the first two years of life, comparing them to T cells from adult organ donors. Our findings reveal that T cell differentiation and regulation are compartmentalized early in life. While adult tissues predominantly contain memory T cells, pediatric blood and tissues are mainly composed of naive recent thymic emigrants. Effector memory T cells are only found in the lungs and small intestine of pediatric individuals. Furthermore, regulatory T cells, which play a role in suppressing immune activation, make up a significant proportion (30-40%) of CD4(+) T cells in pediatric tissues, but are present at much lower frequencies (1-10%) in adult tissues. These pediatric tissue regulatory T cells are able to suppress the activation of other T cells, and early T cell functionality is limited to the mucosal sites with the lowest ratio of regulatory T cells to effector memory T cells. This suggests that immune responses in early life are controlled locally in the mucosal tissues.

title: Circulating microRNAs as biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine whether measuring serum levels of microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-16, miR-195, and miR-199a, either alone or in combination with conventional serum markers, could help differentiate between hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and chronic liver diseases (CLDs). Previous research has suggested a connection between abnormal miRNA expression and HCC.

For this retrospective analysis, we used serum samples from 105 HCC patients, 107 CLD patients, and 71 healthy control subjects. The miRNAs were measured using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. We also measured the conventional HCC markers α-fetoprotein (AFP), lens culinaris agglutinin-reactive AFP (AFP-L3%), and des-γ-carboxyprothrombin (DCP) using commercial kits.

The results showed that serum levels of miR-16 and miR-199a were significantly lower in HCC patients compared to CLD patients and control subjects (P<0.01). When used as individual markers, miR-16 had the highest sensitivity for HCC, followed by miR-199a, AFP, DCP, AFP-L3%, and miR-195. The combination of miR-16, AFP, AFP-L3%, and DCP provided the best combination of sensitivity (92.4%) and specificity (78.5%) for HCC, both overall and when analyzing patients with tumors smaller than 3 cm.

As a secondary marker for HCC, miR-16 correctly predicted HCC in 18 out of 26 (69.2%) patients who had negative results on all three conventional markers, most of whom had tumors smaller than 3 cm. MiR-16 produced false positive results in only 12 out of 96 (12.5%) CLD patients.

In conclusion, adding miR-16 to conventional serum markers improved the sensitivity and specificity for detecting HCC. Further research should explore the use of miR-16 as a second-line test for cases that are considered negative based on conventional HCC markers, in larger prospective studies.

title: Mitochondrial haplogroups and hypervariable region polymorphisms in schizophrenia: a case-control study.
text: Previous research has identified connections between mitochondrial haplogroups and schizophrenia (SZ). However, no studies have explored the correlation between major mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) haplogroups and SZ in the Chinese population. The objective of this study was to investigate the association between mtDNA haplogroups and the development of SZ in the Chinese Han population. A case-control study was conducted, and the mtDNA hypervariable regions (HVR1, HVR2, and HVR3) were sequenced in the Han population. The mtDNA haplogroups and HVR polymorphisms were analyzed in 298 SZ patients and 298 controls. The haplotypes were categorized into 10 major haplogroups: A, B, CZ, D, F, G, M, N, N9a, and R. Statistical analysis revealed that only N9a exhibited a nominally significant association with protection against SZ [1.68% vs. 6.38%, p=0.004, OR=0.251 (0.092-0.680); after adjusting for age and sex: p=0.006, OR=0.246 (0.090-0.669)]. Three HVR polymorphisms were found to be nominally significantly different between individuals with SZ and controls, and all except one (m.204T>C) were linked to the N9a haplogroup. Our findings suggest that mtDNA haplogroup N9a may serve as a protective factor against SZ.

title: Resolution of acute inflammation in the lung.
text: The lung relies on acute inflammation for maintaining good health, but it also requires proper resolution of this inflammation. When the body is invaded by harmful microbes, exposed to harmful substances, or experiences tissue damage, it initiates an acute inflammatory response to protect itself. However, to prevent unnecessary harm to healthy tissue, the lung produces specialized proresolving mediators such as lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins. These immunoresolvents interact with specific receptors on immune cells and structural cells to reduce inflammation and promote the healing process. Unfortunately, this resolution process seems to be impaired in various lung diseases that involve excessive or chronic inflammation. In this article, we examine the molecular and cellular factors that contribute to the resolution of acute inflammation in the lung.

title: The calcium sensor STIM1 is regulated by androgens in prostate stromal cells.
text:
The development and maintenance of the prostate in adults is a result of the interaction between stromal and glandular components. Androgens play a role in this process by directly affecting the stroma. In this study, we aimed to investigate the connection between androgens and another important regulator of stromal cells, intracellular calcium (Ca2+). 

We obtained prostate stromal cells from patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia and compared gene expression in cells treated with dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and untreated cells using Affymetrix gene expression arrays. We identified genes involved in calcium signaling through Gene Ontology analysis. One of the genes, stromal interaction molecule-1 (STIM1), showed significant differential expression and had four associated GO terms. Further analysis revealed putative androgen response element sequences in the promoter region of STIM1, confirming the ability of androgen receptor (AR) to bind to STIM1. Androgens directly regulated the expression of STIM1, and knock-down of STIM1 inhibited its effects on store-operated calcium entry. Reduced STIM1 expression in prostate stromal cells resulted in lower basal Ca2+ levels, decreased Ca2+ release by thapsigargin, and reduced store filling after store depletion induced by TG. 

In conclusion, our findings suggest that androgens modulate intracellular calcium levels by directly regulating the STIM1 gene through AR binding to its promoter.

title: Role of soluble guanylate cyclase in dilator responses of the cerebral microcirculation.
text: The effects of nitric oxide (NO) on cerebral blood vessels are influenced by both soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC)-dependent and potentially sGC-independent mechanisms. One possible sGC-independent mechanism by which NO may cause vasodilation is by inhibiting the production of a vasoconstrictor metabolite through the cytochrome P450 pathway. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether the dilation of cerebral microvessels in response to NO is reliant on the activation of sGC. We measured the diameters of cerebral arterioles (with a baseline diameter of 94+/-5 micrometers) using a closed cranial window in anesthetized rabbits. Under normal conditions, YC-1, an NO-independent activator of sGC, caused vasodilation, which was blocked by ODQ, an inhibitor of sGC. These results suggest that sGC plays a crucial role in cerebral arterioles. Furthermore, acetylcholine, which stimulates the production of NO by the endothelium, caused dilation of cerebral arterioles, which was inhibited by ODQ. For instance, in the absence and presence of ODQ, 1 microM acetylcholine dilated cerebral arterioles by 34+/-7% and 5+/-1%, respectively. The increase in arteriolar diameter in response to sodium nitroprusside (an NO donor) was inhibited by approximately 80% by ODQ, but was unaffected by 17-ODYA or clotrimazole, inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 pathway. Therefore, the dilation of the cerebral microcirculation in response to both exogenously applied and endogenously produced NO is largely dependent on the activation of sGC.

title: Noxa controls Mule-dependent Mcl-1 ubiquitination through the regulation of the Mcl-1/USP9X interaction.
text: The level of the pro-survival protein Mcl-1 is tightly controlled, and reducing Mcl-1 expression promotes cell death. Mcl-1 interacts with various BH3-only proteins, with Noxa playing a key role in regulating Mcl-1 levels. Our study reveals that Noxa induces the breakdown of Mcl-1 specifically at the mitochondria, where Noxa is located. This degradation of Mcl-1 relies on the E3 ligase Mule, which adds multiple ubiquitin molecules to Mcl-1. Interestingly, recent findings have shown that the deubiquitinase USP9X prevents Mcl-1 degradation by removing ubiquitin molecules. To investigate the impact of Noxa on this deubiquitination process, we examined the interaction between Noxa and USP9X. Surprisingly, overexpressing Noxa led to a decrease in the interaction between USP9X and Mcl-1, resulting in an increase in polyubiquitinated forms of Mcl-1. Furthermore, Noxa overexpression enhanced the interaction between Mule and Mcl-1 while reducing the formation of the Mule/USP9X complex. These changes collectively promote the degradation of Mcl-1 by the proteasome. The involvement of Noxa in the regulation of Mcl-1 degradation through the proteasome adds complexity to this process, which is governed by multiple interactions.

title: Paediatric HIV infection.
text: In the year 2000, it is projected that there will be approximately six million pregnant women and five to ten million children who will be infected with HIV-1. Plans for intervention strategies have already been made and implemented in certain cases. However, it is crucial to develop a strategy that is both timely and cost-effective, considering that the majority of HIV-1 infected individuals live in developing nations. Additionally, further research is required to understand the immunological and virological factors that influence the transmission of HIV-1 from mother to child, the varying rates of disease progression in affected children, and the nature of transient infections.

title: Potential role of NF-kappaB in adult neural stem cells: the underrated steersman?
text: Neural stem cells are the precursors of neurons and glial cells. They undergo proliferation, migration, and differentiation during brain development to form specific lineages. Recently, researchers have identified neural stem cells in the adult central nervous system. Studies have revealed that various soluble factors, such as chemokines and cytokines, regulate the proliferation, migration, and differentiation of these stem cells. However, the downstream signal transduction mechanisms of these factors are not well understood. In this article, we explore the potential role of the transcription factor nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kappaB) in these crucial signal transduction processes. NF-kappaB is a transcription factor found in neurons, glia, and neural stem cells. It was initially discovered in lymphocytes by David Baltimore's laboratory. NF-kappaB is involved in various biological processes, including inflammation, innate immunity, development, apoptosis, and anti-apoptosis. Recent studies have shown that NF-kappaB family members are widely expressed in neurons, glia, and neural stem cells. In the nervous system, NF-kappaB plays a critical role in neuronal plasticity, learning, memory consolidation, neuroprotection, and neurodegeneration. Emerging evidence suggests that NF-kappaB also influences the proliferation, migration, and differentiation of neural stem cells. NF-kappaB consists of three subunits: two DNA-binding subunits and one inhibitory subunit. Activation of NF-kappaB occurs in the cytoplasm, leading to the degradation of the inhibitory subunit and allowing the nuclear import of the DNA-binding subunits. Once in the nucleus, several target genes can be activated. In this review, we propose a model to explain the multiple actions of NF-kappaB on neural stem cells. Additionally, we discuss the potential role of NF-kappaB in brain cancer stem cells.

title: Intrauterine factors and risk of breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of current evidence.
text:
The available evidence suggests that there is a link between a woman's prenatal experience and her risk of developing breast cancer later in life. This association may be due to various factors, including differences in levels of maternal hormones and growth hormones, mutations in germ cells, the formation of cancer stem cells, and other genetic or epigenetic events. In order to better understand this relationship, we conducted a quantitative review of the existing data on intrauterine exposures and breast cancer risk.

To conduct our review, we systematically searched for studies that examined the association between perinatal factors and breast cancer risk. We analyzed each perinatal factor separately, including birthweight, birth length, parental age at delivery, gestational age, exposure to diethylstilbestrol in the womb, twin membership, maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, and other factors.

Our review identified 57 studies published between October 1, 1980, and June 21, 2007. We found that higher birthweight (relative risk [RR] 1.15 [95% CI 1.09-1.21]), longer birth length (1.28 [1.11-1.48]), advanced maternal age (1.13 [1.02-1.25]), and advanced paternal age (1.12 [1.05-1.19]) were associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. On the other hand, we observed a decreased risk of breast cancer in women who had experienced maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia (0.48 [0.30-0.78]) or were part of a twin pregnancy (0.93 [0.87-1.00]). We did not find any significant association between breast cancer risk and gestational age at birth (0.95 [0.71-1.26]) or maternal diethylstilbestrol treatment (1.40 [0.86-2.28]).

In conclusion, the prenatal environment plays a role in a woman's susceptibility to breast cancer later in life. However, further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms responsible for this predisposition.

title: Helicobacter hepaticus does not induce or potentiate colitis in interleukin-10-deficient mice.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate whether Helicobacter hepaticus can cause colitis in mice lacking the interleukin-10 gene (IL-10(-/-) mice) and enhance colitis in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) IL-10(-/-) mice. Germfree IL-10(-/-) mice with a mixed or inbred genetic background were exposed to H. hepaticus through oral feeding and rectal enemas. In a separate experiment, germfree IL-10(-/-) mice were colonized with stool from SPF mice that either had or did not have H. hepaticus. After 7 to 9 weeks, the researchers assessed weight loss, mortality, colon histology, IL-12 secretion, and T-cell activation markers in the mesenteric lymph nodes. The results showed that IL-10(-/-) mice monoassociated with H. hepaticus for up to 16 weeks did not exhibit significant colitis or increased IL-12 production. Similarly, SPF IL-10-knockout mice did not show any significant differences in weight loss, mortality, histologic scores, colonic IL-12 secretion, or T-cell activation with or without H. hepaticus. Therefore, the researchers concluded that H. hepaticus does not induce or enhance disease in IL-10(-/-) mice and is not necessary to induce colitis in genetically susceptible hosts.

title: Metabolic interplay between glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidation: The reverse Warburg effect and its therapeutic implication.
text: The Warburg effect, also known as aerobic glycolysis, may contribute to the aggressive nature of hepatocellular carcinoma. However, recent evidence has highlighted the limitations of this effect, including high mitochondrial respiration and low glycolysis rates in cancer cells. To explain these contradictory findings, researchers have proposed a metabolic interplay between glycolytic and oxidative cells, known as the "reverse Warburg effect". Additionally, aerobic glycolysis may occur in the stromal compartment surrounding the tumor, where stromal cells provide cancer cells with lactate, preventing the creation of an acidic environment in the tumor microenvironment. This concept introduces significant heterogeneity in tumors, making it challenging to treat the disease with a single approach. Understanding the metabolic flexibility facilitated by lactate shuttles opens up new possibilities for developing treatments that target the hypoxic tumor microenvironment and overcome the limitations of glycolytic inhibitors.

title: Enhanced waterlogging tolerance in barley by manipulation of expression of the N‐end rule pathway E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6
text: Enhancing the tolerance of crops to low oxygen levels during flooding is crucial for ensuring food security. In Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh., the N-end rule pathway plays a significant role in regulating plant responses to hypoxia by controlling the stability of group VII ethylene response factor (ERFVII) transcription factors. These factors are regulated by the oxidation status of the amino terminal (Nt)-cysteine (Cys). Our study demonstrates that the barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) ERFVII BERF1 is a substrate of the N-end rule pathway in laboratory conditions. Moreover, we found that Nt-Cys acts as a sensor for hypoxia in living organisms, as the stability of the oxygen-sensor reporter protein MCGGAIL-GUS increased in waterlogged transgenic plants. By reducing the expression of the N-end rule pathway N-recognin E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6 (HvPRT6) in transgenic RNAi barley plants, we observed an increase in the expression of hypoxia-associated genes and changes in seed germination patterns. Additionally, these transgenic plants exhibited sustained biomass, improved yield, chlorophyll retention, and enhanced induction of hypoxia-related genes in response to waterlogging. The HvPRT6 RNAi plants also displayed reduced chlorophyll degradation under prolonged darkness, a condition often associated with waterlogged environments. Furthermore, the Barley Targeting Induced Local Lesions IN Genomes (TILLING) lines, which carry mutant alleles of HvPRT6, showed similar phenotypes and increased expression of hypoxia-related genes. In conclusion, targeting the N-end rule pathway is a promising approach for plant breeding to enhance waterlogging tolerance in barley and other cereal crops.

title: A SUMO-Dependent Protein Network Regulates Chromosome Congression during Oocyte Meiosis
text: During the process of oocyte meiosis in Caenorhabditis elegans, a complex made up of multiple proteins, known as the ring complex (RC), is found between homologous chromosomes. This complex plays a role in promoting chromosome congression through the action of a protein called chromokinesin KLP-19. While some components of the RC are known, the process of how the RC is assembled has not been well understood. Our research demonstrates that the SUMO E3 ligase GEI-17/PIAS is necessary for recruiting KLP-19 to the RC. Through proteomic analysis, we have identified KLP-19 as a substrate for SUMO modification in vivo. Further analysis conducted in vitro has shown that KLP-19 is efficiently modified by SUMO in a GEI-17-dependent manner, while GEI-17 itself undergoes extensive auto-sumoylation. Both GEI-17 and another component of the RC, the kinase BUB-1, possess functional SUMO interaction motifs (SIMs), which enable them to recruit SUMO-modified proteins, including KLP-19, to the RC. Therefore, the dynamic process of SUMO modification and the presence of SIMs in RC components create a network that facilitates the assembly of the RC. Our findings emphasize the significance of SUMO-SIM networks in regulating the assembly of protein complexes that undergo dynamic changes.

title: Prediagnostic levels of C-peptide, IGF-I, IGFBP -1, -2 and -3 and risk of endometrial cancer.
text: Conditions such as obesity, noninsulin dependent diabetes mellitus, and polycystic ovary syndrome are linked to a higher risk of endometrial cancer due to chronic hyperinsulinemia. In affluent societies, elevated plasma IGF-I and decreased levels of IGF-binding proteins have been associated with an increased risk of various types of cancer. In this study, we aimed to investigate the association between pre-diagnostic blood concentrations of C-peptide (a marker of pancreatic insulin production), IGF-I, IGFBP-1, -2, and -3 with endometrial cancer risk. The study included 166 women with primary invasive endometrial cancer and 315 matched controls from New York (USA), Umeå (Sweden), and Milan (Italy). Among the participants, 44 cases and 78 controls were premenopausal at recruitment. The results showed that the risk of endometrial cancer increased with higher levels of C-peptide. The odds ratio for the highest quintile was 4.76, indicating a significant association. This association remained even after adjusting for BMI and other confounding factors. On the other hand, higher levels of IGFBP-1 were inversely related to endometrial cancer risk. However, this association weakened and lost statistical significance after adjusting for confounders. Levels of IGF-I, IGFBP-2, and IGFBP-3 were not found to be associated with endometrial cancer risk. Overall, chronic hyperinsulinemia, as indicated by increased circulating C-peptide, is associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer. Decreasing the prevalence of chronic hyperinsulinemia through lifestyle changes or medication is expected to help prevent endometrial cancer.

title: Interactions between SRY and SOX genes in mammalian sex determination.
text: The role of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome in determining testis development in mammals is still not fully understood. Initially, it was believed that SRY directly activates other genes involved in the pathway for testis determination. However, this paper proposes an alternative hypothesis suggesting that SRY indirectly functions by interacting with related genes, namely SOX3 (the precursor of SRY) and SOX9 (which plays a crucial role in vertebrate gonad differentiation). Specifically, the hypothesis suggests that in females, SOX3 inhibits the function of SOX9, whereas in males, SRY inhibits SOX3 and allows SOX9 to carry out its role in testis determination. This hypothesis can be tested by predicting the phenotypes of individuals with deficiencies or overproduction of any of these three genes, both in XX and XY individuals. Furthermore, it provides an explanation for challenging cases such as XX individuals lacking SRY but exhibiting male characteristics, as well as cases of transdifferentiation in the absence of SRY. Additionally, the hypothesis proposes a possible evolutionary pathway from an ancient system relying on SOX3 dosage to the dominant SRY sex-determining system observed in present-day mammals.

title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and microarray-based analysis of protein location
text: Genome-wide location analysis, also referred to as ChIP-Chip, is a technique that combines chromatin immunoprecipitation and DNA microarray analysis to identify interactions between proteins and DNA in living cells. In this method, protein-DNA interactions are captured in vivo through chemical crosslinking. The process involves cell lysis, DNA fragmentation, and immunoaffinity purification of the desired protein, which results in the co-purification of DNA fragments associated with that protein. The enriched DNA population is then labeled and mixed with a differentially labeled reference sample. This mixture is then applied to DNA microarrays to detect signals indicating enrichment. To analyze the data, various computational and bioinformatic approaches are employed. These approaches normalize the enriched and reference channels, connect signals to specific regions of the genome represented on the DNA microarrays, provide confidence metrics, and generate maps of protein-genome occupancy. In this article, we provide a detailed description of the experimental protocols used, starting from the crosslinking of cells to the hybridization of labeled material. We also offer insights into the factors within these protocols that can influence the results. These protocols typically take around one week to complete, assuming a sufficient number of cells are available, and have been successfully utilized to produce reliable and high-quality ChIP-chip results in various cell and tissue types.

title: Spatial and temporal clusters of Barmah Forest virus disease in Queensland, Australia.
text: The aim of this study was to use geographical information systems and spatial scan statistic (SaTScan) to identify clusters of Barmah Forest virus (BFV) disease in Queensland, Australia. Data on BFV cases, population, and statistical local areas (SLAs) boundaries were obtained from Queensland Health and the Australian Bureau of Statistics for the period 1992-2008. A retrospective analysis using SaTScan software was conducted to identify spatial and space-time clusters of high-rate BFV disease. The analysis used a spatial cluster size based on a proportion of the population and a 200 km radius, with varying time windows from 1 to 12 months for the space-time analysis. The results showed a significant purely spatial cluster (including 23 SLAs) and a significant space-time cluster (including 24 SLAs) in approximately the same location. Additional secondary clusters were also identified in various locations. This study provides evidence of statistically significant BFV disease clusters in Queensland, Australia, and demonstrates the usefulness of SaTScan in analyzing surveillance data to develop effective prevention and control strategies for BFV disease in the region.

title: Surfactant Protein B Suppresses Lung Cancer Progression by Inhibiting Secretory Phospholipase A2 Activity and Arachidonic Acid Production
text:
Objective: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of surfactant protein B (SP-B) in radioresistance, which is a major challenge in the treatment of inoperable cancer types such as advanced stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

Methods: We established a ΔSFTPB A549 cell line to study the impact of SP-B on radioresistance. We analyzed the expression of SP-B in A549 and NCI-H441 cell lines in response to ionizing radiation (IR). We also used conditioned media (CM) from NSCLC cells to examine the downstream signaling pathway. To assess the in vivo effects of SP-B, we conducted a mouse xenograft model with intratumoral injection of CM.

Results: Our findings showed that IR led to a decrease in SP-B expression in NSCLC cell lines, which was regulated by the TGF-β signaling pathway. Decreased SP-B expression promoted cell survival and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Treatment with CM from irradiated cells activated sPLA2, enhanced the protein kinase Cδ-MAPKs signaling pathway, and increased arachidonic acid production. We confirmed the role of SP-B in vivo through our mouse xenograft model.

Conclusion: Our study revealed that the down-regulation of SP-B is involved in the radiation-induced metastatic conversion of NSCLC. We provided evidence that SP-B acts as a suppressor of NSCLC progression.

title: Liraglutide improves hippocampal synaptic plasticity associated with increased expression of Mash1 in ob/ob mice
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of daily treatment with the GLP-1 mimetic, Liraglutide, on synaptic plasticity, gene expression in the hippocampus, and metabolic control in obese diabetic mice.

Results: The study found that obese diabetic mice had impaired long-term potentiation (LTP) compared to lean controls. However, treatment with Liraglutide completely rescued this impairment and improved LTP compared to lean controls. The expression of certain genes related to neurotrophic factors was not significantly different between the groups, but the expression of synaptophysin and Mash1 was decreased in obese diabetic mice. Treatment with Liraglutide increased the expression of Mash1 in these mice. Additionally, Liraglutide significantly reduced plasma glucose levels and improved insulin concentrations. It also reduced the glycaemic excursion following a glucose load and enhanced the insulin response to glucose. However, Liraglutide did not affect O2 consumption, CO2 production, respiratory exchange ratio, or energy expenditure. Furthermore, Liraglutide reduced food intake and the number of feeding bouts, but this reduction was not solely due to energy restriction.

Conclusion: Liraglutide has beneficial effects on metabolic control and synaptic plasticity in mice with severe obesity and insulin resistance. These effects are mediated, at least in part, through increased expression of Mash1, which is believed to improve hippocampal neurogenesis and cell survival.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation of IME1 determines initiation of meiosis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The initiation of meiosis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae relies on the IME1 gene. Transcription of IME1 occurs when specific conditions are met, such as nitrogen and glucose starvation, as well as the presence of MATa1 and MAT alpha 2 gene products. However, our research reveals that IME1 is also regulated at the translational level. Translation of IME1 mRNA occurs during nitrogen starvation or G1 arrest. Additionally, constitutively high levels of IME1 transcription in the presence of nutrients are sufficient for IME1 RNA translation. We identified four conditions that lead to the expression of Ime1 protein in vegetative cultures: elevated transcription levels with IME1 on a multicopy plasmid, elevated transcription with a Gal-IME1 construct, G1 arrest induced by alpha-factor treatment, and G1 arrest following mild heat-shock treatment of cdc28 diploids. By utilizing these conditions, we gathered evidence suggesting that starvation is not only necessary for IME1 transcription and efficient translation, but also for the activation of Ime1 protein or the induction/activation of another factor that, either alone or in conjunction with Ime1, triggers meiosis.

title: Targeted proteomics reveals compositional dynamics of 60S pre-ribosomes after nuclear export
text: The construction and targeting of eukaryotic pre-ribosomal particles involve various factors that associate temporarily, enzymes that consume energy, and transport factors. However, measuring the co-enrichment of multiple factors with maturing pre-ribosomal particles is challenging and hinders our understanding of their function and the numerous energy-consuming steps involved in ribosome assembly. To address this issue, we developed a workflow that combines genetic trapping, affinity-capture, and selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (SRM-MS). Using this approach, we investigated the proteome of pre-60S particles after they are exported from the nucleus. We discovered assembly factors that accompany pre-60S particles to the cytoplasm and are released before translation initiation. Additionally, we identified a new factor that aids in the nuclear export of pre-60S particles. Our workflow, which captures and quantifies protein interaction networks of trapped intermediates of macromolecular complexes, is a reliable tool for uncovering the dynamic processes involved in their in vivo assembly and transport.

title: Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea and incident stroke: the sleep heart health study.
text:
RATIONALE: While obstructive sleep apnea is known to increase the risk of hypertension and atherosclerosis, it remains unclear whether it is associated with an increased risk of stroke in the general population.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to determine the incidence of ischemic stroke in a community-based sample of men and women with varying degrees of sleep apnea.

METHODS: Between 1995 and 1998, a longitudinal cohort study was conducted, and baseline polysomnography was performed. The primary focus was on the obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI), and the outcome measured was incident ischemic stroke.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 5,422 participants without a history of stroke and untreated for sleep apnea were followed for a median of 8.7 years. During this period, 193 ischemic strokes were observed. After adjusting for covariates, a significant positive association between ischemic stroke and OAHI was found in men (P = 0.016). Men in the highest OAHI quartile (>19) had an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.86 (95% confidence interval, 1.1-7.4). In the mild to moderate range (OAHI, 5-25), each one-unit increase in OAHI in men was estimated to increase stroke risk by 6% (95% confidence interval, 2-10%). In women, stroke risk was not significantly associated with OAHI quartiles, but an increased risk was observed at an OAHI greater than 25.

CONCLUSIONS: The strong association between ischemic stroke and OAHI in men with mild to moderate sleep apnea suggests that targeting this population for future stroke prevention trials may be appropriate.

title: Reproducibility of 31P cardiac magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 3 T.
text:
The aim of this study was to utilize the higher clinical field strength of 3 T to develop and optimize a chemical shift imaging (CSI) acquisition protocol that can generate high-quality spectra specific to the myocardium within a reasonable scan time. Additionally, a data analysis method based solely on the anatomical location of the spectra was implemented to eliminate any potential bias caused by interpretation of spectral information. 

Twenty healthy male subjects were scanned on two separate occasions using the optimized CSI protocol at 3 T. The data were analyzed to assess both intra- and inter-subject variability, as well as intra- and inter-observer variability. The average phosphocreatine (PCr)/adenosine triphosphate (ATP) value for the first scan was 2.07 +/- 0.38, and for the second scan, it was 2.14 +/- 0.46, indicating no significant difference between the two scans. The intra-subject variability was 0.43 +/- 0.35 (percentage difference 20%), and the inter-subject coefficient of variation was 18%. The intra-observer variability, measured as the absolute difference between analyses conducted by a single observer, was 0.14 +/- 0.24, with no significant difference between the analyses. The inter-observer variability also showed no significant differences in the PCr/ATP value measured by four different observers, as indicated by an intra-class correlation coefficient of 0.763. 

The increased signal strength at 3 T has enhanced spatial resolution and improved myocardial specificity without compromising reproducibility compared to previous studies conducted at 1.5 T. We present an acquisition protocol that consistently produces high-quality spectra and a robust analysis method that eliminates potential user bias.

title: Nuclear HuR accumulation through phosphorylation by Cdk1.
text: HuR, a protein that primarily binds to RNA in the nucleus, moves to the cytoplasm when exposed to stress and signals for cell growth. In the cytoplasm, it either stabilizes or adjusts the translation of specific mRNA molecules. Our study provides evidence that the subcellular distribution of HuR is influenced by its phosphorylation at S202 by the G2-phase kinase Cdk1. We observed that HuR was phosphorylated specifically during the G2 phase of the cell cycle. When Cdk1 activity was inhibited, the levels of HuR in the cytoplasm increased, while activating Cdk1 decreased its cytoplasmic presence. We also discovered that a mutant form of HuR (HuR(S202A)) that cannot be phosphorylated at S202 was mainly located in the cytoplasm, as confirmed by a new antibody specifically targeting phospho-HuR(S202). The increased cytoplasmic presence of unphosphorylated HuR was associated with reduced interaction with 14-3-3 proteins and increased binding to target mRNA molecules. Our findings suggest that Cdk1 phosphorylates HuR during the G2 phase, which helps to keep it in the nucleus by interacting with 14-3-3 proteins, thereby inhibiting its post-transcriptional function and anti-apoptotic effects.

title: Surgical Resection for Patients with Solid Brain Metastases: Current Status
text:
Brain metastases are a common occurrence in cancer patients, affecting up to 40% of individuals. However, recent advancements have significantly transformed their management over the past decade. These developments include enhanced imaging techniques that allow for better detection of metastases, improved systemic treatments that have led to a higher incidence of metastases, and the utilization of advanced surgical methods, such as image-guided surgery, to address metastatic lesions. 

Class 1 data indicates that surgery is a more effective approach for treating metastases compared to whole brain radiation. Additionally, research suggests that even metastases located in critical areas of the brain can be safely removed. The complication rate associated with surgery is low, and the likelihood of recurrence is less than 10%. 

In general, surgery is recommended in several scenarios, including when a mass is present with an unknown primary source, when a symptomatic mass is located in critical areas of the brain, when a mass causes significant edema requiring high dose steroids, when the mass exceeds 3 cm in size, or when the patient prefers surgery over radiosurgery as an alternative option. 

Further evaluation is needed to determine whether radiosurgery or whole brain radiation should be used in conjunction with surgical removal of metastases.

title: Clinical features and treatment of peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum.
text:
The aim of this study was to gain a better understanding of the clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum (PPG), a rare form of pyoderma gangrenosum that is often misdiagnosed and primarily affects patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The study involved a retrospective analysis of seven patients with PPG who were observed in a community setting affiliated with a university between 1988 and December 1999. The main outcomes measured were the clinical and histopathologic features of PPG, associated disorders, and microbiologic findings. 

The results showed that two patients had Crohn's disease, two had ulcerative colitis, and three had abdominal cancer. Five patients experienced at least one relapse of PPG after initial healing. While three out of four patients with IBD had active bowel disease, only one patient experienced a parallel course with PPG. Both patients who had their stoma relocated developed an ulcer at the new site. Effective treatments included the use of topical superpotent corticosteroids, intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetonide at the edge of the ulcer, topical cromolyn sodium, oral dapsone, prednisone, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous infliximab. 

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that although PPG is most commonly seen in patients with IBD, it can also occur in the absence of IBD. Biopsy of the skin lesion is not sufficient for diagnosis but can help rule out other causes. Relocating the stoma may lead to new ulceration and should be avoided. Trauma to the skin of a susceptible patient may trigger the development of pustules or ulcers associated with pathergy.

title: The Tof1p-Csm3p protein complex counteracts the Rrm3p helicase to control replication termination of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The termination of replication forks at the natural termini of the rDNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is regulated in a specific and directional manner. This regulation is achieved through the interaction between the Fob1p replication terminator protein and the tandem Ter sites located in the nontranscribed spacers. Our study utilized 2D gel analyses and chromatin immunoprecipitations (ChIP) to demonstrate the existence of an additional level of control mediated by the Tof1p and Csm3p proteins, which are part of the intra-S-phase checkpoint protein complex. These proteins protect stalled forks at Ter sites from the activity of the Rrm3p helicase, also known as "sweepase". The sweepase has the tendency to release arrested forks by temporarily displacing the Ter-bound Fob1p. In the absence of the two checkpoint proteins, very few replication forks were arrested at the natural replication termini. However, the absence of the Rrm3p helicase slightly increased the arrest of forks at the Ter sites. By deleting both the TOF1 (or CSM3) and RRM3 genes simultaneously, we were able to restore fork arrest by eliminating both the fork-releasing and fork-protection activities. Other genes involved in the MRC1 checkpoint pathway, such as MRC1, WSS1, and PSY2, did not play a role in this global control. This suggests that Tof1p-Csm3p function differently from MRC1 and the aforementioned genes. Furthermore, this mechanism is not limited to the natural Ter sites but was also observed when a replication fork encountered transcription from the opposite direction, leading to fork arrest.

title: Association of hypomethylation of LINE-1 repetitive element in blood leukocyte DNA with an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
text: This study aimed to investigate the association between global hypomethylation in blood leukocyte DNA and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The study included 315 HCC cases and 356 controls matched for age, sex, and HBsAg status. Global methylation was assessed by analyzing long interspersed element-1 (LINE-1) repeats using bisulfite-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and pyrosequencing. The results showed that the median methylation level in HCC cases (77.7% 5-methylcytosine (5mC)) was significantly lower than that in controls (79.5% 5mC) (P=0.004, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). The odds ratios (ORs) for HCC in individuals with different quartiles of LINE-1 methylation were 1.1 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.7–1.8), 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.2), and 2.6 (95% CI 1.7–4.1) (P for trend <0.001), respectively, compared to individuals in the highest quartile. Individuals with LINE-1 methylation below the median had a 1.9-fold (95% CI 1.4–2.6) increased risk of HCC compared to those with higher LINE-1 methylation. This study provides the first evidence that global hypomethylation in LINE-1 repeats in blood leukocyte DNA is associated with an increased risk of HCC. These findings suggest that measuring global hypomethylation in easily obtainable blood leukocyte DNA may help identify individuals at risk of HCC.

title: The ketogenic diet for the treatment of childhood epilepsy: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
The ketogenic diet has been a successful treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy in children since the 1920s. This study aimed to test the effectiveness of the ketogenic diet in a randomized controlled trial. The trial included 145 children between the ages of 2 and 16 who experienced daily seizures or more than seven seizures per week, had not responded to at least two antiepileptic drugs, and had not previously tried the ketogenic diet. The trial took place between December 2001 and July 2006, with children being seen at two hospital centers or a residential center for young people with epilepsy. The children were randomly assigned to receive the ketogenic diet immediately or after a 3-month delay, with no other changes to their treatment (control group). Both the families and investigators were aware of the group assignments. Early withdrawals were recorded, and seizure frequency was assessed after 3 months and compared to the control group. The primary goal was to reduce seizures, and the analysis was based on intention to treat. Tolerability of the diet was assessed through a questionnaire at 3 months. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov under the number NCT00564915. 

Out of the 145 children, 73 were assigned to the ketogenic diet group and 72 to the control group. Data from 103 children were available for analysis: 54 in the ketogenic diet group and 49 in the control group. Some children did not complete the trial for various reasons, including not receiving their intervention, inadequate data, or withdrawal from treatment due to intolerance. After 3 months, the mean percentage of baseline seizures was significantly lower in the diet group compared to the control group (62.0% vs 136.9%, a 75% decrease, 95% CI 42.4-107.4%; p<0.0001). In the diet group, 28 children (38%) experienced more than a 50% reduction in seizures compared to only four children (6%) in the control group (p<0.0001). Additionally, five children (7%) in the diet group had more than a 90% reduction in seizures compared to none in the control group (p=0.0582). The efficacy of the treatment did not significantly differ between symptomatic generalized or symptomatic focal syndromes. The most common side effects reported at the 3-month review were constipation, vomiting, lack of energy, and hunger. 

In conclusion, the results of this trial support the use of the ketogenic diet in children with treatment-resistant epilepsy. The study was funded by the HSA Charitable Trust, Smiths Charity, Scientific Hospital Supplies, and the Milk Development Council.

title: Building-in biosafety for synthetic biology.
text: As synthetic biology advances, practical applications are transitioning from theoretical concepts and laboratory-based research to real-world implementation. One major concern, especially in relation to microbial systems, is the possibility of self-replicating re-engineered cells causing unintended consequences if they escape or overpower their intended environment. To address this issue of biosafety, various methods have been proposed to restrict microbial replication and horizontal gene transfer. These methods include utilizing host-construct dependencies such as toxin-antitoxin pairs, conditional plasmid replication, or the necessity of specific metabolites for cellular function. While the future holds promise for more robust "firewalls" between natural and synthetic cells through genetic code refactoring or the development of orthogonal systems like xeno nucleic acids, our focus here is on what can be accomplished using existing technology. We provide an overview of the current state-of-the-art in designing for biosafety and offer general recommendations, such as minimizing environmental retention times, for ongoing synthetic biology projects to better safeguard against potential negative impacts.

title: Sustained active site rigidity during synthesis by human DNA polymerase μ
text: Pol μ is a human DNA polymerase that plays a crucial role in repairing double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ). In order to understand how Pol μ functions in this process, we conducted a structural analysis of its catalytic cycle for single-nucleotide incorporation. Our findings reveal that, unlike other template-dependent DNA polymerases, Pol μ does not undergo significant conformational changes in its protein subdomains, amino acid side chains, or DNA during dNTP binding or catalysis. Instead, the main conformational change occurs earlier in the catalytic cycle, when the flexible loop 1 region adjusts upon DNA binding. We also observed that Pol μ variants with alterations in loop 1 exhibit modified catalytic properties and are partially impaired in NHEJ. These results suggest that specific residues in loop 1 play a crucial role in Pol μ's unique ability to facilitate template-dependent NHEJ of DSBs with unpaired 3′ ends.

title: Angiopoietin-1 requires p190 RhoGAP to protect against vascular leakage in vivo.
text: The mechanism by which Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) inhibits permeability in the mature vasculature, a ligand of the endothelium-specific receptor Tie-2, is still unknown. However, our study reveals that Ang-1 signals Rho family GTPases to arrange the cytoskeleton in a way that strengthens the junctions, thereby enhancing the barrier function of the endothelium. Ang-1 phosphorylates Tie-2 and its downstream effector phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, leading to the activation of Rac1, an endogenous GTPase, and the inhibition of RhoA, another GTPase. The coordinated regulation of these GTPases is crucial for the vessel-sealing effects of Ang-1, as the loss of either part of this dual effect eliminates the cytoskeletal and anti-permeability actions of Ang-1. p190 RhoGAP, a regulatory protein for GTPases, plays a key role in coordinating these effects. It is phosphorylated by Ang-1 treatment, requires Rac1 activation, and is necessary for RhoA inhibition. Ang-1 counteracts the cytoskeletal and pro-permeability effects of endotoxin, but it relies on p190 RhoGAP to do so. When p190 RhoGAP small interfering RNA is used to inhibit p190 RhoGAP, the ability of Ang-1 to rescue endotoxemia-induced pulmonary vascular leak and inflammation in mice is completely abolished. In conclusion, Ang-1 prevents vascular permeability by regulating the endothelial cytoskeleton through coordinated and opposite effects on the Rho GTPases Rac1 and RhoA. The critical role of p190 RhoGAP in linking Rac1 activation and RhoA inhibition highlights its importance in the protective effects of Ang-1 against endotoxin. These findings provide mechanistic evidence that targeting the endothelium via Tie-2 could be a specific therapeutic approach for life-threatening endotoxemic conditions like sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

title: Vesicular trafficking of semaphorin 3A is activity-dependent and differs between axons and dendrites.
text: The role of secreted semaphorins in the developing nervous system and their potential functions in mature neurons are not well understood. Our study focuses on how neurons transport and secrete semaphorins, specifically semaphorin 3A (Sema3A). We observed that Sema3A is distributed in a punctate pattern in the axons and dendrites of cultured cortical neurons. By using GFP-tagged Sema3A, we found that it shares a similar distribution and co-localizes with proteins found in secretory vesicles. Through live-cell imaging, we discovered that GFP-Sema3A vesicles exhibit dynamic trafficking with distinct characteristics in axons and dendrites, including directionality, velocity, mobility, and pausing time. In axons, most GFP-Sema3A vesicles move rapidly without interruption, primarily in the anterograde direction. In contrast, dendrites contain many stationary GFP-Sema3A vesicles that move equally frequently in both directions. Disrupting microtubules, but not actin filaments, significantly impairs the transport of GFP-Sema3A. Interestingly, depolarization causes a reversible arrest of axonal transport of GFP-Sema3A vesicles, while having little effect on dendritic transport. Conversely, blocking action potentials with tetrodotoxin (TTX) accelerates axonal transport but does not affect dendritic transport. These findings suggest that axons and dendrites regulate the trafficking of Sema3A and potentially other secretory vesicles in distinct ways, with axons specializing in fast, uninterrupted, anterograde transport. Additionally, neuronal activity plays a role in regulating secretory vesicle trafficking in axons through a depolarization-induced arrest of trafficking.

title: Frequency of Intracranial Aneurysms Determined by Magnetic Resonance Angiography in Children (Mean Age 16) Having Operative or Endovascular Treatment of Coarctation of the Aorta (Mean Age 3).
text: This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of intracranial aneurysms (IAs) in 80 children who were treated for coarctation of the aorta (CofA) at an early age. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) was performed when the children were on average 15.7 ± 7.1 years old, while surgical or endovascular treatment for CofA was done at an average age of 2.6 ± 4.4 years. Surprisingly, no IAs were found in any of the children. This contradicts previous findings in adult patients who were treated for CofA later in life, suggesting that the association between CofA and IAs may not be as strong as previously thought.
