Instead, our results suggest that modifiable risk factors such as hypertension may play a role in the development of IAs in CofA patients diagnosed and treated as adults. In conclusion, early treatment of CofA appears to reduce the risk of IAs in children, making MRA screening less necessary for this young population.

title: Transcriptional profiling of the heart reveals chamber-specific gene expression patterns.
text: The normal development and function of the heart rely on the specific gene expression in each cardiac chamber. To explore the genetic foundation of cardiac anatomical specialization, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of gene expression in the four heart chambers and the interventricular septum. Through rigorous statistical analysis, we identified both known and novel members of gene families that play crucial roles in cardiac development and function, such as LIM proteins, homeobox proteins, wnt and T-box pathway proteins, as well as structural proteins like actins and myosins. Furthermore, this study revealed thousands of additional genes with differential expression, for which little is known about their structure or function. By clustering genes with known and unknown functions, we gained insights into the signaling pathways that are vital for the development and maintenance of chamber-specific features. To facilitate future research in this field, we have created a searchable internet database that allows the examination of chamber-specific gene expression for any gene included in this comprehensive microarray. It is expected that further investigation of the genes identified in this study will provide valuable insights into the specialization of heart chamber tissues and their specific roles in cardiac development, aging, and disease.

title: CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cell microRNA expression and function: a circuit diagram of differentiation control.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a newly discovered group of epigenetic elements that consist of small noncoding RNAs. They bind to the 3' untranslated region of mRNAs and decrease their translation into proteins. miRNAs have important roles in various cellular processes such as metabolism, apoptosis, differentiation, and development. In our study, we identified 33 miRNAs expressed in CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cells (HSPCs) from normal human bone marrow and mobilized human peripheral blood stem cell harvests. We combined this information with human HSPC mRNA expression data and miRNA-mRNA target predictions to create a novel miRNA:mRNA interaction database called the Transcriptome Interaction Database. Through in silico predictions from this database, we discovered that miRNAs control hematopoietic differentiation by regulating the translation of mRNAs crucial to hematopoiesis. Based on these predictions, we developed a model that explains how miRNAs control different stages of hematopoiesis. According to our model, HSPCs express many genes involved in hematopoietic differentiation, but these genes are suppressed by miRNAs until differentiation occurs. To validate our findings, we confirmed that miRNAs actually decrease the translation of several target mRNAs. Lastly, we focused on miRNA-155 for further investigation in hematopoiesis because we hypothesized that it regulates both myelopoiesis and erythropoiesis. As expected, introducing miRNA-155 significantly reduced the formation of both myeloid and erythroid colonies in normal human HSPCs.

title: Acute exercise activates nuclear factor (NF)-kappaB signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle.
text: Two studies were conducted to examine the impact of a single session of physical exercise on the nuclear protein kappaB (NF-kappaB) signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle. In the first study, a group of rats (n=6) ran on a treadmill at a speed of 25 m/min and a 5% incline for 1 hour or until exhaustion. They were compared to a second group (n=6) that received two injections of pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (PDTC, 100 mg/kg, i.p.) 24 and 1 hour before the exercise session. Three additional groups of rats (n=6) were injected with either lipopolysaccharide (LPS) at a dose of 8 mg/kg (i.p.), t-butylhydroperoxide (tBHP) at a dose of 1 mmol/kg (i.p.), or saline (C) and were euthanized while at rest. The rats in the exercise group showed higher levels of NF-kappaB binding and P50 protein content in their muscle nuclear extracts compared to the rats in the control group. The levels of cytosolic IkappaBalpha and IkappaB kinase (IKK) were decreased, while the levels of phospho-IkappaBalpha and phospho-IKK were increased in the exercise group compared to the control group. The activation of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway due to exercise was partially inhibited by PDTC treatment. Treatment with LPS, but not tBHP, replicated and intensified the effects observed in the exercise group. In the second study, the researchers examined the time course of NF-kappaB activation following exercise. The highest levels of NF-kappaB binding were observed 2 hours after exercise. Decreased levels of cytosolic IkappaBalpha and increased levels of phospho-IkappaBalpha were found within 0-1 hour after exercise, while P65 levels peaked at 2-4 hours. These findings suggest that the NF-kappaB signaling pathway can be activated in response to muscular contraction in a manner that is sensitive to oxidative stress, likely due to increased production of oxidants. These intracellular events may be the initial steps leading to increased expression of manganese superoxide dismutase, as previously reported. (Pfluegers Arch. 442, 426-434, 2001).

title: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII and the endoribonuclease III coordinately regulate spa gene expression.
text: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII is a large regulatory RNA that plays a crucial role in controlling various virulence genes responsible for producing exoproteins and cell-wall-associated proteins. One of the important functions of RNAIII is to repress the expression of the spa gene, which codes for surface protein A. Our study reveals that spa repression occurs not only at the transcriptional level but also through RNAIII-mediated inhibition of translation and degradation of the stable spa mRNA by the double-strand-specific endoribonuclease III (RNase III). The 3' end domain of RNAIII, which is partially complementary to the 5' part of spa mRNA, effectively binds to spa mRNA through a loop-loop interaction. This binding is sufficient to inhibit the formation of the translation initiation complex in vitro, but in vivo, the coordinated action of RNase III is necessary to degrade the mRNA and halt translation irreversibly. Our findings also suggest that RNase III is recruited to target the paired RNAs. These discoveries add another layer of complexity to the expression of the S. aureus virulon.

title: Fast calcium and voltage-sensitive dye imaging in enteric neurones reveal calcium peaks associated with single action potential discharge.
text: Increased neuronal activity is reflected by slow changes in [Ca(2+)](i). Our study demonstrates that by using single-trial fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging with a sampling rate of at least 200 Hz, we were able to observe peaks that corresponded to single spike discharge recorded by consecutive voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging in enteric neurones and nerve fibres. Additionally, fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging revealed subthreshold fast excitatory postsynaptic potentials. The [Ca(2+)](i) peaks induced by nicotine were reduced by -conotoxin and blocked by ruthenium red or tetrodotoxin. Furthermore, fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging allowed for the direct recording of single action potentials in enteric neurones. The occurrence of [Ca(2+)](i) peaks depended on the opening of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, as well as the release of Ca(2+) from intracellular stores.

title: New colorimetric cytotoxicity assay for anticancer-drug screening.
text:
We have created a fast, accurate, and affordable method for measuring the amount of cellular protein in both adherent and suspension cultures using 96-well microtiter plates. This method is suitable for regular laboratory use as well as large-scale applications, such as the National Cancer Institute's in vitro anticancer-drug discovery screen, which requires millions of culture wells annually. 

To perform the measurement, cultures were treated with trichloroacetic acid and then stained with a solution of 0.4% sulforhodamine B (SRB) in 1% acetic acid for 30 minutes. Any excess dye was removed by washing with 1% acetic acid, and the dye bound to the proteins was extracted using 10 mM unbuffered Tris base. The optical density of the extracted dye was determined using a computer-interfaced, 96-well microtiter plate reader. 

The results of the SRB assay showed a linear relationship with the number of cells and with the protein content measured by both the Lowry and Bradford assays, covering a wide range of cell densities. At a cell density of 1,000 cells per well, the signal-to-noise ratio at 564 nm was approximately 1.5. The sensitivity of the SRB assay was comparable to several fluorescence assays and superior to both the Lowry and Bradford assays, as well as 20 other visible dyes. 

The SRB assay offers a nondestructive, stable, and visible colorimetric endpoint that can be easily observed with the naked eye. It is highly sensitive to drug-induced cytotoxicity, useful for quantifying clonogenicity, and well-suited for high-volume, automated drug screening. Additionally, SRB exhibits strong fluorescence when excited by a laser at 488 nm, allowing for quantitative measurement at the single-cell level using static fluorescence cytometry.

title: A murine model of human myeloma bone disease.
text: Myeloma is a type of bone disease that is both devastating and unique. It leads to the destruction of bones through the activation of osteoclasts, but the exact ways in which myeloma cells increase osteoclast activity are still unknown. To gain a better understanding of these mechanisms, it would be helpful to have an animal model of human myeloma bone disease. Fortunately, multiple myeloma occurs naturally in aging C57 BL/KaLwRij mice and exhibits all the characteristics of the disease in humans, including bone lesions. However, inducing the disease in normal mice is challenging due to the variability in the number of myeloma cells in the preparations derived from bone marrow. To address this, we have developed a cell line from this murine myeloma and have observed that it causes osteolytic bone lesions in mice, similar to human myeloma bone disease. The cell line produces interleukin-6, but does not rely on external interleukin-6 for growth. When we injected the cultured cells intravenously into mice, they consistently developed the same disease as those injected with fresh bone marrow-derived myeloma cells, including monoclonal gammopathy and bone lesions visible on X-rays. Some of the mice also experienced hypercalcemia, and the bone lesions were characterized by increased osteoclast activity. These findings were replicated when we inoculated Nu/Bg/XID mice with the cultured murine myeloma cells. Since we can inject mice with precise cell numbers and accurately predict when they will develop bone lesions, experience hypercalcemia, and eventually die, this model should be convenient for studying the mechanisms through which myeloma cells activate osteoclasts in this human myeloma bone disease model.

title: Ticagrelor vs. clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes and diabetes: a substudy from the PLATelet inhibition and patient Outcomes (PLATO) trial
text:
Patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) who have high platelet reactivity are at a higher risk of ischaemic events and bleeding after acute coronary syndromes (ACS). In the PLATelet inhibition and patient Outcomes (PLATO) trial, ticagrelor was found to reduce the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke, with similar rates of major bleeding compared to clopidogrel. Our aim was to investigate the outcomes of ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in patients with DM or poor glycaemic control. 

In our analysis, we examined patients with pre-existing DM (n = 4662), including 1036 patients on insulin, as well as those without DM (n = 13,951), and subgroups based on admission levels of haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c; n = 15,150). Among patients with DM, ticagrelor showed a reduction in the primary composite endpoint (HR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.76-1.03), all-cause mortality (HR: 0.82, 95% CI: 0.66-1.01), and stent thrombosis (HR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.36-1.17), without an increase in major bleeding (HR: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.81-1.12). These findings were consistent with the overall cohort and did not show any significant interactions between diabetes status and treatment. We also found no differences between patients with or without ongoing insulin treatment. 

Furthermore, ticagrelor reduced the primary endpoint, all-cause mortality, and stent thrombosis in patients with HbA1c levels above the median (HR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.70-0.91; HR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.65-0.93; and HR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.39-1.00, respectively), with similar rates of bleeding (HR: 0.98, 95% CI: 0.86-1.12). 

In conclusion, ticagrelor, compared to clopidogrel, was effective in reducing ischaemic events in ACS patients regardless of their diabetic status and glycaemic control, without an increased risk of major bleeding events.

title: Cardiovascular risk factors and migraine: the GEM population-based study.
text:
The background of this study is that migraine, especially with aura, increases the risk of early-onset ischemic stroke. The reasons for this are not fully understood, but it may be because people with migraines have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease. The authors of this study compared the cardiovascular risk factors of adults with migraines to those without migraines.

The participants in this study were 5,755 individuals aged 20 to 65 years from the Genetic Epidemiology of Migraine (GEM) study in the Netherlands. Among them, 620 were current migraineurs, with 31% experiencing aura, 64% without aura, and 5% unclassified. The control group consisted of 5,135 individuals who had never experienced migraines. The researchers measured various cardiovascular risk factors, including blood pressure, cholesterol levels, smoking, oral contraceptive use, and the Framingham risk score for heart disease.

The results showed that compared to the control group, migraineurs were more likely to smoke and less likely to consume alcohol. They were also more likely to have a family history of early heart attacks. Migraineurs with aura had a higher likelihood of having unfavorable cholesterol levels, high blood pressure, and a history of early-onset heart disease or stroke. Female migraineurs with aura were more likely to use oral contraceptives. The odds of having an elevated Framingham risk score for heart disease were approximately doubled for migraineurs with aura.

In conclusion, individuals with migraines, especially those with aura, have a higher cardiovascular risk profile compared to those without migraines.

title: Th2-mediated host protective immunity to intestinal nematode infections.
text: Despite extensive research, there is still limited knowledge about the mechanisms that combat nematodes residing in the intestine. Most of the current understanding comes from studying laboratory models in rodents. It is evident that when an infection by intestinal helminths occurs, the immune system triggers a strong Th2-mediated response. This response regulates various characteristics of helminth infections, such as eosinophilia, intestinal mastocytosis, and increased production of IgE. The ability to manipulate the host's immune response in vivo using monoclonal antibodies and recombinant cytokines specific to certain cytokines, along with the use of animals with disrupted genes involved in the immune response, has provided valuable tools to investigate the potential mechanisms at play. Without a T-cell compartment, the host is unable to expel the parasite. If a Th1-dominated response is generated, protective immunity is generally compromised. Therefore, it seems that some aspect of the Th2-mediated response controls the effector mechanisms. Although it is evident that mast cells may play a role in protection against certain infections, possibly through the generation of a non-specific inflammatory response, the activation process of these cells remains unclear. Studies using transgenic animals suggest that activation does not occur through the high-affinity receptor for IgE, which also raises doubts about the significance of conventional interactions between effector immune cells and antibodies. There is limited evidence supporting a protective role for eosinophilia in any system. New data also suggest that while interleukin 4 (IL-4) is generally important and can have effects independent of an adaptive immune response, it may not always be sufficient to mediate protection. Other Th2 cytokines, such as IL-13, may require further investigation. It is evident that several potential Th2-controlled effector mechanisms, particularly those relevant to mucosal surfaces, still need to be explored. Overall, worm expulsion is likely the result of a combination of multiple mechanisms, some of which may be more crucial for certain parasite species than others.

title: Wnt/β-catenin signaling defines organizing centers that orchestrate growth and differentiation of the regenerating zebrafish caudal fin.
text: The regeneration of fins in zebrafish occurs through the creation of a group of precursor cells called the blastema. The proliferation of blastemal cells and the arrangement of the epidermis above them rely on the crucial Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Surprisingly, this signaling is not active in the epidermis or the majority of proliferative blastemal cells. Instead, interference with specific pathways in the tissue indicates that Wnt signaling in the nonproliferative distal blastema is necessary for cell proliferation in the proximal blastema. Additionally, signaling in cells lining the osteoblasts guides osteoblast differentiation. Therefore, Wnt signaling indirectly regulates epidermal patterning, blastemal cell proliferation, and osteoblast maturation through secondary signals. Through gene expression profiling, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and functional rescue experiments, it is suggested that Wnt/β-catenin signaling operates through Fgf and Bmp signaling to control epidermal patterning. On the other hand, retinoic acid and Hedgehog signals mediate its effects on blastemal cell proliferation. We propose that Wnt signaling coordinates fin regeneration by establishing organizing centers that instruct the behaviors of neighboring tissues.

title: The utility of cerebrospinal fluid analysis in patients with multiple sclerosis
text: The diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) requires ruling out other possible diagnoses. Therefore, it is recommended to routinely analyze the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in patients who have experienced their first clinical event suggestive of MS. While CSF analysis is no longer mandatory for diagnosing relapsing-remitting MS, as long as the MRI diagnostic criteria are met, caution should be exercised when diagnosing MS in patients with negative MRI results or without CSF analysis. CSF investigation is valuable in eliminating other potential causes of the disease. The presence of oligoclonal IgG bands in the CSF can provide prognostic information and aid in clinical decision-making. Additionally, CSF analysis plays a crucial role in MS research by providing insights into the pathogenesis of the disease and neurodegenerative inflammation. Although not yet validated, new CSF biomarkers have been identified for diagnosing MS, assessing disease activity, predicting prognosis, and evaluating treatment response. With advancements in detection techniques, the number of these biomarkers is likely to increase. This review summarizes the CSF findings that contribute to the differential diagnosis of MS and highlights the potential of novel biomarkers in advancing our understanding of the disease's pathophysiology.

title: Expression of circadian genes correlates with liver metastasis and outcomes in colorectal cancer.
text: Circadian rhythms are daily fluctuations in various biological processes, which are caused by the feedback loops of eight core circadian genes: Per1, Per2, Per3, Cry1, Cry2, Clock, Bmal1, and CKIε. Recent research suggests that these circadian genes play a role in the growth and development of different types of cancer. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between circadian gene expression and clinicopathological factors and outcomes in patients with colorectal cancer. The researchers analyzed surgical samples of cancerous tissue and adjacent normal mucosa from 202 untreated colorectal cancer patients. They used quantitative real-time, reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction to measure the relative expression levels of the circadian genes in the samples. The results showed that the expression of the Clock and CKIε genes in cancerous tissue was significantly higher compared to adjacent normal mucosa. On the other hand, the expression of the Per1 and Per3 genes in cancerous tissue was significantly lower compared to adjacent normal mucosa. Further analysis revealed that high expression of the Bmal1 gene and low expression of the Per1 gene were associated with liver metastasis. Additionally, patients with high expression of the Per2 gene had significantly better outcomes compared to those with low expression of the Per2 gene. Therefore, overexpression of the Bmal1 gene and reduced expression of the Per1 gene could potentially serve as predictors of liver metastasis. Furthermore, reduced expression of the Per2 gene may be indicative of outcomes in patients with colorectal cancer.

title: The Danish prescription registries.
text: This article discusses the establishment of two large prescription registries in Danish pharmacies, namely the Odense University Pharmacoepidemiological Database (OPED) and the Pharmacoepidemiological Prescription Database of North Jutland (PDNJ). The content, coverage, completeness, and data quality of these registries are examined. Additionally, the article presents the conditions for accessing the data. Together, these registries cover approximately one million individuals, which accounts for 18% of the Danish population. The populations included in the registries are stable and representative of the overall Danish population. All reimbursed medications at the individual level are covered by these registries. By registering a unique and permanent personal identifier, it becomes possible to compile longitudinal drug histories and link prescription data to other population-based Danish registries. The Danish prescription registries demonstrate excellent completeness for reimbursed prescription drugs, and a few comparison studies indicate high validity of the register information. Overall, these registries serve as a valuable new data source for pharmacoepidemiological studies.

title: Oridonin, a diterpenoid purified from Rabdosia rubescens, inhibits the proliferation of cells from lymphoid malignancies in association with blockade of the NF-kappa B signal pathways.
text: The study discovered that oridonin, a natural compound derived from Rabdosia rubescens, effectively inhibited the growth of multiple myeloma (MM; U266, RPMI8226), acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia (Jurkat), and adult T-cell leukemia (MT-1) cells. The effective dose that inhibited 50% of the target cells (ED50) ranged from 0.75 to 2.7 microg/mL. Through terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase-mediated dUTP nick end labeling staining, it was observed that oridonin induced apoptosis in MT-1 cells in a time-dependent manner. The study also investigated the impact of oridonin on antiapoptotic Bcl-2 family members and found that it reduced the levels of Mcl-1 and BCL-x(L) proteins in both MT-1 and RPMI8226 cells. However, it did not affect the levels of Bcl-2 protein. Further analysis revealed that oridonin inhibited the DNA-binding activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kappa B) in these cells, as confirmed by luciferase reporter gene, ELISA-based, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays. Oridonin also hindered NF-kappa B activity stimulated by tumor necrosis factor-alpha and lipopolysaccharide in Jurkat cells and RAW264.7 murine macrophages. Notably, oridonin reduced the survival of cells from patients with adult T-cell leukemia (three samples), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (one sample), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (one sample), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (three samples), and MM (four samples) by inhibiting NF-kappa B DNA-binding activity. However, it did not affect the survival of normal lymphoid cells from healthy volunteers. In conclusion, oridonin shows potential as an adjunctive therapy for individuals with lymphoid malignancies, including the fatal disease adult T-cell leukemia.

title: Uncertainty in integrative structural modeling.
text:
Integrative structural modeling involves utilizing various types of input information and progresses through four distinct stages: (i) gathering relevant information, (ii) designing a model representation and converting the gathered information into a scoring function, (iii) sampling models that yield high scores, and (iv) analyzing both the models and the information. 

During the initial stage, uncertainty arises due to sparse, noisy, ambiguous, or heterogeneous data. In the second stage, uncertainty may stem from a representation that is too coarse for the available information or a scoring function that fails to accurately capture the information. The third stage primarily introduces uncertainty through inadequate sampling. Finally, in the fourth stage, techniques such as clustering, cross-validation, and other methods are employed to estimate the precision and accuracy of both the models and the information.

title: Moist occlusive dressing (Aquacel(®) Ag) versus moist open dressing (MEBO(®)) in the management of partial-thickness facial burns: a comparative study in Ain Shams University.
text:
The face plays a crucial role in expressing emotions and conveying individual identity. Facial burns can have devastating physical, emotional, and psychosocial effects on patients. Among these burns, partial thickness burns are particularly common in children. This study aims to compare the effectiveness of two different techniques for managing partial thickness burns of the face: standard moist open technique and moist closed technique.

The study included patients with partial-thickness facial burns who were admitted to the burn unit at Ain Shams University in Cairo, Egypt, between April 2009 and December 2009. The patients were divided into two groups: one group received open treatment with MEBO(®), while the other group received coverage with Aquacel(®) Ag. Various factors such as demographics, length of hospital stay, rate of infections, time to total healing, frequency of dressing changes, pain, cost benefit, and patient discomfort were compared between the two groups. The long-term outcome, specifically the incidence of hypertrophic scarring, was assessed during a follow-up period of up to 6 months.

The results showed no significant differences in demographics between the two groups. However, the group treated with Aquacel(®) Ag had a shorter mean time for re-epithelialization (10.5 days) compared to the MEBO(®) group (12.4 days) (p<0.05). Additionally, the Aquacel(®) Ag group experienced less frequent dressing changes, less pain, and less patient discomfort. There was no significant difference in cost between the two groups. Furthermore, the quality of scarring improved in the Aquacel(®) Ag treatment group. Long-term outcomes were recorded for both groups during the three and six-month follow-up periods.

In conclusion, the use of moist occlusive dressing (Aquacel(®) Ag) significantly improves the management and healing rate of partial thickness facial burns compared to moist open dressing (MEBO(®)). It also leads to better long-term outcomes, including a reduced incidence of hypertrophic scarring.

title: Feedback upregulation of HER3 (ErbB3) expression and activity attenuates antitumor effect of PI3K inhibitors.
text: We investigated the impact of XL147, an inhibitor of PI3K, on human breast cancer cell lines that have constitutive PI3K activation. Treatment with XL147 led to a dose-dependent reduction in cell growth and levels of pAKT and pS6, which are signal transducers in the PI3K/AKT/TOR pathway. In cells that overexpress HER2, inhibiting PI3K resulted in an increase in the expression and phosphorylation of multiple receptor tyrosine kinases, including HER3. When FoxO1 and FoxO3a transcription factors were knocked down, the induction of HER3, InsR, IGF1R, and FGFR2 mRNAs upon PI3K inhibition was suppressed. In HER2(+) cells, knocking down HER3 with siRNA or co-treating with the HER2 inhibitors trastuzumab or lapatinib enhanced XL147-induced cell death and inhibition of pAKT and pS6. Trastuzumab and lapatinib also synergized with XL147 in inhibiting pAKT and growth of established BT474 xenografts. These findings suggest that PI3K antagonists can inhibit AKT and alleviate the suppression of receptor tyrosine kinase expression and activity. However, this relief of feedback limits the sustained inhibition of the PI3K/AKT pathway and weakens the response to these agents. Consequently, PI3K pathway inhibitors may have limited clinical effectiveness if used alone. In patients with HER2-overexpressing breast cancer, it is advisable to combine PI3K inhibitors with HER2/HER3 antagonists.

title: Developmental RacGAP α2-Chimaerin Signaling Is a Determinant of the Morphological Features of Dendritic Spines in Adulthood.
text: The morphological characteristics of dendritic spines are crucial for cognitive ability, but the molecular mechanisms involved in shaping spine morphology during development are not fully understood. Additionally, it is unclear how these developmental mechanisms determine the normal morphology of adult spines. In this study, we present evidence that the α2-isoform of Rac-specific GTPase-activating protein α-chimaerin (α2-chimaerin) plays a role in refining spine morphology during the late postnatal period, and that this developmental function of α2-chimaerin affects adult spine morphology. We conducted experiments using mice with global and conditional knock-out of α-chimaerin isoforms (α1-chimaerin and α2-chimaerin). Disruption of α2-chimaerin, but not α1-chimaerin, in mice resulted in larger and denser spines in the hippocampus. Conversely, overexpression of α2-chimaerin in developing hippocampal neurons led to a decrease in spine size. Disruption of α2-chimaerin inhibited EphA-mediated spine development in cultured hippocampal neurons. When α2-chimaerin disruption began during the juvenile stage, spine size increased in the hippocampus. However, deleting α2-chimaerin only in adulthood did not alter spine morphology. Consistent with these findings, disrupting α2-chimaerin during the juvenile stage increased contextual fear learning in adulthood, while deleting α2-chimaerin only in adulthood had no effect on contextual learning. These results suggest that α2-chimaerin signaling during developmental stages contributes to the determination of adult spine morphology and the establishment of normal cognitive ability. This study has important implications for understanding neurodevelopmental disorders and their impact on cognitive function. Specifically, it highlights the role of Rac and its regulators, such as Rac-specific GTPase-activating proteins and Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factors, in spine morphogenesis and cognitive ability. Our findings provide compelling evidence that α2-chimaerin is involved in refining spine morphology during late postnatal development and that this developmental function of α2-chimaerin affects adult spine morphology. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that α2-chimaerin signaling during late postnatal development is crucial for normal cognitive ability in adult mice.

title: Efficacy and tolerability of amitriptylinoxide in the treatment of chronic tension-type headache: a multi-centre controlled study.
text: Amitriptyline is the preferred medication for treating chronic tension-type headaches. A study was conducted with 197 patients (87 males and 110 females) with a mean age of 38 +/- 13 (ranging from 18 to 68) to compare the effectiveness and tolerability of 60-90 mg of amitriptylinoxide (AO), 50-75 mg of amitriptyline (AM), and a placebo (PL). The study consisted of a four-week baseline phase followed by 12 weeks of treatment, and it was conducted in a double-blind, parallel-group manner. The primary goal of the study was to determine if there was a reduction of at least 50% in the product of headache duration and frequency, as well as a reduction of at least 50% in headache intensity. Statistical analysis was performed using Fisher's exact test and analysis of variance. The results showed no significant difference between AO, AM, and PL in terms of the primary study endpoint. The treatment response rate was 30.3% for AO, 22.4% for AM, and 21.9% for PL. A reduction of at least 50% in headache duration and frequency was observed in 39.4% of the AO group, 25.4% of the AM group, and 26.6% of the PL group (PAO-PL = .1384, PAM-PL = 1.000, PAO-AM = .0973). Similarly, a reduction of at least 50% in headache intensity was found in 31.8% of the AO group, 26.9% of the AM group, and 26.6% of the PL group (PAO-PL = .5657, PAM-PL = 1.000, PAO-AM = .5715). Trend analysis indicated that AO had a superior effect in reducing headache intensity (p < 0.05) and the product of headache duration and frequency.

title: Downregulation of Superoxide Dismutase Activity and Gene Expression in Cultured Rat Brain Astrocytes after Incubation with Vitamin C
text: The presence of reactive oxygen species has been associated with changes in the central nervous system. Studies have shown that antioxidant supplementation can have a positive effect. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an enzyme that naturally scavenges reactive oxygen species. This study aimed to investigate the impact of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) supplementation on SOD changes in cultured neurological cells. Rat brain astrocytes (RBA-1 cells) were treated with vitamin C and divided into four groups: a control group (no vitamin C) and three treatment groups with vitamin C at concentrations of 40, 80, and 160 µmol/l. SOD activity, SOD mRNA levels using Northern blotting, and SOD protein amounts using Western blotting were measured after short-term (2 days) and long-term (7 days) incubation. After 2 days, vitamin C led to a concentration-dependent decrease in SOD activity (Mn-SOD from 14.8 ± 1.2 to 13.2 ± 0.5 U/mg protein and Cu/Zn-SOD from 64.8 ± 1.2 to 51.7 ± 0.9 U/mg protein; p < 0.05). Vitamin C also reduced Cu/Zn-SOD mRNA levels from 100 to 86.3 ± 6.7% (p < 0.01), while the protein amounts of both SODs remained unchanged. After 7 days, RBA-1 cells incubated with vitamin C showed a significant decrease in SOD activity (Mn-SOD from 14.9 ± 0.3 to 11.8 ± 0.3 U/mg protein and Cu/Zn-SOD from 61.8 ± 1.8 to 54.6 ± 0.9 U/mg protein; p < 0.01), and the mRNA levels were also reduced (Mn-SOD from 100 to 86.8 ± 8.7% and Cu/Zn-SOD from 100 to 84.7 ± 4.8%; p < 0.01). These findings suggest that incubation with relatively high concentrations of vitamin C for 2 and 7 days may downregulate SOD activity and gene expression in cultured RBA-1 cells.

title: Lateral Hypothalamic Area Glutamatergic Neurons and Their Projections to the Lateral Habenula Regulate Feeding and Reward.
text: The consumption of high-calorie, tasty foods is believed to be a major factor in the global obesity epidemic. However, the specific neural pathways that directly control pleasurable eating are still not fully understood. In this study, we discovered that glutamatergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA), along with their connections to the lateral habenula (LHb), play a role in regulating the intake of enjoyable food. When we genetically removed these LHA glutamatergic neurons in mice that had access to a high-fat diet, their daily calorie intake increased and they gained weight, without affecting their overall activity levels. We found that anterior LHA glutamatergic neurons send glutamatergic signals to the LHb, a brain region involved in processing negative stimuli and predicting negative rewards. By using optogenetic stimulation, we were able to activate the LHA-LHb circuit and observe the release of glutamate and GABA, which ultimately increased the firing of most LHb neurons. In vivo optogenetic inhibition of LHA-LHb glutamatergic fibers resulted in a preference for a specific location, while stimulation of these fibers had the opposite effect. Additionally, inhibiting LHA-LHb glutamatergic fibers acutely increased the consumption of a pleasurable liquid reward. These findings demonstrate that LHA glutamatergic neurons have the ability to regulate feeding and potentially other behaviors through their connections with the LHb and other brain regions. This study is significant because it provides insight into the functional connectivity and behavioral importance of this circuit in relation to eating and reward-related behavior.

title: Glucose Metabolism Inhibits Apoptosis in Neurons and Cancer Cells by Redox Inactivation of Cytochrome c
text: The precise advantage of glucose utilization by neurons and cancer cells is still not fully understood. Despite being different cell types, both neurons and cancer cells have a heightened control over the apoptotic pathway, enabling them to survive for extended periods. Our study reveals that both neurons and cancer cells effectively prevent cytochrome c-mediated apoptosis by relying on glucose metabolism. We have observed that the pro-apoptotic function of cytochrome c is influenced by its redox state, and an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) triggers the oxidation and activation of cytochrome c during apoptosis. However, in healthy neurons and cancer cells, cytochrome c remains inactive due to its reduction and inhibition by intracellular glutathione (GSH), which is produced as a result of glucose metabolism through the pentose phosphate pathway. These findings highlight a remarkable similarity in the regulation of apoptosis between neurons and cancer cells and shed light on how the Warburg effect, which promotes glucose utilization in cancer cells, allows them to evade apoptosis and enables long-term survival of neurons.

title: mTORC2 Regulates Amino Acid Metabolism in Cancer by Phosphorylation of the Cystine-Glutamate Antiporter xCT.
text: The understanding of how mutations in cancer affect amino acid metabolism and drive tumor growth is limited. However, through an unbiased proteomic screen, we have discovered that mTORC2 plays a crucial role in regulating amino acid metabolism in cancer. This regulation occurs through the phosphorylation of the cystine-glutamate antiporter xCT. Specifically, mTORC2 phosphorylates serine 26 at the cytosolic N terminus of xCT, leading to the inhibition of its activity. By genetically inhibiting mTORC2 or using pharmacologic inhibitors of the mTOR kinase, we observed an increase in glutamate secretion, cystine uptake, and its incorporation into glutathione. This finding establishes a connection between growth factor receptor signaling and the uptake and utilization of amino acids. Ultimately, these results reveal an unexpected mechanism that allows cancer cells to adapt to changes in their environment by regulating amino acid metabolism.

title: Bayesian models leveraging bioactivity and cytotoxicity information for drug discovery.
text:
Finding unique leads in drug discovery is a major challenge, especially for neglected diseases like tuberculosis. To overcome this hurdle, we utilized public high-throughput screening (HTS) data to validate a virtual screening approach. This approach involved using Bayesian models that were built with bioactivity information (single-event model) and both bioactivity and cytotoxicity information (dual-event model). By virtually screening a commercial library, we were able to confirm active compounds with hit rates that were one to two orders of magnitude higher than typical HTS results. 

Using the dual-event Bayesian model, we identified compounds with antitubercular whole-cell activity and low cytotoxicity in mammalian cells from a published set of antimalarials. The most potent hit displayed both in vitro activity and in vitro/in vivo safety characteristics of a potential drug lead. These Bayesian models offer significant time and cost savings in the drug discovery process.

title: A role for interleukin-1β in determining the lineage fate of embryonic rat hippocampal neural precursor cells.
text: Neurogenesis occurs in the hippocampus of both developing and adult brains due to the presence of versatile stem cells and specialized precursor cells at different stages of development. These cells have the potential to be used in cell transplantation methods for neurodegenerative disorders and trauma. The prolonged release of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) from activated microglia has a harmful effect on hippocampal neurons and is associated with impaired neurogenesis and cognitive dysfunction in aging, Alzheimer's disease, and depression. This study aimed to examine the impact of IL-1β on the growth and differentiation of embryonic rat hippocampal neural progenitor cells (NPCs) in a laboratory setting. Our findings demonstrate that proliferating NPCs express IL-1R1 and that treatment with IL-1β reduces cell proliferation and the growth of neurospheres. When NPCs were differentiated in the presence of IL-1β, there was a significant decrease in the percentage of newly-formed neurons and post-mitotic neurons, and a significant increase in the percentage of astrocytes in these cultures. These effects were mitigated by the use of an IL-1 receptor antagonist. These results indicate that IL-1β has an inhibitory effect on the proliferation and neurogenesis of embryonic hippocampal NPCs, while promoting the formation of astrocytes, and this is mediated by IL-1R1. These findings highlight the importance of considering the inflammatory environment during NPC development and suggest that strategies to block IL-1β signaling may be necessary to enhance the effectiveness of cell transplantation methods or in conditions where natural hippocampal neurogenesis is impaired.

title: Bone disease in pediatric patients undergoing dialysis with CAPD or CCPD.
text: The histological characteristics of renal osteodystrophy and the occurrence of bone aluminum deposition in children who undergo regular dialysis have not been documented. A total of forty-four pediatric patients who were undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) or cycling peritoneal dialysis (CCPD) underwent bone biopsies and deferoxamine (DFO) infusion tests. All patients were also taking oral calcitriol. Osteitis fibrosa (OF) was observed in 39% of patients, mild lesions (M) in 25%, normal histology (NH) in 16%, aplastic lesions (AP) in 11%, and osteomalacia (OM) in 9%. Histochemical staining revealed the presence of bone surface aluminum (SA) in 10 out of 20 patients who were administered aluminum-containing phosphate-binding agents, while none of the 24 patients treated with calcium carbonate showed SA. The statistical analysis showed a significant association between SA and the type of phosphate-binding agent used (chi 2 = 15.5, P < 0.0001). Serum biochemistries and DFO infusion tests were not able to predict bone histology, but plasma aluminum levels were significantly elevated in patients with OM, and the highest bone aluminum content was observed in these patients. The bone formation rate (BFR) was positively correlated with serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels (r = 0.55, P < 0.001), and inversely related to bone aluminum content (r = -0.42, P < 0.01), even in patients with OF (r = -0.66, P < 0.05). Patients with SA greater than 30% had normal or reduced BFR compared to those with SA less than 30% (chi 2 = 12.2, P < 0.005). Based on SA greater than 30%, six patients were classified as having aluminum-related bone disease, including three with OM, one with AP, and two with NH. Two-thirds of pediatric patients undergoing CAPD/CCPD continued to experience hyperparathyroidism despite treatment with calcitriol. However, regardless of the histologic lesion or serum PTH level, BFR was adversely affected by aluminum when SA exceeded 30%.

title: Disruption of the immune-checkpoint VISTA gene imparts a proinflammatory phenotype with predisposition to the development of autoimmunity.
text: VISTA, short for V domain-containing Ig suppressor of T-cell activation, is a regulator that inhibits T cell-mediated immune responses. Previous research using a VISTA-blocking antibody has shown that blocking VISTA enhances T-cell activation. This study provides a detailed analysis of mice that have had the VISTA gene deleted. While young mice with VISTA deficiency appear to have normal development of blood cells, they gradually accumulate spontaneously activated T cells and produce various inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Immunization with a neoantigen also leads to increased T-cell responsiveness. Despite experiencing chronic inflammation in multiple organs, aged mice lacking VISTA do not develop autoimmune diseases affecting the entire body or specific organs. However, when these VISTA-deficient mice are bred with 2D2 T-cell receptor transgenic mice, which are prone to developing experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, the incidence and severity of the disease significantly increase. This disease progression is associated with heightened activation of encephalitogenic T cells in the peripheral tissues and increased infiltration into the central nervous system. Overall, these findings suggest that VISTA acts as a negative regulator of immune checkpoints, and its absence lowers the threshold for T-cell activation, leading to an enhanced proinflammatory state and an increased likelihood and intensity of autoimmunity under susceptible conditions.

title: Molecular mechanisms that funnel RNA precursors into endogenous small-interfering RNA and microRNA biogenesis pathways in Drosophila.
text: In Drosophila, there are three types of small RNAs that play a role in RNA silencing: microRNAs (miRNAs), PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs), and endogenous small-interfering RNAs (endo-siRNAs or esiRNAs). While piRNAs are produced independently of Dicer, the biogenesis pathways for miRNAs and esiRNAs require Dicer1 and Dicer2, respectively. Recent research has focused on the isoforms of Loquacious (Loqs), specifically Loqs-PB and Loqs-PD, which are involved in the processing pathways for miRNAs and esiRNAs. However, the exact functions of these Loqs isoforms in their respective small RNA biogenesis pathways are still unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that Loqs-PD specifically associates with Dicer2 through its C-terminal domain. The Dicer2-Loqs-PD complex includes R2D2, another known partner of Dicer2, and is able to remove both exogenous siRNAs and esiRNAs from their precursors in vitro. Interestingly, Loqs-PD enhances the activity of Dicer2, while R2D2 does not. The Dicer2-Loqs-PD complex is able to process esiRNA precursor hairpins with long stems, resulting in the production of small RNAs associated with AGO2. However, small RNAs derived from the terminal hairpins of esiRNA precursors are loaded onto AGO1, indicating that they belong to a new subset of miRNAs. These findings suggest that the structure of the precursor RNA determines the biogenesis mechanism of esiRNAs and miRNAs, with hairpin structures containing long stems playing a role in the evolution of Drosophila miRNAs.

title: Neutralizing antibody responses in acute human immunodeficiency virus type 1 subtype C infection.
text: Studying the evolution and characteristics of neutralizing antibodies in human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection is crucial for identifying potential targets for vaccine development. In this research, we examined the neutralization responses of 14 individuals infected with HIV-1 subtype C, using envelope clones obtained within the first 2 months after infection. Our findings reveal that potent, yet strain-specific, neutralizing antibodies emerge within 3 to 12 months of HIV-1 infection. The strength of this response was linked to shorter envelope lengths in the V1-to-V5 region and fewer glycosylation sites, particularly in the V1-V2 region. Within a year of infection, 4 out of 14 individuals exhibited anti-MPER antibodies, while 12 participants developed high levels of antibodies to CD4-induced (CD4i) epitopes, often before the appearance of autologous neutralizing antibodies. However, neither anti-MPER nor anti-CD4i antibodies demonstrated broad neutralization capabilities. These findings shed light on the timing, potency, breadth, and epitope specificity of neutralizing antibody responses in acute HIV-1 subtype C infection.

title: The cell cycle in polyploid megakaryocytes is associated with reduced activity of cyclin B1-dependent cdc2 kinase.
text: The megakaryocyte, which is the precursor to platelets, undergoes a process called endomitosis where it matures into a polyploid cell through DNA replication without mitosis. We have been able to study the factors that control endomitosis in our megakaryocytic cell line, MegT, which was created by introducing a temperature-sensitive simian virus 40 large T antigen into the megakaryocytes of transgenic mice. Our goal was to determine if endomitosis involves continuous DNA synthesis (S phase) or if it consists of S phases interrupted by gaps. By analyzing the cell cycle in MegT cells, we found that when the large T antigen was deactivated, the cells transitioned from a mitotic cell cycle to an endomitotic cell cycle that included S and Gap phases. The levels of cyclin A, a protein involved in the transition from G1 to S phase, and cyclin D3, a protein involved in the G1 phase, were elevated at the start of DNA synthesis in both MegT cells undergoing mitotic cell cycles and during endomitosis. However, the level of cyclin B1, a protein involved in mitosis, cycled in cells undergoing mitotic cell cycles but was not detectable during endomitosis. The levels of the mitotic kinase protein, Cdc2, remained consistent during both the mitotic cell cycle and endomitosis; however, the activity of the cyclin B1-dependent Cdc2 kinase was greatly reduced in the polyploid cells. Fibroblasts that were immortalized with the same heat-labile oncogene did not show reduced levels of cyclin B1 when exposed to high temperatures, nor did they become polyploid. This suggests that the reduced levels of cyclin B1 are specific to megakaryocytes and not a result of the T-antigen mutation. In conclusion, the cellular programming during endoreduplication in megakaryocytes is associated with decreased levels of cyclin B1.

title: Ghrelin secretion stimulated by {beta}1-adrenergic receptors in cultured ghrelinoma cells and in fasted mice.
text: The hormone ghrelin, which is produced in the stomach, significantly increases in mouse plasma during severe calorie deprivation, a crucial event for survival. However, the exact mechanism behind this increase remains unknown. In this study, we examined the regulation of ghrelin secretion in tissue culture cells derived from mice with ghrelinomas induced by a specific SV40 T-antigen transgene. Our findings revealed that the cells responsible for ghrelin secretion express high levels of mRNA encoding beta(1)-adrenergic receptors. When norepinephrine or epinephrine was added to the culture medium, ghrelin secretion was stimulated. This effect was blocked by atenolol, a selective beta(1)-adrenergic antagonist. Furthermore, when normal mice were treated with reserpine to deplete adrenergic neurotransmitters from sympathetic neurons, the fasting-induced increase in plasma ghrelin was prevented. Similar inhibition was observed after administration of atenolol. In conclusion, our study suggests that ghrelin secretion during fasting is triggered by adrenergic agents released by sympathetic neurons, which directly interact with beta(1) receptors on the ghrelin-secreting cells in the stomach.

title: Dominance relationships between S-alleles in self-incompatible Brassica campestris L.
text: A total of 249 out of 276 possible pair-wise combinations between 24 S-alleles of Brassica campestris were examined in this study. These S-alleles were obtained from two natural populations in Turkey and Japan. To determine the dominance relationships between each pair of S-alleles, reciprocal test-crosses were conducted between the F1 hybrids and their respective parental S-homozygotes. The 24 S-alleles were categorized into two groups on the stigma side and three groups on the pollen side. In the stigma, codominance was frequently observed, while dominance or recessiveness appeared depending on the specific combination of S-alleles. On the other hand, codominance was less common in the pollen, and there seemed to be a hierarchical pattern of dominance relationships overall, although dominance was observed with certain specific combinations of S-alleles. The interactions among the 24 S-alleles differed between the stigma and the pollen. In the pollen, there were 20 pairs that exhibited independent weakening of S-alleles, whereas only two pairs showed this interaction in the stigma. This interaction appears to be associated with the recessiveness of S-alleles.

title: MicroRNA-203 inhibits cellular proliferation and invasion by targeting Bmi1 in non-small cell lung cancer.
text: The role of microRNAs in regulating tumor progression and invasion is widely recognized. However, the significance of miR-203 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between B-cell-specific moloney murine leukemia virus insertion site 1 (Bmi1) and miR-203. The results showed that miR-203 acts as a tumor suppressor by controlling the expression of Bmi1. NSCLC tissues exhibited decreased levels of miR-203, while Bmi1 expression was elevated in both tissues and cell lines. Moreover, reducing Bmi1 or increasing miR-203 expression inhibited the proliferation and invasion of NSCLC cells in laboratory settings. Additionally, a dual-luciferase reporter assay confirmed Bmi1 as a new target of miR-203. In conclusion, this study highlights the tumor-suppressive role of miR-203 and its importance in suppressing NSCLC cell growth by targeting Bmi1. These findings suggest that miR-203 could be a promising therapeutic target for NSCLC.

title: Characterization of the interaction between retinoic acid receptor/retinoid X receptor (RAR/RXR) heterodimers and transcriptional coactivators through structural and fluorescence anisotropy studies.
text: Retinoid receptors, known as RARs and RXRs, are transcription factors that are activated by ligands. They regulate the transcription of target genes by recruiting coregulator complexes at specific promoters. In order to understand how heterodimerization and ligand binding affect the recruitment of coactivators, we conducted a study where we determined the crystal structure of the complex formed by the RARbeta/RXRalpha ligand-binding domain heterodimer, its 9-cis retinoic acid ligand, and a peptide called NR box 2, which is derived from the nuclear receptor interaction domain (NID) of the coactivator TRAP220 and contains an LXXLL motif. Additionally, we measured the binding affinities of the isolated NR box 2 peptide and the full-length NID of the coactivator SRC-1 for retinoid receptors in the presence of different types of ligands. Our analysis of the three-dimensional structures and fluorescence data showed that heterodimerization does not significantly change the structure of the individual subunits or their ability to interact with NR box 2. Similarly, we found that the ability of one subunit to recruit NR box 2 is not affected by the ligand binding status of the partner receptor. However, the strength of the overall association between the heterodimer and the full-length SRC-1 NID is determined by the combination of RAR and RXR ligands, with both receptor agonists needing to be present simultaneously for the highest binding affinity. We discovered that an LXXLL peptide-driven mechanism is responsible for the concerted reorientation of three phenylalanine side chains, creating an "aromatic clamp" that locks the RXR activation helix H12 in the transcriptionally active conformation. Additionally, we observed that variations in helix H11-ligand interactions can alter the communication pathway between helices H11, H12, and the connecting loop L11-12, which leads to the coactivator-binding site. Overall, our findings provide insights into the molecular and structural features that influence the ligand-dependent interaction of the RAR/RXR heterodimer with nuclear receptor coactivators.

title: PRC2 complexes with JARID2, MTF2, and esPRC2p48 in ES cells to modulate ES cell pluripotency and somatic cell reprogramming.
text: The role of the Polycomb repressive complex two (PRC2) in embryonic stem (ES) cell pluripotency is not well understood. It was previously believed that ES cells have the same subunit composition of PRC2 as HeLa cells and Drosophila embryos. However, our research shows that PRC2 in mouse ES cells actually contains three additional subunits: JARID2, MTF2, and a new protein called esPRC2p48. These three subunits are highly expressed in mouse ES cells compared to differentiated cells. When JARID2, MTF2, or esPRC2p48 are knocked down, the level of PRC2-mediated H3K27 methylation is altered, leading to the expression of genes associated with differentiation in ES cells. Interestingly, when JARID2, MTF2, and esPRC2p48 are expressed together, they enhance the reprogramming of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) into induced pluripotent stem cells mediated by Oct4/Sox2/Klf4. On the other hand, knocking down or eliminating JARID2, MTF2, or esPRC2p48 significantly inhibits reprogramming. In MEFs, JARID2, MTF2, and esPRC2p48 modulate H3K27 methylation and help repress the expression of genes associated with specific lineages. They also synergistically stimulate the activity of PRC2's histone methyltransferase in vitro. Therefore, our findings highlight the importance of JARID2, MTF2, and esPRC2p48 as regulatory subunits of PRC2 in ES cells and demonstrate their critical roles in modulating PRC2's activity and gene expression in both ES cells and during the reprogramming of somatic cells.

title: General and abdominal adiposity and risk of death in Europe.
text:
BACKGROUND
Previous research has primarily relied on the body-mass index (BMI) to evaluate the connection between adiposity and mortality risk. However, few studies have investigated whether the distribution of body fat contributes to predicting death.

METHODS
We conducted a study using data from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC), which included 359,387 participants from nine countries. We analyzed the association between BMI, waist circumference, and waist-to-hip ratio with the risk of death. Cox regression analysis was used, with age as the time variable. The models were stratified by study center and age at recruitment, and adjusted for educational level, smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and height.

RESULTS
Over an average follow-up period of 9.7 years, 14,723 participants died. The lowest mortality risks related to BMI were observed at a BMI of 25.3 for men and 24.3 for women. After adjusting for BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio showed a strong association with the risk of death. Men and women in the highest quintile of waist circumference had relative risks of 2.05 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.80 to 2.33) and 1.78 (95% CI, 1.56 to 2.04), respectively. Similarly, those in the highest quintile of waist-to-hip ratio had relative risks of 1.68 (95% CI, 1.53 to 1.84) and 1.51 (95% CI, 1.37 to 1.66), respectively. BMI remained significantly associated with the risk of death even when waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio were included in the models (P<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS
These findings suggest that both overall adiposity and abdominal adiposity are linked to the risk of death. Therefore, waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio should be considered in addition to BMI when assessing mortality risk.

title: Phosphorylation of the autophagy receptor optineurin restricts Salmonella growth.
text: Receptor molecules play a crucial role in selective autophagy by connecting specific cargoes to the autophagosomal membranes, which are adorned with ubiquitin-like microtubule-associated protein light chain 3 (LC3) modifiers. Despite the identification of several autophagy receptors, little is understood about the mechanisms that govern their functions in living organisms. In this study, we discovered that the phosphorylation of an autophagy receptor called optineurin promotes the selective autophagy of cytosolic Salmonella enterica coated with ubiquitin. The protein kinase TANK binding kinase 1 (TBK1) phosphorylates optineurin at serine-177, thereby increasing its affinity for LC3 and facilitating the autophagic clearance of cytosolic Salmonella. Conversely, optineurin mutants that cannot bind to ubiquitin or LC3, as well as the silencing of optineurin or TBK1, hindered Salmonella autophagy, leading to an escalation in intracellular bacterial proliferation. Based on our findings, we propose that the phosphorylation of autophagy receptors may serve as a general mechanism for regulating cargo-selective autophagy.

title: PKD1 Inhibits AMPKα2 through Phosphorylation of Serine 491 and Impairs Insulin Signaling in Skeletal Muscle Cells.
text: The activity of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses energy levels, is inhibited in cases of insulin resistance. Recent research has shown that exposure to high levels of glucose increases the phosphorylation of AMPK at Ser(485/491) of its α1/α2 subunit. However, the mechanism behind this increase is not yet understood. Diacylglycerol (DAG), which is also elevated in muscle exposed to high glucose, activates several signaling molecules including protein kinase (PK)C and PKD1. Our objective was to determine whether PKC or PKD1 is involved in the inhibition of AMPK by causing phosphorylation at Ser(485/491) in skeletal muscle cells. We treated C2C12 myotubes with the PKC/D1 activator phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), which acts as a DAG mimic. This treatment resulted in dose- and time-dependent increases in AMPK Ser(485/491) phosphorylation, leading to a ∼60% decrease in AMPKα2 activity. Expression of a mutant form of AMPKα2 (S491A) that cannot be phosphorylated prevented the reduction in AMPK activity induced by PMA. The phosphorylation and inhibition of AMPK were partially prevented by the broad PKC inhibitor Gö6983 and fully prevented by the specific PKD1 inhibitor CRT0066101. Knocking down PKD1 genetically also prevented the phosphorylation of AMPK at Ser(485/491). Inhibition of previously identified kinases that phosphorylate AMPK at this site (Akt, S6K, and ERK) did not prevent these events. PMA treatment also impaired insulin signaling through Akt, but this was prevented by PKD1 inhibition. Finally, in cell-free conditions, recombinant PKD1 phosphorylated AMPKα2 at Ser(491). These findings reveal that PKD1 is a novel upstream kinase of AMPKα2 Ser(491) that negatively affects insulin signaling in muscle cells.

title: Accuracy of ICD-9-CM codes for identifying cardiovascular and stroke risk factors.
text:
Our objective was to determine which ICD-9-CM codes in Medicare Part A data can identify cardiovascular and stroke risk factors. We conducted a cross-sectional study comparing ICD-9-CM data to structured medical record reviews from 23,657 Medicare beneficiaries aged 20 to 105 years who had atrial fibrillation. Quality improvement organizations used standardized abstraction instruments to assess the presence of 9 cardiovascular and stroke risk factors. We used the chart abstractions as the gold standard to evaluate the accuracy of ICD-9-CM codes in identifying these risk factors. 

The results showed that ICD-9-CM codes for all risk factors had high specificity (>0.95) but low sensitivity (< or =0.76). The positive predictive values were greater than 0.95 for 5 common, chronic risk factors: coronary artery disease, stroke/transient ischemic attack, heart failure, diabetes, and hypertension. Valvular heart disease, the sixth common risk factor, had a positive predictive value of 0.93. For all 6 common risk factors, negative predictive values ranged from 0.52 to 0.91. 

The rare risk factors- arterial peripheral embolus, intracranial hemorrhage, and deep venous thrombosis- had high negative predictive value (> or =0.98) but moderate positive predictive values (range, 0.54-0.77) in this population. 

In conclusion, using ICD-9-CM codes alone, heart failure, coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypertension, and stroke can be identified, but not necessarily ruled out. When possible, additional data such as physician notes or imaging studies should be reviewed to confirm the diagnosis of valvular disease, arterial peripheral embolus, intracranial hemorrhage, and deep venous thrombosis.

title: Modulation of cellular and viral promoters by mutant human p53 proteins found in tumor cells.
text:
Recent studies have demonstrated that wild-type p53 can suppress transcription from various cellular and viral promoters. Given that p53 mutations are commonly observed genetic abnormalities in human cancers, it is crucial to investigate the impact of these mutations on promoter functions. In this study, we examined the effects of both wild-type and mutant human p53 on the promoter of the human proliferating-cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), as well as several viral promoters, such as those of herpes simplex virus type 1 UL9, human cytomegalovirus major immediate-early, Rous sarcoma virus, and human T-cell lymphotropic virus type I. 

To assess the influence of p53 mutations on promoter activity, HeLa cells were co-transfected with an expression vector containing either wild-type or mutant p53, along with a plasmid carrying a reporter gene (chloramphenicol acetyltransferase) under the control of viral or cellular promoters. As expected, the expression of wild-type p53 suppressed promoter function. However, the expression of p53 mutants with amino acid substitutions at positions 175, 248, 273, or 281 resulted in a significant increase in PCNA promoter activity (2- to 11-fold). The viral promoters also exhibited activation, albeit to a lesser extent. 

Furthermore, we demonstrated that the activation by mutant p53 requires a minimal promoter containing only a TATA box. Notably, a more substantial increase (25-fold) in activation was observed when the promoter contained a binding site for the activating transcription factor or cyclic AMP response element-binding protein. Using p53-deficient Saos-2 cells, we confirmed that the activation by mutant p53 is a direct enhancement. Importantly, the mutant p53 forms utilized in this study are commonly found in various cancer cells. The activation of PCNA by these mutant p53s suggests a potential mechanism for increasing cell proliferation. Thus, our findings indicate a possible functional role for p53 mutants in cancer cells, as they activate several critical loci, including PCNA.

title: Valvular interstitial cells suppress calcification of valvular endothelial cells.
text:
BACKGROUND Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is the most prevalent heart valve disease in the Western world. Our previous research suggested that valvular endothelial cells (VECs) replenish damaged adult valve leaflets through a process called endothelial-to-mesenchymal transformation (EndMT). However, it is unclear whether EndMT contributes to valvular calcification. We hypothesized that aortic VECs undergo osteogenic differentiation through EndMT, and that this process can be inhibited by valvular interstitial cells (VICs).

APPROACH AND RESULTS We observed that VEC clones underwent TGF-β1-mediated EndMT, as evidenced by significantly increased mRNA expression of EndMT markers α-SMA, MMP-2, and Slug compared to unstimulated controls. To investigate the effects of VICs on VEC EndMT, we derived clonal populations of VICs from the same valve leaflets, co-cultured them with VECs, and grew them in control or TGF-β1 supplemented media. In the presence of VICs, EndMT was inhibited, as indicated by decreased mRNA expression of α-SMA, MMP-2, and Slug. When cultured in osteogenic media, VECs exhibited osteogenic changes, confirmed by an increase in mRNA expression of osteocalcin, osteopontin, and Runx2. However, the presence of VICs inhibited VEC osteogenesis, as evidenced by decreased expression of osteocalcin and osteopontin. Time course analysis suggested that EndMT precedes osteogenesis, with an initial increase in α-SMA and MMP-2 followed by an increase in osteopontin and osteocalcin.

CONCLUSIONS These findings suggest that EndMT may occur before VEC osteogenesis. Our study demonstrates that VICs inhibit VEC EndMT and osteogenesis, highlighting the importance of VEC-VIC interactions in maintaining valve homeostasis.

title: The HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor simvastatin activates the protein kinase Akt and promotes angiogenesis in normocholesterolemic animals.
text: New research suggests that statins have the ability to protect blood vessels, regardless of their ability to lower lipid levels. In our study, we discovered that statins quickly activate a protein kinase called Akt/PKB in endothelial cells. As a result, simvastatin, a type of statin, increased the phosphorylation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), a natural substrate of Akt. This activation inhibited cell death and sped up the formation of blood vessel structures in laboratory settings, relying on Akt for its effects. Similar to the effects of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) treatment, both simvastatin administration and increased Akt signaling in the endothelium promoted the growth of new blood vessels in ischemic limbs of rabbits with normal cholesterol levels. Therefore, the activation of Akt is a potential mechanism behind some of the positive side effects of statins, such as the promotion of blood vessel growth.

title: Varenicline, an alpha4beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor partial agonist, selectively decreases ethanol consumption and seeking.
text: Alcohol dependence is a widespread disease affecting millions of people worldwide. While there have been advancements in pharmacotherapy for those dependent on alcohol, there is still a crucial need for the development of new and additional therapeutic approaches. It is common for alcohol and nicotine to be abused together, and research indicates that neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) play a role in both alcohol and nicotine dependence. Varenicline, a partial agonist at the alpha4beta2 nAChRs, has been shown to reduce nicotine intake and has recently been approved as a smoking cessation aid. In our study, we investigated the impact of varenicline on ethanol consumption and seeking using three different animal models of drinking. Our findings demonstrate that when varenicline was administered in doses known to reduce nicotine reward, it selectively decreased ethanol seeking but not sucrose seeking in animals using an operant self-administration drinking paradigm. Additionally, in animals that had been chronically exposed to ethanol for two months prior to varenicline treatment, acute administration of varenicline reduced voluntary ethanol consumption but not water consumption. Furthermore, chronic administration of varenicline decreased ethanol consumption without causing a rebound increase in ethanol intake when varenicline was discontinued. These results suggest that the alpha4beta2 nAChRs may play a role in ethanol-seeking behaviors in animals with chronic ethanol exposure. The specific reduction in ethanol consumption by varenicline, along with its reported safety profile and minimal side effects in humans, indicates that varenicline may hold promise as a treatment for alcohol dependence.

title: Targeting TLR4 signaling by TLR4 Toll/IL-1 receptor domain-derived decoy peptides: identification of the TLR4 Toll/IL-1 receptor domain dimerization interface.
text: The initiation of intracellular signaling in TLR4 Toll/IL-1R (TIR) domains is triggered by the dimerization induced by agonists. Therefore, it is crucial to identify the interface responsible for TLR4-TIR dimerization in order to develop therapeutics that can block TLR4 signaling. To achieve this, a collection of decoy peptides that can penetrate cells was designed. Each peptide represents a complete patch of the TLR4 TIR surface. Additionally, these peptides were synthesized together with a cell-permeating Antennapedia homeodomain sequence. The peptides were then tested to determine their ability to inhibit early cytokine mRNA expression and MAPK activation in primary murine macrophages stimulated with LPS. Out of the five peptides tested (4R1, 4R3, 4BB, 4R9, and 4αE), all effectively inhibited TLR4 signaling, but not TLR2 signaling. To investigate their direct binding to TLR4 TIR, Förster resonance energy transfer was used with time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy. The results showed that Bodipy-TMR-X-labeled 4R1, 4BB, and 4αE reduced the fluorescence of TLR4-Cerulean expressed in HeLa or HEK293T cells. 4R3 exhibited partial activity, while 4R9 had the least activity. These findings suggest that the region between the BB loop of TLR4 and its fifth helical region is responsible for TLR4 TIR dimerization. Furthermore, this study provides direct evidence for the effectiveness of the decoy peptide approach. This approach involves initially testing peptides that represent different surface-exposed segments of a protein to inhibit its function. Then, the specific targets of these peptides are identified using Förster resonance energy transfer to define recognition sites in signaling proteins. These sites can be targeted therapeutically to disrupt transient protein interactions and their functions.

title: A paediatric case of sideroblastic anaemia. Ultrastructural studies of erythroblasts cultured from marrow BFU-E in a methylcellulose micromethod.
text: We analyzed the physical and functional traits of erythroblasts obtained from marrow erythroid progenitor cells that were cultivated in a methylcellulose microculture. These cells were taken from a young girl with a rare form of atypical sideroblastic anemia (SA) that only partially responded to pyridoxine. In three consecutive cultures, the formation of colonies was within the normal range (median values: 82.25 CFU-E and 16.4 BFU-E derived colonies/6.6 X 10(4) cells) compared to the growth of normal cells (65-315 CFU-E and 9-40 BFU-E). We assessed the differentiation of these cells in vitro by conducting a biochemical microassay on a cytosol enzyme involved in the production of hemoglobin: uroporphyrinogen I synthase (UROS). The UROS levels in the erythroid colonies from SA marrow were at the lower end of the normal range (median values: 6.7 +/- 0.3 and 14.4 +/- 3.8 pmol uroporphyrinogen/h in CFU-E and BFU-E-derived colonies respectively, compared to 17.4 +/- 7.3 and 25 +/- 7.2 pmol/h in CFU-E and BFU-E colonies from healthy individuals). When we examined the SA erythroblasts from non-cultured bone marrow or those derived from cultured BFU-E under an electron microscope, we observed the characteristic accumulation of iron in mitochondria surrounding the nucleus of most cells (known as ringed sideroblasts). However, the majority of cultured cells displayed significant dyserythropoietic features, including a high number of bilobulated or trilobulated erythroblasts, multiple cytoplasmic vacuoles, numerous abnormalities in the nucleus, and excessive membrane material beneath the plasma membrane. These features were difficult to observe in non-cultured marrows.

title: Innate lymphoid cells: emerging insights in development, lineage relationships, and function.
text: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are a type of immune cells that do not have a specific antigen receptor. However, they are capable of producing a wide range of effector cytokines, similar to T helper cell subsets. ILCs play important roles in various biological processes such as lymphoid organogenesis, tissue remodeling, antimicrobial immunity, and inflammation, especially at barrier surfaces. Their ability to quickly respond to stress-causing microbes suggests that ILCs are crucial in the initial line of defense in the immune system. In this review, we will examine the current data on the developmental requirements, lineage relationships, and effector functions of two families of ILCs: (a) Rorγt-expressing cells involved in the formation of lymphoid tissues, mucosal immunity, and inflammation, and (b) type 2 ILCs that are essential for immunity against helminths. Additionally, we will discuss the potential roles of ILCs in the development of immune-mediated inflammatory and infectious diseases, including allergies.

title: No net renal extraction of homocysteine in fasting humans.
text:
The underlying mechanism of hyperhomocysteinemia in chronic renal failure in humans is not yet understood. It has been suggested that the absence of homocysteine extraction in the kidneys may be a contributing factor, as significant homocysteine uptake has been observed in the kidneys of healthy rats. To investigate this further, we examined homocysteine extraction in the kidneys of normal human subjects. 

In our study, we measured both total (free and protein-bound) and free homocysteine levels in the blood of 20 fasting patients with normal kidney function. Blood samples were taken from the aorta and the right-side renal vein during cardiac catheterization. We calculated renal homocysteine extraction by dividing the arteriovenous difference by the arterial levels and multiplying by 100%. 

Our findings revealed that there was no significant renal extraction of homocysteine in either the total or free form. The percentages were as follows: 0.9% (SD 5.8; 95% CI -1.8 to +3.6) for total homocysteine and -0.2% (11.0; -5.4 to +4.9) for free homocysteine. 

Based on these results, we can conclude that there is no significant net renal uptake of homocysteine in fasting individuals with normal kidney function. Therefore, the absence of such uptake is not responsible for the development of hyperhomocysteinemia in patients with renal failure.

title: Traditional Chinese acupuncture in tension-type headache: a controlled study.
text: A total of thirty patients diagnosed with tension-type headache were selected at random to participate in a trial comparing traditional Chinese acupuncture and sham acupuncture. The severity of symptoms and response to treatment were evaluated using five measures: intensity, duration, and frequency of headache pain episodes, headache index, and analgesic intake.
