This report presents the baseline data for the 3,234 participants who were randomized into three treatment groups: intensive lifestyle modification, standard care plus metformin, and standard care plus placebo. 

The results show that among the participants, 55% were Caucasian, 20% were African-American, 16% were Hispanic, 5% were American Indian, and 4% were Asian-American. The average age at entry was 51 +/- 10.7 years, and 67.7% of the participants were women. Additionally, 16% were under 40 years old, and 20% were 60 years old or older. Among the women, 48% were postmenopausal. Men and women had similar rates of hypercholesterolemia (37% and 33%, respectively) and hypertension (29% and 26%, respectively). Based on fasting lipid measurements, 54% of men and 40% of women met the criteria for abnormal lipid profiles according to the National Cholesterol Education Program. More men than women were current or former smokers or had a history of coronary heart disease. Furthermore, 66% of men and 71% of women had a first-degree relative with diabetes. On average, the participants had a BMI of 34.0 +/- 6.7 kg/m2 at baseline, with 57% of men and 73% of women having a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. The average fasting plasma glucose levels (6.0 +/- 0.5 mmol/l) and HbA1c levels (5.9 +/- 0.5%) in men were similar to those in women (5.9 +/- 0.4 mmol/l and 5.9 +/- 0.5%, respectively). 

In conclusion, the DPP has successfully enrolled a diverse group of participants with varying ages, levels of obesity, and ethnic and racial backgrounds who are at a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. The study aims to investigate the impact of interventions on the development of diabetes.

title: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infections induce gastric mutations in mice.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of Helicobacter pylori infections in causing mutagenic events in gastric epithelial cells, as well as the potential genotoxic risk factor of a high-salt diet. Male mice were inoculated with either H. pylori or Helicobacter felis for 6 and 12 months. The frequency and types of mutations in the stomach were analyzed, along with the inflammatory host response and expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). After 6 months, mice infected with H. pylori had a 4-fold increase in gastric mutant frequency compared to uninfected mice, while mice infected with H. felis had a 1.7-fold increase. These mutations were primarily transversions resulting from oxidative damage. The infected mice also exhibited severe gastritis and high levels of iNOS expression. After 12 months, hyperplasia developed and both the mutagenic effects and iNOS expression decreased in the infected mice. There were no synergistic effects between a high-salt diet and Helicobacter infection on the frequency of gastric mutation. In conclusion, this study demonstrates a direct mutagenic effect of H. pylori infection in the Big Blue transgenic mouse model, which is likely caused by oxidative DNA damage and the resulting inflammatory response.

title: A minimal Tat system from a gram-positive organism: a bifunctional TatA subunit participates in discrete TatAC and TatA complexes.
text:
The Tat system is responsible for transporting folded proteins across bacterial and thylakoid membranes. In Gram-negative organisms, it is believed that a TatABC substrate-binding complex and a separate TatA complex come together to create an active translocon, with all three subunits playing a crucial role in the translocation process. However, most Gram-positive organisms do not possess a tatB gene, indicating significant differences in organization and potentially in the way the system functions. 

In this study, we focused on investigating the Tat complexes encoded by the tatAdCd genes of Bacillus subtilis. When tatAdCd was expressed in a tat null mutant of Escherichia coli, we observed efficient export of a large Tat substrate called TorA, which contains a cofactor. This suggests that the tatAd gene has a dual function in B. subtilis, as it can complement the absence of either tatAE or tatB in E. coli mutants. 

Furthermore, we identified and characterized two distinct Tat complexes that have unique features. The first is a TatAdCd complex, which has a molecular weight of approximately 230 kDa and is considerably smaller than the TatABC complex found in E. coli (approximately 370 kDa on BN gels). The second complex is a separate TatAd complex, which has a molecular weight of approximately 270 kDa according to gel filtration chromatography. This is in stark contrast to the highly heterogeneous TatA complex in E. coli, which can range in size from approximately 50 kDa to over 600 kDa. The heterogeneity of TatA has been associated with the varying sizes of the Tat substrates being translocated. However, the unique nature of the TatAd complex in B. subtilis suggests that discrete TatAC and TatA complexes may come together to form a single translocon.

title: A systemic granulomatous response to Schistosoma mansoni eggs alters responsiveness of bone-marrow-derived macrophages to Toll-like receptor agonists.
text: Macrophages play a crucial role in both the innate and acquired immune responses to Schistosoma mansoni. These cells can be activated into either a classical (M1) or alternative (M2) state, which determines their function in either causing tissue damage through innate immunity or promoting fibrotic remodeling. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether the systemic Th2-type cytokine polarization induced by S. mansoni affects the differentiation and activation of macrophages. To do this, we examined macrophages derived from the bone marrow of mice with S. mansoni egg-induced pulmonary granulomas, as well as macrophages from unchallenged (or naïve) mice. We assessed their activation state and their response to specific Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonists, including S. mansoni egg antigens. We found that macrophages from Th2-polarized mice expressed significantly higher levels of "found in inflammatory zone-1" (FIZZ1) and ST2 (M2 markers), while showing significantly lower levels of NO synthase 2, CCL3, MIP-2, TNF-alpha, and IL-12 (M1 markers), compared to naïve macrophages. Additionally, Th2-polarized macrophages exhibited enhanced responses to specific TLR agonists, leading to increased gene and protein levels of both M2 and M1 markers in these cells. These findings demonstrate that the signals received by bone marrow precursors during S. mansoni egg-induced granuloma responses can dynamically alter the development of macrophages and enhance their responsiveness to TLR activation, potentially influencing the pulmonary granulomatous response.

title: Orai1 and STIM reconstitute store-operated calcium channel function.
text: The functional interaction between the membrane proteins STIM1 and Orai1, which are essential for the activation of store-operated channels (SOC), remains unknown. However, our study demonstrates that when expressed together, STIM1 and Orai1 can reconstitute functional SOCs. When expressed alone, Orai1 significantly reduces store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) in human embryonic kidney 293 cells and the Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) current (I(CRAC)) in rat basophilic leukemia cells. However, when coexpressed with the store-sensing STIM1 protein, Orai1 leads to a substantial increase in SOCE, enhancing the rate of Ca(2+) entry by up to 103-fold. This entry is solely dependent on the presence of stored Ca(2+), as coexpression does not result in any measurable store-independent Ca(2+) entry. Furthermore, this entry can be completely blocked by the SOC blocker, 2-aminoethoxydiphenylborate. Coexpression of Orai1 and STIM1 also significantly enhances CRAC channel function in rat basophilic leukemia cells. STIM2, a closely related protein to STIM1, inhibits SOCE when expressed alone, but when coexpressed with Orai1, it leads to substantial constitutive (store-independent) Ca(2+) entry. STIM proteins are known to mediate Ca(2+) store-sensing and endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane coupling, but they do not possess intrinsic channel properties. Our findings demonstrate a significant increase in SOC function when both Orai1 and STIM1 are present, suggesting that Orai1 contributes to the plasma membrane channel component responsible for Ca(2+) entry. The suppression of SOC function by overexpression of Orai1 likely indicates the importance of a specific stoichiometry between STIM1 and Orai1.

title: Tet and TDG mediate DNA demethylation essential for mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition in somatic cell reprogramming.
text: The functional role of Tet-mediated DNA oxidation, a recently discovered epigenetic modification in mammals, is not well understood in cell-fate transitions. In this study, we investigate the reprogramming capacity of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) lacking all three Tet genes, into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Our results demonstrate that Tet-deficient MEFs cannot be reprogrammed due to a block in the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) step. Similarly, reprogramming is impaired in MEFs deficient in TDG. This block in reprogramming is partially caused by the defective activation of crucial miRNAs, which relies on oxidative demethylation facilitated by Tet and TDG. Restoring the affected miRNAs or reintroducing catalytically active Tet and TDG rescues reprogramming in the knockout MEFs. Therefore, oxidative demethylation, necessary for gene activation, is functionally essential for fibroblast reprogramming to pluripotency. These findings provide valuable insights into the role of epigenetic barriers in cell-lineage conversion.

title: The last and the next hundred years of malariology.
text: The pioneers of malariology were a remarkable group of individuals who possessed scientific innovation, unwavering dedication to research, strong personalities, diverse interests, and a genuine concern for society. Despite significant advancements in research and comprehension over the past century, malaria continues to burden the world heavily. To make progress in the next century, research must embrace specialization while also adopting a holistic approach, necessitating collaborative efforts from multidisciplinary teams. The dynamic nature of malaria, influenced by environmental changes and interventions, has replaced the static patterns of the past. Research has delved into various cycles of the parasite's life, examining them at microscopic, biochemical, and genomic levels, as well as quantifying epidemiological cycles for control purposes. Recent developments include the identification of stage-specific antigens, the consideration of disease cycles rather than just parasites, the study of parasite populations instead of individual cases, and the exploration of genetic variations within the parasite-human host-vector triad. This volume presents a comprehensive overview of the biomedical aspects of fundamental malariology, highlighting the interconnected population genetics of malaria parasites, anophelines, and humans. It offers a cohesive model for addressing the pressing biological challenges of drug resistance, vaccine development, insecticidal and net control, and can contribute, alongside socio-economic research, to the ongoing efforts in disease control. Advancements in understanding the spatial and temporal changes of malaria on a large scale enable us to accurately predict the effects of local and global environmental changes and anticipate epidemics. Future research will focus on bridging the gaps between these different levels of understanding, just as control efforts will aim to connect various levels of the healthcare system. The dire situation in impoverished holoendemic countries also demands practical support, similar to the involvement of the founding fathers of malariology. A comprehensive understanding must inform the new control initiatives, starting with Roll Back Malaria, for the next century.

title: Activation of AMP-activated protein kinase suppresses oxidized low-density lipoprotein-induced macrophage proliferation.
text: The progression of atherosclerosis is influenced by foam cells derived from macrophages. In a previous study, we found that the expression of granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which is dependent on ERK1/2, plays a crucial role in the proliferation of macrophages induced by oxidized low density lipoprotein (Ox-LDL). In this study, we aimed to investigate whether the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) could inhibit macrophage proliferation. We assessed the proliferation of mouse peritoneal macrophages induced by Ox-LDL using [(3)H]thymidine incorporation and cell counting assays. We observed that the AMPK activator 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleoside (AICAR) significantly inhibited proliferation, and this effect was reversed by dominant-negative AMPKalpha1, indicating that AMPK activation suppresses macrophage proliferation. AICAR also partially suppressed Ox-LDL-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation and GM-CSF expression, suggesting the involvement of another mechanism in the AICAR-mediated suppression of macrophage proliferation. AICAR suppressed GM-CSF-induced macrophage proliferation without affecting p38 MAPK/Akt signaling. GM-CSF suppressed the phosphorylation and expression of p53 and induced Rb phosphorylation. Overexpression of p53 or p27(kip) suppressed GM-CSF-induced macrophage proliferation. AMPK activation by AICAR induced cell cycle arrest, increased p53 phosphorylation and expression, and suppressed GM-CSF-induced Rb phosphorylation. Furthermore, AICAR activated AMPK, leading to the expression of p21(cip) and p27(kip), and the suppression of macrophage proliferation was restored by small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting p21(cip) and p27(kip). In conclusion, AMPK activation inhibits Ox-LDL-induced macrophage proliferation by suppressing GM-CSF expression and inducing cell cycle arrest. These findings suggest that targeting AMPK activation could be a potential therapeutic approach for treating atherosclerosis.

title: Evaluation of cortical bone by peripheral quantitative computed tomography in renal transplant recipients.
text:
BACKGROUND: Renal transplant patients have a threefold higher risk of fractures compared to matched controls. The majority of these fractures affect the peripheral bones, indicating a greater compromise of cortical bone. Peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) is a novel imaging technique that allows for separate evaluations of cortical and trabecular bones. In this study, we used pQCT to assess cortical bone in 12 renal transplant patients (seven men and five women) and compared them to 27 normal controls.

METHODS: We performed pQCT scans on the distal radius of the non-dominant forearm using the XCT 960 system (Stratec, Pforheim, Germany). We measured total and cortical bone mineral density (TBMD, cBMD), total and cortical area (TA, cA), cortical thickness (cThk), endosteal and periosteal circumferences, and the buckling ratio (r/cThK).

RESULTS: Compared to normal controls, the transplant patients as a whole showed a significant increase in TA, endosteal circumference (P < .001), and the buckling ratio (P < .001), along with a significant reduction in cThK (P < .001). Female patients exhibited a marked decrease in cA (51.4 vs 69.3 [pixel n]; P < .0001) and cThK (2.08 vs 2.78 mm; P < .0001). Male patients also had a decrease in cThK (2.54 vs 3.30 mm; P = .0001) and an increase in endosteal perimeter (31.2 vs 26.4 mm; P < .0001). The total time on dialysis prior to renal graft correlated negatively with cortical thickness (r = .62; P < .01).

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that the significant thinning of cortical bone may explain the higher incidence of peripheral fractures among renal transplant patients.

title: Ataxia, dementia, and hypogonadotropism caused by disordered ubiquitination.
text:
BACKGROUND
Over a century ago, the combination of ataxia and hypogonadism was first described, but its genetic basis has remained unknown.

METHODS
To investigate this, we conducted whole-exome sequencing in a patient with ataxia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. We then performed targeted sequencing of candidate genes in other patients with similar symptoms. Detailed characterization of neurologic and reproductive endocrine phenotypes was carried out. Additionally, we tested the effects of sequence variants and the presence of an epistatic interaction in a zebrafish model.

RESULTS
In a consanguineous family, we discovered digenic homozygous mutations in RNF216 and OTUD4, which encode a ubiquitin E3 ligase and a deubiquitinase, respectively. These mutations were found in three affected siblings. Further screening revealed compound heterozygous truncating mutations in RNF216 in an unrelated patient, as well as single heterozygous deleterious mutations in four other patients. In zebrafish embryos, knockdown of rnf216 or otud4 resulted in defects in the eye, optic tectum, and cerebellum. Combining the suppression of both genes worsened these phenotypes, which were rescued by nonmutant, but not mutant, human RNF216 or OTUD4 messenger RNA. All patients exhibited progressive ataxia and dementia. Neuronal loss was observed in cerebellar pathways and the hippocampus, with surviving hippocampal neurons containing ubiquitin-immunoreactive intranuclear inclusions. Defects were also detected at the hypothalamic and pituitary levels of the reproductive endocrine axis.

CONCLUSIONS
Our findings demonstrate that inactivating mutations in RNF216 or a combination of mutations in RNF216 and OTUD4 can cause the syndrome of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, ataxia, and dementia. These results establish a link between disordered ubiquitination and neurodegeneration and reproductive dysfunction. Furthermore, they highlight the effectiveness of whole-exome sequencing in combination with functional studies for uncovering genetic interactions that contribute to disease. (This research was funded by the National Institutes of Health and others.)

title: Combination cancer immunotherapies tailored to the tumour microenvironment
text: Evidence suggests that in the near future, cancer immunotherapy will play a significant role in the treatment plans for many patients with various types of cancer. There are multiple immune processes involving different types of cells that either fight against or promote tumor growth, and tumor cells employ various strategies to evade the immune response. The tumor microenvironment plays a crucial role in determining which pathways suppress the immune system's ability to fight against the tumor. This includes the activation of immune checkpoint receptors on certain cells and the release of substances that inhibit the immune response. Therapeutic approaches that target these pathways, particularly immune checkpoint receptors, have shown promising results in patients with advanced-stage cancers like melanoma. However, not all patients respond well to these monotherapy approaches, and alternative strategies are needed to achieve the best therapeutic outcomes. These strategies involve eliminating the majority of tumor cells to trigger the release of tumor antigens and enhance the function of antigen-presenting cells. Additionally, adjuvants can be used to boost the function of antigen-presenting cells, and agents that enhance the activity of effector cells can also be employed. In this review, we explore how the tumor microenvironment can be categorized based on the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression within the tumor. This categorization allows for the development of personalized combination cancer therapies that target specific tumor microenvironments.

title: Cyclic AMP-dependent phosphorylation of thromboxane A(2) receptor-associated Galpha(13).
text: Although it is widely known that cAMP can inhibit platelet activation caused by various agonists, we have discovered that the thromboxane A(2) signal transduction pathway is particularly sensitive to this inhibition. As a result, we decided to investigate whether cAMP-dependent kinase plays a role in phosphorylating the thromboxane A(2) receptor-G-protein complex. Our findings revealed that cAMP induces the labeling of solubilized membrane proteins in the Galpha subunits region (38-45 kDa) with [gamma-(32)P]ATP, and these phosphoproteins co-purify with thromboxane A(2) receptors during ligand affinity chromatography purification. By immunoprecipitating the eluate from the affinity column with a Galpha(13) antibody, we observed that 8-Br-cAMP increased the phosphorylation of thromboxane A(2) receptor-associated Galpha(13) by 87 +/- 27%. Additionally, when we immunopurified Galpha(13) using microtiter wells coated with a different Galpha(13) antibody, we found that 8-Br-cAMP increased Galpha(13) phosphorylation by 53 +/- 19%. Finally, we treated (32)P-labeled whole platelets with prostacyclin and observed a 90 +/- 14% increase in phosphorylated Galpha(13), which was reversed by pretreatment with the adenylate cyclase inhibitor MDL-12. These results provide the initial evidence that protein kinase A is responsible for phosphorylating Galpha(13) both in vitro and in vivo, and they explain why cAMP preferentially inhibits thromboxane A(2)-mediated signaling in platelets.

title: Tet proteins can convert 5-methylcytosine to 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine.
text: The presence of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) in DNA is crucial for regulating gene expression, genomic imprinting, and suppressing transposable elements. The Tet (ten eleven translocation) proteins have the ability to convert 5mC into 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC). In addition to 5hmC, our research demonstrates that the Tet proteins can also produce two other derivatives of cytosine, namely 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC), through an enzymatic process. We have discovered the presence of 5fC and 5caC in the genomic DNA of mouse embryonic stem cells and various mouse organs. By manipulating the expression levels of Tet proteins, we can increase or decrease the amounts of 5hmC, 5fC, and 5caC in the genome. This discovery unveils two previously unknown cytosine derivatives in genomic DNA that are generated by Tet proteins. Our findings suggest that DNA demethylation may occur through a process involving oxidation catalyzed by Tet proteins, followed by decarboxylation.

title: Long-term use of aspirin and age-related macular degeneration.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between regular aspirin use and the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The study was conducted over a 20-year period and involved participants from the Beaver Dam Eye Study in Wisconsin. The participants, aged 43 to 86 years, underwent examinations every 5 years. They were asked about their regular use of aspirin, defined as at least twice a week for more than 3 months, at subsequent examinations. The main outcome measures were the incidence of early AMD, late AMD, and two subtypes of late AMD (neovascular AMD and pure geographic atrophy), assessed through retinal photographs using the Wisconsin Age-Related Maculopathy Grading System. 

The study found that regular aspirin use 10 years prior to the retinal examination was associated with an increased risk of late AMD. The estimated incidence of late AMD was 1.76% in regular users and 1.03% in nonusers. Regular aspirin use 10 years prior was also significantly associated with neovascular AMD, but not pure geographic atrophy. However, aspirin use 5 years or 10 years prior to the retinal examination was not associated with incident early AMD. 

In conclusion, among the adult cohort studied, regular aspirin use 5 years prior to the observed incidence was not linked to the development of early or late AMD. However, regular aspirin use 10 years prior was associated with a small but statistically significant increase in the risk of late and neovascular AMD.

title: Growth control and ribosomopathies.
text: Ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis are two of the most energy-intensive processes in a growing cell. Additionally, any abnormalities in their molecular components can disrupt gene expression patterns. Consequently, cells have developed a surveillance system to monitor the condition of the translational machinery. The identification of causative mutations and gene deletions associated with ribosome biogenesis has led to the classification of a group of related disorders known as ribosomopathies. In the last ten years, significant progress has been made in understanding the connection between growth control and ribosome biogenesis. The discovery of additional functions of certain ribosome proteins outside of ribosomal activity, and their influence on p53 levels, has established a link between ribosome dysfunction and cell cycle regulation. However, there is also evidence suggesting the existence of p53 and/or Hdm2 independent pathways. This review provides a summary of recent advancements in comprehending the mechanisms underlying ribosomopathies and explores the relationship between ribosome production and tumorigenesis.

title: Tunable signal processing through modular control of transcription factor translocation.
text: We investigated the various ways in which signaling pathways can trigger the activation of transcription factors (TFs). Our focus was on understanding how TFs interpret signals to produce different dynamic responses. In our study, we observed that the TF Msn2, which is responsible for responding to general stress in budding yeast, acts as a flexible signal processor. It has the ability to track, filter, or combine signals depending on the input it receives. This adaptability in signal processing is achieved through the dual regulation of nuclear import and export via phosphorylation. Mutants lacking one form of regulation only retained one signal-processing function. The versatility of Msn2 in processing signals is essential for generating distinct dynamic responses to various natural stresses. Our research sheds light on the integration of complex signal-processing functions within a single molecule and offers insights for designing TFs with customizable signal-processing capabilities.

title: Killing by bactericidal antibiotics does not depend on reactive oxygen species.
text: The conventional belief that bactericidal antibiotics kill by modulating their specific targets has been challenged by recent studies proposing an alternative, unified mechanism of killing. According to this mechanism, toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated in the presence of antibiotics. However, our research found no connection between an individual cell's likelihood of survival in the presence of antibiotics and its ROS levels. Interestingly, we discovered that an ROS quencher called thiourea protected cells from antibiotics even at low concentrations, but this effect was observed even under anaerobic conditions. Surprisingly, there was no significant difference in the survival of bacteria treated with different antibiotics under aerobic or anaerobic conditions. These findings suggest that ROS do not play a role in the killing of bacterial pathogens by antibiotics.

title: A naturally occurring mouse model of X-linked congenital stationary night blindness.
text:
The purpose of this study is to describe a naturally occurring mutation called nob, which is an X-linked recessive mutation that affects visual transmission in mice. The researchers used various methods to investigate this mutation, including recording the electroretinogram (ERG) to assess the light-evoked response of the retina and recording cortical potentials with a scalp electrode to evaluate visual transmission. The inheritance pattern of the nob mutation was determined through breeding experiments. Additionally, the researchers performed retinal histologic analysis using light microscopy. 

The results of the study showed that while the photoreceptor-mediated ERG component (a-wave) was normal in nob mice, the major response component reflecting postreceptoral neuronal activity (b-wave) was absent. Furthermore, visually-driven cortical activity was abnormal in nob mice. However, the nob retina appeared to have a normal cytoarchitecture when examined under a light microscope. 

Based on these findings, the researchers concluded that the nob mutation disrupts the transmission of visual information through the retina. They also suggested that these mice could serve as a valuable model for studying outer retinal synaptic function. Additionally, the nob mutant mouse may be a useful animal model for studying congenital stationary night blindness, a human disorder characterized by a severe loss of rod-mediated visual sensitivity.

title: Differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells and embryonic stem cells into steroidogenic cells using steroidogenic factor-1 and liver receptor homolog-1.
text: In previous studies, we have shown that mesenchymal stem cells can be transformed into steroidogenic cells by using steroidogenic factor-1 and 8bromo-cAMP treatment. We also found that the use of liver receptor homolog-1, another member of the nuclear receptor 5A family, along with 8bromo-cAMP, can induce the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells into cells that produce steroid hormones. However, these approaches cannot be applied to other undifferentiated cells like embryonic stem cells or embryonal carcinoma cells, as the over-expression of the nuclear receptor 5A family is toxic to these cells. To overcome this limitation, we developed embryonic stem cells that carry a tetracycline-regulated steroidogenic factor-1 gene at the ROSA26 locus. We first differentiated these embryonic stem cells into a mesenchymal cell lineage by culturing them on collagen IV-coated dishes and treating them with retinoic acid. Only after the expression of steroidogenic factor-1, the differentiated cells were able to convert into steroidogenic cells. These cells exhibited characteristics similar to adrenocortical cells and produced a significant amount of corticosterone. These findings demonstrate that pluripotent stem cells can be transformed into steroidogenic cells through the nuclear receptor 5A family, specifically via the mesenchymal cell lineage. This approach holds promise as a potential source of cells for gene therapy in diseases caused by steroidogenesis deficiencies.

title: Chronic daily headache. A clinical and psychological profile before and after treatment.
text: In order to evaluate the clinical and personality characteristics of patients with chronic daily headache before and after receiving treatment, a study was conducted on a sample of 20 patients. The patients were assessed using the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), specifically the abbreviated 356-item Italian version, and the Strait and Trait Anxiety Index 1,2 (STAI). The patients were divided into two groups: group 1 consisted of 6 patients with a "conversion V" configuration, characterized by elevated hypochondria and hysteria scales, while the depression scale was slightly lower. Group 2 included 13 patients with elevated depression and other MMPI scales. One patient did not show any scale elevation. Both groups exhibited high scores on the STAI 1,2. Almost all patients displayed various psychosomatic symptoms and some migraine features. The frequency, intensity, and duration of the headaches were regularly recorded, and the MMPI and STAI were administered again after the treatment. The results showed an improvement in headaches and a decrease in several MMPI and STAI 2 scores. However, 12 out of the 20 patients still exhibited a conversion V configuration after treatment. The findings suggest that chronic daily headache is often a manifestation of transformed migraine and is accompanied by anxiety in all patients and hysteric traits in some. Over time, these patients may develop a depressive disorder. Even after treatment, patients who initially displayed hysteric traits still exhibited them at a lower level, and those with depression may have their hysteric traits unmasked.

title: Potassium channel structure and function as reported by a single glycosylation sequon.
text: Inwardly rectifying K+ channels (IRKs) are integral membrane proteins that play a crucial role in maintaining the resting membrane potential and cell volume by selectively allowing the passage of K+ ions. These proteins are often N-glycosylated, with the attached carbohydrate located outside the cell and potentially influencing their function. However, the specific effects of glycosylation on IRKs at the molecular level have not been fully understood. ROMK1, a member of the IRK family, is an ideal candidate for studying glycosylation due to its single N-glycosylation consensus sequence. Previous research has demonstrated the expression of functional ROMK1 in the plasmalemma of an insect cell line (Spodoptera frugiperda, Sf9), and it exists in two forms: glycosylated and unglycosylated. To assess its functionality, glycosylation was eliminated through an N117Q mutation or treatment with tunicamycin. Both unglycosylated forms exhibited significantly reduced whole cell currents compared to the wild-type. Analysis of single channel currents revealed a significant decrease in the probability of channel opening as the underlying cause. These findings confirm that the N-glycosylation site is located outside the cell, supporting current topological models of IRKs. Furthermore, we conclude that the presence of carbohydrate at the N-glycosylation site stabilizes the open state of ROMK1.

title: Role of the novel Th17 cytokine IL-17F in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): upregulated colonic IL-17F expression in active Crohn's disease and analysis of the IL17F p.His161Arg polymorphism in IBD.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the role of interleukin (IL)-17F in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). The researchers examined the expression of IL-17F in the intestines and analyzed the effect of a specific genetic variation, IL17F p. His161Arg, on disease susceptibility and phenotype. They also investigated whether this genetic variation interacts with other known IBD-associated genetic variants.

The researchers measured the expression of IL-17F mRNA in inflamed and uninflamed intestinal tissues using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR). They found that IL-17F mRNA expression was significantly increased in inflamed colonic lesions in CD but not in UC. However, the overall expression of IL-17F mRNA was higher in UC compared to CD.

Next, the researchers analyzed the IL17F p. His161Arg genetic variation in a group of 1682 individuals, including CD patients, UC patients, and controls. They found that the frequency of this genetic variation was similar in IBD patients and controls, and it was not associated with a specific disease phenotype. However, they did observe a weak association between the IL17F p. His161Arg variation and a low body mass index (BMI) and earlier age of disease onset in UC.

Finally, the researchers investigated whether there was any interaction between the IL17F p. His161Arg variation and other known IBD-associated genetic variants, specifically variants in the IL23R and NOD2/CARD15 genes. They found no evidence of epistasis between the IL17F p. His161Arg variation and the CD-associated IL23R variants.

In conclusion, this study showed that IL-17F gene expression is increased in active CD, but not in UC. The IL17F p. His161Arg genetic variation is not associated with IBD susceptibility and does not interact with CD-associated IL23R variants.

title: Targeting brain cancer: advances in the molecular pathology of malignant glioma and medulloblastoma
text: Malignant brain tumors remain a significant cause of illness and death among various individuals. The two most prevalent types in adults and children, namely malignant glioma and medulloblastoma, have been extensively studied in the last twenty years. This research has greatly enhanced our understanding of their fundamental biology and how they develop. In this review, we will outline these advancements within the framework of molecular pathology and explore how they impact the development of innovative treatment approaches.

title: Rapid helper T-cell recovery above 200 × 106/l at 3 months correlates to successful transplant outcomes after allogeneic stem cell transplantation
text: The present study examines the significance of quantitatively measuring peripheral lymphocyte subsets, specifically the recovery of CD4+ helper T-cells, in predicting outcomes after allogeneic stem cell transplantation. A total of 69 recipients of allogeneic transplants were included, with the following diagnoses: 42 with acute myeloid leukemia, 5 with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, 15 with chronic myeloid leukemia, 5 with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, and 2 with high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. The counts of peripheral lymphocyte subsets (CD3+ T-cells, CD3+4+ helper T-cells, CD3+8+ cytotoxic T-cells, CD19+ B-cells, and CD56+ natural killer cells) were measured at 3, 6, and 12 months. The recovery of CD4+ helper T-cells at 3 months showed a strong correlation with overall survival (OS) (P<0.0001), non-relapse mortality (NRM) (P=0.0007), and opportunistic infections (P=0.0108) when the cutoff value was set at 200 × 106/l CD4+ helper T-cells. Rapid recovery of CD4+ helper T-cells was also associated with a higher transplant dose of CD4+ helper T-cells (P=0.006) and the type of donor (P<0.001). Early recovery of CD4+ helper T-cells at 3 months was correlated with a faster subsequent recovery of helper T-cells until 12 months, but not with B-cell recovery. In a multivariate analysis, rapid recovery of CD4+ helper T-cells at 3 months, along with a higher transplant dose of CD34+ cells, was found to be a favorable prognostic factor for OS (P=0.001) and NRM (P=0.005).

title: Generating an iPSC bank for HLA-matched tissue transplantation based on known donor and recipient HLA types.
text: The therapeutic potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is limited by the likelihood of immunological rejection due to Human Leukocyte Antigens (HLA) mismatch. However, we have discovered a solution. By utilizing a tissue bank consisting of 150 carefully chosen homozygous HLA-typed volunteers, we can successfully match 93% of the UK population while minimizing the need for immunosuppression. Our model offers a practical method for creating an iPSC stem cell bank by utilizing existing HLA-typed samples, eliminating the need to type a large number of individuals in the future.

title: Promiscuous gene expression and the developmental dynamics of medullary thymic epithelial cells.
text: The structural and functional microenvironment required for the development and quality control of the T cell repertoire is formed by thymic epithelial cells (TEC). These cells also serve as a source of tissue-restricted antigens (TRA) through promiscuous gene expression (pGE). However, the relationship between the regulation of pGE and the cell biology of TEC subsets, including their turnover and developmental interrelationship, is not well understood. It has been observed that pGE is primarily seen in mature medullary TEC (mTEC) that are phenotypically and functionally mature, suggesting that full implementation of pGE depends on mTEC differentiation. In this study, we demonstrate that the emergence of TEC subsets and pGE are closely linked during development, and we provide evidence that mature CD80pos mTEC develop from an immature CD80neg subset. This differentiation process occurs continuously in the postnatal thymus. While mature mTEC have a turnover rate of 2 to 3 weeks, immature mTEC have a smaller cycling pool and a larger non-cycling pool. The non-cycling pool may serve as a reservoir of committed precursors that sustain the renewal process. Our findings highlight the dynamic nature of the mTEC population and suggest that the availability and presentation of TRA in the thymus undergoes constant temporal and spatial reorganization.

title: Evaluation of HER-2/neu amplification and other biological markers as predictors of response to neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy in primary breast cancer: the role of anthracycline dose intensity.
text:
The effectiveness of anthracycline-based chemotherapy in relation to HER-2/neu status is still a topic of debate. We conducted a study to determine the role of HER-2/neu gene amplification and other biological markers in predicting response to different doses of neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy. We reviewed the medical records of 115 patients with primary breast cancer. Of these, 48 received high doses of anthracycline (doxorubicin > or =20 mg/m2/wk; epirubicin > or =30 mg/m2/wk) and 67 received moderate-low doses. Before starting neoadjuvant chemotherapy, we assessed the pathological diagnosis, hormonal receptor status (HR), Ki67, and HER-2/neu status of tumor samples. HER-2/neu status was determined using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). 

We found that HER-2/neu amplification was present in 29 out of 115 (25%) tumors, with 18 in the moderate-low-dose group and 11 in the high-dose group. In the univariate analysis, a high Ki67 index (> or =20%) and positive clinical axillary nodes were predictive of a positive tumor response (P = 0.033 and 0.001, respectively). However, in the multivariate analysis, only Ki67 was found to be a significant predictor of response (OR = 3.08, 95% CI = 1.1-8.5, P = 0.03). HER-2/neu status did not have a significant impact on predicting response to different anthracycline dose intensities. This finding was consistent when considering HR and Ki67 as well. 

In conclusion, our study did not find a significant relationship between HER-2/neu status and response to different doses of anthracycline-based chemotherapy.

title: Radioactive labeling of mitochondrial translation products in cultured cells.
text: The mammalian mitochondrial genome contains 37 genes, with 13 of them responsible for encoding polypeptide subunits in the enzyme complexes of the oxidative phosphorylation system. The remaining genes encode the necessary rRNAs and tRNAs for translation. The mitochondrial translation machinery is located in the mitochondrial matrix and is solely dedicated to synthesizing these 13 enzyme subunits. In humans, mitochondrial disease is often linked to defects in mitochondrial translation. This can result in a decrease in the overall rate of mitochondrial protein synthesis, a reduction in the synthesis of specific polypeptides, the production of abnormal polypeptides, or changes in the stability of certain translation products. To assess these alterations in mitochondrial translation, a simple technique can be employed that takes advantage of the mitochondrial translation machinery's resistance to antibiotics that completely inhibit cytoplasmic translation. By specifically labeling the mitochondrial translation products with radioactivity in cultured cells, the results can be observed on gradient gels. Analyzing mitochondrial translation in cells cultured from patient biopsies is valuable for studying disease-causing mutations in both the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

title: Caenorhabditis elegans cyclin A- and B-type genes: a cyclin A multigene family, an ancestral cyclin B3 and differential germline expression.
text:
We have successfully cloned cDNAs for three cyclins in Caenorhabditis elegans: cyclins A1, B, and B3. While cyclins A1 and B share close similarities with A- or B-type cyclins found in other species, cyclin B3 shows less resemblance to these cyclins. However, we have discovered that cyclin B3 is highly similar to the recently identified chicken cyclin B3. This finding suggests that cyclin B3 has been conserved throughout evolution. 

Cyclin A1 belongs to a multigene family of A-type cyclins. However, when examining northern blots, we found that the cyclin A1 cDNA only recognizes a single band. Similarly, the cyclin B3 cDNA also produces a single-sized RNA. In contrast, the cyclin B cDNA generates three different transcripts. 

Through our analysis using RNAs from germline-defective mutants and populations enriched for males, we have determined that one of the cyclin B transcripts is specific to the paternal germline. The other two cyclin B transcripts, as well as the cyclin A1 and cyclin B3 transcripts, are most abundant in the maternal germline and are only present at low levels in other tissues. 

Furthermore, we have discovered that the 3' untranslated regions of each Caenorhabditis cyclin cDNA contain multiple copies of potential translational control elements. These elements have been shown in Xenopus and Drosophila maternal cyclin mRNAs to play a role during oogenesis and early embryogenesis.

title: A comparison of pharmacological (amitriptyline HCL) and nonpharmacological (cognitive-behavioral) therapies for chronic tension headaches.
text: A total of 41 individuals who frequently experience tension headaches were randomly divided into two groups. One group received cognitive-behavioral therapy, which was administered primarily at home. The other group received amitriptyline therapy, with the dosage adjusted to 25, 50, or 75 mg/day based on individual needs. Both cognitive-behavioral therapy and amitriptyline showed significant improvements in reducing headache activity. Patient daily recordings indicated a 56% reduction in headache index for cognitive-behavioral therapy and a 27% reduction for amitriptyline. Neurologist ratings of clinical improvement showed that 94% of patients in the cognitive-behavioral therapy group and 69% in the amitriptyline group were rated as at least moderately improved. In certain aspects, such as headache index, somatic complaints, and perceptions of control over headache activity, cognitive-behavioral therapy had slightly better outcomes compared to amitriptyline. However, neither treatment completely eliminated headache problems.

title: Homeostasis model assessment: insulin resistance and β-cell function from fasting plasma glucose and insulin concentrations in man
text: The interaction between steady-state basal plasma glucose and insulin concentrations is responsible for their regulation in a feedback loop. A computer model has been utilized to predict the homeostatic concentrations resulting from varying levels of β-cell deficiency and insulin resistance. By comparing a patient's fasting values with the model's predictions, it is possible to quantitatively assess the contributions of insulin resistance and deficient β-cell function to fasting hyperglycemia using the homeostasis model assessment (HOMA). The accuracy and precision of this estimation have been evaluated by comparing it with independent measures of insulin resistance and β-cell function, such as hyperglycemic and euglycemic clamps, as well as an intravenous glucose tolerance test. The estimation of insulin resistance obtained through the homeostasis model assessment showed a strong correlation with estimates obtained through the euglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.88, p < 0.0001), fasting insulin concentration (Rs = 0.81, p < 0.0001), and hyperglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.69, p < 0.01). However, there was no correlation with any aspect of insulin-receptor binding. The estimation of deficient β-cell function obtained through the homeostasis model assessment correlated with the estimation derived from the hyperglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.61, p < 0.01) and the estimation from the intravenous glucose tolerance test (Rs = 0.64, p < 0.05). The precision of the estimates from the model was relatively low, with coefficients of variation of 31% for insulin resistance and 32% for β-cell deficit, which limits its usefulness. Nevertheless, the correlation between the model's estimates and patient data supports the hypothesis that basal glucose and insulin interactions are primarily determined by a simple feedback loop.

title: Clinical benefits and considerations of bisphosphonate treatment in metastatic bone disease.
text: Patients who have metastatic bone disease are at risk of experiencing skeletal-related events that can have a negative impact on their quality of life, leading to a loss of independence and functional abilities. Bisphosphonates have become an essential part of the treatment for patients with bone metastases as they can delay the onset and reduce the risk of skeletal-related events. They also provide relief from bone pain in various types of cancer, thereby preserving the patient's quality of life. Zoledronic acid has been proven to be effective and safe in treating bone lesions caused by breast cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, and other solid tumors, as well as in patients with multiple myeloma. Current research suggests that early treatment with zoledronic acid, even before the onset of bone pain, may offer additional clinical benefits and improve survival rates in certain groups of patients who have high levels of N-telopeptide of type I collagen (NTX), a biochemical marker of bone resorption. Studies have demonstrated that the majority of patients who received zoledronic acid experienced a normalization of their elevated NTX levels in breast cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, and other solid tumors. Moreover, the normalization of NTX values was associated with extended survival.

title: Distinct memory CD4+ T cells with commitment to T follicular helper- and T helper 1-cell lineages are generated after acute viral infection.
text: T cells known as CD4(+) T follicular helper (Tfh) cells play a crucial role in providing signals to B cells during germinal center reactions, which are necessary for the production of long-lasting antibodies. However, it is still unclear whether there are CD4(+) memory T cells that are specifically committed to the Tfh cell lineage once the antigen has been cleared. To investigate this, we conducted adoptive transfer experiments using antigen-specific memory CD4(+) T cell subpopulations in a model of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection. Our findings revealed the existence of distinct memory CD4(+) T cell populations that are committed to either the Tfh or Th1 cell lineages. We reached these conclusions by analyzing gene expression profiles, conducting epigenetic studies, and performing phenotypic and functional analyses. Our results suggest that CD4(+) memory T cells retain the memory of their previous effector lineage even after the antigen has been cleared, and they are primed to regain their lineage-specific effector functions upon encountering the antigen again. These findings have significant implications for the development of effective vaccines, as enhancing the generation and activation of memory Tfh cells could improve vaccine-induced protective immunity.

title: Control of synapse development and plasticity by Rho GTPase regulatory proteins
text:
Synapses are specialized connections between cells that facilitate communication between neurons. In the brain, most excitatory synapses are found on dendritic spines, which are small protrusions extending from dendrites and rich in actin. These spines undergo significant changes in shape and number during development and in response to environmental stimuli, which are believed to be important for processes like learning and memory. However, improper spine development can hinder information processing in the brain and is associated with various brain disorders. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms that regulate spine formation and plasticity, as well as the synapses within them, is crucial for our comprehension of cognition and disease.

Rho-family GTPases, which are key regulators of the actin cytoskeleton, play essential roles in coordinating the development and remodeling of spines and synapses. Precise control of Rho GTPase activity in terms of time and space is crucial for their proper functioning, as abnormal signaling can lead to spine and synapse defects, as well as cognitive impairments. Rho GTPases are activated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and inhibited by GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs). We propose that Rho-family GEFs and GAPs provide the necessary spatiotemporal regulation and signaling specificity for proper Rho GTPase function. This is supported by their multiple presence per Rho GTPase, regulated expression during development, specific localization, ability to organize specific signaling networks, and tightly controlled activity, potentially involving interactions between GEFs and GAPs. Recent studies have identified several Rho-family GEFs and GAPs that contribute uniquely to the formation of spines and synapses. In this article, we highlight some of these proteins and discuss how they occupy distinct biochemical niches that are critical for synaptic development.

title: Rate and molecular spectrum of spontaneous mutations in the bacterium Escherichia coli as determined by whole-genome sequencing.
text: Understanding the rate and characteristics of spontaneous mutations is crucial for comprehending evolutionary and molecular processes. In this study, we examine the accumulation of spontaneous mutations in wild-type Escherichia coli and a defective strain lacking mismatch repair (MMR), which is responsible for correcting replication errors, over numerous generations. The main findings are as follows: (i) the mutation rate in the wild-type E. coli strain is approximately 1 × 10(-3) per genome per generation; (ii) mutations in the wild-type strain exhibit the expected bias towards G:C > A:T mutations, but this bias shifts to A:T > G:C mutations in the absence of MMR; (iii) during replication, A:T > G:C transitions predominantly occur with A as the template on the lagging strand and T as the template on the leading strand, while G:C > A:T transitions predominantly occur with C as the template on the lagging strand and G as the template on the leading strand; (iv) there is a strong preference for transition mutations to occur at 5'ApC3'/3'TpG5' sites (where bases 5'A and 3'T are mutated) and, to a lesser extent, at 5'GpC3'/3'CpG5' sites (where bases 5'G and 3'C are mutated); (v) although the rate of small (≤4 nt) insertions and deletions is high in repeat sequences, these events occur at only 1/10th the genomic rate of base-pair substitutions. MMR activity is genetically regulated, and bacteria found in nature often lack MMR capacity, suggesting that modulation of MMR can be advantageous. Therefore, comparing the results from the wild-type and MMR-defective strains may provide a deeper understanding of the factors influencing mutation rates and spectra, their potential variations among organisms, and how they may be influenced by environmental conditions.

title: Apolipoprotein E4 as a predictor of outcomes in pediatric mild traumatic brain injury.
text:
The APOE epsilon4 allele, which is a variant of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene, has been associated with negative outcomes in adults with traumatic brain injury (TBI) of varying severity. There is some initial evidence suggesting a similar pattern in children. This study aimed to explore the relationship between the APOE epsilon4 allele and outcomes in children with mild TBI. 

The study included 99 children between the ages of 8 and 15 who had experienced mild TBI. These children were recruited from consecutive admissions to Emergency Departments at two large children's hospitals. The researchers assessed the outcomes of the children immediately after the injury in the Emergency Department, as well as at follow-ups after 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months. 

Out of the 99 participants, 28 had at least one epsilon4 allele. There were no demographic differences between children with and without the epsilon4 allele. However, children with the epsilon4 allele were more likely to have a Glasgow Coma Scale score below 15 compared to those without the allele. There were no other differences in measures of injury severity between the two groups. 

Interestingly, children with the epsilon4 allele performed better on a test of constructional skill compared to those without the allele. However, there were no differences between the groups on any other neuropsychological tests. Additionally, there were no differences in post-concussive symptoms between children with and without the epsilon4 allele. 

Overall, the findings of this study suggest that the APOE epsilon4 allele does not consistently impact the outcomes of mild TBI in children.

title: Do physicians follow systemic treatment and funding policy guidelines?
text:
The use of bisphosphonates to prevent skeletal related events in women with bone metastases from breast cancer is well established. We conducted an evaluation of bisphosphonate use in clinical practice at three Canadian cancer centers, as well as assessed whether physicians at these centers are adhering to local treatment guidelines and funding policies.

We retrospectively reviewed the charts and electronic files of patients who received either clodronate or pamidronate between January 2000 and December 2001 at the three cancer centers. 

The results showed a significant improvement in the time between the diagnosis of bone metastases and the initiation of bisphosphonate treatment, decreasing from a median of 155 days in 1998 to 24 days in 2001. However, despite a local funding policy that recommended oral clodronate as the first choice, only 67% of patients received this treatment. Additionally, despite one center's guidelines suggesting that bisphosphonates should be discontinued when the patient's condition worsens, 90% of their patients continued to receive bisphosphonates until death.

In conclusion, while a lot of effort is put into creating evidence-based treatment guidelines, funding policies often impose more restrictions than what the guidelines suggest. This review highlights that physicians still manage a significant number of patients outside of funding policies, but within evidence-based recommendations. Therefore, there is a need to either develop guidelines and policies that physicians will adhere to or implement methods to ensure compliance with restrictive policies.

title: Increased resting energy expenditure and weight loss are related to a systemic inflammatory response in lung cancer patients.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between increased resting energy expenditure (REE) and weight loss in lung cancer patients and a systemic inflammatory response. The researchers used indirect calorimetry to measure REE and various assays to measure inflammatory markers such as soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor 55 (sTNF-R55), soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor 75 (sTNF-R75), soluble intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (sICAM-1), soluble E-selectin (sE-selectin), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), interleukin 6 (IL-6), TNF-alpha, and C-reactive protein (CRP). They conducted a cross-sectional study comparing inflammatory markers between hypermetabolic patients (REE/Harris Benedict [HB] equation ≥ 110%) and normometabolic patients (REE/HB < 110%), as well as between patients who experienced weight loss (more than 10% loss of preillness weight) and those whose weight remained stable. The study included 87 patients with primary non-small-cell lung cancer. The results showed that hypermetabolic patients had significantly higher levels of sTNF-R55, sE-selectin, LBP, and CRP compared to normometabolic patients. Weight loss was associated with increased levels of sTNF-Rs, sICAM-1, IL-6, LBP, and CRP. In conclusion, the presence of a systemic inflammatory response, as indicated by elevated levels of inflammatory markers and acute phase proteins, is related to hypermetabolism and weight loss in patients with primary non-small-cell lung cancer.

title: Exercise capacity and body mass as predictors of mortality among male veterans with type 2 diabetes.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between exercise capacity, BMI, and mortality in a group of male veterans with type 2 diabetes. The research design involved excluding two underweight patients and including 831 consecutive patients with type 2 diabetes who underwent exercise testing between 1995 and 2006. Exercise capacity was measured in metabolic equivalents (METs) and patients were categorized based on BMI and exercise capacity. Cox proportional hazards analysis was used to assess the association between exercise capacity, BMI, clinical variables, and all-cause mortality. The study participants were followed for mortality until June 2006. 

Results showed that during an average follow-up of 4.8 years, 112 patients died, resulting in an annual mortality rate of 2.2%. Each 1-MET increase in exercise capacity was associated with a 10% survival benefit. However, BMI was not significantly associated with mortality. After adjusting for various factors, diabetic patients who achieved less than 5 maximal METs were 70% more likely to die compared to those who achieved 5 or more maximal METs. 

In conclusion, there was a strong inverse relationship between exercise capacity and mortality in this group of men with type 2 diabetes, independent of BMI.

title: Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia: a review.
text: Impaired awareness of hypoglycemia (IAH) is a complication that occurs as a result of insulin therapy. It affects individuals with type 1 and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes mellitus, causing a decrease or absence in their ability to recognize the onset of hypoglycemia. Typically, there is also a deficiency in the body's counter-regulatory hormonal responses to hypoglycemia. This combination of IAH and counter-regulatory failure significantly increases the risk of severe hypoglycemia. To identify individuals at risk of severe hypoglycemia, scoring systems have been developed for use in clinical settings. The primary approach to treating IAH is to diligently avoid hypoglycemia.

title: A chikungunya fever vaccine utilizing an insect-specific virus platform
text: Traditionally, the development of vaccines involves finding a balance between effectiveness and safety. Live-attenuated vaccines provide strong and long-lasting immunity but come with a higher risk compared to inactivated vaccines. On the other hand, inactivated vaccines are safer but may require multiple doses to be effective. To overcome these challenges, we created a vaccine platform using a specific virus called Eilat virus (EILV) that only affects insects. To combat the chikungunya fever pandemic, we used a modified version of EILV that contained the structural proteins of the chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Through advanced imaging techniques, we confirmed that the modified virus closely resembled the wild-type CHIKV and replicated similarly in vertebrate cells. However, the modified virus was completely unable to replicate effectively, ensuring a high level of safety. A single dose of the modified virus produced in mosquito cells triggered a rapid immune response in mice, generating long-lasting neutralizing antibodies that provided complete protection. In nonhuman primates, the modified virus also elicited a strong immune response, protecting against viremia (presence of virus in the bloodstream) and fever. Our use of the EILV platform is the first example of utilizing an insect-specific virus in the development of preclinical vaccines, demonstrating the potential of such viruses in the field of vaccinology.

title: Molecular elements of low-oxygen signaling in plants.
text: The importance of oxygen and its limitations in plant fitness, growth, and development is becoming increasingly evident. Recent studies have uncovered the mechanisms by which plant cells perceive oxygen. This sensory system relies on a specific group of ethylene responsive transcription factors (ERF-VII) that are targeted for degradation through an oxygen-mediated branch of the N-end rule pathway. Additionally, the regulation of ERF-VII proteins is controlled by their sequestration at the plasma membrane and their release when hypoxia occurs. When oxygen is completely absent, reactive hydrogen peroxide temporarily accumulates, leading to the activation of genes involved in signaling and the attenuation of oxidative stress. Furthermore, temporary hypoxic conditions resulting from densely packed cells have been found to influence cell fate determination in maize anthers. Similarly, limited oxygen supply in large fruits or tubers growing in aerobic conditions can stimulate anaerobic-like responses. These discoveries regarding low-oxygen signaling and its impact on cell development emphasize the need to consider hypoxia in agricultural practices and breeding programs.

title: Purification, characterization, and sequence analysis of a potential virulence factor from Porphyromonas gingivalis, peptidylarginine deiminase.
text: The infection of the gingival sulcus by Porphyromonas gingivalis has been linked to the development and progression of adult-onset periodontitis. This particular organism employs various virulence factors to evade the body's defense mechanisms and establish itself as a prominent pathogen in periodontal pockets. One common characteristic shared by many oral pathogens is the production of ammonia, which serves as a protective agent during acidic cleansing cycles in the mouth. Furthermore, the production of ammonia by P. gingivalis has been suggested to be a virulence factor due to its detrimental effects on neutrophil function. In this research, we present the first isolation of a peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) from a prokaryote. PAD possesses biochemical properties and features that indicate its potential as a virulence factor. It catalyzes the deimination of the guanidino group of carboxyl-terminal arginine residues in various peptides, including the vasoregulatory peptide-hormone bradykinin, resulting in the production of ammonia and a citrulline residue. The soluble form of the protein has an apparent mass of 46 kDa, while the DNA sequence predicts a full-length protein of 61.7 kDa. PAD exhibits optimal activity at 55 degrees Celsius, remains stable at low pH levels, and demonstrates the highest activity above pH 9.0. Interestingly, when exposed to stabilizing factors, PAD resists limited proteolysis and retains significant activity even after brief boiling. We propose that PAD, in conjunction with arginine-specific proteinases from P. gingivalis, facilitates the growth of the pathogen in the periodontal pocket by initially enhancing its survival and subsequently aiding the organism in evading the body's humoral defenses.

title: Traumatic encephalopathy: review and provisional research diagnostic criteria.
text:
GOALS: The aim of this study is to determine the frequency of neurobehavioral signs and symptoms reported in all published cases of traumatic encephalopathy (TE) in order to develop clinical diagnostic criteria with predictive validity.

INTRODUCTION: Since 1928, cases of persistent or progressive neurological or neurobehavioral changes following head injuries have been documented. This condition is commonly known as traumatic encephalopathy (TE). However, there are currently no established diagnostic criteria for the clinical diagnosis of TE. It is crucial to establish provisional research diagnostic criteria to enable accurate diagnosis and facilitate further research on the epidemiology, etiology, course, prognosis, imaging and biomarkers, neuropathological features, and potential treatments of TE.

METHODS: A comprehensive review was conducted on all 436 published cases of TE in various languages. All symptoms and signs reported in these cases were categorized and counted.

RESULTS: Out of the 436 cases, 97 met the inclusion criteria, which required sufficient documentation of the history and neurobehavioral examination. Based on the most frequently reported clinical features, provisional research diagnostic criteria for clinically probable and clinically possible TE were developed.

CONCLUSION: The provisional diagnostic criteria presented in this study are the first published criteria for TE that have been derived from a systematic analysis of its clinical characteristics. This marks an initial step towards establishing scientifically derived consensus criteria, which are crucial for advancing research on this significant condition.

title: Hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus infection.
text: Approximately 200,000 individuals in the United States are affected by both hepatitis C virus (HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). With the use of highly active antiretroviral therapy, the lifespan of HIV-infected individuals has increased, but liver disease has become a significant cause of illness and death, particularly in certain environments. HIV infection has a negative impact on all stages of hepatitis C infection, leading to higher viral persistence and faster progression of HCV-related liver disease. Conversely, hepatitis C can complicate the treatment of HIV infection, increasing the occurrence of liver toxicity caused by antiretroviral drugs. The medical management of hepatitis C in HIV-infected individuals is still a subject of debate due to the complexity of both infections and potential drug interactions, as well as the scarcity of published information. Nevertheless, the burden of liver disease is too great to postpone the management of HIV/HCV-coinfected individuals until more data becomes available. Instead, the current approach to managing hepatitis C must rely on data obtained from individuals without HIV and a comprehensive understanding of both infections. Well-designed studies on therapy for HIV/HCV-coinfected individuals are necessary to provide guidance for future patient management.

title: Role of the vascular endothelial growth factor pathway in tumor growth and angiogenesis.
text: Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, plays a crucial role in tumor growth and the spread of cancer. As a result, understanding the molecular basis of tumor angiogenesis has been a major focus in cancer research. The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway is widely recognized as a key regulator of this process. This pathway consists of multiple ligands and receptors that have both overlapping and distinct binding specificities, expression patterns, and functions. Activation of the VEGF-receptor pathway initiates a series of signaling processes that promote the growth, movement, and survival of endothelial cells from existing blood vessels. Additionally, VEGF is involved in vessel permeability and has been linked to malignant effusions. More recently, VEGF has been found to play a crucial role in mobilizing endothelial progenitor cells from the bone marrow to distant sites where new blood vessels are forming. Given the well-established role of VEGF in promoting tumor angiogenesis and the development of human cancers, researchers have designed and developed agents that specifically target this pathway. Studies using various anti-VEGF/VEGF-receptor therapies have demonstrated their ability to effectively inhibit angiogenesis and tumor growth in preclinical models. Recently, the use of an anti-VEGF antibody called bevacizumab, in combination with chemotherapy, has been shown to significantly improve survival rates and treatment response in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. This success validates VEGF pathway inhibitors as an important new approach in cancer therapy.

title: Frozen robust multiarray analysis (fRMA).
text:
The most commonly used preprocessing algorithm for Affymetrix and Nimblegen gene expression microarrays is called Robust Multiarray Analysis (RMA). RMA performs background correction, normalization, and summarization in a modular way. The last two steps require multiple arrays to be analyzed together. This ability to borrow information across samples gives RMA several advantages. For example, the summarization step fits a parametric model that takes into account probe effects, which are assumed to be consistent across arrays, and improves outlier detection. Residuals obtained from the fitted model can be used to create useful quality metrics. However, there are two drawbacks to RMA's dependence on multiple arrays: (1) it cannot be used in clinical settings where samples need to be processed individually or in small batches, and (2) data sets that are preprocessed separately cannot be compared. 

To address these issues, we propose a preprocessing algorithm called frozen RMA (fRMA). This algorithm allows microarrays to be analyzed individually or in small batches and then combines the data for analysis. It achieves this by utilizing information from large publicly available microarray databases. Specifically, estimates of probe-specific effects and variances are precomputed and frozen. With new data sets, these precomputed estimates are used along with information from the new arrays to normalize and summarize the data. We have found that fRMA performs comparably to RMA when the data is analyzed as a single batch and outperforms RMA when analyzing multiple batches. 

The methods described here have been implemented in the R package fRMA and can be downloaded from the software section of http://rafalab.jhsph.edu.

title: Hypoxia in relation to vasculature and proliferation in liver metastases in patients with colorectal cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the presence of hypoxia in liver metastases of colorectal cancer using pimonidazole binding, glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) and carbonic anhydrase IX (CA-IX) expression, proliferation, and vascularity. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the expression of GLUT1 and CA-IX in corresponding primary tumors. 

A total of twenty-five patients with liver metastases of colorectal cancer, who were scheduled for metastasectomy, were included in the study. Before surgery, the patients were administered the hypoxia marker pimonidazole and the proliferation marker iododeoxyuridine. Frozen metastases were then subjected to immunofluorescent staining to analyze pimonidazole binding, vascularity, and proliferation quantitatively. Thirteen paraffin-embedded primary tumors were also stained immunohistochemically for GLUT1 and CA-IX expression, which was analyzed semiquantitatively in both primary tumors and corresponding liver metastases. 

The results showed that pimonidazole binding in liver metastases exhibited a pattern consistent with diffusion-limited hypoxia. The average fraction of pimonidazole-positive areas was 0.146, and the average distance from vessels to pimonidazole-positive areas was 80 micrometers. Co-localization between pimonidazole binding and GLUT1 or CA-IX expression was often observed, but there were also microregional areas where they did not match. There was no correlation between the level of pimonidazole binding and GLUT1 or CA-IX expression. In some patients, a significant proportion (up to 30%) of proliferating cells were found in pimonidazole-stained areas. The expression of CA-IX in primary tumors and metastases showed a significant correlation, whereas there was no correlation observed for GLUT1 expression. 

In conclusion, liver metastases of colorectal cancer contain a substantial number of hypoxic cells compared to other tumor types. However, the lack of correlation between pimonidazole binding and GLUT1 or CA-IX expression raises doubts about the usefulness of these markers as indicators of hypoxia.

title: Unmet needs mediate the relationship between symptoms and quality of life in breast cancer survivors
text: The purpose of this study was to compare the symptoms, unmet needs, and quality of life (QoL) reported by women at different time points following surgery and adjuvant treatment for breast cancer. The study also aimed to examine the relationships between symptoms, unmet needs, and QoL using structural equation modeling. A total of 113 and 137 breast cancer survivors who were 6 months to less than 2 years and 2 to 5 years post-treatment, respectively, completed various surveys during their medical follow-up. The surveys assessed symptoms, unmet needs, and QoL. The average number of symptoms and unmet needs were calculated for each group. The most common symptoms reported were primarily related to physical health. There were no significant differences in symptom scores between the two survivor groups. However, survivors at less than 2 years post-treatment reported higher scores for psychological and health care system/information needs, as well as lower composite scores for physical and mental QoL compared to those at 2 to 5 years post-treatment. The study found that symptom burden had direct and indirect effects on survivors' physical and mental QoL through unmet needs, even after adjusting for survival time. The results suggest that breast cancer survivors continue to experience symptoms regardless of the time since treatment, and that unmet needs play a role in their QoL.

title: Phagocytosis and deposition of vascular beta-amyloid in rat brains injected with Alzheimer beta-amyloid.
text: The presence of beta-amyloid protein deposits outside of cells in the brain is a characteristic feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). To investigate the impact of amyloid in an animal model, the researchers injected amyloid cores obtained from AD brains into the cortex and hippocampus of rats. As a control, they also injected lipofuscin, a major impurity in the plaque core preparation, on the opposite side to induce a similar response in phagocytic cells. The rats were euthanized at 2 days, 7 days, and 1 month after the injections, and the presence of amyloid was detected using four different staining techniques. The amyloid and lipofuscin migrated from the injection site into unaffected neuropil, remaining present for at least 1 month. Both substances were associated with increased staining of glial fibrillary acidic protein and microglia (OX-42). Within a week, many of the amyloid cores were engulfed by phagocytes. Some of these phagocytes containing beta-amyloid migrated towards blood vessels and ventricles, and by 1 month, a significant amount of amyloid was directly associated with the vessels. This suggests that phagocytic cells can internalize amyloid from external sources and attempt to clear it from the central nervous system (CNS). Therefore, the observed distribution of amyloid may not necessarily reflect the initial deposition site.

title: Specific sites in the C terminus of CTCF interact with the SA2 subunit of the cohesin complex and are required for cohesin-dependent insulation activity.
text: New research has revealed that the protein CTCF, which plays a crucial role in organizing chromatin within the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, relies on the cohesin complex for its functions. Our study demonstrates that the interaction between CTCF and the cohesin complex is facilitated by direct connections between the cohesin subunit SA2 and specific regions of CTCF's C-terminal tail. All other components of the cohesin complex are recruited through their interaction with SA2. When we expressed CTCF mutants lacking the C-terminal domain or with mutations in the SA2 binding sites, it disrupted the normal expression of imprinted genes IGF2-H19 and also compromised the insulation activity.
