In the short term, the administration of inflammatory cytokines or activation of the innate immune system can lead to adaptive behavioral responses that conserve energy to fight infection or recover from injury. However, chronic exposure to high levels of inflammatory cytokines and persistent changes in neurotransmitter systems can result in neuropsychiatric disorders and depression. The mechanisms behind the behavioral effects of cytokines involve the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways in the brain, which leads to alterations in monoamine, glutamate, and neuropeptide systems, as well as a decrease in growth factors like brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Additionally, inflammatory cytokines may act as mediators between environmental factors (such as childhood trauma, obesity, stress, and poor sleep) and genetic factors (such as functional gene polymorphisms) that contribute to the development of depression. This review explores the concept that specific gene polymorphisms and neurotransmitter systems can either protect against or make individuals vulnerable to specific symptom dimensions of cytokine-related depression. Furthermore, potential therapeutic strategies that target inflammatory cytokine signaling or the effects of cytokines on neurotransmitter systems in the brain are discussed as a means to prevent or reverse the behavioral effects of cytokines.

title: Sputum inflammation predicts exacerbations after cessation of inhaled corticosteroids in COPD.
text: INTRODUCTION The GOLD guidelines discourage the use of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in patients with mild-to-moderate COPD. However, many patients still use ICS and stopping the treatment can lead to worsened lung function and more frequent exacerbations in some patients. Unfortunately, doctors are unsure which patients can safely stop ICS treatment. AIM The aim of this study was to identify predictors of COPD exacerbations after ICS withdrawal. METHODS This study involved 68 COPD patients who were using ICS. During ICS treatment, the patients underwent post-bronchodilator spirometry, body plethysmography, and health status assessment. The researchers also analyzed sputum cell differentials, leukotriene B(4) levels, eosinophilic cationic protein levels, myeloperoxidase levels, C-reactive protein levels, soluble intracellular adhesion molecule levels, and urinary desmosine levels. The sputum was also examined for mRNA levels of various inflammatory markers. STATISTICS Cox regression analyses were conducted to determine significant factors associated with COPD exacerbations after ICS withdrawal. RESULTS The results showed that higher sputum eosinophil levels, higher sputum myeloperoxidase/neutrophil levels, longer duration of COPD symptoms, smoking less than 40 packyears, and ICS withdrawal in November, December, or January were significant predictors of experiencing a COPD exacerbation after ICS withdrawal in a univariate model. In a multivariate model, all factors except for sputum myeloperoxidase/neutrophil levels remained independent predictors. CONCLUSIONS Assessing sputum inflammation, particularly eosinophil numbers, along with packyears smoking, season, and duration of COPD symptoms can help doctors make informed decisions about whether or not to safely withdraw inhaled corticosteroids in patients with mild-to-moderate COPD.

title: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha activation decreases metastatic potential of melanoma cells in vitro via down-regulation of Akt.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the potential anticancer properties of Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPAR), which are known to regulate lipid and glucose metabolism. Specifically, the researchers focused on the PPARalpha ligand, fenofibrate, and its ability to inhibit metastasis in melanoma tumors. 

The experimental design involved using mouse (B16F10) and human (SkMell88) melanoma cell lines in monolayer cultures, as well as conducting soft agar and cell migration assays. The researchers also analyzed the expression and transcriptional activity of PPARalpha in response to fenofibrate using Western blots and a luciferase-based reporter system. 

The results showed that fenofibrate inhibited the migration of both B16F10 and SkMel188 cells in Transwell chambers, as well as colony formation in soft agar. These effects were reversed when a PPAR inhibitor, GW9662, was used. Further analysis revealed that fenofibrate caused a time-dependent down-regulation of Akt and extracellular signal-regulated kinase l/2 phosphorylation in the treated cells. 

To further investigate the role of Akt in fenofibrate's action, the researchers used a B16F10 cell line that expressed a constitutively active Akt mutant. They found that these cells were resistant to fenofibrate. Conversely, when Akt gene silencing was achieved using siRNA, the migratory ability of B16F10 cells was reduced, mimicking the effects of fenofibrate. Additionally, fenofibrate sensitized BI6FIO cells to the proapoptotic drug staurosporine, suggesting that the down-regulation of Akt function by fenofibrate contributes to its inhibition of metastatic potential. 

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that fenofibrate's antimetastatic activity is dependent on PPAR and involves the down-regulation of Akt phosphorylation. The findings suggest that fenofibrate supplementation may enhance the effectiveness of melanoma chemotherapy.

title: PHC3, a component of the hPRC-H complex, associates with E2F6 during G0 and is lost in osteosarcoma tumors
text: Polyhomeotic-like 3 (PHC3) is a gene that is widely expressed and belongs to the polycomb gene family. It is also a component of the human polycomb complex hPRC-H. Our research has shown that in normal cells, PHC3 interacts with both components of the hPRC-H complex and with a transcription factor called E2F6. In cells that are undergoing differentiation or are in a confluent state, PHC3 and E2F6 are found together in the nucleus in a pattern that resembles the binding of polycomb bodies to heterochromatin. This pattern is not observed in cells that are actively proliferating, suggesting that PHC3 may be involved in an E2F6-polycomb complex that is known to occupy and silence target promoters in a state of cell cycle arrest (G0). Previous studies have shown that the region containing PHC3 frequently undergoes loss of heterozygosity (LoH) in primary human osteosarcoma tumors. When we examined normal bone tissue and osteosarcoma tumors, we discovered that PHC3 expression was lost in 36 out of 56 osteosarcoma tumors. Further analysis of the DNA sequence revealed that PHC3 was mutated in nine out of 15 primary osteosarcoma tumors. These findings suggest that the loss of PHC3 may contribute to the development of tumors by potentially disrupting the ability of cells to remain in a state of cell cycle arrest.

title: Germinal center T follicular helper cell IL-4 production is dependent on signaling lymphocytic activation molecule receptor (CD150).
text: The assistance of CD4 T cells is crucial for the formation and maintenance of germinal centers (GCs), and a specific subset of CD4 T cells called T follicular helper (T(FH)) cells is necessary for this process. The expression of signaling lymphocytic activation molecule (SLAM)-associated protein (SAP [SH2D1A]) in CD4 T cells is essential for the development of GCs. However, mice lacking SAP only show a moderate impairment in T(FH) cell differentiation, as indicated by common T(FH) surface markers. T(FH) cells expressing CXCR5(+) can be found within the GCs, as well as in the boundary regions between T/B cell zones. In this study, we demonstrate that GC-associated T follicular helper (GC T(FH)) cells can be identified by their coexpression of CXCR5 and the GL7 epitope, which allows for the analysis of their phenotype and function. GC T(FH) cells are a distinct subset of polarized T(FH) cells, with an enhanced ability to assist B cells and produce IL-4 in a T(H)2-independent manner. Interestingly, mice lacking SAP do not have the GC T(FH) cell subset, and SAP(-) T(FH) cells are unable to produce IL-4 and IL-21. We also show that SLAM (Slamf1, CD150), a surface receptor that relies on SAP signaling, is specifically required for IL-4 production by GC T(FH) cells. GC T(FH) cells depend on the production of IL-4 and -21 for optimal assistance to B cells. These findings highlight the complexities of SAP-dependent SLAM family receptor signaling, revealing the significant role of SLAM receptor activation in IL-4 production by GC CD4 T cells, but not in the differentiation of T(FH) cells and GC T(FH) cells.

title: High cardiovascular mortality in Russia cannot be explained by the classical risk factors. The Arkhangelsk study 2000
text: Since the early 1990s, Russia has faced a public health crisis characterized by a remarkably high mortality rate and a significant decrease in life expectancy. The leading cause of death has been cardiovascular diseases. Unfortunately, there have been limited large-scale studies conducted in Russia during this time period. However, a health survey conducted in Arkhangelsk, Russia, between 1999 and 2000 included a total of 1968 men and 1737 women aged 18 to 75 years. This investigation focused on assessing traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as family history, smoking, blood pressure, and blood lipids, as well as general health variables. The study provides specific data on the risk factors for coronary heart disease based on gender. Despite the high cardiovascular mortality rate in Russia, the calculated risk for coronary heart disease, as determined by the Framingham risk score and the Norwegian risk score, was lower in all age groups of men and women in Arkhangelsk compared to studies conducted in Western Europe and the USA. These findings suggest that the high cardiovascular mortality rate in Russia may be influenced by factors beyond the traditional risk factors associated with coronary heart disease.

title: Wnt7a/Fzd7 Signalling Directly Activates the Akt/mTOR Anabolic Growth Pathway in Skeletal Muscle
text: The activation of the planar-cell-polarity pathway and the expansion of satellite stem cells in skeletal muscle repair are facilitated by Wnt7a signaling through its receptor Fzd7. In myofibres that have already differentiated, we have observed that the binding of Wnt7a to Fzd7 directly triggers the Akt/mTOR growth pathway, leading to myofibre hypertrophy. Interestingly, the Fzd7 receptor complex is associated with Gα(s) and PI(3)K, and these components are necessary for Wnt7a to activate the Akt/mTOR growth pathway in myotubes. Importantly, the activation of this pathway by Wnt7a-Fzd7 is completely independent of IGF-receptor activation. These experiments collectively demonstrate that Wnt7a-Fzd7 activates different pathways at different stages of myogenic lineage progression, and reveal a non-canonical anabolic signaling pathway for Wnt7a and its receptor Fzd7 in skeletal muscle.

title: Four newly located pseudouridylate residues in Escherichia coli 23S ribosomal RNA are all at the peptidyltransferase center: analysis by the application of a new sequencing technique.
text: A novel technique has been developed to easily locate pseudouridylate (psi) residues in any RNA molecule. This method combines two known modification procedures to specifically identify U residues that have been converted into psi. The first procedure involves reacting U-like and G-like residues with N-cyclohexyl-N'-beta-(4-methylmorpholinium)ethylcarbodiimide p-tosylate (CMC), followed by removing all CMC groups except those linked to the N3 of psi using an alkaline solution. This halts reverse transcription, resulting in a gel band that indicates the presence of a U residue. The second procedure is uridine-specific hydrazinolysis, which breaks the RNA chain at all U residues and produces a gel band during reverse transcription. However, psi residues are resistant to hydrazinolysis and therefore remain intact, allowing reverse transcription to continue without interruption. As a result, no band is observed at psi residues. This combined method can also differentiate psi from other modified bases such as 5-methyluridine, 4-thiouridine, uridine-5-oxyacetic acid, and 2-thio-5-methylaminomethyluridine. This has been demonstrated by treating rRNA and tRNA species known to contain these modified bases at specific sites. Using this technique, four previously unknown psi sites were discovered in Escherichia coli 23S RNA at positions 2457, 2504, 2580, and 2605. Additionally, one previously reported site at position 2555 was disproven. These four new psi residues, located within or near the peptidyltransferase ring, may have functional and/or structural significance at the peptidyltransferase center.

title: Pharmacological characterization of 1-(5-chloro-6-(trifluoromethoxy)-1H-benzoimidazol-2-yl)-1H-pyrazole-4-carboxylic acid (JNJ-42041935), a potent and selective hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor.
text: The hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) enzymes are potential targets for treating various conditions such as anemia, ulcerative colitis, and ischemic and metabolic diseases. We have discovered a new compound called JNJ-42041935, which inhibits PHD through structure-based drug design methods. We conducted studies on enzyme, cellular, and whole-animal systems to understand the pharmacology of JNJ-42041935 and compared it with other known PHD inhibitors. JNJ-42041935 proved to be a potent (pK(I) = 7.3-7.9), reversible, and selective inhibitor of PHD enzymes, competing with 2-oxoglutarate. Furthermore, we used JNJ-42041935 to compare its effects with intermittent, high doses of an exogenous erythropoietin receptor agonist in a rat model of inflammation-induced anemia. Interestingly, JNJ-42041935 (100 μmol/kg, once a day for 14 days) effectively reversed inflammation-induced anemia, while erythropoietin had no impact. These findings highlight JNJ-42041935 as a valuable tool for studying PHD inhibition and suggest that PHD inhibitors hold promise for treating inflammation-induced anemia.

title: Three-Dimensional Modeling and Quantitative Analysis of Gap Junction Distributions in Cardiac Tissue
text:
Gap junctions play a crucial role in facilitating communication between cells in the heart tissue. Changes in the arrangement of these gap junctions have been linked to various heart diseases such as hypertrophy and ischemia. Previous studies have used two-dimensional optical and electron microscopy to visualize the spatial distribution of gap junctions. It has been observed that in healthy heart cells, these gap junctions are primarily located at the ends of the cells, but can also be found in central regions.

In this study, we aimed to enhance these visualization techniques by using high-resolution scanning confocal microscopy and image processing to reconstruct the three-dimensional distribution of gap junctions. We developed methods to quantitatively analyze these distributions by examining the intensity profiles along the main axes of the heart cells. Our analysis focused on characterizing the polarization of gap junctions at cell ends, as well as the statistical properties of the intensity profiles.

To test our methodology, we conducted experiments on rat ventricular myocardium. The results of our analysis provided novel quantitative data on the distribution of gap junctions. Notably, we found that these distributions exhibit significant variability in terms of polarization, skewness, and kurtosis. We believe that our methodology offers a quantitative alternative to the current visually-based approaches, and can be particularly useful in characterizing engineered and diseased heart tissue.

Furthermore, we propose that the data obtained from our analysis can be used to improve computational models of cardiac conduction. By incorporating these quantitative measurements of gap junction distributions, we can enhance our understanding of how electrical signals propagate through the heart and potentially improve the diagnosis and treatment of heart conditions.

title: Clonally derived human embryonic stem cell lines maintain pluripotency and proliferative potential for prolonged periods of culture.
text: We have successfully derived two human embryonic stem (ES) cell lines, H9.1 and H9.2, from blastocysts. These cell lines have the ability to develop into various types of cells from all three embryonic germ layers, even after being cultured for a long period of time. Prior to the derivation of H9.1 and H9.2, the parental ES cell line, H9, had already been cultured for 6 months. After an additional 8 months of culture, H9.1 and H9.2 continued to proliferate actively, express high levels of telomerase, and maintain normal karyotypes. The length of telomeres in these cells varied slightly but remained between 8 and 12 kb in high-passage H9.1 and H9.2 cells. When injected into SCID-beige mice, high-passage H9.1 and H9.2 cells formed teratomas that contained differentiated cells from all three embryonic germ layers. These findings demonstrate the pluripotency of individual human ES cells, their ability to maintain pluripotency during long-term culture, and their capacity for self-renewal. The exceptional developmental potential, proliferative ability, and karyotypic stability of human ES cells distinguish them from adult cells.

title: Autosomal dominant lateral temporal epilepsy: two families with novel mutations in the LGI1 gene.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate mutations in the LGI1 gene in families with autosomal dominant lateral temporal epilepsy (ADLTE). ADLTE is characterized by partial seizures with symptoms suggesting a lateral temporal onset, including frequent auditory aura. Two newly identified families with ADLTE were evaluated through clinical and genetic analyses. The coding sequence of the LGI1 gene was analyzed for evidence of mutation in affected individuals from both families. The results showed that each patient had a history of partial seizures, often with secondary generalization earlier in the course. Approximately two thirds of affected patients in each family reported auditory aura. Novel mutations in the LGI1 gene were detected in both families, including a single-nucleotide deletion at position 329 (del 329C) in one family and a nonsynonymous variation (C435G) in the other family. In conclusion, this study identified two novel mutations in the LGI1 gene and further supported the consideration of LGI1 mutations in patients with a history of partial seizures consistent with lateral temporal lobe onset.

title: Identification of Senescent Cells in the Bone Microenvironment.
text: Cellular senescence is a crucial process in which cells remain metabolically active but stop dividing and undergo specific changes in their characteristics. These changes include an increase in the expression of p16Ink4a, significant alterations in the substances they secrete (known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype or SASP), shortening of telomeres, and decondensation of pericentromeric satellite DNA. As senescent cells accumulate in various tissues as we age, they and the dysfunctional factors they release are being recognized as potential targets for therapies to prevent age-related degenerative diseases like osteoporosis. However, it has been unclear which specific cell type(s) in the bone microenvironment undergo senescence in vivo with aging, mainly because previous studies have focused on senescence in cultured cells. Therefore, we conducted a study in young (6 months old) and old (24 months old) mice to measure senescence and SASP markers in vivo in highly enriched cell populations, all obtained directly from bone/marrow without any in vitro culture. We found that in both female and male mice, the expression of p16Ink4a significantly increased with aging in B cells, T cells, myeloid cells, osteoblast progenitors, osteoblasts, and osteocytes. Additionally, we observed a higher percentage of senescent osteocytes in the bone cortices of old mice compared to young mice (11% versus 2%, p < 0.001) through the quantification of senescence-associated distension of satellites (SADS), which refers to the large-scale unraveling of pericentromeric satellite DNA. Furthermore, primary osteocytes from old mice had six times more telomere dysfunction-induced foci (TIFs) than osteocytes from young mice (p < 0.001). The increased accumulation of senescent osteocytes with age was accompanied by higher expression of multiple SASP markers in osteocytes from old mice compared to young mice, some of which also showed significant upregulation in myeloid cells. These findings demonstrate that with aging, a subset of cells from different lineages in the bone microenvironment become senescent, although senescent myeloid cells and senescent osteocytes are the main contributors to the SASP. Considering the crucial role of osteocytes in bone remodeling, our results suggest that senescent osteocytes and their SASP may contribute to age-related bone loss. This study was conducted by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research in 2016.

title: Changes in white blood cells and platelets in children with falciparum malaria: relationship to disease outcome.
text:
There is limited knowledge regarding the changes in white blood cells and platelets in children with falciparum malaria in areas where the disease is prevalent. To address this, we conducted a study in which we examined the white cell count (WCC) and platelet levels of 230 healthy children from the community, 1369 children admitted to the hospital with symptomatic malaria, and 1461 children with other medical conditions.

Our findings revealed that children with malaria had a higher WCC compared to the healthy community controls. Furthermore, we observed that leucocytosis was strongly linked to younger age, deep breathing, severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and death. Interestingly, we did not find any association between the WCC and a positive blood culture.

In children with malaria, we discovered that high lymphocyte counts and low monocyte counts were independently associated with mortality. Additionally, we found that 56.7% of children with malaria had a platelet count of less than 150 x 109/l, which was associated with age, prostration, and parasite density. However, we did not observe any correlation between platelet count and bleeding problems or mortality. Moreover, the mean platelet volume was higher in children with malaria compared to those with other medical conditions. This suggests that there may be an early release of platelets from the bone marrow in response to peripheral platelet destruction.

In conclusion, our study demonstrated that leucocytosis is associated with both the severity and mortality of falciparum malaria in children, regardless of the presence of bacteraemia. On the other hand, although thrombocytopenia is very common in children with malaria, it is not linked to adverse outcomes.

title: Microenvironmental regulation of biomacromolecular therapies
text: There is currently a lot of interest in using molecular therapies to treat different diseases. This has led to extensive efforts to develop smart drug carriers that can deliver bioactive macromolecules (such as proteins, antibodies, DNA, and small interfering RNA) to specific targets in a controlled manner. However, the impact of the microenvironment where the target cell is located on the success of these therapies has been overlooked. The extracellular matrix (ECM), which is a component of the cellular niche, may play a crucial role in this regard. Many diseases and injuries disrupt the normal architecture of the ECM, as well as the adhesion of cells to the ECM and their subsequent activities. This review will explore the significance of the ECM and the interactions between the ECM and cells in determining the response to bioactive macromolecules. It will also propose how this knowledge can be used to establish new criteria for designing innovative drug delivery systems.

title: Homocysteine Induces Trophoblast Cell Death with Apoptotic Features1
text:
The potential role of hyperhomocysteinemia as a risk factor in women experiencing habitual abortions, placental abruption or infarcts, preeclampsia, and/or intrauterine growth retardation has been suggested. However, the underlying mechanisms by which homocysteine acts are not well understood. This study aimed to investigate the effects of homocysteine on trophoblast gonadotropin secretion and cell death in vitro. 

In primary human trophoblast cells, treatment with homocysteine at a concentration of 20 μmol/L resulted in various cellular changes, including flattening and enlargement, extension of pseudopodia, and vacuolization. The cells also showed detachment, apoptosis, and necrosis. DNA degradation was examined using in situ nick end labeling, and the cytoplasm of apoptotic cells was selectively stained using M30 CytoDEATH. The release of cytochrome c from mitochondria to the cytosol and DNA cleavage in agarose gel were also investigated. 

It was found that homocysteine, but not cysteine, induced trophoblast apoptosis and significantly reduced human chorionic gonadotropin secretion. These findings suggest that trophoblast cell death may be a potential mechanism through which homocysteine contributes to pregnancy complications associated with placental diseases.

title: Intrahippocampal administration of an androgen receptor antagonist, flutamide, can increase anxiety-like behavior in intact and DHT-replaced male rats.
text: The effects of testosterone (T) and its metabolite dihydrotestosterone (DHT) on anxiety-like behavior have not been fully understood. We conducted two hypotheses to investigate these effects. Firstly, we hypothesized that if T reduces anxiety-like behavior through DHT, then removing the testes (gonadectomy or GDX) would increase anxiety-like behavior, which could be reversed by administering DHT systemically. Secondly, we hypothesized that T and DHT reduce anxiety-like behavior by acting on androgen receptors in the hippocampus. To test this, we administered an androgen receptor antagonist called flutamide directly to the hippocampus. We applied inserts containing either flutamide or nothing to the dorsal hippocampus of intact, GDX, or GDX rats replaced with DHT, 2 hours before conducting tests in the open field, elevated plus maze, or defensive freezing tasks. The results showed that GDX rats displayed more anxiety-like behaviors compared to intact or DHT-replaced rats. Intact and DHT-replaced rats that received flutamide in the hippocampus exhibited significantly more anxiety-like behavior than the control groups. However, flutamide did not increase anxiety-like behavior in GDX rats. These findings suggest that androgens can decrease anxiety-like behavior in male rats, partly through DHT's actions on androgen receptors in the hippocampus.

title: Cardiovascular risk and events in 17 low-, middle-, and high-income countries.
text:
BACKGROUND: The reasons behind the majority of deaths from cardiovascular disease occurring in low-income and middle-income countries, estimated to be over 80%, are currently unknown.

METHODS: We conducted a study involving 156,424 individuals from 628 urban and rural communities in 17 countries, including 3 high-income, 10 middle-income, and 4 low-income countries. The participants' cardiovascular risk was assessed using the INTERHEART Risk Score, a validated tool that measures risk-factor burden without the need for laboratory testing. Higher scores indicate a greater burden of risk factors. The participants were followed for an average of 4.1 years to track incident cardiovascular disease and death.

RESULTS: The mean INTERHEART Risk Score was highest in high-income countries, intermediate in middle-income countries, and lowest in low-income countries (P<0.001). However, the rates of major cardiovascular events, such as death from cardiovascular causes, myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure, were lower in high-income countries compared to middle- and low-income countries (3.99 events per 1000 person-years vs. 5.38 and 6.43 events per 1000 person-years, respectively; P<0.001). Case fatality rates were also lowest in high-income countries (6.5%, 15.9%, and 17.3% in high-, middle-, and low-income countries, respectively; P=0.01). Urban communities had a higher burden of risk factors compared to rural communities, but lower rates of cardiovascular events (4.83 vs. 6.25 events per 1000 person-years, P<0.001) and case fatality rates (13.52% vs. 17.25%, P<0.001). The use of preventive medications and revascularization procedures was significantly more common in high-income countries compared to middle- or low-income countries (P<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Despite low-income countries having the lowest burden of risk factors, the rates of major cardiovascular disease and death were significantly higher in these countries compared to high-income countries. The high burden of risk factors in high-income countries may have been mitigated by better control of risk factors and more frequent use of proven pharmacologic therapies and revascularization. (Funded by the Population Health Research Institute and others.)

title: Increased density of tumor-associated macrophages is associated with decreased survival in advanced thyroid cancer.
text: The role of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) in the progression of thyroid cancers is not yet understood. This study aimed to determine the density of TAMs in different types of thyroid cancers and to examine the correlation between TAM density and clinicopathologic parameters. Immunohistochemistry was performed on tissue samples from well-differentiated (WDTC), poorly differentiated (PDTC), and anaplastic thyroid cancers (ATC) using markers specific to macrophages. Clinical and pathologic data were collected from electronic medical records. Follow-up information was available for PDTC patients for up to 12 years. The results showed that a higher density of CD68(+) TAMs (≥10 per 0.28 mm²) was present in 27% of WDTC, 54% of PDTC, and 95% of ATC cases. The density of TAMs was significantly higher in PDTC and ATC compared to WDTC (P=0.03 and P<0.0001, respectively), and in ATC compared to PDTC (P<0.002). In PDTC, a higher density of TAMs was associated with capsular invasion (P=0.034), extrathyroidal extension (P=0.009), and decreased cancer-related survival (P=0.009) compared to PDTC with a low density of TAMs. In conclusion, advanced thyroid cancers have an increased density of TAMs. A high density of TAMs in PDTC is associated with invasion and decreased cancer-related survival. These findings suggest that TAMs may play a role in tumor progression and should be considered when developing novel therapies targeting thyroid tumor cells.

title: Blockade of Tim-1 and Tim-4 Enhances Atherosclerosis in Low-Density Lipoprotein Receptor-Deficient Mice.
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the role of T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain (Tim) proteins in atherosclerosis. Tim proteins are expressed by various immune cells and can recognize phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells. They can function as either costimulators or coinhibitors. Tim-1 is found on activated T cells, dendritic cells, and B cells, while Tim-4 is present on macrophages and dendritic cells. Tim-4 plays a critical role in clearing apoptotic cells and regulating the number of activated T cells expressing phosphatidylserine. It is also genetically associated with low levels of low-density lipoprotein and triglycerides. Given the potential impact of Tim-1 and Tim-4 on atherosclerosis, modulating their activity could have therapeutic value in cardiovascular disease.

To investigate the effects of blocking Tim-1 and Tim-4, ldlr(-/-) mice were fed a high-fat diet for 4 weeks and treated with either control antibodies or monoclonal antibodies that block phosphatidylserine recognition and phagocytosis by Tim-1 (3D10) or Tim-4 (21H12). The results showed that both anti-Tim-1 and anti-Tim-4 treatments increased atherosclerosis by 45% compared to controls. This was attributed to impaired clearance of apoptotic cells and an increase in aortic CD4(+)T cells. Mice treated with anti-Tim-4 also showed higher percentages of activated T cells and late apoptotic cells in the circulation. In vitro experiments further demonstrated that blocking Tim-4 inhibited the clearance of apoptotic macrophages induced by oxidized low-density lipoprotein. Additionally, anti-Tim-4 treatment led to increased T helper cell (Th)1 and Th2 responses, while anti-Tim-1 induced Th2 responses but reduced the percentage of regulatory T cells. Finally, combined blockade of Tim-1 and Tim-4 resulted in a 59% increase in atherosclerotic lesion size.

In conclusion, blocking Tim-4 worsens atherosclerosis by preventing the clearance of phosphatidylserine-expressing apoptotic cells and activated T cells. On the other hand, the effects of Tim-1 on atherosclerosis are related to changes in the balance between Th1 and Th2 responses and a decrease in circulating regulatory T cells.

title: Genetic and physical analysis of double-strand break repair and recombination in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: We conducted an investigation on the recombination and repair of double-strand breaks (DSBs) induced by HO endonuclease in a yeast LACZ duplication plasmid. A 117-bp MATa fragment, present in one copy of LACZ, was used as the site for initiating a DSB upon expression of HO endonuclease. The DSB could be repaired by utilizing wild-type sequences located on a second copy of LACZ, which lacked a promoter, on the same plasmid. Interestingly, gene conversion-associated crossing-over occurred in at least 50% of the cases, in contrast to normal mating-type switching. The proportion of conversion events accompanied by exchange was higher (80%) when the two copies of LACZ were in direct orientation, compared to when they were inverted (50%). Furthermore, plasmid loss was significantly more frequent in the inverted orientation. We also monitored the kinetics of intermediate and final product appearance. Repair of the DSB was found to be slow, taking at least an hour from the detection of HO-cut fragments to completion of repair. Surprisingly, the appearance of the two reciprocal products of crossing over did not occur at the same rate. For instance, when the two LACZ sequences were in direct orientation, the HO-induced formation of a large circular deletion product did not coincide with the appearance of a small circular reciprocal product. We propose that these differences may reflect two distinct processes with different kinetics: one involving only one cut end and the other involving the concerted participation of both ends of the DSB.

title: Nitroxergic nerves mediate vagally induced relaxation in the isolated stomach of the guinea pig.
text:
In this study, we demonstrate that the relaxation caused by stimulating the vagus nerve in the guinea pig's isolated stomach, while cholinergic (muscarinic) and adrenergic receptors are blocked, is mediated by nitric oxide (NO). We support this finding by observing that NG-monomethyl-L-arginine, an inhibitor of NO synthesis, inhibits vagal relaxation. Additionally, we find that the inhibitory effect of NG-monomethyl-L-arginine is partially reversed when co-incubated with L-arginine, but not with D-arginine. We also observe that NO activates soluble guanylate cyclase, and the relaxation induced by vagal stimulation is prevented by methylene blue, an inhibitor of soluble guanylate cyclase, further supporting our conclusions.

Furthermore, we find that hexamethonium, an inhibitor of ganglionic nicotinic receptors, abolishes the relaxant effect of vagal stimulation. This suggests that ganglionic transmission does not rely on NO release from preganglionic neurons. However, hexamethonium does not inhibit the gastric relaxation caused by increasing intragastric pressure, which we have previously described as being mediated by NO. This selective inhibition by hexamethonium indicates the presence of at least two distinct neuronal pathways that can generate NO and facilitate gastric accommodation of food or fluid.

title: Efficient T cell activation requires an optimal dwell-time of interaction between the TCR and the pMHC complex
text: The activation of cytotoxic T cells (CTLs) by antigens relies on the specific recognition of peptide-major histocompatibility class I (pMHC) molecules on the surface of target cells by the T cell receptor (TCR). We investigated how mutations in the antigen-binding site of a Kb-restricted TCR affect T cell activation, antigen binding, and dissociation from the antigen. We also examined these parameters for variants derived from a Kd-restricted peptide that was recognized by a CTL clone. By using these two separate systems, we demonstrate that T cell activation can be hindered by mutations that either decrease or increase the binding half-life of the TCR-pMHC interaction. Our findings suggest that efficient T cell activation occurs within a specific range of dwell-time for the TCR-pMHC interaction. This limited range of dwell-time aligns with the exclusion of T cells with extremely low or high affinity from the expanded population during immune responses.

title: Crystal structure of human insulin-regulated aminopeptidase with specificity for cyclic peptides.
text: Insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP), also known as oxytocinase, is a zinc-metallopeptidase found in the membrane. It plays a role in cleaving neuroactive peptides in the brain and has been found to enhance memory when its activity is inhibited. By studying the crystal structure of human IRAP, we have discovered that it consists of four domains arranged in a closed configuration. Within this structure, there is a large cavity that is mostly hidden and located adjacent to the active site. Interestingly, the GAMEN exopeptidase loop in IRAP adopts a distinct conformation compared to other aminopeptidases. This explains why IRAP specifically targets cyclic peptides like oxytocin and vasopressin. Through computational docking, we have successfully mapped a series of cognitive enhancers that are specific to IRAP onto the crystal structure. This provides valuable insights into the relationship between their structure and activity. Furthermore, it demonstrates the potential of using this structure as a powerful tool in the development of new cognitive enhancers for the treatment of various memory disorders, including Alzheimer's disease.

title: Glutathione and glutathione-dependent enzymes represent a co-ordinately regulated defence against oxidative stress.
text: Elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) within cells, known as oxidative stress, can be harmful and lead to dysfunction of cell membranes, DNA damage, and protein inactivation. Chronic oxidative stress is associated with various diseases including cancer, arthritis, and neurodegenerative disorders. The metabolism of glutathione plays a crucial role in protecting cells against oxidative stress caused by harmful agents. Glutathione, a tripeptide, is a key component of a complex detoxification system that relies on the interdependence of its different components. Glutathione functions at multiple levels to detoxify the cell, including scavenging free radicals, reducing peroxides, and conjugating with electrophilic compounds. Therefore, glutathione provides the cell with multiple defenses against both ROS and their toxic byproducts. This article explores how glutathione biosynthesis, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, and glutathione S-conjugate efflux pumps work together to help cells adapt to oxidative stress. The coordination of this response is partially achieved through the antioxidant responsive element (ARE), which is present in the promoters of genes that can be induced by oxidative and chemical stress. Transcriptional activation through the ARE is mediated by certain transcription factors, such as Nrf and small Maf proteins. The article also discusses the mechanisms by which intracellular sensors detect ROS and thiol-active chemicals that induce gene expression through the ARE. Activation of genes through the ARE is responsible for the increased antioxidant and detoxification capacity observed in normal cells treated with cancer chemopreventive agents. In some cases, it may also explain why tumors develop resistance to cancer chemotherapeutic drugs. Therefore, understanding the regulation of ARE-driven gene expression has significant implications for medical research.

title: Does socioeconomic status matter? A meta-analysis on parent training effectiveness for disruptive child behavior.
text: The effectiveness of parent training programs is often assumed to be diminished for families with a disadvantaged socioeconomic status (SES). However, the influence of initial problem severity on the effects of SES has been largely overlooked. In this meta-analysis, we aimed to determine (a) whether SES has a different impact on parent training effectiveness immediately after treatment and at a 1-year follow-up, while controlling for initial problem severity levels, and (b) whether SES interacts with initial problem severity in its effect on program effectiveness. We included 75 studies that focused on reducing disruptive child behavior through parent training programs. Separate analyses were conducted for the immediate posttreatment period and the approximately 1-year follow-up assessments. Our findings revealed that disadvantaged samples benefited less from parent training immediately after treatment, but only when they had low levels of initial problem severity. At the follow-up assessment, disadvantaged samples benefited less from parent training regardless of initial problem severity. Initial problem severity was a strong predictor of effect sizes both immediately after treatment and at the follow-up assessment. Interestingly, parent training programs were equally effective for disadvantaged and nondisadvantaged families immediately after treatment, particularly when initial problems were severe. However, it was more challenging for disadvantaged families to maintain the treatment gains, suggesting that they may require more sustained family support.

title: Infectiousness of malaria-endemic human populations to vectors.
text: The infectiousness of human populations to mosquitoes, which plays a crucial role in determining the stability and intensity of malaria transmission, has rarely been estimated. In studies analyzing malaria transmission in the field, the prevalence of asexual parasites or gametocytes has often been used as a proxy for infectiousness. In this study, we present empirical data on human infectiousness from Africa and Papua New Guinea. Our findings show that there is little correlation between the infectiousness of human populations to mosquitoes and the intensity of mosquito-to-human transmission, across a wide range of transmission levels. We compare these findings with the predictions of a simulation model of Plasmodium falciparum epidemiology. The model suggests that there is minimal variation in the infectiousness of the human population for entomologic inoculation rates (EIRs) above approximately 10 infectious bites per year. This indicates that the lack of relationship between EIR and the infectious reservoir can be explained without considering the effects of acquired transmission-blocking immunity. However, due to the limited availability of field data from areas with an EIR below 10 per year, we were unable to validate the model predictions for low EIR values. These results suggest that interventions aimed at reducing mosquito-to-human transmission will have little to no impact on human infectiousness in most rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa, where transmission levels are typically high. Unless significant reductions in transmission can be achieved, it is necessary to implement interventions that target the density or infectiousness of blood stage parasites, in addition to measures to prevent mosquito-to-human transmission.

title: Molecular analysis of circulating tumour cells—biology and biomarkers
text: The growing evidence of intratumour heterogeneity suggests that single-site biopsies are insufficient in providing a complete understanding of a tumour's genomic landscape. As targeted therapies become more prevalent in clinical practice, it is increasingly important to screen tumours for genomic abnormalities and investigate resistance mechanisms when the disease progresses. However, obtaining multiple biopsies from different locations and at different times is impractical, uncomfortable for patients, and carries risks. In this article, we explore how circulating tumour cells (CTCs) can be captured through a minimally invasive blood test and easily sampled multiple times, offering potential insights into intratumour heterogeneity and tumour evolution. However, the clinical usefulness of this approach is yet to be determined. The CellSearch® system is a validated technology for detecting and isolating CTCs, but other methods are also gaining recognition. We also discuss how recent discoveries regarding CTCs align with mechanisms of haematological spread observed in preclinical models, including evidence of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, collective cell migration, and the presence of cells with tumour-initiating capabilities in the circulation. Advances in single-cell molecular analysis are improving our understanding of metastasis mechanisms, and the combination of CTC and cell-free DNA assays is expected to provide valuable blood-based biomarkers for real-time patient monitoring and treatment planning.

title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress contributes to beta cell apoptosis in type 2 diabetes
text: The impact of elevated lipid levels on beta cells can lead to their death, contributing to a decrease in beta cell mass in type 2 diabetes. Our study aimed to determine if endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress plays a role in lipid-induced apoptosis in beta cells, and if ER stress is present in both animal models and humans with type 2 diabetes. We examined the expression of genes associated with ER stress in insulin-secreting MIN6 cells exposed to high lipid levels, islets isolated from db/db mice, and pancreas sections from individuals with type 2 diabetes. To assess the effect of reducing ER stress on lipid-induced apoptosis, we increased the production of the ER chaperone heat shock 70 kDa protein 5 (HSPA5, also known as immunoglobulin heavy chain binding protein [BIP]). Our findings revealed that the pro-apoptotic fatty acid palmitate triggered a significant ER stress response in MIN6 cells, while the non-apoptotic fatty acid oleate did not. The mRNA levels of activating transcription factor 4 (Atf4), DNA-damage inducible transcript 3 (Ddit3, also known as C/EBP homologous protein [Chop]), and DnaJ homologue (HSP40) C3 (Dnajc3, also known as p58) increased over time in palmitate-treated MIN6 cells, correlating with increased apoptosis. However, this correlation was not observed in oleate-treated cells. By increasing the production of HSPA5 in MIN6 cells, we were able to significantly protect against lipid-induced apoptosis by reducing ER stress. In islets from db/db mice, we observed an upregulation of various marker genes associated with ER stress. Additionally, we observed increased processing (activation) of X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) mRNA, confirming the presence of ER stress. Finally, in pancreas sections from individuals with type 2 diabetes, we observed increased production of HSPA5, DDIT3, DNAJC3, and BCL2-associated X protein in islet cells. These findings provide evidence that ER stress is present in type 2 diabetes and plays a role in the failure of beta cells.

title: Coactivator SRC-2-dependent metabolic reprogramming mediates prostate cancer survival and metastasis.
text: The reprogramming of metabolic pathways is a key characteristic of cancer cell growth and survival. It enables these rapidly dividing cells to meet their anabolic and energetic needs. While the regulators of tumor metabolism are not fully understood, they hold promise as targets for cancer therapy. In this study, we discovered that the upregulation of the oncogenic transcriptional coregulator SRC-2 (also known as NCOA2) drives the production of lipids from glutamine, supporting the survival and spread of tumor cells. SRC-2 levels were found to be significantly elevated in various tumors, particularly in prostate cancer, where it was amplified and overexpressed in 37% of metastatic tumors. In prostate cancer cells, SRC-2 stimulated a process called reductive carboxylation, which converts α-ketoglutarate into citrate through retrograde TCA cycling. This promotes lipogenesis and alters glutamine metabolism. The activation of SRC-2 by glutamine-mediated nutrient signaling, via mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation, triggers downstream transcriptional responses by coactivating SREBP-1. This, in turn, enhances the expression of lipogenic enzymes. Metabolic profiling of human prostate tumors revealed a significant increase in the metabolic signature driven by SRC-2 in metastatic tumors compared to localized tumors, further highlighting its role as a key coordinator of cancer metastasis. Additionally, inhibiting SRC-2 in mouse models significantly reduced the survival, growth, and spread of prostate cancer. These findings suggest that targeting the SRC-2 pathway could be a potential therapeutic strategy for prostate cancer.

title: In vitro substrate specificity of protein tyrosine kinases
text: Protein tyrosine kinases have long been thought to be promiscuous, phosphorylating synthetic peptides like P60stc autophosphorylation site peptides and angiotensin without much regard for site specificity. However, recent evidence suggests that this belief needs to be reexamined. Researchers have obtained synthetic peptides that show high substrate activity for specific groups of protein tyrosine kinases. By systematically modifying certain substrate peptides, they have found that the determinants for kinase substrate reside in specific amino acid residues near the target tyrosine. Furthermore, it has been discovered that certain protein kinases are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation at specific sites by highly specific protein tyrosine kinases. This review discusses these findings and other biochemical studies that contribute to our evolving understanding of the substrate specificity of protein tyrosine kinases in vitro.

title: Relative effectiveness of clinic and home blood pressure monitoring compared with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in diagnosis of hypertension: systematic review
text:
The objective of this study was to compare the accuracy of clinic measurements and home blood pressure monitoring with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring for diagnosing hypertension. The study design was a systematic review with meta-analysis using hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic models. The quality of the studies was assessed, including validation of blood pressure measurement equipment. The data sources included Medline, Embase, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, DARE, Medion, ARIF, and TRIP up to May 2010. The eligibility criteria for selecting studies were that they examined the diagnosis of hypertension in adults using home and/or clinic blood pressure measurement compared to ambulatory monitoring with clearly defined thresholds for diagnosing hypertension.

The results showed that out of the 20 eligible studies, only seven (clinic) and three (home) studies could be directly compared to ambulatory monitoring. When compared to ambulatory monitoring thresholds of 135/85 mm Hg, clinic measurements over 140/90 mm Hg had a mean sensitivity of 74.6% (95% confidence interval 60.7% to 84.8%) and specificity of 74.6% (47.9% to 90.4%). Home measurements over 135/85 mm Hg had a mean sensitivity of 85.7% (78.0% to 91.0%) and specificity of 62.4% (48.0% to 75.0%).

In conclusion, neither clinic nor home measurement alone had sufficient sensitivity or specificity to be recommended as a single diagnostic test for hypertension. Relying solely on clinic or home blood pressure measurements for treatment decisions may lead to overdiagnosis. It is suggested that ambulatory monitoring be used before initiating lifelong drug treatment to ensure more appropriate targeting of treatment, especially around the diagnostic threshold.

title: Purification and characterization of mouse hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Using a range of phenotypic markers, researchers successfully isolated hematopoietic stem cells from mouse bone marrow. These cells have the remarkable ability to multiply and transform into myelomonocytic cells, B cells, or T cells with nearly perfect efficiency. Remarkably, only thirty of these cells are needed to rescue half of the mice exposed to lethal radiation, while also restoring all types of blood cells in the surviving animals.

title: Regulation of arabinose and xylose metabolism in Escherichia coli.
text: When multiple sugars are provided, bacteria like Escherichia coli often consume them one at a time, a process known as carbon catabolite repression. A well-known example is the consumption of glucose and lactose, where E. coli prioritizes glucose and only starts consuming lactose once all the glucose is consumed. Glucose not only represses lactose consumption but also the consumption of other sugars like arabinose and xylose. In this study, we investigated another hierarchy in E. coli, specifically between arabinose and xylose. Our findings reveal that when E. coli is grown in a mixture of these two pentoses, it consumes arabinose before xylose. This preference is consistent with catabolite repression, as the presence of arabinose represses the expression of xylose metabolic genes. We discovered that this repression is dependent on AraC and involves arabinose-bound AraC binding to xylose promoters to repress gene expression. Overall, our results demonstrate that sugar utilization in E. coli is regulated by multiple layers, with glucose being consumed first, followed by arabinose, and finally xylose. These findings have implications for the metabolic engineering of E. coli strains capable of producing chemicals and biofuels from a mixture of hexose and pentose sugars derived from plant biomass.

title: MicroRNA expression profiling of human metastatic cancers identifies cancer gene targets.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) that do not code for proteins play a role in the development and progression of cancer. They are expressed differently in normal tissues and cancerous tissues. However, their specific role in the spread of cancer is still unknown. In order to identify miRNAs that are associated with the metastatic phenotype of solid tumors, we conducted a miRNA microarray analysis on 43 pairs of primary tumors (including colon, bladder, breast, and lung cancers) and their corresponding metastatic lymph nodes. We discovered a miRNA signature consisting of 15 overexpressed and 17 underexpressed miRNAs in metastatic cancer. Our findings were validated through qRT-PCR analysis. Some of the identified miRNAs, such as miR-10b, miR-21, miR-30a, miR-30e, miR-125b, miR-141, miR-200b, miR-200c, and miR-205, are already known to be associated with cancer progression. To further support our results, we conducted an immunohistochemical analysis on a small sample of paired colon, breast, and bladder cancers, as well as their metastatic lymph nodes, targeting three well-defined miRNA gene targets (PDCD4, DHFR, and HOXD10 genes). We found that the expression of these targets, as determined by immunohistochemistry, closely matched the deregulation of the corresponding miRNAs. Our findings suggest that specific miRNAs may play a direct role in cancer metastasis and could serve as a new diagnostic tool for identifying gene targets in metastatic cancer.

title: Circos: an information aesthetic for comparative genomics.
text:
We have developed a visualization tool called Circos that makes it easier to identify and analyze similarities and differences in genomes. Our tool is highly effective in showing variations in genome structure and any other positional relationships between genomic intervals. This type of data is commonly generated through sequence alignments, hybridization arrays, genome mapping, and genotyping studies. 

Circos utilizes a circular ideogram layout to display relationships between pairs of positions using ribbons. These ribbons encode the position, size, and orientation of related genomic elements. Additionally, Circos can present data in various formats such as scatter plots, line plots, histogram plots, heat maps, tiles, connectors, and text. 

By using GFF-style data inputs and hierarchical configuration files, Circos allows users to create bitmap or vector images. These configuration files can be easily generated using automated tools, making Circos suitable for quick deployment in data analysis and reporting pipelines.

title: Pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and clinical profile of novel antiplatelet drugs targeting vascular diseases.
text: Platelet inhibitors are the primary treatment for patients with vascular diseases. However, the current leading antiplatelet agent, clopidogrel, has certain limitations both in terms of its pharmacological properties and clinical effectiveness. As a result, researchers have been searching for more efficient platelet antagonists. Some potential candidates include blockers of the purinergic P2Y12 receptor, such as prasugrel, an oral irreversible thienopyridine. There are also two adenosine triphosphate analogues, ticagrelor (oral) and cangrelor (intravenous), which bind reversibly to the P2Y12 receptor. Elinogrel is a direct-acting reversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor that can be administered both intravenously and orally, making it unique among antiplatelet compounds. Other options include BX 667, an orally active and reversible small-molecule P2Y12 receptor antagonist, as well as SCH 530348, SCH 205831, SCH 602539, and E5555, which are highly selective and orally active antagonists on the protease-activated receptor 1. Additionally, there are drugs that target new sites, such as terutroban, an oral, selective, and specific inhibitor of the thromboxane receptor; ARC1779, a second-generation, nuclease-resistant aptamer that inhibits von Willebrand factor-dependent platelet aggregation; ALX-0081, a bivalent humanized nanobody that targets the GPIb binding site of von Willebrand factor; and AJW200, an IgG4 monoclonal antibody of von Willebrand factor. The pharmacology and clinical profiles of these new platelet antagonists suggest that they offer more consistent, rapid, and potent platelet inhibition compared to current agents. However, further comparisons in properly powered, randomized, controlled trials are needed to determine if these potential advantages translate into clinical benefits.

title: BLM is required for faithful chromosome segregation and its localization defines a class of ultrafine anaphase bridges.
text: Our study focused on the role of BLM in maintaining accurate chromosome segregation in human cells. Mutations in BLM are responsible for Bloom's syndrome, a disorder linked to an increased risk of cancer and chromosomal instability. To investigate this further, we compared BLM-defective cells to those that expressed the BLM protein. The BLM-defective cells exhibited a higher occurrence of anaphase bridges and lagging chromatin, whereas the corrected cells did not. During mitosis in normal cells, the BLM protein localized to anaphase bridges, along with its partners topoisomerase IIIalpha and hRMI1 (BLAP75). By using BLM staining as a marker, we discovered a type of ultrafine DNA bridge in anaphase that was surprisingly common in normal human cells. These bridges, known as BLM-DNA bridges, also showed staining for the PICH protein and frequently connected centromeric loci. Cells lacking BLM had a higher frequency of these bridges. Based on our findings, we propose that sister-chromatid disjunction is often incomplete in human cells, even after anaphase begins. We have developed a model that explains how BLM ensures complete sister chromatid decatenation during anaphase.

title: Association Between High Serum Soluble Corin and Hypertension: A Cross-Sectional Study in a General Population of China.
text:
The association between Corin and hypertension has been suggested by cell- and animal-based studies. However, there is still a lack of population-based evidence to support this association, which is crucial for translating basic research into clinical and preventive practice. Therefore, our aim was to investigate this association in a general population in China.

Between January and May 2010, we conducted a cross-sectional study involving 2,498 participants aged above 30 years who resided in the Gusu district of Suzhou. We measured serum soluble corin levels and blood pressure.

The results showed that hypertensive participants had higher levels of serum corin compared to nonhypertensive participants (median (interquartile range): 1,836.83 (1,497.85-2,327.87) pg/ml vs. 1,579.14 (1,322.18-1,956.82) pg/ml, P < 0.001). There was a positive association between higher serum corin levels and prevalent hypertension (odds ratio (OR) = 2.01, P < 0.001). In the multiple analysis, participants in the third (OR = 1.43, P = 0.007) and fourth (OR = 1.96, P < 0.001) quartiles of serum corin had significantly increased odds of hypertension compared to those in the lowest quartile. The odds ratios of hypertension also increased significantly with higher serum corin levels (P for trend <0.001). Subgroup analysis revealed that the odds ratios of hypertension associated with high corin levels (above the median level of 1,689.20 pg/ml) remained significant in subgroups based on age, body mass index, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and fasting plasma glucose (all P < 0.05).

In conclusion, our study demonstrated that hypertensive individuals had elevated levels of serum corin compared to those without hypertension. This finding suggests that corin may play a role in the development of hypertension.

title: Shared and distinct genetic variants in type 1 diabetes and celiac disease.
text:
The background of this study involves two inflammatory disorders, type 1 diabetes and celiac disease, which are often found together in populations, indicating a possible shared genetic origin. The HLA class II genes on chromosome 6p21 are associated with both diseases, so the researchers aimed to determine if there are any non-HLA genes that are also shared.

To do this, they conducted genotyping and statistical analyses on DNA samples from 8064 patients with type 1 diabetes, 9339 control subjects, and 2828 families (3064 parent-child trios). They also examined 18 loci associated with type 1 diabetes in 2560 patients with celiac disease and 9339 control subjects.

The results showed that three celiac disease loci (RGS1 on chromosome 1q31, IL18RAP on chromosome 2q12, and TAGAP on chromosome 6q25) were associated with type 1 diabetes. Additionally, a 32-bp insertion-deletion variant on chromosome 3p21 was identified as a new type 1 diabetes locus. This variant was also associated with celiac disease, along with PTPN2 on chromosome 18p11 and CTLA4 on chromosome 2q33. In total, there were seven loci with evidence of a shared association, including SH2B3 on chromosome 12q24. The IL18RAP and TAGAP alleles were found to confer protection in type 1 diabetes but susceptibility in celiac disease.

There were also loci that had distinct effects in each disease. For type 1 diabetes, these included INS on chromosome 11p15, IL2RA on chromosome 10p15, and PTPN22 on chromosome 1p13. For celiac disease, the distinct loci were IL12A on 3q25 and LPP on 3q28.

In conclusion, this study suggests that there is a genetic susceptibility to both type 1 diabetes and celiac disease, with common alleles being shared. This indicates that there may be common biological mechanisms, such as autoimmunity-related tissue damage and intolerance to dietary antigens, that contribute to the development of both diseases.

title: Promotion of tumorigenesis by heterozygous disruption of the beclin 1 autophagy gene.
text: Defects in autophagy, a pathway responsible for breaking down long-lived proteins and cytoplasmic organelles, are often observed in malignant cells. However, there is currently no genetic proof that autophagy genes play a role in suppressing tumors. In human cases of sporadic breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer, the beclin 1 autophagy gene is deleted in one of the two copies in 40-75% of cases. To investigate whether this deletion promotes tumorigenesis, we conducted experiments using a targeted mutant mouse model. Our results show that disrupting one copy of the beclin 1 gene increases the occurrence of spontaneous malignancies and speeds up the development of premalignant lesions induced by the hepatitis B virus. Molecular analysis of tumors in these mice revealed that the remaining intact copy of the beclin 1 gene is not mutated or silenced. Additionally, disrupting one copy of beclin 1 leads to increased cellular proliferation and reduced autophagy in living organisms. These findings demonstrate that beclin 1 acts as a tumor-suppressor gene when only one copy is present, providing genetic evidence that autophagy is a novel mechanism for controlling cell growth and suppressing tumors. Therefore, mutations in beclin 1 or other autophagy genes may contribute to the development of human cancers.

title: Treatment-related mortality with bevacizumab in cancer patients: a meta-analysis.
text: The aim of this study was to determine the overall risk of fatal adverse events (FAEs) associated with the use of bevacizumab, a widely used angiogenesis inhibitor, in cancer patients. A systematic review and meta-analysis of published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. The researchers searched various databases and conference abstracts to identify relevant studies. Eligible studies included RCTs that compared bevacizumab in combination with chemotherapy or biological therapy to chemotherapy or biological therapy alone. The analysis included a total of 10,217 patients from 16 RCTs. The overall incidence of FAEs with bevacizumab was found to be 2.5%. The addition of bevacizumab was associated with an increased risk of FAEs compared to chemotherapy alone. This association varied depending on the chemotherapeutic agents used, but not on tumor types or bevacizumab doses. Bevacizumab was found to increase the risk of FAEs in patients receiving taxanes or platinum agents, but not when used with other agents. The most common causes of FAEs were hemorrhage, neutropenia, and gastrointestinal tract perforation. In conclusion, the meta-analysis showed that bevacizumab in combination with chemotherapy or biological therapy was associated with increased treatment-related mortality compared to chemotherapy alone.

title: Quiescent and active hippocampal neural stem cells with distinct morphologies respond selectively to physiological and pathological stimuli and aging.
text: Throughout a person's life, new neurons are continuously produced in the adult hippocampus by neural stem/progenitor cells (NSCs). This process, known as neurogenesis, is influenced by external stimuli and can be altered. Our research demonstrates that the canonical Notch signaling pathway, specifically through RBP-J, is crucial for neurogenesis in the hippocampus. Notch signaling helps distinguish different types of NSCs, particularly those expressing Sox2. Within these NSC pools, subpopulations can transition between actively dividing or dormant states. Radial and horizontal NSCs respond differently to stimuli that promote neurogenesis. Physical exercise activates the dormant radial NSC population, while epileptic seizures cause an expansion of the horizontal NSC pool. Interestingly, in aged mice, a decrease in neurogenesis is associated with a decline in active horizontal NSCs rather than a complete loss of stem cells. Furthermore, the transition to a dormant state can be reversed, rejuvenating neurogenesis in the brain. These findings, which reveal the existence of multiple NSC populations with Notch dependence but distinct responses to stimuli and reversible dormancy, have significant implications for understanding adaptive learning mechanisms and regenerative therapy.

title: Low serum vitamin D is associated with high risk of diabetes in Korean adults.
text:
The role of vitamin D in glucose metabolism is being investigated, particularly in relation to the risk of diabetes mellitus. While a low vitamin D level has been linked to an increased risk of diabetes, this association has not been confirmed in Asians. Therefore, our objective was to examine the association between serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus in Korean adults, using data from a large population-based survey.

We conducted cross-sectional analyses on 5787 Korean adults (2453 men and 3334 women) aged 20 years or older, who participated in the Fourth Korea NHANES in 2008. Diabetes mellitus was defined as a fasting plasma glucose level of ≥7 mmol/L or current use of oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin. Insulin resistance was assessed using the homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and the quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI).

Compared to individuals with a sufficient serum 25(OH)D concentration of ≥75 nmol/L, the odds ratios (ORs) for diabetes mellitus were 1.73 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.09-2.74), 1.30 (95% CI: 0.91-1.84), and 1.40 (95% CI: 0.99-1.98) for serum 25(OH)D concentrations of <25, 25 to <50, and 50 to <75 nmol/L, respectively, after adjusting for multiple factors (P-trend < 0.0001). Additionally, we found that the serum 25(OH)D level was inversely associated with HOMA-IR (β = -0.061; P = 0.001) and positively associated with QUICKI (β = 0.059; P = 0.001) in overweight or obese participants.

In conclusion, our study suggests that a low serum vitamin D concentration is associated with an increased risk of diabetes mellitus in Korean adults. Furthermore, we found that this concentration is inversely associated with insulin resistance in overweight or obese individuals.

title: When NK cells overcome their lack of education.
text: The immune system's cells have developed different ways to detect their surroundings and respond to changes in the body. NK cells, a type of lymphocyte, have the ability to both regulate and attack, making them highly adaptable to changes within the body. In a recent study published in the JCI, Tarek and his team highlight the positive outcomes of manipulating NK cell adaptation to the body in a new therapy using monoclonal antibodies against neuroblastoma (NB). This groundbreaking approach to treatment should encourage further investigation into the potential of NK cell therapies.

title: Toll-like receptor-3 mediates HIV-1 transactivation via NFκB and JNK pathways and histone acetylation, but prolonged activation suppresses Tat and HIV-1 replication.
text: TLR3 has been implicated in the development of various viral infections, including inflammation and AIDS caused by SIV and HIV-1. However, the specific molecular mechanisms behind these effects mediated by TLR3 remain unknown, and it is unclear whether HIV interacts with cellular TLR3 to influence the disease process. In this study, we aimed to investigate the impact of TLR3 ligands on the activation of HIV-1 using primary human macrophages and cells containing integrated copies of the HIV-1 promoter. Our findings reveal that TLR3 activation leads to an increase in the expression of transcription factors such as c-Jun, CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha (CEBPA), signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)-1, STAT-2, RELB, and nuclear factor kappa-B1 (NFκB1), most of which are known to regulate the activity of the HIV promoter. Additionally, we demonstrate that TLR3 activation enhances HIV-1 transactivation through the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and NFκB pathways. This effect is accompanied by epigenetic modifications, including a decrease in histone deacetylase activity, an increase in histone acetyl transferase (HAT) activity, and an increase in the acetylation of histones H3 and H4 at lysine residues in the nucleosome-0 and nucleosome-1 regions of the HIV-1 promoter. However, prolonged TLR3 activation leads to a decrease in HIV-1 transactivation, a reduction in HAT activity and Tat transcription, and a suppression of viral replication. Overall, our data suggests that TLR3 can function as a viral sensor, mediating viral transactivation, cellular signaling, innate immune response, and inflammation in individuals infected with HIV. This study provides new insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for these TLR3-mediated effects.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus: are current neonatal treatment options better or worse than no treatment at all?
text: There is a lack of consensus regarding the optimal timing for closing a moderate-sized patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in infants. While it is generally agreed that closure should occur by the age of 1-2 years, there is uncertainty about whether it needs to be closed during the neonatal period. Neonatologists mostly agree that a moderate-sized PDA should be closed in premature infants (born before 28 weeks) who still require mechanical ventilation. However, there is significant variation among neonatologists in treating a PDA in infants who do not require mechanical ventilation. The uncertainty is further compounded by the high likelihood of spontaneous ductus closure and the absence of randomized controlled trials specifically addressing the risks and benefits of neonatal ductus closure. Recent evidence suggests that early pharmacologic treatment can provide important short-term benefits for preterm newborns. On the other hand, while ductus ligation can eliminate the negative effects of a PDA on lung development, it may introduce its own set of complications that offset the benefits of closure.

title: A conserved phosphatase cascade that regulates nuclear membrane biogenesis.
text: A newly emerging group of phosphatases, which belong to the haloacid dehalogenase superfamily, contains the catalytic motif DXDX(T/V). One member of this DXDX(T/V) phosphatase family, called Dullard, has recently been identified as a potential regulator of neural tube development in Xenopus [Satow R, Chan TC, Asashima M (2002) Biochem Biophys Res Commun 295:85-91]. In this study, we demonstrate that both human Dullard and the yeast protein Nem1p have similar functions in mammalian and yeast cells, respectively. Not only do Dullard and Nem1p share similarities in their primary sequences, but they also possess similar domains, exhibit similar substrate preferences, and localize to the nuclear envelope. Furthermore, we show that human Dullard can rescue the abnormal nuclear envelope morphology observed in nem1Delta yeast cells, effectively replacing Nem1p. Additionally, it has been reported that Nem1p dephosphorylates the yeast phosphatidic acid phosphatase Smp2p [Santos-Rosa H, Leung J, Grimsey N, Peak-Chew S, Siniossoglou S (2005) EMBO J 24:1931-1941], and we demonstrate that Dullard dephosphorylates the mammalian phosphatidic acid phosphatase, lipin. Based on these findings, we propose that Dullard is involved in a unique phosphatase cascade that regulates the biogenesis of the nuclear membrane, and that this cascade is conserved from yeast to mammals.

title: Increased expression of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 in ovarian/peritoneal endometriotic lesions.
text: Endometriosis is a disease that is influenced by estrogen and affects approximately 10% of premenopausal women. Research suggests that different sites of endometriosis have varying levels of estrogen, possibly due to unique local estrogen metabolism. Our study aimed to investigate whether specific enzymes responsible for estrogen metabolism were regulated differently in biopsy samples and stromal cells from endometrial and endometriotic tissues. We evaluated the expression of Cytochrome P450 (CYP) 1A1 and CYP1B1 mRNA and protein in deep-infiltrating lesions (rectal, retossigmoidal, and uterossacral), superficial lesions (ovarian and peritoneal), and healthy endometrium. Using a cross-sectional study with 58 premenopausal women not undergoing hormonal treatment, we found that CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 mRNA expression was generally higher in superficial lesions compared to healthy endometrium. Additionally, CYP1A1 mRNA expression in superficial lesions was higher than in the eutopic endometrium. Interestingly, we observed a similar pattern of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 expression in stromal cells isolated from ovarian lesions compared to cells from rectum lesions or eutopic endometrium. However, we also found that estradiol had a longer half-life in ovarian endometriotic stromal cells compared to eutopic stromal endometrial cells. These findings suggest that CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 are regulated differently in ovarian/peritoneal lesions and ovarian endometriotic stromal cells, leading to a slower metabolism in these cells.

title: Eset partners with Oct4 to restrict extraembryonic trophoblast lineage potential in embryonic stem cells.
text: Eset, a methyltransferase enzyme responsible for histone H3 Lys 9 (H3K9) methylation, plays a crucial role as an epigenetic regulator in the development of the inner cell mass (ICM). Typically, ICM-derived embryonic stem (ES) cells are unable to differentiate into trophectoderm (TE) cells in blastocysts. However, our study reveals that depletion of Eset using shRNAs leads to differentiation, resulting in the formation of trophoblast-like cells and the activation of trophoblast-associated gene expression. Through chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and sequencing (ChIP-seq) analyses, we have identified Eset target genes that exhibit H3K9 trimethylation dependent on Eset. We have also confirmed that Eset binds to and represses genes preferentially expressed in the TE, such as Tcfap2a and Cdx2. Single-cell PCR analysis demonstrates that the expression of Cdx2 and Tcfap2a is induced in Eset-depleted morula cells. Importantly, Eset-depleted cells are capable of incorporating into the TE of a blastocyst and subsequently developing into placental tissues. Coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP assays further reveal that Eset interacts with Oct4, which in turn recruits Eset to silence these trophoblast-associated genes. Our findings suggest that Eset plays a role in restricting the potential of pluripotent cells to differentiate into extraembryonic trophoblast lineage, and it establishes a connection between an epigenetic regulator and key cell fate decisions mediated by a pluripotency factor.

title: Suicides after pregnancy in Finland, 1987-94: register linkage study.
text:
AIM
To investigate the rates of suicide related to pregnancy based on the type of pregnancy.

METHOD
This study utilized register linkage to analyze data on suicides in women of reproductive age. The Finnish birth, abortion, and hospital discharge registers were used to identify women who had completed a pregnancy in their last year of life.

LOCATION
