In this study, we demonstrate that the acetylation of two lysine residues in p53 facilitates the recruitment of the TFIID subunit TAF1 to the p21 promoter through its bromodomains. When cells are exposed to UV irradiation, p53 is diacetylated at lysines 373 and 382, leading to the recruitment of TAF1 to a distant p53-binding site on the p21 promoter before looping to the core promoter. Disrupting the interaction between acetyl-p53 and bromodomains hinders TAF1 recruitment to both the distant p53-binding site and the core promoter. Additionally, we observe the presence of TFIID subunits TAF4, TAF5, and TBP on the core promoter prior to TAF1, suggesting that different subunits of TFIID may be recruited separately to the p21 promoter in response to DNA damage. Overall, these findings highlight the significance of posttranslational modification of the p53 transcription factor in the transcriptional activation of the p21 gene.

title: Dasatinib inhibits both osteoclast activation and prostate cancer PC-3-cell-induced osteoclast formation.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of dasatinib, a Src family kinase inhibitor, in targeting prostate cancer bone metastases. Previous therapies have had limited effects, so new treatments are focusing on the interaction between cancer cells, bone marrow cells, and the bone matrix. Osteoclasts, which play a role in the development of bone tumors caused by prostate cancer, were targeted in this study.

The results showed that dasatinib inhibited the differentiation of osteoclasts from bone marrow-derived monocytes, with an EC(50) of 7.5 nM. It also inhibited the differentiation of osteoclasts induced by PC-3 cells, a human prostate cancer cell line. Additionally, dasatinib inhibited the differentiation of osteoclasts induced by conditioned medium from PC-3 cell cultures. Even at the lowest concentration tested (1.25 nmol), dasatinib inhibited osteoclast differentiation by 29%. Furthermore, dasatinib inhibited osteoclast activity by 58%, as measured by collagen 1 release.

The experimental design involved in vitro experiments using dasatinib to target osteoclast activation and inhibit prostate cancer bone metastases.

In conclusion, dasatinib was found to inhibit the differentiation of osteoclasts from mouse primary bone marrow-derived monocytes and PC-3 cell-induced osteoclast differentiation. It also inhibited osteoclast degradation activity. Inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and activity may be an effective targeted therapy for patients with prostate cancer bone metastases.

title: BMP receptor ALK3 controls collecting system development.
text:
The precise molecular signals that regulate the growth and branching of the ureteric bud during the formation of the renal collecting system are not well understood. However, it has been observed that members of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) family can inhibit the morphogenesis of ureteric bud and collecting duct cells in laboratory settings by signaling through the type I BMP receptor ALK3. To further investigate the role of the BMP signaling pathway in vivo, researchers created a mouse model with ALK3 deficiency specifically in the ureteric bud lineage (referred to as Alk3(UB-/-) mice).

During the initial stages of branching morphogenesis, Alk3(UB-/-) kidneys displayed an abnormal pattern of primary ureteric bud branches and an increased number of branches. However, as renal development progressed, these mutant kidneys had fewer ureteric bud branches and collecting ducts compared to normal, wild-type kidneys. Postnatally, Alk3(UB-/-) mice exhibited a dysplastic renal phenotype characterized by underdevelopment of the renal medulla, a reduced number of medullary collecting ducts, and abnormal expression of beta-catenin and c-MYC in the medullary tubules. In conclusion, the normal development of the kidney relies on ALK3-dependent BMP signaling, which plays a crucial role in controlling the branching of the ureteric bud.

title: Increased release of ferritin and iron by iron-loaded alveolar macrophages in cigarette smokers.
text: Cigarette smokers have an increased amount of iron in their lower respiratory tract, which is mainly found in alveolar macrophages (AM) but also in alveolar epithelial fluid. This iron, bound to ferritin, could potentially be released by reductants in cigarette smoke and cause damage through the generation of reactive hydroxyl radicals. To investigate if AM are a source of extracellular ferritin and iron in the alveoli, we studied the release of iron, ferritin, and transferrin by AM obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) of 27 healthy individuals, including nine nonsmokers (NS), nine light smokers (LS), and nine heavy smokers (HS). In vitro experiments showed that the release of iron over 20 hours was higher in AM from LS (2.24 +/- 0.21 nmol/10(6) AM/20 h, p < 0.001) and HS (3.11 +/- 0.32 nmol/10(6) AM, p < 0.001) compared to NS (1.28 +/- 0.08 nmol/10(6) AM). Similarly, the release of ferritin over 20 hours was increased in AM from LS (71 +/- 24 ng/10(6) AM, p < 0.05) and HS (176 +/- 35 ng/10(6), p < 0.001) compared to NS (18 +/- 3 ng/10(6) AM). AM from 12 smokers (8 HS, 4 LS) contained more than 10 nmol of iron per 10(6) cells. These iron-loaded AM released a higher percentage of their ferritin stores in vitro over 4 hours (8.4% +/- 1.1, p < 0.01) compared to AM from NS (3.2% +/- 0.6). The release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) over 4 hours was significantly lower (2.9% +/- 0.3, p < 0.001) than ferritin release.

title: The spectrum of retinopathy in adults with Plasmodium falciparum malaria
text: A specific retinopathy has been identified in African children with cerebral malaria, but there has been limited research on this condition in adults. Since the structure and function of the retinal blood vessels closely resemble those of the cerebral blood vessels, studying retinal changes can provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of cerebral malaria. To investigate malarial retinopathy in Bangladeshi adults, a detailed observational study was conducted using high-definition portable retinal photography. The study found that retinopathy was present in 63% of adults with severe malaria and 70% of adults with cerebral malaria. The occurrence of moderate or severe retinopathy was higher in cerebral malaria compared to uncomplicated malaria, bacterial sepsis, or healthy individuals. The spectrum of malarial retinopathy observed in Bangladeshi adults was similar to that seen in African children, but there was no discoloration of the blood vessels. The severity of retinal whitening was found to be correlated with elevated levels of venous plasma lactate upon admission, suggesting that retinal ischemia reflects systemic ischemia. In conclusion, retinal changes associated with microvascular blockage were common in adults with severe falciparum malaria and were linked to disease severity and coma, indicating that compromised microcirculation plays a significant role in the pathophysiology of severe and cerebral malaria. Portable retinal photography shows promise as a valuable tool for studying malarial retinopathy.

title: Prospective randomized open blinded end-point (PROBE) study. A novel design for intervention trials. Prospective Randomized Open Blinded End-Point.
text: Introducing a novel approach to intervention studies, we present the PROBE study (Prospective Randomized Open, Blinded End-point). This innovative design is compared to the traditional double-blind design. The PROBE design offers several advantages, including reduced costs and a closer resemblance to standard clinical practice. Consequently, the results obtained from the PROBE study are more readily applicable in routine medical care. As the evaluation of end-points is conducted by a blinded end-point committee, it is evident that there should be no disparity between the two trial types in this aspect.

title: PSGL-1 function in immunity and steady state homeostasis.
text: The importance of P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) in the movement of white blood cells has become increasingly evident since its initial discovery as a ligand for selectins. PSGL-1 was initially thought to be a simple molecule with a flexible rod-like structure, which allowed it to tether white blood cells to the walls of blood vessels. This interaction between white blood cells and the blood vessel walls, facilitated by selectin-PSGL-1 binding, requires the presence of branched O-glycan extensions on specific amino acid residues of PSGL-1. In some cells, like neutrophils, the enzymes responsible for adding these O-glycans are always present, while in other cells, like T cells, they are only expressed after activation. As a result, PSGL-1 supports the recruitment of white blood cells in both the innate and adaptive immune responses. The selectins engage with multiple sugar residues on the branched O-glycans of PSGL-1, creating velcro-like catch bonds that enable white blood cells to roll along the blood vessel walls. Additionally, binding of PSGL-1 can trigger signaling events that affect the behavior and function of the cells. Further investigation of PSGL-1 has provided a better understanding of its role as a selectin ligand and has revealed unexpected insights into its involvement in processes such as stem cell migration to the thymus and mature T-cell migration to secondary lymphoid organs. PSGL-1 has also been found to bind to homeostatic chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, supporting the movement of cells in response to these chemokines. Interestingly, the O-glycan modifications of PSGL-1 that facilitate rolling in inflammatory conditions interfere with its binding to homeostatic chemokines, limiting the response to chemotactic signals during normal T-cell traffic. The impact of PSGL-1 on cell movement in both inflammatory and normal conditions is largely determined by the addition of O-glycans. However, the regulation of PSGL-1 glycosylation in T cells in vivo is not well understood. The purpose of this review is to summarize the current knowledge and gaps in understanding of PSGL-1 glycosylation and to provide an update on its functional role.

title: Ligand binding determines whether CD46 is internalized by clathrin-coated pits or macropinocytosis.
text: CD46 is a receptor found on the surface of human cells that interacts with complement components C3b and C4b, as well as various pathogens like the measles virus and human herpes virus 6. When ligands bind to CD46, it has several effects: (i) it protects the body's own cells from complement attack by breaking down complement components, (ii) it influences intracellular signals that regulate immune cell function, (iii) it plays a role in antigen presentation, and (iv) it down-regulates the presence of CD46 on the cell surface. Recent evidence suggests that CD46 signaling can connect innate and acquired immune function, but the specific molecular mechanisms and the importance of receptor trafficking within cells are still not fully understood. Our research demonstrates that in nonlymphoid cells, CD46 is constantly internalized through clathrin-coated pits, transported to multivesicular bodies, and then recycled back to the cell surface. However, when CD46 is cross-linked at the cell surface by multivalent antibodies or the measles virus, it triggers the formation of pseudopodia that engulf the ligand, resembling a process called macropinocytosis, and ultimately leads to the degradation of CD46 on the cell surface. Therefore, we have identified two pathways for CD46 internalization, which are regulated by the strength of cross-linking and utilize either clathrin-coated pits or pseudopodial extension. This discovery has significant implications for understanding CD46 signaling, antigen presentation, CD46 down-regulation, and the engulfment of pathogens.

title: A three-dimensional cell biology model of human hepatocellular carcinoma in vitro
text: We developed a three-dimensional (3-D) model of metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) using MHCC97H cells cultured on molecular scaffolds in a rotating wall vessel bioreactor. Through morphological and biochemical analyses, we found that this 3-D HCC model accurately replicated various clinical pathological features of HCC, such as cancer cell appearance, tissue structure, protein production and release, glucose metabolism, tissue-specific gene expression, and programmed cell death. When xenografted into the livers of nude mice, these 3-D HCC spheroids led to the formation of tumors and distant metastasis. Consequently, this 3-D HCC model holds great promise for studying HCC tumor biology, screening anticancer drugs, and establishing animal models for HCC research.

title: Patterns of age-specific mortality in children in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa.
text: Understanding the relationship between age, season, and malaria mortality is crucial for developing epidemiologic models of malaria immunity. However, many studies on malaria mortality have grouped their findings into broad age categories and across seasons, making it difficult to predict the potential impact of interventions targeted at specific age groups of children. In this study, we provide age-specific mortality rates for children under the age of 15 from 2001 to 2005 in seven demographic surveillance sites located in areas of sub-Saharan Africa with stable endemic Plasmodium falciparum malaria. We utilize verbal autopsies (VAs) to estimate the percentage of deaths caused by malaria within each age group, allowing us to calculate malaria-specific mortality rates for each site, age group, and month of the year. Across all sites, a significant proportion of deaths (ranging from 20.1% in a Mozambican site to 46.2% in a site in Burkina Faso) were attributed to malaria. The overall patterns of malaria mortality by age were similar across the different sites. Deaths in infants under three months old were rarely attributed to malaria, but in children over one year old, the proportion of deaths attributed to malaria showed weak age dependence. While most sites experienced peak all-cause mortality rates during the rainy season, the strong seasonality in malaria transmission did not necessarily correspond to strong seasonality in the proportion of deaths attributed to malaria, except in the two sites in Burkina Faso. Improving the accuracy of malaria verbal autopsies would facilitate the interpretation of age and season patterns in this type of data.

title: Obesity due to melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) deficiency is associated with increased linear growth and final height, fasting hyperinsulinemia, and incompletely suppressed growth hormone secretion.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the somatotroph axis in obese individuals with Melanocortin receptor 4 (MC4R) deficiency compared to equally obese controls. Anthropometric measurements and insulin concentrations were obtained from 153 MC4R-deficient subjects and 1392 controls who were matched for age and severity of obesity. In a subset of 33 MC4R-deficient patients and 36 control subjects, fasting levels of IGF-I, IGF-II, IGF binding protein (IGFBP)-1, IGFBP-3, and acid-labile subunit were measured. Pulsatile GH secretion was examined in six adult MC4R-deficient subjects and six obese controls. 

The results showed that height sd score was significantly higher in MC4R-deficient children under 5 years old compared to controls, and this effect persisted throughout childhood. Final height was also greater in MC4R-deficient men and women. Fasting levels of IGF-I, IGF-II, acid-labile subunit, and IGFBP-3 were similar in both groups. GH levels were suppressed in obese controls, but pulsatile GH secretion was maintained in MC4R deficiency. The mean maximal GH secretion rate per burst and mass per burst were increased in MC4R deficiency, indicating increased pulsatile and total GH secretion. Fasting insulin levels were significantly elevated in MC4R-deficient children.

In conclusion, MC4R deficiency leads to increased linear growth in childhood, resulting in greater adult final height than expected based on obesity alone. The maintenance of GH pulsatility in MC4R deficiency suggests a role for MC4R in controlling hypothalamic somatostatinergic tone. Elevated fasting insulin levels in children with MC4R mutations may also contribute to the accelerated growth phenotype observed in MC4R deficiency.

title: The selectivity of beta-adrenoceptor antagonists on isoprenaline-induced changes in heart rate, blood pressure, soleus muscle contractility and airways function in anaesthetized cats.
text:
The effects of several beta-adrenoceptor antagonists, including propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol, and butoxamine, were studied in anaesthetized cats. These were compared to the effects of four synthetic phenylethanolamine derivatives. The study measured the impact of isoprenaline on various parameters in the anaesthetized cat, such as heart rate, blood pressure, soleus muscle contractility, and airway reactance. The researchers also assessed how each antagonist drug modified the dose-response relationship of isoprenaline. 

The study found that propranolol caused parallel shifts in the log dose-response curves for isoprenaline in all parameters. Metoprolol and atenolol had similar effects on all parameters except blood pressure, while butoxamine affected all parameters except soleus muscle and heart rate. To measure the selectivity of action of the antagonists in different organs, the researchers compared DR10 values computed from isoprenaline dose-ratios. Propranolol was the most potent antagonist and showed slight selectivity of action on the soleus muscle compared to the heart. Atenolol and metoprolol were approximately equally potent and only cardioselective at low doses. Butoxamine was the least potent antagonist and had non-beta-adrenoceptor effects on the measured parameters. 

The study also examined four new compounds: 4'-bromo-2'-methoxy-N-isopropyl phenylethanolamine, the 4'-chloro- and 4'-methyl analogues, and 4'-methoxy-N-t-butyl phenylethanolamine. These compounds were found to be potent antagonists but did not exhibit any selectivity of action. 

Overall, the results suggest that there is no clear separation of beta-adrenoceptors into beta 1- and beta 2-subclasses in the organs of the cat. Additionally, there is no apparent separation of beta-adrenoceptor-mediated effects on skeletal muscle and airways.

title: Breast cancer and obesity: an update.
text: The relationship between obesity and breast cancer risk, as well as the behavior of the disease, is complex. In postmenopausal women, especially the elderly, various indicators of obesity have been linked to an increased risk of breast cancer. However, before menopause, higher body weight is actually associated with a lower risk of breast cancer. The impact of body weight and obesity on breast cancer risk in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women is believed to be influenced by estrogenic activity. Obesity has also been linked to more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis and a poorer prognosis in both premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancer cases. When considering the relationship between obesity and breast cancer in African-American women, there are some notable differences compared to white women. However, the high prevalence of obesity among African-American women may contribute to their relatively worse prognosis compared to white American women. While estrogens are often highlighted as the main explanation for the effects of obesity on breast cancer, other factors may be equally or even more important, particularly in relation to the expression of an aggressive tumor phenotype. This review emphasizes the role of insulin, insulin-like growth factor-I, and leptin, as well as their connection to angiogenesis and transcriptional factors.

title: Dietary saturated and unsaturated fats as determinants of blood pressure and vascular function.
text:
The risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) has long been associated with the amount and type of dietary fat. In the development of coronary heart disease (CHD), arterial stiffness and endothelial dysfunction are important risk factors. Nutritional science offers various methods to assess vascular function, such as clinic and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, pulse wave analysis, pulse wave velocity, flow-mediated dilatation, and venous occlusion plethysmography. This review focuses on the impact of dietary fat quantity and type on blood pressure, arterial compliance, and endothelial function.

When it comes to fat quantity, habitual consumption of dietary fat seems to have little influence on vascular function, regardless of fatty acid composition. However, consuming high-fat meals temporarily impairs endothelial function compared to low-fat meals. This is due to increased levels of circulating lipoproteins and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), which can activate pro-inflammatory pathways and increase oxidative stress.

In terms of fat type, cross-sectional data suggests that saturated fat has a negative effect on vascular function, while polyunsaturated fat, particularly linoleic acid (18:2n-6) and n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), have a beneficial impact. Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5n-3) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6n-3) have been shown to reduce blood pressure, improve arterial compliance in individuals with type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia, and enhance endothelium-dependent vasodilation. Understanding the mechanisms behind this vascular protection and the specific physiological effects of EPA and DHA are important areas for future research.

Due to the limited availability of high-quality observational or interventional data on the relationship between dietary fatty acid composition and vascular function, no additional recommendations can be made beyond current guidelines at this time.

title: Very small embryonic-like stem cells with maximum regenerative potential get discarded during cord blood banking and bone marrow processing for autologous stem cell therapy.
text: The loss of very small embryonic-like stem cells (VSELs) during cord blood banking and bone marrow processing for autologous stem cell therapy is likely due to their small size. To investigate this hypothesis, a study was conducted using human umbilical cord blood (UCB) and discarded red blood cell (RBC) fractions from human bone marrow (BM). The study found that VSELs, which are pluripotent stem cells with high regenerative potential, settle with the RBCs during Ficoll-Hypaque density separation. These VSELs are very small (3-5 μm), have a high nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, and express nuclear Oct-4, cell surface protein SSEA-4, and other pluripotent markers such as Nanog, Sox-2, Rex-1, and Tert. Interestingly, a distinct population of slightly larger, round hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with cytoplasmic Oct-4 were found in the "buffy" coat, which is typically used in stem cell therapy. Immunohistochemical studies on umbilical cord tissue sections also revealed the presence of nuclear Oct-4-positive VSELs and fibroblast-like mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) with cytoplasmic Oct-4. These VSELs with nuclear Oct-4, found in UCB, umbilical cord tissue, and discarded RBC fractions from BM processing, may persist throughout life, maintain tissue homeostasis, and undergo asymmetric cell division to self-renew and produce larger progenitor stem cells such as HSCs or MSCs, which differentiate based on the somatic niche. Therefore, it can be concluded that VSELs are the true stem cells in adult body tissues, while HSCs and MSCs are progenitor stem cells that arise from asymmetric cell division of VSELs. These findings may help explain the low efficacy observed in adult autologous stem cell trials, where progenitor stem cells are unknowingly injected instead of pluripotent stem cells with maximum regenerative potential.

title: CNS repair requires both effector and regulatory T cells with distinct temporal and spatial profiles.
text: The role of monocyte-derived macrophages (mo-MΦs) and T cells in spinal cord repair has been well-established. Recently, it was discovered that the brain choroid plexus epithelium (CP) plays a crucial role in recruiting monocytes, and this recruitment is dependent on IFN-γ. In this study, we aimed to understand how the presence of effector T cells can be reconciled with the role of immune cells that resolve inflammation in the repair process. Using a mouse model of acute spinal cord injury, we found that mice lacking IFN-γ-producing T cells did not activate the CP, leading to limited recruitment of inflammation-resolving mo-MΦs to the spinal cord. Additionally, we discovered that mo-MΦs locally regulated the recruitment of thymic-derived Foxp3(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells to the injured spinal cord during the subacute/chronic phase. Importantly, when we reduced the number of Tregs at this stage, tissue remodeling was hindered, whereas transient ablation of Tregs restricted to the 4-day period before the injury promoted repair. This suggests that reducing systemic immunosuppression at the time of injury can enhance central nervous system repair. Our findings highlight the importance of a dynamic immune cell network in the repair process, involving both effector and regulatory T cells, connected by mo-MΦs. However, dysregulation of any of these cell populations can impede the repair process, emphasizing the need for precise temporal and spatial control in therapeutic interventions.

title: Sperm function tests and fertility.
text: Traditionally, the diagnosis of male infertility has relied on evaluating human semen through a descriptive analysis. This analysis focuses on the quantity, movement, and shape of spermatozoa present in the ejaculate. The underlying belief is that male fertility can be determined by surpassing a certain threshold of motile and morphologically normal spermatozoa for successful conception. However, numerous studies have shown that this concept is flawed. In reality, it is not solely the number of spermatozoa that affects fertility, but rather their functional ability. As a result, various in vitro tests have been developed to assess different aspects of sperm function, such as their ability to move, penetrate cervical mucus, undergo capacitation, recognize the zona, undergo the acrosome reaction, and fuse with the oocyte. These functional tests have proven to be fairly accurate in predicting the fertilizing capacity of human spermatozoa both in vitro and in vivo. Recent advancements in this field include tests to evaluate the impact of oxidative stress on human spermatozoa, as well as the integrity of their nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. These assessments not only provide information on the fertilizing capacity of human spermatozoa, but also their ability to support normal embryonic development.

title: Isolation and characterization of the cDNA encoding BKLF/TEF-2, a major CACCC-box-binding protein in erythroid cells and selected other cells.
text: CACCC boxes are important sequences found in the regulatory elements of genes expressed in erythroid cells and some other cell types. While a specific protein called EKLF is necessary for the proper expression of the adult beta-globin gene in erythroid cells, it is not required for the regulation of other globin and nonglobin genes in these cells. In this study, we aimed to identify other transcription factors that bind to CACCC boxes and are active in mouse erythroid cells. We discovered a major gel shift activity called BKLF, which is present in yolk sac and fetal liver erythroid cells and can be distinguished from EKLF using specific antibodies. By using a less strict hybridization method, we obtained the cDNA encoding BKLF, a unique zinc finger protein that shares similarities with EKLF and other Krüppel-like proteins in its DNA-binding domain but is different in other regions. BKLF is expressed in various cell lines, with particularly high levels in the midbrain region of embryonic mice. It seems to correspond to the gel shift activity known as TEF-2, which is a transcriptional activator involved in regulating the simian virus 40 enhancer and other regulatory elements containing CACCC boxes. BKLF binds strongly and preferentially to many CACCC sequences in genes expressed in erythroid cells, often outcompeting Sp1. Therefore, it is likely to play a role in controlling the expression of numerous genes that are not influenced by EKLF.

title: Effect of osteoporosis treatments on risk of non-vertebral fractures: review and meta-analysis of intention-to-treat studies
text: The effectiveness of most osteoporosis treatments in reducing the risk of vertebral fractures is well-established, but the evidence is less clear for preventing non-vertebral fractures. It is important to base conclusions about treatment efficacy on analyses of the intention to treat (ITT) population rather than subgroup analyses. However, the effectiveness of non-vertebral anti-fracture treatments has mainly been determined through post-hoc subgroup analyses. This review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the non-vertebral anti-fracture effectiveness of various osteoporosis therapies, with a more rigorous assessment of the ITT populations. Data on non-vertebral anti-fracture effectiveness, which was a defined endpoint of the ITT analyses and confirmed by radiographs, were collected from randomized, placebo-controlled, phase III clinical trials lasting at least 3 years. Meta-analyses were conducted for two bisphosphonates, alendronate and risedronate. The relative risks (RR), 95% confidence intervals (CI), and statistical significance of active treatment compared to placebo were calculated. Eleven clinical trials met the review criteria, and three of them demonstrated statistically significant non-vertebral anti-fracture effectiveness in the ITT population: two trials with risedronate and one trial with strontium. The meta-analysis revealed significant reductions in the relative risk of non-vertebral fractures for both alendronate (RR=0.86; 95% CI: 0.76–0.97, P =0.012) and risedronate (RR=0.81; 95% CI: 0.71–0.92, P =0.001). Risedronate and strontium ranelate were the only treatments that demonstrated non-vertebral anti-fracture effectiveness in this comprehensive assessment of osteoporosis therapy using ITT populations in trials lasting 3 years or more. Risedronate was the only treatment shown to be effective in more than one trial. The meta-analysis indicated that both alendronate and risedronate provide non-vertebral anti-fracture effectiveness.

title: Islet1 deletion causes kidney agenesis and hydroureter resembling CAKUT.
text: The transcription factor known as Islet1 (Isl1) is temporarily expressed in a specific group of heart and limb progenitor cells. Surprisingly, when Isl1 was conditionally deleted during studies on limb development, it resulted in unexpected kidney abnormalities. This led us to investigate the expression of Isl1 in the kidney and its potential role in kidney development. Through in situ hybridization, we discovered that Isl1 is expressed in the mesenchymal cells surrounding the base of the ureteric bud in mice. Deletion of Isl1 under specific conditions caused kidney agenesis or hypoplasia and hydroureter, a phenotype similar to congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) in humans. The absence of Isl1 led to abnormal branching of the ureteric bud, either branching out from the nephric duct or forming accessory buds. Both of these abnormalities could result in obstruction of the ureter-bladder junction and subsequent hydroureter. The improper elongation and limited branching of the ureteric buds were the likely causes of kidney agenesis or hypoplasia. Additionally, the lack of Isl1 reduced the expression of Bmp4, a gene associated with the CAKUT-like phenotype, in the metanephric region prior to ureteric budding. In conclusion, Isl1 plays a crucial role in the proper development of the kidney and ureter by preventing the abnormal formation of the ureteric bud. These findings warrant further investigation to determine if Isl1 may be a causative gene for human CAKUT.

title: Tissue transglutaminase (TG2)--a wound response enzyme.
text: The repair of tissue after injury relies on a series of coordinated events that occur simultaneously, including inflammation, re-epithelialization, neovascularization, and the synthesis and stabilization of a fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM). This ECM is then remodeled to resemble normal tissue over time. During the healing process, specific members of the transglutaminase (TG) family are upregulated and serve as a unique class of mediators for wound healing. These enzymes, which create crosslinks between proteins using epsilon(gamma-glutamyl) lysine bridges, play a role in wound healing by stabilizing proteins and regulating the behavior of various cell types recruited to the injured area for tissue repair. In this article, we explore the role of the most widely expressed TG family member, known as "tissue transglutaminase" (TG2), in the process of wound repair. By examining both early and recent evidence from the literature, we illustrate how TG2, with its multifunctional properties, influences the stability of the ECM, interactions between cells and the ECM, and consequently, the behavior of cells during the different phases of wound healing. Additionally, we highlight the potential therapeutic applications of TG2 itself.

title: Crystal structures of the glutamate receptor ion channel GluK3 and GluK5 amino-terminal domains.
text: The majority of fast excitatory synaptic neurotransmission in the central nervous system is mediated by ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs). The assembly of iGluRs into different subtypes, such as AMPA, kainate, and N-methyl-d-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptors, is regulated by their extracellular amino-terminal domains (ATDs). Kainate receptors can be further classified into low-affinity receptor families (GluK1-GluK3) and high-affinity receptor families (GluK4-GluK5) based on their affinity for the neurotoxin kainic acid. Although these two families share a 42% sequence identity for the intact receptor, their ATDs only have a 27% sequence identity. In this study, we have successfully determined the high-resolution crystal structures of GluK3 and GluK5 ATDs. Both of these ATDs form dimers, but they exhibit different dimer assemblies at the R1 interface. However, the dimer assembly at the R2 domain is similar to what has been reported for other non-NMDA iGluRs. This finding supports previous reports that GluK4-GluK5 cannot form functional homomeric ion channels and require coassembly with GluK1-GluK3. Our analysis also reveals that the relative orientation of domains R1 and R2 in individual non-NMDA receptor ATDs can vary by up to 10°, whereas the NMDA receptor GluN2B subunit shows a 50° difference. This restricted movement of domains in non-NMDA receptor ATDs is likely due to extensive intramolecular contacts between domain R1 and domain R2, as well as their dimeric assembly, which involves interactions at both R1 and R2 domains. Overall, our results provide valuable insights into the structure and function of GluK4-GluK5, which is the least understood family of iGluRs.

title: Effectiveness of screening older people for impaired vision in community setting: systematic review of evidence from randomised controlled trials.
text:
The objective of this study was to determine if population screening for impaired vision in older individuals in the community leads to improvements in vision. The study design involved a systematic review of randomized controlled trials that assessed vision or visual function in the community, with a follow-up period of at least 6 months. The subjects included adults aged 65 or over. The main outcome measure was the proportion of individuals with visual impairment in the intervention and control groups, using any method of assessing visual impairment. 

The results showed that there were no trials specifically focused on visual screening. However, outcome data on vision were available for 3494 individuals from five trials that used multiphasic assessment. These trials used self-reported measures for vision impairment as both screening tools and outcome measures. The inclusion of a visual screening component did not lead to improvements in self-reported visual problems (pooled odds ratio 1.04: 95% confidence interval 0.89 to 1.22). Although a small reduction (11%) in the number of older individuals with self-reported visual problems cannot be ruled out. 

In conclusion, based on the current evidence, screening asymptomatic older individuals in the community for visual impairment is not justified. Treatment can usually reduce visual impairment in this age group. The reasons for the lack of benefit seen in this study are unclear. Further research is needed to determine appropriate interventions for older individuals with unreported vision impairment.

title: Protein interaction network of the mammalian Hippo pathway reveals mechanisms of kinase-phosphatase interactions.
text: The Hippo pathway plays a crucial role in controlling the size of organs and maintaining tissue balance in response to various stimuli, such as cell density and mechanotransduction. In cell culture, inhibiting phosphatases with certain drugs can also activate Hippo signaling. To understand the protein-protein interactions within the Hippo pathway, we examined the effects of inhibiting serine and threonine phosphatases using okadaic acid. Our analysis revealed 749 protein interactions, including 599 previously unknown interactions. We also found that some interactions involving serine and threonine phosphatases were dependent on phosphorylation. By mutating the T-loop of MST2, a protein kinase, we disrupted its association with STRIPAK, a complex consisting of phosphatases and kinases. Additionally, deleting the amino-terminal forkhead-associated domain of SLMAP, a component of the STRIPAK complex, prevented its interaction with MST1 and MST2. Inhibiting phosphatases caused distinct changes over time in the proteins that interacted with MOB1A and MOB1B, which are involved in activating Mps one binder kinase. These changes also promoted interactions with upstream proteins in the Hippo pathway, such as MST1 and MST2, as well as with the trimeric protein phosphatase 6 complex (PP6). In human cells treated with okadaic acid, mutating three specific amino acids in the phospho-serine- and phospho-threonine-binding domain of MOB1B prevented its interaction with MST1 and PP6. Overall, our findings suggest that phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating the interactions between kinases and phosphatases in the Hippo signaling pathway, providing a potential mechanism for pathway control.

title: Differential Effects of N-Acetylcysteine, Theophylline or Bicarbonate on Contrast-Induced Rat Renal Vasoconstriction
text:
Background: The main factors that cause kidney damage after the injection of contrast media (CM) are vasoconstriction and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this study, we compared the effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), theophylline, and sodium bicarbonate on vasoconstriction and ROS production in a rat model of CM-induced nephropathy. 

Methods: Sprague-Dawley rats were dehydrated for three days and then received either CM (Telebrix) or a sham injection of saline. Some of the rats were given NAC, theophylline, or bicarbonate before the CM injection. Laser Doppler was used to estimate medullar renal blood flow. The rats were sacrificed 1, 15, or 30 minutes after the treatments, and their kidneys were examined for intrarenal STAT-8 isoprostane, PGE2, and NO levels. 

Results: NAC significantly reduced vasoconstriction. Theophylline only had a mild effect on perfusion drop at 15 minutes and was ineffective after 30 minutes. Unlike theophylline or bicarbonate, NAC significantly increased intrarenal PGE2 levels. NAC and theophylline, but not bicarbonate, gradually increased intrarenal NO levels. However, CM-induced ROS accumulation, as indicated by STAT-8 isoprostane estimation, continued to progress regardless of any pharmacologic interventions. 

Conclusions: (1) NAC effectively prevented CM-induced vasoconstriction, while bicarbonate and theophylline did not; (2) NAC's vasodilatory effect was mediated through increased PGE2 synthesis; and (3) ROS accumulation was a primary response to CM-induced kidney injury and was not affected by any pharmacologic interventions.

title: Induction of AMPK activity corrects early pathophysiological alterations in the subtotal nephrectomy model of chronic kidney disease.
text: The rat kidney ablation and infarction (A/I) model, also known as subtotal or 5/6th nephrectomy, is extensively studied as a model for nondiabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD). In this model, the A/I kidney shows reduced kidney function and metabolic efficiency. We investigated the activity of AMPK, a renoprotective enzyme affected by metabolic changes and cellular stress, in this model. Surprisingly, we found that AMPK activity decreases during the early pathophysiological changes. As time progresses, the kidney parameters worsen, leading to extensive structural, functional, metabolic, and fibrotic changes at 4 weeks after A/I. However, we discovered that inducing AMPK activity using metformin or 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide can increase AMPK activity in this model. This induction also corrects kidney metabolic inefficiency, improves kidney function, and reduces kidney fibrosis and structural alterations. Based on our findings, we conclude that AMPK activity is reduced in the subtotal nephrectomy model of nondiabetic CKD. The altered regulation of AMPK coincides with the progression of disease parameters, and restoring AMPK activity can prevent the progressive loss of function seen in this model. Therefore, we suggest that inducing AMPK activity could be an effective therapeutic target for treating nondiabetic CKD.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging for volume estimation of large multinodular goitres: a comparison with scintigraphy.
text: The aim of this study was to assess the use of magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for estimating the volume of large multinodular goitres in patients seeking non-surgical treatment. A total of 20 patients (three males and 17 females; average age 61 +/- 21 years) with multinodular goitres larger than 100 ml were included in the evaluation. The MR measurements were compared to scintigraphic (SC) volume estimations. The intraobserver coefficient of variation (CV) for MR measurements was found to be 2.2 +/- 2.0% (Observer 1), while the interobserver CV was 4.1 +/- 2.2% (Observers 1 and 2). Mechanical complications were observed in all 20 patients through MR imaging. For SC measurements, the intraobserver CV was 7.5 +/- 5.7% (Observer 3) and 5.4 +/- 5.1% (Observer 4), while the interobserver CV was 10.1 +/- 6.1%. The correlation between the measurements obtained from both methods was not strong (r = 0.665), resulting in a CV of 17.3 +/- 14.2%. The underestimation of SC volumes could not be attributed to the presence of cysts on the thyroid surface. In conclusion, MR imaging can be effectively used to estimate the volume of multinodular goitres in vivo. The high precision of MR measurements makes it a valuable technique for evaluating thyroid growth and non-surgical treatment for reducing goitre size. Scintigraphic volume measurements alone are insufficient for this purpose. Additionally, MR imaging provides detailed anatomical information regarding mechanical complications associated with large goitres.

title: Differential role of CbpA and PspA in modulation of in vitro CXC chemokine responses of respiratory epithelial cells to infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
text: Respiratory epithelial cells actively participate in the body's response to respiratory pathogens, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, by releasing chemokines that recruit neutrophils. To study how specific virulence factors of pneumococcus contribute to the production of CXC chemokines, we infected type II pneumocytes (A549) and nasopharyngeal cells (Detroit-562) with S. pneumoniae D39 or mutants lacking choline-binding protein A (CbpA), pneumococcal surface protein A (PspA), or specific domains of these proteins. When exposed to wild-type D39, both A549 and Detroit-562 cells showed a significant increase in CXC chemokine mRNA and interleukin-8 protein. This response was doubled when a cbpA deletion mutant (DeltaCbpA) was used, suggesting that CbpA inhibits the induction of CXC chemokines. All three N-terminal domains of CbpA are necessary for this effect, as deleting any of these regions had the same impact on the CXC chemokine response as deleting cbpA entirely. Infection with a pspA deletion mutant (DeltaPspA) resulted in a twofold decrease in the CXC chemokine response in A549 cells, but not in Detroit-562 cells, compared to infection with D39 after 2 hours. Therefore, PspA seems to stimulate early release of CXC chemokines from A549 cells. Deleting the region of pspA that encodes the first N-terminal alpha-helical domain reduced the ability of S. pneumoniae to elicit a chemokine response to the same extent as deleting pspA entirely. Thus, the N termini of CbpA and PspA have different effects on the induction of CXC chemokines in epithelial cells infected with S. pneumoniae.

title: HIV-1 therapy with monoclonal antibody 3BNC117 elicits host immune responses against HIV-1
text: The antibody 3BNC117 is a powerful and wide-ranging neutralizer of HIV-1. It specifically targets the CD4 binding site on the viral envelope spike. When given passively, this antibody can prevent infection in animal models and reduce the amount of virus in individuals already infected with HIV-1. Our study reveals that a single injection of 3BNC117 as a form of HIV-1 immunotherapy has an impact on the antibody responses of individuals with high levels of virus in their blood. Compared to untreated individuals who showed minimal changes in their ability to neutralize the virus over a six-month period, those who received 3BNC117 saw a significant improvement in their ability to neutralize different strains of the virus. This suggests that 3BNC117-mediated immunotherapy enhances the body's immune response to HIV-1.

title: Safety and efficacy of RNAi therapy for transthyretin amyloidosis.
text:
BACKGROUND: Transthyretin amyloidosis is a condition characterized by the accumulation of transthyretin amyloid in peripheral nerves and the heart. RNA interference (RNAi) therapy has shown potential in reducing transthyretin production.

METHODS: We developed two formulations of lipid nanoparticles, ALN-TTR01 and ALN-TTR02, containing a potent antitransthyretin small interfering RNA. Safety and efficacy of these formulations were evaluated in separate phase 1 trials. ALN-TTR01 was tested in 32 patients with transthyretin amyloidosis, while ALN-TTR02 was tested in 17 healthy volunteers.

RESULTS: Both trials demonstrated rapid, dose-dependent, and long-lasting reduction in transthyretin levels. ALN-TTR01 at a dose of 1.0 mg/kg resulted in a mean reduction of 38% compared to placebo (P=0.01). ALN-TTR02 at doses of 0.15 to 0.3 mg/kg achieved reductions ranging from 82.3% to 86.8%, with reductions of 56.6% to 67.1% at 28 days (P<0.001 for all comparisons). These reductions were confirmed to be RNAi-mediated. Mild-to-moderate infusion-related reactions were observed in 20.8% and 7.7% of participants receiving ALN-TTR01 and ALN-TTR02, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: ALN-TTR01 and ALN-TTR02 effectively suppressed the production of both mutant and nonmutant forms of transthyretin, demonstrating the potential of RNAi therapy in targeting disease-causing genes. (Funded by Alnylam Pharmaceuticals; ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT01148953 and NCT01559077.)

title: The mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 is inhibited by the peptide GsMTx4.
text: Cells have the ability to respond to mechanical stress by activating mechanosensitive ion channels (MSCs). The discovery of Piezo1, a type of MSC that selectively allows the passage of positively charged ions, has provided a new avenue for studying how mechanical signals are transmitted at the cellular level. To determine if the peptide GsMTx4, which inhibits endogenous cationic MSCs, also affects Piezo1 activity, we conducted experiments using transfected HEK293 cells. We found that extracellular GsMTx4 at micromolar concentrations reversibly inhibited approximately 80% of the mechanically induced current in these cells. This inhibition was not affected by voltage changes and was similar to the inhibition observed with endogenous MSCs. The mirror image d enantiomer of GsMTx4 also inhibited Piezo1 activity, indicating that the peptide binds to the channel in a specific manner. Based on the kinetics of Piezo1 current, we determined that the association and dissociation rates of GsMTx4 were 7.0 × 10(5) M(-1) s(-1) and 0.11 s(-1), respectively, with a K(D) of approximately 155 nM, which is consistent with previous reports on endogenous MSCs. GsMTx4 also caused a rightward shift in the pressure-gating curve of Piezo1, indicating its ability to modify the channel's gating behavior. In contrast, streptomycin, a nonspecific inhibitor of cationic MSCs, showed a different pattern of inhibition, suggesting that it blocks the channel when it is open. GsMTx4 did not affect the activity of another mechanical channel called TREK-1. Furthermore, GsMTx4 was able to reversibly inhibit whole-cell Piezo1 currents, although differences in the on rate were observed compared to outside-out patches. These findings demonstrate that GsMTx4 specifically targets the mechanosensitivity of Piezo1, making it a valuable tool for high-throughput screening of drugs and diagnostic assays.

title: Thiazolidinediones improve beta-cell function in type 2 diabetic patients.
text: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) have been shown to enhance glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Recent evidence from both in vivo and in vitro studies suggests that TZDs also improve the function of pancreatic beta cells. The objective of this research was to investigate whether the improvement in glycemic control induced by TZDs is associated with enhanced beta-cell function. The study involved 11 individuals with normal glucose tolerance and 53 patients with T2DM [average age 53+/-2 years; average BMI 29.4+/-0.8 kg/m2; fasting plasma glucose (FPG) 10.3+/-0.4 mM; Hb A1c 8.2+/-0.3%]. The diabetic patients were randomly assigned to receive either a placebo or a TZD for a period of 4 months. The participants underwent two procedures: 1) a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) to measure plasma glucose, insulin, and C-peptide concentrations, and 2) a two-step euglycemic insulin clamp with [3-(3)H]glucose to assess insulin-mediated total body glucose disposal (Rd). Following this, the T2DM patients were further randomized to receive 4 months of treatment with either pioglitazone (45 mg/day), rosiglitazone (8 mg/day), or a placebo. Both pioglitazone and rosiglitazone were found to significantly improve FPG, mean plasma glucose during OGTT, Hb A1c, and insulin-mediated total body glucose disposal (Rd), while also reducing mean plasma free fatty acids (FFA) during OGTT (all P<0.01, ANOVA). The insulin secretion/insulin resistance (disposition) index [DeltaISR(AUC)/Deltaglucose(AUC)/IR] was significantly enhanced in all groups receiving TZDs: +1.8+/-0.7 (PIO+drug-naïve diabetics), +0.7+/-0.3 (PIO+sulfonylurea-treated diabetics), and 0.7+/-0.2 (ROSI+sulfonylurea-withdrawn diabetics) compared to -0.2+/-0.3 in the two placebo groups (P<0.01, all TZDs vs. placebo, ANOVA). The improvement in insulin secretion was positively correlated with increased body weight, fat mass, and Rd, and inversely correlated with decreased plasma glucose and FFA during the OGTT. In conclusion, treatment with TZDs in patients with T2DM leads to enhanced beta-cell function, which is strongly associated with improved glycemic control.

title: A novel Ku70 function in colorectal homeostasis separate from nonhomologous end joining
text: Ku70, a well-known factor involved in nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ), also plays a role in tumor suppression, although the specific molecular mechanism is still unknown. In previous studies, we observed that mice lacking DNA ligase IV (Lig4), another important NHEJ factor, developed aggressive lymphoma when the tumor suppressor p53 was absent. However, when a hypomorphic mutant p53R172P was introduced, which impaired p53-mediated apoptosis but not cell-cycle arrest, the tumor phenotype was prevented. However, Lig4−/−p53R172P mice developed severe diabetes. To further understand the role of NHEJ and p53-mediated apoptosis in vivo, we bred Ku70−/− p53R172P mice. Surprisingly, these mice did not develop diabetes, but 80% of them had abnormally enlarged colons with significant inflammation. Interestingly, most of these mutant mice progressed to dysplasia, adenoma, and adenocarcinoma, which is different from the phenotype observed in Lig4−/−p53R172P mice. This strongly suggests that Ku70 has an NHEJ-independent function. Importantly, our analysis of Ku70−/−p53R172P colonic epithelial cells revealed nuclear stabilization of β-catenin, along with higher expression of cyclin D1 and c-Myc in affected colon sections compared to control samples. This phenotype is not caused by the p53 mutation, as Ku70−/− mice also exhibit it. Our findings not only uncover a new essential function of Ku70 in maintaining colon homeostasis but also provide an excellent in vivo model for studying the mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis and tumor progression in the colon, specifically how chronic inflammation and abnormal cellular proliferation contribute to these processes.

title: Association of Sickle Cell Trait With Hemoglobin A1c in African Americans
text: The significance of Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) in reflecting previous glucose levels may vary between individuals with sickle cell trait (SCT) and those without it. The objective of this study was to assess the relationship between SCT and HbA1c levels based on fasting or 2-hour glucose levels among African Americans. The study utilized data from two community-based cohorts, the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study and the Jackson Heart Study (JHS), with a total of 7938 participants. Participants without SCT data, those without concurrent HbA1c and glucose measurements, and those with specific hemoglobin variants were excluded. The primary outcome was analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to examine the association between SCT and HbA1c levels, while controlling for fasting or 2-hour glucose measures. The presence of SCT was considered as the exposure. The main outcome measure was the stratification of Hemoglobin A1c based on the presence or absence of SCT. The results showed that participants with SCT had statistically significantly lower HbA1c values compared to those without SCT, for a given fasting or 2-hour glucose level. This finding remained consistent even after adjusting for key risk factors. The difference in HbA1c levels between individuals with and without SCT was more pronounced at higher fasting and 2-hour glucose concentrations. Additionally, the prevalence of prediabetes and diabetes was significantly lower among participants with SCT when defined using HbA1c values. These findings suggest that HbA1c may underestimate past glycemia in African American patients with SCT and further evaluation is warranted.

title: PGAP2 mutations, affecting the GPI-anchor-synthesis pathway, cause hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome.
text: A new subclass of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs) has recently been discovered, characterized by mutations in genes involved in the biosynthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. These mutations result in a distinct set of clinical features. So far, six genes (PIGA, PIGL, PIGM, PIGN, PIGO, and PIGV) encoding proteins in the GPI-anchor-synthesis pathway have been found to have mutations in individuals with severe neurological symptoms such as seizures, muscular hypotonia, and intellectual disability. To identify these mutations, we developed a diagnostic gene panel that targets all known genes involved in the GPI-anchor-synthesis pathway. Through this panel, we detected three missense mutations in PGAP2 (c.46C>T, c.380T>C, and c.479C>T) in two unrelated individuals with hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome (HPMRS). These mutations were found to be present in the investigated families. PGAP2 is responsible for fatty-acid GPI-anchor remodeling, a process that takes place in the Golgi apparatus and is necessary for the stable association between GPI-anchored proteins and the cell-surface membrane rafts. When we introduced the altered protein constructs (p. Arg16Trp, p. Leu127Ser, and p. Thr160Ile) into PGAP2-null cells, we observed only partial restoration of GPI-anchored marker proteins (CD55 and CD59) on the cell surface. This demonstrates that impairment of GPI-anchor remodeling also leads to HPMRS. In conclusion, targeted sequencing of genes involved in the GPI-anchor-synthesis pathway is an effective diagnostic method for identifying this specific subclass of CDGs.

title: Screening for Lung Cancer: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
text: The USPSTF provides recommendations on preventive care services for patients without symptoms, based on evidence of benefits and harms. They do not consider costs in their assessments. Clinical decisions should consider evidence but also individualize care for each patient. Policy and coverage decisions should also consider factors beyond clinical evidence. The USPSTF recommends annual lung cancer screening with LDCT for adults aged 55 to 80 with a smoking history. Screening should stop after 15 years of quitting smoking or if there are health issues that limit life expectancy or surgery. Screening for lung cancer can prevent deaths, but there are also risks such as false-positive results and overdiagnosis. The USPSTF concludes that screening is moderately beneficial for high-risk individuals. Screening should be tailored to the patient's age, smoking history, and time since quitting. LDCT is the recommended screening test, and surgical resection is the standard treatment for localized NSCLC. Smoking cessation is the most effective way to prevent lung cancer. Clinicians have resources available to help patients quit smoking.

title: Dual role of interleukin-10 in the regulation of respiratory syncitial virus (RSV)-induced lung inflammation.
text: RSV infections in children often lead to lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) and require hospitalization. These infections can cause acute respiratory failure and are also associated with additional complications such as secondary bacterial infections and reactive airway disease. One notable response in severe RSV-induced LRTI and the development of asthma is an increase in the expression of interleukin (IL)-10. However, there have been conflicting findings on whether IL-10 inhibits asthmatic responses or exacerbates the disease. To address this discrepancy, we conducted a study using a mouse model that over-expresses IL-10 specifically in the lungs. Our results showed that when IL-10 was present during RSV infection, it not only reduced acute inflammation within 24 hours of infection but also mitigated later inflammatory changes characterized by the expression of T helper type 2 (Th2) cytokines and chemokines. Although this finding may seem contradictory to clinical observations of elevated IL-10 levels in asthmatic patients, we also discovered that delaying IL-10 over-expression until the late immune response to RSV infection resulted in additive effects rather than inhibitory effects. Importantly, in non-infected mice with IL-10 over-expression, IL-10 alone induced an increase in Th2 cytokines (IL-13 and IL-5) and Th2-related chemokines (monocyte chemoattractant protein 1, chemokine ligand 3, and regulated upon activation normal T cell expressed and secreted). We identified a specific subset of myeloid cells as the primary source of IL-10-induced IL-13 production. Therefore, the heightened pathological responses observed in our "delayed" IL-10 over-expression model could be attributed to IL-10 over-expression alone. Overall, our study revealed that IL-10 has dual roles in RSV-induced lung inflammation, which depend on the timing of elevated IL-10 expression in the lungs.

title: Latent membrane protein 1 of Epstein–Barr virus coordinately regulates proliferation with control of apoptosis
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) encodes an oncoprotein called latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), which is a membrane protein that functions as a constitutively active receptor. LMP1 plays a crucial role in inducing and sustaining the proliferation of infected B cells. It mimics the signaling of the CD40 receptor and is involved in regulating the proliferation and survival of EBV-infected cells. To understand the immediate-early target genes controlled by LMP1 and its impact on infected human B cells, we created a conditional LMP1 allele within the intact EBV genome. Through functional analysis, we discovered that LMP1 specifically triggers mitogenic activation of B cells by activating c-myc and Jun/AP1 family members. Additionally, LMP1 directly upregulates the expression of multiple genes with opposing functions related to cell survival. The signals from LMP1 are crucial for the G1/S transition in human B cells; cells without LMP1 signals are arrested in the cell cycle and remain quiescent. Interestingly, LMP1 induces both pro- and antiapoptotic genes, creating a balance that allows for survival during its induction and maintenance of proliferation. Importantly, LMP1's activities are not necessary for the survival of nonproliferating cells.

title: Crizotinib in ROS1-rearranged non-small-cell lung cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Rearrangements of the ROS1 gene in non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) create a distinct molecular subgroup that may respond well to ROS1 kinase inhibition. Crizotinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets ROS1, as well as other proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinases.

METHODS: We conducted a study with 50 patients who had advanced NSCLC and tested positive for ROS1 rearrangement. These patients were treated with crizotinib at a standard oral dose of 250 mg twice daily. Safety, pharmacokinetics, and response to therapy were assessed. ROS1 fusion partners were identified using next-generation sequencing or reverse-transcriptase-polymerase-chain-reaction assays.

RESULTS: The objective response rate was 72%, with 3 complete responses and 33 partial responses. The median duration of response was 17.6 months, and median progression-free survival was 19.2 months. Among the tested tumors, 7 ROS1 fusion partners were identified, including 5 known and 2 novel partner genes. The type of ROS1 rearrangement did not correlate with the clinical response to crizotinib. The safety profile of crizotinib was similar to that observed in patients with ALK-rearranged NSCLC.

CONCLUSIONS: Crizotinib demonstrated significant antitumor activity in patients with advanced ROS1-rearranged NSCLC. ROS1 rearrangement defines a second molecular subgroup of NSCLC that is highly responsive to crizotinib. (Funded by Pfizer and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00585195.)

title: The S. cerevisiae Rrm3p DNA helicase moves with the replication fork and affects replication of all yeast chromosomes.
text:
The Saccharomyces cerevisiae DNA helicase Rrm3p plays a crucial role in facilitating the progression of replication forks through over 1000 specific locations in the genome. Our study reveals that the replication of all yeast chromosomes is significantly delayed in cells lacking Rrm3p. Surprisingly, even in a region without any predicted Rrm3p-dependent sites, we observed delayed replication. Analysis of replication intermediates on two-dimensional gels showed that the rate of fork movement in rrm3 cells was similar to that of wild-type cells, except at known Rrm3p-dependent sites. These findings suggest that while Rrm3p is involved in global DNA replication, its activity is primarily required at specific sites that are challenging to replicate.

Using chromatin immunoprecipitation, we found that Rrm3p is associated with both Rrm3p-dependent and -independent sites and moves along with the replication fork through both types of sites. Furthermore, we discovered that Rrm3p interacts with Pol2p, the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon, in living cells. This indicates that Rrm3p is not recruited to its action sites when replication forks stall, but rather is a component of the replication fork machinery.

title: The pathophysiology of protein-overload proteinuria.
text: The study examined the effects of protein overload nephrosis in rats, induced by injecting bovine serum albumin (BSA) into the peritoneum. By conducting fractional clearance studies using inulin and tracer proteins of varying size and charge, the researchers made several observations in proteinuric rats: 1) the glomerular filtration rate and renal plasma flow remained unchanged; 2) the clearance of rat serum albumin increased 34-fold, reaching levels similar to BSA; 3) the clearance of anionic horse radish peroxidase (HRP) increased 2-fold, while neutral and cationic HRP had normal clearance values; and 4) the clearance of heterologous IgG and IgM increased 11-fold and 3-fold, respectively. Degenerative changes were observed in glomerular epithelial cells, but the distribution of anionic sites in the glomerular basement membrane remained unaltered according to polyethyleneimine binding studies. In summary, elevated serum albumin concentration led to increased transcapillary albumin transport, resulting in degenerative changes in glomerular epithelial cells with the development of reversible large pore defects.

title: Effects of aging on central and peripheral mammalian clocks.
text:
The organization of circadian rhythms changes as we age, but we are unsure to what extent these changes are due to alterations in the central pacemakers, peripheral oscillators, or the mechanisms that connect them. To investigate this, we used transgenic rats with a luciferase reporter to study the effects of aging on the expression rhythm of the Per1 gene in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and peripheral tissues. We compared young (2 months) and aged (24-26 months) Per1-luc transgenic rats that were synchronized to light-dark cycles. After sacrificing the rats, we removed and cultured their tissues to measure Per1-luc expression in 10 different tissues. 

In the SCN, which is the central pacemaker in mammals, Per1-luc expression showed a strong rhythmic pattern for over 7 weeks in culture. The only difference between the rhythmicity of the SCN in young and old rats was a small but significant age-related shortening of the free-running period. The circadian rhythmicity in some peripheral tissues was not affected by aging, while in others, it either advanced or disappeared relative to the light cycle. However, we found that the arrhythmic tissues could be induced to oscillate by applying forskolin, indicating that they still had the ability to oscillate but were not being properly regulated in vivo. 

Overall, our findings provide new insights into how aging affects the circadian system in mammals. Aging appears to impact rhythms in some tissues but not others, and it may primarily affect the interactions among circadian oscillators, potentially reducing the ability of the SCN to regulate oscillators in the periphery.

title: CtBP3/BARS drives membrane fission in dynamin-independent transport pathways
text: Membrane fission plays a crucial role in membrane transport. Currently, the only known protein machinery involved in in vivo transport is dynamin, which functions in some but not all transport pathways. This suggests the existence of other fission machineries. In our study, we demonstrate that carboxy-terminal binding protein 3/brefeldin A-ribosylated substrate (CtBP3/BARS) is responsible for fission in basolateral transport from the Golgi to the plasma membrane and in fluid-phase endocytosis. In contrast, dynamin is not involved in these processes. On the other hand, CtBP3/BARS is inactive in apical transport to the plasma membrane and in receptor-mediated endocytosis, both of which are controlled by dynamin. This indicates that CtBP3/BARS regulates membrane fission in endocytic and exocytic transport pathways that are distinct from those requiring dynamin.

title: Influenza A myocarditis developing in an adult liver transplant recipient despite vaccination: a case report and review of the literature.
text: Despite receiving vaccination, solid organ transplant recipients who are on chronic immunosuppressive agents are still at a higher risk of acquiring influenza virus. Influenza infection can lead to myocarditis, although it is a rare complication. We present a case of an adult liver transplant recipient who developed influenza A myocarditis despite receiving prophylactic vaccination. This occurrence is possible in solid organ transplant recipients due to their reduced response to protein vaccines, which makes them more susceptible to infections. Further studies are necessary to determine if antiviral chemoprophylaxis during influenza season would effectively prevent influenza in this high-risk population of solid organ transplant recipients.

title: Extrapulmonary effects of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on physical activity: a cross-sectional study.
text: RATIONALE Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) often experience reduced physical activity. COPD has extrapulmonary effects that can contribute to the severity of the disease. OBJECTIVES This study aimed to investigate how the extrapulmonary effects and comorbidities of COPD are associated with reduced physical activity in patients. METHODS A cross-sectional study was conducted with 170 outpatients with COPD. Physical activity was measured using a multisensor accelerometer armband, which recorded steps per day and physical activity level. Various tests were performed to assess cardiovascular status, mental status, metabolic/muscular status, systemic inflammation, and anemia. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS A multivariate linear regression analysis revealed that N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels, left ventricular diastolic function, and systemic inflammation were independently associated with reduced physical activity in patients with COPD, regardless of their GOLD stages or BODE score. CONCLUSIONS Patients with higher levels of systemic inflammation and left cardiac dysfunction tend to have reduced physical activity in COPD.

title: Cleavage efficient 2A peptides for high level monoclonal antibody expression in CHO cells.
text: By utilizing 2A peptides, the heavy chain (HC) and light chain (LC) genes necessary for monoclonal antibody (mAb) production can be linked on a single cassette. This approach allows for control of the LC and HC ratio and reduces the number of non-expressing cells. Four different 2A peptides, derived from foot-and-mouth disease virus (F2A), equine rhinitis A virus (E2A), porcine teschovirus-1 (P2A), and Thosea asigna virus (T2A), were compared for their ability to express three biosimilar IgG1 mAbs in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell lines. The HC and LC were linked using various 2A peptides, both with and without GSG linkers. By inserting a furin recognition site upstream of the 2A peptide, the 2A residues that would normally be attached to the HC could be removed. The different 2A peptides exhibited varying cleavage efficiencies, which correlated with the level of mAb expression. The relative cleavage efficiency of each 2A peptide remained consistent when expressing different IgG1 mAbs in different CHO cells. Although complete cleavage was not observed with any of the 2A peptides, the presence of GSG linkers did enhance cleavage efficiency and subsequently increased mAb expression levels. The T2A peptide with the GSG linker (GT2A) demonstrated the highest cleavage efficiency and mAb expression level. CHO DG44 pools that were stably amplified using GT2A achieved titers of 357, 416, and 600 mg/L for the three mAbs in shake flask batch cultures. Incomplete cleavage likely resulted in improperly processed mAb species and aggregates, which were eliminated using a chromatin-directed clarification method and protein A purification. Overall, the vector and methods described offer a straightforward process that is advantageous for both mAb development and manufacturing.

title: The complexity of human ribosome biogenesis revealed by systematic nucleolar screening of Pre-rRNA processing factors.
text: The production of mature ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) involves a complex process from polycistronic precursors. This process, known as precursor (pre)-rRNA processing, has been extensively studied in yeast and was believed to be similar in humans. To investigate this further, we studied 625 nucleolar proteins in HeLa cells and found that 286 of them are necessary for pre-rRNA processing. Interestingly, 74 of these proteins do not have a counterpart in yeast. We also discovered that pre-rRNA processing defects are present in different cell types, including primary cells, and are not caused by the activation of a p53-dependent nucleolar tumor surveillance pathway. These defects occur before cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. Additionally, we examined the role of the exosome in processing internal transcribed spacers (ITSs) and found that the maturation of the 3' end of 18S rRNA involves a protein called EXOSC10/Rrp6, which is a known ITS2 processing factor in yeast. Our findings suggest that human cells employ unique strategies and recruit specific factors to carry out essential processing steps, which has important implications for understanding ribosomopathies at a molecular level and developing effective therapeutic treatments.

title: Maximal aerobic capacity in African-American and Caucasian prepubertal children.
text: The aim of this study was to compare the levels of oxygen consumption (VO2) at rest, during submaximal exercise, and at maximal capacity (VO2max) in African-American and Caucasian prepubertal children aged 5-10 years. Resting VO2 was measured using indirect calorimetry while the children were in a fasted state. Submaximal VO2 and VO2max were determined during a progressive treadmill exercise test designed for children. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry was used to measure total fat mass (FM), soft lean tissue mass (LTM), and leg soft LTM. Total energy expenditure (TEE) and activity energy expenditure (AEE) were determined using doubly labeled water. The results showed a significant difference in VO2max between the two ethnic groups (P < 0.01), with African-American children having approximately 15% lower absolute VO2max compared to Caucasian children (1.21 +/- 0.032 vs. 1.43 +/- 0.031 l/min, respectively). This difference in VO2max persisted even after adjusting for soft LTM (1.23 +/- 0.025 vs. 1.39 +/- 0.031 l/min; P < 0.01), leg soft LTM (1.20 +/- 0.031 vs. 1.43 +/- 0.042 l/min; P < 0.01), and soft LTM and FM (1.23 +/- 0.025 vs. 1.39 +/- 0.031 l/min; P < 0.01). Furthermore, the lower VO2max remained significant after adjusting for TEE (1.20 +/- 0.02 vs. 1.38 +/- 0.0028 l/min P < 0.001) and AEE (1.20 +/- 0.024 vs. 1.38 +/- 0.028 l/min; P < 0.001). In conclusion, this study found that African-American and Caucasian children have similar levels of VO2 at rest and during submaximal exercise, but African-American children have a lower VO2max by approximately 15%, regardless of factors such as soft LTM, FM, leg LTM, TEE, and AEE.

title: Penaeus monodon Dscam (PmDscam) has a highly diverse cytoplasmic tail and is the first membrane-bound shrimp Dscam to be reported.
text: The Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule (Dscam) is believed to have a significant role in the "alternative adaptive immunity" observed in invertebrates. Dscam consists of a cytoplasmic tail that facilitates signal transduction and a hypervariable extracellular region that may employ a pathogen recognition mechanism similar to vertebrate antibodies. In a previous study, we discovered a unique form of Dscam without a tail in Litopenaeus vannamei. In this research, we present the first membrane-bound form of shrimp Dscam, known as PmDscam, which was isolated from Penaeus monodon. PmDscam exists in both membrane-bound and tail-less forms. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that while crustacean Dscams from shrimp and water flea did not share a single subclade, they were distinct from invertebrate Dscam-like molecules and insecta Dscams. In the extracellular region, the variable regions of PmDscam were found in N-terminal Ig2, N-terminal Ig3, and the entire Ig7 domain. The different variants of PmDscam in the extracellular region and transmembrane domain were produced through mutually exclusive alternative splicing events. The variants in the cytoplasmic tail were generated through exon inclusion/exclusion. Based on the genomic organization of Daphnia Dscam's cytoplasmic tail, we propose a model illustrating how the shrimp Dscam genomic locus may utilize Type III polyadenylation to generate both the tail-less and membrane-bound forms.

title: The different biological effects of telomestatin and TMPyP4 can be attributed to their selectivity for interaction with intramolecular or intermolecular G-quadruplex structures.
text: The presence of G-quadruplex structures in telomeres of Stylonychia macronuclei and in the promoter of c-myc in human cells has confirmed their potential as targets for drug design. However, it is crucial to determine the selectivity of G-quadruplex-interactive agents for different types of G-quadruplex structures. In this study, we have made progress in linking specific biological effects of these drugs to their interaction with either intermolecular or intramolecular G-quadruplex structures formed in telomeres. Telomestatin, a natural compound derived from Streptomyces anulatus 3533-SV4, has been identified as a potent telomerase inhibitor due to its interaction with G-quadruplex structures. Our findings reveal that telomestatin has a preference for intramolecular G-quadruplex structures over intermolecular ones, and it exhibits a 70-fold selectivity for intramolecular G-quadruplex structures compared to duplex DNA. Telomestatin effectively stabilizes G-quadruplex structures formed from both duplex human telomeric DNA and single-stranded DNA. Notably, telomestatin can stabilize these structures even in the absence of monovalent cations, which sets it apart from other G-quadruplex-interactive compounds. At noncytotoxic concentrations, telomestatin inhibits the proliferation of telomerase-positive cells over a few weeks. In contrast, TMPyP4, a compound that promotes the formation of intermolecular G-quadruplex structures, suppresses the proliferation of both alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT)-positive cells and telomerase-positive cells.
