The presence of impaired glucose regulation suggests that the beta cells in the pancreas are unable to produce enough insulin to compensate for the increased demand caused by insulin resistance. The relationship between insulin production and insulin sensitivity follows a hyperbolic pattern, which can be measured using the disposition index. Any alteration in this relationship increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes. Although there have been no clinical trials specifically targeting individuals with metabolic syndrome, structured lifestyle changes have been tested in individuals with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance and have shown promising results in reducing the incidence of Type 2 diabetes by nearly 50%, as long as a weight loss of at least 5% is achieved. Certain oral antidiabetic and anti-obesity medications have also shown some success, although to a lesser extent. Some fibrates have demonstrated the ability to reduce or delay the onset of diabetes, while extended-release niacin has no significant effect and the use of statins remains controversial. Among antihypertensive agents, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are associated with the lowest risk of incident diabetes.

title: The fallacy of the ecological fallacy: the potential misuse of a concept and the consequences.
text: The "ecological fallacy" has been used to evaluate ecological studies in epidemiological contexts. While there is strong empirical evidence showing a lack of comparability between correlations derived from ecological- and individual-level analyses, the conceptual meaning of the ecological fallacy remains problematic. This paper argues that issues in cross-level inference can be better understood as validity problems, which are not exclusive to ecological-level analyses. Taking this approach increases awareness of potential inference problems in individual-level studies and highlights the unique contributions of ecological variables. Ultimately, this expands the scope for identifying causes of disease and implementing interventions to improve public health.

title: Blocking caspase-activated apoptosis improves contractility in failing myocardium.
text: Apoptosis of cardiac myocytes has been observed in end-stage failing human hearts. However, the potential therapeutic benefits of inhibiting apoptosis in congestive heart failure (CHF) have not been fully understood. This study aimed to investigate the role of caspase activation in the development of CHF, specifically in cardiac contractility and sarcomere organization. Using a rabbit model of heart failure induced by rapid ventricular pacing, we conducted in vivo transcoronary adenovirus-mediated gene delivery of the potent caspase inhibitor p35. Our findings demonstrate that caspase activation is associated with a decrease in contractile force of failing myocytes by disrupting sarcomeric structure. However, gene transfer of p35 in this animal model prevented the increase in caspase 3 activity and DNA-histone formation. Hearts expressing p35 showed significant improvements in left ventricular pressure rise (+dp/dt), reduced end-diastolic chamber pressure (LVEDP), and delayed development of heart failure. To further understand these benefits, we examined the effects of caspase 3 on cardiomyocyte dysfunction in vitro. Injecting activated caspase 3 into intact myocytes resulted in disorganized sarcomeres and decreased contractility. These findings highlight the direct impact of caspases on cardiac function and suggest potential novel therapeutic strategies through antiapoptotic treatments.

title: Development and validation of QRISK3 risk prediction algorithms to estimate future risk of cardiovascular disease: prospective cohort study
text:
The aim of this study was to develop and validate updated prediction algorithms for estimating the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease in both women and men, taking into account potential new risk factors. The study design was a prospective open cohort study, conducted in general practices in England that provided data for the QResearch database. The participants included 1309 QResearch general practices in England, with 981 practices used to develop the scores and a separate set of 328 practices used to validate the scores. The derivation cohort consisted of 7.89 million patients aged 25-84 years, while the validation cohort consisted of 2.67 million patients. All patients were free of cardiovascular disease and were not prescribed statins at baseline.

The methods used in this study involved Cox proportional hazards models in the derivation cohort to derive separate risk equations for men and women, which were then evaluated at 10 years. The risk factors considered included those already included in QRISK2, such as age, ethnicity, deprivation, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, total cholesterol: high density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio, smoking, family history of coronary heart disease, type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, treated hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease. Additionally, new risk factors were considered, including chronic kidney disease, systolic blood pressure variability, migraine, corticosteroids, systemic lupus erythematosus, atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, HIV/AIDS, and erectile dysfunction in men. Measures of calibration and discrimination were determined in the validation cohort for both men and women, as well as for individual subgroups based on age group, ethnicity, and baseline disease status.

The main outcome measures of this study were incident cardiovascular disease recorded on general practice, mortality, or hospital admission records. The results showed that there were 363,565 incident cases of cardiovascular disease identified in the derivation cohort during follow-up, with a total of 50.8 million person years of observation. All of the new risk factors considered met the model inclusion criteria, except for HIV/AIDS, which was not statistically significant. The models demonstrated good calibration, high levels of explained variation, and discrimination. In women, the algorithm explained 59.6% of the variation in time to diagnosis of cardiovascular disease, with a D statistic of 2.48 and Harrell's C statistic of 0.88. The corresponding values for men were 54.8%, 2.26, and 0.86, respectively. Overall, the updated QRISK3 algorithms performed similarly to the QRISK2 algorithms.

In conclusion, this study successfully developed and validated updated QRISK3 risk prediction models. The inclusion of additional clinical variables in QRISK3 can assist doctors in identifying individuals at the highest risk of heart disease and stroke. These variables include chronic kidney disease, systolic blood pressure variability, migraine, corticosteroids, systemic lupus erythematosus, atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, and erectile dysfunction.

title: The importance of engaging policy-makers at the outset to guide research on and introduction of vaccines: the use of policy-maker surveys.
text: Conducting face-to-face surveys with policy-makers and influential leaders is a valuable tool for early identification of (a) key issues related to the introduction of a new vaccine, (b) individuals and groups in a country who hold significant decision-making power or influence in vaccine introduction, (c) potential obstacles to vaccine introduction, and (d) the data needs of policy-makers to overcome these obstacles. By gathering the opinions and beliefs of those responsible for making or influencing decisions on vaccine introduction, these surveys can ensure that research efforts align with the requirements of policy-makers in countries affected by the targeted diseases. Additionally, these surveys can inform vaccine introduction strategies by identifying financially and politically viable approaches for vaccine distribution, targeting, and financing. This article outlines the methodology employed in conducting such surveys, addresses methodological concerns, and shares insights gained from two policy-maker surveys conducted in various Asian countries regarding new-generation vaccines for cholera, typhoid fever, and shigellosis, as well as future vaccines for dengue fever/dengue haemorrhagic fever.

title: Histone acetyltransferase PCAF regulates inflammatory molecules in the development of renal injury.
text: Inflammation is closely linked to kidney diseases, such as chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI), but the exact mechanism behind this connection is not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the role of a protein called p300/CBP-associated factor (PCAF), which is responsible for modifying histones in the kidneys of mice with kidney disease and mice injected with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). We observed that PCAF was overexpressed in these mice, leading to increased histone acetylation and the upregulation of certain inflammatory genes, including ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and MCP-1. Additionally, we found that increased histone acetylation was specifically recruited to the promoters of ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and MCP-1 in LPS-injected mice. In laboratory experiments using human renal cells, we discovered that knocking down PCAF resulted in the downregulation of inflammatory molecules, including VCAM-1, ICAM-1, p50 subunit of NF-κB, and MCP-1 at both the mRNA and protein levels. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in histone acetylation. Conversely, overexpressing PCAF led to an increase in the expression of inflammatory molecules. Furthermore, when PCAF was deficient, the recruitment of histone acetylation to the promoters of ICAM-1 and MCP-1 was reduced, and the upregulation of these inflammatory molecules in response to palmitate was inhibited. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that PCAF plays a crucial role in regulating inflammatory molecules through histone acetylation at a specific site (H3K18ac), suggesting that it could be a potential therapeutic target for kidney diseases associated with inflammation.

title: T1 mapping for myocardial extracellular volume measurement by CMR: bolus only versus primed infusion technique.
text: The objective of this study was to assess the accuracy of the "bolus only" T1 mapping cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) technique in measuring myocardial extracellular volume fraction (ECV). Myocardial ECV can be measured using T1 mapping before and after the administration of a contrast agent, assuming that the distribution of the contrast agent between the blood and myocardium is in equilibrium. Equilibrium distribution can be achieved through a primed contrast infusion (equilibrium contrast-CMR [EQ-CMR]) or approximated by measuring the dynamic equilibration after a bolus injection. The bolus only approach is appealing, but there is limited data supporting its use. In this study, we compared the bolus only technique with two independent standards: collagen volume fraction (CVF) from myocardial biopsy in aortic stenosis (AS) and the infusion technique in five representative conditions. We studied 147 subjects, including healthy volunteers, individuals with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe AS, amyloidosis, and chronic myocardial infarction. We performed and compared ECV measurements using both the bolus only technique (at 15 minutes) and the infusion technique. In 18 subjects with severe AS, we compared the results with histological CVF. The ECV measurements from both techniques correlated with histological CVF. Across all health and disease conditions, there was a strong correlation between the techniques. However, in diseases with high ECV (amyloidosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with late gadolinium enhancement, and myocardial infarction), the Bland-Altman analysis showed that the bolus only technique consistently gave higher ECV values above 0.4, compared to the infusion technique. In conclusion, the bolus only, T1 mapping-derived ECV measurement is sufficient for ECV measurement in a range of cardiac diseases and is validated histologically in AS. However, when ECV is above 0.4, the bolus only technique consistently measures ECV higher compared to the infusion technique.

title: Cytomegalovirus US2 destroys two components of the MHC class II pathway, preventing recognition by CD4+ T cells
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a common herpesvirus that can cause severe illness in individuals who are immunosuppressed due to bone marrow or tissue transplantation or who have AIDS (ref. 1). HCMV establishes latent infections that can reactivate periodically, and it employs a range of immune evasion proteins to survive and replicate in the presence of a strong immune response. Monocyte/macrophages play a crucial role in HCMV infection, acting as a reservoir for latent virus and aiding its spread throughout the body. These cells, along with other HCMV-permissive cells like endothelial and glial cells, can express MHC class II proteins and present antigens to CD4+ T lymphocytes. In this study, we discovered that the HCMV protein US2 is responsible for breaking down two important proteins in the MHC class II antigen presentation pathway: HLA-DR-α and DM-α. This finding was unexpected, as US2 was previously known to degrade MHC class I proteins (refs. 5,6), which are only distantly related to class II proteins. When US2 was expressed in cells, their ability to present antigens to CD4+ T lymphocytes was greatly reduced or completely eliminated. This suggests that US2 may enable HCMV-infected macrophages to evade detection by CD4+ T cells, a characteristic that would be advantageous following virus reactivation.

title: CD169-positive macrophages dominate antitumor immunity by crosspresenting dead cell-associated antigens.
text: The development of cytotoxic T lymphocytes that target tumors is considered crucial for the stimulation of immune responses against tumors. In order to activate these CD8(+) T cells, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) must first acquire antigens associated with tumor cells. Dead tumor cells are the main source of tumor antigens, but little is known about how APCs in lymph nodes that drain from the tumor site acquire and present these antigens. In this study, we demonstrate that CD169(+) macrophages engulf dead tumor cells that are transported through the lymphatic system and subsequently present tumor antigens to CD8(+) T cells. Immunization with irradiated tumor cells under the skin protects mice from tumors that are genetically identical. However, the activation of tumor antigen-specific CD8(+) T cells and the subsequent immune response against tumors are significantly impaired in mice that lack CD169(+) macrophages. Neither migratory dendritic cells (DCs) nor conventional DCs residing in the lymph nodes are necessary for the presentation of tumor antigens. Therefore, we have identified CD169(+) macrophages as APCs residing in the lymph nodes that play a major role in the early activation of tumor antigen-specific CD8(+) T cells.

title: Emerging mechanisms in morphogen-mediated axon guidance.
text: During the early stages of animal development, the secretion of morphogenic molecules such as Sonic hedgehog (Shh), Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp family members creates gradients that regulate cell proliferation and determine the fate and characteristics of target cells. These molecules activate well-known signaling pathways that ultimately control gene transcription. Additionally, Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp signaling also play a crucial role in the assembly of neural circuits, which is conserved throughout evolution. They regulate various processes including neuronal polarization, axon and dendrite development, and synaptogenesis. These processes require rapid and localized changes in the organization of the cytoskeleton and components of the plasma membrane. A significant question arises regarding whether morphogen signaling at the growth cone utilizes similar mechanisms and intracellular pathway components as those involved in morphogen-mediated cell specification. This review explores recent advancements in understanding this issue, highlighting how Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp have either adapted their traditional signaling pathways or adopted alternative and innovative molecular mechanisms to influence different aspects of neuronal circuit formation.

title: Lessons learnt from malaria epidemics in the Islamic Republic of Iran.
text: The Islamic Republic of Iran is currently in the pre-elimination stage of malaria control, but there are still concerns about malaria epidemics in the southern region of the country. This study examines the epidemiological characteristics and factors that contribute to 60 reported malaria epidemics in the Sistan va Baluchestan province between 2005 and 2009. A statistical model called the zero-truncated negative binomial model was used to analyze the relationship between predictor variables and the total number of malaria cases. The majority of malaria epidemics occurred in the southern part of the province, primarily between July and October, with the highest number of cases in August. Most of these epidemics were small-scale, with less than 100 cases, and short in duration, lasting less than a month. Plasmodium falciparum, a type of malaria parasite, was present in 46.7% of the epidemics. The study found that an increase in rainfall and population movements were the most significant factors contributing to these epidemics. These findings can be used to improve the country's epidemic investigation and reporting system as it moves closer to the goal of eliminating malaria.

title: Autoradiography of chromosomal DNA fibers from Chinese hamster cells.
text: Lack of knowledge regarding the actual length of DNA molecules in the chromosomes of complex organisms has consistently hindered the comprehension of chromosome structure. As a result, efforts have been made, often utilizing electron microscopy, to approximate the size of DNA in these organisms. Solari (1) previously documented the longest recorded measurement of such DNA, which was a DNA fiber from a sea urchin sperm that measured at least 93 μ in length.

title: Epigenetic memory and preferential lineage-specific differentiation in induced pluripotent stem cells derived from human pancreatic islet beta cells.
text: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (HiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (HESCs) share a high degree of similarity. In our study, we successfully generated iPSC lines from human pancreatic islet beta cells using two genetic lineage-tracing systems. These reprogrammed cells exhibited pluripotent markers and successfully differentiated into the three embryonic germ layers. Notably, the iPSCs derived from beta cells (BiPSCs) maintained an open chromatin structure at key beta-cell genes and possessed a distinct DNA methylation pattern that set them apart from other PSCs. Additionally, BiPSCs displayed an enhanced capacity to differentiate into insulin-producing cells both in vitro and in vivo, surpassing ESCs and non-beta iPSCs. Our findings suggest that the epigenetic memory of BiPSCs may predispose them to readily differentiate into insulin-producing cells. These results highlight the influence of the cells of origin on the phenotype of HiPSCs and propose that their biased differentiation potential could be advantageous for cell replacement therapy.

title: CCL2/monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 mediates enhanced transmigration of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected leukocytes across the blood-brain barrier: a potential mechanism of HIV-CNS invasion and NeuroAIDS.
text: Encephalitis and dementia associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) are characterized by the infiltration of white blood cells into the central nervous system (CNS), activation of microglia, abnormal expression of chemokines, disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and eventual loss of neurons. It is not well understood how human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) infection affects the ability of white blood cells to migrate in response to chemokines and alter BBB integrity. Our study demonstrates that HIV infection of human white blood cells leads to increased migration across our tissue culture model of the human BBB in response to the chemokine CCL2. Additionally, HIV infection disrupts the BBB by increasing permeability, reducing tight junction proteins, and inducing the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)-2 and MMP-9. When added to our model, HIV-infected cells did not migrate in the absence of CCL2, and this condition did not affect BBB integrity. Other chemokines such as CXCL10, CCL3, and CCL5 did not enhance the migration of HIV-infected white blood cells or BBB permeability. The increased migration of HIV-infected white blood cells in response to CCL2 is associated with their increased expression of CCR2, the chemokine receptor for CCL2. These findings suggest that CCL2, but not other chemokines, plays a crucial role in the infiltration of HIV-infected white blood cells into the CNS and the subsequent development of NeuroAIDS-related pathology.

title: Prostaglandin E2 as an inhibitory modulator of fibrogenesis in human lung allografts.
text:
RATIONALE: The development of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) in human lung allografts is linked to the expansion and fibrotic differentiation of donor mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs). However, the factors that regulate the fibrotic differentiation of these resident MSCs are not well understood.

OBJECTIVES: This study aims to investigate the role of endogenous and exogenous prostaglandin (PG)E2 in modulating the fibrotic differentiation of MSCs derived from human lung allografts.

METHODS: The effects of PGE2 on proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression were examined in lung-resident MSCs (LR-MSCs) obtained from patients with and without BOS. Specific agonists and antagonists were used to elucidate the underlying pathway.

MEASUREMENT AND MAIN RESULTS: Treatment with PGE2 significantly inhibited the proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-SMA expression of LR-MSCs derived from normal lung allografts. The suppressive effects were found to be mediated through the PGE2/E prostanoid (EP)2/adenylate cyclase pathway, as determined by pharmacologic and small-interfering RNA approaches. Stimulation of endogenous PGE2 secretion by IL-1β was associated with a reduction in myofibroblast differentiation in vitro, while inhibition of PGE2 synthesis by indomethacin increased α-SMA expression. LR-MSCs from patients with BOS secreted significantly less PGE2 compared to non-BOS LR-MSCs. Additionally, BOS LR-MSCs exhibited defects in cyclooxygenase-2 induction, leading to impaired PGE2 synthesis in response to IL-1β. These BOS LR-MSCs also demonstrated resistance to the inhibitory effects of PGE2, which was associated with a decrease in the EP2/EP1 ratio.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight the importance of the PGE2 axis in regulating the fibrotic differentiation of LR-MSCs. Failure of this regulatory mechanism is associated with the development of BOS.

title: Association of DNA polymerase mu (pol mu) with Ku and ligase IV: role for pol mu in end-joining double-strand break repair.
text: The biological function of mammalian DNA polymerase mu (pol mu) is not yet fully understood, although it is known to be related to terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. In this study, we demonstrate that exposure of cells to ionizing radiation (IR) leads to an increase in the levels of pol mu protein. Additionally, pol mu forms distinct nuclear foci following IR, which largely overlap with the foci of gammaH2AX, a known marker for DNA double-strand breaks. This suggests that pol mu is involved in the cellular response to such breaks. Furthermore, pol mu associates with the repair factor Ku in cell extracts and requires both Ku and another end-joining factor, XRCC4-ligase IV, to form a stable complex on DNA in vitro. Moreover, pol mu facilitates the recruitment of XRCC4-ligase IV to Ku-bound DNA and promotes ligase IV-dependent end joining. In contrast, the related mammalian DNA polymerase beta does not interact with Ku and XRCC4-ligase IV, and is less effective than pol mu in facilitating joining mediated by these factors. Overall, our findings support the crucial role of pol mu in the end-joining pathway for repairing double-strand breaks.

title: Stromal-epithelial metabolic coupling in cancer: integrating autophagy and metabolism in the tumor microenvironment.
text:
In vivo, cancer cells do not exist as pure and uniform populations. Instead, they are found within clusters called "cancer cell nests," which are surrounded by stromal cells, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts. It is therefore reasonable to suspect that stromal fibroblasts could have an impact on the metabolism of neighboring cancer cells, and vice versa. Based on this concept, we recently proposed that the Warburg effect observed in cancer cells may be a result of culturing them in isolation, outside of their normal stromal context or tumor microenvironment.

In fact, when cancer cells are co-cultured with fibroblasts, the cancer cells increase their mitochondrial mass, while the fibroblasts lose their mitochondria. A detailed analysis of this phenomenon reveals that aggressive cancer cells act as "parasites," utilizing oxidative stress as a "weapon" to extract nutrients from the surrounding stromal cells. The oxidative stress in fibroblasts triggers the destruction of mitochondria through a process called mitophagy. As a result, the stromal cells are compelled to undergo aerobic glycolysis and produce energy-rich nutrients like lactate and ketones to nourish the cancer cells. This mechanism enables cancer cells to thrive and spread without relying on blood vessels as a source of nutrients. They can simply induce oxidative stress wherever they go, which explains their survival during metastasis.

We propose that stromal catabolism, facilitated by autophagy and mitophagy, fuels the anabolic growth of tumor cells, thereby promoting tumor progression and metastasis. We have coined this novel concept as "The Autophagic Tumor Stroma Model of Cancer Metabolism," also known as the "Reverse Warburg Effect." Additionally, we explore how the addiction of cancer cells to glutamine (glutaminolysis) aligns with this new model by promoting oxidative mitochondrial metabolism in aggressive cancer cells.

title: Oxidative stress in renal dysfunction: mechanisms, clinical sequelae and therapeutic options
text: The incidence of cardiovascular events in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) has been increasingly associated with oxidative stress. This is particularly significant as traditional cardiovascular risk factors do not fully explain the high rates of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in this population. Patients with renal impairment experience increased oxidative stress due to heightened oxidant activity and reduced antioxidant capacity. This oxidative stress worsens with worsening renal dysfunction. Inflammation, which is also present in CKD, further exacerbates the generation of oxidants. The detrimental effects of oxidative stress manifest as endothelial dysfunction and left ventricular hypertrophy, both of which have negative cardiovascular implications. Given our improved understanding of oxidative stress, it is crucial to explore treatment options that can reduce it. By doing so, we may be able to reverse endothelial dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, and the associated clinical consequences.

title: Effect of age, sex, and sites on the cellularity of the adipose tissue in mice and rats rendered obese by a high-fat diet.
text: The size of cells and the number of fat pads in Swiss mice were examined in relation to obesity induced by a high-fat diet consisting of 40% lard. Two groups of mothers were given either the high-fat diet or a control diet during pregnancy and lactation, and their offspring were also fed the same diets after weaning. At two weeks old, mice suckled by mothers on the high-fat diet had larger parametrial fat pads, which was solely due to an increase in fat cell size. From weaning until the 18th week, the two groups showed significant differences, with the obese group exhibiting a noticeable enlargement of fat cells. In contrast, the control group did not experience any changes in cell numbers, while the obese mice consistently and continuously increased in cell number until the 52nd week. Hyperplasia, or an increase in cell number, was only observed in adult mice. When adult rats were introduced to the high-fat diet, it also resulted in an increase in fat cell number. At 32 weeks of age, three different fat pad sites were compared in both males and females. All sites showed an increase in weight in the high-fat fed group. This increase was due to hyperplasia in the perirenal site, hypertrophy in the epididymal and subcutaneous sites, and a combination of hyperplasia and hypertrophy in the parametrial site. Therefore, in both males and females, the adipose sites in obese mice responded to the diet in a site-specific manner. It was concluded that the fat content in a diet plays a role in the formation and maturation of new fat cells, as well as in the regulation of fat cell lipid content. These processes may act independently or in conjunction, depending on the specific adipose tissue site.

title: Transcriptional integration of mitochondrial biogenesis.
text: Mitochondrial biogenesis and function rely on gene regulatory factors encoded by the nuclear genome. Some of these factors work exclusively within the mitochondria to regulate mitochondrial transcription, translation, and other functions. Others control the expression of nuclear genes necessary for mitochondrial metabolism and organelle biogenesis. The transcriptional coactivators known as the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator-1 (PGC-1) family play a crucial role in transmitting and integrating physiological signals that govern metabolism, differentiation, and cell growth to the transcriptional machinery that controls mitochondrial functional capacity. Therefore, the PGC-1 coactivators serve as a central component of the transcriptional regulatory network that harmoniously regulates the energy-producing functions of mitochondria in response to changing physiological conditions, aging, and disease.

title: RFID system evaluation against radiated transient noise
text: This paper evaluates a radiofrequency identification system based on the ISO/IEC 14443 type-B standard in the presence of transient noise. The system operates in real time at a frequency of 13.56 MHz and is subjected to controlled interference from various transient bursts with varying levels, frequencies, and durations. The interference is applied to an AC main wire near the system, and its impact on the digital communication system is assessed using two methods. The first method involves directly observing an RFID equipment in the presence of transient signals, while the second method involves capturing the interference in the time domain and evaluating its effect through simulation. The transient noises affect the RFID system, leading to different types of errors. The study highlights the importance of measuring and evaluating transient phenomena in the time domain to ensure that the RFID system is not susceptible to problems.

title: Musculoskeletal pain in Europe: its impact and a comparison of population and medical perceptions of treatment in eight European countries.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the impact of musculoskeletal pain (MP) and compare how it is managed by the general population and primary care physicians. Additionally, the study aimed to identify any misconceptions about treatment. 

To gather data, a total of 5803 individuals with MP and 1483 primary care physicians from eight European countries were randomly selected and interviewed via telephone. A structured questionnaire was used to inquire about the usual management of MP, as well as the perceived benefits and risks of treatment. The participants' current health status was also assessed using the SF-12 questionnaire. 

According to the primary care physicians' perspectives, MP appears to be well managed. All patients who seek treatment are offered some form of treatment, with over 90% of doctors aiming to improve their patients' quality of life. Additionally, most physicians are aware of and concerned about the risks associated with treatment using NSAIDs. 

However, from a population perspective, it was found that up to 27% of individuals with pain do not seek medical help. Among those who do seek help, many wait for months or even years before consulting a doctor. Furthermore, only 55% or fewer of the patients who have seen a doctor are currently receiving prescription treatment for their pain. 

The study also revealed poor communication between doctors and patients, with few patients being provided with information about their condition. Additionally, many patients hold misconceptions about treatment. 

In conclusion, the management of MP is consistent across the eight European countries studied. However, there is a disconnect between the perspectives of physicians and patients regarding care. Some individuals with pain never seek medical help, despite experiencing constant or daily pain. Those who do seek help often receive limited written information or explanation, and many hold misconceptions about the benefits and risks of treatment, which hinders their ability to actively participate in decisions about their care.

title: [Palliative care in Germany].
text: Palliative care in Germany still faces a significant shortage, both for patients in hospitals and those receiving care at home. However, there has been progress in the past 15 years, which is encouraging and has brought more attention to the needs of the terminally ill. Specialized palliative care facilities have been established, particularly for inpatients in hospitals and hospices, although there is still work to be done to ensure full coverage. The situation is more concerning for outpatients, as there is a lack of sufficient financial resources allocated to palliative care. It is crucial to recognize the needs of the terminally ill and their loved ones, and society must prioritize this issue on the healthcare agenda. The current developments at the national and state levels are promising and offer hope for further improvement in the delivery of palliative care to all who require it, not just the sick.

title: A view to a kill: the bacterial type VI secretion system.
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a structure within a cell that is similar in structure and function to a phage tail attached to a membrane inside the cell. Recent research has shown that a rapid change in the shape of a protein complex called a sheath propels the spike and tube components of the T6SS, along with antibacterial and antieukaryotic substances, out of predatory T6SS(+) cells and into prey cells. The contracted structure is then recycled using ATP. The T6SS is controlled at both the transcriptional and posttranslational levels, with the latter involving the detection of changes in the cell membrane in some species. In addition to attacking eukaryotic cells directly, the T6SS can also target other bacteria that are infecting a mammalian host. This emphasizes the importance of the T6SS not only for bacterial survival in the environment, but also in the context of infection and disease. This review focuses on these advancements and others in our understanding of the structure, function, assembly, and regulation of the T6SS.

title: Open Access Increases Citation Rate
text: PLoS Biology has published a research article by Gunther Eysenbach that explores the impact of open-access articles on citations. The study provides strong evidence that open-access articles are more likely to be recognized and cited immediately compared to non-open-access articles. This finding supports the belief that open-access publication facilitates scientific dialogue among researchers and should be implemented across the entire scientific literature as soon as possible. The study compared citations of articles published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) between June 2004 and December 2004. PNAS introduced an open-access option for authors in June 2004, with a publication charge of $1,000. Non-open-access articles in PNAS had a six-month delay before becoming publicly available. The results of the study clearly showed that open-access articles gained a significant citation advantage over non-open-access articles within 4 to 16 months after publication. They were twice as likely to be cited within 4 to 10 months and almost three times as likely between 10 and 16 months. The study also examined the impact of self-archiving non-open-access articles and found that they were cited less frequently compared to open-access articles from the same journal. The article acknowledges the potential conflict of interest, as the author is also an editor of an open-access journal. However, this conflict of interest can actually ensure rigor in the study. The article underwent a thorough evaluation process, including consultation with an academic editor and review by experts in bibliometric analyses, information science, and statistics. The decision to publish the article in PLoS Biology was based on the strength of evidence and the unique comparison of OA and non-OA articles from the same journal while controlling for confounding factors. The study not only provides evidence for the immediate advantage of open access but also highlights challenges to its long-term future. The citation history of authors who chose the open-access option differed from those who did not, suggesting varying attitudes, influence from group leaders, or differences in ability to pay publication charges. The availability of hybrid journals offering open-access options allows for replication of similar experiments. Further studies over longer periods will determine if the citation advantage for open-access articles is sustained. Overall, the study provides tangible evidence supporting the benefits of open access, which has been widely believed but lacked solid evidence until now.

title: Serum immunoglobulin A from patients with celiac disease inhibits human T84 intestinal crypt epithelial cell differentiation.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of celiac disease serum IgA on the communication between mesenchymal and epithelial cells. To do this, T84 epithelial cells were grown in collagen gel cultures with IMR-90 fibroblasts or transforming growth factor beta. The effects of purified celiac IgA and monoclonal tissue transglutaminase antibodies were examined by adding them to the cell cultures. The results showed that celiac disease IgA and antibodies against tissue transglutaminase inhibited epithelial cell differentiation and increased cell proliferation. This suggests that celiac disease-specific autoantibodies may play a role in the development of the mucosal lesion in celiac disease.

title: Pathogenesis of diseases associated with antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies.
text: There is limited knowledge regarding the causes of diseases associated with circulating antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies (ANCA), such as primary vasculitides and inflammatory bowel diseases. However, our understanding of the immune mechanisms potentially involved in the development of these diseases is continuously expanding. In this review, we initially focus on the factors that trigger the formation of ANCA, including the potential role of microbial superantigens and any potential defects in the progression of apoptosis or the clearance of apoptotic cells. We then shift our attention to the impact of ANCA on clinical symptoms and the role they play in causing disease, including the accessibility of ANCA antigens as targets for circulating antibodies and the mechanisms by which ANCA function. The mechanisms by which ANCA activate neutrophils are explored, including the involvement of Fcgamma receptors, the potential ways in which neutrophils cause tissue damage, and the interaction between neutrophils and endothelial cells.

title: The common marmoset as a novel animal model system for biomedical and neuroscience research applications.
text: The common marmoset, a small primate native to the New World, has become a focal point in the fields of biomedical science and neuroscience. This is due to several factors: its ability to react similarly to human cytokines and hormones, its manageable size for experimentation, its high reproductive efficiency, the establishment of essential research tools, and its unique behavioral and cognitive traits. Researchers have successfully developed various models of neurological diseases in the common marmoset, including Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, stroke, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury. Recently, a transgenic common marmoset with germline transmission was created, offering a promising new animal model for studying human diseases. This review aims to provide an overview of the recent advancements in biomedical research and neuroscience utilizing the common marmoset as an exceptional model system.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 regulates the transcription of steroidogenic enzymes and induces the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into steroidogenic cells.
text: Steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), also known as Ad4BP, is a crucial transcriptional regulator of genes related to steroid production. However, liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1), which belongs to the same NR5A nuclear receptor family as SF-1, is expressed at significantly higher levels than SF-1 in the human gonad. Previous studies have shown that SF-1 can induce the differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into steroid-producing cells like Leydig or adrenocortical cells. Similarly, the introduction of LRH-1 into human MSCs (hMSCs) using cAMP also leads to the expression of steroid-producing enzymes, including CYP17, and their differentiation into cells that produce steroid hormones. Further analysis revealed that three LRH-1 binding sites were responsible for the activation of CYP17. Immunohistochemical studies confirmed the presence of LRH-1 protein in human Leydig cells. The CYP17 promoter region was found to be highly methylated in hMSCs, but the introduction of LRH-1 and cAMP treatment resulted in demethylation. These findings suggest that LRH-1 may serve as another important regulator of the steroidogenic lineage in MSCs and play a crucial role in the production of steroid hormones in human Leydig cells.

title: Checkpoint responses to replication fork barriers.
text: Maintaining the accuracy of DNA replication is crucial for preserving the integrity of the genome. When an active replication fork encounters obstacles, various cellular pathways are activated to stabilize the replication machinery and address the underlying issue. However, if the problem persists, the fork may collapse, leaving DNA ends vulnerable to potentially harmful processing. In prokaryotes, the collapse of a replication fork triggers the activation of recombination proteins, which restore the fork. Recent studies have revealed that recombination is also closely associated with replication in eukaryotic cells, with recombination proteins being recruited to collapsed forks but not stalled ones. In this review, we explore different types of barriers that can impede replication forks and how these barriers can lead to distinct DNA structures at stalled forks. The DNA structure checkpoints operating during the S phase respond differently to various barriers, and we delve into the processes regulated by these DNA replication checkpoints, focusing on the role of the intra-S phase checkpoint in stabilizing stalled forks.

title: Ecology, economics and political will: the vicissitudes of malaria strategies in Asia.
text:
The recorded history of malaria in parts of Asia spans over 2,000 years. Throughout this time, the disease has played a significant role in the socioeconomic development of various nation states. Over the past 50 years, there have been notable fluctuations in the prevalence and impact of malaria across different landscapes, such as rice fields, rainforests, mountains, and plains. These diverse environments reflect the vast ecological diversity inhabited by the majority of mankind. This period has also witnessed dramatic changes in social and economic structures, population size, density, and mobility, as well as political systems. All of these factors have contributed to the changing nature of malaria in this extensive region.

Although the majority of global malaria cases currently occur in Africa, Asia had a higher number of cases earlier in the century before successful malaria programs were implemented. Today, Asia poses a global threat due to the emergence of multidrug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, which is gradually spreading throughout tropical regions. This reflects the economic changes that have occurred in recent decades, particularly the movement of populations in search of commerce, trade, and personal fortunes, or as a result of physical conflicts.

From the 1950s to the 1990s, there have been instances of near "eradication" followed by a resurgence of malaria in Sri Lanka, as well as control and resurgence in India. The influence of war and postwar instability has also affected drug resistance in Cambodia, while prolonged political turmoil in Myanmar has led to an increase in severe and cerebral malaria. Vivax malaria has been eliminated from many provinces in central China, except for forested border areas where it remains a challenge. These experiences, both positive and negative, provide valuable lessons in the ongoing debate between eradication and control as alternative strategies.

China has long pursued the goal of "basic elimination," which is essentially eradication under a different name, in defiance of World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. The Chinese experience demonstrates that with community organization, thorough case detection and management, focused elimination efforts, and political will at all levels of society, it is possible to eliminate malaria from large areas of a vast nation and maintain near-eradication status through surveillance. However, China has faced difficulties in the international border regions of the tropical south due to unrestricted population movement, which complicates the malaria control program. Thailand, Malaysia, and to some extent Vietnam have also achieved essential elimination in their rice field plains through robust vertical programs but struggle to do so in their forested border areas.

Economics plays a central role in the rise and fall of nations, as well as in the history of disease among populations. The current emphasis on free market economics as the primary driver of national wealth poses limitations on community involvement in malaria management. The task of malaria control or elimination should be closely linked to the broader macroeconomic processes that governments prioritize, rather than being isolated within the health sector. Historically, malaria has had a significant negative impact on the productivity of nations. Economic models need to be refined and integrated with political, technical, and demographic strategies. The recent history of malaria in China offers some lessons that may be applicable in this context.

title: Global and regional risk of disabling sequelae from bacterial meningitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: There is a lack of available data sources to assess the global and regional risk of complications from bacterial meningitis. Our objective was to estimate the risks of major and minor complications caused by bacterial meningitis, determine the distribution of different types of complications, and compare the risk based on region and income. We conducted a systematic review of published papers from 1980 to 2008. Major complications were categorized according to standard global burden of disease categories (cognitive deficit, bilateral hearing loss, motor deficit, seizures, visual impairment, hydrocephalus). We also included less severe, minor complications (behavioral problems, learning difficulties, unilateral hearing loss, hypotonia, diplopia), as well as multiple impairments. A total of 132 papers were included in our analysis. The median risk of experiencing at least one major or minor complication after being discharged from the hospital was 19.9% (with a range of 12.3-35.3%). The risk of experiencing at least one major complication was 12.8% (with a range of 7.2-21.1%), while the risk of experiencing at least one minor complication was 8.6% (with a range of 4.4-15.3%). In terms of specific types of bacterial meningitis, the median risk of experiencing at least one major complication was 24.7% for pneumococcal meningitis, 9.5% for Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and 7.2% for meningococcal meningitis. The most common major complication reported was hearing loss (33.9%), and 19.7% of individuals had multiple impairments. In a random-effects meta-analysis, the overall risk of experiencing a major complication was twice as high in the African (pooled risk estimate of 25.1% [95% CI 18.9-32.0%]) and southeast Asian regions (21.6% [95% CI 13.1-31.5%]) compared to the European region (9.4% [95% CI 7.0-12.3%]; overall I(2)=89.5%, p<0.0001). The risks of long-term disabling complications were highest in low-income countries, where the burden of bacterial meningitis is greatest. The majority of reported complications could have been prevented through vaccination with Hib, pneumococcal, and meningococcal vaccines.

title: Efficacy of human papillomavirus testing for the detection of invasive cervical cancers and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
BACKGROUND
The effectiveness of cervical-cancer screening policies based on HPV testing was assessed in this study. HPV testing is known to be more sensitive but less specific than cytology for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).

METHODS
Between March 2004 and December 2004, women aged 25-60 years were randomly assigned to either conventional cytology or HPV testing in combination with liquid-based cytology (first phase) or alone (second phase). Randomization was done using a computer in two screening centers and numbered sealed envelopes in the remaining seven centers. Women who tested positive for HPV and were aged 35-60 years were referred to colposcopy during phase one. Women aged 25-34 years were referred to colposcopy only if cytology was abnormal or HPV testing was persistently positive. In phase two, women in the HPV group were referred for colposcopy if the HPV test was positive. Two rounds of screening occurred in each phase, with cytology testing only at the second round. The primary endpoint was the detection of grade 2 and 3 CIN, as well as invasive cervical cancers during the first and second screening rounds. Analysis was done based on intention to screen.

FINDINGS
A total of 47,001 women were randomly assigned to the cytology group and 47,369 to HPV testing for both phases. In the second round of screening, 33,851 women from the cytology group and 32,998 from the HPV-testing group participated. Histological diagnoses from screening done elsewhere were also retrieved. The detection of invasive cervical cancers was similar between the two groups in the first round of screening. However, no cases were detected in the HPV group during the second round, compared to nine in the cytology group. Overall, in the two rounds of screening, 18 invasive cancers were detected in the cytology group versus seven in the HPV group. Among women aged 35-60 years, the relative detection of CIN2, CIN3, and CIN2 and 3 combined was higher in the HPV group compared to the cytology group in the first round. However, in the second round, the relative detection was lower in the HPV group. Among women aged 25-34 years, there was significant heterogeneity between phases in the relative detection of CIN3. The detection ratio of CIN2 for women aged 25-34 years was higher in the HPV group in the first round but lower in the second round.

INTERPRETATION
HPV-based screening is more effective than cytology in preventing invasive cervical cancer by detecting high-grade lesions earlier and providing a longer low-risk period. However, in younger women, HPV screening may lead to over-diagnosis of regressive CIN2.

FUNDING
This study was funded by the European Union, Italian Ministry of Health, Regional Health Administrations of Piemonte, Tuscany, Veneto, and Emilia-Romagna, and Public Health Agency of Lazio.

title: Microcytosis, iron deficiency and thalassaemia in a multi-ethnic community: a pilot study.
text: The high occurrence of microcytosis, defined as a mean cell haemoglobin of less than 27 pg, without any other abnormalities, is a major source of confusion when screening for haemoglobin disorders. In order to address this confusion, we conducted a small pilot study to investigate the use of plasma ferritin and HPLC assay on the original sequestrene blood sample when microcytosis is detected. The study included 1,302 participants who were referred by their General Practitioner (GP) for a full blood count at a North London district general hospital that serves a diverse inner-city population. Ethnicity was determined through a questionnaire. Among individuals of North European descent, microcytosis was found in 3% of males (with half being iron-deficient) and 11% of females (with the majority being iron-deficient). Among ethnic minorities, microcytosis was present in 35% of males (with one tenth being iron-deficient) and 45% of females (with less than half being iron-deficient). The remaining cases could be diagnosed as "probable alpha thalassaemia". Based on our findings, we conclude that routine analysis of the original sequestrene sample using plasma ferritin assay and haemoglobinopathy screening when microcytosis is detected could improve the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of laboratory services for primary care and maternity services.

title: Crystal structure of the human AAA+ protein RuvBL1.
text: RuvBL1 is a highly conserved protein found in eukaryotes that belongs to the AAA(+)-family of ATPases, which are associated with various cellular activities. It plays crucial roles in important signaling pathways like c-Myc and Wnt, involved in chromatin remodeling, transcriptional and developmental regulation, as well as DNA repair and apoptosis. In this study, we present the 3D structure of the selenomethionine variant of human RuvBL1, refined using diffraction data to a resolution of 2.2A. The crystal structure of the hexamer consists of RuvBL1 monomers bound to ADP. These monomers have three domains, with the first and third domains being responsible for ATP binding and hydrolysis. Despite the known requirement of ATPase activity for various in vivo functions, we only observed minimal activity with the purified protein. Through structural homology and DNA binding studies, we discovered that the second domain, unique to AAA(+) proteins and absent in the bacterial homolog RuvB, functions as a novel DNA/RNA-binding domain. We demonstrated that RuvBL1 interacts with both single-stranded and double-stranded DNA/RNA. The structure of the RuvBL1.ADP complex, along with our biochemical findings, suggests that while RuvBL1 possesses the structural characteristics of a molecular motor or ATP-driven helicase, it requires one or more unidentified cofactors for its enzymatic activity.

title: Characteristics of a monoclonal antibody (RM124) against acute myelocytic leukemia cells.
text: We developed a monoclonal antibody against cells from an experimental rat myelocytic leukemia (BNML). The rat leukemia model shares many characteristics with human acute myelocytic leukemia. We characterized the monoclonal antibody (MCA) RM124 by examining its labeling pattern on BNML leukemia cells, normal rat bone marrow cells, and hemopoietic stem cells (HSC) using flow cytometry and complement-dependent cytotoxicity assays. Flow cytometry showed that MCA-RM124 labeled the leukemic cells much more strongly than normal bone marrow cells, including CFU-S and CFU-C. Only a subset of normal granulocytes exhibited some cross reactivity, but at a lower labeling intensity. Cytotoxicity assays demonstrated that the MCA-RM124 selectively killed leukemic cells while sparing normal hemopoietic stem cells (CFU-S).

title: Quantitative assessment of T-cell repertoire recovery after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
text: Increased risks of infection and cancer relapse are associated with delayed T cell recovery and restricted T cell receptor (TCR) diversity after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT). However, accurately measuring TCR diversity after allo-HSCT has been challenging. In this study, we used a combination of 5' rapid amplification of complementary DNA ends PCR and deep sequencing to quantify TCR diversity in 28 allo-HSCT recipients using a single oligonucleotide pair. We confirmed the accuracy of our method by analyzing duplicate blood samples. After 6 months, recipients of cord blood-grafts had TCR diversity similar to that of healthy individuals, while recipients of T cell-depleted peripheral-blood stem cell grafts had significantly lower CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cell diversities. After 12 months, the deficiencies in CD4(+) T cell diversity had improved, but not in CD8(+) T cell diversity. Overall, our method provides valuable insights into T cell repertoire recovery after allo-HSCT and may help identify patients at high risk of infection or relapse.

title: Silver sulfadiazine for the treatment of partial-thickness burns and venous stasis ulcers.
text:
Over the years, silver-containing antibiotics like silver sulfadiazine (SSD) have been commonly used as topical treatment for patients with partial-thickness burns and venous stasis ulcers. This review aims to address the following research question: Does the use of topical SSD compared to nonantibiotic dressings improve mortality, wound healing, re-epithelialization, or infection rates in ambulatory patients with partial-thickness burns or stasis dermatitis ulcers? 

To conduct this review, we searched various databases including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and others. We included trials that enrolled patients of any age with partial-thickness burns or venous stasis ulcers and randomly assigned them to receive either topical SSD or placebo, saline-soaked gauze, paraffin gauze, sterile dry dressing, or nonantibiotic moist dressing. The outcomes we considered were mortality, wound healing, speed of re-epithelialization, and infection rates. 

Our search yielded 400 potential articles related to burns. However, no human studies met the inclusion criteria. We found only 7 animal studies (1 mouse, 4 rat, and 2 pig) that were relevant to our research question. These animal studies provided conflicting results, with some supporting the use of SSD for treating partial-thickness burns and others questioning its effectiveness. 

Regarding stasis dermatitis ulcers, we identified 50 articles for review. After reviewing 20 abstracts, we found only one article that met the inclusion criteria. This study did not show any significant improvement in the rate of complete healing in the SSD group compared to the placebo group, either at 4 weeks or at 1 year of follow-up. 

In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the routine use of SSD for ambulatory patients with either partial-thickness burns or stasis dermatitis ulcers in order to decrease mortality, prevent infection, or enhance wound healing in humans.

title: Putting p53 in Context
text: TP53 is the gene most commonly mutated in human cancer. In terms of its function, p53 is activated by various stress stimuli and subsequently controls a highly intricate transcriptional program that has an impact on a wide range of biological responses. Despite the numerous aspects of the p53 network that have been uncovered, there is still a lack of understanding regarding how and in what circumstances p53 exerts its diverse effects. It is unclear how we can interpret the different activities of p53 and the consequences of its dysfunction in order to comprehend how outcomes are determined by cell type, mutation profile, and epigenetic cell state. Additionally, how can we go about restoring p53's tumor-suppressive activities in cancer?

title: Modeling the evolution of culture-adapted human embryonic stem cells.
text: The continuous cultivation of human embryonic stem (ES) cells is bound to undergo evolution over time, as any advantageous mutations will be selectively amplified. However, the impact of population size, mutation rate, and selection pressure on this evolutionary process is often overlooked. To address this, we have developed a Monte Carlo simulation model that predicts how changes in these factors can affect the emergence and spread of mutant ES cells. We have validated the model by comparing it with in vitro data. This simulation allows us to estimate the rate at which culture-adapted ES cells are generated under different assumptions about the key parameters. Notably, it emphasizes the importance of population size, suggesting that maintaining cells in smaller populations reduces the likelihood of abnormal cultures developing.

title: CD28 delivers a unique signal leading to the selective recruitment of RelA and p52 NF-kappaB subunits on IL-8 and Bcl-xL gene promoters.
text: CD28 plays a crucial role in activating T lymphocytes by acting as a costimulatory receptor. It not only enhances signals from the T cell antigen receptor (TCR), but also delivers its own independent signals. When engaged by B7, CD28 can generate signals that are not dependent on the TCR, resulting in the activation of IkappaB kinase and NF-kappaB. Our study demonstrates that these TCR-independent signals from CD28 lead to the selective transcription of survival (Bcl-xL) and inflammatory (IL-8 and B cell activation factor) genes, but not proliferative (IL-2) genes, in a manner that depends on NF-kappaB. T cells stimulated by CD28 actively secrete IL-8, and the up-regulation of Bcl-xL protects these cells from apoptosis induced by radiation. The transcription of CD28-induced genes is facilitated by the specific recruitment of RelA and p52 NF-kappaB subunits to target promoters. In contrast, p50 and c-Rel, which bind preferentially to NF-kappaB sites on the IL-2 gene promoter after anti-CD3 stimulation, are not involved. Therefore, our findings identify CD28 as a crucial regulator of genes that are important for both survival and inflammation.

title: Netting neutrophils are major inducers of type I IFN production in pediatric systemic lupus erythematosus.
text:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that affects the entire body. It is characterized by a breakdown of tolerance to nuclear antigens and the formation of immune complexes. Recent genomic studies have shown that individuals with SLE have consistently elevated levels of type I interferon (IFN)-induced and neutrophil-related transcripts in their white blood cells. This suggests that increased production and availability of IFN-α, as well as changes in dendritic cell (DC) homeostasis, play a role in the development of lupus.

While the association between neutrophils and lupus has been known for some time, their specific role in the disease has remained unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that mature neutrophils in individuals with SLE are activated by type I IFN in the body and undergo cell death when exposed to anti-ribonucleoprotein antibodies derived from SLE patients. This leads to the release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which contain DNA and high levels of two specific neutrophil proteins called LL37 and HMGB1. These proteins facilitate the uptake and recognition of mammalian DNA by plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs).

Importantly, the SLE NETs activate pDCs to produce large amounts of IFN-α in a manner that depends on DNA and Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9). This finding uncovers a previously unknown role for neutrophils in the development of SLE and establishes a new connection between antibodies that recognize nucleic acids and the production of type I IFN in this disease.

title: Assessment for selection for the health care professions and specialty training: consensus statement and recommendations from the Ottawa 2010 Conference.
text:
The assessment process for selecting candidates for medicine and health professions should adhere to the same quality assurance procedures as in-course assessments. However, the existing literature on selection is limited and lacks strong theoretical or conceptual foundations. Regarding written testing, there is evidence supporting the predictive validity of the Medical College Admission Test (MCAT) for medical school and licensing examination performance. Additionally, grade point average, particularly when combined with MCAT scores, has shown predictive validity for graduate entry programs, but there is little evidence regarding the predictive validity of scores from school leaver exams. Interviews, as a selection measure, have not proven to be reliable. However, studies on multiple mini-interviews have demonstrated good predictive validity and reliability. Among other selection measures, only personality testing has shown potential for future research. 

The priority of widening access to medical and health professional programs aligns with the social accountability mandate of these schools. While traditional selection measures tend to discriminate against certain population groups, there is limited evidence on the impact of non-traditional measures in promoting inclusivity. Preparation and outreach programs have shown the most promise in this regard. In summary, there is a limited consensus on assessment for selection. Recommendations for future action include adopting principles of good assessment and curriculum alignment, utilizing multi-method programmatic approaches, developing interdisciplinary frameworks, and employing sophisticated measurement models. The social accountability mandate of medical and health professional schools necessitates the integration of social inclusion, workforce considerations, and widening access into the principles of good assessment for selection.

title: THE GLYOXAL BIS(2-HYDROXYANIL) METHOD MODIFIED FOR LOCALIZING INSOLUBLE CALCIUM SALTS.
text:
In order to stain insoluble calcium salts with glyoxal bis(2-hydroxyanil) (GBHA), the original solution was altered. The original solution consisted of 2 ml of 0.4% GBHA in absolute ethanol and 0.3 ml of aqueous 5% NaOH, which only allowed for staining of soluble calcium salts. The modifications made were as follows:

Modification I: 2 ml of 0.4% GBHA in absolute ethanol was mixed with 0.6 ml of 10% aqueous NaOH.

Modification II: 0.1 gm GBHA was mixed with 2 ml of 3.4% NaOH in 75% ethanol.

To prevent the diffusion and loss of calcium, the tissues were processed using either the freeze-substitution or freeze-dry method. The sections were stained without removing the paraffin.

Modification I is effective when 1 or 2 drops of the solution are placed on the section and gradually evaporated to dryness. This concentrates the GBHA and NaOH on the insoluble calcium salts.

Modification II is effective when the solution is dried or poured onto the section and allowed to stain for 5 minutes.

After staining, the slides are immersed in 90% ethanol saturated with KCN and Na2CO3 for 15 minutes to enhance specificity to calcium. They are then rinsed and counterstained in 95% ethanol containing 0.1% each of fast...

title: Detecting selective sweeps: a new approach based on hidden markov models.
text: The detection and localization of selective sweeps based on SNP data has recently gained significant attention. In this study, we propose the utilization of hidden Markov models (HMMs) to detect selective sweeps in DNA sequences. Similar to previously published techniques, our HMMs utilize the site frequency spectrum and the spatial diversity pattern along the sequence to identify selection. However, unlike previous approaches, our HMMs explicitly incorporate the correlation structure between linked sites. Our methods exhibit comparable detection power and accuracy in estimating the location of the selected site to competing methods for populations with constant size. Notably, in scenarios involving population bottlenecks, our methods demonstrate a reduced occurrence of false positives.

title: A Balance between Secreted Inhibitors and Edge Sensing Controls Gastruloid Self-Organization.
text:
The earliest stages of human embryogenesis are still not well understood. In order to study the events that shape the human embryo, we conducted experiments using colonies of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) grown on a micropatterned surface and treated with BMP4. These structures, called gastruloids, mimic the arrangement of the germ layers in a developing mammal embryo and provide a way to investigate the mechanisms that determine the structure and signaling patterns in the human gastrula. 

In terms of structure, densely packed hESCs position their receptors for transforming growth factor β on their sides in the middle of the colony, while keeping the receptors at the edges of the colony on the top surface. This relocation of receptors shields the cells in the middle from ligands applied from the top, but still allows them to respond to ligands presented from the bottom. Additionally, BMP4 directly triggers the production of its own inhibitor, NOGGIN, creating a reaction-diffusion mechanism that plays a role in patterning. 

We have developed a mathematical model that combines edge detection and the action of inhibitors to predict the positioning of human cell fates in gastruloids, and potentially in the human embryo as well.

title: Tenectin is a novel alphaPS2betaPS integrin ligand required for wing morphogenesis and male genital looping in Drosophila.
text: The development of adult structures in insects that undergo complete metamorphosis is controlled by ecdysteroids and juvenile hormones. This process involves interactions between cells, which are partly mediated by integrin receptors on the cell surface and their corresponding ligands in the extracellular matrix (ECM). However, the exact role of these adhesion molecules and their regulation by hormones is not well understood. In this study, we investigate a newly discovered ECM protein called tenectin and its gene structure. We show that tenectin is regulated by hormones and is essential for the proper development of the adult wing and male genitalia. Through genetic interactions in flies and cell culture assays, we demonstrate that tenectin functions as a ligand for the PS2 integrins. This interaction relies on specific motifs known as RGD and RGD-like motifs. Furthermore, our experiments on the development of male genitalia reveal that tenectin plays a role in the looping morphogenesis and highlights the involvement of PS integrins in the establishment of left-right asymmetry.

title: Schedule-dependent interaction between anticancer treatments
text: Many cancers exhibit overexpression of the oncogene MDMX, which leads to the suppression of the tumor suppressor p53. In order to reactivate p53 and enhance the effectiveness of DNA-damaging drugs, it may be beneficial to inhibit the oncogene product MDMX. However, our current knowledge lacks a quantitative understanding of how inhibiting MDMX affects the p53 signaling pathway and the sensitivity of cells to DNA damage. Through live cell imaging, it has been observed that depleting MDMX triggers two distinct phases of p53 accumulation in individual cells: an initial pulse after cell division, followed by low-amplitude oscillations. The response to DNA damage differs significantly between these two phases. During the first phase, depleting MDMX in combination with DNA damage leads to cell death, while in the second phase, MDMX depletion inhibits cell death. Therefore, in order to design an optimal schedule for administering dual-drug therapy, it is crucial to have a quantitative understanding of signal dynamics and cellular states.

title: Potent, Selective, and Orally Bioavailable Inhibitors of VPS34 Provide Chemical Tools to Modulate Autophagy in Vivo.
text: Autophagy, a process that controls the degradation of cellular components through lysosomes, has faced challenges in its study due to the absence of dependable pharmacological tools. However, there are now selective inhibitors accessible to regulate the PI 3-kinase VPS34, which plays a crucial role in autophagy. In this article, we present the identification of potent and specific VPS34 inhibitors, along with their pharmacokinetic properties and their ability to hinder autophagy in both cellular and mouse models.

title: The role of neutrophils in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus.
text:
The purpose of this review is to discuss recent findings that suggest neutrophils play a crucial role in regulating innate and adaptive immunity, as well as contributing to organ damage in systemic autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). 

Recent studies have identified several potential biomarkers for SLE that are related to neutrophils, including neutrophil granular proteins and histones that undergo post-translational modifications during the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). In the bone marrow, neutrophils in SLE patients can contribute to abnormalities in B and T cells by producing increased levels of type-I interferons, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα), and B-cell stimulating factors like B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL). These lupus neutrophils, particularly a subset known as lupus low-density granulocytes, also exhibit epigenetic modifications and genomic alterations that may contribute to their harmful effects in SLE. 

Furthermore, proteins and enzymes released by lupus NETs can impact vascular health by inducing endothelial cell apoptosis and oxidizing lipoproteins. In murine studies, inhibiting the formation of NETs through peptidylarginine deiminase inhibitors has been shown to alleviate the lupus phenotype and reduce atherosclerosis. 

In summary, recent discoveries highlight the importance of neutrophils, particularly low-density granulocytes and abnormal NET formation and clearance, in the development of SLE. Future research should focus on finding ways to selectively target these immunostimulatory pathways in order to develop more effective treatments for this disease.

title: Enhancement of proteasome function by PA28α overexpression protects against oxidative stress.
text: The primary role of the proteasome is to degrade proteins within cells. When the proteasome malfunctions, it has been observed in experimental cardiomyopathies and linked to congestive heart failure in humans. Currently, there are no measures to improve the proteasome's ability to break down proteins, but doing so would be beneficial in testing the impact of proteasome dysfunction and could have significant therapeutic potential. The association between the proteasome activator 28 (PA28) and the 20S proteasome may be involved in antigen processing. However, it is unclear if PA28 has any other important roles besides antigen presentation, although increased levels of PA28 have been seen in certain types of cardiomyopathy. In this study, we demonstrate that overexpressing PA28α (PA28αOE) stabilizes PA28β, increases 11S proteasomes, and improves the degradation of a known proteasome surrogate substrate (GFPu) in cultured neonatal rat cardiomyocytes. PA28αOE significantly reduces the protein carbonyls caused by H(2)O(2) and greatly suppresses apoptosis in cultured cardiomyocytes, both under normal conditions and when exposed to H(2)O(2) stress. In conclusion, PA28αOE effectively increases 11S proteasomes, enhances the proteasome's ability to remove misfolded and oxidized proteins, and protects against oxidative stress in cardiomyocytes. This provides a highly sought-after method to enhance the degradation of abnormal cellular proteins by the proteasome.

title: A unified concept of species and its consequences for the future of taxonomy
text: There is a wide range of contemporary species concepts, but they all agree on the basic notion that species are distinct lineages within populations at the biological level. The differences lie in the additional characteristics (such as reproductive isolation, monophyly, and diagnosability) that are considered necessary for identifying lineages as species. A unified species concept can be achieved by recognizing that the essential property of species is being a separately evolving lineage segment, while the secondary properties can be seen as evidence for assessing lineage separation or as defining different subcategories of species (such as reproductively isolated, monophyletic, or diagnosable species). This unified concept has implications for taxonomy, including the recognition that undifferentiated and undiagnosable lineages are still species, species can merge, species can be nested within other species, the species category is not a taxonomic rank, and new practices and conventions are needed to accommodate these conclusions. Accepting a unified species concept brings about significant changes in taxonomy, reflecting a shift in how the species category is understood. Rather than being seen as one rank in a hierarchical classification system, it is now viewed as a natural category representing units at a specific level of biological organization. This change aligns with the broader shift in systematics and taxonomy, where the focus has moved from classifying organisms to testing hypotheses about lineage boundaries and phylogenetic relationships. The unified species concept is a logical outcome of this shift and is crucial for the future of taxonomy, as it recognizes species as fundamental units in biology.

title: Regulation of the small GTP-binding protein Rho by cell adhesion and the cytoskeleton.
text: The ability of serum components, such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), to induce actin stress fibers and focal adhesions in a Rho-dependent manner suggests that they activate the small GTP-binding protein Rho. There has been controversy surrounding whether cell adhesion to extracellular matrices (ECM) also activates Rho, as it is difficult to distinguish changes in Rho activity from the structural contributions of ECM to focal adhesion formation. To address this, we developed a method to measure GTP-bound cellular Rho. When Swiss 3T3 cells were plated on fibronectin-coated dishes, Rho was initially inhibited and then activated, with serum greatly enhancing the activation phase. In serum-starved adherent cells, LPA induced transient Rho activation, while suspended cells showed sustained Rho activation.
