Additionally, suspended cells exhibited higher Rho activity than adherent cells in the presence of serum, suggesting the presence of an adhesion-dependent negative-feedback loop. Interestingly, both cytochalasin D and colchicine triggered Rho activation, despite their opposing effects on stress fibers and focal adhesions. These findings demonstrate that ECM, cytoskeletal structures, and soluble factors all play a role in regulating Rho activity.

title: Core binding factors are necessary for natural killer cell development and cooperate with Notch signaling during T-cell specification.
text: CBFbeta, a subunit of the core binding factors (CBFs), does not bind to DNA. In mice with decreased levels of CBFbeta, there are significant early defects in T-cell development, but not in B-cell development. Our study reveals that CBFbeta is also necessary during the initial stages of natural killer (NK)-cell development. Additionally, we find that T-cell development is disrupted during specification, as the expression of Gata3 and Tcf7, which are crucial regulators of T lineage specification, is greatly reduced, along with functional thymic progenitors. Activation of Notch or IL-7 signaling, or overexpression of Runx1 or CBFbeta, cannot restore T-cell expansion or differentiation in cells lacking sufficient CBFbeta. This suggests that the ability of prethymic cells to respond appropriately to Notch signaling depends on CBFbeta, and both signals work together to activate the T-cell developmental program.

title: VEGF and podocytes in diabetic nephropathy.
text: VEGF-A, a protein secreted by podocytes, plays a crucial role in the survival of endothelial cells, podocytes, and mesangial cells. It regulates slit-diaphragm signaling and podocyte shape through interactions between VEGF-receptor 2, nephrin, nck, and actin. In diabetic nephropathy, chronic hyperglycemia leads to excessive VEGF-A production by podocytes and low levels of endothelial nitric oxide. This abnormal communication between VEGF-A and nitric oxide pathways is exacerbated by the diabetic environment, resulting in heightened oxidative stress. Recent research on these underlying molecular mechanisms has identified potential targets for therapeutic intervention in diabetic renal disease.

title: Detection and distribution patterns of telomerase activity in insects.
text: Most insects have telomeres consisting of pentanucleotide (TTAGG)n repeats. However, Diptera and some other insect species lack these repeats, suggesting that their telomere regions may be maintained without telomerase. To better understand the unique telomere formation in insects, we conducted a study on a potential insect telomerase that has not been previously described. Using a modified telomeric repeat amplification protocol (TRAP), we initially identified telomerase activity in crickets, cockroaches, and two Lepidopteran insects. The telomerase from crickets and cockroaches utilized dATP, dGTP, and dTTP as substrates, but not dCTP, and sequence analysis of the TRAP products confirmed that the (TTAGG)n repeats were synthesized by telomerase. The telomerase in cockroaches was found in both somatic (fat body, muscle, and neural tissues) and germ line (testis) cells, suggesting that the expression of this enzyme is not tissue-specific in adult stages. While we observed high levels of telomerase activity in crickets and cockroaches, we were unable to detect activity in all tissues and cell cultures of the silkworm, Bombyx mori, as well as in two Drosophila and one Sarcophaga cell lines. This supports the hypothesis that Dipteran insects maintain their telomeres without the use of telomerase.

title: Conversion of the lac repressor into an allosterically regulated transcriptional activator for mammalian cells.
text:
Using the Escherichia coli lac repressor, a new regulatory system was developed in mammals. This was achieved by modifying the coding region of the lac repressor to include a nuclear localization signal from the simian virus 40 (SV40) large tumor antigen and the transcription activation domain from the herpes simplex virus type 1 virion protein 16. The resulting fusion protein, known as lac activator protein (LAP), proved to be a potent activator of various promoters containing lac operator sequences. These sequences could be positioned either upstream or downstream of the transcription unit.

Interestingly, transactivation could occur with just a single lac operator, but multiple operators showed a synergistic effect when they were separated by a short distance. Promoters containing 14 or 21 operator sequences exhibited a remarkable induction of at least 1,000-fold in response to LAP. In fact, their activity levels were 20 to 30 times higher than that of the SV40 early promoter in HeLa cells. The activation process was found to be strongly inhibited by isopropyl-beta-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG), indicating that LAP retained the necessary functions for allosteric regulation.

Furthermore, LAP demonstrated a dual functionality as it also acted as a repressor of an SV40 promoter that contained an operator immediately downstream of the TATA box. Finally, genetic selection methods were developed to generate LAP-expressing cell lines at a high frequency. This could be achieved using either established cell lines or primary cells in culture.

title: Antigen availability determines CD8⁺ T cell-dendritic cell interaction kinetics and memory fate decisions.
text: T cells undergo three phases of activation in lymph nodes when they encounter dendritic cells carrying antigens (Ag). The duration of the first phase, which involves brief and repeated interactions between DCs and T cells, is influenced by the amount of Ag. The second phase, characterized by stable interactions between DCs and T cells, was previously thought to be crucial for complete T cell activation. However, our research has shown that this is not always the case. When CD8⁺ T cells interacted with DCs presenting low-dose and short-lived Ag, they did not progress to the second phase. On the other hand, higher Ag doses led to the transition to the second phase. Both scenarios resulted in T cell proliferation and differentiation into effector cells, but they exhibited different gene expression patterns at 12 and 24 hours. T cells that experienced the second phase developed long-lasting memory, while conditions without stable interactions resulted in a loss of immune memory. Therefore, T cells make important decisions about their fate shortly after exposure to Ag, which determines whether they develop long-term memory or abortive effector responses. These decisions are influenced by the kinetics of T cell-DC interactions.

title: BAX/BAK-independent mitoptosis during cell death induced by proteasome inhibition?
text: The rapid death of cancer cells can be induced by proteasome inhibitors. Our study demonstrates that in epithelial cancer cells, this death is accompanied by a significant increase in the levels of various BH3-only proteins, such as BIK, BIM, MCL-1S, NOXA, PUMA, and p53. These elevated protein levels are likely a result of inhibiting their degradation by the proteasome, as well as promoting their transcription and active translation. Interestingly, the subsequent cell death does not rely on BAX and possibly BAK, but instead follows the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. We have identified the series of molecular events that lead to cell death caused by a typical proteasome inhibitor called MG132. These events begin with the rapid accumulation of BH3-only proteins in the mitochondria, followed by the permeabilization of the mitochondrial membrane and the subsequent loss of DeltaPsi(m). Ultimately, irreversible changes occur in the mitochondrial ultrastructure, leading to the degradation of the mitochondrial network and the impairment of crucial mitochondrial functions. Our findings also provide a rationale for using proteasome inhibitors more broadly to eliminate apoptosis-resistant tumor cells that lack functional BAX/BAK proteins.

title: Site of action of a ribosomal RNA methylase responsible for resistance to erythromycin and other antibiotics.
text: The producing organism Streptomyces erythraeus uses an enzyme to provide resistance against erythromycin. This enzyme dimethylates a specific adenine residue in Bacillus stearothermophilus 23 S rRNA. In Escherichia coli 23 S RNA, this corresponds to residue Ade 2058. The same site is targeted by the methylase enzyme in Staphylococcus aureus, which is responsible for resistance against macrolides, lincomycin, and streptogramin B-related antibiotics.

title: 53BP1 nuclear bodies form around DNA lesions generated by mitotic transmission of chromosomes under replication stress
text: The completion of genome duplication is hindered by obstacles that impede the progress of replication forks. This can have a detrimental effect on the integrity of the genome, but it is unclear what happens to DNA that has unresolved replication intermediates. In this study, we demonstrate that mild replication stress increases the occurrence of chromosomal abnormalities that are passed on to daughter cells. These abnormalities are confined to specific areas within the nucleus, marked by a protein called p53-binding protein 1 (53BP1) and other genome caretakers associated with chromatin. We also observe that the number of these nuclear compartments containing 53BP1 increases when a DNA helicase called BLM is removed, as BLM is responsible for untangling DNA. Conversely, when a condensin subunit called SMC2, which is necessary for the stability of mitotic chromosomes, is reduced, the number of 53BP1 nuclear compartments is partially reduced. Finally, we provide evidence that these 53BP1 nuclear compartments protect fragile sites on chromosomes from degradation. Overall, these findings suggest that the preservation of DNA and chromatin integrity at regions prone to replication issues requires their transmission to future generations of cells during mitosis.

title: Targeted inhibition of tumor-specific glutaminase diminishes cell-autonomous tumorigenesis.
text: The role of glutaminase (GLS) in cancer cell metabolism, growth, and proliferation is crucial. Researchers are investigating GLS as a potential target for cancer treatment, but it is unclear whether GLS inhibitors have any effects on cancer cell growth, the surrounding microenvironment, or unintended targets. In this study, we found that reducing the expression of Gls impeded tumor progression in a mouse model of hepatocellular carcinoma driven by the MYC oncogene. Treatment with a GLS-specific inhibitor called BPTES extended survival without causing any noticeable harm in mice with MYC-induced hepatocellular carcinoma. BPTES also hindered the growth of a MYC-dependent human B cell lymphoma cell line (P493) by blocking DNA replication, resulting in cell death and fragmentation. In mice with P493 tumor xenografts, BPTES treatment suppressed tumor cell growth. However, P493 xenografts expressing a BPTES-resistant GLS mutant (GLS-K325A) or overexpressing GLS were unaffected by BPTES treatment. Additionally, a customized Vivo-Morpholino molecule that targeted human GLS mRNA significantly inhibited P493 xenograft growth without affecting the expression of mouse Gls. Conversely, a Vivo-Morpholino molecule targeting mouse Gls had no anti-tumor activity in vivo. Overall, our findings demonstrate the essential role of GLS in tumorigenesis and support the use of small molecules and genetic inhibition of GLS as potential strategies for targeting the cancer cell's dependence on GLS in cancer therapy.

title: Dominant optic atrophy, deafness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dystaxia, and myopathy. A new syndrome.
text: A total of 23 individuals from a family of 96 members displayed a previously undocumented autosomal dominant disorder. This disorder is characterized by a gradual deterioration of the optic nerves, abnormal electroretinography results without any changes in retinal pigmentation, and a progressive loss of hearing that typically becomes noticeable during the first or second decade of life. As individuals reach middle age, they may also experience drooping eyelids, difficulty controlling eye movements, unsteady coordination, and a non-specific muscle weakness.

title: Dynein is required for polarized dendritic transport and uniform microtubule orientation in axons
text: The organization of microtubules and the components they contain differ between axons and dendrites. Our study demonstrates that the motor protein dynein plays a critical role in the transport and orientation of microtubules in Drosophila melanogaster dendritic arborization (da) neurons. Mutations in dynein result in changes in the distribution of organelles within dendritic arbors, causing a shift in the position of dendritic branches towards the cell body. Dynein is also essential for the specific localization of Golgi outposts and the ion channel Pickpocket in dendrites. Normally, axonal microtubules are uniformly oriented with their plus ends distal; however, in the absence of dynein, axons contain microtubules with both plus and minus ends distal. These findings suggest that dynein is necessary for the distinct characteristics of axons and dendrites. Without dynein, dendritic organelles and proteins enter the axon, and the uniform polarity of axonal microtubules is disrupted.

title: Small molecule screening in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived terminal cell types.
text: The desire for improved clinical results has sparked a growing fascination with utilizing human cells that closely mimic physiological conditions in the drug discovery field. Patient-specific human induced pluripotent stem cells have emerged as a promising and practical model for studying human disease physiology, offering relevance, reliability, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. The application of high throughput screening using small molecules in cells derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells is beginning to impact the drug discovery process by identifying innovative therapeutic compounds. Nevertheless, the utilization of these cells poses numerous challenges in the development of high throughput screening methods. This technology holds the potential to revolutionize the approach to drug discovery.

title: Gene expression during gonadogenesis in the chicken embryo.
text:
The study focused on investigating the genes involved in determining and differentiating the sex of vertebrates, specifically in embryonic chicken gonads. The researchers used reverse transcription and the polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to analyze the expression of various genes during the process of gonadal sex differentiation. They examined the expression profiles of AMH, SOX9, SOX3, WT1, SF1, and DAX1 genes, which are known to play a role in sex determination. 

The results showed that some of these genes exhibited sexually dimorphic expression profiles during gonadal development, while others were expressed at similar levels in both sexes. The gene responsible for producing Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) was found to be expressed in both sexes before and during sexual differentiation, with higher levels in males. SOX9 expression was specific to males and increased after the detection of AMH transcripts. SOX3 expression was observed before clear SOX9 expression and was up-regulated in both sexes at the beginning of gonadal sex differentiation, but decreased later in development. The WT1 gene showed high expression in both sexes, while SF1 expression was significantly higher in developing ovaries compared to testes. DAX1 transcripts were present in both sexes at all stages examined, but expression seemed to be slightly higher in developing ovaries. 

These expression profiles were analyzed in relation to current theories of vertebrate sex determination.

title: Organ-resident, nonlymphoid cells suppress proliferation of autoimmune T-helper lymphocytes.
text: The inappropriate expression of Ia determinants by organ-resident cells, leading to the local presentation of autoantigen, has been linked to organ-specific autoimmunity. To study this phenomenon, researchers have used experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis in rats, which involves immunization with retinal soluble antigen and serves as a model for organ-specific autoimmunity. In an in vitro system derived from this model, uveitogenic rat T-helper lymphocytes specific to the retinal soluble antigen were compared to control T-helper lymphocytes reactive to the purified protein derivative of tuberculin. These lymphocytes were cocultured with Ia-expressing syngeneic retinal glial cells (Müller cells) in the presence of the specific antigen. Under normal culture conditions, antigen presentation was not observed, and the Müller cells strongly suppressed the proliferative response of primed T-helper lymphocytes to the antigen presented on conventional antigen-presenting cells. Additionally, the Müller cells inhibited the subsequent expansion of T-helper lymphocytes dependent on interleukin-2 (IL-2). This suppression of proliferation was accompanied by a decrease in IL-2 production in response to the antigen and a reduction in the expression of high-affinity IL-2 receptors. The suppression occurred through direct contact between the Müller cells and the lymphocytes. These findings suggest that local suppression mechanisms play a role in immune regulation and the maintenance of tissue homeostasis.

title: Drug induced refractory headache--clinical features and management.
text:
A study was conducted on two hundred patients who suffered from severe headaches on a daily or near-daily basis, despite taking excessive amounts of daily symptomatic or immediate relief medications. Among these patients, one hundred and sixteen (58%) were also taking prophylactic medications, which proved to be ineffective. All patients were provided with dietary instructions to consume low tyramine and low caffeine, as well as biofeedback training. The study examined the impact of continuing symptomatic medications, discontinuing symptomatic medications, and adding or changing prophylactic medications in different treatment groups. The findings of the study are as follows: 

1.) The daily use of symptomatic or immediate relief medications leads to chronic daily headaches.
2.) Discontinuing the use of daily symptomatic medications alone results in an improvement in headaches.
3.) The concomitant use of symptomatic medications negates the effectiveness of prophylactic medications.
4.) Discontinuing the use of daily symptomatic medications enhances the positive effects of prophylactic medications.

title: Neuromodulation of neurons and synapses.
text: The flexibility of neural circuit operation and behavior is supported by neuromodulation. Neurons can be affected by individual neuromodulators in different ways, as they target various physiological mechanisms. On the other hand, multiple neuromodulators can have similar effects by acting on the same targets. These actions can either work together or oppose each other, but neuromodulation typically involves adjusting membrane and synaptic properties in a balanced manner. This is achieved by targeting ion channels and synaptic dynamics, rather than just excitability or synaptic strength. Furthermore, neuromodulators can have effects over different timescales, ranging from short-term adjustments to long-term regulation. This brief overview highlights the diverse effects of neuromodulators on ion channels and synaptic properties.

title: Mutation frequency and specificity with age in liver, bladder and brain of lacI transgenic mice.
text: The study examined the frequency and specificity of mutations in nuclear DNA from the liver, bladder, and brain of Big Blue lacI transgenic mice aged 1.5-25 months. It was found that mutations increased with age in the liver and accumulated at a faster rate in the bladder. In the brain, there was a slight initial increase in mutation frequency in young mice, but no further increase in adult mice. To determine the origin of these mutations, the researchers analyzed the mutational spectra for each tissue and age. They discovered that there were no significant changes in mutational specificity in any tissue at any age when analyzing the DNA sequence of mutant lacI transgenes. This suggests that the mutations found in aging animals were the result of a common set of DNA lesions that occurred during DNA replication. The data also indicated that there were no significant age-related mutational changes caused by oxidative damage, errors in DNA polymerase fidelity, or inefficiency in DNA repair. Therefore, there is no evidence to support the hypotheses that oxidative damage or accumulation of errors in nuclear DNA significantly contribute to the aging process in these three somatic tissues.

title: Breaching the basement membrane: who, when and how?
text: The basement membrane (BM) is a specialized network of extracellular matrix macromolecules that surrounds various types of cells, including epithelial, endothelial, muscle, fat, and nerve cells. In processes such as development, immune surveillance, and disease conditions like cancer and fibrosis, host cells are able to penetrate the BM by activating tissue-invasive programs. However, the specific identity of these programs is not well understood. It has been commonly assumed that all cells use similar mechanisms to cross BM barriers, but recent evidence suggests that cells may selectively utilize protease-dependent or protease-independent invasion programs. Recent findings indicate that protease-dependent transmigration relies heavily on a group of membrane-anchored metalloenzymes called membrane-type matrix metalloproteinases, which permanently remodel the structure of the BM. On the other hand, the mechanisms enabling protease-independent transmigration are still unclear, but they may involve the reversible disassembly of the BM network. Further investigation into the molecular mechanisms involved in BM transmigration will provide valuable insights into tissue remodeling events in various pathological conditions and may also lead to the development of new therapeutic approaches.

title: Soluble MD-2 is an acute-phase protein and an opsonin for Gram-negative bacteria.
text: Myeloid differentiation factor-2 (MD-2) is a protein that binds to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a component of Gram-negative bacteria. It is typically found in conjunction with Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and is responsible for the LPS responsiveness of immune cells. MD-2 can also be found as a soluble protein. In patients with severe infections or inflamed tissues, levels of soluble MD-2 (sMD-2) in the plasma and other fluids are significantly elevated. Our research shows that sMD-2 is a type II acute-phase protein, meaning its levels increase during an acute-phase response. In mice, both soluble MD-2 mRNA and protein levels are up-regulated in the liver after an acute-phase response is induced. Human hepatocytic cells secrete soluble MD-2, and its production is increased by interleukin-6. Soluble MD-2 specifically binds to Gram-negative bacteria and not Gram-positive bacteria. When hepatocytic cells secrete sMD-2, it acts as an essential cofactor for the activation of TLR4-expressing cells by Gram-negative bacteria. Additionally, soluble MD-2 enhances the phagocytosis of Gram-negative bacteria, primarily by polymorphonuclear neutrophils. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that sMD-2 is a newly identified type II acute-phase reactant, an opsonin for Gram-negative bacteria, and a necessary cofactor for the activation of TLR4-expressing cells. This suggests that sMD-2 plays a crucial role in the innate immune response to Gram-negative infections.

title: Division-coupled astrocytic differentiation and age-related depletion of neural stem cells in the adult hippocampus.
text: The production of new neurons in the adult hippocampus decreases as we age, and this decline may be responsible for age-related cognitive decline. Our study reveals that the continuous depletion of the neural stem cell pool, caused by their division, may contribute to the decrease in hippocampal neurogenesis associated with aging. Our findings suggest that adult hippocampal stem cells, when they exit their dormant state, undergo a series of unequal divisions to generate dividing offspring that will eventually become neurons and then mature into astrocytes. Therefore, the reduction in the number of neural stem cells is a process linked to their division and directly affects the production of new neurons. We propose a model called the "disposable stem cell" model, which outlines the neurogenesis cascade in the adult hippocampus. This model explains the disappearance of hippocampal neural stem cells, the emergence of new astrocytes, and the decline in the production of new neurons that occurs with age.

title: P19 embryonal carcinoma cells.
text: P19 cells are a type of pluripotent embryonal carcinoma that can continuously grow in media supplemented with serum. The differentiation of these cells can be controlled using safe drugs. Retinoic acid is particularly effective in stimulating the development of neurons, astroglia, and microglia, which are cell types typically derived from the neuroectoderm. When aggregates of P19 cells are exposed to dimethyl sulfoxide, they differentiate into endodermal and mesodermal derivatives, including cardiac and skeletal muscle. P19 cells can be easily transfected with DNA containing recombinant genes, and stable cell lines expressing these genes can be readily isolated. These manipulations make P19 cells an ideal material for studying the molecular mechanisms that govern the developmental decisions made by differentiating pluripotent cells.

title: Iguanas and Salmonella marina infection in children: a reflection of the increasing incidence of reptile-associated salmonellosis in the United States.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the clinical aspects and risk factors for Salmonella serotype Marina infection in the United States. In order to achieve this, we analyzed all reported cases of S. Marina in 1994 from the National Salmonella Surveillance System. Patients were interviewed regarding their demographic information, clinical course, diet, travel history, and contact with reptiles prior to illness.

Out of the 32 patients, 26 (81%) were infants under the age of one, and 24 (75%) were male. This is in contrast to other Salmonella isolates reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 1994, where only 14% were infants and 49% were male. Among the patients, 11 (34%) required hospitalization for a median of 3.5 days (range: 2 to 21 days), and unfortunately, one patient died. Out of the 28 patients (88%) who reported exposure to iguanas, only 4 (14%) had direct contact with the reptile, and only 12 respondents (43%) were aware that it could have been the source of infection. Interestingly, 7 (32%) out of the 22 families who owned an iguana at the time of illness still owned one when contacted after a median of 28 weeks. Those who believed the iguana was the source of infection were more likely to have given away or sold the pet compared to those who did not. Additionally, 4 isolates (13%) were obtained from blood samples, and it was found that bacteremia was associated with the use of antibiotics within 30 days prior to S. Marina infection (odds ratio: 24; 95% confidence interval: 1.2-1309).

In conclusion, S. Marina infection is a potentially serious illness linked to exposure to iguanas, highlighting the broader issue of reptile-associated salmonellosis. Many parents are unaware that owning an iguana puts their children at risk of Salmonella infection. Therefore, it is crucial for pediatricians, veterinarians, and pet store owners to educate their patients and customers about the potential risks associated with owning reptiles and provide appropriate preventive education.

title: Siblings with opposite chromosome constitutions, dup(2q)/del(7q) and del(2q)/dup(7q).
text: Chromosome 7q36 microdeletion syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by underdeveloped brain, small head size, abnormalities in the reproductive organs, and difficulties with language. The main features of chromosome 2q37 microdeletion syndrome include developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders, BDMR syndrome, and distinct facial appearance. In a genetic screening of two brothers with global developmental delay, advanced chromosomal analysis and probe amplification revealed rearrangements in specific regions of chromosomes 2q37.2 and 7q35, with one brother having a deletion and the other a duplication. Both brothers exhibited abnormal facial features, severe physical and intellectual disabilities, and differences in their reproductive organs. The rest of the family did not show any abnormal genetic traits. The genetic analysis of the parents suggested that the gene mutation may have occurred through a process called adjacent-1 segregation from the mother. To gain more insight into the related genes and their chromosomal locations, we compared the phenotypes of our patients with those described in previous studies.

title: Methods for quantifying follicular numbers within the mouse ovary.
text:
Accurately estimating the number of ovarian follicles at different stages of development is a crucial indicator of the folliculogenesis process. It helps us understand how endocrine signals and paracrine/autocrine mechanisms control the growth and maturation of oocytes and their supporting follicular cells. However, previous studies using various methods have reported significant differences in follicular numbers per ovary, making it challenging to interpret ovarian function in control versus experimental conditions. 

This study presents unbiased and assumption-free stereological methods for quantifying early and growing follicular numbers in mouse ovaries. The researchers used a fractionator approach to sample a specific fraction of histological sections from adult wild-type ovaries. They independently counted primordial and primary follicles using optical and physical disector methods. These fractionator/disector methods, which are not influenced by follicular size or shape, provided estimations of 1930 +/- 286 (S.E.M.) and 2227 +/- 101 primordial follicles, and 137 +/- 25 and 265 +/- 32 primary follicles per ovary at 70 and 100 days of age, respectively. 

Additionally, by conducting exact counts on serial sections, the researchers estimated that there were 135 secondary and later follicles per ovary at 100 days of age. They also used a fractionator/physical disector approach to estimate the remnants of zona pellucidae (a marker of previous follicular atresia), which were approximately 500 per ovary. 

The application of these quantitative methods described in the study will enhance our understanding of follicular dynamics and the factors that influence their growth and maturation. It will also enable better comparisons between different studies.

title: Identification of functional cooperative mutations of SETD2 in human acute leukemia
text:
The development of full-blown malignancy in acute leukemia, which is characterized by chromosomal rearrangements, requires additional molecular disruptions. However, the specific mechanisms involved in this cooperative process are still unknown. In our study, we used whole-genome sequencing to analyze a pair of monozygotic twins who had different forms of leukemia caused by rearrangements in the MLL (also known as KMT2A) gene. We discovered a fusion gene called MLL-NRIP3 and biallelic mutations in SETD2, which is responsible for encoding a histone H3K36 methyltransferase. Furthermore, we found that loss-of-function point mutations in SETD2 were recurrent in 6.2% of the 241 patients with acute leukemia we examined, and these mutations were associated with multiple major chromosomal abnormalities.

In leukemic blasts with SETD2 mutations, we observed a global reduction in H3K36 trimethylation (H3K36me3). Additionally, when SETD2 was downregulated in the presence of a genetic lesion, it contributed to both the initiation and progression of leukemia by enhancing the self-renewal potential of leukemia stem cells. Therefore, our study provides strong evidence that SETD2 functions as a tumor suppressor. The disruption of the SETD2-H3K36me3 pathway represents a distinct epigenetic mechanism involved in the development of leukemia.

title: Evidence regarding human papillomavirus testing in secondary prevention of cervical cancer.
text: Clinicians now more than ever require regularly updated reviews due to the continuous influx of new information regarding innovative methods for preventing cervical cancer. Recent meta-analyses and systematic reviews provide a summary of three potential clinical applications of human papillomavirus (HPV) testing: triage for women with uncertain or low-grade cytologic abnormalities, prediction of treatment outcomes for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) lesions, and primary screening for cervical cancer and pre-cancer. Consistent evidence suggests that HPV-triage using the Hybrid Capture(®) 2 assay (HC2) is more accurate than repeat cytology in triaging women with equivocal Pap smear results. Other tests show similar accuracy, but mRNA testing with the APTIMA(®) test is more specific compared to HC2. In triaging low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL), HC2 is more sensitive but less specific than repeat cytology. The APTIMA(®) test is more specific without sacrificing sensitivity. Identifying DNA of HPV types 16 and/or 18, or RNA from the five most carcinogenic HPV types, allows for the selection of women at the highest risk for CIN3+, but these markers have lower sensitivity and negative predictive value compared to full-range high-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing. After conservative treatment of cervical pre-cancer, HPV testing is quicker and more sensitive in detecting residual or recurrent high-grade CIN compared to follow-up cytology. Primary screening for hrHPV generally detects more CIN2, CIN3, or cancer compared to cytology, but is less specific. Combined HPV and cytology screening slightly improves sensitivity but significantly reduces specificity compared to HPV testing alone. Randomized trials and cohort studies consistently show a lower cumulative incidence of CIN3+ and cancer in women aged 30 years or older who test negative for hrHPV DNA at enrollment compared to those who test negative cytologically. HC2, GP5+/6+ PCR, cobas(®) 4800 PCR, and Real Time PCR are clinically validated for use in primary screening. The loss in specificity associated with primary HPV-based screening can be compensated for by appropriate algorithms involving reflex cytology and/or HPV genotyping for HPV16 or 18. There is substantial evidence supporting the advantages of HPV testing in triage, surveillance, and primary screening for women aged 30 years or older. However, the benefits of HPV-based screening require a well-organized program with high compliance to screening and triage policies. This article is part of a special supplement titled "Comprehensive Control of HPV Infections and Related Diseases" in Vaccine Volume 30, Supplement 5, 2012.

title: International standards for fetal growth based on serial ultrasound measurements: the Fetal Growth Longitudinal Study of the INTERGROWTH-21st Project.
text: In 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed growth standards for infants and children up to age 5. Following a similar approach, the Fetal Growth Longitudinal Study (FGLS) aimed to create international growth and size standards for fetuses as part of the INTERGROWTH-21(st) Project. The FGLS assessed fetal growth in urban populations across eight countries where mothers received adequate health and nutritional care. Ultrasound measurements were taken from 14 weeks of gestation until birth in a cohort of low-risk women with reliable estimates of gestational age. The study found small differences between observed and smoothed centiles for various fetal growth measures, and international standards for fetal growth were established. These standards are recommended for clinical interpretation of ultrasound measurements and for comparisons across populations. The study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: Role of NF-kappa B in cell survival and transcription of latent membrane protein 1-expressing or Epstein-Barr virus latency III-infected cells.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) latency III infection transforms B lymphocytes into lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) by producing EBV nuclear and membrane proteins, known as EBNAs and latent membrane proteins (LMPs). These proteins regulate transcription through the Notch and tumor necrosis factor receptor pathways. To understand the role of NF-kappa B in LMP1 and overall EBV latency III transcriptional effects, LCLs were treated with BAY11-7082 (BAY11), an NF-kappa B inhibitor. BAY11 effectively inhibited NF-kappa B, leading to a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, induction of apoptosis, and alteration of LCL gene expression. The effects of BAY11 were similar to those of another NF-kappa B inhibitor, Delta N-I kappa B alpha, as observed in decreased JNK1 expression and microarray analyses. A significant number of array elements that decreased with Delta N-I kappa B alpha expression also decreased with BAY11 treatment. Among the newly identified genes induced by NF-kappa B, LMP1, and EBV were pleckstrin, Jun-B, c-FLIP, CIP4, and I kappa B epsilon. Out of 776 significantly changed array elements, 134 were upregulated fourfold in EBV latency III, and 74 were upregulated fourfold with LMP1 expression alone, while only 28 were downregulated more than fourfold by EBV latency III. The gene products regulated by EBV latency III are involved in cell migration, antigen presentation, the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and interferon signaling. When comparing the gene expression of EBV latency III LCLs to immunoglobulin M (IgM)-stimulated B cells, germinal-center B cells, and germinal-center-derived lymphomas, LCLs clustered with IgM-stimulated B cells, separate from germinal-center cells or germinal-center lymphoma cells. The expression of IRF-2, AIM1, ASK1, SNF2L2, and components of IFN signaling pathways further distinguished EBV latency III-infected B cells from IgM-stimulated or germinal-center B cells.

title: Endotoxin tolerance: new mechanisms, molecules and clinical significance.
text: Endotoxin tolerance, a phenomenon known as the refractory state of innate immune cells such as monocytes/macrophages after exposure to small amounts of endotoxin, has been observed. This state, referred to as "endotoxin tolerance," is clinically relevant in sepsis patients, where monocytes/macrophages contribute to immunosuppression and increased mortality. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying endotoxin tolerance are still not fully understood. Recent advancements in understanding inflammation as a self-regulating process, the role of MyD88 and TRIF signaling pathways in inducing activation or tolerance, the flexibility of NF-kappaB function, and the influence of chromatin modification and microRNAs in LPS-induced gene reprogramming have prompted a re-evaluation of endotoxin tolerance. This review aims to integrate these new findings into a comprehensive understanding of endotoxin tolerance, its molecular basis, and its clinical implications in various pathologies.

title: Pancreatic tumor cells with mutant K-ras suppress ERK activity by MEK-dependent induction of MAP kinase phosphatase-2.
text: A high percentage of human pancreatic carcinomas have activating mutations in the K-ras gene. Previous research showed that the presence of oncogenic, activated K-ras in human pancreatic carcinoma cell lines did not lead to constant activation of the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1 and ERK2). In this study, we aimed to further understand the ERK signaling pathway in pancreatic tumor cell lines to determine if it undergoes compensatory downregulation. We discovered that the decrease in serum-induced ERK activation was not due to a delay in ERK phosphorylation kinetics. Treatment with the tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor orthovanadate increased the level of ERK phosphorylation, suggesting that a vanadate-sensitive tyrosine phosphatase is involved in the negative regulation of ERK. Additionally, most of the pancreatic tumor cell lines had elevated expression of a dual specificity phosphatase called mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase phosphatase-2 (MKP-2), which can inactivate ERK. This elevation correlated with the presence of active MAP kinase kinase (MEK). Overall, these findings indicate that pancreatic tumor cells with oncogenic K-ras compensate, at least in part, by increasing the expression of MKP-2 to suppress the ERK signaling pathway.

title: E2F3 is a mediator of DNA damage-induced apoptosis.
text: The E2F transcription factors play a crucial role in apoptosis. In this study, we found that a specific member of the E2F family, E2F3a, can be activated by DNA damage through both transcriptional and posttranslational mechanisms. We discovered that the posttranslational activation of human E2F3a relies on the checkpoint kinases. Additionally, we observed that the checkpoint kinases phosphorylate E2F3a and that mutating the phosphorylation site prevents the protein from being induced by DNA damage. Furthermore, we demonstrated that DNA damage leads to the transcriptional induction of E2F1 and E2F2 in a manner dependent on E2F3. Finally, through experiments conducted in vitro and in vivo, we established that E2F3 is essential for DNA damage-induced apoptosis. These findings highlight the novel role of E2F3 as a key regulator of the DNA damage response.

title: miR-294/miR-302 promotes proliferation, suppresses G1-S restriction point, and inhibits ESC differentiation through separable mechanisms.
text: The miR-294 and miR-302 microRNAs play a role in promoting the shortened G1 phase of the embryonic stem cell (ESC) cell cycle and inhibiting differentiation caused by let-7. In this study, we investigated the involvement of the retinoblastoma (Rb) family proteins in these processes. Under normal growth conditions, miR-294 facilitated a rapid transition from G1 to S phase, regardless of the presence of the Rb family. However, miR-294 hindered the accumulation of cells in G1 in response to nutrient deprivation and cell-cell contact, and this effect was dependent on the Rb proteins. Additionally, we discovered five other miRNAs (miR-26a, miR-99b, miR-193, miR-199a-5p, and miR-218) that suppressed ESC self-renewal when acting alone, but were counteracted by miR-294 and miR-302. Four out of the six miRNAs that induced differentiation caused an accumulation of cells in G1 that was dependent on Rb. However, all six miRNAs still suppressed self-renewal even in the absence of the Rb proteins. These findings demonstrate that the miR-294/miR-302 family regulates the G1 restriction point and the silencing of self-renewal through both Rb-dependent and Rb-independent pathways, respectively.

title: Bacteriophage latent-period evolution as a response to resource availability.
text:
Bacteriophages, also known as phages, have the ability to modify microbial communities by lysing hosts, transferring genetic material, and causing lysogenic conversion. In order to understand the effects on natural communities, it is crucial to develop predictive models. In this study, we examine how variations in different model parameters can influence these predictions. Specifically, we focus on the eclipse period, latent period, adsorption constant, burst size, handling of differences in host quantity and quality, and modeling strategy.

To begin, we compare two existing models of phage growth. These models differ primarily in how they simulate the kinetics of phage adsorption. One model is a computer simulation, while the other is an explicit calculation. When host quantities are high (around 10(8) cells/ml), both models accurately predict the growth rates of phage populations based on experimental data. However, at lower host quantities (10(7) cells/ml), the computer simulation continues to provide accurate predictions, while the explicit model does not.

Next, we focus on predictions of latent-period optima. The latent period is the time it takes for a specific phage to maximize its population growth in the presence of a specific quantity and quality of host cells. Both models predict similar latent-period optima at higher host densities (e.g., 17 minutes at 10(8) cells/ml). However, at lower host densities, the computer simulation predicts much shorter latent-period optima compared to the explicit calculations (e.g., 90 versus 1,250 minutes at 10(5) cells/ml).

Finally, we examine the impact of host quality on phage latent-period evolution. By distinguishing between latent-period phenotypic plasticity and latent-period evolution, we argue that the influence of host quality on phage latent-period evolution may be relatively minor.

title: Neutrophil elastase-mediated lung disease.
text: The initiation and progression of lung disease have been linked to elastases found in both neutrophils and macrophages. While it is unlikely that these proteases evolved with the intention of harming lung tissue, the connective tissue framework of the lungs, which is rich in elastin, seems to be particularly vulnerable to the effects of elastolytic proteases. Neutrophil elastase is believed to play a role in the migration of neutrophils towards sites of inflammation and in the degradation of proteins from invading organisms or other inflammatory response products. Therefore, inhibitors of this protease are responsible for protecting normal tissues from its harmful effects. In cases of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, we observe a natural experiment that disrupts the balance between this protease and its inhibitors, leading to an increased risk of destructive lung disease.

title: Role of TRPML and two-pore channels in endolysosomal cation homeostasis.
text: The transient receptor potential (TRP) channels TRPML1, TRPML2, and TRPML3, also known as mucolipins 1-3 or MCOLN1-3, are nonselective channels that allow the passage of cations. Mutations in the Trpml1 gene lead to mucolipidosis type IV in humans, which is characterized by psychomotor retardation, corneal clouding, and retinal degeneration. On the other hand, mutations in the Trpml3 gene cause deafness, circling behavior, and coat color dilution in mice. No disease-causing mutations have been identified for the Trpml2 gene. Similar to TRPML channels, two-pore channels (TPCs) such as TPC1, TPC2, and TPC3 are located in intracellular organelles, particularly in endosomes and lysosomes. Both TRPML channels and TPCs may act as channels for the release of calcium and cations in endosomes, lysosomes, and related organelles. TRPMLs are activated by phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate and regulated by pH, while TPCs are activated by nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate in a calcium- and pH-dependent manner. They may also play a role in endolysosomal transport and fusion processes, serving as sources of intracellular calcium. However, the precise physiological functions of TRPML channels and TPCs are still not fully understood, and it remains to be determined whether TRPML channels are exclusively found in endolysosomal ion channels or if they are also functionally active at the plasma membrane in vivo.

title: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in London: clinical experience of 21 cases.
text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a rare condition in the United Kingdom and has previously been limited to individuals of Afro-Caribbean descent. From 1981 to 1995, 21 cases were observed at two teaching hospitals in inner London, where 17% of the population is of Afro-Caribbean origin. The clinical presentations resembled those seen in areas where HTLV-I is prevalent. Combination chemotherapy resulted in significant responses (complete response + partial response) in 10 out of 16 patients (63%) who were evaluated. However, the median survival time was only 5.5 months. Disease progression and opportunistic infections were the primary causes of treatment failure and death. In the central nervous system (CNS), three patients (14%) experienced relapse. Our cases confirm the severe immunosuppression associated with ATLL. The unfavorable prognosis of acute and lymphoma types of ATLL emphasizes the necessity for novel treatment approaches, such as zidovudine and alpha-interferon, which include prophylaxis against CNS disease and opportunistic infections.

title: Regeneration, tissue injury and the immune response.
text: The immune system's role in responding to tissue injury has sparked interest in its potential influence on tissue, organ, or appendage regeneration. One theory suggests that inflammation may hinder regeneration, but there is also evidence supporting positive contributions from immune components. The vertebrate eye is a unique site with limited immune activity due to various immunomodulatory mechanisms. In certain newt species, ocular tissues like the lens have regenerative capabilities. Recent studies have revealed that local lens injury triggers the activation of antigen-presenting cells, which migrate to the spleen and return to displace and engulf the lens. This process induces regeneration from the dorsal iris. The activation of thrombin from prothrombin in the dorsal iris plays a crucial role in initiating regeneration. The potential connections between the immune response and regenerative response are explored in relation to the evolutionary variation of regeneration and specifically lens regeneration.

title: Poverty, Hunger, Education, and Residential Status Impact Survival in HIV
text: Despite receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), individuals infected with HIV still experience higher mortality rates compared to those who are not infected. It has been observed that lower socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with increased mortality in various chronic illnesses, but there is limited data on its impact in people with HIV. To address this gap, we conducted a study involving 878 HIV-infected individuals who were followed from 1995 to 2005. We used Cox proportional hazards models to estimate the effects of SES measures and other factors on all-cause mortality. Additionally, we employed mixed effects analyses to examine how SES influences the factors that predict death. Among the 200 individuals who died during the study period, it was found that they were older, had lower CD4 counts, and higher viral loads (VL). Univariate analyses revealed that age, transmission category, education, albumin levels, CD4 counts, VL, hunger, and poverty were all predictors of death. In the multivariable model, age, CD4 counts, albumin levels, VL, and poverty remained significant predictors of mortality. Furthermore, the mixed models demonstrated associations between CD4 counts and education/hunger, albumin levels and education/homelessness/poverty, and VL and education/hunger. These findings suggest that SES plays a role in mortality among individuals infected with HIV, both directly and indirectly. Therefore, addressing socioeconomic disparities should be a priority in health policies targeting this population.

title: The INO80 ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex is a nucleosome spacing factor.
text: The ATP-dependent remodeler INO80 exhibits a distinct mechanism of nucleosome mobilization compared to another remodeler, SWI/SNF, which is also involved in gene activation. Unlike SWI/SNF, INO80 is unable to disassemble nucleosomes when remodeling short nucleosomal arrays. Instead, INO80's nucleosome spacing activity more closely resembles that of ISW2 and ISW1a, which are generally associated with transcription repression, although there are some notable exceptions. INO80 requires a minimum of 33 to 43 base pairs (bp) of extranucleosomal DNA for effective nucleosome mobilization, with 70 bp being the optimal length. Similar to ISW2 and ISW1a, INO80 prefers to move mononucleosomes towards the center of the DNA, but does so with greater precision. Unlike ISW2/1a, INO80 does not rely on the H4 tail for nucleosome mobilization; instead, the H2A histone tail negatively regulates nucleosome movement by INO80. INO80 is capable of bringing arrays of two or three nucleosomes with 50 or 79 bp of linker DNA closer together, resulting in a final length of approximately 30 bp of linker DNA or a repeat length of approximately 177 bp. A minimum length of more than 30 bp of linker DNA is necessary for INO80 to facilitate nucleosome movement and spacing in arrays.

title: Concentrations of tenofovir and emtricitabine in saliva: implications for preexposure prophylaxis of oral HIV acquisition.
text: In order to prevent the transmission of HIV through oral sex, it is necessary for the drugs used for preexposure prophylaxis (Prep) to be present in saliva. We conducted a study where we simultaneously measured the concentrations of tenofovir (TFV) and emtricitabine (FTC) in both the plasma and saliva of 41 HIV-infected patients who were receiving stable antiretroviral treatment. The average ratios of saliva to plasma concentration were found to be 3% (±4%) for TFV and 86.9% (±124%) for FTC. Therefore, it is recommended to use a combination of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and FTC to effectively prevent the acquisition of HIV through oral sex.

title: Increased lean body mass as an early indicator of olanzapine-induced weight gain in healthy men.
text:
Weight gain is a common side effect of many psychiatric medications, but the exact reasons for this are not fully understood. To investigate this further, we conducted a two-week study on the weight gain effects of olanzapine, a medication known to sometimes cause this side effect. Our aim was to determine if the weight gain was unrelated to changes in the psychiatric condition being treated. 

We recruited healthy male volunteers and randomly assigned them to either receive olanzapine (5 mg/day for 7 days, then 10 mg/day for 7 days) or a placebo. Out of the 24 participants, 19 completed the study (13 on olanzapine, 6 on placebo). We measured various factors including body weight, glucose, triglyceride, total cholesterol, lipid, leptin, insulin, and aldosterone levels, resting metabolic rate, body composition, physical activity, and 24-hour dietary intake. 

The results showed a significant increase in weight, as well as triglyceride, insulin, and leptin levels in the olanzapine group as a whole. Among the participants who gained weight while taking olanzapine (8 individuals), there was an increase in lean mass but not fat mass. Additionally, their insulin, fasting glucose, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and non-high-density lipoprotein levels increased, while aldosterone levels decreased. No significant metabolic or endocrine changes were observed in the placebo group or in those taking olanzapine who did not gain weight. 

These findings suggest that early metabolic changes associated with olanzapine use are independent of fat accumulation.

title: QTc interval length and QT dispersion as predictors of mortality in patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes.
text: Patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes (NIDDM) have an increased risk of cardiovascular death, although the exact reasons for this are not fully understood. The objective of our study was to assess the impact of corrected QT interval length (QTc) and QT dispersion (QT-disp) on mortality in a group of 324 Caucasian NIDDM patients. At the beginning of the study, a resting 12-lead ECG was performed. The maximum (QT-max) and minimum QT (QT-min) intervals were measured, and QT-max was adjusted for heart rate (QTc-max). QT-disp was defined as the difference between QT-max and QT-min. The median QTc-max was 454 ms(1/2) and the median QT-disp was 61 ms. Prolonged QTc interval (PQTc), defined as QTc-max > 440 ms(1/2), was present in 67% of the patients, while prolonged QT-disp (PQT-disp), defined as QT-disp > 50 ms, was present in 51%. Over the course of the 9-year follow-up period, 100 patients died, with 52 of those deaths attributed to cardiovascular diseases. Among patients with PQTc, 37% died compared to 17% with a normal QTc interval (p<0.001). The Cox proportional hazard model, which included potential risk factors at the beginning of the study, identified the following independent predictors of all-cause mortality: QTc-max (p<0.05), age (p<0.0001), albuminuria (p<0.01), retinopathy (p<0.01), HbA1c (p<0.05), insulin treatment (p<0.01), total cholesterol (p<0.01), serum creatinine (p<0.05), and the presence of cardiac heart disease based on Minnesota coded ECG (p<0.001). While QT-disp was not a predictor, QTc-max interval was an independent predictor of cardiovascular mortality. Our study revealed a high prevalence of QTc and QT-disp abnormalities and suggested that QTc-max, but not QT-disp, is a significant predictor of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in NIDDM patients.

title: Repriming of DNA synthesis at stalled replication forks by human PrimPol
text: DNA replication forks that collapse during the process of duplicating the entire genome pose a threat to the stability of the genetic material. The likelihood of fork collapse increases when replication inhibitors or UV radiation are present, as these factors cause specific changes in the DNA structure. In such cases, the progression of the fork may be aided by error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS) DNA polymerases. Alternatively, the replisome, which is responsible for DNA replication, may bypass the damaged DNA and leave an unreplicated gap that needs to be repaired after replication. This mechanism requires a priming event downstream of the damaged area. Our research demonstrates that PrimPol, a newly discovered human enzyme with both primase and TLS polymerase activities, utilizes its primase function to ensure uninterrupted fork progression following UV radiation and to restart DNA synthesis when there is a depletion of deoxyribonucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs). Given its role in DNA damage tolerance, PrimPol could potentially be targeted for cancer therapy.

title: Recombinant human tumor necrosis factor administered as a five-day continuous infusion in cancer patients: phase I toxicity and effects on lipid metabolism.
text:
A trial was conducted to evaluate the effects of recombinant human tumor necrosis factor (rH-TNF) on patients. The trial involved a five-day continuous intravenous (IV) infusion of rH-TNF, which was repeated every 28 days. A total of 19 patients received 38 courses of therapy. The initial dose was 5 X 10(4) U/m2/d, and it was gradually increased to 1.0 X 10(5), 2.0 X 10(5), 2.4 X 10(5), and finally 3.0 X 10(5) U/m2/d.

The side effects of the treatment were generally mild and self-limiting. Patients experienced symptoms such as fever, chills, hypotension, fatigue, anorexia, and headaches. However, these effects were not severe. At the highest dose of 3.0 X 10(5) U/m2/d, the main concern was hematologic toxicity, which caused temporary decreases in platelet and white blood cell counts. Additionally, higher doses of rH-TNF led to elevated bilirubin levels.

Lipoprotein analysis revealed changes in lipid levels following the five-day treatment with rH-TNF. High-density lipoproteins decreased, while triglycerides and very-low-density lipoproteins increased.

Pharmacokinetic studies using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) test showed that plasma rH-TNF levels were less than 0.2 U/mL.

Based on the findings, the recommended dose for phase II trials is 2.4 X 10(5) U/m2/d, administered as a five-day continuous infusion.

title: Tissue-specific expression and regulation of sexually dimorphic genes in mice.
text:
We present a comprehensive study on the differences in gene expression between males and females in various somatic tissues of 334 mice. These mice were obtained from a crossbreeding of two inbred mouse strains, C57BL/6J and C3H/HeJ. By analyzing a large number of individuals, we were able to detect even small differences in gene expression between the sexes. The use of an intercross allowed us to investigate the genetic control of sexually dimorphic gene expression.

Using microarray analysis, we examined 23,574 transcripts and discovered that the extent of sexual dimorphism in gene expression was much greater than previously known. In the liver, adipose tissue, and muscle, thousands of genes exhibited sexual dimorphism, while in the brain, hundreds of genes showed this characteristic. These genes displayed tissue-specific expression patterns and were enriched for specific pathways in the Gene Ontology database. Interestingly, we observed chromosomal enrichment not only on the sex chromosomes but also on several autosomes.

Through genetic analyses, we found evidence of global regulation of subsets of sexually dimorphic genes. The transcript levels of many of these genes were controlled by multiple expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) hotspots, which exhibited tissue-specific control. Additionally, we identified an enrichment of tissue-specific transcription factor binding sites in the sexually dimorphic genes.

title: The role of prevention in oncology practice: results from a 2004 survey of American Society of Clinical Oncology members.
text:
The purpose of this study, conducted in 2004 by the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Cancer Prevention Committee, was to assess the involvement of ASCO members in clinical prevention activities. The methods involved sending a survey to a random sample of 2,000 domestic members and a convenience sample of 3,144 international members, with updated questions on genetics, chemoprevention, and survivorship. 

Out of the domestic members contacted, 49.7% responded (n = 851), while 465 international members responded. Nonresponders were found to be younger on average. The results showed that 35% of respondents had received formal instruction in cancer prevention and control. Additionally, most respondents expected an increase in the use of prevention, screening/early detection, and risk reduction/genetic counseling in their practices over the next 5 years. 

The majority of respondents reported caring for cancer survivors and providing general medical care. They also either directly provided or referred patients for cancer prevention and control services such as cancer screening, tobacco and nutrition counseling, risk reduction, and chemoprevention. 

Multivariable modeling revealed that those practicing in an academic setting, seeing a higher proportion of patients without a cancer diagnosis, having formal training in prevention and control, expecting an increase in prevention activities in the next 5 years, and providing community advice on prevention had fewer perceived barriers to including cancer prevention activities in their clinical practice. 

In conclusion, this study identified barriers to the inclusion of cancer prevention and control activities in oncology clinical practice. However, a significant proportion of both domestic and international ASCO members expressed interest in these activities and desired more specific educational programs in this emerging area of oncology practice.

title: Stress-dependent regulation of FOXO transcription factors by the SIRT1 deacetylase.
text: The Sir2 deacetylase plays a role in determining the lifespan of different species, but we still have limited knowledge about the specific molecular mechanisms through which Sir2 promotes longevity. Our research indicates that in mammalian cells, the Sir2 equivalent SIRT1 seems to regulate the cellular response to stress by controlling the FOXO family of Forkhead transcription factors. These proteins act as sensors for the insulin signaling pathway and also regulate the lifespan of organisms. In response to oxidative stress, SIRT1 and the FOXO transcription factor FOXO3 form a complex within cells. SIRT1 is able to deacetylate FOXO3 both in vitro and within cells. The impact of SIRT1 on FOXO3 function is twofold: it enhances FOXO3's ability to induce cell cycle arrest and resistance to oxidative stress, while inhibiting its ability to induce cell death. Therefore, one possible mechanism by which Sir2 proteins may extend organismal lifespan is by shifting FOXO-dependent responses away from apoptosis and towards stress resistance.

title: TLR-Mediated Innate Production of IFN-γ by CD8+ T Cells Is Independent of Glycolysis.
text: CD8(+) T cells have the ability to respond to infections that are not related to their specific antigen in an Ag-independent manner. This rapid innate-like immune response allows these T cells, which have previous exposure to antigens, to alert other types of immune cells to invading pathogens. In this study, we demonstrate that murine CD8(+) T cells can detect TLR2 and TLR7 ligands, resulting in the quick production of IFN-γ but not TNF-α and IL-2. Importantly, T cells that have previous exposure to antigens and are activated by TLR ligands produce enough IFN-γ to enhance the activation of macrophages. Unlike antigen-specific reactivation, the production of IFN-γ by CD8(+) T cells through TLR stimulation relies solely on newly synthesized transcripts and does not induce mRNA stability. Additionally, the transcription of IFN-γ upon TLR triggering depends on the activation of PI3K and serine-threonine kinase Akt, and protein synthesis relies on the activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin. We then investigated the energy source that drives the TLR-induced production of IFN-γ. While the production of antigen-specific cytokines requires a switch to glycolysis for optimal release, the availability of glucose does not affect the rate of IFN-γ production upon TLR-mediated activation. Instead, mitochondrial respiration provides enough energy for TLR-induced IFN-γ production. To our knowledge, this is the first report that describes how TLR-mediated bystander activation leads to a helper phenotype of CD8(+) T cells. It triggers a brief increase in IFN-γ production, which results in a significant but limited activation of CD8(+) T cells with previous exposure to antigens. This activation is sufficient to prime macrophages but restricts T cell responses to unrelated infections.

title: Recommendations for the presurgical psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients.
text: The impact of psychosocial factors on the long-term results of bariatric surgery is significant. These factors include emotional adjustment, adherence to postoperative lifestyle recommendations, weight loss outcomes, and improvement or resolution of co-morbidities. Therefore, it is advisable for bariatric behavioral health specialists with specialized knowledge and experience to be involved in the assessment and care of patients both before and after surgery. The evaluating clinician plays various crucial roles in the comprehensive treatment of bariatric patients. One of the key roles is identifying factors that may hinder optimal surgical outcomes and providing recommendations to the patient and bariatric team on how to address these issues. This document provides recommendations for the psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients, outlines the appropriate qualifications for those conducting these evaluations, emphasizes the importance of communicating evaluation results and suggesting treatment plans, and highlights the need for continuous behavioral healthcare for the bariatric patient throughout the entire surgical and postsurgical process.

title: Simian immunodeficiency virus–induced mucosal interleukin-17 deficiency promotes Salmonella dissemination from the gut
text: Salmonella typhimurium causes a localized infection in healthy individuals, but in those infected with HIV, it can become life-threatening. Our study focuses on simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) infection in rhesus macaques and its impact on the mucosal barrier functions against S. typhimurium. We found that SIV infection leads to a depletion of T helper type 17 (TH17) cells in the ileal mucosa, which impairs the ability to prevent S. typhimurium from spreading. In macaques without SIV infection, the response to S. typhimurium was dominated by TH17 cells, including the production of interleukin-17 (IL-17) and IL-22. However, in SIV-infected macaques, TH17 cells were significantly reduced, resulting in a weakened response to S. typhimurium and increased bacterial spread. We also observed that mice lacking the IL-17 receptor had higher levels of S. typhimurium dissemination, indicating that IL-17 deficiency affects mucosal barrier function. In conclusion, SIV infection impairs the IL-17 axis, which is crucial for preventing the spread of microbes from the gastrointestinal tract.

title: An adoption study of human obesity.
text:
In our study, we investigated the impact of genetic factors and the family environment on the level of fatness in a group of 540 adult Danish adoptees. These adoptees were carefully selected from a larger population of 3580 individuals and were categorized into four weight classes: thin, median weight, overweight, and obese. 

Our findings revealed a significant correlation between the weight class of the adoptees and the body-mass index of their biological parents. This correlation was particularly strong for the mothers (P < 0.0001) and also significant for the fathers (P < 0.02). However, we did not observe any relationship between the weight class of the adoptees and the body-mass index of their adoptive parents. 

When we analyzed the cumulative distributions of the body-mass index of parents, we obtained similar results. There was a clear association between the body-mass index of biological parents and the weight class of the adoptees, while no such association was found with the index of adoptive parents. 

Importantly, this relationship between biological parents and adoptees was not limited to the obesity weight class. It was evident across the entire spectrum of body fatness, ranging from very thin to very fat. 

Based on these findings, we can conclude that genetic influences play a significant role in determining fatness in adults, while the family environment alone does not appear to have a noticeable effect.

title: Redox-dependent downregulation of Rho by Rac
text: Rac and Rho GTPases play crucial roles in regulating the remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton during cell spreading and migration. In this study, we demonstrate that Rac-induced production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leads to a decrease in Rho activity. This redox-dependent reduction in Rho activity is necessary for the formation of membrane ruffles and integrin-mediated cell spreading induced by Rac. The pathway connecting ROS generation to the downregulation of Rho involves the inhibition of a protein called low-molecular-weight protein tyrosine phosphatase (LMW-PTP), followed by an increase in the tyrosine phosphorylation and activation of its target, p190Rho-GAP. Our findings reveal a new mechanism by which changes in cellular redox state are linked to the regulation of actin cytoskeleton rearrangements mediated by Rho GTPases.

title: The epidemiology of trachoma in Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile States, southern Sudan.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence and distribution of trachoma in the states of Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile in southern Sudan. Limited surveys and anecdotal data suggested that trachoma was endemic in these areas, but little was known about the extent of the problem. To gather more information, population-based cross-sectional surveys were conducted in nine sites in southern Sudan between September 2001 and June 2004. The sample was selected using a two-stage random cluster sampling method. Trachoma grading was done using the WHO simplified grading system. 

A total of 17,016 individuals were examined, representing a response rate of 86.1% of the total population. The prevalence of active trachoma signs in children aged 1-9 years was as follows: TF=53.7% (95% CI=52.1-55.3); TI=42.7% (95% CI=41.2-44.2); TF and/or TI=64.1% (95% CI=62.5-65.5). The prevalence of trichiasis (TT) in children under 15 years old was 1.2% (95% CI=0.9-1.4), while the prevalence of TT in individuals aged 15 years and above was 9.2% (95% CI=8.6-9.9). Women were more likely to have trichiasis compared to men (odds ratio (OR)=1.57; 95% CI=1.34-1.84). 

Based on these findings, it is estimated that there is a backlog of 178,250 individuals requiring surgery in the states of Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile. The entire population, estimated to be over 3.9 million, is in need of the SAFE strategy to control blinding trachoma. 

In conclusion, trachoma is a significant public health issue in all nine study sites in southern Sudan. The high prevalence of active trachoma and TT in children highlights the severity of the problem. Urgent action is needed to implement trachoma control interventions in these endemic regions.

title: A single residue determines the cooperative binding property of a primosomal DNA replication protein, PriB, to single-stranded DNA.
text:
PriB is an essential protein in bacteria that plays a crucial role in the re-initiation of replication. In this study, we examined and compared the DNA-binding properties of PriB from Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium LT2 (StPriB) and Escherichia coli (EcPriB). We found that only one amino acid, V6, differed between EcPriB and StPriB, with StPriB having an alanine (A6) in place of valine (V6). Previous structural studies have shown that this residue is located on the potential dimer-dimer interface of PriB and does not participate in binding to single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).

Interestingly, we discovered that the cooperative binding mechanism of StPriB to DNA is distinct from that of EcPriB. While EcPriB forms a single complex with ssDNAs of different lengths, StPriB forms two or more separate complexes. Based on our findings and the available structural information, we propose potential binding modes for the formation of stable complexes between PriB and ssDNA molecules consisting of 25 nucleotides (nt), namely (EcPriB)25 and (StPriB)25.

title: Genomic organization and chromosomal location of the human dsRNA adenosine deaminase gene: the enzyme for glutamate-activated ion channel RNA editing.
text: The structure of the gene responsible for encoding the enzyme DRADA, which is involved in RNA editing for certain types of glutamate-gated ion channel subunits, has been characterized. This enzyme is found in the nucleus. The DRADA gene spans 30 kb pairs and contains 15 exons. Transcription of the gene is initiated at multiple sites, 164 to 216 nucleotides before the translation initiation codon. The putative promoter region does not contain typical TATA or CCAAT box-like sequences. The three dsRNA binding motifs, each consisting of 70 amino acid residues, are encoded by two exons with an intervening sequence that interrupts the motif at the same amino acid position. This suggests that the dsRNA binding domains may consist of two separate functional subdomains. The DRADA gene has been located on the long arm of chromosome 1, in the q21 region, using fluorescent in situ hybridization. The information provided in this study regarding the gene's structure and sequence will aid in investigating the role of DRADA in hereditary diseases that may be caused by malfunctioning glutamate-gated ion channels.

title: "We charge them; otherwise we cannot run the hospital" front line workers, clients and health financing policy implementation gaps in Ghana.
text:
The aim of this study is to analyze the gaps in policy implementation regarding user fees, exemptions, and health insurance in providing financial access to primary clinical care for children under five in Ghana. The methods used in this study included analyzing routine data, conducting focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and administering a structured questionnaire. 

The results of the study showed that providers often modified the implementation of exemptions policy, sometimes not providing full exemptions or none at all. Clients who were aware of their entitlement to exemptions often did not request them due to fear of negative reactions from providers. Providers justified their modifications and negative reactions by citing the threat to the financial viability of their institutions caused by uncertainty and delays in reimbursement. 

During the study, insurance coverage was low and frontline workers did not appear to be modifying implementation arrangements. However, the underlying conflicts in goals, scarcity of resources, working conditions, and relationships between frontline workers and clients that contributed to the gaps in exemptions policy implementation remained unchanged. Therefore, there is a possibility that the health insurance policy may also face implementation gaps, similar to what happened with the exemptions policy. 

In conclusion, policies that do not consider the incentives for frontline worker adherence and fail to align them with policy objectives are likely to experience implementation gaps.

title: EML4-ALK translocation predicts better outcome in lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR.
text:
INTRODUCTION
The fusion of the echinoderm microtubule-associated protein like 4-anaplastic lymphoma kinase (EML4-ALK) is a new target in a specific type of non-small cell lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma. The fusion of EML4-ALK is not found in conjunction with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations. To determine the impact of EML4-ALK on the prognosis of non-small cell lung cancer, we investigated the presence of EML4-ALK fusion in lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR and analyzed their treatment outcomes.

METHODS
We enrolled lung adenocarcinoma patients with malignant pleural effusions who had wild-type EGFR and measurable target lesions for analysis of EML4-ALK fusion using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and direct sequencing. We analyzed demographic data, EML4-ALK status, and survival data. Additionally, we performed fluorescence in situ hybridization on some available tumor samples to confirm the results of the PCR. Furthermore, we analyzed K-ras mutation in patients without EML4-ALK fusion genes.

RESULTS
A total of 116 patients with wild-type EGFR sequencing results had complete clinical data for analysis. None of the patients received ALK inhibitor therapy. Among them, 39 patients (34%) had the EML4-ALK fusion gene. The concordance rate between reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and fluorescence in situ hybridization was 85%. The K-ras mutation rate for patients without EML4-ALK fusion gene was 6.5%. Multivariate analysis showed that patients with better performance status (p < 0.001) and EML4-ALK translocation (p = 0.017) had longer overall survival. There were no significant differences in clinical factors and survival outcome between patients with variant 1 and nonvariant 1 EML4-ALK fusion genes.

CONCLUSION
In lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR, the presence of EML4-ALK translocation is associated with longer overall survival.
