title: Transcriptional Repression of Gata3 Is Essential for Early B Cell Commitment
text:
The exact mechanisms that lead to the suppression of alternative fate potentials in early B cell precursors are still not fully understood. However, through the use of gain- and loss-of-function techniques, as well as a synthetic Zinc-finger polypeptide (6ZFP) designed to prevent transcription factor binding to a specific cis element, we have discovered that the transcription factor EBF1 plays a crucial role in promoting B cell lineage commitment. EBF1 achieves this by directly repressing the expression of the T-cell-lineage-requisite gene Gata3. 

When Ebf1-deficient lymphoid progenitors were examined, we observed an increase in their potential to develop into T cells, along with elevated levels of Gata3 transcript expression. Conversely, when EBF1 expression was enforced, T cell differentiation was inhibited and there was a rapid loss of Gata3 mRNA. 

Interestingly, by using the 6ZFP to disrupt EBF1 binding to a regulatory region of Gata3, we were able to restore Gata3 expression. This disruption also prevented EBF1 from suppressing T cell differentiation and halted B cell differentiation through a mechanism that relies on GATA3. Additionally, we found that EBF1 binding to Gata3 regulatory sites led to repressive histone modifications in that region. 

These findings highlight the importance of a transcriptional circuit in the commitment of B cell lineage.

title: Isolation and partial characterization of an unusual human immunodeficiency retrovirus from two persons of west-central African origin.
text: Two patients with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, originally from West-Central Africa but currently residing in Belgium, were found to be infected with an uncommon retrovirus. This virus exhibited similar biological and morphological properties to human immunodeficiency retrovirus type 1 (HIV-1) and HIV-2, but notable antigenic differences were observed. Additionally, certain viral proteins displayed distinct molecular weights compared to their counterparts in HIV-1 and HIV-2. Chemical cleavage of the most conserved viral proteins resulted in different patterns compared to HIV-1 and HIV-2. Moreover, nucleic acid hybridization experiments successfully distinguished between the different virus types. Sequence analysis of the viral U3 region unveiled a unique enhancer organization not present in other immunodeficiency viruses. The findings indicated that the new isolate is more closely related to HIV-1 than HIV-2, but it clearly differs in several significant aspects.

title: Role of circulating nitrite and S-nitrosohemoglobin in the regulation of regional blood flow in humans.
text: In order to determine the impact of endothelial-derived nitric oxide (NO) and intravascular nitrogen oxide species on the regulation of human blood flow, we conducted a study measuring forearm blood flow and levels of plasma nitrite, LMW-SNOs and HMW-SNOs, and red cell S-nitrosohemoglobin (SNO-Hb). These measurements were taken at rest and during the inhibition of NO synthesis, followed by forearm exercise. Surprisingly, we discovered significant gradients of plasma nitrite between arterial and venous circulation, suggesting a new source of intravascular NO delivery. This finding supports the idea that circulating nitrite is biologically active, as its consumption increased during exercise when regional endothelial NO synthesis was inhibited. The role of circulating S-nitrosothiols and SNO-Hb in the regulation of basal vascular tone is less clear. We found that low-molecular-weight S-nitrosothiols were not detectable, and levels of S-nitroso-albumin were much lower than previously reported. Interestingly, S-nitroso-albumin primarily formed in the venous circulation, even when NO synthase was inhibited. While SNO-Hb was measurable in the human circulation, there were no significant gradients between arterial and venous circulation, and the delivery of NO from SNO-Hb was minimal. In conclusion, our data suggests that circulating nitrite is biologically active and provides a gradient for intravascular NO delivery. Additionally, S-nitroso-albumin does not deliver NO from the lungs to the tissue, but rather forms in the peripheral circulation. Finally, SNO-Hb and S-nitrosothiols have minimal impact on the regulation of basal vascular tone, even during exercise stress.

title: Extra centrosomes and/or chromosomes prolong mitosis in human cells
text: We have conducted experiments using laser microsurgery and cell fusion to investigate the impact of additional centrosomes and/or chromosomes on the length of mitosis in human cells. Our findings revealed that doubling the number of chromosomes extended a 20-minute division by approximately 10 minutes, while doubling the number of centrosomes added an additional 30 minutes. The presence of extra centrosomes and/or chromosomes delays the fulfillment of the spindle assembly checkpoint, resulting in the prolongation of mitosis. Consequently, mitosis can be prolonged through non-genetic mechanisms, and the presence of extra chromosomes and centrosomes likely contributes to the heightened mitotic index observed in numerous tumors.

title: Familial recurrence-pattern analysis of nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate--a Danish Registry study.
text: The discovery of a connection between genetic variation at the TGFA locus and nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate (CP) is a significant breakthrough in our understanding of this condition. This study aimed to determine if there is a link between CP-susceptibility loci, like TGFA, and the occurrence of CP. The researchers examined the recurrence pattern of CP in families to determine the most likely mode of inheritance for the condition. The study took advantage of the comprehensive registration of CP cases in Denmark, ensuring accurate data collection. The researchers used register linkage to estimate the recurrence risks for different degrees of relatives of 1,364 CP patients. The estimated risks were 2.74% for first-degree relatives, 0.28% for second-degree relatives, and 0.00% for third-degree relatives. These estimates align closely with previous findings based on questionnaires and interviews. However, the prevalence of nonsyndromic CP in the population was found to be higher than previously reported. Using the Risch method, the researchers analyzed these and other published data and concluded that CP is unlikely to be caused by a single major locus or additive multilocus inheritance. Instead, the recurrence pattern suggests that CP is influenced by multiple interacting loci. According to the data, a single locus that increases the risk to first-degree relatives by more than six times is unlikely, but a locus that increases the risk by three times fits the data well. Detecting such a locus is feasible with a realistic sample of affected siblings.

title: Gene methylation in gastric cancer.
text: Gastric cancer is a prevalent form of cancer and remains the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. The majority of new cases and deaths occur in developing countries. During the early stages of the molecular biology revolution, cancer research primarily concentrated on genetic changes, including those in gastric cancer. Epigenetic mechanisms play a crucial role in the normal development and maintenance of tissue-specific gene expression patterns in mammals. Disruption of these mechanisms can result in altered gene function and the transformation of normal cells into cancerous ones. Recent advancements in the rapidly evolving field of cancer epigenetics have revealed extensive reprogramming of various components of the epigenetic machinery in cancer, such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, noncoding RNAs, and microRNAs. The most well-established epigenetic hallmark in gastric cancer is the abnormal DNA methylation in the promoter regions of genes, which leads to the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and other genes associated with cancer. The advantages of targeting gene methylation for the detection and diagnosis of cancer in biopsy specimens and non-invasive body fluids like serum and gastric washes have prompted numerous studies in gastric cancer. This review focuses on the most common and significant epigenetic phenomenon, DNA methylation, in gastric cancer, and highlights the impact of epigenetics on this field.

title: Klebsiella aerogenes urease gene cluster: sequence of ureD and demonstration that four accessory genes (ureD, ureE, ureF, and ureG) are involved in nickel metallocenter biosynthesis.
text: The sequence of the region upstream from the Klebsiella aerogenes urease structural genes was analyzed and found to contain a coding sequence capable of producing a 29.8-kDa peptide. Deletions were made in this gene, called ureD, as well as in the genes ureE, ureF, and ureG, which are located immediately downstream of the structural genes. When these mutated plasmids were introduced into Escherichia coli, high levels of urease were produced, but the enzyme was either inactive (due to deletions in ureD, ureF, or ureG) or only partially active (due to deletions in ureE). The purified ureases from the mutated cells were found to be the same as the control enzyme when analyzed using gel filtration chromatography and sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. However, the activity levels of the enzyme correlated with the amount of nickel present, as determined by atomic absorption analysis. The peptides UreD, UreE, UreF, and UreG were tentatively identified by comparing mutant and control cell extracts using gel electrophoresis, by expressing the genes separately in vivo, or by analyzing transcription-translation reactions in vitro. The identities of UreE and UreG were confirmed by sequencing their amino-terminal regions. The levels of UreE and UreG (with apparent molecular weights of 23,900 and 28,500, respectively) were found to be similar to those of the urease subunits, while the amounts of UreF (apparent molecular weight of 27,000) and UreD (apparent molecular weight of 29,300) were significantly reduced, possibly due to the absence of strong ribosome binding sites in the regions upstream of these coding sequences. These findings demonstrate that all four accessory genes are necessary for the proper functioning of the urease metallocenter.

title: Hepatic polyploidy and liver growth control.
text: Cellular polyploidy is observed in all differentiated mammalian tissues, indicating its onset. Polyploidy is commonly observed in the normal liver and in liver conditions that affect its functioning. As our understanding of polyploidy grows, it is becoming evident that cells with higher ploidy levels are more likely to undergo terminal differentiation, cellular senescence, and apoptosis. Genetic abnormalities, such as impaired DNA repair, can contribute to the development of hepatocellular polyploidy. According to current models, extensive polyploidy may lead to organ failure and the activation of precancerous cell clones, potentially resulting in oncogenesis.

title: Disturbances in the positioning, proliferation and apoptosis of neural progenitors contribute to subcortical band heterotopia formation.
text: Cortical malformations are often linked to intractable epilepsy and other developmental disorders. Our research focuses on the tish rat, a genetic model of subcortical band heterotopia (SBH) associated with epilepsy, to understand the developmental processes involved in SBH formation in the neocortex. Our findings reveal that Pax6(+) and Tbr2(+) progenitors are not properly positioned in the tish(+/-) and tish(-/-) neocortex during neurogenesis. Additionally, mislocalized tish(-/-) progenitors have a longer cell cycle compared to wild type or normally-positioned tish(-/-) progenitors, due to an extended G(2)+M+G(1) phase. This misplacement is not caused by breakdown of adherens junctions or loss of radial glial polarity in the ventricular zone (VZ), as confirmed by immunohistochemistry using phalloidin (to detect F-actin), aPKC-λ, and Par3. However, vimentin immunohistochemistry indicates that the radial glial scaffold is disrupted in the tish(-/-) heterotopia region. Furthermore, lineage tracing experiments using in utero electroporation in tish(-/-) neocortex demonstrate that mislocalized progenitors do not maintain contact with the ventricular surface, and ventricular/subventricular zone (SVZ) progenitors generate neurons that migrate into both the heterotopia and cortical plate (CP). Overall, these findings highlight a series of developmental abnormalities contributing to SBH formation that differ from primary errors in neuronal migration.

title: Sex-related differences in the presentation, treatment and outcomes among patients with acute coronary syndromes: the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events.
text: The objective of this study was to determine if there are any differences between men and women in terms of the severity, management, and outcomes of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) as seen on angiography. The study included 7,638 women and 19,117 men with ACS who underwent coronary angiography and were part of the GRACE registry from 1999 to 2006. The severity of disease was categorized as normal/mild or advanced based on the degree of stenosis in the epicardial vessels. The results showed that women were older than men and had a higher prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors. Both men and women presented with chest pain, but women were more likely to experience jaw pain and nausea. Women were also more likely to have normal/mild disease and less likely to have left-main and three-vessel disease or undergo percutaneous coronary intervention. Women with advanced disease had a higher risk of death. After adjusting for age and extent of disease, women had a higher likelihood of adverse outcomes at six months compared to men, although the difference in mortality was not statistically significant. In conclusion, women with ACS had a higher prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors and atypical symptoms, but were more likely to have normal/mild angiographic coronary artery disease. Further research is needed to explore sex differences in disease severity.

title: GITR, a member of the TNF receptor superfamily, is costimulatory to mouse T lymphocyte subpopulations.
text: GITR, also known as glucocorticoid-induced TNFR family related gene, is a member of the TNFR superfamily (TNFRSF) and is expressed in various cell types, including T lymphocytes. We conducted a study to investigate whether GITR plays a role in costimulation of T lymphocyte subpopulations, as it shares a high similarity in its cytoplasmic region with other known costimulatory members of the TNFRSF. Our findings demonstrate that the proliferation response of CD8+ and CD4+ peripheral T cell subpopulations was enhanced when a GITR costimulus was combined with an anti-CD3 stimulus. Additionally, the expression of the main activation-induced receptor (IL-2Ralpha) and the production of IL-2 and IFN-gamma were significantly increased with a GITR costimulus compared to anti-CD3 alone. Furthermore, GITR stimulation resulted in enhanced ERK phosphorylation, indicating its involvement in the activation of the MAPK pathway. Interestingly, the GITR costimulus triggered proliferation of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Treg cells), which was accompanied by the loss of the anergic phenotype and suppressor activity. However, unstimulated GITR(-/-) CD4+CD25+ cells and GITR(+/+) CD4+CD25+ cells exhibited equal suppressor activity on CD4+CD25- responder cells. These findings suggest a novel role for GITR as a costimulatory molecule in T cell subsets.

title: PI3K and cancer: lessons, challenges and opportunities
text: The significant role of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) activation in the biology of tumor cells has led to extensive efforts in targeting PI3K and its downstream kinases, including AKT and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), for cancer treatment. However, recent clinical data indicate limited effectiveness of single-agent inhibitors targeting PI3K, AKT, or mTOR at tolerable doses. One exception is the positive response observed in chronic lymphocytic leukemia patients treated with PI3Kδ inhibitors, where a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic cellular activities contribute to efficacy. In this review, we discuss the main challenges and opportunities in the clinical development of inhibitors that target the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway. By focusing on patient selection, gaining a better understanding of immune modulation, and strategically combining these inhibitors with other agents, we can fully harness the potential of this promising class of targeted anticancer drugs.

title: Sequence-based species delimitation for the DNA taxonomy of undescribed insects.
text: Automated DNA-based approaches have the potential to greatly expedite the cataloging of the numerous undescribed species of insects. However, there is currently a lack of procedures for large-scale species discovery using sequence data. In this study, we utilized mitochondrial DNA variation to define species within a beetle radiation in the genus Rivacindela from arid Australia, which is poorly understood. By analyzing sequence variation in three mtDNA genes, we identified 46 or 47 putative species using quantitative methods that rely on unique genetic characteristics. The differentiation between these groups was also evident in the branching rate of calibrated trees. We developed a new likelihood method that combines stochastic lineage growth models with coalescence theory to determine the transition point from species-level to population-level evolutionary processes. By fitting the switches from speciation to coalescent nodes on the ultrametric tree of Rivacindela, we estimated that this transition occurred approximately 0.43 million years ago, resulting in 48 putative species. These entities defined through our approach exhibited biological properties consistent with traditionally defined species, including coherent geographic ranges, alignment with morphologically recognized species, and levels of sequence divergence typical for closely related insect species. The identification of distinct evolutionary groupings through patterns of sequence variation allows for automated species delineation from DNA surveys of local communities, providing a framework for taxonomy in this poorly understood insect group.

title: CCR6 regulates the migration of inflammatory and regulatory T cells.
text: The roles of Th17 and regulatory T (Treg) cells in autoimmune diseases are opposite, but the mechanisms behind their migration to inflammatory tissues are not well understood. This study reveals that both T cell subsets express CCR6. The expression of CCR6 in Th17 cells is regulated by TGF-beta and requires two nuclear receptors, RORalpha and RORgamma. Th17 cells also produce the CCR6 ligand CCL20, which is induced by TGF-beta and IL-6 in a synergistic manner. This induction requires STAT3, RORgamma, and IL-21. Th17 cells promote the migration of Th17 and Treg cells in vitro by producing CCL20, and this migration is dependent on CCR6. When CCR6 is lacking in Th17 cells, the severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis is reduced, along with the recruitment of Th17 and Treg cells into inflammatory tissues. Similarly, CCR6 is also important for the recruitment of Treg cells into inflammatory tissues. These findings highlight the crucial role of CCR6 in the migration of Treg and Th17 cells.

title: Inhibition of receptor-mediated calcium influx in T cells by unsaturated non-esterified fatty acids.
text: We conducted a study to examine the impact of omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs) on receptor-mediated calcium (Ca2+) entry in a T-cell line called JURKAT. To induce an increase in intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) and Ca2+ influx, we used anti-CD3 antibodies (OKT3). All UFAs, as well as Ni2+ ions and 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol 13-acetate, reduced the sustained increase in [Ca2+]i induced by OKT3 to its basal levels. Previous studies have shown that non-esterified fatty acids activate protein kinase C (PKC). However, our experiments using H-7 and analysis of PKC-dependent phosphorylation of 19 and 80 kDa marker substrates ruled out the involvement of PKC in the UFA-induced inhibition of Ca2+ entry. Flow-cytometry analysis demonstrated that UFAs do not interfere with antibody-receptor binding. The effect of UFAs was reversed when BSA (0.2%, w/v) was added after the fatty acids had decreased the OKT3-induced increase in [Ca2+]i to basal levels. We discussed the significance of these findings and proposed potential mechanisms for the inhibition of receptor-mediated Ca2+ influx by UFAs.

title: Deleted in liver cancer-1 (DLC-1): a tumor suppressor not just for liver.
text: Deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC-1) was initially discovered as a potential tumor suppressor gene that is frequently deleted in hepatocellular carcinoma. Further research has revealed that reduced levels of DLC-1, either due to genetic deletion or DNA methylation, are associated with various cancer types such as lung, breast, prostate, kidney, colon, uterus, ovary, and stomach. Restoring DLC-1 expression in cancer cells has been found to regulate the structure of the actin cytoskeleton and focal adhesions, leading to a significant inhibition of cell growth. This supports the notion that DLC-1 functions as a tumor suppressor. Its tumor-suppressive role is dependent on its RhoGTPase activating protein (RhoGAP) activity and steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR)-related lipid transfer (START) domain, as well as its localization to focal adhesions. The recruitment of DLC-1 to focal adhesions occurs through the Src Homology 2 (SH2) domains of tensins, independent of phosphotyrosine. Therefore, the expression and subcellular localization of DLC-1 could serve as a valuable molecular marker for cancer prognosis. Additionally, DLC-1 and its downstream signaling molecules may represent potential therapeutic targets for cancer treatment.

title: Interaction of Helicobacter pylori with gastric epithelial cells is mediated by the p53 protein family.
text:
BACKGROUND & OBJECTIVES: Despite extensive research on the p53 tumor suppressor, there are still many unanswered questions regarding the biological functions of its homologs, p73 and p63. Recent evidence suggests that both p73 and p63 are involved in the regulation of apoptosis, cell differentiation, and drug sensitivity. In this study, we aimed to investigate the roles of p73 and p63 proteins in gastric epithelial cells during Helicobacter pylori infection.

METHODS: We conducted coculture experiments of gastric epithelial cells with H. pylori and assessed the functions of p73 and p63 proteins using various techniques such as luciferase reporter assays, real-time polymerase chain reaction, immunoblotting, and cell survival assays. To inhibit the activity of p73 and p63 isoforms, we used short hairpin RNA and dominant-negative mutants. Additionally, we analyzed human and murine gastric tissues using immunohistochemistry with p73 and p63 antibodies, as well as the modified Steiner's silver method.

RESULTS: Our results showed that the interaction between H. pylori and gastric epithelial cells led to a significant increase in p73 protein levels both in vitro and in vivo, as observed in human gastritis specimens and H. pylori-infected mice. This increase in p73 resulted in the up-regulation of pro-apoptotic genes, namely NOXA, PUMA, and FAS receptor, in gastric epithelial cells. Furthermore, the inhibition of p73 activity suppressed cell death and FAS receptor induction caused by H. pylori. We also found that bacterial virulence factors within the cag pathogenicity island, c-Abl tyrosine kinase, and interaction with p63 isoforms played a role in controlling the activity of p73.

CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that p73 is involved in H. pylori-induced apoptosis and indicate a potential role for the p53 family in the epithelial cell response to H. pylori infection.

title: Brown and white adipose tissues: intrinsic differences in gene expression and response to cold exposure in mice
text: Brown adipocytes are responsible for dissipating energy, while white adipocytes serve as a storage site for energy. Our research focused on the ability of different white adipose tissue depots to acquire a brown phenotype through exposure to cold temperatures. By comparing genes activated by cold exposure in white fat to those enriched in brown fat, we were able to identify a unique transcription signature, which we referred to as "brite." This signature provided insights into the genes, pathways, and regulatory motifs associated with the process of "browning," offering new targets for further understanding this phenomenon. One such gene, neuregulin 4, was found to be highly expressed in brown adipose tissue and upregulated in white fat upon cold exposure. Our cell studies demonstrated that neuregulin 4 promotes the growth of nerve fibers, suggesting its role in increasing innervation of adipose tissue in response to cold. To study the specific differences between adipose depots at an in vitro level, we developed a cell culture system that accurately replicates the unique properties of each depot. Understanding the key transcriptional events involved in the transition from white to brown adipose tissue is crucial, as it offers potential solutions to combat metabolic disorders such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (CONCEPTT): a multicentre international randomised controlled trial
text:
BACKGROUND
Pregnant women with type 1 diabetes are considered high-risk and are advised to maintain optimal glucose control. However, the outcomes for newborns due to maternal hyperglycemia are not ideal. The purpose of this study was to assess the effectiveness of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) on maternal glucose control and the health outcomes for both mother and baby.

METHODS
This was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial involving women aged 18-40 with type 1 diabetes who had been on intensive insulin therapy for at least 12 months. Participants were either pregnant (up to 13 weeks and 6 days gestation) or planning to become pregnant. The trial took place in 31 hospitals across Canada, England, Scotland, Spain, Italy, Ireland, and the USA. Two parallel trials were conducted, one for pregnant participants and one for those planning pregnancy. In both trials, participants were randomly assigned to either CGM in addition to capillary glucose monitoring or capillary glucose monitoring alone. Randomization was stratified based on insulin delivery method (pump or injections) and baseline glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). The primary outcome was the change in HbA1c from randomization to 34 weeks gestation for pregnant women and to 24 weeks or conception for women planning pregnancy. Secondary outcomes included obstetric and neonatal health outcomes. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov under the number NCT01788527.

FINDINGS
Between March 25, 2013, and March 22, 2016, a total of 325 women (215 pregnant, 110 planning pregnancy) were randomly assigned to either capillary glucose monitoring with CGM (108 pregnant and 53 planning pregnancy) or without (107 pregnant and 57 planning pregnancy). Pregnant women using CGM showed a small improvement in HbA1c levels (mean difference -0.19%; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.03; p=0.0207). They also spent more time within the target glucose range (68% vs 61%; p=0.0034) and less time with hyperglycemia (27% vs 32%; p=0.0279) compared to the control group. The incidence of severe hypoglycemia episodes and time spent hypoglycemic were similar between the two groups. Neonatal health outcomes were significantly better in the CGM group, with a lower incidence of large for gestational age babies, fewer neonatal intensive care admissions lasting more than 24 hours, fewer cases of neonatal hypoglycemia, and a shorter length of hospital stay. No significant benefits of CGM were observed in women planning pregnancy. Adverse events occurred in both the CGM and control groups, with skin reactions being the most common.

INTERPRETATION
The use of CGM during pregnancy in women with type 1 diabetes leads to improved neonatal outcomes, likely due to reduced exposure to maternal hyperglycemia. CGM should be offered to all pregnant women with type 1 diabetes who are on intensive insulin therapy. This study is the first to suggest potential improvements in non-glycemic health outcomes with the use of CGM.

FUNDING
This study was funded by the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation, Canadian Clinical Trials Network, and National Institute for Health Research.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps: Is immunity the second function of chromatin?
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) consist of modified chromatin combined with granular and specific cytoplasmic proteins. These NETs are discharged by neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, potentially as a final effort to manage microbial infections. The release of chromatin occurs through a distinctive form of cell death known as "NETosis." In this article, we will examine our comprehension of the process by which NETs are formed, their role in combating infections and serving as warning signals, as well as their growing significance in autoimmunity and coagulation.

title: Phosphorylation of p35 and p39 by Cdk5 determines the subcellular location of the holokinase in a phosphorylation-site-specific manner.
text: Cdk5 belongs to the cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) family and is activated by neuronal activators p35 or p39. It plays a crucial role in regulating various neuronal activities such as migration, synaptic activity, and neuronal death. The myristoylation of p35 and p39 enables their association with the cytoplasmic membrane, forming p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5 complexes. However, the relationship between cellular localization and different functions is not fully understood. To investigate this, we examined the impact of Cdk5 activity on the subcellular localization of p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5. We discovered that Cdk5 activity influenced the localization of these complexes by phosphorylating p35 or p39. By using mutants of p35 and p39 that were either unphosphorylated or phosphomimetic, we determined that phosphorylation at Ser8, which is common to both p35 and p39, regulated the cytoplasmic localization and perinuclear accumulation of unphosphorylated S8A mutants, as well as the overall cytoplasmic distribution of phosphomimetic S8E mutants. Cdk5 activity was essential for maintaining the cytoplasmic presence of Cdk5-activator complexes, although small amounts of p35 and p39 were also detected in the nucleus. Interestingly, the nuclear levels of p35 and p39 increased when Cdk5 activity was inhibited. Furthermore, p39 exhibited a greater tendency to accumulate in the nucleus compared to p35, and phosphorylation at Thr84, which is specific to p39, regulated the potential nuclear localization activity of the Lys cluster in p39. These findings suggest that the subcellular localization of Cdk5-activator complexes is determined by the kinase activity of Cdk5 and also indicate a potential role for p39-Cdk5 in the nucleus.

title: Interleukin-12 and -23 Control Plasticity of CD127(+) Group 1 and Group 3 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Intestinal Lamina Propria.
text: There are at least three distinct subsets within Human group 1 ILCs: NK cells, CD127(+) ILC1, and intraepithelial CD103(+) ILC1. In patients with Crohn's disease, the number of CD127(+) ILC1 increases while ILC3 decreases in inflamed intestinal tissues. Our research shows that the differentiation of ILC3 to CD127(+) ILC1 can be reversed both in vitro and in vivo. CD127(+) ILC1 can differentiate into ILC3 in the presence of interleukin-2 (IL-2), IL-23, and IL-1β, with the transcription factor RORγt playing a crucial role. This process is further enhanced by retinoic acid. Additionally, we have observed a higher proportion of CD14(+) dendritic cells (DC) in resection specimens from Crohn's disease patients. In vitro, these CD14(+) DCs promote the polarization of ILC3 to CD127(+) ILC1. On the other hand, CD14(-) DCs promote the differentiation of CD127(+) ILC1 into ILC3. These findings suggest that the composition, function, and phenotype of CD127(+) ILC1 and ILC3 in the gut are influenced by environmental cues.

title: Transcriptional regulation of neuronal genes and its effect on neural functions: expression and function of forkhead transcription factors in neurons.
text: FOXO, a mammalian counterpart of DAF-16, is a forkhead box transcription factor that plays a crucial role in regulating the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans. It belongs to a group of forkhead transcription factors including AFX, FKHRL1, and FKHR. FKHR is phosphorylated at three specific sites (Thr-24, Ser-256, and Ser-319) in a manner dependent on phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt, which effectively inhibits death signals. In this study, we observed the dephosphorylation of FKHR after transient forebrain ischemia, leading to its translocation into the nucleus of neurons in gerbil and mouse brains. The activation of FKHR preceded delayed neuronal death in the vulnerable regions of the hippocampus following ischemic brain injury. This activation of FKHR was accompanied by an increase in DNA binding activity for the FKHR-responsive element on the Fas ligand promoter. Additionally, we identified FKHR-induced downstream targets such as Fas ligand and Bim in brain ischemia. Based on these findings, we propose a novel approach to rescue neurons from delayed neuronal death by promoting survival signaling. By inhibiting FKHR-dependent or -independent death signals in neurons, sodium orthovanadate, a protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor, up-regulated Akt activity in the brain and effectively rescued neurons from delayed neuronal death.

title: ERAAP synergizes with MHC class I molecules to make the final cut in the antigenic peptide precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: CD8(+) T cells rely on the major histocompatibility complex class I molecules to detect peptides (pMHC I) on the surface of cells for immune surveillance. These peptides are produced through the breakdown of intracellular polypeptides by the proteasome in the cytoplasm and then in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the ER aminopeptidase associated with antigen processing (ERAAP). To better understand how ERAAP functions in vivo, we examined naturally processed peptides in cells with or without the appropriate MHC I and ERAAP. In the absence of MHC I, ERAAP degraded the antigenic precursors in the ER. However, MHC I molecules were able to bind proteolytic intermediates and were crucial for the production of the final peptide by ERAAP. Therefore, ERAAP and MHC I work together to generate the final pMHC I repertoire.

title: Estimates of animal and plant protein intake in US adults: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1988-1991.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the sources of protein intake in a sample of the US adult population, as well as among subgroups categorized by race-ethnicity, age, and gender. The study utilized data from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted between 1988 and 1991. The survey included a stratified random sample of the civilian noninstitutionalized population from all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Participants reported their dietary intake over a 24-hour period, and the sources of protein and the contribution of each protein type to the total protein intake were determined. The study included a total of 7,924 adult participants.

Statistical analyses were conducted to calculate weighted total, age-specific, and age-adjusted mean protein intakes using SAS and WesVarPC. Differences between groups were assessed using 2-tailed t tests.

The results showed that animal protein was the main source of protein in the American diet, accounting for 69% of total protein intake. Within animal protein, meat, fish, and poultry contributed the most (42%), followed by dairy protein (20%). Plant protein consumption was primarily derived from grains (18%).

Gender differences were observed in protein intake. Women consumed a lower percentage of beef (14%) and pork (7%) protein compared to men (18% and 9% respectively). Conversely, women consumed a higher percentage of poultry (13%), dairy (22%), and fruit and vegetable (11%) protein compared to men (11%, 19%, and 9% respectively).

Race-ethnicity also influenced protein intake. Blacks reported consuming a higher percentage of poultry (18%) and pork (11%) protein, but a lower percentage of dairy protein (14%) compared to whites (12%, 7%, and 22% respectively) and Mexican-Americans (11%, 8%, and 17% respectively). Mexican-Americans consumed a higher percentage of legume (7%) and egg (7%) protein compared to whites (4% and 4% respectively) and blacks (4% and 5% respectively). Whites consumed a higher percentage of grain protein (19%) compared to blacks (16%) and Mexican-Americans (15%).

In conclusion, this study highlights that while the percentage of total energy from protein may be similar across different race-ethnicities and between men and women, the sources of protein differ. These findings emphasize the importance of considering these differences when providing nutrition education tailored to specific populations.

title: CYP18A1, a key enzyme of Drosophila steroid hormone inactivation, is essential for metamorphosis.
text: Ecdysteroids are a type of steroid hormone that play a crucial role in coordinating important developmental changes in insects. The levels of these hormones in the body, both when they increase and decrease, are vital for regulating molting and metamorphosis. Therefore, the production and breakdown of ecdysteroids are of great physiological significance. Our research focuses on the Cyp18a1 gene in Drosophila melanogaster, which encodes a cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for the hydroxylation of ecdysteroids. This enzyme is involved in the breakdown of ecdysteroids, specifically through the conversion of 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) into 20-hydroxyecdysonoic acid. This process occurs in multiple steps, with the formation of 20,26-dihydroxyecdysone as an intermediate. In Drosophila larvae, Cyp18a1 is expressed in various tissues that are targeted by 20E. To understand the importance of Cyp18a1 in Drosophila development, we conducted experiments to inactivate this gene. We generated null alleles by removing a specific DNA element and also used RNA interference to knock down Cyp18a1 expression. Both approaches resulted in pupal lethality, suggesting that the degradation of ecdysteroids is impaired without functional Cyp18a1. Our findings indicate that the inactivation of 20E is crucial for proper development, and CYP18A1 serves as a key enzyme in this process.

title: The sialyltransferase ST3GAL6 influences homing and survival in multiple myeloma.
text: Glycosylation is a process where oligosaccharide chains are covalently attached to proteins or lipids. Changes in this process, specifically increased sialylation, have been linked to the development of cancer and its spread to other parts of the body. However, the impact of altered sialylation on the movement of multiple myeloma (MM) cells has not been previously studied. In this research, we discovered that MM cell lines and patients have high levels of a gene called β-galactoside α-2,3-sialyltransferase, or ST3GAL6. This gene is crucial for the production of functional sialyl Lewis X, which is involved in the synthesis of selectin ligands in humans. In patients with MRC IX, high expression of ST3GAL6 is associated with poorer overall survival. Through our study, we found that reducing the levels of ST3GAL6 led to a significant decrease in the amount of α-2,3-linked sialic acid on the surface of MM cells. This reduction was accompanied by a significant decrease in the cells' ability to adhere to MM bone marrow stromal cells and fibronectin, as well as reduced migration through endothelial cells in vitro. Furthermore, our in vivo experiments showed that MM cells with reduced ST3GAL6 levels had decreased ability to home and engraft in the bone marrow niche, resulting in lower tumor burden and longer survival. These findings highlight the importance of altered glycosylation, particularly sialylation, in the adhesion and movement of MM cells.

title: New developments in the epidemiology of cancer prognosis: traditional and molecular predictors of treatment response and survival.
text: research conducted on the impact of lifestyle choices and behaviors on cancer development. Additionally, limited attention has been given to exploring the influence of genetic predisposition on cancer susceptibility. Despite the extensive studies on epidemiology and somatic changes, the investigation into the role of lifestyle, behavior, and genetics in cancer risk remains insufficient.

title: Behavioral effects of estrogen receptor gene disruption in male mice.
text: The development of brain functions and behaviors that differ between males and females is regulated by gonadal steroid hormones. The nuclear receptors of these hormones provide an opportunity to understand how molecular events in neurons contribute to basic instinctive behaviors in mammals. By studying transgenic mice that lack the estrogen receptor (ER), we have discovered the importance of ER activation by natural estrogen in the development of male-typical behaviors. Surprisingly, despite being unable to reproduce, the ERKO mice still displayed normal motivation to mate with females, but they had fewer successful attempts and almost no ejaculations. Aggressive behaviors were significantly reduced, and the ERKO males rarely exhibited typical male offensive attacks. Additionally, the ER gene disruption led to less masculine open-field behaviors. Interestingly, even though the functional ER protein was clearly absent in the brain, the androgen-dependent system seemed to be unaffected in the ERKO mice. These findings suggest that the expression of the ER gene during development plays a crucial role in organizing not only simple sexual behaviors but also male-typical aggressive and emotional behaviors.

title: High-Density Lipoproteins Exert Pro-inflammatory Effects on Macrophages via Passive Cholesterol Depletion and PKC-NF-κB/STAT1-IRF1 Signaling.
text: The presence of cholesterol in cell membranes plays a role in regulating various cell signaling pathways and functions. Although high-density lipoproteins (HDLs) can reduce inflammation in different cell types by depleting cholesterol, their effects on inflammatory responses in macrophages are not well understood. In this study, we demonstrate that HDL-mediated passive cholesterol depletion and disruption of lipid rafts have clear pro-inflammatory effects on murine and human primary macrophages in laboratory settings. These pro-inflammatory effects were also observed in peritoneal macrophages from mice with elevated HDL levels. Consistent with these findings, mice with low HDL levels showed compromised innate immune responses necessary for clearing P. aeruginosa bacterial infection in the lungs. Through expression analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by polymerase chain reaction (ChIP-PCR), and a combination of pharmacological and genetic interventions, we discovered that both native and reconstituted HDL enhance Toll-like-receptor-induced signaling by activating a PKC-NF-κB/STAT1-IRF1 axis, resulting in increased expression of inflammatory cytokines. The pro-inflammatory activity of HDL supports the proper functioning of macrophage immune responses.

title: Hypoxia of the renal medulla--its implications for disease.
text: The kidney plays a crucial role in land mammals by reabsorbing water to ensure survival in dry environments. This water conservation process is made possible by the renal medulla, which concentrates urine to a level that is up to four times more concentrated than plasma. To achieve this unique concentration gradient, the medulla utilizes a system of vessels and tubules that work in opposition to each other, allowing for active reabsorption of sodium in an oxygen-deprived environment (Figure 1). In this article, we explore the connection between medullary hypoxia and the susceptibility to both acute and chronic renal injuries. We delve into the Renal Medullary Concentrating Mechanism and its implications.

title: Troponin concentrations for stratification of patients with acute coronary syndromes in relation to therapeutic efficacy of tirofiban. PRISM Study Investigators. Platelet Receptor Inhibition in Ischemic Syndrome Management.
text:
Physicians face a significant challenge in determining which patients with acute coronary syndromes would benefit from treatment with glycoprotein-IIb/IIIa-receptor antagonists. To address this, we conducted a study to investigate whether troponin concentrations could be used to stratify patients for treatment with tirofiban.

In our study, we enrolled 2222 patients with coronary artery disease who had experienced chest pain within the previous 24 hours. All patients received aspirin and were randomly assigned to receive either tirofiban or heparin. We measured baseline levels of troponin I and troponin T. We then monitored the occurrence of death, myocardial infarction, or recurrent ischemia after 48 hours of infusion treatment, as well as at 7 and 30 days.

Our findings revealed that 28.3% of patients had troponin I concentrations above the diagnostic threshold of 1.0 microg/L, while 29.0% had troponin T concentrations above 0.1 microg/L. The 30-day event rates (death, myocardial infarction) were significantly higher for troponin-I-positive patients compared to troponin-I-negative patients (13.0% vs. 4.9%, p<0.0001), as well as for troponin T-positive patients compared to troponin T-negative patients (13.7% vs. 3.5%, p<0.001).

At 30 days, tirofiban treatment was found to reduce the risk of death (adjusted hazard ratio 0.25 [95% CI 0.09-0.68], p=0.004) and myocardial infarction (0.37 [0.16-0.84], p=0.01) in troponin-I-positive patients. This benefit was observed in both medically managed patients (0.30 [0.10-0.84], p=0.004) and those undergoing revascularization (0.37 [0.15-0.93], p=0.02) after 48 hours of infusion treatment. However, no treatment effect was observed in troponin-I-negative patients. Similar benefits were seen in troponin-T-positive patients.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that troponin I and troponin T can effectively identify high-risk patients with acute coronary syndromes who would benefit from treatment with tirofiban, whether managed medically or through revascularization.

title: Evolution and function of ubiquitin-like protein-conjugation systems
text: The primary role of ubiquitin is to chemically alter other proteins through covalent modification. Recently, a remarkable number of proteins have been found to possess similar characteristics to ubiquitin, despite their slight resemblance. These proteins are also capable of binding to other proteins. Interestingly, the activation process of ubiquitin and the biosynthesis of specific enzyme cofactors share striking similarities, suggesting a potential evolutionary connection between them.

title: Inflammatory biomarkers and exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text: The adverse effects of exacerbations of respiratory symptoms in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) on patients are significant and long-lasting. This study aimed to test the hypothesis that individuals with stable COPD and elevated levels of inflammatory biomarkers are at a higher risk of experiencing exacerbations. The study involved a prospective cohort of 61,650 participants from the Copenhagen City Heart Study and the Copenhagen General Population Study, with 6574 participants diagnosed with COPD. Baseline levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, and leukocyte count were measured in participants who were not experiencing exacerbation symptoms. Exacerbations were defined as short-course treatment with oral corticosteroids alone or in combination with an antibiotic, or as a hospital admission due to COPD. The results showed that during the follow-up period, 3083 exacerbations were recorded, with a mean of 0.5 exacerbations per participant. Individuals with one high biomarker had a multivariable-adjusted odds ratio of 1.2 for frequent exacerbations, while those with two high biomarkers had an odds ratio of 1.7, and those with three high biomarkers had an odds ratio of 3.7, compared to individuals with no elevated biomarkers. The hazard ratios using maximum follow-up time were 1.4, 1.6, and 2.5, respectively. Adding inflammatory biomarkers to a basic model improved the predictive ability of the model. The relative risks were consistent across different subgroups of COPD patients. The study concluded that elevated levels of CRP, fibrinogen, and leukocyte count in individuals with COPD are associated with an increased risk of exacerbations, even in those with milder COPD and no previous exacerbations. Further research is needed to determine the clinical significance of these biomarkers for risk stratification.

title: Gene supplementation therapy for recessive forms of inherited retinal dystrophies
text: In the past ten years, gene supplementation therapy for inherited retinal degeneration has made significant advancements. Initial studies conducted on animal models of the disease demonstrated modest yet genuine improvements in retinal function and/or survival. Subsequent advancements in the vectors used for gene transfer to the retina have resulted in improved treatment efficacy across various animal models. This progress led to the initiation of three clinical trials in 2008, specifically targeting Leber congenital amaurosis caused by retinal pigment epithelium 65 deficiency. The outcomes of these trials indicate that gene therapy can be a safe and effective treatment for inherited retinal dystrophy. In this article, we will assess the advancements made in gene supplementation therapy for the retina and explore the potential of gene therapy in treating different forms of inherited retinal degeneration.

title: Complex Tissue and Disease Modeling using hiPSCs.
text: The use of human pluripotent stem cells to create genetic models has provided new opportunities for studying disease mechanisms and testing drugs. However, many of these models only consider cell-autonomous factors, overlooking the potential impact of the entire cellular and extracellular environment on disease phenotypes and drug responses. To fully harness the potential of these models, it is crucial to develop complex multicellular structures that accurately mimic tissue niches, including vascular components. In this article, we explore the latest research on creating human tissue mimics and offer recommendations for advancing this field.

title: Reprogramming somatic cells towards pluripotency by cellular fusion.
text: Pluripotent cells originate from the inner cell mass (ICM) of mammals and have the ability to develop into any cell type in the adult organism through a process of commitment and ordered differentiation. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms that govern and stabilize cell fate determination, as well as those that can be manipulated to reverse it, are only partially understood. The reprogramming of somatic cells to a pluripotent-like state can be achieved through various experimental methods, such as nuclear transfer, the introduction of specific transcription factors, or the fusion of somatic cells with pluripotent stem cells. These approaches have been used to demonstrate the remarkable ability of many fully differentiated cell types to undergo epigenetic changes and to identify the factors necessary for pluripotent conversion. In this review, we summarize recent advancements in cell fusion-based studies that contribute to a better understanding of the foundations of pluripotency and the epigenetic mechanisms that facilitate the conversion between different cell types.

title: Anorectic drugs and pulmonary hypertension from the bedside to the bench.
text: For over 30 years, anorectic drugs have been used to assist obese individuals in losing weight. However, the use of certain drugs such as aminorex and fenfluramine led to outbreaks of primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) in Europe during the late 1960s and early 1970s. These drugs were voluntarily removed from the market. The exact cause of PPH in patients treated with these drugs is uncertain, but recent evidence suggests that abnormalities in potassium channels and the vasoactive and proliferative properties of 5-HT (a neurotransmitter) may play a role. Aminorex, fenfluramine, and dexfenfluramine have been found to inhibit potassium channels, leading to vasoconstriction in the pulmonary resistance vessels and potentially causing smooth muscle cell proliferation. Additionally, 5-HT has been linked to pulmonary artery vasoconstriction and smooth muscle cell proliferation, with high levels observed in individuals with fenfluramine-induced PPH. However, a definitive cause-and-effect relationship has not yet been established. One positive outcome of the anorectic-related PPH epidemics is that they have provided valuable insights into the causes of PPH unrelated to anorectic drugs.

title: B-catenin deficiency, but not Myc deletion, suppresses the immediate phenotypes of APC loss in the liver.
text: Approximately 30% of hepatocellular carcinomas exhibit dysregulated Wnt signaling. Therefore, it is crucial to identify the downstream pathways activated by Wnt signaling. In this study, we used cre-lox technology to delete the Apc gene in the adult mouse liver. This deletion resulted in a rapid increase in nuclear beta-catenin and c-Myc, leading to increased proliferation and hepatomegaly within just 4 days. To investigate the pathways responsible for these effects, we examined the impact of inactivating APC in combination with the potential key effectors beta-catenin and c-Myc. Loss of beta-catenin rescued both the proliferation and hepatomegaly phenotypes caused by APC loss. However, deletion of c-Myc, which rescued the phenotypes of APC loss in the intestine, had no effect on the phenotypes of APC loss in the liver. These findings highlight the strikingly different consequences of Wnt pathway deregulation in the liver compared to the intestine. In the liver, the majority of Wnt targets are dependent on beta-catenin but independent of c-Myc.

title: Uncoupling Mitochondrial Respiration for Diabesity.
text: Until recently, it was believed that the mechanism of adaptive thermogenesis was solely attributed to the presence of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in brown and beige adipocytes. UCP1 is responsible for facilitating a leakage of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, resulting in uncoupled oxidative metabolism without the production of adenosine triphosphate and an increase in energy expenditure. Therefore, increasing the amount of brown and beige adipose tissue with enhanced UCP1 expression has been considered a viable target for addressing obesity-related disorders. However, recent research has revealed an alternative pathway to uncouple mitochondrial respiration that is independent of UCP1. This pathway involves a secreted enzyme called PM20D1, which is predominantly found in UCP1+ adipocytes. PM20D1 exhibits both catalytic and hydrolytic activity, allowing it to reversibly form N-acyl amino acids. These N-acyl amino acids serve as natural uncouplers of mitochondrial respiration at physiological concentrations. When PM20D1 or its products, the N-acyl amino acids, are administered to mice with diet-induced obesity, it improves their glucose tolerance by increasing energy expenditure. In short-term studies, the treated animals show no signs of toxicity and experience a 10% reduction in weight, primarily from adipose tissue. Further investigation into this metabolic pathway may lead to the discovery of innovative therapies for diabesity, the disease state associated with diabetes and obesity.

title: A functional polymorphism in the prodynorphin gene promotor is associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: The prodynorphin gene (PDYN), which produces the dynorphin peptide known for its anticonvulsant properties, is a strong candidate as a gene that suppresses seizures and may influence susceptibility to temporal lobe epilepsy. To investigate this, we conducted a study comparing 155 patients with nonlesional temporal lobe epilepsy to 202 controls. Our findings revealed that individuals with low-expression L-alleles in the PDYN promoter region have an increased risk of developing temporal lobe epilepsy, particularly if they have a family history of seizures. Regardless of familial background, those who are L-homozygotes have a higher risk of experiencing secondarily generalized seizures and status epilepticus.

title: Cardiovascular and renal benefits of dry bean and soybean intake.
text: Dry beans and soybeans are rich in nutrients, packed with fiber, and excellent sources of protein. Both dry beans and soybeans have been proven to have protective and therapeutic effects. Research has shown that consuming dry beans can potentially lower cholesterol levels, improve diabetic conditions, and provide metabolic benefits that aid in weight management. Soybeans, on the other hand, contain unique compounds called isoflavones, such as genistein and diadzein, which have various biological functions. Soybeans and soy-based foods have the potential to promote overall health by reducing cholesterol, improving vascular health, maintaining bone density, and alleviating menopausal symptoms. Although the exact effects of soy on renal function are not fully understood, it appears to have positive effects. While populations with high soy consumption have lower rates of certain cancers, there is still a lack of definitive experimental data to confirm soy's protective role. As legume products and resources become more readily available, incorporating dry beans and soyfoods into our diets can be both practical and enjoyable. As more people shift towards a plant-based diet, dry beans and soy will become powerful tools in the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases.

title: Nonuniform probability of glutamate release at a hippocampal synapse.
text: The probability of neurotransmitter release (Pr) is a crucial factor in synaptic plasticity. It is commonly assumed that Pr is consistent across all terminals within a synapse, but this assumption is challenging to reconcile with the varying size and structure of synaptic terminals in the central nervous system. To investigate this, we measured the release probability at excitatory synapses on cultured hippocampal neurons. We analyzed the progressive block of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor-mediated synaptic currents using the irreversible open channel blocker MK-801. Our findings revealed that the release probability was not uniform, ranging from 0.09 to 0.54, for terminals originating from a single axon. The majority of these terminals had a low Pr, while a few had a high Pr. Interestingly, terminals with high Pr are more susceptible to activity-dependent modulation, which is known to occur during long-term potentiation.

title: An autoimmune disease, APECED, caused by mutations in a novel gene featuring two PHD-type zinc-finger domains
text: APECED, also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy, is a unique systemic autoimmune disease that is caused by a single gene defect. It is the first autoimmune disorder to be found outside the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region. The exact biochemical defect responsible for APECED is currently unknown. However, we have discovered a new gene called AIRE, which codes for a potential nuclear protein that contains two PHD-type zinc-finger motifs. This suggests that AIRE may play a role in regulating transcription. So far, five mutations in the AIRE gene have been identified in individuals with APECED. This groundbreaking discovery of a single-gene defect causing a systemic autoimmune disease provides a valuable tool for further investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying autoimmunity.

title: NuA4 lysine acetyltransferase Esa1 is targeted to coding regions and stimulates transcription elongation with Gcn5.
text: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NuA4 is a significant complex responsible for acetylating H4 lysine, a process known as lysine acetyltransferase (KAT). It is recruited to promoters and plays a role in initiating transcription. The subunits of NuA4 contain domains that bind to methylated histones, indicating that histone methylation may direct NuA4 to coding sequences during transcription elongation. Our study demonstrates that NuA4 is recruited during transcription, relying on its physical association with elongating polymerase II (Pol II) that has been phosphorylated on the C-terminal domain by cyclin-dependent kinase 7/Kin28. This recruitment occurs independently of the subunits Eaf1 and Tra1, which are necessary for NuA4's recruitment to promoters. While the histone methylation carried out by Set1 and Set2 is not essential for NuA4's interaction with Pol II or its targeting to certain coding regions, it does enhance the interaction between NuA4 and histones, as well as the acetylation of H4 in vivo. The NuA4 KAT, Esa1, is responsible for increasing H4 acetylation and promoting the occupancy of RSC (Remodels the Structure of Chromatin) and the eviction of histones in coding sequences, thereby enhancing the rate of transcription elongation. Esa1 works together with the H3 KAT in SAGA, Gcn5, to further enhance these functions. Our findings provide insight into the pathway through which acetylation-mediated nucleosome remodeling and eviction occur in coding sequences, ultimately stimulating transcription elongation by Pol II in vivo.

title: Targeting mitotic exit leads to tumor regression in vivo: Modulation by Cdk1, Mastl, and the PP2A/B55α,δ phosphatase.
text: Recent research has suggested that targeting mitotic exit could be a promising therapeutic strategy for treating cancer. In our study using genetically modified mice, we have discovered that the APC/C cofactor Cdc20 is crucial for the initiation of anaphase in both embryonic and adult cells, including progenitor and stem cells. When Cdc20 is eliminated, aggressive tumors regress effectively, whereas current mitotic drugs have limited impact. Interestingly, cells lacking Cdc20 can still exit mitosis when Cdk1 and the kinase Mastl (Greatwall) are deactivated. This mitotic exit relies on the activity of PP2A phosphatase complexes that contain regulatory subunits B55α or B55δ. These findings highlight the importance of key players in mitotic exit in mammals and their implications for the delicate balance between cell death and mitotic exit in tumor cells.

title: DrugBank 5.0: a major update to the DrugBank database for 2018
text: DrugBank (www.drugbank.ca) is an online database that provides comprehensive molecular information on drugs, including their mechanisms, interactions, and targets. Since its inception in 2006, DrugBank has continuously evolved to meet the changing needs of drug research and development, taking advantage of advancements in web standards. The latest update, DrugBank 5.0, is the most significant upgrade in over a decade. The database has seen substantial growth in existing data content, with some categories expanding by over 100%. For example, the number of investigational drugs has increased by almost 300%, drug-drug interactions by nearly 600%, and SNP-associated drug effects by over 3000%. Notable improvements have been made to the quantity, quality, and consistency of drug indications, drug binding data, as well as drug-drug and drug-food interactions. Additionally, DrugBank 5.0 introduces a wealth of new data, including information on the impact of hundreds of drugs on metabolite levels (pharmacometabolomics), gene expression levels (pharmacotranscriptomics), and protein expression levels (pharmacoprotoemics). The update also includes data on the status of numerous new drug clinical trials and existing drug repurposing trials. Furthermore, the DrugBank website has undergone significant enhancements in content, interface, and performance, making it more user-friendly and valuable for various areas of pharmacological research, pharmaceutical science, and drug education.

title: Analyzing mechanisms of alternative pre-mRNA splicing using in vitro splicing assays.
text: The discovery of in vitro assays for analyzing pre-mRNA splicing has provided valuable insights into the characteristics of splicing signals and the machinery involved in this process. These assays can be easily manipulated using different biochemical techniques, allowing for endless possibilities in investigating alternative pre-mRNA splicing. By modifying reaction conditions, researchers can isolate and study reaction intermediates, which is crucial for understanding how the spliceosome removes introns and how regulatory elements contribute to defining splice sites and alternative exons. Despite being independent from RNA transcription and other RNA processing events, the in vitro splicing system has become a standard assay due to its significant experimental advantages. However, it does differ from the natural process of mRNA biogenesis in some aspects. In this article, we provide a comprehensive guide to conducting in vitro splicing assays. We discuss various experimental designs that have been used to gain insights into the mechanisms of splice site recognition and activation in communication with the general splicing machinery. We also present methods for measuring splicing kinetics, observing the formation of pre-spliceosomal complexes, and manipulating the in vitro system to understand the regulatory influences in alternative splicing.

title: New Roles for Pharmacists in Community Mental Health Care: A Narrative Review
text:
Pharmacists have a crucial role to play in the treatment of mental illnesses, especially considering the increasing global burden of these disorders. This review aims to explore the evidence supporting the delivery of pharmacist services in mental health care and address the obstacles and opportunities for expanding the use of these services within the broader mental health care team. The review is divided into three main sections.

The first section focuses on the pharmacist's role within multidisciplinary teams and their contribution to early detection of mental illnesses. It highlights new roles that pharmacists can take on, such as participating in case conferencing and collaborative drug therapy management. Additionally, it emphasizes the importance of pharmacist involvement in the early identification of mental health conditions, the development of care plans, and the follow-up care for individuals with mental health problems.

The second section explores the impact of medication review services and other pharmacist-led interventions aimed at reducing inappropriate use of psychotropic medicines and improving medication adherence. It also discusses potential new roles for pharmacists, including the management of antipsychotic polypharmacy and involvement in patient-centered care.

The final section addresses barriers that may hinder the implementation of mental health pharmacy services. These barriers include pharmacists' attitudes, stigma surrounding mental health, and their skills in caring for patients with mental health problems. The review also discusses strategies to reduce mental health stigma and improve collaboration between pharmacists and physicians.

Overall, this review highlights the importance of pharmacists in mental health care and provides evidence-based recommendations for expanding their role in supporting individuals with mental illnesses.

title: UV light-induced DNA synthesis arrest in HeLa cells is associated with changes in phosphorylation of human single-stranded DNA-binding protein.
text: Our study demonstrates that exposure to UV radiation leads to a decrease in DNA replication activity in human HeLa cells. This reduction in replication activity in vitro corresponds to the UV-induced blockage of cell cycle progression in these cultured cells. Additionally, UV radiation triggers specific changes in the phosphorylation pattern of the 34 kDa subunit of a DNA replication protein known as human single-stranded DNA-binding protein (hSSB). The presence of a hyperphosphorylated form of hSSB is associated with a decrease in in vitro DNA replication activity in UV-irradiated cell extracts. However, the addition of purified hSSB to these extracts restores replication activity, suggesting that the UV-induced arrest of DNA synthesis may be partially mediated by phosphorylation-related modifications in the function of hSSB, a crucial component of the DNA replication machinery.

title: P446L-importin-beta inhibits nuclear envelope assembly by sequestering nuclear envelope assembly factors to the microtubules.
text: The mutant Drosophila importin-beta (P446L-imp-beta), known as P446L-imp-beta, has been found to prevent the assembly of the nuclear envelope (NE) in a dominant negative manner. To understand how P446L-imp-beta works, we conducted a study on NE assembly using Sepharose beads in vitro. While Drosophila embryo extracts supported NE assembly on Sepharose beads coated with Ran, NE assembly did not occur in extracts supplemented with exogenous P446L-imp-beta. Interestingly, NE also formed on beads coated with normal importin-beta. Surprisingly, when P446L-imp-beta was immobilized on Sepharose beads, it recruited NE vesicles as efficiently as normal importin-beta. The difference in behavior between cytoplasmic P446L-imp-beta and bead-bound P446L-imp-beta seems to be due to the increased microtubule (MT) binding ability of P446L-imp-beta compared to normal importin-beta. While wild-type importin-beta can bind to MTs and this binding decreases upon interaction with RanGTP, P446L-imp-beta cannot be released from MTs by RanGTP. Similar to normal importin-beta, P446L-imp-beta binds to certain types of nucleoporins that are known to be necessary for NE assembly at the end of mitosis. It appears that the inhibitory effect of P446L-imp-beta on NE assembly is caused by sequestering some of the nucleoporins required for NE assembly onto the MTs.

title: Histone chaperones and nucleosome assembly.
text: Newly discovered structures of the nucleosome core particle have provided valuable insights into the interactions between histones and DNA, as well as histone-histone interactions. These structures have paved the way for a better understanding of how chromatin is assembled and how it behaves during replication and transcription. Both histone chaperones and chromatin remodeling complexes play crucial roles in these processes. The nucleosome, consisting of the histone octamer and its associated proteins, exhibits a symmetrical structure, which histone chaperones can exploit to bind to the core histones. Recent research suggests that the nucleoplasmin pentamer may play a role in histone storage, sperm chromatin decondensation, and nucleosome assembly by forming a decamer through dimerization. According to this model, histone binding on the chaperone's lateral surface involves specific interactions and a shared symmetrical axis.

title: Intestinal methane production in obese individuals is associated with a higher body mass index.
text:
CONTEXT Obesity is a widespread problem in the United States, affecting approximately one-third of the population. Recent research suggests that the composition of gut bacteria, known as enteric microbiota, may play a significant role in the development of obesity. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between methanogenic archaea and obesity in human subjects.

METHODS The study recruited individuals with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or higher from a weight loss program at a tertiary care medical center. Participants who met the study's criteria completed a questionnaire that included visual analogue scores for the severity of bowel symptoms. They also provided a breath sample to measure methane levels. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to identify associations with BMI.

RESULTS A total of 58 patients were enrolled in the study. Among them, 20% (n = 12) had breath test results indicating the presence of methane (>3 parts per million [ppm]), with an average methane concentration of 12.2±3.1 ppm. Methane-positive individuals had significantly higher BMI (45.2±2.3 kg/m²) compared to methane-negative individuals (38.5±0.8 kg/m²; P=.001). Methane-positive individuals also experienced more severe constipation than methane-negative individuals (21.3±6.4 vs 9.5±2.4; P=.043). Multiple regression analysis revealed a significant association between BMI and methane, constipation, and antidepressant use. Importantly, methane remained an independent predictor of higher BMI even when accounting for antidepressant use (P<.001) and both constipation and antidepressant use (6.55 kg/m² higher BMI; P=.003).

CONCLUSION This study is the first to demonstrate that a higher concentration of methane detected through breath testing is a predictor of significantly greater obesity in overweight individuals.

title: Study of infectious intestinal disease in England: rates in the community, presenting to general practice, and reported to national surveillance. The Infectious Intestinal Disease Study Executive.
text:
The aim of this study was to determine the occurrence and causes of infectious intestinal disease in both the general population and those seeking medical attention from general practitioners. The study utilized a combination of community-based cohort incidence research, general practice-based incidence studies, and linkage of cases to national laboratory surveillance. The study took place in 70 general practices across England and involved a total of 459,975 patients. Community surveillance was conducted on a randomly selected group of 9,776 patients. The main outcomes measured were the incidence of infectious intestinal disease in the community and the number of cases reported to general practice.

The results showed that there were 781 cases of infectious intestinal disease identified in the community cohort, resulting in an incidence rate of 19.4 cases per 100 person years (with a 95% confidence interval of 18.1 to 20.8). In comparison, there were 8,770 cases reported to general practice, resulting in an incidence rate of 3.3 cases per 100 person years (with a confidence interval of 2.94 to 3.75). For every 1.4 laboratory identifications, 6.2 stools sent for laboratory investigation, 23 cases presenting to general practice, and 136 community cases, only one case was reported to national surveillance. The ratio of cases in the community to cases reaching national surveillance was lower for bacterial pathogens (3.2:1 for salmonella and 7.6:1 for campylobacter) compared to viruses (35:1 for rotavirus and 1562:1 for small round structured viruses). Additionally, there were numerous cases where no specific organism was identified.

In conclusion, infectious intestinal disease affects approximately 1 in 5 individuals each year, with 1 in 6 of these cases seeking medical attention from a general practitioner. The proportion of cases that are not captured by national laboratory surveillance is significant and varies greatly depending on the microorganism involved. Therefore, alternative methods of supplementing the national laboratory surveillance system for infectious intestinal diseases should be considered.

title: Venous thrombosis in cancer patients: insights from the FRONTLINE survey.
text: The FRONTLINE study is the first global survey that aims to gather information on the perceptions and management of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in cancer patients. VTE is a common complication in cancer patients and can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. However, there is limited knowledge on how oncologists perceive the risk of VTE and how they manage it. The study collected data on the perceived risk and practices related to VTE in cancer patients undergoing surgical and medical treatment. The findings of the study were compared to existing evidence through literature reviews, and a questionnaire was developed with the guidance of an advisory board. The questionnaire was distributed globally to clinicians involved in cancer care. A total of 3,891 completed responses were analyzed. The study found that brain and pancreatic tumors were considered to have a high risk for VTE, and the use of central venous lines was also associated with a high risk. There were significant differences in the use of thromboprophylaxis between surgical and medical cancer patients, with over 50% of surgeons initiating thromboprophylaxis routinely, while most medical oncologists used it in less than 5% of medical patients. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) was the most commonly used method of thromboprophylaxis, particularly in Europe. However, around 20% of respondents reported using aspirin for prophylaxis, despite lack of evidence for its effectiveness. LMWH was also the most common initial treatment for VTE, with oral anticoagulation therapy being widely adopted for long-term treatment. Many patients were treated on an outpatient basis, and secondary prevention of VTE was typically continued for 3 to 6 months after deep vein thrombosis or longer for pulmonary embolism. The results of the study highlight the need for guidelines to guide clinical practice based on evidence-based data. Oncologists should be educated on the true risks of VTE in different cancers and strategies for prevention and treatment to reduce morbidity and mortality. The study also identified areas for future research.

title: A dual function of the CRISPR-Cas system in bacterial antivirus immunity and DNA repair.
text: The CRISPR-Cas system is a form of adaptive immunity found in prokaryotes that protects against viruses and plasmids. Within this system, the Cas1 protein is present in all prokaryotes with CRISPR, but its exact role is not well understood. Our research focuses on the Cas1 protein from Escherichia coli (YgbT), which we have found to have nuclease activity against various types of DNA, including single-stranded and branched DNAs like Holliday junctions, replication forks, and 5'-flaps. By studying the crystal structure of YgbT and conducting site-directed mutagenesis, we have identified a potential active site. Through genome-wide screens, we have also discovered that YgbT interacts physically and genetically with important DNA repair components such as recB, recC, and ruvB. These findings are supported by the fact that a ygbT deletion strain showed increased sensitivity to DNA damage and impaired chromosomal segregation. Interestingly, similar effects were observed in strains with CRISPR cluster deletions, suggesting that YgbT's role in repair involves interaction with the CRISPRs.
