Our results demonstrate that YgbT belongs to a unique family of nucleases that target branched DNAs and indicate that, in addition to its antiviral function, certain components of the CRISPR-Cas system play a role in DNA repair.

title: Antibodies from patients with rheumatoid arthritis target citrullinated histone 4 contained in neutrophils extracellular traps.
text:
BACKGROUND: Histone deimination plays a role in regulating gene function and contributes to the antimicrobial response by enabling the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), deiminated proteins are targeted by anti-citrullinated peptides antibodies (ACPA).

OBJECTIVE: This study aims to test the hypothesis that sera from RA patients react with deiminated histones found in NETs.

METHODS: Neutrophils from peripheral blood were stimulated with A23187 and treated with acid to induce NETosis. NET proteins were then isolated. Sera were tested using immunoblot on acid-extracted proteins from neutrophils and NETs, as well as ELISA on deiminated histone H4 or H4-derived peptides. Bands that reacted with RA sera were excised from gels, digested with trypsin, and analyzed using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time of flight (MALDI-TOF) to detect citrullinated peptides.

RESULTS: RA sera showed reactivity with an 11 KDa deiminated antigen from activated neutrophils, which was also recognized by anti-H4 and anti-deiminated H4 antibodies. Similar reactivity was observed with NET proteins. MALDI-TOF analysis identified the antigen from neutrophils or NETs as citrullinated H4. ELISA demonstrated that RA sera bound to in vitro citrullinated H4. Antibodies against citrullinated H4 14-34 and 31-50 peptides were detected in 67% and 63% of RA sera, respectively, compared to less than 5% in controls. Antibody titers were correlated with anti-CCP2.

CONCLUSIONS: Citrullinated H4 from activated neutrophils and NETs is targeted by antibodies in RA. Synthetic citrullinated H4-derived peptides can serve as a new substrate for ACPA detection. These findings suggest a novel connection between innate and adaptive immunity in RA, as NETosis can generate antigens for ACPA.

title: Mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo2 is important for enterochromaffin cell response to mechanical forces
text:
The gastrointestinal epithelial enterochromaffin (EC) cell is responsible for synthesizing the majority of the body's serotonin. These cells release serotonin in response to mechanical forces, but the exact mechanism behind this process is unknown. In this study, we discovered that the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo2 is specifically expressed in human and mouse EC cells. When Piezo2 is activated by mechanical forces, it generates a distinct ionic current, triggers serotonin release, and stimulates gastrointestinal secretion. Inhibiting Piezo2 through drugs or molecular knockdown reduces mechanosensitive currents, serotonin release, and the associated physiological effects. These findings suggest that Piezo2 plays a crucial role in EC cell mechanotransduction in the small bowel of humans and mice. 

In summary, the EC cell in the gastrointestinal epithelium is responsible for producing serotonin and responding to mechanical forces. We found that Piezo2, a mechanosensitive ion channel, is expressed in EC cells and is essential for their mechanosensitivity and the subsequent physiological effects.

title: Improved prognosis of thoracic aortic aneurysms: a population-based study.
text: The incidental identification of thoracic aortic aneurysms through advanced imaging techniques presents challenges, particularly in the elderly population. This study aimed to determine if the prognosis for individuals with thoracic aortic aneurysms has improved due to advancements in medical therapies and surgical techniques. The study involved a population-based cohort of 133 patients diagnosed with degenerative thoracic aortic aneurysms in Olmsted County, Minnesota, between 1980 and 1994. The findings were compared to a previously reported cohort of similar patients between 1951 and 1980. The primary outcomes measured were the incidence, cumulative rupture risk, rupture risk based on aneurysm size, and survival rates. The results showed that unlike abdominal aortic aneurysms, which predominantly affect men, 51% of thoracic aortic aneurysms were found in older women (mean age, 75.9 vs 62.8 years for men; P= .01). The overall incidence rate between 1980 and 1994 was more than three times higher than the rate from 1951 to 1980, with an incidence rate of 10.4 per 100,000 person-years (95% confidence interval [CI], 8.6-12.2). The cumulative risk of rupture after five years was 20%, with 79% of ruptures occurring in women (P= .01). The five-year risk of rupture increased with aneurysm size, with a 0% risk for aneurysms less than 4 cm, 16% (95% CI, 4%-28%) for those 4 to 5.9 cm, and 31% (95% CI, 5%-56%) for aneurysms 6 cm or larger. Overall, the five-year survival rate improved to 56% (95% CI, 48%-66%) between 1980 and 1994 compared to only 19% between 1951 and 1980 (P<.01). In conclusion, this study found that elderly women make up a growing proportion of patients with clinically recognized thoracic aortic aneurysms and are more likely to experience rupture. However, the overall survival rate for thoracic aortic aneurysms has significantly improved in the past 15 years.

title: Intravenous valproate is well tolerated in unstable patients with status epilepticus.
text: The hospital records of 13 patients with status epilepticus and hypotension who were treated with IV valproate therapy were reviewed by the authors. The majority of the patients were elderly, with an average age of 74.4 +/- 12.5 (SD) years. They received a loading dose of valproate averaging 25.1 +/- 5.0 mg/kg, with a range of 14.7 to 32.7. The rate of administration was 36.6 +/- 25.1 mg/min, ranging from 6.3 to 100. No significant changes were observed in blood pressure, pulse, or the use of vasopressors. Based on the data, it can be concluded that valproate loading is well tolerated, even in patients with cardiovascular instability.

title: Interplays between ATM/Tel1 and ATR/Mec1 in sensing and signaling DNA double-strand breaks.
text: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) pose a significant threat to the integrity of the genome as they have the potential to cause mutations, rearrangements of chromosomes, and instability in the overall genomic structure. To counteract this danger, cells have evolved signal transduction pathways called DNA damage checkpoints, which are present in both yeasts and humans. These pathways are responsible for detecting DNA damage and transmitting this information to specific cellular targets. These targets, in turn, regulate the cell cycle and facilitate DNA repair. In mammals, the protein kinases ATM and ATR, along with their yeast counterparts Tel1 and Mec1, play a crucial role as the main regulators of the checkpoint response to DSBs. In this review, we focus on the initial stages of DSB processing and the significance of DNA-end structures in activating ATM/Tel1 and ATR/Mec1 in a coordinated and reciprocal manner.

title: The ‘definitive’ (and ‘primitive’) guide to zebrafish hematopoiesis
text: The use of zebrafish as a model organism has greatly advanced the study of blood cell formation and hematological malignancies for hematologists. Despite the significant evolutionary differences between bony fish and mammals, the molecular pathways that govern hematopoiesis have remained highly conserved. This means that most, if not all, of the crucial genes responsible for hematopoietic transcription factors in mammals also have counterparts in zebrafish. Like other vertebrates, teleost blood lineages are believed to originate from a group of pluripotent, self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells. In this article, we provide a comprehensive review of the timing, location, and regulation of both "primitive" and "definitive" hematopoiesis in zebrafish. We also discuss a model of T-cell leukemia and recent advancements in blood cell transplantation. Since many of the regulatory genes that control embryonic hematopoiesis are also involved in oncogenic pathways in adults, understanding the development of blood cells is likely to offer valuable insights into the pathophysiology of human leukemias.

title: Steroid receptor interactions with heat shock protein and immunophilin chaperones.
text:
We have presented a historical overview of research on steroid receptors, specifically focusing on the untransformed 9S receptor. This receptor has been a source of confusion for both novice and expert investigators due to its complex structure and physiological significance. Previous studies faced controversies and uncertainties because the native, hormone-free state of these receptors is a large multiprotein complex that was difficult to describe due to its unstable and dynamic nature. However, studying the untransformed 9S state of steroid and dioxin receptors has provided a unique opportunity to examine the function of the heat shock protein, hsp90, which is ubiquitous, abundant, and conserved.

The control of receptor association with hsp90 through hormones allowed researchers to manipulate the receptor heterocomplex in a physiologically meaningful way. For several steroid receptors, binding to hsp90 was necessary for the receptor to be in its native hormone-binding state. Additionally, hormone binding facilitated the dissociation of the receptor from hsp90 and its conversion to the DNA-binding state. While the complexes between tyrosine kinases and hsp90 were discovered earlier, the hormonal regulation of steroid receptor association with hsp90 enabled a faster and easier study of hsp90 function.

It was observed that hsp90 binds to the receptors through their hormone-binding domains (HBDs), and these domains can be fused to different proteins, allowing their function to be controlled by hormones. This linkage between hormonal regulation of receptor binding to hsp90 and the initial step in steroid hormone action proved to be powerful. By stabilizing the 9S receptor hsp90 heterocomplexes with molybdate, researchers were able to study their protein composition. It became evident that these complexes are multiprotein structures containing unique proteins such as FKBP51, FKBP52, CyP-40, and p23, which were discovered due to their presence in these structures.

Further analysis revealed that hsp90 itself exists in various native multiprotein heterocomplexes independent of steroid receptors and other "substrate" proteins. Cell-free systems are now being used to study the formation of receptor heterocomplexes. The assembly process of the multicomponent receptor-hsp90 heterocomplex is being reconstituted, and the importance of individual proteins like hsp70, p60, and p23 in this process is being recognized.

It is important to note that our understanding of the mechanism and purpose of steroid receptor heterocomplex assembly is still in its early stages. While we can speculate on the roles of receptor-associated proteins in receptor action, both individually and as a group, their actual functions remain unclear or unknown. We can create realistic models of chaperoning and trafficking of steroid receptors, but the processes themselves, such as where chaperoning occurs in the cell and whether it is limited to the cytoplasm or associated with structural elements, are still unknown. Apart from the requirement for hormone binding, we also do not fully understand the extent to which the hsp90-based chaperone system affects steroid hormone action.

The discovery of the hsp90 heterocomplex assembly system has the potential to contribute to a broader understanding of protein processing in cells. Since this assembly system is present in all eukaryotic cells, it likely plays an essential role in the function of many proteins. While the bacterial homolog of hsp90 is not essential, hsp90 is crucial in eukaryotes. Recent studies suggest that the duplication of genes for hsp90 and hsp70 accompanied the development of the cell nucleus from prokaryotic ancestors. However, further research is needed to fully comprehend the implications of this hsp90 heterocomplex assembly system and its impact on protein processing in cells.

title: Molecular Characterization of Oxysterol Binding to the Epstein-Barr Virus-induced Gene 2 (GPR183)*
text: Oxysterols are cholesterol derivatives that have been recognized as an important group of molecules in physiological processes. Despite their role in regulating various cellular functions, only a few proteins that bind to oxysterols have been identified, and our understanding of how they bind is limited. Recently, the family of G protein-coupled seven transmembrane-spanning receptors (7TM receptors) has been included in this group. Specifically, the Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 2 (EBI2 or GPR183) has been found to be activated by several oxysterols, with 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol (7α,25-OHC) being the most potent activator. However, we currently have no knowledge of how these oxysterols bind to the receptor. Through mutational analysis, we have identified four key amino acid residues that are crucial for the binding of 7α,25-OHC: Arg-87 in TM-II, Tyr-112 and Tyr-116 in TM-III, and Tyr-260 in TM-VI. When these residues are substituted with other amino acids, such as Ala or Phe, there is a significant decrease in the binding of the agonist and activation of the receptor. Docking simulations suggest that Tyr-116 interacts with the 3β-OH group of the agonist, Tyr-260 with the 7α-OH group, and Arg-87, either directly or indirectly, with the 25-OH group, although nearby residues may also contribute. Additionally, Tyr-112 is involved in the binding of 7α,25-OHC through hydrophobic interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that position II:20/2.60 is an important residue for ligand binding in receptors that have a positively charged residue at this position. This group of receptors is primarily activated by lipids and nucleotides, as exemplified by the CysLTs, P2Y12, and P2Y14 receptors. In summary, we provide the first molecular characterization of how oxysterols bind to a 7TM receptor and identify position II:20/2.60 as a generally important residue for ligand binding in certain 7TM receptors.

title: Up-regulation of neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1) in the prefrontal cortex of schizophrenic and bipolar patients.
text: Biological psychiatry has long sought to understand the dysfunction of dopamine in individuals with mental illness. This study focuses on a newly identified group of proteins that interact with dopamine receptors, which may contribute to dysfunction in individuals with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Our findings show that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in individuals with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, as observed in the Stanley Foundation Neuropathology Consortium, exhibit significantly higher levels of a protein called neuronal calcium sensor-1, which regulates the desensitization of the D2 dopamine receptor. These elevated levels of neuronal calcium sensor-1 were not influenced by factors such as age, gender, hemisphere, cause of death, postmortem period, alcohol consumption, or the use of antipsychotic and mood stabilizing medications. This study provides support for the idea that abnormalities in dopamine receptor-interacting proteins may be associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

title: c-Abl: activation and nuclear targets
text: The c-Abl tyrosine kinase and its transforming variants have been linked to the development of tumors and various cellular processes. c-Abl is found in both the nucleus and cytoplasm, where it performs different functions. Its effects are influenced by interactions with other proteins and DNA, as well as its tyrosine kinase domain. While some aspects of c-Abl kinase activation and its target proteins and cellular mechanisms have been understood at a biochemical level, the overall outcomes of these molecular events have remained largely unknown. c-Abl has been found to regulate the cell cycle and can cause cell growth arrest and apoptosis under certain conditions. The interaction between c-Abl and p53 and p73 has received significant attention, particularly in relation to ionizing irradiation signaling pathway-induced apoptosis. In this pathway, p73 serves as an important downstream effector. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of these nuclear processes involving c-Abl and discuss their potential implications for cell physiology.

title: Cancer survival increases in Europe, but international differences remain wide.
text: The EUROCARE project examined cancer survival rates across Europe by analyzing data from 45 cancer registries in 17 countries. The study focused on 1,836,287 patients diagnosed with 13 different types of cancer between 1978 and 1989. The data was divided into four regions: Northern Europe (Finland, Sweden, Iceland), UK and Denmark (Denmark, England, Scotland), Western Europe (France, The Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Switzerland), and Eastern Europe (Estonia, Poland). The data was further divided into four time periods. The study found significant variations in cancer survival rates between countries and regions. Overall, survival rates improved over time, particularly for testicular cancer (12% increase), breast cancer, large bowel cancer, skin melanoma (approximately 9-10% increase), and lymphomas (approximately 7% increase). Northern Europe had the highest survival rates for most solid tumors, while Eastern Europe and the UK/Denmark had the lowest rates. Regional differences were less pronounced for lymphomas. Western Europe showed greater improvement in survival rates compared to Northern Europe. The study suggests that the differences in survival rates may be attributed to variations in access to diagnostic and treatment facilities, as well as the effectiveness of healthcare systems.

title: A nuclear translation-like factor eIF4AIII is recruited to the mRNA during splicing and functions in nonsense-mediated decay.
text: Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) is a surveillance mechanism in eukaryotes that degrades mRNA containing a premature-termination codon (PTC). To detect the PTC, NMD relies on translation to read the mRNA frame. During pre-mRNA splicing, the exon-exon junction complex (EJC) is recruited to a region on the mature mRNA, about 20-24 nucleotides upstream of the exon junction. If a PTC is present upstream from the EJC, NMD is triggered. Eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A) III is a nuclear protein that interacts with translation initiation factors eIF4G and eIF4B. It shares a high degree of similarity with the initiation factors eIF4AI/II. Our study demonstrates that siRNA targeting eIF4AIII, but not eIF4AI/II, inhibits NMD. Additionally, eIF4AIII, but not eIF4AI, is specifically recruited to the EJC during splicing. These findings suggest that eIF4AIII may substitute for eIF4AI/II during NMD, as it is loaded onto the mRNA in the nucleus during splicing, possesses properties related to a translation initiation factor, and functions in NMD.

title: Swaddling: a systematic review.
text: Swaddling, a practice that was once widespread in child care before the 18th century, is still observed in certain regions of the Middle East and is gaining popularity in the United Kingdom, the United States, and The Netherlands as a means to reduce excessive crying. In order to assess its potential advantages and disadvantages, we have conducted a comprehensive review of all available articles on swaddling. Generally, swaddled infants experience less arousal and longer periods of sleep. Preterm infants, in particular, have demonstrated improved neuromuscular development, reduced physiological distress, enhanced motor organization, and greater self-regulatory abilities when swaddled. When compared to massage, swaddling has been found to decrease crying in excessively fussy infants and can provide pain relief. It has also proven beneficial in cases of neonatal abstinence syndrome and infants with neonatal cerebral lesions. Swaddling can help regulate body temperature, but improper application can lead to hyperthermia. Another potential drawback is an increased risk of hip dysplasia, particularly when swaddling involves extending and adducting the legs. While swaddling promotes the recommended supine position for infants, combining swaddling with the prone position raises the risk of sudden infant death syndrome, necessitating parents to discontinue swaddling if their infants attempt to turn. There is some evidence suggesting a higher likelihood of respiratory infections associated with the tightness of swaddling. Additionally, swaddling does not impact the onset of rickets or bone properties. Swaddling immediately after birth may result in delayed postnatal weight gain under certain circumstances, but does not appear to affect breastfeeding parameters.

title: Expression of the Norrie disease gene (Ndp) in developing and adult mouse eye, ear, and brain.
text: The gene responsible for Norrie disease, known as Ndp, encodes a protein called Norrin. Norrin activates the canonical Wnt signaling pathway by binding to its receptor, Frizzled-4. This signaling system plays a crucial role in the normal development of blood vessels in the retina and the survival of blood vessels in the cochlea. However, the expression of Ndp beyond the retina in mammals is not well understood due to the limited presence of Norrin mRNA and protein. In this study, we investigate the expression of Ndp during mouse development using a knock-in mouse model that carries the coding sequence of human placental alkaline phosphatase (AP) inserted at the Ndp locus (Ndp(AP)). We find that Ndp(AP) expression becomes apparent in the central nervous system (CNS) by E10.5 and exhibits dynamic and complex patterns. The regions of Ndp(AP) expression in the CNS observed before birth are later replaced by widespread expression in astrocytes in the forebrain and midbrain, Bergman glia in the cerebellum, and Müller glia in the retina. In the developing and adult cochlea, Ndp(AP) expression is closely associated with two highly vascularized regions: the stria vascularis and a capillary plexus between the organ of Corti and the spiral ganglion. These findings suggest that Norrin may have additional developmental and/or homeostatic functions beyond its known roles in the retina and cochlea.

title: Control of NFAT Isoform Activation and NFAT-Dependent Gene Expression through Two Coincident and Spatially Segregated Intracellular Ca2+ Signals
text: Throughout eukaryotes, there is a conservation of excitation-transcription coupling, which connects stimulation at the cell surface to changes in gene expression in the nucleus. However, it is still unclear how closely related coexpressed transcription factors are differentially activated. In this study, we demonstrate that two isoforms of Ca2+-dependent transcription factors, NFAT1 and NFAT4, require distinct sub-cellular signals of InsP3 and Ca2+ for sustained activation in a physiological context. NFAT1 is activated by Ca2+ microdomains near the cell membrane, while NFAT4 requires Ca2+ mobilization from the inner nuclear envelope through nuclear InsP3 receptors. Additionally, NFAT1 is deactivated more slowly than NFAT4 in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, allowing for a longer activation phase. Contrary to previous beliefs, oscillations in cytoplasmic Ca2+ do not play a role in activating either NFAT protein. Instead, sustained physiological activation of NFAT4 is closely linked to oscillations in nuclear Ca2+. Our findings demonstrate how gene expression can be regulated by coinciding yet spatially distinct Ca2+ signals, which are generated by a freely diffusible InsP3 messenger.

title: Brain region-specific up-regulation of mouse apolipoprotein E by pharmacological estrogen treatments.
text: The role of cerebral apolipoprotein E (apoE) in protecting and repairing neurons has been identified. However, the impact of estrogen on apoE and the mechanism behind it can vary in different regions of the brain due to the varying levels and types of estrogen receptors. To investigate this further, female C57BL/6 mice that had undergone ovariectomy were treated with high levels of 17 beta-estradiol or a placebo for 5 days, resulting in abnormally high levels of estradiol in the treated mice's blood. The levels of apoE and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured in the cortex, hippocampus, and diencephalon. In the cortex and diencephalon, 17 beta-estradiol increased apoE levels but had no effect on GFAP levels. However, in the hippocampus, both GFAP and apoE levels were equally increased. When 17 beta-estradiol was administered to mice lacking estrogen receptor (ER) alpha or when C57BL/6 mice were treated with 17 alpha-estradiol, a weak estrogen receptor agonist, apoE was specifically induced in the cortex but not in the diencephalon. These findings suggest that the effects of 17 beta-estradiol on apoE in the diencephalon are mediated either directly or indirectly by ER alpha, while in the cortex, a non-classical mechanism or ER beta may be involved. Analysis of mRNA levels in wild-type mice treated with estrogen or a placebo revealed that the effect of 17 beta-estradiol on apoE was not associated with changes in apoE mRNA levels.

title: ATM and ataxia telangiectasia.
text: The biomedical research community has long been fascinated by Ataxia telangiectasia (AT) due to its wide range of associated defects, such as neurodegeneration, immune dysfunction, radiosensitivity, and cancer predisposition. Once mutations in ATM (ataxia telangiectasia, mutated) were identified as the root cause of the disease, further analysis revealed that this protein kinase plays a crucial role in the cellular response to DNA double-stranded breaks. Numerous important cellular responses that prevent cancer rely on ATM kinase substrates. Consequently, AT is a disease that arises from deficiencies in responding to specific types of DNA damage. Despite being a rare neurodegenerative disorder, studying the biology of AT will enhance our understanding of the fundamental processes underlying cancer and neurodegeneration.

title: A novel immortalized human endometrial stromal cell line with normal progestational response.
text: The scarcity of suitable human material and the inability to culture primary human endometrial stromal cells (HESCs) for extended periods of time limit their use in in vitro studies. Immortalizing these cells would greatly facilitate research; however, the process often leads to abnormal karyotypes and functional characteristics. To address this issue, we introduced telomerase into cultured HESCs to prevent the natural shortening of telomeres that occurs during cell division in adult somatic cells. We have successfully developed and examined a newly immortalized HESC line that does not exhibit any clonal chromosomal abnormalities or numerical abnormalities. Furthermore, when compared to the original unpassaged parent cells, the new cell line demonstrated similar biochemical responses after exposure to ovarian steroids. Both morphologically and at the molecular level, the cells exhibited a classical decidualization response to estradiol and medroxyprogesterone acetate, with progestin regulating the expression of various proteins such as IGF binding protein-1, fibronectin, prolactin, tissue factor, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, and Fas/Fas ligand. In conclusion, we have successfully developed an immortalized HESC line that closely resembles the primary parent cells in terms of karyotype, morphology, and phenotype. This cell line serves as a reliable and valuable resource for in vitro studies.

title: Comparison of the intrinsic kinase activity and substrate specificity of c-Abl and Bcr-Abl.
text: The intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity and substrate specificity of c-Abl and Bcr-Abl protein tyrosine kinases (PTKs) were examined by studying the peptide substrates obtained from a synthetic combinatorial peptide library. Our findings suggest that Bcr-Abl consistently exhibited stronger phosphorylation of these peptides compared to c-Abl. Additionally, Bcr-Abl displayed a preference for peptides containing one or more positive charges.

title: Strong association between respiratory viral infection early after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and the development of life-threatening acute and chronic alloimmune lung syndromes.
text: Alloimmune lung syndromes (allo-LS) are serious complications that can occur after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). These syndromes include idiopathic pneumonia syndrome, bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, and bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia. In our study of 110 pediatric patients, we found that 30 of them had allo-LS, accounting for 27.3% of the cohort. Among these cases, 18 were diagnosed with idiopathic pneumonia syndrome and 12 with bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome. Our analysis revealed that respiratory viral infections occurring shortly after HSCT were significant predictors for the development of allo-LS (P <.0001), regardless of the specific virus involved. Furthermore, our multivariate analysis showed that allo-LS was the only factor associated with higher mortality rates (P = .04). Surprisingly, we observed that prolonged use of immunosuppressive medications to treat acute graft-versus-host disease actually had a protective effect against the development of allo-LS (P = .004). Based on these findings, we propose that early respiratory tract infections caused by common cold viruses may make the lungs more susceptible to alloimmunity.

title: Hepatitis C virus blocks interferon effector function by inducing protein kinase R phosphorylation.
text:
The Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an RNA virus that contains a single strand of genetic material. It encodes a polyprotein that is translated using an internal ribosome entry site (IRES). When a person is infected with HCV, it triggers the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in the liver, which are responsible for fighting against viral infections. However, HCV is able to persist in the body, suggesting that it has the ability to block the function of these ISGs. 

Our research has shown that HCV infection leads to the activation of a protein kinase called PKR, which phosphorylates and activates a protein called eIF2 alpha. This protein is involved in the initiation of translation in eukaryotic cells. As a result, the expression of ISG proteins is reduced, even though the mRNA for these proteins is still being produced. 

Interestingly, when we suppressed the expression of PKR in cells that were treated with interferon, we observed that the expression of ISG proteins was restored and the antiviral effects of interferon were enhanced. This suggests that the activation of PKR by HCV is actually beneficial for the virus, as it selectively suppresses the translation of ISGs. 

It is important to note that while the activation of PKR inhibits the translation of host proteins, including ISGs, it does not affect the translation of HCV proteins that are dependent on the IRES. This finding further supports the idea that HCV has evolved mechanisms to evade the host immune response.

title: The influence of denervation on grafted hindlimb regeneration of larval Xenopus laevis.
text: The objective of this research is to determine whether the independence of nerve function for the regeneration of early stage limbs and the dependence on nerves for late stage limbs, as observed in a previous study (Filoni and Paglialunga, 1990), is influenced by external factors or intrinsic changes occurring within the limb cells during development in larval Xenopus laevis. This paper investigates the regenerative capacity of early and late stage hindlimbs under the same external conditions by grafting them onto denervated hindlimbs of host larvae at the same developmental stage. All grafted limbs are amputated after the host larvae reach stage 57-58 (according to Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956). In experiment I, the grafted limb is amputated at stage 52, specifically at the thigh level. In experiment II, the grafted limb is amputated at stage 54-55, at the tarsalia level. In experiment III, the grafted limb is amputated at stage 57, also at the tarsalia level. In all three experiments, the host limb is amputated at the tarsalia level along with the grafted limb. The results indicate that while grafted limbs amputated at stages 52 and 54-55 can regenerate without nerves, grafted limbs amputated at stage 57 cannot. The inability of late stage grafted limbs to regenerate cannot be attributed to an immune-type inhibiting reaction, as it has also been observed in denervated autografted limbs and host limbs. Since all grafted limbs are subjected to the same environmental conditions, the findings suggest that the nerve-independence for regeneration of early stage limbs and nerve-dependence of late stage limbs in larval Xenopus laevis are not influenced by external factors, but rather by intrinsic changes occurring within the limb cells during development.

title: Adult c-Kit(+) progenitor cells are necessary for maintenance and regeneration of olfactory neurons.
text: The olfactory epithelium contains chemosensory neurons that send odor information from the nose to the brain. In adult mammals, the olfactory epithelium is a unique and strong zone for producing new neurons and other cells, thanks to the presence of germinal basal cells. However, we still don't fully understand the stem and progenitor cells in these germinal layers and how they are regulated. In this study, we discovered that progenitor cells expressing c-Kit, a receptor tyrosine kinase found in stem cells in various embryonic tissues, are necessary for maintaining the adult neuroepithelium. Through genetic fate-mapping experiments in mice, we found that c-Kit(+) cells contribute to the production of olfactory neurons during embryonic development. In adults, there is limited activity of c-Kit(+) progenitor cells (ckPCs) under normal conditions. However, when the neuroepithelium is damaged experimentally, ckPCs become activated and regenerate the neuronal population. Some non-neuronal cells also arise from ckPCs. Furthermore, when we selectively depleted the ckPC population using targeted diphtheria toxin A expression, neurogenesis failed to occur after experimental injury. Our analysis revealed that most ckPCs are located among the globose basal cell populations and act downstream of horizontal basal cells, which can function as stem cells. This discovery of the importance of c-Kit-expressing progenitors in maintaining the olfactory system provides new insights into the mechanisms of adult olfactory neurogenesis. Additionally, we have identified a previously unknown site of c-Kit activity in adults.

title: Neurogenin3: a master regulator of pancreatic islet differentiation and regeneration.
text: The crucial role in the development of endocrine cells in the islets is played by the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor neurogenin-3 (Ngn3, Neurog3). If Ngn3 expression is disrupted or forced early on during pancreas development in mice, the formation of islets is prevented. The timing of Ngn3 expression during the primary and secondary transitions of endocrine cell development determines the four distinct endocrine cell lineages: α, β, PP, and δ cells, which respectively produce glucagon, insulin, pancreatic polypeptide, and somatostatin. In cases of injury to the adult mouse pancreas, such as duct ligation or streptozotocin treatment, Ngn3 is activated in stem/progenitor cells associated with the ducts, leading to their transformation into alpha and/or beta cells (Xu et al, Collombat et al). Given the significant role of Ngn3 as a key regulator of endocrine pancreas development, efforts are being made to explore therapeutic approaches that can enhance Ngn3 expression in diabetes, with the aim of increasing beta cell mass and functionality.

title: Detection of Mycoplasmas in Patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
text: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a degenerative disease that affects the motor neurons and its cause is currently unknown. Various factors, including genetic defects, nutritional deficiencies, head trauma, environmental toxins, autoimmune responses, and viral and bacterial infections, have been identified as potential contributors. Mycoplasmas, which have been linked to various illnesses in humans, were investigated in this study to determine their presence in the bloodstream of ALS patients. Both ALS patients and healthy individuals were included in the study, and blood samples were collected with or without anticoagulant. The presence of mycoplasmas was detected through culture or direct PCR, and the presence of antibodies IgM and IgG against LAMPs (lipid-associated membrane proteins) of these microorganisms was determined through Western blot. Additionally, cultures for aerobic facultative bacteria were conducted. A total of 13 ALS patients and 44 healthy individuals were screened using blood samples. All blood cultures for non-fermentative mycoplasmas and aerobic facultative bacteria yielded negative results. However, cultures for fermentative mycoplasmas were considered positive after identifying mycoplasmal DNA through PCR. Mycoplasma sp. was detected through culture or direct PCR in 6 out of 13 (46%) patients and in 4 out of 44 (9%) healthy individuals. Specifically, M. fermentans was detected through PCR using specific primers in six patients and two healthy individuals. IgM antibodies against LAMPs of M. fermentans were detected in 6 out of 13 (46%) blood samples from patients and in 13 out of 44 (30%) from healthy individuals. IgG antibodies were detected in 4 out of 13 (31%) patients and in 3 out of 44 (7%) healthy individuals. These findings suggest that mycoplasmas may cause a systemic infection and potentially play a role in the development or progression of ALS.

title: Correlation and variable importance in random forests
text: The focus of this paper is on variable selection using the random forests algorithm when dealing with correlated predictors. In situations involving high-dimensional regression or classification frameworks, variable selection can be challenging, especially when there are highly correlated predictors. Initially, we conduct a theoretical analysis of the permutation importance measure for an additive regression model. This analysis helps us understand how the correlation between predictors affects the permutation importance. Based on our findings, we propose the Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) algorithm as a suitable approach for variable selection in such scenarios. The RFE algorithm eliminates variables recursively, using the permutation importance measure as a ranking criterion. We then present several simulation experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the RFE algorithm in selecting a small number of variables while achieving a low prediction error. Finally, we apply this selection algorithm to the Landsat Satellite data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository to validate its performance.

title: An Oct4-Centered Protein Interaction Network in Embryonic Stem Cells
text: The role of transcription factors, like Oct4, is crucial in establishing and maintaining the identity of pluripotent cells. While the genomic locations of several pluripotency transcription factors have been identified, there is limited knowledge about their interaction partners. In this study, we have used an improved affinity protocol to isolate proteins that interact with Oct4 from mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs). By purifying Oct4 partners, including Sall4, Tcfcp2l1, Dax1, and Esrrb, we have identified a total of 166 proteins that form the Oct4 interactome. These proteins include transcription factors and chromatin-modifying complexes that are known to play a role in self-renewal, as well as several factors that were not previously associated with the ESC network. Our findings reveal that Esrrb interacts with the basal transcription machinery and also shows interactions between transcription factors and components of the TGF-beta, Notch, and Wnt signaling pathways. Furthermore, we observed that depletion of Oct4 leads to reduced binding of Tcfcp2l1, Dax1, and Esrrb to their target genes. In summary, our purification protocol has provided a clearer understanding of the regulatory circuitry involved in maintaining pluripotent cell identity.

title: GABA(B) receptor 1 polymorphism (G1465A) is associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.
text:
BACKGROUND: Dysfunction of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors has been linked to the development of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE).

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the genetic contribution of cloned human GABA receptors to TLE.

METHODS: The researchers genotyped 141 patients (78 women and 63 men; mean age = 49.1 +/- 18.0 years) with nonlesional TLE and compared them to 372 age- and sex-matched individuals without epilepsy. They specifically looked for the G1465A polymorphism in the human GABA receptor 1 (GABA[B1]) gene.

RESULTS: The study found a significant overrepresentation of the G1465A heterozygote in TLE patients compared to controls. The A/G genotype was present in 17% of TLE patients and only 0.5% of controls (p < 0.0001). Additionally, patients carrying the A allele had a significantly higher risk (p = 0.003, OR = 6.47, 95% CI = 2.02 to 20.76) of developing drug-resistant TLE. Although the age at seizure onset tended to be lower in patients with the A/G genotype, the difference was not statistically significant.

CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that the GABA[B1] polymorphism (G1465A) greatly increases susceptibility to TLE and may also influence the severity of this common epileptic disorder.

title: Crystal structure, biochemical and cellular activities demonstrate separate functions of MTH1 and MTH2
text: Cancer disrupts the normal balance of redox metabolism, causing damage to important cellular components like deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs). One potential strategy to combat cancer is to target enzymes that sanitize the dNTP pool, such as MTH1. The MTH2 protein, also known as NUDT15, is a human homologue of a bacterial enzyme called MutT, which has the ability to remove a damaged form of dNTP called 8-oxo-dGTP. In this study, we present the first crystal structure of NUDT15 and show that it actually prefers other nucleotide substrates over 8-oxo-dGTP. We identify key structural features that explain the different substrate preferences of NUDT15 and MTH1. Interestingly, depleting NUDT15 has no impact on the incorporation of 8-oxo-dGTP into DNA and does not affect the survival of cancer cells in the cell lines we tested. We also profiled two other enzymes, NUDT17 and NUDT18, and found that they have much less activity against oxidized nucleotides compared to MTH1. Our findings suggest that NUDT15 is not biologically relevant as an 8-oxo-dGTPase, and that MTH1 is the most important enzyme for sanitizing the cellular dNTP pool known to date.

title: De novo expression of Trpm4 initiates secondary hemorrhage in spinal cord injury
text: The role of transient receptor potential M4 (Trpm4), a unique member of the Trp family of ion channels, is not well understood. We conducted a study using rodent models of spinal cord injury to investigate the involvement of Trpm4 in the progressive expansion of secondary hemorrhage, which is caused by capillary fragmentation and is the most damaging mechanism of secondary injury in the central nervous system. We found that Trpm4 mRNA and protein were significantly increased in capillaries before they fragmented and formed petechial hemorrhages. In vitro experiments showed that Trpm4 expression in COS-7 cells made them highly susceptible to swelling and death caused by ATP depletion. In animal models of spinal cord injury, suppressing Trpm4 gene expression in rats treated with Trpm4 antisense or in Trpm4−/− mice preserved the structural integrity of capillaries, eliminated secondary hemorrhage, reduced lesion volume by threefold to fivefold, and greatly improved neurological function. This is the first known example of a Trp channel that needs to be newly expressed in order to cause pathology in the central nervous system.

title: Differential expression of bcl-2 in intestinal epithelia. Correlation with attenuation of apoptosis in colonic crypts and the incidence of colonic neoplasia.
text: The occurrence of both spontaneous and damage-induced apoptosis in epithelial cells was examined in longitudinal sections of the crypts of the small intestine and colon of BDF1 mice. Immunohistochemistry was used to compare this with the expression pattern of bcl-2, a protein that suppresses apoptosis. In the small intestine, apoptosis was highest around cell position 4, which is believed to contain the stem cells. However, in the colon, apoptosis was not limited to the area where the stem cells are found (positions 1 and 2). Instead, apoptosis was reduced and spread throughout the length of the crypt. Some cells at the base of the colonic crypts in mice expressed bcl-2 protein, while bcl-2 was not present in the crypts of the small intestine. Importantly, bcl-2 was absent in small intestinal crypt cells at positions 4-5, which is the region where the stem cells are located. The role of bcl-2 in reducing apoptosis in stem cells was confirmed by studying homozygously bcl-2 null C57BL/6 mice, which showed a significant increase in spontaneous apoptosis, specifically at the base of the colonic crypts, compared to crypts from wild-type mice. However, there was no increase in spontaneous apoptosis in the small intestinal crypts of the bcl-2 null mice. Examination of sections from human colon and small intestine also revealed that bcl-2 expression was limited to the base of the colonic crypt. The reduction of apoptosis by bcl-2 in the region of the stem cells in the colonic crypts may make them more susceptible to developing cancer. In fact, analysis of human carcinomas showed expression of bcl-2, which in some samples was inversely related to the expression of p53.

title: Aortic stiffness, blood pressure progression, and incident hypertension.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between vascular stiffness, central hemodynamics, microvascular function, and blood pressure progression. The study was conducted in Framingham, Massachusetts, using data from the Framingham Offspring study. The study included 1759 participants, with a mean age of 60 years.

The results showed that higher levels of forward wave amplitude (FWA) and carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (CFPWV) during examination cycle 7 were associated with higher systolic blood pressure during examination cycle 8. Additionally, higher FWA, augmentation index, and CFPWV during examination cycle 7 were associated with an increased risk of incident hypertension during examination cycle 8.

Interestingly, blood pressure during examination cycle 7 was not found to be associated with CFPWV during examination cycle 8. Furthermore, higher resting brachial artery flow and lower flow-mediated dilation during examination cycle 7 were also associated with incident hypertension.

In conclusion, this study suggests that higher levels of aortic stiffness, FWA, and augmentation index are associated with an increased risk of incident hypertension. However, initial blood pressure was not independently associated with the risk of progressive aortic stiffening.

title: The EMBL nucleotide sequence database.
text: Europe's main nucleotide sequence resource is the EMBL Nucleotide Sequence Database, available at http://www.ebi.ac.uk/embl.html. This database collects DNA and RNA sequences directly from researchers, genome sequencing groups, scientific literature, and patent applications (Fig. 1). The European Bioinformatics Institute collaborates with DDBJ and GenBank to produce, maintain, and distribute the database. Quarterly releases are distributed on CD-ROM, and EBI's network services provide access to the most current data collection through the Internet and World Wide Web interface. Users can search the database, find sequence similarities, and access numerous additional databases.

title: Anaphase catastrophe is a target for cancer therapy.
text: Neoplastic cells have an inherent genetic instability. By targeting pathways that affect this instability, we can disrupt the growth of tumor cells without significant harm to normal cells. One type of genetic instability, known as chromosomal instability (CIN), is characterized by errors in cell division that lead to mis-segregation of chromosomes. CIN often occurs due to the presence of extra centrosomes, which disrupt the normal structure required for accurate chromosome segregation. Tumor cells are able to survive with extra centrosomes due to biochemical pathways that cluster these structures and promote proper chromosome segregation. However, recent research has shown that inhibiting these pathways prevents centrosome clustering and forces chromosomes to segregate into multiple daughter cells. This triggers a process called anaphase catastrophe, which leads to the death of tumor cells with more than 2 centrosomes. Interestingly, this death program can be induced through the inhibition of cyclin dependent kinase 2 (Cdk2), either genetically or pharmacologically, and is further enhanced when combined with a microtubule inhibitor. Importantly, this proapoptotic effect occurs even in the presence of ras mutations in cancer cells. Anaphase catastrophe represents a previously unrecognized mechanism that can be harnessed for the apoptotic death of cancer cells, making it an attractive target for cancer therapy and prevention.

title: Dishevelled Activates JNK and Discriminates between JNK Pathways in Planar Polarity and wingless Signaling
text: Frizzled family proteins have been identified as receptors for Wnt signaling molecules. In the fruit fly Drosophila, there are two known Frizzled proteins that are involved in different developmental processes. Frizzled is necessary for the formation of epithelial planar polarity, while Dfz2 affects morphogenesis through wingless-mediated signaling. Dishevelled is required in both of these signaling pathways. In this study, we conducted genetic and overexpression experiments to demonstrate that Dishevelled activates JNK cascades. Through rescue analysis, we found that Dishevelled has different requirements for protein domains in each pathway. The C-terminal DEP domain is crucial for rescuing planar polarity defects and inducing JNK signaling. Additionally, we discovered that the planar polarity-specific dsh1 allele has a mutation in the DEP domain. Our findings suggest that different Wnt/Fz signals activate distinct intracellular pathways, and Dishevelled distinguishes between them through specific domain interactions.

title: Genome-wide lineage-specific transcriptional networks underscore Ikaros-dependent lymphoid priming in hematopoietic stem cells.
text: We conducted an investigation into the mechanisms that regulate lineage potential in the early stages of hematopoiesis. Firstly, we identified a series of gene expression signatures that are associated with specific lineages. These signatures were found to be present in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and were differentially passed on to lineage-restricted progenitors. Lymphoid, myeloid, and erythroid transcripts were all found to be primed in HSCs. Although this multilineage priming was resolved as the cells underwent lineage restrictions, we discovered an unexpected co-occurrence of lymphoid and myeloid gene expression and potential beyond a certain myeloid restriction point. Lastly, we demonstrated that the zinc finger DNA-binding factor Ikaros is not only necessary for inducing lymphoid lineage priming in HSCs but also for repressing genetic programs that are compatible with self-renewal and multipotency in cells downstream of HSCs. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the priming and restriction of lineage potentials in early hematopoiesis and highlight the crucial role of Ikaros as a dual regulator in this process.

title: Vitamin D status: measurement, interpretation, and clinical application.
text: Vitamin D, also known as the sunshine vitamin, is now acknowledged for its role in promoting bone health in both children and adults. Additionally, it has been found to have other health benefits, such as reducing the risk of chronic diseases like autoimmune diseases, common cancer, and cardiovascular disease. Vitamin D is produced in the skin or obtained through diet, but in its natural form, it is biologically inactive. It undergoes two hydroxylations to become biologically active. The first hydroxylation occurs in the liver on carbon 25, resulting in the formation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]. The second hydroxylation takes place in the kidney on carbon 1, forming the active form of vitamin D, known as 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)(2)D]. To assess vitamin D levels, methods have been developed to measure these metabolites in the bloodstream. Serum 25(OH)D is considered the indicator of vitamin D status. On the other hand, serum 1,25(OH)(2)D does not provide any information about vitamin D status and may even be normal or increased due to secondary hyperparathyroidism associated with vitamin D deficiency. Experts generally agree that a 25(OH)D level below 20 ng/mL indicates vitamin D deficiency, while a level between 21-29 ng/mL is considered insufficient. The aim should be to maintain both children and adults at a level above 30 ng/mL to fully benefit from the various health advantages provided by vitamin D.

title: Lessons from the past: managing insecticide resistance in malaria control and eradication programmes.
text: Over the past 5 years, there has been a significant increase in the distribution of insecticide-treated bednets in sub-Saharan Africa to combat malaria. Many countries are also considering or have already started indoor residual spraying campaigns. These efforts are positive because vector control has consistently proven effective in reducing malaria transmission. However, the long-term success of these interventions depends on the continued susceptibility of the anopheles vectors to the limited range of insecticides available. It is crucial to continuously monitor for early signs of insecticide resistance and implement carefully planned resistance management strategies. Unfortunately, this monitoring aspect is often overlooked in the rush to achieve high coverage targets. We emphasize the importance of establishing an insecticide resistance surveillance system and urge all those involved in malaria vector control to prioritize these measures. Failing to take action now will inevitably result in a breakdown of disease control and jeopardize efforts to eradicate this significant public health issue.

title: T helper 2 cytokines inhibit autophagic control of intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
text: Autophagy, a recently acknowledged immune defense mechanism against pathogens within cells, has been extensively studied in relation to innate immunity. However, the impact of the adaptive immune response on autophagy regulation remains less understood. The cytokine IFN-gamma, produced by T helper 1 (Th1) cells, has been found to induce autophagy in macrophages, aiding in the elimination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this study, we demonstrate that Th2 cytokines have an effect on autophagy in macrophages and their ability to combat intracellular M. tuberculosis. Both IL-4 and IL-13 hindered autophagy and the subsequent elimination of mycobacteria within murine and human macrophages. The inhibition of autophagy induced by starvation, mediated by IL-4 and IL-13, relied on Akt signaling. On the other hand, the inhibition of IFN-gamma-induced autophagy was Akt independent but dependent on signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6). These findings shed light on how Th1-Th2 polarization differentially impacts the immune control of intracellular pathogens.

title: Lipid-based nutrient supplement increases the birth size of infants of primiparous women in Ghana.
text: The International Lipid-Based Nutrient Supplements Project created a small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplement (LNS) for pregnant and lactating women. The objective of this study was to assess the impact of prenatal LNS supplementation on fetal growth. The study involved 1320 women who were less than or equal to 20 weeks pregnant. They were randomly assigned to receive either 60 mg of iron and 400 μg of folic acid (IFA), 1-2 Recommended Dietary Allowances of 18 micronutrients including 20 mg of iron (MMN), or LNS with the same micronutrients as the MMN group, along with 4 minerals and macronutrients contributing 118 kcal (LNS) daily until delivery. Fetal growth was compared among the groups using intention-to-treat analysis, with birth length as the primary outcome. The analysis included 1057 women (IFA = 349, MMN = 354, LNS = 354). There were no significant differences in mean birth length, length-for-age z score (LAZ), head circumference, or percentage of low birth length among the groups. However, there were differences in mean birth weight, weight-for-age z score (WAZ), and BMI-for-age z score (BMIZ), with a trend towards differences in low birth weight. In pairwise comparisons, the LNS group had higher mean birth weight, WAZ, and BMIZ, and a lower risk of low birth weight compared to the IFA group. The other group differences were not significant. The effect of the intervention was influenced by factors such as mother's parity, age, height, baseline hemoglobin, household food insecurity, and child sex, with parity being the most consistent factor. Among primiparous women, the LNS group had higher mean birth length, LAZ, weight, WAZ, BMIZ, head circumference, and head circumference-for-age z score compared to the IFA group. Similar differences were found when comparing the LNS and MMN groups among primiparous women, and no group differences were found among multiparous women. In conclusion, prenatal LNS supplementation can improve fetal growth in vulnerable women in Ghana, particularly primiparous women. This trial was registered at clinicaltrials.gov as NCT00970866.

title: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor ligand bezafibrate for prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus in patients with coronary artery disease.
text:
Recent studies have indicated that type 2 diabetes can be prevented through lifestyle changes and medications that affect glucose metabolism. However, it is unclear whether medications that impact lipid metabolism can also delay the development of type 2 diabetes. This study aimed to assess the effects of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor ligand bezafibrate on the progression from impaired fasting glucose to type 2 diabetes in patients with coronary artery disease over a 6.2-year period.

The study included 303 patients aged 42 to 74 years who did not have diabetes but had a fasting blood glucose level of 110 to 125 mg/dL. These patients were randomly assigned to receive either 400 mg of bezafibrate retard (156 patients) or a placebo (147 patients) once a day. None of the patients were taking statins, and the use of ACE inhibitors, which also reduce the risk of diabetes, was relatively low. During the follow-up period, 146 patients developed new-onset diabetes, with 80 (54.4%) from the placebo group and 66 (42.3%) from the bezafibrate group (P=0.04). The mean time until the onset of new diabetes was significantly longer in patients taking bezafibrate compared to those taking the placebo: 4.6+/-2.3 years versus 3.8+/-2.6 years (P=0.004). Multivariate analysis revealed that bezafibrate treatment independently predicted a reduced risk of developing new diabetes (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.49 to 0.99). Other significant factors associated with future type 2 diabetes in patients with impaired fasting glucose were total cholesterol level (hazard ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.0 to 1.51) and body mass index (hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.05 to 1.16).

In conclusion, bezafibrate can lower the incidence and delay the onset of type 2 diabetes in patients with impaired fasting glucose. However, further research is needed to determine whether combining bezafibrate with other recommended drugs for secondary prevention, such as statins and ACE inhibitors, would be as effective as suggested by our findings.

title: Familial occurrence of chronic tension-type headache.
text: In a study on chronic tension-type headache (CTTH), the validity of proband report was evaluated. A physician conducted clinical interviews with first-degree relatives to determine the accuracy of the proband report. The study also investigated the occurrence of CTTH in first-degree relatives to understand familial patterns. The population relative risk was calculated to assess the aggregation of CTTH within families. All interviews with probands and their relatives were conducted by a neurological resident, following the diagnostic criteria of the International Headache Society. The study included 122 probands and 377 first-degree relatives. The sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and chance-corrected agreement rate for diagnosing CTTH were found to be 68%, 86%, 53% (PVpos), 92% (PVneg), and 0.48, respectively. The low sensitivity of the proband report suggests that clinical interviews by physicians are necessary in family studies on CTTH. Clinically interviewed parents, siblings, and children showed a significantly increased risk of CTTH (2.1 to 3.9-fold) compared to the general population. The risk of CTTH among first-degree relatives was not influenced by the gender of the probands. The significantly increased familial risk and the absence of increased risk in spouses indicate the involvement of a genetic factor in CTTH.

title: Complex formation of SMAP/KAP3, a KIF3A/B ATPase motor-associated protein, with a human chromosome-associated polypeptide.
text:
We recently discovered a new protein called SMAP (Smg GDS-associated protein), which is associated with Smg GDS (small G protein GDP dissociation stimulator). SMAP contains Armadillo repeats and is phosphorylated by Src tyrosine kinase. It is the human equivalent of mouse KAP3 (kinesin superfamily-associated protein), which is associated with mouse KIF3A/B (a kinesin superfamily protein). KIF3A/B acts as a microtubule-based ATPase motor for organelle transport. 

From a human brain cDNA library, we identified a protein that interacts with SMAP. This protein is a human version of Xenopus XCAP-E (Xenopus chromosome-associated polypeptide), which is a subunit of condensins that regulate the assembly and maintenance of mitotic chromosomes. We named this protein HCAP (Human chromosome-associated polypeptide). 

Analyses of tissue and subcellular distribution showed that HCAP is expressed throughout the body and is highly concentrated in the nucleus, where SMAP and KIF3B are also found. In the presence of Mg-ATP, SMAP forms a complex with HCAP and KIF3B in the nucleus. These findings suggest that SMAP/KAP3 acts as a bridge between HCAP and KIF3A/B, facilitating the interaction between chromosomes and an ATPase motor protein.

title: Surveillance for foodborne-disease outbreaks--United States, 1993-1997.
text:
PROBLEM/CONDITION
Since 1973, the CDC has maintained a collaborative surveillance program to collect and periodically report data on foodborne disease outbreaks (FBDOs) in the United States.

REPORTING PERIOD COVERED
This summary covers data from January 1993 to December 1997.

DESCRIPTION OF SYSTEM
The Foodborne Disease Outbreak Surveillance System examines data on FBDOs, which are defined as the occurrence of two or more cases of a similar illness resulting from consuming the same food. State and local public health departments are responsible for identifying and investigating FBDOs. They use a standardized form to report these outbreaks to the CDC.

RESULTS
From 1993 to 1997, a total of 2,751 foodborne disease outbreaks were reported (489 in 1993, 653 in 1994, 628 in 1995, 477 in 1996, and 504 in 1997). These outbreaks affected a reported 86,058 individuals. Bacterial pathogens were responsible for the majority of outbreaks (75%) and cases (86%). Salmonella serotype Enteritidis caused the most outbreaks, cases, and deaths, with many of these outbreaks linked to egg consumption. Chemical agents caused 17% of outbreaks and 1% of cases, viruses caused 6% of outbreaks and 8% of cases, and parasites caused 2% of outbreaks and 5% of cases.

INTERPRETATION
The number of FBDOs reported to the CDC remained relatively stable during this period and compared to previous years. S. Enteritidis continued to be a significant cause of illness and death. Additionally, outbreaks caused by contaminated produce and Escherichia coli O157:H7 remained prominent.

ACTIONS TAKEN
Methods for detecting FBDOs are improving, and efforts are being made to simplify and expedite the reporting of FBDO data (e.g., through a revised reporting form and electronic reporting methods). State and local health departments continue to investigate and report FBDOs to enhance our understanding of foodborne disease epidemiology in the United States. At the regional and national levels, surveillance data help identify the causes, transmission vehicles, and contributing factors of FBDOs, guiding public health actions to reduce illness and death associated with these outbreaks.

title: Nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of C-ABL tyrosine kinase.
text: The nonreceptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl, which is found in both the nucleus and cytoplasm of proliferating fibroblasts, contains three nuclear localization signals. However, when fibroblasts adhere to a fibronectin matrix, there is a rapid and temporary loss of c-Abl from the nucleus, suggesting the possibility of nuclear export. In a study conducted by Lewis et al. in 1996, it was discovered that the C terminus of c-Abl does indeed have a functional nuclear export signal (NES) with a leucine-rich motif. This NES can complement an NES-defective HIV Rev protein and facilitate the nuclear export of glutathione-S-transferase. The function of the c-Abl NES is affected by the nuclear export inhibitor leptomycin B, and a mutation in a single leucine (L1064A) in the NES eliminates its export function. The mutated c-Abl, known as c-Abl NES(-), is exclusively localized in the nucleus. Treatment with leptomycin B also leads to the nuclear accumulation of wild-type c-Abl protein. Furthermore, the c-Abl NES(-) remains in the nucleus when detached fibroblasts are replated onto a fibronectin matrix. These findings demonstrate that c-Abl continuously shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm, and the rate of nuclear import and export can be influenced by the adherence status of fibroblastic cells.

title: Regulation of embryonic stem cell pluripotency by heat shock protein 90.
text: Understanding the molecular mechanisms behind stem cell pluripotency is crucial for comprehending stem cell biology, early embryonic development, and the clinical application of regenerative medicine. Our study reveals that the molecular chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) plays a vital role in maintaining pluripotency in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) by regulating various pluripotency factors, including Oct4, Nanog, and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3. When Hsp90 was inhibited using either 17-N-Allylamino-17-demethoxygeldanamycin or miRNA, ESCs underwent differentiation. However, overexpressing Hsp90β partially rescued this differentiation, particularly by restoring the levels of Oct4 and Nanog. Interestingly, Hsp90 was found to interact with Oct4 and Nanog in the same cellular complex, protecting them from degradation through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway. This suggests that Oct4 and Nanog may be novel client proteins of Hsp90. Furthermore, Hsp90 inhibition reduced the mRNA levels of Oct4, but not Nanog, indicating that Hsp90 may be involved in Oct4 mRNA processing or maturation. Additionally, inhibiting Hsp90 increased the expression of certain protein markers associated with mesodermal lineages, suggesting that Hsp90 suppresses mesodermal differentiation in ESCs. These findings highlight a new role for Hsp90 in maintaining ESC pluripotency by regulating the levels of multiple pluripotency factors, particularly Oct4 and Nanog.

title: CD4+CD25+Foxp3+Regulatory T Cells Protect Endothelial Function Impaired by Oxidized Low Density Lipoprotein via the KLF-2 Transcription Factor
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to investigate how CD4+CD25+ Regulatory T cells (Tregs) regulate pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules, specifically Krüppel-Like Factor-2 (KLF-2) and its downstream transcriptional targets, in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) that have been impaired by ox-LDL. The study aimed to determine the mechanisms involved in this regulation.

Methods and Results: HUVECs were cultured in the presence of different concentrations of ox-LDL (0 mg/L, 25 mg/L, 50 mg/L, 100 mg/L) for varying durations (4, 6, 12, and 24 hours) to identify early- and late-induced genes. Non-stimulated controls were taken at 0 hours. The expression levels of pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules (vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 [VCAM-1], intracellular adhesion molecule-1 [ICAM-1], E-selectin), KLF-2, and its target genes (eNOS, PAI-1) were determined using real-time RT-PCR and/or western blot analysis. The expression levels of these molecules in HUVECs cultured alone or with anti-CD3 mAbs activated Tregs, followed by the addition of ox-LDL (50 mg/L) for 6 hours, were compared to expression levels in control cultures. Treatment with ox-LDL increased the expression of pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules and PAI-1, while decreasing eNOS expression. Additionally, KLF-2 expression was significantly downregulated in a dose- and time-dependent manner. However, the addition of Tregs reversed the increase in pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules and the inhibition of KLF-2 expression caused by ox-LDL. Further experiments using small interfering RNA showed that reducing endogenous KLF-2 expression partially reversed the suppressive effect of Tregs on HUVECs activation, suggesting that KLF-2 is a transcriptional regulator of the Tregs-mediated effects in endothelial cells. Mechanism studies revealed that Treg-mediated KLF-2 expression in ox-LDL-impaired HUVECs requires both cell contact and soluble factors.

Conclusions: This study demonstrates that Tregs can protect endothelial function by regulating KLF-2 and its downstream transcriptional targets. This regulation involves both cell-to-cell contact and soluble factors.

title: Metformin Normalizes Type 2 Diabetes-Induced Decrease in Cell Proliferation and Neuroblast Differentiation in the Rat Dentate Gyrus
text: This study aimed to investigate the impact of metformin, a commonly prescribed drug for type 2 diabetes, on cell proliferation and neuroblast differentiation in the subgranular zone of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (SZDG) in Zucker diabetic fatty (ZDF) rats, which serve as a model for type 2 diabetes. To achieve this, metformin was administered orally once daily to 14-week-old ZDF rats for a duration of 2 weeks, and the animals were sacrificed at 16 weeks of age. Throughout the study period, blood glucose levels were consistently higher in the ZDF rats treated with a placebo compared to the Zucker lean control (ZLC) rats. However, the administration of metformin significantly reduced blood glucose levels starting from 15.5 weeks of age. In the SZDG, the presence of Ki67 (a marker for cell proliferation) and doublecortin (DCX, a marker for differentiated neuroblasts) immunoreactive cells was notably lower in the ZDF rats treated with a placebo compared to the ZLC rats. Conversely, in the ZDF rats treated with metformin, there was a significant increase in the number of Ki67- and DCX-immunoreactive cells in the SZDG compared to the placebo-treated ZDF rats. These findings suggest that diabetes has a detrimental effect on cell proliferation and neuroblast differentiation in the SZDG, while metformin treatment effectively restores these processes in diabetic rats.

title: Molecular mechanisms underlying tumor dormancy.
text: Research suggests that dormant, tiny tumors are not only common, but also highly prevalent in otherwise healthy individuals. These dormant tumors, due to their small size and non-invasive nature, do not show any symptoms and often go undetected. However, with advancements in diagnostic imaging and molecular biology, it is now evident that these neoplasms can remain in a dormant state for long periods without growing in size. One crucial mechanism behind tumor dormancy is the ability of the tumor population to induce angiogenesis. It is believed that most tumors start as microscopic, non-angiogenic neoplasms that cannot grow until they establish a blood supply. The growth of cancer does not follow a continuous exponential pattern, and clinical symptoms usually appear when tumors reach a significant size. Dormancy can occur in primary tumors, as well as in residual or occult disease from treated tumors or micro-metastases. The existence of dormant tumors has important implications for early cancer detection and treatment. Understanding the regulatory processes involved in tumor dormancy will help identify new biomarkers for early cancer detection and may lead to the development of therapies that promote dormancy. Despite the prevalence of microscopic, dormant tumors in humans and the clinical significance of early detection, this area of cancer research has been underexplored. This mini review summarizes observations, models, and experimental approaches to studying tumor dormancy. It also discusses the similarities and differences between tumor dormancy and cellular dormancy of tumor cells, as well as the transition from tumor dormancy to the onset of angiogenesis.

title: The myeloid transcription factor GATA-2 regulates the viral UL144 gene during human cytomegalovirus latency in an isolate-specific manner.
text: The general consensus is that after initial infection, human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) remains dormant in CD34(+) progenitor cells and other cells derived from the myeloid lineage for the rest of a person's life. In this study, we demonstrate that the viral UL144 gene is active during this dormant phase in two types of myeloid lineage cells: CD34(+) and CD14(+) monocytes. Furthermore, we confirm that the UL144 protein functions in monocytes that are latently infected. However, this expression of UL144 during dormancy only occurs in specific strains of HCMV and relies on the presence of functional GATA-2 transcription factor binding sites in the UL144 promoter. This is in contrast to the viral gene LUNA, which is also regulated by GATA-2 but is uniformly expressed during dormancy regardless of the virus strain. These findings suggest that the transcriptome associated with HCMV dormancy may vary depending on the specific virus strain and the presence of transcription factor binding sites in the promoters of genes associated with dormancy.

title: How to control residual cardiovascular risk despite statin treatment: focusing on HDL-cholesterol.
text: The primary goal in managing dyslipidemia in high-risk cardiovascular disease patients is to lower low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. However, even if patients achieve LDL-C levels below the recommended targets, they may still experience cardiovascular events. This could be due to elevated triglyceride (TG) levels and low levels of high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C). Low HDL-C and high TG levels are common and are considered independent risk factors for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized by low HDL-C levels, high TG levels, and small, dense LDL particles, is a typical form of dyslipidemia in individuals with insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome. Therefore, for patients who have achieved LDL-C levels below the recommended targets but are still at risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), it may be necessary to focus on raising HDL-C levels and lowering TG levels as secondary therapeutic targets. However, it is still uncertain whether increasing HDL-C levels alone can effectively reduce CHD, and there is ongoing debate about whether functional HDL is more important than HDL-C in reducing CHD. Large clinical trials are currently underway to compare combination treatments with statin and niacin, fibrates, or cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors to statin alone treatments, specifically focusing on CHD endpoints and including a significant number of patients with diabetes. In this review, we explore the rationale and significance of increasing HDL-C levels with or without lowering TG levels in the treatment and prevention of cardiovascular events.

title: The prevalence of congenital malformations is still higher in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes despite near-normal HbA1c: a literature review.
text:
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between congenital malformations and maternal hyperglycemia in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes (type 1 or type 2). Additionally, we sought to determine if the rate of congenital malformations in women with near-normal glycemic control was similar to that of the general population. Furthermore, we aimed to investigate the association between congenital malformations and maternal hyperglycemia in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes, with a specific focus on women with near-normal HbA1c levels in early pregnancy.

METHODS: This literature review was conducted through an electronic search of the PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, and Web of Science databases in July 2017. The search terms used were diabetes, pregnancy, HbA1c or glycemic control, and congenital anomaly or congenital anomaly. We included original papers published in English after 1997 that provided data on congenital malformations and HbA1c levels in at least 250 women with pregestational diabetes.

RESULTS: A total of nine papers were included, encompassing 6,225 women with type 1 diabetes and 2,334 women with type 2 diabetes. The prevalence of congenital malformations was found to be 6.4% in women with type 1 diabetes and 4.3% in women with type 2 diabetes. For the combined group of women with pregestational diabetes, the relative risk of congenital malformations compared to the general population was 3.2. Among women with HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy or HbA1c levels between 53-64 mmol/mol (7.0-8.0%), the prevalence of congenital malformations was 4.3% and 3.7%, respectively. The relative risks for these groups were 2.2 and 1.9, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: Pregnant women with pregestational diabetes had a threefold higher prevalence of congenital abnormalities compared to the general population. However, even HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy were associated with a twofold increased risk of congenital malformations compared to the general population.

title: Local and systemic insulin resistance resulting from hepatic activation of IKK-beta and NF-kappaB.
