text: We demonstrate that obesity and a high-fat diet (HFD) activate NF-kappaB and its transcriptional targets in the liver. To mimic this chronic, subacute "inflammation" state, we selectively expressed constitutively active IKK-b in hepatocytes of transgenic mice called LIKK. These LIKK mice exhibit characteristics of type 2 diabetes, including high blood sugar levels, severe insulin resistance in the liver, moderate systemic insulin resistance, and effects on muscle. The LIKK mice also showed increased production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1beta, and TNF-alpha in the liver, similar to the levels induced by HFD in wild-type mice. We observed parallel increases in cytokine signaling in both the liver and muscle of LIKK mice. By neutralizing IL-6 systemically or inhibiting IKK-beta with salicylate, we were able to improve insulin resistance. Additionally, reversing the phenotype of both LIKK mice and wild-type mice on an HFD was achieved by expressing the IkappaBalpha superrepressor (LISR) in the liver. These findings suggest that the accumulation of lipids in the liver triggers subacute hepatic "inflammation" through NF-kappaB activation and subsequent cytokine production, leading to insulin resistance locally in the liver and systemically.

title: Homelessness and health.
text: The issue of homelessness has a significant impact on a large number of Canadians and carries crucial implications for their health. Individuals experiencing homelessness are at a higher risk of premature death and suffer from various health issues, such as seizures, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, musculoskeletal disorders, tuberculosis, as well as skin and foot problems. Additionally, homeless individuals encounter significant obstacles that hinder their ability to access healthcare services. Further research is necessary to discover more effective methods of providing care to this population.

title: Serum metabolomics in animal models and human disease.
text:
The purpose of this review is to discuss recent applications of serum metabolomics in both human and animal studies. The focus is on understanding the variations in human metabolism and using serum metabolomics for disease profiling. 

Recent findings have shown attempts to develop noninvasive biomarkers of disease and track the effects of nutritional and genetic interventions using serum metabolomics. While progress has been made in identifying common changes in aging, menopause, and cancer, there are challenges in interpreting the results. These include small sample sizes in human studies and differences between human and rodent metabolomes. 

However, the Humsermet project, which involved a metabolic screening of over 1000 healthy individuals, has provided valuable insights that can improve the interpretation and design of future human studies. Additionally, the creation of a human serum metabolome database can aid in the design of both human and animal model studies. 

In summary, while some consistent alterations in the serum metabolome have been identified, there are still inconsistencies. The development of a human serum metabolome database will be beneficial for future research in both human and animal models.

title: Differential Requirement of the Extracellular Domain in Activation of Class B G Protein-coupled Receptors.
text: GPCRs from the secretin-like family, known as class B GPCRs, play a crucial role in maintaining hormonal balance and are important targets for drugs used to treat metabolic disorders and neuronal diseases. These receptors consist of a large extracellular domain (ECD) at the beginning and a transmembrane domain (TMD) with seven transmembrane helices, which is the characteristic GPCR signature. Class B GPCRs are activated by peptide hormones that bind to the receptor's ECD at their C termini and to the TMD at their N termini. It is believed that the ECD acts as a trap to bind and localize the hormone to the receptor, allowing the hormone's N terminus to insert into the TMD and trigger changes in its conformation, leading to downstream signaling activation. However, our research challenges this widely accepted model by demonstrating that different human class B GPCRs have varying requirements for the ECD in order to be activated. In one group of receptors, including corticotrophin-releasing factor receptor 1 (CRF1R), parathyroid hormone receptor (PTH1R), and pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide type 1 receptor (PAC1R), the need for the ECD in high affinity hormone binding can be bypassed through induced proximity and mass action effects. On the other hand, another group of receptors, such as glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), require the ECD for signaling even when the hormone is covalently linked to the TMD. Additionally, the activation of GLP-1R by small molecules that interact with the intracellular side of the receptor depends on the presence of its ECD, suggesting a direct involvement of the ECD in GLP-1R activation.

title: Genome-wide maps of histone modifications unwind in vivo chromatin states of the hair follicle lineage.
text: We investigate the remodeling of chromatin in adult stem cells (SCs) found in mouse skin, specifically in hair follicles. These SCs play a crucial role in the regeneration process. Through analyzing the changes in mRNA and chromatin in both inactive and active hair follicle SCs, as well as their progeny, we discover that polycomb-group (PcG)-mediated H3K27-trimethylation is a significant factor in the progression of hair follicle lineage. This mechanism differs from that of embryonic SCs. In hair follicle SCs, PcG represses the development of non-skin lineages and hair follicle differentiation. In the progeny, non-skin regulators remain repressed by PcG, hair follicle SC regulators acquire H3K27me3-marks, and hair follicle lineage regulators lose them. Interestingly, genes that are poised in embryonic stem cells, active in hair follicle SCs, and repressed by PcG in the progeny encode not only important transcription factors but also signaling regulators. We demonstrate the significance of these genes in maintaining the balance between hair follicle SC quiescence, highlighting the importance of chromatin mapping in understanding SC behavior. Our findings provide an explanation for how hair follicle SCs transition between inactive and active states without losing their stemness, and they define the roles of PcG-mediated repression in governing an irreversible fate switch.

title: Two classes of endogenous small RNAs in Tetrahymena thermophila.
text: RNA interference (RNAi) pathways in organisms involve endogenous small RNAs that play a role in guiding RNA cleavage, translational repression, or DNA or chromatin methylation. In the case of Tetrahymena thermophila, a unicellular organism, the process of developmentally regulated DNA elimination is controlled by an RNAi mechanism. This mechanism involves approximately 27-30-nucleotide (nt) RNAs. In our study, we examine the characteristics of these approximately 27-30-nt RNAs, as well as a second RNAi pathway represented by approximately 23-24-nt RNAs. These shorter RNAs accumulate in a strain-specific manner and are found in clusters on the genome that are antisense to predicted genes. These findings demonstrate the presence of distinct endogenous RNAi pathways in T. thermophila, a complexity that was previously thought to exist only in multicellular organisms.

title: The binding of maize DHN1 to lipid vesicles. Gain of structure and lipid specificity.
text: Dehydrins, also known as late embryogenesis abundant D-11 (DHNs), are plant proteins that are produced in response to abiotic stresses like drought, low temperature, and salinity, as well as during the later stages of embryogenesis. When purified, these proteins exhibit spectral and thermal properties that suggest they lack a defined structure. However, DHNs do contain a consensus 15-amino acid sequence called the "K segment," which bears resemblance to a class A2 amphipathic alpha-helical, lipid-binding domain found in other proteins like apolipoproteins and alpha-synuclein. The presence of the K segment raises the question of whether DHNs have the ability to bind to lipids, bilayers, or phospholipid vesicles. In this study, we demonstrate that DHN1 from maize (Zea mays) is capable of binding to lipid vesicles that contain acidic phospholipids. Furthermore, we observe that DHN1 exhibits a stronger affinity for smaller vesicles compared to larger ones, and that its association with vesicles leads to an apparent increase in the protein's alpha-helicity. Therefore, it is possible that DHNs, along with other plant stress proteins in the late embryogenesis abundant and cold-regulated classes, undergo conformational changes at the water/membrane interface that are related to their functional roles in stabilizing vesicles or other endomembrane structures under stressful conditions.

title: Requirement of heterochromatin for cohesion at centromeres.
text: The role of silent chromatin in the function of centromeres during cell division is still unknown. Sister chromatids need to stay together until anaphase, when cohesion mediated by Scc1/Rad21 is broken. In organisms with multiple cells, cohesins in chromosome arms separate during prophase, leaving centromeres as the only connection before anaphase. However, it is unclear what sets centromere cohesion apart from arm cohesion. In fission yeast, Swi6 (a counterpart of Heterochromatin protein 1) is a part of silent heterochromatin. Our study demonstrates that this heterochromatin is specifically necessary for cohesion between sister centromeres. Swi6 is responsible for the association of Rad21-cohesin with centromeres, but not along chromosome arms. Therefore, it distinguishes centromere cohesion from arm cohesion. Consequently, one of the functions of centromeric heterochromatin is to attract cohesin, ensuring proper chromosome segregation and cohesion between sister centromeres.

title: Gene expression in human skeletal muscle: alternative normalization method and effect of repeated biopsies
text:
Recently, the reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) method has gained popularity in assessing transcription and mRNA levels in muscle samples from rodents and humans. However, the conventional practice of using endogenous controls to correct for variability in cDNA content between samples is not ideal. In this study, we explored three main aspects: (1) a novel normalization method based on determining cDNA content using the flourophores PicoGreen and OliGreen, (2) the impact of repeated muscle biopsies on mRNA gene expression, and (3) the spatial heterogeneity in mRNA expression across the muscle.

Our findings demonstrate that both PicoGreen and OliGreen reagents exhibit high sensitivity and linearity when used to measure cDNA content. Standard curves constructed using oligo standards and serial dilutions of representative RT samples consistently showed linearity with R2 values exceeding 0.99. Moreover, PicoGreen reagent effectively detected the RNA:DNA hybrid content in RT samples. Standard curves constructed using double-stranded lambda DNA and serial dilutions of representative RT samples also exhibited linearity with R2 values exceeding 0.99.

Based on our analysis of reversed transcribed human skeletal muscle RNA samples using PicoGreen and OliGreen, we propose that these fluorophores offer a potential alternative normalization procedure for human gene expression studies. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that multiple muscle biopsies obtained from the same muscle do not influence the mRNA response induced by acute exercise for any of the genes examined.

title: The Impact of Location of Progressive Visual Field Loss on Longitudinal Changes in Quality of Life of Patients with Glaucoma.
text: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between progressive loss in different regions of the visual field and changes in quality of life (QoL) over time. The study was a prospective, observational cohort study that included 236 patients with glaucomatous visual field loss. These patients were followed for an average of 4.3±1.5 years. The participants completed the 25-item National Eye Institute Visual Functioning Questionnaire (NEI VFQ-25) annually and underwent standard automated perimetry (SAP) every 6 months. To be included in the study, participants needed to have completed at least 2 NEI VFQ-25 assessments and 5 SAP tests during the follow-up period. The researchers evaluated rates of visual field change using 4 different regions of the integrated binocular visual field (central inferior, central superior, peripheral inferior, and peripheral superior). They then used a joint multivariable longitudinal linear mixed model to investigate the association between changes in NEI VFQ-25 scores and changes in the different regions of the visual field. The main outcome measures were the relationship between changes in QoL scores and changes in mean sensitivity in the different regions of the visual field. The results showed a significant correlation between changes in NEI VFQ-25 scores and changes in the different regions of the visual field. Specifically, a 1 decibel (dB)/year change in binocular mean sensitivity in the central inferior area was associated with a decline of 2.6 units/year in NEI VFQ-25 scores. The associations for the peripheral inferior, central superior, and peripheral superior areas of the visual field had R(2) values of 30%, 24%, and 19%, respectively. The association for the central inferior visual field area was significantly stronger than those of the central superior and peripheral superior areas, but not the peripheral inferior area. The study also found that patients with worse visual field sensitivity at baseline experienced greater declines in NEI VFQ-25 scores. In conclusion, the progressive decline in sensitivity in the central inferior area of the visual field had the strongest association with longitudinal decline in QoL in patients with glaucoma.

title: Use of thiazolidinediones and the risk of bladder cancer among people with type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis.
text:
Patients with type 2 diabetes have a 40% higher chance of developing bladder cancer. Thiazolidinediones, specifically pioglitazone, may contribute to this increased risk. To assess the risk of bladder cancer in adults with type 2 diabetes who take thiazolidinediones, we conducted a thorough review and meta-analysis. 

We searched various biomedical databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus, as well as grey literature sources from the beginning until March 2012. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies that reported incidents of bladder cancer in individuals with type 2 diabetes who were exposed to pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, or any other thiazolidinedione.

Out of the 1787 studies we identified, we selected 4 RCTs, 5 cohort studies, and 1 case-control study. The total number of patients included in these studies was 2,657,365, with 3643 cases of newly diagnosed bladder cancer, resulting in an overall incidence rate of 53.1 per 100,000 person-years. 

The one RCT that examined pioglitazone use did not find a significant association with bladder cancer (risk ratio [RR] 2.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91-6.13). However, the cohort studies on thiazolidinediones (pooled RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.04-1.26; I(2) = 0%) and specifically pioglitazone (pooled RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.07-1.39; I(2) = 0%) showed significant associations with bladder cancer. On the other hand, the two RCTs that evaluated rosiglitazone use did not find a significant association with bladder cancer (pooled RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.34-2.23; I(2) = 0%).

Based on the limited evidence available, it can be concluded that thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, are likely to increase the risk of bladder cancer in adults with type 2 diabetes.

title: Immune signaling by RIG-I-like receptors.
text: The RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), namely RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2, play a crucial role in detecting RNA viruses and initiating and regulating the immune response against them. These receptors identify viral RNA or processed self RNA in the cytoplasm, leading to the activation of innate immunity and inflammation. Additionally, they influence gene expression to control the infection. It is worth noting that RLRs collaborate with Toll-like receptors and other factors to enhance innate immunity and modulate the adaptive immune response. The regulation of RLRs occurs at various levels, including autoregulation, interactions with ligands and cofactors, and posttranslational modifications. Abnormal RLR signaling or dysregulation of RLR expression has been linked to the development of autoimmune diseases. Gaining a better understanding of RLR signaling and response mechanisms will provide valuable insights for the development of RLR-targeted therapeutics for antiviral and immune-modifying purposes.

title: Ionizing radiation-induced long-term expression of senescence markers in mice is independent of p53 and immune status.
text: Exposure to infrared (IR) radiation has been proven to cause the development of senescence markers, which is a characteristic that aligns with the lifelong delay in repair and regeneration of tissues that have been irradiated. Our hypothesis was that these senescence markers induced by IR could persist in vivo for an extended period, potentially leading to a permanent decline in tissue functionality. In this study, we demonstrate that mouse tissues exposed to a non-lethal dose of IR exhibit long-lasting effects, with DNA damage foci and increased expression of p16(INK4a), both of which are indicators of cellular senescence and aging, still present up to 45 weeks after exposure. Through BrdU-labeling experiments, we discovered that damaged cells caused by IR are preferentially eliminated, to some extent, depending on the tissue. Surprisingly, the accumulation of damaged cells was found to be independent of the DNA damage response regulator p53 and an intact immune system, as the levels were similar in both wild-type and Rag2(-/-) gammaC(-/-) mice, the latter lacking T, B, and NK cells. Overall, our findings provide strong evidence that exposure to IR leads to the long-term expression of senescence markers in vivo, which may contribute to the observed decline in tissue functionality among cancer survivors.

title: Cranial neural crest and the building of the vertebrate head
text: The development of the head in vertebrates is a complex process involving various molecular and morphogenetic events. These events work together to create a specific pattern of cartilages, bones, and nerves, resulting in unique craniofacial structures for each species. The neural crest, a specialized cell type originating from the nervous system, plays a crucial role in this process by providing the main source of craniofacial tissue. The extent of patterning information inherent to the neural crest has recently been a topic of debate, and recent advancements have highlighted the influence of environmental signals on the coordination of craniofacial development in both space and time.

title: Tamoxifen resistance in MCF7 cells promotes EMT-like behaviour and involves modulation of beta-catenin phosphorylation.
text: Previously, we have shown that breast cancer cells, after developing resistance to endocrine therapy, exhibit changes in their growth rate and become more aggressive in laboratory settings. We wanted to investigate the role of cell-cell adhesive interactions in promoting this aggressive behavior, so we examined the integrity of a protein complex involved in this process in our model of tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer. In our experiments, tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TamR) formed loosely packed colonies in culture, with a loss of cell-cell junctions and changes in cell shape that are characteristic of a process called epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). When we blocked the function of a protein called E-cadherin, which is involved in cell-cell adhesion, we observed increased invasion and decreased aggregation of endocrine-sensitive MCF7 cells, but this had little effect on the behavior of TamR cells. Furthermore, TamR cells had higher levels of a protein called beta-catenin that was phosphorylated on tyrosine, but lower levels of beta-catenin phosphorylated on serine/threonine. These cells also showed a loss of association between beta-catenin and E-cadherin, increased levels of beta-catenin in the cytoplasm and nucleus, and increased expression of genes that are known to be involved in tumor progression and EMT and are regulated by beta-catenin. When we inhibited the activity of a protein called EGFR in TamR cells, we observed a decrease in tyrosine phosphorylation of beta-catenin, an increase in the association between beta-catenin and E-cadherin, and an increase in cell-cell adhesion. In these treated cells, the association between beta-catenin and another protein called Lef-1, as well as the expression of genes such as c-myc, cyclin-D1, CD44, and COX-2 that are regulated by beta-catenin, were also reduced. These findings suggest that the ability of tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells to adhere to each other is impaired due to EGFR-mediated changes in the phosphorylation of beta-catenin, and this may contribute to their increased aggressiveness and transition to a mesenchymal phenotype in laboratory settings.

title: Expression profiles of Toll-like receptors in non-small cell lung cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
text: The incidence of lung cancer is higher in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), but the role of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) and lung cancer development is not well understood. This study aimed to measure the expression of TLRs in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) of IPF patients, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, and control subjects. The mRNA expression of TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9 was quantitatively measured using real-time reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, and TLR9 protein expression was assessed on BALF T-lymphocytes using flow cytometry. The results showed that TLR3 mRNA expression was significantly higher in NSCLC patients compared to IPF and controls. TLR7 mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls. TLR9 mRNA expression was significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls. TLR2 mRNA expression was significantly higher in IPF patients compared to controls. Flow cytometry analysis revealed decreased TLR3 and TLR9 expression in IPF patients compared to the NSCLC group and decreased TLR9 expression in IPF compared to controls. TLR2 protein expression was significantly higher in IPF patients compared to NSCLC. In conclusion, this study found increased expression of endosomal TLRs in NSCLC patients and elevated expression of TLR2 in pulmonary fibrosis. These findings do not support the hypothesis of a common TLR pathway between NSCLC and IPF.

title: A protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor ameliorates disease in a mouse model of progeria.
text: Progerias are uncommon genetic disorders characterized by premature aging. Certain progeroid disorders are caused by mutations that result in the buildup of a modified form of prelamin A, a protein that plays a role in the structure of the cell nucleus. In progeria, the accumulation of this modified prelamin A disrupts the nucleus's structural support, leading to abnormal nuclei shapes. Previous research has demonstrated that farnesyltransferase inhibitors (FTIs) can reverse this cellular abnormality. To investigate further, we conducted a study using an FTI called ABT-100 in Zmpste24-deficient mice, which serve as a mouse model for progeria. The mice treated with the FTI showed improvements in body weight, grip strength, bone health, and survival rate at 20 weeks of age. These findings suggest that FTIs may have positive effects in individuals with progeria.

title: A rare mutation in UNC5C predisposes to late-onset Alzheimer's disease and increases neuronal cell death
text: A rare coding mutation, T835M (rs137875858), has been discovered in the UNC5C netrin receptor gene. This mutation has been found to be associated with disease in an autosomal dominant pattern in two families with a high prevalence of late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, it has been observed to be linked to the disease in four large case-control cohorts, with an odds ratio of 2.15 and a P-value of 0.0095. The T835M mutation affects a conserved residue in the hinge region of UNC5C. In vitro studies have shown that this mutation leads to increased cell death in human HEK293T cells and rodent neurons. Moreover, neurons expressing T835M UNC5C are more susceptible to cell death caused by various neurotoxic stimuli, including β-amyloid (Aβ), glutamate, and staurosporine. Based on these findings and the fact that UNC5C is highly expressed in the hippocampus of the adult nervous system, it is proposed that one possible mechanism by which T835M UNC5C contributes to the risk of Alzheimer's disease is by increasing vulnerability to neuronal cell death, particularly in regions of the brain affected by Alzheimer's disease.

title: Treatment of active tuberculosis in HIV-coinfected patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
BACKGROUND
Patients who have both human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and tuberculosis are at a higher risk of death, treatment failure, and relapse.

METHODS
To assess the impact of the duration and dosing schedule of rifamycin and the use of antiretroviral therapy in treating active tuberculosis in HIV-positive patients, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials and cohort studies was conducted. The included studies confirmed the initial tuberculosis diagnosis, failure, and/or relapse through microbiological testing, and the patients received standardized regimens containing rifampin or rifabutin. The pooled cumulative incidence of treatment failure, death during treatment, and relapse was calculated using random-effects models. Multivariable meta-regression was performed using negative binomial regression.

RESULTS
After reviewing 5158 citations, 6 randomized trials and 21 cohort studies were included in the analysis. The use of regimens with 2 months of rifamycin was associated with a higher risk of relapse (adjusted risk ratio, 3.6; 95% confidence interval, 1.1-11.7) compared to regimens with rifamycin for at least 8 months. Daily therapy during the initial phase (n=3352 patients from 35 study arms) had lower rates of failure (adjusted risk ratio, 4.0; 95% confidence interval, 1.5-10.4) and relapse (adjusted risk ratio, 4.8; 95% confidence interval, 1.8-12.8) compared to thrice-weekly therapy (n=211 patients from 5 study arms). There were indications of higher relapse rates if rifamycins were used for only 6 months compared to 8 months or longer, or if antiretroviral therapy was not used.

CONCLUSIONS
This review raises concerns about the current recommendations for treating HIV-tuberculosis coinfection. The data suggest that a minimum duration of 8 months of rifamycin therapy, initial daily dosing, and concurrent antiretroviral therapy may lead to better outcomes. However, further well-designed randomized trials are urgently needed to confirm these findings.

title: Crystal structure and association behaviour of the GluR2 amino-terminal domain.
text: The main way that fast excitatory neurotransmission occurs is through ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs). These receptors are made up of tetrameric, ligand-gated ion channel proteins and are divided into three subfamilies: AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors. Each subfamily has a similar modular-domain structure. The active channels for all subfamilies are formed exclusively by subunits within the same subfamily. This process is mainly controlled by the amino-terminal domain (ATD). However, we do not yet understand how the ATD specifically guides the assembly of subfamily-specific receptors. In this study, we demonstrate that the ATDs of AMPA receptor GluR1 and GluR2 form tightly associated dimers. Through the analysis of crystal structures of the GluR2-ATD, we propose mechanisms that explain how the ATD guides the assembly of subfamily-specific receptors.

title: Deficiency in l-serine deaminase results in abnormal growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12.
text: The inability to deaminate l-serine has a severe negative impact on the growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12. A specific strain of this organism, in which the three genes (sdaA, sdaB, tdcG) responsible for coding the three l-serine deaminases, has been deleted, shows good growth in glucose minimal medium. However, when subcultured into minimal medium containing glucose and casamino acids, it produces unusually large and misshapen cells, many of which burst. In Luria-Bertani (LB) broth, with or without glucose, it forms long filaments. The addition of S-adenosylmethionine to LB broth with glucose restores cell division and improves growth in medium with casamino acids. We propose that the replication of E. coli is regulated by methylation. An abnormally high concentration of intracellular l-serine, in the presence of other amino acids, leads to a shortage of S-adenosylmethionine, and the absence of S-adenosylmethionine and/or C1-tetrahydrofolate derivatives hinders normal cell division.

title: Stem cell characteristics in prostate cancer cell lines.
text:
Recent studies have shown that there is a small population of stem-like cells in various human cancers that play a crucial role in tumor growth. The objective of this study was to examine the stem cell properties of six established prostate cancer cell lines (DU145, DuCaP, LAPC-4, 22Rv1, LNCaP, and PC-3) in vitro. The researchers tested the colony-forming efficiency and self-renewal ability of different types of clones using low-density plating and serial passaging. They also examined the expression of the putative stem cell marker CD133 and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) using flow cytometry, and performed immunohistochemical stainings for various markers. 

The results showed that five out of the six cell lines formed distinct types of clones. DU145 holoclones, in particular, could be maintained in culture for multiple passages, indicating their self-renewal ability. CD133(+) cells were detected in a small fraction (0.01%) of DU145 cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis. However, these CD133(+) cells, as well as DU145 BCRP(+) cells (0.15%), were not more clonogenic and did not show increased holoclone formation compared to marker-negative or unselected cells. Immunohistochemistry revealed alpha2-integrin and BCRP as potential stem cell markers, and cytokeratin 5 (CK5) in combination with cytokeratin 18 (CK18) to distinguish transient amplifying cells. 

In conclusion, this study suggests that there may be stem-like cells present in several established prostate cancer cell lines. However, CD133 selection does not effectively enrich for these stem-like cells in these cell lines.

title: Resistance to antimicrobials in humans and animals.
text: Antibiotic overuse is not the sole cause of antimicrobial resistance, and reducing usage alone is not the only solution. The first signs of weakened effectiveness in antibiotics, known as antimicrobial resistance, became apparent in the mid-20th century. By the 1990s, multiple reports highlighted the dangers of excessive or inappropriate antibiotic use in medical settings, as well as the use of antibiotics in animal feed to promote growth. Initially, overuse of antibiotics was identified as the primary culprit, and reducing their usage was seen as the solution. However, the issue is more complex than initially thought. The notion that decreasing antibiotic use would solve the problem was embraced by the United Kingdom government in response to a report from the House of Lords. This response included a public awareness campaign, monitoring resistance throughout the food supply chain, targets for reducing hospital-acquired infections, and the establishment of an advisory body to oversee all aspects of antibiotic use. However, the concept of overuse has proven to be too simplistic. While there is evidence of excessive prescribing in certain cases, it is not the sole factor contributing to antimicrobial resistance.

title: Unmet needs and depressive symptoms among low--income older adults.
text: In previous research, it has been discovered that declining health, reduced social interaction, and insufficient financial resources are significant risk factors for depression in older adults. On the other hand, social support from family and friends, as well as religiosity, have been found to be protective factors. In this study, we aimed to determine if low-income older adults' perception of unmet needs for home- and community-based services for various aging-related issues would independently contribute to their depressive symptoms. We took into account the aforementioned risk and protective factors. A total of 213 older adults living in the community were interviewed to evaluate their depressive symptoms using the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), as well as their unmet needs in areas such as personal assistance, instrumental and environmental support, emotional support, and other enabling services. Our findings revealed a significant positive association between the number of unmet needs and depressive symptoms in these older adults. However, it should be noted that the unmet needs only accounted for a small portion of the variation in GDS scores. We discuss the implications of these findings for future research and practice.

title: A key role for Ctf4 in coupling the MCM2-7 helicase to DNA polymerase alpha within the eukaryotic replisome.
text: The structure of the eukaryotic replisome, which is essential for maintaining genome stability, is not well understood. In previous studies, we discovered that various regulatory proteins gather around the MCM2-7 helicase at yeast replication forks to form the replisome progression complex (RPC). This complex potentially connects MCM2-7 with other components of the replisome. Our latest research reveals that the RPC associates with DNA polymerase alpha, which initiates each Okazaki fragment during the synthesis of the lagging strand. Our findings suggest that the GINS and Ctf4 components of the RPC form a crucial complex that links MCM2-7 to DNA polymerase alpha. Recent studies have also shown that the Mrc1 subunit of RPCs binds to DNA polymerase epsilon, responsible for synthesizing the leading strand at DNA replication forks. Our experiments demonstrate that cells lacking both Ctf4 and Mrc1 continuously activate the DNA damage checkpoint during chromosome replication and fail to complete the cell cycle. These results emphasize the significance of connecting MCM2-7 to replicative polymerases in regulating chromosome replication in eukaryotes, with Ctf4 playing a key role in this process.

title: Data analysis methods for detection of differential protein expression in two-dimensional gel electrophoresis.
text: The advancement of microarray technology has prompted statisticians and bioinformaticians to develop novel statistical approaches for comparing various biological samples. The aim is to identify a limited number of genes that exhibit differential expression among thousands. In the field of quantitative proteomics, the analysis of protein expression through two-dimensional gel electrophoresis shares some similarities with transcriptomic studies. Hence, this study aimed to assess different data analysis methodologies commonly employed in array analysis using diverse proteomic datasets comprising hundreds of proteins. Despite having limited replications, the significance analysis of microarrays method demonstrated greater efficacy in accurately identifying differentially expressed proteins compared to the Student's t-test. This procedure helps prevent wasting time on false positives and avoids losing valuable information through false negatives.

title: A clinical approach to circadian rhythm sleep disorders.
text: Circadian rhythm sleep disorders are characterized by complaints of difficulty sleeping and excessive sleepiness. These issues are primarily caused by disruptions in the internal circadian timing system or a mismatch between sleep timing and the 24-hour social and physical environment. Alongside physiological and environmental factors, maladaptive behaviors often contribute to the development of these disorders. This review will focus on the clinical approach to diagnosing and managing various circadian rhythm sleep disorders, including delayed sleep phase disorder, advanced sleep phase disorder, non-entrained type, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, shift work sleep disorder, and jet lag disorder. Diagnostic tools like sleep diaries and wrist activity monitoring are often helpful in confirming the diagnosis. Since behavioral and environmental factors are often involved in these conditions, a multimodal approach is typically necessary. Interventions may include educating patients on sleep hygiene, timed exposure to bright light, avoiding bright light at inappropriate times, and using medications like melatonin. However, it's important to note that melatonin is not FDA-approved for treating circadian rhythm sleep disorders.

title: SIVrcm infection of macaques.
text: In a previous report, we discussed the discovery and analysis of SIVrcm, a unique lentivirus found in a domesticated Red-Capped Mangabey (RCM) in Gabon. SIVrcm differs from other primate lentiviruses such as HIV-1 and HIV-2/SIV. This report presents additional experiments conducted to study the replication of SIVrcm in vitro and its effects on macaques. The findings reveal that SIVrcm has minimal cytopathic effects on Molt 4 Clone 8 cells, as well as rhesus and human PBMCs. In vivo studies demonstrate that SIVrcm is not pathogenic in rhesus macaques for up to 200 days and in cynomolgous macaques for up to one year, although it does establish a chronic infection in both species.

title: Integrating nutrition security with treatment of people living with HIV: lessons from Kenya.
text:
CONTEXT
There is a need to develop better interventions to improve the nutrition security of individuals receiving antiretroviral treatment due to their increased caloric requirements, potential side effects of treatment, and the negative impact of malnutrition on adherence and drug resistance.

OBJECTIVE
This study aims to highlight the benefits and challenges of interventions aimed at strengthening the nutrition security of people living with HIV who are undergoing antiretroviral treatment.

METHODS
Qualitative research was conducted on a short-term nutrition intervention that provided free antiretroviral treatment to HIV-positive individuals in western Kenya between late 2005 and early 2006.

RESULTS
Patients who participated in the food program while receiving treatment reported improved adherence to medication, reduced side effects, and better ability to satisfy their increased appetite. Many clients also experienced weight gain, regained physical strength, and were able to resume their labor activities while enrolled in the dual program of food supplementation and treatment. These improvements also led to increased support from their families and communities.

CONCLUSIONS
These findings support the need for a comprehensive response to address the coexistence of AIDS epidemics and chronic nutrition insecurity. Future research should focus on bridging the gap between short-term nutritional support for individuals and long-term livelihood security programs for communities affected by AIDS. This interdisciplinary research should be accompanied by collaborative efforts between the agriculture and health sectors in these environments.

title: Acylated and desacyl ghrelin stimulate lipid accumulation in human visceral adipocytes
text: The aim of this study was to examine the effects of obesity and obesity-related type 2 diabetes on the different forms of the hormone ghrelin, and to investigate the potential role of these forms in the regulation of adipogenesis in humans. The concentrations of acylated and desacyl ghrelin in the blood were measured in 80 participants. The expression of the ghrelin receptor in omental adipose tissue was analyzed, and the impact of acylated and desacyl ghrelin on adipogenesis was assessed in vitro using omental adipocytes. The results showed that levels of acylated ghrelin were higher, while levels of desacyl ghrelin were lower, in individuals with obesity and obesity-related type 2 diabetes. Body mass index, waist circumference, insulin, and the HOMA index were positively associated with acylated ghrelin levels. Obese individuals also had lower levels of the ghrelin receptor in omental adipose tissue. In the adipocytes, both forms of ghrelin increased the expression of genes involved in fat storage and stimulated lipid accumulation. These findings suggest that both acylated and desacyl ghrelin contribute to lipid accumulation in visceral adipocytes. The elevated levels of acylated ghrelin observed in obese individuals may therefore play a role in excessive fat accumulation in obesity.

title: Significant correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression and the association with poor recurrence-free survival in rectal cancer after preoperative chemoradiotherapy
text: The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between the gene expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 and the clinical outcome in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who underwent preoperative chemoradiotherapy (CRT). Residual cancer cells were collected from 52 patients who received preoperative CRT for locally advanced rectal cancer. Total RNA was extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens using microdissection. The expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 genes were measured using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemistry. Additionally, in vitro experiments were conducted using colon cancer cell lines to investigate the changes in gene expression levels of LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 (AMPK) after irradiation. Our findings indicate that patients with poor pathological response and tumor recurrence had significantly higher gene expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 compared to those without these outcomes (P < 0.05). Furthermore, there was a significant positive correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression after CRT (Spearman’s ρ: 0.429, P = 0.0023). Patients with high expression levels of both LKB1 and LGR5 had a significantly lower recurrence-free survival compared to the other group (P = 0.0055, 95% confidence interval: 1.39–11.08). Lastly, in vitro experiments demonstrated a similar pattern of sequential gene expression among LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 after irradiation. Our results suggest that the expression of LKB1 and LGR5 may be involved in resistance to CRT, thereby contributing to tumor relapse in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who undergo preoperative CRT.

title: Evaluating the impact of pharmacists in mental health: a systematic review.
text: Efforts to enhance the outcomes of individuals with mental illness have often involved integrating the expertise of various healthcare professionals into collaborative care models. Clinical pharmacists have been actively contributing to these models for more than three decades, assuming roles such as educators, consultants, and providers. This systematic review aims to assess the quantity and quality of medical literature published between 1972 and 2003 that examines the impact of pharmacists in mental health. Out of approximately 35 publications identified on this topic, only 16 met the necessary scientific standards for evaluation and comparison. These 16 studies were evenly split between inpatient and outpatient settings and were conducted in diverse healthcare organizations, including the Veterans Administration, health maintenance organizations, community mental health clinics, and nursing homes. Nine of the studies explored the role of pharmacists in providing treatment recommendations and patient education, five focused on pharmacists as providers with prescribing authority, and the remaining two described the influence of pharmacists in educating psychiatric staff. While six of the 16 studies were prospective, only three of them incorporated randomization procedures for patients or facilities. Overall, the results of these 16 studies were positive, demonstrating improvements in outcomes, prescribing practices, patient satisfaction, and resource utilization. However, it is important to note that most of the investigations were small in scale, and significant limitations in study design hindered further comparisons. Given the extensive history and anecdotal success of pharmacists in mental healthcare settings, additional multicenter cost-effectiveness trials are necessary to further validate the role of psychiatric pharmacists.

title: Multicenter phase II study of lapatinib in patients with brain metastases from HER2-positive breast cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of lapatinib, an inhibitor of epidermal growth factor receptor/HER2, in treating brain metastases in patients with advanced HER2+ breast cancer. Patients who had previously received trastuzumab and cranial radiotherapy and had progressive brain metastases were eligible for the study. The primary goal was to achieve a >or=50% reduction in the volume of CNS lesions without increasing steroid use or experiencing worsening neurologic signs and symptoms or progression of extra-CNS disease.

A total of 242 patients participated in the study, and it was found that lapatinib resulted in CNS objective responses in 6% of patients. Additionally, an exploratory analysis showed that 21% of patients experienced a >or=20% reduction in the volume of their CNS lesions. It was observed that patients who had a reduction in lesion volume also had improved progression-free survival and neurologic signs and symptoms.

Furthermore, a subset of 50 patients who were evaluated in the lapatinib plus capecitabine extension of the study showed that 20% achieved a CNS objective response and 40% had a >or=20% reduction in the volume of their CNS lesions.

In conclusion, this study confirms the limited effectiveness of lapatinib in treating CNS metastases in patients with HER2+ breast cancer. However, there were additional positive responses observed when lapatinib was combined with capecitabine. Further research is needed to explore lapatinib-based treatment regimens for CNS metastases in HER2+ breast cancer patients.

title: Control of signaling-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells by the tumor suppressor p53
text: Abnormal immune responses, such as unresolved inflammation and autoimmune conditions, can occur when dying cells are not efficiently cleared. Our research demonstrates that the tumor suppressor p53 plays a role in the phagocytosis of apoptotic cells through a target called Death Domain1α (DD1α). This suggests that p53 promotes both the pathway leading to cell death and the events that occur after cell death. Unlike typical scavenger receptors that recognize phosphatidylserine on the surface of dead cells, DD1α appears to function as an engulfment ligand or receptor that interacts with other DD1α molecules at the junctions between apoptotic cells and macrophages. In mice lacking DD1α, we observed defects in clearing dying cells in vivo, which resulted in damage to multiple organs and indicated immune dysfunction. The expression of DD1α induced by p53 prevents the persistence of cell corpses and ensures the efficient generation of precise immune responses.

title: Circulating tumor DNA as a non-invasive substitute to metastasis biopsy for tumor genotyping and personalized medicine in a prospective trial across all tumor types.
text: Cell-free tumor DNA (ctDNA) has the potential to revolutionize non-invasive diagnostic tests for personalized medicine by providing molecular information similar to that obtained from invasive tumor biopsies. In the histology-independent phase II SHIVA trial, patients are matched with targeted therapeutics based on screening of multiple somatic mutations using metastatic biopsies. To assess the usefulness of ctDNA in this trial, we conducted a supplementary study comparing the detection of somatic mutations in plasma DNA versus metastasis biopsies in 34 patients with 18 different tumor types. We used a multiplexed next-generation sequencing panel to scan 46 genes and over 6800 COSMIC mutations. In 27 patients, 28 out of 29 mutations identified in metastasis biopsies (97%) were also detected in matched ctDNA. Additionally, one extra mutation was found exclusively in ctDNA. In the remaining seven patients, mutation detection from metastasis biopsy was unsuccessful due to insufficient biopsy material, but all plasma DNA samples successfully provided three more potentially actionable mutations. These findings suggest that ctDNA analysis could serve as a viable alternative or replacement for costly, harmful, and time-consuming tissue biopsies of metastasis. This holds true regardless of cancer type or metastatic site, and allows for multiplexed mutation detection to guide personalized therapies based on the genetic content of the patient's tumor.

title: TGF-beta suppresses tumor progression in colon cancer by inhibition of IL-6 trans-signaling.
text: The molecular consequences of alterations in TGF-beta signaling in colorectal cancer are not well understood. However, our study using transgenic mice that overexpress TGF-beta or a dominant-negative TGF-betaRII reveals that TGF-beta signaling in T lymphocytes infiltrating tumors plays a role in controlling the growth of dysplastic epithelial cells in experimental colorectal cancer. This was determined through histology and a new system for high-resolution chromoendoscopy. At the molecular level, we found that TGF-beta signaling in T cells regulates the activation of STAT-3 in tumor cells through IL-6. Interestingly, IL-6 signaling requires soluble IL-6R derived from tumor cells rather than membrane-bound IL-6R. Furthermore, inhibiting TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling prevented tumor progression in vivo. These findings provide valuable insights into TGF-beta signaling in colorectal cancer and suggest potential therapeutic strategies for the disease by targeting TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling.

title: New opportunities: the use of nanotechnologies to manipulate and track stem cells.
text: Nanotechnologies are rapidly developing tools that have the potential to be valuable in the measurement, comprehension, and manipulation of stem cells. For instance, magnetic nanoparticles and quantum dots can be utilized to label and track stem cells within living organisms. Nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, and polyplexes can be employed for the delivery of genes/oligonucleotides and protein/peptides into the cells. Additionally, engineered nanometer-scale scaffolds can be used to guide stem cell differentiation and facilitate transplantation. This article explores the application of nanotechnologies in tracking, differentiating, and transplanting stem cells. Furthermore, we delve into their usefulness and address any concerns regarding their potential cytotoxicity.

title: The emergence of order in the Drosophila pupal retina.
text: During the process of pupation, the Drosophila eye undergoes a transformation where a well-organized arrangement is established among the ommatidia. This is achieved through the emergence of eight additional cell types: primary, secondary, and tertiary pigment cells, as well as the four cells responsible for forming the bristle. These cells intertwine to form a lattice structure between the ommatidia. The lattice is refined by eliminating excess cells to align neighboring ommatidia. Recent findings indicate that in larval development, the fate of cells is influenced by local contacts. This phenomenon seems to persist during pupal development, as the type of contact a cell makes predicts its eventual cell type. Cells that come into contact with the anterior or posterior cone cells within an ommatidium consistently become primary pigment cells. On the other hand, cells that contact primary pigment cells from different ommatidia develop into secondary and tertiary pigment cells. The development of bristles differs in several ways from ommatidial development. The four cells within each bristle group are believed to originate from a single founder cell. During their early differentiation, these cells do not adhere to a specific pattern of contact with surrounding ommatidial cells, but they do establish specific contacts within the bristle group. Additionally, unlike the surrounding ommatidia, bristle differentiation occurs from the center of the eye towards the edges. As cells are eliminated through programmed cell death in two stages, the bristles are positioned in their final arrangement. Once all cells in the lattice have reached their final positions, a second phase of retinal development commences, resulting in the production of structures unique to each cell type. This paper explores the various stages of pupal development and proposes that local cell-cell contacts play a crucial role in generating the cells necessary for a fully functional retina.

title: Gene expression analysis by cDNA microarray in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
text:
BACKGROUND
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a common type of cancer in humans, but there is limited knowledge about the molecular mechanisms that determine its malignancy. To gain a better understanding of OSCC, it is crucial to conduct comprehensive gene expression profiling.

METHODS
In this study, we used cDNA microarray to analyze the expression patterns of 16,617 genes in nine OSCC patients.

RESULTS
We identified 47 genes with altered expression in all cases. These 47 genes were classified into 10 categories based on their ontology. To validate the microarray data, we performed reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to analyze the expression of genes such as TGFBI, FADD, and DUSP1. Hierarchical clustering analysis divided the nine cases into two clusters.

CONCLUSIONS
The 47 genes identified in this study are suggested to have functional significance in the development of oral squamous cell carcinoma. Furthermore, the gene expression patterns obtained through hierarchical clustering analysis may represent different degrees of differentiation. The patients in this study had a smooth postoperative recovery and remained tumor-free after surgery. In the future, as the number of cases for microarray analysis increases and long-term observations are conducted, the data on 5-year survival rates can be added. This will enable us to better understand the malignancy of OSCC based on these gene expression patterns.

title: Risk factors associated with symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the risk factors for gastroesophageal reflux in the United States, as there is a lack of population-based data on this topic. We conducted a cross-sectional study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, using a random sample of residents aged 25 to 74 years. Participants were sent a valid self-report questionnaire to assess reflux symptoms and potential risk factors. Logistic regression was used to determine the odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for reflux symptoms associated with these risk factors. 

Out of the 2,118 eligible subjects, 1,524 (72%) responded to the questionnaire. Our findings revealed that several factors were independently associated with frequent reflux symptoms (occurring at least weekly). These factors included having a body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m2 (OR = 2.8; CI, 1.7 to 4.5), having an immediate family member with heartburn or esophageal/stomach disease (OR = 2.6; CI, 1.8 to 3.7), having a history of smoking (OR = 1.6; CI, 1.1 to 2.3), consuming more than seven drinks per week (OR = 1.9; CI, 1.1 to 3.3), and having a higher score on the psychosomatic symptom checklist (OR per 5 units = 1.4; CI, 1.3 to 1.6). 

In conclusion, our study highlights obesity as a significant risk factor for gastroesophageal reflux. However, the effectiveness of weight reduction in managing reflux symptoms still needs further investigation. The presence of a family history of reflux suggests a potential genetic component to the disorder.

title: A mathematical investigation of the effects of inhibitor therapy on three putative phosphorylation cascades governing the two-component system of the agr operon.
text: Bacteria commonly utilize two-component systems (TCSs) to detect specific external signals and initiate a suitable response within the cell through a phosphorylation cascade. In the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus, the TCS of the agr operon plays a role in a regulatory process known as quorum sensing. Quorum sensing is a mechanism of cell-to-cell communication used to assess population density. Understanding this process is crucial because S. aureus utilizes this knowledge to coordinate the production of exotoxin virulence factors necessary for infection. In this study, we present three models of the agr operon, each incorporating a different phosphorylation cascade for the TCS, as the exact nature of the cascade remains unclear. By employing numerical and asymptotic techniques, we investigate the impact of inhibitor therapy on these three cascades. Inhibitor therapy is a novel approach to controlling bacterial infection by reducing virulence. Our findings, when compared to relevant experimental data, offer insights into the potential effectiveness of this therapy. Additionally, the TCS models presented in this study have broad applicability, as TCSs are widely conserved across bacterial species.

title: Coregulators in nuclear estrogen receptor action: from concept to therapeutic targeting.
text: Estrogens play a crucial role in regulating the growth, differentiation, and functions of various target tissues, such as the reproductive tracts, breast, skeletal, nervous, cardiovascular, digestive, and immune systems. These biological effects are primarily mediated by two distinct receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta, which act as transcription factors that respond to hormones and other signals. The recruitment of coactivator proteins to these receptors is essential for their transcriptional and biological activities. These coactivator complexes allow the receptors to appropriately respond to hormonal or pharmacological ligands, interpret signals from inside and outside the cell, facilitate chromatin condensation, and interact with the general transcription apparatus at target gene promoters. Additionally, there are corepressors that act as negative regulators of ER activity in different physiological or pharmacological contexts, adding complexity to ER action. This review also discusses ongoing efforts to develop pharmaceutical agents that target the interactions between ERs and cofactors as potential therapeutics for estrogen-related pathologies.

title: Autophagy and mTORC1 regulate the stochastic phase of somatic cell reprogramming
text: During the process of reprogramming mouse fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells using four reprogramming factors (Sox2, Oct4, Klf4, and c-Myc), referred to as 4F, autophagy is robustly induced. This induction occurs independently of p53 activation and is facilitated by the simultaneous downregulation of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and the upregulation of autophagy-related genes. The 4F factors work together to repress mTORC1, but differ in their regulation of autophagy-related genes. Klf4 and c-Myc induce these genes, while Sox2 and Oct4 inhibit them. On one hand, inhibiting mTORC1 promotes reprogramming by facilitating cell reshaping, including mitochondrial remodeling and reduction in cell size. On the other hand, mTORC1 paradoxically hinders reprogramming by triggering autophagy. Autophagy does not play a role in cell reshaping during reprogramming, but instead degrades p62. The accumulation of p62 in cells lacking autophagy actually aids in reprogramming. Our findings demonstrate a complex signaling network involving the inhibition of mTORC1 and the induction of autophagy in the early stages of reprogramming. The delicate balance between these processes ultimately determines the efficiency of reprogramming.

title: Lithium Therapy Improves Neurological Function and Hippocampal Dendritic Arborization in a Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1 Mouse Model
text:
Background: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a neurodegenerative disorder that is inherited dominantly and characterized by progressive motor and cognitive dysfunction. The disease is caused by an expanded polyglutamine tract in a protein called ataxin 1 (ATXN1). The pathogenesis of SCA1 involves a complex process that starts with misfolding of ATXN1, leading to dysregulation of gene expression. Lithium has been shown to have neuroprotective effects in various conditions, possibly by influencing gene expression. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of lithium treatment in a mouse model of SCA1 that closely resembles the human disease.

Methods and Findings: We fed Sca1154Q/2Q mice, which carry the mutant ATXN1 gene, and their normal littermates either regular chow or chow supplemented with 0.2% lithium carbonate. The mice that received lithium showed improvements in motor coordination, learning, and memory compared to those on regular chow. Importantly, these motor improvements were observed when treatment was started before symptoms appeared or after symptom onset. In terms of neuropathology, lithium treatment prevented the reduction of dendritic branching in mutant hippocampal pyramidal neurons. We also found that lithium treatment restored the levels of isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (Icmt), which is down-regulated early in the course of SCA1 and serves as a marker of mutant ATXN1 toxicity.

Conclusions: The positive effects of lithium on early markers of SCA1 pathogenesis, as well as its beneficial effects on behavior and neuropathology in an authentic disease model, suggest that it could be a promising treatment for human SCA1 patients.

title: The progression from hypertension to congestive heart failure.
text: GOALS - The objectives of this study were to examine the relative and population-attributable risks of hypertension in the development of congestive heart failure (CHF), to analyze the progression from hypertension to CHF over time, and to identify risk factors that contribute to the development of overt heart failure in individuals with hypertension. DESIGN - This study utilized an inception cohort design. SETTING - The study took place in a general community. PARTICIPANTS - The participants included individuals aged 40 to 89 years who were originally part of the Framingham Heart Study and Framingham Offspring Study. They were free of CHF at the start of the study, which began on January 1, 1970, to reflect more contemporary experiences. EXPOSURE MEASURES - Hypertension was defined as having a blood pressure of at least 140 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg diastolic, or current use of medications for high blood pressure. Other potential risk factors for CHF were assessed through periodic clinic examinations. OUTCOME MEASURE - The main outcome measure was the development of CHF. RESULTS - A total of 5143 eligible subjects were included in the study, providing 72422 person-years of observation. Over a follow-up period of up to 20.1 years (mean, 14.1 years), 392 new cases of heart failure were identified. In 91% of these cases, hypertension preceded the development of heart failure. After adjusting for age and other heart failure risk factors, the hazard of developing heart failure was approximately 2-fold higher in hypertensive men and 3-fold higher in hypertensive women compared to normotensive individuals. Multivariable analyses showed that hypertension had a significant population-attributable risk for CHF, accounting for 39% of cases in men and 59% in women. Among individuals with hypertension, myocardial infarction, diabetes, left ventricular hypertrophy, and valvular heart disease were predictive of an increased risk for CHF in both men and women. Survival rates following the onset of hypertensive CHF were low, with only 24% of men and 31% of women surviving 5 years. CONCLUSIONS - Hypertension was found to be the most common risk factor for CHF in this population-based sample, contributing to a significant proportion of heart failure cases. Implementing preventive strategies focused on early and aggressive blood pressure control is likely to be the most effective approach for reducing the incidence of CHF and its associated mortality.

title: Association of plasma resistin with glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria in hypertensive adults.
text: We conducted a study to investigate the relationship between resistin, a proinflammatory cytokine, and renal function in hypertensive adults without known coronary heart disease or stroke. We measured resistin levels in the plasma of 1575 participants and estimated their glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria. After adjusting for various risk factors, we found that higher resistin levels were associated with lower glomerular filtration rate in both black and non-Hispanic white participants. This association remained significant even after considering markers of insulin resistance and inflammation, and it was observed in participants with and without diabetes. Additionally, higher resistin levels were associated with higher albuminuria in participants with diabetes, regardless of their ethnicity. These associations were independent of coronary heart disease risk factors, hypertension medication use, and statin use. In conclusion, our findings suggest that higher resistin levels are linked to impaired renal function in hypertensive adults, particularly in those with diabetes.

title: Large-scale candidate gene scan reveals the role of chemoreceptor genes in host plant specialization and speciation in the pea aphid.
text: Understanding the factors that drive speciation is crucial for interpreting patterns of biodiversity. To establish a connection between barriers to gene flow and the origins of divergence, it is necessary to identify the genetic changes that contribute to adaptation and reproductive isolation. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to studying the genetics of speciation, which complements the commonly used methods of mapping quantitative trait loci and conducting genome-wide scans for selection. Specifically, we present a large-scale candidate gene approach using sequence capture to identify the genetic changes associated with reproductive isolation in the pea aphid, a model organism for studying ecological speciation. By employing targeted resequencing, we were able to expand the candidate gene approach and focus on the role of chemosensory gene families in host plant specialization. Through screening for divergence under selection at 172 candidate and noncandidate loci, we discovered a small number of loci that exhibit significant differentiation among host races, primarily involving odorant and gustatory receptor genes. This study provides the first evidence that certain chemoreceptor genes, often found in close proximity in the genome, may play a crucial role in local adaptation and reproductive isolation in the pea aphid, as well as potentially other phytophagous insects. Our approach paves the way for a new avenue of research in the functional genomics of ecological speciation.

title: The cancer stem cell hypothesis: a guide to potential molecular targets.
text: According to prevailing theories, cancer occurs when somatic cells multiply uncontrollably due to the accumulation of random mutations in genes that regulate cell growth. However, there have been conflicting findings regarding this mutation theory. These discrepancies could potentially be explained by the presence of residual tumor cells known as Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs). These CSCs play a crucial role in the development, maintenance, spread, and recurrence of tumors. In this article, we provide an overview of the current knowledge on CSCs, particularly focusing on the potential identification of specific markers for CSCs. Additionally, we explore the clinical implications of targeting CSCs in the treatment of cancer.

title: Serum amyloid A: An acute-phase protein involved in tumour pathogenesis
text: The production of the acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (SAA) is mainly controlled by inflammation-related cytokines. A high level of circulating SAA could serve as an excellent indicator for both acute and chronic inflammatory diseases. However, SAA is also produced in tissues outside the liver, such as human carcinoma metastases and cancer cell lines. A growing body of in vitro evidence supports the idea that SAA plays a role in the development of cancer and neoplastic diseases. Increasing data suggests that SAA could be included in a group of biomarkers that detect a series of physiological events reflecting tumor growth and the body's response. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the various ways in which SAA may contribute to tumor formation, speed up tumor progression and metastasis, and enhance our understanding of this acute-phase protein as a potential link between chronic inflammation and neoplasia.

title: Body size and outcomes on peritoneal dialysis in the United States.
text:
The background of this study is that being overweight is often seen as a reason to not use peritoneal dialysis. The main objective of the study was to determine if the actual mortality rates support this belief. 

The study was conducted as a retrospective cohort study of Medicare patients in the United States who started dialysis between 1995 and 2000. There were a total of 418,021 patients, with 11% of them using peritoneal dialysis. 

The results showed that 7% of the patients were underweight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2), 27% were overweight (BMI 25.0 to 29.9 kg/m2), and 23% were obese (BMI > 29.9 kg/m2) at the start of dialysis. Compared to patients with a normal BMI, the odds of starting peritoneal dialysis were lower for underweight patients and higher for overweight patients, but not significantly different for obese patients. 

Among the patients using peritoneal dialysis, the adjusted mortality rates were higher for underweight patients in the first, second, and third year. For overweight patients, the mortality rates were lower in the first and second year, but not significantly different in the third year. For obese patients, the mortality rates were not significantly different in any of the years. These associations remained similar even after accounting for patients who switched to hemodialysis. 

In terms of transplantation, underweight patients had lower rates, while overweight and obese patients had similar or slightly higher rates compared to patients with a normal BMI. 

For patients who switched to hemodialysis, underweight patients had slightly lower rates, while overweight and obese patients had higher rates. 

In conclusion, although overweight and obese patients are less likely to start peritoneal dialysis, they have longer survival rates compared to underweight patients. This cannot be fully explained by lower transplantation and technique survival rates.

title: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome: a machine designed to destroy
text: The APC/C, also known as the anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome, is a crucial ubiquitin ligase involved in various processes within and beyond the eukaryotic cell cycle. It stands out as the most intricate molecular machinery capable of catalyzing ubiquitylation reactions, comprising over a dozen subunits that come together to form a massive 1.5-MDa complex. Recent findings have shed light on numerous unforeseen mechanisms governing the activity of APC/C, offering initial understanding of how this unique ubiquitin ligase identifies its targets.

title: Regulation of the expression of alkaline phosphatase in a human breast-cancer cell line.
text: Treatment of BC-M1 breast cancer cells with dexamethasone resulted in the production of placental-type alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Both the activity and mRNA levels of ALP in the cells were elevated. The increase in ALP activity by dexamethasone was dependent on the duration and dosage of treatment. The accumulation of ALP mRNA was hindered by actinomycin D and cycloheximide, suggesting that the induction of ALP involves other regulatory proteins. Interestingly, retinoic acid had contrasting effects on ALP expression compared to dexamethasone. Additionally, both retinoic acid and phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate significantly reduced the dexamethasone-induced ALP expression. Analysis of thermostability and sensitivity to amino acid inhibitors revealed that BC-M1 ALP closely resembles the placental form. Northern hybridization analysis confirmed that ALP mRNA transcripts in BC-M1 cells and term placenta are similar in size and distinct from those in choriocarcinoma cells. Furthermore, the degradation of BC-M1 ALP mRNA had a similar half-life of 27 hours in untreated and dexamethasone- or retinoic acid-treated cells. These findings demonstrate that dexamethasone primarily increases ALP gene transcription to induce ALP in BC-M1 cells.

title: Declining tuberculosis notification trend associated with strengthened TB and expanded HIV care in Swaziland.
text: This retrospective observational review examines the efforts made by the Swaziland National Tuberculosis (TB) Control Programme from 2004 to 2014. The aim is to highlight the discrepancy between the actual decrease in reported TB cases and the rise in estimated incidence. The analysis of policies and practices reveals that the most influential factors contributing to the decline in TB case notification are the improved accessibility of antiretroviral therapy for TB patients with co-infections, the successful integration of TB and human immunodeficiency virus services in the country, and enhancements in the implementation of various components such as directly observed treatment, active case finding, and rapid diagnosis through the utilization of new technologies.

title: Advances in techniques of testing mycobacterial drug sensitivity, and the use of sensitivity tests in tuberculosis control programmes.
text:
A paper was published in 1961 following an informal international consultation of tuberculosis bacteriology specialists. The purpose of the consultation was to establish criteria and technical procedures for reliable sensitivity tests of the three main antituberculosis drugs: isoniazid, streptomycin, and p-aminosalicylic acid. The sensitivity tests included the absolute-concentration method, the resistance-ratio method, and the proportion method. 

Seven years later, another consultation was held to review the latest advancements in the field and discuss the practical implementation of sensitivity tests in tuberculosis control programs. During this consultation, the participants agreed on the definition of drug sensitivity and resistance. They emphasized the importance of using a discrimination approach to calibrate sensitivity tests. 

The present paper contains the perspectives of the participants, as well as descriptions of the sensitivity tests used by the Medical Research Council of Great Britain for both first- and second-line drugs (minimal inhibitory concentration and resistance-ratio methods). Additionally, it includes information on the two main variants of the proportion method developed by the Institut Pasteur, Paris, and a method for calibrating sensitivity tests.

title: Time from finding abnormality on mass-screening to final diagnosis of lung cancer.
text:
Mass-screening for lung cancer is a unique system in Japan. This study examines the time it takes from detecting an abnormality on mass-screening to receiving a final diagnosis of lung cancer. Out of the 517 patients with lung cancer admitted to our hospital over a 10-year period until December 2001, 83 (16.1%) were identified through mass-screening. We analyzed the medical records of these 83 patients to determine the time intervals between the mass-screening and the pathological diagnosis with clinical staging.

In 74.7% of cases, the time from the mass-screening to the hospital visit was less than 2 months. However, 6.0% of patients visited the hospital more than 6 months after the mass-screening. There was no significant difference in the time intervals based on gender (p=0.0680) or age (p=0.1532). Among the 60 patients referred from outside, on average, they visited our hospital 0.5 month after seeking medical attention at a nearby clinic, and it took an additional 0.5 month at our hospital to receive a pathological diagnosis of lung cancer with TNM staging.

There was a statistically significant difference in survival between patients diagnosed within 4 months and those diagnosed after 4 months from the screening (p=0.0487). While the majority of cases had an acceptable interval, there is still room for improvement to minimize delays and maximize the benefits of early cancer detection.

title: Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates B-cell reactivity, subset differentiation, and trafficking molecule expression.
text: The role of the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) in B cells is not well understood, although it is known to be important for the normal movement of T lymphocytes. Our study reveals that when KLF2 is specifically lacking in B cells, the expression of trafficking molecules CD62L and β7-integrin is reduced. Surprisingly, the expression of sphingosine-1 phosphate receptor 1, a key target of KLF2 in T cells, is only minimally affected. The absence of Klf2 leads to a significant decrease in the B1 B-cell population and a notable increase in transitional and marginal zone B-cell numbers. Furthermore, KLF2-deficient B cells exhibit increased apoptosis and impaired proliferation after B-cell receptor cross-linking. Analysis of gene expression shows that KLF2-deficient follicular B cells share several characteristics with normal marginal zone B cells, including reduced expression of signaling molecules that may contribute to impaired activation of these cells. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that KLF2 plays a crucial role in determining the differentiation and functional responsiveness of mature B cells.

title: Antibiotics and risk of subsequent first-time acute myocardial infarction.
text: New evidence suggests that certain bacterial infections may be linked to an increased risk of developing acute myocardial infarction (heart attack). If this causal association exists, individuals who have used antibiotics that are effective against these bacteria, regardless of the reason for use, may have a lower risk of experiencing a heart attack compared to non-users.
