The objective of this study was to investigate whether previous use of antibiotics reduces the risk of developing a first-time heart attack. The study involved a population-based case-control analysis using data from the General Practice Research Database in the United Kingdom, which included 350 general practices. The study included 3,315 case patients aged 75 years or younger who had experienced a first-time heart attack between 1992 and 1997, as well as 13,139 controls without a history of heart attack who were matched to the cases based on age, sex, general practice attended, and calendar time. The main outcome measures were the use of antibiotics among individuals with and without a history of heart attack. The results showed that individuals with a history of heart attack were significantly less likely to have used tetracycline antibiotics or quinolones. However, no significant effect was found for the previous use of macrolides, sulfonamides, penicillins, or cephalosporins. These findings provide further evidence, although indirect, for a potential association between bacterial infections susceptible to tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics and the risk of heart attack. Further research is needed to better understand the role of infections in the development of heart attacks.

title: Thrombopoietin/MPL signaling regulates hematopoietic stem cell quiescence and interaction with the osteoblastic niche.
text: The maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) relies on their interaction with a specific environment known as the niche. In this study, we demonstrate that a subset of long-term (LT)-HSCs in the adult bone marrow (BM) express a receptor called MPL, which binds to thrombopoietin (THPO). These LT-HSCs are in a dormant state and are closely associated with osteoblastic cells that produce THPO. When THPO binds to MPL, it activates a signaling pathway that increases the expression of beta1-integrin and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors in HSCs. We found that inhibiting or stimulating the THPO/MPL pathway using an anti-MPL neutralizing antibody (AMM2) or THPO treatment, respectively, had opposite effects on the quiescence of LT-HSCs. Treatment with AMM2 reduced the number of dormant LT-HSCs and allowed the engraftment of exogenous HSCs without the need for irradiation. On the other hand, exogenous THPO temporarily increased the population of dormant HSCs and subsequently induced their proliferation in vivo. Taken together, these findings indicate that THPO/MPL signaling plays a crucial role in the regulation of LT-HSCs within the osteoblastic niche.

title: Interlaboratory reproducibility and proficiency testing within the human papillomavirus cervical cancer screening program in Catalonia, Spain.
text: In 2006, Catalonia implemented a screening protocol for cervical cancer that included testing for human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA using the Digene Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) assay. To ensure consistency between laboratories, a proficiency testing (PT) survey of HPV samples was conducted starting in 2008. The purpose of this study was to assess the reliability of the HC2 assay. Each participating laboratory provided 20 samples annually, with 5 samples randomly selected from each of the following relative light unit (RLU) intervals: <0.5, 0.5 to 0.99, 1 to 9.99, and ≥10. Kappa statistics were used to measure the agreement between the original and PT readings. Discrepant results were analyzed using bootstrapping. A total of 946 specimens were retested. The kappa values were 0.91 for positive/negative classification and 0.79 for the four RLU intervals. Upon retesting, the RLU values were consistently lower than the original test (P<0.005), regardless of the time elapsed between the two determinations (median, 53 days), possibly due to freeze-thaw cycles. The probability of obtaining discrepant results upon retesting depended on the RLU value; samples with RLU values in the 0.5 to 5 interval had a 10.80% probability of yielding discrepant results (95% confidence interval [CI], 7.86 to 14.33), compared to 0.85% probability for samples outside this interval (95% CI, 0.17 to 1.69). Overall, the HC2 assay demonstrated high consistency between laboratories. We have identified different confidence thresholds and proposed guidelines for future interlaboratory PT, as ensuring the quality of HPV DNA detection remains crucial for cervical cancer prevention screening programs.

title: The role of regulatory variation in complex traits and disease
text: We are currently experiencing an unprecedented period of advancement in the identification of genetic loci that contribute to variations in traits. These traits can range from growth and fitness in simple organisms to diseases in humans. However, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of how these loci actually impact these traits for the majority of cases. To bridge this gap, studies on the genetics of gene expression have emerged as a crucial tool for connecting variations in DNA sequences to observable characteristics. In this article, we will examine recent discoveries regarding the molecular nature of regulatory variants and explore how they influence the transcriptome and proteome. We will also delve into the conceptual progress made through studies on model organisms and provide examples of complete chains of causality that connect specific genetic variations to changes in gene expression. These changes, in turn, lead to physiological alterations and ultimately affect the risk of developing diseases.

title: Adhesion disengagement uncouples intrinsic and extrinsic forces to drive cytokinesis in epithelial tissues.
text: Cell invagination during cytokinesis is facilitated by a contractile actomyosin ring. However, in epithelial cells, the presence of E-cadherin-mediated adhesion between the cell cortices raises questions about the process of invagination, the formation of new junctions, and the maintenance of tissue integrity. Research conducted on Drosophila embryos has revealed that apicobasal cleavage is polarized, with invagination occurring more rapidly from the basal side compared to the apical side. The contraction of the ring is regulated by septin filaments and Anillin, but its polarized constriction is not. Instead, the polarized cleavage is attributed to the mechanical attachment of the ring to E-cadherin complexes. The formation of the new junction involves the disengagement of local adhesion in the cleavage furrow, followed by the formation of new E-cadherin complexes at the newly formed interface. The disengagement of E-cadherin is influenced by the tension exerted by the cytokinetic ring and neighboring cells. Through our research, we have identified both intrinsic and extrinsic forces that are essential for cytokinesis and have developed a framework for understanding how tissue cohesion is maintained during epithelial division.

title: The epithelial inward rectifier channel Kir7.1 displays unusual K+ permeation properties.
text: We isolated cDNAs from rats and humans that encoded a polypeptide consisting of 360 amino acids. This polypeptide had a tertiary structure similar to inwardly rectifying K+ channel (Kir) subunits. We named these new proteins Kir7.1. They were less than 37% identical to other Kir subunits and had unique residues at conserved sites, particularly near the pore region. We found high levels of Kir7.1 transcripts in the brain, lung, kidney, and testis of rats. In rat brain sections, we used in situ hybridization to show that Kir7.1 mRNA was not present in neurons and glia, but it was strongly expressed in the secretory epithelial cells of the choroid plexus. We confirmed this expression pattern using in situ patch-clamp measurements. When we injected cRNA of Kir7.1 into Xenopus oocytes, we observed macroscopic Kir currents that had a very shallow dependence on external K+ concentration ([K+]e). This was different from all other Kir channels. At a holding potential of -100 mV, the inward current through Kir7.1 averaged -3.8 +/- 1.04 microA with 2 mM [K+]e and -4.82 +/- 1.87 microA with 96 mM [K+]e. In the pore region, Kir7.1 had a methionine at position 125, whereas other Kir channels had an arginine at that position. When we replaced this methionine with the conserved arginine in mutant Kir7.1 channels, the pronounced dependence of K+ permeability on [K+]e, which is characteristic of other Kir channels, was restored. Additionally, the sensitivity to Ba2+ increased by a factor of approximately 25 (Ki = 27 microM). These findings suggest that this specific site plays an important role in the regulation of K+ permeability in Kir channels by extracellular cations.

title: Oral fingolimod (FTY720) for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
text:
BACKGROUND: Fingolimod (FTY720) is a novel oral immunomodulating drug being studied for the treatment of relapsing multiple sclerosis.

METHODS: A total of 281 patients were randomly assigned to receive either oral fingolimod at a dose of 1.25 mg or 5.0 mg, or a placebo once daily. These patients were followed for 6 months with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical evaluations (core study, months 0 to 6). The primary endpoint was the total number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions recorded on T(1)-weighted MRI at monthly intervals for 6 months. In an extension study (months 7 to 12), the investigators and patients remained unaware of the dose assignments, and patients who initially received placebo were randomized again to one of the fingolimod doses.

RESULTS: A total of 255 patients completed the core study. The median total number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions on MRI was significantly lower with 1.25 mg of fingolimod (1 lesion, P<0.001) and 5.0 mg of fingolimod (3 lesions, P=0.006) compared to placebo (5 lesions). The annualized relapse rate was also significantly lower in the group given 1.25 mg of fingolimod (0.35, P=0.009) and 5.0 mg of fingolimod (0.36, P=0.01) compared to the placebo group (0.77). In the extension study, the number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions and relapse rates remained low in the groups that received continuous fingolimod, and both measures decreased in patients who switched from placebo to fingolimod. Adverse events included nasopharyngitis, dyspnea, headache, diarrhea, and nausea. Clinically asymptomatic elevations of alanine aminotransferase levels were more frequent with fingolimod (10 to 12%, vs. 1% in the placebo group). One case of the posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome occurred in the 5.0-mg group. Fingolimod was also associated with an initial reduction in heart rate and a modest decrease in forced expiratory volume in 1 second.

CONCLUSIONS: This proof-of-concept study demonstrated that fingolimod reduced the number of lesions detected on MRI and clinical disease activity in patients with multiple sclerosis. Further evaluation in larger, longer-term studies is warranted. (Clinicaltrials.gov numbers, NCT00333138 [core study] and NCT00235430 [extension].)

title: Nonoverlapping functions of DNA polymerases mu, lambda, and terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase during immunoglobulin V(D)J recombination in vivo.
text: The enzymes DNA polymerases mu (pol mu), lambda (pol lambda), and terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase (TdT) belong to the pol X family. They have similar sequences and functional domain organization. Previously, we discovered that pol mu is involved in light chain gene rearrangement but not heavy chain gene rearrangement, which was surprising. In this study, we found that immunoglobulin heavy chain junctions in animals lacking pol lambda are shorter in length but have normal N-additions. This suggests that pol lambda is recruited during heavy chain rearrangement before TdT comes into play. Contrary to previous laboratory studies, when we analyzed animals with all three enzymes deactivated, we found no overlapping or compensatory activities for V(D)J recombination between pol mu, pol lambda, and TdT. This intricate use of polymerases with different catalytic specificities may correspond to the specific role that the third hypervariable region plays in each immunoglobulin chain. Pol lambda maintains a wide range of heavy chain junctional diversity, while pol mu ensures a limited light chain junctional variability.

title: Moderate regular exercise increases basal production of nitric oxide in elderly women.
text: Vascular endothelial cells generate nitric oxide (NO), a powerful substance that dilates blood vessels and is believed to possess properties that can prevent the development of atherosclerosis. Consequently, it has been suggested that NO could be utilized to regulate vascular tone and hinder the progression of atherosclerosis. However, NO activity declines with age. In a previous study, we observed a significant increase in the concentration of plasma nitrite/nitrate (NOx), the stable end product of NO, in healthy young individuals following intense aerobic exercise training. Based on this, we hypothesized that lifestyle modifications, such as even mild regular exercise training, could enhance NO production in older individuals who were previously sedentary. To test this hypothesis, we measured the plasma NOx concentration before and after a 3-month regimen of mild aerobic exercise training (cycling on a leg ergometer at 80% of the ventilatory threshold for 30 minutes, 5 days a week) in elderly women. Additionally, we evaluated the plasma concentration of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), a second messenger of NO, in the same samples. The individual ventilatory threshold significantly increased after the 3-month exercise training, and there was a significant decrease in resting blood pressure. These findings suggest that the 3-month exercise training had favorable physiological effects in older women. The exercise training led to a significant increase in the plasma concentration of NOx, and there was also an increase in the plasma concentration of cGMP. This study indicates that even mild regular aerobic-endurance exercise can enhance NO production in older individuals who were previously sedentary, potentially resulting in beneficial effects (such as lowering blood pressure and preventing atherosclerosis through endogenous NO) on the cardiovascular system.

title: Competition between target sites of regulators shapes post-transcriptional gene regulation
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) play a crucial role in post-transcriptional gene regulation (PTGR) by controlling mRNA turnover, localization, and translation. These regulators achieve their effects by binding to specific sequences on their target mRNAs. Recent evidence suggests that competition for binding is a fundamental aspect of PTGR. Not only can miRNAs be rendered ineffective by the targets they interact with, a process known as 'sponging', but competition between binding sites on different RNAs can also result in regulatory crosstalk between transcripts. In this article, we present a quantitative model of competition effects under normal physiological conditions and examine the significance of endogenous sponges in PTGR, considering the key features that arise from these interactions.

title: Primary prevention of ischemic stroke: A statement for healthcare professionals from the Stroke Council of the American Heart Association.
text: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States, with over 700,000 incident strokes occurring annually and 4.4 million stroke survivors. In 1999, the economic burden of stroke was estimated to be $51 billion in direct and indirect costs. Despite advancements in treatment, prevention remains the best approach to reducing the burden of stroke. Identifying and targeting high-risk individuals for interventions is crucial, as there has been a leveling off of previous declines in stroke-related mortality and a possible increase in stroke incidence. To provide a comprehensive overview of established and potential stroke risk factors, the Stroke Council of the American Heart Association formed a writing group. This group utilized literature review, reference to guidelines, and expert opinion to summarize existing evidence and make recommendations. Risk factors for a first stroke were classified based on their potential for modification and the strength of evidence supporting them. Tables were provided to show the prevalence, population attributable risk, relative risk, and risk reduction with treatment for each factor. Population attributable risk indicates the proportion of ischemic strokes in the population that can be attributed to a specific risk factor.

title: Chimeric live, attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis (ChimeriVax-JE): phase 2 clinical trials for safety and immunogenicity, effect of vaccine dose and schedule, and memory response to challenge with inactivated Japanese encephalitis antigen.
text: ChimeriVax-JE is a vaccine designed to protect against Japanese encephalitis. It is made using the yellow fever (YF) 17D vaccine as a carrier. In a phase 2 trial, 99 adults were given either the ChimeriVax-JE vaccine, a placebo, or the YF 17D vaccine (YF-VAX). The ChimeriVax-JE vaccine was well tolerated, and there were no differences in side effects between the different groups. The presence of the ChimeriVax-JE and YF-VAX viruses in the bloodstream was brief and at low levels. Out of 87 subjects who received varying doses of ChimeriVax-JE, 82 (94%) developed neutralizing antibodies. A second dose given 30 days later did not enhance the immune response. Previous vaccination with YF did not interfere with ChimeriVax-JE, but there was a suggestion (although not statistically significant) that ChimeriVax-JE interfered with the effectiveness of YF-VAX given 30 days later. Another study looked at the immune response in individuals who had received ChimeriVax-JE 9 months prior and in those who had not received it before and were given the JE-VAX vaccine. Preimmune individuals showed a strong immune response. Overall, ChimeriVax-JE appears to be a safe vaccine that provides sufficient levels of neutralizing antibodies after a single dose.

title: Global prevalence of anxiety disorders: a systematic review and meta-regression.
text:
The prevalence of anxiety disorders worldwide is described in a highly variable manner in the literature. To address this, a systematic review and meta-regression were conducted to estimate the prevalence of anxiety disorders and identify factors that may influence these estimates. The results of this study will be used to inform the new Global Burden of Disease study.

To gather data, a systematic review was conducted on prevalence studies of anxiety disorders published between 1980 and 2009. Various sources, including electronic databases, reference lists, review articles, and monographs, were searched. Additionally, experts were contacted to identify any missing studies. Meta-regression analyses were then used to identify substantive and methodological factors associated with inter-study variability. The global prevalence of anxiety disorders was calculated, taking into account study methodology.

The findings of this study were based on 87 studies conducted in 44 countries. Current prevalence estimates ranged from 0.9% to 28.3%, while past-year prevalence estimates ranged from 2.4% to 29.8%. Substantive factors such as gender, age, culture, conflict and economic status, and urbanicity were found to account for the majority of variability. Methodological factors, including prevalence period, number of disorders, and diagnostic instrument, explained an additional 13% of variance between studies in the final multivariate model. After adjusting for methodological differences, the global current prevalence of anxiety disorders was estimated to be 7.3% (with a range of 4.8-10.9%). The prevalence varied across cultures, with African cultures having a prevalence of 5.3% and Euro/Anglo cultures having a prevalence of 10.4%.

In conclusion, anxiety disorders are common worldwide, and the factors identified in this study explain much of the variability in prevalence estimates. It is important to consider cultural differences in responses to survey instruments when studying anxiety disorders.

title: Expression of optineurin, a glaucoma-linked gene, is influenced by elevated intraocular pressure.
text: A recent study has linked Optineurin (OPTN), a protein associated with optic neuropathy, to 16.7% of families affected by primary open-angle glaucoma. Although the exact function of OPTN in the eye is still unknown, it is found in the trabecular meshwork, which plays a crucial role in maintaining intraocular pressure (IOP). To better understand the involvement of OPTN in glaucoma development, we examined its expression in response to factors known to be associated with the disease: elevated IOP, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha), and dexamethasone (DEX). These treatments were conducted on human organ cultures under conditions that mimic physiological pressure. Our findings reveal a significant upregulation of OPTN after 2, 4, and 7 days of sustained elevated IOP. Additionally, OPTN expression was induced 2.3-fold by TNFalpha and 2.6-fold by prolonged DEX treatment. These results provide evidence that OPTN is part of the transcriptome that responds to glaucomatous insults and support the protective role of this protein in the trabecular meshwork.

title: Prevention of malaria in long-term travelers.
text: This text discusses the challenges faced by long-term travelers in preventing malaria and the need for updated guidelines. The objective is to examine the risk of malaria in long-term travelers, recent developments in protective measures, and the safety of malaria prevention methods. The evidence was acquired through a comprehensive search of scientific publications, including MEDLINE, and additional references were obtained from various sources. The synthesis of evidence reveals that long-term travelers have a higher risk of malaria and often do not adhere to preventive measures. Different strategies are used, such as discontinuation of chemoprophylaxis, sequential regimens, emergency self-treatment, and seasonal prophylaxis. However, each strategy has its advantages and drawbacks. The issue of counterfeit drugs in malaria-endemic countries is also highlighted. Vivax malaria poses a significant risk to travelers, and current preventive regimens do not prevent relapses. Consensus guidelines are necessary for the prevention of malaria in long-term travelers. In conclusion, expert advice from travel medicine specialists is crucial, and prevention strategies should be tailored to individual travelers.

title: Activation of AMPKα2 in adipocytes is essential for nicotine-induced insulin resistance in vivo
text: Smoking cigarettes has a contradictory effect on the human body, as it promotes weight loss while also causing insulin resistance (IR) and high levels of insulin in the blood. However, the reasons behind these effects are not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that nicotine, a major component of cigarette smoke, specifically activates AMP-activated protein kinase α2 (AMPKα2) in fat cells. This activation leads to the phosphorylation of MAP kinase phosphatase-1 (MKP1) at serine 334, triggering its degradation through the proteasome. The reduction of MKP1 caused by nicotine leads to abnormal activation of both p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase and c-Jun N-terminal kinase. This, in turn, increases the phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) at serine 307. The phosphorylation of IRS1 leads to its degradation, inhibition of protein kinase B, and the loss of insulin's ability to inhibit the breakdown of fats. As a result, nicotine promotes lipolysis, leading to weight loss. However, this increase in lipolysis also raises the levels of free fatty acids in the bloodstream, causing insulin resistance in tissues that are sensitive to insulin. These findings establish AMPKα2 as a crucial mediator of nicotine-induced insulin resistance throughout the body, despite reductions in body fat.

title: Availability of evidence of benefits on overall survival and quality of life of cancer drugs approved by European Medicines Agency: retrospective cohort study of drug approvals 2009-13
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the availability of data on overall survival and quality of life benefits for cancer drugs approved in Europe. The study design was a retrospective cohort study, and the data was obtained from publicly accessible regulatory and scientific reports on cancer approvals by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) from 2009 to 2013. The main outcome measures included the design features of pivotal and postmarketing trials, such as randomisation, crossover, and blinding, as well as the comparators and endpoints used. The availability and magnitude of benefit on overall survival or quality of life were determined at the time of approval and after market entry. The European Society for Medical Oncology Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale (ESMO-MCBS) was used to assess the clinical value of the reported gains in published studies of cancer drugs.

The results of the study showed that between 2009 and 2013, the EMA approved the use of 48 cancer drugs for 68 indications. Out of these, eight indications (12%) were approved based on a single arm study. At the time of market approval, there was a significant prolongation of survival in 24 out of the 68 indications (35%). The magnitude of the benefit on overall survival ranged from 1.0 to 5.8 months, with a median of 2.7 months. Additionally, there was an improvement in quality of life in seven out of the 68 indications (10%) at the time of market approval. In the postmarketing period, out of the 44 indications that initially showed no evidence of a survival gain, three (7%) showed evidence for extension of life, and five (11%) reported a benefit on quality of life. Overall, out of the 68 cancer indications with EMA approval and a median follow-up of 5.4 years, only 35 (51%) showed a significant improvement in survival or quality of life, while 33 (49%) remained uncertain. Among the 23 indications associated with a survival benefit, less than half (11/23, 48%) were judged to have a clinically meaningful benefit according to the ESMO-MCBS tool.

In conclusion, this study found that most cancer drugs approved by the EMA between 2009 and 2013 entered the market without evidence of benefit on survival or quality of life. Even after a minimum of 3.3 years after market entry, there was still no conclusive evidence that these drugs either extended or improved life for most cancer indications. When there were survival gains, they were often marginal compared to existing treatment options or placebo.

title: A cluster randomized, controlled trial of breast and cervix cancer screening in Mumbai, India: methodology and interim results after three rounds of screening.
text: Cervix and breast cancers are prevalent among women worldwide and have a significant impact on developing countries. In May 1998, the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, India, initiated a screening trial for these cancers with the support of a grant from the NCI (US). The trial employed trained primary health workers to provide health education, visual inspection of the cervix using 4% acetic acid-VIA, and clinical breast examination in the screening group, while the control group only received health education. The trial consisted of four rounds of screening every two years, followed by eight years of monitoring for incidence and mortality rates of cervix and breast cancers. This article presents the methodology and interim results after three rounds of screening. The screening and control groups were well-randomized, with 75,360 participants in the screening arm and 76,178 in the control arm. In the screening arm, high participation rates, low attrition, and good compliance with diagnostic confirmation were observed. Additionally, there was a significant decrease in the stage of cancer at diagnosis, a high rate of completion for treatment, and improving case fatality ratios. Participants in the screening arm who had been screened and those who had never been screened showed notable differences in religion, language, age, education, occupation, income, and health-seeking behavior for gynecological and breast-related issues. During the same period, the control arm demonstrated excellent participation in health education, low attrition, and a substantial number of symptomatic referrals for both cervix and breast concerns.

title: Evidence for energy-dependent accumulation of paraquat into rat lung
text: The herbicide paraquat, also known as N,N′-dimethyl 4,4′-bipyridilium, has the potential to cause widespread oedema and fibrosis in the human lung if accidentally ingested. In cases where death occurs several weeks after ingestion, there are no visible changes in the lungs during the initial days. Various animal experiments have demonstrated that the lung is the primary organ affected by paraquat. When administered to animals, paraquat initially accumulates in the lung and remains there. This retention is believed to be linked to the development of lung damage, although the exact mechanism is currently unknown.

title: Role of gut commensal microflora in the development of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
text: Mucosal tolerance has been recognized as a potentially significant pathway for treating autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis in humans and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). However, there is limited knowledge about the ability of commensal gut bacteria to induce and sustain peripheral immune tolerance. To investigate this, we administered a broad spectrum of antibiotics orally to inbred SJL and C57BL/6 mice in order to reduce their gut microflora. The reduction of commensal bacteria in the gut hindered the development of EAE. Interestingly, mice treated with antibiotics intraperitoneally did not experience a significant decline in gut microflora and developed EAE similar to untreated mice. This suggests that the decrease in disease activity was linked to changes in the gut bacterial population. The protection observed was associated with a decrease in proinflammatory cytokines and an increase in IL-10 and IL-13. We conducted an adoptive transfer of a small number of IL-10-producing CD25(+)CD4(+) T cells (>75% FoxP3(+)) that were purified from cervical lymph nodes of mice with commensal bacteria. This transfer reduced EAE symptoms, and in vivo neutralization of CD25(+) cells indicated the role of regulatory T cells in maintaining peripheral immune homeostasis. Our findings demonstrate that modifying gut commensal bacteria with antibiotics can modulate peripheral immune tolerance, providing protection against EAE. This approach may present a new therapeutic strategy for treating multiple sclerosis and potentially other autoimmune conditions.

title: Epidemiology of surgically managed pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence.
text:
AIM: This study aims to determine the occurrence of surgically treated pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence in a population-based group and describe their clinical characteristics.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted, including all patients who underwent surgical treatment for prolapse and incontinence in 1995. The study population consisted of 149,554 women aged 20 or older who were members of Kaiser Permanente Northwest. A standardized data-collection form was used to review the medical records of the 395 identified women. Variables examined included age, ethnicity, height, weight, vaginal parity, smoking history, medical history, and surgical history. Analysis involved calculating age-specific and cumulative incidences, as well as determining the number of primary and repeat operations performed for prolapse or incontinence.

RESULTS: The incidence of prolapse and incontinence increased with age. The lifetime risk of undergoing a single operation for these conditions by age 80 was 11.1%. The majority of patients were older, postmenopausal, parous, and overweight. Almost half were current or former smokers, and one-fifth had chronic lung disease. Reoperation was common, accounting for 29.2% of cases, and the time intervals between repeat procedures decreased with each subsequent repair.

CONCLUSION: Pelvic floor dysfunction is a significant health concern for older women, as evidenced by the 11.1% lifetime risk of undergoing surgery for pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence, as well as the high proportion of reoperations. Further epidemiologic research is needed to determine the causes, natural progression, and long-term treatment outcomes of these conditions.

title: Antihypertensive classes, cognitive decline and incidence of dementia: a network meta-analysis.
text: The aim of this study was to assess the impact of different types of antihypertensive drugs on the occurrence of dementia and cognitive function. A systematic review was conducted, including 19 randomized trials and 11 studies, which analyzed the effects of antihypertensive treatment on cognition and dementia incidence in hypertensive patients without prior cerebrovascular disorders. Network meta-analysis was used to compare the different classes of antihypertensive drugs. The results showed that regardless of the drug class, antihypertensive treatment had positive effects on overall cognition and most cognitive functions, except for language. It also reduced the risk of all-cause dementia by 9% compared to the control group. Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) were found to have the greatest benefits on overall cognition compared to placebo, β-blockers, diuretics, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. The change in blood pressure did not significantly differ between the different drug classes. In conclusion, this study supports the idea that antihypertensive treatment can help prevent cognitive decline and dementia, and suggests that ARBs may be the most effective class of drugs for this purpose.

title: Abnormal hemoglobins in a quarter million people.
text: Erythrocyte hemolysates from over 250,000 individuals in Alabama were subjected to electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.4. Samples showing abnormalities were further electrophoresed in citrate agar at pH 6.0. Mutant globin chains, excluding Hb S and C, were electrophoresed in urea-mercaptoethanol buffers at both pH 8.9 and pH 6.0. Additionally, 60 of these samples were structurally analyzed. Among approximately 6,000 samples from Caucasians, only three contained abnormal hemoglobins, namely Hb D Los Angeles, Hb J Baltimore, and one unidentified variant. Out of 249,000 samples from African Americans, around 29,000 exhibited detectable abnormalities through electrophoresis, with the majority associated with Hb S or C, occurring at frequencies of approximately 9% and 3% respectively. Roughly 1,000 samples displayed patterns of potential clinical significance. Twenty other mutant hemoglobins were identified in 164 families, with four of them (Hb Alabama, Montgomery, Titusville, and Mobile) being previously unknown. The methods employed in this study were rapid, cost-effective, and suitable for large-scale surveys. They provided precise characterizations of numerous mutant hemoglobins, and there were no discrepancies between the presumptive identifications based on these characterizations and the definitive identifications obtained from structural analyses.

title: Cellular adaptation to mechanical stress: role of integrins, Rho, cytoskeletal tension and mechanosensitive ion channels.
text: In order to comprehend how cells detect and adjust to mechanical stress, we conducted an experiment where we applied tensional forces to magnetic microbeads that were attached to integrin receptors on the cell surface. We then used optical microscopy to measure the displacement of the beads with high precision, down to the sub-micrometer level. The cells displayed four distinct types of mechanical responses: (1) an immediate viscoelastic response; (2) an early adaptive behavior characterized by a decrease in response to oscillatory forces over time; (3) a later adaptive response where the cells became stiffer under sustained static stresses lasting more than 15 seconds; and (4) a large-scale repositioning response that occurred when the stress was prolonged for over a minute. Importantly, these adaptation responses had different biochemical characteristics. The immediate and early responses were influenced by dissipating the cytoskeletal prestress (isometric tension) chemically, whereas the later adaptive response was not affected by this. The repositioning response could be prevented by inhibiting tension through interference with Rho signaling, similar to the immediate and early responses. However, it could also be prevented by blocking mechanosensitive ion channels or inhibiting Src tyrosine kinases. Cooling the cells to 4 degrees Celsius to slow down biochemical remodeling suppressed all adaptive responses. Therefore, cells employ multiple mechanisms to detect and react to changes in mechanical stress levels applied to integrins, both static and dynamic in nature.

title: Cutting edge: Candida albicans hyphae formation triggers activation of the Nlrp3 inflammasome.
text: The role of the proinflammatory cytokine IL-1beta in antifungal immunity is important, but how fungal pathogens trigger IL-1beta secretion is not well understood. In this study, we found that Candida albicans infection activates the Nlrp3 inflammasome, leading to the release of IL-1beta. The ability of C. albicans to transition from a single-celled yeast form to a filamentous form is crucial for Nlrp3 inflammasome activation. Mutants of C. albicans that cannot form hyphae were unable to induce IL-1beta secretion in macrophages. Additionally, mice lacking Nlrp3 showed increased susceptibility to C. albicans infection, indicating the important role of Nlrp3 in the innate immune response to this pathogen.

title: Type 2 diabetes and subsequent incidence of breast cancer in the Nurses' Health Study.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the potential link between type 2 diabetes and the incidence of invasive breast cancer. Previous research has suggested that insulin resistance, a characteristic of type 2 diabetes, may increase the risk of breast cancer. We conducted a prospective study using data from the Nurses' Health Study, which followed 116,488 female nurses aged 30-55 years old from 1976 to 1996 for the occurrence of type 2 diabetes and until 1998 for incident invasive breast cancer. Medical records and pathology reports were used to verify breast cancer cases. 

During the follow-up period of 2.3 million person-years, we identified 6,220 women with type 2 diabetes and 5,189 cases of invasive breast cancer. Our findings showed that women with type 2 diabetes had a slightly higher incidence of breast cancer compared to those without diabetes (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.17; 95% CI 1.01-1.35). This association remained significant even after adjusting for factors such as age, obesity, family history of breast cancer, history of benign breast disease, reproductive factors, physical activity, and alcohol consumption. However, the association was only observed among postmenopausal women (HR = 1.16; 0.98-1.62) and not premenopausal women (HR = 0.83; 0.48-1.42). Furthermore, the association was more pronounced among women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer (HR = 1.22; 1.01-1.47). 

In conclusion, our study suggests that women with type 2 diabetes may have a slightly increased risk of developing breast cancer, particularly among postmenopausal women and those with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer.

title: Virus-encoded microRNAs.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have attracted significant attention due to their crucial role in various cellular processes such as immune function, apoptosis, and tumorigenesis. Numerous virus families have been found to encode miRNAs, and our understanding of their involvement in the viral infectious cycle is expanding. However, despite the identification of over 225 viral miRNAs, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of their functions. In this article, we focus on a few well-studied viral miRNAs to extract common themes in their activities, including self-regulation of viral gene expression, evasion of host defenses, and their likely role in maintaining latent and persistent infections. We propose that while the molecular mechanisms and machinery may be similar, most viral miRNAs may have evolved to target viral-encoded transcripts or unique networks of host genes. This includes a potentially abundant class of viral miRNAs that specifically regulate one or a few key host genes. We also discuss the future directions for the field, emphasizing the importance of additional functional studies using targeted viral miRNA mutants in relevant infection models.

title: Wolfram syndrome 1 and adenylyl cyclase 8 interact at the plasma membrane to regulate insulin production and secretion
text: The dysfunction of pancreatic β-cells and the progression of type 2 diabetes are caused by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Wolfram syndrome 1 (WFS1) is known to regulate the ER stress signalling pathway, but its role in β-cell function is not well understood. In this study, we present evidence that WFS1 is crucial for the production of cyclic AMP stimulated by glucose and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), as well as the regulation of insulin biosynthesis and secretion. When stimulated by glucose, WFS1 moves from the ER to the plasma membrane, where it forms a complex with adenylyl cyclase 8 (AC8), an enzyme essential for generating cAMP in β-cells and integrating glucose and GLP-1 signals. ER stress and mutant WFS1 hinder the formation of this complex and the activation of AC8, resulting in reduced cAMP synthesis and insulin secretion. These findings demonstrate that a protein related to ER stress plays a distinct role outside the ER by regulating both insulin biosynthesis and secretion. The decrease in WFS1 protein on the plasma membrane during ER stress contributes to β-cell dysfunction and the progression of type 2 diabetes.

title: Two Rice GRAS Family Genes Responsive to N-Acetylchitooligosaccharide Elicitor are Induced by Phytoactive Gibberellins: Evidence for Cross-Talk Between Elicitor and Gibberellin Signaling in Rice Cells
text: This study presents data that demonstrates the rapid induction of two genes, CIGR1 and CIGR2, from the GRAS family in rice. These genes, known as chitin-inducible gibberellin-responsive genes, are activated by the powerful elicitor N-acetylchitooligosaccharide (GN) and exogenous gibberellins. The level of mRNA accumulation depends on the dose and activity of the gibberellins, indicating that a specific biological receptor is involved in recognizing and transmitting signals upon exposure to these phytoactive compounds. Pharmacological analysis further reveals that the accumulation of CIGR1 and CIGR2 mRNA in response to gibberellin treatment relies on protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events. Interestingly, in rice calli derived from two different mutants, slender rice 1 and d1, CIGR1 and CIGR2 are induced by the GN elicitor but not by gibberellin. This suggests that the signal transduction pathway triggered by gibberellin is separate from that activated by GN. Additionally, it implies that CIGR1 and CIGR2 have distinct roles in defense and development, respectively, indicating their dual functionality.

title: Ghrelin's second life: from appetite stimulator to glucose regulator.
text: Ghrelin, a hormone produced by the stomach, was the first hormone discovered to stimulate appetite. It is made up of 28 amino acids and requires a specific modification at Ser³, which is facilitated by an enzyme called ghrelin O-acyltransferase (GOAT), in order to be biologically active. Ghrelin works by binding to its receptor (GRLN-R) on neurons in the hypothalamus, specifically in the arcuate nucleus, to increase food intake. It is found throughout the body and is involved in various physiological functions, including the release of growth hormone, gastric emptying, and regulation of body weight. Ghrelin and its receptor are also present in the pancreas, suggesting a local role in physiological processes. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of ghrelin and its receptor in the regulation of blood glucose levels, which is the main focus of this review. Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain how ghrelin regulates blood glucose, with one possibility being its impact on insulin secretion. While there is some debate, most studies suggest that ghrelin inhibits insulin secretion, leading to elevated glucose levels in the bloodstream. This suggests that ghrelin may contribute to the development of diabetes. Given the increasing prevalence of obesity-related type 2 diabetes, there is a need for new therapies that target both energy balance and glucose regulation. Antagonists of the ghrelin-GOAT signaling pathway show promise as potential treatments for this disease.

title: Histone acetylation and deacetylation in yeast
text: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, histone acetylation and deacetylation take place through the recruitment of acetyltransferase and deacetylase enzymes to gene promoters. Additionally, these processes can affect most nucleosomes in a widespread manner. Recent discoveries have revealed that histone acetylation plays a role not only in transcription but also in DNA replication, repair, and the formation of heterochromatin. Interestingly, certain lysines that can be acetylated serve as binding sites for regulatory factors. Furthermore, it is worth noting that histone deacetylation is not solely repressive but can also be necessary for gene activity.

title: Neuroinflammation in spinal cord injury: therapeutic targets for neuroprotection and regeneration.
text: The occurrence of a traumatic spinal cord injury initiates a complex inflammatory reaction in the local area, which can either enhance the healing process or worsen the damage. The cellular and molecular immune cascade that occurs after the injury changes over time and distance from the site of the injury. During this process, various substances like cytokines, proteases, and growth factors are produced, creating dynamic environments that can either lead to the death, damage, repair, or growth of neurons and glia. The cells present in this environment play a crucial role in determining whether repair or pathology will occur. In order to promote healing, it is important to manipulate the composition and characteristics of the cells involved in the neuroinflammatory response to the injury. This article examines how the neuroinflammatory response can influence outcomes such as pain, regeneration, and functional recovery.

title: Evaluation of systemic amyloidosis by scintigraphy with 123I-labeled serum amyloid P component.
text: In systemic amyloidosis, it has been challenging to monitor the distribution and progression of the disease as it can only be demonstrated through biopsy. However, we conducted a study to investigate whether labeled serum amyloid P component (SAP) could be utilized to locate amyloid deposits. We administered iodine-123 labeled SAP intravenously to 50 patients with biopsy-proven systemic amyloidosis, including 25 with the primary (AL) type and 25 with the secondary (AA) type. Additionally, we administered it to 26 control patients with disease and 10 healthy individuals. After 24 hours, we obtained whole-body images and regional views, which were then analyzed in a blinded manner. The results showed that in patients with amyloidosis, the 123I-SAP quickly and specifically localized in amyloid deposits. The scintigraphic images obtained were distinct and appeared to accurately identify the extent of amyloid deposition in all 50 patients. Conversely, there was no uptake of 123I-SAP in the control patients or healthy subjects. Among patients with AA amyloidosis, the spleen was consistently affected, while patients with the AL type showed uptake in the heart, skin, carpal region, and bone marrow. Notably, positive images were observed in six patients with previously negative or unsuccessful biopsies, and subsequent biopsies or autopsies confirmed the presence of amyloid. Furthermore, progressive amyloid deposition was observed in 9 out of 11 patients who were studied serially. In conclusion, scintigraphy using 123I-SAP can be employed for the diagnosis, localization, and monitoring of systemic amyloidosis.

title: The Neurovascular Unit Coming of Age: A Journey through Neurovascular Coupling in Health and Disease
text: The idea of the neurovascular unit (NVU) was established during the 2001 Stroke Progress Review Group meeting of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. It highlights the close connection between the brain and its blood vessels. Since then, the NVU has captured the attention of the neuroscience community, leading to significant advancements in the field. This article aims to evaluate the current understanding of the NVU, with a specific focus on its crucial role in linking neural activity and blood flow. The available evidence suggests a shift in the understanding of neurovascular coupling mechanisms. Previously, it was believed to be a one-dimensional process involving signaling between neurons, astrocytes, and local blood vessels. However, recent findings indicate that multiple cells release mediators, which engage distinct signaling pathways and effector systems throughout the entire cerebrovascular network in a highly coordinated manner. Although the dysfunction of the NVU in neurodegenerative diseases is not yet fully comprehended, it supports emerging theories that maintaining neurovascular health is essential for promoting brain health.

title: Effects of MAL61 and MAL62 overexpression on maltose fermentation of baker's yeast in lean dough.
text: Maltose is the primary fermentable sugar found in lean dough. In order to enhance the leavening capability of baker's yeast in lean dough, it is necessary to improve maltose metabolism. Two key factors involved in maltose metabolism are maltase (alpha-glucosidase, encoded by MAL62) and maltose permease (encoded by MAL61). However, the main factor that limits the rate of maltose metabolism and the leavening ability of baker's yeast is still unknown. To address this, we constructed strains that overexpressed MAL61 and/or MAL62 to determine the decisive factor for maltose metabolism in industrial baker's yeast in lean dough. Our findings indicate that increasing maltose permease activity through MAL61 overexpression resulted in less improvement in maltose fermentation compared to increasing maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression. Notably, a significant increase in maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression led to a 44% enhancement in the leavening ability of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough and a 39% increase in maltose metabolism in a medium containing glucose and maltose. Therefore, maltase is the limiting factor in maltose fermentation for industrial baker's yeast in lean dough. This study provides a basis for the development of industrial baker's yeast strains that facilitate rapid dough leavening.

title: Human papillomavirus genotype 31 does not express detectable microRNA levels during latent or productive virus replication.
text: Recent evidence suggests that several harmful DNA viruses produce their own microRNAs in infected cells. MicroRNAs have been found in various human and animal herpesviruses, as well as in polyoma- and adenoviruses. While the exact functions of these viral microRNAs are still unclear, it is likely that they play a crucial role in viral replication within the host. In this study, we examined the microRNAs expressed in human cells during different phases of the human papillomavirus genotype 31 (HPV31) replication cycle. Despite identifying over 500 cellular microRNAs, we did not find any HPV31-specific microRNAs. Based on this, we concluded that HPV31, and possibly other human papillomaviruses, do not produce viral microRNAs.

title: Integrated genomic profiling of endometrial carcinoma associates aggressive tumors with indicators of PI3 kinase activation.
text: We conducted a comprehensive analysis of primary endometrial carcinomas to identify features that can predict recurrent disease. Our analysis included genome-wide expression and copy-number data, as well as extensive clinical and histopathological information. By analyzing the expression data, we identified two distinct clusters with different phenotypes, including significant differences in disease-free survival. To understand the underlying mechanisms, we also examined amplifications, deletions, and loss of heterozygosity across the genome. We found 11 significantly amplified and 13 significantly deleted regions. Notably, amplifications of the oncogene PIK3CA in the 3q26.32 region were associated with poor prognosis and were found in the aggressive transcriptional cluster. Additionally, tumors with PIK3CA amplification showed signatures of PI3 kinase (PI3K) activation, which was also observed in aggressive tumors without PIK3CA amplification. Tumors with loss of PTEN expression or PIK3CA overexpression, but without PIK3CA amplification, also exhibited the PI3K activation signature, high protein expression of the PI3K pathway member STMN1, and an aggressive phenotype. However, mutations in PTEN or PIK3CA did not show the same expression profile or aggressive phenotype. STMN1 expression was found to have independent prognostic value. These findings highlight the importance of systematically characterizing the cancer genome in clinically annotated specimens and suggest that the PI3K pathway plays a crucial role in aggressive endometrial cancer.

title: Alteration of the Antitumor Immune Response by Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts
text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), a type of activated fibroblast found in the tumor microenvironment, play a crucial role in the complex interaction between tumors and surrounding tissues. CAFs are a prominent population of stromal cells in most human carcinomas and have been implicated in various processes such as tumor growth, angiogenesis, cancer stemness, remodeling of the extracellular matrix, tissue invasion, metastasis, and even resistance to chemotherapy. Over the past decade, research has shown that these activated fibroblasts also have a role in modulating the immune response against tumors. In this article, we provide an overview of our current understanding of how CAFs accomplish this task and discuss the potential therapeutic implications of targeting these cells.

title: Confusion and memory loss from capsular genu infarction: a thalamocortical disconnection syndrome?
text: We analyzed six patients who experienced a sudden change in behavior following an infarction in the inferior genu of the internal capsule. The acute syndrome displayed fluctuating alertness, lack of focus, memory loss, lack of motivation, difficulty making decisions, and slowed movement, indicating dysfunction in the frontal lobe. Contralateral weakness on one side of the body and difficulty speaking were generally mild, unless the infarction extended into the posterior limb. Five patients with left-sided infarctions underwent neuropsychological testing, which revealed severe verbal memory loss. Four patients also exhibited additional cognitive deficits consistent with dementia. A right-sided infarction caused temporary impairment in visuospatial memory. Functional brain imaging of three patients showed a localized decrease in blood flow in the same hemisphere, particularly in the inferior and medial frontal cortex. We conclude that the infarction in the capsular genu disrupted the inferior and anterior thalamic peduncles, leading to reduced activity in the frontal cortex on the same side. These findings suggest that one mechanism for cognitive decline resulting from a small infarction is the disconnection of white matter tracts between the thalamus and cortex, which can sometimes lead to "strategic-infarct dementia."

title: Neoadjuvant androgen ablation before radical prostatectomy in cT2bNxMo prostate cancer: 5-year results.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of 3 months of androgen deprivation on the positive margin rate in patients with prostate cancer. We conducted a multi-institutional prospective randomized trial between February 1992 and April 1994, involving patients with stage cT2b prostate cancer. A total of 138 patients received 3 months of leuprolide plus flutamide before radical prostatectomy, while 144 patients underwent radical prostatectomy only. We followed these patients for 5 years, which is the longest follow-up period for any neoadjuvant trial to date.

During the follow-up period, patients were monitored every 6 months with serum prostate specific antigen (PSA) testing. Biochemical recurrence was defined as a PSA level greater than 0.4 ng/ml. After 5 years, there was no significant difference in the biochemical recurrence rate between the two groups. In the neoadjuvant androgen ablation plus prostatectomy group, 64.8% of patients had a PSA level below 0.4 ng/ml, compared to 67.6% in the prostatectomy only group (p = 0.663).

Based on these findings, we conclude that although 3 months of androgen deprivation before radical prostatectomy appeared to decrease positive surgical margins, a 5-year follow-up does not show any difference in the recurrence rate. Therefore, until further studies demonstrate improved outcomes with longer periods of treatment, there is no indication for induction androgen deprivation before radical prostatectomy.

title: Full-length transcriptome assembly from RNA-Seq data without a reference genome.
text: The use of massively parallel sequencing of cDNA has greatly enhanced our ability to study transcriptomes in a thorough and efficient manner. However, current methods for reconstructing transcripts from this data often rely on aligning reads to a reference genome, which poses a problem when working with samples that have a partial or missing reference genome. In this study, we introduce the Trinity method, which allows for de novo assembly of full-length transcripts, and evaluate its effectiveness on samples from fission yeast, mouse, and whitefly, where a reference genome is not yet available. By constructing and analyzing sets of de Bruijn graphs in an efficient manner, Trinity is able to fully reconstruct a significant portion of transcripts, including those from alternatively spliced isoforms and recently duplicated genes. In comparison to other de novo transcriptome assemblers, Trinity is able to recover more full-length transcripts across a wide range of expression levels, with a sensitivity similar to methods that rely on genome alignments. Our approach offers a comprehensive solution for reconstructing transcriptomes in any sample, particularly when a reference genome is absent.

title: Growth restricted in vitro culture conditions alter the imprinted gene expression patterns of mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: The improper development of clones and chimeras derived from embryonic stem (ES) cells is often linked to growth abnormalities in the fetus. This can result in the production of offspring that are either over or underweight, with increased rates of neonatal mortality and morbidity. The blame for these issues is often placed on the incorrect epigenetic reprogramming of cells used in the procedures, particularly the role of imprinted genes in controlling fetal growth. To investigate this further, we examined the expression patterns of two growth regulatory imprinted genes, insulin-like growth factor II (Igf2) and H19, in mouse ES cells that were cultured under conditions that restricted growth and after being aged in vitro. We found that culturing the cells with serum-depleted media (starvation) and at high cell density (confluence) increased the expression of both imprinted genes and caused abnormal methylation profiles in specific regulatory regions of Igf2 and H19. These findings support the idea that restricting the growth of ES cells in culture can lead to changes in the methylation of regulatory domains and the expression patterns of imprinted genes, potentially contributing to the loss of developmental potential.

title: When is antipsychotic polypharmacy supported by research evidence? Implications for QI.
text: The use of multiple antipsychotic medications, known as antipsychotic polypharmacy, is becoming more common among both inpatients and outpatients. However, it is unclear whether this practice is appropriate or not. To address this, a review of research studies comparing the effects of multiple antipsychotics versus a single antipsychotic was conducted. The studies were divided into two groups based on whether the prescribing followed guideline recommendations for multiple-antipsychotic use. The results showed that there is no evidence supporting the use of antipsychotic polypharmacy in patients who have not previously shown resistance to monotherapy. However, in patients with a history of treatment resistance, there is limited data supporting antipsychotic polypharmacy, particularly when clozapine is combined with a second-generation antipsychotic. It is recommended to avoid antipsychotic polypharmacy in patients who do not meet guideline-recommended indications. The Joint Commission is implementing measures to assess and document the appropriateness of antipsychotic polypharmacy in hospital-based psychiatric services.

title: The Liverpool uveal melanoma liver metastases pathway: outcome following liver resection.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the outcomes of patients who underwent liver resection for metastases from uveal melanoma. The study included patients referred with uveal melanoma metastases over a period of 9 years. High-risk patients, after treatment of primary uveal melanoma, were given the option to participate in a 6-monthly non-contrast liver magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) surveillance. If liver metastases were detected, patients underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI, computer tomography (CT) of the thorax, and staging laparoscopy. 

Out of the 155 patients referred with uveal melanoma liver metastases, 17 (11.0%) underwent liver resection, and one patient received percutaneous radio-frequency ablation. Most patients who underwent liver resection had multiple metastectomies (n = 8), and three patients had major liver resections. The overall median survival for patients who underwent surgery/ablation was 27 (14-90) months, which was significantly better than the median survival of patients who received palliative treatment [median = 8(1-30) months, P < 0.001]. Among the patients who underwent surgery, 11 experienced recurrent disease [median = 13(6-36) months]. Patients who had a major liver resection had significantly poorer disease-free survival (P = 0.037). 

In conclusion, patients who are eligible for surgical resection of metastatic uveal melanoma have a more favorable survival compared to those who do not undergo surgery.

title: Smooth muscle lineage diversity in the chick embryo. Two types of aortic smooth muscle cell differ in growth and receptor-mediated transcriptional responses to transforming growth factor-beta.
text: Studies in the avian embryo have identified two types of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the tunica media of large elastic arteries. One type originates from the cardiac neural crest and is ectoderm in origin (referred to as Ect), while the other type arises from local mesenchyme of mesodermal origin (referred to as Mes). To investigate if differences in their primary embryonic lineage can lead to stable differences in growth and differentiation properties, we isolated Ect and Mes SMCs from the aorta of Day 14 chick embryos. Our findings show that despite their different origins, Ect and Mes SMCs express nearly identical levels of seven SMC differentiation markers in vitro, indicating their common smooth muscle developmental fates in vivo. However, Ect SMCs have a greater capacity for growth in serum-free medium compared to Mes SMCs, but only when short-range cell-cell interactions are permitted. Various peptide growth factors, such as PDGF-AA, PDGF-BB, basic FGF, EGF, and activin, stimulate DNA synthesis to similar extents in both Ect and Mes SMCs, suggesting that they do not account for the serum-independent growth observed in Ect SMCs. However, we observed significant lineage-dependent differences in SMC responses to transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta). TGF-beta 1 consistently increased DNA synthesis in Ect SMCs, while it inhibited growth in paired cultures of Mes SMCs. Further analysis revealed that Ect and Mes SMCs express similar levels of types I, II, and III TGF-beta receptors. However, Mes SMCs produce a fully glycosylated form of the type II TGF-beta receptor, whereas Ect SMCs only produce an unglycosylated form. These findings indicate that Ect and Mes SMCs exhibit lineage-dependent differences in growth and receptor-mediated transcriptional responses to TGF-betas. This suggests that different SMC populations within the same vessel wall may respond differently to signals involved in the formation of the tunica media during embryonic development and in the progression of vascular disease later in life.

title: THE USE OF LEAD CITRATE AT HIGH pH AS AN ELECTRON-OPAQUE STAIN IN ELECTRON MICROSCOPY
text: Preparing lead citrate involves the use of aqueous solutions of lead salts and saturated solutions of lead hydroxide as stains in electron microscopy. These stains enhance the electron-scattering properties of biological materials. However, lead hydroxide stains form insoluble lead carbonate when exposed to air, leading to contamination of the stained surfaces. To avoid this, elaborate procedures have been developed to exclude air or carbon dioxide during staining. Recently, modifications of Watson's lead hydroxide stain have been introduced, which utilize high pH and small amounts of tartrate as a weak complexing agent in addition to lead. These modified stains are less likely to contaminate the section surfaces with precipitated stain products. The stain described here differs from previous alkaline lead stains in that it contains an excess of the chelating agent citrate to sequester all the lead present. Lead citrate is soluble in basic solutions and has a high association constant with the lead ion. Tissue binding sites in biological components have a greater affinity for lead citrate, resulting in the sequestration of lead from the staining solution. Alkaline lead citrate solutions do not form precipitates when exposed to air for up to 30 minutes, making them less likely to contaminate sections. The resulting staining is intense and highlights various cellular structures. The stain solution is prepared by...

title: Amylase, Lipase, and Acute Pancreatitis in People With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Liraglutide: Results From the LEADER Randomized Trial.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the levels of serum amylase and lipase and the occurrence of acute pancreatitis in patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk who were randomly assigned to receive either liraglutide or a placebo and observed for a period of 3.5-5.0 years. 

A total of 9,340 patients with type 2 diabetes were included in the study and were randomly assigned to receive either liraglutide or a placebo. The median observation time was 3.84 years. Fasting serum lipase and amylase levels were monitored throughout the study. The occurrence of acute pancreatitis was determined through a blinded assessment.

The results showed that patients treated with liraglutide had a 28.0% increase in serum lipase levels and a 7.0% increase in serum amylase levels compared to the placebo group. These levels increased at 6 months and remained stable thereafter. During the study period, 18 liraglutide-treated patients (0.4% [1.1 events/1,000 patient-years of observation]) and 23 placebo patients (0.5% [1.7 events/1,000 patient-years of observation]) were confirmed to have acute pancreatitis through adjudication. Most cases of acute pancreatitis occurred at least 12 months after randomization. Patients treated with liraglutide who had a previous history of pancreatitis (n = 147) were not more likely to develop acute pancreatitis compared to similar patients in the placebo group (n = 120). Elevations in amylase and lipase levels did not predict the future risk of acute pancreatitis (positive predictive value <1.0%) in patients treated with liraglutide.

In conclusion, among patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, there were fewer cases of acute pancreatitis in those treated with liraglutide (regardless of previous history of pancreatitis) compared to the placebo group. Liraglutide was associated with increases in serum lipase and amylase levels, but these increases did not predict the occurrence of subsequent acute pancreatitis.

title: Zoledronic acid is unable to induce apoptosis, but slows tumor growth and prolongs survival for non-small-cell lung cancers.
text:
Although zoledronic acid (ZOL), a third-generation bisphosphonate, has shown promise as a therapeutic agent for various types of cancer, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, multiple myeloma, and small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), its potential anti-tumor effect on non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has not been thoroughly investigated. This study aimed to examine the effects of ZOL on line-1 tumor cells, which are similar to human lung adenocarcinoma cells. 

In vitro experiments were conducted to assess the anti-tumor effects of ZOL on line-1 tumor cells. This included measuring cellular proliferation using an MTT assay, analyzing the cell cycle using flow cytometry, and evaluating apoptosis levels using annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) and 4'-6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining. Additionally, an animal model was used to study the growth and survival of line-1 tumor cells after ZOL treatment. The in vivo cell cycle pattern was also examined using lacZ-expressing line-1 cells (line-1/lacZ). 

The results showed that ZOL significantly inhibited the growth of line-1 tumor cells in a dose-dependent manner in vitro. The treated cells were mainly arrested at the S/G2/M-phase of the cell cycle, but no apoptotic cells were observed. When ZOL was removed, the inhibited cells resumed proliferation, and the cell cycle prolongation caused by the drug disappeared. Within 72-96 hours after drug removal, the cell cycle distribution of the treated cells returned to a similar pattern as the untreated controls. In vivo studies confirmed that ZOL effectively slowed the growth of line-1 tumors and increased the lifespan of mice compared to untreated mice. The in vivo cell cycle distribution of line-1 tumor cells after ZOL exposure matched the in vitro findings. 

In conclusion, ZOL has the potential to reduce tumor burden and prolong survival in murine pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Although further research is needed to confirm the clinical relevance of these results in human lung cancer patients, combining ZOL with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy could be a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of NSCLC.

title: A central role for central tolerance.
text: Our understanding of self/nonself discrimination has been transformed by recent discoveries about central tolerance and its role in preventing organ-specific autoimmunity. This shift in our thinking can largely be attributed to the identification of tissue-restricted self-antigens (TRAs) being expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) in a promiscuous manner. These TRAs are expressed in mTECs in a way that mirrors the tissues found throughout the body, regardless of their developmental or spatio-temporal expression patterns. In this review, we will summarize the current knowledge about how TRA expression is regulated at the cellular and molecular level in mTECs. We will also discuss the mechanisms of antigen presentation and the ways in which tolerance is induced. Furthermore, we will explore the implications of these findings for understanding the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases, as well as their relevance to other biological processes such as fertility, pregnancy, puberty, and tumor defense.

title: Contribution of traditional healers to a rural tuberculosis control programme in Hlabisa, South Africa.
text:
The study took place in the rural health district of Hlabisa, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The objective was to evaluate the acceptability and effectiveness of traditional healers as supervisors of tuberculosis (TB) treatment in an existing directly observed treatment, short-course (DOTS) program. The design of the study involved comparing treatment outcomes between new TB patients in three intervention sub-districts who had the option of traditional healers for directly observed treatment (DOT) supervision, and those in the rest of the district who had the standard options for DOT supervision (health facility, community health worker, and lay persons). The study also compared treatment outcomes between different options for DOT supervision. 

A total of 3461 TB patients were registered in Hlabisa District between April 1999 and December 2000, with 2823 being discharged from the hospital to the ambulatory DOT program. Outcomes were known for 1816 patients in Hlabisa District, with 275 patients in the intervention area and 1541 patients in the control area. There was no significant difference in treatment outcome between the intervention and control areas. Among the 275 patients in the intervention area, 48 were supervised by traditional healers and 227 were supervised by other individuals. Treatment completion rates were not significantly higher among patients supervised by traditional healers compared to those supervised by other categories of DOT supervisors. Interviews with 41 of the 51 traditional healer patients who completed treatment showed high levels of satisfaction with the care they received. 

In conclusion, traditional healers were found to be effective in contributing to the performance of the TB program in this pilot scheme in Hlabisa district. Further evaluation will be necessary as this approach is expanded.

title: Alzheimer's disease: the two-hit hypothesis.
text: There is ample evidence to suggest that oxidative stress and abnormal changes in cell division play significant roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the relationship between these two events and their contribution to the disease's progression has only recently become clear. Early on, before any cellular damage occurs, both oxidative stress and cell cycle-related abnormalities are observed. Based on our research into the signaling pathways involved in cell division and oxidative stress in AD, we have proposed a "two-hit hypothesis." According to this hypothesis, either oxidative stress or abnormalities in cell division can independently initiate the disease, but both processes are necessary for its progression. In this article, we will present the evidence supporting the involvement of oxidative stress and abnormal cell division in AD and explain the two-hit hypothesis by demonstrating how both mechanisms are essential and consistent features of the disease.

title: Toll-like receptor 7 mediates pruritus
text: In order to regulate innate immunity, Toll-like receptors are commonly found in immune cells. However, our research discovered that Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is also present in C-fiber primary sensory neurons and plays a crucial role in causing itchiness (pruritus). Interestingly, TLR7 is not required for inducing mechanical, thermal, inflammatory, and neuropathic pain in mice. These findings suggest that TLR7 specifically mediates itching and could be a promising target for developing treatments to alleviate itchiness in skin diseases.

title: Antigen presentation by major histocompatibility complex class I-B molecules.
text: The majority of MHC class I loci are composed of Class I-b genes. These genes, found in various organisms, are either monomorphic or oligomorphic. The mouse, in particular, has a significant number of potentially intact Class I-b genes and is well-studied in this regard. Class I-b molecules differ from Class I-a molecules in two main ways: they have limited polymorphism and lower cell surface expression. These distinct characteristics provide insights into the evolution and function of this class. Additionally, Class I-b proteins often have shorter cytoplasmic domains, may be secreted, or may use a lipid anchor instead of a transmembrane domain. Some are also expressed in specific cells or tissues. At least six mouse MHC Class I-b molecules have been found to present antigens to alpha beta or gamma delta T cells. Recent advancements have shed light on the physiological function of H-2M3a and have identified the natural peptide-binding motif of Qa-2. Furthermore, significant progress has been made in understanding other Class I-b molecules, such as Qa-1, TL, HLA-E, HLA-G, and the MHC-unlinked Class I molecule CD1. However, we argue that the classification of MHC genes as Class I-a and I-b is conceptually misleading, despite its historical basis and practical usefulness. With this in mind, we then delve into the discussion of antigen presentation by MHC Class I-b molecules, focusing on their structure, polymorphism, requirements for peptide antigen binding, and tissue expression.

title: Pdgfrβ+ Mural Preadipocytes Contribute to Adipocyte Hyperplasia Induced by High-Fat-Diet Feeding and Prolonged Cold Exposure in Adult Mice.
text: The expansion of white adipose tissue (WAT) in obesity involves the creation of new fat cells, but we are still unsure where these cells come from. In this study, we used Zfp423(GFP) reporter mice to study a specific type of cell in adipose tissue called adipose mural (Pdgfrβ(+)) cells, which have different levels of a factor called Zfp423 that determines their commitment to becoming fat cells. We discovered that there are different populations of mural cells in adipose tissue, and the levels of Zfp423 can distinguish between cells that are likely to become fat cells and cells that have an inflammatory-like function. Using our "MuralChaser" system, we found that adipose perivascular cells are the precursors for fat cells formed during obesity, and the formation of fat cells and the abundance of these precursors are regulated differently depending on the location in the body. Interestingly, Pdgfrβ(+) cells do not play a significant role in the initial recruitment of beige fat cells in WAT when exposed to cold temperatures; it is only after prolonged exposure to cold that these cells transform into beige fat cells. These findings provide genetic evidence that fat cells in obesity originate from a specific type of cell called mural cells and suggest that beige fat cell formation may come from multiple sources.

title: Effect of clinical guidelines on medical practice: a systematic review of rigorous evaluations.
text: Despite the growing interest in clinical guidelines, there remains uncertainty regarding their effectiveness.
