This uncertainty has been exacerbated by the lack of a thorough and comprehensive overview. To address this, we have identified 59 evaluations of clinical guidelines that met strict scientific criteria. Of these evaluations, 24 focused on guidelines for specific clinical conditions, 27 examined preventive care, and 8 explored guidelines for prescribing or support services. Remarkably, all but 4 of these studies observed significant enhancements in the process of care following the implementation of guidelines. Additionally, 9 out of the 11 studies that assessed the outcome of care reported significant improvements. Based on these findings, we can conclude that explicit guidelines do enhance clinical practice, particularly when introduced alongside rigorous evaluations. However, it is important to note that the extent of these improvements varied significantly.

title: Threonine as a carbon source for Escherichia coli.
text: Mutants of Escherichia coli K-12 have the ability to utilize threonine as the sole source of carbon and energy under aerobic conditions. This metabolic pathway involves the conversion of threonine to aminoketobutyric acid through the action of threonine dehydrogenase. Aminoketobutyric acid is then further metabolized by aminoketobutyric acid ligase, resulting in the formation of acetyl coenzyme A and glycine. In a strain lacking serine transhydroxymethylase, this pathway is utilized and glycine is excreted as a byproduct. The activity of aminoketobutyric acid ligase was confirmed by passing crude extracts through Sephadex G100.

title: Protein S-nitrosylation: a physiological signal for neuronal nitric oxide
text: The role of nitric oxide (NO) in various physiological and pathophysiological events cannot be fully explained by its known effects on soluble guanylyl cyclase. While it is known that exogenous NO can S-nitrosylate cysteine residues in proteins, it is unclear if this is an important function of endogenous NO. In this study, we used a new proteomic approach to identify a group of proteins that are naturally S-nitrosylated. We also observed the loss of this modification in mice lacking neuronal NO synthase (nNOS), suggesting that nNOS is involved in this process. The targets of NO include metabolic, structural, and signaling proteins that may act as effectors for NO produced by neurons. These findings highlight protein S-nitrosylation as a physiological signaling mechanism for nNOS.

title: Hypoxia‐Sensitive COMMD1 Integrates Signaling and Cellular Metabolism in Human Macrophages and Suppresses Osteoclastogenesis
text: The mechanisms by which hypoxia enhances inflammatory responses and osteoclastogenesis are not fully understood. However, our study has identified COMMD1 as a cell-intrinsic negative regulator of osteoclastogenesis that is suppressed under hypoxic conditions. In human macrophages, COMMD1 inhibits the induction of NF-κB signaling and a metabolic pathway dependent on the transcription factor E2F1, which is stimulated by the cytokine RANKL. Hypoxia reduces the expression of COMMD1 protein, leading to increased expression of inflammatory and E2F1 target genes, as well as enhanced osteoclastogenesis. These E2F1 targets include genes involved in glycolysis and metabolism, such as CKB, which enable cells to meet metabolic demands in challenging environments, as well as genes driven by inflammatory cytokines. Analysis of gene expression in rheumatoid arthritis patients revealed that increased COMMD1 expression is associated with decreased bone erosion. Furthermore, deletion of Commd1 in myeloid cells resulted in increased osteoclastogenesis in models of arthritis and inflammatory osteolysis. These findings highlight the importance of COMMD1 and the E2F-metabolic pathway in regulating osteoclastogenic responses in pathological inflammatory conditions, and provide insight into how hypoxia contributes to inflammation and bone destruction.

title: Production of tyrosol by Candida albicans biofilms and its role in quorum sensing and biofilm development.
text: The role of tyrosol and farnesol, two molecules involved in quorum sensing, in the morphological transition of Candida albicans from yeasts to hyphae was investigated in this study. The secretion of tyrosol by C. albicans and its potential role in biofilm development were explored. Tyrosol was found to be produced by both suspended cells and biofilms of four C. albicans strains, including three mutants with defects in the Efg 1 and Cph 1 signaling pathways. The production of tyrosol correlated with biomass for both cell types, but biofilm cells secreted significantly more tyrosol than suspended cells when adjusted for cell dry weight. The addition of exogenous farnesol inhibited biofilm formation by up to 33% in a wild-type strain after 48 hours. Exogenous tyrosol did not appear to have an effect, but scanning electron microscopy revealed that it stimulated the production of hyphae during the early stages of biofilm development. Experiments with different concentrations of tyrosol and farnesol suggested that farnesol had a dominant effect, resulting in biofilms consisting mostly of yeast cells. Testing biofilm supernatants showed that tyrosol had a greater inhibitory effect on germ tube formation by suspended cells after 14 hours, but farnesol's activity increased significantly during the later stages of biofilm development. Overall, these findings support the conclusion that tyrosol acts as a quorum-sensing molecule for both biofilms and suspended cells, with its most significant impact occurring during the early and intermediate stages of biofilm formation.

title: Regulated nucleo/cytoplasmic exchange of HOG1 MAPK requires the importin beta homologs NMD5 and XPO1.
text: The role of MAP kinase signaling modules in eukaryotic cells is to transmit signals from the extracellular environment to the nucleus. However, there is limited knowledge about how these signals cross the nuclear envelope. When yeast cells are exposed to increased extracellular osmolarity, the HOG1 MAP kinase cascade is activated. This cascade consists of three tiers of protein kinases: SSK2, SSK22, and STE11 MAPKKKs, PBS2 MAPKK, and HOG1 MAPK. By using green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusions of these kinases, we discovered that HOG1, PBS2, and STE11 are located in the cytoplasm of unstressed cells. However, following osmotic stress, only HOG1 translocates into the nucleus, while PBS2 and STE11 remain in the cytoplasm. The translocation of HOG1 is rapid, temporary, and coincides with its phosphorylation and activation by its MAPKK. Phosphorylation of HOG1 is both necessary and sufficient for its nuclear translocation, as a kinase with impaired catalytic activity is translocated to the nucleus as effectively as the wild-type kinase. Under stress conditions, the nuclear import of the MAPK relies on the activity of the small GTP binding protein Ran-GSP1, rather than the NLS-binding importin alpha/beta heterodimer. Additionally, HOG1 import necessitates the function of a gene called NMD5, which encodes a novel importin beta homolog. Similarly, the export of dephosphorylated HOG1 from the nucleus requires the involvement of the NES receptor XPO1/CRM1. Our findings establish the requirements for the controlled nuclear transport of a stress-activated MAP kinase.

title: FBW7 regulates endothelial functions by targeting KLF2 for ubiquitination and degradation
text: The F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7 (FBW7) protein, which is a component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase SCFFBW7 complex, plays important roles in various physiological and pathological processes. While the role of FBW7 in vascular development is known, its function in the endothelium has not been investigated. In this study, we demonstrate that FBW7 is a crucial regulator of endothelial functions, including angiogenesis, leukocyte adhesion, and maintenance of the endothelial barrier. Through RNA interference, we observed that depletion of FBW7 significantly impairs angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo. We also identified the zinc finger transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) as a physiological target of FBW7 in endothelial cells. Knockdown of FBW7 led to the accumulation of endogenous KLF2 protein in endothelial cells. We further discovered that FBW7-mediated degradation of KLF2 depends on the phosphorylation of KLF2 by glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) at two specific sites. Mutations in these phosphorylation sites prevented FBW7-mediated degradation and ubiquitination of KLF2. Knockdown of FBW7 using siRNA confirmed that KLF2 is an essential target of FBW7 in the regulation of endothelial functions. Additionally, we found that FBW7-mediated degradation of KLF2 is critical for angiogenesis in teratomas and zebrafish development. Overall, our study highlights the role of FBW7 in endothelial cell migration, angiogenesis, inflammation, and barrier integrity, and provides new insights into the regulation of KLF2 stability in vivo.

title: Role of RhoA-specific guanine exchange factors in regulation of endomitosis in megakaryocytes.
text: The development of aneuploidy in cancer can be preceded by polyploidization. However, in the case of megakaryocytes (Mks), polyploidization is a tightly regulated process that is crucial for efficient platelet production, although the exact mechanisms involved are still unknown. Through our study using primary cells, we have found that the guanine exchange factors GEF-H1 and ECT2, which are often overexpressed in cancer and play a vital role in RhoA activation during cytokinesis, need to be downregulated for Mk polyploidization to occur. Specifically, GEF-H1 downregulation is necessary for the first endomitotic cycle (2N-4N), while ECT2 downregulation is required for subsequent cycles (>4N). When both GEF-H1 and ECT2 are artificially expressed, endomitosis is prevented, leading to the proliferation of 2N Mks. Additionally, our research has revealed that Mks lacking Mkl1, a gene mutated in megakaryocytic leukemia, have elevated GEF-H1 expression, which is responsible for preventing polyploidization. However, we have also found that knocking down GEF-H1 alone using shRNA can rescue this ploidy defect. These findings provide valuable insights into the differences between normal and malignant megakaryocytopoiesis, as well as the abnormal mitosis observed in aneuploid cancers.

title: Optimal therapy for reduction of lipoprotein(a).
text: The atherogenic and pro-thrombotic potential of Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) and its role in coronary heart disease and stroke are supported by experimental and clinical evidence. This article discusses new strategies for reducing Lp(a) levels. Previous efforts have focused on identifying therapies for hyperlipoproteinemia(a), such as apheresis techniques, nicotinic acid, and statins. However, none of these approaches have proven to be definitively effective or convenient for patients, prompting the exploration of alternative strategies. Recent studies have shown promising results with interventions targeting inflammatory pathways, such as inhibiting Interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling using natural compounds like Ginko biloba or the IL-6 receptor antibody Tocilizumab. These interventions have the potential to lower Lp(a) levels and reduce cardiovascular risk. Additionally, aspirin, in addition to its antiplatelet effects, may also decrease plasma Lp(a) concentration and modulate its impact on platelets. In conclusion, this article emphasizes the limitations of current approaches to lowering Lp(a) and highlights new insights that may lead to improved treatment options.

title: Early gastric cancer and dysplasia.
text:
The treatment of early gastric cancer has undergone significant changes since it was first discovered in Japan in 1962. Initially, the main approach was curative surgical resection, but over time, endoscopic resection techniques have become more prevalent. Initially, polypectomy was the preferred method, but recently, endoscopic submucosal dissection has gained popularity.

As these endoscopic techniques have been used more widely around the world, studies have shown that they are just as effective as traditional surgical methods for carefully selected patients. This has led to an expansion of the criteria for endoscopic resection, allowing more patients to benefit from improved quality of life without the risks associated with surgery.

In this article, we will discuss the evolution of endoscopic and surgical therapy in the treatment of early gastric cancer.

title: The impact of homelessness on children.
text: In this article, we examine and evaluate research conducted within communities regarding the impact of homelessness on children. The challenges faced by homeless children pose significant obstacles to their future success and overall welfare. Of particular worry are issues related to health, such as illnesses, hunger, insufficient nutrition, delays in development, anxiety, depression, behavioral difficulties, and academic struggles. Various factors that could influence these outcomes include inadequate living conditions, instability in housing and shelters, insufficient support services, and obstacles in accessing available assistance. It is crucial to implement public policy initiatives that address the specific needs of homeless children.

title: Strategies of microbial cheater control.
text: The advantages of collaboration among microorganisms may be hindered by genetic discord within social groups, known as 'cheating'. In order for collaboration to thrive as an evolutionary tactic, the detrimental consequences of this conflict must be addressed or lessened. To establish a foundation for future studies in microbial behavioral ecology, we present various hypothetical methods that could potentially restrict the actions of cheaters.

title: Golden Hours in Severe Paraquat Poisoning-The Role of Early Haemoperfusion Therapy.
text:
INTRODUCTION
Paraquat is a commonly ingested poison, particularly in Southern India, and its consumption often leads to fatal outcomes. The main causes of death are acute lung injury or multi-organ failure.

AIM
This study aims to assess the effectiveness of early haemoperfusion as a treatment for patients poisoned with paraquat.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients admitted to a Tertiary Medical College Hospital between January 2012 and December 2015, who had a history of paraquat consumption. The outcomes of patients who received only gastric lavage and symptomatic treatment were compared to those who received haemoperfusion as a therapy. Additionally, the role of early haemoperfusion (within 6 hours) versus late haemoperfusion (after 6 hours) in paraquat poisoned patients was also examined. Patient data, including age, sex, mode of treatment, and outcomes of those who received early and late haemoperfusion, were extracted and analyzed.

RESULTS
A total of 101 patients were included in the study, with 62 of them dying. The mortality rate was higher in patients who received only gastric lavage and symptomatic treatment compared to those who received haemoperfusion (92.1% versus 42.9%, respectively). Furthermore, it was observed that the survival rate was better in patients who received early haemoperfusion.

CONCLUSION
Early haemoperfusion proved to be beneficial in managing severe paraquat poisoning and significantly improved the survival rate in these patients.

title: Changes in the prevalence of cerebral palsy for children born very prematurely within a population-based program over 30 years.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the changes in the prevalence rates of cerebral palsy (CP) among extremely premature infants over a 30-year period. The study was conducted in Northern Alberta and included 2318 infants born between 1974 and 2003 with gestational ages ranging from 20 to 27 weeks and birth weights between 500 and 1249 g. By the age of 2, 1437 infants had died, 23 were lost to follow-up, and 858 had received neurodevelopmental assessments. The main outcome measure was the population-based prevalence rates of CP. Logistic regression with linear spline was used to analyze changes in CP prevalence over time.

At the age of 2, 122 (14.2%) of the 858 survivors were diagnosed with CP, and this diagnosis was confirmed for each child by the age of 3 or older. Among infants with gestational ages of 20 to 25 weeks, the population-based survival rate increased from 4% to 31%, while the prevalence of CP per 1000 live births increased from 0 to 110 until the years 1992-1994 and then decreased to 22 in the years 2001-2003. Among infants with gestational ages of 26 to 27 weeks, the population-based survival rate increased from 23% to between 75% and 80%, while the prevalence of CP per 1000 live births increased from 15 to 155 until the years 1992-1994 and then decreased to 16 in the years 2001-2003. For all survivors born in the years 2001-2003, the prevalence of CP was 19 per 1000 live births.

In conclusion, the study found that the population-based prevalence rates of CP among extremely premature infants with gestational ages of 20 to 27 weeks and birth weights between 500 and 1249 g have been steadily decreasing in the last decade, while mortality rates have remained stable or decreased. This is a reversal of the trends observed prior to 1992-1994.

title: Desferrioxamine treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda in a patient with HIV and chronic renal failure.
text: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) has been observed in individuals with HIV. Current research suggests that HIV infection may disrupt the hepatic cytochrome oxidase system, leading to impaired porphyrin metabolism. Additionally, individuals undergoing chronic hemodialysis for renal failure may have an increased risk of developing PCT. Alongside the factors associated with PCT in HIV patients, it is possible that the accumulation of porphyrins due to renal failure may contribute to the manifestation of this disease. We present a case of PCT in an individual infected with HIV-1 who is undergoing blood dialysis. This case has proven resistant to antimalarial treatment but has been effectively managed with desferrioxamine.

title: Mutations in G protein beta subunits promote transformation and kinase inhibitor resistance
text: Mutations in genes that encode G protein α (Gα) subunits are found in approximately 4-5% of all human cancers. However, there is currently no defined understanding of oncogenic alterations in Gβ subunits. In this study, we present evidence that recurrent mutations in Gβ proteins GNB1 and GNB2 promote cytokine-independent growth and activate canonical G protein signaling. Multiple mutations in GNB1 affect the protein interface that binds Gα subunits, as well as downstream effectors, disrupting Gα interactions with the Gβγ dimer. These mutations in Gβ proteins are clustered based on lineage, with specific mutations found in myeloid neoplasms and B cell neoplasms. When patient-derived GNB1 variants were expressed in Cdkn2a-deficient mouse bone marrow and transplanted, they resulted in either myeloid or B cell malignancies. Treatment with the dual PI3K-mTOR inhibitor BEZ235 suppressed GNB1-induced signaling and significantly improved survival in vivo. In several human tumors, mutations in the gene encoding GNB1 were found to co-occur with oncogenic kinase alterations, such as the BCR-ABL fusion protein, the V617F substitution in JAK2, and the V600K substitution in BRAF. Coexpression of patient-derived GNB1 variants with these mutant kinases led to resistance to kinase inhibitors in each case. Therefore, alterations in GNB1 and GNB2 confer transformed and resistance phenotypes in various human tumors and may be targeted with inhibitors of G protein signaling.

title: Isolation of major pancreatic cell types and long-term culture-initiating cells using novel human surface markers.
text: We have created a new set of markers on the surface of cells that can be used to isolate and study the different types of cells in the human pancreas. We used a technique called subtractive immunization to select hybridomas from Balb/C mice that reacted specifically with certain cell types and their surface markers. We confirmed the specificity and reactivity of these antibodies using immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry. These antibodies were able to bind to surface antigens on both islet and nonislet pancreatic cells, allowing us to isolate and study different populations of alpha, beta, exocrine, and duct cells from human pancreas samples. By using a technique called fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), we were able to separate these cell populations and analyze their composition in detail. We also used these antibodies to demonstrate that human islet expansion cultures originated from nonendocrine cells and that by sorting specific subpopulations and overexpressing certain transcription factors (Pdx-1 and ngn3), we could increase insulin expression levels to up to 1% of normal islet cells. This is an improvement over previous results using this culture system. These methods allow for the analysis and isolation of distinct pancreatic cell populations that could potentially be used in cell therapy.

title: Re-engineered CD40 receptor enables potent pharmacological activation of dendritic-cell cancer vaccines in vivo
text: The modest results of clinical trials for dendritic-cell (DC) vaccines highlight the need for improvements in their design. While many potential antigens have been identified, the development of methods to enhance antigen presentation by DCs has been slow. To address this, we have created a powerful, drug-inducible CD40 (iCD40) receptor that allows for controlled activation of DCs in lymphoid tissues. The iCD40 receptor consists of a fusion of the cytoplasmic domain of CD40 with drug-binding domains, enabling it to respond to a lipid-permeable, high-affinity dimerizer drug. This design bypasses negative-feedback mechanisms associated with the extracellular domain of CD40, resulting in prolonged activation of iCD40-expressing DCs in vivo. As a result, these DCs generate stronger CD8+ T-cell responses, including the elimination of established solid tumors, compared to traditional ex vivo activation methods used in most clinical DC protocols (P < 0.01). Furthermore, iCD40-mediated DC activation surpasses the activation achieved by stimulating the full-length, natural CD40 receptor both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. Since iCD40 is shielded from the external environment and can be activated within the immunological synapse, iCD40-expressing DCs have an extended lifespan and hold promise for more potent vaccines, potentially benefiting immune-compromised patients as well.

title: Effect of homocysteine lowering on mortality and vascular disease in advanced chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
In observational studies of patients with chronic kidney disease, high plasma homocysteine levels have been found to increase the risk of mortality and vascular disease. Folic acid and B vitamins have been shown to lower homocysteine levels in this population, but it is unclear whether they can reduce mortality. 

The objective of this study was to determine whether daily administration of high doses of folic acid and B vitamins can reduce mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease. The study was a double-blind randomized controlled trial conducted between 2001 and 2006 in 36 US Department of Veterans Affairs medical centers. The participants included 2056 individuals aged 21 years or older with advanced chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease and high homocysteine levels. 

The intervention involved the participants receiving a daily capsule containing 40 mg of folic acid, 100 mg of pyridoxine hydrochloride (vitamin B6), and 2 mg of cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), or a placebo. The primary outcome measured was all-cause mortality, and secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction, stroke, lower extremity amputation, a composite of these three outcomes plus all-cause mortality, time to initiation of dialysis, and time to thrombosis of arteriovenous access in hemodialysis patients. 

The results showed that the mean baseline homocysteine levels were similar in both the vitamin and placebo groups. At 3 months, the homocysteine levels decreased significantly in the vitamin group compared to the placebo group. However, there was no significant effect on mortality between the two groups. The secondary outcomes and adverse events also did not show any significant differences between the vitamin and placebo groups. 

In conclusion, the treatment with high doses of folic acid and B vitamins did not improve survival or reduce the incidence of vascular disease in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease. The trial was registered under clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00032435.

title: Treated individuals who progress to action or maintenance for one behavior are more likely to make similar progress on another behavior: coaction results of a pooled data analysis of three trials.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare the likelihood of taking effective action on one behavior and its relationship to taking effective action on a second behavior in treatment and control groups. The researchers analyzed data from three randomized trials of Transtheoretical Model (TTM) tailored interventions, which were conducted in the U.S. in 1999 and involved a total of 9461 participants. The behaviors examined were diet and sun protection, diet and smoking, and sun protection and smoking. The researchers used odds ratios (ORs) to compare the likelihood of taking action on a second behavior compared to taking action on only one behavior.

The results showed that, across all behavior pairs, the treatment group had higher ORs at 12 and 24 months compared to the control group. Two of these differences were statistically significant. Specifically, the combined ORs at 12 and 24 months were 1.63 and 1.85 for the treatment group, and 1.20 and 1.10 for the control group.

Based on these findings, the researchers concluded that the results of this study were consistent with previous studies that applied TTM tailoring to energy balance behaviors. They also noted that there was more coaction within the treatment group across all studies. The researchers suggested that future research should focus on identifying predictors of coaction in interventions targeting multiple behavior changes.

title: Trabecular bone score as an indicator for skeletal deterioration in diabetes.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the use of lumbar spine trabecular bone score (TBS) as an indicator for skeletal deterioration in individuals with diabetes. The study collected cross-sectional data from participants in a community-based cohort study from 2009 to 2010. The participants included 1229 men and 1529 postmenopausal women over the age of 50. The study measured biochemical parameters, lumbar spine TBS, and bone mineral density (BMD) from dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry images. 

The results showed that men with diabetes had lower lumbar spine TBS compared to men without diabetes, while their lumbar spine BMD was higher. In women, lumbar spine TBS was lower in those with diabetes only in an unadjusted model. However, among women under 65 years old, those with diabetes had lower TBS even after adjusting for covariates. Diabetes was not associated with BMD at femur sites in either gender. 

The study also found that TBS was negatively correlated with glycated hemoglobin, fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, and homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance in both genders. However, there was no correlation with homeostasis model assessment for β-cell function. 

In conclusion, the study suggests that the inverse association between lumbar spine TBS and insulin resistance could make TBS a useful indicator for determining skeletal deterioration in diabetic patients with high BMD.

title: Full activation of the T cell receptor requires both clustering and conformational changes at CD3.
text: The process of triggering the T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) involves both clustering of the receptor and changes in the structure of the CD3 subunits at their cytoplasmic tails. However, the exact mechanism by which ligand binding to TCRalphabeta induces these changes in CD3 is still unknown. In our study, we used specific ligands to demonstrate that the conformational change in CD3 requires both multiple interactions with the ligand and the restriction of TCR-CD3 mobility by the plasma membrane. This change in conformation occurs through coordinated rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not involve any alterations in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains. Importantly, this conformational change in CD3 is reversible upon ligand dissociation and is necessary for the activation of T cells. Therefore, our model, which allows for a permissive geometry, provides a molecular explanation for how information from ligand binding to TCRalphabeta is transmitted to the CD3 subunits and the intracellular signaling machinery.

title: Class III PI3K Vps34 plays an essential role in autophagy and in heart and liver function.
text: The Class III PI3K Vps34, also known as PIK3C3, is a crucial regulator of autophagy. While its role in autophagy in yeast is well-established, its function in mammals remains unclear. To better understand the physiological role of Vps34 and its specific involvement in autophagy, we created Vps34(f/f) mice. These mice have a deletion of exon 4 of Vps34 and a frame shift that results in the removal of 755 out of 887 amino acids of Vps34 when Cre recombinase is expressed. When Vps34 is acutely removed in MEFs through adenoviral Cre infection, there is a decrease in the localized production of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate, as well as a blockage of both endocytic and autophagic degradation. Starvation-induced autophagosome formation is also hindered in Vps34-null MEFs and liver. In liver-specific Albumin-Cre;Vps34(f/f) mice, hepatomegaly, hepatic steatosis, and impaired protein turnover are observed. Similarly, ablation of Vps34 in the heart of muscle creatine kinase-Cre;Vps34(f/f) mice leads to cardiomegaly and reduced contractility. Furthermore, while mTOR activation in response to amino acids is suppressed in the absence of Vps34, the steady-state level of mTOR signaling remains unaffected in Vps34-null MEFs, liver, and cardiomyocytes. Overall, our findings demonstrate that Vps34 is essential for regulating functional autophagy and is crucial for normal liver and heart function.

title: Sex-based differences in the effect of digoxin for the treatment of heart failure.
text:
The Digitalis Investigation Group trial found that digoxin treatment did not reduce overall mortality in patients with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function, but it did slightly decrease hospitalizations. However, the study did not evaluate the differences in the effect of digoxin between men and women, despite the varying characteristics and outcomes of heart failure in each gender. 

To address this, we conducted a post hoc subgroup analysis on the 6800 patients from the Digitalis Investigation Group study to determine if there were any sex-based differences in the impact of digoxin therapy. We used Mantel-Haenszel tests of heterogeneity and a multivariable Cox proportional-hazards model, adjusting for demographic and clinical variables, to assess the interaction between sex and digoxin therapy in relation to the primary endpoint of death from any cause. 

Our analysis revealed a significant absolute difference of 5.8 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 0.5 to 11.1) between men and women in the effect of digoxin on the rate of death from any cause (P=0.034 for the interaction). Specifically, women who were randomly assigned to digoxin had a higher death rate compared to women assigned to placebo (33.1 percent vs. 28.9 percent; absolute difference, 4.2 percent, 95 percent confidence interval, -0.5 to 8.8). On the other hand, the death rate was similar between men assigned to digoxin and men assigned to placebo (35.2 percent vs. 36.9 percent; absolute difference, -1.6 percent; 95 percent confidence interval, -4.2 to 1.0). 

In the multivariable analysis, digoxin was associated with a significantly higher risk of death among women (adjusted hazard ratio for comparison with placebo, 1.23; 95 percent confidence interval, 1.02 to 1.47), but it had no significant effect among men (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.93; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.85 to 1.02; P=0.014 for the interaction). 

In conclusion, the effect of digoxin therapy differs between men and women. Women with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function who receive digoxin treatment have an increased risk of death from any cause, while men do not experience the same effect.

title: Recipient-type specific CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells favor immune reconstitution and control graft-versus-host disease while maintaining graft-versus-leukemia.
text: CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells, also known as Treg's, play a crucial role in preventing autoimmune diseases that target specific organs and in promoting tolerance to organ transplants from different individuals. Recent studies, including our own, have shown that a high number of Treg's can also help manage graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) when combined with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in mice. However, obtaining enough freshly purified Treg's from a single donor for therapeutic purposes is impractical in a clinical setting. Therefore, we conducted ex vivo expansion of regulatory T cells by stimulating them with allogeneic antigen-presenting cells (APCs), which not only increased their numbers but also generated Treg's that specifically target alloantigens. Our findings demonstrate that recipient-specific Treg's effectively control GVHD while promoting immune reconstitution. On the other hand, irrelevant Treg's only offer partial protection against GVHD. Furthermore, grafted animals showed a higher survival rate of specific Treg's compared to irrelevant Treg's. Importantly, the use of recipient-specific Treg's did not interfere with the potential graft-versus-tumor effect. These results suggest that recipient-specific Treg's could be preferentially utilized in future clinical trials to manage GVHD.

title: Expression of the gene encoding the chemorepellent semaphorin III is induced in the fibroblast component of neural scar tissue formed following injuries of adult but not neonatal CNS.
text: This study examines the presence of a chemorepellent called semaphorin III (D)/collapsin-1 (sema III) in the rat central nervous system (CNS) after lesions. Scar tissue formed after injuries to various parts of the CNS contained many spindle-shaped cells that expressed high levels of sema III mRNA. The researchers focused on investigating these cells in the lesioned lateral olfactory tract (LOT). Most of the sema III mRNA-positive cells were found in the core of the scar and exhibited characteristics of fibroblast-like cells. The sema III receptor, neuropilin-1, was expressed in injured neurons projecting to the lesion site, a subset of scar-associated cells, and blood vessels surrounding the scar. In contrast to lesions in mature CNS, cutting the LOT in neonates did not induce sema III mRNA expression in the lesioned cells and resulted in robust axonal regeneration. The co-expression of sema III and neuropilin-1 in the scar suggests that sema III/neuropilin-1-mediated mechanisms play a role in CNS scar formation. The expression of sema III, a chemorepellent released after CNS injury, provides the first evidence that chemorepulsive semaphorins may contribute to the inhibitory effects of scars on the regrowth of injured CNS nerve fibers. The robust regrowth of injured axons in the absence of sema III following early neonatal lesions supports this idea. Inactivating sema III in scar tissue through antibody perturbation, genetic manipulation, or pharmacological intervention could be a powerful approach to promote long-distance regeneration in the adult CNS.

title: The relationship of the level of cyclic amp to differentiation in primary cultures of chick muscle cells.
text: This study aimed to investigate the impact of increased levels of cAMP on the differentiation of primary cultures of chick myoblasts. To achieve this, either 0.1 mM But 2 cAMP or 1 mM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine was added to the cultures 24 hours after plating and maintained throughout the 70-hour culture period. The results showed that both reagents significantly delayed the fusion of the myoblasts, but did not affect the increase in creatine phosphokinase activity. Morphological analysis revealed no difference in the relative numbers of myoblasts and fibroblasts between the control group, But 2 cAMP group, and 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine group. However, the latter reagent seemed to inhibit cell proliferation to some extent.

title: Intact endothelial autophagy is required to maintain vascular lipid homeostasis.
text: The exact role of autophagic flux in the vascular endothelial layer is not well understood. However, our study demonstrates that in primary endothelial cells, both oxidized and native LDL can stimulate the formation of autophagosomes. Furthermore, through confocal and electron microscopy, we observed that excessive amounts of native or modified LDL are engulfed by autophagic structures. When we temporarily reduced the expression of the essential autophagy gene ATG7, we found higher levels of intracellular (125) I-LDL and oxidized LDL accumulation, suggesting that autophagy may play a crucial role in regulating excessive external lipids in endothelial cells. To assess the physiological significance of these findings, we conducted experiments on mice with a conditional deletion of ATG7 specifically in the endothelium. After intravenous infusion of fluorescently labeled oxidized LDL, we observed that mice lacking endothelial expression of ATG7 had prolonged retention of oxidized LDL in the retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal endothelium of the eye. In a chronic model of lipid excess, we examined the atherosclerotic burden in ApoE(-/-) mice with or without endothelial autophagic flux. The absence of endothelial autophagy significantly increased the atherosclerotic burden. Therefore, in both acute and chronic in vivo models, endothelial autophagy appears to be crucial in limiting lipid accumulation in the vessel wall. Consequently, strategies that promote autophagy or prevent the age-related decline in autophagic flux may be particularly beneficial in the treatment of atherosclerotic vascular disease.

title: Induction of circadian gene expression in human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate whether human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) can be used as an in vitro model to study the activity of the core circadian transcriptional apparatus. Primary cultures of undifferentiated or adipocyte-differentiated ASCs were treated with dexamethasone, rosiglitazone, or 30% fetal bovine serum. The response of undifferentiated ASCs to dexamethasone was further examined in the presence of lithium chloride, which inhibits glycogen synthase kinase 3, a key component of the circadian apparatus. Total RNA was collected at 4-hour intervals over 48 hours and analyzed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). 

The results showed that adipocyte-differentiated cells responded more quickly to treatments compared to undifferentiated controls, but the period of the circadian gene oscillation was longer in the adipocyte-differentiated cells. Dexamethasone induced circadian gene expression patterns with mean periods of 25.4 and 26.7 hours in undifferentiated and adipocyte-differentiated ASCs, respectively. Both rosiglitazone and serum shock resulted in a significantly longer period in adipocyte-differentiated ASCs compared to undifferentiated ASCs. The Bmal1 profile was shifted by approximately 8 to 12 hours relative to Per1, Per3, and Cry2, which is consistent with their expression in vivo. Lithium chloride inhibited adipogenesis and significantly lengthened the period of Per3 and Rev-erbalpha gene expression profiles by more than 5 hours in dexamethasone-activated undifferentiated ASCs. 

In conclusion, these findings support the initial hypothesis and demonstrate that ASCs can serve as an in vitro model for studying circadian biology in human adipose tissue.

title: BCL9 promotes tumor progression by conferring enhanced proliferative, metastatic, and angiogenic properties to cancer cells.
text: The Wnt signaling cascade plays a crucial role in oncogenesis, with certain components acting as either tumor suppressors or oncogenes in various human cancers. This highlights the significance of investigating Wnt signaling components as potential targets for cancer therapy. In this study, we utilized expression profiling analysis, as well as in vitro and in vivo functional studies, to demonstrate that BCL9, a component of the Wnt pathway, functions as a novel oncogene in multiple myeloma and colon carcinoma. We found that BCL9 enhances beta-catenin-mediated transcriptional activity, independent of the mutational status of other Wnt signaling components. Additionally, BCL9 promotes cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and metastasis by inducing a transition from an epithelial to a mesenchymal-like phenotype. Importantly, knocking down BCL9 significantly improved the survival of xenograft mouse models of cancer by reducing tumor load, metastasis, and host angiogenesis. This was achieved through the down-regulation of c-Myc, cyclin D1, CD44, and vascular endothelial growth factor expression in tumor cells. These findings highlight the crucial role of BCL9 in tumor progression and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for various malignancies associated with dysregulated Wnt signaling.

title: Programmed cell death pathways in cancer: a review of apoptosis, autophagy and programmed necrosis.
text: Programmed cell death (PCD) is the term used to describe the death of a cell through various mechanisms such as apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis. It occurs in pathological conditions when there is an intracellular program guiding the cell's demise. These three forms of PCD can determine the fate of cells in malignant neoplasms. Apoptosis and programmed necrosis always lead to cell death, while autophagy can either promote cell survival or contribute to cell death. Recent research has provided a wealth of evidence that enhances our understanding of cancer development and progression through these distinct types of cell death. By deciphering the signaling pathways involved in PCD, we may be able to develop targeted anti-cancer therapies. This review provides an overview of apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis pathways, as well as the regulation of apoptosis-related microRNAs in cancer. By comprehending PCD and the intricate interplay between apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis, scientists and clinicians may eventually harness these mechanisms to discover novel drug targets for future cancer treatments.

title: Loss of gametophytic self-incompatibility with evolution of inbreeding depression.
text: The prevalence of gametophytic self-incompatibility (SI) in plants serves as a mechanism to prevent self-fertilization and the resulting negative effects of inbreeding depression. However, this SI often evolves into self-compatibility. In this study, we examine the genetic mechanisms behind the breakdown of gametophytic SI. We utilize a dynamic model to explore the evolution of inbreeding depression, allowing for the partial elimination of nearly recessive lethal mutations through selfing. Additionally, we take into account pollen limitation and sheltered load associated with the S-locus. We consider two potential mechanisms for the breakdown of gametophytic SI: a nonfunctional S-allele and an unlinked modifier locus that deactivates the S-locus. Our findings demonstrate that self-compatible alleles can successfully invade a self-incompatible population under a wide range of conditions. The conditions for invasion are consistently less strict for a nonfunctional S-allele compared to a modifier locus. The spread of self-compatible genotypes is facilitated by extremely high or low selfing rates, a small number of S-alleles, and pollen limitation. Based on observed parameter values, it appears that the maintenance of gametophytic SI is a result of a combination of high inbreeding depression in self-incompatible populations, intermediate selfing rates in self-compatible genotypes, and sheltered load associated with the S-locus.

title: The oncogenic microRNA miR-22 targets the TET2 tumor suppressor to promote hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal and transformation.
text: Cancer often leads to the disruption of microRNAs. In this study, we discovered that miR-22 is overexpressed in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and leukemia, and its abnormal expression is linked to a lower chance of survival. To investigate its impact on hematopoietic stem cell function and cancer, we created transgenic mice that selectively expressed miR-22 in the hematopoietic system. These mice exhibited decreased levels of global 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) and increased self-renewal of hematopoietic stem cells, along with impaired differentiation. Conversely, inhibiting miR-22 hindered the proliferation of leukemic cells in both mice and humans. Over time, the transgenic mice developed MDS and hematological malignancies. Additionally, we identified TET2 as a crucial target of miR-22 in this context. Introducing TET2 expression counteracted the effects induced by miR-22. The reduced levels of TET2 protein also correlated with unfavorable clinical outcomes and increased miR-22 expression in MDS patients. Consequently, our findings establish miR-22 as a potent proto-oncogene and suggest that abnormalities in the miR-22/TET2 regulatory network are prevalent in hematopoietic malignancies.

title: Transmission of atherosclerosis susceptibility with gut microbial transplantation.
text:
New research suggests that there is a connection between atherosclerotic heart disease and the way certain dietary nutrients are metabolized by the intestinal microbiome, resulting in the production of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO). In order to test this hypothesis, scientists conducted a study using gut microbial transplantation to see if it could transmit TMAO production and increase susceptibility to atherosclerosis.

The study began by observing a strong correlation between atherosclerotic plaque and plasma TMAO levels in a group of mice (consisting of 22 different strains). This association was statistically significant, indicating a potential link between TMAO and atherosclerosis. Two strains of mice were then selected for the transplantation experiment: one strain that was prone to atherosclerosis and produced high levels of TMAO (C57BL/6J), and another strain that was resistant to atherosclerosis and produced low levels of TMAO (NZW/LacJ).

The researchers suppressed the resident intestinal microbes in apolipoprotein e null mice using antibiotics before transplanting the cecal microbes from the donor mice. Initially, the recipients who were on a choline diet and received cecal microbes from the C57BL/6J mice had higher levels of trimethylamine (TMA) and TMAO. However, these differences in TMA/TMAO levels did not persist until the end of the study.

Interestingly, the mice who received cecal microbes from the C57BL/6J mice showed an increase in atherosclerotic plaque burden when on a choline diet, compared to the mice who received cecal microbes from the NZW/LacJ mice. Analysis of microbial DNA in the feces and cecum revealed that the donor microbial community features were successfully transmitted to the recipients, with some variations in taxa proportions between the donor strains. These variations tended to align with TMAO levels. Additionally, specific taxa proportions were identified that correlated with plasma TMAO levels in both donors and recipients, as well as with the size of atherosclerotic lesions in recipients.

In conclusion, this study suggests that atherosclerosis susceptibility can be transmitted through gut microbial transplantation. This finding opens up the possibility of targeting the gut microbiota as a novel therapeutic approach for modulating atherosclerosis susceptibility.

title: The complete primary structure of the spermadhesin AWN, a zona pellucida-binding protein isolated from boar spermatozoa.
text: AWN is a protein found in the secretions of the male accessory glands and becomes associated with the surface of sperm after ejaculation. It is believed to play a role in sperm adhesion to the zona pellucida of the egg through a carbohydrate-recognition mechanism. AWN may be involved in the early stages of fertilization in pigs. In this study, we provide a detailed description of its primary structure using protein-chemical and mass spectrometric methods. AWN exists in two forms, AWN-1 and AWN-2, with AWN-2 being acetylated at the N-terminus. The amino acid sequence of AWN consists of 133 residues and includes two disulphide bridges between neighboring cysteine residues. Comparison of the amino acid sequence of AWN with other boar spermadhesins, specifically AQN-1 and AQN-3, revealed significant similarity.

title: What influences government adoption of vaccines in developing countries? A policy process analysis.
text: This paper presents a framework for analyzing how governments in developing countries consider and adopt new vaccines. It specifically focuses on the cases of early Hepatitis B vaccine adoption in Taiwan and Thailand to explore the factors that influence this process. The study emphasizes the importance of looking beyond individual variables and considering the policy context and decision-making process in determining the speed and extent of vaccine adoption. The cases demonstrate the feasibility and significance of modeling "causal diversity," which refers to the complex conditions that lead to specific decision outcomes, in various country contexts. By gaining a better understanding of how government decision-makers filter information and the arenas where critical decisions are made, analysts can predict the institutionalization of new vaccines, and advocates can develop targeted strategies to accelerate their diffusion.

title: Benzodiazepines and injurious falls in community dwelling elders.
text:
BACKGROUND: Benzodiazepines are commonly prescribed medications for elderly individuals, but they are known to increase the risk of falling, which can have serious consequences.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to determine the impact of benzodiazepine-related injurious falls in the elderly population.

METHOD: A nested case-control study was conducted using data from the French PAQUID cohort, which followed participants for 10 years. The main outcome measure was the occurrence of an injurious fall, defined as a fall resulting in hospitalization, fracture, head trauma, or death. Controls were selected at a ratio of 3:1 to cases. Benzodiazepine exposure was determined based on self-reported use in the two weeks prior to the follow-up visit preceding the fall.

RESULTS: The study found a significant association between benzodiazepine use and injurious falls, with a notable interaction with age. The adjusted odds ratio for injurious falls in individuals exposed to benzodiazepines was 2.2 for those aged 80 years or older and 1.3 for those younger than 80 years. The population attributable risk for injurious falls in benzodiazepine-exposed individuals aged 80 years or older was 28.1%. The incidence of injurious falls in this population was 2.8 per 100 person-years, and approximately 9% of these falls resulted in death. Based on these findings and population estimates, benzodiazepine use may be responsible for nearly 20,000 injurious falls and approximately 1,800 deaths in individuals aged 80 years or older in France each year.

CONCLUSION: Given the significant morbidity and mortality associated with benzodiazepine use in the elderly, and the limited effectiveness of current guidelines in preventing misuse, new strategies are needed to reduce benzodiazepine use in this population.

title: Effect of women's nutrition before and during early pregnancy on maternal and infant outcomes: a systematic review.
text:
New research suggests that a woman's nutritional status before and during early pregnancy can have a significant impact on the development of the fetus and the overall success of the pregnancy. To explore this further, we conducted a thorough review of existing evidence, analyzing 45 articles that included intervention trials and observational studies. These articles were sourced from PubMed and EMBASE databases, as well as review articles.

The findings from both intervention trials and observational studies indicate that taking folic acid supplements during the periconceptional period (before 12 weeks gestation) can greatly reduce the risk of neural tube defects. Additionally, observational studies suggest that taking vitamin and mineral supplements before and during early pregnancy can lower the chances of delivering low birthweight or small-for-gestational age (SGA) babies, as well as reduce the likelihood of preterm deliveries (PTD). Some studies also suggest that factors such as maternal prepregnancy size, low stature, underweight, and overweight can increase the risks of PTD and SGA.

While the available data highlight the importance of women's nutrition in the first trimester of pregnancy, there is a need for more well-designed prospective studies and controlled trials in developing countries. These studies should focus on examining the relationships between nutrition and outcomes such as low birthweight, SGA, PTD, stillbirth, and maternal and neonatal mortality. Additionally, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of periconceptional interventions, including food supplements, multivitamin-mineral supplements, and specific micronutrients like iron, zinc, iodine, vitamin B-6, and B-12. It is also crucial to explore the connection between measures of prepregnancy body size and composition and the health outcomes of both the mother and the child.

title: Kinesin-2 controls development and patterning of the vertebrate skeleton by Hedgehog- and Gli3-dependent mechanisms.
text: The Hedgehog signaling pathway is crucial for the proper formation of the vertebrate skeleton. In this study, we provide evidence that when the Kif3a subunit of the kinesin-2 intraflagellar transport motor is conditionally deactivated in mesenchymal skeletal progenitor cells, it leads to significant defects in craniofacial patterning, split sternum formation, and the development of polydactyly. These abnormalities resemble those observed in mice with disrupted hedgehog signaling. Our findings indicate that the absence of Kif3a in mesenchymal tissues impairs both the repressor function of the Gli3 transcription factor and the activation of the Shh transcriptional targets Ptch and Gli1. Through quantitative analysis of gene expression, we observe a dramatic decrease in Gli1 transcript levels, while Gli3 expression remains largely unaffected by kinesin-2 depletion. However, our results suggest that the motor is necessary for the efficient cleavage of the full-length Gli3 transcription factor into its repressor form.

title: Ablation of NF1 function in neurons induces abnormal development of cerebral cortex and reactive gliosis in the brain.
text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a common genetic disorder that affects the growth properties of cell populations derived from the neural crest. Additionally, around half of NF1 patients experience learning disabilities. To study NF1 function in both laboratory settings and living organisms, we have developed a method to create a conditional mutation in the NF1 gene using Cre/loxP technology, which allows us to bypass the embryonic lethality seen in NF1 null mouse embryos. By introducing a transgenic mouse strain with a Cre gene driven by the Synapsin I promoter into the NF1 background, we have successfully eliminated NF1 function in most mature neuronal populations. These mice exhibit abnormal development of the cerebral cortex, indicating that NF1 plays a crucial role in this aspect of central nervous system development. Additionally, although these mice do not develop tumors, they do show extensive astrogliosis without noticeable neurodegeneration or microgliosis. These findings suggest that NF1-deficient neurons can trigger reactive astrogliosis through a mechanism that does not involve direct cell-to-cell communication.

title: Pathology of postprimary tuberculosis in humans and mice: contradiction of long-held beliefs.
text: Tuberculosis continues to be one of the leading causes of death worldwide. The majority of cases, around 80%, are caused by postprimary tuberculosis in the lungs. However, there is a lack of available tissues from developing lesions, making it difficult to study this form of tuberculosis. In the past, before the use of antibiotics, researchers described early postprimary tuberculosis as a type of pneumonia characterized by the presence of lipids, which is different from the caseating granulomas commonly seen today. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a study using histopathologic, immunohistochemical, and acid fast stains to examine tissues from individuals with untreated primary and postprimary tuberculosis, and compared the findings with mice that had reactivation tuberculosis. The results confirmed that developing postprimary tuberculosis starts as a lipid pneumonia with bronchial obstruction, where the infection is limited to foamy alveolar macrophages. The formation of cavities is a result of both caseation of tuberculous pneumonia and microvascular occlusion, which is characteristic of delayed type hypersensitivity. Reactivation tuberculosis in mice also begins as a similar lipid pneumonia with bronchial obstruction and evidence of involvement of delayed type hypersensitivity. In both species, the development of necrosis is associated with the localization of the bacteria within lipid droplets. These findings suggest that reactivation tuberculosis in mice can serve as a valuable model for studying the development of postprimary tuberculosis in humans.

title: Secondary aerosolization of viable Bacillus anthracis spores in a contaminated US Senate Office.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the secondary aerosolization of Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) spores in indoor environments. The study focused on the Hart Senate Office Building and other facilities in the vicinity of the US Capitol, which had been contaminated during bioterrorist attacks involving letters and mail-handling systems in Washington, DC. 

To gather data, stationary and personal air samples, surface dust, and swab samples were collected under two different conditions: semiquiescent (minimal activities) and simulated active office conditions. The researchers aimed to estimate the extent of secondary aerosolization of B anthracis spores by evaluating the nominal size characteristics, airborne concentrations, and surface contamination of the spores.

The results showed that viable B anthracis spores reaerosolized under semiquiescent conditions, with a significant increase in reaerosolization during simulated active office conditions. The researchers observed increases in B anthracis collected on open sheep blood agar plates (P<.001) and personal air monitors (P =.01) during active office conditions. Furthermore, more than 80% of the B anthracis particles collected on stationary monitors were within a respirable size range of 0.95 to 3.5 micro m.

In conclusion, the study found that Bacillus anthracis spores used in a recent terrorist incident can reaerosolize under common office activities. These findings have important implications for respiratory protection, remediation, and reoccupancy of contaminated office environments.

title: Fingolimod provides long-term protection in rodent models of cerebral ischemia.
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the therapeutic effects of fingolimod, a sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor agonist, in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia. Previous clinical trials have shown that fingolimod is effective in treating advanced multiple sclerosis, as it reduces reperfusion injury in the heart, liver, and kidney. To determine the translational significance of these findings, the researchers examined the long-term behavioral outcomes of fingolimod treatment, the effectiveness of delayed treatment, and whether neuroprotection could be achieved in a different species. 

The researchers utilized rodent models of middle cerebral artery occlusion and cell-culture models of neurotoxicity and inflammation to assess the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of neuroprotection by fingolimod. The results showed that fingolimod reduced infarct size, neurological deficit, edema, and the number of dying cells in the core and periinfarct area in a transient mouse model. This neuroprotection was accompanied by a decrease in inflammation, as fingolimod-treated mice had fewer activated neutrophils, microglia/macrophages, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)-positive blood vessels. Fingolimod-treated mice also exhibited a smaller infarct and performed better in behavioral tests up to 15 days after ischemia. Interestingly, the protective effects of fingolimod were still observed in a permanent model when treatment was administered 4 hours after ischemic onset. Additionally, fingolimod reduced infarct size in a rat model of focal ischemia. However, fingolimod did not protect primary neurons against glutamate excitotoxicity or hydrogen peroxide. Instead, it decreased ICAM-1 expression in brain endothelial cells stimulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha. 

In conclusion, these findings suggest that the beneficial effects of fingolimod after stroke are primarily mediated through anti-inflammatory mechanisms and possibly vasculoprotection, rather than direct effects on neurons. Therefore, S1P receptors represent a promising target for stroke treatment.

title: Induced regeneration—the progress and promise of direct reprogramming for heart repair
text: The potential to revolutionize cardiovascular medicine lies in the regeneration of cardiac tissue. Remarkable advancements in stem cell biology and direct reprogramming techniques have provided us with potent tools to achieve this objective. This review delves into the significant strides made in generating new cardiomyocytes in laboratory settings, as well as the thrilling progress made in reprogramming cardiac tissue within living organisms. Additionally, we tackle the controversies and obstacles that pose challenges to this field.

title: "Sandwich"-type immunoassay of carcinoembryonic antigen in patients receiving murine monoclonal antibodies for diagnosis and therapy.
text: Some patients who were receiving injections of monoclonal antibody experienced a significant increase in blood levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA). The levels of CEA were measured using a monoclonal antibody-based double-determinant enzyme immunoassay. In this assay, untreated plasma samples were diluted with a buffer containing mouse serum. As the CEA levels increased, there was also a simultaneous increase in levels of human antibody against mouse Ig (HAMA). To determine the cause of the false-positive CEA levels, the sera were treated with solid-phase anti-human IgG or Protein A, which restored the CEA levels to their original values. This suggested that HAMA was most likely responsible for the false-positive results. Attempts to eliminate HAMA interference by adding undiluted mouse serum to the assay mixture or heating plasma samples to 70 degrees C were not effective. However, protein precipitation with polyethylene glycol (130 g/L) or heating plasma samples to 90 degrees C successfully eliminated the false-positive CEA levels caused by HAMA, without affecting the authentic CEA levels.

title: Mutant dynactin in motor neuron disease
text: The impaired transportation of axons in motor neurons has been suggested as a potential cause of neuronal degeneration in motor neuron disease. In this study, we have identified a connection between a lower motor neuron disease and a specific region on chromosome 2p13, spanning 4 Mb. Through mutation analysis of a gene within this region, which codes for the largest subunit of the axonal transport protein dynactin, we have discovered a single base-pair alteration that leads to an amino-acid substitution. This substitution is predicted to disrupt the folding of dynactin's microtubule-binding domain. Furthermore, binding assays have demonstrated a decrease in the binding capacity of the mutant protein to microtubules. These findings highlight the role of dysfunctional dynactin-mediated transport in the development of motor neuron disease in humans.

title: Thioredoxin mediates oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2 and growth cone collapse.
text: The repulsive guidance molecule Semaphorin3A (Sema3A) plays a crucial role in axon guidance by causing growth cone collapse. This process is mediated by the phosphorylation of Collapsin Response Mediator Protein 2 (CRMP2). In our study, we have discovered that CRMP2 oxidation and the presence of Thioredoxin (TRX) are involved in the regulation of CRMP2 phosphorylation and subsequent growth cone collapse. Upon stimulation by Sema3A, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is produced through the action of Molecule Interacting with CasL (MICAL), leading to the oxidation of CRMP2. This oxidation enables CRMP2 to form a homodimer through cysteine-504. The oxidized CRMP2 then transiently interacts with TRX, forming a disulfide-linked complex. This complex further stimulates the phosphorylation of CRMP2 by glycogen synthase kinase-3, ultimately resulting in growth cone collapse. To validate our findings, we conducted in vitro experiments using a limited set of purified proteins, successfully reconstituting the oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2. Our study not only sheds light on the significance of H2O2 and CRMP2 oxidation in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse but also highlights the previously unrecognized role of TRX in connecting CRMP2 oxidation to phosphorylation.

title: Pathologic indicators of degradation and inflammation in human osteoarthritic cartilage are abrogated by exposure to n-3 fatty acids.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation on the metabolism of osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage, compared to treatment with n-6 polyunsaturated or other fatty acid supplements. The metabolic profile of human OA cartilage was assessed before and after exposure to n-3 PUFAs or other fatty acids for 24 hours, followed by a 4-day explant culture with or without interleukin-1 (IL-1). Various parameters were measured, including glycosaminoglycan release, activity of aggrecanase and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP), and levels of messenger RNA (mRNA) expression for inflammation mediators, aggrecanases, MMPs, and their natural tissue inhibitors (TIMPs).

The results showed that supplementation with n-3 PUFA, but not other fatty acids, dose-dependently reduced the release of proteoglycan metabolites from articular cartilage explants, both endogenously and IL-1-induced. It also specifically inhibited the proteolytic activity of endogenous aggrecanase and collagenase. Furthermore, n-3 PUFA supplementation specifically suppressed the expression of mRNA for ADAMTS-4, MMP-13, and MMP-3, but not TIMP-1, -2, or -3. Additionally, it suppressed the expression of mRNA for inflammation mediators (cyclooxygenase 2, 5-lipoxygenase, 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein, tumor necrosis factor alpha, IL-1alpha, and IL-1beta), without affecting the expression of other proteins involved in normal tissue homeostasis.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that exposure of human OA cartilage to n-3 PUFA can significantly alter pathological indicators, while other classes of fatty acids do not have the same effect.

title: Interactive effects of oligofructose and obesity predisposition on gut hormones and microbiota in diet-induced obese rats.
text: The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of oligofructose (OFS), a prebiotic, on energy intake and fat mass in relation to gut satiety hormones and microbiota. The study aimed to determine if the effects of OFS varied depending on predisposition to obesity. Adult male rats, both diet-induced obese (DIO) and diet-resistant (DR), were divided into two groups: one group was fed a high-fat/high-sucrose (HFS) diet, while the other group was fed the HFS diet supplemented with 10% OFS for a period of 6 weeks. The researchers measured body composition, food intake, gut microbiota, plasma gut hormones, and cannabinoid CB(1) receptor expression in the nodose ganglia. The results showed that OFS significantly reduced body weight, energy intake, and fat mass in both DIO and DR rats. There were differences in gut microbiota between the two phenotypes, but these differences were eliminated by OFS. OFS did not have an effect on plasma ghrelin or CB(1) expression in the nodose ganglia, but it did reduce GIP levels and increase PYY levels in the plasma. In conclusion, OFS was effective in reducing body weight and adiposity in both prone and resistant obese phenotypes. The changes in gut microbiota profiles and gut hormone levels induced by OFS likely contributed to the sustained lower body weights observed.

title: RKIKK motif in the intracellular domain is critical for spatial and dynamic organization of ICAM-1: functional implication for the leukocyte adhesion and transmigration.
text: There is currently no direct evidence to suggest a connection between the spatial organization of ICAM-1 on the cell surface and its physiological function in terms of leukocyte adhesion and transendothelial migration (TEM). However, our observations indicate that ICAM-1 plays a direct role in the elongation of microvilli and becomes clustered on these structures. When the intracellular domain of ICAM-1 is truncated, it results in a uniform distribution of ICAM-1 on the cell surface. Through mutation analysis, we have determined that the C-terminal 21 amino acids are not necessary for ICAM-1 function, but a segment of 5 amino acids ((507)RKIKK(511)) in the NH-terminal third of the intracellular domain is crucial for proper localization and dynamic distribution of ICAM-1. This segment is also involved in the association of ICAM-1 with F-actin, ezrin, and moesin. Importantly, deletion of the (507)RKIKK(511) segment significantly delays LFA-1-dependent membrane projection, reduces leukocyte adhesion, and hinders subsequent TEM. Treatment of endothelial cells with cell-permeant penetratin-ICAM-1 peptides containing the ICAM-1 RKIKK sequences inhibits leukocyte TEM. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the (507)RKIKK(511) motif is essential for the presentation of ICAM-1 on microvilli and suggest a novel regulatory role for ICAM-1 topography in leukocyte TEM.

title: Immunology of the tick-host interaction and the control of ticks and tick-borne diseases.
text: The initial trial for a tick vaccine took place six decades ago, but progress has been sluggish since then. However, the recent introduction of a recombinant vaccine for Boophilus microplus is a significant development. Our understanding of naturally acquired immunity against ticks, especially in domesticated ruminant hosts, is still limited. Although some progress has been made in identifying "hidden" antigens, the characterization of naturally acquired immunity antigens remains restricted. There are still crucial questions regarding the impact of tick-induced immunosuppression and the effect of immunity on the transmission of tick-borne diseases. Peter Willadsen and Frans Jongejan discuss these intriguing and important recent findings in this article.

title: Rapid method for the isolation of lipoproteins from human serum by precipitation with polyanions.
text: This text describes procedures for isolating lipoproteins from human serum using precipitation with polyanions and divalent cations. By using heparin and either MnCl(2) or MgCl(2) plus sucrose, a mixture of low and very low density lipoproteins can be prepared without the need for ultracentrifugation. The precipitation in both cases is reversible, selective, and complete. The isolated lipoproteins are highly concentrated and free from other plasma proteins, as confirmed by immunological and electrophoretic methods. To separate the low density and very low density lipoproteins from each other, ultracentrifugation is employed. The method offers the advantage of producing large quantities of lipoproteins with just one preparative ultracentrifugation. In addition to heparin, other polyanions such as dextran sulfate and sodium phosphotungstate can be used to achieve precipitation of the low and very low density lipoproteins, followed by the precipitation of high density lipoproteins by increasing the concentrations of the reagents. These lipoproteins, which may contain small amounts of protein contaminants, can be further purified by ultracentrifugation at d 1.22. By performing a single preparative ultracentrifugation, immunologically pure high density lipoproteins can be isolated from large volumes of serum.

title: The role of oral antidiabetic agents: why and when to use an early-phase insulin secretion agent in Type II diabetes mellitus
text: The evidence gathered in the 1990s strongly supports the idea that controlling blood sugar levels is crucial not only for individuals with Type I diabetes who require insulin, but also for those with Type II diabetes who do not. While measuring HbA1c is the standard method for assessing the impact of glucose control on the occurrence and prevention of diabetic complications, recent evidence suggests that other glucose parameters are also significant. Peaks in blood sugar levels after meals and challenges appear to be potential indicators of vascular damage in early Type II diabetes. Currently, there is no universally accepted approach for the pharmacological management of Type II diabetes. The United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study has demonstrated the critical importance of achieving a near-normal blood sugar target, but treating this progressive disease with medication is challenging. The study also confirmed that the loss of natural insulin production contributes to the progression of Type II diabetes. However, early insulin treatment did not prove to be more beneficial than other forms of therapy. In recent years, the use of multiple medications, known as polypharmacy, has greatly improved the treatment of this disease. This approach has been further enhanced with the introduction of early-phase insulin secretion agents. Two such agents, nateglinide and repaglinide, can be used alone or in combination with metformin to reduce post-meal blood sugar spikes and HbA1c levels. Their potential in managing diabetes is comparable to the combination treatment of glibenclamide and metformin. Further research is needed to confirm their long-term effects on improving life expectancy and reducing complications in individuals with Type II diabetes.

title: Layered hydrogels accelerate iPSC-derived neuronal maturation and reveal migration defects caused by MeCP2 dysfunction.
text: To explore various cellular characteristics in neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Rett syndrome, patient-derived neural progenitor cells (NPCs) are best examined using 3D assays. Unlike 2D systems, these assays can better replicate the cell arrangement found in the brain. In this study, we have developed a novel 3D migration and differentiation assay using layered hydrogels to investigate how these processes are impacted in neurodevelopmental disorders. Our soft 3D system mimics the brain environment and expedites the maturation of neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived NPCs, resulting in electrophysiologically active neurons within a short span of 3 weeks. By utilizing this platform, we have discovered that methyl-CpG-binding protein-2 (MeCP2) dysfunction has a genotype-specific effect on iPSC-derived neuronal migration and maturation in 3D layered hydrogels, leading to reduced neurite outgrowth and fewer synapses. Therefore, this 3D system broadens the scope of neural phenotypes that can be studied in vitro, encompassing those influenced by physical and mechanical stimuli or necessitating specific arrangements of multiple cell types.

title: Inducible gene expression: diverse regulatory mechanisms
text: In this Review, we explore the mechanisms behind the swift and targeted activation of gene expression in response to external stimuli. The primary driver of this process is the regulation of RNA polymerase II-dependent transcription, which leads to the rapid activation of gene expression. We delve into the various events that take place during the transcription cycle in eukaryotes, shedding light on their significance in facilitating this rapid response. Alongside the controlled recruitment of the transcription machinery to the promoter, recent findings have revealed that chromatin remodeling and the release of paused polymerase are additional crucial steps in this process. Furthermore, emerging research suggests that certain components of signal transduction cascades also play a vital role in activating transcription at specific target genes.

title: On the origins of ultra-fine anaphase bridges.
text: The article titled "Replication stress induces sister-chromatid bridging at fragile site loci in mitosis" by Chan KL, Palmai-Pallag T, Ying S, and Hickson ID, published in Nature Cell Biology in 2009, discusses the occurrence of sister-chromatid bridging at fragile site loci during mitosis as a result of replication stress.

title: Resistance to gefitinib in PTEN-null HER-overexpressing tumor cells can be overcome through restoration of PTEN function or pharmacologic modulation of constitutive phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase/Akt pathway signaling.
text: The purpose of this study is to investigate the use of tyrosine kinase (TK) inhibitors for the treatment of HER overexpressing tumors. The optimal use of these inhibitors depends on a better understanding of the downstream signaling pathways that mediate their effects. Previous research has shown that the EGFR-selective TK inhibitor gefitinib is effective in treating EGFR- and Her2-overexpressing tumors by down-regulating Akt. However, MDA-468 cells, which lack PTEN function, are resistant to gefitinib. This resistance is due to EGFR-independent constitutive Akt activation caused by the loss of PTEN function. By reintroducing PTEN or using a pharmacologic approach to down-regulate the PI3K/Akt pathway, the sensitivity of MDA-468 cells to gefitinib can be restored. These findings have important implications for predicting and treating resistance to TK inhibitors.
