title: Transcriptome analysis reveals human cytomegalovirus reprograms monocyte differentiation toward an M1 macrophage.
text: Monocytes are the primary targets for human CMV (HCMV) infection and are believed to be responsible for spreading the virus through the bloodstream. When monocytes undergo polarization, they can develop into either proinflammatory M1 macrophages or anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages. We hypothesized that HCMV infection induces the development of proinflammatory M1 macrophages, which helps the virus spread by enabling infected monocytes to move from the blood into the tissue. To test this hypothesis, we used Affymetrix Microarray to analyze the gene expression profile of infected monocytes at a specific time point that is crucial for regulating the infection. Our findings showed that HCMV significantly increased the expression of 583 genes (5.2% of total genes) and decreased the expression of 621 genes (5.5% of total genes) by at least 1.5-fold after 4 hours of infection. Further analysis revealed that HCMV infection stimulated genes associated with classical M1 macrophage activation. Specifically, 65% of genes related to M1 polarization were up-regulated, while only 4% of genes related to M2 polarization were up-regulated. Additionally, analysis of the monocyte chemokinome at the transcriptional level showed that 44% of M1 macrophage chemokines and 33% of M2 macrophage chemokines were up-regulated. Proteomic analysis using chemokine antibody arrays confirmed the secretion of these chemotactic proteins from HCMV-infected monocytes. Overall, our results demonstrate that HCMV infection leads to a unique gene expression profile in monocytes, indicating a bias towards the classical M1 activation phenotype.

title: Antithymocyte globulin treatment for patients with recent-onset type 1 diabetes: 12-month results of a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
text:
BACKGROUND: Type 1 diabetes occurs when T-cells destroy β cells. Previous studies indicate that antithymocyte globulin (ATG) may reduce this autoimmune response. We conducted a clinical trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of rabbit ATG in preserving islet function in individuals with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Here, we present the 12-month results.

METHODS: In this phase 2 trial, we enrolled patients aged 12-35 with recent-onset type 1 diabetes and a peak C-peptide of 0.4 nM or higher. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 6.5 mg/kg ATG or placebo over four days. The primary endpoint was the change in 2-h area under the curve C-peptide response from baseline to 12 months. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis. This is an interim analysis of an ongoing trial that will continue for 24 months. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00515099).

FINDINGS: Between Sept 10, 2007, and June 1, 2011, we screened 154 individuals, randomly assigning 38 to ATG and 20 to placebo. There was no significant difference in the primary endpoint between the two groups. Participants in the ATG group had a mean change in C-peptide area under the curve of -0.195 pmol/mL (95% CI -0.292 to -0.098), while those in the placebo group had a mean change of -0.239 pmol/mL (-0.361 to -0.118) (p=0.591). Most participants in the ATG group experienced cytokine release syndrome and serum sickness, which led to a temporary increase in interleukin-6 and acute-phase proteins. T-cell depletion occurred in the ATG group, but effector memory T cells were not affected, and the ratio of regulatory to effector memory T cells declined initially and then stabilized. ATG-treated patients had 159 grade 3-4 adverse events, primarily related to T-cell depletion, compared to 13 in the placebo group. However, there was no significant difference in the incidence of infectious diseases between the two groups.

INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that a short course of ATG does not preserve β-cell function in patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes after 12 months. Generalized T-cell depletion without specific depletion of effector memory T cells and preservation of regulatory T cells appears to be an ineffective treatment for type 1 diabetes.

title: The nucleosome family: dynamic and growing.
text: Since the nucleosome was discovered in 1974, scientists have found various particles in which DNA is wrapped around different histone complexes. These particles include octasomes, hexasomes, tetrasomes, "split" half-nucleosomes, and recently discovered hemisomes. The existence of all these particles in vivo and the conditions under which they exist are still uncertain. Understanding their physiological significance in the complex DNA transactions within the eukaryotic nucleus and their dynamics is crucial. This review summarizes research conducted over more than three decades and redefines the concept of a "nucleosome." It emphasizes that the nucleosome is not a single static entity but rather a family of particles with distinct structural and dynamic properties, each serving different functions.

title: Association between serum corin levels and risk of acute myocardial infarction.
text:
BACKGROUND: There is growing evidence suggesting that corin plays a crucial role in regulating salt-water balance, blood pressure, and cardiac function by activating natriuretic peptides. This case-control study aimed to assess the association between serum soluble corin and acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

METHODS: A total of 856 consecutive AMI patients and 856 control subjects were enrolled in this study. We used a logistic regression model to investigate the potential relationship between serum corin levels and AMI risk.

RESULTS: AMI patients exhibited higher BMI, lower physical activity levels, and a higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking compared to the control group. Serum corin levels were significantly lower in AMI patients (825±263pg/ml) compared to healthy controls (1246±425pg/ml). After adjusting for body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and physical activity, the odds ratios of ST elevation (STEMI) and non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) were significantly reduced with increasing levels of serum corin in both men and women (P for trend, <0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates a significant decrease in serum corin levels in AMI patients, and it reveals an inverse association between corin levels and the incidence of STEMI and NSTEMI in both men and women.

title: Crosstalk between the estrogen receptor and the HER tyrosine kinase receptor family: molecular mechanism and clinical implications for endocrine therapy resistance.
text: Breast cancer progression and the evolution of tumors are influenced by the intricate interactions between steroid receptors (estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor) and growth factor receptors. In recent years, the field of cancer treatment has seen the emergence of various approaches targeting these specific pathways and key molecules (such as ER and growth factor receptors) to halt tumor growth and achieve complete eradication. However, the success of these treatments has been inconsistent, with both initial resistance and acquired resistance posing significant challenges. Recent studies on ER biology have provided new insights into its role in breast cancer and have emphasized the importance of a close interplay between the ER and HER family signaling pathways in the development of resistance to endocrine therapies targeting the ER pathway. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of the mechanisms through which breast cancer cells develop resistance to endocrine therapies due to the crosstalk between the ER and HER growth factor receptor signaling pathways. Additionally, it explores potential therapeutic strategies that could extend the duration of response and overcome resistance to endocrine therapies.

title: Nuclear PTEN functions as an essential regulator of SRF-dependent transcription to control smooth muscle differentiation
text: The progression of vascular disease is linked to significant changes in the phenotype and function of vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs). The expression of genes responsible for SMC contraction and differentiation is controlled by a transcription factor called serum response factor (SRF). However, the precise mechanisms that regulate SMC phenotype are not fully understood. In this study, we discovered a new role for the lipid and protein phosphatase PTEN in the nucleus. PTEN works together with SRF to maintain the differentiated smooth muscle (SM) phenotype. PTEN interacts with the N-terminal domain of SRF, which enhances SRF's ability to bind to important promoter elements in genes specific to SM. When factors induce a switch in phenotype, PTEN is translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, resulting in reduced activity of SRF in promoting muscle development, but increased activity in promoting the proliferation of cells. We observed a decrease in PTEN expression in the intimal SMCs of atherosclerotic lesions in humans, suggesting that these findings may have clinical significance.

title: SEROSURVEY FOR FELINE LEUKEMIA VIRUS AND LENTIVIRUSES IN CAPTIVE SMALL NEOTROPIC FELIDS IN SÃO PAULO STATE, BRAZIL
text: Feline leukemia virus (FeLV), Gammaretrovirus, and feline immunodeficiency virus, a Lentivirus, are part of the Retroviridae family and can cause persistent infections in domestic cats (Felis catus). These infections can lead to cytoproliferative and cytosuppressive disorders. The morbidity and mortality rates associated with these viruses are high in domestic cats worldwide. If endangered neotropic small felids become infected with these viruses, it could have devastating consequences. To determine the prevalence of FeLV and feline lentiviruses in neotropic small felids kept in captivity in São Paulo state, Brazil, we tested serum samples from 104 animals of the species Leopardus pardalis, Leopardus tigrinus, Leopardus wiedii, Herpailurus yaguarondi, and Oncifelis geoffroyi using commercially available immunoassays. All results were negative, indicating that retrovirus infection is not a significant clinical issue in these populations. However, since domestic cats in São Paulo city are naturally infected with these pathogens and feral cats are commonly found in zoologic facilities in Brazil, preventive measures should be implemented to prevent the transmission of retroviruses to naive populations of wild and captive neotropic felids in Brazil.

title: Comparing the metabolism of quercetin in rats, mice and gerbils
text:
The metabolism of quercetin in vivo is investigated using various species of rodents. However, it is uncertain if these animals are suitable as animal models. Therefore, we compared the metabolism of quercetin in Wistar rats, Balb/c mice, and Mongolian gerbils. We analyzed the levels of quercetin metabolites (quercetin-3-glucuronide, quercetin-3′-sulfate, and methyl-quercetin isorhamnetin) in the plasma, lungs, and livers of these animals using high-performance liquid chromatography. We also examined the metabolic enzyme activities in the intestinal mucosal membrane and liver. 

Initially, we observed that gerbils had the highest level of Q3′S after acute quercetin administration. However, after long-term supplementation (20 weeks), Q3G became the dominant metabolite in the plasma, lungs, and livers of all animals, followed by IH and Q3′S. Gerbils still exhibited a higher Q3′S conversion ratio. The average concentrations of total quercetin in the plasma of gerbils were the highest in both short- and long-term studies. The activities of uridine 5′-diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase, phenolsulfotransferase, and catechol-O-methyltransferase were induced by quercetin in a dose- and tissue-dependent manner in all animals. 

Overall, the metabolism of quercetin is similar in all animals after long-term supplementation and comparable to that of humans. However, gerbils have a higher accumulation of quercetin and Q3′S conversion ratio compared to the other animals.

title: Cytokinesis failure generating tetraploids promotes tumorigenesis in p53-null cells
text: We conducted an experiment to investigate the long-standing hypothesis that cell division failure, resulting in genetically unstable tetraploid cells, contributes to the development of aneuploid malignancies. To test this idea, we temporarily blocked cytokinesis in p53-null (p53-/-) mouse mammary epithelial cells (MMECs), allowing us to isolate diploid and tetraploid cultures. We found that the tetraploid cells exhibited a higher frequency of whole-chromosome mis-segregation and chromosomal rearrangements. Interestingly, only the tetraploid cells were transformed in vitro when exposed to a carcinogen. Additionally, when transplanted subcutaneously into nude mice, only the tetraploid cells gave rise to malignant mammary epithelial cancers in the absence of a carcinogen. These tumors displayed numerous non-reciprocal translocations and an 8–30-fold amplification of a chromosomal region containing a cluster of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) genes. Overexpression of MMP has been associated with mammary tumors in both humans and animal models. Therefore, our findings suggest that tetraploidy increases the occurrence of chromosomal alterations and promotes tumor development in p53-/- MMECs.

title: Claspin, a Chk1-regulatory protein, monitors DNA replication on chromatin independently of RPA, ATR, and Rad17.
text: In Xenopus egg extracts containing incompletely replicated DNA, Claspin is necessary for the activation of Chk1 through ATR. Our study reveals that Claspin binds to chromatin in a controlled manner during S phase. This binding is dependent on the pre-replication complex (pre-RC) and Cdc45, but not on replication protein A (RPA). This suggests that Claspin binds to chromatin around the time of initial DNA unwinding at replication origins. On the other hand, both ATR and Rad17 require RPA to associate with DNA. Claspin, ATR, and Rad17 all independently bind to chromatin. These findings indicate that Claspin has a role in monitoring DNA replication during S phase. Claspin, ATR, and Rad17 may work together in regulating checkpoints by detecting different aspects of a DNA replication fork.

title: Cold-related respiratory symptoms in the general population.
text:
INTRODUCTION
Respiratory symptoms related to cold weather are frequently experienced by individuals living in northern regions, particularly those with pre-existing respiratory conditions. However, there is limited knowledge regarding the prevalence of these symptoms in the general population and the specific temperatures at which they begin to occur.

OBJECTIVES
This study aimed to determine the prevalence and threshold temperatures for self-reported respiratory symptoms associated with cold weather, both in healthy individuals and those with respiratory diseases.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
A total of 6,591 men and women aged 25 to 74 years from the national FINRISK study were surveyed regarding their experience of cold-related respiratory symptoms. The results were analyzed using age-adjusted prevalence rates and coefficients obtained from multivariate regressions.

RESULTS
Individuals with asthma (69% in men, 78% in women) and chronic bronchitis (65% in men, 76% in women) reported cold-related respiratory symptoms more frequently compared to healthy individuals (18% in men, 21% in women). Binomial regression analysis revealed that symptom prevalence increased with age and was higher by 4%, 50%, and 21% in females, individuals with asthma, and those with chronic bronchitis, respectively. The reported threshold temperature for cold-related symptoms was -14 degrees Celsius for males and -15 degrees Celsius for females, with a slight increase observed with age (0 to 5 degrees Celsius), asthma (2 degrees Celsius), and chronic bronchitis (3 degrees Celsius). Notably, the threshold temperature for mucus production decreased with age (2 to 5 degrees Celsius) and asthma (2 degrees Celsius). The effects of smoking and education were found to be minimal.

CONCLUSION
Cold-related respiratory symptoms are prevalent among individuals with chronic respiratory diseases and can manifest at relatively low temperatures. In cold climates, these symptoms may significantly impact an individual's health-related quality of life.

title: Carvedilol for children and adolescents with heart failure: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
CONTEXT: While beta-blockers have been shown to be effective in improving symptoms and survival in adults with heart failure, their effects in children and adolescents remain unclear.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of carvedilol in children and adolescents with symptomatic systemic ventricular systolic dysfunction.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted involving 161 children and adolescents with symptomatic systolic heart failure from 26 US centers. Patients were assigned to receive either placebo or carvedilol in addition to conventional heart failure medications. The study began in June 2000 and concluded in May 2005, with each patient receiving medication for 8 months.

INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly assigned to receive placebo, low-dose carvedilol, or high-dose carvedilol, with dosages based on the patient's weight and whether their systemic ventricle was a left ventricle or not.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome measure was a composite measure of heart failure outcomes in patients receiving carvedilol compared to those receiving placebo. Secondary efficacy variables included individual components of the composite measure, echocardiographic measures, and plasma b-type natriuretic peptide levels.

RESULTS: The study found no statistically significant difference between the groups in terms of the composite end point. Among patients assigned to placebo, 56% improved, 30% worsened, and 15% remained unchanged. Among patients assigned to carvedilol, 56% improved, 24% worsened, and 19% remained unchanged. The rates of worsening were lower than expected. The odds ratio for worsened outcome in the carvedilol group compared to the placebo group was 0.79, indicating no significant difference. However, a subgroup analysis revealed a significant interaction between treatment and ventricular morphology, suggesting a possible differential effect of carvedilol based on the type of ventricle.

CONCLUSIONS: These preliminary results suggest that carvedilol does not significantly improve clinical heart failure outcomes in children and adolescents with symptomatic systolic heart failure. However, due to lower than expected event rates, the study may have been underpowered. There may be a differential effect of carvedilol based on ventricular morphology in this population.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: This trial was registered on clinicaltrials.gov with the identifier NCT00052026.

title: The circadian clock gene BMAL1 is a novel therapeutic target for malignant pleural mesothelioma.
text:
Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive cancer that originates from the cells lining the parietal pleura. It has a poor prognosis, and while there have been advancements in treatment, more effective therapeutic approaches are needed. Recent studies have shown that BMAL1, a key component of the circadian clock, is overexpressed in MPM. In this study, we aim to investigate BMAL1 as a potential molecular target for MPM.

We found that the majority of MPM cell lines and some clinical specimens expressed higher levels of BMAL1 compared to a non-cancerous mesothelial cell line and normal pleural specimens, respectively. Additionally, we observed that the circadian rhythm pathway is disrupted in MPM cells, as a serum shock did not induce the expected rhythmic expression of BMAL1 in MPM cells.

To further explore the role of BMAL1 in MPM, we conducted experiments using two MPM cell lines and the non-cancerous cell line. Knocking down BMAL1 in the MPM cell lines resulted in suppressed proliferation and clonal growth, while no significant effects were observed in the non-cancerous cell line. Furthermore, BMAL1 depletion caused disruptions in the cell cycle, leading to increased apoptosis and polyploidy in MPM cells. We also observed downregulation of cell cycle regulators and upregulation of cyclin E expression upon BMAL1 knockdown.

Interestingly, the MPM cell line with the highest level of BMAL1 showed the most significant effects upon BMAL1 knockdown. These cells exhibited mitotic catastrophe, characterized by disrupted cell cycle regulators and drastic morphological changes such as micronucleation and multiple nuclei.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that BMAL1 plays a critical role in MPM and could be a promising therapeutic target for this aggressive cancer. Further research is needed to explore the potential of targeting BMAL1 in MPM treatment.

title: Mechanism and Regulation of DNA-Protein Crosslink Repair by the DNA-Dependent Metalloprotease SPRTN
text: Until recently, not much was known about the repair mechanisms specific to covalent DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs), which are harmful DNA lesions that disrupt important chromatin processes like replication and transcription. However, a DPC-processing protease in yeast has been identified, shedding some light on the subject. While it is believed that higher eukaryotes also possess a DPC protease based on data from Xenopus laevis egg extracts, its exact identity has yet to be determined. In this study, we have identified the metalloprotease SPRTN as the DPC protease in metazoans. When SPRTN is lost, DPCs cannot be repaired and the organism becomes hypersensitive to agents that induce DPCs. SPRTN carries out DPC processing through a unique DNA-induced protease activity, which is regulated by several intricate mechanisms. Through cellular, biochemical, and structural studies, we have discovered a DNA switch that triggers its protease activity, a ubiquitin switch that controls SPRTN's accessibility to chromatin, and a regulatory autocatalytic cleavage process. Additionally, our findings offer a molecular explanation for how SPRTN deficiency leads to the premature aging and cancer predisposition disorder known as Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome.

title: 'Zero is not good for me': implications of infertility in Ghana.
text: This study examines the impact of infertility on women in Ghana, West Africa, considering its implications for mental health, marital stability, social interaction, and gendered experiences. The research involved analyzing semi-structured interview data from 107 women seeking treatment in gynecological and obstetric clinics in Accra, Ghana. The findings reveal that infertile women face significant social stigma, strain in their marriages, and various mental health difficulties. They often feel unfairly blamed for their infertility, leading to greater social consequences compared to their male partners. Even women who do not identify as infertile acknowledge the severe social consequences of infertility, particularly for women. Overall, infertility in Ghana has far-reaching effects on social interactions, marital stability, and mental health, with these consequences being perceived as unequal between Ghanaian men and women.

title: Ethical dilemmas in a randomized trial of asthma treatment: can Bayesian statistical analysis explain the results?
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate whether the use of bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation could reduce the need for endotracheal intubation, length of hospital stay, and hospital charges in patients with status asthmaticus. However, the presence of physician treatment bias made it challenging to enroll patients. To address this bias, Bayesian statistics were employed to analyze the study results. 

The study was conducted as a prospective, randomized controlled clinical trial over a period of 34.5 months at an urban university hospital with an emergency department that had an annual census of 94,000 visits. Patients who remained in status asthmaticus after initial treatment with inhaled beta-agonists and steroids were randomly assigned to receive either BiPAP ventilation in addition to standard treatment or standard treatment alone (non-BiPAP). Intubation was performed as necessary for both groups. Patients with concurrent cardiac or other pulmonary diseases were excluded from the study. The primary outcome measures were the rate of endotracheal intubation and length of hospital stay. Secondary outcome measures included vital signs (respiratory rate, pulse rate, blood pressure), changes in expiratory peak flow, changes in pulse oximetry values, and hospital charges. Data analysis involved the use of Fisher's exact test, Mann-Whitney tests, and Bayesian statistics. Only data from the first enrollment were included in the analysis for patients who were enrolled multiple times. 

Nineteen patients were enrolled in the BiPAP group, while 16 patients were enrolled in the non-BiPAP group. Due to physician treatment bias, enrollment significantly decreased, leading to an early termination of the study. Demographic characteristics showed that the groups were similar in terms of age, sex, initial peak flow rate, and arterial blood gas measurements. The non-BiPAP group had a 7.3% increase (95% CI = -22 to +45) in the intubation rate compared to the BiPAP group. There was no significant difference in length of hospital stay or hospital charges, although there was a favorable trend in favor of the BiPAP group. One patient in the BiPAP group experienced discomfort associated with the nasal BiPAP mask. Bayesian analysis revealed that in order for the collected data to be convincing at a 95% confidence level, the treating physicians would have needed to have a prior conviction of 98.9% that BiPAP was an effective treatment. 

In conclusion, this study found that BiPAP ventilation did not have any harmful effects in patients with status asthmaticus. There was a trend towards a decreased rate of endotracheal intubation, shorter hospital stays, and reduced hospital charges. However, further research with a larger sample size is necessary to determine the clinical and statistical significance of this intervention. Ethical concerns regarding withholding BiPAP treatment from the control group led to the premature termination of the study at the authors' institution.

title: Mental health in prison populations. A review--with special emphasis on a study of Danish prisoners on remand.
text:
The aim of this study is to examine existing literature on mental health and psychiatric disorders in prison populations and apply the findings to a specific Danish study on individuals awaiting trial. The methodology involves a review of the literature, which is then divided into several sections: the validity of psychometrics in prison populations, the prevalence of psychiatric disorders prior to imprisonment, the incidence of psychiatric disorders during imprisonment, the relationship between psychopathy and psychiatric comorbidity, and the different methods of heroin use (smoking vs. injection) and their association with dependence syndromes. The results are compared to a longitudinal Danish study that focuses on individuals in solitary confinement or non-solitary confinement. 

The findings highlight the importance of considering various factors when addressing mental health in prison populations, such as international differences, the prison environment, demographics, and methodological issues. The global prison population is increasing, and psychometrics may yield different results in prison populations compared to the general population. For example, the General Health Questionnaire-28 has low validity in remand prisoners. Psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, are more prevalent in prison populations and may be on the rise. Dependence syndromes, particularly related to drug use, are the most common disorders observed. The early stages of imprisonment are particularly vulnerable, with a higher incidence of adjustment disorders, especially in individuals in solitary confinement. The prevalence of psychopathy is lower in European prisons compared to North American prisons, and higher scores of psychopathy are associated with greater psychiatric comorbidity. Opioid dependence is the most frequent drug disorder, and individuals who use injection as their method of administration tend to have more severe dysfunction compared to those who smoke the drug. Many mentally ill prisoners go undetected and receive inadequate treatment. 

In conclusion, there is a growing population of mentally ill prisoners who are not being adequately identified and treated.

title: Why females live longer than males: control of longevity by sex hormones.
text: In many species, including humans, females tend to live longer than males. Researchers have discovered a potential explanation for this phenomenon, which involves the positive effects of estrogens. Estrogens bind to estrogen receptors and enhance the expression of genes associated with longevity. These genes include those responsible for producing antioxidant enzymes like superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase. Consequently, mitochondria in females generate fewer harmful reactive oxygen species compared to males. However, the use of estrogens as a solution has significant drawbacks. They have feminizing effects, making them unsuitable for males, and may even increase the risk of serious diseases like uterine cancer in postmenopausal women. On the other hand, phytoestrogens found in soy or wine could potentially offer some of the beneficial effects of estrogens without the undesirable consequences. By studying the differences in lifespan between genders, we can gain insights into the fundamental processes of aging and develop practical strategies to enhance the longevity of both females and males.

title: The pre-B-cell receptor: selector of fitting immunoglobulin heavy chains for the B-cell repertoire
text: In this Opinion article, I discuss the significance of the pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) in the formation of antigen-specific B cells. This involves the selection of immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) variable-region repertoire, differentiation and proliferation of precursor B cells, and the exclusion of IgH allelic. Comparisons with the pre-T-cell receptor (pre-TCR) in T-cell development raise thought-provoking inquiries. Why do both B- and T-cell lineages utilize a surrogate chain, such as the surrogate light chain and the pre-TCR α-chain, respectively, to develop their repertoires of cells capable of recognizing antigens? What roles do the pre-BCR and pre-TCR play in the differentiation of lymphocytes and the exclusion of antigen-receptor alleles? This article, along with the accompanying piece by Harald von Boehmer, aims to shed light on these questions.

title: Helicobacter species methods and protocols. Introduction.
text: The Helicobacter infection is a long-lasting condition that is primarily responsible for causing gastric and duodenal ulcers, as well as gastric cancer. The understanding of this bacteria, its interaction with the host, and the immune response of the host has greatly improved due to the standardization of culture techniques and animal models. In the upcoming chapters, we will delve into the clinical aspects of this infection and highlight the crucial techniques for conducting thorough investigations.

title: Effectiveness of statin-eluting stent on early inflammatory response and neointimal thickness in a porcine coronary model.
text:
The purpose of this study was to assess the effectiveness of stent-based cerivastatin delivery in reducing inflammatory responses and adverse effects on endothelial function, as well as inhibiting neointimal hyperplasia in a porcine coronary model. Drug-eluting stents (DES) are commonly used during coronary revascularization due to their ability to reduce restenosis and target lesion revascularization compared to bare metal stents (BMS). However, DES have limitations, including late thrombosis caused by delayed healing and persistent local inflammation. Statins have been shown to inhibit cell proliferation, inflammation, and restore endothelial function. 

In this study, pigs were randomly assigned to receive either a cerivastatin-eluting stent (CES) or a BMS in their coronary arteries. All animals survived the procedure without any adverse effects. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a significant decrease in inflammatory cell infiltration in the treated vessels on day 3 after stenting. Endothelial function, assessed by intracoronary infusion of bradykinin, was preserved in both the CES and BMS groups at day 28. Volumetric intravascular ultrasound images showed a decrease in intimal volume in the CES group. Histomorphometric analysis demonstrated a reduction in neointimal area in the CES group despite similar injury scores. 

In conclusion, the use of CES in porcine coronary arteries resulted in a significant decrease in neointimal hyperplasia, with a reduced early inflammatory response and no endothelial dysfunction.

title: Genetic variation in West Nile virus from naturally infected mosquitoes and birds suggests quasispecies structure and strong purifying selection.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the genetic diversity of West Nile virus (WNV) in naturally infected mosquitoes and birds. The researchers collected samples from ten infected birds and ten infected mosquito pools during the peak of the 2003 WNV transmission season in Long Island, NY, USA. They focused on a specific fragment of the WNV genome and sequenced 20 clones per specimen.

The results showed that WNV infections in nature come from a genetically diverse population of genomes. Within individual specimens, the average nucleotide diversity was 0.016%, and around 19.5% of clones differed from the consensus sequence. Interestingly, WNV sequences in mosquitoes were found to be more genetically diverse than those in birds. There was no bias towards specific types of mutations in either host, and the genetic diversity estimates did not differ significantly between the two coding regions analyzed.

The researchers also found evidence that WNV genetic diversity may be maintained throughout the enzootic transmission cycle, rather than arising independently during each infection. This was supported by the similarity of non-consensus clones obtained from two avian specimens. Additionally, the study revealed signs of purifying selection within and between WNV populations.

Overall, these findings suggest that WNV populations may exist as a quasispecies and undergo strong purifying natural selection.

title: Overlapping patterns of IGF2 and H19 expression during human development: biallelic IGF2 expression correlates with a lack of H19 expression.
text: During certain stages of human embryonic/fetal and early postnatal development, the spatial patterns of IGF2 and H19 gene expression show remarkable similarities. However, there are notable exceptions in the ciliary anlage of the embryonic retina and the choroid plexus/leptomeninges, where only transcripts from the IGF2 locus can be detected, not from the H19 locus. Additionally, unlike other tissue samples examined, the choroid plexus/leptomeninges express both parental IGF2 alleles. Although RNase protection analysis indicates weak activity of the P1 promoter in the choroid plexus/leptomeninges, the P2, P3, and P4 promoters are active wherever IGF2 is expressed. These findings are discussed in relation to a proposed coordinated control of the reciprocally imprinted and closely linked IGF2 and H19 loci.

title: Intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation after balloon catheter injury. The role of basic fibroblast growth factor.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the localization and synthesis of basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) in the rat carotid artery during chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation. Immunocytochemical staining revealed the presence of bFGF in the uninjured arterial wall. However, after balloon injury, the cellular staining of bFGF decreased. Western and northern blot analyses confirmed a decrease in both bFGF protein and mRNA levels following injury. To further explore the role of bFGF, a neutralizing antibody was administered 4 and 5 days after injury. Surprisingly, this antibody had no effect on intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation. These findings suggest that an increase in bFGF expression is not necessary for the observed chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation after balloon catheter injury. Additionally, bFGF does not appear to be the primary mitogen responsible for intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation.

title: Prevention of central venous catheter-associated thrombosis: a meta-analysis.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the use of anticoagulant prophylaxis in patients with central venous catheters, as there is controversy surrounding its effectiveness. The researchers conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on this topic. They searched MEDLINE and EMBASE databases up to May 2006, and also manually searched conference proceedings and bibliographies for additional relevant studies. 

The results of the analysis included fifteen trials, which evaluated the use of unfractionated heparin infusion, oral fixed low-dose vitamin K antagonist, and subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin. The summary relative risks for all catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis (both symptomatic and asymptomatic) ranged from 0.31 to 0.73, indicating a statistically significant reduction in risk. However, for symptomatic deep vein thrombosis, the summary relative risks ranged from 0.28 to 0.72, but did not achieve statistical significance for any specific regimen. 

In conclusion, the researchers found that anticoagulant prophylaxis is effective in preventing all catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis in patients with central venous catheters. However, its effectiveness in preventing symptomatic venous thromboembolism, including pulmonary embolism, remains uncertain.

title: Long-term efficacy of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation in adolescents: a randomized controlled trial.
text: A study was conducted to examine the effectiveness of nicotine patches compared to placebo patches in helping Dutch adolescents quit smoking. The results showed that nicotine patches were effective in promoting smoking cessation at the end of the treatment period, but only in participants who were highly compliant. The study also investigated whether the effects of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) persisted at 6- and 12-month follow-up assessments. Adolescents between the ages of 12 and 18, who smoked at least seven cigarettes a day and were motivated to quit, were recruited from school yards and randomly assigned to receive either a nicotine patch or a placebo patch. A total of 257 participants attended an information meeting and underwent a 6- or 9-week treatment. Smoking cessation, compliance, and other factors were measured using online questionnaires. Biochemical validation of smoking cessation at the 12-month follow-up was done using saliva cotinine. The results showed that at the 6-month follow-up, 8.1% of participants in the nicotine patch group and 5.7% in the placebo patch group were abstinent. At the 12-month follow-up, the abstinence rates were 4.4% and 6.6% respectively. However, when analyzing the data using an intention-to-treat approach, there were no significant effects of NRT on abstinence rates at either follow-up period, even after considering compliance and adjusting for other factors. In conclusion, NRT was not effective in helping adolescents quit smoking at the 6- and 12-month follow-ups. This suggests that a more intensive approach is needed to support young people in their efforts to quit smoking.

title: Interferon gamma in autoimmunity: A complicated player on a complex stage.
text: Initially, autoimmune disease was perceived to regard IFNγ as a prime example of a pro-inflammatory factor. However, it is now evident that IFNγ possesses the ability to exhibit both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects, with the specific outcome being influenced by the particular physiological or pathological context being investigated. This article aims to examine the primary immune modulatory functions of IFNγ and provide an overview of the current evidence regarding its influence on the development and regulation of various autoimmune diseases and disease models.

title: The first gene of the Bacillus subtilis clpC operon, ctsR, encodes a negative regulator of its own operon and other class III heat shock genes.
text: The regulation of the Bacillus subtilis clpC operon involves two stress induction pathways. These pathways are activated by either sigmaB or a class III stress induction mechanism that acts on a sigmaA-like promoter. When the clpC operon was placed under the control of the isopropyl-beta-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG)-inducible Pspac promoter, the natural clpC promoters fused to a lacZ reporter gene were significantly repressed after IPTG induction. This repression strongly suggests that one of the gene products of the clpC operon acts as a negative regulator. The first gene of the clpC operon, ctsR, encodes this negative regulator and contains a predicted helix-turn-helix DNA-binding motif. Deletion of ctsR eliminated the negative regulation and led to high expression of both the clpC operon and the clpP gene under nonstressed conditions. However, an increase in clpC and clpP mRNA levels was still observed after heat shock, even in the absence of sigmaB, indicating the presence of a second induction mechanism at the vegetative promoter. Further analysis revealed that the deletion of ctsR partially influenced the expression of other class III stress genes. Through experiments with different clpC promoter fragments and the purified CtsR protein, a potential target region where the repressor binds in vivo and in vitro was identified. Our findings demonstrate that the CtsR protein acts as a global repressor of the clpC operon and other class III heat shock genes. It prevents transcription from both the sigmaB- and sigmaA-dependent promoters under normal conditions and may become inactive or dissociate under inducing stress conditions.

title: Role for c-myc in activation-induced apoptotic cell death in T cell hybridomas.
text: When immature T cells and certain T cell hybridomas are stimulated through the T cell receptor complex, they undergo cell death known as apoptosis. This phenomenon is likely linked to the elimination of developing T cells in response to antigens. The apoptosis triggered by this activation relies on the synthesis of proteins and RNA in the dying cells, although the specific genes involved in this process have not been identified before. By using antisense oligonucleotides that target c-myc, the constitutive expression of c-Myc protein in T cell hybridomas can be blocked. This interference with c-myc expression hampers all aspects of activation-induced apoptosis, while leaving lymphokine production unaffected in these cells. These findings suggest that c-myc expression is an essential component of activation-induced apoptosis.

title: Examining BCL-2 family function with large unilamellar vesicles.
text: The BCL-2 family, consisting of around twenty proteins, plays a role in cell survival and apoptosis. When cells experience stress, such as DNA damage, the pro-apoptotic proteins BAK and BAX become activated and disrupt the outer mitochondrial membrane, a process known as mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP). This allows pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c to enter the cytoplasm, activate caspases, and trigger apoptosis. BAK and BAX require interactions with BH3-only proteins like BID to induce MOMP. Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins like BCL-xL and MCL-1 regulate cell survival by controlling the interactions between BAK/BAX and the BH3-only proteins that activate them. Sensitizer/de-repressor BH3-only proteins like BAD and PUMA inhibit anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins. The decision between cell survival and MOMP is determined by multiple BCL-2 family interactions at the outer mitochondrial membrane. Large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) are a useful model for studying these interactions and membrane permeabilization. LUVs are made up of specific lipids found in Xenopus mitochondria and can mimic the outer mitochondrial membrane. A modified version of this model allows for kinetic analysis of protein interactions and real-time measurement of membrane permeabilization using a dye and quencher system. This article describes the use of LUVs containing the dye and quencher to study various combinations of recombinant BCL-2 family proteins and control experiments.

title: The Hippo pathway effector YAP controls mouse hepatic stellate cell activation.
text:
The activation of hepatic stellate cells is a response to liver injury, but prolonged activation during chronic liver damage leads to excessive matrix deposition and the formation of pathological scar tissue, ultimately resulting in fibrosis and cirrhosis. While the importance of sustained stellate cell activation in this process is well known, the mechanisms that initiate and drive the early stages of activation are not well understood. 

In this study, we identified the Hippo pathway and its effector YAP as a key pathway that controls stellate cell activation. YAP, a transcriptional co-activator, was found to drive the initial changes in gene expression during stellate cell activation. Activation of stellate cells in mice through CCl4 administration or in vitro led to rapid activation of YAP, as evidenced by its movement into the nucleus and the induction of YAP target genes. YAP was also activated in stellate cells of fibrotic livers in humans, as indicated by its presence in the nucleus. 

Importantly, when YAP expression was knocked down or pharmacologically inhibited, hepatic stellate cell activation was prevented in vitro. In addition, pharmacological inhibition of YAP hindered fibrogenesis in mice. 

In conclusion, the activation of YAP is a crucial driver of hepatic stellate cell activation, and inhibiting YAP presents a new approach for treating liver fibrosis.

title: Human Monocytes Engage an Alternative Inflammasome Pathway.
text: The bioactivity of Interleukin-1β (IL-1β), a cytokine, is regulated by the activation of the inflammasome. However, when exposed to lipopolysaccharide, human monocytes secrete IL-1β independently of the usual inflammasome triggers. This response is specific to humans and is not observed in mice. In human monocytes, lipopolysaccharide activates an "alternative inflammasome" that relies on NLRP3-ASC-caspase-1 signaling. However, this alternative inflammasome does not exhibit the typical characteristics of the classical inflammasome, such as pyroptosome formation, pyroptosis induction, and K(+) efflux dependency. By studying a monocyte transdifferentiation system, we discovered that the TLR4-TRIF-RIPK1-FADD-CASP8 signaling pathway is responsible for propagating the activation of the alternative inflammasome upstream of NLRP3. It is important to note that this signaling cascade is only involved in alternative inflammasome activation and does not extend to classical NLRP3 activation. Given that the alternative inflammasome activation is sensitive and promiscuous to TLR4, we propose that this signaling cascade plays a crucial role in TLR4-driven, IL-1β-mediated immune responses and immunopathology in humans.

title: The use of biosimilars in immune-mediated disease: A joint Italian Society of Rheumatology (SIR), Italian Society of Dermatology (SIDeMaST), and Italian Group of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IG-IBD) position paper.
text: Biological agents are commonly used in the fields of rheumatology, dermatology, and inflammatory bowel disease. Over the past decade, there has been an increase in evidence supporting their effectiveness and safety for these therapeutic purposes. Biosimilar agents are monoclonal antibodies that are similar to previously approved biologics. In the European Union, they have been approved for the management of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), although currently, data is only available for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. However, it is essential to have direct evidence on the efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity of biosimilars in conditions such as psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and in children. Taking into account the existing literature, we present the official position of the Italian Societies of Rheumatology, Dermatology, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease on the use of biosimilars in IMIDs.

title: The coordination of cyclic microtubule association/dissociation and tail swing of cytoplasmic dynein.
text:
The dynein motor domain consists of a tail, head, and stalk. It is believed that the tail swings against the head during its ATPase cycle to generate a force on microtubules. In order for this "power stroke" to occur, dynein must coordinate the tail swing with the association and dissociation of microtubules at the tip of the stalk. While we have a better understanding of the tail swing process, the coordination of microtubule interaction remains unclear. 

To investigate this, we used the single-headed recombinant motor domain of Dictyostelium cytoplasmic dynein. We aimed to answer questions about how the motor domain's interaction with a microtubule is influenced by ATPase steps, how the two mechanical cycles (microtubule association/dissociation and tail swing) are coordinated, and which ATPase site in the motor domain regulates this coordination. 

Through steady-state and pre-steady-state measurements, we discovered that the two mechanical cycles occur simultaneously in most of the intermediate states of the ATPase cycle. In the poststroke state, the motor domain strongly binds to the microtubule with a K(d) of approximately 0.2 microM. However, in the prestroke state, most motor domains weakly bind to the microtubule with a K(d) of >10 microM. 

Interestingly, our results indicate that the timing of the microtubule affinity change and tail swing is staggered during the recovery stroke step, where the tail moves from the poststroke to the prestroke position. We also found that the ATPase site in the AAA1 module of the motor domain is responsible for coordinating these two mechanical processes.

title: A conserved modified wobble nucleoside (mcm5s2U) in lysyl-tRNA is required for viability in yeast.
text: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) that are specific for Gln, Lys, and Glu in all organisms (except Mycoplasma) and organelles contain a modified nucleoside called 2-thiouridine derivative (xm(5)s(2)U) as the wobble nucleoside. These tRNAs are responsible for reading the A- and G-ending codons in the split codon boxes His/Gln, Asn/Lys, and Asp/Glu. In eukaryotic cytoplasmic tRNAs, the conserved constituent in position 5 of uridine is 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl (mcm(5)). A protein called Tuc1p, found in yeast, is similar to the bacterial protein TtcA and is essential for the synthesis of 2-thiouridine in the wobble position (position 34) of tRNA, rather than the synthesis of 2-thiocytidine in position 32. This suggests that an ancient member of the TtcA family has evolved to modify U34 in tRNAs of organisms from the Eukarya and Archaea domains. When the TUC1 gene is deleted along with the ELP3 gene, which results in the absence of the mcm(5) side chain, all modifications are removed from the wobble uridine derivatives of cytoplasmic tRNAs specific for Gln, Lys, and Glu, leading to cell death. Interestingly, the double mutant elp3 tuc1 can be rescued by an excess of the unmodified form of these three tRNAs, indicating that the primary function of mcm(5)s(2)U34 is to enhance the efficiency of reading the correct codons rather than preventing mis-sense errors. Surprisingly, the viability of the double mutant can be restored by overexpressing the tRNA(Lys) lacking mcm(5)s(2)U alone.

title: The molecular requirements for cytokinesis.
text: Animal cells undergo cytokinesis after anaphase onset by forming an actomyosin contractile ring. This ring constricts the plasma membrane, resulting in the formation of two daughter cells connected by a cytoplasmic bridge. Eventually, this bridge is severed to complete the process of cytokinesis. Various techniques have been employed to identify proteins involved in cytokinesis in vertebrates, insects, and nematodes. In most animal cells, a core group of approximately 20 proteins play individual roles in cytokinesis. These proteins can be found in the contractile ring, central spindle, RhoA pathway, and vesicles responsible for expanding the membrane and severing the bridge. While additional proteins are involved in cytokinesis, they are not conserved among animal cells or necessary for the process.

title: Ibuprofen for the treatment of patent ductus arteriosus in preterm or low birth weight (or both) infants.
text:
The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness and safety of ibuprofen with indomethacin, placebo, or no treatment for closing a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in premature, low birth weight infants. The researchers conducted a search of various databases to identify relevant studies. They included 33 studies involving 2190 infants in their analysis.

Two studies compared intravenous ibuprofen with placebo, and one study compared oral ibuprofen with placebo. The results showed that ibuprofen reduced the incidence of failure to close a PDA and the composite outcome of infant mortality, dropouts, or the need for rescue treatment. Another study comparing oral ibuprofen with placebo also found a significant reduction in failure to close a PDA.

Twenty-one studies compared the failure rates for PDA closure with ibuprofen and indomethacin. There was no significant difference between the two groups. However, the risk of developing necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) was lower with ibuprofen, and the duration of ventilatory support was shorter.

Eight studies compared oral ibuprofen with indomethacin, and the results showed no significant difference in failure rates for PDA closure. However, the risk of NEC was lower with oral ibuprofen compared to indomethacin. There was also a decreased risk of failure to close a PDA with oral ibuprofen compared to intravenous ibuprofen.

The researchers concluded that ibuprofen is as effective as indomethacin in closing a PDA and is currently the preferred drug. Ibuprofen also reduces the risk of NEC and transient renal insufficiency. Oro-gastric administration of ibuprofen is as effective as intravenous administration. However, further studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of different doses and administration methods of ibuprofen, as well as its long-term effects on infants with PDA.

title: A gradient of template dependence defines distinct biological roles for family X polymerases in nonhomologous end joining.
text: Three members of the Pol X family have been associated with nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) in mammals. Template-independent TdT plays a role in promoting diversity during NHEJ-dependent repair of V(D)J recombination intermediates. However, the functions of template-dependent polymerases mu and lambda in NHEJ are still not well understood. Our study demonstrates that both pol mu and pol lambda are recruited by NHEJ factors to fill gaps in cases where ends have partially complementary overhangs. This suggests that they have similar roles in promoting accuracy in NHEJ. However, only pol mu is involved in promoting accuracy during immunoglobulin kappa recombination. This unique role in vivo is linked to the TdT-like ability of pol mu, but not pol lambda, to act when primer termini lack complementary bases in the template strand. Interestingly, unlike TdT, pol mu primarily relies on a template from another DNA molecule for synthesis in this context. This difference in template dependence is mainly due to a small structural element that is present but distinct in all three polymerases.

title: Involvement of sympathetic nervous system and brown fat in endotoxin-induced fever in rats.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the role of brown adipose tissue (BAT) and the sympathetic nervous system in the increase in heat production during endotoxin-induced fever. Over a 4-hour period, oxygen consumption (VO2) was found to be significantly higher (28%) after two doses of endotoxin (Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide, 0.3 mg/100 g body weight) given 24 hours apart. When a mixed beta-adrenoceptor antagonist (propranolol) was injected, VO2 decreased by 14% in rats treated with endotoxin. Selective beta 1- (atenolol) or beta 2- (ICI 118551) antagonists reduced VO2 by 10%. These drugs did not affect VO2 in control animals. The thermogenic activity of BAT, assessed by measuring guanosine 5'-diphosphate (GDP) binding in mitochondria in vitro, increased by 54% in the interscapular BAT and by 171% in other BAT depots. Surgical denervation of one lobe of the interscapular depot prevented these responses. Endotoxin did not stimulate GDP binding in rats fed protein-deficient diets. This could be due to the fact that BAT thermogenic activity was already elevated in control rats on these diets or because endotoxin significantly reduced food intake in the protein-deficient animals. These findings suggest that the activation of BAT by the sympathetic nervous system plays a role in the thermogenic responses to endotoxin and that dietary manipulation can modify these responses.

title: Metabolic, Epigenetic, and Transgenerational Effects of Gut Bacterial Choline Consumption.
text: Choline is a vital nutrient and methyl donor that plays a crucial role in regulating epigenetics. In this study, we investigated how the metabolism of choline by gut microbes affects the fitness of bacteria and the biology of the host. To do this, we engineered a microbial community that lacked a specific enzyme needed for choline utilization. Our findings demonstrate that bacteria that use choline compete with the host for this nutrient, leading to significant changes in the levels of methyl-donor metabolites in the blood and liver. This disruption in choline availability mimics the biochemical characteristics of choline deficiency. Additionally, mice with high levels of choline-consuming bacteria were more susceptible to metabolic diseases when fed a high-fat diet. Moreover, the reduction in methyl-donor availability caused by the bacteria influenced DNA methylation patterns in both adult mice and their offspring, resulting in behavioral changes. These results highlight the impact of bacterial choline metabolism on host metabolism, epigenetics, and behavior, which is often overlooked. Therefore, when determining the optimal intake of nutrients, it is important to consider individual differences in microbial metabolism.

title: Genome-wide analysis reveals SR protein cooperation and competition in regulated splicing.
text: SR proteins are well-known RNA binding proteins that enhance the inclusion of exons by binding to exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs). However, it has been unclear whether the rules governing the activities of SR proteins on model genes can be applied universally to their functions in cells. In this study, we conducted comprehensive analyses of two typical SR proteins, SRSF1 (SF2/ASF) and SRSF2 (SC35), using splicing-sensitive arrays and CLIP-seq on mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs). Surprisingly, we discovered that these SR proteins promote both the inclusion and skipping of exons in vivo, despite their binding patterns not explaining these opposing effects. Further investigations revealed that the loss of one SR protein is accompanied by a coordinated loss or compensatory gain in the interaction of other SR proteins at the affected exons. Therefore, the specific impact of one SR protein on regulated splicing actually relies on a complex network of relationships with multiple other SR proteins in mammalian genomes.

title: Human tuberculous granulomas induce peripheral lymphoid follicle-like structures to orchestrate local host defence in the lung.
text: The human tuberculous granuloma is crucial for the local immune processes that determine the outcome of tuberculosis. However, there is limited information available about these processes in human patients. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to gain a better understanding of the functional and structural properties of the infiltrated tissue. The researchers investigated the mycobacterial load in lesions and its spread to different tissue locations. They also examined the distribution, biological functions, and interactions of the host immune cells. By analyzing the early formation of granulomas in previously healthy lung tissue, they observed a sequential infiltration of cells to the sites of mycobacterial infection. They identified a general structure of the developing granuloma, which consisted of an inner cell layer with few CD8(+) cells surrounding the necrotic center, and an outer area of lymphocyte infiltration containing antigen-presenting cells that harbor mycobacteria. Additionally, they found CD4(+), CD8(+), and B cells in active follicle-like centers that resemble secondary lymphoid organs. The researchers concluded that the follicular structures in the outer rim of granulomas play a crucial role in coordinating the long-lasting host response in pulmonary tuberculosis.

title: Eosinophil pathogenicity mechanisms and therapeutics in neuromyelitis optica.
text:
The presence of eosinophils in inflammatory demyelinating lesions in neuromyelitis optica (NMO) was investigated using various methods such as cell culture, ex vivo spinal cord slices, and in vivo mouse models. The aim was to understand the role of eosinophils in NMO development and explore the potential of eosinophil inhibitors as a therapeutic option. 

Eosinophils derived from mouse bone marrow were cultured and found to exhibit antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) when exposed to NMO autoantibody (NMO-IgG) in cell cultures expressing aquaporin-4. Additionally, in the presence of complement, eosinophils significantly increased cell killing through a complement-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CDCC) mechanism. 

To further investigate the impact of eosinophils, NMO pathology was induced in spinal cord slice cultures treated with NMO-IgG by including eosinophils or their granule toxins. The use of second-generation antihistamines cetirizine and ketotifen, known for their eosinophil-stabilizing properties, effectively reduced NMO-IgG/eosinophil-dependent cytotoxicity and NMO pathology. 

In live mice, NMO lesions characterized by demyelination, induced by continuous intracerebral injection of NMO-IgG and complement, exhibited significant infiltration of eosinophils. Transgenic hypereosinophilic mice showed increased severity of lesions, while mice with reduced eosinophil levels achieved through anti-IL-5 antibody treatment or gene deletion, as well as normal mice receiving oral cetirizine, experienced reduced lesion severity. 

These findings suggest that eosinophils play a role in NMO pathogenesis through ADCC and CDCC mechanisms, and approved eosinophil-stabilizing drugs may hold therapeutic potential for NMO treatment.

title: Association of cystic fibrosis with abnormalities in fatty acid metabolism.
text:
Patients with cystic fibrosis exhibit changes in plasma fatty acid levels. Previous research has shown that arachidonic acid levels are elevated and docosahexaenoic acid levels are reduced in affected tissues of cystic fibrosis-knockout mice. This study aimed to determine if humans with mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene also have a fatty acid defect in CFTR-expressing tissues. 

The study analyzed fatty acids in nasal and rectal biopsy specimens, nasal epithelial scrapings, and plasma from 38 cystic fibrosis patients. The results were compared to those of 13 obligate heterozygotes, 24 healthy controls, 11 individuals with inflammatory bowel disease, 9 individuals with upper respiratory tract infection, and 16 individuals with asthma. 

The findings revealed that the ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was increased in mucosal and submucosal nasal biopsy specimens (P<0.001) and rectal biopsy specimens (P=0.009) of cystic fibrosis patients with both pancreatic sufficiency and insufficiency, compared to healthy controls. This change in nasal tissue was attributed to elevated arachidonic acid levels and reduced docosahexaenoic acid levels. In nasal mucosa cells, the ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was also increased in cystic fibrosis patients (P<0.001) compared to healthy controls, with obligate heterozygotes showing intermediate values (P<0.001). However, this ratio was not increased in individuals with inflammatory bowel disease. Asthma and upper respiratory tract infection patients had values between those of cystic fibrosis patients and healthy controls. 

In conclusion, these findings suggest that fatty acid alterations similar to those observed in cystic fibrosis-knockout mice are present in CFTR-expressing tissues of cystic fibrosis patients.

title: Actin dynamics and cell-cell adhesion in epithelia.
text: Recent advancements in intercellular adhesion research have emphasized the significance of the association between adherens junctions and the actin cytoskeleton. In skin epithelial cells, the formation of adherens junctions involves a dynamic process that includes the extension of filopodia into the neighboring cell membrane. This physical interaction triggers the clustering of adherens junction protein complexes at the tips of the filopodia. Consequently, actin polymerization is stimulated at the cytoplasmic interface of these complexes. Although the exact mechanism is not yet fully understood, it appears that the VASP/Mena family of proteins plays a role in organizing actin polymerization at these specific sites. In vivo, the formation of adherens junctions relies on filopodia in processes where epithelial sheets need to be brought closer together to establish stable intercellular connections. Examples of such processes include ventral closure during embryonic development and wound healing in postnatal animals.

title: Lamin A-dependent nuclear defects in human aging.
text: The premature aging syndrome Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (HGPS) is caused by mutations in the nuclear structural protein lamin A. However, it is unclear whether lamin A has any role in normal aging. Our study reveals that the same molecular mechanism responsible for HGPS is also active in healthy cells. We found that cell nuclei from older individuals develop similar defects to those seen in HGPS patient cells, such as changes in histone modifications and increased DNA damage. These age-related nuclear defects occur due to sporadic activation of the same cryptic splice site in lamin A, which is responsible for HGPS when constitutively activated. Interestingly, when we inhibit this splice site, the nuclear defects associated with aging are reversed. These findings suggest that lamin A is involved in the process of physiological aging.

title: Zmpste24 deficiency in mice causes spontaneous bone fractures, muscle weakness, and a prelamin A processing defect.
text: Zmpste24, an essential metalloproteinase found in the endoplasmic reticulum, plays a crucial role in the processing of CAAX-type prenylated proteins. Through biochemical studies on Zmpste24-deficient mice (Zmpste24(-/-)), we have discovered the pathological consequences of Zmpste24 deficiency. These mice experience slow weight gain, malnourishment, and progressive hair loss. The most notable pathological feature is the occurrence of multiple spontaneous bone fractures, similar to those seen in mouse models of osteogenesis imperfecta. Zmpste24(-/-) mice also exhibit significant reductions in both cortical and trabecular bone volumes. Additionally, they display muscle weakness in the lower and upper extremities, resembling mice lacking the farnesylated CAAX protein prelamin A. Prelamin A processing is impaired in fibroblasts lacking Zmpste24 and the CAAX carboxyl methyltransferase Icmt, but remains normal in fibroblasts lacking the CAAX endoprotease Rce1. While the muscle weakness in Zmpste24(-/-) mice can be attributed to defective prelamin A processing, the brittle bone phenotype suggests a broader role for Zmpste24 in mammalian biology.

title: Human and other faeces as breeding media of the trachoma vector Musca sorbens.
text: The fly Musca sorbens Wiedemann is believed to be a carrier of Chlamydia trachomatis, which causes trachoma in humans. Previous studies have shown that M. sorbens primarily breeds in isolated human feces on the surface of the soil, rather than in covered pit latrines. In order to determine the breeding media of M. sorbens in a rural Gambian village where trachoma is prevalent, we conducted experiments using soil-filled buckets as test breeding media and monitored the emergence of adult flies. We found that M. sorbens emerged from human feces in 6 out of 9 trials, as well as from calf (3/9), cow (3/9), dog (2/9), and goat (1/9) feces. However, no flies emerged from horse feces, composting kitchen scraps, or a soil control. When adjusted for the mass of the medium, the highest number of flies emerged from human feces, with an average of 1426 flies per kilogram. The median time for emergence was 9 days after oviposition, with an interquartile range of 8-9.75 days. Of all the flies that emerged from feces, 81% were M. sorbens. Male and female flies that emerged from human feces were significantly larger than those from other sources, indicating that they would likely be more fertile and have a longer lifespan. Female flies captured from children's eyes were similar in size to those from human feces, but larger than those from other sources. Based on our findings, we conclude that human feces are the most suitable breeding medium for M. sorbens, although some breeding also occurs in animal feces. The removal of human feces from the environment through the implementation of basic sanitation measures is likely to significantly reduce the density of flies, minimize eye contact, and consequently reduce the transmission of trachoma. However, if feces from other animals are present, M. sorbens will continue to persist.

title: Current Health and Environmental Status of the Maasai People in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: The AIDS pandemic continues to surge, impacting approximately 38.6 million individuals worldwide as time goes by. In light of this, two Cal Poly students are currently developing a satellite health clinic to cater to the Maasai people residing in the Kajiado district of Southern Kenya. Traditionally, the Maasai have led a pastoralist lifestyle, relying on their cattle for sustenance and sharing water sources with them, which increases the risk of contamination. However, with the growing population in Kenya, the grazing land that the Maasai have traditionally used is diminishing. Consequently, some have turned to farming as a means to sustain their livelihoods. These factors have led to the desertification and deforestation of their region. As the Maasai way of life evolves, they increasingly depend on maize rather than meat and dairy products for their nutritional needs. All of these changes have influenced the transformation of Maasai culture. In order to gain a better understanding of the Maasai and to identify potential areas where further assistance may be required to support their survival, we will address these changes.

title: Identification and characterization of a widely expressed form of adenylyl cyclase.
text: Using degenerate primers based on a conserved region of previously described adenylyl cyclases (Premont, R. T. (1994) Methods Enzymol. 238, 116-127), researchers have identified a novel mammalian adenylyl cyclase through reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction amplification. The full-length cDNA sequence obtained from mouse brain indicates that this adenylyl cyclase is a 1353-amino acid protein with a 12-membrane span topology. It contains two regions that show high similarity to the catalytic domains of adenylyl cyclases. Comparing this novel adenylyl cyclase with the eight previously described mammalian enzymes, it is evident that this type 9 adenylyl cyclase sequence is the most divergent, establishing a sixth distinct subclass of mammalian adenylyl cyclases. The AC9 gene has been located on human chromosome band 16p13.3-13.2. The 8.5-kb mRNA encoding the type 9 adenylyl cyclase is widely distributed, being present in all tested tissues, and is particularly abundant in skeletal muscle and brain. AC9 mRNA is found throughout the rat brain, with higher levels in the hippocampus, cerebellum, and neocortex. An antiserum targeting the carboxyl terminus of the type 9 adenylyl cyclase can detect native and expressed recombinant AC9 protein in tissue and cell membranes. The AC9 protein is most abundant in mouse brain membranes. Further analysis of expressed recombinant AC9 demonstrates that it is a functional adenylyl cyclase that is stimulated by Mg2+, forskolin, and mutationally activated Gsalpha. AC9 activity is not affected by Ca2+/calmodulin or G protein betagamma-subunits. Therefore, AC9 represents a functional G protein-regulated adenylyl cyclase present in the brain and most somatic tissues.

title: Expression of Golli mRNA during development in primary immune lymphoid organs of the rat
text: The Golli-MBP transcription unit consists of three Golli-specific exons and eight exons from the "classical" myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. This results in the production of alternatively spliced proteins that share an amino acid sequence with MBP. Unlike MBP, which is only expressed in the nervous system, Golli gene products are expressed both before and after birth in various locations. In this study, we used RT-PCR and 5' RACE to determine the sequence of Golli in rats. We found that Golli sequences are expressed in primary lymphoid organs as early as e16.5, which may explain the lack of T cell response observed in rats with Golli-induced meningitis.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of single baseline measurement of Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in emergency department: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to obtain summary estimates of the accuracy of a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay (Roche Diagnostics) for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction in patients presenting to the emergency department.

DESIGN: This study involved a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies.

DATA SOURCES: The researchers searched Medline, Embase, and other relevant electronic databases for papers published between January 2006 and December 2013.

STUDY SELECTION: Studies were included if they evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a single baseline measurement of Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction in patients presenting to the emergency department with suspected acute coronary syndrome.

STUDY APPRAISAL AND DATA SYNTHESIS: The first author screened all titles and abstracts identified through the searches and selected all potentially relevant papers. Two reviewers independently conducted the screening of the full texts, data extraction, and methodological quality assessment using the adapted QUADAS-2 tool. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or arbitration. If appropriate, meta-analysis was conducted using the hierarchical bivariate model.

RESULTS: Twenty-three studies reported the performance of the evaluated assay at presentation. The results for cut-off values of 14 ng/L and 3-5 ng/L were pooled separately. At 14 ng/L, the summary sensitivity was 89.5% (95% confidence interval 86.3% to 92.1%) and the summary specificity was 77.1% (68.7% to 83.7%). At 3-5 ng/L, the summary sensitivity was 97.4% (94.9% to 98.7%) and the summary specificity was 42.4% (31.2% to 54.5%). This means that if 21% of 100 consecutive patients have acute myocardial infarction, 2 (95% confidence interval 2 to 3) of those patients will be missed (false negatives) if 14 ng/L is used as a cut-off value, and 18 (13 to 25) of the patients without acute myocardial infarction will test positive (false positives). If the 3-5 ng/L cut-off value is used, less than 1 (0 to 1) patient with acute myocardial infarction will be missed, and 46 (36 to 54) patients without acute myocardial infarction will test positive.

CONCLUSIONS: The results suggest that a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay can be used to rule out acute myocardial infarction if lower cut-off values such as 3 ng/L or 5 ng/L are used. However, this method should be part of a comprehensive triage strategy and may not be appropriate for patients who present less than three hours after symptom onset. Care must also be taken due to the higher imprecision of the evaluated assay and the greater effect of lot-to-lot reagent variation at low troponin concentrations.

SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration number CRD42013003926.

title: Pericyte differentiation.
text: Pericytes are identified in their natural environment by their location within the basement membrane of microvessels. They are an essential component of the microvascular wall and are thought to play a role in angiogenesis, although their specific function is not fully understood. Pericytes derived from the retinal microvasculature have been cultured and distinguished from other stromal cells, such as smooth muscle cells, based on distinct phenotypic characteristics. In laboratory settings, pericytes form clusters of cells rich in extracellular matrix, which can mineralize when exposed to growth medium containing serum, without the need for external beta-glycerophosphate. These findings suggest that pericytes are primitive mesenchymal cells capable of transforming into an osteogenic phenotype. The differentiation of pericytes is also characterized by changes in their response to transforming growth factor beta 1 and alterations in the production and deposition of various extracellular matrix proteins, including laminin, Type IV collagen, tenascin, Type X collagen osteonectin, and thrombospondin-1. Mineralization is commonly associated with angiogenesis, indicating that pericytes may play a role in this process in their natural environment.

title: Membrane association of the CD3ε signaling domain is required for optimal T cell development and function.
text: The TCR:CD3 complex plays a crucial role in transmitting signals that are essential for the proper development of T cells and adaptive immunity. In T cells at rest, the CD3ε cytoplasmic tail attaches to the plasma membrane through a nearby stretch of basic-rich amino acids known as the proximal basic-rich stretch (BRS).
