In this research, we demonstrate that mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS experienced significant decreases in the number of cells in the thymus and had limited transition from double-negative (DN) 3 to DN4 thymocytes. This was due to heightened signaling from DN4 TCR, which resulted in increased cell death and downregulation of TCR in subsequent populations. Additionally, the absence of a functional CD3ε-BRS affected positive T cell selection but not negative selection. As a result, mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS had impaired peripheral T cell function and were significantly less responsive to influenza infection. These findings collectively indicate that the attachment of the CD3ε signaling domain to the membrane is necessary for optimal development of thymocytes and proper functioning of peripheral T cells.

title: A new era in ovulation induction.
text:
The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of aromatase inhibitors in inducing ovulation, promoting superovulation, and improving outcomes in IVF. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using relevant keywords in MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of systematic reviews. 

The results showed that letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, achieved ovulation rates ranging from 70% to 84% and pregnancy rates of 20% to 27% per cycle. In comparison to anastrazole, letrozole appeared to have higher rates of ovulation and pregnancy. When used for superovulation, letrozole was associated with a smaller number of developing follicles and a thicker endometrium. Additionally, the pregnancy rate with letrozole for superovulation was higher than with the use of clomiphene citrate (CC) (16.7% vs. 5.6%). Furthermore, the addition of letrozole to FSH treatment reduced the required FSH dosage. The pregnancy rate for letrozole and FSH treatment was similar to that of FSH alone.

In conclusion, aromatase inhibitors are equally or more effective than CC in inducing ovulation and promoting superovulation. Unlike CC, they do not have an antiestrogenic effect on the endometrium. Considering these advantages, aromatase inhibitors can be considered as a replacement for CC in ovulation induction. However, their role in IVF treatment still requires further investigation.

title: Of lineage and legacy: the development of mammalian hematopoietic stem cells
text: The development of the hematopoietic system is one of the earliest and most complex processes in mammals. Researchers are particularly interested in understanding where adult bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells come from during development. However, tracing their origin is challenging due to the mobility of blood and the fact that hematopoietic cells emerge from various embryonic sites. The origin of the adult mammalian blood system is still a subject of active debate and intense research. Scientists are also studying the signals that trigger the development of adult hematopoietic stem cells, as these signals could be used to generate and expand these important cell populations outside of the body. This article provides a historical overview and the latest findings on the developmental origins of hematopoiesis.

title: Long crocidolite asbestos fibers cause polyploidy by sterically blocking cytokinesis.
text: The carcinogenic effects of asbestos are primarily attributed to the dimensions of its fibers. It is believed that long asbestos fibers can disrupt the distribution of chromosomes during cell division, resulting in genetic alterations that lead to cell transformation and the development of cancer. Through the use of advanced microscopy techniques, we have observed the impact of individual crocidolite asbestos fibers on cytokinesis, the final stages of cell division, in LLC-MK2 epithelial cells. This is the first study to provide a detailed account of their effect on cytokinesis. Our findings indicate that long fibers (15-55 micrograms) can physically obstruct cytokinesis by becoming trapped in the cleavage furrow, occasionally resulting in the formation of a binucleated cell. The ends of these obstructing fibers are typically found within invaginations of the newly formed nuclei. We have also observed instances where the fiber attaches to the nuclear envelope, as evidenced by a chromatin strand running alongside the fiber into the intercellular bridge. These strands may break, leading to structural rearrangements of chromosomes. Our data demonstrates that individual crocidolite fibers can induce genetic changes by physically blocking cytokinesis, and that the length of the fiber and its affinity for the nuclear envelope are crucial factors. These genomic alterations may be among the initial events that contribute to asbestos-related cancers.

title: Neural induction and early patterning in vertebrates.
text: Signals from a specific region of the early embryo trigger the development of the nervous system in vertebrates. This process, known as neural induction, was first discovered by experimental embryologists studying amphibian embryos. Further research on the molecular mechanisms involved in neural induction, using the same model system, revealed that the absence of ongoing transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signaling in the outer layer of cells is a key factor in acquiring an anterior neural fate. This discovery led to the establishment of the 'default' model of neural induction. Endogenous neural inducers are proteins that are released and inhibit TGFβ ligands in the upper layer of cells. In the lower layer, where the inhibitors are not present, a non-neural fate is induced. It has been shown that inhibiting the TGFβ pathway is enough to directly induce neural fate in mammalian embryos, as well as in pluripotent mouse and human embryonic stem cells. This suggests that the molecular process that distinguishes neural from non-neural cells is conserved across various organisms in the evolutionary tree. The availability of embryonic stem cells from mice, primates, and humans will aid in further understanding the role of signaling pathways and their downstream mediators in neural induction in vertebrate embryos.

title: What's in the 'treatment gap'? Ethnographic perspectives on addiction and global mental health from China, Russia, and the United States.
text: In recent years, there has been a growing focus on addressing mental illnesses in low- and middle-income countries through evidence-based interventions, known as the 'global mental health' agenda. However, anthropologists and cultural psychiatrists have engaged in lively debates regarding the appropriateness of this agenda. This article reflects on these debates by drawing on ethnographic fieldwork conducted in China, Russia, and the United States, specifically examining the management of substance use disorders. The authors argue that the prevailing concept of 'treatment gaps' in global mental health research and interventions only partially reveals the intricate networks of institutions, therapies, knowledge, and individuals involved in addressing addiction and other mental health issues in specific contexts.

title: Generation of mice deficient in both KLF3/BKLF and KLF8 reveals a genetic interaction and a role for these factors in embryonic globin gene silencing.
text: The transcriptional regulators KLF3 and KLF8, also known as Krüppel-like factors 3 and 8, have a strong relationship and bind to similar DNA sequences. Previous research has shown that in erythroid cells, there is a hierarchical regulation within the KLF family. KLF1 drives the expression of both Klf3 and Klf8 genes, and KLF3, in turn, represses Klf8 expression. While the roles of KLF1 and KLF3 in erythroid cells have been studied, the contribution of KLF8 to this regulatory network has remained unknown. To investigate this, we created a mouse model with disrupted KLF8 expression. These mice are viable but have a shorter lifespan. However, mice lacking both KLF3 and KLF8 die around embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5), indicating a genetic interaction between these two factors. In the fetal liver, embryos with mutations in both Klf3 and Klf8 show greater dysregulation of gene expression compared to either single mutant. Specifically, we observe the activation of embryonic globin expression, but not adult globin expression. These findings suggest that KLF3 and KLF8 have overlapping roles in vivo and are involved in silencing embryonic globin expression during development.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis phagosome maturation arrest: selective targeting of PI3P-dependent membrane trafficking.
text: The ability of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to enter host macrophages and reside in a phagosome, which fails to mature into a phagolysosome, is crucial for the widespread transmission of tuberculosis and the resulting global pandemic affecting billions of people. Tuberculosis can be seen as a disease that heavily involves intracellular trafficking and the formation of cellular structures. The current understanding of the blockage in the maturation of M. tuberculosis phagosomes also provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms of phagolysosome formation. This maturation blockage occurs due to interference with the recruitment and functioning of rabs, rab effectors (such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases and tethering molecules like EEA1), SNAREs (such as Syntaxin 6 and cellubrevin), and Ca2+/calmodulin signaling. M. tuberculosis counterparts of mammalian phosphatidylinositols disrupt these systems and their associated processes.

title: SvpA, a novel surface virulence-associated protein required for intracellular survival of Listeria monocytogenes.
text:
Researchers have discovered a previously unknown protein called SvpA (surface virulence-associated protein) that plays a role in the virulence of the intracellular pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. This protein, weighing 64 kDa and encoded by svpA, is found both in culture supernatants and on the surface of the bacteria. Immunogold labeling with an anti-SvpA antibody confirmed its presence on the bacterial surface. Analysis of the peptide sequence revealed that SvpA contains a leader peptide, a predicted transmembrane region at the C-terminal, and a positively charged tail similar to the surface protein ActA. This suggests that SvpA may partially reattach to the bacterial surface through its C-terminal membrane anchor. 

To study the function of SvpA, researchers created a mutant strain by disrupting svpA in the wild-type strain LO28. The mutant strain showed significantly reduced virulence in mice, with a 2 log decrease in the LD50 and limited bacterial growth in organs compared to the wild-type strain. This decrease in virulence was not due to a loss of adherence or a decrease in the expression of known virulence factors, which remained unaffected in the svpA mutant. Instead, it was caused by a restriction of intracellular growth of the mutant bacteria. 

Further investigation using confocal and electron microscopy revealed that most svpA mutant bacteria remained trapped within phagosomes in bone-marrow-derived macrophages, while wild-type bacteria quickly escaped into the cytoplasm. The regulation of svpA was found to be independent of PrfA, the transcriptional activator of virulence genes in L. monocytogenes. Instead, SvpA was down-regulated by MecA, ClpC, and ClpP, which are proteins highly similar to those found in Bacillus subtilis and form a regulatory complex controlling the competence state of this saprophyte. 

In summary, the findings suggest that SvpA is a novel factor involved in the virulence of L. monocytogenes, promoting the escape of bacteria from phagosomes in macrophages. SvpA is partially associated with the bacterial surface and its regulation is independent of PrfA, but controlled by a MecA-dependent regulatory network.

title: Measuring adherence to highly active antiretroviral therapy: implications for research and practice.
text: The introduction of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) has had a profound impact on the progression of HIV disease, leading to significant reductions in both the severity of HIV-related symptoms and the number of deaths caused by the virus. However, the daily HAART regimen is quite complex, and strict adherence to the treatment is crucial for achieving long-term suppression of the virus and preventing the development of drug resistance. Due to the intricacy of HAART, accurately assessing medication adherence has become extremely important. Although various methods are currently being used, each method only captures a portion of adherence behaviors, and their ability to predict adherence is limited. Given the importance of adherence to HAART for both individual and public health, it is necessary to continue developing and validating measures to assess medication adherence.

title: Survival rates of tropical and temperate passerines: a Trinidadian perspective.
text: Data collected over a 10-year period in Trinidad using mist nets were analyzed to estimate adult survival rates for 17 species of forest passerines. The survival rates in Trinidad (mean 65%, range 45%-85%) were found to be significantly higher than the published estimates for European (mean survival 52%, range 32%-71%) and North American (mean survival 53%, range 29%-63%) passerines of similar body size. This translates to a 45% higher mean life expectancy in Trinidad. These results were confirmed even after accounting for phylogeny using a method of independent contrasts. The presence of transient and/or young birds was an important factor in the Trinidad data, and studies that do not consider these birds may underestimate adult survival rates. This study provides evidence supporting the hypothesis that avian survival rates are higher in the humid tropics, although the difference may not be as large as previously believed.

title: P0 glycoprotein peptides 56–71 and 180–199 dose-dependently induce acute and chronic experimental autoimmune neuritis in Lewis rats associated with epitope spreading
text: Two peptides derived from the synthetic peripheral nerve myelin P0 protein were studied in relation to their ability to induce experimental autoimmune neuritis (EAN) in Lewis rats. The first peptide, P0 180-199, was found to induce an acute course of EAN when administered at low doses (50-100 microg/rat), while the second peptide, P0 56-71, induced a chronic course of EAN when given at a high dose (250 microg/rat). The onset of clinical signs was delayed by 1-3 days in P0 56-71 induced EAN compared to P0 180-199 induced EAN, but the peak of the disease occurred at a similar time point post immunization. Intramolecular epitope spreading, as measured by delayed type hypersensitivity response, was observed in both types of EAN, but only at high antigen doses for P0 180-199 induced EAN. Interferon-gamma production was higher in P0 180-199 induced EAN compared to P0 56-71 induced EAN. Histopathologic evaluation showed similar levels of mononuclear cell infiltration in the sciatic nerves of both types of EAN, but more severe demyelination was observed in P0 180-199 induced EAN. These findings support the idea that high dose autoantigen immunization leads to extensive determinant spreading and a chronic course of autoimmune diseases.

title: Interaction between broad-spectrum antibiotics and the combined oral contraceptive pill. A literature review.
text: Opinions on the importance of drug interactions between the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) and broad-spectrum antibiotics vary significantly. Clinical practices differ greatly, particularly between doctors in Europe and those in the US. Rifampicin and griseofulvin are known to induce hepatic enzymes and have a genuine interaction with the COCP, resulting in reduced effectiveness. However, the situation with broad-spectrum antibiotics is less clear. There are limited prospective studies on the pharmacokinetics of using COCP and antibiotics concurrently, and few, if any, provide convincing evidence for reduced contraceptive efficacy. Nevertheless, there is evidence that variable handling of contraceptive steroids could make certain women more susceptible to COCP failure at certain times. To protect the few unidentified women who may be at risk, it may be justified to take a cautious approach and use additional or alternative contraception during short courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics and the initial weeks of long-term antibiotic administration, considering the serious consequences of unwanted pregnancy. Conflicting opinions and advice can be confusing for both professionals and patients, and instructions for additional precautions during and after using COCP and antibiotics together can be complicated. Many women are unaware of or confused about the circumstances that can lead to COCP failure. Healthcare professionals prescribing the COCP should continue to educate women about its mode of action and the times when the risk of failure is highest. Professionals who believe that concurrent antibiotic use poses a genuine threat to the contraceptive efficacy of the COCP should be prepared to provide simple and consistent advice on additional contraceptive precautions, supported by written information and reinforced regularly.

title: CLIP-170 interacts with dynactin complex and the APC-binding protein EB1 by different mechanisms.
text: CLIP-170 is a protein found in the cytoplasm that plays a role in the interaction between endosomes and microtubules, as well as in controlling the dynamics of microtubules. It is known to localize to the growing ends of microtubules, where it colocalizes with dynactin and EB1, proteins involved in activating dynein and binding to the APC protein, respectively. This suggests that CLIP-170 may interact with both dynactin and EB1. To investigate this further, we conducted experiments using site-specific mutagenesis of CLIP-170 and a transfection/colocalization assay in mammalian tissue culture cells. Our results indicate that CLIP-170 does indeed interact with both dynactin and EB1, either directly or indirectly. We discovered that the interaction between CLIP-170 and dynactin is mediated by a specific part of the CLIP-170 tail that binds to metals. On the other hand, the interaction between CLIP-170 and EB1 does not require any metal binding motifs. Additionally, our experiments suggest that the CLIP-170/dynactin interaction occurs through a specific subcomplex of dynactin called the shoulder/sidearm subcomplex, and it can happen in the cytosol without the need for microtubule binding. These findings have implications for how dynactin and EB1 are targeted to the growing ends of microtubules. Our data suggests that the CLIP-170/dynactin interaction can help target the dynactin complex to microtubule plus ends, although dynactin can also directly target microtubule plus ends through the microtubule binding motif of the p150(Glued) subunit. Furthermore, we found that CLIP-170 mutants affect the localization of p150(Glued) but not EB1, indicating that EB1 can target microtubule plus ends independently of dynactin.

title: Subcapsular encounter and complement-dependent transport of immune complexes by lymph node B cells
text: The understanding of how B cells encounter antigens in lymphoid tissues is still incomplete. Additionally, it is not clear how immune complexes are transported to follicular dendritic cells. However, our study using real-time two-photon microscopy observed that immune complexes are rapidly delivered through the lymph to macrophages in the subcapsular sinus of the lymph node. B cells captured these immune complexes from macrophage processes that entered the follicle and transported them to follicular dendritic cells. Moreover, B cells that recognized the specific antigen captured antigen-containing immune complexes from macrophage processes and migrated to the T zone. Our findings highlight the subcapsular sinus macrophages as a crucial location for B cell interaction with immune complexes and demonstrate that intrafollicular B cell migration facilitates the transport of immune complexes and encounters with specific antigens.

title: Exercise training-induced adaptations in the coronary circulation.
text: Aerobic exercise training leads to an increase in the capacity of blood flow in the coronary arteries. This increase is associated with changes in the control of resistance in the coronary blood vessels, which affects the flow of blood. The control systems that regulate resistance in the coronary arteries, such as metabolic, myogenic, endothelium-mediated, and neurohumoral systems, vary in importance throughout the arterial tree. These control systems work together to regulate resistance at different levels in the arterial tree. Additionally, the adaptations induced by exercise training are not uniform throughout the coronary tree, but rather vary spatially. Therefore, it is important to examine these adaptations throughout the entire arterial tree. The changes in endothelium-mediated control play a role in the alterations in resistance control induced by exercise training. There is evidence suggesting that the effects of training may differ between large coronary arteries and the microcirculation. The mode, frequency, intensity, and duration of exercise training can also influence the changes in endothelial function. Exercise training also affects the response of smooth muscle in the coronary arteries to vasoactive agents and alters the control of intracellular calcium in the smooth muscle cells. It also enhances the reactivity of resistance arteries in the coronary system. The effects of exercise training on smooth muscle differ between large coronary arteries and the microcirculation. For example, adenosine sensitivity increases in large arteries after training but remains unchanged in small resistance arteries. Although there is still much to be studied, evidence shows that chronic exercise alters the characteristics of endothelial and smooth muscle cells in the coronary arteries. This cellular plasticity plays a role in the adaptation of the cardiovascular system to exercise training.

title: Hepatic intra-arterial versus intravenous fotemustine in patients with liver metastases from uveal melanoma (EORTC 18021): a multicentric randomized trial.
text: The impact of intrahepatic treatment on survival in uveal melanoma (UM) patients with liver metastases is not known. We conducted a prospective study to compare the effectiveness and side effects of hepatic intra-arterial (HIA) and systemic (IV) fotemustine in these patients. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either IV or HIA fotemustine at a dose of 100 mg/m(2) on days 1, 8, 15 (and 22 in the HIA arm only) as induction, followed by a 5-week rest period and then every 3 weeks as maintenance. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS), and secondary endpoints included response rate (RR), progression-free survival (PFS), and safety. After randomizing 171 patients, accrual was stopped based on the results of a futility OS analysis. Of the total patients, 155 died and 16 were still alive, with a median follow-up of 1.6 years (range 0.25-6 years). HIA did not improve OS (median 14.6 months) compared to the IV arm (median 13.8 months), with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.09 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.79-1.50. However, HIA showed a significant benefit in PFS compared to IV, with a median of 4.5 months versus 3.5 months, respectively (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.45-0.84). The 1-year PFS rate was 24% in the HIA arm and 8% in the IV arm. HIA treatment also resulted in an improved RR of 10.5% compared to 2.4% in the IV arm. The most common grade ≥3 toxicity in the IV arm was thrombocytopenia (42.1%) and neutropenia (62.6%), while in the HIA arm, it was catheter complications (12%) and liver toxicity (4.5%), along with two toxic deaths. In conclusion, HIA treatment with fotemustine did not lead to improved OS compared to IV treatment, despite better RR and PFS. Intrahepatic treatment should still be considered experimental. The study was registered under EUDRACT NUMBER 2004-002245-12 and CLINICALTRIALSGOV IDENTIFIER NCT00110123.

title: Comparison of survival between cerebellar and supratentorial glioblastoma patients: surveillance, epidemiology, and end results (SEER) analysis.
text:
BACKGROUND
Cerebellar glioblastoma multiforme (cGBM) is a rare form of brain tumor. While it is generally believed that cGBM has a worse prognosis compared to supratentorial GBM (sGBM), there is limited research to support this belief.

OBJECTIVE
This study aims to investigate the impact of cerebellar location on survival by comparing the overall survival time of cGBM and sGBM patients using a case-control design.

METHODS
The researchers used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) registry to identify 132 cGBM patients from 1973 to 2008. Each cGBM patient was matched with an sGBM patient from a pool of 20,848 sGBM patients based on age, extent of resection, decade of diagnosis, and radiation therapy using propensity score matching.

RESULTS
Among the cGBM patients, 37% were over 65 years old, 62% were male, and 87% were white. Most patients underwent surgery and radiation (74%), while only 26% underwent surgical resection alone. The median survival time for the matched cohort of cGBM and sGBM patients was 8 months, but the survival distributions were different (log-rank P = .04). At 2 years, the survival rate for cGBM was 21.5% compared to 8.0% for sGBM, and at 3 years, it was 12.7% for cGBM and 5.3% for sGBM. Multivariate analysis of survival among cGBM patients showed that younger age (P < .0001) and radiation therapy (P < .0001) were significantly associated with a lower risk of mortality. Among all patients, multivariate analysis showed that tumor location (P = .03), age (P < .0001), tumor size (P = .009), radiation (P < .0001), and resection (P < .0001) were associated with survival time in the unmatched cohort.

CONCLUSION
The median survival time for cGBM and sGBM patients was 8 months, but cGBM patients had a survival advantage as the study progressed. These findings suggest that cGBM patients should receive aggressive treatment, including surgical resection and radiation therapy, similar to sGBM patients.

title: Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans infection (animal experiments).
text: During a specific period of the infection course in white mice that were injected with a pure culture of a Candida albicans strain that breaks down proteins, both Staphylococcus aureus and C. albicans were simultaneously found in the peritoneal abscesses. This was particularly evident in abscesses attached to the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, and upper part of the small intestine. The presence of these two pathogens together was further confirmed through histopathological examination, which showed a large number of staphylococci near Candida cells, typically in the center of the granulomas caused by the fungus. Considering that the protein breakdown products of C. albicans can provide a favorable environment for the growth of S. aureus, and the latter can be found in the intestinal tract of seemingly healthy mice, possibly as part of the temporary microflora, the coexistence of these two significant causes of endogenous infections, as observed in this study, is of great clinical interest. Additionally, these findings highlight the importance of controlling the bacterial population in mice for accurate mycological research.

title: Three common functional polymorphisms in microRNA encoding genes in the susceptibility to hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: New evidence suggests that certain genetic variations in microRNAs may be linked to the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, previous studies have produced inconclusive results. The purpose of this review and meta-analysis is to determine whether common single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in microRNA genes are associated with susceptibility to HCC and the clinicopathologic characteristics of hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related HCC. We conducted a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and China BioMedicine (CBM) databases to identify relevant articles published before January 1st, 2013. Ten case-control studies, involving a total of 3437 cases and 3437 healthy controls, were included in the analysis. We identified three common functional SNPs in miRNA genes: miR-146a G>C (rs2910164), miR-196a-2 C>T (rs11614913), and miR-499 T>C (rs3746444). Our meta-analysis revealed that the miR-146a C variant was associated with a decreased risk of HCC, particularly among Asian and male populations. Conversely, the miR-196a-2 T variant was associated with an increased susceptibility to HCC among Caucasian populations. However, we did not find any significant correlations between the miR-499 C polymorphism and HCC risk. When we further analyzed the data based on HBV status, we observed a similar trend of association between the three SNPs and HBV-related HCC risk. However, due to small sample sizes, these results were not statistically significant. Overall, our meta-analysis suggests that SNPs in miR-146a and miR-196a-2 genes may play a significant role in genetic susceptibility to HCC.

title: Isonicotinamide enhances Sir2 protein-mediated silencing and longevity in yeast by raising intracellular NAD+ concentration.
text: Sirtuins are a family of protein deacetylases that play a crucial role in gene transcription, cellular metabolism, and aging. They rely on an adequate level of NAD(+) in the cell, which is maintained through NAD(+) biosynthesis and salvage pathways. Nicotinamide (NAM) is an important precursor of NAD(+) but also inhibits the deacetylation reaction. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NAM is converted to nicotinic acid (NA) by the enzyme nicotinamidase Pnc1, which is then used by the NAD(+) salvage pathway enzyme NA phosphoribosyltransferase (Npt1). Isonicotinamide (INAM) is a compound similar to NAM that stimulates the activity of yeast Sir2 deacetylase by counteracting NAM inhibition. Our study found that INAM not only stimulates Sir2 in vitro but also increases the intracellular NAD(+) concentration in vivo. INAM improved normal gene silencing at the rDNA locus and partially restored silencing defects in an npt1Δ mutant. Yeast cells grown without NA had a shorter lifespan, but this was extended by INAM in a SIR2-dependent manner, accompanied by increased NAD(+). The increase in NAD(+) induced by INAM relied heavily on Pnc1 and Npt1, suggesting that INAM enhances flux through the NAD(+) salvage pathway. Additionally, INAM influenced the expression of multiple NAD(+) biosynthesis and salvage pathways, promoting homeostasis during the stationary phase.

title: Similar activation of signal transduction pathways by the herpesvirus-encoded chemokine receptors US28 and ORF74.
text: The chemokine receptors US28 from human cytomegalovirus and ORF74 from human herpesvirus 8 are both constantly active. Our study demonstrates that both receptors activate the transcription factors nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) and cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) on a continuous basis, and that their respective endogenous receptor ligands regulate these pathways. By using specific modulators against various components of the signaling pathways, such as the G protein subunit Galphai, phospholipase C, protein kinase C, calcineurin, p38 MAP kinase, and MEK1, we discovered that both receptors utilize multiple yet similar pathways for their constitutive and ligand-dependent activations. NFAT and CREB transcription factors, along with their upstream activators, are known to induce both host and virally encoded genes. We propose that these virally encoded chemokine receptors play a role in coordinating the expression of host and potentially viral genes in a similar manner. Since ORF74 is associated with the development of neoplasia, these findings may have significant implications for the pathogenicity of cytomegalovirus.

title: The therapeutic promise of the cancer stem cell concept.
text: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a specific group of cells within tumors that possess the unique ability to initiate and renew tumors, as well as generate non-tumorigenic cancer cells through differentiation. These cells have been identified in various human cancers and their presence in clinical cancer samples has been linked to the progression of the disease in patients. Recent research suggests that the failure of current therapies to effectively eliminate tumors may be due to the influence of CSCs. Therefore, targeting CSCs in cancer treatment could be a promising approach to improve therapy outcomes, especially for cancers that are resistant to traditional anti-cancer drugs that primarily target the bulk of tumor cells.

title: 3'-End processing of pre-mRNA in eukaryotes.
text: The generation of 3'-Ends in most eukaryotic mRNAs involves the cleavage of the RNA strand and the addition of a poly(A) tail. In mammalian cells, this process relies on specific sequences, including AAUAAA upstream of the cleavage site, a GU-rich sequence element downstream of the cleavage site, and stimulatory sequences before AAUAAA. Six factors have been identified to carry out these reactions, and except for one, they have been purified and their cDNAs cloned. Some interactions between RNA and protein, as well as protein-protein interactions within the processing complex, have been studied, but many details, such as the identity of the endonuclease, remain unknown. Researchers are currently investigating various cases of regulated polyadenylation at the molecular level. In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the sequences involved in cleavage and polyadenylation are less specific compared to metazoans, and a downstream element has not been identified. Although the list of processing factors may now be complete with around twelve polypeptides, their specific roles in the reaction are still largely unknown. It is known that 3'-processing is linked to transcription, and this connection is believed to involve interactions between processing factors, the mRNA cap, and RNA polymerase II.

title: Structure and developmental regulation of Golli-mbp, a 105-kilobase gene that encompasses the myelin basic protein gene and is expressed in cells in the oligodendrocyte lineage in the brain.
text: A new transcription unit, known as the Golli-mbp gene, has been discovered. This unit spans 105 kilobases and includes the mouse myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. Within this gene, there are three distinct exons that can be alternatively spliced into MBP exons and introns. This splicing process generates a variety of MBP gene-related mRNAs, each of which is regulated during different stages of development. These mRNAs are expressed in cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage as they progress through various stages of differentiation. Therefore, the MBP gene is part of a more intricate gene structure, and its products may have a role in promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation before myelination occurs. Additionally, one specific Golli-mbp mRNA, which codes for a protein closely related to MBP, is also expressed in non-neural tissues such as the spleen.

title: Cardiovascular effects of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes.
text: The purpose of this study was to determine if an intensive lifestyle intervention for weight loss would have long-term effects on cardiovascular disease in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes. The study randomly assigned 5145 participants to either an intervention group, which focused on weight loss through decreased caloric intake and increased physical activity, or a control group, which received diabetes support and education. The primary outcome measured was a combination of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for angina over a maximum follow-up period of 13.5 years. The trial was stopped early after a futility analysis at a median follow-up of 9.6 years. The intervention group showed greater weight loss throughout the study, as well as improvements in glycated hemoglobin, fitness, and other cardiovascular risk factors. However, there was no significant difference in the occurrence of the primary outcome between the intervention and control groups. In conclusion, an intensive lifestyle intervention for weight loss did not reduce the rate of cardiovascular events in overweight or obese adults with type 2 diabetes.

title: Early loss of interneurons and delayed subunit-specific changes in GABA(A)-receptor expression in a mouse model of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: The injection of kainic acid (KA) into the dorsal hippocampus of adult mice causes spontaneous recurrent partial seizures and mimics the histopathological changes seen in human mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) (Bouilleret V et al., Neuroscience 1999; 89:717-729). In this mouse model of MTLE, the effects on pre- and postsynaptic components of GABAergic neurotransmission were examined using immunohistochemistry at various time points (1-120 days). The markers for GABAergic interneurons (parvalbumin, calbindin-D28k, and calretinin), the type-1 GABA transporter (GAT1), and major GABA(A)-receptor subunits in the hippocampal formation were analyzed. The acute administration of KA resulted in a significant loss of hilar cells, but only limited damage to CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells. Additionally, the staining of parvalbumin and calbindin-D28k in interneurons was irreversibly lost in CA1 and the dentate gyrus (DG), while calretinin staining remained unaffected. The staining of the GABA(A)-receptor alpha1 subunit in interneurons also disappeared after KA treatment, indicating acute degeneration of these cells. Similarly, GAT1 immunoreactivity showed degenerating terminals in CA1 and DC at 24 hours post-KA, which then subsided almost completely. The loss of CA1 neurons, and to a lesser extent CA3 neurons, became evident at 7-15 days after KA administration. This loss was more pronounced after 1 month, accompanied by a corresponding decrease in GABA(A)-receptor staining. In contrast, the granule cells in the DG showed significant enlargement and dispersion in the molecular layer, along with an increase in GABA(A)-receptor subunit staining. After 4 months, the dorsal CA1 area was almost completely lost, CA3 was reduced, and the DG represented the majority of the remaining dorsal hippocampal formation. No significant morphological changes were observed on the opposite side. These findings suggest that the loss of hilar cells and GABAergic neurons contribute to the development of epilepsy in this MTLE model. On the other hand, the long-term degeneration of pyramidal cells and the dispersion of granule cells may represent distinct responses to recurrent seizures. Finally, the upregulation of GABA(A)-receptors in the DG may be a compensatory response that persists for several months in epileptic mice.

title: Cardiorespiratory adaptation during sleep in infants and children.
text: After birth, the cardiorespiratory control system goes through a process of functional maturation. During this time, the system is unstable, which puts infants at risk for disturbances in their heart and breathing, especially when they are sleeping. In recent years, researchers have focused on understanding how different states of alertness affect respiratory and cardiac control. Of particular importance is the impact of rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep on the mechanisms involved in cardiorespiratory control, as newborns spend a significant amount of time in this sleep state. In fact, REM sleep makes up more than half of the total sleep time for full-term newborns, and even more for preterm newborns. However, as infants grow from term to six months of age, the proportion of REM sleep decreases. Since respiratory and cardiac disturbances tend to occur during REM sleep, the high prevalence of this sleep state may increase the risk of abnormal sleep-related events in early infancy. It is crucial for clinicians to be aware of these developmental changes in sleep patterns, as they are relevant to conditions such as apparent life-threatening events (ALTE), sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), and the cardiorespiratory responses to respiratory disorders. Our current understanding of respiratory and cardiac control is primarily based on studies conducted during the first few months of life, and there is a lack of data on late infancy and early childhood. This paper aims to review the available information on how sleep affects various aspects of cardiorespiratory control, including ventilatory mechanics, gas exchange, chemoreceptor function, arousal responses, changes in heart rate and heart rate variability, and the occurrence and mechanisms of bradycardia.

title: A Common Signal Patch Drives AP-1 Protein-dependent Golgi Export of Inwardly Rectifying Potassium Channels.
text: The majority of inwardly rectifying potassium (Kir) channel family members possess a cytoplasmic domain structure that functions as an unusual Golgi export signal in one specific Kir channel, Kir2.1 (KCNJ2). This raises the question of whether Kir channels share a common mechanism for Golgi export. In this study, we investigate this idea by focusing on two structurally and functionally distinct Kir family members, Kir2.3 (KCNJ4) and Kir4.1/5.1 (KCNJ10/16), which have approximately 50% amino acid identity. Our results show that the Golgi export of both channels is hindered when the AP-1 γ subunit is knocked down using siRNA, as expected for a shared AP-1-dependent trafficking process. Through a comprehensive mutagenic analysis, guided by homology mapping in atomic resolution models of Kir2.1, Kir2.3, and Kir4.1/5.1, we have identified a common structure that acts as a recognition site for AP-1 binding and controls Golgi export. This signal, which is larger than previously thought based on studies with Kir2.1, is formed by a cluster of residues located at the junction of the cytoplasmic N and C termini. The signal consists of a stretch of hydrophobic residues from the C-terminal region that create a hydrophobic cleft, an adjacent cluster of basic residues within the N terminus, and a potential network of salt bridges that connect the N- and C-terminal regions. Since the formation of this patch and AP-1 binding rely on proper folding of the cytoplasmic domains, the signal serves as a common quality control mechanism at the Golgi for Kir channels. These findings reveal a novel proteostatic mechanism that links protein folding of channels to their forward trafficking in the secretory pathway.

title: Statins in the treatment of polycythaemia vera and allied disorders: an antithrombotic and cytoreductive potential?
text: Thrombohaemorrhagic complications are a major concern in the classical chronic Ph-negative myeloproliferative disorders (CMPDs), which include polycythaemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythaemia (ET), and idiopathic myelofibrosis (IMF). These complications significantly contribute to both morbidity and mortality. The pathophysiology of these disorders involves clonal myeloproliferation, myeloaccumulation, and a tendency to develop myelofibrosis and neoangiogenesis in the bone marrow and spleen. This review focuses on the potential clinical benefits of statin therapy in patients with CMPDs, based on in vitro and in vivo studies that have demonstrated the antithrombotic, antiproliferative, proapoptotic, and antiangiogenic effects of statins.

title: Metabolic analysis of senescent human fibroblasts reveals a role for AMP in cellular senescence.
text: Cellular senescence is a significant mechanism for suppressing tumors in mammals. Various oncogenic insults, such as the activation of the ras proto-oncogene, can trigger the initiation of senescence. While it is known that the senescence program involves the up-regulation of cell-cycle regulators like p16INK4A and p21CIP-1, the specific mechanisms underlying the senescence response are still unclear. In stress-induced premature senescence, reactive oxygen species are believed to be important contributors to the phenotype. Additionally, alterations in cellular carbohydrate metabolism have been linked to oncogenic transformation, particularly aerobic glycolysis. These findings suggest that metabolic changes are involved in both tumor formation and suppression, although the specific metabolic pathways involved are not well understood. To investigate this further, we studied age-dependent changes in cellular carbohydrate metabolism using a human fibroblast model of in vitro senescence. Our results show that senescent fibroblasts experience a metabolic imbalance, characterized by a significant decrease in ribonucleotide triphosphates, including ATP, which are necessary for nucleotide biosynthesis and cell proliferation. The depletion of ATP in senescent fibroblasts is caused by dysregulation of glycolytic enzymes, ultimately leading to a substantial increase in cellular AMP, which we demonstrate induces premature senescence. These findings suggest that metabolic regulation plays a crucial role in cellular senescence and tumor suppression.

title: Identification of an H2-M3-restricted Listeria epitope: implications for antigen presentation by M3.
text: We have used expression cloning to discover a specific epitope of the intracellular bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes that is restricted by H2-M3. By studying this epitope, we found that a hexapeptide called fMIGWII, which has an amino-terminal N-formyl group, can effectively target cells for lysis by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. In contrast, the nonformylated version of the peptide was much less active, around 100 times less potent. The protein source of this epitope is a 185 amino acid protein that is predicted to be a transmembrane protein. It retains its N terminus and has an N(out)-C(in) topology. This membrane orientation helps protect the epitope from deformylases found in the bacterial cell. Additionally, it suggests a possible explanation for how phagocytes are able to present H2-M3-restricted bacterial epitopes through a vacuolar TAP-independent mechanism.

title: High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomographic imaging of cortical and trabecular bone microarchitecture in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: The aim of this study was to use high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography to examine the microarchitecture and biomechanics of the peripheral skeleton in female patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The study was conducted as a cross-sectional study in patients with T2DM recruited from a diabetic outpatient clinic. Elderly female patients with T2DM and age- and height-matched controls were recruited for the study. The participants were imaged using high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography at the distal radius and tibia, and quantitative measures of bone mineral density, cross-sectional geometry, trabecular and cortical microarchitecture were calculated. Compressive mechanical properties were also determined using micro-finite element analysis. The results showed that compared to the controls, the T2DM cohort had higher trabecular bone mineral density adjacent to the cortex and higher trabecular thickness in the tibia. Cortical porosity differences were consistent with impaired bone strength, particularly in the radius. These findings suggest that T2DM may be associated with impaired resistance to bending loads due to inefficient redistribution of bone mass, characterized by loss of intracortical bone offset by an elevation in trabecular bone density. This pilot investigation provides a potential explanation for the increased fracture incidence in patients with T2DM that cannot be explained by standard bone mineral density measures.

title: Critical role of CD28 in protective immunity against Salmonella typhimurium.
text: Both TCR signals and costimulatory signals are necessary for efficient T cell activation. CD28 is a molecule that provides costimulatory signals for T cells. In order to understand the role of CD28 in the immune response against Salmonella typhimurium, the bacterium responsible for murine typhoid fever, we conducted experiments using mice that lacked CD28 expression (CD28-/- mice). These mice were found to be highly susceptible to infection with wild-type S. typhimurium and were unable to control infection with attenuated aroA- S. typhimurium. Further analysis revealed that CD28-/- mice did not produce T-dependent antibodies and had impaired production of IFN-gamma. Therefore, CD28 cosignaling is crucial for immunity against S. typhimurium. This is the first report to describe the essential role of CD28 in protective immunity against an intracellular microbial pathogen.

title: D3 phosphoinositides and outside-in integrin signaling by glycoprotein IIb-IIIa mediate platelet actin assembly and filopodial extension induced by phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate.
text: Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) causes a small number of actin filaments in human blood platelets to grow faster, resulting in the slow assembly and extension of filopodia. These reactions also occur when the integrin glycoprotein (GP) IIb-IIIa is perturbed immunologically, and they can be inhibited by the phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor wortmannin. Platelets that lack GPIIb-IIIa integrins or have inhibited GPIIb-IIIa function due to calcium chelation or the peptide RGDS show reduced responsiveness to PMA. In contrast, stimulation of the thrombin receptor with high doses of thrombin receptor-activating peptide (TRAP) leads to rapid and extensive actin assembly and extension, which is not affected by wortmannin. However, we have discovered that wortmannin can inhibit the formation of filopodia when the thrombin receptor is activated with suboptimal doses of TRAP. In vitro studies have shown that phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate inhibits the severing and capping of actin filaments by human gelsolin. These findings suggest that D3 polyphosphoinositides and integrin signaling play a role in PMA-induced platelet stimulation, and that D3-containing phosphoinositides generated in response to protein kinase C activation and GPIIb-IIIa signaling act as intermediates in the assembly of filopodial actin.

title: `Gain of function' phenotype of tumor-derived mutant p53 requires the oligomerization/nonsequence-specific nucleic acid-binding domain
text: Mutations in the p53 gene found in tumors can activate the expression of genes involved in cell proliferation. Interestingly, these mutant forms of p53 do not bind to the same DNA sites as the normal, wild-type p53 protein, indicating a different mechanism of activation. In this study, we investigated the specific domains of mutant p53 required for activating the promoters of three genes: epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), multiple drug resistance 1 (MDR-1), and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA). Additionally, we identified a structural domain essential for the "gain of function" property of a specific mutant p53 variant, known as p53-281G. This gain of function was measured by the ability of cells expressing this mutant to form tumors in nude mice. We created deletion mutants of p53-281G that removed conserved domains I, II, III, IV, and V individually, as well as a mutant that eliminated amino acids 100 to 300, removing four out of the five conserved domains (II-V). Another deletion mutant, p53-281G del 393-327, removed the oligomerization and nonsequence-specific nucleic acid-binding domains of p53. Our results showed that all these deletion mutants had significantly lower transactivation ability compared to intact p53-281G when it came to activating the EGFR and MDR-1 promoters. However, these deletion mutants still effectively activated the PCNA promoter, suggesting a different mechanism of transactivation for this gene. Furthermore, when expressed constitutively in cells, the p53-281G del 393-327 mutant was unable to induce tumor formation in nude mice, unlike intact p53-281G. This indicates that structural domains near the C-terminus of p53 are crucial for its gain of function property.

title: Banana contains a diverse array of endogenous badnaviruses.
text:
Banana streak disease is caused by multiple types of badnavirus, including Banana streak Obino l'Ewai virus. This particular virus has had a significant impact on international banana breeding programs, as it frequently infects new hybrids, preventing further development. It is believed that this infection occurs when viral DNA becomes integrated into the nuclear genome of Musa balbisiana (B genome), one of the wild species that contributes to many of the currently cultivated banana varieties.

To investigate whether other badnavirus species' DNA is integrated into the Musa genome, PCR-amplified DNA fragments from Musa acuminata, M. balbisiana, Musa schizocarpa, as well as the cultivars 'Obino l'Ewai' and 'Klue Tiparot', were cloned. A total of 103 clones were sequenced, and all showed similarity to open reading frame III in the badnavirus genome. However, there was significant variation, with 36 distinct sequences identified that had less than 85% nucleotide identity to each other.

No common sequences were found between M. acuminata and M. balbisiana, indicating that integration occurred after these species diverged. Analysis of non-synonymous and synonymous substitution rates suggested that the integrated sequences evolved under strong selective pressure, as expected for a living badnavirus. Furthermore, each distinct sequence appeared to result from an independent integration event.

title: Pregnancy in women with type 1 diabetes: have the goals of St. Vincent declaration been met concerning foetal and neonatal complications?
text:
The aim of this study was to assess whether the goals set by the St. Vincent declaration in 1989, which aimed to improve pregnancy outcomes for women with type 1 diabetes, have been met. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of twelve population-based studies published in the last decade, which included a total of 14,099 women with type 1 diabetes and 4,035,373 women from the general population. We compared the prevalence of four complications related to fetal and neonatal health.

The results showed that women with type 1 diabetes had a higher risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes compared to the general population. The occurrence of congenital malformations was 5.0% in women with type 1 diabetes, compared to 2.1% in the general population. The relative risk for congenital malformations was 2.4. Perinatal mortality was also higher in women with type 1 diabetes, with a rate of 2.7% compared to 0.72% in the general population. The relative risk for perinatal mortality was 3.7. Preterm delivery was more common in women with type 1 diabetes, with a rate of 25.2% compared to 6.0% in the general population. The relative risk for preterm delivery was 4.2. Additionally, the delivery of large for gestational infants was more prevalent in women with type 1 diabetes, with a rate of 54.2% compared to 10.0% in the general population. The relative risk for delivering large for gestational infants was 4.5. Furthermore, higher levels of HbA1c in early pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

In conclusion, our findings indicate that the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes is significantly higher in women with type 1 diabetes compared to the general population. Unfortunately, the goals set by the St. Vincent declaration have not been achieved.

title: BP control and left ventricular hypertrophy regression in children with CKD.
text: The association between hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy in children with CKD has not been definitively established, unlike in adult patients. To investigate this relationship, we analyzed data from the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children cohort. A total of 478 subjects were enrolled, with 435, 321, and 142 subjects remaining enrolled at years 1, 3, and 5, respectively. Echocardiograms were conducted one year after study entry and then every two years, while blood pressure measurements were taken annually. We utilized a linear mixed model to examine the impact of blood pressure on left ventricular mass index, which was measured at three different visits. Additionally, a mixed logistic model was employed to assess left ventricular hypertrophy. These models were part of a joint longitudinal and survival model to account for informative dropout. Predictors of left ventricular mass index included systolic blood pressure, anemia, and the use of antihypertensive medications other than angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers. Predictors of left ventricular hypertrophy included systolic blood pressure, female sex, anemia, and the use of other antihypertensive medications. Over a span of four years, the adjusted prevalence of left ventricular hypertrophy decreased from 15.3% to 12.6% in the systolic blood pressure model and from 15.1% to 12.6% in the diastolic blood pressure model. These findings suggest that a decrease in blood pressure may indicate a reduction in left ventricular hypertrophy in children with CKD. Furthermore, they highlight additional factors that should be investigated as potential predictors of left ventricular hypertrophy in these patients.

title: Nicotinic Acid Adenine Dinucleotide 2'-Phosphate (NAADP) Binding Proteins in T-Lymphocytes.
text: The messenger known as Nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) plays a role in regulating the release of calcium from acidic stores within cells. While several channels, such as two-pore channels (TPC), ryanodine receptor (RYR), and mucolipin (TRP-ML1), have been linked to NAADP's regulation of calcium signaling, the specific receptor for NAADP has not yet been identified. This study aimed to use a photoaffinity probe called [32P]-5-azido-NAADP ([32P]-5-N3-NAADP) to investigate proteins that bind to NAADP in extracts from NAADP-responsive Jurkat T-lymphocytes. The photolabeling of Jurkat S100 cytosolic fractions with [32P]-5-N3-NAADP resulted in the labeling of at least ten different proteins. Some of these S100 proteins, including a doublet at 22/23 kDa and a small protein at 15 kDa, showed a preference for NAADP as the labeling was protected when unlabeled NAADP was included, whereas the structurally similar NADP required much higher concentrations for protection. Interestingly, the labeling of several S100 proteins (60, 45, 33, and 28 kDa) was enhanced by low concentrations of unlabeled NAADP, but not by NADP. The effect of NAADP on the labeling of the 60 kDa protein was biphasic, reaching a peak at 100 nM with a five-fold increase and showing no change at 1 µM NAADP. When the P100 membrane fraction from Jurkat cells was examined, several proteins were also photolabeled. Similar to the results with S100, a doublet at 22/23 kDa and a 15 kDa protein appeared to be selectively labeled. However, NAADP did not increase the labeling of any P100 proteins as it did in the S100 fraction. The photolabeled S100 and P100 proteins were successfully separated using two-dimensional gel electrophoresis. The combination of [32P]-5-N3-NAADP photolabeling and two-dimensional electrophoresis provides a suitable strategy for identifying and characterizing NAADP binding proteins.

title: Loss of subcellular lipid transport due to ARV1 deficiency disrupts organelle homeostasis and activates the unfolded protein response.
text: The protein encoded by ARV1 facilitates the transport of sterols from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the plasma membrane. Mutations in yeast ARV1 lead to the accumulation of multiple lipids in the ER and sensitivity to drugs that affect sterol and sphingolipid metabolism. Through the use of fluorescent and electron microscopy, we observed sterol buildup, expansion of subcellular membranes, increased formation of lipid droplets, and fragmentation of vacuoles in ARV1 mutants. Analysis of ARV1 deletion transcription profiles revealed the activation of Hac1p, a key component of the unfolded protein response (UPR). We confirmed this by observing constitutive splicing of HAC1 transcripts, induction of a UPR reporter, and elevated expression of UPR targets in ARV1 mutants. Additionally, we found that the gene IRE1, which encodes the unfolded protein sensor in the ER lumen, has a lethal genetic interaction with ARV1, indicating that the UPR is necessary for the survival of cells lacking ARV1. Surprisingly, ARV1 mutants expressing a variant of Ire1p that is defective in sensing unfolded proteins are still viable. These strains also exhibit constitutive HAC1 splicing, which interacts with DTT-induced disruption of protein folding. These findings suggest that a component of UPR induction in arv1Δ strains is unrelated to protein misfolding. In murine macrophages, decreased expression of ARV1 also leads to UPR induction, particularly an up-regulation of activating transcription factor-4, CHOP (C/EBP homologous protein), and apoptosis. Loading cholesterol or inhibiting cholesterol esterification further increases CHOP expression in ARV1 knockdown cells. Therefore, the loss or down-regulation of ARV1 disrupts membrane and lipid homeostasis, leading to a breakdown of ER integrity and subsequent induction of the UPR.

title: IL-28, IL-29 and their class II cytokine receptor IL-28R
text: The innate and adaptive immune systems are regulated by cytokines, which play a crucial role. In this study, we have discovered a group of three cytokines, known as interleukin 28A (IL-28A), IL-28B, and IL-29, in the human genomic sequence. These cytokines are distantly related to both type I interferons (IFNs) and the IL-10 family. Our research revealed that IL-28 and IL-29, similar to type I IFNs, are induced during viral infections and exhibit antiviral properties. However, IL-28 and IL-29 interact with a heterodimeric class II cytokine receptor composed of IL-10 receptor β (IL-10Rβ) and a previously unidentified class II receptor chain called IL-28Rα. This newly discovered cytokine family could potentially offer an alternative to type I IFNs in conferring immunity against viral infections.

title: High-dose recombinant tumor necrosis factor alpha in combination with interferon gamma and melphalan in isolation perfusion of the limbs for melanoma and sarcoma.
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the toxicity and effectiveness of a combination treatment using recombinant tumor necrosis factor alpha (rTNF alpha), recombinant interferon gamma (rIFN-gamma), and melphalan for in-transit metastases of melanoma and recurrent sarcoma. The combination was chosen based on previous reports of synergistic antitumor effects. 

A total of 23 patients, 19 females and four males, with either multiple progressive in-transit melanoma metastases or recurrent soft tissue sarcoma, received a total of 25 isolation limb perfusions (ILPs) with the triple combination. The treatment involved injecting rTNF alpha as a bolus in the arterial line, with a total dose ranging from 2 to 4 mg, under hyperthermic conditions for 90 minutes. rIFN-gamma was given subcutaneously on days -2 and -1, and also included in the perfusate with rTNF alpha at a dose of 0.2 mg. Melphalan was administered in the perfusate at a concentration of 40 micrograms/mL. 

During the study, only two severe toxicities were observed in the pilot study with rTNF alpha, including severe hypotension with tachycardia and transient oliguria, as well as moderate hypotension followed by severe kidney failure with complete recovery. In the ILPs performed with the triple combination, patients received continuous infusion of dopamine and showed only mild hypotension and transient chills and temperature. Minimal regional toxicity was observed. Hematologic toxicity, including neutropenia and neutropenia with thrombocytopenia, was observed in 11 cases. 

Out of the 23 patients, 21 achieved complete responses (CRs) with a range of 4 to 29 months, two had partial responses (PRs) with a range of 2 to 3 months, and no failures were reported. The overall disease-free survival and survival rates at 12 months were 70% and 76%, respectively. Softening of the nodules was observed within 3 days after ILP, and the time to definite response ranged from day 5 to 30. 

In conclusion, this preliminary analysis suggests that high-dose rTNF alpha can be administered with acceptable toxicity using ILP with dopamine and hyperhydration. The combination of rTNF alpha, rIFN-gamma, and melphalan appears to be highly effective with minimal toxicity, even after prior therapy with melphalan alone.

title: Methanosphaera stadtmaniae gen. nov., sp. nov.: a species that forms methane by reducing methanol with hydrogen
text:
Methanosphaera stadtmaniae is a spherical-shaped organism that does not have the ability to move. It is classified as Gram-positive and obtains energy for growth by using hydrogen to convert methanol into methane. This organism cannot produce methane from hydrogen and carbon dioxide, formate, acetate, or methylamines. It also cannot grow with hydrogen and carbon monoxide, nitrate, fumarate, sulfate, or choline. 

The pH range in which Methanosphaera stadtmaniae thrives is between 6.5 and 6.9, while its optimal temperature is between 36° and 40° C. It is not affected by bile salts, inhibitors of folic acid coenzyme synthesis, cephalothin, or clindamycin. However, it is inhibited by metronidazole, bacitracin, monensin, lasalocid, and bromoethanesulfonate. 

For growth, Methanosphaera stadtmaniae requires acetate, carbon dioxide, isoleucine, ammonium, and thiamin. Biotin stimulates its growth. This organism does not contain cytochromes, and the mol % G+C of its DNA is 25.8. The composition of its cell wall, 16 S rRNA, and its immunological fingerprint indicate that it belongs to a new genus within the Methanobacteriaceae family. 

The natural habitat of the type strain of Methanosphaera stadtmaniae is the human large intestine.

title: Generation of induced pluripotent stem cells from Asian patients with chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
text: We have successfully created induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from Asian patients suffering from chronic degenerative diseases of the nervous system, such as spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). These iPS cells were generated by introducing four factors (KLF4, SOX2, OCT4, and c-MYC) into the patients' cells. Our findings demonstrate that these iPS cells possess pluripotency similar to human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and can differentiate into various types of cells both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. Notably, these iPS cells can also be directed to differentiate into neural cells, which are specifically affected in chronic degenerative diseases. As a result, the patient-specific iPS cells we have created serve as a valuable tool for studying disease mechanisms, testing new drugs, and developing innovative therapies for chronic neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Embryonic-like stem cell derived from adult bone marrow: immature morphology, cell surface markers, ultramicrostructure and differentiation into multinucleated fibers in vitro.
text: Embryonic-like stem cells (ELSC), which express some of the surface markers found in human embryonic stem cells, may be a more suitable option for treating degenerative muscular diseases compared to mesenchymal stem cells (MSC). We obtained ELSC and MSC from bone marrow and conducted a comparison of their characteristics and ability to differentiate into muscle cells. The results demonstrated that ELSC could be successfully isolated from three adult bone marrow samples using a serum-free medium supplemented with 10ng/ml basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF). Similarly, MSC could also be isolated from the same samples using DMEM/F12 medium containing 10% new cattle serum. However, ELSC appeared smaller and more slender in morphology, exhibited an upregulated expression of SSEA-4, and appeared more immature under ultramicroscopic examination compared to MSC derived from the same samples. Immunofluorescent staining and RT-PCR analysis revealed that ELSC weakly expressed Oct-4, Nanog-3, and Sox-2. Furthermore, both ELSC and MSC could be induced to form long, multinucleated muscle fibers expressing myogenin and myosin heavy chain (MHC) in a myogenic differentiation medium. However, by day 10, the proportion of multinucleated fibers positive for MHC was 25.0%+/-6.9% and 13.8%+/-7.6% in ELSC and MSC cultures, respectively. These findings suggest that ELSC derived from bone marrow are an excellent candidate for cell therapy in degenerative muscular diseases.

title: Kinetic evidence for rapid oxidation of (-)-epicatechin by human myeloperoxidase.
text: Apocynin, a compound known to inhibit leukocyte NADPH oxidase, has been found to require dimerization by myeloperoxidase (MPO). A dietary flavan-3-ol called (-)-Epicatechin has been identified as a 'prodrug' of apocynin-like metabolites that can inhibit endothelial NADPH oxidase activity and increase the level of nitric oxide in cells. We conducted a study to investigate the oxidation of (-)-Epicatechin by MPO, as it has been suggested that (-)-Epicatechin may be a substrate for MPO. Using a multi-mixing stopped-flow technique, we discovered that (-)-Epicatechin is one of the most effective electron donors for heme peroxidases that has been studied thus far. The rate constants for the conversion of MPO-compound I to compound II and compound II to resting enzyme, mediated by (-)-Epicatechin, were estimated to be 1.9 x 10(7) and 4.5 x 10(6) M(-1)s(-1), respectively, at pH 7 and 25 degrees Celsius. These findings indicate that (-)-Epicatechin can undergo rapid one-electron oxidation mediated by MPO.

title: Using the yeast gene deletion collection to customize gene expression.
text: Despite the ease of manipulating the genome in S. cerevisiae, researchers are constantly seeking more convenient and rapid methods for substituting yeast promoters. By replacing a gene's original promoter with a different promoter of choice, researchers can achieve regulated expression and simplify the process of determining functional relevance. While various clever strategies for inserting chromosomes have been described over the years, the S. cerevisiae Genome Deletion Project offers an incredibly valuable resource for a more streamlined workflow. The strategy, as explained by Liko et al. on page 728, is refreshingly simple. Through the genome deletion project, a collection of strains has been created in which a single ORF is replaced with a kanamycin resistance module. Although the primary purpose of this collection is to provide a comprehensive resource of nearly all possible knockouts, the authors note that there will likely be a strain available for almost any yeast promoter of interest in which the ORF is replaced.

title: Tyrosine phosphorylation and regulation of the AMPA receptor by SRC family tyrosine kinases.
text: The phosphorylation of AMPA receptors plays a crucial role in regulating receptor function and is involved in various forms of synaptic plasticity in the central nervous system (CNS). While the serine and threonine phosphorylation of AMPA receptors has been extensively studied, the potential impact of tyrosine phosphorylation on these receptors remains unexplored. In this study, we demonstrate that the GluR2 subunit of AMPA receptors undergoes tyrosine phosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo, specifically on tyrosine 876 near its C terminus, by Src family tyrosine kinases. Furthermore, treatment with GluR agonists in cultured cortical neurons leads to an increase in the phosphorylation of tyrosine 876. Tyrosine phosphorylation of GluR2 results in a decrease in its association with the GluR2-interacting molecules GRIP1/2, while its interaction with PICK1 remains unaffected. Additionally, mutation of tyrosine 876 abolishes the internalization of the GluR2 subunit induced by AMPA and NMDA. These findings highlight the significance of tyrosine phosphorylation of tyrosine 876 by Src family tyrosine kinases in regulating AMPA receptor function and suggest its potential role in synaptic plasticity.

title: tBid induces alterations of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation flux by malonyl-CoA-independent inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1
text: Recent research indicates a strong connection between cell metabolism and apoptosis. We conducted a study to examine changes in lipid metabolism in permeabilized hepatocytes that were treated with truncated Bid (tBid) in the presence of caspase inhibitors and exogenous cytochrome c. By measuring the flux of β-oxidation using labeled palmitate, we found that tBid inhibits β-oxidation, leading to an increase in palmitoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) levels and a decrease in acetyl-carnitine and acylcarnitines. These changes are characteristic of the inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1). Interestingly, we discovered that tBid reduces CPT-1 activity through a mechanism that is not influenced by malonyl-CoA, the primary inhibitory molecule of CPT-1, or Bak and/or Bax. However, it does depend on a decrease in cardiolipin. When Bcl-2, which interacts with CPT-1, is overexpressed, it counteracts the effects of tBid on β-oxidation. This unexpected role of tBid in regulating lipid β-oxidation suggests a model in which tBid-induced metabolic decline leads to the accumulation of harmful lipid metabolites like palmitoyl-CoA, which may play a role in the apoptotic pathway.

title: CD8+ T cells are activated in an antigen-independent manner in HIV-infected individuals.
text: The excessive activation of T cells, specifically CD8(+) T cells, is a defining characteristic of chronic HIV-1 infection. The mechanisms through which HIV-1 triggers the activation of CD8(+) T cells and the specific antigens involved are not well understood. Our study reveals that CD8(+) T cells are activated during in vivo HIV-1 replication regardless of their antigen specificity. Cytokines present during untreated HIV-1 infection, particularly IL-15, induce proliferation and expression of activation markers in CD8(+) T cells without the need for TCR stimulation. Additionally, CD8(+) T cells are stimulated by LPS or HIV-1-activated dendritic cells (DCs) in an IL-15-dependent manner, independent of antigen specificity. We found that IL-15 expression is significantly increased in DCs isolated from viremic HIV-1 patients, suggesting that inflammatory cytokines activate CD8(+) T cells in untreated HIV-1 patients regardless of antigen specificity. In contrast, CD4(+) T cells appear to be preferentially activated by specific persistent antigens. These findings explain the higher prevalence of activated CD8(+) T cells compared to CD4(+) T cells in untreated HIV-1 infection.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts promote hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis through chemokine-activated hedgehog and TGF-β pathways.
text: Fibroblasts are abundant in the surrounding microenvironment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) due to the prevalence of fibrotic or cirrhotic livers in most HCC cases. However, the role of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in HCC metastasis is not well understood. In this study, we found that CAFs promote the migration and invasion of HCC cells in laboratory settings and facilitate HCC metastasis to the bone, brain, and lung in NOD/SCID mice. Analysis using the RayBio human chemokine antibody array revealed that CAFs secrete higher levels of CCL2, CCL5, CCL7, and CXCL16 compared to peri-tumor fibroblasts. CCL2 and CCL5 specifically increase the migration of HCC cells, while CCL7 and CXCL16 promote both migration and invasion. Furthermore, CCL2 and CCL5 stimulate the activation of the hedgehog (Hh) pathway, while CCL7 and CXCL16 enhance the activity of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) pathway in HCC cells. When neutralizing antibodies against these chemokines were used, the effect of CAFs on HCC metastasis was notably reduced, and the activation of Hh and TGF-β pathways in HCC cells was compromised. In conclusion, CAF-secreted CCL2, CCL5, CCL7, and CXCL16 play a role in promoting HCC metastasis by coordinating the activation of Hh and TGF-β pathways in HCC cells.

title: Mortality risk in patients with dementia treated with antipsychotics versus other psychiatric medications.
text:
The aim of this study was to compare mortality rates in the year following the initiation of new antipsychotic medication for neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia with rates after starting other psychiatric medications. The study used retrospective data from the Department of Veterans Affairs on patients aged 65 and older who began outpatient treatment with psychiatric medication following a dementia diagnosis. The study included a total of 10,615 patients. The researchers used multivariate models and propensity-scoring methods to control for confounding factors. Secondary analyses were conducted, including a group of patients not taking any medication and an examination of mortality causes.

The results showed that all groups taking antipsychotics had significantly higher mortality rates (ranging from 22.6% to 29.1%) compared to patients taking nonantipsychotic medications (14.6%). The adjusted mortality risks for atypical antipsychotics and combined atypical and conventional antipsychotics were similar to those for conventional antipsychotics. Nonantipsychotic medications had a significantly lower mortality risk compared to conventional antipsychotics. Except for anticonvulsants, the adjusted risks for all individual classes of nonantipsychotics were significantly lower than the risk for antipsychotics. The mortality risks did not change over the course of 12 months. The proportions of patients taking antipsychotics who died from cerebrovascular, cardiovascular, or infectious causes were not higher than rates for those taking nonantipsychotic psychiatric medications.

In conclusion, the study found that antipsychotic medications taken by patients with dementia were associated with higher mortality rates compared to most other medications used for neuropsychiatric symptoms. The exact relationship between mortality and antipsychotics is not well understood and may be attributed to either a direct effect of the medication or the underlying pathophysiology of the neuropsychiatric symptoms that lead to antipsychotic use.

title: Glutathione: overview of its protective roles, measurement, and biosynthesis.
text: This review serves as an introduction to a special issue focused on glutathione (GSH), a compound synthesized in cells that is the most abundant low molecular weight thiol. GSH plays crucial roles in safeguarding cells against oxidative damage and the toxicity of foreign electrophiles, while also maintaining redox homeostasis. This article briefly discusses the functions of GSH, the sources of oxidants and electrophiles, and the mechanisms by which GSH eliminates these harmful substances through reduction and conjugation. Additionally, methods for assessing GSH levels in cells are described. The synthesis and regulation of GSH are explored, as well as therapeutic approaches for manipulating GSH content that have been proposed.
