The aim of this overview is to provide a concise summary of key aspects of glutathione metabolism, as part of a larger special issue that will offer a comprehensive review of the current understanding of this vital molecule.

title: A wellness class for inpatients with psychotic disorders.
text:
The aim of this project was to educate patients with psychotic disorders, many of whom were taking second-generation antipsychotics, about lifestyle changes that can help combat weight gain. To achieve this, all inpatients on a Veterans Affairs acute inpatient schizophrenia treatment unit were invited to attend a 30-minute presentation led by a medical student and a psychology student, supervised by the primary investigator. The presentation covered various topics, including the importance of maintaining an ideal body weight by following the USDA Food Pyramid, determining appropriate food portions, making healthy choices when eating out, and starting and sticking to an exercise program. To assess the effectiveness of the presentation, subjects completed a 13-item quiz on food and nutrition before and after the session. 

Results showed that 50 patients completed both the pre- and post-presentation tests. The average percentage of correct answers on the pre-test was 85.6%, which increased to 89.3% on the post-test. This difference of 3.7% was statistically significant (t = 2.43, df = 49, p < 0.02), indicating that the presentation had a positive impact on patients' understanding of the material. On average, there was a 6.1% improvement in test scores.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that individuals with psychotic disorders can benefit from educational presentations on nutrition and healthy lifestyle choices. The statistically significant improvement in test scores suggests that patients gained a better understanding of fundamental concepts related to food choices and fitness.

title: Heterochromatin integrity affects chromosome reorganization after centromere dysfunction.
text: The centromere is crucial for passing on genetic information in eukaryotic chromosomes. The epigenetic regulation of centromere identity has been linked to genome stability, changes in chromosome structure, and the formation of new species. However, we have limited knowledge about how problems with the centromere impact the structure of chromosomes. In this study, we demonstrate that in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, deleting the centromere under certain conditions leads to the survival of cells that have either acquired a new centromere near the end of the chromosome or have fused two chromosomes together without a centromere. The ratio of new centromere formation to chromosome fusion is significantly reduced when genes involved in the formation of heterochromatin through RNA interference are deactivated. By influencing how chromosomes reorganize, the distribution of heterochromatin throughout the genome may play a role in determining the outcome of changes in chromosome structure.

title: Expansion and deletion of CTG repeats from human disease genes are determined by the direction of replication in E. coli
text: The expansion of CTG repeats is linked to several hereditary neurological and neurodegenerative diseases in humans. Our study reveals that the occurrence of genetic expansions or deletions in Escherichia coli is influenced by the direction of replication. We found that large expansions are more likely to happen when the CTGs are present in the leading strand template, rather than the lagging strand. On the other hand, deletions are more prominent when the CTGs are in the opposite orientation. Interestingly, most deletions resulted in products of specific sizes. These observations suggest that strand slippage, combined with non-classical DNA structures, could explain these phenomena and may be relevant to the expansion-deletion mechanisms observed in disease genes on eukaryotic chromosomes.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps capture and kill Candida albicans yeast and hyphal forms.
text: Neutrophils have the ability to engulf and destroy microbes through the fusion of phagolysosomes. Recent research has shown that activated neutrophils can also create extracellular fibers composed of granule proteins and chromatin. These structures, known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), are capable of breaking down virulence factors and eliminating both Gram positive and negative bacteria. In this study, we present evidence for the first time that Candida albicans, a eukaryotic pathogen responsible for fungal infections in immunocompromised individuals, can induce the formation of NETs and is susceptible to NET-mediated killing. C. albicans is known for its ability to switch between budding cells and filamentous hyphae, which contributes to its virulence. Our findings demonstrate that NETs can effectively eliminate both forms of C. albicans, and that the granule components play a key role in this fungal killing process. Overall, our data suggests that neutrophils are capable of trapping and killing ascomycetous yeasts by forming NETs.

title: Katanin p60-like1 promotes microtubule growth and terminal dendrite stability in the larval class IV sensory neurons of Drosophila.
text: The shape of dendrites is an important factor in determining how neurons function. However, we still don't fully understand the mechanisms that control the different shapes of dendrites and how these shapes affect their function. In this study, we show that a protein called Kat-60L1 is necessary for regulating the complex shape and function of dendrites in a type of neuron found in Drosophila larvae. Mutant flies lacking Kat-60L1 are less responsive to painful mechanical and thermal stimuli. Additionally, the number and length of dendrite branches are reduced in these mutants, suggesting a link between neuronal function and the overall complexity of the dendritic arbor. These defects in dendrite shape occur mainly during the later stages of larval development, and live imaging reveals that Kat-60L1 is needed for stabilizing newly forming branches that resemble filopodia. Mutant dendrites also have fewer microtubules labeled with a protein called EB1-GFP, indicating that Kat-60L1 promotes the growth of microtubules to establish stable terminal branches and a complex dendritic arbor. Interestingly, another protein called Spastin, which also severs microtubules, reduces the complexity of the dendritic arbor in the same type of neuron, but does not affect microtubule growth within dendrites. On the other hand, overexpression of Spastin destroys stable microtubules in these neurons, while Kat-60L1 has no effect. This suggests that Kat-60L1 and Spastin have different roles in shaping dendrites through their regulation of microtubules. Our findings support the idea that microtubule-severing proteins play distinct roles in controlling the shape and function of neurons, and that the development of dendritic arbors involves multiple pathways acting at different stages of development.

title: Update on technical issues concerning complementary feeding of young children in developing countries and implications for intervention programs.
text:
This paper presents an updated version of the 1998 WHO/UNICEF report on complementary feeding. Recent research findings generally align with the guidelines outlined in the previous report. However, the adoption of new energy and micronutrient requirements for infants and young children will lead to revised recommendations on minimum meal frequency and energy density of complementary foods. Additionally, the list of "problem nutrients" will be modified.

In the absence of fortification, complementary foods often lack sufficient levels of iron, zinc, and vitamin B6. Furthermore, the intake of other nutrients may also be insufficient in certain populations. The paper discusses strategies for addressing these nutrient deficiencies and emphasizes the importance of optimizing breastmilk intake when introducing other foods into the diet.

The impact of complementary feeding interventions on child growth has shown variability, highlighting the need for more comprehensive programs. To address this, the paper recommends a six-step approach for planning, implementing, and evaluating such programs.

title: Decrease of learning capacity in offspring with increasing paternal age in the rat.
text: The study involved using 15 male Wistar rats of different ages (2.5, 6, 10, 14, 18, and 22 months) to mate with 2.5-month-old females. Additionally, another experiment was conducted using 15 male Wistar rats at the ages of 2.5 months and 23 months, which were randomly mated with 2.5-month-old females. The offspring were then assessed for various factors such as litter size, sex ratio, external malformations, growth, mortality within the first 13 weeks, reproductive capacity at 13 weeks, spontaneous activity, emotionality, and learning capacity. The results showed that only the learning capacity of the offspring, measured by success rate, decreased significantly as the father's age increased. However, this effect was not observed in females. The implications of these findings on genetics are briefly discussed.

title: Processing of the beta-amyloid precursor. Multiple proteases generate and degrade potentially amyloidogenic fragments.
text: The processing of beta-amyloid precursor proteins (APP) is necessary for the release and deposition of the beta/A4 protein into amyloid plaques, which are characteristic of aging and Alzheimer's disease. In this study, we investigated the role of acidic intracellular compartments in APP processing using cultured human cells. By using acidotropic agents and inhibitors specific to lysosomal proteases, along with metabolic labeling and immunoprecipitation techniques, we discovered that APP is broken down within an acidic compartment, resulting in the production of at least 12 COOH-terminal fragments. Nine of these fragments likely contain the entire beta/A4 domain and have the potential to form amyloid plaques. Treatment with E64 or Z-Phe-Ala-CHN2 effectively blocked the activity of lysosomal cysteine proteases cathepsins B and L, but had no effect on the lysosomal aspartic protease cathepsin D or the production of potentially amyloidogenic fragments. Instead, these inhibitors prevented further degradation of the fragments. Consequently, a large number of potentially amyloidogenic fragments of APP are regularly generated by noncysteine proteases within an acidic compartment, and then eliminated by cysteine proteases within lysosomes. Immunoblot and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed that chronic inhibition of cysteine proteases leads to the accumulation of potentially amyloidogenic APP fragments in lysosomes. These findings provide additional evidence supporting the hypothesis that an acidic compartment may play a role in amyloid formation, and begin to elucidate the proteolytic processes that may be crucial for amyloidogenesis.

title: Pharmaceutical Public-Private Partnerships in the United States and Europe: Moving from the Bench to the Bedside
text:
Regulators in the United States and the European Union have taken significant steps to bridge the gap between academic research and patient care in order to address medical needs and improve industry competitiveness. One effective tool in the pharmaceutical sector is the pharmaceutical public-private partnership (PPPP), which involves a legally binding contract between a private pharmaceutical company and a public or privately funded research university. This partnership can lead to more efficient outcomes in the highly regulated pharmaceutical industry.

By establishing a well-structured binding contract and promoting positive social norms, the parties involved in a PPPP can move away from an inefficient prisoners' dilemma Nash Equilibrium and towards the Pareto Optimal Frontier. Additionally, by coordinating the actions of interdependent actors, a PPPP arrangement can incentivize successful commercialization, surpassing the incentives provided by traditional contracts. While PPPPs are more common in the United States than in Europe, this article aims to provide a roadmap for universities, private firms, and EU policy makers to create efficient PPPPs that promote innovation in the European pharmaceutical industry.

Furthermore, this article suggests amendments to U.S. laws governing the patenting of government-funded technology to prevent unnecessary obstacles in sharing upstream medical discoveries and research tools. Our analysis not only compares different approaches, but also combines game theory, law, and management principles to enhance for-profit PPPPs.

title: Chronic stress and psychological well-being: evidence from Thailand on household crowding.
text: In this study, we investigate the impact of household crowding, a form of chronic stress, on psychological well-being. We analyze data from a large random sample of households in Bangkok, Thailand, which experiences higher levels of crowding compared to the United States. Our objective is to determine whether household crowding negatively affects psychological well-being, taking into account various background characteristics. We find that objective crowding has a detrimental effect on well-being, and this effect is mediated by subjective crowding. Subjective crowding consistently and directly harms well-being. Gender does not appear to play a role in these effects. We also find that the effects of objective and subjective crowding are similar across different types of households, including extended family households. We reject the notion that subjective crowding is a consequence rather than a cause of psychological well-being. Our findings indicate that chronic crowding poses a significant threat to psychological well-being. While our analysis is based on data from one city, we provide a historical and theoretical context to suggest which cultural settings are most likely to be affected by the detrimental effects of household crowding on psychological well-being.

title: Age- and sex-specific genomic profiles in non-small cell lung cancer.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the differences in the biology of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) based on patient age and sex. The researchers conducted a retrospective analysis of 787 patients with early stage NSCLC at Duke University. They divided the patients into subgroups based on age and sex and analyzed gene expression signatures to identify patterns of pathway activation. The main outcome measures were patterns of pathway activation that correlated with 5-year recurrence-free survival. The results showed that there were low- and high-risk patient clusters within the age and sex subgroups, with the high-risk patients having the shortest recurrence-free survival. These high-risk patients demonstrated increased activation of specific pathways compared to the low-risk patients. The researchers confirmed the clinical relevance of these pathway-based subphenotypes in women and patients younger than 70 years. However, further validation is needed in independent patient data sets. Overall, this study suggests that different pathway activation profiles are associated with recurrence-free survival in NSCLC patients.

title: Amelioration of colitis by genetically engineered murine regulatory T cells redirected by antigen-specific chimeric receptor.
text: The scarcity of antigen-specific regulatory T cells (Tregs) limits their therapeutic application for inflammatory diseases. To address this issue, chimeric immune receptors with antibody-type specificity can be used to redirect effector T cells (Teff) to sites of inflammation. This approach has the potential to alleviate a wide range of diseases characterized by uncontrolled inflammatory responses. In this study, we present a novel protocol for the genetic modification and expansion of murine naturally occurring Tregs (nTregs) using a 2,4,6-trinitrophenol-specific tripartite chimeric receptor. The transduced Tregs maintained their Foxp3 level, could undergo repeated expansion upon encountering their cognate antigen, and specifically suppressed Teff cells. Adoptive transfer of a small number of transduced nTregs resulted in antigen-specific amelioration of trinitrobenzenesulphonic acid colitis. These findings demonstrate that nTregs can be efficiently transduced to express functional, antigen-specific chimeric receptors, enabling the specific suppression of Teff cells both in vitro and in vivo. This approach holds promise for future cell-based therapies in inflammatory bowel disease and other inflammatory disorders.

title: Purification and activation properties of UreD-UreF-urease apoprotein complexes.
text: The presence of UreD, UreF, and UreG accessory proteins, along with UreE, is necessary for the in vivo assembly of the Klebsiella aerogenes urease nickel metallocenter. Previous research has shown that the urease apoprotein can exist in an uncomplexed form, as well as in UreD-urease and UreD-UreF-UreG-urease complexes. This study reveals the existence of a new series of complexes consisting of UreD, UreF, and the urease apoprotein. These complexes have unique activation properties that differ from both urease and UreD-urease complexes. Unlike the previously described complexes, the UreD-UreF-urease complexes are not deactivated by NiCl2. The activation of UreD-UreF-urease apoenzyme is less dependent on bicarbonate concentration compared to urease and UreD-urease apoproteins. Immunoblot analyses using anti-urease and anti-UreD antibodies indicate that UreD is concealed in the UreD-UreF-urease complexes, likely by UreF. We propose that the binding of UreF alters the activation properties of UreD-urease apoprotein by preventing nickel ions from binding to the active site until the carbamylated lysine metallocenter ligand is formed.

title: Coordinate regulation of the IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 cytokine cluster in Th2 clones revealed by allelic expression patterns.
text: The cytokines IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 are used as markers to identify the Th2 subset of effector T cells, and they are often expressed together. These cytokine genes are located close to each other within 140 kb of DNA in both mice and humans. By studying IL-4-expressing CD4+ T cell clones from F1 mice, we discovered genetic variations for each of these cytokines and determined which parent's genes were responsible for producing the cytokine mRNAs. We found that both monoallelic (expression from one allele) and biallelic (expression from both alleles) expression occurred for each gene, as well as for an additional gene called IL-3, which is located over 450 kb away from GM-CSF on the same chromosome. When IL-4 was expressed in T cell clones, it was usually expressed from the same allele as IL-13 or IL-5 in 81% of cases. However, there was only a 52% agreement at the allelic level among clones that expressed IL-3. This suggests that while independent expression of cytokine alleles is common in T cells, the cluster of genes containing IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 is regulated in a coordinated manner.

title: Effect of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass: a meta-analysis of randomized trials.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the effects of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass. A meta-analysis was conducted, analyzing postoperative blood loss in randomized clinical trials comparing hydroxyethyl starch to albumin for fluid management in adult cardiopulmonary bypass surgery. The study also assessed the impact of hydroxyethyl starch molecular weight and molar substitution. Additionally, randomized trials comparing different hydroxyethyl starch solutions were included in the analysis.

The results of the study included 18 trials with a total of 970 patients. Compared to albumin, hydroxyethyl starch was found to increase postoperative blood loss by 33.3% of a pooled standard deviation (95% confidence interval, 18.2%-48.3%; P < .001). The risk of reoperation for bleeding was more than doubled with the use of hydroxyethyl starch (relative risk, 2.24; 95% confidence interval, 1.14-4.40; P = .020). Hydroxyethyl starch also led to increased transfusion of red blood cells by 28.4% of a pooled standard deviation (95% confidence interval, 12.2%-44.6%; P < .001), fresh-frozen plasma by 30.6% (95% confidence interval, 8.0%-53.1%; P = .008), and platelets by 29.8% (95% confidence interval, 3.4%-56.2%; P = .027). There were no significant differences in these effects between hydroxyethyl starch 450/0.7 and 200/0.5. However, there was insufficient data available for hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 versus albumin, although no significant differences were found in head-to-head comparisons of hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 with 200/0.5. Albumin was found to improve hemodynamics, but there were no differences observed in fluid balance, ventilator time, intensive care unit stay, or mortality.

In conclusion, the use of hydroxyethyl starch in cardiopulmonary bypass surgery was associated with increased blood loss, reoperation for bleeding, and blood product transfusion. Lower molecular weight and substitution did not appear to mitigate these risks.

title: Downstream of Mutant KRAS, the Transcription Regulator YAP Is Essential for Neoplastic Progression to Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive cancer with low survival rates and is often associated with the presence of an oncogenic KRAS mutation. However, targeting KRAS has not been successful in treating this disease. Our research has revealed that the levels of YAP mRNA, which encodes Yes-associated protein (YAP), are elevated in human PDAC tissue compared to normal pancreatic tissue. YAP is a protein that is regulated by the Hippo pathway during tissue development and homeostasis. In mouse models with genetically engineered KrasG12D and KrasG12D:Trp53R172H mutations, deleting Yap specifically in the pancreas halted the progression of early neoplastic lesions to PDAC without affecting normal pancreatic development and function. While Yap was not necessary for the initial step of acinar to ductal metaplasia (ADM) in the development of PDAC, it played a critical role in the proliferation of mutant Kras or Kras:Trp53 neoplastic pancreatic ductal cells in culture and their growth and invasion in mice, leading to PDAC. Yap acted as a crucial transcriptional switch downstream of the oncogenic KRAS-MAPK pathway, promoting the expression of genes that encode secretory factors, which collectively sustained neoplastic proliferation, a tumorigenic response in the tumor microenvironment, and PDAC progression in Kras and Kras:Trp53 mutant pancreas tissue. Overall, our findings have identified Yap as a significant oncogenic KRAS effector and a promising target for therapeutic intervention in PDAC and potentially other types of KRAS-mutant cancers.

title: Rho, Rac and Cdc42 regulate actin organization and cell adhesion in macrophages.
text: The functions of Rho family proteins in haematopoietic cells have not been extensively studied, although they are known to regulate actin organization in fibroblasts. Bac1.2F5 cells, a murine macrophage cell line dependent on colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1), were used in this study. CSF-1 promotes the proliferation and motility of these cells and acts as a chemoattractant. When CSF-1 was applied to Bac1 cells, it rapidly induced actin reorganization. This stimulation resulted in the formation of filopodia, lamellipodia, and membrane ruffles at the plasma membrane, as well as the appearance of fine actin cables within the cell interior. Microinjection of a constitutively activated form of Rac1 (V12Rac1) stimulated the formation of lamellipodia and membrane ruffling. On the other hand, the dominant inhibitory Rac mutant (N17Rac1) inhibited CSF-1-induced lamellipodium formation and caused cell rounding. The activation of Cdc42 (V12Cdc42) induced the formation of long filopodia, while the dominant inhibitory mutant (N17Cdc42) prevented CSF-1-induced filopodium formation but not lamellipodium formation. Activation of RhoA (V14RhoA) stimulated the assembly of actin cables and cell contraction, while inhibition of Rho (C3 transferase) led to the loss of actin cables. Bac1 cells exhibited adhesion sites to the extracellular matrix, which contained beta1 integrin, pp125FAK, paxillin, vinculin, and tyrosine phosphorylated proteins. These adhesion sites, known as "focal complexes," were present in growing cells and CSF-1-starved cells but disassembled in cells injected with N17Cdc42 or N17Rac1. Interestingly, beta1 integrin did not disperse until long after the disappearance of focal phosphotyrosine and vinculin staining. In conclusion, Cdc42, Rac, and Rho play distinct roles in regulating the formation of actin filament-based structures in Bac1 macrophages, and Cdc42 and Rac are also necessary for the assembly of adhesion sites to the extracellular matrix.

title: Visualizing the function and fate of neutrophils in sterile injury and repair
text: Neutrophils have been implicated as harmful cells in various inflammatory conditions where they harm the host, resulting in neutrophil death and subsequent phagocytosis by monocytes and macrophages. However, our study reveals that in a fully healing sterile thermal hepatic injury, neutrophils also infiltrate the injury site and play a crucial role in dismantling damaged blood vessels and creating pathways for new vascular regrowth. Surprisingly, these neutrophils do not die or get phagocytosed at the injury site. Instead, a significant number of these neutrophils reenter the bloodstream and follow a predetermined path that involves a stopover in the lungs to increase the expression of CXCR4 (C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4) before migrating to the bone marrow, where they undergo apoptosis.

title: The effect of mass screening on incidence and mortality of squamous and adenocarcinoma of cervix uteri.
text:
The aim of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of the Finnish mass screening program for cervical squamous carcinoma and adenocarcinoma by analyzing changes in incidence and mortality rates. The data used in this study were obtained from the Finnish Cancer Registry, which has been collecting data since 1953. The nationwide mass screening program was initiated in the mid-1960s and is currently managed by a centralized organization. Women between the ages of 30 and 60 are invited for screening every 5 years.

The results of this study show that the average incidence of cervical carcinoma in the early 1960s was 15.4 per 10(5) woman-years. However, by 1991, this number had significantly decreased to only 2.7 per 10(5) woman-years. The mortality rate has also decreased proportionally since the implementation of the mass screening program. In the early 1960s, the mortality rate was 6.6 per 10(5) woman-years, whereas in 1991, it had dropped to 1.4 per 10(5) woman-years. It is important to note that the decrease in incidence is primarily observed in squamous cell carcinomas. On the other hand, the mortality caused by adenocarcinoma has decreased in the screened birth cohorts, but the incidence rate has remained unchanged.

Based on these findings, it can be concluded that the Finnish mass screening program has been highly effective in reducing the incidence and mortality rates of cervical carcinoma. Therefore, it is crucial to continue this program in the future. Additionally, more attention should be given to detecting glandular cell atypias in cervical smears, as this may contribute to further reducing the incidence of cervical adenocarcinoma.

title: Role of 5-HT in the regulation of the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis: effects of 5-HT on adrenocortical cells.
text: Serotonin, also known as 5-HT, plays a crucial role in regulating the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis. It has been found that 5-HT controls the activity of hypothalamic CRF neurons and pituitary corticotrope cells by activating specific receptor subtypes, namely 5-HT1A and/or 5-HT(2A/2C). Additionally, 5-HT can stimulate the renin-angiotensin system by triggering renin secretion, leading to increased aldosterone production. At the adrenal level, locally produced 5-HT acts as a paracrine messenger, stimulating the secretory activity of adrenocortical cells. The presence of 5-HT in the adrenal gland has been confirmed through immunohistochemical and biochemical studies in various species. In frogs, rats, and pigs, chromaffin cells synthesize 5-HT, while in mice, it is contained in nerve fibers within the adrenal cortex. In humans, 5-HT is found in perivascular mast cells. Both in vivo and in vitro studies have demonstrated that 5-HT stimulates corticosteroid secretion in different species, including humans. However, the specific receptor involved in the mechanism of action of 5-HT varies among species. In frogs and humans, the stimulatory effect on adrenocortical cells is mediated by a 5-HT4 receptor subtype, which activates adenylyl cyclase and calcium influx. In rats, the effect on aldosterone secretion is mediated through activation of 5-HT7 receptors. Clinical studies have shown that 5-HT4 receptor agonists stimulate aldosterone secretion in healthy individuals and in patients with corticotropic insufficiency and primary hyperaldosteronism. The local serotonergic control of corticosteroid production may play a role in the physiological regulation of adrenal cortex activity, as well as in the pathophysiology of cortisol and aldosterone disorders.

title: Effect of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor/cachectin on glucose turnover in the rat.
text:
We conducted a study to examine the impact of recombinant human interleukin-1 beta (IL-1) and recombinant human tumor necrosis factor alpha/cachectin (TNF) on glucose metabolism in healthy rats. We used a method called primed constant infusion of D-(6-3H)glucose and D-[U-14C]glucose to measure glucose kinetics. During the infusion of isotopes for 6 hours and monokines for 4 hours, we also measured the levels of glucagon and insulin in the plasma and analyzed their correlation with changes in glucose metabolism.

We found that only IL-1 caused an increase in the rates of glucose appearance (Ra) and disappearance (Rd). This increase was accompanied by a rise in glucagon levels and a decrease in the ratio of insulin to glucagon. Additionally, the administration of IL-1 led to an early increase in plasma glucose concentration, which coincided with the peak in Ra. The metabolic clearance rate (MCR) and the percentage of glucose oxidized were also enhanced by IL-1, indicating that this monokine promotes the utilization of glucose as a substrate.

On the other hand, TNF administration did not have any effect on Ra, Rd, the percentage of glucose oxidized, or MCR. However, TNF-treated rats showed an increase in the percentage of glucose recycling without affecting the overall rate of glucose production.

Based on these findings, we conclude that endogenous macrophage products, such as IL-1, play a role in the various changes observed in carbohydrate metabolism during injury and/or infection.

title: Human and murine very small embryonic-like cells represent multipotent tissue progenitors, in vitro and in vivo.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the development of human and murine very small embryonic-like (HuVSEL or MuVSEL) cells both in laboratory conditions and in living organisms. In laboratory conditions, HuVSEL and MuVSEL cells were observed to differentiate into cells from all three embryonic germ layers. HuVSEL cells were found to generate robust mineralized tissue of human origin in calvarial defects, surpassing the control group. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed that HuVSEL cells gave rise to neurons, adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts within the calvarial defects. Similarly, MuVSEL cells were also capable of differentiating into similar lineages. In the first round of serial transplants, approximately 60% of MuVSEL cells maintained their VSEL cell characteristics, while other cells differentiated into multiple tissues within 3 months. Secondary transplants did not detect donor VSEL cells, indicating limited self-renewal, but did demonstrate VSEL cell derivatives in the original location for up to 1 year. Teratomas were not observed at any point during the study. These findings demonstrate that VSEL cells have the ability to generate various types of cells both in laboratory settings and in living organisms, providing a basis for future regenerative therapies targeting osseous, neural, and connective tissue disorders.

title: High frequency of p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A) inactivation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
text: Multiple genetic mechanisms can deactivate the tumor suppressor gene p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A). We examined 29 invasive primary head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC) to assess p16 inactivation using a new monoclonal antibody (mAb), DCS-50, in immunohistochemistry. We correlated p16 staining in the primary lesions with genetic analysis, including: (a) detailed microsatellite analysis of markers at the p16 locus to identify homozygous deletion; (b) sequence analysis of p16; and (c) Southern blot analysis to determine the methylation status of the 5' CpG island of p16. Among the 29 HNSCC tumors, 24 (83%) showed no p16 nuclear staining in immunohistochemistry. Out of these 24 tumors, we discovered that 16 (67%) had homozygous deletions, 5 (21%) were methylated, 1 had a rearrangement at the p16 locus, and 1 had a frameshift mutation in exon 1. These findings indicate that: (a) p16 tumor suppressor gene inactivation is a common occurrence in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas; (b) p16 is deactivated through various distinct and exclusive events, including homozygous deletion, point mutation, and promoter methylation; and (c) immunohistochemical analysis of the p16 gene product expression is an accurate and relatively straightforward method for assessing p16 gene inactivation.

title: Genome-wide RNAi screen of Ca(2+) influx identifies genes that regulate Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) channel activity.
text: Recent research conducted by our team and others has shown that Stim plays a crucial and consistent role in store-operated Ca(2+) influx and Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) (CRAC) channel activity. Through an unbiased genome-wide RNA interference screen in Drosophila S2 cells, we have now identified 75 factors that significantly hindered Ca(2+) influx when the stores were depleted by thapsigargin. Among these factors, 11 were predicted to be transmembrane proteins, including Stim, and one called olf186-F. When olf186-F was suppressed through RNA interference, there was a significant decrease in thapsigargin-induced Ca(2+) entry and CRAC current. Conversely, overexpression of olf186-F led to a three-fold increase in CRAC current. When olf186-F was co-transfected with Stim, CRAC currents were further amplified to eight times higher than the control, and they developed more rapidly. olf186-F belongs to a highly conserved family of proteins with four transmembrane spans, and homologs of this protein can be found from Caenorhabditis elegans to humans. The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca(2+) pump sarco-/ER calcium ATPase (SERCA) and the single transmembrane-soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive (NSF) attachment receptor (SNARE) protein Syntaxin5 were also found to be necessary for CRAC channel activity. This supports the idea of a signaling pathway in which Stim detects Ca(2+) depletion within the ER, moves to the plasma membrane, and interacts with olf186-F to initiate CRAC channel activity.

title: Wedelolactone induces growth of breast cancer cells by stimulation of estrogen receptor signalling.
text: Wedelolactone, a compound found in plants, has been found to have anti-cancer properties against breast and prostate carcinomas both in laboratory tests and in living organisms. It targets various cellular proteins, including androgen receptors, 5-lipoxygenase, and topoisomerase IIα. In laboratory tests, it has shown cytotoxic effects on breast, prostate, pituitary, and myeloma cancer cell lines at concentrations of micromoles per liter. However, this study has revealed a new biological activity of wedelolactone at nanomolar doses. It acts as an agonist of estrogen receptors (ER) α and β, as evidenced by its ability to activate the estrogen response element (ERE) in cells expressing either ERα or ERβ, and by its molecular docking into the ligand binding pocket of both receptors. In breast cancer cells, wedelolactone promotes the growth of estrogen receptor-positive cells, increases the expression of estrogen-responsive genes, and activates rapid non-genomic estrogen signaling. These effects can be blocked by pre-treatment with the pure ER antagonist ICI 182,780, and they are not observed in breast cancer cells lacking ER. In conclusion, wedelolactone acts as a phytoestrogen in breast cancer cells by stimulating both genomic and non-genomic signaling pathways of ER.

title: Subpopulations of mouse blood monocytes differ in maturation stage and inflammatory response.
text: The study aimed to characterize different subsets of mouse monocytes based on their expression of certain markers. The researchers found three distinct subpopulations of monocytes that could be distinguished by their expression of Ly-6C, CD43, CD11c, MBR, and CD62L. These subsets exhibited similar phagocytic abilities, expressed the M-CSF receptor (CD115), and could develop into macrophages when stimulated with M-CSF. By depleting monocytes using liposomes loaded with dichloromethylene-bisphosphonate and observing their repopulation, the researchers demonstrated a developmental relationship between the subsets. The Ly-6C(high) subset, similar to bone marrow monocytes, was the first to reappear in the circulation after depletion. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that Ly-6C expression on these cells was down-regulated while in circulation. Inflammatory conditions caused an increase in immature Ly-6C(high) monocytes, resembling the inflammatory left shift of granulocytes. Acute peritoneal inflammation preferentially recruited Ly-6C(med-high) monocytes. Overall, these findings highlight the existence of distinct subpopulations of mouse monocytes with varying maturation stages and abilities to be recruited to inflammatory sites.

title: Proteogenomics to discover the full coding content of genomes: a computational perspective.
text: Proteogenomics is a burgeoning field that combines genomics and proteomics. It encompasses various technologies that enable the identification and characterization of protein-coding genes by searching tandem mass spectra against genomic databases. The peptides obtained through proteogenomics offer invaluable insights for gene annotation, which are often challenging or impossible to determine using conventional annotation methods. These insights include confirming translation, determining reading frames, identifying gene and exon boundaries, providing evidence for post-translational processing, identifying splice forms (including alternative splicing), and predicting novel genes. However, for proteogenomics to fulfill its potential, it must overcome several technological obstacles, such as improving the speed and accuracy of peptide identification, developing specialized databases, addressing sampling bias, and more. This article provides an overview of the current state of the field, highlighting its achievements and the role of computational approaches in overcoming these challenges. It discusses how technological and algorithmic advancements have facilitated large-scale proteogenomic studies in various model organisms, including arabidopsis, yeast, fly, and human. Additionally, it offers a glimpse into the future of the field, discussing ongoing efforts to tackle complex gene structures, search against genomes of related species, and reconstruct immunoglobulin genes.

title: The in vitro phosphorylation of p53 by calcium-dependent protein kinase C--characterization of a protein-kinase-C-binding site on p53.
text:
In our study, we have demonstrated that Ca2+-dependent protein kinase C (PKC) can phosphorylate recombinant murine p53 protein in vitro. This phosphorylation occurs on multiple residues within a conserved basic region of 25 amino acids, located at the C-terminal part of the protein. Specifically, PKC phosphorylates the synthetic p53-(357-381)-peptide at several Ser and Thr residues, including Ser360, Thr365, Ser370, and Thr377.

Furthermore, we have found that the p53-(357-381)-peptide, when present at micromolar concentrations, can enhance the sequence-specific DNA binding ability of p53. However, this stimulation is lost when the peptide is phosphorylated by PKC.

To better understand the mechanisms involved in PKC-dependent phosphorylation of the p53-(357-381)-peptide, we compared the phosphorylation of recombinant p53 and the p53-(357-381)-peptide by PKC. Our results indicate that the phosphorylation of full-length p53 at the C-terminal PKC sites is highly dependent on the accessibility of the phosphorylation sites. Additionally, we have identified a separate domain on p53, distinct from the p53-(357-381)-peptide, that is involved in binding PKC. This domain is located within a conserved 27-amino-acid peptide, p53-(320-346)-peptide, adjacent to residues 357-381.

Interestingly, the interaction between the p53-(320-346)-peptide and PKC inhibits PKC autophosphorylation and the phosphorylation of various substrates, including p53-(357-381)-peptide, neurogranin, and histone H1. We observed that conventional Ca2+-dependent PKC alpha, beta, and gamma, as well as the catalytic fragment of PKC (PKM), were similarly susceptible to inhibition by the p53-(320-346)-peptide. However, the Ca2+-independent PKC delta was less sensitive to inhibition.

These findings provide valuable insights into the in vivo phosphorylation of p53 by PKC and its regulation.

title: Role of ocular pigment epithelial cells in immune privilege
text: The ocular microenvironment has both immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory characteristics. Cells called pigment epithelial (PE) cells, which are found in the eye, have the ability to inhibit the activation of T cells and the production of regulatory T cells in a laboratory setting. This ability is dependent on the cells' ability to produce molecules that inhibit immune responses, such as CD86 (B7-2), transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, thrombospondin-1, programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1/B7-H1), and cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 2α. PE cells from different parts of the eye, such as the iris, ciliary body, and retina, can each suppress T-cell activation through similar mechanisms. Additionally, regulatory T cells derived from PE cells have functions that contribute to immune regulation in the eye. The eye employs multiple strategies to control inflammation caused by the immune system. This phenomenon, known as immune privilege, is crucial in preventing damage to nearby cells and ultimately avoiding blindness. This review focuses on the immunosuppressive properties and role of PE cells in immune privileged areas of the eye.

title: Drug-resistant Salmonella in the United States: an epidemiologic perspective.
text: Salmonellosis is a significant health issue in the United States, with over 40,000 reported cases, 500 deaths, and financial costs exceeding $50 million annually. The emergence of antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella strains is a concerning development with implications for public health. While the transmission of these bacteria can be complex, advancements in molecular biology and combined epidemiologic and laboratory studies now allow for the identification of the primary source of antimicrobial-resistant salmonellae - animal-based foods. These studies indicate that the use of antimicrobial drugs in food animals creates selective pressure, leading to the emergence and persistence of resistant strains.

title: Glutamine-specific N-terminal amidase, a component of the N-end rule pathway.
text:
The N-terminal Gln deamidation by Nt(Q)-amidase, an amidohydrolase located at the N-terminus, is a crucial component of the protein degradation pathway known as the N-end rule. In our research, we have successfully identified and characterized the Nt(Q)-amidase activity, referred to as Ntaq1, in various mouse tissues. Additionally, we have purified Ntaq1 from bovine brains, identified its corresponding gene, and initiated the analysis of this enzyme.

Ntaq1 exhibits a high degree of conservation among animals, plants, and certain fungi. However, its sequence differs significantly from other amidases. Interestingly, we have discovered that a previous mutation in the Drosophila Cg8253 gene, which we have now determined encodes Nt(Q)-amidase, leads to impaired long-term memory.

Furthermore, our investigations have unveiled the protein ligands of the previously uncharacterized human C8orf32 protein, which we have identified as Ntaq1 Nt(Q)-amidase. Notably, recent "high-throughput" studies have successfully elucidated the crystal structure of C8orf32 (Ntaq1).

Through site-directed mutagenesis of Ntaq1 and analysis of its crystal structure, we have determined that the active site and catalytic mechanism of Nt(Q)-amidase closely resemble those of transglutaminases.

title: Brahma-related gene 1-dependent STAT3 recruitment at IL-6-inducible genes.
text: IL-6 is a cytokine that plays various roles in the immune system, cell growth, and tumor development. It activates a protein called STAT3, which then binds to specific regions of DNA and activates gene transcription. We wanted to investigate if another protein called BRG1, which is involved in DNA remodeling, is also necessary for STAT3 recruitment. Our study demonstrates that BRG1 is indeed required for the activation of certain genes in response to IL-6. BRG1 is always present at these gene regions and is crucial for STAT3 recruitment, as well as for modifying the surrounding DNA structure. Interestingly, while BRG1 is necessary for IL-6-induced STAT3 recruitment, it is not required for STAT1 recruitment in response to another cytokine called IFN-gamma. Additionally, BRG1 enhances the expression of certain genes even without STAT3 involvement. These findings highlight the broad role of BRG1 in regulating STAT protein access to different gene promoters and reveal specific differences in its effects on DNA accessibility and STAT protein recruitment.

title: High and low fat consumers, their macronutrient intake and body mass index: further analysis of the National Diet and Nutrition Survey of British Adults.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the characteristics of individuals who consume high and low amounts of fat, specifically in terms of their macronutrient intake and body mass index (BMI). The researchers reanalyzed data from the Dietary and Nutritional Survey of British Adults, comparing two groups of participants: high fat consumers and low fat consumers. The classification of these groups was based on 7-day weighed food records that were considered valid for measuring energy intake. Participants were classified based on the percentage of energy from fat (FAT%) and the absolute amount of fat consumed (FATg). The criteria for the high FAT% group were those who consumed more than 45% of their energy from fat, while the low FAT% group consumed less than or equal to 35% of their energy from fat. For the FATg group, the threshold for the high fat group was consuming more than 138 g/day for men and more than 102 g/day for women, while the low fat group consumed less than 85 g/day for men and less than 70 g/day for women.

The dietary data was collected from private households in Great Britain between 1986 and 1987. Participants who were slimming, ill, or had an energy intake to basal metabolic rate ratio (EI: BMR) of less than 1.2 were excluded from the analysis in order to focus on habitual energy intakes. From the remaining 1240 subjects, 10.8% (6.1% of the total population) were classified as low fat consumers (76 men and 58 women) and 15.4% (8.7% of the total population, 93 men and 98 women) were classified as high fat consumers.

The main outcomes measured in this study were macronutrient consumption and BMI. The results showed that 30% of the participants changed their fat group classification when the criteria for defining high and low fat groups were altered from FAT% to FATg. Nutrient intakes varied depending on the definition of the groups. The high fat FATg group consumed significantly more of all nutrients compared to the low fat FATg group. However, this difference was not observed in the FAT% analysis, where the high fat group consumed more fat and less carbohydrate. On average, the BMI tended to be higher in the high fat groups, particularly in the FATg analysis. However, the high fat group included individuals with a wide range of BMIs. Further examination of BMI in the high fat groups revealed that age was the only variable that distinguished individuals in the top and bottom quartiles of BMI, with an 11-year difference.

In conclusion, high and low fat consumers differ in various aspects, and this is influenced by how these groups are defined (FAT% or FATg). High fat consumers generally have a higher BMI than low fat consumers, but not all high fat consumers are overweight or obese.

title: Quantitative, genome-wide analysis of eukaryotic replication initiation and termination.
text: Our understanding of various important aspects of DNA replication, such as the specific locations where DNA synthesis starts and ends, the frequency of origin usage, and the influence of transcription on fork progression, is limited. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of replication fork directionality in the S. cerevisiae genome using deep sequencing of Okazaki fragments. This approach allowed us to systematically examine initiation, origin efficiency, fork progression, and termination. Our findings reveal that the initiation of leading-strand synthesis primarily occurs in nucleosome-free regions at replication origins. Additionally, we demonstrate that replication termination is mainly a passive process that does not rely on specific DNA sequences or fork pausing. By studying the kinetics of origin firing, we were able to reconstruct timing profiles for the entire chromosome from an asynchronous culture.

title: The murine H19 gene is activated during embryonic stem cell differentiation in vitro and at the time of implantation in the developing embryo.
text: The in vitro differentiation of murine embryonic stem cells to embryoid bodies replicates the events that occur naturally in vivo just before and after embryonic implantation. By utilizing this system and conducting differential cDNA cloning, we have successfully identified genes that are regulated during early embryogenesis. In this study, we present the discovery of several cDNA clones, including one that corresponds to the H19 gene. This particular gene becomes active in extraembryonic cell types during implantation, suggesting its potential role in this stage of development. Furthermore, it is subsequently expressed in all cells of the mid-gestation embryo, except for most cells in the developing central and peripheral nervous systems. However, after birth, the expression of this gene either stops completely or is significantly reduced in all tissues.

title: Localization of Sir2p: the nucleolus as a compartment for silent information regulators.
text: The proteins encoded by SIR3, SIR4, and RAP1 in wild-type budding yeast strains are found together with telomeric DNA in a limited number of foci within interphase nuclei. Immunostaining of Sir2p reveals that, in addition to staining that aligns with Rap1 foci, Sir2p is also present in a specific region of the nucleolus. The presence of Sir2p at both the spacer of the rDNA repeat and telomeres is confirmed through formaldehyde cross-linking and immunoprecipitation using anti-Sir2p antibodies. In strains lacking Sir4p, Sir3p becomes concentrated in the nucleolus through a pathway that requires SIR2 and UTH4, a gene responsible for regulating yeast lifespan. The unexpected localization of Sir2p and Sir3p in the nucleolus is consistent with the observed effects of sir mutations on rDNA stability and yeast longevity, thus identifying a new site where silent information regulatory factors exert their influence.

title: Optogenetics reveal delayed afferent synaptogenesis on grafted human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural progenitors.
text:
The reprogramming of somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells has opened up new possibilities for cell replacement therapy and disease modeling in various neurological disorders. However, it is still unclear to what extent the transplanted human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) differentiate into functional neurons and integrate into the existing neural circuitry. In this study, we provide a detailed analysis of the functional properties and synaptic integration of hiPSC-derived neurons transplanted into an in vitro model of hyperexcitable epileptic tissue called organotypic hippocampal slice cultures (OHSCs), as well as in adult rats in vivo.

To begin, the hiPSCs were differentiated into long-term self-renewing neuroepithelial stem (lt-NES) cells, which are known to primarily give rise to GABAergic neurons. After being differentiated in OHSCs for six weeks, the lt-NES cell-derived neurons exhibited typical neuronal characteristics such as tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium currents, action potentials, and both spontaneous and evoked postsynaptic currents, indicating the presence of functional synaptic inputs. However, the grafted cells displayed distinct electrophysiological properties compared to the host cells in the OHSCs, including higher input resistance, lower resting membrane potential, and action potentials with lower amplitude and longer duration.

To investigate the source of synaptic inputs to the grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons, the host neurons were genetically modified to express Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) and were optogenetically activated using blue light. Simultaneous recordings of synaptic currents in the grafted neurons, six weeks after transplantation, revealed limited synaptic connections from the host neurons. However, longer differentiation times, up to 24 weeks after transplantation in vivo, resulted in more mature intrinsic properties and extensive synaptic inputs from the host neurons to the lt-NES cell-derived neurons, suggesting that these cells require an extended period of time for differentiation, maturation, and synapse formation. Nevertheless, even at this later time point, the grafted cells maintained a higher input resistance, indicating that they receive sufficient synaptic inputs from the host brain.

Given that the lt-NES cells used in this study have a strong tendency to differentiate into GABAergic neurons, the synaptic inputs from the host-to-graft neurons may facilitate the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters and help normalize hyperexcitable neuronal networks in brain disorders such as epilepsy.

title: Anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody in new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus.
text:
BACKGROUND
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is a chronic autoimmune disease caused by T lymphocytes attacking insulin-producing beta cells. Previous clinical studies have shown that continuous immune suppression can temporarily slow down the loss of insulin production. Preclinical studies have suggested that a monoclonal antibody targeting CD3 could reverse hyperglycemia and induce tolerance to recurrent disease.

METHODS
We conducted a study to examine the effects of a nonactivating humanized monoclonal antibody against CD3, called hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala), on insulin production in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Within 6 weeks of diagnosis, 24 patients were randomly assigned to receive either a 14-day course of treatment with the monoclonal antibody or no antibody. The patients were then monitored during the first year of the disease.

RESULTS
After one year, treatment with the monoclonal antibody resulted in maintained or improved insulin production in 9 out of 12 patients in the treatment group. In contrast, only 2 out of 12 patients in the control group showed a sustained response (P=0.01). The positive effects of the treatment on insulin responses lasted for at least 12 months after diagnosis. Additionally, glycosylated hemoglobin levels and insulin doses were reduced in the monoclonal antibody group. The most common side effects were fever, rash, and anemia, but no severe side effects were observed. Clinical responses were associated with changes in the ratio of CD4+ T cells to CD8+ T cells 30 and 90 days after treatment.

CONCLUSIONS
Treatment with hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala) helps prevent the decline in insulin production and improves metabolic control during the first year of type 1 diabetes mellitus in the majority of patients. The mechanism of action of the anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody may involve direct effects on pathogenic T cells, the induction of regulatory cell populations, or both.

title: Establishment and in vitro differentiation of a new embryonic stem cell line from human blastocyst.
text: The purpose of this study was to create a human embryonic stem cell line. Embryonic stem cells have the unique ability to stay undifferentiated and multiply indefinitely in a laboratory setting, while also having the potential to develop into various types of cells. This makes them valuable for studying differentiation, gene function, and other related areas. To achieve this, the inner cell mass of a human blastocyst was isolated and cultured on mouse embryonic fibroblasts using specific medium and additives for embryonic stem cells. The resulting cell line, named Royan H1, was assessed through various methods including examining its appearance, passaging, freezing and thawing, alkaline phosphatase activity, expression of Oct-4 and surface markers like Tra-1-60 and Tra-1-81, as well as its karyotype and ability to undergo spontaneous differentiation. The differentiated cells, such as cardiomyocytes and neurons, were further analyzed using transmission electron microscopy and immunocytochemistry. Our study successfully derived a new embryonic stem cell line (Royan H1) from a human blastocyst. These cells maintained their undifferentiated morphology even after more than 30 passages, had a normal XX karyotype, remained viable after freezing and thawing, and expressed alkaline phosphatase, Oct-4, Tra-1-60, and Tra-1-81. They also remained undifferentiated when grown on mouse embryonic fibroblast feeder layers, with or without recombinant human leukemia inhibitory factor. Additionally, Royan H1 cells could differentiate into various cell types in vitro without the need for feeder cells, forming embryoid bodies that could further develop into beating cardiomyocytes and neurons. These findings establish Royan H1 cells as a novel human embryonic stem cell line.

title: Lactate Metabolism in Human Lung Tumors
text: Cancer cells in culture consume glucose and release lactate, but it is unclear if lactate plays a role in energy metabolism in living tumors. Our previous research showed that human non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) use glucose in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. In this study, we demonstrate that lactate is also a carbon source for the TCA cycle in NSCLC. We observed the highest evidence of lactate utilization in NSCLC tumors with high 18fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and aggressive behavior. When we infused NSCLC patients with 13C-lactate, we found extensive labeling of TCA cycle metabolites. In mice, removing monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT1) from tumor cells eliminated lactate-dependent metabolite labeling, confirming that tumor cells autonomously take up lactate. Interestingly, when we directly compared lactate and glucose metabolism in vivo, lactate was found to be the predominant contributor to the TCA cycle. These findings suggest that tumors, including human NSCLC, can use lactate as a fuel source in vivo.

title: Increased lipid peroxidation as a mechanism of methionine-induced atherosclerosis in rabbits.
text: The transmethylation/transsulfuration pathway converts methionine into homocysteine, which can potentially cause atherosclerosis through various mechanisms, including lipid peroxidation. Therefore, excessive intake of dietary methionine may lead to the development of atherosclerosis. To investigate this hypothesis, we measured the levels of thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) in plasma and aorta, as well as the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase (GPX) in the aorta and erythrocytes of rabbits fed a diet enriched with 0.3% methionine for 6 or 9 months. We also conducted histological examinations of the aortas. Rabbits fed a methionine-enriched diet for 6 or 9 months showed significant increases in plasma and aortic TBARS levels, as well as increased activities of aortic antioxidant enzymes. However, there was a decrease in plasma antioxidant activity. In erythrocytes, SOD activity increased, catalase remained unchanged, and GPX decreased in the treated animals. Histological examination of the aortas revealed typical atherosclerotic changes, such as thickening of the intima, cholesterol deposition, and calcification in the methionine-fed rabbits. These findings confirm that a high-methionine diet can induce atherosclerosis in rabbits and suggest that disturbances in lipid peroxidation and antioxidant processes may be potential mechanisms underlying its atherogenic effects.

title: Sex differences in sex chromosome gene expression in mouse brain.
text: One major question is whether genes on the sex chromosomes directly influence the development and function of non-reproductive tissues, or if all sex differences in somatic tissues are caused by secretions from the gonads. To explore this, we investigated whether pairs of genes on the mouse X and Y chromosomes are expressed differently in the brain based on sex. Using RT-PCR and northern blot analysis, we examined the mRNA expression of eight Y-linked genes and their X-linked counterparts in the brain at three different stages: 13.5 days after fertilization, the day of birth, and adulthood. We found that six Y genes were expressed at one or more stages: Usp9y, Ube1y, Smcy, Eif2s3y, Uty, and Dby. Interestingly, these genes were also expressed in the brains of XY females, indicating that their expression does not rely on secretions from the testes. Additionally, all six X-linked homologues (Usp9x, Ube1x, Smcx, Eif2s3x, Utx, and Dbx) were expressed in the brain, and in adulthood, the levels of these transcripts were significantly higher in females compared to males, regardless of X-inactivation status. However, for five of these gene pairs, the expression of the Y-linked gene in males was not enough to compensate for the female bias in X gene expression. Three gene pairs, Usp9x/y, Ube1x/y, and Eif2s3x/y, showed different patterns of regulation in the brain, suggesting that they may not have the same functions. These sex differences in X-Y gene expression provide insights into the potential mechanisms through which these genes contribute to sex differences in brain development and function.

title: Genome architecture, rearrangements and genomic disorders.
text: There is a growing understanding that many human diseases are caused by repeated changes in DNA that occur in unstable parts of the genome. These conditions are known as genomic disorders, and they occur when the abnormal amount of certain genes within the changed parts of the genome leads to clinical symptoms. These changes can happen within or between chromosomes, and they are made possible by the presence of specific repetitive DNA sequences called low-copy repeats (LCRs). These LCRs are very similar in sequence, spanning about 10-400 kilobases of DNA, and they serve as the building blocks for the rearrangements through a process called nonallelic homologous recombination (NAHR). The presence of LCRs makes the region more prone to these rearrangements. Additionally, it has been suggested that the arrangement of LCRs in the genome plays a significant role in the evolution of primate species.

title: painDETECT: a new screening questionnaire to identify neuropathic components in patients with back pain.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the presence of nociceptive and neuropathic components in pain and the importance of accurate pain diagnosis for effective treatment. The study focused on chronic low back pain (LBP) patients and aimed to achieve the following objectives: (i) develop a reliable screening tool to identify neuropathic pain components in chronic LBP patients, (ii) determine the prevalence of neuropathic pain components in a large-scale survey of LBP patients, and (iii) assess the impact of neuropathic pain components on the severity of co-morbidities in LBP patients. 

The painDETECT questionnaire (PD-Q) was developed and validated in collaboration with the German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain. The questionnaire was administered to approximately 8000 LBP patients. The results showed that the PD-Q is a reliable screening tool with high sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive accuracy. In the cohort of chronic LBP patients, 37% were found to have predominantly neuropathic pain. These patients reported higher levels of pain intensity and experienced more severe co-morbidities such as depression, panic/anxiety, and sleep disorders. This also had a negative impact on their functionality and use of healthcare resources. Based on the prevalence of LBP in the general population, it was estimated that 14.5% of all female and 11.4% of all male Germans suffer from LBP with a predominant neuropathic pain component. 

In conclusion, the study highlights the importance of accurate pain diagnosis in choosing appropriate therapy for LBP patients. Simple and easy-to-use screening questionnaires can effectively identify neuropathic pain components in both individual LBP patients and larger cohorts. Since neuropathic pain is associated with more intense pain, severe co-morbidities, and poorer quality of life, accurate diagnosis is crucial for effective treatment.

title: Scoring of dual fluorescein and ICG inflammatory angiographic signs for the grading of posterior segment inflammation (dual fluorescein and ICG angiographic scoring system for uveitis)
text: The purpose of this study is to propose a scoring system for uveitis that combines dual fluorescein angiography (FA) and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA). This scoring system would be useful in monitoring disease progression and evaluating the effectiveness of treatment. The methodology involved using existing FA scoring systems, a standardized ICGA protocol, and previous interpretations of ICGA findings in posterior uveitis. Scores were assigned to various angiographic signs that indicate ongoing inflammation in the posterior segment of the eye. Each sign was rated based on its impact on the assessment of intraocular inflammation. To allow for direct comparison between FA and ICGA, the total ICGA score was multiplied by a coefficient of 2 to adjust to the total FA score. The results showed that a maximum score of 40 was assigned to FA signs, including optic disc hyperfluorescence, macular edema, retinal vascular staining and/or leakage, capillary leakage, retinal capillary nonperfusion, neovascularization of the optic disc, neovascularization elsewhere, pinpoint leaks, and retinal staining and/or subretinal pooling. A maximum score of 20 was assigned to ICGA signs, including early stromal vessel hyperfluorescence, choroidal vasculitis, dark dots or areas (excluding atrophy), and optic disc hyperfluorescence. In conclusion, this combined scoring system using FA and ICGA can help estimate the extent of retinal and choroidal inflammation, monitor disease progression and treatment response, and provide comparable data for clinical studies. However, further testing in clinical settings and determination of intra- and interobserver variations are needed to assess the applicability of this system.

title: Improving outcomes of acute kidney injury: report of an initiative
text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a complicated condition that occurs in various settings and has multiple causes. It presents with a range of symptoms, from slight increases in serum creatinine levels to complete renal failure. In this article, we discuss the establishment of a collaborative network dedicated to AKI. This network, known as the Acute Kidney Injury Network, has developed standardized criteria for diagnosing and classifying AKI. These criteria will require further validation through future research, a process that will be supported by the Acute Kidney Injury Network. This network serves as a platform for sharing knowledge and improving patient outcomes.

title: A Screen for Endocytic Motifs
text: The signals used to sort cargo into coated vesicles are typically short linear motifs. In the case of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, three motifs have been identified: YXXPhi, [D/E]XXXL[L/I], and FXNPXY. To discover new endocytic motifs, we created a library of CD8 chimeras with random sequences in their cytoplasmic tails. We then employed a novel fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based assay to select constructs that were internalized. Among the top five efficiently internalized tails, only one contained a conventional motif. Two of them had dileucine-like sequences that seemed to be variations of the [D/E]XXXL[L/I] motif. The remaining tail contained a unique internalization signal, YXXXPhiN, which was functional even in cells expressing a mutant mu2 unable to bind YXXPhi. This indicates that it is not a variation of the YXXPhi motif. Similar sequences can be found in endogenous proteins, including a functional YXXXPhiN motif (in addition to the classical YXXPhi) in cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4). Therefore, the repertoire of endocytic motifs is more diverse than the three well-known sorting signals.

title: Microtubule stabilization reduces scarring and causes axon regeneration after spinal cord injury.
text: Spinal cord repair is often hindered by hypertrophic scarring and limited axon growth. These processes are controlled by microtubule dynamics. By stabilizing microtubules to a moderate extent, scar formation can be reduced after spinal cord injury in rodents. This stabilization has various cellular effects, including reducing transforming growth factor-β signaling. It also prevents the buildup of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and creates a favorable environment for axon regeneration in sensory neurons. Additionally, microtubule stabilization promotes the growth of central nervous system axons and leads to functional improvement. In summary, stabilizing microtubules decreases fibrotic scarring and enhances axon growth capacity.

title: Histone tails: Directing the chromatin response to DNA damage.
text: Significant amounts of energy are dedicated to modifying large sections of chromatin near DNA double strand breaks (DSBs). As soon as a DSB occurs, numerous changes are made to histones to create a foundation for the assembly of DNA repair protein complexes near the damaged DNA. This intricate signaling network is crucial for repairing DNA damage and coordinating with cellular processes that occur both locally and throughout the genome. Failing to properly carry out these chromatin changes in response to DNA damage has been linked to developmental abnormalities, immunodeficiency, and cancer in humans and genetically modified mice. This review will explore our current understanding of the histone modifications that occur in response to DNA damage in mammalian cells, emphasizing their role in maintaining genome integrity.

title: Sestrin2 inhibits uncoupling protein 1 expression through suppressing reactive oxygen species.
text: The protein known as Uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1) is found in the inner membrane of the mitochondria in brown adipose tissue (BAT) in mammals. Its main function is to generate heat by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation. When exposed to cold temperatures or when there is an abundance of nutrients, sympathetic neurons stimulate BAT to produce Ucp1, which leads to energy dissipation and thermogenesis. This increase in Ucp1 expression has been shown to reduce obesity in mice and is associated with leanness in humans. However, the molecular regulation of Ucp1 expression is not well understood. In this study, we investigate the role of Sestrin2 and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the regulation of Ucp1 expression. By overexpressing Sestrin2 in adipose tissues, we observed a decrease in both basal and cold-induced Ucp1 expression in BAT, resulting in reduced thermogenesis and increased fat accumulation. We also found that endogenous Sestrin2 plays a role in suppressing Ucp1 expression, as BAT from mice lacking Sestrin2 showed significantly higher levels of Ucp1 expression. Furthermore, we discovered that a mutant form of Sestrin2 that is unable to reduce ROS accumulation was ineffective in regulating Ucp1 expression. Similarly, the use of antioxidant chemicals that suppress ROS also inhibited Ucp1 expression. We identified p38 MAPK as a signaling mediator required for cAMP-induced Ucp1 expression, and both Sestrin2 overexpression and antioxidant treatments inhibited its activity. These findings suggest that Sestrin2 and antioxidants inhibit Ucp1 expression by suppressing ROS-mediated p38 MAPK activation, highlighting the importance of ROS in BAT metabolism.

title: The non-catalytic function of XPG protein during dual incision in human nucleotide excision repair.
text: XPG belongs to the FEN-1 structure-specific endonuclease family and is responsible for cutting at the 3'-junction of bubble substrates. It plays a crucial role in the human dual incision repair system by making the 3'-incision. In order to understand XPG's precise function in nucleotide excision repair, we conducted mutagenesis on two amino acid residues believed to be involved in DNA binding and catalysis. The mutant proteins were then overproduced using a baculovirus/insect cell system, purified, and characterized. The D77A mutation had a minor impact on junction cutting and excision activity, resulting in uncoupled 5'-incision by mammalian cell-free extracts. On the other hand, the D812A mutation completely eliminated XPG's junction cutting and 3'-incision abilities. However, when the excision nuclease was reconstituted with XPG (D812A), it successfully performed normal 5'-incision at the 23rd-24th phosphodiester bonds 5' to a (6-4) photoproduct without any 3'-incision. This suggests that Asp-812 is a crucial residue in XPG's active site and that, apart from its role in making the 3'-incision, XPG's physical presence in the protein-DNA complex is necessary for subsequent non-catalytic 5'-incision by XPF-ERCC1.

title: A 40-Hz auditory potential recorded from the human scalp.
text: Computer techniques can easily extract a sequential pattern of brain potentials from brainwaves in response to sound stimuli. These potentials, occurring between 8 and 80 milliseconds after the stimulus, resemble 3 or 4 cycles of a 40-Hz sine wave. We have discovered that these waves combine to create a single, stable composite wave when the sounds are repeated at a rate of approximately 40 per second. This phenomenon, known as the 40-Hz event-related potential (ERP), possesses several intriguing properties. Firstly, it has been observed to vanish under surgical anesthesia, and it shares similarities with similar phenomena in the visual and olfactory systems. These findings suggest that the effective processing of sensory information may necessitate cyclical brain events within the 30- to 50-Hz range. Secondly, by measuring the latency and amplitude of the 40-Hz ERP, valuable information regarding the number and location of auditory nerve fibers stimulated by a specific tone can be obtained. Lastly, this response is present even at sound intensities very close to the normal thresholds for adult hearing at various frequencies. This discovery could potentially have applications in clinical hearing tests.

title: Bile acids: natural ligands for an orphan nuclear receptor.
text: The molecular mechanisms by which bile acids regulate the transcription of genes controlling cholesterol homeostasis are not well understood. However, it has been found that certain bile acids, such as chenodeoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, and deoxycholic acid, can activate the farnesoid X receptor (FXR; NR1H4), which is an orphan nuclear receptor. These bile acids and their conjugates act as ligands and affect the interaction between FXR and a peptide derived from steroid receptor coactivator 1. These findings suggest the existence of a nuclear bile acid signaling pathway that may play a role in regulating cholesterol homeostasis.

title: The yeast ribosomal protein L32 and its gene.
text: The yeast ribosomal protein gene RPL32 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is of particular interest for two reasons. Firstly, it is located next to another ribosomal protein gene, RP29, which may have divergent transcription controlled by the same sequences. Secondly, it seems that the splicing of RPL32's transcript is regulated by the product of the gene, ribosomal protein in L32. RPL32 has been thoroughly analyzed and is crucial for cell growth. Its sequence suggests that L32 is a protein consisting of 105 amino acids. It is slightly basic near the NH2 terminus and acidic near the COOH terminus. Additionally, it shares similarities with ribosomal protein L30 found in mammals. The reading frame has been confirmed through partial NH2-terminal analysis of L32. The nucleotide sequence also indicates the presence of a 230-nucleotide intron, which starts with the unusual sequence GTCAGT and ends 40 nucleotides after the consensus sequence TAC-TAAC. The intron's existence has been verified by determining the sequence of a cDNA clone. Transcription begins 58 nucleotides before the AUG initiation codon, and the polyadenylation site is located 100 nucleotides after the termination codon. The regulation of ribosomal protein gene transcription has been associated with two related consensus sequences. Examination of the intergenic region between RP29 and RPL32 reveals the presence of three copies of these sequences. When all three sequences are deleted, the synthesis of a L32-LacZ fusion protein decreases by over 90%. However, there is still some residual activity.

title: Derivation conditions impact X-inactivation status in female human induced pluripotent stem cells.
text: Variability in X-inactivation status is observed in female human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines. Most hiPSC lines maintain one active X chromosome (Xa) and one inactive X chromosome (Xi) from the donor cells. However, there are rare instances where hiPSC lines have two active X chromosomes, suggesting sporadic epigenetic changes in the inactive X during reprogramming. In this study, we demonstrate that the X-inactivation status in female hiPSC lines is dependent on the conditions used for derivation.
