HiPSC lines generated using the Kyoto method (retroviral or episomal reprogramming) with leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF)-expressing SNL feeders frequently exhibit two active X chromosomes. Early passage hiPSC lines with one active and one inactive X chromosome, generated on non-SNL feeders, convert to lines with two active X chromosomes after several passages on SNL feeders. Additionally, supplementation with recombinant LIF leads to the reactivation of some X-linked genes. Therefore, the type of feeders used significantly influences the X-inactivation status. The efficient production of hiPSC lines with two active X chromosomes presents unprecedented opportunities to study human X-reactivation and -inactivation.

title: Loss of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein expression in malignant melanoma.
text: Recent studies have revealed a significant decrease in the levels of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in various types of cancers, including breast, liver, lung, pancreatic, colon, prostate, brain, and myeloid cancers. In our research, we examined benign compound nevi (BCN, n=17), dysplastic compound nevi (DCN, n=15), superficial spreading melanomas [SSM, categorized as <1 mm (n=19) and >4 mm (n=18) Breslow tumor thickness], and cutaneous metastatic disease (CMD, n=24). Immunohistochemistry was conducted using specific antibodies targeting 5hmC, 5-methylcytosine (5mC), and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein (TET2). The immunohistological scoring revealed significantly higher median levels of 5hmC in BCN and DCN compared to thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD (P<0.0001). There was no significant difference in 5mC immunoreactivity between nevi and melanoma (P=0.15). TET2 expression was predominantly weak but was significantly more frequent in nevi than in thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD (P<0.0001). Our findings demonstrate that advanced melanomas exhibit reduced levels of 5hmC and TET2 expression compared to nevi and thin melanomas. This suggests that 5hmC and TET2 may play a crucial role in the epigenetic regulation of melanoma development and progression.

title: Estimation of the dietary requirement for vitamin D in healthy adults.
text: There is significant variation among international dietary recommendations for vitamin D due to knowledge gaps. The objective of this study was to determine the amount of dietary vitamin D needed to maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentrations above different proposed cutoffs during winter, while accounting for the impact of summer sunshine exposure and diet. The study involved a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind intervention conducted over 22 weeks in men and women aged 20-40 years. Different supplemental doses of vitamin D(3) (0, 5, 10, and 15 microg/d) were administered throughout the winter. Serum 25(OH)D concentrations were measured at the beginning and end of the study. The results showed a clear dose-dependent increase in serum 25(OH)D with higher supplemental vitamin D(3) doses. The slope of the relationship between vitamin D intake and serum 25(OH)D was 1.96 nmol x L(-1) x microg(-1) intake. The study found that a vitamin D intake of 8.7 microg/d was needed to maintain serum 25(OH)D concentrations above 25 nmol/L in 97.5% of the participants. This intake varied from 7.2 microg/d for those with sun exposure, 8.8 microg/d for those with occasional sun exposure, and 12.3 microg/d for those who avoided sun exposure. The vitamin D intakes required to maintain serum 25(OH)D concentrations above 37.5, 50, and 80 nmol/L in 97.5% of the participants were 19.9, 28.0, and 41.1 microg/d, respectively. In conclusion, the recommended range of vitamin D intakes to maintain winter vitamin D status in the majority of 20-40-year-old adults (considering different sun exposure preferences) is between 7.2 and 41.1 microg/d.

title: Rapid purification of homodimer and heterodimer HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by metal chelate affinity chromatography.
text: We have made modifications to an Escherichia coli vector that now allows for the simultaneous expression of both the 66-kDa HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (p66) and the pol-coded protease. This twin expression cassette produces large quantities of both reverse transcriptase and protease. However, when expressed under these conditions, 50% of the over-expressed p66 reverse transcriptase undergoes processing, resulting in the accumulation of significant amounts of p66/p51 enzyme. Additionally, by adding a poly(histidine) affinity label at the beginning of the reverse-transcriptase-coding sequence (His-p66), we are able to easily and quickly purify milligram quantities of either p66 or p66/p51 enzyme from a crude lysate using metal chelate affinity chromatography. The purified His-p66 and His-p66/His-p51 reverse transcriptase demonstrate both reverse transcriptase and RNase H activity. Furthermore, the purification of a p66/p51 enzyme, where only the p66 component is labeled, using metal chelate chromatography further supports the existence of a heterodimer.

title: Polyphenols of Cocoa: Inhibition of Mammalian 15-Lipoxygenase
text: Theobroma cacao, a plant that produces cocoa and chocolate, contains compounds called epicatechin and procyanidins. These compounds were found to inhibit rabbit 15-lipoxygenase-1, with the larger procyanidins being more effective. The decamer fraction of procyanidins had an IC50 value of 0.8 M. Among the individual flavanols, epigallocatechin gallate and epicatechin gallate were more potent inhibitors than epicatechin. Epicatechin and procyanidin nonamer also inhibited the formation of 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid in rabbit smooth muscle cells. However, inhibition of the lipoxygenase pathway in J774A.1 cells was only observed when the cells were sonicated, suggesting a barrier for flavanols in these cells. Additionally, epicatechin and the procyanidin decamer inhibited human platelet 12-lipoxygenase. These findings suggest that flavanols and procyanidins have a general inhibitory effect on lipoxygenase, which may contribute to their potential cardiovascular benefits. This could explain why procyanidins have been shown to decrease the leukotriene/prostacyclin ratio in humans and human aortic endothelial cells.

title: Quality of life in patients with advanced heart failure.
text: Evaluation of the treatment of congestive heart failure typically relies on objective clinical outcomes. However, there is growing recognition of the importance of patient self-assessment in the evaluation process. To explore this further, a study was conducted to assess the quality of life of 134 patients with advanced heart failure symptoms who were being considered for heart transplantation. The assessment included a combination of subjective and objective measures, such as functional status, physical symptoms, emotional state, and psychosocial adaptation. Surprisingly, there was no significant correlation between patients' cardiac ejection fraction and any quality-of-life measures. However, the results did reveal significant associations between the 6-minute walking test, New York Heart Association classification, self-reported functional status, and psychosocial adjustment. In fact, self-reported functional status, depression, and hostility accounted for 43% of the variance in total psychosocial adjustment to illness. These findings highlight the importance of including quality of life as an outcome measure in treatment evaluations. They also suggest that interventions aimed at improving the quality of life for patients with advanced heart failure should focus on reducing depression and hostility while increasing daily activity levels.

title: Regional vascular resistance during exercise: role of cardiac afferents and exercise training.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate whether cardiac vagal afferents have a suppressive effect on the increase in regional vascular resistance during exercise, and whether endurance exercise training enhances this suppressive effect. We conducted the study on 12 rabbits, measuring changes in regional vascular resistance at rest and during running at a speed of 12.6 m/min and a 20% incline. We performed reversible denervation of cardiac afferents using intrapericardial procainamide HCl (2%), and repeated the procedures in five rabbits after an 8-week endurance exercise training program. Since procainamide injections affect both the efferent and afferent innervation to the heart, we needed to determine the impact of blocking the efferent innervation on the regulation of regional vascular resistance during exercise. We equipped the rabbits with Doppler ultrasonic flow probes around the renal, mesenteric, ascending, and terminal aortic arteries. We also inserted catheters in the central ear artery and vein, as well as the pericardial sac. We measured mean arterial pressure, heart rate, cardiac output, and resistances in the renal, mesenteric, ascending, terminal aortic, and systemic arteries. During exercise, we observed increases in resistances in the renal (+37 +/- 4%), mesenteric (+88 +/- 9%), and systemic (-34 +/- 3%) arteries, while the resistance in the terminal aortic artery decreased (-62 +/- 6%). Blocking only the cardiac efferent innervation did not have a significant effect on regional vascular resistance during exercise. However, when both the efferent and afferent innervation were blocked, we observed significant increases in resistance in the renal (+62 +/- 6%) and mesenteric (+134 +/- 13%) arteries, while the resistance in the terminal aortic artery (-51 +/- 4%) and systemic arteries (-27 +/- 2%) remained unchanged during exercise. Endurance exercise training significantly enhanced the suppressive effect of cardiac afferents on regional vascular resistance in the renal and mesenteric arteries.

title: Serum Soluble Corin is Decreased in Stroke.
text:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: The levels of soluble corin have been found to be reduced in individuals with coronary heart disease. Given the link between cardiac dysfunction and stroke, it is plausible that circulating corin could serve as a potential marker for stroke risk. However, there is currently a lack of research on the association between circulating corin and stroke in humans. Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate this association in patients with stroke and healthy individuals from the community.

METHODS: A total of 481 patients with ischemic stroke, 116 patients with hemorrhagic stroke, and 2498 healthy controls were included in the study. Serum levels of soluble corin, as well as conventional risk factors for stroke, were examined. As previous studies have shown variations in circulating corin between men and women, the association between serum soluble corin and stroke was evaluated separately for each gender.

RESULTS: Both male and female patients with ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke exhibited significantly lower levels of serum soluble corin compared to the healthy controls (all P values, <0.05). In multivariate analysis, men in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were found to have a higher likelihood of experiencing ischemic (odds ratio [OR], 4.90; 95% confidence interval, 2.99-8.03) and hemorrhagic (OR, 17.57; 95% confidence interval, 4.85-63.71) stroke compared to men in the highest quartile. Similarly, women in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were also more likely to have ischemic (OR, 3.10; 95% confidence interval, 1.76-5.44) and hemorrhagic (OR, 8.54; 95% confidence interval, 2.35-31.02) stroke compared to women in the highest quartile. The odds ratios for ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke significantly increased with decreasing levels of serum soluble corin in both men and women (all P values for trend, <0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: The findings of this study indicate that patients with stroke have lower levels of serum soluble corin compared to healthy controls. These results suggest that serum soluble corin may play a role in the pathogenesis of stroke.

title: Topical application of chlorhexidine to neonatal umbilical cords for prevention of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in a rural district of Pakistan: a community-based, cluster-randomised trial.
text:
In low-resource settings where home deliveries are common, umbilical cord infection (omphalitis) poses a risk for neonatal sepsis and mortality. Our objective was to evaluate the impact of cleansing the umbilical cord with a 4% chlorhexidine (CHX) solution, with or without handwashing using antiseptic soap, on the incidence of omphalitis and neonatal mortality. 

We conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Dadu, a rural area of Sindh province, Pakistan. Clusters were defined as the population served by a traditional birth attendant (TBA) and were randomly assigned to one of four groups (groups A to D) using a computer-generated random number sequence. The implementation and data collection teams were unaware of the group assignments. Newborns delivered by participating TBAs who received birth kits were eligible for enrollment. 

One intervention involved birth kits containing 4% CHX solution for application to the cord at birth by TBAs and once daily by family members for up to 14 days, along with soap and educational messages promoting handwashing. Another intervention included CHX solution only, while a third intervention focused on handwashing only. The control group promoted standard dry cord care. The primary outcomes were the incidence of neonatal omphalitis and neonatal mortality. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (number NCT00682006). 

A total of 187 clusters were randomly assigned to the study groups. Among the 9,741 newborns delivered by participating TBAs, factorial analysis showed a reduced risk of omphalitis with CHX application (risk ratio [RR]=0.58, 95% CI 0.41-0.82; p=0.002), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing (RR=0.83, 0.61-1.13; p=0.24). We found strong evidence of a reduction in neonatal mortality in neonates who received CHX cleansing (RR=0.62, 95% CI 0.45-0.85; p=0.003), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing promotion on neonatal mortality (RR=1.08, 0.79-1.48; p=0.62). No serious adverse events were recorded. 

In conclusion, the application of 4% CHX to the umbilical cord was effective in reducing the risk of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in rural Pakistan. Providing CHX in birth kits could be a valuable strategy for preventing neonatal mortality in high-mortality settings. This study was funded by the United States Agency for International Development.

title: The IKK complex, a central regulator of NF-kappaB activation.
text: The IKK kinase complex serves as the central component of the NF-kappaB cascade. It consists primarily of two kinases, IKKalpha and IKKbeta, along with a regulatory subunit known as NEMO/IKKgamma. While there may be additional components that exist, their characterization remains uncertain. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there are two distinct NF-kappaB pathways, which depend on the activating signal and the type of cell. These pathways include the canonical pathway, which relies on IKKbeta and NEMO, and the noncanonical pathway, which solely relies on IKKalpha. The primary question that remains partially answered is how an NF-kappaB activating signal triggers the activation of the kinase subunits, enabling them to phosphorylate their targets and ultimately induce the nuclear translocation of NF-kappaB dimers. In this review, I will examine the genetic, biochemical, and structural data accumulated over the past decade regarding the function of the three IKK subunits.

title: Cognitive predictors of young children's readiness for powered mobility.
text: The development of cognitive and psychosocial skills in early childhood has been linked to independent mobility. However, children with physical disabilities may face challenges in moving independently, which can lead to delays in these areas. Providing powered mobility at an early stage can give these young children the opportunity to move independently. However, there is limited information available to determine when a child has the cognitive abilities required to operate a powered wheelchair safely. This research aims to identify these skills. To achieve this, a cognitive assessment battery and a program for wheelchair mobility training and assessment were created. Twenty-six children between the ages of 20 and 36 months, who had physical disabilities, were evaluated using the cognitive assessment and participated in the wheelchair training and assessment program. A stepwise regression analysis was conducted to determine which cognitive skills predicted wheelchair mobility performance. The study found that spatial relations and problem-solving skills were significant predictors and accounted for 57% of the variance in wheelchair skills. The study also presents developmental cut-off points on these scales in relation to wheelchair skills and discusses their clinical applications.

title: Knockdown of the co-chaperone Hop promotes extranuclear accumulation of Stat3 in mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: Phosphorylation, dimerisation, and translocation to the nucleus of the signal transducer and activator of transcription3, Stat3, are crucial events in maintaining the pluripotency of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs). To investigate this mechanism, we used RNAi to reduce the levels of the co-chaperone Hsp70/Hsp90 organising protein (Hop) in an mESC line. The knockdown of Hop resulted in a 68% decrease in Stat3 mRNA levels, a reduction in soluble pYStat3 levels, and an accumulation of Stat3 outside the nucleus. We observed that Hop's main binding partner, Hsp90, co-localised with a small fraction of non-nuclear Stat3 in mESCs, and both Stat3 and Hop were found to co-precipitate with Hsp90. Interestingly, the depletion of Hop did not affect the levels of Nanog and Oct4 proteins, but it did lead to a decrease in Nanog mRNA levels. Furthermore, we discovered that mESCs lacking Hop lost their ability to form embryoid bodies with a basement membrane, indicating a loss of pluripotency. These findings suggest that Hop plays a crucial role in facilitating the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of Stat3, highlighting the involvement of the Hsp70/Hsp90 chaperone heterocomplex machinery in pluripotency signaling.

title: B-cell self-tolerance in humans.
text:
The generation of the human antibody repertoire is facilitated by two mechanisms. The first mechanism is V(D)J recombination, which occurs during the early stages of B-cell development in the bone marrow. The second mechanism is somatic mutation of immunoglobulin genes, which takes place in mature B cells that respond to antigens in the periphery. V(D)J recombination creates diversity by randomly joining gene segments, while somatic mutation introduces random point mutations. Both mechanisms are necessary to achieve the level of diversity in antigen receptors that is crucial for immune protection. Defects in either mechanism can lead to increased susceptibility to infections.

However, the downside of generating such a vast array of random diversity in the antibody repertoire is the production of autoantibodies. To prevent autoimmunity, B cells that express autoantibodies are regulated by strict mechanisms. These mechanisms either modify the specificity of the autoantibodies or determine the fate of the cells that express them. Abnormalities in B-cell self-tolerance are associated with numerous autoimmune diseases, although the exact nature of these defects is not well-defined. In this article, we provide a summary of recent data on the self-reactive B-cell repertoire in both healthy individuals and patients with autoimmune conditions.

title: JMJD6 Promotes Colon Carcinogenesis through Negative Regulation of p53 by Hydroxylation
text: The role of Jumonji domain-containing 6 (JMJD6) within the Jumonji C domain-containing protein family remains unclear, and its biological function is largely unexplored. However, our research has discovered a physical association between JMJD6 and the tumor suppressor p53. We have determined that JMJD6 functions as a lysyl hydroxylase, dependent on α-ketoglutarate and Fe(II), to catalyze the hydroxylation of p53. This hydroxylation primarily occurs on lysine 382 of p53, and we have observed the presence of hydroxylated p53 in vivo. Additionally, JMJD6 counteracts p53 acetylation, facilitates the interaction between p53 and its negative regulator MDMX, and suppresses p53's transcriptional activity. Depleting JMJD6 enhances p53's transcriptional activity, induces cell cycle arrest in the G1 phase, promotes cell apoptosis, and increases sensitivity to cell death induced by DNA damaging agents. Importantly, reducing JMJD6 levels inhibits p53-dependent colon cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in vivo. Furthermore, the expression of JMJD6 is significantly up-regulated in various types of human cancer, particularly in colon cancer. High levels of nuclear JMJD6 protein are strongly associated with aggressive clinical behaviors in colon adenocarcinomas. These findings highlight a novel posttranslational modification of p53 and suggest that JMJD6 could serve as a potential biomarker for colon cancer aggressiveness and a target for intervention.

title: Spread of chloroquine resistance in Plasmodium falciparum.
text: More than 40 countries have now confirmed the presence of malaria that is resistant to chloroquine. Although the drug was introduced in 1934, it did not see widespread use until the early 1950s. There are anecdotal reports suggesting that resistance to chloroquine emerged as early as 1957 in Colombia and along the Cambodia-Thailand border. However, it was not until 1960 that resistance in these areas was officially confirmed, and it is possible that there were two separate instances of resistance. The spread of resistance was rapid, with a new area of resistance identified in East Africa by 1977. The resistance to chloroquine poses a significant problem for both the prevention and treatment of malaria. In this article, David Payne examines the spread of resistance and discusses some of its implications.

title: Obesity occurring in apolipoprotein E-knockout mice has mild effects on fertility.
text: The Apolipoprotein (Apo) family is involved in lipid metabolism. There are five types of Apo: Apoa, Apob, Apoc, Apod, and Apoe. Apoe plays a crucial role in the metabolism of lipoproteins and is necessary for the efficient clearance of chylomicron remnants and VLDL remnant particles by the liver through receptor-mediated plasma clearance. Apoe-deficient (Apoe(-/-)) mice spontaneously develop atherosclerotic plaques, followed by obesity. In this study, we examined whether the absence of Apoe affects reproduction in female mice by causing lipid deposition. The results showed that Apoe(-/-) mice had extremely high cholesterol levels, disrupted cholesterol metabolism, and increased lipid accumulation in the ovaries, resulting in heavier ovaries compared to the WT counterparts. Additionally, estrogen and progesterone levels significantly decreased at D 100. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that at D 100, the expression of cytochromeP450 aromatase (Cyp19a1), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (Hsd3b), mechanistic target of rapamycin (Mtor), and nuclear factor-κB (Nfkb) significantly decreased, while the expression of BCL2-associated agonist of cell death (Bad) and tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (Tsc2) significantly increased in the Apoe(-/-) mice. However, there was no difference in fertility rates between the Apoe(-/-) and WT mice, indicating that obesity resulting from Apoe knockout does not significantly affect reproduction. However, the deletion of Apoe did increase the number of ovarian follicles and the ratio of ovarian follicle atresia and apoptosis. This study contributes to our understanding of the role of Apoe in reproduction.

title: Lipid metabolism and toxicity in the heart.
text: The heart requires the highest amount of calories and has the most efficient breakdown of fatty acids (FAs). However, in cases of obesity and type 2 diabetes, the heart's ability to take up and break down FAs becomes imbalanced, resulting in the accumulation of lipids and potential cardiac lipotoxicity. This article will first examine the pathways through which the heart obtains FAs from the bloodstream and stores them as triglycerides within its cells. It will then discuss studies conducted on mouse models to investigate the negative effects of excessive lipid accumulation on heart function and the efforts made to mitigate this toxicity. Lastly, the article will provide an overview of the known connections between heart lipid metabolism and dysfunction in humans.

title: Malaria eradication back on the table.
text: After nearly four decades, the global health agenda has once again turned its attention to eradicating malaria. Inspired by the Gates Malaria Forum in October 2007, various organizations are now discussing the advantages and disadvantages of redefining eradication as a clear objective of malaria control efforts. Previous attempts to eliminate malaria in southern Africa and Pacific Island states, as well as the World Health Organization's (WHO) Global Malaria Programme agenda and field manual for malaria elimination, indicate a growing movement towards a global eradication campaign. As we celebrate 60 years of WHO's commitment to fighting malaria, it is important to reflect on what has been accomplished and what lessons we can learn from the past. We now possess a wealth of knowledge about the biology of parasite-host responses, the factors that contribute to endemicity and transmission dynamics, the social and economic implications of malaria at various levels, and the challenges faced by health systems in endemic countries. However, we have yet to determine how to effectively synthesize and integrate this knowledge to achieve elimination in different settings. Regional malaria elimination campaigns were first conducted in the late 1940s, paving the way for the Global Malaria Eradication Program in 1955. This program successfully eliminated malaria from Europe, North America, the Caribbean, and parts of Asia and South-Central America. However, sub-Saharan Africa, which currently bears 80% of the malaria burden, did not experience significant success. The main reasons for failure, particularly in Africa, were the technical challenges associated with executing the eradication strategy. From 1969 to 1991, the focus shifted to technical issues, research and development for new tools, and advancements in drug and vaccine development, vector control, and insecticide-treated nets. These decades also provided a better understanding of the social, economic, and cultural dimensions of malaria. Unfortunately, little global support was specifically provided for malaria control in the newly independent states of Africa, which were struggling to establish comprehensive health systems and primary healthcare. In 1992, due to a worsening malaria situation and promising technical advancements, global attention once again turned to malaria control. The Roll Back Malaria initiative, launched by WHO in 1998, led to the Abuja Declaration in 2000, which set targets for progressive intervention coverage aimed at eliminating malaria as a public health problem. It emphasized the need for significantly strengthened local health systems to achieve this goal. Increased resources from organizations such as the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the World Bank's Booster Program, and the US President's Malaria Initiative have contributed to rising intervention coverage. Against this backdrop, the call for elimination/eradication emerges. However, the challenges ahead are significant. It is widely acknowledged that elimination in Africa is not currently feasible with existing tools. Efforts must go beyond developing better tools and focus on strategically combining existing and future tools for maximum effectiveness within the health and social systems of endemic areas. Achieving elimination and eradication also necessitates effective surveillance strategies to monitor progress, which poses a challenge for health systems. This, in turn, requires a deeper understanding of malaria transmission heterogeneity in a globalized world with rapidly changing environmental, climate, migration, and transnational cooperation dynamics. Sustaining momentum in the long term, especially in the face of regional elimination successes, while waiting to achieve final eradication, will be a major challenge. Starting with the "easy-to-eliminate" settings on the margins of malaria prevalence may initially boost morale but may not provide significant benefits to areas with the highest malaria burden. Any strategic plan must be a globally synchronized effort, tailored to the specific needs of all endemic areas. Although we currently lack the knowledge, systems, and tools to eradicate malaria, we do have a window of opportunity in terms of political will and financial resources to refocus on the goal of effective control through universal coverage of appropriate interventions. The prerequisites for a successful start are inclusive discussions to establish a global vision, goals, and strategy, as well as a global plan for all endemic areas outlining how, where, and when to transition from control to elimination. What must set this new era apart, particularly in Africa, is a genuine emphasis on health systems rather than mere rhetoric.

title: CI-994 (N-acetyl-dinaline) in combination with conventional anti-cancer agents is effective against acute myeloid leukemia in vitro and in vivo.
text:
N-acetyl-dinaline (CI-994) is a promising experimental cancer drug that works by inhibiting histone deacetylases. We conducted a study to assess how CI-994 interacts with conventional chemotherapeutic drugs commonly used to treat acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in both a rat model for AML and Brown Norway rat acute myelocytic leukemia (BNML).

In our in vitro experiments, we found that combining CI-994 with cytarabine (ara-C), daunorubicin, and mitoxantrone resulted in a moderate synergistic effect. When tested in vivo, higher doses of CI-994 led to complete remissions. Specifically, the combination of CI-994 and ara-C showed significant activity against BNML. Additionally, the combinations of CI-994 with daunorubicin and mitoxantrone also demonstrated effectiveness against BNML.

Overall, our study highlights the favorable interactions between CI-994 and conventional anti-cancer drugs used in the treatment of AML, both in laboratory settings and in live animal models.

title: CTCF and Cohesin in Genome Folding and Transcriptional Gene Regulation.
text: The cell cycle heavily relies on the dynamic structural organization of chromosomes for genome function, replication, integrity, and propagation. During interphase, the folding of the genome plays a crucial role in regulatory segmentation, ensuring proper transcriptional control, facilitating orderly replication, and preventing illegitimate recombination, thus maintaining genome integrity. In this review, we examine recent studies utilizing high-resolution chromosome conformation capture and functional analysis to gain insights into the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes. Additionally, we discuss mechanistic models that elucidate how CTCF and cohesin proteins govern the functional architecture of mammalian chromosomes.

title: Melatonin synthesized by T lymphocytes as a ligand of the retinoic acid-related orphan receptor.
text: Melatonin has a wide range of effects on the immune system, influencing various physiological events. While the importance of specific melatonin membrane receptors is well known for many biological functions, there is evidence suggesting that retinoic acid-related orphan receptor alpha (RORα) may play a role in nuclear melatonin signaling. However, more research is needed to confirm a direct interaction between melatonin and RORα, as it is possible that melatonin has downstream effects. In this study, we found that RORα is primarily located in the nucleus of human Jurkat T-cells and is co-immunoprecipitated with melatonin. Additionally, immunocytochemistry studies confirmed that melatonin and RORα are found in the same cellular locations. Melatonin caused a time-dependent decrease in nuclear RORα levels, indicating that it may affect RORα's transcriptional activity. Interestingly, RORα is involved in the generation of Th17 and Treg cells, which play opposing roles in immune conditions like autoimmunity or acute transplant rejection. Therefore, the discovery that melatonin can modulate RORα has significant therapeutic potential for various clinical disorders.

title: Age- and infection intensity-dependent cytokine and antibody production in human trichuriasis: the importance of IgE.
text: We examined the immune response to Trichuris trichiura infection in a group of 96 individuals living in an area with high parasite prevalence and a pattern of infection that increases with age. When exposed to T. trichiura antigen, a small percentage of the participants (7%) produced interleukin (IL)-4, IL-9 (5%), and IL-13 (17%). However, a larger proportion (97%) produced IL-10, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha (93%), and interferon (IFN)-gamma (32%). Interestingly, the levels of TNF-alpha (P =.016) and IFN-gamma (P =.012) increased significantly with age, indicating a shift towards a more chronic infection. The most common parasite-specific antibodies detected were IgG1, IgG4, IgA, and IgE. Unlike the other antibody subclasses and IgA, parasite-specific IgE showed a negative correlation with infection intensity, as measured by egg output (P =.008), and a positive correlation with host age (P =.010). These findings suggest a mixed cytokine response in trichuriasis and a protective role for IgE.

title: The cryoprotective effect of trehalose supplementation on boar spermatozoa quality.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of trehalose on the success of cryopreservation of boar sperm, with the goal of improving sperm quality during the frozen-thawed process. We assessed the freeze-thawing tolerance of boar spermatozoa in a cooling extender with varying concentrations of trehalose (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200mmol/l), in order to determine the optimal concentration. We used parameters such as sperm motility, acrosome integrity, membrane integrity, and cryocapacitation to evaluate the cryopreservation capacity of boar spermatozoa. The results showed that the best outcomes were achieved with extenders supplemented with 100mmol/l of trehalose, with motility at 49.89%, acrosome integrity at 66.52%, and membrane integrity at 44.61%. However, freeze-thawing tolerance significantly decreased with 200mmol/l of trehalose. The CTC score for semen diluted with extender containing 100mmol/l of trehalose was 3.68% before capacitation and 43.82% after capacitation. In conclusion, trehalose can enhance the cryoprotective capacity of boar spermatozoa. The supplementation of trehalose at a concentration of 100mmol/l in the basic extender can significantly improve parameters such as sperm motility, membrane integrity, and acrosome integrity, while reducing cryocapacitation during the cryopreservation process.

title: Roads to polyploidy: the megakaryocyte example.
text: Polyploidy, characterized by multiple copies of the haploid chromosome number, has been observed in plants, insects, and mammalian cells such as platelet precursors, specifically megakaryocytes. Various cell types achieve high ploidy through distinct cell cycles. Megakaryocytes undergo an endomitotic cell cycle, which involves an S phase interrupted by a gap. During this gap, the cells enter mitosis but skip anaphase B and cytokinesis. In this review, we examine the mechanisms that drive this cell cycle and polyploidy in megakaryocytes, comparing them to other systems that achieve high ploidy. Overall, polyploidy is associated with coordinated changes in gene expression. Some of these changes may be a consequence of high ploidy and contribute to new cell physiology, while others may induce polyploidization. Future research will focus on further investigating these two groups of genes.

title: Central memory and effector memory T cell subsets: function, generation, and maintenance.
text: The memory T cell pool serves as a constantly evolving collection of T lymphocytes that have encountered antigens throughout an individual's life. Recent research suggests that memory T lymphocytes can be categorized into two distinct groups: central memory (TCM) and effector memory (TEM) cells. These groups differ in their ability to migrate and their functions as effectors. This review explores the diversity of TCM and TEM, their various stages of development, and the existing models that explain how they are generated and sustained in both humans and mice.

title: The Werner and Bloom syndrome proteins help resolve replication blockage by converting (regressed) holliday junctions to functional replication forks.
text: Cells have mechanisms to deal with obstacles that prevent the progression of replication forks. These mechanisms ensure that DNA synthesis is completed and minimize the risk of genomic instability. One model for resolving blocked replication involves the regression of forks to form Holliday junction structures. The human RecQ helicases WRN and BLM, which are deficient in Werner and Bloom syndromes respectively, play a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability and are believed to be involved in accurately resolving replication blockages. Supporting this idea, WRN and BLM localize to sites of blocked replication following certain DNA-damaging treatments and exhibit increased activity on replication and recombination intermediates. In this study, we investigate the actions of WRN and BLM on a specific Holliday junction substrate that reflects a regressed replication fork. Our results show that, in reactions requiring ATP hydrolysis, both WRN and BLM primarily convert this Holliday junction substrate into a four-stranded replication fork structure, indicating that they target the Holliday junction to initiate branch migration. Consistently, the Holliday junction binding protein RuvA inhibits the conversion reactions mediated by WRN and BLM. Importantly, this converted product is suitable for replication, with its leading daughter strand easily extended by DNA polymerases. Additionally, the binding to and conversion of this Holliday junction are most effective at low concentrations of MgCl(2), suggesting that WRN and BLM preferentially act on the open conformation of Holliday junctions. Our findings suggest that, following regression events, WRN and/or BLM could restore functional replication forks to overcome blockages. This function aligns well with the phenotypes observed in cells deficient in WRN and BLM.

title: Do Montelukast Sodium and N-Acetylcysteine Have a Nephroprotective Effect on Unilateral Ureteral Obstruction? A Placebo Controlled Trial in a Rat Model.
text: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the protective effects of montelukast sodium and N-acetylcysteine on secondary renal damage caused by unilateral ureteral obstruction in a rat model. A total of 30 Wistar albino male rats were randomly assigned to three groups: placebo, N-acetylcysteine, and montelukast sodium. Three rats were included as the control group. The left ureter of the rats was surgically sutured using 4-zero polyglactin sutures. The medications were administered three days prior to the obstruction and continued for 15 days. Renal scintigraphy using dimercaptosuccinic acid was performed before the obstruction and on day 15. On day 15, the rats were sacrificed and histopathological examinations were conducted. Oxidative stress markers (myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde), sulfhydryl and total nitrite levels were biochemically assessed to evaluate lipid peroxidation, oxidative protein damage, and antioxidant levels, respectively. The results showed that the N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium groups exhibited less inflammation and tubular epithelial damage compared to the placebo group (p <0.05) on pathological examination. No differences were observed in normal kidneys. The N-acetylcysteine group had lower levels of myeloperoxidase, malondialdehyde, and total nitrite, while the montelukast sodium group had lower levels of myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde compared to the placebo group (p <0.05). There were no significant differences in sulfhydryl levels (p >0.05) or among the N-acetylcysteine, montelukast sodium, and placebo groups on scintigraphy (p >0.05). No differences were observed in pathology, chemistry, and scintigraphy among the N-acetylcysteine, montelukast sodium, and sham treated groups (p >0.05). In conclusion, N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium demonstrated a protective effect against obstructive kidney damage. However, further investigations are required.

title: Oxidative phosphorylation: synthesis of mitochondrially encoded proteins and assembly of individual structural subunits into functional holoenzyme complexes.
text: In higher eukaryotes, the majority of ATP used in cellular processes is produced by five protein complexes (I-V) located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This process, called oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), plays a crucial role in maintaining energy balance in the body. When OXPHOS fails to meet the changing energy demands of cells, it often leads to human diseases. Except for Complex II, the components of OXPHOS complexes are encoded by both the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes. This means that the expression of the 13 mitochondrial polypeptides must be coordinated with the relevant nuclear-encoded partners to form functional enzyme complexes. The assembly of these complexes is a highly organized process, involving various nuclear-encoded factors that work at different stages.

title: Familial gastroesophageal reflux and development of Barrett's esophagus.
text: The medical team investigated the family of an elderly man who had Barrett's esophagus to determine if there was a link between gastroesophageal reflux and the development of Barrett's esophagus. Out of the five children who are still alive, all of them have either gastroesophageal reflux or esophagitis, or both, and three of them have confirmed cases of Barrett's esophagus. Additionally, two members of the third generation also have gastroesophageal reflux. This pattern suggests that the trait of gastroesophageal reflux is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Furthermore, the family has a high occurrence of cancer, which could potentially be indicative of the cancer family syndrome.

title: The effect of folate fortification on folic acid-based homocysteine-lowering intervention and stroke risk: a meta-analysis.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the effects of folic acid supplementation on homocysteine levels and stroke risk in different folate fortification settings. Previous studies have shown conflicting results on the impact of folic acid supplementation on stroke risk. We conducted a meta-analysis of relevant randomized controlled trials to investigate this further.

We identified fourteen randomized controlled trials through a literature search. The participants included a total of 39,420 patients. We compared homocysteine reduction in subgroups categorized by folate fortification status. We used relative risks with 95% confidence intervals to assess the association between folic acid supplementation and stroke risk.

The results showed that homocysteine reductions were 26.99% in the subgroup without folate fortification, 18.38% in the subgroup with folate fortification, and 21.30% in the subgroup with partial folate fortification. There was a significant difference between the subgroups with and without folate fortification. The relative risk of stroke was 0.88 in the subgroup without folate fortification, 0.94 in the subgroup with folate fortification, and 0.91 in the subgroup with partial folate fortification. However, these differences were not statistically significant.

In conclusion, folic acid supplementation may have a modest benefit in preventing strokes in regions without folate fortification.

title: On the origin and impact of mesenchymal stem cell heterogeneity: new insights and emerging tools for single cell analysis.
text: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibit significant variability from cell to cell. This diversity is observed among different donors, tissue sources, and even within cell populations. This widespread variation complicates the use of MSCs in regenerative therapies and may limit their effectiveness. Traditional assays typically measure MSC properties in bulk, which masks this cell-to-cell variability. However, recent studies have discovered extensive variability among and within clonal MSC populations. This variability encompasses functional differentiation capacity, molecular state (such as epigenetic, transcriptomic, and proteomic status), and biophysical properties. The origins of these variations are still not fully understood, but potential mechanisms include micro-anatomical heterogeneity in vivo, epigenetic bistability, and transcriptional fluctuations. New tools for analyzing gene and protein expression at the single-cell level in MSCs offer the potential for further insights into the mechanisms and implications of this cell-to-cell variation. Ultimately, these advancements may enhance the clinical utility of MSCs in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. This review provides an overview of the dimensions in which MSC heterogeneity exists, describes some of the known mechanisms that govern this variability, and highlights emerging technologies that could improve our understanding and application of this unique cell type in clinical settings.

title: Altered microRNA expression in bovine skeletal muscle with age.
text: The decline in skeletal muscle function that occurs with age can lead to various muscular disorders in elderly individuals, both inherited and acquired. The levels of microRNAs (miRNAs) may be altered during the maintenance and repair of muscle. To investigate this further, we conducted a comprehensive study on miRNAs in bovine skeletal muscle development using next-generation small RNA sequencing. We identified a total of 511 miRNAs, including one potentially new miRNA. Thirty-six miRNAs showed differential expression between prenatal and postnatal stages of muscle development, including several myomiRs (miR-1, miR-206, and let-7 families). When comparing miRNA expression in different muscle tissues, we found that 14 miRNAs were up-regulated and 22 miRNAs were down-regulated in postnatal muscle. Additionally, we predicted and submitted a novel miRNA, bta-mir-10020, to the miRBase database. Through a dual luciferase reporter assay, we demonstrated that bta-mir-10020 directly targeted the 3'-UTR of the bovine ANGPT1 gene. Overexpression of bta-mir-10020 significantly reduced DsRed fluorescence in the wild-type expression cassette compared to the mutant type. Using three computational approaches (miranda, pita, and rnahybrid), we predicted that these differentially expressed miRNAs targeted 3609 bovine genes. Analysis of disease and biological function, as well as the KEGG pathway, revealed that these targets were statistically enriched in functions related to muscle growth and disease. Our findings on miRNA expression during different stages of muscle development and aging expand the knowledge of bovine miRNAs expressed in muscle and could contribute to further research on growth and developmental disorders in this tissue.

title: Apoptosis occurs predominantly in bystander cells and not in productively infected cells of HIV- and SIV-infected lymph nodes
text: Despite the identification of human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) as the cause of AIDS 13 years ago, we still lack knowledge about how HIV-1 kills the primary target, the CD4 antigen-carrying T cell. Our research, along with others, has observed an increase in the percentage of apoptotic cells among circulating CD4+ (and CD8+) T cells in individuals with HIV, and this frequency of apoptosis increases as the disease progresses. However, it remains unclear whether this apoptosis occurs in infected or uninfected T cells. Our study, using in situ labeling of lymph nodes from HIV-infected children and SIV-infected macaques, reveals that apoptosis primarily occurs in bystander cells rather than the infected cells themselves. These findings have significant implications for understanding the disease's progression and developing effective therapies. Specifically, they suggest that rational drug therapy should involve combination agents that target viral replication in infected cells and induce apoptosis in uninfected cells.

title: Neuronal origin of a cerebral amyloid: neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease contain the same protein as the amyloid of plaque cores and blood vessels.
text: The protein part of Alzheimer's disease amyloid, which includes neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid plaque core, and congophilic angiopathy, is a clumped polypeptide with a subunit mass of 4 kd (known as the A4 monomer). The amyloid is initially deposited in the neuron and later in the extracellular space, based on the extent of N-terminal heterogeneity. By using synthetic peptide-based antisera, we have discovered that the N terminus of A4 (residues 1-11) contains an epitope for neurofibrillary tangles, while the inner region of the molecule (residues 11-23) contains an epitope for plaque cores and vascular amyloid. The non-protein part of the amyloid (aluminum silicate) may serve as the foundation for the deposition or amplification (potentially self-replication) of the clumped amyloid protein. Although the subunit size and composition of Alzheimer's disease amyloid resemble those of the scrapie-associated fibril and its constituent polypeptides, their sequences are not the same. Furthermore, the sequence and composition of neurofibrillary tangles are not similar to any known components of normal neurofilaments.

title: Pregnancy characteristics and maternal risk of breast cancer.
text: During pregnancy, hormone levels such as estrogen and progesterone are significantly higher than during other stages of life. These hormones are primarily produced in the placenta, and signs of placental impairment can indicate hormone exposure during pregnancy. However, the association between these markers and the risk of breast cancer in mothers has been inconsistent. This study aims to examine the relationship between indirect markers of hormonal exposure, such as placental weight and other pregnancy characteristics, and the risk of developing breast cancer in mothers. The study is a population-based cohort study that utilizes data from various Swedish registers. The participants are women included in the Swedish Birth Register who delivered singletons between 1982 and 1989, with complete information on date of birth and gestational age. The women were followed up until the occurrence of breast cancer, death, or the end of the follow-up period in 2001. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the associations between hormone exposures and the risk of breast cancer. The main outcome measure is the incidence of invasive breast cancer. Out of the 314,019 women in the cohort, 2216 (0.7%) developed breast cancer during the follow-up period, with 2100 (95%) being diagnosed before the age of 50. The study found that women whose placentas weighed between 500 and 699 g in their first pregnancy and at least 700 g in their second pregnancy (or vice versa) had an increased risk of breast cancer compared to women with placentas weighing less than 500 g in both pregnancies. Similarly, women with placentas weighing at least 700 g in both pregnancies had a doubled risk of breast cancer. However, a high birth weight in two successive births was only associated with an increased risk of breast cancer before adjusting for placental weight and other factors. These findings suggest that placental weight is positively associated with the risk of breast cancer in mothers, supporting the hypothesis that pregnancy hormones play a role in modifying maternal breast cancer risk.

title: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a category or a continuum? Genetic analysis of a large-scale twin study.
text:
The aim of this study was to examine the heritability and the continuum versus categorical approaches to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) using a large sample of twins. A total of 1,938 families with twins and siblings between the ages of 4 and 12 were recruited from the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council Twin Registry. ADHD was assessed using a maternal rating scale based on the DSM-III-R criteria. Probandwise concordance rates and correlations were calculated for monozygotic and dizygotic twins and siblings, and heritability was analyzed using the De Fries and Fulker regression technique. 

The results showed a strong genetic influence on ADHD, with a narrow heritability estimate ranging from 0.75 to 0.91. This heritability was consistent across different familial relationships (twins, siblings, and twin-siblings) and across different definitions of ADHD, whether viewed as a continuum or as a disorder with specific symptom cutoffs. There was no evidence of nonadditive genetic variation or shared family environmental effects. 

In conclusion, these findings suggest that ADHD should be considered as an extreme manifestation of a behavior that is genetically influenced throughout the entire population, rather than as a disorder with distinct causes. This has important implications for the classification of ADHD, the identification of genes associated with this behavior, as well as for diagnosis and treatment strategies.

title: Antiapoptotic BCL-2 is required for maintenance of a model leukemia.
text: Resistance to apoptosis, which is often achieved by the overexpression of proteins that prevent cell death, is a common occurrence in the development of cancer. However, it is still uncertain whether defects in the process of apoptosis are necessary for the maintenance of tumors. In order to investigate this, we created mice that had a conditional BCL-2 gene and constitutive c-myc, which led to the development of lymphoblastic leukemia. When we eliminated BCL-2, the leukemic cells rapidly died and the survival of the mice was significantly prolonged. This confirmed that BCL-2 is a valid target for cancer therapy. The loss of this single molecule resulted in cell death, despite the presence of other oncogenic events. This suggests that cancer cells have inherent abnormalities that generate signals for cell death, which would normally kill the cell if not counteracted by defects in the apoptotic process.

title: Cellular and histopathological changes in the infrapatellar fat pad in the monoiodoacetate model of osteoarthritis pain.
text:
OBJECTIVE: Our objective was to investigate the changes in the infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) in rats undergoing the monoiodoacetate (MIA) model of degenerative joint disease, which exhibits similarities to osteoarthritis (OA). We aimed to analyze the development of weight bearing asymmetry and examine the inflammatory infiltrate and histopathological changes in the IPFP.

METHODS: Rats were intra-articularly injected with MIA and their weight bearing asymmetry was monitored for 21 days. IPFPs were collected from both the affected and unaffected joints for analysis. We assessed the inflammatory infiltrate and histopathological changes in the IPFP.

RESULTS: The injection of MIA resulted in significant weight bearing asymmetry. The wet weights of the IPFP in the affected joints were significantly increased on days 1 and 3 in MIA-treated rats. MIA treatment also led to significant increases in the total white blood cells, monocytes, and neutrophils in the IPFP on various days. Histopathological findings showed adipocyte necrosis, IPFP fibrosis, patellar cartilage and subchondral bone necrosis, and synovial hyperplasia at different time points.

CONCLUSIONS: Our study clearly demonstrated marked inflammatory changes in the IPFP during the early stage of the MIA model of OA, which may contribute to the observed pain. Further investigation is needed to understand the role of the IPFP in later stages of the model.

title: Angiogenesis therapy: amidst the hype, the neglected potential for serious side effects.
text:
A decade ago, angiogenesis therapy was relatively unknown as a treatment concept. However, it has now gained significant attention in the field of cardiology. It is difficult to come across a cardiology journal, attend a cardiology meeting, or read a newspaper without encountering the excitement surrounding the potential impact of angiogenesis therapy on patients with atherosclerotic lesions that block arteries supplying the heart or legs. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge that powerful therapeutic interventions often come with the risk of harmful effects, and angiogenesis therapy is no exception.

Despite the lack of primary end-point efficacy demonstrated in reasonably powered, randomized, double-blind clinical studies so far, there has been a noticeable absence of serious consideration of the potential side effects in scientific communications. However, the lay media recently shifted from unbridled enthusiasm to profound skepticism after the tragic death of a young man caused by the injection of a large amount of an adenoviral vector into the hepatic artery (unrelated to angiogenesis therapy). On the other hand, the scientific community has generally failed to engage in in-depth discussions about the inherent dangers of angiogenesis interventions.

It is crucial to have a comprehensive discussion about the potential complications of angiogenesis therapy, not only because of the aforementioned event but also because there is a wealth of mechanistic data available that allows us to anticipate specific side effects that may arise from this treatment. In this discussion, we will primarily focus on the biological activities of two powerful angiogenic cytokines: vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF). Angiogenic agents have the ability to induce neovascularization in various tissues, which is significant in clinical settings.

title: Body mass index and magnetic resonance markers of brain integrity in adults.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between obesity and being overweight during adulthood and the risk of developing dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease, later in life. Additionally, the study aimed to investigate the impact of adiposity on cognitive function and brain structure in healthy adults. The researchers utilized magnetic resonance imaging and proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging data from 50 middle-aged participants who were scanned as control subjects for another study. 

The results showed that higher body mass indices (BMIs) were associated with lower concentrations of N-acetylaspartate, a marker of neuronal viability, in the frontal, parietal, and temporal white matter. Lower N-acetylaspartate levels were also observed in the frontal gray matter, and lower concentrations of choline-containing metabolites, related to membrane metabolism, were found in the frontal white matter. These findings suggest that increased BMI in midlife is linked to abnormalities in neuronal and/or myelin function, particularly in the frontal lobe. As the frontal white matter is more susceptible to the effects of aging, these results may indicate accelerated aging in individuals with high levels of adiposity. Consequently, a higher BMI may increase the likelihood of developing age-related diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease.

title: Characteristics of medial temporal lobe epilepsy: II. Interictal and ictal scalp electroencephalography, neuropsychological testing, neuroimaging, surgical results, and pathology.
text:
A retrospective evaluation was conducted on sixty-seven patients with temporal lobe epilepsy who underwent temporal lobectomy and achieved seizure freedom. These patients did not have specific epileptogenic lesions. The evaluation focused on preoperative scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) findings, neuropsychological test results, neuroimaging findings, surgical outcomes, and pathology of the resected tissue.

During prolonged monitoring, paroxysmal abnormalities were observed in the interictal scalp EEG of 64 patients (96%). These abnormalities were mainly localized in the anterior temporal region of 60 patients (94%). Bilateral independent paroxysmal activity was found in 42% of the patients, with a tendency to be more prominent on the side of seizure origin in half of these cases. Ictal EEG changes were rarely detected at the onset of clinical seizures, but a lateralized buildup of rhythmic seizure activity was observed in 80% of patients during the seizure. However, in 13% of cases, the scalp EEG seizure buildup was contralateral to the side of seizure origin, as confirmed by depth EEG and curative surgery. Lateralized postictal slowing, when present, reliably indicated the side of seizure origin. 

Neuropsychological testing provided concordant lateralizing findings with the side of seizure origin in 73% of patients. In cases where neuropsychological testing yielded discordant or nonlateralizing results, the patients were usually found to have right temporal seizure origin. Intracarotid amobarbital (Amytal) testing revealed absent or marginal memory functions on the side of seizure onset in 63% of patients, while 37% had intact memory bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in some patients and proved to be highly sensitive in detecting subtle medial temporal abnormalities. These abnormalities were observed in 23 out of 28 MRI images and corresponded to mesial temporal sclerosis upon pathological examination, except in two patients.

In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the preoperative evaluation of patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, highlighting the significance of scalp EEG, neuropsychological testing, intracarotid amobarbital testing, and MRI in determining the side of seizure origin and identifying potential abnormalities.

title: OPA1-dependent cristae modulation is essential for cellular adaptation to metabolic demand.
text: The structure of cristae, which are organized invaginations of the inner membrane of mitochondria, is responsive to the cell's energy demands. However, the regulation of these dynamic changes and their consequences are not well understood. OPA1, a mitochondrial GTPase, is responsible for both fusing the inner membrane and maintaining the structure of cristae. In our study, we found that OPA1 can dynamically respond to changes in energy conditions to regulate the structure of cristae. Interestingly, this regulation is independent of OPA1's role in mitochondrial fusion. We discovered that even a mutant form of OPA1, which can still form oligomers but lacks fusion activity, was able to maintain the structure of cristae. Importantly, OPA1 was found to be essential for resistance to cell death caused by starvation, mitochondrial respiration, growth in galactose media, and the assembly of ATP synthase. These functions were independent of OPA1's fusion activity. We also identified mitochondrial solute carriers (SLC25A) as interactors of OPA1 and demonstrated that blocking their function, either pharmacologically or genetically, inhibited OPA1's oligomerization and function. Therefore, we propose a new mechanism by which OPA1 senses the availability of energy substrates, which in turn modulates its role in regulating the architecture of mitochondria in a protein-dependent manner involving SLC25A.

title: Phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke.
text:
The use of phenylpropanolamine in appetite suppressants and cough or cold remedies has been linked to hemorrhagic stroke in case reports. To further investigate this association, a case-control study was conducted. Participants included men and women aged 18 to 49 who had experienced a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage within 30 days prior to enrollment and did not have a previously diagnosed brain lesion. Two matched control subjects were identified for each patient using random-digit dialing. 

The study included 702 patients and 1376 control subjects. Among women, the adjusted odds ratio for the association between the use of appetite suppressants containing phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke was 16.58 (95% CI, 1.51 to 182.21; P=0.02), and 3.13 (95% CI, 0.86 to 11.46; P=0.08) for the association with the first use of a product containing phenylpropanolamine. All first uses of phenylpropanolamine were in cough or cold remedies. When considering both men and women, the adjusted odds ratio for the association between the use of a product containing phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke was 1.49 (95% CI, 0.84 to 2.64; P=0.17), 1.23 (95% CI, 0.68 to 2.24; P=0.49) for the association with the use of cough or cold remedies containing phenylpropanolamine, and 15.92 (95% CI, 1.38 to 184.13; P=0.03) for the association with the use of appetite suppressants containing phenylpropanolamine. No increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke was found in men who used cough or cold remedies containing phenylpropanolamine, and no men reported using appetite suppressants. 

In conclusion, the findings suggest that phenylpropanolamine in appetite suppressants, and possibly in cough and cold remedies, is an independent risk factor for hemorrhagic stroke in women.

title: The safety of intravenous fluorescein for confocal laser endomicroscopy in the gastrointestinal tract.
text:
Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) is a rapidly growing tool for gastrointestinal endoscopic imaging. To enhance imaging with CLE, fluorescent contrast agents are used, with intravenous fluorescein being the most commonly used agent. While fluorescein is FDA-cleared for diagnostic angiography of the retina and has a well-documented safety profile for these indications, its use with CLE has not been cleared. The aim of this study was to determine the rate of serious and total adverse events associated with intravenous fluorescein when used for gastrointestinal CLE. 

A cross-sectional survey was conducted at 16 International Academic Medical Centres that had active research protocols involving intravenous fluorescein for CLE. These centres actively monitored adverse events related to the use of intravenous fluorescein for CLE. 

A total of 2272 gastrointestinal CLE procedures were performed at the 16 centres. The most common dose of contrast agent used was 2.5-5 mL of 10% sodium fluorescein. No serious adverse events were reported. Mild adverse events occurred in 1.4% of individuals, including nausea/vomiting, transient hypotension without shock, injection site erythema, diffuse rash, and mild epigastric pain. It is important to note that only immediate post-procedure events were actively monitored. 

In conclusion, the use of intravenous fluorescein for gastrointestinal CLE appears to be safe, with few acute complications.

title: Metabolic DNA as the origin of spontaneously released DNA?
text:
Living cells, excluding dead or dying ones, have the ability to release a DNA fraction. This phenomenon has been observed in various organisms such as humans, mammals, birds, amphibians, plants, and prokaryotes. The spontaneously released DNA fraction possesses several characteristics: (a) it is found in both actively dividing and nondividing, specialized cell populations; (b) it is unstable; (c) it is associated with DNA-dependent RNA or DNA polymerase; (d) it is linked to an RNA fraction; (e) it has a smaller molecular weight compared to the typical genetic DNA fraction; and (f) it contains an increased proportion of Alu repeat sequences compared to a unique gene found in plasma or serum.

Conversely, early studies involving autoradiography, biochemistry, quantitative cytochemistry, and cytophysics have allowed the identification of a DNA fraction that shares certain characteristics: (1) it is present in both actively dividing and nondividing, specialized cell populations; (2) it is unstable; and (3) it has a smaller molecular weight than the typical genetic DNA fraction. This particular DNA fraction is referred to as metabolic DNA (m-DNA) and it was proposed to potentially generate additional gene copies for the rapid production of m-RNA, which would subsequently be destroyed. Therefore, it is suggested that the metabolic DNA fraction may serve as the precursor to the spontaneously released DNA fraction.

title: The flavivirus precursor membrane-envelope protein complex: structure and maturation.
text: Before being transmitted to another host, many viruses undergo a maturation step in the final stages of assembly. In the case of flaviviruses, this maturation process is guided by the proteolytic cleavage of the precursor membrane protein (prM), which transforms the virus from an inert state to infectious particles. Our research has successfully determined the crystal structure of a recombinant protein, with a resolution of 2.2 angstroms, where the dengue virus prM is connected to the envelope glycoprotein E. This structure represents the prM-E heterodimer and fits accurately within the cryo-electron microscopy density of immature virus at a neutral pH. The beta-barrel structure of the pr peptide covers the fusion loop in E, effectively preventing fusion with host cell membranes. By studying this structure, we can identify the different stages of its pH-induced conformational changes during maturation, ultimately leading to the release of pr when the virus buds from the host.

title: Peptide and non-peptide G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in skeletal muscle.
text: GPCRs, also known as G-protein coupled receptors, are a diverse group of cell surface receptors that play a crucial role in various cellular functions. While numerous GPCRs and associated proteins have been identified in skeletal muscle, their systematic analysis has been relatively limited compared to other muscle tissues such as cardiac and vascular smooth muscle cells. In this study, we have gathered a comprehensive list of GPCRs expressed in skeletal muscle and examined their known functions in both skeletal muscle tissue and cultured skeletal muscle cells.

title: Characterization of complete genome and small RNA profile of pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus, a novel badnavirus in China.
text: High throughput sequencing of small RNAs revealed the discovery of a new badnavirus in pagoda trees. The virus caused yellow mosaic symptoms on the leaves and had a complete genome consisting of 7424 nucleotides. It shared 40.4-45.1% identity with other badnaviruses. The genome contained five open reading frames (ORFs), including three conserved badnaviral ORFs. Based on these findings, the virus was classified as a new member of the Badnavirus genus in the Caulimoviridae family and given the tentative name pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus (PYMAV). Phylogenetic analysis showed that PYMAV, along with gooseberry vein banding virus (GVBV) and grapevine vein-clearing virus (GVCV), formed a distinct group separate from other well-known badnaviral groups. The viral derived small RNA (vsRNA) profile of PYMAV was compared to other viruses in the same family. It was found that PYMAV had a higher abundance of 21-nt vsRNAs, while other viruses had a predominance of 22- or 24-nt vsRNAs. The sense and antisense PYMAV vsRNAs were almost equally distributed, unlike other viruses in the family that showed a preference for the sense strand of their genome. Additionally, PYMAV vsRNAs were evenly distributed along the genome without any specific vsRNA generating hotspots.

title: Experimental approaches for the treatment of malignant gliomas.
text: This review focuses on the subject of malignant gliomas, which are the most common primary brain tumors and include glioblastomas and anaplastic astrocytomas. In the past three decades, the standard treatment for these tumors has evolved to include maximal safe surgical resection, radiation therapy, and temozolomide chemotherapy. Although the median survival rate for patients with glioblastomas has increased from 6 months to 14.6 months, the majority of patients still succumb to these tumors. However, there has been significant recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms behind tumor development and growth. This review explores the translation of genetic, epigenetic, and biochemical discoveries into potential therapies that have been tested in clinical trials.

title: Reversal of hyperglycemia in mice by using human expandable insulin-producing cells differentiated from fetal liver progenitor cells.
text: The most promising method for treating type 1 diabetes is replacing beta cells. However, the widespread use of this approach is hindered by a shortage of cells available for transplantation. To address this issue, researchers have explored the activation of insulin production, storage, and regulated release in stem/progenitor cells as a potential solution. In this study, we investigated whether fetal human progenitor liver cells (FH) could be induced to differentiate into insulin-producing cells by introducing the pancreatic duodenal homeobox 1 (Pdx1) gene, a key regulator of pancreatic development and insulin expression in beta cells. FH cells have a high replication capacity, which was further enhanced by introducing the gene for the catalytic subunit of human telomerase. The immortalized FH cells expressing Pdx1 activated multiple beta-cell genes, produced and stored significant amounts of insulin, and released insulin in a regulated manner in response to glucose. When these cells were transplanted into immunodeficient mice with high blood sugar levels, they successfully restored and maintained normal blood sugar levels for extended periods of time. Measurement of human C-peptide in the mouse serum confirmed that the transplanted human cells normalized blood sugar levels. This approach presents a potential new source of cells for transplantation in patients with type 1 diabetes.

title: A review of the methods for human iPSC derivation.
text: The ability to convert somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) presents an opportunity to create patient-specific cell lines that can be used to study human diseases. These iPSC lines can also be valuable tools for drug discovery and the development of cellular transplantation therapies. While there are various methods available for generating iPSC lines, the most suitable ones for studying human diseases and developing therapies should have high efficiency in producing iPSCs from limited samples, be capable of reprogramming both skin fibroblasts and blood cells, and be free from any genetic modifications. Several reprogramming techniques meet these criteria and can be used to derive iPSCs for projects with both scientific and therapeutic objectives. By combining these reprogramming methods with small molecule modulators that affect signaling pathways, it is possible to successfully generate iPSCs even from challenging patient-derived somatic cells.

title: EB virus-encoded RNAs are recognized by RIG-I and activate signaling to induce type I IFN.
text: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) produces small nonpolyadenylated RNAs called EBERs. These untranslated RNAs are most abundant in cells infected with latent EBV and are known to have secondary structures with multiple short stem-loops. The cytosolic protein Retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) detects viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) within cells and triggers signaling pathways that lead to the activation of protective cellular genes, including type I interferons (IFNs). Our study aimed to investigate whether EBERs are recognized by RIG-I as dsRNA. We found that transfection of RIG-I plasmid induced the production of IFNs and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) in EBV-positive Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) cells, but not in their EBV-negative counterparts or EBER-knockout EBV-infected BL cells. Additionally, transfection of EBER plasmid or in vitro-synthesized EBERs induced the expression of type I IFNs and ISGs in RIG-I-expressing, EBV-negative BL cells, but not in RIG-I-deficient cells. EBERs activated RIG-I's substrates, NF-kappaB and IFN regulatory factor 3, which were essential for the activation of type I IFNs. Furthermore, we observed that EBERs co-precipitated with RIG-I. These findings demonstrate that RIG-I recognizes EBERs and triggers signaling pathways to induce type I IFN production in EBV-infected cells.

title: Pregnancy in dialysis patients: a review of outcomes, complications, and management.
text: Pregnancy can occur in women who are undergoing chronic dialysis, although it is not very common. In 1980, the occurrence of pregnancy in women on dialysis was only 0.9%. However, studies conducted between 1992 and 2003 have shown that pregnancy occurred in 1-7% of women on chronic dialysis. Unfortunately, only half of the infants born to these women survive. It has been found that "intensive dialysis" for 16-24 hours per week can improve infant survival rates. This article provides a comprehensive review of the incidence, duration, complications for both the mother and fetus, and outcomes of pregnancy in women on chronic dialysis. It also summarizes the management of anemia, hypertension, electrolyte imbalances, bone mineral issues, and acid-base parameters in pregnant dialysis patients. Additionally, recommendations are made regarding the dialysis prescription for pregnant women undergoing either hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD). Due to the complex and delicate nature of the pregnant woman on dialysis, it is crucial for the patient, nephrologist, dialysis staff, obstetrician, and neonatologist to work closely together in order to maximize the chances of a successful pregnancy.

title: Potent immunosuppressive activities of cytomegalovirus-encoded interleukin-10.
text: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) possesses advanced strategies to evade detection by the host immune system. Recently, a new gene was discovered in the genomes of human and primate CMV. This gene consists of segments from noncontiguous open reading frames and shows limited similarity to the natural cellular interleukin-10 (IL-10). In this study, we explore the biological effects of the CMV IL-10-like gene product and reveal its potent immunosuppressive properties. Both purified recombinant CMV IL-10 derived from bacteria and CMV IL-10 expressed in human cell supernatants were found to hinder the proliferation of mitogen-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), exhibiting similar effectiveness to recombinant human IL-10. Furthermore, CMV IL-10 expressed by human cells inhibited the synthesis of cytokines. Treatment of stimulated PBMCs and monocytes with CMV IL-10 resulted in a significant reduction in the production of proinflammatory cytokines.
