Additionally, CMV IL-10 was observed to decrease the expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and class II molecules on the cell surface, while simultaneously increasing the expression of the nonclassical MHC allele HLA-G. These findings provide the first evidence that CMV possesses a biologically active IL-10 counterpart, which may aid in immune evasion during viral infections.

title: Evidence for the presence of urease apoprotein complexes containing UreD, UreF, and UreG in cells that are competent for in vivo enzyme activation.
text: The activation of Klebsiella aerogenes urease, an enzyme that contains nickel, requires the presence of functional accessory proteins UreD, UreF, and UreG, and is further aided by UreE. These accessory proteins are believed to be involved in the assembly of the enzyme's active center. In cells with high levels of ureD expression, three UreD-urease apoprotein complexes are present, and these complexes are crucial for activating the enzyme in vivo. In this study, we investigated the impact of deleting the accessory genes on the formation of the urease complex. We found that the products of the ureE, ureF, and ureG genes are not necessary for the formation of UreD-urease complexes. However, the complexes from the ureF deletion mutant showed a delay in elution during size exclusion chromatography. Despite this delay, the size of these complexes remained consistent with UreD-urease complexes according to native gel electrophoretic analysis, suggesting that UreF alters the conformation of the complexes. Additionally, we discovered a new series of urease apoprotein complexes that are only present in cells containing ureD, ureF, ureG, and the urease subunit genes. These complexes were found to contain urease, UreD, UreF, and UreG. We propose that these UreD-UreF-UreG-urease apoprotein complexes represent the active form of urease apoprotein in the cell.

title: Human somatic cell nuclear transfer using adult cells.
text: The potential use of patient-specific human pluripotent stem cells derived through somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) in various therapeutic contexts has been explored. However, achieving successful SCNT with human cells has proven to be challenging, with only fetal or infant somatic cells being reported thus far. In this study, we present the application of a recently developed method for generating human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) through SCNT, using dermal fibroblasts obtained from males aged 35 and 75. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of using SCNT with adult human cells and support further investigation into its potential as a strategy for regenerative medicine.

title: "Natural" killer cells in the mouse. I. Cytotoxic cells with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells. Specificity and distribution according to genotype.
text: Naturally occurring killer lymphocytes with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells can be found in the spleens of young and adult mice. These lymphocytes exhibited lytic activity against both syngeneic and allogeneic Moloney leukemia cells, but their effectiveness was primarily observed when tested against leukemia cells grown in vitro. Two non-Moloney leukemias and the mastocytoma line P815 were resistant to the lytic activity. Competition experiments using unlabeled Moloney or other tumor cells as inhibitors in the cytotoxic assays confirmed that the specificity of lysis remained consistent across different strains of mice. The capacity to compete and the sensitivity to lysis by the killer cells were strongly correlated. Analysis of the kinetics of the cytotoxic assay showed that lysis occurred rapidly within one to four hours, suggesting that there was no conventional in vitro induction of immune response. There was no evidence to suggest that soluble factors played a role in the cytolytic assay.

title: Dose-response study on thyrotoxic patients undergoing positron emission tomography and radioiodine therapy
text:
Due to the known difficulties in accurately assessing thyroid mass and radiation dose, our previous policy was to administer 75 MBq of iodine-131 every six months to patients with Graves' disease until they achieved a euthyroid state. However, with the introduction of positron emission tomography (PET) at our hospital, we are now able to calculate the radiation dose to the thyroid with approximately 20% accuracy. This is achieved by determining the thyroid mass through an iodine-124 PET scan.

To further investigate the effects of radiation dose, we conducted a study involving 65 patients who received either a single or cumulative radiation dose of less than 80 Gy. The results revealed that patients who received a low radiation dose (less than 20 Gy) during their initial treatment had a high likelihood of remaining toxic after 12 months. Conversely, patients who received higher radiation doses (over 40 Gy) during their initial treatment had a high probability of achieving control. The probability of achieving a euthyroid state increased more rapidly with higher radiation doses compared to the probability of becoming hypothyroid.

Based on the findings of this dose-response study, we have implemented a new treatment protocol. Prior to 131I therapy, a 124I PET tracer study will be conducted to determine the appropriate thyroid dose of 50 Gy for patients with Graves' disease. Further 131I therapy will only be considered if patients are still experiencing toxicity after 12 months.

title: Increased serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy is associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
text:
The objective of this study was to examine the levels of soluble corin in the circulation before hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP). The study focused on serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy in patients with HDP and their age- and gestational weeks-matched controls. A total of sixty-eight pairs of cases of HDP and controls were included in the study. Blood samples were collected between 16 and 20 gestational weeks, and serum soluble corin was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay methods. The relationship between serum soluble corin and HDP was analyzed using conditional logistic regression models. 

The results showed that serum soluble corin levels in mid pregnancy were higher in cases with HDP compared to controls. Participants were divided into quartiles based on the distribution of serum soluble corin levels in controls. Those in the highest quartile had a significantly increased risk for HDP compared to the lowest quartile, even after adjusting for other factors. However, there was no significant increase in risk for participants in the second and third quartiles. When the first three quartiles were combined as a reference group, individuals in the highest quartile still had a significantly increased risk for HDP. 

In conclusion, increased serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy was associated with an increased risk for HDP. These findings suggest that elevated levels of serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy could serve as an indicator for HDP.

title: The in vitro effect of dandelions antioxidants on microsomal lipid peroxidation.
text: Dandelions have been utilized in traditional medicine for their ability to stimulate bile production, increase urine output, reduce inflammation, stimulate appetite, and promote bowel movements. It is believed that their therapeutic effects may be attributed to their antioxidant properties. To investigate the mechanism of action, researchers studied the effects of dandelion extracts on a specific part of rat liver cells. The extracts were found to decrease the breakdown of lipids caused by enzymes and also reduced the levels of cytochrome c, both with and without the presence of NADPH, in a manner that depended on the concentration of the extracts.

title: Local Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels stimulates production of an intracellular messenger and an intercellular pro-inflammatory signal.
text: The production of the pro-inflammatory molecule leukotriene C4 (LTC4) from mast cells is driven by Ca2+ entry through store-operated Ca2+ channels. This process involves the activation of Ca2+-dependent protein kinase C, mitogen-activated protein kinases ERK1/2, phospholipase A2, and 5-lipoxygenase. In this study, we investigate whether local Ca2+ influx through store-operated Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels in the plasma membrane stimulates this signaling pathway. By manipulating the amplitude and spatial extent of Ca2+ entry, either by altering chemical and electrical gradients for Ca2+ influx or changing the Ca2+ buffering of the cytoplasm, we observed significant impacts on protein kinase C and ERK activation, generation of arachidonic acid, and LTC4 secretion. Interestingly, these changes occurred without significant alterations in the overall cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels. When comparing the activation of CRAC channels in different external Ca2+ concentrations, we found that despite achieving similar bulk cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentrations, protein kinase C activation and LTC4 secretion were larger in conditions with higher Ca2+ and the inhibitor La3+. This suggests that a subplasmalemmal Ca2+ rise plays a central role in these processes. Furthermore, we discovered that the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase Syk is involved in coupling CRAC channel opening to protein kinase C and ERK activation. Additionally, we found that recombinant TRPC3 channels also activate protein kinase C, indicating that subplasmalemmal Ca2+ rather than a microdomain exclusive to CRAC channels is the trigger. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a subplasmalemmal Ca2+ increase in mast cells is highly versatile, as it can trigger both cytoplasmic responses through the generation of intracellular messengers and long-distance changes through increased secretion of paracrine signals.

title: Cytokine production patterns and lymphoproliferative responses in volunteers orally immunized with attenuated vaccine strains of Salmonella typhi.
text:
This study investigated the immune responses triggered by new recombinant strains of attenuated Salmonella typhi used as live oral vaccines. Specifically, the study examined the cytokine production and proliferation patterns in individuals who were orally immunized with attenuated S. typhi vaccines CVD 906, CVD 908, and CVD 908 expressing the circumsporozoite protein of Plasmodium falciparum. 

Following immunization, the researchers found sensitized lymphocytes in the subjects' blood, which showed significantly increased proliferative responses and interferon-gamma production to purified S. typhi flagella compared to preimmunization levels. Additionally, the study revealed significant negative correlations between interleukin-4 production and both interferon-gamma production and proliferation to S. typhi flagella. 

These findings demonstrate that oral immunization with attenuated S. typhi strains, either alone or carrying a foreign gene, induces robust systemic cell-mediated immunity to purified S. typhi antigens. This immune response includes the production of cytokines consistent with T1-type responses.

title: Molecular interplay of the noncoding RNA ANRIL and methylated histone H3 lysine 27 by polycomb CBX7 in transcriptional silencing of INK4a.
text: The regulation of the INK4b/ARF/INK4a tumor suppressor locus in normal and cancerous cell growth is influenced by the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me), which is controlled by the Polycomb group proteins. The role of the antisense noncoding RNA ANRIL in the expression of protein-coding genes within the INK4b/ARF/INK4a locus has been unclear. However, our findings demonstrate that chromobox 7 (CBX7), a component of the polycomb repressive complex 1, binds to ANRIL. Both CBX7 and ANRIL are present at higher levels in prostate cancer tissues. In addition to recognizing H3K27me, CBX7's function is influenced by its interaction with RNA, and disruption of either interaction affects CBX7's ability to repress the INK4b/ARF/INK4a locus and control senescence. Through a structure-guided analysis, we have uncovered the molecular interplay between noncoding RNA and H3K27me, facilitated by the conserved chromodomain. Our study provides insight into how noncoding RNA directly participates in epigenetic transcriptional repression.

title: Tumor necrosis factor alpha mediates apoptosis of brown adipocytes and defective brown adipocyte function in obesity.
text: Obesity often leads to severe defects in both the quantity and quality of brown adipocytes. In order to investigate the role of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) in the functional decline of brown fat in obesity, we conducted a study using genetically obese (ob/ob) mice with targeted mutations in the genes responsible for TNF receptor expression. By eliminating both TNF receptors or just the p55 receptor, we observed a significant decrease in brown adipocyte apoptosis and an increase in the expression of beta(3)-adrenoreceptor and uncoupling protein-1 in obese mice. Additionally, obese mice lacking TNF-alpha function exhibited a higher number of active brown adipocytes with multiple lipid droplets, as well as improved thermoregulation. These findings highlight the crucial role of TNF-alpha in various aspects of brown adipose tissue biology and its involvement in the abnormalities observed in obesity.

title: Engineered FGF19 eliminates bile acid toxicity and lipotoxicity leading to resolution of steatohepatitis and fibrosis in mice
text:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a common chronic liver disease that currently lacks approved treatments. Despite extensive research, the specific cellular mechanisms that contribute to the development and progression of NAFLD are not well understood. While obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome are all known risk factors for NAFLD, recent studies suggest that dysregulated bile acid metabolism may also play a role in the disease. In particular, NAFLD patients often have low levels of fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19), a hormone that regulates bile acid synthesis, lipogenesis, and energy balance in the gut-liver axis. 

To investigate this further, researchers used a mouse model that mimics the progression of NAFLD in humans, from simple fat accumulation in the liver to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and advanced NASH with liver cancer. They found that both FGF19 and a modified version called M70 were able to improve liver health by reducing bile acid toxicity and lipotoxicity. Analysis of liver samples showed that treatment with FGF19 or M70 led to a decrease in harmful lipid species and an increase in unoxidized cardiolipins, an important component of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Additionally, FGF19 and M70 treatment improved liver enzyme levels, resolved NASH-related tissue damage, and enhanced insulin sensitivity, energy balance, and lipid metabolism. 

While prolonged exposure to FGF19 led to liver cancer in the mice, those treated with M70 did not develop tumors. These findings suggest that M70, an engineered FGF19 hormone, has the potential to be a promising therapeutic option for patients with NASH. By targeting multiple pathways, M70 can provide anti-steatotic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic effects. Further research is needed to explore the clinical potential of M70 in treating NASH. (Hepatology Communications 2017;1:1024-1042).

title: Leptin deficiency contributes to the pathogenesis of alcoholic fatty liver disease in mice.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of alcohol on adipokines and the connection between adipokine dysregulation and alcoholic fatty liver disease. Mice were given alcohol for different durations to observe changes in adipokines over time. The results showed that alcohol reduced white adipose tissue (WAT) mass and body weight, leading to the accumulation of lipids in the liver. The concentration of plasma adiponectin initially increased after 2 weeks of alcohol exposure but returned to normal levels after 4 and 8 weeks. Alcohol also suppressed the expression of the leptin gene in WAT and decreased the plasma leptin concentration throughout the study. There was a strong positive correlation between plasma leptin concentration and WAT mass or body weight. To investigate whether leptin deficiency played a role in alcohol-induced hepatic lipid imbalance, mice were given alcohol for 8 weeks with or without leptin administration during the last 2 weeks. Leptin administration normalized the plasma leptin concentration and reversed alcoholic fatty liver. Leptin also restored the levels of phosphorylation of signal transducer Stat3 and adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase, which were reduced by alcohol. These findings suggest that leptin deficiency, along with a reduction in WAT mass, contributes to the development of alcoholic fatty liver disease.

title: Three-dimensional chemical imaging of skin using stimulated Raman scattering microscopy
text: This abstract discusses the use of Stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS) microscopy to generate three-dimensional images of native skin, focusing on its microanatomical features and the penetration of topically applied materials. The study collected image depth stacks at different wavelengths corresponding to proteins, lipids, and water in the skin. The findings reveal that corneocytes in the stratum corneum are clustered together, forming groups with diameters ranging from 100 to 250 μm. These clusters are separated by microanatomical skin-folds called canyons, which are 10- to 25-μm wide. Interestingly, these canyons can extend to depths comparable to the dermal-epidermal junction, even below the flat surface regions of both porcine and human skin. SRS imaging also provides insights into the distribution of chemical species within the cell clusters and canyons. Water is primarily found within the cell clusters, with its concentration increasing rapidly at the transition from the stratum corneum to the viable epidermis. On the other hand, canyons do not contain detectable levels of water but are rich in lipid material. Additionally, the study shows that oleic acid-d34, when applied to the skin surface, lines the canyons up to a depth of 50 μm below the skin's surface. These findings have potential implications for evaluating the penetration profiles of bioactive materials using traditional methods like tape-stripping.

title: Familial amyloidosis: a study of 52 North American-born patients examined during a 30-year period.
text: The Mayo Clinic examined 52 patients born in North America with biopsy-proven familial amyloidosis between 1961 and 1990. At the time of diagnosis, 83% of these patients had peripheral neuropathy, 33% had autonomic neuropathy, and 27% had cardiomyopathy. Renal disease was observed in less than 10% of patients, and liver involvement was rare. The median age at diagnosis was 64 years. Diagnostic biopsies showed similar sensitivity to primary amyloidosis, with amyloid deposits found in 77% and 78% of subcutaneous fat aspirates or rectal biopsy specimens, respectively, and in 41% of bone marrow specimens. The median survival duration for patients with inherited amyloidosis was 5.8 years, which was better than that for patients with primary amyloidosis. Even when stratified by organ involvement, patients with familial amyloidosis had superior survival rates. Cardiomyopathy and the combination of age and autonomic neuropathy were strong predictors of survival. Out of the 52 patients, 22 died, with 55% of them dying from cardiac failure or cardiac arrhythmia. Inanition, along with progressive peripheral or autonomic neuropathy, was the cause of death for 41% of patients. Immunohistochemical studies identified transthyretin in 31 out of 34 tested tissue specimens, with a transthyretin mutation found in 24 of those 31 patients. Additionally, five more patients had a transthyretin mutation, but tissue was unavailable for immunostaining.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the environment within the phagosome.
text: Macrophages serve as the primary defense against microbial invasion once they cross the epithelium barrier. The acidic and hydrolytically competent environment of the phagolysosome is usually sufficient to kill most microbes. However, our understanding of the lumenal environment within the phagosome is still being revealed through real-time functional assays. These assays measure pH change, fusion between phagosomes and lysosomes, proteolysis, lipolysis, and beta-galactosidase activity. This information is crucial for comprehending pathogens that successfully exploit the endosomal/lysosomal continuum. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects macrophages by interrupting the normal maturation process of the phagosome, causing it to remain at pH 6.4 and exhibit characteristics similar to an early endosome. Current research is focused on studying the bacterium's transcriptional response to the changing environment in the macrophage phagosome. By manipulating environmental cues, such as preventing the pH drop to 6.4 using concanamycin A, the majority of the bacterium's transcriptional response can be eliminated. This demonstrates that pH is the primary signal that the bacterium detects and reacts to. These approaches represent our ongoing efforts to unravel the communication between the pathogen and its host cell.

title: High density DNA methylation array with single CpG site resolution.
text:
We have created a cutting-edge DNA methylation BeadChip that revolutionizes the process of profiling the human genome. This advanced BeadChip has a high density and can analyze over 480K CpG sites, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of twelve samples. Our innovative design includes probes for 99% of RefSeq genes, with multiple probes per gene, as well as coverage for 96% of CpG islands from the UCSC database, CpG island shores, and additional content selected from whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data and input from DNA methylation experts.

To analyze CpG methylation, we utilize the well-established Infinium® Assay, which uses bisulfite-converted genomic DNA. We applied this technology to study DNA methylation in both normal and tumor DNA samples and compared the results with whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) data obtained from the same samples. Remarkably, the array and sequencing methods produced highly similar DNA methylation profiles, with an average R2 value of 0.95. This breakthrough allows researchers to rapidly uncover genome-wide methylation patterns, greatly advancing methylation research.

title: Acentrosomal Microtubule Assembly in Mitosis: The Where, When, and How.
text: During mitosis, the cell constructs a bipolar spindle, which is a structure made up of microtubules that separates the duplicated chromosomes into two daughter cells. Most animal cells enter mitosis with duplicated centrosomes, which act as a source of dynamic microtubules. However, it has been discovered that spindle assembly also relies on the formation of microtubules without centrosomes, which occurs around the chromosomes after the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. Additionally, pre-existing microtubules play a role in this process. The specific locations where microtubules are formed, the timing of microtubule amplification, and how these two pathways work together are still subjects of debate. In this study, we analyze the available data and propose a comprehensive model that explains the assembly of microtubules without centrosomes in dividing cells.

title: Molecular mechanisms of mammalian DNA repair and the DNA damage checkpoints.
text: DNA damage is a common occurrence in cells and can result in mutations, cancer, and cell or organism death. When DNA is damaged, cells have various responses to either repair or eliminate the damage, including activating programmed cell death to remove cells with harmful mutations. These responses include repairing the damaged DNA, halting the cell cycle to allow for repair and prevent the transmission of damaged chromosomes, causing changes in gene expression that benefit the cell, and eliminating heavily damaged or abnormal cells through apoptosis. DNA repair mechanisms involve different processes such as direct repair, base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, double-strand break repair, and cross-link repair. The DNA damage checkpoints use proteins like ATM, ATR, the Rad17-RFC complex, and the 9-1-1 complex to detect DNA damage and initiate signaling pathways involving Chk1 and Chk2 kinases and Cdc25 phosphatases. These signaling pathways activate p53 and inhibit cyclin-dependent kinases, preventing cell cycle progression at different checkpoints. This review examines the molecular mechanisms of DNA repair and the DNA damage checkpoints in mammalian cells.

title: Characterization of serotonin 5-HT2C receptor signaling to extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1 and 2.
text: The study focused on understanding how serotonin 5-HT2C receptors (5-HT(2C)Rs) interact with extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) 1/2. These receptors are mainly found in the central nervous system and are associated with conditions like obesity, depression, and schizophrenia. The researchers used a Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell line that expressed the receptor at levels similar to those in the brain. They observed that the non-RNA-edited form of the 5-HT(2C)R led to constitutive phosphorylation of ERK1/2, which could be influenced by full, partial, and inverse agonists. Interestingly, the agonists DOI and quipazine showed different effects on phosphoinositide accumulation, intracellular Ca2+ levels, and ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Further analysis revealed that ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to 5-HT stimulation required phospholipase D, protein kinase C, and activation of the Raf/MEK/ERK pathway, but did not involve receptor- or non-receptor tyrosine kinases, phospholipase C, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, or endocytosis. These findings highlight the potential of selectively targeting specific pathways to modulate neuronal signaling in both normal and abnormal conditions.

title: Short-term medical service trips: a systematic review of the evidence.
text: Short-term medical service trips (MSTs) have the objective of addressing the healthcare needs of low- and middle-income countries. However, the lack of thoroughly reviewed empirical evidence on the activities and outcomes of these trips is a cause for concern. In order to develop evidence-based recommendations for healthcare delivery, it is crucial to conduct systematic research reviews. In my study, I specifically focused on MST publications that presented empirical results. In May 2013, I conducted searches and identified 67 studies that had been published since 1993. Surprisingly, these studies accounted for only 6% of all the articles published on this topic in the past two decades. Furthermore, nearly 80% of the studies reported on surgical trips. Despite the growth of the MST field, the medical literature in this area is lacking, with the majority of scholarly publications lacking significant data collection. By incorporating data collection into service trips, organizations can validate their practices and gather information on areas that require improvement.

title: Comparison of Beck Depression Inventories -IA and -II in psychiatric outpatients.
text: A total of 140 psychiatric outpatients with various psychiatric disorders completed the revised versions of the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-IA; Beck & Steer, 1993b) and the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; Beck, Steer, & Brown, 1996) as self-administered assessments. The coefficient alphas for the BDI-IA and BDI-II were .89 and .91, respectively. Comparing the two inventories, the mean rating for Sadness was higher on the BDI-IA, while the mean ratings for Past Failure, Self-Dislike, Change in Sleeping Pattern, and Change in Appetite were higher on the BDI-II. The mean total score for the BDI-II was approximately 2 points higher than that of the BDI-IA, and the outpatients endorsed approximately one more symptom on the BDI-II compared to the BDI-IA. The correlations between the BDI-IA and BDI-II total scores with sex, ethnicity, age, the diagnosis of a mood disorder, and the Beck Anxiety Inventory (Beck & Steer, 1993a) were similar, differing by no more than 1 point for each variable.

title: Tumor engraftment in nude mice and enrichment in stroma- related gene pathways predict poor survival and resistance to gemcitabine in patients with pancreatic cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to prospectively evaluate the engraftment rate, factors influencing engraftment, and predictability of clinical outcome of low-passage xenografts from patients with resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA). Additionally, the study aimed to establish a bank of PDA xenografts. Patients with resectable PDA scheduled for resection at the Johns Hopkins Hospital were included in the study. Representative pieces of tumor were implanted in nude mice, and the status of the SMAD4 gene and content of tumor-generating cells were determined. Gene expression analysis was conducted using a U133 Plus 2.0 array. Patients were followed for progression and survival. 

The results showed that out of 94 patients with PDA who underwent resection, 69 tumors were successfully implanted in nude mice, and 42 (61%) of them engrafted. Engrafted carcinomas were more frequently associated with SMAD4 mutation and exhibited a metastatic gene expression signature, indicating a worse prognosis. Tumors from patients resistant to gemcitabine, a commonly used chemotherapy drug, showed enrichment in stroma-related gene pathways. On the other hand, tumors sensitive to gemcitabine were enriched in cell cycle and pyrimidine gene pathways. Patients with xenografts sensitive to gemcitabine had a longer time to progression when treated with the drug for metastatic disease compared to those with xenografts resistant to gemcitabine. 

In conclusion, this study successfully generated xenografts in 61% of attempted patients, resulting in a pool of 42 PDA xenografts with valuable biological information and annotated clinical data. Patients with PDA and SMAD4 inactivation had a higher engraftment rate. Engraftment was found to be a poor prognosis factor, and engrafted tumors exhibited a metastatic gene expression signature. Tumors from gemcitabine-resistant patients showed enrichment in stromal pathways.

title: The MCM8-MCM9 complex promotes RAD51 recruitment at DNA damage sites to facilitate homologous recombination.
text: The proteins MCM8 and MCM9, which are similar to the minichromosome maintenance protein, have previously been linked to DNA replication elongation and the formation of prereplication complexes. Our research has shown that MCM8 and MCM9 physically interact with each other, and that MCM8 is necessary for the stability of MCM9 protein in mammalian cells. When MCM8 or MCM9 is depleted in human cancer cells, or when there is a loss of function mutation in MCM9 in mouse embryo fibroblasts, the cells become more sensitive to the DNA interstrand cross-linking agent cisplatin. This suggests that MCM8 and MCM9 play a role in repairing interstrand cross-links through homologous recombination. Knocking down MCM8 or MCM9 significantly reduces the efficiency of homologous recombination repair. Our analysis using human DR-GFP cells and Xenopus egg extract shows that MCM8 and MCM9 proteins are quickly recruited to sites of DNA damage and help in the recruitment of RAD51. Therefore, these two specific MCM homologs found in metazoans are new components of homologous recombination and could be potential targets for cancer treatment when used in combination with DNA cross-linking agents.

title: The 5TMM series: a useful in vivo mouse model of human multiple myeloma.
text: The present invention introduces a unique sink and dishwashing apparatus that combines a sink and a cabinet with a shared side wall. This cabinet creates a closed space and includes a wire basket for holding and washing multiple dishes. The shared side wall, which is part of the cabinet, serves as one side of the sink and can be opened to allow the wire basket to slide from the cabinet into the sink for loading and unloading dishes. Inside the cabinet, the invention features a motor-powered pump that sprays water through a rotatably mounted spray arm to wash the dishes, similar to traditional dishwashing machines. Additionally, the invention includes a motor-powered garbage disposal. In an alternative version, two cabinets, as described earlier, can be positioned on opposite sides of the sink.

title: Ionic protein-lipid interaction at the plasma membrane: what can the charge do?
text: Phospholipids play a crucial role in cell membranes, but they also have other functions aside from forming lipid bilayers. Specifically, acidic phospholipids create microdomains in the plasma membrane and can interact with proteins through polybasic sequences, which can affect the protein's function. The number of proteins influenced by ionic protein-lipid interaction is rapidly increasing and now includes membrane proteins, cytoplasmic soluble proteins, and viral proteins. In this review, we examine how acidic phospholipids in the plasma membrane control protein structure and function through ionic interactions, as well as how Ca(2+) regulates these interactions through direct and indirect mechanisms.

title: A20 is overexpressed in glioma cells and may serve as a potential therapeutic target.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the expression of the primary response gene OBJECTIVE A20 in human glioma tissues and cell lines, and its impact on the development of glioma cells and a mouse tumor model. The methods used included reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR), western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and flow cytometry. Additionally, a xenograft tumor model in mice was utilized to assess the effects of specific A20 siRNAs on tumorigenesis. The results showed that A20 was overexpressed in clinical glioma tissue samples and correlated with the stage of the disease. All four human glioma cell lines also expressed A20, with U87 displaying the highest expression levels. Inhibiting A20 expression using siRNAs in vitro led to reduced growth rates of glioma cells, G1/S arrest, and increased apoptosis. In the mouse tumor model, local administration of siRNA significantly suppressed solid tumor growth. These findings suggest that A20 plays a role in the development of human glioma and may be a potential therapeutic target in the future.

title: Prevalence and size of directly detected patent foramen ovale in migraine with aura.
text: In this study, researchers used transesophageal contrast echocardiography to assess the prevalence and size of right-to-left shunts in patients with migraine with aura compared to healthy controls. They found that 47% of migraine with aura patients had a patent foramen ovale, compared to 17% of control subjects. While the prevalence of small shunts was similar between the two groups, moderate-sized or large shunts were more common in the migraine group. The presence of a shunt increased the odds of having migraine with aura. Other echocardiographic differences were not found between the groups, and there were no differences in headache and baseline characteristics between migraine patients with and without a shunt. In conclusion, nearly half of migraine with aura patients have a right-to-left shunt, with larger shunt sizes compared to controls. The clinical presentation of migraine is the same regardless of the presence of a patent foramen ovale.

title: A Live Attenuated Chimeric West Nile Virus Vaccine, rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30, Is Well Tolerated and Immunogenic in Flavivirus-Naive Older Adult Volunteers
text: West Nile virus (WNV) is a significant cause of mosquito-transmitted illness in the United States. The disease can range from mild fever to severe and fatal neurological infection. Individuals over the age of 60 are particularly vulnerable to developing neuroinvasive disease, which can have a high mortality rate or result in long-term neurological complications. A vaccine called rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30, which is a combination of live attenuated West Nile virus strains, has been proven to be safe and effective in healthy adults between the ages of 18 and 50. This study aimed to assess the safety and effectiveness of rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30 in adults between the ages of 50 and 65 who have not been previously exposed to flaviviruses. The results showed that the vaccine was both safe and capable of inducing an immune response. Given the unpredictable nature of WNV outbreaks, having a safe and effective vaccine is crucial for public health.

title: Localization and requirement for Myosin II at the dorsal-ventral compartment boundary of the Drosophila wing.
text: During the development of organisms, their tissues can undergo a separation into different cell populations by forming compartment boundaries. These boundaries have been observed in various tissues, but the molecular processes that divide cells in many cases are not well understood. In the Drosophila wing, a specific area of Notch activation is responsible for maintaining the boundary between the dorsal and ventral compartments. This process relies on the actin cytoskeleton. Our research reveals that the dorsal-ventral boundary shows a distinct accumulation of Myosin II, which is regulated by Notch signaling. In contrast, the Par-3 homologue Bazooka is depleted at this boundary. Additionally, we found that mutations in the Myosin heavy chain subunit encoded by zipper can disrupt the dorsal-ventral compartmentalization without affecting the anterior-posterior compartmentalization. These findings highlight the unique accumulation and importance of Myosin activity in the dorsal-ventral compartmentalization and propose a new mechanism in which contractile tension along an F-actin cable at the compartment boundary contributes to the process.

title: The cause of hepatic accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate on fructose loading.
text: The study examined the changes in metabolite content in freeze-clamped livers of fed rats when perfused with 10mm-d-fructose. The most notable effects of fructose were the accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate, reaching up to 8.7mumol/g of liver within 10 minutes, a decrease in total adenine nucleotides (up to 35% after 40 minutes) with a corresponding decrease in ATP content to 23% within 10 minutes, a sevenfold increase in IMP concentration to 1.1mumol/g, and an eightfold increase in alpha-glycerophosphate to 1.1mumol/g. There was a temporary decrease in P(i) from 4.2 to 1.7mumol/g, but it recovered to normal levels within 40 minutes, likely due to P(i) uptake from the perfusion medium. The degradation of adenine nucleotides beyond AMP can be explained by the decrease in ATP and P(i). Since ATP inhibits 5-nucleotidase and P(i) inhibits AMP deaminase, any AMP present in the tissue is likely to undergo dephosphorylation or deamination under the conditions following fructose loading. The lactate content increased to 4.3mumol/g at 80 minutes, while pyruvate also increased, and the [lactate]/[pyruvate] ratio remained within normal limits. The concentration of free fructose within the liver remained significantly lower than in the perfusion medium, indicating that the rate of fructose penetration into the tissue was slower than its utilization rate. Liver aldolase, responsible for the cleavage of fructose 1-phosphate, is inhibited by various phosphorylated intermediates, particularly IMP, in a competitive manner with a K(i) of 0.1mm. The maximal rates of the enzymes involved in synthesizing and splitting fructose 1-phosphate are approximately equal. The accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate during fructose loading is caused by the inhibition of its cleavage by IMP resulting from the degradation of adenine nucleotides.

title: Reported side effects to chloroquine, chloroquine plus proguanil, and mefloquine as chemoprophylaxis against malaria in Danish travelers.
text:
The purpose of this study was to gather information on the frequency of reported symptoms in travelers using different antimalarial drugs. The study was conducted as an open, nonrandomized study, where self-reported events were recorded from travelers recruited from two travel clinics in Copenhagen, Denmark. The main measures of interest were the proportion of travelers reporting specific symptoms in three different prophylaxis groups, as well as compliance, hospitalization, and premature termination of travel.

Between May 1996 and April 1998, a total of 5,446 travelers were included in the study, and 4,158 questionnaires (76.3%) were returned. Compliance was found to be significantly better in mefloquine users, with 83.3% of short-term travelers compared to 76.3% in chloroquine plus proguanil users. Additionally, 84.8%, 59.3%, and 69.5% of those using chloroquine, chloroquine plus proguanil, and mefloquine respectively reported no symptoms, while 0.6%, 1.1%, and 2.8% reported "unacceptable" symptoms. Mefloquine users had a significantly higher risk of reporting depression (RR 5.06, 95% CI 2.71 - 9.45), "strange thoughts" (RR 6.36, 95% CI 2.52 - 16.05), and altered spatial perception (RR 3.00, 95% CI 1.41 - 6.41) compared to chloroquine users.

In conclusion, overall, mefloquine is tolerated at least as well as chloroquine plus proguanil and has better compliance. However, symptoms related to the central nervous system are more common in mefloquine users, and when symptoms do occur, they are perceived as more severe.

title: Ubiquitinylation of the cytosolic domain of a type I membrane protein is not required to initiate its dislocation from the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) proteins US2 and US11 have the ability to target newly synthesized class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) heavy chains for rapid degradation. This process, known as dislocation, involves the proteasome. When US2 is present, it leads to the formation of class I MHC heavy chain conjugates with higher molecular weight. These conjugates can be detected by a specific monoclonal antibody called W6/32, indicating that the class I MHC molecules maintain their proper structure. These conjugates consist of properly folded glycosylated heavy chains that have been modified with one, two, or three ubiquitin molecules. In contrast, control cells and cells transfected with US11 do not show the presence of folded ubiquitinated class I MHC heavy chains. This suggests that US2 and US11 use different mechanisms to target class I MHC heavy chains for dislocation. Furthermore, US2 and US11 have different requirements in terms of the conformation of the heavy chain molecule. Although ubiquitin conjugation can occur on the cytosolic tail of the class I MHC molecule, replacing lysines in this region with arginine does not prevent degradation by US2. In an in vitro system that mimics US2-mediated dislocation, heavy chains lacking these lysines still undergo ubiquitin modification, but in the soluble cytoplasmic fraction. This indicates that ubiquitin conjugation can only occur on the lumenal domain of the class I MHC molecule, after it has been released from the endoplasmic reticulum. Therefore, it is concluded that ubiquitinylation of class I MHC heavy chains is not necessary during the initial step of the US2-mediated dislocation process.

title: The adaptor protein Tks5/Fish is required for podosome formation and function, and for the protease-driven invasion of cancer cells.
text: Tks5/Fish is a protein that acts as a support structure, consisting of five SH3 domains and one PX domain. In cells that have been transformed by Src, Tks5/Fish is found in podosomes, which are distinct protrusions on the underside of the cell membrane. To investigate the role of Tks5/Fish, we created Src-transformed cells with reduced levels of this protein. As a result, these cells were no longer able to form podosomes, were unable to break down gelatin, and showed poor invasive capabilities. We observed the presence of Tks5/Fish in podosomes of invasive cancer cells, as well as in samples from human breast cancer and melanoma. Additionally, Tks5/Fish expression was found to be necessary for protease-driven invasion of matrigel in human cancer cells. Lastly, when Tks5/Fish and Src were coexpressed in epithelial cells, podosomes were observed. Therefore, it appears that Tks5/Fish is essential for the formation of podosomes, degradation of the extracellular matrix, and invasion of certain cancer cells.

title: Corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain.
text:
BACKGROUND: Shoulder pain is a common issue, and while there are many treatments available, few have been proven to be effective. This review focuses on corticosteroid injections as a treatment for shoulder pain, and is part of a series of reviews on different interventions for shoulder disorders.

OBJECTIVES: The goal of this review is to determine the effectiveness and safety of corticosteroid injections in treating shoulder pain in adults.

SEARCH STRATEGY: We conducted a search of various databases up until June 2002, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Central, and Science Citation Index.

SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomized and pseudo-randomized trials in any language that compared corticosteroid injections to placebo or another intervention. We also considered trials that examined different types and dosages of steroid injections in adults with shoulder pain. We excluded trials that involved shoulder pain lasting less than three weeks, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and fractures.

DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two independent reviewers assessed the inclusion criteria and methodological quality of each trial. We present the results separately for different shoulder conditions, such as rotator cuff disease and adhesive capsulitis, and where possible, we combine the results in a meta-analysis.

MAIN RESULTS: We identified 26 trials that met our inclusion criteria. The number, site, and dosage of injections varied greatly between studies. The number of participants in each trial ranged from 20 to 114, with a median of 52 participants. The methodological quality of the trials varied. For rotator cuff disease, some trials showed a small benefit of subacromial steroid injection compared to placebo, but no benefit over nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) was demonstrated based on the pooled results of three trials. For adhesive capsulitis, two trials suggested an early benefit of intra-articular steroid injection over placebo, but there was not enough data to combine the trials in a meta-analysis. One trial suggested a short-term benefit of intra-articular corticosteroid injection over physiotherapy (success at seven weeks relative risk = 1.66).

REVIEWER'S CONCLUSIONS: Despite the numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain, the small sample sizes, variable methodological quality, and heterogeneity of the studies mean that there is limited overall evidence to guide treatment. Subacromial corticosteroid injection for rotator cuff disease and intra-articular injection for adhesive capsulitis may have some benefit, although the effect may be small and not long-lasting. Further trials are needed to investigate the efficacy of corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain. Additionally, important questions remain unanswered, such as the impact of needle placement accuracy, anatomical site, frequency, dose, and type of corticosteroid on efficacy.

title: IL-2 receptor signaling is essential for the development of Klrg1+ terminally differentiated T regulatory cells.
text: The functional and phenotypic characteristics of thymic-derived natural T regulatory cells (Tregs) are diverse. Recently, a small portion of peripheral Tregs has been found to express Klrg1, but it is still unclear if Klrg1 defines a unique subset of Tregs. In this study, we demonstrate that Klrg1(+) Tregs are a distinct subset that originates from Klrg1(-) Tregs. This subset consists of Tregs that are responsive to recent antigen exposure, highly activated, and short-lived. They express higher levels of molecules involved in Treg suppression and are predominantly found in mucosal tissues. The development of Klrg1(+) Tregs also relies on extensive IL-2R signaling. This activity of IL-2 is separate from its role in Treg homeostasis and competitive fitness. These characteristics resemble terminally differentiated short-lived CD8(+) T effector cells. Our findings suggest that a crucial pathway involved in antigen-activated conventional T lymphocytes also operates in Tregs.

title: The aurora B kinase promotes inner and outer kinetochore interactions in budding yeast.
text: In the process of chromosome segregation, the macromolecular protein complex known as the kinetochore plays a vital role. One of its essential components, Dsn1, is responsible for assembling the kinetochore and undergoes phosphorylation by the Aurora B kinase. Our research has revealed that the phosphorylation of Dsn1 by Aurora B facilitates the interaction between outer and inner kinetochore proteins in budding yeast.

title: AMP-activated/SNF1 protein kinases: conserved guardians of cellular energy
text: The AMPK family, known as the SNF1/AMP-activated protein kinase, plays a crucial role in maintaining the equilibrium between ATP production and consumption in all eukaryotic cells. These kinases consist of heterotrimers, consisting of a catalytic subunit and regulatory subunits that detect cellular energy levels. In situations where energy levels are compromised, this system activates catabolic pathways and inhibits the synthesis of proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids, as well as the growth and proliferation of cells. Surprisingly, recent findings suggest that the AMPK system also has additional functions beyond regulating energy balance, such as ensuring the preservation of cell polarity in epithelial cells.

title: Mammographic density, plasma vitamin D levels and risk of breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
text: The underlying biology for the association between mammographic density and breast cancer risk is still unknown. However, studies have suggested that vitamin D may play a role in reducing breast cancer risk, as dietary intake of vitamin D has been linked to lower breast density. To investigate this further, we conducted a case-control study within the Nurses' Health Study cohort, involving 463 postmenopausal cases and 497 controls. Our aim was to examine the relationship between mammographic density and plasma levels of two vitamin D metabolites: 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)(2)D]. We also wanted to determine if these vitamin D metabolites modify the association between breast density and breast cancer risk. We measured percent mammographic density from digitized film mammograms and used statistical models to analyze the data. Our findings showed no significant association between circulating levels of 25(OH)D or 1,25(OH)(2)D and mammographic density. However, we did observe that women in the highest tertile of mammographic density and lowest tertile of plasma 25(OH)D had a four-fold higher risk of breast cancer compared to women with the lowest mammographic density and highest plasma 25(OH)D levels. This suggests that the association between mammographic density and breast cancer risk is independent of plasma vitamin D metabolites in postmenopausal women. Further research is needed to explore the relationship between vitamin D, mammographic density, and breast cancer risk.

title: Finding the right niche: B-cell migration in the early phases of T-dependent antibody responses.
text: The humoral immune responses rely on B cells encountering antigens, interacting with helper T cells, and then either proliferating and differentiating into low-affinity plasma cells or organizing into a germinal center (GC) to become high-affinity plasma cells and memory B cells. Interestingly, each of these events takes place in specific areas of the lymphoid tissue, associated with distinct stromal cells. To mount a successful response, B cells must move swiftly and in a highly regulated manner from one niche to another. The chemokine CXCL13 plays a crucial role in guiding B cells to follicles, while T-zone chemokines direct activated B cells to the T zone. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) aids in cell egress from the tissue and positions marginal-zone B cells in the spleen. Recent research has revealed the importance of the orphan receptor EBV-induced molecule 2 (EBI2; GPR183) in guiding activated B cells to specific follicular niches, and down-regulating this receptor is necessary for organizing cells into GCs. In this review, we explore the current understanding of how chemokines, S1P, and EBI2 contribute to the migration events that drive humoral immune responses.

title: Arginine Starvation Impairs Mitochondrial Respiratory Function in ASS1-Deficient Breast Cancer Cells
text: Autophagy is the primary response to nutrient deprivation and is crucial for removing dysfunctional or damaged organelles. However, excessive autophagy can be harmful to cells and contribute to cell death. Depending on the availability of enzymes involved in molecule production, cells may rely on external nutrients for these molecules. Argininosuccinate synthetase 1 (ASS1) is a vital enzyme in arginine production, and its levels are reduced in many solid tumors, making them vulnerable to arginine depletion from outside sources. Our study demonstrated that prolonged arginine deprivation using ADI-PEG20 (pegylated arginine deiminase) led to autophagy-dependent death in breast cancer cells lacking ASS1. These cells rely on external arginine and died when exposed to ADI-PEG20 or cultured without arginine. Arginine deprivation caused oxidative stress in mitochondria, impairing their energy production and integrity. Moreover, breast cancer cells only died in vivo and in vitro from arginine deprivation if they were capable of autophagy. Therefore, the primary mechanism behind the lethal effects of prolonged arginine deprivation was cytotoxic autophagy triggered by mitochondrial damage. Lastly, ASS1 was found to be low or absent in over 60% of 149 random breast cancer samples, suggesting that patients with such tumors could benefit from arginine deprivation therapy.

title: A prospective natural-history study of coronary atherosclerosis.
text:
BACKGROUND: Atherosclerotic plaques that cause acute coronary syndromes often occur in areas of mild coronary artery stenosis. The factors that contribute to these events are not well understood.

METHODS: In a prospective study, 697 patients with acute coronary syndromes underwent coronary angiography and intravascular ultrasonographic imaging after receiving percutaneous coronary intervention. Major adverse cardiovascular events, such as cardiac death, cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction, or rehospitalization due to unstable or progressive angina, were categorized as being related to either the originally treated (culprit) lesions or untreated (nonculprit) lesions. The patients were followed for a median period of 3.4 years.

RESULTS: The cumulative rate of major adverse cardiovascular events over three years was 20.4%. These events were attributed to culprit lesions in 12.9% of patients and to nonculprit lesions in 11.6%. Most nonculprit lesions responsible for subsequent events were initially mild based on angiography (mean diameter stenosis of 32.3±20.6%). However, multivariate analysis showed that nonculprit lesions associated with recurrent events were more likely to have a plaque burden of 70% or greater, a minimal luminal area of 4.0 mm(2) or less, or be classified as thin-cap fibroatheromas based on intravascular ultrasonography.

CONCLUSIONS: In patients who experienced acute coronary syndromes and received percutaneous coronary intervention, major adverse cardiovascular events during follow-up were equally attributable to recurrence at the site of culprit lesions and nonculprit lesions. Although nonculprit lesions responsible for unexpected events were often mild based on angiography, they were frequently characterized by a large plaque burden, a small luminal area, or thin-cap fibroatheromas based on intravascular ultrasonography. (Funded by Abbott Vascular and Volcano; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00180466.)

title: What do medical schools teach about women's health and gender differences?
text:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the inclusion of women's health and gender-specific information in the curricula of medical schools in the United States. The authors used data from the Association of American Medical Colleges' Curriculum Management and Information Tool (CurrMIT) to conduct a search of schools that offered courses or clerkships related to women's health or gender-specific topics. They also analyzed the relationship between the frequency of these topics and various institutional characteristics.

The authors identified 95 schools that offered related courses or clerkships, with nine schools meeting the criteria for an interdisciplinary women's health course or clerkship. Among a subset of 60 schools with comprehensive CurrMIT information, they identified 18 specified women's health topics and 24 topics on gender-specific content, totaling 42 topics. The number of topics taught varied from zero to 26, with an average of 11 topics. More than 50% of these schools taught 11 of the specified topics, while less than 30% included gender-specific topics. In bivariate analysis, there was no association between the mean number of topics taught and schools' characteristics. However, a women's health program and a female dean were positively associated in a regression model.

In conclusion, the study found that only a few medical schools offer interdisciplinary women's health courses or include gender-specific information in their curricula. The presence of a designated women's health program may increase the inclusion of this content in schools' curricula.

title: A molecular framework for plant regeneration.
text: The ability of plants and certain animals to regenerate organs from adult tissues is well-known. However, the molecular mechanisms behind this process have not been extensively studied. In this study, we focus on investigating a specific regeneration response in the roots of Arabidopsis plants. By using laser-induced wounding, we disrupt the flow of auxin, a plant hormone that instructs cell fate, in the root tips. Our findings show that changes in cell fate resulting from this disruption require the involvement of three transcription factors: PLETHORA, SHORTROOT, and SCARECROW. These transcription factors control the expression and positioning of PIN proteins, which facilitate the efflux of auxin across cell membranes, thus restoring auxin transport in the regenerated root tips. In summary, our research reveals that a regeneration mechanism, utilizing factors involved in the patterning of embryonic root stem cells, first responds to changes in hormone distribution and then stabilizes a new distribution pattern.

title: Cocoa flavonols and procyanidins promote transforming growth factor-beta1 homeostasis in peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
text: Research indicates that certain flavan-3-ols and procyanidins (FP) may have a positive impact on cardiovascular well-being. Previous studies have shown that FP derived from cocoa can potentially regulate the levels and production of various signaling molecules linked to immune function and inflammation, including cytokines and eicosanoids. In this particular investigation, we aimed to determine whether different FP fractions, ranging from monomers to decamers, can influence the secretion of the cytokine transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta(1) from resting human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC). Thirteen healthy participants were included in the study and categorized based on their baseline TGF-beta(1) production. When PBMCs from individuals with low baseline TGF-beta(1) levels (n = 7) were stimulated with individual FP fractions (25 microg/ml), there was an increase in TGF-beta(1) release ranging from 15% to 66% compared to baseline (P < 0.05; monomer, dimer, and tetramer). The smaller FP fractions (<or=pentamer) were more effective in enhancing TGF-beta(1) secretion compared to the larger fractions (>or=hexamer), with the monomer and dimer inducing the greatest increases (66% and 68%, respectively). In contrast, TGF-beta(1) secretion from individuals with high baseline TGF-beta(1) levels (n = 6) was inhibited by individual FP fractions (P < 0.05; trimer through decamer). The inhibition was most significant with trimeric through decameric fractions (28% to 42%), while monomers and dimers moderately inhibited TGF-beta(1) release (17% and 23%, respectively). Considering the vascular effects associated with TGF-beta(1), we propose that in healthy individuals, the regulation of its production by FP provides an additional mechanism through which FP-rich foods can potentially promote cardiovascular health.

title: BMP receptor IA is required in mammalian neural crest cells for development of the cardiac outflow tract and ventricular myocardium.
text: The neural crest is a group of cells that can develop into various types of cells and migrate from the border of the neural and surface ectoderm. In mice, these migratory neural crest cells first appear at the five-somite stage. Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), specifically BMP2 and BMP4, have been identified as regulators of neural crest cell induction, maintenance, migration, differentiation, and survival. In mice, there are three known BMP2/4 type I receptors, with Bmpr1a being expressed early in the neural tube and potentially involved in neural crest development. However, its exact role in the neural crest is unclear due to its earlier functions in other areas. To investigate this, we specifically removed Bmpr1a in the neural crest starting at the five-somite stage. We observed that most aspects of neural crest development proceeded normally, suggesting that BMPRIA is not necessary for many early neural crest processes. However, mutant embryos exhibited a shortened cardiac outflow tract with defective septation, a process that requires neural crest cells and is crucial for survival after birth. Surprisingly, these embryos died in mid-gestation due to acute heart failure, which was accompanied by reduced proliferation of ventricular myocardium. This myocardial defect may be caused by reduced BMP signaling in a small group of neural crest derivatives in the epicardium, which is known to provide signals for ventricular myocardial proliferation. These findings demonstrate the essential role of BMP2/4 signaling in the development of neural crest derivatives in mammals, particularly in the formation of the outflow tract, and its potential regulation of a critical proliferation signal for the ventricular myocardium.

title: Early intermittent noninvasive ventilation for acute chest syndrome in adults with sickle cell disease: a pilot study
text: Alveolar hypoxia and hypoxic vasoconstriction result in the entrapment of sickle cells in the pulmonary vasculature. Enhancing alveolar ventilation and oxygenation may enhance the outcome of acute chest syndrome (ACS). A study was conducted from November 1998 to February 2002 to compare the effectiveness of noninvasive ventilation (NIV) versus oxygen alone in improving oxygenation on day 3 in adults with ACS, and to assess the impact on pain, transfusion requirements, and length of hospital stay. A total of 71 consecutive ACS episodes in 67 patients were randomly assigned to receive either oxygen (n = 36) or NIV (n = 35) for 3 days in a medical step-down unit. The NIV group had higher baseline respiratory rate and pain scores. NIV promptly reduced the respiratory rate, increased $$ {\text{Pa}}_{{\text{O}_{2}}} $$ , and decreased the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient $$ (({\text{A}} - {\text{a}})_{{{\text{O}}_{ 2} }} ) $$, while these parameters remained unchanged with oxygen alone. However, $$ {\text{Pa}}_{{{\text{CO}}_{ 2} }} $$ significantly worsened only in the oxygen group. On day 3, there was no significant difference between the groups in terms of the proportion of episodes with normal $$ {\text{Pa}}_{{{\text{O}}_{ 2} }} $$ (35% with NIV and 25% with oxygen; P = 0.5) or $$ (({\text{A}} - {\text{a}})_{{{\text{O}}_{ 2} }} ) $$ . Patient satisfaction and compliance were lower with NIV. There were no differences observed in pain relief, transfusions, or length of hospital stay. In the subgroup of patients with severe hypoxemia $$ ( {\text{Pa}}_{{{\text{O}}_{ 2} }} \le 6 5\,{\text{mmHg)}} $$ , physiological variables also improved more rapidly with NIV, although the differences were slightly more pronounced. Respiratory rate and gas exchange improved more quickly with NIV. However, NIV did not significantly reduce the number of patients who remained hypoxemic on day 3 and was associated with greater patient discomfort.

title: Serum Exosome MicroRNA as a Minimally-Invasive Early Biomarker of AML
text: Relapse continues to be the primary cause of death among patients diagnosed with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). The advancement in monitoring minimal residual disease (MRD) offers the potential for timely adjustments in treatment to prevent relapse. However, current surveillance techniques are ineffective in detecting MRD during the early stages of relapse, as they primarily identify circulating blasts that are associated with advanced disease. In this study, we explore the use of exosomes as a minimally invasive tool for identifying a microRNA (miRNA) biomarker. We have identified a specific set of miRNA that is abundant in AML exosomes and have monitored the levels of circulating exosome miRNA to differentiate between leukemic xenografts, non-engrafted samples, and human CD34+ controls. Through the development of biostatistical models, we have discovered that circulating exosomal miRNA can be detected even at low levels of marrow tumor burden, before the presence of circulating blasts. Interestingly, both leukemic blasts and marrow stroma contribute to the presence of exosome miRNA in the serum. Based on our findings, we propose the development of serum exosome miRNA as a novel and sensitive biomarker for the early detection and prospective tracking of AML recurrence.

title: Human cytomegalovirus encodes an MHC class I-like molecule (UL142) that functions to inhibit NK cell lysis.
text: In addition to the previously known UL18, clinical and low passage strains of human CMV (HCMV) also contain an extra MHC class I-related molecule called UL142. The UL142 gene is located within the ULb' region, which is absent in many commonly used high passage laboratory strains. To investigate the effects of UL142, cells were transfected with UL142 or infected with a recombinant adenovirus expressing UL142. These cells were then used to test the response of both polyclonal NK cells and NK cell clones in a system that mimics the body's own immune response. Analysis of 100 NK cell clones from five donors revealed that 23 clones were inhibited by fibroblasts expressing UL142 alone. When UL142 mRNA expression was reduced using small-interfering RNA in HCMV-infected cells, their sensitivity to lysis increased. Based on these findings, we conclude that UL142 is a newly discovered MHC class I-related molecule encoded by HCMV, which inhibits NK cell killing in a manner that depends on the specific clone of NK cells.

title: Identification of the conserved serine/threonine residues important for gibberellin-sensitivity of Arabidopsis RGL2 protein.
text: The DELLA proteins GAI, RGA, RGL1, and RGL2 in Arabidopsis act as inhibitors of plant growth, suppressing various developmental processes. Previous research has shown that gibberellin (GA) reduces the inhibitory function of DELLA proteins by promoting their breakdown through the proteasome pathway. However, it is unclear if GA-induced protein degradation is the sole mechanism for regulating the effectiveness of DELLA proteins. In this study, we demonstrate that tobacco BY2 cells are a suitable model system for investigating GA signaling. RGL2, one of the DELLA proteins, exists in a phosphorylated state in BY2 cells. GA triggers the degradation of RGL2, and this process is hindered by proteasome inhibitors and serine/threonine phosphatase inhibitors. Interestingly, serine/threonine kinase inhibitors do not appear to affect the degradation of RGL2, suggesting that dephosphorylation of serine/threonine residues is likely necessary for the proteasome-mediated breakdown of RGL2. Through targeted substitutions of all 17 conserved serine and threonine residues, we identified six mutants (RGL2(S441D), RGL2(S542D), RGL2(T271E), RGL2(T319E), RGL2(T411E), and RGL2(T535E)) that mimic constitutive phosphorylation and are resistant to GA-induced degradation. These findings suggest that these sites may serve as potential phosphorylation sites. Additionally, a functional assay using the expression of GA 20-oxidase revealed that RGL2(T271E) is likely a non-functional mutant, while RGL2(S441D), RGL2(S542D), RGL2(T319E), and RGL2(T411E) only retain 4-17% of the activity of the wild-type RGL2. In contrast, RGL2(T535E) retains approximately 66% of the wild-type RGL2 activity. Importantly, the expression of GA 20-oxidase in BY2 cells expressing these mutant proteins remains responsive to GA, indicating that the stabilization of RGL2 protein is not the sole mechanism for regulating its effectiveness.

title: A chart review of cyproheptadine for stimulant-induced weight loss.
text: Weight loss is a common issue for young people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) who take stimulant medications. This can make it difficult to find the right dosage and ensure compliance. However, studies have shown that cyproheptadine can help stimulate weight gain. To further investigate this, we reviewed the medical records of 28 pediatric psychiatry outpatients who were prescribed cyproheptadine for weight loss or insomnia while taking stimulants. Out of these patients, 4 did not consistently take cyproheptadine and 3 stopped taking it within the first week due to side effects. We analyzed the data of the remaining 21 patients (aged 4-15 years) who continued taking 4-8 mg of cyproheptadine every night for at least 14 days (average duration of 104.7 days). Most of these patients had experienced weight loss while taking stimulants alone (average weight loss of 2.1 kg, average weight velocity of -19.3 g/day). However, all 21 patients gained weight when they started taking cyproheptadine alongside the stimulants, with an average weight gain of 2.2 kg (paired t = 6.87, p < 0.0001) and an average weight velocity of 32.3 g/day. Additionally, 11 out of 17 patients who initially experienced insomnia while taking stimulants alone reported significant improvements in sleep when cyproheptadine was added. Based on these findings, we believe that cyproheptadine may be a useful treatment option for young people with ADHD who experience weight loss due to stimulant medications. However, further randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these results.

title: Life course breast cancer risk factors and adult breast density (United Kingdom)
text: The objective of this study was to investigate whether risk factors in childhood and early adulthood have an impact on mammographic breast density later in life. The study included 628 women who had a medical examination at the University of Glasgow Student Health Service between 1948 and 1968. These women also completed a questionnaire in 2001 and had a screening mammogram in Scotland between 1989 and 2002. The mammograms, taken at a median age of 59 years, were classified using a six-category classification system for breast density percent. Logistic regression was used to analyze the associations between risk factors and the likelihood of having a high-risk mammogram (≥25% dense). The results showed that high-risk mammograms were associated with parity (adjusted odds ratio (OR) per child: 0.77 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.61–0.99)), age at first birth (OR per year: 1.05 (0.99–1.11)), smoking at university (OR smokers versus non-smokers: 0.58 (0.36–0.92)), and body mass index (BMI) while at university (OR per 1kg/m2: 0.75 (0.69–0.82)). However, no significant associations were found between breast density and age at menarche, birth weight, oral contraceptive (OC) use, height, leg length, or exercise at age 20. In conclusion, this study confirms previous findings that reproductive events and certain anthropometric measures can affect breast density, but most of the risk factors examined throughout the life course were not closely related to adult breast density.

title: Osteoclast nuclei of myeloma patients show chromosome translocations specific for the myeloma cell clone: a new type of cancer-host partnership?
text:
Bone destruction is a major clinical manifestation of bone cancers. It is widely believed that this destruction is not caused by the cancerous cells themselves, but rather by osteoclasts. Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells of monocytic origin that are known to be the only cells capable of breaking down bone. 

A recent study has shown that osteoclasts from patients with myeloma, a type of bone cancer, contain nuclei with translocated chromosomes from the myeloma B-cell clone. These nuclei, which originate from the cancerous cells, are actively transcribing genes and are fully integrated with the other nuclei in the osteoclasts. The study found that over 30% of the osteoclast population analyzed in this study consisted of nuclei from the malignant cells. 

Furthermore, the study discovered that osteoclast-myeloma clone hybrids, which contain more nuclei than normal osteoclasts, were present in close proximity to the myeloma cells. Similar hybrid cells were also generated in laboratory co-cultures of myeloma cells and osteoclasts. These findings suggest that the fusion of myeloma cells and osteoclasts can give rise to these hybrid cells. 

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that malignant cells play a significant role in the formation of bone-resorbing osteoclasts in multiple myeloma. The presence of osteoclast-myeloma clone hybrids reveals a previously unknown mechanism of bone destruction, in which the cancerous cells directly participate. This suggests that the transfer of malignant DNA from cancer cells to host cells may have a greater impact on cancer development than previously thought.

title: Frequency modulation entrains slow neural oscillations and optimizes human listening behavior.
text: The ability of humans to continuously track and process dynamic environmental stimuli, such as speech, is believed to be enhanced through a process called "entrainment" of internal brain oscillations. This involves reorganizing the phase of these oscillations to align with expected critical events, resulting in improved processing. This study aims to address two unanswered questions in this field. Firstly, how widespread is neural entrainment to environmental rhythms? Can neural oscillations be entrained by the temporal patterns of ongoing rhythmic stimuli without sudden changes? Secondly, does neural entrainment optimize the performance of the perceptual system? Does human auditory perception benefit from the reorganization of neural phases? In this experiment using electroencephalography, participants were asked to detect short gaps in a frequency-modulated sound that were distributed evenly across the phase angle of a 3-Hz stimulus. The ability to detect these gaps was not evenly distributed across time, but instead clustered around specific preferred phases of the modulation. Furthermore, the optimal phase of the stimulus was determined individually by the neural delta oscillation entrained by the stimulus. Lastly, the delta phase of the brain activity predicted participants' performance better than the phase of the stimulus or the event-related potential after the gap. This study demonstrates the behavioral advantages of realigning neural phases in response to frequency-modulated auditory stimuli, suggesting that fluctuations in natural environmental input serve as a pacing signal for internal brain oscillations, influencing perceptual processing.

title: Interventions by pharmacists in out-patient pharmaceutical care.
text: The healthcare community has always recognized the valuable contributions of pharmacists in patient care. Pharmacists play a crucial role in reducing medication errors, optimizing therapy, and lowering treatment costs. This study aimed to retrospectively determine the number and types of medication errors addressed by dispensing pharmacists at the OPD pharmacy in Khoula Hospital in 2009. The interventions made by pharmacists and assistant pharmacists at the OPD pharmacy were collected, categorized, and analyzed in detail. The findings revealed that 72.3% of the interventions were minor, with 40.5% involving changes to medication orders. Female patients received more interventions compared to male patients. Notably, 98.2% of the interventions were accepted by the prescribers, indicating their recognition of the importance of pharmacy practice. Among the 688 interventions related to prescribing errors, 40.5% involved changing medication orders or clarifying the medicine. Administrative issues accounted for 14.9% of the interventions, while 8.7% were related to medication selection and errors due to lack of patient history knowledge. Additionally, 8.2% of the interventions addressed medication overdoses. Moderately significant interventions were observed in 19.4% of cases, with 7.5% having a major impact on medication errors. Pharmacists intervened in 20.8% of prescriptions to prevent complications, 25.1% to optimize treatment, and 7.9% to improve compliance. Based on these results, it is evident that pharmacists play a vital role in improving the healthcare system. We recommend conducting more research studies to raise awareness among healthcare professionals, address prescription and dispensing issues, improve documentation systems, reduce prescribing errors, and enhance the knowledge of pharmacists and other healthcare professionals.

title: Biochemical studies on Mycobacterium tuberculosis UreG and comparative modeling reveal structural and functional conservation among the bacterial UreG family.
text:
Nickel is an essential micronutrient for cellular life, but it becomes toxic when present in soluble form at concentrations that are not natural. This contradiction has led living organisms to develop efficient systems for managing nickel utilization and maintaining balance within the body. One such system involves the incorporation of nickel into the active site of urease, a process that requires the coordination of various accessory proteins and is tightly regulated. Understanding this activation mechanism could have medical applications in combating ureolytic bacteria, including the deadly pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The focus of this study is UreG, a crucial chaperone that plays a role in the in vivo activation of urease by facilitating the insertion of Ni2+ into the active site.
