To reduce the number of refinement parameters, collective variables can be used instead of independent atomic variables. One example of this is the TLS parameterization, which describes the translation, libration, and screw-rotation displacements of a pseudo-rigid body. This article focuses on the implementation of the TLS parameterization in the macromolecular refinement program REFMAC. The derivatives of the residual with respect to the TLS parameters are expanded based on the derivatives with respect to individual anisotropic U values, which are calculated using a fast Fourier transform technique. As a result, TLS refinement is fast and can be routinely used. The article provides examples of TLS refinement for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) and a transcription activator GerE. Both cases have data only up to 2.0 A, making individual anisotropic refinement impractical. GAPDH has been refined with one to four TLS groups in the asymmetric unit, while GerE has been refined with six TLS groups. In both cases, the inclusion of TLS parameters leads to improved refinement statistics, particularly in terms of R and free R values, which show a several percent improvement. Additionally, both GAPDH and GerE have multiple molecules in the asymmetric unit, and the TLS parameterization effectively accounts for significant differences in displacement parameters between molecules. This leaves residual local displacements that are similar between molecules and can be restrained using NCS restraints.

title: Sequence features surrounding the translation initiation sites assigned on the genome sequence of Synechocystis sp. strain PCC6803 by amino-terminal protein sequencing.
text:
In order to understand the characteristics of the sequences surrounding the translation initiation sites in the genome of Synechocystis sp. strain 6803, we conducted a study. First, we extracted total proteins from the cells and separated them using two-dimensional electrophoresis. Then, we determined the amino-terminal sequences of the proteins that were relatively abundant. By comparing these sequences with the nucleotide sequence of the entire genome, we successfully identified the translation initiation sites for a total of 72 proteins on the genome.

From our analysis, we discovered several sequence features at and around the translation initiation sites. Firstly, we found evidence that, in addition to the commonly known initiation codons ATG, GTG, and TTG, the codon ATT was also occasionally used as a rare initiation codon. Secondly, we identified the core sequences (GAGG, GGAG, and AGGA) of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence in the appropriate position preceding 35 of the initiation sites (48.6%). Lastly, we formulated the preferential sequence surrounding the initiation codons as 5'-YY[...]R-3', where Y represents pyrimidine nucleotides, R represents purine nucleotides, and the three dots represent the initiation codons.

These findings are valuable for improving gene-finding software and our approach can be applied to comprehensively analyze the expression profiles of cellular proteins.

title: Deregulated DNA polymerase beta induces chromosome instability and tumorigenesis.
text: In order for cancer to develop, the genetic makeup of tumor cells must undergo changes that increase their susceptibility to mutations. This is typically caused by a malfunction in the network of systems responsible for maintaining the stability of the genome, such as cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and accurate DNA synthesis during replication. One common genetic alteration found in many solid tumors is aneuploidy, which refers to an abnormal numeric imbalance in the chromosomes. Our study reveals that the introduction of DNA polymerase beta, an enzyme known for its error-prone nature and frequent over-regulation in human tumors, into cells leads to aneuploidy. This abnormality is accompanied by the misplacement of the centrosome-associated gamma-tubulin protein during cell division, a defective mitotic checkpoint, and the promotion of tumor growth in immunodeficient mice. Therefore, our findings suggest that changes in the expression of polymerase beta can cause significant genetic alterations associated with a malignant phenotype.

title: Combinatorial signaling by Sonic hedgehog and Wnt family members induces myogenic bHLH gene expression in the somite.
text: Previously, we have shown that the combined signals from the neural tube and the floor plate/notochord complex work together to stimulate the expression of myogenic bHLH genes and myogenic differentiation markers in unspecified somites. In this study, we demonstrate that Sonic hedgehog (Shh), found in the floor plate/notochord, and a specific group of Wnt family members (Wnt-1, Wnt-3, and Wnt-4), found in the dorsal regions of the neural tube, have the ability to mimic the muscle-inducing activity of these tissues. When Shh is combined with either Wnt-1 or Wnt-3, it is enough to induce myogenesis in somitic tissue in a laboratory setting. Therefore, we propose that the formation of myotome in living organisms may be guided by the combined effects of Shh secreted by ventral midline tissues (floor plate and notochord) and Wnt ligands secreted by the dorsal neural tube.

title: Advances in osteoclast biology: old findings and new insights from mouse models
text: The maintenance of sufficient bone mass relies on the controlled and timely removal of old, damaged bone. This intricate process is carried out by a specialized type of cell called osteoclast, which has multiple nuclei. In the past 15 years, researchers have gained a comprehensive understanding of the origins, differentiation pathways, and activation stages that contribute to the normal functioning of osteoclasts. This knowledge has mainly been acquired through the creation and examination of genetically modified mouse models. These mice have mutations in specific genes that result in bone defects due to abnormalities in the recruitment, formation, or function of osteoclasts. These studies have revealed important information, such as the identification of the RANK-RANKL-OPG system as a key regulator of osteoclast formation, the characterization of mechanisms involved in ion transport and cellular attachment, and the recognition that enzymes responsible for breaking down the bone matrix are crucial for resorption. This review article focuses on the main findings in osteoclast biology obtained from genetic mouse models and highlights emerging concepts that explain how osteoclasts contribute to maintaining adequate bone mass and integrity throughout life.

title: DNA methylation in embryonic stem cells.
text: Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are versatile cells that have the ability to develop into different types of cells. They are used in various applications such as cell therapy, drug development, disease modeling, and studying cellular differentiation. Understanding how these cells function and differentiate through the interplay of epigenetics, genetics, and gene expression is crucial. One important epigenetic factor is DNA methylation, which plays a major role in regulating gene expression. DNA methylation is particularly significant in imprinted genes and X-chromosome inactivation, where it represses gene expression by modifying promoter regions. Differences in DNA methylation have been observed in genes associated with pluripotency, such as Nanog and Oct4/Pou5f1, between pluripotent and differentiated cells. It is evident that precise regulation of DNA methylation is essential for normal development. With the increasing number of reported associations between abnormal DNA methylation and diseases, there is a growing demand for high-throughput methods to analyze DNA methylation. This article focuses on these methods and discusses recent studies on DNA methylation in ESCs.

title: Reserves, functional, immunoregulatory, and cytogenetic properties of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes.
text: The role of bone marrow (BM) stroma in supporting hematopoiesis has been linked to the development of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). This study aims to investigate whether the progenitor cells of BM stroma, known as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), are primarily affected in MDS. The reserves, functional properties, and cytogenetic characteristics of MSCs were evaluated in comparison to BM hematopoietic cells in patients with de novo MDS (n = 13). The number, differentiation potential, and immunosuppressive function of patient MSCs did not significantly differ from normal MSCs (n = 20). Patient MSCs did not exhibit abnormalities in the production of proinflammatory or growth-promoting cytokines, nor did they have the cytogenetic abnormalities found in hematopoietic cells. However, some patient and normal MSC cultures did develop irrelevant chromosomal alterations (trisomies 5 and 7) of uncertain significance. Compared to controls, patient MSCs showed impaired proliferative and clonogenic potential, which may be a nonspecific abnormality associated with the chronic inflammatory process in the patients' BM. These findings suggest that MSCs from MDS patients are not part of the abnormal clone and do not contribute significantly to the inflammatory microenvironment in the bone marrow.

title: Symmetric signalling within asymmetric dimers of the Staphylococcus aureus receptor histidine kinase AgrC.
text: The accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum-sensing system plays a major role in controlling the virulence of Staphylococcus aureus. Within this system, the AgrC receptor histidine kinase detects its autoinducing peptide (AIP) ligand and generates a signal that leads to the secretion of virulence factors. Despite being well-studied, the activation mechanism of AgrC remains poorly understood. Through co-immunoprecipitation analysis and intermolecular complementation of receptor mutants, we discovered that AgrC forms dimers independently of ligands and undergoes trans-autophosphorylation upon interaction with AIP. Interestingly, when specific AIPs were added to AgrC mutant dimers with only one functional sensor domain, both kinase domains were symmetrically activated, despite the sensor asymmetry. Additionally, mutant dimers involving one constitutive protomer exhibited ligand-independent activity, regardless of which protomer was kinase deficient. These findings indicate that signaling through either individual AgrC protomer leads to symmetric activation of both kinase domains. We propose that this signaling mechanism across the dimer interface is crucial for dimeric quorum-sensing receptors to rapidly initiate a response upon detecting a signal.

title: Attachment of the ubiquitin-related protein Urm1p to the antioxidant protein Ahp1p.
text: Urm1p is a protein that is related to ubiquitin and is involved in modifying other proteins after they have been synthesized. Urm1p conjugation has been found to play a role in the process of budding and in sensing nutrients. In this study, we have discovered the first target of the urmylation pathway in living organisms, which is a protein called Ahp1p that acts as an antioxidant. The attachment of Urm1p to Ahp1p requires the presence of a protein called Uba4p, which is part of the urmylation pathway. When the components of the urmylation pathway are lost, the cells become more sensitive to a specific type of oxidant that affects thiol groups. This sensitivity is also observed when Ahp1p is absent, suggesting that urmylation is involved in the response to oxidative stress. Additionally, when cells are treated with thiol-specific oxidants, the levels of Ahp1p-Urm1p conjugates change, indicating that the attachment of Urm1p to Ahp1p may regulate the function of Ahp1p in the response to antioxidant stress in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

title: Sulfasalazine in the treatment of spondylarthropathy. A randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
text:
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of sulfasalazine (SSZ) in treating spondylarthropathy. The study was conducted over a period of 6 months and involved a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with patients who had active spondylarthropathy despite previous treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Patients were either given SSZ (3 gm/day) or a placebo. The primary measures of effectiveness were assessments by the physician and patient, pain levels, and morning stiffness. The study analyzed the results based on the intention-to-treat and completer patient populations, and also examined the time course of the treatment's effects in the completer patient population. 

Out of the 351 patients enrolled, 263 (75%) completed the full 6-month treatment period. The withdrawal rates were 20% in the placebo group and 30% in the SSZ group. In terms of effectiveness, the analysis of the intention-to-treat population showed a statistically significant difference between the two groups for only one of the four primary outcome variables: the patient's overall assessment of disease activity. 60% of patients taking SSZ showed improvement of at least 1 point on a 5-point scale, compared to 44% of patients taking the placebo. Laboratory markers of inflammation also showed a statistically significant improvement in favor of SSZ. Subgroup analysis revealed that the most notable effects were observed in patients with psoriatic arthritis, both in terms of the primary efficacy variables and secondary efficacy variables such as the number of inflamed joints. 

Adverse events were more common in the SSZ group compared to the placebo group, but all were temporary or reversible after discontinuation of treatment. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that SSZ is more effective than a placebo in treating active spondylarthropathy, particularly in patients with psoriatic arthritis.

title: A randomized trial of aspirin to prevent colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of regular aspirin use on the occurrence of colorectal adenomas, which are known to be precursors to most colorectal cancers. To do this, a randomized, double-blind trial was conducted involving 635 patients who had previously been diagnosed with colorectal cancer. These patients were randomly assigned to receive either a daily dose of 325 mg of aspirin or a placebo. The study then assessed the proportion of patients who developed adenomas, the number of recurrent adenomas, and the time it took for adenomas to develop between randomization and subsequent colonoscopic examinations. The relative risks were adjusted for various factors such as age, sex, cancer stage, the number of colonoscopic examinations, and the time to the first colonoscopy. The study was terminated early by an independent data and safety monitoring board due to statistically significant results found during a planned interim analysis. 

The results showed that out of the 517 patients who underwent at least one colonoscopic examination, 17 percent of those in the aspirin group had one or more adenomas, compared to 27 percent in the placebo group (P=0.004). The mean number of adenomas was also lower in the aspirin group (0.30+/-0.87) compared to the placebo group (0.49+/-0.99) (P=0.003). After adjusting for various factors, the relative risk of any recurrent adenoma in the aspirin group was 0.65 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.46 to 0.91) compared to the placebo group. Additionally, the time it took for a first adenoma to be detected was longer in the aspirin group (hazard ratio for the detection of a new polyp, 0.64; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.43 to 0.94; P=0.022). 

In conclusion, the findings of this study suggest that daily aspirin use is associated with a significant reduction in the occurrence of colorectal adenomas in patients who have previously been diagnosed with colorectal cancer.

title: The Wilms tumour suppressor protein WT1 (+KTS isoform) binds alpha-actinin 1 mRNA via its zinc-finger domain.
text: Mutations in the WT1 gene are linked to developmental syndromes that impact the urogenital system and various types of cancer, such as Wilms tumor, acute myeloid leukemia, breast cancer, and prostate cancer. The WT1 protein is a member of the zinc-finger transcription factor family known as early growth response. Unlike other members of this family, WT1 undergoes a unique alternative splicing event that inserts the tripeptide KTS between its third and fourth zinc fingers. The isoforms without KTS efficiently bind to DNA and regulate transcription, while the isoforms with KTS have reduced DNA binding ability and interact with splice factors and RNA. Although some potential DNA targets have been identified, the specific mRNA targets of WT1 in physiological contexts are still unknown. In this study, we investigated the distribution of WT1 in ribonucleoprotein complexes in nuclear extracts from M15 cells, a mouse fetal kidney cell line. We observed that WT1 coexisted with the splice factor PSF in large ribonucleoprotein particles of at least 2 MDa. Additionally, we found that PSF co-immunoprecipitated with WT1, suggesting a functional interaction between these two multifunctional proteins. By using a yeast three-hybrid library constructed from the co-immunoprecipitated RNA, we discovered that WT1 (+KTS) binds to the region near or at the start codon of alpha-actinin 1 (ACTN1) mRNA. This binding was further confirmed through a band shift assay, which demonstrated the ability of the WT1 zinc-finger domain (+KTS) to bind to this specific sequence in vitro. Therefore, ACTN1 is likely the first identified physiological mRNA target of WT1.

title: How safe are psychiatric medications after a voluntary overdose?
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the potential lethality of psychiatric medications in a representative sample of suicide attempts. The study was conducted in a general hospital in Madrid, Spain, between 1996 and 1998. A total of 563 suicide attempts were analyzed, with medication overdose being the method used in 456 attempts (81%). The toxicity of the medications was evaluated by comparing the dose taken to the maximum recommended prescription dose.

The results showed that benzodiazepines were the most commonly used drugs in cases of self-poisoning, accounting for 65% of overdoses. This was followed by new antidepressants (11%), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) (10%), and antipsychotics (8%). It was found that patients who were prescribed these medications were more likely to overdose on them. In the case of TCAs, 47% of the overdoses were potentially lethal. However, all patients who overdosed on psychiatric medications recovered well and were discharged without any long-term effects.

The study suggests that psychiatric medications, particularly benzodiazepines, new antidepressants, and antipsychotics, are relatively safe when used for self-poisoning. It emphasizes the importance of properly treating patients with mental illnesses, as under-treatment can increase the risk of suicide. Therefore, it is recommended to prescribe psychiatric medications, especially the newer ones, rather than withholding them out of an exaggerated fear of a lethal overdose.

title: Health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of earlier eligibility for adult antiretroviral therapy and expanded treatment coverage: a combined analysis of 12 mathematical models.
text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recently released new guidelines recommending the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for individuals with HIV and CD4 cell counts of 500 cells/µL or lower. This is a higher threshold than the previous recommendation. As a result, decision makers in each country must determine whether to expand ART eligibility accordingly.

To evaluate the potential impact, costs, and cost-effectiveness of different adult ART eligibility criteria, multiple independent mathematical models were used in four settings: South Africa, Zambia, India, and Vietnam. These models projected results over a 20-year period and considered scenarios of current and expanded treatment coverage.

The analyses compared extending eligibility to include individuals with CD4 counts of 500 cells/µL or lower, or all HIV-positive adults, to the previous recommendation of initiation with CD4 counts of 350 cells/µL or lower. Costs were assessed from a health system perspective, and the incremental cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted was calculated to compare different strategies. Strategies were considered "very cost-effective" if the cost per DALY averted was less than the country's per capita gross domestic product (GDP), and "cost-effective" if it was less than three times the per capita GDP.

In South Africa, the cost per DALY averted of extending ART eligibility to CD4 counts of 500 cells/µL or lower ranged from $237 to $1691, compared to the 2010 guidelines. In Zambia, expanded eligibility ranged from improving health outcomes while reducing costs to $749 per DALY. Similar results were found in scenarios with substantially expanded treatment access and for expanding eligibility to all HIV-positive adults. Expanding treatment coverage in the general population was deemed cost-effective.

In India, eligibility for all HIV-positive individuals ranged from $131 to $241 per DALY, and in Vietnam, eligibility for CD4 counts of 500 cells/µL or lower cost $290 per DALY. In concentrated epidemics, expanded access among key populations was also found to be cost-effective.

In conclusion, earlier ART eligibility is estimated to be very cost-effective in low- and middle-income settings. However, further research and information are needed to revisit these findings. Scaling up ART should be considered alongside other high-priority health interventions when allocating health budgets.

This study was funded by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the World Health Organization.

title: Chronic daily headache: long-term prognosis following inpatient treatment with repetitive IV DHE.
text:
We conducted a retrospective study to examine the long-term outcomes of 50 consecutive patients who were admitted to our inpatient headache program due to chronic daily headache (CDH) caused by the excessive use of analgesics, ergotamine, or both. These patients underwent detoxification, received repetitive intravenous dihydroergotamine (IV DHE) and prophylactic medications as part of the program, and achieved freedom from headaches with this treatment regimen. 

Upon admission, 37 out of the 50 patients had transformed migraine (TM), 12 had new daily persistent headache (NDPH), and 1 had chronic tension-type headache. Among the patients with TM, 29 also had coexisting migraine, while 7 of those with NDPH and the single patient with chronic tension-type headache had coexistent migraine. The substances abused, either alone or in combination, included: caffeine in 39 patients (average daily intake of 441 mg), acetaminophen in 32 patients (average daily intake of 2187 mg), aspirin in 24 patients (average daily intake of 1807 mg), ibuprofen in 9 patients (average daily intake of 1156 mg), narcotics in 7 patients (average daily intake of 10.1 mg morphine equivalents), and ergotamine in 11 patients (average daily intake of 2.3 mg).

At the time of admission, 20 patients were already using preventive medication. Follow-up evaluations were conducted at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after discharge. At the 3-month mark, 43 patients were assessed, with 44% reporting an excellent or good outcome, 28% reporting a fair outcome, and 3 patients still overusing analgesics. At the 24-month mark, 39 patients were analyzed, with 59% reporting a good or excellent outcome, 28% reporting a fair outcome, and 5 patients still overusing analgesics, 4 of whom were not doing well. title: Survival in a case of massive paraquat ingestion.
text: A case study is presented involving a 59-year-old man who attempted suicide by ingesting the herbicide paraquat. This herbicide is known to have severe consequences, often resulting in death due to damage to the gastrointestinal tract, shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or the development of pulmonary fibrosis. In this particular case, the patient exhibited many indicators of a poor prognosis. However, prompt treatment was initiated, including decontamination of the digestive system and hemodialysis, followed by antioxidant therapy involving deferoxamine and acetylcysteine. Surprisingly, the patient only experienced nonoliguric acute renal failure, mild liver test abnormalities, and impaired CO transfer factor without any respiratory issues. The renal and hepatic disturbances resolved completely within a month, but the CO transfer factor remained altered even after 14 months. This case suggests that early administration of antioxidant therapy, such as deferoxamine and acetylcysteine, along with measures to prevent absorption or enhance elimination, can be beneficial in limiting systemic toxicity and potentially saving lives in cases of paraquat poisoning.

title: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase is a cytosolic DNA sensor that activates the type I interferon pathway.
text: The presence of DNA in the cytoplasm of mammalian cells acts as a signal that triggers immune responses in the host, such as the production of type I interferons. This activation occurs through the production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cyclic GMP-AMP or cGAMP) by cytosolic DNA. cGAMP then binds to and activates the adaptor protein STING. By using biochemical fractionation and quantitative mass spectrometry, we have identified a cGAMP synthase called cGAS, which belongs to the nucleotidyltransferase family. When cGAS is overexpressed, it activates the transcription factor IRF3 and induces interferon-β in a STING-dependent manner. On the other hand, when cGAS is knocked down, it inhibits IRF3 activation and interferon-β induction caused by DNA transfection or DNA virus infection. cGAS binds to DNA in the cytoplasm and catalyzes the synthesis of cGAMP. These findings demonstrate that cGAS serves as a sensor for cytosolic DNA, leading to the induction of interferons through the production of the second messenger cGAMP.

title: Eating pathology, emotion regulation, and emotional overeating in obese adults with Binge Eating Disorder.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the connection between emotional regulation, emotional overeating, and general eating pathology in a group of adults seeking treatment for Binge Eating Disorder (BED). The sample consisted of 326 obese adults (248 women, 78 men) who met the DSM-IV-TR criteria for BED. Before receiving treatment, participants completed various assessments, including the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Emotional Overeating Questionnaire (EOQ), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and Eating Disorder Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q). The results of hierarchical regression analyses revealed that difficulties in emotion regulation were a significant factor in both emotional overeating and general eating pathology, even after controlling for sex and negative affect. These findings suggest that emotion regulation may play a crucial role in the perpetuation of emotional overeating and eating pathology in obese adults with BED.

title: Monoallelic expression and methylation of imprinted genes in human and mouse embryonic germ cell lineages.
text: Imprinting is a type of epigenetic modification that results in the expression of certain genes from only one allele. Disrupted imprinting is thought to hinder the success of human stem cell transplantation, as studies have indicated that epigenetic marks are unstable in mouse embryonic germ (EG) and embryonic stem (ES) cells. However, the direct examination of stem cell imprinting in humans has not been conducted previously. Our research reveals that three imprinted genes, TSSC5, H19, and SNRPN, exhibit monoallelic expression in human EG-derived cells that have been differentiated in vitro. Additionally, we observed that a fourth gene, IGF2, displays partially relaxed imprinting at a ratio ranging from 4:1 to 5:1, which is similar to the ratio found in normal somatic cells. Furthermore, we discovered that an imprinting control region (ICR) responsible for regulating H19 and IGF2 imprinting maintains normal methylation, suggesting that imprinting may not pose a significant epigenetic obstacle to human EG cell transplantation. Lastly, we successfully constructed an in vitro mouse model of genomic imprinting by generating EG cells from 8.5-day embryos of an interspecific cross. In this model, undifferentiated cells exhibit biallelic expression and acquire preferential parental allele expression after differentiation. This mouse model enables the experimental manipulation of epigenetic modifications in cultured EG cells, which may not be feasible in human stem cell research.

title: Functional in vivo interactions between JNK1 and JNK2 isoforms in obesity and insulin resistance.
text: The c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNKs) play a crucial role in inflammation and interfere with insulin action in both cultured cells and whole animals. Obesity leads to an increase in overall JNK activity, but only JNK1 deficiency, not JNK2 deficiency, results in reduced fat accumulation and improved insulin sensitivity. Interestingly, Jnk2(-/-) mice exhibit higher-than-normal levels of JNK activation, particularly in the liver, suggesting an interaction between the isoforms that may have masked the metabolic effects of JNK2 in isolated mutant mice. To investigate the role of the JNK2 isoform in metabolic balance, we bred Jnk1(-/-) and Jnk2(-/-) mice and examined body weight and glucose metabolism in the resulting mutant allele combinations. Among all the viable genotypes studied, only Jnk1(-/-) and Jnk1(+/-)Jnk2(-/-) mice showed reduced body weight and increased insulin sensitivity. These two groups of mice also displayed lower overall JNK activity and cytokine expression in liver tissue compared to the other genotypes examined. These findings suggest that the JNK2 isoform is also involved in metabolic regulation, but its function is not readily apparent when JNK1 is fully expressed due to regulatory interactions between the two isoforms.

title: The immunological synapse of CTL contains a secretory domain and membrane bridges.
text: CTLs are known for their rapid destruction of target cells. However, our research demonstrates that despite the quick demise of target cells within 5 minutes of contact with CTLs, CTLs also form an immunological synapse similar to CD4 cells. This synapse consists of a ring of adhesion proteins surrounding an inner signaling molecule domain. Interestingly, lytic granule secretion takes place in a separate domain within the adhesion ring, ensuring the organization of signaling proteins during exocytosis. Through live and fixed cell studies, we have observed the transfer of target cell plasma membrane markers to the CTLs as the cells separate. Furthermore, electron microscopy has revealed the presence of membrane bridges between the CTLs and target cell membranes, suggesting a potential mechanism for this transfer.

title: Compromised intestinal epithelial barrier induces adaptive immune compensation that protects from colitis.
text: Mice that do not have junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A) experience increased permeability in the intestinal epithelium, bacterial translocation, and higher numbers of lymphocytes in the colon. However, they do not develop colitis. To understand the role of adaptive immune compensation in response to increased intestinal permeability, we studied the susceptibility of mice lacking both F11r and Rag1 to acute colitis. While mice with normal F11r and lacking Rag1 showed minimal contributions from adaptive immunity, mice lacking both F11r and Rag1 experienced increased colitis that was dependent on the presence of microflora. By eliminating specific T cell subsets and analyzing cytokines, we discovered that CD4(+) T cells producing TGF-β played a protective role in mice lacking F11r. Furthermore, the absence of JAM-A led to higher levels of mucosal and serum IgA, which depended on CD4(+) T cells and TGF-β. In mice with normal F11r but lacking Igha, the absence of IgA did not affect the disease. However, mice lacking both F11r and Igha were significantly more susceptible to acute injury-induced colitis. These findings demonstrate that adaptive immune-mediated protection is important in preventing acute colitis when the intestinal epithelial barrier is compromised.

title: Apoptosis and chemoresistance in transgenic cancer models
text: Multidrug resistance remains a problem that has not been resolved in clinical oncology. More than ten years ago, it was discovered that genes encoding cellular efflux pumps could make cancer drugs ineffective even before they reached their intended targets. Recently, it has been realized that many drugs activate a common program that leads to cell death, and mutations in this program can also cause multidrug resistance. However, it is difficult to thoroughly evaluate the role of apoptotic defects in this drug-resistant phenotype because of technical complications. This has created uncertainty about the importance of apoptosis in cell death caused by therapy. For example, analyzing patient specimens is limited because of unknown mutations in the biopsy material, and using cancer cell lines can be biased because of unnatural conditions. To overcome these limitations, we used a transgenic cancer model to study the impact of apoptosis on treatment outcomes. In this article, we discuss the potential drawbacks of cell culture assays, highlight the advantages of genetically engineered mice as model systems, and describe a transgenic mouse model that can be used to study how drugs affect primary lymphomas with specific genetic mutations at their natural location.

title: NC-100717: a versatile RGD peptide scaffold for angiogenesis imaging.
text: The use of in vivo imaging technologies has great potential in detecting disease pathology by targeting the molecular pathways involved in angiogenesis. The process of angiogenesis requires the activation and movement of endothelial cells to promote the growth of new blood vessels. These endothelial cells interact with the extracellular matrix through specific cell adhesion receptors called integrins. Peptides that contain the tripeptide sequence RGD have a strong affinity for the integrins alphavbeta3 and alphavbeta5, which are associated with angiogenesis. In this study, we synthesized and tested the binding affinity of the RGD-containing peptide NC-100717 and various molecular probes derived from it in vitro.

title: Dose-dependent effect of statins on the incidence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether statin treatment can reduce the occurrence of acute kidney injury (AKI) after cardiac surgery. The study included 2,104 patients who underwent coronary artery bypass graft or valve surgery at the Minneapolis Veterans Administration Medical Center. AKI was defined as a significant increase in serum creatinine levels within 48 hours after surgery or the need for postoperative hemodialysis. Propensity scores were used to account for differences between the statin and non-statin treatment groups. The patients were divided into high-dose (≥40 mg) and low-dose (<40 mg) statin groups based on equivalent-dose simvastatin. Out of the 2,104 patients, 68% were taking statins, and 24% developed AKI. The results showed that statin treatment was not associated with a lower incidence of postoperative AKI after adjusting for propensity scores. Additionally, statins did not have an effect on the occurrence of postoperative hemodialysis. In conclusion, this study suggests that statin treatment does not reduce the risk of AKI after cardiac surgery.

title: Comparison of allogeneic vs autologous bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stem cells delivered by transendocardial injection in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy: the POSEIDON randomized trial.
text: The safety and effectiveness of allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) compared to autologous MSCs in patients with left ventricular dysfunction due to ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) were evaluated in a phase 1/2 randomized comparison study. The study took place at a US tertiary-care referral hospital between April 2, 2010, and September 14, 2011, with a 13-month follow-up period. Transendocardial stem cell injection was used to deliver either 20 million, 100 million, or 200 million cells to 10 left ventricular sites. The main outcome measures included the incidence of treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) within 30 days post-catheterization. Efficacy assessments included various tests and measurements related to heart function. The results showed that both allogeneic and autologous MSC therapies had low rates of treatment-emergent SAEs, including immunologic reactions. MSC injection had a positive impact on patient functional capacity, quality of life, and ventricular remodeling. The study concluded that both allogeneic and autologous MSCs were safe and effective in treating patients with ICM.

title: Periosteal bone formation--a neglected determinant of bone strength.
text: Smaller life forms can easily search for food on the undersides of branches or steep cliffs without being affected by gravity. However, larger animals must move quickly against gravity in order to find dinner and avoid becoming prey. To meet this need, their long bones serve as lever mechanisms, which are remarkable examples of biomechanical engineering. These bones achieve the seemingly contradictory qualities of being both stiff and flexible, strong and lightweight, thanks to their material composition and structural design. The stiffness of the bones comes from the presence of hydroxyapatite crystals encrusting the triple-helical structure of collagen type I, which provides...

title: Triglyceride depletion of brown adipose tissue enables analysis of mitochondrial respiratory function in permeabilized biopsies.
text:
Recent research has provided increasing evidence that mitochondria, the powerhouses of cells, play a crucial role in the development and progression of obesity and related diseases in fat cells. Traditionally, scientists have assessed mitochondrial function in brown adipose tissue (BAT) by measuring the levels and activity of mitochondrial enzymes, or by studying respiration in isolated mitochondria. However, isolating mitochondria is time-consuming, requires a large amount of tissue, and disrupts the natural connections between mitochondria within the cell.

In this study, we present a new and efficient method for analyzing mitochondrial respiratory states in BAT biopsies. This method involves depleting intracellular triglycerides and then permeabilizing the tissue. By using this protocol, we were able to analyze all mitochondrial respiratory states, including phosphorylation (OXPHOS), no-phosphorylation (LEAK), and uncoupled (ETS) states. We were also able to study the use of substrates for complex I, complex II, and cytochrome c, which confirmed the integrity of the mitochondria and the effectiveness of the preparation.

By reducing the amount of tissue required to approximately 17 mg wet weight, our protocol allows for the analysis of small regions of BAT in both human and animal models. This opens up new possibilities for investigating the mechanisms that regulate mitochondrial function in both healthy individuals and those with diseases. Ultimately, this research will contribute to a better understanding of mitochondrial function and its role in maintaining health or contributing to disease.

title: HES-1 preserves purified hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo and accumulates side population cells in vivo.
text: The c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (KSL) cell population in mice contains long-term hematopoietic reconstituting cells. Among these cells, the CD34(low/-) cells are the most purified population of hematopoietic stem cells in the adult bone marrow. In this study, we demonstrate that introducing the HES-1 gene into CD34(low/-)c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (34-KSL) cells using retrovirus-mediated transduction preserves their long-term reconstituting activity in vitro. We also observe that cells derived from the HES-1-transduced 34-KSL population produce progenies with characteristics such as negative Hoechst dye staining (side population) and a CD34(low/-) profile in the bone marrow KSL population in recipient mice. These progenies are produced at significantly higher ratios compared to nontransduced 34-KSL-derived competitor cells. Based on these findings, we conclude that HES-1 preserves the long-term reconstituting hematopoietic activity of 34-KSL stem cells in an ex vivo setting. Up-regulating HES-1 protein in the 34-KSL population without retrovirus transduction could potentially be a powerful method for expanding hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Measuring Absolute RNA Copy Numbers at High Temporal Resolution Reveals Transcriptome Kinetics in Development.
text: Transcript regulation plays a crucial role in the functioning of cells, and any misregulation can result in diseases. Despite the availability of technologies to study the transcriptome, our understanding of transcript kinetics is still incomplete, which hampers quantitative biology. This is particularly challenging in embryonic development, where rapid changes in gene expression determine the fate of cells. To address this, we conducted extensive sampling of Xenopus embryos at high frequencies and normalized the sequence reads to obtain accurate gene expression trajectories in absolute transcript numbers. Our findings reveal that during a developmental period equivalent to the first 8 weeks of human gestation, transcript kinetics vary significantly, spanning eight orders of magnitude. By organizing genes based on their expression dynamics, we discovered that genes with similar temporal expression patterns often share common functions. Interestingly, we observed that a single parameter, the characteristic timescale, can effectively classify transcript kinetics on a global scale and differentiate genes involved in development from those associated with cellular metabolism. In summary, our analysis provides unprecedented insights into the rearrangement of maternal and embryonic transcripts, revolutionizing our ability to conduct quantitative biology.

title: Inflammasome activation by adenylate cyclase toxin directs Th17 responses and protection against Bordetella pertussis.
text: The production of IL-1beta through the inflammasome is crucial in the development of certain autoinflammatory diseases and may also be linked to the creation of IL-17-producing CD4(+) T (Th17) cells that cause autoimmunity. However, the impact of the inflammasome on adaptive immunity to infection has not been explored. This article demonstrates that inflammasome-mediated IL-1beta plays a vital role in the generation of Ag-specific Th17 cells and in providing protective immunity against Bordetella pertussis infection. Through a respiratory challenge model in mice, it was observed that B. pertussis infection was significantly worse in IL-1R type I-defective (IL-1RI(-/-)) mice. It was discovered that adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA), a key virulence factor secreted by B. pertussis, stimulated the production of IL-1beta by dendritic cells through the activation of caspase-1 and the NALP3-containing inflammasome complex. Mutant toxins were used to show that CyaA-induced caspase-1 activation did not rely on adenylate cyclase enzyme activity but rather on the pore-forming ability of CyaA. Additionally, CyaA facilitated the development of Ag-specific Th17 cells in wild-type mice but not in IL-1RI(-/-) mice. Furthermore, IL-17-defective mice had a higher bacterial load. These findings demonstrate that CyaA, a virulence factor of B. pertussis, stimulates innate IL-1beta production through the NALP3 inflammasome, thereby influencing T cell responses towards the Th17 subtype. In addition to its known role in evading host immunity, these findings suggest that CyaA can promote IL-1beta-mediated Th17 cells, which aid in clearing the bacteria from the respiratory tract.

title: Infection and apoptosis as a combined inflammatory trigger.
text: Although there is extensive research on the inflammatory phagocytosis of microbial pathogens and the non-inflammatory phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, the consequences of the innate immune system recognizing host cells undergoing apoptosis as a direct result of infection remain unclear. In this scenario, the innate immune system is faced with conflicting signals from both apoptotic cells and the infecting pathogen. Activation of nuclear receptors has been linked to the recognition of apoptotic cells, while Toll-like receptors are the primary inflammatory receptors engaged during infection. When these two signals combine, a series of events occur, starting with the suppression of a specific subset of genes involved in the inflammatory response and culminating in the activation of a T helper-17 adaptive immune response. This immune response is particularly effective in eliminating the infecting pathogen and facilitating the repair of damaged host tissue caused by the infection.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia with t(14;19)(q32;q13) is characterized by atypical morphologic and immunophenotypic features and distinctive genetic features.
text: The t(14;19)(q32;q13) is a rare chromosomal abnormality that involves the IGH@ and BCL3 loci and is often found in B-cell malignancies. In this study, we provide a detailed analysis of 14 cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) with this translocation. The patients, consisting of 10 men and 4 women, all exhibited lymphocytosis, with 10 also experiencing lymphadenopathy. The blood and bone marrow lymphocytes were predominantly small, but displayed atypical cytological and immunophenotypic features. The t(14;19) was present in the neoplastic stem line in all cases, and was the only abnormality in 4 of them. Additional cytogenetic abnormalities were observed in 10 cases, including trisomy 12 in 9 and complex karyotypes in 7. Fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed the presence of the IGH@/BCL3 fusion gene in all cases. Furthermore, all cases had unmutated IGHV genes, with only 7 expressing ZAP70. IGHV4-39 was preferentially used in 7 cases. Our findings suggest that the t(14;19)(q32;q13) identifies a distinct subset of CLL/SLL with unique clinicopathological and genetic characteristics. Additionally, this translocation may represent an early, potentially primary, genetic event.

title: Risk factors for the development of gallstone recurrence following medical dissolution. The British-Italian Gallstone Study Group.
text:
AIM: To evaluate the risk factors for gallstone recurrence after non-surgical treatment.
METHODS: A prospective follow-up study was conducted on a multicentre cohort of patients who had undergone gallstone dissolution without surgery. The study was conducted in six gastroenterology units in the UK and Italy. A total of 163 patients were included in the study and were followed up with ultrasound scans and clinical assessments every 6 months for up to 6 years. Various factors such as patient characteristics, gallstone characteristics, treatment modalities, and follow-up variables were assessed as potential risk factors for gallstone recurrence using univariate and multivariate analysis.
RESULTS: During the follow-up period, 45 cases of gallstone recurrence were observed. The presence of multiple primary gallstones and a longer time taken for complete gallstone dissolution were found to be significantly associated with an increased risk of recurrence. The appearance of biliary sludge during follow-up was also significantly related to the development of gallstone recurrence. The use of statins or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents did not provide protection against recurrence.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients with primary single stones are the most suitable candidates for non-surgical treatment of gallstones due to their low risk of recurrence. The association between recurrence and biliary sludge formation, as well as the time taken for dissolution of primary stones, indirectly supports the role of impaired gallbladder motility in the development of gallstones.

title: Deletion of the developmentally essential gene ATR in adult mice leads to age-related phenotypes and stem cell loss.
text: Defects in the DNA damage response (DDR) have been linked to developmental abnormalities, cancer, and premature aging. Mutations in the ATR checkpoint regulator have been found to cause developmental defects in both mice (resulting in pregastrulation lethality) and humans (leading to Seckel syndrome). In this study, we demonstrate that the elimination of ATR in adult mice results in disruptions in tissue homeostasis and the rapid onset of age-related characteristics, such as hair graying, hair loss, kyphosis, osteoporosis, thymic involution, fibrosis, and other abnormalities. Through histological and genetic analyses, we have determined that the deletion of ATR causes immediate cellular loss in tissues that rely on continuous cell proliferation for maintenance. Notably, the thymic involution, hair loss, and hair graying observed in ATR knockout mice were accompanied by significant reductions in tissue-specific stem and progenitor cells, as well as the depletion of tissue renewal and homeostatic capacity. Taken together, these findings suggest that the diminished regenerative ability in adults resulting from the deletion of a DDR gene essential for development is enough to trigger the premature manifestation of age-related characteristics.

title: Conventional and monocyte-derived CD11b(+) dendritic cells initiate and maintain T helper 2 cell-mediated immunity to house dust mite allergen.
text: The role of dendritic cells (DCs) in allergic airway inflammation is crucial, but it remains unclear which specific subset of DCs is responsible for this process. In this study, we used CD64 and MAR-1 staining to effectively distinguish between CD11b(+) monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) and conventional DCs (cDCs). We then examined the uptake, migration, and presentation of antigens by lung and lymph node (LN) DCs in response to inhaled house dust mite (HDM). Our findings indicate that CD11b(+) cDCs, rather than CD103(+) cDCs, are primarily responsible for inducing T helper 2 (Th2) cell immunity in HDM-specific T cells both in vitro and in vivo, leading to the development of asthma. Additionally, our studies in Flt3l(-/-) mice, which lack all cDCs, revealed that moDCs alone were sufficient to induce Th2 cell-mediated immunity, but only when a high dose of HDM was administered. The main function of moDCs was found to be the production of proinflammatory chemokines and the presentation of allergens in the lung during the challenge. Therefore, we have identified migratory CD11b(+) cDCs as the primary subset responsible for inducing Th2 cell-mediated immunity in the LN, while moDCs play a crucial role in orchestrating allergic inflammation in the lung.

title: Interplay between the dividing cell and its neighbors regulates adherens junction formation during cytokinesis in epithelial tissue.
text: The formation of adherens junctions (AJs) during cell division is not well understood. In our study, we discovered that AJ formation is synchronized with cytokinesis and involves interactions between the dividing cell and its neighboring cells. As the cytokinetic ring contracts, neighboring cells accumulate Myosin II and generate cortical tension, which establishes the initial shape of the daughter cell interface. However, the presence of neighboring cell membranes hinders the formation of AJs. Once the midbody is formed and neighboring cells withdraw, actin polymerization, guided by Arp2/3, maintains the geometry of AJs and regulates their final length, as well as the arrangement of epithelial cells after division. We propose that cytokinesis in epithelial tissues is a collaborative process, where the dividing cell and its neighbors work together to control the spatial and temporal aspects of AJ formation, while also preserving tissue cohesion.

title: Cancer stem cells in solid tumours: accumulating evidence and unresolved questions
text: Solid tumors pose a significant challenge in cancer treatment and are a major burden on patients. The hypothesis of cancer stem cells (CSCs) offers a compelling explanation for the resistance to therapy and dormant nature observed in many of these tumors. It is becoming increasingly evident that various solid tumors are organized in a hierarchical manner and sustained by a unique subset of CSCs. Recent studies using mouse models of epithelial tumor development have provided direct evidence supporting the CSC hypothesis, although other models of tumor heterogeneity also appear to be applicable. The clinical significance of CSCs is still a matter of debate, but initial findings suggest that targeted therapies may be feasible.

title: The structure of the follistatin:activin complex reveals antagonism of both type I and type II receptor binding.
text: The stimulation of various cellular differentiation and growth responses is achieved by TGF-beta ligands through the activation of type I and II receptors. To regulate these physiological responses, ligand antagonists like follistatin are crucial. In this study, we present the structure of activin A, a TGF-beta ligand, when bound to the high-affinity antagonist follistatin. By encircling activin, two follistatin molecules effectively neutralize the ligand by burying a significant portion of its residues and receptor binding sites. Previous research had suggested that follistatin does not block type I receptor binding. However, the crystal structure reveals that the N-terminal domain of follistatin has an unexpected fold that mimics a universal type I receptor motif and occupies the receptor binding site. The formation of follistatin:BMP:type I receptor complexes can be explained by the stoichiometric and geometric arrangement of the activin:follistatin complex. The manner in which follistatin binds to ligands has significant implications for its ability to neutralize both homo- and heterodimeric ligands within this growth factor family.

title: The activity of siRNA in mammalian cells is related to structural target accessibility: a comparison with antisense oligonucleotides.
text: We conducted a study to examine the relationship between local target accessibility and the effectiveness of siRNA in inhibiting the target gene. We used a computational approach to assess target accessibility, which has been previously validated through experimental probing of target RNA. We selected two sites on ICAM-1 mRNA that were predicted to be accessible and one site predicted to have an inaccessible structure. We tested siRNA constructs targeting these sites to suppress ICAM-1 gene expression in ECV304 cells. We compared the effectiveness of siRNA with antisense oligonucleotides (asON) in a target-dependent manner. The concentration-dependent suppression of siRNA indicated a significant difference in activity between active siRNAs (IC50 approximately 0.2-0.5 nM) and an inactive siRNA (IC50 > or = 1 microM), which aligns with the activity pattern of asON when considering predicted target accessibility. The exceptional activity of siRNA si2B (IC50 = 0.24 nM) suggests that not all siRNAs active at typical concentrations of >10-100 nM belong to this highly active category. These findings propose a method to assess target accessibility for siRNA and support the design of effective siRNA constructs. This approach can be automated, work at high throughput, and incorporate additional parameters relevant to siRNA's biological activity.

title: Rapid accumulation of mutations during seed-to-seed propagation of mismatch-repair-defective Arabidopsis.
text: Throughout the numerous cell divisions that occur before the formation of plant gametes, the apical-meristem and floral antecedents are constantly exposed to both internal and external mutagenic threats. While some harmful recessive mutations may be eliminated during the growth of haploid gametophytes and early embryos, indicating a quality-checking process called "haplosufficiency," the presence of multiple plant genome-maintenance systems suggests the need for rigorous quality control during prior diploid growth. In order to investigate the hypothesis that prior mismatch repair (MMR) plays a crucial role in safeguarding plant genetic accuracy, we conducted a study using Arabidopsis. We simultaneously propagated 36 lines with MMR deficiencies (Atmsh2-1) and 36 wild-type lines. The Atmsh2-1 lines exhibited a rapid accumulation of various mutations: by the fifth generation (G5), the plants displayed abnormalities in morphology, development, fertility, germination efficiency, seed/silique development, and seed set. Only two Atmsh2-1 lines appeared normal at G5, while all 36 wild-type lines remained unaffected. Analysis of insertion/deletion mutations at six repeat-sequence (microsatellite) loci revealed that each Atmsh2-1 line had developed its own unique "fingerprint," resulting from as many as 10 microsatellite mutations in a single line. Therefore, MMR during diploid growth is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the plant genome.

title: Archaeal chromatin and transcription.
text: Archaea possess a range of DNA binding proteins that can bind to DNA sequences independently, indicating the evolution of multiple solutions to the problem of compacting the genome. Some of these proteins undergo specific modifications, such as lysine acetylation or methylation, similar to the modifications seen in histones that regulate chromatin structure and transcription in eukaryotes. The process of transcription initiation in Archaea closely resembles that of eukaryotes, specifically RNA polymerase II (RNAPII). However, Archaea lack the multi-subunit complexes found in eukaryotes that remodel chromatin and activate RNAPII initiation. Instead, they have specific regulators that can repress or activate transcription in a manner similar to the bacterial paradigm of regulating promoter binding by RNAP. Repressors compete with the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) and TFB for the TATA-box and TFB-recognition elements (BRE) of the archaeal promoter, or with the archaeal RNAP for the site of transcription initiation. The regulation of transcription initiation by repressors binding to specific sites is consistent with the lack of sequence conservation in these regions. However, most Archaea have only one TBP and/or TFB, which suggests that they must bind to similar TATA-box and BRE sequences upstream of most genes. Repressors that compete with TBP and/or TFB binding must therefore also interact with transcript-specific regulatory sites near or distant from the TATA-box/BRE region. The fate of the archaeal TBP and TFB after transcription initiation is still unknown. Based on their functional similarity to their eukaryotic counterparts in the RNAPII system, it is expected that archaeal TBP and possibly TFB remain bound to the TATA-box/BRE region after transcription initiation. However, this seems unlikely as it may limit repressor competition at this site to only the first round of transcription initiation.

title: Temporal segregation of 4-1BB versus CD28-mediated costimulation: 4-1BB ligand influences T cell numbers late in the primary response and regulates the size of the T cell memory response following influenza infection.
text: This report demonstrates that CD28(-/-) mice have a severe impairment in the initial expansion of D(b)/NP366-374-specific CD8 T cells when infected with influenza virus. On the other hand, 4-1BB ligand (4-1BBL)(-/-) mice do not show any defect in primary T cell expansion in response to influenza virus. However, 4-1BBL(-/-) mice do show a decrease in D(b)/NP366-374-specific T cells later in the primary response. When these mice are challenged with influenza virus for a second time, 4-1BBL(-/-) mice have a lower number of D(b)/NP366-374-specific T cells compared to wild-type mice. This reduction brings the level of CD8 T cell expansion during the secondary response down to the level of a primary response, resulting in a decrease in CTL effector function. In contrast, the antibody responses and secondary CD4 T cell responses to influenza are not affected by 4-1BBL deficiency. Therefore, CD28 is crucial for the initial expansion of T cells, while 4-1BB/4-1BBL signaling affects T cell numbers later in the response and is necessary for the survival and/or responsiveness of the memory CD8 T cell pool.

title: Functional role of high-affinity anandamide transport, as revealed by selective inhibition.
text: Anandamide, a natural substance that binds to cannabinoid receptors in the central nervous system, is released by neurons when they become stimulated and is quickly deactivated. The process by which anandamide is deactivated is not fully understood, but it is believed to occur either through transport into cells or through enzymatic breakdown. In laboratory studies, a compound called N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)arachidonylamide (AM404) was found to prevent the accumulation of anandamide in rat neurons and astrocytes, suggesting that this accumulation is due to transport facilitated by a carrier. Although AM404 does not activate cannabinoid receptors or inhibit the breakdown of anandamide, it does enhance the response of these receptors to anandamide both in laboratory settings and in living organisms. These findings suggest that carrier-mediated transport may play a crucial role in ending the biological effects of anandamide and could potentially be targeted by drugs.

title: Silibinin inhibits the invasion of IL-6-stimulated colon cancer cells via selective JNK/AP-1/MMP-2 modulation in vitro.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of silibinin on cell invasion in IL-6-stimulated LoVo colon cancer cells. Silibinin is a flavonoid with antihepatotoxic properties and various anticancer capabilities. The study found that silibinin reduced the expression of matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), which is involved in cell invasion. Western blot data showed a 1.6- or 1.7-fold decrease in MMP-2 protein expression when treated with silibinin or a JNK inhibitor. Zymography and confocal microscopy also confirmed these results. Silibinin was found to inhibit the binding activity of activator protein-1 (AP-1) and the promoter activity of MMP-2 via AP-1 binding. Further experiments demonstrated that silibinin inhibited cell proliferation and invasion in IL-6-stimulated LoVo cells. These findings suggest that silibinin could be used as a novel antimetastatic treatment for colon cancer.

title: Immigration cohorts and residential overcrowding in southern California
text: How much do immigrants reduce their high rates of residential overcrowding as they spend more time in the United States? This question is answered using a "double cohort" method that includes both birth cohorts and immigration cohorts. This method allows us to separate the effects of duration of immigration from the effects of aging, as cohorts go through different stages of life where family sizes may change. The analysis shows that trends among cohorts are different from the overall pattern observed at a single point in time. The increase in income among cohorts is found to be a significant factor in the decrease of overcrowding over time. However, trends among Hispanic immigrants diverge from those of other groups, indicating less reduction in overcrowding and even increases in certain age groups.

title: Expression of green fluorescent protein in the ureteric bud of transgenic mice: a new tool for the analysis of ureteric bud morphogenesis.
text:
The process of ureteric bud growth and branching is complex and crucial for the development of the collecting duct system and the number of nephrons in the metanephric kidney. Although we have started to understand the genes involved in regulating this process, our knowledge of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying ureteric bud morphogenesis is still limited. Additionally, the timing and sequence of branching and elongation that lead to the formation of the kidney's collecting system can only be inferred from retrospective staining or microdissection of fixed samples.

To address these issues, we have created transgenic mice strains that express a green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the ureteric bud under the control of the Hoxb7 promoter. In these mice, GFP is present in every branch of the ureteric bud during renal development and in the epithelial cells derived from it in the adult kidney. The GFP fluorescence can be easily observed in living tissue, allowing us to track the dynamic growth and branching of the ureteric bud over several days when the kidneys are cultured in vitro. By using confocal microscopy, we can analyze the branching of the ureteric bud in all three dimensions.

These transgenic mice are a powerful tool for studying the normal patterns of ureteric bud morphogenesis and investigating how the bud responds to growth factors, matrix elements, and other agents that regulate its growth and branching.

title: Biological properties of herpes simplex virus 2 replication-defective mutant strains in a murine nasal infection model.
text:
In this study, we utilized a mouse nasal model to investigate the characteristics of different strains of herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) in vivo. The main focus was on the wild-type (wt) strain, the TK-negative strain, and the replication-defective strains. We found that the nasal septa tissue is the primary site for viral replication after intranasal (i.n.) inoculation.

When the wt strain 186 syn(+)-1 virus was administered at doses of 10(4) PFU or higher per nostril, it caused lethal encephalitis. At lower doses, no neurons in the trigeminal ganglia showed positivity for the latency-associated transcript, indicating the absence of latent infection.

The TK-negative mutant virus 186DeltaKpn replicated in the nasal septa tissue but only showed low-level replication in the trigeminal ganglia at one specific timepoint. In contrast, in situ hybridization of the trigeminal ganglia revealed that the number of LAT-positive neurons was directly proportional to the inoculum dose, ranging from 10(3) to 10(6) PFU per nare.

The replication-defective mutant virus 5BlacZ did not replicate in the nasal septa tissue and did not persist in viral DNA at the inoculation site or the trigeminal ganglia. However, when 5BlacZ or the double-mutant dl5-29 were inoculated at distal sites, they reduced acute replication and latent infection of 186DeltaKpn following intranasal challenge.

This infection model serves as a valuable biological system for studying the characteristics of HSV-2 strains. It also demonstrates that replication-defective mutant strains do not persist at the sites of inoculation or in sensory ganglia. However, they can induce immune protection, leading to a reduction in the latent viral load of a challenge virus.

title: The sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor agonist FTY720 modulates dendritic cell trafficking in vivo.
text: FTY720, a pro-drug, is currently in phase III clinical trials to prevent allograft rejection. Once phosphorylated, FTY720 targets the G protein-coupled-sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) on lymphocytes, inhibiting their movement from lymphoid organs and their circulation to sites of inflammation. However, the impact of FTY720 on dendritic cell (DC) trafficking has not been assessed. In this study, we demonstrate that murine DCs express all five S1PR subtypes (S1PR1-5). When administered to C57BL/10 mice, FTY720 significantly reduced circulating T and B lymphocytes within 24 hours, but did not affect blood-borne DCs, which were actually increased for up to 96 hours. However, DCs in lymph nodes and spleen were reduced. The number of syngeneic or allogeneic DCs transferred into the blood was significantly increased in FTY720-treated animals, while donor-derived DCs and allostimulatory activity for host naïve T cells in the spleen were reduced. Administration of the selective S1PR1 agonist SEW2871 also increased circulating DC numbers. Flow analysis showed that FTY720 administration downregulated the expression of CD11b, CD31/PECAM-1, CD54/ICAM-1, and CCR7 on blood-borne DCs. Additionally, transendothelial migration of FTY720-P-treated immature DCs to the CCR7 ligand CCL19 was reduced. These findings suggest that FTY720's immunosuppressive effects may be attributed to its modulation of DC trafficking.

title: Sustained survivin expression from OX40 costimulatory signals drives T cell clonal expansion.
text: The T cell receptor (TCR) and costimulatory molecules play a crucial role in generating a high number of effector T cells. Our study reveals that OX40 cosignaling controls the expression of Survivin in peripheral T cells through sustained activation of PI3k and PKB. Interestingly, OX40 induces Survivin independently of mitotic progression in late G1 phase. When Survivin is blocked, it inhibits the transition to S-phase and division of T cells, ultimately leading to apoptosis. On the other hand, the expression of Survivin alone is sufficient to restore proliferation and counteract apoptosis in T cells lacking costimulation. Additionally, Survivin can rescue T cell expansion in vivo. While Survivin allows effector T cells to accumulate in large numbers, the survival of T cells after active division requires the presence of Bcl-2 family proteins. Therefore, sustained expression of Survivin through costimulatory signaling is crucial for maintaining T cell division over time and regulating the extent of clonal expansion.

title: The Combination of Exercise and Respiratory Training Improves Respiratory Muscle Function in Pulmonary Hypertension
text: This prospective study aimed to evaluate the impact of exercise and respiratory training on respiratory muscle strength and 6-minute walking distance (6MWD) in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Seven PAH patients, confirmed through invasive methods, participated in a 3-week in-hospital training program, followed by 12 weeks of continued training at home. Medication remained unchanged throughout the study. Blinded observers assessed efficacy parameters at baseline, after 3 weeks, and after 15 weeks. Respiratory muscle function was evaluated using twitch mouth pressure (TwPmo) during nonvolitional supramaximal magnetic phrenic nerve stimulation. The training program was well-tolerated and feasible, with excellent compliance from all patients. TwPmo values increased from 0.86 ± 0.37 kPa at baseline to 1.27 ± 0.44 kPa at the final assessment. Similarly, 6MWD improved from 417 ± 51 m to 498 ± 39 m. Both TwPmo and 6MWD showed significant increases between baseline and the final assessment. These findings suggest that exercise and respiratory training, when used alongside medical therapy, may effectively enhance respiratory muscle strength and exercise capacity in PAH patients. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these results.

title: Dual role of the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis in the development of autoimmune myocarditis: induction by IL-12 and protection by IFN-gamma.
text: The reciprocal regulation between IL-12 and IFN-gamma, as well as their involvement in type 1 inflammatory responses, is known to contribute to tissue damage in autoimmune diseases. To understand the role of the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis in autoimmune myocarditis, we conducted a study. We found that mice lacking IL-12p40, a component of IL-12, were resistant to myocarditis. In the absence of IL-12, CD4(+) T cells specific to self-antigens exhibited reduced proliferation and increased production of Th2 cytokines. On the other hand, mice lacking IFN-gamma developed severe autoimmune disease, and blocking IL-4R signaling did not make IL-12p40-deficient mice susceptible to myocarditis. This indicates that IL-12 triggers autoimmunity through a mechanism that is independent of the effector cytokines IFN-gamma and IL-4. In summary, our findings suggest that the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis has a dual role in the development of autoimmune myocarditis. While IL-12 promotes disease by promoting the expansion of Th1-type cells, IFN-gamma production from these cells limits the progression of the disease.

title: Somatic and Germline Diversification of a Putative Immunoreceptor within One Phylum: Dscam in Arthropods.
text: Arthropod Dscam is a receptor utilized by the nervous and immune systems, similar to the human Down Syndrome cell adhesion molecule. However, unlike in vertebrates, arthropods have a wide range of Dscam isoforms that play a crucial role in determining neuronal identity during nervous system development. This chapter explores the various ways in which Dscam diversifies in arthropods' evolution and its controversial role in the immune system. In insects and crustaceans, the Dscam gene undergoes mutually exclusive alternative splicing, resulting in three clusters of duplicated exons that encode the variable parts of the receptor. This process generates over 10,000 isoforms of Dscam. In more primitive arthropods like centipedes, Dscam diversity arises from a combination of numerous germline genes (over 80), with alternative splicing affecting only one exon cluster in about half of these genes. In even more primitive arthropods such as chelicerates, no alternative splicing occurs, but there are dozens of germline Dscam genes. Compared to controlling the expression of multiple germline genes, somatic alternative splicing within a single gene offers a simpler way to express a diverse repertoire of Dscam. Dscam is expressed by hemocytes and is considered a phagocytic receptor, although it is also found in solution. Further research is needed to understand its binding to pathogens, its role in phagocytosis, its potential involvement in determining hemocyte identity, its expression kinetics, and the regulation of its RNA splicing in order to fully comprehend the relationship between Dscam diversity and immunity.

title: Epidemiology, health-related quality of life and economic burden of binge eating disorder: a systematic literature review
text:
The purpose of this study was to conduct a systematic review on the epidemiology, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and economic burden of binge eating disorder (BED). The researchers performed a literature search of English-language articles using various databases. The search for epidemiology studies was limited to those published between 2009 and 2013. The cost data were adjusted to 2012 US$ purchasing power parities. The quality of all included studies was assessed.

A total of 49 articles were included in the review. Out of these, 31 reported data on the epidemiology of BED, 16 focused on the HRQoL burden, and 7 examined the economic burden. The diagnosis of BED was made using the 4th Edition of The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) criteria in 46 studies. The lifetime prevalence of BED in the general population (according to DSM-IV) ranged from 1.1% to 1.9%.

The findings revealed that BED was associated with significant impairment in both physical and mental aspects of HRQoL. The mean scores for the Short Form 36 Physical and Mental Component Summary varied between 31.1 and 47.3, and 32.0 and 49.8, respectively. Compared to individuals without an eating disorder, those with BED had higher healthcare utilization and costs. The annual direct healthcare costs per BED patient ranged from $2,372 to $3,731.

In conclusion, BED is a serious eating disorder that negatively affects HRQoL and is associated with increased healthcare utilization and costs. However, the limited literature on this topic highlights the need for further research, particularly to gain a better understanding of the long-term HRQoL and economic burden of BED.

title: Subcellular steroid/nuclear receptor dynamics.
text: Steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, retinoic acids, and vitamin D attach to their receptors, now known as steroid/nuclear receptors. Once bound, these receptors move either within the cell or into the nucleus and form large protein complexes with cofactors. This process either activates or suppresses gene transcription, making steroid/nuclear receptors ligand-dependent transcription factors. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its variants has revealed that the subcellular distribution of many steroid/nuclear receptors is more dynamic than previously believed. Some receptors shuttle between the cytoplasm and nucleus. Unliganded steroid/nuclear receptors can be categorized into three groups based on their distribution: primarily in the nucleus, in the cytoplasm, or with a mixed distribution. However, the addition of a ligand causes the receptors to almost entirely relocate to the nucleus. Hormonal stimulation causes the receptors to transition from a uniform pattern to a heterogeneous dot-like image within the nucleus. Ligand binding to steroid/nuclear receptors recruits numerous proteins, including cofactors, which triggers the redistribution of receptor complexes in the nucleus. This focal organization may involve more complex processes than simple DNA binding sites for transcription. The activities and interactions of steroid/nuclear receptors can be visualized and localized within a single cell.

title: EMT, the cytoskeleton, and cancer cell invasion
text: The spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body, known as the metastatic process, relies on the cancer cells leaving the original tumor and acquiring the ability to migrate and invade. This is achieved through a process called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), where the cancer cells undergo changes in their adhesive properties and utilize developmental processes to gain migratory and invasive characteristics. This involves a significant reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and the formation of membrane protrusions necessary for invasive growth. However, the molecular mechanisms behind these cellular changes are still not well understood, and further research is needed to better understand the different migratory organelles involved, such as lamellipodia, filopodia, invadopodia, and podosomes. Importantly, there is currently a lack of direct experimental evidence linking the formation of migratory membrane protrusions to the process of EMT and tumor metastasis. In this review, we provide a summary of recent advancements in understanding the molecular processes and factors involved in EMT and the formation of invasive membrane protrusions.

title: Different response of human glioma tumor-initiating cells to epidermal growth factor receptor kinase inhibitors.
text:
We conducted a study to assess the sensitivity of human glioma tumor-initiating cells (TICs) to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase inhibitors, specifically erlotinib and gefitinib. These TICs are believed to play a crucial role in the development, progression, and recurrence of tumors. We isolated cells from seven glioblastomas and cultivated them under conditions that promote neural stem cell growth.
