title: Adapting the WHO package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions, Samoa
text:
Samoa has been facing challenges in addressing the burden of noncommunicable diseases at various levels, including the health system, community, and individuals. In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) implemented a package of essential interventions for noncommunicable diseases in low-resource settings in seven villages across Samoa. The National Steering Committee Members took the lead in designing and implementing a screening process, with the help of local facilitators and healthcare workers who collected health and lifestyle data. The WHO/International Society of Hypertension risk assessment was used to identify individuals over the age of 40 who were at high risk of noncommunicable diseases. 

Samoa is a small island developing state that has been experiencing an increase in morbidity and mortality due to noncommunicable diseases. A national survey revealed that 50.1% of the adult population in Samoa, which amounts to 595 out of 1188 individuals, is at high risk of developing such diseases. Unfortunately, a significant number of noncommunicable diseases remain undiagnosed or untreated due to a shortage of healthcare staff and a lack of awareness about risk factors. 

During the screening campaign, the teams collected data from 2234 adults. Among individuals over the age of 40, 6.7% were identified as being at high risk and were encouraged to seek treatment or manage their risk factors. The community members also developed an awareness program to enhance understanding of lifestyle risk factors. 

One of the key lessons learned from this initiative was the importance of engaging community members in the screening campaign. By identifying individuals at high risk of developing noncommunicable diseases, early intervention became possible. Additionally, education played a crucial role in raising awareness about the symptom-free nature of early-stage noncommunicable diseases.

title: Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016
text: In the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2016, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of alcohol use and its impact on health. We gathered data from 195 locations between 1990 and 2016 to estimate alcohol consumption, alcohol-related deaths, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). Our methods included analyzing individual and population-level alcohol consumption data from 694 sources, as well as studying the risks associated with alcohol use from 592 studies. We made improvements to previous estimates by adjusting for unrecorded consumption, conducting a new meta-analysis of health outcomes, and developing a method to determine the optimal level of alcohol consumption for individual health. Our findings revealed that globally, alcohol use was the seventh leading risk factor for both deaths and DALYs in 2016. It accounted for 2.2% of female deaths and 6.8% of male deaths. Among individuals aged 15-49, alcohol use was the leading risk factor, with 3.8% of female deaths and 12.2% of male deaths attributable to alcohol. For this age group, the main causes of alcohol-related deaths were tuberculosis, road injuries, and self-harm. In individuals aged 50 and older, cancers accounted for a significant proportion of alcohol-related deaths. We also found that the level of alcohol consumption that minimizes harm is zero. These results suggest the need for global alcohol control policies to focus on reducing overall consumption. The study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: The Dual Immunoregulatory function of Nlrp12 in T Cell-Mediated Immune Response: Lessons from Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
text: Although the cause of multiple sclerosis (MS) is still unknown, T cells play a crucial role in this disease. Immune cells respond to pathogens and danger signals through pattern-recognition receptors (PRR). Studies have suggested that Nlrp12, an intracellular PRR, is involved in the development of a mouse model of MS called Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis (EAE). In this research, we used induced and spontaneous models of EAE, as well as T cell assays in the lab, to investigate whether Nlrp12 inhibits the Th1 response and prevents T-cell mediated autoimmunity. Our findings indicate that Nlrp12 has a protective effect in induced EAE by reducing the IFNγ/IL-4 ratio in lymph nodes, but it promotes the development of spontaneous EAE in 2D2 T cell receptor (TCR) transgenic mice. Further investigation into the mechanism of Nlrp12's activity in T cell response revealed that it inhibits T cell proliferation and suppresses the Th1 response by reducing the production of IFNγ and IL-2. Upon TCR activation, Nlrp12 inhibits Akt and NF-κB phosphorylation, while having no effect on S6 phosphorylation in the mTOR pathway. In conclusion, we propose a model that explains the dual immunoregulatory function of Nlrp12 in EAE, as well as a model that explains the molecular mechanism of Nlrp12-dependent regulation of T cell response.

title: Acute and chronic exercise in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: evidence of structural and functional plasticity and intact angiogenic signalling in skeletal muscle
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) responses to acute submaximal exercise and training effects in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Six patients and six healthy matched controls participated in knee-extensor exercise (KE) at 50% of maximum work rate before and after KE training. Muscle biopsies were taken to assess skeletal muscle structure and the angiogenic response. Before training, patients with HFrEF exhibited higher leg vascular resistance and greater noradrenaline spillover during submaximal KE exercise. However, skeletal muscle structure and VEGF response were generally not different between groups. After training, resistance and noradrenaline spillover were reduced in the patients. Although VEGF did not respond to acute exercise in the trained state, capillarity was increased. Muscle fiber cross-sectional area and percentage area of type I fibers increased, and mitochondrial volume density exceeded that of controls. These findings suggest that patients with HFrEF exhibit structural/functional plasticity and appropriate angiogenic signaling in skeletal muscle. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the response to acute submaximal exercise and the effects of training in patients with HFrEF.

title: 2017 revisions of McDonald criteria shorten the time to diagnosis of multiple sclerosis in clinically isolated syndromes
text: We conducted a retrospective analysis on 137 patients with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) and dissemination in space (DIS) of demyelinating lesions to examine the impact of the 2017 revisions of McDonald criteria on the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS). These patients were from two MS centers in Italy. Our findings revealed that the application of the 2017 revisions of McDonald criteria resulted in a diagnosis of MS in 82.5% of the patients who would not have been diagnosed with MS based on the previous criteria at the time of their initial demyelinating event. Following a follow-up period of 3.8 ± 2.9 years, 85.8% of these patients eventually met the previous (2010) criteria as well. Therefore, the use of the 2017 revisions of McDonald criteria allows for an earlier diagnosis of MS in a significant proportion of CIS patients who are likely to develop MS.

title: Efficacy of PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors and PD-L1 expression status in cancer: meta-analysis
text:
AIM: To compare the effectiveness of PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors with conventional drugs in cancer patients who were either PD-L1 positive or PD-L1 negative. 

METHODS: A meta-analysis was conducted using randomized controlled trials. Data was collected from PubMed, Embase, Cochrane database, and conference abstracts from the American Society of Clinical Oncology and European Society of Medical Oncology up to March 2018. Studies that included PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors (avelumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab, nivolumab, and pembrolizumab) and had available hazard ratios for death based on PD-L1 positivity or negativity were included. The threshold for PD-L1 positivity or negativity was defined as PD-L1 stained cells accounting for 1% of tumor cells or tumor and immune cells, assessed through immunohistochemistry staining methods. 

RESULTS: A total of 4174 patients with advanced or metastatic cancers from eight randomized controlled trials were included. Compared to conventional agents, PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors were associated with significantly longer overall survival in both PD-L1 positive patients (n=2254, hazard ratio 0.66, 95% confidence interval 0.59 to 0.74) and PD-L1 negative patients (n=1920, 0.80, 0.71 to 0.90). However, the effectiveness of PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade treatment differed significantly between PD-L1 positive and PD-L1 negative patients (P=0.02 for interaction). Furthermore, the long-term clinical benefits of PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade were consistently observed across different interventional agents, cancer histotypes, randomization stratification methods, immunohistochemical scoring systems, drug targets, control groups, and median follow-up times in both PD-L1 positive and PD-L1 negative patients. 

CONCLUSIONS: PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade therapy is a preferable treatment option compared to conventional therapy for both PD-L1 positive and PD-L1 negative patients. This suggests that PD-L1 expression alone is not sufficient to determine which patients should receive PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade therapy.

title: Global cancer statistics 2018: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 36 cancers in 185 countries.
text: This article presents an update on the global burden of cancer worldwide, using data from the GLOBOCAN 2018 estimates of cancer incidence and mortality provided by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. The focus is on the variation in cancer rates across 20 different regions around the world. In 2018, it is estimated that there will be 18.1 million new cases of cancer (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer) and 9.6 million cancer-related deaths (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer). Among both males and females, lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer, accounting for 11.6% of all cases, and the leading cause of cancer death, responsible for 18.4% of all cancer-related deaths. Female breast cancer (11.6%), prostate cancer (7.1%), and colorectal cancer (6.1%) are also significant in terms of incidence, while colorectal cancer (9.2%), stomach cancer (8.2%), and liver cancer (8.2%) are notable causes of mortality. Among males, lung cancer is the most frequent cancer and the leading cause of cancer death, followed by prostate and colorectal cancer (for incidence), and liver and stomach cancer (for mortality). Among females, breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer death, followed by colorectal and lung cancer (for incidence), and vice versa (for mortality). However, it is important to note that the most frequently diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer death can vary significantly between countries and within each country, depending on economic development and associated social and lifestyle factors. It is worth mentioning that most low- and middle-income countries lack high-quality cancer registry data, which is crucial for planning and implementing evidence-based cancer control programs. The Global Initiative for Cancer Registry Development is an international partnership that aims to improve estimation and promote the collection and use of local data to prioritize and evaluate national cancer control efforts. This article is published in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians 2018;0:1-31 and is copyrighted by the American Cancer Society.

title: Gut Microbiota Is a Key Modulator of Insulin Resistance in TLR 2 Knockout Mice
text: The interaction between environmental factors and host genetics plays a crucial role in controlling the gut microbiota, which can impact the development of obesity and insulin resistance. When TLR2-deficient mice are kept in a germ-free environment, they are protected from diet-induced insulin resistance. However, the presence of gut microbiota can reverse this protection and induce insulin resistance in genetically predisposed animals, such as TLR2 knockout mice. In this study, we examined the effects of gut microbiota on metabolic parameters, glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and TLR2 signaling in non-germ free TLR2 knockout mice. Our findings revealed that the loss of TLR2 in conventionalized mice led to a phenotype resembling metabolic syndrome. These mice exhibited changes in their gut microbiota, with a significant increase in Firmicutes and a slight increase in Bacteroidetes compared to control mice. These alterations in gut microbiota were accompanied by increased absorption of LPS, subclinical inflammation, insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, and eventually, obesity. Furthermore, we found that this sequence of events could be replicated in wild-type mice through microbiota transplantation and reversed by antibiotic treatment. At the molecular level, the mechanism involved activation of TLR4, ER stress, and JNK activation, but not the IKKβ-IκB-NFκB pathway. Additionally, our data indicated a reduction in regulatory T cells in visceral fat of TLR2 knockout mice, suggesting that this modulation may contribute to their insulin resistance. Overall, our results highlight the significant role of microbiota in the intricate network of molecular and cellular interactions that connect genotype to phenotype. These findings have potential implications for understanding and managing common human disorders such as obesity, diabetes, and other immunological conditions.

title: TGF‐β‐mediated exosomal lnc‐MMP2‐2 regulates migration and invasion of lung cancer cells to the vasculature by promoting MMP2 expression
text: Previous research has shown that microRNAs (miRNAs) carried by exosomes, which are regulated by transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, play a role in controlling the migration and invasion of lung cancer cells. However, it is still unclear whether and how TGF-β-mediated exosomal long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are involved in regulating the migration and invasion of lung cancer cells. In this study, we conducted coculture experiments and observed that pretreatment with TGF-β increased the migration and invasion abilities of lung cancer cells. Additionally, TGF-β pretreated A549 cells were found to enhance vascular permeability. Furthermore, we discovered that TGF-β-mediated exosomes, which serve as carriers for intercellular communication, play a role in regulating lung cancer invasion and vascular permeability. Through transcriptional analysis, we identified lnc-MMP2-2 as being highly enriched in TGF-β-mediated exosomes. This lncRNA may function by enhancing the expression of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)2, as demonstrated by ectopic expression and silencing experiments of lnc-MMP2-2, which affected lung cancer invasion and vascular permeability. We also conducted semiquantitative assessments of lnc-MMP2-2 and MMP2 expression, and evaluated the correlations between these two molecules in specific tissues. Our findings suggest that exosomal lnc-MMP2-2 may regulate the migration and invasion of lung cancer cells into blood vessels by promoting MMP2 expression. Therefore, this lncRNA could potentially serve as a novel therapeutic target and predictive marker for tumor metastasis in lung cancer.

title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2016
text:
Objective: The objective of this study was to provide an update to the guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock, known as the "Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock: 2012."

Design: A consensus committee consisting of 55 international experts from 25 international organizations was formed. Nominal groups were created at important international meetings attended by committee members. A conflict-of-interest policy was established and strictly followed throughout the process. A dedicated meeting was held in December 2015 for all panel members. Teleconferences and electronic-based discussions were used extensively for communication and collaboration.

Methods: The panel was divided into five sections: hemodynamics, infection, adjunctive therapies, metabolic, and ventilation. Population, intervention, comparison, and outcomes (PICO) questions were reviewed and updated as necessary, and evidence profiles were created. Each subgroup formulated a list of questions, conducted thorough searches for the best available evidence, and utilized the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system to assess the quality of evidence. Recommendations were categorized as strong or weak, and best practice statements were provided when appropriate.

Results: The Surviving Sepsis Guideline panel developed a total of 93 statements on the early management and resuscitation of patients with sepsis or septic shock. Out of these, 32 were strong recommendations, 39 were weak recommendations, and 18 were best practice statements. Four questions did not receive any specific recommendation.

Conclusions: This study demonstrates a high level of agreement among a large group of international experts regarding many strong recommendations for the optimal care of sepsis patients. While some aspects of care have limited supporting evidence, evidence-based recommendations for the acute management of sepsis and septic shock are crucial for improving outcomes in these critically ill patients with high mortality rates.

title: Mitochondrial genome variation and the origin of modern humans.
text:
The study of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has greatly contributed to our understanding of human evolution. This is due to its unique characteristics, such as its high copy number, lack of recombination, high substitution rate, and maternal mode of inheritance. However, most studies on human evolution using mtDNA sequencing have focused only on the control region, which makes up less than 7% of the entire mitochondrial genome. These studies are complicated by the significant variation in substitution rate between different sites, as well as the challenges posed by parallel mutations, which make it difficult to accurately estimate genetic distance and draw reliable phylogenetic conclusions.

Previous comprehensive studies on the human mitochondrial molecule have primarily relied on restriction-fragment length polymorphism analysis. While this approach provides valuable data, it is not well-suited for estimating mutation rates and determining the timing of evolutionary events. In order to enhance our understanding of human evolution using mitochondrial DNA, we conducted a study that analyzed the complete mtDNA sequence of 53 individuals from diverse backgrounds. By comparing our mtDNA data with a parallel study on the Xq13.3 region in the same individuals, we were able to gain a comprehensive perspective on human evolution, particularly in relation to the age of modern humans.

title: Deficiency of Interleukin-15 Confers Resistance to Obesity by Diminishing Inflammation and Enhancing the Thermogenic Function of Adipose Tissues
text: The objective of this study is to investigate the role of IL-15, an inflammatory cytokine, in promoting obesity. Previous studies have shown that IL-15 is produced during physical exercise and can reduce weight gain in mice. However, our findings on IL-15 knockout mice suggest that IL-15 actually promotes obesity. To understand the mechanisms behind this, we conducted experiments using control and IL-15 knockout mice fed a high fat diet or normal control diet. After 16 weeks, we evaluated body weight, adipose tissue and skeletal mass, serum lipid levels, and gene/protein expression in the adipose tissues. We also studied the effect of IL-15 on thermogenesis and oxygen consumption in adipocytes. Our results show that IL-15 deficiency prevents diet-induced weight gain and accumulation of lipids in various adipose tissues. Gene expression analysis revealed increased expression of genes associated with adaptive thermogenesis in the brown and subcutaneous adipose tissues of IL-15 knockout mice. Additionally, oxygen consumption was higher in the brown adipocytes from IL-15 knockout mice. Furthermore, IL-15 knockout mice had decreased expression of pro-inflammatory mediators in their adipose tissues. In conclusion, the absence of IL-15 leads to reduced fat accumulation in white adipose tissues and increased lipid utilization through adaptive thermogenesis. IL-15 also promotes inflammation in adipose tissues, which may contribute to obesity-associated metabolic syndrome.

title: Chromatin signatures of pluripotent cell lines.
text: The modification of the genome through epigenetics is believed to play a crucial role in determining the lineage and developmental stage of cells in a multicellular organism. In this study, we demonstrate that the epigenetic characteristics of pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ES) differ significantly from those of embryonic carcinoma cells, haematopoietic stem cells (HSC), and their differentiated offspring. Genes that are specific to a particular lineage and remain silent are replicated earlier in pluripotent cells compared to tissue-specific stem cells or differentiated cells. Surprisingly, these genes also exhibit high levels of acetylated H3K9 and methylated H3K4, which are markers of open chromatin. Additionally, in ES cells, some non-expressed genes display a combination of these markers with H3K27 trimethylation. This unique epigenetic profile characterizes the pluripotency of ES cells, where lineage-specific genes may be accessible but are accompanied by repressive H3K27 trimethylation modifications. The methylation of H3K27 plays a crucial role in preventing the expression of these genes in ES cells, as their premature expression occurs in ES cells lacking the embryonic ectoderm development (Eed) protein. Our findings suggest that lineage-specific genes in ES cells are poised for expression but are restrained by opposing chromatin modifications.

title: Regulation of Hippo pathway transcription factor TEAD by p38 MAPK-induced cytoplasmic translocation
text: The Hippo pathway is responsible for controlling the size of organs and maintaining tissue balance. When this pathway is disrupted, it can lead to the development of cancer. In mammals, the core components of the Hippo pathway include Mst1/2, MAPK4Ks, and Lats1/2, which are serine/threonine kinases that regulate the pathway. When these kinases are deactivated, it results in the dephosphorylation, stabilization, and movement of the major functional transducers of the Hippo pathway, YAP and TAZ, into the nucleus, where they become activated. YAP and TAZ are transcription co-activators that primarily control gene expression by interacting with a family of transcription factors called TEAD. The current understanding of the regulation of the Hippo pathway focuses on the phosphorylation-dependent movement of YAP and TAZ between the nucleus and cytoplasm, but the regulation of TEAD's movement has been largely overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate that environmental stress causes TEAD to move from the nucleus to the cytoplasm through the activation of p38 MAPK, independently of the Hippo pathway. Importantly, this stress-induced movement of TEAD inhibits YAP's activity and selectively suppresses the growth of cancer cells driven by YAP. Our findings uncover a mechanism that controls the movement of TEAD and highlight the importance of TEAD's localization in determining the output of the Hippo pathway.

title: How do I perform a lumbar puncture and analyze the results to diagnose bacterial meningitis?
text: The purpose of this study was to review the evidence on diagnostic lumbar puncture (LP) techniques that can reduce the risk of adverse events and to assess the accuracy of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in adult patients suspected of having bacterial meningitis. The researchers searched various databases to identify relevant studies and included randomized trials that examined interventions to improve the success of LP or reduce adverse events. They also identified studies that evaluated the accuracy of CSF analysis for diagnosing bacterial meningitis. The researchers independently assessed study quality and extracted relevant data. They found 15 randomized trials and used a random-effects model for quantitative synthesis. The results showed that atraumatic needles and reinsertion of the stylet before needle removal were associated with a decrease in the risk of headache. Mobilization after LP also showed a nonsignificant decrease in headache. In terms of CSF analysis, certain criteria accurately diagnosed bacterial meningitis. The study concluded that small-gauge, atraumatic needles can reduce the risk of headache after diagnostic LP, and reinsertion of the stylet before needle removal is recommended. Bed rest after the procedure is not necessary. Future research should focus on interventions to improve the success of diagnostic LP and enhance procedural skills training.

title: Guidelines for the use and interpretation of assays for monitoring autophagy.
text:
In 2008, we published the initial guidelines for standardizing research on autophagy. Since then, there has been a significant increase in research on this topic, with many new scientists entering the field. Our knowledge base and relevant technologies have also expanded. Therefore, it is crucial to update the guidelines for monitoring autophagy in different organisms. Several reviews have discussed the range of assays used for this purpose. However, there is still confusion regarding acceptable methods to measure autophagy, particularly in multicellular eukaryotes.

One important point to emphasize is the distinction between measurements that monitor the numbers or volume of autophagic elements (such as autophagosomes or autolysosomes) at any stage of the autophagic process and those that measure flux through the autophagy pathway (i.e., the complete process). It is necessary to differentiate between a block in macroautophagy that leads to autophagosome accumulation and stimuli that increase autophagic activity, defined as increased autophagy induction coupled with increased delivery to and degradation within lysosomes or vacuoles.

In other words, it is crucial for new investigators in the field to understand that an increase in autophagosomes does not necessarily indicate more autophagy. In many cases, autophagosomes accumulate due to a block in trafficking to lysosomes without a simultaneous change in autophagosome biogenesis. Conversely, an increase in autolysosomes may indicate a decrease in degradative activity.

In this article, we present a set of guidelines for selecting and interpreting methods to study macroautophagy and related processes. These guidelines are intended for investigators who aim to examine autophagy and for reviewers who need to provide constructive critiques of papers focused on these processes. It is important to note that these guidelines are not rigid rules, as the appropriate assays depend on the specific research question and system being used. We also emphasize the importance of using multiple assays to monitor autophagy, as no single assay is guaranteed to be the most suitable in every situation.

Throughout these guidelines, we discuss various methods for assessing autophagy and the information that can or cannot be obtained from them. By highlighting the strengths and limitations of specific autophagy assays, we hope to inspire technical innovation in the field.

title: Subversion of Systemic Glucose Metabolism as a Mechanism to Support the Growth of Leukemia Cells.
text: From an organismal perspective, cancer cells can be seen as parasites that compete with the host for vital resources like glucose. In this study, we used leukemia models and samples from leukemia patients to observe a type of adaptive balance, where malignant cells alter the body's physiology by impairing both insulin sensitivity and insulin secretion. This alteration allows tumors to obtain more glucose. Mechanistically, tumor cells stimulate the production of IGFBP1 from adipose tissue, which affects insulin sensitivity. Additionally, leukemia disrupts the gut microbiota, causes serotonin loss, and inactivates incretins, all of which suppress insulin secretion. Significantly, by disrupting this adaptive balance induced by leukemia, we were able to slow down disease progression and extend survival. Our findings offer a new approach to managing leukemia on a systemic level.

title: Tumor-derived exosomes induce N2 polarization of neutrophils to promote gastric cancer cell migration
text:
Exosomes are small vesicles that play a role in cellular communication during both health and disease. Tumor cells have the ability to polarize neutrophils into a pro-tumor phenotype, but the specific function of tumor-derived exosomes in this process is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of exosomes derived from gastric cancer cells (GC-Ex) on the activation of neutrophils and the underlying mechanisms involved.

Our results showed that GC-Ex prolonged the survival of neutrophils and induced the expression of inflammatory factors in these cells. Furthermore, GC-Ex-activated neutrophils were found to promote the migration of gastric cancer cells. We discovered that GC-Ex carried a protein called high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1), which interacted with a receptor called TLR4 to activate the NF-κB pathway. This activation led to an increased autophagic response in neutrophils. When we blocked the interaction between HMGB1 and TLR4, as well as the NF-κB pathway and autophagy, we observed a reversal of the GC-Ex-induced neutrophil activation. Silencing HMGB1 in gastric cancer cells further confirmed its role as a key factor in GC-Ex-mediated neutrophil activation.

Additionally, we found that HMGB1 expression was upregulated in gastric cancer tissues and was associated with a poor prognosis in patients with gastric cancer. Furthermore, exosomes derived from gastric cancer tissues had a similar effect on neutrophil activation as those derived from gastric cancer cell lines.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that exosomes derived from gastric cancer cells induce autophagy and pro-tumor activation of neutrophils through the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of neutrophil regulation in cancer and highlight the multifaceted role of exosomes in shaping the tumor microenvironment.

title: ROS-induced R loops trigger a transcription-coupled but BRCA1/2-independent homologous recombination pathway through CSB
text: Transcription-coupled DNA repair mechanisms, such as transcription-coupled homologous recombination (TC-HR), play a vital role in safeguarding actively transcribed regions of the genome. In this study, we utilized reactive oxygen species (ROS) to induce and investigate TC-HR at a transcribed site in human cells. Similar to canonical HR, RAD51 is essential for TC-HR. However, unlike canonical HR, the recruitment of RAD51 to damaged sites during TC-HR does not rely on BRCA1 and BRCA2 but instead depends on RAD52 and Cockayne Syndrome Protein B (CSB). During TC-HR, CSB recruits RAD52 through an acidic domain. Interestingly, CSB is recruited by R loops, which are significantly induced by ROS in transcribed regions. Importantly, CSB exhibits a strong affinity for DNA:RNA hybrids in vitro, suggesting its role as a sensor for ROS-induced R loops. Consequently, TC-HR is initiated by CSB in response to R loops and executed by the CSB-RAD52-RAD51 axis, establishing an alternative HR pathway independent of BRCA1/2 that safeguards the transcribed genome.

title: Autophagy and its potent modulators from phytochemicals in cancer treatment
text: Autophagy is a process found throughout the body that breaks down and recycles damaged or harmful parts of cells. It is crucial in treating cancer. When used in therapy, autophagy primarily helps cells survive, but excessive autophagy can cause non-apoptotic cell death, known as autophagic cell death. Many plants and herbs contain natural compounds that are commonly used to treat various types of cancer. Recent evidence suggests that these compounds, which target the autophagy process, show promise as cancer treatments. However, these compounds have different effects on autophagy. In this review, we explore the role of autophagy in cancer development and treatment, with a focus on understanding how phytochemicals, particularly those found in plants, can modulate autophagy to fight cancer. Importantly, we propose a new idea that the dynamic effects of phytochemicals on autophagy in cancer should be carefully evaluated.

title: Exosomal miR-99a-5p is elevated in sera of ovarian cancer patients and promotes cancer cell invasion by increasing fibronectin and vitronectin expression in neighboring peritoneal mesothelial cells
text: This study aimed to identify the specific exosomal microRNAs (miRNAs) produced by epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) cells, determine if serum miRNA levels can distinguish EOC patients from healthy individuals, and investigate the role of exosomal miRNAs in ovarian cancer progression. Exosomes were collected from the culture media of two EOC cell lines, TYK-nu and HeyA8. A miRNA microarray revealed elevated levels of miR-99a-5p in EOC-derived exosomes. The expression of serum miR-99a-5p was measured in EOC patients, patients with benign ovarian tumors, and healthy volunteers. The effect of exosomal miR-99a-5p on peritoneal dissemination was examined by treating human peritoneal mesothelial cells (HPMCs) with EOC-derived exosomes. Additionally, miR-99a-5p mimics were transfected into HPMCs to analyze their impact on cancer invasion using a 3D culture model. Proteomic analysis was performed on HPMCs transfected with miR-99a-5p to identify potential target genes. The results showed significantly increased serum miR-99a-5p levels in EOC patients compared to benign tumor patients and healthy volunteers. Serum miR-99a-5p expression levels decreased after EOC surgeries, indicating its association with tumor burden. Treatment with EOC-derived exosomes increased miR-99a-5p expression in HPMCs. Transfection of miR-99a-5p into HPMCs promoted ovarian cancer invasion and upregulated fibronectin and vitronectin expression. In conclusion, serum miR-99a-5p is elevated in ovarian cancer patients and exosomal miR-99a-5p promotes cell invasion by affecting HPMCs through fibronectin and vitronectin upregulation, making it a potential target for inhibiting ovarian cancer progression.

title: The Pfam protein families database.
text: Pfam is a widely utilized database that contains over 13,000 protein families that have been carefully curated. The current release, 26.0, provides access to Pfam through servers located in the UK, the USA, and Sweden. In this report, we will discuss the changes that have taken place since our 2010 NAR paper, which was based on release 24.0. In the past two years, we have created 1840 new families and expanded the coverage of the UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) to almost 80%. An important development is our decision to involve the Wikipedia community in annotating our families. We have linked Pfam families to relevant Wikipedia pages and encouraged both communities to enhance and expand those pages. Additionally, we have made improvements to the Pfam website and introduced new visualizations, such as the 'sunburst' representation of the taxonomic distribution of families. In this work, we also address two topics that will be of particular interest to the Pfam community. Firstly, we explain the definition and usage of family-specific gathering thresholds that have been manually curated. Secondly, we discuss the characteristics of domains of unknown function (DUFs), which are a rapidly growing group of families within Pfam.

title: Exercise as a therapeutic approach to improve blood pressure in patients with peripheral arterial disease: current literature and future directions.
text:
INTRODUCTION Patients who have symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) experience a decrease in their ability to function and an increase in mortality rates due to cardiovascular disease. While exercise has been a key component in clinical treatment to enhance walking capacity in these patients, its impact on cardiovascular parameters has not been thoroughly examined. 

Areas covered: This review focuses on the role of exercise in improving blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD and provides an overview of the current evidence regarding the immediate (single session of exercise) and long-term effects of walking and resistance exercise on blood pressure and its determinants. 

Expert commentary: Exercise has been found to result in immediate and long-term reductions in blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD. These effects were particularly noticeable after walking and resistance exercise. Further research is needed to explore the effects of other types of exercise, especially those that are not painful, on cardiovascular function in patients with symptomatic PAD.

title: Morin Exhibits Anti-Inflammatory Effects on IL-1β-Stimulated Human Osteoarthritis Chondrocytes by Activating the Nrf2 Signaling Pathway
text:
Objective: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of morin on inflammation in osteoarthritis chondrocytes stimulated by IL-1β and to understand the underlying mechanism.

Methods: The levels of NO and PGE2 were measured using the Griess method and ELISA, respectively. The levels of MMP1, MMP3, and MMP13 were also measured using ELISA. 

Results: The results showed that IL-1β significantly increased the production of NO, PGE2, MMP1, MMP3, and MMP13. However, treatment with morin significantly reduced these increases. Additionally, morin suppressed IL-1β-induced NF-κB activation. Moreover, morin increased the expression of Nrf2 and HO-1. Knockdown of Nrf2 prevented the anti-inflammatory effects of morin.

Conclusion: In conclusion, this study suggests that morin can alleviate IL-1β-induced inflammation by activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway.

title: Impact of blood pressure variability on cardiovascular events in elderly patients with hypertension.
text: Blood pressure variability is a common characteristic of hypertension in older individuals, but its clinical significance is still uncertain. To address this, we investigated the impact of blood pressure variability on the occurrence of cardiovascular events in elderly patients with hypertension. We followed 106 consecutive hypertensive patients over the age of 60 (mean age, 73.9 +/- 8.1 years; male, 54%) who underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. The follow-up period lasted a median of 34 months (range, 3-60 months), during which we observed 39 cardiovascular events, including 14 cases of cerebral infarction and 7 cases of acute myocardial infarction. We used the coefficient of variation (CV) of 24-hour systolic blood pressure (SBP) values as a measure of blood pressure variability. The patients had an average CV value of 10.6% and were divided into two groups based on this mean value: a high CV group (n = 46) and a low CV group (n = 60). Although the baseline characteristics were similar between the two groups, Kaplan-Meier plots for event-free survival showed a significantly higher rate of cardiovascular events in the high CV group compared to the low CV group (p < 0.05). Cox's proportional hazards analysis revealed that increased blood pressure variability (indicated by a high CV value of 24-hour SBP) was an independent predictor of cardiovascular events. Additionally, the CV value of daytime SBP and the standard deviation (SD) value of both 24-hour SBP and daytime SBP were positively correlated with the occurrence of cardiovascular events. These findings suggest that increased blood pressure variability may be an independent risk factor for cardiovascular events in elderly patients with hypertension.

title: Reprogramming committed murine blood cells to induced hematopoietic stem cells with defined factors.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for maintaining blood formation throughout a person's life and are crucial for bone marrow transplantation. Our study reveals that by temporarily expressing six specific transcription factors (Run1t1, Hlf, Lmo2, Prdm5, Pbx1, and Zfp37), we can confer the ability for multilineage transplantation onto lymphoid and myeloid progenitors and myeloid effector cells that were previously committed to a specific lineage. Additionally, the inclusion of Mycn and Meis1, along with the use of polycistronic viruses, enhances the effectiveness of this reprogramming process. The resulting reprogrammed cells, known as induced-HSCs (iHSCs), possess the ability to differentiate into multiple lineages, regenerate stem/progenitor compartments, and can be transplanted multiple times. Through single-cell analysis, we discovered that iHSCs generated under optimal conditions exhibit a gene expression profile that closely resembles that of natural HSCs. These findings demonstrate that the expression of a specific set of factors is enough to activate the gene networks responsible for HSC functionality in committed blood cells. As a result, our research suggests that reprogramming blood cells could be a viable strategy for producing transplantable stem cells with clinical applications.

title: Genetic variability in a frozen batch of MCF-7 cells invisible in routine authentication affecting cell function
text:
The current recommendations for cell line authentication, annotation, and quality control do not adequately address genetic heterogeneity. Our research within the Human Toxome Project has shown that a single batch of the human breast adenocarcinoma cell line MCF-7, obtained directly from a cell bank, can exhibit significant cellular and phenotypic heterogeneity. This heterogeneity cannot be detected using the usual cell authentication method of short tandem repeat (STR) markers. STR profiling is only effective in identifying cross-contamination and misidentification of cell lines, but it does not capture the extent of heterogeneity present. Therefore, additional methods must be employed to examine heterogeneity.

The presence of heterogeneity in cell lines can have serious implications for the reproducibility of experiments, as evidenced by differences in morphology, estrogenic growth dose-response, whole genome gene expression, and untargeted mass-spectroscopy metabolomics in MCF-7 cells. Comparative Genomic Hybridization (CGH) was used to trace these differences back to genetic heterogeneity present in the original frozen vials from the same ATCC lot. However, the STR markers did not differ from the ATCC reference for any of the samples. These findings highlight the importance of implementing additional quality assurance measures in Good Cell Culture Practice and cell characterization. Specifically, other methods such as CGH should be utilized to uncover potential genomic heterogeneity and genetic drifts within cell lines.

title: The Mammalian-Specific Protein Armcx1 Regulates Mitochondrial Transport during Axon Regeneration
text: The importance of mitochondrial transport in the functioning of neurons and axons is well recognized. However, its impact on neuronal injury responses, such as the survival of neurons and the regeneration of axons, is not well understood. In a mouse model known for its strong ability to regenerate axons, we have discovered that a gene called Armcx1, which is specific to mammals and encodes a protein localized in mitochondria, is upregulated after axotomy in this highly regenerative condition. By overexpressing Armcx1 in adult retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), we have observed an enhancement in mitochondrial transport. Significantly, Armcx1 also promotes both the survival of neurons and the regeneration of axons after injury, and these effects are dependent on its localization in mitochondria. Additionally, when Armcx1 is suppressed, both neuronal survival and axon regeneration are compromised in this highly regenerative model, further confirming the crucial role of Armcx1 in regulating neuronal injury responses in the adult central nervous system (CNS). Our findings indicate that Armcx1 plays a critical role in controlling mitochondrial transport during the process of neuronal repair.

title: A diversity of beta diversities: straightening up a concept gone awry. Part 1. Defining beta diversity as a function of alpha and gamma diversity
text: Beta diversity is a term that has been used to describe various phenomena, all of which involve differences in composition between different places. However, these phenomena are often unrelated and unpredictable. This review aims to provide a unified conceptual framework for understanding the different interpretations of beta diversity and what they measure. The first part of the review focuses on defining the beta component of diversity, which involves determining how diversity is measured and how it is divided into alpha and beta components. The ecological literature has used various definitions of beta diversity resulting from these decisions. True beta diversity is achieved when the total effective number of species in a dataset (true gamma diversity) is divided into the effective number of species per distinct composition.

title: A cross-cultural study of wine consumers with respect to health benefits of wine
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the preferences and consumption habits of wine consumers in two culturally diverse groups: Koreans and Australians. Participants had to be over 18 years old and regular wine consumers. Data was collected through an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that Australians perceived red wine to have more health benefits compared to Koreans. Additionally, Australian consumers had a greater knowledge of the health benefits of wine compared to Korean consumers. Both Korean and Australian consumers preferred red wine, but the proportion of preference for red wine was significantly higher among Koreans. Both groups preferred to spend between AUD$11-$19 on wine products. The results also showed that Korean consumers were more attracted to health-oriented wine compared to Australian consumers. In terms of gender, Korean women had a similar preference for red wine as men, while Australian women consumed significantly more white wine than men. These findings provide valuable insights for winemakers and marketers, suggesting that emphasizing the health aspects of wine could maximize consumer interest.

title: DIASPORA BONDS: TAPPING THE DIASPORA DURING DIFFICULT TIMES
text: Tapping into the wealth of their diaspora communities, India and Israel have successfully raised more than US$35 billion. These diaspora bonds serve as a reliable and cost-effective means of obtaining external financing, particularly when countries face limited access to international capital markets. For diaspora investors, these bonds not only present an investment opportunity but also allow them to contribute to their country of origin. Many countries with sizable diasporas abroad stand to benefit greatly from the potential of diaspora bonds. However, nations with weak governance and high sovereign risk may require assistance in terms of institutional capacity building and credit enhancement from multilateral or bilateral agencies. Take Haiti, for example, which could potentially generate hundreds of millions of dollars through diaspora bond issuance, provided a guarantee structure is established to instill trust in the country's public institutions.

title: Peroxisome Proliferator Activated Receptor gamma (PPARγ) Agonist Rosiglitazone Ameliorate Airway Inflammation by Inhibiting Toll-Like Receptor 2 (TLR2)/Nod-Like Receptor with Pyrin Domain Containing 3 (NLRP3) Inflammatory Corpuscle Activation in Asthmatic Mice
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role and mechanism of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonist (PPARγ) in the toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2)/nod-like receptor with pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammatory corpuscle pathway in asthmatic mice. Eighteen female mice (C57) were divided into four groups: control group, asthma model group challenged with ovalbumin (OVA), rosiglitazone group, and PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone treatment group. The infiltration of inflammatory cells around the bronchial tubes, as well as the proliferation and mucus secretion of bronchial epithelial goblet cells, were observed using staining techniques. Western blots were used to measure the expression levels of TLR2, PPARγ, nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kappaB), NLRP3, and ASC. The results showed that the number of inflammatory cells and eosinophils, as well as the levels of OVA-specific IgE, interleukin-4 (IL-4), and IL-13, were significantly higher in the asthma group compared to the control group and treatment group. In the treatment group, the infiltration of inflammatory cells, thickening of the bronchial walls, hyperplasia of goblet cells, and mucus secretion were significantly reduced compared to the asthma group. PPARγ expression was significantly higher in the treatment group compared to the asthma group and control group. The protein expression levels of TLR2, NF-kappaB, NLRP3, and ASC were significantly lower in the treatment group compared to the asthma group, but higher compared to the control group. In conclusion, PPARγ rosiglitazone improves airway inflammation by inhibiting NF-kappaB expression in asthmatic mice and further inhibits the activation of TLR2/NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscles.

title: Omi/HtrA2 Participates in Age-Related Autophagic Deficiency in Rat Liver
text: The liver is a crucial organ that performs many important functions, and it is essential to maintain its normal function for overall health. Autophagy, a process that helps maintain cellular balance, plays a significant role in ensuring proper organ function. Research has shown that a decline in liver function with age is linked to a deficiency in autophagy, although the exact reasons behind this are still unclear. Omi/HtrA2, a serine protease belonging to the HtrA family, promotes cell death through different pathways. Mice lacking Omi/HtrA2 displayed symptoms of premature aging, similar to those seen in cases of autophagic insufficiency. In this study, we found that the levels of Omi/HtrA2 protein in the liver decreased as rats aged, and this reduction was correlated with a decline in liver function. Additionally, several proteins related to autophagy (LC3II/I, Beclin-1, and LAMP2) were significantly reduced in the rat liver as they aged. When Omi/HtrA2 was inhibited, autophagy decreased, and liver function was impaired. In conclusion, our findings suggest that Omi/HtrA2 contributes to age-related autophagic deficiency in the rat liver. This study provides new insights into the mechanisms involved in liver aging.

title: Macrosomia and Hyperinsulinaemic Hypoglycaemia in Patients with Heterozygous Mutations in the HNF4A Gene
text: The association between macrosomia and negative outcomes for both the baby and mother is well-known. However, the factors that contribute to macrosomia are not well understood. One factor that has been identified is increased fetal insulin secretion, which is seen in pregnant women with diabetes and congenital hyperinsulinemia. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of two key regulators of pancreatic insulin secretion in the development of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia. We examined birthweight and the incidence of neonatal hypoglycemia in patients with heterozygous mutations in the maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) genes HNF4A and HNF1A/TCF1. Additionally, we studied the effects of pancreatic deletion of Hnf4a on fetal and neonatal insulin secretion in mice.

title: ART adherence clubs: A long-term retention strategy for clinically stable patients receiving antiretroviral therapy
text: The ART-adherence club model described in this article offers a patient-friendly approach to accessing antiretroviral therapy (ART) for stable patients. It aims to alleviate the burden on healthcare facilities by freeing up clinical resources for new patients and those who are clinically unstable or at risk of treatment failure. Under this model, 30 patients are assigned to an ART club, which meets every two months for less than an hour at a facility or community venue. The meetings are led by a lay club facilitator who conducts a brief clinical assessment, makes referrals if necessary, and dispenses pre-packaged ART. Between January 2011 and December 2012, the Western Cape Government successfully implemented this model, establishing over 600 ART clubs in Cape Town and providing ART care to more than 16,000 patients. This widespread and rapid rollout demonstrates the enthusiastic participation of both patients and facility staff. South Africa should consider adopting a similar model for nationwide implementation.

title: Exercise-linked FNDC5/irisin rescues synaptic plasticity and memory defects in Alzheimer’s models
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disorder characterized by the failure of synapse and memory, which has been linked to defective brain hormonal signaling. Irisin is a myokine that is released during exercise when the membrane-bound precursor protein fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) is cleaved. It is also expressed in the hippocampus. Our study reveals that levels of FNDC5/irisin are reduced in the hippocampi and cerebrospinal fluid of individuals with AD, as well as in experimental AD models. When we decreased the expression of brain FNDC5/irisin in mice, it resulted in impaired long-term potentiation and memory for recognizing novel objects. On the other hand, increasing the levels of FNDC5/irisin in the brain rescued synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mouse models. Overexpression of FNDC5/irisin in the peripheral system also rescued memory impairment, while blocking either peripheral or brain FNDC5/irisin weakened the neuroprotective effects of physical exercise on synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mice. Our findings demonstrate that FNDC5/irisin plays a crucial role in the beneficial effects of exercise in AD models, making it a potential novel agent for counteracting synapse failure and memory impairment in AD.

title: Influence of antidepressant therapy on sick leave in primary care: ADAS, a comparative observational study
text:
Background: In comparison to other European countries, Sweden's annual expenses for sick leave are considered moderate. Common mental disorders (CMD) affect a significant portion of the adult population, accounting for 10-15% of sick leave cases. A study based on Swedish registers suggests that patients on long-term sick leave for CMD who receive antidepressant therapy experience longer periods of sick leave and a higher frequency of non-time-limited sickness compensation compared to those receiving psychotherapy, work-oriented rehabilitation, or other therapies.

Aim: The aim of this study is to determine whether patients on antidepressant therapy for depression, anxiety, and stress-related mental disorders, who are on long-term sick leave, have a longer duration of sick leave compared to patients treated with alternative therapies.

Method: This study is a prospective, observational study conducted at 28 primary health care centers in the Region Västra Götaland, Sweden. It includes 192 patients who are on sick leave due to CMD. The outcome measures are the total number of sick leave days and the net number of sick leave days.

Interpretation: The study found no significant differences in sick leave days (total or net) due to CMD between patients treated with antidepressants and those not receiving antidepressant therapy during the 12-month observation period. The only difference observed at baseline was a higher frequency of exhaustion disorder in the group not receiving antidepressants. Analysis of other potential factors associated with shorter or longer sick leave revealed that the patient's perception of their ability to return to work in the near and distant future was the only significant factor. Additionally, the patient's perception of their ability to return to their current workplace was found to be a significant factor associated with longer sick leave. Given the impact of CMD on sick leave and associated costs, future research on the rehabilitation process should emphasize this factor.

title: CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling via transactivation of GSK-3β and Axin2 expression
text: The role of CDX2, a specific nuclear transcription factor found in the intestines, in the development and progression of colorectal cancer (CRC) is not well understood. This study aimed to investigate the effects of CDX2 on colon cancer cells. The findings showed that reducing CDX2 levels in these cells increased cell proliferation and tumor formation, while overexpressing CDX2 inhibited cell proliferation. The study also revealed that CDX2 knockdown or overexpression affected Wnt signaling activity, with downstream targets of this pathway being up-regulated or down-regulated accordingly. Furthermore, suppressing Wnt signaling reversed the enhanced cell proliferation caused by CDX2 knockdown, while activating this pathway enhanced the inhibited cell proliferation caused by CDX2 overexpression. The study also confirmed that CDX2 directly activates the expression of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) and axis inhibition protein 2 (Axin2) by binding to their respective promoters. In conclusion, these findings suggest that CDX2 suppresses Wnt/β-catenin signaling, thereby inhibiting the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells.

title: Prostaglandin E2 mediates sensory nerve regulation of bone homeostasis
text: The ability of sensory nerves to detect bone density or metabolic activity in order to regulate bone homeostasis is currently unknown. However, our research has discovered that prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which is secreted by osteoblastic cells, activates the PGE2 receptor 4 (EP4) in sensory nerves. This activation helps to regulate bone formation by inhibiting sympathetic activity through the central nervous system. We have observed that the secretion of PGE2 by osteoblasts increases when bone density decreases, as seen in osteoporotic animal models. The removal of sensory nerves leads to a decline in skeletal integrity. Specifically, when the EP4 gene in sensory nerves or cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) in osteoblastic cells is knocked out, there is a significant reduction in bone volume in adult mice. Models of sensory denervation show an increase in sympathetic tone, but this bone loss can be rescued by propranolol, a β2-adrenergic antagonist. Additionally, the injection of SW033291, a small molecule that locally increases PGE2 levels, significantly enhances bone formation. However, this effect is hindered in EP4 knockout mice. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that PGE2 serves as a mediator between sensory nerves and bone homeostasis, promoting regeneration.

title: The Bone and Joint Decade 2000-2010.
text: The Bone and Joint Decade, from 2000 to 2010, has been officially declared by the World Health Organisation. This is a timely and appropriate decision, considering the large number of individuals worldwide who suffer from disabilities related to the musculo-skeletal system, caused by trauma, ageing, degeneration, and other factors. Thanks to advancements in orthopaedic surgery and rheumatology, those with bone and joint disabilities have greatly benefited from pharmacological advancements, improved imaging techniques, surgical procedures, and man-made materials that can replace damaged bone and cartilage. However, these man-made materials are prone to wear and tear and can become loose within the body. As we enter the Bone and Joint Decade, it is crucial to focus on further advancements in bone and cartilage research to enhance the treatment of these diseases. The Human Genome Project has provided us with a better understanding of disease genes and the potential for gene manipulation to prevent and treat specific conditions. The culture and transplantation of cartilage cells are already a reality, and tissue engineering, which involves growing cells in three-dimensional substrates, will be used in the future to replace damaged bone and cartilage with living tissues. Although progress has been made, more research is needed. It is reasonable to anticipate a significant breakthrough in the treatment of bone and joint diseases by the end of this decade.

title: Prevalence of late-life depression and gap in mental health service use across European regions.
text:
The purpose of this study was to examine the prevalence and utilization of mental health services for late-life depression in four regions of Europe (Western Europe, Scandinavia, Southern Europe, and Central and Eastern Europe). Additionally, the study aimed to identify socio-demographic, social, and health-related factors associated with mental health service use. 

The study utilized a cross-sectional design and analyzed data from the Survey on Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. The sample consisted of 28,796 individuals (53% women) residing in Europe, with a mean age of 74 years. Mental health service use was determined based on self-reported diagnosis or treatment for depression. 

The findings revealed that the overall prevalence of late-life depression was 29%, with the highest rates observed in Southern Europe (35%), followed by Central and Eastern Europe (32%), Western Europe (26%), and the lowest rates in Scandinavia (17%). Several factors were strongly associated with depression, including the number of chronic diseases, pain, limitations in daily activities, grip strength, and cognitive impairment. 

Furthermore, the study identified a significant gap in mental health service utilization, with only 21% of individuals with late-life depression receiving treatment. 

In conclusion, the study suggests that interventions to address late-life depression should focus on individuals with chronic somatic comorbidities and limitations in mental and physical functioning. Additionally, promoting help-seeking behavior among older adults, reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, and providing education to general practitioners may help bridge the gap in mental health service utilization.

title: Impedance and Interface Properties of Al/Methyl-Red/p-InP Solar Cell
text: A solar cell made of Al/methyl-red/p-InP was created using a solution-processing method and analyzed using current-voltage (I-V) and capacitance-voltage-frequency (C-V-f) measurements at room temperature. The ideality factor and barrier height of the device were determined to be 1.11 eV and 2.02, respectively, based on the dark I-V characteristics. The device demonstrated good photovoltaic behavior, with a maximum open circuit voltage of 0.38 V and short-circuit current of 2.8 nA under 200 lx light intensity. The barrier height and acceptor carrier concentration values for the Al/methyl-red/p-InP devices were obtained as 1.27 eV and from the linear region of its characteristics, respectively. The difference between the I-V and C-V measurements for the Al/methyl-red/p-InP device was attributed to their different nature. Additionally, the energy distribution curves of the interface states and their time constants were determined from the conductance properties of the Al/methyl-red/p-InP structure at room temperature. The interface state densities and relaxation times of the device ranged from to s at (1.11-) eV to and s at (0.79-) eV, respectively. The experimental results showed that both the interface state density and relaxation time of the interface states decreased with bias voltage.

title: R: A Language for Data Analysis and Graphics
text: This article presents our journey in creating and executing a statistical computing language. Our aim was to merge beneficial elements from two established computer languages while developing this novel language. We believe that the resulting language offers numerous benefits in terms of portability, computational efficiency, memory management, and scoping.

title: The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates
text:
"The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates" is the most widely referenced and utilized atlas of the mouse brain available in print. It serves as a valuable resource for researchers and students, offering precise stereotaxic coordinates for laboratory experiments, as well as comprehensive delineations and indexing of brain structures for reference purposes. The accompanying DVD provides detailed drawings of brain structures that can be used as templates for creating figures in scientific publications.

The 3rd edition of this atlas represents a significant update and expansion compared to previous editions. In addition to the existing coronal and sagittal series, the inclusion of delineations and photographs in the horizontal plane of section enhances the comprehensiveness of the atlas. Furthermore, all tissue sections are now presented in high-resolution digital color photography, ensuring optimal visual clarity. The DVD accompanying the atlas contains the same high-resolution photographs of the sections and intermediate sections in JP 2000 format.

The delineations of brain structures have been thoroughly revised in this edition, aligning the naming conventions with Paxinos and Watson's "Rat Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates, 6th Edition". To enhance practicality for laboratory use, the 3rd edition is now available in a more convenient 14"x11" format. Moreover, the atlas is presented in full color throughout, providing a visually engaging experience. The included CD contains all plates and diagrams, along with Adobe Illustrator files of the diagrams, offering additional flexibility for users. Additionally, the atlas features updated and redesigned coronal and sagittal diagrams. Notably, for the first time in mammals, sagittal figures now include rhombomeric borders. Lastly, microscopic plates have been scanned using an improved method, resulting in significantly higher quality images.

title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
text: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis is a recent addition to the UseR! series published by Springer, which is currently one of the fastest-growing sources of computational statistics resources. This series focuses on R, either introducing new packages developed by the authors or explaining how to utilize various R packages for statistical techniques. ggplot2 is an R implementation of The Grammar of Graphics (Wilkinson 2005), a systematic approach to creating statistical graphics that was previously discussed in a book reviewed by Cox (2007) in the Journal of Statistical Software. Hadley Wickham, the author of this book, is also the developer of ggplot2.

title: Multiple Imputation For Nonresponse In Surveys
text: You can find multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys in our book collection, and it is accessible online for public use, enabling instant downloads. Our book servers are located in multiple places, ensuring minimal latency when downloading any of our books, including this one. In simple terms, the multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys can be read on any device as it is universally compatible.

title: Inhibition of the dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) reveals IL-33-dependent eosinophil-mediated control of tumor growth
text:
The dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) is responsible for post-translational modification of chemokines, which negatively regulates lymphocyte trafficking. However, inhibiting DPP4 has been found to enhance T cell migration and tumor immunity by preserving functional chemokine CXCL10. In our study, we extended these findings to pre-clinical models of hepatocellular carcinoma and breast cancer and discovered a new mechanism by which DPP4 inhibition improves anti-tumor responses.

When we administered the DPP4 inhibitor sitagliptin, we observed higher concentrations of the chemokine CCL11 and increased migration of eosinophils into solid tumors. This led to enhanced tumor control, which was still present in mice lacking lymphocytes but disappeared after depleting eosinophils or using degranulation inhibitors. We also found that the alarmin IL-33, expressed by tumor cells, was necessary and sufficient for eosinophil-mediated anti-tumor responses. This mechanism also contributed to the effectiveness of checkpoint-inhibitor therapy.

These findings shed light on the role of IL-33 and eosinophils in tumor control, which becomes apparent when the endogenous mechanisms of DPP4 immunoregulation are inhibited. Eosinophils have traditionally been associated with allergies but are now recognized to play a role in other aspects of immunity. In our study, we used a clinically approved DPP4 inhibitor to recruit eosinophils to mouse tumors, where they were crucial for tumor destruction.

title: Cycling Quiescence in Temozolomide Resistant Glioblastoma Cells Is Partly Explained by microRNA-93 and -193-Mediated Decrease of Cyclin D
text: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a deadly cancer that affects the central nervous system and is often resistant to chemotherapy. Temozolomide (TMZ) is the primary chemotherapy drug used, but there have been extensive studies on its resistance. These studies have focused on genes involved in mismatch repair, drug efflux, and alterations in the cell cycle. However, the exact mechanism by which TMZ causes cell cycle arrest is still unclear. Researchers have discovered a link between TMZ-resistant GBM cells and microRNA (miRNA) and exosomes. By analyzing miRNA arrays, they identified specific miRNAs present only in exosomes from TMZ-resistant GBM cells and primary spheres. Further investigation revealed that miR-93 and miR-193 were responsible and that they targeted Cyclin D1, a key regulator of cell cycle progression. Experimental studies confirmed that these two miRNAs reduced the expression of Cyclin D1, leading to a decrease in cell cycling quiescence and increased resistance to TMZ. These findings demonstrate how GBM cells can develop resistance to TMZ through miRNA-mediated targeting of Cyclin D1. The data also suggest potential therapeutic strategies to overcome chemoresistance by targeting miRNAs, exosomes, and the cell cycle.

title: Longitudinal changes in maternal corin and mid-regional proatrial natriuretic peptide in women at risk of pre-eclampsia
text: The objective of this study was to examine the changes in maternal plasma levels of corin and midregional proatrial natriuretic peptide (MR-PANP) in pregnancies that develop preeclampsia (PE) and gestational hypertension (GH). A nested case control study was conducted using data from a larger prospective longitudinal study in singleton pregnancies at high risk for PE. Blood samples were collected every four weeks until delivery. The values were compared in pregnancies that developed preterm-PE, term-PE, GH, and those that remained normotensive. The distribution of maternal plasma corin and PANP levels were transformed using log 10 transformation. A multilevel mixed-effects linear model was used for analysis. A total of 471 samples from 122 women were analyzed. In the normotensive group, log10corin levels were associated with gestational age. In the GH and term-PE groups, corin levels did not differ significantly from the normotensive group. However, MR-PANP levels were significantly higher in pregnancies that developed preterm-PE and GH compared to the normotensive group. Maternal plasma corin and MR-PANP could potentially serve as biomarkers for predicting preterm-PE. The author, A. Khalil, has received research support from USCOM, Roche, Alere, NICOM, and Q-fFN, and has also served as a speaker for Roche.

title: Children's Exercise Physiology
text: The second edition of "Children's Exercise Physiology" has been reorganized and revised to provide the most current research, methodology, and approaches regarding children's physiological responses to exercise. This book not only explores the major issues that differentiate children from adults, but also delves into the underlying mechanisms behind these differences. Readers will gain an understanding of the physiological distinctions between children and adults, including size, biochemical variances, neuromuscular disparities, and the absence of sexual and hormonal maturation, as well as the reasons behind these distinctions. Professionals involved in working with young athletes, disease management, and health promotion will find valuable insights into the physiological factors that influence exercise performance. The field of children's exercise physiology is constantly evolving, and in the eight years since the publication of the first edition, new information has emerged. This updated edition features a streamlined structure with 13 chapters, an introduction, and enhanced features such as chapter objectives, discussion questions and research directions, and a glossary of terms to facilitate learning. The table of contents has been reorganized to improve the flow between chapters, and a new final chapter has been added to cover the role of the central nervous system. Additionally, there is in-depth discussion on the determinants of aerobic fitness and VO2 kinetics, as well as the significance of maximal aerobic power in children. With improved chapters on thermoregulation and metabolic and endocrinologic responses to exercise, readers can be confident that they are receiving the most up-to-date information in "Children's Exercise Physiology, Second Edition."

title: Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines.
text: As the average weight of women of childbearing age has increased, it has become more challenging to find a balance between the health of both the mother and the child during pregnancy. In response to this, Weight Gain During Pregnancy aims to reevaluate the 1990 Institute of Medicine guidelines for weight gain during pregnancy. This book builds upon the original framework of the guidelines and seeks to update them by conducting a thorough review of existing literature and analyzing independent databases. It explores the connections between weight gain during pregnancy and various factors such as the mother's pre-pregnancy weight and height, all within the context of the health of both the mother and the infant. The book provides updated target ranges for weight gain during pregnancy and offers guidelines for accurate measurement. Notably, it includes specific recommendations for weight gain in obese women. Weight Gain During Pregnancy is a valuable resource for healthcare practitioners, policymakers, educators, researchers, and pregnant women themselves. Its goal is to enhance understanding of the role of gestational weight gain and equip individuals with the necessary tools to promote optimal outcomes during pregnancy.

title: To err is human. Building a safer health system
text: Mistakes are made by human beings, and the healthcare services industry is a complex field that is prone to accidents. According to the IOM Report [1], certain systems are more susceptible to accidents than others. When a system fails, there are often multiple factors at play. In healthcare, human errors are the main contributors to accidents, but these errors are often a result of failures within the system. These failures exist in the system even before the error occurs, similar to latent errors that are difficult to detect as they may be hidden in computers or within different levels of management. Many of these errors can be prevented by designing systems that make it difficult for people to make mistakes and easy for them to do the right thing. In healthcare, this means creating processes that ensure patient safety and prevent accidental injuries. As healthcare and its delivery system become more complex, the opportunities for errors increase. The IOM report "To Err is Human" suggests an approach to reduce medical errors and improve patient safety. The environment in which this occurs plays a crucial role in quality. This influence can be divided into two dimensions: the first is the domain of quality, which includes practices consistent with current medical knowledge. The second dimension consists of external forces that can drive improvements in the delivery system's quality. Despite the fact that the risk of dying from a medical error far exceeds the risk of dying in an airline accident, public attention has been more focused on improving safety in the airline industry rather than in healthcare systems. Due to the lack of standardized terminology, it is important to define what constitutes an error and what qualifies as an adverse event. The IOM Report defines an error as the failure of a planned action to be completed as intended or the use of an incorrect plan to achieve a goal. An adverse event, on the other hand, refers to an injury caused by medical management rather than the patient's underlying condition. An adverse event that can be attributed to an error is considered a "preventable adverse event."

title: Advanced Human Nutrition
text: The second edition of Advanced Human Nutrition offers a comprehensive exploration of the human body and explains the significance of nutrients from a biochemical, physiological, and molecular standpoint. The inclusion of figures helps to visually depict the information and enhance the reader's comprehension. Complex pathways are presented in a manner that is easy for students to understand, and diagrams are used to illustrate metabolism and the molecular functions of nutrients. Throughout the text, there are various elements such as "Here's Where You Have Been" and "Here's Where You Are Going" that reinforce key points from each chapter and provide real-life examples to make the content more relatable. The book covers a wide range of topics including cell aging, damage and repair systems, human nutrition and digestion, absorption in relation to organs, exocrine and endocrine functions, histology, and absorptive activities. It also explores microflora and satiety/hunger mechanisms, the role of macronutrients during exercise, and the importance of liquids and sports drinks. Additionally, prevalent diseases in western cultures such as coronary heart disease, cancer, and osteoporosis are discussed. Instructors can access an Instructor's Manual, PowerPoint Presentations, and a TestBank as free downloads.
